Living with dampness and mold in your home can harm your health in several ways. Some of the problems that may be linked to a damp, moldy environment are described below.

Respiratory problems: Mold and damp conditions can lead to coughing, wheezing, and trouble breathing. People who have asthma or other breathing conditions may react more strongly.

Allergic reactions: Mold can trigger allergy symptoms such as sneezing, itchiness, and a runny nose. Those with allergies or asthma may be especially sensitive.

Skin irritation: Mold and damp can also irritate the skin and cause rashes, particularly in people who have eczema or other skin disorders.

Weakened immunity: Some research indicates that being exposed to mold and dampness may dampen the immune system, leaving people more vulnerable to infections and other illnesses.

Keep in mind that the exact effects of a damp, moldy living space depend on several factors, including which types of mold are present, how long and how heavily a person is exposed, and the person's age, overall health, and genetic makeup. If you are worried about how such conditions might affect you, it is wise to consult a healthcare professional who can give you advice tailored to your situation.

Honestly, they often couldn't avoid it, and friendly fire happened a lot. Soldiers did have some tricks to tell friend from foe, though.

The biggest help was the flag. Each army carried big flags and banners, and soldiers kept their eyes on them. If you could see your side's flag, you knew which way to face and where your friends were. Armies also tried to dress differently. Some wore bright colors, like the red coats of British soldiers, so they stood out from the enemy in blue or gray. But many armies wore similar colors, or the smoke and dust made everyone look the same.

They also used passwords and battle cries. A soldier might shout a special word, and if the person next to him didn't answer correctly, he knew to be careful. Some wore armbands, sashes, or sprigs of leaves in their hats.

Mostly, though, they relied on order. Soldiers stood shoulder to shoulder in neat lines, so everyone near them was usually on their own side. Officers gave orders with drums and bugles, and everyone moved together. If you were fighting in a line, the people in front of you were probably the enemy and the people behind and beside you were probably friends.

Even with all this, mistakes still happened, and sometimes they were very costly. During the American Civil War, for example, the famous general Stonewall Jackson was accidentally shot by his own men in the confusion of a battle at night.

Okay, so the human body has over 600 muscles, and they do a lot more than just let you move. They handle posture, circulation, digestion, breathing, and plenty else. The big categories are skeletal, smooth, and cardiac. Skeletal muscles attach to your bones and are what you use to move around. There are over 200 of them, spread across your arms, legs, and torso. Smooth muscles line the walls of your organs and blood vessels, and they work on their own without you thinking about it, which is why your digestion keeps going while you're asleep. Cardiac muscle is found only in the heart, and its whole job is pumping blood through your body. On top of those, there are smaller muscles doing specific jobs, like the ones in your eye that move it around and the tiny ones in your ear that help you keep your balance.

The Vanguard Dividend Growth Fund may simply not have increased its dividends over the past few years. Several explanations are possible, including a market downturn, a shift in the fund's investment approach, or the fact that the securities it holds have not raised their own dividends. Another possibility is that the figures displayed on Yahoo Finance are outdated or do not capture the fund's dividend payments correctly. Keep in mind that a mutual fund's results, dividend growth included, change over time and cannot be guaranteed. Before you decide to invest, it is wise to read through the fund's prospectus and other disclosure materials carefully, and to speak with a financial advisor as well.

Yep, you can keep tabs on when execs or other leaders dump big chunks of stock by watching insider trading activity. In the US, insiders at public companies (executives, directors, and so on) have to report their trades to the SEC within two business days. Those filings end up in the SEC's EDGAR database, where anyone can look them up for free.

If digging through EDGAR sounds like a chore, plenty of financial news sites and tracking services pull those filings together for you. Many of them let you set alerts for specific executives or companies, so you find out right away when someone sells. Just don't read too much into one sale. Insider selling can be a useful signal about a company's prospects, but it's only one piece of the puzzle, and people sell for all sorts of reasons, like paying taxes or diversifying. Do your own homework, and maybe run any big decisions past a financial advisor before you act.

Back in the late 1800s, two camps were fighting over the future of electricity. Thomas Edison backed direct current (DC), while Nikola Tesla pushed alternating current (AC). DC flows in one direction, from a positive terminal to a negative one. You'll find it in batteries, phones, and plenty of other electronics. AC switches direction over and over, usually 50 or 60 times a second (that's the hertz part), and it's what runs most homes and businesses.

So what was the fight about? Mostly, how to get power across long distances. Edison figured DC was simpler to distribute and use. Tesla argued AC was the better bet because it could travel much farther and at higher voltages, which made it more efficient. AC ended up winning and is now the standard for the grid. DC never went away, though. It's still everywhere in batteries and electronics, so both have stuck around.

Kennywood isn't technically within Pittsburgh's city limits. It's in West Mifflin, a borough just southeast of the city, at 4800 Kennywood Boulevard, West Mifflin, PA 15122. The park sits on a bluff overlooking the Monongahela River, roughly 8 to 10 miles from downtown Pittsburgh, near the communities of Duquesne, Homestead, and Munhall.

By car, the trip from downtown usually takes about 20 to 30 minutes depending on traffic. A common route is to take the Parkway East (I-376) or head through the Homestead area via Route 837, then follow signs to the park. Parking is available on site for a fee. Some Pittsburgh Regional Transit bus routes also serve the area, but service can be limited, so it's worth checking current schedules before relying on public transportation.

A persistent cough after a cold is common. Viral infections can leave the airways inflamed for three to eight weeks, and thick white phlegm usually means the lining of the airways is still producing mucus. The nagging pain under your right shoulder blade is most often muscle strain from hard, repeated coughing, which can pull on the muscles and ribs around the shoulder blade. Inflammation of the lining of the lung (pleurisy) or a small chest infection can also cause pain in that area, and sometimes lung problems refer pain to the back or shoulder.

Because the cough has lasted since before Christmas and the pain is ongoing, I'd recommend getting it checked by your GP or a pharmacist soon, especially if you haven't been examined recently. They can listen to your chest and decide whether you need a chest X-ray or other tests. Seek urgent help the same day if you develop a high temperature, breathlessness, chest pain that gets worse when you breathe in, coughing up blood, or feel generally unwell.

About the Nolotil: its active ingredient is metamizole, which is a painkiller and fever reducer. The leaflet lists rare but serious side effects, mainly a sudden drop in white blood cells (agranulocytosis) and severe allergic reactions. Stop taking it and contact a doctor straight away if you get a sore throat, fever, mouth ulcers, unusual bruising or bleeding, or a rash, swelling, or difficulty breathing. Metamizole is not widely used in the UK, so it's worth asking the prescriber or pharmacist to explain why it was chosen for you, how long to take it, and whether it's safe with any other medicines you use. Take it exactly as directed and don't exceed the recommended dose. If you're unsure at any point, your pharmacist can go through the leaflet with you.

Sesame seeds come from the sesame plant, Sesamum indicum, a flowering herb in the family Pedaliaceae. The plant is grown mainly for its seeds, which form inside small pods that split open when ripe. Sesame is one of the oldest oilseed crops known, and it is thought to have been first domesticated in the Indus Valley or parts of Africa several thousand years ago. Today the largest producers include India, Myanmar, Tanzania, Sudan, and China, and the seeds are harvested, hulled, and processed for use in foods, oil, and other products.

Ok so ensemble averaging is basically when you combine predictions from a bunch of models to get a more accurate result. Usually you train several models on the same data and then average what they predict. Why bother? A few reasons. First, it can cut down on overfitting. Each model might latch onto different noise in the training data, so when you average them, those quirks tend to cancel out. Second, it often generalizes better. The ensemble can pick up on the real patterns more reliably, which usually means better predictions on data it hasn't seen. Third, it makes things more stable. If you tweak a hyperparameter or swap out one model, the averaged result won't swing around as much.

There are a few ways to do it. Simple averaging is the easiest: every model's prediction counts equally and you just take the mean. Weighted averaging gives better-performing models more say, so each prediction gets a weight based on how well that model did, and then you average with those weights. Voting is another option, especially for classification, where each model casts a vote and the most popular answer wins.

It's honestly one of the more reliable tricks in machine learning for squeezing out extra accuracy and stability, so it shows up a lot in both practice and competitions.

Long short-term memory, usually abbreviated LSTM, is a type of recurrent neural network architecture designed to learn from sequences of data, such as text, speech, time series, or video frames. Standard recurrent neural networks process a sequence one element at a time and carry a hidden state forward, but in practice they struggle to learn relationships that span many steps because the gradients used in training tend to either shrink toward zero or blow up as they are propagated backward through time. This is known as the vanishing or exploding gradient problem, and it makes it hard for a plain recurrent network to remember information from far back in a sequence.

LSTM, introduced by Sepp Hochreiter and Jürgen Schmidhuber in 1997, addresses this problem by adding a separate memory channel called the cell state, along with a set of learned gates that control how information flows into, out of, and within that memory. Each LSTM unit has three main gates. The forget gate decides which parts of the existing cell state should be discarded. The input gate decides which new information from the current input should be written into the cell state. The output gate decides which parts of the cell state should be exposed as the unit's output at the current step. Each gate is a small neural network layer that outputs values between zero and one, acting like a soft switch, and the gates are trained along with the rest of the network through backpropagation.

Because the cell state is updated mostly through addition and gated multiplication rather than repeated transformation, gradients can flow across many time steps without vanishing as quickly, allowing the network to capture long-range dependencies. For example, an LSTM language model can remember the subject of a sentence while generating a verb many words later.

LSTMs were widely used for tasks such as machine translation, speech recognition, handwriting recognition, and time series forecasting before the rise of transformer models, which now dominate most sequence tasks. Variants such as the gated recurrent unit (GRU), which uses a simpler gating structure, are also common.

Totally normal for babies to get stiff in the neck and shoulders as they grow, and it can come from a bunch of things. Muscle tension, teething, and just being uncomfortable or in pain can all do it. Your little guy's recent infections and antibiotics could be part of it too. Constipation is another possibility, since it can make a baby fussy and tense up. If the stiffness hangs around or gets worse, though, definitely check in with his doctor so they can take a proper look. Until then, gentle massages and some easy stretches might help him loosen up. Also make sure he's getting enough fluids and eating well, since that supports how he's growing and developing.

A switchblade drone is an unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) capable of changing from a compact, folded form into a larger, fully extended one. The name "switchblade" alludes to how rapidly the drone can shift between these two configurations. Such drones are generally small and light, which makes them simple to transport and put into use in many different circumstances. They can carry a range of sensors and other onboard gear, including cameras, radar, and communication systems, allowing them to handle a broad variety of missions. Certain models are built specifically for military or law enforcement purposes, whereas others are meant for civilian work like search and rescue, inspection, or mapping. Switchblade drones have a reputation for being versatile and for completing tasks in conditions where other drones would be impractical or risky. They can usually function in tight spaces and other difficult environments, and they can be launched quickly and efficiently to collect information or carry out additional duties.

Sounds like you might be dealing with asthma. It's a chronic lung condition that causes coughing, wheezing, and trouble breathing, and it's definitely worth getting checked out if you're having these symptoms. The good news is it's very manageable with the right treatment. Usually that means medication to calm inflammation and open up your airways, plus steering clear of whatever sets your symptoms off.

There are a few main types of meds. Inhaled corticosteroids are the daily preventers. They cut down inflammation in your airways so you're less likely to have flare-ups. Long-acting bronchodilators relax the muscles around your airways, so breathing gets easier. You'd typically take these once or twice a day. Short-acting bronchodilators are the rescue inhalers you use when symptoms hit, and they work fast.

Your doctor is the one to help you figure out what's right for you, so don't try to sort it out alone. Triggers matter too. Tobacco smoke, air pollution, and certain chemicals can all make things worse.

If you're around mold at work, bring it up with your employer and your doctor. They can help you figure out next steps. And if you're getting chest pain along with the asthma stuff, don't wait on that. Get medical help right away, since chest pain can point to something more serious. A provider can pin down what's going on and sort out the right treatment.

Yes, slight pain and discomfort can be a symptom of a hernia, and given your history it's worth paying attention to. Recurrence is a real possibility after hernia repair, and the area above a previous repair is one where new bulges or weakness sometimes appear. Pain from a light workout is also common after surgery, though, especially when the abdominal wall is still healing or when muscles are being used in a new way. A pain level of 1 out of 10 that appeared after exercise is often just muscle or soft tissue strain, but it's hard to tell the two apart from symptoms alone.

A few things can help you judge. A hernia usually produces a bulge or lump that you can see or feel, particularly when you cough, strain, or stand for a while, and it may be more noticeable at the end of the day. Pain that gets worse with coughing, lifting, or straining, or a dull heaviness or pressure in the groin or abdomen, points more toward a hernia. Pain that is tender to the touch in the muscle, improves with rest, and is clearly linked to the workout points more toward a strain. Lying down and gently pressing on the area can also help, since a hernia often softens or disappears when you're flat.

Because you've had two repairs in a short time, I'd recommend letting your surgeon or GP know about this, even though it's mild. They can examine you, which is often more reliable than self-checking. Seek care promptly, without waiting, if you notice a firm, painful or non-reducible lump, nausea or vomiting, fever, or pain that rapidly increases or spreads. Those can signal a complication that needs urgent attention.

In the meantime, avoid heavy lifting, straining, and strenuous core work until you've been checked, and keep an eye on whether the discomfort is stable, improving, or growing.

A graphical model is basically a way of showing how a bunch of variables relate to each other using a graph. Each variable gets a node, and the edges between nodes show how those variables are connected. The neat part is that the graph also encodes conditional independencies, so you don't need to spell out the whole probability distribution. You just specify things for the variables that are directly linked by edges, and that keeps it compact.

People use these models to reason about messy, complex systems where the relationships are uncertain or hard to pin down with numbers. They're handy for modeling and analyzing data, especially in machine learning, statistical modeling, and AI.

There are two main flavors. Directed graphical models, which you'll also hear called Bayesian networks, and undirected ones, also known as Markov random fields. With the directed kind, the edges are meant to show a causal relationship between variables. With the undirected kind, the edges just show a statistical relationship.

They're a pretty powerful framework for this sort of thing, and they've been used on all sorts of problems: speech recognition, image classification, natural language processing, and plenty more.

Entropy is basically a measure of how disordered or random a system is. People bring it up a lot in thermodynamics, which is the study of how heat moves between things. Picture two containers of gas. In one, the molecules are packed tightly and kind of organized. In the other, they're spread out all over the place in a messy way. The packed-together one has lower entropy since everything's neatly arranged, and the spread-out one has higher entropy because it's more chaotic.

So why does this matter for heat? Well, when two objects are at different temperatures, heat flows from the hot one to the cool one until they match. That's thermal equilibrium. How much heat actually moves depends on the temperature gap between them, but entropy plays a part too, since the whole process tends to push a system toward more disorder overall.

If you want the simple version: entropy is a way of measuring how mixed up or jumbled something is. Scientists use it to figure out how heat travels and why things end up at the same temperature.

ARB drugs, short for angiotensin receptor blockers, are a group of medications prescribed for high blood pressure (hypertension) and heart failure. They function by obstructing the effects of angiotensin II, a chemical that narrows blood vessels and raises blood pressure. When this chemical is prevented from acting, the blood vessels can widen and blood pressure drops. These medicines are typically swallowed as tablets. Some common ARB drugs are losartan, candesartan, irbesartan, olmesartan, telmisartan, and valsartan. Keep in mind that ARB medications are not right for everyone and may cause side effects. Anyone considering them should consult a healthcare professional to determine whether they are appropriate and to raise any concerns or questions.

Yes, Netflix earns revenue from programs it produces, such as House of Cards. The company's main source of income is subscriptions to its streaming service, for which viewers pay a monthly charge to watch the full library of TV series, films, and other titles. Netflix also brings in money through advertising, which includes product placement in its original series and movies. Product placement means a business pays to have its goods shown within a TV show or film. If a character on a program sips a Coca-Cola, for instance, that is an example of product placement, and Netflix may be paid by the brand whose product appears on screen. In short, Netflix makes its money from subscription fees for its streaming service and from advertising, including product placement, in its original shows and movies.

The regimen your husband's doctor prescribed, doxycycline 100 mg twice daily, is the standard adult dose for Lyme disease. Current guidelines from the Infectious Diseases Society of America recommend 10 days for early localized disease such as the typical expanding rash, and 14 to 21 days for early disseminated disease, such as multiple rashes, facial palsy, or mild heart involvement. Three weeks is at the longer end of the usual range for non-neurologic disease, so it is a reasonable and adequate course for most people. Larger doses are not more effective and mainly increase side effects. Longer courses have not been shown to help in studies, and prolonged antibiotics carry real risks, so extending treatment is generally not recommended unless the doctor sees a specific reason.

Some things depend on his particular situation. If he has neurologic symptoms like meningitis, nerve problems beyond a facial palsy, significant heart block, or Lyme arthritis, the treatment plan can differ, sometimes involving intravenous ceftriaxone or a 28-day course for arthritis. If you are unsure which stage he is in, it is worth asking his doctor directly. It is also normal for some symptoms, such as fatigue, aches, or joint discomfort, to linger for weeks or even a few months after treatment ends. That does not necessarily mean the infection is still active. If symptoms worsen or new ones appear, he should go back to the doctor.

For taking doxycycline safely, he should swallow each capsule with a full glass of water and stay upright for at least thirty minutes afterward, since the drug can irritate or injure the esophagus. Taking it with food helps with nausea. Dairy, calcium, iron, magnesium, antacids, and multivitamins with minerals can block absorption, so these should be separated from the dose by about two to three hours. It also makes the skin much more sun-sensitive, so he should use sunscreen and cover up outdoors. Watch for severe diarrhea, which can signal a C. difficile infection, and for severe headache or vision changes.

The probiotic is a sensible addition. It is best taken a couple of hours apart from the doxycycline and may reduce antibiotic-related diarrhea. Turmeric is generally fine in food, but supplements deserve a little caution at his age. High-dose curcumin can have mild blood-thinning effects, occasionally affects the liver, and is sometimes poorly tolerated by the stomach. Some turmeric products also contain calcium or other minerals that could interfere with absorption if taken at the same time. Mention it to his doctor or pharmacist, and keep it well separated from the antibiotic doses.

A few other practical points: he should finish the full course even if he feels better, check himself for ticks in the future, and avoid assuming that repeat antibody tests will turn negative, as they often stay positive for years after successful treatment. If you would like reassurance, a short call to his prescribing doctor or pharmacist to confirm the stage of disease and the plan for follow-up is a good idea.

The Navier-Stokes equations describe how fluids move, whether that's air, water, or anything else that flows. They're named after Claude-Louis Navier, a French engineer and physicist, and George Gabriel Stokes, an Anglo-Irish scientist. Basically, they tie together a fluid's velocity, pressure, and other properties and show how all of those change over time. People use them for all sorts of things: designing airplane wings and engines, forecasting weather, figuring out how blood moves through your body, or modeling what oceans and rivers are doing. They're built on conservation of mass, momentum, and energy, and they come as a set of coupled partial differential equations that have to be solved together to get an accurate picture of the flow. That's the hard part. Solving them is notoriously tough, and mathematicians and engineers are still working on it. Even with how much we rely on them, plenty of fluid dynamics is still not fully understood and is very much an open question.

Mary Matalin's a political consultant and commentator, and she's married to James Carville, the Democratic strategist. They're pretty famous for being on opposite sides of the aisle, since she's a Republican and he's a Democrat. Somehow it works, though. They've been married since 1993 and have two kids together. She's also written a few books and shows up as a commentator on different news programs now and then.

Your sister's regimen sounds complicated, and a review by her doctor or a pain team would be worthwhile. I can't safely prescribe, but I can point out what to ask about.

Some of the entries are unclear. "MST Continus 5mg plus one morphine tab" and "one morphine sulphate" may be duplicate morphine products, and MST Continus doesn't usually come in a 5mg strength, so the exact doses and names should be checked against her pharmacy labels. Zimovane (zopiclone) is a sleeping tablet rather than a painkiller, but combined with morphine it can add to drowsiness and slow breathing, so it's worth asking whether it's still needed. Diclofenac is an anti-inflammatory that can irritate the stomach and affect the kidneys, and whether it's appropriate depends on her other conditions and medicines. Paracetamol taken regularly is a sensible base, but the total daily amount should be confirmed so she doesn't exceed the safe maximum, particularly if she also takes cold or flu remedies that contain it.

Pain after a lung biopsy is often sharp and worse on breathing or movement, and it can sometimes respond better to scheduled rather than as-needed dosing, or to adjustments in timing. A doctor might consider whether the pain is mainly pleuritic, whether a different opioid or a long-acting formulation would give steadier cover, or whether a nerve-targeted medicine such as gabapentin or pregabalin would help if there's a nerve component. Some patients benefit from regular bowel softeners, since constipation is a common problem with morphine, and from a clear written plan for when to take extra doses.

It would be reasonable to ask her GP, hospital team, or a specialist pain or palliative care team to review the whole list, and to ask specifically whether the regimen can be simplified and whether the pain is being controlled well enough for her to rest and eat. Her sister should seek urgent medical help if she becomes very drowsy or confused, has slow or shallow breathing, or has pain that suddenly worsens or is accompanied by fever, breathlessness, or coughing up blood.

Process calculus is a family of formal languages used to model and reason about concurrent systems, in which many independent computational processes interact with one another. Rather than describing a program as a sequence of steps operating on data, a process calculus describes a system as a collection of agents that communicate and synchronize by exchanging messages or by sharing channels. The central idea is that the behavior of a system can be captured by a small set of algebraic operators, such as parallel composition, choice between alternatives, sequencing, and restriction, which combine simple processes into more complex ones.

The field grew out of work in the late 1970s and early 1980s, most notably Robin Milner's Calculus of Communicating Systems (CCS) and Tony Hoare's Communicating Sequential Processes (CSP). Later developments include Milner's pi-calculus, which allows the names of channels themselves to be sent as messages, meaning that the communication topology of a system can change during execution. Other variants target specific domains, such as the join calculus, the ambient calculus for mobile computing, and stochastic process calculi for modeling performance.

Process calculi are valuable because they provide a precise mathematical semantics for concurrency, which is notoriously difficult to reason about informally. Researchers use them to state and prove properties such as deadlock freedom, safety, and equivalence between systems, often through notions like bisimulation, which asks whether two processes can match each other's observable behavior step by step. These techniques have been applied to communication protocols, security protocols, hardware design, distributed algorithms, and business process modeling, and they also influenced the design of practical languages and verification tools.

Basically, error messages pop up when the operating system or some specific program hits a problem. Say you try to open a file that isn't there. The OS will probably throw up something like "File not found" or "No such file or directory."

They can come from all kinds of causes. Sometimes it's hardware, like a flaky network card or a hard drive that's on its way out. Other times it's software: a bug in the program, or two pieces of software that just don't get along.

The people who build the OS or the program write these messages, and the point is to tell you what went wrong and maybe how to fix it. Some are in plain English and some are full of technical jargon. It usually depends on who they expect to be reading it and how tricky the problem is.

So really, they're there to help you figure out what's broken and start troubleshooting. They're part of the system's error handling, and honestly they're pretty handy when something goes sideways.

Program semantics is basically the meaning of a program in a given language: what it's supposed to do and how it's meant to be used. You can pin that down in a few ways. Plain English works, and so does math notation, or a formal system built for the job. A few common approaches come up a lot. Operational semantics describes the steps a program takes when it runs. Denotational semantics maps a program to a mathematical function that gives its value. Axiomatic semantics uses a set of axioms to describe what the program does. Structural operational semantics defines rules for how a program's syntax gets transformed step by step. Why bother? Knowing the semantics helps you see how a program should behave, write code that's correct and dependable, and reason about things like correctness and performance.

Okay so on Facebook, a tag is basically how you mention someone or a page in a post, comment, or message. When you tag someone, it links to their profile, and they (and their friends, depending on settings) can see the post. You can tag people in posts, photos, and pretty much anything else. To do it, just type "@" and start typing their name. A list pops up, and you pick the person you want. Same deal for pages: type "@" and then the page's name.

Tagging is handy for pointing something out to a specific person, and it can help a post get seen by more people. The tagged person also gets a notification, which can bump up engagement and send some traffic your way. Just don't go overboard. Only tag people or pages when it actually makes sense for the post, or people get annoyed fast.

To find trailing five-year stock returns for the 1980s, first pick a data source that includes dividends, since price-only figures understate total return. Robert Shiller's publicly shared dataset provides monthly S&P 500 prices, dividends, and earnings back to 1871, which makes it a convenient free option for index-level work. Aswath Damodaran's site also publishes annual historical returns for U.S. stocks, bonds, and bills. For individual securities or broader market portfolios, the Center for Research in Security Prices (CRSP) database, accessed through WRDS if you have a university or institutional subscription, is the standard source. Yahoo Finance can work for some indices and funds, but check that you are using a total return series (for example, the ^SP500TR index) rather than the plain price index, and confirm how far back the data actually goes, since some series start only in the late 1980s or later.

Once you have monthly or daily total return data, the calculation is straightforward. For each ending date, identify the price or total return index value from exactly five years earlier. The cumulative return is the ending value divided by the starting value, minus one. To express it as an annualized figure, which is usually more useful for comparisons, take that ratio, raise it to the power of one divided by five, and subtract one. For example, if an index rose from 100 in January 1980 to 175 in January 1985, the cumulative return is 75 percent and the annualized return is about 11.8 percent.

If you are building a series rather than a single number, use a spreadsheet or a short script. In Excel or Google Sheets, you can place dates in one column, look up the value 60 months earlier with a lookup function, and compute the annualized return in the next column. In Python with pandas, you can sort the data by date, use a shift of 60 rows for monthly data (or 1,260 rows for daily data, approximately 252 trading days per year), and apply the annualization formula to the result. Make sure to note whether you are using monthly or daily observations and whether your figures include reinvested dividends, because those choices can change the results noticeably.

Attempting to time the stock market is a hard and hazardous approach, since it means guessing when to purchase and sell shares based on current conditions, headlines, or other considerations. Countless elements can move a stock's price, and forecasting how the market will behave over the near term is rarely possible with confidence. Consequently, many people who attempt to time the market wind up losing money instead of building wealth. Part of the reason so many investors lose money is that the market can be erratic, with prices capable of swinging sharply within a brief span. Such instability makes it difficult for investors to judge well when to buy or sell, and they often make errors that lead to losses. Another factor is that the market responds to a broad mix of influences, such as economic conditions, corporate announcements, and events around the world. These influences can shift quickly and are hard to foresee, which makes sound decisions about the market a real challenge. Lastly, some investors attempt to time the market by chasing the newest trends or hot tips instead of conducting their own research and relying on solid analysis. This tends to be risky, since it is frequently unclear which trends will last and which will fade. In short, timing the stock market is a difficult and perilous strategy that suits few investors. A better path is generally to build a long-term investment plan and keep your focus on your goals, rather than pursuing quick profits.

In 1877, the American astronomer Asaph Hall found the two moons of Mars, Phobos and Deimos. At the time he was employed at the United States Naval Observatory in Washington, D.C., where he studied Mars through a 26-inch refracting telescope. He spotted Deimos on August 12, 1877, and Phobos six days later, on August 18. The moons took their names from Greek mythology. Phobos, meaning "fear," was named for a son of Ares, the Greek counterpart of the Roman god Mars, while Deimos, meaning "terror," was named for a son of the goddess Aphrodite.

Yes, balance transfers can be a legitimate way to avoid interest for a period of time, though they come with conditions worth understanding.

Many major credit card issuers offer introductory 0% APR promotions on balance transfers, typically lasting anywhere from about 12 to 21 months, sometimes longer. During that window, the balance you move over accrues no interest, so every payment goes toward principal. The key is to pay down the transferred amount before the promotional period ends, because any remaining balance then starts accruing interest at the card's regular rate, which is often in the high teens or twenty percent range.

Most issuers charge a balance transfer fee, usually 3 to 5 percent of the amount transferred, and that fee is added to your balance immediately. On a $5,000 transfer at 3 percent, for example, you would pay $150 up front, which is often still far less than the interest you would otherwise pay. Some cards advertise no-fee transfers, which are worth seeking out if you can find one with a good promotional rate.

A few other points matter. Your credit limit constrains how much you can move, and the transfer usually must be completed within a set number of months after account opening. Purchases you make on the new card may not get the same promotional rate, and payments may be applied to the lower-rate balance first, so check the terms. Also, opening a new card triggers a hard credit inquiry and lowers your average account age slightly, which can cause a small, temporary dip in your score.

The strategy works best if you have a realistic plan to pay off the balance within the promotional period, meaning you divide the total, including the fee, by the number of months available and make at least that payment every month. Avoid running up new charges on the old card, since that can quickly erase the benefit. Reading the cardholder agreement for the specific promotion before applying is essential, since terms vary considerably between issuers.

Starting a side business slowly is one of the most sensible ways to test an idea without risking your income or your sanity. The key is to treat the first stage as an experiment rather than a launch. Before spending money on a website, equipment, or inventory, try to sell something to a few real people. You might offer your service to a friend of a friend, post a simple listing, or pre-sell a product to a small group. If strangers are willing to pay, you have evidence worth building on. If they aren't, you've learned that cheaply.

Once you have some early interest, set a realistic pace. Many people do well with a fixed number of hours each week, such as five or six, protected on their calendar the way they would protect a meeting. Consistency matters more than intensity, because a side business that gets a little attention every week will usually outlast one that gets bursts of enthusiasm followed by long gaps. Keep a simple record of what you spend, what you earn, and how much time you put in. Those numbers will tell you far more about whether the business is working than how busy you feel.

Finally, grow only when the demand justifies it. Reinvest modest profits into the things that clearly bring in customers, and be willing to drop the parts that don't. Keep your day job's security in mind, set a clear point at which you would reconsider the project, and talk with someone who knows your finances. A slow start gives you time to learn what customers actually want, and that knowledge is the foundation for any business that eventually becomes full-time, if you choose to make it so.

Prison rape is common for a few connected reasons, and the answer is more about people and money than about the buildings themselves.

Think of a prison like a school with thousands of kids, lots of them grown-ups who have done bad things, and not enough teachers. Prisons are often badly overcrowded, so there are far more people than staff can watch at any moment. A guard might be responsible for a whole hallway or dormitory, and much of that space is out of sight. Cameras help, but they only work if someone is watching the screens, and there are rarely enough staff to do that around the clock. Many prisons also have blind spots, like showers, corners, and bunks, where bad things can happen quietly.

Some prisons have a rough unwritten rule where stronger inmates push weaker ones around. Staff sometimes don't notice, don't have time to step in, or, in the worst cases, look the other way. Victims are often afraid to speak up because they worry they will be punished or attacked for "snitching," and it can be hard to prove what happened. So it stays hidden.

Why not just add more guards and cameras? Mostly because it costs a lot of money, and many governments don't spend enough on prisons. Hiring and training good staff is hard, and prisons often have high turnover and low pay. Some places are doing better, using things like separate housing for vulnerable people, better training, and reporting systems that protect victims, but progress is uneven.

So it isn't that people don't know how to stop it. It's that stopping it takes enough watchful, well-trained people, fewer people crammed into each space, and a real commitment to caring about what happens to the people inside.

Numbness in the lower back, hip, leg, and neck can come from a bunch of things. Pinched or irritated nerves, muscle strain, spinal stenosis, degenerative disc disease, and other health issues can all do it. Your MRI might tell you a lot about what's going on, so hang tight for those results.

MS is one possibility worth knowing about. It's a chronic autoimmune disease that messes with the central nervous system, and numbness and tingling in different parts of the body are common symptoms. That said, it's far from the only explanation, so don't jump to conclusions. Your doctor is the one who can actually pin down the cause and figure out the right treatment.

Also, plenty of numbness isn't serious at all and clears up by itself with some rest and taking it easy. Still, if it's sticking around or getting worse, get it checked out.

So a flexible spending account (FSA) lets you set aside part of your paycheck before taxes to cover certain medical costs. Lots of employers offer them, and you can use the money for things like copays, deductibles, and prescriptions. Here's the basic idea. You sign up and pick how much to put aside from each paycheck. That amount comes out before taxes get calculated, so your taxable income drops and you pay a bit less in taxes overall. Then you spend the money on eligible expenses, like doctor copays, prescriptions, and other medical services. Some FSAs also cover over-the-counter meds and stuff like contacts or bandages.

You do have to keep track of what you spend and submit receipts or other paperwork to your employer or the FSA administrator to get reimbursed. The catch is that whatever you set aside and don't use by the end of the plan year usually gets forfeited. So plan your contributions carefully. A few plans let you roll over a small amount into the next year, but it depends on the plan.

Don't mix these up with health savings accounts (HSAs), though. HSAs also offer tax breaks and pay for medical costs, but you need a high-deductible health plan to qualify. They have looser rules about what counts as eligible, and your unused money carries over from year to year.

The expression "to make your first million" typically refers to reaching a net worth of one million dollars, whether through wages, investment returns, or other money-making ventures. Many people regard this as an important financial landmark and use it as a target or yardstick for measuring personal financial achievement. It comes up frequently in discussions of personal finance and building wealth, where it serves as shorthand for the gradual accumulation of substantial assets over the course of a lifetime.

Season 2 of Project Runway, which aired in 2005 on Bravo, was won by Chloe Dao. She beat out the other finalists to take the title and the prize package, which included a spread in Elle magazine and a cash prize of $100,000 toward starting her own fashion line.

The pattern you're describing, with pain worsening a week after the injury, a warm red hard lump, spreading bruising, and swelling into the foot, needs to be checked by a doctor soon, ideally today or tomorrow at an urgent care clinic or your primary care office. Warmth and redness around a lump that is getting worse can mean an infection or a collection of blood or pus under the skin. Bruising that spreads down the foot in a line can happen when a fracture or a deeper tendon or ligament injury lets blood travel along the tissue planes. A doctor can examine the area and, if needed, order an X-ray or ultrasound to look for a fracture or fluid collection.

Until you're seen, keep the leg elevated above heart level when you're resting, and avoid putting heavy weight on the foot if walking hurts. You can use ice wrapped in a cloth for 15 to 20 minutes at a time, but don't press hard on the lump. Over-the-counter pain relievers like acetaminophen can help with discomfort. Avoid massaging or squeezing the lump, since that can worsen an infection or bleeding.

Go to an emergency department right away if you develop a fever or chills, red streaks spreading up the leg, numbness or tingling in the foot, toes that look pale, blue, or feel cold, or if you can't move your toes or bear any weight on the foot. Also tell the doctor about the softball impact so they can consider whether anything was broken.

A chronograph is basically a watch with a stopwatch built in. You get all the usual timekeeping stuff, plus a way to time things. The name comes from Greek: "chronos" means time and "graphein" means to write, so it's sort of "time writer." People who do sports or any kind of timing work tend to love them, but plenty of regular folks just like having one around for timing anything that needs it. Most have a start/stop button and a reset button to run the stopwatch. Some also have a tachymeter, a scale on the bezel or dial that lets you work out speed or distance from elapsed time. And they come in different flavors: mechanical ones run on a wound spring, quartz ones run on a battery, and some are digital, showing the time and stopwatch readings as numbers.

Foamy stool with mucus after a course of strong antibiotics is common, but it can also signal something that needs prompt medical attention, so it's worth raising with his GP or the hospital team soon.

The most frequent cause is antibiotic-associated diarrhoea. Antibiotics kill off many of the normal gut bacteria, which upsets digestion and can make stools loose, frothy, and mucus-rich. The foam often comes from gas produced by fermenting food that isn't being absorbed properly. Because he has had several antibiotics, including a second course at home, this is the most likely explanation, but it still needs checking.

The most important thing to rule out is Clostridioides difficile, a bowel infection that often follows broad-spectrum antibiotics. It typically causes frequent watery diarrhoea, mucus, sometimes a strong smell, abdominal cramping, fever, and loss of appetite. It is treatable, but it can become serious if left untreated, so a stool test is worth requesting if the diarrhoea persists or he has any of these symptoms.

Other possibilities include a stomach bug such as norovirus or Giardia, which can follow hospital stays. Fat malabsorption can also cause pale, frothy, greasy stools, and reduced mobility or changes in diet during illness can contribute to altered bowel habits. Multiple sclerosis itself can affect bowel control and transit, and some medicines, such as laxatives, magnesium, or certain supplements, can loosen stools too.

Please contact his GP, the pharmacist, or NHS 111 (or local equivalent) soon, and seek urgent help if he has blood in the stool, black or tarry stools, a fever, severe or worsening abdominal pain, signs of dehydration (dizziness, very dark urine, little urine passed), more than about three watery stools a day, or if he becomes confused or very unwell. Meanwhile, keep him well hydrated, and check with a pharmacist or doctor before giving any anti-diarrhoea medicine, since these can be harmful if C. difficile is present. Let the clinician know the full antibiotic history, including the home course, as this will shape the tests and treatment they recommend.

Yeah, there's some evidence that commodity futures and stocks can be negatively correlated, meaning when one goes up the other tends to drop, and the reverse. Part of the reason is that they respond to different things. Commodity prices tend to swing with supply and demand, while stocks are more about company earnings and how the economy is doing. Different players are involved too: producers and consumers of raw materials on one side, investors on the other. But don't count on it. The relationship shifts over time, and sometimes the two move together, or there's no clear link at all.

Several elements may have played a part in gold's price decline in 2011. Stronger worldwide economic conditions may have boosted investor confidence and lowered the need for safe havens such as gold. Gold prices often move opposite to economic growth, since investors tend to take on more risk when the economy is healthy. Another possibility is that the push for deficit reduction and fiscal tightening across many nations made gold less attractive as protection against inflation. The strength of the U.S. dollar, which is generally positively correlated with gold's price, may also have been a factor. The dollar typically gains ground during periods of economic expansion and market calm, which could have pushed gold's price down. Because gold's price responds to many influences, the 2011 drop was likely the result of several of these factors acting together, along with others.
