Finally, if you have an undescended testicle, you should raise it with your doctor, because it could impact both fertility and general health.

Being a U.S. resident alien does not by itself bar you from treaty benefits, but whether you can claim an exemption under Article 21 depends on the kind of income, which country is taxing it, and how the savings clause applies.

Article 21 of the India-U.S. treaty, as I understand it, is the "other income" article. It generally assigns taxing rights over income not covered by the treaty's other articles to your country of residence. If you are a U.S. tax resident and the income arises in India, that usually means the United States has the right to tax it, and India should not, so you could argue for relief from Indian tax on that income. I'm working from memory on the article numbering and wording, so please verify the current text of the treaty and its protocol before relying on it.

There are important limits. The treaty contains a savings clause that lets the United States tax its citizens and residents as if the treaty did not exist, with only a few listed exceptions, such as certain relief-from-double-taxation provisions. This means a green card holder usually cannot use the treaty to reduce U.S. tax on U.S.-source or worldwide income. Treaty relief mainly matters for you on the Indian side, where India may tax Indian-source income, and on the U.S. side it typically works through the foreign tax credit (Form 1116) for Indian tax you pay.

If you take a return position based on the treaty that reduces your U.S. tax, you generally must disclose it on Form 8833. Failing to disclose can trigger a penalty. You should also check whether India considers you a resident under its own rules. If both countries claim you as a resident, the tie-breaker rules in Article 4 (permanent home, center of vital interests, habitual abode, nationality) determine which country is treated as your residence for treaty purposes, and that can change which exemptions apply.

Because the outcome depends on the specific income and your facts, I'd recommend having a cross-border tax professional review your situation, ideally with the actual treaty text and your Indian tax residency status in hand.

Honestly, there are a handful of reasons people keep buying a stock after it's already gone up. The first is that they think it still has room to run. If a company's been posting strong numbers, sits in an industry that's looking good, or has been getting positive news, some investors figure the climb isn't over yet.

Then there's diversification. Plenty of folks spread their money across lots of different stocks so that one company tanking doesn't wipe them out, and adding a winner to the mix is just part of that plan.

Some people are really in it for the income. If the company pays dividends, you get a regular payout just for holding on, and that can be the main draw regardless of what the share price does.

And then there's plain speculation. Some buyers hope to sell at an even higher price later on. It's a riskier bet, though, because nothing guarantees the stock keeps climbing, and it can just as easily reverse.

Adversarial machine learning is the study of how machine learning systems can be attacked, manipulated, or deceived by deliberately crafted inputs, and how to defend them against such attacks. It sits at the intersection of machine learning and computer security, and it starts from a simple observation: most machine learning models are built on the assumption that the data they see at test time will resemble the data they were trained on, but a malicious actor can break that assumption on purpose.

The most famous illustration involves image classifiers. Researchers discovered that adding a tiny, carefully computed perturbation to an image, often invisible to the human eye, can cause a highly accurate neural network to misclassify it with great confidence. A picture of a panda might be labeled a gibbon, or a stop sign with a few stickers placed on it might be read as a speed limit sign by a self-driving car's vision system. These manipulated inputs are called adversarial examples, and their existence revealed that models which appear to perform well may be relying on fragile patterns quite different from the ones humans use.

Attacks in this field are usually grouped by when and how they occur. Evasion attacks happen at deployment time, when an attacker modifies an input so the model gets it wrong, as with spam emails crafted to slip past a filter or malware altered to avoid detection. Poisoning attacks happen during training, when an attacker injects corrupted or mislabeled data so the resulting model learns incorrect behavior or contains a hidden backdoor that activates on a specific trigger. Other attacks target privacy or intellectual property rather than accuracy: model extraction attempts to copy a model by repeatedly querying it, membership inference tries to determine whether a particular person's data was used in training, and model inversion seeks to reconstruct sensitive training data from the model's outputs. With large language models, related concerns include prompt injection and jailbreaking, where inputs are designed to make the system ignore its instructions or produce prohibited content.

Researchers also distinguish attacks by how much the attacker knows. In a white-box setting the attacker has full access to the model's architecture and parameters and can use gradients to efficiently find damaging perturbations. In a black-box setting the attacker can only observe outputs, yet attacks often still succeed, partly because adversarial examples tend to transfer between different models trained on similar tasks.

On the defensive side, common approaches include adversarial training, where models are trained on adversarial examples so they learn to resist them, input preprocessing and detection methods that try to spot or neutralize manipulated inputs, robust optimization techniques, certified defenses that mathematically guarantee correct behavior within a bounded range of perturbations, and careful data validation to guard against poisoning. Many proposed defenses have later been broken by stronger attacks, so the field has developed something of an arms race dynamic, and robustness often comes at some cost to standard accuracy or computational efficiency.

The topic matters because machine learning is increasingly used in high-stakes settings such as autonomous driving, medical diagnosis, fraud detection, facial recognition, and content moderation. Understanding adversarial vulnerabilities helps engineers build systems that are not only accurate on average but also reliable when someone is actively trying to make them fail, and it has also deepened scientific understanding of what neural networks actually learn.

Persistent redness around the penis is not considered normal, so it's worth discussing with a healthcare provider. Petroleum jelly can offer short-term comfort, but it doesn't address the root problem, which needs to be identified. Possible explanations include irritation of the skin, fungal or bacterial infections, sexually transmitted infections (STIs), and allergic reactions. A medical professional can make an accurate diagnosis and suggest treatment. Depending on the situation, they might order additional tests or prescribe creams or oral medication. Meanwhile, keeping the area clean by washing it every day with warm water and avoiding snug clothing can help reduce further irritation.

I'm sorry you're dealing with this. Losing coverage through no fault of your own is stressful, especially when you depend on medications. There are several ways to keep your prescriptions going while you sort out longer-term coverage, and some legal protections that may help you recover costs later.

For immediate medication needs, start by calling your prescriber's office and explaining the situation. Doctors can often switch you to a cheaper generic or therapeutic equivalent, write prescriptions for larger quantities, or give you free samples, especially for brand-name drugs. At the pharmacy, ask for the cash price and compare it against discount programs like GoodRx, SingleCare, or RxSaver, which are free to use and can cut costs dramatically. Many big-box retailers such as Walmart, Costco (whose pharmacy you can use without a membership in most states), and Kroger offer low-cost generic lists, and Mark Cuban's Cost Plus Drug Company sells many generics at close to manufacturer cost by mail. If you take a brand-name drug, check the manufacturer's website for a patient assistance program. Most major drug companies provide medications free or at steep discounts to uninsured people who meet income guidelines, and your doctor's office can often help with the paperwork. NeedyMeds.org and Medicine Assistance Tool (medicineassistancetool.org) are good places to search these programs. Federally qualified health centers and community health clinics also offer sliding-scale care and often have discounted pharmacy access through the 340B program; you can find one at findahealthcenter.hrsa.gov. If you're running out of something critical like insulin, seizure medication, or heart medication, many states allow pharmacists to dispense an emergency supply, and insulin makers have capped out-of-pocket costs for uninsured patients through their own programs.

For replacement coverage, losing employer-based insurance is a qualifying life event that opens a 60-day special enrollment period on the ACA marketplace at healthcare.gov or your state's exchange. Coverage lost due to an employer's failure to pay premiums generally counts, and depending on your income you may qualify for substantial subsidies. You should also check Medicaid eligibility, since you can apply any time of year and in some states coverage can be retroactive up to three months, which could reimburse recent medical expenses. If you have a spouse or parent with employer coverage, losing your own plan likely lets you join theirs mid-year as well. COBRA may or may not be available, because it depends on the underlying plan still existing, but it's worth asking the insurer directly.

On the fraud itself, if your employer deducted premiums from your paycheck but didn't pay the insurer, that is a serious violation. Contact the U.S. Department of Labor's Employee Benefits Security Administration at askebsa.dol.gov or 1-866-444-3272. They handle these cases, help workers recover benefits, and can sometimes get claims paid retroactively. Your state insurance commissioner and state labor department are also worth contacting, and if you've incurred large medical bills, an employment or ERISA attorney may take the case on contingency. Keep your pay stubs showing deductions, any notices from the insurer, and receipts for medical and pharmacy costs, since these will be important if you seek reimbursement.

If you tell me which medications you take or what state you're in, I can point you toward more specific programs or options.

Crocodiles live in tropical regions across Africa, Asia, the Americas, and Australia. They are found mostly in warm climates because, as cold-blooded reptiles, they depend on their surroundings to regulate their body temperature.

Most crocodiles inhabit freshwater environments such as rivers, lakes, swamps, marshes, and wetlands. The Nile crocodile, for example, is widespread throughout sub-Saharan Africa, while the mugger crocodile lives in India, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, and nearby countries. In the Americas, the American crocodile can be found in southern Florida, the Caribbean, Mexico, Central America, and northern South America.

Some species are comfortable in brackish or salt water as well. The saltwater crocodile, the largest living reptile, ranges from eastern India through Southeast Asia to northern Australia and is known for traveling long distances across open ocean between islands and coastlines. It often lives in estuaries, mangrove swamps, and river mouths where fresh and salt water mix.

In general, crocodiles prefer habitats with slow-moving or still water where they can hunt, along with nearby banks or sandy areas where they can bask in the sun and lay their eggs.

Honestly, a bunch of stuff can move a stock's price. The most common reason one goes up is that the company's doing well and the future looks good for it. That could be strong sales and profits, a tight operation, or solid management. Other things can push it up too, like a healthy economy, lots of demand for what the company sells, or good trends across the whole industry. Investors will also pay more if they think the company has real room to grow, or if they figure it'll start paying dividends down the road. That said, the market's driven by a ton of tangled-up factors, so it's really hard to know for sure what a particular stock or the market overall will do. Do your own homework, and maybe talk to a financial pro before you put money into anything.

Computer gaming, often shortened to PC gaming when referring specifically to personal computers, is the activity of playing games on a computer rather than on a dedicated console or handheld device. The term covers an enormous range of experiences, from simple browser-based puzzles and mobile-style titles to demanding three-dimensional worlds that require powerful graphics hardware. Players interact with these games using a keyboard and mouse, a game controller, or sometimes specialized peripherals such as flight sticks or racing wheels, and the games run on the computer's processor, graphics card, memory, and storage.

One of the defining features of computer gaming is its openness. Because personal computers are highly configurable, players can upgrade components, adjust graphics and performance settings, and install mods that alter or extend a game's content. The platform is also known for hosting a wide variety of genres, including strategy, role-playing, simulation, shooters, and independent titles made by small teams or even individuals. Games are commonly bought and downloaded through digital storefronts such as Steam, Epic Games Store, or the developer's own launcher, though physical discs and direct downloads remain options too.

Computer gaming also has a strong social and competitive side. Multiplayer games let people play together over the internet, and many communities form around shared interests, online servers, streaming, and esports tournaments. Because of its flexibility and broad reach, computer gaming is one of the largest and most influential segments of the overall video game industry.

Cambridge is a collegiate public research university in Cambridge, England, founded way back in 1209. It's the second-oldest university in the English-speaking world and the fourth-oldest surviving one in the world. Most of the day-to-day stuff like housing and social life runs through the colleges, while the academic departments handle lectures and labs and the like. It's in the Russell Group of research-heavy UK universities, and it's also part of LERU, a group of top European research universities. It was a founding member of the Europaeum network too. Cambridge has a long reputation for both research and teaching, and it pops up near the top of world rankings pretty much every year. There's a real push toward interdisciplinary work, and the faculties cover everything from the sciences and engineering to the humanities, social sciences, and business. It's produced loads of famous alumni and staff, including more than 100 Nobel laureates. Some of the well-known research centres and institutes include the Cavendish Laboratory, the Judge Business School, and the University Library.

Choosing an investing services company comes down to a few questions you can check for yourself. Start with what kind of help you want. Some firms simply execute trades on a platform you control, some manage a portfolio for you, and some offer ongoing financial planning. Knowing which of these you need narrows the field quickly.

Next, look at how the firm is paid, because that shapes its incentives. Fee-only advisers charge a flat fee, an hourly rate, or a percentage of assets under management and do not earn commissions on products they sell you. Commission-based advisers may earn money from the funds or insurance products they recommend, which can create a conflict of interest even when they act in good faith. Ask any adviser directly, "Are you a fiduciary at all times, and how exactly do you get paid?" A good answer is clear and specific. A vague or evasive one is a warning sign.

Verify credentials and registration. In the United States, you can search the SEC's Investment Adviser Public Disclosure database or FINRA's BrokerCheck to confirm that a firm or individual is registered and to see any disciplinary history. Other countries have comparable regulators. Common professional credentials such as CFP, CFA, or CPA indicate training, though you should still check that the designation is current.

Compare total costs. Management fees, fund expense ratios, trading commissions, and account minimums all add up. Over decades, a difference of one percentage point in annual fees can meaningfully reduce your final balance, so ask for a written estimate of all costs.

Evaluate fit and communication. Pick a firm whose investment philosophy you understand and whose services match your goals, whether that is retirement, a home purchase, or building wealth. Meet with two or three candidates, ask how they would handle a market downturn, and notice whether they explain things in terms you can follow and are willing to answer questions patiently.

Finally, check the firm's background. Look for a clear written disclosure document, which in the U.S. is called Form ADV Part 2 for advisers, and read the sections on conflicts of interest and disciplinary history. Ask for client references if you want more reassurance. Taking your time at this stage is worthwhile, since the right firm can serve you for many years.

The term "Mansfield Amendment" most commonly refers to a provision in United States law, sponsored by Senator Mike Mansfield of Montana, the Senate Majority Leader at the time. It was added as Section 203 of the Military Authorization Act for fiscal year 1970, which was passed in 1969. The amendment prohibited the Department of Defense from using its funds to support any research project or study unless that work had "a direct and apparent relationship to a specific military function or operation."

The amendment emerged during the Vietnam War, when many in Congress and the public were uneasy about the military's growing influence over American science and universities. Since the Second World War, agencies such as the Office of Naval Research and the Advanced Research Projects Agency had become major sponsors of basic, open-ended academic research in fields like physics, mathematics, computer science, and the social sciences. Mansfield and his supporters argued that the Pentagon should not be the main patron of general scientific inquiry and that such research belonged instead with civilian agencies, particularly the National Science Foundation. Antiwar sentiment on campuses also made military-funded research politically contentious.

The practical effect was significant. Defense agencies began scrutinizing their research portfolios and cutting or redirecting projects that could not show an obvious military payoff. Some areas, including early artificial intelligence research supported by ARPA, came under pressure to justify themselves in terms of concrete applications, contributing to a shift toward more mission-oriented funding. Responsibility for basic research gradually moved toward the National Science Foundation and other civilian bodies, although these agencies did not always receive enough additional money to fully replace what the military had provided.

The strict wording lasted only briefly. In the following year's authorization act, Congress softened the language so that research needed only to have, in the opinion of the Secretary of Defense, a "potential relationship" to a military function or operation. Even so, the original amendment had a lasting cultural influence, encouraging defense research managers to emphasize applied, mission-relevant work and shaping debates about the proper relationship between the military and academic science for decades afterward.

It is worth noting that the same name is sometimes used for a different proposal Mansfield championed around 1971, which sought to cut the number of American troops stationed in Europe roughly in half. That measure was debated vigorously during the Cold War but was defeated in the Senate. When people mention the Mansfield Amendment in discussions of science policy or research funding, however, they almost always mean the 1969 restriction on Defense Department research.

Trying to conceive while on anti-tuberculosis (TB) medication, Rcinex 600 included, is generally considered safe. Even so, you should tell your physician that you plan to get pregnant and raise any risks or worries you have. Certain TB drugs can produce side effects that might harm a developing fetus, including birth defects or a low birth weight. Talk with your physician about the possible benefits and risks of staying on your current treatment, and ask whether any alternative therapies would be safer during pregnancy. Your physician can give you the latest and most reliable information on using TB drugs while trying to conceive or while pregnant. To give you and your baby the best chance at a good outcome, always follow the treatment advice and instructions your physician gives you.

"Mazel tov" comes from Hebrew and translates to "good luck" or "congratulations." People commonly say it to celebrate a joyful event like a marriage, the arrival of a baby, or a major accomplishment. In general, the expression conveys delight and hopes for a bright future.

Speech recognition is basically computers turning spoken words into written text. It's what lets a machine make sense of what you're saying, and you'll find it in voice assistants, transcription tools, and call center systems all the time. There are two main flavors. The first is isolated speech recognition, which handles single words or short phrases said one at a time, with a little pause in between. You'll see this in voice command setups like smart home gadgets or virtual assistants. The second is continuous speech recognition, which deals with normal, flowing speech with no breaks between words. That one's the go-to for transcription software and call centers, where people need the text showing up in real time. Under the hood, these systems rely on a mix of machine learning algorithms and acoustic models. They get trained on huge piles of recorded human speech, which lets them pick up on the patterns in how we pronounce things and what words tend to show up in which situations.

An artificial intelligence system is a computer-based system designed to perform tasks that normally require human intelligence, such as recognizing speech or images, understanding and generating language, making predictions, planning actions, or solving problems. Rather than following only a fixed set of hand-written instructions for every situation, an AI system typically learns patterns from data or is guided by models that let it adapt its behavior to new inputs.

An AI system is usually made up of several parts working together. There is a model, which is the mathematical structure that captures the relationships the system has learned, such as a neural network with millions or billions of adjustable parameters. There is training, the process by which the model is adjusted using large amounts of data so that its outputs become more accurate or useful. There is also the software and infrastructure around the model that receives inputs, runs the computations, and delivers results to a user or another program. In many modern systems, these components are combined with data pipelines, user interfaces, and safety or monitoring mechanisms.

AI systems are often grouped by how capable or specialized they are. Narrow AI systems are built for a specific task, like a spam filter, a translation tool, or a medical image classifier, and they make up nearly all AI in use today. General AI, which would match or exceed human ability across a wide range of tasks, remains a research goal and has not been achieved. Within narrow AI, approaches include rule-based expert systems, machine learning, and deep learning, with the last two being dominant in recent years.

In everyday life, AI systems appear in recommendation engines on streaming and shopping sites, voice assistants, navigation and route planning, fraud detection in banking, and chatbots that answer questions or write text. Because these systems learn from data, their quality depends heavily on the data used to train them, and they can reflect biases or make errors that users should understand and check.

Dear Huma, I understand how worrying this is, especially after eight months of trying. Your reports being clear is a good sign, and a single low result does not mean your husband cannot father a child.

Low rapid progressive motility, at 2%, means that only a small share of his sperm move forward quickly and in a straight line. That is a real finding and it can make natural conception harder. However, a semen analysis has several other measures, including sperm count, total motility (all movement combined), shape of the sperm, and semen volume. A low count of rapidly moving sperm is often still enough for pregnancy when the other numbers are reasonable. So the next step is to make sure the doctor sees the complete report, and it is usually wise to repeat the semen test after about three months, because sperm take roughly that long to develop and results can vary a lot from one test to another.

As for your chances, most healthy couples conceive within about one year of regular intercourse, and at eight months you are still within the normal window. Male factors contribute to roughly half of infertility cases, so this is common and treatable. Many men with reduced motility do conceive naturally, especially if the sperm count is good. Your chances depend on the full semen picture and on your own ovulation and tubal health, which your doctor has already checked.

Several things may help. Your husband should avoid smoking, tobacco, and excess alcohol, keep a healthy weight, and avoid keeping a laptop on his lap or wearing very tight underwear, since heat reduces sperm quality. A balanced diet rich in fruits and vegetables, adequate sleep, and lower stress also support sperm health. Some doctors recommend antioxidant supplements such as coenzyme Q10, zinc, folic acid, or vitamin E, though the evidence for these is modest, so only take them under medical advice. He should also be checked for a varicocele, which is a swelling of veins around the testicle and is a common, treatable cause of poor sperm quality. Hormone tests and a urine or semen infection screen may also be advised.

For timing, intercourse every two to three days around ovulation, which is usually about fourteen days before your next period, gives the best chances. Your doctor can confirm your ovulation with a simple ultrasound or blood test if needed.

If the repeat test still shows low motility after several months, there are effective options. Intrauterine insemination (IUI) places washed, concentrated sperm directly into the uterus and can help when motility is moderately low. For more severe problems, IVF with ICSI is very effective, because a single healthy-looking sperm is injected directly into an egg, so motility is no longer a barrier. Good urologists, andrologists, and infertility specialists are available in major cities like Lahore, Karachi, and Islamabad, and many government teaching hospitals also have fertility clinics with lower costs. Please avoid unqualified clinics that promise guaranteed cures.

Please discuss these options with your doctor, and do not lose hope. Many couples in your situation go on to have healthy children.

Mortgage rates and yields on 10-year Treasury bonds tend to move together because they respond to many of the same forces, including the balance between the supply of and demand for credit, expectations about inflation, and the general level of interest rates across the economy. When 10-year Treasury yields rise, investors are usually asking for a larger return, perhaps because they expect higher inflation or see greater risk that a borrower will fail to repay. Lenders may then raise mortgage rates to offset the added risk and cost of lending. On the other hand, when Treasury yields fall, this often suggests that investors are less worried about rising prices or default, and mortgage rates may follow them down. Still, mortgage rates do not move in lockstep with Treasury yields. A lender's cost of funds and the profit it hopes to earn also shape the rates it offers. Even so, because the 10-year Treasury yield serves as a common reference point for many other interest rates, including mortgage rates, it can meaningfully affect how much a home loan costs to borrow.

Silent letters are just letters you write but don't actually say out loud. They stick around for a few reasons. Sometimes they hint at where a word came from, and sometimes they help tell apart words that would otherwise look pretty similar.

Take the "k" in "knife." It's silent, and the idea is that it helps set the word apart from "nife," which isn't a word anyway. Or the "g" in "gnome," which supposedly points to the word's French roots, since it comes from "gnome" over there too.

I'll admit they can be a real headache if you're learning a new language, because they don't follow the usual pronunciation patterns and you just have to memorize them. Still, they're a neat leftover from the history of a language. They show where words came from and how they've changed over the years.

Okay so modern art basically covers anything made from the late 1800s up to today. It's a huge mix of stuff: paintings, sculptures, photos, and plenty more. The big thing is that it usually ditches traditional techniques, so it can look nothing like the old stuff you'd find in a museum. Lots of modern artists aren't trying to paint people or objects realistically at all. They're messing around with shapes, colors, and textures to come up with their own look. A lot of it also carries a message, whether that's about politics or society or something really personal to the artist. Some folks make work just to say something or get their feelings out there. I'll admit it can be hard to get into at first, but it's basically artists trying out new ideas and expressing themselves in whatever way they can.

Brett Favre started 297 straight regular season games at quarterback in the NFL. The streak kicked off on September 27, 1992 and ran all the way to December 12, 2010. He played for the Packers, the Jets, and the Vikings along the way, and plenty of people would put him in the conversation for greatest QB ever.

A virtual assistant is a software program that understands spoken or typed requests and carries out tasks on a user's behalf. Common examples include Siri, Google Assistant, Amazon Alexa, and Microsoft's Cortana, though many chatbots and customer service helpers also function as virtual assistants. They typically rely on natural language processing and speech recognition to interpret what a person says or writes, and then use that understanding to respond, answer questions, or perform actions.

The range of tasks a virtual assistant can handle is broad. People use them to set alarms and timers, send messages, play music, check the weather, control smart home devices like lights and thermostats, look up information, or make reservations. Behind the scenes, the assistant connects to online services, databases, and the user's connected apps and devices to get the job done. Many also learn from patterns in a user's behavior over time, which can make suggestions or responses more personalized.

The term can also refer to human workers. A human virtual assistant is a remote contractor who performs administrative or support work, such as managing email, scheduling appointments, handling data entry, or doing research, typically working from their own location and communicating with clients online.

The term "processed food" refers to any food that has been changed in some manner before reaching shoppers. That might involve mixing in additional ingredients, cooking the food, freezing it, or putting it into packaging. In general, processed foods are less nutritious than whole, unprocessed ones, since they may contain added sugars, unhealthy fats, and other components that do the body no favors. They can also provide fewer nutrients than whole foods, because a good portion of those nutrients may be lost as the food is processed and prepared. Consuming large amounts of processed food can harm your health, as it may cause weight gain, raise your chances of developing certain diseases, and leave you feeling worse overall. To keep your body strong and healthy, it's important to eat a range of whole, unprocessed foods, including fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and lean proteins.

A brute-force attack is a method of breaking into a protected system by systematically trying every possible possibility until the correct one is found. It most commonly targets passwords, encryption keys, or PINs. Rather than exploiting a flaw in the software or tricking a person, the attacker relies on raw computing effort and persistence, essentially guessing over and over at high speed.

The basic idea is simple. If a password is four digits long, there are only 10,000 possible combinations, so a program can try all of them in a fraction of a second. If the password is twelve characters drawn from uppercase letters, lowercase letters, digits, and symbols, the number of combinations becomes astronomically large, and trying them all could take centuries with current hardware. This is why the difficulty of a brute-force attack grows exponentially with the length and complexity of the secret being guessed.

There are several common variations. A simple brute-force attack tries every combination in order. A dictionary attack is a smarter version that tries likely candidates first, such as common words, leaked passwords, and predictable patterns like "Password123". Credential stuffing takes username and password pairs leaked from one breach and tries them on other services, betting that people reuse passwords. Password spraying tries a few very common passwords against many accounts, which avoids triggering lockouts on any single account. Offline attacks work against stolen databases of hashed passwords, where the attacker can guess at enormous speed using GPUs without alerting anyone, while online attacks must go through a login page and are slowed by the server.

Defenses focus on making each guess costly or limiting the number of guesses. Long, unique passwords or passphrases greatly expand the search space. Account lockouts, rate limiting, and CAPTCHAs slow down online attempts. Multi-factor authentication means a correct password alone is not enough. For stored passwords, developers use salted hashes with deliberately slow algorithms such as bcrypt, scrypt, or Argon2, which make offline guessing much more expensive. Monitoring for unusual login patterns can also reveal an attack in progress.

Brute-force attacks are a standard concept in security testing as well, where authorized professionals use them to check whether systems have weak passwords. Using them against systems without permission, however, is illegal in most jurisdictions.

Honestly, it's mostly detective work with old texts. Linguists dig through whatever writing survived from those times: poems, stories, laws, letters, even boring receipts. Reading enough of it shows them how the grammar works, how sentences get put together, and what words and sounds people actually used. Related languages help a lot too, since you can compare words and spot patterns that carry over. And every now and then, if a living language is close enough to the old one, researchers can pick up useful clues from people who still speak it.

HIV, the human immunodeficiency virus, causes acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS) if left untreated. The virus infects and destroys CD4 cells, a type of white blood cell that coordinates the immune system's response to infections. As these cells decline, the body becomes increasingly vulnerable to opportunistic infections such as pneumocystis pneumonia, tuberculosis, and certain cancers like Kaposi sarcoma and lymphoma. HIV is transmitted through contact with certain body fluids, including blood, semen, vaginal fluid, and breast milk, most commonly through unprotected sex, sharing needles, or from mother to child during pregnancy, birth, or breastfeeding. Antiretroviral therapy can suppress the virus so effectively that people with HIV live near-normal lifespans and cannot transmit the virus sexually, though the infection itself is lifelong.

Yeah, pain in the spot where your gallbladder used to be after a cholecystectomy isn't that unusual. People call it phantom pain a lot of the time. It usually comes from nerve endings that got hurt during surgery, and those nerves can keep sending pain signals to the brain even though the gallbladder's gone. But it's also possible your pain has nothing to do with the surgery. The liver sits in the upper right part of your belly, so if that's where it hurts, the liver could be part of the picture. Plenty of other things can cause belly pain too, like digestive issues, muscle strains, or kidney stones. If it's bugging you or getting worse, get it checked by a doctor. They can look at your symptoms and figure out what's really going on.

Windshield wipers are sold one at a time because the two wipers on a car are usually different lengths, so each one is a different part. The driver's side is often longer than the passenger's side, and the rear wiper on many cars is its own separate size too. Since the parts don't match, a store can't sell one "pair" that works for every car. Instead, you buy the exact length each side needs.

Many people do replace them one at a time. Wipers don't wear out at the same rate. The driver's side does most of the work, since it's the side that sweeps across the area you look through most, so it often gets worn out sooner. Some people only replace the one that's streaking or chattering, and that's perfectly fine. Others replace both at once because they're already in the car, both are the same age, and it saves a trip later. Neither way is wrong.

So you're not doing anything unusual. Replacing both at the same time is a very common choice, and it's a good one if you want fresh wipers all around. It just means you'll buy two separate parts, which is why the packaging looks like singles.

Pancytopenia means that all three main blood cell types are low at the same time: red cells (which carry oxygen, and are reflected in your hemoglobin of 6.9), white cells (which fight infection, and are low at 2800), and platelets. It is a finding, not a single disease, so the underlying cause has to be identified. Common causes include deficiencies of vitamin B12, folate, or iron, problems within the bone marrow, certain medicines, infections, and autoimmune conditions. I can't tell you your exact diagnosis from these numbers. Your doctor would confirm it with a complete blood count with peripheral smear, reticulocyte count, vitamin B12 and folate levels, iron studies, and sometimes a bone marrow test.

Regarding the medicines, leucovorin is a form of folic acid that is often used when folate is deficient or to counter certain drug toxicities. Livogen is a hematinic, a supplement meant to support blood formation. Vitcofol injection usually contains vitamin B12 and folic acid. Taken together, this regimen is a reasonable approach for some types of nutritional anemia, and short courses of these drugs are generally well tolerated. However, one safety point matters: high-dose folate can partly correct the blood count in vitamin B12 deficiency while nerve damage continues silently, so it is important that B12 status is checked and that B12 is kept up if it is low. Your doctor will presumably know this, but you should ask whether your B12 level has been measured.

Because your hemoglobin is 6.9, which is quite low, and your white cell count is reduced, you should be monitored closely. Ask your doctor whether you need a transfusion, when your blood count will be rechecked, and what the cause is. Seek medical care urgently if you develop chest pain, shortness of breath at rest, fainting, a racing heartbeat, fever or signs of infection, unusual bleeding or bruising, or new numbness, tingling, or confusion.

Several over-the-counter (OTC) medicines contain dextromethorphan, a cough suppressant, which may help ease a cold-related cough. Among them are Robitussin DM, which combines dextromethorphan with guaifenesin, an expectorant that thins and loosens mucus in the airways; Vicks DayQuil Cough, which adds acetaminophen, a pain reliever, to dextromethorphan and guaifenesin; and NyQuil Cough, which pairs dextromethorphan with doxylamine succinate, a sedating antihistamine, and acetaminophen. Delsym is a liquid form of dextromethorphan that can be swallowed directly or mixed with water and used as a throat spray. It is important to follow the directions on the packaging and avoid going over the recommended dose. Because dextromethorphan can cause drowsiness, you should not drive or use heavy machinery while taking it. If you have questions about these medications, or if your cough continues despite treatment, speaking with a healthcare professional is always advisable.

No ETF I'm aware of tracks a long straddle directly, so the closest matches depend on which side of the trade you want. A long straddle, which buys an at-the-money call and put, profits from a large move in either direction, and it gains from rising volatility. For long-volatility exposure, ProShares VIX Short-Term Futures ETF (VIXY) and similar VIX-futures funds are the usual choice, though they suffer from futures roll costs and decay over time, so they're better suited to short-term hedging than long-term holding. For a more options-based approach, some tail-risk or "crisis alpha" funds use put options to profit from sharp market drops, which captures part of the straddle's payoff.

If you want the opposite, a short straddle that earns premium when markets stay calm, Simplify Volatility Premium ETF (SVOL) is a known option-selling fund, though it sells VIX-related call options rather than straddles on the S&P 500 itself. Several issuers, including NEOS and Cboe Vest, also run options-income funds that sell index calls or put spreads, but these are not true straddle replicas.

Because fund holdings and strategies change, check the current prospectus or a screener such as ETF.com or Morningstar for the latest details, or consult a financial advisor if you're considering options exposure.

People always start harping on saving money when the economy gets shaky, and honestly it makes sense. When things are rough, everybody feels a bit more exposed. You start worrying about whether your job's safe, groceries and rent keep creeping up, and whatever you've got invested might be worth less next month than it is today.

That's where a savings cushion really helps. If the car dies or your hours get cut or you lose your paycheck for a while, you've got something to lean on instead of panicking or putting it all on a credit card. Families especially tend to sleep better knowing there's a little buffer there.

And it's not just a recession thing. Building up savings over time makes you more stable and better able to handle whatever gets thrown at you, good economy or bad.

The honest answer is that there's no single current figure I can state with confidence, because the numbers come from periodic surveys and change over time. The most-cited source is the Federal Reserve's Survey of Consumer Finances, which is conducted every three years. Its 2022 results, the most recent I'm aware of, showed a median retirement account balance of roughly $87,000 among households that had any retirement account, while the median for all households (including those with none) was much lower, around $25,000 to $30,000. Those figures differ a lot depending on whether you count households with no retirement savings at all, and they also vary sharply by age. Households near retirement age typically have substantially higher balances than younger ones.

If you need a precise, up-to-date number, I'd recommend checking the latest Survey of Consumer Finances release on the Federal Reserve's website, or data from the Employee Benefit Research Institute, which publishes detailed retirement savings statistics by age group.

I'm sorry you're worried about your son's swollen lymph nodes. Given your own recent experience with lymphoma, it's natural to fear the worst. Still, swollen lymph nodes have many possible causes, and in most cases they don't point to anything serious. In children, the usual culprit is a viral illness like a common cold or the flu, since the nodes swell as the immune system responds to the infection. Bacterial infections, allergies, and minor injuries can also cause this, too. Because your son recently had a cold and is teething, his swollen nodes most likely stem from one of these ordinary causes. Even so, if you have any lingering concerns about his health, it's worth speaking with a healthcare provider. His doctor can examine him, identify the reason for the swelling, and suggest any treatment that's needed. If your worries persist, bring them up with his doctor again, and consider getting a second opinion from another professional, such as a pediatrician or a pediatric specialist.

Definitely follow your doctor's advice on this one and get whatever tests or treatment they recommend. A liver function test (LFT) is just a blood draw that checks levels of certain substances your liver makes, called liver enzymes. If your liver isn't working right, those numbers can come back higher than normal. High bilirubin, which you mentioned, can point to liver damage or disease, but it's not always the liver. Certain medications or conditions that speed up the breakdown of red blood cells can push it up too, so there's more than one possible explanation. Your doctor will want to track down the cause and talk through next steps. They might order imaging or even a liver biopsy to narrow it down. Also, don't skip the TB treatment. They'll likely have you on medication to clear the bacteria and stop it spreading, and you need to finish the whole course so the infection actually goes away.

Think of internet like a water pipe. The speed is how wide the pipe is, so a wider pipe lets more water flow through at once. Internet companies sell you a certain pipe width, and they charge based on how wide it is, because that's the thing they are really building and maintaining in your neighborhood. A fast pipe needs better wires and equipment, and it costs more to run.

Cell phones work differently. Think of them more like a big water tank that gets refilled each month. The phone company has a set amount of signal they can send through the air, and it is shared with lots of people nearby. What you pay for is how much total water you pull out of the tank over the month. Each time you watch a video or load a page, you use up some of your tank, so the company charges by how much you took.

So the difference comes down to what's being sold. Home internet sells the pipe itself, and phone plans sell the total amount you use. No Illuminati needed, just different ways of selling the same kind of water.

Yep, "folio" works as a contraction of "portfolio." It comes from the Latin "folium," meaning "leaf," and people use it for a book made of bound sheets of paper. Applied to a portfolio, it can mean a set of documents, images, or other materials presented together in a bound format, kind of like a book. You'll also see it used as a shortened form of "portfolio" in professional settings, whether that's a portfolio of work or a portfolio of investments.

It seems the individual you're describing may be experiencing abdominal pain and headaches that haven't been explained by any neurological or circulatory problems. If so, it would make sense to look into other possible explanations for these symptoms. For example, a kidney stone could cause abdominal pain and, at times, headache. Inflammatory conditions like Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis, or a gastrointestinal infection, could also account for both kinds of symptoms. To pin down the cause, further tests may be needed, such as a CT scan or MRI of the abdomen, along with blood and urine tests to look for infection or inflammation. Taking a thorough medical history and conducting a physical exam may also reveal additional clues.
