You can very likely have your breast MRI safely. By 1996, titanium and titanium alloy plates and screws were already the standard for orthognathic surgery. Titanium miniplate fixation became widespread in the 1980s, and by the mid-1990s it was the norm in most practices. Some surgeons used stainless steel or Vitallium (a cobalt-chromium alloy) in earlier decades, but titanium was overwhelmingly the most common choice by your surgery date. Biodegradable plates were only beginning to be used experimentally around then.

Titanium is non-ferromagnetic, so the MRI magnet won't pull on it, and it heats very little. Vitallium is also considered MRI-safe in practice. Even stainless steel fixation in the jaw is generally not a barrier to MRI, because the plates are small, firmly anchored in healed bone, and surrounded by tissue that holds them in place. Radiologists routinely scan patients with facial and jaw hardware. The main practical effect of metal is image distortion, or "artifact," near the implant, and because your jaw is far from your breasts, that shouldn't affect the quality of a breast MRI.

To find out exactly what was used, you have a few options. Contact the oral and maxillofacial surgeon who did the operation, or their practice if they've retired, since records are often transferred to another surgeon or kept for many years. You can also request your operative report from the hospital where the surgery was done. Operative notes usually name the fixation system and manufacturer, and hospitals often keep implant logs or stickers from the packaging. Even if records from 1996 have been destroyed, which is possible given retention policies, that's usually not a problem.

The most important step is to tell the MRI facility about your jaw hardware when you schedule and again on the safety screening form. Radiology staff deal with this question all the time. If records can't be found, they may simply proceed based on the type and location of the implant, or occasionally take a quick plain X-ray to look at the hardware. In the very rare case of real uncertainty, the radiologist makes the final safety call, but jaw plates from that era are almost never a reason to cancel a scan. Telling them ahead of time is the most reliable way to avoid surprises on the day of your appointment.

Even when a company does not send you a 1099-MISC, you must still report any income of more than $600 that you received from it. This money should be listed as general income on your tax return. To do so, you will fill out the return and place the income on the proper form, for example Form 1040 if you file as an individual or Form 1120 if you file for a business. The amount you were paid by the company goes in the other income section, which can cover wages, salaries, tips, and various other kinds of earnings. Reporting all of your income accurately matters, whether or not a 1099-MISC arrives. If you leave income off your return, you could be charged penalties and interest. Should you be unsure how to report this income, you can talk to a tax professional or look at the IRS instructions for the relevant tax form.

Good question! The water itself doesn't really go bad. Water is pretty tough, and it's mostly just water. The date is there for the bottle and for the taste.

Over time, the plastic bottle can slowly let tiny bits of air in and let tiny bits of the water's flavor or the plastic's flavor leak out. So the water might start to taste a little flat, or like plastic, even though it's still safe to drink. Sometimes tiny bacteria can get in if the bottle wasn't sealed perfectly at the factory, and those can grow over a long time. The date is the company's promise that it will still taste fresh and be clean until then.

So think of it like a juice box or a bag of chips. Nothing dangerous happens right at the date, the company just wants you to get the best taste. Plus, the date helps stores rotate their shelves so the oldest bottles get sold first.

Honestly, swelling in the ankle and foot plus a lump in the groin could be a blood clot. If you think that's what's going on, get her seen as soon as you can. Clots can get serious fast if nobody deals with them.

That said, it might be something else. Inflammation, an injury, or just fluid building up can all make an ankle and foot swell. A doctor really needs to look at it to figure out which one it is, and then she can get the right treatment.

The other thing is that the lump in the groin could be tied to the stent procedure your mom had. That's a common spot where they go in, so it's worth keeping in mind. I'd follow whatever instructions her care team gave her, and if anything new or weird shows up, call them and let them know. They know her situation best and can check her out properly.

A pyramid scheme is an investment arrangement in which every participant brings in new people, and the money those recruits pay in is passed upward to the members above them. The name comes from the typical shape of the structure: a single person sits at the top, two people form the second tier, four form the third, and the pattern continues downward. Consider how one might operate. The founder at the peak persuades two people to join by assuring them of big profits. Each of those two then signs up four more, making the same promise, and each of those four brings in eight others, and so forth. The underlying assumption is that as the pyramid grows, cash will continue to move up toward the top. In the end, though, the structure falls apart, because there aren't enough fresh recruits to keep it going. When it collapses, those at the bottom, who joined most recently, lose everything they put in. Many countries outlaw pyramid schemes, since they are fraudulent and offer investors no genuine value. Their only function is to enrich the person at the top by deceiving others into handing over their money.

It doesn't sound weird at all. White coat hypertension is common, and the usual approach is less about treating it and more about working around it so your true readings are recognized.

The most useful step is to make your home readings count. Use a validated upper-arm cuff (the British and Irish Hypertension Society and the US-based validatebp.org list tested models), and bring it to a visit so the clinic can compare it with their own device. Take readings properly: sit quietly for five minutes with your back supported, feet flat, arm at heart level, no caffeine or exercise beforehand, and take two readings a minute apart, morning and evening, for a week. Keep a log and share it. Many doctors will also order ambulatory blood pressure monitoring, where you wear a cuff for 24 hours that measures automatically during normal life. This is the standard way to confirm white coat hypertension and rule out the opposite problem, masked hypertension, so it's worth asking for.

At the appointment itself, a few tactics help. Tell the nurse up front that you get anxious and that your readings are normal at home. Ask to sit quietly for five to ten minutes before the measurement, and ask them to repeat it at the end of the visit, when you've calmed down. Arrive early so you aren't rushing, since a hurried walk in raises pressure. Skip caffeine beforehand, and use the bathroom first because a full bladder pushes numbers up. Some clinics will let you take the reading yourself, or leave you alone in the room while an automatic cuff runs.

To reduce the anxiety itself, slow breathing works well: in for four seconds, out for six to eight, for a few minutes before and during the measurement. Muscle relaxation, focusing on a neutral thought or music through headphones, and not watching the numbers can all help. If anxiety around medical settings is severe in general, brief cognitive behavioral therapy can be very effective, and it's reasonable to mention to your doctor.

It's also worth knowing that white coat hypertension isn't always entirely harmless. Some research suggests a slightly higher chance of developing sustained hypertension later, so it's sensible to keep checking at home occasionally, maintain a healthy weight, stay active, limit salt and alcohol, and have a yearly review. Medication is generally not recommended just because of clinic readings when home and ambulatory readings are normal.

If you tell your doctor all this and they still want to act on the clinic numbers, ask specifically for ambulatory monitoring or a review of your home log before any decisions are made.

Action selection is the process by which an agent decides what to do in a particular situation. It may mean choosing among several alternatives, or working out the best course of action given the present state of the environment or system. Many factors can shape this choice, such as the agent's goals and objectives, the resources it has and the constraints it faces, and the outcomes it expects from each possible action. The process can become quite complicated, especially when several objectives conflict or compete, or when the results of various actions are uncertain or difficult to foresee. Within artificial intelligence, action selection is a central part of decision-making, and it is commonly tackled with methods like planning, reinforcement learning, and decision trees. Within cognitive psychology, it is regarded as a core component of cognitive control and executive function, and researchers examine it in relation to decision-making, problem-solving, and goal-directed behavior.

Okay, so the big choice is between buying physical gold and buying a gold ETF, and each one has its tradeoffs.

With physical gold, you actually own the metal. You can store it somewhere safe, like a safe deposit box, and you always know exactly where your money is sitting, which a lot of people find reassuring. Gold also has a long track record as a store of value, so if you think the price is headed up, owning the real thing is a straightforward way to play it. The downsides are real, though. Storage costs money and is a hassle, and selling a big chunk of gold quickly can be tough. You have to find a buyer willing to pay what you want, and that gets harder when markets are rough.

A gold ETF flips most of that. It trades on a stock exchange, so you can buy or sell in seconds, which is handy when things get volatile. You don't have to deal with storage or insurance, so costs are usually lower, and it's an easy way to add gold to a portfolio without the physical stuff. The catch is that you're trusting the fund to actually hold the gold and manage it properly, so you're taking on counterparty risk. And since the ETF is only trying to follow the gold price, its performance can drift a bit from the metal's actual price. That's called tracking error.

So which one makes sense really comes down to what you want. If you want something tangible you can hold and don't mind the hassle, physical gold works. If you'd rather have something liquid and low-maintenance, an ETF is probably the better pick. Either way, it's worth talking to a financial advisor before you commit.

Fox News isn't the only one that carried the Benghazi hearings live. CNN and MSNBC covered them live too, while they were happening. Fox may have put more airtime into it because they thought it was a big story, or because their audience was especially interested. Maybe a bit of both.

Quick background: the Benghazi hearings were a series of congressional investigations into the September 11, 2012, attacks on the U.S. diplomatic mission in Benghazi, Libya. Four Americans died in the attacks, including the U.S. Ambassador to Libya. Lawmakers wanted to figure out what happened and whether anyone screwed up along the way. Because the hearings reached high-level officials, including then-Secretary of State Hillary Clinton, they got tons of media attention. Some people felt the attacks could have been prevented and that the government didn't do enough to protect its diplomats in Libya. Others saw the whole thing as politically motivated, a way to go after Clinton and the Obama administration.

Direct marketing is a form of advertising in which businesses communicate directly with specific individuals or groups of potential customers, rather than reaching a broad audience through mass media such as television, radio, or general print publications. The goal is to prompt a immediate response, such as a purchase, a visit to a website, a phone call, or a request for more information.

Common examples include postal mail such as catalogs and promotional letters, email campaigns, text messages, telemarketing calls, and door-to-door distribution of flyers. Because the message is sent to a targeted recipient, direct marketing typically relies on customer data, such as names, addresses, purchase histories, or demographic details, to identify who is most likely to be interested in a product or service.

One of the main advantages of direct marketing is that its results are often measurable. A company can track how many people responded to a particular offer, which makes it easier to evaluate the return on investment and refine future campaigns. It also allows for personalization, so messages can be tailored to a recipient's interests or past behavior.

Direct marketing is subject to various legal and ethical rules, particularly concerning consent and privacy. Many regions require businesses to obtain permission before sending unsolicited emails, texts, or calls, and recipients usually have the right to opt out of future communications.

Measuring as much as 100 feet (30 meters) long and weighing up to 200 tons, the blue whale holds the title of the largest animal on the planet. Its range covers every ocean in the world, and it is easily recognized by its blue-gray coloring and long, slim body. As a member of the baleen whale group, the blue whale has no teeth. Instead, its mouth contains long, flexible keratin plates that strain tiny prey, such as krill, out of the water. The species is endangered, since hunting and other human activity have drastically cut its numbers. For all their immense size, blue whales are typically gentle animals and are not dangerous to people.

The Atanasoff–Berry Computer (ABC) was an early electronic machine designed and partly built during the 1930s by physicist John Atanasoff and engineer Clifford Berry. It was the first computer to carry out calculations with electronic switches (vacuum tubes) rather than mechanical ones (like relays or mechanical calculators), and it was also the first to represent data using binary digits (bits). The ABC was meant to solve systems of simultaneous linear equations, a frequent kind of problem in scientific and engineering work. Data was fed in and programs were stored on punched cards, and a set of vacuum tube circuits handled addition, subtraction, and multiplication. The machine was never finished, yet the concepts Atanasoff and Berry worked out while designing it went on to shape the development of modern computers. In 1973, the US Patent Office credited the ABC as "the first computer to use electronic switches and binary digits in its calculations, and the first machine to use punched cards as a program medium." That same year, Atanasoff and Berry were awarded the US National Medal of Technology and Innovation for their work on the ABC.

I'm sorry you made an error while paying your income taxes. If you've already submitted your return with a wrong account number, you'll have to reach out to the Internal Revenue Service (IRS), tell them about the error, and ask them to fix it. The IRS's toll-free line for individual tax questions is 1-800-829-1040. Should the problem not get resolved by phone, you might have to send the IRS written documentation that explains what went wrong and asks for a correction. If you haven't filed yet but have entered the wrong account number, fix it before you submit your return. You can change your return through the IRS "Free File" service, or you can complete and send in an amended return (Form 1040-X). Accurate account details matter when you file, since the IRS relies on them to process your payment and apply it to your account. If you still have questions or concerns, contact the IRS for more help.

When a store asks whether you want "debit or credit," it is really asking which card you intend to use for the payment. A debit card draws directly from your checking or savings account at a bank or credit union, so purchases move money out of your account and into the merchant's account. A credit card, by contrast, is essentially a loan from the card issuer: when you buy something with it, you borrow the money and must repay it later, along with any interest charges. Therefore, the choice should depend on your circumstances. If the funds are sitting in your checking or savings account and you prefer to settle the purchase immediately, debit is often the better option. If you lack the cash on hand right now, or you would like to earn the rewards or other perks your credit card provides, credit may suit you better.

The apple in your hand is not biologically dead, even though its form of life differs from that of an animal or a person. It remains a living organism, with its cells still working and carrying out their normal tasks, such as generating energy and repairing harm. Yet the apple's life effectively ended the moment it was harvested from the branch. Once separated from the tree, it lost its link to the roots, which had been supplying water, nutrients, and other essentials for survival. Deprived of these, the fruit will gradually begin to rot and break down. That decline, however, unfolds over a span of time, so the apple can still be enjoyed well before it spoils. In short, the apple you are eating is not alive as you are, but it is still a living thing. It died when picked, yet it remains edible and pleasant for some time before it turns bad.

A storytelling device is any technique or element a writer, filmmaker, or other narrator uses to shape how a story is told, as distinct from the events of the story itself. Where the plot is what happens, the device is how the material is presented to the audience so that it becomes engaging, clear, or emotionally powerful. Common examples include foreshadowing, where early hints suggest what is to come; flashbacks and flashforwards, which move the timeline backward or ahead; the unreliable narrator, whose account the audience has reason to doubt; and dramatic irony, where the audience knows something the characters do not. Other devices include a frame narrative, where one story is nested inside another as in The Arabian Nights; a cliffhanger, which ends a scene on an unresolved tension to pull the audience forward; and the use of symbols or recurring motifs that carry meaning across the work.

Devices also include choices of point of view, such as first person versus third person, and the pacing decisions that determine how long a scene lingers or how quickly events move. In visual media, the equivalents include camera angles, editing rhythms, voice-over, and the deliberate withholding of information. Because devices shape the audience's experience, they can be used to build suspense, create sympathy, reveal character gradually, or invite interpretation. Writers often discuss them when analyzing or critiquing a work, asking not only what happens but why the story is arranged the way it is and what effect that arrangement produces.

The liver is one of the few organs that can regenerate, and when the cause of mild to moderate inflammation is something you can remove, such as a medication or alcohol, enzyme levels often come back to normal over several weeks to a few months. Since your February results were normal and you have since stopped the medications, there is a good chance yours will improve. But I'd treat that as a likely outcome, not a guarantee, and I'd want it confirmed with a repeat blood test.

The main thing to know is that Tylenol (acetaminophen) is a common cause of liver injury, especially when taken often or in combination with other products. Many prescription pain medicines and cold or sleep products contain acetaminophen too, so it is easy to take more than you realize. The usual maximum for healthy adults is about 3,000 to 4,000 mg per day, and lower if you drink alcohol or have liver problems. Other drugs, supplements, and herbal products can also affect the liver, so make a full list of everything you took, including doses and dates, and bring it to your doctor.

Treatment depends on the cause. If a medication is responsible, the plan is usually to stop it, avoid alcohol, avoid acetaminophen and anything else that stresses the liver until your doctor says otherwise, and recheck liver tests in a few weeks. There is no pill that speeds healing in most cases. If the numbers do not improve, or if they were very high to begin with, your doctor may look for other causes such as viral hepatitis, fatty liver, autoimmune disease, or bile duct problems. That could involve more blood tests and an ultrasound.

Ask your doctor which specific numbers were high (ALT, AST, bilirubin, and so on) and how high, because that affects how urgent this is. Also ask what you can safely take for headaches in the meantime, since you shouldn't just go without pain relief or guess at alternatives.

Seek care promptly if you develop yellowing of the skin or eyes, dark urine, pale stools, severe abdominal pain, persistent nausea or vomiting, unusual fatigue, or confusion. Those suggest more significant liver trouble and should not wait for a routine follow-up.

Peter Thiel is an American entrepreneur, venture capitalist, and political figure, best known for his role in founding PayPal and for being one of the first outside investors in Facebook. Born in 1967 in Frankfurt, West Germany, he moved to the United States as a child and grew up in California. He studied philosophy at Stanford University and earned a law degree from Stanford Law School before entering the technology sector.

In 1998, Thiel co-founded Confinity, which later merged with X.com to form PayPal. He served as the company's chief executive before it was acquired by eBay in 2002 for about $1.5 billion. Afterward, he used his gains to become an influential investor. In 2004 he invested in Facebook when it was still a young company, and he later made early investments in firms such as LinkedIn, Airbnb, and SpaceX. He also co-founded Palantir Technologies, a data analytics company that works with government agencies and private organizations.

Thiel is also known for his investment firm, Founders Fund, which he established in 2005 with other PayPal alumni, and for his book "Zero to One," which argues that the most valuable businesses create genuinely new products and markets rather than competing in existing ones. He has been a prominent libertarian-leaning voice in Silicon Valley, supporting causes such as limited government and certain forms of technological and scientific innovation. He funded the Thiel Fellowship, which pays young people to skip or leave college and pursue entrepreneurial projects, and he backed the Hulk Hogan lawsuit against Gawker Media, which led to that outlet's closure. In 2016 he publicly endorsed Donald Trump and spoke at the Republican National Convention, and he later became a supporter of various conservative political candidates.

Buying a house in Germany can feel like a lot, but you can make it a lot smoother by tackling it in steps. Here's roughly how I'd go about it.

Start by figuring out your budget. You need to know what you can actually spend before you start browsing, so look at your income, savings, and debts. Don't forget the ongoing costs too: mortgage payments, property taxes, and maintenance add up fast.

Next, get pre-approved for a mortgage. A lender will review your finances and tell you how much they'd be willing to lend. It makes house hunting easier, and sellers take you more seriously when they know you've already been vetted.

Then start looking. Check listings, go to open houses, and get a feel for what your money buys in the areas you like. It's also worth digging into local trends like average prices and how much demand there is for different property types.

A good real estate agent can save you a lot of headaches. They know the local market, can point you toward places that fit what you need, and will negotiate for you. Worth the commission, in most cases.

Before making an offer, get a professional home inspection. It'll flag any nasty surprises, and it helps you decide whether to go ahead. If the inspector finds problems, you can also use them to push the price down.

When you find the right place, make your offer. Your agent can help you word it based on current market conditions, the property's condition, and anything else that matters in your situation.

Last step: once your offer is accepted and your financing is locked in, you sign the contract and pay. This usually means working with a lawyer or notary to sort out the legal paperwork.

I'm so sorry your dad is going through this. Pus in the chest after surgery plus a fever is something he needs looked at right away, since it could mean an infection or another complication from the operation. What happens next depends on what's causing it and the details of his case, so his care team will need to examine him and run some tests before they can settle on a plan. That could mean antibiotics, draining the pus, or going back in to remove any infected tissue. In the meantime, he should rest, drink plenty of fluids, and tell his nurses or doctors if he's in pain so they can manage it properly. Please don't wait on this one. Getting him seen quickly makes a big difference. I really hope he gets the help he needs and bounces back soon.

Biological vision is the process by which living organisms detect and interpret light from their surroundings in order to build a useful picture of the world. It is one of the most widespread senses in nature, found in animals from simple single-celled organisms that sense light intensity to humans and other mammals with complex, high-resolution eyes. The basic task is always the same: convert light energy into signals that the nervous system can process, so the organism can find food, avoid predators, navigate, and coordinate its behavior.

The process generally begins with photoreceptors, specialized cells that contain light-sensitive molecules such as opsins, which are paired with a light-absorbing chromophore like retinal. When a photon is absorbed, the molecule changes shape, triggering a chemical cascade inside the cell that alters its electrical state. This change is then passed on to other neurons, which combine, filter, and organize the signals. In vertebrates, this processing begins in the retina, where neurons detect contrast, motion, and edges before sending information along the optic nerve to the brain, mainly to areas in the thalamus and visual cortex.

Biological vision varies greatly across species. Some animals see only light and dark, while others perceive color, polarized light, or ultraviolet and infrared wavelengths that humans cannot see. Eye structures also differ, from simple light-sensitive pits and pinhole eyes in some invertebrates to camera-type eyes with lenses in vertebrates and compound eyes made of many small units in insects. Despite these differences, the field of biological vision draws on neuroscience, biology, and physics to understand how evolution has shaped these systems and how they transform raw light into the rich visual experience that guides behavior.

The answer depends on which group you look at, because the figures vary a lot.

The most widely cited source is the Federal Reserve's Survey of Consumer Finances, last released for 2022. It found that the median retirement account balance among all families was about $87,000, but that figure includes only families who have retirement accounts. Roughly half of American families had no retirement account at all, so the median across all families, counting those with zero, is far lower. The mean (average) among account holders was much higher, around $333,000, because a relatively small number of households hold very large balances.

By age, the 2022 survey showed median balances among account holders of roughly $40,000 for those under 35, about $60,000 for ages 35 to 44, around $100,000 for ages 45 to 54, about $185,000 for ages 55 to 64, and roughly $200,000 for ages 65 to 74. These figures are approximate and are for households that have accounts, such as 401(k)s and IRAs.

Other sources give somewhat different pictures. Vanguard's data on its own plan participants showed a median 401(k) balance of around $35,000 and an average near $134,000 for 2023, though that covers only one plan type at one provider. Balances have likely risen since then thanks to strong stock market returns, but newer comprehensive federal data is not yet available.

The key takeaway is that typical Americans have saved far less than common retirement guidelines suggest, such as having several times your annual salary saved by your 60s. Many households rely heavily on Social Security, and a sizable share has little or no dedicated retirement savings. Home equity and traditional pensions also contribute to retirement security for some, but they are not captured in these account-balance figures.

Blood in your spit that shows up only after lying down for a while, and then clears once you are up and moving, is most often coming from the nose, sinuses, throat, or mouth rather than the lungs. While you lie flat, small amounts of blood or mucus from irritated tissue can pool in the back of the throat, and the first spit after getting up brings it out. Common causes include dry air, nasal or sinus irritation, allergies, a recent cold, postnasal drip, acid reflux irritating the throat, gum problems such as gingivitis, and dry or cracked nasal lining. Sleeping with your mouth open, using a CPAP machine, or taking blood thinners or aspirin can make it more likely.

Because it happens only briefly and then stops, it is often minor. Still, it is worth mentioning to a doctor if it keeps happening, since a pattern that repeats over days or weeks deserves a look. A simple exam of your nose, mouth, and throat may find the source. Meanwhile, you can try a humidifier at night, saline nasal spray, good hydration, gentle brushing and flossing, and checking whether your gums bleed.

Please get seen promptly, and do not wait, if you notice any of the following: coughing up blood that is bright red or frothy, more than a teaspoon of blood, blood that continues after you are up, a cough lasting more than a few weeks, unexplained weight loss, night sweats, fever, chest pain, shortness of breath, easy bruising or bleeding elsewhere, or if you are a smoker or have smoked heavily, since lung causes need to be ruled out. If you have any trouble breathing or heavy bleeding, seek emergency care right away.

If you take blood thinners, tell your prescriber about this. Otherwise, make a routine appointment with your primary care provider in the next week or two, and note how often it happens, how much blood you see, and whether it looks like it comes from your nose, gums, or deeper in the chest.

This is a common and frustrating situation, and it often comes from scammers rather than real creditors. SEO and "business listing" operators frequently send official-looking invoices or past-due notices to businesses, hoping someone will pay without checking whether they actually signed up for the service. If you don't recall agreeing to anything with these companies, don't pay yet.

Start by checking your records. Search your email, bank and credit card statements, and accounting software for the company names and any earlier contact. If you find a signed contract or an order you placed, you may have a real obligation, and you should review its terms, cancellation window, and billing dates. If you find nothing, you most likely aren't a customer.

Next, verify each company independently. Look up their official website yourself rather than using links or phone numbers in the invoice, and check whether their business registration exists in your state's Secretary of State database. Be wary of invoices that pressure you with urgent deadlines, threaten collections or legal action within days, or ask for payment by gift card, wire, or cryptocurrency. Those are classic warning signs.

If you're confident you don't owe them, reply in writing (email is good, so you have a record) stating that you have no record of a contract or purchase, that you dispute the invoice, and that you ask them to send proof of the agreement and an itemized account. Keep copies of everything and don't confirm any payment details. Avoid calling back on numbers printed on the invoice, since those can be fake.

If they keep contacting you, you can report them to the Better Business Bureau, your state attorney general's consumer protection office, and the FTC at reportfraud.ftc.gov. If a company has your payment information or you've already paid, contact your bank or card issuer right away to dispute the charge or block future payments.

If you tell me roughly what the invoices say, such as the amounts, the service described, and how they reached you, I can help you judge whether they look legitimate or fraudulent and draft a dispute letter.

Committing a crime in a country where you don't live can have grave consequences. Depending on how serious the offense is, the penalties might include fines, time in prison, or in some cases even the death penalty. Anyone accused of wrongdoing abroad should promptly consult a lawyer and seek assistance from their embassy or consulate, which can offer legal support and explain what to expect in the process. Even as a visitor, it is essential to obey the local laws of the country you are in so that you can stay out of trouble.

The number depends on the tradition. The Protestant Bible has 66 books: 39 in the Old Testament and 27 in the New Testament. The Catholic and Orthodox Bibles include additional books in the Old Testament, such as Tobit, Judith, Maccabees, and Sirach, so the Catholic count is 73. Some Orthodox traditions include even more, and the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo canon has around 81 or 88 books depending on how it is counted.

A peptide sequence refers to the ordered chain of amino acid residues that forms a peptide or protein. Amino acids serve as the fundamental units from which proteins are assembled, and peptide bonds link them into chains. The order in which amino acids appear within a protein dictates how it folds in three dimensions and what job it performs. Researchers commonly express this order using one-letter abbreviations for each residue. As an illustration, the sequence "MVHLTPEEK" describes a peptide built from methionine, valine, histidine, leucine, threonine, proline, glutamic acid, and lysine, in that order. The length of a peptide can range from only a handful of residues up to several hundred. Such molecules may be made through chemical synthesis or generated naturally by cells during protein synthesis. Peptides are involved in numerous bodily processes, such as cell signaling, immunity, and catalysis by enzymes. Beyond their biological roles, they also find use in laboratory research and in designing medicines and other therapies.

Inflation isn't a fixed number; it changes over time and differs by country. As a rough guide, many developed economies have targeted around 2 percent per year, which is the goal set by central banks such as the U.S. Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank. Recent figures have varied widely, with inflation spiking above 8 percent in some countries in 2022 before easing in many places during 2023 and 2024.

For the current rate in your country, the most reliable sources are the national statistics agency (such as the Bureau of Labor Statistics in the United States or the Office for National Statistics in the United Kingdom) or the central bank's website. If you tell me which country you're interested in, I can explain what I know about its recent trends, though my information may not reflect the latest monthly release.

Whether you can deduct car or home costs depends largely on how you use them and what kind of return you file, so it helps to split the two.

For a car, the main deduction is for business use. If you're self-employed or a business owner, you can deduct the business portion of your vehicle expenses, either by using the IRS standard mileage rate (65.5 cents per mile for 2024, adjusted yearly) or by deducting the actual costs such as gas, insurance, repairs, depreciation, and interest, multiplied by the business-use percentage. You need a mileage log showing business trips, dates, destinations, and purposes to support the claim. Commuting from home to a regular workplace is generally not deductible. W-2 employees can no longer deduct unreimbursed job expenses for federal purposes, though some states and certain professions such as armed forces reservists, performing artists, and some government employees are exceptions. Electric vehicles may also qualify for federal tax credits, which are separate from deductions and subject to income and vehicle eligibility rules.

For a home, the picture is different. If you own your home and itemize deductions, you can generally deduct mortgage interest on up to $750,000 of acquisition debt (for loans taken after December 2017), and state and local property taxes within the SALT cap, which is currently $10,000 for most filers but is scheduled to rise under recent legislation. Points paid on a purchase may also be deductible. Because the standard deduction is high, many homeowners no longer benefit from itemizing, so check whether your total itemized deductions exceed it. If you use part of your home regularly and exclusively for business, you may claim a home office deduction, either using the simplified method ($5 per square foot up to 300 square feet) or the actual expense method, which allocates a share of mortgage interest, utilities, insurance, repairs, and depreciation. Rental property owners can deduct a broad range of expenses and depreciation against rental income.

Rules change frequently and depend on your state, filing status, and specific circumstances. If you tell me whether you're self-employed, an employee, a homeowner or renter, and roughly what you spend, I can point you to the most likely options. A tax professional can confirm the details for your situation.

Ronald Reagan is polarizing because he did a lot of things that people judged very differently depending on their values and their view of what government should do. He was president from 1981 to 1989, and his record touches on taxes, the economy, the Cold War, and the role of government, so people who care most about those areas tend to have strong opinions about him.

Imagine a big sandbox with two groups of kids who disagree about how the sandbox should be run. Reagan was a leader who believed the sandbox worked best when the grownups stepped back and let kids build what they wanted. He cut taxes and reduced many regulations, and supporters say this helped the economy grow, with several years of strong growth and falling inflation after a rough stretch in the late 1970s. They also credit him with standing firm against the Soviet Union and helping bring the Cold War to a peaceful end, which many people see as a huge win for freedom. For those who share his instincts about small government and a strong national defense, he represents a hero who made them proud and gave them hope.

Other kids looked at the same sandbox and worried about the kids who got left out. Critics point out that his tax cuts tended to benefit wealthier people more, that federal deficits grew considerably during his presidency, and that the economy's gains were not shared equally. They also point to his administration's slow response to the AIDS crisis, his handling of some foreign conflicts, such as the Iran-Contra affair, and his cuts to social programs. For people who believe government should do more to help those in need, he looks like a leader whose policies made life harder for many Americans.

So people disagree about Reagan partly because they disagree about the facts and mostly because they weigh the same facts differently. Some judge him by the economy and the end of the Cold War, while others judge him by inequality, deficits, and the people his policies did not help. Historians also debate how much credit he deserves for events that had many causes. Reagan himself remains popular in many circles, and his legacy is still a live argument about what kind of country we should be.

When people discuss entitlement nowadays, they typically mean the belief that one is owed something without having earned it or without regard for the emotions and requirements of other people. Someone might be described as having a "sense of entitlement" if they consistently expect preferential treatment or demand their own way, paying no attention to how their choices affect those around them.

Information mining, sometimes called data mining, refers to the work of finding patterns and connections within vast collections of data. Using sophisticated methods and algorithms, it pulls and examines data from many different sources in order to reveal useful knowledge and insights. Organizations and researchers rely on it to guide choices, spot trends, and address challenges in fields such as commerce, science, and medicine. The process generally draws on machine learning approaches, including clustering, classification, and regression, to sift through large datasets and surface meaningful information. As a core component of data analytics, it is frequently paired with other tools, such as data visualization, to make the findings easier to understand and interpret.

New Guinea lies in the western Pacific Ocean, just north of Australia. It is the second-largest island in the world after Greenland. The island is divided politically between two countries: the eastern half forms the independent nation of Papua New Guinea, while the western half is part of Indonesia, where it is known as Papua and West Papua provinces. The Torres Strait separates its southern shores from the northern tip of Australia, and the Coral Sea and Solomon Sea lie to its east and southeast.

Douglas Bruce "Doug" Lenat (1950–2023) was an American computer scientist and artificial intelligence researcher best known for creating Cyc, a long-running project to build a comprehensive knowledge base of common-sense facts and the reasoning rules needed to use them. Lenat began the effort in 1984 while working at the Microelectronics and Computer Technology Corporation in Austin, Texas, and later continued it through Cycorp, the company he founded in 1994. The central idea behind Cyc was that many AI systems failed because they lacked the basic background knowledge humans take for granted, such as the understanding that water is wet, that people generally die once and stay dead, or that a sentence about a cup on a table implies the cup is supported by the table. Lenat and his team spent decades hand-entering millions of these assertions and encoding them in a formal logical language so that a computer could draw inferences from them.

Before Cyc, Lenat earned recognition in the 1970s and early 1980s for programs that explored automated discovery and heuristic search, most notably the AM and EURISKO systems. AM was designed to generate and test mathematical concepts, and EURISKO attempted to learn new heuristics about its own reasoning. EURISKO also gained public attention for winning the Traveller tabletop war game tournament, after which its rules were changed to prevent a repeat.

Lenat received the Computers and Thought Award from the International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence in 1987 and was honored for his contributions to the field over many years. He was also known for his ambitious, long-term outlook, and he argued that symbolic, knowledge-based approaches deserved a central role in AI even as statistical and neural network methods rose to dominate the field. Lenat died in August 2023, and his work on Cyc remains one of the most sustained attempts to give machines a broad foundation of general knowledge.

Nephrotic syndrome is basically a cluster of symptoms you get when your kidneys aren't doing their job right and can't filter waste and extra fluid out of your blood properly. Usually it comes down to damage to the glomeruli, which are the tiny filters in your kidneys that clear out that stuff.

How it's treated really depends on what's causing it, but here's what you'll commonly see.

Medications are a big one. Your doctor might put you on something to control blood pressure, bring down the swelling, and help prevent complications like infections.

Diet matters too. They'll often suggest cutting back on salt, which helps with both blood pressure and swelling.

Speaking of blood pressure, high blood pressure is really common with this condition, and you want to keep it in check so your kidneys don't get hurt any more than they already have.

If an autoimmune problem is behind it, immunosuppressive therapy is a possibility. It calms down the inflammation and helps protect the kidneys from further damage.

And if the kidneys are badly damaged, you may end up needing dialysis to clear the waste and extra fluid from your blood.

Whatever the plan is, stick with it and keep going to your follow-up appointments. That's how your doctor keeps an eye on things and tweaks the treatment when it needs it.

Martin Luther King Jr. was shot on the balcony of the Lorraine Motel in Memphis, Tennessee, on April 4, 1968. He was standing outside Room 306 on the second-floor balcony when he was struck by a single rifle shot at about 6:01 p.m. He had come to Memphis to support striking Black sanitation workers. He was taken to St. Joseph's Hospital, where he was pronounced dead a little after 7 p.m.

James Earl Ray was convicted of the assassination after pleading guilty in 1969, though he later recanted his plea. The Lorraine Motel is now part of the National Civil Rights Museum, which preserves the balcony and Room 306 as a memorial.

Movies that weren't filmed in 3D can be turned into 3D through a process called conversion. Think of it like a magic trick where a flat drawing gets made to look like it has depth.

Here's the basic idea. Your two eyes see the world from slightly different spots, so each eye sees a slightly different picture. Your brain mixes those two pictures together and tells you how far away things are. 3D movies work by showing each eye a slightly different picture, so your brain thinks things are popping out at you.

When a movie was filmed with just one camera, there's only one picture. So artists have to make a second picture themselves. They do this by going through the movie frame by frame, which means one still picture at a time. Movies play about 24 pictures every second, so a two hour movie has hundreds of thousands of frames. That's a huge amount of work, and for The Lord of the Rings, the conversion team had to do it for the whole film.

For each frame, the artists first trace the important things in the picture, like people, trees, and buildings, and cut them out into separate layers, a bit like paper dolls. They then decide how far away each layer should be. Next, they slide each layer a tiny bit left or right to create the second eye's view. Things meant to be close get shifted more, and things far away get shifted less. Where a layer moved and uncovered empty space, the artists fill in the gap by painting in what would be hidden behind it, which is the hardest and slowest part.

Computers help a lot with this today, figuring out depth automatically and doing some of the shifting, but people still check and fix the results by hand. Once both eye pictures are ready, the film is shown in a way that sends one picture to each eye, and your brain does the rest.

An existential risk is a danger that puts the continued survival of humanity, or of any other intelligent life, in jeopardy. Such threats are especially hard to evaluate and reduce, since they could wipe out the human species entirely or stop it from achieving its full potential. Nuclear war, pandemics, bioterrorism, and artificial intelligence that goes wrong are all commonly cited examples. Discussion of the idea takes place mainly in philosophy, ethics, and risk management, and it also comes up among those who shape policy and make decisions. What sets existential risks apart from other kinds of risk is their capacity to inflict devastating and irreversible damage on humankind. They also tend to involve events that are unlikely to occur but would have an enormous impact if they did, and this combination makes preparation and mitigation particularly challenging. Because of how large and serious these risks are, individuals, organizations, and governments should weigh the possible consequences and act in advance to confront and prevent them.

In psychology, the term affect describes the emotional side of experience. It covers a spectrum of emotional conditions, such as feelings, moods, and emotions. Affect may be pleasant, like joy or happiness, or unpleasant, like sorrow or anger. Some affective states are fleeting and last only briefly, while others persist for a longer stretch of time. Affect shapes the way people perceive and react to their surroundings. It guides how people think, feel, and act, and it can have consequences for physical health and overall well-being. Several theories attempt to explain how affect arises and how it steers behavior. One holds that affect is a reaction to environmental stimuli, such as positive or negative events and experiences. Another suggests that affect stems from internal influences, including thoughts, beliefs, and attitudes. Grasping affect and its effect on behavior matters across many disciplines, including psychology, psychiatry, and counseling. It is also pertinent to education, where awareness of students' emotional states can help teachers foster a supportive learning environment.

Many factors determine why some words are seen as improper or off-limits in particular settings. A few explanations for why "butt" might be judged more acceptable than "ass" in certain situations are as follows. First, connotation: the two words carry somewhat different associations. "Butt" tends to be used in a playful, lighthearted manner, whereas "ass" often carries a harsher tone and is sometimes employed as an insult. As a result, "butt" can seem suitable in more settings, while "ass" may strike people as crude or offensive. Second, historical usage: both words have been part of English for centuries, yet their uses have shifted. "Butt" has long been applied in a neutral or even friendly sense, while "ass" has more often been used in a demeaning way. This history can make "butt" easier to accept in various contexts. Third, cultural norms: different groups and communities set their own standards for which words are appropriate, so "butt" might be preferred in some places while "ass" is more common in others. In the end, these judgments differ from place to place and person to person, so it is wise to pay attention to both your word choice and the setting in which you speak.

Imperfect information is when one or more players in a game or decision don't know everything they'd need to know. They might not be sure what options are open to them, or what will happen if they pick one. So they have to make calls based on partial info. You see this all over the place. In poker, you can't see the other players' cards, so you're betting on guesses and whatever you can read from how they act. Stock investors never have the full picture on how a company will do, so they're working with incomplete data. Honestly, everyday life is full of this too: you rarely know every possible outcome or what the other people involved actually want. It makes decisions messier and less predictable, and it can totally change how things turn out, in games and in the real world. It's a big deal in game theory and economics, and in any field that looks at how people decide when they're uncertain.

Imagine a big toy store where kids can play with lots of toys at once. Some toy stores are really just a counter where you pick up a toy and take it home. Others are like a giant playground where everybody is playing the same game together at the same moment, and the playground has to keep track of every single kid, every toy, and every rule all the time.

Blizzard's Battle.net, especially for games like World of Warcraft, is like that giant playground. The game world itself lives on Blizzard's computers, not on yours. Every time you swing a sword or pick up treasure, their computers have to decide what happened and tell everyone else. That is a lot of work, and the computers doing it need to be fixed, cleaned, and updated from time to time. Some of those fixes can't be done while the game is running, just like you can't repaint a swing while kids are swinging on it. So Blizzard picks a regular time, usually Tuesday, when fewer people are playing, and says, "Everybody out of the playground for a little while so we can fix things."

PSN and Xbox Live are more like the front desk of the toy store. They mostly handle things like logging you in, keeping your friends list, and letting you buy games or chat. Those jobs are simpler and can be split across many computers, so workers can fix a few at a time while the others keep going. The actual games you play on those services usually run on their own servers made by each game company, and those companies do their own maintenance, which you may not notice or which happens at odd times.

The truth is that PSN and Xbox Live do go down for maintenance too, just less often and sometimes in small pieces, or with announcements you didn't see. Blizzard just likes to do it on a regular schedule so everyone knows when to expect it, which is kind of like having a set cleaning day instead of surprise closures.

I can't recommend a specific dentist without knowing your city, but I can help you think through the options and how to find someone trustworthy.

First, the mismatch you noticed matters. An X-ray can show decay that isn't visible or painful yet, and a clinical exam can show problems the X-ray misses, so the two should be weighed together. Before accepting root canal treatment, ask the dentist what exactly the X-ray shows: whether the decay is close to the nerve (pulp), whether there is infection at the root tip, and whether the nerve itself appears healthy or damaged. Ask her to show you the image and point out the problem. You can also ask whether the pain is coming from this tooth at all, since referred pain, a cracked tooth, gum disease, or bite stress can mimic a nerve problem.

If the nerve is still healthy, several pulp-preserving options may be possible. Selective or stepwise caries removal removes only the softest decay and leaves a thin layer over the nerve, with a temporary filling and a recheck in a few months. Indirect or direct pulp capping places a medicated material over the nerve to encourage it to heal. Silver diamine fluoride can arrest some decay without drilling. A simple filling or crown may be enough if the decay is shallower than it looks. Some of these are less predictable in certain cases, so a dentist should judge whether your tooth is a good candidate.

Waiting is not always safe. If the nerve is already infected or dying, delaying treatment can lead to an abscess, bone loss, or the tooth being lost. Get urgent care promptly if you develop facial swelling, fever, pain that wakes you at night, trouble swallowing or breathing, or pus or a bad taste from the gum.

To find a competent and honest provider in your area, consider these steps. Ask your general dentist for a referral to an endodontist, a specialist in root canal treatment, who can give an independent diagnosis. Get a second opinion before any irreversible treatment, and ask for a copy of your X-rays so another dentist can review them. Dental schools near you often provide evaluations at lower cost. Your local or state dental association can also provide referrals. Signs of an honest dentist include explaining the diagnosis clearly, showing you images, offering more than one option with honest trade-offs, not pressuring you into same-day treatment, and being willing to answer "what happens if we wait?"

If you tell me your city or country, I can suggest what kinds of specialists and resources are typically available there.

Yes, your results look normal, and nothing in them suggests you can't get pregnant.

Your FSH of 5.20 mIU/ml on day 2 is in a healthy range. Early-cycle FSH is mainly used to check ovarian reserve, and values below about 10 are generally considered reassuring. Your LH of 5.80 mIU/ml is also normal for this phase, which typically falls somewhere around 2 to 10. Your prolactin of 6.98 ng/ml is well within normal limits (usually below about 25 in women), so there's no sign of the high prolactin that can interfere with ovulation.

On LH versus FSH, your doctor is essentially right. In the early part of the cycle the two are often similar, and LH being slightly higher than FSH is not a problem. The ratio matters mainly when doctors are considering polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), where LH is sometimes two to three times higher than FSH. Your ratio is about 1.1, which is not a concern. Even then, PCOS is diagnosed from irregular periods, signs of excess male hormones, and ovary appearance on ultrasound, not the ratio alone. With regular periods and these numbers, PCOS seems unlikely.

It also helps to know that seven months without conceiving is still within the normal range for someone your age. About 80 to 85 percent of couples conceive within a year of regular unprotected intercourse, so many doctors don't consider it a fertility problem until a full year has passed for women under 35. Many healthy couples simply take a bit longer.

Since hormones are only one part of fertility, your doctor may suggest other steps if you haven't done them already. Ovulation predictor kits or tracking can confirm you're ovulating and help you time intercourse in the few days before and on ovulation. A thyroid test (TSH) is often checked because thyroid imbalance can affect fertility. An AMH test gives another view of egg reserve. If things still don't happen, an HSG (a dye X-ray) can check that your fallopian tubes are open. It's also important that your partner has a semen analysis, since male factors account for roughly 40 to 50 percent of cases where couples have difficulty conceiving, and the test is simple and inexpensive.

Meanwhile, general measures like taking folic acid, keeping a healthy weight, avoiding smoking and excess alcohol, and managing stress all support your chances. Your results are encouraging, so try to stay positive and keep following up with your doctor.

South Park is able to mock well-known figures and steer clear of legal trouble largely because the First Amendment to the United States Constitution protects it, guaranteeing freedom of speech and expression. In practical terms, the show's creators, Trey Parker and Matt Stone, are free to voice their views and ideas, even when some audiences find them critical or offensive. The series also frequently relies on satire, a comedic style that takes real events or people and exaggerates them in order to make a point or critique something. Since the show plainly does not portray its satirical targets in a serious or literal way, it is hard for anyone to convincingly claim that the program defamed them or caused them other harm. Lastly, each episode typically opens with a disclaimer declaring the show to be fiction and noting that any similarity to real people, living or deceased, is purely accidental. This disclaimer further signals that the program should not be taken seriously and is intended simply as a comedic take on current events and culture.

Joe's Crab Shack was a casual seafood chain here in the US, kind of a beachy, themed restaurant thing. It got started back in 1991, and then Ignite Restaurant Group bought it in 2006. Ignite ended up filing for bankruptcy in 2017, and after that Landry's picked up the Joe's Crab Shack chain. Landry's owns and runs a whole bunch of restaurants and hospitality businesses, and it's privately held by billionaire Tilman Fertitta.

Long-term investing means buying assets that are anticipated to grow in value across several years or even decades. Examples include shares of stock, bonds, mutual funds, property, and certain commodities such as gold and other precious metals. Long-term investing offers a number of benefits. A longer holding period gives an investment more time to appreciate and lets compound returns build up. Such investments tend to carry greater risk, yet they can also deliver higher gains over the long haul. Spreading money across a range of assets lets you diversify your holdings and distribute risk among various sectors and industries. Many long-term options, including mutual funds and exchange-traded funds (ETFs), are professionally managed, which can be valuable for people who lack expertise in investing. Keep in mind that every investment involves some degree of risk, and positive returns are never guaranteed. Before making any investment decisions, it is wise to seek guidance from a financial advisor or other professional.

Pain in your right groin when you stand and talk in a higher pitch than usual could point to a hernia. Hernias often bring pain, soreness, or a sense of pressure in the groin. Standing and speaking can make the discomfort more noticeable, since both raise the pressure inside the abdomen and may push the hernia further outward. That said, the pain and lump might instead stem from a different problem, such as a strained inguinal ligament or a pulled muscle. You should see a healthcare provider so the source of your pain can be identified and you can get the right treatment. A provider can examine you physically and may order imaging tests to pinpoint what is causing your symptoms.

Sorry to hear you're dealing with body pain and can't get your hands on Inergy. I can't really recommend a specific medication, though. That's a call for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your history. There are plenty of options for body pain, and which one works best depends on what's causing it, what other conditions you have, and what else you're taking. A pharmacist is a good first stop since they can look at your full med list and tell you what's safe. Your doctor can also help figure out the root cause and map out a plan. If you've already tried some things, mention those too, because it helps them narrow it down fast.

Yeah, recycling can actually get you some tax perks, mostly if you're running a business. A few ways it tends to work:

Tax credits are one. Some governments will give businesses a credit if they recycle a certain percentage of their waste, or if they use recycled materials in what they make.

Deductions are another. You might be able to write off recycling-related costs, like buying recycling equipment or paying to transport recycled materials.

Then there's property tax exemptions. In some places, if your business hits a certain recycling rate or uses recycled materials in its products, you could get a break on property taxes too.

That said, what's available depends a lot on where you live and what kind of recycling you're actually doing, so there's no one-size-fits-all answer. If you're serious about going after any of this, talk to a tax pro or dig into the tax rules for your area.

Whether you should buy from your landlord depends on your finances, your plans, and the specific deal, but there are some useful ways to think it through.

Start with whether you can afford it on your own terms. Buying means more than the price. You'll need a down payment, closing costs (often 2 to 5 percent of the price), and money for repairs and maintenance, which renters usually don't pay for. Compare your likely monthly mortgage payment, property taxes, insurance, and upkeep against what you pay in rent now. If buying would stretch your budget thin, leaving you with no emergency fund, that's a serious warning sign.

It also helps to know the house's condition. Ask whether there have been recent inspections, and get your own independent inspection before committing. Your landlord may be willing to sell "as is," and you should find out about roof, foundation, plumbing, electrical, and any history of water damage or pests before you're locked in.

The landlord relationship can be an advantage. You already know the home, the neighborhood, and how the building has been maintained. Some landlords will sell below market value, offer flexible terms, or let you apply part of your rent toward the purchase. Those are worth asking about, but get any such arrangement in writing with a real estate attorney reviewing it, since verbal side agreements can fall apart.

Be careful about the mixing of roles. Because you're dealing with someone who is also your landlord, make sure you still have a clear, fair negotiation and that you're not pressured by the fact that you might lose your home if you say no. You're entitled to walk away, and you should be sure you could find another place to live if you did.

Finally, consider whether you plan to stay at least five years or so. Buying makes the most financial sense when you'll be in the home long enough to recover the transaction costs. If you might move soon, renting may be the better choice.

If you share your rough numbers, your location, and how long you expect to stay, I can help you think through the comparison more concretely. A consultation with a mortgage advisor and a real estate attorney would also be worth it before you commit.

A directed acyclic graph (DAG) is a directed graph with no cycles. So you can't start at some vertex, follow the arrows, and end up back where you started. People use them for all sorts of things. One big use is modeling dependencies: in a build system, for instance, the edges can show which source files depend on which, and each node can stand for compiling one particular file. They also show up in data processing pipelines. Think of a machine learning setup where the nodes are preprocessing or feature engineering steps and the edges track how data flows from one to the next. And they're handy for scheduling, like a job scheduler where each node is a job and the edges capture which jobs have to finish before others can start. The no-cycles rule is what makes these work. Nothing can loop forever, so a process built on a DAG always has a clear end. Since the edges have direction, the order of steps is baked into the structure, which matters a lot when one thing has to happen before another.

Options are financial agreements that grant the buyer the freedom, though not the requirement, to purchase or sell an underlying asset at a fixed price on or before a set date. An option holder may choose to exercise this right at any point before expiration, provided the option remains in the money. The expiration date marks the final day on which exercise is permitted. Should the holder fail to exercise by that date, the option lapses and becomes worthless. Investors generally use options either to protect themselves against risk or to bet on how the price of an underlying asset will move. A call option gives its holder the right to buy the asset, whereas a put option gives its holder the right to sell it. Underlying assets may take many forms, including stocks, bonds, currencies, commodities, or futures contracts.
JFK ran against Richard Nixon, the Republican candidate, in the 1960 presidential election. It was a pretty close race, but Kennedy came out on top and became the 35th President of the United States.

There are a few possible explanations for swelling and a sore at the corner of the mouth. One is angular cheilitis, an inflammation at the mouth's corners that is usually driven by a fungal or bacterial infection. Another is cold sores, also called fever blisters, which result from the herpes simplex virus and may appear on or near the lips. Swelling and sores in this area can also stem from an allergic reaction to a product such as toothpaste or lip balm. Finally, shortages of certain nutrients, particularly iron or vitamin B2 (riboflavin), can bring on angular cheilitis. A healthcare provider should examine the swelling and sore to identify the cause and recommend suitable treatment. Until then, applying a lip balm or cream can calm the area and keep it moisturized. If the swelling becomes severe or the sore is painful, contact the healthcare provider who prescribed the penicillin for further advice.

A soft bump on the bridge of the nose after a blow is usually a small collection of blood or fluid under the skin, or swelling from bruising. Your doctor's advice to use ice for 10 to 15 minutes twice a day is sensible. Keep using it for the next day or two, always wrapping the ice pack in a thin cloth rather than placing it directly on the skin. After about 48 hours, a warm compress may help the body reabsorb the blood and fluid, though you can ask your doctor whether to switch. Keep your head elevated, especially when sleeping, to reduce swelling. Acetaminophen (paracetamol) is a safer choice for pain than ibuprofen or aspirin, which can increase bruising, but confirm with your doctor first. Avoid pressing on the area, blowing your nose forcefully, or wearing glasses that rest on the bridge until it settles. Gentle cleaning with mild soap and water is fine. Topical arnica gel is often used for bruising, though the evidence for it is limited.

Most swelling and bruising like this improves within one to two weeks, and a small bump can take up to three or four weeks to fully flatten. Bruising may change color from purple to green or yellow as it heals, which is normal.

Contact your doctor promptly, or seek urgent care, if you notice any of the following: the nose looks crooked or shifted, you have persistent or heavy bleeding, one or both nostrils become blocked and stay blocked, the bump becomes firm, very tender, or keeps growing, you have trouble breathing through your nose, you develop vision changes, double vision, or swelling around the eyes, or you have fever, spreading redness, or drainage, which could signal infection. These signs can point to a fracture or a septal hematoma, which needs prompt attention.
