A stock market index reflects the combined prices of many companies, and those prices are essentially collective bets about future profits and the risks attached to them. A terrorist attack changes both of those things almost instantly, or at least changes what investors believe about them, so prices adjust.

The first and most immediate driver is uncertainty. Markets can price in bad news fairly well when its scope is known, but an attack raises questions nobody can answer right away: Is this an isolated event or the start of a campaign? Will there be more attacks? How will the government respond, and could it lead to military conflict? When investors cannot estimate risk, they tend to demand a higher return for holding risky assets, which means they are only willing to buy stocks at lower prices. Many also move money into assets seen as safer, such as government bonds, gold, or certain currencies, and that selling pushes the index down.

There are also direct economic effects. An attack can destroy property, shut down businesses, disrupt transportation and supply chains, and in some cases close the exchanges themselves, as happened in New York for several days after September 11, 2001. Certain industries are hit especially hard because their future earnings depend on people feeling safe. Airlines, hotels, tourism companies, and restaurants often see sharp drops, while insurers face the prospect of large claims. Because these companies are part of broad indexes, their declines pull the overall number down.

Psychology and herd behavior amplify the reaction. Fear spreads quickly through news coverage and social media, and many investors sell simply because they see others selling or want to limit losses before prices fall further. Automated trading systems and stop-loss orders can accelerate this, turning a moderate decline into a steep one within minutes or hours.

Expectations about broader economic consequences matter too. Investors may anticipate that consumers will spend less, that businesses will delay investment, that security costs will rise, or that governments will increase military spending and borrowing. Some sectors can actually rise in response, such as defense contractors and security firms, which is why the effect on an index is a net result of winners and losers.

Historically, the impact on major indexes has usually been sharp but relatively short-lived in large, stable economies. Markets often recover within weeks or months once it becomes clear the economy's fundamental capacity is intact, and central banks may help by cutting interest rates or providing liquidity, as the Federal Reserve did after 9/11. The size and duration of the drop tend to depend on the scale of the attack, its location relative to financial centers, whether it seems likely to be repeated, and how strong the economy and financial system were beforehand. Smaller or less developed markets, or countries facing repeated attacks, can experience more lasting effects because the risk becomes part of investors' long-term outlook.

Okay, so Bayesian inference is basically a way of doing statistics where you use Bayes' theorem to keep updating how likely a hypothesis is as new evidence rolls in. Bayes' theorem is just a formula for working out the probability of something given what you already knew about related conditions. The main difference from classical (frequentist) stats is that frequentists treat the hypothesis as fixed and use the data to test it, whereas Bayesians let the probability of the hypothesis itself change as data comes in. The core idea is that both the data and the hypothesis can be treated as random variables, and probability theory tells you how they relate. That means you can make probabilistic predictions from the data and then revise them whenever new data shows up. You'll see it a lot in machine learning and data analysis, where it helps make predictions about complicated systems even when you don't have much data. It pops up in economics, psychology, biology, and plenty of other fields too, anywhere people want to draw conclusions about uncertain stuff from what they've observed.

Optimal control theory is a mathematical optimization technique for identifying the control inputs, often referred to as "controls" or "control actions," that give a given system the best achievable performance while respecting certain constraints. It forms a branch of control theory concerned with improving control systems. In these problems, the goal is to determine a control strategy that either minimizes or maximizes a performance measure across a specified time horizon. That performance measure is frequently a cost function, capturing the balance between the advantages of strong performance and the expenses incurred by applying the controls. The time horizon is the interval during which the control inputs act and the system's behavior is assessed.

The approach is applied across many disciplines, such as engineering, economics, and computer science, and it finds use in manufacturing, transportation, finance, and robotics. Consider a few examples: a manufacturing process seeking to reduce production costs while meeting quality standards, a self-driving car working to use as little fuel as possible while keeping a safe and efficient speed, or an investment portfolio designed to earn the highest returns with minimal risk.

At its core, optimal control theory relies on dynamic optimization, which means finding the best solution to a problem involving variables that change over time. The optimal solution is whichever one maximizes or minimizes the performance measure over the time horizon. Engineers and researchers typically rely on optimization algorithms or mathematical methods such as the calculus of variations or dynamic programming to locate it. I hope this helps! Black swan theory is a concept popularized by Nassim Nicholas Taleb, a statistician, former trader, and author of the 2007 book "The Black Swan." It describes rare, unpredicted events that carry extreme impact and that people tend to rationalize after the fact as if they had been foreseeable. The name comes from the old European assumption that all swans were white, a belief that was overturned when black swans were discovered in Australia in the seventeenth century.

Taleb identifies three defining traits of a black swan event. First, it is an outlier, lying outside the realm of regular expectations because nothing in the past convincingly points to its possibility. Second, it carries a massive impact. Third, despite its strangeness, people concoct explanations for it after the fact, making it seem predictable in hindsight. Examples often cited include the rise of the internet, the 9/11 attacks, the 2008 financial crisis, and the COVID-19 pandemic, though whether each truly qualifies is debated.

The theory also critiques how humans and institutions handle uncertainty. Taleb argues that people rely too heavily on models based on normal distributions, which assume that extreme events are vanishingly rare, when many real-world phenomena, such as financial markets, wealth distribution, and natural disasters, follow fat-tailed distributions where extreme events occur more often than expected. He also points to narrative fallacy, our tendency to build tidy stories that make past events look inevitable, and to confirmation bias, which leads us to ignore evidence that challenges our assumptions.

From this, Taleb draws practical lessons. Rather than trying to predict black swans, which is essentially impossible, individuals and organizations should build resilience, maintain safety margins, avoid excessive debt and fragile structures, and position themselves to benefit from positive surprises. He distinguishes between "Mediocristan," where outcomes are predictable and averages matter, and "Extremistan," where a few extreme events dominate outcomes, and argues that we increasingly live in the latter.

Normally the ex-dividend date comes first, followed by the record date and then the payment date. But the payable date can fall before the ex-dividend date in certain situations, and it usually comes down to how the company and its exchange set the timeline.

The most common reason is that the dividend is declared with a payment date that is set without regard to the trading calendar. Companies sometimes announce a payable date that is earlier than the ex-dividend date, which can happen when the board approves the dividend with a schedule that was determined before the record date was finalized, or when a company is trying to pay shareholders quickly. In these cases, the date of record and ex-dividend date are set after the payment is already scheduled, so the order looks reversed on paper.

Another factor is the difference between the declaration, record, and payment steps and the way brokers and data providers publish them. Some financial websites list the payable date as the date the company expects to pay, while the ex-dividend date is calculated under exchange rules based on the settlement cycle. If a company changes its timetable or if the data is updated late, the published dates can end up out of their usual sequence.

Finally, there are situations involving foreign companies, special dividends, or corporate actions such as spin-offs, where the payment and the ex-date are governed by different rules or jurisdictions, and the dates may not follow the normal pattern.

In practice, if you see this, the key question is which date the company itself announced in its official notice. The ex-dividend date is the one that determines whether you receive the dividend: you must own the stock before that date to be entitled to the payment. If the payable date comes first, the company's announcement or the exchange's listing is the authoritative source to check.

Kernel methods are a family of algorithms for pattern analysis and machine learning. The basic idea is to take data points from a low-dimensional input space and map them into a higher-dimensional feature space, where they're often much easier to separate. A kernel function does the work here. It takes two data points and spits out a single number measuring how similar they are.

The big payoff is that kernel methods can handle data that isn't linearly separable in its original form. Once you map things into a higher-dimensional space, you can often find a straight dividing line (or plane) between classes that wasn't possible before. That's handy for stuff like image classification or natural language processing, where the raw inputs are usually a messy tangle.

You'll see the approach in a few well-known algorithms: support vector machines (SVMs), kernel principal component analysis (KPCA), and kernel ridge regression. Each one leans on a kernel function to shift the data into that richer feature space, which makes tasks like classification, regression, or clustering a lot more manageable. People have used them for all sorts of things, from sorting data and reducing dimensions to approximating functions. Pretty versatile tool to have in the toolbox.

A feedforward neural network is an artificial neural network commonly applied to classification and prediction problems. It is built from several layers of linked "neurons" that handle and pass along information. Every layer takes in data from the layer before it, performs its processing, and forwards the result to the layer after it. The last layer's output represents the network's forecast or label for the input.

The opening layer, known as the input layer, contains the neurons that take in the raw data. The intermediate layers, referred to as hidden layers, transform that data through the use of weights and biases. The concluding layer, the output layer, generates the final prediction or categorization.

These networks get the name "feedforward" from the way information moves: strictly one way, from input to output, with no loops back. Other designs, such as recurrent neural networks, differ in that they can cycle information through themselves. Feedforward networks see broad use in areas like image and speech recognition, natural language processing, and predictive analytics. Being capable tools for tackling difficult problems, they have played a key role in building many of today's artificial intelligence systems.

Radiation therapy is often used for painful or weakened bones, and in some cases surgery or a brace is needed to stabilize a bone.

About the medications: ketorolac is an NSAID, and NSAIDs are generally avoided or used cautiously in myeloma because they can harm the kidneys and increase bleeding risk, especially if he has kidney involvement or high calcium. Please ask his doctor whether it should be continued at all. Aventyl (nortriptyline) commonly causes drowsiness and fatigue, particularly at the start or when the dose is high. Don't stop it abruptly on your own, since that can cause withdrawal symptoms. Ask his prescriber whether the dose can be lowered, the timing changed (for example, taken only at bedtime), or an alternative used for his pain or nerve symptoms.

While he waits, it's reasonable to ask his care team to check his blood counts (anemia is a common cause of fatigue), calcium, kidney function, and pain control. Ask them, too, for a clear timeline for the biopsy results and treatment start, and whether he should be referred to a myeloma specialist or a center that offers transplant evaluation if that isn't already in place. Keeping a simple log of when he feels most tired and which medications he's taken can help the team adjust his regimen.

The cerebral cortex is the outermost layer of the brain, a thin sheet of gray matter that covers the two large hemispheres of the cerebrum. In humans it is only about two to four millimeters thick, but because it is extensively folded into ridges called gyri and grooves called sulci, its surface area is large enough to fit inside the skull. Its gray color comes from the dense concentration of neuron cell bodies, while the white matter beneath it consists mainly of the myelinated axons that connect cortical regions to one another and to deeper structures.

The cortex is responsible for most of the brain's higher-order functions. It processes sensory information such as vision, hearing, touch, and smell, with each sense having dedicated primary areas, for example the visual cortex at the back of the brain. It also controls voluntary movement through the motor cortex in the frontal lobe, and it supports language, memory, reasoning, planning, decision-making, attention, and conscious awareness. Association areas integrate information from multiple senses so that a person can recognize a face, understand speech, or judge the meaning of a situation.

Anatomically, the cortex is commonly divided into four lobes on each side: frontal, parietal, temporal, and occipital. Histologically, the neocortex, which is the most recently evolved part and makes up most of the cortex in mammals, typically has six layers of neurons that differ in their connections and roles. Its development and expansion are considered a major factor in the advanced cognitive abilities of humans and other mammals.

Lenders earn their income from loans by collecting interest on the money they advance. Were that practice outlawed, lending would probably become hard to find for individuals and companies alike, since there would be no profit motive behind handing out funds. Access to capital needed to launch or expand a venture would shrink, and this could slow overall economic development. The consequences would be milder in a small nation, where the economy is modest and fewer people and firms depend on borrowing. In a superpower such as the United States, however, the effects would be far greater, given the sheer size and intricacy of its economy and the large number of borrowers involved. A worldwide ban would magnify these effects even further, reaching every national economy at once. Borrowing would become harder across all countries, likely dragging down growth globally. In short, prohibiting interest on loans would probably harm economies and the spread of wealth, as it would restrict the financing that individuals and businesses rely on to get started or grow.

I'm so sorry about your dad's diagnosis. Cancer in the chest and near the aorta is serious, and what happens next really depends on the type and stage, plus his overall health and what he wants. Usually the first step is a biopsy, where they take a small tissue sample from the tumor and look at it under a microscope. That tells the team what kind of cancer it is and how far along it is, which shapes the whole plan.

There are a few main options. Surgery is sometimes possible to remove the cancerous tissue. That might be a traditional open operation, or it might be laparoscopic, which uses small incisions and special instruments. Radiation therapy uses high-energy beams, like X-rays, to kill cancer cells, and it's sometimes paired with chemo or used on its own. Chemotherapy uses drugs that go after cancer cells. They can be given by mouth or through an IV, and they're often combined with surgery or radiation.

Every case is different, though, so the best route will depend on a lot of specifics. Your dad's care team can walk him through the options, the risks, and what to expect from each one. If he's feeling unsure, getting a second opinion is totally reasonable.

Particle swarm optimization (PSO) is a computational technique for locating the global minimum or maximum of a function. Its design draws on the behavior of social animals like birds or bees, which share information and work together toward a common aim. In PSO, a population of "particles" travels through a search space, adjusting its positions according to both its own experience and that of the other particles. Every particle stands for a candidate solution to the optimization problem and is described by its position and velocity within the search space. A particle's position is updated by combining its own velocity with the best position it has found so far (its "personal best") and the best position found by the whole swarm (the "global best"). Its velocity, in turn, is updated through a weighted blend of its present velocity and these position-based adjustments. Because the positions and velocities are revised again and again, the swarm gradually gathers around the function's global minimum or maximum. PSO is able to optimize many kinds of functions, and it has been used on numerous optimization problems in areas including engineering, finance, and biology.

So a solar eclipse happens when the Moon slides between the Sun and Earth and its shadow lands on us. If the Moon covers the Sun's disk completely, you get a total eclipse. If it only covers part of it, that's a partial one. It can only happen at new moon, when the Sun, Earth and Moon line up in a straight row. Well, with the Moon in the middle, I mean. There's a name for that alignment, syzygy, which is a fun word to throw around. Line it up perfectly and you get totality, but if it's a little off, you only get a partial.

You might wonder why we don't get one every month. The Moon's orbit around Earth is tilted compared to Earth's orbit around the Sun, so most of the time the Moon's shadow just misses us. Roughly twice a year though, things line up well enough for an eclipse to be possible.

Then there are annular eclipses. Those happen when the Moon is farther out in its orbit, so it looks smaller in the sky and can't cover the whole Sun. What you see is a bright ring of sunlight, called an annulus, glowing around the Moon's dark silhouette.

It's a good puzzle, because you'd think 70 degrees is 70 degrees no matter what month it is. The secret is that your body doesn't feel the number on the thermostat. The thermostat only measures the air, but your body is feeling lots of other things too.

The first big thing is the walls and windows. Your body is always giving off a little bit of warmth, like a tiny campfire. In winter, the walls and windows are cold because it's freezing outside, so your little campfire's warmth gets sucked toward them, even if the air in the middle of the room is warm. That's why you can feel chilly sitting next to a window in winter. In summer, the sun has been baking the walls and roof all day, so they're warm and send a little heat back toward you. Same air temperature, but in winter you're losing heat to the room, and in summer the room is giving some heat to you.

The second thing is how wet or dry the air is. Winter air is very dry, and dry air pulls moisture off your skin. When water leaves your skin, it takes some heat with it, which is the same reason you feel cold getting out of a bath. Summer air is usually more humid, so sweat and moisture don't leave your skin as easily, and you feel warmer and stickier.

The third thing is drafts. Cold air from outside sneaks in around doors and windows in winter, and little cold breezes make you feel colder than the thermostat says.

The fourth thing is what your body is used to. When you come inside from a snowy day, your hands and feet are cold and your body wants to warm up, so a warmer room feels cozy. In summer, after being in the heat, a cooler room feels like a relief. Your body also slowly adjusts to each season, so you're kind of "tuned" differently in January than in July.

So people turn the thermostat up in winter not because they actually want hotter air, but because they want to feel the same comfortable amount of warm, and in winter it takes a higher number on the thermostat to get that feeling.

David Chalmers is an Australian philosopher, best known for his work on consciousness and the philosophy of mind. He was born in 1966 and has spent much of his career at New York University, where he is a University Professor and co-director of the Center for Mind, Brain, and Consciousness. He also holds an appointment at the Australian National University.

Chalmers gained wide recognition in 1995 when he presented a paper at a conference in Tucson, Arizona, that introduced the phrase "the hard problem of consciousness." He distinguished this from the "easy problems," which concern explaining cognitive functions such as perception, memory, and attention. The hard problem asks why physical processes in the brain give rise to subjective experience at all, why there is "something it is like" to see red or feel pain. He argued that standard physical and functional explanations seem to leave this question unanswered, and this idea has shaped debates across philosophy, neuroscience, and cognitive science.

His book The Conscious Mind (1996) developed these ideas at length and defended a form of property dualism, the view that consciousness is a fundamental feature of reality not reducible to physical facts, while remaining compatible with a naturalistic worldview. He has also written on topics including the metaphysics of possibility, personal identity, the extended mind, virtual reality, and the philosophical implications of artificial intelligence. His more recent work includes Reality+ (2022), which examines whether virtual worlds can be as real as the physical one.

Chalmers is widely regarded as one of the most influential living philosophers of mind, and he is known for engaging seriously with popular and interdisciplinary audiences as well as with academic colleagues.

Honestly, you should probably get a doctor or dentist to look at a torn frenulum, even though it might heal on its own. The frenulum is a sensitive little strip of tissue in your mouth, so it's worth making sure it's healing right. If the tear is small and isn't bugging you much, it may well close up by itself. Still, a pro can check it out and tell you what's best. Sometimes they'll clean it up and stitch it if needed. Your job in the meantime is keeping it clean and leaving it alone so it doesn't get irritated or reinjured. An over-the-counter wound care product might help too. But if the pain gets bad, or it doesn't seem to be getting better, don't wait around. Get seen as soon as you can.

Yeah, there's a real difference in risk between the two. A physical ETF actually holds the stuff in the index, or at least a basket built to track it. A synthetic one doesn't. It uses derivatives, usually a swap, to get the index's return.

The big one is counterparty risk. With a synthetic ETF you're counting on whoever's on the other side of that derivative to actually pay up. If that counterparty gets shaky or defaults, you could have a problem. Physical ETFs don't have that issue, since they're sitting on the real assets.

Tracking error is the other thing. That's just the gap between how the ETF performs and how the index performs. Physical funds usually track more tightly, because they own what's in the index, so they should move pretty much in lockstep with it. Synthetic funds can drift a bit more, since the derivative might not match the underlying assets perfectly.

That said, neither one is automatically the "bad" choice. Either can work fine depending on what you're after and how much risk you're comfortable with. I'd just read up on how a particular fund is built before you buy it, and decide from there which one fits your portfolio.

It is deeply troubling to learn that your brother has intense anger problems and has been acting violently. Getting professional help promptly is essential, both to tackle the problem and to protect your brother and the people around him. Anger problems and violent conduct can stem from many sources. Your brother may be dealing with stress, depression, anxiety, or some other mental health concern that is fueling his rage. Substance use, previous trauma, or a physical condition such as a brain injury or hormone imbalance may also play a part. Having a mental health expert, such as a psychiatrist or psychologist, assess him is important for uncovering what lies beneath his anger and building a suitable plan for care. That plan might involve therapy, medication, or both. Your brother should also learn practical ways to manage anger, like slow breathing, counting to ten, or stepping away when he feels overwhelmed. Remember that reaching out for help with anger is a constructive move toward better mental health and overall well-being. Urge your brother to talk with a mental health professional, and give him your support as he pursues treatment.

It's unfortunate that gaining weight has been such a struggle for you. When your body burns energy quickly or tends to shed pounds easily, adding weight can be hard. Still, several approaches may help you put on weight in a healthy manner. Eat more often: rather than sticking to three big meals a day, spread your food out over smaller meals and snacks. Doing so can raise your total calorie intake and keep your body steadily fueled. Pick nutrient-dense foods: concentrate on items that offer plenty of calories along with nutrients, including nuts, seeds, nut butters, avocados, olives, and cheese. They let you add weight without filling up on empty calories. Include plenty of protein: your body relies on protein to build and repair tissue, and good sources include meat, poultry, fish, eggs, dairy, beans, and legumes. Drink your calories: smoothies blended from milk, yogurt, and fruit, or milkshakes made from ice cream and milk, can add a lot to your daily total. Consider supplements: if you continue to have difficulty, a weight gain product such as protein powder or a mass gainer might be worth a try, since it can raise your calorie and protein intake. Before beginning any new supplement, though, talk with a healthcare professional. Keep in mind that healthy weight gain requires time and consistency, and it often takes several months or longer before your weight changes noticeably. Also remember that weight is only one piece of your overall health. Maintaining a balanced, nutritious diet and exercising regularly matter more than hitting a particular number on the scale.

OCD is a chronic mental health condition, and it can really mess with your day-to-day life. It comes down to two things: obsessions and compulsions. Obsessions are those unwanted, intrusive thoughts, images, or urges that spike your anxiety or just make you miserable. Compulsions are the repetitive behaviors or mental rituals you feel driven to do in response to them.

Treatment usually means medication plus therapy. Fluoxetine is one of the common meds for it. It's an antidepressant, specifically an SSRI (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor), and it works by raising serotonin levels. Serotonin's a chemical messenger in your brain tied to mood and behavior.

There's no known "cure" for OCD, but treatment can work really well at cutting down symptoms and making life better. Definitely get a psychiatrist or psychologist involved so you can figure out what plan fits you. On the therapy side, the main options are cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) and exposure and response prevention (ERP), and both have a good track record with OCD.

Lots of people with OCD end up needing treatment long-term, and that's pretty common. Still, some folks eventually taper off their medication or go to therapy less often. Whatever you do, stick close to your treatment team and follow what they recommend.

Gordon Plotkin is a British theoretical computer scientist, born in 1946, who is widely regarded as one of the most influential figures in the semantics of programming languages. He spent most of his career at the University of Edinburgh, where he became a professor in the School of Informatics and a central member of its Laboratory for Foundations of Computer Science. He earned his PhD at Edinburgh in 1972, with a thesis on automatic methods of inductive inference, and he has been elected a Fellow of the Royal Society and of the Royal Society of Edinburgh in recognition of his contributions.

Plotkin's work focuses on giving precise mathematical meaning to programs, so that one can reason rigorously about what software does. One of his best-known contributions is structural operational semantics, introduced in his 1981 Aarhus lecture notes "A Structural Approach to Operational Semantics." This approach describes how programs execute by means of inference rules defined over the syntax of the language, and it became a standard tool for specifying and studying programming languages. He also wrote the seminal 1977 paper "LCF Considered as a Programming Language," which introduced the language PCF and studied the relationship between its operational behavior and its denotational (mathematical) meaning, raising the famous full abstraction problem that occupied researchers for decades.

His contributions extend across many other areas. Early in his career he worked on inductive logic programming and introduced the idea of least general generalization, also known as anti-unification. He developed the call-by-name and call-by-value distinction in the lambda calculus in a precise form, contributed to domain theory through constructions such as the Plotkin powerdomain for modeling nondeterminism, and, together with John Power and later Matija Pretnar, developed the theory of algebraic effects and effect handlers, which has influenced the design of modern programming languages and libraries. He has also worked on logical frameworks, probabilistic computation, and the semantics of differentiable programming.

Plotkin has received numerous honors, including the Milner Award from the Royal Society and the Royal Medal from the Royal Society of Edinburgh, and he has been named an ACM Fellow. In later years he has also been associated with research at Google. Overall, his name is closely tied to the foundations of how computer scientists understand and formally describe programming languages.

There are a few different ways people go about buying stocks on a monthly basis, and you've got options. The first is dollar-cost averaging, which just means putting a fixed amount into a stock or portfolio on a regular schedule no matter what the price is doing. It smooths out the bumps and keeps you from buying everything at the wrong moment. The second is strategic rebalancing. Say you want 60% stocks and 40% bonds, and stocks have had a great run and now make up 70% of your portfolio. You'd sell some stocks and buy bonds to get back to your target. The third is market timing, where you try to guess short-term moves and buy or sell accordingly. Honestly, that one's risky, because nobody predicts the market consistently well. The best pick really depends on your goals, how much risk you can stomach, and your financial situation. Do your own digging, and if you're not sure, talk to a financial advisor who can look at your specific circumstances.

Assuming you mean James Butler "Wild Bill" Hickok, the famous lawman and gunfighter of the American West, his father, William Alonzo Hickok, died of illness in 1852 in Troy Grove (then called Homer), Illinois, when James was about fifteen. He was in his early fifties, and the death was not violent. Contemporary records don't give a precise medical cause, though it is generally described as a sickness that came on after years of hardship and financial struggle.

William Alonzo Hickok is often remembered as an abolitionist who reportedly helped run a station on the Underground Railroad, hiding people escaping slavery on the family farm. Family lore holds that young James sometimes went along on these trips, and a frequently repeated story claims the two were once chased and shot at by men hunting runaways. Some accounts suggest this dangerous work and its stress contributed to his declining health, but that connection is more tradition than documented fact.

His death left the family in difficult circumstances, and within a few years James headed west to Kansas, beginning the life that would make him a legend. If you meant a different "Wild Bill," let me know and I can look at that person instead.

Blood that shows up in your spit after lying down and then clears once you're upright often comes from the upper airway rather than the lungs. The most common causes are a small nosebleed or irritated nasal lining overnight, with blood trickling down the back of the throat while you sleep. Postnasal drip, sinus inflammation, dry air, mouth breathing, or nose picking can all cause this. Bleeding gums from brushing or a sore spot in the mouth can also do it, since blood collects while you're lying flat and mostly clears once you're up and swallowing or rinsing.

Even so, blood in your spit should be checked by a doctor, not just assumed to be harmless, especially if it keeps happening. Coughed-up blood from the lungs or airways needs evaluation, and a doctor can usually tell the difference with a few questions and an exam. They may look in your nose and throat, check your blood pressure and oxygen levels, and order a chest X-ray or blood tests if needed. This is worth doing soon if you smoke or have smoked in the past, are over about 40, take blood thinners, or have had this more than a few times.

Get medical care right away if the bleeding is more than a streak, if you cough up bright red blood or frothy blood, if you have trouble breathing, chest pain, fever, night sweats, unexplained weight loss, a persistent cough, or lightheadedness, or if you see blood in your urine or stool. Until you're seen, it helps to note how often it happens, how much blood you see, and whether you've had a cough, cold, or nosebleeds recently, since those details will help your doctor narrow down the cause.

The Kanab ambersnail (Oxyloma haydeni kanabensis) is a small snail native to the Kanab Creek drainage, which spans parts of Arizona and Utah in the United States. In 1990, the US Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) designated it an endangered species. This status reflects the snail's extremely restricted habitat, which is susceptible to damage and loss from several causes, among them water development, livestock grazing, and the use of off-road vehicles. To address the problem, the FWS created a recovery plan for the Kanab ambersnail, which calls for safeguarding and restoring its habitat as well as monitoring the species' population.

Red eye in photographs happens when light bounces off the blood vessels at the back of the eye. During a flash photo, light from the flash strikes the retina at the rear of the eye and reflects back into the camera lens. Because the flash illuminates those blood vessels, they show up as red in the picture, which explains why people's eyes so often look red in flash photos. Several conditions make red eye more likely. The first is how close the flash sits to the lens: the nearer it is, the greater the chance of the effect. The second is the size of the subject's pupils. Dilated pupils admit more light, raising the odds of red eye. Red eye also tends to appear in dim settings, since the pupils naturally widen in low light. There are a few ways to lessen the problem. Placing the flash farther from the lens helps, as does using a flash fitted with a diffuser, which spreads the light more evenly. Many cameras also offer a red-eye reduction mode, which fires a brief preliminary light before the main flash. This makes the pupils contract, limiting how much light enters the eye and reducing the red glow.

A loan you take out to cover an expense is usually called a personal loan or a consumer loan. People use them for things like fixing up the house, paying medical bills, or dealing with some surprise cost that popped up. You can get them from banks, credit unions, or other lenders, and the interest rate can be fixed or variable. Before you sign anything, look hard at the interest rate, how long you have to pay it back, and any fees attached. Those details decide whether the loan is actually affordable for you.

A number of things could explain feeling dizzy and having blurred vision while taking an antidepressant. The most likely is that the medication itself is responsible, since dizziness and blurred vision are known side effects of certain antidepressants. However, another condition might be the culprit instead, such as low blood pressure, a disorder of the inner ear, or a problem with the eyes. Because of this, you should talk to a healthcare provider if these symptoms appear. They can work out what is behind them and suggest suitable treatment. Until then, it may be worth cutting out chocolate and fizzy drinks to see whether that makes a difference.

Sudden paleness with pale lips and new fatigue is something to take seriously, and I'd have her seen by a doctor promptly, ideally today. If she also has trouble breathing, a bluish or gray tint to the lips, a racing heart, dizziness or fainting, chest pain, confusion, or is very hard to wake, go to the emergency room or call emergency services.

There are several possible explanations. One is anemia, meaning low red blood cells or hemoglobin. It can come from iron or B12 deficiency, blood loss (including slow bleeding in the gut that you wouldn't see), or a drop in blood cell production. Needing extra effort to do things she normally does easily fits this picture. Risperidone and topiramate are not common causes, but rarely some medicines can lower blood counts, so a complete blood count is worth asking for. Clonazepam and topiramate can also cause sedation and fatigue, and topiramate can occasionally cause metabolic acidosis, which can make a person tired and affect breathing.

Another possibility is low oxygen from an asthma flare. Paleness plus exertional fatigue can mean her lungs aren't moving air well even if she isn't wheezing loudly. A pulse oximeter reading would help if you have one; a reading below about 92 percent warrants urgent care. Also consider infection, dehydration, low blood pressure, or low blood sugar. Risperidone can cause low blood pressure when she stands up, and topiramate can reduce sweating and raise body temperature, which matters in warm weather. Heart problems, thyroid issues, and rarely a more serious blood disorder are less common but are the reason a prompt evaluation matters.

Since she is autistic, she may not be able to tell you how she feels, so a change in her usual abilities is meaningful information. Note any other changes: appetite, fluid intake, stool color (black or bloody stools matter), vomiting, fever, cough, bruising, headaches, or sleep.

When you call or go in, bring a list of her medications and doses, and mention when the paleness started and that dressing has become tiring. Reasonable tests include a physical exam, oxygen level, blood pressure and heart rate, a complete blood count, iron studies, a metabolic panel (including bicarbonate), and possibly a peak flow or lung check. Don't change or stop any of her medications on your own, especially clonazepam or topiramate, since stopping them abruptly can cause problems like seizures. Let her doctor decide on any adjustments.

Because it has already been several days, I wouldn't wait for it to resolve on its own. Call her pediatrician or primary doctor today, and if you can't be seen quickly, use urgent care.

I'm sorry about your father's diagnosis. A new discharge with a strong smell in the middle of cancer treatment should be reported to his care team today, not at his next scheduled visit.

Mucus discharge is fairly common with rectal cancer and with radiation to the pelvis, since radiation can inflame the rectal lining and tumors often produce mucus. A milky or white discharge can come from that. But a foul smell suggests something more, such as infection, dying tumor tissue breaking down, an abscess, or a fistula (an abnormal channel forming between the rectum and nearby organs or the skin). Chemotherapy can also weaken his ability to fight infection, so these problems can progress quickly.

He should contact his oncology team or surgeon right away and describe exactly what he is seeing and smelling. He should go to the emergency room without waiting if he develops a fever or chills, severe or worsening abdominal or rectal pain, a swollen or hard belly, confusion or unusual drowsiness, dizziness or fainting, heavy bleeding, or trouble urinating. Those can signal a serious infection that needs urgent treatment.

It would help to tell the team when the symptoms started, whether he has had a fever, and whether he has noticed any bleeding or changes in bowel movements. They can examine him and, if needed, order tests or imaging to find the cause and treat it.

It makes sense that your friend is worried about cancer, but a biopsy is a routine step doctors often take to find out what is causing an unusual bump or sore in the mouth. The circumvallate papillae are small, raised bumps on the back of the tongue, and they are a normal part of its anatomy. Your friend's sore spot may be connected to these papillae, though it could also be something else entirely. Only a biopsy can reliably determine what is behind it. Stitches may be needed afterward, but the procedure is fairly minor, usually done in a doctor's office or as an outpatient, recovers quickly, and is generally well tolerated. Your friend should talk with his healthcare provider about the risks and benefits of the biopsy and think carefully about what could happen if he skips it. Feeling anxious about a medical procedure is common, but a biopsy is an important diagnostic tool for identifying and treating many conditions, cancer among them.

Lots of people with RA and fibromyalgia end up dealing with dizziness, shortness of breath, or a slow heart rate, and it can come from things like inflammation, being wiped out, or stress. Yesterday's symptoms could easily have been one of those or a mix. That said, a BP of 119/65 is totally fine, but a pulse of 35 is really low and isn't something to brush off. If it happens again, or if you're feeling faint, short of breath, or just off, get it checked out soon, ideally by a doctor or urgent care, and don't wait it out. They can figure out what's actually going on and what to do about it.
Elvis Presley came into the world on the 8th of January, 1935.

As a freelancer, you need to know what you owe in taxes and set money aside throughout the year instead of waiting until year's end to pay. Doing so helps you dodge a large bill and possible penalties when you file. One way to handle this is to have tax amounts taken from your income in advance, which you can accomplish through estimated tax payments. These are payments you send to the government during the year to cover the tax you expect to owe. They are usually made in four installments and are based on your projected income and tax liability for the year. To make them, you must complete and submit Form 1040-ES, Estimated Tax for Individuals. The form contains a worksheet that helps you work out your expected tax for the year based on anticipated income and deductions. Payments are then sent with the form and a payment voucher. Keep in mind that if your estimated payments during the year fall short, you could face a penalty. You can avoid this by paying at least 90% of the current year's tax or 100% of the previous year's tax. Another possibility is to ask your clients to withhold taxes from what they pay you. Some clients will agree to this when requested, especially if you have worked with them for a long time. To arrange it, you must give the client a Form W-9, Request for Taxpayer Identification Number and Certification, which includes your Social Security number or Individual Taxpayer Identification Number (ITIN). The client can then deduct the proper amount from your payments and remit it to the government for you.

Sleep paralysis is a condition that may strike as you drift off or come out of sleep. While it happens, your muscles are temporarily immobilized, leaving you unable to move or talk. This is a natural feature of the sleep cycle, as it keeps you from physically acting out your dreams. Occasionally, though, this paralysis happens while you are awake, which can be frightening and disturbing. A very common sign is the sensation that someone or something is nearby, even though you are certain you are alone. Often called a "sleep intruder," this presence can seem vivid and menacing. Others have hallucinations or different sensory disturbances, such as hearing odd sounds or seeing flashes of light. Several factors can trigger sleep paralysis, among them insufficient or irregular sleep, stress or anxiety, certain medications or substances, and medical conditions like narcolepsy or sleep apnea. If you experience sleep paralysis, consult a healthcare professional to find the underlying cause and talk through your treatment options. Meanwhile, good sleep habits can help, including getting adequate rest, managing stress, and steering clear of substances that interfere with sleep.

Honestly, cash in lieu of dividends inside an IRA usually isn't taxed on its own. IRAs are tax-deferred, so you don't owe anything on income earned in the account until you pull money out. But that's where things get trickier. If you take a cash distribution, it could still get taxed depending on your situation. Take it out before 59 1/2 and you'll likely owe an early withdrawal penalty on top of regular income tax. And if you have a traditional IRA and the distribution is bigger than your deductible contributions, part of it may be taxable. For anything specific to your case, I'd talk to a tax pro or check the IRS guidance, since the details can get messy.

Pluto didn't suddenly become a dwarf planet. Its status changed in 2006, when astronomers agreed on a definition of what a "planet" is. Before that, there was no official rule, so anything that looked like a planet got called one.

Think of it like this. When Pluto was discovered in 1930, scientists knew very little about it. It looked like a small dot of light, and they had no idea how big it was or what else was out there. They thought it might be as big as Earth, so calling it a planet made sense. The word "dwarf planet" didn't even exist yet. Nobody had a special box for small, round things orbiting the Sun beyond Neptune.

Later, astronomers got better telescopes and started finding many other icy objects far out past Neptune, in a region called the Kuiper Belt. Some were close to Pluto's size, and one, named Eris, was even a little bigger. If Pluto counted as a planet, then these other objects would have to count too, and the list of planets could grow very long. Astronomers wanted a clear, sensible rule instead.

In 2006, the International Astronomical Union made three simple rules. A planet has to orbit the Sun, be round because of its own gravity, and have cleared the area around its orbit of other big objects. Pluto is round and orbits the Sun, but it shares its neighborhood with lots of other icy bodies, so it doesn't meet the third rule. That's why it was moved into a new group called dwarf planets, which are round but haven't cleared their path.

So the change wasn't about Pluto itself getting smaller. It was about people learning more and deciding to organize our solar system's family more carefully. Pluto is still the same wonderful icy world it always was. It just has a different label now.

Smart key systems, often called keyless entry or push-button start, are available on a wide range of vehicles today. Most manufacturers offer them on many models, and they have become standard on a large share of new cars, especially in the mid-range and luxury segments. Brands that commonly include them include Toyota, Honda, Ford, Chevrolet, Hyundai, Kia, Nissan, Subaru, Mazda, Volkswagen, Audi, BMW, Mercedes-Benz, Lexus, Acura, Infiniti, Volvo, Tesla, and most other major automakers.

Whether a particular car has one depends on the model year and trim level. A base model may use a traditional key, while a higher trim of the same car includes a smart key fob that lets you unlock the doors and start the engine without taking it out of your pocket. To check a specific vehicle, look at its features list on the manufacturer's website, the window sticker, or the owner's manual, or search for the model and year along with "smart key" or "keyless entry."

Several software applications can support value investing. A few well-known choices are as follows. Yodlee Money Center lets you monitor your portfolio, examine your holdings, and build tailored reports. Personal Capital is a money management tool offering investment tracking, budgeting, and financial planning features. Quicken, a widely used personal finance program, provides investment tracking and analysis along with budgeting and bill management. Stock Rover offers value investors a variety of instruments, such as fundamental analysis, portfolio monitoring, and screeners that help locate undervalued stocks. ValueLine gives access to the ValueLine Investment Survey, a highly regarded source of financial data and commentary. Even so, these programs are helpful only as aids; they cannot replace a solid grasp of value investing principles and a disciplined method for choosing investments. Investors should always conduct their own research and due diligence before making decisions.

So an anteroseptal infarct on an ECG basically means blood flow got blocked to the front and middle part of the heart muscle, the septum. Usually that's a clot in one of the coronary arteries that feed the heart. If it doesn't get treated quickly, the muscle tissue in that area can get damaged or die off, and that's what a heart attack (myocardial infarction) really is.

If your ECG shows signs of an anteroseptal infarct more than once, and an echocardiogram also shows a thickened septum, it's pretty likely the infarct really did happen. People who've had a heart attack often keep having symptoms or ECG changes afterward, since the damage to the muscle isn't always fully reversible.

If you're having anything that could be heart attack stuff, like chest pain, shortness of breath, or discomfort in your neck, jaw, arms, or back, get checked out. Don't just wait it out. Doctors will also want to rule out things like indigestion or other non-heart causes of chest discomfort, because getting the cause right is what lets them treat it properly.

Biomarkers of aging are biological indicators you can use to track how the aging process is going. They tell you something about the health and function of different organ systems and tissues, and they can show how aging is affecting the body. Some common ones: telomere length (telomeres are the protective caps on the ends of chromosomes, and they shorten every time a cell divides; shorter ones are linked to more age-related disease and a shorter lifespan), inflammation (chronic, low-grade inflammation is a hallmark of aging and shows up in heart disease, cancer, and neurodegenerative disorders), and DNA methylation (a chemical tag on DNA that helps control which genes get switched on, and the patterns shift as we get older, which may play a role in aging). Mitochondrial function matters too. Mitochondria are the cell's powerhouses, and they tend to get less efficient with age, which is tied to a bunch of age-related diseases. Hormone levels like testosterone and estrogen drop over time, affecting all sorts of things. Bone density falls with age, which raises the odds of osteoporosis and fractures. Grip strength is another one, since it's a handy proxy for overall muscle strength and function, and it usually declines as we get older. There are plenty more, and researchers are always hunting for new and better markers to understand aging.

Computational creativity is a field of research that studies whether and how computers can produce work that people would regard as creative. It sits at the intersection of artificial intelligence, cognitive science, philosophy, and the arts. Researchers in this area build software that generates poems, music, paintings, stories, designs, scientific hypotheses, and other outputs, and they try to understand what makes such outputs original and valuable.

The field asks two broad kinds of questions. The first is practical: how can we design systems that help people be more creative, or that come up with novel solutions on their own? The second is theoretical: what does creativity actually consist of, and could a machine ever genuinely possess it? Scholars in computational creativity often distinguish between creativity that is judged by an audience and creativity that arises from a process the system itself carries out. A system might produce something that looks surprising and useful, but whether we credit it with creativity depends on how we define the term and on whether we consider the mechanism behind the output.

To evaluate creative systems, researchers often look at properties such as novelty, which asks whether the output differs meaningfully from what already exists, and value, which asks whether it is appropriate or useful for its purpose. Some also consider whether the system can explain or justify its choices, and whether it can reflect on and revise its own work. Early examples include programs that composed music in the style of classical composers and story generators that followed structured rules to write simple narratives. More recent work uses large machine learning models, which raises new questions about authorship, originality, and how much credit belongs to the programmer, the training data's human creators, or the system itself.

Computational creativity matters both for understanding human creativity, since building models of it can clarify how ideas form, and for practical applications in art, design, science, and entertainment.

A storytelling device is a technique or element that writers and speakers use to communicate a message or theme, give a narrative structure and organization, or hold the audience's interest. Several common examples follow. Plot is the series of events that forms a story. It usually has a beginning, a middle, and an end, and the events are linked by cause and effect. Characters are the people or creatures who inhabit a story. A character may be the protagonist, who is the central figure, or the antagonist, who opposes the protagonist or stands in the way. Setting is the time and place in which the story unfolds. It may be real or invented, and it can strongly shape the narrative. Point of view is the perspective from which the story is told. It may be first person, narrated by a character within the story; third person, narrated from outside; or omniscient, narrated by a voice that knows everything. Dialogue is the exchange of words between characters. It can expose their traits, move the plot forward, and generate conflict or tension. Symbolism is the use of objects, actions, or events to stand for something beyond their literal meaning. These are only a few of the devices that can appear in many kinds of stories, such as novels, plays, and films.

A quasi-judicial agency is a governmental body empowered to issue decisions that carry the force of law and that shape the rights and duties of private individuals and organizations. Like courts, these agencies can interpret and apply laws and regulations, yet they are not part of the judicial branch. Instead, they sit within the executive branch or operate as independent agencies, and they are generally tasked with enforcing particular laws or rules in a defined area of authority. Administrative law judges, zoning boards of appeals, and labor relations boards are all examples. Such agencies frequently have the ability to conduct hearings, collect evidence, and issue rulings that bind the parties to a dispute. Sometimes a court can review an agency's decision on appeal, while in other situations the decision is final and cannot be challenged further.

Cancer is a condition in which the body's cells multiply and grow without any control. When these malignant cells gather into a mass, known as a tumor, surgeons can often treat it by cutting the tumor out. Yet cancer cells are also capable of traveling to distant areas of the body, a process called metastasis, and in such situations taking out the tumor by itself might not be enough to eliminate the disease. Consider a person with testicular cancer that has already reached other organs, such as the lymph nodes or the lungs. Removing the testicles through an operation called orchiectomy would not be enough to deal with the illness. That individual would instead require further therapies, such as chemotherapy or radiation, to destroy any cancer cells left behind and reduce the chance of a recurrence. Notably, testicular cancer is frequently detected at an early stage, where surgery alone may be sufficient. Still, anyone facing a diagnosis should talk through every available option with a medical professional in order to settle on the most suitable plan.

Springer Nature is one of the world's largest academic publishing companies, formed in 2015 through the merger of Springer Science+Business Media and Nature Publishing Group. Springer had its roots in a German bookseller and publisher founded in Berlin in 1842 and later became a major force in scientific, technical, and medical literature. Nature Publishing Group was the publisher of the prestigious journal Nature, one of the most widely read and cited scientific journals in the world. The combined company, headquartered in Berlin and with significant operations in London and New York, is owned by the German private equity firms Holtzbrinck Publishing Group and BC Partners, which hold majority stakes.

The company publishes a wide range of content, including thousands of peer-reviewed journals, books, reference works, and databases across fields such as biology, medicine, physics, chemistry, computer science, engineering, and the social sciences. Its portfolio includes well-known titles such as Nature, Scientific American (which it acquired in 2019), and the Springer book series. It also operates an open access publishing model through its journals and has been a major participant in debates over academic publishing costs, subscription pricing, and the accessibility of research. Like other large academic publishers, it has faced criticism over high article processing charges and profit margins, while also being recognized for the scale and reach of the scientific knowledge it disseminates.

Pinpointing what is causing a rash is hard without additional details or a chance to look at it directly. A rash on the cheeks can stem from many things, such as allergic reactions, infections, or irritation caused by something in the environment. If you think it might be connected to something your son came into contact with at the science center, try to work out what it was and keep him away from it in the future. Should the rash be severe, or come with other symptoms like fever, trouble breathing, or intense discomfort, get medical help as quickly as you can.

For now, you can keep the affected skin clean and dry and put on a moisturizing cream or lotion to soothe it. If it itches, an over-the-counter antihistamine such as Benadryl may ease the itching. Try to stop your son from scratching, since scratching can irritate the skin further and may even cause an infection. It's also wise to watch the rash for any shift in how it looks or how bad it is. If it fails to get better, or if it spreads or gets worse, reach out to a healthcare provider so it can be evaluated and treated.

Radiation works on cancer because it kills cancer cells or keeps them from growing and splitting. When those cells get hit, they can get damaged enough to die off. The catch is that healthy cells get hit too, so doctors try hard to aim the beams right at the tumor. Tighter aim means fewer side effects and a better shot at the treatment actually working.

A Canadian company that goes public with a dual listing on the Toronto Stock Exchange and the New York Stock Exchange gains access to two of the deepest equity markets in the world, and that access carries several practical consequences. The most immediate is broader investor reach. Canadian pension funds and retail investors can buy the shares in their home currency on the TSX, while U.S. institutions and individuals can trade them on the NYSE in U.S. dollars, often without the friction of cross-border settlement. Many large institutional mandates, index funds, and sector funds are tied to U.S. benchmarks, so a NYSE listing can make the stock eligible for inclusion in indices that would otherwise be out of reach, which can drive sustained demand and support valuation.

The dual listing also affects liquidity and price discovery. Trading is split between two venues, so the company will want to monitor how volume and spreads behave on each, since a thinly traded TSX line can sometimes lag the NYSE price, creating arbitrage opportunities that market makers exploit. Over time, however, most of the trading usually migrates to whichever market offers better depth, typically the U.S. venue for a company with significant American shareholders.

Regulatory obligations multiply. The company must comply with Canadian securities law administered by provincial regulators and the Canadian Securities Administrators, including continuous disclosure requirements, insider trading rules, and the national instrument governing financial reporting. Because the NYSE is a U.S. exchange, the company also falls under the U.S. Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and must file reports with the Securities and Exchange Commission. Foreign private issuers can use Form 40-F and Form 20-F with some accommodations, but a company that loses foreign private issuer status, for example because a majority of its shareholders are American and its management or business is principally in the United States, faces the full domestic reporting regime, including Form 10-K and 10-Q filings. Canadian issuers listed in the U.S. may also be subject to the Sarbanes-Oxley Act, which imposes internal control requirements and personal certification duties on executives, adding meaningful compliance cost.

Governance expectations shift as well. NYSE listing standards require an audit committee made up of independent directors, a code of conduct, and shareholder approval for certain equity issuances, and some of these rules differ from TSX requirements. The company may need to reconcile two sets of governance practices and disclose where it departs from NYSE rules, relying on foreign private issuer exemptions where available.

Accounting and reporting choices matter too. Canadian issuers have moved to IFRS, and a U.S. listing may require reconciliation to U.S. GAAP unless the company is a foreign private issuer that reports under IFRS as issued by the IASB, which the SEC accepts. Currency exposure is another consideration, since the company reports in Canadian dollars but its NYSE shares are priced in U.S. dollars, and investors on each exchange experience exchange-rate effects differently.

Finally, costs and strategic considerations weigh heavily. Dual listing means paying listing fees to two exchanges, duplicating investor relations work, and funding legal and audit work for two regulatory regimes. Management must also think about how dual listing affects takeover dynamics, executive compensation (since U.S.-style equity plans may be more competitive), and the company's public profile. For many firms the visibility, valuation benefits, and access to U.S. capital justify these costs, but the decision requires careful weighing against the ongoing administrative burden and the risk of greater exposure to U.S. litigation and enforcement.

A line of credit for investment purposes is a revolving loan that lets you borrow money, up to an approved limit, to buy securities or fund other investments. You pay interest only on the amount you actually draw, and as you repay the balance, the credit becomes available again. Common forms include margin loans from a brokerage, which are secured by the securities in your account, and securities-based lines of credit offered by banks or wealth managers, which are also backed by a pledged portfolio. Unsecured personal lines of credit are another option, though they usually carry higher interest rates and stricter qualification requirements.

The main appeal is leverage. If the investments you buy rise in value by more than the interest you pay, the gain is magnified. However, leverage works in both directions. If your investments fall, you still owe the borrowed amount, and losses are magnified too. With a secured line, a sharp market decline can trigger a margin call, requiring you to deposit more collateral or sell holdings quickly, often at unfavorable prices. Interest rates on these lines are typically variable, so rising rates can increase your costs over time.

Before opening one, consider your risk tolerance, your ability to cover payments if your investments underperform, and the tax treatment of the interest, which may be deductible in some cases when the borrowed funds are used for taxable investments, though rules vary and you should consult a tax professional. Compare interest rates, collateral requirements, and maintenance thresholds across lenders, and be clear on what happens in a downturn. If you are new to leveraged investing, speaking with a fee-only financial advisor can help you judge whether it fits your situation.

Donating to charity is a great way to make a difference, but it helps to be a little strategic about it. Start by researching the organization. Make sure its mission lines up with what you care about and that it's actually doing good work in that area. Look for groups that are open about their finances and have a solid track record of using donations well.

Next, think about how you want to give. You can do a one-time gift, set up monthly donations, or even leave a planned gift in your will. Pick whatever fits your budget and what you hope to achieve.

Also check the tax side of things. Depending on where you live, your donations may be tax-deductible, so hang onto your receipts and records in case you need them at tax time.

Watch out for scams, too. Sadly, some groups pose as real charities just to get your money. Before you give, do some digging and make sure the group is legit.

And remember, money isn't the only way to help. You can volunteer your time, spread the word about a cause, or speak up for issues you care about. Any of those can make a real difference, and doing a few of these things together can make your giving go even further.

An economic feature is a trait or element of an economy that sets it apart from others. These features span a broad range, including the kinds of goods and services produced, how developed the economy is, the degree of technological sophistication, the extent of international trade, how income and wealth are spread across the population, the economic system that is in operation, and how much the government steps in to regulate economic activity. Such features can strongly shape how an economy works and how well it performs, which is why they are frequently used when comparing different economies.

Chicken is by far the most eaten bird, mostly because it's cheap and easy to farm, and there's just a huge demand for it. Farms can raise chickens in big numbers, and you get both meat and eggs out of the deal. Pigeons and crows don't really show up on menus for the same reasons. They're harder to farm, nobody's buying them in bulk, and a lot of people simply don't find the idea appealing. That said, some cultures do eat pigeon, and it's considered a delicacy in certain places.

A vetting process is basically a close look at someone or something to figure out whether they're a good fit or can be trusted. The goal is to collect and weigh information about a person or organization so you can decide how credible they are, whether they're trustworthy, or whether they're right for a specific role. You'll see vetting in plenty of places: hiring, security clearances, joining clubs or groups, and so on. Say an employer is hiring. They might vet the candidates to see who actually fits the job best. A government agency handing out a security clearance does something similar, since the person will be dealing with sensitive material and they need to know who they're dealing with. Usually the process digs into someone's background: where they studied, what jobs they've held, whether they have a criminal record, and anything else that matters. That info often comes from interviews, reference checks, and other sources. What comes out of it then gets used to decide whether that person or group gets the privilege or role they're after.

Numbness in the lower back, down the left hip and leg to the toes, plus numbness in the neck and upper back, can have several causes. The most common is pressure on nerves. A disc bulge or herniation in the lower spine can press on the nerve roots that supply the left leg, and narrowing of the spinal canal (spinal stenosis) can do the same. In the neck, a similar problem with the cervical spine can cause numbness that spreads into the shoulders, arms, or upper back. Less often, nerve damage from diabetes, vitamin B12 deficiency, or other conditions causes numbness in the legs and feet.

Multiple sclerosis is one possibility, and your doctors may be considering it, especially since you had a contrast MRI. Contrast helps show active inflammation and lesions, and MS can cause numbness that moves around the body, affects both sides, or comes and goes. However, MS is only one of many explanations, and the spine findings you describe are more typically caused by a structural problem in the spine. Only your doctor can tell you what the scan actually shows and what it means for you. Keep in mind that the MRI report may describe findings that are common and not necessarily the cause of your symptoms.

Please don't wait until May 10 if any of the following happen: loss of bladder or bowel control, new numbness in the groin, inner thighs, or the area around the anus, sudden or rapidly worsening weakness in a leg, trouble walking or keeping your balance, numbness spreading into both legs or your arms, or difficulty with hands or fine movements. These can signal nerve compression that needs urgent treatment, so contact your doctor or go to an emergency department right away.

Until your appointment, it may help to write down when the numbness started, how it changes through the day, what makes it better or worse, and any other symptoms such as weakness, vision changes, fatigue, or bladder problems. Ask your doctor or the imaging center for a copy of the MRI report and to explain the findings, and ask whether you need blood tests or a neurology referral sooner. Bring your questions to the appointment, including what the diagnosis is and what the next steps would be.

So a commonwealth is basically a political community where the people have a say in how things are run and the government answers to them. In the US, it's just a state with a republican form of government, meaning folks elect representatives to make decisions for them. Some states use "commonwealth" instead of the more formal-sounding "state" or "republic," but that's really just a name. It isn't a separate class of state and doesn't come with any special legal status.

Four states call themselves commonwealths right now: Kentucky, Massachusetts, Pennsylvania, and Virginia. All four have a long history of self-government and played big roles in how the country developed.

Puerto Rico is also called a commonwealth, but that's a different situation. It's an unincorporated territory of the US, so it falls under federal jurisdiction without being an actual state. People there get a fair amount of self-government, and the territory has a non-voting delegate in Congress.

An upper ontology, also called a top-level or foundational ontology, is a general-purpose framework that defines the most basic and abstract categories of things that exist, along with the relationships among them. Its purpose is to provide a common structure within which more specific, domain-level ontologies can be organized. Concepts such as object, event, process, time, space, attribute, quantity, and relation are typical examples of the kinds of notions an upper ontology tries to capture, because they apply across almost every field of knowledge.

The central idea is that while a medical ontology might define concepts like "disease" or "symptom," and a legal ontology might define "contract" or "liability," both can be linked back to shared top-level notions like "process" or "agent." This shared backbone makes it easier for different systems to interoperate, since they can map their terms onto common foundations rather than building incompatible vocabularies from scratch. It also helps ensure consistency, so that the same word is not quietly used to mean different things in different parts of a knowledge base.

Several upper ontologies have been developed over the years. Examples include SUMO (the Suggested Upper Merged Ontology), DOLCE (the Descriptive Ontology for Linguistic and Cognitive Engineering), BFO (Basic Formal Ontology), and the Cyc upper ontology. They differ in philosophical commitments, such as whether they treat time and change in the same way or how they distinguish between continuants like objects and occurrents like events. Because of these differences, choosing an upper ontology often involves trade-offs between simplicity, philosophical rigor, and practical usability.

Upper ontologies are used in fields such as artificial intelligence, the semantic web, natural language processing, knowledge representation, and biomedical informatics. They are generally considered a foundational tool rather than a complete description of reality, and their value lies largely in enabling clarity, reuse, and integration of knowledge across many domains.

Okay so here's the thing about coffee before bed. The caffeine keeps you awake, plain and simple. It wakes up your brain and makes it harder to drift off, and it takes a few hours to wear off, so an evening cup can easily mess with your sleep. But there's a flip side. If you've had coffee at bedtime every night for years, your body can start to link that cup with winding down. That's the Pavlovian part: the habit itself starts cueing relaxation, so you might feel sleepy right after you drink it.

So which one wins? It really depends on you. Some people are super sensitive to caffeine and will be wired no matter what their habit says. Others have such a strong routine that the coffee almost works like a bedtime signal, and the caffeine barely bothers them. Most of us land somewhere in between, where the two effects partly cancel out. Honestly, the easiest way to find out is to try cutting the evening coffee for a week and see whether you sleep better.

When an in-the-money stock option reaches its expiration date, the underlying stock is priced above the option's strike price. As a result, the option carries intrinsic value, and its holder may exercise it to buy or sell the stock at the strike price. The decision to exercise rests entirely with the holder. If they choose to exercise, the broker carries out the transaction and the option is recorded as exercised. If they choose not to, the option lapses and the holder loses the right to exercise it. At that point it has no value, and the holder can no longer buy or sell the stock at the strike price. Importantly, the holder is entitled to exercise the option but is never required to do so. Depending on their investment strategy and prevailing market conditions, they can either exercise the option or allow it to expire.

Data visualization means producing graphical depictions of information so that it can be conveyed clearly and efficiently. This work involves choosing suitable visual encodings, such as position, length, angle, area, or color, to stand for the data, and then combining these encodings into graphics that a viewer can readily understand. It plays a key role in data analysis, where it helps people investigate and make sense of large collections of data, spot patterns and trends, and share their conclusions with others. The technique can produce many kinds of output, including charts, plots, maps, and diagrams. A range of tools and methods exist for this purpose, from software like Excel, Tableau, and D3 to programming languages such as R and Python. With them, users can build everything from straightforward bar charts and line plots to more intricate forms like heat maps and tree diagrams. In short, data visualization is a strong means of understanding and communicating data, and it is a valuable skill for anyone who works with data.

Imagine your brain is like a movie theater that keeps playing even when your body is asleep. While you sleep, your brain is still awake and busy, making up stories and pictures. Sometimes it makes up a story where you fall, and because your brain is the one making it, it can make the feeling seem just as real as when you're awake. Your brain doesn't always know the difference between a pretend fall and a real one, so it gives you the same whooshing, tummy-dropping feeling.

There's also a reason you wake up right when you fall. When you drift off to sleep, your muscles relax, and sometimes your brain gets confused by that. It thinks, "Uh oh, are we falling?" and it sends a little zap to your body to wake you up and catch yourself. Scientists call this a hypnic jerk.
