Day to day, they use tools like CAD software, oscilloscopes, and other test gear. A typical job might involve designing a system, testing it, hunting down whatever's broken, writing up technical reports and specs, or running a project. Some people also handle maintenance and repairs or give technical support to other folks on the team.

It's a huge field with subfields like power engineering, control engineering, electronics, and computer engineering. Lots of engineers pick one lane, like power transmission, while others bounce between projects.

It is typically advisable to see a doctor after a bee or wasp sting, particularly when the person has run a fever and developed a headache following the sting. Benadryl and Motrin may ease some of the symptoms, but they do not replace proper medical care. A doctor needs to rule out any possible complications that might call for more targeted treatment. Anyone who has trouble breathing, marked swelling, or a serious allergic reaction (anaphylaxis) should get medical help right away. In those situations, an epinephrine auto-injector (EpiPen) should be used if one is on hand, and emergency services should be called without delay. Even when the reaction seems milder, such as fever and headache, it remains wise to get checked out, so that underlying problems can be excluded and suitable treatment started. A doctor might prescribe a steroid or another medication to reduce inflammation and relieve symptoms. Meanwhile, the person should be watched closely for any changes, and medical attention should be sought if symptoms get worse or new ones appear.

Several elements have driven the extended decline in Treasury yields and corresponding rise in bond prices across the U.S. market, a phenomenon often called a "secular bull market." The main contributors include the following.

Economic growth and inflation: When the economy expands robustly and inflation runs high, borrowing demand tends to rise, which can push rates upward. On the other hand, sluggish growth and low inflation typically weaken credit demand, potentially driving rates down.

Central bank policy: Institutions like the Federal Reserve shape interest rates through monetary policy. Raising its benchmark rate tends to lift Treasury yields, while cutting it tends to lower them.

International demand: As the largest and most liquid bond market globally, the U.S. Treasury market is frequently viewed as a safe haven during periods of uncertainty. Consequently, foreign investor demand for Treasuries can play a major role in setting yields.

Government debt: Years of federal budget deficits have expanded the supply of Treasuries. This larger supply can exert downward pressure on yields, since more bonds are available for investors to purchase.

Taken together, these and other forces have sustained the long-term decline in interest rates and rise in Treasury prices. However, this trend is not guaranteed to persist indefinitely, and periods of volatility or shifts in the direction of rates remain possible.

Howard Hathaway Aiken (March 8, 1900 – March 14, 1973) was an American physicist and computer scientist, best remembered for the Harvard Mark I, a groundbreaking machine constructed at Harvard University during the 1930s and 1940s. Born in Hoboken, New Jersey, Aiken earned his bachelor's degree in electrical engineering from Columbia University in 1923, and later received his doctorate in physics from Harvard in 1939. Keen on applying computing machinery to scientific and engineering problems, he collaborated closely with IBM on the design and construction of the Mark I, which was finished in 1944. This electromechanical computer served a range of scientific and military purposes, including work related to the first hydrogen bomb. Aiken went on to pursue further computing projects at Harvard and was also linked to the development of UNIVAC, the first commercial computer. As a pioneer of computer science, he shaped the field's growth during the twentieth century through his work on the Mark I. He is regarded as a central figure in computing history, and numerous awards and honors have acknowledged his contributions.

Scientific creationism is a view held by some Christians. Its central claim is that God brought the universe into being, along with everything in it, including living beings such as humans and animals. Some who hold this view take the account of creation in the Bible's book of Genesis to be historically accurate and believe science can confirm it. Others who accept scientific creationism read the Genesis account as a metaphor, or as a way of conveying truths that cannot be fully grasped. Is there anything about scientific creationism you'd like me to help clarify?

Google Voice Search lets you talk to Google instead of typing. You speak into your device's mic, ask a question or give a command, and it answers either on screen or out loud. Say "Ok Google, what's the weather today?" and it'll pull up or read out the forecast for wherever you are. It works on phones, tablets, and computers, as long as you've got internet and the Google app or Chrome. Smart speakers like Google Home and Nest Hub are built around it, so that's the main way you use them. You'll need a Google account, and the feature has to be turned on in your settings.

Basically, errors and residuals are both about how far off a prediction is from what actually happened. Say you've got a model that guesses a response variable, Y, from a predictor, X. You plug in an X value, get a predicted Y, and then compare it to the Y you actually observed. That gap is the residual (or the error, depending on who you ask and how the textbook is written).

Here's a quick example. Imagine a simple linear regression where you're predicting Y from X. If the model spits out 10 for a given X but the real Y came in at 12, the residual is 2. Why bother with this? Because residuals tell you how well the model is doing. Big, patterned residuals can point to a bad fit or some hidden bias, and they're also the go-to tool for checking whether the model's assumptions actually hold up and where it needs fixing.

Store cars, meaning vehicles financed through a retailer or dealer's own finance arrangement, usually come with insurance requirements that are set by the lender rather than by the store itself. In most cases the finance agreement obliges you to carry comprehensive insurance for the full term of the loan, not just the minimum third-party cover required by law. The lender is financing an asset that secures the debt, so it wants the car protected against theft, accidental damage, and write-off. Some agreements also require you to name the finance company as an interested party or loss payee on the policy, which means that if the car is written off, any insurance payout goes first to settling the outstanding balance.

Many store finance providers specify a minimum level of cover, sometimes including a requirement that the policy be for the car's full market value or replacement value, and they may restrict certain policy features such as high excesses. Some will ask for proof of insurance before handing over the keys and may require you to provide annual renewal documents. If you let the policy lapse, the lender can typically buy insurance on your behalf, often at a much higher premium, and add the cost to your balance, so it is worth checking that your renewals are set up correctly.

Before signing, read the finance agreement carefully for the exact insurance clause, confirm whether you can choose your own insurer or must use one the store nominates, and ask whether the finance company needs to be noted on the policy. If you already have a policy, call your insurer to confirm they can add the lender as a loss payee and that the cover meets the stated requirements. If you are unsure about any term, the lender or an independent consumer advice service can explain your obligations in plain language.

The British Empire didn't fall apart all at once. Over many decades, the countries it ruled slowly decided they wanted to run themselves, and Britain gradually let go. A few big things helped this happen.

First, after World War Two, Britain was very tired and very poor. The war had cost a huge amount of money and many lives, so Britain didn't have the strength to keep control of faraway places by force.

Second, people in the colonies wanted to be in charge of their own homes. Many people who lived under British rule began to protest, organize, and push for independence. Some of these movements were peaceful, and some involved fighting. Leaders like Mahatma Gandhi in India showed that large numbers of people refusing to cooperate could make a colony very hard to govern.

Third, the world's attitudes were changing. After the war, many people believed that one country shouldn't rule over another against its will. The United Nations was formed in 1945 to encourage countries to respect each other's independence, and the two biggest powers of the time, the United States and the Soviet Union, were both pushing against old European empires.

So, in simple terms, Britain got tired and poor, the people it ruled wanted to be free, and the world started to think that was the right thing. India became independent in 1947, and many African and Caribbean countries followed in the 1950s and 1960s. Most of the empire was gone by the 1970s. Today, the countries that were once part of it are independent, and many of them are members of an organization called the Commonwealth, where they still have friendly ties with Britain.

Two people who both test negative for sexually transmitted infections (STIs) and then have unprotected sex can still end up infected. Tests are not perfectly accurate, and a person can carry an STI without realizing it, since many infections cause no noticeable symptoms. Some infections, HIV among them, also may not appear on a test until several weeks after exposure, so someone can get a negative result and still be capable of passing the infection to a partner. To lower the chance of transmission, using protection such as condoms during sex is essential. Regular testing and open conversations with a partner about their STI status are also important ways to safeguard both people's health.

Imagine you run a lemonade stand, and you notice that when you sell plain lemonade, a few people stop by, but when you sell lemonade with a silly hat on, way more people stop and buy. Pretty soon you're wearing the silly hat every day, because more customers means more money. That's basically what happened to these channels.

Discovery and National Geographic are businesses, and they make most of their money from advertisers who pay to show commercials. Advertisers pay more when more people are watching. Starting around the early 2000s, the channels noticed that shows like Deadliest Catch, Gold Rush, or Ice Road Truckers pulled in much bigger audiences than a documentary about volcanoes or deep sea fish. People like watching other people, especially when there's drama, money on the line, danger, or colorful personalities. So the channels made more of what worked.

There's also the cost side. A really good science documentary is expensive and slow to make. You might need scientists, special cameras, travel to remote places, animation, and months or even years of filming. Something like Planet Earth costs a fortune. A reality show is cheaper: you follow a few guys around a junkyard or a gold mine with a small camera crew, and you can crank out a whole season quickly. And once a reality show is popular, you can keep making new seasons for years with the same people, which is very reliable for a business.

Another big change was competition. Back in the 1990s, if you wanted nature or science shows, cable channels were one of the few places to get them. Then the internet, YouTube, Netflix, and other streaming services came along and started offering lots of educational content, often for free or on demand. Cable channels had to fight harder for viewers, so they leaned even more into whatever got the biggest ratings. Ownership changes and corporate pressure to grow profits pushed things in the same direction, and the same thing happened to History Channel and TLC, which originally stood for The Learning Channel.

So it's not that nobody wanted science shows anymore. It's that the channels found something cheaper that more people would watch, and they followed the money. The good news is that high quality science and nature content still exists, it just mostly moved elsewhere, like big BBC productions, streaming documentaries, PBS programs such as Nova, and a lot of excellent science creators on YouTube.

Noam Chomsky works as a linguist, philosopher, cognitive scientist, historian, and social commentator, and many consider him one of the most important living intellectuals. His work has substantially shaped linguistics, cognitive psychology, and philosophy. Born in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, in 1928, he earned his bachelor's degree from the University of Pennsylvania in 1949 and his doctorate from the same institution in 1955. That same year he began teaching at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), where he now holds the title of Institute Professor Emeritus. He is chiefly famous for his investigations into the nature of language and the architecture of the human mind. His theory of transformational grammar transformed linguistics and also influenced psychology, philosophy, and computer science. Beyond this, he has examined how the mind functions and what thought is, and he has written at length about the social and political consequences of language and communication. Alongside his scholarly career, he is well known as an activist and critic of society, speaking and writing on many subjects, among them war, civil liberties, and the media.

A semicolon is a punctuation mark that separates clauses within a sentence. It resembles a period, but its job is to join clauses that share a close connection in meaning. For example: "I went to the store; I needed to buy some milk." Here, "I went to the store" and "I needed to buy some milk" are the two clauses. The semicolon links them because they are closely tied together and form a single idea. Semicolons make writing clearer and better organized. They can join clauses that lack a conjunction such as "and" or "but," and they signal a pause that is longer than a comma but shorter than a period. I hope this is helpful! Feel free to ask if you have any other questions.

Lean manufacturing is a production philosophy and set of practices aimed at maximizing customer value while minimizing waste. Waste, in this context, includes anything that does not add value from the customer's perspective, such as excess inventory, overproduction, waiting time, unnecessary transport, defects, unused employee talent, extra motion, and over-processing. The approach emphasizes smooth, continuous flow of work, producing only what is needed when it is needed, and continuously improving processes through small, incremental changes. Common tools associated with lean include just-in-time production, kanban pull systems, value stream mapping, 5S workplace organization, and standardized work.

The core ideas were developed primarily at Toyota in Japan. Taiichi Ohno, an engineer and executive at Toyota, is widely credited as the main architect of the Toyota Production System, from which lean manufacturing grew. Ohno drew on earlier influences, including the ideas of Sakichi Toyoda, the founder of Toyoda's textile machinery business, whose principle of jidoka (automation with a human touch, allowing machines to stop when defects occur) became a foundation of the system. Shigeo Shingo, an industrial engineer who worked with Toyota, contributed significantly through techniques such as single-minute exchange of die and poka-yoke, or error-proofing.

The term "lean manufacturing" itself was coined in the late 1980s by John Krafcik, a researcher at MIT, and was popularized by the 1990 book The Machine That Changed the World by James Womack, Daniel Jones, and Daniel Roos, which compared Toyota's methods with Western mass production.

Stopping drinking is one of the most helpful things you can do, but it is not the only way to bring your liver enzymes down, and it is definitely not too late for it to help. The liver has a remarkable ability to heal, and even after many years of hepatitis C and drinking, removing alcohol lowers inflammation, slows scarring, and reduces your risk of cirrhosis and liver cancer. Alcohol and hepatitis C together damage the liver much faster than either one alone, so quitting matters a great deal.

It may also help to know that a liver enzyme level of 50 (usually the ALT) is only mildly elevated. Normal ranges vary by lab but often top out somewhere around 35 to 55. So while it is a sign your liver is under stress, it is not an alarmingly high number. Enzyme levels also don't tell the whole story, since they don't reliably show how much scarring is present. Your doctor can check that with a simple ultrasound-based test called a FibroScan or with blood test scores such as FIB-4. Knowing your degree of scarring is more important than the enzyme number itself.

The most important thing to ask your doctor about is treating the hepatitis C itself, because the virus is probably the main cause of the elevated enzymes. Hepatitis C is now curable in most people. Modern treatment is usually a pill taken once a day for 8 to 12 weeks, with cure rates above 95 percent and generally mild side effects, very different from the older interferon treatments some people remember. After a cure, liver enzymes often return to normal, and the liver can partly recover. If no one has offered you this, ask directly about direct-acting antiviral treatment or a referral to a liver specialist or infectious disease clinic, and ask about assistance programs if cost is a concern.

Beyond that, a few other things support your liver: getting vaccinated against hepatitis A and B if you aren't already immune, avoiding large doses of acetaminophen (Tylenol) and checking with your doctor before starting supplements or herbal products, and keeping a healthy weight, since fatty liver adds further strain.

One caution about quitting alcohol: if you have been drinking heavily or daily, stopping suddenly can cause dangerous withdrawal, so talk with your doctor about how to stop safely. There are also medications and support programs that make quitting easier, and asking for that help is a strong step, not a weakness.

Your fear is understandable, but your situation is very treatable. Stopping alcohol and getting your hepatitis C cured together give you an excellent chance of protecting your liver for the long term.

I'm sorry you're going through this, Tracey. Two weeks of intense cramps and poor sleep would wear anyone down, and it makes sense that you're feeling vulnerable.

Leg and foot cramps after Mirena removal are plausibly connected, though the evidence is mostly anecdotal rather than well studied. The Mirena releases a progestogen (levonorgestrel) that acts mainly on the womb, but a small amount enters the bloodstream. When it's removed, your own hormones have to re-establish their rhythm. Estrogen and progesterone shifts can affect fluid balance, nerve and muscle excitability, and the levels of minerals like magnesium, calcium, and potassium. Many women report cramps, joint aches, headaches, mood changes, and insomnia in the weeks after removal, and these tend to settle as the cycle returns, often within a few weeks to a couple of months.

Other things can add to it. Poor sleep and stress make cramps and pain feel worse. Dehydration and low magnesium or potassium are common triggers. Heavier bleeding or a return of periods after removal can also lower iron and fluids. Some people also find the cramps are worse at night when lying still.

There are free or cheap things you can try. Gently stretching your calves and feet before bed, and when a cramp hits, pulling your toes up toward your shin, can help. A warm bath, a hot water bottle, or a warm wet towel on the muscle can ease tightness. Drinking enough water and eating foods rich in magnesium and potassium, such as bananas, potatoes, beans, nuts, oats, and leafy greens, can help. Keeping the bedclothes loose so your feet aren't pointed downward is a small but useful trick. Cutting out caffeine in the afternoon may help your sleep too.

It's worth seeing a doctor or calling a nurse line if the cramps are severe or not improving, because a few things need ruling out. Get seen urgently if one leg is swollen, red, warm, or tender in the calf, or if you have chest pain or breathlessness, since a blood clot is uncommon but serious. Also seek help if you have fever, heavy bleeding, severe pelvic pain, or signs of infection after removal. In the UK, your GP is free, and NHS 111 is free by phone if you aren't sure how urgent it is. A pharmacist can also give advice at no cost.

Most of these symptoms do ease as your body adjusts, so there's good reason to hope this is temporary. I hope you get some rest soon.

Arthur Samuel was an American computer scientist, and honestly one of the real pioneers of AI. He lived from 1901 to 1990. He's mostly remembered for machine learning, which is basically the idea of getting computers to learn from data and get better at things over time without being spelled out step by step. In 1959 he built a checkers-playing program that did exactly that, and people still point to it as one of the first real examples of machine learning in action. A lot of what came later traces back to that work. He also taught electrical engineering and computer science at Stanford for years, researching and teaching while he was there.

Bryophytes are basically the small, non-vascular plants, so think mosses, liverworts, and hornworts. They've got a few things in common.

For starters, they're tiny. Most only get a few centimeters tall. They also don't have vascular tissue, which means no specialized plumbing for moving water and nutrients around the plant. No seeds either. They reproduce with spores instead.

They don't have true roots, just little hair-like things called rhizoids that anchor them to the ground. And since they've got no vascular system, they really depend on water, both to move nutrients around and to reproduce.

That's why you usually find them in damp or wet spots, like forests, along streams, or on rocks.

I'm sorry your sister is going through this while waiting for her results. Her regimen is fairly extensive, and there is probably room to improve it, but any changes need to come from her prescribing doctor or a palliative care or pain team, because several of these drugs interact and the details matter.

Looking at what she takes: MST Continus is slow-release morphine, which provides background pain control. Oral morphine 10 mg every 4 to 6 hours is the "breakthrough" or immediate-release dose for pain that gets through. Paracetamol, taken as two tablets three times daily, is a sensible baseline, and the total of about 3 g a day is within safe limits (the maximum is 4 g, lower if she is underweight or has liver problems). Diclac Retard is diclofenac, an anti-inflammatory. Zimovane (zopiclone) is a sleeping tablet.

There are several things worth raising with her doctor. First, the morphine list seems to include extra "one morphine tablet" doses in the morning and with another dose. Make sure the team knows the total morphine she takes in 24 hours, since a clear written schedule helps avoid both under-treatment and accidental overdose. If she needs breakthrough doses often (more than about three a day), the long-acting dose probably needs adjusting rather than adding more ad hoc tablets.

Second, combining morphine and zopiclone increases drowsiness and slows breathing. That matters especially with a lung condition. If she is unusually sleepy, confused, or breathing slowly, that needs urgent attention. The doctor may want to review whether the zopiclone dose is still appropriate.

Third, diclofenac carries risks of stomach bleeding, kidney strain, and raised blood pressure or heart risk, particularly with long use or in older people. It is usually taken with food and often with a stomach-protecting medicine such as omeprazole. Ask whether she has that protection and whether kidney function has been checked.

Fourth, morphine causes constipation in nearly everyone, so she should be on a regular laxative, and nausea may need treatment too. Poorly managed constipation can itself cause a lot of discomfort.

Fifth, depending on the type of pain, other options may help. Nerve-type pain (burning, shooting) may respond to medications like gabapentin, pregabalin, or amitriptyline. Pain at the biopsy site or chest wall pain may respond to local measures such as heat, or a nerve block. If pain is from bone involvement, other treatments can be added. Non-drug approaches like relaxation and positioning also help.

I'd suggest asking her doctor for a medication review, ideally with a pain or palliative care specialist, and bringing a diary of when she has pain, how severe it is, and which doses she takes. Palliative care teams manage pain regardless of diagnosis and are not only for end of life, so a referral is reasonable even before results arrive.

Please seek urgent help if she becomes very drowsy, hard to wake, confused, has very slow or shallow breathing, black stools, or vomiting blood. I hope the results come back with good news.

When someone gets tasered, the taser shoots two small darts attached to thin wires, and they deliver rapid electrical pulses into the body. Those pulses travel along the nerves, which normally carry tiny electrical messages from the brain to the muscles telling them what to do. The taser's pulses are much stronger and faster than the body's own messages, so they overwhelm the nerves and cause them to fire over and over, all at once.

Think of it like a radio that gets flooded with so much static that it can't play the real song. The muscles get so many confusing signals that they clench up hard and can't respond to the brain's instructions. Because the muscles are locked in this tight, jumping state, a person usually falls down and can't move well for a few seconds. This is why the effect is called temporary paralysis.

Once the electricity stops, the nerves settle back down, the muscles relax, and the brain's messages start working again. That's why the person can usually move normally again soon after.

Your apple is alive, in a way! Apples are made of tiny living parts called cells, and those cells keep doing their jobs after the apple is picked. They breathe in a little oxygen and use up sugar to keep going, a bit like you do when you're sleeping.

The apple doesn't die all at once. Over days and weeks, its cells slowly wear out. Keeping it cold, like in a fridge, slows this down a lot, so it can stay crunchy for a long time. Eventually the cells stop working, and that's when the apple gets mushy and brown. Scientists don't agree on one exact moment when it dies, because it happens little by little.

The seeds inside are a little different. They're alive but sleeping, waiting to grow into new apple trees if you plant them.

In machine learning, the learning rate is a hyperparameter that sets how large a step the optimizer takes when it updates the model's parameters. It plays a central role in neural network training, since it governs how quickly or slowly the model learns. Typically, the learning rate is chosen before training begins and stays fixed for the entire run. When it is large, each training step produces bigger adjustments to the parameters; when it is small, the adjustments are more modest. There are several ways to choose it. One option is to pick a fixed value by hand, though this is often hard, because the best value can differ considerably from one model and dataset to another. A more widespread method is a learning rate schedule, which changes the rate over time in response to how the model is performing. For instance, the rate might begin high and then decline steadily as training goes on. Selecting a suitable rate matters a great deal: if it is too high, the model may diverge, and if it is too low, training becomes slow and inefficient. Striking the right balance is essential to training a machine learning model successfully.

Okay, so the multi-armed bandit problem is a classic one in reinforcement learning. Basically, you've got a decision-maker (the "agent") who has to pick from several options (the "arms") to get the biggest reward. Each arm pays out according to its own probability distribution, but the agent doesn't know those distributions up front. So it has to figure them out by trial and error.

The "bandit" name comes from slot machines, since you're stuck choosing between levers. The real tension is between exploring, where you try different arms to learn what they pay, and exploiting, where you just keep pulling whichever arm looks best so far. Explore too little and you might miss a better arm. Explore too much and you leave money on the table. The goal is finding that sweet spot so you rack up as much reward as possible over time.

It's a simple setup, but it shows up everywhere. People use it for online ads, clinical trials, and deciding how to split resources. It's also been used to study how humans and animals handle similar choices, which is pretty neat.

Pain in the kidney region and the testicle may stem from a number of different sources. Frequent culprits include kidney stones, urinary tract infections, testicular torsion, and swelling of the prostate gland, known as prostatitis. Seeing a physician is essential so that the problem can be correctly identified and managed. Kidney stones, for instance, are often extremely painful and sometimes need a medical procedure to be removed. Urinary tract infections likewise cause significant discomfort but usually respond well to antibiotic treatment. Testicular torsion, in contrast, is an emergency that calls for prompt surgery to avoid lasting harm to the testicle. Prostatitis is typically managed with medication and changes to daily habits. Antacid medicine may bring short-term relief, since stomach acidity can occasionally add to discomfort in the kidney area and testicle. Even so, a doctor should be consulted to find the root cause of the pain and arrange suitable treatment.

You can have another person invest for you and divide the gains and losses with you, and this kind of setup is called a partnership. In a partnership, two or more people or entities join together to create a business, and the profits and losses are distributed as laid out in the partnership agreement. Still, several factors deserve attention before you commit to one.

The first is legal structure. Partnerships come in several forms, including general partnerships, limited partnerships, and limited liability partnerships. Each carries its own legal and tax consequences, so you should understand how they differ and pick the one that suits your situation best.

The second is risk. As a partner, you are personally liable for the partnership's debts and obligations. If the business racks up losses or gets sued, you could be held personally accountable.

The third is decision-making. Partnerships usually mean making decisions jointly, and they demand strong communication and trust among the partners. If working closely with another person or sharing control of the business makes you uncomfortable, a partnership may not suit you.

In short, a partnership can be a sound way to invest in a business, but you should weigh all the possible risks and rewards carefully before joining one.

Setting a price that ends in "99" is known as "charm pricing," a popular tactic retailers rely on to make goods look more affordable. The approach rests on the notion that a price such as "99 cents" seems to fall just short of a full dollar figure, which leads shoppers to perceive it as a sweeter bargain. Take an item listed at $9.99: it registers as almost $10, yet it sits a bit below that mark, so it appears more attractive than the same item at $10. Retailers use this psychological effect to make their merchandise more enticing to buyers. Charm pricing also serves some practical purposes. A store that wants an item to bring in $10 but would rather avoid the look of a high cost might list it at $9.99 instead. That small change can make the product feel more reasonably priced and can also boost sales. In short, charm pricing helps retailers present their products as more appealing and affordable, and it can be an effective way to drive sales.

A put option is basically a contract that gives you the right, but not the obligation, to sell some amount of an asset at a set price (the strike price) on or before a certain date, the expiration. The person on the other side, the one who sells the put, is called the writer.

If you buy a put, you're betting the asset's price is going to drop below the strike before it expires. Say you buy a put on a stock with a $50 strike that expires in three months. If the stock tanks below $50 in that time, you can exercise the option and sell at $50 even though the market price is lower. That's where your profit comes from. But if the stock stays above $50, you just let it lapse and you're out the premium you paid for the option.

The writer is betting the opposite, that the price stays above the strike. If it does, the option expires worthless and the writer pockets the premium. If the price drops below the strike, though, the writer's stuck. They have to buy the asset at the strike price from the holder, which is more than it's worth on the market, so that's a loss for them.

Smell is tiny bits of stuff floating through the air. Think of a flower or a cookie: it gives off super-small pieces of itself, called molecules, that are too little to see. These pieces are so light and spread out that they drift away from the source, kind of like how a puff of bubble-gum smoke or a drop of food coloring spreads out in water. So smell is more like floating than like radiating.

It is not like sound, though. Sound is a wiggle that travels through the air, like ripples on a pond. Smell doesn't wiggle. It actually has to arrive: the molecules physically move from the cookie to you. They get there by bumping around in the air, pushed by the wind, or by spreading out on their own, until some of them reach your nose.

When they reach your nose, they land on a soft, wet patch high up inside it. There are special sensors there, a bit like tiny locks, and each smell molecule fits into a lock of a certain shape. When it fits, the sensor sends a message up to your brain saying "cookie!" That's how you know what you're smelling.

So the trip from point A to point B works like this: the cookie lets out tiny floating pieces, the wind and bumping carry them through the air, and they drift into your nose, where they fit into sensors that tell your brain what it is.

A defibrillator (often spelled "defibulator" but properly "defibrillator"), and especially the automated external defibrillator, or AED, found in public places, should be used when someone is in sudden cardiac arrest. In practical terms, that means the person has collapsed, is unresponsive when you shout and tap them, and is not breathing normally. Gasping, irregular breaths don't count as normal breathing, so treat that the same as no breathing. If you see these signs, call emergency services right away, start CPR, and have someone bring an AED as quickly as possible.

You don't need to diagnose the heart rhythm yourself. Once you turn on an AED and attach the pads to the person's bare chest as shown in the pictures on the pads, the device analyzes the heart and will only deliver a shock if it detects a shockable rhythm, such as ventricular fibrillation. If no shock is needed, it will tell you to continue CPR. The machine gives spoken step-by-step instructions, so untrained bystanders can use it safely, and in many places Good Samaritan laws protect people who help in good faith.

You should not use it on someone who is conscious, breathing normally, or has a pulse and is responsive. A few precautions apply. Make sure nobody is touching the person when the shock is delivered. Wipe the chest dry if it's wet, and move the person out of standing water. Remove medication patches from where the pads go. Place pads slightly away from any implanted pacemaker, which usually shows as a bump under the skin. AEDs can also be used on children and infants, ideally with pediatric pads or a child setting. If those aren't available, adult pads are still better than nothing.

The key point is that speed matters enormously. Survival drops significantly with each minute without CPR and defibrillation, so if you suspect cardiac arrest, don't hesitate to get and use an AED. Taking a CPR and AED course from an organization like the Red Cross or American Heart Association is a great way to build confidence.

Some websites conceal a product's price until it goes into the cart for several reasons. First, the site may want shoppers to pile more items into their carts before they learn the total, which works especially well when larger orders earn discounts. Second, hiding the price can make it harder to compare with what rival sites charge, a tactic that is most effective when the product is rare or cannot be found elsewhere. Third, withholding the price can create an impression of exclusivity or scarcity, leading buyers to believe they have found a special deal or that demand for the item is high. Fourth, the site may be trying to cut down on distractions and keep the shopper focused on one particular item, which is useful when the catalog is large. Let me know if you would like more information on any of these points.

Birds vocalize for many different purposes. Certain species sing to draw in potential partners, whereas others use their calls to guard a patch of land or to keep in touch with fellow flock members. Vocalizing also lets birds maintain contact with one another, which is especially useful when they travel together in a group. Some birds, parrots among them, may make sounds purely for amusement or as a way of showing how they feel. How much energy a bird spends on calling depends on the kind of sound it produces and how long it keeps going. Singing is demanding, but many birds manage their energy by pausing to rest between songs. Giving away their position to predators is certainly a hazard for birds. Still, most species have evolved strategies to reduce that danger, such as perching high in a tree where they are harder to spot, or singing during periods when predators are less active.

Edsger W. Dijkstra (1930–2002) was a Dutch computer scientist who made foundational contributions to the field of programming and software engineering. He is best known for developing Dijkstra's algorithm in 1956, a method for finding the shortest path between nodes in a graph, which remains a standard technique in computer science and is widely used in network routing and mapping software. He also made important contributions to the design of operating systems, including the THE multiprogramming system, and to concurrent programming, where he introduced the semaphore concept for managing access to shared resources and formulated classic problems such as the dining philosophers problem.

Beyond specific inventions, Dijkstra was an influential advocate for rigorous, mathematically grounded approaches to programming. He argued that programs should be developed alongside their proofs of correctness, and he promoted structured programming, famously criticizing the use of the goto statement in a 1968 letter titled "Go To Statement Considered Harmful." His book "A Discipline of Programming" and his many published essays, often written by hand and circulated as manuscripts called EWDs, shaped how generations of researchers and educators think about software quality. He received the 1972 ACM Turing Award for his fundamental contributions to programming languages, and he spent much of his career at institutions including the Eindhoven University of Technology and the University of Texas at Austin.

An operational definition is basically how you pin down a concept or variable so it can actually be measured in a study. Why bother? Because it gives you a clear, specific, objective way to measure something, which means different researchers measuring it are more likely to be doing the same thing. Say you're studying intelligence. You might define it as whatever score someone gets on a standardized IQ test. That's your operational definition, and it tells everyone exactly how intelligence was measured in your study. This matters a lot for replication. If another team uses the same definition, they can redo the study and see whether they get similar results, and that's how people come to trust the findings.

The defensive line in football is the group of defensive players who line up closest to the line of scrimmage, directly facing the offensive line. It is often just called the "D-line," and its players are known as defensive linemen. Their main jobs are to stop the run, pressure or sack the quarterback, and disrupt the offense's blocking.

The line is usually made up of defensive tackles, who play on the interior, and defensive ends, who line up on the outside edges. In a typical four-man front there are two tackles and two ends, while a three-man front, as in a 3-4 defense, uses a nose tackle in the middle flanked by two defensive ends. Players just behind the line, called linebackers, often work closely with it, and some linebackers rush the passer as well.

If you're asking about a different kind of football, such as soccer, the equivalent group is simply called the defenders or the back line, and it typically includes center-backs and full-backs.

Lots of big US cities sit right on state lines, and it usually comes down to a few things. Plenty of them grew up around rivers or railways, since those were the easiest ways to move people and goods between places. St. Louis is a good example: it sits on the Mississippi and was a major shipping hub in the 1800s. Kansas City sits near where the Missouri and Kansas Rivers meet, and Omaha is on the Missouri too.

Some cities just got founded as border towns. Cincinnati is one of them. It was started in 1788, back when Ohio was still part of the Northwest Territory, and it sat across from Kentucky, which was then part of Virginia. Other cities simply spread out over time until they covered land on both sides of the line. Memphis is a case like that. It's on the Tennessee-Mississippi border and has grown into parts of both states.

So it's a mix of things: where the rivers and rail lines ran, how the borders got drawn back when the country was young, and how the cities kept growing over the decades.

Americans of Japanese descent are commonly called Japanese Americans. The term Nikkei is also widely used, especially in historical and community contexts, to refer to Japanese emigrants and their descendants living outside Japan. Within this group, people are often identified by generation: the first generation, who immigrated from Japan, are called Issei, the second generation, their children born in the United States, are Nisei, and the third generation are Sansei.

Mangos originated in South Asia, specifically the region that is now India, Myanmar, and Bangladesh. The tree has been cultivated there for at least four to five thousand years, and it holds deep cultural significance in the region, appearing in ancient texts and art. From India, mango cultivation spread eastward to Southeast Asia and later westward through Persian and Arab traders, eventually reaching East Africa, and then Brazil and the Caribbean after European colonization in the 16th century. Today India is by far the largest producer of mangos, and the fruit is grown in tropical and subtropical regions around the world, including Mexico, China, Indonesia, Pakistan, and parts of Africa and South America.

Existential risk refers to a threat that could cause the extinction of humanity or permanently and drastically curtail its potential. The term was popularized by the philosopher Nick Bostrom in the early 2000s, though concern about humanity-ending catastrophes is much older. What distinguishes an existential risk from an ordinary disaster is not just its scale but its irreversibility: a terrible war or pandemic that kills millions is a catastrophe, but if civilization eventually recovers, it is not existential in the strict sense. An existential catastrophe is one from which there is no coming back, either because no humans remain or because humanity is locked into a permanently diminished state, such as an unrecoverable collapse or an inescapable global totalitarian regime.

Researchers usually divide these risks into natural and anthropogenic (human-caused) categories. Natural risks include large asteroid or comet impacts, supervolcanic eruptions, and, more speculatively, nearby stellar explosions. Because humanity has survived hundreds of thousands of years of exposure to such hazards, many scholars argue that the annual probability of natural extinction is quite low. Anthropogenic risks are generally considered more pressing because they are new and growing. Commonly discussed examples include nuclear war and the resulting "nuclear winter," engineered pandemics made possible by advances in biotechnology, extreme climate change scenarios, and the development of advanced artificial intelligence whose goals are not aligned with human interests. Some thinkers also include unforeseen risks from technologies not yet invented.

The concept carries significant ethical weight. Proponents argue that preventing extinction is uniquely important because it would destroy not only everyone alive today but also all the future generations who might otherwise exist, potentially trillions of lives over the coming millennia. This reasoning, associated with movements such as effective altruism and longtermism, suggests that even small reductions in the probability of extinction could be enormously valuable. Institutions such as the Future of Humanity Institute at Oxford (which operated until 2024), the Centre for the Study of Existential Risk at Cambridge, and the Future of Life Institute have studied these questions.

The idea also attracts criticism. Some argue that estimates of the probabilities involved are highly speculative, that focusing on distant hypothetical futures can distract from present-day suffering and injustice, or that the framework can be used to justify extreme measures. Others question whether certain risks, such as those from artificial intelligence, are as serious as advocates claim. Despite these debates, the concept of existential risk has become an influential lens for thinking about how humanity manages powerful technologies and long-term global threats.

Your son might have pulled a muscle in his stomach, but it could be something else too, so keep an eye on his symptoms and get him checked out if you're worried. Until then, a few things can help. Let him rest and skip anything that could aggravate it. Put a cold pack on the sore spot for 15 to 20 minutes every two or three hours to bring down swelling. Acetaminophen (Tylenol) or ibuprofen (Advil) can help with the pain, just follow the dosing on the package. Make sure he's drinking plenty, water or something with electrolytes, so he doesn't get dehydrated. If the pain gets worse or hangs around, or he starts vomiting or having trouble breathing, get him seen right away. Better safe than sorry. Call his doctor or head to the ER if anything feels off.

Noam Chomsky is an American linguist, philosopher, cognitive scientist, and political commentator, born in 1928 in Philadelphia. He is widely regarded as one of the most influential thinkers of the twentieth and twenty-first centuries, and he is often called the father of modern linguistics. In the late 1950s he introduced generative grammar, a theory proposing that human beings possess an innate, universal capacity for language, and that the ability to produce and understand an unlimited number of sentences rests on a finite set of underlying rules. This idea challenged the dominant behaviorist account of language learning and helped launch the cognitive revolution in psychology and related fields.

Chomsky spent most of his career at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, where he became a professor of linguistics and remains a professor emeritus. Beyond linguistics, he has made substantial contributions to the theory of computation, most notably the Chomsky hierarchy, a classification of formal grammars that is still used in computer science.

He is also known as a prominent critic of United States foreign policy, corporate media, and neoliberal economics. His political writings, including books such as Manufacturing Consent, written with Edward Herman, and Hegemony or Survival, have made him a leading voice on the left, and he is among the most cited scholars in the world. Supporters praise his intellectual rigor and moral seriousness, while critics argue that some of his linguistic theories have been revised or superseded and that his political views are sometimes one-sided.

Steam trading cards are digital cards earned by playing particular games on the Steam platform. Many people enjoy gathering them, either to display their favorite titles or simply for the pleasure of building a collection. Others take part in swapping cards with fellow players in hopes of completing sets they are missing. As for why anyone would spend real money on these digital cards, the reason is that some collectors place value on them as a means of showcasing favorite games or as a collectible in their own right. In the same way that people amass physical trading cards, stamps, or other keepsakes, others find satisfaction in gathering virtual items. Much as someone might pay a premium for a scarce paper trading card, someone else might pay for a rare digital one. Another motive is that these cards can be combined to create badges on Steam, which then appear on a player's profile. Such badges may reflect a person's achievements or passions, and some view them as a way to express devotion to a specific game or to connect with others who share the same interests. Lastly, it is worth noting that Steam trading cards do not all carry the same worth. Common cards tend to be fairly inexpensive, whereas scarcer ones can command higher prices, and as with any collectible, a card's value depends on a range of different factors.

Supervised learning is basically when you train a model on data that already has the right answers attached. Each example has inputs and a correct output label, and the model's job is to figure out the mapping between them so it can guess labels for data it's never seen. Say you want to predict house prices from size and location. You'd grab a bunch of houses with known sale prices, feed the model the size and location of each one alongside its price, and let it learn the pattern. Once it's trained, you can throw in a house that hasn't sold yet and get an estimate. There are two main flavors. Classification is when you're picking a category, like whether a photo shows a cat or a dog. Regression is when you're predicting a number on a continuous scale, like that house price. Either way, the core idea is the same: learn from labeled examples, then generalize to new ones.

A surname is your family name, the part of your name you share with your relatives and usually inherit from a parent. It is also called a last name in many English-speaking countries because it typically comes at the end. For example, in the name John Smith, "Smith" is the surname.

A given name is the personal name chosen for you, usually by your parents at birth. It is also called a first name or forename because in many Western cultures it comes first. In the name John Smith, "John" is the given name. If you have a middle name, that is also considered a given name, though forms often ask for it separately.

The order isn't the same everywhere. In China, Japan, Korea, Hungary, and Vietnam, the surname traditionally comes first. In the Chinese name Wang Wei, for instance, "Wang" is the surname and "Wei" is the given name. That's why forms ask for "surname" and "given name" instead of "first name" and "last name," which avoids confusion across cultures.

When filling out a form or passport application, put your family name in the surname field and your personal name or names in the given name field, regardless of the order you normally say them in.

Claiming HST compensation on your personal income tax return in Ontario requires you to file a return with the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA). The general process works like this:

Collect your paperwork. Have on hand any receipts or invoices showing the HST you paid. You might also be asked to show proof of any credits or rebates you were given.

Check that you qualify. You have to satisfy certain conditions before claiming HST compensation on your personal return. For instance, you must have been living in Ontario on December 31st of the tax year, and the HST must have been paid on eligible expenses.

Work out the amount. Total the HST you paid on eligible expenses over the course of the tax year, then deduct any credits or rebates that you received.

Enter the claim on your return. While filing, record the HST amount you paid along with the credits or rebates you received. The HST can then be claimed as a tax credit on your return.

Send in your return. After finishing the return, deliver it to the CRA, either online or by mailing a paper copy.

If you still have questions about claiming HST compensation on your personal income tax return in Ontario, consider reaching out to the CRA or a tax professional for more help.

Sinemet is the most likely cause. It contains levodopa, which commonly lowers blood pressure, especially when standing up. This is called orthostatic or postural hypotension, and it is a well-known side effect of Parkinson's medicines. The timing fits: your pressure is normal when you wake, then drops after you take the tablets, which is typical of levodopa's effect.

Hydrocortisone is less likely to be the cause. It usually raises or maintains blood pressure, and it is often used to treat low blood pressure from adrenal insufficiency. Thyroxine rarely causes a sudden drop in blood pressure after a dose. Too much thyroxine tends to speed up the heart rather than lower pressure, though the levels of all three medicines still matter.

Please don't stop or change any of these medicines on your own. Stopping hydrocortisone suddenly can be dangerous, and stopping Sinemet can bring on severe Parkinson's symptoms. Instead, contact your doctor or neurologist soon and tell them about this pattern. They may adjust the timing or dose of Sinemet, suggest measuring your blood pressure before and about one to two hours after the morning tablets, or check whether your hydrocortisone and thyroxine doses are right. In the meantime, sitting or lying down after taking your morning medicines, standing up slowly, and drinking water as advised can help.

Seek urgent medical care if you feel faint, have a fall, become confused, have chest pain, or notice a very rapid or irregular heartbeat.

Paying off a car loan within a year can be smart, but whether it actually makes sense really depends on your situation. A few things to think about:

Interest first. If your rate is high, clearing the loan fast can save you real money, since the longer it runs, the more interest piles up. If the rate is low, though, the savings are smaller.

Make sure you're stable. Before you throw everything at the loan, check that you've got enough cash left over for emergencies and regular bills. Paying off the car can leave you short if something goes wrong, so an emergency fund matters here.

Look at your other debts. If you're carrying credit card debt or student loans, those might be the better target, especially if they charge higher interest. Generally, it makes more sense to tackle the most expensive debt first.

Think about what else the money could do. If you could earn more by investing that cash than you'd save on interest, holding onto it might be the better move. It's worth comparing the two numbers.

In the end, it comes down to your own finances and what you care about most. Weigh the pros and cons before you commit.

Solar panels don't actually work by absorbing heat, and that's the key thing to fix in your picture. They work with light, not heat. Sunlight is made of tiny packets of energy called photons, and when those photons hit a solar panel, they knock electrons loose inside it. That's the magic step.

Here's the simple version. A solar panel is made of special material, usually silicon, that's been treated so it has two layers with a slight difference in how they hold onto electrons. One layer is a bit eager to give electrons away, and the other is a bit eager to grab them. Think of it like a hill with a slide on one side: when sunlight kicks an electron loose, the built-in slope of the material pushes it in one direction.

Once you have lots of electrons all being pushed the same way, you have an electric current flowing. Wires on the front and back of the panel collect that flow, and it comes out as direct current, or DC, which is a steady flow of electricity that always goes in one direction. Batteries and many electronic gadgets use DC.

So the heat isn't really what gets turned into power. Heat is actually a bit of a nuisance: panels work slightly less efficiently when they get very hot, which is why they're often mounted so air can flow behind them. The power comes from the light itself, shaking loose electrons, and the electrons flowing through wires is what runs your lights, phone chargers, and the rest.

Imagine every letter lives inside an invisible box, like a little room. Font size is the height of that room, not the height of the letter itself. The size is measured in a unit called points, and one point is about 1/72 of an inch. So a 12 point font means the invisible box is 12 points tall, which is about one sixth of an inch.

Here is where it gets confusing. The person who designs a font gets to decide how big the letter is inside its box. One designer might draw tall letters that almost fill the room. Another might draw smaller letters with lots of empty space around them. Both fonts live in a 12 point box, so both are "size 12," but one looks bigger than the other. It is like two kids sharing same-sized bedrooms, where one kid has a giant bed and the other has a tiny one. The rooms match, but what's inside doesn't.

So yes, the numbers are a real measurement, but they measure the box, not what you actually see. The part of the letter that looks big or small is mostly the height of a lowercase letter like x, which designers call the x-height. Fonts with a big x-height look larger at the same point size. That is why Verdana looks huge next to Times New Roman even when both are set to 12.

As for why 12 is the standard, there is no magic rule. It comes from the days of printing, when 12 points was a comfortable size for reading a page held at arm's length. It is big enough for most eyes to read easily but small enough to fit plenty of words on a page. Typewriters also produced text close to that size, so people got used to it, and schools and offices kept using it as the default. It is mostly habit and comfort, not science.

One more wrinkle: on screens, the points are not always exactly 1/72 of an inch, because screens have different sizes and sharpness. The computer makes a guess about how big things should be, so 12 on your phone and 12 on a printed page can look different too.

Lee Sedol is a professional Go player from South Korea. Go is an old Chinese board game played on a grid of intersecting lines, using black and white stones, and it is famous for its complexity and the high level of skill needed to play it well. Lee took up Go when he was 5 years old and turned professional at 12. Over his career he has captured many tournament titles, and he is regarded as one of the finest Go players in the world. In 2016, he drew widespread attention by facing the artificial intelligence program AlphaGo in a heavily publicized match of five games. Although he was seen as the likely winner, Lee lost the series 4-1. Even so, his play against AlphaGo earned considerable admiration, as did the gracious manner in which he accepted his loss.

"A Change Is Gonna Come" is a track written and sung by Sam Cooke. Issued in 1964 on the album "Ain't That Good News," it became an anthem of the civil rights era. Cooke drew on his own encounters with discrimination and segregation, along with the broader civil rights struggle of that period, when crafting the song. Many artists have recorded their own versions over the decades, and it still stands as a moving call for social and political change.

U.S. grocery stores provide cash back for a few reasons. For one, it is a convenient option for shoppers who pay with cash but lack enough to cover their total, sparing them a separate stop at an ATM or bank. It can also cut down on the coins a store must keep in its registers, since customers may take extra money back as bills instead of loose change. Lastly, it can shorten checkout lines, making the shopping trip more pleasant and leaving customers happier.

Your question is ambiguous, since "Article 5" appears in many documents. The most famous is Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty (NATO's founding treaty, signed in 1949). It states that an armed attack against one or more member countries in Europe or North America shall be considered an attack against them all. Each member then agrees to take whatever action it deems necessary, including the use of armed force, to assist the attacked party. It is the only time the clause has been invoked: the United States called for it after the September 11, 2001 attacks.

Article 5 also appears in other important texts. In the U.S. Constitution, the Fifth Amendment (not Article 5) covers rights such as due process and protection against self-incrimination, while Article V describes how the Constitution can be amended. In the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, Article 5 prohibits torture and cruel, inhuman, or degrading treatment. In the European Convention on Human Rights, Article 5 protects the right to liberty and security.

If you tell me which document you mean, I can explain that article in more detail.

In physics, a system's configuration space is an abstract mathematical space that captures every possible arrangement (positions, shapes, and so on) the system can adopt. It encodes the possible positions and orientations of all the particles in the system. The concept is central to classical mechanics, where it serves to describe how a collection of particles moves. Take a single particle moving through three-dimensional space: its configuration space is just three-dimensional space itself, with each point corresponding to one possible location of the particle. For more intricate systems, the configuration space may have many more dimensions. Two particles in three-dimensional space, for instance, would form a six-dimensional configuration space, where each point represents a particular pair of positions and orientations. The concept also appears in quantum mechanics, where it describes the possible states of a quantum system. There, the configuration space is frequently called the "Hilbert space" or "state space" of the system. In short, configuration space is a valuable tool for understanding and forecasting how physical systems behave, and it occupies a key position across many branches of physics.

Dear Kay, I'm sorry you're dealing with this, and I understand why it's frightening. Because the swelling is getting worse, spreading up your legs, and affecting your whole body, please contact your doctor today rather than waiting for your next scheduled visit.

Edema, which is fluid collecting in the tissues, has many possible causes. The most common involve the heart, since a weakened heart may not pump well and fluid backs up into the legs. Kidney problems can cause the body to hold on to salt and water, and liver disease, particularly when it affects protein levels in the blood, can lead to swelling throughout the body. Problems with the veins in the legs, such as poor circulation or a blood clot, can cause swelling in one or both legs. Thyroid problems, low protein levels from poor nutrition, and certain medications can also cause it. Some common medications that cause swelling include certain blood pressure drugs (such as amlodipine), steroids, anti-inflammatory pain relievers like ibuprofen or naproxen, and some hormones. Prolonged stress can contribute indirectly, through changes in salt intake, drinking, sleep, and activity levels, but stress alone usually does not explain swelling that is spreading. Xanax (alprazolam) is not a typical cause of swelling, but tell your doctor about everything you take, including over-the-counter products.

Because swelling that is spreading and affecting the whole body needs evaluation, your doctor will likely want blood tests for kidney, liver, and thyroid function, a check of your heart, and possibly a urine test and an ultrasound of your legs. Please mention to them that the swelling has moved up your legs, that your shoes no longer fit, and that it is affecting your whole body.

Seek emergency care right away, by calling 911 or going to the nearest emergency room, if you have shortness of breath or trouble breathing, especially when lying down, chest pain or pressure, a racing or irregular heartbeat, fainting, sudden confusion, a leg that suddenly becomes painful, red, warm, or much more swollen than the other, coughing up blood, or very little urine.

While you wait to be seen, try to keep your legs raised above heart level when sitting or lying down, limit salt, and avoid standing or sitting for long periods. Do not start compression stockings or take extra pain relievers without checking with your doctor first.

Lots of empires have tried to take Afghanistan over the years, but the two biggest attempts were by the British and the Soviets. The British went after it in the 1800s and early 1900s because they wanted to keep their grip on India and limit influence in the area. They fought several campaigns there, including the First Anglo-Afghan War (1839-1842) and the Second (1878-1880). They did win some early battles, but they never really managed to control the country, and Afghan fighters gave them a rough time. The Soviets tried again in the 1900s. They invaded in 1979 and stayed for nearly ten years. Plenty of Afghans fought back, and the whole thing became known as the Soviet-Afghan War. In the end the Soviets pulled out in 1989, after taking heavy losses and without getting what they wanted.

Arthur Samuel (1901–1990) was an American computer scientist and electrical engineer who is widely regarded as a pioneer of artificial intelligence and machine learning. He worked for much of his career at IBM, where he made lasting contributions to the field during the 1950s and 1960s.

Samuel is best known for creating a checkers-playing program that could improve its performance by learning from experience. Rather than being given explicit instructions for every possible board position, the program evaluated positions using a scoring function whose weights were adjusted as it played against itself and against human opponents. Over many games, the program got better, eventually reaching a level where it could beat respectable amateur players. In 1959 he published a paper describing this work, and it is from this work that he is credited with coining the term "machine learning," defined as giving computers the ability to learn without being explicitly programmed for a specific task.

Beyond the checkers program, Samuel contributed to early work on computer memory and programming, and he was an influential figure in establishing the research agenda for artificial intelligence. He also played a role in the early development of computer science as an academic discipline, and he later became a professor at Stanford University. His ideas about learning from data and improving through experience laid groundwork for many later developments in modern machine learning.

Using a line of credit to invest means borrowing money, usually from a bank, and putting it into stocks, real estate, a business, or another asset in hopes that the returns will exceed the cost of borrowing. Common sources include a personal line of credit, a home equity line of credit (HELOC), a securities-based line of credit secured by an existing investment portfolio, or a business line of credit. Because you only pay interest on the amount you draw, a line of credit can be more flexible than a lump-sum loan, and HELOCs and portfolio-backed lines often carry lower interest rates than unsecured credit.

The main appeal is leverage. If you borrow at 7 percent and your investment earns 10 percent, you keep the 3 percent difference, which amplifies your returns. In some jurisdictions, interest on money borrowed to earn investment income may be tax-deductible. In Canada, for example, interest is generally deductible when borrowed funds are used to earn income from investments, and in the United States investment interest expense can be deductible up to your net investment income if you itemize. Rules vary, so it is worth confirming with a tax professional, and keeping borrowed funds clearly separated from personal spending helps preserve any deduction.

The risks are significant. Leverage magnifies losses just as much as gains. If your investment falls in value, you still owe the full amount borrowed plus interest. Most lines of credit carry variable rates, so rising interest rates can turn a profitable strategy into a losing one. With a HELOC, your home is the collateral, so a combination of market losses and an inability to make payments could put your house at risk. Securities-based lines can trigger a margin-call-like demand to repay or add collateral if your portfolio drops, forcing you to sell at the worst possible time. Lenders can also reduce or freeze a line of credit during economic downturns, exactly when you might need flexibility.

Several factors determine whether this approach makes sense. Your income should be stable enough to cover interest payments comfortably without relying on investment returns. Your time horizon should be long, since short-term market swings can be severe. The expected return should realistically exceed the after-tax borrowing cost by a comfortable margin, keeping in mind that stock market returns are never guaranteed. You also need the emotional discipline to hold through a downturn without panic selling while still owing money.

Many people who use this strategy start with a modest amount relative to their net worth, favor diversified, low-cost investments rather than speculative ones, pay at least the interest monthly, and have a clear plan for repaying the principal. Before proceeding, it is wise to speak with a fee-only financial advisor and a tax professional who can evaluate your specific situation, because borrowing to invest can build wealth faster but can also deepen losses in ways that are hard to recover from.

Yes, your results look normal, and nothing in them suggests you can't get pregnant.

For a woman tested on day 2 or 3 of her cycle, a typical FSH is roughly 3 to 10 mIU/ml, and yours is 5.20. This is a good sign, because a high FSH (usually above about 10) would suggest a lowered egg reserve, and yours is well within the healthy range. A typical early-cycle LH is roughly 2 to 10 mIU/ml, so your 5.80 is normal too. Prolactin is usually considered normal up to about 20 to 25 ng/ml in non-pregnant women, so 6.98 is comfortably normal. A high prolactin can interfere with ovulation, but that isn't the case for you.

About what you heard: the concern behind it is the LH to FSH ratio, which doctors look at mainly when considering polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS). In PCOS the LH is often noticeably higher than FSH, sometimes with a ratio of 2:1 or more. Your ratio is about 1.1 to 1, which is essentially balanced and not in the range that raises suspicion. So it's not true that LH must be lower than FSH. A slightly higher LH than FSH is not abnormal by itself, and your doctor is right that you shouldn't read too much into it. The ratio is only one small clue and is never used alone to diagnose anything. Your regular periods are also reassuring, since they usually mean you are ovulating.

Seven months of trying is still within the normal range. Even for healthy couples, only about 80 to 85 percent conceive within a year, and the chance in any single month is only around 20 to 25 percent. Doctors usually begin a fuller fertility workup after 12 months of trying at your age, so it's good that you're already being checked.

Some things that may help: timing intercourse around ovulation, which is typically about 14 days before your next period starts (every other day during the several days before and including that point works well); tracking ovulation with test kits; and taking folic acid daily. It's also worth knowing that fertility is a two-person issue, so a semen analysis for your partner is a simple and important test that is often done early. Your doctor may also suggest other checks, such as a mid-luteal progesterone level to confirm ovulation, thyroid function (TSH), and possibly an ultrasound or a test of whether the fallopian tubes are open if you don't conceive after a longer time.

Please follow up with your doctor about the next steps, but based on these three numbers, there's no cause for worry.

Honestly, it's not always possible for a distressed plane to ditch in water. It really comes down to where the plane is and what the water looks like. If it's too high or too far from the water, the pilot may not have enough time or distance to glide down safely. And even when it's close, the water might be too choppy to land on, or there could be ships or buildings in the way.

Planes do sometimes land on water with people surviving, though. The Hudson River landing is the classic example. Captain Chesley "Sully" Sullenberger put a plane down on the Hudson in New York City, and everyone got out. That one worked partly because the plane was low and nothing was in the way. Passengers and crew also got off the plane fast.

That said, a lot of water landings don't end well. The impact can be too violent, the plane might sink before everyone gets out, or the water can be cold and rough enough to make survival tough. And honestly, most crashes don't happen on water at all. Plenty happen on land, and your odds really depend on the details of each one.

A programming language is basically a formal language with a set of instructions you can use to get a computer to produce some kind of output. People use them to write programs that carry out specific algorithms. Those programs can run on a computer or other device and handle a task or a bunch of tasks. There are tons of them, and each one has its own rules and syntax. C, C++, Java, Python, and Ruby are some popular examples. Every language has its strengths, so it's really about picking the right one for the job. Python gets used a lot for web development and data analysis, while C and C++ are more of a go-to for systems programming and low-level stuff. To write a program, you type out instructions in a text file following the language's syntax. The instructions can be dead simple, like printing a message to the screen, or they can get pretty involved, like sorting a list of numbers. Once that's done, you run a compiler or interpreter to turn your code into machine code the computer can actually execute. Programming languages are kind of everywhere in modern computing, from operating systems and mobile apps to websites and beyond.

Okay, so here's the deal with the Fair Credit Reporting Act (FCRA) in the US. It's a federal law that controls how creditworthiness data gets collected, shared, and used. You've got the right to see your credit report and dispute anything wrong on it, which is huge. You can also opt out of having your data shared with certain outfits, like credit card companies and insurers. To do that, head to the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) website and follow their steps.

Keep in mind that states have their own rules on top of the FCRA. Some even run their own credit reporting setups and hold data to tougher standards. So it's worth checking what applies where you live.

Honestly, the best move is to stay on top of your rrights. Pull your credit report regularly, and if you spot a mistake, dispute it right away. And be careful about handing out your Social Security number to anyone you don't know, since that's exactly the kind of info someone could use to get at your credit data.

It's usually wise to set aside part of your earnings for later, yet it's equally worth enjoying what you earn today and using it to make your life better. Finding the right mix depends on your personal money goals and situation. A few factors can guide how much you decide to spend. First, consider your financial objectives: are you saving toward something specific, like a house, clearing debt, or retirement? If your goals stretch far into the future, putting more aside and spending less may make sense. Second, look at your income and outgoings: can you cover your present costs comfortably, or do you find it hard to get by? If you can save a portion and still meet your obligations, boosting savings may be a good move. But if bills are already a struggle, you might need to earn more or trim your spending. Third, think about what matters most to you. If experiences and time with loved ones are a priority, you may want to put more of your money toward them. If financial stability and independence weigh heavier, saving more could suit you better. In the end, the balance between saving and spending comes down to your own goals and circumstances. Drawing up a budget that reflects your priorities can help you get the most out of what you earn.

So basically in Sweden the ombudsman is an independent government body that looks out for people's rights when they deal with government agencies and public authorities. If you think a agency has violated your rights, you can file a complaint and the ombudsman can look into it. The system is split across several offices, each with its own focus. There's one for children, one for elderly care, and one for discrimination issues, for example. There's also a public sector ombudsman that handles complaints about what government agencies and authorities actually do. Their job is to review complaints, run investigations, and recommend ways to settle disputes. They can't make binding decisions or hand down orders, though. What they have is influence and reputation, which can push agencies toward change and make things fairer and more effective.
