For this reason, modern navigation systems rely heavily on probabilistic methods that represent uncertainty explicitly, and increasingly on machine learning to interpret sensor data and anticipate the behavior of people and other agents.

Oil rigs are what people use to drill for oil and natural gas, the stuff that heats homes and runs cars and other machines. There are different kinds, but the ones you see sitting out in empty fields are usually called "land rigs." They've got a tall metal structure on the ground with a big drill bit at the bottom that digs deep into the earth.

Before anything gets drilled, workers have to figure out where to dig. They use special tools to test the ground and look for signs of oil or gas. If they think there's something worth going after, they set up a land rig right on that spot. The rig holds a long pipe called a "drill string," which is really a bunch of smaller pipes that fit inside each other, with the drill bit attached at the end.

To get going, workers use a big engine to spin the drill bit. The bit is made of super hard stuff like diamonds or tungsten, so it can chew through rock and soil as it turns. As it goes deeper, the crew uses the rig to raise and lower the string. That lets them control how deep they're going, and it also means they can pull the bit back up to swap it out or fix it.

Once the hole is deep enough, they pump a mix of water, sand, and chemicals down the drill string. It's called "drilling mud," and it keeps the bit cool and clean while also stopping the walls of the hole from caving in. If they hit oil or gas, they slide in a pipe called a "casing" to line the hole, which keeps the stuff from leaking out into the ground. After that, they put a pump at the bottom to bring the oil or gas up to the surface.

Hope that helps make sense of how it all works! Let me know if you've got more questions.

The Oxford English Dictionary, usually abbreviated as the OED, is the most comprehensive and authoritative dictionary of the English language. Published by Oxford University Press, it traces the history of English words, showing not only what they mean today but how their meanings, spellings, and pronunciations have changed over time. For each entry, it provides dated quotations from books, newspapers, letters, and other sources, illustrating how a word was used in each period and when it first appeared in writing.

The dictionary began in 1857 when the Philological Society proposed a new dictionary that would record the entire vocabulary of English. The first installment appeared in 1884 under the editorship of James Murray, and the complete first edition was published in 1928, long after its original planned completion date. Since then, it has been revised and expanded continually, and much of its content is now available online, with updates added quarterly. It contains hundreds of thousands of entries, and its coverage extends beyond standard English to include regional, historical, and borrowed words from around the world.

Because of its scale and its focus on historical evidence, the OED is widely used by scholars, writers, translators, and researchers who need to know the precise origin and development of a word. It is often described as the definitive record of the English language.

Whether it's worth investing somewhere because dividends aren't taxed there really depends on your own situation, so it's smart to look at taxes before you buy. If you live in a country that taxes dividends, a place with no dividend tax can let you keep more of what you earn. But don't stop there. Capital gains tax, interest income tax, and withholding taxes can all take a bite too, and they don't always work the way you'd expect. Tax rules for investment income also vary a lot from country to country, so check what applies where you're actually investing. And if things get complicated, a tax pro or financial advisor can help you sort out the details.

A Jacquard loom is a mechanical loom that automates the weaving of intricate patterns into fabric. Joseph Marie Jacquard invented it in the early 1800s, and people still use it today to make things like brocade, damask, and tapestry. The clever part is the punched cards. They work a lot like the cards in early computers: you string them together in a sequence that matches the pattern you want, and as the loom runs, it reads each card and moves the harnesses and needles to match. So the pattern gets woven right into the cloth.

What makes it so useful is how precise and repeatable it is. You can get complicated, detailed designs that would be a nightmare to produce by hand, or that you couldn't really pull off at all. That's why you see Jacquard looms churning out so much of the fancy, high-end decorative fabric.

Waiting until the very last moment to settle your credit card bills is usually unwise, since it can result in late fees and harm your credit score. Paying on time matters, and in most cases the best approach is to pay as early as you are able. Doing so helps you steer clear of penalties and of any negative effect on your credit rating. If your goal is to save as much money as possible, consider clearing your full balance every month instead of carrying part of it forward. That way you won't be charged interest, which can add up to a considerable expense over time. Comparing different cards and choosing one with a low interest rate is also smart, because it can reduce what you pay in interest. To sum up, you are generally better off paying your credit card bills in full and by the due date instead of leaving them until the final moment. This protects you from late fees and credit score damage, and it can lower your interest costs as well.

The false positive rate is a measure used in statistics, medical testing, machine learning, and security to describe how often a test or model wrongly signals that something is present when it is actually absent. In other words, it is the proportion of truly negative cases that get incorrectly classified as positive.

Formally, it is calculated as the number of false positives divided by the total number of actual negatives, which is the sum of false positives and true negatives. If a spam filter examines 1,000 legitimate emails and wrongly flags 20 of them as spam, the false positive rate is 20 divided by 1,000, or 2 percent. It is also equal to one minus the specificity of the test, since specificity measures the proportion of actual negatives correctly identified.

A few examples help make the idea concrete. A medical screening test with a false positive rate of 5 percent will tell about 5 out of every 100 healthy people that they might have the disease. A fraud detection system may flag legitimate transactions as fraudulent, inconveniencing customers. In hypothesis testing, the false positive rate corresponds to the Type I error rate, which is the probability of rejecting a true null hypothesis. The significance level, often set at 0.05, is essentially the false positive rate you are willing to tolerate.

It is important not to confuse the false positive rate with the false discovery rate or with the probability that a positive result is wrong. The false positive rate is conditioned on the case being truly negative, while the share of positive results that are wrong depends also on how common the condition is. If a disease is very rare, even a test with a low false positive rate can produce many more false alarms than true detections, so most positive results may turn out to be wrong. This is a common source of misunderstanding, related to the base rate fallacy.

There is usually a trade-off with the false negative rate. Making a test more sensitive, so it misses fewer real cases, often raises the false positive rate, and vice versa. Tools such as the ROC curve plot the true positive rate against the false positive rate across different thresholds, helping people choose a balance suited to the costs of each type of error.

Hey, there are a few reasons your follicles might not be growing the way they should even with IUI. One is ovarian dysfunction, which can come from hormonal imbalances, age-related decline in fertility, or certain medical conditions that mess with how the ovaries work. Another is just not responding well to the meds. Some people don't react much to certain fertility drugs, and Ovitrop HP 75 could be one of those cases, which would hold back follicle growth. Problems with the uterus or cervix can also get in the way of getting pregnant, though that's more about conceiving than growth itself. Lifestyle stuff plays a part too. Too much exercise, a lot of stress, or poor nutrition can all affect your fertility and how your follicles develop. Honestly, your best bet is to talk to your fertility specialist so they can figure out what's going on in your specific case. They might change the dose or switch you to a different medication, or they could suggest another type of fertility treatment altogether.

The full order book for a stock is usually called Level 2 or market depth data, and in practice there are a few places to get it, depending on how deep you need it to be.

Most brokerages offer Level 2 quotes, often free or for a modest monthly fee. Platforms such as Interactive Brokers, Fidelity's Active Trader Pro, Charles Schwab's thinkorswim, E*Trade's Power E*Trade, and Webull show the bids and asks at multiple price levels, along with the size at each level and often the market maker or exchange posting it. Some require a funded account and a market data subscription, and non-professional rates are typically a few dollars a month.

One important caveat is that the "full book" doesn't really exist in one place in the US. Stocks trade across many exchanges (NYSE, Nasdaq, Cboe, IEX and others) plus dark pools, and each exchange has its own order book. Consolidated Level 2 from a broker usually combines the Nasdaq TotalView feed or similar, but it may not capture everything. For the most complete view, you would want the depth-of-book feeds directly from each exchange, such as Nasdaq TotalView, NYSE OpenBook, or Cboe depth feeds. These are paid products aimed at professionals and cost more, though some brokers and data vendors resell them.

Other options include charting and data platforms like TradingView, which offers depth-of-book for some assets with paid add-ons, and Bookmap, which visualizes order book history. For programmatic access, data vendors such as Polygon.io, Databento, and IEX Cloud alternatives provide order book data via APIs, with Databento in particular offering full-depth historical and live market-by-order data.

Also note that IEX publishes its own order book data (DEEP) for free, but it represents only IEX's share of trading, which is a small percentage of total volume. Hidden orders, iceberg orders, and dark pool liquidity won't appear in any of these feeds, so even the deepest data shows only displayed liquidity.

If you tell me which market (US stocks, other countries, crypto) and whether you want live viewing or data for analysis, I can point you to a more specific option.

Doctors have you cough during a testicular exam for a couple of reasons. The main one is to see how things move. When you cough, your testicles should shift up and in a little toward your body. If they don't move that way, or if there's swelling or pain, the doctor may want to look into it more closely. The other reason is to check the scrotum, the skin sac that holds the testicles. They're looking for swelling, lumps, or anything else that seems off. That's why it's a normal part of a routine physical. It helps catch potential problems early, and the cough just gives the doctor a better look at everything.

So the Berlin Blockade was a diplomatic and military crisis that ran from 1948 to 1949, and it's usually seen as one of the first big flashpoints of the Cold War. Its roots go back to 1945. After the war, the Allies (the US, the UK, and the Soviet Union) split Germany into four occupation zones, and Berlin, the capital, got chopped up into four sectors too. At first the Western powers and the Soviets actually worked together running things, but it didn't last. They just couldn't agree on how to rebuild and govern the place.

Reparations were a big sticking point. The Soviets wanted huge payments from Germany, and the Western powers pushed back on that. The Soviets also hated the Marshall Plan, the American program to rebuild Western Europe, Germany included. From Moscow's side, it looked like a way for the West to grab economic and political control over the continent.

Reunification was another fight. The Western powers wanted Germany put back together as one country, but the Soviets weren't keen. Given Germany's track record of aggression, they worried a united Germany would be a threat to them. Put all that together and the mistrust just kept piling up, until it boiled over into the blockade.

So a PRAM is basically an idealized parallel computer, mostly used by theorists to figure out how fast an algorithm could possibly run. You've got a bunch of processors all hooked up to one shared memory, and any of them can grab any memory cell whenever it wants. They run instructions at the same time, which is the whole point.

There are a few flavors depending on how you handle collisions. The CRCW version (concurrent-read, concurrent-write) lets multiple processors read and write the same cell at once. The EREW version (exclusive-read, exclusive-write) is stricter and only lets one processor touch a given cell at a time. People design PRAM algorithms to squeeze out as much parallelism as they can, and some of them do end up working on real hardware like clusters or supercomputers. Just don't expect real machines to behave like the model. It's pretty idealized, so the numbers can look a lot rosier than what you'd actually get.

Sudden paleness, especially when the lips are also pale and a normally independent task like getting dressed has become an effort, deserves prompt medical attention rather than watchful waiting. I'd recommend calling her doctor today, and if she seems to be getting worse, going to urgent care or the emergency room.

Several things could be behind this. Because she has asthma, the first concern is whether she is getting enough oxygen. A flare-up doesn't always cause dramatic wheezing. Sometimes it shows up as tiredness, paleness, faster breathing, or working harder to breathe. If you have a pulse oximeter at home, check her oxygen level. A reading below about 94 percent is a reason to call her doctor, and anything around 90 or lower, or lips or fingertips that look bluish or gray, is an emergency.

Anemia is another common cause of new paleness and fatigue, especially pale lips, gums, or inner eyelids. It can come from low iron, from slow blood loss (for example, through the stomach or intestines, or heavy periods if she is old enough to menstruate), or from other conditions. A simple blood count can check for this. Even though Geritol contains iron, it doesn't rule anemia out.

Her medications are also worth considering. Topiramate can cause metabolic acidosis, a shift in the body's chemistry that can lead to fatigue, faster breathing, and a generally unwell appearance. It can also contribute to kidney stones and reduced sweating, which can lead to overheating. Clonazepam can cause sedation and, especially combined with other sedating medicines or during illness, can slow breathing. Risperidone can occasionally cause low blood pressure, particularly when standing up, which can make someone look pale and tired. If any dose was recently changed or a new medicine or supplement was added, tell the doctor. Fish oil in high doses can mildly affect bleeding, though that is less likely to be the main issue.

Other possibilities include a brewing infection or virus, dehydration or not eating well, low blood sugar, or less commonly a heart problem or something more serious like a blood disorder. Because she is autistic, she may not be able to describe symptoms like dizziness, chest discomfort, stomach pain, or shortness of breath, so changes in her behavior, energy, appetite, sleep, or bathroom habits are important clues to share.

When you talk to her doctor, mention when you first noticed the paleness, whether it has stayed the same or worsened, her breathing and any rescue inhaler use, her energy level, whether she has had a fever, vomiting, unusual stools (especially black or bloody), bruising, or nosebleeds, and the exact doses of all her medications. The doctor will likely want to examine her and may order blood tests such as a complete blood count and a metabolic panel.

Go to the emergency room or call emergency services right away if she has trouble breathing, bluish or gray lips, confusion or unusual drowsiness that makes her hard to wake, fainting, a seizure, a racing heart, or if her rescue inhaler isn't helping. Otherwise, a same-day call to her pediatrician or doctor is the right next step.

A dividend stock is a share that delivers regular cash payments to its owners. These payouts usually arrive every quarter, and their size is typically either a set dollar figure or a fixed share of the company's profits. Investors who hunt for dividend stocks commonly focus on several defining traits. The first is solid financial health: dividend-paying firms tend to show strong earnings and cash flow, since they must generate a steady stream of profit to keep paying shareholders. The second is dividend yield, which expresses the annual payment as a percentage of the share price; a higher yield is usually seen as more appealing because it offers a bigger return on the money invested. Third, some investors favor companies with a track record of raising their dividends year after year, as this often signals financial strength and room to grow. Fourth is the payout ratio, meaning the portion of earnings handed out as dividends. A high ratio suggests that much of the profit is being distributed, which may leave less money to reinvest in the business and could weigh on future growth. Finally, sector matters, because dividend levels vary across industries. Utilities and telecommunications firms are known for generous payouts, whereas technology companies rarely pay dividends. Investors can locate dividend stocks with screening tools that filter by criteria such as yield, payout ratio, and sector. Still, it is essential to conduct independent research and assess a company's financial condition and growth prospects before buying any stock.

So a GPU (graphics processing unit) is basically specialized hardware that can crunch a ton of calculations really fast. It's especially good when you've got huge piles of data to chew through, like rendering graphics, running simulations, or training machine learning models. That's why a rig full of graphics cards beats a rig full of processors for certain kinds of work. GPUs are just built to be way faster at those particular calculations.

Here's the thing: a GPU can do loads of math operations at the exact same time, so it plows through big chunks of data quickly. A regular CPU can only handle a limited number of calculations at once, so it's not nearly as efficient when the data gets huge.

So if what you're doing is mostly heavy number-crunching, say rendering a 3D animation or training a machine learning model, a multi-GPU rig is going to be a lot faster than one stacked with CPUs.

The Starving Time was a devastating period in Jamestown, Virginia, during the winter of 1609 to 1610, when the English colony nearly collapsed. The settlers had arrived in 1607 with little knowledge of farming or the local environment, and they relied heavily on supplies from England and on trade with the neighboring Powhatan people. Relations with the Powhatan deteriorated after a series of conflicts, and the colonists were cut off from much of the food they had been obtaining. At the same time, a severe drought hit the region, ruining crops and reducing the game and fish available. The colony's leadership was also in disarray, since Captain John Smith had been injured in a gunpowder accident and returned to England in late 1609.

Over the following months, hunger became extreme. Colonists ate whatever they could find, including horses, dogs, rats, snakes, and even leather, and there are accounts of people consuming the dead. Of the roughly 500 people living in the colony in the fall of 1609, only about 60 were still alive by spring 1610. When survivors prepared to abandon Jamestown and sail back to England, they were met by a supply fleet under Thomas West, Lord De La Warr, which arrived in time to persuade them to stay. The colony survived, but the Starving Time remains one of the most grim episodes in early American colonial history and shaped later English efforts to establish more self-sufficient settlements.

A colleague's three-month-old son has been diagnosed with a right-sided inguinal hernia, and the question is whether surgery is needed right away or whether it can wait, and if it can wait, how long. Inguinal hernias in infants are generally treated surgically. When the operation should happen depends on the hernia's size and position and on whether it is causing any symptoms. As a rule, repair is recommended promptly to avoid complications such as incarceration, where the hernia becomes trapped, or strangulation, where the blood supply to the trapped bowel is interrupted. Even so, a pediatric surgeon should be consulted to decide the most suitable approach for this child. The surgeon will weigh the particular features of the hernia along with the infant's general health and medical history before settling on a plan.

Yes, some bank accounts exist specifically to take in deposits while blocking withdrawals and debit card use. People usually refer to these as "savings accounts" or "deposit accounts," and they can be found at conventional banks, credit unions, and internet-only banks. Savings accounts generally serve long-term goals, letting money grow through interest. Opening one may require a minimum initial deposit, and keeping a minimum balance may also be required. Certain savings accounts charge fees for withdrawals, while others cap how many withdrawals you can make in a single month. Deposit accounts, by contrast, are intended for short-term use, such as setting aside funds for a particular purpose or holding money you expect to spend on a purchase or investment soon. These accounts often come with smaller minimum balance requirements and typically do not charge withdrawal fees. Both types of accounts are protected by the FDIC, which insures deposits up to $250,000 per depositor at each institution. If a bank collapses, depositors get their money back up to that insured limit.

Facial and lip flushing, a feeling of warmth accompanied by redness, may arise from a variety of sources. Among the more frequent triggers are alcohol and caffeine, which widen blood vessels and bring on flushing. Spicy food works in a similar way, dilating vessels and producing the same effect. Menopause is another common cause, since flushing is a typical symptom once estrogen levels decline. Rosacea, a chronic skin condition, also leads to facial redness and flushing. In addition, allergies can produce flushing as one component of an allergic response. Certain drugs, including niacin (vitamin B3) and some blood pressure medications, may list flushing among their side effects. Occasionally, flushing points to an underlying health problem such as an infection or an autoimmune disorder. Anyone who experiences frequent flushing, or flushing alongside other symptoms, should consult a healthcare provider to identify the cause and get suitable treatment.

A dredge is basically a machine that digs sediment like sand, mud, and gravel off the bottom of a body of water. Most of them work by sucking or scooping the stuff up and dumping it somewhere else. The classic one is the suction dredge, which has a big hose that pulls up sediment and water from the bottom. That hose hooks up to a pump, which shoves the mix through pipes into a hopper or barge. Once it's there, the sediment gets separated from the water and hauled off to a designated spot, and the water goes back into the body of water.

Then there's the cutter suction dredge. This one has a spinning cutter head on the front that chews up the sediment so it's easier to vacuum away. The suction system grabs the loosened material and pumps it through pipes into a hopper or barge, same as before.

You'll also run into trailing suction hopper dredges, which drag suction pipes along the bottom while holding the sediment in a big onboard hopper as they go. Bucket dredges are another option. They use a chain of buckets to scoop material up and dump it into a hopper or barge. Different designs, but the core idea is the same: mechanically pull sediment off the bottom and move it somewhere else.

Hi Ayesha, thank you for asking. Your concern is understandable, and the good news is that most cousin couples have healthy children. Let me explain the facts so you can plan with confidence.

When two people are related, they share some of the same gene versions inherited from a common ancestor. This means that if either of you carries a rare harmful gene variant, there is a higher chance that your child could inherit the same variant from both of you, which can cause a recessive genetic condition. For first cousins like you, the overall risk of a birth defect or genetic disorder is somewhat higher than in unrelated couples, roughly from about 2 to 3 percent up to around 4 to 6 percent. That means the great majority of babies, around 94 to 98 percent, are born healthy. The increase comes mainly from rare recessive conditions, and many of these are not visible until later in childhood.

Since you and your husband are healthy, you are already in a good position. Here are some steps that can help:

1. See a genetic counselor before you conceive. They can review your family history on both sides, and discuss whether any carrier screening tests would be useful for you and your husband. Carrier screening can check for many common recessive conditions.

2. See your gynecologist or doctor for a preconception checkup. Make sure you are up to date on vaccinations such as rubella, and discuss any medicines you take. Start folic acid supplements, usually 400 micrograms daily, at least a month before trying to conceive, as this lowers the risk of neural tube defects.

3. Keep your blood sugar, blood pressure, and weight in a healthy range, and avoid smoking, alcohol, and any drugs not prescribed by your doctor.

4. During pregnancy, attend all your antenatal visits. Routine ultrasound scans and blood tests can detect many problems early. If you want more information, your doctor can offer additional prenatal screening or diagnostic tests such as NIPT or amniocentesis, which can be discussed if needed.

Most cousin marriages result in healthy, normal children, and with proper medical guidance you can greatly improve your chances. Please speak with a genetic counselor or your obstetrician soon, so they can give advice specific to your family history. Wishing you and your husband a healthy pregnancy.

So when a helicopter loses power to the main rotor, it starts dropping pretty fast. But the pilot isn't out of luck, because there's a technique called autorotation that lets them put it down safely.

Basically, the pilot cuts the engine (or disconnects it from the rotor) and lets the helicopter come down. As it falls, air rushes up through the main rotor blades and keeps them spinning. That's the autorotation part. The pilot uses the tail rotor to keep the nose pointed where they want it and steers toward a decent spot to land. Right before touchdown, they pull back on the controls to flare the helicopter, which slows the descent and softens the landing.

So really, the pilot is just using the helicopter's own motion and gravity to get it down in one piece when the engine isn't driving the rotor anymore.

Okay, so pattern recognition is basically spotting regularities in data and using them to sort or classify things. You take sensory input, like pictures, sound, or text, and figure out what it is based on certain criteria. It's a big deal in machine learning and AI because it lets computers make decisions from what they've picked up. You'll see it with visual patterns, audio patterns, and text patterns, and it's behind stuff like identifying objects in photos, recognizing spoken words, or spotting trends in financial data.

The process usually goes through a few steps. First you collect raw data from sensors or wherever it comes from. Then you preprocess it, which just means cleaning it up and organizing it so it's easier to work with. Next comes feature extraction, where you pull out the most useful characteristics to classify things with. Last, you actually classify the data based on the patterns you've found.

It shows up everywhere: image and speech recognition, natural language processing, anomaly detection. Honestly, it's one of the core pieces of most machine learning and AI systems, and people are still working hard on improving it.

Silent letters are mostly leftovers from the past. English spelling was largely fixed centuries ago, but the way words are pronounced kept changing afterward, so the spelling stayed behind while the sounds moved on.

Think of it like an old toy box. Long ago, people said these words differently. In "knife" and "gnome," the K and G were actually pronounced at the start, the way you'd say them in "kite" or "go." Over time people stopped pronouncing those first sounds, but writers kept the letters because the spelling was already written down in books and dictionaries. The same thing happened to the L in "walk" and "talk," and the B in "comb" and "lamb."

Some silent letters came from other languages. "Pterodactyl" comes from Greek, where the P was pronounced. "Gnome" also comes from Greek, and "Django" is a name from a language where the D sound is different from how English speakers say it. When English borrowed these words, it often kept the original spelling.

Some letters were added on purpose, too. In the 1500s, scholars wanted spellings to look like their Latin or Greek roots, so they put in letters like the B in "doubt" even though it was never said there. That's why it's a bit of a puzzle.

So there's no clever plan behind them. They're like old footprints left in cement: the ground moved, but the marks stayed.

A Pooled Registered Pension Plan (PRPP) is a retirement savings option open to people in Canada. These plans help Canadians put money aside during their working years and give them a stream of income once they retire. Like defined benefit and defined contribution plans, PRPPs aim to deliver regular retirement income. They differ, though, in that the assets are pooled together and managed by a professional pension plan administrator instead of being sponsored by an employer. As a result, a person can join a PRPP even when no pension plan is offered at their workplace. Employees, self-employed people, and business owners are all eligible.

Money goes into a PRPP through payroll deductions or through voluntary contributions. Each individual chooses how much to contribute, subject to limits set by the government. The plans also carry tax advantages: both the contributions and the investment earnings inside the plan are untaxed until the money is withdrawn. PRPPs fall under federal regulation and are run by financial institutions or other approved organizations. Because they are meant to be inexpensive and simple to establish and operate, they are an appealing choice for anyone without access to a workplace pension plan.

Short answer: in the US it's illegal pretty much everywhere. All 50 states, DC, and the territories treat prostitution as a crime. The one exception is certain rural counties in Nevada, where it's legal in licensed brothels. So when people say it's legal in some places, that's mostly other countries, plus that Nevada carve-out.

Also, prostitution and sex work aren't quite the same thing. Sex work is the broader term, basically trading sexual services, intimacy, or affection for money or some other compensation. Some people do it by choice. Others get pushed into it through coercion or exploitation, and that's a very different situation.

Some countries treat sex work as a legitimate job and the government regulates it. The US mostly doesn't. Here it generally isn't recognized as real work, and there's no regulation of it.

Honestly, bad pain under the shoulder blade and in the armpit can come from a bunch of things: a pulled or spasming muscle, a pinched or irritated nerve, or something going on with your spine or nearby joints. If it's lasting a while or really intense, get it checked by a doctor or other healthcare provider so they can figure out what's actually going on. The right treatment depends on the cause, but some common options are:

Over-the-counter or prescription pain meds, which can take the edge off and calm down inflammation.

Physical therapy, where exercises and stretches help loosen things up, build strength, and ease muscle tension.

Massage, which can relax tight muscles and get blood moving.

Chiropractic care, where adjustments aim to realign the spine and improve movement.

Acupuncture, an old Chinese practice where thin needles go into specific points on the body to help with pain.

Whatever plan your provider lays out, try to stick with it, since that's the best way to get your pain under control and feel better overall. And if your symptoms worry you or the pain isn't getting better with treatment, let them know right away.

Thinking about putting money into USD as a Eurozone resident? There are a few things to sort out first. Start with the exchange rate, since it changes what your investment is worth in dollars and what your returns will look like when you convert back. If the rate looks good, now might be a decent time to buy in. If it doesn't, you could hold off for a better rate or look at something else entirely.

Economic conditions matter too, on both sides of the Atlantic. Strong US conditions might make dollar investments more appealing, while weak ones could be a reason to wait or explore other options. Don't forget your own situation. Are you comfortable with the risk? Is the USD part of a broader, diversified portfolio, or would it be most of your money? And is this a short-term play or something you're holding for years? Your answers to those questions will tell you a lot about whether it's the right move for you.

Rich Fields, the longtime announcer on The Price Is Right, was a fixture of the show for decades. After Barker retired in 2007, Fields continued to serve as announcer under host Drew Carey, who took over the show in 2007.

Fields was known for his warm, booming introductions and his catchphrase-style delivery of prices and contestant names, and he remained a recognizable voice to viewers for many years. He stepped away from the show in the years following Carey's tenure began, and the announcing duties eventually passed to other performers. Fields has since largely retired from regular television work, though he has remained a respected figure among fans of the program.

Brink's is a recognized company that offers secure transport and storage, including for high-value goods like currency and precious metals. Path planning is the problem of finding a feasible route for a moving object from a starting position to a goal while avoiding obstacles and satisfying constraints. It is a core capability in robotics, autonomous vehicles, drones, computer games, and computer-aided design, wherever something needs to move through an environment in a purposeful way.

The problem usually starts with a model of the environment, often a map or grid, that marks where obstacles are and where the free space lies. The planner then searches this model for a sequence of positions or motions that connects start and goal. Classic approaches include graph-search algorithms such as Dijkstra's algorithm and A*, which find shortest paths on a discretized grid or graph by systematically expanding the most promising options. For high-dimensional spaces, such as a robot arm with many joints, sampling-based methods like Rapidly-exploring Random Trees (RRT) and Probabilistic Roadmaps are more practical, because they randomly sample configurations and connect the feasible ones rather than enumerating every possibility.

Good path planning is more than finding any route. Planners often aim to optimize criteria such as travel distance, time, energy use, or safety margin from obstacles. They also must respect the physical limits of the system, such as a car's turning radius or a robot's maximum joint speed, which is why some methods plan within the vehicle's dynamics rather than just in pure geometry. Because real environments change and sensors are imperfect, path planning is typically paired with motion control and re-planning, so that the robot can adjust when it encounters an unexpected obstacle.

Homeschooling means a family teaches kids at home instead of sending them to a public or private school. How it works varies a lot. Some families follow a set curriculum with textbooks and lesson plans, much like a school would. Others use a more relaxed approach, learning through books, museums, projects, and everyday life. Many states require parents to tell the local school district or state that they're homeschooling, and some require keeping records of what's been taught or testing the child at certain ages. Other states ask very little. Parents usually act as the teachers, though some families use online classes, tutors, or co-ops where several families share teaching.

Yes, you can get an official high school diploma while homeschooling. Often the parent issues it, and the family keeps records of the courses and grades, sometimes called a transcript. Some states also let homeschoolers earn a diploma through a recognized church-affiliated or private online program, or by passing a high school equivalency test like the GED, which is accepted by most employers and colleges as an alternative to a diploma.

Colleges do accept homeschooled students. Most schools look at the whole picture: a transcript showing the courses taken, grades or a portfolio of work, standardized test scores like the SAT or ACT, and sometimes letters of recommendation. Many colleges have specific admissions guidelines for homeschoolers, and some ask for extra documentation, but being homeschooled is not a barrier by itself.

Homeschooling does not automatically hurt your chances. Admissions officers generally care about how strong your academic record is, not where you learned it. A homeschooled student with solid grades, good test scores, and interesting activities can be just as competitive as anyone else. The main challenge is that homeschoolers have to put together their own records and sometimes explain their education more clearly, so it helps to keep good documentation from the start. If a homeschooled student has a clear record of challenging coursework, it can actually stand out.

An exchange-traded fund (ETF) generally mirrors changes to its underlying index as quickly as it can. Index reconstitution is the act of altering which securities an index contains, whether by adding some or dropping others. Providers may do this to keep pace with shifts in the market or to make sure the index still represents its intended segment accurately. Once the index changes, the ETF that follows it usually revises its portfolio to match the new lineup. This adjustment, often called rebalancing, means buying or selling the fund's holdings so they line up with the revised index. How quickly this happens varies by fund and by index. Some ETFs adjust their holdings every day, while others do so at longer intervals. Either way, the fund's goal is to track the index closely, including any changes to its makeup.

Yep, a US citizen can buy rental property in Canada, but there's a fair bit to sort out first. You'll need the right paperwork to enter and stay in Canada for the purchase, so a valid passport and probably a temporary resident visa, depending on your situation. Check that early so it doesn't trip you up later.

Then get to know the local market. Look at what similar places rent for, how fast units go, and what prices have been doing. Don't forget the ongoing costs: property taxes, insurance, and repairs can eat into your returns faster than you'd think.

It's worth talking to a local real estate agent and a lawyer who handles this kind of deal. They can walk you through the buying process and flag any rules that apply to foreign owners, which vary by province and city.

The tax side is the part people tend to underestimate. As a non-resident owner, you'll likely owe Canadian tax on rental income, and you may also need to file in the US. A cross-border tax pro is a good call here so you don't end up out of compliance in either country.

Circumvallate papillae are normal structures. They are the largest taste bumps on the tongue, arranged in a V shape near the back, each sitting in a small trench lined with taste buds. Because they are prominent and sit in a fold, they can look irregular or become tender, especially when irritated by sharp teeth, rubbing from dentures or dental work, or stomach acid that refluxes into the mouth. Inflammation of these papillae, sometimes called papillitis, is a recognized cause of soreness in that area, and it fits your friend's story well. Filing down a tooth edge helped a little, and reducing antacids helped too. Antacids may seem like they would only reduce acid, but changes in their use can shift symptoms, and the improvement suggests irritation from mechanical or chemical sources is at least part of the picture.

Still, the fact that the spot improved does not rule out a more serious cause, and that is why the doctor recommended a biopsy. Cancer of the back of the tongue can start as a sore that seems minor, may not hurt much, and may be mistaken for irritation. The key clinical questions are how long the spot has been there, whether it is healing or staying the same or growing, and whether he has risk factors such as tobacco or heavy alcohol use or HPV infection. A sore that persists beyond about two to three weeks despite removing irritants is generally considered worth evaluating, and a doctor who recommends a biopsy is usually doing so because something about the spot does not look like simple irritation.

On the stitches concern, it helps to know that many small tongue biopsies are done under local anesthetic and often heal without stitches, or with dissolvable ones. Some are done with brush sampling or a tiny punch. Your friend could ask the doctor directly whether stitches are always needed, what the procedure involves, and what the alternatives are, including referral to an ear, nose and throat specialist or oral surgeon if the first doctor's approach feels uncertain. Most people who have a biopsy learn the result is benign, and getting a definite answer is far less stressful than living with an unexplained sore.

So your instinct to keep investigating is sound. It would be reasonable to encourage your friend to see the biopsy as the fastest way to get certainty rather than a sign that cancer is assumed. In the meantime, he should avoid tobacco and alcohol, keep the area clean, and notice whether the spot changes. If it does not clearly resolve within a couple of weeks, or if he develops a lump, bleeding, difficulty swallowing, or numbness, he should return to the doctor promptly.

A continuous function is, intuitively, a function whose graph you can draw without lifting your pencil from the paper. There are no sudden jumps, gaps, or breaks: if you change the input by a small amount, the output also changes by only a small amount. This idea of "small changes in, small changes out" is the heart of continuity, and it makes continuous functions predictable and well behaved.

To make the idea precise, mathematicians first define continuity at a single point. A function f is continuous at a point a if three things hold: f(a) is actually defined, the limit of f(x) as x approaches a exists, and that limit equals f(a). In other words, the value the function approaches as you get close to a is exactly the value it takes at a. A function is called continuous on an interval, or simply continuous, if it is continuous at every point in its domain or in the interval being considered.

The most rigorous version is the epsilon-delta definition. The function f is continuous at a if, for every positive number epsilon, no matter how small, there exists a positive number delta such that whenever x is within delta of a, f(x) is within epsilon of f(a). You can read this as a challenge and response: someone demands that the output stay within some tiny tolerance epsilon of f(a), and you can always meet the demand by keeping the input close enough to a, within delta.

Many familiar functions are continuous. Polynomials such as f(x) = x squared plus 3x minus 1 are continuous everywhere. The sine and cosine functions, the exponential function, and the absolute value function are also continuous everywhere. Rational functions like 1/x are continuous at every point where they are defined, though they cannot be continuous at x = 0 because they are not defined there. Examples of discontinuous functions include a step function that equals 0 for negative inputs and 1 for inputs of zero or more, which jumps at zero, and the function 1/x squared, which shoots off to infinity near zero. Discontinuities are often classified as removable (a single hole in the graph that could be filled in), jump discontinuities (the graph leaps from one value to another), and infinite discontinuities (the function blows up).

Continuous functions have several important properties that make them central to calculus and analysis. Sums, differences, products, and compositions of continuous functions are continuous, and so are quotients wherever the denominator is not zero. The Intermediate Value Theorem says that if a function is continuous on a closed interval from a to b, it takes every value between f(a) and f(b), which is why a continuous function that goes from negative to positive must cross zero somewhere. The Extreme Value Theorem says that a continuous function on a closed, bounded interval always attains a maximum and a minimum value. Continuity is also a prerequisite for differentiability: every differentiable function is continuous, although a continuous function need not be differentiable, as the absolute value function shows with its sharp corner at zero.

Beyond real-valued functions, the concept generalizes to much broader settings, such as functions between metric spaces and topological spaces, where continuity is described in terms of open sets: a function is continuous if the preimage of every open set is open. Despite this abstraction, the underlying intuition remains the same, namely that nearby inputs lead to nearby outputs.

A reader writes in at gleixia@163.com with a question: despite eating healthy food, her face structure isn't improving. She says she has been eating two eggs a day, yet her eyes look sunken, and she wants a better facial structure and brighter, more attractive eyes. She is 6'2" and weighs 70 kg.

In response, the advice explains that diet alone may not be the only thing that determines how skin or facial structure looks. A healthy diet supports overall health and may have some effect on skin appearance, but several other factors matter as well. Genetics shape facial structure and skin type. Aging makes skin less elastic and can reduce collagen production, leading to fine lines and wrinkles. Excessive sun exposure damages skin and can cause fine lines, wrinkles, and uneven tone. Hormonal changes, such as those during menopause or pregnancy, can also alter how skin looks. High stress can impair the body's ability to keep skin healthy. Finally, a consistent routine of cleansing, moisturizing, and sun protection helps preserve skin's health and appearance.

The answer also suggests that anyone worried about their skin or facial structure consult a dermatologist or another healthcare provider, who can evaluate their overall health and recommend lifestyle changes or treatments.

Cracking a Rubik's Cube at high speed depends on memorized sequences of moves and well-practiced methods. Here is a rough outline of the process. The solver first scans the cube for faces that are already finished, meaning every sticker on them is the same color, such as a white face. Then the solver works to place the edge pieces, the cubies showing two colors, in their correct spots, often by lining them up with the center pieces, which show only one color, on that white face. After the edges are settled, attention turns to the corner pieces, the cubies with three colors, which are positioned relative to the centers and edges already in place. Last, the solver applies algorithms, which are fixed sequences of moves, to shuffle the remaining pieces until the entire cube is solved.

Many approaches exist for fast solving. The Fridrich method uses a set of specific algorithms applied in a set order. Another popular technique is CFOP, an acronym for Cross, F2L (First Two Layers), OLL (Orient Last Layer), and PLL (Permute Last Layer). Finishing the puzzle in under ten seconds requires exceptional skill with these sequences, along with the ability to perform them both rapidly and accurately. Becoming a quick solver takes sustained practice and commitment.

Soft computing is a discipline concerned with building computational systems and algorithms modeled on, or imitating, the way humans think, perceive, and act. The label "soft" reflects the fact that these systems are meant to be flexible and adaptable, and to cope well with uncertainty, imprecision, and partial truth. They stand in contrast to conventional "hard" computing, since they are intended for problems that are complex, poorly defined, or not well understood, and for data that is noisy, incomplete, or uncertain. The field draws on many methods, such as artificial neural networks, fuzzy logic, evolutionary algorithms, probabilistic reasoning, and machine learning. These techniques see broad use in areas like pattern recognition, data mining, image processing, natural language processing, and control systems. They are especially valuable for tasks where information is incomplete or ambiguous, or where a system must adjust and learn from experience.

Formal reasoning is basically logical argument that sticks to a strict set of rules. You start from statements you take as true (the premises) and make logical moves from there. There are two main flavors. Deductive reasoning goes from a general principle down to a specific conclusion, while inductive reasoning goes the other way, starting from specific observations and building toward a general claim. You'll see it all over math, computer science, philosophy, and law. It's really handy for untangling complicated systems and making decisions you can actually justify.

I'm sorry you're dealing with this. Pain in the neck plus weakness in both hands is exhausting. I can't examine you, so treat this as background to discuss with your surgeon and therapist.

Your new herniations sit just above and just below your fused segments, which is common. When several levels are fused, the neighboring discs take on more motion and stress, which is often called adjacent segment degeneration. That may be part of why turning your head hurts. The upcoming EMG matters because it will help separate how much of your hand weakness comes from the neck roots and how much from the radial nerves in the arms, and that guides treatment for each.

Your pain when turning your neck is not necessarily a reason to skip physical therapy, but it is a reason to make sure the therapy fits you. Tell the therapist about your fusion levels, the C3 and C7 herniations, and how much rotation hurts. Good therapy for a neck like yours usually starts gently, with pain-free isometric exercises (pressing your head lightly against your hand without moving), deep neck flexor activation such as gentle chin tucks, shoulder blade and upper back strengthening, posture work, and soft tissue work for the muscles that tend to guard and spasm. Forceful stretching into painful rotation, chiropractic-style manipulation, and cervical traction should generally not be done above or below a multilevel fusion without your surgeon's explicit approval. A good therapist will work within a tolerable range and progress slowly. If a session leaves you significantly worse for more than a day or two, report it so the plan can be adjusted.

Several things can make therapy more bearable. Your doctor may consider an anti-inflammatory if your stomach, kidneys, and other medications allow, or a short course of a muscle relaxant for spasm. For nerve-type pain such as burning, shooting, or tingling, medications like gabapentin, pregabalin, or duloxetine are often used. Heat before exercise and ice afterward help many people. If pain still blocks progress, ask about injections. An epidural steroid injection or selective nerve root block can calm an irritated nerve root from the C3 or C7 herniation, and facet or medial branch blocks can help if the pain comes from the joints next to the fusion. These are often used specifically to create a window in which therapy becomes possible.

Day to day, try to avoid long periods looking down at a phone or reading, raise screens to eye level, and turn your whole body rather than just your neck when you can, for example when backing up a car. A supportive pillow that keeps your neck neutral, sleeping on your back or side rather than your stomach, and breaking up long sitting periods can reduce flare-ups.

For the radial nerve side, avoid pressure on the backs of your upper arms, such as leaning on armrests or sleeping with an arm draped over a chair or under your body. If you have wrist drop or trouble extending your wrist or fingers, a wrist cock-up splint can protect the hand and improve function while the nerve recovers. It's worth asking whether a referral to an occupational or certified hand therapist makes sense alongside the neck therapy.

Questions for your doctor could include whether the C3 or C7 herniation is compressing the spinal cord or only a nerve root, whether the EMG will also test for other entrapments, whether injections are an option before or during PT, and what your restrictions are for neck movement and lifting.

Contact your doctor promptly or seek urgent care if you notice worsening weakness, new numbness spreading into your legs, trouble walking or balance problems, loss of hand coordination such as difficulty buttoning or dropping things more often, or any change in bladder or bowel control. These can signal pressure on the spinal cord, which needs faster attention than ordinary neck pain.

Many people with your combination of problems do improve, especially once the source of each symptom is clarified and the arm nerves are given a chance to recover.

If someone with a serious mental illness commits a crime that would carry the death penalty for a sane offender, the legal system generally handles the case differently because of that illness. Many jurisdictions hold that a person is not criminally responsible if, as a result of mental illness, they could not grasp the nature or consequences of what they were doing. This principle, called the insanity defense, can lower the charges or the sentence for anyone shown to have been clinically insane when the offense occurred. When such a person is judged insane and therefore not responsible, a court may order them into a psychiatric treatment facility rather than prison. The purpose of that arrangement is to give the person the care they need to manage their condition and to reduce the chance of reoffending. In short, a clinically insane person who commits a crime punishable by death for a sane person is typically treated differently under the law, and the insanity defense may reduce their charges or sentence, potentially leading to commitment to a mental health facility instead of imprisonment.

Yeah, a star can totally exist outside a galaxy, though it's not the usual setup. A galaxy is basically a huge bunch of stars, gas, and dust all tied together by gravity, and most of them have millions or even billions of stars. But not every star is part of one. Some are free-floating, meaning they aren't really attached to any galaxy and just drift through space on their own. These loners tend to be smaller and less massive than the ones in galaxies. They're also a pain to spot. They're so far off, and they don't have a bright galaxy behind them to make them stand out. So yeah, it happens, just rarely, and they're tough to find.

Subjective experience is the first-person, felt quality of being conscious: what it is like, from the inside, to see red, taste coffee, feel pain, or be anxious about tomorrow. The word "subjective" signals that these experiences belong to a particular subject, a someone for whom things appear a certain way. The philosopher Thomas Nagel captured the idea in his 1974 essay about bats, arguing that an organism has conscious states only if there is something it is like to be that organism. You could know every physical fact about a bat's echolocation, he suggested, and still not know what it is like to perceive the world that way.

Philosophers often use the term "qualia" for the specific qualitative character of such experiences: the redness of red, the sting of a pinprick, the particular flavor of mint. These are distinguished from the functional or physical story about what happens when you encounter those things, such as light of a certain wavelength striking the retina, signals traveling to the brain, and behavior following. The puzzle is that the physical description seems complete without ever mentioning why any of it should be accompanied by felt experience. David Chalmers called this the hard problem of consciousness, contrasting it with the "easy" problems of explaining things like attention, memory, and reportability, which are difficult scientifically but at least seem to be tractable through mechanisms.

Subjective experience is distinct from mere information processing. A thermostat responds to temperature, and a computer can classify images, but whether there is anything it is like to be such a system is exactly what is in dispute. Likewise, it differs from objective facts, which can be checked by anyone from outside. Your experience is directly accessible only to you, which is why the problem of other minds arises: you infer that others have experiences from their behavior and similarity to you, but you cannot observe their experience directly.

There are several broad positions on how to understand it. Physicalists hold that experience is ultimately a brain process, perhaps one that seems mysterious only because of how we think about it. Some illusionists go further and say that the sense of ineffable inner qualities is a kind of misrepresentation by the brain. Dualists claim that experience is something over and above the physical. Panpsychists suggest that experience is a fundamental feature of matter. Others, like those favoring functionalist or higher-order theories, try to explain experience in terms of how information is organized or represented.

The topic matters beyond philosophy. It bears on questions about animal sentience, anesthesia and disorders of consciousness, and whether artificial systems could ever have experiences, all of which depend on what subjective experience is and what gives rise to it.

Timeshares are vacation properties you can buy or rent for a set chunk of time each year. They make the most sense if you go to the same place every year and like the idea of having a spot that feels like yours. Timeshare presentations are the sales pitches companies use to get you to buy one, and they usually come with a sweetener like a free trip or a discount just for showing up. The salesperson will walk you through all the perks and features of the property, trying hard to make it sound like a no-brainer. Timeshares work out well for some folks, but they're definitely not for everybody. Do your homework and think it through before you sign anything. Plenty of people end up feeling pressured during a presentation, or they find out later that reselling is a real headache. Still, if you weigh the costs against the benefits and do your due diligence, a timeshare can be worth it.

Rule-based programming is basically a way of building software where the behavior comes from a bunch of rules saying what to do when certain things happen. Usually they're written as if-then statements: the "if" part sets up a condition or trigger, and the "then" part says what to do when that condition is met. You'll see these a lot in AI and expert systems, where the goal is to take what a domain expert knows and encode it so a computer can work with it. They also pop up in natural language processing, where rules can describe a language's grammar, and in automated decision-making, where the system checks data against predefined rules and picks an outcome.

The big perk is flexibility. You can change or add rules as new information comes in or things shift, so these systems work well in environments that keep changing. That said, they can get messy fast. Once you've got hundreds or thousands of rules, keeping them organized and making sure they don't conflict with each other becomes a real headache.
