If you're thinking of a New York congressman with a sex-related scandal, Chris Lee resigned from the House in 2011 after shirtless photos he had sent to a woman he met on Craigslist became public. Vito Fossella, who represented Staten Island, was arrested for drunk driving in 2008 while on his way to visit a woman in Virginia with whom he had a child, and he did not seek reelection.

Imagine your whole class agreed on a set of rules at the start of the year, like "nobody brings candy to school." Canada signed up to a few of those kinds of rules with almost every other country. They are three United Nations drug treaties, from 1961, 1971, and 1988, and they say countries should keep marijuana illegal except for medical and scientific uses. If Canada decides to let people buy and use pot anyway, it is breaking a promise it made to the rest of the class.

So what could go wrong? Mostly it comes down to reputation and relationships, because there is no playground monitor who can punish Canada directly. The UN's drug watchdog, called the International Narcotics Control Board, can publicly scold a country and say it is not following the rules. That is embarrassing, and it can make Canada look like a country that does not keep its word, which matters when Canada wants other countries to follow agreements it cares about, like trade deals, human rights rules, or climate promises.

Some countries might also be annoyed. The United States, for example, still has federal laws against marijuana, and a neighbor changing the rules could cause friction at the border, such as extra questions for travelers or worries about pot crossing over. Other countries that strongly oppose drug legalization might complain loudly, and that could make working together on other things a little harder.

There is also a bigger worry that if Canada breaks the rules and nothing happens, other countries might think they can ignore treaties they do not like too, which weakens the whole system of promises between countries.

Canada has a few ways to handle this. It could try to change the treaties, it could withdraw from them and rejoin with an exception, or it could argue that the treaties are outdated and that protecting people's health is a good reason to try something new. In real life, Canada went ahead and legalized in 2018 and mostly faced criticism rather than serious penalties, so the consequences turned out to be more about words and image than anything harsher.

Okay so the light independent reactions (aka the Calvin cycle or dark reactions) don't actually need light directly. They run on energy that's already stored in ATP and NADPH, which the light dependent reactions made earlier. Basically, CO2 gets locked into organic molecules during this stage. It all happens in the stroma of the chloroplast and it's a long chain of enzyme-driven steps.

Here's the rough version. CO2 gets attached to a molecule called RuBP, and the enzyme doing that job is RuBisCO (ribulose bisphosphate carboxylase/oxygenase, which is a mouthful). That makes 3-phosphoglycerate, or 3-PGA. From there, a few reactions involving glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate dehydrogenase and triose phosphate isomerase turn it into G3P. Some G3P goes back to regenerate RuBP so the cycle keeps going, and the rest gets used to build stuff like glucose, amino acids, and lipids.

So yeah, this is what lets plants grow and build their tissues. It's also a big deal for the carbon cycle, since it's how plants pull CO2 out of the air and lock it up in organic compounds.

Okay so there are a few ways to get into US stocks from India. You can open a brokerage account with a firm that takes foreign investors and trades US stocks. Charles Schwab and Interactive Brokers are two people usually mention. Another route is buying a mutual fund or ETF that tracks a basket of US stocks. Those trade on Indian exchanges, so you can grab them through your regular broker or app. You could also go the ADR route through your Indian brokerage account. ADRs are certificates representing shares of a foreign company, and they trade on US exchanges. Lastly, there are cross-border platforms like DealTimer or TradeZero that let you open an account and trade US stocks from India. Just know that international stocks come with extra risks, like currency swings and political stuff. Think about your goals and how much risk you can actually stomach before you jump in.

Words get their "bad" feeling mostly from how people use them, not from the things they point to. A word becomes taboo when lots of people agree it's rude, and that agreement usually grows from history, from who used the word and how, and from what feels polite in the moment.

Think of it like a secret club. Some words are invited to the grown-up party and some are kept out because the grown-ups decided they sounded too rough or too private. "Butt" got invited because it was used in lots of everyday, silly, friendly ways, like "butterfly" or "stubborn as a mule" or just "sit on your butt," and it sounded more like a cartoon than a body. "Ass" got kept out partly because it was used more often as an insult, like calling someone a jerk, and partly because it sounds a bit harsher and more direct when you say it.

Here's the funny part: "ass" actually means the same animal as "donkey," and it was once a totally normal word in old books and churches. Over time, people started using it more rudely, and the polite grown-ups decided to keep it out of schools and offices. Nobody voted on it, it just slowly happened, like a game of telephone where the message changed.

So the body part isn't the problem. The problem is the feeling people attach to the word, and that feeling changes from place to place and from time to time.

Corpus Christi is a Roman Catholic feast day celebrated in honor of the Eucharist, the sacrament in which Catholics believe the bread and wine become the body and blood of Christ. The name is Latin for "Body of Christ." The feast falls on the Thursday after Trinity Sunday, which is the Sunday following Pentecost, so it usually lands in late May or June. Some countries and dioceses have moved the observance to the following Sunday for convenience.

The feast was established in the 13th century, largely after a Belgian nun named Juliana of Liège reported visions urging the Church to honor the Eucharist with a dedicated festival. Pope Urban IV extended it to the whole Church in 1264, and it became more widespread after the 14th century.

Traditions vary by region, but many communities hold processions in which the consecrated host is carried through the streets in a monstrance, often accompanied by hymns, prayers, and decorated altars or streets. In parts of Latin America, Spain, Italy, and the Philippines, the day is marked with elaborate parades, flower carpets, and public festivities. In some countries, such as Austria, Germany, and Poland, it is an official public holiday.

Buying from shops in your own town is good for a few reasons. When you spend money at a local store, that money tends to stay nearby. The shop owner uses it to pay their workers, who then spend it at other local businesses, like the bakery or the hardware store. It's a bit like passing a ball around a playground: the more it gets passed among friends, the more fun everyone has.

Local shops also help make your town a nice place to live. They keep the streets busy, they often sponsor the soccer team or the school fair, and they give people jobs close to home. If every store closed and everything came from far away, your town would be quieter and a little less special.

Buying locally can also mean fresher food and more interesting things. A farmer selling tomatoes at the market may have picked them that morning, and a local toymaker might make something you can't find in a big store. You can also ask the person who made or sold it questions, and they usually know their stuff and care about getting it right for you.

Finally, when things are made or grown nearby, they often travel a shorter distance to reach you. That means fewer trucks and planes burning fuel, which is kinder to the air we all breathe.

So buying locally helps your neighbors, keeps your town lively, gives you fresh and special things, and takes care of the planet a little bit too.

Honestly, you should tell your doctor about any new or weird symptoms, especially if you're on medication. That lump in your armpit and the pins and needles in your arm might be side effects from the methotrexate, but they really need to be checked out so someone can figure out what's going on and what to do about it. Until then, keep taking your meds the way your doctor told you to. If you're not sure whether you should keep going, call them and ask. They know your situation and can tell you what makes sense for you.

Premature ejaculation (PE) is a widespread sexual concern that can stem from many sources. Psychological factors such as stress, anxiety, and depression can play a role, as can physical causes like hormonal imbalances, nerve damage, and some medications. If you are dealing with PE, several strategies may help you gain better control over ejaculation. One approach is to practice techniques that delay climax, such as the "squeeze" method and the "stop-start" method. Both involve stimulating the penis until you sense that ejaculation is near, pausing the stimulation for a few seconds, and then resuming once the urge has faded. Another option is to use a condom, since it can reduce sensitivity and may help you last longer. You might also consider medication, either over the counter or by prescription. Antidepressants, phosphodiesterase inhibitors, and topical anesthetics are among the options that have been used for PE, but it is important to consult a healthcare provider before starting any medication. Relaxation practices can also help, because stress and anxiety may contribute to the problem. Deep breathing, meditation, or yoga may ease your symptoms over time. Finally, if psychological factors such as stress, anxiety, or depression are behind your PE, therapy can be an effective way to address the root cause. Speaking with a healthcare provider is an important step whenever you experience PE, as they can help identify what is causing it and suggest the most suitable treatment.

The universal law of gravitation is a scientific principle that explains the gravitational attraction between any two objects. According to the law, the force pulling two objects together grows in direct proportion to the product of their masses, and it shrinks in proportion to the square of the distance separating them. In equation form, this is expressed as: F = G * ((m1 * m2) / r^2). In this equation, F stands for the gravitational force between the two objects. G is the gravitational constant, a value found through experiment that is roughly 6.674 x 10^-11 N * (m^2 / kg^2). The terms m1 and m2 represent the masses of the two objects, and r is the distance between them. Sir Isaac Newton first set out the universal law of gravitation in 1687, and it is still a core principle in the study of gravity and celestial mechanics today.

Honestly, it's a good idea to decide ahead of time how much you're willing to lose on any one trade, and keep that to a small slice of your total trading capital. That's basically what people mean by a risk management strategy.

How big a slice is up to you. It depends on how much risk you can stomach and how risky the trade itself is. If you're more of a cautious trader, you'd probably risk less per trade, while someone more aggressive might be fine going bigger. Neither is wrong, they just fit different people.

The one rule I'd stick to no matter what is never risking money you can't afford to lose. Trading is risky by nature, so you want to be careful about how much of your pile is on the line at any given time.

Honestly, if the fluid in your dad's lungs is causing symptoms or making it hard for him to breathe, draining it is usually something doctors consider. But it really depends on the person. Things like what's causing the fluid, how bad his symptoms are, and his overall health and history all matter a lot. Doctors weigh the benefits against the risks for each patient, so there's no one-size-fits-all answer.

The best move is to sit down with his healthcare provider and ask what they recommend for him specifically. Ask about the risks and complications of the procedure too, not just the upside. They can walk you through what to expect and help you figure out the right call for your family.

A discipline of study is a recognized branch of knowledge, a field with its own subject matter, methods, vocabulary, and standards for deciding what counts as good evidence or sound reasoning. Physics, history, economics, philosophy, and literature are all disciplines. Each one carves out a particular set of questions and develops accepted ways of investigating them. A historian, for example, works with archives and primary sources and weighs them critically, while a chemist designs controlled experiments and measures how substances interact.

What makes something a discipline rather than just a topic is that it has an organized community and tradition behind it. There are scholars who train others, journals and conferences where work is shared and checked by peers, and a body of accumulated theory that newcomers must learn. Universities reflect this by organizing themselves into departments and degree programs, each corresponding to a discipline or a cluster of closely related ones.

The word also carries a sense of training and rigor. To study within a discipline is to learn not only facts but a way of thinking: how to ask questions, how to argue, and how to recognize error within that field's norms.

Disciplines are usually grouped into broad families, such as the natural sciences, the social sciences, the humanities, the formal sciences like mathematics and logic, and the applied or professional fields like engineering, law, and medicine. The boundaries are not fixed, though. Many modern areas of work are interdisciplinary, blending approaches from several fields, as in biochemistry, cognitive science, or environmental studies. Over time, such blends can themselves harden into new disciplines with their own traditions and institutions.

Your results look normal. Your FSH of 5.20 mIU/mL and LH of 5.80 mIU/mL fall within the usual early-cycle range, and your prolactin of 6.98 ng/mL is well below the usual upper limit of about 25 ng/mL. Reference ranges vary slightly between labs, so your lab's printed range is the one to check, but nothing here suggests a hormone problem.

The rule that LH should be lower than FSH is a common simplification. The LH-to-FSH ratio is sometimes used as a clue for conditions like polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), where LH is often noticeably higher than FSH, sometimes two or three times higher. A ratio close to 1, as yours is, is not a concern on its own. PCOS is diagnosed from a combination of irregular cycles, signs of high androgens, and ultrasound findings, not from this ratio alone. Your doctor is right that these two numbers are not strictly dependent on each other.

Your regular periods are also encouraging, since they suggest you are ovulating. Seven months of trying is not long. Many healthy couples take up to a year to conceive, and fertility evaluations are usually recommended after 12 months of trying if you are under 35, or after 6 months if you are 35 or older.

If you want to move forward, the next steps your doctor might consider include:

- Confirming ovulation with a progesterone test about seven days before your expected period, or with ovulation predictor kits.
- Checking your ovarian reserve with an AMH test and an ultrasound of your ovaries.
- Having your partner's semen analysis, since male factors contribute to about half of fertility problems.
- Checking that your fallopian tubes are open, usually with a hysterosalpingogram (an X-ray dye test), if the earlier tests are normal and you have not conceived.

In the meantime, having intercourse every two to three days around ovulation, and especially in the days just before it, gives the best chance each cycle. Keep discussing these results and next steps with your doctor, who can interpret them in the context of your full history.

To find the excess cash on a balance sheet, subtract the amount of cash needed to keep the company running from its total cash balance. The result is the excess cash, which is also known as "free cash."

Calculating excess cash requires looking at several considerations, such as the company's financial standing, its operating costs, and its prospects for growth. Some specific items worth weighing include the following. Current liabilities are debts and obligations due in the short term, such as accounts payable and taxes owed. Non-current liabilities are obligations due over the long term, such as long-term debt and pension commitments. Operating expenses are the day-to-day costs of running the business, such as salaries, rent, and utilities. Capital expenditures are outlays for long-term growth, such as buying new equipment or constructing new facilities.

After weighing these factors, subtract the cash needed to meet these obligations from the company's total cash balance to arrive at the excess cash. For instance, if a company holds $100,000 in cash and has $50,000 in current liabilities and operating expenses, its excess cash would be $50,000. Keep in mind that excess cash is only one part of assessing a company's enterprise value. Other factors, such as the asset base, revenue, and profitability, deserve consideration as well.

The United Nations (UN) is a global organization formed after the Second World War with the aim of fostering cooperation among nations and working to avert armed conflict between them. Its many bodies and agencies tackle a broad range of concerns, such as peace and security, the protection of human rights, and economic and social development. A central part of its approach to preventing conflict is encouraging diplomacy and open dialogue, bringing nations to the table so they can discuss their disputes and reach peaceful settlements. The organization also runs peacekeeping missions, deploying troops to regions at risk of fighting or already caught in violence. These missions observe the situation on the ground and work to stop further bloodshed. Even with these efforts, conflicts and wars continue to break out across the world. The UN is not always able to stop them, particularly when one or more countries refuse to cooperate or ignore its recommendations. Nevertheless, it still provides aid in such circumstances, delivering essentials like food, water, and medical supplies to those harmed by fighting, and pushing for a peaceful end to the hostilities.

SD card "class" refers to the minimum sustained write speed the card guarantees, which matters most for recording video, shooting bursts of photos, or running applications that write data continuously. SDHC cards (capacities from 4 GB up to 32 GB) use the Speed Class ratings, where the number inside the "C" symbol is the minimum sustained write speed in megabytes per second. Class 2 guarantees at least 2 MB/s, Class 4 at least 4 MB/s, Class 6 at least 6 MB/s, and Class 10 at least 10 MB/s. There is also a UHS Speed Class, shown as a U inside a circle with a 1 or 3 (guaranteeing 10 MB/s or 30 MB/s), and a Video Speed Class, marked V6, V10, V30, and so on, which is intended for higher-bitrate video. Choosing a higher class gives smoother performance in demanding tasks, though for ordinary photo storage or light use, Class 4 or Class 10 is usually sufficient.

Nadoxin gel is a topical product prescribed for acne. As with any drug, it may cause adverse effects, though the majority of users never notice any. Typical reactions include dry skin, itchiness, and skin irritation. Such effects tend to be minor and usually fade without intervention within a few days of starting treatment. Another possibility is that you have an allergic response to a component of the formula. If your reactions are severe, or if your skin does not get better after several days of use, stop applying the gel and consult your healthcare provider. The bumps you have noticed could be linked to the acne treatment, but they might also stem from an unrelated cause. If they are bothering you or worrying you, arrange a visit with a healthcare provider who can assess them and advise on next steps.

I can't safely recommend a specific medicine or dose for your father without a doctor examining him, because the right treatment depends on the cause of his vertigo, and at 83 with a past stroke, several common vertigo medicines carry real risks. I can explain what doctors usually consider so you can have a more informed conversation with his neurologist or physician.

The first priority is ruling out a new stroke or TIA. His 1997 infarct was in the posterior circulation, the same blood supply that serves the brain's balance centres. New or worsening vertigo in someone with that history should be evaluated promptly, not just treated with symptom relief. Take him to emergency care immediately if the vertigo comes with double vision, slurred speech, facial droop, weakness or numbness on one side, trouble swallowing, inability to walk or stand unaided, sudden severe headache, or new loss of vision. A CT scan often misses small fresh strokes in the back of the brain. An MRI with diffusion-weighted imaging, and sometimes an MR angiogram or a Doppler of the neck and vertebral arteries, gives much better information. The CT findings you describe, small old lacunar infarcts, white matter changes, and atrophy, are common at his age and point to long-standing small vessel disease. They don't by themselves explain the vertigo, though they can contribute to imbalance.

Many vertigo episodes in elderly people have other, very treatable causes. The most common is benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, a brief spinning sensation triggered by turning in bed, lying down, or looking up. It is treated not with tablets but with a simple head-repositioning manoeuvre (the Epley manoeuvre) done by a doctor or physiotherapist, often with quick relief. Other frequent culprits are a drop in blood pressure on standing, side effects of blood pressure or other medicines, dehydration, low blood sugar, anaemia, heart rhythm problems such as atrial fibrillation, and thyroid or vitamin B12 problems. A good evaluation would include lying and standing blood pressure, an ECG, blood sugar, blood count, and a review of all his current medications.

Regarding the medicines themselves, doctors commonly prescribe betahistine, which is generally well tolerated, or short-term vestibular suppressants such as prochlorperazine, meclizine, or cinnarizine. In older adults the suppressants should usually be limited to a few days. They can cause drowsiness, confusion, and falls, and cinnarizine in particular can cause Parkinson-like stiffness and tremor in the elderly. Long-term use also slows the brain's natural recovery of balance. For lasting improvement, vestibular rehabilitation exercises with a physiotherapist are often more effective than pills.

Given his scan, the most important medical treatment is probably preventing further strokes. That typically means an antiplatelet such as aspirin or clopidogrel, a statin, and good control of blood pressure, sugar, and cholesterol, as decided by his doctor. If he is already on these, make sure he takes them consistently. At home, have him get up slowly from lying or sitting, keep him well hydrated, keep floors clear and well lit, and consider a walking aid if he is unsteady, since falls are a major danger at his age.

Please take the CT report and a short diary of his vertigo episodes to a neurologist. Note how long each lasts, what triggers it, and any other symptoms. That information will help them choose the safest and most effective treatment for him.

Singapore uses the Singapore dollar (SGD), usually written as S$, and it's split into 100 cents. It's the legal tender there, and it's also accepted in Brunei, where it works as a secondary currency. The Monetary Authority of Singapore is the central bank, so it's the one that issues and manages the money. The exchange rate floats with the market, but it's pretty stable, which is why people like using it for trade and investment.

This is a really understandable worry, and the honest answer is that you shouldn't have to make this decision on your own. Please contact your midwife, obstetrician, or GP today, or a pharmacist, and tell them exactly what you've told me: that you were advised to stop, that you've now missed two nights, and that you're struggling to sleep. Given how close you are to your due date, it's worth getting a clear answer quickly rather than waiting for your next appointment.

It may help to understand why you've heard two different things, because both have some basis. The reason you were probably told to stop is that when a baby is exposed to amitriptyline right up until birth, they can sometimes show temporary symptoms in the first few days, such as jitteriness, irritability, feeding difficulties, sleepiness, or mild breathing problems. These are usually mild and short-lived, and hospitals are familiar with monitoring for them. The reason you've also read that it's not safe to stop is that suddenly stopping after taking it for four years can cause discontinuation effects in you, including poor sleep, irritability, nausea, flu-like feelings, and a return of anxiety. Stopping abruptly right before birth also raises the risk of anxiety or depression in the postnatal period, which matters a great deal for both you and your baby. Because of this, many current guidelines don't recommend routinely stopping antidepressants in late pregnancy. Instead, they generally recommend continuing if the medication is working well, letting the delivery team know so they can keep an eye on the baby after birth. If a change is made, it's usually done gradually rather than all at once.

So the trouble sleeping you're having may well be discontinuation symptoms, anxiety, late pregnancy itself, or a mix. A professional who knows your history can weigh these up and tell you whether to restart at your usual dose, at a lower dose, or to stay off it with a plan for support. It's also worth knowing that amitriptyline is generally considered compatible with breastfeeding, if that's something you're planning, so this decision doesn't have to affect that.

Whatever is decided, make sure the team who will be with you during labour and after the birth knows you've been taking amitriptyline, so they can watch your baby appropriately and also check in on your own mental health afterwards. If at any point your anxiety becomes severe, you feel unable to cope, or you have any thoughts of harming yourself, please contact your maternity unit or emergency services straight away. You've done really well managing your anxiety through the whole pregnancy, and asking this question is a sensible thing to do.

Biggest Jewish populations are in Israel and the US, no contest. Israel has the most, with over 6 million Jews, which works out to roughly 75% of the country. The US is second with around 7.5 million, though that's only about 2% of the total population since it's such a big country. You'll also find sizable communities in France, Canada, the UK, and Russia. Add it all up and there are roughly 14 million Jews around the world.

Bile duct strictures after gallbladder surgery usually come from injury or scarring during the operation. The duct can be damaged by the surgical instruments, by the heat or clips used to remove the gallbladder, or by stitches placed too tightly. Healing at the injury site then produces scar tissue, which contracts over time and narrows the duct. Sometimes a small leak of bile after surgery also contributes, because the body responds to the irritation with more fibrosis. Each time the ERCP stretches the narrowed area, the scar can re-form, especially if the stretch was short-lived. This is why a stricture can keep coming back even after repeated dilations.

There is no single minimum diameter that defines a stricture. Doctors look at the whole picture: how narrow the duct appears on imaging, whether bile is still draining well, your blood tests (especially bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, and liver enzymes), and whether you have symptoms like jaundice, itching, fever, or pain. A duct that is quite narrow but still draining without infection may be managed differently from one that is blocking flow.

Because the stricture has returned after many dilations, it may be time to ask whether ERCP alone is still the right tool. Some people do better with longer-term plastic or metal stents placed for several months, which keep the duct open while scar tissue remains soft. Others are better served by surgical repair, most often a hepaticojejunostomy, in which the bile duct is connected directly to a loop of small intestine, bypassing the narrowed section. Surgery for refractory strictures has good long-term results in experienced hands, and many people find it ends the cycle of repeat procedures.

I'd suggest asking your gastroenterologist for a referral to a hepatobiliary or biliary surgeon, ideally at a tertiary or specialist center that treats post-surgical bile duct injuries. A second opinion from a team that handles these cases regularly can help you compare stenting, repeat endoscopy, and surgical reconstruction. Bring a copy of your operative report, your imaging, and a list of the complications you had with previous procedures so the new team understands your history.

If you develop fever, chills, worsening yellowing of the skin or eyes, severe abdominal pain, or dark urine with pale stools, seek care promptly, since these can signal infection or blockage.

Surgery might help improve movement in a leg affected by polio, but whether it will, and which procedure would be suitable, depends on the person's particular condition and how much of the leg is paralyzed. A qualified medical professional, such as a physical therapist or an orthopedic surgeon, should be consulted to decide on the best course of treatment. After evaluating your fiancee's condition, they can suggest the most fitting options, which may or may not involve an operation. Generally, physical therapy and rehabilitation exercises can help people with polio move better and function more effectively. Such approaches are often paired with other measures, including medications, braces, or assistive devices, to further support mobility and function. It also matters that your fiancee lives healthily, eating a balanced diet and staying regularly active, since this supports recovery and benefits overall health and well-being.

When a company's shares are removed from a stock exchange, they can no longer be bought or sold there. Reasons for this range from the company falling short of the exchange's listing standards to filing for bankruptcy. If the shares later reappear on the exchange under a different ticker, that generally signals the company has resolved the problems behind the removal and gained approval to trade there again. Anyone who held shares when the delisting occurred may have seen their value change. To learn what became of your holdings and which courses of action are available, reach out to the company or your brokerage.

Duavent is a combination of ipratropium and salbutamol, two medicines that open up narrowed airways. It is a prescription drug, and it helps when the airways are tight or constricted, as in asthma, wheezing from a viral infection, or bronchospasm. It does not treat the infection, and it does not loosen phlegm. So whether it is appropriate for your daughter depends on whether her airways are actually narrowed, which a doctor can check by listening to her chest for wheezing. She doesn't need an asthma diagnosis to benefit from it, since some children wheeze during colds or bronchitis, but it also shouldn't be given just because a cough is bothersome. It can cause side effects such as a fast heartbeat, shakiness, restlessness, trouble sleeping, and dry mouth, and the right dose depends on her age and weight. I'd advise against using it at home unless a doctor has examined her and told you to, or has prescribed it for her before with a specific dose. If you have a nebulizer, plain saline (sodium chloride 0.9%) is generally safe and can help moisten and loosen mucus while you wait to see the doctor.

A temperature of 37.3°C is normal or at most very slightly warm. It is not considered a fever, which usually starts around 37.5 to 38°C depending on how it's measured. Body temperature also naturally rises a little in the afternoon or after activity, so that reading by itself is not worrying.

A week of cough with phlegm that wakes her at night is very common after a cold, and many of these coughs settle within two to three weeks. Still, it's reasonable to have her checked by a pediatrician, especially since the cough sounds tight, which can sometimes mean wheezing or a chest infection. In the meantime, give her plenty of fluids and raise her head slightly when she sleeps. Clean, humid air can help too. If she is older than one year, a teaspoon of honey before bed has been shown to ease nighttime cough. Never give honey to babies under one.

Seek care promptly, or go to the emergency room, if she breathes fast or with effort, if the skin between her ribs or below her neck pulls in with each breath, if you hear wheezing or a whistling sound, if her lips look bluish, if she develops a fever of 38.5°C or higher or a fever lasting more than two to three days, or if she becomes unusually sleepy, refuses to drink, or seems very unwell. You should also see a doctor if the cough lasts beyond about three weeks or keeps getting worse instead of better.

If you can share her age, I can give you more specific guidance.

An associate of arts degree is an undergraduate credential usually obtained at a community college or another two-year school. It is a general qualification intended to give students a wide grounding in the liberal arts and sciences, covering areas like English, mathematics, history, and the social sciences. Typically comprising 60 credits and requiring about two years of full-time study, it is generally regarded as equivalent to the first half of a four-year bachelor's program. Some learners earn this degree as a stepping stone before moving on to a four-year university to finish their bachelor's, while others treat it as a complete program in its own right.

"Girls Just Want to Have Fun" was released in 1979 as a single by American singer Robert Hazard, and it became a much bigger hit when Cyndi Lauper recorded her version for her 1983 debut album, *She's So Unusual*.

Several kinds of events can trigger significant swings in the foreign exchange (forex) market. Among them are decisions by central banks, such as the Federal Reserve in the United States or the European Central Bank, whose monetary policy choices can shift currency values; for instance, altering interest rates can change how much demand there is for a given currency. Political developments also matter, since instability or major policy shifts, including elections or Brexit, can meaningfully affect exchange rates. Economic data releases, such as gross domestic product (GDP) or employment numbers, reveal how healthy a country's economy is, and so they can influence its currency's worth. Natural disasters like hurricanes or earthquakes can likewise disrupt an economy and move its currency. Finally, broader global market trends, such as a surge in oil prices or a worldwide recession, can ripple through forex markets. Because the market is highly volatile and responds to a wide variety of factors, traders need to watch conditions closely and stay ready for sudden changes.

Perpetual motion refers to a device that would keep moving or doing work forever without receiving any energy from outside. Such a thing cannot exist, because it conflicts with both the first and second laws of thermodynamics. The first law concerns energy, and it states that energy can neither be created nor destroyed, only converted from one form into another. That raises a question: if an object keeps moving or working with no energy supplied to it, what is the source of that energy? The second law concerns heat. It holds that heat naturally travels from warmer objects to cooler ones, and that it cannot move from a cooler object to a warmer one unless some work is done. Consider a perpetual motion machine that is meant to run endlessly. Where would its heat go? It would accumulate until the machine could no longer function. For these reasons, perpetual motion cannot be achieved, since it would break fundamental laws of physics!

Imagine you live in a little town, and there's a nice lady down the street who bakes bread. When you buy bread from her, the money you give her stays in your town. She might use it to buy apples from the farmer nearby, and the farmer might use it to buy shoes from the shoe shop. Your money keeps going around and around your town like a ball being passed between friends, and that helps everyone there have jobs and take care of their families.

Now think about how the food gets to you. If you buy strawberries grown far, far away, they have to ride in big trucks, boats, or airplanes for a very long time. Those trucks and planes burn fuel and make the air dirtier. But if the strawberries grow on a farm close to your house, they only take a short little trip to get to you. That's kinder to the Earth.

Food from nearby can also taste better. When fruits and veggies have to travel far, they're often picked before they're ripe so they don't go bad on the long trip. Food from close by can be picked when it's ready, so it's often fresher, juicier, and yummier.

Buying locally also helps you get to know people. You can meet the farmer who grew your carrots or the person who made your toy, and you can ask them questions about how they made it. It makes your town feel friendlier, like a big neighborhood where people help each other.

Finally, local shops make your town special. If everyone only bought things from giant stores far away, all the little shops might close, and every town would look the same. When you buy from them, you help keep your town unique and fun.

To be fair, buying locally can sometimes cost a bit more, and some things just can't be made nearby, like bananas if you live somewhere cold. So it's not about buying everything locally, but choosing local when you can is a nice way to help your neighbors, your town, and the planet.

A subsidy refers to financial help or backing that a government or another body gives to a company or a person. Its purpose is usually to boost a certain kind of economic activity or to assist a specific group, for example farmers or students. The support may come in several forms, including direct payments, reduced taxes, or loans with low interest rates. Subsidies frequently serve to motivate companies to manufacture particular goods, or to make certain products and services more affordable for individuals. They may also shield local industries from competition abroad, or contribute to solving social or environmental problems.

Renting an apartment comes with a few money things you should keep an eye on. The big one, obviously, is rent: that's what you pay the landlord or property manager every month to live there. Most places will also ask for a security deposit up front, a one-time payment they hold in case you trash the place or skip rent. If you've got a pet, expect a pet deposit on top of that, usually one-time too, to cover any damage the critter causes. Some landlords or management companies charge an application fee just to process your paperwork, so don't be surprised if you see one. Renters insurance isn't always required, but it's smart to have it. It covers your stuff if it gets stolen or damaged, and it's usually pretty cheap. Then there are the random extras: move-in fees, late payment penalties, and a hefty charge if you bail on your lease early. Read your rental agreement closely before signing and make sure you actually understand every cost you're on the hook for.

Psych was an American comedy-drama that ran on the USA Network from 2006 to 2014. It lasted eight seasons and 120 episodes, and the finale wrapped up on March 26, 2014. If you meant a different show with a similar name, let me know which one and I can dig into that instead.

Sorry you're having a hard time putting weight on. It's frustrating when your body burns through everything or just loses weight easily. There are a few things that might help, though, and you can do them in a healthy way.

First, eat more often. Rather than three big meals, try smaller meals and snacks spread through the day. That bumps up your calories and keeps a steady supply of energy coming in.

Second, go for foods that pack a lot of calories and nutrients, like nuts, seeds, nut butters, avocados, olives, and cheese. You get the extra calories without filling up on junk.

Protein matters too, since your body uses it to build and repair tissue. Meat, poultry, fish, eggs, dairy, beans, and other legumes are all good sources.

You can also drink your calories. Smoothies made with milk, yogurt, and fruit work well, and so do milkshakes with ice cream and milk.

If none of that does it, a weight gain supplement like protein powder or a mass gainer could help you get more calories and protein. Talk to a doctor or other healthcare professional before you start any new supplement, though.

Keep in mind that gaining weight the healthy way takes time and consistency. It's pretty normal for it to take several months or longer before you see a real change. And weight is only one piece of your health. Eating a balanced diet and staying active matters more than hitting a particular number on the scale.

I'm doing well, thanks, and I'm sorry you've had such a rough recovery. Glad the dry socket pain has settled.

A small lump at a surgical site three weeks out is not unusual, but significant pain in it is not something I'd just wait out. Several things can cause it. The most common is a retained or partly buried suture. Stitches are usually dissolvable, but they can take several weeks to break down, and sometimes the knot or a fragment lingers and irritates the gum or cheek tissue. Another possibility is granulation tissue, a firm, tender, reddish bump that forms as the wound heals, especially if there is a bit of debris or suture material underneath. Swelling from the healing flap itself can also feel like a firm knot. Less commonly, a small localized infection or abscess can form, particularly after a dry socket, and a small bone fragment working its way to the surface (a sequestrum) can create a sore lump as well. A true cyst this soon is unlikely, though a blocked small gland or a fluid pocket can feel similar.

Because it is painful rather than just a bit tender, I'd have it looked at by your oral surgeon or dentist in the next few days. It is a quick exam, and often the fix is simple, such as removing the leftover suture or cleaning out the area. They may take an X-ray if they suspect something deeper.

See someone promptly, the same day if possible, if you develop fever, increasing swelling of the cheek or face, a bad taste or pus draining from the area, redness spreading, trouble opening your mouth or swallowing, or pain that is getting worse instead of better.

In the meantime, rinse gently with warm salt water a few times a day, especially after eating, keep the area clean with careful brushing nearby, avoid poking or pressing on the lump, and use over-the-counter pain relief like ibuprofen or acetaminophen if you can take them safely. Please don't try to cut or pull out any stitch yourself.

It is probably something minor and easily treated, but a painful knot at three weeks deserves a quick check rather than waiting.

Google Voice Search is a Google feature that lets people search the web, find information stored on their device, and carry out a range of other tasks using spoken commands. By speaking into the microphone on their device, users can pose a question or give an instruction, and the device replies either in writing or aloud. If you say "Ok Google, what's the weather today?", for instance, Google Voice Search will show or read out the current forecast for your area. The feature works on many kinds of hardware, such as smartphones, tablets, and computers, provided they are connected to the internet and have the Google app or the Google Chrome browser. It can also be used with smart home products like Google Home and Nest Hub, which are built specifically for voice control. Before using Google Voice Search, you must have a Google account and turn the feature on in your device's settings.

This is a common situation, and the good news for your boyfriend is that in most places a co-owner generally can't be forced to stay in shared ownership forever. The details depend heavily on where the property is located and how the title is held, so take what follows as general background rather than legal advice.

The first thing to figure out is how they own the house. If they hold it as tenants in common or joint tenants, each typically owns a share and has certain rights to exit. It's also worth checking whether there's any written agreement between them, such as a co-ownership agreement or terms in a will or trust if they inherited the house, because that document might spell out what happens when one wants to sell, including a right of first refusal or a required buyout process.

The most practical route is usually a buyout. If his sister wants to keep the house, she could buy his share at fair market value, which typically means getting an independent appraisal and then working out his portion of the equity after accounting for any mortgage. She may need to refinance to do this, and if there's a joint mortgage, he'd want to make sure he's actually released from it rather than just signing over his ownership. Alternatively, she might agree to sell if she has time to plan, or they could agree to rent it out and split the income. Mediation can be really helpful here, especially since this is family and emotions about a shared home, possibly a parent's home, can run high.

If they truly can't agree, most jurisdictions in the US, UK, Canada, Australia and elsewhere allow a co-owner to go to court. In the US this is usually called a partition action; in England and Wales it's typically an application under the Trusts of Land and Appointment of Trustees Act, often called a TOLATA claim. A court can order the property sold and the proceeds divided, and sometimes gives the other owner a chance to buy out the share first. Courts will also sort out who paid for what, such as the mortgage, taxes, and improvements, which can shift how the money gets split. The downside is that litigation can be expensive, slow, and hard on family relationships, and a forced sale sometimes brings a lower price, so it's usually best treated as a last resort or as leverage to encourage a negotiated deal.

Practically, your boyfriend should gather the deed, any mortgage documents, records of what each of them has paid toward the house, and any agreements, then talk to a local real estate or property lawyer. Many offer an initial consultation, and a lawyer's letter laying out his options sometimes nudges a reluctant co-owner toward a buyout or sale without needing to go to court. It may also help to understand why his sister wants to keep it, since knowing whether it's emotional, financial, or about having somewhere to live can open up compromises that work for both of them.

Explainable AI (often abbreviated XAI) refers to methods and techniques that make the behavior and decisions of artificial intelligence systems understandable to humans. Many modern AI systems, especially deep neural networks, operate as "black boxes": they can produce accurate predictions or recommendations, but their internal reasoning is so complex that even their designers may struggle to say why a particular output was produced. Explainable AI aims to address this gap by providing insight into how and why a system reached its conclusions.

The motivation for XAI comes from several practical needs. In high-stakes areas such as medicine, lending, criminal justice, and autonomous driving, people affected by a decision often have a right to understand it, and professionals need to verify that the system is working correctly. Explanations also help developers debug models, detect bias or reliance on irrelevant features, and comply with regulations such as the European Union's provisions on automated decision-making. Trust is another factor: users are more likely to rely on a system whose reasoning they can inspect and question.

Approaches to explainability generally fall into two categories. Some models are inherently interpretable, such as simple decision trees or linear regression, where the logic can be read directly from the model's structure. Others are complex models to which post-hoc explanation techniques are applied after training. Popular post-hoc methods include feature importance scores, which indicate how much each input contributed to a prediction; saliency maps, which highlight the regions of an image that influenced a classification; and surrogate models, which approximate a complicated system with a simpler one that is easier to understand locally.

There is also an ongoing tension between accuracy and interpretability, since the most powerful models are often the least transparent. Researchers debate how faithful post-hoc explanations are to what a model actually does, and what kind of explanation is useful to a given audience, whether a data scientist, a regulator, or an everyday user. Explainable AI is therefore both a technical field and a question of how humans and machines should communicate.

Camera resectioning, also called camera calibration or pose estimation in some contexts, is the process of determining the parameters of a camera that produced a given image. It works in the reverse direction of the usual imaging process: rather than projecting a three-dimensional scene onto a two-dimensional image plane, it starts from known points in the 3D world and their observed locations in the image, and works backward to recover how the camera was positioned and how its lenses and sensor transformed the scene.

The parameters fall into two groups. The intrinsic parameters describe the camera itself, including the focal length, the coordinates of the principal point (where the optical axis meets the image plane), the pixel scaling along each axis, and any skew between the sensor's axes. These are typically collected into a 3 by 3 calibration matrix. The extrinsic parameters describe the camera's position and orientation in the world, namely a rotation and a translation that map world coordinates into the camera's own coordinate frame. Together, the intrinsic and extrinsic parameters form a single 3 by 4 projection matrix that maps any 3D world point to its 2D pixel location.

To perform resectioning, one needs a set of correspondences, meaning known 3D points in the scene paired with their measured 2D image coordinates. Each correspondence yields linear equations involving the entries of the projection matrix, and with enough correspondences (at least six points in the general case) the matrix can be solved, commonly through a direct linear transformation followed by refinement that minimizes reprojection error. Practical systems often use a calibration target with a known pattern, such as a checkerboard, to supply these points easily.

Camera resectioning is foundational in computer vision and photogrammetry. It is used for tasks such as 3D reconstruction, augmented reality, robotic navigation, measuring objects from photographs, correcting lens distortion, and aligning virtual objects with real camera footage.

Continuous improvement is basically the habit of always looking for ways to make things work better in a business or organization. You spot something that could be smoother or more efficient, change it, and then check whether the change actually helped. Lots of companies build this into bigger plans like total quality management or lean manufacturing, and it can touch everything from a single task on the factory floor to how the whole company runs. The point is to keep boosting productivity and efficiency so customers end up with better products and service.

Hives (welts) on the cheeks and body after an outing like this are most often an allergic reaction, though a viral illness or an insect bite can cause similar marks. Something he touched, ate, or breathed at the science center could be the trigger, such as a food, a plant, an animal, a cleaning product, or latex. Hives usually come and go within a day or so, and the rosy color can linger for a while after the welts fade, so it's reassuring that the Benadryl calmed things down.

Call 911 or go to the nearest emergency room right away if he has any trouble breathing, wheezing, noisy or hard breathing, swelling of the lips, tongue, or throat, drooling or difficulty swallowing, a hoarse voice, repeated vomiting, unusual sleepiness or difficulty waking, pale or bluish skin, or dizziness or fainting. These can signal a serious allergic reaction, and they need immediate care even if the Benadryl seemed to help.

Because the swelling on one cheek was quite pronounced and the rash is still present, I'd also call his pediatrician today rather than waiting. Tell them what happened, the timing, and the medicine you gave. They can advise whether he needs to be seen and can confirm the Benadryl dose for his age and weight. Also check the box for the dosing instructions, and don't give more than the label allows in 24 hours. Benadryl can make children very drowsy, so watch him closely, especially if he's napping.

Get seen promptly if the swelling on one side of his face becomes warm, hard, painful, or spreads, or if he develops a fever. That pattern can sometimes point to a skin infection rather than an allergy.

In the meantime, write down everything he ate, drank, and touched at the science center, and note whether anyone else in your group had a similar reaction. That information will help his doctor figure out the cause and whether he should avoid it in the future.

A capital market is a financial market where long-term funds are raised and traded. It brings together those who have money to invest, such as individuals, companies, and institutions, with those who need funds for long-term purposes, such as businesses expanding operations, governments financing infrastructure, or entrepreneurs starting new ventures. Unlike the money market, which deals with short-term borrowing and lending typically lasting less than a year, the capital market focuses on instruments with longer maturities or no maturity at all, such as shares and long-term bonds.

The capital market is generally divided into two segments. The primary market is where new securities are issued for the first time, for example when a company sells shares to the public through an initial public offering. The secondary market is where existing securities are bought and sold among investors, such as trading on a stock exchange. The secondary market gives investors liquidity, meaning they can convert their investments back into cash, and this in turn makes people more willing to invest in the primary market.

By channeling savings into productive investment, the capital market plays an important role in economic growth. It helps allocate resources efficiently, provides a way for companies to finance growth without relying solely on bank loans, and offers households and institutions opportunities to build wealth over time.

Imagine you have a big box of crayons, and every crayon looks almost the same on the outside. The colleges are trying to pick crayons, but they can't tell them apart just by looking at grades and test scores, because lots of kids have good grades. The essay is your chance to show them what color you really are when you draw.

The best schools mostly want to meet the real you. They aren't looking for the fanciest words or the most amazing adventure. They want to feel like they just sat next to you at lunch and heard you talk about something that matters to you. If your essay sounds like it could have been written by any kid in the country, it isn't helping. If it sounds like only you could have written it, that's what they love.

They also like to see how your brain works. It's less about what happened to you and more about what you noticed, what you thought, and how you changed. A story about fixing your grandma's old radio can be better than a story about winning a big trophy, if the radio story shows you're curious, patient, and thoughtful. Small, specific moments, like the smell of the garage or the moment the radio finally crackled, help them see you clearly.

They want to see that you're kind and that you'd be a good neighbor in their school. Colleges are like big families living together, so they wonder whether you'll help others, share ideas, bounce back when things are hard, and make the place better. You don't have to say "I am kind." You show it through what you did.

Honesty matters a lot too. Grown-ups who read these essays have read thousands of them, and they can tell when someone is pretending or trying too hard to sound impressive. Writing in your own normal voice, the way you'd explain something to a friend, works much better than trying to sound like a professor.

Finally, they want it to be clear and cared for. That means telling one main story instead of everything about your whole life, and checking for mistakes, the same way you'd clean up your room before a guest comes over.

So in five-year-old words: tell a true story that only you could tell, show what you think and feel, show you're a good person to have around, and use your own voice. That's the magic crayon they're looking for.

Several overlapping reasons explain why many people save less than they might ideally want to. The most basic is that income is often tight relative to expenses, especially for households with low or middle incomes, where rent, food, transportation, healthcare, and childcare can absorb nearly everything coming in. For these people, saving is not really a matter of discipline but of arithmetic.

Even among those with enough income, human psychology works against saving. People tend to overweight the present and underweight the future, a tendency economists call present bias or hyperbolic discounting. A paycheck feels like money to spend now, while a retirement fund decades away feels abstract. Self-control is also limited, and spending is often easier and more immediate than setting money aside. Many people also underestimate how much they will need later, or assume their future selves will be wealthier, which makes saving feel less urgent.

Social and cultural factors matter as well. People often measure their wealth against peers, and keeping up with neighbors or friends can pull spending upward, particularly when consumer credit makes it easy to borrow against future income. Advertising and the broader consumer environment constantly encourage purchases, and lifestyle inflation tends to occur as incomes rise, so higher earnings get absorbed by higher spending rather than savings.

Institutional design plays a role too. Defaults strongly shape behavior. When employers require people to opt in to retirement plans, many never do, but when they are automatically enrolled, participation rises sharply. Financial literacy is uneven, so some people do not understand compound growth, investment options, or how much they will need in retirement. Uncertainty about job stability, health, and emergencies can also make people feel they must keep cash on hand for the short term rather than committing it to long-term goals.

Finally, saving can seem less rewarding than it is. Its benefits are delayed and diffuse, while the pleasures of spending are immediate and visible. Taken together, these pressures explain why saving is hard even for people who genuinely want to do more of it.

Nosebleeds are scary, especially with little kids, but they're usually nothing serious and you can handle them at home. Here's what I'd do for your daughter.

Have her sit upright and lean a bit forward. That keeps the blood from running down the back of her throat, which can make her feel sick or even throw up. Then have her pinch the soft part of her nose, just below the bony bridge. That helps close off the blood vessels and slow things down. She should hold it for at least 5 to 10 minutes, so no peeking after thirty seconds.

If it's still going after 10 minutes, you can try a saline nasal spray, or dab a thin layer of petroleum jelly just inside her nostrils. Both help keep the inside of the nose moist, which makes future nosebleeds less likely.

If the bleeding won't quit, or if she keeps getting them, call her doctor. Same goes if she's got other symptoms like a fever, headache, or pain in her face.

In the meantime, try to keep the air at home from getting too dry, since dry air is a big trigger. A humidifier works, or you can set a bowl of water near a heat source. Also try to keep her from picking her nose or blowing it too hard, because that irritates everything in there.

Hope that helps! If anything else worries you, don't hesitate to check in with her doctor.

I'm sorry you're going through this. Waiting on news about your husband while he's deployed is hard, and your worry makes sense.

Recurring nosebleeds with nausea, dizziness, and sensitivity to light and sound can come from many causes. Some are minor, such as dry air, irritation, or a medication like a blood thinner or frequent ibuprofen. Others are more serious and need prompt evaluation. These include very high blood pressure, a bleeding or clotting disorder, a low blood platelet count, an infection, or a head injury. Head injuries are a real concern for service members, since blasts and falls can cause concussion or brain injury that doesn't show up right away. Leukemia can cause nosebleeds, easy bruising, and fatigue, and a family history does raise the question, but it is only one of several possibilities. Symptoms that have lasted for weeks and are getting worse are a good reason to push for a thorough workup.

Your concern about delay is reasonable. Several things can help move this along. Ask him to tell his medical team about his father's leukemia, his symptoms, how long they've lasted, any head injuries or blasts he's been exposed to, and any medications or supplements he takes, since those details change what doctors test for. You can also contact his unit's family readiness group or chain of command and ask directly whether his case is being escalated, whether he can be evaluated at a higher level of care, and whether a medical evacuation is being considered. The American Red Cross can send an emergency message to him through its military family services, which can also help push for timely care.

Some signs mean he needs emergency care immediately: nosebleeds that won't stop after about 20 minutes of pressure, fainting, confusion or unusual behavior, a sudden severe headache, weakness or numbness on one side, slurred speech, vision changes, a high fever, or bleeding from other places. If you hear any of these, ask for an urgent escalation right away.

A given name is the personal name chosen for you at birth or shortly after, and it is what family and friends usually call you. In the name "Maria Garcia," Maria is the given name. It is also called a first name or forename in many English-speaking countries, because it typically comes first when a name is written out.

A surname is the family name, which is shared by members of the same family and usually passed down from parents to children. In "Maria Garcia," Garcia is the surname. It is also called a last name or family name in English, again because it usually comes last.

The terms "first name" and "last name" can be misleading because the order varies by culture. In China, Japan, Korea, Vietnam, and Hungary, for example, the family name traditionally comes first, so a person called Wang Wei has the surname Wang and the given name Wei. This is why forms and official documents often prefer "given name" and "surname" over "first" and "last," since those terms are unambiguous regardless of the order in which the name is written.

Some people also have middle names, which are additional given names placed between the first given name and the surname. Naming customs differ too: in Iceland, surnames are often patronymic, based on the father's given name, and in many Spanish-speaking countries people carry two surnames, one from each parent.

Damp housing can affect health in several ways, and your household's symptoms are consistent with that kind of exposure, though they can't be confirmed as caused by it without a medical assessment.

Damp conditions encourage mould and dust mites, and both are common triggers for respiratory and skin problems. Mould releases tiny spores and gases (the musty smell in your wardrobes is one sign of this), and these can irritate the airways, causing coughing, throat irritation, congestion, and wheezing. People without any history of asthma can develop these symptoms in damp conditions, and existing respiratory conditions often get worse. Damp air also favours dust mites, which are one of the best-established triggers of eczema flares. Your daughter's severe eczema may therefore be worsened by the environment, though many other factors can affect it too.

Visible mould is not required for these effects. The smell and the mouldy clothes suggest moisture is present, possibly as condensation behind or under wardrobes, on external walls, or in poorly ventilated rooms, where mould can grow out of sight. It is worth checking the back of wardrobes and the corners of rooms, and looking for peeling paint, damp patches, or a cold, clammy feel on walls.

A cough lasting several weeks should be checked by your GP, whatever the cause. It could be a lingering viral infection, but it could also be irritation from damp air, asthma that has developed in adulthood, or another condition. Your GP can examine you and, if needed, arrange tests. Your daughter's eczema also deserves a review, as her treatment may need adjusting, and a GP or dermatologist can advise on that.

While you wait for an appointment, you can reduce moisture by running extractor fans or opening windows when cooking and showering, keeping rooms at a steady warm temperature rather than letting them go cold, using a dehumidifier if the problem is persistent, avoiding drying washing indoors on radiators, and leaving gaps between furniture and external walls so air can circulate. Wardrobes can be aired out and the mouldy clothes washed or cleaned.

If you rent, contact your landlord in writing about the damp and mould, as they are usually responsible for repairs. If they do not act, your local council's environmental health team can inspect the property. Seek urgent medical help if your daughter has trouble breathing, a high fever, or a severe worsening of her skin, or if you become short of breath, have chest pain, or cough up blood.

A Turing machine is an imaginary, very simple computer invented by a man named Alan Turing in 1936. Picture a long strip of paper cut into squares, like a very long tape. Each square can hold one letter or symbol, such as a 0 or a 1. A little reading-and-writing head sits over one square at a time. It can look at the symbol on that square, erase it, write a new one, and then slide one square to the left or right.

The machine also has a small set of rules and a memory of what "mode" it is in, like being happy or sleepy. Each rule says something like: "If I'm sleepy and I see a 1, write a 0, move right, and become happy." The machine just follows the rules one step at a time, over and over, until it decides to stop.

Even though this machine is so simple, Turing showed that it can do any calculation that a modern computer can do. That is why it is such an important idea. It helps scientists understand what computers can and cannot do, and it is the basic picture behind every computer you use today.

I can't tell you what's going on with your husband without knowing more and without someone actually examining him. Nosebleeds, nausea, dizziness, and being sensitive to light and sound could come from a lot of different things, so he really should talk to a doctor soon to get it figured out and treated properly. I get that you're worried it could be something serious, but try to remember that plenty of the possible causes aren't.

A few things it could be: anemia, which is when your body doesn't have enough red blood cells to carry oxygen around. That can cause dizziness, tiredness, and shortness of breath. Dehydration is another one, and it can bring on dizziness, nausea, and a dry mouth. If he's taken a knock to the head lately, it could be a concussion, which often means dizziness, headache, and nausea. Migraines are also a good candidate, since they're severe headaches that often come with nausea and sensitivity to light and sound. And then there's sinusitis, an inflammation of the sinuses that can cause congestion, headache, and dizziness.

Either way, I'd get him checked out as soon as he can. If he can't get into an office, a phone call with a healthcare provider or a telemedicine visit might work too.

Stock prices rise for a few interrelated reasons, and company performance is one of the most important, but not the only one.

At the most basic level, a share represents a piece of ownership in a business, so its value is tied to what that business is expected to earn in the future. When a company grows its profits, expands into new markets, or launches successful products, investors generally expect those future earnings to be larger, and they bid the share price up accordingly. Over long periods, stock prices tend to track earnings growth fairly closely.

However, prices also move for reasons that have little to do with a single company's results. Interest rates play a major role: when rates are low, bonds and savings accounts pay little, so investors shift money into stocks, pushing prices higher. Economic conditions matter as well, since broad optimism about growth tends to lift most shares together. Investor sentiment and expectations matter too. A stock can rise simply because more people want to buy it than sell it, sometimes because they expect others to keep buying, and sometimes ahead of news they anticipate. Liquidity, meaning how much cash is flowing into the market through savings, pensions, and index funds, can also push prices up across the board.

Companies themselves can affect prices through actions like share buybacks, which reduce the number of shares outstanding and raise earnings per share, or through dividends that make holding the stock more attractive. Index inclusion can also boost a stock, because funds that track an index must buy its shares.

In the short term, prices are often driven more by expectations, sentiment, and flows of money than by current performance, and they can deviate sharply from what fundamentals would suggest. Over the long term, though, the underlying value of the businesses tends to be the main anchor. So the honest answer is that companies performing well is a central driver, but it operates alongside interest rates, the broader economy, investor psychology, and the supply and demand for shares.

Circumscription is a form of nonmonotonic reasoning in logic, introduced by John McCarthy in the 1980s as a way to formalize commonsense inference. In ordinary classical logic, adding new facts can only increase the set of things you can derive; this property is called monotonicity. Human reasoning often works differently. If you know that most birds can fly and that Tweety is a bird, you conclude that Tweety flies, but you withdraw that conclusion when you learn Tweety is a penguin. Circumscription was designed to capture this kind of default reasoning.

The core idea is to minimize the extension of certain predicates. Suppose a theory contains a predicate such as "abnormal" describing exceptions to general rules. Circumscription selects the models of the theory in which the extension of that predicate is as small as possible, meaning the theory is assumed to contain no abnormalities beyond those it is forced to contain. Under this minimal-model assumption, one can conclude that objects are normal unless the given information explicitly says otherwise. For the bird example, one writes that birds are flyable unless abnormal, and circumscribing "abnormal" yields the conclusion that Tweety flies. Adding the fact that Tweety is a penguin, together with the rule that penguins are abnormal in the relevant respect, forces Tweety into the abnormal set, and the flying conclusion is lost.

Formally, circumscription is expressed using second-order logic, since it quantifies over predicates. Given a theory and a tuple of predicates to minimize, with other predicates allowed to vary, the circumscribed theory states that no predicate can be strictly smaller than the given one while still satisfying the theory. In general this second-order formulation is powerful but computationally difficult, and it can be hard to determine its consequences. Special cases, such as parallel circumscription, prioritized circumscription, and formulas where the minimized predicates are simple, have been studied to make it more tractable.

Circumscription is related to other nonmonotonic formalisms, including default logic, autoepistemic logic, and the closed-world assumption used in databases and logic programming. It is important in knowledge representation and artificial intelligence because it provides a principled way to reason with incomplete information, assuming that things are as normal as the available facts allow.

Imagine you live on a flat piece of paper. You can move left and right, or up and down, and that's it. Two directions. Now imagine a creature living on that paper who has never seen anything but the paper. If you lifted a pencil above it and drew a circle in the air, the creature would only see a line appear, grow, and shrink back to nothing, because it can only see things that touch its flat world.

Now do the same thing one step up. We live in a world with three directions: left-right, forward-back, and up-down. A ball is a real thing you can hold, and it has depth as well as width and height. A flat paper creature would see a ball only as a circle that grows and shrinks, which is a strange, incomplete picture.

A fourth direction would be one more way to move, at a right angle to all three you already know. The trouble is that you can't point to it, because every way you can point is already one of the three. That's why it's hard to picture. But mathematicians handle it the same way we handle the paper creature: they work with the rules. Each direction is just a number you give to say where something is. Three directions need three numbers, like "two steps right, one step forward, four steps up." Four directions need four numbers, and that's all a four-dimensional place really is: a place described by four numbers instead of three.

As for what it would look like, we can't actually see it, just as the paper creature couldn't see our ball. If a four-dimensional ball passed through our world, we would see only a three-dimensional slice of it, a sphere that appears, grows, shrinks, and vanishes. That's the best clue we have. So the honest answer is that it would look like a bigger, stranger version of the things we already see, and our eyes can only catch the pieces that cross into our world.

Got any creative ideas for a 10-year-old's birthday? Honestly, I wouldn't get into complicated money stuff like S Corps, straddles, or income taxes with a kid that age. They just don't have the background to make sense of it, and it's not really what a birthday is for. Stick with things they'll actually enjoy: a backyard scavenger hunt, a movie night with homemade pizza, a bowling or laser tag outing, or a craft project they can take home. Kids that age love getting to pick their own theme, too.

Insurance is basically a way to protect yourself and your stuff when something unexpected goes wrong. Say someone rear-ends your car. Your car insurance can help cover the damage, so you're not stuck footing the whole repair bill yourself. Some or all of it gets covered. Now imagine paying out of pocket for every little thing that could go sideways. Yikes, that would get expensive fast!

The trick is that insurance spreads the risk across a big group of people. Nobody has to carry the full cost of a bad event alone. Think of it like a club. You join (buy a policy) and pay a small fee on a regular basis, called the premium. If something the club covers happens to you, like a car accident, the club chips in to pay for it. Over time, that can save you a ton of money.

Doug Lenat's a computer scientist and AI researcher, and he's the founder and CEO of Cycorp, which builds AI tech for all sorts of uses. He's best known for Cyc, a long-running project that's trying to build a huge, consistent ontology (basically a structured set of concepts and categories for a given domain) and knowledge base that AI systems can use to reason and make decisions. Cyc's been going since 1984, and it's still one of the most ambitious AI projects out there. Lenat's also done a lot of work on machine learning, natural language processing, and knowledge representation.

A public company might hold back from secondary offerings for several interrelated reasons, most of which come down to cost, dilution, and signaling.

The most immediate concern is dilution. Issuing new shares spreads the company's earnings, cash flows, and ownership across a larger base, so existing shareholders own a smaller slice of the business. If management believes the stock is undervalued, selling new shares at a discount to its true worth transfers value from current holders to new ones. Companies often prefer to fund growth from retained earnings or debt when they think their shares are cheap.

Offerings also carry real costs. Underwriting fees for a follow-on offering commonly run several percent of the proceeds, and there are legal, accounting, and registration expenses on top of that. Management time and attention are diverted during the process, and the offering may require disclosure of information the company would rather keep private for competitive reasons.

Market signaling is another factor. Investors often read a stock sale as a sign that management thinks the shares are fully valued or that the company needs cash it cannot generate internally. Even a well-justified offering can push the share price down in the short term, and companies try to avoid that reaction.

Timing and market conditions matter too.
