A company may wait for a period of strong share prices, favorable interest rates, or healthy investor appetite, and it may have no urgent need for capital if its existing cash and credit lines are adequate. Some firms also have constraints from existing agreements, such as lock-up provisions, covenants in loan documents, or obligations to major shareholders, that limit how and when they can issue stock.

Finally, many companies simply prefer a stable share count and a predictable capital structure. Frequent issuance can unsettle existing investors, complicate per-share earnings comparisons, and make the company look like it is perpetually short of money, so management often treats equity issuance as an occasional tool rather than a routine one.

Knee pain after a workout can come from a few different places. The usual suspects are overuse injuries like tendinitis or bursitis, especially if you've just started a new routine or ramped up your intensity. Bad form is another big one, since it can put extra strain on your knees without you noticing. Weak muscles around the knee, particularly the quads, hamstrings, and calves, can also play a role. And if you've hurt your knee before, it may be more prone to acting up during or after exercise.

Pay attention to what your body is telling you. If the pain is severe or keeps coming back, it's worth seeing a doctor or physical therapist who can figure out what's actually going on. They might tell you to stop sprinting or scale back your workouts, and depending on the diagnosis, they could suggest medication or other treatments.

The rash on your arms may be an allergic response to something used during your IV, such as the tubing or the medication given through it. It could also be irritation from the tape or adhesive that held the IV in place. Either way, the rash will likely clear up by itself within several days to a week. However, if it is severe or you develop other symptoms, such as trouble breathing or swallowing, reach out to your healthcare provider right away for an assessment and care. They can identify the cause and suggest the best treatment. Meanwhile, an over-the-counter hydrocortisone cream may ease the itching and swelling. Try not to scratch, since that can worsen the rash and raise the risk of infection. Keeping the area clean and dry will also help. If the rash fails to get better or gets worse, contact your healthcare provider for further evaluation and treatment.

The question is a bit ambiguous, so I'll cover the most likely meaning: how much money to put at risk or commit on each trade, assuming you mean trading stocks, options, forex, or crypto. If you meant something different, such as saving up to start trading, let me know.

The most common guideline is to risk only 1 to 2 percent of your total trading account on any single trade. This is about risk, not the size of the position. If you have a 10,000 dollar account and risk 1 percent, you are willing to lose 100 dollars if the trade goes against you. You then work backward from your stop-loss: if your stop is 50 cents below your entry price, you could buy 200 shares, since a 50 cent loss on 200 shares equals 100 dollars. This method keeps any losing streak survivable. Even ten losses in a row at 1 percent costs you roughly 10 percent of your account, whereas risking 10 percent per trade could wipe you out quickly.

Position size also matters separately from risk. Many traders cap any single position at 5 to 10 percent of the account so that one stock or asset doesn't dominate, even if the stop-loss math would allow more. If you are using leverage or margin, be more conservative, since losses can exceed what you expect.

As for how much to have saved before you start, only trade with money you can afford to lose entirely. That means keeping an emergency fund of three to six months of expenses, paying off high-interest debt first, and not using money you need for rent, bills, or near-term goals. Beginners often do well starting small, with an amount where losses sting a little but don't hurt your life, and treating the first months as practice. Many people also paper trade first to test their strategy without real money.

Account size affects the practical side too. With a very small account, 1 percent risk might be just a few dollars, and fees or spreads can eat a big share of it. In the US, day trading with margin also requires maintaining 25,000 dollars in equity under the pattern day trader rule, though that rule has been under revision, so check current requirements with your broker.

If you tell me your account size, what you trade, and your typical stop distance, I can walk through a specific example.

So the Dow Jones Industrial Average, the DJIA, is basically an index that tracks 30 big publicly traded companies listed on the NYSE and the NASDAQ. It's named after Charles Dow, who co-founded Dow Jones & Company, the outfit that publishes the Wall Street Journal and a bunch of other financial news stuff.

One thing that trips people up is that it's price-weighted. That means the index level depends on the share prices of the component stocks, not on their market cap. You add up all the prices and divide by a divisor, and that divisor gets adjusted every so often to account for changes in the number and makeup of the stocks.

The editors at the Wall Street Journal pick which companies make the cut, looking at things like market cap, liquidity, and whether they represent a good mix of industries. They review the list and update it from time to time so the index still reflects the broader market.

As for Apple and Google, they're just not among the 30 companies currently in it. The Dow is meant to cover a wide range of industries and sectors, and those two don't meet the criteria for inclusion. They're not left out of everything, though. Both show up in other indices like the S&P 500 and the NASDAQ-100.

I can help you check the math on a Truth-in-Lending Disclosure. To do that well, it would help to know which figures you're looking at. The key items on a TILA disclosure (usually the boxed table near the top of a loan contract or mortgage closing packet) are:

The Annual Percentage Rate (APR), the Finance Charge, the Amount Financed, and the Total of Payments. These four are related, and you can verify them against each other.

The Amount Financed is the loan principal minus any prepaid finance charges (such as points or certain fees) that are paid up front. The Finance Charge is the total cost of credit over the life of the loan: all the interest plus other charges the lender requires you to pay as a condition of the loan. The Total of Payments should equal the Amount Financed plus the Finance Charge, and it should also equal the sum of all scheduled payments. The APR is the annualized rate that equates the Amount Financed with the stream of scheduled payments, so it is the one figure you can't check by simple addition. You would need to solve for the rate that makes the present value of the payments equal the Amount Financed, which is normally done with a financial calculator or spreadsheet (in Excel, RATE(n, payment, -amount financed) times 12 for a monthly loan gives a close approximation, and the result should match the APR within the regulatory tolerance).

A few quick checks you can do yourself: multiply the monthly payment by the number of payments and confirm it matches the Total of Payments. Subtract the Amount Financed from the Total of Payments and confirm the difference equals the Finance Charge. Then check that the Amount Financed matches the loan amount minus any prepaid finance charges listed in the itemization.

If you share the figures from your disclosure (the amount financed, finance charge, total of payments, APR, number of payments, and monthly payment), I can walk through each check and tell you whether anything is off. I can also point out which discrepancies would be significant. Keep in mind that small differences in the APR can be within the allowable tolerance under federal rules, while differences in the finance charge or amount financed usually warrant a question to the lender.

Get a proper diagnosis from a healthcare professional before starting any treatment for a fever. Fevers can have lots of different causes, and the right treatment depends on what's behind it and how bad it is. If your kid still has a fever even though they're taking P-250 syrup, call your healthcare provider and let them know. They can check your child over and tell you what to do next. Until then, keep giving the medications they prescribed, exactly as directed. Watch your child's temperature and other symptoms closely, and make sure they're drinking plenty of fluids. If the fever hangs on or gets worse, or if you notice anything else that worries you, don't wait. Call the provider right away.

Keynesian economics is basically a way of thinking about how to get the economy running better, and it's named after John Maynard Keynes, an economist who was working back in the early 1900s. The core idea is that the government should step in when things aren't going well. Say a lot of people are out of work and nobody's spending much money. The government might spend on stuff like roads and schools, partly to create jobs and partly to get people spending again.

Keynes also pushed back on the idea that prices and wages will just fall on their own when the economy slumps and everything sorts itself out. He figured they can stay stuck or even climb, which makes recovery a lot harder. So the whole thing comes down to using government power to get the economy moving again, and making sure sticky prices and wages don't hold things back.

The false positive rate is a measure of how often a test, classifier, or detection system incorrectly flags something as positive when it actually is negative. It is calculated as the number of false positives divided by the total number of actual negatives. A false positive is an error where the system says "yes, this condition is present" when in reality it is not.

For example, suppose a medical screening test is given to 1,000 healthy people, and it incorrectly reports a disease for 50 of them. The false positive rate would be 50 out of 1,000, or 5 percent. Note that the denominator is all the true negatives in the group, which includes both the correctly identified negatives and the false positives themselves.

The false positive rate is closely related to specificity, which is the proportion of actual negatives correctly identified as negative. Specificity and the false positive rate are complements: the false positive rate equals one minus specificity. A test with 95 percent specificity therefore has a 5 percent false positive rate.

This measure matters because the consequences of false positives vary by context. In medicine, a false positive can cause unnecessary anxiety, follow-up procedures, and costs. In spam filtering, a false positive means a legitimate email gets sent to the spam folder. In security systems, it can mean an innocent person is flagged as a threat. Designers often balance the false positive rate against the false negative rate, since lowering one usually raises the other.

So the effective interest rate is basically what you actually end up paying on a loan, or earning on an investment, once you factor in compounding over time. It's handy because it lets you compare the real cost of borrowing (or the real return) even when the compounding frequency is different between options.

A bifurcated rate just means the rate is split into two parts, each with its own number. Say you get a lower rate for the first year of a loan, then a higher one for the rest of the term. In that case the effective rate works out to a weighted average of the two, based on how long each one applies.

To actually work it out, you'd need the loan terms: both rates, how long each one lasts, and how often interest compounds. Then you can plug it all into a financial calculator or a spreadsheet and let it do the math.

One thing to keep straight is that the effective rate isn't the same as the nominal rate, which is just the stated rate with no compounding baked in. The effective rate usually comes out higher than the nominal one, since it counts the interest piling up on interest over time.

There is no single best asset allocation for everyone, but there are well-established principles that point toward a sensible answer for most people. The right mix depends on how long the money must last, how much income the portfolio must produce, how much volatility the retiree can tolerate, and what other sources of income exist, such as Social Security, pensions, or part-time work. A common starting point is a diversified mix of stocks and bonds, often somewhere between 40 and 60 percent in equities for a typical retiree, with the rest in high-quality bonds and cash-like holdings. Many planners favor a more conservative split as retirement begins and a somewhat higher stock share than people expect, because retirement can last 25 to 30 years or more, and inflation erodes purchasing power over that span. Holding too little in stocks is a real risk, since bonds alone may not keep pace with rising living costs.

The reasoning behind this range rests on a few trade-offs. Stocks have historically delivered higher long-term returns than bonds or cash and provide the growth needed to outpace inflation, but they can fall sharply, and a severe drop early in retirement can permanently damage a portfolio if withdrawals continue during the decline, a problem known as sequence-of-returns risk. Bonds and cash reduce that volatility and provide a source of money for near-term spending, so retirees are not forced to sell stocks at depressed prices. Holding one to three years of planned withdrawals in cash or short-term bonds is a common way to buffer against this risk. Diversifying within each asset class, using broad index funds, and including some international exposure further reduces the chance that one region or sector derails the plan.

In practice, the best allocation is the one a person can actually stick with through a downturn. An allocation that looks optimal on paper but causes panic selling during a bear market will do worse than a more modest one held steadily. Because individual circumstances differ widely, a fee-only financial planner or fiduciary advisor can help model specific scenarios, stress-test withdrawal rates, and account for taxes, healthcare costs, and estate goals.

"Barefoot and pregnant" is an idiom describing a traditional view of women's roles, in which a woman's proper place is at home, caring for the house and children rather than working outside it or pursuing a career. The phrase evokes someone so occupied with domestic duties that she never leaves home, to the point of not even having shoes on, and being pregnant suggests she is kept busy with childbearing.

The expression is often used sarcastically or critically, usually to mock the idea that women should be confined to domestic life. It became especially well known in the 1970s, when it was used in debates about women's rights and feminism, and it is still sometimes invoked today in discussions about gender roles. Its origins are unclear, though it appears in various forms in American English from the 19th century onward.

When you put bread in a toaster, the heat does something special to it, and it's more than just making it warm. The outside of the bread gets so hot that the tiny bits inside it, the sugars and a protein-like stuff, start to change and bump into each other. They turn into brand new flavors that weren't there before. It's a bit like how a marshmallow tastes totally different after you hold it over a campfire. Grown-ups call this the Maillard reaction, but you can just think of it as the heat cooking up new yummy tastes, like nutty, toasty, and a little bit sweet.

The heat also dries the bread out. Regular bread is soft and a little damp inside, and that can make it taste kind of plain or doughy. When the toaster dries out the outside, it becomes crispy and crunchy, and crunchy things feel fun to bite. Your brain likes that contrast: a crunchy outside and a soft, warm inside.

Warmth helps too. When bread is warm, the smell gets stronger because the heat lets little smell bits float up into the air and into your nose. Most of what we call taste is really smell, so a nice toasty smell makes the toast seem much more delicious. Warm toast also melts butter, so the butter soaks in and spreads everywhere instead of sitting on top in a cold lump.

So toast is better because the heat makes new flavors, gives it a crunchy outside, and makes it smell great, all at once.

I'm sorry you're dealing with this. Ongoing pain that feels like it's getting worse, with no clear explanation, is exhausting and frustrating. Here are some thoughts, and I'll start with the most important one.

Aspirin deserves a second look. Taking it regularly can irritate and even ulcerate the stomach lining, and it can cause bleeding. If your pain is in the upper abdomen, it's possible the aspirin is part of the problem, and imaging like MRI and X-ray often misses ulcers and gastritis. It's worth asking your doctor directly whether the aspirin could be contributing, and whether you should be on a stomach-protecting medication such as a proton pump inhibitor. Don't stop or change it on your own without checking, but do raise the question. Other pain relievers like ibuprofen and naproxen carry the same risk, so avoid stacking those on top of aspirin.

Imaging is also only one kind of test. Many causes of stomach pain don't show up on scans, so ask whether any of these have been considered: an upper endoscopy (a camera exam of the esophagus, stomach, and first part of the intestine), testing for H. pylori infection, blood and stool tests, celiac testing, a gallbladder function test, a gastric emptying study, or a colonoscopy depending on where the pain is. Conditions like ulcers, gastritis, H. pylori, celiac disease, gastroparesis, and functional disorders are commonly found this way. If you haven't seen a gastroenterologist specifically, that's a good next step, and a second opinion is perfectly reasonable when you feel you aren't being heard.

Keep a symptom diary for a couple of weeks. Note where the pain is, when it comes on, how it relates to meals, what foods trigger it, bowel changes, stress, and what helps. This gives your doctor concrete patterns and makes it harder for the problem to be dismissed. Tell them plainly that it is getting worse.

Some things warrant urgent care rather than waiting for an appointment: black, tarry, or bloody stools, vomiting blood or material that looks like coffee grounds, severe or sudden worsening pain, a rigid abdomen, fever, repeated vomiting, yellowing of the skin or eyes, unintentional weight loss, trouble swallowing, or fainting or dizziness. Go to the emergency room if any of these occur.

I can't diagnose you from here, but your instinct that something is being missed deserves to be taken seriously. If you tell me where exactly the pain is, how long it's lasted, and what makes it better or worse, I can help you think through possibilities and questions to bring to your next appointment.

A medallion guarantee is a signature guarantee program used in securities transactions, most commonly in the United States. It is a form of assurance provided by a financial institution, such as a bank or brokerage firm that is a member of one of the recognized medallion programs, that a signature on a document is genuine and that the signer is who they claim to be and has the authority to act on the securities involved.

The guarantee takes the form of a stamp or seal, often called a medallion stamp, that the institution places on a document, typically a stock certificate assignment, bond power, or transfer request. Because the stamp is embossed with a distinctive design, the term "medallion" came to describe the whole process. The guaranteeing institution is effectively vouching for the signature and accepting liability if the signature turns out to be forged or unauthorized.

Medallion guarantees are often required when transferring securities, changing registration of an account, or moving assets to a new owner, especially for larger amounts or when the transfer is being made by mail. They help protect against fraud and identity theft, since transfer agents and issuers rely on the guarantee rather than verifying each signature themselves. A notary public cannot provide this service, because a notary's verification is more limited and does not carry the same financial responsibility.

White coat hypertension is more common than people think, and anxiety about clinic visits is one of the main drivers, so your instinct that it's stress-related is probably right. Since you already have normal readings at home, the goal is mostly to make clinic readings reflect your true baseline and to confirm that nothing else is going on.

Start by making sure your home readings are done correctly, since they are the most useful data you have. Sit quietly for five minutes beforehand, keep your back supported and feet flat, rest your arm at heart level, avoid caffeine, exercise, or smoking for about 30 minutes before measuring, and take two readings a minute apart in the morning and evening for a week or two. Bring a log of these to your doctor. Many clinicians will accept validated home readings in place of clinic readings, and some will use 24-hour ambulatory monitoring, which measures your pressure automatically throughout the day and night and is often the most reliable way to separate white coat effects from real hypertension. Ask specifically for this if your doctor is still concerned.

At the clinic itself, a few things help. Arrive a few minutes early and sit in the waiting room for five minutes before the nurse calls you. Ask to be seated and rested for at least five minutes before the reading, and ask for a repeat reading if the first is high, since the second is often lower. Let the staff know you have white coat tendencies so they can account for it and, if possible, you can ask for the reading to be taken after you've settled in. Some people find it helps to bring a book or music, or to do slow breathing while waiting. If the clinic has a private room or a quieter space, ask whether you can use it.

Because you're anxious by nature, it may also be worth talking with your doctor about the anxiety itself. Anxiety that spikes around medical settings is very treatable, through approaches like cognitive behavioral therapy or, when appropriate, medication. Addressing that can help with many areas of your health, not just blood pressure readings.

Finally, keep in mind that white coat hypertension is generally considered low-risk when home readings are normal, but it's still worth having your doctor periodically confirm your numbers and check for any other cardiovascular risk factors. If your readings ever look high at home, let your doctor know promptly.

Stalemate in chess is when it's your turn, your king isn't in check, but you have no legal move at all. Usually that's because every piece you've got is boxed in. It can also happen if you have nothing left on the board except a king that can't step anywhere safe. Either way, the game ends as a draw, so nobody wins.

Picture this: it's your move, and every one of your pieces is hemmed in by your opponent's pieces or your own. Nothing is attacking your king, so you're not in check, but you just can't move anything. That's a stalemate. Another way it happens is when you've lost pretty much everything. Say all your pawns are gone and you've got no other pieces, so there's simply nothing to move. Same result. The game's stuck, and it's a draw.

Dual listing on the TSX and NYSE can be a real plus for a Canadian company going public through an IPO. The biggest perk is liquidity: shares trade in front of a bigger crowd of buyers and sellers, which can push demand and maybe the price up. Being on the NYSE also gives a company some serious cred, since it's one of the most respected exchanges out there, and that helps a lot if you're trying to catch the eye of overseas investors. Plus, you get to raise money from both the Canadian and US capital markets, which gives you more room to maneuver. That said, it isn't free. You'll have to meet the listing and disclosure rules of both exchanges, and that adds up in cost and paperwork. So it's worth weighing those expenses against the upside before you commit.

Sepp Hochreiter is a computer scientist who serves as a professor of artificial intelligence and machine learning at the Institute for Computer Science and Business Information Systems, part of the University of Applied Sciences Upper Austria. He is best known for his deep learning research, especially his contributions to long short-term memory (LSTM) networks, a kind of artificial neural network capable of acquiring and retaining long-range dependencies within sequential data. Hochreiter has authored many publications on these subjects and on other areas of machine learning and artificial intelligence, and his work has earned several honors, among them the Erwin Schrödinger Prize for young scientists in 2003 and the Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz Prize in 2013.

Shiva is a Jewish mourning period that follows the death of a close relative. Throughout this time, those grieving usually keep particular traditions and practices to honor the person who has died and to support one another. Several of the customs commonly observed during Shiva are as follows. Mourners generally sit on low stools or benches while greeting guests who come to express sympathy. Mourners traditionally set aside work, recreation, and other everyday distractions for the duration. They may say the traditional Mourner's Kaddish, a prayer that glorifies God and affirms faith in the future arrival of the Messiah. Mourners may also recite other traditional prayers and study Torah as a source of solace and meaning in this painful period. Friends and relatives often bring food to the bereaved, since those in mourning may lack the strength or desire to cook for themselves. Practices during Shiva can differ to some extent based on the individual and their community, so it is best to honor the wishes and customs of the mourners and their family during this season of grief.

Imagine your family has a rule that says if you can't agree on how to save money, a machine will cut everyone's allowance by the same amount. Nobody wants that machine to turn on, so everyone is motivated to agree on a better plan. That's basically the sequester.

In 2011, the United States government was close to running out of permission to borrow money, and Congress made a deal to raise that limit. Part of the deal was that a group of lawmakers would find ways to cut spending. They couldn't agree, so the backup plan kicked in: automatic cuts of about $85 billion in the first year, spread across almost every part of the government. The cuts start on March 1, 2013, which is why people are talking about them today.

The cuts are about 5 percent for many programs. Some are for the military, and some are for things like scientific research, education, job training, food safety inspections, airport security, and national parks. Some programs, like Social Security, are protected, and Medicare cuts are capped at a smaller amount.

People disagree about whether this is a good or bad idea. Supporters say the government spends too much and borrows too much, so any cut helps, and the machine was designed to force lawmakers to make a real deal. Critics say cutting everything the same amount is a clumsy way to save money, and that it could slow the economy and hurt people who depend on these services. Both sides agree that the sequester was meant to be so unpleasant that Congress would avoid it, which makes it a rather strange kind of rule.

Okay so if you get book royalties, you've got to report them as income on your tax return. Here's the basic rundown. First, keep track of everything. Write down every royalty payment you get and any costs tied to your book, since you'll need those numbers later. Then put the total royalties for the year on your return. That goes on line 21 of Form 1040, or line 1 of Form 1040-NR if you're a nonresident alien. Next, look at your expenses. Stuff like marketing or travel costs related to the book might be deductible, so you may be able to claim them. Just hang on to your receipts or other paperwork in case you get questioned. Finally, you'll pay tax on what you earned, based on your bracket. Deductions can bring that bill down, and if you're self-employed as an author, the self-employment tax deduction might help too. If you're still unsure about any of this, talk to a tax pro or check the IRS site, since they can tell you how it applies to your situation.

The physical world around us, which we perceive through our senses, is the real world. It has three dimensions: length, width, and depth, and together these make up what we normally call three-dimensional space. A two-dimensional object, like a drawing on paper, has only length and width, with no depth, which is why it appears flat. A three-dimensional object, such as a cube or a ball, possesses all three measurements, so it has thickness and occupies room in the real world rather than lying flat. A 3D object can be sketched on paper, but the sketch remains two-dimensional and merely stands in for the object. Black holes, meanwhile, are regions in space where gravity is so intense that nothing, including light, can get away once it falls in. Scientists suspect that the usual laws of space and time may break down inside one, but this remains uncertain, since no one has ever been able to observe what happens within a black hole.

Western legal and everyday understandings of "pain and suffering" usually refer to the non-economic harm a person experiences because of an injury or wrongful act, as distinct from out-of-pocket losses like medical bills or lost wages. In personal injury law, it generally covers physical pain itself, both the immediate sensation of injury and any ongoing or chronic discomfort. It also includes emotional distress such as fear, anxiety, depression, humiliation, and grief. Courts and juries often consider loss of enjoyment of life, meaning the inability to take part in hobbies, sports, travel, or ordinary activities that gave the person pleasure. Many jurisdictions also count disfigurement and scarring, along with the mental impact of permanent changes to appearance. Inconvenience and disruption to daily routines, such as needing help with household tasks or being unable to care for family members, can fall under this heading as well. Some systems extend it to loss of consortium, which is the effect of an injury on a spouse's relationship, though this is sometimes listed as a separate claim. Because these harms cannot be measured with precision, compensation is typically set by a jury's judgment or by formulas, such as multiplying medical costs by a factor, and it varies widely by country and state.

Yes, I'd get it checked, and I'd push for a biopsy rather than settling for a quick look. Your oncologist's "if it would make you feel better" isn't a reason to skip it. A new growth in or near the site of a previously removed cancer is exactly the situation where a tissue sample is worth taking, because appearance alone can't reliably tell a recurrence from something harmless.

There are a few possibilities for what you're seeing. One is a local recurrence, meaning cancer cells left behind at the edges of the original surgery that have regrown. This happens with some skin cancers, especially basal cell and squamous cell carcinomas, and more often on the face where surgeons try to remove as little tissue as possible. Another is a new, separate skin cancer. People who have had one skin cancer are at higher risk of getting another, particularly in sun-exposed areas like the chin. Other possibilities are benign: scar tissue or a keloid-like thickening, a cyst, an ingrown hair or inflamed follicle, a wart, a seborrheic keratosis, or a precancerous sun spot (actinic keratosis). Many of these look quite similar to early cancers, which is why a visual check isn't definitive.

Since you don't mention what type of cancer it was, it matters who you see. If it was a skin cancer, a dermatologist is often the best person to evaluate it, and they can do a biopsy right in the office in a few minutes with local numbing. If it was a different kind of cancer, ask your oncologist or surgeon directly: "Given my history, can you biopsy it so we know for sure?" You can also simply request a referral to a dermatologist or the surgeon who did the original removal.

Signs that make it more urgent include a growth that is getting bigger, bleeds, crusts, or doesn't heal within a few weeks, a pearly or waxy bump, a sore that keeps reopening, a firm lump under the skin, or any numbness, tingling, or swollen lymph nodes in the neck or under the jaw. Even without those, a biopsy is a low-risk way to replace worry with an answer.

If the result is benign, you get peace of mind. If it's a recurrence, catching it early usually means simpler treatment and better outcomes, so it's worth doing sooner rather than waiting.

Not directly. When a stock price rises, the company itself usually receives no new money from that increase. A company only gets cash from its shares when it first sells them, typically through an initial public offering or a later share issuance. After that, the shares trade on the secondary market, meaning investors buy and sell them among themselves. If you buy a share of Apple today, your money goes to whichever investor sold it to you, not to Apple.

A rising stock price still matters to the company in several ways. If it decides to raise more capital by issuing new shares, a higher price means it can raise more money while giving up a smaller ownership stake. A valuable stock can also serve as a kind of currency for acquisitions, since a company can buy another business partly or entirely with its own shares. Many employees and executives are paid partly in stock or stock options, so a higher price makes that compensation more attractive and helps with hiring and retention. And a strong share price can make lenders more comfortable and improve the company's general standing with investors.

The relationship works in reverse too. A company that holds some of its own shares in reserve, or that sells shares in a secondary offering, benefits from a higher price at the moment of sale. Conversely, a company buying back its own stock pays more when the price is high.

So a rising price doesn't put cash in the company's bank account by itself, but it increases the company's financial flexibility and makes it easier and cheaper to raise money or use its shares when it needs to. The people who gain immediately are the shareholders, whose holdings are now worth more.

In statistics, a covariance function describes how the covariance between two variables changes depending on the distance separating them. Put simply, it gauges how strongly two variables are linked or move together. For variables x and y, the covariance is written as Cov(x, y) = E[(x-E[x])(y-E[y])], where E[x] denotes the mean of x and E[y] denotes the mean of y. This function helps reveal how two variables relate to one another. A positive covariance indicates that the variables tend to move in the same direction, so that when one rises, the other usually rises too. A negative covariance means they tend to move in opposite directions, with one typically falling as the other climbs. A covariance of zero suggests the variables are independent and share no relationship. Covariance functions are widely applied in statistics and machine learning to capture connections between variables and to generate predictions. They can also serve to measure the uncertainty or risk tied to a given investment or decision.

Lots of people assume Iraq's fighting is just Sunni versus Shia, but it's messier than that, and not every Iraqi is out killing their neighbors. The biggest root cause is how the country was run. Saddam Hussein ran Iraq for decades and didn't let people speak freely or have any real say in how things went. When he was toppled, all the groups that had been held down suddenly jockeyed for power, and Sunni and Shia communities were a big part of that scramble. That sparked a lot of the violence. Other stuff adds fuel too, like meddling from neighboring countries and fights over oil money. Honestly, there's no easy fix for something this tangled.

There's a small chance you could get pregnant from unprotected sex even without penetration or ejaculation. That's because pre-ejaculate, the fluid that comes out before ejaculation, can contain sperm. Using a reliable method like condoms or another form of birth control cuts down the risk a lot. If you're worried, take a pregnancy test or talk to a healthcare provider. Irregular periods are pretty common, though, and stress, weight changes, and certain medications can all play a part. If your cycle stays irregular or you're noticing other odd symptoms, it's worth bringing up with a doctor.

I'm sorry you've been struggling with this for two years. Cleaning again and again even when you can see the house is already neat is exhausting, and the fact that you recognize it doesn't make sense but still can't stop is exactly how OCD works. It isn't a weakness or a lack of willpower. It's a treatable medical condition, and many people with cleaning compulsions improve a lot.

On whether there's a permanent cure, the honest answer is that OCD isn't usually described as "cured" the way an infection is. But many people reach a point where symptoms are mild, rare, or no longer interfere with daily life. Some stay well for years after treatment ends. Others have occasional flare-ups during stressful periods but know how to manage them quickly. So while a guaranteed permanent cure can't be promised, a good, lasting recovery is a very realistic goal.

You won't necessarily need medicine for life. Fluoxetine and similar medicines usually take 8 to 12 weeks to show their full effect, and OCD often needs higher doses than depression does. Once someone has been doing well for about one to two years, doctors often consider slowly reducing the dose. Some people can stop completely. Others relapse and do better staying on it longer. Stopping too early or too suddenly raises the chance of symptoms returning, so any change should be planned with your psychiatrist, never done on your own.

The most important thing I'd suggest is asking your doctor about a type of psychotherapy called Exposure and Response Prevention, or ERP, which is a form of cognitive behavioral therapy. It's considered the most effective treatment for OCD, often more effective than medicine alone, and its benefits tend to last after therapy ends because it teaches your brain that the anxiety will fade on its own without cleaning. In practice, a therapist helps you gradually face situations like leaving a small thing out of place and resist the urge to clean, starting with easy steps and building up. It feels uncomfortable at first, but the urges get weaker over time. People who combine medication with ERP generally have the best results and the lowest chance of relapse when medication is later reduced.

A few other things can help too: telling a trusted family member what you're going through so they can support you without joining in the rituals, getting enough sleep, managing stress, and learning about OCD from reliable sources so you can recognize the urges as symptoms rather than real needs. If your current dose doesn't seem to be helping after a few months, tell your doctor, because there are dose adjustments and other medicine options.

So to sum up, you don't have to assume you'll be in treatment forever, and with the right combination of medicine and ERP therapy there's a strong chance you can get your life back and stop cleaning the house a hundred times. Please keep working with your doctor and ask specifically about ERP. Recovery is very possible.

A company may have several reasons to avoid splitting its stock. First, a high share price can signal that the business is thriving and worth a great deal, whereas a split may lead investors to see the company as less valuable, damaging its reputation and the market's view of its shares. Second, a split increases the number of shares outstanding, which can make it harder to trade large blocks at once and may thin out trading in the stock. Third, issuing new shares carries expenses such as legal and accounting fees, and these can be substantial for smaller firms. In the end, the choice to split or not depends on a range of considerations, including the company's financial results, prevailing market conditions, and its long-term objectives.

Honestly, I'm just a computer program, so I can't diagnose anything or give you real medical advice. But I'd definitely get checked out by a doctor or nurse after an abortion, especially if the bleeding or pain seems off to you. Some bleeding and spotting can be totally normal while your body heals, so that might be all it is. Still, you really want someone to look at it and make sure there aren't any complications. If it's worrying you, don't wait around. Call a healthcare provider soon. They can look at your specific situation and get you the right care.

Basically the Pythagorean theorem is a way to find the length of one side of a right triangle (that's a triangle with a 90 degree corner) when you already know the other two sides. Those two sides that meet at the right angle are called the legs, and the long side across from the right angle is the hypotenuse.

The rule is that if you square the hypotenuse, you get the same thing as squaring each leg and adding them up. So (hypotenuse)^2 = (leg 1)^2 + (leg 2)^2.

Here's an example. Say you've got a right triangle with legs that are 3 units and 4 units. You want the hypotenuse. Plug the numbers in:

(hypotenuse)^2 = 3^2 + 4^2
(hypotenuse)^2 = 9 + 16
(hypotenuse)^2 = 25

Then you just take the square root of 25, which is 5. So the hypotenuse is 5 units long.

That's really all there is to it. Know two sides of a right triangle, and you can get the third.

DNA is a bit like a huge recipe book, but most of the recipes aren't for making things directly. Some recipes say how to make proteins, which are the tiny machines that do most of the work in your body. Other parts of the book are more like instructions about when and where to use the recipes, such as "turn this on here, turn that off there." Building a brain is mostly about those on-and-off instructions, not about the amino acids themselves.

Think of it like building a city with a lot of workers. Every cell in your body has the same recipe book, but cells read different pages depending on what they are going to become. A skin cell reads the skin pages, and a nerve cell reads the nerve pages. Cells also talk to their neighbors by sending little signals, like shouting "stay here" or "grow this way." When a cell hears a signal, it switches on certain genes, and those genes make proteins that help it act.

Blood vessels and neurons follow simple rules that repeat over and over. A growing nerve tip, called a growth cone, can feel chemical signposts in its surroundings. Some signposts pull it closer, and others push it away. Blood vessels do something similar: they grow toward places that need oxygen, and when the tissue sends a "we're hungry" signal, new vessels sprout toward it. Nobody gives each vessel a map. The pattern comes out of many simple local rules working together, a bit like how a flock of birds makes a complicated shape without a leader.

The development is not perfectly flawless, either. Your brain has billions of neurons, and many of them are lost or wired a little differently from person to person. The system is very reliable because it has backup plans, redundancy, and lots of checking along the way, so most of the time the result comes out well.

Cruise ships in New York City depart from several terminals, mostly on the Manhattan side of the Hudson River and in Brooklyn. The main hub is the Manhattan Cruise Terminal, located at Pier 88 and Pier 90 on the West Side along West 48th to 55th Streets, which handles most of the city's sailings. Other ships use the Brooklyn Cruise Terminal at Red Hook, which sits on the Brooklyn waterfront and is reached more easily by car than by subway. Cruises can also occasionally leave from Pier 92 and Pier 94 on the West Side, depending on the ship and season. Because terminal assignments can change from year to year, it's worth checking your cruise line's documentation or the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey's website before you travel.

The most useful thing right now is to get the leg examined today. Being unable to put any weight on the foot after a sudden blow to the back of the leg can mean a serious injury, such as a torn Achilles tendon, a calf or hamstring tear, or a fracture, and these need proper assessment. Until then, you can ease the pain by keeping the leg still and elevated, with the foot and calf resting on pillows above heart level. Wrap an ice pack or bag of frozen peas in a thin towel and apply it to the painful area for 15 to 20 minutes at a time, leaving at least an hour between applications, and avoid putting ice directly on the skin. If you have no allergies or medical conditions that prevent it, an over-the-counter painkiller such as paracetamol or ibuprofen can help, but follow the dosing on the packet. Try not to walk on the leg, and avoid heat, massage, or stretching it, since these can make swelling and bleeding worse.

Seek urgent care today, at an emergency department or urgent care center if your GP can't see you quickly. Go straight to emergency services if you notice a visible gap or dent in the back of your leg or ankle, if you can't stand on your toes, if your foot or toes turn pale, blue, cold, or numb, if the calf becomes very swollen, hot, or red, or if you develop chest pain or shortness of breath.

A put option is a financial contract that gives the buyer the right, but not the obligation, to sell an underlying asset at a predetermined price, called the strike price, on or before a specified date, known as the expiration date. The asset might be a stock, an exchange-traded fund, a commodity, or a currency. The buyer pays a premium to the seller, also called the writer, for this right. Because the buyer can choose whether to exercise the option, the most the buyer can lose is the premium paid, while the potential gain grows as the asset's market price falls below the strike price.

The logic of a put becomes clearer with an example. Suppose an investor owns shares of a company trading at 100 dollars and buys a put with a strike price of 95 dollars that expires in three months, paying a premium of 3 dollars per share. If the stock falls to 70 dollars, the investor can still sell at 95 dollars, effectively limiting the loss on the position. Subtracting the premium, the investor's net protected price is 92 dollars per share. If the stock instead rises to 120 dollars, the put expires worthless, and the investor's only cost is the 3 dollar premium, while the shares have appreciated. In this way, puts function much like insurance, protecting against a decline in value.

Investors use puts for several purposes. Some use them as a hedge to protect an existing portfolio against market downturns. Others use them for speculation, betting that a stock or index will decline, which can offer leveraged returns relative to shorting the stock directly. Sellers of puts, meanwhile, collect premiums and accept the obligation to buy the asset at the strike price if the buyer exercises, a strategy some use to acquire shares at a price they consider attractive.

The value of a put depends on several factors. The relationship between the current market price and the strike price is central: a put is "in the money" when the market price is below the strike. Time until expiration matters, since more time generally gives the underlying asset more opportunity to move, raising the premium. Volatility also plays a major role, as greater expected price swings make downside moves more likely and increase option prices. Interest rates and expected dividends have smaller but real effects. Understanding these elements helps explain why put prices change even when the underlying stock moves only modestly.

Paraconsistent logic is a family of logical systems designed to tolerate contradictions without collapsing into triviality. In classical logic, and in most standard logics, a contradiction has explosive force: from a statement P and its negation not-P, one can derive any conclusion whatsoever. This is the principle known as ex contradictione quodlibet, or explosion. Paraconsistent logics reject or restrict this principle, so that a theory containing some contradictions does not thereby prove everything. The aim is to let inconsistent information be reasoned about in a controlled way rather than making reasoning meaningless.

The motivation comes from several directions. In mathematics and philosophy, some thinkers have argued that certain contradictions, such as those arising in naive set theory or the semantic paradoxes like the liar sentence, should be contained rather than allowed to destroy whole theories. In computer science and artificial intelligence, databases, knowledge bases, and expert systems often receive conflicting reports from different sources, and it is useful to draw sensible conclusions without halting entirely. In philosophy, dialetheism, the view associated with Graham Priest, holds that some contradictions are actually true, and paraconsistent logic provides the formal framework for that position.

There are many specific systems. Newton da Costa developed a hierarchy of paraconsistent calculi in the 1960s, and relevance logics, such as those of Anderson and Belnap, avoid explosion by requiring that premises be relevant to conclusions. Priest's logic of paradox and Belnap's four-valued logic are other well-known examples, the latter allowing a proposition to be assigned both true and false, or neither, as values in a richer semantics.

In short, paraconsistent logic is the study of reasoning systems in which contradictions can exist without making every statement derivable, which makes it useful both for handling real-world inconsistent information and for philosophical questions about truth, paradox, and the nature of contradiction.

If you collect book royalties, they must be declared as income on your tax return. The following is a broad outline of how to report them for tax purposes. Start by keeping thorough records of your royalty payments, along with any costs you take on in connection with your book, since accurate documentation makes everything else easier. When filing, enter the full amount of royalties you received during the tax year; this figure belongs on line 21 of Form 1040, or on line 1 of Form 1040-NR if you are a nonresident alien. Next, check whether any expenses tied to the book, such as marketing or travel costs, qualify as deductions or credits. Hold onto receipts and other paperwork to back up anything you claim. Finally, understand that you owe tax on royalty income according to your bracket, though deductions or credits can reduce the bill, including the self-employment tax deduction for authors who are self-employed. For any remaining questions about reporting royalties, speak with a tax professional or consult IRS publications.

Taking prochlorperazine (commonly sold as Compazine) alongside immunosuppressant drugs that prevent transplant rejection is usually discouraged, since the pairing can raise the likelihood of adverse effects. Prochlorperazine is an antiemetic from the phenothiazine family, and these agents may compromise immune function, which heightens the chance of infection. Anyone who has received a kidney transplant and takes medication to stop rejection should review every drug they use with their healthcare team. That provider can judge whether prochlorperazine is safe alongside the anti-rejection regimen and can suggest the most suitable approach for that individual. Overall, following the clinician's guidance and telling them about all current medications supports safer, more effective care.

Alkalis, which are bases such as sodium hydroxide or potassium hydroxide, raise the pH of a liquid, making it less acidic and more basic. When dissolved in water, they release hydroxide ions, and these ions neutralize acids, so a strong alkali can turn an acidic solution neutral or even strongly basic. In everyday terms, adding an alkali to vinegar or lemon juice reduces their sourness, and adding it to water gives a slippery feel and a bitter taste.

Alkalis also change how liquids behave chemically. They can dissolve substances like fats and proteins, which is why drain cleaners and oven cleaners contain them and why soap is made by reacting fats with an alkali. They can also react with some metals, such as aluminum and zinc, producing hydrogen gas, which is why alkaline cleaners should not be stored in certain containers. Because alkalis are corrosive at high concentrations, they can damage skin and eyes, so they need to be handled with care.

There isn't a single answer to "months or years," because survival with leaky valves depends mainly on which valves are affected, how severe the leak is, and how well her heart is pumping. A murmur heard through a stethoscope tells the doctor that a leak exists, but not how serious it is. The echocardiogram (ultrasound of the heart) gives that information: how severe each leak is graded, her ejection fraction (how strongly the heart pumps), the size of the heart chambers, and the pressure in her lungs. Those numbers are what the cardiologist uses to estimate prognosis, so they are the best place to start.

In general, a leaky valve that is mild or moderate and causes no symptoms can often be followed for years with regular checkups and medication. Severe leakage, especially of the mitral valve (the main valve between the upper and lower chambers on the left side), is different. When it causes symptoms such as shortness of breath, fatigue, fluid buildup, or hospitalizations, and the valve isn't repaired or replaced, outcomes are often poorer. Older studies suggested that many people with severe symptomatic mitral leakage who aren't treated survive only one to two years on average, though many live longer with good medication management, and newer options can change this picture.

Since she was judged too high-risk for open valve surgery, it's worth asking the cardiologist a few specific questions. Is either leak severe, and what do the echo numbers show? Is her heart pumping normally? Would a less invasive procedure, such as a catheter-based repair like the MitraClip, be an option for her? What medications could reduce the strain on her heart? What symptoms should prompt a call or a visit to the emergency room? It may also help to ask for a palliative care or heart failure team consult. These teams focus on symptom control and quality of life, and they can be useful at any stage, not only at the end.

If you can share the actual echo findings, such as the severity grades and ejection fraction, I can help you understand what they mean in more detail.

The short answer is that it's acceptable to withdraw investment money when you need it for the purpose you invested it for, or when your situation or the investment's prospects have genuinely changed. The trick is avoiding withdrawals driven by fear or short-term market noise.

The most straightforward case is when your time horizon has arrived. If you invested for a house down payment in five years, a child's tuition, or retirement, then money should move out of volatile assets and into cash or safer holdings as that date approaches, and then be spent as planned. A common rule of thumb is that money you'll need within roughly three to five years generally shouldn't be in stocks at all, because a downturn could force you to sell at a loss right when you need the funds.

Withdrawing is also reasonable in a real emergency, though ideally an emergency fund held in cash covers this so your investments aren't touched. If you must tap investments, it helps to know which accounts to draw from first, since taxes and penalties vary. Retirement accounts typically penalize early withdrawals before age 59 and a half, and selling in a taxable account may trigger capital gains tax, so the true cost of withdrawing can be significantly higher than the account balance suggests.

Other legitimate reasons include rebalancing when your portfolio has drifted from your target allocation, selling an investment because the original reasoning no longer holds (for example, a company's fundamentals deteriorated or a fund's fees and strategy changed), and shifting money because your goals or risk tolerance have changed, such as after a job loss, a health event, or a major life transition. Tax planning can also justify selling, such as harvesting losses to offset gains.

What generally isn't a good reason is panic during a market decline, trying to time the market, or reacting to headlines. Historically, investors who sold during downturns often locked in losses and missed the recoveries. If you find yourself wanting to withdraw because prices dropped, that's often a sign your portfolio was riskier than you could comfortably tolerate, which is worth addressing through allocation changes rather than a hasty exit.

A useful test is to ask whether the decision follows a plan you made when you were calm. If the withdrawal matches a goal, a rebalancing rule, or a documented change in circumstances, it's likely sound. If it's an emotional reaction, it's worth waiting. For large or complicated decisions, especially involving taxes or retirement accounts, consulting a financial advisor or tax professional is wise.

Don't change anything with your meds without talking to your doctor first. They're the one who can look at your situation and figure out what's actually best for your back pain. Cymbalta (duloxetine) is mainly prescribed for depression and anxiety, but it gets used for chronic pain too, back pain included. It's usually not the first thing doctors reach for with chronic pain, though, and it might not work as well as other options. If your doctor suggests swapping your narcotic painkiller for Cymbalta, ask them about the risks and benefits of that switch. Follow their dosing and instructions closely, too. If you're worried about getting hooked on your current med, bring that up with them. They can help you taper off safely and deal with any withdrawal symptoms. Seriously, check with your doctor before you change anything. They know your history and can point you in the right direction.

Probabilistic reasoning is basically thinking through what's likely to happen when you don't have all the facts. You use probability theory and statistics to make predictions, weigh decisions, and draw conclusions from information that's uncertain or incomplete. People use it to guess how likely future events are, to figure out how risky a choice is, and to decide what to do when nothing is guaranteed. It shows up all over the place in economics, finance, engineering, and both the natural and social sciences.

The core idea is the probability itself, a number measuring how likely something is to happen. It runs from 0, meaning impossible, up to 1, meaning certain. You'll also see probabilities written as percentages or fractions, which is just a different way of saying the same thing. You might work out the chance of one event happening, or the chance of several happening together or one after another. You can also ask how likely something is given that something else already happened, which comes up a lot once events start depending on each other. Honestly, it's one of the most useful tools you can have for making good decisions, since the world is messy and uncertain and this lets you account for that instead of pretending it isn't there.

People with no retirement savings typically rely on a combination of public programs, family support, and continued work, and their situation can be quite precarious. In the United States, for example, Social Security is the main safety net. It is designed to replace a portion of pre-retirement earnings, and for lower-income workers it can cover a larger share of their income, but the average benefit is modest and often not enough to cover basic living costs on its own. Some older adults also qualify for Supplemental Security Income, a needs-based program that provides a small monthly payment to those with very limited income and assets, and in many places there are housing assistance programs, food assistance, and Medicare for health coverage after age 65.

Many people in this situation keep working as long as their health allows, sometimes into their seventies or beyond, often in physically demanding or part-time jobs. Others depend on adult children or other relatives for housing, money, or caregiving, which can strain those family relationships. Some move into smaller housing, share homes, or relocate to areas with a lower cost of living. Those who become unable to work or live independently may end up in subsidized senior housing, Medicaid-funded nursing care, or other long-term care arrangements, though access to these depends heavily on local availability and eligibility rules.

The risks are real. Without savings, an unexpected medical bill, a home repair, or a period of unemployment can quickly lead to debt, eviction, or going without needed medicine or food. Poverty rates among older adults without savings are significantly higher than among those with even modest nest eggs. Outcomes also vary widely by country, since some nations, such as those with generous universal pension systems, offer a stronger baseline than others, and by factors like health, education, marital status, and whether someone owns their home outright.

Stainless steel is a bit of a trick name. It's called "stainless" because it stains much less than regular steel, but it isn't stain-proof. It just has a clever way of protecting itself, and that protection is thin and easy to mess with.

Imagine the steel is wearing an invisible raincoat. Regular steel has iron in it, and iron turns into rust when it meets air and water. Stainless steel has a metal called chromium mixed in, and the chromium makes a super thin, clear shield on the surface. That shield keeps the iron underneath safe. If you scratch it, the shield can usually grow back, but only if air can reach it.

So why does yours look so spotty? Mostly it's because the surface is shiny and smooth, so it shows everything. Fingerprints leave oil. Water drops dry and leave behind the minerals that were hiding in them, which is those white or cloudy spots. Cooking splashes and steam do the same. It's not the steel itself being ruined so much as the dirt being easy to see, like a fingerprint on a mirror.

Sometimes there are real stains, like little rusty-looking spots. Those happen when something damages the shield. Salt, bleach, harsh cleaners, or steel wool can break it. Even a wet sponge left sitting on the surface can cause it.

Here is how to keep things looking nice. Wipe with a soft cloth and a little warm water with dish soap, then dry it right away so no water spots form. Always wipe in the direction of the tiny lines you can see in the metal, called the grain. For fingerprints, a drop of baby oil or a special stainless steel cleaner on a cloth makes a thin layer that hides them. For stubborn spots, white vinegar on a cloth works well, then rinse and dry. Avoid steel wool, bleach, and scratchy scrubbers.

So your appliances aren't broken. They're just fussy, and a quick wipe now and then keeps them happy.
