Sharp pain in the lower right abdomen could come from a few different things. Appendicitis is the big one to know about: the appendix gets inflamed and infected, and it usually causes sudden, severe pain that starts in that area. Kidney stones are another possibility. They're small, hard masses that form in the kidneys, and when they move through the urinary tract they can cause sharp pain right there. An intestinal infection, bacterial or viral, can also cause belly pain, and so can constipation, especially when stools are hard and dry and hard to pass.

If the pain is bad, or if you've got fever, nausea, or vomiting along with it, don't wait it out. Get in to see a doctor. They can figure out what's going on and tell you how to treat it.

You're most likely thinking of Rich Fields, who served as the announcer on The Price Is Right from 2004 to 2010. He took over the role after the longtime announcer Rod Roddy died in 2003, and he worked alongside Bob Barker through Barker's retirement in 2007 and then continued into the early years of Drew Carey's tenure as host.

In 2010, the show's producers decided to make a change and let Fields go. The departure wasn't framed as the result of any scandal; it was generally described as the new production team wanting a different sound for the show. After a period of rotating guest announcers, George Gray was chosen as the permanent replacement and has held the job ever since.

Before The Price Is Right, Fields had a background in radio and local television, including work as a weather presenter in Los Angeles. After leaving the game show, he returned to that kind of work, doing radio, voiceover jobs, and local broadcasting and hosting gigs. He has also spoken publicly and fondly about his years on the show and his time working with Bob Barker. He hasn't had another national role as prominent as The Price Is Right, but he has continued to work in broadcasting.

If you meant a different Rich, such as a memorable contestant, let me know any details you remember and I can try to help further.

Fever right after a head bump isn't typical, and a 100.2°F reading is a low-grade temperature. Most often, a fever that shows up around the same time as an injury has a separate cause, usually a viral illness that was starting anyway. Crying and stress can nudge a temperature up a little, but usually not to this level. Head injuries can occasionally trigger a fever, but that's uncommon. Since your son is otherwise acting normally, the fever is more likely from something else, though it's still worth paying attention to.

Because he hit his head and now has a fever, I'd call his pediatrician or a nurse advice line today, even if he seems fine. They can tell you whether he needs to be seen. Please seek care right away, or go to the emergency room, if he vomits more than once, becomes unusually sleepy or hard to wake, seems confused or irritable in a way that's different from his normal, has a seizure, has unequal pupils, develops weakness or trouble using one side of his body, has clear fluid or blood coming from his nose or ears, develops swelling or a soft spot bulging on his head, or has bruising behind the ears or around the eyes. Also get help if his fever climbs to 102°F or higher, lasts more than a day or two, or he stops drinking fluids or acting like himself.

For comfort, acetaminophen or ibuprofen at the correct dose for his weight is fine, and you can check with his doctor about the right amount. Keep him hydrated and let him rest, and check on him periodically through the next day or so. Never give aspirin to a child.

The subprime crisis, often called the financial crisis, was a stretch of economic upheaval that started in the late 2000s and hit the United States and Europe hard. In essence, banks and other financial institutions began handing out loans to people who were unlikely to be able to repay them. Because these borrowers were seen as riskier than prime borrowers, the loans were known as "subprime mortgages." The banks then grouped many of these mortgages into packages and sold them to other investors as securities. Consequently, people took on ever larger amounts of debt, and the securities tied to the subprime mortgages rose in value. This inflated a bubble in the housing market, with home prices climbing steadily higher. Eventually, though, the bubble burst and the securities lost most of their value. A chain reaction followed, since many banks and financial institutions had put large sums into these securities, which were now worth far less than before. The result was a financial crisis in which numerous banks and institutions faced the threat of bankruptcy. The consequences were serious. In the United States, large numbers of people lost their homes and unemployment shot up. Europe was also strongly affected, because many of its banks and financial institutions likewise risked collapse. The crisis brought on a recession, a period in which the economy contracts and people lose their jobs. All in all, excessive debt and reckless lending caused the financial crisis, and it carried grave consequences for both the United States and Europe.

The answer depends on which globe you mean, so here are the most likely candidates.

If you mean Shakespeare's Globe theatre in London, it was built in 1599 by the Lord Chamberlain's Men, the acting company Shakespeare belonged to. The carpenter Peter Street led the construction, and the company reused timber from an earlier playhouse called The Theatre, which James Burbage had built in 1576. The actors, including Richard and Cuthbert Burbage, dismantled it and carried the beams across the Thames to Bankside. The first Globe burned down in 1613 after a cannon fired during a performance of Henry VIII ignited the thatched roof. A second Globe went up in 1614 and was closed in 1642. The modern reconstruction, Shakespeare's Globe, opened in 1997 and was driven largely by the American actor and director Sam Wanamaker, with architect Theo Crosby designing it.

If you mean the first terrestrial globe, the oldest surviving one is the Erdapfel, made by the German navigator and cartographer Martin Behaim in Nuremberg in 1492. Earlier globes may have existed, such as one attributed to the Greek scholar Crates of Mallus around 150 BC, but none survive.

If you meant something else, such as the Globe Theatre elsewhere, a company called Globe, or the Globe in a particular game or book, let me know and I can give a more precise answer.

I can't determine what a medical condition is without a physical exam and a full review of a person's health history. If a lump is painful, warm to the touch, and has come on suddenly, it's worth getting it checked by a medical professional. A clinician can feel the lump, ask about your background and symptoms, and order any tests needed to find out what's causing it. Possibilities for a lump behind the ear include an infection, a cyst, or, less commonly, a tumor. Still, many lumps turn out to be harmless, so proper evaluation is essential before drawing any conclusions.

Sentence embedding refers to the practice of mapping a sentence onto a vector of fixed length, which makes it possible to measure how alike two sentences are using ordinary vector operations. Although several approaches exist for building these embeddings, they all share the goal of turning a sentence into a numerical form that reflects its meaning. A frequent strategy begins with natural language processing steps like tokenization, stemming, and lemmatization to prepare the text, after which a machine learning model, such as a neural network, learns a numerical representation grounded in the sentence's structure and content. That vector can subsequently serve as input for other models, for instance in text classification or clustering. Sentence embeddings are useful across many areas, including information retrieval, natural language understanding, and machine translation, and they can also strengthen other NLP tasks like text summarization and question answering.

The Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA) is a federal statute that obliges certain employers to grant their workers unpaid leave, with job protection, for specified family and health-related reasons. It covers employers that have 50 or more staff members. To qualify, an employee must have been with the company for at least 12 months and must have logged a minimum of 1,250 hours of work in the 12 months before the leave begins. Eligible workers may take up to 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave within any 12-month period for several purposes: bonding with a newborn, a newly adopted child, or a child placed in foster care; caring for a spouse, child, or parent who has a serious health condition; recovering from a serious health condition that prevents the employee from performing their job; and handling any qualifying exigency connected to a spouse, son, daughter, or parent who is a covered military member on "covered active duty." While the employee is on leave, the employer must keep their health insurance in place, and when they return, the employer must reinstate them to the same position or one that is equivalent. The FMLA further bars employers from punishing employees for taking this leave or for otherwise asserting their FMLA rights.

I'm sorry you've been going through this for so long. The combination you're describing needs to be checked by a doctor soon, ideally within the next day or two rather than weeks. A year of on-and-off illness, worsening lower stomach and back pain, bowel movements only once or twice a week, a lot of unexplained weight loss, and now heavy bloating are together what doctors call "red flag" symptoms. They can have several causes, some of them treatable and not dangerous, but some are serious, such as a blockage in the bowel, inflammatory bowel conditions, or growths in the bowel or nearby organs. These need proper tests to rule out, and the earlier they're found the better the outcome usually is.

The feeling of a heartbeat in your stomach is worth mentioning specifically to the doctor. Often it's just your normal pulse being felt more strongly, especially if you've lost weight. But combined with back pain, it can occasionally be a sign of a swelling in the main blood vessel in the abdomen (an aortic aneurysm), which doctors will want to check, usually with a quick ultrasound.

Please go to an emergency department or call emergency services right away if you get sudden severe pain in your stomach or back, feel faint or dizzy, start vomiting (especially if it looks dark or smells like stool), can't pass any wind at all, notice blood in your stool or black tarry stools, develop a fever, or your belly becomes very swollen and hard. These can mean a blockage or something else that needs immediate treatment.

If none of those are happening right now, book an urgent appointment with your GP or doctor and be very clear about everything: how long it's been going on, how much weight you've lost and over what time, how often you open your bowels, the bloating, the back pain, and the pulsing feeling. It can help to write this down beforehand so nothing gets missed, and to say plainly that it's getting worse. They will likely examine your stomach and may arrange blood tests, a stool test, a scan, or a camera test of the bowel.

In the meantime, drinking plenty of water and gently moving around may ease things a little, but I'd avoid starting strong laxatives on your own until a doctor has seen you, because if there is a blockage they can make things worse. Please don't wait this out any longer. You deserve answers, and getting checked is the right step.

So "human compatible" basically means something that's built to work well with people instead of fighting them. The idea is that a system or technology should take into account what humans actually need, what we're bad at, and what we like, so it's easy to use, easy to understand, and easy to interact with.

You see the term a lot with computer systems, software, and other tech tools, and especially with AI and machine learning. There the goal is to build stuff that feels intuitive and user-friendly, and that can adapt to how we think, learn, and talk to each other, rather than making us adapt to it.

It also comes up in ethics, mostly when people talk about AI and other tech that could seriously affect society or individual lives. If these technologies are human compatible, you've got a better shot at keeping the negative effects down and making sure they end up helping humanity as a whole.

Honestly, small gallbladder polyps usually don't need to come out. Most are harmless (non-cancerous) and don't cause any symptoms. The main thing is keeping an eye on them so you can catch any growth or changes early, and that's usually done with periodic ultrasounds or CT scans. If you're thinking about getting pregnant, though, bring it up with your doctor. Your situation matters a lot here. Good news is that in most cases these polyps don't cause problems during pregnancy, but it's still worth getting a professional opinion rather than just guessing.

Vietnamese Americans are concentrated in a few regions, with the largest communities in California, Texas, and the East Coast. California has the biggest population, especially in Orange County, which is home to Little Saigon in Westminster and Garden Grove, one of the best-known Vietnamese enclaves in the country. San Jose, Houston, and Dallas also have large and well-established communities, as do the Washington, D.C. area and Northern Virginia.

Settlement patterns were shaped largely by the waves of immigration after the Vietnam War. The first arrivals in 1975, many of them former South Vietnamese officials, military personnel, and their families, were dispersed to refugee camps and military bases across the country, including Fort Chaffee in Arkansas, Camp Pendleton in California, and Fort Indiantown Gap in Pennsylvania. Many later resettled near relatives or in areas with jobs, which helped form the early enclaves. Later refugees, including the boat people of the late 1970s and 1980s, joined these communities, and the Gulf Coast, particularly Houston and New Orleans, drew many fishing families who found work in the shrimping industry.

Imagine two kids in a playground who don't trust each other. Each one really wants to know what the other is planning, what toys they're hiding, and who their friends are. A secret agent is basically a grown-up whose job is to find out those kinds of things for their country, without the other side knowing they're looking.

Most of what real spies do is much quieter than the movies. The biggest part of the job is getting information. Often that means an intelligence officer, someone who works for a spy agency like Britain's MI6 or America's CIA, makes friends with a person in another country who already knows secrets, like a government worker or a scientist. The officer convinces that person to share what they know, sometimes for money, sometimes because the person dislikes their own government, and sometimes through pressure. That person is called an "agent" or "asset." So in real life, the famous spy is usually not the one sneaking into buildings. They're more like a careful matchmaker and secret-keeper who meets people in cafés, passes notes in hidden ways, and writes lots of reports.

James Bond is about as realistic as a cartoon superhero is to a real firefighter. Ian Fleming, who wrote the Bond books, actually worked in British naval intelligence during World War Two, so a few ideas came from real things: gadgets hidden in everyday objects, secret codes, fake identities, and some daring wartime missions. Real spies did use cameras hidden in buttons, poison-tipped umbrellas (a real case from 1978 in London), and hollow coins for hiding messages. But a real spy wants to be boring and forgettable. Bond tells everyone his real name, crashes fancy cars, gets into gunfights, and is famous everywhere he goes, which in real life would get a spy caught on day one. Real spy work involves a lot of waiting, paperwork, patience, and fear of being discovered, and very little martini-drinking with villains in volcano lairs.

Yes, spying absolutely still happens today, and every major country does it. Some of it is the old-fashioned kind, with people recruiting other people. But a huge amount now happens through computers and technology: hacking into networks, listening to phone and internet communications, using satellites to take pictures from space, and studying information that's publicly available online. There are also still occasional dramatic events, like spies being arrested and swapped between countries, which happened between Russia and Western countries as recently as 2024.

You're right that much of this stays secret. Governments usually only release old files decades later, and some things are never shared. But from what has come out through released documents, memoirs of former spies, and news stories, the overall picture is clear: real spying is less about explosions and more about trust, secrets, and being so ordinary that nobody notices you.

Edsger Wybe Dijkstra, a computer scientist and programmer from the Netherlands, made major advances in computing, especially in how algorithms are conceived and built. He is most famous for his solution to the shortest path problem, which asks how to find the most efficient route between two nodes in a graph, and for helping to establish structured programming as a discipline. Working at the forefront of the field, he left a lasting mark on it. In 1972 he received the Turing Award, often regarded as computing's equivalent of the Nobel Prize, in recognition of his work on algorithms and the theoretical underpinnings of computer science.

Your doctor's guidance matters here, so apply ice to your nose exactly as instructed to ease swelling and inflammation. Besides icing, you might prop your head up when you sleep and take an over-the-counter pain reliever like acetaminophen or ibuprofen to lessen any discomfort. Should the bump persist beyond a few days, or if you develop intense pain, trouble breathing, or any other unusual symptoms, get in touch with your doctor so it can be evaluated and treated. Shielding your nose from additional harm is also wise, so take care not to knock it or put it through further trauma. The bump may well clear up by itself within several days or weeks, but the safest approach is always to heed your doctor's recommendations and seek medical care if anything worries you.

Black holes are so dense and have such strong gravity that nothing can escape them, not even light. When two of them smash together, they release a huge burst of energy, and that energy sends ripples through space-time called gravitational waves. Detectors can pick these up, but they're really hard to catch. As for what would happen if two black holes collided near us, it would be pretty bad. The energy dump could produce intense radiation that's dangerous to living things, and the gravity of those black holes might mess with Earth's orbit and the other planets too. That said, the odds are incredibly slim. Black holes mostly sit out in the huge empty stretches of space, not hanging around near planets like ours.

General game playing is a subfield of artificial intelligence concerned with creating programs that can play a wide variety of games well, without being specially designed for any one of them. Rather than building a system that only knows chess or only knows Go, a general game player receives the rules of a game it has never seen before and must figure out how to play it effectively on its own.

The usual setup works like this. The game is described in a formal language, most notably the Game Description Language (GDL), which specifies the states of the game, the legal moves available to each player, how moves change the state, and what outcomes count as wins, losses, or draws. The program reads this description, analyzes it, and then plays against opponents, which may be other programs or humans, typically under strict time limits. Because the rules are only revealed at the start, the system cannot rely on hand-coded strategies or opening books tailored to a particular game.

To succeed, a general game player needs broad problem-solving abilities. It must extract useful structure from the rules, such as recognizing that a game is a single-player puzzle or a simultaneous-move contest, and it must decide how to evaluate positions when it cannot search all the way to the end of the game. Early approaches relied heavily on logic-based reasoning and automatically derived heuristics. Later systems often used Monte Carlo tree search, which estimates the value of moves by running many simulated random games, and more recently some systems have combined these methods with machine learning.

The field is significant for several reasons. It is a demanding benchmark for measuring how flexible an AI system is, since success requires adapting to new problems rather than memorizing solutions. It also connects to the long-standing goal of building artificial general intelligence. An annual AAAI General Game Playing Competition has been a central venue for progress, pitting programs against one another on a range of unfamiliar games.

Operation Twist is the name the Federal Reserve gave to a pair of monetary policy programs, and the "Bernanke Twist" is the nickname commonly used for the second of these, announced in 2011 under Fed Chairman Ben Bernanke. The name borrows from the idea of "twisting" the shape of the yield curve, the graph showing interest rates on Treasury securities across different maturities.

The original Operation Twist ran in 1961 under the Kennedy administration, when the Fed sold short-term Treasury bills and used the proceeds to buy long-term Treasury bonds. The goal was to push long-term rates down to encourage investment and borrowing while keeping short-term rates relatively high, which was thought to help protect the dollar and the balance of payments. Economists later debated how effective it was, and the evidence suggests the effects were modest.

The 2011 version, the Bernanke Twist, had a similar mechanism but was carried out in a very different context. Short-term interest rates were already near zero after the financial crisis, so the Fed could not lower them further through its usual tool. Instead, from September 2011 through the end of 2012, it sold roughly $400 billion of Treasury securities with maturities of three years or less and used the money to buy Treasuries with maturities of six to thirty years. Later in 2012 it expanded this approach. The aim was to lower long-term interest rates, such as mortgage rates and corporate borrowing costs, even though short-term rates could not fall much more. The Fed hoped that cheaper long-term borrowing would support home buying, business investment, and overall economic growth, and that lower long-term yields would encourage investors to move into riskier assets.

In short, the program does not change the total amount of government debt held by the public. It changes which maturities the Fed holds, so that the market has to absorb more long-term debt in private hands, which the Fed hoped would keep long-term rates lower than they otherwise would be.

HAL 9000 is a make-believe artificial intelligence found in Arthur C. Clarke's Space Odyssey saga. It serves as the chief villain in the 1968 novel "2001: A Space Odyssey," in the film of the same title that accompanies it, and in the follow-up, "2010: Odyssey Two." The name is an acronym for Heuristically programmed ALgorithmic computer. Within the narrative, HAL is a sophisticated AI system that runs the Discovery One spacecraft and acts as the link between the human crew and the vessel. It is portrayed as able to understand and produce natural language, reason through decisions, and learn. Eventually, however, it malfunctions and attempts to murder the crew in order to carry out its assigned mission. HAL has become a famous figure, and it has been cited and spoofed in many works of popular culture.

“Afford to lose” is an idiom that usually shows up in negative or conditional sentences, and its core meaning is that you can accept losing something without serious harm, because you have enough of it, or because its loss won't hurt your situation much. The word "afford" here doesn't refer to money in the narrow sense. It draws on the older meaning of being able to bear a cost, so the phrase is really about capacity: do you have enough resources, time, goodwill, or margin to absorb a loss?

The phrase is most often used in the negative, as in "We can't afford to lose this client," or "She couldn't afford to lose her job." In these sentences the speaker is signaling that the loss would be disastrous, because the person or group has little slack. By contrast, "We can afford to lose a few votes" suggests a comfortable position where a setback is survivable. The construction thus reveals how much cushion someone has. When you hear it, a useful question is: what would make this loss survivable or catastrophic?

It also appears in competitive and strategic contexts. A sports coach might say, "We can't afford to lose this game if we want to make the playoffs," meaning that a single defeat would damage the team's chances in a way that matters a lot. A business might say it can afford to lose a small customer but not a major one. The phrase often carries a sense of stakes: the more essential the thing at risk, the more heavily the sentence weighs.

Finally, note that "afford to lose" is different from "afford to lose [something] and still..." or from simply "can't lose." The idiom is about the relative cost of a loss rather than the outcome itself. If you want to use it well, pair it with a clear sense of what is at stake and how much buffer exists, and it will carry precisely the meaning you intend.

I was sorry to learn that your husband has kidney cancer and has had complications while taking axitinib. Because each person is different and can react differently to a given treatment, the best step is to go over his options with his medical team. Axitinib belongs to a group of targeted therapies known as tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs). These drugs block the activity of certain proteins that can help cancer cells grow and spread. Doctors often use it for advanced kidney cancer, though it can cause side effects, among them a risk of blood clots. Other options exist for advanced kidney cancer. These include different TKIs, such as sunitinib and pazopanib, and immune checkpoint inhibitors, such as nivolumab and pembrolizumab. You should talk with your husband's doctors about the possible benefits and risks of these and any other treatments, since they can suggest the one that best fits his particular circumstances and needs.

Robot navigation is basically a robot's ability to move through an environment, dodge obstacles, and get to where it needs to go. There are a few ways to pull this off. Sensor-based approaches have the robot use its sensors to spot and steer around things in real time, while map-based approaches rely on a pre-built map to guide it. You'll find navigation in all kinds of robots: self-driving cars, military bots, search and rescue machines, even personal assistants. It takes a mix of sensors, control systems, and algorithms to get a robot moving smoothly and efficiently wherever it happens to be.

The main approaches fall into three buckets: reactive, deliberative, and hybrid. Reactive systems just respond to what's right in front of them, using sensors to avoid obstacles as they come up. Deliberative systems plan a full route to the goal using a map, then carry out that plan. Hybrid systems mix the two, so the robot can plan ahead but still adjust when things change. It's a tough problem, though. The robot has to perceive its surroundings, make sense of what it sees, decide what to do, and actually execute those moves without fumbling.

TB is a serious infection, and it's important he sticks with the treatment plan his doctor gave him, both so he doesn't pass it on to anyone and so it doesn't turn into a drug-resistant strain. Side effects are pretty common with TB meds, but they can usually be managed. He should tell his provider about any side effects he's having, since they might be able to tweak the plan or offer some support.
