Meta-learning in computer science refers to approaches in which a system learns how to learn. Rather than training a model to perform one specific task from scratch, a meta-learning system is trained across a distribution of related tasks so that it acquires general knowledge about the learning process itself. Once that knowledge is in place, the system can adapt to a new task quickly, often from only a handful of examples, with far less data and computation than a conventional model would need.

The core idea is a two-level structure. At the inner level, a model learns a particular task from a small amount of task-specific data. At the outer level, a meta-learner observes many such learning episodes and adjusts something about the inner learning procedure, such as its starting parameters, its update rule, its hyperparameters, or its architecture, so that future inner-level learning becomes more efficient. Training therefore operates over tasks rather than over individual data points.

Several families of methods are commonly distinguished. Optimization-based approaches, of which Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning (MAML) is the best known, seek an initialization from which a few gradient steps produce good performance on any new task. Metric-based approaches, such as prototypical networks and matching networks, learn an embedding space in which new examples can be classified by comparing them to a few labeled references. Model-based approaches use architectures, often with memory or recurrent components, that internally store and update information as they process a new task. Some researchers also work on learning the learning algorithm itself, for example by training neural networks to output update rules, or on automating the choice of hyperparameters and neural architectures.

Meta-learning is motivated by the observation that humans learn new concepts from very few examples, whereas standard deep learning typically requires large datasets. It is therefore central to few-shot learning, and it appears in areas such as automated machine learning (AutoML), where systems learn which architectures or settings tend to work well, in reinforcement learning, where agents must adapt quickly to changing environments, and in personalization, where a model must adjust to a new user with limited data.

The field also faces challenges. Meta-learning requires large collections of tasks for meta-training, which can be expensive to assemble. Optimizing the outer loop is often computationally costly and can be unstable. There is also the risk of meta-overfitting, where a system performs well on the training tasks but fails to generalize to tasks that differ substantially from them. Current research addresses these issues by improving efficiency, designing more diverse task distributions, and developing theory about when and why meta-learned systems generalize.

That slam comes from the idea that the middle class cares more about guarding its perks and social standing than about what's good for everyone else.

Dark spots on the heart, sometimes called myocardial abnormalities or heart muscle abnormalities, can result from a number of different causes. Some stem from problems with the heart's blood supply, including blocked coronary arteries or inflammation of the heart muscle. Past heart attacks, viral infections, and certain inherited conditions can also lead to these abnormalities. If your twin brother has been told he has dark spots on his heart and his cardiologist is worried, he should stick closely to the treatment plan he has been given. That plan might involve more testing, such as a cardiac catheterization (cath) or further imaging, to pinpoint what is causing the spots and to decide on the best course of treatment. He should also work with his healthcare provider to manage any underlying medical conditions, and he should adopt habits that support his heart, such as eating a healthy diet, exercising regularly, and avoiding smoking. As for you, talking over any health worries with a healthcare provider is always wise. If you have mitral valve prolapse (MVP) with regurgitation and an enlarged left ventricle, you should follow your recommended treatment plan and keep these conditions under control to protect your heart. Keeping up a healthy lifestyle matters too, as does getting medical care if you notice any new or worsening symptoms.

From what you've shared, your chest X-ray doesn't appear to show pneumonia, which is a lung infection. The doctor instead diagnosed asthmatic bronchitis, a condition where asthma causes the airways of the lungs (the bronchi) to become inflamed. The X-ray may have revealed a slight coarsening of the bronchovascular markings. These are the fine lines and patterns on the image that represent the bronchi and the blood vessels within the lungs. The costophrenic angles, meaning the corners where the ribs meet the lining of the lung, were described as sharp, which is a normal result. The heart is not enlarged, and the aorta, the major vessel that carries oxygen-rich blood from the heart out to the rest of the body, is described as uncoiled, meaning it isn't twisted or bent in an unusual way. All in all, the X-ray seems not to have shown any significant abnormalities or causes for concern. Keep in mind, though, that X-rays only display the structure of the body's organs and tissues, so they cannot always pick up certain conditions or diseases. It's always wise to keep in touch with your doctor and raise any questions or worries you have about your health.

A medallion guarantee is a stamp or signature placed on a document to confirm that it is authentic and genuine. It usually appears on financial papers like checks, money orders, and drafts, and banks and other financial institutions often require it to keep financial transactions secure. It is generally issued by a financial institution or another authorized organization, with the purpose of guarding against fraud and forgery. To obtain one, the document must satisfy specific standards of authenticity and security, and the institution may charge fees or other costs for providing the guarantee.

So when you pay by debit or credit at a restaurant, the server usually brings the card reader to your table and runs the payment right there, before you head out. If you want to tip, just tell them how much you're adding and they'll punch it into the machine. That tip gets tacked onto the total on your card, so the meal and the tip go through together. Say your meal comes to $20 and you want to leave $3 (that's 15%). The reader charges $23 to your card, covering both the food and the tip in one go. Make sense?

Nonparametric statistics is a branch of statistics that makes few or no assumptions about the shape or form of the underlying probability distribution that generates the data. Classical methods, by contrast, often assume the data follow a specific distribution, such as a normal (Gaussian) distribution, and then estimate a fixed set of parameters like the mean and variance. Nonparametric methods drop or relax these assumptions, which makes them more flexible and more robust when the assumptions are doubtful, when the sample is small, or when the data are ordinal or otherwise not well described by a standard family of distributions.

The name can be a little misleading. Nonparametric methods do not mean that there are no parameters at all; rather, the number and nature of the parameters are not fixed in advance. In a nonparametric model, the amount of structure the model can capture typically grows with the amount of data available. For example, a histogram or a kernel density estimate can approximate almost any shape of distribution, and its complexity adapts to the sample.

Several common nonparametric tools illustrate the idea. The sign test and the Wilcoxon signed-rank test compare the location of two related samples by using only the signs or ranks of differences rather than their actual values. The Mann-Whitney U test does a similar job for two independent samples. The Kruskal-Wallis test extends this idea to comparing several groups, and Spearman's rank correlation measures monotonic association between variables without assuming linearity or normality. Other important methods include the empirical cumulative distribution function, bootstrap resampling, and kernel density estimation, as well as nonparametric regression techniques such as local polynomial smoothing and splines.

The main advantages of nonparametric methods are their robustness to outliers and to departures from assumed distributions, and their applicability to data types that do not naturally fit numerical or normal models. Their main drawbacks are that they can be less statistically powerful than correctly specified parametric methods when the parametric assumptions actually hold, and that they can require larger samples or more computation to give precise estimates, especially in high-dimensional settings.

Computation time is the amount of time a computer or program takes to carry out a task or process. It is usually measured in seconds, milliseconds, or other units of elapsed time, and it reflects how long the processor spends executing instructions, as opposed to waiting for input, reading from disk, or communicating over a network. In some contexts, the term is used more loosely to mean the total wall-clock time from start to finish, which can include those waiting periods.

The concept is central to evaluating software and algorithms. Developers use computation time to compare the efficiency of different approaches, to identify slow sections of code that need optimization, and to estimate how a program will perform as the size of its input grows. In theoretical computer science, analysts often describe computation time in terms of asymptotic complexity, such as whether the time required grows linearly, quadratically, or exponentially with the input size, rather than measuring it in seconds on a particular machine.

Computation time also depends on many factors beyond the algorithm itself, including the speed of the hardware, the efficiency of the programming language and compiler, the load on the system from other processes, and the characteristics of the data being processed. For this reason, careful benchmarking typically involves running the same task multiple times under controlled conditions and reporting averages or ranges.

Race and gender are two different things, and people's experiences with them can be pretty different too. Gender is about who you feel like you are on the inside, and it doesn't always match the sex you were assigned at birth. Race is about physical traits like skin color, eye shape, and hair texture. Those usually get passed down from your parents, and you can't really change them. Someone can choose to identify with a gender other than the one they were assigned at birth, but they can't choose a different race, since that's not something they can switch.

A put option is a contract that gives its buyer the right, but not the obligation, to sell a specific asset at a fixed price, called the strike price, on or before a certain expiration date. The asset is most often a stock, but it can also be an index, commodity, currency, or exchange-traded fund. The buyer pays an upfront fee called the premium to the seller, also known as the writer, who takes on the obligation to buy the asset at the strike price if the buyer chooses to exercise.

People buy puts mainly for two reasons: to profit from an expected price decline, or to protect an asset they already own. Suppose you own shares trading at 100 and buy a put with a strike of 95 for a premium of 3 per share. If the stock falls to 70, you can still sell at 95, so your loss is limited to the drop from 100 to 95 plus the 3 premium. Used this way, a put works like insurance, and the strategy is often called a protective put. As a speculative bet, the buyer profits when the underlying falls well below the strike. In the same example, if the stock drops to 70, the put is worth about 25 at expiration, so the net gain is 22 per share after subtracting the premium. The break-even point at expiration is the strike minus the premium, here 92.

The buyer's maximum loss is the premium paid, which occurs if the stock stays at or above the strike at expiration and the option expires worthless. The buyer's maximum gain is large but finite, since a stock cannot fall below zero; it equals the strike price minus the premium, times the number of shares, which is normally 100 per contract.

The seller sees the opposite picture. The seller collects the premium and hopes the option expires worthless. The risk is substantial if the stock collapses, since the seller must buy at the strike regardless of how low the market price has fallen. Many sellers write cash-secured puts, setting aside enough money to buy the shares, sometimes because they would be happy to own the stock at that price.

Several factors determine a put's price. Intrinsic value is the amount by which the strike exceeds the current stock price, if at all. A put is in the money when the stock is below the strike, at the money when they are about equal, and out of the money when the stock is above the strike. Time value reflects the chance the option becomes more valuable before expiration, and it decays as expiration approaches, a effect known as theta. Implied volatility also matters: higher expected price swings raise option prices. Interest rates and dividends have smaller effects.

American-style puts can be exercised any time before expiration, while European-style puts can be exercised only at expiration. Most traders do not exercise at all; they close the position by selling the option before expiration to capture its remaining value.

Puts carry risks worth remembering. Buyers can lose their entire premium quickly, especially if they choose short expirations. Sellers face large potential losses and may face margin calls. Because options are leveraged and complex, they suit investors who understand how pricing, time decay, and volatility interact.

Symbolic computation, also called symbolic algebra or algebraic manipulation, is a branch of math where you work with algebraic expressions and equations by simplifying and transforming them symbolically. Instead of plugging in numbers, you treat the quantities as symbols. That lets you tackle all sorts of problems, from algebraic and differential equations to integral equations. You can also do operations on polynomials, matrices, and other mathematical objects. The big upside is that it often shows you more about how a problem is structured and how its pieces relate than numerical methods do. That's especially handy with complex or abstract stuff, where crunching numbers alone can leave you guessing about what's really going on. There are plenty of programs built for this, like Mathematica, Maple, and Maxima. You type in expressions or equations and manipulate them symbolically to find solutions or simplify things.

The Netflix Prize was a data science contest Netflix ran to make its movie recommendations better. It went from 2006 to 2009 and pulled in more than 50,000 people from 186 countries. Netflix put up $1 million for whoever could build the best algorithm for predicting how users would rate films, using their past ratings. The target was to beat Netflix's own recommendation accuracy by at least 10%, which would've made a real difference to the company's bottom line since happier customers stick around longer. In the end, a team called "BellKor's Pragmatic Chaos" hit that mark and took the prize. The money got split among the members, who were researchers from AT&T Labs and the University of Toronto. The contest had a big effect on data science and machine learning, and it showed people how well large-scale collaborative competitions could push research forward.

Lots of big American cities sit on state lines because rivers and rivers' geography made them good places to settle. Many state borders were drawn along rivers, like the Mississippi, the Missouri, and the Ohio. Think of a river as a long, wet highway. Boats could carry goods up and down it, so towns grew up on its banks where people could trade, unload cargo, and swap things with farmers. When a river marks a border, a town built at a good spot on its bank ends up right on the line between two states.

Cities also grew where rivers met or where land was easy to cross. Kansas City and Omaha sit on the Missouri River, which was a main route for boats heading west. St. Louis became a busy hub because it was near where the Missouri meets the Mississippi, so boats from many directions stopped there. Memphis sits on a high bluff above the Mississippi, a good, dry, safe place to build a town and a port. Cincinnati grew on the Ohio River for the same kind of reason.

So it's a bit like a lemonade stand: people set up where the most people walk by. The river was the busiest street around, and the border just happened to run down the middle of it.

Yes, you should take this seriously, and I would strongly encourage you not to wait for your GP appointment tonight. New weakness or heaviness in one arm, especially together with feeling light-headed and spaced out, can be a sign of a stroke or a transient ischaemic attack (a "mini-stroke"), and your family history of strokes and a brain haemorrhage makes this more concerning. Please call emergency services now (999 in the UK, 112 in Europe, 911 in the US) or have someone take you to an emergency department straight away. Do not drive yourself.

Stroke treatment is very time-sensitive. Some of the most effective treatments only work within a few hours of symptoms starting, and even if that window has passed since yesterday afternoon, symptoms that are ongoing or changing need same-day hospital assessment with a brain scan, which a GP surgery cannot provide. If this turns out to be something less serious, such as a trapped nerve, a migraine variant, or a problem with blood pressure or blood sugar, that is a good outcome, and emergency staff would much rather see you and reassure you than have you wait.

Call for help immediately, if you haven't already, if you notice any of the warning signs summed up as FAST: your face drooping on one side, being unable to lift both arms and keep them up, slurred or confused speech, or difficulty finding words. The same applies to sudden severe headache, vision changes, trouble walking or balancing, numbness spreading to your face or leg, or worsening confusion. If you are alone, tell someone nearby or phone someone so you are not by yourself, and note the time your symptoms began and any changes so you can tell the medical team.

You know your own body, and the fact that you are worried enough to ask is itself a good reason to get checked urgently. Please seek emergency care now rather than waiting until this evening.

A vetting process is a systematic check of a person, organization, or proposal to confirm that it is trustworthy, qualified, or suitable before someone is allowed to take on a role, receive access, enter a partnership, or move forward with a decision. The word comes from the idea of closely examining or "vetting" something, much like a veterinarian examines an animal's health.

In practice, vetting can take many forms depending on the context. For employment, it often includes verifying references, confirming educational and professional credentials, checking criminal or financial records, and sometimes conducting interviews designed to assess character and reliability. For government security clearances, vetting may involve detailed background investigations into a person's associations, finances, and personal history. Businesses use vetting when selecting suppliers or investors, reviewing whether a company is financially sound, legally compliant, and free of red flags. Vetting is also used for volunteers working with children, for tenants applying to rent property, and for candidates seeking political office or membership in certain organizations.

The goal is to reduce risk by gathering reliable information before committing to something. A good vetting process follows consistent standards so that everyone is evaluated fairly, and it respects privacy and legal limits on what information may be collected.

Pancytopenia just means your counts are low across all three blood cell types: red cells, white cells, and platelets. There's no single cause. It can come from bone marrow problems, autoimmune conditions, or certain medications. Leucovorin and Livogen both get used for anemia, which is a low red cell count. Leucovorin is a form of folic acid, and your body needs folate to make red blood cells. Livogen contains iron and is mainly for anemia caused by iron deficiency. Most people take both safely when their doctor says so, but any medication can cause side effects. With Leucovorin you might get stomach pain, diarrhea, or nausea. Livogen can cause constipation, nausea, or stomach pain. Don't ignore side effects. Tell your doctor about them so they can keep an eye on things and tweak your treatment if needed. Keep up with your appointments too, so they can check that the plan is working and catch any changes early.

In science and research, a discovery is the process of making fresh observations or findings that deepen our understanding of the world. It might mean recognizing a previously unknown phenomenon, revealing new connections among phenomena we already know about, or obtaining new evidence that either supports or challenges an existing hypothesis. Discoveries can arise from many kinds of scientific and research work, such as running experiments, analyzing data, carrying out observations, and reviewing existing literature. Because it lets us broaden our knowledge of the world around us, discovery is a vital part of the scientific process. It can generate new insights, ideas, and theories, and it frequently drives major progress in areas like medicine, technology, and the environment. Discovery may also have practical uses, including the creation of new products or the adoption of new policies or practices. In short, discovery is a key element of scientific and research endeavors, since it teaches us more about the world and how it functions, and it allows us to make well-informed decisions and take suitable actions grounded in that understanding.

Computational complexity is a branch of computer science concerned with how much in the way of resources, such as time and memory, an algorithm needs to solve a problem. It serves as a gauge of how efficient an algorithm is and helps establish whether a given algorithm is practical for a particular problem. Within this field, the resources most often examined are running time, counted in steps or operations, and storage space, measured in the amount of memory consumed. An algorithm is regarded as efficient when it solves a problem within a sensible span of time and memory relative to the size of the input. By contrast, an algorithm that demands excessive time or memory to reach a solution is regarded as inefficient. Several distinct measures exist, among them time complexity, space complexity, and overall complexity. Time complexity captures how long an algorithm takes to solve a problem, whereas space complexity captures how much memory it requires. Overall complexity considers both of these together. Computational complexity theory matters greatly within computer science because it reveals the boundaries of what can be computed efficiently and guides the creation of algorithms that perform as well as possible. It also clarifies the trade-offs among competing algorithms and assists in selecting the most suitable one for a given task.

Insects can walk up glass because their feet are not as smooth as they look. Each foot has tiny, sticky pads and very fine hairs, and these let them grip surfaces that seem perfectly flat to us.

Think of it like this: if you press your hand against a window, it might stick a little bit. That happens because of a very gentle pull between your skin and the glass. An insect's foot works in a similar way, but it has many thousands of tiny hairs on its pads, each one splitting into even tinier tips. Those tips touch the glass in lots of little spots, and at those spots a weak, invisible attraction holds the foot in place. Because the hairs are so small and so many, they can grab on even though the glass looks slick.

Insects also have a sticky fluid on their pads, a bit like a drop of oil, which helps the hairs stay close to the glass. When the insect wants to move, it simply lifts a foot away, and the hairs let go easily. So it sticks, lets go, sticks, and lets go with each step, which is how it climbs up.

So the glass is not really something the insect hangs onto with a hook or a claw. It is more like the insect is gently holding on with millions of tiny sticky fingertips.

Engines are usually mounted at the front of most cars since that placement works well. It keeps the vehicle's weight evenly distributed, which improves how easily it drives, and it also simplifies repairs when a problem arises under the hood. Some luxury models instead place the engine at the rear, which can boost acceleration. With the engine's mass resting over the rear wheels, those wheels grip the road better when the car speeds up. The drawback is that the weight is less evenly balanced, so handling can become more difficult. Ultimately, the choice depends on what the designers believe suits a specific vehicle. They weigh factors such as the intended top speed, how the car will handle, and how comfortable the people inside will be.

Steam is a digital distribution platform run by Valve Corporation, and it handles digital rights management, multiplayer gaming, and social networking. Valve launched it in 2003 mainly so they could push automatic updates to their own games, but it's grown into a storefront for tons of games from other developers. You can get it on Windows, macOS, and Linux. You buy games through the store, then download and play them via the Steam client. Sure, there's plenty of single-player stuff, but there are also multiplayer titles, plus tools for streaming and broadcasting your gameplay. There's also user reviews, forums, and community groups, so you can hang out with other players.

Erie, Colorado sits in two counties. Most of the town is in Weld County, but the western portion lies in Boulder County. The town is located in the northern Front Range area, roughly between Boulder and Longmont to the west and Brighton to the southeast, and it has grown quickly as a suburban community in the Denver metropolitan area. Because it straddles the county line, residents' property taxes, voting, and some services can depend on which side of the line their address falls on.

Multi-level marketing (MLM) is a commercial arrangement in which a firm distributes its goods through a web of self-employed sellers, known as "distributors." These individuals earn money not just from their own sales, but also from the sales of the people they bring into the business, and from the sales of those people's recruits. Because of this layered payout structure, the arrangement is often called a "pyramid." Those near the top, a small group who have signed up large numbers of others, often appear to earn substantial incomes, whereas the many people at the bottom, who have recruited no one, typically earn little or nothing.

Critics regard MLM as a scam, arguing that the company's real priority is expanding its roster of distributors rather than moving products to customers. In their view, the firm cares more about persuading people to join as sellers than about generating genuine consumer demand. Others accept MLM as a legitimate business model that is simply very hard to make work. They contend that earning money through it is possible but demands considerable effort and commitment, and that most who attempt it end up earning little or nothing. Overall, anyone weighing an MLM, like any business opportunity, should proceed carefully: research thoroughly, ask pointed questions, and weigh the possible risks and rewards before committing.

Sorry to hear you're dealing with pain in your testicles and your belly. If it's persistent or really bad, please get it checked out, since it could point to something that needs treatment. Testicular pain has a few common causes, like infection, injury, or conditions such as testicular torsion or epididymitis. Torsion is an emergency: the spermatic cord, which supplies blood to the testicle, twists, and it causes severe pain and swelling. If it isn't treated fast, you can lose the testicle. Epididymitis is inflammation of the epididymis, the tube that carries sperm away from the testicle. It's usually from a bacterial infection, which can include an STI, though other things can trigger it too. Belly pain is even more varied. It could be digestive trouble, an infection, or something like appendicitis or a kidney stone. Try to see a doctor soon if the pain sticks around or gets worse. They can figure out what's going on and tell you how to treat it. Until then, skip whatever seems to make it worse and take an over-the-counter painkiller as the label says.

So the Kanab ambersnail (Oxyloma haydeni kanabensis) is this tiny snail that's native to the Kanab Creek drainage, which runs through parts of Arizona and Utah. The US Fish and Wildlife Service put it on the endangered list back in 1990. The big reason is that its habitat is really limited, so it doesn't take much to hurt it. Things like water development, livestock grazing, and off-road vehicles can all degrade or wipe out the places it lives. The FWS did put together a recovery plan for it, and that plan covers protecting and restoring the habitat and keeping tabs on how the population is doing.

I'm sorry your daughter is dealing with this. A rash that follows a cold in a toddler is often a viral rash, which usually fades on its own within a few days to a week or so. Still, because she is so young, it's worth having her doctor look at it soon, ideally within the next day or so, especially since it appeared after she was already sick.

In the meantime, a few things can help her feel more comfortable. Keep her skin cool and her clothing loose and soft, since heat and tight fabric can make itching worse. A lukewarm (not hot) bath or a gentle wash with a mild, fragrance-free soap can soothe her, and patting the skin dry rather than rubbing it helps too. A plain, fragrance-free moisturizer like petroleum jelly or a thick cream applied after bathing can ease dryness and itch. For itching, you can give a children's antihistamine such as diphenhydramine or cetirizine, but check the dose carefully for her weight and age and confirm with her doctor or pharmacist first, since some of these are not recommended for very young children. Try to keep her from scratching by keeping her nails short and trimmed.

Please avoid putting Vicks VapoRub on her chest and stomach right now, since it can irritate broken or itchy skin, and it is not recommended for children under two. Also, she should not use the Hyland's cold and cough product unless her doctor says it is appropriate, since many of these products are not recommended for young children, and a rash can sometimes be a reaction to a medicine.

Seek medical care promptly, or go to urgent care or the emergency room, if she develops a fever that is high or lasts more than a couple of days, has trouble breathing or wheezing, has swelling of the face, lips, or tongue, seems unusually drowsy or hard to wake, becomes very fussy or stops eating and drinking, or if the rash looks like bruising or small purple or red spots that do not fade when you press a clear glass against them.

Since she is almost two and a half and had a recent cold, please call her pediatrician and describe the rash, the itching, and the medicines she has been taking. They can tell you what is most likely causing it and whether she needs to be seen.

gleixia@163.com Q. I can't get my face to look better no matter how healthy I eat. Why?

Hi doctor, I've been eating well, but my face structure still isn't changing. I used to eat two eggs a day. My eyes look sunken, and I really want a better structure and brighter-looking eyes and face. I'm 6'2" and 70 kg. Diet alone probably isn't the whole story here. Good food helps your overall health and can have some effect on your skin, but it's not the only thing that shapes how your face looks. Genes matter a lot, since they determine your facial structure and skin type. Aging plays a part too: skin gets less elastic and makes less collagen over time, so fine lines and wrinkles show up. Sun exposure is a big one, because too much of it damages skin and leads to lines, wrinkles, and uneven tone. Hormones matter as well, and they shift during things like menopause or pregnancy. Stress can also take a toll, since heavy stress makes it harder for your body to keep skin healthy. A steady routine of cleansing, moisturizing, and sun protection helps a lot with how your skin looks. If you're really worried about your face, see a dermatologist or another healthcare provider. They can look at your overall health, suggest lifestyle changes, and talk through treatment options that might help.

A level (short for Advanced level) is a qualification you can take in the UK, Isle of Man, and Channel Islands, usually between the ages of 16 and 18. You can study all sorts of subjects, like maths, science, English, history, or languages. Universities and employers see them as a solid measure of academic ability, and in the UK they're often what you need to get into uni. The whole thing splits into two parts: AS (Advanced Subsidiary) level, which you usually do in the first year and which covers about half the material, and the A2 level, with exams normally sitting at the end of year two. Grades run from A* down to E. A* is the top, and A and A* are seen as really good. B, C, and D are good too, just not quite as impressive. An E counts as a pass, but it's not exactly a strong result. If A levels aren't your thing, you can also go for the International Baccalaureate (IB) or the Cambridge Pre-U. Universities accept those as well.

Disney's Magic Kingdom is a theme park at the Walt Disney World Resort near Orlando, Florida. It opened on October 1, 1971, as the first park at the resort, and it is widely considered the flagship of Disney's U.S. parks. It is also one of the most visited theme parks in the world, drawing well over 17 million guests in a typical year.

The park is organized into themed areas, or "lands," arranged around a central hub. Visitors enter along Main Street, U.S.A., a nostalgic recreation of an early twentieth-century American town, and at its end stands Cinderella Castle, the park's iconic centerpiece. From there guests can go to Adventureland, Frontierland, Liberty Square, Fantasyland, Tomorrowland, and, more recently, areas themed to newer stories such as the Seven Dwarfs Mine Train in an expanded Fantasyland.

Attractions include classic rides like Pirates of the Caribbean, the Haunted Mansion, Jungle Cruise, Space Mountain, Big Thunder Mountain Railroad, "it's a small world," and Peter Pan's Flight. The park is also known for its live entertainment, including parades, character meet-and-greets, and the evening fireworks shows over the castle.

Magic Kingdom is based on the original Disneyland in California, which opened in 1955, but it is larger and has some differences in layout and rides. The park sits alongside other Walt Disney World parks, including EPCOT, Disney's Hollywood Studios, and Disney's Animal Kingdom, and it is connected to resort hotels by monorail, boat, and bus. Similar Magic Kingdom-style parks exist elsewhere, such as Tokyo Disneyland, Disneyland Paris, and Shanghai Disneyland, though each has its own variations.

Honestly, there are a few meds people usually end up trying for hair loss, and finasteride and minoxidil are the big two. Finasteride is a prescription pill that's mainly for male pattern hair loss. Minoxidil is a topical you rub onto your scalp, and it works for both men and women. If your hair loss is tied to hormones, your doctor might bring up hormone replacement or other meds that target that root cause.

That said, you really want a dermatologist or your regular doctor to figure out what's actually causing it, because the right treatment depends on that. They can walk you through the risks and benefits of each option and help you pick what fits your situation. Hair loss can come from genetics, certain medical conditions, or some medications, and sometimes fixing the underlying issue is enough to stop it or even bring some hair back.

I can't really suggest substitutes for the meds you mentioned since I don't know your history or what's going on with you specifically. Just don't change anything on your own without checking with your provider first.

Yes, it is possible to have a concussion without noticeable symptoms, although it is less common than having symptoms. Many people who sustain a concussion experience at least some signs, such as headache, dizziness, confusion, sensitivity to light or noise, or difficulty concentrating. However, some people feel fine right after the injury, or their symptoms are so mild that they dismiss them or never connect them to the bump or blow to the head. Symptoms can also be delayed, appearing hours or even a day or two later.

The chances of having no symptoms at all are hard to pin down precisely, because many mild concussions go unreported and there is no single test that confirms one. Factors such as the force of the impact, a person's age, and individual differences in how the brain responds all play a role. Some research suggests that a meaningful portion of people with head impacts, particularly in contact sports, report no symptoms even when studies look closely at them, but these numbers vary widely between studies.

Because of this, it is wise to take any blow to the head seriously, even if you feel fine. If you have been hit in the head or had your head shaken hard, watch for changes over the following days and rest from activities that could cause another impact. Seek medical care promptly if you develop worsening headache, repeated vomiting, unusual drowsiness, trouble waking, confusion, slurred speech, weakness or numbness, or if you lose consciousness. A doctor can evaluate you and advise on the appropriate level of rest and return to activity.

Font size is measured in a unit called a "point," and in modern digital typography one point is 1/72 of an inch. So a 12-point font is, in theory, 12/72 of an inch, which is one sixth of an inch. The number really is a measurement, but it measures something sneakier than you might expect.

Back when printing was done with metal type, every letter was carved onto the end of a little metal block. The font size described the height of that block, not the height of the letter on it. The block had to be tall enough to fit the tallest parts of any letter, like the top of a "b" or "h" and the tail hanging down from a "g" or "y," plus a little breathing room. Think of it like shoe boxes: every box for a size 12 shoe is the same size, but the shoes inside can be chunky boots or skinny sandals. The box is standardized, the shoe isn't.

Digital fonts kept this idea. When a designer makes a font on a computer, they draw the letters inside an invisible box called the "em square," and the font size sets how big that box is. But each designer decides how much of the box the letters fill. One might draw big, tall lowercase letters that nearly fill the space, while another might draw small, delicate letters with lots of empty room around them. Both are "12 point" because their invisible boxes are the same size, but the letters you actually see look bigger or smaller. That's why 12-point Verdana looks much larger than 12-point Times New Roman or Garamond. The most noticeable difference is usually the "x-height," which is how tall the lowercase letters like x, a, and e are compared to the capitals.

As for why 12 is the standard, there's no magic reason. It's just a size most people find comfortable to read on a printed page held at a normal distance, not so big that it wastes paper and not so small that it strains your eyes. Typewriters and early printing had similar common sizes, and when word processors came along, programs like Microsoft Word set 12 as the default, especially paired with Times New Roman. Schools and offices then wrote "12-point font" into their rules for essays and documents, which locked it in as a habit. Interestingly, because fonts vary so much, a rule like "12-point font" doesn't actually guarantee the same amount of text per page, which is why students have long been able to stretch essays by picking a font with bigger-looking letters.

Data from the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) shows that in 2019 the United States spent an average of $10,739 on healthcare for each person. That amount makes up a considerable share of the nation's gross domestic product (GDP), the combined value of all goods and services the economy produces. American healthcare spending is among the highest anywhere in the world, and costs are still climbing. Several factors help explain why healthcare is so expensive in the country. Among them are steep prescription drug prices, expensive hospital stays and medical procedures, and the heavy administrative expenses built into the healthcare system. The country's population is also large and getting older, which adds further pressure on the system and pushes costs higher. Many efforts are under way to bring these costs down, such as reforming the healthcare system, negotiating lower drug prices, and encouraging the use of cost-effective treatments. Even so, finding answers to the problem of high healthcare costs is still a complicated and difficult task.

A redshirt freshman is basically a college football player who sat out their first year, so they didn't play in any games, but they're still a freshman as far as eligibility goes. They've been enrolled at the school for a year by then, they just haven't suited up for a game yet.

The "redshirt" part comes from holding a guy out of competition for a season so he keeps that year of eligibility. Coaches usually do it with players who aren't quite ready for the college level, or who could use the extra time to practice and develop. It's not a punishment or anything, it's more like a head start.

The idea is that it lets a player end up with four full seasons of eligibility instead of just three.

Ayn Rand called her philosophy Objectivism, and you can think of it as resting on a few big ideas that fit together like building blocks.

The first idea is that the world is real and is what it is, no matter what anyone wishes or feels. A rock is a rock even if you really want it to be a cookie. The second idea is that people understand that real world by using their own minds and thinking carefully, which she called reason. Not by guessing, not by feelings alone, and not by just believing what someone else tells them.

The third idea is about how to be good. Rand thought each person's own life and happiness is the most important thing for them to take care of, and that it's right to work hard for what you want. She called this rational self-interest. She didn't mean being mean or stealing, because she thought taking from others was wrong too. She meant you shouldn't be expected to give up your own dreams just because someone else wants you to. People should trade fairly, like swapping a toy you made for a toy someone else made, and both of you are happy.

The fourth idea is about rules for living together. Rand believed the best system is one where people are free to make things, own what they make, and trade it, which is a kind of capitalism with very little government control. She thought the government's job is mainly to keep people from hurting or forcing each other.

You've already seen a lot of this in Anthem. That story is about a world where the word "I" has been erased and everyone must live only for the group. When the hero discovers his own mind and his own wants, it's a celebration of the individual. The other two books grow that same seed into bigger stories.

The Fountainhead is about an architect named Howard Roark who designs buildings his own way, even though everyone tells him to copy old styles and do what's popular. People laugh at him and try to stop him, but he refuses to give in. The book's main theme is being true to your own vision and creativity instead of living to please others or win their approval.

Atlas Shrugged is a much bigger story about a country falling apart. The people who invent things, run businesses, and keep everything working are treated badly and asked to keep giving and giving. So, led by a mysterious man named John Galt, they quietly go on strike and disappear. Without them, the world starts to stop working. The title imagines Atlas, the giant from old myths who holds up the sky, deciding to shrug and set it down. The theme is that creative, productive people hold up the world, and that society depends on minds that are free to think and work.

So, put very simply, all three books share the same heartbeat: your mind is your most important tool, your life belongs to you, and the world works best when people are free to think, create, and trade for themselves.

A propositional formula is an expression in propositional logic, the branch of logic that deals with statements that are either true or false and with how such statements combine. The basic building blocks are propositional variables, often written as letters like p, q, and r, each standing for a proposition that can take either the value true or the value false. These variables are combined using logical connectives such as negation (not), conjunction (and), disjunction (or), implication (if...then), and biconditional (if and only if). Parentheses are used to group subexpressions and make the structure unambiguous.

The formal definition is recursive. Every propositional variable is a formula. If A is a formula, then its negation, written not A or ¬A, is also a formula. If A and B are formulas, then combining them with any binary connective, such as (A ∧ B), (A ∨ B), (A → B), or (A ↔ B), produces a new formula. Nothing else counts as a formula. So an expression like (p ∧ ¬q) → r is a formula, while something like p ∧ → q is not, because it is not built according to these rules.

The meaning of a formula is determined by its truth value under a given assignment. An assignment gives each variable a truth value, and the truth value of the whole formula is then computed step by step from the truth values of its parts, using the standard truth tables for each connective. For example, under an assignment where p is true and q is false, the formula p ∧ ¬q evaluates to true, since ¬q is true and both conjuncts hold.

Propositional formulas are central to logic, mathematics, computer science, and electronics. They are used to model reasoning and arguments, to express conditions in programming, to design digital circuits, and to study problems such as satisfiability, where one asks whether some assignment makes a formula true. A formula that is true under every assignment is called a tautology, while one that is false under every assignment is a contradiction.

A Master Limited Partnership (MLP) is a business structure that blends the tax advantages of a partnership with the liquidity and ownership rights associated with a publicly traded company. These entities are frequently set up to run and manage energy-sector assets like pipelines, storage facilities, and natural resource extraction operations. Like ordinary stock, MLP units trade on a public exchange, so investors can freely buy and sell them. Still, MLPs differ from ordinary stock in several important ways.

The first difference is tax treatment. An MLP does not pay corporate income tax at the entity level. Rather, its income flows through to the individual partners, who must pay tax on their respective shares. For this reason, MLP investors may face a smaller overall tax burden than people who hold ordinary stock.

The second difference concerns payouts. MLPs must give a portion of their income to their partners in the form of "distributions." Though these resemble the dividends that ordinary stock pays, they receive different tax treatment. Distributions are regarded as a return of capital rather than ordinary income. They lower the cost basis of the MLP units, which can create a tax liability when the units are eventually sold.

The third difference involves ownership rights. MLP units give partners an ownership stake much like that granted by ordinary stock. However, voting rights attached to MLP units may be weaker, because the general partners usually keep control over management and decision-making.

Before investing in an MLP, it is wise to weigh its tax consequences and ownership rights with care. Speaking with a financial advisor or tax professional can also help you understand the possible advantages and disadvantages of these investments.

Okay, so semi-supervised learning is basically training a model on a mix of labeled and unlabeled data. Quick refresher: supervised learning uses fully labeled data, so every example comes with the right answer. Unsupervised learning gets no labels at all and has to find patterns on its own. Semi-supervised sits in the middle. You've got a small pile of labeled examples and a big pile of unlabeled ones, and the model tries to use what it learns from the labeled stuff to make sense of the rest.

Why bother? Labeling data is often expensive or slow. Think medical scans that need a specialist to mark them up. If you only have a handful of labels, semi-supervised methods can still get you a lot further than ignoring the unlabeled data entirely.

One common way to do it is self-training. You train a model on the small labeled set, use it to guess labels for the unlabeled examples, keep the guesses it's confident about, add those to the training set, and retrain. Then you repeat that loop until the model is labeling most of the data well. It's not magic, though. If the early guesses are wrong, the errors can snowball.

People use it for all sorts of things, like natural language processing, image classification, and speech recognition. It also plays nicely with other techniques, transfer learning being a popular pairing, and that combo can give your model a real boost.

A mortgage is a kind of loan that helps people pay for a house. The property being bought serves as collateral, so the lender keeps a legal claim on it until the debt is completely repaid. Each month, the borrower sends the lender a payment that covers both the principal, meaning the original sum borrowed, and the interest, which is what the lender charges for letting the borrower use that money. A home loan is simply another name for a mortgage, since both refer to borrowing specifically to purchase a residence, and people frequently use the two phrases as if they meant the same thing. Because a mortgage or home loan is a major financial commitment that can shape your finances for decades, it is wise to examine its terms closely before agreeing to it. Comparing offers from several lenders and reading the conditions of each loan carefully can help you determine whether it truly suits your circumstances.

Automated decision-making refers to the use of technology, often software, algorithms, or artificial intelligence, to make decisions about people or situations with little or no human involvement. Instead of a person reviewing information and judging the outcome, a system processes data according to predefined rules or learned patterns and produces a result, such as approving a loan, screening a job applicant, setting an insurance premium, or flagging a transaction as fraudulent.

These systems can operate in fully automated form, where the decision is executed immediately without any human review, or in semi-automated form, where the system recommends an outcome and a person makes the final call. The distinction matters because the more a decision relies on the machine's output alone, the greater the concern about errors, bias, and lack of accountability.

Because automated decisions can significantly affect people's lives, many legal frameworks now regulate them. The European Union's General Data Protection Regulation, for example, gives individuals the right not to be subject to decisions based solely on automated processing that have legal or similarly significant effects, unless certain conditions are met. Such rules typically require transparency about how the system works, the right to request human intervention, and the right to contest the outcome.

In short, automated decision-making is the delegation of decisions to computational systems, offering speed and consistency at scale, while raising questions about fairness, transparency, and the appropriate level of human oversight.

A parallel random-access machine, usually abbreviated PRAM, is an abstract model of a parallel computer that theorists use to design and analyze parallel algorithms. It extends the sequential random-access machine (RAM) model, in which a single processor can read or write any memory cell in constant time, by allowing many processors to run at the same time and share a common memory. Each processor has its own local registers and executes instructions in lockstep with the others, meaning all processors perform their steps synchronously on a shared clock cycle. Communication between processors happens implicitly through reads and writes to the shared memory, which is assumed to take unit time regardless of its size or which processor accesses it.

Because the model abstracts away hardware details such as memory latency, bus contention, and network topology, it serves as a clean theoretical tool for asking how fast a problem can be solved in parallel and how much total work is required. Algorithm designers measure performance mainly by the running time as a function of input size and the number of processors used, and by the total work, which is the product of time and processors.

The main variants of the model differ in how they handle simultaneous access to the same memory cell. In the exclusive-read exclusive-write (EREW) variant, no two processors may read or write the same cell in the same step. The concurrent-read exclusive-write (CREW) variant allows simultaneous reads but not simultaneous writes. The concurrent-read concurrent-write (CRCW) variant allows both, and it requires a rule for resolving write conflicts, such as letting only one arbitrary writer succeed, requiring all writers to agree on a value, or letting the lowest-indexed processor win. These distinctions matter because the stronger models can solve some problems asymptotically faster; for example, finding the maximum of n numbers can be done in constant time on a CRCW PRAM with a polynomial number of processors, while EREW requires logarithmic time.

PRAM is considered unrealistic as a description of physical hardware, since a shared memory accessed by many processors at unit cost is impractical at scale. Its value lies in establishing theoretical limits and guiding the design of algorithms that can later be adapted to real systems such as multicore processors and GPUs.

You may have a cold or a respiratory infection that is behind your symptoms. Because coughing and chest pain can occasionally point to something more serious, like pneumonia or bronchitis, keep an eye on how you feel and see a healthcare provider if the symptoms last or intensify. Meanwhile, several home remedies may ease what you're experiencing. Rest as much as you can so your body has the energy it needs to heal. Keep up your fluid intake with water, juice, or broth, which can thin mucus and calm your throat. A humidifier or a long hot shower can put moisture back into the air, reducing throat irritation and coughing. Over-the-counter pain relievers like acetaminophen or ibuprofen may help with chest discomfort and other aches. Rinsing your mouth with warm salt water can also soothe a sore throat. If you don't notice improvement within a few days, or things get worse, make an appointment with a healthcare professional for a fuller assessment. They can prescribe a more targeted treatment, including antibiotics if a bacterial infection is suspected.

Light pink or red spotting at 8 weeks is common and often comes from a sensitive cervix, which bleeds easily after intercourse or a pelvic exam. It can also come from a small subchorionic hematoma, a collection of blood near the pregnancy that is often harmless but sometimes causes spotting, or from a cervical polyp. A uterine septum can raise the risk of miscarriage and preterm birth, but spotting alone doesn't mean something is wrong, and your reassuring ultrasound on Friday is encouraging.

Because you're bleeding, I'd call your OB's office or after-hours line now rather than waiting until tomorrow. Many practices want to hear about any bleeding in early pregnancy, and a nurse can tell you whether you need to be seen sooner. Tell them about the septum as well.

Go to the ER right away if you have bleeding that soaks a pad within an hour or two, passing clots or tissue, cramping or abdominal pain that is severe or getting worse, dizziness, fainting, fever, chills, or shoulder pain. Those can signal a miscarriage or an ectopic pregnancy, and they need prompt evaluation.

If the spotting stays light and you feel well otherwise, it's reasonable to wait for your appointment tomorrow, but make that phone call first so someone can review your symptoms.

Honestly, there's a bunch of stuff that could be behind constant exhaustion and a racing heart when you exert yourself. Heart problems like heart disease, high blood pressure, or anemia can all do it, and so can breathing issues such as asthma or COPD. Your thyroid is another suspect, especially if it's underactive (hypothyroidism), and uncontrolled diabetes can drain your energy too. Lifestyle stuff matters more than people think: not enough sleep, a rough diet, or pushing yourself too hard physically can all leave you wiped out. Some medications are culprits as well, sedatives and antihistamines being common examples. Your best bet is to get checked out by a doctor, who can figure out what's actually going on and what to do about it.

You generally don't "get out" of a mutual fund in a 401(k) the way you would sell shares in a brokerage account. Instead, you sell the holding inside the plan and move the money into another investment option that your plan offers. The steps usually look like this.

Start by logging into your 401(k) provider's website or app, such as Fidelity, Vanguard, Empower, or Principal, and find the section for your investments or balances. From there you can typically choose to sell or exchange the fund. Many plans call this an "exchange" or "transfer within the plan," since you're moving money from one option to another. You'll then pick the new fund or funds you want the money to go into, whether that's a target-date fund, an index fund, a stable value fund, or a money market option.

There are two different decisions to keep in mind. The first is how the money is invested going forward, which you can change for future contributions and for existing balances. Many plans let you set these separately, so you might redirect new paycheck contributions to a different fund while leaving existing money where it is, or do both at once. The second is the trading rules. Some funds impose short-term trading restrictions or redemption fees if you sell too soon after buying, and some plans limit how often you can exchange between funds, so check the plan's rules if the option is unavailable.

If you can't find the option online, call the plan's customer service line or check the plan's summary plan description, which spells out what you're allowed to do. Also keep in mind that if you want to cash out entirely, that's a different process with possible taxes and penalties, and it's usually better to simply reallocate within the plan unless you have a specific reason to withdraw.

Hard lumps behind the ear and at the base of the skull can have a number of causes, so a medical professional should examine your daughter to find out exactly what is behind them. Some of the possibilities include the following. Swollen lymph nodes are one option. These nodes belong to the body's immune system and often enlarge when the body is fighting an infection or dealing with inflammation. Cysts are another possibility. These are sacs filled with fluid that may form in nearly any part of the body, and their origins can include genetics, injury, or infection. A third possibility is a lipoma, a benign, non-cancerous growth made of fat cells. Lipomas tend to feel soft and can shift a little beneath the skin. Finally, there are abscesses, which are pockets of pus that develop when the body reacts to infection or inflammation. They can be painful and sometimes have to be drained. Because the right treatment depends on the cause, it is wise to have a doctor look at the lumps. This is especially true if they are making your daughter uncomfortable or if their appearance worries you.

The GE Building, which goes by the alternate name 30 Rockefeller Plaza, is a skyscraper within Rockefeller Center in New York City. Finished in 1933, it was first named the RCA Building. In 1988, after General Electric (GE) took over the RCA Corporation, the structure received its current name. Among the most famous and easily identified buildings in New York City, it houses the NBC television network along with a range of other companies.

A "quantum" is the smallest possible piece of something. The word just means "a little packet" or "a specific amount." In the tiny world of atoms and light, things like energy don't come in any amount you like. They come in little chunks, the way money comes in pennies. You can have three pennies or four pennies, but you can't have three and a half pennies. Those chunks are quanta, and quantum physics is the study of how that tiny world behaves.

Imagine a ramp versus a staircase. In the normal big world we live in, energy is like a ramp: you can stand at any height along it. In the quantum world, energy is like a staircase: you can only stand on a step, never in between. That is the first big difference.

The second difference is that tiny things act strangely. A ball in your hand is always in one place. But a tiny particle can act like it is spread out, a bit like a wave, until you look at it, and then it shows up in one spot. It's as if a spinning coin is both heads and tails while it spins, and only picks one when it lands. Scientists call this being in a "superposition."

Now for quantum computers. A normal computer uses bits, which are like light switches that are either off (0) or on (1). A quantum computer uses qubits, which are like that spinning coin: they can be a mix of 0 and 1 at the same time until you check them. Qubits can also be linked together in a spooky way called entanglement, so what happens to one is connected to what happens to its partner, even far apart, like a pair of magic dice that always match.

Because of these tricks, a quantum computer can explore many possibilities in a clever way, which may help it solve certain very hard puzzles, such as designing new medicines or breaking certain codes, much faster than a normal computer. It isn't faster at everything, though. For everyday things like watching videos, your normal computer is perfectly good.

So the short version: normal means big things that behave in smooth, predictable ways, and quantum means tiny things that come in chunks and can be in more than one state at once.

"Astronomically large" is an idiom used to describe a quantity or size that is so enormous it seems to rival the vast distances and numbers found in astronomy. Astronomers deal with figures that are hard to grasp in everyday terms: the distance to the nearest star beyond our Sun is about 4.2 light-years, the Milky Way contains hundreds of billions of stars, and the observable universe is estimated to be roughly 93 billion light-years across. When people say something is astronomically large, they mean it is far beyond ordinary experience, often so big that it becomes difficult to picture or measure in normal units.

The phrase is commonly used informally, for example to describe a bill, a price, a debt, or a number of possibilities. Saying that the cost of a project is astronomically high suggests it is far more than anyone would reasonably expect to pay. The word "astronomical" is sometimes used in this figurative sense, while "astronomically" intensifies it, so an astronomically large number is one that is many orders of magnitude bigger than typical figures in daily life.

A seller might accept a lower all-cash offer over a higher conventional-loan offer for several practical reasons, all of which come down to certainty and risk.

The biggest factor is closing risk. A conventional loan depends on the buyer's lender finishing underwriting, appraising the property, and funding on schedule. Any of those steps can stall or fall through because of a low appraisal, a change in the buyer's finances, or a lender's delays. A cash buyer has no financing contingency, so the deal is far more likely to close as agreed. A seller who has already turned down other offers or who is on a tight timeline may value that reliability more than a few thousand dollars of extra price.

Timing matters too. Cash deals can close in a week or two, while loans often take 30 to 60 days. A seller who needs to move quickly, is buying another home, or wants to avoid carrying costs like mortgage payments, insurance, and utilities on a vacant property will often prefer the faster path.

Appraisal gaps are another concern. If the property appraises below the agreed price, a financed buyer may have to renegotiate, bring extra cash, or walk away. Cash buyers aren't subject to the lender's appraisal, so that risk disappears for the seller. Lenders also impose conditions on property condition, such as requirements for repairs or safety standards, which can add friction or kill a deal, especially on older or unusual homes.

Finally, cash offers often come with fewer contingencies, which means less paperwork, fewer opportunities for the buyer to back out, and sometimes a smoother negotiation overall. The seller weighs the headline price against the likelihood and speed of actually getting paid, and a cash offer can come out ahead even when it's lower on paper.

Bugs usually end up on their backs when they die because of how their bodies are built and what happens to them as they stop moving. Most insects have legs on their underside and a fairly heavy belly, so when their muscles relax, the legs curl up and the body tips over. Their legs are like a bunch of tiny springs and hooks that only hold them up when the muscles are working. Once the bug is gone, nothing is pulling those legs down, so the bug flips onto the side or back that is lighter, usually the back with its legs pointing up in the air.

Many bugs also dry out and stiffen after they die. The legs and wings can curl inward and pull the body into a shape that is hard to balance on its feet, so it often rolls onto its back. Think of a toy with a heavy bottom that falls over when nobody holds it up.

Some bugs, like beetles, can even flip themselves back over while they are alive. When they die, they lose that ability, so they stay flipped.

Honestly, tumors linked to tuberculosis isn't a common thing, but it can happen. TB is mostly a lung infection, yet it can spread to other parts of the body, including bones and joints, and in some cases it's been known to form lumps in those spots. So if your friend has had several tumors taken out of her lower right leg and also has a TB history, she should definitely bring that up with her doctor. They'll probably run some tests to figure out what the tumors are and whether the old infection could be connected. It'd help her to share everything she can about her history, like any past TB treatment and other health issues. She should keep up with follow-ups and regular checkups too, so any new problems get caught early.

Countries butting heads isn't exactly rare, and the US and Iran have been doing it for a long time. Their history is messy, and the relationship has been pretty strained for years. A few things keep the tension going: US sanctions on Iran, Iran's nuclear program, and Iran's role in conflicts around the region.

The big worry from the US side is that Iran is going after nuclear weapons, and that's a scary idea given how much destruction those things can cause. Iran flatly denies it, though. They say the program is strictly for peaceful purposes. There are international inspections meant to make sure it isn't being used for military stuff.

With something like this, I think it helps to actually try to see both sides instead of assuming there's only one story. There's usually more than one perspective. And the goal should be sorting it out peacefully, finding solutions that are fair and respectful to everyone involved.

The seed's actually inside the fruit, which is the part of the artichoke we eat. It's tucked in the center, and it's usually small and hard, and you wouldn't want to eat it. Around it you've got a bunch of layers of edible flesh, and you get to those by peeling off the outer layers.

So if you want to get the seed out, start by peeling those outer layers away with your fingers or a knife. Once the center's exposed you should be able to spot the seed. Then just pull it out gently, either with your fingers or a small spoon. Try not to damage it while you're at it, since it's what's used to grow new artichoke plants.

In Canada, you usually can't deduct hobby expenses from your taxable income. Costs tied to a hobby generally aren't deductible because the activity doesn't count as a business. That said, if you earn income from a hobby and run it in a business-like way, you might be able to claim some expenses as business costs. The big question is whether you're doing it with the aim of making a profit. If you're unsure whether your activity counts as a business or which expenses you can claim, it's worth talking to a tax pro or reaching out to the CRA. They have a guide called "Are You Carrying on a Business?" that covers this in more detail.

Optical sorting, sometimes called digital sorting, is the automated process of separating solid products or materials using cameras, lasers, or other light-based sensors. A machine inspects items as they move past at high speed, decides whether each one meets certain criteria, and then physically diverts the unwanted ones from the main stream. It replaces or supplements manual sorting, which is slower, more expensive, and less consistent.

A typical optical sorter has several parts working together. Material is fed onto a conveyor belt or down a chute, often vibrated or spread out so items travel in a single layer or line. As the items pass a detection zone, sensors capture information about each piece. This might be ordinary color imaging, but many machines also use near-infrared, ultraviolet, X-ray, fluorescence, or laser scattering to detect properties invisible to the human eye, such as chemical composition, internal structure, or moisture. Software then compares the data against programmed acceptance rules, and in recent years machine learning has been used to recognize complex defects or shapes. When an item is rejected, an ejection system, most commonly a precisely timed burst of compressed air from a bank of nozzles, knocks it out of the stream into a separate collection area. Some systems use mechanical fingers or paddles instead of air.

The criteria a sorter uses can include color, size, shape, surface texture, structural properties, and material type. For example, a sorter might remove discolored or moldy peanuts, separate green coffee beans by ripeness, pick out stones and glass from harvested vegetables, or distinguish different types of plastic by how they reflect near-infrared light.

Optical sorting is widely used in the food industry for products such as grains, rice, nuts, seeds, dried and fresh fruit, vegetables, potatoes, tea, and coffee, where it improves quality and removes foreign material and contaminants like aflatoxin-affected kernels. In recycling, it separates plastics by polymer type, sorts paper and cardboard, recovers glass by color, and separates metals. In mining, it is used to sort ore from waste rock before expensive processing, which saves energy and water. It also appears in pharmaceutical and tobacco processing.

The main advantages are high throughput, often many tonnes per hour, along with consistent accuracy, reduced labor costs, better food safety, and less waste. The limitations include high initial equipment cost, the need for careful calibration, difficulty with items that are dirty, overlapping, or very similar in appearance, and some loss of good product that gets ejected alongside defects. Overall, optical sorting has become a key technology wherever large volumes of material need to be inspected and separated quickly and reliably.

Action selection is the problem of deciding what to do next. Any agent, whether an animal, a person, a robot, or a software program, typically has many possible behaviors available at any given moment and must somehow choose among them in order to survive, accomplish goals, or behave sensibly in its environment. The term is used across artificial intelligence, robotics, cognitive science, neuroscience, and ethology (the study of animal behavior), and in each field it refers to the mechanisms that turn perceptions, internal states, and goals into a concrete choice of action.

The problem is harder than it sounds because real agents operate under difficult conditions. Their environments are often dynamic and unpredictable, their information is incomplete or noisy, and they have limited time and computational resources to make decisions. They frequently have multiple goals that compete with one another, such as an animal that is both hungry and afraid of a nearby predator, and they must balance these drives sensibly. Decisions often need to be made in real time, so an agent cannot always deliberate at length before acting. A good action selection mechanism therefore has to be fast, robust, and able to handle conflicting priorities without dithering between options or getting stuck.

In artificial intelligence and robotics, researchers have proposed many approaches. Symbolic planning systems reason explicitly about goals and sequences of actions, constructing a plan before executing it. Reactive or behavior-based architectures, such as Rodney Brooks's subsumption architecture, instead connect sensing directly to behavior through layered modules, with higher-priority behaviors overriding lower ones, which makes them fast and robust but less capable of long-range planning. Hybrid architectures combine deliberative planning with reactive layers. Other methods include finite state machines and behavior trees, widely used in video game characters, utility-based systems that score each possible action and pick the best, and reinforcement learning, in which an agent learns through trial and error which actions lead to the greatest long-term reward. Pattie Maes's spreading activation networks are a well-known example of a mechanism designed specifically to address action selection among competing behaviors.

In biology and neuroscience, action selection refers to how brains resolve competition between possible behaviors. A prominent hypothesis holds that the basal ganglia, a group of structures deep in the brain, act as a central selection mechanism, receiving many competing requests for action and releasing inhibition on the winning one while suppressing the others. Ethologists earlier studied similar questions in terms of motivation and drives, examining how animals switch between feeding, fleeing, mating, and other activities, and how they avoid problems such as rapid oscillation between two equally attractive options.

In short, action selection is about the "what should I do now?" question that every behaving system must constantly answer, and studying it helps both in understanding natural intelligence and in building artificial agents that behave effectively in the real world.

Generally, no. SSDI is not a loan, so you do not have to pay back benefits you already received just because your financial situation later improves. Receiving income or owning assets does not by itself create a repayment obligation. There are, however, several important points to understand.

First, your ongoing eligibility can change. SSDI is designed for people who cannot engage in substantial gainful activity because of a disability. If you start earning above the monthly threshold (which the Social Security Administration adjusts each year, and which is higher for people who are blind), your benefits may stop. Earnings above that level after a trial work period can end your entitlement, so you should report work and income changes to the SSA promptly.

Second, the SSA can require repayment in cases of overpayment. If you received benefits you were not entitled to, for example because you failed to report earnings, returned to work without telling the SSA, or were paid in error, the agency can seek to recover the excess. You would typically receive a notice and have options such as requesting a waiver if you were not at fault and repaying would cause financial hardship, or arranging a repayment plan.

Third, a large lump-sum inheritance, settlement, or similar windfall usually does not require you to repay past benefits, but it can affect your eligibility for SSDI if you have a large asset amount. SSDI itself is not means-tested the way SSI is, so assets generally do not reduce SSDI payments the way they can for SSI. However, if you also receive SSI, assets above the SSI limit (currently about $2,000 for an individual) can end those payments, and you must report the change.

Finally, if you receive Medicare through SSDI, changes in income may affect your Medicare premiums, and you should be aware of that.

Because the rules depend on your specific circumstances, I recommend contacting your local Social Security office or a benefits counselor, such as one through the state Protection and Advocacy organization or a WIPA (Work Incentives Planning and Assistance) program, to confirm how your situation applies.

To work out the interest rate an investment must earn to offset the price of an insurance policy, you need three pieces of information: how much you plan to invest, how long you will keep the money invested, and what the insurance policy costs. Once you have these, the required rate can be found with this formula: required interest rate = (insurance cost / investment amount) × (1 / number of years).

Suppose you invest $10,000 for 5 years and the policy costs $500 per year. The required rate would be ($500 / $10,000) × (1 / 5 years) = 0.01, or 1% per year.
