In other words, the investment would need to earn at least 1% annually to cover the insurance cost. This calculation ignores any taxes or fees tied to the investment or the policy, and it assumes the policy remains in force for the whole investment period. It is also worth weighing the investment's risk, since riskier investments are more likely to suffer losses that could cancel out the gains they produce.

Overlapping toes, sometimes called crossed toes, is a pretty common birth defect. It changes the shape of the toes and can make walking uncomfortable or awkward. In kids, it's often caused by there not being enough room in the womb, so the toes end up bent and sitting on top of each other. There are a few ways to deal with it. Splinting is one: a splint or special shoe inserts can help straighten things out and get the foot lined up better. Stretching exercises can also help loosen things up and improve how far the toes move. Custom orthotics, like insoles or arch supports, can realign the foot, which may help the toes line up too. Massage can get the blood moving and ease stiffness. Surgery is the last resort. Doctors usually only go that route if the other stuff hasn't worked or if the toes are causing real pain or trouble walking. How it's handled really depends on how bad it is and how old your kid is, so it's worth talking to a pediatrician or a podiatrist about what makes sense for your child.

Feeling pressure or pain when you laugh can have several explanations. Some of the more likely ones are listed here.

Muscle strain: Laughing puts a lot of muscles to work, especially those in the abdomen and chest. If one of these muscles is strained, laughing can make it hurt or feel uncomfortable.

Chest infection: Conditions like pneumonia or bronchitis can make laughing painful, because laughter puts extra pressure on an already affected chest and lungs.

Acid reflux: People with reflux may find that laughing worsens their symptoms, since it presses on the stomach and can push acid up into the esophagus.

Heart problems: Rarely, chest pain during laughter points to something more serious, such as angina or a heart attack. If the pain is severe or won't go away, or if it comes with other symptoms like shortness of breath, nausea, or dizziness, you should get medical help as quickly as you can.

In general, whenever you have unusual or lingering pain or discomfort, it's wise to talk with a healthcare professional so the cause can be identified and properly treated.

High bilirubin readings may stem from many different causes, and liver disease is one of them. Your liver could be starting to deteriorate, but other factors may also be behind the changes in your bilirubin levels. Several possible explanations exist. Liver disease is one: raised bilirubin can indicate liver damage or illness, including conditions like hepatitis or cirrhosis. A blockage in the bile ducts, which normally carry bile from the liver into the small intestine, is another; when flow is obstructed, bilirubin can accumulate in the body and push levels up. Hemolysis, the breakdown of red blood cells, is a third. As red cells break apart, they release bilirubin into the bloodstream, which can raise the level. Finally, certain medications, including some antibiotics and anti-seizure drugs, are known to increase bilirubin. Because the cause determines the right treatment, it is important to talk through these elevated readings with your healthcare provider. They may order additional tests, such as liver function tests or imaging studies, to pinpoint the reason.

Certainly! Rugby is played by two squads of 15 athletes each, using an oval ball. Victory goes to whichever side accumulates the greater number of points. The match opens with a kickoff: one team boots the ball toward its rivals, who attempt to catch it and advance it toward the far end of the pitch. Ball carriers can advance by running with it, handing it off to a teammate, or kicking it ahead to a player. Points are earned by carrying the ball across the opponent's goal line and grounding it there. Such a score, known as a "try," is worth 5 points. Following a try, the scoring team may attempt a conversion, kicking the ball between the posts for 2 additional points. When a player commits an infraction, the opposing side is awarded a free kick or a penalty kick. The contest is split into two halves, and whichever team has the higher total at the final whistle is declared the winner. I hope this clears things up! Is there anything else you'd like to know about rugby's rules?

Logical consequence, also called logical entailment, is the relation between statements when one statement necessarily follows from others. A statement is a logical consequence of a set of premises when there is no possible situation in which all the premises are true and the conclusion is false. In other words, if the premises are true, the conclusion must also be true, purely in virtue of the logical form of the statements, regardless of what the statements are about or whether they happen to be true in the actual world.

A classic example is the inference from "All humans are mortal" and "Socrates is human" to "Socrates is mortal." The conclusion follows because of the structure of the argument: any situation where the first two claims hold and the last fails is impossible. By contrast, "It is raining, so the streets are wet" is not a case of logical consequence in this strict sense, since one could imagine rain without wet streets, for instance if the rain were very light and evaporated immediately, or if someone had cleaned the streets.

The concept is central to logic, mathematics, and philosophy. Logicians study it formally by defining precise languages and semantics, so that consequence can be checked systematically. Alfred Tarski gave an influential account in the 1930s, defining consequence in terms of truth preservation across all interpretations of the non-logical terms. Another common approach uses proof theory, where a conclusion is a consequence of premises if it can be derived from them using valid rules of inference. Philosophers continue to debate deeper questions, such as whether consequence depends on necessity, on form, or on some combination, and which expressions count as logical constants in the first place.

Imagine you and a friend are holding opposite ends of a long jump rope. If you flick your end, a bump travels down the rope to your friend. The rope itself stays mostly in place, but the bump carries energy from your hand to your friend's hand. Waves work the same way: water mostly bobs up and down in place while the push of energy moves along.

A tsunami is a very special wave. Most ocean waves are made by wind blowing across the top of the water, so they only reach down a little way. A tsunami is made by something huge happening on the sea floor, usually an earthquake where one slab of rock suddenly slips and shoves the water above it. Imagine pushing your whole bathtub's water with a giant hand all at once. That push creates a wave that reaches all the way from the bottom of the ocean to the top.

The energy comes from the earth itself. Deep inside the planet, huge pieces of rock are constantly pushing and rubbing against each other, and they store up a lot of energy like a stretched rubber band. When the rock suddenly snaps into a new position, that stored energy is released. Some of it shakes the ground, and a big part of it gets passed into the water as the wave.

How much energy is that? A large tsunami can carry an amount of energy comparable to many nuclear bombs, though scientists measure it in very large units that are hard to picture. What matters most is that the energy spreads out as it travels. The wave gets wider and flatter as it moves, so the same energy is spread over a bigger and bigger area.

Where does the energy go? Mostly it travels across the ocean, and when the wave reaches shallow water near a coastline, it slows down and piles up into a tall wall of water. That is when it crashes onto land and does damage. Eventually, the energy is used up by friction and churning, turning into a tiny bit of warmth in the water and the shore.

How fast does it move? In the deep ocean, a tsunami can race along at speeds of around 500 miles per hour, which is about as fast as a jet airplane. That is much faster than a surfer's wave. But out in the deep sea, a tsunami is so low and stretched out that a ship might not even feel it pass. It only becomes dangerous when it slows down near the coast.

Yes, nail changes like these are a common feature of psoriatic arthritis, so your doctor's explanation is plausible. Psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis often affect the nails, causing small pits or holes in the nail plate, thickening, crumbling, and separation of the nail from the nail bed. The yellowish material you can squeeze out from under or at the base of the nail, and the odor, however, are not typical of psoriasis alone. Those features often mean a secondary infection, usually a fungal or bacterial one, has developed in the damaged nail. Nail infections can happen more easily when the nail is already injured or lifted, and some people with psoriasis or arthritis are on medications that suppress the immune system, which raises that risk.

Because of this, it is reasonable to ask your doctor or a dermatologist to look at the nail specifically, and possibly take a small sample to test for fungus or bacteria. Treating an infection, if one is present, can make a real difference in comfort and in how the nail heals. Please contact your doctor sooner rather than later if the area becomes more painful, red, swollen, warm, or starts draining more, or if you develop fever, since those signs suggest the infection needs prompt treatment.

Many people hold the belief that a bigger penis makes a man more appealing as a sexual partner, yet research offers no support for this notion. In practice, penis size does not determine how well someone can satisfy a partner. Far more important are the techniques a person uses during sex and their willingness to talk openly with a partner about what they enjoy. Bodies vary widely, too, so what one individual finds arousing or attractive may differ considerably from what another person does.

A file-based system is a way of arranging and keeping data on a computer. Information is held in separate files, which are grouped together in directories (sometimes referred to as folders). Every file carries a distinct name and occupies a particular spot within the directory hierarchy. Users of such a system can make, change, and remove files and directories whenever necessary. They are also able to relocate files between directories, duplicate them, and carry out other actions on them. Operating systems like Windows, macOS, and Linux commonly rely on file-based systems to handle how data is stored and organized on a machine. Because they offer a flexible, user-friendly way to store and retrieve information, these systems form a core part of many computers.

Okay, so life insurance basically pays out a chunk of money to whoever you name as your beneficiary when you die. That's the whole point, really: it's there so your family isn't left scrambling to cover the bills if you're gone. There are two main flavors. Term life covers you for a set stretch, usually 10, 20, or 30 years. If you die during that window, the insurer pays out. If you make it past the end, the policy just expires and that's that. Permanent life, often called whole life, lasts your entire life as long as you keep paying. It also has a savings piece that builds cash value over the years, which you can use to help cover premiums, borrow against, or pull out. The payout can go toward a lot of things: funeral costs, paying off debts or the mortgage, keeping the household running for whoever depended on you, or even paying for things like college or retirement down the road.

Imagine you have a box of toys and you dump them on the floor. There are only a few ways they can be arranged if you want them neatly stacked, but there are tons of messy ways they could land. Entropy is a way of counting how many of those different arrangements (called "microscopic arrangements") could look the same from the outside. When you see a messy room, there are many ways the toys could be scattered that all look "messy," so the messy state has high entropy. The neat, stacked state is one special arrangement that's hard to hit by chance, so it has low entropy.

In thermodynamics, which is the study of heat and energy, the "toys" are tiny particles like atoms and molecules bouncing around. A hot cup of cocoa has its particles zipping around fast in many different ways. A cold cup has them moving more slowly and in fewer ways. Heat spreading out from the hot cocoa into the cold air means energy gets shared among more particles in more ways, so the total number of possible arrangements goes up. That increase is what physicists call entropy increasing.

This is why things naturally tend to go from ordered to mixed up. It's not that nature loves chaos. It's simply that there are far more messy arrangements than neat ones, so things drift toward the messy ones, just like the toys ending up scattered rather than stacking themselves back into a tower.

People who deny that HIV causes AIDS usually start from a few real-sounding observations and then stretch them too far.

One big reason is history. When AIDS first appeared in the early 1980s, nobody knew what caused it. It showed up mostly in gay men and injection drug users, so some people, including a respected virologist named Peter Duesberg, argued that the cause must be lifestyle things like drug use, heavy partying, and the medicines people took, not a virus. Once HIV was discovered, a few people simply never let go of that first idea, even as the evidence piled up against it.

A second reason is that some of the arguments sound clever. Denialists point out that HIV doesn't kill everyone right away, and that people can carry it for ten years before getting sick. To a five-year-old brain, that seems odd: a germ that takes forever? But many viruses work slowly, so this isn't actually strange. They also say the tests don't prove the virus is there, or that AIDS is just a label for many old diseases. Both claims have been checked and don't hold up.

A third reason is distrust. Early AIDS drugs like AZT were given in very high doses and did have nasty side effects. Governments and drug companies have also done bad things before, such as the Tuskegee syphilis study. So some people feel the whole story is a cover-up to sell expensive pills. If you already don't trust authorities, it's easy to believe they're lying.

A fourth reason is that it feels better. Being told a virus is in your body and you'll need medicine forever is scary. Believing it's all a mistake, or that you can fix things with healthy living, is comforting. Some people also feel angry about being blamed or stigmatized, and rejecting the idea of a sexually transmitted virus can feel like rejecting that blame.

Finally, a few charismatic voices and communities keep the idea alive. Once friends, websites, and books all say the same thing, it feels true, and anyone who disagrees looks like part of the conspiracy.

The trouble is that the evidence for HIV is very strong. Scientists can see the virus, and medicines that attack it keep people healthy. When countries like South Africa listened to denialists in the early 2000s, hundreds of thousands of people died who could have been saved. That is why this particular myth is considered so harmful.

Both approaches have their advantages and drawbacks, and which one suits you best will hinge on your own circumstances and finances. A few points are worth weighing.

Taking out a loan: If your credit is strong and you qualify for a loan with a low interest rate, borrowing to pay for a move could work well. It lets you hold on to your other property and still have the money you need to relocate. That said, you should read the loan terms closely and confirm that you can comfortably handle the monthly payments.

Selling property: Liquidating property can give you a single lump sum to put toward a move. This route may not be practical, however, if much of your wealth is locked up in those assets or if you aren't willing to let them go.

In the end, whether to borrow or sell will depend on your specific situation and financial picture. Consulting a financial advisor can help you understand your options more clearly and identify the best path forward.

Think of American football as a game of taking turns trying to carry a ball into the other team's end of the field. The field is 100 yards long, with a special zone at each end called the end zone. If your team gets the ball into the other team's end zone, you score a touchdown, worth 6 points. That's the main goal of the whole game.

Each team has 11 players on the field at a time. One team has the ball and is trying to move forward; that's the offense. The other team is trying to stop them; that's the defense. Teams don't both attack at once like in soccer. One side attacks, the other defends, and then they switch.

The game isn't one continuous run. It's broken into short bursts called plays, or downs. Before each play, everyone lines up facing each other. Then the ball is snapped backward to the quarterback, the leader of the offense, and the action starts. The play lasts only a few seconds and ends when the player with the ball gets tackled, runs out of bounds, scores, or a thrown ball hits the ground without being caught. Then everyone stops, walks back, and lines up again. That stop-and-start rhythm is why it can look confusing at first.

The most important rule is the "ten yards in four tries" idea. The offense gets four plays, called downs, to move the ball forward at least 10 yards. If they make it, they get a fresh set of four tries to go another 10 yards. This keeps repeating, chunk by chunk, as they march down the field. When you hear an announcer say "third and 4," it means it's their third try and they still need 4 more yards to earn a new set of downs. The yellow line you see on TV marks where they need to reach.

If they fail to go 10 yards in four tries, the other team gets the ball right where they failed. That's bad for the offense, because it hands the opponent good field position. So if a team is on its fourth try and still far from the 10 yards, it usually punts, meaning it kicks the ball far down the field. It gives up the ball on purpose but makes the other team start much farther from scoring. That's why you often see a kick on fourth down.

The offense moves the ball in two basic ways. It can run, where the quarterback hands the ball to a running back who tries to push through the defenders. Or it can pass, where the quarterback throws the ball forward to a teammate who has run down the field, called a receiver. If the receiver catches it, the team gains those yards. If nobody catches it, it's an incomplete pass, the ball goes back to where the play started, and that try is used up. If a defender catches it instead, that's an interception, and the defense's team takes over the ball.

The big players in front, called linemen, act like a wall. On offense they protect the quarterback and push defenders out of the way for runners. On defense they try to break through and tackle the quarterback or the runner. Tackling the quarterback before he can throw is called a sack, and it's a big win for the defense.

There are a few other ways to score. After a touchdown, the team gets a bonus try: usually an easy kick through the tall yellow goalposts for 1 extra point, or they can try to get the ball into the end zone again from close range for 2 points. If a team gets close but can't quite reach the end zone, it can kick the ball through the goalposts for a field goal, worth 3 points. And rarely, if the defense tackles the offense's ball carrier inside the offense's own end zone, that's a safety, worth 2 points to the defense.

The game is 60 minutes of clock time, split into four 15-minute quarters, but the clock stops a lot, which is why a game takes around three hours. The team with the most points at the end wins.

So if you watch a game, just keep track of three things: who has the ball, which down it is, and how far they need to go. Each play is basically a little puzzle, with the offense trying to gain yards and the defense trying to stop them. Once you see it as "get 10 yards in four tries, keep doing that until you reach the end zone," everything else starts to make sense. Madden is hard to learn from because it expects you to already know this and throws a hundred play choices at you, so watching a real game with this in mind, maybe with someone who can answer questions, is a much easier way in.

Honestly, putting business stuff on your personal card is pretty convenient, especially if you don't have a business card yet or you need to buy something right now. But there are a few catches worth thinking about first.

Interest is the big one. Personal cards usually charge higher rates than business cards, so if you carry a balance you'll end up paying more than you would otherwise.

Then there's your credit utilization, which is just how much of your available credit you're actually using. Run a bunch of business purchases through your personal card and that number can jump, and a high ratio can drag your credit score down.

Record-keeping gets annoying too. You've got to separate personal and business purchases yourself, and that makes it harder to track your business expenses accurately when tax time rolls around.

And on liability, you could be personally on the hook for any unpaid balance or debt that comes from the business, since it's your name on the card.

So yeah, it works fine in a pinch, but weigh the pros and cons. A dedicated business card might suit you better in the long run.

Imagine you're standing on a long straight line, like a number line painted on the playground. Regular numbers tell you how far to walk forward or backward along it. Three means take three steps forward, and minus three means take three steps backward. But that line only lets you go two ways. What if you want to go sideways? Complex numbers are like adding a second line that crosses the first one, so now you can walk anywhere on the whole playground, not just back and forth.

The "imaginary" part, usually written with the letter i, is simply the sideways direction. The name "imaginary" is a bit of a historical accident and makes it sound fake, but it's no more made-up than negative numbers. Here is the neat trick: multiplying by i means "turn a quarter of the way around." If you're facing forward and multiply by i, you're now facing sideways. Do it again and you're facing backward, which is the same as multiplying by minus one. That's why i times i equals minus one. It's two quarter-turns making a half-turn. So complex numbers are really numbers that know how to describe both size and direction, and especially turning.

That turning is why they show up everywhere in the real world, because lots of things spin, wave, wiggle, or go round and round. The electricity in your house doesn't flow in one steady direction. It sloshes back and forth many times a second, like a swing. Engineers use complex numbers to keep track of where the swing is in its motion, which makes designing power grids, chargers, and radios much easier.

Sound and music are waves too. When your phone records your voice or a music app shows bouncing bars, it uses a method called the Fourier transform, built on complex numbers, to split a sound into all the separate notes inside it. The same idea helps compress pictures into JPEG files, clean up blurry images, and let Wi-Fi and phone signals carry information through the air.

In physics, the rules that describe tiny things like electrons, called quantum mechanics, are written with complex numbers. Nature at its smallest scale seems to work in terms of these little arrows that spin and add together. Without them we couldn't have explained how atoms work, and we wouldn't have computer chips or lasers.

They also help engineers check whether things will stay steady or shake apart, like airplane controls, bridges, or the system that keeps a drone balanced. Complex numbers can tell them whether a wobble will calm down or grow bigger and bigger.

So the simple version is this: regular numbers let you move back and forth, and complex numbers let you move around and turn. Since so much of the world spins and wiggles, complex numbers turned out to be the perfect language for describing it.

It can make sense, but the details matter a lot. First, check whether the 0% offer is really a cash advance. Credit card cash advances usually carry a fee of 3 to 5 percent of the amount and a higher APR that starts accruing immediately, with no grace period. A 0% promotion is more often a balance transfer offer, which typically charges a transfer fee of 3 to 5 percent, or a special promotional rate on new purchases. Read the terms or call the issuer to confirm exactly what you're getting and what it costs.

Assuming the fee is small, the math is simple. If the loans you'd pay off charge more than the fee works out to per year, you save money. For example, a 4 percent fee on $5,000 costs $200 once, and paying off a loan at 12 percent saves roughly $600 a year in interest. The savings shrink if your loans are already at low rates, like a 4 percent car loan.

The bigger risks are these. Eight months is a deadline, and when the promotion ends, any remaining balance usually jumps to a regular APR that is often 20 percent or more. Some promotions also use deferred interest, where if you don't pay off the full amount in time, you owe all the interest that would have accrued from the start. Missing a payment can cancel the promo rate. And the debt doesn't disappear; you've moved it from a loan with a fixed payoff schedule to a revolving card balance, which can tempt you to borrow again.

It works best if you can calculate the monthly payment needed to clear the balance before the promo ends, set up automatic payments, and commit to not adding new charges to the card. If you can't realistically pay it off in eight months, a fixed-rate personal loan with a lower rate is often safer.

If you tell me the promo terms, the fee, and the rates on the loans you'd pay off, I can run the numbers for you.

Natural-language understanding (NLU) is a branch of natural-language processing (NLP) concerned with a computer's capacity to analyze, comprehend, and interpret human language. It works by taking unstructured written or spoken input and drawing meaning from it, so that the system can complete tasks like answering questions, producing replies, or executing commands. To examine how language is structured and what it means, NLU systems generally draw on a mix of methods from linguistics, computer science, and artificial intelligence. These methods may include determining the grammatical structure of sentences, identifying and interpreting the meanings of words and phrases, and pulling information out of text or speech. NLU is used in many settings, such as chatbots, voice assistants, machine translation systems, and information retrieval systems. It remains an active field of research within computer science and artificial intelligence, and it could transform the way people and computers interact.

Totally get why you're worried about your daughter being referred to a rheumatologist and her test results. Here are some questions you might want to bring up at her appointment: Why was she referred to a rheumatologist in the first place? What tests have been done so far, and what did they show? Based on those results and the doctor's exam, what's the likely diagnosis? What's the plan for treatment? Is there anything she can do at home, like changes to diet, activity, or routine, to help manage things? What are the possible risks or side effects of the treatment? And how will they keep an eye on how it's working, and when will you come back in? It's also a good idea to bring a list of her current medications and copies of any recent records or test results. Don't feel shy about asking anything else that's on your mind. You should walk out feeling like you actually understand what's going on with her.

Showering is fine, and you didn't need to skip one. Showering doesn't wash away or interfere with the medication in any meaningful way, and keeping clean is helpful. For a plain bath, most people can resume once the medicine has had time to work, generally a day or two after the dose, so you're likely fine by now. Keep the water plain and warm rather than hot, skip bubble baths, bath oils, scented soaps, and douching, since these can irritate the area and encourage yeast to come back. Afterward, pat yourself completely dry and wear breathable cotton underwear. Because you're at 9 months, it's worth checking with your doctor or midwife about baths in general. If your water breaks or you think you might be leaking fluid, you should switch to showers only and call your provider.

There's also something your provider should know. The one-day treatments like Monistat 1 aren't usually the first choice during pregnancy. Guidelines for pregnant women generally recommend a longer course, usually the 7-day version of a vaginal cream such as miconazole or clotrimazole, because yeast infections in pregnancy tend to be more stubborn and more likely to return with shorter treatments. Monistat 1 isn't considered harmful to the baby, since very little is absorbed, and it's good that your symptoms have cleared. But the infection could linger without symptoms or come back. Oral fluconazole (Diflucan) is typically avoided in pregnancy, so the vaginal creams remain the standard option. If you use an applicator this late in pregnancy, insert it gently and not too deeply, or ask about using the cream without the applicator.

Please let your doctor or midwife know you had a yeast infection and what you used, especially since you're so close to delivery. A yeast infection present during birth can sometimes pass to the baby and cause thrush in the mouth or diaper rash. Your provider may want to confirm it has fully cleared or recommend the longer treatment. Also contact them if the itching, burning, or unusual discharge returns, if the discharge has a strong odor or a gray or green color (which could mean a different infection), or if you have fever or pelvic pain.

Using pads during treatment was a good idea, just avoid tampons. Congratulations, and best wishes for your delivery.

The question seems to be asking what's really going on between the U.S. and Iran, so here is a simple version.

Imagine a playground where two kids stopped being friends a long time ago. In 1953 the U.S. helped remove Iran's elected leader and put the Shah, a king, back in charge. Many Iranians were angry about that. In 1979 they had a revolution and kicked the Shah out, and then some Iranians took Americans hostage at the U.S. embassy. Since then the two countries have mostly been enemies, and each has done things that made the other more suspicious and angry.

Now for the nuclear part. You're right that U.S. intelligence has generally said Iran stopped its organized nuclear weapons program around 2003 and had not made the decision to build a bomb. But that's only part of the picture. Iran has enriched uranium to levels much higher than any peaceful power plant needs, and it has limited inspectors' access at times. So it's like a kid who says "I'm only building a toy" while gathering parts that could also build something scarier. Many countries worry about that, not just the U.S. Iran says its program is peaceful, and the 2015 deal limited it, until the U.S. left that deal in 2018 and Iran began enriching more again.

As for the "outlandish" accusations, some are backed by solid evidence and some are not. Iran really does support armed groups like Hezbollah and the Houthis, and it has sent drones to Russia. There have also been credible assassination plots tied to Iran. But the U.S. has also made claims that turned out wrong, most famously about Iraq's weapons in 2003, so people are right to want good evidence before believing big claims.

The simple truth is that both sides have reasons for the fight. The U.S. and its allies, like Israel and Saudi Arabia, see Iran as a threat to their safety. Iran sees the U.S. as a bully that interferes in its region and punishes it with sanctions. Politicians in both countries also find it useful to have an enemy. So it isn't a story with one bad guy and one good guy. It's two sides with a long history of distrust, each doing some things that are worrying and some things that are exaggerated.

Think of them as two close cousins made of the same building blocks. Both are made of nitrogen and oxygen. The only difference is the count of oxygen pieces: a nitrate has three oxygens stuck to one nitrogen, and a nitrite has two. That one missing oxygen makes them behave quite differently.

Nitrates are the calmer, more stable one. You find them naturally in vegetables like spinach, beets, celery, and lettuce. On their own they don't do much to meat. Nitrites are the more active one, and they are the ones that actually do the work in ham. They keep the meat pink instead of turning gray, give it that familiar cured flavor, and, most importantly, stop dangerous bacteria like the one that causes botulism from growing.

The two are also linked. Bacteria in your mouth, and in some curing processes, can turn nitrates into nitrites by pulling off one oxygen. So some old-fashioned cures used nitrates as a slow-release source, which would gradually become nitrites. Modern ham is usually cured by adding sodium nitrite directly, so the kid at the store was probably right.

You may also see ham labeled "no nitrites added" or "uncured." That usually means it was cured with celery juice or celery powder, which is naturally high in nitrate. Bacteria turn that nitrate into nitrite, so the ham still ends up with nitrite in it, just from a plant source instead of a packet.

As for health, the amounts in cured meats are small and regulated, but eating lots of processed meat has been linked to higher cancer risk, partly because nitrites can form compounds called nitrosamines when meat is cooked at high heat. Vegetables contain far more nitrate than ham does, but they also come with vitamin C and other things that discourage those harmful compounds from forming. So the short version for a five-year-old: nitrate is the sleepy one, nitrite is the busy one, and ham uses the busy one to stay pink and safe.

A covariance function, also called a kernel in many machine learning contexts, is a function that describes how the values of a random process or random field at two different points are related to each other. Given a stochastic process X(t), its covariance function C(s, t) is defined as the covariance between the random variables X(s) and X(t), that is, C(s, t) = E[(X(s) − μ(s))(X(t) − μ(t))], where μ denotes the mean function. The idea is to quantify how much the value of the process at one location or time tends to move together with its value at another.

The covariance function has several important properties. It is symmetric, meaning C(s, t) = C(t, s). It is also positive semidefinite, which means that for any finite collection of points, the matrix of covariances between them has no negative eigenvalues. This property is essential, because it guarantees that the covariance function corresponds to a valid variance structure for some random process. When the process is stationary, the covariance depends only on the distance or lag between the two points, so C(s, t) can be written as a function of s − t alone. When it further depends only on the magnitude of that distance, the process is called isotropic in the spatial setting.

Covariance functions appear across many fields. In time series analysis, the autocovariance function measures how a signal correlates with a lagged version of itself, and it is central to methods like autoregressive modeling and spectral analysis. In spatial statistics and geostatistics, covariance functions such as the exponential, Gaussian, and Matérn families describe how measurements at nearby locations resemble each other, and they underpin techniques like kriging. In Gaussian process regression and other kernel methods, the choice of covariance function encodes assumptions about smoothness, periodicity, and length scale of the functions being learned.

Having two urinary openings can happen. It may be a congenital variation, such as a duplicated urethra or a split opening, or a small pouch or channel connected to the urethra. Sperm appearing in the urine or leaking with arousal has a few common explanations. One is retrograde ejaculation, where semen travels backward into the bladder instead of out of the penis, which can occur with certain nerve or bladder conditions, some medications, or after some prostate or bladder procedures. Another is leftover semen or prostatic fluid draining out of a pouch or the second opening after ejaculation or arousal. Infection or inflammation of the prostate or urethra can also cause discharge that you may mistake for sperm. Sometimes what looks like sperm is mucus or prostatic fluid, which is normal in small amounts.

I'd suggest seeing a urologist, preferably one who handles male reproductive and urinary problems. They will usually take a history, examine you, and may order a urine test, a semen analysis, a urine test after ejaculation to check for sperm in the bladder, an ultrasound, or imaging of the urinary tract. Once the cause is clear, treatment can range from simple measures or medication for infection or nerve-related problems, to surgery if there is a structural abnormality such as a duplicated channel. If you have pain, burning, blood in the urine, weak urine flow, fever, or difficulty with fertility or sexual function, please mention these at the appointment, since they help the doctor narrow down the cause.

The Italian ocean liner SS Andrea Doria sank on July 26, 1956. She had collided the previous evening, July 25, with the Swedish liner MS Stockholm in heavy fog off the coast of Nantucket, Massachusetts. The Stockholm's reinforced bow struck the Andrea Doria's starboard side, tearing a large hole and causing the ship to list heavily, which made many of her lifeboats unusable.

The ship stayed afloat for about eleven hours after the collision, which gave time for a large rescue effort involving the Stockholm and other vessels, including the Ile de France. Of roughly 1,700 people aboard the Andrea Doria, most were saved, but 46 people died as a result of the collision, along with five on the Stockholm. The Andrea Doria went under at about 10:09 a.m. on July 26 and now rests in around 240 feet of water, making her a famously dangerous and popular wreck for expert divers.

So basically diplomatic immunity is a set of rules that says certain foreign government officials, and their families too, don't have to follow the same laws as everybody else while they're in another country. The idea is that these people are representing their own country, and the rules let them do their jobs without worrying that the host country might punish them for it. Family members usually get covered because they live with the official and might be involved in the work somehow.

A lot of people think it means you can rob a bank or kill someone and just walk away, but that's not how it works. It's there to stop officials from being unfairly targeted by the host country, not to give them a free pass to break the law. If someone with immunity does something serious like robbery or murder, the host country can ask their home country to waive the immunity. Once that happens, the person can be charged and punished in the host country like anyone else.

Matrix decomposition is a way of writing a matrix in a particular structured form. Several kinds exist, each serving its own purpose and suited to different applications. Among the most widely used are the following. Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) splits a matrix into three components, U, S, and V, in which U and V are unitary and S is diagonal; it is frequently employed for reducing dimensionality and compressing data. Eigenvalue Decomposition (EVD) breaks a matrix into two components, D and V, where D is diagonal and V is unitary; it is commonly applied to obtain a matrix's eigenvalues and eigenvectors, which help in understanding how linear systems behave. QR Decomposition factors a matrix into Q and R, with Q unitary and R upper triangular; it is often used to solve systems of linear equations and to find least squares solutions. Cholesky Decomposition expresses a matrix as L and its transpose L^T, where L is lower triangular; it is typically used for solving linear equations and for calculating a matrix's determinant. Across science, engineering, and data analysis, matrix decomposition is a valuable tool, since it makes matrices easier to manipulate and examine.

Lower back pain that comes on when you're hungry and shifts between sides is worth investigating further, because the location can be misleading. Pain from the stomach, duodenum (the first part of the small intestine), or pancreas often radiates to the back. An empty stomach with stronger acid exposure can irritate the stomach lining or an ulcer, and a duodenal ulcer in particular is classically felt in the upper or mid back and eased by eating. Gallbladder or pancreatic problems can also cause back pain that changes with meals. Less commonly, kidney stones or a kidney infection cause flank pain, though those usually don't follow a hunger pattern. Muscle or spine problems can be aggravated by posture or by the way you sit or bend when you're not eating, and low blood sugar can contribute to a general feeling of unease.

Bacterial overgrowth can also play a role. Excess bacteria in the small intestine produce gas and bloating, which stretch the bowel and can refer discomfort to the back, and they can worsen digestion and bowel habits. Treating it with metronidazole is reasonable, but partial improvement is common, and SIBO often recurs or has an underlying cause such as slowed gut motility, previous abdominal surgery, or conditions like irritable bowel syndrome. A doctor may consider a different antibiotic such as rifaximin, dietary changes, or a search for the cause.

Because your symptoms have not fully resolved, I'd recommend follow-up with your doctor. They may want to check for an ulcer or H. pylori infection (which can be tested for and treated), review whether omeprazole at 40 mg is still needed and for how long, and possibly order blood tests, a urinalysis, or an abdominal ultrasound to look at the gallbladder, pancreas, and kidneys. Keep a short diary of when the pain starts, what you eat, and what relieves it, since that will help your doctor.

Seek medical care promptly if you have fever, vomiting, black or bloody stools, unintended weight loss, yellowing of the skin or eyes, pain that is severe or constant, pain that wakes you at night, or any urinary changes such as blood in the urine or pain on urinating.

The Cambridge Computer Laboratory is part of the University of Cambridge in England, where it carries out research and provides teaching in computer science. Regarded as one of the world's foremost centers for the discipline, it hosts a range of significant research groups and projects. Its home is the William Gates Building, found on the University's West Cambridge site, and it forms part of the broader University of Cambridge School of Technology. Established in the early 1980s, the laboratory has contributed substantially to the creation of numerous major technologies and innovations in computer science.

There are a number of possible explanations for sudden numbness and weakness in the arms and legs. One is stroke, a medical emergency that happens when blood supply to the brain is interrupted. Besides numbness and weakness in the limbs, it may bring difficulty speaking, vision problems, and a sudden, intense headache. Another possibility is a pinched nerve, which can produce numbness and weakness in the affected region. This often results from a herniated spinal disc or other structural problems in the spine. A transient ischemic attack (TIA), sometimes called a "mini-stroke," is a brief interruption of blood flow to the brain. Its symptoms resemble those of a stroke, but they typically clear up within 24 hours. Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a long-term autoimmune condition affecting the central nervous system. It can cause numbness and weakness in the limbs, along with fatigue, trouble with balance and coordination, and vision problems. Guillain-Barré syndrome is an uncommon autoimmune disorder that attacks the nerves. It may lead to weakness and numbness in the arms and legs, as well as difficulty speaking and swallowing and problems controlling the bladder and bowels. Peripheral neuropathy refers to damage to nerves outside the brain and spinal cord. It can cause numbness, tingling, and weakness in the limbs. Your wife should see a doctor as soon as possible to identify the cause of her symptoms and begin appropriate treatment. Beyond the tests already completed, the doctor may order additional studies, such as an electroencephalogram (EEG), electromyography (EMG), or nerve conduction studies, to help pinpoint the cause of the numbness and weakness.

So sado-masochism, which people often lump in with BDSM, is basically about getting into activities that involve giving or receiving pain, and getting some kind of pleasure out of that. People tend to misunderstand it, and yeah, it's controversial for plenty of folks. But for some people it's a real part of who they are and how they express themselves sexually. The big thing is that it has to be consensual and respectful, every time. Anything non-consensual or abusive isn't sado-masochism, it's just abuse.

A wiki platform is software that lets people create, edit, and organize a collection of interlinked web pages, usually collaboratively and often with little or no technical knowledge required. The name comes from the Hawaiian word "wiki," meaning quick, reflecting the idea that pages can be created and changed fast in a web browser. Wikipedia is the most famous example, but wiki platforms are also widely used by companies, schools, and open-source communities for internal documentation, project notes, knowledge bases, and how-to guides.

Most wiki platforms share a few core features. They provide a simple editing interface, often using lightweight markup or a visual editor, so that contributors can format text without writing HTML. They keep a version history of every page, so edits can be compared and reverted if needed. They also make it easy to link pages to one another, and they usually include search, categories or tags, and permission settings that control who can view or change content.

Some popular wiki platforms include MediaWiki, which powers Wikipedia; Confluence, a commercial product popular in businesses; and open-source options such as DokuWiki, Dokuwiki alternatives like Wiki.js, and Outline. Choosing one depends on whether you need a free self-hosted tool, a managed cloud service, or an integrated team workspace.

The Cash and Carry arrangement was a clause within the Lend-Lease Act of 1941, which let the United States supply military assistance to its Allies during the Second World War. Under this arrangement, the United States would sell or lease military hardware, food, and other supplies to nations battling the Axis powers, but only if those nations paid in cash up front and organized their own shipping. Cash and Carry was adopted so that the United States could aid its Allies while avoiding direct entry into the conflict. It was later superseded by the Lend-Lease Act itself, which offered military aid to the Allies on more generous terms.

His death hit the music world and his fans really hard, and a lot of people still see him as one of the most important musicians of the '90s.

Your question is brief, so I'll cover the most likely meanings and you can tell me which one fits.

If you mean placing a bid on an auction (like eBay) and winning at less than your maximum, that's normal. On proxy-bidding systems you enter the most you're willing to pay, and the system only raises your bid as much as needed to stay ahead of the next-highest bidder. So if your maximum is 100 dollars and the runner-up stops at 60, you pay just above 60, not 100. This is why bidding your true maximum is generally the best strategy.

If you mean trading stocks or other securities, a bid price is what buyers are offering, and the ask is what sellers want. If you place a buy limit order at a price, it executes at that price or better, meaning you can end up paying less than your limit if sellers are willing to sell lower. A market order, by contrast, fills at the best available price, which is usually the ask. You can't normally buy below the current bid unless you place a limit order below the market and wait for the price to fall to you, which may never happen.

If you mean buying a house, offering under the asking price is common, and a lower accepted offer just means you got a deal. In a competitive market, sellers often counter or choose higher offers, so lowball bids can lose out.

If you mean ad bidding, such as Google Ads, your bid is the maximum you'll pay per click, and you usually pay less than that because of the auction mechanics, which charge just enough to beat the next competitor's ranking.

Which of these is your situation? If you tell me the platform and what you're trying to accomplish, such as paying less, understanding why you paid less than expected, or figuring out why an order didn't fill, I can give more specific advice.

There isn't a clean, direct way to short San Francisco home prices. Residential real estate doesn't trade on an exchange, and there are no SF-specific home price futures for ordinary investors. So the practical approach is to take a position through a proxy that moves with the thing you think will fall.

The most direct proxies are San Francisco office properties and the companies that own them. Office values in SF fell sharply after 2020 because of remote work, and some of the most exposed publicly traded REITs have large Bay Area holdings. Hudson Pacific Properties is one example that has historically been concentrated in San Francisco and Los Angeles offices. Shorting or buying puts on such names lets you bet on Bay Area commercial real estate weakness, though it's a different market from homes, and company-specific news (asset sales, mergers, refinancing) can dominate the stock price.

For residential exposure, you can buy put options or short broad homebuilder and housing-related ETFs, or use an inverse real estate fund. These are national, not local, so they only partly reflect what happens in San Francisco. San Francisco is a high-priced, relatively supply-constrained market, and its prices can diverge from national trends for long stretches, so a national short can be a poor match for a local view.

Whatever you choose, keep several risks in mind. Options lose value through time decay and can expire worthless even if you're directionally right. Shorting stock carries borrowing costs and the risk of a squeeze, and it has unlimited theoretical loss. Real estate prices are also sticky: sellers often refuse to cut asking prices, and transactions slow down rather than prices falling sharply, so a bearish thesis can take years to play out. Timing and sizing matter a lot.

If your underlying concern is a personal one, such as overpaying for a home or owning a concentrated position in SF property, the more effective hedge may be to reduce that exposure directly, for example by renting instead of buying, selling a property, or diversifying your other assets, rather than trying to construct a short. It's also worth talking with a fee-only financial advisor or a derivatives-savvy broker before putting real money into any of these trades.

The deep purple line is the control line. It appears whenever a test has absorbed enough urine and is working properly, so it tells you the test is valid but says nothing about pregnancy on its own. The faint line in the test window is the result line, and on most home pregnancy tests any visible line there, however pale, counts as a positive. It means the test has detected hCG, the hormone produced after a fertilised egg implants. A faint line usually just means you are testing early, when hormone levels are still low. Since you got the same result on two tests and your period is late, the most likely explanation is that you are in the very early stages of pregnancy.

There are a few things that can cause confusion. If a faint line only appears after the time limit in the instructions (often 3 to 10 minutes), it may be an evaporation line rather than a true positive, so check that you read it within the stated window. A faint positive can also occasionally reflect a very early pregnancy that doesn't continue, sometimes called a chemical pregnancy, which can look like a slightly late period. Coming off the pill can also make your cycles irregular for a while, so a late period alone wouldn't prove anything. However, stopping the pill does not cause a false positive test, because the pill contains no hCG.

To be more certain, repeat the test in two or three days using your first urine of the morning, when hormone levels are most concentrated. In a healthy early pregnancy hCG roughly doubles every couple of days, so the test line should look darker. A digital test that displays "pregnant" or "not pregnant" can also remove the guesswork about faint lines.

If the repeat test is positive, book an appointment with your GP or a midwife to confirm the pregnancy and arrange antenatal care. In the meantime, it's sensible to start taking a folic acid supplement (400 micrograms daily is the usual recommendation), avoid alcohol and smoking, and check with a pharmacist before taking any medicines. If you have severe one-sided abdominal pain, shoulder-tip pain, heavy bleeding or feel faint, seek medical help promptly, since these can be signs of a problem such as an ectopic pregnancy.

To add your earnings to your personal finance balance, you can take a few steps. Next, log each payment in a finance app, spreadsheet, or notebook, noting the date, the amount, and where it came from. After recording it, revise your budget so it reflects the extra funds, which will show you how much you can spend and how much you can set aside. Keep watch on your expenses as well to confirm you're sticking to your budget, which helps prevent overspending and makes sure you're putting enough toward savings. Finally, look over your income and spending on a regular schedule, such as every month or every three months, so you can stay informed about your finances and adjust your budget when needed.

I'm sorry you're dealing with this. Neck pain that hurts just to turn your head, after fusions at C4 through C7 and with herniations at C3 and C7, needs a plan that protects the spine while easing pain. Please bring these suggestions to your surgeon or pain specialist before starting anything, since your situation is complex.

Pain that is severe and focused near the fused segments is often related to the levels above and below the fusion. Adjacent segment stress is common after multilevel fusion, and it can add to the nerve irritation from your herniations. Ask your doctor whether imaging or a flexion-extension X-ray has been done to check the segments next to the fusion, since that could change how your pain is managed.

For pain relief right now, options to discuss with your doctor include acetaminophen on a regular schedule, and an NSAID such as ibuprofen or naproxen if your kidneys and stomach tolerate them. For nerve-type pain from radiculopathy, medications like gabapentin, pregabalin, or duloxetine are often used, and they can help with the burning, shooting, or tingling you may have in your arms. A short course of a muscle relaxant may help spasm, though it can cause drowsiness. Topical lidocaine or diclofenac patches can help localized neck pain with fewer systemic effects. Ice in the first day or two after a flare, and moist heat afterward, can both help. Supporting your neck with a pillow that keeps it neutral and avoiding prolonged looking down at a phone can reduce strain.

Regarding physical therapy, your doctor's recommendation is reasonable, but the approach matters a great deal. Look for a therapist who has experience with post-surgical spines and cervical radiculopathy, and tell them exactly what you told me: the fusion levels, the herniations, and that turning your head hurts. A good therapist will start with very gentle, pain-guided work, such as gentle isometrics, postural retraining, scapular and upper back mobilization, and breathing exercises, and will avoid forceful neck manipulation or end-range rotation, which can be unsafe around fused levels and herniated discs. Aquatic therapy is often easier to tolerate when movement is painful. Ask your surgeon for any movement restrictions so the therapist knows what to avoid.

If pain stays high, a referral to a pain management clinic is worth considering. Options there can include a cervical epidural steroid injection to calm irritated nerve roots, which may also make therapy more tolerable. Some people benefit from nerve blocks or medial branch procedures if the pain seems to come from the facet joints near the fusion.

Some symptoms need prompt medical attention rather than waiting for a scheduled visit. Seek urgent care if you notice new or rapidly worsening weakness or numbness in your arms or hands, loss of balance or trouble walking, new bowel or bladder changes, fever with neck pain, a severe headache, or neck pain after a fall or injury. Since you are waiting for an EMG and your hand function may recover, tell your doctor promptly if your hands are getting weaker rather than stable.

A search algorithm is a step-by-step procedure for finding a particular piece of information, or a path to it, within a larger collection of data or a space of possibilities. The thing being sought might be a value in a list, a record in a database, a route between two cities, or a solution to a puzzle. What unifies these cases is that there is a set of candidates, a way to test whether a candidate is the target, and a strategy for deciding which candidates to examine and in what order.

The simplest example is linear search, which checks each item in a collection one after another until it finds the target or runs out of items. It works on any collection and needs no preparation, but it can be slow, since in the worst case it looks at every element. Binary search is faster but requires the data to be sorted. It compares the target with the middle element, discards the half that cannot contain it, and repeats on the remaining half. Because it halves the problem each time, it takes time proportional to the logarithm of the collection's size, which is dramatically quicker for large datasets.

Other search algorithms operate on structures such as graphs and trees. Breadth-first search explores all nodes at one distance from the starting point before moving farther out, so it finds the shortest path in an unweighted graph. Depth-first search follows one branch as far as it can before backtracking, which uses little memory and suits problems like maze solving or exploring game states. Informed or heuristic searches, such as A*, use an estimate of how far each node is from the goal to guide the search, so they typically examine far fewer nodes than uninformed methods while still finding optimal paths when the heuristic is well behaved. Dijkstra's algorithm handles weighted graphs by always expanding the cheapest known route first.

Hash-based lookup is another important approach: it computes a position for an item directly from its key, giving near constant-time retrieval on average. There are also search methods for optimization problems where checking everything is impossible, including hill climbing, simulated annealing, and genetic algorithms. These trade guaranteed optimality for practicality.

Search algorithms are usually compared on several criteria: completeness (does it always find a solution if one exists), optimality (is the solution it finds the best), time complexity, and memory use. The right choice depends on how the data is organized, how large it is, whether it changes, and how important it is to get the best answer rather than merely a good one. The term also applies, more loosely, to web search engines, which combine indexing, retrieval, and ranking algorithms to find relevant documents among billions of pages.

Montargis is a town in the Loiret department of the Centre-Val de Loire region in France. Centre-Val de Loire lies in the middle of the country and is celebrated for its scenic rural landscapes, its castles, and its many historic sites. To the west it meets Pays de la Loire, to the northwest Brittany, to the north Normandy, to the east Île-de-France, and to the south Bourgogne-Franche-Comté. It is widely regarded as safe to take soy isoflavones alongside metformin. Still, anyone considering a new supplement should speak with a healthcare professional first, particularly if they are trying to get pregnant or already take other medications. Soy isoflavones are plant compounds that resemble the hormone estrogen. They occur naturally in soybeans and other legumes and are also sold as supplements. Certain research has indicated that these compounds might help normalize menstrual cycles and boost fertility in women with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), a frequent cause of reproductive difficulties. The evidence, however, is limited, and further studies are required before these findings can be confirmed. Metformin is a drug often prescribed for type 2 diabetes and PCOS. It lowers blood sugar by reducing the glucose the liver releases and by making muscle cells more responsive to insulin. It is generally regarded as safe and effective for these uses, though it is essential to take it exactly as a healthcare provider directs in terms of dose and timing. Before altering any medication or supplement routine, it is always wise to talk with a healthcare provider. They can help you weigh the possible risks and benefits and decide on the most appropriate approach for your individual circumstances.

A terrorist attack moves a stock index mainly because it changes what investors expect about the future, and prices are essentially a bet on future earnings and the risk attached to them.

The first effect is uncertainty. An attack raises questions nobody can answer right away. Will there be more attacks? Will governments respond with military action? Will travel, trade, or consumer spending be disrupted? Investors generally dislike not knowing, so many of them sell riskier assets like stocks and move into safer ones such as government bonds, gold, or cash. That wave of selling pushes the index down, and it can feed on itself when others see prices falling and join in.

The second effect is a reassessment of corporate profits. Some sectors are hit directly. Airlines, hotels, tourism, restaurants, and retail tend to fall because people may travel and spend less. Insurers can drop if they face large claims. Other sectors may rise, such as defense and security companies, so the index reflects the net result of these opposing moves, though broad indexes usually fall at first.

The third effect is physical or operational damage. If an attack hits financial infrastructure, as on September 11, 2001, when markets in the United States closed for several days, trading itself is disrupted, and firms lose people, offices, and communications. Even attacks elsewhere can interrupt supply chains, energy supplies, or transport.

The fourth effect is the wider economic and political reaction. Investors worry about higher security spending, tighter borders, rising oil prices if the attack is in a key producing region, or a drop in consumer and business confidence. Central banks may also step in, by cutting rates or supplying liquidity, which becomes part of the market's reaction.

Historically, though, these drops are often short-lived unless the attack significantly harms the real economy. After many attacks, including those in Madrid in 2004 and London in 2005, markets recovered within days or weeks, because the lasting economic damage was limited. The September 11 attacks produced a larger and longer decline, partly because of the market closure, the scale of the shock, and the subsequent wars and economic weakness already under way. So the initial fall reflects fear and uncertainty, while the later path depends on whether the attack actually changes economic fundamentals.

Sears Holdings is struggling for a few main reasons, and the stores you see in Southern California are not the whole picture.

Imagine a toy shop that used to be the only place in town to buy toys. For a long time, people had to go there. Then other toy stores opened, and later a giant online store started selling toys cheaper and delivering them to your door. The old toy shop still has customers, but fewer of them, and it has to keep paying rent on a lot of big buildings. If it sells fewer toys than it needs to cover all those costs, it starts losing money.

That is roughly what happened to Sears. It was once America's biggest store chain, selling almost everything. Over the years, Walmart, Target, and Amazon took away many of its customers. Sears also made some decisions that didn't help, like spending years cutting back on fixing up its stores and letting its products feel old. Many of its stores were in old malls that lost shoppers too.

Its owner, Eddie Lampert, also used a lot of the company's money to pay off debts and to buy back its own stock, instead of investing in better stores and products. When the company got into trouble, it sold off valuable pieces like Kenmore and Craftsman to raise cash, and it closed many stores to save money.

As for why you keep hearing about its demise while your local stores seem fine, there are a few reasons. Sears has closed hundreds of stores, so the ones left in places like Southern California may be the healthier locations that still make money. The company also has a lot of debt, and each new round of bad news, like missed payments or bankruptcy filings, gets reported. Finally, a store looking busy on a given day doesn't tell you whether the whole company is making enough money to survive.

John Templeton was a well-known investor and mutual fund manager, famous for a pretty sensible, practical way of investing. The line "this time it's different" gets pinned on him a lot, and it's basically a warning: don't assume the rules that held up in the past are suddenly going to stop working. If you catch yourself getting swept up in the hype around some hot investment or market trend, that's your cue to slow down and think hard about the risks and what you could lose before you put money in.

Templeton himself was a cautious guy and leaned toward value investing, meaning you hunt for assets that are undervalued or that everybody else is overlooking, and you wait for them to grow in value over time. So the quote fits his whole outlook. When people say "this time it's different," they're usually convinced some investment or trend is exempt from the normal laws of economics and markets. Templeton's point was that it isn't. Something can look special or exceptional, but it's still subject to the same forces and risks every other investment has always faced. So whatever you're thinking of buying, weigh the downside honestly before you jump in.

The female symbol, also called the Venus symbol or the female sign, is a circle with a small cross underneath it. Some versions have the cross attached to the bottom of the circle instead. It's the go-to marker for the female gender, and you'll see it a lot in women's studies and feminist writing. People also use it to point to female anatomy, especially the reproductive system. It's basically the partner to the male symbol, which is a circle with an arrow pointing up and to the right. Put the two together and you get a way of talking about gender as a pair, or about a mixed group, though that pairing doesn't really capture non-binary identities.

Non-monotonic logic is a form of reasoning that permits conclusions to be overturned when new information arrives. Classical monotonic logic, by contrast, treats a conclusion once reached as permanently fixed, whereas non-monotonic logic leaves room for conclusions to be reconsidered as more facts come to light. Several varieties exist, among them default logic, autoepistemic logic, and circumscription. Researchers in artificial intelligence, philosophy, and linguistics use these systems to model reasoning under uncertainty and to deal with information that is either incomplete or contradictory. Default logic reaches conclusions by treating a set of default assumptions as true unless some evidence points the other way, so that conclusions may be withdrawn once new data appears. Autoepistemic logic is a non-monotonic system for modeling reasoning about one's own beliefs; its conclusions can be revised as new information arrives, and this revision follows the principles of belief revision. Circumscription models reasoning about incomplete or inconsistent information by restricting attention to a subset of the available information, aiming to reach the most reasonable conclusion the limited information allows. Non-monotonic logics are especially valuable where information is uncertain or incomplete and where conclusions must be open to revision as new evidence emerges. Their application spans artificial intelligence, philosophy, and linguistics, where they support modeling of uncertain reasoning and the handling of incomplete or inconsistent information.

Think of a game like a toy box that comes with its own little notebook. Some old games, like the original Legend of Zelda on the NES, had a tiny battery and a tiny bit of memory built right into the game cartridge. When you saved, the game wrote down your spot in that notebook, and the battery kept the notebook from being erased when you turned the console off. So the game carried its own save space with it.

Memory cards came along because of a change in how games were made and sold. Games on discs, like the PlayStation's, are a bit like a book you can only read and never write in. A disc is made at a factory, and the console can only look at what is printed on it. It cannot scribble new things onto it. So where do you put your progress? You need a separate notebook, and that is the memory card. It is a little thing you plug into the console, and every disc game can share it.

Discs were popular because they were cheap to make and could hold lots of stuff like music and movies. Cartridges were expensive, and adding a battery and save memory made each one cost even more. So using a disc plus one memory card was a good deal for the companies and for players.

Now, you mentioned the Nintendo 64. Most of its games did save on the cartridge itself, either with a battery or a special memory chip, so those were like Zelda. But the N64 also had a memory card, called the Controller Pak, that plugged into the controller. Some games used it because they needed extra room to save, or so you could carry your saves to a friend's house. Some games used it instead of putting save memory in the cartridge, which kept the cartridge cheaper.

So the short answer is this: cartridges could carry their own notebook, discs could not, so discs needed a separate notebook, the memory card.

The brain has no "voice" in the way people tend to imagine. What feels like a voice in your head is really just your own thinking. You perceive those thoughts as originating inside your skull because that is where the brain sits. The brain governs every thought, movement, and sensation you have, so it is natural to feel that your thoughts come from within your head. You also can't shift the apparent location of your thoughts, since they are simply electrical and chemical processes taking place in the brain. You have no direct command over those processes, which means you can't decide where your thoughts appear to originate. The frontal lobe takes part in activities such as reasoning, planning, and making decisions, but it isn't the sole region involved. Thoughts and perceptions arise from activity spread across many areas of the brain, not just that one. Nor is this a question of discipline. Because you can't control where your thoughts seem to come from, neither willpower nor a lack of it plays any role.
