Some people write about themselves in the third person on LinkedIn or their personal websites because they feel it comes across as more polished and formal. Rather than writing "I have a degree in computer science," they might write "John has a degree in computer science." This can give the impression of greater distance and objectivity, as opposed to a more personal and subjective tone. Others choose the third person to steer clear of repeating "I" over and over, since frequent use of the word can make writing seem self-absorbed or egotistical. Switching to the third person lets the writer avoid that overuse and creates a sense of balance and objectivity. In the end, whether to write about oneself in the third person comes down to personal taste and what the writer feels sounds best. Some prefer the first person for its warmth and authenticity, while others favor the third person for its formal, professional tone. Ultimately, the choice is yours, and it should reflect what works best for you and your personal brand.

A commonwealth state is a state whose constitution or official name uses the term "commonwealth" to describe its form of government. The word comes from the old English phrase "common weal" or "common good," and in political usage it refers to a polity organized around the public welfare and the shared interests of its people rather than the private interests of a ruler.

In the United States, four states officially call themselves commonwealths: Kentucky, Massachusetts, Pennsylvania, and Virginia. Legally and in practice, these states are no different from the other forty-six. They are full states with the same powers, the same representation in Congress, and the same status under the federal constitution. The label is largely historical and symbolic, a reflection of the political philosophy of their colonial and revolutionary era, when the idea of government serving the common good was widely discussed.

The term also appears in other contexts. Puerto Rico is formally the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico, a self-governing territory associated with the United States, and it has its own constitution and governor while remaining under U.S. sovereignty. Australia has states that are not commonwealths in that sense, but the country as a whole is the Commonwealth of Australia. Several other nations, including the United Kingdom as a loose association, and the Commonwealth of Nations, a voluntary association of mostly former British territories, use the word in their names as well.

A video game engine is the software behind a video game. It gives developers the tools and technology they need to build the game, covering areas such as graphics, physics, audio, and artificial intelligence. Many engines exist, and each comes with its own mix of features and strengths. Certain engines excel at particular genres, while others suit different kinds of projects better. Take the Frostbite engine, created by Dice, which is renowned for its polished visuals and lifelike physics. That makes it a strong fit for titles demanding rich detail and realism, like the Battlefield series. The Call of Duty engine, by contrast, may lag behind Frostbite in graphics and physics, yet it is likely tuned for fast, action-packed play, which is central to the Call of Duty franchise. In short, some engines outperform others because they are built around the specific needs of the games they support. Since every game has different requirements, the ideal engine for a given project depends on what that game requires.

Your situation is common, and having no bleeding or pain at this stage is reassuring. Dry socket (alveolar osteitis) affects roughly 2 to 5 percent of simple extractions overall, and molars, especially lower ones, are more prone to it. Upper molars carry a lower risk than lower ones. Your risk goes up if you smoke, use straws, have a history of dry socket, or are taking hormonal contraceptives. A clot that has partly come out doesn't always mean dry socket will develop, though. Dry socket usually shows up around days 2 to 4 with a throbbing pain that often radiates toward the ear, jaw, or neighboring teeth, along with a bad taste or smell and a visibly empty socket with exposed bone. Since you're not in pain, the socket may simply be healing, as the clot can reform or the gum tissue can gradually close over it.

The most useful things you can do now are to stop rinsing vigorously and avoid spitting forcefully, since both can dislodge the clot further. Gentle rinsing with warm salt water after meals is fine if it doesn't disturb the area. Avoid smoking, drinking through straws, and alcohol for at least the next few days, and try not to poke at the socket with your tongue or fingers. Stick to soft, lukewarm food, chewing on the opposite side, and keep your head elevated when resting.

Contact your dentist or oral surgery clinic if you develop increasing or severe pain, especially after day three, an unpleasant taste or smell, swelling, fever, or bleeding that won't stop. They can check the socket and, if needed, place a medicated dressing, which usually brings quick relief. If everything stays calm, the socket should continue to heal over the next one to two weeks.

Warehouse spreadsheets are used to track, organize, and analyze the information needed to run a storage and distribution operation, especially in smaller or mid-sized businesses that don't have a dedicated warehouse management system, or as a supplement to one.

The most common use is inventory tracking. A spreadsheet can list every item by SKU or product name, along with its quantity on hand, storage location, unit cost, and reorder point. Staff update it as goods are received, moved, or shipped, which gives a running picture of what is in stock and helps prevent both shortages and overstocking. Many warehouses add formulas or conditional formatting so that items fall below a minimum level are highlighted automatically.

Spreadsheets are also used for receiving and shipping records. These log incoming deliveries, purchase order numbers, suppliers, dates, and condition of goods, as well as outgoing orders, carriers, tracking numbers, and delivery dates. This creates a paper trail that helps resolve disputes about missing or damaged shipments.

Location and layout management is another use. Warehouses often map out aisles, racks, shelves, and bins in a sheet so workers can quickly find where a product is stored and so managers can see how much space is free.

Spreadsheets also support planning and analysis. Managers can calculate inventory turnover, carrying costs, order lead times, and demand trends, then use charts and pivot tables to forecast needs or spot slow-moving items. Labor scheduling, productivity tracking, and cost comparisons between suppliers or carriers are commonly handled the same way.

Other typical uses include cycle count and audit sheets, where physical counts are compared against recorded quantities to find discrepancies, as well as tracking equipment maintenance, safety inspections, and returns.

The main advantages of spreadsheets are low cost, flexibility, and ease of use. The drawbacks are that they depend on manual data entry, can develop errors, are hard to keep in sync among multiple users, and don't scale well as order volume grows. At that point, many businesses move to dedicated warehouse or inventory management software.

Imagine a city in the desert, where the land is dry and sandy and almost nothing green grows. Now imagine a giant garden built high in the air, like a stack of big flowerpots or a wedding cake, with trees, bushes, and flowers growing on each layer. That's what people long ago described as the Hanging Gardens of Babylon.

The story says a powerful king named Nebuchadnezzar II built it in the city of Babylon, in what is now Iraq, around 2,600 years ago. The tale goes that his wife missed the green, leafy hills of her homeland, so he built her a garden that looked like a little piece of those hills. Other stories say the king built it just to show how rich and powerful he was.

It was impressive for a few reasons. Growing plants in a hot, dry place was very hard, so a garden full of greenery would have looked almost magical. Since the garden was built on stacked terraces, it would have looked like it was floating or hanging in the sky, which is where the name comes from. And people had to carry water up to the top layers, probably with some kind of pump or water-lifting machine, which was a clever piece of engineering for its time.

One important thing to know is that no one has ever found clear proof that the gardens really existed. They're known mostly from writings by Greek and Roman travelers who visited hundreds of years later, and some historians think the stories may be exaggerated or even mixed up with other places. So it's a bit like a famous legend: it's a wonderful picture in our minds, even if no one can point to the exact spot where it stood.

Insomnia is basically a sleep disorder that makes it hard to fall asleep or stay asleep. Stress, anxiety, and medical conditions can all cause it. Lots of people with it lie there because their brain won't shut off, or because they're anxious or stressed. Others wake up over and over because of physical discomfort or trouble breathing. Obviously, if you're not getting real rest, school gets harder. Your body and brain use sleep to recover, so without it you might struggle to focus, remember stuff, or make decent decisions.

So yeah, it's worth getting enough sleep when you can and reaching out for help if it keeps happening. Your friend scrolling social media might just be a way to kill time or take their mind off not sleeping. Everyone deals with it differently, though. Some people swear by breathing exercises or meditation, while others find it helps to talk to a therapist or, in some cases, get medication to help them sleep.

Median household income in the US was about $68,703 in 2020, according to Census Bureau data. That's the midpoint, so half of households made more and half made less. But it swings a lot depending on where you live and what you do for work. Some states sit well above the national number, others well below, and some jobs pay way more or less than average. Income is only part of the picture, though. Savings, debt, and what you spend each month matter just as much when you're figuring out how you're really doing.

It is widely regarded as safe for first cousins to conceive children together, though their offspring face a modestly elevated chance of certain inherited genetic conditions. The reason is that related parents are more likely to carry the same inherited gene variants, which raises the odds that a child receives two copies of a harmful one. How large that risk is depends on the particular genetic background of you and your husband. Certain conditions occur more frequently in some ethnic or cultural populations, so your family's medical history is worth examining too. Anyone considering a pregnancy should consult a healthcare professional, who can explain possible risks and advise on ways to support a healthy pregnancy. A provider may also suggest genetic counseling, which can clarify those risks and help you make well-informed choices. Ultimately, the central goal is a healthy pregnancy and a healthy baby, which can be supported through steps such as prenatal care, a nutritious diet, and avoiding activities that could harm the baby.

Look, the men in those ISIS execution videos are usually in a awful spot, and honestly they don't have many good options. Most of them figure they've got no shot in a fight against armed captors, and they're scared that trying anything, even running, could bring on worse violence. Some were probably drugged or otherwise out of it, which doesn't help with thinking straight. And ISIS is a terrorist group that runs on extreme violence and fear, so the people in those videos were likely threatened with something even worse if they didn't go along. It's hard to judge why people do or don't do things when they're facing that kind of danger. Everyone handles stress and terror differently, so it's worth cutting them some empathy.

Sounds like you're dealing with some soreness and stiffness after your trigger finger release. Hope it's not too miserable. A few things that might help:

Give your hand a break. It needs time to heal, so try to avoid gripping or lifting anything heavy for a while.

Try ice. A cold pack wrapped in a towel works well, about 15 to 20 minutes at a time, several times a day. It helps with swelling and pain.

Over-the-counter pain relievers like ibuprofen or naproxen can take the edge off inflammation. Just follow the label and check with your doctor before you start anything new.

Gentle stretches help too. Make a loose fist, then spread your fingers wide, or slowly bend and straighten them. It'll feel stiff at first, but moving it keeps things from locking up more.

If it's still rough, a physical therapist can show you specific exercises and may offer massage or other treatments for pain and swelling.

Definitely keep your doctor in the loop, though, especially about that knot in your finger and any pain you're having. They might suggest a different treatment or tweak your recovery plan.

An IT manager oversees the complete planning, organization, and carrying out of all information technology activities in a company. The role covers installing and keeping up computer systems, both hardware and software, and supervising the building and upkeep of the organization's IT infrastructure. The manager also controls the IT budget and makes sure that technology systems and resources are put to good, efficient use. In many cases, the position involves partnering with other departments and stakeholders to pinpoint and rank technology needs and initiatives, as well as creating and putting into practice rules and procedures governing how IT resources are used. Exactly what the job entails can differ based on how large the organization is and what kind of work it does, but it typically includes leading a group of IT specialists, coordinating with other teams, and keeping pace with the newest technological developments.

The Uberman sleep schedule is a way of sleeping where you take lots of short naps instead of one long sleep at night. The idea is that you sleep for about 20 to 30 minutes every four hours, which adds up to roughly two and a half hours of sleep in a day, spread across six naps. Some people who try it say they feel fine, but most experts think it's very hard to keep up and can leave you tired and foggy, because your body needs longer stretches of deep sleep to recover properly.

Here's a simple way to picture it. Normally, you sleep like a big bear in a cave all night in one long piece. The Uberman way is more like a squirrel who keeps popping out for quick little naps all day and night. The naps are short so the squirrel doesn't get too sleepy, and the timing is set so there's always a nap coming up soon.

If you're curious, the most important thing to know is that a regular sleep schedule with a good amount of sleep at night is what most people need to feel healthy and awake. If you ever want to try something new with your sleep, it's a good idea to talk with a doctor first.

Oral thrush is a common side effect of inhaled corticosteroids like Flovent (fluticasone), and it's especially likely after a long illness when you've been using the inhaler regularly. The good news is that it's usually easy to treat, and there are some steps you can start tonight.

The most important one is rinsing your mouth well after every dose of Flovent. Swish with water for several seconds and spit it out, without swallowing. Rinsing also helps clear medication from your mouth and throat. Brushing your teeth and tongue gently, and cleaning any dentures if you wear them, can help remove the fungus as well. Many people also find that using a spacer with the inhaler reduces how much medication lands in the mouth.

For a home remedy, some people rinse with a salt water solution, made by dissolving about half a teaspoon of salt in a glass of warm water, several times a day. Plain yogurt with live cultures may help some people, though the evidence is limited. Avoid sugar and sweets for now, since they can feed the yeast.

Over-the-counter antifungal options are available, such as clotrimazole lozenges (sold as Mycelex troche) or miconazole oral gel. These are usually worth getting from a pharmacy, and a pharmacist can help you choose one. Home remedies alone often aren't enough for a established infection, so it's a good idea to see a doctor or pharmacist soon, especially if the thrush doesn't start improving within a few days, if it spreads, or if you have trouble swallowing or eating. A prescription antifungal such as fluconazole is the usual next step in that case.

Please don't stop using your Flovent on your own, since it's controlling your airway inflammation. Instead, ask your doctor whether a lower dose or a different inhaler might be an option, and let them know about the thrush. If you have a fever, trouble breathing, or a sore throat that's getting worse rather than better, get medical care promptly.

I Bonds are savings bonds issued by the U.S. Department of the Treasury. They carry little risk and suit people aiming to build savings over many years while earning some interest. Their interest rate has two parts: a fixed rate that stays the same for the bond's entire life, and an inflation-linked rate that moves with the Consumer Price Index (CPI). The Treasury sets the fixed rate at the time a bond is issued, based on current market conditions and how much money the government needs to borrow, and that rate never changes afterward. It is usually announced twice a year, in May and November, and covers bonds issued during the following six months. The inflation-linked rate is also set by the Treasury and is recalculated every six months to reflect CPI changes. Its purpose is to preserve the value of the money invested by raising the bond's interest as inflation pushes up prices. To summarize, the fixed rate is chosen by the Treasury according to market conditions and borrowing needs and remains unchanged for the bond's life, while the inflation-linked rate is updated every six months in line with the CPI.

Groin pain that comes on with standing and certain activities is very often related to a hernia, and what you describe fits that pattern well enough that it's worth taking seriously. An inguinal hernia happens when tissue, usually a loop of intestine or fatty tissue, pushes through a weak spot in the abdominal wall in the groin. Pressure inside the abdomen rises when you stand for long periods, and it also rises when you strain, cough, or bear down. Speaking loudly or at a higher pitch can involve bracing your core and increasing abdominal pressure, which may be enough to make a small hernia bulge out and become uncomfortable. A lump that is sometimes tender, especially when the discomfort flares, is a typical description of this kind of hernia.

Other possibilities exist, including a swollen lymph node from a minor infection, a muscle or tendon strain in the groin or lower abdomen, or occasionally a problem with the testicle or the cord running to it if you are male. Because these can look and feel similar, it is hard to be certain without an examination.

I would recommend seeing a doctor soon rather than waiting, mainly because a hernia that becomes trapped can cause serious problems. Seek urgent care right away if the lump becomes hard, very painful, discolored, or cannot be pushed back in, or if you develop nausea, vomiting, fever, or severe pain with a racing heartbeat. A primary care doctor or a general surgeon can examine the area, often by having you stand and cough, which usually confirms a hernia quickly. In the meantime, avoid heavy lifting and straining, and notice whether the lump changes in size or position as you rest or stand.

The Pooled Registered Pension Plan (PRPP) is a Canadian retirement savings option, established under federal legislation (the Pooled Registered Pension Plans Act) and launched in 2021. It was designed to give employers and individuals a low-cost, professionally managed way to save for retirement, particularly for people whose employers do not offer a workplace pension.

PRPPs are administered by licensed administrators, which are typically financial institutions, and they are regulated by federal and provincial pension regulators. Contributions are pooled across many members, which allows the plan to keep investment and administrative fees low. Members are generally able to choose from a range of investment options, and contributions are typically made through payroll deduction when set up through an employer, or directly when an individual joins on their own.

Contributions are tax-deductible, similar to registered pension plans and RRSPs, and investment growth is tax-sheltered until withdrawal. Contribution room is tied to the individual's RRSP limit, so it is generally in line with other registered retirement savings vehicles. Funds are locked in until retirement, though certain circumstances may allow earlier access. At retirement, members typically convert their savings into a retirement income product, such as an annuity or a registered retirement income fund, depending on the plan's rules.

Employers who choose to offer a PRPP are generally not required to contribute, though they may choose to match employee contributions. Employers also avoid many of the administrative and fiduciary responsibilities that come with sponsoring their own pension plan, since the administrator takes on much of that role.

Availability and specific features vary by province and by administrator, and some provinces have their own rules or have chosen to participate differently. If you are considering a PRPP, it is worth comparing the fees, investment choices, and withdrawal rules offered by the available administrators, and checking the current details with the administrator or a financial advisor, since the program's terms may have changed since my information was last updated.

The Matrix was written and directed by Lana and Lilly Wachowski, known at the time as the Wachowski brothers, and it was released in 1999. Joel Silver produced it, and it was distributed by Warner Bros. in partnership with Village Roadshow Pictures. The film starred Keanu Reeves as Neo, Laurence Fishburne as Morpheus, Carrie-Anne Moss as Trinity, and Hugo Weaving as Agent Smith. The Wachowskis went on to make two sequels, The Matrix Reloaded and The Matrix Revolutions, both released in 2003, and Lana Wachowski later directed a fourth film, The Matrix Resurrections, in 2021. The visual effects, including the famous "bullet time" sequences, were overseen by John Gaeta, and the action choreography was handled by Yuen Woo-ping.

There are several ways to compensate your employees beyond standard hourly or salaried pay. Consider the following options. Bonuses can be granted to workers who reach specific targets or perform exceptionally well, which is an effective means of motivating people and recognizing their efforts. If your company works on commission, you can make commission part of an employee's pay, which helps tie their financial interests to the company's and encourages them to close more sales. If your business is publicly traded, stock options are another possibility; they give staff a stake in the company's success and can help you recruit and hold on to strong talent. Beyond wages, you can provide benefits such as health insurance, retirement plans, and paid time off, all of which can make up a significant portion of the total package employees receive. Finally, perks like flexible hours, the ability to work remotely, or chances for professional growth can add value and show support for your staff. Deciding which compensation structure suits your business and your people best is important, and consulting a financial or HR professional can help you choose the right approach.

Stomach pain and cramps during dialysis can come from a few different things. Electrolyte shifts are a big one. Dialysis pulls potassium, sodium, and calcium around in the body, and when those levels get out of whack, cramping can follow. Meds can be a culprit too, especially phosphate binders and acid reducers, since they often upset the stomach. Infection is possible as well, whether bacterial or viral. And then there's ulcers, which are sores in the lining of the stomach or intestine and can definitely cause pain.

If your husband's getting stomach pain or cramps during dialysis, he should bring it up with his healthcare team. They're the ones who can figure out what's actually going on and what to do about it. Sometimes that means tweaking his meds or adding something to help with the pain.

A greedy algorithm is a problem-solving approach that makes the best local choice at every step, hoping that these individual decisions will add up to a globally optimal result. Put differently, at each stage it picks whatever seems most beneficial in the moment, with the aim of arriving at the best overall solution. Consider, for instance, a set of tasks, each with its own deadline and the time it takes to finish, where the objective is to complete as many of them as possible before their deadlines. A greedy method would tackle this by always choosing the task that takes the least time to complete. That strategy does not always yield the best outcome, since it can sometimes be better to take on a longer task first when it has an earlier deadline. Still, there are situations where the greedy choice does produce the optimal answer. Overall, greedy algorithms are easy to write and can be quite efficient for certain classes of problems, but they are not a universal solution because they do not always find the optimum. Before adopting one, it is worth examining the particular problem closely and judging whether a greedy strategy is likely to work.

A person can certainly respect and value the teachings of several religions, but fully following the beliefs and practices of more than one at once is usually not feasible. The reason is that many faiths hold core doctrines and observances that can clash with those of other traditions. Judaism, Islam, and Christianity, for instance, each take a distinct position on who or what God is, what part Jesus plays, and how people ought to conduct their lives. Because these positions may not be reconcilable, wholeheartedly accepting all three at the same time is hard to do. Many religions also ask adherents to take on particular obligations, such as joining in specific rituals or observing certain dietary rules, and these can conflict with what other religions demand. In short, appreciating and respecting the teachings of many religions is possible, yet completely embracing the beliefs and practices of several simultaneously tends to be difficult.

Okay so apparently Indonesia has the most Muslims of any country, somewhere over 225 million based on the latest estimates. Yeah, it's the biggest one. Pakistan, India, and Bangladesh come after it and have huge numbers too. Put those four together and you're looking at more than half of all Muslims on the planet.

Yep, an ETF usually moves to match its index's new lineup pretty quickly after a reconstitution. Basically, the index gets reshuffled, with companies added or dropped for reasons like market shifts or keeping the index true to the segment it's meant to cover. The fund that tracks it then has to adjust its holdings to match. That's the rebalancing part: it buys and sells the underlying stocks so its portfolio lines up with the new makeup. How often this happens depends on the fund and the index. Some ETFs sync up daily, others take their time. Either way, the goal is to stay as close as possible to the index's performance, changes included.

Computation time, sometimes called run time or execution time, is the span a computer needs to carry out a particular job or group of jobs. People express it in different units, such as seconds, milliseconds, or microseconds. Several elements shape how long it takes, among them how intricate the job is, how fast the processor runs, how much memory is on hand, and how well the underlying algorithms and software are designed. Generally speaking, work that demands more processing capacity or simply runs longer will show a greater computation time. This measure matters a great deal in computer science and engineering, since it can strongly influence how well and how efficiently a system functions. When performance targets must be met or the user experience needs improving, engineers may need to refine algorithms and programs so that computation time is reduced.

Ho Chi Minh was a Vietnamese communist revolutionary who served as both prime minister and president of Vietnam. He played a central role in the Vietnam War, a conflict fought across Vietnam, Laos, and Cambodia between the late 1950s and the early 1970s. On one side stood the communist forces of the Democratic Republic of Vietnam, which he led; on the other were the anti-communist forces of the Republic of Vietnam, backed by the United States and other Western nations. Born in Vietnam in 1890, Ho devoted much of his life to the struggle for national independence and social justice. Drawn to communism, he was strongly shaped by the thinking of Karl Marx and Vladimir Lenin. He established the Vietnamese Communist Party and directed its forces throughout the war. Although he endured many setbacks and defeats, he and his followers ultimately triumphed and brought Vietnam together under communist rule. He passed away in 1969, only a few years before the war came to an end.

Lower back pain with tingling in your back and legs can come from a bunch of different things. Pulled muscles or sprains are pretty common, and so is a pinched or irritated nerve, or some kind of problem with the bones or joints in your spine. It could also be spinal stenosis (basically the spinal canal getting narrower), degenerative disc disease, or, more rarely, a spinal infection or tumor. And sometimes it's not even a back thing. Diabetes, multiple sclerosis, or a vitamin deficiency can cause similar symptoms too.

Honestly, you'll want to get it looked at by a doctor so you get a real diagnosis and the right treatment. They'll go over your symptoms and history, and they might send you for an MRI or CT scan to figure out what's going on. From there, treatment could be medication, physical therapy, or changes like exercising more and paying attention to your posture. Surgery is sometimes needed, but that's not the usual route.

Think of killing someone as a very big wrong, and the law sorts those wrongs into bins based on what was going on inside the person's head when it happened. Murder is the bin for the most serious kind: the person meant to kill, or meant to seriously hurt someone so badly that death was likely, and didn't have a good excuse. Manslaughter is the bin for killings that are still wrong and still punished, but the person either didn't mean to kill or was pushed into it by something that makes the act a little more understandable, so the law treats it as less blameworthy.

So manslaughter isn't just an accidental murder, though accidents are one kind of it. Involuntary manslaughter is the accidental kind. Someone causes a death by being really careless, like driving recklessly or handling a dangerous thing without caution, but they never wanted anyone to get hurt.

Voluntary manslaughter is the tricky one, because the word "voluntary" here means the person did intend to do the act that caused the death, but the situation made it less bad in the eyes of the law. The classic example is a person who suddenly finds out someone is hurting their child and, in a rush of rage, hurts that person fatally. They meant to do it, but they were overwhelmed by a provoking event, so the law says it's not as bad as a calm, planned killing.

The main difference from murder is the state of mind. Murder is a planned or cold-blooded killing, or one done with a plain intent to harm badly, without a strong excuse. Voluntary manslaughter involves intent too, but the anger or emotional shock was strong enough that the law reduces the punishment. Involuntary manslaughter has no intent to kill at all.

The exact definitions and punishments differ from place to place, so if this is for a real situation, a lawyer or the local law would give you the precise rules.

A nonresident alien generally pays no U.S. federal income tax on capital gains from selling stocks, bonds, or other investments that are not U.S. real property and are not connected with a U.S. trade or business. The main exceptions are gains on U.S. real estate, which are taxable, and gains from someone present in the U.S. for 183 days or more in a tax year, which can be taxed as a nonresident. So the usual strategy is to sell appreciated non-U.S.-situs assets before your U.S. residency start date.

The timing depends on how you become a resident. If you get a green card (lawful permanent resident status), you become a resident for tax purposes on the first day you are physically present in the U.S. as a green card holder, and that day starts your residency. If you qualify under the substantial presence test, residency generally begins on the first day of the 31-day period in which you meet the 183-day threshold, counting weighted days from the current and prior two years. In either case, the year of change is a dual-status year: you are a nonresident before the start date and a resident after it, and you file a dual-status return. Gains realized before the residency start date are generally not subject to U.S. tax, while gains after it are.

Be careful about the basis issue. When you become a resident, your original cost basis generally carries over, and there is usually no automatic step-up to market value. That means any unrealized appreciation accumulated while you were a nonresident could be taxed as U.S. gain if you sell after becoming a resident. Selling before the start date avoids this, although you should confirm the current rules and any exceptions with a professional.

Several other points matter. Your home country may tax the gain when you sell, and a tax treaty may affect where the gain is taxed and whether you can claim credits. Selling a large position in a single year may also trigger high taxes in your home country, so the timing should be coordinated across both countries. Finally, be careful with the substantial presence test, since the days you spend in the U.S. before the green card or before meeting the threshold can change your start date, and your travel plans should be planned around it. Because the rules are technical and the consequences are significant, it is wise to consult a cross-border tax advisor who can model the sale, your residency start date, and your home-country obligations before you act.

Meta-learning, sometimes called learning to learn, is a machine learning model's capacity to quickly adjust to new tasks or settings by drawing on what it has gained from earlier tasks. In computer science, it works by exposing a model to a large number of tasks so that it becomes skilled at learning and adapting to unfamiliar problems more efficiently. Typically, the model is first trained on a collection of related tasks and then fine-tuned on a new task using only a handful of examples. This approach can enhance machine learning performance across many domains, such as robotics, natural language processing, and computer vision. Because it can substantially cut the data and computation needed to master new tasks, meta-learning stands out as a promising path toward intelligent systems that can adapt and learn in real-world environments.

A dim sum restaurant serves a Cantonese style of meal built around many small dishes rather than one large entrée per person. The tradition comes from southern China, especially Guangzhou and Hong Kong, where it grew out of teahouses serving snacks alongside tea. Because of that history, dim sum is usually eaten in the morning or around lunchtime, and many restaurants serve it only until mid-afternoon. The whole experience is often called "yum cha," which means "drink tea."

When you arrive, you'll typically be seated at a table, often a large round one if you're with a group, and one of the first things that happens is someone asks what kind of tea you'd like. Common choices include jasmine, oolong, pu-erh, and chrysanthemum. The tea is usually refilled throughout the meal, and a common custom is that if your teapot is empty, you leave the lid propped open or flipped so staff know to bring more. Some people also tap two or three fingers on the table to say thanks when someone pours tea for them.

The food itself is ordered in one of two ways, depending on the restaurant. In the traditional style, servers push carts around the dining room loaded with steamer baskets and plates. As a cart passes, you can look at what's on it or ask, then point to whatever you want. The server puts the dish on your table and marks your order on a card that stays at your table, often with a stamp or a check in a category based on the dish's size or price. Many modern restaurants have replaced carts with a paper menu or checklist where you write down quantities of each item and hand it to a server, or with ordering by tablet or QR code. Some places use a mix of both systems.

The dishes come in small portions, usually three or four pieces per plate or basket, so the idea is to order a variety and share everything with the table. Popular items include har gow (shrimp dumplings in a translucent wrapper), siu mai (open-topped pork and shrimp dumplings), char siu bao (fluffy buns filled with barbecued pork), cheung fun (rice noodle rolls with sauce), lo mai gai (sticky rice wrapped in lotus leaf), turnip cakes, spring rolls, chicken feet, and spare ribs. For dessert, egg tarts, mango pudding, and sesame balls are common. Dishes tend to arrive as they're ready rather than in courses, so the meal has a relaxed, ongoing pace where you keep ordering until everyone is full.

When you're finished, you ask for the check, and the staff total it up from your card or order record. Prices are often grouped into tiers like small, medium, large, and special, which is why cart restaurants mark categories rather than individual dish names. Dim sum is generally meant to be a social, leisurely meal, so it's common to see families and friends lingering for an hour or more, especially on weekends when the restaurants can be loud, busy, and full of energy.

ESPP stands for Employee Stock Purchase Plan, and if you're in one and moving from Europe to the US, the tax side of things can change quite a bit. Here's what to keep in mind. In the US, ESPP benefits are usually taxable when you buy, whether you sell right away or hang onto the shares. People often call this the "qualifying disposition" tax treatment. If you sell within two years of the grant date or within one year of the purchase date, you might owe an "early disposition" tax. That's basically the gap between the stock's fair market value at purchase and what you paid, taxed at your ordinary income rate. Hold on longer, though, more than one year after purchase and more than two after the grant date, and you may qualify for the friendlier long-term capital gains rates. If your home country has a tax treaty with the US, that could help too. Depending on the treaty, you might get a lower rate on ESPP income or even an exemption. The rules here get messy and really depend on your situation, so I'd talk to a tax pro or financial advisor before you make any moves, especially around the move itself.

You're not an idiot, and this one got tangled up in politics, so it's easy to get lost. One correction first: the person killed was not a Libyan ambassador. It was the American ambassador to Libya, Chris Stevens. The event is usually called the Benghazi attack, and it happened on September 11, 2012.

Here's the simple version. A few years earlier, Libya's dictator, Muammar Gaddafi, was overthrown in a civil war. The US and its allies helped with airstrikes. Afterward, Libya didn't have a strong government or army, so many armed militias controlled different areas. Benghazi, a city in the east, was one of the messiest places. Stevens was there working at a small American diplomatic compound, and it wasn't heavily guarded.

That night, armed attackers broke into the compound and also attacked a nearby CIA annex. Stevens and three other Americans were killed: Sean Smith, Glen Doherty, and Tyrone Woods. Why it happened is still partly debated. Some of the attackers may have been militant extremists who saw the Americans as targets. Others may have taken advantage of protests that had broken out in the region that day over an anti-Islam video made in the US. Investigators have found that the attack was likely not just a spontaneous protest that got out of hand.

It became a presidential issue for two reasons. First, it happened just weeks before the 2012 election, when Barack Obama was running for reelection against Mitt Romney. Second, in the days after the attack, US officials, including UN Ambassador Susan Rice, publicly said it grew out of a protest over the video. Critics said that was wrong or misleading and that the administration was covering up a planned terrorist attack. Supporters said the officials were giving the best information they had at the time. Congress held many hearings, including a long investigation by a House committee, and the issue was fought over repeatedly in politics, including in Obama's and Romney's campaigns.

So the short answer is: an American ambassador was killed by armed militants in a chaotic country, and the government's explanation of why it happened became a political fight.

The liver is one of the few organs with a strong ability to repair and regenerate itself, so there is genuinely good reason to be hopeful. When liver inflammation is caused by medications, including acetaminophen (Tylenol) and many prescription drugs, the most important "treatment" is usually exactly what you have already done, which is stopping the substances that were stressing it. In many cases of drug-related liver injury, liver enzyme levels begin to improve within a few weeks of stopping and often return to normal over one to three months, though it can take longer depending on how much damage occurred and for how long.

That said, it is important not to assume the cause without confirming it with your doctor. Elevated liver numbers can also come from viral hepatitis, fatty liver disease, alcohol, certain supplements or herbal products, autoimmune conditions, iron overload, gallbladder or bile duct problems, and other causes. Your doctor will likely want to repeat your liver blood tests in several weeks to see whether the numbers are trending down. If they are not improving, or if they were very high to begin with, you may be asked to do additional testing such as hepatitis screening, an ultrasound of the liver, or other blood work. It would help to tell your doctor honestly and specifically which medications you were taking, how much, and how often, including the amount of Tylenol, because that information makes a big difference in figuring out what happened. If you were taking more than the recommended dose of acetaminophen, or combining it with other products that also contain acetaminophen, mention that clearly.

While your liver recovers, there are practical steps that support healing. Avoid alcohol completely, since it adds direct stress to the liver. Avoid Tylenol and any combination cold, flu, or pain products that contain acetaminophen unless your doctor says otherwise, and check with a doctor or pharmacist before taking any new medication, supplement, or herbal remedy, since some of these can also harm the liver. Eating a balanced diet, staying hydrated, getting adequate rest, and maintaining a healthy weight all help. If you have been vaccinated against hepatitis A and B, that is useful protection; if not, your doctor may recommend it.

Since you mentioned taking a lot of prescription drugs, if any of that use was beyond what was prescribed or involved medications that were hard to stop, it is worth bringing up with your doctor as well, both for your liver and for your overall wellbeing. They can help you find safer ways to manage headaches and pain going forward.

Seek medical care promptly rather than waiting for a follow-up appointment if you develop yellowing of the skin or eyes, dark urine, pale or clay-colored stools, pain in the upper right side of your abdomen, ongoing nausea or vomiting, unusual bruising or bleeding, swelling in your belly or legs, or confusion or unusual sleepiness, since these can signal more serious liver injury.

In short, there is a good chance your liver will heal now that you have stopped the medications, but the right plan is to follow up with your doctor for repeat testing to confirm the numbers are improving and to rule out other causes.

Information processing is basically the stuff your mind does when it takes in, stores, and works with information. Humans and other animals both do this. It covers noticing and making sense of sensory input, holding onto stuff and pulling it back up from memory, and then using all of that to make choices or figure things out. Lots of cognitive pieces are involved here, like perception, attention, memory, and decision-making, and they all kind of team up so we can get around in the world. Say you spot an object: your brain picks up on its size, shape, and color, then uses those clues to figure out what it is. Hear a sound and your brain processes it so you can follow what someone's saying. Reading or writing works the same way, with your brain handling language so you can talk to people. Cognition as a whole is the umbrella term for how we take in, process, store, and use information, and information processing is a big chunk of that. It's messy and always shifting, too, shaped by what you already know, what you've been through, how you're feeling, and what's going on around you when you take the information in.

Given what you're describing, I'd encourage your husband to see a doctor soon rather than rely on home remedies alone. A week of persistent pain after a fall, along with numbness and tingling running into the arm and red bumps spreading along the arm, goes beyond a simple bruise or muscle strain. Numbness and tingling can come from a pinched nerve, but they can also signal a more significant injury, such as a fracture, a dislocation, or nerve or blood vessel involvement, and a clinician needs to examine him to rule these out. The red bumps also deserve evaluation, since they could be a skin reaction, an infection, or something else, and a change in skin condition after an injury should be checked. If he develops increasing weakness, loss of grip strength, severe swelling, a cold or pale or bluish hand, fever, or pain that worsens quickly, he should be seen urgently or go to an emergency department.

While he arranges an appointment, some general measures may help with the soreness itself. He can rest the shoulder and avoid activities that aggravate it, use ice wrapped in a towel for 15 to 20 minutes at a time several times a day during the first few days, and take an over-the-counter pain reliever such as ibuprofen or acetaminophen as directed on the label, keeping in mind that some people shouldn't take ibuprofen, so he should check with a pharmacist if unsure. A sling for short-term comfort can be useful, but he shouldn't keep the arm immobilized for long, because stiffness can develop. Gentle movement within a comfortable range is generally better than complete stillness once the acute pain settles.

A doctor will likely want to check the shoulder's range of motion and nerve function and may order X-rays or other imaging. Please don't delay that visit on the assumption that it's only a pinched nerve, since sorting out the cause is what will ultimately lead to the fastest and safest recovery.

Question answering is a natural language processing task in which a system automatically produces an answer to a question written in everyday language. The system might pull the answer from a large body of documents, such as a database or a text corpus, or it might build the answer from some other form of knowledge or information. Sometimes these systems can merge details drawn from several sources, or apply heuristics and similar techniques to arrive at an answer that the input data never states directly. Such systems are widely used in many settings, among them information retrieval, customer service, and educational tools.

Of course! In typography, which is the art and craft of arranging type, the size of a font is usually given in points, and a single point equals 1/72 of an inch. A 12-point font, then, stands 12/72 of an inch tall. Twelve points is also the usual default size for documents, since it strikes a good balance: the text is compact enough to get plenty of words onto a page, yet big enough to read comfortably. That said, fonts labeled as size 12 do not all look the same size, because each typeface has its own design features. Some have broader or more narrow letterforms, for instance, while others leave extra room between lines. Because of these differences, 12-point text in one typeface can look bigger or smaller than 12-point text in a different one.

Raphael, the Italian Renaissance painter and architect, was born on April 6, 1483, in Urbino, Italy. Some sources give March 28, 1483, as an alternative date, but April 6 is the one most commonly cited. He died in Rome on April 6, 1520, his 37th birthday.

Several factors can explain why a small area might contain a large number of mattress stores. First, people regularly need mattresses, since everyone requires a place to sleep and a quality mattress contributes to comfortable, restful nights, which keeps demand steady. Second, mattresses come in many varieties, including memory foam, innerspring, and hybrid, and because individual preferences differ, stores often focus on particular types. Third, the market is competitive, so each retailer tries to draw shoppers through sales, discounts, and other promotions. Finally, clustering stores together is convenient for consumers, who can quickly compare prices and styles to find the right match. Taken together, these factors explain how so many mattress stores can remain profitable in one small location.

Good Friday is the Friday before Easter and marks the day Christians commemorate the crucifixion of Jesus Christ at Golgotha, near Jerusalem. For believers, it is the most solemn day in the Christian calendar. Churches typically hold services of mourning rather than celebration, and many observe it with fasting, prayer, and quiet reflection on Christ's suffering and death.

The central significance of the day lies in the Christian belief that Jesus's death was a sacrifice that atoned for human sin. Christians hold that through his crucifixion, he took on the penalty for humanity's wrongdoing and reconciled people to God. The name "Good" is often understood in this sense, meaning holy or pious, though some suggest it reflects an older usage of "good" as "God" in the phrase "God's Friday."

Good Friday also carries a bridge to Easter Sunday, which celebrates the resurrection. The events of Good Friday are seen as incomplete without the resurrection, so the day is understood as the darkest point in a story that ends in hope and new life. Traditions associated with the day include the Stations of the Cross, readings of the Passion narratives from the Gospels, veneration of the cross, and in some countries, processions and reenactments. Many Christian communities also observe a day of rest, and in several countries, including the United Kingdom and much of Europe, it is a public holiday.

President George W. Bush signed the No Child Left Behind Act (NCLB) into federal law on January 8, 2002. Its goal was to raise the academic standards of public schools across the United States by strengthening accountability, granting states and school districts greater freedom in how they operated, and expanding the educational choices available to parents. The law also sought to narrow the achievement gap between disadvantaged students and their better-off classmates. To do this, it required states to establish measurable targets for student performance and to take action in schools that failed to reach them. Although the law generated considerable debate, it was ultimately superseded in 2015 by the Every Student Succeeds Act (ESSA).

Yes, there can be significant differences, though the details depend on your country and local rules. I'll assume you're in the United States, since that's where the distinctions are most commonly discussed, but let me know if you're elsewhere.

The biggest issue is how the income is classified. A traditional long-term rental is generally reported on Schedule E as passive rental income, and it is not subject to self-employment tax. Short-term rentals like Airbnb can change that. If the average guest stay is seven days or less, the IRS generally doesn't treat it as a rental activity at all. If you also provide substantial services, such as regular cleaning during stays, meals, or concierge-type help, the income may be treated as a business reported on Schedule C, which means self-employment tax of about 15.3 percent on net profit. A short-term rental where you mainly provide the space and basic turnover cleaning often stays on Schedule E, but the line is fuzzy, so it's worth checking.

Passive activity rules also matter. Long-term rental losses are usually passive and limited in how they offset other income, with a partial allowance for moderate earners who actively participate. Short-term rentals where you materially participate can sometimes produce non-passive losses, which is why cost segregation and accelerated depreciation strategies are popular with short-term rental owners. This can be a real advantage, but it requires meeting participation tests and keeping good records.

Occupancy taxes are another difference. Most cities and states impose lodging or transient occupancy taxes on short-term stays, and many don't apply to long-term tenants. Airbnb collects and remits these in many jurisdictions, but not all, so you may be responsible for registering and paying. You may also owe sales tax in some places.

If you rent out your home for fewer than 15 days a year, the income is generally tax-free under the so-called Augusta rule, and you can't deduct rental expenses. That applies to short-term rentals only and is a nice perk for occasional hosting.

Deductions are similar in both cases: mortgage interest, property taxes, insurance, repairs, depreciation, and management fees. Short-term rentals tend to have more deductible operating costs, like platform fees, furnishings, supplies, utilities, and cleaning. If you also live in the property, you'll need to allocate expenses between personal and rental use.

Finally, check local regulations and licensing. Many cities require permits, cap the number of nights, or ban short-term rentals, and those can affect both legality and your tax filings. Mortgage terms, HOA rules, and your insurance policy may also restrict short-term use.

Because the classification can change your tax outcome noticeably, a brief consult with a tax professional familiar with rental property is worthwhile before your first year of hosting.

Producing a single TV episode demands a great deal of time and work, which is why a number of different people handle different episodes. Think of assembling a puzzle: the job goes faster when several people each take on a section. To keep the series feeling unified, those leading the production, such as the showrunner, check that every episode fits with the others and contributes to one coherent story. They also work to ensure that the characters and the show's world remain consistent from one episode to the next.

I'm sorry you're dealing with this. Living with OCD for two years, with compulsions like cleaning over and over even when things are already neat, is exhausting, and it's understandable to wonder whether you'll need medication forever.

To answer your questions directly: there is no guaranteed permanent cure for OCD, but it is very treatable, and many people reach a point where their symptoms are small enough that they barely interfere with daily life. Whether you need fluoxetine for life is something only your own doctor can decide, and it depends on how you respond, how long you've been stable, and what your symptoms look like over time. Many people take it for a long period, and some eventually taper off under medical supervision once they're doing well. Please don't stop or reduce fluoxetine on your own, because abrupt changes can cause withdrawal symptoms or a return of the OCD.

The most effective non-medication treatment for OCD is cognitive behavioral therapy with a specific method called exposure and response prevention (ERP). It works by gradually facing the urges to clean without giving in to the compulsion, and over time the urge weakens. Research shows ERP often produces lasting improvement, and combining it with medication tends to work better than either alone. If you're not already seeing a therapist who offers ERP, ask your doctor for a referral.

It would also help to tell your prescribing doctor how the medication is working for you, including whether the cleaning urges have decreased at all. Your dose may need adjusting, and they can discuss the long-term plan with you.

If the urges ever become overwhelming or you start feeling hopeless, please reach out to your doctor or a mental health professional promptly.

The University of Cambridge is a public research university with a collegiate structure, located in Cambridge, England. Established in 1209, it is the second-oldest university in the English-speaking world and the fourth-oldest surviving university globally. Its colleges supply most of the accommodation and social amenities for students, while its many academic departments deliver lectures and other teaching resources. The university belongs to the Russell Group, a body of research-intensive British universities, and to the League of European Research Universities (LERU), a network of leading European research institutions. It is also a founding member of the international Europaeum network. Cambridge has a long-standing reputation for excellence in both research and teaching and regularly appears among the world's leading universities. Its emphasis on interdisciplinary work is strong, and its faculties span a broad range of fields, including the sciences, engineering, the humanities, the social sciences, and business. The institution has produced many distinguished alumni and staff, among them more than 100 Nobel laureates. It also hosts well-known research centers and institutes, including the Cavendish Laboratory, the Judge Business School, and the University Library.

If you run a business and have a disagreement with an airline about a schedule change, you have several options for resolving it. Start by reaching out to the airline directly. Call or email its customer service team, lay out what happened, and ask for help. They may offer a fix such as rebooking you onto another flight or issuing a credit toward a later trip. If the airline can't settle the matter, you can lodge a complaint with the Department of Transportation (DOT). Its Aviation Consumer Protection Division takes complaints about airline problems, including delays, cancellations, and fare disagreements. If neither approach works and you believe the airline has treated you unfairly, consider hiring a lawyer. An attorney who has handled airline disputes can help you pursue a remedy. Keep in mind that every case is different, so the right course of action will depend on your particular circumstances.

Ever read The Master Algorithm by Pedro Domingos? It's about the idea of one single learning algorithm that could, in theory, pick up and do pretty much any task a computer can be programmed for. The thinking goes like this: that algorithm would take in data, learn from it, and then make predictions, sort things into categories, optimize outcomes, or handle whatever else machine learning can do today. Domingos walks through the history of the field and the current state of things, and he makes a case that approaches like decision trees, neural networks, and support vector machines are really just special cases of some more general learning method. He also gets into what a true master algorithm would mean for fields like medicine, finance, and science. I found it a fun, thought-provoking read that makes you wonder where machine learning and AI are headed.

Four Loko is a flavored malt beverage that got pretty big in the US in the late 2000s and early 2010s. It came in a can that looked a lot like an energy drink, which was part of the appeal, and it packed a serious alcohol punch. People started calling it a "blackout in a can," and not as a joke. It was really easy to drink a lot of it fast without feeling how drunk you were getting. The drink caused plenty of drama over the dangerous drinking and alcohol-related accidents it was linked to. In 2010 the FDA said mixing caffeine with alcohol like this was a public health risk, and a bunch of states banned it outright. Then in 2013 the maker pulled the caffeine from the recipe and started selling it as a "malt beverage" instead.

Paying employees in ways other than a standard cash salary can help you attract talent, manage costs, or tailor compensation to what your team values. The most common alternatives fall into a few categories.

Equity compensation is often the first option that comes to mind for startups and growing companies. Stock options or restricted stock units give employees a share of the company's future value, which can be powerful for retention, though it requires careful legal structuring, valuation, and communication about the risks, since equity is worth nothing if the company fails to grow or be sold.

Profit sharing and bonuses tie pay to company performance. A profit-sharing plan distributes a percentage of profits to staff, while performance bonuses reward individual or team targets. These keep fixed costs lower in lean years, but employees may feel uneasy if payouts are inconsistent, so clear formulas help.

Non-cash benefits are another route. Health insurance, retirement contributions such as a 401(k) match, paid time off beyond the legal minimum, flexible or remote work, professional development budgets, and wellness stipends all carry real value. Many employees weigh these more heavily than small salary increases, and some of them are tax-advantaged for both sides.

Some employers offer commission or revenue-share arrangements, especially in sales, where pay rises directly with results. Others use pay-in-kind options such as company products, housing, meals, or transportation, though these can have tax implications that need checking.

Finally, flexible compensation structures let employees choose their mix, for example trading some salary for extra vacation days or a higher retirement contribution. Such cafeteria-style plans can increase satisfaction without raising your total payroll cost.

Before implementing any of these, it's worth consulting an accountant or employment attorney in your jurisdiction, since tax treatment, wage-and-hour rules, and securities regulations for equity vary considerably. If you tell me your industry, company size, and what you hope to achieve, such as cutting costs, improving retention, or competing for specific roles, I can suggest which options fit best.

It is worrying that your baby has been running a fever for four days and that it returns even after you've given medicine. Please contact a healthcare provider promptly so they can figure out what is causing the fever and decide on the right treatment. Recurring fevers in infants can stem from many sources, such as viral or bacterial infections, or other underlying health problems. In some cases, the fever may be the immune system's reaction to a recent vaccine or medication. A provider can examine your child and may order tests to pinpoint the cause. Until then, keep giving the medications exactly as instructed and watch your baby's temperature and general condition closely. Keep them well hydrated by offering plenty of fluids. If the fever doesn't go away or you notice other troubling signs, such as trouble breathing, a rash, or unusual drowsiness and lack of responsiveness, get medical help immediately.

Imagine marriage is like a special promise between two people, and the government keeps a big book of who has made which promise. When you marry someone, you get lots of grown-up rules attached: they can make medical decisions for you if you're sick, they inherit your stuff if you die, they share your money and your house, and you both have to take care of any kids. Bigamy is when someone makes that same big promise to a second person without ending the first one.

The trouble is that the rules only work cleanly with one spouse at a time. If a man is married to two women, who gets to decide about his hospital care? Who gets the house when he dies? Who gets his pension? The government would have to untangle a knot, and somebody would end up hurt and surprised.

That's the second big reason. Bigamy usually involves lying. Most of the time the person hides the first marriage from the second spouse, who thinks they're in a real marriage but actually isn't, legally. That person can lose money, property, and years of their life. So the law treats it a lot like fraud, a kind of cheating that harms someone who trusted you.

There's also history. Western countries built their marriage laws on traditions, especially Christian ones and older Roman law, that defined marriage as two people. Over the centuries, the law was built around that idea, with divorce, inheritance, and taxes all designed for pairs.

Some people argue that if everyone involved is honest and agrees, the government should stay out of it, and that is a real debate. Living together or having a spiritual ceremony with several partners is often not a crime in many places. What's illegal is getting more than one official marriage on paper. Other countries do allow multiple spouses, but they have to write special rules to handle who gets what, which Western legal systems have mostly chosen not to do.

So the short version: one marriage at a time keeps the rules simple, protects people from being tricked, and matches how the laws were built long ago.

Left ventricular (LV) diastolic dysfunction is when the left ventricle of the heart has trouble relaxing and filling with blood during diastole, the phase of the heartbeat when the heart fills up. Grade 1 is the mildest form. How it's treated depends on how serious it is and what's causing it. Doctors often use a few approaches. Medications are one. Diuretics can help your body get rid of extra fluid and bring down blood pressure, and drugs like ACE inhibitors or ARBs may ease the strain on your heart and improve blood flow. Lifestyle changes matter a lot too. Eating better, moving more, and managing stress can all help your heart and keep symptoms in check. Cardiac rehab, a program of supervised exercise and education, can also cut your risk of future problems. Surgery is usually only considered in severe cases, when damaged heart tissue needs repair or replacement. Whatever the plan, stick with what your doctor recommends and keep your follow-up appointments so they can track how things are going and adjust treatment if needed.

"Priced in" is a phrase used in finance and investing to describe information that is already reflected in the current price of an asset, such as a stock, bond, currency, or commodity. When people say something is priced in, they mean the market has already anticipated it and adjusted the price accordingly, so when the event actually happens, the price may not move much, or at all.

The idea rests on the notion that markets are forward-looking. Investors constantly buy and sell based on what they expect to happen, not just on what has already happened. If analysts widely expect a company to report strong earnings next week, investors may buy the stock in advance, pushing its price up before the announcement. When the earnings are released and match expectations, the stock might barely move, because the good news was already accounted for. In that case, the strong earnings were priced in.

This explains why markets sometimes react in ways that seem counterintuitive. A company can announce record profits and see its stock fall, because investors had expected even better results. Likewise, a stock can rise on bad news if the news was less bad than feared. What moves prices is usually the gap between what actually happens and what was expected, often called the surprise.

The same concept applies to broader economic events. If the market is nearly certain that a central bank will raise interest rates by a quarter of a percentage point, bond yields and currency values will typically adjust well before the decision. The announcement itself then has little effect unless the central bank does something different or signals a change in its future plans.

The phrase is also used more loosely outside finance to mean that something is already expected or accepted, so it no longer causes surprise or reaction. For example, someone might say a politician's controversial behavior is priced in, meaning voters already know about it and further examples are unlikely to change their opinions.

When you bring on a freelancer, you need to be aware of your responsibilities as a business owner when it comes to taxes. Generally, you must hold back and remit taxes on any money you pay a freelancer for their work. These taxes cover federal income tax, Social Security, and Medicare. In the United States, if you pay a freelancer $600 or more over the course of a calendar year, you are required to send them a Form 1099-MISC. The form reports miscellaneous income to the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) and must be submitted by January 31 of the following year. When the freelancer is neither a U.S. citizen nor a resident alien, you might also have to withhold and pay taxes on what you pay them, a process called "backup withholding." For guidance on your particular tax duties when hiring freelancers, speak with a tax professional or consult the IRS website.

I'm sorry your daughter is dealing with discomfort. Itchy sores on her legs and arms may stem from several causes, such as insect bites, allergic reactions, or skin disorders. Prurigo is one skin condition that produces itchy bumps or sores, but only a healthcare professional can confirm the cause and recommend the right treatment. Meanwhile, there are a few things you can do to ease her symptoms. Keep the sores clean and dry by gently washing them with mild soap and water, then patting them dry with a clean towel. Try to discourage scratching, since it can worsen irritation and raise the risk of infection. You might also apply an over-the-counter cream or ointment, such as one containing hydrocortisone, to reduce inflammation and itching. An over-the-counter anti-inflammatory like ibuprofen, a type of NSAID, may help with swelling and discomfort. Cold compresses or ice packs placed on the affected skin can also soothe itching and swelling. Always follow the recommended dose and schedule for any medication, and check with her healthcare provider before giving her any of them. If her symptoms don't get better or she develops new ones, seek medical care as soon as possible.

It is quite common for infants to develop stiffness in their muscles, particularly around the neck and shoulders, during periods of growth. Several things can contribute to this, such as muscle strain, teething, and an attempt to ease discomfort or soreness. Your baby's recent illnesses and the antibiotics he has taken may also have played a part in the tightness. Constipation is another possibility, since it can bring on discomfort that leads to tense muscles. Switzerland's national anthem is called the "Schweizerpsalm," which translates to "Swiss Psalm." It's a German-language hymn that Alberich Zwyssig wrote back in 1841. The lyrics are basically a prayer asking for the country and its people to be looked after and kept safe. You'll hear it at official ceremonies and events pretty often, so it's a big part of how the Swiss mark occasions like that.
