Truth is, the saying may have been floating around before him and he just made it stick. The point is pretty simple, though: one good image can get across something complicated or tell a whole story faster than a wall of text ever could.

A redshirt freshman is a college athlete in their second year of eligibility who did not play in any games during their first season on the team. In American college sports, most athletes have five years to play four seasons, so a player who sits out a year, typically to develop physically and learn the system without using a season of eligibility, is said to have "redshirted." That year of inactivity preserves their four years of competition. So a redshirt freshman is someone who is in their second calendar year of school but still has their first year of game eligibility, since they did not compete the year before. The term is used in NCAA football and other college sports, and the practice is sometimes called a redshirt year.

An economic feature is basically a trait of an economy that sets it apart from others. These can cover a lot of ground: what goods and services get made, how developed the economy is, how advanced its technology is, how much it trades with other countries, how income and wealth are spread out, what kind of economic system it runs on, and how much the government steps in. They can shape how well an economy works, which is why people often compare economies using them.

A discipline is basically a field of study, an area of knowledge built around a particular subject. You'll find them everywhere: the arts, the humanities, social sciences, natural sciences, you name it. Think psychology, biology, history, economics, literature, that kind of thing. Each one usually has its own theories, concepts, and methods that people use to dig into whatever they're studying. They overlap a lot too, and plenty of folks end up studying or working in more than one so they can get a fuller picture of a topic.

Category theory is a branch of mathematics that studies mathematical structures in terms of the relationships between them rather than their internal makeup. It was introduced in the 1940s by Samuel Eilenberg and Saunders Mac Lane, who were working on algebraic topology and needed a language to describe how constructions in one area of mathematics translate systematically into another. Today it serves as a unifying framework across algebra, topology, logic, and theoretical computer science.

The basic idea is simple. A category consists of objects and morphisms (also called arrows) between those objects. Each morphism goes from a source object to a target object. Morphisms can be composed: if one arrow goes from A to B and another from B to C, there is a composite arrow from A to C. Composition must be associative, and every object must have an identity morphism that leaves other arrows unchanged when composed with them. That is the whole definition, which is why so many different things qualify. Sets with functions form a category, as do groups with homomorphisms, topological spaces with continuous maps, and vector spaces with linear maps. Even a single partially ordered set can be viewed as a category, with an arrow from x to y whenever x is less than or equal to y.

The central shift in perspective is to characterize things by how they interact with other things. Instead of describing the product of two sets by listing pairs of elements, category theory defines a product by a universal property: it is the object equipped with two projection arrows such that any other object with arrows to the two factors maps to it in a unique way. This definition works equally well for groups, spaces, or order structures, and it determines the product up to unique isomorphism. Constructions like coproducts, limits, colimits, and free objects are described the same way.

Two further notions carry much of the theory. A functor is a mapping between categories that sends objects to objects and morphisms to morphisms while preserving composition and identities. For example, the fundamental group turns topological spaces into groups, and continuous maps into homomorphisms. A natural transformation is a way of comparing two functors, giving for each object a morphism in a manner compatible with all arrows. Eilenberg and Mac Lane originally created the subject to make precise what "natural" means in mathematics.

Other important ideas include adjoint functors, which capture a pervasive kind of optimal correspondence, such as between free and forgetful constructions, and monads, which model algebraic structure and have become important in functional programming. Toposes, a special kind of category, generalize the notion of a universe of sets and connect geometry with logic.

Critics sometimes call the subject "abstract nonsense," but its defenders point out that it reveals hidden similarities between distant fields and often makes proofs more conceptual and shorter. In computer science it informs type theory, programming language design, and the semantics of computation, and it is increasingly applied in areas like databases, quantum physics, and network modeling.

Yes, it's quite possible. A fall down the stairs can worsen an existing labral tear, enlarge it, or cause new injuries around the hip, and the fact that your pain became much worse the evening after the fall is a reason to take this seriously. It's very common to feel okay right after a fall because adrenaline masks pain, then have swelling, bruising, and muscle spasm set in over the following hours. That alone could explain a lot of the pain, but it can't be assumed to be harmless.

Beyond the labrum, a fall like this can cause a fracture of the pelvis, the hip socket, or the top of the thigh bone, which is more likely if your bones are thinner or you're older. It can also cause deep bruising, a muscle or tendon strain, or injury to the cartilage in the joint. Some fractures, especially small ones in the hip region, still allow people to walk a little, so being able to bear weight doesn't rule one out.

I'd recommend being seen today rather than waiting, either at an urgent care or emergency department, since you'll likely need an X-ray and possibly a CT or MRI. Go straight to emergency care if you can't put weight on the leg, if the leg looks shortened or turned outward, if you have severe pain with any movement of the hip, if you hit your head, or if you notice numbness, weakness, or a cold or discolored foot. Also seek urgent help for any loss of bladder or bowel control, or numbness in the groin area, or if pain is spreading into your back.

Regarding the tramadol, please don't take more than your prescribed dose to chase the pain, as tramadol carries a risk of seizures and other serious effects at higher doses, and the usual maximum is 400mg in 24 hours for adults. If your current dose isn't controlling the pain, that's another reason to be examined, and a clinician can adjust your pain plan safely. In the meantime, rest, avoid putting full weight on the leg if it hurts, and use ice for short periods. Please also ask about a walking aid or help with the stairs, since another fall is the thing to avoid most. If your hip specialist is following you for the tear, let them know about the fall too.

Banks do this more often than you'd think, and it usually comes down to a few things.

First, speed. A cash offer can close fast because nobody has to wait on a mortgage approval or an underwriter deciding whether they like the property's condition and value. If the place has been sitting on the market for a while, the bank probably just wants it gone, and quick cash looks pretty good.

Then there's risk. A higher offer with a conventional loan hangs on a lot of things going right. The buyer has to actually get financed, and the house has to appraise high enough to back the loan. If either one falls apart, the deal dies, the sale gets pushed back, and the bank may have to relist and start the whole process over. That's a real cost, so a smaller sure thing can beat a bigger maybe.

There can be other stuff going on too. Maybe the cash buyer has a solid financial track record, or they're offering something that isn't about the price, like a longer closing window or taking on some repairs or renovations themselves.

In the end it depends on the specific sale and how the bank weighs the risks and benefits of each offer.

Cruise ships serving New York City use two main terminals within the city, plus a third nearby in New Jersey that's often considered part of the New York cruise market.

The Manhattan Cruise Terminal is on the west side of Midtown Manhattan along the Hudson River, roughly between West 46th and West 54th Streets on 12th Avenue. Ships dock at Piers 88 and 90, with Pier 92 also part of the complex. Its location is convenient, close to the Theater District and Hell's Kitchen and near the Intrepid Sea, Air & Space Museum. Lines such as Norwegian Cruise Line, Carnival, and several luxury brands commonly use it.

The Brooklyn Cruise Terminal is at Pier 12 in the Red Hook neighborhood of Brooklyn, facing the Statue of Liberty and Lower Manhattan. It handles larger ships, and Cunard's Queen Mary 2 is closely associated with it, along with some Carnival and Princess sailings. It's a bit less accessible by subway than Manhattan, so many passengers arrive by taxi, rideshare, or the NYC Ferry.

Cape Liberty Cruise Port is in Bayonne, New Jersey, across the harbor from Manhattan. It isn't technically in New York City, but it's marketed as a New York-area departure point and is used heavily by Royal Caribbean and Celebrity Cruises. Driving there from Manhattan usually takes thirty to forty-five minutes depending on traffic.

If you're booking a cruise or meeting someone, check your cruise documents for the specific terminal, since the three are in different boroughs or states and are not close to each other.

Sudden, severe pain on the outer thigh with no injury, especially pain that wakes you at night and has lasted two days, needs prompt medical evaluation. I can't tell from a description what is causing it, but several possibilities are worth raising with a doctor.

The pain may be coming from somewhere other than the thigh itself. Hip problems, such as arthritis or inflammation of the bursa on the outside of the hip, often cause pain felt down the outer thigh. Irritation of a nerve in the lower back (a pinched nerve root) can also refer pain into the thigh, sometimes with burning, tingling, or numbness. Meralgia paresthetica, compression of the nerve that supplies skin on the outer thigh, is another possibility, though it usually causes burning or numbness more than severe pain. A muscle strain or cramp in the vastus lateralis, the large muscle on the outer thigh, can also cause significant pain even without a clear injury.

Because the pain is worse at night and is deep and severe, your doctor will want to rule out bone-related causes. A stress fracture of the femur, a bone infection, or, less commonly, a bone lesion can all cause pain that is worse at rest and at night. Since you've had knee surgery, your doctor may also want to check the surgical site and the surrounding bone.

Deep vein thrombosis, a blood clot in a deep vein of the leg, is also important to exclude, particularly if you notice swelling, warmth, redness, or pain in the calf or the whole leg.

Seek emergency care right away if you develop chest pain, shortness of breath, fever, rapidly increasing swelling or redness, numbness or weakness in the leg, an inability to bear weight, or loss of bladder or bowel control. Also contact a doctor urgently if you have a history of cancer or unexplained weight loss.

For the next step, see your primary care doctor or an orthopedic surgeon soon, ideally within a day or two given how severe the pain is. They will likely examine your hip, knee, and back, and may order X-rays of the femur and hip, and possibly an MRI or blood tests depending on what they find. In the meantime, you can use ice, rest the leg, and take an over-the-counter pain reliever as directed on the label, provided you have no contraindications to those medications.

A file-based system is a way of storing and managing data in which information is kept in separate files on a storage device, such as a hard drive or server, and programs access those files directly to read, write, and process the data. Each file typically holds a collection of related records, and each application that needs the data often has its own set of files for that purpose.

This approach was common in early computing and is still used for many simple tasks. For example, a small business might keep customer details in one spreadsheet, invoices in another, and inventory in a third. Each file is independent, and the programs that use them are written to understand each file's particular structure.

The main drawback of file-based systems is that the same data often ends up duplicated across several files, which can lead to inconsistencies when one copy is updated and others are not. They also make it difficult to share data safely among many users, enforce rules about what the data must look like, or retrieve information that spans multiple files. These limitations are a major reason why database management systems were developed, since databases centralize data, reduce redundancy, and provide controlled, structured access to it.

It is hard to pinpoint one person who invented medicine, since its development spans countless cultures and eras. Nearly every society on Earth has practiced some form of healing, and each has built its own body of medical knowledge and techniques. Among the oldest documented medical traditions is that of ancient Egypt, where practitioners were working as early as 2500 BCE. Egyptian thinkers held that the body should maintain balance and harmony, and their approach to treatment relied on herbs, minerals, and other natural materials to cure disease and support well-being. Other ancient peoples, including the Greeks and Romans, likewise built medical systems of their own. Hippocrates, a Greek physician who worked in the 5th century BCE, is frequently called the "father of modern medicine" because of his lasting influence, including the Hippocratic Oath that physicians still take today. Still, many people have contributed meaningfully to medicine over the centuries, so no single "first inventor" can be named.

A flashbang, another name for a stun grenade, is an explosive device built to confuse and briefly immobilize people through a loud bang and an intense burst of light. Within its casing sits a small explosive charge which, once set off, produces both the loud report and the bright flash. These effects are intended to shock people and leave them unable to reason clearly or make out their surroundings. A stun grenade is typically tossed into a room or area where people are gathered. The blast and flash can be highly jarring and bewildering for anyone close by. Depending on the person and the situation, the disorienting effects may fade within seconds or persist for several minutes. Police and military units sometimes employ these devices to manage crowds or take suspects into custody, though they may also be deployed in other circumstances calling for rapid disorientation. Keep in mind that stun grenades carry risks and can injure people if handled or used incorrectly.

It's more complicated than a fight over whose prophet is bigger, though religion is part of the story. Sunni and Shia Muslims do disagree about who should have led the Muslim community after the Prophet Muhammad died, and that old split still shapes identity, but for most people today it works more like a family or team label than a theological argument they lose sleep over.

Think of Iraq like a big house where several families were forced to share rooms, and then the people in charge for a long time were mostly from one family, who kept the best rooms for themselves. When that ruler fell in 2003, the rooms were suddenly up for grabs. Groups that had been left out wanted power, and groups that had been on top were afraid of losing everything. Nobody trusted anybody, and when people feel scared, they grab onto whoever seems most like them and blame whoever seems most different.

Then came the real trouble. The American invasion broke the army and the government apart, so many armed men were suddenly out of work and looking for a side. Outside countries also picked favorites and sent money and weapons, which made the fights bigger. Terrorist groups like al-Qaeda and later ISIS moved in and tried to stir up hatred between communities, because violence helped them grow. Militias formed to protect neighborhoods, and some of them became criminal gangs or political machines that profited from the chaos.

So the simple version is this: people were scared, the country's leaders had fallen, some of the most dangerous people in the world saw an opening, and religious differences were a handy label that made it easier to see neighbors as enemies. Most Iraqis, of every background, have said they are tired of it and simply want to live in peace.

Yep, when you sell stocks for a profit, you can end up owing capital gains tax on that profit. How much depends on how long you held them and what tax bracket you're in.

If you held the stock for more than a year, you usually get the long-term capital gains rate, which is lower than what you'd pay on regular income. That's the good scenario. If you sold after a year or less, it's the short-term rate instead, and that's just taxed like your ordinary income, so it tends to sting more.

Keep good records of your trades, and especially your cost basis (basically what you paid for the shares), because you'll need those numbers to figure out your gains or losses come tax time. Also look into any deductions or credits you might qualify for, since those can knock down what you owe.

If your situation's at all complicated, talk to a tax pro, or just read through the IRS guidelines. They'll explain how it all applies to you better than a forum post can.

A bicuspid aortic valve doesn't usually cause leg tingling directly, but a few related issues are worth considering. Your sitting is a plausible explanation. Prolonged sitting, especially with crossed legs or a wallet in a back pocket, can compress the sciatic or peroneal nerve, which runs near the outside of the knee and often causes tingling on one side. Lower back issues such as a irritated disc can also send symptoms down one leg. If the tingling is light, comes and goes, and eases when you stand and move around, a nerve pinch from sitting is the most likely cause.

Because you have a bicuspid valve, though, it's wise to get it checked rather than assume. The valve is linked to a higher risk of aortic enlargement and, less commonly, problems with blood vessels in the legs or clots traveling from the heart. Tingling that persists for several days, even if mild, deserves a call to your doctor or cardiologist, who can examine your legs, check your pulses, and consider whether your aortic imaging is up to date. Routine follow-up imaging is standard for people with this condition, so ask when your last echocardiogram or aortic scan was.

Seek emergency care right away if the leg becomes cold, pale, or painful, if you notice sudden weakness or numbness that spreads, if you have chest pain, shortness of breath, dizziness, or fainting, or if you develop fever along with new symptoms, since infection of the valve is a serious concern in people with bicuspid valves.

You can't really measure resistance strength from an EMA alone, since an EMA is a smoothed price average rather than a price level where sellers have historically clustered. What it can do is give you a rough sense of where price is likely to meet supply, and how much that zone matters, if you read it in a few specific ways.

Start by treating an EMA as a candidate resistance line when price is trading below it and rallies up into it. The 50-day and 200-day EMAs are the most widely watched, so a rally that stalls at either one carries more weight than a stall at a shorter period like the 9 or 20. Next, look at how price has interacted with the EMA over time. If the stock has been rejected by that EMA several times, each touch from below followed by a drop, the level is acting as resistance and its strength rises with each confirmed rejection. If price has spent long stretches above the EMA, it is more likely to be support than resistance, so a recent break above should weaken the case for resistance there.

The slope and position of the EMA matter too. A declining EMA that price keeps failing to reclaim signals persistent overhead supply, which is stronger evidence than a flat or rising EMA that price briefly touches. The distance between price and the EMA also helps: a stock that bounces off a far-away EMA after a steep fall shows the average is pulling in buyers or sellers, whereas a stock hugging the EMA without a clear reaction shows little.

Volume is the most useful complement. Rejections at the EMA on heavy volume suggest real selling pressure and a stronger level, while rallies into the EMA on thin volume that fade quietly suggest weaker resistance. Using several EMAs together can also help. When the 20, 50, and 200 converge near the same price, that confluence often marks a zone of stronger resistance than any single line.

Finally, remember that EMA-based resistance is a probabilistic guide, not a guarantee. Confirm the reading against a horizontal price level such as a prior swing high, and consider the broader market trend and any news, since fundamentals can override technical levels. Backtesting how the stock has reacted to the same EMA in the past gives you the most reliable sense of how strong that level really is.

Yep, there's a name for that: "receivables," or more specifically "accounts receivable." It's basically the money customers or clients owe you for stuff you've already delivered or work you've already done, but they haven't paid yet. Businesses count it as an asset since it's cash they should be bringing in later. It usually shows up on the balance sheet as a current asset, because most of it gets collected within a year or so.

Dizziness during pregnancy has plenty of possible causes. Low blood pressure, low blood sugar, and dehydration are the usual suspects. Sometimes it's a sign of something more serious, like pre-eclampsia, which is a high blood pressure disorder that only shows up in pregnancy. If your daughter feels lightheaded, the first thing is to get her to lie down and take it easy. Have her drink some fluids and eat something, since that can help bring her blood sugar back up. If it doesn't go away, or she gets chest pain, trouble breathing, or anything else that worries you, she needs to call her healthcare provider right away. Rest helps, and so does avoiding long stretches of standing. If she can't keep fluids down, she should get checked out too.

Disulfide bonds are most commonly associated with the tertiary structure of proteins. A disulfide bond is a covalent link (S–S) formed when the sulfhydryl (–SH) groups of two cysteine residues are oxidized. Because these cysteines are often far apart in the amino acid sequence but brought close together when the polypeptide folds, the bond helps lock the chain into its overall three-dimensional shape, which is the defining feature of tertiary structure.

Disulfide bonds can also contribute to quaternary structure when they form between cysteines on two separate polypeptide chains, holding the subunits together. Insulin is a classic example: its A and B chains are joined by two interchain disulfide bonds, and the A chain also has one intrachain disulfide bond. Antibodies are another example, with disulfide bridges linking their heavy and light chains.

They are not part of primary structure, which refers only to the sequence of amino acids joined by peptide bonds, and they are not what defines secondary structure, which is stabilized by hydrogen bonds along the backbone in alpha helices and beta sheets. So the short answer is tertiary structure, with a role in quaternary structure when they connect different chains.

Inverse problems are basically about working backwards: you want to figure out some property of an object or system, but all you can actually measure is a different, related property. People run into these all the time in science and engineering when they need to know what's going on inside something they can't open up. Geophysicists, for instance, look at tiny variations in the Earth's gravitational and magnetic fields and try to guess what the interior is made of and how it's laid out. Doctors and engineers do something similar with medical imaging. A CT scan or MRI doesn't hand you a picture of an organ directly. The machine collects raw measurements, and then software has to reconstruct the image from them. In electrical engineering, you might measure how a device responds to a signal and work backwards to pin down the electrical properties of the materials inside it. Solving these usually means leaning on a mix of math and stats: optimization methods, machine learning, statistical models, and so on, depending on how messy the data is.

There are a bunch of things that can narrow the bile duct after gallbladder surgery or an ERCP. Scarring or inflammation is a big one. Tumors or other abnormal growths can do it too, and so can stones or debris building up inside the duct. Sometimes the duct is just naturally narrow, or someone's born with an abnormality that makes it more likely to narrow down.

Narrowing after an ERCP isn't unusual, especially if the whole point of the procedure was to clear out stones or debris. The procedure itself can cause inflammation or scarring that tightens things up. And if new stones or debris form afterward, that can narrow it again.

As for what counts as normal, it varies a bit, but the duct should generally be at least 6-8 mm across. If it gets much narrower than that, bile has a hard time flowing through properly, and that can lead to all sorts of symptoms and complications.

If you're dealing with complications, or you're just sick of going through ERCP after ERCP, talk to your doctor about it. There may be other treatment options worth looking at. They can also tell you more about what's actually causing your narrowing and what they'd recommend.
Richard Nixon held the office of United States President from January 20, 1969, until August 9, 1974. He stepped down before completing his second term because of the Watergate scandal.

Casey Anthony faced multiple criminal charges over the 2008 death of her two-year-old daughter, Caylee. Prosecutors brought first-degree murder, aggravated child abuse, and aggravated manslaughter of a child. Anthony was acquitted of both the first-degree murder and aggravated child abuse counts, though a jury convicted her on four counts of lying to police. Her sentence was four years in prison, but because she received credit for time already served, she walked free in July 2011. The case drew enormous media coverage and close public attention. The outcome was contested, sparking considerable debate about the justice system and the evidence heard at trial.

"The sulfas" usually refers to sulfa drugs, more formally called sulfonamides. They were the first widely used synthetic antibiotics. Their history goes back to the 1930s, when the German researcher Gerhard Domagk found that a red dye called Prontosil could cure bacterial infections in mice. Scientists soon learned that the body breaks Prontosil down into sulfanilamide, the compound that actually fights bacteria. Domagk received the Nobel Prize in 1939, and sulfa drugs saved many lives during World War II, before penicillin became widely available.

Sulfonamides work by blocking bacteria from making folic acid, which they need to grow and reproduce. Bacteria must make their own folic acid, while humans get it from food, so the drugs can target bacteria without blocking the same process in human cells. Because they stop bacterial growth rather than killing bacteria outright, they are described as bacteriostatic.

The best-known sulfa drug today is sulfamethoxazole, usually combined with trimethoprim and sold under names such as Bactrim and Septra. This combination is commonly used for urinary tract infections, certain types of pneumonia (especially Pneumocystis pneumonia in people with weakened immune systems), some skin infections, and other bacterial illnesses. Other sulfa drugs include sulfadiazine, used for toxoplasmosis, and silver sulfadiazine, a cream applied to burns. Sulfasalazine is used for inflammatory conditions like ulcerative colitis and rheumatoid arthritis.

Sulfa drugs are known for causing allergic reactions fairly often, and "sulfa allergy" is one of the most commonly reported drug allergies. Reactions range from mild rashes to rare but serious conditions such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome. Other possible side effects include sensitivity to sunlight, nausea, and, less commonly, effects on the blood or kidneys. A sulfa allergy is not the same as an allergy to sulfites (food preservatives) or to sulfur itself. Some non-antibiotic drugs, such as certain diuretics, also contain a sulfonamide group, though cross-reactivity with the antibiotics appears to be uncommon.

If you meant something else by "the sulfas," such as a band, a place, or a term from another field, let me know and I can address that instead.

Automated reasoning refers to the use of software to derive new conclusions on its own from a collection of given statements or axioms. Falling under artificial intelligence and computer science, it focuses on building algorithms and systems capable of logical inference and of making decisions grounded in deductions drawn from known facts or axioms. Its applications span theorem proving, diagnosis, planning, and natural language processing. Fields such as mathematics, computer science, engineering, and artificial intelligence rely on it to carry out work that would be impractical or impossible for people to perform by hand. Several approaches exist, including rule-based systems, resolution-based systems, model-based systems, and hybrid systems that merge several of these methods. To represent and reason about knowledge, these systems may employ different logical formalisms, among them propositional logic, first-order logic, and higher-order logics. To sum up, automated reasoning means using a computer program to reason logically and reach decisions from established facts or axioms, and it is a powerful tool for tackling complex problems and tasks beyond human manual capability.

If you're a contractor, go with TurboTax Business. It's built for businesses, whether you're a sole proprietor, a partnership, or a corporation. You get the stuff that matters for business owners, like filing a Schedule C (Form 1040) to report your business income and expenses, or a Form 1065 (Partnership Return of Income) if you've got a partnership. TurboTax Basic is really meant for people with simple returns and no business income or expenses. It probably won't have all the forms and features you need to report contractor income and expenses properly. Just make sure you pick the version that fits your situation and the IRS requirements. If you're not sure which one to get, a tax pro can point you in the right direction, or you can check the IRS website.

Hillary Rodham Clinton is an American politician, lawyer, and diplomat, born on October 26, 1947, in Chicago, Illinois. She graduated from Yale Law School and built a career in law and advocacy, with a focus on children's and family issues. She became First Lady of the United States when her husband, Bill Clinton, served as the 42nd president from 1993 to 2001. During that time she took on a prominent role in policy debates, most notably an effort to reform the nation's health care system.

She later represented New York in the United States Senate from 2001 to 2009, and then served as Secretary of State under President Barack Obama from 2009 to 2013. In that role she traveled extensively, promoted diplomatic initiatives, and was a significant figure in American foreign policy. She also ran for the Democratic presidential nomination in 2008, losing to Obama, and later became the Democratic Party's nominee for president in 2016, losing the general election to Donald Trump. She was the first woman to win a major party's presidential nomination in the United States.

Beyond elected and appointed office, Clinton has written several books, including memoirs and works on public policy, and she has remained an active figure in national politics and public life. Her career has made her one of the most widely recognized and often debated political figures in modern American history.

Whether $250,000 in five years is realistic depends mostly on what you're starting with, so the math is the place to begin. If you invest in a broad stock market index fund and earn a historically typical return of around 7 to 10 percent a year, you'd need roughly $160,000 to $180,000 invested today to reach $250,000 in five years. If you're starting from little or nothing, you'd need to contribute about $3,300 to $3,600 a month at those returns, since compounding does relatively little over such a short period. In most cases, then, the money will come mainly from what you earn and save, not from investment returns. Investing preserves and grows money you already have, but it rarely creates large sums quickly from a small base.

Trading is the path most people are drawn to, and it deserves a frank warning. Studies of retail day traders consistently find that the large majority lose money over time, and only a very small percentage earn more than they could at an ordinary job. Turning a few thousand dollars into $250,000 through trading would require extraordinary returns sustained for years, which is statistically very unlikely and usually involves leverage, options, or crypto speculation that can wipe out an account entirely. If you want to trade, treat it as a small slice of your money you can afford to lose, not as your primary plan.

Raising your income is usually the most reliable lever. Some people get there by moving into higher-paying fields like software, sales with strong commissions, skilled trades such as electrical or plumbing work, nursing or other healthcare roles, or by negotiating raises and switching employers, which often brings bigger pay jumps than staying put. If you can earn enough to save $40,000 to $50,000 a year and invest it steadily, you would plausibly reach your target in five years. Living well below your means while your income rises is what makes this work.

Starting a business offers the highest upside and the widest range of outcomes. Service businesses with low startup costs, such as cleaning, landscaping, pressure washing, bookkeeping, consulting, freelance design or development, or a skilled trade you already know, tend to be more dependable than product or app ideas because they can become profitable quickly and don't need much capital. Many people start these on the side while keeping their job, reinvest early profits, and grow by hiring help once demand exceeds what they can handle. A service business netting $60,000 to $100,000 a year in profit is achievable for many motivated people within a few years, though it takes real work and some failures along the way. Real estate is another route people use, through house hacking (buying a small multi-unit property, living in one unit, and renting the others) or improving and reselling properties. It can build equity fairly fast but carries debt, market, and execution risks.

For most people, the strongest plan combines these. Increase your earning power through your career or a side business, keep expenses low, put the savings into diversified low-cost index funds, and avoid gambling the core of your money on speculative trades. If you share your current savings, income, skills, and how much risk you can tolerate, I can help sketch a more specific path and run the numbers for your situation.

A measuring wheel, sometimes called a surveyor's wheel or hodometer, is a handheld instrument that surveyors and other professionals use to gauge distance. It has a wheel fitted with a handle and a counter that tallies how many times the wheel turns as it rolls across the ground. To find the space between two locations, or the length of a straight or winding route, surveyors push the wheel along the path. The user works out the distance covered by multiplying the revolution count by the wheel's circumference. These wheels are especially handy for covering long stretches of rough or uneven land, and they are used in many places, such as building sites, woodlands, and farm fields.

A backdoor is a way of getting around the normal login or security checks on a computer system, program, or app. Someone can use one to sneak into a system they shouldn't have access to, or to do things inside it that they're not allowed to do. Backdoors show up in a few different ways. A developer might build one in on purpose, an attacker might plant one after breaking in, or it might just be a flaw nobody fixed. Bad actors use them for all sorts of things, like grabbing sensitive data or taking remote control of a machine. They can also let someone skip past protections that are supposed to block certain actions. Finding and removing them matters a lot, since they're a serious risk. The usual approach is running regular security audits, testing the system, and keeping software patched and up to date.

The phrase "I think, therefore I am" comes from the French philosopher René Descartes. People often refer to it as the "Cogito," since the Latin word "cogito" means "I think," and that is how the original statement begins. The point of the quote is that thinking itself shows you exist. Even if you cannot be certain of anything else in the world, you can be certain of your own existence, because you are able to think about it. Doubting or questioning anything requires someone to carry out that doubt, so there must first be a being that exists. In other words, "I think, therefore I am" means that your ability to think proves you exist. Does that make sense?

Spain won the most recent FIFA Women's World Cup, held in 2023 in Australia and New Zealand. They beat England 1-0 in the final in Sydney on August 20, 2023, with Olga Carmona scoring the only goal. It was Spain's first Women's World Cup title. The next tournament is set for 2027 in Brazil, so if you're asking after that, there may be a newer champion.

A flame is basically fire you can see burning bright. It's a mix of gases, like oxygen and some kind of fuel (wood, gasoline, whatever), and once that mix catches, it starts to burn. The burning gives off heat and light. You can cook dinner with that heat, stay warm on a cold night, or even run machines. The light helps when it's dark out, and people have used it as a signal for ages. Flames are gorgeous to watch, but they can really hurt you if you don't respect them. So be careful around them and follow the safety rules, especially if you're the one holding the lighter.

Imagine a family that kept borrowing money from its neighbors so it could buy lots of toys and treats, and it kept doing this for many years, even when it wasn't earning enough to pay the money back. That's a lot like what happened to Greece.

For a long time, the Greek government spent more money than it collected. The money it collected comes mostly from taxes, and Greece often didn't collect as much of it as it should have, partly because many people and businesses didn't pay all the taxes they owed. Meanwhile, the government spent a lot on things like paying large numbers of workers, giving out pensions to people who retired early, and running its public services. When you spend more than you bring in, you have to borrow the difference, and the borrowing piles up over time.

Greece also had some tricky things happen with its numbers. Before it joined the euro, a shared money used by many European countries, it had problems keeping its finances honest. Later, it was found that Greece had been reporting figures that made its debt look smaller than it really was. Once the truth came out around 2009, lenders became worried and stopped lending to Greece, or demanded much higher interest.

Then came a big world event, the 2008 financial crisis, which hurt economies everywhere and made it even harder for Greece to earn and borrow. The country could no longer pay back what it owed on its own, so other European countries and the International Monetary Fund stepped in with rescue loans. Those loans came with strict conditions, like cutting government spending and raising taxes, which made life hard for many Greek people for years, with lots of job losses and shrinking incomes.

So, in short: Greece spent and borrowed more than it could afford, didn't collect all the taxes it should have, hid how bad the numbers really were, and then got hit by a global crisis that made the problem impossible to ignore.

Toast tastes different from plain bread mostly because the heat changes it in a few ways at once. The outside gets crispy and crunchy, and that contrast with the softer middle is a big part of why it's nicer to eat. It's like you get two textures in one bite instead of just one.

The color changes too. It goes golden brown, which looks way more appealing, and honestly that affects how good something tastes more than people think. Then there's the smell. Once it's toasting you get that slightly nutty, toasty aroma, and smell is a huge part of flavor anyway.

So it's really the look, the feel, and the smell all shifting together, and that adds up to bread that just tastes better.

Written by J.J. Cale, the song "Cocaine" was originally recorded by Cale himself and appeared on his 1972 debut album, Naturally. Many other musicians have since performed their own versions, and one of the most successful came from Eric Clapton, whose 1977 recording reached the charts.

Persistent diarrhoea in toddlers around his age often has a few likely explanations. One is an infection, such as giardia or another gut bacterium, which can linger for weeks and needs a stool test to identify. Another is a temporary loss of the enzyme that digests lactose, which often follows a stomach bug. This would fit with lactose-free milk not helping much, since the problem may be less about lactose itself. A third is an intolerance or allergy to cow's milk protein, which is common in this age group and is the reason doctors often suggest soya formula. Soya is a reasonable next step for that, though some children with cow's milk protein sensitivity also react to soya, so it's worth watching how he responds over a few weeks. Gluten-related problems (coeliac disease) can also appear once wheat is introduced, and in less common cases there may be a problem with how the gut absorbs nutrients. Many toddlers also have "toddler diarrhoea," which is harmless, causes frequent loose stools with bits of undigested food, and is often linked to large amounts of fruit juice or sugary drinks. If he is growing well and otherwise happy, this is a common and benign explanation, but his doctors will want to rule out the others first.

A few things would be useful to ask his doctor. Ask whether stool tests have been done to check for infection and whether any blood or fat malabsorption tests are planned. Ask whether his weight and growth have been checked, since that tells you a lot about how much he is absorbing. Ask how long to trial the soya formula before judging whether it's working, and whether a dietitian or paediatric gastroenterologist should be involved if things don't improve. It's also worth asking about his fluid intake, and how much juice or sweet drinks he has.

Seek medical advice promptly if he shows signs of dehydration, such as fewer wet nappies, a dry mouth, sunken eyes, unusual sleepiness or crying without tears. You should also be concerned about blood or mucus in the stool, vomiting, fever, weight loss or poor weight gain.

Imagine two kids who each run a big toy box at school where anyone can drop things off and anyone else can come take a copy. Both toy boxes sometimes end up with stuff that was swiped from someone else. The teacher doesn't punish either kid just for that, because the rule is: if someone says "hey, that's mine, it was stolen," you have to take it out right away and you can't be trying to collect stolen stuff on purpose. As long as you follow that rule honestly, you're allowed to keep running your toy box.

MediaFire is like the kid who follows the rule. When a movie studio or music company says "that file is ours," MediaFire removes it. It doesn't pay people for uploading popular stuff, and over time it leaned more toward being a regular storage service for personal files, like a digital backpack. So it gets protection under the law (in the US this is called the DMCA "safe harbor").

MegaUpload, according to the US government, was like the kid who pretended to follow the rule but was secretly cheating. Prosecutors said it paid people rewards when their uploads got downloaded a lot, and the most downloaded things were usually pirated movies, shows, and music, so it was basically paying people to bring in stolen stuff. When a company asked for a file to be removed, MegaUpload allegedly just deleted that one link while keeping the actual file and other links to it, so the stolen copy stayed available. Investigators also said they found internal emails showing the people running it knew exactly what was going on, and even shared pirated files themselves. On top of that, it was enormous, reportedly a few percent of all internet traffic, and the government claimed it made around 175 million dollars, much of it from people paying to download pirated content faster. Its founder, Kim Dotcom, was also very flashy and public, which made it an obvious target.

So the government shut down MegaUpload in 2012 and charged its owners with crimes, not just because pirated stuff was on it, but because they believed the whole business was built on piracy and the owners were knowingly helping it happen. MediaFire stayed open because it played by the rules closely enough. After MegaUpload went down, a lot of similar sites got scared and either changed how they worked or shut themselves down, which was partly the point of making an example of one big, bold player.

Several elements can drive shifts in both rent and home prices. For rent, one key influence is how many people want rental units in a given area. When renters are plentiful relative to available units, landlords can often command higher rents. When demand is weak, however, they may need to reduce rents to fill vacancies. Costs also matter: when landlords pay more for property taxes, utilities, or repairs, they frequently raise rents to offset those expenses.

Home prices, meanwhile, respond to a different set of forces. The general condition of the housing market plays a central role. Strong demand paired with limited inventory tends to push prices up, while weak demand or an abundance of listings tends to pull them down. Interest rates are another major factor. Low rates make mortgages cheaper, encouraging more buyers and pushing prices higher, whereas high rates raise borrowing costs, dampening demand and often leading prices to fall. The broader economy also matters, since a healthy economy tends to boost housing demand and prices, and a sluggish one tends to reduce them. Finally, location shapes value, as homes in some neighborhoods attract more buyers than others. School quality, job opportunities, and the general appeal of an area all affect how much demand exists for homes there.

In short, many variables contribute to changes in rent and home prices, and the reasons behind any particular movement can differ widely from one market and location to another.

The Oxford English Dictionary (OED) is a huge dictionary of the English language, put out by Oxford University Press. Lots of people consider it the most authoritative English dictionary out there, and language scholars lean on it all the time. It's a historical dictionary, so it tracks how words and their meanings have changed over the centuries. With more than 600,000 main entries, it gives definitions, etymologies, and quotations showing words in actual use. You'll also find pronunciation, grammar notes, and info on regional variations. It comes in print and online, and it gets updated regularly to keep up with how English changes. Writers, editors, linguists, and anyone else curious about the language end up using it as a reference.

So to claim HST compensation on your personal return in Ontario, you've got to file a tax return with the CRA. Here's roughly how it goes.

First, get your paperwork together. You'll want any receipts or invoices showing the HST you paid, and maybe proof of any credits or rebates you already got.

Next, check that you're actually eligible. There are some criteria. For example, you have to be an Ontario resident on December 31st of the tax year, and you have to have paid HST on eligible expenses.

Then work out your claim. Add up all the HST you paid on eligible expenses during the year, and subtract any credits or rebates you've received.

After that, when you file, you enter the HST you paid and the credits or rebates you got. That lets you claim the HST as a tax credit on your return.

Last step is sending it in to the CRA. You can file online or mail in a paper copy, whichever you prefer.

If you're still unsure about any of it, it's worth calling the CRA or talking to a tax professional. They can sort out the specifics for your situation.

Blind individuals rely on either a white cane or a guide dog to get around and locate objects. The cane is a slender, lightweight rod held in the hand and swept back and forth along the ground while walking. Through this tapping, the person senses bumps or shifts in the surface, which signal obstacles ahead or the boundaries of features such as curbs and steps. When searching for a sign that has Braille on it, a blind person may sweep the cane across the area to find the sign. They can also draw on their other senses, such as hearing and smell, to narrow down its location. For instance, they might listen for sounds emanating from the sign or notice any scents nearby. After finding the sign, they run their fingertips over its raised dots. Braille uses patterns of raised dots to stand for letters, numbers, and symbols, and readers identify these patterns by moving their fingers across them. Finding and reading a Braille sign may take a blind person somewhat longer than it would take a sighted person, but with practice and the aid of a cane or guide dog, they can accomplish the task just as effectively as anyone else.

Flies can zip around and switch direction in an instant, thanks to the many small muscles in their wings that produce rapid adjustments. Their eyesight is also excellent, so they spot danger early and steer clear of it. On top of that, flies are extremely nimble and can shift their body weight swiftly to turn mid-flight. As you swing at one, it detects your motion and takes off before you make contact, which is why it often looks as though the fly is deliberately dodging your strikes. In short, flies have evolved to be highly skilled at escaping danger and staying safe, which explains why they can slip away even when you feel certain you have them trapped.

Joseph Boakye Danquah, a Ghanaian politician, was among the founders of the United Gold Coast Convention (UGCC), a party that contributed greatly to Ghana's fight for independence. Born in 1909 in Bekwai, a town in Ghana's Ashanti Region, he studied at Achimota College and the University of London. Danquah became a leading figure in Ghanaian politics and played a key part in the negotiations that ended British colonial rule and brought independence in 1957. He sat in parliament and held several ministerial positions, among them Minister of Justice and Attorney General. He died in 1965.

When the stock market takes a big dive, what people call a crash, it tends to shake up other investments too, bonds included. Usually, when stocks tank, folks pull their money out and park it somewhere safer, and bonds are a go-to for that. They're seen as safer than stocks because they pay a fixed return, and the issuer generally has to pay back the principal and interest on a set date down the road. So when everyone rushes toward bonds, demand goes up, and that tends to push bond prices higher. More demand for something usually means its price climbs. That said, the bond-stock relationship isn't always so neat. It depends on a bunch of stuff, like how the economy is doing and where interest rates are sitting. If you're thinking about making moves with your money, it's worth talking to a financial advisor before you pull the trigger.

Imagine a big pizza that a whole town owns together. Each slice is a tiny piece of ownership in a company, and those slices are called stocks, or shares. When you buy a share of a company like a toy maker or a shoe company, you own a tiny little piece of it. If the company does well and makes lots of money, your slice often becomes worth more, and some companies even share a bit of their money with their owners as a thank-you called a dividend. If the company does badly, your slice can become worth less, so there is always a risk.

The place where people trade these slices is called the stock market. Think of it like a giant marketplace where buyers and sellers meet. Prices go up and down all day based on what people think a company is worth and what they expect it to do in the future.

To start, you need a brokerage account. A brokerage is a company that lets you buy and sell stocks. Some popular ones in the United States include Fidelity, Charles Schwab, Vanguard, and Robinhood, and many banks have their own too. You sign up online, give some basic information like your name, address, and Social Security number, link a bank account to put money in, and then you can buy shares through their app or website. Many brokers now let you start with very small amounts, even a few dollars, and let you buy partial shares.

Once you are set up, search for a company by its ticker symbol, which is a short code like AAPL for Apple, type in how much you want to buy, and place your order. Many beginners start with a broad index fund, which is a single investment that holds tiny pieces of hundreds of companies at once. That spreads out your risk, so if one company struggles, the others can help balance it out.

Go slowly, only put in money you won't need soon, and remember that the market goes up and down. Learning as you go is a good idea, and it can help to read beginner resources from places like Investor.gov, which is run by the U.S. government and is free.

If the underlying stays below the strike price, a put option is in the money, and at expiration its value equals its intrinsic value: the strike price minus the underlying's price. For example, if you hold a put with a $50 strike and the stock is trading at $42 at expiration, the put is worth $8 per share. Since a standard equity option contract covers 100 shares, that comes to $800 per contract.

Before expiration, the put is worth more than that intrinsic amount because it also carries time value, which reflects the chance the underlying could fall further before the option expires. Time value depends on how much time is left, how volatile the underlying is, and interest rates. It shrinks as expiration approaches and disappears entirely at expiry. For deep in-the-money puts, time value is often small, and in some cases, particularly with American-style puts where early exercise is allowed, the option may trade very close to its intrinsic value.

Value and profit are different. Your actual profit is the put's value minus the premium you paid. If you paid $3 for that $50 put and the stock ends at $42, your profit is $8 minus $3, or $5 per share. The breakeven point at expiration is the strike minus the premium, so in this case the stock needs to be below $47 for you to come out ahead. If the stock is below the strike but above breakeven, say at $48, the put is worth $2, but you still lose $1 per share overall.

If you sold the put instead of buying it, the picture is reversed. The underlying staying below the strike means the option will likely be exercised against you, obligating you to buy the shares at the strike price. Your loss is the strike minus the market price, offset by the premium you collected.

Okay so if you're getting hounded by student loan collectors, you've got a few options. First, if payments are killing you, look into a repayment plan. There are several, including income-driven ones that base your monthly payment on how much you make and how big your family is. Your loan servicer can walk you through what's available.

If you're only temporarily unable to pay, you might be able to pause things through deferment or forbearance. Deferment works if you're back in school, in the military, or going through economic hardship. Forbearance lets you lower or skip payments during financial trouble, but heads up, interest keeps piling up on your loans the whole time.

Got more than one student loan? Consolidating them into a single loan can make life easier to manage and might lower your monthly payment.

Forgiveness is another possibility in some cases. If you work in public service, teach in a low-income area, or serve in the military, you could qualify.

And if you think you don't actually owe the debt being collected, you can dispute it. Put your challenge in writing to the collector and include whatever evidence you've got. They have to verify the debt and prove you owe it. If they can't, they have to stop collecting.

Also, collectors have to follow federal and state rules about how they behave. If one is acting shady or illegal, file a complaint with the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB). They can investigate and step in if needed.

College students are generally wise to begin planning how they will save and invest for the future. Still, before settling on how much to put into stocks, several considerations deserve attention. The first is your financial footing: a solid base should be in place before investing, which means keeping an emergency fund, clearing any high-interest debt, and sticking to a budget. The second is what you want your investments to accomplish. Are you building a retirement nest egg, or do you need income in the near term? Your objectives will shape both the amount you commit and the kinds of assets worth considering. The third is your tolerance for risk. Stock investing always carries some uncertainty, so you should be at ease with the risk you take on. Newcomers may prefer a more cautious approach, usually a blend of stocks and bonds. Overall, starting small and raising your contributions gradually tends to be sensible, since it lets you learn how markets behave without exposing yourself to excessive danger. Consulting a financial professional can also help, as they can build a personalized plan suited to your circumstances and goals.

Pinning down the precise count of registered vehicles in the United States is hard, since the figure shifts constantly as new vehicles are bought and registered while older ones are retired from use. Still, Federal Highway Administration (FHWA) data indicates that roughly 263 million vehicles were registered across the country as of December 2020. That total covers passenger cars, trucks, buses, and motorcycles. Because the FHWA revises these statistics regularly, the present-day number of registered vehicles in the U.S. could differ somewhat.

A stye is basically an infection in one of the oil glands along your eyelid. A high white blood cell (WBC) count can point to infection, but it doesn't really cause a stye on its own. Other stuff can make you more likely to get one, like poor hygiene, a weakened immune system, or some underlying medical conditions. If you've got one, it's worth getting it checked by a healthcare provider so you know what you're dealing with. They'll often suggest warm compresses and gently cleaning the area with an antibacterial solution. Sometimes they'll prescribe antibiotic eye drops or ointment to clear it up. Now and then a stye has to be drained surgically, but that's not the usual route. Good hygiene helps keep things from spreading: wash your hands often and don't share towels or makeup. If you keep getting styes or notice other eye problems, definitely get that looked at too.

The green on the Mexican flag is supposed to stand for hope, joy, and love, and it also nods to the independence movement. There are three colors up there, green, white, and red, and they run in vertical stripes, not horizontal ones like people sometimes assume. Green is on the left, white sits in the middle, and red is on the right. Since all three stripes are the same size, it's a tricolor with equal bands. The colors and symbolism tie back to Mexico's coat of arms, which shows an eagle perched on a cactus with a serpent in its beak. You'll also hear that the colors reflect the country's landscape, with green for the lush forests and red for the soil.

The prostate is a gland in the male reproductive system, tucked just below the bladder and wrapped around the urethra, the tube that carries urine and semen out of the body. Its main job is making a fluid that forms part of semen. When you get sexually aroused, the prostate contracts and squeezes some of that fluid into the urethra, where it mixes with sperm and other fluids. That fluid helps feed and protect the sperm and gives them a better shot at getting through the female reproductive tract. Problems like an enlarged prostate or prostate cancer can mess with peeing and sex, so it's worth getting checked out by your doctor now and then.

Pain at the back of the lower ribs after a blow usually comes from one of a few sources, and a cracked rib is definitely one of them. The most common causes are a rib bruise (contusion), a cracked or fractured rib, a strain of the intercostal muscles that run between the ribs, or a sprain of the small joints where the ribs attach to the spine. All of these can produce sharp, on-and-off pain that flares when you sit a certain way, twist, stretch, take a deep breath, cough, or sneeze. Bruises and muscle strains tend to improve noticeably within one to three weeks, while a cracked rib often takes around four to six weeks to heal and may stay tender to direct pressure over one specific spot for a while. The fact that your pain has eased somewhat is a good sign, but it doesn't rule out a small crack, since those also gradually get better. Honestly, the treatment for a simple bruise and a simple hairline rib fracture is largely the same, which is why doctors don't always X-ray uncomplicated cases, and small cracks often don't show up on X-ray anyway.

Because your pain is on the lower left side of the back, there are two organs worth keeping in mind. The left kidney sits right beneath those lower back ribs, and a hard hit there can bruise it. Signs of that include blood in your urine (pink, red, or cola-colored), pain that feels deep rather than on the surface, or flank pain that worsens rather than improves. The spleen also sits under the lower left ribs, and it can be injured by trauma, sometimes with delayed symptoms. Warning signs of a spleen injury include worsening pain in the left upper abdomen, pain that spreads to the left shoulder tip, dizziness or lightheadedness, fainting, a fast heartbeat, or feeling pale and clammy. Any of those, or significant shortness of breath, coughing up blood, or pain that gets steadily worse, should be treated as an emergency.

If none of those warning signs are present, home care usually works well. Rest from heavy lifting and contact activities, apply ice for 15 to 20 minutes at a time in the first few days (heat can help later for muscle tightness), and use over-the-counter pain relief such as acetaminophen or ibuprofen if they're safe for you. One important point with suspected rib injuries is to keep breathing deeply and to cough when needed, even though it hurts. Holding a pillow against the area can make this easier. Shallow breathing to avoid pain can lead to chest infections like pneumonia. Avoid wrapping or binding your ribs tightly for the same reason.

It's reasonable to see a doctor if the pain isn't clearly improving after a couple of weeks, if one specific point on a rib is very tender to press, if you felt or heard a crack or crunch, or if you simply want peace of mind. They can examine you, check your urine for blood, and decide whether imaging is needed.

Dishwashers are really good at cleaning, but they can be rough on knives in a few ways. Inside the machine, your knife gets bounced around and knocks against plates, glasses, and other metal things. That banging can dull the edge or even chip it, like how a crayon gets broken if you toss it in a box full of toys. The water jets also push hard, so a thin blade can get shoved into other dishes and get nicked.

The soap is a bigger problem than it sounds. Dishwasher detergent is much stronger than the gentle dish soap you use by hand, and it has chemicals that can slowly eat away at the metal and make it dull or spotty. Wood handles are even worse off, because the hot water and strong soap can dry them out, crack them, and make them loosen over time.

When you wash by hand, you hold the knife yourself, you can see exactly where the blade is, and you can dry it right away so water doesn't sit on it and cause rust. That's why hand washing keeps a sharp knife sharp for much longer.

Picture yourself in a room. You can go forward or back, left or right, up or down, so that's three directions. Now try adding a fourth one that's totally separate from those three. Honestly, it's hard to picture, since our brains are built for three dimensions and anything beyond that kind of breaks our intuition. One way people try to wrap their heads around it is by treating time as the fourth dimension. You can move forward into the future or back into the past, same as you move through space. But time isn't really a space you walk through the way you walk across a room. It's more like a way of keeping track of how things change and happen in order. Beyond time, you could imagine other kinds of extra directions, but coming up with a concrete example gets tricky fast. Some scientists and philosophers have floated the idea of extra dimensions past the three we live in, but nobody can say for sure what they'd look like or how they'd work.

Ensemble averaging is a statistical method that merges the outputs of several models to produce more precise predictions. Typically, multiple models are trained on the same dataset, and their predictions are then averaged. The approach offers several benefits. First, it can curb overfitting, since each model trained on the same data is less likely to memorize the same noise or random fluctuations, so their combined behavior is less tied to the training set. Second, it can strengthen generalization: by pooling the predictions of several models, the ensemble may capture the underlying structure of the data more effectively, which tends to yield better results on new, unseen inputs. Third, it can make predictions more stable, because averaging reduces sensitivity to the particular model chosen or the exact hyperparameter settings used. Several techniques exist for combining predictions, including simple averaging, weighted averaging, and voting. Simple averaging takes the mean of all models' predictions. Weighted averaging assigns each model a weight according to its performance and averages the weighted predictions. Voting lets each model cast a ballot for the final outcome, with the option receiving the most votes becoming the ensemble's prediction. Overall, ensemble averaging is a powerful way to improve both the accuracy and reliability of predictions in machine learning and data analysis.

The answer depends on what you mean by "tick level," because most retail platforms don't stream every trade and quote change. They send throttled or conflated updates, often several times per second, which looks real-time but isn't true tick-by-tick data. If you need every print and every quote change, you'll often get better value from a dedicated data vendor alongside a cheap or free broker.

Among brokers, Interactive Brokers is usually the strongest value for serious traders. Its standard feed is filtered and snapshotted at intervals of a few hundred milliseconds, but its API offers a genuine tick-by-tick request type, limited by how many market data lines you have. Non-professional US data bundles run roughly ten dollars a month or less and are often waived if you generate enough commissions. Depth-of-book feeds like Nasdaq TotalView cost extra, typically in the mid-teens per month for non-professionals.

Charles Schwab's thinkorswim platform gives free real-time streaming quotes, Level II, and time and sales to account holders, which is hard to beat if you trade manually. Its API is also free but conflated and rate-limited, so it suits retail use better than high-fidelity tick capture.

TradeStation has long been popular with active and algorithmic traders for its tick-based charting and historical tick data, and data fees are often waived with modest activity. Tastytrade offers free streaming quotes and a reasonable API through its DXFeed-based infrastructure, mainly for options and futures traders. Webull and moomoo give free real-time quotes and cheap or promotional Level II subscriptions, but their feeds are aggregated and not suited to precise tick analysis. Tradier and Alpaca are developer-oriented brokers with streaming APIs. Alpaca's free tier uses only the IEX exchange feed, a small slice of total volume, and full SIP consolidated data costs about a hundred dollars a month.

If you want true tick-level fidelity, look beyond brokers to data providers. Databento sells exchange-native tick and order book data on usage-based or subscription pricing and is widely regarded as excellent for quality per dollar. Polygon, which has rebranded under the name Massive, offers consolidated real-time tick streams on flat monthly plans starting in the tens of dollars. DTN IQFeed has long been the standard for unfiltered tick data for retail charting software like Sierra Chart and NinjaTrader, at roughly eighty to a hundred dollars a month with exchange fees. For futures specifically, Rithmic and CQG feeds through brokers like AMP Futures or EdgeClear provide unfiltered ticks very cheaply, often a few dollars a month plus CME exchange fees.

A practical setup for many people is to execute at a low-cost broker like Interactive Brokers or Schwab and pay a specialist vendor such as Databento, Polygon/Massive, or IQFeed for clean tick data. For futures, a Rithmic-connected broker is hard to beat. Exchange fees differ greatly depending on whether you qualify as a non-professional, so classify yourself correctly. Pricing changes often, so check current rate cards before committing.

Puce is basically a dark reddish-brown, though you'll see it called a purplish-brown or a brownish-purple too. It's one of those muted, understated colors that sits somewhere between red and brown. Some folks would say it looks more like a reddish-gray, or even a dull, washed-out pink. You run into it a lot in interior design and fashion, and it shows up in all sorts of stuff, like paint, fabric, and wallpaper.

Many brokerages provide streaming quotes, and their prices vary widely. When deciding which one to choose, you may want to weigh several factors. The first is cost: what does the brokerage charge for streaming quotes, and are there extra fees for particular features or data feeds? The second is data quality, meaning how fast and accurate the quotes are, and whether the data comes straight from the exchanges or is pulled together from several sources. The third is platform features: is the interface easy to use for viewing and analyzing streaming quotes, and does it include tools or indicators that help you make better-informed trading decisions? The fourth is customer service: does the brokerage respond promptly to questions and problems, and does it offer assistance in multiple languages and time zones?

Brokerages known for their streaming quote services include Interactive Brokers, E*TRADE, TD Ameritrade, and Charles Schwab. It's a good idea to compare the features and pricing of a few different brokerages so you can find the one that suits your needs best.

Windows XP was released to manufacturing in August 2001 and became generally available on October 25, 2001. That makes it over 23 years old as of 2025. Microsoft ended mainstream support in 2009 and stopped providing security updates for most editions in April 2014, though it extended support for some embedded versions until 2019 and a few later ones.

Interstate 70 runs east-west across the country, from Cove Fort, Utah all the way to Baltimore, Maryland. Along the way it passes through Utah, Colorado, Kansas, Missouri, Illinois, Indiana, Ohio, West Virginia, Pennsylvania, and Maryland. It's a big deal for both travelers and trucks, linking a lot of major cities and popular getaway spots. You'll get through the Rockies, the Great Plains, and the Appalachians, and it runs by or close to several national parks and monuments, like Arches, the Colorado National Monument, Black Canyon of the Gunnison, the Appalachian Trail corridor, and the C&O Canal National Historical Park.

Judgment as a matter of law, also called a directed verdict, is what a judge issues during a trial when they decide one side has won without the jury needing to weigh in on the facts. Basically, the judge concludes the evidence from one party is so strong that the other side can't realistically win, no matter what the jury thinks. It can happen when one party's evidence simply isn't legally enough to back up their claims or defenses. It can also happen when the other side's evidence is so overwhelming that no reasonable jury could land anywhere else. Judges can also step in if both sides have agreed on the facts and the only questions left are legal ones. Usually it's saved for cases where there's no real fight over the facts or the law, and it's a way to wrap things up early once it's obvious who should win. Don't confuse it with a judgment on the merits, though. That's the final ruling on who has which rights and who owes what, based on the evidence and the law.

Visible light is a form of electromagnetic radiation that our eyes can detect. Its wavelengths lie roughly between 400 and 700 nanometers (nm), and this range is the reason it receives the name visible light. Light with a shorter wavelength carries more energy and looks more blue, while light with a longer wavelength carries less energy and looks more red. Visible light occupies only a narrow band of the electromagnetic spectrum, which also covers radio waves, microwaves, infrared, ultraviolet, X-rays, and gamma rays. Such radiation surrounds us constantly, yet our eyes can perceive just a tiny fraction of it. Visible light matters greatly in daily life: it allows us to see our surroundings and is put to use in many fields, including lighting, communication, and photography.

Yeah, unpaid taxes can definitely get in the way of getting a business license. A lot of states and cities want you squared away on taxes and other financial stuff before they'll sign off on one. The thinking is that they want businesses to be run responsibly and actually pay what they owe.

So if you've got back taxes hanging over you, you'll probably have to deal with that first. Sometimes that means paying the whole thing off, and other times you can set up a payment plan with the tax agency and that's enough to get you through.

I'd sort it out sooner rather than later, though. Letting it sit just piles on penalties and interest, and it can eventually turn into legal trouble too. If you're not even sure whether you owe anything, or you don't know how to fix it, talking to a tax pro or an attorney is worth it. They can tell you what makes the most sense for your situation.

Biomarkers of aging are measurable biological indicators that reflect the progression of aging within an organism, going beyond chronological age, which is simply the number of years a person has lived. Two people born on the same day can have very different biological ages, meaning their bodies may be functioning as though they are older or younger than their calendar years suggest. Biomarkers aim to capture these differences by tracking the underlying processes that drive aging, such as cellular damage, declining organ function, and changes in metabolism or the immune system.

Researchers look at many kinds of biomarkers. Some are molecular, such as patterns of chemical modifications on DNA known as epigenetic clocks, which can estimate biological age with surprising accuracy by analyzing methylation at specific sites in the genome. Others include telomere length, which tends to shorten as cells divide, and markers of inflammation like elevated levels of certain blood proteins. Clinical and physiological measures also play a role, including blood pressure, grip strength, lung capacity, cognitive performance, and blood chemistry values such as glucose, cholesterol, and kidney or liver function indicators. Combining many such measures into a single score is a common approach, since no single marker captures the full complexity of aging.

The value of these biomarkers lies in several areas. They can help scientists understand why organisms age and how interventions might slow the process. They may allow doctors to identify people at higher risk for age-related diseases like heart disease, dementia, or diabetes before symptoms appear. They are also used to test whether treatments, such as diet changes, exercise programs, or experimental drugs, actually slow biological aging rather than just treating individual diseases.

Despite their promise, biomarkers of aging are still an active area of research. There is no universally accepted standard, and different tests can give different results for the same person. Researchers continue to work on validating these markers, confirming that they reliably predict health outcomes and respond meaningfully to interventions.

Hi Amit, I'm sorry you've been dealing with this. Pigmentation after laser hair reduction is a known complication, called post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation. It happens when the skin is irritated or mildly burned by the laser, and the pigment cells respond by making extra melanin. It is more common in medium to darker skin types, and in people who get sun exposure around the time of treatment. The good news is that it is usually treatable, though after two years it will likely need patience and a consistent routine, and it is best supervised by a dermatologist who can examine your skin in person.

The most important step is strict sun protection. Ultraviolet and even visible light keep the pigment active and make it darker.
