Imagine you're trying to describe someone you can't see, touch, or fully understand, and the only words you have were made for describing people. That's the problem religions ran into with God. Most of the big monotheistic traditions actually teach that God is not a man or a woman at all, because God doesn't have a body. But languages like Hebrew, Arabic, Greek, and Punjabi sort almost every word into "he" or "she," and there's no good word for a person who is neither. So people had to pick one, and they mostly picked "he."

Why "he"? A big part of the answer is history. These religions grew up in societies where fathers and kings were in charge. When people wanted to say God is powerful, protects us, makes the rules, and takes care of us like a family, the most natural pictures were "King" and "Father." Jesus called God "Father," and that word became central to Christian prayer, so Christians feel they should keep using the words Jesus gave them. In Judaism, God is called "King of the Universe" in many prayers. Using "he" also helped these religions stand apart from neighboring religions that had goddesses tied to fertility and nature, so calling God "he" was partly a way of saying "our God is different from those."

Now here's the interesting part: the religions themselves often say the "he" is just a placeholder. In Judaism, the Bible says humans, both male and female, were made "in God's image," which many teachers read as meaning God includes qualities of both. Jewish mystics even speak of the Shekhinah, a feminine word for God's presence. Islam is very firm that God, Allah, is nothing like any created thing, so God is definitely not male; the Arabic word "huwa" is just grammar. In fact, one of God's most important names, ar-Rahman, comes from the same root as the word for a mother's womb. Sikhism teaches that God is formless and beyond gender, and the Guru Granth Sahib calls God both mother and father, though in everyday translation people often say "He."

Christianity also has female pictures of God tucked into the Bible: God is compared to a mother who comforts her child, a mother eagle, and a woman searching for a lost coin, and Jesus compares himself to a hen gathering her chicks.

So how do modern theologians explain all this? They mostly fall into a few groups. Many traditional thinkers say "Father" and "he" are not claims that God is a boy, but they should still be kept because they come from scripture and from Jesus himself, and because changing them might change the faith. Others say these words are like metaphors, little pictures pointing at something too big to see, and that it's fine and even good to also use female pictures, or to avoid gendered words when possible, so nobody thinks God is "more like" men than women. Some feminist theologians go further and argue that always calling God "he" made people think men were closer to God, and that this hurt women, so the language should change. And many Muslim and Sikh scholars simply say the problem is mostly an English-translation issue, since their traditions never believed God had a gender in the first place.

So the short version for a five-year-old would be this: most of these religions say God isn't a boy or a girl, but people needed a word to talk about God, they lived in a world where dads and kings were in charge, and "he" is the word that stuck. Today, grown-ups who study religion argue about whether to keep that word because it's tradition, or to use other words too so it's clear that God is bigger than any one kind of person.

A cryptographic hash function is a mathematical algorithm that takes an input of any size, such as a password, a file, or a message, and produces a fixed-length string of characters called a hash or digest. The same input always produces the same output, but even a tiny change to the input, such as altering a single letter, produces a completely different-looking output. This property makes it easy to check whether data has been changed.

What distinguishes a cryptographic hash function from an ordinary hash function, such as those used in programming to organize data in tables, is that it is designed to meet several strict security requirements. First, it should be computationally infeasible to reverse the process, meaning that given a hash value, you cannot practically work backward to find the original input. This is called preimage resistance. Second, it should be extremely difficult to find two different inputs that produce the same hash, which is known as collision resistance. Third, given one input and its hash, it should be hard to find a different input that yields that same hash, a property called second preimage resistance.

These functions are widely used in modern computing. They help verify file integrity, so you can confirm a downloaded file matches the version the publisher intended. They are central to digital signatures, where a hash of a document is signed rather than the whole document. They also underpin password storage, where systems store hashes of passwords instead of the passwords themselves, often combined with a random value called a salt to resist precomputed attacks. Blockchains such as Bitcoin rely on them to link blocks together and secure the chain.

Common examples include SHA-256, which is part of the SHA-2 family and widely used today, and SHA-3, a newer standard. Older algorithms like MD5 and SHA-1 are no longer considered secure because researchers have found practical ways to generate collisions in them.

Think of the movie rating system like a grown-up group that looks at every movie before letting it into the "official" list. The people in that group are called the Classification and Rating Administration in the United States, and they're the ones who give movies ratings like G, PG, PG-13, or R. Until they've watched the whole movie and made their decision, the honest thing to say is "not yet rated," even if everybody can guess what it will get.

Why does it take so long? Imagine your teacher had to watch a long video and then fill out a careful checklist about every scary moment, bad word, and kissing scene before deciding how old kids should be to see it. That takes time. The movie studio sends a finished copy, a small group of raters watches the entire thing, they talk about it together, and sometimes the studio is asked to trim a scene or two and send it back for another look. Each step adds days or weeks.

As for the guessing game, a movie that looks like a cartoon for families might still get an R if it has a lot of swearing or violence, and a movie that looks grown-up might surprise everyone. That's why the group doesn't guess; they just wait until they've seen it.

Yeah, a supraclinoid aneurysm can cause symptoms that look a lot like trigeminal neuralgia (TN), but they're really two different things, so getting the right diagnosis matters a lot for treatment. TN is facial pain from irritation or damage to the trigeminal nerve, the one that handles sensation in your face. It usually shows up as brief, severe jolts of pain, often set off by things like talking, chewing, or just touching your face. People often describe it as sharp and stabbing, and it can be bad enough to mess with your day.

An aneurysm, on the other hand, is a bulge in a blood vessel that can happen pretty much anywhere in the body. Supraclinoid aneurysms sit in vessels above the clinoid process, a bony bit inside the skull. They can cause headache, neck pain, and vision changes, and if one ruptures it can be life-threatening.

If you're having symptoms and think it might be one of these, see a neurosurgeon or another doctor for a proper workup. They can figure out what's actually going on and what treatment makes sense for you.

An itch is that prickly, annoying feeling on your skin that makes you want to scratch. Think of your skin as having tiny helper messengers called nerves. These nerves run from your skin up to your brain, and they carry messages like "hot," "cold," "ouch," and "tickle" or "itch."

Sometimes something bothers the skin. It might be a bug bite, a bit of dry skin, a scratchy sweater, sweat, or a little rash. When that happens, special cells in your skin release chemicals, and one famous one is called histamine. Histamine wakes up the itch messengers, and they send a signal up to your brain that says, "Hey, something is bugging me down here!"

Your brain doesn't like that bothersome feeling, so it tells your hand to scratch. Scratching works because it creates a different, stronger feeling, a little bit of pain or pressure, and that feeling pushes the itch signal out of the way for a moment. It's a bit like shouting over a noisy buzzing bee so you stop hearing the buzz.

That's also why scratching can feel so good, and why it sometimes makes the itch come back later. Scratching can irritate the skin even more, which sends more itch messages, so the cycle keeps going. The best help is to gently pat or rub the spot, or use a cool cloth, and let the skin calm down on its own.

Your understanding is pretty close. "Bourgeois" comes from French and originally meant town-dweller or property-owning citizen, and in the 1800s it came to describe the middle class: people who owned businesses, property, and money, as opposed to the working class who sold their labor, or the old aristocracy who inherited wealth and status.

It became an insult mostly because of Karl Marx and other socialist writers. They argued that the bourgeoisie, the owners of factories and capital, got rich off the work of everyone else, and that their values, like caring a lot about money, property, respectability, and keeping things the way they are, were really tools to protect their own advantage. So calling someone bourgeois became a way of saying they're comfortable and self-satisfied while ignoring the struggles of people below them.

Over time the word spread beyond that technical meaning. Today it often suggests someone who is conventional, materialistic, fussy about manners, or more concerned with appearances than with real principles. Some people also use it simply to mean "middle class" in a neutral way, so it depends a lot on who is speaking and how.

So, like you're five: a "bourgeois" person is someone who likes their nice house and tidy rules, and people use the word as a bit of a dig because they think those nice things come at the expense of others.

Yes, in many cases you can, and it's a popular strategy. Many credit cards offer elevated rewards at grocery stores, often 3% to 6% back depending on the card, and most grocery stores sell third-party gift cards for retailers like Amazon, Home Depot, Starbucks, restaurants, and gas stations. If the purchase codes as a grocery transaction, you earn the grocery rate on money you would have spent elsewhere anyway, which can beat the rate your card gives at the final merchant.

There are some important caveats. First, card issuers decide how to classify purchases, and the rules vary. Some cards explicitly exclude gift cards or purchases at superstores and warehouse clubs, so check your card's terms. Even at a regular supermarket, the transaction is usually coded by the merchant category of the store, so it often counts, but a few issuers have excluded gift card purchases from bonus categories or capped them.

Second, watch for fees. Third-party gift cards typically carry an activation or purchase fee, commonly $4 to $7 per card, which can wipe out the benefit. A fee of $5 on a $100 card is 5%, which erases most of the extra rewards. Higher-denomination cards dilute the fee, and some stores run promotions with bonus fuel points or waived fees, which makes the trade more attractive.

Third, stores often limit how many gift cards you can buy at once or per day, and some cap total dollar amounts. Frequent large purchases can also trigger fraud alerts or, rarely, an account review, since issuers watch for patterns resembling manufactured spending.

Fourth, the cards need to be for something you will actually spend. Buying cards for stores you use regularly, such as gas, dining, or home improvement, is sensible. Buying cards you won't use, or ones with expiration or dormancy fees, defeats the purpose.

Finally, compare against alternatives. If your card already earns a good flat rate, or earns more directly at the destination merchant, buying a gift card adds effort for little gain. Do the math: rewards rate at the grocery store minus the fee, versus the rate you'd get paying directly.

So it works when the card terms allow it, the fee is small or waived, and you'd use the cards anyway.

"Mama Told Me Not to Come" was sung by Randy Newman. He released it in 1966 on his debut album, *Randy Newman*, and it became a bigger hit in 1970 when Three Dog Night recorded a version that reached number 1 on the Billboard Hot 100.

Honestly it's not that home internet is "priced by speed" and phone data is "priced by amount." They're just two different kinds of service, usually sold by different companies, so they end up priced differently.

With home internet, you usually get a menu of speed tiers, and the faster ones cost more. Faster speeds let you do more at once, like streaming HD video or gaming online, since those things need a lot of data moved in a short window. On the phone side, plans are mostly priced by how much data you can use each month. The carriers have to pay to run and maintain the networks that get your phone online, and they've got to cover those costs somehow. The more data you burn through, the more it costs them, so they charge you more for bigger buckets.

So it's not really a clean "speed vs. data" split. It's just two services with different costs behind them and different ways people use them, and the pricing follows from that.

Honestly, a rear spoiler on a FWD car is mostly there to cut rear lift and add a bit of downforce back there, which helps the car feel planted at speed. A front wing could do something similar, but it really depends on how it's shaped and how it plays with the rest of the car. Most people put wings and spoilers on the back because that's where lift tends to be the biggest problem, thanks to how the weight is spread out.

Your description fits a hyperextension injury, where your elbow was forced straight, past its normal range, while your arm was loaded by the other player's weight. That kind of force can damage several structures at once. The most likely possibilities are a sprain of the ligaments that stabilize the elbow, particularly the ones on the inner or outer side; a strain or partial tear of the triceps or the tendons around the joint; a bruise or small fracture of the bone, most often the tip of the ulna (olecranon) or the head of the radius; or, less commonly, a partial or full dislocation.

The swelling comes from your body's inflammatory response. Small blood vessels in the injured tissue leak fluid and blood, and when that happens inside the joint, it can cause noticeable swelling and stiffness. Swelling that appears quickly, or a lot of blood in the joint, often points to a more serious injury such as a fracture or a significant ligament tear. Pain that comes and goes is common with sprains and bruises, since it tends to flare when you move or put weight on the arm.

Because I can't examine you, I can't tell which of these you have, and some of them, especially fractures and dislocations, need prompt treatment to heal well. I'd recommend seeing a doctor, urgent care, or a sports medicine clinic within the next day or so, sooner if you notice any of the following: you can't fully straighten or bend the elbow, the arm looks deformed, you can't bear weight on it or grip something, you have numbness, tingling, or coldness in your hand or fingers, the swelling is rapidly getting worse, or the pain is severe or constant.

In the meantime, you can rest the arm and avoid using it to push, lift, or brace yourself. Ice it for about 15 to 20 minutes at a time with a cloth between the ice and your skin, and keep it elevated above heart level when you can. An over-the-counter pain reliever such as ibuprofen or acetaminophen may help, as long as it's safe for you to take. Avoid trying to test the joint by forcing it straight or bending it hard.

Soda loses its fizz over time because the carbon dioxide responsible for it can slip out of the can, even when the can has been sealed. The gas is dissolved in the liquid, and whenever it gets the opportunity, it tends to leave the solution and enter the surrounding air. Opening a can lowers the pressure inside, which lets some of the dissolved carbon dioxide break free from the liquid and form bubbles. If the can is left open for an extended period, an increasing amount of the gas escapes into the air, and that gradual loss is what leaves the soda flat.

Counting cards is basically a way to get an edge at certain card games by keeping track of which cards have already been played and which ones are still left in the deck. The idea is to figure out whether the next card is more likely to be high or low, then bet bigger when the odds swing your way. Using a device or any kind of outside help to do it is illegal and counts as cheating. Just counting in your head, though, generally isn't illegal. Casinos fight back in a few ways: they throw multiple decks into the shoe, shuffle more often, or kick out anyone they catch doing it. People still try it anyway, even with those precautions in place.

Bob Seger was born on May 6, 1945, in Dearborn, Michigan. As of my most recent information, he is in his late seventies, so if you're asking about today's date, you can subtract 1945 from the current year (adjusting for whether his birthday has passed yet that year) to get his exact age.

Formal reasoning is the practice of drawing conclusions from premises by following explicit rules of inference, where the validity of the conclusion depends only on the structure or form of the argument rather than on the meaning of the particular words or the truth of the content. Its defining feature is that the rules are stated precisely enough that anyone can check each step mechanically, and a conclusion counts as correct whenever it follows from the premises under those rules.

A simple example is the classic syllogism: all men are mortal, Socrates is a man, therefore Socrates is mortal. The argument is valid because of its form, which might be written as "all A are B, x is A, therefore x is B." Any argument with that same form is valid, regardless of what A, B, and x stand for. Formal reasoning studies these forms and the rules that govern them.

The field is most developed in logic and mathematics. Formal systems consist of a language with defined symbols and grammar, a set of axioms or starting assumptions, and rules of inference that specify how new statements may be derived from old ones. A proof is a finite sequence of statements in which each one is either an axiom or follows from earlier lines by an allowed rule. Because every step is explicit, proofs can be verified without relying on intuition or interpretation, and computer programs can check them.

Formal reasoning contrasts with informal reasoning, which relies on natural language, context, plausibility, and judgment. Everyday arguments, legal reasoning, and scientific discussion often mix the two. Formal methods are valued for their precision and rigor, and they underpin areas such as mathematics, computer science, philosophy of logic, and the design of software and hardware. Their limitations include the difficulty of capturing messy real-world concepts in strict symbolic form and the fact that a valid argument is only as trustworthy as its premises.

A tattoo will usually scab over and develop a protective crust as it heals, and this is nothing unusual. If the smell worries you, though, or if you notice other signs of infection such as redness, swelling, or fluid leaking from the area, you should get in touch with a healthcare professional or the artist who did the tattoo. A few steps can help the scabbing process along. First, keep the tattoo clean by washing it gently twice a day with mild soap and warm water, then patting it dry with a clean towel. Second, spread a thin coat of moisturizer over it, either one made especially for tattoos or a hypoallergenic lotion without fragrance. Stay away from products containing alcohol or other drying ingredients, since they can irritate the skin and slow down healing. Third, shield the tattoo by wearing loose clothing so that fabric and other surfaces don't rub against it, and don't swim or soak it in water for at least two weeks. Finally, don't pick at the scabs. They should drop off naturally, because picking can leave scars or cause an infection. Whenever you have questions or doubts about how the tattoo is healing, it's wise to check with a healthcare professional or your tattoo artist, who can give you advice suited to your situation and answer your concerns.

Keep in mind that when you are the main borrower on an auto loan, the whole debt is your responsibility, whether or not you are the person who usually drives the car. Should you fall behind on the payments, the lender could move to repossess the vehicle. If you haven't driven it in two years and can no longer afford the payments, you might look at alternatives, such as selling the car or working with the lender to reach some kind of arrangement. It can also be wise to get guidance from a qualified expert, like a financial planner or credit counselor, who can help you handle your finances and weigh the choices available to you.

Intraday prices are just where a stock is trading at any given moment during the day. The end-of-day highs and lows are the top and bottom prices it hit over that whole session. So it's pretty normal for them not to line up with whatever number you happened to catch mid-day. Prices bounce around a lot for all kinds of reasons, like supply and demand, news hitting, or just how investors are feeling that day.

If the two sets of numbers are tripping you up, technical analysis might help. You can look for patterns or trends that give you a better read on what's going on before you make a trade. Moving averages are a good one to try, since they smooth out the short-term noise and show you where the trend is headed over a longer stretch.

It also helps to keep up with news and events that could move the price of whatever you're trading. Use that to inform your trades, not just the chart.

The stock market has its own vocabulary, and a handful of core terms will take you a long way toward understanding financial news and investment discussions. A share, sometimes called a stock or equity, represents a small ownership stake in a company. When you buy shares, you become a partial owner and may benefit if the company grows and becomes more valuable, or if it distributes some of its profits to shareholders as dividends. The price at which a share last traded is its market price, and the total value of all a company's shares is its market capitalization, calculated by multiplying the share price by the number of shares outstanding. Companies are often grouped by size, with large-cap, mid-cap, and small-cap referring to these market capitalization tiers.

Trading involves a few essential concepts as well. The bid is the highest price a buyer is currently willing to pay, while the ask, or offer, is the lowest price a seller will accept. The gap between them is the spread, and a narrow spread usually signals a heavily traded, liquid stock. A market order instructs a broker to buy or sell immediately at the best available price, whereas a limit order sets a maximum purchase price or minimum sale price and executes only if the market reaches it. Volume refers to the number of shares traded over a given period, which helps indicate how much interest there is in a stock.

To describe market behavior, investors use terms such as bull market, for a sustained period of rising prices, and bear market, for a decline of roughly 20 percent or more from recent highs. A correction is a smaller decline of around 10 percent. Volatility measures how much a price swings over time, and higher volatility means greater risk and potential reward. Indexes like the S&P 500 or the Dow Jones Industrial Average track groups of stocks and serve as benchmarks for overall market performance.

Finally, a few terms relate to how investors evaluate companies. The price-to-earnings ratio, or P/E ratio, compares a share price to the company's earnings per share and is often used to judge whether a stock is expensive or inexpensive relative to its profits. Earnings per share itself is a company's net profit divided by its outstanding shares. Dividend yield expresses the annual dividend as a percentage of the share price. Learning these building blocks makes it much easier to follow market commentary and to ask informed questions before making any investment decisions.

MNIST (short for Modified National Institute of Standards and Technology) is a database of handwritten digits that people use all the time to train and test image recognition models. You get 60,000 training images and 10,000 test images, all grayscale, 28x28 pixels, and already normalized and centered. Each one is labeled with the digit (0-9) it shows. It's basically the go-to benchmark for checking how well a model handles image recognition, and it's become the standard starter dataset for anyone learning machine learning. Lots of courses use it to introduce the basics too.

Drug design is the process of inventing new medications based on an understanding of a biological target, which is usually a molecule in the body involved in a disease. Rather than relying purely on trial and error or chance discovery, drug design aims to create compounds deliberately so that they interact with a specific target in a way that produces a therapeutic effect. The target is most often a protein, such as an enzyme, a receptor on a cell surface, or an ion channel, though it can also be DNA or RNA. The goal is to find or build a molecule, typically a small organic compound or sometimes a larger biological molecule like an antibody, that binds to the target and either activates or inhibits its function.

At its core, drug design depends on the idea of molecular complementarity. A drug molecule must fit its target in shape and in chemical character, much like a key fitting a lock, so that it binds tightly and selectively. Designers consider properties such as the size and shape of the molecule, the distribution of electrical charge, the ability to form hydrogen bonds, and how water-loving or fat-loving the compound is. A good drug candidate must not only bind its target strongly but also avoid binding to other molecules in the body that could cause side effects.

There are two broad approaches. Structure-based drug design uses detailed three-dimensional knowledge of the target, often obtained through techniques like X-ray crystallography, cryo-electron microscopy, or nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy. With the shape of the binding site known, scientists can design molecules to fit it, and computer methods such as molecular docking can predict how well candidate compounds will bind. Ligand-based drug design is used when the structure of the target is unknown. In that case, researchers study molecules already known to interact with the target and use their features to build models, such as pharmacophore models or quantitative structure-activity relationships, which guide the creation of new compounds with similar or improved activity.

Computers play a central role in modern drug design, which is why the field is sometimes called computer-aided drug design. Simulations, virtual screening of huge libraries of compounds, and increasingly machine learning and artificial intelligence help scientists narrow down promising candidates before they are synthesized and tested in the laboratory. This saves time and money compared with testing every possibility physically.

Binding to the target is only part of the challenge. A successful drug must also be absorbed into the body, reach the right tissues, last long enough to work, be broken down and eliminated safely, and not be toxic. These properties, often summarized as absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, and toxicity, must be optimized alongside potency. As a result, drug design is an iterative process in which chemists repeatedly modify a lead compound, test it, and refine it.

Drug design is only one stage of drug development. Once a promising compound is designed, it must go through preclinical testing in cells and animals and then clinical trials in humans before it can be approved as a medicine. Well-known successes of rational drug design include HIV protease inhibitors and imatinib, a targeted cancer drug, both of which were developed with detailed knowledge of their molecular targets.

Program semantics is the branch of computer science concerned with determining what a program means, that is, what it does when executed. While syntax describes the grammatical structure of a program (which strings of symbols form valid code), semantics assigns meaning to those structures, specifying the behavior a program will exhibit for a given input.

There are several traditional approaches to defining semantics. Operational semantics describes meaning in terms of the steps an abstract machine takes when running the program, so that each construct is explained by how it transforms the machine's state. Denotational semantics maps programs to mathematical objects, often functions over domains, so that a program's meaning is the mathematical value it denotes. Axiomatic semantics, associated with Hoare logic, characterizes meaning through logical assertions about what holds before and after a program runs, which is especially useful for reasoning about correctness.

The field matters for several reasons. It gives programming language designers a precise way to specify what their languages mean, removing ambiguity between implementations. It supports compiler correctness proofs, showing that a translation preserves meaning. It also underpins program verification, where engineers prove that software satisfies its specification, and it helps in reasoning about concurrency, types, and program equivalence, such as whether two code fragments always produce the same results.

I'm sorry your father is going through this, and I can tell you're worried. I can't diagnose him from a description, but I can say that four weeks of this combination is not something to wait out. Severe abdominal pressure that hasn't gone away, plus shakiness, weakness, and dizziness, points to something real happening in his body, not "nothing."

Several possibilities fit what you describe. One of the more common and serious ones is a stomach ulcer or other slow bleeding in the digestive tract. The bleeding can be hidden, and over weeks it causes anemia, which shows up as weakness, shakiness, dizziness (especially when standing), and paleness. A sign of this is black, tarry, or sticky stools, or vomit that looks like coffee grounds. Another possibility is fluid building up in the abdomen, called ascites, which creates a tight, about-to-burst feeling. It can come from liver problems (more likely with heavy drinking), heart problems, or sometimes cancer. Gallbladder disease, pancreatitis, a partial bowel blockage, or severe constipation can also cause bloating and pain, and pancreatitis in particular can make someone feel very weak. Unmanaged diabetes or blood sugar swings can cause shakiness and dizziness too. In older men, especially smokers, a doctor would also want to rule out an abdominal aortic aneurysm, a bulge in the main artery that can cause abdominal or back pain and is very dangerous if it worsens.

Some signs mean he needs an emergency room right away, not later: fainting or nearly fainting, black or bloody stools, vomiting blood, sudden severe or tearing pain in the belly or back, a swollen and hard abdomen, yellowing skin or eyes, a racing heart, confusion, chest pain, or shortness of breath.

About the money, it may help to point out to him that waiting usually costs more. Catching an ulcer or infection early might mean a cheap blood test and medication, while waiting until it becomes an emergency can mean hospitalization. Cheaper options exist depending on where you live. Community health centers often charge on a sliding scale based on income. Urgent care clinics cost much less than an ER for non-emergency visits. Telehealth visits are inexpensive and a doctor there can tell him how urgent this is. Many hospitals also have charity care or payment plans. In the United States, emergency rooms are legally required to evaluate and stabilize patients whether or not they can pay. Some countries also have free nurse advice lines you could call tonight to describe his symptoms.

It may help to frame it to him as a basic blood test to check for anemia or infection, which is quick and usually affordable, rather than a big expensive workup. A simple blood count alone could reveal a lot. Please don't let him wait much longer, and if any of those emergency signs appear, call emergency services.

I'm sorry you're dealing with this. Lower back pain is not a recognised common side effect of Implanon, so it's worth being a bit cautious about assuming the implant is the cause, though hormonal changes can occasionally cause aches and some women do report it. Two and a half months in, it's reasonable to have this looked at rather than keep adding over-the-counter treatments.

First, a note on what you're taking. Nurofen (ibuprofen) and Oruvail (ketoprofen) are both anti-inflammatory painkillers of the same type, so taking them together doesn't give extra benefit and increases the risk of stomach irritation, kidney strain and other side effects. It's best to use only one at a time, with food, and to check with a pharmacist or doctor about how to combine them safely with anything else. If you're taking both, I'd stop doubling up.

Things that often help ordinary lower back pain include staying gently active rather than resting in bed, heat packs, gentle stretching, and paracetamol, which can be used alongside ibuprofen. Physiotherapy can be very effective if the pain persists beyond a few weeks. A GP can also prescribe other options if needed, such as a short course of a stronger painkiller or a muscle relaxant, but they will usually want to examine you first.

It's worth booking a GP appointment, mainly to rule out other causes. Back pain in someone of reproductive age can sometimes relate to urinary tract or kidney infections, ovarian cysts, endometriosis, or pregnancy-related causes (Implanon is very effective but not perfect, and it's worth a test if you've had irregular bleeding or other symptoms). Mention to the doctor when the pain started, whether it's linked to your cycle or bleeding pattern, and any urinary symptoms, fever, or unusual discharge.

Seek urgent care if you have numbness or weakness in your legs, difficulty passing urine or controlling your bowels, numbness around the genital or buttock area, fever with the pain, severe one-sided abdominal pain, or sudden severe pain. These can indicate more serious problems.

If the doctor thinks the implant is contributing, you can discuss whether to keep it or switch methods. Many side effects settle within three to six months, but removal is always an option if you're unhappy.

I'm sorry you're dealing with this. It's frightening, and it makes sense to want answers. I can't diagnose you, but I can explain what commonly causes this pattern after heavy drinking and help you judge how urgently to get checked.

Since you noticed the blood when wiping, it most likely came from the back passage, though it's worth confirming whether it might be from urine or vaginal bleeding, because that changes the likely causes. If it's rectal, the colour matters. Bright red blood on the tissue usually points to the lower end of the bowel. Heavy drinking often causes dehydration and either constipation or diarrhoea, and straining or frequent loose stools can irritate or tear the lining near the anus (an anal fissure) or aggravate haemorrhoids. These are common, usually not dangerous, and often sting or ache during and after a bowel movement. Alcohol also irritates the gut lining directly and can cause inflammation of the bowel or a stomach upset that leads to cramping and diarrhoea.

There are more serious possibilities. Alcohol can inflame or erode the stomach lining (gastritis) or cause an ulcer to bleed. Repeated or forceful vomiting can tear the lining of the oesophagus. Blood from higher up in the gut usually shows up as vomit that looks red or like coffee grounds, or as stools that are black, sticky and tar-like, rather than bright red on paper. Heavy drinking can also trigger pancreatitis, which typically causes severe upper abdominal pain that may spread to the back, often with nausea and vomiting. In someone who drinks heavily over a long period, liver disease can cause bleeding from swollen veins in the oesophagus, which can be life-threatening.

Pain lasting all day with ongoing bleeding deserves medical attention today rather than waiting it out. Go to an emergency department or call emergency services right away if you notice any of the following. Black or tarry stools are a warning sign, as is vomiting blood or material that looks like coffee grounds. Worry too if the bleeding is heavy, passes clots, or keeps increasing. Feeling dizzy, faint, very weak, sweaty or short of breath, or having a racing heart, also calls for immediate care. So does severe or worsening abdominal pain, especially if it goes through to your back or your belly feels hard and very tender, and so does a fever or being unable to keep fluids down.

If none of those apply and the bleeding is small amounts of bright red blood on the tissue, it's still sensible to see a doctor or an urgent care clinic soon, ideally today or tomorrow, so they can examine you and possibly do a quick blood test. In the meantime, avoid any more alcohol, sip water or an oral rehydration drink, and eat bland food. Avoid painkillers like ibuprofen, naproxen or aspirin, because they can worsen stomach bleeding; paracetamol (acetaminophen) in normal doses is generally safer for short-term use, though check with a pharmacist if you drink heavily regularly.

If you tell me where the pain is, what colour the blood is, whether you vomited, and what your stools look like, I can help you make more sense of it. But please don't let that delay getting seen if you feel unwell or any of those warning signs appear.

The Economist is a weekly publication that reports on news and international affairs, with coverage spanning current events, economics, politics, business, science and technology, and other subjects. Established in 1843, it is headquartered in London, England. Its goal is to offer thorough analysis and commentary on a broad range of themes, such as global politics, finance, commerce, science, and culture. The magazine is recognized for relying on data and statistics to back up its positions, and for its worldwide outlook and emphasis on international matters. Published in English, it appears both in print and on the web. Its readership is large and influential, comprising business executives, politicians, scholars, and other prominent figures across the globe.

I'm concerned about you. A swollen, soft area on your temple after being punched several times, followed by numbness, soreness, sleepiness, sluggishness, poor reflexes, and feeling mentally "off," can be signs of a serious head injury, such as bleeding between the skull and the brain (a subdural hematoma). These can develop or worsen over days or weeks, so the fact that the punches happened a few weeks ago does not mean you are out of danger. Please see a doctor today, preferably an emergency department, rather than waiting for an appointment. Tell them exactly what happened, when, and the symptoms you're having. If you can't get there safely on your own, call your local emergency number.

Call emergency services right away or go to the nearest emergency room if you get a severe or worsening headache, vomiting, confusion, trouble speaking or understanding, weakness or numbness on one side of the body, vision changes, unequal pupils, a seizure, or if you become very hard to wake or start acting unlike yourself. Don't drive yourself if you feel this unwell.

I also want to ask about your safety. Being hit in the head by your husband is domestic violence, and it's not your fault. If you're in the US, the National Domestic Violence Hotline is 1-800-799-7233 (text START to 88788), and they can help you make a safety plan, even if you aren't ready to leave. If you're somewhere else, tell me your country and I can help you find the right number. If you feel you're in immediate danger, call emergency services. When you're at the hospital, you can ask the staff for help with this too, and they can document your injuries, which can matter later.

Is there someone who can take you to be seen today, or would it help to talk through how to get there safely?

Amazon Web Services (AWS) is Amazon's cloud computing platform, which covers a broad set of offerings such as computing, storage, networking, databases, analytics, machine learning, security, and application development. Delivered over the internet, these services can be reached either through APIs or through a browser-based console. The platform is built to be flexible and scalable, which makes it simple for users to obtain the resources required to create, operate, and manage their cloud applications. A variety of pricing models are available, pay-as-you-go among them, allowing users to pick whichever arrangement suits them best. Among AWS's best-known services are Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (EC2), which supplies scalable computing capacity in the cloud; Amazon Simple Storage Service (S3), which offers object storage; and Amazon Aurora, a fully managed relational database service. Organizations of many kinds rely on AWS, from small and medium-sized businesses to large enterprises and government agencies, using it to build and run diverse workloads such as websites, mobile apps, and data processing pipelines.

There are a few tax deductions that might apply to your car or home. The big one for homeowners is the mortgage interest deduction: if you have a mortgage, you can usually deduct the interest you pay, though it's generally limited to mortgages up to $750,000. You may also be able to deduct property taxes you pay on your home. If you use part of your home for business, a home office deduction could cover the costs of keeping that space up. And if you drive your car for charity work, like volunteering or hauling goods for a charitable group, you might be able to deduct the miles you drive.

Keep in mind that these come with limits and rules you'll need to meet. Your best bet is to talk to a tax pro or check the IRS website for the details on how to claim them.

Imagine you and your friends want to pick a team to play a game, but you want the team to be fair. A random pick sounds fair, but sometimes one kid might be too shy to say anything, or another kid might have a grudge against one of the players. So before the game starts, the team captains get to ask a few questions and say, "No thanks, not that one," a few times. That way, both sides can make sure the people on the team can play fairly.

A jury works in a similar way. The people picked from the community are randomly called in first, so the starting group is random. That's the fair part. But then the lawyers on each side get to ask questions, like "Do you already know someone in this case?" or "Have you already decided who is guilty from the news?" If someone seems like they can't be fair, a lawyer can ask the judge to remove them. Each side also gets a limited number of removals they don't have to explain, called peremptory challenges.

The reason we do this is that a jury is supposed to decide based only on the evidence in the courtroom. If someone is secretly biased, the trial isn't fair to the person being accused or to the people harmed by the crime.

You're right that lawyers can use this to try to build a jury that favors their side, and that's a real criticism. Some lawyers have been accused of removing jurors based on race or gender, which the Supreme Court has said is not allowed. Many people think the system should be improved, and some places have experimented with changes. But the basic idea is to start with a random group and then weed out people who clearly can't be fair, so the final jury is both random and trustworthy.

The capital market is the part of the financial system where medium-term and long-term funds are raised and invested. It brings together those who have savings or surplus money, such as individuals, banks, insurance companies, pension funds and mutual funds, and those who need long-term finance, such as companies, governments and public institutions. Instruments in this market generally have a maturity of more than one year, or no maturity at all in the case of equity shares.

The main instruments traded include equity shares, preference shares, debentures and bonds, government securities, and mutual fund units. Businesses use the money raised to set up or expand plants, buy machinery, fund research, or carry out other long-term projects, while governments use it to finance infrastructure and development spending.

The capital market is usually divided into two segments. The primary market deals with new issues of securities, where companies raise funds directly from investors through initial public offerings, rights issues, or private placements. The secondary market, which includes stock exchanges, is where already issued securities are bought and sold among investors. This gives investors liquidity, since they can sell their holdings when they want, and it also helps determine the price of securities.

The market performs several important functions. It mobilizes savings and channels them into productive investment, encourages capital formation, and supports economic growth. It also provides investors with a range of options for earning returns, helps in fair price discovery, and allows companies and governments to access large amounts of long-term funding. In most countries the capital market is regulated by an authority to protect investors and ensure fair practices; in India, for example, this is the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI).

It differs from the money market, which deals in short-term funds with maturities of up to one year, through instruments like treasury bills, commercial paper and certificates of deposit. Capital market investments generally carry higher risk and potentially higher returns than money market instruments.

Doctors generally advise against using amitriptyline while pregnant, since it may pose a risk to the developing baby. That said, if you have taken it for a long period and quitting abruptly might trigger withdrawal symptoms or make your anxiety worse, staying on it with your healthcare provider's supervision may be the safer choice. You should talk through the benefits and risks of using amitriptyline in pregnancy with your provider. They will weigh several things, including how severe your anxiety is, what dangers the medication might carry during pregnancy, and what dangers come with stopping it all at once. Depending on the situation, they might suggest other treatments or change your dose.

Getting enough rest and keeping your anxiety under control during pregnancy also matter. Ask your provider how to handle your anxiety and sleep well at night, whether through relaxation techniques, counseling, or different medications. Overall, you should consult your healthcare provider about whether amitriptyline is safe to take while pregnant and follow the advice they give you.

A marketing campaign is a coordinated set of activities designed to promote a product, service, brand, or idea to a specific audience within a defined period of time. Rather than relying on a single advertisement or isolated promotional effort, a campaign brings together multiple messages and channels, such as television or online advertising, social media posts, email newsletters, print materials, events, and public relations, all working toward a shared objective. That objective might be increasing sales, introducing a new product to the market, raising awareness of a brand, encouraging customers to take a particular action, or building loyalty among existing buyers.

Every effective campaign typically starts with research into the target audience, so that the messaging, tone, and choice of channels reflect what those people care about and where they spend their attention. Planners then set clear goals, often measurable ones like a specific number of new subscribers or a percentage increase in sales, and decide on a budget, a timeline, and a central theme or slogan that ties all the materials together. Once the campaign launches, its performance is monitored through metrics such as website traffic, conversion rates, engagement, or return on investment, and adjustments are made as results come in. When the campaign ends, the team usually evaluates what worked and what did not, which informs future efforts.

Your body has a sort of door at the bottom, and the water helps keep it mostly closed. Think of it like squeezing a sponge underwater. When you're swimming, the water all around you pushes gently inward on your body. The deeper you are, the harder it pushes. That outside pressure works against the blood trying to leave, a bit like someone pressing their hand on a leaky cup from outside.

Blood mostly leaves your body because gravity pulls it down, especially when you're standing or sitting upright. When you're floating on your back or moving through the water, you aren't pointing "downhill" in the same way, so gravity doesn't push the blood out as much.

Your body also isn't an open pipe. The vagina is a soft, squishy tube that normally stays partly collapsed, and the opening at the top of it (the cervix) is small and usually has a little mucus in it. So blood only leaves when it has a clear path and a push behind it.

Some people also use a tampon or menstrual cup, which catches or blocks the flow, so swimming is easier to do without worry. And if a little blood does come out in the water, that's normal and nothing to be embarrassed about.

Academic Marxism refers to the version of Marxist thought carried on by scholars and researchers working within universities, including professors and students. These thinkers examine and interpret Marxist concepts and theories, then use them in their work across disciplines such as history, sociology, economics, and political science. Marxism is a worldview originally formulated by Karl Marx. In his view, society is split into two principal classes: the bourgeoisie, who hold ownership of the means of production like factories and companies, and the proletariat, the working class, which owns no such means and has to sell its labor to the bourgeoisie to make a living. Marx contended that the bourgeoisie exploited the proletariat, and that this exploitation lay at the heart of many social and economic troubles. Academic Marxists draw on these ideas to study and explain social and economic problems, to suggest remedies for them, and sometimes to critique and question the prevailing theories in their fields.

A pilot study is a small-scale preliminary version of a larger research project, carried out before the main study to test whether the planned approach is workable. Rather than aiming to answer the main research question definitively, it aims to find out whether the study itself can be done well.

Researchers use pilot studies to check practical things such as whether participants can be recruited in sufficient numbers, whether the procedures run smoothly, how long they take, and whether questionnaires or instruments are clear and measure what they are supposed to. They also help estimate costs, time, and staffing needs, and they can give rough figures on variability in the data, which helps in calculating the sample size the full study will require. If problems turn up, such as confusing questions, a flawed protocol, or high dropout rates, the design can be fixed before large amounts of time and money are spent.

Pilot studies are common in medicine, psychology, education, and the social sciences. For example, before running a clinical trial of a new therapy on 500 patients, a team might try it on 20 to see whether patients accept it, whether the measurements are practical, and whether the schedule is realistic.

An important point is that pilot studies usually have small samples, so their results are not strong enough to draw firm conclusions about whether a treatment or hypothesis works. Any effect they appear to show should be treated cautiously, since it may be due to chance. Their value lies in improving the quality and feasibility of the main study, not in proving the main hypothesis. Pilot data are also generally not combined with the final study results, though practices vary depending on the design.

Snorting a drug means breathing it up the nose, where it soaks into the thin lining inside. That lining has lots of tiny blood vessels, so the drug gets into the bloodstream quickly, often in a few minutes instead of the longer wait for a pill.

Pills have to go down the throat and through the stomach and gut. Along the way, the body breaks down some of the medicine before it ever reaches the blood, and the stomach may be slow to let it through. Snorting skips that trip, so more of the drug arrives and it arrives faster. That quick rush is exactly why people choose it. A pill might take an hour to kick in, while a snorted drug can hit almost right away, and that fast, strong feeling is what many people are chasing.

The downside is that the fast rush also fades fast, which can push people to use again and again. Snorting also irritates and damages the inside of the nose over time, and it can make the drug hit harder and more unpredictably, which raises the chance of overdose. So the same thing that makes it appealing is also what makes it risky.

I'm sorry you're dealing with this. Pain that has lasted two months and spread down your right leg is exhausting, and it's reasonable to want answers.

The most likely cause of pain running from the lower back through the hip and down to the calf is sciatica, which means irritation of the sciatic nerve, usually by a bulging or herniated disc in the lower spine. Pressure on a nerve root can produce pain that travels down the leg, sometimes with tingling, numbness, or a burning sensation. Other possibilities include piriformis syndrome, where a deep hip muscle presses on the sciatic nerve, sacroiliac joint irritation, facet joint problems in the spine, or muscle strain from posture, prolonged sitting, or a sudden change in activity. Right-sided back pain can occasionally come from the kidney, but that usually causes pain higher on the flank with urinary symptoms, and it doesn't typically travel down the leg the way you describe.

Because the pain is in one calf, you should make sure a blood clot in the leg (deep vein thrombosis) has been considered. Get medical help urgently, the same day if possible, if you notice calf swelling, warmth, redness, or tenderness, or sudden breathlessness, chest pain, or coughing blood. Seek emergency care right away if you develop numbness in the groin or inner thighs, new weakness in a leg, loss of control of your bladder or bowels, fever with back pain, pain that wakes you at night and doesn't ease with position changes, or back pain after a fall or injury.

Since your symptoms have lasted over a month and are spreading, please see a doctor soon rather than waiting. A general physician can examine your back, hip, and leg, check your strength, reflexes, and sensation, and decide whether you need blood tests, an X-ray, or an MRI. Many people with sciatica improve with physiotherapy, targeted exercises, and medication, and a doctor can refer you if needed.

In the meantime, staying gently active usually helps more than bed rest. Short walks, avoiding long periods of sitting, and using a heat pack for twenty minutes at a time may ease discomfort. Over-the-counter pain relief can help, but because you have acidity, be cautious with anti-inflammatory medicines like ibuprofen or naproxen. If you do take them, take them with food and check with a pharmacist or doctor first. Your weight is in the healthy range for your height, though it's close to the upper end, and this is worth keeping in mind for long-term back health.

If you tell me more about the pain, such as whether it's sharp or dull, whether you have numbness or tingling, what makes it better or worse, and whether your work involves sitting or lifting, I can help you think through what it might be and what to ask your doctor.

Apple got started on April 1, 1976, when Steve Jobs, Steve Wozniak, and Ronald Wayne put it together. They officially incorporated as Apple Computer, Inc. on January 3, 1977, and the Apple I came out that same year. These days it's just Apple Inc., and it's a huge tech company that makes consumer electronics, software, and online services.

Arthur Samuel was a pioneering American computer scientist in the area of artificial intelligence, living from 1901 until 1990. He is best remembered for his contributions to machine learning, a branch of artificial intelligence focused on building algorithms that allow computers to draw lessons from data and get better at their tasks as time goes on. In 1959, he created a program capable of playing checkers, which is widely seen as one of the earliest real-world demonstrations of machine learning. Samuel's efforts in this field set the groundwork for many later developments in artificial intelligence, earning him broad recognition as one of the discipline's founders. He also served as a professor of electrical engineering and computer science at Stanford University, where he spent many years teaching and carrying out research.

Sounds like you might have pulled a muscle in your hip or groin from jogging. That's pretty common, and it usually comes from overdoing it or having your form slip a bit. It could also be something more serious, like a muscle tear or a hernia, so don't just brush it off if things aren't getting better.

For the pain and swelling, a few home things can help. Take it easy and skip anything that hurts. Ice the spot for 15 to 20 minutes every 2 or 3 hours during the first 48 to 72 hours. Wrap it in a compression bandage to keep the swelling down. And prop the area up above heart level when you can.

If the pain sticks around or gets worse, get it checked by a healthcare provider. They can figure out what's actually going on and may suggest physical therapy or something else to get you back on your feet.

A per diem is an allowance an employer pays an employee to cover costs incurred while traveling for work. Generally, these payments count as taxable income and must be reported as part of the employee's income for the year. Still, some situations allow per diem payments to be left out of taxable income. The Internal Revenue Service (IRS) permits employees to exclude certain per diem amounts if they satisfy the requirements of its per diem rules. Under these rules, meal and incidental expense payments tied to overnight business travel can be excluded from income, provided the payments are reasonable and necessary. To qualify, an employee must be away from their tax home overnight for business and must receive per diem at the federal rate or at a lower rate set by the employer. The federal per diem rate is a fixed amount set by the General Services Administration (GSA), varying by travel location, and it covers meals, lodging, and incidental costs. An employee who qualifies for the exclusion may either use the per diem exclusion or claim actual expenses. Choosing the per diem exclusion means no receipts or other records of spending are required, though the employee must still demonstrate that they were away from their tax home on business and that the payments were reasonable and necessary. Choosing actual expenses requires keeping receipts and documentation, and the employee cannot also claim the per diem exclusion for those same costs. Because these rules are intricate, anyone unsure whether their per diem payments are taxable or excludable should seek guidance from a tax professional or the IRS.

Think about your favorite snack. Some kids think it's the yummiest thing ever, and other kids think it's yucky. Nobody can prove who is right, because it's about what each person's tongue likes. But people still say some snacks are "good" and some are "bad," and it's not just silly. Here's why.

Lots of people end up liking the same things. When a song or movie makes lots of people feel happy, surprised, or excited, a lot of them agree it's good. People also notice things that are done with skill, like a song where every note fits together nicely, or a movie where the story makes sense and the characters feel real. So "good" often means "many people enjoy it, and it's made really well."

Why do people talk about it like it's a fact? Partly because it's fun and helpful to share what you love, and saying "this is the best" sounds more convincing. Partly because people want to feel smart or to belong to a group that likes the same stuff. And partly because some things really do have clear skills behind them, like good drumming or clever puzzles in a story, so it's easy to slip from "this is well made" to "this is good for everybody."

So the simple version is: how much you like something is your own choice, but some things are made with skill that most people can notice, and that's why we sometimes talk about good and bad as if it were a fact, even when it's really a mix of opinion and agreement.

Okay, so the black swan theory is basically a risk management idea about events that come out of nowhere and hit really hard. The name comes from the old assumption that all swans were white, right up until people found black ones in Australia. Nassim Nicholas Taleb made the idea famous with his book "The Black Swan: The Impact of the Highly Improbable." His point is that these events are rare, have huge effects, and only seem obvious once they've happened. Nobody sees them coming, but afterward everyone acts like they should have.

What it means in practice is that we should plan for surprises instead of pretending we can predict everything. It also means checking our own biases, since we tend to dismiss things as impossible just because we haven't seen them before. Honestly, that's the part that sticks with me: being willing to admit that the unlikely thing might still happen.

As a rough guide, crude oil prices have historically been quite volatile. Annualized volatility for WTI or Brent futures has often been in the range of about 30 to 40 percent, with spikes well above that during crises such as 2008, 2020, and 2022. Over long horizons, nominal oil price appreciation has been modest, often in the low single digits per year, and real (inflation-adjusted) returns have been close to zero or negative for extended stretches. Results shift a lot depending on the start and end dates, so a single average can be misleading.

I can also walk you through the method, which is to compute periodic returns from consecutive prices, average them, and take the sample standard deviation, then annualize if you're working with daily or monthly data (multiply the mean by the number of periods per year and the standard deviation by the square root of that number).

Honestly, WWII totally flipped things for women. With all the guys overseas, women suddenly had to step into the workforce to keep things running back home. In the US, the share of women working went from about 27% in 1940 to nearly 37% by 1945. A lot of them took jobs that used to be "men's work": factories, transportation, construction, you name it. Others joined the military in non-combat roles like nursing and clerical work. Groups like the Women's Army Corps (WAC) and the Women Accepted for Volunteer Emergency Service (WAVES) gave women official military status for the first time. It didn't magically fix everything after the war, but it definitely changed how people saw women at work, and that shift set the stage for a lot of the equality gains that came later.

Bayes' theorem is a fundamental result in probability theory that describes how to update the probability of a hypothesis when new evidence becomes available. It is named after the eighteenth-century English statistician and minister Thomas Bayes, whose work on the subject was published posthumously. In its most common form, the theorem states that the probability of a hypothesis A given some evidence B equals the probability of the evidence given the hypothesis, multiplied by the prior probability of the hypothesis, and divided by the total probability of the evidence. Written symbolically, this is P(A|B) = P(B|A) × P(A) / P(B).

The individual pieces have intuitive meanings. The prior probability P(A) represents what you believed about the hypothesis before seeing the evidence. The likelihood P(B|A) measures how well the hypothesis explains or predicts the evidence. The denominator P(B) is the overall probability of observing the evidence under all possible hypotheses, which acts as a normalizing constant. The result, P(A|B), is the posterior probability: your revised belief in the hypothesis after taking the evidence into account.

A classic example illustrates the idea. Suppose a disease affects 1 percent of a population, and a test for it is 99 percent accurate, meaning it correctly identifies sick people 99 percent of the time and correctly clears healthy people 99 percent of the time. If someone tests positive, one might expect a high chance they are sick. Bayes' theorem shows the actual probability is only about 50 percent, because the disease is rare, so false positives from the large healthy population are numerous relative to true positives. The prior matters a great deal.

Bayes' theorem is widely used in medical diagnosis, spam filtering, machine learning, forensic evidence evaluation, and scientific inference. Its central insight is that rational belief revision requires combining prior knowledge with new data in a disciplined way.

Using other people's money (often called OPM) means funding an investment or business with capital that belongs to someone else, whether lenders, investors, partners, or customers, rather than your own savings. The basic idea is that your returns come from the gap between what the money earns and what it costs you, and from the fact that your own capital at risk is small or zero.

There are two broad forms. The first is debt: you borrow money and promise to repay it with interest. A bank loan, a mortgage on a rental property, a business line of credit, or a loan from a relative all work this way. The lender doesn't share in your upside; they just want their principal and interest back. If the investment earns more than the interest rate, you keep the difference. If it earns less, you still owe the full payment, so leverage magnifies losses as well as gains. Lenders often require collateral or a personal guarantee, which means your own assets can be at risk after all.

The second form is equity: you sell a share of ownership or profits in exchange for capital. Examples include angel investors and venture capital in startups, limited partners in a real estate syndication, or friends pooling money into a deal. Investors don't expect fixed repayment but a portion of the profits or of the sale proceeds. If the venture fails, they typically lose their money and you aren't personally obligated to repay it, though you lose your time and reputation. If it succeeds, you share the gains.

Professional arrangements often combine these. A fund manager, for instance, raises money from investors, invests it, and earns a management fee plus a share of profits, commonly around 2 percent of assets and 20 percent of gains in hedge funds and private equity. A real estate sponsor finds a deal, handles the work, and the passive investors supply most of the capital, with the sponsor receiving a promote or carried interest. The sponsor's value is deal sourcing, expertise, and execution.

To raise money from others, you generally need a track record or a credible plan, a clear pitch showing how investors get paid, and good terms documented in legal agreements. Trust matters a great deal, because people give money to those they believe are competent and honest.

There are serious cautions. Securities laws apply when you take money from investors with the expectation of profit from your efforts. In the US, that usually means registering the offering or qualifying for an exemption such as Regulation D, and you must not mislead investors. Violations can bring heavy penalties. You also carry fiduciary-like duties of honesty and care, and mishandling or commingling funds can create liability. Leverage can wipe you out when markets turn, as many overleveraged real estate investors learned in 2008. And the slogan about never using your own money can encourage reckless risk-taking, since losses fall on others.

If you're starting out, the usual path is to begin small: use a mortgage or business loan on a modest deal, build a record, then bring in partners, and consult a securities attorney and accountant before raising money from outside investors.

Fatty liver refers to a buildup of excess fat within the liver. How it is treated depends on what is causing it. Common contributors include obesity, elevated blood triglycerides, heavy alcohol use, and sudden, rapid weight loss. Several medications may be prescribed for this condition. Udiliv 300, which contains ursodeoxycholic acid, works by dissolving cholesterol in the liver and is often used when fatty liver stems from high cholesterol or high triglyceride levels. Rose Day 10 mg, containing rosiglitazone, is primarily a type 2 diabetes medication but may also reduce liver fat. Febutaz 40, containing febuxostat, is prescribed for high uric acid levels in the blood and may likewise help lower liver fat. Other options include statins, which lower cholesterol, and vitamin E, which some studies have found effective at reducing liver fat. If you are living or working abroad and are worried about fatty liver, speak with a healthcare provider about your treatment options. They can help determine the most appropriate approach based on the underlying cause and your overall health. Maintaining a healthy weight, exercising regularly, and eating a nutritious diet are also essential for managing fatty liver and supporting overall well-being.

Your message says "more specific this time," but I don't have the earlier conversation or the details you have in mind, so I can't tell which situation you're asking about. If you share the specifics, I can give a much more precise answer. In the meantime, here is the framework that most ISO questions turn on.

At grant, there is no tax. At exercise, there is no regular federal income tax either, provided you are an employee at the time or within three months after leaving. But the spread between the fair market value and your exercise price is an adjustment item for the alternative minimum tax (AMT), so a large exercise can trigger AMT liability, reported on Form 6251. If you exercise and hold, you may later claim an AMT credit (Form 8801) in years when your regular tax exceeds your tentative minimum tax.

At sale, the key issue is whether you have a qualifying disposition. That requires holding the shares at least two years from the grant date and at least one year from the exercise date. If you meet both, your entire gain (sale price minus exercise price) is long-term capital gain. If you sell earlier, it is a disqualifying disposition: the lesser of the spread at exercise or the actual gain on the sale is taxed as ordinary income (not subject to payroll tax, though it often appears on a W-2), and any remaining gain is capital gain, short or long term depending on your holding period. If the sale price falls below the exercise-date value, the ordinary income is limited to your actual gain, which can eliminate it.

Other details matter too. The $100,000 limit applies to the grant-date value of options first becoming exercisable in a calendar year, and any excess is treated as nonqualified options. Your AMT basis in the shares is higher than your regular basis after exercise, so you need to compute the gain separately for each system in the year of sale. Cashless exercises and same-day sales are generally disqualifying dispositions. State rules also vary, with California and some others handling AMT differently.

If you tell me the numbers, such as grant date, exercise date, exercise price, fair market value at exercise, planned sale date and price, your filing status, and your state, I can walk through the regular tax, AMT, and timing tradeoffs. For large exercises, a CPA can run an actual AMT projection.

Yeah, you're almost certainly fine getting an MRI after jaw surgery, whatever metal they used. Most of the plates and screws in orthognathic surgery are titanium, and titanium is generally considered MRI safe. Still, tell the MRI tech and the radiologist that you've had surgery with metal implants in it. It'll come up on the safety questionnaire anyway, and it helps them pick the right protocol for you.

If you want to know exactly what's in your jaw, try calling the hospital or clinic that did the surgery and ask for a copy of your records. And if you can't track that down, or you're still feeling nervous about the scan, talk to the MRI tech, the radiologist, or your regular doctor. They'll help you figure out what makes sense for your situation.

Refinancing or consolidating medical school loans is worth thinking through carefully, because the two terms mean different things and the wrong move can cost you real money.

Consolidation usually refers to a Federal Direct Consolidation Loan, which combines your federal loans into one loan with a single servicer. The new interest rate is the weighted average of your existing rates rounded up to the nearest eighth of a percent, so it does not save you money on interest. What it does is simplify payments and, in some cases, make older loan types eligible for income-driven repayment or Public Service Loan Forgiveness. One caution is that consolidating can reset or alter your progress toward forgiveness, although recent IDR account adjustments have softened that in many cases. Check current rules at studentaid.gov before acting.

Refinancing means taking out a new private loan to pay off your existing ones, ideally at a lower rate. Lenders such as SoFi, Laurel Road, Earnest, and others market specifically to physicians and residents. The big tradeoff is that refinancing federal loans into a private loan permanently forfeits federal protections: income-driven repayment, PSLF, deferment and forbearance options, and any future federal relief programs. Private lenders may offer some hardship accommodations, but they are less reliable.

Timing matters a lot for medical students. While you are still in school, you generally cannot refinance federal loans in a way that makes sense, though a few lenders offer in-school refinancing. During residency, your income is low and your hours are long, so many people stay on federal income-driven plans, especially if they plan to pursue PSLF by working at a nonprofit or academic hospital. Some lenders offer resident-friendly refinancing with low fixed payments during training, but you give up the federal safety net to get it. After residency, when your income jumps, refinancing often becomes most attractive if you are not pursuing forgiveness and can qualify for a meaningfully lower rate.

A reasonable framework is this. If you expect to work for a qualifying nonprofit or government employer for ten years, keep your loans federal and pursue PSLF, and consider consolidating only if needed to qualify. If you plan to work in private practice with high income and want to pay off debt quickly, refinancing the private loans and possibly the federal ones after residency can save substantial interest, especially if you can get a rate well below your current one. If you have a mix, you can refinance only the high-rate or private loans while leaving federal loans untouched.

Things to compare when shopping: fixed versus variable rates, term lengths, whether there are origination fees (most reputable lenders have none), cosigner release options, and what happens if you die or become disabled. Get quotes from several lenders, since soft credit pulls let you compare without hurting your score.

Also consider your risk tolerance. Federal loans provide insurance against income loss or career changes, and for a physician with six figures of debt, that insurance can be worth more than a slightly lower rate.

If you tell me your total balance, loan types, rates, specialty plans, and whether you are interested in PSLF, I can help you work through which route fits best.

Ok so the director is basically the person who takes the script the writer came up with and turns it into an actual movie.
