There's no single interest rate at which debt becomes a useful tool, because the answer depends on what the borrowed money earns or saves you relative to what it costs. The core principle is that borrowing makes sense when the expected after-tax return on the investment or purchase exceeds the after-tax cost of the debt, adjusted for risk. If a business can earn 12 percent on a project and borrow at 6 percent, the spread creates value. If the same money earns 4 percent, the loan destroys value even though 6 percent might sound modest in isolation.

Rough thresholds help in practice. For a household, low-rate fixed debt such as a long-term mortgage at a rate near or below expected long-run returns on diversified investments is often reasonable, while high-interest consumer debt above roughly 10 to 20 percent is usually expensive enough that paying it down beats most investment alternatives. For businesses, the relevant comparison is the weighted average cost of capital, and borrowing is sensible when a project's return clears that hurdle with a margin of safety for downside scenarios. For governments, the question shifts to whether borrowing rates sit below nominal economic growth, since debt-to-GDP ratios tend to stabilize when growth outpaces interest costs.

Two additional factors matter as much as the rate itself. The first is the certainty of cash flows: variable-rate debt or debt with a refinancing deadline can become painful if rates rise or credit tightens, even when today's rate looks cheap. The second is the ability to service the debt in a bad year. A rate that is manageable when income is strong can become a crisis during a recession. So the sensible test is not just whether the rate is below the expected return, but whether the borrower could still pay comfortably if conditions turned against them.

A Turing machine is a hypothetical device created by Alan Turing, the well-known mathematician and computer scientist. It offers a way of picturing how a computer could operate, relying on a sequence of basic instructions that direct its actions. Picture a long strip of paper that you plan to use for storing information. You can write items on it, such as numbers or letters, and look back at them later. Now suppose a small machine can travel along that strip, reading what is written there or adding new marks. That machine is what we call a Turing machine. It decides what to do at each step by following a set of rules, known as an "algorithm." For instance, it could be instructed to read a number from the strip, increase it by one, and write the result back in place. By repeating this process again and again with the same rules, the machine can carry out increasingly complex tasks. The central idea is that, given the proper instructions, a Turing machine can be programmed to perform any task a computer is capable of. That is why Turing machines matter so much in computer science: they help us grasp how computers function and how we can apply them to solve problems.

Of course! Synesthesia is a trait in which a person's senses are linked in ways that most people's aren't. Some individuals, for instance, perceive colors when they listen to music, or experience flavors when they look at numbers. It resembles picturing an apple with your eyes closed, except that for someone with synesthesia, the color appears as vividly as if they were actually looking at the fruit with their eyes open. This is not an illness or a flaw; it simply reflects a different way some brains are wired. For those who have it, it can be fascinating and enjoyable, though it may also be puzzling when others don't grasp how they experience the world. In brief, synesthesia means your brain links things that most people keep separate, such as hearing sounds and seeing colors, or seeing numbers and tasting words.

Imagine you want to join a group of kids playing on the playground, but walking up alone feels scary. A wingman is like a buddy who walks over with you, says "Hey, can we play too?", and makes the whole thing feel normal instead of weird. That's basically the job.

When you're trying to meet women, walking up alone to a stranger can feel like a big, risky move, and to her it can sometimes feel a little intense, like you're singling her out. With a friend beside you, it's just two guys being social, which feels more casual and less like a high-stakes pitch. Your wingman can start a conversation, keep it going when there's an awkward pause, tell a funny story that makes you look good ("this guy once fixed my car in the rain at midnight"), or tell people things about you that would sound like bragging if you said them yourself.

A big part of the job is handling the friend. Women often go out in pairs or groups, and if you're talking to one woman, her friend might feel left out and want to leave, or might pull her away. A good wingman chats with the friend so everyone's having a good time and nobody feels abandoned. He's also there for moral support, giving you a little push when you're nervous and helping you laugh it off if things don't go well.

As for feeling awkward in front of him, that's a fair worry, but the trick is picking the right person. A good wingman is a friend you're already comfortable with, someone who's on your side and isn't judging you. If you do say something clumsy, he can jump in and smooth it over, and later you two can laugh about it together. That actually takes a lot of the sting out of rejection, because it becomes a shared, funny night out rather than you failing alone. If the only friend available would make you more self-conscious, then he's not the right wingman for you, and going solo or just hanging out in social settings with a relaxed group might work better.

Okay so the tingling in your left leg could be from your bicuspid aortic valve, or it could be something totally different. Honestly, the best move is to get it checked by a doctor so they can figure out what's actually going on. A bicuspid aortic valve is a heart condition you're born with. The aortic valve controls blood flowing out of the heart to the rest of your body, and normally it has three leaflets. With a bicuspid valve there are only two, which can make the valve narrow or leak and cause heart problems. That said, tingling in the legs isn't really a typical symptom of it. A more likely suspect is peripheral neuropathy, which is damage to the nerves that carry signals between the brain and spinal cord and the rest of the body. It has lots of possible causes, like diabetes, low vitamin levels, or a nerve getting pinched. Sitting for long stretches can play a part too, since it can reduce blood flow to your legs. Again, a doctor is the one to sort this out. They might suggest simple stuff like getting up and stretching every so often when you're sitting for a while, or they might recommend something else depending on what's causing it.

How you report software subscriptions depends on whether you mean financial accounting, tax, or internal expense tracking. Here's an overview focused mainly on accounting.

Most software subscriptions, such as SaaS products like Microsoft 365, Salesforce, or Adobe Creative Cloud, are treated as service contracts rather than assets. You don't own the software; you're paying for access. The subscription fee is generally recorded as an operating expense over the period you receive the service. If you pay monthly, you simply expense each payment in the month it covers. If you pay annually or multiple years upfront, you record the payment as a prepaid expense, a current asset, and then recognize a portion each month, for example one-twelfth of an annual fee. This keeps your expenses matched to the periods that benefit from them.

Under US GAAP, ASC 350-40 addresses cloud computing arrangements that are service contracts. The subscription fees are expensed, but certain implementation costs, such as configuration, integration, data conversion, and testing during the application development stage, can be capitalized and amortized over the term of the hosting arrangement, including reasonably certain renewals. These capitalized implementation costs are presented in the same balance sheet line as a prepayment for the service, and the amortization appears in the same income statement line as the subscription fees, not as depreciation or amortization of intangibles. Training and data cleanup costs are generally expensed as incurred. If the contract actually gives you the right to take possession of the software and run it yourself without significant penalty, it may instead be treated as an internal-use software intangible asset.

Under IFRS, the IFRS Interpretations Committee concluded in 2019 that a typical SaaS arrangement does not give the customer control of an intangible asset, so fees are expensed as the service is received. A follow-up 2021 agenda decision held that configuration and customization costs are usually expensed too, either when incurred or over the contract term if the supplier is performing distinct services that are not separate from the access itself. Capitalization is only possible in limited cases where the customer creates a separate intangible asset it controls, such as custom code it owns.

For tax purposes in the United States, subscription fees are typically deductible as ordinary and necessary business expenses. Prepaid amounts may be deductible immediately under the 12-month rule if the benefit doesn't extend beyond 12 months from when the right begins or the end of the following tax year, whichever is earlier; longer prepayments are usually deducted ratably. Purchased off-the-shelf software that you own, as opposed to subscribe to, may be depreciated over 36 months or expensed using Section 179 or bonus depreciation. Other countries have their own rules, and sales tax or VAT on digital services may also apply depending on jurisdiction.

On the practical side, many businesses maintain a subscription register listing each vendor, cost, billing frequency, renewal date, owner, and the general ledger account used, often something like "software subscriptions" or "IT services." This helps with accrual and prepaid schedules, budget review, and catching unused or duplicate licenses. Tools such as expense management platforms or SaaS management software can automate much of this.

If you let me know whether you're asking about GAAP, IFRS, tax filing, a particular country, or simply how to track subscriptions for budgeting, I can go into more specific detail, including sample journal entries.

There are a number of possible explanations for upper abdominal pain that worsens when a person coughs, laughs, or sneezes. One is a strained or spasming muscle: these actions place extra tension on the abdominal muscles, which can lead to discomfort. Another is gastroenteritis, an inflammation of the digestive tract usually triggered by a virus or bacteria, which can bring abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. Gallbladder problems, such as gallstones, may also be responsible, especially when the pain appears after a meal. Finally, pancreatitis, meaning inflammation of the pancreas, can produce abdominal pain along with nausea and vomiting. Because the cause is not always clear, it is important to consult a healthcare provider, who can examine you, order tests if needed, and recommend a diagnosis and treatment plan.

Metal feels cold because it is very good at pulling heat out of your skin. When you touch something, heat moves from your warmer hand into the cooler object, and your brain reads that flow of heat as "cold." Wood or plastic feels less cold, even when it is sitting in the same room and is the same temperature, because those materials don't pull heat away from your hand nearly as quickly.

Think of it like a line of kids passing a ball of warmth. Metal has lots of tiny helpers inside it, called electrons, that zip around and pass energy along super fast. So when your warm finger touches the metal, the metal grabs your warmth and carries it away in a hurry. Your skin loses heat fast, and that feels cold.

The metal itself isn't really colder than the wooden table next to it. If a steel bar and a wooden stick have been sitting in the same room for hours, they are both the same temperature. The steel just feels colder because it steals heat from you much faster.

American football pits two teams of eleven players against each other. The teams alternate possession of an oval ball and try to advance it along a lengthy field, either by passing it or by carrying it. The team on offense aims to score by getting the ball into the opposing team's end zone, while the defense works to stop that advance and win possession of the ball. An offense gets four attempts, known as "downs," to gain at least ten yards. If it manages this, it earns a fresh set of four downs to cover another ten yards. If it fails, possession goes to the opposing team, which then tries to move the ball itself. There are several ways to put points on the board. A touchdown, worth six points, happens when a player runs the ball over the opponent's goal line or catches a pass in the end zone. A field goal, worth three points, is made when a player kicks the ball between the goalposts. An extra point, worth one point, is earned by kicking the ball through the goalposts after a touchdown. Whichever team has accumulated the most points when the game ends is the winner. Would you like to know anything else about the game?

Gastritis is basically inflammation of your stomach lining. You'll usually get stomach pain, nausea, bloating, and that annoying feeling of being full even when you haven't eaten much. If you think that's what you've got, go see a doctor so you get a real diagnosis and the right treatment. In the meantime, a few things might take the edge off.

Stay away from stuff that irritates your stomach, like spicy or fatty foods. Smaller meals more often tend to go easier than a few big ones. Cut out the smoking and the alcohol if you can. An over-the-counter antacid or acid reducer like omeprazole (Prilosec) can help bring down the stomach acid. Ranitidine (Zantac) used to be the other go-to, though it's been pulled from a lot of shelves, so check what's actually available. A warm bath or a heating pad on your belly can help your muscles relax and ease the pain. And drink plenty of fluids, water especially, to help flush out whatever's bugging your digestive system.

Keep in mind none of this is a fix, just a way to get through the rough patch. If the symptoms stick around, or something just feels off to you, get it checked out.

Premature ejaculation (PE) is more common than people think, and it can come from all sorts of things. Stress, anxiety, and depression can play a part, and so can physical stuff like hormone imbalances, nerve damage, or certain meds. If it's happening to you, there are a few things worth trying.

First, the squeeze and stop-start techniques are pretty popular for a reason. The idea is to stimulate yourself or your partner until you feel close to coming, then stop for a few seconds and start again once the urge fades. Doing this a few times can help you get better at holding off.

Condoms can also help. They dull sensation a bit, which sometimes means you last longer.

Some people look into medication. Antidepressants, PDE5 inhibitors, and numbing creams or sprays are all options that come up a lot. Talk to a doctor before you take anything, though, especially since some of these have side effects or don't mix well with other drugs.

Relaxation stuff can help too, since stress makes PE worse for a lot of people. Deep breathing, meditation, or yoga might take the edge off and make a difference over time.

If anxiety or depression seems to be behind it, therapy can be a big help. Working on the root issue often does more than trying to fix the symptom alone.

And honestly, it's worth seeing a healthcare provider no matter what. They can figure out what's going on and suggest the right approach for you.

I can't recommend a specific medication or dose without examining your father, but I can explain what doctors usually consider. Because he is 83, has had a posterior circulation stroke (PCA infarct), and his scan shows lacunar infarcts and chronic small-vessel changes, his doctor should evaluate the vertigo before any treatment is chosen. Frequent dizziness in someone with this history can come from several causes, including reduced blood flow to the brainstem or inner ear, a new small stroke or transient ischemic attack, benign positional vertigo, inner ear problems, low blood pressure on standing, or side effects of his current medicines. The right treatment depends on which of these is responsible, so a neurologist or his primary doctor should ideally assess him, and a repeat MRI may be useful since CT is less sensitive for small posterior circulation strokes.

Some medicines are commonly considered for vertigo, such as betahistine (used in many countries, though evidence is modest), and short-term use of antivertigo drugs like meclizine. However, these are often avoided or used very cautiously in elderly people because they can cause drowsiness, confusion, dry mouth, urinary problems, and falls. More important in his case is secondary stroke prevention, which often includes blood pressure control, cholesterol management, and an antiplatelet agent or other antithrombotic therapy if none is already prescribed. Please don't start or stop any blood thinner or blood pressure medicine on your own, and check with his doctor before adding any sedating drug.

Several things can help in the meantime. Ask his doctor to check his blood pressure both lying and standing, review all his current medications for dizziness-causing effects, and make sure he gets enough fluids and eats regularly. Vestibular rehabilitation exercises, or repositioning maneuvers if he has positional vertigo, are often effective and safe. Keep his home safe from falls by using grab bars, good lighting, and a walker or cane if he needs one.

Seek emergency care immediately if the dizziness is sudden and severe, or comes with new weakness or numbness, facial drooping, slurred speech, double vision, trouble swallowing, loss of balance or inability to walk, confusion, a severe headache, chest pain, or fainting. These can signal a new stroke, which needs urgent treatment.

The speed class printed on an SDHC (Secure Digital High Capacity) card indicates the least amount of data it can consistently write over a period of time. These ratings are shown as a number, usually between 2 and 10, and the larger the number, the quicker the card writes. As a rough reference, Class 2 guarantees 2 MB/s, Class 4 guarantees 4 MB/s, Class 6 guarantees 6 MB/s, Class 8 guarantees 8 MB/s, and Class 10 guarantees 10 MB/s. Keep in mind that these figures are only minimums, so a given SDHC card may actually write faster than its class suggests. When selecting a card, the class rating deserves close attention, especially if you plan to record high-definition video or move large files. A higher rating helps the card keep pace with such demands and lowers the chance of dropped frames or other problems.

Nasal congestion in a 6-week-old is common, but because babies this young breathe mainly through their noses and can tire quickly or have feeding trouble when blocked, it deserves prompt medical attention. The safest step is to call your pediatrician or a nurse advice line today rather than waiting, since a doctor should check a baby this age who has had symptoms for three days. Seek emergency care right away if he breathes fast or with visible effort (the chest pulling in between or below the ribs, flaring nostrils, grunting), has pauses in breathing, turns bluish or pale around the lips, feeds poorly or refuses feeds, has fewer wet diapers than usual, seems unusually sleepy or hard to wake, or has a fever. In babies under three months, a fever of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher is an emergency on its own.

Please do not use nasal sprays or decongestant drops unless a doctor specifically prescribes them. Many over-the-counter products are unsafe for infants, and some can cause harm at this age. Saline drops or a saline spray used before feeds and sleep, followed by gentle suction with a bulb syringe, is generally considered safe and helpful. Use only a few drops of plain saline in each nostril, wait a minute, then suction gently. Keeping the air moist with a cool-mist humidifier and keeping him upright during and after feeds can also make breathing easier. Smoke exposure should be avoided entirely.

As for the lungs, a stuffy nose on its own usually does not cause lasting lung problems in healthy babies. However, if a blocked nose is caused by an infection that spreads to the chest, such as bronchiolitis or pneumonia, it can affect breathing, which is another reason to have him examined. Most babies recover fully with appropriate care. Trust your instincts: if you feel something is wrong, get him seen promptly.

Hydrogen, denoted by the symbol H, is the chemical element with atomic number 1. It ranks as the lightest and most plentiful element in the cosmos, accounting for roughly 75% of the universe's elemental mass. At standard temperature and pressure it exists as a gas, though it can be chilled and compressed into a liquid or a solid. It is extremely flammable and burns with a faint blue flame. As the simplest of all elements, its atom contains just one proton and one electron. Hydrogen is found in nature mainly as molecules, such as water (H2O), or as a component of larger molecules like hydrocarbons. It serves many important purposes in industry and science. Numerous vehicles run on it as fuel, including fuel cell vehicles that convert it into electricity. It also plays a role in manufacturing chemicals such as ammonia and methanol, in refining petroleum, in steel production, and in purifying certain metals. Beyond these, it finds use in the food industry and in making some kinds of plastics.

I'm sorry you're feeling this way, and I believe you. Your history matters here, so let me lay out what I think is most important.

The combination you describe, a tender abdomen, body aches, night sweats, fatigue, a rash, slow-healing cuts, and a body that hasn't felt right since a serious IUD infection, deserves a proper medical workup rather than a home remedy. A pelvic infection can sometimes linger, come back, or leave complications such as an abscess, scarring, or ongoing inflammation. If the IUD is still in place, it can also be a source of persistent infection. Your temperature of 96.5 is actually a bit low, not a fever, and a low or unstable temperature together with feeling cold, sweating, and being very unwell can sometimes be a sign that the body is struggling with infection, so it shouldn't be brushed off.

Please get seen in person soon. If you have any of the following, go to an emergency room today: severe or worsening abdominal pain, a rigid or very tender belly, a fever of 100.4 F or higher, shaking chills, confusion, a racing heart, dizziness or fainting, vomiting you can't stop, foul-smelling or unusual vaginal discharge, heavy bleeding, or a rash that spreads quickly or looks purple or bruise-like. Those can signal sepsis or a serious pelvic infection, which need urgent treatment.

If none of those are present, still try to be seen within a day or two, by your regular doctor, an urgent care clinic, or a gynecologist. When you go, it helps to say directly: "I had a serious IUD infection in October and have not recovered. I now have abdominal tenderness, night sweats, body aches, a rash, and slow-healing cuts. I'd like a pelvic exam, ultrasound, and blood work." Reasonable tests include a complete blood count, inflammatory markers like CRP, a metabolic panel, blood sugar and A1c (slow wound healing and sweats can point to blood sugar problems), thyroid tests, STI and pelvic infection testing, and a pregnancy test. Write your symptoms down with dates so you can be taken seriously, and bring someone with you if you can. If one clinician dismisses you, it is fine to ask for another opinion.

Until you're seen, you can ease symptoms safely. Drink plenty of fluids, rest, and eat what you can. Acetaminophen can help with aches and headache, taking it as directed on the label. Avoid heavy use of ibuprofen if your stomach is tender. Keep cuts clean with mild soap and water and covered, and watch for redness, warmth, swelling, or pus. For the rash, avoid new soaps or creams, and take a photo each day so a doctor can see how it changes. Please don't start leftover antibiotics on your own, since that can mask the problem and make testing harder.

You are right to push for answers. I hope you get care quickly and start feeling better.

Object detection is a computer vision task where you figure out what objects are in an image or video, where they are, and what type they are. It's a big deal for driver assistance systems and self-driving cars, and it shows up in plenty of other places too, like video surveillance, image search, and robotics. There are lots of ways to do it, but most of them come down to training a machine learning model on a big pile of annotated images, meaning pictures where someone has marked where each object is and what it is. Once the model is trained, it can spot objects in new images or videos it has never seen. People sometimes mix this up with object recognition, which only asks what something is from a fixed list of categories. Recognition might tell you that a thing in a photo is a chair. Detection goes further and also tells you where that chair sits in the frame. The field has moved fast in the last few years thanks to deep learning and convolutional neural networks (CNNs). Those tools made it possible to build detection models that are really accurate and work across all sorts of applications.

Sequence mining is basically a way of digging through data to find patterns and links between things that happen in order. You might be looking for patterns that keep repeating, or for weird sequences that signal something big is going on. It's used all over the place, like in finance, healthcare, and marketing, to make sense of huge piles of data. In finance, people use it to spot patterns in stock prices or trades that could point to a trend or a risk. Hospitals might use it to notice patterns in patient records that hint at a particular condition or how well a treatment is working. Marketers look at customer behavior to see what might lead to a sale or keep someone coming back. There are plenty of techniques for this, including hidden Markov models, sequential pattern mining, and time series analysis. They're handy for untangling complicated, constantly changing systems that would be a nightmare to figure out by hand.

Belize is a small country on the eastern coast of Central America. You've got Mexico up north, Guatemala to the west and south, and the Caribbean Sea running along the east side. It's a tropical place with gorgeous beaches, and the culture is a real mix of Indigenous, Maya, and Afro-Caribbean influences. English is the official language, but you'll hear Spanish, Kriol, and several Indigenous languages too. The capital is Belmopan, though the largest city is actually Belize City.

Thomson came up with the plum pudding model of the atom back in 1904. The idea was that an atom is basically a positively charged sphere with negative electrons stuck inside it, kind of like raisins in a pudding. Rutherford later reworked that picture. He showed the positive charge and nearly all the mass sit in a tiny, dense nucleus at the center, with electrons zipping around it.

A social network is a structure made up of individuals or organizations, called nodes, connected by relationships such as friendship, collaboration, kinship, or shared interests. The concept comes from sociology and social science, where researchers study how these connections shape the flow of information, influence, resources, and behavior among people. In this sense, a social network can be a family, a workplace, a group of friends, or the broader web of ties linking members of a community.

In everyday usage, the term more often refers to online social networks, which are digital platforms such as Facebook, Instagram, LinkedIn, X, and TikTok. These services let users create profiles, form connections with other users, share content like text, photos, and videos, and interact through comments, messages, and reactions. They typically rely on algorithms that decide which posts and people users see, and they have become major channels for communication, news, marketing, and community building.

Social networks offer real benefits, such as staying in touch with distant friends, finding professional opportunities, and joining groups with shared interests. They also raise concerns, including privacy and data collection, the spread of misinformation, harmful effects on mental health, and the potential for online harassment. Understanding social networks therefore involves looking both at the human relationships they represent and at the technologies that now mediate many of them.

Kids and teens often start smoking for reasons that feel important to them at the time, even if they don't look smart from the outside. Many want to fit in with friends, look older or cooler, or feel grown up. Some are curious, or they see parents, movie stars, or others doing it and think it looks fun or relaxing. Others start because they're stressed, bored, or sad, and a cigarette seems like a quick way to feel better, even though it doesn't really help in the long run.

The tricky part is that nicotine, the drug in cigarettes, is very good at hooking people. It works fast, so the brain learns to want it again and again. After a while, a person may smoke not to feel good but just to stop feeling bad, like when they're grumpy because they need another one. That's why it can be so hard to quit, even for people who really want to.

Another reason is that the bad things from smoking don't show up right away. Someone who smokes today usually doesn't feel sick tomorrow, so it's easy to think, "It won't happen to me." Young people especially tend to feel invincible and believe they'll quit later, before any real harm happens.

So you're right that the trade is a bad one: lots of money, health problems later, and a habit that's hard to break. Lots of people who start later wish they hadn't, and many of them work hard to quit. The best choice is simply to never start.

Optical character recognition, usually abbreviated as OCR, is a technology that converts images of text into machine-readable text. The input might be a scanned page, a photograph of a sign or document, or a frame from a video, and the output is editable, searchable characters that a computer can store, copy, or process. Without OCR, a scanned book or a photo of a receipt would just be a picture, with the words visible to people but invisible to software.

The process generally begins with preprocessing, where the image is cleaned up by adjusting brightness and contrast, removing noise, straightening skewed pages, and converting it to black and white. The software then performs layout analysis to find regions containing text, separating paragraphs, columns, tables, and images. Next comes character recognition itself. Early OCR systems matched shapes against stored templates of known letters, while modern systems typically use machine learning, and especially deep neural networks, trained on huge collections of text images. These models can recognize characters across many fonts, sizes, and handwriting styles, and they often use language context to correct likely mistakes, such as distinguishing an "l" from a "1" based on the surrounding words.

OCR is used in many everyday settings. Libraries and archives use it to digitize books and historical documents, banks use it to read checks, postal services use it to sort mail by address, and smartphone apps let people copy text from photos or translate signs. It also supports accessibility by helping visually impaired users hear printed material read aloud. Accuracy depends heavily on image quality, font clarity, and language, so poor lighting, unusual typefaces, or messy handwriting can still cause errors. Even so, OCR has become a foundational tool for turning the large body of printed and photographed text into data that can be searched and analyzed.

I'm not a doctor, but I can share some general information. Topical acne gels can cause side effects such as dryness, peeling, stinging, and itching, and some people develop contact dermatitis, a reaction to an ingredient in the product. Because the gels you used contain different ingredients, I can't tell from the names alone which one, if any, is responsible. Your pharmacist or a dermatologist can check the active ingredients on the labels.

The bumps you describe, small, mostly on the nose and cheeks, not red, and sometimes itchy, could have several causes. One possibility is folliculitis, an irritation or infection of hair follicles, including a yeast-type form that often appears after acne treatments and can be itchy. Another is irritation or allergic contact dermatitis from one of the tubes. Skin can also stay sensitive and dry for a few months after isotretinoin, and small bumps can simply be residual acne or tiny clogged pores. Since the bumps have no redness and only sometimes flare, a bacterial skin infection seems less likely, but I can't rule it out from a description alone.

For now, it would help to stop all the tubes for a few days, or at least the most recent one you started, and see whether the bumps settle. Use a gentle, fragrance-free moisturizer and a mild cleanser, avoid touching or squeezing the bumps, and try not to scratch. Avoid putting steroid creams on your face without a doctor's advice, since they can make some of these conditions worse.

You should see a dermatologist soon, especially since the bumps are itchy and changing. Seek care sooner if you notice spreading redness, pus, warmth, pain, fever, or bumps that are getting larger or more numerous. A dermatologist can examine the skin, tell whether the bumps are fungal, irritant, or acne-related, and recommend the right treatment, which may be different from what you were using before.

Adenosine deaminase (ADA) is an enzyme that helps break down purines, the building blocks of DNA and RNA. When someone has an ADA deficiency, it's usually because of a genetic mutation that leads to the enzyme being inactive or not made in enough quantity. You can inherit that mutation from your parents, or it can happen spontaneously during fetal development. It's a rare inherited disorder, and it hits the immune system hard. People with it struggle to fight off infections and tend to get serious, repeated ones. How bad it gets really varies. Some folks have pretty mild symptoms, while others end up with severe, life-threatening infections. Treatment often includes enzyme replacement therapy, where the body gets ADA supplements to make up for what it can't produce. For some patients, though, doctors recommend a bone marrow transplant instead.

Use adjusted close for backtesting. Regular (unadjusted) close prices jump on dates when a stock splits or pays a dividend, which makes it look as though the price dropped or spiked when nothing economically happened. Adjusted close retroactively scales historical prices to account for splits and dividends, so the series reflects the true total return an investor would have earned and gives you a consistent basis for calculating returns, moving averages, and other indicators.

There are a few caveats worth keeping in mind. Adjusted prices are backward-adjusted, so they change whenever a new dividend or split occurs, which means you should re-download the data rather than mixing old and new snapshots. Adjusted close also doesn't capture everything: it generally doesn't account for trading costs, taxes, or slippage, so your backtest should model those separately. And if your strategy depends on the actual prices a trader would have seen at a given moment, such as checking order fill levels or computing position sizes in share counts, you may need the unadjusted open, high, low, and close, using adjusted data only for return calculations.

Linear network coding is a technique for sending data through a network that lets intermediate nodes carry out coding operations on the information they receive, instead of just passing it along unchanged to the next node. Depending on the design, this can speed up data delivery or reduce the rate of transmission errors, thereby improving overall network efficiency. The approach rests on linear transformations, which are mathematical operations applied to a collection of data values to yield a new set of values. Such transformations can blend or merge the data in different ways, and the resulting coded data is then sent across the network. Its central benefit is that intermediate nodes are not limited to forwarding packets; they can process what they receive, which may raise the network's capacity by moving data more efficiently. As an illustration, when two nodes send information to a third node, linear network coding can merge both streams into one coded message that travels across the network more effectively. The technique has found use in wireless communications, peer-to-peer networks, and distributed storage systems. Studies have shown it can boost the capacity and efficiency of these networks, and it remains an active research topic in computer science and networking.

You should speak with a healthcare professional about the symptoms you're experiencing. A slow heartbeat (bradycardia) and lightheadedness can stem from many sources, such as certain medications, existing health problems, or everyday habits. A medical provider can work out what is behind your symptoms and suggest the right course of action. Be sure to also bring up your past episodes of shortness of breath and any chance that you've been around cleaning products at work. Those factors might be tied to an underlying illness or to the substances you came into contact with. Until you've been evaluated, try to rest well, drink enough fluids, and steer clear of activities that could make things worse. However, if you notice serious or ongoing symptoms like fainting, chest pain, or trouble breathing, get medical help right away.

Businesses are typically permitted to decline credit cards as a payment method. That said, once a business chooses to take credit cards, it has to abide by the card issuer's rules, which might include not singling out particular card brands or adding surcharges for paying by card. Some companies opt out of card payments because the processing fees they owe the card company are costly, or because they simply favor other payment options. Still, companies should weigh what their customers want before making that decision. Plenty of shoppers assume they can pay by card, so a store that refuses them could lose sales to rivals who accept cards.

A buttoned-down shirt is a dress shirt with a collar whose points are fastened to the shirt body by small buttons. This style originated in the late 19th century in England, where polo players reportedly buttoned their collars down to keep them from flapping during matches. It later became a staple of American and British menswear, valued for its relaxed yet polished look that works well for both business and casual occasions.

Because the collar stays flat and in place, a button-down shirt is often considered less formal than a standard point-collar shirt, which is typically worn with a tie in more formal settings. The term is also sometimes used more loosely to describe any shirt with a button-down collar, or to mean someone who is conservative, orderly, or restrained in behavior or style.

Interstate 70 (I-70) is a principal east-west highway in the United States, stretching from Cove Fort, Utah, to Baltimore, Maryland. Along its route it passes through Utah, Colorado, Kansas, Missouri, Illinois, Indiana, Ohio, West Virginia, Pennsylvania, and Maryland. The highway is a vital corridor for both travel and freight, linking numerous major cities and recreation destinations. Its path crosses the Rocky Mountains, the Great Plains, and the Appalachian Mountains, and it runs through or close to several national parks and monuments, such as Arches National Park, Colorado National Monument, Black Canyon of the Gunnison National Park, the Appalachian National Scenic Trail, and the C&O Canal National Historical Park.

The Montreal Expos were a Major League Baseball (MLB) club located in Montreal, Quebec, Canada. From 1969 through 2004 they competed in the National League (NL). In 2005 the franchise relocated to Washington, D.C., where it took the name Washington Nationals. The Expos began as an expansion franchise in 1969 and took the field for their first season in 1970. Competing in the NL East, they played their home games at Olympic Stadium in Montreal. Their first few seasons were marked by losing, but the club grew into a contender during the late 1970s and early 1980s. In 2004 Major League Baseball took ownership of the Expos and planned to transfer them to Washington, D.C. for the 2005 campaign. The relocation drew criticism, yet it was carried out, and the team emerged as the Nationals. Since 2005 the Nationals have called Washington, D.C. home and have also played in the NL East.

Usually you don't pay tax on the balance itself. Having money sitting in a savings account isn't taxable in most countries. What can be taxed is the interest the money earns. In the UK, for example, you get a Personal Savings Allowance (up to £1,000 of interest a year for basic-rate taxpayers, less for higher earners, and nothing for additional-rate taxpayers), and interest above that is taxed at your income tax rate. In the US, interest is taxable as ordinary income regardless of amount, and your bank will send you a Form 1099-INT if it pays more than a small threshold. Other countries have their own rules, and some have wealth taxes that do count the balance itself, so the answer depends on where you live.

If you tell me your country and roughly how much interest you earn, I can give you a more specific picture.

I'm sorry you're dealing with a toothache. Getting it looked at promptly matters, since an unfinished root canal can allow infection to spread and cause more damage to the tooth. You could try a few things to ease the discomfort. Swishing with warm salt water may help bring down swelling and irritation. Over-the-counter pain relievers like acetaminophen or ibuprofen can also help, as long as you follow the directions on the label. Holding a cold compress against the outside of your cheek, near the sore tooth, can reduce swelling and dull the sensation. It's also wise to steer clear of very hot or very cold foods and drinks, since they may aggravate the pain. If the discomfort continues or becomes severe, please contact a dentist right away so they can find the source and recommend proper treatment. Until then, keep away from extreme temperatures and avoid biting down on the affected tooth. I hope these tips bring you some relief.

Honestly, there are a few things a white spot inside the nostril could be. It might be a harmless growth like a nasal polyp or a wart. It could also be an infection, either fungal or bacterial. Sometimes it's leukoplakia, which is basically a thickened patch of skin inside the nostril. Really, though, you'll want a doctor to take a look so they can figure out what it is and how to treat it.

A deviated septum usually wouldn't cause a white spot by itself. The septum is the bit of bone and cartilage dividing your nostrils, and when it's crooked, it doesn't typically leave spots like that. That said, if the misalignment is irritating or inflaming the area, it could be part of the picture. If your dentist suggested a more specific scan to get a better look, I'd go ahead and do it. That's the best way to find out what's actually going on and get the right treatment.

Drilling in deep water involves two separate depths: how deep the water is above the seafloor, and how far the drill can then go down into the rock beneath it. Both have pushed into remarkable territory.

For oil and gas, modern drillships and floating rigs routinely work in what the industry calls ultra-deep water, generally more than about 1,500 meters (5,000 feet). The records for water depth sit at a little over 3,000 meters, roughly 10,000 to 11,000 feet, set by drillships working off India, in the Gulf of Mexico, and off Brazil and West Africa. Once on the seabed, these wells can go very deep into the rock. The well often cited as among the deepest ever drilled is BP's Tiber well in the Gulf of Mexico, drilled in 2009 by the Deepwater Horizon rig. It reached a total depth of about 10,685 meters (around 35,000 feet), with about 1,260 meters of that being water and the rest rock.

Scientific drilling has gone to even greater water depths, though usually not as far into the seafloor. In the 1970s and 1980s, the research ship Glomar Challenger took core samples from parts of the Mariana Trench region in water close to 7,000 meters deep. In 2012, the Japanese drilling vessel Chikyu drilled through about 6,900 meters of water in the Japan Trench to study the fault that caused the 2011 Tohoku earthquake, then went more than 800 meters into the seafloor. Chikyu also holds the record for scientific drilling below the seabed, reaching about 3,260 meters into the Nankai Trough off Japan in 2018. The deepest hole into true oceanic crust, Hole 504B off Costa Rica, goes a little over 2,100 meters.

Several factors limit how deep these operations can go. In very deep water, a riser, the large pipe connecting the ship to the well that carries drilling mud and controls pressure, becomes extremely heavy and difficult to manage, so very deep scientific work often drills without one. Long strings of drill pipe have to support their own enormous weight. Deep in the rock, rising temperatures and pressures damage equipment and make the borehole unstable, the same problems that stopped the deepest land hole, the Kola Superdeep Borehole in Russia, at about 12,262 meters. A long-standing scientific goal is to drill all the way through the ocean crust into the Earth's mantle, about 6 to 7 kilometers below the seafloor in the thinnest areas, but that has not yet been achieved.

In short, humans can drill in water a bit over 3 kilometers deep for oil and nearly 7 kilometers deep for science, and can reach total depths beyond 10 kilometers below the sea surface.

A graphical model is a way of representing and reasoning about the relationships among a set of random variables using a graph. In this graph, each node stands for a variable, and the edges (connections between nodes) encode how the variables depend on or relate to one another. The main appeal of this representation is that it makes complicated joint probability distributions easier to understand, store, and compute with. Instead of specifying the probability of every possible combination of variables, which grows exponentially with the number of variables, a graphical model shows which variables directly influence which others, and the joint distribution can then be factored into smaller pieces that depend only on small groups of connected variables.

There are two main families of graphical models. The first is directed graphical models, often called Bayesian networks, which use arrows to show that one variable is conditionally dependent on its parents. For example, if rain influences whether the sidewalk is wet, and the sidewalk being wet influences whether someone slips, the network would draw arrows following that chain of influence. The second family is undirected graphical models, often called Markov random fields, which use plain edges to show symmetric associations without a notion of cause and effect. These are common in areas such as image processing, where neighboring pixels tend to have similar values.

Graphical models are useful for several tasks. They support inference, meaning computing the probability of some unknown variables given observed ones, such as diagnosing a disease from symptoms. They also support learning, where the structure and parameters of the model are estimated from data. Because the graph reveals conditional independence relationships, algorithms can exploit that structure to make calculations far more efficient. Graphical models appear throughout machine learning, statistics, natural language processing, computer vision, genetics, and error-correcting codes, and they provide a unifying language for many probabilistic methods, including hidden Markov models and many variants of neural probabilistic systems.

Born in New York City on March 30, 1979, Norah Jones is the daughter of Sue Jones and the late Indian sitar master Ravi Shankar. She works as an American singer, songwriter, and actress, and her music has earned her many honors, among them nine Grammy Awards. Her catalog includes a number of hit albums, notably "Come Away With Me," which sold more than 26 million copies around the world and took home five Grammys. Jones is recognized for her distinctive voice and for her knack for mixing musical styles such as jazz, pop, and country.

Yes, but the drop is usually smaller than the dividend itself and it is not a loss of value for shareholders in the way it might first appear. On the ex-dividend date, the day the buyer of the stock is no longer entitled to the upcoming payment, the share price typically falls by roughly the amount of the dividend. The reason is that the company has moved cash out of its treasury and into shareholders' hands, so the company is worth that much less. A shareholder who owned the stock before the ex-date receives the dividend in cash, and the lower share price offsets it, so their total wealth is essentially unchanged before taxes and trading costs.

In practice the price adjustment is often less than the full dividend. Markets are not perfectly efficient, and factors such as taxes play a role. In many jurisdictions dividends are taxed differently from capital gains, so investors in higher tax brackets may prefer that value come through price appreciation, which can make the drop smaller than the payout. Other forces, including the general upward drift of the market over the day, can also obscure the effect on any given day.

The dividend drop is a standard consequence of how dividends work and is central to pricing models in finance. It is also why dividend capture strategies, which try to buy just before the ex-date and sell afterward, generally do not earn a free profit once taxes and transaction costs are accounted for.

Think of a file-sharing website like a big library where people can drop off books and let others borrow them. The question is why one library got shut down and another didn't.

Megaupload was run in a way that made it look like the library was doing more than just providing shelves. The people who ran it were accused of encouraging visitors to copy popular movies and music that the owners hadn't given permission for, and they made a lot of money from people paying for faster access. In 2012, U.S. authorities arrested the founders and shut the site down. The founders were charged with crimes related to copyright, and the case was long and complicated.

MediaFire is also a file-hosting site, but it has generally followed the rules that these sites are expected to follow. When someone reports a copyrighted file, it removes that file. It also doesn't have a history of its owners being accused of directing people to pirate things. Because of that, it hasn't been targeted the same way.

As for why authorities don't go after every site, there are a few reasons. They have limited time and money, so they tend to focus on the biggest or most obviously harmful cases. A site that quickly removes illegal material when asked is usually treated differently from one that seems to be built around piracy. Also, the law generally protects websites from being blamed for what users upload, as long as they respond properly to complaints, so going after a site takes strong evidence that its operators knew and encouraged the illegal activity.

A stop loss is basically an order to sell a security once it hits a certain price. When the price reaches that level, the order turns into a market order and gets filled at whatever the best available price is. So if you set one at your purchase price, you're telling your broker to sell if the stock drops back to where you bought it. People use this to cap how much they can lose on a trade. Just keep in mind that the stop price isn't guaranteed. If the market is moving fast, you could end up selling for noticeably more or less than the level you picked.

Okay so the Expos were an MLB team out of Montreal, Quebec, Canada. They played in the National League from 1969 to 2004, then in 2005 the team moved to Washington, D.C. and became the Washington Nationals. They started out as an expansion team in 1969 and actually played their first season in 1970, in the NL East. Home was Olympic Stadium in Montreal.

Early on they really struggled, but they got competitive in the late '70s and early '80s. Then in 2004 MLB bought the team, and it was supposed to move to D.C. for the 2005 season. People were pretty upset about it, and it was a messy process, but it happened anyway. The Nationals have been in D.C. ever since, still in the NL East.

Yes. Several free and paid online repositories collect the financial statements of publicly traded companies. The most authoritative free source in the United States is the SEC's EDGAR database (sec.gov/edgar), where companies file annual reports (10-K), quarterly reports (10-Q), and other disclosures, all searchable by company name or ticker and available at no cost. Many other countries have equivalent systems, such as the UK's Companies House and Financial Conduct Authority filings, Canada's SEDAR+, and the European Securities and Markets Authority's filing system for certain issuers.

For more convenient access, financial data aggregators offer standardized statements and historical data. Yahoo Finance, Google Finance, and MarketWatch show income statements, balance sheets, and cash flow statements for most listed companies, often with several years of history. Macrotrends and Companies Market Cap provide long-run charts and data series. Paid services such as S&P Capital IQ, Bloomberg Terminal, FactSet, Morningstar, and Refinitiv (LSEG) offer deeper, cleaned, and comparable datasets, typically used by professionals and often available through university or library subscriptions.

For bulk or research use, the SEC publishes structured financial data from EDGAR's XBRL filings, and academic resources such as Compustat (accessible through many university libraries) and WRDS (Wharton Research Data Services) provide standardized historical panels for research.

Securities orders on a stock exchange are paired up either by an electronic platform or by a specialist working on the trading floor. Once an investor submits a buy or sell order, it is routed to the exchange's trading system, which looks for a counterpart order already entered by another investor. When a match turns up, the system carries out the trade, completing the deal by moving the security to the buyer and the payment to the seller. If no counterpart exists, the system keeps the order on hold until one arrives. Such a pending order is called an "open order" or an "order on the book." The investor may cancel an open order at any point before it is filled. On the floor, specialists handle the matching for a particular security or group of securities. Drawing on their understanding of supply and demand, they pair buyers with sellers and work to make sure trades happen at a fair price. Whether the matching is done electronically or by a floor specialist, the aim is identical: connect buyers and sellers so that securities and money change hands efficiently and transparently.

Capacitors work somewhat like miniature batteries, holding electrical charge. Inside each one are two metal plates, and electricity is stored on those plates when it is applied. Picture two metal plates with charge placed between them: a large amount of charge forms what looks like a tall mound of electricity between the plates, while a smaller amount forms a low mound. Now imagine a stretchy rubber sheet fitted between the two plates. Stretching that sheet squeezes the charge mounds closer together, which makes it more difficult for electricity to pass between the plates. That is essentially how a capacitor stores energy: a rubber-like material, known as a "dielectric," is placed between the metal plates. To use the stored charge, a capacitor is connected to a circuit, and the electricity drains out into the circuit much as water drains from a bucket. Many electronic devices rely on capacitors to even out the flow of electricity and to hold energy for future use.

The destructive force of a bomb is generally gauged by how much explosive material it holds. The Hiroshima weapon, nicknamed "Little Boy," carried roughly 64 kilograms (141 pounds) of uranium. A device with 1,000 times that quantity of explosive material would be far bigger and heavier than Little Boy and would most likely produce a much wider blast radius, meaning the zone hit by the explosion. Still, the reach of the blast also hinges on other variables, including the kind of explosive used, the height at which the device goes off, and the surroundings. A detonation over a city, for instance, would create a different blast pattern than one set off at ground level in an open field. Nuclear weapons are extremely destructive and can cause terrible harm to people and the environment. The attacks on Hiroshima and Nagasaki during World War II killed hundreds of thousands of people and left lasting damage to the environment. A weapon 1,000 times as powerful as Little Boy would probably be more destructive still.

Peter Thiel, a businessman, investor, and donor, was born in Germany but holds American citizenship. He gained widespread recognition as a co-founder of PayPal, the online payments firm, and as an early backer of LinkedIn and Facebook. He also established Mithril Capital Management, a venture capital firm, and Palantir Technologies, which specializes in analyzing data. Beyond his commercial work, Thiel has taken part in political advocacy and a range of causes. His views are generally libertarian, and he has openly criticized the prevailing culture and social attitudes within Silicon Valley.

Business credit is a financial track record that a company builds separately from its owners' personal credit, and it is useful for securing vendor accounts, business loans, and lines of credit. The process usually begins with getting the business properly set up: registering the company with the state, obtaining an Employer Identification Number (EIN) from the IRS, opening a business bank account, and listing a physical address and phone number that match public records. Lenders and credit bureaus want to see that the business is a distinct legal entity, so an LLC or corporation is generally preferred over a sole proprietorship for this purpose.

Once the foundation is in place, the next step is establishing a credit file with the major business credit bureaus, such as Dun & Bradstreet, Experian Business, and Equifax Business. Many small companies start with net-30 vendor accounts, which are suppliers that allow the business to buy goods or services now and pay within thirty days without a formal credit check. Paying these invoices on time is one of the most effective ways to build a positive history. Some vendors also report to business bureaus, so consistent payment can gradually produce a credit profile that outside lenders will recognize. Secured business credit cards, which require a cash deposit, and retail store accounts can serve as additional early steps.

When the business is ready to apply for a loan or larger credit line, the lender will typically review the business's credit reports, time in operation, annual revenue, cash flow, existing debts, and bank statements. Many lenders also ask the owner for a personal guarantee, which makes the owner personally responsible if the business cannot repay. Applicants should prepare recent financial statements, tax returns, a business plan or description of how the funds will be used, and documentation of the legal structure. Comparing options from banks, credit unions, online lenders, and Small Business Administration (SBA) backed programs can reveal differences in interest rates, fees, repayment terms, and approval requirements.

After approval, managing the credit responsibly is what sustains it over time. Keeping utilization low, making every payment on schedule, avoiding unnecessary applications that create multiple hard inquiries, and regularly checking the business credit reports for errors all help maintain a strong profile. Over time, a good business credit history can lead to higher limits, better interest rates, and easier access to capital as the company grows.

Space appears dark, but the reason is not that light can't travel through a vacuum; it's that space contains no air. On Earth, sunlight passes through the atmosphere and reaches our eyes, which is how we see the world around us. Out in space, however, there is no atmosphere to carry that light to us, so the surroundings look black. It is also true that regions nearer the Sun seem brighter, but only because the Sun is so luminous that it illuminates everything nearby. Consequently, if you could travel to the Sun, you would find it intensely bright, and you would be able to make out everything around you.

A long, long time ago, people lived in tiny groups, and everybody knew everybody. If you wanted your friend Og, you just shouted "Og!" and he came. There was only one Og, so one name was enough. Even that probably started small, with people using sounds or little nicknames like "the tall one" or "the one who runs fast."

Then people started living in bigger villages and towns. Now there might be three different Ogs in the same place, and it got confusing. Imagine a whole classroom where every kid was named Tom. Nobody would know which Tom you meant! So people began adding extra words to tell them apart.

Those extra words came from many places. Some told what a person did for a job: a man who made things from iron was called Smith, a baker was Baker, and a miller was Miller. Some told where a person lived or came from: someone who lived by a hill might be called Hill, and someone from a place called York might be called York. Some told who your parent was: Johnson means "John's son," and in other places you see the same idea in names like Fitzgerald, O'Brien, Ivanov, or Andersen. And some were nicknames about how a person looked or acted, like Short, Brown, or Strong.

At first these extra names only lasted for one person's life. If Tom the baker had a son, the son might be called by something else. But later, around the Middle Ages in Europe, and at different times in places like China, Japan, and the Middle East, rulers and tax collectors wanted to keep lists of who lived where and who owed what. It was much easier with names that stayed the same. So families began passing their last names down from parents to children, and the names stuck.

So in short: names were added because there got to be too many people to keep straight, and they were kept the same from parent to child because it helped everyone keep track of who was who.

Honestly, you can't really pin down a rash like this without someone looking at it in person and asking about his history, so he should get it checked by a doctor. There are a bunch of possible causes for an itchy rash that starts on the thighs and spreads. Allergic reactions are one: a chemical, a plant, or something he ate can set it off. It could also be an infection like chickenpox, shingles, or a fungal thing. Eczema is another common culprit, causing itching, redness, and dry, scaly patches. Insect bites from mosquitoes, fleas, or bedbugs can do it too. And heat rash is a possibility, which happens when sweat ducts get blocked and sweat gets trapped under the skin, especially in warm, muggy weather.

Anyway, he should really see a provider to figure out what it is. In the meantime, an over-the-counter antihistamine might help with the itch, and try not to scratch, since that just makes things worse. If it's not getting better, or if he starts running a fever or having trouble breathing, don't wait around. Get medical help right away.

The United States spends more on health care per person than any other country. In 2022, national health expenditures were about $4.5 trillion, which works out to roughly $13,500 per person. Figures for 2023 were higher, at about $4.9 trillion or around $14,500 per person, according to the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services. Spending has been growing at roughly 4 to 7 percent a year, so the current figure is likely a bit above that.

That total includes everything: spending by individuals, private insurers, employers, and federal and state governments. Out-of-pocket costs such as copays, deductibles, and uncovered services make up only a modest share, around 10 to 11 percent of the total, or roughly $1,400 to $1,500 per person on average. The rest is paid through insurance premiums, taxes, and government programs like Medicare and Medicaid. Government programs finance close to half of all spending.

For comparison, other wealthy countries spend far less. Countries like Germany, Switzerland, Canada, and the United Kingdom typically spend between about $6,000 and $8,500 per person, with Switzerland and Germany at the higher end. The U.S. also spends about 17 to 18 percent of its gross domestic product on health care, compared with about 10 to 12 percent in most peer nations.

Researchers generally attribute the higher U.S. costs less to people using more care and more to higher prices for drugs, hospital services, and physician pay, along with higher administrative costs. Despite the spending, U.S. life expectancy and some health outcomes lag behind many comparable countries.

Ehud Shapiro is an Israeli computer scientist and professor, best known for his contributions to logic programming, machine learning, and computational biology. He earned his PhD at Yale University and has held positions at the Weizmann Institute of Science in Israel, where he has led research groups in computer science and, more recently, has been involved in work on molecular computing and synthetic biology.

Among his most influential work is the development of Model Inference Systems and algorithms for inductive logic programming, which allow computers to learn logical rules from examples. He is also known for his research on "Shapiro's algorithm" for debugging logic programs and for his work on concurrent logic programming languages, such as the language Concurrent Prolog, which helped shape approaches to parallel programming.

In more recent years, Shapiro has explored the idea of computing with biological molecules, including building molecular machines and DNA-based computing systems that can perform logical operations inside living or chemical environments. He has also been a founder or contributor to projects connecting computer science with biology, and he has received numerous awards for his scientific achievements, including recognition from the Association for Computing Machinery and other scientific bodies.

A random variable is basically a variable whose value depends on chance. It's a function that hands a number to each outcome of a random experiment. Say you roll a single die. The possible outcomes are 1 through 6, so you could define a random variable X that equals whatever number comes up. If you roll a 1, X = 1, if you roll a 2, X = 2, and so on.

There are two main types. Discrete random variables take on a finite or countably infinite set of values, like the number of heads you get flipping a coin three times. Continuous ones can land on any value in a range, like how long it takes someone to run a mile. Pretty much anything you can measure on a smooth scale falls into that second group.

Probability distributions tell you which values a random variable can take and how likely each one is. For the die example, it's a uniform distribution, since every face has the same chance of coming up.

So when you go scuba diving, the water pressure around you goes up the deeper you swim, and that pressure squeezes the air in your lungs. That's actually what lets you breathe down there. The trouble starts when you head up too fast. The pressure outside drops quickly, and the air in your lungs wants to expand, sometimes more than your lungs can handle.

Think of a balloon. Hold one underwater and the pressure squishes it smaller. Bring it up too quickly and the air inside swells, and it might pop. Your lungs can get hurt the same way. That rapid expansion can damage lung tissue and blood vessels, and doctors call the result barotrauma. You might get chest pain, trouble breathing, or coughing up blood, and in bad cases it can be life-threatening. So take your time coming up. Slow ascents give your body a chance to adjust to the pressure change, and that's the best way to avoid it.

Hans Moravec is a Austrian-born roboticist and computer scientist, born in 1948, who has spent much of his career at Carnegie Mellon University in Pittsburgh, where he worked on mobile robots and computer vision. He is best known for his early work on autonomous robot navigation, including the Stanford Cart and the CMU Rover, which helped pioneer techniques for robots to perceive and move through their surroundings. He also developed occupancy grid mapping, a method for representing the environment as a grid of probabilities, which became an important tool in robotics.

Beyond his technical contributions, Moravec is widely known for his thinking about artificial intelligence and the future of machine intelligence. He wrote influential books such as Mind Children (1988) and Robot: Mere Machine to Transcendent Mind (1999), in which he speculated that human minds might eventually be transferred into robotic or computer systems, and that machines would surpass human intelligence within a few decades. He also helped articulate what is now called Moravec's paradox: the observation that tasks requiring high-level reasoning are comparatively easy for computers, while tasks like perception and motor skills that humans perform effortlessly are very difficult to replicate.

Moravec is also associated with the Robotics Institute at Carnegie Mellon and has been a prominent voice in discussions about transhumanism and the long-term trajectory of artificial intelligence.

You can, and people do. Partnerships, profit-sharing arrangements, and hedge funds all work this way. But the arrangement runs into several practical problems.

The biggest is that the person investing your money has different incentives from yours. If he keeps part of the gains but his share of losses is capped by what he can actually pay, he can take bigger risks than you would, since you bear most of the downside. Even with an honest manager, you have to monitor what he does, and that monitoring is hard and costly, especially for someone who doesn't know the investment world well. Managers can also take excessive fees, make trades that benefit them more than you, or simply misreport results.

Loss-sharing is also less symmetrical than it sounds. If the money is lost, the manager usually doesn't have enough personal wealth to cover his half, so in practice you absorb most of the loss. Profit-sharing, by contrast, is real money he gets to keep.

Finding a trustworthy person with real skill is hard too. Many people who claim to be good investors aren't, and some are outright frauds. The arrangement that sounds fair on paper can be the setup for a Ponzi scheme, which is why regulators pay close attention to informal pooled-money deals.

Legal and tax issues add friction. In many jurisdictions, managing other people's money for a share of profits requires registration as an investment adviser or fund manager, and informal partnerships can expose you to unlimited personal liability. Taxes on shared profits can also get complicated.

So the idea isn't unworkable, but it works best with formal structures, clear written terms, transparency, and a manager whose money is invested alongside yours so his incentives line up with yours.

Rockets look slow for a few reasons, and none of them mean they're actually slow.

The first reason is distance. A rocket is very far away from you, even when it looks close. Things that are far away always look like they're moving slowly. A airplane flying high in the sky looks like it barely moves, even though it's zooming along. Your brain judges speed by how much something moves across your view, and a rocket covers only a small slice of the sky each second.

The second reason is that the rocket starts out heavy and slow. At the very beginning it has to push itself up off the ground while carrying huge amounts of fuel and weight. It takes a while to build up speed, so the first few seconds look almost like it's just hovering or creeping upward. Then it gets faster and faster, and by the time it's far up, it's zooming.

The third reason is that the speed needed to escape gravity is reached over a long stretch of time. The rocket keeps pushing and speeding up for several minutes. It doesn't need to reach its top speed right away, it just needs to keep gaining speed the whole way up.

So a rocket is like a kid on a swing that starts slow and gets faster and faster. At the beginning it looks sleepy, but it's really working hard to get going.

David Rumelhart was a cognitive psychologist and computer scientist who did a ton of work in AI and cognitive modeling. He was born in 1941 and got his PhD in psychology from Stanford in 1967. He's probably best known for his work on artificial neural networks, which are basically programs built to mimic how the human brain handles information. He was one of the leaders of the connectionist movement, which tried to figure out how the brain works by building computer models of the neural connections behind thinking. Rumelhart also helped develop backpropagation, a method that's still widely used for training neural networks. He co-wrote the hugely influential book "Parallel Distributed Processing," which pushed the idea of distributed representation: the notion that the brain spreads information across many neurons and connections instead of parking it in one spot. He taught at UC San Diego and won the National Medal of Science, the top scientific honor in the US, in 1990. He died in 2011.

I'm sorry you're dealing with an allergic reaction and struggling to get relief. There are several things you can try. First, consider an antihistamine. Besides Benadryl, other over-the-counter options such as loratadine (Claritin), cetirizine (Zyrtec), and fexofenadine (Allegra) may help, and if one doesn't work for you, it may be worth switching to another. Second, place a cool, damp cloth on the affected skin, which can ease swelling and itchiness. Third, over-the-counter products like hydrocortisone cream, calamine lotion, or a menthol-based ointment can offer short-term itch relief. Fourth, try to resist scratching, since it can aggravate the rash and cause more irritation and swelling. Finally, if you know what set off the reaction, such as a certain food or medication, do your best to steer clear of it. If your symptoms are severe or don't improve with over-the-counter care, please see a healthcare provider, who can identify the cause of the rash and suggest the right treatment.

Think of it like learning to write with a pencil that was first made by a pencil-maker who used an older pencil. Java didn't start out fully made of Java. Long ago, the very first Java compiler was written in another language, probably C, and people used that to build the first Java tools. Once Java could compile itself, the people who made it wrote a new Java compiler in Java, and then used the old one to build the new one. Now the Java compiler is "bootstrapped," meaning it has pulled itself up by its own bootstraps.

Here is the trick for why it still works. A compiler is just a program that turns the words of a language into instructions a computer understands. Once you have a working compiler, you can keep using it to build newer versions of itself, so you never need the original one again. It's like a recipe that was first cooked on a stove you borrowed from a friend, and later you cooked the next batch on your own stove, which you built using the first batch of cookies to pay for the bricks.

As for NetBeans, it is a Java program, but it doesn't run directly on your computer's chip. The Java compiler turns the NetBeans code into a special middle language called bytecode. Your computer doesn't speak bytecode either, so it has a helper program called the Java Virtual Machine, which is itself a native program written in C and C++. The JVM reads the bytecode and translates it on the fly into instructions your machine understands. That's why you see a Java process in Task Manager: it's the JVM running NetBeans.

So the short version is: the first version was built with something else, every later version was built with an earlier Java compiler, and NetBeans runs on a translator program that was built long ago from a non-Java foundation.

Yes, "folio" is an acceptable shortened form of "portfolio." "To make your first million" means to earn your first million units of money, usually a million dollars (or pounds, euros, or another currency), typically through work, business, investing, or some other income-generating activity.
