This applies to real cash economy (RCE) games, where players can earn actual money by selling virtual goods or currency. If you are uncertain whether earnings from an RCE game are taxable, speak with a tax professional or review the IRS's guidance on how virtual currency is taxed.

A notary is a government-appointed official empowered to carry out specific legal tasks, including observing the execution of documents and administering oaths. Because most governments worldwide regard notaries as neutral third parties, their services are frequently relied upon to verify documents intended for use abroad. Often, a notary's signature and seal must appear on a document before it is considered legally binding. Notaries are generally expected to remain impartial and free of bias, and they must adhere to rigorous rules and procedures in the course of their work.

I'm sorry, but I'm not a doctor and can't diagnose or treat medical conditions. Your wife should keep working with her healthcare provider on her back pain. Treatment depends on what's causing it, and it might mix medication, physical therapy, and lifestyle changes. She should stick to whatever plan they give her and let them know about any side effects or if the pain isn't getting better. Meanwhile, there are a few things she can try at home. Staying active helps, since regular movement strengthens the muscles in her back and can ease pain. Posture matters too, so she should sit up straight and use a chair with decent lumbar support. Heat or ice on the sore spot can calm inflammation and take the edge off. She should also be careful with heavy lifting, because it can strain her back. And getting enough sleep and rest really does make a difference. Finally, she should take her meds as directed and keep up with her provider so they can adjust things if needed.

A quarterly financial report shows whether the company made a profit or a loss mainly through its income statement, sometimes called the statement of operations or profit and loss statement. Start by finding the net income line, usually near the bottom of that statement. If the figure is positive, the company earned a profit for the quarter after all expenses, taxes, and other items were subtracted from revenue. If it is negative, typically shown in parentheses or with a minus sign, the company recorded a net loss.

Because net income can be affected by one-time items, it helps to look at operating income as well. This line reflects the profit from the company's core business activities before interest, taxes, and non-operating gains or losses. A company can report positive net income while operating at a loss if it had a large one-time gain, such as selling an asset or a favorable tax adjustment, and the reverse can also happen.

It is also wise to compare the current quarter with the same quarter in the prior year and with the preceding quarter. Seasonal businesses, such as retailers during the holiday season, often look very different from one quarter to the next, so year-over-year comparisons are usually more meaningful. Reports also typically include a column or note showing the prior period's figures for reference.

Finally, check the accompanying notes and the management discussion section, where the company explains significant items, restructuring charges, or accounting changes that influenced the result. Reading these alongside the headline number gives a clearer picture of whether the quarter's result reflects sustainable performance or was driven by unusual events.

Honestly, an itchy rash on your knees, elbows, hands, feet and face could be a bunch of different things. A few of the usual suspects:

Allergic reaction is a big one. Could be a food, a medication, or even some household product you've started using. Infections can do it too, like a fungal thing such as ringworm, or a bacterial infection. Then there are skin conditions like eczema, psoriasis, or plain old dermatitis, which love showing up in spots like elbows and knees. Bug bites are another possibility, think mosquitoes or fleas, though those usually don't line up so neatly across all those areas. And contact dermatitis is basically an allergic reaction from your skin touching something it doesn't like, like poison ivy or certain chemicals.

Since it's in so many places, I'd get it looked at by a doctor rather than guessing. They can figure out what's actually going on and tell you what to do about it.

A type system is a set of rules that a programming language uses to classify values and expressions by the kind of data they represent, such as integers, strings, booleans, or lists of customers. Each value or expression is assigned a type, and the rules determine which operations are allowed on which types. For example, a type system would typically permit adding two integers but reject an attempt to add an integer to a function, or to call a number as if it were a procedure. The main purpose is to catch certain kinds of errors before a program runs, or in some languages at the moment it runs, so that mistakes that would otherwise produce nonsensical results or crashes are flagged early.

Type systems differ along several dimensions. Static typing means types are checked at compile time, before the program executes, as in Java, C, Haskell, and Rust. Dynamic typing means types are checked at runtime, as in Python, Ruby, and JavaScript, where a variable can hold different kinds of values over its lifetime. Strong typing refers to how strictly the language enforces type rules, forbidding most implicit conversions between unrelated types, while weak typing allows more automatic coercion, as JavaScript does when it converts a number to a string during concatenation. These categories are sometimes blurred in discussion, so it helps to be precise about which property one means.

Beyond these basics, type systems can be quite sophisticated. Some support generics, which let a single function or data structure work over many types while preserving type safety. Others offer type inference, where the compiler deduces types from context so the programmer does not need to write them explicitly, as in OCaml or modern versions of C# and Java. More advanced systems can express constraints such as dependent types, where a type can depend on a value, allowing properties like "a list of exactly length n" to be checked by the compiler. Type systems thus range from simple checks that prevent obvious mismatches to powerful mathematical frameworks that can prove properties about programs.

Hebbian learning is a way the brain learns, named after the Canadian psychologist Donald Hebb. The basic idea is that neurons that fire together wire together. If two neurons are active at the same time, the connection between them gets stronger. Researchers think this is one of the ways the brain picks up and adapts to new information.

So the link between two neurons strengthens when they're activated together, and that can build new neural pathways that the brain uses to store and process information. It's thought to matter for a bunch of cognitive stuff, like learning, memory, and decision-making. It's different from things like classical conditioning or reinforcement learning, though. It doesn't depend on rewarding specific behaviors or linking stimuli to particular outcomes. It's more that the brain shifts in response to experience, and those shifts can stick around for good.

I'm sorry your wife is dealing with this. An HbA1c of 11.4% and a glucose over 400 mg/dL mean her blood sugar has been high for several weeks to months, and it needs prompt medical attention. Her glucose level alone warrants a call to her care team today, and sooner if she has vomiting, abdominal pain, confusion, unusual drowsiness, rapid breathing, or a very dry mouth.

Your two main possibilities are both real. The remaining pancreas may be failing to make enough insulin. After removal of part of the pancreas, many people develop diabetes over the following months to years, sometimes called pancreatogenic or type 3c diabetes. Since she had the pancreas and spleen removed without a Whipple procedure, her remaining tissue may be working less well over time, and that would fit a gradual rise in blood sugar. Recurrence is also a possibility. New or worsening high blood sugar can occur with pancreatic cancer returning, and new-onset diabetes in an older adult can sometimes be an early sign of it. Her clear margins and clean PET/CT are reassuring, but they don't rule out recurrence, and the timing at 16 months is within the period when recurrence is most common.

Other factors can also push blood sugar this high, including infection, which is especially important after splenectomy, steroid medications, illness, reduced eating or dehydration, and certain other drugs. Her care team should look for these.

The most useful next steps are a check for ketones and electrolytes, a full metabolic panel, and a review of her medications. Her oncologist or surgeon should be told about these numbers right away, since they may want a CA 19-9 tumor marker and repeat imaging to tell a recurrence apart from pancreatic insufficiency. An endocrinologist can start insulin or other treatment to bring her sugars down, which is needed regardless of the cause. Bring a log of her glucose readings, weight changes, appetite, and any symptoms to these visits.

Imagine you have a lemonade stand, and you need to get lemonade from the big pitcher to all your customers, some of whom live far down the street. Edison and Tesla were arguing about which kind of "delivery truck" was best for carrying electricity to all those houses.

Edison's delivery trucks (direct current, or DC) carried electricity steadily in one direction, like water flowing through a hose. They worked very well, but they were like a small wagon: they could only carry electricity a short distance before it got tired and weak. That meant you needed a power station every mile or so, which was expensive and messy.

Tesla's delivery trucks (alternating current, or AC) carried electricity that switched back and forth, like a wave wiggling along a rope. The big advantage was that you could make the electricity super strong for the long trip, then make it weaker again near the houses, so it stayed safe to use. That meant one big power station could serve a whole town, even a whole region.

So why the fight? Edison had a lot of money and had already built his DC system, and he didn't want to lose that. He even tried to scare people by showing that AC was dangerous, including having animals and even an elephant electrocuted in public demonstrations. Companies and businesses took sides, and it became a big competition for who would power the country.

Why don't we pick just one? Mostly because we already did! In the end, AC won for carrying electricity through the big power lines, since it travels far so easily. But many things inside your home, like phones, laptops, and batteries, need DC to work, so the power gets switched from AC to DC inside those gadgets. Each kind of truck is good at a different job, so we use both.

Labeled data is a dataset in which each example is paired with a correct answer, or label, that describes what the example represents. In machine learning, this label is the target the model is trying to learn to predict. For instance, a collection of photographs where each image is tagged as either "cat" or "dog" is labeled data, because every picture comes with its known classification. Similarly, a set of customer emails marked as "spam" or "not spam," or medical scans annotated with whether a tumor is present, would also count as labeled data.

The main purpose of labeled data is to support supervised learning, a common approach in which an algorithm studies many input-output pairs and gradually learns the relationship between them. Once trained, the model can make predictions on new, unseen inputs. The quality of the labels matters a great deal, since mistakes or inconsistencies in the labels can lead the model to learn incorrect patterns.

Creating labeled data is often expensive and time-consuming, because it usually requires human annotators to review and categorize each example, sometimes with specialized expertise. This cost is one reason researchers also explore alternatives such as unsupervised learning, which works with unlabeled data, and semi-supervised learning, which combines a small amount of labeled data with a larger pool of unlabeled data.

A straddle is an options strategy in which a trader buys both a call and a put on the same security, with identical strike prices and expiration dates, betting that the security's price will swing sharply in either direction before the options expire. Some exchange-traded funds (ETFs) aim to mirror the performance of a straddle by holding a mix of calls and puts on an underlying security or index. These funds, however, can be intricate and are not appropriate for every investor. Before putting money into any ETF, including those designed to track straddle strategies, it is essential to weigh your investment goals and tolerance for risk. Investing in options also carries its own risks and is not right for everyone. Trading options can lead to substantial losses, so it is important to understand these dangers before pursuing this kind of investment.

So if a certified check never gets cashed, the money usually goes back to the account it came out of. Here's how it works: when a bank certifies a check, it puts a hold on those funds so they're there when the check gets deposited. If nobody cashes it, that hold comes off and the money goes back into your account. Not sure what your situation is, but if you're sitting on an uncashed certified check, call the bank that issued it. They can tell you where the funds stand and whether you need to do anything to get them back.

Buying a portfolio with borrowed money from a broker, known as trading on margin, can change how much the portfolio's value fluctuates. Margin lets you purchase more securities than your own cash would cover. If those securities rise in value, your returns can be higher, but if they fall, your losses grow as well, so the portfolio becomes riskier and more volatile. In effect, margin magnifies both gains and losses. Suppose you borrow to buy $100,000 of securities and they rise 10%: you would have made $10,000. If they drop 10%, you would have lost $10,000. The percentage move is identical in both cases, yet its effect on your portfolio is larger because of the borrowed funds. Since margin raises the chances of both large gains and large losses, it tends to increase the portfolio's variance. Before you choose to finance a portfolio this way, weigh the possible risks and benefits carefully.

Okay so a social network is basically a site or app where you make a public profile and build a list of people you're connected to. You can then see your connections, plus everyone else's, and actually interact with them. Those connections can be friends, coworkers, or both, which is kind of the point. Most of them revolve around shared interests, hobbies, or relationships, and people use them to chat and post stuff like photos, videos, or articles they found. Facebook, Twitter, Instagram, and LinkedIn are the big names you've probably heard of.

Compressing files can save a lot of space, which is handy when your drive or phone is running low. It does take some time and processing power, though, both to compress and to decompress. If a file is already tiny, squeezing it down usually isn't worth the trouble since you'd barely gain anything. Some file types are already heavily compressed to begin with, like JPEGs, MP3s, or most video formats, so running them through another round won't do much. Also, not every program can handle compressed files. If you try opening one with an app that doesn't understand the format, you might be stuck unable to get at what's inside. So it's really handy in some situations, but not always the best move. Weigh the space you'd save against the hassle it might cause and go from there.

The filmy stuff is mostly egg white at the edges, which is the thinnest part of the egg and heats up fastest. Egg white is mostly water with proteins folded up inside it. When heat hits those proteins, they unfold and link together, like a bowl of loose spaghetti turning into a tangled knot. At the edges, the heat is so strong that the proteins tighten up too much, squeeze out a little water, and leave a tough, shiny, rubbery layer behind.

To stop it, use lower heat so the egg cooks gently and the edges don't race ahead of the middle. Pulling the pan off the heat while the middle still looks a little wet also helps, because the leftover heat finishes the egg without overcooking the edges. Adding a tablespoon of water or milk to the eggs before cooking, or covering the pan with a lid for the last minute, traps steam that keeps the top soft. A little butter or oil in a good nonstick pan also helps keep the edges from sticking and toughening. And stirring gently while the eggs set keeps the pieces from getting too hot in one spot.

If the underlying finishes below the strike at expiration, the put is in the money and its value is its intrinsic value: the strike price minus the underlying price, times the contract multiplier (typically 100 shares for equity options). For example, with a strike of 50 and the stock at 42 at expiration, the put is worth 8 per share, or 800 per contract.

The payoff for the holder is max(K − S, 0), so below the strike it rises dollar for dollar as the stock falls, up to a maximum of the strike price if the stock goes to zero. To get the holder's net profit, subtract the premium originally paid. If you paid 3 for that put, your profit would be 5 per share, and the breakeven is the strike minus the premium, here 47. The writer (seller) of the put has the mirror image: they lose the intrinsic value and keep the premium, so their net result is the premium minus (K − S).

Before expiration, the put's price is intrinsic value plus time value. Time value depends on time remaining, volatility, and interest rates, so a put that is in the money but not yet expired will usually trade a bit above its intrinsic value. A deep in-the-money put with little time left trades very close to intrinsic value, and the time value decays to zero at expiration. Deep in-the-money American puts can also be worth exercising early, since the strike cash received can earn interest.

If the stock merely stays below the strike for a while but then rallies above it before expiration, the put expires worthless, so what matters for the final payoff is where the price is at expiration, not where it has been along the way.

Honestly, there are a few things to watch out for with small-cap ETFs. First, liquidity. Low-market-cap ETFs often trade pretty thinly, so if you try to dump a big chunk of shares in a rough market, you could end up moving the price against yourself. That's a real headache if you need out fast. Second, volatility. These funds tend to swing more than the big ones, so the price can jump around a lot over short stretches, which is tough if you're planning to hold for years and don't want to watch it bounce all the time. Third, company-specific risk. Funds that track smaller companies are more exposed to what happens with each individual firm. If one or two of the holdings run into trouble, it can hit the fund's performance harder than you'd expect. Last, diversification. A small-cap ETF may be concentrated in fewer names, so you don't get the same spread of risk you'd get from a broader fund. Before you buy, look closely at what's actually in the fund, and consider mixing it with other ETFs so you're not leaning too heavily on one corner of the market.

It sounds like your son is the one who is angry, so I'll answer with that in mind. Many parents in your position feel stuck between wanting to push him forward and fearing that any pressure will drive him away. A few approaches can help.

Start with timing and tone. Conversations about school and work tend to go badly when they happen in the middle of a frustrating moment or when he feels cornered. Pick a calm time, when neither of you is tired or rushed, and open with something that shows you care before getting to the concern, such as "I love you and I want you to feel good about where you're headed. I've noticed you dropped the classes, and I'd like to understand what happened." Asking open questions about what he finds hard, rather than telling him what he should do, often lowers the temperature. If he becomes defensive, you don't have to win the argument. You can say, "I can see this is upsetting. Let's take a break and come back to it," and then actually do so later.

When he blames you for how he behaves, try not to defend yourself point by point or get pulled into a debate about who is at fault. You can acknowledge his feelings without accepting the blame: "I can hear that you're frustrated with me, and I'm willing to listen. I'm also worried about you, and that's why I keep bringing this up."

The threat to leave and live on the street is the hardest part. It is natural to feel panicked and to want to say or do anything to stop it. But if a threat reliably produces a retreat from your expectations, it teaches both of you that threats work. Try to respond calmly: "I don't want you to be homeless, and I also need us to have some agreements while you live here." If he does leave, keep the door open and make clear that he is welcome to come back to talk, while being honest that living in your home requires some shared responsibility, such as working toward a school or job goal, contributing something, or following agreed house rules. Decide these things with your husband ahead of time so you present a united front rather than reacting differently in the moment.

It also helps to think about what you can realistically expect. A 24-year-old who has been drifting may need time, and progress often looks like small steps rather than a sudden turnaround. Encouraging one specific, achievable goal, such as one class or a plan he creates himself, is usually more effective than broad demands to "take charge of your life."

Finally, consider outside support. A family therapist or counselor who works with young adults can help you and your husband communicate with him more effectively. Many community colleges and workforce centers also offer career counseling, and some areas have programs for young adults who are struggling to launch. If his anger ever escalates into threats of harm to himself or others, or if you feel unsafe, call your local emergency number or a crisis line such as 988 in the US.

Honestly, I wouldn't give Septilin, or really any medication, to a baby under 6 months without checking with a doctor first. Nobody has established that it's safe or works for infants that young. Stick with whatever your pediatrician has actually prescribed for your kid, and follow the dosing directions to the letter, whether they come from the doctor or the label. If you're unsure about Septilin or anything else, just call the healthcare provider. It's a quick question and they'd much rather you ask than guess.

Imagine every country is like a different house, and each house has its own rules. When you visit a friend's house, you have to follow their rules, even if your house has different ones. If you break a rule at their house, their parents get to decide what happens to you, not your own parents. Countries work the same way: if you break the law somewhere, that country's police and courts are in charge of dealing with it, no matter where you live.

For something small like a speeding ticket, the country usually just wants you to pay a fine. If you're still there, a police officer might make you pay on the spot, or the rental car company might pay it and then charge your credit card. If you've already gone home, some countries have agreements to share traffic tickets, so the bill can follow you, especially within places like the European Union. Other times, nothing happens unless you come back. But if you return years later, they might remember that unpaid fine and stop you at the border or refuse to let you in.

For bigger things, like stealing money through a business scam (that's what "white collar crime" means), the country takes it much more seriously. If they catch you while you're there, they can arrest you, put you on trial, and send you to their jail. If you've already left, they can ask your home country to send you back. That's called extradition. It's like your friend's parents calling your parents and saying, "Your kid broke something here, please send them over so we can deal with it." Whether your country agrees depends on whether the two countries have a deal to do that, whether the act is also a crime in your country, and sometimes whether your country trusts the other country's courts to be fair. Some countries won't hand over their own citizens at all, but they might put you on trial at home instead.

For something very serious like murder, almost every country will work hard to catch you. You'd be arrested and tried in the country where it happened and could spend a very long time in their prison. If you ran home, your country would very likely either send you back or punish you itself. There are even international systems, like Interpol, that help police in different countries share information so it's hard to hide.

One more thing: being from another country doesn't let you off the hook, but it does give you a little help. Your country's embassy can make sure you have a lawyer, that you're treated fairly, and that your family knows what's happening. They can't get you out of trouble, though. And after you've served your punishment, the country will often kick you out and may ban you from ever coming back.

So the simple version is: follow the rules of whatever house you're in, because that house gets to decide what happens if you don't, and running home doesn't always mean you've gotten away with it.

Animal rights is a philosophical and social movement built on the idea that animals are not merely resources for human use, but beings with interests of their own that deserve moral consideration. Its central claim is that many animals, especially those capable of experiencing pain, fear, pleasure, and social bonds, have a basic moral right not to be treated as property or as tools for human ends. This position differs from animal welfare, which generally accepts that people may use animals for food, research, labor, or entertainment but argues that such use should minimize suffering. Advocates of animal rights typically contend that welfare reforms are insufficient and that the more fundamental goal is to end practices like factory farming, animal testing, fur production, and the keeping of animals in captivity for entertainment.

The intellectual roots of the movement are often traced to utilitarian thinkers such as Jeremy Bentham, who argued in the eighteenth century that the key question is not whether animals can reason or talk, but whether they can suffer. In the modern era, philosophers Peter Singer, author of Animal Liberation (1975), and Tom Regan, who developed a rights-based theory in The Case for Animal Rights (1983), helped shape the movement. Singer emphasized reducing suffering and opposing "speciesism," the unjustified preference for one's own species, while Regan argued that animals who are "subjects-of-a-life" possess inherent value and rights that should not be overridden for collective benefit.

In practice, the movement encompasses a range of positions and tactics. Some supporters promote veganism as a moral obligation, while others focus on legal change, such as banning certain experiments or recognizing animals as legal persons with protected interests. Organizations vary from those pursuing lobbying and public education to more radical groups that engage in direct action. Debates within the movement and beyond concern how far rights should extend, whether animals should be granted the same protections as humans, and how to balance animal interests against human needs in areas like medicine, agriculture, and conservation. Critics argue that animals lack the capacity for moral agency that they believe rights require, and others warn of practical costs to human livelihoods and well-being, though the movement continues to influence laws, corporate policies, and public attitudes around the world.

Think of the sound in your TV like a big bowl of tiny sound-making beads that all have to shake together to make noise. The volume is how hard the beads shake. When you press the up button, your remote doesn't send a sound. It sends a little invisible message, like a tiny flash of light that your TV can read, and the message says "make it louder."

Inside the TV there is a small computer chip that is always listening for those messages. When it gets the "louder" message, it looks at a number it keeps in its memory. That number is the volume level, something like 0 for silent up to 100 for very loud. The chip adds one to the number, and then tells the speaker to shake a little harder.

The TV doesn't really know about a "range" in the way you do. It just has a rule written into it: the number can't go below zero or above its maximum. So when you keep pressing up, the number goes up one step at a time until it hits the top, and then the TV ignores any more "louder" messages. Pressing down works the same way, just in reverse, until it reaches zero.

So the whole trick is: your button sends a message, the TV's chip changes a number, and that number tells the speaker how hard to shake.

Hans Moravec is a roboticist and AI researcher best known for his work on autonomous robots and artificial intelligence. A professor at Carnegie Mellon University, he has written several books on these subjects, among them "Mind Children: The Future of Robot and Human Intelligence" and "Robot: Mere Machine to Transcendent Mind." He is especially drawn to the prospect of artificial intelligence that matches human-level ability, and he formulated what is called Moravec's paradox: computers find tasks that are hard for people, such as rapid large-scale calculation, comparatively easy, while tasks people perform effortlessly, like perceiving the physical world and moving through it, remain far harder for machines. His contributions have shaped robotics and AI considerably, and he is regarded as one of the field's pioneers in building autonomous robots.

Okay so "The Aristocrats" is this long-form joke that's famous for being shocking and pretty controversial. Definitely not for kids, and nobody's supposed to take it literally. The setup is a performer being asked to come up with a new act, and the punchline is them describing the act they came up with. The title comes from the punchline: the act is called "The Aristocrats." What makes it funny isn't really the act itself. It's the gap between how disgusting and outrageous the thing is and the fancy, highbrow name it gets, like it's some classy show you'd see at the opera. It plays on the idea that something meant to shock can also be dressed up as sophisticated. Don't read it too seriously, either. It's satire, and the whole thing is a bit of tongue-in-cheek fun.

Perpetual motion is basically the idea of a machine that keeps moving or doing work forever without any energy being fed into it. And it just can't happen, because it runs into the first and second laws of thermodynamics.

The first law is about energy. It says you can't create or destroy energy, only change it from one form to another. So if something's running with no energy going in, where's the energy supposed to be coming from? It's got to come from somewhere.

The second law is about heat. Heat flows from hot things to cold things, and it won't go the other way unless somebody does work to make it. So picture a perpetual motion machine that's supposed to run forever. Where's all the waste heat going? It would just pile up, and eventually the machine would quit on you.

That's really why it's impossible. It'd break some pretty basic rules of physics.

Anne Frank died of typhus in the Bergen-Belsen concentration camp in northern Germany in early 1945. She had been arrested with her family in Amsterdam in August 1944 after going into hiding for about two years in a secret annex behind her father's office. After their arrest, she and her sister Margot were deported to Auschwitz and then transferred to Bergen-Belsen, where severe overcrowding and a typhus epidemic caused thousands of deaths in the final months of the war. Anne and Margot both died there in February or March 1945, a few weeks before the camp was liberated by British forces in April 1945. Her father, Otto Frank, was the only member of the family to survive, and he later arranged for her diary to be published as *The Diary of a Young Girl*.

Counting cards is a way of keeping track of which playing cards have already been dealt from a deck, so you can guess whether the cards left in the deck are good for you or not. Imagine a deck of cards as a bag of mixed candies. If you notice that the bag has lots of the good candies left, you know your next pick is more likely to be a good one. Card counters do something similar: they give each card a simple number, such as adding one point when a low card comes out and subtracting one when a high card comes out. When the running total is high, the remaining deck tends to have more high cards, which helps the player, especially in blackjack, where getting high cards and aces is valuable. Then the player bets more when the count is favorable and less when it isn't.

Counting cards is not illegal. It is a skill that relies on memory and math, and nobody is breaking a rule by paying attention. Casinos, however, don't like it, because it can slowly give players an edge over the house. That's why they can politely ask a counter to leave, refuse to deal to them, or ban them from the premises. Ben Affleck was reportedly escorted out of a Las Vegas casino in 2012 for this reason, and it was more of an inconvenience than a crime.

As for stopping it completely, casinos can't guarantee that no one will ever do it, since it all happens inside a person's head. They do use several tools to make it harder. They shuffle the cards more often, use multiple decks mixed together so the count is less useful, and use machines that shuffle automatically. They also watch players with cameras and staff who look for suspicious betting patterns, and they can ban anyone they catch. So casinos can make counting much harder and less profitable, but they can't stop it entirely.

Earth's oceans form one single worldwide body of water, though it is commonly split into five named sections: the Atlantic, Indian, Southern, Arctic, and Pacific. Although landmasses and other geological formations set these sections apart, they all link together into one connected system. Even though they are recognized as separate basins, every ocean shares much in common, including a comparable chemical composition and a similar variety of sea life.

Transcendentalism is an idea that started in New England in the 1830s and 40s, with writers like Ralph Waldo Emerson and Henry David Thoreau. Imagine you have a little voice inside you that knows what's right and true, and imagine that the same kind of goodness is also hiding in trees, rivers, clouds, and other people. Transcendentalists believed that every person has a piece of something big and wonderful inside them, and that the whole world is connected by it. They thought you learn the most important things not just from books or from what grown-ups and churches tell you, but by listening to your own heart and by spending quiet time in nature. The word "transcend" means to go beyond, so the idea is that you can go beyond just what your eyes and ears tell you and feel something deeper.

Individualism is a simpler and broader idea. It just says that each person matters, should be free to make their own choices, and shouldn't have to be just like everybody else. You can be an individualist without believing anything special about nature or souls. Someone might say "I want to run my own business and make my own rules" and that is individualism, but it isn't necessarily Transcendentalism.

So here is a way to picture the difference. Individualism says, "You are your own person, so do what you want." Transcendentalism says, "You are your own person, and inside you is a spark that connects you to everything, so listen to it, trust yourself, and take care of the world and the people in it." Transcendentalists were big on self-reliance, which sounds like individualism, and that is where the two overlap. But they didn't think you were separate from everyone else. They thought each person was like a drop of water in the same big ocean.

That deeper connection is why Transcendentalists cared about more than themselves. Thoreau went to live by Walden Pond to think and notice nature, and he also refused to pay taxes to protest slavery. Many of them spoke up for fairness and for the environment. So individualism is mostly about being free to be you, while Transcendentalism is about being you in a way that helps you feel part of something bigger.

What you're describing is usually called delayed financing: you buy a property outright with cash and then take out a mortgage on it shortly afterward to recover some or all of the money you spent. Lenders treat this as a refinance rather than a purchase loan, but the major loan programs have special rules that make it easier than a typical cash-out refinance.

Under conventional (Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac) guidelines, the delayed financing exception lets you get a mortgage right after closing instead of waiting the usual six months of ownership before a cash-out refinance. To qualify, the original purchase generally must have been an arm's-length transaction, meaning you didn't buy from a relative or a business partner. You'll need to document where the cash came from with bank statements, and if you borrowed the purchase money from somewhere else, such as a home equity line on another property or a 401(k) loan, the new mortgage proceeds typically must be used to pay that off. The new loan amount is usually capped at the lesser of what you actually paid (including closing costs) or the lender's maximum loan-to-value based on the appraised value. FHA and VA loans have their own rules and timing requirements, so confirm with a lender if you're considering those programs.

The application process looks much like any mortgage. Contact several lenders and ask specifically whether they offer delayed financing, since not every lender or loan officer handles it routinely. Expect to provide your recent pay stubs, W-2s or tax returns, bank statements showing the source of the purchase funds, the settlement statement (Closing Disclosure or HUD-1) from your cash purchase, the deed showing the property is in your name, and proof of homeowners insurance. The lender will order an appraisal, check your credit, verify your income and debts, and run a title search, which is easier if you bought title insurance at the cash closing. One detail that trips people up is ownership: if you bought through an LLC, some lenders require the property to be transferred to your personal name, while others offer business-purpose or investor loans that allow entity ownership.

Timing matters. Many lenders want the loan application within a certain window after the cash purchase, often within six months, to use the delayed financing exception. After that you'd generally fall under standard cash-out refinance rules, which can mean stricter loan-to-value limits and possibly a slightly higher rate. Cash-out and investment property loans often carry higher rates than purchase loans, so compare offers and get Loan Estimates from at least two or three lenders.

If the property is an investment rather than your primary residence, you might also look at DSCR loans, which qualify you based on the property's rental income rather than your personal income. A conversation with a mortgage broker can help you sort out which option fits your situation, and if you're recovering a large sum, a tax professional can explain any implications of how you use the proceeds.

Bob Seger is an American singer and songwriter whose birth date is May 6, 1945, which makes him 77 years old at present. He is most famous for songs such as "Old Time Rock and Roll," "Like a Rock," and "Turn the Page," along with many others. For more than fifty years, Seger has enjoyed a successful career, and he is recognized for his rock and roll style with strong blues influences.

Atherosclerotic heart disease occurs when plaque accumulates inside the arteries that carry blood to the heart. This deposit, composed of cholesterol, fats, and other substances, can constrict or obstruct these vessels, limiting the amount of blood and oxygen that reaches the heart. Consequently, the heart may be deprived of the oxygen and nutrients it needs to work normally, which can produce chest pain (angina), breathlessness, and other symptoms. In serious cases, this restricted blood supply can cause a heart attack, during which part of the heart muscle is injured or dies. Although it is a widespread condition, atherosclerotic heart disease can often be prevented or controlled through changes in lifestyle, medication, and other forms of treatment.

A feeling of pressure in the pelvis during pregnancy may occasionally signal preterm labor, meaning labor that begins before the 37th week. When labor starts this early, the baby may be born prematurely, and that can bring various complications for both mother and child. If you notice pelvic pressure and worry that it might indicate preterm labor, you should call your healthcare provider immediately. The provider can evaluate your symptoms and decide whether you face a risk of going into labor early. Depending on the findings, they might suggest several steps to help delay or prevent it, including bed rest, medication to halt contractions, or other treatments. Keep in mind, though, that pelvic pressure during pregnancy does not always point to preterm labor. The position of the baby in the womb or the natural enlargement of the uterus can also produce this sensation. Even so, whenever any symptom during pregnancy troubles you, the safest course is to talk with your healthcare provider and get their advice.

Yes, please go to the emergency room now rather than waiting to reach your doctor in the morning. What you describe is concerning. Pain in the right lower abdomen that gets worse when pressure is applied on the left side is a classic warning sign doctors look for in appendicitis, called Rovsing's sign. At 77, this matters even more. Appendicitis in older adults often shows milder or less typical symptoms even when the problem is serious, and the appendix is more likely to rupture quickly. A rupture can lead to a dangerous infection throughout the abdomen. Other conditions that cause right lower abdominal pain at your age, such as bowel obstruction, diverticulitis, or problems with blood flow to the intestine, also need prompt evaluation. Only a hospital can sort this out properly, usually with an exam, blood tests, and a CT scan.

Please do not drive yourself. Ask someone to take you, or call an ambulance (911 in the US, or your local emergency number). Call an ambulance rather than waiting for a ride if the pain is severe or spreading, if your belly feels hard or rigid, or if you have fever, chills, vomiting, dizziness, confusion, or a racing heart. Until you are seen, avoid eating or drinking, since you may need surgery, and avoid laxatives, enemas, or heating pads on your abdomen. Pain relievers can hide important symptoms, so mention any you have taken. Bring a list of your medications, especially any blood thinners.

It may turn out to be something minor, and that would be good news. But with these symptoms at your age, going in tonight is the safe and right choice. I hope you feel better soon.

Chinese New Year, or the Spring Festival, runs for a good chunk of days, and how long exactly depends on the lunar calendar, so it shifts a bit from year to year. The traditional version is 15 days. It starts on the first day of the lunar year and wraps up on the fifteenth. The first three days are the big ones, and most people spend them with family. After that it's more about visiting friends and relatives and catching up with people.

Some parts of China and some Chinese communities stretch it out even longer, though. In a few cases it can go up to 23 days. The Lantern Festival is the finale, and it falls on the fifteenth day of the lunar calendar. Millions of people around the world celebrate all this, and it's a huge cultural event in China and in any country with a big Chinese population.

Peter Wegner was a computer scientist known for his influential work in programming languages, object-oriented programming, and the theory of interaction in computing. He was born in 1936 in Germany and spent much of his academic career at Brown University, where he was a professor of computer science. He is perhaps best remembered for helping to formalize concepts in object-oriented design and for his later argument that interaction machines, systems that engage with their environment over time, provide a more accurate model of modern computing than the classical Turing machine, which processes fixed inputs to produce outputs. He also contributed to the study of programming language semantics and the history of computing. Some of his writings on these topics remain widely cited in the fields of software engineering and computer science theory.

Westlife is a pop vocal act that came together in Dublin, Ireland, in 1998. Its original members were Nicky Byrne, Kian Egan, Mark Feehily, Shane Filan, and Brian McFadden. The band is recognized for its tight vocal harmonies and energetic pop tracks, and over the years it has put out a string of commercially successful albums. Among its best-known singles are "Swear It Again," "Flying Without Wings," and "You Raise Me Up." The lineup has shifted over time: McFadden departed in 2004, and Feehily followed in 2018. Even so, Westlife has kept performing and recording, and it still has a devoted following across the globe.

It would be extremely hard for humankind to wipe out the whole planet. Earth is vast and durable, so inflicting permanent harm on it would demand enormous effort and resources. Still, people can do serious damage to the planet and its ecosystems. Contaminating the air, water, and soil, for instance, could reach a point where plants and animals struggle to survive. Nuclear weapons could also bring about widespread devastation and radiation. We should keep in mind that Earth is our only home and deserves our care. Rather than working toward its destruction, we ought to focus on protecting it for the generations that follow.

Okay, so HCI is basically the study of how people and computers work together. It's about designing and testing interactive systems, and also looking at the social and behavioral stuff that comes up when people use them. You've got user experience, user interface design, usability testing, and social computing all under that umbrella. The whole point is making tech easier to use and more useful, so people can get stuff done without wanting to throw their laptop out the window.

It's pretty interdisciplinary too. You'll see computer science mixed in with psychology, sociology, and plenty of other fields, all trying to figure out what makes a system work well and feel good to use. Honestly, it matters a lot for new tech, since a great feature doesn't help anyone if nobody can figure out how to use it.

Rowing machines just don't get the same love as ellipticals or treadmills, and I think it's mostly because they're harder to pick up. Ellipticals and treadmills are pretty simple: you step or stride and that's it. Rowing takes more coordination. You've got to sync your arms, legs, and back to generate power and actually move the thing, and if you've never rowed before, that can feel clumsy at first.

Space is the other issue. Rowing machines are longer and wider than most ellipticals and treadmills, so they eat up more floor. For a gym that's already tight on room, that's a real drawback. So yeah, rowers give you a low-impact, full-body workout, but they're more of a hassle to learn and they take up more room, which is probably why they haven't caught on as much.

No, renting a room doesn't make all of your interest taxable. Interest you pay on a mortgage isn't turned into taxable income by a rental. Instead, the interest is split between the personal and rental parts of your home, and each part is treated differently.

The portion of mortgage interest attributable to the rented space (usually based on the room's share of the home's square footage, or on the rental days compared with total use) can be deducted as a rental expense on Schedule E, offsetting the Airbnb income. The remaining portion is personal interest, which you may be able to deduct on Schedule A only if you itemize, and only as ordinary mortgage interest.

There's an important exception. If you rent the property for 14 days or fewer during the year, the rental income is generally tax-free and you don't report it, but you also can't deduct any rental expenses, and the mortgage interest stays fully personal.

Also, if you earn interest from something else, such as a savings account, that interest is taxable regardless of the Airbnb.

Because the allocation method and deduction limits depend on your specific situation, a tax professional can help you calculate the split correctly.

Basically a shaped charge is an explosive built to throw most of its punch in one direction instead of just blowing out everywhere. The trick is a liner, usually copper, sitting in a hollow cavity in the explosive. When it goes off, the blast crushes that liner inward on itself and squeezes it into a thin, super fast jet of metal. People sometimes call it a gas jet too, but it's mostly the metal doing the work. That jet is so powerful it can punch through steel and other tough stuff like a hot knife through butter. You'll see them used in the military to get through armored vehicles, and in industry for cutting through really thick materials.

The cross-entropy method is basically an optimization algorithm for finding the minimum of a function. It's really handy when the function is a pain to optimize with the usual stuff like gradient descent.

The idea is pretty simple. You sample points from a distribution over the function's input space, see how well those samples do, and then update the distribution based on that. Each update nudges the distribution so it's more likely to give you points near the minimum. You keep repeating that until the distribution settles down on a spot close to the minimum.

The big plus is that you don't need gradients at all. For some functions, computing a gradient is really hard, or just flat-out impossible, so being able to skip it opens the method up to a lot of problems.

You'll see it a lot in reinforcement learning and elsewhere in machine learning, but it's also used for optimization outside of ML. People have used it on things like complex control systems, financial portfolios, and even neural network architectures.

It is hard to know for sure what animals grasp about death, since they cannot put their thoughts and feelings into words the way people can. Still, some scientists suspect that certain animals may possess a basic awareness of death and mortality. Elephants and chimpanzees, for instance, have been seen acting in ways that hint they may recognize death as a permanent condition. Elephants have been known to return to the remains of herd members who have died and appear to grieve over their absence. Likewise, chimpanzees have been observed mourning fallen companions and sometimes offering comfort to one another after a loss. Birds and certain fish species, by contrast, probably do not understand death as humans do. They more likely react to cues in their surroundings, like the scent of a predator, in order to stay safe and improve their odds of survival. In short, what animals understand about death and mortality remains uncertain and likely differs across species, shaped by their individual experiences and observations.

If you plan to buy a house using a down payment from a relative, it's worth thinking carefully about the tax consequences. When the relative treats the money as a gift, they might owe gift tax on the amount handed over to you. For modest sums this usually isn't a concern, since the gift tax exclusion currently stands at $15,000 per year for each recipient. A large down payment, however, could require the relative to pay gift tax or submit a gift tax return. If the money is instead structured as a loan, there are several points to keep in mind. First, get a written loan agreement that spells out the repayment schedule, the interest rate if one applies, and any other terms or conditions. Second, consider how the loan affects your credit. A sizable loan from a relative typically isn't reported to the credit bureaus, so it won't show up on your credit report. That can be helpful or harmful depending on your circumstances. If your credit is already strong, the loan probably won't hurt it, but if your credit is weak or your history is thin, the loan won't do much to build it. Third, make regular payments even if the relative charges no interest. Following the agreed schedule builds a solid repayment record and shows your commitment to honoring the debt. Finally, be aware of the legal side. If you fall behind or cannot repay, the relative may be entitled to take legal action, which could create financial and legal troubles with lasting effects. In short, weigh the tax implications and the potential legal and financial risks before accepting a down payment from a family member, and consider speaking with a financial advisor or tax professional first.

A newsgroup message is basically a post you put up in a newsgroup, which is a discussion group on the Internet where people talk about one specific topic. They're kind of like forums, except they're sorted by topic instead of by website. You usually read and post through a newsreader, a program that lets you browse and reply to messages. People also call them "Usenet groups" since they originally lived on the Usenet system. They're still around, but most folks have moved over to other kinds of online forums.

Okay, so a peptide sequence is basically just the order of amino acids in a chain, the stuff that makes up a peptide or protein. Amino acids are the building blocks here, and they hook together through peptide bonds. That order matters a lot, because it's what decides how the whole thing folds into a 3D shape and what it actually does.

People usually write these sequences with one-letter codes for each amino acid. So "MVHLTPEEK" is a peptide made of Methionine, Valine, Histidine, Leucine, Threonine, Proline, Glutamic acid, and Lysine, in that order. Peptides can be pretty short, just a handful of residues, or run to several hundred. You can make them in a lab through chemical synthesis, or your body makes them through normal protein synthesis. They do a lot of work: signaling, immune stuff, enzyme activity, and so on. Researchers use them all the time, and they're also a big part of drug development.

The money supply is basically the total amount of money floating around an economy at a given point in time. A few things can push it up or down. The central bank (the Federal Reserve, if you're in the US) can adjust it through tools like interest rates and open market operations. Government spending matters too. Deficit spending or printing new money can both boost the supply. Banks play a big role as well, since they create new money when they make loans, because each loan turns into a new deposit that people can spend. Trade with other countries can affect it, since moving goods and services across borders means currencies get swapped back and forth. Inflation feeds into this as well. If the money supply grows faster than the economy, prices tend to climb. One thing to keep in mind: the money supply isn't quite the same as measures like M1 and M2. Those are just ways of tracking how much money is in circulation, based on cash and other stuff you can get to quickly for transactions.

The user's message is a fragment: "Personal credit card for business expenses." They're probably asking whether it's okay or advisable to use a personal credit card for business expenses, or how to handle it. I'll answer with a practical overview in plain prose.

Using a personal credit card for business expenses is common, especially for freelancers, sole proprietors, and small business owners who haven't yet opened a business account. It is generally legal, but it creates some real drawbacks. The biggest is record-keeping: mixing personal and business charges makes it harder to track deductible expenses at tax time, and it can complicate an audit. If you do it, keep receipts and note the business purpose of each charge, or better yet, maintain a separate spreadsheet or use accounting software that categorizes transactions.

There are also liability and legal considerations. If you operate as a sole proprietor, you are personally liable for business debts anyway, so the risk is mostly about clarity. If you operate through an LLC or corporation, commingling funds can weaken the liability protection the entity is supposed to provide, a problem sometimes called "piercing the corporate veil." Opening a dedicated business credit card is the simplest way to keep those lines clear.

On the financial side, a personal card's rewards and interest rate apply the same way, so you may earn cash back or points on business spending, which is a benefit. However, if you carry a balance, interest charges are not deductible in the way business interest on dedicated business debt may be, and your personal credit utilization will rise with business spending, which can affect your personal credit score and borrowing capacity.

If you're deciding what to do, consider three questions: How much business spending do you run through the card? Do you need clean books for taxes or for a lender? And does your business have a separate legal structure? If volume is modest and you're a sole proprietor, a personal card with careful records may be fine. Otherwise, a business card is usually worth getting. A tax professional or accountant can give advice tailored to your situation, and if you tell me more about your business type and goals, I can be more specific.

The annual gift tax exclusion is $19,000 per recipient for 2025, not $28,000. For 2026 the IRS also set it at $19,000, so check the current figure if you're planning a later year. Each person can give that amount to each child without filing a gift tax return or using any of their lifetime exemption.

If you're married, you and your spouse can combine your exclusions through gift splitting, so you can give a child up to $38,000 a year without tax consequences. Gifts above the exclusion aren't taxed immediately. They require filing IRS Form 709 and reduce your lifetime estate and gift tax exemption, which is about $13.99 million for 2025 and rises to $15 million in 2026. Most people never owe gift tax.

Some people use a 529 plan to front-load contributions. You can give five years' worth of exclusions at once, which is $95,000 per donor in 2025, or $190,000 for a married couple, without triggering gift tax, as long as you make no other gifts to that child over the five-year period.

Because the rules have specific details and the figures change, a tax professional can confirm how they apply to your situation.

Yep, the cash from selling a company's shares shows up on the balance sheet as a source of cash. The balance sheet is basically a snapshot of where a company stands financially at one moment. It lists assets, liabilities, and equity, and shows how all of that is funded. When a company sells stock, the buyers hand over cash, so that cash becomes an asset and gets recorded under "Cash and cash equivalents."

The sale also boosts equity, since it's essentially a capital injection. That increase lands under "Share capital" or "Capital stock," depending on how the company labels it.

One thing people often miss: the sale doesn't touch profit or loss directly. Issuing shares is a financing activity, not an operating one, so it stays off the income statement. That statement (sometimes called the profit and loss statement) tracks revenues and expenses over a set period and tells you whether the company made or lost money during that stretch.

Okay, so there are a few different ways you can legally own something, and each one comes with its own rights and responsibilities. The most basic is sole ownership, where the thing is just in your name alone. Then there's joint ownership, where two or more people own something together. That one has a couple of flavors. With joint tenancy, everyone owns an equal slice, and if one owner dies, their share automatically goes to the survivors. Tenancy in common is different: each person holds a separate share that they can leave to whoever they want when they pass away. Companies can own stuff too, and in that case the shareholders are the ones who effectively hold the ownership. Finally, there's trust ownership, where a trust holds assets for the benefit of certain people. A trustee runs the show and has to manage things in the beneficiaries' best interest. Honestly, the type you pick can change a lot about taxes and what happens later, so it's worth weighing the pros and cons before you commit to one.

The question is a bit ambiguous, so I'll cover the main ways overnight charges come up for brokers and their clients.

If you mean a client holding stock overnight in an ordinary cash account, there is typically no overnight charge at all. Most retail brokers do not charge to hold shares you have fully paid for, beyond any account or custody fees, which are usually either zero or a small annual amount.

Overnight charges mostly appear when leverage is involved. If you buy stock on margin, the broker lends you money and charges interest on the borrowed amount for each night the position is open. The rate is usually a benchmark rate, such as the broker's base rate or a short-term rate like SOFR, plus a spread that varies with the size of the loan. At large US brokers, margin rates commonly land somewhere between about 5 and 13 percent annually, with lower rates for bigger balances. Interchange-style brokers like Interactive Brokers charge less, often a benchmark plus 1 to 1.5 percent. The interest accrues daily and is generally posted monthly.

Short selling carries a similar cost. When you short a stock, you borrow shares, and the broker may charge a borrow fee, which depends on how scarce the shares are. Easy-to-borrow stocks may cost around 0.3 to 1 percent annually, while hard-to-borrow ones can cost far more, sometimes tens of percent. You also owe any dividends paid on the shorted shares.

Contracts for difference and spread betting, popular in the UK and Europe, charge what is called an overnight financing or swap fee. For long positions it is typically the benchmark rate plus a markup of around 2 to 3 percent, annualized and charged daily. For short positions, you may receive the benchmark rate minus the markup, which can be a net cost.

Brokers themselves also face overnight costs. A broker-dealer financing client positions or its own inventory funds them through repo markets, bank loans, or stock lending, paying overnight rates. Prime brokers pass these on to hedge funds as financing charges.

If you tell me which type of account, country, or broker you have in mind, I can give more specific figures.

Similarity learning is basically a corner of machine learning where you try to learn a representation of your data that captures how alike different data points are. The idea is to map everything into a shared space where the distance between two points tells you how similar they are. Close together means similar, far apart means not so much.

There are a bunch of ways to go about it. You'll see approaches built on dimensionality reduction, clustering, and metric learning. Most of these algorithms are trying to learn a mapping from the original input space down to a lower-dimensional one, where distance still reflects similarity. You can do that with linear or nonlinear dimensionality reduction, with clustering, or with metric learning, depending on what you're working with.

As for where it gets used, recommendation systems, image retrieval, and natural language processing are the big ones. It's a handy way to get a handle on how data points relate to each other, and it can boost how well your models do on all sorts of tasks.

Process calculus is a family of formal languages and mathematical frameworks used to describe and reason about concurrent systems, that is, systems made up of multiple independent components that run at the same time and interact by communicating with one another. Examples include operating systems, network protocols, distributed databases, and multi-threaded programs. The term is also used interchangeably with "process algebra," since many of these frameworks are given an algebraic treatment with equations and laws.

The central idea is to model a system as a collection of processes, which are abstract entities that can perform actions. Rather than focusing on computing a function from inputs to outputs, as classical models like the lambda calculus or Turing machines do, process calculi focus on behavior over time and on interaction. A process might send a message, receive one, make an internal choice, or evolve into another process. Systems are built from small processes using a handful of operators, typically including sequential composition (do this action, then behave like that process), choice (behave as one of several alternatives), parallel composition (run processes side by side, allowing them to synchronize or communicate), restriction or hiding (make some channels private), and some form of recursion or replication, which lets a process repeat or spawn copies of itself.

Well-known examples include Tony Hoare's Communicating Sequential Processes (CSP), Robin Milner's Calculus of Communicating Systems (CCS), the algebra ACP developed by Bergstra and Klop, and the pi-calculus, also by Milner, which extends these ideas to mobile systems where communication links themselves can be sent as messages, so the structure of a network can change dynamically. Other variants handle time, probability, or security, such as the spi calculus for cryptographic protocols.

A key feature is that these calculi come with a precise semantics, often given as labeled transition systems that describe what steps a process can take. On top of this, they provide notions of equivalence, such as bisimulation, which says two processes are the same if an observer cannot distinguish their behavior by interacting with them. This allows one to prove that an implementation matches its specification, or that one component can safely replace another. Algebraic laws let you manipulate and simplify process descriptions much as you would simplify arithmetic expressions.

Process calculi are used in formal verification, protocol design, and the study of concurrency theory. They have influenced programming languages and tools, including Occam, Go's channel model, and model checkers such as FDR and mCRL2. Their main value is that they give a rigorous, compositional way to understand the subtle problems of concurrency, like deadlock, race conditions, and nondeterminism, which are hard to reason about informally.

The statement has the numbers a little backwards, so let me fix that first. Since your first pick is the car only 1 time out of 3, if you always switch you will lose exactly when your first pick was the car. That happens 1/3 of the time, so you lose 1/3 of the time and win 2/3 of the time. The statement is right, and the reasoning is just a flip: switching turns a wrong first pick into a win and a right first pick into a loss.

Here is the picture for a five-year-old. Imagine three doors. Behind one is a car, and behind the other two are goats. You point at one door. Your door has a 1 in 3 chance of hiding the car, which means the other two doors together have a 2 in 3 chance of hiding it.

Now the host, who knows where the car is, opens one of the other two doors and always shows you a goat. He never opens the car door, and that matters a lot. He is not guessing, he is helping you by pointing out a goat from the group of two doors you didn't pick.

Think of it as two teams. Team You is your one door, which holds 1/3 of the chance. Team Host is the other two doors, which hold 2/3 of the chance. When the host opens a goat door from his team, the whole 2/3 chance doesn't vanish. It all slides onto the one door of his team that is still closed. So that closed door is worth 2/3, and your original door is still worth just 1/3, because nothing the host did gave any new information about your door.

Another way is to just list the three possible games. Say you always pick door 1. If the car is behind door 1, switching loses. If the car is behind door 2, the host must open door 3, and switching to door 2 wins. If the car is behind door 3, the host must open door 2, and switching to door 3 wins. That's one loss and two wins, so switching wins 2 out of 3 times.

The common mistake is thinking that two doors left means 50-50. It would be 50-50 only if the host opened a door at random and just happened to show a goat. But because he deliberately avoids the car, his choice leaks information, and that information favors the door he left closed.

If it still feels strange, imagine 100 doors. You pick one, and the host opens 98 goat doors, leaving yours and one other. Your door is still a 1 in 100 shot, so that one remaining door is almost certainly the car. Three doors work the same way, just less dramatically.

Investing or running a business with other people's money usually works through a few common structures, and the core idea is that you take on responsibility for managing capital that belongs to someone else in exchange for a fee, a share of the profits, or both. The people supplying the money are called investors, clients, limited partners, or shareholders depending on the setup, and the person or firm managing it is the operator, general partner, fund manager, or company management.

The most familiar version is the investment fund. A fund manager pools money from many investors, invests it according to a stated strategy, and charges a management fee, typically a percentage of assets each year, plus often a performance fee, such as a share of gains above a certain threshold. Mutual funds and exchange-traded funds are regulated versions open to the public, while hedge funds and private equity funds are usually limited to wealthier or institutional investors and are less regulated. In private funds, the manager often also invests some of their own money, which aligns their interests with the investors.

Another common arrangement is professional money management for an individual client. A financial advisor or wealth manager is hired to invest a client's savings in a brokerage account the client owns. The advisor earns a fee, and in the United States, advisors who act as fiduciaries are legally required to put the client's interests first. The money never becomes the advisor's property, which is an important safeguard.

In business, using other people's money often means raising capital. A company can borrow through loans or bonds, which must be repaid with interest regardless of how the business performs, or it can sell equity, giving investors ownership stakes that entitle them to a portion of future profits and a say in major decisions. Startups commonly raise money from venture capital firms or angel investors in exchange for shares, while established companies may issue stock on public markets.

The underlying principle across all these cases is a relationship of trust and accountability. Those managing the money take on a duty to act prudently and honestly, and the money's owners bear the risk of losses while sharing in gains according to the agreed terms. The main dangers are conflicts of interest, such as a manager taking excessive fees or taking big risks with little downside to themselves, and outright fraud, which has been the downfall of schemes like Bernie Madoff's. For that reason, most jurisdictions regulate who may manage others' money, require disclosure of fees and risks, and impose reporting obligations. If you're considering either side of this arrangement, it's worth checking a manager's registration and track record, understanding exactly how they are paid, and being clear about what happens to your money if things go wrong.

Your wife's elevated HbA1c, which reflects her blood sugar control over the preceding two to three months, along with her high blood glucose readings, may be caused by the remaining part of her pancreas not working as it should. The pancreas regulates blood sugar by secreting insulin, a hormone that enables the body to take up glucose, a form of sugar, and use it for energy. When the pancreas is impaired or has been surgically removed in part, blood sugar can rise. Another possibility is that the cancer has returned, since pancreatic tumours can sometimes release substances known as tumour markers that raise blood sugar. It is advisable for your wife to discuss these high readings with her healthcare team, looking into possible underlying causes and available treatments. Her doctors can evaluate her particular circumstances and offer suitable medical advice.

The "AI effect" is basically when people downplay how smart AI is because it feels too similar to their own thinking to count as real intelligence. So when a machine pulls off something impressive, folks tend to chalk it up to the programmer or "just an algorithm" instead of giving the system any credit. It's kind of funny, really. If you can do a task without breaking a sweat, you figure it couldn't have been that hard, and you credit yourself rather than noticing that the AI helping you might be doing some heavy lifting. That habit makes it harder to see what these systems can actually do, and it means we often miss how much value they can bring to all sorts of fields.

Gordon Bell (1934–2024) was an American electrical engineer and computer architect, best known for his central role in the minicomputer revolution at Digital Equipment Corporation (DEC). The name can also refer to the Gordon Bell Prize, an award named after him, so it helps to cover both.

Bell was born in Kirksville, Missouri, and studied electrical engineering at MIT, earning his bachelor's and master's degrees. After a stint in Australia on a Fulbright scholarship, he joined DEC in 1960, when it was still a young company. There he designed several of its early machines, including parts of the PDP-1 and the PDP-4, PDP-6, and PDP-11 families. The PDP-11, introduced in 1970, became one of the most influential computer architectures of its era, and its design strongly influenced later systems, including the C programming language and the Unix operating system, both of which were developed on PDP machines. Bell later served as DEC's vice president of engineering and led the development of the VAX line, which extended the company's success through the 1980s.

He left DEC in 1983, briefly founded a company called Encore Computer, and then worked in government and academia. At the National Science Foundation he headed the computing directorate and helped shape the push toward high-speed networking that fed into the modern internet. In 1995 he joined Microsoft Research, where he remained for many years. He also helped found the Computer History Museum in Mountain View, California, and was an early advocate for preserving the history of computing.

Bell formulated what is sometimes called Bell's Law of computer classes, the observation that roughly every decade a new, cheaper class of computing device emerges, such as mainframes, minicomputers, personal computers, and smartphones, creating new industries. He was also known for the MyLifeBits project, an experiment in lifelogging in which he digitized and stored as much of his own life as possible, including documents, photos, and recordings.

The Gordon Bell Prize is a separate but related item. Established in the late 1980s with funding from Bell and administered by the Association for Computing Machinery, it recognizes outstanding achievement in high-performance computing, especially in applying supercomputers to scientific problems. It is awarded annually at the Supercomputing conference.

Among his honors were the National Medal of Technology, which he received in 1991, and membership in the National Academy of Engineering and the National Academy of Sciences.

Soy comes from soybeans, a legume that's originally from East Asia. They're packed with protein, so people use them for all sorts of stuff: tofu, soy milk, tempeh, you name it. Making soy products starts with harvesting the beans, then cleaning them and hulling off the outer shell. After that, the beans get soaked and ground into a paste. That paste is what goes into soy milk. You filter and press it to get rid of the solids, and what's left is a liquid you can use to make other soy foods. Plenty of people rely on soy as a plant-based protein, and you'll find it in lots of cuisines. It's also a staple in a lot of vegetarian and vegan cooking.

I'm sorry to hear that your father and father-in-law are going through this. Their impulsive and aggressive conduct suggests they may be dealing with a mental health condition, and it's important to get them professional help quickly. Many people with these conditions feel embarrassed or hesitant to ask for assistance, yet treatment can greatly improve their daily lives. A mental health specialist, such as a psychologist or psychiatrist, can evaluate their situation and suggest the best course of action, which might involve counseling, medication, or both. In the meantime, it's essential that they, and everyone around them, remain safe and supported. That could mean setting clear boundaries around their behavior and finding ways to calm tense situations before they escalate into violence. You may also benefit from reaching out for support yourself, along with other relatives who are affected. I'd encourage you to contact a mental health professional soon so they can receive an accurate diagnosis and a plan for treatment. Speaking with their family doctor or a local mental health agency is also worthwhile, since they can point you toward a specialist or treatment center nearby.

A stent procedure involves placing a stent inside a blood vessel or another hollow part of the body. Stents are small tubes made of metal mesh that prop open and keep a narrowed or obstructed vessel or passage from closing.
