Shrinking files can free up room on a computer or phone, which is especially useful when storage is tight. That said, compressing and decompressing files takes time and processing power. Compressing a file that is already small may not be worthwhile, since it would save very little space. Files are also not compressed automatically for another reason: some programs cannot work with compressed files. If a program does not recognize the compression format, you may be unable to read the contents. In short, compression is a handy tool in many cases, but it is not always the best choice. Weighing its advantages against its possible downsides is up to you.

Once inside the account, your funds can increase in value, and you have the flexibility to place them in various investment vehicles, including mutual funds, stocks, and bonds. When retirement arrives and you begin taking money out, the withdrawals are not taxed, since the taxes were already settled on the amounts you originally put in. There are several approaches you could weigh when purchasing stocks each month. One is dollar-cost averaging, where you put a set sum into a specific stock or portfolio at regular intervals no matter what the price is. This tends to soften the effects of market swings and lowers the chance of buying at a poor moment. Another is strategic rebalancing, which means periodically readjusting your holdings to keep them aligned with a target mix of assets. Suppose your goal is 60% stocks and 40% bonds, but a strong rally has pushed stocks higher; you could sell some equities and purchase bonds to restore that balance. A third approach is market timing, which attempts to forecast short-term price movements and trade accordingly. Because consistently predicting the market is so hard, this can be a risky path. In the end, the most suitable strategy depends on your investment objectives, tolerance for risk, and financial circumstances. If you're uncertain which method fits your situation, it's wise to conduct your own research and seek guidance from a financial advisor or other professional.

Keep in mind that donations may need to be declared as income on your tax return. Accepting them could also give the impression of a professional or business arrangement with the giver, which might carry legal and ethical consequences. If you are weighing this option, consulting a legal or financial expert is the safest course.

Imagine three doors. Behind one is a car, and behind the other two are goats. You pick a door, but before it's opened, the host, who knows where the car is, opens one of the other doors to show you a goat. Then he asks whether you want to stick with your door or switch to the other closed one.

The statement you're puzzled by works like this. If you always switch, there's only one way you can lose: your first pick was the car. If you started on the car and switch, you move away from it and get a goat. So the chance of losing by switching is exactly the chance that your first pick was the car, and since you picked one of three doors with no information, that chance is 1 in 3.

The other side of this is what makes switching so good. If your first pick was a goat, which happens 2 out of 3 times, something useful happens. There are two goats, and you're standing on one of them. The host has to open a door with a goat behind it, and he can't open yours, so he opens the other goat. The only door left is the car. Switching then wins every time. So whenever you started on a goat, switching wins, and you start on a goat 2 out of 3 times.

Here's an even simpler way to picture it. Suppose there were 100 doors. You pick one, and the host, who knows where the car is, opens 98 doors that all have goats, leaving your door and one other. Would you believe your random first pick was right, a 1 in 100 chance? Or would you suspect the host carefully avoided the car, and it's sitting behind that one door he left closed? Your first pick stays a 1 in 100 guess. The other door holds the remaining 99 in 100 chance.

So the key idea is that the host isn't opening doors randomly. He's giving you information. Your first guess stays as weak as it was, a 1 in 3 chance, and switching gets you everything else, a 2 in 3 chance. That's why switching loses only 1/3 of the time: it loses only when your very first lucky guess was right.

Yes, it can happen, but it's rare, and you should never count on it.

Your body is made of trillions of tiny building blocks called cells. Normally they follow the rules: they grow when they're supposed to, stop when they're supposed to, and die when they get old or broken. Cancer is when some cells break the rules and keep copying themselves without stopping, crowding out the healthy cells around them.

The good news is that your body already has a security team, your immune system. Its job is to find and destroy cells that are acting wrong, and it does this all the time. Scientists think your body probably catches and kills many would-be cancer cells over your lifetime before they ever become a problem. In that sense, lots of people "beat" cancer without ever knowing it was there.

Sometimes even a cancer big enough for doctors to find goes away on its own. This is called spontaneous remission or spontaneous regression. It's been seen most often in certain cancers, like neuroblastoma in babies, some skin cancers such as melanoma, and some kidney and blood cancers. Sometimes it seems to happen after a bad infection or fever revs up the immune system so it finally notices the cancer and attacks it. Other times nobody knows why.

There's also a second way to "survive" cancer without treatment: some cancers grow so slowly that they never cause harm. Many older men, for example, have small prostate cancers that would never have bothered them, and they die of something else entirely. That's why doctors sometimes recommend "watchful waiting" for certain slow cancers instead of treating right away.

The important catch is that these cases are the exception. For most cancers, especially aggressive ones, the rule-breaking cells grow faster than the body can stop them, and without treatment they spread and become deadly. Spontaneous remission is estimated to happen in only a tiny fraction of cases, something like one in many thousands. That's why surgery, chemotherapy, radiation, and newer treatments matter so much. In fact, one of the newest kinds of treatment, immunotherapy, works by helping the body's own security team do the job it sometimes manages naturally.

So the simple answer: your body can sometimes fight off cancer by itself, and it probably does so quietly more often than we realize, but once a real cancer is growing, betting on that alone is a very risky gamble.

Honestly it's pretty simple. Edge is Microsoft's own browser, so of course they want people using it. It's like Chrome, except Microsoft made it instead of Google. The more people who use it, the more data and feedback they get to make it better, and a more popular browser usually means more money coming in for the company too. Think of a toy maker. They want kids to actually buy the toy and play with it, right? Same idea here. Microsoft built something and wants you to use it and like it.

Target date funds are not unsafe in the sense of being fraudulent or structurally broken, but the post-quantitative-easing era has exposed real risks that many investors did not appreciate, so the answer is that they are riskier than their reputation suggests, though not necessarily unsafe for their intended purpose.

The main concern comes from bonds. Target date funds shift toward bonds as the target year approaches, on the theory that bonds are the stable part of a portfolio. During the long period of falling rates and central bank asset purchases, that held up well. Then in 2022, when inflation surged and rates rose sharply, stocks and bonds fell together. Broad bond indexes lost around 13 percent, and funds with 2025 targets, meant for people about to retire, often lost 15 percent or so. That surprised people who thought a near-retirement fund would be gentle. The assumption that bonds reliably offset stock losses depends on the inflation and rate environment, and QE-era experience had made it look more dependable than it is.

A second issue is that the funds vary a great deal. Two funds with the same target year can hold very different stock allocations, from roughly 30 percent to over 60 percent at the target date, and different glide paths continue after retirement. Investors often assume the date alone defines the risk, when it does not. Fees also differ widely, and some funds hold proprietary underlying products.

Third, the funds are one-size-fits-all. They assume age is the main driver of risk tolerance, ignoring your other savings, pension, home equity, spending needs, or health. Someone with a large pension might be too conservative in one, while someone relying solely on it might be exposed to sequence-of-returns risk, meaning a bad market just before or after retirement does outsized damage.

There are also some structural points. Large target date funds are now significant holders of many assets, and in taxable accounts they can generate capital gains distributions, though this is mostly a problem outside retirement accounts. Liquidity or run risk is generally modest, since they hold mainstream index funds or liquid securities.

On the positive side, they enforce diversification, automatic rebalancing, and disciplined behavior, which is often the biggest factor in investor outcomes. Studies suggest they have helped people avoid costly mistakes. Low-cost versions from large providers remain reasonable defaults.

Practical steps: check the actual stock and bond mix and the glide path, compare fees, consider whether you want a "to" or "through" retirement design, and think about whether short-term or inflation-protected bonds should be part of your holdings if you are close to retiring. If you have complex circumstances, a custom allocation may suit you better. This is general information, not personal advice.

Lots of science fiction does make humans look like the underdogs, and there are a few good reasons for it. The biggest one is storytelling. If humans are the audience's stand-in, a story works better when the characters we're rooting for are newcomers who have to learn how the bigger universe works. Being underestimated is a classic setup: the hero is dismissed, makes mistakes, and then proves everyone wrong. Think of a kid who is told to sit in the back of the class and then turns out to be the smartest one in the room.

Another reason is that writers like to show how strange and advanced aliens could be. If the aliens are far ahead, they look impressive, and humans look small by comparison. That makes the universe feel big and mysterious, which is a lot of the fun of sci-fi.

There's also a bit of humor in it. Many writers poke fun at human behavior, like our squabbling, our rush to make mistakes, and our funny habits, because it's a way to hold a mirror up to ourselves. Douglas Adams's Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy is a famous example, where Earth is literally a joke to the galaxy's other species.

Finally, there's an older tradition behind it. Early science fiction often used aliens as a way to comment on human society, and making humans look foolish from an outside view was a way to criticize our wars, pride, and arrogance. H.G. Wells's War of the Worlds is a good example, where the mighty British Empire is helpless against Martians.

But it's not universal. Plenty of stories show humans as clever, dangerous, or even the most feared species in the galaxy, like Star Trek's Federation or the Culture novels. So the pattern you've noticed is common, but it's a choice writers make, not a rule.

Degenerative disc disease has several possible remedies, both without surgery and through operative procedures. Conservative approaches might involve physical therapy, medications for pain, and other pain-control techniques like epidural steroid injections or radiofrequency ablation. Such measures can ease the discomfort that comes with the condition and often allow people to keep up their daily routines. When these conservative methods fail to bring relief, or when the disease is serious, a surgeon may suggest an operation. Options include spinal fusion, where the injured disc is taken out and the bones directly above and below it are joined, or laminectomy, where part of a vertebra is cut away to take pressure off the spinal cord or nerve roots. Because every case is different, it is essential to consult a healthcare provider to choose the most suitable approach. They can explain the available choices and help you decide on the course that best fits your needs and situation.

So a linear classifier basically sorts data points into classes (two or more) by drawing a straight-ish dividing line in the feature space. Each side of that line, or plane if you've got more dimensions, is a different class. The big assumption is that your data is linearly separable, meaning you can actually draw such a line or plane between the groups. If that's true, the decision boundary is just a linear function of your inputs. You'll see logistic regression, linear discriminant analysis, and SVMs mentioned most often as examples. They're quick to train and pretty easy to set up, and they hold up well on lots of problems. They're especially handy when you've got tons of features and high-dimensional data, since they cope with that efficiently. Where they fall down is when the real boundary is curved or messy. Then you'll probably need something more powerful and non-linear, like a neural network.

Food packaging serving sizes are set by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA), a government agency that works to make sure the food we eat is safe and accurately labeled. These sizes are intended to show people how much of a given food to eat in one sitting. They are generally based on what people typically consume at one time, though they don't always match what individuals actually eat, particularly when someone is very hungry or is trying to cut back and eat smaller portions. Serving sizes are only guidelines, and people can eat more or less depending on their own needs and tastes. It's also worth looking at the other details on the label, such as the calories and the amount of nutrients per serving, to make healthier choices.

Competitive learning is a learning rule for artificial neural networks where the network learns to classify inputs by tweaking the weights on its connections. The neurons basically compete with each other for the input. Each neuron gets input from the previous layer, and whichever one responds most strongly (the most activated one) wins and gets to pass its activation on to the next layer. Then the weights get adjusted so the network gets better at sorting the inputs. It's a pretty handy trick, and people often pair it with other learning algorithms to boost performance. Self-organizing maps are a common example. They take high-dimensional data and squash it onto a lower-dimensional output space while keeping the topological structure intact, so the network ends up clustering the data based on how things relate to each other.

Gordon Bell's a computer scientist and electrical engineer, mostly known for his work in computer architecture and digital hardware design. If you've heard the name, it's probably because of the VAX line of computers, which he was a big part of, and he's also tied to the SPEC benchmarks, the ones people use to measure how well computer systems perform. He's had a big hand in high-performance computing too, and he's picked up a lot of awards over the years, including the IEEE Computer Society's Computer Pioneer Award and the ACM SIGARCH Maurice Wilkes Award. These days he's a researcher at Microsoft Research, and he's a professor emeritus at Carnegie Mellon.

Burning Man is a big gathering that happens once a year in the middle of a dry, flat desert in Nevada. It lasts about a week, and it's named after the huge wooden statue that gets set on fire near the end. People from all over the world come to camp together in a temporary city that appears out of nothing and disappears again when the week is over. The whole place is built by the people who show up, and when everyone leaves, they're supposed to pack up all their trash so the desert is left clean.

Many people there spend their time making art, and it's everywhere: giant sculptures, metal dragons, glowing installations, and cars or bikes decorated to look like something out of a dream. Some people bring their own camps with things like free food, music, or hot tubs for anyone who wanders by. Others just walk around, look at the art, dance, and talk to strangers. There are music parties that go late into the night, and lots of people dress up in costumes, sometimes very colorful or very little. Hula hoops are a common sight, as are bicycles, art cars, and people riding around on strange vehicles.

The gathering runs on a few guiding ideas. One is gifting, which means giving things to others without expecting anything back. Another is radical self-expression, where people do whatever feels meaningful to them as long as they don't hurt anyone. There's also a rule about leaving no trace, so everything you bring in you take back out with you.

The desert can be harsh, so the most important thing is to prepare well. It's very hot during the day, very cold at night, and dust storms can roll in quickly. People bring plenty of water, sun protection, warm clothes, and goggles, and they plan carefully for their shelter and food. Tickets sell out fast and cost a fair amount, and there's a lot involved in getting ready, so it's wise to learn more and talk to people who have been before before you commit.

A long time ago, in 1692, there was a little village called Salem in a place that would later become part of the United States. The people living there were called Puritans. They were very, very serious about religion. They believed God was watching everything they did, and they also believed the Devil was real and was always trying to sneak in and trick people into being bad. To them, the Devil wasn't a story; he was as real as a neighbor down the road.

Now imagine a group of people who are already a little scared all the time. Then lots of extra scary things start happening at once. That's what Salem was like.

First, there was fighting nearby. The settlers had been in wars with Native American groups and with the French, and some families in Salem had run away from towns that had been attacked. People were frightened and sad, and many felt like God might be angry with them.

Second, the grown-ups in charge were in a mess. England, the faraway country that ruled them, had taken away their rules for running things, and for a while nobody was quite sure who was really in charge or whose laws counted. When people don't know who the boss is, they get nervous and grumpy.

Third, the people of Salem didn't get along with each other. Salem was split into two parts: the busy town by the water, where people were getting richer from trade, and the farm village a little farther away. The village families argued about land, about money, and especially about their minister, a man named Samuel Parris. Some families liked him and some really didn't, and they fought about whether to pay him. So neighbors were already mad at neighbors, like kids on a playground who have picked sides.

Then, in the winter of 1692, something strange happened in the minister's own house. His daughter Betty and his niece Abigail started acting very oddly. They screamed, twisted their bodies, hid under furniture, and said they felt like they were being pinched and poked. Nobody today knows for sure why. Maybe they were sick, maybe they were scared, maybe they were copying each other, or maybe they were pretending and then couldn't stop. But a doctor looked at them and said the only explanation he could think of was witchcraft.

Once someone said "witch," everyone's fears came rushing out at once. The girls were asked who was hurting them, and they named people. The first ones named were the kind of people the village already didn't like or trust: a slave woman from the minister's house named Tituba, a poor woman who begged for food, and an older woman who didn't go to church much. Then more girls started having fits and naming more people. Because people believed the Devil was real and sneaky, and because they were already angry at certain neighbors, it became very easy to believe the accusations.

The courts made things worse by allowing something called "spectral evidence." That meant if a girl said she saw someone's ghostly shape hurting her in a dream or vision, the judges counted that as proof. You can't really prove you weren't someone's ghost, so it was almost impossible to defend yourself. And oddly, people who said "yes, I'm a witch" were often spared, while people who told the truth and said "no, I'm not" could be hanged.

By the time it was over, about two hundred people had been accused, and twenty were killed. Later, many people, including some of the judges and one of the accusing girls, said they were sorry and that they had made a terrible mistake.

So the simple version is this: a group of very religious people who truly believed the Devil was nearby were already scared because of war, already confused because nobody was sure who was in charge, and already angry at their neighbors because of old fights. When some girls got mysteriously sick, all of that fear and anger found a target, and things spun out of control.

So the Egg McMuffin is basically a breakfast sandwich: a round slice of Canadian bacon, a freshly cracked egg, and a slice of American cheese, all piled on a toasted English muffin. Herb Peterson came up with it. He was running a McDonald's franchise in Santa Barbara, California, and it hit the menu in 1972.

Exchange-traded products (ETPs) charge ongoing fees, typically through a management fee or expense ratio that is deducted from the fund's assets over time. The market doesn't adjust for these fees in a single discrete step. Instead, the cost is built into the fund's economics and gradually reflected in its price relative to the assets it holds.

The main mechanism is the net asset value. Because the expense ratio is accrued daily and deducted from the fund's assets, the NAV per share falls slightly each day relative to what the underlying holdings would otherwise be worth. For physically backed products, such as a gold ETF, the sponsor may sell a small amount of the underlying asset each month to pay fees, so the holder's share of the metal shrinks over time. For synthetic products that use swaps or futures, fees are often embedded in the pricing of the derivative or the roll yield, which has a similar effect.

On the trading side, arbitrage between the ETP's market price and its NAV keeps the two closely aligned. Authorized participants can create or redeem shares in large blocks, so if the price drifts above or below NAV after accounting for fees, they can profit by trading the difference, which pushes the price back toward NAV. This means the fee is effectively priced in through the continuous erosion of NAV rather than through a visible jump in the share price.

Investors who want to see the fee's effect can compare the fund's total return against its underlying index or benchmark. The gap between the two, after adjusting for tracking differences and any securities lending income, approximates the cost of the fee over that period.

So if your career is kind of all over the place, it's worth picking a retirement setup that's flexible and lets you keep contributing even when you switch jobs or take a break. Here's what's out there.

401(k) plans are the usual employer option. You put part of your paycheck in before taxes, and lots of employers will match some of it, which is basically free money, so it's worth finding out what yours offers.

IRAs are accounts you open yourself, so they follow you from job to job. There are a few flavors: traditional IRAs, Roth IRAs, and SEP IRAs if you're self-employed. Each one has its own tax rules, so it's worth reading up on which fits you.

Pension plans are less common than they used to be, but some employers still offer them. They pay you a guaranteed income in retirement, which is nice if you can get into one.

Social Security is the government program that pays retirement, disability, and survivors' benefits. Don't count on it covering everything, though. For most people it won't be enough on its own to live comfortably, so you'll want other savings too.

Really, the best choice depends on your income, goals, and how much risk you're okay with. A financial advisor can help you sort through it if you're feeling stuck.

Kernel regression is a non-parametric statistical technique for estimating the relationship between a dependent variable and one or more independent variables without assuming a fixed functional form, such as a straight line or a polynomial. Instead of fitting a predetermined equation to the data, it estimates the value of the target at any given point by taking a weighted average of the observed outcomes, where the weights depend on how close each observation is to the point of interest. The basic intuition is that data points near the location you care about should tell you more about the outcome there than data points far away.

The "kernel" in the name refers to the weighting function that determines how much influence each observation has. A kernel is typically a smooth, symmetric function that peaks at zero distance and decreases as distance grows. Common choices include the Gaussian kernel, which uses the familiar bell-shaped curve, the Epanechnikov kernel, which has a parabolic shape and drops to zero beyond a certain range, and the uniform or box kernel, which gives equal weight to all points within a window and none outside it. In practice the specific kernel shape usually matters less than one might expect.

The most widely known form is the Nadaraya-Watson estimator, proposed independently by Èlizbar Nadaraya and Geoffrey Watson in 1964. For a new input x, it predicts the output as the sum over all training points of K((x minus x_i) divided by h) times y_i, divided by the sum over all training points of K((x minus x_i) divided by h). Here K is the kernel function, x_i and y_i are the observed inputs and outputs, and h is a parameter called the bandwidth. The denominator simply normalizes the weights so they add up to one, making the prediction a proper weighted average of the observed y values.

The bandwidth is the single most important choice in kernel regression because it controls how smooth the resulting curve is. A small bandwidth means only very close neighbors receive meaningful weight, so the estimate follows the data closely and can become wiggly and sensitive to noise, which corresponds to low bias but high variance. A large bandwidth spreads the weight over many points, producing a smoother curve that may wash out genuine features of the relationship, which corresponds to high bias but low variance. Analysts commonly choose the bandwidth through cross-validation, testing which value gives the best predictions on held-out data, or through rule-of-thumb formulas derived from statistical theory.

There are refinements of the basic idea. Local linear regression, and more generally local polynomial regression, fits a small weighted line or polynomial around each target point rather than just a weighted constant, which reduces bias near the edges of the data and in regions where the inputs are unevenly spread. Methods like LOESS and LOWESS, often used to draw smooth trend lines through scatter plots, are based on this local fitting principle.

Kernel regression has clear strengths. It is flexible enough to capture nonlinear patterns without requiring the analyst to guess the right equation in advance, it is conceptually simple, and it makes few assumptions about the underlying data. Its weaknesses are also notable. Prediction can be computationally expensive because every new estimate requires looking at all the training data, and it suffers from the curse of dimensionality, meaning that as the number of input variables grows, data points become sparse and the notion of a nearby neighbor loses usefulness, so performance degrades quickly in high-dimensional settings.

It is worth distinguishing kernel regression from kernel ridge regression and support vector machines, which also use the word kernel but in a different sense. In those methods the kernel is a similarity function that implicitly maps data into a higher-dimensional feature space so that linear techniques can model nonlinear relationships. The two ideas are related in spirit, since both rely on measuring similarity between points, but the classic smoothing-based kernel regression described here is primarily about local weighted averaging.

Sadomasochism, often abbreviated as S&M or BDSM when including related practices, is a set of sexual and erotic behaviors and interests that involve giving or receiving pleasure from power exchange, pain, restraint, or psychological dominance and submission. The term combines "sadism," named after the Marquis de Sade, and "masochism," named after Leopold von Sacher-Masoch, both of whom wrote about these themes in literature.

In practice, sadomasochism covers a wide range of activities. A "sadist" or dominant partner typically directs or controls the encounter, while a "masochist" or submissive partner consents to being controlled, and may enjoy sensations such as spanking, bondage, or impact play. Participants often use safewords to signal when something is too intense or should stop, and consent, negotiation, and clear boundaries are considered central to healthy practice.

It's worth distinguishing this from abuse. The defining features of consensual sadomasochism are informed, enthusiastic consent from all adults involved, agreed-upon limits, and the ability to withdraw at any time. Many people who practice it describe it as a consensual exploration of trust, role-play, and intense sensation.

Clinically, the term is also used in psychology. Sadomasochistic interests become a concern in diagnostic terms only when they cause distress or involve non-consenting people, which is how the distinction between a sexual preference and a disorder is typically drawn.

Fixed income ETF prices move around for a few main reasons. The big one is the value of the bonds the fund holds. A bond's value depends on the issuer's creditworthiness, its coupon rate, when it matures, and where interest rates are sitting. So if the issuer's finances get better or rates drop, the bonds usually gain value and the ETF price tends to go up. If the issuer gets shakier or rates climb, the bonds lose value and the ETF usually slides.

Supply and demand matter too. When more people want to buy the ETF than sell it, the price can climb, and when sellers outnumber buyers, it can fall. Broader market conditions feed into this as well. When things look good, investors tend to pile into fixed income funds and push prices up. When things look rough, they often pull back, and prices can drop as a result.

Turkey is a country that spans two continents. Most of its land lies in Western Asia, in the Anatolian peninsula, while a smaller portion sits in Southeastern Europe, in the region known as East Thrace. Its capital is Ankara, and its largest city is Istanbul.

Taking Lactare capsules while nursing is usually considered safe, since they are made with lactose and other ingredients believed to pose no problem for breastfeeding mothers or their babies. Even so, caution is wise with any medication, including those sold without a prescription. Before you begin something new, Lactare capsules included, it's a good idea to check with your healthcare provider to confirm that it suits both you and your baby. Little is known about how safe Lactare capsules are over the long term, because they were not designed for extended use. The usual advice is to take them briefly to help boost your milk supply instead of staying on them for a prolonged stretch. If you have worries about the safety of Lactare capsules or any other medicine during breastfeeding, raise them with your healthcare provider. They can help you consider the possible risks and benefits so you can make an informed choice that is best for you and your baby.

Honestly, you couldn't run across water at the speed of sound, and it's not even close. Sound moves about 343 meters per second, which works out to roughly 767 miles per hour. Most people top out somewhere around 6 or 7 meters per second when sprinting, so that's way off. And even if you could somehow hit that speed, you'd still sink. Water can't hold up a body the way solid ground does, so you'd just go under and end up soaked!

A boat or raft is a different story. Those sit on top of the water, so the water supports them, and with a powerful enough engine you could really move across the surface fast. So if speed on water is what you're after, grab a boat instead of trying to run for it.

In chess, stalemate describes a position where the player to move is not in check yet has no legal move available. It can arise when every one of that player's pieces is obstructed and unable to move, or when the player has nothing left on the board to move. A stalemate ends the game as a draw, so neither side is declared the winner. Picture yourself in a game with the move in your hands. Surveying the board, you find that each of your pieces is hemmed in by your opponent's pieces and has nowhere to go. Yet none of your opponent's pieces attacks your king, so you are not in check. Since every piece you own is blocked, you have no legal move, and the game is therefore a stalemate. Stalemate can also happen when a player runs out of pieces entirely, such as when all of their pawns have been captured and no other pieces remain. With nothing to move, that player again has no legal option. In short, stalemate is a standstill in which neither side can make a legal move, and the result is a draw.

A lot of religions picture God as male mostly because of the language they use. The words used for God tend to be masculine, and masculine terms have usually been the default for anything seen as powerful or superior. So it's more a cultural and linguistic habit than something baked into the religion itself. Plenty of people think God is beyond gender altogether and that human categories just don't fit. Others say God is male because God is the creator and sustainer of everything, and in a lot of cultures those have been seen as male roles.

Not every religion does this, though. Hinduism and Wicca, for example, see the divine as both male and female, or as having masculine and feminine qualities. Buddhism and Taoism don't really give God a gender at all.

These days, some theologians and scholars are pushing back on the traditional male image. They argue we should recognize how diverse and complicated the divine really is. Some also say that always picturing God as male can do harm, since it reinforces gender stereotypes and leaves out people who don't identify as male.

Formal verification is a technique that uses logical reasoning and mathematical proof to establish that a system, whether a software program or a hardware design, is correct. It confirms that a system adheres to its specifications and operates as expected, while also locating and removing faults or weaknesses that might lead to failure or unpredictable behavior. The process begins by defining a formal set of specifications or requirements for the system, from which a collection of logical assertions, known as proof obligations, is derived. These obligations are then checked using mathematical techniques and automated theorem provers, with the aim of showing that the system meets its specifications and behaves correctly. Formal verification finds application across computer science, engineering, and mathematics, and it can be used on many kinds of systems, such as pure software, pure hardware, or combined software-hardware systems. It is a strong means of safeguarding the reliability and security of complicated systems, and it is especially valuable for mission-critical applications where even a minor error could have grave consequences.

Pain that feels like your old gallbladder pain after 18 years is unusual, but it does happen, and it deserves a medical evaluation. Your gallbladder is gone, so the pain is coming from somewhere else, even if it feels the same. Pain in the upper right abdomen is often felt in the same place no matter which organ is involved, so the sensation alone doesn't tell you the cause.

Your liver is a reasonable suspect, since it sits right where the gallbladder used to be and shares its drainage system. Gallstones or sludge can form in the bile ducts even after the gallbladder is removed, and a stone passing through the bile duct can cause pain very similar to a gallbladder attack. Scarring or narrowing of the bile duct, or a problem with the muscle at its outlet (sphincter of Oddi dysfunction), can cause the same thing. Liver inflammation or fatty liver can also cause a dull, persistent ache in that area.

Other possibilities include the pancreas (pancreatitis can cause pain that radiates through to the back), peptic ulcers or severe reflux, a hernia at one of your old surgical port sites, the right kidney, the colon near the liver, the right lung or the lining around it, and muscle or rib pain from the abdominal wall. Each of these can mimic gallbladder pain.

You should see a doctor soon, and sooner rather than later if the pain is severe, lasts more than a few hours, or comes with fever, chills, yellowing of the skin or eyes, dark urine, pale stools, persistent nausea or vomiting, or pain that spreads to your back or shoulder. Those signs can point to a blocked bile duct or infection, which need prompt care. A basic workup usually includes blood tests for liver function and pancreatic enzymes (lipase), and often an abdominal ultrasound. If something still isn't clear, a specialist may order an MRI of the bile ducts or a procedure to look at them directly.

People who engage in cyberstalking rely on the internet and other digital tools to harass, frighten, and threaten the people they target. Their conduct can take many forms, such as sending abusive or menacing messages, circulating rumors or false claims about the victim, watching the victim's activity online, collecting personal details, or trying to harm the victim's reputation or personal connections. Some cyberstalkers also use technology to follow the victim's whereabouts or to break into the victim's personal accounts or devices. The consequences for victims can be serious, including emotional distress, a loss of privacy, and harm to both their personal and professional relationships. It is important to take measures to guard yourself against cyberstalking and to look for help if you are being targeted.

A traditional dim sum restaurant is built around small shared dishes served with tea, usually eaten from morning through early afternoon. The Cantonese term is yum cha, which literally means "drink tea," and tea is central to the experience. When you sit down, someone will ask what kind you want, such as jasmine, oolong, pu-erh, or chrysanthemum, and a pot is brought to the table. You pour for others before yourself, and if your pot runs empty you leave the lid slightly ajar to signal that you want a refill. A common courtesy is to tap two fingers on the table when someone pours for you, as a quiet thank you.

The food is served in one of a few ways. In the classic style, servers push carts around the dining room, each loaded with steamer baskets and plates. They call out or show what they have, and you point to what you want. Items might include shrimp dumplings (har gow), pork and shrimp shumai, barbecue pork buns (char siu bao), rice noodle rolls (cheung fun), turnip cake, steamed spare ribs, chicken feet, egg tarts, and sesame balls. The server places the dishes on your table and stamps a card with marks showing what you took. Some restaurants have moved away from carts and instead give you a paper menu with checkboxes. You mark what you want, hand it in, and the dishes come fresh from the kitchen. Others use tablets or QR codes, and a few do a hybrid with carts for some items and made-to-order for others.

Dishes are generally small, typically three or four pieces each, so the idea is to order many things and share them. Prices are tiered by size categories, such as small, medium, large, and special, and the cost depends on which category each dish falls into. The card or order sheet is tallied at the end, and you usually pay at the table or at the front counter. Tipping practices vary, and the tea often carries a small per-person charge.

Eating order is flexible, but people often start with lighter steamed items, move to fried or baked dishes, and finish with sweets like egg tart or mango pudding. Popular places can be crowded, especially on weekends, so you may need to take a number and wait. Going with a group is helpful, because more people means you can try more dishes. Soy sauce, chili oil, and sometimes mustard are on the table for dipping, and you can ask for extras.

Yes, it's accurate that receiving hospital care in the United States can carry a steep price tag, particularly when major treatment like surgery is required. Several factors contribute to this. For one, medical care in the U.S. typically costs more than in many other nations. Part of the reason lies in the expense of cutting-edge medical technology and the substantial pay earned by healthcare workers. Additionally, the American healthcare system is structured differently from those found elsewhere. Most Americans obtain health insurance either through their job or by purchasing a policy independently. Premiums can be quite high, especially for people with pre-existing conditions or those who are older. Without insurance, or when a policy leaves a large portion of treatment costs uncovered, patients may end up paying substantial sums themselves. For those already struggling financially, this burden can be especially hard to bear. Government programs like Medicaid and Medicare offer some help, providing coverage to low-income people and seniors respectively. Still, these programs don't reach everyone, and their benefits may fall short of covering the full expense of treatment.

Richard Nixon served as President of the United States for about five and a half years. He took office on January 20, 1969, after winning the 1968 election, and he was re-elected in 1972. He resigned on August 9, 1974, in the face of almost certain impeachment over the Watergate scandal, so his presidency lasted roughly 5 years and 6 months. Vice President Gerald Ford then became president.

So a pyramid scheme is basically an "investment" where everybody who's in has to recruit more people to join, and the money the new folks put in gets pushed up to the people above them. It's called a pyramid because that's the shape it ends up taking. One person at the top, then two under them, then four, and it just keeps widening.

Here's how it might go. The guy who starts it recruits two people and tells them they'll make a ton of money. Those two each go out and get a few more people, promising the same thing. Then each of those people recruits even more, and on and on. The pitch is that as long as more people keep piling in, the cash keeps flowing up to the top.

The problem is it can't last. Eventually you run out of new people to bring in, and the whole thing falls apart. The ones who get burned are the folks at the bottom, the last ones in, who lose everything they put in.

That's why pyramid schemes are illegal in a lot of countries. They're fraud, and they don't create any real value for the people investing. All they really do is let whoever's at the top get rich by tricking everyone else into handing over their money.

A reading of 133/88 is above the normal range. The standard guideline threshold for elevated blood pressure is a systolic under 120 and diastolic under 80, and 133/88 would be classified as stage 1 hypertension by the American Heart Association and ACC criteria if it holds up over repeated measurements. A single reading, though, tells you very little on its own. Blood pressure swings a lot with caffeine, stress, a full bladder, talking during the measurement, arm position, cuff size, or having just come from the gym or a flight of stairs. Many people get a higher number the first time they check it, and it drops on a calm recheck.

Your gym habit is a good sign in general, since regular exercise lowers blood pressure over time, so training alone is unlikely to be the cause of a persistently high reading. Creatine has been reported to raise blood pressure slightly in some studies, though the evidence is mixed and the effect is usually small. Protein supplements are not a typical cause. Pre-workout supplements containing stimulants like caffeine, or a lot of salt in your diet, can push numbers up too, so those are worth thinking about if you use them.

My suggestion is to recheck it a few times over a week or two. Sit quietly for five minutes first, rest your arm at heart level, and take two or three readings a minute or so apart in the morning and evening, then write them down. If the average stays around 130/85 or higher, that's worth raising with a doctor. Since you haven't had a checkup in a while, now is a good time to book one anyway. A basic visit usually includes a blood pressure check, a look at your blood sugar and cholesterol, and kidney function, which is also relevant if you take creatine. Bring your home readings with you.

If you ever get a reading well above 180/120, or you have chest pain, severe headache, shortness of breath, vision changes, or weakness or numbness, seek medical care promptly. Otherwise, there's no need to panic, but don't ignore it either.

Several things could explain this, and given your fall and your MS history, it's worth getting evaluated soon rather than waiting it out.

One possibility is an MS-related symptom. MS can cause brief, stereotyped, electric or stabbing pains called paroxysmal symptoms, which last seconds and recur many times a day, followed by burning or tingling (dysesthesia) in the limb. These come from demyelinated nerve pathways misfiring. The fact that yours is short, sudden, and then followed by burning fits this pattern fairly well. A new lesion in the spinal cord or brain, or a pseudo-relapse triggered by stress, infection, heat, or injury, could be behind it. A fall can also be a trigger, or the fall itself may have been caused by an MS-related problem with balance or leg weakness.

Another possibility is a peripheral nerve injury from the fall. The outer upper thigh is supplied by the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve, and irritation of it (meralgia paresthetica) causes burning, tingling, or sharp pain on the outer thigh. Bruising or swelling can compress or injure that nerve or others nearby. However, that typically stays in the thigh and wouldn't explain burning in the lower leg and foot, so a branch of the sciatic or peroneal nerve, or the nerve roots in the lower back, may also be involved.

A third possibility is a lumbar spine problem, such as a pinched nerve root (radiculopathy) or disc injury from the fall. Pain in the outer thigh with burning down to the lower leg and foot can follow a nerve root pattern, often L4 or L5. Spine injury is also relevant because a fall can cause a problem that mimics or overlaps with MS.

Other causes to keep in mind include a deep bruise or hematoma pressing on a nerve, a small stress fracture or other injury near the hip or femur that was missed, and a blood clot in the leg, which can follow a fall and cause pain, though that usually brings swelling, warmth, or constant pain rather than brief stabbing episodes.

I'd contact your neurologist or doctor within the next few days. They can examine you and may order an MRI of the spine and possibly the brain to look for new MS activity or a pinched nerve, and sometimes nerve conduction studies or an X-ray. If it's MS-related, there are medications that work well for these brief pains, such as carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, or gabapentin, and if it's a relapse, steroids may be considered.

Seek urgent care right away if you develop new weakness, numbness in the groin or saddle area, loss of bladder or bowel control, swelling, redness or warmth in the leg, trouble walking, or fever, or if you have another fall.

Wheezing and breathlessness that flare with colds and dust, and that now need Levolin three times a day, suggest that your airways are inflamed and not well controlled. Needing a reliever this often is usually a sign that a daily controller medicine is needed, so please arrange a review with your doctor or a respiratory specialist soon. Do not wait for your next routine visit. The usual treatment for this pattern is a regular low-dose inhaled corticosteroid, which reduces the underlying inflammation so that the rescue inhaler is needed less. Your doctor may also check your lung function with a spirometer or peak flow meter to confirm the diagnosis and track your progress. Keep using your inhaler as prescribed in the meantime, and do not stop or cut back any medicine on your own.

To reduce your triggers, focus on dust. Use dust-mite covers on your pillows and mattress, wash bedding weekly in hot water, and keep the bedroom as free of dust as possible by removing carpets, soft toys, and clutter where you can. Vacuum with a machine fitted with a HEPA filter, or ask someone else to do it, and wear a well-fitting mask while cleaning or sweeping. Keep windows closed on dusty or windy days, and avoid smoke, incense, strong fumes, and cold dry air where possible. If you have pets, keep them out of the bedroom. Good hand hygiene and an annual flu vaccine can lower the chance of colds triggering an attack. If you have a runny or blocked nose, treating allergic rhinitis with a nasal steroid spray often helps your chest as well, since the two conditions are closely linked.

Check that you are using your inhaler correctly. A spacer device improves delivery, and your pharmacist can show you the technique. Keep a diary of when your symptoms occur and how often you use the reliever, and bring it to your appointment.

Seek urgent medical help without delay if you become very short of breath at rest, struggle to speak in full sentences, have blue or grey lips, feel chest tightness that does not ease after your reliever, or if the inhaler gives less and less relief. These can be signs of a serious attack.

TMZ doesn't stand for anything official. The name is widely said to come from the address of the Los Angeles studio where the celebrity news site and TV show were first based, the Thousand Oaks... rather, it is commonly traced to Thousand Oaks Boulevard? The more accurate account is that it draws on the Pacific Time Zone idea, but the founders have never confirmed a single origin. In practice, TMZ is just the name of the brand, with no expansion.

Long ago, people didn't need family names because everyone in a small village knew everyone else. If you were called Tom, that was enough. But as villages grew into towns and cities, there were lots of Toms, so people started adding extra words to tell them apart. Someone might be called "Tom the baker" or "Tom who lives by the big oak tree." Over time, those extra words stuck around and got passed down to children.

Many family names started this way. A man who worked as a smith, which means he made metal tools, might be called John Smith, and his children became the Smiths. A person who lived near a hill might be called Hill, and a person whose father was named Robert might become Robertson, meaning "Robert's son." Some names came from where a family lived, some from the color of their hair, and some from the job they did.

People started using family names for practical reasons. They helped with taxes, because governments wanted to know who owed money. They helped with keeping track of who owned land, and who was related to whom. Over many generations, a name that started as a nickname became something a family kept forever, so that everyone in the family shared the same name and could be recognized as belonging together.

Scholars can reconstruct how long-dead and no-longer-spoken languages functioned by examining surviving manuscripts and other written materials from those eras. Such sources might include verse, narratives, legal codes, and various other documents composed in the original tongue. Through close analysis of these materials, researchers can uncover the language's grammatical structure and sentence patterns, along with its vocabulary and pronunciation. Familiarity with languages related to the ancient one also helps them interpret it more accurately. Occasionally, linguists may even locate communities that speak a descendant or close relative of the ancient language, offering further insight into how it was once used.

Imagine a company is like a lemonade stand, but a really big one with billions of customers. At first, the stand wants everyone to love its lemonade, so it gives you lots of choices: more sugar, less sugar, add ice, whatever you like. But as the stand grows, the people running it start caring about different things than just making you happy.

The first thing is that you are not always the customer the way you think you are. With YouTube, the real customers are advertisers, and you and your attention are what's being sold to them. So the company wants you to watch as long as possible. A "top viewed videos" list lets you find what you want and leave. A recommendation feed that guesses what you'll like keeps you scrolling. Features that help you leave or choose for yourself get buried or removed, because they don't make money.

The second thing is that Windows and iOS have their own goals. Microsoft wants people using its online services, like its account system, cloud storage, and search, and it collects data to improve ads and products. Giving you a lot of control over privacy and updates gets in the way of that. Updates are also forced partly for a good reason: unpatched computers get hacked, and a hacked computer makes the company look bad. So control gets traded away for "safety" and simplicity.

The third thing is that simple is cheaper. Every setting is something the company has to build, test, and fix forever. If only a few people use a feature, it's easier to cut it. Designers also like making things look the same on phones, tablets, and computers, so features that don't fit the new look get dropped. Also, the average user is a beginner who gets confused by many options, so the company designs for them, and power users like you lose out.

The fourth thing is that people inside companies get rewarded for launching something new, not for leaving something good alone. Nobody gets promoted for saying "we kept everything the same." So there's a constant push to change things, even when the old way worked fine. Some changes are also tests: the company tries them on millions of people and keeps whatever raises numbers like watch time or sign-ups, which isn't always what makes your experience better.

So it's not that the software is getting worse by accident. It's getting better at the company's goals, which sometimes aren't the same as yours. If you want more control, you can sometimes find it in alternatives: Linux or privacy-focused tools for computers, or browser add-ons and other apps for YouTube.

There are a few possible causes for swelling and a sore at the corner of the mouth. The most common one is angular cheilitis, which is inflammation at the mouth corners usually caused by a fungal or bacterial infection. Cold sores are another option. They're caused by the herpes simplex virus and can show up on or around the lips. Allergic reactions can also do it, often to something like toothpaste or lip balm. And low levels of certain nutrients, like iron or vitamin B2 (riboflavin), can lead to angular cheilitis too.

Honestly, the best move is to get a healthcare provider to take a look and figure out what's going on so you get the right treatment. Until then, a lip balm or cream can help soothe the area and keep it from drying out. If the swelling gets bad or the sore really hurts, reach out to whoever prescribed the penicillin, since they'll want to know.

I'm afraid I can't evaluate particular investments, since I'm a language model without access to live data or the internet. Giving tailored investment recommendations is also outside what I should do, as I lack the credentials for that. Real estate in particular carries complexity and risk, so weighing your personal finances and objectives carefully is essential before committing any money. Consulting a licensed financial advisor or a real estate professional is generally a wise step before making any decision.

It sounds like you could be dealing with asthma, a long-term lung condition that brings on coughing, wheezing, and trouble breathing. If you notice these signs, it's worth getting checked by a doctor, since asthma is manageable with the right care. Typically, treatment combines medication that reduces airway swelling and opens the passages with steps to steer clear of whatever sets off symptoms. Several medications are commonly prescribed. Inhaled corticosteroids lower inflammation in the airways and are generally used every day to head off symptoms. Long-acting bronchodilators relax the muscles surrounding the airways so breathing becomes easier, and they are usually taken once or twice daily for ongoing control. Short-acting bronchodilators provide fast relief and are used only when symptoms flare up. Finding the approach that suits you best is something to work out with your healthcare provider. Beyond medication, avoiding triggers matters a great deal. Tobacco smoke, air pollution, and certain chemicals can all make asthma worse. If your job exposes you to mold, talk with your employer and your doctor so you can decide on the right next steps. Finally, chest pain alongside asthma symptoms warrants prompt medical attention, because it can point to a more serious problem. A healthcare provider can identify the cause and recommend suitable treatment.

AIDS is what you get when HIV, the Human Immunodeficiency Virus, has done enough damage to the immune system. And no, mosquitoes don't spread HIV. They can't pass it from one person to another. HIV moves through certain bodily fluids like blood, semen, vaginal fluids, and breast milk, and it has to get directly into another person's body through those fluids to infect them. A mosquito bite just doesn't work that way. It won't carry the virus over. The main routes are sex, sharing needles or other injection gear, and mother to baby during pregnancy, birth, or breastfeeding. Safer sex, not sharing needles, and other basic precautions are what actually cut the risk.

Ronald Reagan remains a divisive figure largely because, as President of the United States, his convictions and conduct frequently clashed with the views of many liberals. Many conservatives regard him as a decisive leader whose choices strengthened the economy and bolstered national security, whereas a number of liberals reject his policies and contend that they produced harmful outcomes, especially for particular segments of the population. Reagan, for instance, enacted a series of measures that shrank the scale and reach of government, something many conservatives welcomed as a move toward limited government and greater personal liberty. Liberals countered that these measures harmed low-income families and disadvantaged communities by cutting the public resources and assistance available to them. His approach to foreign affairs also fueled the debate over his legacy. Certain conservatives argue that his determination to stand up to the Soviet Union and advance democracy abroad helped end the Cold War and created a safer world. Certain liberals, by contrast, argued that his policies were excessively aggressive and contributed to armed conflicts and human rights violations in various regions. In sum, Reagan's presidency brought major shifts and controversies, which together account for his reputation as a polarizing figure.

The Halting Problem is a question from computer science that asks whether someone could write a computer program able to examine any other program and determine whether it will run endlessly or eventually finish. Picture a toy robot that you can program to perform various tasks, with a small computer inside that carries out the instructions you supply. Suppose you wanted to create a program for this robot that could tell you, for any program you hand it, whether that program will loop forever or stop at some point. The Halting Problem is about whether such a program can exist. It cannot. This may sound surprising, but the reason is that some programs run forever and others stop, yet there is no general method to know in advance which group a given program belongs to without actually running it. Because of this, the Halting Problem matters greatly in computer science: it shows us the boundaries of what computers are capable of doing.

Yes, it can, and the way it happens is worth understanding because the underlying principle is sound while its misuse is common.

The principle is that money already spent and unrecoverable shouldn't influence a forward-looking decision. What matters is whether the additional cost from here on is justified by the additional benefit from here on. Applied honestly, this stops people from throwing good money after bad.

The distortion comes from how you draw the line around the decision. If a project has consumed $8 million and needs $2 million more to finish, a sponsor can say the only relevant question is whether $2 million buys more than $2 million in value. That framing can make the project look like an easy yes, even when the whole undertaking was a poor idea and will never earn back its total cost. Taken to the extreme, you can keep approving small completion increments on a doomed project because each one looks reasonable in isolation.

There are several related ways this gets abused. One is slicing a large investment into stages, so that each stage is evaluated only on its incremental economics once earlier stages are sunk. Another is mislabeling costs as sunk when they are not, for example calling a commitment sunk when it could actually be cancelled, resold, or redeployed, which hides the real opportunity cost. A third is ignoring sunk costs selectively: the sponsor discards past spending when it hurts the case but cites it when it helps ("we've already built the foundation, so we have momentum"). Finally, ignoring sunk costs can also hide a pattern of poor judgment, since a team that keeps overrunning budgets gets evaluated only on the latest increment, never on its track record.

Note that in a strictly rational sense, the incremental analysis is still correct for the decision at hand. The problem is that it answers a narrower question than the one stakeholders often care about, such as whether to have started, whether the organization's estimates can be trusted, or whether the capital would be better used elsewhere. A sound check is to compare the incremental option against every real alternative, including abandoning, selling, or redirecting the resources, and to review forecasts against the project's history of cost estimates. It also helps to have someone independent of the project's sponsors build the forward-looking case, since sponsors have an incentive to frame it favorably.

So the idea isn't wrong, but like any framing device it can be used to steer a conclusion, and the remedy is to scrutinize what is being counted as sunk and what alternatives are being left off the table.

Yeah, dreams can feel super real, and falling is probably one of the most common things people dream about. Basically your brain is taking in whatever your body and the room around you are doing while you sleep, stuff like touch, sound, movement, even a bit of light, and it weaves that into the dream. So with your recurring one, where you're tipping backwards in a chair, my guess is your brain is picking up on that sense of falling backwards and just running with it like it's actually happening. That's why it feels so vivid even though you're lying there fine.

It could also be tied to something going on in your life. If you're afraid of falling, or you took a bad fall at some point, your brain might be using that memory or feeling as a way to work through it while you sleep. Either way, falling dreams are really normal. Pretty much everybody gets them at some point, and it's just your brain chewing on sensory input and old experiences while you're out.

Enigma is a German music project that Michael Cretu started back in 1990. He's a Romanian-born musician and producer, and he's basically the brains behind the whole thing. The sound is mostly electronic, but it mixes in dance, ambient and new age stuff, and a lot of people call it "ethereal" or "mysterious." What really made them stand out was the Gregorian chants and other samples worked into the songs, pulled from all kinds of sources.

The name comes from the Enigma machine, the electromechanical rotor cipher device the German military used to encrypt messages during World War II. Cool nod, I think.

They've put out a bunch of albums over the years. The big ones people usually mention are MCMXC a.D. (1990), The Cross of Changes (1993), Le Roi est mort, vive le Roi! (1996), and The Fall of a Rebel Angel from 2016.

Gibraltar's a tiny peninsula on Spain's southern coast, and Britain's had it since 1713. So why would the UK hang on to it? Mostly for three reasons. The first is location: it sits right at the mouth of the Mediterranean, which makes it a handy spot for the military to park ships, planes, and troops. The second is the people. Most folks who live there see themselves as British and don't want to become Spanish, so handing it over would go over badly with a lot of them. The third is history. The UK and Spain have a long, messy relationship, and giving up Gibraltar could look like backing down, which nobody in London really wants to be seen doing. Put together, it's about keeping a foothold and not looking weak in the region.

Okay so there are a couple of ways to fake zero gravity inside a closed space. The most common one is a centrifuge. It's basically a machine that spins really fast, and the spinning pushes everything outward and creates a simulated gravity pull. If you're inside and it's spinning fast enough, you'd feel like you're floating in a low-gravity environment, kind of like being in orbit.

Another option is a zero-g airplane. These things fly a special curved path called a parabolic arc, climbing up and then diving down. While the plane is coming down over the top of the arc, everyone inside gets about twenty or thirty seconds of weightlessness. It feels pretty wild, honestly.

But here's the catch: neither of these actually gets rid of gravity. They just cancel it out or mimic it. Real gravity only goes away if you're somewhere with no nearby mass pulling on you, which basically means deep out in space, far from any planet or star.

Yep, there are plenty of places online to pull up public companies' financial statements. The big one in the US is EDGAR, the SEC's database. You can search it at https://www.sec.gov/edgar/searchedgar/companysearch.html and get pretty much any filing a public company has submitted, financial statements included. Another option is the investor relations page on the company's own website. Most publicly traded companies post their annual and quarterly reports there, so you don't have to dig far. If you can't find the link, just check the main site or search the company name plus "investor relations."

During the Second World War, women's place in society underwent a major transformation. With male soldiers deployed overseas, large numbers of women were asked to take up paid work to sustain the war effort. The result was a dramatic rise in the female labor force and a gradual change in how society viewed women's employment. In the United States, the share of women working climbed from about 27 percent in 1940 to almost 37 percent by 1945. Women moved into occupations that had long been reserved for men, including work in factories, on transit systems, and at construction sites. Others served in the armed forces in support roles that did not involve combat, such as nursing and clerical work. The conflict also gave rise to groups like the Women's Army Corps (WAC) and the Women Accepted for Volunteer Emergency Service (WAVES), which gave women a more formal military presence. The wartime shifts in women's roles left a lasting mark on society, as their greater presence in the workforce helped lay the groundwork for expanded equality and opportunity in the decades that followed.

The World of Coca-Cola is a museum and attraction in Atlanta, Georgia, dedicated to the story, promotion, and manufacturing of the Coca-Cola brand. It first welcomed visitors in 1990 and has since been renovated and enlarged on several occasions. Its displays trace the company's history, and it includes a 4D theater show, a tasting room where guests can try Coca-Cola beverages from around the globe, and a gift shop. Drawing more than two million people annually, it is one of Atlanta's most visited tourist spots.

The US subprime mortgage market collapsed beginning in 2007 and fully unfolded through 2008. Subprime loans, which were made to borrowers with weak credit or limited ability to document income, had grown rapidly in the early 2000s, fueled by low interest rates, lax lending standards, and a booming housing market that encouraged the belief that home prices would keep rising. Many of these loans carried adjustable rates or other features that became unaffordable once introductory terms expired, and as home prices peaked and began falling in 2006, borrowers found they could neither refinance nor sell their way out of trouble.

Delinquencies and foreclosures climbed through 2007, and the trouble spread quickly because subprime mortgages had been bundled into mortgage-backed securities and collateralized debt obligations held by banks, investment funds, and institutions worldwide. As the true value of these securities became uncertain, credit markets froze. Several major financial firms suffered heavy losses, and the crisis reached a turning point in 2008 with the near-collapse and rescue of Bear Stearns in March, the government takeover of Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac in September, and the bankruptcy of Lehman Brothers later that month. The resulting panic prompted a broad government response, including the Troubled Asset Relief Program, and the episode triggered the deepest recession since the Great Depression, with millions of Americans losing their homes and jobs.

The IEEE Computer Society is the largest of the technical societies within the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE), which is itself the world's largest professional organization dedicated to advancing technology. The Computer Society focuses specifically on computing, computer science, and computer engineering, and it serves researchers, educators, students, and practicing professionals in these fields. It is headquartered in Washington, D.C., with a major operations office in Los Alamitos, California, and it has tens of thousands of members worldwide.

The society traces its roots to 1946, when a group of computing pioneers formed a committee under the American Institute of Electrical Engineers, one of the predecessors of the IEEE. It grew alongside the computer industry itself and became a formal IEEE society as the field matured. Today it covers a wide range of topics, including software engineering, artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, computer architecture, networking, graphics, and data management.

One of its central activities is publishing. It produces a large portfolio of magazines and scholarly journals, such as Computer, IEEE Software, IEEE Security & Privacy, IEEE Computer Graphics and Applications, and the IEEE Transactions series on topics like software engineering, computers, and pattern analysis. Many of these are among the most cited publications in their areas. Its articles and conference papers are made available through the IEEE Computer Society Digital Library.

The society also sponsors or co-sponsors many conferences and workshops each year, including well-known events in areas such as computer vision, software engineering, and high-performance computing. These meetings are important venues for presenting new research and for professional networking.

Another major role is the development of standards and professional credentials. The society has contributed to standards work through the IEEE Standards Association and has been involved in defining bodies of knowledge, such as the Software Engineering Body of Knowledge (SWEBOK). It has also offered certifications, including the Certified Software Development Professional program, and it participates in curriculum guidelines and accreditation-related efforts for computing education.

Membership offers benefits such as access to publications, training materials, career resources, and local chapters where members meet and collaborate. The society also gives out awards recognizing achievements in computing, including the Computer Pioneer Award and the W. Wallace McDowell Award, and it names fellows and other honorees for significant contributions to the field.

As of my most recent information, Louisiana's two U.S. senators are Bill Cassidy, a Republican who has served since 2015, and John Kennedy, also a Republican, who has served since 2017. Since officeholders can change through elections, resignations, or appointments, it's a good idea to check the U.S. Senate website or Louisiana's official government pages to confirm the current senators.

Honestly, there are a few ways you could tackle high-interest student loans, and the right one depends on your situation. Refinancing is the first one most people think of. You can often get a lower rate by shopping around with banks, credit unions, or online lenders, and that can save you a lot in interest over the life of the loan. Consolidation is another route. If you've got several loans at different rates, rolling them into one loan at a lower rate can make things simpler and might drop your monthly payment too. If you have federal loans, don't overlook the repayment plans. Income-driven plans and extended plans can shrink your monthly bill based on your income and family size. Then there's deferment and forbearance, which can help if money is tight right now. Just know that interest may keep piling up while you pause, so it can cost you more down the road. Finally, some loan forgiveness programs cover part of your balance if you work in a particular field or for a certain employer and meet the requirements. Pick whatever fits your finances best. Talking to a financial advisor or a student loan counselor can also help you figure out your next move.

American English is the set of varieties of the English language spoken and written in the United States. It is the dominant form of English in North America and one of the most widely used English standards in the world, shaped by the country's history, immigration, and cultural influence.

Its origins go back to the colonial period, when English settlers arrived in the seventeenth century, bringing with them dialects from England, especially from the southern and eastern regions. Over time, contact with Dutch, Spanish, French, German, Native American languages, and later many immigrant languages introduced new vocabulary and influenced pronunciation. Once the United States became independent, there was a conscious effort among some writers and lexicographers, most notably Noah Webster, to establish a distinctly American identity in language. Webster's dictionaries and spelling reforms helped standardize forms such as "color" instead of "colour" and "center" instead of "centre."

Differences between American and British English appear in several areas. In spelling, American English often drops the British "u" in words like "honour" and changes "-re" endings to "-er." Vocabulary differs as well, with terms such as "elevator" for "lift," "apartment" for "flat," and "sidewalk" for "pavement." Pronunciation varies considerably too, particularly in features like the pronunciation of the letter "r" after vowels, which is generally pronounced in American English but often dropped in many British accents. Grammar and idiom also show differences, such as the American preference for "gotten" as the past participle of "get" and different patterns in the use of present perfect tense.

It is important to recognize that American English is not a single uniform dialect. It includes many regional varieties, such as Southern, New England, Midwestern, and African American Vernacular English, each with its own distinct features. Despite this diversity, a broadly shared standard exists and is used in media, education, government, and business, which is why American English is so widely recognized across the country and beyond.

Anne Frank died of typhus in Bergen-Belsen in 1945, just a few weeks before the camp was liberated. She was only 15. She and her family had spent two years hiding in a secret annex in Amsterdam to dodge the Nazis during World War II, but they were found and arrested in 1944. Anne and her sister Margot ended up in the camp, and both caught typhus there. Margot died first, and Anne followed a few days later. Anne's diary, written while she was in hiding, is still one of the most haunting firsthand accounts of the Holocaust and of what Jewish families went through during those years.

Yeah, pregnancy is possible if a condom breaks during sex. Unwanted 72 can help, but how well it works depends on timing. If she's worried, she should talk to a healthcare provider asap. They can look at her situation and tell her whether she needs more emergency contraception or a pregnancy test. In most countries, abortion is generally legal early on, but the rules and how easy it is to get one vary a lot from place to place, so check what applies where you live.
