Yes, a fall down the stairs can certainly cause further damage to a hip that already has a labral tear. A sudden impact or an awkward twisting movement as you fall can extend the existing tear, create a new tear, or irritate the surrounding joint lining so that it becomes inflamed and fills with fluid. It's also very common for pain to be fairly mild immediately after a fall and then become much worse over the following hours or overnight. Adrenaline masks pain at first, and inflammation, swelling and muscle spasm take time to build. So the pattern you're describing fits with a significant injury, though it doesn't by itself tell you exactly what has happened.

The labrum isn't the only thing that may have been hurt. A fall onto the hip can also cause deep bruising, muscle or tendon strains around the hip and groin, inflammation of the bursa on the outside of the hip, and occasionally a fracture of the hip, pelvis or the top of the thigh bone. Fractures are worth taking seriously even if you managed to walk afterwards, because some hip fractures are small or incomplete at first and still allow some movement. Because your mobility was already reduced and your pain is now horrendous rather than just somewhat worse, I'd strongly encourage you to get checked today rather than waiting to see if it settles.

You should go to an emergency department, or call emergency services if you can't get there safely, if you can't put weight on the leg, if the leg looks shorter or is turned outward, if there's significant swelling or bruising, if you hit your head during the fall, if you feel numbness or tingling in the leg, or if the pain is not controlled by your usual medication. If none of these apply, an urgent appointment with your GP or an urgent care or minor injuries clinic the same day is still sensible. They can examine the hip and decide whether you need an X-ray to rule out a fracture or an MRI to look at the labrum and soft tissues.

On the medication side, please be careful not to take extra tramadol beyond what you've been prescribed in an attempt to manage the new pain. Tramadol has a maximum daily limit, usually 400mg in total for most adults, and going over it raises the risk of seizures and other serious side effects. It also interacts with some antidepressants and other medicines. If your current dose isn't touching the pain, that's a reason to seek medical help, not to increase the dose yourself. In the meantime, rest the hip, use a cold pack wrapped in a cloth for 15 to 20 minutes at a time, and avoid the stairs where possible or have someone with you when you use them.

Once you've been assessed, it's also worth raising with your doctor or physiotherapist the fact that your hip problem has led to a fall. Things like a stair rail on both sides, a walking aid, or a review of your treatment plan for the labral tear could help reduce the chance of this happening again.

Yes, a reading of 230 deserves attention, and I'd encourage you to see a doctor about it rather than just watching it.

For a 58-year-old, the typical maximum heart rate is around 160 to 165 beats per minute (roughly 220 minus age, though individuals vary by 10 to 15 beats either way). A true rate of 230 is far above that, and it is higher than almost anyone's sinus rhythm can reach, which is the heart's normal rhythm driven by its natural pacemaker. So there are two main possibilities.

The first is that the reading is wrong. Wrist-based optical monitors are notorious for errors during exercise. Race walking involves a distinctive arm swing, and the sensor can lock onto your arm cadence or a harmonic of your step rate instead of your pulse. Sudden spikes lasting 10 to 20 seconds, followed by normal readings, are a classic signature of this. A chest strap, which measures electrical activity, is much more accurate, so if you are using a wrist device, try a chest strap for a few sessions.

The second possibility is that the reading is real, in which case it would likely be a rhythm disturbance such as supraventricular tachycardia, atrial fibrillation or flutter, or rarely a ventricular arrhythmia. These can start and stop abruptly, which fits what you describe. Many are not dangerous, and some are very treatable, but they should be identified, and a few can be serious. Being healthy and fit does not rule them out, and endurance athletes actually have a somewhat higher rate of atrial arrhythmias.

I'd suggest booking an appointment with your doctor, ideally a cardiologist or sports cardiologist, and mentioning the readings and your training. They will probably do an ECG, possibly an exercise stress test, and perhaps a wearable monitor or event recorder to capture an episode. Bring the data from your device.

Meanwhile, until you've been evaluated, it makes sense to ease off the hardest efforts. Stop and seek emergency care if you ever feel chest pain, faintness, severe shortness of breath, near-fainting, or if a racing heartbeat doesn't settle. Also notice whether you feel anything during the spikes, such as pounding, fluttering, or lightheadedness, since that helps distinguish a real rhythm problem from a device glitch.

Most likely this turns out to be benign or a measurement artifact, but with a number this high it's worth confirming.

Removing small gallbladder polyps is usually unnecessary, since they are typically noncancerous and produce no symptoms. Even so, they should be watched over time to confirm they are not enlarging or turning malignant, which is commonly accomplished with periodic imaging such as ultrasound or CT. Anyone hoping to start a family and worried that gallbladder polyps could affect a pregnancy should discuss their individual circumstances and possible risks with a physician. Generally, these polyps cause no complications during pregnancy, though seeking medical guidance is the wisest approach.

The effective interest rate from a bifurcated interest rate is the single rate that would produce the same economic result as the two-part rate structure, so it is the rate you use to measure the true cost (or yield) of the financing over its life. A bifurcated rate typically arises when a debt instrument carries a rate that is split into two components, such as a fixed portion and a variable or contingent portion, or when a stated rate applies to one period and a different rate applies afterward. Because the components behave differently, you cannot simply add them together or average them without distorting the answer. Instead, you compute the effective rate by finding the discount rate that equates the present value of all expected cash flows, under both components, to the amount borrowed or the carrying value at inception.

In practice, the calculation proceeds in a few steps. First, lay out the cash flow schedule for each period, including the fixed portion, the expected value of the variable portion (using the current index or a forward curve), and any principal repayments or fees. Second, solve for the internal rate of return of that combined stream, which is the rate r satisfying the equation that sets the initial net proceeds equal to the sum of the discounted cash flows. Third, if the rate changes at a known point, you may need to apply the IRR across the entire term rather than treating each segment separately, since the effective rate reflects the blended result. Where the variable component is uncertain, many accounting frameworks, such as those under IFRS 9 or US GAAP, require the effective rate to be re-estimated when expectations change, with the carrying amount adjusted accordingly.

As an illustration, suppose a loan of 1,000 carries 5 percent interest for the first two years and then switches to a rate equal to a benchmark plus 2 percent for the remaining three years, and the benchmark is expected to be 4 percent. You would project the annual payments under each phase, discount them back using a trial rate, and adjust the trial rate until the present value equals 1,000. The resulting rate would be the effective interest rate, which will fall somewhere between the two stated rates, weighted by their duration and timing.

If you tell me the specific structure of your instrument, such as whether the split is by time period or by fixed and floating components, and whether you need the figure for accounting or for a financial analysis, I can walk through the exact calculation with your numbers.

Generally, no. When a stock price rises on the open market, the company itself doesn't receive any money from that increase. Most trading happens between investors. If you buy a share from another shareholder, your payment goes to that seller, not to the company. The company only receives money when it sells new shares directly, such as in an initial public offering or a later offering of additional stock. That is the point where the share price translates into cash for the business.

That said, a higher stock price can benefit a company in indirect ways. A rising price increases the company's market value, which makes it easier and cheaper to raise money later by issuing new shares, since each share sells for more. It can also make it easier to borrow, because lenders may view a company with a strong valuation as less risky. Companies can use their stock as currency to acquire other businesses, and a higher price means they give up fewer shares to do so. Stock-based pay for employees and executives also becomes more valuable, which helps with hiring and retention.

There are some other effects worth knowing about. If a company pays dividends, a higher price doesn't automatically mean a bigger dividend, since that is set by the board. If the company buys back its own shares, a higher price actually makes that more expensive. Executives and early investors who hold shares or options may gain personally, but that is separate from the company's finances.

So the price itself is mostly a scoreboard of what investors think the company is worth, and it affects the company's opportunities more than its bank balance.

A monarch is an individual who occupies the top position in a monarchy, a system of government in which one person, most often a king or queen, has ultimate control over a nation. Typically, the role passes from one generation to the next within a royal family, and the monarch acts as the country's head of state, speaking for it in foreign affairs and performing ceremonial functions. Depending on the particular governmental arrangement, the monarch may hold some executive and lawmaking authority as well, though the extent differs from one system to another. Generally, the monarch receives counsel from a group of ministers or other officials, and their power may also be restricted by constitutional rules.

Phobos and Deimos were discovered by the American astronomer Asaph Hall in August 1877. He was working at the United States Naval Observatory in Washington, D.C., using its 26-inch refracting telescope, which was the largest refractor in the world at the time. Hall found Deimos first, on August 12, 1877, and then spotted Phobos a few days later, on August 18.

Hall was reportedly close to giving up the search when his wife, Angeline Stickney Hall, encouraged him to keep looking. The largest crater on Phobos was later named Stickney in her honor. The names Phobos and Deimos, meaning "fear" and "dread," come from Greek mythology, where they were the sons and companions of Ares, the Greek counterpart of Mars. The names were suggested by Henry Madan, a science master at Eton College in England.

Bloemfontein lies in South Africa's Free State province, where it serves as the provincial capital. Roughly 300 kilometers to the southwest of Johannesburg, it sits in the country's central region. It is also recognized as one of South Africa's three national capitals, alongside Cape Town and Pretoria.

For a child with urticaria, the usual oral prednisolone dose is 1 mg/kg/day, up to a maximum of about 40 to 60 mg a day. For your daughter at 19 kg, that works out to about 19 mg per day, which is commonly rounded to 20 mg once daily in the morning after food, or split into two doses of about 10 mg each. Some clinicians use a range of 0.5 to 2 mg/kg/day depending on severity, so the range for her would be roughly 10 to 38 mg a day, with 1 mg/kg being the typical choice.

For duration, short courses of 3 to 5 days are standard for acute urticaria. If you are continuing steroids after deflazacort, the total steroid exposure is what matters, so a further 3 to 5 days is usually reasonable. If the course stays under about 10 to 14 days in total, it can generally be stopped without tapering. If it runs longer, or the rash returns as soon as the steroid stops, a taper is usually used and the cause needs to be looked into.

For Omnacortil, the liquid comes as 5 mg/5 ml (1 mg/ml) and 15 mg/5 ml (3 mg/ml), and tablets come in 5, 10, 20 and 40 mg. So 19 mg would be about 19 ml of the 5 mg/5 ml syrup, or about 6.3 ml of the 15 mg/5 ml syrup. Check the strength on your bottle carefully, because mixing these up is a common cause of dosing errors.

A few points are worth raising with your doctor. Urticaria lasting 7 days that has not responded to an antihistamine or to deflazacort is unusual, so it is worth looking for a trigger such as an infection, a new medicine or a food. Deflazacort and prednisolone are the same class, so switching between them is unlikely to add benefit unless the first dose was too low. Deflazacort 4 days at an adequate dose should have helped, so confirm that dose was right. The antihistamine can also be optimized: a non-sedating one such as cetirizine or levocetirizine is often used regularly, and in resistant cases the dose can be increased under medical advice. Hydroxyzine at 3.5 ml twice daily may also be worth checking against the syrup strength (10 mg/5 ml), which gives about 7 mg per dose, roughly 0.37 mg/kg, a modest dose.

Please seek urgent care if she develops swelling of the lips, face or tongue, difficulty breathing, wheezing, repeated vomiting, abdominal pain, dizziness or drowsiness, or if the rash becomes painful, bruise-like or blistering, or lasts more than a day at the same spot with joint pain or fever. Since you have not yet had the rash assessed in person for a cause, it would be best to confirm the dose with her pediatrician or dermatologist before starting.

Equity just means ownership in the company, usually as stock options or actual shares. So if your employer's offering you equity, they're basically letting you own a piece of the business. A few things are worth thinking about before you say yes.

First, figure out what it's actually worth. That usually depends on what the company is valued at right now, and that number moves around with how the company's doing financially, what's happening in its industry, and the market in general.

Then look hard at the terms. Check the vesting schedule, which is how long you have to stay before you can exercise your options or sell your shares. Also check whether there are limits on selling or transferring the equity, and whether any other strings are attached.

Don't forget it's a gamble, too. The value can go up or down depending on how the company does, so think about the risks and the possible payoff, and whether that fits with the rest of your finances.

And think about where you see yourself long term. If you plan to stick around, equity can be a nice way to tie your interests to the company's. If you're not sure you'll stay, it might not be worth much to you.

Whatever you decide, take your time and weigh all of it before committing. If you're unsure about anything, talking to a financial advisor or a lawyer probably isn't a bad idea.

Brazil is not Spanish-speaking, so the answer comes down to Argentina and Uruguay, which are both Spanish-speaking nations and both have won the tournament. Argentina has three World Cup titles (1978, 1986, and 2022), while Uruguay has two (1930 and 1950). Spain, the only other Spanish-speaking country with a title, won its first in 2010, giving it one, which puts it behind Argentina and Uruguay. So Argentina leads the Spanish-speaking nations with three titles, followed by Uruguay with two and Spain with one.

Lower back pain together with tingling in the back and legs can stem from a wide range of sources. Frequent culprits include strained or sprained muscles, pinched or irritated nerves, and disorders affecting the bones or joints of the spine. Less common explanations include spinal stenosis, which is a narrowing of the spinal canal, as well as degenerative disc disease and spinal infections or tumors. The symptoms you describe might also be tied to a different health condition altogether, for example diabetes, multiple sclerosis, or a shortage of certain vitamins. Because of this, you should consult a doctor or another healthcare professional to get a correct diagnosis and suitable treatment. A provider will review your symptoms and medical background, and might suggest additional tests such as an MRI or CT scan to pinpoint what is behind the pain and tingling. Treatment options can include medication, physical therapy, and changes to daily habits, such as regular exercise and good posture. Occasionally, surgery may be required.

Okay, so David Lorge Parnas is a computer scientist and software engineer, mostly known for his work on modularity and information hiding. He's a professor emeritus at the University of Waterloo in Canada, but he's also taught at MIT and some other schools. He's picked up a bunch of awards over the years, including the ACM SIGSOFT Outstanding Research Award and the ACM SIGPLAN Robin Milner Young Researcher Award. He's a Fellow of both the ACM and the IEEE. His big claim to fame is the idea of modularity in software design: you break a huge system into smaller chunks that can be built and tested on their own. It makes code easier to maintain and reuse, which is why people still talk about it decades later.

"Errors and residuals" is a distinction that comes up in statistics and regression analysis, and the two terms describe closely related but different quantities.

An error is the difference between an observed value and the true, underlying value that a model is trying to capture. In a statistical model, we often assume that each observation is generated by some systematic relationship plus a random component, and that random component is the error term. Errors are theoretical: because the true relationship and the true population parameters are typically unknown, we cannot directly observe the errors. They represent the natural variability or noise in the data that the model cannot explain, and in many theoretical treatments they are assumed to have a mean of zero and a particular distribution, often a normal distribution.

A residual, by contrast, is the observable counterpart of an error. Once you fit a model to a sample of data, the residual for each data point is the difference between the actual observed value and the value predicted by the fitted model. Residuals are computed from the data and the estimated model, so they can always be calculated after fitting. Because they depend on estimated parameters rather than true ones, residuals are only estimates of the underlying errors. In a simple linear regression, for instance, the residual for observation i is the observed y-value minus the fitted y-value from the regression line.

The practical importance of residuals lies in diagnosis. Since errors cannot be seen, analysts examine residuals to check whether the model's assumptions hold. If residuals show a pattern, such as curvature, changing spread across the range of predictions, or extreme outliers, this suggests the model may be misspecified, that the relationship is not linear, or that the variance is not constant. Plots of residuals against fitted values, or quantile plots of residuals against a normal distribution, are standard tools for this purpose.

In short, errors are the true, unobservable deviations assumed by a model, while residuals are the observed, computed deviations from a fitted model, used to estimate and check those errors.

General Warren lost his life during the Battle of Bunker Hill on June 17, 1775, a clash of the American Revolutionary War. Records indicate that he was struck by gunfire and killed while directing his soldiers in the fighting. The engagement pitted British troops against colonial militiamen, and although the colonists were eventually compelled to withdraw, historians regard the battle as a pivotal moment in the conflict, since it showed the resolve and courage of the colonial fighters.

So Pluto got called a planet back when it was found in 1930, mostly because people figured it was a lot like the other planets in size and makeup. Then we learned more about it, and we started finding other stuff way out at the edge of the solar system, and it became pretty clear Pluto didn't really fit in.

The big thing is size. Earth and Mars are thousands of kilometers across, but Pluto's only about 2,377 km (1,475 miles) wide. It's tiny by comparison.

Its orbit is weird too. The other planets travel in paths that are pretty close to circles, but Pluto's is stretched out and tilted. That means it's often way farther from the Sun than the rest of them, and one trip around takes it a lot longer.

Between the small size and the odd orbit, scientists reclassified it as a dwarf planet in 2006. It still orbits the Sun, it just isn't counted as a full-on planet like the other eight.

Dry skin is super common, so don't stress about it. It happens to pretty much everyone at some point, whatever your age. Usually it comes down to the weather or your surroundings, your genes, or sometimes a medical condition.

A few things that've helped a lot of people: moisturize regularly, and pick one that suits your skin type. The trick is to put it on right after you get out of the shower or bath, while your skin's still a little damp, since that locks the moisture in. Also, go easy on the hot water. It feels great, but it strips out your skin's natural oils, so lukewarm showers are better. Same goes for soap. Harsh ones do the same stripping thing, so switch to a gentle, pH-balanced cleanser instead.

Protect your skin too. Throw on gloves when you're doing the dishes or cleaning, and wear sunscreen of SPF 30 or higher whenever you're outside, because the sun does a number on it. Food matters a bit as well. Plenty of fruits, veggies, and healthy fats can help your skin look and feel better.

If your skin stays dry no matter what you try, go see a dermatologist. There could be an underlying issue that needs actual treatment.

There are tons of brokerages that offer streaming quotes, and the prices vary a lot, so it pays to shop around. A few things I'd look at when you're picking one.

Cost is the obvious one. How much are they charging for streaming quotes? And are there extra fees for certain features or data feeds? Those can sneak up on you.

Then there's data quality. What's the latency and accuracy like? It also matters whether the data comes straight from the exchanges or gets pulled together from a bunch of different sources.

Platform features count too. Is the interface easy to use for pulling up and analyzing quotes? Does it come with tools or indicators that actually help you make better trading decisions?

Last, customer service. Do they respond when you've got a question or something breaks? And do they offer support in multiple languages and time zones, if that matters to you?

As for who's known for streaming quotes, Interactive Brokers, E*TRADE, TD Ameritrade, and Charles Schwab are the usual names. I'd compare features and pricing across a few of them and see which one fits what you need.

Yeah, the yellow stuff with holes in your fingernails could be tied to your psoriatic arthritis. It's an inflammatory kind of arthritis, and it often messes with the nails. You might see pitting, thickening, or yellowing, and the nails can also grow slower or get brittle and snap easily. Worth mentioning to your doctor, though, since nail changes can sometimes point to something else going on. They can figure out what's causing it and what to do. Sometimes you'd need to treat the arthritis itself, and other times just treating the nails is enough.

Sir James Lighthill was a British scientist and mathematician whose work greatly advanced fluid dynamics and applied mathematics. Born in London in 1924, he studied mathematics and physics at Cambridge University, receiving his bachelor's degree in 1945 and his Ph.D. in 1950. His research centered on the mathematical analysis of fluid flow, and he played an important part in developing computational methods for studying how fluids behave. He also explored a range of other subjects, such as the theory of sound waves, the stability of aircraft, and the movement of ocean waves. Beyond his research, Lighthill was a well-respected teacher and mentor, and over the course of his career he occupied several prestigious academic posts. He was a Fellow of the Royal Society, a Fellow of the Royal Academy of Engineering, and a member of the Order of the British Empire. His contributions to science and engineering earned him many awards and honors, among them the Royal Society's Hughes Medal, the Royal Academy of Engineering's James Watt Medal, and the Gold Medal of the Institute of Mathematics and its Applications. He died in 1998, aged 73.

Within the criminal justice system, an arraignment is the formal stage at which a defendant hears the criminal charge or charges brought against them. During this proceeding, the defendant is told what they are accused of and is asked to answer with a plea of guilty, not guilty, or no contest. This step matters because it gives the defendant a formal opportunity to reply to the allegations and sets in motion the preparations for trial, should one be needed. The arraignment also provides a chance to ask for legal representation and to request bail or other release conditions.

Soy isoflavones are generally considered low-risk at food-level amounts, and there's no well-known dangerous interaction between them and metformin. The evidence that they help people with PCOS conceive is weak, though. A few small studies have reported improvements in some hormone levels or cycle regularity, but none has shown a clear increase in pregnancy rates, and the supplements aren't a proven fertility treatment. Concentrated isoflavone supplements also act weakly like estrogen, and their long-term effects during conception and early pregnancy haven't been well studied. So they're probably not harmful for most people, but your doctor should know you're taking them, and you should check the dose on the label rather than stacking several products.

Because you've been trying for five years, I'd put more energy into a fuller fertility evaluation than into supplements. Metformin takes a few months to show its full effect on ovulation, so three months in is early to judge it. Still, five years is a long time, and it's reasonable to ask your doctor whether you should see a reproductive endocrinologist. A workup usually includes confirming whether and when you ovulate, checking hormone levels, looking at your fallopian tubes and uterus, and having your partner's semen analysis done. PCOS medications that are often more effective for ovulation than metformin alone, such as letrozole or clomiphene, can be discussed at that point. Fertility treatment for PCOS is very effective for many people, and you don't have to wait longer to start looking into it.

Intractability is a concept in computational complexity theory describing problems for which no efficient algorithm is known, or for which one provably cannot exist in practice. An "efficient" algorithm is usually taken to be one whose running time grows polynomially with the size of the input, so that doubling the input size increases the work by at most a fixed power. A problem is called intractable when the best known algorithms require time that grows exponentially or faster, so that even moderately sized instances become infeasible on any realistic computer.

The distinction matters because computer scientists separate problems into tractable and intractable classes based on how their difficulty scales. A problem with an exponential-time algorithm may still be solvable for small inputs, but as the input grows, the running time quickly becomes astronomical. For example, an algorithm that takes 2^n steps on an input of size n is fine for n = 20 but hopeless for n = 300, since the count of steps exceeds the number of atoms in the observable universe.

Some intractable problems are proven to be intractable in a strong sense. Certain problems provably require exponential time, meaning no polynomial-time algorithm exists, regardless of how clever future researchers are. Such results are rare and often rely on the time hierarchy theorem or similar arguments. Far more common are problems that are believed to be intractable but for which no proof exists. The most famous example is the P versus NP question: many important problems, such as the traveling salesman problem and Boolean satisfiability, are NP-complete, meaning that if any of them had a polynomial-time solution, all of them would. Since decades of effort have failed to find such a solution, most researchers believe these problems are intractable, though this remains unproven.

In practice, intractability shapes how people work with hard problems. Instead of seeking exact optimal solutions, practitioners often use approximation algorithms, heuristics, randomized methods, or solve special cases that have useful structure. Cryptography also depends on intractability: the security of many encryption schemes relies on the assumption that certain problems, such as factoring large integers, cannot be solved efficiently.

The learning rate is one of the most important hyperparameters in training machine learning models, especially neural networks. It is a number, typically small, that controls how much the model's parameters (such as weights and biases) are adjusted in response to the error it makes on training data. Training usually works by computing the gradient of a loss function, which indicates the direction in which the parameters should move to reduce the error, and then taking a step in that direction. The learning rate determines the size of that step. If the step is multiplied by a learning rate of 0.01, for example, each update moves the parameters by one hundredth of the gradient's value.

The choice of learning rate involves a trade-off. A value that is too large can cause the training process to overshoot the optimal parameter values, leading to oscillations or even divergence, where the loss grows instead of shrinking. A value that is too small makes learning very slow, requiring many more iterations to converge, and it may leave the model stuck in a poor solution or a region where progress is extremely gradual. Because of this sensitivity, practitioners often experiment with several values, use learning rate schedules that decrease the rate over time, or employ adaptive optimizers such as Adam, which adjust the effective step size for each parameter automatically.

Capacitors are basically little batteries that store electricity. Inside, there are two metal plates, and when you push electricity into the thing, it piles up on those plates. Picture it like this: pump in a lot of charge and it's like a big mountain of electricity sitting between the plates. Pump in less and you get a smaller mountain. Now imagine stretching a rubber sheet between the two plates. That sheet pushes the electricity mountains closer together, which makes it harder for the charge to jump across. That's the basic idea. The sheet is called a dielectric, and it's what lets the capacitor hold charge. When you want that stored electricity back, you hook the capacitor up to a circuit and the charge flows out, kind of like water draining from a bucket. You'll find capacitors in tons of electronics, smoothing out the flow of power and holding energy for when it's needed.

Sesame seeds come from the sesame plant, Sesamum indicum, a flowering annual that grows about three to six feet tall. The plant produces small tubular flowers, typically white or pale pink, and after these flowers are pollinated they develop into elongated seed pods called capsules. Each capsule holds dozens of tiny seeds arranged in rows. When the pods mature and dry, they naturally split open, which is thought to be the origin of the famous phrase "open sesame" from the tale of Ali Baba.

The plant is one of the oldest oilseed crops known to humanity, with evidence of cultivation going back more than 3,000 years, likely originating in the Indian subcontinent or Africa, where many wild relatives of sesame still grow. It thrives in hot climates and tolerates drought well, which is part of why it became so widespread in tropical and subtropical regions.

Today the largest producers include Sudan, Myanmar, Tanzania, India, Nigeria, and China, with significant production elsewhere in Africa and Asia. Because the pods tend to shatter and scatter their seeds when ripe, much of the harvesting is still done by hand in many regions, with workers cutting the stalks, drying them upright in bundles, and then shaking or beating out the seeds. Newer varieties bred to resist shattering have made mechanical harvesting more practical in places like the United States.

The seeds come in several colors, including white, tan, brown, and black, depending on the variety. They are eaten whole, toasted, ground into pastes like tahini, or pressed to make sesame oil, which is prized in many cuisines for its rich, nutty flavor.

Selling a call against a stock you already own is called a covered call. Here's how it works in practice.

When you sell a call option, you collect a premium up front, paid to you by a buyer. In return, you give that buyer the right to buy your shares from you at a set price (the strike price) on or before an expiration date. Each option contract covers 100 shares, so if you own 100 shares, you can sell one call.

Your outcome depends on where the stock trades at expiration:

If the stock stays below the strike price, the option expires worthless. You keep the premium and your shares, and you can sell another call later.

If the stock rises above the strike, the buyer will likely exercise, and you must sell your shares at the strike price. You keep the premium plus any gain up to the strike, but you miss out on any further upside.

If the stock falls, the premium you collected cushions the loss a little, but you still hold shares that have dropped in value. The premium is not protection against a large decline.

Since you describe a stock that has been doing poorly, a few points matter. The premium is usually larger when the market expects more volatility or a bigger move, so the price you receive partly reflects that expectation. Your real concern is whether you'd be happy selling the shares at the strike if the stock recovers. Pick a strike you'd accept as a sale price, not just one that pays the most premium. Also, if you believe the stock may rise, selling a call caps your gain, which works against that view. Selling a call makes the most sense when you expect the stock to stay flat or drift modestly, or when you're willing to sell at the strike.

Finally, check your brokerage's options approval level, since covered calls usually require basic approval, and consider the tax consequences of having your shares sold, especially if you've held them at a gain or loss.

Computer Go is the field of artificial intelligence concerned with creating programs that play the board game Go. Go is an ancient game, originating in China more than two millennia ago, in which two players alternately place black and white stones on a grid, usually 19 by 19 lines, with the aim of surrounding more territory than their opponent. Although its rules are simple, the game has enormous strategic depth, and it has long been considered one of the hardest challenges for machines.

The difficulty comes mainly from the size of the game's search space. On a 19 by 19 board there are far more legal positions than there are atoms in the observable universe, and the number of possible moves at each turn is much larger than in chess. Traditional chess programs relied on brute-force search combined with hand-crafted evaluation functions, an approach that works poorly in Go because it is hard to write down rules that judge a position's strength and because the branching factor is so high. Human players often rely on intuition and pattern recognition about global influence, which were difficult to capture in code.

For decades, the strongest Go programs played only at an amateur level. Progress accelerated dramatically in the 2010s when researchers combined Monte Carlo tree search with deep neural networks. In 2016, DeepMind's AlphaGo defeated the professional champion Lee Sedol, a milestone that many experts had expected to be decades away. Later systems, such as AlphaGo Zero and AlphaZero, learned to play through self-play without human game data and surpassed earlier versions. Open-source programs like Leela Zero and KataGo have since become widely used tools for both research and study.

Computer Go matters beyond the game itself because it serves as a testbed for general techniques in AI, including search, reinforcement learning, and the evaluation of positions under uncertainty. Its history also offers a notable example of how a problem thought to require human intuition can yield to machine learning approaches.

Ezekiel was a Hebrew prophet and priest who lived during the sixth century BCE and is traditionally regarded as the author of the Book of Ezekiel, one of the major prophetic books of the Hebrew Bible and the Christian Old Testament. He was the son of a priest named Buzi and was among the Judeans deported to Babylon in 597 BCE, when King Nebuchadnezzar took King Jehoiachin and many of Jerusalem's leading citizens into exile. Ezekiel lived among the exiles near the Chebar canal in Babylonia, and it was there, around 593 BCE, that he received his call to prophesy.

His ministry falls into two broad phases. Before the destruction of Jerusalem in 586 BCE, his message was largely one of judgment, warning that the city and its temple would fall because of the people's idolatry, injustice, and unfaithfulness to God. After the city's fall, his tone shifted toward hope and restoration, promising that God would gather the scattered people, renew their hearts, and restore them to their land.

Ezekiel is especially known for his vivid and often strange visions and symbolic actions. His opening vision describes God's glory appearing on a throne-chariot carried by four living creatures with wheels full of eyes. He also acted out prophecies dramatically, such as lying on his side for extended periods to represent the siege of Jerusalem and shaving his head to symbolize the fate of its inhabitants. Perhaps his most famous passage is the vision of the valley of dry bones in chapter 37, where God brings scattered bones back to life as a picture of Israel's national revival. The book closes with an elaborate vision of a restored temple and a renewed land, with a river flowing from the temple that brings life wherever it goes.

Theologically, Ezekiel emphasized God's holiness and sovereignty, the idea that God's presence was not confined to Jerusalem, and the principle of individual responsibility, teaching that each person is accountable for their own righteousness or wickedness. He also spoke of God giving the people a new heart and a new spirit, an idea that later influenced both Jewish and Christian thought. His imagery has had a lasting impact on later apocalyptic literature, including the Book of Revelation in the New Testament.

No, they are different measures, although both involve net income in some form and are sometimes confused because each expresses profitability as a percentage.

The capitalization rate, or cap rate, is a real estate metric. It is calculated by dividing a property's net operating income (NOI) by its current market value or purchase price. For example, a building that generates 100,000 dollars a year in net operating income and sells for 1,250,000 dollars has a cap rate of 8 percent. It tells you the unlevered annual return the property produces relative to what it is worth, and it is widely used to compare properties and to estimate value: if you know a market's typical cap rate and a property's NOI, you can divide NOI by the cap rate to approximate the property's value. Net operating income here excludes financing costs like mortgage interest, as well as income taxes and depreciation, so the cap rate reflects the property's performance independent of how it is financed.

Net profit margin is a general business metric. It is calculated by dividing net income by total revenue. If a company brings in 1,000,000 dollars in revenue and keeps 80,000 dollars after paying all expenses, including cost of goods, operating costs, interest, and taxes, its net profit margin is 8 percent. It tells you how much of each dollar of sales the business keeps as profit, so it measures operating efficiency and pricing power rather than return on an asset's value.

The key distinction lies in the denominator and the numerator. A cap rate compares income to the value of an asset, making it a return-on-investment measure, while net profit margin compares income to revenue, making it an efficiency measure. The income figures also differ: NOI is before debt service and taxes, while net income is after all expenses. A rental property could have a high profit margin on its rental revenue but a low cap rate if it is very expensive relative to the income it produces, which illustrates that the two numbers answer different questions.

So the USA PATRIOT Act, which stands for "Uniting and Strengthening America by Providing Appropriate Tools Required to Intercept and Obstruct Terrorism" (yeah, someone worked hard on that acronym), got signed by George W. Bush on October 26, 2001. That was just weeks after the September 11 attacks. The whole idea was to hand law enforcement more tools for stopping and fighting terrorism, and it ended up changing a bunch of federal laws along the way, including FISA (the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act) and the ECPA (Electronic Communications Privacy Act). It's been pretty controversial ever since, mostly because people worry about what it does to civil liberties and privacy.

Looking for info on corporate bonds? There are a bunch of places to check. Financial news sites like Bloomberg and CNBC cover corporate bonds in depth, including the "junk" ones, and you'll usually find current and historical prices and ratings there.

For more detailed data, look at online databases like the Bloomberg Terminal, Thomson Reuters Eikon, or S&P Global Market Intelligence. Most of these require a subscription, but your local library or even your bank might give you free access, so it's worth asking.

Research firms like Moody's, Standard & Poor's, and Fitch Ratings publish ratings and reports on bonds too. Those reports often cost money, though you may be able to read them for free through a library or your financial institution.

Brokerage firms are another option. Plenty of them have bond info on their websites, or you can just call and ask.

On the junk bond question: these are also called high-yield bonds, and they're riskier than investment-grade bonds because the companies issuing them have lower credit ratings. That's why they pay higher yields, to make up for the extra risk. If you're thinking about buying some, do your homework on the issuer's creditworthiness and the risks before you jump in.

Imagine you have a toy car on a long straight road, and you can only say how far forward or backward it is. That is like the regular numbers you know: three steps forward, two steps back. Now imagine the car is on a big playground instead, where it can also go left and right. To say where it is, you need two numbers instead of one. A complex number is just a way of keeping those two numbers together in a single package. One part says how far one way, and the other part says how far the other way.

The special trick is that these packages have a neat rule built in: multiplying by a certain special number, called i, makes things turn a quarter turn, like spinning in a circle. Do it twice and you have turned all the way around to face backward, which is why i times i equals minus one. That is the secret of why people say i is "imaginary," even though it is really just a name for "turn a corner." So the physical meaning of complex numbers is that they describe things that both have a size and a direction of turning, or things that go round and round, like a spinning wheel, a swinging swing, or a wave in water.

Because so many things in the world wiggle, spin, or wave, complex numbers turn up everywhere. Electricians use them to understand the electricity in the wall of your house, which goes back and forth in waves. Radios, phones, and Wi-Fi use them to send and catch signals, because those signals are waves too. Music software uses them to figure out which notes are in a song, and the same idea helps compress pictures and sounds so they fit on your phone. Engineers use them to make sure bridges, airplanes, and buildings do not shake too much. Doctors use them in MRI machines to make pictures of the inside of your body. And in quantum physics, the science of the tiniest things in the universe, the whole description of how particles behave is written with complex numbers, so without them we would not have modern computers or lasers.

So in five-year-old terms: regular numbers tell you how far to walk in a line, and complex numbers tell you how far to walk and also how to spin. Since nature loves to spin and wiggle, these numbers help us understand and build lots of the things we use every day.

Not necessarily. Where you enter it depends on what kind of work produced the income, not on whether you received a form. All income is taxable whether or not a 1099 is issued. The $600 threshold only determines when the payer is required to file a 1099. It doesn't affect whether you owe tax. (Also, since 2020, payments to independent contractors are reported on Form 1099-NEC rather than 1099-MISC, so the company may simply be using the wrong form name or may be overlooking its obligation. That's their issue, not yours.)

If you earned the money as an independent contractor, freelancer, gig worker, or through any activity you do regularly with the intent to make a profit, it's self-employment income. It belongs on Schedule C as business income, not as general "other income." This matters because self-employment income is subject to self-employment tax (Social Security and Medicare, roughly 15.3 percent) on top of income tax. On the plus side, Schedule C lets you deduct related business expenses. Most tax software lets you enter business income directly without a 1099, often under an option like "other self-employment income" or "cash/income not reported on a 1099."

If the income was truly occasional and not connected to any business or trade, such as a one-time payment or a hobby activity, it generally goes on Schedule 1 as "other income." That avoids self-employment tax but doesn't allow expense deductions. The IRS looks closely at people who label recurring work income this way, so use it only when it genuinely fits.

If the company controlled how, when, and where you did the work, like an employer would, you may actually have been misclassified and should have received a W-2. In that case, look into Form 8919.

Whichever applies, keep records of what you were paid, such as bank deposits, invoices, or payment app statements, in case the IRS ever asks.

A common form of legal ownership is sole proprietorship, in which a single individual owns and operates a business and is personally responsible for its debts and obligations. Other forms of legal ownership include partnerships, where two or more people share ownership and management, and corporations, which are separate legal entities owned by shareholders whose personal liability is generally limited to their investment. Limited liability companies, or LLCs, blend features of partnerships and corporations by offering owners limited personal liability along with flexible management. In the context of property rather than businesses, legal ownership is often described as fee simple, which gives the owner the most complete set of rights over real estate, including the right to use, sell, lease, or pass it on to heirs.

Inference rules are logical principles that let you reach conclusions from information you already have. Logicians and mathematicians use them to derive new statements from existing ones, whether to demonstrate that a logical argument holds up or to work through a mathematical problem. They fall into two broad categories: deductive and inductive. Deductive rules yield conclusions that must be true if the starting information is true. Suppose you accept that every mammal is warm-blooded and that a certain animal is a mammal; you can then conclude with certainty that the animal is warm-blooded. This reasoning is an instance of a deductive rule known as modus ponens. Inductive rules, by contrast, produce conclusions that are probably true given the evidence. If a coin lands heads up ten times in a row, for example, you might suspect it is weighted toward heads. This kind of reasoning illustrates an inductive rule. In short, inference rules are a vital part of logic and mathematics because they allow us to build new knowledge from what we already know.

Usually, yeah, when a company announces it made a profit, the share price tends to go up. Investors see the profit and figure the company's in good shape, so more of them want to buy in. More buyers means more demand for the shares, and that pushes the price higher.

It's not a guarantee, though. Plenty of other stuff moves a stock too, like the overall economy, what the market's doing at the moment, and how other companies in the same industry are performing. So a profit announcement can give the price a bump, but it's definitely not the only thing at work.

Riverfront Stadium in Cincinnati opened on June 30, 1970, with the Reds hosting the Atlanta Braves. The first home run in the ballpark was hit by Atlanta's Hank Aaron, who connected in that opening game. The Braves won that night, 8-2, with Aaron's homer being a notable moment given that he was closing in on the major milestones of his career. Aaron went on to hit many more home runs in the park during his career.

The first Reds home run at the stadium came from Johnny Bench, who hit one later in the same period, but the very first overall belonged to Aaron.

A continuous function is basically one with no sudden jumps, breaks, or holes. If you graphed it, you'd get one unbroken curve with no gaps. A few things have to hold for that to be true. The function has to be defined at every point in its domain. It also needs a finite limit at each of those points, and that limit has to match the function's actual value there. The "draw it without lifting your pencil" rule is a handy way to picture it, though it's more of a rule of thumb than a strict definition.

The reason people care so much is that calculus works nicely on continuous functions. You can differentiate them and integrate them, which lets you figure out how they behave, find the slope of the graph at a point, or work out the area under a curve. Polynomials, trig functions, and exponentials are all good examples. You'll see them everywhere, like modeling real-world stuff, solving engineering problems, and even trying to predict financial trends.

The multi-armed bandit is a classic problem in probability theory and decision-making under uncertainty. It takes its name from a hypothetical gambler facing a row of slot machines, often called "one-armed bandits" because they take your money. Each machine, or "arm," pays out according to its own hidden probability distribution, and the gambler does not know which arm is the most rewarding. With a limited number of pulls, the gambler must decide which arm to play at each step.

The central difficulty is the tradeoff between exploration and exploitation. Exploitation means pulling the arm that currently appears to pay best, which earns reward based on what you already know. Exploration means trying other arms to gather information, which may sacrifice short-term reward but could reveal a better option for the future. Too much exploitation risks locking onto a suboptimal arm, while too much exploration wastes pulls on poor options. The goal is to maximize total reward over time, or equivalently to minimize "regret," which measures how much worse your choices performed compared with always picking the best arm in hindsight.

Several strategies address this tradeoff. The epsilon-greedy approach usually exploits the best-known arm but occasionally chooses one at random. Upper confidence bound methods favor arms whose estimated values are uncertain, giving them an optimistic bonus so they get tried. Thompson sampling maintains a probability belief about each arm's payout, samples from those beliefs, and plays the arm that the sample favors. Each method balances the tradeoff differently, and theoretical guarantees exist for how quickly they approach optimal behavior.

Multi-armed bandits have wide practical use. Online advertising systems use them to decide which ads or headlines to display, clinical trials use them to allocate patients to treatments that appear to work better, recommendation systems use them to balance showing popular content with discovering new interests, and websites use them for A/B testing that adapts traffic toward winning variants as evidence accumulates. The framework is also a foundation for the broader field of reinforcement learning, where an agent must learn from rewards while its actions also affect future situations.

So "deep structure" in linguistics is basically the underlying meaning and structure of a sentence, the thing the surface structure comes from. The surface structure is just how the sentence actually gets expressed when somebody says or writes it. Noam Chomsky and his followers came up with the idea as part of transformational grammar, which says the deep structure gets turned into the surface structure by a series of rules.

The way the theory works, deep structure is made up of the syntactic and semantic relationships between the words and phrases in a sentence. One deep structure can end up as a bunch of different surface structures, depending on the context and on which rules you apply to it.

Take "The cat sat on the mat." Its deep structure is pretty simple: a subject ("the cat"), a verb ("sat"), and an object ("the mat"). The surface structure is the specific form you actually see, with the words in a certain order and the verb carrying particular inflections.

Why does it matter? Well, it helps explain how a sentence gets its meaning across, and how different surface forms can come from a single deep structure. It also shows up as a key piece in a lot of theories about language and how the brain processes it.

There are 66 books in the Bible, 39 in the Old Testament and 27 in the New Testament. The Old Testament is basically the Hebrew Bible, and the New Testament covers Jesus's teachings and the early church. People often split it into two groups: the Old Testament, which is the Jewish scriptures, and the New Testament, which is the Christian ones. You'll find law, history, poetry, and prophecy in the Old Testament, while the New Testament has the Gospels, letters, and Revelation.

Some swelling or soreness after getting wisdom teeth out is pretty normal, but if you've got pain or swelling that won't go away, tell your dentist or oral surgeon. That knot you're feeling could be a cyst, sure, but it could just as easily be part of the healing process or even a stitch poking at you. There's really no way to know without someone looking at it, so get it checked out. I know it's tempting to google it and play doctor, but it's better to be safe than guess wrong.

Until you can get in, a warm compress on the area might take down some of the swelling and ease the ache. Over-the-counter pain meds can help too, just stick to the directions on the label. But if the pain gets bad, the swelling gets worse, or anything else seems off, don't wait around. Call your dentist or surgeon right away. They can tell you what to do next and make sure everything's healing the way it should.

A stock's price can climb even when there is no good news or strong earnings behind it, and a number of things may be responsible. One is market demand. When many people want to buy a particular stock, their eagerness alone can push the price higher, even without any news or favorable results. Investor mood or speculation about how the company will perform later on often lies behind this.

Another is a short squeeze. Sometimes a large group of investors bets that a stock will fall, a practice called short selling. If positive news suddenly arrives or buying picks up, the price can jump sharply as those investors are forced to buy back shares. This is what people call a short squeeze.

A third possibility is market manipulation. A price can sometimes be inflated artificially through tactics such as insider trading or "pump and dump" schemes. These practices are illegal, and anyone involved in them may face serious penalties.

Keep in mind that countless factors shape stock prices, and forecasting their movements is not always possible. Investors should do their own research and stay aware of the risks that come with buying stocks.

Chemotherapy is a form of treatment that relies on medications to destroy cancer cells. It is frequently given for kidney (renal) cancer, yet how much it prolongs survival for these patients differs considerably based on several considerations. Generally speaking, chemotherapy can be a useful option for advanced kidney cancer, since it may reduce tumor size and slow how quickly malignant cells multiply. Even so, it does not cure the disease, and its usefulness depends on the cancer's stage and type, as well as the patient's general health and age. Certain research has found that chemotherapy can raise overall survival among people with advanced kidney cancer, though these gains tend to be small, and the extra time gained varies. Typically, for people with advanced kidney cancer, chemotherapy may add anywhere from a few months to a few years to life. Importantly, chemotherapy carries possible side effects, which differ from person to person and depend on the particular drugs used. Such side effects may include tiredness, nausea, vomiting, and a greater susceptibility to infection. Anyone considering this treatment should talk through its likely benefits and drawbacks with a healthcare provider to decide whether it suits their situation.

Continuous improvement is an ongoing effort to find and carry out ways of raising the efficiency, effectiveness, and quality of a business or organization. It entails pinpointing where things can get better, introducing changes to tackle those weak spots, and then assessing the outcomes to confirm that the changes are genuinely beneficial. Frequently, it forms part of a broader business approach, such as total quality management or lean manufacturing, and it may touch every level of an organization, from single work processes to the company's overall way of operating. Its aim is to keep boosting productivity and efficiency while delivering superior products and services to customers.

The vas deferens, also called the ductus deferens, is the tube that carries sperm from the testicles up to the ejaculatory ducts. When you ejaculate, its muscles squeeze and push the sperm along so it can mix with other fluids and leave the body through the urethra. It doesn't make hormones itself, though. Its job is mostly transport, and it helps keep the rest of the reproductive system running smoothly.

Yes, you can take emergency contraception again, even if you have not had a period since the last time you used it. Emergency contraceptive pills are considered safe to use more than once, including more than once in the same menstrual cycle. Taking them again will not harm your health or your future fertility. What matters most is timing: the pill works best when taken as soon as possible after unprotected sex.

The time limit depends on the type of pill. Levonorgestrel pills (such as Postinor, Plan B, or Norlevo) should be taken within 72 hours (3 days) of unprotected sex and are more effective the sooner you take them. Ulipristal acetate (ella or ellaOne) works for up to 120 hours (5 days) and is generally a bit more effective, especially later in that window. If more time has passed, a pharmacist or clinic may still be able to help. A copper IUD inserted by a health provider within 5 days of unprotected sex is the most effective form of emergency contraception, and it can then remain as ongoing birth control.

Repeated use can upset your cycle. Your period may come earlier or later than expected, be heavier or lighter, and you may have spotting in between. Nausea, headache, breast tenderness, and tiredness are also common for a day or two. These effects are temporary.

Because emergency pills can shift your cycle, a late period does not necessarily mean you are pregnant. Still, if your period is more than about a week late, or if about three weeks have passed since your last unprotected sex, take a home pregnancy test, which will be reliable by then. If it is negative but your period still does not come, test again or see a health provider.

Emergency contraception works well, but it is less effective than regular birth control and is not meant to be your main method. If you are having sex regularly, a clinic, pharmacist, or doctor can help you choose something more reliable, such as the daily pill, an injection, an implant, or an IUD, and using condoms as well protects against sexually transmitted infections. It is understandable to feel scared, but acting quickly as you are doing gives you the best chance of preventing pregnancy, and a health provider can support you if you have any further worries.

Okay so artificial neural networks are basically computer programs built to imitate how the brain works. Your brain has billions of tiny cells called neurons that hook up to each other and pass signals around. An artificial network does something similar with a bunch of connected "neurons" that take in and send along information. They're stacked into layers: the input layer takes the data in, the hidden layers do the crunching, and the output layer spits out an answer. Feed it some data and it runs through everything and makes a prediction or decision based on what it's picked up so far. Say you train one on pictures of animals. Show it a new photo and it can guess what animal it is, based on all the examples it saw before. People use these for all sorts of stuff, like recognizing images and speech, translating languages, or even beating people at chess. They're honestly pretty great for problems that would be way too messy for a person to work out by hand.

A Pooled Registered Pension Plan (PRPP) is a Canadian retirement savings vehicle created under the federal Pooled Registered Pension Plans Act, which came into force in 2013, with matching provincial legislation in most provinces. It was designed mainly for employees of small and medium-sized businesses and for self-employed people who do not have access to a workplace pension plan.

The plan is run by a licensed administrator, usually a financial institution such as an insurance company, trust company, or investment firm. The administrator takes on the fiduciary responsibility for managing the plan, handling regulatory compliance, and selecting investment options, so that employers do not carry that burden. Many contributions from many employers and individuals are pooled together, which is meant to lower costs through economies of scale. Investment fees are generally expected to be lower than typical retail products.

Contributions are made by the member and, optionally, by the employer. Employers are not required to contribute under the federal framework, though some provinces have rules about participation, and an employer who offers a PRPP must generally enroll eligible employees automatically, with employees able to opt out. Contributions are tax-deductible and growth is tax-sheltered until withdrawal, much like an RRSP. Contribution limits fall under the same room rules as RRSPs, so contributions to a PRPP reduce the available RRSP room, and employer contributions are treated as a deductible expense for the business and not a taxable benefit to the employee.

Funds are locked in, meaning they are generally intended for retirement income and cannot be withdrawn freely, though there are exceptions such as financial hardship, shortened life expectancy, or non-residency. At retirement, members can typically draw income through a variable benefit, similar to a life income fund, or purchase an annuity. Plans are portable, so a member can keep the account or transfer it when changing jobs.

Uptake has been modest. Quebec has its own version, the Voluntary Retirement Savings Plan, which requires employers with a certain number of employees and no existing plan to offer one. Some other provinces have also implemented their own PRPP legislation. For current details such as limits, fees, and available providers, check the Canada Revenue Agency, the Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions, or your provincial pension regulator, since rules and offerings change.

Yeah, Netflix does make money off shows like House of Cards that they produce. Mostly it's subscriptions. People pay a monthly fee to get access to all the TV shows, movies, and other stuff on the service. But they also bring in cash from ads, including product placement in their original shows and movies. That's when a company pays to have its product show up on screen. Say a character cracks open a Coke on a show: that's product placement, and Netflix may well get paid by Coca-Cola for it. So the short version is that Netflix earns from both subscriptions and from selling ads and placements inside its own shows and movies.

Puce is a deep, dark shade of brownish purple, often described as a mix between brown and purple, sometimes with a reddish or grayish tint. The name comes from the French word for "flea," reflecting the insect's dark, reddish-brown color. The term was first used in English in the late 18th century, and it was especially popular in fashion during the 1700s and 1800s. Today it is still used to describe clothing, paint, and other colored materials, and it often appears in color charts as a muted, dusky tone.

Erie, Colorado sits in two counties, Weld County and Boulder County. The town straddles the county line, and most of its land area and population lie on the Weld County side. Erie is located in the northern Denver metropolitan area, roughly between Boulder and Interstate 25.

Karma (Sanskrit, from the root kr, "to do" or "to act") means action, and more specifically the moral consequences that intentional actions set in motion. In Buddhist thought, every intentional deed of body, speech, or mind leaves a trace that shapes future experience. Wholesome actions rooted in generosity, kindness, and wisdom tend to bring pleasant results, while unwholesome actions rooted in greed, hatred, and delusion tend to bring suffering. The emphasis falls on intention, since the Buddha taught that it is volition (cetana) that makes an action karmic in the first place.

Karma is not a fixed destiny or a system of divine reward and punishment. Buddhism holds that present circumstances result from many causes, including past karma but also physical conditions, natural laws, and the choices one makes now, so one is never simply locked into a predetermined fate. Because karma is always being created through ongoing choices, individuals have real agency to change the direction of their lives and their future rebirths.

The concept is closely tied to rebirth and to the aim of liberation. Karma keeps beings cycling through existence (samsara) as long as craving and ignorance drive unwholesome actions. Awakening, or nirvana, ends this cycle by removing the defilements that generate new karma. Different Buddhist traditions explain the mechanics in varying detail, but the core idea is that ethical action shapes the course of one's life and the path toward freedom from suffering.

Type 1 diabetes occurs when the immune system wrongly targets and destroys the insulin-producing cells of the pancreas. Insulin is a hormone that helps control the amount of sugar (glucose) circulating in the blood, and it matters because it allows the body to use glucose as fuel. Without enough insulin, the body cannot make use of the glucose in the bloodstream, and blood sugar levels climb too high. Because the pancreas of someone with type 1 diabetes does not make sufficient insulin, they must replace it through injections or an insulin pump, which lets the body handle blood glucose properly. Even with this treatment, though, the body may sometimes fail to use blood glucose efficiently. This can happen when a person's insulin requirements shift, such as during exercise or sickness, or when they consume more sugar than the body can process at that moment. In such cases, a person with type 1 diabetes may have to eat sugar or other carbohydrate-containing foods to help keep their blood sugar balanced. I hope this is useful! Feel free to ask if you have further questions.

People may fail to save more of their earnings for a variety of reasons. Several of the most frequent ones are these. First, some individuals have a low income that cannot cover their essential costs and still leave money to set aside. Second, heavy spending on necessities such as housing, food, and transportation can leave very little to put away. Third, many people carry large debts, including credit card balances or student loans, and they must repay these before they can begin building savings. Fourth, a lack of financial knowledge means some people do not understand how to save effectively or how to put their money to productive use. Fifth, a focus on the short term can lead people to favor immediate goals or enjoyment over preparing for the future. Finally, unplanned costs like a medical emergency or a car repair can catch those without enough set aside, forcing them to draw on their savings or borrow. In short, numerous factors can keep people from saving more of what they earn, and it is worth keeping them in mind when you try to strengthen your own saving habits.

Okay so derivatives and integrals are basically the two big tools for dealing with change. A derivative tells you how fast a function is changing at any particular point, and an integral tells you the total change piled up over an interval, or equivalently the area under the curve. The derivative of x^2 is 2x, and you can see why: x^2 grows at a rate of 2x at every point. So if x nudges up a little, x^2 nudges up about twice as much.

The derivative of sin^2 x is where people often trip up. It's not 2 sin x. It's actually 2 sin x cos x. The reason is that sin^2 x doesn't grow at a steady rate like x^2 does. Its speed depends on where you are. When sin x is big and cos x is small, sin^2 x is moving fast, and when sin x is small and cos x is big, it's crawling. The derivative just keeps track of that shifting speed.

On the integral side, the integral of x is x^2/2. You can picture the total change as a triangle with base x and height x, which has area x^2/2. The integral of sin x or cos x doesn't work out to anything that simple, though. You won't get a neat polynomial for it, so you end up with more involved expressions to describe the total change over an interval.

Lazy evaluation is a programming technique that postpones computing an expression until its result is genuinely required. Programmers rely on it to boost efficiency by skipping calculations that turn out to be unnecessary, and it also makes it possible to work with infinite data structures. Most languages evaluate an expression immediately when the program reaches it. Under lazy evaluation, by contrast, that work waits until the value is truly needed. Special constructs such as lazy variables or lazy functions can achieve this, running their computation only at the moment they are accessed or invoked. A typical benefit is performance: when a program handles a large data set, it can be more efficient to compute just the elements it actually uses, instead of processing the whole set and throwing away what goes unused. Lazy evaluation also enables infinite structures, such as streams or lists that can be walked through without end. Here, each element is calculated only when the traversal reaches it, so the structure takes shape gradually as it is consumed. In short, lazy evaluation is a powerful tool for making programs faster and more expressive, since they compute only what is actually needed.

Honestly, stomach pain plus dizziness could be a bunch of different things, and nobody can really pin it down without your dad getting checked out by a doctor. But here are some of the usual suspects.

It could be a gut issue, like indigestion, acid reflux, or even an ulcer. It could also be an infection, say food poisoning or a stomach bug, which can easily make you queasy and lightheaded at the same time. Dehydration is another big one, since it'll cause both symptoms pretty reliably. Stress and anxiety can do it too, because they mess with your stomach and can leave you feeling woozy.

The scarier possibility is something with the heart or blood vessels, like angina or even a heart attack. Those can show up as stomach discomfort and dizziness, which is why I wouldn't just wait it out.

So yeah, get your dad in to see a doctor so they can figure out what's going on and treat it properly. I wouldn't try to diagnose or treat it at home, because some of the causes behind this stuff are pretty serious.

Scottsdale is a municipality in eastern Maricopa County, Arizona, in the United States. Situated within the Greater Phoenix region, it forms part of the broader Phoenix metropolitan area. Visitors and residents also have access to numerous art galleries, museums, and other points of interest. With roughly 255,000 inhabitants, the city lies about 20 miles northeast of Phoenix.
