Imagine your brain is like a big toy box. Words are one kind of toy in there, but they're not the only kind. There are also pictures, sounds, smells, feelings, memories of how things move, and the sense of what your body is doing. You can think with any of those toys, not just the word toys.

Think about a baby. A baby can't talk, but it still knows its mom's face, gets excited when it sees a bottle, and figures out that pushing a cup off the table makes a fun crash. That's thinking! Dogs do it too. A dog doesn't say "I wonder where my ball went" in its head, but it still remembers the ball, pictures where it might be, and goes looking. So thinking without words looks a lot like that: pictures, feelings, "this goes with that," and "if I do this, that happens."

Now, about deaf people, there's a little mix-up worth fixing. Most deaf people do have a language. Sign languages, like American Sign Language, are real, complete languages with their own grammar, jokes, and poetry. Many deaf people who sign say they "think in sign," kind of seeing or feeling hands moving in their mind, the same way you "hear" words in your head. Some think in pictures, some in written words, some in a mix. So a deaf person who grew up signing thinks with language just like you do, it just isn't made of sounds.

Also, not everyone hears a voice in their head, even hearing people. Some people say their thoughts are mostly pictures or feelings, and they only turn them into words when they need to talk. So the inner voice is common, but it isn't the only way brains work.

The really rare case is someone who grew up with no language at all, like a child raised away from people, or a deaf child nobody ever taught to sign. There's a famous story about a deaf man named Ildefonso who didn't learn any language until he was an adult. Later, when he could explain it, he said that before language he could still see, remember, feel, and figure things out, but it was very lonely and confusing. He couldn't easily think about things that weren't right in front of him, like "yesterday," "next week," or ideas like "fair" or "why." When he finally learned that things have names, it was like a light turned on, and he cried because suddenly everything had a name.

So here's the simple version: people without language still think, using pictures, feelings, and memories, like babies and animals do. Language is like a super handy tool that lets you think about bigger and trickier things, like the past, the future, and ideas you can't touch. And that tool can be made of sounds, hand shapes, or anything else, as long as it's a real language.

Swelling that persists weeks after bilateral wide excisions and skin grafts on both shins is worth a prompt call to your surgeon, even though some swelling after this kind of surgery is expected. Removing skin and tissue from the anterior legs can disrupt the lymphatic channels that drain fluid from the feet and ankles, and a graft can scar and tighten in ways that limit normal drainage. Your history of edema probably makes you more prone to this, since fluid that was already hard to clear now has fewer routes out. Still, persistent swelling on both sides needs to be evaluated rather than assumed to be routine, because a few other causes need to be ruled out.

The most important thing to rule out is a blood clot in the deep veins of the legs, which can cause swelling in the foot, ankle, and calf, often on one side but sometimes on both. Clots are a particular risk after surgery and reduced mobility. Seek emergency care right away if you develop sudden or worsening swelling, calf or leg pain or tenderness, warmth or redness, shortness of breath, chest pain, or a rapid heartbeat. Infection of the grafts or surrounding tissue is also important to exclude, so report any increasing redness, heat, pus or drainage, a foul smell, fever, or chills, and any graft that looks dark, separated, or unusually painful. Heart, kidney, or liver problems can also cause bilateral leg swelling, so if the swelling is spreading upward, you have new shortness of breath when lying flat, or your weight is climbing quickly, that needs urgent attention too.

If those concerns have been checked and the swelling is mainly from lymphatic or venous causes, the usual approach is a stronger and more consistent compression program than ACE wraps alone. A fitted, medical-grade compression garment or a bandaging regimen applied by a certified lymphedema therapist is often much more effective, and your surgeon or a lymphedema clinic can refer you. Manual lymphatic drainage, a gentle massage technique done by a trained therapist, is commonly used alongside compression for this kind of swelling. Ask your surgeon whether you should wait for the grafts to mature before starting compression over them, since the timing and pressure depend on how the skin is healing.

At home, elevate your legs so your feet are above the level of your heart for part of the day, not just propped slightly, and try to do this for regular periods rather than occasionally. Move your ankles and toes through full circles and pumps several times an hour when you are sitting, and walk short distances as your surgeon permits, since muscle contraction is what drives fluid back toward the body. Limiting salt can reduce fluid retention. Do not start or change diuretic (water pill) medication on your own, but ask your doctor whether one would be appropriate for you.

Because this is weeks out from surgery and the swelling is not improving with what you are doing, please contact your surgeon's office soon and describe the swelling exactly as you have here, including when it started, whether it is the same on both sides, and what you have already tried. Ask for a referral to a lymphedema specialist or vascular provider if the surgeon's office does not offer one. If any of the warning signs above appear, do not wait for a scheduled appointment.

So you got paid, but no 1099-MISC showed up? Doesn't matter. That income still has to go on your return. It's usually called "miscellaneous income," and the place to put it is Form 1040, the standard personal return. Your total income goes on line 1, and that includes the misc. stuff.

If you're self-employed or a sole proprietor, it goes on Schedule C (Form 1040) instead, since that's where business income and losses get reported. Leaving income off because no form came in is a bad idea. The IRS can catch it, and you could end up with fines or penalties. If you're not sure where it belongs, a tax pro can sort it out quickly, or you can check the IRS instructions.

Earning $250,000 in five years is achievable for many people, but there is no guaranteed method, and the most reliable paths depend heavily on your starting capital, skills, and risk tolerance. The honest truth is that the sum comes from some combination of earning more, saving a high share of income, and investing that savings at a reasonable rate of return. Trading for quick gains is the riskiest route and the one most likely to lose money, so it is usually better to build on steadier foundations.

Consider the arithmetic first. If you have no savings, reaching $250,000 in five years means saving roughly $4,000 per month, or about $50,000 per year, before any investment growth. If you can invest that money in a broad index fund averaging around 7 to 8 percent annually, the monthly target drops to something closer to $3,300 to $3,500. Starting with some capital, even $20,000 to $50,000, lowers the monthly requirement considerably. Knowing your starting point and how much you can realistically save is the first step.

The most dependable approach for most people is to raise income and direct as much of it as possible into low-cost diversified investments, such as broad index funds or retirement accounts where taxes are deferred or reduced. Earning more might mean pursuing a promotion, changing employers for a higher salary, acquiring a certification in a high-demand field, or building a side income through freelancing or consulting. Living below your means and avoiding high-interest debt matter as much as the investment returns, because debt payments quietly consume the money you would otherwise be growing.

If you want to start a business, the path is less predictable. Many small businesses take years to become profitable, and some never do. A business can produce large returns, but it requires significant time, and you should be prepared for the possibility that it earns little or fails. Testing a business idea on a small scale while keeping your job is a sensible way to limit risk.

Active trading deserves particular caution. Most individual traders underperform simple index investing over time, and leverage or options can wipe out an account quickly. If you are drawn to trading, consider limiting it to a small portion of your money you could afford to lose entirely, and track your results honestly.

A reasonable plan would be to calculate your current net worth, set a monthly savings target, invest it consistently in diversified funds, and look for ways to increase your income over the period. If you share more details about your current income, savings, skills, and how much risk you can tolerate, I can help you work out a more specific plan. Consider also speaking with a fee-only financial planner, who can review your situation without earning commissions on products they recommend.

So an artificial immune system is basically a computer system built to copy how your body's immune system works. Your immune system protects you from infection and disease by spotting foreign stuff like bacteria and viruses and getting rid of it. An AIS does something similar, but for a computer, a network, or some other artificial environment. It looks for threats and reacts to them.

Under the hood, it uses algorithms and machine learning to pick up on patterns and oddities in data that might mean there's a threat or a weak spot somewhere. That covers a pretty wide range of things, like viruses, malware, and other cyber attacks.

One of the big perks is that it can run nonstop. It keeps watching the system and responds in real time, so you've got ongoing protection even when nobody's actually using the machine.

There's no single way to build one, either. People have come up with lots of different approaches, and you'll see them used in cybersecurity, medical diagnosis, and pretty much anywhere else that catching and responding to threats matters.

A painful lump at a stitch site three weeks after wisdom tooth surgery isn't typical of normal healing, so it's worth having your oral surgeon or dentist look at it soon. Healing often causes some tenderness and firmness for a while, but a lump that hurts and feels cyst-like can have several causes. A knot of suture material or a stitch that hasn't dissolved can irritate the tissue around it. Sometimes a small pocket of fluid, a localized infection or abscess, or a granuloma (a small inflamed tissue reaction) forms. Occasionally a tiny bone fragment works its way out and causes irritation.

Please contact the office promptly if the lump is getting larger, if you notice pus, a bad taste, or drainage, if the area is red or hot, if you have a fever, or if the swelling is spreading or making it harder to open your mouth, swallow, or breathe. Those signs suggest infection and need same-day attention. If you're not in the office's hours, an urgent care or emergency dental service can help.

Until you're seen, avoid pressing or poking at the lump, keep the area clean with a soft toothbrush and gentle salt-water rinses if your surgeon has cleared that, and use an over-the-counter pain reliever as directed. Most of the time this is easily fixed, often by removing a stitch or draining a small pocket, so don't hesitate to call.

Left ventricular (LV) diastolic dysfunction is a condition in which the heart's left ventricle has trouble relaxing and filling with blood during diastole, the phase of the cardiac cycle in which the heart fills. Grade 1 diastolic dysfunction is its mildest form. How it is managed depends on how severe the condition is and what is causing it. Common approaches include medication, where diuretics may be given to reduce fluid buildup and lower blood pressure, and drugs such as angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors or angiotensin receptor blockers may be used to enhance blood flow and ease the workload on the heart. Lifestyle adjustments, including changes to diet, physical activity, and stress management, can support overall heart health and help control symptoms. Cardiac rehabilitation, a structured program of exercise and education, can also strengthen heart health and lower the chance of future complications. In serious cases, surgery might be needed to repair or replace damaged heart tissue. Patients should follow the plan their doctor recommends and keep up with regular follow-up visits so the condition can be monitored and the treatment adjusted as needed.

A 14-year-old can experience pain in the lower rib region for a wide range of reasons. One category involves the musculoskeletal system, where strains, sprains, or other injuries to the muscles, ligaments, or tendons nearby may be responsible. Digestive problems are another possibility, such as indigestion, constipation, or inflammatory bowel disease. Breathing-related conditions, including pneumonia, bronchitis, and pleurisy, can also produce discomfort in this area. Beyond these, a number of other medical conditions may be to blame, among them kidney stones, liver disorders, and nerve problems. Because the cause can be hard to pin down, it is important to have your child seen by a healthcare provider who can identify the source of the pain and recommend appropriate treatment. The provider will typically ask detailed questions about the child's history, carry out a physical exam, and possibly request further tests to help reach a diagnosis.

Your body makes heat mostly by burning fuel, a lot like a campfire does, but much more slowly and carefully. The food you eat contains energy stored in sugars and fats. Inside your cells, tiny parts called mitochondria act like little power plants. They take that stored energy and break it apart step by step, using oxygen from the air you breathe. When this breakdown happens, some of the energy is used to build and run things your body needs, like muscles moving or your heart beating, and a lot of it leaks out as warmth.

That warmth is the "thermic reaction" you're asking about. Every single cell is doing this all the time, so the heat adds up across your whole body. Your blood is warm because it travels everywhere and picks up that heat from the cells it passes, then carries it around to spread it out evenly.

Your body also has a thermostat in your brain that keeps the temperature near 37 degrees Celsius, or about 98.6 degrees Fahrenheit. If you get too cold, it can make you shiver, which means your muscles move quickly and burn extra fuel to make heat. If you get too hot, it makes you sweat so the water cooling on your skin takes heat away.

Think of it like this. A battleship is a giant boat that sits out on the water and shoots very far with huge cannons. For a long time, whoever had the biggest battleships won. But then airplanes and missiles came along, and they could reach the battleship from very far away and sink it before it could do anything. A battleship is also very expensive and very easy to find, since the ocean is wide but a big ship still sticks out, and it can't hide well. So the navy mostly switched to aircraft carriers, submarines, and missile ships that can hit from far away.

A tank is a bit like a battleship on land, but it has some important differences. On land, there are lots of places to hide: hills, trees, buildings, ditches, and smoke. A tank can drive behind a hill and only poke its gun out to shoot, while a battleship in the open sea has nowhere to duck. Tanks also don't have to go it alone. They travel with soldiers, trucks, and other vehicles, and the soldiers can go where tanks can't, like into towns, forests, and rough ground. Ships can't walk onto a beach and take the land; someone has to do that job, and tanks help with it.

Tanks have also changed a lot to survive. Modern tanks have armor that is hard to punch through, systems that spot incoming missiles and shoot them down, and sensors that help them see in the dark or through smoke. They're also small enough to move quickly and can be fixed in the field. Land is also where most of the fighting over territory happens, because you have to physically hold a place to win it. A ship can sink another ship, but it can't stay on a piece of land and keep it.

So the short version is: tanks can hide, they work with soldiers, they can move over land where ships can't, and they've gotten better at surviving the same threats that sank battleships.

Your skin has tiny holes called pores, and each one has a little oil factory attached to it. That oil, called sebum, is supposed to keep your skin soft and protected. A pimple happens when a pore gets clogged with oil and dead skin cells, and then bacteria that normally live on everyone's skin start growing in the trapped gunk. Your body notices and sends in its defense team, which causes the redness, swelling, and pus. So you need three things for a pimple: lots of oil, pores that clog easily, and a strong reaction from your body.

The big reason some people get lots of acne and others get almost none is that everyone's skin is built a little differently, mostly because of genes, the instructions you inherited from your parents. Some people's oil factories are set to "high," some people's pores shed dead skin in a way that clogs more easily, and some people's immune systems react more strongly to the bacteria, making pimples bigger and more painful. If one of your parents had bad acne, there's a good chance you would too. Your friends with clear skin probably just won the genetic lottery on this one. It isn't something they're doing better than you.

Hormones matter a lot too. Hormones like testosterone, which everyone has in different amounts, tell the oil factories to work harder. That's why acne often starts at puberty, and why some people keep getting it into their twenties and beyond while others grow out of it early. Bodies are sensitive to these hormones in different amounts, so two people with similar hormone levels can have very different skin.

Other things can make acne a bit better or worse, like stress, certain medications, heavy or greasy skin products, picking at pimples, and for some people certain foods such as sugary things or lots of dairy. But these are usually smaller nudges, not the main cause. Acne is not caused by being dirty, and scrubbing hard usually makes it worse.

The good news is that bad acne is very treatable. Over-the-counter products with benzoyl peroxide or adapalene help many people, and a dermatologist can prescribe stronger options like prescription creams, antibiotics, hormonal treatments, or isotretinoin for severe cases, which works extremely well for a lot of people. Since yours sounds pretty rough, seeing a doctor is really worth it, both to clear it up and to prevent scarring. It isn't your fault, and you don't have to just put up with it.

Okay, so a stock dividend is basically when a company hands out extra shares of its own stock to shareholders. People call it a dividend because it comes out of the company's profits or earnings. A stock split is different. It's just a change in how many shares are floating around, and no profits actually get paid out. The company does it to bump up the share count and bring the price per share down. Say a company announces a 2-for-1 split: you get one more share for every share you already own, so you end up with twice as many shares and each one is worth about half as much. That's really the key difference. A stock dividend moves profits to shareholders, while a stock split doesn't.

Bleeding and swelling after a tooth pull are pretty normal, so don't freak out too much. Just stick to whatever aftercare instructions your dentist or oral surgeon gave you, since that's what helps things heal right. Mostly that means keeping the spot clean and not doing stuff that can knock the blood clot loose: no vigorous rinsing or spitting, no sucking on straws, and no smoking. If you think the clot has come out, call your dental office and ask what to do next.

The thing to watch for is dry socket. That's when the clot is lost or never forms properly, and it can hurt quite a bit and slow down healing. Your dentist can tell you how to handle it if it happens. In the meantime, a gentle rinse with warm salt water can keep the area clean and take the edge off swelling or soreness. Keep taking any meds you were prescribed as directed, and follow the rest of the aftercare steps your dental team gave you.

If you want protection in case the stock market falls, you could consider putting money into assets that often hold their value when stocks are under pressure. Treasury bonds, issued by the federal government, are generally regarded as relatively secure, and they often perform well during periods of market turbulence since investors tend to move their money toward safer holdings. Gold is another long-standing safe haven that frequently does well when the economy is uncertain, and it can help diversify a portfolio and cushion against stock losses. Real estate may also serve as a hedge, since it is a physical asset that doesn't swing with the stock market as sharply, though property values can still be shaped by broader economic conditions. Keep in mind that no investment is entirely free of risk, and putting everything into a single asset is usually unwise. Spreading your money across different asset classes is a key principle of sound investing and generally helps lower overall risk.

Debt can be handy for buying things or funding investments, but you've got to look closely at the terms before signing anything. The interest rate is probably the biggest one. It decides how much you'll end up paying back on top of what you borrowed, so lower is almost always better. A low rate cuts what borrowing really costs you and makes the payments easier to handle. Don't stop there, though. The loan length matters, since a longer repayment period can mean smaller monthly payments but more interest over time. Why you're borrowing matters too, and so does whether you can actually make the payments. Taking on debt for stuff you don't really need, or when your budget can't cover the payments, is a bad idea. You could default or land in real financial trouble, and that risk can easily outweigh whatever you were hoping to gain.

Sometimes, but not reliably, and neither Google nor Yahoo documents a clear policy on it. The answer depends on how the correction reaches their data vendors and which part of the site you're looking at.

When an exchange or FINRA busts a trade under the clearly erroneous execution rules, or when a trade is corrected after the fact, the change is sent through the consolidated tape (the SIP feeds) as a cancel or correction message referencing the original trade. A professional system built on that feed is expected to remove or amend the trade and recalculate the day's high, low, last, and volume. Google Finance and Yahoo Finance don't process the raw tape themselves. They license data from third-party providers, and the quality of that handling varies. In practice, the official daily open, high, low, close, and volume in their historical tables often end up reflecting the cleaned data, because vendors typically pull end-of-day summaries from the exchanges' official records after corrections are applied. Intraday charts and real-time quotes are much less dependable. A spike from a trade that was later busted can stay visible for the rest of the session, and sometimes it persists in intraday or short-range historical charts.

There are well-known cases where errors simply stay put. Yahoo's historical data in particular has long had a reputation among quants and hobbyists for occasional bad prints, missing days, and odd values that are never fixed, and there is no formal channel for reporting them that guarantees a correction. Events with mass cancellations, like the May 2010 Flash Crash, produced inconsistencies across free sites, with some showing the busted extremes and others not.

If by "adjusted" you mean corporate-action adjustments, both services handle those retroactively. Yahoo's historical data includes an "Adj Close" column that is recalculated for splits and dividends, and both sites back-adjust price history for stock splits, so older prices will change after a split. That process is separate from trade corrections and is applied far more consistently.

For anything where accuracy matters, such as backtesting, compliance, or disputes over a specific print, it's better to rely on the exchange's own data, the SIP or FINRA records, or a paid vendor that explicitly documents how it applies cancels, corrections, and trade-condition filters, rather than on free consumer finance portals.

The fixed rate on a Treasury I bond is set when you buy the bond and stays the same for the bond's entire life. What changes over time is the inflation component, which is reset every six months, in May and November, based on the Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U). When consumer prices rise over the prior six-month period, the semiannual inflation rate goes up, and that raises the composite rate, which combines the fixed rate and the inflation rate. Because of this, I bond returns move with inflation.

The fixed rate itself is not changed by inflation or by the bond's age. The Treasury announces a new fixed rate twice a year, usually in May and November, and that rate applies only to bonds issued during the following six months. So a bond you buy at a higher fixed rate keeps that rate, while bonds bought later may carry a different one. Any increase in the fixed rate therefore reflects the Treasury's prevailing real interest rate policy at the time of issue, not a change to your existing bond.

I'm sorry you've been dealing with this for five years. Frequent illness, chest pain, and trouble breathing after coughing are serious, and because of your symptoms and your exposure to mold at work, you should see a doctor soon, ideally within the next week or two. If you become short of breath at rest, have chest pain that is severe or spreading to your arm, jaw, or back, feel faint, or have blue or gray lips or fingertips, call emergency services right away.

Your doctor will likely want to confirm whether this is asthma or something else. Asthma is a possibility, especially since you react to cleaning products and sprays, but several other conditions can cause similar symptoms, including chronic bronchitis, a lung infection, reactive airway problems from irritant or mold exposure, hypersensitivity pneumonitis (an immune reaction to mold that can cause lasting lung damage), and sometimes heart problems, which can also cause chest discomfort and breathlessness in women your age. Because chest pain on one side can come from the heart, lungs, muscles, or ribs, it's important to have it evaluated rather than assume the cause.

Useful tests typically include spirometry (a breathing test, sometimes repeated before and after an inhaled medication), a chest X-ray or CT scan, blood tests, and possibly an ECG to check your heart. Allergy testing may be recommended too.

Common treatments for asthma, if that's the diagnosis, include inhaled corticosteroids to reduce airway inflammation, which are often the mainstay for long-term control, and short-acting rescue inhalers such as albuterol for sudden symptoms. Some people need a long-acting bronchodilator or other add-on medicine. Your doctor may also prescribe an action plan so you know what to do when symptoms flare. If an infection is causing repeated illness, treating it promptly matters. For chest pain after coughing, the doctor may suggest treating the cough and inflammation, and they can advise on pain relief that is safe for you.

The most important step for your health is reducing exposure. Since you work in a building with mold, talk with your employer about remediation, a move to a different space, or a leave of absence. Keeping a record of when symptoms happen and whether they improve on weekends or vacations can help your doctor and may be useful for workplace or workers' compensation discussions. Avoiding cleaning sprays and smoke, using a HEPA air purifier at home, keeping humidity below about 50 percent, and getting the flu, pneumonia, and COVID vaccines can also help reduce flare-ups and infections.

Please don't start or change any medications without a clinician's guidance, and make an appointment with your primary care doctor, who may refer you to a pulmonologist or an allergist if needed.

Thunder and lightning happen when electrical charges move around inside a cloud or travel between a cloud and the earth. Snow consists of frozen water vapor, whereas rain consists of liquid water. In a snowstorm, the air is usually so cold that the snowflakes do not melt into raindrops, which means that no electrical charges shift around and, as a result, there is no thunder or lightning. It helps to compare ice with water. Ice is solid and water is liquid. Leave a piece of ice in a warm room and it will gradually melt into water. In the same way, snow turns into rain when the air is warm enough. When the air stays cold, though, the snow remains frozen, and thunder and lightning do not occur.

Driving tires you out even though your body is mostly sitting still, for a few reasons. Your brain is working the whole time. It's watching the road, checking mirrors, judging how fast other cars are moving, and reacting to surprises like a sudden stop or a car cutting in front of you. All that careful watching is hard work, and brains get tired from it just like legs get tired from running.

Your body is also holding itself in one position for hours. Your muscles in your back, neck, and legs stay tensed a little to keep you steady, and that slowly wears you out. Sitting still can be more tiring than moving around, because your body never gets to stretch or shift.

Road trips add some extra tiredness too. The car hums and vibrates, which is soothing in a sleepy way, and the air inside can get dry or stuffy. Staring at a long straight road for hours can make your eyes work hard and your mind go foggy. Plus, you may have been sitting in the same spot without drinking much water or getting fresh air.

So the simple answer is that your brain worked hard, your muscles stayed tense, and the car made the air and noise a bit draining. Stretching, drinking water, and taking short breaks to walk around can help you feel more like yourself again.

Common side effects of these medicines include:

Aspirin and a statin are often prescribed to protect the heart and blood vessels, and stopping them suddenly can increase risk, especially after a heart problem or stroke. Pantoprazole is often prescribed to protect the stomach while he takes aspirin, so stopping it could bring back stomach problems.

Feeling fed up with medicines is very common, and it is a reasonable thing to raise with his doctor. Ask whether all three are still needed, whether the doses can be simplified, whether any can be combined or switched, or whether a once-daily timing would make the routine easier. The doctor or pharmacist can review his full list and decide what is safe for him.

Warren Buffett is an American businessman, investor, and philanthropist, often regarded as one of the greatest investors of all time. He serves as chairman, chief executive, and the largest shareholder of Berkshire Hathaway, a multinational conglomerate headquartered in Omaha, Nebraska. He started out in the 1950s working as a stockbroker before setting up his own investment partnership, which in time grew into Berkshire Hathaway. Buffett is famous for practicing value investing, a strategy of identifying companies trading below their true worth that have strong growth prospects, and then holding them over many years. Throughout his career, he has achieved notable success with investments in firms like Coca-Cola, American Express, and Wells Fargo. He has also carried out several profitable acquisitions, such as buying GEICO, Duracell, and the railroad operator Burlington Northern Santa Fe. Beyond his investment work, Buffett earns income from his salary as Berkshire Hathaway's CEO, as well as from dividends and share buybacks the company provides. Despite his wealth, he is known for a modest way of life and for devoting a large share of his fortune to charitable causes.

Totally normal for LH and FSH to bounce around during your cycle. LH usually spikes mid-cycle, right around ovulation, and FSH tends to be higher early on in the cycle. From the numbers you gave, nothing looks out of range to me.

That said, things like your age, weight, and general health can nudge those levels around, so a single reading doesn't tell you everything. And hormones aren't the whole fertility story anyway. Lifestyle, overall health, and any underlying medical conditions all play a part too.

If you're worried about it, I'd run your specific numbers by a doctor or other healthcare provider. They can actually walk you through what your levels mean and help you figure out a plan that fits what you're hoping for with your fertility.

When you change an order, the usual practice is to cancel the existing one and place a fresh order that carries the updated details. The reason is that the revised order can then be processed and executed independently of the original. Still, how modifications are managed depends on the exchange or trading platform in use. A few exchanges or platforms let you alter an order without cancelling it first, though this isn't universal. For that reason, it's wise to confirm with your platform how it treats order changes.

Banks generally want small businesses in business accounts for reasons tied to risk, regulation, and cost. A personal account is governed by the account holder's personal identity and typically assumes that money is being spent on household needs, not used to run a company that takes in customer payments, pays vendors, and handles payroll. When business activity flows through a personal account, the bank's risk models and compliance systems no longer reflect what is actually happening, so the bank would be misjudging the account's risk profile.

Regulation is a major part of this. Banks must verify who owns and controls a business and monitor accounts for money laundering and fraud. Business accounts involve additional know-your-customer steps, such as collecting formation documents, an employer identification number, and information about beneficial owners. Those checks are much harder to apply if a business quietly runs through an account opened as a consumer.

Pricing also matters. Business accounts often carry higher fees, but they include services that small companies need, such as higher transaction volumes, merchant services, payroll and check handling, wire transfers, and credit card processing. Personal accounts are priced for lower volume and simpler use, so a business running heavy activity through one would cost the bank more than the account's fees cover.

Finally, there is a separation argument. Keeping business and personal funds apart protects the owner's limited liability, since courts may disregard a corporation or LLC if its finances are commingled with the owner's. Separate accounts also make bookkeeping, tax filing, and audits far easier. Banks benefit from this clarity, and the business owner does too.

To deposit a cheque made out to an associate, the associate usually has to sign it over to your business first. Ask them to sign the back of the cheque, and if your bank requires it, to write "Pay to the order of" followed by your business account name. Some banks also want the associate's name and contact details written on the back or a statement that they authorize the transfer. Then take it to your business bank, either at a branch or through the mobile or ATM deposit service if the bank allows it. Most banks will ask who is depositing it, and some will want the associate present, or at least to confirm the endorsement by phone.

Check the front of the cheque before you do this. If it says "account payee only" or "A/C payee," it can generally only be paid into the named payee's own account, and your bank may refuse it. In that case, the associate should deposit it into their own account and then transfer the funds to your business account. If the cheque is made out to your business name exactly, you can usually deposit it without any endorsement.

Finally, keep a record of the transaction, including who issued the cheque, why it was issued, and the endorsement, so your accounts clearly show where the money came from. If the associate is a partner, employee, or contractor, your accountant can tell you how the payment should be recorded.

Your body has little sensors inside it that tell your brain where things are and how they're moving. Some of them are in your ears, which is how you know which way is up, but others are scattered deep in your belly and pelvis, around your organs. Your guts aren't bolted down tightly. They hang inside you on stretchy attachments, kind of like water balloons dangling from rubber bands.

When you drop suddenly, your whole body falls, but your insides lag behind for a split second and then float upward a bit relative to your body, the way your stomach seems to rise on a roller coaster. That makes the stretchy attachments go slack and then tug differently. The sensors in there notice the change and send a "whoa, something's weird!" message to your brain. Your brain isn't great at labeling signals from that area, so it just feels like a funny tickle or swoop.

The reason the tingle seems to show up in your wiener and nearby areas is that the nerves from your genitals, bowels, and lower belly all travel through the same neighborhood in your lower spine and pelvis. Their signals get mixed together, so your brain has trouble telling exactly which one is talking. A strange sensation from the pelvic area can get felt as a tingle in several places at once. Also, being scared or surprised makes your body release adrenaline, which changes blood flow and muscle tension down there, adding to the feeling.

As for why falling does it more than speeding up: when you accelerate forward or upward, you get pushed firmly into your seat, and your insides get pressed down and held in place, which feels solid and normal. When you fall, that support suddenly disappears. Your body briefly feels weightless, and your insides stop being pressed down. That loss of the usual pushing and pulling is what the sensors notice most, so the swoopy tickle happens with drops rather than with simply going fast.

So the short version is that your insides are a bit floaty, your nerves down there share a phone line, and a quick drop makes everything go slack all at once, so your brain says "tingle!"

The Ten Commandments appear in two places in the Bible, both in the first five books. The first and most commonly cited version is in Exodus 20:1-17, where God speaks them to the Israelites at Mount Sinai after bringing them out of Egypt. A second version appears in Deuteronomy 5:6-21, in Moses' farewell speech to the people as they prepare to enter the Promised Land. The two lists are very similar, though they differ in a few details, such as the reason given for keeping the Sabbath.

No, pulling on your arm wouldn't heal a broken bone the way it does in the games. In Far Cry, the character just snaps back together instantly, but in real life bones take weeks to knit back together. When a bone breaks, your body has to grow new bone tissue across the crack, and that takes time and a lot of work from your cells.

Pulling hard can actually make things worse. The broken ends can slide further apart, tear the muscles and blood vessels around them, or push a sharp piece through the skin. That's why doctors sometimes have to gently line the bones up themselves, using an X-ray to check, and then hold them still with a cast, a splint, or sometimes metal screws or rods if the break is serious.

So the short answer is: the game is pretend, and real bones need a doctor to set them and then a lot of patient resting while your body does the slow repair work. Your English is great, by the way!

Laws tied to age are usually meant to shield people from harm. Because physical, emotional, and mental maturity tend to change as people grow, the law often sets different rules for different age groups. The age of consent is one example: it reflects the belief that young people have not yet developed the maturity needed to make well-informed choices about sexual activity. Age minimums for drinking and smoking work similarly, since those activities can damage health, and society generally holds that individuals should reach a certain age before deciding for themselves whether to take part. In short, age-based laws exist to protect people from harm and to make sure they are mature enough to make informed decisions in particular areas of life.

Yes, you should be seen tonight, and I would go to the emergency room rather than wait to reach your doctor in the morning. At 77, appendicitis and other serious abdominal problems can be harder to catch and can progress faster than in younger people. Older adults often have milder or less typical symptoms, less fever, and less obvious tenderness, even when the appendix is inflamed or close to rupturing. That means you shouldn't be reassured just because the pain feels tolerable.

The specific thing you describe is important. Pain in the right lower abdomen that gets worse when pressure on the left side is applied is a recognized sign, often called Rovsing's sign, and it points toward appendicitis. Combined with bloating and pain in that location, this is exactly the kind of picture that warrants prompt evaluation, usually with an exam, blood tests, and a CT scan or ultrasound. Other conditions can cause similar symptoms in your age group, such as diverticulitis, a bowel obstruction, a hernia, or problems with the colon, and these also need timely attention.

Calling your doctor's after-hours line is reasonable if you can reach someone within a few minutes, but don't let that delay you. If you have any of the following, go right away and consider calling an ambulance rather than driving yourself: fever or chills, vomiting, pain that suddenly worsens or spreads across the abdomen, a hard or rigid belly, dizziness or fainting, a fast heartbeat, or inability to pass gas or stool.

In the meantime, avoid eating or drinking much in case you need surgery or a scan, and don't take laxatives or heating pads, since those can make things worse if the appendix is inflamed. Avoid strong pain medication that might mask symptoms before you are examined, though it's fine to tell the staff what you've taken. If you live alone, try to have someone drive you or let someone know you are going.

It is far better to go in and learn it is something minor than to wait and risk a rupture. I hope it turns out to be nothing serious.

General game playing (GGP) is a branch of artificial intelligence concerned with building computer programs that can independently play many different kinds of games. Its aim is to create one program capable of playing any game, rather than one tailored to a specific title. A typical GGP system has two principal parts: a game description language and a general game-playing agent. The game description language is a formal notation for specifying a game's rules, including the moves available to players, the possible states of the game, and what counts as a win or a loss. The general game-playing agent takes this description, uses it to analyze the current situation, assesses possible moves, and chooses what to do. GGP systems have been applied to board games, card games, and video games, and they have also served as tools for studying decision-making and strategic reasoning in fields such as economics, politics, and military strategy.

LSTM stands for long short-term memory, and it's basically a kind of recurrent neural network that's really good with sequential stuff like time series or natural language. Like any RNN, it reads an input sequence one element at a time and keeps an internal state that holds onto info about what it's already seen. The big difference is that LSTMs were built to get around the vanishing and exploding gradient problems that make regular RNNs a pain to train, so they can actually pick up on longer-term dependencies in the data.

The way it works is you've got a bunch of "cells" processing the input, and each cell has three kinds of gates: input, output, and forget. Those gates let the network choose what to keep and what to toss from its internal state, and they control what flows into and out of the cell.

People have used LSTMs for all sorts of things, like language translation, speech recognition, and time series prediction. They've also been used to generate text and music, and even to model biological sequences like DNA.

Polio being gone from most of the world doesn't mean we can quit vaccinating. A few reasons why.

For one, if we stop, the disease can just come back. Vaccines don't only protect the person getting the shot, they protect the people around them too. When enough people in a community are vaccinated, the disease has a hard time spreading at all. That's herd immunity. Take that away and it can start moving again, and the folks who can't be protected by the vaccine, like tiny babies or people with weak immune systems, are the ones who could get really sick.

Also, polio is still out there in other parts of the world. If we stopped vaccinating, a traveler could bring it in, and then you've got an outbreak in your own town.

And there's no cure for polio. If someone catches it and survives, they can end up with long-term problems like paralysis. Keeping up with vaccines means people don't have to deal with that.

There are really two different questions tangled together here, and both have simple answers.

First, the IDE. NetBeans is a program written in Java, and it runs on the Java Virtual Machine, which is why you saw a Java process in your task manager. But the IDE itself isn't the thing that compiles your code. It is more like a fancy notepad with buttons. When you press "build", it calls a separate tool, the Java compiler (javac), and hands it your files. The compiler happens to also be a Java program, and that's fine, because the JVM is a separate piece of software that can run any Java program, including the compiler.

Now the chicken-and-egg part: if the compiler is written in Java, who compiled the compiler? Imagine you want to build a machine that makes tools, and you need a tool to make the machine. The trick is to do it in stages. The very first Java compiler was written in another language, C. That first compiler was used to compile a Java compiler written in Java. Once that worked, you had a Java compiler made of Java. From then on, each new version of the compiler is compiled by the previous version. This is called bootstrapping, like pulling yourself up by your own bootstraps.

Think of it like a kid learning to talk. At first, grown-ups explain words using gestures and pictures. Once the kid knows enough words, you can explain new words using words the kid already knows. You don't need the gestures anymore. The first Java compiler was the gestures, and later compilers are the words explaining new words.

Many languages do this: C compilers are written in C, and Rust's compiler is written in Rust. It's a nice proof that the language is good enough to build serious tools, including itself.

One more detail: Java doesn't turn your code straight into something the computer's chip understands. The compiler turns it into bytecode, a simpler in-between language, and the JVM reads that bytecode and runs it. So the JVM is the one common helper that runs NetBeans, the compiler, and your own programs alike.

Rocker arms are basically little levers in some internal combustion engines that carry motion from the camshaft over to the valves. They get the name because they rock, or pivot, on a shaft or pivot point while the camshaft lobes push on them. In a typical setup the camshaft sits in the cylinder head, and its lobes are shaped to open and close the valves at just the right moments in the engine's cycle. The rocker arms hook up to the camshaft through a pushrod, and their job is to pass the force along to the valves. So as the cam turns, it pushes the pushrod, the pushrod pushes the rocker arm, and the arm pivots and opens the valve.

You'll see a few different kinds: solid, hydraulic, and roller rockers. Solid ones are the simplest, just a single piece of metal. Hydraulic ones use oil pressure to cut down on friction and wear in the valve train. Roller rockers put a little roller on the tip to cut friction and wear even more. Whichever type you've got, rocker arms matter a lot in an engine, and they're built to handle some serious loads and high speeds.

The right approach depends mostly on whether your company is publicly traded, because that determines whether you can sell shares at the moment you exercise.

If the company is public, this is usually easy. Most brokers that administer employee stock plans offer a cashless exercise, sometimes called a same-day sale. The broker fronts the money to exercise, immediately sells enough shares to cover the exercise price, taxes, and fees, and gives you the rest in cash or shares. A variant called sell-to-cover sells only enough to pay the costs, so you keep the remaining shares. Either way you don't need much cash up front. Your plan administrator, often a firm like Fidelity, Schwab, E*Trade, or Morgan Stanley, will have this as a standard option in its online portal.

If the company is private, it's harder because no market exists to sell into, and the costs include both the strike price and potentially a large tax bill. For non-qualified options, the spread between the strike price and the current fair market value is taxed as ordinary income when you exercise. For incentive stock options, that spread can trigger the alternative minimum tax. You may owe tax on paper gains you can't sell, so estimate the total cash requirement, including taxes, before deciding anything.

In that situation you have several possibilities. You can exercise only part of your grant, picking the number of shares you can afford and leaving the rest for later. You can ask whether the company offers a loan, a cashless exercise program, or a net exercise, where the company withholds some shares to cover the cost. You can look into option financing companies such as Secfi, EquityBee, or ESO Fund, which pay your exercise costs and sometimes the taxes in exchange for a share of the eventual proceeds. These deals are often non-recourse, meaning you owe nothing if the company fails, but they can take a large portion of the upside, so read the terms carefully. Some companies also allow or arrange secondary sales or tender offers, where you sell some vested shares or options to investors, and that money can fund the exercise of the rest.

Timing matters too. If you're still employed, you often don't need to exercise until a liquidity event like an IPO or acquisition, at which point a cashless exercise becomes possible. The pressure usually comes when you leave the company, since many plans give you only 90 days after departure to exercise before the options expire. Check your plan documents, because some companies offer extended post-termination exercise windows of several years, and some will negotiate an extension. Also, if your company allows early exercise of unvested options while the strike price and fair market value are still close, exercising early and filing an 83(b) election can greatly reduce costs and taxes, though that mainly helps with future grants rather than solving the current problem.

Finally, because the tax consequences can be large and depend on option type, your income, and your state, it's worth spending an hour with a tax professional familiar with equity compensation before committing money, particularly for a private company where the shares could end up worth nothing.

Nonparametric statistics is an area of statistics concerned with methods that make no assumptions about the probability distribution underlying the data. Such methods are usually applied when the data fail to satisfy the requirements of parametric tests, or when the distribution is simply not known. A familiar example is the Wilcoxon rank-sum test, which compares two groups of data. Because it does not demand normally distributed data, it is frequently chosen when samples are small or when the data are not normal. Other nonparametric tests include the Mann-Whitney U test, the Kruskal-Wallis test, and the Spearman rank correlation coefficient. These techniques are widely employed in disciplines like psychology, biology, and economics, where data often fail to meet parametric assumptions. They are also helpful when samples are limited or when the data are ordinal instead of continuous. On the other hand, nonparametric tests tend to have less statistical power than their parametric counterparts, so they may be less likely to pick up real differences between groups, yet they remain valuable across many different circumstances.

A pilot study is basically a mini version of a bigger research project. You run it first to see if the whole thing is even doable, and to figure out what might go wrong before you've sunk a ton of time and money into the real deal. If something's off with the design or the method, you catch it early and tweak it.

You see them a lot in medicine, psychology, and the social sciences, but they show up in engineering, education, and business too. What you actually do depends on the project. Maybe you collect data from a small group of people, maybe you run a tiny experiment, or maybe you just test out a new questionnaire, measuring tool, or intervention to see how it holds up.

The big payoff is knowing whether the larger study has a decent shot at working, and getting a chance to polish the design along the way. You also pick up useful clues about things that could affect your results later, like who your participants are, how big your sample needs to be, and which measurement techniques work best.

El Morro, or Castillo San Felipe del Morro if you want the full name, is a 16th-century citadel sitting in Old San Juan, Puerto Rico. It's a UNESCO World Heritage site and one of the island's biggest tourist draws. Built to keep attackers from coming in by sea, it sits on a rocky point right at the mouth of the harbor. It's huge, too, with six levels, a moat, and a bunch of artillery batteries that once fired on any ship trying to sneak past. You can take a tour if you're visiting, and honestly it's worth it for the history of both the fort and the city.

You're right that it's very early, and pain in the lower back and abdomen is unlikely to be a sign of pregnancy this soon. Implantation, when a fertilized egg attaches to the uterine lining, generally happens about 6 to 12 days after ovulation. Some women feel mild cramping or twinges around then, but hormone levels (hCG) are still too low to cause most pregnancy symptoms at that stage. So a period-like ache with no period is more likely to come from something else, though it's not impossible that it's early pregnancy.

Several other things can explain it. Ordinary premenstrual symptoms such as cramping and back pain can start days before a period, and they can be mistaken for it, especially when you're watching your body closely. Ovulation itself can cause one-sided lower abdominal pain, and if your cycle runs a bit differently than you expect, you may simply be earlier in your cycle than you think. Constipation, gas, and bloating are very common causes of lower abdominal and back discomfort. Stress and anticipation can also shift the timing of a period, and trying to conceive often makes people notice every sensation. A urinary tract infection or other pelvic infection can cause similar pain too, so burning with urination, unusual discharge, or fever would be worth mentioning.

For timing, a home pregnancy test is most reliable from the first day of a missed period, or about 14 days after ovulation. Testing earlier can give a false negative, because hCG may not yet be detectable. If your period is late, test with first-morning urine, and if it's negative but your period still hasn't come after a few days, test again.

Some symptoms should not wait. Seek prompt medical care for severe or sharp pain, especially if it is on one side, or for heavy bleeding, dizziness, fainting, or shoulder pain. These can signal an ectopic pregnancy or another urgent problem. Fever or pain that keeps worsening also warrants a visit.

If the pain is mild and your period or a positive test is still pending, it's reasonable to wait a few days and test. If a test is positive, or the pain persists beyond your expected period, check in with a doctor or midwife. Starting a prenatal vitamin with folic acid while you're trying to conceive is also a good idea.

Imagine a giant spinning monster that eats everything in its path. The middle of a tornado is the monster's mouth, and nobody wants to stand in it. That's the simple reason: it's incredibly dangerous. The wind inside a strong tornado can rip houses off their foundations, toss cars like toys, and turn ordinary things like boards and bricks into flying missiles. Any camera that got close enough to look straight down the middle would almost certainly be smashed or carried away, along with whoever was holding it.

There's also a problem with seeing. A tornado isn't a clean tube you can peek into. The air around the center is full of dirt, water, and chunks of debris, so even if a camera survived, it would mostly record a blur of dark mess. Tornadoes also move fast and unpredictably, so you can't just plant a camera and wait for the center to pass over it exactly.

People do wonder about it, though, and a few have tried. In 1928 a Kansas farmer named Will Keller said he looked up into a tornado that passed right over his storm cellar, and he described a hollow, glowing tube with small lightning flashes, but that was only his story, not a video. In 2011, a storm chaser named Brandon Sullivan filmed what looked like the inside of a tornado, and in 2013 the chaser Tim Samaras and his team died while studying a tornado in Oklahoma. Samaras had earlier managed to place a probe in front of a tornado's path, and in 2003 he got readings from inside one, including a sudden drop in air pressure. Scientists also use special mobile radar trucks, which can see inside a tornado from a safe distance by bouncing radio waves off the debris. Those give pictures of wind speed rather than regular photos.

So the answer in kid terms is this: the inside of a tornado is too dangerous, too dirty, and too hard to aim at for a normal camera to get a good look. We know a bit about it from brave people, tough instruments, and radar, but a clear movie of the center is still very rare.

Talk to your doctor before you start taking anything for your brain or memory. They can look at your situation and point you toward options that actually fit you. There's only limited evidence that some supplements help with brain function, so don't expect miracles. A few that come up a lot: omega-3s, which you'll find in fatty fish like salmon, and which may have anti-inflammatory effects on the brain. Ginkgo biloba, an herb people have used for memory for ages, though the research on whether it works is mixed. B vitamins, especially B6, B12, and folic acid, which matter for brain health and might help with memory if you're low on them. Acetyl-L-carnitine, an amino acid that some studies have linked to better memory and thinking. And curcumin, the compound in turmeric, which has anti-inflammatory properties and may help cognition. Keep in mind none of these work for everyone, and they can cause side effects or interact with other meds. So check with a healthcare professional before adding anything new.

So a PRPP, or Pooled Registered Pension Plan, is basically a retirement savings option in Canada. The idea is to help people save up and have some income once they stop working. It's a bit like the more familiar defined benefit and defined contribution plans, since the end goal is the same: a regular income in retirement. The difference is that a PRPP is pooled and run by a professional pension administrator instead of being sponsored by one employer. That means you can join one even if your job doesn't offer a pension at all.

It's open to employees, self-employed people, and business owners. You put money in either through payroll deductions or by making voluntary contributions. You decide how much to contribute, though there are government limits on the max. There's a nice tax perk too. Your contributions and any investment income inside the plan aren't taxed until you actually take the money out.

The federal government regulates them, and they're run by financial institutions or other approved organizations. They're meant to be cheap and pretty easy to set up and manage, which makes them a good fit if you don't have a workplace pension to lean on.

Honestly, the three-blade design comes down to a few things. For one, three blades catch wind energy more efficiently than two, since the load gets split evenly and each blade doesn't have to work as hard, so it can be lighter. Two blades also spin faster, which sounds like a plus but actually makes the rotor harder to balance and more prone to wobble. Three blades keep things steadier because their weight is spread evenly around the hub, so the turbine sits upright and stays calm in gusty wind. And noise is a big one. Three blades give off a smoother, more even whooshing rhythm that people living nearby tend to find less irritating than the choppier sound of fewer blades. So that's pretty much why you see three of them on almost every turbine: better efficiency, better stability, and quieter operation.

Yes. Financing a portfolio on margin increases its variance, and it does so in a specific way that is worth understanding.

When you borrow to buy additional securities, you effectively scale up your exposure to the underlying assets. If you have equity of 100 and borrow 50 to invest 150 in risky assets, your portfolio's returns are determined by the 150 invested, but the gains and losses are measured against only your 100 of equity. The volatility of your equity return is therefore amplified by the leverage ratio. In the simple case where the borrowing is risk-free and the asset return has standard deviation sigma, a leverage factor L (total assets divided by equity) produces an equity return standard deviation of L times sigma. Variance rises with the square of the leverage factor, so doubling leverage quadruples the variance of your returns.

The borrowing itself does not add randomness if the rate is fixed and known, since the debt obligation is a deterministic claim. What creates the added risk is that the debt is a fixed claim against a variable asset, which makes the equity residual more sensitive to asset movements. In practice, if the loan rate floats, or if there is a risk of forced liquidation through margin calls, the variance picture becomes more complicated, and the real risk includes the possibility of losses large enough to trigger a margin call and force sales at unfavorable prices.

Margin financing also has a second-order effect on variance through the correlation structure. If you hold a diversified portfolio, leverage scales the whole portfolio's variance by the square of the leverage factor, so the diversification benefits you had are preserved proportionally but the overall level of risk is magnified. Leverage does not change the relative weights in your portfolio, only the scale.

In short, margin financing increases portfolio variance roughly in proportion to the square of the leverage ratio, and it adds the tail risk of forced liquidation that a simple variance calculation does not capture.

Business intelligence (BI) refers to the set of technologies, processes, and practices that organizations use to collect, integrate, analyze, and present business data so that people can make better-informed decisions. The goal is to turn raw information from sources such as sales records, customer databases, financial systems, and operational logs into insights that managers and employees can act on.

A typical BI setup involves several stages. Data is first gathered from different internal and sometimes external systems and then cleaned, standardized, and stored in a central location such as a data warehouse. From there, analysts and tools query and transform the data to answer questions like which products are most profitable, where costs are rising, or how customer behavior is changing over time. The results are commonly displayed through dashboards, reports, charts, and interactive visualizations that make patterns easy to spot.

BI tools range from traditional reporting software to modern self-service platforms that let non-technical users explore data on their own. Popular examples include Microsoft Power BI, Tableau, and Looker. Many BI systems also incorporate forecasting and basic statistical analysis, and increasingly they use machine learning to highlight anomalies or predict future outcomes.

In essence, business intelligence helps organizations move from relying on intuition or outdated information to making decisions grounded in timely, accurate data, which can improve efficiency, reveal new opportunities, and reduce risk.

Swelling of the feet and legs, known as edema, can have many different causes. These include remaining in the same standing or sitting position for too long, pregnancy, menstruation, and certain drugs such as nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) or some blood pressure medications. Problems with the heart, liver, kidneys, or thyroid can also be responsible. Another cause is venous insufficiency, in which the veins struggle to carry blood from the legs back up to the heart. Disorders of the lymphatic system, such as lymphoma or lymphedema, can produce swelling as well.

In your situation, the swelling may be connected to the stress you have been under. Stress can raise levels of the hormone cortisol, which may cause the body to hold on to fluid. However, it could just as easily result from one of the other causes mentioned above. Because swelling can signal a more serious underlying condition, you should have it checked by a medical professional. A doctor can run tests to identify the cause and suggest suitable treatment.

Until then, raising your legs whenever you sit or lie down may bring some relief, as may avoiding long periods in a single standing or sitting position. Compression stockings can also help reduce the swelling.

Interactive Brokers and Questrade are both popular discount brokers in Canada, so you've got two solid options. Here's how they stack up.
