Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty, also called the Washington Treaty, is the backbone of NATO. It lays out the mutual defense commitment: if one member gets attacked, every member treats it as an attack on all of them. The text reads: "The Parties agree that an armed attack against one or more of them in Europe or North America shall be considered an attack against them all and consequently they agree that, if such an armed attack occurs, each of them, in exercise of the right of individual or collective self-defence recognised by Article 51 of the Charter of the United Nations, will assist the Party or Parties so attacked by taking forthwith, individually and in concert with the other Parties, such action as it deems necessary, including the use of armed force, to restore and maintain the security of the North Atlantic area." It's been invoked just once, after the September 11, 2001 attacks on the United States. Afterward, NATO allies gave the US military and logistical help and joined the wider fight against terrorism.

A redshirt freshman is a college football player who is in his second year at a school but only his first year of playing eligibility used in games. The term comes from "redshirting," a practice in which an athlete sits out a season of competition, usually practicing with the team but not playing in games, so that he preserves a year of eligibility.

Under NCAA rules, athletes generally have four seasons of competition they can use. By redshirting during his first year on campus, a player can spend that year practicing, learning the system, lifting weights, and adding size and strength without losing one of those four seasons. The name is said to come from the red jersey that scout team or non-competing players often wear in practice to distinguish them from the starters.

Teams redshirt players for several reasons. A young player may not be physically ready to compete at the college level, or there may be older players ahead of him on the depth chart, so it makes more sense to develop him for a year rather than use up a season on limited playing time. Players may also redshirt because of an injury that keeps them out for most or all of a season.

So in his second year, a redshirt freshman is academically a sophomore but still has the athletic standing of a freshman, with four years of eligibility remaining. Under more recent rules, players can also appear in a limited number of games, currently up to four, and still keep the redshirt, which has made the practice more flexible. Some players also redshirt later in their careers, usually because of injury, and then they are called redshirt sophomores, juniors, or seniors depending on how many years they have been in the program.

The right choice depends on whether you value low cost, flexibility, or protection more, because each of these options trades one of those off against the others.

Parent PLUS loans are federal loans parents take out for a dependent undergraduate. Their main advantage is protection rather than price. The rate is fixed (8.94 percent for loans disbursed in the 2025–26 year), and there is an origination fee of roughly 4.2 percent taken off the top, so the effective cost is often higher than home equity borrowing. In exchange, you get things no bank offers. The debt is discharged if the parent dies or becomes totally and permanently disabled, or if the student dies. Deferment and forbearance are available during hardship. Your house is never at risk. Approval depends only on not having an adverse credit history, not on income or a credit score. Interest may qualify for the student loan interest deduction of up to $2,500 a year, subject to income limits. Keep in mind that federal law changed in 2025. For new Parent PLUS loans made on or after July 1, 2026, borrowing is capped at $20,000 per year and $65,000 total per student. Those loans will also lose access to income-driven repayment, which removes one of the program's former safety valves, so check the current rules before you borrow.

A HELOC is a revolving line of credit secured by your home. It is usually cheaper up front, with minimal or no closing costs and rates that often run a bit below PLUS rates for borrowers with good credit and solid equity. It is also flexible, since you draw only what you need each semester and pay interest only on what you've drawn. The downsides are significant, though. The rate is almost always variable, so a four-year college plan plus a ten- or twenty-year repayment period exposes you to rate increases. Many HELOCs also have an interest-only draw period followed by a sharp jump in payments when repayment begins. Most importantly, your home is the collateral, so if a job loss or illness makes payments impossible, you risk foreclosure rather than simply entering forbearance. Under current tax law, interest on home equity debt used for tuition is generally not deductible, because the deduction applies only when the money buys, builds, or substantially improves the home.

A second mortgage, usually called a home equity loan, is also secured by your house but pays out a lump sum at a fixed rate with a fixed payment schedule. That predictability is its main appeal over a HELOC, and its rates are often competitive with or lower than PLUS. However, you borrow everything at once and pay interest on the full amount immediately, even though tuition is due over several years. Closing costs can be higher than a HELOC's, and it carries the same foreclosure risk and the same lack of tax deductibility for education use.

A few broader points apply across all three. Home equity is not counted as an asset on the FAFSA, but cash you've borrowed and left sitting in a bank account can be, so timing draws close to when bills are due can matter. You should also compare private parent loans and, ideally, exhaust the student's own federal Direct Loans first. Those carry lower rates, no credit check, and stronger repayment protections, and they put some of the responsibility on the student.

As a general rule of thumb, a HELOC or home equity loan makes the most sense for parents with stable, secure income, substantial equity, a clear plan to pay the balance off within a few years, and enough cushion that the house would never be at real risk. Parent PLUS tends to be the better choice when income is less certain, when the parent is nearing retirement, or when the death and disability discharge and hardship options are worth the higher cost. Between the two home equity products, choose a HELOC if you want to borrow gradually and can tolerate rate risk, and choose a fixed home equity loan if you want certainty and need most of the money soon. Running the total cost of each option over your realistic payoff timeline, including fees, is the best way to make the decision concrete.

Okay, so data visualization is basically turning numbers into pictures so people can actually get what the data is saying. You pick the right visual encoding (position, length, angle, area, color, that kind of thing) and use those to build something a viewer can read without much effort. It's a big deal in data analysis. People use it to dig into huge datasets, spot patterns or trends, and then explain what they found to others. You can make all sorts of things with it: charts, plots, maps, diagrams, you name it.

As for tools, there's a ton to choose from. Excel and Tableau are popular, D3 is great if you're comfortable with code, and R and Python are everywhere for this stuff. You can start with simple bar charts or line plots and work your way up to heat maps or tree diagrams. Honestly, if you work with data at all, getting good at visualizing it is worth the time.

I'm assuming you mean "rovers," since Land Rover is a car brand, and no Land Rovers have been to Mars. The number of rovers that have successfully landed on Mars is five, all sent by NASA, plus one from China.

NASA's first was Sojourner, which landed in 1997 as part of the Mars Pathfinder mission. Spirit and Opportunity followed in 2004. Spirit operated until 2010, while Opportunity kept going until 2018. Curiosity landed in 2012 and is still operating. Perseverance arrived in February 2021 and carried the Ingenuity helicopter, which made dozens of flights before its mission ended in 2024.

China's Zhurong rover landed in May 2021 as part of the Tianwen-1 mission and operated for a time before going dormant in 2022. That brings the total to six successful Mars rovers: five American and one Chinese.

If you count only those still working, Curiosity and Perseverance are the active ones, as far as I know. Other countries have attempted Mars landings, such as the Soviet Union's Mars 3 in 1971, which briefly transmitted from the surface and carried a small rover that was never deployed, but no other rovers have operated there.

There's a bunch of stuff you can do to protect yourself from identity theft, and most of it isn't hard.

First off, keep your personal info locked down. Your social security number, birth date, that kind of thing. Only hand it over when you really have to, and only to people or places you trust.

Passwords matter a lot too. Use a strong, different one for every account, and don't share them with anybody. Turn on two-factor authentication wherever it's offered. It's a bit annoying, but it works.

Be careful online. Don't click links or open attachments from people you don't know, and run some decent security software on your computer and phone so malware doesn't sneak in.

Check your bank and credit card statements regularly for charges you don't recognize. You can also set up alerts so you get pinged if something looks off, which saves you from having to catch it yourself.

When you're shopping or doing anything with money online, make sure the site is secure. Look for "https" at the start of the URL and a little padlock in the address bar.

Don't forget your physical mail. A locked mailbox helps, or you can get a P.O. box. And shred anything with personal info on it before you toss it.

Finally, be wary of giving out personal details over the phone or online, especially to outfits you've never heard of. If you stick with all this, you'll cut your risk of getting hit by identity theft by a lot.

Nitrates and nitrites are close cousins. Both are made of a nitrogen atom stuck to some oxygen atoms. The only real difference is how many oxygen atoms are attached. A nitrate has three oxygens, and a nitrite has two. You can remember it this way: nitrATE has more letters in the ending sound and more oxygen, while nitrITE is the "lighter" one with one less.

They can turn into each other. When a nitrate loses one of its oxygens, it becomes a nitrite. Tiny bacteria do this all the time, including the ones in your mouth when you eat vegetables like spinach, celery, and beets, which are naturally full of nitrates. So your body is already used to handling both.

For your ham, nitrite is the one that does the actual work. It keeps dangerous germs from growing, especially the one that causes botulism, a very serious kind of food poisoning. It also gives ham its pink color and its familiar "cured" flavor. Without it, ham would look grayish-brown like plain cooked pork. In the old days people cured meat with nitrate (saltpeter), and over a long time bacteria slowly turned it into nitrite. Today makers mostly skip that slow step and add nitrite directly, which is easier to control. So the kid at the store was right: modern ham usually has nitrite, not nitrate.

One extra thing worth knowing: if you see ham labeled "uncured" or "no nitrites added," it often contains celery powder or celery juice instead. Celery is loaded with natural nitrates that get turned into nitrites, so it ends up doing basically the same job. It's not really nitrite-free, just nitrite from a different source.

As for health, eating a lot of processed, cured meat has been linked to a higher risk of some cancers, partly because nitrites can form harmful compounds when meat is cooked at high heat. That's a reason to enjoy ham in moderation rather than a reason to panic about a sandwich.

Okay so this is a classic thought experiment about infinity, and it's kinda fun. Picture a turtle on a tiny island somewhere in the sun, standing on top of a pillar that's so tall it runs up into the sky. The turtle is holding a feather. It lets go, and as the feather drifts down, the turtle takes one tiny step down the pillar. Now the question: will the feather ever hit the ground before the turtle does?

Surprisingly, the answer is no. No matter how long the feather falls, the turtle can always take one more tiny step before the feather lands. There's no end to the number of tiny steps it can take, so the feather never catches up. That's the whole point of the puzzle. It's meant to get you thinking about infinity, the idea of something with no end or limit. Here the steps never run out, so the feather never gets the turtle.

I'm sorry your baby is unwell. Several things could explain this combination, and some are common and minor while others need prompt medical attention, so it's worth having a doctor look at him soon.

Green, loose, smelly stools are very often caused by an infection, especially a viral gut infection (gastroenteritis), which can follow or occur alongside a cold. Feeding changes can also contribute: when a baby is congested, he may struggle to breathe and suck at the same time, which leads to smaller feeds, less food intake, and sometimes milk that is digested differently. Green color itself is often just bile in the stool and is not always a sign of danger on its own. Vomiting a small amount of food with mucus is frequently caused by swallowing the mucus that drains from a blocked nose during a cold, which can irritate the stomach and trigger gagging or spitting up.

Still, a baby who is refusing feeds, not finishing bottles, and has loose stools with vomiting needs to be watched closely for dehydration, which can become serious quickly in infants. Signs to act on right away include fewer wet diapers than usual (for example, fewer than about four or five in 24 hours), a dry mouth, crying without tears, a sunken soft spot on the head, unusual sleepiness or floppiness, vomiting that becomes forceful or green, blood in the stool, a swollen or hard belly, breathing that is fast or labored, or a fever developing. Any of these means he should be seen the same day or go to emergency care.

Even without these signs, I'd recommend contacting your pediatrician or a health clinic today rather than waiting. They can check his hydration, listen to his chest and ears, and decide whether he needs stool testing or other evaluation. In the meantime, keep offering small, frequent feeds, try to clear his nose with saline drops and gentle suction before feeds, keep him upright for a while after feeding, and offer extra fluids in small amounts if he is taking them, while continuing to watch his wet diapers closely.

Solar panels generate electricity by harnessing the sun's energy. They rely on special materials that take in sunlight and turn it into electrical power. The process goes like this: sunlight strikes the panels, and the materials within them absorb it. The absorbed energy dislodges electrons from their atoms, and this movement of electrons produces an electric current. The current then travels to an inverter, which changes it into a form suitable for running a home or business. In short, solar panels capture the sun's energy and transform it into electricity that can run your electronic devices.

To sell mutual fund holdings inside your 401(k), start by signing in to your account via your employer's benefits site or the website of the third-party administrator that manages the plan. Go to the investments area and locate the fund you wish to dispose of. Choose that fund, then press the "Sell" option. The system will ask how many shares you'd like to part with, and you'll need to verify the order. If your holding is substantial, the plan might cap how much can be withdrawn in a single transaction, meaning you could have to split the sale across multiple orders. Once the sale settles, the cash will show up in your account, where you can reinvest it in other options or take it out. Keep in mind that selling funds within a 401(k) can carry tax consequences, so speaking with a financial planner or tax professional before adjusting your investments is wise.

ImageNet is a huge image database built for object recognition research. Every year since 2010, the ImageNet project has run the ImageNet Large Scale Visual Recognition Challenge (ILSVRC), where teams train image classification and object detection models on the dataset and then test them. It's become one of the biggest events in computer vision. The dataset has over 14 million images spread across more than 22,000 categories. The pictures come from the internet and get labeled with whatever objects or concepts show up in them. Teams train on a chunk of the data, called the training set, then check how well their model does on a separate chunk, the validation set. Accuracy gets measured by top-1 error rate, which is just the fraction of validation images the model gets wrong. The competition has pushed a lot of new techniques forward, and plenty of the winning models ended up everywhere in industry and academia. It also turned ImageNet into the go-to benchmark for judging image recognition models.

I can't tell you the cause from these symptoms alone, but some of them together are worth taking seriously, especially the missed period combined with stomach pain.

The most important thing to do first is take a home pregnancy test. Many early pregnancies cause no obvious symptoms, and a missed period is a common sign of pregnancy even when you feel normal. Stomach pain, loss of appetite, food sensitivities, and headaches can all occur in early pregnancy too. If the test is positive, or if it's negative but your period still hasn't come after a few more days, see a doctor. Missed periods can also come from hormonal changes, stress, thyroid problems, significant weight change, or other causes.

The stomach symptoms themselves could have several explanations. Sharp pain that is worse in the morning, along with reduced appetite and sensitivity to certain foods, is often linked to gastritis (inflammation of the stomach lining), acid reflux, or a peptic ulcer. Stress, irregular eating, and some medications such as painkillers can bring these on. Gallbladder problems, which often cause pain after meals, and irritable bowel syndrome are other possibilities. Mild headaches alongside these symptoms can come from stress, dehydration, skipped meals, or poor sleep.

See a doctor soon, ideally within the next few days, since you have several symptoms that have persisted and a missed period. Seek urgent care right away if you have severe or worsening abdominal pain, pain on one side of your lower abdomen, vomiting blood or material that looks like coffee grounds, black or bloody stools, fainting or dizziness, heavy vaginal bleeding, fever, or yellowing of your skin or eyes. Pain on one side with a possible pregnancy can sometimes signal an ectopic pregnancy, which is a medical emergency.

A doctor can examine you, run a pregnancy test and blood tests, and if needed arrange further tests such as an ultrasound or an endoscopy. Until then, try eating smaller, bland meals, avoid alcohol, caffeine, spicy and fatty foods, and NSAID painkillers like ibuprofen, and keep track of which foods seem to trigger your pain.

Multiple myeloma is a cancer of the plasma cells, the immune cells that live in your bone marrow. It often causes bone lesions (areas of abnormal bone), and those can lead to fractures and pain. Treatment usually mixes several approaches: chemo, radiation, meds to strengthen bones, and pain control. What works best depends on things like the stage of the disease, your general health, and any other conditions you have.

Here's what's commonly used. Chemotherapy uses drugs to kill cancer cells. They can be taken as pills or given through an IV, and they're often combined with other treatments. Radiation therapy aims high-energy beams at the cancer to destroy it, and doctors often use it on bone lesions, sometimes alongside chemo. Bone-strengthening drugs like bisphosphonates can cut the risk of fractures and help improve bone density. And for pain, people might take NSAIDs or opioids, depending on how bad things are.

Definitely talk through all your options and the possible side effects with your care team. They're the ones who can figure out what makes sense for your particular situation.

Emergency contraceptive pills such as Postinor-2 are meant to serve as a backup against pregnancy when a regular method fails, for example if a condom breaks or birth control pills are missed. They are not designed for ongoing, routine use. When taken as directed after unprotected intercourse, Postinor-2 should help prevent pregnancy, though it is less effective than consistent methods like the pill, patch, or ring. If you have had unprotected sex after taking Postinor-2 and are worried about a pregnancy, speak with a healthcare professional or get medical advice promptly. Using Postinor-2 more than once within two weeks is discouraged, since it raises the likelihood of side effects including nausea, vomiting, and irregular bleeding. To avoid unplanned pregnancies and reduce the risk of sexually transmitted infections (STIs), it is important to rely on dependable contraception. If you are sexually active and not using a regular method, a healthcare provider can explain the options that suit you.

A processor, also called a central processing unit (CPU), is the main component of a computer responsible for most of its processing work. It carries out the instructions of a computer program by repeatedly retrieving instructions from memory, interpreting them, and then executing them. Because the processor governs how quickly a computer can complete tasks, it is an essential part of any computer system. A faster processor runs instructions more rapidly, which improves overall performance. Today's processors are also built to consume less power, which extends battery life in laptops and other portable devices. Processors come in a wide range of types, from entry-level chips in budget laptops to powerful chips used in gaming PCs and servers. Their performance is usually described using clock speed, meaning how many instructions they can execute each second, and core count, which is the number of processing units inside a single processor. Beyond running instructions, processors also handle input/output (I/O) operations, manage memory, and respond to interrupts. These responsibilities are divided among the processor's control unit, which retrieves and decodes instructions from memory, and the arithmetic/logic unit (ALU), which carries out arithmetic and logical calculations.

Romani people, sometimes called Gypsies, are a group of families who have lived in many countries for a very long time. Their story began a long, long time ago in India, and many of them travelled from place to place, which is why they now live in lots of different countries, including parts of Europe, and some live in America too.

Romani people have their own language, called Romani, and they often have their own music, dances, and stories. Many families have traditions they love, like celebrating weddings with lots of music and dancing, and sharing food and holidays with their relatives.

Sometimes people have treated Romani people unfairly, and some people used the word "Gypsy" in a mean way. That's why many Romani people prefer to be called Romani, which is the name they use for themselves. It's always kind to ask people what they like to be called.

So, the most important thing to know is that Romani people are families with their own language, music, and traditions, just like many other families around the world.

99-cent stores keep their prices so low largely because they purchase merchandise in large quantities and negotiate discounts with their suppliers. They also stock products that are less in demand or have small flaws, since suppliers will sell these at a reduced price. On top of that, they hold down operating expenses with a compact, no-frills store design, and they pass the resulting savings along to shoppers. Computer art is basically any art made with software and hardware, so it covers a lot: illustration, graphic design, video, animation, you name it. People make it with all sorts of tools, from 2D and 3D modeling to vector and raster graphics, and even straight-up code. It often relies on specialized techniques that just aren't possible with paint, pencil, or clay. It's blown up over the past few years, mostly because more people can get their hands on decent hardware and software. You'll see it in ads, movies and games, classrooms, and so on. It's also showing up more in contemporary art, and you'll find it hanging in galleries and museums right next to the traditional stuff.

A life insurance policy is a contract between you and an insurance company. You pay premiums, either monthly or annually, and in return the insurer pays a sum of money, called the death benefit, to the people you name as beneficiaries when you die. The main purpose is to protect people who depend on your income, such as a spouse, children, or business partners, by helping them cover living expenses, debts, funeral costs, or future needs like education.

There are two broad categories. Term life insurance covers you for a fixed period, commonly 10, 20, or 30 years. If you die during that time, the benefit is paid; if you outlive the term, coverage ends and nothing is paid out. Because it is pure protection, it is generally the cheapest option and is a good fit for people who need coverage during working years or while raising a family. Permanent life insurance, which includes whole life, universal life, and variable life, lasts your entire life as long as premiums are paid. These policies also build cash value that you can borrow against or withdraw, but they cost considerably more, and the fees and complexity can be significant.

When choosing a policy, the first question is how much coverage you need. A common rule of thumb is ten to twelve times your annual income, but a better approach is to add up your debts, the income your family would need to replace, future expenses such as college, and final costs, then subtract existing savings and other insurance. Next, consider the term length, which should last until your dependents are financially independent or your mortgage is paid off.

Premiums depend on your age, health, tobacco use, occupation, hobbies, and the amount of coverage. Buying younger and healthier locks in lower rates. Most insurers require an application and often a medical exam, though some offer no-exam or simplified issue policies at higher prices. Be honest on the application, since misstatements can lead to a denied claim.

Other things to know include naming and periodically updating your beneficiaries, understanding the contestability period (usually two years, during which the insurer can investigate claims more closely), and the suicide clause that often applies in the early years. Riders can add features such as waiver of premium if you become disabled, accelerated death benefits for terminal illness, or the ability to convert a term policy to permanent coverage. Death benefits are generally income-tax-free to beneficiaries in the United States, though large estates may face estate tax.

It is wise to compare quotes from several insurers, check their financial strength ratings from agencies like AM Best, and consider speaking with an independent agent or fee-only financial planner. So under federal gift tax rules in the US, you can give up to $15,000 per recipient per year without owing any gift tax. That means you can hand $15,000 in cash or other assets to each of your kids and you're in the clear. Go over that amount and you'll need to file a gift tax return, and you might owe tax, but the lifetime exclusion is $11.7 million per person, so unless you're planning to give your kids well over that, you probably won't actually pay anything. One thing people miss: the kids aren't automatically tax-free on what they receive. If a gift is big enough, they could face taxes on it, but those thresholds sit way above $15,000, so a gift that size almost certainly won't create a tax bill for them.

The MNIST database (Modified National Institute of Standards and Technology database) is a widely used collection of handwritten digit images, designed for training and testing image processing and machine learning systems. It contains 70,000 grayscale images of the digits 0 through 9, each 28 by 28 pixels in size. The set is split into 60,000 images for training and 10,000 for testing. The images were drawn from a mix of sources, including American Census Bureau employees and American high school students, and were normalized and centered so that the digits appear in a consistent format.

Because it is small, clean, and easy to work with, MNIST became a standard benchmark in the machine learning community, particularly for developing and comparing classification algorithms. It is often the first dataset that students encounter when learning about neural networks and computer vision. Early work on convolutional neural networks, such as Yann LeCun's LeNet models, was evaluated on MNIST, and modern models now achieve error rates well below one percent on it. Although it is considered too simple to be a meaningful challenge for state-of-the-art research today, it remains a popular teaching and prototyping tool. It is freely available and is included in many machine learning libraries, which makes it simple to load and experiment with.

Okay, so Benjamin Graham, the guy basically everyone calls the father of value investing, laid out his stock-picking approach in "The Intelligent Investor." He had this idea of the "defensive investor," someone who mostly wants to avoid losing money and still come away with a decent return. One of the main rules he gave that person was to look for stocks with a high earnings-per-share (EPS) ratio. His rule of thumb was that the earnings yield should be at least twice the current long-term bond yield, which is basically what you'd get on long-term government bonds. So if bonds are paying 3%, you'd want the earnings yield to be at least 6%.

Graham also liked stocks with a solid dividend yield, a strong balance sheet, and a long history of being stable and reliable. None of that guarantees anything, but it can cut down on risk and make a good return more likely.

Institutional racism is basically when societal institutions end up treating certain groups of people unfairly. It shows up in lots of ways, but a few examples people often point to in the US are:

Drug laws: A lot of folks argue that drug laws get enforced much more heavily against racial minorities, which leads to way higher incarceration rates for those groups.

Voter suppression: Some laws, like voter ID requirements or purges of voter rolls, have been criticized for hitting racial minorities harder and making it tougher for them to cast a ballot.

Immigration policies: Detention and deportation practices have drawn criticism for falling disproportionately on racial and ethnic minorities.

Redlining: Back in the day, banks and other lenders would refuse loans or financial services to people in certain neighborhoods, based on the race or ethnicity of those areas. That helped entrench segregation and made it much harder for people of color to get credit and build wealth.

Drilling depth under the sea depends on two things: how deep the water is, and how far the drill goes into the rock below the seafloor.

For water depth, modern drillships can operate in roughly 3,000 to 3,600 meters (about 10,000 to 12,000 feet) of water for commercial oil and gas work. Some vessels are rated for even deeper, and the record for a drilled well in water is around 3,400 meters or more. Scientific drilling ships such as the JOIDES Resolution and the Japanese vessel Chikyu have worked in water nearly 7,000 meters deep. Chikyu, with its riser system, can drill in about 2,500 meters of water, and without a riser it can go much deeper.

For depth below the seafloor, commercial wells commonly reach 6,000 to 10,000 meters total depth measured from the rig, and some have gone beyond 10,000 meters. For instance, the Deepwater Horizon drilled the Tiber well to about 10,685 meters (35,055 feet) total depth in the Gulf of Mexico, in roughly 1,260 meters of water. Scientific drilling has reached about 3,000 meters or more below the seafloor; Chikyu set a record of around 3,250 meters below the seafloor off Japan, and it has aimed for greater depths.

The limits come from heat, pressure, and equipment. Temperatures rise with depth, often 25 to 30 degrees Celsius per kilometer, and high pressure can damage tools and drilling fluids. Very long drill strings also become heavy and prone to twisting or breaking, and in deep water the riser pipe connecting the ship to the seafloor must withstand strong currents and its own weight. Keeping the borehole stable is another challenge, since rock can collapse or fluids can surge in unexpectedly.

For comparison, the deepest hole ever drilled on land is the Kola Superdeep Borehole in Russia at about 12,262 meters, which shows that the practical limit with current technology is around 12 kilometers, and underwater drilling is usually shallower than that.

Gastritis refers to an inflammation of the stomach lining, and it may bring about abdominal pain, nausea, bloating, and a sense of fullness. Anyone who suspects they have it should see a doctor to get an accurate diagnosis and appropriate treatment. While waiting for that appointment, several steps may ease the discomfort. Stay away from foods likely to irritate the stomach, including spicy and fatty dishes. Choose smaller meals eaten more often rather than a few large ones. Give up smoking and avoid alcohol. An over-the-counter antacid or acid blocker, such as omeprazole (Prilosec) or ranitidine (Zantac), can lower the amount of stomach acid. A warm bath or a heating pad placed on the abdomen may relax the muscles and soothe pain. Drinking plenty of fluids, water in particular, can help wash irritants out of the digestive tract. Keep in mind that these measures only offer short-term relief, and you should see a doctor if the symptoms continue or if you have any worries.

Adversarial machine learning is a subfield of machine learning that studies how models can be deceived, manipulated, or attacked, and how to make them more robust against such attacks. The core observation driving the field is that many machine learning systems, especially deep neural networks, can be surprisingly fragile. A small, often imperceptible change to an input, such as adjusting a few pixels in an image, can cause a model to produce a confident but incorrect prediction. A photo of a panda, for example, might be altered with noise invisible to a human so that the classifier labels it as a gibbon with high confidence.

The field generally considers several categories of attack. Evasion attacks occur at inference time, when an attacker crafts inputs designed to slip past a model, such as malware modified to avoid detection or altered road signs that confuse a self-driving car's vision system. Poisoning attacks happen during training, when an adversary inserts malicious or mislabeled data into the training set so that the resulting model behaves incorrectly on certain inputs or contains a hidden backdoor. Model extraction or stealing attacks involve querying a deployed model repeatedly to reconstruct a copy of it or approximate its behavior. Privacy attacks, such as membership inference and model inversion, aim to learn sensitive information about the training data from the model's outputs.

On the defensive side, researchers pursue several strategies. Adversarial training augments the training process with adversarial examples so the model learns to resist them. Certified defenses try to provide mathematical guarantees that a model's prediction will not change within a given range of input perturbations. Other approaches include input preprocessing, detection of suspicious inputs, differential privacy for protecting training data, and careful data curation to guard against poisoning.

The field matters because machine learning is increasingly used in security-sensitive settings such as fraud detection, content moderation, autonomous driving, and medical diagnosis. Understanding these vulnerabilities is essential for building systems that remain reliable when facing not just random errors but deliberate efforts to exploit them.

I cannot say with any accuracy when the world will come to an end. People have offered forecasts of doomsday, but none of them rest on scientific or trustworthy evidence. A large number of these past forecasts have failed to materialize, and there is little reason to think the planet will cease to exist on May 21 or on any other particular day. It helps to keep in mind that Earth has existed for billions of years, so there is no justification for expecting its end in the near future.

Peter Wegner is a computer scientist and professor, and he's best known for his work on programming language design and implementation. He got his PhD in computer science from UC Berkeley in 1969. After that he taught at a few schools, including the University of Arizona, Brown, and UC San Diego. A lot of his work centers on how programming languages get designed and built, and he's contributed to ALGOL 68 along the way. He's also written plenty of papers on software engineering, programming language design, and the history of computing.

Film colorization is the process of adding color to black-and-white or monochrome footage, photographs, or other visual media that were originally recorded without color. Because the original image contains only brightness information, the colorist must estimate and supply the hues, saturation, and tonal values that would have been present in the real scene, and this estimation is what makes the process both artistically interesting and historically controversial.

The earliest forms of colorization were manual and labor-intensive. In the early twentieth century, some silent films were hand-tinted, with individual frames painted or dyed, and stencil techniques were used to apply color to prints. Later, in the 1980s, computer-assisted methods emerged. Colorists would digitize each frame, select regions of the image, and assign color values to those areas, often working with reference photographs, period costume records, and knowledge of set design. Modern approaches increasingly rely on machine learning, where neural networks trained on large collections of color and black-and-white images predict plausible colors automatically, though human artists typically review and correct the results.

The practice has drawn considerable debate. Supporters argue that colorization makes older works more accessible to modern audiences, can restore a sense of how the past actually looked, and offers a creative way to reinterpret classic material. Critics, including many film directors, historians, and preservationists, contend that colorization alters the artistic intent of filmmakers who deliberately chose black-and-white photography, and that the colors added are necessarily guesses that may misrepresent history. A notable controversy arose in the 1980s when Ted Turner's company colorized numerous classic Hollywood films, prompting protests and advocacy for legislation to protect the integrity of original works.

Founded in 1821, The Guardian is a British newspaper recognized for a left-leaning editorial position. Its coverage spans many subjects, among them politics, world affairs, business, science, technology, the environment, culture, and the arts. The paper has earned a name for independent, high-quality journalism, and many people admire the depth of its reporting and analysis. Available both in print and on the internet, it attracts a large readership around the world. Beyond straight news, The Guardian carries opinion columns and other editorial material, along with various multimedia offerings such as podcasts and videos.

I'm sorry your son has been going through this. A swelling under the scrotum that follows a boil, needs antibiotics, and then drains is most often a skin infection that has spread into deeper tissue, such as an abscess or a deeper soft tissue infection. Sometimes these are caused by staph bacteria, and sometimes a boil in the groin area can lead to a collection of pus that needs to be opened and drained. The antifungal treatment he received suggests the doctors also considered a fungal cause, which is sometimes seen in warm, moist skin folds like the groin. The drainage and the dehydration point to an infection that is significant enough to need closer monitoring.

I can't tell from here exactly what he has, and the details matter a lot, so the most useful step is to ask his care team directly. Good questions to ask include what the diagnosis is, whether the swelling was ever drained or needs to be, what the drainage culture showed, which antibiotic he is on and how long he should take it, and what signs would mean he needs to return right away. It's also worth asking whether he needs a follow-up visit, an ultrasound, or a referral to a urologist or surgeon if the swelling persists.

In the meantime, several things generally help with infections like this. He should keep the area clean and dry, change dressings as instructed, avoid tight underwear or clothing that rubs, and make sure he drinks enough fluids, since dehydration can make him feel worse and affects recovery. Over-the-counter pain relievers can ease discomfort, but check with the doctor first about which one is appropriate. Warm compresses are sometimes recommended for swelling, but only if his doctor agrees, since they can be wrong for some conditions.

He should be seen urgently if he develops a fever or chills, worsening pain, redness that spreads, new swelling, pus or bleeding that increases, trouble urinating, confusion, dizziness, very little urine, or if he seems unusually drowsy or unwell. Those signs can mean the infection is spreading or he is becoming dehydrated again.

Under United States federal gift tax rules, you may transfer a certain amount of c 
money or other property to a person without incurring gift tax. This yearly exemption, known as the annual exclusion, is presently $15,000 for each recipient in each year. Accordingly, you can hand over up to $15,000 in cash or other assets to each child without owing any gift tax. Should you wish to exceed the annual exclusion for a child, you are free to do so, though you would need to file a gift tax return and might owe tax. The current lifetime gift tax exemption stands at $11.7 million per individual, so barring plans to give your children far more than that figure, you are unlikely to owe any gift tax. Keep in mind that gifts are not necessarily tax-free for the recipients either. Children who receive cash or property might owe taxes on its value if it surpasses certain limits. Those limits, however, are generally well above the annual exclusion, so it is improbable that a child would owe tax on a gift of $15,000 or less.

Imagine you have a tiny bit of stuff, like a crumb of cookie. Einstein figured out that even a small crumb of stuff holds a huge hidden amount of energy, which is energy that is locked inside it and just sitting there, not moving or glowing. The formula tells you how much. The "m" is how much stuff you have, and the "c" is the speed of light, which is incredibly fast, about 300,000 kilometers every second. Because c is multiplied by itself (that little 2 means "times itself"), the number gets enormous very quickly. So a crumb of stuff, multiplied by that giant number, turns into a gigantic amount of energy.

Think of it like a secret piggy bank. Matter, the stuff all around us, is like a bank that has a huge pile of energy saved up inside, even though we rarely see it spend any. Most of the time nothing happens to unlock it, so we never notice. But in some special situations, like inside the Sun or inside a nuclear power plant, a little bit of matter gets converted into energy, and that releases an amazing amount of heat and light. The Sun shines because it keeps turning a small amount of its mass into energy, and that energy travels all the way to Earth to keep us warm.

It is also how atomic bombs work, which is why the formula is famous. A tiny change in the weight of atoms during a nuclear reaction releases a massive burst of energy, and the formula explains where that energy came from.

So the big idea is this: mass and energy are two forms of the same thing. Stuff can be turned into energy, and energy can, in a sense, be stuff. The formula is just the exchange rate between them, and because the speed of light is so enormous, even a tiny amount of mass is worth a tremendous amount of energy.

People who reach retirement age with no savings usually end up depending on some combination of government programs, continued work, family support, and a significantly reduced standard of living. The exact picture depends a lot on the country, but in the United States, which is where this question comes up most often, the main safety net is Social Security. Most workers who have paid into the system for at least ten years qualify for a monthly benefit, and for a large share of older Americans it makes up most or all of their income. The average retirement benefit is roughly two thousand dollars a month, though people with lower lifetime earnings receive less. That amount can cover basic needs in some areas but is often tight, especially for renters in expensive cities.

Beyond Social Security, people with very low income and assets may qualify for Supplemental Security Income, which provides a small additional monthly payment, as well as Medicaid, food assistance through SNAP, housing subsidies, and help with utility bills. Medicare kicks in at sixty-five and covers much of health care, though it leaves gaps in areas like dental, vision, hearing, and especially long-term care. Medicaid is what ends up paying for nursing home care for many people who have exhausted their resources.

Many people without savings keep working well past the traditional retirement age, sometimes full time and sometimes in part-time or lower-paying jobs. This works for those who stay healthy, but illness, disability, caregiving duties, or age discrimination can push people out of the workforce earlier than they planned, which is one of the main risks of relying on work as a retirement strategy.

Family often fills the gaps as well. Older adults may move in with adult children, share housing with relatives or roommates, or receive regular financial help. Others downsize, relocate to cheaper regions, or in some cases move abroad to countries with lower living costs.

The harder outcomes include persistent financial stress, difficulty affording medications or unexpected expenses, falling behind on rent, and in the worst cases homelessness, which has been rising among older adults in the US. Women, people who had low-wage or irregular work, and those who live alone tend to be the most vulnerable.

In countries with stronger public pension systems, such as much of Western Europe, Canada, or Australia, the situation is generally less precarious because government pensions and guaranteed minimum incomes for seniors are more generous and health care is universal, so a lack of personal savings is less likely to lead to deprivation, though it still typically means a modest lifestyle.

If you're asking because you're worried about your own situation, it's worth knowing that starting late still helps, that checking your projected Social Security benefit at ssa.gov gives a useful baseline, and that delaying benefits past full retirement age increases the monthly amount permanently.

Interbank electronic transfers can take several days to settle for a few reasons. For one, banks handle incoming and outgoing transactions at different speeds, and some institutions move money through their systems faster than others, which can create holdups. Additionally, banking networks do not run in a constant, real-time flow. Instead, most banks group transactions together and process them in batches at set times during the day, so a transfer may have to wait for the next batch cycle before it is finalized. Lastly, electronic transfers often undergo extra security screening, especially when the amount is large or the money is crossing international borders, and these checks take time and add to the total duration. Overall, interbank transfers usually finish within a few business days, though the timeline can stretch longer depending on the details of a particular transfer.

Yes, there are several reasons, though they depend on who the buyer is and what alternatives they have.

The most important point is that a bond with a 0% coupon is not necessarily a bond with a 0% yield. Zero-coupon bonds pay no interest but are sold at a discount to face value, so the investor earns a return through the price rising to par at maturity. If you truly mean a 0% yield, where you pay par and get back only par, then the reasons become more specialized but still exist.

One reason is safety relative to other options. In periods when yields are zero or negative, as happened with German, Swiss, and Japanese government debt in the 2010s, a 0% bond can be the better deal compared with bank deposits that charge fees or negative rates, or with other bonds that guarantee a loss. Large institutions cannot easily hold billions in physical cash, which has storage, insurance, and security costs, so a government bond returning exactly what you put in can be the cheapest safe place to park money.

Another reason is regulation and mandates. Banks, insurers, pension funds, and money market funds are often required to hold high-quality liquid assets or to match liabilities with government securities. They buy these bonds because they must hold something of that type, not because the yield is attractive. Central banks buying under quantitative easing programs were also major purchasers regardless of yield.

A third reason is expected price gains. Bond prices rise when yields fall, so a trader who expects rates to go negative or deflation to deepen might buy a 0% bond hoping to sell it later at a higher price. Relatedly, in a deflationary environment a 0% nominal yield is a positive real return, because the money you get back buys more than it did when you invested.

Currency is another factor. A foreign investor might buy a 0% bond denominated in a currency they expect to appreciate, such as the Swiss franc, earning a return through the exchange rate. Hedging arrangements can also make a bond that yields nothing in its home currency produce a positive yield for an investor once currency hedging costs or gains are included.

Finally, bonds serve as collateral in repo markets and derivatives trading, and as a hedge within a portfolio, since high-quality government bonds tend to rise in value during stock market crashes. Their usefulness for these purposes can justify holding them even when they pay nothing.

For an ordinary individual investor with access to an insured savings account or money market fund paying positive interest, a 0% yield bond usually makes little sense. But for institutions and in unusual economic conditions, there are real and rational motivations.

K-Cups are single-serve coffee pods designed for use in Keurig brewers. Every pod holds a set amount of ground coffee and is enclosed in a wrapper made of plastic and foil. Operating one is straightforward: insert the pod into the Keurig, shut the lid, and hit the start button. The machine pierces the pod and pushes hot water through the grounds, so a freshly brewed cup is ready within seconds. Because they are so convenient and simple to prepare, K-Cups appeal to many people who want a fast, uncomplicated way to make coffee at home.

A biological neural network is a collection of neurons in a living organism that are connected to one another and work together to process information. The most familiar example is the brain and the wider nervous system of animals, but the term also covers much smaller systems, such as the few hundred neurons of a nematode worm or the ganglia that control a snail's feeding movements.

The basic unit is the neuron, a cell specialized for electrical and chemical signaling. A typical neuron has a cell body, branching fibers called dendrites that receive incoming signals, and a long fiber called an axon that sends signals onward. Neurons meet at junctions called synapses. When a neuron is stimulated enough, it fires an electrical impulse called an action potential, which travels down the axon. At most synapses this impulse triggers the release of chemical messengers known as neurotransmitters, which cross a tiny gap and either excite or inhibit the next neuron. Whether that neuron fires depends on the combined input from all of its connections, which can number in the thousands.

What makes these networks powerful is not any single neuron but the pattern of connections among them. The human brain has roughly 86 billion neurons and trillions of synapses, organized into circuits and regions that handle functions like vision, movement, memory, language, and emotion. Some circuits are feedforward, passing signals along in one direction, while many others contain loops and feedback that allow sustained activity, rhythms, and complex dynamics.

A key property is plasticity. The strength of synapses changes with experience, becoming stronger or weaker depending on how they are used, and new connections can form while others are pruned away. This is the basis of learning and memory. A common summary, sometimes phrased as "neurons that fire together wire together," describes the idea that correlated activity strengthens connections.

Biological neural networks are also the inspiration for artificial neural networks in computing. Artificial versions borrow the idea of simple units connected by adjustable weights, but they are greatly simplified. Real neurons have diverse types, complex dendritic processing, many kinds of neurotransmitters, timing-dependent behavior, and are influenced by supporting cells such as glia and by hormones and body chemistry. Biological networks also operate with remarkable energy efficiency and learn in ways that are still not fully understood, which is why neuroscience and artificial intelligence continue to inform each other.

Your skin has tiny holes called pores, and under each one there's a little oil factory. The oil is supposed to keep your skin soft. Pimples happen when a pore gets clogged with that oil and old dead skin, and then tiny germs that live on everyone's skin start to party in there and make it red and puffy.

The reason it's different for different people is mostly that everyone's bodies are built a little differently. Some people were born with oil factories that work extra hard and make lots of oil, and those people get clogged pores more easily. Some people's skin is also more grumpy and swollen when the germs show up, so even a small clog turns into a big red bump, while their friends' skin just shrugs it off.

A lot of this comes from your parents. If they had bad acne, you're more likely to have it too, the same way you might get their hair color or their height. That means it isn't your fault, and it doesn't mean you're dirty. Scrubbing harder usually makes it worse, because it makes skin angrier.

Hormones are also like little messengers in your body that tell the oil factories how much to work. They go up and down during the teen years, but for many people they keep bouncing around into their twenties and beyond, which is why you can still have acne at 21. Stress, poor sleep, some medicines, and certain skin or hair products can nudge things too. For some people, a lot of sugary foods or milk seems to make a difference, though that's less clear and varies from person to person.

So your friends with clear skin mostly just won the genetic lottery on oil and swelling. The good news is that you aren't stuck. Gentle washing, over-the-counter creams with things like benzoyl peroxide, adapalene, or salicylic acid can help a lot. If it's really bad, a doctor or dermatologist has stronger tools, like prescription creams, pills, or other treatments, and they work well for most people. It's worth booking a visit rather than just waiting it out.

A bumpy, raised, itchy rash appearing a few days after a cold is very common in toddlers, and it's usually not serious. There are a few likely explanations. Many viruses that cause colds are followed by a viral rash a few days later, often on the chest, belly, and back. These rashes can be bumpy and mildly itchy and usually fade on their own within a week or so. Another strong possibility is hives, which often show up after a viral infection. Hives are raised, itchy welts or bumps that may come and go or shift location over hours. A third possibility is a skin reaction to the vapor rub itself. Baby Vicks contains fragrance and ingredients such as eucalyptus and rosemary oils that can irritate sensitive skin, so if the rash is mainly where you applied the rub, that is a likely cause.

For now, I would stop using both the Vicks and the Hyland's cough product. Her cold is mostly over, and stopping them removes them as possible triggers. Gently wash the area with lukewarm water and a mild, fragrance-free soap, pat dry, and apply a plain fragrance-free moisturizer such as petroleum jelly or a sensitive-skin cream. Dress her in loose, soft cotton clothing, keep her cool since heat and sweating make itching worse, and keep her nails short so scratching doesn't break the skin. A cool compress or a lukewarm bath can soothe the itch.

If the itching is bothering her, an oral antihistamine can help, especially if this is hives. Cetirizine (children's Zyrtec) is approved for children her age, but please check the correct dose for her weight with your pediatrician or pharmacist before giving it. A thin layer of over-the-counter 1% hydrocortisone cream once or twice a day for a few days can also calm itchy patches, but avoid broken skin and the face.

For the lingering cough, it's normal for a cough to hang on for two to three weeks after a cold. Plenty of fluids, a cool-mist humidifier in her room, and a half to one teaspoon of honey before bed (safe at her age) can all help.

Please call her doctor if the rash is still there or getting worse after a few days, if it spreads quickly, blisters, or looks infected, or if she develops a fever. You can press a clear drinking glass against the spots. If the rash doesn't fade under the pressure, or it looks like tiny purple or red pinpoint dots or bruises, she needs to be seen right away, especially if she also has a fever. Seek emergency care immediately if she has swelling of the lips, face, or tongue, trouble breathing or wheezing, repeated vomiting, or seems unusually drowsy or limp.

Most likely this is a harmless post-viral or irritation rash that will settle within several days. But since she is scratching, a quick call or visit to her pediatrician for a look is always reasonable and can give you peace of mind.

Great question! Okay, so the stock market is basically a place where people buy and sell shares of public companies. When you buy a share, you're getting a tiny ownership stake in that company. Say you pick up one share of a company's stock: you own a very small slice of it. There are lots of ways to get into this, but the most common route is opening a brokerage account. Think of it like a bank account, except it's for trading stocks. You'll pick a brokerage firm and follow their sign-up process, which usually means filling out some paperwork and showing some ID. Once that's done, you can buy and sell through their website or app.

Buying a stock is basically a bet that the company will do well down the road. If it does, and the price climbs, you can sell for a profit. But if it tanks, you could lose money, and that's a real possibility you need to be ready for. Do your own digging before you put money in, and it's worth talking to a financial advisor if you're unsure.

Honestly, a tooth or gum infection really needs a dentist, or an oral surgeon or periodontist if it's more involved. Don't wait on it. These can spread and get nasty if you let them sit. Antibiotics might knock it back for a bit, but they usually won't clear it up on their own, so you'll still need someone to actually diagnose and treat the source. If it's hurting and swollen, an over-the-counter painkiller like ibuprofen (Motrin) can help take the edge off, just follow the label. Keep the area clean and skip hard or crunchy stuff that'll irritate it. Please don't swap out your antibiotics on your own, though. Check with a healthcare provider first. They can figure out the best move for your situation. If you can't get in to see a dentist right away, keep taking the antibiotics as prescribed and call your provider if things get worse or you've got questions.

Sadomasochism is a term for sexual or erotic practices in which a person gets pleasure from giving or receiving pain, humiliation, control, or submission. It combines two words: sadism, named after the Marquis de Sade, an 18th-century French writer whose works depicted deriving pleasure from inflicting suffering, and masochism, named after Leopold von Sacher-Masoch, an Austrian author whose fiction featured pleasure in being dominated or made to suffer. The psychiatrist Richard von Krafft-Ebing coined both terms in the late 19th century.

In everyday use, sadism refers to enjoying causing pain or exerting power over a partner, while masochism refers to enjoying receiving pain or being controlled. Many people who engage in these activities do both, and the practice is often grouped under the broader umbrella of BDSM, which stands for bondage and discipline, dominance and submission, and sadism and masochism. Activities can range widely, from light spanking, restraint, or role-play involving power dynamics, to more intense practices.

In the modern understanding, the key distinction is consent. Healthy participation among adults is typically based on negotiation beforehand, clear boundaries, and often a "safe word" that lets someone stop the activity immediately. Communities that practice BDSM often emphasize the phrase "safe, sane, and consensual" or "risk-aware consensual kink."

Psychologically, mental health professionals today generally distinguish between consensual kink, which is not considered a disorder in itself, and sexual sadism or masochism disorder, a diagnosis reserved for cases where the interest causes significant distress or impairment, or involves harming non-consenting people. Research suggests that people who practice BDSM are not more likely to have psychological problems than others, and many report that it enhances intimacy, trust, and communication with partners.

The term is also sometimes used more loosely or metaphorically to describe someone who seems to seek out suffering or enjoys inflicting cruelty, though in that sense it moves away from the sexual meaning.

British Energy Nuclear Power Notes are financial instruments put out by British Energy Group, a firm that runs nuclear power stations in the UK. Several things influence what the notes are worth, among them how creditworthy British Energy Group is, the interest rates currently prevailing in the market, and how much investors want to buy the notes. If you want to know what the notes are presently worth, you could look at financial news sites or ask a financial advisor or broker. Details about their value may also be available on the British Energy Group website or from providers of financial market data.

So Casey Anthony got charged over the death of her 2-year-old daughter Caylee back in 2008. The charges were first-degree murder, aggravated child abuse, and aggravated manslaughter of a child. She ended up acquitted of the murder and child abuse counts, but the jury convicted her on four counts of lying to police. She got four years, but since she'd already served that time while waiting for trial, she walked out in July 2011. The whole thing was huge in the media and people argued about it nonstop. A lot of folks were pretty angry about the verdict, and it sparked plenty of debate about the justice system and what the evidence actually showed.

Think of writing a program like giving very detailed instructions to a helper who does exactly what you say and nothing more. Imagine you're telling someone how to make a peanut butter sandwich. You say "put peanut butter on bread," but you forgot to mention that the bread is still in its bag. Your helper dutifully tries to spread peanut butter on the plastic bag. That gap between what you meant and what you actually said is where a bug comes from. Programmers make these mistakes all the time, usually because they forgot a step, mixed up two similar instructions, or didn't think about a situation that only happens sometimes, like when the bread is already empty.

Bugs are hard to avoid for a few reasons. First, a program can have thousands or millions of instructions, and they all have to work together, so a small mistake in one place can cause a strange problem somewhere else. Second, computers follow instructions with perfect literalness, so they don't guess what you meant the way a person would. Third, there are an enormous number of possible situations a program might face. Someone might type something unexpected, use the program on an old device, or click two buttons at the same moment. It's almost impossible to imagine every one of those cases ahead of time. Finally, people make mistakes, and the people writing programs are no exception.

That's why programmers spend so much time testing, reading each other's work, and fixing problems after they're found. Software is rarely perfect on the first try, and fixing bugs is a normal part of the job.

A foul smell from under a toenail in an 85-year-old diabetic woman should be taken seriously, even if the nail looks normal from the top. Because she is blind and may have reduced sensation in her feet from diabetic neuropathy, she may not feel pain or notice a problem that is developing. The most likely causes are a fungal infection of the nail, a bacterial infection (often with a greenish or dark discoloration and a strong smell), a small ingrown edge of the nail, or a hidden sore or break in the skin under or beside the nail. Moisture trapped in the folds around the nail, or in the skin between the toes, can also produce odor. In diabetics, these can progress quickly to cellulitis, an abscess, or even a bone infection, so it is better not to wait.

I would recommend having her seen by her doctor or a podiatrist within the next few days, and sooner if you notice redness, swelling, warmth, pus, drainage, black or dark skin, increased pain, fever, or red streaks spreading up the foot. Those signs mean she needs urgent care the same day. The clinician will examine under and around the nail, may trim or lift part of the nail to look underneath, take a swab or nail clipping for testing, and check her circulation and sensation. Treatment depends on the cause: antifungal medicine, antibiotics, or removing the infected part of the nail.

In the meantime, you can do some simple things. Wash her feet daily with lukewarm water and mild soap, check the water temperature with your hand or elbow because she may not sense burns, and dry thoroughly, especially between the toes. Look at both feet carefully every day, including the soles and around all the nails. Give her clean cotton socks each day and well-fitting, breathable shoes, and never let her walk barefoot. Please avoid cutting into the nail, digging under it, or using strong chemicals, home remedies, or over-the-counter medicated products without advice, since a small injury can turn into a serious wound in diabetes. Also make sure her blood sugar is well controlled, as high sugars make infections more likely and slower to heal.

Since she is blind, regular professional foot checks, ideally every few months, along with a family member's daily inspection, are an important part of her diabetes care.

Lazy evaluation is a strategy in which the computation of a value is postponed until that value is actually needed. Instead of calculating an expression as soon as it is encountered, the program creates a kind of placeholder, often called a thunk, that records how the value would be computed. The work is performed only when some other part of the program tries to use the result. If the value is never needed, the computation never happens at all.

A simple way to picture this is a restaurant where the kitchen waits for an actual order before cooking. Under eager evaluation, by contrast, every dish would be prepared the moment the menu was printed, whether or not anyone ordered it.

Lazy evaluation offers several practical benefits. It allows programmers to work with infinite data structures, such as an endless list of prime numbers, because only the portion that is requested gets generated. It can avoid unnecessary work, which may improve performance when many computed values are discarded. It also lets programs separate the description of a computation from its execution, so that a program can be written in a more modular and declarative style, with control flow determined by demand rather than by the order of statements.

The approach has costs as well. Because evaluation happens at unpredictable moments, it can be harder to reason about time and memory usage. Unevaluated thunks can accumulate and consume significant memory, sometimes causing what is called a space leak. Debugging can also be more difficult, since errors may surface far from the code that caused them.

Lazy evaluation is the default in languages such as Haskell, and it is available in many others through features like generators in Python, streams in Scala, or lazy sequences in Clojure. Many languages, including Python, JavaScript, and Java, use eager evaluation by default but provide lazy constructs for specific situations.

Slugging percentage (SLG) is a baseball statistic used to gauge how much power a hitter has. To find it, you divide the total bases a player has earned from hits by his number of at-bats: SLG = (Hits + 2B + (2 * 3B) + (3 * HR)) / At-Bats. Here is a sample calculation. Suppose Player A has 50 hits, 10 doubles, 3 triples, and 5 home runs over 250 at-bats. His slugging percentage would work out like this: SLG = (50 + (10 * 2) + (3 * 3) + (5 * 4)) / 250 = (50 + 20 + 9 + 20) / 250 = 99 / 250 = .396. That means Player A's slugging percentage is .396. Note: Because it also accounts for extra-base hits like doubles and triples, slugging percentage is usually regarded as a better indicator of a player's power than home run totals alone.

Doug Lenat is a computer scientist and AI researcher who founded Cycorp, where he serves as chief executive and which builds artificial intelligence tools for a range of uses. He is most closely associated with the Cyc project, a long-running effort to build a broad, coherent ontology (a structured collection of concepts and categories within a given area) and a knowledge base that AI systems can draw on to reason and make decisions. Work on Cyc began in 1984, and it remains one of the most ambitious and widely recognized AI research endeavors anywhere. Lenat has also contributed substantially to the field through his studies of machine learning, natural language processing, and knowledge representation.

The visual cortex is the part of the brain that processes visual information. It occupies the occipital lobe, at the back of the head, and it receives signals that originate in the eyes and are relayed through the thalamus, specifically a region called the lateral geniculate nucleus. From there, visual information travels to the primary visual cortex, also called V1 or the striate cortex, which is the first major stage of cortical processing for sight.

Beyond V1, the visual cortex is organized into a series of higher areas, often labeled V2, V3, V4, and V5 (also known as MT, for middle temporal area), along with many others. Information flows through these areas in a hierarchy, with each stage extracting more complex features. Early areas detect simple things like edges, orientation, and contrast. Later areas combine these into shapes, faces, objects, motion, and color. Processing is generally split into two broad streams: a dorsal pathway that runs upward toward the parietal lobe and handles spatial location and movement, often described as the "where" or "how" pathway, and a ventral pathway that runs downward toward the temporal lobe and handles object and face recognition, the "what" pathway.

The visual cortex also has a notable property called retinotopy, meaning that neighboring points in the visual field are represented by neighboring neurons in the cortex. This creates a kind of map of the visual world on the cortical surface, and it is why damage to a specific part of the visual cortex can cause blindness in a corresponding portion of the visual field.

I'm sorry you're going through this. Being in pain, sick from withdrawal, and without a doctor you trust is exhausting and frightening, and you deserve real help.

Your most urgent need is the withdrawal.
