Read through any contract or agreement you sign with a company, and go over your bills and invoices closely, so that you can spot any charge you never agreed to. If a charge worries you, a sensible first step is to get in touch with the company and try to settle the matter in a friendly way. Should that fail, you may have to obtain legal help or think about submitting a complaint to a consumer protection agency.

Automated decision-making describes the reliance on computer algorithms and other technologies to reach conclusions with no human involvement. Such determinations rest on data and pre-programmed rules, and they can be produced more quickly and more uniformly than when people make them. This approach appears across many fields, such as finance, insurance, healthcare, and criminal justice. Organizations typically adopt it to boost productivity, lower the chance of mistakes, and achieve greater impartiality. Yet it also gives rise to ethical worries, especially when the algorithms or underlying data contain bias or when the outcomes carry serious weight. In such situations, human supervision and review of the automated process may be essential to make sure the results are equitable and fair.

The question is about the order of events when a market opens, specifically whether the bid or the ask gets established first. The short answer is that neither comes first in a strict sense; they are posted together, and the spread appears as soon as there are resting orders on both sides of the book.

Before the open, many electronic markets accept orders during a pre-open or call auction period. Buy orders (bids) and sell orders (asks) accumulate without trading, and the exchange computes an indicative opening price from the overlap. When the auction uncrosses, a single opening price is set, and the continuous market begins with the remaining unfilled orders forming the bid and ask. Because limit orders on both sides arrive during the same pre-open window, the best bid and best ask typically appear at essentially the same moment.

In markets without a call auction, the first quotes come from market makers or liquidity providers who post two-sided quotes as the session starts. A market maker usually posts a bid and an ask simultaneously, since offering only one side would expose them to one-directional risk. Some quotes may be stale or wide in the first seconds, and the spread often narrows as more participants enter.

If you are asking about a specific exchange or a particular data feed, the exact sequence can vary, so the venue's trading rules and opening procedures are the authoritative reference.

Hard to say for sure from here, but there are a few things that could cause sharp pain in your thigh plus burning in your lower leg.

One is a muscle strain or injury. If you took a fall a month ago and had a lot of bruising on that leg, you could've pulled or damaged a muscle in your thigh or lower leg and it just hasn't healed right.

Another is nerve irritation or compression. That burning feeling in your lower leg and foot sounds a lot like a nerve being irritated or pinched. It could come from an injury, a pinched nerve, or a condition like multiple sclerosis.

A blood clot is also possible. Clots can form in the leg veins and usually cause pain, swelling, and warmth in the area, so if you notice any of that, don't wait around on it.

There's also a long list of other stuff that could do this, like myositis (inflamed muscles), tendinitis (inflamed tendons), or arthritis (inflamed joints).

Honestly, you should get it looked at by a doctor so they can figure out which it is and get you treated. They'll ask about your history and examine the leg, and sometimes they'll want more tests to nail down the problem.

The sequester is an automatic spending reduction mechanism created by the U.S. government to shrink the money allocated to certain programs. Its purpose is to help bring down the national debt and narrow the budget deficit. Once the sequester takes effect, specific federal agencies must cut their expenditures. Those reductions may be applied evenly, so every program within an agency loses the same share of funding, or they may be aimed at particular programs, which then absorb deeper cuts than the rest. A broad array of initiatives can be touched by the sequester, including those in education, defense, and healthcare. The effects can also reach the services these initiatives deliver, such as fewer teachers in classrooms or a smaller number of military personnel. Because it can cause serious harm to vital programs and to the people who depend on them, the sequester is typically regarded as a measure of last resort.

Russia and Ukraine are two neighboring countries. Ukraine used to be part of the Soviet Union, which was a big country led by Russia, but it became its own independent country in 1991 when the Soviet Union broke apart. Russia's leader, Vladimir Putin, has never really accepted that Ukraine is a separate country, and he feels Ukraine should be closer to Russia or under its control. In 2014, Russia took over a part of Ukraine called Crimea and supported fighting in eastern Ukraine. Then in February 2022, Russia invaded Ukraine with a huge army, trying to take more of the country. Ukraine has been fighting back, and many countries, including the United States and European countries, have been sending Ukraine weapons and money to help it defend itself. Russia has also faced many sanctions, which are penalties like bans on trade, to pressure it to stop. The war has caused a lot of death, destruction, and people fleeing their homes, and it is still going on as of my most recent information.

Multimodal sentiment analysis is basically sentiment analysis that looks at more than one channel at once. Instead of just reading someone's words, it also pulls in things like audio, video, and other media. The idea is that a person's tone of voice, facial expressions, and body language can say a lot about how they feel, and those signals often don't show up in the text alone. Sarcasm is a classic example: the words say one thing, but the tone says another. Combining channels catches that kind of thing and picks up on subtle or mixed emotions that a single-channel approach would miss. People use it for all sorts of stuff, like watching social media chatter, handling customer service, doing market research, and tracking how a crowd feels over time or how opinions shift after some big event.

A flexible spending account (FSA) is a tax-advantaged account offered through an employer that lets you set aside part of your paycheck, before income taxes, to pay for eligible out-of-pocket expenses. Because the money comes out of your pay before taxes are calculated, you lower your taxable income and save on taxes on whatever you put in.

You decide at the start of each plan year how much to contribute, and that amount is divided evenly across your paychecks. Once the year begins, you can generally use the full elected amount right away, even before it has all been deducted from your pay. You then submit receipts or claims to the FSA administrator for eligible costs such as deductibles, copayments, prescription drugs, dental and vision care, and certain medical equipment. Many plans also issue a debit card linked to the account so you can pay for qualifying purchases directly.

The main catch is that FSAs are "use it or lose it." Any money left in the account at the end of the plan year may be forfeited, though some employers offer a grace period of a few months or allow a limited amount (a carryover) to roll into the next year, but not both. Because of this, it helps to estimate your expected expenses carefully before choosing a contribution amount. Your employer may also have a deadline for submitting claims after the plan year ends.

There are annual contribution limits set by the IRS, which change periodically, and your employer may set a lower cap. Leaving your job usually ends your ability to use the account, so unused funds can be lost unless you use COBRA-style continuation coverage, which is available for some health FSAs.

There are also dependent care FSAs, which work similarly but cover childcare and elder care expenses instead of medical costs, with their own limits.

I can share the usual reference doses so you can discuss them with her doctor, but please confirm the plan with the doctor who is treating her before starting, especially since she is already on deflazacort.

For acute urticaria in children, prednisolone is commonly given at about 1 mg per kg per day. For your daughter at 19 kg, that works out to roughly 20 mg once a day, taken in the morning after breakfast. Some doctors use a range of 0.5 to 1 mg/kg/day, so anywhere from 10 to 20 mg daily is within the usual range. The course is usually short, about 3 to 5 days, occasionally up to 7. A course this short generally does not need to be tapered, but if her combined steroid use (deflazacort plus prednisolone) goes past about 10 to 14 days, the doctor will likely want a gradual taper. Omnacortil comes as 5, 10, and 20 mg tablets and as a syrup. The plain syrup is 5 mg per 5 ml, so 20 mg would be 20 ml. The Forte syrup is 15 mg per 5 ml, so 20 mg would be about 6.7 ml. Check which strength you have before measuring. When switching, deflazacort should be stopped rather than given together with prednisolone, since both are steroids. Roughly 6 mg of deflazacort equals 5 mg of prednisolone, so the doctor may simply convert her current dose.

The antihistamine may also be worth reviewing, because steroids are an add-on while antihistamines remain the main treatment. If her Atarax syrup is the usual 10 mg per 5 ml, then 3.5 ml twice daily gives about 14 mg a day. The usual pediatric hydroxyzine dose is about 1 to 2 mg/kg/day, which for her would be around 19 to 38 mg a day, so her current dose may be on the low side. Many doctors now prefer a non-sedating antihistamine such as cetirizine or levocetirizine given regularly every day rather than only when itching. For stubborn urticaria, specialists sometimes increase it above the standard dose under supervision. Giving it regularly for a couple of weeks, even after the rash settles, helps prevent relapse.

In children, hives lasting a week are very often triggered by a viral or other infection. Less common triggers include a new food or a medicine such as an antibiotic or ibuprofen. It is worth thinking back to anything new before the rash started.

Seek urgent medical care if she develops swelling of the lips, tongue, eyes, or throat, difficulty breathing or swallowing, hoarse voice, repeated vomiting, dizziness, or drowsiness. See the doctor promptly if she has fever, joint pain or swelling, or individual spots that last more than 24 to 48 hours, look like bruises, or leave dark marks, as these can point to something other than simple urticaria. If the rash continues beyond about six weeks, it is considered chronic urticaria and is best evaluated by a pediatrician or dermatologist.

Salesforce.com is a cloud-based customer relationship management (CRM) platform offering a variety of tools and services that let companies oversee and monitor customer interactions, sales and marketing activities, and other business operations. Built for organizations of every size, it aims to strengthen customer relationships while boosting efficiency and productivity. Its main features and capabilities include the following. Contact and lead management: the platform gives businesses a way to organize data on customers and prospects, such as contact details, account histories, and sales and marketing activity. Sales force automation: sales teams can use it to handle their accounts, leads, opportunities, and related tasks, and it offers forecasting and pipeline management so teams can plan and follow their sales work. Marketing automation: marketing teams can build, run, and track campaigns and programs, with functions like lead management, email marketing, and social media marketing. Customer service and support: businesses can manage their service and support work through case management, knowledge management, and customer portal solutions. Analytics and reporting: a set of analytics and reporting tools allows companies to track and gauge how well their sales, marketing, and customer service efforts are performing. All in all, Salesforce.com is meant to help companies simplify and refine their customer-facing processes, build better relationships with customers and prospects, and foster growth and success.

Malaysia Airlines flight MH370 vanished on March 8, 2014, somewhere between Kuala Lumpur and Beijing. There were 227 passengers and 12 crew on board, and nobody has ever found the plane. Search teams combed huge stretches of ocean, and still nothing conclusive turned up, so what happened to everyone on it is still an open question. People have floated plenty of theories over the years, but none of them has been confirmed. Honestly, it's one of the strangest unsolved mysteries in aviation history.

There are a number of possible explanations for persistent bad breath, even when you brush regularly. Several factors are worth examining. First, oral hygiene matters: you should brush for a full two minutes, two times daily, with fluoride toothpaste, and floss every day to clear plaque and food debris from between your teeth. If these habits are lacking, they may be what is causing the odor. Second, diet plays a role. Pungent foods like onions and garlic can make your breath smell, and sugary or acidic foods encourage bacterial growth in the mouth, which also leads to bad breath. Third, a dry mouth, medically called xerostomia, can be a problem, since saliva normally washes away bacteria and food particles. Certain medications, dehydration, or particular medical conditions can reduce saliva and make bad breath more likely. Finally, some health conditions, including sinus infections, bronchitis, and diabetes, can produce bad breath. If the odor continues despite regular brushing and good oral care, consult your dentist or doctor to check for an underlying health problem. They can identify the source and suggest suitable treatments.

The multivariate normal distribution, sometimes called the multivariate Gaussian distribution, describes a random vector whose components are jointly continuous and each normally distributed. It extends the univariate normal distribution, which governs a single normally distributed random variable. For a multivariate normal with mean vector μ and covariance matrix Σ, the probability density function (PDF) is: f(x) = [1 / ((2π)^(n/2) |Σ|^(1/2))] exp(−½ (x−μ)^T Σ^(−1) (x−μ)), where x = (x_1, x_2, …, x_n)^T is the random vector, n is the number of components, and |Σ| denotes the determinant of the covariance matrix. The mean vector μ fixes where the distribution is centered, while the covariance matrix Σ governs its shape. Because it is flexible enough to represent a broad variety of dependencies among variables, the multivariate normal is widely employed in statistical modeling and machine learning. It also appears frequently in Bayesian inference, since the posterior distributions of many Bayesian models are often roughly multivariate normal.

Smart traffic lights are basically regular traffic lights with extra gear bolted on: sensors, cameras, and other tech that lets them react to what's actually happening on the road and keep things moving. They can talk to other lights nearby and to cars, which helps shave off waiting time and cut down on jams. The lights use sensors to pick up vehicles, pedestrians, and bikes rolling up to an intersection, then tweak the green light timing based on how much traffic there is, how fast things are moving, and so on. Say a road is jammed and a bunch of cars are stuck at a red. The light might stretch out the green so more of them can get through. They can also chat with nearby lights and vehicles through things like DSRC, a wireless standard built for transportation. That lets everything coordinate, which makes traffic flow better and can make intersections safer. The whole point is smoother driving, less congestion, and better safety for everyone, whether you're in a car, on a bike, or walking. You're seeing them pop up in more cities lately, partly because towns want to ease traffic and cut down on vehicle emissions.

I'm sorry you're going through this. It's pretty common not to see much on an ultrasound in the early weeks, especially before 8 weeks. The gestational sac and the baby inside it can change size and position fast in those first few weeks, so the fetus can be hard to make out until it's bigger. A single scan also isn't the whole picture. Things like where the uterus is sitting, how much abdominal fat there is, or fibroids can all affect what the tech sees.

That said, if you're worried about losing the baby, please call your provider rather than sitting with it. They can look at your specific situation, tell you what the scan did and didn't show, and decide whether you need another scan or some bloodwork to keep an eye on things. Try to take it easy while you wait. Get some rest, eat decently, and do something that actually helps you unwind, even if it's just a walk or a show you like. Stick with whatever prenatal care plan they've given you, including any meds or supplements.

Long short-term memory (LSTM) networks are a form of recurrent neural network (RNN) that works especially well for sequential data like time series or natural language. As with other RNNs, an LSTM reads an input sequence one element at a time and keeps an internal state that records information about the elements it has already seen. LSTMs, however, were built to avoid the vanishing and exploding gradient problems that often arise when training conventional RNNs, which lets them capture dependencies that span longer stretches of the data. An LSTM is made up of several "cells" that handle the incoming data, and every cell has three kinds of gates: input, output, and forget gates. Through these gates, the network can choose which parts of its internal state to keep or drop, and can control how information enters and leaves the cell. LSTMs have been applied across many areas, such as machine translation, speech recognition, and forecasting of time series. They have also been used to produce text and music and to model biological sequences like DNA.

Mortgage rates come down to a few things. First, what it costs the lender to get the money to lend you in the first place. That depends on the market, and mostly on where interest rates are across the whole economy. When rates are high everywhere, lenders pass that along and charge you more for a mortgage too.

Then there's you. Your credit score and financial history matter a lot, because lenders see a borrower with a high score and a solid track record as less risky. Lower risk usually gets you a lower rate.

The type of loan matters too. Adjustable-rate mortgages (ARMs) usually start out with a lower rate than fixed-rate ones, but that rate can move over time as the market does. So depending on when you look, an ARM could end up cheaper or more expensive than a fixed loan.

One more thing: rates can differ quite a bit from lender to lender, even for two people with nearly identical credit and finances. So shop around and compare a few lenders before you commit. It can really pay off.

Yes. Several countries and territories use a currency called the dollar, or a dollar-named unit, whose subdivision is not the cent. The clearest example is Zimbabwe's currency history, but the more lasting case is found among several Caribbean and Pacific territories. Some of these use the dollar with a subunit that is not the cent. Jamaica's dollar is divided into 100 cents, so it does not qualify, but a few others illustrate the pattern more directly. Brunei's ringgit is not a dollar, though its English name is the Brunei dollar, which is divided into 100 sen. Many people are surprised to learn that the Liberian dollar is divided into 100 cents, so that example does not fit either.

The strongest examples come from places where the dollar has no subunit at all in practice. The Mauritanian ouguiya and the Mongolian tögrög are not dollars, but they show how some currencies skip the usual decimal division. Among dollar-named currencies, the Zimbabwean bond notes and the Zimbabwean dollar of the early 2000s were issued in forms that were sometimes stated without cents in everyday use, since prices were rounded to whole units because the smallest denominations had so little value.

To be accurate, I cannot name with full confidence a current country whose dollar has no fractional unit whatsoever, and I would recommend checking a current reference such as the ISO 4217 list or a central bank website, since currency arrangements change over time.

Honestly there are a handful of reasons someone might skip an umbrella policy. The first one is cost. They can get pricey, especially if you've got a lot of assets to protect, and some folks just decide the extra protection isn't worth what they'd be paying.

Then there's the "do I even need this?" angle. If you're not doing anything that makes you likely to get sued, or you just don't have much to lose, an umbrella policy can feel like overkill.

Coverage limits are another thing. These policies often won't cover stuff like professional liability or business-related claims, so if that's what you're really worried about, an umbrella isn't going to do much for you.

And some people figure their home and auto insurance already have them covered well enough, so they don't bother with another policy on top.

In the end it's a personal call. It really comes down to your own situation and how much risk you're comfortable with.

Puce is a deep reddish-brown shade, occasionally characterized as a purplish-brown or a brownish-purple. The color is soft and understated, and it is usually placed somewhere in the range between red and brown. Certain people see it instead as a reddish-gray or a dull, faded pink. Puce turns up frequently in interior design and fashion, and it is available in many different materials, including paint, fabric, and wallpaper.

Dry skin that has lasted since childhood, and that runs in your family, is very common, and in most cases it can be managed well, though it is usually a long-term condition rather than something that disappears completely. Your father and brother having the same problem suggests your skin type is inherited, often a tendency toward a dry skin barrier or conditions like eczema or ichthyosis-type dryness, so it helps to know that you are not doing anything wrong.

Olive oil is not a good choice for most people. It is heavy, can feel greasy, and does not hold water in the skin well, which may explain why it has not helped. A better approach is to use a thick, fragrance-free moisturizer such as one containing petroleum jelly, ceramides, glycerin, or urea. Ointments and creams work better than lotions, which contain more water and evaporate quickly. Apply the moisturizer within two or three minutes of washing, while your skin is still slightly damp, and reapply during the day, especially on your hands and legs.

Cut back on hot showers and long baths, since hot water strips natural oils. Use lukewarm water, keep washing short, and use a gentle, soap-free cleanser. Pat your skin dry rather than rubbing it, and avoid harsh soaps, strong detergents, and alcohol-based products. Wearing gloves for household chores and cotton clothing can also help, and using a humidifier in dry or heated rooms makes a noticeable difference.

If your skin is cracked, itchy, bleeding, or inflamed, or if it does not improve after several weeks of consistent care, please see a dermatologist. They can tell whether you have eczema, a thyroid-related problem, or a specific skin condition, and they can prescribe stronger treatments if needed. Since your skin is quite severe and runs in your family, this is a worthwhile visit, and it may bring real relief much sooner than trying products on your own.

I'm sorry, that's stressful, but it's usually fixable if you act quickly. I'll assume you're in the United States, so let me know if you're elsewhere, since the details differ by country.

Start by contacting your bank or the payment service you used right away. If the payment hasn't settled yet, they may be able to cancel or recall it. If it has gone through, ask whether they can request a reversal from the receiving bank. Where the wrong account belonged to a real person or business, the bank can often contact that institution on your behalf, though recovery can take time and isn't guaranteed.

Next, figure out where the money actually went. If you used IRS Direct Pay, EFTPS, or a debit or credit card through an IRS-approved processor, the payment usually goes to the IRS regardless, and the "account number" might simply be your bank account from which funds were drawn. In that case, a wrong number typically means the payment fails and is returned, and the real issue is whether it was made on time. If instead you sent a wire or transfer to a wrong destination account, the funds may be sitting with someone else.

Then protect yourself on the tax side. Check your IRS online account at irs.gov to see whether a payment posted. If it didn't, make the payment again as soon as possible through Direct Pay or another official method so that penalties and interest stop accruing. Keep records of the failed attempt, including confirmations and bank communications. If you get a penalty notice, you can request penalty abatement for reasonable cause, and the IRS also has a first-time penalty abatement option if your record is otherwise clean. Interest generally can't be waived, but it is usually small over a short period.

If you're unsure which situation you're in, tell me how you paid and what the account number was for, and I can give more specific steps. You can also call the IRS at 800-829-1040 to confirm what they've received.

Imagine a group of kids who all promise each other they'll follow the same playground rules. Canada is one of those kids, and it's usually known as the one who follows the rules and tells others they should too. Three big international agreements from 1961, 1971, and 1988 say countries should only allow drugs like marijuana for medical or scientific use, not for fun. If Canada makes recreational marijuana legal, it's breaking a promise it made to the other kids.

The biggest problem isn't really punishment, because there isn't much. The group that watches over these treaties, the International Narcotics Control Board, can scold a country, write reports criticizing it, and recommend that other countries be cautious, but it can't fine Canada or send in police. Uruguay legalized marijuana in 2013 and mostly just got stern words. So the real cost is about trust and reputation.

Here's why that matters. Canada likes to tell other countries, "You should follow international agreements on human rights, trade, the environment, and so on." If Canada picks and chooses which promises it keeps, another country could say, "Why should we follow the rules you care about when you ignore the ones you don't like?" That makes it harder for Canada to be taken seriously when it wants something from the world. It's like the kid who always reminds everyone about the rules getting caught breaking one: people stop listening to him as much.

There were also some practical worries. The United States, Canada's closest neighbour and biggest trading partner, still treats marijuana as illegal at the federal level, so there were concerns about tighter border checks or Canadians being questioned or even banned from entering the US for being involved in the legal cannabis industry. Some also worried that if lots of countries ignored the treaties, the whole system that coordinates fighting dangerous drug trafficking around the world could get weaker.

Canada had a few ways to handle this. It could formally leave the treaties and rejoin with an exception for marijuana, which Bolivia did for coca leaves. It could try to get the treaties changed, which is very hard because many countries would have to agree. Or it could argue that legalizing and regulating marijuana actually fits the treaties' main goal of protecting people's health better than prohibition did. Canada mostly went with that last argument when it legalized in 2018, accepted some criticism, and the consequences ended up being mostly embarrassment and diplomatic grumbling rather than anything serious.

Honestly, there are a few usual reasons someone might not feel anything the first time they try weed. First off, bodies are all different. Some people are just more sensitive to THC than others, so the same amount can hit one person hard and barely register with another. Second, potency varies a lot. Strains differ, and even two batches from the same strain can have different amounts of the active stuff, so what you felt last time might not match this time. And third, you might not have had enough or taken it in a way that actually got it into your system. Smoking or vaping usually works faster than eating it, since it gets absorbed through the lungs, while edibles take longer and can be easy to underestimate. So if you took a small hit or a tiny bite and waited a few minutes, you could easily have missed it. Hope that clears things up a bit. Happy to answer anything else if you're curious.

Internet traffic is the volume of data moving across the internet at any particular moment. That data might consist of emails, web pages, video and audio files, or any other kind of information sent between devices that are connected to the network. Analysts gauge internet traffic in several ways, such as counting the bits or bytes sent each second, the number of packets transferred, or the number of connections opened to a specific website or service. The amount of traffic at any given time depends on many variables, including how many people are online, what kind of content they are accessing, and the hour of the day. Traffic typically peaks when large numbers of users are online simultaneously and drops during quieter off-peak periods. Grasping these patterns matters for several reasons. Internet service providers must manage their networks so they can cope with the load at any moment, while website operators may need to refine their sites to handle the visitors they attract. Moreover, studying traffic trends helps businesses and organizations see how people use the internet and how they can more effectively reach and engage their intended audience online.

Norah Jones is Ravi Shankar's daughter, the sitar player who passed away in 2012, and her mom is Sue Jones. She was born March 30, 1979, in New York City. She's an American singer, songwriter and actress, and she's picked up a ton of awards over the years, nine Grammys in total. Her big breakout was the album "Come Away With Me," which sold over 26 million copies worldwide and took home five Grammys by itself. What people really notice about her is that voice, and the way she mixes jazz, pop and country without it ever sounding forced.

"Stand by Me" was written by Ben E. King along with Jerry Leiber and Mike Stoller. King recorded it first and it came out as a single back in 1961. Since then tons of artists have covered it, and it's pretty much a classic at this point. There's also the 1986 coming-of-age movie Stand By Me, directed by Rob Reiner, which took its title from the song and used it on the soundtrack.

Camera resectioning is basically figuring out where a camera was and which way it was pointing when it took a picture. You start with some 3D points in the scene whose real-world locations you know, plus the spots where those points show up as 2D coordinates in the image. From that, you can work out the camera's position and orientation at the moment the shot was taken. People use it for all sorts of things: augmented reality, 3D reconstruction, robot localization, that kind of thing.

You need those known points, often called control points or feature points, with their matching 2D projections in the image. The math boils down to solving a set of equations that link the 3D coordinates to where they land in the picture. You can tackle that with linear least squares, or with nonlinear optimization if you want more accuracy. Once you've got the pose, you can build a 3D model of the scene, run AR stuff, or figure out where the camera sits relative to landmarks around it.

Brain development refers to the processes by which the brain forms, grows, and matures, beginning shortly after conception and continuing well into early adulthood. It covers both the physical construction of the brain, such as the creation of neurons and the wiring that connects them, and the gradual refinement of those structures in response to genetic instructions and life experience. Because the brain underlies thought, emotion, movement, and behavior, the way it develops shapes nearly every aspect of who a person becomes.

The process starts very early in pregnancy. Around the third week after conception, a flat sheet of cells in the embryo folds to form the neural tube, which eventually becomes the brain and spinal cord. Cells along this tube multiply rapidly in a phase called neurogenesis, producing billions of neurons. These newly formed neurons then migrate to their proper locations, guided by chemical signals and supporting cells, and begin to specialize into the many types of nerve cells found in different brain regions. By the time a baby is born, most of the neurons it will ever have are already in place.

Once neurons reach their destinations, they start forming connections with one another through structures called synapses. This phase, known as synaptogenesis, is especially intense during late pregnancy and the first few years of life, when the brain forms connections at an extraordinary rate. In fact, young children have far more synapses than adults do. Over time, the brain trims away connections that are rarely used while strengthening those that are used often, a process called synaptic pruning. This "use it or lose it" principle allows the brain to become more efficient and tailored to the environment a person actually lives in.

Another important process is myelination, in which nerve fibers become coated with a fatty substance called myelin. Myelin acts like insulation on an electrical wire, allowing signals to travel faster and more reliably. Myelination proceeds gradually, starting with areas responsible for basic functions like sensation and movement and finishing with areas involved in complex reasoning. The prefrontal cortex, which handles planning, impulse control, and decision making, is among the last regions to fully mature, typically not until the mid-twenties. This helps explain why teenagers may struggle more with risk assessment and self-regulation than adults.

Brain development is shaped by both nature and nurture. Genes provide the basic blueprint, but experiences such as nutrition, sleep, physical activity, social interaction, language exposure, and emotional care strongly influence how the brain is wired. Certain periods, often called sensitive or critical periods, are times when the brain is especially responsive to particular kinds of input; for example, early childhood is a particularly favorable time for learning language and developing vision. Conversely, harmful factors like chronic stress, neglect, malnutrition, or exposure to alcohol and drugs during pregnancy can disrupt development and have lasting effects.

Although the most dramatic changes happen before adulthood, the brain never becomes completely fixed. Throughout life it retains a degree of plasticity, meaning it can reorganize itself, form new connections, and adapt to learning or injury. In this broader sense, brain development is a lifelong process, even though its foundations are laid in the earliest years.

Honestly, accepting personal donations usually isn't a great idea. It can get messy fast and make your finances harder to untangle. If you need money or support, a crowdfunding campaign or a non-profit setup might be a better route. If you go ahead anyway, be upfront about what the money is for and how you'll spend it. Keep in mind that donations can count as income on your tax return, so you may owe taxes on them. Also, taking money from people can make it look like you have a business or paid arrangement with them, which can bring up legal and ethical headaches. If you're leaning toward this, talk to a lawyer or accountant first. They can walk you through your specific situation.

Honestly, it's hard to say what's causing a lump on your stomach without seeing it in person, so it's worth getting it checked by a doctor, especially if you're also noticing twitching or spasms. There are a few usual suspects. A lipoma is a harmless (noncancerous) lump made of fat cells. A hernia happens when something pushes through a weak spot in the abdominal wall muscles. An abscess is a pocket of pus from an infection. A cyst is a fluid-filled sac that can pop up pretty much anywhere in the body. The twitching could also just be a muscle spasm or some other muscle issue. Either way, a provider can sort out what's going on and tell you what to do next.

Computational science is a field that spans several disciplines and relies on computers and algorithms to model, examine, and make sense of intricate systems and natural or artificial phenomena. Its practitioners build and apply computational models and simulations to tackle questions in science, engineering, and beyond. The field pulls together knowledge from mathematics, computer science, physics, chemistry, biology, and engineering, and its methods can be brought to bear on a broad range of problems. It might be used, for instance, to investigate how fluids move, how materials are structured, how living organisms change over time, how economies behave, or many other phenomena. As problems have grown in complexity and size, beyond what conventional analytical techniques can handle, reliance on computers and algorithms has become ever more essential. Through computational science, researchers can carry out virtual experiments and analyze data in ways that would be unfeasible or impossible with traditional approaches. The discipline has also opened the door to understanding systems that once resisted analysis, such as large-scale biological processes or the dynamics of financial markets.

The female symbol, sometimes called the Venus symbol or the female sign, consists of a circle with a small cross beneath it, or a small cross with a circle attached to one end. It stands for the female gender and appears frequently in women's studies and feminist writing. It can also refer to female anatomy, particularly the reproductive system. It commonly serves as the counterpart of the male symbol, a circle with an arrow extending upward and to the right. Taken together, the two symbols are often used to express the idea of gender, or to indicate a group that is mixed or non-binary.

Caffeine is a real stimulant, and it usually wins. It blocks a chemical in your brain called adenosine, which normally builds up during the day and makes you sleepy. When caffeine blocks it, your brain stays more alert even though you feel ready for bed. Caffeine also has a half-life of several hours, so even half of an evening coffee can still be active in your body when you try to fall asleep.

The "coffee, then sleep" habit is a Pavlovian link, like a bell that tells a dog it's dinner time. Your brain can learn some cues that mean "time to wind down," and that can help you feel sleepy or relaxed. But a learned cue is generally much weaker than a drug acting directly on your brain chemistry. So the caffeine's effect is the stronger one, and the habit doesn't cancel it out.

They don't really cancel each other. Some people do adapt over time and sleep reasonably well after evening coffee, but that usually means their sleep is still being somewhat reduced without them noticing. If you want to find out, try cutting out the evening coffee for a week or two and see whether you fall asleep faster or wake up feeling more rested.

I can't really recommend a specific medication for your kid's rash, but here's what I can tell you about Acutret. It's isotretinoin, a prescription drug mainly used for severe acne, and it isn't usually the go-to for rashes. Please don't start it without a doctor's say-so. Before anything goes into your child, talk through the risks and benefits with their provider. They'll look at age, weight, overall health, and exactly what kind of rash it is before picking a treatment. If Acutret has already been prescribed, stick to the instructions, follow any diet or other restrictions they give you, and let the doctor know about any side effects or weird reactions right away.

F1 visa holders in the United States have fewer investment options than U.S. citizens or permanent residents, mainly because of restrictions tied to their nonimmigrant status and the expectation that they will not rely on U.S. income. The most important point is that F1 students are generally permitted to hold investments, but they must not earn income from unauthorized employment, and any investment strategy should be checked against their visa conditions and tax obligations.

Bank accounts, including savings and checking accounts, are the simplest starting point, and many international students keep funds in U.S. banks while also using high-yield savings accounts or certificates of deposit. Students can also invest in publicly traded stocks, exchange-traded funds, and mutual funds through a U.S. brokerage account. Opening a brokerage account typically requires a Social Security Number or Individual Taxpayer Identification Number, and some brokers will accept an ITIN or a passport alone, so it is worth comparing providers. Bonds, including U.S. Treasury securities, are another option for more conservative investors.

Investing in real estate is possible but requires care. F1 students can buy property, but mortgage approval is harder without a credit history or Social Security Number, and many lenders require a permanent residence or a substantial down payment. Some students instead purchase property through cash or seller financing. Owning rental property can also create income, and that income is generally taxable in the United States, so it must be reported properly.

Students should be cautious about running a business or earning income from their investments in ways that could be considered unauthorized employment. Passive investment income such as dividends and interest is generally acceptable, but actively operating a business or working as a self-employed consultant without authorization can violate status. Students who want to start a company should consult an immigration attorney first.

Tax matters deserve attention. Nonresident aliens and resident aliens are taxed differently, and F1 students are often nonresidents for tax purposes during their first five calendar years in the U.S. unless they pass the substantial presence test. Dividends, capital gains, and interest may have different withholding and reporting rules, and some foreign investors face withholding on U.S.-source income. Consulting a tax professional familiar with international students is strongly advised. Foreign investments held outside the U.S. may also carry reporting requirements, such as the FBAR if foreign accounts exceed certain thresholds.

Finally, students should keep their investments consistent with their financial needs, since tuition, housing, and living costs must be covered, and they should avoid sending funds through informal channels that could complicate their records. Speaking with a qualified financial advisor, a tax professional, and, where business or employment questions arise, an immigration attorney, will help ensure that investment decisions support both financial goals and lawful status.

Ever wonder what's actually happening when you hit the volume button on your TV? It's pretty simple, really. You're changing how much electricity gets sent to the speakers, and that's what makes the sound louder or quieter. Press "up" on the remote (or on the TV itself) and the TV sends more power to the speakers, so things get louder. Hit "down" and it cuts the power, so it gets softer. The TV has a whole range of levels it can hit, and it figures out how far to go based on the signal from your remote or buttons. Most sets move in small steps, so you can dial it in right where you want it. Hope that helps! Shoot me a message if you've got more questions.

SWIFT, which stands for the Society for Worldwide Interbank Financial Telecommunication, is a network that lets financial institutions across the globe exchange details of financial transactions securely and in a uniform format. When a bank issues a SWIFT, it transmits a message over this network to another financial institution, usually in order to start a financial transaction. If you want to know exactly when a bank issued a particular SWIFT, you should either get in touch with that bank or look through the records or systems it relies on to keep track of its SWIFT messages. The bank ought to be able to tell you the date and time of issue. Another option is to look at the message itself, since it should contain information on when it was sent.

A tsunami is a massive wave produced by a disturbance beneath the ocean surface, such as an earthquake or an erupting volcano. That underwater event pushes the water into motion, generating a wave that spreads outward across the sea. Because tsunami waves are extremely long and tall, they carry a great deal of energy. They can move at up to 500 miles per hour, faster than a commercial jet. This energy originates from whatever triggered the wave: an earthquake or volcanic eruption releases a huge amount of power, which passes into the water and forms the wave. When a tsunami arrives at the coast, its enormous energy can wreck buildings and infrastructure. It can also flood low-lying land and wear away the shoreline. Tsunamis are highly destructive and dangerous, so anyone living in an area where they are likely should be prepared and know how to respond.

Co-owners usually can't sell a property without the agreement of the others listed on the title, so his sister's refusal is a real obstacle. The first step is to find out exactly how they hold the house. The deed will say whether they own it as tenants in common, which lets each owner's share be sold or passed on separately, or as joint tenants with right of survivorship. It will also show whether both names are actually on the title, since sometimes one sibling is only on a mortgage or was never added.

If she won't agree, there are a few common paths. They can talk through her reasons, because she may be worried about where she would live, the price, or money she has put into the house. Practical compromises often work: one person buys out the other at an appraised value, they agree on a set date to list, or one of them rents the place for a while. A mediator, which is often much cheaper than litigation, can help when the conversation keeps stalling.

If nothing works, a co-owner in most US states, and in many other places, can ask a court for a partition action. The court can order the property sold and the proceeds divided, or in some cases order one owner to buy the other out. This process can be slow, costly, and damaging to the relationship between siblings, so it's usually a last resort. Any co-owner with a mortgage or a claim on the house also has to be considered.

Because the details depend heavily on your location and the wording of the deed, it's worth a consultation with a local real estate attorney before he takes any formal step. Many will offer a short initial meeting. If you tell me the country or state and how the title is held, I can give you more specific information.

Kurt Cobain died on April 5, 1994, at his home in Seattle, Washington. He was 27 years old. His body was found a few days later, on April 8, above the garage of his house. Medical examiners determined that he had died from a self-inflicted gunshot wound, and the death was ruled a suicide.

Imagine your brain has a sleepy switch and a busy switch, and when you have insomnia, the sleepy switch gets stuck in the wrong spot. Your body feels tired and wired at the same time, like a car with the engine running but the wheels stuck in mud. Scrolling on Facebook or Tumblr is easy because it asks almost nothing from your brain. You just look at pictures and tap, and your brain can do that even when it's foggy and worn out.

Studying is different. It takes focus, memory, and careful thinking, and a brain that hasn't slept well has a hard time holding onto ideas. It's like trying to carry a stack of books when your arms are shaky. Your friend might also feel anxious or frustrated about not sleeping, and that worry takes up space in her head that could have gone to schoolwork.

Being awake at night also doesn't mean she's ready to do hard things. Her body is still in "rest mode" even though her eyes are open, so the parts of her brain that help with learning and planning aren't working at their best. So she reaches for the easy stuff, the way you might want a snack instead of cooking a big dinner when you're tired.

If you want to help her, you could suggest she do something gentle and quiet at night, or talk with a doctor, since lots of sleep trouble can be treated.

Google Finance and Yahoo Finance usually give you historical stock prices that already account for stuff like splits, dividends, and mergers. So the numbers are "adjusted," and they should line up pretty well with what the stock actually traded at back then. Just keep in mind that they're built from publicly available info, so they're not perfect. Sometimes the data's just wrong, or it hasn't caught up with something that happened recently. If you're seeing numbers that look off, or you need something you can really rely on, go check the company's own filings or financial statements. That's where the accurate, up-to-date stuff lives.

Bond funds can definitely drop in value, just like any other investment. But the swings are usually a lot smaller than what you see with stocks or other riskier stuff, since bonds are generally seen as the steadier option.

There are a few reasons you don't see huge sell-offs in them. For one, a bond fund usually holds a whole bunch of different bonds, so if one of them defaults, it doesn't hurt the fund much. The risk gets spread around. Bond values also tend to react less to shifts in the economy and the market than stocks do, which helps keep things calmer.

A lot of people buy bond funds to protect their money and bring in some income, not to chase quick gains. So they're less likely to panic and bail when the market gets jumpy in the short term. That alone cuts down on big sell-offs compared to other kinds of investments.

Still, think about what you're actually trying to do with your money and how much risk you can stomach before you jump in. Every investment has its upsides and downsides. If you're not sure, talking to a financial advisor or doing some solid research first is a good move.

Could be that the Vanguard Dividend Growth Fund just hasn't grown its dividends much lately. There are a few reasons that might happen. Maybe the market took a dip, maybe the fund changed its investment strategy, or maybe the stocks it holds simply haven't raised their payouts. It's also possible the numbers you're looking at on Yahoo Finance are out of date or just aren't showing the dividends right, so I wouldn't take them as gospel.

Keep in mind that a mutual fund's performance, dividend growth included, moves around over time, and nobody can promise it'll go up. If you're thinking about putting money in, read through the fund's prospectus and the other disclosure documents first. Talking to a financial advisor wouldn't hurt either before you make the call.

Geothermal is basically heat that's stored in the Earth, and it counts as renewable. The heat comes from the core, and a lot of that is kept going by radioactive elements slowly decaying down there. It makes its way up to the surface through conduction, convection, and radiation, and we can tap it to make electricity or to heat and cool buildings.

There are a few ways to do that. Geothermal power plants use the heat from deep underground to generate electricity. Geothermal heat pumps work differently: they take advantage of the fact that the ground near the surface stays at a pretty constant temperature, so you can use it to warm a building in winter and cool it in summer. Then there are geothermal reservoirs, which are natural underground pools of water heated from below. You can use those for power, for heating buildings, or even for thermal baths and spas.

It's a reliable, sustainable source of energy, and it could end up playing a big part in the shift to renewables.

The right path depends mostly on how much you're starting with, because the gap between your starting capital and $250,000 determines how much return you need. If you start with $10,000, you would need roughly a 90 percent annual return for five years, which is unrealistic and usually leads to blowing up an account. If you start with $100,000, you need about 20 percent a year, which is still very aggressive for investing. If you can contribute regularly, say $3,000 a month, then a normal market return of 7 to 10 percent gets you to around $220,000 to $250,000 even starting from zero. So the most reliable lever is usually your savings rate, not your trading skill.

For investing, the dependable route is steady contributions into low-cost diversified index funds, using tax-advantaged accounts first. Run the math with a compound interest calculator to see what monthly amount reaches your goal at 7 percent. Active trading is where most people lose money. Studies of retail day traders consistently show that the large majority underperform or lose, so I would not build a five-year plan around it. If you want to trade, do it with a small portion of your money that you can afford to lose.

The other lever is growing your income, which is where a business or high-value skill comes in. A business can produce a far larger return on a small amount of capital than markets can, but it carries risk and takes real work. Realistic options include service businesses such as agencies, consulting, trades, or freelancing that you can start with little money, then systemize and scale. Others include buying a small existing profitable business, which is slower to start but less risky than building from scratch, or building a product or software if you have the skills. Whichever you choose, aim to validate demand quickly with paying customers before investing much.

A practical plan would be to first decide your starting capital and monthly savings capacity. Second, increase your income through a raise, a better job, a side business, or new skills, since that raises the amount you can invest. Third, put the bulk of your savings in index funds automatically. Fourth, reinvest some business profits back into the business while it is growing, then move surplus into investments.

Be wary of anything promising fast, guaranteed returns, such as signal groups, crypto schemes, forex courses, or leveraged strategies sold by influencers. Leverage in particular can wipe out your capital quickly.

If you tell me your starting amount, monthly savings, income, skills, and risk tolerance, I can sketch a more specific plan and show what numbers would be needed to reach $250,000 in five years.

The human body contains more than 600 muscles, which handle movement and posture and also support processes such as blood flow, digestion, and breathing. The main categories include skeletal muscles, which are connected to bones and drive voluntary motion; there are over 200 of them, found in the arms, legs, and trunk. Smooth muscles line the walls of internal organs and blood vessels, where they carry out involuntary actions like moving food through the gut and regulating circulation. Cardiac muscle, which exists only in the heart, contracts to pump blood through the whole body. Beyond these three types, many smaller muscles serve specialized roles, such as the ones in the eye that move it and the ones in the ear that aid balance.

A millwright is a skilled tradesperson who installs, maintains, and repairs industrial machinery and equipment. These workers are trained to handle a broad range of equipment, such as conveyor systems, pumps, motors, and generators. They also take charge of setting up and servicing machine tools and other manufacturing equipment. Most millwrights are employed in factories, power plants, and similar industrial facilities, where they may have to work in tight spaces, at elevated heights, or under other demanding conditions. Their tools range from hand tools and power tools to precision measuring instruments. To do this work well, millwrights generally need a solid grasp of mechanical and electrical systems, strong problem-solving abilities, and careful attention to detail. They also need to be able to read blueprints and technical drawings. Depending on the job, some millwrights must hold formal training or certification in a specialized field, such as welding or pneumatics.

Imagine you want to send a secret note to your friend, but you don't want anyone to know it came from you. So you pass the note through a chain of helpers. Each helper only knows who gave them the note and who to hand it to next, so nobody along the way knows the whole story.

Tor is a system on the internet that works like this. When you use it, your computer sends your internet traffic through several volunteer computers around the world. Each of these volunteer computers is called a "Tor node," which is just a fancy name for one of the helpers in the chain.

The last helper in the chain is called the "exit node." It is the one that finally delivers the note to where it's going on the regular internet, like a website. The website sees the exit node's address instead of yours, so it doesn't know exactly who asked for the page.

Some people run these helpers from their homes or offices, and they do it to help protect people's privacy. Because the exit node is the last stop, it can see the note itself, though it can't see who wrote it. That's why it's a good idea to still use secure websites that scramble the message, so the helper can't read what's inside.

The outlook for stomach cancer, which is also called gastric cancer, hinges on several considerations, including how advanced the disease is, where the tumor sits, the kind of cells involved, and the patient's general state of health. As a rule, catching and treating the cancer sooner leads to a more favorable outlook. Staging plays a major role here, since it describes how large the cancer has grown and whether it has reached other areas of the body. Stomach cancer is usually classified into four stages. In Stage 0, cancer cells are found only in the innermost lining of the stomach. In Stage I, the cells have moved past that lining but remain within the stomach wall. In Stage II, the cancer has extended beyond the stomach and may have made its way to nearby lymph nodes. In Stage III, it has reached lymph nodes farther away or other organs. Five-year survival rates vary by stage at diagnosis: roughly 95% for Stage 0, 70 to 80% for Stage I, 40 to 50% for Stage II, and 20 to 30% for Stage III. These figures are broad estimates only, and any individual's actual prognosis may differ. For a prognosis specific to a particular person, it is best to consult a medical professional.

Sore throat, stuffy nose, and cough are pretty classic signs of a viral infection like a cold or the flu. Allergies can cause the same stuff, though, and so can irritants like smoke or air pollution. As for the crusty eyes you mentioned, that could be conjunctivitis, which is basically inflammation of the thin, clear lining of your eyelid and the white part of your eye. It can come from a virus, bacteria, allergies, or irritants. Sometimes it's a sign of something else going on, like dry eye or blepharitis (inflammation of the eyelid). If the symptoms stick around or get worse, though, get it checked out by a healthcare provider. They can figure out what's actually going on and point you toward the right treatment.

Bigamy means entering into a marriage with one person while still legally married to another. Many countries make it a crime, since it involves deception and can cause real harm to those affected. Picture yourself married to someone you love and trust, and then discovering that your spouse has secretly wed another person. You would likely feel deeply hurt, and your faith in your spouse would be shaken. The second spouse would also be left bewildered and misled, having had no idea that your partner was already married. Bigamy can create legal difficulties as well. For instance, when couples have children, it may be unclear who the legal parents are, and disputes can arise over who is entitled to property such as a house or a car. All in all, bigamy is prohibited because it is regarded as a deceitful and damaging act that brings confusion and legal trouble to everyone it touches.

Bugs can crawl up vertical glass because their feet are covered in tiny hairs that grip the surface. You can't see these hairs with the naked eye, but they're strong enough to keep the bug stuck as it walks. Kind of like how a rubber band grabs onto things, except the bug's hairs do the gripping instead.

Ah man, sorry you messed up the account number on your tax payment, that's a stressful one. If you've already filed and put in the wrong number, you'll want to get in touch with the IRS, tell them what happened, and ask them to fix it. The number for individual tax questions is 1-800-829-1040, and it's toll-free. If you can't get it sorted out over the phone, you might have to send them something in writing explaining the mistake and asking for the correction.

Now, if you haven't filed yet, that's easier. Just fix the number before you submit anything. You can do that through the IRS "Free File" service, or if you've already sent a return and need to change it, you'd fill out an amended return, which is Form 1040-X.

Really worth double-checking your account info when you file, because the IRS uses it to process your payment and credit it to your account. Get it wrong and things can get messy. And if you've got more questions after all this, just call the IRS again and they should be able to help you out.

I'm sorry you're dealing with this. Employer fraud that causes a coverage lapse is stressful, but there are several ways to bridge the gap, and some of them can work within days.

The first step is to look into a Special Enrollment Period. Losing coverage, especially through no fault of your own, generally qualifies you to enroll in a marketplace plan at healthcare.gov or your state exchange, typically within 60 days of the loss. Some states also allow enrollment for up to 60 days after. Also check whether you qualify for Medicaid, which you can apply for at any time of year, and which can sometimes be retroactive up to three months. If you have a documented fraud situation, keep all of that paperwork, since it supports your eligibility and may matter for any later claims.

For medications right now, talk to your prescriber and pharmacist today. Explain the situation and ask for a short emergency supply. Many states allow pharmacists to dispense an emergency refill of a maintenance medication, usually a few days to a month, even without a new prescription. Ask your doctor about samples, and whether any of your drugs have cheaper generic equivalents.

Pharmacy discount cards like GoodRx, SingleCare, or Cost Plus Drugs often make generics very cheap, sometimes under ten dollars a month, and Walmart, Costco, and some grocery chains have low-cost generic lists. Compare prices, because they vary widely. For brand-name drugs, check the manufacturer's patient assistance program, which often provides free or reduced-cost medication to uninsured people, and sites like NeedyMeds.org can help you find these. For insulin specifically, manufacturers have capped-price programs.

Community health centers (federally qualified health centers) charge on a sliding scale and often have in-house pharmacies with discounted drugs. You can find one at findahealthcenter.hrsa.gov. Free clinics and local health departments may also help.

Also ask your former insurer or the plan administrator whether coverage can be reinstated retroactively, since fraud by an employer sometimes triggers that. Contact your state insurance department and the Department of Labor's Employee Benefits Security Administration (866-444-3272), which handles cases of misused premiums and can sometimes help recover claims or restore coverage. If you paid claims out of pocket during the gap, keep receipts.

To open an online stock trading account in the United States, take the following steps. First, decide which kind of account suits you. Options include individual accounts, joint accounts, and retirement accounts such as traditional or Roth IRAs. Next, research and compare online brokerage firms, weighing factors like fees, available investments, quality of customer service, and ease of use. Then gather the required paperwork. Depending on the firm and account type, you may need to supply personal details such as your name, address, and Social Security number, financial details such as your employment, income, and net worth, and identification like a driver's license or passport. After that, complete the online application by following the brokerage's instructions and accepting its terms and conditions. Once the application is in, fund the account, typically through an electronic transfer from your bank or by mailing a check. Finally, begin trading. After your account is funded and approved, you can buy and sell stocks online. Before placing your first trade, learn how the brokerage's platform works and note any applicable fees or restrictions. Keep in mind that some brokerages have extra requirements or procedures, so read and follow their instructions carefully. It is also wise to speak with a financial advisor or tax professional before making investment decisions.

Several things could be contributing here, and the pattern you describe (dizziness, blurry vision, and numb or cold tingling in the hands, feet and face) is worth taking seriously, though it is often explained by fairly ordinary causes.

Antidepressants are a common culprit. Many of them, especially SSRIs and SNRIs such as sertraline, citalopram, fluoxetine, venlafaxine and duloxetine, can cause dizziness, blurred vision and tingling sensations (paresthesia) as side effects. Tricyclics and mirtazapine can also cause blurred vision and lightheadedness, partly through effects on blood pressure and on the muscles that focus the eye. Side effects can appear or worsen after a dose change, after missing doses, or when another substance interacts with the medication. Caffeine is a good example: chocolate and many fizzy drinks contain it, and caffeine can heighten the jittery, tingling, dizzy feelings that some antidepressants already produce. Some fizzy drinks also contain a lot of sugar, which leads me to the next point.

A rapid rise and then fall in blood sugar after sugary foods or drinks can cause dizziness, blurred vision, shakiness and a cold, tingly feeling. This is sometimes called reactive hypoglycemia, and it is worth mentioning to your doctor, who can check your blood sugar. Anxiety and panic symptoms are another possibility. Stimulants like caffeine can trigger rapid breathing, which lowers carbon dioxide in the blood and causes exactly this kind of numbness and tingling in the hands, feet and around the mouth, along with lightheadedness and visual disturbance. Low blood pressure, dehydration, low iron or B12, and thyroid problems can also produce similar symptoms.

Because the symptoms have lasted weeks and are tied to a medication, I would arrange an appointment with your doctor soon rather than waiting. They may check your blood pressure, blood sugar, blood count, B12, and thyroid function, and review your antidepressant and dose. Please do not stop the antidepressant suddenly on your own, as that can cause its own dizziness and sensory symptoms, and can worsen your mood. In the meantime, it is reasonable to cut back on chocolate, caffeine and fizzy drinks to see whether the symptoms ease, to eat regular balanced meals, and to stay hydrated. Keeping a short diary of when episodes occur, what you ate or drank, and when you took your medication can help your doctor spot the pattern.

Seek urgent care if you ever have sudden vision loss, facial drooping, weakness on one side, trouble speaking, severe headache, chest pain, fainting, or numbness that is persistent and one-sided, as these could signal something more serious.

Yes, a blood test can sometimes point toward cancer, but it usually can't confirm it on its own. A complete blood count and a comprehensive metabolic panel can show abnormalities such as anemia, unusual white blood cell counts, high calcium, or abnormal liver or kidney values, and these can prompt further investigation. Some newer tests look for tumor markers or fragments of tumor DNA circulating in the blood, but these are not reliable enough to screen for cancer in people without symptoms, and a definite diagnosis generally requires imaging or a biopsy.

What you describe concerns me and deserves prompt medical attention. Losing about two pounds a week while eating normally or even eating more is called unintentional weight loss, and it is one of the symptoms doctors take most seriously. It can have many causes, including thyroid disease, diabetes, infections, digestive disorders, and cancer, and many of these are treatable. Combined with six months of dizziness, blood pressure swings, and shortness of breath, it's important to be evaluated soon rather than waiting.

Please see a doctor within the next few days, and sooner if you feel faint, have chest pain, severe shortness of breath, fainting, or confusion, in which case go to an emergency room or call your local emergency number right away. When you go, tell the doctor exactly what you told me: the timeline, the weight loss amount, the dizziness, and the blood pressure changes. Bring a log of your weight and any blood pressure readings if you have them. Your doctor can order blood work and other tests to find the cause.

The mind-body problem is basically the question of how the mind and body relate to each other, and philosophers have been chewing on it for centuries. It matters because it touches on consciousness, what a self even is, and how all of that fits with the physical world. One approach is to ask whether the mind is its own distinct thing or just what the body's physical processes amount to. Dualists say the mind and body are separate and can interact, but they aren't the same thing. Monists take a different tack. They think there's really just one kind of stuff here, and mind and body are two ways of describing the same thing. Plenty of theories have been put forward to crack this, and honestly, none has settled it. It's still very much an open debate.

Honestly it's tough to pin down an exact number, since it's always shifting. People buy and register new vehicles every day, and older ones get pulled off the road. But the Federal Highway Administration (FHWA) had a figure for December 2020, and it came out to roughly 263 million registered vehicles in the US. That covers passenger cars, trucks, buses, and motorcycles. The FHWA updates its numbers regularly, so if you look today you'll probably see something a little different.

Oil's mean return and volatility swing a lot from year to year, honestly. Prices get pushed around by all sorts of things: the global economy, politics, OPEC decisions, hurricanes, you name it. So returns on oil can be really hard to predict. Volatility is the big one to watch. WTI crude futures have had annualized standard deviations hitting 50% in some years, which is wild. Average returns bounce around just as much, with some years looking great and others taking a serious beating. Oil is a high-risk bet, and it's not for everyone. Figure out your goals and how much loss you can stomach, and maybe talk to a financial advisor before you put money in.

Of course! Throughout history, people have needed ways to tell individuals apart, particularly in bigger communities where many people share the same first name. Family names offer one solution. A family name is a particular type of surname handed down from one generation of a family to the next. These names let people follow their ancestry and learn about their origins. They have also served to signal a person's social or economic standing, or to indicate the group or community someone is part of. Most likely, family names came about because they gave people a practical, convenient means of identifying themselves and their relatives.
