Basically solar panels turn sunlight into electricity. They're made of materials, usually silicon, that soak up the light. When sunlight hits the panel, that energy knocks electrons loose inside the material, and all those moving electrons make an electric current.

That current isn't quite ready to use yet, though. It gets sent to an inverter, which changes it into the kind of electricity your home or business actually runs on. After that you can power your lights, your devices, whatever you've got plugged in. So it's just sunlight in and usable electricity out.

So you're selling ESPP shares and wondering about the tax hit. Basically, you'll owe tax on whatever profit you made, which is the capital gain. If you held the stock for more than a year before selling, that gain gets taxed at the long-term capital gains rate, and that's usually lower than your regular income tax rate. Held it a year or less? Then it's short-term, and it gets taxed at your ordinary income rate instead. Either way, you'll need to report the sale on your US return and pay whatever's due. If you're a US citizen or resident alien living abroad, you might be able to exclude some or all of your foreign earned income and housing costs, too. With all these moving parts, it's worth talking to a tax pro who can look at your situation and tell you what you actually qualify for.

Technically, yeah, some people do survive cancer without any medical treatment, but it's rare and doctors really don't recommend going that route. Cancer can kill you if it's left alone. Your best shot is actually getting treated, whether that's surgery, chemo, radiation, or some mix of them. Those treatments kill off cancer cells, shrink tumors, and keep the thing from spreading to other parts of your body.

If you've got symptoms that could point to cancer, like a cough that won't go away, weight loss you can't explain, or changes in your bowel habits, go see a doctor. Catching it early makes it a lot easier to treat and your odds are much better.

And if you've been diagnosed and you're thinking about skipping treatment, talk it over with your doctor first. They can walk you through the risks and benefits of each option so you can make a decision that fits your situation.

Computer Go is basically what it sounds like: programs that play Go. If you haven't run into it, Go is a really old board game from China, played on a 19x19 grid, where the goal is to surround more territory than your opponent. The rules are dead simple, but the strategy runs incredibly deep.

That depth is exactly why it's been such a headache for AI. You need long-term planning and real strategic thinking, and you have to judge who's ahead in a position that's hard to read. To build a decent Go program, people have had to mix a bunch of techniques, like machine learning, search, and pattern recognition.

It's come a long way in the last several years, too. The best programs can now beat the strongest human players. Still, Go is far from a solved problem for AI, and there's plenty of room left to make these programs better.

Honestly, a spinning feeling plus pressure in the head could come from a bunch of things. One common culprit is BPPV, where tiny crystals in the inner ear get knocked out of place and make you feel dizzy when you move your head a certain way. Inner ear problems in general, like inflammation or damage, can cause the same spinning sensation. Migraines are another possibility, since they often bring dizziness and head pressure along with the headache. High blood pressure can sometimes cause that pressure feeling too. Your grandmother really should see a doctor to figure out what's going on, because the treatment depends on the cause. Until then, she should move her head slowly and skip anything that might set off the dizziness, like reading in a car or jumping up from a chair too fast.

Imagine you want to join a club, and the club says you have to pay five dollars to get in. Once you're in, the club tells you that the way to get your money back is to bring in two new friends, and each of them pays five dollars too. Part of what your friends pay goes to you. Then those two friends are told to go find two friends of their own, and so on. That's the basic idea.

The trick is that nobody is actually selling anything useful. The only way money comes in is from new people joining. The people at the top get paid with the money from the people below them, and those people hope to get paid by the people below them.

Here is why it gets big so fast. If you bring in two people, and each of them brings in two, and so on, the numbers double at every step: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32. After about twenty steps you would need over a million people, and after thirty steps you would need over a billion. The scheme looks like it's working great in the early stages because each new level is only a little more work to recruit, and the people near the top make real money. That success is what convinces others to join, and the stories of early winners are used as advertising.

But here is the problem. The world runs out of people. Every level has to be twice as big as the one before it, so the scheme hits a wall very quickly, usually long before anyone expects. When there is nobody left to recruit, the money stops flowing, and the people at the bottom, who are always the largest group, lose everything they paid. In any pyramid scheme, the majority of people, roughly nine out of ten or more, end up losing money, because there must always be far more people at the bottom than at the top.

Why do people keep falling for it? Often the scheme is dressed up to look legitimate. It might pretend to sell vitamins, makeup, or an investment product, but the real money comes from recruiting, not from selling to actual customers. Friends and family are the ones who recruit you, so you trust them. And the early winners are very convincing, because they honestly got paid.

That's also why pyramid schemes are illegal in most places. They aren't a clever business. They're a game of musical chairs where the music always stops and most people are left standing with nothing.

Semi-supervised learning is a machine learning method that trains a model on a mixture of labeled and unlabeled data. Supervised learning relies on a labeled dataset in which every training example comes with its correct output. Unsupervised learning, by contrast, receives no labeled examples at all and has to discover structure in the data by itself. Semi-supervised learning sits between these two extremes: it uses a small quantity of labeled data together with a large pool of unlabeled data. The underlying idea is that the model can draw on what it learns from the labeled examples to make predictions about the unlabeled ones. This is particularly helpful when labeling a large dataset is costly or slow, or when only a few labeled examples exist.

One way to carry this out is self-learning. The model is first trained on a small labeled set, then applies its predictions to label more examples from the unlabeled pool. These new labels are incorporated into the training data, and the model is retrained. The cycle can be repeated several times until the model predicts labels accurately for most of the dataset. Semi-supervised learning has proven effective in many areas, such as natural language processing, image classification, and speech recognition. It can also be combined with other techniques, including transfer learning, to further boost model performance.

Hi Angie. Thanks for the detail. Difficulty urinating after sex can have several causes, and most are treatable. In men, the urethra can become irritated or inflamed from friction during intercourse, and that swelling can temporarily narrow the flow. A urinary tract infection or prostatitis (inflammation of the prostate) can also cause a weak stream, sometimes with burning or a feeling of incomplete emptying. Less commonly, a sexually transmitted infection such as gonorrhea or chlamydia can irritate the urethra and cause similar symptoms, and these are worth ruling out since you had unprotected sex. Sometimes the cause is simply temporary muscle tension or anxiety, which can make it harder to start or maintain a stream.

Because he is drinking plenty of fluids, that is a good sign, but it does not rule out an infection. Since symptoms began only two days after intercourse, calling his doctor is a sensible step. He should mention the timing, the unprotected sex, and that the stream is weaker, and he should ask for a urine test and possibly STI testing. Prompt treatment matters, since untreated infections can spread or become more complicated, and an STI would also affect you both.

Some things to watch for that mean he should be seen urgently rather than waiting for an appointment: fever or chills, severe pain in the lower back or abdomen, blood in the urine, inability to pass urine at all, or swelling or severe pain in the testicles.

It would also be wise for you to get tested as well, even if you feel fine, since many STIs cause no symptoms. Your doctor or a clinic can advise you on the right tests. Best wishes to you both.

There is no single best asset allocation for a retirement portfolio, because the right mix depends on your time horizon, your other sources of income, how much you need the portfolio to produce, and how well you can tolerate watching its value fall without selling in a panic. That said, there are well-established principles that lead most people toward a reasonable answer, and understanding them matters more than any specific formula.

The core tradeoff is between growth and stability. Stocks have historically delivered the highest long-term returns, roughly 6 to 7 percent per year above inflation for broad U.S. markets over the past century, but they can drop 30 to 50 percent in a bad bear market and take years to recover. High-quality bonds return less but fluctuate far less and often hold up or rise when stocks fall. Cash and short-term instruments are the most stable but barely keep pace with inflation. A retirement portfolio has to balance the need to grow enough to last perhaps 30 years against the need to avoid being forced to sell stocks at a deep loss to pay the bills.

For people still decades away from retirement, a heavily stock-weighted portfolio, often 80 to 100 percent equities, is usually sensible because they have time to recover from downturns and their future paychecks act like a bond-like asset. As retirement approaches, the danger shifts to what is called sequence-of-returns risk: a large market decline in the first few years of retirement, while you are withdrawing money, can permanently damage a portfolio in a way that the same decline twenty years later would not. This is why most target-date funds and planners gradually shift toward bonds, typically landing somewhere between 40 and 60 percent stocks around the retirement date. Some research, notably by Wade Pfau and Michael Kitces, suggests a "rising equity glide path" in retirement, starting more conservatively and then increasing stock exposure as the early danger years pass, can actually improve outcomes.

A commonly cited middle-of-the-road allocation for a new retiree is something like 50 to 60 percent stocks and 40 to 50 percent bonds and cash. Historical studies behind the well-known 4 percent withdrawal guideline found that portfolios in roughly this range survived 30-year retirements in nearly all historical periods, while portfolios with too few stocks were more likely to run out because they failed to keep up with inflation. Being too conservative is a real risk, not just being too aggressive.

Your personal circumstances can justify moving away from that middle. If Social Security, a pension, or an annuity covers most of your essential expenses, your portfolio is funding discretionary spending and can afford to hold more stocks. If you rely on the portfolio for basic living costs, more stability is warranted. Some retirees use a "bucket" approach, holding two to five years of spending in cash and short-term bonds so they never have to sell stocks during a downturn, with the rest invested for growth. Your health, longevity expectations, desire to leave an inheritance, and honest emotional reaction to losses all matter too; the best allocation on paper is useless if you abandon it during a crash.

Within each asset class, diversification and cost matter a great deal. Low-cost broad index funds covering domestic and international stocks, along with a mix of government and high-quality corporate bonds, often including inflation-protected Treasury securities, give wide exposure at minimal expense. Rebalancing periodically, perhaps once a year or when the mix drifts significantly, keeps risk in line with your plan and enforces a discipline of selling high and buying low.

In short, the best allocation is the one that provides enough growth to outpace inflation over a long retirement, enough stability to get you through bad markets without forced selling, and a level of volatility you can actually live with. For many people that lands around a balanced stock and bond mix at retirement, adjusted for their guaranteed income and risk tolerance. Because the stakes are high and individual situations vary, it can be well worth consulting a fee-only fiduciary financial planner who can model your specific numbers.

Market cap is basically how much a publicly traded company is worth according to the stock market. You get it by multiplying the stock price by the number of shares out there. So if a company's trading at $50 a share and has 1 million shares outstanding, its market cap is $50 million. Pretty simple.

People mostly use it as a quick way to gauge how big a company is, and it plays a big part in how a company's stock gets valued too. You can zoom out with it as well. Add up the market caps of every public company in a country and you get a rough sense of how big that country's stock market is, and some folks even use that as a stand-in for the size of the economy.

One thing to keep straight though: market cap isn't the same as the value of the company's assets, and it's not the same as how much revenue it brings in. It's just what investors are collectively willing to pay for the company, based on the stock price at that moment.

Mouth sores with blood clots can come from a bunch of different things, so I'd get a doctor or dentist to look at it and figure out what's actually going on. A few possibilities:

Canker sores are small, shallow ulcers that show up inside your mouth, usually on the tongue, gums, or inner cheek. They're round or oval with a red border, and they can hurt enough to make eating or talking a pain.

Cold sores, or fever blisters, are little painful blisters that tend to pop up on the lips or around the mouth. They come from the herpes simplex virus, so they're contagious. Most clear up by themselves in a few days to a week.

Oral cancer is the scary one, and yes, a sore with blood clots can be a sign of it. It covers cancers of the mouth, throat, and head and neck. Other things to watch for are a sore throat that won't go away, trouble swallowing, and a lump or mass in your mouth or throat.

If you've got a sore with blood clots, don't wait around too long to get it checked. In the meantime, you can ease the pain a bit. Rinse with warm salt water, take something like acetaminophen or ibuprofen, and stay away from acidic, spicy, or salty foods. A topical anesthetic or a pain-relieving mouthwash can help too.

Good oral hygiene helps as well, so brush and floss regularly and try to cut back on tobacco and alcohol. That won't guarantee you never get sores, but it makes problems less likely.

The CEO of Facebook is Mark Zuckerberg. He co-founded the company in 2004 while he was a student at Harvard University and has led it ever since. In 2021 the parent company was renamed Meta Platforms, and Zuckerberg remains its chief executive.

The Great Chicago Fire broke out on the night of October 8, 1871, and burned for about two days, until October 10. It started in or near a barn on DeKoven Street on the city's West Side, though the popular story that a cow kicked over a lantern there has never been confirmed. The fire destroyed roughly 3.3 square miles of the city, left an estimated 100,000 people homeless, and killed around 300 people.

HIV/AIDS denialists are people who reject the scientific consensus that HIV is the cause of AIDS, or who deny that HIV causes AIDS at all. Their reasoning usually rests on a handful of ideas that sound plausible on the surface, so it helps to see what those ideas are and why scientists found them unconvincing.

Think of it like a detective story where someone has decided the wrong suspect did it. The denialists point to a few clues they think don't fit. One clue is that AIDS was first noticed in the early 1980s among gay men, injection drug users, and others, and some argue that drug use, poor nutrition, or the stress of poverty must be the real cause. Another is that many people who have HIV stay healthy for years without treatment, which they see as evidence that the virus can't be the main culprit. A third is that some people with AIDS have no detectable HIV, which seems to contradict the idea that the virus is always responsible.

Some denialists also point to controversial figures and past mistakes. Peter Duesberg, a respected virologist, argued in the late 1980s that HIV was a harmless passenger virus and that AIDS was caused by recreational drugs and anti-HIV medications. His reputation lent weight to the movement. Others point to the fact that the drug AZT was expensive and had serious side effects, and they conclude that the whole medical establishment is profiting from a false story. Some also distrust governments and pharmaceutical companies, especially given the real history of abuses like the Tuskegee study, and they feel that suspicion is justified.

Here is why scientists rejected these ideas. Researchers have found HIV in nearly every person with AIDS, and they can show how the virus destroys the immune system's T cells over time. The "healthy for years" pattern is explained by the slow, long course of the infection, and the "no virus detected" cases were usually explained by testing limits or late-stage disease. Most importantly, antiretroviral drugs that stop HIV from copying itself stop the progression to AIDS, and when HIV is blocked, people's immune systems recover. Also, people who get HIV through contaminated blood or needles, without any drug use, still develop AIDS. Those results are hard to explain if HIV is not the cause.

So in simple terms, denialists look at some puzzling details and a history of mistrust, and they conclude that the main explanation must be wrong. Scientists looked at the same puzzles, tested them, and found that the virus explanation holds up, while the alternative ideas did not survive the evidence.

I'd get your son checked by his pediatrician in the next day or two. Lumps like these are usually harmless, but a doctor should look at them, especially since they're new and you're concerned.

The most likely explanation, given that he just recovered from hand, foot, and mouth disease, is swollen lymph nodes. Lymph nodes often enlarge after a viral infection as the immune system responds, and they can feel like firm, rubbery lumps under the skin. Nodes on the side of the head, near the ear, and toward the back of the scalp are common places for this. They're often tender at first and then shrink over a few weeks. The itching could be part of the healing process or a mild skin reaction.

Other possibilities include cysts or small fatty lumps (lipomas), which are usually soft, movable, and painless. Scalp folliculitis or an insect bite can also cause itchy bumps, though those usually come with redness or a visible spot. Less commonly, a skin reaction or a rash left over from the illness could be involved.

Call the doctor promptly, or seek same-day care, if you notice any of the following: fever, redness or warmth spreading over the lumps, pain when touched, pus or drainage, lumps that are hard, fixed in place, or growing quickly, or any headache, stiff neck, vomiting, unusual sleepiness, confusion, or swelling around the eye. Those signs need prompt attention.

If the lumps are soft, not painful, and he otherwise seems like himself, a visit in the next day or two is reasonable. The doctor can usually tell what they are by feel and may simply recommend watching them. Many lymph nodes take two to four weeks to go back to normal, so if they're still there after that, let the doctor know.

Your husband's readings, an average of 107/63, are actually on the low side rather than high. That matters here, because the fatigue you're describing is more likely linked to blood pressure running low, or to something else entirely, than to high blood pressure. High blood pressure itself usually causes no symptoms, so fatigue is not a typical sign of it. When hypertension does cause tiredness, it is usually because the condition or its treatment is affecting the body in other ways.

Lisinopril is the more likely connection. It lowers blood pressure by relaxing blood vessels, and at 20 mg daily, especially in a 69-year-old, it can push pressure lower than the body is comfortable with. Readings in the 100s over the 60s can leave some people feeling lightheaded, drained, or unusually tired, particularly if they stand up quickly or are dehydrated. Lisinopril can also occasionally cause a dry cough, dizziness, and in some people fatigue, and kidney function and potassium levels can be affected, which may also contribute to tiredness. Because he is still working and feeling more tired than usual, it is worth looking at whether the timing of his dose, his fluid intake, or his activity level has changed.

Several other common causes of new fatigue at his age deserve consideration too. These include thyroid problems, anemia, sleep disturbance (including sleep apnea, which is common in older men and is linked to blood pressure), blood sugar changes, depression, medication side effects from other drugs he may take, and the simple cumulative effects of a demanding job and summer heat.

Since the change is recent and noticeable, I'd encourage a visit to his doctor soon. Bring your log of readings, including the timing and whether he felt lightheaded when they were taken. The doctor may want to check blood work for kidney function, potassium, thyroid, and blood count, and may consider whether the lisinopril dose should be adjusted. Please do not stop or change his medication on your own. Seek urgent care if he faints, has chest pain, severe shortness of breath, confusion, or a sudden severe headache.

Okay, so the saying "the exception proves the rule" is kind of confusing at first. Basically, it means that when something breaks a rule, that exception ends up backing up the rule somehow. Think about it like this: say everyone assumes all birds can fly. Then you point out penguins can't. That penguin thing doesn't kill the rule, it actually shows the rule is there in the first place, since you need a rule before an exception can stand out. Honestly, the whole idea is a bit of a mess, and people argue about what "prove" was even supposed to mean back then. Anyway, hope that helps! Let me know if anything's still unclear.

Of course! Picture the internet as an enormous city filled with countless houses. Every house has its own address, much as every website on the internet has its own address known as an "IP address." Suppose you want to go to a friend's home. You might try to memorize where they live, but that gets difficult when you have many friends. A phone book would make things simpler, since it would list each friend's name next to their address, and you could just search for the name to get the address. DNS acts as a phone book for the internet. Rather than flipping through pages, your computer uses DNS to find the IP address that belongs to a website. Because of this, you never need to memorize the IP addresses of all the sites you like to visit. You simply enter the website's name into your browser, and DNS helps your computer locate the right IP address. Does that make things a little clearer? Feel free to ask if you have any more questions!

Circumpolar constellations are groups of stars that seem to remain above the horizon at all times for someone standing at a given latitude on Earth. In other words, they can be seen in the night sky during every season and never dip below the horizon. Which constellations qualify depends on how far north or south the observer is. The Big Dipper, also called Ursa Major, is circumpolar for anyone north of 44 degrees north latitude. The Southern Cross, or Crux, by contrast, stays visible year-round for observers south of 30 degrees south. Other examples include Cassiopeia, which is circumpolar above 74 degrees north, Draco, visible year-round above 65 degrees north, and Polaris, the North Star, which is circumpolar above 89 degrees north.

Aerospace engineering is basically the branch of engineering that designs, builds, tests, and runs aircraft and spacecraft. It pulls together physics, materials science, and general engineering principles to make vehicles that can handle both the atmosphere and outer space. You'll see aerospace engineers working on all sorts of stuff: commercial and military planes, space probes, satellites, rockets, you name it.

It's a pretty specialized field, so you need a strong background in math and science before you even get started. Once you're in, you'll lean heavily on CAD software to draw up and analyze designs, and you'll often run tests in wind tunnels or other facilities to check that things actually perform and stay safe. The field splits into a few subdisciplines. Aeronautical engineering covers aircraft, and astronautical engineering covers spacecraft.

Where you end up working can vary a lot. Some people go to government agencies, others to the military, aerospace companies, or universities. The day-to-day might be research and development, testing, manufacturing, or maintenance and repair, depending on the job.

Pain in the back of your ribs after an injury could be a cracked or bruised rib. Pulled muscles or sprains in that area can hurt like that too. Sometimes it's something internal, or an underlying medical issue, so it's worth getting looked at. I'd see a doctor. They'll examine you, ask about your symptoms, and maybe order imaging to figure out what's going on, and then they can tell you how to treat it.

Until then, take it easy and don't do anything that makes the pain worse. That means skipping the strenuous stuff, putting ice on the spot, and taking an over-the-counter pain reliever if you need one. Try not to put pressure on the injured area either. Lifting heavy things or playing contact sports is a good way to hurt it again, so stay away from that for now.

Rowing machines have a smaller following than ellipticals or treadmills mainly because they demand more coordination and skill to operate properly. Most people find ellipticals and treadmills simpler, since their repetitive motions are quick to pick up. A rowing machine, by contrast, calls for synchronized work from the arms, legs, and back in order to produce force and move the apparatus. Those who have never rowed before may find this harder to master.

Space is another factor working against rowing machines. They tend to be longer and broader than ellipticals and treadmills, so they need more room. For gyms and fitness centers with limited floor area, this can be a real constraint. In short, although rowing machines provide a low-impact, full-body workout, their steeper learning curve and larger footprint keep them less popular than ellipticals and treadmills.

A hyperspectral imager is a remote sensing device that measures how much light a target object or scene reflects across many wavelengths, usually spanning the visible and near-infrared (NIR) parts of the electromagnetic spectrum. Such instruments are commonly carried by satellites, aircraft, or other platforms, and they capture images of the Earth's surface or other areas of interest. What sets a hyperspectral imager apart is its capacity to record reflectance over a broad wavelength range with fine spectral resolution. This enables it to recognize and measure the substances in a scene by their distinctive spectral fingerprints. For instance, it can locate and chart minerals, plant cover, water bodies, and other materials across the ground. These imagers serve many purposes, such as mineral prospecting, crop monitoring, land use charting, environmental observation, and military reconnaissance. By analyzing spectral properties, they can identify and categorize objects and substances, supplying detailed insight into the makeup and spatial arrangement of materials within a scene.

Osteophytic lipping refers to small bony outgrowths, often called bone spurs, that form at the edges of joints. The body typically produces them in response to wear and tear or arthritis, when cartilage thins and the bone around the joint remodels. On an X-ray they look like a small lip or beak of bone along the joint margin. In the feet, they are common around the big toe joint (where they are sometimes called hallux rigidus or a bunion-related spur), the ankle, and the midfoot. The spur itself is not usually the cause of pain. Pain tends to come from the inflamed joint, the stiffness it causes, or pressure from the spur against shoes or nearby tissue.

Whether surgery is worthwhile depends on several things that only your treating foot or orthopaedic specialist can judge properly. These include which joint is affected, how severe the changes look on imaging, how much the pain limits your daily life, and how well you have responded to non-surgical treatment so far. Surgery is generally considered when pain remains significant despite conservative measures such as supportive footwear with a stiff sole or rocker profile, custom or off-the-shelf insoles, activity modification, anti-inflammatory medication, physiotherapy, or injections. Many people with spurs never need surgery, while others gain real relief from a well-chosen procedure.

Your situation deserves careful thought. Standing for more than nine hours a day on joints that are already painful is a significant load, and it may be what has made walking so difficult. Before deciding, it would be reasonable to ask your surgeon which joint is being treated and what the procedure involves, what recovery looks like and how long you would be off your feet, what the realistic chance of pain relief is, and whether the surgery would let you return to long periods of standing. It is also worth asking whether your job could be adjusted in the meantime, for example with sit-stand options, anti-fatigue mats, or regular breaks, and whether a second opinion would help.

I cannot examine you or see your scans, so this is general information rather than a recommendation for your particular case. Please discuss these questions with the specialist who has assessed your feet. If the surgery is offered, you are entitled to understand the benefits and risks clearly before agreeing to it.

Blood pressure often varies over the course of a day, so one reading doesn't necessarily tell the full story about your typical levels. That said, a jump of the size you mentioned deserves attention, particularly if you have peripheral artery disease (PAD) and take lisinopril for hypertension. You should bring this change to your healthcare provider's attention, since they might need to modify your medication or suggest lifestyle adjustments. They could also track your readings more closely to identify any trends or underlying problems. Until then, keep taking your medication as directed and follow any other guidance your provider has given you for controlling your blood pressure.

The Institution Owned number on Google Finance is basically the share of a company's outstanding stock that big institutional investors hold. We're talking investment firms, pension funds, insurance companies, mutual funds, that kind of crowd. Google pulls ownership info from regulatory filings and other public sources, then divides the shares institutions own by the total shares outstanding. That percentage is what shows up on the company's profile page. Keep in mind it's just an estimate, so it might not be perfectly accurate. Do your own digging and maybe talk to a financial advisor before you put money anywhere.

"Leaving Las Vegas" featured Nicolas Cage and Elisabeth Shue in its main roles. Cage portrayed Ben Sanderson, a Hollywood screenwriter who relocates to Las Vegas intending to drink himself to death, and Shue played Sera, a prostitute who develops a bond with Ben as he sets out on this path. Mike Figgis directed the film, which came out in 1995. Critics praised it highly, and it earned a number of awards, among them the Academy Award for Best Actor, which went to Cage for his performance.

Subjective experience refers to what it is like, from the inside, to undergo a mental state. When you taste coffee, feel a sharp pain, see the color red, or feel a wave of nostalgia, there is something it feels like for you to have that experience. That felt, first-person quality is what philosophers and scientists mean by subjective experience. It is often contrasted with objective descriptions, which explain events from a third-person standpoint, such as how light of a certain wavelength strikes the retina or which neurons fire when you are hurt.

The term "subjective" here does not mean biased or merely a matter of opinion, as it does in everyday speech. It means that the experience belongs to a subject, a someone who has it, and that it is directly available only from that subject's point of view. You can tell another person that you are in pain, and they can observe your behavior and even scan your brain, but they cannot have your pain as you have it. This privacy, or first-person access, is one of the defining features of subjective experience.

Philosophers sometimes use the word "qualia" (singular "quale") for the individual qualitative features of experience, such as the particular redness of red or the specific bitterness of coffee. The philosopher Thomas Nagel captured the idea in his famous 1974 essay "What Is It Like to Be a Bat?", arguing that even if we knew everything about a bat's echolocation system, we would still not know what it is like for the bat to perceive the world that way. A creature has subjective experience, on this view, if there is something it is like to be that creature.

Subjective experience is central to what David Chalmers called the "hard problem of consciousness." Science has made progress on the so-called easy problems, such as explaining how the brain processes information, discriminates stimuli, and controls behavior. The hard problem asks why any of this processing is accompanied by felt experience at all, rather than happening "in the dark." Why should certain brain activity feel like anything? There is no consensus answer. Some thinkers hold that experience is ultimately identical to physical brain processes, others believe it is a fundamental feature of reality, and still others argue that our sense of a hard problem is a kind of illusion generated by how our minds represent themselves.

The concept matters in many practical areas too. In medicine, it shapes how we think about pain and about patients in comas or vegetative states. In ethics, the capacity for subjective experience, especially for suffering, is often treated as the basis for moral consideration, which informs debates about animal welfare. And in discussions of artificial intelligence, a recurring question is whether a machine that behaves intelligently might also have subjective experience, or whether it could process information without anything being felt at all. Because subjective experience is known directly only from the inside, these questions remain some of the most difficult and intriguing in philosophy and science.

Association rule mining is a data mining technique for discovering interesting relationships, or associations, between items in large collections of data. It is most famously applied to transaction data, such as the purchases recorded by a supermarket, where the goal is to find patterns like "customers who buy bread and butter often also buy milk." Each such pattern is expressed as a rule of the form "if A, then B," where A and B are sets of items.

The technique works by first identifying frequent itemsets, which are combinations of items that appear together in a sufficiently large share of the transactions. The strength of a frequent itemset is measured by its support, the proportion of transactions containing it. From these frequent itemsets, candidate rules are generated and evaluated using metrics such as confidence, which is the proportion of transactions containing A that also contain B, and lift, which compares the observed co-occurrence of A and B to what would be expected if they were independent. A lift greater than one suggests a positive association, while a value near one suggests little relationship.

Because the number of possible itemsets grows exponentially with the number of items, practical algorithms rely on pruning strategies. The Apriori algorithm, proposed by Agrawal and Srikant in 1994, uses the principle that every subset of a frequent itemset must also be frequent, allowing it to discard large portions of the search space. The FP-Growth algorithm offers a more efficient alternative by compressing the data into a tree structure and avoiding repeated candidate generation.

Beyond retail market basket analysis, association rule mining is used in areas such as web usage analysis, medical diagnosis support, bioinformatics, and intrusion detection. Its main strength is that it produces human-readable rules, though it can generate very large numbers of rules, many of which may be trivial or spurious, so evaluating and filtering them is an important part of the process.

Google Cloud Platform is basically Google's cloud computing setup for building, deploying, and running apps and services. You get a pile of cloud services out of it: computing, storage, networking, analytics, machine learning, security, and app development, plus more. Developers and businesses use it to run apps, websites, and services on Google's infrastructure. It's meant to scale easily, it's pretty flexible, and it's not too painful to use. You can get at it through a web console or through APIs.

A few of the main features:

Computing options like virtual machines, containers, and serverless stuff (Google Cloud Functions, for example)

Storage options including block storage, object storage, and BigQuery, which is a fully managed data warehouse

Networking tools like virtual private clouds, load balancers, and edge caching

Analytics and machine learning tools, including BigQuery, Google Cloud Machine Learning Engine, and Google Cloud AI Platform

Security and compliance features like encryption at rest and in transit, identity and access management, and security key management

Companies of all sizes use it, from scrappy startups to huge enterprises. It's especially popular with teams who want the scalability and flexibility of the cloud without the cost headaches.

Honestly, nobody knows for sure why Reddit leans liberal, but there are a few theories floating around. One is that liberals are just more likely to post about politics there in the first place, so they end up more visible. Reddit's culture might also just appeal more to liberal folks, for whatever reason. Then there's the age thing: Reddit skews young, and younger people tend to lean more liberal, so that could be part of it. It's also a global site, and politics looks really different from one country to the next, so who's posting depends a lot on where they live. And don't forget that the loudest voices online aren't always the typical ones. Reddit might not reflect the general population at all, or it could just be that its liberal users are the ones who speak up the most.

Steam trading cards are virtual cards you pick up by playing certain games on Steam. Plenty of people collect them to show off their favorite games, or just because the collecting itself is fun. Some folks also trade them with other players to fill gaps in their collection.

As for why anyone would pay real money for them, it's pretty much the same reason people buy physical cards, stamps, or other collectibles. Some people just like owning virtual stuff. A rare card can be worth cash to someone, the same way a rare baseball card can be.

Cards also have a practical use: you can combine them into badges, which show up on your profile. Those badges can say something about what you've accomplished or what you're into, and they can be a good conversation starter with people who share your interests. That's a big draw for some buyers.

Not every card is worth much, though. Common ones usually go for pennies, while rarer ones can fetch a lot more. Like any collectible, the price depends on how rare a card is and how much people want it.

Imagine you and your friends each have a favorite team. If everyone agrees there is only one real champion, then anyone who picks a different team is clearly wrong, and it can feel like a big deal to let them keep cheering. Many monotheistic religions work a bit like that. They teach that there is one true God and that the way to know Him is specific, so people sometimes feel they have to convince others or stop them from going the wrong way. That can lead to arguments, and sometimes fights.

Polytheistic religions, like the old Greek, Roman, or Hindu traditions, often had lots of gods who could all exist together. If your neighbor prayed to a different god, you could shrug and think, "Okay, that's their god. Mine is over here." Romans even added the gods of the people they conquered to their own collection. It was easier to live side by side when no one insisted that only one answer was allowed.

It's also worth knowing that polytheistic societies did have wars, and not all religious fighting comes from monotheism. Religion often gets mixed up with land, power, and money, and people can use religion as a reason for fights that are really about other things. Some of the biggest conflicts that get labeled "religious" are also tangled up with politics and ethnicity. So the difference is real, but religion is rarely the only ingredient.

Your resting heart rate at 24 is usually considered normal if it's somewhere between 60 and 100 beats per minute. That said, everyone's a little different. Things like fitness level, sex, and general health can all shift where your number lands. If you're regularly sitting well above 100 at rest, though, it's worth getting it checked out by a doctor, since that can sometimes point to an underlying issue.

I can't diagnose this from a description, but I can tell you what it might be and why it's worth getting checked promptly.

A feeling of the brain being "frozen" for about 20 minutes, in someone who is 71 and has had it a few times, can have several causes. One possibility is a migraine variant. Some people who had migraines earlier in life later develop what is called a late-life migraine aura, which causes temporary neurological symptoms such as numbness, a strange or frozen sensation, visual changes, or difficulty with speech, sometimes without any headache at all. Your history of right-sided migraines makes this plausible, and it is a common explanation.

However, at your age the same symptoms can also be a transient ischemic attack, often called a mini-stroke. This is a brief interruption of blood flow to part of the brain that resolves on its own, usually within minutes to an hour. It matters because a TIA is a warning sign, and the risk of a full stroke is highest in the days and weeks afterward. Other possibilities include small seizures, which can begin later in life, irregular heart rhythms such as atrial fibrillation that send small clots to the brain, blood pressure or blood sugar problems, and carotid artery narrowing.

Because you have had this more than once and it happened just yesterday, I would not wait for a routine appointment. Contact your doctor today and tell them exactly what you told me, or go to an urgent care or emergency department if you can't be seen quickly. They will likely check your blood pressure, heart rhythm, and blood sugar, and may order blood tests, an ECG, imaging of the brain, and an ultrasound or scan of the arteries in your neck. If it is a TIA, treatments such as blood thinners, cholesterol medication, or blood pressure control can greatly lower your stroke risk. If it turns out to be a migraine aura, you can be reassured and given guidance.

If it happens again, call emergency services right away rather than waiting it out, especially if you notice any of these: weakness or drooping on one side of the face, weakness or numbness in an arm or leg, trouble speaking or understanding, sudden vision loss, confusion, loss of balance, or a sudden severe headache. Try to note the time it starts and how long it lasts, and write down what you felt, since that will help the doctor.

It is quite possible this turns out to be benign, but at 71 it deserves a prompt evaluation. I hope you get answers soon.

Ezekiel's one of the prophets in the Hebrew Bible, and the Book of Ezekiel is named after him. Tradition says he wrote it himself, and it's in both the Hebrew Bible and the Christian Old Testament.

He was a priest and prophet living in the 6th century BC. Born in Jerusalem, he ended up among the Jews Nebuchadnezzar II carted off to Babylon after Jerusalem fell in 586 BC. It was there, in exile, that he started getting visions from God and was told to prophesy to the Israelites living in Babylon.

A lot of what he said was about judgment. God was going to come down on the Israelites for their sins. But there was a hopeful side too, because he also talked about the nation being restored, the temple in Jerusalem being rebuilt, and the Jews eventually going back home.

The book itself is a real mix. You get straight prophecies, parables, and these symbolic actions he'd act out to get God's message across. It's a big deal in both Judaism and Christianity, and it's had a lot of influence on each.

Outstanding tax debts may stand in the way of getting a business license. In many states and localities, a business has to satisfy particular financial and tax requirements before a license is granted. Governments impose these conditions because they want companies to operate responsibly with their finances and to contribute the taxes they rightfully owe. Anyone with unpaid taxes might have to settle the matter first, either by paying the full balance or by setting up a payment plan with the relevant tax agency. Dealing with the problem quickly is important, since unpaid taxes can lead to extra penalties and interest charges, and may even result in legal action. If you can't tell whether you owe back taxes, or you don't know how to clear them up, it makes sense to speak with a tax professional or an attorney who can recommend the most suitable way forward.

Action selection is the problem of deciding which action an agent should perform at a given moment, especially when several possible actions compete for the agent's limited resources or when the agent has multiple goals that cannot all be pursued at once. It appears in many fields, including artificial intelligence, robotics, and the study of animal behavior, and it is central to any system that must act autonomously in a changing environment.

The core difficulty is that an agent constantly receives information from its surroundings and has internal needs, such as hunger, safety, or a task to complete. It must weigh these against one another and choose a single course of action, or a coherent sequence of them, rather than trying to do everything simultaneously. A simple example is an animal that must decide whether to flee from a predator, eat, or rest. Choosing to flee when a predator is near is usually the right decision, even though the animal is also hungry, because survival takes priority. Action selection is the mechanism that makes this kind of prioritization happen.

In robotics and artificial intelligence, researchers have developed several approaches to the problem. Some use fixed priority schemes, in which certain behaviors always override others, such as obstacle avoidance overriding a navigation goal. Others use utility or reward-based methods, in which each possible action is scored according to how well it serves the agent's goals, and the highest-scoring action is chosen. Still others rely on hierarchical structures, in which high-level goals are broken into subgoals and then into concrete actions, or on learning-based methods, in which the agent improves its choices through experience.

Ethologists and neuroscientists also study action selection in animals, asking how brains resolve conflicts between competing drives. Proposed mechanisms often involve networks in which different behaviors inhibit one another, so that the strongest activated behavior wins and suppresses the rest. The basal ganglia in vertebrate brains are frequently discussed in this context.

In short, action selection is the process by which an agent resolves competing possibilities and commits to one action at a time, balancing urgency, goals, and environmental conditions to behave effectively.

Inductive programming is an area within artificial intelligence and machine learning in which computer programs are used to automatically build and improve machine learning models from data. Its purpose is to streamline the work of constructing and choosing models, and to produce models that are more precise and perform better on unseen data. To do this, it draws on methods such as genetic programming, neural networks, and decision trees, which sift through large volumes of data to uncover patterns and relationships that can forecast outcomes or categorize new inputs. The central aim is to yield models capable of accurate predictions or decisions without requiring users to perform heavy manual tuning or feature engineering. The approach is applied widely, including in natural language processing, image and video recognition, and predictive modeling across areas like finance, healthcare, and marketing. It could greatly speed up the development of machine learning models and open them up to people with limited technical skill.

Sorry to hear about your neck pain and the other health stuff you're dealing with. That sounds rough.

Neck pain can come from a bunch of different things: a strained muscle, a pinched nerve, or wear and tear or an injury in the spine. The best move is to see a doctor or other healthcare pro who can figure out what's actually going on, because the right treatment depends on the cause.

Usually the options include physical therapy, medications, injections, and sometimes surgery. PT is often the first thing people try. It stretches and strengthens the muscles in your neck and upper back, which can ease the pain and help you move more freely. For meds, doctors commonly go with NSAIDs to bring down inflammation, or muscle relaxants if you've got spasms. If that doesn't cut it, there are injections like corticosteroids or nerve blocks, which can calm the inflammation and dull the pain.

If things are really bad, or nothing conservative is working, your provider might bring up surgery. There are a few kinds. One is fusion surgery, where they join two or more vertebrae together to stabilize the spine.

Whatever plan you end up on, stick with it and tell your provider if something changes or worries you. And try to head off future flare-ups too. Keep decent posture, set up your workspace so it's easier on your neck, and take breaks from anything that puts strain on it.

Imagine you have a big sandbox at school, and the bigger your part of the sandbox is, the more room you have to build castles and keep your toys. Countries are kind of like that. A leader might want more land because more land means more people live there, and more people means more helpers, more soldiers to keep things safe, and more workers to grow food and make things. A bigger country can also feel stronger, so other countries are less likely to bother it.

Land is also useful for practical reasons. Good farmland grows lots of food, and having your own food means you don't have to depend on someone else. Rivers and lakes give water for drinking and farming. Mountains and oceans can act like walls that keep enemies away. Some leaders want land near the sea so their boats can reach faraway places, or land on hills where they can see enemies coming.

Sometimes a leader wants land because of their history or pride. Maybe their grandparents once lived there, or their country used to own it long ago, and they want to make things "right" again. Other times they just like the feeling of being in charge of more things, the same way a kid feels proud when they have the biggest pile of blocks on the playground.

Still, taking land from someone else usually makes them very upset, and they may fight back. So a leader has to weigh whether the reward is worth the trouble, and whether they can win without everyone getting hurt.

That's a fun question! Evolution doesn't really work by animals deciding to get "better" or "worse." It works through natural selection: animals that are better suited to their surroundings tend to survive and have babies, and those babies inherit the traits that helped their parents out. Over many generations, those traits can spread through the whole population. So some animals might have ended up less scary because it gave them an edge. Maybe they could sneak up on prey more easily, or maybe being less intimidating helped them find mates. On the other hand, some animals probably didn't need to be scary at all, since they already had other ways to defend themselves or find food.

As for sharks, yeah, some species, like the megalodon, were way bigger and more intimidating than anything swimming around today. But the smaller sharks we have now might just be better suited to their environment than the megalodon was. Honestly, we can't know for sure without more evidence.

Oklahoma's down in the Great Plains and South Central part of the US. Farming's a big deal there, mostly wheat, cotton, and cattle. It's also a major oil and natural gas state, and those industries matter a lot to the economy. You'll find food processing, aerospace and defense, and general manufacturing too. And beyond all that, there's a pretty wide mix of other businesses, things like healthcare, education, finance, and tourism.

Term life insurance covers you for a set stretch, usually 10, 20, or 30 years. If the insured person dies during that window, the policy pays a death benefit to whoever is named as beneficiary. If the young adult has no dependents, though, the parents probably wouldn't get much financial benefit from the policy, since losing them wouldn't create a big money hole for the family. Parents might still push for it anyway. It can help cover funeral and burial costs, or give some support to a spouse or other people who rely on the young adult. Term is also way cheaper than permanent life insurance, which lasts your whole life. So even if mom and dad don't end up cashing in, it could still make sense for the kid, especially if they plan to have dependents someday or just don't want to pay the higher premiums that come with permanent coverage.

The Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA) gives qualifying employees the right to take up to 12 weeks of unpaid leave for specific family and medical reasons while keeping their job secure. Beyond job security, the law offers eligible workers several additional safeguards. For one, employers must keep up the worker's group health insurance during the leave, so the employee retains the same coverage as before and does not need to arrange or pay for replacement insurance. The law also permits leave for several purposes, such as caring for a seriously ill relative, welcoming a newborn or newly adopted child, or recovering from the employee's own serious health problem. Such leave helps workers manage the pressures of job and family, giving them the time and support required to look after themselves and those who depend on them. Finally, FMLA guarantees that an eligible employee who returns from leave can resume the same job or one comparable to it. Knowing this, workers can step away from their duties without fearing they will lose their position and have to search for a new one.

There are roughly 285 to 290 million registered vehicles in the United States, depending on the source and year. The Federal Highway Administration, which compiles state registration data, reported about 283 million registered vehicles for 2022, a figure that includes passenger cars, SUVs, pickup trucks, motorcycles, buses, and commercial trucks. Industry analysts such as S&P Global Mobility, which track "vehicles in operation," estimated the light-vehicle fleet alone at around 286 to 289 million in 2023 and 2024.

The total has grown steadily for decades, generally by a few million vehicles each year, and the average vehicle on the road is now more than 12 years old, a record high. Light trucks, a category that includes SUVs, pickups, and minivans, make up a large and growing majority of the fleet compared with traditional cars. Among the states, California has the most registered vehicles, with well over 30 million, followed by Texas and Florida.

Because states report registrations differently and some vehicles are registered in more than one place or remain registered after they stop being driven, any national total should be treated as a close estimate rather than an exact count.

Mary Matalin is married to James Carville, the Democratic political strategist best known for leading Bill Clinton's successful 1992 presidential campaign. Matalin, a Republican strategist who worked for George H. W. Bush's 1992 reelection effort and later served as an adviser to Vice President Dick Cheney, married Carville in 1993, just after that campaign in which they were on opposing sides.

Their marriage has drawn attention for decades because of their sharply different political affiliations. They co-wrote a book about the 1992 campaign called "All's Fair: Love, War, and Running for President," and later "Love & War: Twenty Years, Three Presidents, Two Daughters and One Louisiana Home." The couple has two daughters, Matty and Emerson, and they moved from the Washington area to New Orleans in 2008.

Ovex is generally considered safe for a 4-year-old with threadworm. Its active ingredient, pyrantel, is licensed for children from around 2 years old, and it works in the intestine, where threadworms live, not in the stomach. Always check the leaflet or packet for the correct dose for his age and weight, and never give more than the label says.

Ovex doesn't work quickly in the way you might expect. It paralyses the worms so they pass out in the stools, usually within a day or two, but it doesn't kill the eggs. Eggs laid around the bottom before treatment can keep causing itching for a week or two afterwards, even though the treatment has worked. So waking with itching on the night after a dose doesn't necessarily mean it has failed, and you shouldn't give an extra dose just because the itching continues.

The usual approach is a second dose two weeks after the first. This kills any worms that have hatched from eggs in the meantime, which is important because the first dose doesn't clear everything. If you're unsure whether this is threadworm at all, your GP or pharmacist can advise, since the itching could have other causes. It's worth seeing a doctor if the itching continues well beyond two weeks after the second dose, if he has a fever, stomach pain, weight loss or blood in his stools, or if he seems unwell.

While you're treating him, it helps to keep his nails short and discourage scratching, wash his hands after using the toilet and before eating, and change and wash his pyjamas and bedding at a hot temperature. Wash bath towels separately and try to avoid shaking bedding, since eggs can spread into the air. If the infection has spread, other family members may need treating at the same time, and your GP or pharmacist can advise on that too.

Prednisolone for kids is usually dosed by weight, so the exact amount depends on how much your child weighs and what's being treated. For hives (urticaria), the usual range is about 1 to 2 mg/kg a day, split into a couple of doses. That can shift though, depending on how bad the hives are and how your kid responds.

I'd run it by your doctor before starting anything, prednisolone included. They know your child's history and can set the right dose and figure out how long the course should be. Then stick to the schedule they give you, and finish the whole course even if the symptoms clear up early. If you stop too soon, the hives can come right back.

Keep an eye out for side effects too, and tell your doctor if something worries you. The common ones are an upset stomach, a bigger appetite than usual, and trouble sleeping. If you notice mood or behavior changes, don't wait on that one. Call your doctor right away.

I can't see your reports, so I can't say exactly what is happening in your case, but I can explain the common reasons follicles grow slowly during an IUI cycle and what usually happens next.

Ovitrop HP 75 contains menotropin, which is FSH and LH activity, and it is given to push the ovaries to develop follicles. Response to it varies a lot between women and even between cycles in the same woman. The most common reasons for a slow response are a lower ovarian reserve (low AMH or low antral follicle count), which often goes with age over about 35, though it can happen earlier. Polycystic ovary syndrome can cause either a sluggish or an exaggerated response, depending on the dose. Other causes include a starting dose that is too low for your body, thyroid problems, high prolactin, high BMI or insulin resistance, and sometimes the timing of when the injections were started in the cycle. Previous ovarian surgery, endometriosis, or an ovarian cyst can also reduce response. Sometimes no cause is found, and the ovaries simply respond slowly in a particular cycle.

Needing 8 or more days of injections is not unusual. Many women need 8 to 12 days, and growth is typically about 1 to 2 mm a day once follicles are established. Your doctor is monitoring you with scans, so the plan is likely to be adjusted based on how the follicles look. Options include continuing the same dose, increasing it, adding more days, or, if the response stays poor, cancelling or converting the cycle and trying a different protocol next time. When the lead follicle reaches about 18 to 20 mm, a trigger injection is given and the IUI is timed 24 to 36 hours later.

It would help to ask your doctor a few things: what your AMH and antral follicle count are, what size the follicles are now, whether your dose will be changed, and what the plan is if growth is still inadequate. Also ask whether your thyroid, prolactin, and blood sugar have been checked.

Please don't change or stop the injections on your own. Follow the scan schedule, and contact your clinic promptly if you get severe abdominal pain, bloating, vomiting, or breathlessness, as these can signal overstimulation. A poor response in one cycle doesn't mean future cycles will fail, since protocols can be adjusted.

Association rule mining is a data mining method for uncovering connections between variables in large collections of data. It helps reveal recurring patterns that can be used to anticipate future events or guide decisions. These relationships are usually expressed as "if-then" statements: the "if" portion lists a group of items (an "itemset") that appear together in a transaction, while the "then" portion names an item or itemset likely to be bought alongside them. For instance, a rule might state that a customer who buys bread and milk is also likely to buy butter.

To find such rules, algorithms rely on a measure of how strongly the items on each side of the rule are linked. This measure, known as support, counts how many transactions in the dataset contain those items together. A rule with high support is regarded as more dependable, since the pattern shows up more often. Association rule mining has many uses, such as market basket analysis, fraud detection, and recommendation systems. As a result, it serves as a valuable tool for understanding relationships in data and offering insights that can shape business strategy.

Fleas are these tiny wingless bugs that can jump surprisingly far for their size. They mostly live on mammals and birds and feed on their blood. They're ectothermic, so they can't control their own body temperature and depend on their surroundings to stay warm. That's why you usually find them in warm, humid places where hosts are easy to come by. They also turn up wherever their hosts hang out a lot, like homes, animal shelters, and kennels. And they don't only stay on the animal itself. Plenty of them live in the environment too, like in grass, leaves, or any other spot where their hosts spend time.

Random optimization is a family of search methods for finding the best value of a function when you cannot easily compute its gradient or when the function is noisy, discontinuous, or otherwise poorly behaved. Instead of relying on calculus to determine which direction leads uphill or downhill, these methods explore the space of possible solutions using randomness, sampling candidate points and keeping those that perform better.

The simplest version is pure random search. You repeatedly pick points at random from the feasible region, evaluate the objective function at each one, and remember the best point found so far. Although this is crude, it has a surprising advantage: it makes no assumptions about smoothness, and with enough samples it will eventually get close to the optimum. Its weakness is inefficiency, since it wastes effort on regions that are clearly poor.

A more refined approach is random local search, sometimes called stochastic hill climbing. Here you start from a current candidate, perturb it by adding a small random change, and accept the new point if it improves the objective. Repeating this gradually climbs toward a good solution. Many variants adjust the size of the random steps over time, taking larger jumps early on to explore broadly and smaller ones later to refine the answer.

Other well-known methods build on the same idea. Simulated annealing sometimes accepts worse solutions, with a probability that decreases over time, so the search can escape local optima. Evolutionary strategies and genetic algorithms maintain a population of candidates, combine and mutate them randomly, and select the fittest to form the next generation. The Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy (CMA-ES) is a particularly successful example that learns the shape of promising regions as it goes. Random restarts are another common tactic, in which the search is launched repeatedly from different random starting points to reduce the risk of being trapped in a single poor local optimum.

Random optimization is especially useful in settings such as hyperparameter tuning, engineering design, simulation-based models, and reinforcement learning, where evaluating the objective is expensive or the function is a black box. Its main drawbacks are that it can require many function evaluations, convergence is often slow compared with gradient-based methods on smooth problems, and results depend on the quality of the random sampling and tuning choices. Even so, its robustness and simplicity make it a valuable tool when more principled methods are not applicable.

I'm sorry you're dealing with stomach pain. There are many possible reasons for it, and a proper diagnosis is important before any treatment begins. Your discomfort may be related to gastric trouble, though numerous other conditions could be responsible. Among the likely causes are indigestion, food poisoning, a viral or bacterial infection, inflammatory bowel disease, and constipation. If your pain is severe, please see a doctor without delay. A physician can examine you and may order tests to pinpoint the source. Until then, a few measures might ease your symptoms. Steer clear of spicy, greasy, or acidic foods, since they can inflame the stomach and make the pain worse. Keep up your fluid intake, particularly water, which may help your body clear out anything contributing to the problem. An over-the-counter pain reliever like acetaminophen or ibuprofen may also take the edge off. Rather than large meals, try eating smaller portions more often, which can be gentler on your digestion. A probiotic supplement is another option, since it may help restore healthy bacteria in your gut and relieve symptoms. I hope these suggestions help, and I strongly encourage you to consult a doctor soon so the cause can be identified and treated properly.

Direct marketing is basically when a business talks straight to its customers instead of going through some middleman, usually by email, text, or social media. The point is to get people's attention and nudge them to buy something or do some other specific thing, like signing up or clicking through to a page.

Most campaigns start with a targeted list of people who've already shown some interest in a product or service. Companies build those lists from all sorts of places: their own customer databases, website traffic data, purchase history, that kind of thing.

One big upside is that you can actually measure how it's going. You can look at open rates, click-through rates, and conversion rates, so you can see pretty quickly what's working and what's flopping, then tweak things.

There are a few main flavors. Email marketing means sending promos or newsletters to a list of addresses. SMS marketing is the same idea but with text messages to phone numbers. Social media marketing is promoting stuff on Facebook, Twitter, Instagram and the like. Direct mail is the old-school physical stuff, like brochures and catalogs sent through the post. And telemarketing is calling people up to pitch them products or services.

Done right, it can work really well for reaching and engaging customers. You just have to respect their privacy and what they actually want to hear about, or it goes sideways fast.

COMPAS, short for Correctional Offender Management Profiling for Alternative Sanctions, is a proprietary software tool developed by a company called Northpointe, which later became part of Equivant (now Constellation Justice Systems). It is used in the United States criminal justice system to assess the likelihood that a defendant or offender will reoffend, and to help identify their needs for supervision and treatment. It was first developed in the late 1990s and has been adopted by courts, probation departments, and corrections agencies in a number of states, including New York, Wisconsin, California, and Florida.

The software works by taking in answers to a questionnaire of around 137 questions, some drawn from interviews with the person being assessed and some from criminal records. These cover things like criminal history, age at first arrest, employment, education, residential stability, substance use, social environment, and attitudes toward crime. The tool then produces scores on several scales, most notably risk of general recidivism, risk of violent recidivism, and risk of failure to appear in court. Scores are presented as decile ratings from 1 to 10, grouped into low, medium, and high risk. The specific algorithm is a trade secret, so defendants and often courts cannot examine exactly how the scores are calculated.

COMPAS became widely known in 2016 after a ProPublica investigation analyzed scores for thousands of defendants in Broward County, Florida. The journalists concluded that the tool was biased against Black defendants: Black defendants who did not go on to reoffend were nearly twice as likely as white defendants to have been labeled high risk, while white defendants who did reoffend were more often mislabeled as low risk. Northpointe disputed this, arguing that the tool was fair because its scores were equally accurate in predicting reoffending across racial groups, meaning a given score corresponded to roughly the same actual recidivism rate regardless of race.

This disagreement sparked a major academic debate. Researchers showed that when the underlying rates of recorded reoffending differ between groups, it is mathematically impossible to satisfy several intuitive definitions of fairness at once, such as equal error rates and equal predictive accuracy across groups. The case thus became a standard example in discussions of algorithmic fairness and machine learning ethics. Other studies questioned how accurate the tool really is, with one finding that untrained online volunteers predicted recidivism about as well as COMPAS did, and that a simple model using just a couple of variables performed comparably.

Legal challenges have also arisen. In State v. Loomis (2016), the Wisconsin Supreme Court allowed the use of COMPAS in sentencing but said it could not be the determinative factor and that judges should be given written warnings about its limitations, including its proprietary nature and concerns about group-based predictions. Critics continue to raise issues of transparency, due process, and whether such tools reinforce existing disparities in policing and prosecution, since the data they rely on reflects past enforcement patterns.

Yes, quite a few places. In the United States, personal finance has been taught in high schools for decades, and a growing number of states now require it for graduation. Utah was one of the earliest to mandate a personal finance course, and by the early 2020s many other states had followed, with some requiring a standalone course and others folding the material into math or social studies. The Council for Economic Education tracks these requirements and has reported steady growth in the number of states that mandate it.

Other countries have taken similar steps. Australia includes financial literacy in its national curriculum, and several Canadian provinces teach money management within math or other required courses. In the United Kingdom, financial education appears in the citizenship and math curricula, and the government has promoted it in schools for years. Countries such as New Zealand, Singapore, and several in Europe and Asia also include financial literacy in their schooling, though the depth and format vary considerably.

The quality and consistency of these courses differ widely. Some are a single semester covering budgeting, credit, taxes, and saving, while others are a brief unit within a broader class. Whether a student encounters the subject often depends on where they live and which school they attend.

If you're hoping to conceive and your periods are irregular, tracking your menstrual cycle may help you spot patterns and estimate when you're most likely to ovulate. Ovulation is when an egg is released from the ovary, and pregnancy cannot happen without it. There are a few ways to follow your cycle and estimate your ovulation window. One is to keep a menstrual calendar, noting how long each cycle lasts and when your periods start. Most cycles run about 28 days, though anywhere from 21 to 35 days is considered normal. In a 28-day cycle, ovulation usually happens around day 14, but the timing shifts depending on how long your cycle is. Another option is ovulation predictor kits, which you can buy at pharmacies. They work by detecting luteinizing hormone (LH) in your urine, since LH rises sharply just before ovulation. A third approach is charting your basal body temperature, which is your resting temperature. It usually goes up slightly after ovulation. Taking your temperature each morning before getting out of bed and recording it over several weeks can reveal patterns that point to your most fertile days. You should also speak with your doctor about any concerns regarding your cycle or fertility. They may recommend treatments or medications that can regulate your periods and improve your chances of conceiving. For instance, clomiphene (sold as Fertyl) is commonly prescribed to treat infertility in women with irregular periods. Any medication, including this one, should be taken only under the direction of a healthcare provider.

A healthcare provider should evaluate any rash so it can be properly diagnosed and treated. Without further information, it's hard to recommend a specific treatment, since a rash on the arms and stomach can have many causes, and the right approach depends on which one is responsible. Several common causes include the following. Allergic reactions may produce a rash as one of their symptoms, and it can be itchy, red, or bumpy. The triggers vary widely and include medications, foods, and things in the environment. Infections, whether bacterial or fungal, can also lead to a rash on these areas. It may look red and bumpy and could come with other symptoms such as fever, chills, and tiredness. Skin conditions such as eczema, psoriasis, and dermatitis are another possibility, and these can arise from genetics, environmental influences, and stress, among other factors. A healthcare provider can pinpoint what is behind the rash and suggest suitable treatment. Meanwhile, your partner could try over-the-counter creams or ointments to ease the itching and discomfort. It is also worth telling the provider that your partner had troubling symptoms (nausea, sweating, and feeling faint) after taking cocodamol. The medication may have caused them, so this should be raised with a healthcare provider too, who might suggest a different drug or change the dose.

Any website can potentially be hacked, though some are better protected than others. How secure a site is depends on the quality of its design and the care taken in maintaining it. Making a site completely secure, immune to every attempt at intrusion, is extremely hard and probably impossible. Attackers keep discovering fresh methods of breaking in, while developers keep working to close the gaps and strengthen their sites. Even the best-protected website can fall to a hacker who has enough skill, time, and resources. The situation resembles a game of cat and mouse: hackers constantly look for a way in, and developers constantly try to keep them out. Site owners should therefore review their security on a regular basis and repair any weaknesses they uncover, which makes success as difficult as possible for attackers. To sum up, no website is entirely safe, but some are safer than others, and owners should do everything they can to protect their sites as well as possible.

Race and gender are distinct concepts, and each shapes people's lives in its own way. Gender refers to a person's internal sense of who they are, which may or may not match the sex they were recorded as at birth.
