Race, by contrast, concerns observable physical traits such as skin tone, eye shape, and hair texture. Such traits are typically passed down from parents and are not something a person can alter. While someone may choose to identify with a gender other than the one assigned to them at birth, race is not a matter of personal choice in the same way, since it is not something a person can change.

Yeah, a blood test can sometimes show signs of cancer or at least raise a flag that something might be going on. But it's usually not enough on its own to diagnose it. Cancer is tricky to pin down, so doctors often need a bunch of different tests to confirm it or rule it out. There are several kinds of blood tests used for this. Some check levels of certain proteins or substances that tend to go up in people with cancer. Others look for cancer cells or bits of abnormal DNA floating around in the blood, which can sometimes be one of the earliest clues. If you've been dealing with things like dizziness, blood pressure that's either too high or too low, trouble breathing, or weight loss you can't explain, get in to see a healthcare provider soon. Those symptoms can come from lots of different causes, so you really want a proper diagnosis. They'll probably examine you and might order a blood test or other work-up to figure out what's going on.

Magic Kingdom is the big flagship park at Walt Disney World, down in Lake Buena Vista, Florida, just outside Orlando. It's actually the most visited theme park in the world, pulling in over 20 million people a year. The whole place is built around classic Disney stories and characters, so you get rides, shows, and attractions based on all those old favorites. Cinderella Castle is the one everybody knows, but Pirates of the Caribbean and Space Mountain are huge draws too. The park's split up into themed lands like Adventureland, Frontierland, Fantasyland, and Tomorrowland, so there's a pretty different vibe depending on which part you're wandering through.

Long short-term memory, usually abbreviated LSTM, is a type of recurrent neural network architecture designed to learn from sequences of data while remembering relevant information over long stretches of time. It was introduced by Sepp Hochreiter and Jürgen Schmidhuber in 1997 to address a central weakness of ordinary recurrent neural networks, namely the vanishing gradient problem.

In a standard recurrent network, the model processes a sequence one step at a time, carrying a hidden state forward from each step to the next. When training with backpropagation through time, the error signals must travel backward through many steps, and they are repeatedly multiplied by numbers that are often smaller than one. As a result, the gradients shrink toward zero, and the network struggles to learn dependencies between events that are far apart, such as a word at the start of a paragraph that determines the correct form of a verb at the end.

The LSTM solves this by adding a separate memory pathway called the cell state, which runs through the sequence with only small, controlled modifications. Information can flow along this pathway almost unchanged, which lets gradients survive across many time steps. The flow of information into and out of the cell state is regulated by gates, each of which is a small neural layer with a sigmoid activation that outputs values between zero and one, acting like a soft switch.

There are three main gates. The forget gate decides how much of the existing cell state to keep or discard. The input gate decides how much new candidate information, computed from the current input and the previous hidden state, should be written into the cell state. The output gate decides how much of the updated cell state is exposed as the hidden state, which is passed to the next step and used for predictions. Because these gates are learned during training, the network figures out for itself what is worth remembering and what can be forgotten.

Several variants exist. The most popular is the gated recurrent unit, or GRU, which simplifies the design by merging some gates and the cell and hidden states. Bidirectional LSTMs read a sequence in both directions, and stacked LSTMs layer several on top of each other for greater capacity.

LSTMs were the dominant approach for many sequence tasks from the 2000s through the mid-2010s, including speech recognition, handwriting recognition, machine translation, language modeling, and time series forecasting. Since around 2017, Transformer models, which rely on attention rather than recurrence, have replaced LSTMs in most large-scale language applications because they train more efficiently in parallel and handle very long contexts better. Still, LSTMs remain useful for smaller datasets, streaming data, and settings where compact, low-latency models are important.

Happy hour got its name a long time ago, when a bar might have offered a special drink deal for just one hour each day, usually in the late afternoon when the place was quiet. The name stuck even after the idea changed. Today many places stretch that time out to two or three hours, or even all afternoon, because it helps bring in customers for longer. People still call it happy hour out of habit, a bit like how we still say "sunrise" even though the sun doesn't really rise.

Think of it like a nickname that got older than the thing it describes. Your grandma might still call the TV "the radio" even though it shows pictures now. Happy hour is the same: the name is from the old days, but the fun part, cheaper snacks and drinks, is still there, and it can last as long as the restaurant wants it to.

Sure thing! So big games fit on one disc because they're on Blu-ray, which just holds way more data than a DVD. That's why a season of a show can end up spread across several DVDs while a game squeezes onto one Blu-ray. Think of it like buckets. A Blu-ray is a big bucket and a DVD is a smaller one. If you've got a ton of water to store, you'll need a bunch of small buckets, but a big bucket can hold the same amount in one go. Make sense?

US airliners typically maintain a cabin pressure altitude of about 6,000 to 8,000 feet, which corresponds to roughly 11.0 to 12.2 pounds per square inch of air pressure, compared with about 14.7 psi at sea level. The aircraft's pressurization system keeps the cabin at this level even when the plane is cruising at 35,000 feet or more, where outside pressure is only around 3.5 psi. Regulations from the Federal Aviation Administration set a maximum cabin altitude of 8,000 feet under normal conditions at the aircraft's maximum certified altitude, and many modern jets, such as the Boeing 787 and Airbus A350, are designed to hold a lower cabin altitude of around 6,000 feet, which is easier on passengers and crew.

Greek is an Indo-European language with one of the longest recorded histories of any language in the world, with written evidence stretching back more than three thousand years. It is the official language of Greece and one of the two official languages of Cyprus, and it is spoken by roughly thirteen to fifteen million people today, including substantial communities in the diaspora in places like the United States, Australia, Germany, and Canada.

The language is traditionally divided into several major phases. Mycenaean Greek, written in the Linear B script, is the earliest attested form, dating to around the fifteenth to twelfth centuries BCE. After a gap in the written record, the alphabet was adapted from Phoenician in roughly the eighth century BCE, and Ancient Greek developed through several dialects such as Attic, Ionic, Doric, and Aeolic. Ancient Greek was the language of Homer, of the philosophers Plato and Aristotle, of the historians Herodotus and Thucydides, and of the New Testament. Its classical form, centered on the Attic dialect of Athens, became the standard for literature and learning.

Medieval and modern Greek developed from the Koine, the common Greek spoken across the Hellenistic and Roman worlds, and later from Byzantine Greek. Modern Greek is written with the Greek alphabet, a script of twenty-four letters that also gave rise to the Latin and Cyrillic alphabets. Today the language is commonly distinguished as Modern Greek, which has a standardized form based on the Athenian dialect, and it retains a rich vocabulary that has contributed many terms to English and other languages, especially in science, medicine, philosophy, and mathematics.

Simulation-based optimization is an approach for finding the best values of a system's controllable inputs when the system's behavior is too complex to describe with a closed-form mathematical model. Instead of writing down an equation that links decisions to outcomes, the analyst builds a simulation model that imitates how the system behaves, such as a factory floor, a supply chain, a queueing network, or a financial portfolio under random market movements. The simulation is run with different input settings, and an optimization algorithm uses the results to search for the settings that perform best according to a defined objective, such as minimizing cost, maximizing throughput, or reducing waiting times.

The central difficulty is that the objective function is typically not available in explicit form. Each evaluation requires running the simulation, which may be computationally expensive, and the outputs are often noisy because the simulation involves random elements. Because of this, simulation-based optimization draws on specialized techniques. Common methods include response surface methodology, which fits a simple statistical model to a set of simulation runs and uses it to guide the search; ranking and selection procedures, which statistically identify the best option among a small set of alternatives; metaheuristics such as genetic algorithms, simulated annealing, and tabu search, which explore the solution space without needing gradient information; and stochastic approximation methods, which adjust inputs iteratively using noisy estimates of gradients.

The field is widely used in manufacturing scheduling, logistics, healthcare capacity planning, call center staffing, energy systems, and military planning, wherever decisions must be evaluated under uncertainty and direct experimentation on the real system would be costly, risky, or impossible. Its main challenges are managing the computational budget, handling noise in the results, and ensuring that the simulation model is an adequate representation of the real system.

There are a few ways you can get your hands on foreign government bonds. First, some governments let individuals and institutions buy directly from their central bank or treasury. You can usually find the steps on that agency's website, so it's worth a look. Second, a brokerage with international investment services can get you into a wide range of foreign securities, government bonds included. Third, if picking individual bonds sounds like a hassle, you could go with a mutual fund or ETF that holds a mix of foreign government bonds. That's an easy way to get exposure without doing all the research yourself.

Whichever route you take, keep the risks in mind. If the bond is denominated in a foreign currency, exchange rates can eat into your returns. You're also taking on the risk that the foreign government's finances or stability take a turn for the worse. Look into both of these before you commit any money.
In the 1960 U.S. presidential election, John F. Kennedy, often called JFK, competed against the Republican nominee, Richard Nixon. Kennedy came out on top and became the nation's 35th president.

Sunlight is a source of energy that originates from the sun, and it can be turned into electricity by means of solar panels. These panels consist of cells made from a specialized substance known as silicon. When light from the sun strikes the panels, the cells absorb its energy, prompting electrons within the silicon to begin circulating. As these electrons travel, they generate an electrical current, much like water flowing through a river. That current can supply power to houses, companies, and other structures. Before it can be used, however, the electricity must be adjusted in voltage, a process carried out by a component called an inverter. The inverter converts the direct current (DC) produced by the panels into alternating current (AC), the form of electricity found in homes and workplaces. Once it has been converted, the electricity travels through wiring to operate lights, appliances, and other electrical equipment in a building. In short, solar panels turn sunlight into electricity, and an inverter transforms that electricity into a usable form, which together make it possible to convert solar energy into electrical energy for homes and businesses.

Chest pain that moves around and comes with brief dizzy spells can have many causes, and some of them are serious, so it's worth having a doctor evaluate it soon rather than waiting to see if it passes.

Many cases turn out to be harmless. Pain that shifts across the upper ribcage and chest is often musculoskeletal, such as inflammation of the cartilage where the ribs meet the breastbone (costochondritis) or strain from posture, coughing, or exercise. Acid reflux and esophageal spasm can cause pain in the middle of the chest that wanders. Anxiety and panic can cause chest discomfort along with lightheadedness, often in episodes that come on suddenly and fade within minutes. Dizziness lasting 10 to 20 seconds can result from brief drops in blood pressure, dehydration, standing up too quickly, low blood sugar, or anemia.

However, chest pain together with dizziness also needs to be taken seriously, because heart rhythm problems or reduced blood flow to the heart can cause exactly these symptoms. Irregular heartbeats or brief episodes of abnormal rhythm can produce a sensation of lightheadedness, and cardiac causes are important to rule out, particularly if you have risk factors such as high blood pressure, high cholesterol, diabetes, smoking, a family history of heart disease, or you are over about 40. A doctor can check with an electrocardiogram (ECG), blood tests, and possibly a heart rhythm monitor worn for a few days or weeks, which is often the best way to catch intermittent episodes.

Please seek emergency care right away if the chest pain becomes crushing or pressure-like, spreads to your arm, jaw, neck, or back, or comes with shortness of breath, sweating, nausea, fainting, or a racing or irregular heartbeat. Similarly, go urgently if a dizzy spell doesn't resolve or you lose consciousness.

If none of those apply, book an appointment with your primary care doctor within the next few days and describe what you've told me, including how often the episodes happen, what you were doing when they started, and whether anything seems to bring them on or relieve them. Keeping a simple log of episodes can be very helpful.

Four Thirds (often written 4/3) is a digital camera sensor standard and lens mount system developed jointly by Olympus and Kodak, with the first specification published in 2002. The name refers to the sensor size, which measures roughly 18 by 13.5 millimeters, giving a 4:3 aspect ratio. That is smaller than a full-frame sensor but larger than the sensors in most compact cameras, and it was designed to allow compact, lightweight camera bodies and lenses while still producing good image quality.

A defining feature of the system is its lens mount, which has a short flange focal distance (the distance between the lens mount and the sensor). This short distance allowed lenses to be built smaller and lighter, and it also made adapting other lenses to the system easier. Cameras using the standard include Olympus E-series DSLRs such as the E-510 and E-620, and Panasonic Lumix models like the GH series, which were especially popular with videographers.

Because the sensor is smaller than full frame or APS-C, the system has a crop factor of 2, meaning a lens produces the same field of view on a Four Thirds body as a lens twice its focal length would on a full-frame camera. This gives telephoto reach in a smaller package, though it also makes achieving shallow depth of field harder than on larger sensors.

In 2008 Olympus and Panasonic introduced Micro Four Thirds, a mirrorless variant that keeps the same sensor size but uses a shorter flange distance and a smaller mount. Micro Four Thirds became the more widely adopted successor, and the original DSLR-based Four Thirds system is now largely discontinued, though its lenses can still be used on Micro Four Thirds bodies with an adapter.

An AI accelerator is a hardware device or software library built to speed up artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) workloads, including both training and inference. Because these workloads are computationally demanding and need substantial processing power, an accelerator helps by supplying hardware or software tailored to them. Several kinds of AI accelerators exist. Graphics processing units (GPUs) are specialized processors originally meant to handle the complicated calculations behind graphics rendering, though they can also speed up AI and ML work. Tensor processing units (TPUs) are custom chips Google developed specifically to accelerate machine learning, for example training and running deep neural networks. Field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs) are hardware devices that can be programmed to carry out a particular set of tasks, and they speed up AI and ML work by performing the necessary calculations more efficiently. Application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs) are custom chips built for a defined set of tasks, and like FPGAs, they accelerate AI and ML workloads by offering a more efficient way to do the required calculations. AI accelerators can shorten the time needed to train machine learning models, and they can also help during inference, when a trained model makes predictions on new data. They are especially valuable for workloads that depend on heavy parallel processing, such as those involving large datasets or complex models.

Meningitis is inflammation of the membranes around the brain and spinal cord. In babies, it is usually caused by an infection that reaches the brain through the bloodstream or nearby tissue. Newborns and infants under about three months are especially vulnerable because their immune systems are still developing. The most common bacterial causes in this age group are Group B streptococcus, E. coli, and Listeria, which babies often pick up around the time of birth. Older infants are more likely to get meningitis from Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis, or, before routine vaccination, Haemophilus influenzae. Viral meningitis is more common overall and is most often caused by enteroviruses, which spread through respiratory droplets and contact with feces, and sometimes by herpes simplex virus, which is usually acquired during birth.

Methamphetamine does not directly cause meningitis, and drug use cannot transmit it by itself. The association you have heard about is indirect. People who use injection drugs or who have poor hygiene, limited medical care, or crowded living conditions have higher rates of serious infections, and some of those infections can spread to the brain. Infants in households with these risks may also have more exposure to germs, but that is a matter of risk, not a deliberate act.

Whether the baby's infection was viral or bacterial, and where it came from, will be determined by the medical team through testing of the spinal fluid and blood, and sometimes through information about the mother's health during pregnancy and delivery. Early treatment is critical, and the doctors are best placed to explain what they find. If you have specific concerns about the baby's safety or care, you can share them directly with the hospital's staff or social worker, who are trained to look into those questions appropriately. In the meantime, it is understandable to be worried, and it may help to focus on supporting the family while the baby receives care.

Genetic algorithms are basically optimization methods modeled on natural evolution, and people use them to hunt for good solutions to search and optimization problems. The way it works is you take a bunch of candidate solutions (called "individuals" or "chromosomes") and encode each one as a string of bits or numbers. Then you push them around with a few operators: selection, crossover (also called recombination), and mutation.

Each individual gets scored by a fitness function that tells you how good the solution it represents actually is. Fitter individuals have a better shot at being picked for the next round. The chosen ones get paired up for crossover, where chunks of bits or numbers from two parents get swapped or mixed to make an offspring. Then mutation randomly tweaks a few of those bits or numbers, just to keep things from getting stale. You repeat this over many generations and, with any luck, the population drifts toward better and better answers.

What's nice about them is that they can dig through huge search spaces and turn up decent solutions even when the problem is messy and hard to model. The catch is that they eat a lot of computing power, and there's no guarantee they'll actually land on the true best solution.

Okay so Siddhartha Gautama, aka the Buddha, was a spiritual teacher who lived around 2,500 years ago in ancient India. He's basically the founder of Buddhism, which is all about reaching enlightenment through meditation and good moral conduct. He grew up as a prince and had a pretty posh life. But he got really bothered by all the suffering he saw around him, so he walked away from that life to figure out how to end it. He spent years doing strict asceticism, basically denying himself everything and disciplining his body hard, hoping that would get him enlightenment. It didn't. He eventually realized that punishing himself wasn't the way to go, and he landed on a middle path somewhere between indulgence and self-denial. That became the Eightfold Path, a set of guidelines for ethical and spiritual growth. Funny enough, even though he was an ascetic, he's often shown as a chubby, round figure in Buddhist art. That's meant to symbolize enlightenment and spiritual nourishment. The idea is that you don't get there by starving yourself, but through inner wisdom and understanding.

Okay so if you're just getting into the stock market, here's a quick rundown of some terms you'll run into. A stock is basically a slice of ownership in a company, so when you buy one, you're buying a small piece of that business. A share is just one unit of that ownership. If you own 100 shares, you own 100 units of the company.

Market cap is how people gauge how big a company is. You get it by multiplying the total number of outstanding shares by the current price of one share. So if a company has 1 million shares out and each one trades at $50, the market cap is $50 million.

A bull market is when prices are climbing and people feel good about where things are headed. It usually means businesses are doing well and investors are confident. The bear market is the flip side: prices are falling, folks are nervous, and it can point to a slowdown or some kind of uncertainty in the economy.

Last one is dividends. That's a payout a company sends to its shareholders, usually in cash but sometimes in extra shares. They're often paid on a schedule like every quarter or once a year.

Hope that clears up the basics. Ask away if anything's still confusing.

I'm sorry your wife is going through this. A year of severe back pain is exhausting for her and for you, and it's reasonable that the current treatment isn't controlling it well enough. Here is some general guidance, but her own treatment team needs to direct the specifics.

Spinal tuberculosis (often called Pott's disease) is treated with a long course of anti-TB medicines, usually for six to twelve months or more. Pain in this condition comes from inflammation and from pressure or instability in the affected bones, so the medicines take time to bring it under control. Pain can persist for a while even when the infection is responding. That said, uncontrolled pain for a year is a clear sign that the plan needs to be reviewed, not just endured.

Please contact her consultant soon and tell them plainly that her pain is not controlled. Ask whether her pain medicines need to be changed or strengthened, whether she needs a scan (such as an MRI) to check how the infection and the spine are doing, and whether a spine specialist should be involved, since bone involvement sometimes needs bracing or, occasionally, surgery. Ask also whether physiotherapy can be added, as guided movement and support can ease pain and protect the spine.

Some practical steps can help in the meantime. She should rest in positions that support her spine and avoid heavy lifting, bending, or twisting. Using a firm mattress and a supportive pillow, and getting help with daily tasks, can reduce strain. Warm packs may ease muscle tightness, though they should not be used over an area with reduced sensation.

Seek urgent medical care right away if she develops weakness or numbness in her legs, difficulty walking, loss of control of bladder or bowels, a high fever, or sudden worsening of back pain. These can signal pressure on the spinal cord and need emergency treatment.

If you can share which medicines she is taking and what her doctors have said about her scans, I can help you understand them and prepare questions for her next visit.

Sudden, stabbing pain in the lower back when you sneeze or cough may stem from several possible causes, such as a pulled muscle, kidney stones, or a urinary tract infection (UTI). Because you have a history of interstitial cystitis and recurrent UTIs, your symptoms could be linked to one of these issues, though they might also have an entirely different origin. If the pain is severe or doesn't go away, you should consult a healthcare professional, who can identify the underlying cause and suggest suitable treatment. Until then, applying a heating pad to the sore area, using an over-the-counter pain reliever, and staying well hydrated may help ease your discomfort.

Four Thirds cameras are digital cameras built around the Four Thirds system, an open standard for sensors and lenses introduced in 2002 by Olympus and Eastman Kodak. The name comes from the sensor format, which uses a 4:3 aspect ratio and a sensor measuring roughly 17.3 by 13 millimeters. That makes it smaller than APS-C and full-frame sensors but considerably larger than the sensors in most compact cameras and smartphones. Because the sensor is smaller than a 35mm film frame, lenses have a crop factor of about 2, so a 25mm lens gives a field of view similar to a 50mm lens on a full-frame camera.

The original Four Thirds system was designed for digital single-lens reflex cameras, meaning they used a mirror and an optical viewfinder. Olympus made most of these bodies, including the E-series like the E-1, E-3, and E-5, with Panasonic and Leica also producing some models. Because the standard was open, lenses from different manufacturers could work across bodies from different brands, which was unusual at the time.

In 2008 Olympus and Panasonic introduced Micro Four Thirds, which kept the same sensor size but removed the mirror box, creating a mirrorless system. This shortened the distance between the lens mount and the sensor, allowing much smaller and lighter cameras and lenses. Micro Four Thirds largely replaced the original DSLR-based system, which is now discontinued. Today the format is used by OM System (the successor to Olympus's camera business), Panasonic with its Lumix G and GH lines, and several other companies, including makers of cinema and video cameras such as Blackmagic Design. Original Four Thirds lenses can still be used on Micro Four Thirds bodies with an adapter.

The main appeal of the format is portability, a wide selection of compact lenses, strong in-body image stabilization, and excellent video features, which has made it popular with travelers, wildlife photographers who value the extra reach of the crop factor, and videographers. The trade-offs compared with larger sensors are generally somewhat more noise in low light and less ability to achieve very shallow depth of field at equivalent framing.

Darkening of the skin between the thighs, in the groin, and over the buttocks is common, and it usually has a benign cause. The most likely reasons are friction and sweat, which irritate the skin over time and leave it darker and duller. Tight clothing, thigh rubbing while walking, heat, humidity, and shaving or waxing in these areas all contribute. The skin in the genital and buttock region is also naturally darker than the skin on the arms or face, so some difference in tone can be normal. A fungal infection of the groin (tinea cruris) or a long-standing skin irritation can also leave a darker patch after it heals, and this is called post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation.

A less common cause to think about is acanthosis nigricans, a condition where the skin becomes darker, thicker, and velvety, often in the folds of the body. It is linked to insulin resistance, weight gain, or prediabetes, and it is worth mentioning to a doctor because it can be an early sign of diabetes. A simple blood sugar test (fasting glucose or HbA1c) can rule this out. Hormonal changes and, rarely, other medical conditions can also cause patchy darkening.

For care, wear loose cotton underwear and breathable clothing, and avoid tight pants or leggings for long periods. Keep the area clean and dry, especially after sweating, and pat it dry rather than rubbing. Use a gentle, fragrance-free cleanser, and consider a moisturizer with urea, lactic acid, or niacinamide, which can help with dullness and dryness. Stop or reduce shaving or waxing in the area for a while, since these can irritate the skin. If you notice itching, redness, scaling, or a ring-shaped rash, an antifungal cream such as clotrimazole may help, but see a doctor first to confirm the diagnosis. Avoid bleaching creams or strong steroid creams unless a doctor prescribes them, because they can thin the skin or worsen the pigmentation.

Since the change has lasted and you describe dull skin in these areas, I'd recommend seeing a doctor or dermatologist. They can examine the skin, check for fungal infection or acanthosis nigricans, and, if needed, order a blood sugar test. Most of these causes improve well once the friction and moisture are controlled and the underlying cause is treated.

The exact fees depend on your country and even your state or region, so I'll describe the typical picture in the United States and note where things differ elsewhere.

When selling, the largest cost is usually agent commissions, which historically total around 5 to 6 percent of the sale price, split between the listing agent and the buyer's agent. Recent industry changes have made commissions more negotiable, so it's worth discussing them up front. Sellers also commonly pay transfer or recording taxes (which vary widely by state and sometimes city), title and escrow fees, attorney fees in states where lawyers handle closings, and prorated property taxes and any homeowners association dues up to the closing date. You may also pay for repairs negotiated after the buyer's inspection, staging, cleaning, professional photos, and the payoff of your existing mortgage, which can include a prepayment penalty on rare loans. In total, sellers often budget 8 to 10 percent of the sale price.

When buying, you'll have closing costs that typically run 2 to 5 percent of the purchase price, separate from your down payment. These include loan origination or underwriting fees, the appraisal, a credit report fee, title search and title insurance, escrow or settlement fees, recording fees, and sometimes attorney fees. You'll also prepay certain items such as homeowners insurance, property taxes, and mortgage interest for the partial first month, and lenders often require an initial escrow deposit for taxes and insurance. If you put down less than 20 percent on a conventional loan, expect private mortgage insurance. FHA loans carry upfront and ongoing mortgage insurance premiums, VA loans have a funding fee, and USDA loans have their own guarantee fees. You can choose to pay discount points to lower your interest rate.

Buyers also pay for items outside the closing statement, including the home inspection (often a few hundred dollars), optional tests for radon, termites, sewer lines, or mold, an earnest money deposit that gets credited toward your purchase, moving costs, and immediate repairs or utility setup. In some places a buyer's agent is paid by the buyer directly, depending on the agreement you sign.

Outside the US, costs differ. In the UK, buyers pay Stamp Duty Land Tax, solicitor fees, and survey costs, while sellers pay estate agent fees, often 1 to 3 percent. In Canada, land transfer taxes can be significant for buyers. In many European countries, notary fees and transfer taxes add several percent to the buyer's costs.

To get accurate numbers, ask your lender for a Loan Estimate early on, which itemizes expected costs, and compare it with the Closing Disclosure you receive before closing. Many fees are negotiable, and you can shop around for title services, insurance, and lenders. Sellers can also ask a local agent for a net sheet estimating what they'll walk away with. If you tell me your location, I can give more specific figures.

Random forests are an ensemble learning method used for classification, regression, and other tasks. They work by building a whole bunch of decision trees during training, then spitting out either the most common class (for classification) or the average prediction (for regression) across all those trees. The big reason they exist is that single decision trees tend to overfit their training data, and forests help fix that. Each tree gets trained on a bootstrap sample, meaning a random draw from the training set taken with replacement. And when a tree splits a node, it doesn't look at every feature anymore. It only considers the best split within a random subset of features. That usually bumps the bias up a little compared to one unrestricted tree, but averaging all the trees cuts the variance way down, and that drop tends to outweigh the bias increase, so you end up with a better model. People have used them successfully for all sorts of things, like recommending products on shopping sites, banking, diagnosing diseases, and classifying images.

Excessive alcohol use can cause a range of health problems, among them stomach pain and bleeding. You should see a doctor as soon as you can so the source of your symptoms can be identified and you can receive appropriate treatment. Abdominal pain and bleeding following a bout of heavy drinking may have several explanations. One is alcoholic liver disease, in which heavy drinking damages the liver and may produce pain in the abdomen along with bleeding. Another is gastritis, where alcohol irritates the stomach lining, causing inflammation and sometimes bleeding. A third is alcoholic pancreatitis, in which heavy drinking inflames the pancreas, potentially resulting in abdominal pain and bleeding. Ulcers are also possible, since alcohol can help bring about sores in the stomach or intestines that cause pain and bleeding. Again, getting medical attention promptly is important so that the cause can be determined and properly treated. Until then, you should stop drinking alcohol and have plenty of fluids to remain hydrated.

Several things could explain this, and given your history, more than one may be involved at once. Only an exam can sort it out, but here are the most likely possibilities.

The pattern you describe, a sudden, intense pain lasting only seconds followed by burning further down the leg, sounds neuropathic, meaning it comes from a nerve rather than muscle or bone. Nerve pain tends to be sharp, electric, or stabbing and is often followed by burning, tingling, or pins and needles in the area that nerve supplies.

Multiple sclerosis is a strong candidate. MS can cause "paroxysmal symptoms," brief attacks of pain or abnormal sensation lasting seconds, sometimes many times a day, caused by misfiring in damaged nerve pathways in the brain or spinal cord. Burning dysesthesia in the legs and feet is also one of the most common MS pain types. A new symptom like this could reflect a relapse or new lesion, or a pre-existing lesion that the stress of the fall and injury has made more noticeable, since MS symptoms often flare with physical stress, pain, heat, or infection.

The fall itself could also have injured a peripheral nerve. Heavy bruising can mean a sizable hematoma, a collection of blood in the tissue, which can press on nearby nerves as it organizes and heals. The common peroneal (fibular) nerve wraps around the outer side of the leg just below the knee and is especially vulnerable to bruising or compression; irritation there classically causes pain and burning down the outer lower leg and the top of the foot. The lateral femoral cutaneous nerve, which supplies the skin of the outer thigh, can cause burning or sharp sensations in the area you describe, a condition called meralgia paresthetica.

A fall can also jar the lower back. Irritation of a lumbar nerve root, particularly L5, can send shooting pain along the outer thigh and burning into the lower leg and foot, and this can happen even if your back doesn't hurt much.

A blood clot (deep vein thrombosis) is less likely given how brief your pain is, but it's worth keeping in mind after a leg injury, especially if your mobility has been reduced. Signs would be swelling in one calf or leg, warmth, redness, or a constant aching tenderness rather than brief jolts.

I'd recommend contacting your neurologist soon, ideally within the next several days, since a new neurological symptom in someone with MS deserves evaluation. They may examine your strength, reflexes, and sensation and possibly order an MRI or nerve conduction studies. If it is MS-related paroxysmal pain or nerve pain from the injury, it is often quite treatable, sometimes with medications such as carbamazepine, gabapentin, or pregabalin.

Seek urgent care right away if you develop weakness in the leg, trouble lifting your foot or toes (foot drop), tripping or dragging your foot, new swelling, warmth, or redness in the leg, loss of bladder or bowel control, numbness in the groin or inner thighs, chest pain or shortness of breath, or other new MS symptoms such as vision changes or significant numbness elsewhere.

Thinking doesn't need words. Words are just one tool your brain uses to think, like a flashlight is one tool for seeing in the dark. You can think with pictures, sounds, feelings, movements, and ideas that have no word attached at all.

Try this: imagine how to get from your bed to the kitchen. You probably saw a little map or movie in your head, not a sentence. Or think about the taste of ice cream. There's no talking in that thought, just the taste. Babies do this too. Before they know any words, they already figure out that if they cry, someone comes, and that a dropped toy falls down. That's thinking without language.

Deaf people are a good example, but with a twist. Many deaf people do use language in their heads, just not a spoken one. If someone grew up using sign language, they think in signs. They may "see" their hands moving in their mind, or have a picture of the signs, the way you hear your inner voice. Deaf people who grew up with sign language also dream in sign. So they aren't without language at all, because sign language is a full, real language. Deaf people who grew up with no access to any language for years are a different case, closer to what you're asking about.

Feral children, or children raised with almost no human contact, are sadly very rare and hard to study. From the cases we know, they could still think in basic ways. They could solve problems, remember places, want things, and feel scared or happy. What they struggled with was complicated thinking, like planning far into the future, talking about the past, or understanding abstract ideas such as "fairness" or "next Tuesday." Words help us hold those big ideas, like handles on a heavy bag. Without handles, the bag is much harder to carry. Also, if a child doesn't learn language early, their brain has a hard time learning it later, which is why those children often never become fully fluent.

So to sum up: you think with whatever tools you have. Words are a very strong tool, but not the only one. Pictures, feelings, sounds, and body movements can all carry thoughts. Language just makes thinking bigger, faster, and easier to share.

Visible light is the slice of electromagnetic radiation our eyes can actually pick up. It runs from roughly 400 nanometers (nm) to 700 nm, which is where the name comes from. Shorter wavelengths carry more energy and look bluer, while longer ones carry less energy and look redder. That's a small chunk of the whole electromagnetic spectrum, which also includes radio waves, microwaves, infrared, ultraviolet, X-rays, and gamma rays. All of those are around us constantly, but we only see one little window of them. Still, that window matters a lot. It's how we see anything at all, and people use it for everything from lighting rooms to sending data to taking photos.

John Williams is the composer behind the music of the Star Wars films. He wrote the soundtracks for all nine principal entries in the saga, along with a range of other Star Wars productions. Williams' compositions have become a defining element of the franchise, earning wide praise from both reviewers and fans. Among the most celebrated and recognizable pieces from these films are "The Main Title," "The Imperial March," and "Duel of the Fates."

Shazam is an app that helps you figure out what song is playing around you. You open it, it listens for a few seconds, and then it tells you the title and artist if it recognizes the tune. Here's roughly how it goes. First, you open the app and tap the button to start listening. Your phone's mic grabs a short clip of whatever's playing. That clip gets sent to a server, which is basically a powerful computer that can crunch a ton of data really fast. The server compares the clip against a huge database of songs, looking for a match in the sound patterns. If it finds one, it sends the song info back to your phone, and the app shows you the name and artist on screen. Pretty neat, right? Let me know if you want more details on any part of it.

If you hold several student loans from different lenders, consolidating or refinancing them can make sense, since it can streamline your monthly payments and may reduce your interest rate. Keep a few points in mind as you weigh this choice.

First, look at the interest rate. Qualifying for a lower rate through consolidation or refinancing can reduce the total amount you pay across the life of the loan.

Second, think about the loan term. Stretching the repayment period may shrink your monthly payment, but you will end up paying more in interest overall.

Third, check for fees. Certain lenders charge for consolidating or refinancing, so compare what different lenders ask for to be sure you get the most favorable terms.

Fourth, consider your repayment situation. If you already struggle to keep up with your monthly payments, consolidating or refinancing might not be the right move. An income-driven repayment plan or a loan forgiveness program could suit you better.

Before you commit, it is wise to weigh every option carefully. Talking with a financial advisor or a student loan specialist can also help you reach the best decision for your circumstances.

Starbucks is a widely loved coffee chain across the United States, recognized for reliably good coffee and a broad menu of beverages and snacks. Much of its appeal comes from its premium ingredients and tight quality controls over how each drink is prepared, so customers can count on a satisfying cup no matter which store they visit. I'm sorry you're going through this. Five months of cough is exhausting, and it's understandable to feel discouraged. A clear X-ray is reassuring, but it doesn't rule out many causes of a lingering cough, and there are good ways to find out what's going on.

A cough that lasts for weeks after an infection is common. Once the infection clears, the airways can stay irritable for a long time, and a cough can persist for several months. Your cough never fully went away and has now flared again, so it's worth looking for something that is keeping the airways inflamed. Possibilities include asthma, sometimes appearing for the first time after a chest infection, or a cough-variant form of it. Bronchitis can also become persistent, and in some people an infection leaves behind bronchiectasis, a condition where the airways are permanently widened and prone to infection. Acid reflux, where stomach acid irritates the throat and airways, is another common cause of a long-standing cough, as is post-nasal drip from sinus problems. Some blood pressure medicines, particularly ACE inhibitors, cause a dry cough, so it's worth checking your medication list. Irritants such as smoke, damp or mould, dust, and chemical fumes at home or work can also keep a cough going.

The smoky smell is a separate question, though it may be related. After a respiratory infection, some people develop a distorted or phantom sense of smell, where they perceive smoke or other odours that aren't there. This is a recognised effect of viral illness and sinus inflammation. Sometimes the sensation is felt as a breathing or chest feeling rather than a smell, and anxiety about your breathing can make it more noticeable.

It would be worth seeing your GP soon, and if you haven't already, asking for a full review rather than a repeat of the earlier tests. Useful steps might include lung function testing (spirometry), a test of airway inflammation (such as a FeNO breath test), a trial of asthma treatment, a review of reflux and sinus symptoms, a check of your medications, and a referral to a respiratory clinic or ENT specialist if the cause isn't clear. A CT scan of the chest is sometimes done when X-rays are normal but symptoms persist. If the smell changes persist, your doctor can also discuss whether a referral for smell assessment is appropriate.

Seek medical attention promptly if you cough up blood, have fever, night sweats, unexplained weight loss, increasing breathlessness, chest pain, wheezing, or a change in the colour or amount of phlegm.

Five months is a long time, but many causes of persistent cough are treatable, and finding the right one often takes a few steps. Please don't give up on getting a proper answer.

Optical sorting is basically using cameras and sensors plus some pretty clever software to sort stuff automatically based on how it looks. You see it a lot in manufacturing and recycling, where it sorts things like plastics, metals and other materials by color, shape, size, and similar visual traits.

A typical setup has a conveyor belt (or some other moving surface) carrying the items past a row of cameras or sensors. The sensors grab images and send them to a computer, which analyzes them and decides where each item should go based on criteria someone programmed in ahead of time. Then mechanical arms or some other automated mechanism push the items into the right bins or send them off to different spots.

It's fast, and it handles huge volumes without breaking a sweat. It's usually more accurate and consistent than people sorting by hand, too. It's also friendlier to the environment than sorting methods that rely on chemicals or other hazardous stuff.

The downsides? These systems can cost a lot to buy and keep running. And if the things you're sorting are hard to tell apart just by looking at them, optical sorting probably won't work well for you.

Brain development is the process through which the brain grows and matures. It starts in the womb and carries on through childhood and adolescence into adult life. During fetal development, the brain begins to take shape within the first few weeks of pregnancy. At that point it consists of three main regions: the forebrain, the midbrain, and the hindbrain. Each of these regions differentiates and grows at its own pace, and each has a distinct part to play in the development of both the brain and the body. Once a baby is born, the brain keeps developing and changing. In the first few years of life it grows rapidly, and new connections form between neurons, the cells of the brain. This process, called neuroplasticity, lets the brain adjust and change in response to new experiences. Throughout childhood and adolescence, maturation continues. Connections between neurons become stronger, new neurons develop, and synapses, the junctions linking neurons, are both reinforced and pruned. In adulthood the brain still changes and adapts, though more slowly than in youth. Even so, it retains the ability to respond to new experiences across the whole lifespan. In short, brain development is a complex, ongoing process that is essential to the growth of the body and to a person's thoughts, behaviors, and abilities.

No, renting out a room on Airbnb doesn't make all of your interest taxable, and it doesn't cause you to lose your mortgage interest deduction. I'm assuming you're in the United States and asking about mortgage interest. What it does is change how that interest is reported, because part of your home is now being used to earn income.

When you rent out a room, the IRS expects you to split your home expenses, including mortgage interest, between personal use and rental use. The split is usually based on the share of the home's square footage that the rented room represents, and sometimes also on the number of days it was actually rented. The rental share of the interest goes on Schedule E as an expense that reduces your taxable rental income. The personal share stays on Schedule A as an itemized deduction, assuming you itemize. Since the interest is just divided between two places, you generally don't lose any of the benefit. If you take the standard deduction, moving part of the interest to Schedule E can actually help, because that portion now offsets rental income even though you aren't itemizing.

There's one important exception. If you rent the space for fewer than 15 days in the year, the rental income isn't taxable at all and you don't report it. In that case you also don't deduct any rental expenses, so your mortgage interest is treated entirely as personal.

A few related points are worth knowing. Renting part of your home can affect the capital gains exclusion when you sell, and if you claim depreciation on the rented portion, that depreciation is generally recaptured and taxed when you sell, even if the rest of the gain is excluded. Airbnb income is also reported to the IRS through Form 1099-K once you pass the reporting thresholds, so you should keep good records of the income and the expenses you allocate to the rental.

Think of it like a playground fight that happened on a different playground. The rules of the playground where something happens usually come first. Mexico does not have the death penalty, but a murder conviction there can mean many decades in prison.

The United States can also get involved, but usually not as the main judge. Under certain federal laws, the US can sometimes prosecute its own citizens for crimes committed abroad, especially when the victim was an American. So it's possible for both countries to have a claim on the case.

The two countries also have a treaty called an extradition treaty, which is a promise to hand over certain people when the other country asks. If you were in the US, Mexico could ask the US to send you there to stand trial. If you were in Mexico, the US could ask Mexico to send you back to face charges in America. Which country actually ends up trying you depends on the lawyers, the governments, and the facts of the case.

Your history teacher might find it interesting that this situation is a real example of a legal idea called "territorial jurisdiction," which means the place where a crime happens usually gets the first say. If you're asking because of a real situation, please talk to a lawyer who knows both US and Mexican law, because the details matter a lot.

Soft computing is a collection of computational techniques that aim to handle problems involving uncertainty, imprecision, partial truth, and approximation, in ways that are tolerant of these imperfections. Rather than demanding exact answers from precisely defined models, soft computing accepts approximate solutions in exchange for tractability, robustness, and low cost, much as the human mind routinely reasons and makes decisions with vague or incomplete information.

The field was popularized by Lotfi Zadeh in the early 1990s, and its core components are fuzzy logic, neural networks, evolutionary computation (such as genetic algorithms), and probabilistic reasoning. Fuzzy logic lets a system express degrees of truth, so that a statement like "the room is warm" can be true to a degree between zero and one rather than simply true or false. Neural networks learn patterns from data by adjusting many weighted connections, which makes them effective for recognition and prediction tasks where explicit rules are hard to write. Evolutionary methods borrow ideas from biological evolution, generating candidate solutions, keeping the better ones, and recombining them over successive generations to search large or poorly understood solution spaces. Probabilistic methods, including Bayesian approaches, quantify uncertainty and update beliefs as new evidence arrives.

What distinguishes soft computing from traditional "hard" computing is its emphasis on exploiting tolerance for imprecision. Hard computing seeks exact, provably correct results from precise models, which works well for problems like arithmetic or well-specified engineering calculations. Soft computing is better suited to real-world problems such as image recognition, control of complex machinery, medical diagnosis, financial forecasting, and natural language processing, where the data are noisy and the underlying relationships are too complicated to model exactly.

In practice, these techniques are often combined into hybrid systems, such as neuro-fuzzy controllers that use neural learning to tune fuzzy rules. The overall goal is systems that are practical, adaptable, and affordable, even if they do not always produce perfectly exact outputs.

A biological neuron model is a mathematical or computational description of how a real nerve cell works. Neurons are the basic signaling units of the nervous system, and they process information by receiving electrical and chemical inputs, integrating them, and sending outputs to other cells. Models aim to capture these behaviors at a level of detail suited to the question being studied, ranging from highly simplified abstractions to elaborate simulations of individual ion channels and cell geometry.

The most detailed models are biophysical. The classic example is the Hodgkin-Huxley model, developed in 1952 from experiments on the giant squid axon. It describes the membrane as an electrical circuit with a capacitor and several voltage-dependent conductances, one for sodium, one for potassium, and a leak channel. Differential equations govern how the gating variables for these channels open and close, which in turn determines how the membrane voltage rises into an action potential and then recovers. Later extensions add more channel types, dendrites, and branching morphology, producing multi-compartment models that can reproduce a neuron's complex firing patterns.

Simplified models trade biological realism for tractability. The leaky integrate-and-fire model treats the neuron as a capacitor that accumulates input current and leaks charge over time; when its voltage crosses a threshold, it emits a spike and resets. The FitzHugh-Nagumo and Izhikevich models reduce the Hodgkin-Huxley equations to two variables while still reproducing a wide range of firing behaviors such as bursting and adaptation. These simpler models are widely used in neuroscience research and in large network simulations because they are computationally cheap.

Neuron models also inform artificial intelligence. The artificial neuron used in neural networks, which computes a weighted sum of inputs and passes it through an activation function, is a far more abstract idea inspired by biological neurons. It captures the notion of integrating inputs and producing a graded output, but it omits spikes, timing, and the detailed biophysics. Spiking neural networks sit closer to biology by using integrate-and-fire style units.

In short, a biological neuron model is any formal representation of neuronal function, chosen to balance accuracy against simplicity depending on whether the goal is understanding real cells, simulating circuits, or building computational systems.

It's natural to feel nervous about receiving an injection and undergoing wisdom tooth extraction, but several measures can help you feel more at ease during the procedure. A stent surgery, more precisely called stenting or stent placement, is a procedure used to open up narrowed or blocked blood vessels or other tubular structures in the body. A stent is a small mesh tube, usually made of metal such as stainless steel or cobalt chromium, though some are made of fabric or biodegradable material. It acts as a scaffold that holds the vessel open so blood or other fluids can flow through more freely.

The most common use is in the heart, where stents treat coronary artery disease. Over time, fatty deposits called plaque can build up along the artery walls and narrow the passage, reducing blood supply to the heart muscle and causing chest pain or increasing the risk of a heart attack. In many cases, a stent is placed during a procedure called angioplasty. The doctor threads a thin catheter through a blood vessel, usually starting at the wrist or groin, guides it to the blocked area, and inflates a small balloon to widen the vessel. The stent is then left in place, often mounted on the balloon, to keep the artery open. Many stents are coated with medication that slowly releases over time to reduce the chance the artery narrows again.

Stents are also used in other parts of the body, including the legs (to treat peripheral artery disease), the carotid arteries in the neck (to reduce stroke risk), the kidneys, and the biliary or esophageal tracts, where they keep passages open that have been narrowed by disease or tumors.

Because the procedure is minimally invasive, most patients go home within a day or two and recover relatively quickly. Patients who receive a coronary stent typically take antiplatelet medication for a period afterward to keep blood from clotting on the device. As with any procedure, there are risks, such as bleeding, infection, or the vessel narrowing again, but for many people stents greatly improve symptoms and quality of life. If you are facing this procedure, your doctor can explain which type of stent and approach fit your situation.

Self-determination theory (SDT) is a framework for understanding human motivation and personality. It accounts for how the satisfaction of people's fundamental psychological needs for autonomy, competence, and relatedness connects to their well-being and mental health. The theory rests on the premise that individuals are born with a natural tendency to grow and mature, and that this tendency can be either supported or obstructed by the social and physical surroundings they inhabit. SDT identifies three core psychological needs. Autonomy refers to the desire to feel in charge of one's life and to make decisions that align with one's values and objectives. Competence is the desire to feel capable and effective in what one undertakes. Relatedness is the desire to feel close to and backed by other people. According to SDT, when these needs are fulfilled, people tend to experience more positive emotions, greater well-being, and better mental health. Conversely, when these needs go unmet, people are more prone to negative emotions, diminished well-being, and mental health difficulties. The theory has been put to use in many areas, such as education, healthcare, and the workplace, to better understand and foster well-being and psychological health.

"Human Compatible" most commonly refers to the 2019 book "Human Compatible: Artificial Intelligence and the Problem of Control" by Stuart Russell, a computer science professor at the University of California, Berkeley, and coauthor of "Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach," one of the most widely used AI textbooks. The book argues that the way artificial intelligence has traditionally been designed is fundamentally flawed and could become dangerous as AI systems grow more capable, and it proposes a different foundation for building machines that remain beneficial to people.

Russell's central critique targets what he calls the "standard model" of AI. In that model, engineers give a machine a fixed objective, and the machine works to achieve it as effectively as possible. He points out that humans are bad at specifying objectives completely and correctly, and a sufficiently powerful system pursuing a slightly wrong goal could produce harmful outcomes, much like the King Midas story, where getting exactly what you asked for turns out to be a disaster. He also notes that a machine with a fixed goal has an incentive to resist being switched off, since it cannot achieve its objective if it is turned off. Today's recommendation algorithms illustrate the point on a small scale: systems built to maximize clicks or engagement can end up shaping and polarizing users' preferences in ways nobody intended.

To address this, Russell proposes three principles for what he calls provably beneficial AI. First, the machine's only objective should be to maximize the realization of human preferences. Second, the machine should be initially uncertain about what those preferences are. Third, the ultimate source of information about human preferences should be human behavior. The key insight is that uncertainty about the objective makes a machine humble and deferential. A machine that knows it might be wrong about what we want has a reason to ask permission, accept correction, and allow itself to be switched off, because a human stopping it is evidence that it was about to do something undesirable. Technically, this connects to approaches like inverse reinforcement learning and "assistance games," in which the AI learns preferences by observing and interacting with people.

The book also discusses the difficulties this approach raises, such as the fact that humans are irrational, inconsistent, and differ from one another, so aggregating and interpreting preferences is philosophically and practically hard. Russell addresses misuse of AI, autonomous weapons, surveillance, effects on employment, and the risk of humans becoming overly dependent on machines. He responds to skeptics who dismiss concerns about advanced AI, arguing that the risks deserve serious attention even if superhuman AI is decades away.

The book was well received as an accessible yet rigorous introduction to the AI alignment problem and has influenced public and academic discussion of AI safety. Russell also founded the Center for Human-Compatible Artificial Intelligence (CHAI) at Berkeley, which researches these ideas. The better strategy for most people is usually dollar-cost averaging: investing a fixed amount on a regular schedule regardless of market conditions. This approach removes the pressure of trying to time the market, reduces the risk of investing a large sum right before a downturn, and builds a disciplined habit. Because you buy more shares when prices are low and fewer when they are high, your average cost tends to smooth out over time.

The main alternative is lump-sum investing, where you invest all available money at once. Historically, lump-sum investing has come out ahead more often than not, because markets tend to rise over long periods and money sitting in cash waits on the sidelines. If you have a large sum ready and can tolerate the possibility of an early drop, investing it all at once is statistically the stronger choice.

For a monthly strategy specifically, the real answer depends on your situation. If you are investing a portion of each paycheck, dollar-cost averaging is simply the natural approach and works well. If you have a lump sum to deploy over several months, the math favors investing it quickly, though spreading it out can help you sleep at night if a big drop would cause you to panic and sell. Whichever you choose, low-cost diversified index funds, consistent contributions, and a long time horizon matter far more than the exact timing of each purchase.

Zelenskyy announced his candidacy for president on New Year's Eve 2018, running as an outsider with an anti-corruption and anti-establishment message. He defeated the incumbent, Petro Poroshenko, in the April 2019 runoff, winning about 73 percent of the vote. His party later won an outright majority in the parliamentary elections that same year.

His presidency has been defined above all by Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, which began on February 24, 2022. Zelenskyy chose to remain in Kyiv as Russian forces advanced toward the capital, and his decision to stay, along with his frequent video addresses to Ukrainians and to foreign parliaments, made him an internationally recognized symbol of Ukrainian resistance. He has worked to secure military, financial, and humanitarian aid from Western countries and has pushed for Ukraine's eventual membership in the European Union and NATO.

His time in office has also drawn criticism and controversy. Before the war, critics questioned his political inexperience and his ties to oligarch Ihor Kolomoisky. He was also caught up in the 2019 phone call with U.S. President Donald Trump that led to Trump's first impeachment. During the war, presidential elections that would normally have been held in 2024 were postponed under martial law, which is required by Ukrainian law during wartime but has been a subject of political debate. Overall, he remains one of the most prominent world leaders of the 2020s, closely associated with Ukraine's struggle for sovereignty.

Back pain that spreads, tingles, and runs down the legs usually points to a nerve being irritated or compressed. The most common cause is a herniated or bulging disc in the lower spine, which can press on the nerve roots and send pain, tingling, or numbness into the buttock, thigh, or leg. This is often called sciatica. Narrowing of the spinal canal (spinal stenosis), degenerative changes in the spinal joints, and muscle strain can also cause similar symptoms. Pain that moves from one side to the middle of the back, or that changes over time, is common with these problems too.

Some of what you describe is less typical for simple back problems, though. Bone pain in the arms, leg pain that wakes you at night, and ongoing fatigue together with back pain deserve a proper medical evaluation rather than a guess. Several possible causes fall into this group, including inflammatory conditions, infections of the spine or bone, blood disorders, and, less commonly, tumors or conditions affecting the bone marrow. Most people with these symptoms do not have anything that serious, but a doctor should check, ideally within the next week or so. A primary care doctor can examine you, check your reflexes, strength, and sensation, and order blood tests (such as a complete blood count, inflammatory markers, and kidney and calcium levels). They may also order an X-ray, MRI, or other imaging depending on what they find.

Seek urgent care right away if you develop any of the following: loss of control of your bladder or bowels, numbness in the groin or inner thighs, rapidly worsening leg weakness or trouble walking, fever with back pain, unexplained weight loss, pain that is severe after a fall or injury, or pain that is constant and unrelenting even when you rest.

In the meantime, keep track of when the pain gets worse, what position or activity triggers it, and when the night pain and fatigue occur. That information will help your doctor narrow things down quickly.

Heart disease (or cardiovascular disease, if you want the formal name) is basically a bunch of conditions that mess with your heart and blood vessels. It's the number one killer worldwide, so it's worth knowing what raises your risk.

High blood pressure is a big one. It makes your heart and vessels work harder than they should, which ups your odds of a heart attack or stroke. High cholesterol is similar. Too much of it in your blood can build up in your arteries and cause atherosclerosis, and that also pushes up heart attack and stroke risk.

Smoking wrecks your blood vessels, plain and simple. Diabetes is another one, especially if your blood sugar isn't well controlled. Being overweight or obese counts too, since extra body fat tends to bring along high blood pressure, high cholesterol, and diabetes.

Then there's lifestyle stuff. If you barely move, you're missing out on the exercise that keeps your heart and vessels in good shape. A diet heavy on saturated and trans fats, salt, and sugar doesn't help either. Chronic stress can play a part by raising your blood pressure and shifting your cholesterol levels. And if heart disease runs in your family, your own risk is higher.

The good news is you can do a lot about most of this. Eat decently, get some regular exercise, don't smoke, keep stress in check, and keep an eye on any risk factors you've got.

Defibrillators are medical devices designed to deliver a shock that restores a normal heartbeat. They are commonly employed during cardiac arrest, a sudden event in which the heart abruptly ceases to pump. When this happens, the brain and other vital organs can be deprived of adequate oxygen, which is extremely hazardous and may prove fatal. To counter this, a defibrillator sends an electrical current through the chest and into the heart in an attempt to get it beating again. The device relies on two pads positioned on the patient's chest, which are linked to the unit. Through these pads, it releases an electric jolt meant to reset the heart's rhythm so that it can resume beating on its own. A defibrillator cannot be used to repeatedly halt and restart someone's heart. Its use is limited to emergencies in which the heart has already stopped, and it is not intended for routine use or for regulating heart rate. I hope this clarifies how defibrillators function. Please let me know if you have any further questions.

Yes, it could be, though there are a few different ways this plays out, and some of them are worth acting on quickly.

First, the dose. If she is prescribed 6 mg a day (1½ tablets of 4 mg) and is taking 6 tablets, that is 24 mg a day, four times the intended dose. Methylprednisolone 24 mg is roughly equivalent to 30 mg of prednisone, which is a meaningful dose. Higher doses of corticosteroids are well known to cause mood changes, including depression, anxiety, irritability, and sometimes agitation or insomnia. Fatigue and weakness can also occur, particularly from muscle weakness or poor sleep. Many people feel wired rather than lethargic on too much steroid, but the opposite can happen too.

Second, and this matters: if she has been on steroids for a while, her body may have reduced its own cortisol production. If she then suddenly cut back, ran out of pills early, or had gaps because she was taking them too fast and ran out, she could be experiencing adrenal insufficiency or steroid withdrawal, which causes profound fatigue, low mood, weakness, nausea, dizziness, and body aches. Running out early is a real possibility if she has been taking four times as many as prescribed, so check how many tablets are left compared with what you would expect.

Other possibilities include high or low blood sugar, low potassium, or the underlying condition being treated flaring up, all of which can cause exhaustion.

What I would do is call her prescriber or pharmacist today, tell them exactly what you think she has been taking and for how long, and let them advise. Do not simply stop the medication abruptly on your own, especially if she has been on it for more than a couple of weeks, because that can cause the withdrawal problem described above. Bring the pill bottle with you or have it in hand so the count can be checked.

Seek urgent care or call emergency services if she has severe weakness, fainting or dizziness on standing, persistent vomiting, confusion, severe abdominal pain, a very low or very high blood sugar, thoughts of harming herself, or any marked change in behavior. Depression on steroids should be taken seriously, so ask her directly how she is feeling and tell the doctor about it.

It would also help to set up a pill organizer or have you dispense the doses, so the mix-up does not recur. A pharmacist can show you how to read the label if the tablet count was the source of confusion.

Honestly, P/E ratios for small caps and large caps don't line up well over time, so comparing them directly can be misleading. Small caps (roughly anything under $2 billion in market cap) are usually riskier and jumpier than large caps ($10 billion and up). That means investors often pay more per dollar of earnings for small caps, betting on growth that might pay off. Big, established companies are different. They've got longer track records of earnings and revenue, so people don't usually pay a premium for growth, and their P/E ratios tend to sit lower. Still, a P/E number alone won't tell you much. You've got to look at the company's financial health, what's happening in its industry, and the broader economy too.

Tony Hoare is a computer scientist from Britain who helped pioneer the discipline. He is most widely recognized for his role in developing the ALGOL programming language and for his work on the CTSS operating system. His contributions extend further into programming methods, the theoretical foundations of computing, and the establishment of software engineering as a field of study. In 1980 he received the ACM Turing Award, frequently described as the "Nobel Prize" of computing, recognizing his work on CSP and his foundational contributions to how programming languages are defined and designed. Hoare is also a Fellow of the Royal Society and a member of the Order of the British Empire.

The conductor's basically the boss of the musicians. They stand up front and use their hands and arms to tell everyone when to come in, when to stop, and how fast or slow to go. They also keep things together so everyone stays in time and in tune. Could an orchestra play without one? Sure, maybe, but it probably wouldn't sound as good. Nobody's really leading, so entrances get ragged and the different sections drift apart. A good conductor is what keeps the whole thing sounding tight and polished.

Communism is both a form of government and a way of organizing society, in which people work together and share what they produce. Under communism, the state owns the means of production, such as factories, farms, and offices, and private property, including houses, cars, and phones, does not exist. The thinking behind it is that everyone should be equal and hold everything in common, so no one is excluded or ends up with more than anyone else. The aim is a society in which everyone has what they need and no one is either poor or rich. In such a society, the government decides how the country's resources are used, while the people cooperate to produce what the nation requires. The state also supplies education, healthcare, and other services. In theory, this gives everyone an equal opportunity to succeed, and nobody needs to worry about going hungry or being unable to pay for a doctor. In practice, though, communist governments have frequently run into serious problems and have not always succeeded. Some argue that communism fails because it conflicts with human nature, since people are unwilling to share on an equal basis. Others contend that it has failed because it was carried out badly, or because other countries suppressed it.

Cold reading is basically a trick people use to seem psychic or like they can read minds. The reader asks vague questions and makes general observations that could fit almost anyone, then tightens things up based on how the other person reacts. Say a cold reader opens with "I sense you've been through a lot of changes lately." That could describe pretty much anybody. If the person nods, the reader might get more specific: "I get the sense you recently moved or started a new job." Agree again, and it gets sharper still: "I feel like you're struggling a bit to adjust to your new surroundings and feeling kind of overwhelmed." It works so well because it's really hard to prove someone isn't psychic, and people often want to believe in special abilities. But it's just a trick, not an actual psychic power.

So basically, phones put out radio waves, and those can mess with the electronics on a plane. We're talking stuff like navigation and communication gear, the things the pilots really need working to fly safely. When your phone's on, it's constantly sending out a signal trying to find a nearby cell tower, and that signal is what can cause interference. That's why they tell you to shut it off (or at least switch to airplane mode) during the flight. That said, some of the newer planes have special systems built in that block interference from phones and other gadgets, so it might not be long before you can actually use your phone up there.

On the risk: receptive anal sex carries one of the highest per-act risks of HIV transmission among sexual activities, because the lining of the rectum is thin and can tear easily, giving the virus direct access to the bloodstream. Still, the per-encounter risk varies widely. If the partner had HIV, the chance of transmission from a single act is commonly estimated at roughly 1 in 50 to 1 in 100 for receptive anal intercourse without a condom, and it is substantially lower if the partner has an undetectable viral load (under effective treatment, transmission is essentially not possible, per the U=U consensus). If the partner's status is unknown, the overall risk depends on his prevalence and his viral load, which you can't determine from here. A short exposure is still an exposure, so it's reasonable to take it seriously rather than assume it's nothing.

The most important step is post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP). PEP is a course of antiretroviral medicines that can prevent HIV if started as soon as possible, ideally within 72 hours of exposure and never later than that. You are two days out, so you may still be within the window, but time is short.
