Please go to an emergency department, a sexual health or STI clinic, or your doctor today or first thing tomorrow and tell them the exact timing. Don't wait for test results before deciding on PEP. It is typically taken for 28 days and has few serious side effects for most people, though they will check your kidney function and other health factors first.

On testing: a standard HIV test taken too early can miss an infection. A lab test (fourth-generation antigen/antibody test) generally becomes reliable about 4 to 6 weeks after exposure, and a rapid test may be less sensitive early on. If you test now, get a repeat test at around 4 to 6 weeks and again at 3 months to be fully confident. Some other infections can be tested sooner. Gonorrhea, chlamydia, and syphilis tests are useful now, and throat and rectal swabs may be needed because anal sex can transmit infection there, which a standard urine test would miss. Hepatitis B and C tests are also worth asking about. Many of these infections are curable, and treating them promptly reduces complications.

Please also tell the clinic if you develop fever, rash, swollen glands, sore throat, or unusual fatigue in the coming weeks, since these can be early signs of HIV and deserve prompt testing.

A social network is an online service or site where people can set up a public profile, compile a roster of people they are linked to, and look at and engage with their own links as well as the links of others on the same system. These ties may be friendships, work relationships, or a mix of the two. Such networks are typically organized around shared interests, pursuits, or bonds, and they give members a way to talk to one another and post material like pictures, clips, and news stories. Facebook, Twitter, Instagram, and LinkedIn are well-known examples.

Civil engineering is basically the branch that handles designing, building, and maintaining the stuff we all rely on: roads, bridges, water and sewage systems, buildings. Civil engineers plan, design, build, and run these systems, and they also deal with managing natural resources and the environment. Some of them work on transportation projects like roads, bridges, and airports. Others focus on water, so think treatment plants, irrigation, and flood control. Plenty work on buildings, structures, and foundations, and some go into environmental work, like building systems to handle waste and pollution. They use a lot of tools these days, including CAD software, to crunch the numbers and design things. In the field, they'll also grab specialized gear like surveying instruments to collect data and take measurements. Technical chops matter, sure, but you also need solid problem-solving, communication, and project management skills if you want to get anywhere in the job.

Yuval Noah Harari is an Israeli historian, public intellectual, and author best known for his popular books on the history of humankind and the future of civilization. He is a professor in the Department of History at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, where he has taught world history since the early 2000s and specialized in medieval and military history before turning to broader, big-picture questions.

He gained international fame with *Sapiens: A Brief History of Humankind* (2011, English translation 2014), which traces the story of Homo sapiens from the emergence of early humans through the agricultural, scientific, and industrial revolutions. The book argues that shared myths, such as religions, nations, money, and human rights, allow large numbers of strangers to cooperate, and it became a global bestseller. He followed it with *Homo Deus: A Brief History of Tomorrow* (2015), which speculates about how technology, biotechnology, and artificial intelligence might reshape humanity's goals and identity, and with *21 Lessons for the 21st Century* (2018), which addresses contemporary challenges such as technological disruption, nationalism, terrorism, and climate change. He has also written children's versions of his histories and *Nexus* (2024), a book on how information networks shape human societies, from ancient clay records to modern artificial intelligence.

Harari is known for his accessible, provocative style, and his work has drawn both wide admiration and criticism. Supporters praise his ability to connect vast historical periods into engaging narratives, while critics argue that his broad generalizations sometimes oversimplify complex history or make speculative predictions with more confidence than the evidence warrants. He is also a vegan and a meditation practitioner, and he has spoken publicly about his personal practice of Vipassana meditation, which has influenced some of his writing.

Prepayment penalties are charges that certain lenders impose when a borrower repays a mortgage before the agreed term ends. Their purpose is to make up for the interest income the lender had anticipated earning over the entire life of the loan. Such penalties are neither standard nor rare. A lender may write a prepayment clause into the mortgage agreement to safeguard its investment. Still, many lenders do not charge them, and certain states restrict or outright ban them. Anyone thinking about a mortgage who worries about facing this kind of fee should ask the lender what its policy is and read the contract closely before committing. Lenders are sometimes open to renegotiating the agreement, prepayment clause included, to give the borrower more favorable terms.

Paul Avery was a San Francisco Chronicle crime reporter during the period when the Zodiac Killer was active in the Bay Area in the late 1960s and early 1970s. He was one of the journalists who received letters from the killer, who often wrote to newspapers to boast about his crimes, send cryptograms, and taunt police and reporters. Avery became something of a figure in the case because the Zodiac corresponded with him directly on several occasions, and he was among the reporters who helped publicize the cipher messages, which the public was invited to try to decode. Avery also had a personal connection to the story: he was in contact with the killer in ways that put him under some attention, and he later co-wrote books about the case with David Toschi, the San Francisco police inspector who worked on the investigation, and with Paul Avery's colleague and co-author Michael Sims... (Avery's most notable book on the subject, written with Toschi and others, is "The Zodiac Killer" and later "Zodiac Unmasked" was written by Robert Graysmith, not Avery, so I should be careful here.) The Zodiac case remains unsolved, and Avery's role was primarily that of a reporter who covered the killings and served as a conduit for the killer's communications.

White-box testing is a software testing approach in which the tester has full knowledge of the internal structure, code, and logic of the system under test. Rather than treating the software as a black box that is judged only by its inputs and outputs, the tester examines how the code is written and designs test cases to exercise specific paths, conditions, branches, loops, and statements within it. The name reflects the idea that the internals are visible, or "transparent," to the person performing the test.

The main goal of white-box testing is to verify that the internal logic works correctly and to uncover errors that might not be apparent from external behavior alone. For example, a tester might ensure that every branch of an if-else statement is executed at least once, that loops terminate correctly, that boundary conditions are handled, and that no dead or unreachable code is hiding defects. Common techniques include statement coverage, branch or decision coverage, condition coverage, path testing, and data flow testing, each of which measures how thoroughly the code has been exercised.

White-box testing is typically performed by developers or specialized testers who can read and understand the source code. It is most useful during unit testing and integration testing, where the focus is on individual components and how they interact. Its strengths include thoroughness in covering code logic, the ability to find hidden errors early, and the identification of security vulnerabilities or inefficient code. Its main limitations are that it requires technical expertise, can be time-consuming for large systems, and may miss requirements that the code fails to implement at all, which is why it is often combined with black-box testing for more complete coverage.

Second Life is an online virtual world created by Linden Lab, a company based in San Francisco, and launched to the public in 2003. Users, often called "residents," create customizable digital avatars and use them to explore a vast three-dimensional environment, socialize with other people, attend events, and participate in a wide range of activities. Unlike a traditional video game, Second Life has no set objectives, levels, or winning conditions. Instead, it is an open-ended space where the experience is largely shaped by what users choose to do and build.

One of the most distinctive features of Second Life is that nearly all of its content is created by its users. Residents can design and build objects, clothing, buildings, vehicles, animations, and entire landscapes using built-in tools and scripting languages. Because creators retain intellectual property rights to what they make, many people have turned their creations into businesses, selling virtual goods and services to other residents.

The world has its own economy based on a virtual currency called the Linden dollar, which can be bought and sold for real money through an official exchange. This has allowed some users to earn genuine income from activities such as fashion design, real estate development, and event hosting within the platform. Users can also purchase or rent virtual land, where they can build homes, shops, clubs, or other spaces.

Beyond entertainment and commerce, Second Life has been used for many other purposes. Universities have held classes and built virtual campuses there, businesses and governments have experimented with virtual offices and embassies, artists have staged exhibitions and performances, and support communities have formed around shared interests, identities, and experiences, including groups for people with disabilities who find in it a space for social connection.

Second Life drew enormous media attention in the mid-2000s, when it was seen as a glimpse of the future of the internet. Although public hype faded after that peak, the platform never disappeared and continues to operate with a dedicated community of active users. It is often cited as an early example of what is now called the "metaverse," and it remains an important reference point in discussions about virtual worlds, digital identity, and online economies.

Jaywalking is basically crossing a street somewhere other than a crosswalk, or crossing in a way that ignores the pedestrian rules. In a lot of countries it's illegal, mostly because it's dangerous for both walkers and drivers. Drivers just aren't expecting someone to step out in a random spot, so they might not be watching for you.

Another thing is that outside a crosswalk you usually don't have the right of way. That means drivers don't have to stop for you, and that's how people end up in accidents or getting hurt.

If you're just wandering around a new city and not crossing any streets, you're obviously not jaywalking. But the moment you cross outside a marked crosswalk, or you're not following the pedestrian rules, you could be doing it. So keep an eye on what's around you and stick to the rules when you're walking somewhere unfamiliar. It's an easy way to stay safe.

Computer art is the name given to any kind of digital art or media produced with the help of computer software and hardware. This category spans many forms, such as illustration, graphic design, video, and animation. Artists may rely on numerous programs and methods to make it, among them 2D and 3D modeling, vector and raster graphics, and programming. Frequently, it calls for specialized instruments and approaches to generate images, animations, and other digital works that could not be made with conventional artistic materials. In recent years, computer art has grown steadily more popular, as powerful hardware and software have become available to a broader public. Industries such as advertising, entertainment, and education make use of it, among others. It is also taking on a larger role in contemporary art, and it is now commonly displayed in galleries and museums next to traditional works.

Atherosclerotic heart disease is basically what happens when plaque builds up in the arteries that feed your heart. That plaque is a mix of cholesterol, fats, and other gunk, and it can narrow or even block those arteries. Less blood and oxygen gets through, so the heart doesn't always get what it needs to work right. You might feel chest pain (angina), get winded easily, or notice other symptoms. If a blockage gets bad enough, part of the heart muscle can get damaged or die, which is a heart attack. The good news is it's really common and you can often prevent it or keep it under control with lifestyle changes, meds, and other treatments.

Honestly, there are a few things that could be going on here. The most obvious one is the antidepressant itself, since dizziness and blurry vision are known side effects for some of them. But it could also be something totally unrelated, like low blood pressure, an inner ear problem, or an issue with your eyes. Hard to say from the outside.

I'd talk to your doctor or pharmacist about it, because they can actually figure out what's causing it and tell you what to do next. Don't just sit on it. In the meantime, you could try cutting out chocolate and fizzy drinks for a bit and see if that makes any difference.

Nexen Tires are made by Nexen Tire Corporation, a South Korean company headquartered in Seoul. The company was founded in 1942 as the Heung-A Tire Company and later became known as Woosung Industrial, then Nexen Tire in 2000 (the name was adopted as the brand and company identity). It is a subsidiary of the Nexen Corporation, formerly known as Nexen Holdings, which grew out of the original business.

Nexen produces its tires at several plants. The company operates factories in Yangsan and Changnyeong in South Korea, in Qingdao in China, and in Žatec in the Czech Republic, which serves the European market. These facilities allow it to supply original equipment and replacement tires to markets around the world.

Nexen is also an original equipment supplier for a number of automakers, including some European and North American brands, and it has sponsored motorsport and sports teams to build its global profile. In the United States, its tires are sold under the Nexen name, and it has also used the Roadstone brand in some markets. Overall, Nexen is generally regarded as a value-oriented brand that offers a range of passenger car, SUV, light truck, and performance tires.

Google Cloud Platform is a cloud computing platform and infrastructure developed by Google to help people construct, launch, and oversee applications and services in the cloud. Its offerings span many areas, such as computing, data storage, networking, analytics, machine learning, security, and application development. Developers and companies use it to create and operate apps, websites, and services on Google's infrastructure. The platform is built to be scalable, adaptable, and simple to use, and users can reach it either through a web console or by way of APIs. Among its most notable capabilities are a variety of computing choices, including virtual machines, containers, and serverless computing through Google Cloud Functions; several storage types, such as block storage, object storage, and BigQuery, a fully managed data warehouse; networking tools like virtual private clouds, load balancers, and edge caching; analytics and machine learning resources, including Google BigQuery, Google Cloud Machine Learning Engine, and Google Cloud AI Platform; and security and compliance features such as encryption at rest and in transit, identity and access management, and security key management. Businesses of every size, from young startups to major enterprises, rely on Google Cloud Platform, and it is especially appealing to organizations seeking the scalability, flexibility, and cost savings that cloud computing provides.

You can try several approaches to make scars and acne marks on your face less noticeable. Over-the-counter topical creams with ingredients like salicylic acid, glycolic acid, or retinoids may help, since they exfoliate the skin and encourage new, healthy skin cells to grow. A gentle, non-abrasive facial scrub or an alpha hydroxy acid (AHA) product can also be used to slough off dead skin cells and improve the texture and tone of your complexion. Another option is a chemical peel, in which a solution strips away the upper layers of skin so that newer, smoother skin shows underneath. To fade hyperpigmentation and uneven tone, you might use a skin-lightening product containing hydroquinone or kojic acid. Resist the urge to pick at or squeeze pimples, because doing so can make acne worse and cause scarring. You should also shield your skin from the sun with a broad-spectrum sunscreen of SPF 30 or higher, as sun exposure can darken hyperpigmentation and make scars more noticeable. For stronger results, consider consulting a dermatologist or another skin care professional about options such as laser therapy, microdermabrasion, or other medical procedures. These can reduce the look of scars and acne marks more effectively, though they tend to cost more and often require several sessions. Keep in mind that scars and marks fade slowly, and outcomes differ from person to person. Patience and a consistent skin care routine matter, since visible improvement can take several weeks or even months.

Honestly there are a few reasons sites do this. One is to get you to toss more stuff in your cart before you see the total, which works well if they run bigger discounts on larger orders. Another is to make price comparison a pain, since you'd have to click through to each item just to see what it costs, and that's easier to pull off when the product is hard to find somewhere else. Some sites also do it to create a bit of exclusivity or scarcity, so you feel like you're getting a special deal or that the item is in demand. And a last one is just to cut down on distractions: if a site has tons of products, hiding prices can keep your focus on the one you're looking at. Hope that helps, and let me know if you want to dig into any of these.

Mortgage points are upfront charges a borrower pays the lender to secure a reduced interest rate on the home loan. One point costs 1% of the loan's total value. So, on a $200,000 mortgage, purchasing two points would require a payment of $4,000 to the lender. Borrowers often use points to bring down their monthly payments, since a smaller interest rate can add up to substantial savings across the loan's duration. Still, paying points raises the initial cost of borrowing, because the borrower pays more at closing in return for smaller payments later. Before deciding, borrowers should weigh whether points suit their situation by considering their financial objectives, the specifics of the mortgage, and whether they can comfortably cover the upfront expense.

The attack on Pearl Harbor on December 7, 1941, was part of the Pacific War, which was the Asian-Pacific theater of World War II. It did not arise from a single conflict but grew out of the Second Sino-Japanese War, which Japan had been fighting against China since 1937. Japan's expansion into China, along with its aim of securing natural resources such as oil and rubber, led to economic sanctions from the United States, Britain, and the Netherlands. Those sanctions, especially the American oil embargo, pushed Japan's leaders to plan a wider war in Southeast Asia. The Pearl Harbor attack was meant to neutralize the American Pacific Fleet so Japan could move freely in that region, and it drew the United States into World War II.

Stevie Wonder's real name is Stevland Hardaway Morris, so that's the name you'd find on his birth certificate. He's an American singer, songwriter, and producer, and he's been massively successful for decades. People talk about his voice all the time, and honestly it's hard to argue with them. He writes his own stuff, and he plays a bunch of instruments too. Lots of folks put him right up there with the best musicians ever, and he's collected 25 Grammys along the way.

As of the 2020 U.S. Census, Memphis, Tennessee had a population of about 633,000 people. Estimates since then have put the city's population at roughly 610,000 to 630,000, as it has seen a gradual decline in recent years. The wider Memphis metropolitan area, which includes parts of Mississippi and Arkansas, is home to more than 1.3 million people.

Using a 0% credit card to pay off other debts sounds great, especially when monthly payments are squeezing you. Just make sure you check a few things first.

Fees come first. Lots of cards charge a balance transfer fee, usually a percentage of whatever you move over. Read the fine print and add that fee into your math before you decide it's worth it.

Then there's what happens when the promo ends. The 0% rate won't last forever, and once it's over the interest usually jumps up. Can you realistically pay the whole balance before that happens? If not, you could end up paying a higher rate than you had before.

Also, opening a new card and adding debt can dent your credit score for a bit. That matters if you're planning to apply for a mortgage or another loan soon, so it's worth thinking about the timing.

In the end it really comes down to your own situation. If you're unsure, talking to a financial advisor or a nonprofit credit counselor can help you see the risks and benefits for your numbers.

Congrats on the first real job. Relocating for it is a big step, but it's also one of the most common ways people launch their careers, so you're in good company. Whether it's the right move depends a lot on your situation, so here are some questions and considerations that might help you think it through.

Start with the job itself. Does it offer a path you actually want, or is it mainly a stepping stone? Look at what people in similar roles at the company went on to do, and whether the skills you'd build there will transfer elsewhere. A job that gives you real responsibility and mentorship early on is often worth more than a slightly higher salary at a place where you'd be doing busywork.

Then think about the money. Compare the salary against the cost of living in the new city, especially rent, transportation, and taxes. A raise that looks good on paper can disappear once you factor in a much higher rent. Also check whether the company offers relocation assistance, a signing bonus, or help with temporary housing. Many employers will negotiate on this if you ask, and it's reasonable to do so.

Consider your support network too. Moving somewhere where you know no one can be exciting, but it can also be lonely, especially in the first few months when work is demanding and your social life is starting from scratch. Think about whether you have friends, family, or alumni connections in the area, and how you'd build a community there. Some people find it easier to move with a friend or to join clubs, sports leagues, or groups tied to their interests right away.

It also helps to ask how reversible the decision is. If the job doesn't work out, could you move back or relocate again without too much damage? Most first jobs aren't permanent, and you'll likely change roles or cities several times, so this one doesn't need to be your forever choice. Still, it's worth knowing your fallback plan.

Finally, notice your gut reaction. Are you excited about the city and the work, or mostly relieved to have an offer at all? Both are normal, but your honest enthusiasm is a useful signal.

If you tell me the city, the role, and what's pulling you toward or away from the move, I can help you weigh the specifics or work through a salary and budget comparison.

Learning a language with someone who speaks a different one can be tricky, but it's totally doable! Here's one way to go about it. Start with gestures and drawings. If one of you wants to say "I'm hungry," just sketch a person with a little line coming out of their stomach, and you'll get the idea across. Next, try a translation app or website. These can handle words and phrases pretty well, so you can actually have basic conversations. Finally, consider taking a language class together. You'll pick up the basics of each other's languages and get real practice listening and speaking. It'll take some patience, sure, but you'll get there.

The sigmoid function is a mathematical function that takes any real number as input and squashes it into a value between 0 and 1, producing an S-shaped curve. It is commonly written as σ(x) = 1 / (1 + e^(-x)), where e is the base of the natural logarithm. When x is a large positive number, e^(-x) becomes very small, so the output approaches 1. When x is a large negative number, e^(-x) becomes very large, so the output approaches 0. At x = 0, the output is exactly 0.5, which marks the midpoint of the curve.

The sigmoid function is widely used in statistics, machine learning, and neural networks. One of its main roles is in logistic regression, where it converts a linear combination of input features into a probability that an outcome belongs to a particular class. In neural networks, it has historically been used as an activation function, introducing nonlinearity so that the network can learn complex patterns. Because its output lies between 0 and 1, it is also useful for representing probabilities or for gating signals.

The function has some useful mathematical properties. Its derivative can be expressed in terms of the function itself: σ'(x) = σ(x)(1 − σ(x)). This makes gradient calculations efficient during training. However, the sigmoid also has a drawback: for inputs with large absolute values, the curve becomes very flat, so the gradient becomes extremely small. This is known as the vanishing gradient problem, and it can slow or stall learning in deep networks. For this reason, activation functions such as ReLU and its variants are often preferred in hidden layers of modern deep networks, though sigmoid remains common in output layers for binary classification.

Certainly, I can help clarify this idea. The number of photons a light source emits each second is tied to the light's frequency. Frequency and wavelength are inversely related: a shorter wavelength means a higher frequency, and a longer wavelength means a lower one. Therefore, when two light sources have equal power, the one with the shorter wavelength emits more photons per second because of its higher frequency, while the one with the longer wavelength emits fewer photons per second because of its lower frequency. I hope this makes things clearer. Please feel free to ask if anything else comes to mind.

Pattern matching is a technique for checking whether a piece of data has a particular structure or form, and for extracting parts of it when it does. Instead of writing a series of manual checks that inspect values one at a time, you describe the shape you expect, and the system determines whether the data fits that description. If it does, the matching parts can be bound to names and used in the code that follows.

The idea appears in many contexts. In programming languages, pattern matching often takes the form of a switch or match expression, where each case lists a pattern such as a specific value, a range, a type, or a nested structure with placeholders. Functional languages like Haskell, Rust, and Scala rely on it heavily, and newer versions of languages like Python and C# have added it as well. Pattern matching also underlies the destructuring of tuples, lists, or objects, where a single statement both tests the shape of a value and pulls out its components.

Outside of programming, the term is closely tied to regular expressions, which are compact notations for describing text patterns. A regular expression such as one matching email addresses or dates can be run against strings to find, validate, or replace the portions that fit. Similar ideas appear in search tools, file globbing like *.txt, and in fields such as computer vision and machine learning, where algorithms recognize recurring structures in images, signals, or data.

In short, pattern matching is the practice of comparing data against a described form so that you can decide what to do based on its structure, and often pull out the relevant pieces in the same step.

Renting out a unit through Airbnb can have tax consequences, since money earned from letting a property is typically taxable. The exact consequences, though, depend on your personal situation and on the laws where you live. Generally, any rental income should be declared on your tax return. If you list your property on Airbnb, you should also keep track of what you earn and of the costs connected to the rental, such as cleaning or repairs. Some of those costs may be deductible when you file, which can lower the amount of tax you owe. Keep in mind that how rental income is treated for tax purposes can differ based on the length of time you rent the property and how frequently you do it. For instance, if you only now and then rent out a room in your home on Airbnb, the money may count as "rental income" and be taxed at your regular income tax rate. By contrast, if you rent out your property on Airbnb often, the earnings may have to be classed as "business income," which follows a different set of tax rules. To understand what using Airbnb means for your taxes, it's wise to speak with a tax professional or look over the tax rules in your jurisdiction.

Imagine your school bus drove through lots of different towns, and each town had its own rules about what you could bring inside. Some towns would say, "No toys that can hurt anyone, ever." A cargo ship is like that bus. It sails through the waters and ports of many countries, and each country has its own rules about guns.

When a ship pulls into a port, the country that owns that port gets to decide whether guns are allowed on board. Lots of countries say no, or they make you fill out a mountain of paperwork, or they take the guns away and keep them until you leave. A ship might visit a dozen ports on one trip, so keeping track of all those rules is really hard and costs a lot of money.

There are other grown-up reasons too. The ship's crew are sailors, not soldiers, so they haven't been trained to fight. If a sailor shoots at pirates, the pirates might shoot back with bigger guns, and then everyone is in more danger. Pirates often have fast little boats and rocket launchers, so a few guns on a big slow ship might not even win. Insurance companies, who pay if something goes wrong, also worry that a gunfight could make things worse and cost more.

Ships also carry things that can explode or burn, like fuel, so bullets flying around can be very dangerous.

Instead of guns, ships often use other tricks. They can go very fast, spray water hoses at the pirates, put up sharp wire on the sides so it is hard to climb aboard, or hide in a safe room. Many ships today also hire trained armed guards, who work for special security companies and follow careful rules. That became more common after the time of the Captain Phillips story, which happened in 2009. So the answer is that it is not always against the rules, but it is complicated, risky, and expensive, which is why many ships back then did not have weapons.

Pinning down an exact count of Muslims in the United Kingdom is hard, since the country does not gather official statistics on religious affiliation. Even so, figures from bodies such as the Office for National Statistics and the Pew Research Center place the Muslim share of the population at roughly 5 percent. Applied to the national total, that works out to about 3.45 million people. It is also important to recognise that British Muslims are far from uniform, drawing on many different ethnic and national origins.

When you sell a call option on a share you own, you grant the buyer the right to purchase that share from you at a fixed price, known as the strike price, on or before a set date, called the expiration date. This arrangement is referred to as writing a call option. If investors believe the share price is heading up, the call you have written may gain in value, since the buyer becomes more inclined to exercise the right to buy from you at the agreed strike price when they expect the stock to trade above it. Should the share climb and the buyer choose to exercise, you must sell the stock to them at the strike price. Should the share fail to appreciate, the option lapses unused and you keep your shares. Writing calls can generate income from a stock that has underperformed, because you collect the premium at the time you sell the option. Nevertheless, there is a risk that you could be forced to part with the stock for less than its prevailing market value if the option is exercised. For that reason, it is essential to weigh the possible risks and benefits carefully before writing calls on a stock.

To work out the volatility (standard deviation) of a stock's price, first collect a series of daily closing prices covering the period you care about. Such data is usually available on financial websites or can be downloaded from a financial database. With the data in hand, follow these steps to compute the standard deviation. Start by finding the mean price over the period: add together all the daily closing prices and divide by the total number of days. Next, subtract the mean from each daily closing price to get the deviation for each day. Then square each of those deviations and sum the squared values. Divide that sum by one less than the number of days in the period; the result is the variance. Finally, take the square root of the variance to arrive at the standard deviation.

To determine the return on investment (ROI) of a stock, you need two figures: the amount you initially invested and the value of that investment at the close of the period you are examining. The ROI can then be found with this formula: ROI = (final value - initial investment) / initial investment. For instance, suppose you put $1,000 into a stock and, after one year, your holding was worth $1,200. The ROI would be (1200 - 1000) / 1000 = 0.2, or 20%. In other words, your investment earned a 20% return over that year.

Several sources offer historical data for the S&P 500 index. Among the options are the following. On Yahoo Finance, you can view the index's history at https://finance.yahoo.com/quote/%5EGSPC/history?p=%5EGSPC, and the "Date" field lets you narrow the results to a particular date range. Google Finance is another option: searching for "S&P 500 index historical data" at https://www.google.com/search?q=S%26P+500+index+historical+data brings up a chart of the index's performance over time, which can be adjusted using the controls on the right side. FRED (Federal Reserve Economic Data), a database run by the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis, holds a broad range of economic and financial figures, including S&P 500 history, and is available at https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/SP500. Quandl, a financial data platform with many financial and economic datasets, also carries S&P 500 historical data at https://www.quandl.com/data/YAHOO/INDEX_GSPC-S-P-500-Index. Finally, Bloomberg, a financial news and data service, provides this history as well; through the Bloomberg Terminal, you can search for "SPX Index" or "S&P 500 Index" to retrieve it.

In psychology, affect is the emotional side of experience. It's an umbrella term covering feelings, moods, and emotions. Affect can be positive, like joy or happiness, or negative, like sadness or anger. Some of it is fleeting, lasting just a moment, while other kinds hang around much longer. It shapes how people take in the world and react to it, and it shows up in how people think, feel, and act. It can even affect physical health and well-being.

Researchers have a few ideas about where affect comes from and how it drives behavior. One view is that it's a reaction to things happening around us, like good or bad events. Another holds that internal stuff, such as thoughts, beliefs, and attitudes, plays a big part. Either way, it matters across a lot of fields, from psychology and psychiatry to counseling. Teachers care about it too, since knowing how students are feeling can help them build a better classroom.

Timeshares are not automatically scams, but they are a product that works well for very few people, and the way they are usually sold is designed to make buyers feel better about the deal than the numbers support. Here is the basic idea. Imagine a fancy condo that you can use only for one week each year. A timeshare lets you buy the right to that week, and you share the place with many other owners who each have their own week. The developer builds the resort, sells these slices, and collects a lot of money up front. After that, owners pay yearly maintenance fees, which often rise over time to cover repairs, staff, and taxes.

Who makes the money? Mainly the developer and the sales company, since they get the big upfront payment. Resale is the weak spot. Once someone owns a timeshare, it is very hard to sell it for anything close to what they paid, because the market is flooded with used weeks and few buyers want them. Many owners end up stuck paying fees for something they no longer want. Some companies make money from resale scams or "exit" services that charge fees to help owners get out, and some of those are fraudulent too.

A savvy person can benefit in a narrow case: if you would truly use the same place at the same time every year, you plan to keep it for decades, and you buy it at a low price with fees you understand, it can be like prepaying for vacations. Even then, you could often rent a similar place for less. Many experienced travelers avoid them entirely, or buy resale units only at deep discounts with full knowledge of the fees.

As for presentations, these are the sales pitches you are often invited to attend, usually in exchange for a free gift, cheap meal, or discounted vacation. The presentation is typically a long, friendly sales event where a salesperson builds excitement, talks about "investing" in your family's future, and pushes you to sign that day, often with offers that seem to expire quickly. The free gift is the bait, and the room is set up to make saying no feel awkward. Your best protection is to go in knowing what you want, take your time, never sign on the spot, and read everything, including the fee schedule and the right to cancel, which in many places lets you back out within a few days.

Functional programming is a style of writing software in which programs are built primarily by composing and applying functions, in the mathematical sense of the word. A mathematical function takes some input and always produces the same output for that input, without changing anything else in the world. Functional programming tries to bring that same predictability to code. Instead of describing a sequence of steps that modify data stored in variables, as you typically do in imperative languages like C or early Java, you describe transformations: this data goes in, that result comes out.

One of the central ideas is the pure function. A pure function depends only on its arguments and has no side effects, meaning it doesn't modify global variables, write to files, print to the screen, or alter the objects passed into it. Because of this, calling a pure function with the same arguments will always give the same result, which makes such functions easy to test, reason about, and reuse. Real programs obviously need to interact with the outside world, so functional programmers usually try to isolate side effects into small, clearly marked parts of the program while keeping the bulk of the logic pure.

Closely related is the idea of immutability. In functional programming, data is generally not changed after it is created. If you want a list with an extra element, you create a new list rather than altering the old one. This eliminates a whole category of bugs where one part of a program unexpectedly changes data that another part relies on, and it makes concurrent and parallel programming much safer, since multiple threads can share data without worrying that someone will modify it underneath them.

Functional programming also treats functions as first-class values. This means functions can be stored in variables, passed as arguments to other functions, and returned as results. Functions that take or return other functions are called higher-order functions. Familiar examples are map, which applies a function to every element of a collection, filter, which keeps only the elements that satisfy a condition, and reduce (sometimes called fold), which combines all the elements into a single value. Using these, a task like "sum the squares of all even numbers in a list" can be expressed as a clear pipeline of transformations rather than a loop with counters and accumulators.

Because loops typically rely on changing a counter variable, functional languages often favor recursion, where a function calls itself on a smaller piece of the problem until it reaches a simple base case. Many functional languages also emphasize function composition, the practice of building complex behavior by chaining small, simple functions together, much like connecting pipes.

Some languages are designed around this paradigm from the ground up, such as Haskell, which is strictly pure, as well as Erlang, Elixir, Clojure, F#, OCaml, and Scala. However, functional ideas have spread widely into mainstream languages, so you can write in a functional style in JavaScript, Python, Java, C#, Kotlin, Rust, and others, using features like lambdas, map and filter, and immutable data structures.

The main benefits people cite are code that is easier to understand in isolation, easier to test, less prone to hidden-state bugs, and better suited to concurrency. The trade-offs are that the style can feel unfamiliar at first, some algorithms are more naturally expressed with mutable state, and creating new data instead of modifying existing data can carry performance costs, although modern languages use clever techniques to minimize them. In practice, many developers blend functional and imperative or object-oriented approaches, using functional techniques wherever they make the code clearer and more reliable.

Double jeopardy is basically the rule that you can't be tried again for the same crime once you've been acquitted or convicted. So if a jury finds you not guilty, the government can't just take another swing at you, even if someone turns up new evidence that makes you look guilty as heck. Same goes for a conviction: once it's done, you can't be retried, even if new evidence later shows you didn't do it. It's there to stop the government from throwing people back into court again and again until it gets the result it wants, and it protects people from being harassed by the system.

Sepp Hochreiter is an Austrian computer scientist and researcher, widely known for his contributions to machine learning and artificial intelligence. He is best known as the co-inventor, together with Jürgen Schmidhuber, of the Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network, a type of recurrent neural network introduced in 1997. Hochreiter had earlier identified the vanishing gradient problem in his 1991 diploma thesis, which explained why standard recurrent networks struggled to learn dependencies across long sequences. LSTM addressed this by using gated memory cells that let information persist over many time steps, and it became one of the most influential architectures for tasks such as speech recognition, language modeling, and machine translation before transformer models rose to prominence.

Hochreiter has held academic positions in Germany and Austria, including work at the Technical University of Munich and later at Johannes Kepler University Linz, where he leads the Institute for Machine Learning and the LIT AI Lab. His research spans deep learning, bioinformatics, and the application of machine learning in fields such as drug discovery and the natural sciences. He has also been involved in developing methods like FABIA for biclustering and contributed to work on self-normalizing neural networks. His work on LSTM is considered foundational, and he has received numerous awards for his contributions to the field.

White coat hypertension, sometimes called office hypertension, describes a pattern in which a person's blood pressure is regularly higher when measured in a medical environment, like a doctor's office, than when it is checked at home or elsewhere outside a clinical setting. Anxiety or stress about being in a medical setting can be the cause. If your case is severe enough that you cannot get a normal reading at any clinic, you should work closely with your healthcare provider to decide on the most suitable treatment. Several approaches can help manage the condition. One is monitoring your blood pressure at home, since a home monitor can give you more accurate readings and a fuller view of your blood pressure over time. Another is relaxation techniques, such as deep breathing or progressive muscle relaxation, which can ease anxiety and stress. Lifestyle changes can also help, including a healthy diet, regular exercise, and stress management, all of which can lower blood pressure and benefit your general health. Finally, medication is sometimes recommended to bring blood pressure down, and your healthcare provider can help you settle on the plan that best fits your particular needs. You should also keep working with your provider over the long term to track and manage your blood pressure. Regular check-ups and blood pressure measurements help confirm that your treatment is working and allow any needed changes to be made.

Commodities are a rich topic, and good resources span books, data sources, and online communities. For foundational reading, Jeffrey Harvey's and others' writings on commodity markets are a starting point, but a widely recommended pick is "Commodities: Markets, Performance, and Strategies" and Kevin Dowd's work on commodity risk, which cover pricing, hedging, and market structure in accessible terms. For a more historical and narrative perspective, Jeffrey Sachs and Andrew Warner's papers on the "resource curse" offer insight into how commodities shape economies.

For live market data and analysis, the CME Group website provides futures contract specifications, settlement prices, and educational materials on oil, metals, grains, and livestock. The U.S. Energy Information Administration publishes detailed energy data and free outlook reports, and the World Bank's Commodity Markets Outlook, released periodically, is excellent for macro trends and price forecasts. The FAO's Food Price Index is valuable if your interest leans toward agricultural goods.

For ongoing reading, Reuters and Bloomberg cover commodities daily, and the Financial Times has strong sector coverage. Specialist newsletters and podcasts, such as those from major investment banks' commodity research desks (many publish summaries publicly), can also keep you current.

If you tell me whether you're interested in investing, trading, economics, or a specific commodity like oil, gold, or coffee, I can point you to more targeted resources.

Linear network coding is a technique for transmitting information through a network in which intermediate nodes, rather than simply forwarding the packets they receive, combine them mathematically before passing them on. The combinations are typically linear, meaning each outgoing packet is a linear combination of incoming packets, with the coefficients drawn from a finite field such as GF(2) or a larger field like GF(2^8). The receiver then recovers the original data by solving a system of linear equations, which works as long as it collects enough independent combinations.

The idea was formalized in 2000 by Ahlswede, Cai, Li, and Yeung, who showed that network coding can achieve the multicast capacity of a network, a rate that routing alone cannot always reach. The classic illustration is the butterfly network, in which two sources must send information to two receivers through a shared bottleneck link. Routing can carry only one bit per time unit across that bottleneck, but if the middle node XORs the two bits and sends the result, each receiver can recover both bits by combining the coded bit with the one it received directly.

Random linear network coding, proposed by Ho and colleagues, simplifies practical implementation. Instead of carefully designing coefficients, each node chooses them at random from a large field. With high probability the resulting combinations are linearly independent, so the destinations can decode successfully without centralized coordination. This property makes the approach robust to network changes, packet losses, and distributed operation.

Applications include content distribution and peer-to-peer file sharing, wireless and mesh networks where broadcast advantages can be exploited, distributed storage systems that tolerate node failures, and streaming systems that benefit from reduced retransmissions. Practical deployments often use random linear codes because they are efficient and need little coordination, though computational cost and the overhead of coding coefficients remain design considerations.

Dogs aren't really born wanting footwear, so it can feel weird for them to have something on their feet. Their paws are packed with sensitive nerves, and shoes muffle that feel for the ground and cut down on grip. Balance matters a lot to them too, so a pair of shoes can make them feel wobbly. Plenty of dogs do a little dance or shuffle when they first get shoes on. Maybe they're getting used to the sensation, or maybe they're just trying to kick the things off. Some dogs also hate the clicking or scraping sound shoes make on hard floors. Bottom line, pay attention to how your dog's doing. If they seem miserable in shoes, try something else or skip them altogether.

The vas deferens, sometimes called the ductus deferens, is a duct within the male reproductive tract that conveys sperm from the testes to the ejaculatory ducts. When ejaculation occurs, the smooth muscle in its walls tightens and pushes the sperm onward, where it combines with other secretions and leaves the body through the urethra. This structure additionally contributes to the generation and movement of hormones and other compounds that aid the overall operation of the male reproductive system.

I can't say for certain whether you will conceive normally, because that depends on what is causing the irregular periods and on your partner's health too. But there are reasons for real hope. Many women with irregular cycles conceive, and regular periods after treatment are a good sign that your body is responding to the medicines.

Here is what the medicines you mentioned generally do. Ovacare is usually given to help the ovaries release an egg, so regular cycles are a sign it may be working. Ovashield is typically taken for a few days in the cycle to support the early stage of the cycle and the development of the egg. Folic acid (Fol Fort) is important for every woman trying to conceive, and it helps protect the baby's early development, so keep taking it as prescribed. Duphaston (dydrogesterone) is a progesterone tablet that is usually taken in the second half of the cycle to support the uterine lining so a pregnancy can implant and continue.

Some practical steps can improve your chances. Try to have intercourse every two to three days around the time of ovulation, which is usually about two weeks before your next period starts. Keep a note of your cycle dates so your doctor can time the treatment well. Maintain a healthy weight, avoid smoking and heavy alcohol, and limit caffeine. Ask your partner to get a basic semen test if it has not been done, since male factors play a role in about half of fertility problems.

Please go back to your doctor if you do not conceive after a few months of this treatment, or sooner if your periods become irregular again, you have severe pain, very heavy bleeding, or other new symptoms. Your doctor can run tests such as hormone levels or an ultrasound to see exactly what is needed. Most couples in your situation are able to conceive with proper follow-up, so keep following your doctor's plan and try not to be discouraged if it takes some time.

Zach Thomas played college football at Texas Tech University, where he was a standout linebacker for the Red Raiders from 1992 to 1995. He was a two-time first-team All-American and was named the Southwest Conference Defensive Player of the Year. Despite that production, he was considered undersized for an NFL linebacker, which caused him to slip in the 1996 draft. The Miami Dolphins selected him in the fifth round, and he went on to have a celebrated career, earning multiple Pro Bowl selections and All-Pro honors and later being inducted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame.

Planes don't really balance by counting seats on each side. The plane is built like a mirror image, with the aisle down the middle, so a row of three on one side matches a row of three on the other side. Even when a row has an odd number of seats, the airline sells seats across the whole plane, and the seats on the left and right add up to about the same total. A few people sitting a bit more on one side barely matters, because a plane carries many tons of stuff and the pilots can make small adjustments.

The bigger balancing problem is front to back, not left to right. A plane has to stay balanced like a seesaw, so the crew cares about where the weight sits between the nose and the tail. That's why the ground crew loads heavy bags in specific spots, why they sometimes ask people to move to different seats, and why the plane carries fuel in tanks that can be pumped around to keep things level.

The Seminole Wars ended in three stages across the nineteenth century, though the final conflict did not produce a formal peace treaty with all Seminole people.

The Second Seminole War, which lasted from 1835 to 1842, was the longest and most costly of the three, and it was the one that brought the fighting to a close in its main phase. Frustrated by the expense and by the Seminoles' guerrilla tactics in the Everglades and swamps, the United States government adopted a policy of capturing Seminole leaders under flags of truce, and by 1842 the army had largely given up on forcing the remaining Seminoles out. Secretary of War John Bell and his successors declared the war effectively over, and the government withdrew most of its troops. A relatively small group, often estimated at around three hundred people, remained in the Everglades and refused to be removed to Indian Territory. Many of the Seminole people had already been forced west, and the conflict ended with an uneasy standoff rather than a negotiated settlement.

The Third Seminole War, from 1855 to 1858, was a smaller conflict sparked by surveying expeditions and continued pressure on the holdouts. It ended when the army, under Colonel William Harney, conducted a campaign that pushed the remaining Seminoles deeper into the swamps, and the government ceased active operations in 1858 without securing a formal surrender from most of them. Those who stayed in Florida became the ancestors of the modern Seminole Tribe of Florida, which gained federal recognition and reservation lands later in the twentieth century.

A personal computer, or PC, is a computer built for one person's everyday use. Most are either desktop or laptop machines, and people rely on them for things like writing documents, surfing the web, gaming, and keeping track of their money. At the heart of a PC is a microprocessor, the central processing unit (CPU) that carries out program instructions and handles calculations. A typical PC also contains memory such as RAM, storage like a hard drive or solid state drive, a display or monitor, and input tools including a keyboard and mouse. Some models add extras such as touchscreens, built-in cameras, or speakers.

Certainly! Attention Deficit Disorder (ADD) is a condition that can make it difficult for someone to focus and maintain concentration. It may also interfere with the ability to stay still and regulate one's actions. Individuals with ADD often struggle to pay attention in classrooms or at jobs, and they may find it challenging to follow directions or finish assignments. Every person's brain functions somewhat differently, and for some, the brain may have more difficulty with attention and self-control than for others. Some people are born with brains that operate differently and may have ADD, whereas others may not develop it until later in life. It's essential to keep in mind that each person is unique, and that those with ADD are not "bad" or "lazy." They simply require additional help and support to handle their condition and achieve success in school and beyond.
Oregon State University is located in Corvallis, Oregon.

Sparse coding is a way of representing data efficiently in machine learning and AI. The basic idea is that most data can be built from a fairly small number of "atoms," or basis functions, instead of a huge pile of individual pieces. You take a dataset and write each example as a linear combination of a fixed set of basis functions, where the coefficients are what represent the data. The trick is finding basis functions that capture the important stuff using as few nonzero coefficients as possible. Most of the coefficients end up zero or close to it, and that's where the "sparse" part comes from. It's handy for a few reasons: it's computationally cheaper, it takes up less storage, and it tends to generalize better to new data. People have used it for image and video analysis, natural language processing, and even neuroscience.

Over the course of his National Football League career, quarterback Brett Favre made 297 straight regular season starts. The run began on September 27, 1992, and came to a close on December 12, 2010. Favre suited up for the Green Bay Packers, the New York Jets, and the Minnesota Vikings, and many people consider him among the best quarterbacks the NFL has ever seen.

A battery is made up of one or more electrochemical cells, and each cell contains three basic components: an anode (the negative electrode), a cathode (the positive electrode), and an electrolyte, which is a substance that allows ions to move between the two electrodes while keeping them electrically separated. Many batteries also include a separator, a thin porous barrier that prevents the electrodes from touching and short-circuiting while still letting ions pass through. The electrodes are made from materials chosen for how readily they give up or accept electrons; for example, common alkaline batteries use zinc and manganese dioxide, while lithium-ion batteries typically use a graphite-based anode and a lithium metal oxide cathode. The electrolyte may be a liquid, a gel, or a solid, and in lithium-ion cells it is usually a lithium salt dissolved in an organic solvent. The whole assembly is enclosed in a casing, often metal or plastic, with terminals that let the stored energy flow out to a device.

Imagine you have a favorite toy, and the kids you play with all have that same toy too. Lots of people had a Nintendo 64 when they were little, so lots of people remember it fondly. It was the box in the living room where a whole group of friends or family gathered, and those happy memories stick around for a long time.

The games were also special. Super Mario 64 was one of the first times Mario ran around in a big 3D world, which felt like magic when it came out. GoldenEye 007 and Mario Kart 64 let you and your friends crowd around the TV, yelling and laughing, which is the kind of fun people remember most. The controller was odd and shaped like a trident, with a little handle in the middle, and that weirdness is part of why it's so memorable.

Even kids today can feel that nostalgia because they see it in things they love. Lots of YouTubers, streamers, and games pay tribute to the N64 look and sound, and older brothers, sisters, parents, and friends pass the excitement down. So a child who never owned one can still feel like they know it, the way you might feel fond of a grandparent's old record player you've only heard about.

Finally, it was in a sweet spot. It was one of the first consoles where games moved into 3D, which made everything feel new and exciting. Many people's favorite childhood memories happened around that time, and that's why the N64 holds such a warm place in so many hearts.

Multivariate statistics is a branch of statistics concerned with analyzing data that involves multiple variables measured simultaneously on each subject or observation. Where univariate statistics looks at one variable at a time, multivariate methods examine how several variables relate to one another, and how they jointly behave. This matters because in most real-world settings, outcomes are influenced by many factors at once, and studying them in isolation can miss important patterns, such as correlations between variables or combined effects that only appear when the variables are considered together.

The field draws on linear algebra and probability theory, since many techniques represent data as vectors or matrices and rely on distributions such as the multivariate normal. Common methods include multiple regression, which models one outcome as a function of several predictors; multivariate analysis of variance (MANOVA), which tests group differences across several outcomes at once; principal component analysis, which reduces many correlated variables to a smaller set of uncorrelated components that capture most of the variation; factor analysis, which seeks latent variables that explain observed correlations; and discriminant analysis and logistic regression, which classify observations into groups. Cluster analysis, which groups similar observations without predefined labels, is also often considered part of this area.

Multivariate statistics is widely used in fields such as psychology, where researchers measure personality or ability traits; marketing, for customer segmentation; biology and ecology, for comparing species across many measurements; finance, for modeling portfolios of correlated assets; and machine learning, where many modern methods have multivariate roots. Working with these techniques requires care, because high-dimensional data can introduce problems like multicollinearity, overfitting, and the difficulty of interpreting many variables at once, so analysts must check assumptions and validate their findings carefully.

Water that starts out cold can turn to ice sooner than water that starts out hot, and the reason is not simply that hot molecules resist freezing. Hot water contains molecules carrying more energy that zip around more quickly, which makes it harder for them to settle into the ordered lattice that ice requires. Slower-moving molecules in cold water, by contrast, can more easily lock into that arrangement. This counterintuitive result, called the Mpemba effect, was first noticed in the 1960s by a schoolboy named Erasto Mpemba. Scientists still do not completely explain it and continue to investigate it. Some suspect it arises from differences in how heat escapes from the water into the surrounding air, or from impurities dissolved in the water. The effect does not appear consistently, and under some circumstances hot water does freeze first. It is most likely to show up when the water is pure and the gap between the starting temperatures of the hot and cold samples is modest.

Doritos and Mountain Dew have long been linked with gaming culture. Several factors explain why these brands are so popular with gamers. First, both companies have poured money into marketing aimed at this audience, sponsoring events, producing ads for gaming platforms, and working with well-known gaming influencers to get their products noticed. Second, the two products are sold almost everywhere, including convenience stores, supermarkets, and other retailers, so gamers can easily buy them and enjoy them during a session. Third, Doritos and Mountain Dew are recognized for their bold, distinctive flavors, which can be appealing to players who want something savory or sweet to snack on while they game. Finally, Mountain Dew's high caffeine content may help gamers stay sharp and focused, which is especially attractive to competitive players or anyone gaming for long stretches. In short, the brands' popularity among gamers comes from a mix of aggressive marketing, easy availability, and a good fit with what gamers want and need.

Okay, so Lebesgue integration is basically a way to define and compute the integral of a real-valued function on a measure space. It's a generalization of the Riemann integral, which only really works for functions on a finite interval. The whole thing is named after the French mathematician Henri Lebesgue, who came up with it in his dissertation back in 1902. Today it's a standard tool in analysis, and you'll run into it all over functional analysis, probability theory, and PDEs.

It's built on measure theory, which is the branch of math dealing with "measure," basically a way of assigning a size or length to sets. The specific measure used here is the Lebesgue measure, which gives sets on the real line their size. So you start with a measure space, meaning a set with a measure attached. For the Lebesgue integral, that's the real numbers with Lebesgue measure. Then you need a real-valued function on that space, something that spits out a real number for each point.

The trick is how you slice things up. Instead of chopping the domain into intervals like Riemann does, you split the range of the function into pieces based on measurable sets, sometimes called "measurable partitions." You assign each piece a value, and the integral becomes the limit of the sums of those pieces as the partition gets finer. That's the part that feels different from Riemann, and it's what lets you handle way messier functions.

And messy is where it shines. You can integrate functions that aren't continuous, and it copes fine with functions that jump around or have singularities. It's also really good for proving convergence results for sequences and series of functions, which is a big reason people love it.

Bernoulli numbers are a sequence of rational numbers, usually denoted B_0, B_1, B_2, and so on, that arise naturally in number theory and analysis. They were named after the Swiss mathematician Jacob Bernoulli, who studied them in the early 1700s in connection with sums of powers of integers.

The standard way to define them is through a generating function. The Bernoulli numbers are the coefficients in the power series expansion of x divided by (e^x minus 1), so that x/(e^x − 1) equals the sum over n of B_n x^n / n!. From this definition, the first few values are B_0 = 1, B_1 = −1/2, B_2 = 1/6, B_4 = −1/30, and B_6 = 1/42. Every odd-indexed Bernoulli number beyond B_1 is zero, and the even-indexed ones alternate in sign and grow rapidly in size.

Their most famous historical role is in formulas for sums of powers. The sum of the k-th powers of the first n positive integers can be written as a polynomial in n whose coefficients involve Bernoulli numbers, a result known as Faulhaber's formula. Bernoulli himself used this connection to compute such sums explicitly.

Bernoulli numbers also appear in many other areas. They occur in the Taylor series of functions such as the tangent and cotangent, in the Euler–Maclaurin formula, which relates sums to integrals and is used for numerical approximation, and in the value of the Riemann zeta function at even positive integers. For example, the sum of the reciprocals of the fourth powers of the positive integers equals π^4/90, and formulas of this type come from Bernoulli numbers. They are also tied to topology and to the study of certain algebraic structures, which is why they remain an important object in modern mathematics.

"Bones" most likely refers to the character Leonard "Bones" McCoy, the ship's chief medical officer on the USS Enterprise in the original Star Trek series, played by DeForest Kelley. He's known for his gruff, skeptical manner and his frequent line "I'm a doctor, not a..." (usually followed by some form of "engineer" or "physicist").

If you meant someone else named Bones, such as the character from the TV show Bones, the forensic anthropologist Temperance "Bones" Brennan, let me know and I can tell you about that one instead.

Okay, so a logical consequence is basically a statement that has to be true if the statements it comes from are true. Think of it this way: if you start with some premises and they're all true, whatever logically follows from them can't be false. Here's a quick example. All cats are mammals. Fluffy is a cat. So Fluffy is a mammal. Nobody has to take that on faith, it just falls out of the first two statements, which makes it a logical consequence of them.

It matters more than it sounds like it does. It's how we draw conclusions and make inferences from what we already know, which is pretty much what reasoning is. Mathematicians rely on the same idea constantly, since proving a theorem is really just showing that it's a logical consequence of the axioms and earlier results.

Degenerative disc disease can be handled with plenty of non-surgical options first. Physical therapy, pain meds, and things like epidural steroid injections or radiofrequency ablation can take the edge off the pain and let you keep doing your usual stuff. If those don't cut it, or the condition is pretty bad, surgery might come up. Spinal fusion is one route: the damaged disc comes out and the vertebrae above and below get fused together. Another is laminectomy, where part of the vertebra is removed to ease pressure on the spinal cord or nerve roots. Honestly, your best bet is to sit down with a doctor or spine specialist who can look at your specific situation. They can walk you through what's available and help you figure out what makes the most sense for you.

The iconic Star Wars main theme, often called the "Star Wars Main Title" or "Star Wars Theme," was composed by John Williams. He wrote the score for the original 1977 film *Star Wars* (later retitled *Star Wars: Episode IV – A New Hope*), and his music for the franchise has become one of the most recognizable in film history.

Opening several new credit cards with generous limits and then leaving them unused is not necessarily the best way to raise your credit score. A high limit can help, but lenders care more about whether you handle credit responsibly and pay on time. Your credit utilization ratio, meaning how much of your available credit you are currently using relative to your total limits, is one of the factors that goes into your score. Generally, a lower ratio works in your favor because it signals that you are not relying heavily on the credit you have. So if you open new cards with large limits and keep their balances at zero, your utilization may drop, which could improve your score. Still, this approach may not be sustainable or helpful over the long run. A better strategy is to use credit responsibly: pay every account on time and never borrow more than you can realistically repay. It is also wise to check your credit report regularly for accuracy and currency, since doing so can reveal problems that might be hurting your score and give you the chance to correct them.

Degenerative disc disease is usually treated in stages, starting with conservative care and moving to procedures or surgery only if symptoms don't improve or if nerve function is threatened. But your symptoms are unusually serious: ataxia (loss of coordination), numbness in the legs, feet, and hands, weakness in both arms and legs, and significant muscle loss. Those signs can mean that nerves in the spinal cord or the spinal canal are being compressed, which is a different situation from ordinary back pain. Please see a spine specialist or neurologist soon, and ask for a full MRI of the spine (cervical and lumbar) plus nerve conduction studies if they haven't already been done. If you notice loss of bladder or bowel control, numbness in the groin or inner thighs, or rapidly worsening weakness, go to an emergency department the same day.

Once the cause is clear, conservative treatment usually includes physiotherapy focused on core and postural strengthening, gentle mobility work, and adapted exercise rather than rest, since prolonged inactivity worsens deconditioning. Medications may include anti-inflammatories for flares, nerve-pain medicines such as gabapentin or pregabalin, and duloxetine, which is often helpful for both nerve pain and fibromyalgia. Injections such as epidural steroid injections or facet joint blocks can reduce pain and guide further treatment. If facet joint pain is confirmed, radiofrequency ablation of the nerves supplying those joints is an option. Surgery, such as decompression, fusion, or disc replacement, is generally considered when there is progressive neurological damage, persistent weakness, or ataxia that isn't responding to other measures.

Some of your other conditions also need attention. Vitamin D and folate deficiencies should be corrected under medical supervision, and your doctor should also check vitamin B12, since deficiency can cause numbness, unsteadiness, and weakness and is easy to miss. Thyroid function, blood sugar, and inflammatory markers are also worth testing if they haven't been. For fibromyalgia, the most evidence supports regular graded low-impact exercise such as water therapy or cycling, good sleep habits, and pacing your activity to avoid boom-and-bust cycles. Given the muscle loss and your recent fractures, a referral to an occupational therapist and a falls-prevention program would also be valuable, along with adequate protein intake and possibly a supervised resistance training program once you are medically cleared.

Because you have had several fractures and now have weakness and unsteadiness, you are at high risk of falls, so it would help to review your home for hazards and consider walking aids. A rehabilitation or pain clinic that works with a multidisciplinary team can coordinate all of this, which is often the most effective approach for a combination of spinal, neurological, and musculoskeletal problems like yours.

I can't recommend specific changes for your sister, because that depends on things only her medical team knows, such as the cause and type of her pain, her kidney and liver function, her breathing, and how she is responding to what she takes now. But there may well be room for better pain control, and some observations can help you have a useful conversation with her doctor.

The basic structure of her regime is standard. She has a slow-release morphine (MST Continus) for steady background control, immediate-release oral morphine (Oramorph) for breakthrough pain, and paracetamol and diclofenac, which work differently from morphine and often help alongside it. The MST Continus dose of 5mg is quite low, though, and it is unclear from your description whether the extra "morphine tab" is an additional dose or part of the same prescription. That is worth clarifying, because doubling up by mistake or missing doses can both cause problems.

The most useful question is how often she needs the Oramorph. If she is taking breakthrough doses regularly, say two or more times most days, her background dose is probably too low. Doctors usually add up the breakthrough morphine used over 24 hours and raise the slow-release dose to cover it, which gives smoother relief with fewer peaks and troughs. Keeping a simple diary of each Oramorph dose, the time, and her pain score before and an hour after would help the doctor adjust things accurately. The breakthrough dose is also usually set in proportion to the total daily background dose, so it may need adjusting as well.

Paracetamol "two tablets three times daily" is usually 1g three times a day. Many people can safely take it four times a day, up to 4g in 24 hours, unless they are of low body weight or have liver problems, so ask whether a fourth dose is appropriate.

Diclofenac can be very effective, especially for pain from the chest wall, bone, or inflammation, but it can irritate the stomach and affect the kidneys and heart. Check whether she is also taking a stomach-protecting medicine such as omeprazole or lansoprazole, which is normally prescribed alongside it.

The type of pain matters too. If her pain is burning, shooting, or tingling, or follows a nerve, it may respond better to medicines such as gabapentin, pregabalin, or amitriptyline than to more morphine. Pain from the biopsy site itself may settle over time, so a review once the wound has healed is sensible.

There are also some safety and comfort points to raise. Morphine almost always causes constipation, so she should be on a regular laxative, and if she isn't, ask for one. Nausea is common early on, and anti-sickness medicine can help. Zopiclone combined with morphine can add to drowsiness and slow breathing, which matters more for someone with a lung problem. Contact a doctor promptly if she becomes very sleepy or confused, her breathing becomes slow or shallow, or she has pinpoint pupils or muscle twitching.

If her pain remains hard to control, ask for a referral to the hospital pain team or a palliative care or symptom control team. This does not mean anything about her diagnosis or prognosis. These teams specialise in pain management and are often very good at fine-tuning regimes like this one, and her GP or the community pharmacist can also do a medication review in the meantime.

I hope the biopsy results bring some clarity soon, and that she gets more comfortable.

You really should get in to see a doctor about the shortness of breath, anxiety, and headache, so they can figure out what's going on and what to do about it. They'll probably do a physical exam and go over your medical history and test results, including the TMT (stress test). If the TMT came back positive but you don't have high blood pressure, diabetes, or anything like that, they might want to dig further to find out why. That could mean an echocardiogram, a cardiac MRI, or other tests looking at how your heart and blood vessels are working.

What they do next depends on what's causing things. If there's underlying heart disease or another cardiovascular issue, they may suggest medication or lifestyle changes. If the anxiety is part of the picture, therapy or medication can help.
