For the headaches, they might recommend an over-the-counter or prescription pain reliever, or talk through ways to handle stress or other possible triggers. Stick with whatever plan they give you, and if things get worse or you're worried about anything, don't wait to get checked out again.

Imagine that everything around you, a rock, a toy, your own hand, is secretly packed full of energy, like a tightly squeezed spring. The equation E = mc^2 says that mass and energy are really two forms of the same thing. Mass is just energy that is locked up and sitting still. The "c squared" part is a gigantic number (the speed of light multiplied by itself), which tells you how much energy is hiding in even a tiny bit of stuff. A paperclip, if you could unlock all of its hidden energy, would have about as much as a big explosion.

So the equation is like an exchange rate between two kinds of money. One kind is "stuff" (mass) and the other kind is "energy." The exchange rate is enormously generous: a tiny bit of stuff turns into a huge amount of energy. But you can't normally cash it in. When you burn a log, you only release a minuscule fraction of the log's hidden energy, and the rest stays locked inside.

Where it actually gets used is in the few cases where we can unlock a little more. The sun is one example. Deep inside it, tiny hydrogen atoms squish together to make helium. The helium weighs a tiny bit less than the hydrogen that went into it. That missing bit of mass didn't vanish; it turned into energy, which is the light and warmth that reaches you. Nuclear power plants do something similar by splitting heavy atoms apart, and the pieces weigh slightly less than the original, with the difference becoming heat that makes electricity. Nuclear bombs use the same idea, but release the energy all at once.

It also works in reverse. In giant machines called particle accelerators, scientists smash particles together very fast, and the energy of the crash can turn into brand new particles, so energy becomes stuff. Medical PET scans also depend on this: a particle and its opposite twin meet and turn completely into energy in the form of light, which the scanner can see.

So the simple version is this: stuff is frozen energy, energy can become stuff, and because the speed of light is so enormous, a little bit of stuff holds a mind-boggling amount of energy. That's why stars shine and why atomic power is so strong.

Solar eclipses happen when the Moon passes between the Sun and Earth, blocking some or all of the Sun's light from reaching parts of our planet. This alignment can only occur at new moon, when the Moon is positioned roughly between Earth and the Sun. However, a new moon usually doesn't produce an eclipse, because the Moon's orbit is tilted about five degrees relative to Earth's orbit around the Sun. Most months, the Moon passes slightly above or below the Sun from our perspective. An eclipse requires the new moon to fall near one of the two points where the Moon's orbit crosses the plane of Earth's orbit, called nodes, which is why solar eclipses happen only a few times a year at most.

There are several types. A total solar eclipse occurs when the Moon completely covers the Sun's bright disk, briefly revealing the outer atmosphere, or corona. A partial eclipse happens when the Moon covers only part of the Sun, and it is visible from a much wider area. An annular eclipse occurs when the Moon is farther from Earth and too small to cover the Sun entirely, leaving a bright ring of sunlight around its edge. Hybrid eclipses change between total and annular along their path.

Because the Moon's shadow is small, a total or annular eclipse is visible only along a narrow track on Earth's surface, typically less than 200 kilometers wide, while partial phases can be seen across a much larger region. Observers should never look directly at the Sun during an eclipse without proper eye protection, except during the brief moment of totality in a total eclipse.

What you're describing is quite common with large, densely worked tattoos, and in most cases it isn't a cause for alarm. A fresh tattoo is essentially a big abrasion, and over the first week or so it weeps plasma, lymph fluid, a little blood, and excess ink. That fluid dries into the scabs and gets trapped under clothing or ointment. Combined with dead skin cells and the natural bacteria that live on everyone's skin, this can produce a distinctive musty, slightly metallic, or "buggy" smell. Some people also notice that certain inks, especially in heavily saturated areas, have their own faint odour while healing. Thick layers of ointment can make it worse, because they hold moisture against the skin and give odour-causing bacteria a warm, damp place to thrive.

To manage both the smell and the scabbing, wash the tattoo gently two or three times a day with lukewarm water and a mild, fragrance-free antibacterial or gentle liquid soap, using clean hands rather than a cloth or sponge. Pat it dry with a clean paper towel and let it air out for a few minutes before applying anything. Then use only a very thin layer of a fragrance-free moisturiser or the aftercare product your artist recommended. If you've been using a heavy ointment like petroleum jelly, switching to a lighter lotion often reduces the odour noticeably. Wear loose, breathable cotton clothing over the area and change your bedsheets regularly, since stale fabric can contribute to the smell.

Leave the scabs alone, however tempting it is. Don't pick, scratch, or peel them, because pulling them off early can lift ink out and leave patchy spots or scarring. Avoid soaking the tattoo in baths, pools, or hot tubs until it's fully healed, since soggy scabs tend to come off prematurely. Short showers are fine. If the itching becomes intense, a gentle slap or a cool compress can help without damaging the skin.

You should be concerned if the smell becomes genuinely foul or rotten, or if it comes with other changes. Warning signs of infection include increasing redness that spreads beyond the tattoo, swelling or heat that gets worse rather than better after the first few days, pain that intensifies, yellow or green pus, red streaks extending from the area, or fever and chills. If you notice any of these, see a doctor promptly, as infections in large tattoos can need antibiotics.

Since yours seems to be healing well and the smell is merely unpleasant rather than putrid, it's most likely just part of the normal healing process and should fade as the scabs naturally flake off over the next week or two. If you're unsure, it's always reasonable to show it to your tattoo artist, who will have seen plenty of healing tattoos and can tell you whether it looks on track.

Yes, a blood clot is possible, and her symptoms need prompt medical attention. Because she had a catheter threaded through the groin, the swelling and lump could also come from the puncture site itself. Common causes include a hematoma (a collection of blood under the skin or in the tissue around the artery), a pseudoaneurysm (a small leak in the artery wall that forms a pulsating sac), or a small abnormal connection between the artery and the vein. A deep vein thrombosis (DVT) in the leg is also a real possibility, especially after a procedure when someone has been lying still. Swelling in the foot and ankle on one side fits with a clot in the leg veins, and a hematoma or pseudoaneurysm can also press on veins and cause that swelling. Since the procedure was attempted on that same side, the catheter may have irritated the artery or vein there, which is one reason the doctors should look at it.

Please call her cardiologist's office or the catheterization team today and tell them exactly what you've described: the swelling in the right ankle and foot, and the knot in the groin on the side where the procedure was attempted. Ask whether she needs an ultrasound of the leg and groin, which is a quick, painless test that can check for both a clot and a pseudoaneurysm. Don't wait for a routine follow-up.

Take her to the emergency room right away, or call 911, if you notice any of the following: the groin lump is pulsing or you can feel a whooshing or buzzing when you touch it, the lump is getting bigger quickly, the groin or thigh is bleeding or the dressing soaks through, her leg becomes pale, cold, blue, or numb, the swelling spreads quickly up the leg, or she develops chest pain, shortness of breath, a racing heartbeat, coughing up blood, or lightheadedness. Those can signal serious complications, including a clot that has traveled to the lungs.

Yoshua Bengio is a computer scientist who teaches at the University of Montreal. He is among the leading figures in deep learning, a branch of artificial intelligence in which neural networks allow computers to learn from data and reach decisions. His work has substantially advanced artificial neural networks, natural language processing, and machine learning more broadly. In 2018, he shared the Turing Award with Yann LeCun and Geoffrey Hinton in recognition of their deep learning research. This award, frequently called the "Nobel Prize of Computing," honors people who have made major contributions to computer science.

Jack LaLanne died on January 23, 2011, at 96. He was an American fitness, exercise, and nutrition guy who got nicknamed the "Godfather of Fitness" and the "First Fitness Superhero," and honestly, it fit. He was known for being full of energy and enthusiasm, and he put that into everything he did for fitness and health. He hosted "The Jack LaLanne Show," which ran from 1953 to 1985 and was one of the first fitness programs on TV. He also wrote a ton, with plenty of books and articles on fitness, exercise, and nutrition.

The symptoms you describe may be due to an excessive intake of Methylprednisolone. This corticosteroid is prescribed for many conditions, such as inflammation, allergies, and disorders of the immune system. Because overuse can lead to serious side effects, it should only be taken the way a healthcare professional directs. If your wife has been taking more than the dose she was prescribed, she should stop the medication and speak with her healthcare provider as soon as she can. Side effects of taking too much Methylprednisolone can include weight gain, a higher risk of infections, weakened bones (osteoporosis), high blood pressure, and mood changes such as depression and anxiety. Should she notice any of these symptoms, she needs to get medical attention right away, since a healthcare provider can evaluate her condition and decide on the right treatment. Until then, she should drink plenty of fluids and rest as much as possible. She should also avoid taking any more Methylprednisolone, or any other medication, unless her healthcare provider has approved it first.

Imagine you have a lemonade stand and your friend wants to borrow a dollar to buy lemons. If it were against the rules to ask for any extra money back, your friend might pay back just the dollar, which sounds fair. But then you would have less reason to lend, because you'd be waiting for your money to come back with nothing extra for taking the risk that your friend might not pay you at all. So fewer people would lend, and lots of little businesses that need money to start or grow would have a hard time finding it. Some people would find sneaky ways around the rule, like charging a "fee" with a different name, or giving a smaller loan so the extra money is hidden somewhere else.

Think of it like a big toy box shared by the whole neighborhood. Interest is a bit like the price of borrowing a toy for a while. If nobody could charge for toys, the people who own lots of toys might keep them at home instead of sharing, and the kids who never had toys to begin with would still have none. Over time, the people who already had lots of toys would probably end up with even more, because they could afford to wait and use their own toys for their own projects, while everyone else would have to save up their own pennies with no help.

A small country would feel this quickly. If its banks and lenders could not charge interest, foreign lenders would probably stop lending to it, and local people with savings might move their money abroad where they could earn something. Families wanting to buy a house or a farm would struggle, and the country could find itself with little money to build roads or schools. Prices might not change much, but fewer things would get built.

In a big, rich country like the United States, the effect would be larger in scale but might be cushioned by a huge pool of savings and many different lenders. Still, the financial system is built around interest, so banks, pension funds, and the government's own borrowing would all be disrupted. Rich people with lots of money to lend might do fine by finding other ways to earn returns, such as owning shares in companies, while ordinary workers who rely on loans for homes, cars, and school might find credit harder to get or be pushed toward riskier workarounds. Wealth could become more concentrated in the hands of people who own businesses and property outright.

If the whole world did this at once, there would be no place to escape the rule, so the effects would be the largest. Global trade, which depends on loans to ship goods and build factories, would slow down. Countries that borrow a lot to grow would have trouble, and the world's savings would have fewer ways to flow to the places that need them most. Many economists think growth would slow, and wealth could be shaped by who already owns capital and land, though some people argue that it could reduce debt traps for poor families. Nobody can say for sure, because no country has ever tried it on a large scale, and people respond to rules in surprising ways.

Leonard Lipton and Peter Yarrow composed "Puff, the Magic Dragon." The trio Peter, Paul and Mary, of which Yarrow was a member, released the first recording in 1962. Since then, the song has grown into a beloved children's standard, and many other musicians have recorded their own versions.

There are a bunch of ways people and companies can use other people's money to invest or run a business. Here are the main ones.

Partnership: two or more people start a business together and split the profits and losses. Everybody puts something in, whether that's cash, property, work, or a particular skill, and the split follows whatever the partnership agreement says.

LLC: this is a business structure that gives you the liability protection of a corporation but the tax treatment of a partnership. Members put in money or property and share profits and losses based on the operating agreement.

Joint venture: a couple of people or organizations team up for one specific project or business activity. They each chip in money, property, or other assets, and the profits and losses get divided according to the joint venture agreement.

Crowdfunding: you raise money by asking lots of people for small amounts, usually through an online platform. Backers generally get either a reward or a bit of equity in the project for chipping in.

Angel investing: an angel investor is just an individual who backs a startup or small business financially. In return they usually get an ownership stake in the company.

Venture capital: this is financing from investors for startups and small businesses that could grow fast. VC firms tend to put in big sums and get ownership equity in the companies they fund.

Public offerings: here a company sells securities to the general public. Basically, it raises money by selling stocks or bonds to investors.

Both nitrites and nitrates are chemical compounds made up of nitrogen and oxygen atoms. Food manufacturers frequently add them to products such as cured meats, including ham, to keep the food from spoiling and to give it a particular taste. What mainly sets the two apart is how many oxygen atoms each one has: nitrites contain two, whereas nitrates contain three. Although this difference in structure seems minor, it can cause the compounds to affect the body in different ways once they are eaten. In cured meats, nitrites are added in small quantities to maintain the meat's color and flavor. Nitrates are less effective as preservatives for meat, so the food industry uses them less often. Therefore, if the ham you purchased lists nitrites, it contains a certain kind of preservative that helps keep it fresh and gives it a distinctive flavor.

Cyberstalkers use the internet, phones, and other digital tools to repeatedly harass, monitor, intimidate, or frighten a specific person. What sets it apart from ordinary online rudeness is the pattern: it's persistent, targeted, and usually makes the victim fear for their safety or feel they can't escape the attention.

A common behavior is relentless unwanted contact, such as sending floods of messages, emails, or comments, creating new accounts after being blocked, or reaching out through friends, family, or coworkers to keep a line to the victim. Many cyberstalkers also monitor their targets closely by tracking social media activity, check-ins, and tagged photos to piece together where someone lives, works, or spends time. In more invasive cases, they install stalkerware on a victim's phone or computer, misuse shared accounts, or hide GPS trackers or devices like AirTags to follow someone's location.

Cyberstalkers often try to damage or control the victim's life and reputation. They may spread rumors or false accusations, impersonate the victim online, post private information like a home address or phone number (known as doxxing), or share intimate images without consent. Some make direct or veiled threats, sometimes hinting that they know where the person is or what they've been doing to show they're watching. Others contact employers or landlords to cause trouble, or sign the victim up for unwanted services and subscriptions.

Many cyberstalkers know their victims, often a former partner, acquaintance, or coworker, though some target strangers or public figures. Their motives vary and can include obsession, a desire for control, revenge after a breakup, or resentment. Online stalking sometimes escalates into in-person stalking, which is one reason it's taken seriously.

Cyberstalking is a crime in many places, including under U.S. federal law and most state laws. If you're dealing with it, it helps to document everything with screenshots and dates, avoid engaging with the stalker, tighten privacy settings, check your devices and accounts for unfamiliar access, and report it to the platforms involved and to police. Organizations such as the National Domestic Violence Hotline or the Cyber Civil Rights Initiative can also offer guidance and support.

The expression "afford to lose" describes how much money or resources a person or organization can give up without suffering serious harm. People commonly use it when discussing gambling, investing, or other ventures that carry a real chance of losing money or valuable assets. Suppose someone walks into a casino and resolves to bet a set sum; they might remark, "I can afford to lose $100." By saying this, they mean they accept the possibility of losing that amount and would not be left in financial or emotional ruin if it disappeared. Conversely, a person who says, "I can't afford to lose any more money" is signaling that they will take no further chances and would prefer to stop gambling or investing. Overall, before committing to any risky undertaking, it is wise to ask whether you can truly absorb the loss. Doing so requires an honest assessment of your finances and your capacity to cope with setbacks. Keep in mind, too, that no investment or bet is entirely free of risk, so losing some or all of your money is always a possibility.

Salesforce is an American cloud software company, headquartered in San Francisco, best known for customer relationship management (CRM) software. CRM software helps businesses manage their interactions with current and potential customers, tracking sales leads, deals, customer communications, support cases, and marketing campaigns in one place. Founded in 1999 by Marc Benioff and others, Salesforce popularized the "software as a service" model, delivering business applications over the internet by subscription rather than as programs installed on company computers.

Its core products are organized into "clouds" for different business functions. Sales Cloud helps sales teams manage pipelines and close deals, Service Cloud supports customer service and help desk operations, Marketing Cloud handles email campaigns, advertising, and customer journeys, and Commerce Cloud powers online storefronts. It also offers analytics, data integration, and industry-specific versions for sectors such as healthcare, financial services, and government.

Over the years Salesforce has grown through major acquisitions, including Tableau for data visualization, MuleSoft for connecting different software systems, and Slack for workplace messaging. It also provides a development platform that lets companies and outside developers build custom applications, plus an app marketplace called AppExchange. More recently the company has invested heavily in artificial intelligence, first through its Einstein features and now through Agentforce, which lets businesses deploy AI agents that can handle tasks like answering customer questions or qualifying sales leads.

Salesforce is one of the largest enterprise software companies in the world, serving businesses of all sizes, from small startups to large multinational corporations.

Given an unstable career, the most useful retirement strategy is one that stays flexible, doesn't lock you into a single employer, and keeps working even when your income doesn't. Start by understanding what you can access. If you're an employee, your employer may offer a 401(k) or similar plan, and if you're in the US, you may be able to contribute to a traditional or Roth IRA regardless of your employment situation. An IRA is portable: it stays with you when you change jobs, and you control the investments. If you change jobs often, avoid cashing out an old 401(k) when you leave, since that triggers taxes and penalties. Roll it into an IRA or your new employer's plan instead.

If your income is irregular, as with freelancing, gig work, or contract roles, look at self-employed options. A Solo 401(k) can allow high contributions if you have no full-time employees besides a spouse, and a SEP IRA is simpler to set up and can be funded in years when you earn more. A SIMPLE IRA is another option for small businesses. Because these contributions are usually calculated as a percentage of net self-employment income, you can contribute heavily in good years and little or nothing in lean ones, which fits variable earnings well.

Since your income may swing, the Roth IRA deserves special attention. You fund it with after-tax money, so you pay taxes now and withdrawals in retirement are generally tax-free. It also lets you withdraw your contributions (not earnings) at any time without penalty, which gives you a bit of a safety valve. Also, if your income is low in a given year, your tax rate is low too, which makes Roth contributions more attractive during those years.

Beyond account type, a few habits matter more than the specific plan. Build an emergency fund of several months of expenses before pushing hard on retirement contributions, because an unstable career makes a cash cushion essential, and it keeps you from raiding retirement accounts during a dry spell. Automate contributions when income is strong, but make them adjustable so you can pause or reduce them without penalty. Keep an eye on fees and choose low-cost index funds where possible, since fees compound over decades. And consider consulting a fee-only financial planner or tax professional once, especially to choose between a Roth and traditional contribution and to set up a self-employed plan correctly.

If you tell me your country, whether you're an employee or self-employed, and roughly how much your income varies, I can get more specific.

Roger Penrose is an English mathematician and physicist, and he's best known for his work on the math behind general relativity and cosmology. He's been a professor at Oxford for a long time and has been part of the Mathematical Institute there since 1972. His most famous work is probably on singularities in general relativity. He and Stephen Hawking came up with the Penrose-Hawking singularity theorems, which show that singularities pop up in certain solutions to Einstein's field equations. He's also done a lot in quantum mechanics and the foundations of quantum theory, and he's even had a hand in the early ideas behind quantum computing. He's picked up plenty of awards along the way, including the 1988 Wolf Prize in Physics, the 2004 Nobel Prize in Physics, and the 2020 Abel Prize.

Kernel regression is a nonparametric technique for estimating the relationship between a predictor variable and a response variable without assuming that the relationship has a particular functional form, such as a line or a polynomial. Instead of fitting a global model with a fixed number of parameters, it estimates the expected value of the response at any given point by taking a weighted average of the observed responses, where observations whose predictor values lie closer to the point of interest receive larger weights.

The weights come from a kernel function, which is a symmetric, non-negative function that peaks at zero and decays as the distance grows. Common choices include the Gaussian kernel, the Epanechnikov kernel, and the uniform kernel. The most widely known estimator is the Nadaraya-Watson estimator, introduced in 1964. For a query point x, it computes the prediction as the sum of K((x − x_i)/h) times y_i, divided by the sum of K((x − x_i)/h), where the sums run over all observations. The denominator normalizes the weights so they add to one, which makes the prediction a local average of the observed y values.

The parameter h is called the bandwidth, and it matters far more than the specific kernel. A small bandwidth makes the estimate depend only on very nearby points, producing a wiggly curve that follows the noise and has high variance but low bias. A large bandwidth averages over a wide neighborhood, giving a smooth curve that may miss real structure, which means low variance but high bias. Bandwidth is usually chosen by cross-validation, or by rules of thumb and plug-in methods that aim to minimize an error measure such as the mean integrated squared error.

There are refinements of the basic idea. Local linear regression fits a weighted straight line around each query point rather than a constant, which reduces bias near the boundaries of the data and handles uneven spacing of the predictors better. Local polynomial regression generalizes this to higher degrees. Other variants include the Gasser-Müller estimator and adaptive methods that let the bandwidth vary across the input space.

Kernel regression is flexible and intuitive, and it can capture nonlinear patterns without prior knowledge of their shape. Its weaknesses are computational cost, since each prediction uses the whole dataset, and the curse of dimensionality: with many predictors, data become sparse in the neighborhood of any point, so convergence is slow and large samples are needed. It is also related to other methods, including k-nearest neighbors regression, which uses a neighborhood defined by count rather than distance, and kernel ridge regression and support vector methods, which use kernels differently, to implicitly map data into high-dimensional feature spaces rather than to compute local averages.

Yes, blood tests can sometimes point to a different diagnosis, but being sent for them is a completely normal and expected part of diagnosing MS, and it usually doesn't mean your neurologist has changed their mind. There is no single blood test that confirms MS. Instead, doctors diagnose it by combining your symptoms, your neurological exam, MRI findings, and sometimes a lumbar puncture, and then ruling out other conditions that can look similar. Blood work is one of the main ways they do that ruling out, so it's a standard step even when the doctor is already fairly confident.

Your friend is right that several conditions can mimic MS, which is why this step matters. Vitamin B12 deficiency can cause numbness, tingling, balance problems, and changes in the spinal cord. Thyroid problems can cause fatigue and other overlapping symptoms. Infections such as Lyme disease, syphilis, and HIV can affect the nervous system. Autoimmune conditions like lupus, Sjögren's syndrome, antiphospholipid syndrome, and sarcoidosis can produce lesions or symptoms resembling MS. Two conditions are especially important to check for: neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (NMOSD), tested with an aquaporin-4 antibody blood test, and MOG antibody disease (MOGAD), tested with an anti-MOG antibody test. Both can look a lot like MS on MRI and in symptoms, but they are treated differently, and some MS medications can actually make NMOSD worse. That is a big reason neurologists test carefully before starting treatment. Many doctors also check vitamin D, since low levels are common in people with MS and worth correcting either way.

So if your neurologist says they are about 97% sure, the blood tests are most likely aimed at covering that remaining few percent and making sure nothing treatable or differently managed is being missed. Most of the time these results come back normal and the MS diagnosis stands. If something does turn up, that's genuinely useful information, because getting the diagnosis right means getting the right treatment.

It's completely reasonable to ask your neurologist directly what they are testing for and whether anything specific prompted it. Many people find that hearing "this is routine" from their own doctor eases a lot of the worry. Waiting for results during a diagnosis like this is stressful, so be kind to yourself in the meantime.

Green and orange patches on the tongue can come from a bunch of things: infections, allergies, or some other underlying health issue. Honestly, the best move is to get your son checked by a doctor or pediatrician so they can figure out what's going on and how to treat it. Thrush is one common culprit. It's a fungal infection that causes white or yellow patches on the tongue, cheeks, and gums, and it shows up a lot in infants. It's usually cleared up with antifungal medication. If he's had thrush before and the patches keep coming back, it could be a recurring infection or something else entirely.

Other possibilities include:

Allergic reactions: certain foods or substances can cause red or white patches on the tongue.

Oral lichen planus: a chronic inflammatory condition that can leave white or red patches on the tongue and elsewhere in the mouth.

Geographic tongue: a harmless condition where small bumps (papillae) go missing or get inflamed, leaving red or white patches that move around over time.

Vitamin deficiencies: low folic acid or vitamin B12 can change how the tongue looks, including patches or color shifts.

Again, the real answer depends on what a provider sees. They might just examine his mouth, but they could also order lab work or other tests to pin it down.

A loan used to cover an expense is generally classed as a personal loan or a consumer loan. Such loans are commonly taken out to fund individual costs like remodeling a house, paying medical bills, or meeting other unforeseen outlays. Banks, credit unions, and other lenders may provide them, with either fixed or variable interest rates. Before borrowing, it is wise to examine the terms closely, including the interest rate, the length of the repayment schedule, and any associated fees, so you can judge whether the loan is truly affordable.

A file-based system is basically a way of organizing and storing data on a computer. The data lives in individual files, and those files sit inside directories (folders, as most people call them). Every file gets its own name and a specific spot in the directory structure. You can create, change, and delete files and folders whenever you want, and you can move or copy files from one folder to another. Operating systems like Windows, macOS, and Linux rely on this approach to handle storage, and it's a big reason why managing data on a computer feels so easy. It's flexible and simple to use, which is why most computer systems depend on it.

Ugh, that really sucks about the insurance thing, especially with your employer being the cause. Getting meds without coverage is rough, but you do have some options.

First, check with the manufacturer of your medications. A lot of drug companies run patient assistance programs for people who can't afford what they're prescribed, so it's worth a call or a quick look on their website.

You could also try your local health department or a community health center. Some of them can get you low-cost or even free meds through government-funded programs.

Ask about generics too. They're usually way cheaper than the brand names and work just as well. And look into prescription discount programs, because there are a bunch out there that knock down the price if you don't have insurance.

If money's still tight, talk to your doctor about alternatives that cost less. They might have a cheaper option that does the job.

Whatever you do, don't just go without your meds because you can't pay for them. That can get serious for your health fast, so reach out for help as soon as you can.

Tim and Eric get called funny by plenty of people because their stuff is so weird. They go for absurd, unexpected bits, and a lot of their sketches poke fun at infomercials, public access TV, and cheap-looking commercials. Those spoofs land for some folks because the ridiculous, off-kilter stuff they throw in is just so bizarre. That said, comedy is super subjective. What cracks one person up might leave the next person totally cold. Lots of people just don't get Tim and Eric, and that's fine. Everyone's got their own taste in what's funny.

A 30% stake in a business generally means the portion of the company that a person or organization owns. Suppose a company has 100 shares of stock and one investor holds 30 of them; that investor would hold a 30% stake. This ownership percentage can shape the holder's rights and obligations within the company. In a corporation, for instance, shareholders usually may vote on certain issues affecting operations, such as electing directors or approving significant business decisions, and their voting power typically matches their percentage of shares. Ownership share may also dictate how much of the company's profits or losses the holder receives or bears, and how much responsibility they carry for its debts. Since the arrangements governing ownership can differ considerably and may rest on various legal and contractual terms, anyone with questions about their rights and duties as a shareholder should consult a lawyer.
