Spain won the 2010 FIFA World Cup, which was held in South Africa. They beat the Netherlands 1–0 in the final on July 11, 2010, at Soccer City in Johannesburg. The only goal came from Andrés Iniesta in the 116th minute of extra time. It was Spain's first World Cup title.

The Manhattan Project was a wartime research and development effort carried out during World War II with the goal of creating the first atomic bombs. Historians regard it as a pivotal moment, since it produced a novel kind of weapon with enormous destructive power. While the world was engulfed in conflict, nations raced to build better and more advanced arms in hopes of outmatching their adversaries. Seeing that atomic weapons could change the course of the war, the United States, joined by partners such as the United Kingdom and Canada, committed substantial time and resources to their development. Because the effort was conducted in deep secrecy and hidden from the public, it has become the subject of many conspiracy theories. Much of the population knew little about the work underway, which allowed rumors and guesses about its nature to spread widely, and these have fueled various theories about the project and its real aims.

I'm sorry you're going through this. It's stressful to watch someone you love in the hospital, and I'll explain what might be going on, though I can't diagnose him, and his medical team knows details I don't.

There are several common reasons blood pressure stays high despite treatment. One is that the underlying cause hasn't been addressed. Kidney disease, narrowed kidney arteries, adrenal gland problems (such as excess aldosterone), thyroid disease, sleep apnea, and rarely hormone-secreting tumors can all keep pressure elevated. Another is that he may have long-standing hypertension with blood vessels that have become stiff, so they respond slowly. Pain, anxiety, a full bladder, lack of sleep, or the stress of being in the hospital can also push readings up. Some substances matter too: anti-inflammatory painkillers like ibuprofen, decongestants, steroids, alcohol, stimulants, and heavy salt intake. Finally, if he has missed or stopped his usual blood pressure medicines, pressure can rebound and take time to come back under control.

It is also worth knowing that doctors usually do not want to bring very high pressure down too quickly. Lowering it too fast can reduce blood flow to the brain, heart, and kidneys and cause harm. So a drop from 160/140 to 150/110 may be an intended, careful first step, and further reduction often happens gradually over hours to days with oral medicines. The diastolic number of 140 was very high, so the improvement to 110 is meaningful progress even if it doesn't feel like it.

Questions worth asking his doctors include: Is there any sign of damage to his heart, kidneys, brain, or eyes? What tests are being done to look for a cause, such as blood and urine tests, kidney function, an ECG, or imaging? What is the target pressure and over what timeframe? Which medicines is he on now, and will they be adjusted? Should anything he was taking at home be changed or avoided?

Please tell the nurse right away if he develops a severe headache, chest pain, shortness of breath, confusion, vision changes, weakness or numbness, trouble speaking, or vomiting, since these can signal complications that need urgent attention.

You can help by sharing his full medication list, any supplements or painkillers he uses, and his history of blood pressure, kidney, or heart problems with the team. Being in the hospital means he's being monitored closely, which is the safest place for this. I hope he improves soon.

Default reasoning is a form of non-monotonic reasoning in which a conclusion is drawn on the basis of typical or normal circumstances, even though the available information is incomplete and the conclusion might later turn out to be false. Instead of requiring proof that something holds in every possible case, a reasoner assumes that things are as they usually are unless there is evidence to the contrary. The classic example is that birds typically fly. If you learn that Tweety is a bird and nothing else, you conclude that Tweety can fly. If you later learn that Tweety is a penguin, you withdraw that conclusion.

This withdrawal of conclusions in light of new information is what makes default reasoning non-monotonic. In classical logic, adding premises never invalidates a previous conclusion; the set of consequences only grows. Everyday human reasoning does not work this way. We constantly make plausible assumptions, such as that a car left parked will still be there, or that a colleague who says they will attend a meeting will do so, and we revise them when we learn of exceptions. Default reasoning tries to capture this pattern formally.

Several formal frameworks have been developed. Raymond Reiter's default logic, introduced in 1980, adds default rules of the form: if a prerequisite is believed and it is consistent to assume a justification, then conclude a consequent. In the bird case, the rule says that if Tweety is a bird and it is consistent to assume Tweety flies, then conclude that Tweety flies. Reasoning produces sets of conclusions called extensions, and a theory can have several extensions when defaults conflict, as in the well-known Nixon diamond, where Nixon is a Quaker (typically a pacifist) and a Republican (typically not a pacifist). Other approaches include circumscription, which minimizes the set of abnormal things, autoepistemic logic, which reasons about what the agent does or does not know, and preferential or conditional logics that model "normally, if A then B." Logic programming with negation as failure is also closely related, since it concludes something is false when it cannot be proven.

Default reasoning matters in artificial intelligence because real-world knowledge bases cannot list every exception to every rule. This is related to the frame problem and the qualification problem, where specifying all conditions needed for an action or rule to apply is impractical. Defaults provide a compact way to represent general knowledge and handle exceptions as they arise.

There are challenges. Determining whether a justification is consistent can be computationally expensive, sometimes undecidable in full generality. Conflicting defaults require ways to prioritize or choose among them, such as specificity, where the more specific rule (penguins don't fly) overrides the more general one. There is also ongoing debate about whether to accept conclusions common to all extensions (skeptical reasoning) or those found in at least one (credulous reasoning).

Yes, it is possible to get pregnant from sex during bleeding, and in your situation the chance is probably higher than it would be with a normal period.

With a regular cycle, pregnancy during true menstruation is unlikely but not impossible. Sperm can survive in the reproductive tract for up to five days, so if you ovulate early, sperm from intercourse near the end of a period can still be present when the egg is released. This is more likely with shorter cycles.

Your case is different because bleeding that has gone on since June 11th is not a normal period. Irregular or prolonged bleeding often means your cycle is disrupted, and ovulation may be happening at unpredictable times. That makes it hard to say which days are "safe." Bleeding that looks like a period can also be something else, such as breakthrough bleeding around ovulation, hormonal imbalance, or even a sign of early pregnancy complications like a threatened miscarriage or an ectopic pregnancy. So you cannot assume you are protected just because you are bleeding.

If you are having sex and do not want to become pregnant, use reliable contraception such as condoms, or another method you have discussed with a clinician, every time. If there is any chance you could be pregnant, take a pregnancy test. Tests on urine are fairly reliable if done at least a couple of weeks after unprotected sex, and a blood test can be done sooner.

More importantly, you should see a doctor soon about the bleeding itself. Having two periods in one month and then bleeding for weeks can lead to anemia, and it needs to be evaluated. Common causes include hormonal imbalances, thyroid problems, polycystic ovary syndrome, fibroids or polyps, infections, side effects of contraceptives, and stress or weight changes. A doctor will likely do a pregnancy test, blood count, possibly hormone tests, and a pelvic ultrasound. Treatment is often simple once the cause is found.

Seek urgent care if you have very heavy bleeding (soaking a pad every hour or two), dizziness, fainting, severe abdominal pain, or a racing heartbeat, especially if pregnancy is possible.

You still have to report the income even if no 1099-MISC arrives. The form is a courtesy document for the IRS's records; your obligation to report earnings comes from the fact that you received them, not from whether someone sent you a form. Income is reportable whether or not a 1099 was issued, and whether or not the payer met the threshold for issuing one, which for most payments is $600 or more in a calendar year (the threshold for many types of payments was scheduled to rise to $2,000 for payments made after 2025 under recent legislation, so check the current rule if your payments are near that level).

Start by gathering your own records. Look through your bank deposits, PayPal, Venmo, Stripe, or other payment platform statements, invoices you sent, and any emails or contracts that show what you were paid and for what work. Total the gross amount you received for the year. If you had any reimbursements, be sure to separate out true reimbursements of expenses the client paid on your behalf, since those generally are not income in the same way, but keep documentation to back that up.

Next, determine how the income should be reported. If you were an independent contractor or sole proprietor, the income goes on Schedule C (Form 1040), Profit or Loss From Business. You list gross receipts there, then subtract your ordinary and necessary business expenses such as supplies, software, mileage, a home office deduction if you qualify, and similar costs. The net profit flows to your Form 1040 and is also subject to self-employment tax, reported on Schedule SE, if the net is $400 or more. If the income was a hobby rather than a business, it still must be reported, generally as other income on Schedule 1, though hobby expenses are generally no longer deductible for federal purposes.

If the income is from a side activity like rental property, royalties, or a one-time sale, different schedules apply, such as Schedule E or Schedule D. Choose based on the nature of the activity.

You should also make quarterly estimated tax payments using Form 1040-ES if you expect to owe at least $1,000 in tax for the year after withholding and credits. Unreported self-employment income can lead to underpayment penalties, so setting aside money for taxes as you earn it is wise.

Finally, keep your records for at least three years from the filing date, and ideally longer. If you're unsure how to classify the income or whether you have deductible expenses, a tax professional or the IRS's free VITA program can help, especially if the amount is significant or your situation is complicated.

The answer depends on which President Bush you mean.

Under George W. Bush (2001 to 2009), the first National Security Advisor was Condoleezza Rice, who served from 2001 to 2005. When Rice became Secretary of State in Bush's second term, her deputy Stephen Hadley succeeded her and served as National Security Advisor from 2005 until the end of the administration in 2009.

Under his father, George H.W. Bush (1989 to 1993), the National Security Advisor was Brent Scowcroft, who held the post for the entire term. Scowcroft had also served in the same role under President Gerald Ford, making him one of the few people to hold the position twice.

Dying is what happens when the body slowly stops being able to do the jobs that keep it running. Think of your body like a big team where everyone passes along the energy and air that everybody else needs. When some team members get too tired or too sick to work, the others lose their supply, and eventually the whole team stops.

The details depend a lot on why someone is dying, but a gentle, illness-related death often goes like this. In the weeks or days before, a person gets very sleepy and tired. They want to eat and drink less, because the body doesn't need as much fuel and the stomach has a harder time handling food. This isn't usually painful, and doctors and nurses can give medicine to help with any discomfort. The person may talk less and want to be left quiet, or they may drift in and out of sleep.

Closer to the end, the blood doesn't flow as strongly, so the hands and feet can feel cool and the skin may look a bit pale or blotchy. Breathing changes too. Sometimes it gets slow, sometimes it has pauses, and sometimes it sounds a bit rattly because of fluid in the throat that the person is too sleepy to swallow. This can sound scary to listeners, but the person is usually not struggling or aware of it. People often seem peaceful, and many are not awake at this point.

Then the breathing stops, and soon after, the heart stops. Without a heartbeat, blood can't carry oxygen to the brain. Within a few seconds the person loses consciousness, and within a few minutes the brain cells begin to be damaged beyond repair. After that, the body gradually cools, the muscles stiffen for a while, and the body no longer feels anything.

As for how it feels, we can't know for certain, since no one can report back. But people who care for the dying say that most of the time the final stage is calm, with the person unaware and comfortable. Sudden deaths, like from a heart attack or accident, are different and can be quicker, with the person losing consciousness very fast.

If you're asking because someone you love is ill, or because you're feeling worried, it can help to talk with a doctor or a hospice nurse. They're very good at explaining what to expect and making sure the person is comfortable.

When intraday data and end-of-day data disagree on highs and lows, the first step is to understand why, because the cause determines the fix. The most common reason is that the two sources aggregate different things. Intraday feeds are often built from consolidated tape or a single venue, while EOD highs and lows may come from the official exchange record, which can include auction prints, late-reported trades, or exclude odd lots and out-of-sequence ticks. Other causes include bad ticks in the intraday stream, differences in session definitions (regular hours versus extended hours), time zone or bar-boundary misalignment, corporate action adjustments applied to one series but not the other, and trade corrections or cancellations that were issued after your intraday data was captured.

Next, decide which source is your authority for each purpose. For official daily bars, the EOD vendor or exchange record is usually the better reference, since it incorporates corrections and the closing auction. For intraday analysis, the intraday data is the reference, but you should not expect its daily aggregate to match exactly. Document that choice so everyone downstream knows which number is canonical.

Then build a reconciliation check. Aggregate your intraday bars to daily using the same session definition as the EOD source, then compare the highs and lows. Allow a small tolerance, perhaps a few basis points or a tick or two, and flag anything outside it. When the intraday high exceeds the EOD high, suspect a bad tick or an extended-hours print. When the EOD high exceeds the intraday high, suspect missing intraday data, a gap in your feed, or a late-reported trade. Looking at the timestamp and volume of the offending print often settles it quickly, since a spike on tiny volume that reverses immediately is typically an error.

For cleaning, apply filters rather than manual edits where possible: remove trades flagged with condition codes for out-of-sequence, odd lot, or cancelled; use median or neighbor-based spike filters; and apply corrections the exchange publishes. If you must override, clip the intraday high and low to the EOD values only when you have confirmed the EOD source is trustworthy, and keep the raw data alongside the adjusted data so you can audit changes.

Finally, handle timing. EOD data is often revised overnight, so rerun reconciliation the next morning and let the revised values replace provisional ones. Log every discrepancy with the symbol, date, both values, and the resolution, which lets you spot patterns, such as a particular vendor or exchange that is consistently off, and decide whether to switch sources or add a rule. For backtesting, consistency matters more than perfection, so pick one rule set, apply it uniformly, and avoid mixing sources within one study.

Category theory is a branch of mathematics that studies structure by focusing on relationships between things rather than on the internal makeup of the things themselves. It was introduced in the 1940s by Samuel Eilenberg and Saunders Mac Lane, originally as a language for algebraic topology, but it has since grown into a general framework that cuts across nearly all of mathematics and has found applications in computer science, logic, and even physics.

The central notion is a category, which consists of two kinds of ingredients: objects and morphisms (often called arrows). A morphism goes from one object to another, and morphisms can be composed. If you have an arrow from A to B and another from B to C, you can combine them into an arrow from A to C. This composition must be associative, and every object must have an identity arrow that does nothing when composed with other arrows. Those few rules are essentially the whole definition, which is what makes the idea so flexible.

Many familiar mathematical worlds fit this pattern. Sets with functions between them form a category. Groups with group homomorphisms form another, as do vector spaces with linear maps and topological spaces with continuous functions. The insight of category theory is that a great deal of what matters about a mathematical object can be understood through how it maps to and from other objects. Instead of asking what an object is made of, you ask how it interacts with everything else in its category.

Category theory then goes a level higher by studying maps between categories, called functors. A functor sends objects of one category to objects of another and arrows to arrows, while respecting composition and identities. For example, there is a functor that takes a topological space and produces its fundamental group, turning geometric problems into algebraic ones. Going higher still, natural transformations are ways of relating two functors to each other, and it was precisely to make the informal idea of a "natural" construction rigorous that Eilenberg and Mac Lane invented the subject.

Several unifying concepts emerge from this viewpoint. Universal properties describe objects by the role they play rather than by explicit construction; the product of two sets, the direct sum of vector spaces, and the product of topological spaces all turn out to be instances of the same categorical idea. Limits and colimits generalize many constructions like intersections, unions, and quotients. Adjunctions capture pairs of functors that stand in a precise kind of dual relationship and appear almost everywhere, often explaining why certain constructions are canonical. The Yoneda lemma, perhaps the most celebrated result, formalizes the idea that an object is completely determined by its relationships with all other objects.

Because of its high level of abstraction, category theory is sometimes jokingly called "general abstract nonsense," but this abstraction is exactly its strength. It reveals that seemingly different results in different fields are really the same theorem in disguise, and it gives mathematicians a common vocabulary for transferring ideas between areas. In computer science it has shaped the design of functional programming languages such as Haskell, where concepts like functors and monads come directly from category theory, and it underlies type theory and the semantics of programming languages. In short, category theory is a mathematics of structure and composition, a way of thinking that emphasizes how things connect rather than what they are made of.

A U.S. default on its public debt would likely send shockwaves through both the stock and bond markets, because Treasury securities serve as the foundation of the global financial system. In the bond market, the most immediate effect would be a sharp rise in yields on Treasuries, particularly those maturing around the date of a missed payment, as investors demand compensation for the newly recognized risk of nonpayment. Because Treasuries are used as benchmark risk-free assets for pricing nearly every other debt instrument, yields on corporate bonds, municipal bonds, mortgages, and consumer loans would also tend to climb, raising borrowing costs across the economy. Prices of existing Treasury bonds would fall as their yields rose, inflicting losses on banks, pension funds, insurers, and money market funds that hold them. Treasuries are also used as collateral in repo markets, so a default could disrupt short-term funding and force institutions to sell assets, potentially freezing liquidity much as happened during the 2008 financial crisis.

In the stock market, a default would most likely trigger a broad sell-off as investors reassess risk, reduce exposure to equities, and seek safety in cash or other assets. Higher interest rates and borrowing costs would weigh on corporate earnings and valuations, since future cash flows become less valuable when discount rates rise. Economic uncertainty would also dampen consumer and business spending, further pressuring company profits. Sectors particularly sensitive to interest rates, such as real estate, utilities, and financials, could be hit especially hard, while volatility indices would likely spike. The severity would depend on how long the default lasted. A brief technical default resolved quickly might produce a sharp but temporary market reaction, whereas a prolonged default could lead to a deeper recession, credit rating downgrades, a weaker dollar, and lasting damage to the United States' standing as the world's preeminent safe-haven issuer.

The last president with any facial hair was William Howard Taft, who had a mustache and left office in 1913. Before him, lots of presidents had beards or mustaches, especially in the late 1800s, when facial hair was very fashionable. Abraham Lincoln had his famous beard, and Ulysses S. Grant, Rutherford Hayes, and Benjamin Harrison all had them too.

Here is the simple version. Think of how kids all want to wear the same kind of shoes because everybody else is wearing them. Grown-ups do that too. Back then, beards were the cool thing. Then around the early 1900s, a new idea took over: being clean-shaven looked neat, modern, and tidy. One big reason was the safety razor, which King Gillette made popular. Before that, shaving yourself was hard and a bit scary, because the razors were very sharp and could cut you. Once shaving became quick and easy, most men did it every day, and a smooth face became the normal look.

Another reason is that, as time went on, people started to think of beards as a little bit unusual or even a bit untrustworthy, especially for someone who wants to win a lot of votes. Candidates and their helpers worry about every little thing that might make some voters like them less. Since nobody has won with a beard in a long time, they figure it's safer to just shave. A few candidates with mustaches or beards, like Thomas Dewey, who had a mustache and lost in 1948, have tried and not won, which made people believe it was a bad idea. That may just be a coincidence, but it stuck in people's minds.

So it's mostly like a fashion rule that everyone started following, and no one wants to be the first to break it. If a popular candidate with a beard came along and did well, that could change quickly, just like the styles of clothes and haircuts change.

Pulmonary hypertension is a condition in which the blood pressure in the arteries of the lungs is abnormally high. These arteries carry blood from the right side of the heart to the lungs, where it picks up oxygen. When they become narrowed, stiffened, or blocked, the right side of the heart has to work harder to push blood through, and over time this can weaken the heart and lead to heart failure.

The condition can develop for many reasons. It may arise on its own without a clear cause, or it may be linked to other conditions such as chronic lung disease, COPD, sleep apnea, blood clots in the lungs, heart valve or left heart disease, certain autoimmune disorders, HIV, liver disease, or exposure to some medications and toxins. Genetic factors also play a role in some families.

Symptoms often develop slowly and are easy to mistake for other problems. The most common include shortness of breath, especially during physical activity, fatigue, dizziness or fainting, chest pressure, swelling in the ankles and legs, and a racing or pounding heartbeat. Because these symptoms are nonspecific, the condition is sometimes diagnosed late.

Diagnosis usually involves an echocardiogram as an initial test, followed by right heart catheterization, which is the definitive way to measure pressures in the lungs. Additional tests may look for the underlying cause, such as lung function tests, imaging, or blood tests.

Treatment depends on the type and cause. Options may include oxygen therapy, diuretics to reduce fluid, anticoagulants, and targeted medications that relax or widen the pulmonary arteries. In some cases, treating the underlying condition is the priority, and for severe or advanced disease, lung transplantation may be considered. Anyone with persistent unexplained shortness of breath or fatigue should see a doctor, since early diagnosis improves outcomes.

Banknotes tend to take a rectangular form for practical reasons, since this shape is simpler to keep and manage. Square or triangular notes would be harder to pile up or slide into a wallet. Rectangles are also quicker to tally, as they can be arranged in neat, even rows. Lastly, this format leaves room for security elements like watermarks and specialized inks that make forgery more difficult.

Common sense reasoning is the ability to make sensible judgments and inferences about everyday situations using the vast body of background knowledge that most people share without ever being explicitly taught it. It covers things humans find so obvious that we rarely notice we know them: if you drop a glass on a tile floor it will probably break, a person cannot be in two places at once, water makes things wet, people usually eat when they are hungry, and if someone is crying at a funeral they are likely sad rather than happy. Common sense lets us fill in gaps, anticipate consequences, and interpret ambiguous statements in ways that fit how the world normally works.

This kind of reasoning draws on several broad areas of knowledge. One is intuitive physics, the understanding of how objects behave, such as that unsupported things fall, solid objects cannot pass through each other, and containers hold things. Another is intuitive psychology, the grasp of how people think and act, including their beliefs, desires, emotions, and intentions. A third involves social norms and conventions, like knowing that you pay before leaving a restaurant or that interrupting someone is generally rude. There is also knowledge about time, causation, and typical sequences of events, for instance that you open a door before walking through it, or that a cake must be baked before it can be eaten.

In psychology and philosophy, common sense reasoning is studied as a fundamental part of human cognition. People rely on it constantly and effortlessly, and it is often fast, approximate, and based on defaults that can be revised when new information appears. If you hear that Tweety is a bird, you assume Tweety can fly, but you readily drop that assumption if you learn Tweety is a penguin. This flexible, defeasible quality distinguishes common sense from strict logical deduction, where conclusions follow with certainty from premises.

The term is especially prominent in artificial intelligence, where common sense reasoning has long been considered one of the hardest problems in the field. Early AI researchers such as John McCarthy recognized in the 1950s and 1960s that intelligent machines would need this kind of knowledge, and projects like Cyc attempted to encode millions of everyday facts and rules by hand. The difficulty is that common sense knowledge is enormous, mostly unstated, highly context dependent, and full of exceptions. A classic illustration is the Winograd schema, a type of test sentence such as "The trophy didn't fit in the suitcase because it was too big," where understanding what "it" refers to requires knowing something about sizes and containers rather than just grammar.

Modern large language models have made notable progress on many common sense benchmarks because they absorb patterns from huge amounts of human-written text, but researchers still debate how deeply these systems understand the world versus how well they mimic statistical regularities. They can still make surprising errors on questions any child could answer, particularly ones involving physical situations, spatial relationships, or novel scenarios unlike their training data.

In short, common sense reasoning is the everyday practical intelligence that allows us to understand and navigate the world by drawing on shared, mostly implicit knowledge about how things and people usually behave. It is so natural to humans that it seems trivial, yet replicating it in machines has proven to be one of the most persistent challenges in the study of intelligence.

Technical debt is a metaphor used in software development to describe the future cost of shortcuts, quick fixes, or suboptimal design choices made during the building of a system. The term was coined by Ward Cunningham in 1992, who compared it to financial debt: a team can take on debt by choosing an easier or faster solution now, much as a person borrows money to get something sooner. Like financial debt, it can be worthwhile in moderation, for example when a team needs to ship a product quickly to meet a market opportunity or to learn what users actually want. However, the debt accrues "interest" over time, because every new feature built on top of a hasty implementation tends to take longer, introduce more bugs, and require more workarounds than it would on a cleaner foundation.

Technical debt takes many forms. It can be deliberate, such as knowingly skipping tests or hardcoding a value to meet a deadline, or it can be unintentional, arising from a team's evolving understanding of the problem, outdated libraries, or code that was reasonable when written but no longer fits the current requirements. Common examples include duplicated code, poor documentation, missing automated tests, convoluted architecture, and dependencies that have fallen out of support.

Managing technical debt means recognizing it, measuring its impact, and deliberately paying it down through refactoring, updating systems, or redesigning weak components. Many teams allocate a portion of each development cycle to this work, so that the debt does not grow unchecked. Left unmanaged, technical debt can slow development to a crawl, make systems fragile and hard to change, and raise the risk of failures, which is why it is an important concern for both engineers and the managers who set priorities.

Computational creativity examines how algorithms and systems can be built to produce outputs that people judge to be creative. The discipline draws on computer science, artificial intelligence, philosophy, psychology, and the arts. Its central aim is to create systems capable of generating new and original ideas, products, or solutions. Such work may involve producing artistic pieces like music or visual art, or devising fresh approaches to problems in science and engineering. Researchers pursue this goal in several ways: some apply machine learning to examine existing data for patterns and trends and then generate new material from them, while others rely on older AI methods like rule-based systems and decision trees. Significant obstacles remain, including building algorithms whose output people find beautiful or meaningful, and designing systems that work effectively within the limits of a specific domain or field of expertise.

When something goes wrong on a computer, the operating system or a particular program typically produces an error message. Suppose you attempt to open a file that isn't there: the operating system may respond with a notice such as "File not found" or "No such file or directory." Error messages come in many varieties and can stem from a range of causes. Some originate from hardware trouble, such as a network card that isn't working properly or a hard drive that is on the verge of failing. Others come from software issues, for instance a bug in a program or a clash with another piece of software. The developers who build an operating system or program generally write these messages so that users can grasp what happened and work out how to resolve it. Depending on who the message is meant for and how complicated the problem is, the wording may be simple and everyday or full of technical terminology. Overall, error messages exist to help users pinpoint and diagnose problems with their machines. They form a key part of a computer's broader error-handling system and can be extremely useful when something breaks.

Yes, it's very normal, and it's one of the most well-documented patterns in how people handle money. Behavioral economists call it "mental accounting," a term popularized by Richard Thaler. The idea is that even though money is technically interchangeable (a dollar is a dollar no matter where it came from), people tend to sort it into separate mental categories based on its source, its intended use, or the situation they're in.

You can see this everywhere. Someone might treat a tax refund or a bonus as "fun money" while being careful with their regular paycheck. People often keep a vacation fund they won't touch even while carrying credit card debt at a high interest rate. Spending $8 on coffee might feel extravagant at home but trivial at an airport. Casino winnings get called "house money" and are spent more freely than wages. A $20 bill found in an old coat feels different from $20 earned at work. Many people also think differently about cash versus cards, or about money in a checking account versus a retirement account.

This habit has real benefits. Separating money into categories makes budgeting simpler, helps people resist temptation, and supports goals. If you've labeled certain money "rent" or "emergency fund," you're less likely to spend it on impulse. Many budgeting methods, like the envelope system, deliberately use this tendency.

It can also lead to choices that don't hold up on closer inspection. Keeping savings earning 1% while paying 20% interest on a credit card costs money, even if it feels responsible. Treating windfalls as less "real" can lead to wasting them, and judging prices by context rather than value can mean overspending in some situations and being needlessly stingy in others.

So thinking about money in contexts is a normal and often useful part of human psychology. The helpful move isn't to eliminate it but to notice when you're doing it and occasionally ask whether the categories are serving your actual goals or just making a decision feel more comfortable than it should.

There are a number of Quicken alternatives worth looking into. Among them are Mint, a free web-based tool for tracking expenses, setting up budgets, and keeping an eye on investments; Personal Capital, a full-featured financial management platform that includes budgeting, investment tracking, and retirement planning features; YNAB (You Need a Budget), a budgeting program that helps you prepare for future costs by setting money aside and working toward financial goals; Pocketbook, a personal finance app that lets you monitor spending, build budgets, and follow your investments; and Moneydance, a personal finance software package offering the same core abilities of tracking spending, creating budgets, and monitoring investments. The right choice ultimately depends on your particular needs and preferences, so it may be worth testing a few of these to find the one that suits you best.

A personal computer, usually abbreviated PC, is a computer designed for use by a single person, typically at a desk or in a home or office setting. It is built to handle everyday tasks such as word processing, web browsing, email, media playback, gaming, and software development, without needing the shared resources or specialized staff that larger mainframe and minicomputer systems once required. Common examples include desktop towers paired with monitors, keyboards, and mice, as well as laptops, which package the same kinds of components into a portable form.

A personal computer is made up of several core parts working together. The central processing unit, or CPU, carries out instructions and performs calculations. Random access memory, or RAM, provides fast temporary storage for data and programs that are in active use. Long-term storage, such as a solid-state drive or hard disk, keeps the operating system, applications, and files even when the power is off. The motherboard connects these components, and a graphics processor handles images and video for the display. Input devices like keyboards and mice let the user interact with the machine, while output devices such as monitors and speakers present information back to the user.

The software side is equally important. An operating system, such as Windows, macOS, or Linux, manages the hardware and provides the interface through which the user runs applications. Because the hardware is standardized and the software is widely available, personal computers can be adapted to a huge range of purposes, from simple home use to professional design, scientific work, and entertainment.

The personal computer became widespread in the late 1970s and 1980s, with machines such as the IBM PC and the Apple II helping to popularize the concept. Today it remains one of the most familiar and versatile technologies in daily life.

There is indeed a name for the total sum of money that others owe you: it is known as "receivables," or sometimes "accounts receivable." This refers to the amounts a company is owed by its customers or clients for products or services already provided but not yet paid for. Because the business can expect to collect these funds later, they count as assets. They usually appear on the balance sheet as current assets, since collection is generally anticipated within a year or less.

If you're asking about trading stocks, forex, crypto, or similar markets, the most widely used guideline is to risk no more than 1 to 2 percent of your total trading account on any single trade. The key word is risk, not position size. If you have a $10,000 account and follow the 1 percent rule, you'd structure each trade so that if your stop-loss is hit, you lose no more than $100. The position itself might be much larger than $100, but your exit point limits the actual loss.

To turn that into a position size, divide the dollar amount you're willing to risk by the distance between your entry price and your stop-loss. For example, if you buy a stock at $50 and set a stop at $48, you're risking $2 per share, so with a $100 risk limit you'd buy 50 shares, about $2,500 worth. This keeps any single loss small enough that a losing streak, which every trader experiences, won't wipe you out. Ten consecutive losses at 1 percent leaves you down about 10 percent, which is recoverable, while ten losses at 10 percent each would cost you about 65 percent of your account.

As for how much to save before you start trading at all, the general advice is to use only money you can afford to lose entirely without affecting your rent, bills, emergency fund, or retirement savings. Many people suggest having an emergency fund of three to six months of expenses in place first. If you plan to day trade US stocks frequently in a margin account, be aware of the pattern day trader rule, which has required a $25,000 minimum balance, though a cash account or a smaller swing-trading approach avoids that requirement. Beginners are often well served by starting small, even a few hundred to a couple thousand dollars, or paper trading first, since early trades tend to be more about learning than profit.

If you meant something else, such as saving up to learn a skilled trade like plumbing or welding, or a trade in the sense of bartering or a trade-in, let me know and I can tailor the answer to that.

Sorry to hear about the kidney stone after taking OxyELITE Pro, that sounds miserable. There's no way to know for sure whether the supplement caused it, though. Kidney stones can come from all sorts of things: what you eat, how much water you drink, and some underlying health issues. Still, it's smart to be careful with any new supplement and keep an eye out for side effects. If you're thinking about trying OxyELITE Pro or something similar again, talk to a doctor or pharmacist first. They know your history and can tell you whether the risks are worth it for you. In the meantime, drinking plenty of water, eating well, and staying active go a long way toward keeping stones away.

Both Interactive Brokers (IBKR) and Questrade are popular with Canadian investors, but they suit different people. Questrade is a Canadian firm, so it's the simpler choice for most Canadians. Its account types are straightforward: RRSP, TFSA, RESP, RRIF, and non-registered accounts, all in Canadian dollars, with full support for registered plans and Canadian tax reporting. Its trade commissions are low, at around $4.95 to $9.95 per ETF trade depending on the plan, and it offers commission-free ETF purchases on a limited list of its own ETFs. Its trading platform is clean and beginner-friendly, and phone and chat support are based in Canada. The main drawbacks are a relatively limited selection of international markets and somewhat wider currency conversion spreads than the most cost-conscious options, plus a fee for some account services.

Interactive Brokers is a much larger, global firm aimed at active and sophisticated traders. Its strength is breadth: access to stock exchanges in dozens of countries, a wide range of products including options, futures, bonds, and forex, and some of the lowest commissions and currency conversion rates available, especially for high-volume traders. Its platforms, such as Trader Workstation and the web-based Client Portal, are powerful but considerably more complex, and the interface can feel overwhelming to a beginner. IBKR also offers registered accounts in Canada, including RRSP and TFSA, though the setup and service experience is generally less hand-holding than Questrade's. Its commission structure can be less intuitive, with tiered pricing and various minimums and data fees that catch new users off guard.

In short, if you're a long-term, buy-and-hold investor who wants simple registered accounts, Canadian-dollar trading, and easy support, Questrade is usually the better fit. If you trade frequently, need international markets or derivatives, or want the lowest possible costs and are comfortable with a more technical platform, Interactive Brokers is worth considering. It's also worth comparing current fee schedules directly on each firm's website, since commissions and promotions change often.

Yes, both actions can affect your credit, though usually in modest and temporary ways.

Opening a new card typically triggers a hard inquiry, which can lower your score by a few points for a few months. The new account also lowers the average age of your accounts, which matters somewhat, and it increases your total available credit. That last effect often helps, since a higher limit lowers your credit utilization ratio (the share of your limits you're using), and utilization is one of the biggest factors in your score.

Closing a card can hurt in a couple of ways. It removes that card's credit limit from your total, which can push your utilization up if you carry balances elsewhere. It can also eventually shorten your average account age and reduce the variety of credit you have, though a closed account in good standing generally stays on your report for up to about ten years and keeps helping your history for a while.

If you're considering both, the usual advice is to avoid closing an older card with no annual fee, since its age and limit are valuable. If the card you're closing has a fee you don't want to pay, closing it after opening the new one can soften the utilization hit. Keeping balances low on all your cards matters more than either move in the short run.

Okay so a balance sheet is basically a financial statement that shows a company's assets, liabilities, and equity at one specific point in time. Think of it as a snapshot of where the company stands financially. The net change is just how much those numbers moved over a stretch of time. If assets, liabilities, or equity went up overall, that's a net increase. If they went down, that's a net decrease.

Say a company has a net increase in assets. That means its assets grew more than its liabilities and equity did. Maybe it bought some new equipment or the stuff it already owns got more valuable. Flip it around and a net decrease in assets means its liabilities and equity grew faster than its assets did. That could happen if the company sold off some assets or watched what it owns lose value.

Insomnia is a sleep disorder that makes it hard for someone to either drift off or remain asleep through the night. Many things can trigger it, such as stress, anxiety, and various medical conditions. Those affected may struggle to fall asleep because their thoughts are racing or because worry and tension keep them awake. Staying asleep can be just as difficult if they experience physical discomfort or trouble breathing. Lacking adequate rest also makes it hard for people with insomnia to keep up with their schoolwork. Sleep is when the body and mind recover and restore themselves, so without enough of it, concentration, memory, and decision-making can suffer. For this reason, anyone dealing with insomnia should make an effort to get sufficient sleep and reach out for help when sleep problems persist. It is also possible that your friend turns to social media to pass the time and take their mind off not being able to sleep. Keep in mind that every person is different and there are many approaches to managing insomnia. Some people find relaxation methods like deep breathing or meditation helpful, while others may gain from speaking with a therapist or using medication to aid sleep.

Honestly, most doctors will tell pregnant women to skip medications unless they really need them, since some can affect the baby. That said, sometimes the benefit of a drug is worth the risk. Ofloxacin is an antibiotic usually seen as fairly safe in pregnancy, but the FDA hasn't approved it for pregnant women. A few studies have hinted at a higher chance of birth defects with it, though we need more research before anyone can be sure.

Isoniazid (INH) is used to treat TB and is generally considered safe during pregnancy, even though the FDA hasn't approved it for pregnant women either. There have been some reports of birth defects in babies exposed to it, but it's unclear whether the medication caused them or something else did.

Ethambutol is another TB drug, and it's usually not recommended during pregnancy because of the risk of birth defects. Reports have linked it to problems with the eyes, ears, and brain in exposed infants.

If you're pregnant and on any of these, talk to your healthcare provider before changing anything. They can weigh the risks and benefits for your specific situation and tell you whether to keep going.

Hi all, I'm hoping someone can help me make sense of my pelvic wash cytology report. I had it done before my hysterectomy and the pathology wording is confusing me. It mentions atypical cells, described as reactive mesothelial cells, with enlarged and crowded nuclei. It also says they're positive for calretinin and negative for Ber-EP4. My big worry is whether these could be metastatic breast cancer cells, since I had TNBC before.

Honestly, I don't think anyone can say for sure from just that summary. You'd need the full report and your medical records to get a real read on it. Still, here's what the terms mean. Reactive mesothelial cells line the internal organs and body cavities, including the pelvis. They can look enlarged and crowded when there's inflammation or injury, so seeing them doesn't automatically mean cancer. The calretinin and Ber-EP4 results are markers that pathologists use to tell mesothelial cells apart from carcinoma cells. Calretinin positive and Ber-EP4 negative leans toward mesothelial cells, but that's the pathologist's call to make.

Breast cancer can spread to the pelvis, so your worry is reasonable. Still, the report alone doesn't tell you whether those atypical cells are breast cancer. Take it to your gynecologist or oncologist and ask them to walk you through the markers and what they mean for you specifically. Ask whether you need further testing too. Your hysterectomy pathology should help answer this as well, so ask them to compare the two.

When you don't get a paycheck you were counting on, you might be able to deduct the unpaid wages on your tax return, though the exact rules depend on your particular circumstances. If you're an employee who wasn't paid for work you completed, the unpaid wages may qualify as a miscellaneous itemized deduction. To claim it, you need to satisfy several conditions. The wages must be for work you actually did. You must have reported them properly to your employer. They cannot be for work performed in an earlier year. And you must have received a Form W-2 from your employer for the year the work took place, even though the paycheck never arrived.

If all of these conditions apply, you can take the deduction as an itemized deduction on Schedule A of Form 1040. Keep in mind that it is limited by a threshold of 2% of your adjusted gross income (AGI), so you can deduct only the portion that goes beyond 2% of your AGI.

Self-employed people who weren't paid for work they did may be able to deduct the unpaid amount as a business expense instead. In that case, it is reported on Schedule C of Form 1040.

Whenever you claim deductions, it's wise to talk with a tax professional or check IRS guidance. They can tell you whether you qualify for a deduction for unpaid wages and show you how to claim it correctly.

DHA (Defence Housing Australia) investment properties are homes leased to the Australian Department of Defence for military personnel and their families. They can work well for some people, but there are a few downsides worth thinking about.

First, they usually cost more upfront than similar places nearby. They tend to be newer and better finished, so you'll likely pay a premium to get in.

Second, you don't really get to pick your tenants. Since Defence is the one leasing the place, you can't screen occupants the way you would with a regular rental.

Third, demand depends on the military being in the area. If troops get moved out or a base shrinks, demand can drop and your rental returns might take a hit.

Last, the leases run for a minimum of 10 years. That's a long commitment, so selling early or moving your money into something else can be harder than with a standard rental.

Weigh these carefully before you buy one.

A straddle, for federal tax purposes, is a set of offsetting positions in personal property, such as options, futures, or forward contracts, where holding one position reduces the risk of loss on another. When an S corporation holds straddle positions, the tax treatment has two layers: the rules that apply at the corporate level, and the pass-through rules that determine how the results reach the shareholders.

At the corporate level, Internal Revenue Code Section 1092 governs straddles. Its main rule defers losses on one leg of a straddle to the extent of unrecognized gain in the offsetting leg, so the corporation cannot recognize a loss in the current year if it still holds an offsetting position with a built-in gain. Deferred losses carry forward until the offsetting position is closed. The rules also require capitalization of interest and carrying charges allocable to positions in a straddle under Section 263(g), which means those costs are added to the basis of the property rather than deducted currently. Holding period rules can also reset in ways that convert short-term gain into short-term loss treatment, so the corporation needs to track the holding periods of each leg carefully.

Some positions are exempt from the straddle rules. Section 1256 contracts, such as regulated futures contracts and certain nonequity options, are marked to market at year end, with 60 percent of the gain or loss treated as long-term and 40 percent as short-term. If a straddle includes both Section 1256 contracts and non-1256 positions, the corporation may make a mixed straddle election under Treasury Regulation 1.1092(b)-6 to identify and govern how those positions are treated. Making or failing to make this election can significantly change the result, so it should be considered before the positions are entered into, where the rules allow.

At the pass-through level, the corporation's gains and losses retain their character under Section 1366(b). Capital gains and losses, Section 1256 amounts, and other separately stated items are reported on each shareholder's Schedule K-1 and netted on the shareholder's own return. Form 6781 is used for Section 1256 contracts and straddles, and Form 8949 and Schedule D report the capital transactions. Shareholders can deduct losses only to the extent of their stock and debt basis under Section 1366(d), and those losses are then subject to the at-risk rules of Section 465 and the passive activity rules of Section 469 at the shareholder level. Interest expense that is not capitalized may be subject to the investment interest limitation of Section 163(d).

If the S corporation also holds accumulated earnings and profits from a prior C corporation period, or if it has significant passive investment income, it should also check the rules under Sections 1362(d)(3) and 1375, since excessive passive income can jeopardize S status and trigger corporate-level tax.

Because straddle rules interact with the pass-through rules, holding period, basis, and elections, the specific facts of the positions matter a great deal. It would be worth reviewing the actual contracts, the corporation's trading records, and any elections already made with a tax professional who works with partnerships and S corporations.

Slugging percentage measures how much total bases a hitter produces per at-bat. You calculate it by adding up the total bases from all hits, where a single counts as one base, a double as two, a triple as three, and a home run as four, and then dividing that total by the number of at-bats. The formula is (singles + 2 × doubles + 3 × triples + 4 × home runs) divided by at-bats.

For example, if a player has 100 hits in 400 at-bats consisting of 60 singles, 20 doubles, 2 triples, and 18 home runs, his total bases would be 60 + 40 + 6 + 72, which equals 178. Dividing 178 by 400 gives a slugging percentage of .445.

Unlike batting average, slugging percentage gives extra credit for power hitting, since extra-base hits are weighted more heavily. Walks and hit-by-pitch plays are not counted as at-bats or bases in this calculation, and sacrifices are excluded from the at-bat total as well.

Imagine the world used to be one big, wiggly set of connected puddles, and then it changed shape over time. That's really the heart of the answer: lakes that look separate today often weren't separate in the past, and fish have had a very long time to spread out.

The biggest helper was ice. During the last ice age, which ended roughly ten to twelve thousand years ago, huge sheets of ice covered much of northern North America and Eurasia. When the ice melted, enormous amounts of meltwater formed giant temporary lakes and rivers that flowed across the land and linked up places that aren't connected now. Fish simply swam along these new waterways into fresh territory. As the ice shrank further, the water drained away and left behind thousands of separate lakes, with the fish already inside them. So the lakes got their fish the way a bathtub gets its toys: the fish were there when the water arrived or while it was still connected.

Northern pike also got help from geography. Long ago, North America and Eurasia were joined by a land area around the Bering Strait, called Beringia, which had rivers and wetlands. Pike living in rivers that drained toward the Arctic could move between the two continents along those freshwater routes, and they can tolerate slightly salty water in places like the Baltic Sea and Arctic river mouths, which makes traveling along coasts easier.

Rivers themselves also move around. Over thousands of years, streams change course, and a flood can link one river system to another. Sometimes one river captures the headwaters of its neighbor, and fish in one get a free ride into the other.

Animals can sometimes help too, though this is a smaller effect. Fish eggs can be sticky, and it's possible some travel on the feet or feathers of water birds. People have helped a great deal in recent times as well, moving pike and many other fish to new lakes for fishing.

So the simple version is this: the world's water used to be connected in ways it isn't now, fish swam wherever the water let them, and when the ice melted and the land changed, the fish were left behind in lakes that look separate today.

So say you own a stock and you sell a call option on it. You're basically handing the buyer the right to buy that stock from you at a set price (the strike price) any time up until a certain date (the expiration date). That's what writing a call means. If people think the stock is headed up, your call gets more valuable, since the buyer is more likely to want to lock in that strike price if they figure the stock will be worth more later. If the price does climb and they decide to use that right, you've got to sell them your shares at the strike, no matter what the market price is at that point. If the stock stays flat or drops, the option just expires worthless and you keep your shares. Writing calls can be a decent way to pull in some income from a stock that's been dragging, since you get the premium up front. The catch is you could end up selling for less than the stock is actually worth if it takes off. So think it through before you start writing calls on something you own.

There's no magic number, but the right amount for a college student usually depends more on your cash flow and safety net than on any fixed dollar figure. Before investing, it helps to have an emergency fund covering a few months of expenses in a savings account, and to have paid off any high-interest debt like credit cards, since those charge rates that far exceed what the stock market typically returns. Once those are in place, the question becomes how much you can set aside each month without straining your budget. Many students start with as little as 25 to 100 dollars a month, and that's a meaningful start because the habit and time in the market matter more early on than the initial sum.

It's also worth knowing that most brokerages today have no account minimums and let you buy fractional shares, so you don't need hundreds of dollars to buy into a company. Index funds or broad exchange-traded funds are a common starting point for beginners because they spread your money across many companies, which reduces the risk of any single stock hurting your returns. Money you'll need within the next few years, such as funds for tuition or a move, generally shouldn't be in stocks at all, since the market can drop sharply in the short term.

The core problem is that the same dollars can reach the IRS through two different forms. A payer sends you a 1099-MISC (or 1099-NEC) for work you did, and if that payer used a credit card or a platform like PayPal, Stripe, or Square, the processor may also send you a 1099-K covering the same payment. The IRS matches both forms to your Social Security number, so if you only report one, or if you report both in full, you can get a mismatch notice or pay tax twice on the same money.

The rule of thumb is that you report each dollar of income once, but you must be able to show how the forms reconcile. Start by gathering every 1099 you received, plus your own records such as invoices, bank deposits, and platform statements. Add up the gross amounts on the 1099-MISC or 1099-NEC forms, then look at the 1099-K gross total. Determine how much of the 1099-K amount is the same payments already included on the 1099-MISC. Many 1099-K totals also include refunds, fees, sales tax, tips, and personal transfers that are not income, so the 1099-K number is often not simply your earnings.

Next, report your true total business income on Schedule C (or the appropriate schedule). Your gross receipts should equal actual income from all sources, counting overlapping payments only once. For example, if a client paid you 10,000 dollars by card through a processor, the client may issue a 1099-NEC for 10,000 and the processor a 1099-K that includes that 10,000. Your gross receipts are 10,000, not 20,000. If you also had 3,000 of other card sales that appear only on the 1099-K, your total is 13,000.

Keep a simple reconciliation worksheet showing each form, its amount, the overlap, and any non-income items you subtract. You do not usually need to file it, but it protects you if the IRS sends a CP2000 notice. If you want the return itself to reflect the adjustment, you can include the full 1099 amounts in gross receipts and then back out the duplicated or non-taxable portion as a negative adjustment, with a clear label, though how this is done depends on the software and form you use. Personal items, such as splitting a dinner bill or selling a used couch at a loss, can be handled by explaining them as nonbusiness or nontaxable. Note that for Schedule 1, the usual place for such an offset is the "other income" adjustments line, with a description.

Finally, ask payers or the processor for corrected forms if they are clearly wrong. A corrected 1099-K is the cleanest fix. Payers are supposed to exclude card payments from the 1099-NEC or 1099-MISC because those are reported on the 1099-K, so a client who sends both has probably made an error. If you are unsure about a specific case, a tax professional can help you document it properly.

Imagine you want to float a toy car in the air using magnets. The trouble is that the Earth's magnetic field is incredibly weak. It's about the strength of a tiny fridge magnet's push, spread out over the whole planet. If you hold two fridge magnets near each other, they push or pull hard because they are close together and strong. But the Earth is a giant, far-away magnet whose push on anything near the ground is very, very small. To lift even a small car using it, you would need a magnet so enormous and powerful that it would be impossible to build and carry around.

There is another problem. Magnets that push against each other are unstable. If you try to balance one magnet floating over another, it always wants to flip over or slide off to the side, kind of like trying to balance a ball on top of another ball. Scientists even have a rule about this, called Earnshaw's theorem, which says you can't hold something steady in the air using only ordinary magnets. You need special tricks, like super cold materials called superconductors or computers that constantly adjust the magnets many times a second.

Those tricks do exist. Some trains in Japan and China, called maglev trains, really do float above their tracks using magnets. But they need special tracks built under them, because the magnets push against the track, not against the Earth. Also, the Earth's magnetic field points sideways near the equator and goes up and down near the poles, so it would not work the same everywhere anyway.

As for real antigravity like in Halo, nobody has found a way to do it. Gravity is a very different thing from magnetism. You can block or switch off magnetism, but we have never found any material or machine that can shield or cancel gravity. It's like wishing for a button that turns off the ground pulling you down. Scientists don't know of any way to make one, and our best theories say it may not be possible at all.

We do have hovercraft, though. They just cheat by using fans to blow a cushion of air underneath them. Helicopters and drones also cheat by pushing air downward. It's loud and uses lots of energy, but it works. So the answer is that magnets are too weak, too wobbly, and gravity is too stubborn, so for now we hover by blowing air instead.

Dimples are tiny dips in the skin that certain people have on their cheeks, chin, or lower lip. They form because of a small built-in fold, or "double," of skin that a person is born with. This fold is connected to the muscles and tissue underneath, so when those muscles contract, the skin pulls inward and forms the dimple. Not everyone shows dimples, since not everyone has this extra fold. The trait is genetic and runs in families, passed along from parents to children. A person may receive it from just one parent, or from both. Because dimples come from each individual's genes, they can show up in different spots from one person to the next: some people have them in their cheeks, while others have them in the chin or lower lip. Where a dimple appears depends on where that extra fold of skin sits, so, much like fingerprints, every person's dimples are one of a kind.

Dr. Carter G. Woodson, an African American historian, author, and journalist often called the "Father of Black History," passed away on April 3, 1950. Born in 1875, he devoted his career to studying, writing about, and encouraging the study of African American history and culture. He established the Association for the Study of Negro Life and History, today called the Association for the Study of African American Life and History (ASALH), and he started Negro History Week, the observance that eventually grew into Black History Month.

Here's a surprise: solar actually has gotten much, much better. It just happened quietly, so it's easy to miss.

Imagine solar panels are like a toy that used to cost a whole lot of money. Back when you were little, one panel was so expensive that only rich people, space satellites, or calculators used them. Since then the price has dropped enormously. Solar electricity now costs roughly a tenth of what it did around 2010, and in many places it's the cheapest way ever invented to make electricity. That's like a toy that once cost a hundred dollars now costing about ten.

So why doesn't it feel like it's everywhere? Think about your house. Even if someone invents a much better kind of light bulb, you don't throw away your lamps, wires, and walls the next day. Power plants, wires, and electricity systems are huge and expensive, and they were built to last forty or fifty years. Swapping them out takes a long time, even when the new thing is better.

There's also the nighttime problem. The sun goes to sleep every night and hides behind clouds, but people still want their lights and fridges on. So we need giant batteries to save sunshine for later, and those batteries only recently became cheap enough. They're getting better fast, just like the panels did.

Another reason is that grown-ups argue about it. Companies that sell coal, oil, and gas make lots of money and don't always want things to change quickly. Rules, permits, and connecting new solar farms to the power lines can also take years of paperwork.

But here's the good news: solar is now growing faster than any other kind of electricity in the world. Lots of new power built every year is solar. In some places, like parts of China, Australia, California, and Europe, you can see panels on roofs and fields everywhere. So the story isn't that solar failed. It's that it started very expensive, got cheap slowly and then suddenly, and the world is in the middle of catching up right now.

No, not directly. When a stock price rises, the company itself usually receives no new cash. The stock price is set by trades between investors on the stock exchange, so when you buy shares from another investor, your money goes to that investor, not to the company. The company's only direct cash from its stock comes from the initial public offering or from later share sales it makes itself, such as secondary offerings or employee stock option exercises, and those transactions happen at a price the company chooses or negotiates, not from the day-to-day market movement.

A higher share price can still benefit the company indirectly. It makes it easier and cheaper to raise money by issuing new shares later, since each new share can be sold for more. It also raises the value of stock-based pay for employees, which can help with recruiting and retention, and it can make acquisitions cheaper, because the company can offer its own inflated shares as payment. Shareholders benefit directly, since the value of their holdings rises, but the company's bank account does not change just because its shares trade higher.

A test is basically a way to check what someone knows, what they can do, how fit they are, or where they fit into some category. You'll see them all over the place: schools, job certifications, psychology, the military. Usually the point is to figure out how good someone is at something or to spot the stuff they still need to work on. Tests come in all kinds of shapes. Some are written, some are spoken, and some just have you actually perform a task. They can cover pretty much anything, like how much you remember about a subject, how well you solve problems, or how physically capable you are. And the results often end up deciding things, like whether you get the job, get into the program, or qualify for the course you wanted.

Think of dimensions as directions you can move. A line has one dimension: you can only go forward or backward, like walking along a string or a number line. That's the first dimension.

A flat piece of paper has two: you can go left-right and up-down, like a checkerboard or a map. When you draw a 3-D box on paper, the paper is still flat. You're just using tricks, like slanted lines and shading, to make your eyes think there's depth. The drawing is only 2-D, but it's a picture of something 3-D.

The real world, the one you live in, has three dimensions: left-right, up-down, and front-back. You can hold a ball because it has all three. Some grown-up scientists also count time as a fourth dimension, because you can't go back to yesterday, but that's a special kind of direction.

Black holes are very strange. A black hole is a place where gravity is so strong that nothing, not even light, can escape once it gets close enough. The edge of that zone is called the event horizon. Once something crosses it, it must keep falling inward, a bit like how you can't avoid getting to tomorrow. At the very center is something called a singularity, where the squeezing is so extreme that scientists' math stops working. Nobody knows for sure what's really happening there, and that's one of the biggest mysteries in science.

Assuming you mean the American Civil War (1861–1865), the immediate trigger was the Confederate attack on Fort Sumter in Charleston Harbor, South Carolina, on April 12, 1861. Confederate forces bombarded the federal fort after President Abraham Lincoln moved to resupply its Union garrison, and the fort surrendered the next day. Lincoln then called for 75,000 volunteers to put down the rebellion, which prompted four more Southern states (Virginia, Arkansas, North Carolina, and Tennessee) to join the Confederacy.

The deeper cause was slavery. For decades the North and South had clashed over whether slavery would expand into new western territories, through the Missouri Compromise of 1820, the Compromise of 1850, the Kansas-Nebraska Act of 1854 and the violence of "Bleeding Kansas" that followed, and the Dred Scott decision of 1857, which held that Congress could not ban slavery in the territories. Tensions sharpened further with John Brown's raid on Harpers Ferry in 1859.

The breaking point came with Lincoln's election in November 1860. He ran on a platform opposing the spread of slavery into the territories, and Southern leaders saw his victory as a threat to the institution's future. South Carolina seceded in December 1860, and six more Deep South states followed by early 1861, forming the Confederate States of America. Their own secession declarations cited the protection of slavery as their central motive. Arguments about states' rights and economic differences were also part of the debate, but they were largely bound up with the slavery question.

Derivatives and integrals are operations that measure, respectively, how quickly a function is changing and the area beneath its graph. A derivative tells us the function's rate of change at any particular point, while an integral gives the total change accumulated over a given interval. The derivative of x^2 is 2x, since x^2 grows at a rate of 2x at every point. Put another way, a small increase in x produces an increase in x^2 that is twice as large. The derivative of x^2 expresses this relationship as 2x. By contrast, the derivative of sin^2 x is not 2 sin x. It is 2 sin x cos x. Unlike x^2, sin^2 x does not grow at a steady rate, so its rate of change depends on the values of sin x and cos x at each point. When sin x is large and cos x is small, sin^2 x rises rapidly, and when sin x is small and cos x is large, it rises more gradually. The derivative of sin^2 x accounts for this shifting rate. Similarly, the integral of x is x^2/2, since the total change in x over an interval can be pictured as the area of a rectangle with base x and height x/2. The integrals of sin x and cos x, however, cannot be written as simple polynomials such as x^2/2. These functions instead call for more complicated mathematical expressions to capture their total change over an interval.

The method depends on where you're tracking your money. If you use a bank account, most income such as a paycheck arrives automatically through direct deposit, and your balance updates on its own once it clears. If you need to record income by hand, you can enter it as an income transaction in your budgeting app, usually by choosing "add transaction" or "add income," entering the amount and date, and assigning it to an income category or account. In a spreadsheet, add a row with the date, a description, and the amount as a positive number, then either keep a running total with a formula that adds each new income row to the previous balance, or sum the income column to get your total. If you simply keep a running balance on paper or in a note, add the amount to your current balance and write down the new total. Whichever method you use, record income when it actually lands in your account, not when you expect it, so your balance stays accurate.
