A steam engine turns the energy stored in heated water into mechanical motion. The basic idea is that water boiled into steam takes up far more space than the liquid it came from, and if that expansion is confined, it pushes hard against whatever surrounds it.

The process begins in a boiler, a sealed vessel where a fire heats water until it becomes steam. The steam collects under pressure in the boiler and is then released through a valve into a cylinder. Inside the cylinder sits a piston, a disk that slides back and forth. The high-pressure steam pushes the piston to one end of the cylinder. Then a valve, often controlled by a mechanism called valve gear, redirects the steam to the opposite side of the piston, pushing it back the other way. This back-and-forth motion is the engine's power stroke.

The piston is connected to a crankshaft by a connecting rod, which converts the straight-line push and pull into rotation, much like the pedals and crank of a bicycle. That rotation can drive wheels, a propeller, or a generator. In many designs, a flywheel attached to the shaft smooths out the uneven pulses of force so the motion stays steady.

After the steam has done its work, it is exhausted from the cylinder. In early engines it was simply vented to the air, while later designs often condensed it back into water in a separate chamber, which lowered the pressure on the far side of the piston and made the engine more efficient. The water could then be pumped back to the boiler to be reheated, completing the cycle.

Steam engines powered the Industrial Revolution, running factories, pumping water out of mines, and driving locomotives and steamships. Their main drawback is that much of the fuel's energy is lost as heat, which is why they were gradually replaced by internal combustion engines and electric motors, though steam turbines still generate most of the world's electricity today.

Traditionally, new TV seasons kick off in the fall because that's when the big networks (ABC, CBS, NBC, Fox, and so on) hold their upfronts. Those are presentations to advertisers about the shows they'll be running in the coming season. Upfronts usually happen in May, and the new seasons start in September, which gives networks all summer to hype their shows so people are primed to tune in when things kick off. Still, there are good reasons a show might land in spring or summer instead. For one, there's usually less competition for eyeballs at those times, since fewer new shows are premiering. That can really help a show trying to build a following, especially one that might get buried in the crowded fall lineup. Nicer weather plays a part too. People are often outside more in spring and summer, but when they do sit down to watch, it's a different mood. Honestly, it comes down to the show itself and what the creators and networks think is the best window. Some shows do better in the fall, and others find their audience in the warmer months.

Colleges evaluating applicants want students who will suit their institution and add something to campus life. Reading an applicant's admission essay, sometimes called a personal statement, is one way they learn more about who that person is. In this essay, you should aim to show the admissions committee what kind of person you are and why their school would suit you. Here are several things colleges may look for. Your personality: Committees want to know you as an individual, so let your personality come through in your writing. Your goals and interests: What are you passionate about? What do you hope to study in college, and what draws you to it? Your experiences: Have any meaningful events shaped you into who you are today? These might be a personal experience, a community service project, or a job. Your writing skills: The essay also gives you a chance to demonstrate how well you write. Use correct grammar and punctuation, and aim for a style that is clear and engaging. Your fit with the school: Why do you want to attend this specific college? Which of its programs, its campus, or its community appeals to you? In short, the admission essay lets you show the committee who you are and why you belong at their school. Be honest and sincere, and keep your focus on your strengths and experiences.

A formal language is basically a set of strings that get made by following a specific set of rules. You'll see them in theoretical computer science, linguistics, and math, where they're used to pin down the syntax of a programming language, the grammar of a natural language, or the rules of a logical system. In computer science, it's a set of strings a formal grammar can generate. That grammar is just a list of rules for building strings, and it's what defines a programming language's syntax or the structure of a document. Linguists use the same idea for human language. The grammar spells out how to build sentences in English or French, covering word categories, word order, and how words and phrases hang together. Mathematicians look at it a bit differently: the strings come out of a formal system, which is a set of rules for shuffling symbols around using axioms and inference rules. That's how logic gets represented and theorems get proven. So, put simply, a formal language is a well-defined collection of strings produced by a fixed set of rules, and it's a precise way to describe programming languages, natural languages, and logic.

Here's the thing: they mostly have figured it out, and the problem was never really that your phone might make the plane fall out of the sky.

Think about how your phone normally works. It's always quietly shouting "Hello, I'm here!" to the nearest cell tower, like a kid calling out to a nearby grown-up. On the ground, there are only a few towers close enough to hear you, so one of them answers and everything is calm. But when you're 35,000 feet up in the sky, your phone can suddenly "see" dozens or even hundreds of towers at once, and it's flying past them really fast. So it shouts louder and louder, and lots of towers all try to answer at the same time. That's like a kid yelling in a huge room full of grown-ups who all turn around at once. It confuses the phone network on the ground. That's actually a big reason the rule exists, and in the United States it's partly a rule from the agency that manages radio signals, not just the aviation folks.

There's also a smaller worry about the airplane itself. Planes have lots of radios and instruments, and pilots wear headsets. Sometimes a phone searching hard for a signal makes a little buzzing noise in those headsets, the same "dit-dit-dit" sound you might have heard near a speaker when a phone rings. It's not dangerous by itself, but during takeoff and landing, when pilots need to hear everything clearly, nobody wants extra noise. Testing every possible phone on every kind of airplane to prove it's totally safe is expensive and slow, so the easy, careful answer was "just turn the phone part off."

That's why "airplane mode" exists. It doesn't turn your phone off; it just stops the shouting. You can still play games, watch movies, listen to music, and on many airlines you can turn Wi-Fi and Bluetooth back on and use the plane's internet and your wireless headphones. Some airlines, especially in Europe, now even put a tiny cell tower inside the plane so phones can talk to it calmly instead of yelling at the ground, and regulators there have started allowing regular phone service in the air.

One last reason the rules change slowly is people. Lots of passengers don't love the idea of sitting next to someone talking loudly on the phone for five hours, so some airlines and lawmakers aren't in a hurry to allow calls even where the technology works. So your phone can mostly stay on; it just has to stop shouting.

Artificial selection is basically when humans breed plants and animals for particular traits. People pick which individuals get to reproduce based on what they want, and that's the big difference from natural selection, where traits that help an organism survive and reproduce just tend to stick around over generations. We've been doing this for thousands of years. Farmers and breeders have pushed animals and crops toward bigger size, better flavor, or nicer looks. Cattle got bred for meat, milk, and leather. Dogs got bred for hunting, herding, and guarding. Crops got bred for yield, taste, and disease resistance. It's also used in labs now to make genetically modified organisms. Scientists can use gene editing to add a specific trait to an organism's genome, or move genes from one species to another with genetic engineering. Honestly, it's a pretty powerful tool, and it's shaped a lot of the plants and animals we see around us today. It's still a big area of research in biology.

Market capitalization, usually shortened to market cap, is the total market value of a publicly traded company's outstanding shares. You calculate it by multiplying the current share price by the total number of shares that investors hold. For example, if a company has 100 million shares outstanding and each share trades at $50, its market cap is $5 billion.

The figure gives a quick sense of a company's size as the market sees it. Analysts and investors commonly group companies by market cap: large-cap companies are generally valued at $10 billion or more, mid-cap companies fall roughly between $2 billion and $10 billion, and small-cap companies are below that range. These cutoffs are conventions rather than strict rules, and they vary somewhat among data providers.

Market cap is not the same as the amount of money a company holds or the price it would cost to buy the whole business. Acquiring a company typically requires paying a premium above its market cap, and the company's debt and cash also affect what a buyer would actually pay, a figure known as enterprise value. Market cap also changes constantly as share prices move throughout the trading day.

Nobody can say for certain whether now is a good or bad moment to put money into stocks. Share prices can swing sharply over short periods, and how an investment has done in the past does not guarantee how it will do going forward. Even so, investing with a long-term outlook is usually wiser than trying to time the market, since staying invested can keep you from missing out on potential growth.

Diversification matters as well, because it helps manage risk. Rather than placing all your money in one kind of investment, you can spread it across several types of assets, including stocks, bonds, and cash. Doing so distributes the risk and may soften the effect of market swings on your portfolio as a whole.

In the end, whether to invest in equities, or in any other asset, should depend on your own goals, your tolerance for risk, and your financial circumstances. Speaking with a financial advisor or other professional can help you work out which investments suit you.

Thunderstorms need a lot of energy, and that energy comes from warm, wet air rising very fast. Think of it like a bubble of warm air shooting up into the sky. As it rises, the water vapor in it cools and turns into droplets, and when those droplets get pushed higher into the freezing cold, they become ice. The bumping, tumbling, and rubbing of all these ice bits and water drops inside the cloud is what builds up static electricity, like rubbing a balloon on your hair. When the charge gets big enough, it jumps across the cloud or to the ground as lightning, and the sudden heat from that jump makes the air expand fast and boom, that's thunder.

Rain and snow are not exactly the same thing, even though they both fall from clouds. Rain forms when water droplets get big and heavy enough to fall. Snow forms when water vapor freezes directly into ice crystals high up, and those crystals stick together into flakes. Snowstorms are usually made of gentler, steadier clouds that don't have the strong rising warm air needed to build up that electric charge. So it's not just that snow is colder. It's that snowstorms usually don't have the big, bouncy, fast-moving air that makes thunder happen.

Sometimes it does happen, though. Thundersnow is a real thing, and it shows up when a powerful storm has strong updrafts and enough of that rising air to make the sparks fly.

Technical analysts generally distinguish leading indicators, which try to anticipate price moves, from lagging indicators, which confirm trends after they have begun. Among the indicators most often described as leading are the Relative Strength Index (RSI) and the Stochastic Oscillator, both of which measure momentum and can flag overbought or oversold conditions before a price reversal occurs. Traders also watch divergences, where price makes a new high or low that is not matched by the indicator, since this can signal weakening momentum ahead of a turn. The Williams %R and the Commodity Channel Index (CCI) work on similar principles and are used for the same purpose.

Volume-based measures are another group often considered leading. On-Balance Volume (OBV) and the Accumulation/Distribution line try to show whether buying or selling pressure is building beneath the surface of price, which can hint at a coming move. Rising volume during a price rise, or accumulation while prices are flat, is read as a sign that a breakout may follow.

It is worth noting that the line between leading and lagging is not absolute. Moving averages, MACD, and trendlines are generally classed as lagging because they are derived from past prices, yet traders often use short-term crossovers from them as early signals. Also, no technical indicator reliably predicts the market, and leading indicators in particular tend to produce false signals, so most practitioners combine several of them with other analysis and risk controls.

There are numerous approaches to deepening your understanding of finance. A few recommendations follow. First, keep abreast of financial news and commentary, since this will show you the newest trends and shifts in the industry. You might read pieces in publications like The Wall Street Journal or Bloomberg, or follow financial analysts and experts on social media. Second, consider online courses or a professional credential. These offer an organized path into the subject and are particularly useful for newcomers. Possibilities include pursuing a financial planning designation such as the Certified Financial Planner (CFP) or Chartered Financial Analyst (CFA), or enrolling in individual classes on subjects like corporate finance, investment management, and financial modeling. Third, join a professional organization such as the Financial Planning Association or the Association for Financial Professionals. These groups offer resources, networking chances, and continuing education to help you keep your skills current. Fourth, seek out internships or job shadowing. Practical experience is a strong way to learn the field and sharpen your abilities. Look for opportunities at financial firms or companies where you can get hands-on exposure and see how financial professionals spend their working days. Finally, build your professional network. Connecting with others in finance lets you learn from their experience, receive advice and guidance, and stay informed about new developments. Attending industry events or joining professional groups and forums are good ways to make these connections.

It's not unusual for a bruise to fade while the area stays tender and firm for weeks or even months. After a significant impact, blood can pool under the skin or in the muscle and form a clot that the body slowly reabsorbs, and the surrounding tissue can remain swollen, thickened, or scarred during that process. Mild tenderness and a firm feeling often improve gradually over several months.

However, two months is a long time for a forearm injury this painful to still be hard and sore to press, and because a bad fall on the forearm can involve bone, I'd recommend seeing a doctor rather than waiting. They can examine the area and, if needed, order an X-ray. Forearm fractures, including small cracks or ones that healed slightly out of position, can leave a firm lump and ongoing tenderness that might not be obvious from the bruise alone. Other possibilities include a hematoma that organized into a firm mass, a small muscle injury that calcified (myositis ossificans), or a fatty tissue injury that formed a hard nodule. Most of these are manageable, but they're easier to sort out with an exam and imaging.

Seek care sooner if you notice increasing swelling or pain, numbness or tingling in your hand, weakness or trouble gripping or turning your wrist, a change in the shape of your arm, fever, or redness and warmth over the area.

It seems like you may be dealing with anxiety. Feeling anxious is a natural reaction to stress, and in certain situations it can even be useful, but when it persists over time it can get in the way of everyday life. Several treatments are available, such as therapy, medication, and self-care practices. If your symptoms are intense or make it hard to get through your day, reaching out to a mental health professional is important. A therapist or counselor can help you pinpoint what is driving your anxiety and build strategies for handling it. They can also teach you relaxation methods like deep breathing, progressive muscle relaxation, or mindfulness, all of which can help ease anxiety. Medication is another effective option. Your doctor or a mental health provider can assess whether it suits your situation and, if so, recommend a suitable prescription. Alongside professional care, a number of self-care habits can make a real difference: getting regular exercise, which lowers stress and lifts mood; eating well and sleeping enough; practicing relaxation techniques such as deep breathing, meditation, or yoga; cutting back on caffeine and alcohol, which can heighten anxiety; staying connected with others and making time for enjoyable activities; and reducing exposure to things that trigger your anxiety, such as certain news coverage or social media. Patience and consistency matter in treatment, since improvement can take time. If you are not seeing progress, be sure to tell your therapist or doctor, because your treatment plan may need adjusting.

Pearl Harbor is a natural harbor on Oahu, in Hawaii, and it's best known for the surprise attack the Imperial Japanese Navy launched there on December 7, 1941. A CFD, short for "contract for difference," is a financial product that lets traders bet on whether the price of an asset will rise or fall without ever holding that asset. These contracts are bought on margin, so a trader can control a larger position using only a fraction of the full amount as capital. Leverage like this can magnify gains, yet it also magnifies danger, since a sharp move against the trader can cause losses greater than the funds they initially put down. Profiting from CFDs depends on accurately forecasting which way the underlying asset's price will go. When the market moves as predicted, the trader earns a gain; when it moves the other way, the trader takes a loss. Because CFD trading carries substantial risk, it does not suit every investor. Anyone considering it should thoroughly grasp those risks and develop a well-founded strategy before placing any trades.

For a 24-year-old, a resting heart rate between 60 and 100 beats per minute is generally considered normal. Okay, so the ex-dividend date is the day a stock starts trading without the upcoming dividend attached to it. If you buy on or after that day, you won't get the dividend, even though it's been declared. The payable date is when the money actually gets paid out to shareholders.

People often wonder how the payable date can come before the ex-dividend date, but it can happen. The ex-dividend date is tied to the record date, which is when the company checks its books to see who qualifies for the dividend. That record date is usually set a few days before the ex-dividend date so the company has time to put together the list of eligible shareholders. Since the payment can go out on its own schedule, it's possible for it to land before the ex-dividend date too. Hope that clears it up! Let me know if anything else is confusing.

Green stool in infants can stem from several sources. One is diet: if a baby eats a lot of green vegetables or formula with a green tint, the stool may take on that color. Another is infection, since bacterial or viral infections of the digestive tract can produce green stool along with vomiting. A third is food intolerance or allergy, where a reaction to a particular food can bring on digestive symptoms such as green stool and vomiting. Vomiting and diarrhea can also point to something more serious, such as an intestinal blockage or a metabolic disorder. If the symptoms continue, or if the baby becomes unusually sleepy or shows signs of dehydration, a pediatrician should evaluate and treat the child.

Description logic (DL) is a family of formal languages for representing knowledge, basically the concepts and relationships in some domain you care about. You use it to describe concepts, individuals, and how they connect, then reason about what follows from those descriptions. A concept is really just a set of individuals (often called instances) that share some properties. So "dog" might pick out every individual that's a dog and has things like "has four legs" and "barks."

You can also build more complicated concepts with logical operators like "and," "or," and "not." Take "small dog": you could define it as a dog that's small and weighs under 20 pounds. Relationships work the same way. "Is a parent of" could link "person" and "child," for instance. That lets you capture hierarchies, like how a poodle is a kind of dog, and a dog is a kind of mammal.

DLs show up in AI, natural language processing, and information retrieval. They're especially handy for messy domains full of tangled-together concepts, like biology or the legal system.

Ever wonder why a bank transfer can take a few days to show up? It's mostly down to a few things. First, banks don't all handle incoming and outgoing transactions at the same speed, so one side can lag behind the other. Second, bank systems aren't really connected in real time. Most of them process transfers in batches at set times during the day, so if your transfer misses the cutoff, it just waits for the next run. Third, there are often extra security checks, especially for big amounts or transfers going overseas, and those take time too. Usually it wraps up in a few business days, but it can drag on longer depending on the details of your transfer.

Preferences in music, movies, and other artistic works are personal, so one individual's favorites may differ from another's. A variety of influences shape what people enjoy, such as their own life experiences, the culture they grew up in, and the era and location they inhabit. Although taste is a matter of individual perception, people frequently speak of "good" and "bad" taste as though it were a fact, largely because their feelings about what they enjoy or reject run deep. It is perfectly natural to want to share one's views and talk about beloved musicians, films, or artworks. At times, people may describe their likes and dislikes using labels such as "good" or "bad" taste, though these labels may not be entirely fair since they rest on personal judgment. Keep in mind that everyone's tastes vary, and it is fine to enjoy or dislike something others may not. It is also acceptable to hold firm opinions about what you love or reject, provided you show respect for the views and preferences of others.

Most cars have their engines in the front because of a mix of practical reasons that built up over time, rather than one big decision. Early cars were basically horse carriages with motors added, and engineers put the engine up front because that's where the horse used to be and where the steering and driver could easily reach the controls. As cars got more popular, front engines made them simpler to build and service, and they left room in the back for passengers and luggage. Over the decades, nearly everyone copied this layout because it worked well and factories were already set up to build it that way.

Some luxury and sports cars put the engine in the back, which is called rear-engine or mid-engine placement, because it can make the car handle and feel different. When the heavy engine sits near the back wheels, those wheels get more grip for pushing the car forward, which helps with acceleration. Putting the weight in the middle of the car, as with many supercars, helps it turn quickly and stay balanced in corners, a bit like how it's easier to spin a baseball bat by holding it near the middle.

Each placement has tradeoffs. Front engines are cheaper to build, leave more room for people and things, and are easier to repair, and they're also safer in a crash because the engine can absorb impact in front of the passengers. However, they can make the car tend to push wide in sharp turns. Rear engines can give great acceleration and grip on the drive wheels, but they can make the car feel tricky to control, especially for beginners, since the back end can slide out more easily. They also usually leave less space for luggage and can be noisier inside. Mid-engine cars try to get the best of both, offering excellent handling and balance, but they cost more to build and often have very little room for storage.

A tequila sunrise is pretty simple: tequila, orange juice, and grenadine. You usually serve it in a tall glass with an orange slice and a cherry on top.

Here's what you need: 1 1/2 ounces of tequila, 4 ounces of orange juice, and 1/2 ounce of grenadine.

Fill a tall glass with ice, pour in the tequila and OJ, and give it a stir. Then slowly pour the grenadine in and let it sink to the bottom. That's what gives you the "sunrise" look, with the red bleeding up into the orange as it mixes. Toss in the orange slice and cherry and you're done.

People make all kinds of versions of this too. Some add lime juice, some add triple sec, and some even throw in a splash of soda water. So play around with it and see what you like best.

Alcohol poisoning occurs when someone drinks enough alcohol to become harmful to the body. The liver normally handles alcohol by breaking it down and clearing it out, but it can only keep up with a limited amount at once. When a person drinks too much in a short period, the surplus alcohol accumulates in the blood and can lead to dangerous complications. Warning signs include vomiting, trouble breathing, confusion, seizures, and in severe cases, coma or death. These effects occur because alcohol interferes with brain function and bodily processes such as heart rate and respiration. Drinking carefully and never consuming excessive amounts is essential. If you plan to drink, it's also wise to arrange a designated driver or another safe ride home. If you suspect someone is suffering from alcohol poisoning, call 911 or take them to a hospital immediately.

Okay, so regret in game theory is basically that sinking feeling you get when you realize you could've picked a different move and done better. Players feel it when they look back and see another option would've paid off more. People use it as a way to judge how good a decision was: choices that leave you with little regret are usually seen as the smarter ones, and the ones that leave you kicking yourself are seen as weaker.

The usual way to measure it is pretty simple. You take what you actually got and compare it to what you would've gotten with another choice. Say you stick with a strategy in some game and it flops. If you then notice a different strategy would have won, that gap is your regret. It's a handy idea because it puts a number on the cost of a bad call. It also shows how people change over time. You make a mistake, you feel the regret, and next time you try something else so you don't feel it again.

Even with these obstacles, plenty of people remain interested in solar power, since it offers a clean, renewable way to generate energy.

Your granddaughter should stick with whatever plan her doctor gave her for the concussion. Spots on the penis may stem from several causes, such as bacteria, irritated skin, or sexually transmitted infections (STIs). Because certain STIs can cause serious harm when untreated, it is wise to see a doctor if you're worried about these spots. There are several steps you can take to clear them up. First, keep the area clean and dry by washing it softly with lukewarm water and a gentle soap, and skip scented products, which can aggravate the skin. Second, choose loose clothing so the skin can breathe and irritation is less likely. Third, press a warm, damp cloth against the area for a few minutes to ease swelling and discomfort. Fourth, consider over-the-counter creams containing benzoyl peroxide or salicylic acid, which can dry out the bumps and lessen redness. Finally, if the spots persist or you notice other symptoms like pain, discharge, or trouble urinating, see a healthcare provider, who can identify the cause and recommend suitable treatment. Keep in mind that these spots can sometimes signal an STI, so practicing safe sex and getting tested regularly is important for protecting your own health and that of your partners.

Asthalin contains salbutamol, a bronchodilator that opens the airways. Doctors usually prescribe it when a baby is wheezing or has a condition that narrows the airways, not for an ordinary cough and cold. At 2.5 months, a baby's airways are very small, so a doctor normally has a specific reason before recommending it. Your doctor may have heard wheezing through the stethoscope or judged that the baby's breathing needed it. Still, it's completely reasonable to ask him directly: "What did you hear or see that made you suggest this, and how long should we use it?" Ask him too about the exact dose, how often to give it, and whether you need a spacer with a mask, since inhalers are not meant to be used by infants without one. Do not give it at a dose or frequency other than what he prescribed, and do not switch to an adult or older child's inhaler.

Watch for side effects such as a racing heartbeat, jitteriness, trembling, or unusual irritability. Tell the doctor if you notice any of these.

Most importantly, a baby this young with a cough and cold should be checked promptly, because infants can worsen quickly. Seek urgent care right away if your baby has fast or noisy breathing, visible pulling in of the chest or ribs with each breath, pauses in breathing, bluish lips or face, feeding poorly or refusing feeds, unusual sleepiness or difficulty waking, fewer wet diapers than usual, or a fever (especially a temperature of 100.4°F / 38°C or higher in a baby under 3 months, which needs same-day medical review).

Also avoid giving any over-the-counter cough or cold medicines to a baby this age unless a doctor specifically tells you to, as many are unsafe for infants.

The metric system is pretty much the standard almost everywhere, and it's built on the International System of Units (SI), which sets up standard units for things like length, mass, and time. People often argue it's better than the imperial system (the one the US still mostly uses). The biggest reason is that it runs on base 10, so it's really easy to work with. The basic unit of length is the meter, and everything scales by powers of 10. Need something longer than a meter? Use kilometers, which are 1000 meters. Need something smaller? Go to centimeters (100 to a meter) or millimeters (1000 to a meter).

It's also tied to science. Units in the metric system are defined using things like the speed of light and properties of atoms, so scientists don't have to juggle different systems. And converting is simple. Want meters to kilometers? Just divide by 1000. Imperial units like feet, inches, and pounds don't scale neatly like that, so converting between them is a lot more annoying. That's really the core of the argument: it's easy to learn, grounded in science, and a breeze to convert.

Your LDL of about 168 mg/dL is in the "high" range, and at your age it deserves a real decision rather than being ignored. However, whether you should take a cholesterol-lowering medicine depends mainly on your overall 10-year risk of heart attack or stroke, not on the LDL number alone. Your doctor can estimate that using a standard risk calculator, such as the ASCVD risk estimator, which uses your age, sex, total cholesterol, HDL, blood pressure, diabetes status, smoking history, and whether you take blood pressure medicine.

Some of your numbers are reassuring. Your blood pressure and blood sugar are normal, your weight is healthy, you walk regularly, you practice yoga, and you have no family history of early heart disease. Your ratios are a mixed picture. A total cholesterol to HDL ratio of 5.29 is on the higher side, since many clinicians aim for below about 4.5 and ideally below 3.5. Your LDL to HDL ratio of 3.47 is also moderately elevated. These ratios support taking your cholesterol seriously, but they do not by themselves mean you need a drug.

For someone your age with these numbers, guidelines generally suggest that a statin is considered when the estimated 10-year risk is around 7.5 percent or higher, or when certain risk-enhancing factors are present, such as a very high lipoprotein(a), persistently high triglycerides, or chronic inflammatory disease. If your calculated risk is lower than that, your doctor may first recommend lifestyle changes and recheck your numbers in a few months. If your risk is intermediate, a coronary artery calcium scan can help clarify whether medicine is worth it. Your doctor may also want to check triglycerides, lipoprotein(a), and a fasting panel to get a complete picture.

Whatever the decision, lifestyle measures help. Reducing saturated fat from red meat, butter, and fried or processed foods, eating more soluble fiber from oats, beans, fruits, and vegetables, and keeping up your walking and yoga all lower LDL to some degree. Not smoking, if that applies to you, matters a great deal.

So my advice is not to start a medicine on your own, but to bring these exact numbers to your doctor and ask for your estimated 10-year cardiovascular risk and whether a statin is recommended for you specifically. Those answers will tell you whether medication makes sense now or whether a period of diet change and monitoring is the better next step.

Generally, workers cannot choose to pay their own federal and state taxes instead of letting their employer handle them. Instead, the employer must deduct the correct amount of taxes from each employee's paycheck and remit that money to the government on the employee's behalf. This arrangement is called payroll tax withholding. In the United States, federal law requires employers to withhold federal income tax, Social Security tax, and Medicare tax from workers' wages, and to contribute an equal matching amount of the Social Security and Medicare taxes themselves. Some states and localities also mandate that employers withhold state and local taxes from pay.

On rare occasions, an employee may ask the employer to pay taxes directly rather than deducting them from wages. A person with a very high income or several income streams, for instance, might make such a request in order to prevent under-withholding and avoid owing a large sum when filing the annual return. Even so, this is generally a voluntary agreement reached between the worker and the employer, not a legal entitlement the worker can insist upon.

It's worth pointing out that not every teenage boy is preoccupied with phallic imagery, and people of every gender often take an interest in bodies and their parts. Still, some teenage boys do show a special fascination with phallic imagery, and there are several possible explanations. One is puberty, a period of substantial physical and hormonal change, during which people often become more curious about their own bodies and those of others. That curiosity can sometimes turn into a fixation on particular body parts, the genitals among them. Some boys may also be drawn to such imagery as a way of projecting masculinity or gaining acceptance from their peers. In certain cultures, boys face social expectations about how to act and what to care about, and phallic imagery can become part of that picture. In short, the motives behind a teenage boy's interest in phallic imagery are varied and differ from one person to the next. Everyone is different, and it's perfectly acceptable to be drawn to different things.

A self-driving car, also called an autonomous vehicle or driverless car, is one that can sense what's around it and get from A to B without a human steering or pedaling. Most of them rely on a mix of cameras, radar, and lidar to collect information about the road, then use AI software to figure out what to do with it. The big promise is safer, smoother travel. Plenty of crashes come down to human error, so taking the driver out of the equation could cut those down, traffic could flow better, and people who can't drive because of age, a disability, or something else would get a lot more freedom. That said, lots of folks are nervous about whether these cars are actually reliable enough, and people still argue about how much regulation and oversight they should face.

Jaywalking means crossing a street or road somewhere other than a marked crosswalk, or crossing in a manner that breaks the rules meant for pedestrians. Many countries make it illegal, since it puts both walkers and drivers at risk. Drivers often don't anticipate that someone will step into the road at an unexpected spot, which makes crossing outside a crosswalk hazardous. Pedestrians who cross away from a crosswalk may also lack the right of way, so drivers have no obligation to stop for them, and this can result in collisions and injuries. Simply strolling through an unfamiliar city to see the sights, without crossing the street, is not jaywalking. But if you cross outside a designated crosswalk, or ignore the rules that apply to pedestrians, you may be jaywalking. To stay safe while walking somewhere new, always stay aware of what is around you and obey the pedestrian rules.

A data warehouse is a centralized repository that stores large volumes of data collected from many different sources, such as transactional databases, customer systems, sales platforms, and external feeds, and organizes it so that it can be analyzed efficiently. Its main purpose is to support business intelligence, reporting, and decision-making, rather than to handle the day-to-day operations of applications. Where an operational database is optimized for recording individual transactions quickly, a data warehouse is optimized for answering broad analytical questions, such as how sales trends have changed over the past three years across regions and product lines.

The process of getting data into a warehouse typically follows an extract, transform, and load pattern, often abbreviated ETL (or ELT when transformation happens after loading). Data is pulled from its original sources, cleaned, standardized so that the same concept is represented consistently, and then loaded into the warehouse. This step matters because data from different systems often uses different formats, naming conventions, and definitions of the same metric, and the warehouse must reconcile these differences so that analysts can trust the results.

Data warehouses usually store historical data over long periods and are structured for reading rather than frequent updating. Many use a dimensional design, such as star or snowflake schemas, which organizes information into central fact tables (for example, sales amounts or order counts) linked to descriptive dimension tables (for example, dates, customers, or products). This structure makes queries that summarize and slice data fast and understandable to business users.

Modern data warehouses are offered as cloud services by providers such as Snowflake, Google BigQuery, Amazon Redshift, and Azure Synapse, among others, and they often scale storage and computing power independently. Organizations use them alongside related tools like data lakes, which store raw data in its native form, and business intelligence dashboards, which present the results to decision-makers.

Imagine you have a special box of toys, and each toy is a feeling or a picture. A poem is like a box where the toys are arranged in a pretty way, with the rhymes and the beats making them sparkle. When someone wants to share the box with friends who speak another language, they can't always keep the exact same toys or the exact same arrangement. So the translator does something clever: they look inside the box, figure out which toys matter most, and then build a new box with different toys that make the same feeling happen.

Sometimes the translator keeps the rhyme, sometimes they keep the beat, and sometimes they let those go and find a new kind of music that works in the new language. Every language has its own sounds, so a rhyme in one language might be a different sound in another, and the translator finds a new one that still makes your ears happy.

The reason a translated poem can still feel beautiful is that the most important part of a poem is usually not the exact words or the syllable count. It's the feeling, the picture it paints, and the surprise it gives you. Those things can travel across languages, even when the wrapping paper changes. People everywhere have feelings like joy, sadness, and wonder, so when a translator gets the feeling right, the poem can make someone's heart jump in any language.

Elk don't have sex with any regular frequency the way the question might imply, because their mating is seasonal and concentrated into a short window. Elk (also called wapiti in North America) breed once a year, during the autumn rut, which typically runs from late August or September through October or early November depending on the population and latitude. During this period, bulls become intensely active, bugling, wallowing in mud, and rounding up groups of cows, and they may mate with several females over the course of the rut. A single cow is usually receptive for only about a day during her estrous cycle, and if she isn't bred, she may come back into heat roughly three weeks later, which is why some copulation can continue for a few weeks.

Outside the rut, elk don't mate at all. Bulls are generally too exhausted and depleted from fighting and chasing cows to do much else, and they often lose a substantial amount of body weight during the season. Cows give birth the following late spring, usually in May or June, which fits the timing of the autumn breeding.

Lee Sedol is a South Korean professional player of Go, the ancient board game of strategy, and he is widely regarded as one of the greatest players of the modern era. He was born in 1983 on Biggeumdo, a small island off the southwest coast of South Korea, and showed exceptional talent as a child. He became a professional at the age of twelve, in 1996, and went on to win eighteen international titles, a record that for years placed him among the very top players in the world. He was known for a creative, aggressive, and often unpredictable style, and in Korea he earned the nickname "The Strong Stone" or sometimes "The Beast" for his fighting spirit. He reached the highest rank of 9 dan.

He became famous well beyond the Go world in March 2016, when he played a five-game match in Seoul against AlphaGo, a computer program developed by Google DeepMind. Go had long been considered much harder for computers than chess because of its enormous number of possible positions and the importance of intuition and judgment in evaluating them. Many experts expected a human champion to win easily, but AlphaGo won the first three games and took the match. Lee won the fourth game with a brilliant and unexpected move, often called the "hand of God" or move 78, which exploited a weakness in the program. The final score was 4 to 1 in favor of AlphaGo. This match is widely seen as a landmark moment in the history of artificial intelligence, comparable to Deep Blue defeating Garry Kasparov at chess in 1997.

Lee retired from professional play in November 2019. He said that the rise of AI, which he described as an entity that cannot be defeated, was one of the reasons he decided to stop. In 2019 he also played a farewell game against a Go program and lost, though he has remained a respected figure in discussions about the relationship between humans and artificial intelligence. The 2017 documentary "AlphaGo" tells the story of the 2016 match and his role in it.

Steam is a digital distribution service created by Valve Corporation that provides digital rights management (DRM), online multiplayer gaming, and social networking. Valve originally introduced it in 2003 to deliver automatic updates for its own games, but it has since grown to carry a broad selection of titles from many other publishers. The service runs on Windows, macOS, and Linux. Through the Steam client, people can buy games, download them, and play them. Alongside single-player titles, it hosts a variety of multiplayer games and offers tools for streaming video and broadcasting gameplay. Its community features include user reviews, discussion forums, and groups where players can get in touch with one another.

So to work out overnight commissions on a CFD at Interactive Brokers, you need two things: how many units you're holding, and the overnight financing rate for the underlying asset. That rate is what you get charged (or credited) for keeping a position open past the close. It's set by the market, so it moves around depending on the asset and how long you hold.

The formula looks like this: Overnight commission = Number of units * Overnight financing rate * Number of nights.

Here's a quick example. Say you've got a CFD on ABC stock, 10,000 units, and the overnight rate for ABC is 0.005%. Hold it for two nights and you get:

10,000 * 0.005% * 2 nights
= 10 * 0.005 * 2
= $0.10

That's just a toy number, though. Your actual rate and charge will depend on the asset and whatever the market is doing that day. Don't forget there's more to CFD costs than overnight financing, either. Other fees can pile up, so it's worth reading through your account terms and checking what applies to your trades before you dive in.

Today's cars can feel less thrilling than older models or concept cars for several reasons. First, safety rules have grown far stricter over time, so vehicles must be built to satisfy those requirements, which can leave them looking more "conservative" or less eye-catching. Second, manufacturers have to weigh practicality and cost when designing new models, so they often cannot include the elaborate features seen on concept cars, which tend to be more of a "showpiece" meant to demonstrate future possibilities. Finally, concept cars are, as the name suggests, just ideas. They are not intended for mass production and are usually prototypes built to test new designs or technologies. Their purpose is to look bold and futuristic, attract attention, and build excitement, but they are not necessarily practical or affordable for everyday driving.

A hard, tender, red bump that burns when touched, without itching, is most often an infected hair follicle, a boil, or an infected ingrown hair or small cyst. Those are common in the pubic area because of hair and friction. Since it started as a small bump that has grown and become painful, that is the most likely explanation. Less commonly, painful lumps or sores in this area can be related to a sexually transmitted infection, so it's worth having it looked at rather than guessing.

For now, you can apply a warm, clean compress for 10 to 15 minutes two or three times a day, which often helps a boil drain or heal. Wash the area gently with mild soap and water, and keep it covered with loose clothing to reduce friction. Over-the-counter ibuprofen or acetaminophen can ease the pain. Try not to squeeze or pop it, since that can spread the infection. A plain antibiotic ointment may help a little, but it usually won't clear a established boil on its own.

I can't prescribe medication, and an antibiotic is often needed if the infection is deeper or spreading. Please see a doctor, urgent care, or a pharmacist soon, especially if the lump is getting bigger, you have a fever or chills, the redness is spreading, it's draining pus, you notice more bumps, or it isn't clearly better within a few days. Get seen promptly if you've had recent sexual contact or the sores are blistering or very painful, since those need proper testing and treatment.

A processor, in computing, is the component of a computer that carries out instructions. It is the part of the machine that performs the basic operations of arithmetic, logic, comparison, and data movement that together make up any program. Modern processors are typically called central processing units, or CPUs, and they are built as integrated circuits containing billions of tiny transistors etched onto a piece of silicon.

A processor works by repeatedly following a cycle often described as fetch, decode, and execute. It fetches an instruction from memory, determines what that instruction asks it to do, and then carries out the operation, such as adding two numbers, moving a value between locations, or deciding which instruction to run next based on a condition. Each instruction belongs to the processor's instruction set architecture, a defined vocabulary of operations that the chip understands. Common examples include the x86 family used in many personal computers and the ARM architecture found in most smartphones and an increasing number of laptops.

Processors rely on several internal parts to do this work. The arithmetic logic unit handles calculations and logical comparisons. Registers are small, very fast storage locations that hold the data currently being worked on. A control unit coordinates the sequence of operations, and caches keep frequently used data close at hand so the processor does not have to wait on slower main memory. A clock signal sets the rhythm of the processor, and its speed is often measured in gigahertz, meaning billions of cycles per second.

Over time, processors have grown more capable through techniques such as multiple cores, which allow several instruction streams to run in parallel on one chip, and pipelining, which overlaps the stages of different instructions. Beyond the general-purpose CPU, the term processor is also applied to specialized chips such as graphics processing units, which excel at parallel workloads like rendering images, and digital signal processors, which handle audio and sensor data. Together, these devices are the engines that turn software into action.

Mathematical optimization is the branch of mathematics concerned with finding the best possible choice from a set of available alternatives, according to some criterion that can be measured numerically. In its simplest form, an optimization problem asks you to maximize or minimize a function, called the objective function, by choosing values for one or more variables, often while respecting certain restrictions called constraints. For example, a company might want to minimize its production costs while still meeting customer demand, or an engineer might want to maximize the strength of a bridge while keeping the amount of steel below a fixed budget.

Every optimization problem has three basic ingredients. The decision variables are the quantities you are free to choose, such as how many units of each product to make or which route a delivery truck should take. The objective function assigns a numerical value to each possible choice, representing what you care about, such as profit, cost, time, error, or energy. The constraints describe which choices are allowed, such as limits on resources, physical laws, or logical requirements. The set of all choices that satisfy the constraints is called the feasible region, and the goal is to find the point in that region where the objective function is as large or as small as possible. That point is called an optimal solution.

Optimization problems come in many varieties, and the type of problem largely determines how hard it is to solve. When the objective and constraints are all linear, the problem is called linear programming, and very efficient methods such as the simplex algorithm and interior point methods can solve problems with millions of variables. When some variables must take whole number values, as in deciding whether to build a factory or not, the problem becomes integer programming, which is generally much harder. Nonlinear optimization deals with curved objective functions or constraints, and an important special case is convex optimization, where the problem has a shape guaranteeing that any local best solution is also the global best, making it reliably solvable. Non-convex problems can have many local optima, so algorithms may get stuck in a solution that is good nearby but not the best overall.

The methods used to solve optimization problems are equally varied. Calculus provides the classical approach: at a smooth minimum or maximum without constraints, the derivative of the function is zero, and with constraints, techniques such as Lagrange multipliers extend this idea. Iterative algorithms like gradient descent repeatedly take small steps in the direction that improves the objective, and this family of methods is the backbone of training machine learning models, where the objective is to minimize prediction error. For problems that are too complex for exact methods, heuristic and metaheuristic approaches such as genetic algorithms, simulated annealing, and local search are used to find good, though not necessarily perfect, solutions in reasonable time.

Mathematical optimization is used almost everywhere quantitative decisions are made. Airlines use it to schedule crews and flights, logistics companies use it to plan routes, financial firms use it to build investment portfolios that balance return and risk, power companies use it to decide which generators to run, and scientists use it to fit models to data. In essence, whenever a problem can be phrased as making the best decision under given limitations, mathematical optimization provides the language to describe it precisely and the tools to solve it.

Of course! The double slit experiment is a well-known physics experiment that sheds light on how light behaves. Picture a wall with two narrow slits cut into it. When you aim a flashlight at the wall, light goes through the slits and forms two beams on the far side. Next, suppose you set up a screen behind the wall to catch those beams. With the flashlight shining on the wall, you would see two bright spots on the screen where the beams land. Now suppose you run the experiment again, but with one slit covered. This time, shining the flashlight at the wall leaves just one bright spot on the screen. Up to this point, everything is simple and makes sense. But now let's try something odd. Imagine that you cover both slits, and you also aim the flashlight at the wall extremely slowly. You would probably expect the screen to stay blank, since no light is getting through the slits. Yet when you check the screen, something surprising appears. Rather than nothing, there is a pattern of alternating light and dark bands. This is the strange, puzzling heart of the double slit experiment. Even when light is not passing through the slits, it still produces a pattern on the screen. This shows that light acts in odd and unexpected ways, and it is one reason physicists keep studying light and trying to work out how it operates.

Visual servoing is a control technique that directs a robot or another system toward a target position or orientation by relying on visual input from sensors. A camera or similar visual sensor observes a target or landmark in the surroundings, and the information it gathers is used to determine the control commands needed to bring the system to the intended location. The control commands are derived from the discrepancy between the system's present position and its goal position, as revealed by the visual data. This discrepancy serves as the basis for a control signal, which is sent to the system to nudge it nearer to the goal. Visual servoing has broad uses in robotics, automation, and machine vision. It proves especially valuable when a robot must move with high accuracy, as in manufacturing or assembly work, or when conditions shift and the robot must modify its motions to keep pace.

Selecting a provider for investing services requires weighing a number of considerations. The following points are worth keeping in mind.

Reputation: Seek out a firm that is well regarded within the industry. Read online reviews, ask friends or financial advisors for recommendations, and look into the firm's past performance.

Fees: Because investing can get costly, compare what different firms charge. Choose one whose prices for its services are reasonable.

Investment options: Confirm that the firm provides a variety of investments suited to your needs and objectives. If you want a particular kind of investment, such as index funds or individual stocks, check that it is available.

Customer service: Good support matters, since you will want help when a problem arises. Look for a firm whose knowledgeable employees can readily answer your questions.

Convenience: Think about whether the firm's website and mobile app are simple to use and fit the way you want to manage your money.

If you weigh these factors, you can find a firm that fits your needs and supports your investment goals. It is also wise to consult a financial advisor or other professional before making any investment decisions.

So Michigan doesn't have any specific law requiring landlords to pay interest on security deposits. That said, landlords still have to handle deposits carefully. You're required to give the tenant a written receipt for the deposit, and within 14 days of move-in you need to provide a written statement describing the unit's condition. Miss that step and the tenant could be owed damages equal to twice the deposit, so it's worth getting right.

When a tenant moves out and you want to keep some or all of the deposit, you've got 30 days from move-out to send an itemized written statement covering damages and repair costs. If you don't, the tenant may be able to get the full deposit back. Deposits belong to the tenant, too, so they should be kept separate from your own money. Whatever's left after legitimate deductions has to go back to the tenant within those same 30 days.

If you've got more questions, a local attorney is your best bet, or you can reach out to the Michigan Department of Licensing and Regulatory Affairs.

It could well be a bruised or strained abdominal muscle, which is common after a fall onto hard objects and usually improves within a few days. Pain that gets worse with standing, sitting up, or reaching, but eases when he's sitting still, fits a muscle injury. Even so, a belly injury in a child should be checked by a doctor, because a blow to the abdomen can sometimes damage internal organs like the liver, spleen, or intestines, and those problems aren't always obvious at first. Since he's still crying with ordinary movement, I'd call your pediatrician or a nurse advice line today and describe what happened. They can tell you whether he needs to be seen.

Go to the emergency room right away if he vomits more than once or vomits green or bloody material, has a belly that becomes swollen or hard, gets pale, becomes unusually sleepy or hard to wake, breathes fast, seems dizzy or faints, has blood in his urine or stool, can't urinate, complains of pain in his left shoulder tip, or develops a fever. Also seek care if the pain worsens rather than improves over the next few hours.

If a doctor confirms it's a muscle injury, you can help him feel better at home. Let him rest and choose whatever position is most comfortable, and avoid rough play for a few days. A cold pack wrapped in a thin towel for 15 to 20 minutes at a time can ease soreness. For pain, acetaminophen dosed by his weight is generally the safer choice until he's been examined, and it's best to check with the doctor before giving ibuprofen after a belly injury. Keep an eye on him over the next day or two, and trust your instincts if he seems worse than a simple bump would explain.

Raytheon Company was a major American aerospace and defense contractor headquartered in Waltham, Massachusetts. Founded in 1922 as the American Appliance Company, it took the name Raytheon in 1925, a combination of "ray" and "theon," a Greek word meaning "of the gods." The company grew significantly during World War II, when it produced radar and magnetron technology, and it later became one of the largest suppliers of missiles, radar systems, electronics, and other military hardware to the United States government and its allies. Its well-known products included the Patriot air defense missile, the Tomahawk cruise missile, the Standard Missile family, and various sensor and radar systems, as well as commercial products such as the microwave oven, which was popularized through Raytheon's Amana subsidiary.

In 2020, Raytheon merged with United Technologies Corporation, the parent of Pratt & Whitney, Collins Aerospace, and Otis Elevator. The combined company was renamed Raytheon Technologies Corporation, and in 2023 it was renamed RTX Corporation. The defense business that had been Raytheon Company continues as Raytheon, operating within RTX as one of its major segments, so the name remains in use even though the original independent company no longer exists in its former form.

Sharp, brief pain that comes and goes, followed by burning in the lower leg and foot, can come from several sources. Given your MS history and the fall a month ago, a few are worth taking seriously.

The fall matters most. A month is enough time for a deep bruise or hematoma to press on a nerve in the thigh, such as the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve, which supplies the outer thigh. Nerve injury or compression can cause sharp, shooting pains and later burning or tingling. A fall can also cause a fracture, including a small hairline or stress fracture of the femur or hip, which sometimes doesn't show on early X-rays. Less obviously, a fall can injure the lower back and irritate a nerve root, sending pain down the leg. Blood clots are another concern: a leg that was bruised, then less mobile, can develop a deep vein clot, which typically causes thigh or calf pain, swelling, warmth, or a feeling of tightness.

Your MS may also be involved. MS can cause paroxysmal pains, which are sudden, brief, electric-like or stabbing pains that last seconds and recur, often triggered by movement or touch. It can also cause neuropathic burning in the feet and legs, and spasticity or muscle spasms. Sometimes a flare or new lesion shows up as a new symptom, and the fall could have contributed to one. Certain MS medications or other drugs can also cause nerve-related side effects.

Because of the fall and your MS, I'd recommend seeing your doctor or neurologist soon rather than waiting, and telling them exactly what you described: the timing, the location, and the burning that follows. They will likely examine your leg and back, check your nerve function and reflexes, and may order X-rays to look for a fracture, an ultrasound to rule out a clot, or an MRI if they suspect a nerve problem or MS activity.

Seek emergency care right away if you develop a swollen, warm, red, or very tender leg, sudden chest pain or shortness of breath, leg weakness or numbness that is spreading or prevents you from standing, loss of bladder or bowel control, numbness in the groin area, or a sudden severe headache. Also get urgent care if you can't bear weight on the leg after the fall.

There are a number of free online services you can use to keep tabs on your cash flow. A few of them are worth a look. Mint is a well-known money management platform that lets you connect your bank accounts, credit cards, and investment accounts all in one spot. It sorts your transactions automatically and provides a summary of your overall financial condition, cash flow included. Personal Capital is comparable to Mint, though it adds budgeting and investment tracking. It can point out where you're overspending and offer ideas for strengthening your cash flow. YNAB, short for You Need a Budget, is a budgeting program centered on building a plan for your money and keeping to it. It records your income and expenses as they happen and provides advice and resources for improving your cash flow. Pocketbook is a personal finance app that tracks your spending, helps you set and monitor a budget, and shows your cash flow as it changes. It also includes features for keeping track of bills and debts. Goodbudget is a budgeting app built on the envelope method, in which you allocate a set amount of money to categories such as groceries or entertainment and monitor what you spend within each one. It can show you where your money goes and highlight places where your cash flow could be improved. These tools are especially useful if you are just beginning to track your cash flow, since they help you get a grip on spending and find opportunities to save. They may fall short, however, for more advanced financial planning or for more complicated situations. In those cases, a more powerful financial management tool or a financial planner may be a better fit.
