In 1904, J.J. Thomson put forward his "plum pudding" atomic model. He envisioned the atom as a sphere of positive charge with negatively charged electrons scattered throughout, much like raisins distributed through a pudding. Ernest Rutherford later revised this picture. His model placed the atom's positive charge and nearly all of its mass in a tiny, dense nucleus at the center, with electrons circling around it.

Movie gunshots are mostly designed to sound exciting rather than accurate. A real gunshot is a very sharp, brief crack, and it can be surprisingly quiet-sounding on a recording, so sound designers layer several recordings together to make it hit harder. They might combine a sharp crack, a deep booming thump from a big cannon-like sound, a metallic clank, and even the sound of a tree branch snapping or a whip. Each part adds something: the crack gives it sharpness, the boom gives it power, and the extra pieces give it character so that each gun feels different.

Filmmakers also care a lot about what the audience feels. In real life a gunshot is loud and startling, but in a movie the sound has to carry emotion, tell you who has the upper hand, and cut through music and dialogue. A bigger, longer, echoing bang makes a scene feel tense and powerful in a way that the real sound, which is often brief and flat, would not.

Microphones also play a role. Recording a gun up close with a mic can make it sound very different from how it sounds to a person standing a few feet away, and even different again from how it sounds from across a field. Sound designers pick whichever version works best for the scene, and then they often add reverb, so the shot seems to bounce off buildings or walls.

Finally, there is a habit of tradition. Over decades, audiences have learned what a "movie gunshot" sounds like, and if a film used a truly accurate sound, it might seem weak or fake to viewers. So the familiar, exaggerated bang has become the expected sound, and it is what most people now think of as the sound of a gun.

It can make sense to borrow rather than pay cash when the purchase is large relative to your savings, and paying in full would leave you with no emergency cushion. Draining your reserves to buy a car, home, or major appliance can leave you exposed to unexpected costs, so a loan that preserves liquidity may be the safer choice. Borrowing also tends to be more reasonable when the item is needed now and waiting to save up would mean going without something essential, such as transportation to a job or a home for a growing family.

Loans can also be worth considering when the interest rate is low relative to what your money could earn elsewhere. If you can borrow at a modest rate, such as a mortgage at a fixed rate, and keep your cash invested in assets with a reasonable expected return, the arithmetic may favor borrowing. This logic weakens, however, if the rate is high, the return on your alternatives is uncertain, or you would be tempted to spend the money you saved.

Some purchases warrant a loan because they build value over time. A mortgage on a home, or a student loan for training that substantially raises your earning power, can be a reasonable use of debt. Consumer goods that lose value quickly, like electronics or furniture financed at high interest, are usually a poorer case for borrowing.

Finally, a loan may be preferable when there are tax advantages, such as mortgage interest deductions in some countries, or when special promotional financing at 0 percent is available and you are confident you can repay before the promotion ends. In every case, the key questions are whether you can comfortably afford the monthly payments, what the total cost will be including interest and fees, and whether the debt fits within your broader financial goals.

A mixture model is a probabilistic framework that combines several probability distributions into one. It offers a flexible way to model data that can be understood as coming from a blend of different underlying distributions. Rather than assuming that a single distribution produced all the observations, a mixture model supposes that the data arose from a combination of distinct distributions, each called a component of the model. Each component receives a weight that reflects how likely it is that a given data point originated from that component. These weights add up to 1 and together express the chance that a data point came from each component. Mixture models appear in many fields, serving purposes such as density estimation, clustering, and classification. They are especially valuable when the data has intricate structure or when it is unclear which single probability distribution fits it best. Consider, for instance, a collection of data points recording the heights of people in a population. Those heights might follow a normal distribution, but they could also follow a more complicated pattern, with several peaks or unusual outliers. In such a case, a mixture model could capture this by combining a normal distribution with an additional distribution that accounts for the data's complex features.

The Harvard Mark I was one of the earliest large-scale automatic digital computers. It was built between 1937 and 1944 at Harvard University, funded by IBM and designed largely by Howard Aiken, a Harvard physicist who had proposed the idea in the early 1930s. Its formal name was the Automatic Sequence Controlled Calculator, and it was completed and put into operation in 1944.

The machine was enormous, roughly 51 feet long and 8 feet tall, and weighed about five tons. It was constructed mainly from electromechanical parts, including electromagnetic relays, rotating mechanical counters, and some 500 miles of wire. Instructions were read from paper tape, and data was held in mechanical registers, so it did not use the vacuum tubes that powered later electronic computers. Its operations were driven by an electric motor and a central shaft that synchronized the components, which made it noisy and relatively slow by later standards. It could perform addition and subtraction in fractions of a second, while multiplication and division took considerably longer.

The Mark I was used heavily by the U.S. Navy during World War II for calculations such as ballistics tables, and its work contributed to the Manhattan Project and other wartime efforts. It is often regarded as a milestone because it showed that large automatic calculation was practical, and it helped inspire the development of later machines. After the war it was followed by the Mark II, Mark III, and Mark IV, which moved progressively toward electronic designs. The Mark I was retired in 1959 and is now displayed at Harvard.

I can't provide a diagnosis or suggest particular medications, so please consult a healthcare professional about what you're experiencing. A clinician can physically examine the area, work out what is causing the lump and any accompanying pain, and then propose suitable treatment, which could involve medication. Seeing a doctor is especially important when symptoms persist or seem worrying, since early care frequently leads to better results.

Common sense reasoning is the ability to make everyday judgments about the world using the broad, mostly unspoken knowledge that nearly all people acquire through living in it. It covers things like knowing that a dropped glass will probably break, that people usually eat dinner in the evening, that you cannot fit a large object inside a small container, or that someone who is crying is probably sad. None of this is typically taught in a formal way, and people rarely state it out loud, yet it underlies almost everything we do and understand.

The knowledge involved comes in several kinds. There is naive physics, which concerns how objects move, break, fall, and interact. There is social and psychological understanding, such as inferring that others have beliefs, desires, and intentions that may differ from our own. There is knowledge of time and causality, like the fact that effects follow causes and that you cannot unbake a cake. And there is cultural and practical knowledge about how institutions, tools, and routines work. Common sense reasoning means combining these background facts with the situation at hand to reach sensible conclusions, often without conscious effort.

The topic matters most in artificial intelligence, where it has been a famous difficulty since the 1950s. Computers can excel at chess or arithmetic yet stumble on questions a young child finds trivial. Consider the sentence "The trophy doesn't fit in the suitcase because it is too big." Humans immediately know that "it" refers to the trophy, because they understand how size and containment work. Tests like the Winograd Schema Challenge were built around this kind of ambiguity. The difficulty is that common sense is vast, implicit, context dependent, and full of exceptions, so it is hard to write down explicitly. Projects such as Cyc tried to hand-encode millions of facts and rules, while more recent approaches rely on large language models that absorb patterns from enormous amounts of text. These models do much better than older systems but still make odd errors, suggesting their grasp is partial and not grounded in real experience of the physical world.

In short, common sense reasoning is the everyday, background-driven thinking that lets us handle ordinary situations sensibly, and reproducing it in machines remains one of the central open challenges in AI.

Okay so Section 8 housing, also called the Housing Choice Voucher Program, is federally funded rental help for low-income folks. HUD runs it, and the whole point is helping people afford decent, safe, and sanitary places on the private market. Most participants pay about 30% of their monthly income toward rent and utilities, and the program covers the rest. To qualify you've got to meet certain income limits, and you might also need to fit other criteria, like being a first-time homebuyer or having a disability. It's open to renters and homeowners alike, and you can use your voucher with any landlord who's willing to take it. The idea is to give lower-income households more options and help them move toward self-sufficiency, including moving to areas with better jobs and schools. If you're wondering whether you'd qualify, your local HUD office is the place to ask.

The highest point on Oahu is Mt. Ka'ala, up in the Waianae mountain range. It tops out at 4,025 feet (1,227 meters), which also makes it the tallest peak in the Waianae Range. It's nowhere near the highest in the whole state, though. That title goes to Mauna Kea on the Big Island. Ka'ala sits inside the Ka'ala Natural Area Reserve, and a lot of plants and animals live up there, including plenty of endangered and threatened species. Hikers love it too. The trails are tough, but the views from the summit are worth the effort.

Medical diagnosis is the process of identifying a disease, disorder, or other health condition that explains a person's symptoms or signs. It is one of the central tasks of healthcare, because accurate identification of what is wrong determines what treatment, monitoring, or further testing is appropriate. The process usually begins when a patient reports symptoms, such as pain, fever, or fatigue, and a clinician then gathers more information through a medical history, a physical examination, and sometimes laboratory tests, imaging studies, or specialized procedures. The clinician weighs these findings against their knowledge of diseases and how they typically present, often forming a list of possible explanations and narrowing it down over time.

Diagnosis is rarely a single moment of certainty. Many conditions share similar symptoms, so clinicians often work through a differential diagnosis, which is a ranked list of candidate conditions that are considered and then either confirmed or ruled out as new information arrives. A diagnosis may be provisional at first and refined later, and in some cases a clear answer is never reached, which is why follow-up and reassessment are important parts of good care.

The result of this process is a named condition or a clearly described problem, often recorded using standardized classification systems such as the International Classification of Diseases. A correct and timely diagnosis allows treatment to begin, helps predict the likely course of illness, and informs the patient about what to expect. Errors in diagnosis, whether delayed, missed, or incorrect, can cause serious harm, so diagnostic accuracy is a major focus of medical training, research, and patient safety efforts.

Okay, so a Solo 401(k) (some people call it a self-employed 401(k) or individual 401(k)) is basically a retirement plan made for self-employed folks and small business owners who don't have any employees besides a spouse. It works a lot like a regular 401(k), just set up for people running their own show. You can put money in as both the employer and the employee, which is the part that makes it pretty powerful. As the employer, you can contribute up to 25% of your net self-employment income, capped at $58,000 for 2021 ($64,500 if you're 50 or older). As the employee, you can put in up to $19,500 for 2021 ($26,000 if you're 50+).

Here's the catch if you also have a job with a 401(k) through an employer. Your total contributions across all 401(k) plans can't go over the annual employee limit, which is $19,500 in 2021 ($26,000 if you're 50 or older). That cap covers everything you put in, whether it's coming from your paycheck as an employee or from the business side as the employer. If you've got Schedule C income, you can base your Solo 401(k) contributions on your net self-employment income from that business, but you'll need to keep both the Solo 401(k) limits and the overall 401(k) limits in mind when you figure out how much to put away. The rules for Solo plans can be different from traditional 401(k)s, so it's worth reading up on the specifics. If you're unsure how any of this shakes out for your situation, talk to a financial planner or tax pro. They can save you from a messy surprise come tax time.

Companies that sell things often use delivery services like UPS, FedEx, or DHL to get packages to people. Those delivery companies are good at bringing packages right to a house or office, where a person can sign for them or where they can be left safely at the door. A P.O. Box is different. It is a small locked mailbox inside a post office building, and it belongs to the post office, not to the delivery company. So a UPS or FedEx driver usually can't drop a package there. Their trucks go to street addresses, and they don't have the keys or the permission to put things into the post office's boxes.

Because of that, many companies only ship to street addresses when they use these private delivery services. Some companies also worry that a P.O. Box makes it harder to check whether an order is real. A street address tells them where a house or business is, and a P.O. Box can be hard to connect to a real person, which can make it easier for scammers to order things with stolen credit cards.

Some companies do accept P.O. Boxes, but they usually send the package through the regular postal service, like USPS, which can deliver to P.O. Boxes. So if a store won't send to your box, it may be because it only uses delivery services that can't reach it. Looking for a shipping option labeled USPS, or asking the company directly, can often solve the problem.

Bottled water costs more than soda at a lot of restaurants, and it's mostly about production and shipping. Every bottle has to be filled, sealed, and labeled, which takes more materials and labor than a can of soda. Then there's the trip to the restaurant, which adds to the price too. Soda, on the other hand, gets made and packaged in huge batches, so the cost per unit stays low. The ingredients are cheap too. Sweeteners and flavorings cost less than purified water, which is weird when you think about it. And honestly, people tend to pay more for bottled water because it feels healthier than soda, so restaurants know they can charge a bit extra for it.

Index investing tends to be tax-friendly because it usually means purchasing and holding a wide range of stocks instead of frequently buying and selling individual shares. Holding in this way can keep taxable capital gains to a minimum. By contrast, active stock trading tends to trigger capital gains more often, which can raise your tax bill. Index funds also typically turn over their holdings less than actively managed funds do, which further lowers the chance of realizing gains. That said, index funds can still produce capital gains, since they sometimes have to sell securities to rebalance or to pay out investors who redeem shares. These gains are generally passed along to fund shareholders rather than kept by the fund itself. If your index fund sits in a taxable account, you will owe taxes on those distributed gains. Overall, index investing can be a tax-efficient approach, but you should stay mindful of possible capital gains and weigh the tax consequences as part of your overall strategy.

Multilinear subspace learning is a family of dimensionality reduction techniques designed to work directly with multidimensional data, known as tensors, rather than flattening that data into long vectors. Many real-world datasets have natural multi-way structure. A grayscale image is a two-way array, a color video is a higher-order array with spatial height, width, color channel, and time dimensions, and a collection of face images captured under different lighting conditions and viewpoints has modes for people, illumination, and pose. Classical methods such as principal component analysis or linear discriminant analysis require vectorizing such data, which destroys the original structure and often produces very high-dimensional vectors with relatively few samples.

The core idea of multilinear subspace learning is to find a separate low-dimensional projection for each mode of the tensor. Instead of learning one large transformation applied to a vector, the method learns a set of smaller matrices, one per dimension, and projects the tensor along each of its modes. The result is a compact core tensor that preserves much of the important information while using far fewer parameters. This approach is motivated by the mathematics of multilinear algebra, particularly tensor decompositions such as the Tucker decomposition, and it generalizes linear subspace methods to the multilinear setting.

Several well-known algorithms fall under this umbrella. Multilinear principal component analysis, sometimes called MPCA or the tensor extension of PCA, seeks projections that maximize captured variance across all modes. Multilinear discriminant analysis extends linear discriminant analysis to tensors by seeking projections that separate classes. Tensor-based methods such as the general tensor discriminant analysis and tensor rank-one decompositions are also commonly discussed. These techniques are typically solved with iterative alternating optimization, where the projection for one mode is updated while the others are held fixed, cycling through the modes until convergence.

The benefits include preserving spatial or structural relationships in the data, reducing the number of parameters that must be estimated, which helps when training samples are limited, and often improving recognition or classification performance. Applications span face recognition, gait recognition, action recognition in video, biomedical signal analysis such as EEG data, and hyperspectral image analysis. Overall, multilinear subspace learning provides a principled way to extract meaningful low-dimensional features from data whose natural form is multidimensional.

Taxes matter in fiscal policy because they're the main way a government gets the money to pay for stuff like schools, roads, hospitals, and social services. Broad-based taxes hit a wide range of goods, services, or activities. Sales tax is a classic example since it applies to most purchases, and value-added taxes (VAT) and other consumption taxes work the same way. Progressive taxes, on the other hand, take a bigger slice of income from people who earn more. So someone making $50,000 a year might pay a lower rate than someone making $100,000. The thinking is that people with more money can afford to chip in a higher share, which can help narrow the gap between rich and poor. Honestly, there's no clear winner between the two. It really depends on what a government is trying to do and what its people care about. Both can raise revenue and hit policy goals, and both come with their own tradeoffs. The best mix usually comes down to a country's specific needs and priorities.

Flank pain, meaning pain in the side of the back between the lower ribs and the hip, has many possible sources, and it helps to sort them by where they come from.

Muscles and ligaments are a very common cause. Strains from lifting, twisting, prolonged poor posture, or an unusual workout can produce a dull ache on one or both sides of the back, and it often worsens with movement or pressing on the area. Irritated spinal joints and discs in the lower back or lower thoracic spine can refer pain out to the flanks as well.

The kidneys sit in this region, so they are a major consideration. Kidney stones usually cause sharp, colicky pain that comes in waves and may spread toward the groin, often with blood in the urine or nausea. A kidney infection (pyelonephritis) typically brings fever, chills, and flank tenderness, and usually a urinary infection beforehand. Less commonly, kidney swelling from other causes can produce a constant dull ache. Since your urine test and bloodwork were normal, some of these are less likely, though a normal urine test doesn't rule out everything, particularly a stone that has not yet caused changes in the urine.

Other organs can refer pain here too. The gallbladder and liver are on the right side, the spleen and pancreas on the left, and the colon can be involved, especially with constipation or inflammation. Pain from the lungs or the lower lung lining can occasionally be felt in the back at the lower rib level. Gynecologic causes, such as ovarian problems in women, can also contribute.

Less often, aortic problems, shingles (which can cause pain before the rash appears), or inflammatory conditions affecting the spine or kidneys are considered.

For your appointment, it may help to note when the pain started, whether it is constant or comes and goes, whether it changes with position, breathing, eating, or urination, and whether you have any fever, nausea, bowel or bladder changes, or unexplained weight loss. Your doctor may want further tests such as a urine culture, an ultrasound, or a CT scan, depending on your history and exam. Seek care promptly if you develop high fever, severe or worsening pain, blood in the urine, vomiting, or difficulty urinating.

No, not in any meaningful way, and the idea runs into several problems. When you buy shares from yourself, the trade doesn't create real demand. You're moving shares between accounts you control, so the market only sees a price that you set. Other investors don't necessarily change their view of the company because of it, and the last trade price can end up being a number that nobody else is willing to pay.

Even if a small trade does lift the quoted price briefly, the price you can sell at depends on the buyers who are actually there. Selling a large block usually pushes the price back down, often sharply, because each sale absorbs the available bids. Stocks that are thinly traded are especially vulnerable to this, which is why a few trades can make a quote look high while the real liquidity is minimal.

The practice is also illegal in most markets. Trading with yourself to create a false appearance of activity or a higher price is called wash trading, and in the United States it's a form of market manipulation under securities law. Regulators such as the SEC and FINRA actively look for patterns like this, and the penalties can include fines, disgorgement of profits, trading bans, and criminal charges. Exchanges and brokers also monitor for it, and cross-account trades between related parties tend to get flagged.

If your goal is to get a good price for shares you hold, the legitimate routes are placing limit orders at the price you want, selling in smaller pieces over time, or, for a large or illiquid holding, finding a buyer through a private sale or a block trade arranged through a broker. If you're trying to understand a specific situation, such as shares in a private company or a stock you think is undervalued, tell me more and I can walk through the options.

Data scraping, also called web scraping, is the automated process of extracting information from websites or other digital sources and converting it into a structured format that can be stored and analyzed. Instead of a person manually copying text, numbers, or images from a web page, a program called a scraper or crawler requests the page, reads its underlying code (usually HTML), and pulls out the specific pieces of data that are needed, such as product prices, news headlines, contact details, or sports statistics. The results are then saved in a spreadsheet, database, or other file for further use.

The technique is widely used for purposes like price comparison, market research, monitoring competitors, aggregating job listings, gathering research data, and training machine learning models. Scrapers can be built with general-purpose programming languages like Python, which offers libraries such as BeautifulSoup and Scrapy, or with point-and-click tools that require little or no coding. Many websites also offer official application programming interfaces (APIs) that provide data in a cleaner, more reliable way, and these are often preferable to scraping when available.

Data scraping raises legal and ethical questions. Website owners may prohibit automated access in their terms of service, and scraping personal information can conflict with privacy laws such as the GDPR. Excessive requests can also overload a server and disrupt a site for other users. Responsible scrapers typically check a site's robots.txt file, which states which parts of the site automated tools may visit, limit the rate of their requests, and respect copyright and data protection rules.

Honestly there are a bunch of reasons cars end up sitting unsold. Dealers might've ordered too many, people's tastes shift, or the market just goes sideways for a while. When that happens, the cars don't just vanish. A lot of them sit on the dealership lot, or get parked at a manufacturer or distributor warehouse, or some other storage place until somebody buys them. Sometimes the dealer gives up waiting and sells them off to wholesalers or runs them through an auction. And every so often a car goes back to the manufacturer or distributor for one reason or another. The thing is, having some unsold stock around is totally normal in the car business. It just takes a while to get supply and demand lined up.

You generally don't need the full cash amount up front. There are several common ways to exercise options when you can't afford the strike price, and which one fits depends on whether your options are listed (publicly traded) or employee stock options.

The most straightforward route for listed options is a cashless exercise, sometimes called a "sell-to-close" or simply selling the options. Instead of exercising and buying the shares, you sell the option contracts themselves on the market. You keep the difference between the sale price and what you paid, and you never need to come up with the strike price. Because an in-the-money option has intrinsic value, its market price already reflects most of what you would have gained by exercising. If you want to own the shares, you can also use a cashless exercise through your broker, where the broker sells just enough of the shares received to cover the strike cost and taxes, and you keep the rest.

Another option is a margin loan or a short-term borrowing arrangement. Many brokers will lend you the money to exercise, secured by the shares or other assets in your account. Be careful here, since margin interest and the risk of a forced sale can erode gains quickly.

For employee stock options, companies often offer a "same-day sale" or "exercise and sell" program, where a broker lends the exercise cost, sells the shares immediately, repays the loan, and gives you the net proceeds. Some companies also allow a "net exercise," where you receive fewer shares, with the value of the withheld shares covering the strike price and taxes. Check your plan documents or ask your equity administrator what is permitted.

Whatever method you choose, be aware of taxes. Exercising nonqualified options typically creates ordinary income equal to the spread between the market price and the strike price, even if you sold nothing. Incentive stock options can trigger alternative minimum tax. Your options also expire, so don't wait too long. A tax professional or financial advisor can help you compare the costs of each approach for your specific situation.

When you sell a stock for more than you paid for it, the profit is called a capital gain, and in most countries it's taxable. The explanation below focuses on the United States, but many countries follow similar principles.

The gain is the sale price minus your cost basis. Your cost basis is generally what you paid for the shares plus any commissions or fees, adjusted for things like stock splits or reinvested dividends. If you sell for less than your basis, you have a capital loss instead.

How long you held the stock matters a great deal. Shares held for one year or less produce a short-term capital gain, which is taxed at your ordinary income tax rate, the same as wages, ranging from 10% up to 37% federally. Shares held for more than one year produce a long-term capital gain, which gets preferential rates of 0%, 15%, or 20% depending on your taxable income. Many middle-income taxpayers pay 15%, and those with lower incomes may pay nothing at all on long-term gains. Higher earners may also owe an additional 3.8% Net Investment Income Tax, and most states tax capital gains as regular income.

Losses can work in your favor. Capital losses first offset capital gains, and if your losses exceed your gains, you can deduct up to $3,000 of the excess against ordinary income each year, carrying any remainder forward to future years. Selling losing positions to offset gains is a strategy known as tax-loss harvesting. However, the wash sale rule disallows the loss if you buy the same or a substantially identical security within 30 days before or after the sale.

If you bought shares of the same stock at different times and prices, the shares you choose to sell affect your gain. Brokers often default to first in, first out, but you can usually designate specific lots, such as the highest-cost shares, to reduce the taxable gain.

Your broker will send Form 1099-B after the year ends showing your sales, and you report them on Form 8949 and Schedule D of your tax return. If you expect a large gain, you may need to make estimated tax payments during the year to avoid underpayment penalties.

Selling inside tax-advantaged accounts like a 401(k), traditional IRA, or Roth IRA doesn't trigger capital gains tax at all. Inherited stock generally gets a "stepped-up" basis equal to its value at the original owner's death, which can eliminate much of the gain. Gifted stock, by contrast, usually carries over the giver's original basis.

If you tell me your country, roughly how long you've held the shares, and your approximate income, I can give you a more specific sense of what you might owe. For large or complicated sales, consulting a tax professional is worthwhile.

Brink Money has advertised high-yield savings rates, and a 5% APY is an unusually high rate, so it's worth checking the fine print. Back in the old messy wars, soldiers had a few ways of showing who was on their side. Flags and banners were a big one, and so were distinctive uniforms or colors you could spot from a distance. They also tried to stick with their own units and follow their commanders' orders, which helped everybody keep track of who was who.

It didn't always work, of course. Things got chaotic, people misread what they were seeing, and sometimes soldiers ended up hurting or killing their own guys by accident. Still, nobody was trying to do that. Most of the effort went into avoiding it as best they could.

Having a bit of pain, swelling, or bruising after a blood draw is fairly common, and these effects typically clear up by themselves in a few days. That said, if the pain gets worse, or the swelling or redness increases, or anything else about your condition worries you, it's wise to reach out to your healthcare provider for an evaluation and advice. They can look at your symptoms and decide on the most appropriate next steps for your particular circumstances.

The first electronic handheld calculator was the "Cal Tech," a prototype developed by Texas Instruments in 1967. It was created by a team led by Jack Kilby, the co-inventor of the integrated circuit, along with Jerry Merryman and James Van Tassel. The Cal Tech could add, subtract, multiply, and divide, and it printed its results on a paper tape instead of using a display screen. It was never sold to the public, but it demonstrated that integrated circuits could make a calculator small enough to hold in the hand.

The first handheld calculators sold commercially appeared shortly afterward. The Canon Pocketronic, released in 1970, was based on the Texas Instruments design. The Busicom LE-120A "HANDY," introduced in 1971, is often credited as the first truly pocket-sized electronic calculator, since it used a single calculator chip and an LED display.

Onions and garlic get their punch from sulfur compounds, and those are the culprits behind the smell. After you eat them, the compounds get absorbed into your bloodstream, then travel to your lungs and come out when you breathe, so your breath stinks. Some of it also leaks out through your sweat, which is why you can sometimes smell like garlic a few hours after dinner. Brushing and rinsing won't fully fix it, and chewing parsley or mint only masks it for a bit. The problem is that these compounds are really volatile, so they float off easily and hit your nose even when nobody's standing right next to you.

I'm sorry you and your husband are going through this. I can't confirm what caused his clots without knowing his full medical history, but I can explain what's known and what options are usually considered next.

Axitinib belongs to a group of drugs called VEGF inhibitors, which block blood vessel growth in tumors. Blood clots, including clots in the lungs (pulmonary embolism), are a recognized side effect of axitinib and are listed in its official prescribing information, although they occur in a small percentage of patients. Cancer itself also raises the risk of clots, as do reduced mobility, recent surgery, and some other conditions. So axitinib may well have contributed, and his doctors were reasonable to stop it, but often the clot results from several factors together. Because his doctors know his situation, their judgment on the cause is likely the most reliable.

There isn't a single "better" medication for everyone with metastatic kidney cancer. The best next choice depends mainly on what he has already received and how his body handles each drug. Today, many patients start treatment with an immunotherapy drug such as nivolumab or pembrolizumab, sometimes combined with another drug. If your husband was on axitinib alone and has never had immunotherapy, an immunotherapy such as nivolumab may be a strong option. Immunotherapy works differently from axitinib and is not particularly associated with blood clots, though it has its own side effects related to the immune system.

Another newer option is belzutifan (brand name Welireg), approved for kidney cancer that has progressed after both immunotherapy and a VEGF-type drug like axitinib. It works through a different pathway and is not known for causing clots. Its main side effects are anemia and low oxygen levels, which his doctors would monitor carefully given his lung history.

Other drugs used after axitinib include cabozantinib, lenvatinib combined with everolimus, tivozanib, and everolimus alone. Cabozantinib in particular often works well after axitinib. However, most of these belong to the same drug family as axitinib and can also carry a risk of clots, so his oncologist would weigh that carefully. In some cases, doctors continue or restart this type of drug while the patient takes a blood thinner, depending on how serious the clot was and how well the cancer was responding.

Some useful questions to ask his oncologist: Has he had immunotherapy before, and if not, is he a candidate? Would belzutifan be appropriate for him? Is it possible to treat the clot with blood thinners and later resume a similar drug, since axitinib was working? And are there clinical trials he could join? Large cancer centers often offer trials of promising new treatments, and you can search for them at clinicaltrials.gov.

It's encouraging that axitinib was helping him for over a year, because it shows his cancer responds to treatment. I hope his oncology team finds a good next step, and please don't hesitate to ask them for a clear explanation of the options and the reasons behind their recommendation.

TED (short for Technology, Entertainment, Design) is a worldwide series of conferences where speakers give brief presentations, typically no longer than 18 minutes, covering subjects such as science, technology, business, education, and the arts. Run by the private non-profit TED organization, these events take place in cities across the globe. They are celebrated for their strong content and varied lineup of presenters, who come from many different professional backgrounds and are often recognized leaders in their fields. The talks are generally filmed and posted online via the TED website and other channels, where they have drawn millions of views from viewers worldwide. Beyond its flagship conferences, TED backs a number of smaller gatherings, including TEDx, TEDWomen, and TEDGlobal, which local groups organize independently using a similar structure. The organization also provides educational materials such as TED-Ed and TED-Ed Clubs, intended to help teachers and students explore a broad range of subjects.

A single tablespoon of water measures roughly 15 milliliters (mL), which is about 0.5 fluid ounces (fl oz). That said, the precise amount can differ a little based on conditions such as temperature and humidity, since these influence the water's density.

Imagine you and your friends each have a pile of candy, and someone says, "Give me one piece of your candy, and I'll let you join my club. Then you can get your friends to give you candy too, and you'll get a share of everything they give." Lots of kids say yes, because it sounds like a fun deal.

Here's the trick. The people at the top of the club get candy from everyone under them. The people at the bottom only get candy if they bring in new kids. Each new kid has to find even more kids to join, and those kids have to find more, and so on. It's like a tower of blocks where every new layer needs a lot more blocks than the one before it.

The problem is that there are only so many kids in the world. Soon, there aren't enough new friends left to recruit, and the kids at the bottom, who joined last, are left with no one to bring in. They lose the candy they gave away, and nobody gives them any back. The people at the top got their candy early and walk away with it, while the bottom layer gets nothing.

That's why they get so big so fast. Each kid who joins is excited to make candy from others, and they recruit their friends, who recruit their friends, spreading very quickly like a rumor. But the money or candy never really comes from selling anything useful. It only comes from new kids joining. So the whole thing eventually runs out of new kids, and most of the people who joined last lose their candy.

Real pyramid schemes work the same way, just with money instead of candy. That's why they're illegal in most places, and why if someone asks you to pay to join and promises you'll get rich by recruiting friends, it's a good idea to say no.

As of December 2021, Twitter had about 330 million monthly active users. Pretty wild number when you think about it. It's basically a place where people fire off short posts called "tweets," which can have text, pictures, or links to pretty much anything online. People use it to swap ideas, catch the latest news, post about their day, or find others into the same stuff they are. A lot of journalists, politicians, and other public figures lean on it too, so it's kind of become a go-to spot for hearing what's going on straight from the source.

I can't determine what is causing your husband's symptoms without more information and a physical exam. Nosebleeds, nausea, dizziness, and sensitivity to light and sound can stem from many different conditions, so he should see a medical professional as soon as he can to find the cause and get appropriate treatment. It's natural to worry about his health and fear something serious, but keep in mind that these symptoms have numerous possible explanations, and not all of them are dangerous. Some possible causes include the following. Anemia is a condition in which the body lacks enough red blood cells to deliver oxygen to its tissues, and it can lead to dizziness, tiredness, and shortness of breath. Dehydration, meaning too little fluid in the body, can bring on dizziness, nausea, and a dry mouth. A head injury or concussion, which can result from a blow to the head, may produce dizziness, headache, and nausea. Migraines are severe headaches that frequently come with nausea and sensitivity to light and sound. Sinusitis, an inflammation of the sinuses, can cause congestion, headache, and dizziness. Again, your husband should consult a healthcare professional promptly so the cause of his symptoms can be identified and treated properly. If he can't get to a doctor in person, he may be able to talk to a provider by phone or through a telemedicine appointment.

A notary is basically a public official who's allowed to handle certain legal tasks, like watching someone sign a document or swearing in a witness. People often end up needing one when they have paperwork that has to be authenticated for use in another country, since most governments recognize notaries as neutral third parties. A lot of the time, a notary's signature and seal are what make a document legally valid. They're expected to stay impartial, and they have to follow pretty strict rules every time they do their job.

Mechanical calculators are devices that do arithmetic with gears, levers, and dials instead of circuits. They were actually the first calculators ever built, long before electronic ones showed up, going back several centuries. The earliest ones appeared in the early 1600s, and they really took off in the 1800s and early 1900s. People used them for all sorts of math: adding, subtracting, multiplying, dividing. Most were run by hand, usually with a crank or lever that turned the gears to get the job done. Eventually electronic calculators took over, since they're smaller, faster, and way easier to use. Still, you'll find mechanical ones here and there, mostly in classrooms or on collectors' shelves.

An island is basically a piece of land that has water all the way around it. That's the main rule. Nobody has a strict official size where land becomes an island, but people usually expect it to be smaller than a continent.

You're not dumb at all, and yes, your thinking is right in a way. Continents are surrounded by water, so in the simplest sense they are very big islands. Australia is a good example. It's surrounded by ocean on every side, so geographers often call it the world's smallest continent, and some people would say it's also the largest island. The difference is mostly about convention. We call the big ones continents and the smaller ones islands, the way we call a very tall hill a mountain and a short one a hill. There's no sharp line between them.

Think of it like this: if you could walk from a piece of land to every other place without getting your feet wet, it's part of the same big land. Australia is cut off by water from every other big land, so it stands alone, and that makes it an island in the simplest sense, just one so huge that we give it its own special name.

A Roth IRA is a special savings account for retirement. The big perk is that you pay taxes on the money you put in now, and in exchange the money can grow over the years and come out later, when you retire, without any tax on the growth. So you get to keep all the gains.

Think of it like a piggy bank with a magic rule. You put in money you've already been taxed on, and it's allowed to grow inside the bank. When you're older (generally after age 59 and a half, and after the account has been open for at least five years), you can take the money out and owe no tax on it. There are also some rules about how much you can put in each year, and your income can affect whether you're allowed to open one.

A mutual fund is a way of pooling money with lots of other people so you can buy a little piece of many different investments at once. Imagine a big bag of marbles that many kids chip in to buy, and each kid gets a share of the whole bag. If the marbles go up in value, your share goes up too. This spreads out the risk, so if one marble breaks, it doesn't ruin everything.

Your Roth IRA is the piggy bank, and mutual funds are some of the things you can put inside it. The insurance agent will likely suggest specific funds to fill it with.

Some questions you could ask at your meeting: What fees do you charge, and what do the funds themselves cost? Are the funds index funds or actively managed? How much risk do they carry, and how does that fit my age and goals? What happens if I need the money early? Asking these will help you follow the conversation and make sure you understand what you're signing up for.

Imagine your belly is like a backpack full of squishy water balloons. Those balloons are your stomach, your intestines, and other soft organs. They're not glued tightly in place. They hang from stretchy straps and sit on top of each other, and all day long gravity pulls them down so they rest on the bottom of the backpack. Your body has gotten used to that feeling, so you don't notice it.

When a roller coaster suddenly drops or a plane dips, you start falling, and for a moment you feel almost weightless. Your bones and muscles are held firmly together, so they drop all at once. The squishy balloons inside don't, though. They lag behind a tiny bit and kind of float up inside you, tugging on their stretchy straps. Your belly is full of little nerve sensors that normally say "everything's sitting where it should be." When the organs float, those sensors shout "hey, something's different!" That shout is the swoopy, tickly feeling.

The tingle down in your private parts comes from a couple of things. The nerves in your lower belly and groin are wired close together and share some of the same pathways to your brain, so when the belly nerves get excited, the feeling can spill over into nearby areas. Also, your body thinks falling might be dangerous, so it quickly releases adrenaline, the "get ready!" chemical. That makes your heart race, changes where your blood flows, and makes a little muscle pull the testicles up closer to your body to protect them. That tightening and the rush of nerve signals together feel like a tingle.

Speeding up forward is different because when a car or plane zooms ahead, the seat pushes against your whole back. Your organs get pressed back along with you, so they're still squished in place and supported. It's like holding the backpack tight against a wall. Falling is the opposite. The thing that normally holds you up, the ground or the seat underneath you, suddenly isn't pushing as hard, so your insides lose their support and get floaty. Your body is very used to gravity pulling down and very sensitive to that pull suddenly going away, so up-and-down changes feel much stranger than forward-and-back ones.

So the tingle is your floaty insides, your busy belly nerves, and your body's "whoa, are we okay?" alarm all happening at once.
