Seek care urgently, the same day if possible, if you notice any of the following: spreading redness or swelling, warmth, pus or fluid, a dark or black toe, severe pain, a open wound, fever, chills, confusion, or feeling generally unwell. These can signal a serious infection that needs prompt treatment.

The term "Mansfield Amendment" refers to a few different pieces of U.S. legislation sponsored by Senator Mike Mansfield of Montana, who served as Senate Majority Leader from 1961 to 1977. The two best known are tied to the Vietnam War era.

The most widely discussed is the 1969 Mansfield Amendment to the Military Procurement Authorization Act for fiscal year 1970. It barred the Department of Defense from using appropriated funds for research unless the research had a direct and apparent relationship to a specific military function or operation. Before this, the Pentagon had funded a great deal of basic research at universities and in other settings, including work in fields with little obvious military connection. Mansfield and others in Congress were concerned about the military's growing influence over academic science and about whether defense money was being spent on projects unrelated to defense needs. The amendment pushed agencies like the Advanced Research Projects Agency (ARPA) to tie their funding more closely to practical military applications. Many historians of science and technology note that it shifted the character of defense research toward more applied work and contributed to a decline in military support for open-ended basic research. A narrower version appeared in the following year's legislation, softening the original language, but the episode had lasting effects on how defense research was justified. Some also argue it indirectly encouraged more civilian science funding through agencies like the National Science Foundation.

The second is a set of Mansfield Amendments from 1971 related to the Vietnam War. These were nonbinding or limited measures urging the president to withdraw U.S. forces from Indochina within a set period, tied to the release of American prisoners of war. A version passed in the Senate and later appeared in modified form in a defense bill as a statement of congressional policy, though it did not force a withdrawal. It reflected growing congressional pressure to end the war.

Mansfield was also behind earlier proposals to reduce the number of U.S. troops stationed in Europe, sometimes called Mansfield resolutions, which argued that European allies should carry more of the defense burden. These were not enacted but influenced later debates on burden sharing within NATO.

Which one people mean usually depends on context. In discussions of science policy, it is nearly always the 1969 research-funding amendment.

In gaming, the term "meta" describes the leading tactics and approaches that players widely adopt in competitive matches. Over time, these approaches tend to appear and mature as players work out the most effective ways to play. Sometimes, game creators deliberately shape certain features to nudge players toward particular styles or tactics. They might, for instance, adjust the abilities of various characters so that some combinations prove stronger than others. Still, the meta can also develop naturally, as players test different tactics and pass along what they learn. This pattern shows up in every competitive title, from a fighting game such as Street Fighter to a team shooter such as Overwatch. In the end, the players taking part are the ones who define the meta. They constantly experiment with new tactics and hunt for any edge over their rivals. Consequently, the meta can shift rapidly as new strategies are found and spread, and developers sometimes have to step in with changes to keep the game balanced and fair.

In Buddhism, karma describes the principle of cause and effect: every deed, whether carried out with the body or the mind, produces results that shape the future of the one who performed it. Buddhist teaching holds that these results are not dictated by a supreme being or deity but follow from the inherent workings of the universe. Each action sets off a sequence of events that may bring either benefit or harm, both to the doer and to the people around them. Because Buddhists accept rebirth, in which a person's consciousness passes into a new body after death, these consequences are not confined to one lifetime and may carry over into future existences. As a result, the choices made in this life can influence what comes later. Karma is understood as a natural law, much like gravity, rather than a system of reward or punishment administered by a god; it is simply the outcome of one's conduct. Rather than trying to pile up good karma, the aim in Buddhism is to pay close attention to one's actions and to develop a compassionate, caring attitude toward all living beings, a path that can ultimately lead to enlightenment.

Cardiovascular disease, commonly called heart disease, refers to a range of conditions that damage the heart and the body's blood vessels, and it is the world's leading cause of death. Several factors can raise a person's chances of developing it. High blood pressure, also known as hypertension, forces the heart and blood vessels to work harder, which makes a heart attack or stroke more likely. High cholesterol is another factor, since excess cholesterol in the blood can accumulate in the arteries and cause atherosclerosis, again raising the likelihood of heart attack and stroke. Smoking harms the blood vessels and adds to the risk of heart disease. People with diabetes are also more vulnerable, particularly when their blood sugar is poorly controlled. Being overweight or obese raises the risk as well, because extra body fat can bring about high blood pressure, high cholesterol, and diabetes. A sedentary lifestyle contributes too, since regular exercise helps keep the heart and blood vessels in good condition. Likewise, a diet rich in saturated fats, trans fats, salt, and sugar can increase the danger. Long-term stress may play a part by elevating blood pressure and altering cholesterol levels. Finally, having relatives with heart disease may put you at higher risk of developing it yourself. To lower your chances of getting heart disease, it is important to live healthily and deal with any risk factors you have. That means eating a nutritious diet, exercising regularly, avoiding tobacco, and managing stress.

Your kidneys are two bean-shaped organs located in the back of your abdomen, one on each side of your spine. They sit just below your rib cage, roughly at the level of your lower back, with the right kidney typically a little lower than the left because the liver takes up space on the right side. They are tucked behind the main abdominal organs, which is why they are considered retroperitoneal, and they are protected by the lower ribs and surrounding fat and muscle.

A Boolean network is a mathematical model used to represent systems whose components can be in one of two states, typically written as on and off, or 1 and 0. Each component, called a node, has a rule that determines its next state based on the current states of other nodes connected to it. Because every node updates according to a logical function, such as AND, OR, or NOT, the whole system evolves in discrete time steps. The structure of the network is usually described by a directed graph, where an arrow from one node to another indicates that the first node influences the second.

These networks were introduced by Stuart Kauffman in the late 1960s as a simplified model of gene regulation, where genes switch each other on or off. Despite their simplicity, they capture important behaviors of complex systems. Starting from a given configuration of all nodes, the network moves through a sequence of states until it reaches a cycle, called an attractor. Some networks settle into a single fixed point, while others oscillate through a repeating set of states. The set of starting states that lead to a particular attractor is called its basin of attraction.

Boolean networks are studied in systems biology, to model gene regulatory and signaling pathways, and in computer science and physics, where they relate to cellular automata and complex systems. Researchers use them to explore questions such as how robust a system is to perturbations, how many stable patterns it can produce, and how its structure determines its dynamics. Extensions include random Boolean networks, which generate rules and connections at random to study typical behavior, and probabilistic Boolean networks, where update rules are chosen with certain probabilities.

Income you receive that does not appear on a 1099-MISC form must still be included on your tax return. This category is commonly called "miscellaneous income." To report it, you would complete Form 1040, the standard individual income tax form. Your total income, including any miscellaneous income, goes on line 1 of that form. Self-employed people and sole proprietors must also list this income on Schedule C (Form 1040), the schedule used for reporting business income or losses. Reporting every dollar you earn is essential, even when no 1099 form was issued, because leaving income off your return can lead to fines and penalties. If you are uncertain how to handle your miscellaneous income, consider speaking with a tax professional or checking IRS guidance.

Imagine someone discovers that tiny pieces of stuff, called atoms, have a huge amount of hidden energy locked inside them, like a giant spring folded up tight. During World War II, the United States was worried that Nazi Germany might figure out how to unlock that energy and build a super-powerful weapon first. So the government gathered a huge team of scientists and engineers, and they worked in secret for several years to build the first atom bombs. In 1945 they dropped two of them on Japan, and the war ended soon after. Because that was the first time anyone had used a weapon that could destroy a whole city in one blast, people everywhere realized the world had changed forever.

It matters so much for a few reasons. The bombs changed how countries think about war, since a single weapon could now do what used to take an entire army. They also started the nuclear age, which led to nuclear power plants that make electricity, and to medicines and tools that use radiation. And for decades afterward, the United States and the Soviet Union built enormous piles of these weapons, which shaped world politics and made people fear that the world could end in an afternoon.

As for the conspiracies, a big reason is secrecy. The project was so hidden that even many people working on it didn't know the whole story, and the government kept its files locked away for years. When people are kept in the dark, they start to imagine what's being hidden. There was also real spying: some scientists did pass secrets to the Soviet Union, so people learned that secrets could be stolen, which made everyone suspicious. Later, the government's treatment of scientists like J. Robert Oppenheimer, who lost his security clearance after being accused of being a risk, made it seem like the official story might not be the whole truth. Add to that the fact that the government did run some tests that exposed people to radiation without telling them, and it became easy for people to believe that other things were being covered up too. Mix all of that with the scary feeling of a brand-new power, and it's no surprise that stories grew around it.

A defibrillator, or AED (automated external defibrillator), is a device that shocks the heart to get it back into a normal rhythm when someone's in cardiac arrest. That's the life-threatening situation where the heart stops beating properly and the person passes out. You don't have to be a medical pro to use one, either. They're built for trained regular folks as well as healthcare workers. You'll usually spot them in airports, schools, and gyms or rec centers, and of course ambulances and hospitals have them too.

If you're going to use one, get proper training first and do what the device tells you. Most of them talk you through each step with voice prompts, so you're not left guessing. You also don't want to use one when it isn't called for, since that can actually hurt the person.

So say you're trained and you come across someone who's unconscious and not breathing. Call emergency services right away, then follow the AED's instructions and give a shock if it says to. Don't dawdle, because survival chances drop a lot with every minute that goes by.

Root beer's basically a carbonated soft drink flavored with a mix of roots and spices. Most folks make it by stirring together water, sugar, and a root beer concentrate or extract, then carbonating it and serving it cold. If you want to try it at home, here's a simple recipe I've used.

You'll need 2 cups granulated sugar, 1 cup water, 2 tablespoons root beer extract, 2 quarts cold water, and 1 teaspoon vanilla extract if you like. Dry ice is optional.

Start by dissolving the sugar in the 1 cup of water in a small saucepan over medium heat, stirring constantly until it's clear. Take it off the heat and let the syrup cool to room temperature. Meanwhile, grab a big pitcher and mix the root beer extract, the 2 quarts of cold water, and the vanilla if you're using it. Stir in the cooled syrup.

Pour everything into bottles or a pitcher and seal it up. If you're using dry ice, drop a small piece into each bottle or into the pitcher, and please handle it with tongs or gloves. It's seriously cold and can burn your skin. The dry ice is what carbonates the drink. No dry ice? You can add a little champagne yeast to each bottle before sealing, which works too. Let it sit at room temp for a few hours so the flavors come together and the fizz builds up, then move it to the fridge until you're ready to drink it.

It makes about 2 quarts, and you can easily scale it up or down. Once you've got the basics down, feel free to play around with different spices and roots to make your own blend.

The Kanab ambersnail, a small land snail found in a few spring-fed wetland sites in southern Utah and northern Arizona (including Vasey's Paradise in Grand Canyon), was first given emergency endangered status by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service in August 1991. That protection was made permanent with a final listing under the Endangered Species Act in 1992. It therefore held endangered status for roughly three decades.

That status has since changed, though not because the snail recovered. Later genetic and morphological studies found that the Kanab ambersnail was not a distinct subspecies but belonged to a more widespread and common ambersnail group. On that basis, the Fish and Wildlife Service moved to remove it from the endangered species list because of a taxonomic error rather than any change in its population. If you need the exact effective date of the delisting, check the Federal Register or the Fish and Wildlife Service's species profile, since my information on when the removal was finalized may not be fully current.

MS-DRGs kicked in on October 1, 2007, and they're basically how Medicare decides how much to pay a hospital for an inpatient stay. CMS uses them to sort stays into groups based on the diagnosis, the procedure, the patient's age and sex, and how the patient was discharged. The idea is to pay more for cases that take more work and resources, and less for simpler ones. They get updated every year too, so they keep up with new treatments and changes in how medicine is practiced.

Charles Dickens lived from February 7, 1812, to June 9, 1870. He was born in Landport, Portsmouth, in England, and died at his home, Gad's Hill Place, near Rochester in Kent. He is remembered as one of the most celebrated novelists of the Victorian era, known for works such as *Oliver Twist*, *A Christmas Carol*, and *Great Expectations*.

Kennywood is an amusement park located in West Mifflin, Pennsylvania, a borough just southeast of downtown Pittsburgh in Allegheny County. It sits on a hillside above the Monongahela River, roughly 10 miles from the city center, and the address is 4800 Kennywood Boulevard.

Most visitors drive there from Pittsburgh by taking Interstate 376 east, then connecting to Route 885 or following signs along Route 51 and Kennywood Boulevard. The trip usually takes about 20 to 25 minutes depending on traffic. The park has large on-site parking lots, so you can park right at the entrance. Public transit options are more limited, though some Pittsburgh Regional Transit bus routes serve the West Mifflin area, so it's worth checking current routes if you don't plan to drive.

Kennywood opened in 1898 and is known as a classic American amusement park, with historic wooden roller coasters such as the Jack Rabbit and the Thunderbolt, along with a carousel and other vintage attractions. It's a National Historic Landmark and a longtime local favorite, typically open seasonally from late spring through early fall, with special events like Phantom Fall Fest in autumn. Hours and dates vary, so check the park's website before you go.

Warren Buffett built his fortune mainly through investing, not through running a single business the way most founders do. He started young, buying stocks as a boy and filing his first tax return at around age 13, and he later studied under Benjamin Graham, the value investing pioneer, at Columbia Business School. His core approach was to find companies he believed were trading for less than their intrinsic worth and hold them for the long term, relying on patience and compounding returns.

His main vehicle became Berkshire Hathaway, a struggling textile maker that he took control of in 1965. Over the following decades he transformed it into a holding company that owned whole businesses outright, such as the insurer GEICO, the railroad BNSF, and the utility operations, and that held large stakes in publicly traded firms like Apple, Coca-Cola, and American Express. Insurance was especially important, because the float, the premiums collected before claims are paid, gave Berkshire a large pool of cheap capital to invest.

Buffett's wealth also grew from the steady compounding of Berkshire's share price over more than fifty years. Much of his net worth remains tied to his Berkshire shares, which is why he became one of the richest people in the world while living modestly in Omaha, Nebraska. He has pledged to give away the bulk of his fortune, much of it through the Gates Foundation and his own family foundations.

When you put bread in a toaster, the heat doesn't just warm it up. It actually changes what the outside of the bread is made of, kind of like a little bit of magic cooking.

Bread has tiny bits of sugar and protein in it. When those get really hot, hotter than boiling water, they start bumping into each other and turning into brand new things. Grown-ups call this the Maillard reaction. Those new things are brown, which is why toast changes color, and they taste and smell yummy, kind of nutty and roasty and a little sweet. It's the same thing that happens when a marshmallow gets golden over a campfire, when cookies brown in the oven, or when a burger gets a tasty crust on the grill. Plain bread never got hot enough on the inside to make those flavors, so toasting adds a bunch of new tastes that weren't there before.

The heat also dries out the outside of the bread. Bread has water in it, and when the water leaves, the bread gets stiff and crunchy instead of soft and squishy. Crunchy food is fun to eat, and the crunch makes it feel more exciting in your mouth. The inside often stays a little soft, so you get crunchy and soft at the same time.

Warm food also smells stronger, and a lot of what we call "taste" is really smell. So warm toast sends lots of good smells up your nose, which makes it seem even more delicious. And because toast is a little dry and warm, butter melts right into it and soaks in, which makes it even better.

So toast tastes better because the heat makes new yummy brown flavors, makes it crunchy, makes it smell stronger, and helps butter melt in.

Honda's first automobile was the T360, a small pickup truck that Honda Motor Co., Ltd. launched in 1963. Its 356 cc inline four-cylinder engine was designed for light commercial work. The sports car that came next, the S500, debuted in 1964 with a 492 cc four-cylinder engine in a straight line, and it was the first Honda automobile sold in the United States. Today, Honda is a leading automaker, building many types of vehicles, among them sedans, hatchbacks, sport utility vehicles, and trucks.

"Nature Boy" was composed by eden ahbez, but it was Nat King Cole who recorded it and brought it to a wide audience. Released in 1948, the single soared to No. 1 on the Billboard chart. Since then, many other performers have recorded their own versions, and the tune is now considered a standard in both jazz and pop music.

Though prostitution is lawful in some countries, and in certain parts of the United States, it is generally against the law across the U.S. and is treated as a punishable crime. All 50 states, the District of Columbia, and every U.S. territory prohibit it, with one exception: some rural counties in Nevada, where it is permitted in licensed brothels. It is worth noting that prostitution and sex work are not identical concepts. Sex work describes trading sexual services, intimacy, or affection in return for money or some other kind of payment. Some people enter sex work voluntarily, whereas others are pushed into it through coercion or exploitation. Certain countries regard sex work as a legitimate occupation and oversee it through government regulation. In the United States, however, it is usually not accepted as legitimate work, and no regulation of it exists.

"Level of agreement" most often refers to how much people, sources, or measurements agree with one another. The phrase shows up in several fields, but the core idea is the same: it describes the degree to which two or more things match or concur.

In statistics and research, it is often measured with tools like Cohen's kappa or the intraclass correlation coefficient, which quantify how consistently different raters or methods reach the same conclusions beyond what chance alone would produce. For example, if two doctors independently diagnose the same set of patients, their level of agreement tells you how reliable the diagnoses are. In surveys, it can describe how strongly respondents agree with a statement, often measured on a scale such as "strongly disagree" to "strongly agree." In a Bland-Altman analysis, it indicates how closely two measurement methods produce the same results.

In everyday usage, it can simply mean how much two people share the same view on something. If you and a friend both think a movie was excellent, you have a high level of agreement; if you disagree on most points, the level is low.

If you tell me the context where you came across the term, such as a textbook, a study, or a survey, I can explain what it means there more specifically.

Stephen Hawking (1942–2018) was a British theoretical physicist and cosmologist, widely regarded as one of the most influential scientists of the late twentieth century. He was born in Oxford, England, and studied at the University of Oxford and then the University of Cambridge, where he spent most of his career and eventually held the prestigious Lucasian Chair of Mathematics, a position once held by Isaac Newton.

Hawking's most celebrated scientific work concerned black holes and the origins of the universe. Working with other physicists, he showed that black holes are not entirely black but should emit radiation, now called Hawking radiation, which implies that black holes slowly lose mass and can eventually evaporate. He also helped develop the theory that the universe had a beginning in a singularity, the Big Bang, and his research connected general relativity with quantum mechanics in ways that continue to shape modern physics. His 1988 book A Brief History of Time, written for a general audience, became an international bestseller and made complex ideas about cosmology accessible to millions of readers.

Hawking was diagnosed in his early twenties with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), a progressive motor neuron disease. He was expected to live only a few years, but he survived for more than five decades, though his physical abilities gradually declined until he communicated mainly through a speech-generating device and relied on a wheelchair. Despite these challenges, he remained an active researcher and public figure, lecturing, writing, and appearing in popular media. He is often seen as an symbol of perseverance and of the power of human curiosity. He died in 2018 in Cambridge, England, and was buried near Isaac Newton in Westminster Abbey.

Diplomatic immunity is a rule that says some government workers who represent their country in another country can't be arrested or put on trial there. It exists so that diplomats can do their jobs without worrying that a foreign government will harass them, arrest them to make a point, or trick them into a fake crime. Imagine if you were sent to play a game at a friend's house on behalf of your whole team. If the other kids could grab you whenever they were angry at your team, you'd never want to go, and talking things out would become impossible. Countries agreed to this rule so they could keep talking to each other even when they disagree.

Family members are covered because diplomats often move to a new country with their husbands, wives, and kids, and the family would be in a tough spot if they could be arrested while the diplomat was protected. The rule is meant to keep the household running smoothly, so the diplomat isn't distracted or pulled away from work. Some family members get full immunity and others get less, depending on the agreement between the countries.

As for robbing a bank and hurting people, no, that is not a free pass. Diplomatic immunity is much narrower than TV shows make it seem. A diplomat who commits a serious crime usually can't be arrested or jailed, but the sending country can choose to waive the immunity so the case can go forward. Often the country instead recalls the person home, where they might face punishment. The host country can also declare the person "persona non grata," which means they must leave. Diplomats also are still expected to obey local laws, and immunity doesn't stop someone from being sent away. It's more like a shield that keeps you from being dragged off to jail by the other country, not a license to break the law and walk free forever.

There are several reasons a person might decide against buying a personal umbrella policy. The most common is cost. Although premiums are often modest relative to the coverage they provide, they are still an added expense, and someone with a tight budget may see it as a lower priority than paying down debt or building savings. Some people also feel they have little to protect. If their net worth is small, they may reason that a judgment exceeding their underlying coverage is unlikely, or that a creditor could only collect so much from them anyway, so the extra protection seems unnecessary.

Others may believe their existing policies are sufficient. Many people already carry auto and homeowners or renters insurance with liability limits, and they may assume those limits are enough for the risks they face. Because an umbrella policy only begins to pay after the underlying limits are exhausted, a person who has never looked closely at those limits may not recognize the gap.

Some people avoid umbrella coverage because they do not fully understand it. The policy's role, how it coordinates with underlying coverage, and what it excludes can be confusing, and a person who is unfamiliar with the product may dismiss it rather than investigate.

Finally, a person whose risk profile is low may simply feel comfortable going without it. If they rarely drive, have no pool or dogs, do not host guests, and have modest assets, they might judge the chance of a large liability claim to be small enough to accept. That judgment is not unreasonable in every case, though it does mean accepting the possibility of a costly uninsured judgment that could affect savings, future wages, and property.

Sharp pain that flares when you tighten the muscles around your bottom, especially during a bowel movement or while sitting on the toilet, usually comes from one of a few common causes. The most likely one is an anal fissure, which is a small tear in the lining of the anus. It often causes sharp pain with bowel movements, and the muscle that surrounds the anus can go into spasm in response, which may be why you feel the urge to clench. Fissures can come back again and again, which fits with your history.

Another possibility is pelvic floor muscle dysfunction, where the muscles that control the anus and rectum tighten when they should relax during a bowel movement. This can cause pain when sitting or straining, and it is often linked to constipation or long periods of sitting on the toilet. Hemorrhoids can also cause pain, particularly if one becomes swollen or develops a clot, though they more often cause itching, bleeding, or a feeling of fullness. Less commonly, the pain could be proctalgia fugax, a brief, intense cramp in the rectum or anus that comes on without warning and passes within seconds to minutes, or coccydynia, which is pain in the tailbone that worsens when sitting.

Because the pain has lasted for years, it's worth seeing a doctor, ideally a general practitioner first, who can refer you to a colorectal specialist if needed. They can examine the area and determine the cause, which usually makes treatment much more effective. You should seek medical care sooner if you notice bleeding, pus or discharge, a lump or swelling that is warm or getting bigger, fever, a change in your bowel habits, or unintended weight loss.

In the meantime, you can reduce strain by eating more fiber, drinking plenty of water, and avoiding long sessions on the toilet or pushing hard. Warm sitz baths (sitting in a few inches of warm water for 10 to 15 minutes) can ease muscle spasm and soothe the area. Keeping the area clean and dry also helps.

The highest point on Oahu is Mount Kaʻala, which rises to about 4,025 feet (1,227 meters) above sea level. It sits in the Waiʻanae Range on the western side of the island. The summit is a flat plateau covered by a rare montane bog, which is protected as part of the Mount Kaʻala Natural Area Reserve. A Federal Aviation Administration radar facility also sits on top, and a paved access road leads to it, though that road is closed to the public. Hikers can reach the summit by trail, most commonly from Waialua on the north side. The route is steep and challenging, with sections that require using fixed cables.

Imagine you go to a store and buy a toy for a few dollars, but the store charges you a fortune for a plastic spoon. That feels unfair, and hospitals work in a similar way, though the reasons are a little more complicated.

Part of the answer is that the electricity is the cheapest thing in the whole picture. A machine might use about as much power as a light bulb, but the price tag on it reflects the years of engineering, the testing needed to prove it is safe, and the cost of making it in small numbers. Each one has to meet strict rules, and the company that makes it has to pay back all that research and paperwork, usually from a small number of big customers like hospitals. Also, a lot of hospital equipment is sold with service contracts, so you are paying for the technicians who keep it working, not just the power it uses.

The bill you get also includes much more than the machine. It covers the nurse who sat with you, the doctor who looked at your scans, the room, the cleaning, the sterile supplies that get thrown away after one use, the insurance the hospital carries in case something goes wrong, and the staff who handle billing. Hospitals also charge different prices to different payers, and the sticker price is often much higher than what insurance actually pays, which makes the whole system confusing.

So the short version is that the device itself may be a small piece of the cost. Most of the money goes to skilled people, safety rules, supplies, and the expense of keeping a building open around the clock. It is still fair to be angry about it, and many people think the system should be more transparent about prices, which is a debate that is still going on.

Sore throat, stuffy nose, and occasional cough often come from the same source: irritation and inflammation in the upper airway. When allergens like pollen, dust, or pet dander land on the lining of your nose and throat, your immune system releases chemicals such as histamine. Those chemicals make the blood vessels swell and the tissue produce extra mucus, which causes congestion and that "stuffy" feeling. Mucus dripping down the back of the throat (postnasal drip) irritates the throat and triggers coughing, and the inflamed tissue itself can feel sore or scratchy. If the sickness also involved a cold virus, the same pattern of inflammation and mucus would occur, so the symptoms can overlap whether the trigger was allergens, a virus, or both.

The crusty eyes you describe are a common companion to this kind of allergy or cold. The eyes share the same immune response: histamine and other inflammatory chemicals irritate the conjunctiva, the thin membrane covering the eye and inside the eyelids. That irritation makes the eyes water, and the tears mix with oil from the eyelid glands and dried mucus. As you sleep, your eyes produce less blinking and tear flow, so this mixture dries into a crust that can glue the lids shut by morning. Rubbing the eyes during the day can spread irritants and worsen the cycle. The crusting tends to ease as the inflammation settles.

It is worth seeing a doctor if the discharge becomes thick, yellow or green and persistent, if one eye is much worse than the other, if you have pain, redness that is intense, light sensitivity, or vision changes, or if symptoms last more than about ten days or keep returning. Warm compresses, gentle eyelid cleaning with a clean damp cloth, saline rinses for the nose, and an over-the-counter antihistamine can help in the meantime.

Several factors explain why certain companies decline to deliver to P.O. boxes. For one, P.O. boxes tend to have less room than a street address, so bulky or irregularly shaped products may not fit. Carriers that rely on aircraft, in particular, can also impose size and weight limits that make P.O. box delivery impossible. Verification is another concern. A courier delivering to a street address can check that the location exists and that the person accepting the parcel is the one meant to receive it, whereas a P.O. box can be opened by anyone who knows the number. Lastly, some businesses do not offer P.O. box delivery at all, either because their systems cannot support it or because it does not fit their broader business strategy.

Imagine you have a wall with two little doors cut into it, side by side, and behind that wall is a big board that catches whatever comes through. Scientists wanted to see what happens when they send tiny things, like bits of light or super tiny particles called electrons, toward those two doors.

First, think about throwing marbles. If you throw lots of marbles at the wall, some go through the left door and some go through the right door. On the board behind, you'd see two piles of marble marks, one behind each door. That makes sense, right? Marbles are little balls, and each one goes through one door or the other.

Now think about water instead. If you make waves in a bathtub and they hit the wall, the wave squeezes through both doors at the same time. On the other side, the two waves spread out and bump into each other. Where a high part meets a high part, the wave gets bigger. Where a high part meets a low part, they cancel out and the water goes flat. So on the board, you'd see a pattern of stripes: strong, weak, strong, weak, many of them, not just two.

Here's the surprising part. When scientists shot tiny electrons at the two doors, one at a time, you'd expect them to act like marbles and make two piles. But they didn't. Little by little, the dots built up into the stripy pattern, the wave pattern. It's as if each tiny electron went through both doors at once, like a wave, and bumped into itself on the other side.

Then it gets even stranger. The scientists said, "Let's watch closely and see which door each electron really goes through." So they put a little detector by the doors to peek. As soon as they did that, the stripes went away, and the electrons made just two piles, like marbles. It's like the tiny things behave one way when nobody checks which door they used, and a different way when someone does.

One small clarification: "watching" doesn't mean a person's eyes have magic powers. It means that to find out which door the electron used, you have to bump into it with something, like a bit of light, and that bump leaves a record of which way it went. Once that information exists anywhere, the wave pattern disappears.

So the big lesson is this: very, very tiny things don't act like the marbles and balls we know. They can act like waves, spreading out and going many ways at once, but when we measure where they are, they show up as single little dots in one spot. Scientists find this weird too. Even grown-up physicists say this experiment holds the main mystery of how the tiny world works, so if it feels confusing, you're in very good company.

If you've got belly pain and bloating, and it's bad or coming with other stuff like fever, vomiting, or diarrhea, get seen as soon as you can. Appendicitis can get serious fast and needs treatment quickly, and what you're describing could be that or something else that's just as worrying. If you can't get hold of your doctor, or you don't have one, just head to the nearest ER or an urgent care center and let them check you out. Don't sit on it, especially if the pain's really intense or it keeps getting worse. Better to go in and find out it's nothing than wait around and end up in worse shape.

The palatine canal is a narrow passage found within the palate, the roof of the oral cavity. It extends from the incisive foramen, a tiny opening near the front teeth in the palate, to the nasopalatine duct, a small passage linking the palate with the nasal cavity. Running through this canal are the nasopalatine nerve and its accompanying blood vessels, which supply sensation and circulation to the palate and nearby tissues. Within the head and neck, this canal is significant, contributing to functions such as taste, speech, and swallowing.

Hair sheds as a normal part of its growth cycle. Each time a strand drops out, another one develops to take its place, which is why the overall volume on your scalp typically stays fairly constant from one day to the next. Still, certain factors can lead some individuals to lose hair, including inherited traits, underlying health conditions, and particular medications. If hair loss is worrying you, consulting a healthcare provider is a sensible step. They can work out what is causing the problem and recommend suitable ways to address it.

Pregnancy can still happen when a condom tears or slips off during sex. How well emergency contraception such as Unwanted 72 works depends on several things, with timing being one of the most important. When it is taken within 72 hours of unprotected intercourse, Unwanted 72 can substantially lower the chance of pregnancy, but it does not guarantee prevention, so a small risk remains. If your girlfriend is worried about becoming pregnant, she should contact a healthcare professional right away. That provider can evaluate her circumstances and advise on what to do next, such as whether another dose of emergency contraception is appropriate or whether a pregnancy test should be done. In most countries, abortion is generally legal in the early weeks of pregnancy, yet access and the specific conditions attached to it differ widely from one region to another, so it is worth learning the rules that apply where you live. Because decisions about pregnancy and abortion are both complicated and deeply personal, it is wise to weigh every option carefully and to lean on trusted people for support and guidance, such as a doctor or counselor.

Imagine your class is picking snack helpers, and the teacher draws the groups on the playground. If the teacher wants a certain kid's friends to win, she can draw the lines so that the other side's friends get all squished into one group and lose everywhere else. That is gerrymandering. In the United States, the people who draw the lines for voting districts are often politicians, and they sometimes draw them so their own party wins more seats than it really deserves.

There are several ways to fix it. One is to take the line-drawing job away from politicians and give it to an independent commission, a group of regular citizens and experts who are not allowed to pick favorites. States like California, Michigan, and Colorado do this. Another is to set clear rules the lines must follow, such as keeping districts compact, keeping towns and counties together, and not splitting neighborhoods for no reason. Some people suggest using computers to draw fair maps, since a computer does not care who wins. Courts can also strike down maps that are too unfair, though in 2019 the U.S. Supreme Court said federal courts will not decide cases about partisan gerrymandering, so state courts and state laws matter a lot now. A different idea is to change how we vote, such as using multi-member districts or proportional representation, so that the lines matter much less. Congress could also pass a national law with rules for every state.

Other countries do have versions of this problem, but many handle it better. Canada, the United Kingdom, and Australia use independent commissions, so line-drawing is less of a fight. Places that use proportional representation, where seats are handed out by the share of votes a party gets, have little to gerrymander at all. Still, unfair districts, or districts that were uneven in size, have shown up in other places too, such as Malaysia, and the U.K. had "rotten boroughs" long ago.

It is not new in the U.S. The word comes from 1812, when Massachusetts governor Elbridge Gerry signed a map with a district shaped so strangely that a newspaper cartoon said it looked like a salamander. Gerry plus salamander became "gerrymander." So it has been around for over 200 years. What has changed is that modern computers and detailed voter data let mapmakers draw unfair lines much more precisely than before, which is why many people worry about it more today.

Existential risk is a term for any threat that could either cause the extinction of humanity or permanently and drastically destroy its long-term potential. The idea was developed most prominently by the philosopher Nick Bostrom, who defined it as a risk where an adverse outcome would either annihilate Earth-originating intelligent life or permanently and drastically curtail its prospects for future flourishing. The key feature is irreversibility: an existential catastrophe is not one that humanity can learn from and recover from, because it closes off the future altogether.

This differs from ordinary disasters, even very terrible ones. A war, a pandemic, or a regional famine can kill millions and still leave civilization able to rebuild. An existential catastrophe would be of a different category, either ending the human story entirely or locking in a permanently diminished state, such as a global totalitarian regime that could never be overthrown, or a collapse so severe that technological civilization could never re-emerge.

Researchers usually separate existential risks into natural and anthropogenic ones. Natural risks include large asteroid or comet impacts, supervolcanic eruptions, and nearby supernovae. These have been present throughout human history, and the fact that we have survived for hundreds of thousands of years suggests their annual probability is quite low. Anthropogenic risks, those created by human activity, are generally considered far more dangerous in the present era. They include nuclear war, engineered pandemics made possible by biotechnology, severe climate change, and the possible development of advanced artificial intelligence whose goals are not aligned with human values. Some estimates, such as those by Toby Ord in his book The Precipice, put the total chance of existential catastrophe this century at around one in six, though such numbers are highly uncertain and debated.

The topic matters to many thinkers because of the scale of what is at stake. If humanity could survive for millions of years and spread beyond Earth, the number of future lives, and the amount of potential value, would be enormous. On this view, even a small reduction in the probability of extinction could be worth more than almost any other benefit we could provide. This reasoning is central to the philosophy of longtermism, though critics argue that it can justify neglecting present suffering, relies on speculative probabilities, or gives too much weight to unlikely scenarios.

Work on existential risk is carried out by academic groups such as the Future of Humanity Institute at Oxford (now closed), the Centre for the Study of Existential Risk at Cambridge, and various other organizations. Their efforts include studying specific threats, improving forecasting, and proposing policies like biosecurity safeguards, arms control, and AI safety research.

The two most common strategies are the avalanche method and the snowball method, and the right choice depends on what motivates you. The avalanche method has you make minimum payments on all your debts, then put every extra dollar toward the one with the highest interest rate. Once that's paid off, you roll its payment into the next-highest rate, and so on. Mathematically, this saves you the most money in interest. The snowball method works similarly, but you target the smallest balance first regardless of interest rate. You get quick wins as individual accounts disappear, which can keep you motivated if you've struggled to stick with a plan before.

Beyond choosing a method, a few steps make a big difference. Start by listing every debt with its balance, interest rate, and minimum payment so you can see the full picture. If you have a budget gap, look for ways to free up cash, such as cutting subscriptions or reducing spending in a few categories. Consider whether you qualify for a lower interest rate through a balance transfer card or a debt consolidation loan, but watch for transfer fees and make sure the new payment schedule actually fits your budget. If your credit card interest is very high and you're behind, a nonprofit credit counselor (often affiliated with the National Foundation for Credit Counseling in the US) can help you build a debt management plan at little or no cost.

Whatever method you pick, automate your minimum payments so you never miss one, since late fees and penalty rates can undo your progress. Then direct any extra income, such as a raise, tax refund, or side earnings, toward the target debt. Consistency over months matters more than the exact order you choose. If you tell me your approximate debts, rates, and monthly budget, I can help you map out a specific payoff timeline.

There are numerous avenues for giving to charity and creating meaningful change in the world. To make sure your contributions are effective and worthwhile, consider the following steps. Start by investigating the organization you're considering: confirm that its mission matches your values and that it is producing real results in the area you care about. Favor groups that openly share their financial details and have a solid history of putting donations to good use. Next, decide which kind of giving suits you best. Options include one-time gifts, recurring monthly contributions, and planned gifts, so weigh which one fits your budget and what you hope to accomplish. It's also wise to understand the tax implications. Depending on your country's laws, charitable donations may be deductible, so keep careful records to claim them when you file your return, where applicable. Stay alert to fraud as well. Some groups falsely present themselves as legitimate charities in order to take people's money, so proceed carefully and verify any organization before you give. Finally, remember that money is not the only form of support. Volunteering your time, spreading awareness of an organization's work, or speaking up for causes you believe in can all make a substantial difference. Following these steps will help ensure your giving has a real impact and advances the causes that matter most to you.

Automatic cars include the gear positions 1, 2, and 3, which are mainly meant for unusual driving conditions or for getting better fuel economy. First gear suits very slow travel, for example climbing a steep hill or trying to gain grip on a slick surface. It sends the greatest amount of power to the wheels, making it easier for the vehicle to move in those situations. Second gear is meant for somewhat faster speeds, such as cruising along level ground or pulling away from a stop. It delivers slightly less power to the wheels than first gear, yet it remains handy for getting the car going. Third gear is intended for faster speeds still, like driving on the highway. It supplies less wheel power than the first two gears, but it lets the car move at higher speeds while burning less fuel. For most situations, the best choice in an automatic car is the "D" (drive) setting, which lets the transmission pick the right gear for the conditions on its own. Selecting 1, 2, or 3 yourself can help in certain circumstances, but ordinary everyday driving generally doesn't call for it.

Variable annuities are financial products commonly bought by people who want to build savings for retirement or other long-range money goals. They come with several advantages, such as the chance for invested money to grow tax-deferred, a range of investment choices, and the ability to later collect guaranteed income payments. Many buyers turn to them to boost income in retirement, while others use them to spread out their portfolio and possibly earn better returns than conventional investments would provide. Keep in mind that variable annuities carry investment risk and are not right for every person. Before making any investment decision, it is wise to weigh your financial objectives and how much risk you can comfortably accept.

This sounds like a chicken-and-egg puzzle, but the trick is that the first chicken didn't have to hatch from the same kind of egg. Imagine you want to build a really good hammer, but to make it you need a hammer. The answer is that you first make a crummy hammer out of a rock and a stick, use that crummy hammer to build a decent hammer, and then use the decent hammer to build an even better one. After that you never need the rock again, because each new hammer can make the next one.

Programming languages work the same way, and this process is called bootstrapping. The very first Java compiler was not written in Java, because Java didn't exist yet. It was written in another language, C. Once that first compiler worked, people could write a Java compiler in Java and then use the old C-based compiler to turn it into a working program. From that point on, the Java compiler could compile its own next version, and the old one could be thrown away. If you go back far enough, every language traces to something simpler, all the way down to people writing raw machine code by hand, the ones and zeros the processor understands directly.

There's another piece to your NetBeans observation. Java programs don't run directly on your computer's processor. When Java code is compiled, it becomes "bytecode," which is like instructions written for an imaginary computer. The Java Virtual Machine, the "Java environment" you saw in Task Manager, is a real program that pretends to be that imaginary computer and runs the bytecode. The JVM itself is mostly written in C and C++, not Java, and it was compiled into normal machine code your computer can run directly. So NetBeans, written in Java, sits on top of the JVM, which sits on your actual hardware.

So when NetBeans compiles your Java code, here's what's happening: a Java compiler, which is itself a Java program that was compiled long ago, is running inside the JVM, reading your Java text and turning it into bytecode. Nothing magical. It's just a program that reads text and writes out instructions, and it doesn't matter what language that program was originally written in, as long as something was already around to compile it first. Java compiling Java is like a cookbook that contains the recipe for printing more cookbooks. You just needed one cookbook to start with.

Imagine two kids each have a favorite toy, and each one says, "My toy is the only real toy, and yours is fake." That's going to start a fight pretty fast. Now imagine two other kids who each have a big box of toys. One says, "I have a dragon toy," and the other says, "Cool, I have a horse toy, maybe your dragon and my horse are friends." They're much less likely to fight over it.

That's part of the answer. Monotheistic religions like Christianity, Islam, and Judaism believe there is one true God, and many of their followers have historically believed that other gods are false. Christianity and Islam also try to spread their faith and bring new people in. When two groups both believe they have the only truth and both want everyone else to join them, they bump into each other a lot. Many polytheistic traditions, like ancient Greek and Roman religion, were more relaxed about other people's gods. The Romans would often just add a conquered people's gods to their own collection or say, "Your god is probably just our god with a different name."

But the bigger answer is that your question's starting idea isn't quite right. Polytheistic and non-monotheistic religions have been involved in plenty of conflicts. The Romans persecuted Christians and Jews. The Aztecs fought wars partly to capture people for sacrifices to their gods. There has been violence between Hindus and Buddhists, and Buddhist-majority Myanmar has carried out terrible violence against Rohingya Muslims. Japan used Shinto, which has many gods, to support its wars in the 1900s.

The reason you mostly hear about monotheistic conflicts is that Christianity and Islam are the two biggest religions in the world, together covering more than half of all people, and they've spread across huge areas where they meet each other. More people and more contact means more chances for fights, and more news stories. Many old polytheistic religions also simply aren't around in big numbers anymore, so they're not in today's headlines.

And one last thing: most "religious" wars aren't really only about religion. They're usually also about land, money, power, and which group gets to be in charge. Religion often acts like a team jersey that tells people which side they're on, even when the real fight is about something else.

Dr. Carter G. Woodson died on April 3, 1950, in Washington, D.C. He was 74 years old and is believed to have died of a heart attack. Often called the "Father of Black History," he founded the Association for the Study of Negro Life and History in 1915 and launched Negro History Week in 1926, which later grew into Black History Month. He was also the second African American, after W.E.B. Du Bois, to earn a PhD from Harvard University.

The "Rule of 9s" is a mnemonic used in trauma medicine to estimate the percentage of a adult's total body surface area (TBSA) affected by burns. The body is divided into regions, each representing roughly 9 percent or a multiple of 9 percent of the total. The head and neck together make up 9 percent, each arm 9 percent, the front of the torso and the back of the torso each 18 percent, each leg 18 percent, and the genitals about 1 percent. By adding up the percentages of the areas burned, a clinician can quickly estimate the extent of the injury, which helps guide fluid resuscitation and treatment decisions. The rule is adapted for children, whose heads are proportionally larger and legs smaller, and it is a rapid estimate rather than a precise measurement.

A redshirt freshman in college football is an athlete who has spent a year with the team without appearing in any games, and who still has eligibility remaining. Such a player earns the label after completing a first year at the school but before taking part in any competition. The word "redshirt" comes from the custom of keeping an athlete out of games for a season so that the clock on their eligibility is stretched out. Coaches often use this approach with players who aren't quite prepared for the demands of college play, or who would gain from another year of practice and development. By redshirting, a player gets a head start on their career and ends up with four seasons of eligibility rather than only three.

Kobe Bryant claimed the NBA Most Valuable Player (MVP) honor a single time during his career. That recognition came in the 2007-2008 campaign, a season in which he guided the Los Angeles Lakers to the top record in the Western Conference and topped the league in scoring. Before earning that MVP distinction, Bryant had already won four NBA championships and been selected to the All-Star game fifteen times.

Okay so the subtractive color model uses cyan, magenta, and yellow as its primaries. You see this stuff in printing, painting, and dyeing, where mixing them soaks up certain wavelengths of light and leaves you with a whole range of colors.

It works like this: when light hits something, the object absorbs some wavelengths and bounces the rest back to your eyes. Those absorbed wavelengths are basically subtracted from what's reflected, which is where the name comes from. Cyan, magenta, and yellow are the go-to primaries because mixing them in different amounts knocks out different chunks of the spectrum. Mix cyan and magenta equally and you get blue. Magenta and yellow together give you red.

Yeah, it's true that hospital visits in the US can get really expensive, especially if you need something major like surgery. A few things drive that. US medical prices are generally higher than in other countries, partly because of pricey new technology and the salaries doctors and other staff earn. The system itself is also set up differently. Most people get insurance through their job or buy it on their own, and that can cost a lot, particularly if you have a pre-existing condition or you're older. If you don't have insurance, or your plan doesn't cover everything, you could be stuck paying a big chunk out of pocket, which is brutal if money's already tight. Government programs like Medicaid and Medicare help with costs. Medicaid covers low-income folks and Medicare covers seniors. But they don't reach everyone, and the coverage often isn't enough to take care of the whole bill.

There are several approaches to imitating the absence of gravity inside an enclosed space like a chamber. One method relies on a centrifuge, a machine that rotates at high speed so that the resulting force produces a simulated gravitational pull. If a person sat inside a centrifuge spinning quickly enough, they would sense that they were in an environment with very little gravity, much like being in orbit. Another option is a so-called zero gravity airplane, which follows a curved route known as a parabolic flight path, climbing and then descending in an arc. While the aircraft is rising, the people on board get a few seconds of weightlessness, similar to what astronauts experience. Still, these techniques merely mimic weightlessness and do not genuinely eliminate gravity from the chamber. True removal of gravity would require a location with no mass or matter nearby to generate a gravitational field, like the enormous void of outer space.

Intellectual property, often abbreviated as IP, refers to legal rights that protect creations of the mind. These creations can be inventions, literary and artistic works, designs, symbols, names, and images used in commerce. The core idea is that a person who creates something new through their intellect should be able to control how it is used and to benefit from it, much as owners of physical property can control and profit from their belongings.

The main categories of intellectual property include patents, copyrights, trademarks, and trade secrets. A patent gives an inventor exclusive rights to make, use, and sell a new and useful invention for a limited period, typically around twenty years, in exchange for publicly disclosing how the invention works. Copyright protects original works of authorship such as books, music, films, software, and paintings, generally for the life of the author plus a number of years. A trademark protects words, logos, slogans, or other signs that distinguish the goods or services of one business from those of others, and it can last indefinitely as long as it remains in use and is renewed. Trade secrets cover confidential business information, such as formulas, customer lists, or manufacturing processes, that gives a company an advantage because it is kept secret.

The purpose of intellectual property law is to encourage innovation and creativity by giving creators a way to earn returns on their efforts, while also balancing the public's interest in access to knowledge and culture. For this reason, protections are usually limited in duration, and certain uses such as education, criticism, and parody may be permitted through exceptions like fair use or fair dealing. Intellectual property rights are enforced through courts and government agencies, and they can be bought, sold, or licensed to others.

Distributed artificial intelligence (DAI) is a subfield of AI concerned with systems in which intelligence is spread across multiple interacting components rather than concentrated in a single central program. These components, often called agents, nodes, or modules, each have some degree of autonomy: they perceive or hold their own piece of information, make local decisions, and communicate or coordinate with one another to solve problems that are too large, too complex, or too geographically dispersed for one system to handle alone.

The field is usually divided into two main branches. The first is distributed problem solving, in which a problem is deliberately split into subtasks that are assigned to different processors or agents, which then work on their parts and combine their results. The second is multi-agent systems, in which several agents, which may have their own goals and even compete or cooperate with one another, interact in a shared environment. Research in this area addresses questions such as how agents should divide work, how they negotiate and resolve conflicts, how they share knowledge, and how a group can reach coherent collective behavior without a central controller.

Distributed AI has practical applications in areas like traffic control, where vehicles or intersections act as local agents; power grid management; robotics teams performing search and rescue; supply chain coordination; and large-scale sensor networks. Its appeal lies in robustness, since the system can keep functioning if one part fails; scalability, since adding more agents can increase capacity; and the ability to respect privacy or organizational boundaries, since each agent can keep its own data local while still contributing to a shared outcome.

John Templeton's warning reflects a conviction that runs through much of market history: investors repeatedly convince themselves that a new environment has rendered old lessons obsolete, and that conviction tends to be expensive. When people say "this time it's different," they are usually pointing to some novel feature of the moment, such as a new technology, a new monetary regime, a structural shift in the economy, or a valuation metric that seems to justify prices that would otherwise look absurd. Some of these claims contain a grain of truth, since economies do change and genuine innovations do occur. The danger lies in treating that sense of novelty as a reason to abandon the discipline of checking prices against fundamentals, assessing risk, and remembering how earlier bubbles and busts unfolded.

Templeton's point was that the phrase is most dangerous precisely when it feels most reasonable. Manias and crashes rarely announce themselves as foolish. Investors in the 1920s, the dot-com era, and the housing boom of the mid-2000s each had persuasive explanations for why the usual constraints no longer applied. Those explanations encouraged people to extrapolate recent gains, lower their guard on leverage, and dismiss warning signs as relics of an outdated way of thinking. When the reversal came, as it always eventually did, the investors who had embraced the phrase were often the most heavily exposed.

Underlying the warning is a broader lesson about human psychology. Markets are driven partly by emotion and herd behavior, and the story that everyone is telling tends to feel uniquely true at the top of a cycle. Templeton, a famously contrarian investor, believed that the safest course was to maintain humility about what one knows, to stay skeptical of narratives that justify excess, and to focus on valuation and the durable principles of sound investing. Recognizing that some things really have changed is wise, but assuming that history has stopped applying is a costly error.

Red eye in photos happens when flash light bounces off the blood vessels at the back of your eye. The retina is basically lit up by the flash, and the camera catches that reddish glow. That's why people's eyes look red in flash shots so often.

A few things make it more likely. The big one is how close the flash sits to the lens. The nearer it is, the more likely you'll get red eye. Pupil size matters too. Dilated pupils let in more light, so they make the problem worse. And since pupils open up wider in dim rooms, red eye tends to show up more in low light.

You can cut down on it in a few ways. Moving the flash farther from the lens helps, and so does using a diffuser, which spreads the light out more evenly. Plenty of cameras also have a red-eye reduction mode that fires a quick burst of light before the main flash. That makes your pupils shrink so less light gets into the eye, and it usually does the trick.

Sorry to hear you've got abdominal pain, back pain, and itching all at once, that sounds miserable. I can't diagnose you or tell you what to take, since I'm only a text-based AI and can't see your history or examine you, but these are worth getting checked by a doctor. If the pain is severe or keeps going, don't wait on it. Plenty of things can cause belly and back pain, like gallbladder trouble, kidney stones, a UTI, or a muscle strain. If you've been told you need your gallbladder out, ask your provider about the risks and benefits, and it's totally fair to get a second opinion if something feels off. If the pain is bad, ask your doctor what's safe for you to take. And again, get seen soon if things are severe or not letting up.

Bogleheads, the followers of Vanguard founder John Bogle's philosophy, usually hold broad, low-cost index funds. The most common global option is Vanguard's Total World Stock Index, which comes as the ETF VT and as a mutual fund (VTWAX for Admiral shares, VTSAX's global counterpart). It holds thousands of companies across developed and emerging markets, with the U.S. making up roughly 60 percent. Other popular choices include iShares MSCI ACWI (ACWI), which tracks a similar all-country index, and Vanguard's FTSE All-World ex-US funds if you want to add international exposure alongside a separate U.S. fund. Fidelity offers a zero-expense-ratio global option, FZROX for U.S. total market and FZILX for international, and Schwab has low-cost broad-market index funds too.

You can buy these at any major brokerage, such as Vanguard, Fidelity, Schwab, or E*Trade, and many smaller brokers also list the ETFs. If you want a simpler setup, Vanguard's Target Retirement funds (such as VTINX or the Target Retirement 2060 fund) bundle global stock and bond index funds into one product that rebalances automatically.

Before buying, confirm the current ticker symbols, expense ratios, and minimum investments on the provider's website, since these change over time.

A boil with swelling under the scrotum, in the perineal area, is most often an abscess, which is a pocket of pus from a bacterial infection, commonly staph. When an abscess drains on its own, that is often part of healing, because the pus is coming out. It does mean the infection was real and sizeable, and that someone needs to make sure it has fully drained and isn't spreading. Antibiotics alone often don't clear an abscess, since the drug struggles to reach inside the pus pocket. Many abscesses need to be opened and drained by a clinician. Sometimes a deeper cavity remains and keeps draining, or there is a tract connecting to the skin, which is why follow-up matters.

The dehydration is probably a result of being sick with infection: fever, poor eating and drinking, sweating, perhaps vomiting or diarrhea from the antibiotics. It is usually treated with fluids. But it also tells you he was ill enough that the infection should be taken seriously.

Some things worth asking the medical team: Was a swab or culture taken from the drainage, and what bacteria grew? Is the antibiotic the right one for that bacteria, including resistant staph (MRSA)? Was an ultrasound done to check for a remaining collection of pus, and to confirm the testicle and epididymis aren't involved? Was the fungal treatment based on a test, or was it a precaution? Does he have any underlying condition such as diabetes, a weak immune system, or skin problems that makes infections more likely? If he is a child or teen, ask about hygiene-related causes like ingrown hairs or friction.

At home, while following the doctors' instructions, keep the area clean with gentle washing, use warm compresses if the doctor approves, cover draining areas with clean dressings, change them often, wash hands thoroughly, avoid squeezing the area, and don't share towels. Finish all antibiotics as prescribed, and make sure he drinks plenty of fluids.

Go back to the hospital right away if he has fever or chills, redness spreading outward, rapidly increasing pain or swelling, skin that turns dark, blistered, or very tender, a foul smell, crackling under the skin, trouble urinating, vomiting, unusual sleepiness or confusion, or severe testicular pain. A rare but serious infection called Fournier's gangrene affects this area and needs emergency surgery, so quick action on those signs matters.

If the drainage continues for more than a few days, or the swelling isn't clearly shrinking, ask for a recheck with a surgeon or urologist instead of waiting. If you tell me his age, whether he has a fever, what the drainage looks like, and which medications he's on, I can help you tailor your questions for the doctor.

Libya's been a mess for years now, and it's hard to keep track of who's who. Back in 2011, people rose up against Muammar Gaddafi, who'd been running the place for over 40 years. That uprising was part of the Arab Spring, when folks across several Middle Eastern and North African countries pushed for more democracy and freedom.
