The cheapest route depends mainly on your state, because sales tax and title fees vary widely, and some states exempt certain transfers between co-owners. Start by finding out whether your state charges sales tax on a transfer between existing co-owners. A few states exempt it, and many others tax the price paid, so call your DMV or check its website before you agree on a number. Also ask whether transfers tied to divorce, separation, or a deceased owner's estate are exempt, since those often have their own rules.

Next, agree on a fair price. Get the vehicle's value from a source like Kelley Blue Book or NADA, adjusted for mileage and condition, and write the agreed price on a bill of sale signed by both of you. Keep in mind that a price far below market value can be treated as a partial gift. That is usually harmless for amounts under the federal annual gift exclusion, which is $19,000 per recipient for 2025, but it can complicate matters in a divorce or estate. Paying the other owner their fair share is the cleanest approach, and it also protects you if the transfer is ever questioned.

If the vehicle has a loan, you will need to either pay it off or refinance it in your name alone, and the lender will usually require the title to be updated as part of that. Some lenders charge a modest fee for changing the borrower.

To complete the transfer, the departing owner signs off on the title, often in a designated "transfer of ownership" section, and both signatures may need to be notarized. Take the signed title, bill of sale, and any required forms to your DMV or county title office. Filing promptly protects both parties, because the departing owner remains partly liable for tickets, tolls, and accidents until the title is changed.

On the tax side, you generally pay no federal income tax on the purchase itself. The departing owner might owe tax on a gain only if they sold the car for more than their adjusted basis, which rarely happens with personal-use vehicles. Losses on personal vehicles are not deductible.

Finally, update the insurance policy to show you as the sole owner, which may lower premiums if the other person was a named driver or the policy was structured around both of you. Doing these steps in the right order, with the correct state exemption and a documented fair price, will keep both taxes and fees as low as the law allows.

An angiogram is basically an x-ray test that lets doctors see your blood vessels, both arteries and veins, from the inside. People usually get one when something's off with blood flow, like a blockage or a narrowed spot. They thread a thin, flexible tube called a catheter into a vessel, usually in the arm or leg, then inject a dye that shows up on the x-rays.

Warfarin is a blood thinner. It keeps clots from forming by interfering with some of the proteins involved in clotting. Doctors tend to prescribe it to folks who are at higher risk of clots, like people who've had a heart attack or stroke or certain heart rhythm problems.

So if your dad has been on warfarin for a long time and recently stopped it ahead of the angiogram, his blood might clot a bit more easily than usual. That doesn't mean the procedure is going to go badly, though. The team doing it will keep a close eye on him, check his vitals, and give meds if needed. Just make sure he sticks to whatever pre-procedure instructions they gave him and tells them every medication he's taking, warfarin included.

Biological vision refers to how living organisms detect and make sense of visual information through their visual system. The process is intricate, relying on the eye, the brain, and the network of neural pathways linking the two. The eye is a specialized organ whose job is to collect light and convert it into electrical signals the brain can interpret. At the back of the eye sits the retina, a thin layer of cells containing photoreceptors known as rods and cones. Rods respond to light and dark and allow the detection of simple shapes and motion. Cones handle color vision, and they respond most strongly to light from the middle of the visible spectrum, around yellow-green. The retina's electrical signals travel to the brain along the optic nerve, and the brain then works on those signals to build a visual image. Doing so engages multiple neural pathways and brain areas, among them the primary visual cortex and the visual association areas. Vision underlies many everyday activities, such as finding one's way around, recognizing objects and people, and communicating with others. Because of its complexity and sophistication, it has received considerable attention from researchers in biology, psychology, and neuroscience.

A soft bump that appears a day or so after a blow to the bridge of the nose is most often a small collection of blood and fluid under the skin (a hematoma) along with general swelling of the soft tissues. In most cases this resolves on its own, and your doctor's advice to use ice is sensible.

In the first 48 to 72 hours after the injury, cold is the most helpful treatment because it narrows blood vessels and limits further bleeding and swelling. Wrap ice or a cold pack in a thin cloth and apply it gently for 10 to 15 minutes at a time, without pressing hard on the nose. Using it a few times a day is fine, and your doctor's twice-daily schedule is reasonable. Keeping your head elevated, such as sleeping on an extra pillow, also helps reduce swelling. If you need pain relief, acetaminophen (paracetamol) is a good choice. Ibuprofen also helps with swelling, though some people prefer to avoid it for the first day or two because of its mild effect on bleeding, so follow your doctor's guidance on this.

Once about three days have passed and the swelling is no longer increasing, many people find that switching to gentle warm compresses, a warm (not hot) damp cloth for 10 to 15 minutes a few times a day, helps the body reabsorb the trapped blood more quickly. It is worth confirming this switch with your doctor since he is already following your case. During recovery, avoid massaging or squeezing the bump, avoid resting glasses on that spot if possible, protect the area from further knocks, and avoid strenuous activity for several days.

As for timing, most of the swelling usually goes down within one to two weeks, and any bruising fades over a similar period, often changing color from purple to green to yellow as it heals. Sometimes a small, firmer lump remains after the softness goes away. This happens when the hematoma organizes into scar-like tissue, and it can take several weeks to a few months to flatten out completely. Occasionally a small lump persists, and a doctor can assess whether anything needs to be done.

You should go back to your doctor, or see an ear, nose and throat specialist, if certain warning signs appear. These include the bump growing larger or becoming more painful, redness, warmth, pus, or fever (which could suggest infection), difficulty breathing through one or both nostrils, or a swollen, bluish bulge inside the nose on the central wall (a septal hematoma, which needs prompt drainage). Other reasons to return are a nose that looks crooked or flattened once the swelling settles, repeated or heavy nosebleeds, clear watery fluid draining from the nose, or problems with vision, severe headache, or dizziness. If there is any question of a broken nose, it is best assessed within about 7 to 10 days, because any realignment is easiest to do in that window.

If the bump stays soft, slowly shrinks, and none of these warning signs appear, it is very likely to resolve on its own with ice early on, possibly warmth later, and some patience.

Dynamic programming is a method for solving complex problems by breaking them down into smaller, overlapping subproblems, solving each subproblem once, and storing its result so it never has to be recalculated. The approach applies when a problem has two key properties: optimal substructure, meaning the best solution to the whole problem can be built from the best solutions to its parts, and overlapping subproblems, meaning the same smaller problems come up again and again during the computation.

Consider the Fibonacci sequence, where each number is the sum of the two before it. A naive recursive program computing the 50th Fibonacci number would recompute the same values an enormous number of times, taking exponential time. Dynamic programming fixes this in one of two ways. In the top-down approach, called memoization, you keep the recursive structure but cache each result the first time it is computed, so later requests return instantly. In the bottom-up approach, called tabulation, you skip recursion entirely and fill a table starting from the smallest cases, using earlier entries to compute later ones. Either way, the work drops from exponential to linear in this example.

The technique is widely used in computer science and operations research for problems such as finding the shortest path in a graph, computing the longest common subsequence of two strings (important in tools like diff), determining the minimum number of coins needed to make change, optimizing resource allocation, and aligning DNA sequences. The main cost is memory, since the stored results must be kept, but in return the method turns problems that would be computationally infeasible into ones that can be solved efficiently.

That big square box on the front of the camera is called a matte box, and it does a few helpful jobs, kind of like the brim of a baseball cap does for your eyes.

The first job is blocking stray light. When you're outside and the sun is off to the side, you squint or put your hand over your eyes so you can see better. A camera lens has the same problem. If sunlight or a bright lamp hits the front of the lens from an angle, it bounces around inside and makes the picture look hazy, washed out, or full of streaks and bright spots called flares. The matte box acts like a big hand shading the lens so only the light from the scene you're filming gets in. It usually has little flaps on the sides and top, called "flags" or "French flags," that can be moved to block light coming from exactly where it's causing trouble.

The second job is holding filters. Filmmakers often put flat pieces of glass in front of the lens to change how the picture looks. Some act like sunglasses and make everything darker so the camera can be set up a certain way, some make the sky darker at the top but leave the bottom alone, and some make things look softer or more dreamy. Those filters are often square or rectangular, and the matte box has slots to slide them in and out quickly without screwing anything onto the lens.

It's square instead of round because the picture the camera records is a rectangle, so a rectangular box can shade the lens closely without cutting off the corners of the image, and the square filters fit neatly inside it.

On a regular DSLR you'd normally use a small round lens hood, but when people use those cameras for serious filmmaking, they add a matte box because it gives them more control over light and makes swapping filters faster. It also just looks very "movie camera," which doesn't hurt.

Prurigo nodularis is a skin condition where hard, itchy bumps pop up on the skin, and it can be a real pain to get under control. Treatment really depends on the person and what's causing it. Doctors often start with antihistamines to take the edge off the itch, plus creams or ointments to calm inflammation. Corticosteroids sometimes come in to bring down swelling, and light therapy (phototherapy) helps some people too.

If you're already doing homeopathic treatment, keep at it if it's working for you, but do let your healthcare provider know what you're using so they can factor it in. Questions or worries are worth bringing up with them too. Try not to scratch or pick at the bumps, since that tends to make things worse and can leave scars. If the itching is really bad or nothing seems to be helping, talk to your doctor about other options. They can help figure out what makes sense for your situation.

Although computers are capable of carrying out a wide range of activities, there are plenty of things they simply cannot accomplish. Certain tasks demand abilities that resemble human qualities, and computers lack these. To illustrate, machines cannot think, feel, or undergo experiences the way people do. Nor can they make choices or work through problems in the manner that humans can. Their capabilities are also bounded by the directions they receive: they can only execute what they have been programmed to perform and cannot reason independently or generate original ideas by themselves. Moreover, computers are restricted to handling the information and data supplied to them. They cannot acquire or comprehend new material unless a person or another machine explicitly instructs them to do so. In short, although computers are highly powerful and able to perform numerous jobs, they cannot match everything humans are capable of, as their abilities are constrained by their programming and by their inability to think, feel, and experience the world as people do.

Pakistan, India, and Bangladesh follow, and together these countries contain a large share of the world's Muslims. Indonesia's position is notable because the Arab world, which is often associated with Islam, is not where most Muslims live; the majority of the global Muslim population is in Asia.

It's understandable to be watching your body closely when you're trying to conceive, and your instinct that it may be too early is probably right. Lower back pain and abdominal cramping can happen in early pregnancy, but they're among the least specific signs, because they're also exactly what many people feel in the days before a period. Progesterone rises after ovulation whether or not an egg was fertilized, and it causes cramping, bloating, breast tenderness, and back aches in both cases, so these sensations can't tell you much either way.

The timing matters too. After sex, it can take several days for ovulation and fertilization to happen, and then another six to twelve days for the fertilized egg to implant. Pregnancy hormones only start building after implantation. If you only started trying two weeks ago, any pregnancy would be very new, and most people don't notice clear symptoms until around the time of a missed period or after. Some people do report mild cramping or light spotting around implantation, but it's usually subtle and hard to tell apart from premenstrual symptoms.

The most reliable approach is to wait until your period is actually late, or at least until the day it's due, and then take a home pregnancy test, ideally with your first morning urine. Testing earlier often gives a negative result even when someone is pregnant, which can be discouraging. If it's negative but your period still hasn't come, test again in a few days to a week.

Do get prompt medical attention if the pain becomes severe, is concentrated on one side, or comes with heavy bleeding, fever, dizziness, fainting, pain in your shoulder, or burning when you urinate. Those can point to something like an infection, an ovarian cyst, or rarely an ectopic pregnancy, which need to be checked.

While you're trying, it's a good idea to start a prenatal vitamin with folic acid if you haven't already, since it helps protect against certain birth defects in the earliest weeks, often before you know you're pregnant. And keep in mind that even for healthy couples, conception often takes several months, so not getting pregnant in the first cycle or two is completely normal.

The right move depends mostly on whether your loans are federal or private, where you are in training, and whether you plan to pursue Public Service Loan Forgiveness. Consolidating and refinancing sound similar but work very differently.

A Federal Direct Consolidation Loan combines multiple federal loans into one, with a fixed rate equal to the weighted average of your existing rates, rounded up to the nearest eighth of a percent. It doesn't lower your interest cost. Its value is administrative and strategic: one servicer, one payment, and sometimes eligibility for repayment plans or PSLF that certain older loan types, such as FFEL or Perkins loans, wouldn't otherwise qualify for. Many medical graduates consolidate right after school to end the grace period early and start making qualifying payments during residency, since residency payments under an income-driven plan are usually small and can count toward PSLF's 120-payment requirement. One caution is that federal repayment rules changed significantly with 2025 legislation, which introduces a new Repayment Assistance Plan and phases out several older income-driven plans for loans made or consolidated after mid-2026. The timing of a consolidation can affect which plans you can access, so check the current rules on studentaid.gov or with your servicer before consolidating.

Refinancing means taking a new loan from a private lender, such as SoFi, Laurel Road, Earnest, Splash, or a credit union, to pay off your existing loans, ideally at a lower rate. For physicians, the savings can be substantial because balances are often $200,000 to $400,000 or more, and Grad PLUS rates have historically been high. Several lenders offer physician-specific products that let residents and fellows pay a token amount, often around $100 a month, until training ends. The major downside is that refinancing federal loans into private ones is irreversible. You permanently lose access to income-driven repayment, PSLF, federal forbearance and deferment options, discharge protections for death or disability (though some private lenders offer this), and any future federal relief programs.

A common framework looks like this. If you plan to work at a nonprofit or academic hospital, keep your loans federal, consolidate if needed, and pursue PSLF, because forgiveness after ten years of mostly residency-level and modest attending payments usually beats any refinancing deal. If you're headed into private practice or a high-paying for-profit setting and plan to pay off aggressively, refinancing often makes sense, frequently right after residency once your attending income qualifies you for the best rates. If you're unsure, staying federal keeps your options open, since you can always refinance later but can never go back. Private loans you already hold carry no federal benefits to lose, so refinancing them whenever you find a better rate is generally low-risk.

Some practical tips: get rate quotes from several lenders, since soft credit checks don't hurt your score. Compare fixed and variable rates, though fixed rates are generally safer on large balances. Look for refinancing cash bonuses, which are common through physician-focused sites. Confirm whether the lender offers death and disability discharge. Partial refinancing is also an option, such as refinancing only your highest-rate loans while keeping the others federal. If your situation is complicated, especially with a high balance, a spouse with loans, or uncertainty about PSLF, a one-time consultation with a student loan specialist familiar with physicians, such as Student Loan Planner, can pay for itself.

If you share where you are in training, your approximate balance and rates, and your likely career path, I can help you think through which approach fits best.

Maxing the HSA after the Roth IRA is a reasonable order, and for many people the HSA is the better account to fund first. It's the only common account that is tax-deductible going in, grows tax-free, and comes out tax-free when used for qualified medical expenses. A Roth gets tax-free growth and withdrawals but no upfront deduction. Your HSA limit is roughly $4,300 for self-only coverage or $8,550 for family coverage in 2025, with an extra $1,000 catch-up contribution once you're 55 or older. Check the current IRS figures, since they change yearly.

To get the most from an HSA, invest the balance rather than leaving it in cash, and if you can afford it, pay current medical bills out of pocket and save the receipts. You can reimburse yourself from the HSA years later, tax-free, which lets the money keep compounding. After age 65, you can withdraw HSA money for any purpose and pay only ordinary income tax, like a traditional IRA, so the account works as a retirement backup as well.

The Roth still has advantages. Contributions can be withdrawn at any time without tax or penalty, and it has no required minimum distributions. So if you're unsure whether you'll have medical costs or want more flexibility, that's a reason to keep some money in the Roth. Also make sure you're capturing any employer 401(k) match before either account, since that's usually the best return available.

Chronic pain in the upper left chest, neck, and upper back often has a musculoskeletal source, but your combination of findings suggests a few possibilities worth discussing with your doctor.

The most common cause is muscle and joint strain in the neck and upper back, such as the trapezius, levator scapulae, or rhomboids, or the small joints of the cervical and upper thoracic spine. Poor posture, desk work, stress, and poor sleep can keep these muscles tight for months. Costochondritis, which is inflammation where the ribs meet the breastbone, can cause left-sided chest wall pain that worsens with movement or pressing on the area. Nerve irritation from the neck, sometimes from a disc or joint problem, can also spread pain into the chest and shoulder blade, so a cervical spine evaluation may be useful.

Your mild mitral valve prolapse and frequent sinus tachycardia deserve attention too. MVP is often linked to atypical chest pain and fatigue, and a fast resting heart rate is commonly associated with postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS) or other forms of dysautonomia. These conditions frequently overlap with chronic widespread pain, headaches, and IBS, and they are more common in people with hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome or hypermobility spectrum disorders. That combination is worth raising with your doctor, because it can change how the pain is managed. Fibromyalgia is largely a diagnosis of exclusion and pattern, so it is reasonable to make sure other contributors have been looked at.

Useful next steps might include blood tests for thyroid function, iron stores (ferritin), vitamin D, B12, and inflammatory markers, a physical therapy evaluation for posture and muscle or joint problems, and a discussion about whether you should be assessed for POTS or hypermobility. If the tachycardia persists, a cardiology or autonomic specialist may help.

Seek prompt medical care if the pain comes on with exertion, is accompanied by shortness of breath, sweating, nausea, fainting, or palpitations that feel different from your usual pattern, or if you develop fever, unexplained weight loss, arm weakness or numbness, or a sudden severe headache. Those symptoms need to be evaluated urgently rather than attributed to your ongoing condition.

Action selection is basically just how an agent picks what to do next in a given situation. Sometimes that means choosing between a few options, sometimes it's figuring out the best move based on whatever the environment or system is doing right now.

A bunch of things can shape the choice: what the agent is trying to achieve, what resources and limits it's working with, and what it expects each action to lead to. It can get pretty messy, especially when goals conflict with each other or when nobody can really predict what an action will cause.

In AI, it's a big part of decision-making, and people tackle it with stuff like planning, reinforcement learning, and decision trees. In cognitive psychology, it ties into cognitive control and executive function, and researchers look at it through decision-making, problem-solving, and goal-directed behavior.

Could be a few things honestly. The most common one is a strained muscle. Laughing works your abs and chest muscles a lot more than you'd think, so if you pulled something there (from working out, coughing a ton, lifting something awkward), it's gonna hurt when you crack up.

A chest infection can do it too. Stuff like bronchitis or pneumonia makes your chest and lungs sore, and laughing puts extra pressure on them, so it stings.

Acid reflux is another one. Laughing squeezes your stomach a bit and can push acid up your esophagus, so if you already deal with reflux you might notice it flaring up when you laugh.

Then there's the scarier but much rarer possibility, something heart-related like angina or even a heart attack. If the pain is bad or won't go away, or you've also got shortness of breath, nausea, or dizziness, don't wait around, get seen right away.

Honestly, if it keeps happening or just feels off to you, it's worth having a doctor take a look so you actually know what's causing it and can get it treated.

Imagine three kids who all have the same great-grandpa, a man named Abraham. They're cousins, so they share a lot: the same old family stories, the same belief that there's one God, and many of the same heroes like Noah, Moses, and Abraham himself. But even though they come from the same family, each cousin tells the most important part of the story differently, and those differences don't fit together.

The biggest disagreement is about Jesus. Christians believe Jesus is God's son, that he died and came back to life, and that this is the center of everything. Jews believe Jesus was a man, not God and not the Messiah, the special savior they're still waiting for. Muslims believe Jesus was a very important prophet, a messenger from God, but not God's son, and they believe he didn't actually die on the cross. You can't believe Jesus is God and also believe he isn't. It's like saying the cookie jar is both full and empty at the same moment.

There's a second disagreement about who had the last word. Muslims believe Muhammad was God's final prophet and that the Quran is God's complete, corrected message. Jews and Christians don't accept Muhammad as a prophet. So if you believe Muhammad is God's last messenger, you're a Muslim; if you don't, you can't really be one.

Each religion also says, in its own way, that its version is the true and complete one. Being a member is less like joining three clubs on different days and more like choosing which answer you believe on a test question with only one right answer. Picking one answer means not picking the others.

That said, people do share a lot across these faiths. Many respect each other, celebrate together, and borrow ideas. Some groups, like the Bahá'í Faith, teach that all these religions came from the same God at different times. And a few individuals mix practices from all three in a personal way. But by the rules each religion sets for itself, you can't fully be all three at once, because their most important beliefs contradict each other.

A grist mill stone is one of the large, heavy stones used to grind grain into flour or meal. In a traditional gristmill, two circular stones were stacked on top of each other. The bottom one, called the bedstone, stayed fixed, while the top one, called the runner stone, turned against it, usually powered by water or wind. Grain was fed through a hole in the center of the upper stone, and as it moved outward between the two grinding surfaces, it was crushed and ground into fine particles.

These stones were typically made from hard, durable rock such as granite, sandstone, or French buhr stone, a porous silica rock prized for its grinding qualities. The faces of the stones were dressed with grooves or furrows, which helped move the grain outward and guided the flour toward the edges where it could be collected. Because the stones wore down over time, millers had to periodically re-dress them by chiseling fresh grooves.

The term can also refer to a grist mill stone as a decorative or historical object, such as a millstone displayed at a historic site or garden, or the name of a particular millstone kept as a relic of an old mill.

Major General Joseph Warren was killed at the Battle of Bunker Hill on June 17, 1775, but the historical record does not name a single individual who shot him. He was a prominent Patriot leader and a physician, and he had been commissioned a major general only days before the battle. As British regulars stormed the redoubt on Breed's Hill during the final assault, Warren was shot in the head at close range. Accounts agree that the killing shot was fired by a British soldier, but the identity of that soldier was never recorded in any reliable source. Some later stories claimed a specific officer or private had done it, but these are generally regarded as unverified.

Triumph motorcycles are made by Triumph Motorcycles Ltd., a British company headquartered in Hinckley, Leicestershire, England. The brand traces its roots to Triumph Engineering Company, founded in Coventry in 1886 by Siegfried Bettmann and Mauritz Schulte, and it has been producing motorcycles under the Triumph name since 1902. Today the company manufactures its bikes at a modern factory in Thailand, while its design and engineering remain based in the UK.

The Netflix Prize was a data science contest run by Netflix, an American company that provides media services and produces content, with the aim of making its movie recommendation engine more accurate. Held between 2006 and 2009, it drew more than 50,000 entrants from 186 nations. Netflix promised $1 million to whichever team could build the best algorithm for forecasting how users would rate films, using their past ratings as the basis. The target was to raise the accuracy of Netflix's recommendations by at least 10 percent, a gain expected to meaningfully boost the company's profits by making customers happier and more likely to stay. The winning entry came from a team named "BellKor's Pragmatic Chaos," whose algorithm exceeded the 10 percent improvement. The prize was divided among its members, a group of researchers from AT&T Labs and the University of Toronto. The Netflix Prize strongly influenced data science and machine learning and helped establish large-scale collaborative competitions as a popular way to move research forward in those fields.

Typically, a new nation comes into being when a group of people decide they want to govern themselves and set their own rules. Their motivation may be dissatisfaction with their current government, or a desire to safeguard a distinct culture and set of traditions. To establish the nation, its founders must work out a plan for how they will run their affairs and look after the people living within its borders. That plan could involve drafting a constitution (a set of rules describing how the government will operate), building a system for choosing leaders, and putting laws in place to protect public safety. After the plan is settled, the new nation must announce its existence to the rest of the world, a step known as "recognition." Other countries may choose to recognize it if they consider the idea sound and if the residents appear content with their new government. Once the nation is up and running, it faces a long list of duties. These can include shielding its population from harm, offering services such as education and healthcare, and ensuring that everyone has enough food and a place to live. It must also build good relations with other countries so that it can trade and work together with them.

I'm sorry you're going through this. Withdrawal on top of chronic pain is miserable, and it makes sense that you feel lost. Let me take the urgent part first and then the bigger question.

Right now, the most important step is to call the pain management practice that prescribed the Suboxone today and tell them plainly that you are in withdrawal and the medication isn't controlling your pain. They can adjust the dose, change the formulation (there are film and tablet versions, and also a long-acting monthly injection that avoids the taste problem), or go back to a different plan. If you can't reach them, call your primary doctor. If you feel very sick, with vomiting you can't stop, severe diarrhea, a racing heart, confusion, or you can't keep fluids down, go to an urgent care or emergency room. Withdrawal from opioids is rarely life-threatening on its own, but dehydration can become serious, and an ER can give you medication to ease it. You can also call SAMHSA's helpline at 1-800-662-4357, which is free, confidential, and open 24/7, and can help you find a prescriber near you.

One important safety point: Suboxone contains buprenorphine, which can cause sudden, worse withdrawal if it's started while methadone is still in your system. Whether that happened to you, or whether you simply stopped methadone abruptly, tell the doctors exactly what you took and when. Please don't go back to methadone or any other opioid on your own, and don't mix in street drugs or someone else's pills, because that is how people get hurt.

As for a permanent cure for back pain, honestly there isn't one single cure, because back pain has many causes. What helps depends on the cause. Some pain, like a disc problem or pinched nerve, can improve a great deal with time, targeted physical therapy, or sometimes procedures such as epidural injections or surgery. Long-term pain often responds best to a combination: physical therapy and gradual strengthening, weight and activity changes, non-opioid medicines (such as certain nerve-pain drugs or anti-inflammatories if safe for you), heat, and sometimes counseling that teaches pain-coping skills. Ask your doctor whether you've had up-to-date imaging and whether a spine specialist, such as a physiatrist or orthopedic or neurosurgeon, should review your case. Many people with chronic back pain feel better over time, even if it isn't a one-time fix.

When you call, it can help to say something like: "I'm in withdrawal, Suboxone isn't working for my pain, and I need an urgent plan today." You deserve a doctor who works with you on both the withdrawal and the underlying pain. Please reach out today rather than waiting it out.

Sorry to hear about your uncle, that's rough. It makes sense that you want to know what he's facing and what the options are.

What they do for a tumor in the esophagus mostly comes down to what type of cancer it is, how far along it is, and how healthy he is otherwise. Surgery to take the tumor out is one route. Chemo is another, and that's basically drugs to kill the cancer cells. Radiation can shrink the tumor too. Plenty of people end up getting a mix of these rather than just one.

As for how long he's got, honestly that's really hard to predict. Every person and every cancer is different, so nobody can give you a solid number without knowing a lot more about his case.

The best thing he can do is stay in close contact with his care team, both to settle on the right plan and to get help with any symptoms he's dealing with. And if you've got specific questions about his treatment or outlook, ask them directly. They know his situation and can give you real answers instead of general stuff like this.

The Kanab ambersnail was listed as endangered under the U.S. Endangered Species Act in 1992, when the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service added it to the federal list. It had been recognized as a distinct species in the years before that, and its status has been reviewed periodically since, so it has now been formally protected as endangered for more than three decades.

The Rhine starts out in the Swiss Alps and winds its way through a bunch of countries before finally spilling into the North Sea. Switzerland, Liechtenstein, Austria, Germany, France, and the Netherlands all get a slice of it. If you pull up a map of Europe, you'll see it cutting right through the middle of the continent, from those mountain beginnings all the way out to the sea.

Stink bombs are constructed from an assortment of substances engineered to release a powerful, foul smell once triggered. Several typical components found in them include rotting eggs or other spoiled foods, which are a frequent source of foul odors and can generate an intensely sickening stench. Ammonia, a chemical famous for its sharp, biting scent and common in cleaning supplies, is another possibility; when combined with other compounds, it can give off an especially repellent smell. Garlic also appears among the ingredients, since its potent aroma is hard to eliminate and can be highly offensive to many people. Skunk spray, the defensive secretion skunks release when threatened, is sometimes imitated through a synthetic version that produces a comparable odor. Additionally, various other chemicals can yield intense, disagreeable smells, such as butyric acid, which is present in vomit, and cadaverine, a compound formed as animal or plant matter decays. It is worth remembering that stink bombs carry risks, since some of their chemical ingredients can cause harm if swallowed or breathed in, so they should be handled and used with care.

Think of a disease like polio as a fire that has gone out in your neighborhood. Nobody has it anymore, so it feels like we could stop keeping the fire extinguishers ready. But the reason the fire went out is that everyone kept those extinguishers ready. If we put them away, the sparks that still exist elsewhere in the world could start a new fire, and since nobody around here has any protection left, it would spread fast.

Polio still exists in a few places in the world, like parts of Pakistan and Afghanistan. Planes, trains, and tourists move between countries every day, so a child who catches it in one place can carry it to another. If the children in your town weren't vaccinated, that visitor could infect them, and those children could pass it on to others. The vaccine works because it teaches each child's body to fight the virus, and when enough people are protected, the virus has nowhere to go. Scientists call this herd immunity.

There's also a practical reason. The people who are most at risk are babies too young to be vaccinated yet, and people whose bodies can't fight off the vaccine well. They depend on the people around them being vaccinated to keep the virus away.

So vaccines are like keeping the fire extinguishers on the wall. Once the fire is out everywhere, we keep the extinguishers ready so it stays out. Your kids getting their shots is exactly what keeps that fire from coming back.

Honestly, you probably shouldn't mix prochlorperazine (Compazine) with immunosuppressants used to prevent transplant rejection. The combo can raise the chance of side effects. Prochlorperazine is an anti-nausea drug from the phenothiazine family, and those can dial down the immune system a bit and make infections more likely, which is the last thing you want when your immune system is already being suppressed on purpose.

If you've had a kidney transplant and you're on rejection meds, tell your doctor or pharmacist about every single thing you take, including over-the-counter stuff. They can tell you whether prochlorperazine is safe for you specifically and suggest something else if it isn't. Don't just stop or start anything on your own. Following your care team's advice and keeping them in the loop on all your meds is the best way to keep things safe.

A nautical mile is defined as exactly 1,852 meters, which works out to about 6,076 feet or roughly 1.15 statute (land) miles. This international definition was adopted in 1929 by the International Hydrographic Conference, and the United States and United Kingdom later adopted it as well, in 1954 and 1970 respectively.

The unit originally came from the geometry of the Earth: one nautical mile corresponds approximately to one minute of arc of latitude, or one sixtieth of a degree, along a meridian. Because of this, it is especially convenient for navigation at sea and in the air, since distances on charts relate directly to latitude and longitude. It is also the basis for the knot, a speed of one nautical mile per hour.

Sitting behind the wheel for hours still takes a lot out of you. Your brain has to stay on high alert the whole time, watching the road, the other cars, and the mirrors, and that kind of focus wears you down. Long stretches of the same view don't help either. Being stuck in one seat for ages can make you feel drained even when you haven't really done anything physical. If you've got a long drive ahead, stop every couple of hours, get out, and stretch your legs. It makes a real difference to your energy.

Egocentric vision describes the view of the surroundings that a person holds from their own vantage point. This view depends on where the person is standing and which way they are facing, and it governs what they can see and notice at any moment. An allocentric, or external, perspective, by contrast, observes the world from an outside, objective position. The egocentric viewpoint, however, is subjective and colored by a person's own experiences and outlook, which can shape how they make sense of the events and objects around them. Psychology and cognitive science treat this concept as significant because it clarifies how people perceive and engage with their environment. It also plays a central role in developing spatial awareness and in the capacity to move through and orient oneself within a space.

Think of a TV show like a big school project that takes a long time to finish. Each episode is one chapter of the same storybook, but a lot of people have to write and draw all those chapters, and not everyone can do every chapter at the same time.

Different directors and writers are used for a few simple reasons. Making a show takes many months, so one person can't do every episode alone. Some people are great at funny episodes and others are great at scary or sad ones. And sometimes a show needs several people working at once so it gets finished on time.

To keep everything matching, the show has a kind of rulebook and a team of helpers. There is usually a head writer or creator who decides what the big story is and what the characters are like, kind of like the person who made the storybook's main idea. Writers get notes about what has already happened, so they don't accidentally make a character forget something. There are also script supervisors, costume and set designers, and actors who keep playing the same character the same way. Sometimes the director even watches earlier episodes to copy the look and feel.

So the episodes come from different people, but they all follow the same map, the same characters, and the same style guide, so the whole show still feels like one story.

There are a bunch of tests that can help figure out why you're having trouble conceiving. Ovulation testing checks for hormones like LH and FSH that show you're ovulating. A semen analysis looks at your husband's sperm count, shape, and how well they move. An HSG is an X-ray where they inject a special dye into the uterus and fallopian tubes to look for blockages or other abnormalities. A pelvic ultrasound uses sound waves to make a picture of your reproductive organs, which can show if anything's off. An endometrial biopsy takes a tiny sample of the uterine lining (the endometrium) to check for problems there. And a laparoscopy is a surgical procedure where they put a small camera into your abdomen to look at the uterus, tubes, and ovaries.

About the pus cells in your husband's semen, that doesn't automatically mean he has an STI. They can show up for all sorts of reasons, like inflammation or irritation. He should talk to his doctor to find out what's causing it and what the best treatment would be. If it does turn out to be an STI, you both need to get treated so it doesn't get passed back and forth. Treatment might improve your chances of conceiving, but nobody can promise it'll happen. Keep working with your doctor on a plan that fits the two of you.

In financial markets, the bid-ask spread refers to the gap between the price a market maker will pay to buy a security (the bid) and the price at which they will sell it (the ask). The bid is the highest price any buyer is prepared to pay for the security, whereas the ask is the lowest price any seller will accept. When the market opens, the spread can shift quickly, since traders are still gauging market conditions and revising their bids and asks. Even so, the bid is usually below the ask, because market makers aim to buy at a lower price and sell at a higher one so they can earn a profit. For this reason, the bid generally appears ahead of the ask at the open. Suppose a security has a bid of $50 and an ask of $51. The spread is then $1, meaning the market maker would purchase the security at $50 and sell it at $51.

Serving sizes on food packaging come from the FDA, the government agency that oversees food safety and labeling. The idea is to give you a rough sense of how much to eat in one sitting. They're based on what people typically eat at one time, but that doesn't always match reality, especially if you're really hungry or trying to eat smaller portions. Think of them as guidelines, not rules. You can eat more or less depending on your own needs. It's also worth checking the other stuff on the label, like calories and nutrients per serving, if you're trying to make healthier choices.

Heart disease is a broad term, but most of the time people mean coronary artery disease, which is the most common form and a leading cause of death worldwide. It develops mainly through a process called atherosclerosis, in which fatty deposits, cholesterol, calcium, and inflammatory cells build up in the walls of the arteries that supply the heart. Over years these plaques narrow and stiffen the arteries, reducing blood flow to the heart muscle. If a plaque ruptures, a blood clot can form on it and suddenly block the artery, causing a heart attack.

Several risk factors drive this process. High blood pressure strains and damages artery walls. High levels of LDL cholesterol (often called "bad" cholesterol) supply the material for plaques, while low HDL cholesterol reduces the body's ability to clear it. Smoking damages blood vessels, promotes clotting, and lowers oxygen in the blood. Diabetes and chronically high blood sugar accelerate artery damage. Obesity, especially fat around the abdomen, is linked to many of these problems, as are physical inactivity and diets high in saturated and trans fats, salt, refined carbohydrates, and processed foods. Heavy alcohol use, chronic stress, and poor sleep can also contribute.

Some risk factors can't be changed. Risk rises with age, men tend to develop heart disease earlier than women (though women's risk increases after menopause), and a family history of early heart disease raises your own risk. Genetics can also cause conditions like familial hypercholesterolemia, which leads to very high cholesterol from birth.

Other types of heart disease have different causes. Heart valve problems can result from congenital defects, aging, or infections such as rheumatic fever. Cardiomyopathy, a disease of the heart muscle itself, can be inherited or caused by alcohol, viral infections, certain medications, or long-standing high blood pressure. Heart rhythm disorders can stem from structural damage, electrolyte imbalances, thyroid problems, or inherited electrical abnormalities. Some people are born with structural heart defects.

The encouraging part is that many of the major causes are modifiable. Not smoking, staying physically active, eating a diet rich in vegetables, fruits, whole grains, legumes, and healthy fats, maintaining a healthy weight, and keeping blood pressure, cholesterol, and blood sugar under control can substantially lower the risk. Regular checkups help catch these problems early, and a doctor can advise on whether medications like statins or blood pressure drugs make sense for your individual situation.

Sorry to hear you're dealing with an allergic reaction and can't get any relief. A few things might help. First, antihistamines: Benadryl isn't your only option. Loratadine (Claritin), cetirizine (Zyrtec), and fexofenadine (Allegra) are all over-the-counter and might work better for you. If one doesn't do much, try another. A cool, wet cloth on the affected spot can calm down the swelling and itch. Over-the-counter creams like hydrocortisone, calamine lotion, or anything with menthol can also take the edge off for a while. Try not to scratch, though I know that's easier said than done. Scratching just makes the rash angrier and can irritate it even more. And if you've figured out what set it off, whether it's a food or a medication, it's worth steering clear of it. If things get worse or the over-the-counter stuff isn't cutting it, get in to see a healthcare provider. They can figure out what's causing the rash and point you toward something that will actually work.

A sociopath is a person who has a hard time caring about other people's feelings, and who often hurts others to get what they want without feeling much guilt or sorrow about it. "Sociopath" is an informal word. Doctors and psychologists more often talk about antisocial personality disorder, which is a real condition that shows up in how a person thinks and acts over many years.

Imagine you have a friend who always wants to win at games. Most kids feel sad when they hurt a friend's feelings, and they want to say sorry and make things right. A sociopath might not feel that tug inside. They might tell small lies, break rules, or take things from others, and they may not feel bad about it afterward. They often understand what other people are feeling, but that understanding doesn't make them want to be kind. It's a bit like knowing where the cookie jar is without caring whether anyone else gets a cookie.

Some common traits people notice are lying often, even when the truth would be easy; charming others at first and then using them; not feeling sorry after hurting someone; getting angry or aggressive quickly; ignoring rules or promises; and acting impulsively without thinking about what might happen next. These traits can show up in other people too, sometimes just because they're having a bad day, so one sign alone doesn't tell you much.

Spotting one is not easy. Sociopaths can seem friendly, funny, and very convincing, especially at the start. Many people who have these traits never hurt anyone, and many people who hurt others are not sociopaths. Only a trained professional can tell whether someone has antisocial personality disorder, and that takes a careful look at their whole life over time.

So the best thing to do is pay attention to how someone treats others, especially people who can't do much to protect themselves. If someone seems to hurt people again and again and never feels bad about it, it's a good idea to keep your distance and talk to a grown-up you trust.

A loss payable clause, usually added to a homeowners policy as a "mortgagee clause" (sometimes called a "loss payee" endorsement), names your mortgage lender as a party with a financial interest in the property. Its main purpose is to protect the lender's collateral. If the home is damaged or destroyed by a covered event, the insurer must include the lender on any claim payment, so the lender can make sure the money goes toward repairing or rebuilding the home rather than being paid only to you.

In practice, the clause works like this. Your lender requires it as a condition of the loan, and the lender is listed on your declarations page with its name and loan number. When a covered claim is paid, the check is typically made out to both you and the lender, or the lender may hold the funds in escrow and release them in stages as repairs progress. For small claims below a set threshold, the insurer may pay you directly. If you pay off the mortgage, the lender's interest ends, and you should ask your insurer to remove the lender from the policy.

The clause also has a useful feature for the lender called the "standard" or "union" mortgage clause. Under it, the lender's coverage can remain valid even if you do something that would otherwise void the policy, such as committing fraud or leaving the home vacant for an extended period. The insurer then pays the lender directly and seeks reimbursement from you. This is why lenders insist on the clause, and it is worth knowing that your own coverage may be affected differently than the lender's.

If you have questions about your specific policy, check the declarations page for the mortgagee listing, or contact your insurance agent and your lender's escrow or insurance department.

China has a long, rich tradition of innovation and invention. Among its most important contributions are the following. Paper is attributed to the Chinese, who created it during the Han Dynasty (202 BC – 220 AD). Printing also began there, as the Chinese built the world's first printing press and used it to produce books, posters, and other materials. The compass is another Chinese achievement, serving as a navigational instrument and a vital aid to exploring the seas. Gunpowder first appeared in China under the Tang Dynasty (618 – 907 AD) and was eventually applied to the making of firearms. Silk production, too, is associated with China, where it originated in the Shang Dynasty (c. 1600 BC – c. 1046 BC). Tea was first grown in China and has been a significant element of Chinese culture for thousands of years. Porcelain, a fine type of ceramic used for dishes, vases, and other ornamental items, is likewise a well-known Chinese product. Acupuncture, a branch of traditional Chinese medicine, involves placing thin needles at particular points on the body to ease pain and encourage healing. Kung Fu, also called Chinese martial arts, is a system of physical, mental, and spiritual training that began in China. The Chinese further created several martial arts weapons, including the staff, spear, and sword, which served both for self-defense and in ceremonies.

TMZ stands for "thirty-mile zone." The term comes from the entertainment industry in Los Angeles, where it refers to a roughly 30-mile radius historically centered on the intersection of West Beverly Boulevard and North La Cienega Boulevard. Film and television studios and labor unions have long used this zone to set work rules. For example, crew members working within it are treated as local hires, while shoots outside it can require extra travel pay or per diem.

The celebrity news website and TV show took the name because the zone is the heart of Hollywood's entertainment world, which is exactly what the outlet covers. TMZ was launched in 2005 by Harvey Levin and became known for breaking celebrity news and gossip stories, often ahead of traditional media outlets.

A sudden fall in a stock's or other security's bid price may stem from several different causes. Among the likely explanations are negative news or rumors concerning the company or its industry, a lowered credit rating for the company, shifts in overall market conditions or investor mood, technical forces such as a large surge of sell orders, and insider selling or other out-of-the-ordinary trading activity. It is worth keeping in mind that the bid price is the most a buyer is prepared to pay for a security, whereas the ask price is the least a seller will accept. The gap between these two figures is called the "spread." A sharp decline in the bid price may signal weaker demand for the security, while a sharp rise may signal stronger demand.

Your husband may have a pinched nerve in his shoulder or arm following his fall. There are several ways to ease a pinched nerve in these areas. First, he should rest the affected limb by steering clear of movements that strain the shoulder or arm. Second, an ice pack applied to the area for 15 to 20 minutes at a time, several times daily, can ease swelling and discomfort. Third, over-the-counter nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), such as ibuprofen or naproxen, may lessen pain and inflammation. Fourth, gentle stretching and strengthening exercises can improve flexibility and range of motion in the limb while also potentially reducing pain. Finally, a heating pad on the affected spot may relax the muscles and boost circulation, which can help with pain. Keep in mind that these measures might not fully resolve the problem. If the pain continues, or if he notices other symptoms such as weakness or loss of function in the limb, he should see a doctor, who can identify the underlying cause and recommend suitable treatment.

Signal processing is the field of engineering and applied mathematics concerned with analyzing, modifying, and extracting useful information from signals. A signal is any quantity that varies over time, space, or some other dimension and carries information, such as a sound wave, a radio transmission, a medical reading from an electrocardiogram, an image, or a stock price series. The goal of signal processing is to take these raw signals and make them more useful, whether by cleaning up noise, compressing data for storage, detecting particular patterns, or converting the signal into a form that is easier to interpret.

The field rests on a combination of mathematical tools, including Fourier analysis, which breaks a signal into the frequencies that compose it, and filtering, which selectively keeps or removes certain frequency components. Engineers also use sampling theory to convert continuous, or analog, signals into discrete digital form without losing essential information, and they use techniques such as convolution, correlation, and wavelet transforms to study how signals behave and interact with systems. Many modern applications rely on digital signal processing, where these operations are carried out by computers or specialized chips.

Signal processing appears throughout everyday technology. Audio systems use it to equalize sound and reduce background hiss, cell phones use it to encode and decode voice and data, medical imaging devices such as MRI and ultrasound use it to reconstruct pictures of the body, and image and video compression formats like JPEG and MP4 depend on it to shrink files while preserving quality. It is also central to radar, sonar, seismology, telecommunications, and the speech recognition systems found in virtual assistants.

There are numerous Christian denominations, and they vary in what they believe and how they worship. Among the most prominent are the following. Baptists hold that baptism is an important sign of a person's faith and devotion to God, and they give the Bible central authority as the guide for their beliefs and conduct. Catholics adhere to the teachings of the Roman Catholic Church, led by the Pope. They affirm the doctrine of the Holy Trinity (God the Father, Jesus the Son, and the Holy Spirit) and regard the sacraments, including baptism and communion, as essential. Methodists stress the value of social justice and of efforts to improve the world. They also emphasize personal faith and grace, the conviction that God's love and forgiveness are offered freely to everyone. Protestants are a varied group who follow the teachings of the Protestant Reformation, a 16th-century movement that aimed to reform the Roman Catholic Church. Protestant congregations treat the Bible as the final authority on truth and encourage each believer to interpret scripture individually. Pentecostals focus on experiencing the Holy Spirit and its gifts, such as speaking in tongues and divine healing. They place great weight on prayer and on cultivating a close, personal relationship with God. These examples represent only some of the many Christian denominations, and numerous others exist. Additional major ones include the Orthodox Church, the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints (Mormons), and Seventh-day Adventists.

A faint line on an at-home pregnancy test may mean you are pregnant, but it could also be a false positive or a positive picked up very early on. If you suspect you could be pregnant, you should confirm the result, either with a more sensitive test such as a blood test or by testing again in a few days. For the repeat, use the first urine of the morning, since that is when levels of the pregnancy hormone human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) tend to be highest. The deep purple line in the other window has nothing to do with whether you are pregnant. Most likely it is a control line, which shows up to indicate that the test is working as it should. If you have had unprotected sex and are noticing possible signs of pregnancy, such as a missed period, tender breasts, nausea, or tiredness, it is wise to see a healthcare provider, who can give you a definite diagnosis and talk through your options. Looking after your reproductive health matters, particularly when you are sexually active.

Plenty of things can shake up the forex market. The big one is central bank decisions. When the Fed or the ECB changes interest rates, it can shift demand for a currency pretty quickly. Political stuff matters too: elections, sudden policy shifts, or something like Brexit can send currency values swinging. Economic data is another driver. GDP numbers or employment reports tell people how a country's economy is doing, so they move the currency accordingly. Natural disasters like hurricanes or earthquakes can hit a country's economy hard and drag its currency down with it. And global trends, like oil prices jumping or a worldwide recession starting, ripple through the market as well. Forex is pretty jumpy to begin with, so traders really need to keep an eye on conditions and expect sudden moves.

A dynamic Bayesian network (DBN) is a kind of probabilistic graphical model that captures how a group of variables and their possible values evolve over time. It extends the standard Bayesian network, a graphical model that describes probabilistic links among variables and their potential values, so that it can account for dependencies that unfold across time. Within a DBN, every variable corresponds to a node in the graph, and the connecting edges indicate how the variables depend on one another. The nodes are organized into layers, where the variables in each layer describe the state of the system at a particular moment. Edges within a single layer capture dependencies among variables at that same moment, whereas edges linking different layers capture dependencies across different moments. Because DBNs model temporal dependencies between variables, they are well suited to systems that change over time and can be used to forecast future states. Such networks see broad use in fields including natural language processing, bioinformatics, and finance.

Online referral systems allow businesses to motivate their customers to recommend the business to friends and relatives. The core concept is simple: the company gives a customer a reward each time that customer's recommendation leads to a successful sale or sign-up. Although these programs can be built in many different ways, they generally follow a few basic stages. First, a customer joins the program and receives a distinctive referral code or link to pass along to people they know. Next, the customer distributes that code or link through social media, email, or personal conversation. When a recipient clicks the link or types in the code, they land on the business's website. If that person then buys something or completes another desired step, such as subscribing to a newsletter, the system records that the referral originated with the existing customer. Once the referral satisfies the program's requirements, usually by making a purchase, the referring customer receives a discount, credit, or some other benefit. Certain programs add tiers, so that customers can unlock greater rewards as they bring in more referrals. Exactly how any given program operates depends on the business and the way it has chosen to configure the system.

Basically, an island is just a chunk of land with water all the way around it. It can be huge or tiny, and it doesn't have a bridge or anything else linking it to other land. A continent, on the other hand, is a big landmass that isn't completely surrounded by water, so it's connected to other land somewhere, whether that's by bridges, tunnels, or some other link. Australia counts as an island. It's a big piece of land with water on every side, and nothing like a bridge ties it to any other land.

Hello, and thank you for reaching out. Brushing three times a day is a good habit, but persistent bad breath (halitosis) often has causes that brushing alone doesn't fix. The most common one is the back of the tongue, which harbors bacteria and food debris. Gently brushing your tongue or using a tongue scraper every morning and night can make a noticeable difference. Flossing once a day is also important, since food caught between the teeth can cause odor that brushing misses. Be sure to clean your toothbrush regularly and replace it every three months or so.

Other common causes include dry mouth, which reduces saliva's natural cleaning effect. Drinking plenty of water, chewing sugar-free gum, and avoiding alcohol and tobacco can help. Some foods such as garlic and onions affect breath for hours, and coffee can contribute as well. Dental problems like gum disease, cavities, or infected gums can also cause odor, so a dental checkup and cleaning is worthwhile if you haven't had one recently. Sinus infections, postnasal drip, tonsil stones, and acid reflux can sometimes cause bad breath too.

If you have tried these steps for a few weeks without improvement, please see a dentist or your primary care doctor. They can find the source and recommend treatment. In Tampa, you can contact a local dental office or a community health clinic for an affordable evaluation.

The GE Building at 30 Rockefeller Plaza was originally called the RCA Building, after the Radio Corporation of America, which was its main tenant and had its headquarters there when the building opened in 1933. The name changed to the GE Building in 1988, when General Electric acquired RCA and took over the naming rights. It has since been renamed again, and is now commonly called 30 Rockefeller Plaza, though many people still know it by its GE or RCA names.

Quantum particles like electrons and photons can act really weird when someone's looking at them or measuring them. One of the best-known quirks is that a particle can be in several states or places at once. Physicists call this superposition. But the moment you measure it, the particle seems to "pick" one specific state or spot. That's the so-called "collapse of the wave function." Basically, looking at it forces it to settle into a single definite state instead of staying in all of them at once. Here's the thing though: none of this really touches everyday life. It only happens at tiny scales with super small particles. It's a fascinating, kind of mind-bending part of the quantum world, but you won't notice it affecting your day in any way.

Think of your body like a house with a bunch of doors. Women's bodies have one special room called the ovary, where eggs are made, and a tube that carries an egg down to a place where a baby can grow. Birth control pills work by keeping that egg from ever leaving its room, so no egg is ready to meet a sperm. Women have the egg part, so the pill goes to the place where the egg lives.

Men make sperm in a different place, and sperm are made all the time, millions every day. That's a bit like a factory that never stops, so you'd have to stop the whole factory, not just one room. Scientists have been working on male versions of the pill for a long time, and some are being tested now, but they're harder to make because the factory keeps running and the medicine has to shut it down safely without causing other problems.

As for the gun idea, you're right that it would be neat to stop the bullet at the source. For birth control, the trouble is that the pill has to work on the body's own systems, and a man's system is more complicated to switch off. There are other options for men already, like condoms and a procedure called a vasectomy, which blocks the sperm's path out of the body. Those are a bit like unloading the gun, and they work well.

The "Starving Time" is what people call the brutal stretch at Jamestown, Virginia, during the winter of 1609-1610. The English colonists had only been there since 1607, and they were already in trouble: not enough food, not enough supplies, lots of people dying from disease and hunger, and fights with the Powhatan people nearby. That winter things got so bad that folks were eating whatever they could scrounge up, including rats, snakes, and, horrifyingly, each other. Many didn't make it. A lot of the suffering came down to bad planning. They hadn't stockpiled enough food or built decent shelter before the cold hit. The nightmare finally ended in spring 1610, when a supply ship showed up from England with food. Even so, Jamestown kept struggling for years, with disease outbreaks and other problems popping up again and again. The colony didn't really start to thrive until the mid-1700s.

So a vector space is basically a bunch of objects called vectors that you can add together and scale by numbers (those numbers are called scalars). Most of the time the scalars are real numbers, but you can also use complex numbers, rationals, or really any field. The adding and scaling have to follow a set of rules called axioms, and those rules are what let you prove most of the basic results in linear algebra.

More formally, a vector space over a field F (people say "over F", or just "vector space" if it's obvious which field) is a set V with two operations that satisfy eight axioms. Here's the list as I know it. Addition: V is an abelian group under vector addition. Scalar multiplication: for any v in V and any c in F, the product cv is still in V. Distributive laws: for u and v in V and c and d in F, (c + d)v = cv + dv, c(u + v) = cu + cv, and (cd)v = c(dv) = d(cv). Additive identity: there's a zero vector 0 in V where v + 0 = v for every v. Additive inverse: every v has a −v in V so that v + (−v) = 0. Multiplicative identity: 1v = v for all v. Compatibility with field multiplication: c(dv) = (cd)v. Compatibility with field addition: c(u + v) = cu + cv for all u, v in V and c, d in F.

Vector spaces are what linear algebra is all about. They're pretty well pinned down by their dimension, which is just the number of vectors in any basis, and by the transformations between them, a.k.a. linear maps.

"I think, therefore I am" is a famous idea from a French philosopher named René Descartes, who lived about 400 years ago. He originally wrote it in Latin as "Cogito, ergo sum."

Imagine you decided to play a game where you try to doubt everything. You ask yourself, "How do I know my bed is real? Maybe I'm dreaming right now. How do I know my eyes aren't tricking me? How do I know a sneaky wizard isn't fooling me about everything I see and hear?" Descartes played exactly this game. He wanted to find at least one thing he could be totally, completely sure about, something nobody could ever trick him on.

He doubted his body, the world around him, even math, because he imagined a powerful trickster could be fooling him about all of it. But then he noticed something. Even while he was doubting everything, he was still doing the doubting. Doubting is a kind of thinking. And if something is thinking, there has to be a "someone" there doing the thinking. You can't have thinking happening with nobody home.

So he realized that even if everything else is fake, the fact that he's thinking proves that he exists in some way. Even if a trickster is fooling him, there has to be a "him" to be fooled. That's the one thing he couldn't doubt.

Here's a simple way to picture it. If you're wondering "Do I exist?", the very fact that you're wondering means you do. A rock doesn't wonder anything. The question itself answers itself.

Descartes used this as a solid starting point, like the first brick in a building, and then tried to work his way back up to figuring out what else he could know for sure. People still argue about how well the rest of his building holds up, but that first brick is one of the most famous ideas in all of philosophy.

Okay, imagine a big family story that spans many years, and it's all about one question: who gets to decide what the world believes and does?

It starts with a woman called The Boss, who is a super soldier and the mother of special soldiers. She trained a man named Snake, who was her student. Long ago, during the Cold War, she pretended to betray her country, and Snake was ordered to kill her. He did, and he became a hero called Big Boss. But it was all a secret trick: she died for her country, and the government lied about it. This made Big Boss very sad and angry, and he decided he could never trust governments again.

So Big Boss started his own army of soldiers who didn't belong to any country, a place where soldiers could just be soldiers. But over time, he got more and more bitter, and his plans grew bigger and scarier. Eventually he fought his own best friends and even his own followers.

Then there's a group called the Patriots, who are like a secret club of very powerful people who secretly control the world's information, and later it turns out they are really just computers (AI) that decide what everybody sees and thinks. Big Boss's old friend and others started this group, but it got out of control.

Big Boss made clones of himself, which are like copies. One of them is Solid Snake, who is a hero. Solid Snake fights Big Boss, who is basically his dad, to stop giant walking tank robots called Metal Gear. These robots can launch nuclear missiles from anywhere. Solid Snake stops them again and again, but each time, it turns out someone bigger was secretly pulling the strings.

Another character, Raiden, is a young soldier who thinks he's a hero in a fake training game but actually is being controlled by the Patriots. He learns that being told what to do isn't the same as choosing for yourself, and he becomes a cyborg ninja.

In the end, Solid Snake gets old very fast because he's a clone, and he teams up with friends to shut down the Patriot computers with a special virus. Big Boss, who was dying, helps one last time, and the two have a final talk. Snake gets to live out his short life in peace.

So the big lesson is: don't let anyone, not governments, not computers, tell you what to believe. Think for yourself, take care of the people you love, and pass on what you've learned to the next generation.

An Army specialist is an enlisted rank in the United States Army, abbreviated SPC, and it sits at pay grade E-4. It is the same pay grade as a corporal, but the two ranks differ in an important way: a corporal is a noncommissioned officer with formal leadership authority, while a specialist is not considered an NCO. Specialists are valued mainly for their technical skills and job proficiency rather than for supervising other soldiers, although in practice they often help guide newer privates and may be given informal leadership responsibilities.

Most soldiers reach specialist after serving as a private first class (E-3). Promotion typically comes after about two years of service and at least six months as a PFC, though waivers can speed this up. Soldiers who enter the Army with a college degree or certain civilian qualifications may start directly at the specialist rank. Because so many soldiers pass through or remain at this grade, specialist is one of the most common ranks in the Army.

The insignia for a specialist is a shield-like shape, sometimes jokingly called the "sham shield," featuring an eagle. It is worn centered on the chest of the uniform.

The rank has its roots in a broader system the Army created in the 1950s, when there were multiple specialist grades running parallel to the NCO ranks from E-4 up to E-9 for technically skilled soldiers. Over time the higher specialist grades were phased out, and by 1985 only the E-4 specialist remained. From specialist, a soldier who demonstrates leadership potential is usually promoted to sergeant (E-5), the first full NCO rank, sometimes moving through corporal first if assigned to a leadership position.

It looks like the specific details didn't come through with your message, so I only see the subject line. I'm happy to dig into your ISO situation once I know what you're dealing with.

The details that usually matter most are your grant price (the strike price), the fair market value of the shares when you exercised or plan to exercise, how many shares are involved, and the relevant dates: when the options were granted, when you exercised, and when you sold or plan to sell. It also helps to know whether you're worried about the alternative minimum tax in the year of exercise, whether you're trying to figure out if a sale counts as a qualifying or disqualifying disposition, or whether you're trying to read your Form 3921 or report something on your return. If the company is private, or if you did an early exercise with an 83(b) election, mention that too, because both change the analysis.

For context while you gather that, the general framework is this. Exercising ISOs and holding the shares doesn't create regular income tax, but the spread between the strike price and the fair market value at exercise counts as an adjustment for the alternative minimum tax. If you hold the shares at least two years from the grant date and at least one year from the exercise date, the whole gain from strike price to sale price is long-term capital gain. If you sell before meeting both holding periods, it's a disqualifying disposition. Part of the gain, generally the spread at exercise, or the actual gain if that's smaller, is taxed as ordinary compensation income, and any remaining gain is capital gain. Also, your cost basis for regular tax and for AMT purposes can differ, which often causes confusion when people sell in a later year.

Send along your numbers and what you're trying to decide or calculate, and I'll walk through it with you.
Kirstie Alley played Rebecca Howe on *Cheers* from 1987 to 1993. She joined the show in its fifth season, replacing Shelley Long as the bar's manager, and stayed through the series finale in 1993.

The Human Brain Project (HBP) is a research initiative designed to deepen our knowledge of the human brain and to create new technologies grounded in that knowledge. Funded by the European Union and started in 2013, it is a major international undertaking that brings together scientists and researchers from fields such as neuroscience, computer science, and engineering. Its central aim is to construct a detailed, multilevel model of the human brain, drawing on information and insights from many sources, including brain imaging, electrophysiology, genetics, and behavioral research. Researchers will use this model to simulate how the brain is active and to examine hypotheses about how it functions. The project also seeks to produce new tools and technologies for studying the brain, among them brain-machine interfaces and computing systems modeled on the brain.
