A key priority is gaining a better grasp of brain diseases and disorders, including Alzheimer's disease, stroke, and depression, so that new treatments and therapies can be developed. In addition, the HBP hopes to push artificial intelligence forward by designing algorithms and systems that take their inspiration from the structure and workings of the human brain.

Machine perception is the ability of a computer system to interpret data from the world in a way that resembles how humans and animals use their senses. Rather than simply receiving raw input such as pixels, sound waves, or sensor readings, a machine with perception can recognize objects, understand speech, detect patterns, and build a meaningful picture of its surroundings.

The field draws on sensors, which gather the raw signals, and on algorithms, which transform those signals into useful information. A camera captures light as an array of numbers, for example, but machine perception turns those numbers into conclusions such as "this is a pedestrian crossing the street" or "this is a handwritten digit seven." Similar processes apply to microphones feeding speech recognition, lidar and radar feeding autonomous vehicles, and tactile sensors feeding robotic grippers.

Modern machine perception relies heavily on machine learning, especially deep neural networks, which learn to extract features from large collections of labeled examples. Earlier approaches depended more on hand-crafted rules and feature detectors designed by engineers. Today the two approaches are often combined, with learned models working alongside geometric reasoning and explicit knowledge about the environment.

Machine perception underpins many everyday technologies, including face unlock on phones, medical image analysis, quality inspection in factories, voice assistants, and navigation systems for drones and self-driving cars. It is closely related to computer vision and speech recognition, which can be viewed as its major subfields, and it connects to robotics, since a robot must perceive its environment before it can act within it.

Cancer is not really one lump in one place. It is made of cells that started growing out of control, and sometimes those cells have already traveled through the body before anyone knows they are there. Cutting out the spot you can see is like pulling one weed when the roots have spread under the whole garden.

Here is a simple way to picture it. Your body is made of tiny building blocks called cells, and each cell has instructions telling it when to grow, when to rest, and when to stop. Sometimes a cell gets a mix-up in its instructions and starts making copies of itself without stopping. If those copies stay in one spot, a doctor can often cut them out and that really is the end of it. But some of the copies can break loose, float through the blood or the fluid in your body, and settle somewhere else to start a new group. Those tiny travelers are often too small to see on a scan or feel with your hands.

That is why doctors sometimes do more than surgery. They might use medicine that travels through the whole body to hunt down cells that wandered off, or radiation that targets a particular area. For testicular cancer specifically, it is often caught early and removing the testicle is the main treatment, and many people are cured that way, sometimes with extra medicine to catch any stray cells. So surgery is often a big part of the answer, but it is not always the only part.

Stomach pain combined with dizziness can stem from a wide range of causes, and an accurate diagnosis isn't possible without a full examination by a healthcare provider. Several conditions could account for these symptoms. Digestive issues such as indigestion, acid reflux, or an ulcer may produce both stomach pain and lightheadedness. Infections, including food poisoning or a stomach virus, can also trigger them. Problems involving the heart or blood vessels, for example angina or a heart attack, may cause dizziness along with abdominal discomfort. Dehydration is another possible culprit, as is psychological strain like stress or anxiety. Your father should see a healthcare provider to get a proper diagnosis and appropriate treatment. Attempting to diagnose or treat these symptoms on his own is unwise, since they may point to any of several serious medical conditions.

Surgery cannot cure polio itself, because the damage to the nerves that control the leg muscles is permanent. But surgery and related treatments can often make a real difference in how well someone with post-polio leg problems walks, and at 31 your fiancée is very much still a candidate for them. The realistic goal is better function, balance, and appearance, not restoring the leg to how it would have been.

The options depend on what exactly is wrong, and an orthopedic surgeon with experience in polio or neuromuscular conditions is the right person to sort that out. For a leg length difference, the choices include limb lengthening, where the bone is gradually stretched using an external frame or an internal lengthening nail, or sometimes shortening the longer leg, which is less common. Lengthening is a long process lasting months, with risks such as infection, stiffness, and nerve or joint problems, and it works best when the muscles are strong enough to support the longer limb. If the muscles are very weak, lengthening can sometimes make walking harder.

Other procedures address weak or imbalanced muscles and deformities. Tendon transfers move a working muscle's tendon to take over the job of a paralyzed one, for example to help lift the foot or stabilize the knee. Surgeons can also correct foot or ankle deformities, or stabilize an unstable joint. Often these are combined with bracing.

Non-surgical help matters a lot and is often part of the plan even after surgery. A shoe lift or built-up shoe can fix a modest length difference immediately and cheaply. A lightweight brace, such as an ankle-foot orthosis or a knee-ankle-foot orthosis, can improve stability and reduce fatigue. Physiotherapy to strengthen the remaining muscles, and gait training, can improve walking noticeably. Many people find that a shoe lift plus a brace gets them most of the benefit with no surgical risk, so it is worth trying these first or alongside any surgical plan.

Before deciding, I would suggest she have a full assessment, including muscle strength testing, X-rays of the legs and spine, a measurement of the exact length difference, and a gait analysis. Ask the surgeon what specifically they expect to improve, how long recovery takes, what the risks are, and what happens if the result is only partial. Getting a second opinion is reasonable for a major procedure. It is also worth knowing that people who had polio sometimes develop new fatigue and weakness decades later, so the surgeon should consider her long-term picture.

On the confidence side, the decision should be hers, made because she wants it, not because others think she should. Many people in her situation find that better mobility, a well-fitted shoe, and good support from a partner help their confidence a great deal. Your supportive attitude is already valuable. If her low confidence is affecting her daily life, talking with a counselor can help alongside any physical treatment.

A stop sign is a traffic sign telling drivers they must come to a full halt at a stop line, a crosswalk, or before entering a through street or intersection. Usually eight-sided and red, it is commonly fixed to a tall post beside the roadway. Upon reaching one, a driver has to stop the vehicle completely before moving on. Any pedestrians or other vehicles already in the intersection or crosswalk take priority over the driver. Even when the intersection looks clear, the driver may continue only after checking for hazards or vehicles that could be coming toward them. Stop signs appear at intersections and other spots where collisions are likely or where people on foot may be crossing. As a key element of traffic control, they keep vehicles moving in an orderly way and protect everyone using the road.

Price history graphs take their shape from the interplay of supply and demand, which is the fundamental force behind almost every price movement. When buyers want more of a good than sellers are willing to provide at the current price, prices tend to rise, and when sellers have more to offer than buyers want, prices tend to fall. Each shift in either curve, whether caused by a change in consumer tastes, production costs, technology, or the number of participants in a market, produces a new equilibrium and therefore a new point on the chart.

Beyond these basic economic forces, the particular shape of a graph depends on the characteristics of the asset or good itself. Commodities such as oil or wheat often show cyclical patterns tied to harvests, weather, and geopolitical events, while stocks tend to reflect expectations about future earnings and the broader health of the economy. Currencies respond to interest rates, inflation, and trade balances, and collectibles or housing can be shaped heavily by speculation, scarcity, and local conditions.

Finally, the way the graph is drawn matters as much as the underlying data. The time span chosen, whether daily, monthly, or decades, determines whether short-term volatility or long-term trends dominate the picture. The scale of the vertical axis, whether linear or logarithmic, can make the same movement look dramatic or modest. Adjustments for inflation, dividends, or currency changes further alter the appearance of the line. So the shape reflects both the real economic forces at work and the choices made in presenting them.

Escrow is like a neutral referee holding something valuable until everyone has done what they promised. Imagine you and a friend agree to trade baseball cards, but you don't trust each other to go first. So you both hand your cards to a trusted grown-up, who keeps them safe. Once you both agree the trade is fair, the grown-up hands each person the other's card. Nobody can cheat, because nobody gets anything until everything is ready.

When you buy a house, escrow works the same way. The money you're paying, and the paperwork that proves the seller is giving up ownership, are both held by a neutral third party, usually an escrow company or a title company. You send your down payment and loan money there, and the seller signs the deed and other documents there too. The escrow officer checks that everything is correct, like making sure the title is clear and no unpaid bills are attached to the house. When every condition is met, the escrow officer pays the seller and records the new deed in your name. Then the house is officially yours.

Escrow matters because buying a house involves a lot of money and a lot of trust. Without it, you might pay before getting the keys, or the seller might hand over the house before getting paid. The neutral holder protects both sides. It also catches problems you might miss, like old liens or errors in the title, before they become your headache.

Your escrow period usually lasts about 30 to 60 days, and during that time you'll typically also do inspections and get your loan finalized. Your real estate agent or lender can tell you who your escrow officer is, and it's fine to ask them questions anytime. Good luck with your new home!

A biological neuron model is a mathematical or computational depiction of how a neuron, a kind of cell within the animal nervous system, is structured and how it operates. Neurons serve as the fundamental building blocks of the nervous system and are central to conveying and processing information. They take in signals from other cells, combine those signals, and produce outgoing electrical and chemical messages. Researchers have developed many ways to describe neuron behavior, spanning everything from simple linear approaches to far more intricate nonlinear ones. Such models make it possible to simulate how neurons respond under varying circumstances, including when exposed to different stimuli or at different points in development. They also help clarify how neurons communicate with one another and how their combined activity supports the nervous system as a whole. These models have a wide range of uses, such as uncovering the mechanisms behind neurological disorders, designing new treatments for those conditions, and building artificial neural networks for machine learning and artificial intelligence.

Baguettes go stale so fast because they're basically just flour, water, yeast, and salt. No butter, no oil, nothing to hold onto moisture. You shape the dough into that long skinny loaf, bake it, and that's pretty much it. The thin crust and all that exposed surface area mean moisture escapes quickly, so the bread dries out and turns hard in a hurry. Sourdough and enriched breads, on the other hand, hang on to their softness longer. They tend to have more moisture inside and a sturdier crust that slows the drying down.

Most solar panels, the kind on roofs and calculators, actually don't use heat at all. They use light. That's the first thing to fix, and it makes the whole story simpler.

Here is the five-year-old version. Sunlight is made of tiny packets of energy called photons. Think of them as teeny tiny balls zooming down from the sun. A solar panel is made of a special material, usually silicon, which is the same stuff found in sand. Inside the silicon there are little particles called electrons, and they are like marbles sitting in holes. When a photon hits the silicon, it bonks an electron and knocks it right out of its hole, like a marble popping out of a bumpy tray.

Now you have a loose marble, but a loose marble that just wanders around doesn't help anybody. So the panel is built with a kind of slope inside it. The silicon is treated in two layers, one that has extra electrons and one that is a bit short on them. Where the two layers meet, there is a built-in push that works like a hill. The freed electrons roll down the hill in one direction only.

Then wires are attached to the top and bottom of the panel. The electrons that rolled to one side want to get back to the other side, so they travel through the wire to get there. That moving stream of electrons is electricity. If you put a light bulb, a phone charger, or a calculator in the path of the wire, the electrons run through it on their way back and make it work. When they finish the trip, they return to the other side of the panel, and sunlight knocks them loose again, so the loop keeps going as long as the sun shines.

One thing to note is that the electricity from a panel flows in one steady direction, which is called direct current. Your house outlets use a back-and-forth kind, so rooftop systems include a box called an inverter that converts it. Batteries can also store the electricity for night time.

As for heat, it is actually a bit of a nuisance. Panels get warm in the sun, and that wasted heat makes them slightly less efficient. There are separate devices called solar thermal collectors that do use the sun's heat, usually to warm water, and some power plants use mirrors to boil water into steam that spins a generator. But the ordinary solar panel skips heat entirely and turns light straight into electricity.

Intractability, also called complexity, basically means a problem is really hard to solve with a computer algorithm. Some problems are easy and finish in no time, but others can take forever or just aren't doable with current tech. The cause might be the size of the problem, how many steps it takes, or how much time or memory you need. Sometimes it's baked into the problem itself, like when it demands a ton of computation or isn't clearly defined to begin with. Classic examples include the traveling salesman problem, the shortest path problem, and the knapsack problem. They're tough because either there's a huge amount of computing involved or there are so many possible answers you'd have to check. It's a big deal in computer science, since it shapes how we design algorithms and systems. Knowing how complex a problem is helps researchers and engineers figure out whether it's worth attacking with today's tools, and it pushes them to come up with new approaches for the stubborn ones.

The first electronic handheld calculator was the Canon Pocketronic, released in 1970 (it was publicly announced in 1970 and went on sale in 1971). Texas Instruments followed shortly after with its own handheld calculator, the Cal Tech prototype in 1967 being an earlier handheld design that never reached the market as a commercial product.

An Associate of Arts (A.A.) degree is a two-year undergraduate degree, typically earned at a community college or junior college in the United States. It is usually awarded after completing about 60 semester credit hours of coursework, which is roughly half of what a bachelor's degree requires. The focus is on the liberal arts and general education, covering subjects such as English composition, history, social sciences, mathematics, foreign languages, humanities, and the arts.

The main purpose of an A.A. is to provide a foundation for transferring to a four-year college or university to complete a bachelor's degree. Many students earn an A.A. and then transfer, often with the credits applying toward the first two years of a bachelor's program, which can reduce overall college costs. Some community colleges also have articulation agreements with state universities that guarantee transfer of the A.A. credits.

An A.A. can also be valuable on its own, as it qualifies graduates for some entry-level jobs and demonstrates completion of college-level study. It differs from an Associate of Science (A.S.), which places more emphasis on math, science, and technical subjects, though the two often serve similar transfer and career purposes.

Cu is just the chemical symbol for copper, so you'll see it on the periodic table. Copper's a soft, bendy metal with that reddish-orange color you probably recognize. It's great at carrying heat and electricity, which is why it shows up everywhere in wiring and electronics. Your body and plants both need a little bit of it, too, though only in trace amounts. It's pretty common in the ground and comes out of ores like chalcopyrite, bornite, and chalcocite. People have been using it for ages for coins, jewelry, and decorative stuff. It also turns up in construction, gets mixed into alloys, and works as a catalyst in plenty of chemical reactions.

"Cake and underwear" stocks is a nickname for companies that sell everyday consumer staples, the kinds of things people keep buying whether the economy is booming or struggling. The phrase captures the idea that people will still celebrate birthdays with a cake and still need to replace their underwear even when money is tight, so demand for these products stays relatively steady through recessions.

The label is most associated with the investor Peter Lynch, who managed the Fidelity Magellan Fund and popularized the idea of investing in businesses you understand from everyday life. The term points to a style of investing that favors dull, dependable businesses with predictable revenue over flashy growth stories. Companies in categories like packaged food, household products, basic clothing, toiletries, and similar low-glamor goods fit the description.

The appeal is defensiveness and stability. Because sales don't swing wildly with the business cycle, these stocks tend to hold up better in downturns, and they often pay regular dividends. The tradeoff is that they usually grow more slowly and may lag the broader market during strong rallies, when investors prefer more cyclical or high-growth sectors. In modern sector terms, "cake and underwear" stocks overlap heavily with consumer staples and, to a lesser degree, some basic consumer discretionary names.

Gottlob Frege (1848–1925) was a German mathematician, logician, and philosopher who is widely regarded as one of the founders of modern logic and the philosophy of language. He taught at the University of Jena for most of his career and worked largely in obscurity during his lifetime, but his ideas came to shape much of twentieth-century philosophy, particularly analytic philosophy.

His most important contribution was his 1879 book Begriffsschrift, often translated as "concept-script," which introduced a formal notation for logic. In it he developed a system of quantifiers and variables that allowed logical relationships to be expressed with precision, going well beyond the traditional Aristotelian logic that had dominated for centuries. This innovation made it possible to analyze complex statements and inferences in a rigorous way, and it laid the groundwork for modern mathematical logic.

Frege also wanted to show that arithmetic could be derived from purely logical principles, a project known as logicism. He pursued this in his two-volume work Grundgesetze der Arithmetik. Late in the second volume, however, Bertrand Russell pointed out a contradiction in Frege's system, now called Russell's paradox, which undermined the project. Frege was deeply disappointed by this discovery, though he acknowledged it honestly in an appendix.

In the philosophy of language, Frege is known for his distinction between sense (Sinn) and reference (Bedeutung). In his essay "Über Sinn und Bedeutung" (1892), he argued that the meaning of a name or expression includes not only the object it refers to but also a mode of presentation of that object. His example of "the morning star" and "the evening star," which both refer to Venus but present it differently, remains a central illustration in discussions of meaning and belief.

Frege's influence is considerable. Russell and Wittgenstein drew heavily on his work, and his ideas remain foundational in logic, semantics, and the philosophy of mathematics.

When you sleep on a plane, your body keeps making oil and sweat the whole time, just like it does at home. The difference is what happens to that oil. When you are awake, you touch your face, rub your eyes, fidget, and move around, and that spreads the oil away or wipes it off. When you fall asleep, your hands rest in your lap or on the armrest, and your face sits against a pillow, a seat, or the window. The oil and sweat stay put and build up, so when you wake up your skin feels greasy and your hair may look flat or oily.

Airplanes make this worse in a few ways. The air inside a cabin is very dry, which can make your skin feel tight and uncomfortable, and your body may respond by making more oil to compensate. The air is also recycled, so it's not very fresh, and you may be breathing warm, stuffy air while you sleep. Your body also gets warm while it sleeps, and warmth makes you sweat a little more. Add in a head pressed against a headrest that may have other people's oil on it, and you can see why you wake up feeling gross.

Your body is not doing anything wrong. It is just doing its normal oily, sweaty thing while you are not around to wipe it away. A quick face wash, a little moisturizer, and a sip of water when you wake up will usually make you feel much better.

Pain in the shoulder and arm together with numbness, pins and needles, and weakness in the hand usually points to a nerve being irritated or compressed somewhere between the neck and the hand. The most common cause is a pinched nerve in the neck (cervical radiculopathy), where a disc or the bony joints of the spine narrow the opening where a nerve root leaves the spinal column. The pain often radiates down the arm, and the numbness and tingling follow the nerve's path into the hand. Other possibilities include carpal tunnel syndrome, which mainly affects the thumb, index, and middle fingers, and thoracic outlet syndrome, where nerves or blood vessels are compressed as they pass under the collarbone. A shoulder problem such as a rotator cuff injury or frozen shoulder can add to the pain, and sometimes more than one of these is present at once. Your physiotherapy may have eased the pain without addressing the underlying nerve pressure, which is why the relief has been temporary.

On motor neurone disease, I understand why the programme worried you, but your symptoms fit a compressed nerve much better than MND. MND typically causes progressive weakness and muscle wasting, often with muscle twitching, and it usually does not cause the kind of persistent numbness and pins and needles you describe. Sensation is normally preserved in MND, and the condition is rare, so these symptoms are far more likely to have a more treatable cause. That said, only a doctor who examines you can rule things out.

I would recommend seeing your GP soon rather than waiting, since three months of symptoms with lost hand strength warrants a proper neurological examination. The doctor may arrange nerve conduction studies, which measure how well the nerves are conducting signals, and an MRI of the neck or shoulder to look for compression. If a nerve root or nerve is clearly being pinched, there are effective treatments, including targeted injections, specialist physiotherapy, and surgery in some cases.

Seek medical attention urgently if you notice weakness that is getting worse quickly, dropping things more often, wasting or visible shrinking of the muscles in your hand or arm, twitching in the tongue or other muscles, difficulty swallowing or changes in your speech, weakness spreading to the other arm or to your legs, loss of balance, or any change in bladder or bowel control.

Transfer learning is basically when you take a model that's already been trained on one task and reuse it for a different but related one. You start with a pre-trained model and fine-tune it on your new data by updating its weights. The neat part is that whatever the model picked up on the first task often carries over. Say a model has learned to spot patterns in pictures of animals. You could fine-tune it to pick out plants too, and it wouldn't have to learn image recognition from zero. It'd just build on what it already knows. This comes in handy when your dataset is small and you don't have enough examples to train something from scratch. It can also boost performance on the new task by leaning on what was learned earlier. Honestly, it's one of the most useful tricks out there for getting decent models when you're short on data.

Building financial knowledge is easiest when you combine a few steady habits with some reading you return to over time. On the reading side, a good starting point is "The Intelligent Investor" by Benjamin Graham, which lays out the principles of value investing and remains a touchstone for how to think about risk and price. "A Random Walk Down Wall Street" by Burton Malkiel offers a readable tour of market theory and index investing, while "Common Stocks and Uncommon Profits" by Philip Fisher is useful if you want to understand growth investing and how to evaluate businesses. For a broader view of how markets and economies behave, "Against the Gods" by Peter Bernstein traces the history of risk and probability, and "Thinking, Fast and Slow" by Daniel Kahneman helps you recognize the psychological biases that affect financial decisions. Once you have the basics, you might move to annual shareholder letters from companies or investors such as Berkshire Hathaway, which teach a great deal about business analysis in plain language.

Beyond books, a few habits keep your knowledge growing. Reading financial news regularly, from sources like the Wall Street Journal, the Financial Times, or Bloomberg, builds familiarity with current events and terminology. Following a few well-regarded economists or analysts, and reading their reasoning rather than just their conclusions, sharpens your judgment. Many people also find it valuable to keep an investment journal, where they record why they made each decision and later compare the outcome to their expectations. This turns experience into a real learning loop.

Finally, practice with real numbers. Reading a company's annual report or 10-K filing, tracking your own budget and net worth over time, or building a simple spreadsheet model of a stock or a retirement plan will teach you more than any single book. Pairing this hands-on work with occasional courses, such as those offered free through Coursera, edX, or the Khan Academy, gives you structure and fills gaps in areas like accounting, statistics, or economics. Consistency matters more than intensity, so a little reading and practice each week will serve you better than occasional bursts of study.

Philip K. Dick was a science fiction author celebrated for his provocative and often unsettling stories that probe questions of reality, awareness, and what it means to exist. Born in Chicago, Illinois, in 1928, he spent his childhood in California. He started publishing science fiction in the 1950s, and his output soon attracted a loyal readership. Over the course of his career he produced more than 44 novels and 121 short stories, many of which later became films, television shows, and other media. Among his best-known titles are "Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?", which became the film "Blade Runner," and "The Man in the High Castle," which was turned into a television series with the same name. His fiction often employs the "unreliable narrator," leaving readers unsure whether to trust the story they are told, and it frequently delves into metaphysical and philosophical ideas. Dick exerted considerable influence on the science fiction field, and his books have earned many awards and honors. He passed away in 1982, yet his lasting legacy endures through fiction that continues to provoke thought.

Orange and green discoloration on a baby's tongue is most often caused by something he has eaten or touched rather than an infection. Orange often comes from carrots, sweet potato, squash, or other orange-colored purees, and green usually comes from peas, spinach, green beans, or pear and other green-tinted foods. Colored medications, vitamin drops, teething gels, or toys and pacifiers with dyes or paint can leave similar marks. If the patches appear shortly after feeding and fade within a few hours, or they wipe off easily with a damp cloth, food or an external substance is the most likely explanation. Keep a quick record of what he ate or was given before the patches showed up, since that can help you spot a pattern.

Thrush itself usually looks different. It typically forms white, cottage-cheese-like patches that don't wipe away and may look like milk curds, sometimes with redness underneath. It is not usually green or orange, so these colors point away from thrush, though the two can occur together.

Because his thrush was slow to clear and has now come back within a couple of weeks, I would mention it to your pediatrician even if the colors turn out to be from food. Recurrent thrush in an infant can have several causes, including a recent antibiotic course, use of a steroid or other medication, a nursing mother who also has yeast on her nipples, or, less commonly, an immune issue that needs evaluation. A doctor can examine his mouth, check whether the patches are thrush or something else, and sample them if needed. Consider calling sooner or seeking care promptly if he has a fever, is feeding poorly or refusing feeds, seems to be in pain, has fewer wet diapers than usual, or if the patches are spreading, bleeding, or accompanied by a rash elsewhere.

High blood pressure, also known as hypertension, may leave some individuals feeling tired. Other possible signs include breathlessness, head pain, and lightheadedness. If your husband feels worn out and takes lisinopril to control his blood pressure, the medication could be the reason. He should talk with his doctor or another healthcare professional about what he is going through, since they can advise on the right next step. Depending on the situation, the provider might change the dose or switch him to a different drug. It also helps for him to live healthily by eating well, staying physically active, and getting adequate sleep, all of which support both his blood pressure control and his overall well-being.

Anorexia is a complex and serious psychiatric condition that can affect anyone, regardless of age or background. Its defining features are a powerful fear of putting on weight and a preoccupation with weight, body size, and shape. Individuals with anorexia frequently have a distorted body image, perceiving themselves as bigger or heavier than they actually are. As a result, they may drastically limit what they eat and adopt other harmful habits, such as exercising excessively, in order to lose weight. The exact cause of anorexia is not fully understood, but experts believe it arises from a mix of genetic, environmental, and psychological influences. Some studies indicate that people with relatives who have mental health conditions, such as anxiety or depression, are more prone to developing the illness. Additional risk factors include past trauma or abuse, trouble managing stress, and societal and cultural pressure to be slim. Within the brain, anorexia may be linked to unusual activity in regions that govern thoughts, emotions, and behaviors concerning food and weight. Certain chemical imbalances in the brain are also believed to contribute to its development. Because anorexia is a grave condition that can threaten life, it demands treatment from professionals. Anyone who is struggling with anorexia or another eating disorder, or who knows someone that is, should reach out to a mental health professional or a qualified treatment facility.

Okay, so in plants, the feedback thing during respiration kicks in when ATP builds up in the cell. ATP is basically the main energy currency of cells, and cellular respiration is what makes it. Respiration eats up oxygen and gives off carbon dioxide as a byproduct, so that part's pretty standard. When ATP levels go up, they set off ATP-sensitive potassium channels, which open and let potassium ions out of the cell. That release then activates rubisco, the enzyme that kicks off the Calvin cycle in the chloroplasts and is responsible for making glucose. The whole loop helps tune how fast respiration runs. Make more ATP when the plant needs it, ease off when it doesn't. That keeps production and use roughly balanced, so the plant has enough energy for everything it has to do.

Another is infection, which can affect the shunt or the area around it and lead to pain. A third is obstruction, where a blockage in the shunt can cause pressure to build up and create pain. Several common conditions fit this pattern.
