Yes, sometimes it is. Some cancers have gone away on their own, a rare event called spontaneous regression. Your body has a defense system called the immune system, which works like a team of tiny cleanup workers that can spot and destroy abnormal cells. Now and then, that team wins without any help from doctors. Some kinds of skin cancer, certain kidney cancers, and a few childhood cancers have been known to disappear this way, and some people have recovered after infections that happened to stir up their immune system.

But this is the exception, not the rule. Most cancers keep growing if nobody treats them, and doctors cannot tell in advance which ones will vanish on their own. So waiting and hoping is risky. Treatments like surgery, medicine, and radiation are the tools that reliably help people get better.

So the simple answer is: the body can sometimes beat cancer by itself, but it rarely does, and that's why doctors are so important.

Nigeria is home to more than 500 languages, and the four most commonly spoken are Hausa, Yoruba, Igbo, and Fulani. Hausa is chiefly used in the north, where it serves as a lingua franca across the region. Yoruba is concentrated in the southwest and also has many speakers in neighboring Benin. Igbo is mainly found in the southeast. Fulani is spread across the whole country, though it is especially common in the north and the central areas. Beyond these four major tongues, numerous others are spoken in Nigeria, such as Kanuri, Edo, Efik, Ijaw, and Tiv, along with many more.

"Nature Boy" was written by Eden Ahbez, an American musician and spiritual seeker who lived a largely unconventional life in Los Angeles. He composed the song in the 1940s, and it became widely known after Nat King Cole recorded it in 1948, turning it into a major hit. The song has since been covered by many other artists, including David Bowie, who recorded a version in the 1970s.

Honestly, I'd steer clear of squeezing or trying to treat a cyst yourself. Get it checked by a healthcare provider so they can figure out what it is and how to handle it. A cyst is basically a closed sac that can hold fluid, pus, or other stuff. They can show up pretty much anywhere on your body, and they usually come from infection, inflammation, a blocked duct, or an injury. What happens next depends on the type, where it is, how big it is, and what's causing it. Sometimes a doctor will drain it, sometimes they'll prescribe antibiotics or something for inflammation, and sometimes they'll just cut it out. If it's really painful, keeps getting bigger, or comes with fever, redness, or swelling, don't wait around. Go in soon. They can take a proper look and tell you what to do.

Volodymyr Zelenskyy is a Ukrainian politician and former comedian who has served as the President of Ukraine since May 2019. He was born in 1978 in Kryvyi Rih, a city in central Ukraine, and before entering politics he was best known as an actor, writer, and producer. He gained widespread fame for playing the lead role in the television comedy series "Servant of the People," in which he portrays a history teacher who unexpectedly becomes president after a viral video of his rant against corruption spreads online. Life imitated art when he ran for the real presidency in 2019 under a political party that took its name from the show, and he won a decisive victory in the runoff election.

His presidency has been dominated by Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, which began in February 2022. Zelenskyy became an internationally prominent figure for refusing offers to evacuate from Kyiv during the early days of the invasion and for rallying his country's defense and seeking military and financial support from Western allies. He has traveled abroad frequently to address parliaments and build international coalitions, and he has been named Time magazine's Person of the Year, among other honors. He has also pursued domestic reforms tied to Ukraine's aspirations for closer integration with the European Union, while facing criticism at various points from opponents and observers over issues such as corruption allegations, media freedom, and the postponement of elections during wartime.

A terrorist attack tends to push stock market indexes down for several overlapping reasons, though the effect is often brief.

The most immediate cause is uncertainty. Investors dislike not knowing what will happen next, and an attack raises questions about whether more violence is coming, how severe the damage will be, and how governments will respond. To reduce their exposure to these unknowns, many investors sell stocks, especially riskier ones, and move money into safer assets such as government bonds, cash, or gold. When many people sell at once, prices fall, and the index, which is a weighted average of those prices, falls with them.

Attacks also threaten economic activity directly. If the attack damages infrastructure, disrupts transportation, closes businesses, or frightens consumers into staying home and spending less, companies may earn less than expected. Analysts then revise their earnings forecasts downward, and since stock prices reflect expected future profits, prices adjust lower.

Certain sectors are hit harder than others. Airlines, hotels, tourism, insurance companies facing large claims, and businesses tied to the affected area or event often drop sharply, and because some of these are large companies, they can pull the broader index down noticeably.

Finally, there is a psychological component. Fear can spread quickly through media coverage, and sentiment can feed on itself, causing selling beyond what the economic facts alone would justify.

Markets often recover within days or weeks, however, as investors reassess the actual economic damage, which is frequently smaller than first feared, and as central banks or governments step in to stabilize conditions.

If the US defaulted on its public debt, the stock and bond markets would take a serious hit. A default means the government can't pay what it owes when it's due, and that would wreck confidence in how it manages its money. The dollar could slide, and both stocks and bonds could get dumped. Stocks would probably fall, since investors would worry about what a default does to the economy. Selling could snowball, and prices would keep sliding. Bonds would take a hit too. Buyers would want higher yields to make up for the extra risk of lending to Washington, so prices would drop and rates would climb. Demand for Treasuries could weaken, pushing their value down even further. Put it all together and you get a big, ugly hit to both markets, plus a shaky economy on top of it.

Vietnamese immigrants have made homes across many parts of the United States, with the largest concentrations found in California, Texas, and Washington. Sizable Vietnamese communities also exist in other states, including Georgia, Illinois, Louisiana, and Virginia. Numerous Vietnamese newcomers have settled in cities such as San Francisco, New York City, and Houston. The initial wave of Vietnamese migration to the U.S. started in the late 1970s, after the Vietnam War ended. A large share of these arrivals were refugees who left Vietnam to escape political persecution or financial hardship. As the years passed, the Vietnamese American community expanded and became more firmly rooted, and today many second- and third-generation Vietnamese Americans live across the country.

Okay, so Form 7004 is basically the form you use to ask the IRS for more time to file. It's not tied to any one type of business, so an LLC can use it too. But here's the thing: if your LLC's only members are a husband and wife, the IRS generally treats it as a partnership, which means you file Form 1065 (the U.S. Return of Partnership Income), and you'd use Form 7004 to get the extension on that one.

The deadline to file 7004 is the original due date of the return, which for calendar-year filers is usually March 15. You can file it electronically through the IRS e-file system or mail it in. Don't skip the payment side, though. Any tax you owe still has to be paid by that original due date, since the extension only buys you time to file, not time to pay. Miss it and you could be hit with late filing and/or late payment penalties, so it's worth getting both pieces handled on time.

Hovercraft already exist, and you may have seen one on a beach or at a museum. A hovercraft pushes a huge cushion of air down underneath itself, so it floats on that air like a boat floating on water. The catch is that the air cushion needs a big fan and a lot of power to keep blowing, and it can't really fly high or go over tall things. So they're useful, but they're not like the cars in Halo.

The idea of using magnets to float is also real. Trains called maglev trains use powerful magnets to lift themselves off the track and zoom along with almost no friction. Some are running in Japan and China today. They work because the magnets on the train push against magnets built into the track, and that push holds the train up. But this needs a special track all along the route, which is expensive to build.

The magnet idea you mentioned, using Earth's own magnetic field, doesn't work well for a simple reason. Earth's magnetic field is very weak. It's strong enough to turn a compass needle, but it isn't strong enough to lift anything heavier than a tiny speck. Pushing against it would be like trying to push a boat by blowing on the water. To lift a car, you'd need a magnet far stronger than the one pulling on it from the ground, and nothing you could carry on the car would do that.

Antigravity, the kind of thing Halo has, is different. Nobody has found a way to cancel gravity or to push against it without something to push against. Gravity is the pull between things that have mass, and we don't yet know how to switch it off. Scientists are still studying it, so it's possible we'll learn something new someday, but for now the vehicles in Halo are science fiction.

So a storytelling device is basically any technique or element a writer uses to get a message or theme across, give the story some structure, or just keep the audience hooked. There are a ton of them, but here are some of the common ones.

Plot is the sequence of events that makes up the story. Usually it's got a beginning, a middle and an end, and one thing leads to the next in a cause-and-effect way.

Characters are the people or creatures living in the story. You've got your protagonist, who's the main character, and the antagonist, who's the person or thing standing in their way.

Setting is just the time and place where it all happens. It can be real or made up, and it can really shape how the story feels and plays out.

Point of view is the angle the story's told from. First person means a character in the story is telling it, third person is more of an outside view, and omniscient is when the narrator knows everything about everyone.

Dialogue is the conversation between characters. It can show you what someone's like, push the plot forward, and stir up conflict or tension.

Symbolism is when an object, action or event stands for something bigger than what it literally is.

Those are only a few examples, and you'll find them in all kinds of stories, from novels and plays to films and more.

Sensitivity and specificity are two measures used to evaluate how well a diagnostic test, screening tool, or classification method performs. They describe the test's accuracy in identifying the presence or absence of a particular condition, such as a disease, infection, or other target state.

Sensitivity, also called the true positive rate, is the proportion of people who actually have the condition who are correctly identified as positive by the test. For example, if a test has a sensitivity of 90 percent, it will correctly detect 90 out of every 100 people who truly have the disease, while missing the remaining 10. A highly sensitive test is valuable when the goal is to catch as many cases as possible, such as in an initial screening, because it rarely misses someone who is affected.

Specificity, also called the true negative rate, is the proportion of people who do not have the condition who are correctly identified as negative by the test. If a test has a specificity of 95 percent, it will correctly clear 95 out of every 100 healthy individuals, while incorrectly flagging the other 5 as positive. A highly specific test is valuable when false alarms are costly or harmful, such as when a positive result leads to invasive follow-up procedures or unnecessary treatment.

The two measures often trade off against each other. Adjusting the cutoff point for a positive result to catch more true cases usually increases false positives, which lowers specificity. Conversely, making the criteria stricter tends to improve specificity but may miss some real cases. Because of this tradeoff, sensitivity and specificity are typically reported together, and they are often visualized using a receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve to choose an appropriate threshold for a given purpose.

Okay so context in language basically means all the stuff around a conversation or piece of writing. That includes where it's happening, who's talking, why they're talking, and whatever background knowledge people bring with them. It matters more than you'd think because it can totally change what words mean. Take "I'm going to the store." If you're at home, that's probably the corner grocery. If you're on vacation somewhere abroad, it might mean a souvenir shop. Same sentence, different picture.

Context also shapes how people talk. A chat with your friends at a casual get-together is going to sound way looser than a business meeting, right? Word choice and formality shift with the setting. Getting the context is pretty key if you want to read something correctly and respond without stepping on toes. It also keeps you out of a lot of misunderstandings.

Honestly, there are a few reasons updates sometimes feel like they break stuff or take features away. One is that developers are usually trying to improve things in other ways, so they'll cut a feature they figure nobody uses much or that keeps causing bugs. Other times they add something new they think is a big deal, and it turns out to be useless for a lot of people, or it actually causes headaches for them.

Another thing is that software gets updated to work with newer devices and tech. Say a new version of a phone operating system comes out. It might have features that only run on the latest phones, which means older phones can lose stuff they used to have, because it's just not supported anymore.

Then there are security updates. Sometimes a patch is needed to close a hole that hackers could exploit, or to fix some other nasty bug. That's good for keeping the software secure and stable, but it can still change how things work or throw a wrench into your routine.

So the intention is usually to make things better for users, but it doesn't always play out that way. Reading the release notes before you update is a good habit, since it tells you what's changing and what might bite you.

A pacemaker is a small device that gets implanted in the chest to help keep the heart beating at the right rate and rhythm. It sends electrical signals to the heart when needed. People often get them to treat arrhythmias, which are abnormal heart rhythms that can cause dizziness, fainting, or shortness of breath. But a pacemaker isn't always the right move for someone with congestive heart failure and atrial fibrillation. Sometimes the rhythm problem doesn't come from the heart's natural pacemaker (the sinoatrial node) or the electrical wiring, so a device wouldn't fix much. Sometimes medications can keep the rhythm under control just fine. Other conditions, like a bleeding disorder or an active infection, can rule it out entirely. And if the heart is too weak to handle the extra strain, a pacemaker might not help and could make things worse. Honestly, the best thing is to talk it through with a doctor. They'll look at your full medical history and how bad your symptoms are before deciding whether it's worth it.

Okay so synesthesia is basically when your senses get mixed up in a way most people's don't. Some folks hear music and see colors, or look at numbers and taste something. It's kind of like picturing an apple with your eyes shut, except for synesthetes it's more like they actually see that red with their eyes open. It's not a disorder or anything broken, just a different way the brain wires things together. Lots of people with it find it fun and interesting, though it can get confusing when others don't get what they're experiencing. So yeah, your brain links up stuff most people keep separate, like sound to color or words to flavor.

Generally, no. A company that bills you for services you never asked for and never received is usually making an improper charge, and in many cases it is breaking the law. Under basic contract principles, a charge needs an agreement behind it, and you cannot be bound to pay for something you did not order. Consumer protection laws add further limits. In the United States, for example, the Federal Trade Commission has rules against unauthorized charges and "negative option" billing, where a company treats your silence or failure to cancel as consent. Many states have their own statutes against deceptive billing, and similar protections exist in the UK, the EU, Canada, and Australia.

There are exceptions to keep in mind. If you signed up for something in the fine print, agreed to a trial that converted to a paid plan, or previously accepted the service and then failed to cancel, the company may have a stronger claim. Sometimes a charge is simply a billing error, a duplicate, or a mix-up with another customer, and those are usually fixed with a phone call.

If you find a charge you don't recognize, a practical approach is to gather your records, including statements, emails, and any contract or terms you accepted. Then dispute the charge directly with the company in writing and ask for an itemized explanation and proof of authorization. If that fails, you can dispute it with your bank or credit card issuer, which often has a chargeback process and strong protections for unauthorized transactions. You can also file a complaint with a consumer protection agency, such as the FTC in the US or your country's equivalent, or pursue the matter in small claims court. Acting promptly matters, since card disputes often have deadlines, sometimes as short as 60 days from the statement date.

Foot and ankle pain that moves between joints, affects both sides, and comes and goes can have several causes, so the right treatment depends on which one is behind it. Gout usually strikes one joint at a time, often the big toe, and flares are typically sudden and intense. A pattern that shifts around both feet and ankles is more often seen in inflammatory arthritis, such as rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, or reactive arthritis, which can follow an infection. Because the picture is unclear, it's worth asking your doctor what tests they have done or plan to do. Blood tests for uric acid, inflammatory markers such as CRP and ESR, rheumatoid factor, and anti-CCP antibodies can help, and X-rays or ultrasound may show joint changes. If fluid can be drawn from a swollen joint, it can be checked for uric acid crystals, which would confirm gout.

Treatment depends on the diagnosis. For pain flares of any type, anti-inflammatory painkillers such as ibuprofen or naproxen often help, but they can affect the stomach, kidneys, and blood pressure, so check with your doctor or pharmacist, especially if you have other conditions or take other medicines. For confirmed gout, colchicine or steroids can treat flares, and if attacks are frequent, medicines such as allopurinol can lower uric acid over time. For inflammatory arthritis, doctors often prescribe disease-modifying drugs such as methotrexate or sulfasalazine, sometimes with newer biologic medicines, because these protect the joints from long-term damage. Rest during flares, ice or heat, supportive footwear, and physiotherapy to maintain movement and strength can help whatever the cause.

Please see a doctor promptly if you develop fever, a joint that is hot, red, or very swollen, difficulty walking, a rash, eye redness or pain, lower back pain, or pain in the heel or along the tendons. Those signs can point to conditions that need quick treatment. Since your symptoms have lasted since May and your diagnosis has changed, asking for a referral to a rheumatologist is reasonable if the cause still isn't clear.

Skyrim is an enormous, richly detailed game offering an abundance of activities. Players can take on countless quests, traverse varied regions, and battle a wide range of foes. Its expansive setting is also populated by numerous characters and cultures, which give the game much of its depth and character. A major reason Skyrim holds players for hundreds of hours is its open-world structure, which lets them tackle objectives and explore in any sequence they like. Because of this, people can proceed at their own pace and pursue whatever captures their interest, instead of hurrying to see everything. Beyond the central storyline, the game offers many side quests, minigames, and other pursuits. Players might gather ingredients to brew potions, prepare meals, or forge weapons and armor, among many other options. Numerous secrets and concealed locations also await discovery, giving people plenty to keep them occupied. In short, Skyrim's vast content comes from its intricate world, its wide variety of activities, and its many hidden secrets. These qualities explain why it remains so popular and enduring, with players able to return for hundreds of hours and still uncover something new.

It is hard to pinpoint what is causing a lump on your stomach without more details and a chance to examine you directly. If the lump worries you, especially when it comes with other signs like twitching or spasms, it is worth having a healthcare provider evaluate it. Several conditions can produce a lump on the stomach. One is a lipoma, a harmless (noncancerous) growth composed of fat cells. Another is a hernia, which happens when an organ or tissue pushes through a weak spot in the abdominal wall muscles. An abscess is also possible; this is a pocket of pus that develops in the body due to an infection. A cyst, a fluid-filled sac that can appear in many different areas of the body, is another option. The lump and the twitching might also be linked to a muscle spasm or some other muscle problem. Once again, seeing a healthcare provider is important so you can get an accurate diagnosis and a suitable treatment plan.

If you used a debit card with insufficient funds to pay for something online, your bank or card issuer will most likely reject the transaction. As a result, the payment won't process and the purchase won't go through. That said, the charge may still appear as pending on your account or on the merchant's side. When that occurs, the merchant hasn't received the money yet and is still waiting for it to clear. To stop the transaction in that case, you'll need to sort things out with the merchant or your bank. To avoid this kind of situation, always confirm you have enough money in your account before making any online purchase. Without sufficient funds, your bank or card issuer could charge an overdraft fee, which may be expensive. If you can't resolve the problem with the merchant or your bank, consider speaking with a financial professional or a consumer protection agency. They can advise you on how to deal with the situation and safeguard your rights as a consumer.

Common sense reasoning is the capacity to draw on everyday knowledge and a basic grasp of how the world works in order to form judgments and make choices across many different circumstances. It means recognizing and using fundamental principles, including cause and effect, non-contradiction, and sufficient reason, to work through problems and reach decisions. This kind of reasoning matters because it lets us find our way through our surroundings and choose well, guided by what we understand about how things operate. It supports critical thinking and helps us link separate pieces of information in a logical way, so that we can arrive at conclusions grounded in evidence and sound reasoning.

I'm sorry you're dealing with pain below your chest. Any pain that persists deserves medical evaluation, since it may point to a range of underlying conditions. Tuberculosis is a serious infection that can attack the lungs and other organs, so sticking with the treatment your healthcare provider has prescribed is essential for a complete recovery. If you've recently completed tuberculosis treatment and still have pain, reach out to your provider so you can talk through your symptoms and work out what is causing it. They might order further tests or suggest treatments to relieve the pain and address any related health problems. Also, it's generally advisable to avoid alcohol or keep intake moderate, because alcohol can interfere with how some medications work and may worsen certain conditions. If you're worried about how much you drink, a healthcare provider or a substance use treatment specialist can offer guidance and support.

Not necessarily. Large recent gains by themselves are a weak signal about what happens next, and the research on this is fairly consistent. Markets at or near all-time highs have historically delivered returns that look broadly similar to other starting points, partly because markets spend a lot of time near highs during long bull runs. Waiting for a pullback has often meant missing further gains, and many people who sit out after a rally never find a moment that feels comfortable to enter.

That said, it isn't a free pass. After big gains, valuations are usually higher, which tends to mean lower expected returns over the following five to ten years, and it leaves less cushion if something disappoints. Short-term risk is also real: you could buy and see a 10 to 20 percent drop soon after, and that can happen at any starting point, not just after rallies. The practical question is less "is the market too high?" and more "can I tolerate a sharp decline without selling, and when will I need this money?"

A few things help with the decision. If your horizon is long, say ten years or more, the entry point matters much less than staying invested and keeping costs low. If you're worried about timing, you can spread your purchases over several months, which reduces the regret of investing right before a drop, though on average lump-sum investing has beaten gradual entry because markets tend to rise more often than they fall. Diversification matters too: a broad index fund is a very different bet from piling into whichever sector or stocks just surged. And your asset allocation should reflect your goals and risk tolerance rather than recent performance, so if you'd have wanted 70 percent in stocks anyway, the recent rally doesn't change that target.

The riskiest behavior is usually chasing performance: buying because prices rose, then panicking and selling when they fall. If a 25 percent decline would cause you to bail out, scale your equity exposure down to a level you can actually hold through. If the money is needed within a few years, equities are a poor fit regardless of recent gains.

This is general information rather than personal advice, and your own situation, including time horizon, emergency savings, and other holdings, should drive the decision.

A market close order is basically an order that gets filled at the end of the trading day. You use it to get out of a position, or to get into one, by buying or selling a security right at the close. Day traders often use these to make sure they're flat by the bell, and some investors use them to cut their exposure before the market shuts down. It's a pretty handy tool if you don't want to be holding something overnight.

Pus-filled itchy bumps after getting a tattoo can mean an allergic reaction or an infection, so it's worth paying attention to. Here's what's helped people I know (and what the usual advice says). Wash the tattoo gently with soap and water, then pat it dry with a clean towel. Skip baths and swimming for the first week, since soaking can make things worse. Put on a thin layer of fragrance-free, hypoallergenic moisturizer to keep the skin from drying out and to take the edge off the itch. Try hard not to scratch it, because scratching can lead to infection or make the ink fade. If the itching is really bad, an over-the-counter antihistamine might help.

That said, go see a doctor if you notice fever, spreading redness, swelling, or any discharge, or if things keep getting worse even though you're taking care of it. Don't wait on an infection. Catching it early makes a big difference.

The mango originated in South Asia, in an area that today covers eastern India, Bangladesh, Nepal, and the eastern part of Pakistan. Scientists think its origins lie in the eastern portion of this region, where the warm, moist tropical climate suits mango cultivation particularly well. Today, mango trees thrive across many tropical and subtropical areas worldwide, such as Central and South America, the Caribbean, Africa, and Southeast Asia.

The Human Brain Project was a large European research initiative launched in October 2013 with the aim of advancing neuroscience, medicine, and computing by building a detailed scientific infrastructure for studying the brain. It was funded mainly by the European Union as one of two inaugural Future and Emerging Technologies Flagship programs, with a planned budget of around one billion euros over ten years. It formally ended in September 2023.

The project was conceived largely by the neuroscientist Henry Markram of the École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne, who had earlier led the Blue Brain Project, an effort to simulate parts of the rodent cortex in detail. The original vision was ambitious: to integrate neuroscience data from around the world and use supercomputers to build biologically realistic computer models of the brain, eventually simulating the whole human brain. Hundreds of researchers at over a hundred institutions across Europe took part.

The project was controversial early on. In 2014, hundreds of neuroscientists signed an open letter criticizing its narrow focus on large-scale simulation, which many considered premature given how little was known about the brain, and its governance. After an independent review, the leadership was restructured, Markram stepped back from his central role, and the scientific scope was broadened to include cognitive neuroscience, neuroinformatics, and other areas.

Over time the work was organized around creating shared research tools rather than a single whole-brain simulation. The central result was EBRAINS, a digital research infrastructure offering brain atlases, data-sharing services, modeling and simulation tools, and access to high-performance computing. Other efforts included neuromorphic computing, meaning hardware that mimics neural circuits (the SpiNNaker and BrainScaleS systems), neurorobotics, and medical informatics for studying brain diseases. The project also produced detailed multilevel brain atlases, such as the Julich-Brain atlas, and contributed to models of brain activity like The Virtual Brain.

Assessments of its legacy are mixed. Critics argue it never delivered on the promise of simulating a human brain and that the initial hype was misplaced. Supporters point to the lasting data platforms, tools, and collaborations it created. EBRAINS continues as a permanent research infrastructure after the project's end.

It is sometimes confused with other brain initiatives, such as the US BRAIN Initiative, the Allen Institute's work, and China's and Japan's brain projects, which have different structures and goals.

The Arctic Circle is an imaginary line of latitude that runs around the Earth at roughly 66 degrees 34 minutes north of the equator. It sits about 2,600 kilometers (1,600 miles) from the North Pole, and it marks the southern boundary of the area where the sun can stay above or below the horizon for a full 24 hours at certain times of year. North of this line, there is at least one day around the June solstice when the sun never sets (the midnight sun) and at least one day around the December solstice when it never rises (the polar night). The farther north you go, the longer these periods last.

The latitude of the circle is tied to the tilt of the Earth's axis, which is about 23.4 degrees. Because that tilt varies very slightly over thousands of years, the exact position of the circle shifts by a small amount, moving a few meters each year.

The circle passes through or near eight countries: Norway, Sweden, Finland, Russia, the United States (Alaska), Canada, Greenland (a territory of Denmark), and Iceland, where it only touches the small island of Grímsey just off the northern coast. Well-known places near it include Rovaniemi in Finland, which is just south of the line, and Fairbanks in Alaska, which lies a bit below it. Much of the region inside the circle is ocean, namely the Arctic Ocean, along with northern parts of the continents that surround it.

Kennywood is an amusement park in West Mifflin, Pennsylvania, a suburb of Pittsburgh. Situated roughly 10 miles south of downtown Pittsburgh, it sits close to Route 837 and the Parkway East (Interstate 376). Because the park is so easy to reach from the city, it draws many families and tourists. Visitors know it for its assortment of thrill rides, attractions suited to the whole family, and classic amusement park fare.

Some currencies are widely regarded as refuges during periods of upheaval, since they are seen as fairly stable and dependable stores of value. The US dollar, the Japanese yen, and the Swiss franc are among those most frequently named in this role. Investors and traders often turn to these currencies in moments of uncertainty or crisis, viewing them as comparatively secure and steady places to hold their money. Several factors explain this reputation. For one, these currencies come from nations with robust, stable economies, which lowers the chance of devaluation or default. Moreover, these countries typically maintain strong, transparent regulatory frameworks that offer investors additional confidence. Lastly, central banks across the globe hold these currencies as reserves, so they enjoy broad acceptance and extensive trading, which tends to make them steadier and less prone to sharp swings. Still, no currency is entirely free of risk, and its relative stability can shift over time as economic and political conditions evolve. For that reason, investors should weigh their decisions carefully and remain mindful of the risks attached to any investment.

Fun fact, Mars's two moons, Phobos and Deimos, were found by an American astronomer named Asaph Hall back in 1877. He was working at the United States Naval Observatory in Washington, D.C., and he spotted them using a 26-inch refracting telescope pointed at Mars. Deimos came first on August 12, and then Phobos showed up on August 18. Both names come from Greek mythology. Phobos means "fear" and was the son of Ares, who's the Greek version of the Roman god Mars. Deimos means "terror," and he was also a son of Ares, though the original answer said Aphrodite, so double-check that if it matters to you.

The Fourth of July commemorates the adoption of the Declaration of Independence by the Second Continental Congress on July 4, 1776, which formally severed the thirteen American colonies from Great Britain. The document was largely drafted by Thomas Jefferson, with edits from the committee and Congress, and it announced that the colonies were free and independent states. Although the vote for independence itself took place on July 2, and the signing of the engrossed copy occurred mostly on August 2, July 4 became the date Americans associated with the nation's birth.

Early celebrations were held almost immediately. In Philadelphia, bells rang, and the Declaration was read aloud in public squares, and there were bonfires, parades, and toasts. Over the following decades the day grew into an annual patriotic holiday, with fireworks, military parades, speeches, and public picnics becoming common traditions. The date gained further importance when John Adams and Thomas Jefferson both died on July 4, 1826, the fiftieth anniversary of the Declaration, which added a sense of national destiny to the occasion.

Congress made July 4 a federal holiday in 1870, though it was not until 1941 that it became a paid holiday for federal employees. Today the day is marked with fireworks, barbecues, parades, and displays of patriotism across the United States.

Fixing a live electrical pylon is seriously dangerous work, and you need special gear and training just to do it safely. Insulated tools and gloves are a basic must to keep people from getting shocked. Helicopters that do this kind of repair often carry "arcing horns" or "arcing chains," which are built to pull electrical current away from the aircraft. They give the current a controlled path to follow, so it can run through the device and ground out without frying the helicopter or the crew. Electricity doesn't mess around, so cutting corners on safety procedures is a terrible idea.

Arthur C. Clarke was a British science fiction writer, science writer, and futurist, born in 1917 and gone since 2008. He's mostly famous for his sci-fi novels and short stories, and a lot of them ended up as movies and TV shows. He also made a name for himself in science, especially satellite communication and space exploration. Clarke gets credit for co-writing the screenplay for "2001: A Space Odyssey," the Stanley Kubrick film that changed the genre. He wrote plenty of novels too, like "Childhood's End," "Rendezvous with Rama," and "The Fountains of Paradise." His stuff has been translated and published all over the world. He was a member of the British Interplanetary Society, and he picked up loads of awards for his work in sci-fi and science.

I can't tell what's causing this from a description alone, and pain that is severe, wakes you from sleep, and has returned worse needs a prompt in-person evaluation rather than home treatment. Please contact your doctor today and tell them the pain has come back stronger. Since the urine test was negative, ask them to look at other causes. Pain under the right breast that spreads to the right shoulder blade and armpit can come from the gallbladder, the liver, a kidney stone, the lower lung or lining of the lung, the pancreas, or a nerve problem such as shingles. Each of these needs a different workup, so it helps to be specific. Useful tests may include blood work for liver function, pancreatic enzymes, and blood counts, plus an abdominal ultrasound or CT scan. Describe when the pain started, what makes it worse or better, whether it comes in waves, and whether you have any nausea, vomiting, fever, or changes in your bowel movements or urine.

While you wait for that visit, an over-the-counter pain reliever such as ibuprofen or acetaminophen may ease discomfort if you have no stomach ulcers, kidney disease, liver disease, bleeding problems, or allergies to these medicines, and if you are not pregnant. Follow the package directions and check with a pharmacist if you are unsure. A heating pad on the area may relax muscle tension if the pain feels muscular. Avoid heavy lifting, and try not to rely on a pain reliever to mask a problem that is getting worse.

Go to an emergency department right away if you develop fever or chills, yellowing of the skin or eyes, vomiting that won't stop, a rash of blisters along one side of the body, chest pain, shortness of breath, fainting, blood in your urine or stool, or pain so severe that you cannot sit still or get comfortable. These can signal a serious condition that needs urgent care.

Honestly, this sounds like it could be levator ani syndrome. That's a chronic pelvic pain thing where the pelvic floor muscles, including the levator ani (the ones holding up your rectum and anus), get stuck in spasm. It's often set off by things like going to the bathroom, sex, or sitting for a long stretch, and it tends to show up as pain in the rectum, anus, or the perineum (the area between your anus and your scrotum or vulva). That said, it could also be something else, like a strained muscle or irritated nerves down there. Your best bet is to see a healthcare provider who can figure out what's actually going on and get you sorted out.

Sounds like you might've bruised or hurt your tailbone, the little triangle-shaped bone at the very bottom of your spine, just above your butt. Landing hard on your backside can do that, and it usually hurts when you sit, stand up, or even just move around. It could also be that you pulled a muscle in your abdomen when you fell. Either way, take it easy for a while and skip anything that makes it hurt until things calm down. If the pain hangs around or gets really bad, go get it looked at by a doctor. They can figure out what's actually going on and tell you what to do about it, which might be rest, ice or heat, over-the-counter painkillers, or some physical therapy.

TED is a nonprofit organization devoted to spreading ideas, most often in the form of short, powerful talks lasting 18 minutes or less. The name stands for Technology, Entertainment, and Design, reflecting the fields that originally inspired the conference when it began in 1984 in California as a one-time event. Since then, it has grown into a global platform that covers an enormous range of subjects, including science, business, education, the arts, health, and social issues.

The organization is best known for its flagship conference, held annually in Vancouver, and for its many spin-off events such as TEDx, which allows independent groups around the world to host their own local TED-style gatherings under a license. TED also makes its talks freely available online through its website and YouTube channel, where many videos have been viewed hundreds of millions of times. This openness is a central part of its mission, which is to share ideas worth spreading with as wide an audience as possible.

TED talks are known for a distinctive style: speakers are typically given a short window to present a single compelling idea, often using storytelling, visual aids, and clear, accessible language rather than dense academic presentation. Speakers have included scientists, writers, activists, entrepreneurs, artists, and public figures. Over the decades, the format has influenced how many people think about public speaking and communicating complex topics to general audiences.

Welt-like, raised, itchy patches that appear fairly suddenly and that improve with Benadryl are most often hives, which are an allergic-type reaction. In kids the most common triggers are a viral infection (very common), a food or something touched or ingested, an insect bite, or contact with something in the environment. A science center has lots of shared surfaces, play materials, and sometimes animals or art supplies, so a contact trigger is possible, but a virus he picked up there or around the same time is just as likely. Hives often come and go over hours to a few days, and that's normal.

There is another possibility worth knowing about. Very red cheeks, sometimes described as "slapped cheek," can be fifth disease, a common mild viral illness in children. It typically causes bright red cheeks, and then a lacy rash on the body and limbs. It's usually not itchy or welt-like the way hives are, but the two can be confused, and the fact that Benadryl helped points more toward hives. Lingering rosy cheeks after the hives calm down can also just be residual irritation or flushing.

What to do now: you can keep an eye on him and, if he's itchy or uncomfortable, continue an antihistamine as directed on the label for his age and weight. Benadryl every 6 hours is within typical dosing, but don't give more than the label allows, and check with a pharmacist or his doctor if you're unsure of the dose. Many pediatricians prefer a non-drowsy one like cetirizine for hives lasting more than a day. Cool compresses and loose clothing help. Think back over what he ate, touched, or was around, and note any new foods, soaps, or sick contacts, since that helps identify a cause.

Call his pediatrician today or tomorrow, mainly to confirm the diagnosis, especially since the cheek swelling and persistent redness are present, and because he needs repeated medication to keep it down. Let them know if he has a fever, since that would point toward a viral cause.

Go to the emergency room or call 911 right away if you see any of these: swelling of the lips, tongue, or face (more than mild cheek puffiness), trouble breathing, wheezing, a hoarse voice or drooling, repeated vomiting, unusual sleepiness or limpness, dizziness or fainting, or a widespread rash along with any of those. Those can signal anaphylaxis, which is an emergency.

If he is breathing normally, acting like himself, eating and drinking, and the rash is fading, it's likely a benign hive reaction, but a quick call to his doctor is a sensible next step.

Yes, you can, and for many freelancers it's the smarter approach. As a freelancer you generally don't have an employer withholding income tax from your pay, so you're responsible for paying it yourself, usually through quarterly estimated payments to the IRS (and your state, if it has an income tax). Paying as you go means you don't face a large bill in April, you avoid underpayment penalties, and you're less likely to be caught short when you have a slow month.

There are a few practical ways to do it. The most common is to make quarterly estimated payments, due roughly in April, June, September, and January, based on your expected income. You can also set aside a fixed percentage of every payment you receive in a separate savings account, which many freelancers do with somewhere around 25 to 30 percent, depending on their income and location, since that covers both income tax and self-employment tax (the Social Security and Medicare contributions, which are about 15.3 percent on net earnings). A third option is to adjust your own W-4 if you have a part-time job alongside freelancing, so the extra withholding from that job covers some of your freelance tax liability.

Keep in mind that the self-employment tax is the part people often underestimate. A tax professional or a tool like the IRS Form 1040-ES worksheet can help you calculate a figure specific to your situation. If your income is uneven, you can also use the "safe harbor" rule, which generally protects you from penalties if you pay at least 100 percent of last year's total tax (110 percent if your prior-year income was above a certain threshold) spread across the year.

A Canadian company going public through an initial public offering (IPO) can gain several advantages from listing on both the Toronto Stock Exchange (TSX) and the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE). Among these is greater liquidity, since its shares become accessible to a wider base of investors across both markets. That broader access may boost demand for the shares and, in turn, push the share price higher. A dual listing can also raise the company's profile and standing, because the NYSE is widely regarded as one of the most prestigious and respected exchanges globally. This is particularly useful for firms hoping to draw in overseas investors. In addition, the company may find it easier to raise funds and manage its capital, since it can draw on the capital markets of both Canada and the United States. Still, a dual listing brings added expenses and regulatory obligations, as the company must meet the listing and disclosure rules of both exchanges. Before choosing this path, the company should weigh these potential costs against the benefits with care.

A biological neural network is a group of interconnected nerve cells, called neurons, that communicate with one another to process information and control behavior. These networks exist in the brains and nervous systems of animals, from simple worms with a few hundred neurons to humans with roughly 86 billion. Within a network, each neuron receives electrical and chemical signals from many others through junctions called synapses, integrates those inputs, and sends its own signal onward if the combined input is strong enough. Through this pattern of firing, the network supports functions such as perception, memory, movement, emotion, and thought.

The term is often used in neuroscience to refer to a specific circuit, such as the networks in the visual cortex that detect edges and motion, or the networks in the spinal cord that coordinate walking. It is a biological counterpart to the artificial neural networks used in computing, which were loosely inspired by how real neurons connect and learn. Unlike artificial networks, biological ones are shaped by physical growth, chemistry, and experience, and their connections strengthen or weaken over time in a process called synaptic plasticity, which is widely thought to underlie learning and memory.

Everybody has an accent, even if it doesn't feel like one to you. An accent is just the way someone's voice sounds when they talk, and it comes from where and how they learned to talk as a little kid. Babies listen to the grown-ups around them and copy the sounds they hear. If the people around you say words a certain way, you learn to say them that way too.

Think of it like learning a song from your friends at school. If all your friends sing a little differently from kids in another town, you'll pick up their style without even trying. Over time, groups of people who live near each other end up sounding alike, and groups who live far apart drift into different ways of talking.

That's why people from one city, country, or family can sound different from people somewhere else. Some sounds get shortened, some get stretched out, and some words get said with a little bounce or a different tune. None of these ways is right or wrong. They're just different ways of saying the same things, like how different families have their own way of making pancakes.

Talking to a healthcare professional about any worrying symptoms is always wise, particularly when strokes run in your family. A weak, heavy-feeling arm, along with dizziness and a spaced-out sensation, might point to a stroke or another medical problem. Getting an accurate diagnosis and treatment quickly matters, so it is good that you already have a GP appointment booked. Until then, try to remain calm rather than panic. Rest as much as you can, and steer clear of anything that could lead to a fall or other injury. Call your local emergency number straight away if you notice any of these symptoms: sudden weakness or numbness on one side of the body; sudden confusion, or trouble speaking or understanding what others say; sudden trouble seeing with one or both eyes; sudden trouble walking, or a loss of balance or coordination; or a sudden, severe headache with no known cause. To repeat, you should see a healthcare professional about your symptoms as soon as you can so that the cause can be identified and you can get the right treatment.

David Rumelhart (1942–2011) was an American psychologist and cognitive scientist who made major contributions to our understanding of human cognition and to the development of artificial neural networks. He earned his doctorate in mathematical psychology at Stanford University and spent much of his career at the University of California, San Diego, where he was a founding member of the Institute for Cognitive Science.

He is best known for his work in the 1980s on parallel distributed processing, a framework that models mental processes as emerging from the interactions of many simple, interconnected units rather than from rule-based symbol manipulation. With James McClelland and the PDP Research Group, he co-edited the influential two-volume book "Parallel Distributed Processing: Explorations in the Microstructure of Cognition" (1986), which helped revive interest in connectionist models of the mind.

Rumelhart is also credited, together with Geoffrey Hinton and Ronald Williams, with popularizing the backpropagation algorithm, a method for training multilayer neural networks by adjusting connection weights to reduce errors. Backpropagation became foundational to modern machine learning and deep learning.

Beyond these contributions, he worked on models of reading, story comprehension, and memory, and he proposed influential theories such as schema theory, which describes how prior knowledge structures guide understanding. He received the prestigious Warren Medal and other honors for his work. In 1998 he was diagnosed with Pick's disease, a neurodegenerative condition, and he died in 2011.

Raphael was an Italian painter and architect, born April 6, 1483 in Urbino. He's easily one of the big names of the High Renaissance, mostly known for his paintings and frescoes, though he did architectural work too. His stuff had a huge pull on art all through the Renaissance and into the Baroque period, and a lot of people would put him on the short list of the greatest artists in Western history.

Honestly there are a bunch of things that can make your whole body feel sore, wiped out, and achy. Overdoing it is a common one, especially if you've hit the gym harder than usual or started something new and your muscles aren't used to it. Not drinking enough water can do it too, and so can not eating enough, since your body just isn't getting the fuel it needs. Lack of sleep is another big culprit. Even a few rough nights in a row can leave you dragging and sore. Stress is sneaky as well, because chronic stress often shows up as tight muscles and that constant tired feeling. And of course, you could be coming down with something like the flu, which often brings body aches along with fatigue.

If it keeps going or you're not sure what's behind it, it's worth seeing a doctor so they can figure out the actual cause and tell you what to do about it. In the meantime, getting some rest, drinking plenty of water, and eating reasonably well can go a long way toward helping you feel better.

ECML PKDD stands for the European Conference on Machine Learning and Principles and Practice of Knowledge Discovery in Databases. It is one of the leading annual academic conferences in the fields of machine learning and data mining, held in Europe. The conference was created by combining two long-running European meetings: ECML, which focused on machine learning, and PKDD, which focused on knowledge discovery and data mining. The two merged into a single joint event in 2001, and it has been held yearly since then, with the location rotating among European cities.

The conference brings together researchers, students, and industry practitioners to present papers on new algorithms, theoretical foundations, and real-world applications of learning from data. Topics typically include supervised and unsupervised learning, deep learning, reinforcement learning, graph mining, time series analysis, and the ethical and practical challenges of applying data-driven methods. Accepted papers are usually published in the Springer Lecture Notes in Artificial Intelligence series (Lecture Notes in Computer Science in earlier years), and the event also features workshops, tutorials, and a discovery challenge in some years.

Within the research community, ECML PKDD is regarded as a prestigious venue, alongside conferences such as NeurIPS, ICML, and KDD, and it is especially known for strong European participation and its emphasis on connecting theory with practical data mining problems.

Currency markets, often called foreign exchange or forex markets, are the venues where currencies are traded. Trades always involve a pair, meaning one currency is purchased while another is sold in the same transaction. A currency's value is set by supply and demand, and a number of factors shape those forces.

Interest rates matter because higher rates make a currency more appealing to investors, who can earn greater returns, so currencies offering higher rates tend to gain value. Inflation works in the opposite direction: when a country's inflation runs above that of its trading partners, its currency often loses value, since rising prices erode its purchasing power and make it less attractive to hold. Economic growth can strengthen a currency, since expanding economies signal an ability to repay debts. Political stability also plays a major role, as countries seen as stable tend to draw more investment, pushing their currencies upward.

On the other side, heavy government debt can weaken a currency, because investors may doubt the government's capacity to meet its obligations. Central banks affect values through monetary policy, including setting interest rates and buying or selling government bonds. The exchange rate regime matters too: a currency pegged to another, such as the US dollar, will generally move in step with that anchor. Finally, trade balances have an effect. A large trade surplus, where exports exceed imports, can push a currency's value higher because the country sells more goods and services abroad.

Eliezer Yudkowsky is a prominent name in artificial intelligence (AI) and in the study of rational thinking. He co-founded the Machine Intelligence Research Institute (MIRI), a nonprofit that investigates the long-term risks and benefits of AI. He also writes and blogs extensively, producing many essays on AI, rationality, and the possible dangers and advantages of advanced technology. He is best known for his work on "friendly AI," the notion of building AI systems whose goals match human values and intentions, and which can be relied upon to act for humanity's genuine benefit.
