The idea is that widely watched EMAs (commonly the 20, 50, 100, 200) act as dynamic resistance because many traders and algorithms react to them, and the strength of that resistance depends on a handful of observable features.

Start with which EMA it is. A 200-day EMA that price is approaching from below carries more weight than a 20-day, because more capital references it and it reflects a longer-term trend. A 20 or 21 EMA is mostly relevant for short-term pullbacks inside a trend, while the 50 sits in between. As a rough hierarchy, the longer the period, the stronger the resistance.

Next, look at the slope. A downward-sloping EMA that price is rising into is much stronger resistance than a flat or rising one, because it signals that sellers have been in control and each prior rally has been sold. A steeply falling EMA means rallies are likely to stall at it. A flat EMA is weaker and more likely to be crossed.

Third, count and examine prior rejections. If price has touched the EMA several times and reversed with long upper wicks or strong bearish closes, the level is respected and probably stronger. Too many touches, however, can wear it down, since each test absorbs some sellers. Two or three clean rejections is a good sign; five or six with progressively shallower pullbacks suggests a breakout is near.

Fourth, check for confluence among EMAs. When several EMAs cluster in the same area, for example the 50 and 100 converging, the zone becomes a thicker band of resistance. A bearish stack, where shorter EMAs sit below longer ones in descending order (20 below 50 below 200), reinforces that the trend is down and that rallies into the longer EMAs will probably fail.

Fifth, consider the angle and speed of approach. A slow grind up into the EMA with shrinking candles and fading momentum often fails. A sharp, high-volume thrust that closes decisively above the EMA suggests resistance is weakening. Though you asked for EMA only, volume is a natural companion, and if you want to stay strictly with EMAs, use the distance between price and the EMA: a stock stretched far above a falling EMA is less likely to be stopped by it than one that has crept up to it.

Finally, judge the reaction to a break. A close above the EMA that holds for two or three sessions, followed by a successful retest where the EMA acts as support, means the resistance has flipped and was weak. A quick close back below it (a failed breakout) confirms strength.

A simple scoring approach: give a point each for a long-period EMA (100 or 200), a downward slope, at least two clean past rejections, EMA clustering, and a bearish EMA stack. Four or five points suggests strong resistance; two or fewer suggests it is likely to give way. Treat this as a framework to test on past charts of your stock before relying on it, and pair it with a stop-loss, since EMAs are lagging and can be overrun in news-driven moves.

Okay, so a caliber is basically how big a bullet is, or how wide the inside of a gun's barrel is. Bigger caliber means bigger bullet and a wider barrel. So a .40 caliber round is smaller than a .50 caliber one. That's why a handgun firing .40s has a skinnier barrel than a rifle shooting .50s. The handgun's smaller barrel is easier to carry and handle with one hand, while the rifle needs that wider bore to shoot a bigger, heavier bullet accurately over longer distances. Hope that clears up the difference! Let me know if anything's still confusing.

White-box testing is when you test software with full knowledge of how it's built inside. You can see the code, the structure, and the logic. That's the opposite of black-box testing, where you only know what goes in and what comes out and have no idea what happens in between. People often mix the two, since white-box testing is great for poking at specific parts or checking that internal processes behave, while black-box testing covers the user's side of things. Together they make a pretty solid strategy.

To do white-box testing well, you really need to understand the code and the algorithms behind it. You write test cases that hit different parts of the code and check that the output is what you expect. That might mean walking through specific paths, poking at edge cases, or making sure error handling actually works. The big upside is that you can dig deep into internal logic and catch sneaky bugs that would be almost impossible to spot from the outside, and you can test at a very low level. The downside? It eats up time, and you often need specialized skills or tools to pull it off.

William J. Rapaport is an American philosopher and computer scientist who is a professor at the State University of New York at Buffalo. He holds appointments in the Department of Computer Science and Engineering, the Department of Philosophy, the Center for Cognitive Science, and the Department of Linguistics, reflecting the interdisciplinary nature of his work. His research sits at the intersection of philosophy of mind, philosophy of language, artificial intelligence, and cognitive science.

Rapaport is best known for his work on computational theories of cognition and language understanding. He has written extensively on the philosophy of computer science, including questions about what it means for a computer to implement an algorithm, how computation relates to semantics, and whether machines can genuinely understand language. He is particularly associated with the idea of "syntactic semantics," the view that semantic interpretation can be understood in terms of relationships among symbols and their internal structure, without requiring direct connections to the external world. He has applied this perspective to natural language understanding and to models of how a cognitive agent builds up a mental representation of a text or situation.

He has also contributed to discussions about the nature of Turing machines and computational implementation, and he has been involved in the study of philosophical issues surrounding John Searle's Chinese Room argument. In addition to his research, he has taught courses in philosophy of computer science, artificial intelligence, and cognitive science, and he maintains a substantial online presence with lecture notes and writings that are widely used by students and researchers in these fields.

Your body is like a busy city where every part needs energy, and that energy comes from oxygen carried around by your blood. Your heart is the pump that moves the blood, your lungs bring in the oxygen, and your brain is the boss that keeps everything running. Dying is what happens when that system slows down and eventually stops, so the parts of the city can't get the energy they need anymore.

When someone dies slowly, like from old age or a long illness, it usually happens in steps. Weeks before, the person often gets very tired and sleeps a lot. They stop feeling hungry or thirsty, because the body doesn't need much fuel anymore and digesting food becomes hard work. This sounds sad, but it usually isn't uncomfortable for them. It's a bit like how you don't want a big dinner when you're really sleepy.

In the last few days, the body starts saving its energy for the most important parts, the heart and brain. So the hands and feet can get cool, and the skin might look pale or a little blotchy and purple. The person may get confused, talk about things that aren't there, or seem far away, like they're half dreaming. Their breathing often changes, sometimes fast, then slow, sometimes with long pauses, and sometimes with a rattly sound because they can't clear their throat anymore. That rattle sounds scary to the people nearby, but doctors believe the dying person usually isn't bothered by it, because by then they're mostly asleep.

Near the very end, most people are unconscious, meaning they're in something like a very deep sleep and aren't really aware of what's happening. Hearing seems to be one of the last senses to fade, so many nurses suggest talking gently to the person even if they can't answer. Then the breathing stops, and the heart stops pumping. Without fresh oxygen, the brain stops working within a few minutes, and that's when a person has died.

As for how it feels, nobody can tell us for sure, but the signs are mostly reassuring. The brain tends to release natural calming chemicals, the person drifts into sleepiness and then unconsciousness, and doctors and nurses can give medicine to take away pain or trouble breathing. Many people who came close to dying and were brought back describe feeling calm or peaceful rather than scared.

Sudden death, like from a heart attack or a bad accident, is different because it skips the slow steps. The heart might stop all at once, and the person usually passes out within seconds, so there's very little time to feel anything.

After death, the body slowly cools down, the muscles get stiff for a while and then loosen again, and the tiny cells in the body stop working one by one over the next hours. But the person themselves, their thoughts and feelings, are no longer there to notice any of it.

Water sounds like a soft place to land, but it's actually almost as hard as concrete when a plane hits it at high speed. Water doesn't squish out of the way the way sand or grass might, so a plane coming down on it can break apart. Sully's landing on the Hudson worked because he kept the plane's speed and nose angle just right, and the plane was big and sturdy enough to float for a while. Most planes aren't built to float, and the waves, the cold, and the chance of the fuselage splitting open make a water landing very dangerous. Pilots also almost never have a choice of where they come down. A runway, a field, or a flat patch of ground is usually a much safer bet than the open ocean, and there is often no nearby water to aim for.

As for why survivors seem rare, it's mostly because the crashes that make the news are the most terrible ones. When a plane goes down far out at sea or hits the ground at high speed, the forces are so great that few people can live through it. The stories of survivors, like Sully's flight where everyone got off safely, get shared a lot too, so it can feel like they're uncommon. In fact, many plane crashes do have survivors. Crashes during takeoff and landing, when planes are moving more slowly, often leave a lot of people alive. Seatbelts, staying low to the ground, and getting out fast all help, which is why flight attendants give those safety instructions before every trip.

The female symbol is called the Venus symbol. It is a circle with a small cross beneath it, and in biology it represents the female sex. Its name comes from the Roman goddess of love and beauty, and the same symbol was also used to represent the planet Venus and the element copper in alchemy.

Yes, this is a popular strategy often called "gift card churning" or "gift card arbitrage," and it can work well, though the benefit depends on the store and the card program. Many grocery chains offer their own rewards programs, and some also sell gift cards to other retailers, restaurants, or services. If you pay with a credit card that earns bonus points on groceries or gift cards, or if the store runs a promotion where you earn extra fuel points or grocery rewards for buying certain gift cards, you can effectively earn more than you would by shopping directly. Some people also use cards like the Amex Gift Card Mall or similar promotions tied to specific cards.

Keep a few caveats in mind. Some credit cards classify gift card purchases at grocery stores as groceries, while others treat them as general merchandise or exclude them from bonus categories entirely. Retailers sometimes limit how many gift cards you can buy at once, and some cards charge fees or have restrictions on which gift cards qualify for promotions. Also, promotions change frequently, so check the current terms before you buy. Finally, make sure you actually plan to use the gift cards at the stores they're for, since unused balances can go to waste. If you're considering this, look at the store's current fuel or loyalty promotions and your credit card's bonus category details to see which combination gives you the best return.

It's hard to pinpoint the exact cause of your symptoms without more details and a hands-on examination. Several conditions could explain a swollen inner cheek that is peeling and sore. One possibility is an oral infection, such as a bacterial or fungal infection like a staph infection or thrush. Another is an allergic reaction to something you ate or touched, which can lead to swelling and irritation in the cheek. Physical injury is also a common cause; if you accidentally bit your cheek or otherwise injured your mouth, that could produce swelling and tenderness. Finally, dry mouth can leave the cheeks swollen and peeling because of a lack of moisture. Seeing a doctor or dentist is important so the cause can be identified and treated properly. Until then, rinsing with a warm saltwater solution may help clean your mouth and ease inflammation, and it's wise to avoid spicy or acidic foods that could aggravate the area.

Chronic runny nose that has lasted for years, starting in childhood, usually has an underlying cause that hasn't been fully controlled. Since you already have allergies, allergic rhinitis is a likely contributor. Allergies to pet dander and dust mites are often perennial, meaning they cause symptoms year round rather than only in certain seasons, and even a mild, ongoing exposure can keep the nasal lining inflamed. Allergy medicine taken as needed may not be enough. Intranasal corticosteroid sprays such as fluticasone or mometasone are generally the most effective treatment for persistent allergic congestion and drainage, and they work best when used every day rather than only during bad days.

Another possibility is nonallergic rhinitis, where the nasal lining is overly reactive to things like temperature changes, strong odors, smoke, perfumes, cleaning products, or spicy food, without any allergy being involved. This is common and often overlooked, and it can coexist with allergies. If you have been using decongestant nasal sprays such as oxymetazoline for more than a few days at a time, rebound congestion, sometimes called rhinitis medicamentosa, can keep your nose stuffy and runny in a cycle that feels permanent.

Structural factors can also play a role. A deviated septum, enlarged turbinates (the bony structures inside the nose that swell when irritated), or nasal polyps can block airflow and cause chronic congestion with drainage. Chronic sinusitis, which can follow repeated inflammation, may produce ongoing mucus even when you aren't sick. Some people also have post-nasal drip caused by acid reflux, where stomach acid irritates the throat and nasal passages, or by hormonal changes, certain medications such as some blood pressure drugs, or irritants in the home or workplace.

Because your symptoms have persisted for about seventeen years, it would be worthwhile to see an allergist or an ear, nose, and throat specialist. They can perform skin or blood testing to identify specific triggers, examine your nasal passages with a scope, and determine whether structural problems or sinus disease are involved. Let a doctor know promptly if you notice thick colored discharge with facial pain or fever, a bloody discharge, loss of smell, or congestion that is only on one side, since these can point to conditions that need different care.

Natural-language understanding (NLU) is a branch of artificial intelligence and computational linguistics concerned with enabling computers to interpret the meaning of human language, whether written or spoken, in a way that is useful for a given purpose. Where broader natural-language processing covers everything from tokenizing text to generating sentences, NLU focuses specifically on comprehension: working out what a person actually means when they say or write something.

Human language is full of ambiguity, so this is a difficult problem. The same word can carry different meanings depending on context ("bank" as a financial institution or a riverside), sentences can be structured in multiple ways, and much of what people communicate is implied rather than stated. A system performing NLU must therefore identify the grammatical structure of an utterance, resolve references such as pronouns, recognize named entities like people, places, and dates, and grasp the intent behind the request.

In practical applications, NLU appears in virtual assistants that respond to spoken commands, chatbots that route customer questions, search engines that interpret queries rather than matching keywords, and tools that extract information from documents or classify emotional tone in reviews. Early systems relied on hand-written rules and carefully defined vocabularies, while modern approaches typically use statistical models and large neural networks trained on vast amounts of text, which have greatly improved the ability to handle the variety and nuance of real language.

What you're describing sounds like aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease (also called Samter's triad or N-ERD): nasal polyps, asthma, and sensitivity to aspirin and similar anti-inflammatory drugs. So yes, the aspirin challenge and desensitization your doctors recommended was appropriate, and it's a well-established treatment for this condition rather than just an allergy test. After repeated polyp surgeries, daily high-dose aspirin is one of the options that can slow polyp regrowth and improve breathing, so the fact that you feel good on it is a good sign.

What you're noticing at lower doses also fits the pattern. Desensitization only works while you keep taking aspirin continuously. If the dose drops or you miss doses, tolerance fades and symptoms like nasal blockage can return, sometimes within a couple of days. That's why the nasal congestion comes back when you decrease it. The hives at 60 mg are less typical, since AERD usually shows up as nose and chest symptoms rather than skin reactions. It could mean you have some additional skin sensitivity, or that the dose was in a range where you were not yet fully tolerant. Either way, it's something your allergist needs to know about specifically.

My practical advice is not to adjust the dose yourself. Stay on the dose that controls your symptoms and keep taking it every day without gaps. If you have to stop for more than a few days, for illness or surgery, tell your doctor, because you may need to be re-desensitized under supervision. Contact your allergist soon to discuss the hives and whether 600 mg twice daily is the right long-term dose. Many people do well on lower maintenance doses, such as 300 to 650 mg a day, but that should be a supervised step-down, not a trial on your own.

Also watch for the side effects of long-term aspirin, mainly stomach irritation or bleeding, so report black stools, persistent stomach pain, or easy bruising. Your doctor may suggest a stomach-protecting medicine. Keep avoiding other NSAIDs like ibuprofen or diclofenac unless your doctor says otherwise, and continue your nasal steroid spray and asthma medications.

Seek urgent care if you ever get facial or throat swelling, trouble breathing, wheezing that doesn't settle, or widespread hives with dizziness. For the hives alone, mention them at your next contact with your allergist, and sooner if they spread or recur regularly.

In mathematics, the range of a function is the collection of every output value that the function can generate. For a function f(x), where x is the input and f(x) is the output, the range consists of all the values f(x) takes as x moves across the entire domain. As an illustration, when f(x) = x^2, the range is every non-negative real number, because squaring any real x never produces a negative result. The range can also be written as an interval on the real number line. Take the function f(x) = x^2 restricted to inputs in [-3,3]: its range is [0,9], since outputs for inputs between -3 and 3 always fall between 0 and 9. Beyond functions, the word "range" may also describe the possible values a variable can hold. If a variable x is limited to the values 1, 2, and 3, its range is the set {1, 2, 3}.

Carlos Pena Jr. is an actor and singer, and most people know him as Carlos Garcia from the Nickelodeon show "Big Time Rush." The series ran from 2010 to 2013 and follows four hockey players who get picked to form a boy band. Pena Jr. played Carlos, a talented musician and dancer who's the wild card of the group. Before that show, he'd done a bunch of stage work and guest spots on TV, including "ER" and "Judging Amy." He's also put out music, both on his own and with the band Big Time Rush.

It's totally understandable that your friend is worried about cancer, but a biopsy is pretty routine. Doctors order them all the time to figure out what's behind weird bumps or sores in the mouth. The bumps on the back of the tongue called circumvallate papillae are normal, though. They're just part of how the tongue is built. So that sore spot might be related to them, or it might be something else entirely. Honestly, a biopsy is the only real way to know for sure.

Yeah, it may need a stitch or two, but it's usually a quick thing done in a doctor's office or outpatient clinic. Recovery is normally pretty short and most people handle it fine. Your friend should still talk through the risks and benefits with his doctor, and think about what happens if he skips it. Getting nervous about procedures is super common, but a biopsy is one of the best tools doctors have for catching and treating things like cancer early.

Duavent (that's ipratropium and albuterol) is usually considered safe to nebulize, but it's really meant for COPD or asthma symptoms, not just a bad cough. So if your daughter doesn't have either of those, it probably isn't the best fit for what she's dealing with. I'd run it by a doctor before you start anything new. They can actually look at her and figure out what makes sense for her situation.

As for the temperature, 37.3°C (about 99°F) is normal for both kids and adults, so I wouldn't worry about that. But if she's got other symptoms along with the cough, or the cough hangs on even after treatment, get her checked out so someone can take a closer look.

No secret society here, just plumbing. Think of internet service like water pipes.

Your home internet comes through a wire, either a cable or fiber line, that runs straight to your house. That wire is like a big pipe that's all yours, or shared with only a few neighbors. Wires can carry a huge amount of data, and adding more capacity is fairly cheap because the company can upgrade equipment at either end. The main thing they can control is how wide they let your pipe be, so they charge by speed. A fatter pipe costs more, but once you have it you can mostly run the water as much as you want.

Cell phones don't have a wire. They talk to a tower through the air using radio waves, and the air is like one small shared pipe that everyone near that tower has to use at the same time. There's only so much radio space available. Governments sell slices of it to phone companies for billions of dollars, and building more towers is expensive and slow. If everyone near a tower streamed movies all day, it would clog up and nobody's phone would work well. So phone companies charge by how much data you use, which nudges people to share that limited air more carefully. It's like a cafeteria with only one soda fountain: if it's free and unlimited, a few kids hog it, so the lunch lady hands out a set number of cups.

That said, the line between the two is blurring. Many phone plans now say "unlimited," but they slow you down after a certain amount, and some home internet plans have data caps too. Part of the pricing is also just business: companies charge whatever people are willing to pay, and since people really want their phones everywhere, they'll pay for data. But the main reason is that wires have lots of room and the shared airwaves don't.

Spotting or bleeding during pregnancy can have all sorts of causes, and it's scary no matter what. If you've got a uterine septum and you're seeing pink spotting, call your provider soon rather than waiting it out. A uterine septum is a congenital thing where a wall of tissue splits the uterus into two cavities. It can make getting pregnant harder and can raise the chances of miscarriage, preterm labor, or problems with the placenta. Your provider can figure out what's going on and tell you what to do next. If you can't get hold of them, or if the bleeding gets heavy or comes with bad belly pain or cramping, head to the ER and don't wait.

Serotonin and dopamine are the brain chemicals that help control mood, emotion, and pleasure. Here's the thing though: being serious or strict doesn't mean someone gets less of a kick from these. Everybody's brain has its own baseline levels, and those shift around depending on genetics, surroundings, and how you live day to day. Some folks just naturally run higher or lower, and that can shape their mood and what they go looking for in terms of fun. But you can't really pin it on one personality trait. Being a serious person doesn't tell you much about how good someone feels when something nice happens.

Birds make noise for all sorts of reasons. Plenty of them sing to win over mates, while others use calls to mark their turf or keep in touch with the rest of the flock. That chatter is handy when a group is on the move, since nobody wants to lose track of the others. Parrots are famous for it, and they'll often squawk just for fun or to show how they're feeling.

As for the energy cost, it really depends on what kind of noise we're talking about and how long the bird keeps at it. Singing can wear a bird out, but most of them take breaks between songs so they don't burn through everything they've got. Giving away their position is a real concern too, no question. Still, birds have figured out ways to cut that risk down. Many sing from high perches where they're harder to spot, and plenty of them pipe up at times when predators are usually less active.

A reader asks whether their pelvic wash cytology, taken before a hysterectomy, shows metastatic breast cancer cells. The report describes atypical cells that were read as reactive mesothelial cells, with enlarged, crowded nuclei, positive for calretinin and negative for Ber-EP4. The reader has a prior history of triple-negative breast cancer. The response explains that it cannot accurately interpret the report without more information or the full medical record. A cytology report is a lab test in which cells are examined under a microscope for abnormalities. Here, the atypical cells were classified as reactive mesothelial cells because of their marker profile: calretinin positivity and Ber-EP4 negativity. Mesothelial cells line the body's internal organs and cavities, including the pelvis, and they can enlarge and crowd together in response to inflammation or injury. Their presence in a sample does not by itself mean cancer is present. Given the reader's breast cancer history, spread to the pelvis is a possibility in general, but the information provided is not enough to say whether these particular cells are metastatic breast cancer. The reader should go over the findings with their doctor and, if needed, pursue further testing to reach an accurate diagnosis.

Andrew Ng's a computer scientist and entrepreneur, and he's best known for his work in AI and machine learning. He co-founded Google Brain, and he used to be Vice President and Chief Scientist at Baidu. He was also an Associate Professor at Stanford for a while. People tend to associate him with online machine learning and large-scale distributed systems, and he helped build Coursera, which is probably how most folks have heard of him. He also founded the AI Fund, a venture capital firm that backs and supports AI projects. Beyond all that, he's a really well-respected speaker and teacher who's given tons of talks and lectures on AI and machine learning. He's seen as one of the top experts in the field, so you'll see him quoted a lot in articles and interviews whenever AI and its effect on society come up.

"ARB" most commonly refers to angiotensin II receptor blockers, a class of blood pressure and heart medications. They work by blocking angiotensin II, a hormone that narrows blood vessels, so the vessels relax and blood pressure falls. They are also used to protect the heart and kidneys, especially in people with diabetes, heart failure, or chronic kidney disease.

Common ARBs include losartan (Cozaar), valsartan (Diovan), irbesartan (Avapro), candesartan (Atacand), olmesartan (Benicar), telmisartan (Micardis), and azilsartan (Edarbi). Some combination products pair an ARB with another blood pressure drug, such as a diuretic or amlodipine, for example Hyzaar, Diovan HCT, or Azor.

ARBs are generally well tolerated, but they can cause dizziness, high potassium levels, and, rarely, kidney changes. They should not be used during pregnancy because they can harm the developing baby. If you were asking about something else by "arb," such as a specific brand name or a different drug, let me know and I can help with that.

An itch is a funny feeling on your skin that makes you want to scratch. Think of it like a tiny alarm bell that your skin rings to tell your brain, "Hey, something is bothering me here! Please take care of it!"

Your skin is covered in teeny tiny nerves, like very thin invisible wires that send messages up to your brain. Some of those nerves are special itch detectors. When something tickles or irritates them, they send the "itch" message. That something might be a mosquito bite, a bit of dry skin, a scratchy wool sweater, or a little bug crawling on you. When your body notices something that might be harmful, it releases a tiny chemical called histamine, which is like a little messenger that shouts at the itch nerves to wake up. That's why bug bites and allergies make you so itchy.

The reason itching exists is probably to protect you. Long ago, an itch told people to brush off bugs, spiders, or prickly plants before they could bite or hurt them. So the itch is your body's way of saying, "Get that off me!"

Scratching feels good because it gives your skin a tiny bit of mild pain, and your brain pays attention to that instead of the itch for a moment. It's like your brain can only listen to one loud thing at a time, and the scratch is louder. But scratching too much can actually make things worse. It can hurt your skin and cause your body to release even more itch chemicals, so the itch comes back, which is why you want to scratch again. That's the itch-scratch cycle.

Sometimes itches come from other things too, like very dry skin in winter, a rash, or an allergy. If an itch won't go away, a grown-up or doctor can help find out why.

Existential risk is basically anything that could wipe out humanity, or any other intelligent life out there, for good. What makes these risks so hard to deal with is that they could either destroy us completely or permanently stop us from ever reaching our potential. Think nuclear war, pandemics, bioterrorism, or AI that goes badly wrong.

You'll see the idea come up a lot in philosophy, ethics, and risk management, and policy people and decision-makers talk about it too. It's not like other risks, because the harm isn't just bad, it's catastrophic and can't be undone. There's no bouncing back afterward.

They also tend to be low-probability, high-impact events. That's a big part of why they're so tough to prepare for. It's hard to get people worked up about something that probably won't happen, even when the stakes are enormous. But given how huge the consequences could be, it makes sense for individuals, organizations, and governments to actually think it through and take steps now to head these things off, instead of waiting until it's too late.

Google Finance does not publish a detailed formula for its "Institution Owned" figure, so the exact method is not fully documented. The figure is generally understood to be based on institutional holdings reported in SEC Form 13F filings. Institutional investment managers with at least $100 million in qualifying securities must file these quarterly, listing their holdings as of quarter end. Data aggregators, which Google draws on, add up the shares reported by these institutions for a given stock and divide that total by the company's shares outstanding. The result is the percentage of the company that institutions own.

Because of this approach, the number is a snapshot tied to the most recent filing period, so it can lag actual ownership by up to about 45 days after quarter end. It also tends to exclude holders below the reporting thresholds, such as smaller advisers, and it may not fully capture shares held through certain structures. Differences in share count denominators, such as using basic versus diluted shares outstanding, can also make the figure differ from what other sites report. For the precise methodology, you would need to check Google's own help documentation or the data provider's notes.

Predictive analytics is the practice of using historical and current data, combined with statistical techniques, machine learning, and data mining, to make informed estimates about future events or unknown outcomes. Rather than simply describing what has already happened, it tries to answer the question of what is likely to happen next, and with what probability.

The basic idea is that patterns found in past data can help forecast future behavior. For example, if a bank has records of thousands of past loans along with information about which borrowers repaid and which defaulted, it can build a model that identifies the characteristics associated with default. When a new applicant comes along, the model can estimate how likely that person is to repay. The output is usually a score or probability rather than a certainty, which helps decision makers weigh risks and choose actions.

The process typically begins with defining a clear question or goal, such as predicting which customers might cancel a subscription. Analysts then gather relevant data, clean and prepare it, and select variables that might influence the outcome. Next they build models using methods like regression analysis, decision trees, neural networks, or time series forecasting. These models are trained on historical data, tested on data they have not seen before to check their accuracy, and then deployed to generate predictions on new information. Because conditions change over time, models are usually monitored and retrained periodically to keep them reliable.

Predictive analytics is used across many fields. Retailers use it to forecast demand and manage inventory, and to recommend products customers are likely to buy. Insurance companies use it to price policies and detect fraudulent claims. Hospitals use it to identify patients at risk of readmission or complications. Manufacturers apply it to predict when equipment is likely to fail so they can perform maintenance before a breakdown occurs, a practice often called predictive maintenance. Marketing teams use it to target the people most likely to respond to a campaign, and financial institutions use it for credit scoring and market forecasting.

It is often discussed alongside related forms of analytics. Descriptive analytics summarizes what happened in the past, diagnostic analytics looks at why it happened, predictive analytics estimates what will happen, and prescriptive analytics goes a step further by recommending what action to take based on those predictions.

While powerful, predictive analytics has limitations. Its accuracy depends heavily on the quality and relevance of the data used; incomplete or biased data can lead to misleading or unfair predictions. Models can also fail when circumstances shift in ways not reflected in historical data, such as during an economic crisis or pandemic. There are ethical concerns as well, particularly around privacy and the risk that models reinforce existing discrimination, for instance in hiring or lending decisions. For these reasons, predictive analytics works best when its results are interpreted carefully and combined with human judgment.

David Chalmers is a philosopher and cognitive scientist whose research centers on the nature of consciousness and the idea of the "hard problem of consciousness." He serves as a professor of philosophy and heads the Centre for Consciousness at the Australian National University, and he has also taught at institutions including the University of Arizona and New York University. He is perhaps most famous for his 1996 book "The Conscious Mind: In Search of a Fundamental Theory," where he introduced the notion of the "hard problem of consciousness." Chalmers contended in that work that although existing scientific theories can account for many features of the mind and brain, they fail to adequately explain how and why we have subjective experiences. He suggested that the existence of subjective experience, or "qualia," presents a basic mystery that current scientific theories may never fully resolve. Chalmers has also made important contributions to the philosophy of language and the philosophy of mind, publishing many articles and books on these subjects. Widely respected and influential in philosophy, his work has provoked considerable debate among philosophers and scientists alike.

Statistical noise refers to the random, unexplained variation in data that obscures the underlying pattern or signal you are trying to detect. Whenever you measure something, collect a sample, or observe a process, the values you get will fluctuate for reasons that have nothing to do with the effect you care about. That fluctuation is the noise, and the meaningful pattern beneath it is often called the signal.

Noise arises from many sources. Measurement instruments are never perfectly precise, so repeated readings of the same quantity will differ slightly. Sampling introduces noise too: if you survey 500 people about their voting intentions, a different random group of 500 would give somewhat different results simply by chance, even if public opinion hadn't changed at all. Natural variability among individuals, uncontrolled environmental factors, recording errors, and countless small influences that are too numerous or subtle to account for all contribute to the random scatter in a dataset.

A simple way to picture it is to imagine flipping a fair coin ten times. You might get seven heads, even though the true probability is fifty percent. That deviation from five heads isn't evidence that the coin is biased; it is just noise from a small sample. If you flipped it ten thousand times, the proportion would settle very close to one half, because noise tends to average out as the amount of data grows.

The central challenge in statistics is distinguishing signal from noise. Tools like confidence intervals, hypothesis tests, and p-values exist largely to answer the question of whether an observed difference or trend is large enough relative to the background noise that it is unlikely to have occurred by chance alone. For example, if a new drug lowers blood pressure by an average of two points in a small trial, researchers must ask whether that improvement is real or whether ordinary patient-to-patient variation could easily produce a difference that size.

Noise matters because ignoring it leads to common mistakes. People often read meaning into random fluctuations, such as a sports team's short winning streak, a single month's rise in a stock price, or a small uptick in crime statistics. Conversely, in machine learning and modeling, a model that fits its training data too closely can end up memorizing the noise rather than learning the true pattern, a problem known as overfitting, which makes it perform poorly on new data.

In short, statistical noise is the random variability inherent in real-world data, and much of statistical thinking is about recognizing it, measuring how large it is, and making sure conclusions are based on genuine patterns rather than chance.

There are a few things to think about before deciding whether to buy the place from your landlord. First, can you actually afford it? Look at your income, debts, and other bills and see whether you can comfortably cover the monthly mortgage plus the extras that come with owning a home.

Next, how are you going to pay for it? If you need a mortgage, check whether you'd qualify and what the terms would look like. If you can pay cash, that changes things a lot.

Location matters too. Do you want to live there long-term? Think about how close it is to work, schools, and the stuff you use every day.

Then there's the condition of the house. Is it in good shape? If it needs work, are you ready and able to handle repairs or renovations?

Finally, take a look at the local market. Is it a buyer's market or a seller's market? That affects what the house is worth and how much room you'll have to negotiate.

If the money works, the location suits you, and the house is in decent shape, buying from your landlord can be a solid move. Just take your time and weigh all of this before you commit.

I'm sorry you're not feeling well. What you describe could be the symptoms of an illness or infection, so it's a good idea to see a healthcare professional who can identify the cause and recommend the right treatment. Meanwhile, a few things may ease your discomfort. Rest as much as you can, since this gives your body the chance to heal and recover. Keep up your fluid intake with water and drinks rich in electrolytes to guard against dehydration. Over-the-counter pain relievers can also help: acetaminophen (Tylenol) or ibuprofen (Advil), often grouped with anti-inflammatory drugs, can bring down a fever and soothe body aches. If your fever runs high, one of these same fever-reducing medications may be useful. Running a humidifier adds moisture to the air, which may ease cold sweats and make your symptoms less severe. It also helps to stay in a comfortable, moderate-temperature space rather than exposing yourself to extreme heat or cold, which could make things worse. Keep in mind that these steps offer only short-term relief. If your symptoms last or get worse, get medical care, and if you are worried about your health, talk to a healthcare professional as soon as you can.

If someone has swallowed a potentially poisonous substance, such as toilet cleaner, it is essential to get medical help right away. Swallowing toilet cleaner is extremely hazardous and may lead to serious complications, such as burns to the mouth and throat, abdominal pain, vomiting, breathing trouble, and, in the worst cases, death. When a person has taken in a large quantity of the cleaner, doctors may perform a procedure known as gastric lavage, or stomach pumping, to clear the substance from the stomach. During this process, a tube is passed through the mouth or nose into the stomach, and a special liquid is used to flush it out. Depending on the symptoms and the amount swallowed, other treatments might also be needed. These could include drugs to ease nausea and vomiting, supportive measures to assist breathing and keep vital signs stable, and in some cases surgery to repair injuries caused by the cleaner. Anyone who has swallowed a possibly toxic substance should follow the advice of the healthcare team caring for them and seek medical care immediately.

Section 8, formally called the Housing Choice Voucher Program, is a federal initiative that offers rent subsidies to people and households with low incomes. The U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) oversees it, and its purpose is to make safe, decent, and sanitary homes affordable within the private rental market. Under the program, participants generally contribute 30% of their monthly income toward rent and utilities, while the program pays the rest. Applicants must satisfy specific income limits and may also need to meet other conditions, such as being a first-time buyer or having a disability. Both renters and homeowners can take part, and voucher holders are free to lease from any landlord who agrees to accept the voucher. Beyond providing more housing choices for low-income families, the program aims to foster economic independence by letting them relocate to neighborhoods with stronger employment prospects and better schools. For questions about the program and whether you qualify for rental help, your local HUD office can provide further details.

Bounded rationality is the idea that people's decision-making is limited by the information they have, the cognitive capacity they can bring to bear, and the time available to them. Rather than assuming humans are perfectly rational optimizers who gather all relevant information and calculate the best possible choice, this concept recognizes that real decisions are made under constraints. Because of these limits, people tend to make choices that are good enough rather than optimal.

The term was introduced by Herbert Simon in the 1950s, and he later received the Nobel Prize in Economics partly for this work. Simon argued that classical economic models, which depicted decision-makers as having complete information and unlimited computational ability, did not describe how people actually behave. He proposed that individuals instead engage in "satisficing," a blend of satisfying and sufficing, in which they search through options until they find one that meets an acceptable threshold, and then stop searching. For example, someone looking for an apartment may not inspect every listing in the city. They may set criteria for price, location, and size, and accept the first place that meets them.

Bounded rationality has influenced many fields, including economics, psychology, political science, and artificial intelligence. It helps explain phenomena such as heuristics and rules of thumb, which speed up decisions but can sometimes lead to systematic errors, and it provides a more realistic foundation for understanding organizational behavior and policy design. Later work in behavioral economics, such as research by Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky, built on these ideas by documenting the specific shortcuts and biases that shape human judgment.

I can't predict the size of your penis, since it depends on factors like genetics, hormone levels, and general health. Penis size also doesn't determine masculinity or how attractive someone is. Being healthy and comfortable with your body matters far more. Losing body fat may make a flaccid penis look longer because less of it is hidden under fat, but it typically doesn't change the size of an erect penis. Size varies widely between individuals and can shift over a lifetime with aging and hormonal changes. Many people worry about their genitals, but there is a broad range of normal. Size is also far from the most important factor in sexual satisfaction for either partner. Open communication, trust, and mutual respect contribute much more to a healthy and fulfilling sexual relationship.

Sorry you're dealing with shoulder and chest pain, that's scary, and it makes sense you'd jump to heart attack. Chest and shoulder pain has lots of possible causes though, and plenty of them have nothing to do with the heart. Heartburn (acid reflux) is a really common one. When stomach acid creeps back up into your esophagus, you get a burning feeling in your chest and throat, and it can sometimes radiate into the shoulder or neck. Muscle strains, pinched nerves, and even stress or anxiety can cause it too. That said, if the pain is severe, comes on suddenly, or comes with shortness of breath, sweating, or nausea, get medical help right away. Those can be signs of a heart attack, and you don't want to guess on that one. In the meantime, try to slow your breathing and relax, since stress can make everything feel worse. If it does sound like heartburn, an antacid or acid blocker from the drugstore might help. If the symptoms stick around or get worse, or you're just not sure what's going on, see a doctor and get it checked out.

Trading with settled and unsettled funds is a central concern for cash account investors, because the settlement cycle determines when proceeds from a sale become fully available for reuse. Under the standard T+3 cycle that applied to most equity trades until the move to T+2 in 2017 and later to T+1 in the United States in 2024, a trade executed on day zero settled on the third business day afterward. Many people still encounter the T+3 terminology in older materials, in certain non-U.S. markets, or in discussions of cash account rules, so it remains worth understanding.

Settled funds are cash that has completed the settlement process and can be withdrawn or used to purchase new securities without restriction. Unsettled funds are proceeds from a sale that have been received on paper but have not yet cleared. Until a sale settles, that cash is typically tagged as unsettled and cannot be used to buy new securities in a cash account, at least not without risking a violation of the rules. Buying a security with unsettled proceeds and then selling that new security before the original sale settles is known as a good faith violation, and repeated violations can lead a brokerage to restrict the account, often requiring that purchases be paid for in full with settled funds for a period of time, commonly ninety days.

Investors commonly manage this by planning their cash flow around the settlement calendar. If you sell a position on a Monday under T+3, the proceeds will not be fully settled until Thursday, so a purchase made on Tuesday or Wednesday using those proceeds would be funded by unsettled cash. Waiting until the funds settle, or using only money that was already settled before the sale, avoids the issue. Some brokerages display separate figures for settled cash, unsettled cash, and buying power, and it is wise to check these before placing orders, particularly near holidays, where the count of business days can extend the wait.

Margin accounts operate under different rules. Because a margin account can borrow against the portfolio, unsettled proceeds may often be used for new purchases without triggering a good faith violation, though the investor still bears the risk of a margin call if the position moves against them. Retirement accounts and some other account types have their own treatment of unsettled funds as well.

In practice, the key habits are to confirm the settlement date of any sale, distinguish settled from unsettled cash in your account view, and avoid relying on proceeds until they have cleared. Checking your specific brokerage's policies is important, since terms and account restrictions can vary.

Blood-tinged mucus with a productive cough usually comes from irritation of the airways. Forceful coughing can rupture tiny blood vessels, and the most common cause of this pattern in a healthy adult is acute bronchitis, often following a cold or other viral infection. Post-nasal drip, sinus irritation, dry air, and dehydration can also contribute. The dizziness is probably related to the coughing itself, since intense coughing fits can briefly reduce blood flow to the brain, and it may also reflect dehydration or just feeling run down.

Some less common causes are worth knowing about, though they tend to come with other signs. Pneumonia usually causes fever, chest pain, or shortness of breath. A blood clot in the lung can cause blood-streaked sputum and lightheadedness, but it typically comes with sudden shortness of breath, sharp chest pain, a racing heart, or leg swelling, and it is more likely with recent surgery, long immobility, travel, or hormonal medications. Because you are feeling well otherwise, these seem less likely, but the combination of blood in your sputum and dizziness is the part that deserves a medical check.

As for duration, a cough from acute bronchitis commonly lasts two to three weeks, and it can linger for several weeks after the infection itself has cleared. A cough that is still going strong after three weeks, or that lasts beyond eight weeks, should be evaluated.

You should seek medical care promptly, and emergency care if it's severe, if you cough up more than a small streak of blood or sputum that is mostly red, if you develop fever, chest pain, shortness of breath, a racing or pounding heartbeat, wheezing, or fainting, or if the dizziness becomes persistent or worsens. Given that you have blood in your sputum and dizziness, it would be sensible to contact your doctor soon even if you feel fine, so they can listen to your lungs and decide whether a chest X-ray or other tests are needed.

In the meantime, rest, drink plenty of fluids, use a humidifier or steam to ease irritation, and avoid smoking and smoke exposure. Honey and warm liquids may soothe the cough. Stand up slowly if you feel dizzy, and sit down right away if you feel faint.

A Switchblade drone is a small, portable loitering munition made by the American defense company AeroVironment. A loitering munition is a weapon that sits somewhere between a reconnaissance drone and a guided missile: after launch it can fly over an area for a period of time, letting an operator watch through its camera and search for a target, and then it dives into that target and detonates its warhead. Because it destroys itself in the attack, it is often called a "kamikaze drone" or "suicide drone," though manufacturers and militaries prefer the term loitering munition.

The name comes from its design. The drone is stored in a compact launch tube with its wings folded against its body. When fired, it is ejected from the tube, and the wings spring open, much like the blade of a switchblade knife, allowing it to fly under electric propulsion. A soldier controls it using a handheld ground control unit, seeing live video from the drone and choosing when and where to strike. An important feature is that the operator can abort an attack at the last moment and send the drone back into a holding pattern if, for example, civilians appear near the target.

There are two main versions. The Switchblade 300 is very small and light, weighing only a few pounds, and can be carried in a backpack by a single soldier. It has a range of roughly 10 kilometers and flies for around 15 to 20 minutes, carrying a small warhead intended for targets such as personnel or lightly protected vehicles. The larger Switchblade 600 weighs around 50 pounds, can fly for about 40 minutes, has a range of roughly 40 kilometers or more, and carries an anti-armor warhead capable of destroying tanks and other armored vehicles.

The Switchblade was first used by US forces in Afghanistan in the early 2010s, giving small infantry units their own precision strike capability without needing to call in aircraft or artillery. It gained much wider public attention in 2022 when the United States sent Switchblade drones to Ukraine as part of military aid following Russia's invasion. Its use there, alongside many other drones, has highlighted how inexpensive, portable, precision-guided weapons are changing modern warfare by giving small groups of soldiers the ability to find and attack targets far beyond their line of sight.

Subjective experience is the personal, first-person way an individual encounters the world, including their own thoughts, feelings, and sensations. It is called subjective because it is a person's own view of what they go through, which is unique to them and may differ from one individual to the next. It is frequently set against objective experience, which concerns the external reality that exists regardless of how any one person perceives it. For instance, the color of an object is treated as an objective property, separate from any individual's subjective experience of seeing it. Because subjective experience bears on how people perceive, interpret, and make sense of their surroundings, it is a significant subject of study in psychology, neuroscience, and philosophy. Researchers in these disciplines try to learn how factors like biology, culture, and individual differences shape subjective experience, and how it can be affected by outside stimuli as well as by internal mental states.

Nope, as far as I know (my info stops around September 2021), nobody's landed a Land Rover on Mars, or any other regular Earth car for that matter. The only things that have made it to the surface are spacecraft and rovers sent up by space agencies like NASA and the European Space Agency. Those are built just for Mars, so they're pretty different from something like a Land Rover you'd drive around here.

In Canada, hobby expenses typically cannot be subtracted from your taxable income. Costs tied to a hobby are usually not deductible, since the activity is not regarded as a business. That said, if income comes from a hobby and the activity is run in a businesslike way, some expenses may qualify as business deductions. For an activity to count as a business, it must be pursued with the aim of earning a profit. If you are unsure whether your hobby qualifies as a business or which expenses you can claim, speak with a tax professional or the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA). The CRA's publication "Are You Carrying on a Business?" offers further guidance on this subject.

The trick is that decibels aren't counting "how much sound there is" the way you'd count apples. They're comparing a sound to a chosen starting point, and that starting point isn't "no sound at all."

Imagine you measure how tall your friends are, but instead of measuring from the floor, you measure from the top of your own head. A friend taller than you is "plus 3 inches," a friend your exact height is "zero," and a friend shorter than you is "minus 2 inches." Your shorter friend still has height. They're just below your reference point.

Decibels work the same way. Scientists picked "0 dB" to be roughly the quietest sound an average young person with healthy ears can just barely hear, a very faint sound, around the level of a mosquito buzzing about three meters away. Anything louder gets a positive number, like a normal conversation at about 60 dB. Anything quieter than that faint sound gets a negative number. So -9 dB doesn't mean "less than nothing." It means the room is even quieter than the faintest sound most people can hear. There's still a tiny bit of sound energy, just very little.

The "A" in dBA means the measurement is adjusted to match how human ears work. Our ears are better at hearing some pitches than others, so the meter gives more weight to the sounds we notice and less to the ones we don't.

To measure it, people use a sound level meter, which has a very sensitive microphone. Sound is just air wiggling back and forth in tiny pressure waves, and the microphone feels those wiggles and turns them into an electrical signal. The meter compares the size of those wiggles to the size at the 0 dB reference and turns that into a decibel number. For something as quiet as -9 dBA, ordinary meters aren't good enough, so engineers use extremely sensitive lab microphones and special equipment that makes very little electrical noise of its own. Otherwise the gadget's own hum would drown out the quiet they're trying to measure.

One more fun fact: decibels go up in a "multiplying" way, not an "adding" way. Every 10 dB is about ten times more sound energy, so a room at -9 dB has only about a tenth of the sound energy of a 0 dB whisper of a sound. That's why people in those rooms say they can hear their own heartbeat and blood flowing.

Information processing is the process by which a system takes in information, transforms it, stores it, and produces some output or response. The term is used across several fields, most notably psychology, computer science, and information theory, and while the details differ, the core idea is the same: input goes in, a series of operations is applied to it, and something useful comes out.

In psychology, information processing refers to a framework for understanding the human mind as a kind of computational system. Researchers in this tradition, which grew prominent in the 1950s and 1960s, describe how people perceive stimuli, attend to some details while ignoring others, encode what they notice into memory, retrieve stored knowledge, and make decisions or take actions based on it. This model compares the mind to a flow of stages, and it is used to study questions such as how attention works, why some information is remembered and other information is forgotten, and how people solve problems.

In computer science, information processing describes what computers do. A program receives data, such as numbers, text, or sensor readings, performs calculations and logical operations on it, stores intermediate and final results, and outputs new data or triggers actions. Nearly all computing can be understood in these terms.

In information theory and related fields, the term covers any manipulation of data, including compressing, encoding, transmitting, or filtering it. A central principle is that processing cannot create information out of nothing; it can only preserve, reorganize, or lose what was already present.

Across all these uses, information processing emphasizes that minds, machines, and other systems respond to the world not directly but by interpreting and transforming the signals they receive.

Imagine a group of kids who all agree on one big idea: the toys in the playroom shouldn't belong to just a few kids who hog them while everyone else does the cleanup. Instead, everybody should share the toys, and eventually there won't even need to be a grown-up in charge of the playroom because everyone will just get along. That big dream is communism. The different "isms" are basically different kids arguing about how to get there and what to do along the way.

Marxism comes from Karl Marx, a German thinker in the 1800s. He was mostly the kid who explained why the playroom is unfair. He said that throughout history, people have been split into groups, those who own things and those who do the work, and that these groups always fight. He believed the workers would eventually get fed up, take over the toys (factories, land, and so on), share them, and over time the need for anyone to be in charge would fade away. Marx wrote a lot about what was wrong and why change would come, but he didn't leave a very detailed instruction manual for running things afterward.

Leninism comes from Vladimir Lenin, who led the Russian Revolution in 1917. He said the workers won't just rise up on their own and figure it out; they need a team of dedicated, organized leaders, a "vanguard party," to plan the takeover and guide everyone. After winning, that party would run the country firmly for a while to protect the revolution from enemies. So Lenin added the idea of a strong, tightly controlled party leading the way.

Stalinism comes from Joseph Stalin, who took over after Lenin died. Stalin took the "strong leaders in charge for now" idea and made it extreme. He became the one boss everyone had to obey, used secret police, prison camps, and fear to keep control, and pushed the country to build factories and farms very fast no matter how many people suffered. He also said communism should be built first in one country, the Soviet Union, rather than waiting for the whole world to join. Many people see Stalinism as the point where "temporary" control turned into a permanent dictatorship.

Trotskyism comes from Leon Trotsky, who helped Lenin lead the revolution but lost the power struggle to Stalin, was kicked out, and was eventually killed on Stalin's orders. Trotsky argued that communism couldn't survive in just one country; the revolution needed to keep spreading around the world, which he called "permanent revolution." He also criticized Stalin for creating a bossy group of officials who cared more about their own power than about the workers.

So, put simply: Marx described the problem and the dream, Lenin said a disciplined party needed to lead the way, Stalin turned that party rule into one man's harsh rule focused on his own country, and Trotsky said Stalin had betrayed the idea and that the revolution should go worldwide instead.

The Il Divo members are Urs Bühler, a Swiss tenor; Sébastien Izambard, a French tenor; David Miller, an American tenor; and Carlos Marín, a Spanish singer. The group was formed in 2003 by Simon Cowell and has become known for blending operatic and pop styles. (Note that the group's name is spelled "Il Divo," and Carlos Marín was the original Spanish member, while Urs Bühler and Sébastien Izambard have also been part of its lineup over the years.)

Sounds like your husband might be dealing with racing thoughts, which can come from things like anxiety, bipolar disorder, or ADHD. If he hasn't already, he should really see a doctor or mental health provider to figure out what's going on and build a plan. There are a few medication types that often help with this stuff. SSRIs and SNRIs are antidepressants that can calm anxiety and lift mood. You'll hear names like paroxetine (Paxil), sertraline (Zoloft), and venlafaxine (Effexor). Benzodiazepines can give short-term relief from anxiety, think lorazepam (Ativan) or clonazepam (Klonopin). For bipolar disorder, mood stabilizers like lithium or valproate (Depakote) are common, since they smooth out the mood swings. If it's ADHD, stimulants such as amphetamines (Adderall) or methylphenidate (Ritalin) can help with focus. All of these can cause side effects and won't suit everyone, though, so he'll want to talk through the risks and benefits with a doctor before starting anything.

I can't tell what is causing your child's symptoms without examining him and learning more about his medical history and general health. These symptoms could stem from many different sources, so a doctor should see him to identify the cause and decide on the right treatment. In children, nosebleeds, headaches, and vomiting may be linked to things like viral illnesses such as colds or the flu, allergies, sinus inflammation, migraines, a concussion or other head injury, high blood pressure, motion sickness, or food poisoning. Less commonly, they can point to something more serious, such as a brain tumor or an aneurysm, which is why prompt medical evaluation matters. During the visit, the doctor can carry out a physical exam, order any tests that are needed, and work out what is going on. Depending on the findings, they might suggest medication, changes to daily habits, further testing, or a referral to a specialist.

Flank pain, meaning pain in the area on either side of the spine between the bottom of the ribcage and the pelvis, can stem from a number of different sources. Among the possibilities are the following. Kidney stones are among the most frequent culprits; these hard deposits form inside the kidneys and become painful as they travel through the urinary tract. A urinary tract infection (UTI) may also produce flank pain, often accompanied by a frequent need to urinate, pain or burning while urinating, and urine that looks cloudy or smells unpleasant. Problems affecting the muscles, bones, or joints of the back or pelvis, such as a pulled muscle, a herniated disk, or osteoarthritis, can likewise lead to pain in this area. Digestive and abdominal conditions, including inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) and diverticulitis, are another possible source. Because the cause can vary so widely, you should see a healthcare provider to get an accurate diagnosis and appropriate treatment. A provider can examine you, arrange any tests that are needed, and work out what is behind your pain.

Swallowing is just how food or drink gets from your mouth down to your stomach. Say you take a sip of water: it fills your mouth, and your tongue pushes it back toward your throat. That kicks off a reflex your body runs on its own, the "swallow reflex," which carries the water down. It's a big deal because it keeps you from choking, and it also keeps you from gulping down too much air, which can leave you feeling bloated or uncomfortable.

Once the liquid's in motion, the muscles in your throat and tongue team up to push it into your esophagus, a long tube running from your mouth to your stomach. The walls of that tube squeeze and relax in waves to shove everything along. When the water finally lands in your stomach, it mixes with stomach acid and other digestive juices that break it into smaller bits your body can actually use for energy and nutrients.

So basically, we swallow because it's how our bodies move food and drink from mouth to stomach, where the real digesting happens.

Timeshares are holiday homes that buyers can either purchase or rent for a set span of time each year. They tend to suit people who return to the same destination annually and appreciate having a dependable place to stay that feels like their own. Timeshare presentations are sales meetings run by timeshare firms that aim to convince attendees to buy in. To draw people in, these companies often dangle perks like complimentary trips or price reductions. At the presentation, a salesperson typically works to persuade you by highlighting the property's advantages and features. Although timeshares can work well for certain people, they are not a universal fit. Before deciding, it's wise to research thoroughly and weigh whether one suits your circumstances. Some buyers have walked away unhappy, reporting pressure to sign during the presentation or trouble selling the property later. Still, with careful evaluation of the costs and benefits and proper diligence, owning a timeshare can be worthwhile.

Things are still very dangerous in parts of Mexico, but the number of killings has come down from its peak. Around 2018 and 2019, Mexico recorded its worst years on record, with more than 30,000 homicides a year. Three years ago, in 2022, the count was still roughly 30,000 or more. Official figures for 2024 and 2025 showed a clear drop, with the government reporting a decline of about a fifth or more. Those numbers are still very high by world standards, and the drop has been uneven. Some states have improved, while others, especially Sinaloa, have seen violence rise since 2024, when two factions of the Sinaloa cartel began fighting each other.

Think of the cartels like rival gangs fighting over street corners. When a leader gets arrested or killed, the gangs fight over who takes over, and that causes new violence. Mexico's government has also been under heavy pressure from the United States to crack down on the drug trade, especially fentanyl, which has led to large transfers of cartel prisoners to the U.S.

As for the news, the coverage probably didn't disappear because nobody cares. Newsrooms have many more stories competing for attention, like wars in Ukraine and the Middle East, and American politics. When violence drops a little, or stays at a steady high level, it often gets less headline space than a sudden shocking event. Mexico-focused reporting has also become harder and more dangerous, since many journalists there have been killed or threatened, so there's less on the ground to report from.

I can't see the very latest news, so for the newest numbers, check recent reports from Mexico's national statistics agency or respected outlets that cover the region closely.

A sociopath is someone with a personality disorder marked by little or no empathy, a inclination to manipulate and take advantage of other people, and an absence of guilt or remorse. Such individuals can also be irresponsible, and they often struggle to obey rules and to keep relationships stable. Identifying a sociopath is not always simple, since they can be adept at hiding what they really intend and at steering other people's behavior. Still, several traits and habits are commonly associated with them. One is a lack of empathy: a sociopath may find it hard to understand, or to care about, what others feel. Another is manipulation: they may try to bend people to their will and readily turn to lies or deception to get what they want. Impulsivity is also typical, meaning they may follow their urges without thinking about what might result. Irresponsibility is another sign, as they may have trouble abiding by rules or fulfilling their duties. Finally, they may show a lack of remorse, feeling no guilt when they hurt others or break the law. Keep in mind that people differ widely, and showing a few of these traits does not automatically make someone a sociopath. If you are worried about another person's behavior, it is wise to consult a mental health professional.

Imagine you're at a birthday party, and the room used to be so hot and crowded that everyone was bumping into each other and making a big noise. Over a long time, the room cooled down and got quieter, but a faint hum of that old noise is still there, floating everywhere, even though you can't see it. That hum is the cosmic microwave background.

About 13.8 billion years ago, the whole universe started out incredibly hot and dense, like the hottest oven you can imagine. Light was bouncing around and couldn't travel far, because everything was so crowded with hot particles that it kept getting bounced off. Then, after about 380,000 years, the universe had stretched out and cooled enough that particles could finally settle down and let light zoom freely in straight lines. That first light has been traveling ever since.

As the universe kept growing, it stretched that light out, the way a rubber band stretches when you pull it. Light that started out bright and hot became longer and weaker, and by now it's so stretched that it's a type of light called microwaves, the same kind your microwave oven uses, except far, far weaker. Our eyes can't see it, but special antennas can pick it up. It comes at us from every direction in the sky, and it's the oldest light we can ever detect.

So the cosmic microwave background is like a baby picture of the universe, a snapshot of what it looked like when it was young and first let its light shine through.

Capital gains are calculated as the sale price minus your "cost basis," which is usually what you paid plus certain costs like commissions or improvements. If you don't know the original purchase price, you still have to report a basis, and the details depend on the asset and the country. I'll describe how it generally works in the United States, since the rules differ elsewhere.

The first step is to try to reconstruct the basis. For stocks and funds, your brokerage may have the records, since brokers have been required to track basis for most shares bought since 2011 (and for mutual funds since 2012). If the shares were transferred from another firm, ask both. Old account statements, trade confirmations, tax returns, and dividend reinvestment records can help. Some companies and transfer agents keep historical records, and historical price data is available for publicly traded securities, so if you know roughly when you bought, you can use the closing price on that date as a reasonable estimate. For real estate, look at the closing statement, county property records, old mortgage documents, or a past appraisal, and add the cost of capital improvements like a new roof or addition. For other assets such as collectibles or a business, receipts, insurance appraisals, or records of comparable sales can support an estimate.

If you truly can't establish a basis, the IRS can treat it as zero, which means the entire sale price is taxable gain. That is the worst-case outcome, so it is worth making a good-faith effort to document a reasonable figure. Estimates are acceptable if they are reasonable and you can explain how you arrived at them, but be prepared to defend them in an audit.

Special rules can also help. If you inherited the asset, the basis is generally the fair market value on the date of the original owner's death, which is often easier to document than the original purchase price, and the gain is automatically treated as long-term. If it was a gift, you generally take over the giver's basis, so you may need their records, though special rules apply if the value had dropped below that basis at the time of the gift. Also, whether the gain is short-term or long-term depends on your holding period, and if you can't prove how long you held it, that can matter too.

For a large or complicated sale, especially real estate or a business, it's worth talking to a tax professional, who can help you assemble a defensible basis. If you tell me the asset type and country, I can be more specific.

You generally don't need to report the original refund again as new income. It counts as income only in the year you received it, and only if you itemized deductions the prior year and deducted state income taxes. If you took the standard deduction, the refund wasn't taxable at all.

If the refund was taxable and you received it last year, it should have been reported on last year's return, and the amount you paid back is handled as follows. If you repaid it in the same year you received it, you simply report the net amount. If you repaid it in a later year, the repayment generally doesn't add income now. Federal rules let you deduct a repayment of previously taxed income in the year you repay it, but only if it's over $3,000 and the rules are complicated, and smaller repayments generally aren't deductible under current law.

Your state refund form (Form 1099-G) shows the amount of refunds issued, so check whether it shows the full original amount or the amount net of your repayment, and compare it to what you reported. If you're unsure whether your refund was taxable or how to handle the repayment, a tax preparer or your state's tax agency can confirm based on your specific return.

Religious conflicts stem from a range of causes, and it would be inaccurate to claim that most of them involve followers of monotheistic faiths. Although some clashes have indeed taken place between monotheistic groups, polytheistic traditions have also seen conflict, both with one another and with other belief systems. We may hear more about disputes among monotheistic religions partly because these faiths have a broader worldwide reach and a longer recorded history than many polytheistic ones. That wider presence creates more occasions for tension to develop between their adherents. Monotheistic religions also frequently hold their doctrines with great conviction, which may make their followers more inclined to see other faiths as opposing their own. Finally, it is worth remembering that religion is not the sole source of conflict. Political, social, and economic problems can also drive disputes, whatever the religious beliefs of those involved.

Switzerland's national hymn goes by the name "Schweizerpsalm," which translates to "Swiss Psalm." Written in German, it was set to music by Alberich Zwyssig in 1841. Its verses petition for the welfare and safeguarding of the nation and its citizens. Official ceremonies and public occasions across Switzerland frequently feature its performance.
