Wild Bill Hickok's father, Howard Hickok, died in 1852 when Bill (James Butler Hickok) was about fifteen years old. He was a farmer in Troy Grove, Illinois, and the family's farm was also a stop on the Underground Railroad, where Howard helped shelter escaping slaves. He died of an illness, often described as a brain or lung ailment brought on by overwork and exposure, though sources vary on the exact cause. He had been struggling with debts on the farm at the time, and his death left the family in financial difficulty. Young Bill, as one of the older sons, took on much of the responsibility of helping support his mother and siblings, which included hunting and working to keep the farm going. Some accounts say the illness followed a period of strenuous labor and stress, but there is no well-documented medical record, so the precise cause remains somewhat uncertain.

Charcoal and ordinary coal share some common ground: both are derived from carbon-heavy materials and both can serve as fuel. Still, several distinctions make charcoal a less workable energy source. To begin, charcoal is produced by heating wood without oxygen, a method known as pyrolysis. This treatment drives off water and impurities, leaving a black, porous substance high in carbon. When burned, charcoal releases less smoke than wood and burns more gradually, so it is well suited to grilling and other uses that call for a clean, sustained flame. Regular coal, by contrast, is a fossil fuel that took millions of years to form from the remains of plants and animals that once lived in swamps and wetlands. It packs far more energy per unit than wood or charcoal, so it yields considerably more heat when burned. That quality makes it a more practical option for large-scale energy generation, such as powering electricity plants. Environmental factors also matter when comparing the two. Although wood is renewable, turning it into charcoal can demand a lot of energy and generate harmful emissions. Moreover, producing charcoal on a large scale can lead to deforestation and degraded land. Coal, on the other hand, is a non-renewable resource mined from the ground, and burning it releases greenhouse gases and other pollutants into the air. Overall, although charcoal is a usable fuel, it falls short of regular coal in practicality and environmental friendliness when it comes to large-scale energy production.

Montargis is a town in the Loiret department, up in the Centre-Val de Loire region of France. If you've never been, it's a pretty central spot, known for its countryside, castles, and loads of history. The region borders Pays de la Loire to the west, Brittany to the northwest, Normandy to the north, Île-de-France to the east, and Bourgogne-Franche-Comté to the south. Montargis sits roughly 100 kilometers south of Paris, so you can get there by train or car without much hassle.

Speech recognition is the automated conversion of spoken language into written text. This technology enables computers to comprehend and make sense of human speech, and it is widely employed in applications like voice assistants, transcription tools, and customer service call centers. It comes in two principal forms. The first, isolated speech recognition, identifies single words or short phrases that are uttered separately, with a brief silence between each one. It is often found in voice command systems, such as those in smart home gadgets or virtual assistants. The second, continuous speech recognition, handles words and phrases delivered in an uninterrupted flow, with no gaps between them. It is typically used in transcription software and call centers, where it converts speech into text as it happens. To analyze and interpret what is said, speech recognition systems rely on a mix of machine learning algorithms and acoustic models. They learn from vast collections of human speech, allowing them to pick up on patterns in pronunciation and the surrounding context in which words appear.

It's not clear from your message whether you're the one owed money or the one who cosigned, so here's how the situation generally works in each case.

If you're the creditor or lender, start by reviewing the loan or cosigner agreement. It will say what counts as default and whether you can demand the full balance early. Then send a written demand letter by a trackable method, stating the amount owed, the deadline, and that you'll pursue legal remedies if it isn't paid. If the debt is secured by an asset, such as a car or equipment, the security agreement usually gives you the right to repossess or require surrender of that asset, and in many places you can do this without going to court as long as you don't breach the peace. For unsecured debts, you can file in small claims court or civil court, and once you have a judgment you can pursue wage garnishment, bank levies, or a lien on property, depending on your jurisdiction. If the person is refusing to share financial information, a court can order them to disclose it through discovery or a debtor's examination, and refusing can bring contempt sanctions. A process server or asset search service can also help locate assets.

If you're the cosigner, you are generally fully liable for the debt, just as the primary borrower is, even if you didn't receive the money. You have the right to request account statements, payment history, and the loan documents from the lender, and many lenders must provide these by law. You can also ask the primary borrower in writing to pay or transfer the asset, and if you end up paying, you typically have a right to recover that money from them, possibly through a small claims suit. If the lender is threatening you and you believe the debt is invalid or was misrepresented, a consumer protection attorney or your state attorney general's office can advise you.

Tell me which side you're on, the type of debt or asset involved, and your state or country, and I can give more specific steps.

Bush had two national security advisors while he was president. Condoleezza Rice had the job first, from January 2001 to January 2005. Then Stephen Hadley took over and stayed on until January 2009, when Bush's term ended. Rice moved over to Secretary of State after her stint, which is why Hadley got the slot.

A ferritin of around 930 is well above the usual range, which is roughly 15 to 200 ng/mL for women (a bit higher after menopause). Ferritin is a protein that stores iron, so it can reflect true iron overload, but it is also an "acute phase reactant," meaning it rises with inflammation, liver problems, and other conditions even when iron stores are normal. That is why doctors don't interpret it alone.

The change from 930 to 937 is not meaningful. Lab results vary by a few percent from test to test, and a 7-point difference is well within that normal variation. In other words, the level essentially stayed the same, which isn't surprising. Ferritin falls slowly, and after stopping supplements it can take months to come down, even if the supplements were the cause. So the lack of a drop after one month doesn't tell you much either way.

The main possibilities are these. One is iron overload from supplements, though a level this high from supplements alone would be unusual unless she took a lot for a long time. Another is hereditary hemochromatosis, a genetic condition where the body absorbs too much iron. Others include chronic inflammation (arthritis or other inflammatory conditions, infections), fatty liver disease or other liver conditions, alcohol use, metabolic syndrome, kidney disease, certain blood disorders, and some cancers. Hypertension and metabolic issues are linked to fatty liver, which commonly raises ferritin, so that is worth considering. Plantar fasciitis by itself isn't a typical cause.

The key next step is a fuller workup, which her doctor will likely order or may already have. Transferrin saturation (iron divided by total iron binding capacity) is the most helpful test: if it is above about 45 percent, true iron overload is more likely, and genetic testing for HFE mutations would follow. If it is normal, inflammation or liver disease is more likely. Other useful tests include liver enzymes (AST, ALT), a C-reactive protein, a complete blood count, blood sugar, and sometimes liver imaging or an MRI to measure iron in the liver.

It's reasonable to keep her off iron supplements, and also to avoid vitamin C supplements and excess alcohol until this is sorted out. She shouldn't start any treatment like blood removal (phlebotomy) unless a doctor confirms iron overload. Because untreated iron overload can damage the liver, heart, and other organs, I'd encourage a prompt follow-up, and sooner if she has fatigue, joint pain, abdominal pain, darkening skin, or shortness of breath. It's also worth asking why she was on iron in the first place, since that history helps interpret the result.

A shaped charge is a specialized explosive built to concentrate the energy of a blast along one chosen direction. It achieves this with a shaped liner placed inside the explosive. The liner is typically made from a material that transmits the blast's force well, copper being a common example. Once the explosive is set off, the blast pressure makes the liner fold inward on itself, producing a thin, extremely fast jet made up of gas and metal. The jet is so powerful that it can slice through metal and other substances much as a heated knife passes through butter. Because of this ability, shaped charges are frequently employed in military and industrial settings, both to cut through heavy, thick materials and to pierce armored vehicles.

South Beach is located on the southeastern tip of Miami Beach, which is a barrier island separated from the mainland city of Miami by Biscayne Bay. It occupies the southern portion of Miami Beach, roughly from around 5th Street in the south up to about 23rd Street in the north, and it is bordered by the Atlantic Ocean on the east and Biscayne Bay on the west. Although it is technically part of Miami Beach rather than the city of Miami proper, it is often thought of as a distinct neighborhood, famous for its Art Deco Historic District, sandy beaches, and vibrant nightlife.

Mutual funds are honestly a pretty solid way to build toward long-term stuff like retirement or just growing your money over time. The basic idea is that a bunch of investors pool their cash, and the fund uses it to buy a mix of stocks, bonds, or other securities. So you get a professional managing it, you're not stuck with one or two bets, and you still get a piece of whatever growth the markets deliver.

In India you've got a few main types. Equity funds put most of their money in stocks. They can pay off well over the long haul, but they're also the riskier option and can swing around a lot. Debt funds go for fixed-income things like bonds. They're steadier and less risky than equity funds, though you'll usually earn less. Then there are hybrid funds, which mix stocks and bonds, so you get a bit of both, some growth potential and some cushion.

When you're picking one, think about what you're actually saving for, how much risk you can stomach without panicking, and what the fund charges and offers. Some people talk to a financial advisor, others just do their own digging, and either can work as long as the fund fits your goals and the rest of your finances. Also, don't dump everything into a single fund or one type of asset. Spreading it out helps keep the risk down and could get you better results in the long run.

If you live in the United States or are a US citizen and have profits from selling shares in Indian companies, you must declare those gains on your American tax return and pay tax on them. The rate you pay depends on your income bracket and how long you owned the shares before selling. Gains on shares held for a year or less are considered short-term and are taxed at your regular income tax rate, while gains on shares held longer than a year are long-term and taxed at a reduced rate. Keep in mind that India may also tax these gains. Even so, the US has tax agreements with many nations, India among them, designed to prevent the same income from being taxed twice. Under the US-India tax treaty, profits from selling shares are usually taxed in the country where the seller is a resident. This means that if you are a US resident or citizen, you will generally owe tax on those gains only in the US and not in India. For further questions about reporting and paying tax on share sale profits from India, it is a good idea to speak with a tax professional or contact the Internal Revenue Service (IRS).

Delta Force is an elite unit within the United States Army, trained for missions such as counterterrorism, direct action, and special reconnaissance. Also called the 1st Special Forces Operational Detachment-Delta (1st SFOD-D), it falls under the United States Special Operations Command (USSOCOM), the body that oversees all of the American military's special operations forces. Its members are highly trained and skilled, equipped to carry out a wide range of intricate and delicate operations. The unit operates with considerable secrecy and is widely regarded as one of the most elite military organizations anywhere in the world.

Ghana scams and direct deposit scams are two forms of financial fraud aimed at both individuals and businesses. Ghana scams, sometimes called "419 scams," take their nickname from the part of the Nigerian criminal code that addresses fraud. Typically, a fraudster posing as someone from Ghana or another West African nation reaches out by email or social media and promises a substantial amount of money if the target will help move the funds out of the country. The scammer may then request personal or financial details, or ask the victim to pay fees or expenses supposedly tied to the transfer. In reality, the money and the person offering it are both fictitious, so the victim loses cash or sensitive information to the con artist.

In a direct deposit scam, one person or a group poses as a legitimate employer or government agency and asks an employee or individual to redirect their direct deposit to another account. The fraudster might demand personal or banking information, or ask the victim to log into their online banking or payroll account to make the switch. After that information is handed over or the change is made, the scammer can divert the victim's pay and take the money.

Caution is essential when responding to unsolicited requests for personal or financial information or to offers of large sums, particularly from people or businesses you do not know. If you believe you have been targeted by either scam, report it to the appropriate authorities and take steps to safeguard your personal and financial data. The debt-to-GDP ratio is a useful gauge of how large a government's debt is relative to the size of its economy, and it shapes the economy in several interrelated ways. When the ratio is low or moderate, a government can borrow cheaply, finance public investment such as infrastructure, and respond to recessions with spending or tax cuts without alarming investors. Lenders are confident the government will repay, so interest rates on government bonds stay low, and those low rates often spill over into cheaper credit for businesses and households.

As the ratio rises, the main concern is the cost of servicing the debt. A larger share of tax revenue must go toward interest payments, which leaves less room for schools, healthcare, defense, or other priorities. If interest rates rise or the economy slows, this burden can grow quickly, sometimes creating a cycle in which borrowing to pay interest pushes the ratio higher still.

High debt can also influence interest rates and investment. If investors begin to doubt a government's ability or willingness to repay, they demand higher yields, which raises borrowing costs across the economy and can crowd out private investment. In extreme cases, a loss of confidence can trigger a currency crisis, a sovereign debt default, or sharp austerity measures that deepen a recession.

Economists disagree about where danger thresholds lie. Some earlier research pointed to around 90 percent of GDP as a level associated with slower growth, though later analyses found the relationship weaker and more dependent on circumstances. Much depends on factors such as whether the debt is held in the country's own currency, how long its maturities are, who owns it, the strength of institutions, and whether the economy is growing faster than the interest rate on the debt. A country that borrows in its own currency and has a credible central bank can sustain higher ratios than one that borrows in foreign currency.

In short, the debt-to-GDP ratio affects the economy mainly through its influence on borrowing costs, the flexibility of fiscal policy, and investor confidence. Its effects are not automatic; the same ratio can be manageable in one country and dangerous in another, depending on growth prospects, interest rates, and institutional credibility.

Think of a battery as a tiny storage tank for energy that gets used up by a chemical reaction. Inside a battery there are two materials that want to trade electrons with each other, and the flow of those electrons through your flashlight or toy is what makes it work. When the materials have traded all the electrons they are willing to trade, the battery is "empty."

A rechargeable battery is built so that the reaction can be run backwards. When you plug it into a charger, electricity pushes the electrons back the other way, so the materials return to their starting state, ready to trade again. Think of it like a ball on a hill that you can roll back up by pushing it, over and over.

A regular AA battery, usually called alkaline, is built differently. Its chemistry is designed to go in one direction only. When it runs down, the materials inside have changed into different substances that don't easily turn back. Pushing electricity into it tends to cause other problems instead: gas can build up, the casing can leak or swell, and in the worst cases it can overheat or burst. That's why the labels warn you not to recharge them. It's a bit like trying to unscramble an egg. The reaction just doesn't reverse neatly.

So the short version is that rechargeable batteries use chemistry that can run both ways, and ordinary batteries use chemistry that only runs one way.

Long short-term memory, usually abbreviated LSTM, is a type of recurrent neural network architecture designed to learn from sequences of data, such as text, speech, time series, or video frames. It was introduced by Sepp Hochreiter and Jürgen Schmidhuber in 1997, and it became one of the most widely used tools in deep learning for sequential tasks before transformer models rose to prominence.

To understand why LSTMs were invented, it helps to know the problem they solve. A standard recurrent neural network processes a sequence one step at a time, passing a hidden state from each step to the next so that it can, in principle, remember earlier information. In practice, these simple networks struggle to learn relationships between events that are far apart in a sequence. During training, the error signals that flow backward through many time steps tend either to shrink toward zero or to grow uncontrollably, problems known as vanishing and exploding gradients. As a result, a plain recurrent network might easily learn that a word depends on the word right before it, but fail to connect a pronoun with a noun mentioned several sentences earlier.

The LSTM addresses this by introducing a component called the cell state, which acts like a conveyor belt running through the entire sequence. Information can travel along this cell state with only small, controlled modifications, which allows gradients to flow across many time steps without fading away. The name "long short-term memory" reflects this idea: the network's short-term memory, meaning its running internal state, is able to persist over long stretches of time.

What makes the cell state controllable is a set of structures called gates. Each gate is a small neural network layer, typically using a sigmoid function that outputs values between zero and one, which act as dials determining how much information passes through. The forget gate decides how much of the existing cell state should be kept or discarded. The input gate decides how much new information, computed from the current input and the previous hidden state, should be written into the cell state. The output gate decides how much of the cell state should be exposed as the hidden state, which is the output passed to the next time step and to subsequent layers. By learning the parameters of these gates during training, the network figures out on its own what to remember, what to forget, and what to reveal at each moment.

For example, when reading a sentence, an LSTM might learn to store the grammatical number of a subject, singular or plural, in its cell state, keep it there while processing intervening words, use it to choose the correct verb form, and then forget it once a new subject appears.

LSTMs were highly successful in many applications, including speech recognition, machine translation, handwriting recognition, language modeling, music generation, and forecasting of financial or sensor data. Systems from companies such as Google, Apple, and Amazon relied on them for years in products like voice assistants and translation services. Several variants exist, including the gated recurrent unit, or GRU, which simplifies the design by merging some gates and combining the cell and hidden states, often performing comparably with fewer parameters.

Today, transformer architectures have largely replaced LSTMs in large-scale language tasks because transformers can process entire sequences in parallel and capture long-range dependencies through attention mechanisms. Nevertheless, LSTMs remain useful in settings where data arrives step by step, computational resources are limited, or sequences are modest in length, and they remain an important milestone in the history of neural networks.

I can't examine your mouth, so I can only describe the common possibilities, but a sore with blood clots usually comes from one of a few causes.

The most common is injury. Biting your cheek or tongue, burning it on hot food, scraping it with sharp food like chips, or irritation from braces, dentures, or a rough tooth edge can break the tissue and cause a bleeding sore with a clot on top. Canker sores (aphthous ulcers) are another frequent cause; they are painful round or oval ulcers with a white or yellow center and red edge, and they may bleed if irritated. Other possibilities include a blood blister (angina bullosa hemorrhagica), which is a dark red or purple blister that pops and leaves a raw, bleeding spot, gum infection or inflammation, a recent tooth extraction (where a clot in the socket is normal and protective), cold sores or other viral infections, and side effects of some medicines. Less often, persistent sores can be related to low platelets, vitamin deficiencies, or other blood or immune conditions.

For care at home, rinse gently with warm salt water (half a teaspoon of salt in a cup of warm water) a few times a day. Try not to pick at the clot or scrape it off, since that restarts bleeding and slows healing. Avoid spicy, acidic, salty, hard, or very hot foods until it heals. Brush gently with a soft toothbrush and keep the area clean. If it bleeds, press a clean damp gauze or cloth against it for 10 minutes. Over-the-counter pain relief such as paracetamol (acetaminophen) or ibuprofen, or a numbing gel made for mouth sores, can help.

You should see a dentist or doctor if the sore has lasted more than two weeks, keeps coming back, is getting larger, or has a hard, raised, or lumpy edge. Persistent sores need checking because, rarely, mouth cancer can look like a non-healing ulcer, and the risk is higher with smoking, tobacco, or heavy alcohol use. Also get seen if you have bleeding that won't stop after 10 to 15 minutes of pressure, multiple sores or sores elsewhere in the body, fever, swollen glands, trouble swallowing or eating, easy bruising, or bleeding gums without a clear reason. If you have lots of bleeding and feel faint, or have trouble breathing or swallowing, seek urgent care.

If you tell me where the sore is, how long you've had it, whether it hurts, and whether you have any recent injury, dental work, or medicines, I can help narrow down what's most likely.

A stop sign tells you to come to a full stop at a stop line, crosswalk, or before entering a through street or intersection. They're usually red and octagonal, mounted on a tall post at the side of the road. When you see one, you've got to stop completely before going on. Any pedestrians or cars already in the intersection or crosswalk get the right of way. If it's clear, you can go ahead, but keep an eye out for hazards or someone coming in from another direction. You'll find them at intersections and other spots where crashes are likely or people are walking around. They keep traffic moving in an orderly way and help keep everyone safer on the road.

Slugging percentage measures a hitter's power by calculating the average number of bases they earn per at-bat. Unlike batting average, which treats every hit the same, slugging gives more weight to extra-base hits.

To calculate it, you first find the player's total bases. A single counts as one base, a double as two, a triple as three, and a home run as four. You then divide the total bases by the number of at-bats. Written out, the formula is total bases divided by at-bats, where total bases equals singles plus two times doubles plus three times triples plus four times home runs.

For example, suppose a player has 100 at-bats with 20 singles, 6 doubles, 1 triple, and 5 home runs. Their total bases would be 20 plus 12 plus 3 plus 20, which equals 55. Dividing 55 by 100 gives a slugging percentage of .550.

Walks, hit-by-pitches, and sacrifices are not counted, because they are not official at-bats. Despite the name, slugging percentage is not really a percentage. It ranges from .000 to a theoretical maximum of 4.000, which would mean a home run in every at-bat. A mark around .400 is roughly league average in Major League Baseball, while anything above .500 is considered very strong. Slugging percentage is also combined with on-base percentage to produce OPS, a popular overall measure of offensive performance.

Your hair doesn't all grow at the same time, and that's the key to the whole puzzle. Each hair on your head sits in a tiny pocket in your skin called a follicle, and every follicle goes through a cycle. First it grows for a few years, like a little tree getting taller. Then it rests for a few months, and during that rest the old hair loosens and eventually falls out. After that, the follicle starts making a brand new hair and the cycle begins again.

Because your roughly 100,000 follicles are all on different timers, only a small group is resting at any one moment. While some hairs are falling out, plenty of others are busy growing. So you lose a few dozen a day, which sounds like a lot, but your head is making new ones at about the same rate, and the total never gets noticeably smaller.

Why do people notice more in the shower? Water and shampoo help loose hairs let go, and when you rub and rinse, they all end up in one spot where you can see them. Women often notice it more because their hair is usually longer, so the shed hairs are easier to spot and tend to stay tangled in the strands. Hair that falls out in the shower was going to fall out anyway. It's just being counted all at once.

Stems do a lot for a plant. They hold it up so it can grow tall and reach for light, and they move water, nutrients, and sugars around the whole plant. Size, shape, and structure change quite a bit depending on the plant, though.

Here's a rundown of the main parts. The epidermis is the outer layer, made of cells that protect the stem from damage and keep water from escaping. Right under that you've got the cortex, a layer of cells that stores water and nutrients. Then there's the vascular tissue, which handles all the transporting. It's made up of xylem and phloem, specialized cells that carry water and sugars, respectively. At the very center is the pith, a spongy core of loosely packed cells that gives some support and stores nutrients too.

Then there's stuff attached to the stem. Leaves do photosynthesis, which is how plants use sunlight to turn carbon dioxide and water into energy. Buds are small, undeveloped leaves or flowers that'll eventually grow into new branches or blooms. Some plants have stipules, little leaf-like bits at the base of a leaf that help support it and protect it from damage. Some, like cacti, have spines or thorns to keep herbivores away. And nodes are just the spots on the stem where leaves, buds, or flowers attach.

It is usually advisable to have a real estate agent when purchasing a house, since they can help with negotiations and guide you through the legal and financial details of the deal. Still, if you decide to go it alone, you have several ways to manage the paperwork. You could retain a real estate lawyer to prepare the legal documents and advocate for you during the transaction, including reviewing the purchase contract, examining the title, and overseeing the closing. Alternatively, you might rely on an online platform or software to draft and finalize the required documents, as some of these services offer templates and instructions for the purchase agreement and closing steps. Even so, you should review any forms from such a service with care and consult a lawyer whenever you have questions or doubts. A third route is to engage a title company or escrow company to run the closing and handle the legal paperwork. A title company can perform a title search, draft the closing documents, and distribute funds at closing, while an escrow company can also manage the closing and paperwork but typically does not perform a title search. Whichever path you take, check every document thoroughly and seek legal counsel when needed, because buying a home is a major financial commitment and you want to protect yourself and ensure the deal is handled correctly.

In most cases you cannot simply deposit a cheque made out to another person into your own business account, even if that person works with you or the money really belongs to the business. Banks check that the name on the cheque matches the name on the account it is going into, and depositing a cheque payable to someone else without proper authority can be treated as fraud. That said, there are several legitimate ways to handle the situation.

The cleanest solution is usually to ask whoever wrote the cheque to cancel it and reissue it in the exact legal or registered trading name of your business. If the payment was meant for the business all along, the issuer generally has no objection, and this avoids any question about whose money it is. When the business is paid regularly, make sure your invoices clearly state the name cheques should be made payable to so the problem doesn't recur.

A second option is for your associate to deposit the cheque into their own account and then transfer the funds to the business account by bank transfer. This is simple and fully legitimate, but keep a written record, such as an email or short note, explaining that the funds were received on behalf of the business. Your bookkeeper or accountant can then record the income correctly, and your associate won't be taxed on money that was never theirs.

A third route is third-party endorsement. Your associate signs the back of the cheque and writes something like "Pay to the order of [your business name]" above their signature, and you then deposit it. Many banks in the US still accept this occasionally, but often only if the payee comes to the branch with identification, and many banks refuse third-party cheques entirely. In the UK and several other countries, most cheques are crossed "account payee," which legally means they can only be paid into the named payee's account, so endorsement isn't an option. Call your bank first to ask whether they accept endorsed third-party cheques and what they require.

If the cheque is made out to a trading name or variation of your business name that differs slightly from how your account is titled, your bank may be able to add that name as an alias on the account, after which such cheques can be deposited normally.

Whichever method you use, make sure your associate agrees in writing that the money belongs to the business, and keep documentation for your accounting records. If significant sums are involved or this happens often, a quick conversation with your bank and accountant is worthwhile.

As a US H-1B holder, you are probably a US tax resident and an NRI (non-resident Indian) for Indian tax purposes, as long as you spent fewer than 182 days in India in the relevant year. That status determines most of the answer.

India taxes an NRI's capital gains only on income that arises in India. If you sell shares listed on an Indian exchange (NSE or BSE), such as Reliance or Infosys, the gain is taxable in India, and the broker typically deducts TDS on the sale. If you sell US-listed stocks through a US brokerage, Indian tax generally does not apply to you as an NRI, because the asset is not situated in India. If you are or become an Indian tax resident (for example, after returning to India), your worldwide gains become taxable in India.

For Indian-listed equity, the rates set by the 2024 budget (effective July 23, 2024) are 20 percent on short-term gains (held 12 months or less) and 12.5 percent on long-term gains (held longer than 12 months), with long-term gains above ₹1.25 lakh per financial year exempt. A 4 percent health and education cess applies on top, and surcharge may apply at higher income levels. Check these figures, since rates and thresholds change, and some earlier rules still apply to sales made before the change.

Because you are a US taxpayer, the US taxes your worldwide income, including gains from Indian shares. The India-US tax treaty gives India the right to tax gains on Indian shares, and you can usually claim a foreign tax credit on your US return using Form 1116 for the Indian tax you paid. This generally prevents double taxation, though the credit is limited to the US tax attributable to that income, and the timing and currency conversion can create mismatches.

Several reporting obligations also apply. If your foreign financial accounts (Indian bank accounts, Indian brokerage accounts, or US accounts held abroad) exceed certain thresholds, you may need to file an FBAR (FinCEN 114) and Form 8938. Be careful with Indian mutual funds, which are generally treated as passive foreign investment companies (PFICs) for US purposes. PFIC rules are punitive and require Form 8621, so it is often better to avoid holding them or to get specialist advice before selling.

Given the interaction between the US and Indian rules, it is worth working with a cross-border tax professional, such as a US CPA with Indian tax experience or an Indian chartered accountant familiar with NRI matters, before you sell or file.

Medical diagnosis refers to figuring out what lies behind a patient's symptoms and signs. Typically, a healthcare professional such as a doctor, nurse practitioner, or physician assistant carries it out by examining the patient physically, asking about their medical background, and sometimes requesting a range of diagnostic tests. The goal is to pinpoint the particular illness or condition responsible for the patient's complaints so that suitable treatment can be given. The process generally follows several stages. First comes gathering information, which means taking a detailed medical history, conducting a physical exam, and looking over any pertinent records or test results. Next is identifying the problem: using the collected information, the professional weighs possible diagnoses and reduces the list to the most probable candidates. Then comes confirming the diagnosis, which can require extra tests such as laboratory work, imaging studies like X-rays or CT scans, or other diagnostic procedures. The final stage is providing treatment: once the diagnosis is settled, the professional suggests a treatment plan tailored to the specific condition or disease identified. It is worth remembering that diagnosis is not always simple. It can take several steps and draw on the input of multiple healthcare professionals. Sometimes the cause is not obvious at first, and additional testing or follow-up may be needed.

Calling a word "loaded" means that, on top of its dictionary definition, it carries a good deal of additional meaning or feeling. That added charge can be favorable or unfavorable, and it may vary from one person to another. Take the word "home," for instance: for some people it evokes warmth and security, a place of safety and comfort, while for others it brings up memories of a hard or miserable place. The same is true of "love." To some it signals deep affection and emotional closeness, but to others it may recall painful or troubling experiences. In short, loaded words carry substantial emotional or cultural weight, and they can strongly shape how we perceive and feel about the things they describe.

Yes, you can close out a short sale using shares you already hold. Shorting a stock means borrowing shares from another party and selling them on the open market. You expect the price to drop, so you can repurchase the shares later at a lower cost, return them to the lender, and keep the difference as profit. If the price rises instead, buying the shares back costs more than you received, which produces a loss. Covering the position requires returning the same number of shares you borrowed. If you already own those shares, you can hand over the borrowed ones and keep your own, which ends the short position and completes the transaction. If you do not own the shares, however, you must purchase them on the market to cover the short.

I'm sorry you're dealing with this. A two-week shooting chest pain, followed by a new hard, itchy lump on your back this evening, is worth taking seriously, and I think your instinct to go back to A&E is a sound one.

Chest pain that shoots, a new lump, and any change in how you feel are the kind of combination that should be looked at in person today rather than after the holidays. The heart being checked earlier is reassuring, but it doesn't rule out other causes. Shooting pain in the chest can come from the nerves or the muscles and bones of the chest wall, and a shingles infection can cause exactly this kind of pain for days before a rash appears. A hard lump can be a number of things, from an infected or inflamed skin cyst or a swollen lymph node to, less commonly, something that needs investigation. Your chest pain disappearing doesn't necessarily mean it has resolved; it may have changed, or the two things may be unrelated.

Please go to A&E or call your local emergency number now, rather than waiting, if you develop any of the following: chest pain that returns or becomes crushing or pressing, pain spreading to your arm, jaw, neck or back, shortness of breath, sweating, nausea, dizziness or fainting, a fever, the lump becoming rapidly larger, redder, hotter or more painful, or a rash or blisters appearing near the area of the pain. Those would mean you should not wait at all.

If you do go, tell the staff everything you've told me: the two weeks of shooting pain, the earlier heart checks, and the new lump that appeared this evening. Mention if you have any other symptoms, recent illness, or a history of cancer. It would also help to take a photo of the lump now, so you can show whether it changes.

Even if you feel better by morning, I'd still arrange to see your doctor soon after the holidays, or sooner if it's possible, so the persistent pain and the lump are properly examined. Is there anything else you've noticed, such as fever, a rash, or any change in breathing?

Movie gunshots usually aren't recorded from a real gun going off, at least not on their own. A real shot often sounds weaker than you'd expect on screen, so sound designers layer things together to make it hit harder. They'll grab sounds from different guns, sometimes toss in explosions or a bit of metal clanging, and blend it all until it feels right. Real guns don't sound the same either. It depends on the gun, the ammo, and where you're standing when it goes off, so the movie version is really just a more punchy take on something that already varies a lot.

A climbing stock price signals that the market now values the company more highly. Several things can cause this, including stronger financial results, favorable news about the business, or a rise in demand for its shares. Even so, the company does not directly take in any extra money when its share price goes up. The stock's price simply mirrors how the market perceives the company's worth. Anyone who holds shares when the price increases may be able to sell them at a profit. The company, though, receives no additional funds from that increase in price.

An image sensor is a component that turns an optical image into an electrical signal. Digital cameras, scanners, and other image-capturing devices rely on it to record pictures. Its core is a grid of photodiodes, light-sensitive elements that transform incoming light into electric current. When light passes through the lens and strikes the sensor, the photodiodes absorb it and produce a current whose strength tracks the light's intensity. That current is then converted into digital data, which the camera's image processing unit assembles into a finished digital picture. Sensors come in two principal varieties: CCD (charge-coupled device) and CMOS (complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor). CCDs cost more to make but typically yield higher-quality images with less noise, while CMOS sensors are cheaper to produce and draw less power, though their images can be noisier. Overall, the image sensor is a vital part of any image-capturing device, since it converts incoming light into a digital representation of the scene that can be stored and edited.

I'm sorry you've been going through this for a year, and I can understand how frustrating it is to keep getting negative results despite seeing many doctors. Here is some general information that may help you think about it.

Yes, delayed or irregular ovulation can happen even when periods arrive on time. Some women have cycles where ovulation occurs later than the typical day 14, for example on day 18, 21, or even later, and sometimes ovulation is skipped entirely in a given cycle. Stress, illness, recent changes in weight, intense exercise, travel, and sleep disruption can all shift the timing. Conditions such as polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) can also cause irregular or absent ovulation without causing obvious period changes, since some women with PCOS still bleed regularly. So a negative result on days 12 to 19 does not necessarily mean something is wrong, but it is a reasonable reason to look more closely.

Some practical points about the testing itself may be useful. Ovulation kits detect the LH surge, which typically comes one to two days before ovulation, so testing once a day in the afternoon or evening is common. If you only tested through day 19, a late ovulation could fall outside that window, so continuing testing for several more days, or using a basal body temperature chart or tracking cervical mucus, can help confirm when ovulation happens. Some women also find that certain kits are less sensitive, and a few conditions can cause a constant or misleading LH pattern, so a doctor can help interpret results.

Because you have been trying for a year, it is generally advisable to have a clear picture of ovulation itself. Useful tests include a progesterone blood test taken about seven days before your expected period to confirm ovulation, and hormone testing such as AMH, FSH, LH, prolactin, and thyroid levels. A pelvic ultrasound to track follicles across a cycle can show whether and when an egg is released. Since you mention reports are normal and semen analysis is fine, a fertility specialist can review whether further evaluation, such as tubal patency testing, is needed. Many clinicians consider evaluation after one year of trying, and you have already reached that point, so seeing a reproductive endocrinologist or fertility specialist would be a sensible next step if you have not already.

Please discuss these specifics with your doctor, who can review your actual reports and history. I hope you get clear answers soon.

The US Constitution was written in 1787, and delegates signed it in Philadelphia on September 17 of that year. It didn't actually take effect until March 4, 1789, though. People still call it the oldest written constitution of any sovereign state, which is pretty wild when you think about it. It's the supreme law of the land and sets up how the federal government works. You've got three branches (legislative, executive, and judicial) each with their own powers and jobs. It also lays out the basic rights Americans have. It's been amended 27 times since then, so it's been tweaked a fair bit, but the core is still the same document from over two centuries ago.

The false positive rate is a measure of how often a test, classifier, or decision rule incorrectly signals "yes" when the true answer is actually "no." In other words, it captures the proportion of genuinely negative cases that get mistakenly labeled as positive.

To calculate it, you take the number of false positives and divide it by the total number of actual negatives. The total number of actual negatives is the sum of false positives (negatives wrongly flagged as positive) and true negatives (negatives correctly identified as negative). So the formula is FPR = FP / (FP + TN). For example, if a medical test is given to 1,000 healthy people and 50 of them are incorrectly told they have the disease, the false positive rate is 50 divided by 1,000, or 5 percent.

The false positive rate is closely related to specificity, which is the proportion of actual negatives that are correctly identified. The two always add up to one, so a test with 95 percent specificity has a 5 percent false positive rate. In statistical hypothesis testing, the false positive rate corresponds to the Type I error rate, often denoted by alpha, which is the probability of rejecting a null hypothesis that is actually true.

The concept matters because false positives carry real costs. A spam filter with a high false positive rate sends legitimate emails to the junk folder. A fraud detection system with a high false positive rate blocks honest customers' transactions. A medical screening test with a high false positive rate causes unnecessary anxiety and follow-up procedures. There is usually a tradeoff between the false positive rate and the true positive rate (also called sensitivity or recall): making a system more aggressive at catching real positives tends to also increase false alarms. This tradeoff is commonly visualized with an ROC curve, which plots the true positive rate against the false positive rate across different decision thresholds.

It is also worth distinguishing the false positive rate from the false discovery rate, which people sometimes confuse. The false positive rate asks, "Of all the truly negative cases, what fraction did we wrongly flag?" The false discovery rate asks, "Of all the cases we flagged as positive, what fraction were actually negative?" These can differ dramatically, especially when the condition being tested for is rare, because even a small false positive rate applied to a large population of negatives can produce many false alarms relative to the true positives.

Pain in the lower left rib area that gets worse with movement and deep breathing, with no fever and no injury, is most often musculoskeletal in a teenager. A few possibilities are worth knowing about, along with some signs that would mean he needs to be seen promptly.

The most common cause is a strained intercostal muscle (the small muscles between the ribs). A cough, even a slight one, a twisting motion, sports, or heavy lifting can irritate these muscles without any memorable injury. Another frequent cause is costochondritis, which is inflammation of the cartilage where the ribs attach to the breastbone. That is usually felt toward the front, and the spot is often tender when you press on it. A related and less well known cause in teens is slipping rib syndrome, or "rib tip syndrome," where the cartilage at the lower ribs (the ones not attached to the breastbone) is loose and slips or irritates nearby nerves. It causes sharp pain in the lower rib area with certain movements, and it is often mistaken for something more serious. Teenagers who are growing quickly can also have this kind of pain.

Because the pain also hurts when he breathes in and he has a cough, a few other things should be considered. Pleurisy, which is irritation of the lining around the lung, often follows a viral illness and causes sharp pain with breathing. A mild pneumonia can do the same, even without much fever. A pneumothorax (collapsed lung) is uncommon but happens in tall, thin teens; it is less likely at his build, but sudden sharp pain with shortness of breath would make it a concern. On the left side below the ribs, the spleen can also be involved, for example if it is enlarged after mono (infectious mononucleosis), which is common at this age. Pain from an enlarged spleen can be a reason to avoid contact sports until a doctor clears him, since the spleen can rupture. Less often, stomach, kidney, or bowel problems can cause pain in this area, including constipation or a kidney stone.

I would take him to see a doctor in the next day or two, since the pain is persistent enough to limit movement and affects breathing. A physical exam, and possibly a chest X-ray, will usually sort this out quickly.

Go to urgent care or the emergency room right away if he has trouble breathing or shortness of breath, pain that is severe or getting worse, a fever, coughing up blood, a rapid heartbeat, dizziness or fainting, pain that spreads to the left shoulder, a swollen or very tender belly, blood in the urine, or if he has recently been hit in the area. Until he is seen, he can rest, avoid contact sports and heavy lifting, and use acetaminophen or ibuprofen as directed for his weight if he has no reason to avoid them.

Yes, a blood clot is one of the possibilities, and because of the timing and location, she should be evaluated promptly rather than waiting to see if it settles.

The right groin is where the catheter was inserted, and the swelling and lump are on the same side. After a catheter procedure there are several things that can cause this. The most common is a hematoma, which is a collection of blood under the skin from bleeding at the puncture site. It usually feels like a firm, tender knot and can cause bruising and some swelling down the leg. A more serious cause is a pseudoaneurysm, where blood leaks from the artery and forms a pulsating pocket next to it. It may feel like a lump that throbs, and sometimes there is a whooshing sound over it. Another possibility is a deep vein thrombosis, a clot in a leg vein, which can cause swelling of the ankle and foot. The vein can be irritated or compressed by a hematoma or pseudoaneurysm, which also contributes to swelling. Less commonly, an arteriovenous fistula (an abnormal connection between the artery and vein) or reduced blood flow in the leg can occur. Also, an attempt that failed on that side can mean more manipulation of the vessel, which raises the chance of a groin complication.

Some swelling and bruising is common after these procedures, but a lump together with ankle and foot swelling should be checked. An ultrasound of the groin and leg is simple and painless and can tell these causes apart quickly.

She should call her cardiologist's office or the hospital that did the procedure today, and be seen the same day. Go to the emergency room or call emergency services right away if the lump is growing quickly, is very painful, or is pulsating, if there is active bleeding, if the leg becomes cold, pale, blue, numb, or weak, if the calf is very painful or red, or if she has chest pain, shortness of breath, coughing blood, a racing heart, or lightheadedness. Those could signal serious bleeding or a clot that has traveled to the lungs.

In the meantime she should rest, avoid heavy lifting or straining, and keep the leg elevated when sitting. If bleeding occurs at the site, press firmly on it and call for emergency help. She also shouldn't stop her blood-thinning medications, such as aspirin or clopidogrel, on her own, since they protect the new stents, unless her doctor tells her to. Let the medical team decide about any changes.

Earth is made up of distinct layers: the crust, the mantle, and the core. The outermost of these, the crust, is solid rock and is broken into a number of tectonic plates. These plates, sections of crust, drift gradually across the planet's surface. Their constant motion underlies many geological phenomena, including earthquakes, volcanoes, and the formation of mountain chains. Beneath the crust lies the mantle, which consists of molten rock. At the center is the core, which has a solid inner portion surrounded by a liquid outer portion. Heat escaping from the core drives convection within the mantle, rising toward the surface, and this convection is what propels the movement of the tectonic plates.

Processed food is any food that has been changed from the way it was when it came from a plant or an animal. Think of an apple. If you pick it off a tree and eat it, that's not processed at all. If you cut it into slices, that's a tiny bit processed. If you cook it down into applesauce, that's more processed. And if a factory takes apple flavoring, lots of sugar, colors, and other ingredients and turns them into a gummy snack shaped like a cartoon character, that's very processed. So processing isn't one thing. It's more like a ladder, and some foods are much higher up the ladder than others.

Not all processed food is bad. Frozen peas, canned beans, plain yogurt, cheese, and bread are all processed, and they can be perfectly healthy. Freezing, canning, and cooking help keep food safe and make it last longer. When people say processed food is bad, they usually mean the foods at the very top of the ladder, which scientists call ultra-processed foods. These include things like chips, candy, soda, many sugary cereals, hot dogs, frozen pizzas, and packaged cookies. They're usually made in factories from ingredients you wouldn't find in a normal kitchen.

Those foods can be a problem for a few reasons. First, they often have lots of sugar, salt, and certain fats, because those make food taste really good. Eating too much of them over a long time can make it harder for your body to stay healthy and can lead to problems with your heart, your weight, and your teeth. Second, a lot of the good stuff from the original plant gets taken out, like fiber, which helps your tummy work well and keeps you feeling full, and many vitamins your body needs to grow strong. Third, these foods are often designed to be so tasty and easy to eat that it's hard to stop. You can eat a whole bag of chips without feeling full, but it would be hard to eat that many potatoes if they were just baked. So people end up eating more than their bodies really need.

A good way to think about it is that your body is like a car that runs best on good fuel. Foods close to how nature made them, like fruits, vegetables, eggs, nuts, and plain meats, are the good fuel. Very processed foods are more like treats. Having them sometimes is fine and can be fun, but if they're most of what you eat, your body doesn't get everything it needs to feel and work its best.

I Confess is a 1953 film noir directed by Alfred Hitchcock, featuring Montgomery Clift as Father Michael William Logan, a Catholic priest drawn into a murder investigation after he hears the confession of a man who later dies. The cast also includes Anne Baxter as Ruth Grandfort, the victim's wife, and Karl Malden as Inspector Larrue, a detective who suspects Father Logan of the crime. O.E. Hasse plays Otto Keller, the man who confesses to the murder, and Brian Aherne appears as Father Michael's lawyer, William Logan.

A specialist, abbreviated "SPC," holds a rank in the United States Army that sits between private first class and corporal. It is the fourth enlisted grade in the Army. Although specialists are sometimes regarded as non-commissioned officers (NCOs), their responsibilities differ from those of higher-ranking NCOs, such as sergeants and above. Within their particular job field, specialists carry out a range of tasks, including operating and maintaining equipment, handling administrative work, and offering technical support. They can also be asked to supervise and train junior soldiers and to take part in training exercises held at the unit level. The Army expects specialists to show greater technical skill and accountability than privates first class, and they may be called upon to fill leadership positions in their unit.

Category theory is basically a way of describing math in terms of "objects" and "arrows" (the arrows are also called morphisms). It's pretty abstract, and the whole point is to give you one framework that ties together a bunch of different things, like groups, rings, and topological spaces.

An object is just whatever kind of thing you're studying in a given setting. So in the category of groups, the objects are groups and the arrows are group homomorphisms. In the category of topological spaces, the objects are topological spaces and the arrows are continuous functions. Pretty straightforward once you see a couple of examples.

The big idea is that you focus on how objects relate to each other through the arrows connecting them, instead of poking around inside the objects themselves. That lets you work at a much more general level, and it's led to some genuinely new insights and results along the way.

You'll see it show up all over math: algebra, geometry, topology, logic. It's also turned up in computer science and physics. Fair warning though, it's a pretty technical subject. You really need a solid math background and a knack for abstract thinking, which is why most people don't run into it until grad school.

A 529 plan is a tax-advantaged savings account designed specifically for education costs, and it helps in several ways.

The biggest benefit is tax treatment. Your contributions go in after tax, but the money grows free of federal income tax, and withdrawals are also tax-free as long as they are used for qualified education expenses. Those include tuition, fees, books, required supplies, and room and board for students enrolled at least half time. Over many years, tax-free growth can make a meaningful difference compared with a regular taxable investment account. Many states also offer a state income tax deduction or credit for contributions, usually if you use your own state's plan, though a handful of states give the benefit regardless of which plan you pick.

There are two main types of plans. Savings plans let you invest in a menu of mutual funds or similar portfolios, and the balance rises and falls with the market. Many offer age-based options that start out aggressive when your child is young and shift toward conservative investments as college approaches. Prepaid tuition plans, offered by some states, let you lock in today's tuition rates at participating public schools, which protects against tuition inflation but is less flexible.

Flexibility is another strength. You, as the account owner, keep control of the money, not your child. You can change the beneficiary to another family member, including yourself, a sibling, or a future grandchild, without penalty. Contribution limits are high, often exceeding $300,000 per beneficiary depending on the state, and relatives like grandparents can contribute too. Gift tax rules allow you to front-load up to five years of annual gift exclusions at once, which can accelerate growth.

Funds can also be used beyond traditional college. Qualified uses include up to $10,000 per year toward K-12 private school tuition, apprenticeship programs, and up to $10,000 lifetime toward student loan repayment. Under recent rules, unused funds in a long-held account may be rolled into a Roth IRA for the beneficiary, subject to limits and a 15-year account age requirement.

The main downside is that withdrawals not used for qualified expenses are subject to income tax on the earnings plus a 10 percent penalty, though the penalty is waived in some cases such as the beneficiary receiving a scholarship. Investment options are also limited to what the plan offers, and you can typically change them only a couple of times a year.

To get started, compare your own state's plan, including fees and investment performance, with other states' plans, open an account with a small amount, and set up automatic monthly contributions. Starting early matters most, since even modest regular deposits can grow substantially over 18 years. A financial advisor or your state's plan website can help you confirm current limits and rules.

Honestly, there are a bunch of things that could be behind random pain in your wrists, arms, and hands. One common one is repetitive strain injury, which happens when you do the same motion over and over, like typing or mousing around for hours. Carpal tunnel is another big suspect. That's when the median nerve gets squeezed as it runs through the wrist, and you end up with pain, numbness, and tingling in the wrist, hand, and fingers. Tendinitis is also possible. That's inflammation in the tendons, the fibrous cords connecting muscle to bone, and it usually comes from overuse or an injury. A fracture can cause pain too, obviously, and so can arthritis, which inflames the joints and can leave them sore and swollen.

If this has been going on and it's bugging you, get it checked by a healthcare provider so they can figure out what's actually happening. And definitely mention the POTS, since it could matter for how they approach your treatment.

When his time at Texas Tech ended, the Miami Dolphins selected him in the fifth round of the 1996 NFL Draft. A steam engine turns the heat energy in steam into mechanical energy. It works by using steam pressure to push against a piston or turbine, which then moves some kind of load. Basically, you heat water in a boiler until it boils and becomes steam. That steam gets piped into a cylinder where it shoves a piston back and forth. The piston is hooked up to a crankshaft, which turns that back-and-forth motion into spinning motion you can actually use to do work. As the steam pushes the piston, it expands and cools, and eventually it condenses back into water. That water goes back to the boiler to get reheated and turned into steam all over again. The heat comes from burning fuel like coal, wood, or oil. There are plenty of types, too: stationary engines, marine engines, locomotive engines, and so on. Steam engines used to power ships, trains, and all sorts of other vehicles, but they've mostly been swapped out for internal combustion engines and electric motors, which are just more efficient.

Start by talking through your symptoms with your healthcare provider, since they can work out what is behind your lower back pain and suggest the best way to treat it. After an Implanon insertion, the pain might stem from a strained or spasming muscle, an irritated nerve, or a reaction to the implant itself. When the pain is severe or won't go away, your provider may suggest pain medication, either over-the-counter or prescription, to keep your symptoms under control. They might also propose physical therapy or another form of rehabilitation aimed at building up the muscles in your back and improving your general mobility. Sometimes, if the implant is causing considerable discomfort or other side effects, your provider may advise having it taken out. Be sure to follow the guidance your provider gives you for handling the pain, and get medical help if your symptoms get worse or you notice any other unusual changes.

Mind-body dualism is basically the idea that your mind and your body are two separate things. On this view, the mind is an immaterial substance that doesn't follow the same physical rules as the body. People often call it Cartesian dualism, after René Descartes, who developed it. He argued that the mind is non-physical and can think, feel, and perceive, while the body is physical and works according to the laws of physics. Descartes figured the two still somehow interact, even though they're fundamentally different. There are plenty of versions of this idea, and philosophers still argue about whether it holds up. Some think you need an immaterial mind to explain conscious experience. Others figure it's simpler to say the mind just comes from the physical brain and what it does.

A grist mill stone is one of the large, heavy stones used in a grist mill to grind grain, such as wheat, corn, rye, or oats, into flour or meal. The word "grist" simply means grain that has been separated from the chaff and is ready to be ground.

Millstones almost always work in pairs. The lower stone, called the bedstone, stays fixed in place, while the upper stone, called the runner stone, rotates above it. Grain is fed through a hole in the center of the runner stone and works its way outward between the two surfaces. The grinding action crushes the kernels, and the resulting flour is pushed out to the edges, where it is collected.

The faces of the stones are not smooth. They are cut with a pattern of grooves called furrows, along with the flat areas between them called lands. The furrows help channel the grain and flour outward and keep the stones cool by letting air circulate, while the lands do most of the crushing and shearing. Millers had to re-dress, or re-cut, these patterns regularly as they wore down.

Different materials were used depending on the region. French buhrstone, a hard, quartz-rich stone with a honeycomb-like texture, was prized for making fine wheat flour. Granite and sandstone were also common, particularly for coarser grinding of corn and other grains. Some stones were made from several pieces bound together with iron bands, while others were cut from a single block.

Millstones were powered by water wheels, windmills, animals, or later by steam and electricity. Many old stones survive today as decorative features, garden pieces, or monuments, and some traditional mills still use them to produce stone-ground flour, which many people value for its flavor and retention of the grain's germ and bran.

Synesthesia is when your brain mixes up its signals, so one sense sets off another. Imagine your senses are different rooms in a house, and usually each room has its own door that only opens from the inside. In someone with synesthesia, some of the doors are connected by a secret hallway, so when someone walks into the "hearing" room, somebody also wanders into the "color" room and turns on the lights.

For example, a person with synesthesia might hear a musical note and see a flash of red at the same time. Or they might look at the letter B and always think of it as being blue, even though it's just black ink on a page. Some people taste words when they hear them, or feel shapes in their hands when they listen to a song. The mix-up happens the same way every time for that person, so the color of the letter B is always blue for them, and it's not a guess or a pretend thing.

Nobody is sure exactly why it happens, but scientists think the wires in the brain that carry messages between the senses are a little more connected in people with synesthesia. It's a bit like having an extra hallway that most people don't have. It's not a sickness. Many people with synesthesia say it's just a normal part of how they experience the world, and some even think it makes things more colorful and fun.

Honestly, messing with your period timing on your own usually isn't a great idea. It can throw off your cycle's natural rhythm, and some methods carry real health risks. If you want to shift when your period comes or just want more control over it, talk to a doctor or nurse first. They can figure out what's going on and suggest something that actually fits you.

Irregular periods can have a bunch of different causes, and a provider can pin down the reason and recommend treatment. Sometimes medication is used to regulate cycles, but that should always happen under a provider's watch. And for what it's worth, there's no single "normal" cycle. Length and regularity vary a lot from person to person, so don't panic if yours doesn't match what you read somewhere else. If something feels off, though, get it checked out and get advice based on your own body.
