The main obstacles are less about money than about the mechanics of living across two economies. Pensions and social security are the first problem. Many high-income countries pay state pensions only to people who live there, or they freeze or reduce payments abroad, and some countries have no totalization agreements with the retirement destination, so years of contributions may never add up to a usable benefit. Healthcare is another. Medicare in the United States, for instance, generally does not cover care outside the country, and many expatriate retirees end up buying private international insurance, which becomes expensive and sometimes unavailable with age or pre-existing conditions. Even when care is cheap locally, serious illness often requires a return home, which is costly and disruptive.

Taxes create further friction. Citizens of some countries, notably the United States, are taxed on worldwide income regardless of where they live, which complicates retirement accounts, investment income, and filing obligations. Moving assets abroad can trigger reporting requirements or unfavorable treatment, and a retiree's home country may not extend the tax treaty benefits they expected.

Practical barriers add up as well. Long-term residency visas in many lower-cost countries require proof of steady income, bank balances, or minimum pension amounts, and visa rules can change with little notice. Banking is often harder for foreigners, since some banks refuse accounts for nonresidents or citizens of certain countries, and transferring money can incur poor exchange rates and fees. Property ownership may be restricted for foreigners, and inheritance and estate rules can be confusing or unfavorable for families.

Finally, there are personal and social costs. Retirees leave behind family, friends, familiar healthcare providers, and a support network that matters more with age. Language barriers, cultural adjustment, dependence on a new legal system, and the difficulty of returning quickly in an emergency all weigh on the decision. Currency risk also matters: a pension paid in a strong currency is attractive now, but exchange rate swings can change its real value substantially. Taken together, these factors mean that the cost savings, which look large on paper, are often offset by complexity, risk, and loss of security.

Freelancing from the UK for a Swiss company is common and usually straightforward, provided you do the work from the UK. Here is how the main issues typically fit together.

You'll need to decide whether to operate as a sole trader or through a limited company. As a sole trader, you register for Self Assessment with HMRC (by 5 October after the end of the tax year in which you start), keep records, and pay Income Tax and Class 4 National Insurance on your profits. Class 2 contributions are no longer compulsory, though some people pay them voluntarily to protect State Pension entitlement if profits are low. A limited company adds admin and accountancy costs but can be more tax-efficient at higher profit levels and may look more professional to some Swiss clients. If you use a company, note that the off-payroll working rules (IR35) work differently when the client has no UK presence: the responsibility for assessing employment status generally falls on your own company, not the Swiss client.

Because you are UK resident, you are taxed in the UK on your worldwide income, including your Swiss fees. If you do the work physically in the UK, Switzerland normally has no right to tax that income, and the UK–Switzerland double taxation agreement supports this. Swiss withholding tax doesn't usually apply to payments to genuinely independent foreign contractors. If a Swiss client tries to deduct tax, ask why, and point to the treaty.

VAT is often misunderstood. Business-to-business services supplied to a client based outside the UK generally have their place of supply in the customer's country, so they fall outside the scope of UK VAT. You don't charge UK VAT, and that income doesn't count toward the UK registration threshold (currently £90,000). Your invoices should note that the supply is outside the scope of UK VAT. You can still register voluntarily if it helps you reclaim VAT on business costs. On the Swiss side, the client usually handles any import tax on services through its own reverse-charge mechanism, and you normally don't need to register for Swiss VAT unless you start supplying services within Switzerland at significant volume.

On social security, the UK and Switzerland have a convention, in force since late 2021, that coordinates which country's system applies. If you are self-employed and work only in the UK, you remain in the UK National Insurance system. Swiss companies are sometimes cautious about whether a foreign freelancer might be treated as their employee under Swiss rules. They may ask for evidence of your self-employed status, such as your UTR, proof of other clients, or a certificate of coverage from HMRC. Having several clients, using your own equipment, setting your own hours and invoicing for deliverables all help show genuine independence.

If you plan to travel to Switzerland to work on site, the position changes. UK nationals can generally provide services in Switzerland for up to 90 working days per calendar year, but this usually requires advance online notification to the Swiss authorities, and some sectors have extra restrictions. Longer or regular stays may need a permit. Days worked in Switzerland could also create Swiss tax or social security exposure, so track them carefully.

On the practical side, have a written contract covering scope, fees, payment terms, currency, ownership of intellectual property, confidentiality, liability limits, termination, and governing law and jurisdiction. Swiss clients often propose Swiss law, which is fine but worth understanding before you sign. If you'll be paid in Swiss francs, a multi-currency account from a provider like Wise or Revolut Business can save a lot on conversion fees compared with high-street banks. For your UK tax return, convert income to sterling using a consistent method, such as the actual amount received or HMRC's published exchange rates. Professional indemnity insurance is worth considering, and some Swiss clients will require it. If you'll handle personal data, both UK GDPR and the Swiss Federal Act on Data Protection may apply, so a short data processing agreement can be useful.

A one-off consultation with a UK accountant who handles international clients is usually money well spent at the start, especially for deciding between sole trader and company and for confirming your VAT treatment. If you tell me more about the type of work, your expected income, and whether you'll ever work in Switzerland in person, I can go into whichever area matters most.

Automated decision-making is basically when computer algorithms and other tech make calls without a person stepping in. The systems work from data and rules someone programmed in, and they churn through decisions way faster and more consistently than people usually can. You'll see it everywhere: banks, insurers, hospitals, even the criminal justice system. Companies love it because it speeds things up, cuts down on mistakes, and (in theory) takes some of the human bias out of the picture. But it's not all good news. If the algorithm is trained on skewed data, or if the decision hits someone hard, like denying a loan or flagging someone for parole, things can go badly wrong. That's why a lot of people argue there should always be a human checking the process, so someone can catch unfair outcomes before they stick.

In biology, a family is a rank in the hierarchical system used to classify living things, a system known as taxonomy. It sits between order and genus. The standard sequence of major ranks runs from domain, kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, and finally species. A family therefore groups together one or more related genera that share a common ancestry and a set of broad characteristics, while being distinct from other families within the same order.

Family names follow conventions that make them easy to recognize. In zoology, family names end in "-idae," as in Felidae (the cat family) or Canidae (the dog family). In botany, and also for algae and fungi, family names typically end in "-aceae," as in Rosaceae (the rose family) or Poaceae (the grasses). There are a few traditional exceptions in botany, such as Asteraceae sometimes being called Compositae, though modern usage favors the standardized endings. The name of a family is usually built from the name of a type genus, the genus that serves as its reference point. Felidae, for example, is based on the genus Felis. Family names are capitalized but not italicized, unlike genus and species names.

Families are meant to reflect evolutionary relationships. Modern classification aims for groups that are monophyletic, meaning that they include a common ancestor and all of its descendants. Historically, families were defined mostly by shared anatomy and appearance, but molecular data, especially DNA sequencing, has led to many revisions. Species have been moved between families, families have been split or merged, and some traditional groupings have been shown not to reflect true ancestry.

The rank is not absolute or uniform in meaning. There is no fixed rule about how much diversity or evolutionary age a family should represent, so families in different groups of organisms can vary widely in size and age. Some contain thousands of species, such as the orchid family Orchidaceae, while others contain just one genus or even a single species. Taxonomists sometimes also use intermediate ranks such as superfamily, subfamily, and tribe to express finer levels of relationship. Superfamilies sit above families, with names ending in "-oidea" in zoology, while subfamilies sit below, ending in "-inae."

Families are useful because they provide a convenient level of generalization. Knowing that a plant belongs to the mint family, for instance, tells you something about its likely square stems, opposite leaves, and aromatic oils. The same is true for animals, where family membership suggests shared body plans, behaviors, and ecological roles.

Stopping the medications you were taking is an important first step, and in many cases the liver can recover on its own once the cause is removed. Recovery depends on what caused the inflammation, how much damage there is, and whether other causes are also involved. Because your levels were normal in February and abnormal in September, something changed in that window, and the timing makes the medications and the acetaminophen (Tylenol) the leading suspects. Taking acetaminophen regularly above the recommended limit, which is generally no more than 3,000 mg a day unless a doctor has told you otherwise, is a well-known cause of liver injury, and the risk rises with alcohol use or with several prescription drugs that also stress the liver.

Still, you should not assume it will resolve without follow-up. Your doctor will likely want to repeat your liver blood tests, often including ALT, AST, alkaline phosphatase, bilirubin, and sometimes a clotting test (INR), to see whether the numbers are falling. They may also order tests for hepatitis viruses, check for fatty liver or other causes, and possibly order an ultrasound. If the levels keep rising or stay high, you may be referred to a hepatologist (a liver specialist). Treatment is mostly supportive: avoiding the causative substances, avoiding alcohol, managing any underlying condition, and monitoring until the tests normalize. There is no single medication that "fixes" the liver, and you should not start any new drug or supplement, including herbal products, without checking with your doctor first.

Until you have spoken with your doctor, avoid acetaminophen unless they approve a safe amount, check labels on cold and sleep products since many contain it, and do not restart the prescription medications you stopped without talking to the prescriber. Bring a complete list of everything you have taken in the past year, including doses and over-the-counter products, to your appointment.

Seek medical care promptly, and go to an emergency room if you develop yellowing of the skin or eyes, dark urine, pale stools, pain in the upper right abdomen, nausea or vomiting that won't stop, unusual bruising or bleeding, confusion, or marked fatigue or swelling in the legs or belly.

A CMM, or coordinate measuring machine, is a precision instrument used to measure the physical geometry of an object with very high accuracy. It works by using a probe to touch points on the surface of a part, recording each point's position in three-dimensional space along the X, Y, and Z axes. By collecting many such points, the machine can determine dimensions, shapes, angles, and positions of features such as holes, edges, and surfaces, and then compare them against the design specifications, typically from a CAD model or engineering drawing.

CMMs are widely used in manufacturing, particularly in aerospace, automotive, and medical device industries, where parts must meet tight tolerances. The probes can be contact types, which physically touch the part, or non-contact types, which use lasers or optical sensors. Many modern machines are computer-controlled and can run automated inspection routines, which improves speed and repeatability. Because they can verify that parts are made correctly, CMMs play an important role in quality control and in confirming that components will fit and function as intended.

Utah was admitted to the Union as the 45th state on January 4, 1896. Its path to statehood was long: the Mormon pioneers who settled the region in 1847 first sought recognition as the State of Deseret, and later territorial status was established in 1850. Statehood came only after Congress required Utah to outlaw polygamy and write that prohibition into its constitution.

In the short run, an economy can expand by producing more goods and services, yet sustained growth over the long run depends on using resources more efficiently and finding substitutes for those that are becoming depleted. This is comparable to a person's height: eating more may help a child grow for a while, but growth eventually ends once the body reaches its mature size. Likewise, an economy cannot expand indefinitely, since the resources available to it are finite. Still, by managing our resources carefully and developing new methods of production, we can keep our economy strong.

No, it isn't riskless, and the gap between the market price and the tender price is essentially the market's way of pricing the risks involved. Buying shares below a tender offer price in hopes of capturing the difference is a well-known strategy called merger arbitrage or risk arbitrage, and the word "risk" in that name is earned.

The biggest danger is that the offer fails or is withdrawn. Tender offers usually come with conditions, such as a minimum number of shares being tendered, regulatory or antitrust approval, financing being secured, or no material adverse change in the target's business. If any condition isn't met, the bidder can walk away, and the stock often falls back to where it traded before the offer, or even lower. That loss can be far larger than the small spread you were trying to capture. You might risk losing twenty or thirty percent to make two percent.

Proration is another common issue, especially in partial tender offers or company self-tender buybacks. If the company offers to buy only a certain number of shares and more are tendered than it wants, it accepts shares pro rata. You might tender 1,000 shares and have only 400 accepted at the offer price, leaving you holding 600 shares that may drop once the offer closes, since the price was often propped up by the offer itself.

Timing also matters. Your money is tied up until the deal closes, which can take months or longer if regulators extend their reviews. A two percent spread earned over a year is a modest return, and you bear opportunity cost the whole time. Delays also give more time for something to go wrong.

There are smaller considerations too. Your broker may charge fees for tendering, there are deadlines you must meet, and taxes apply to any gain. In some cases the consideration isn't all cash but includes the acquirer's stock, which exposes you to that company's price movements. In Dutch auction tender offers, the final price isn't fixed in advance and may end up below what you hoped.

The spread itself is informative. A very small spread suggests the market sees the deal as highly likely to close soon. A wide spread signals real doubt about regulatory approval, financing, or shareholder support. Professional arbitrageurs analyze these factors carefully, and they still sometimes lose money when deals collapse.

So the strategy can be reasonable and is sometimes profitable, but it's a calculated bet on the deal completing as announced, not free money.

Title insurance protects you if something goes wrong with the title to your property. Think of problems like someone else claiming ownership, unpaid liens, or old encumbrances nobody caught. Lenders almost always require it when you're buying with a mortgage, but it's mainly there to protect their stake. You can buy an owner's policy too, and plenty of people do. Whether it's worth it really depends on your situation and how risky your property's history looks. If you're worried about title defects or want protection against those financial hits, it's probably worth a look. Talking to a real estate attorney is a smart move too, since they can tell you whether it makes sense for your case.

Honestly, there are a lot of things that can make someone feel nervous and not very confident, and feeling that way now and then is totally normal. Most people go through it. But if it sticks around and starts getting in the way of your everyday life, it's worth talking to a mental health professional. They can help you figure out what's going on underneath and give you ways to deal with it.

It could be anxiety, or social anxiety in particular, which tends to make people jittery and unsure of themselves around others. Other things can feed into it too, like something rough that happened in the past, low self-esteem, or just a stressful stretch in your life.

As for the crying, that's a normal, healthy way to let feelings out and work through them, so don't beat yourself up over it. If it feels like too much, though, or it's messing with your day-to-day, a therapist can help you dig into why and find some ways to cope.

And it's okay to ask for help if your emotions are getting the better of you. That's what those folks are there for. They can support you and guide you, and you'll probably feel a lot better for it.

Yes, you've got it right on both counts. A compiler is a program that reads instructions written in a language people can understand, like "add these two numbers," and turns them into machine code, the long strings of 1s and 0s that a computer's chip actually follows. And yes, a compiler is itself a program, so it was written by people too.

The very first programs didn't need a compiler at all. Long ago, people programmed computers by flipping switches or plugging wires into boards, and later by typing the 1s and 0s directly. Imagine trying to tell a friend exactly how to build a tower by only saying "block, block, block" in a secret code. It was slow and easy to mess up.

Then came a clever idea: let the computer help. Early pioneers wrote small programs that could translate simpler, word-like instructions into the numbers the machine needed. Grace Hopper's team in the 1950s built some of the first such translators, and the first compiler is often credited to her work on the A-0 system. Other people created languages like FORTRAN, which let scientists write math in something close to ordinary English-like formulas.

So the story goes like this: people first talked to computers in the computer's own language, then built a translator to make it easier, and then used that translator to build even better translators. Each step made the next one easier, a bit like how you learned to read simple words first, then used reading to learn bigger and harder ones.

Michael I. Jordan is an American scientist known for his foundational work in machine learning, statistics, and artificial intelligence. He is a professor at the University of California, Berkeley, where he has held appointments in both the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Sciences and the Department of Statistics. He is often recognized as one of the most influential researchers in the field of modern machine learning.

His research spans a wide range of topics, including probabilistic graphical models, Bayesian nonparametrics, variational inference, and optimization for large-scale data analysis. He has also worked on the theoretical foundations of statistical learning and on how machine learning systems can be designed to operate reliably in real-world settings. In recent years he has written and spoken about the societal and economic implications of AI, arguing for a broader engineering perspective on building systems that serve human needs.

Jordan has trained many students and postdoctoral researchers who have gone on to become leading figures in academia and industry. His contributions have earned him numerous honors, including election to the National Academy of Sciences and the National Academy of Engineering.

It is worth noting that he shares his name with the famous basketball player Michael Jordan, so the two are often confused. The scientist is a different person entirely.

During a period, blood travels from the uterus through the cervix into the vagina and then leaves the body through the vaginal opening. The vagina is not a sealed tube, so the blood does not stay trapped inside it. When a woman swims, the pressure of the surrounding water does not stop menstrual flow, so it can still leave the body as usual. A tampon or menstrual cup, however, can catch or absorb the blood while she is in the water, which keeps it from escaping. These products are made to be worn during physical activity, swimming included, so they are a practical choice for women who want to stay active during their periods.

Okay, so the thing that makes your body produce heat is metabolism. Basically, metabolism is how your body turns food into energy. Your body needs that energy for everything it does, including staying warm. When you eat, your body breaks down the molecules in your food and uses them to make energy, and that process gives off heat as a side effect. That heat is what keeps you near your core temperature of about 98.6°F (37°C). So yeah, metabolism is the answer: you burn food for energy, and the heat from that is what keeps you warm.

I'm sorry you've been through so many procedures and complications. Here is what is generally known, though your own team has the details of your anatomy.

Why strictures keep coming back: A bile duct injury during gallbladder surgery can come from a clip, cautery heat damage, a partial or complete cut, or loss of blood supply to the duct. The body heals the injured area with scar tissue (fibrosis), and scar tissue naturally contracts over time. Stretching or stenting the duct opens it temporarily, but the scar can tighten again, especially if the injury was severe, the stricture is high up near the liver, the duct has poor blood supply, or the stent was too small or removed too early. Repeated inflammation or infection (cholangitis) can also feed more scarring. Each ERCP can itself irritate the duct and sometimes add to the problem.

Typical size: A normal common bile duct is about 4 to 6 millimeters wide, and can be a bit larger after gallbladder removal. Strictures are often just 1 to 3 millimeters at their narrowest. Bile can flow through quite a narrow opening, so there is no single minimum number. What matters is whether bile drains well, meaning your liver tests stay normal and you don't get jaundice, itching, fevers, or infections. Treatment aims to get the duct to a functional size, often by placing several plastic stents side by side or a fully covered metal stent, for around 12 months.

When ERCP keeps failing: If a stricture returns after about a year of well-done multi-stent therapy, guidelines generally favor a different approach, since repeated ERCPs bring complication risks such as pancreatitis, infection, and bleeding. The main alternatives are:

Surgical repair, usually a hepaticojejunostomy (Roux-en-Y). A surgeon connects the healthy bile duct above the scar directly to a loop of small intestine, bypassing the damaged part. It has good long-term success rates, often above 80 to 90 percent, when done by an experienced hepatobiliary surgeon. It is generally considered the definitive fix for a stubborn post-surgical stricture.

Percutaneous approaches, where a radiologist goes through the skin and liver to dilate or stent the duct. These are sometimes used when ERCP can't reach the stricture.

Other options include a longer course of fully covered metal stents in selected cases, though these are less commonly used for benign strictures near the liver.

What I'd suggest: Ask your doctor directly whether you are a candidate for surgical bypass, and request referral to a high-volume hepatobiliary or liver surgery center if you haven't had one. Ask where exactly the stricture sits, how severe it is on imaging (such as MRCP), and what the long-term plan is. Also ask whether the stents you've had were multiple and left in long enough. Getting a second opinion is reasonable given ten procedures.

Please also seek prompt care if you develop fever, chills, yellow skin or eyes, dark urine, pale stools, or severe abdominal pain, since these can signal a blocked duct or infection.

Yeah, you can totally have someone invest for you and split the profits and losses with you. It's usually called a partnership. Basically two or more people (or entities) team up to run a business and share the wins and losses however the partnership agreement says they will.

Before you jump in, though, there are a few things worth thinking about.

First, the legal structure. Partnerships come in different flavors, like a general partnership, a limited partnership, or a limited liability partnership. Each one has its own legal and tax stuff attached, so it really pays to learn the differences and pick the one that fits what you're doing.

Then there's risk. In a general partnership, you're personally on the hook for the partnership's debts and obligations. So if the business racks up losses or gets sued, they can come after you personally, not just the business.

Decision-making is the other big one. Partnerships mean sharing decisions, and that takes a lot of communication and trust. If you don't like working closely with someone or you'd rather not share control, this probably isn't the setup for you.

So a partnership can be a solid way to get into a business, but think hard about the risks and the upsides before you sign anything.

A key-agreement protocol is a cryptographic method that lets two or more participants create a common secret key while communicating over a channel that is not secure. Once established, this key can protect later exchanges between the participants through symmetric-key encryption. To arrive at the shared key, the parties usually send each other a series of messages. Many such protocols draw on public-key cryptography, where every participant holds both a public key and a private key. Messages are encrypted with the public key and decrypted with the private one. Diffie-Hellman key exchange is a well-known example. In it, two parties, Alice and Bob, send each other messages containing their public keys along with some further information, and each then computes the shared secret key from those values using a mathematical function. Other protocols of this kind include Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman (ECDH), Secure Remote Password (SRP), and Authenticated Key Exchange (AKE). Modern communication systems rely heavily on key-agreement protocols to set up secure channels for transmitting sensitive information.

Doctors typically advise people with liver conditions, hepatitis C among them, to steer clear of alcohol so that the liver is protected and the chance of additional harm is lowered. Drinking can inflame the liver, leave it scarred, and make existing damage worse. For that reason, giving up alcohol will probably be good for your liver and could help bring your enzyme levels down. Keep in mind, though, that your enzyme levels can also be influenced by other things, including how advanced your liver disease is and whether you have other medical problems. It's important to follow your healthcare provider's guidance and to work closely with them in managing your hepatitis C along with any other health issues you have.

Greenland and Mexico are both huge, but they're not anywhere close to the same size, and Greenland is actually way smaller. The reason it looks bigger on a map is the Mercator projection, which most maps use. It keeps shapes roughly right, but it stretches things near the poles, so Greenland ends up looking enormous. Honestly, Greenland is about the size of Alaska, which is big, sure, but still well short of Mexico.

Flies are so quick because their eyes and nervous system are built for seeing and reacting very fast. A fly's eyes are made of thousands of tiny lenses, and each one looks at a slightly different part of the world. Together they give the fly a wide view all around its head, so it notices movement almost everywhere at once, including your hand coming toward it.

The fly also processes what it sees much faster than we do. Our brains take a moment to notice something, decide what it means, and tell our muscles to move. A fly's brain works on a much shorter timeline, so by the time your hand is moving, the fly has already sensed the motion and started to react. Scientists have found that flies can react to a threat in a few hundredths of a second, which is quicker than a blink.

Flies also have very good control over their wings and legs. When they sense danger, they can launch into the air in an instant and change direction in the middle of a flight. Because of this, a swat that looks perfectly aimed to you is often aimed at where the fly was a moment ago, not where it is when your hand arrives.

So the trick is not that the fly is smarter than you. It simply sees the danger sooner and moves sooner, and it is built to get out of the way in a hurry.

John Williams did the music for the Star Wars films. He's scored all nine main movies, plus a bunch of other Star Wars stuff. Honestly, his work is a huge part of why the franchise feels the way it does, and critics and fans have loved it for decades. The big ones people always bring up are "The Main Title," "The Imperial March," and "Duel of the Fates."

Head lumps can arise from many different sources, and pinpointing the exact one usually requires a physical exam by a healthcare professional, since the text alone doesn't reveal enough. Some common possibilities include infections like abscesses, cellulitis, or folliculitis; inflammatory conditions such as sebaceous cysts or dermatitis; and trauma, particularly if your son has recently hurt his head. Less often, the lumps may be tumors, which can be either cancerous or benign. Because of this range of causes, it is important to take your son to a healthcare provider so they can identify the source and recommend the right treatment.

Yeah, it's possible the chest pain is coming from the clindamycin or the oxycodone. Both can cause side effects, so it's not a crazy guess. But chest pain can also be your heart or some other health issue that has nothing to do with the meds, and you really can't tell which from the couch.

So I'd call your doctor about it, and soon. Chest pain isn't something to wait on, since it could turn out to be serious. Until you talk to them, keep taking things the way they told you to, and let them know about any weird side effects you notice.

And if the pain gets severe or you're having trouble breathing, don't mess around. Get medical help right away.

The American Civil War kicked off on April 12, 1861, when Confederate forces opened fire on Fort Sumter in South Carolina. It dragged on until April 9, 1865, when the Confederacy surrendered and the Union was back together. Honestly, it's one of the biggest events in American history, and historians are still arguing about its causes and what it led to.

Yeah, a fever after a bump to the head isn't unusual, even when the hit was from something as simple as a metal table. Your body's immune system can kick off inflammation after an injury, and that can push temperature up a bit. Still, keep an eye on your son and get him seen if the fever hangs around or other stuff starts showing up. Honestly, with any head injury, especially in kids, it's worth having a doctor check him out just to make sure nothing more serious is going on. They might suggest rest, some over-the-counter pain relief, and plenty of fluids to help with the fever and whatever else is bugging him.

Some signs mean you should get emergency help right away: he passes out or seems confused, he has a headache that won't quit, he's weak or numb in his arms or legs, he keeps throwing up, his speech sounds slurred, he's having trouble breathing, or he has a seizure. When it comes to head injuries in kids, it's always better to be overly careful. If you're worried about how he's doing or how bad the bump really is, call a healthcare provider and talk it through.

Okay so the Manhattan Project was basically the US-led effort during WWII to build the first atomic bombs. People often forget it wasn't just America, though. The UK and Canada were involved too. Everyone was racing to build better weapons back then, and once the people running it realized atomic bombs could be a total game-changer, they poured huge amounts of money and manpower into it.

Part of why it's so full of conspiracy theories is that it was super secret. Most people had no clue what was going on, so rumors just filled the gap. Some of the theories are wild, but I get why they stuck. When something that big is hidden from the public, people start making up their own explanations for what it was really about.

A duvet cover is a detachable, ornamental sheath that shields a duvet, the soft, puffy bedding insert stuffed with down, feathers, or synthetic filling. It slides over the duvet and is fastened with buttons, snaps, or a zipper. Because it comes off easily and can be washed on its own, the duvet underneath stays guarded against dirt, stains, and everyday wear. Most covers are crafted from pleasant, breathable fabrics like cotton, linen, or a mix of synthetic and natural fibers. They are sold in an enormous range of hues, prints, and designs, letting you pick one that coordinates with your bedroom or brings a burst of color to your bed. Swapping covers is a simple, inexpensive way to refresh your bedding without buying a new duvet. They also travel well, since a light cover can be packed easily and brought along on any trip.

Kobe Bryant only won the NBA MVP once, and that came in the 2007-2008 season. He carried the Lakers to the best record in the Western Conference that year and led the whole league in scoring. Before that MVP trophy, he'd already picked up four championships and made 15 All-Star teams.

John von Neumann (1903–1957) was a Hungarian-American mathematician and polymath who made foundational contributions to many fields, including mathematics, physics, computer science, economics, and statistics. Born in Budapest, he showed exceptional talent early on and later moved to the United States, where he spent most of his career, becoming one of the most influential scientists of the twentieth century.

In mathematics, he developed the rigorous axiomatic foundations of quantum mechanics and wrote a influential book on the subject, "Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics." He also made significant contributions to functional analysis, including the theory of operator algebras, which are now called von Neumann algebras, and he worked on set theory and the foundations of mathematics.

His work in computing is also highly celebrated. He contributed to the design of the stored-program architecture, described in a 1945 report on the EDVAC computer, which is why modern computers are often said to follow the "von Neumann architecture," where instructions and data are held in the same memory. He was also a pioneer in numerical analysis and helped develop early electronic computers.

During World War II, von Neumann worked on the Manhattan Project, where he contributed to the mathematics of implosion-type nuclear weapons. He also helped develop the mathematical basis of game theory, co-writing "Theory of Games and Economic Behavior" with Oskar Morgenstern in 1944, which became foundational for modern economics and strategic decision-making.

He is remembered for his sharp intellect, his wide-ranging influence, and his role in shaping modern science and technology.

Bile duct narrowing after gallbladder surgery or endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) can arise from a number of causes. These include scarring or inflammation of the duct, abnormal growths or tumors, and stones or other debris that build up inside it. Sometimes the duct is narrow from birth, or has a congenital abnormality that makes it more likely to constrict. Narrowing after ERCP is fairly common, particularly when the procedure was done to clear stones or debris from the duct. Inflammation or scarring brought on by the procedure itself can also constrict the duct, and new stones or debris that form afterward may have the same effect. What counts as a normal duct size varies, but generally the duct should measure at least 6-8 mm across. When it becomes much narrower than that, bile may have trouble flowing through, which can cause a variety of symptoms and complications. If you are having complications, or you are weary of repeated ERCP procedures, you should raise these concerns with your doctor and talk about other treatment options. Your doctor can explain more about what is causing your particular narrowing and suggest the most suitable treatment.

Short answer: it's usually okay to try for a baby while you're on TB meds, and that includes Rcinex 600. But I'd still talk to your doctor before you start trying. Tell them what you're planning and ask about any risks that might apply to you.

Some TB drugs can cause side effects that could affect a developing baby, things like birth defects or low birth weight. So it's worth having a real conversation about whether to stay on your current treatment, and whether there's an alternative that's safer during pregnancy. Your doctor will know the latest guidance and can tell you what makes sense for your situation, which I can't do from here.

Whatever you decide, keep following the treatment plan they give you. Stopping or changing meds on your own can backfire, and untreated TB is bad for both you and the baby. Good luck!

Netflix relies on a range of algorithms and methods to suggest shows and movies to its subscribers. One approach is to examine the viewing patterns and tastes of people who have watched similar titles. For instance, if many viewers who finished "Revenge" also went on to watch "Clifford the Big Red Dog," the recommendation system may propose "Clifford the Big Red Dog" to someone who has just completed "Revenge."

Another method is to look at the genres and themes of the programs a person has already viewed. If someone has watched many titles categorized as "dramas" or "thrillers," Netflix may recommend other shows or films in those same categories. "Clifford the Big Red Dog" is a children's program, so the system could be factoring in your viewing of "Revenge," a drama, and offering "Clifford" as a different-genre pick you might enjoy. It's also possible that Netflix is recommending it because it is a popular, all-ages show, and the company wants to suggest content that appeals to a broad audience. I hope this helps! Is there anything else you'd like to know?

MyloCORT cream and Allergex Mepryamine Cream aren't really meant for allergic reactions, so it's worth knowing what they actually do. MyloCORT is a topical corticosteroid that calms inflammation and itching on the skin. Allergex Mepryamine is a combo cream with an antihistamine (mepyramine) and a corticosteroid (hydrocortisone), and it's usually used for things like eczema, dermatitis, and insect bites.

If your mom is getting a bad rash or itching from Risperdal, call her doctor soon and don't wait it out. They might switch her to something else or tweak the dose. Until then, calamine lotion or plain OTC hydrocortisone cream can take the edge off the itch. I'd hold off on using MyloCORT and Allergex together without checking with a provider first, since combining them may not be safe for her situation. Stick to whatever the doctor tells you and follow the directions on the package. If the rash gets worse or isn't improving, get her back in front of the provider right away.

Yeah, you can totally do this. A lot of grocery stores have rewards programs that give you points or cash back on everything you spend, and the earning rate often changes depending on what you're buying. Gift cards can be a way to bump that rate up.

Say the store's program gives you a higher rate on certain categories, like groceries, household stuff, or personal care. If you buy gift cards that count toward those categories, you might end up with more rewards than you'd get just buying the items straight up.

That said, every program works a little differently, and the earning rates can vary a lot from one store to the next. I'd read through the terms and conditions for yours so you know exactly how to squeeze the most rewards out of it.

Equity offers vary a lot, so the most useful first step is figuring out what kind you're being offered, because the tax treatment, risk, and value differ sharply between types. Stock options (incentive stock options or non-qualified options) give you the right to buy shares at a fixed strike price, usually the fair market value on the grant date. Restricted stock units (RSUs) are a promise to deliver actual shares once they vest, and they have value as long as the company has value. Restricted stock awards and profits interests are less common at larger companies but show up in startups. Each of these has different rules for when you owe tax and how much.

The offer letter or grant documents should spell out the number of shares or the percentage of the company, the strike price if it's an option, the vesting schedule (a typical arrangement is four years with a one-year cliff, meaning nothing vests until you've stayed a year, then it vests monthly or quarterly), and what happens to unvested equity if you leave or the company is acquired. Pay attention to the post-termination exercise window for options, since many companies give only 90 days to buy your vested options after you leave, which can be expensive if you have to pay the strike price and possibly tax out of pocket.

Be realistic about value. Private company equity is illiquid, and the stated value on paper is often based on a 409A valuation that may not reflect what shares would sell for. Many startups fail or sell for less than their last funding round, and preferred shares held by investors often sit ahead of common shares, which are usually what employees receive, in the payout order. Ask what share count is outstanding and what the fully diluted number is, so you can judge what your percentage really means. If the company is public, your RSUs are easier to value, but still subject to stock price swings and vesting.

Some practical steps: ask for a written summary of the terms, ask about the company's latest valuation and funding history, and ask whether there's a tender offer or secondary sale program that would let you sell some shares. Consider the tax consequences with an accountant or tax professional before exercising options, especially if you might owe alternative minimum tax on incentive stock options. It's also reasonable to negotiate: you can often ask for more shares, a shorter cliff, a longer exercise window, or a larger base salary in place of some equity.

Finally, treat equity as a possible bonus rather than guaranteed compensation. Decide how you'd feel if it ended up worth nothing, and make sure your base pay and benefits are acceptable on their own. If you tell me the type of equity, whether the company is public or private, and the size of the grant, I can help you think through the specifics.

The USA PATRIOT Act was enacted on October 26, 2001, when President George W. Bush signed it into law. It was passed about six weeks after the September 11, 2001 attacks. The full name is the Uniting and Strengthening America by Providing Appropriate Tools Required to Intercept and Obstruct Terrorism Act of 2001.

Don't panic too much about the IRBBB diagnosis, it's pretty common on ECGs and usually isn't a big deal. Basically, the electrical signals that tell the right side of the heart when to squeeze get a little delayed on one pathway, so the heart's timing is slightly off. Most people with it have zero symptoms and go about their lives just fine. Some do get things like shortness of breath, tiredness, or chest pain, but that's the exception rather than the rule. Your doctor's the best person to tell you how worried to be, so stick with their follow-up schedule and get regular check-ups so they can keep an eye on things. As for sports, he's usually fine to keep playing as long as he feels good doing it. If he ever gets chest pain, dizziness, or gets short of breath in a way that seems off during exercise, he should stop right away and get it checked out.

I'd recommend seeing a doctor or urgent care soon rather than trying to treat this at home. A cyst that has been present for two years, became infected after you squeezed it, and is now large, hard, painful, and draining tan fluid and blood is probably an infected cyst or abscess. These often need to be opened and drained by a clinician, and sometimes antibiotics. Because the lump has been there for a long time and is now hard and enlarging, a doctor should also look at it to confirm what it is, since a few other things, including a swollen lymph node, can look similar.

Please stop squeezing or pressing on it, since that pushes infection deeper and can make it worse. In the meantime, you can apply a warm, damp washcloth for 10 to 15 minutes a few times a day, which may help it drain on its own and eases discomfort. Keep the area clean, avoid tight collars or anything rubbing against it, and use an over-the-counter pain reliever such as ibuprofen or acetaminophen if you can take them.

Go to an emergency department right away if you develop fever or chills, redness that spreads quickly, increasing swelling, difficulty swallowing or breathing, a change in your voice, drooling, or confusion or feeling very unwell. Those signs can mean the infection is spreading and need prompt treatment.

For backtesting, adjusted closing prices are generally the better choice. These prices account for corporate actions like dividends and stock splits, which can meaningfully affect a stock's price. Relying on unadjusted closing prices can produce misleading outcomes, since those figures do not reflect the effects of such events. Adjusted closes also help avoid look-ahead bias, a problem that can arise when a corporate action is announced after the market closes but before a backtest is run on unadjusted data. Keep in mind that data providers may calculate adjusted closes in slightly different ways, so it is important to use a consistent, trustworthy source for your backtesting.

Because money is so central to everyday life and touches so many parts of both our personal and working worlds, it's perfectly natural for it to come up in our thoughts in a variety of settings. Most people consider it in terms of what they earn and spend, what they set aside as savings, where they invest, what they owe, and what they hope to achieve financially. They may also focus on what money is worth, how much it can buy, and how its exchange rate shifts between countries and currencies. Money carries cultural and social meaning as well, since it serves not only as a medium of exchange but also as a yardstick for success or standing.

Water does add moisture to your skin, but it doesn't stay there for long, and it can actually pull some natural oils out with it. Your skin has a thin protective layer made of natural oils and fats, and this layer works like a raincoat. It keeps the water inside your skin from slipping out into the air. When you spend a long time in warm water, especially hot water, that raincoat gets washed off and softened, so the moisture underneath escapes faster.

Think of it like a sponge. A sponge full of water feels wet, but if you leave it out in the sun it dries out quickly. Your skin is similar. The water you soak up in the shower soon evaporates, and the drying feeling you notice is that water leaving.

Soap makes this worse, because soap is designed to wash away oil and dirt, and it takes some of your skin's natural oils along with it. Once those oils are gone, your skin loses water more easily and starts to feel tight, rough, and ashy.

That's why moisturiser helps. It puts oils and fats back on top of your skin, like putting a lid on a cup of warm tea so it stays warm. The lid traps the water your skin already has, so it stays soft and comfortable.

A faint line can mean a few things. Sometimes it's a real positive that's just showing up early, and sometimes it's a false positive, so it's hard to say for sure from the line alone. If you think you could be pregnant, the best move is to retest in a couple of days with your first pee of the morning, since that's when the pregnancy hormone (hCG) is usually most concentrated. A blood test is more sensitive too, if you want a clearer answer sooner.

That deep purple line in the other window isn't part of your result. It's most likely the control line, which just shows the test is working like it should.

They can give you a proper answer and walk you through what your options are. Looking after your reproductive health matters, especially if you're sexually active, so don't just sit on it.

There are a bunch of usual suspects. Lifestyle stuff like eating a lot of salt, carrying extra weight, or not moving around much can all push it up.
