A faint, odd smell at day five on a large, dense tattoo is very common and usually not a sign of trouble. Your arm is dealing with a big area of broken skin, and what you're smelling is most likely a mix of dried plasma and lymph (the fluid that weeps out and forms scabs), the ointment or lotion you're using, and bacteria that live harmlessly on the skin breaking down those residues. Ointments such as petroleum-based products or heavily scented lotions can also turn slightly rancid or take on a sour, metallic or "crushed bug" note when they mix with weeping fluid and sit under a bandage or clothing. A heavily scabbed tattoo traps that mixture, so the smell can be more noticeable than on a small piece.

What would make it a concern is a change in the picture: a foul or sweet, rotten smell, yellow or green pus, spreading redness beyond the tattoo edges, increasing swelling or heat, throbbing pain that gets worse after the first few days, red streaks running up the arm, or fever and chills. Any of those means you should see a doctor promptly. Since you have none of these, you're probably fine, but keep checking.

For the scabbing itself, the aim is to keep scabs thin and flexible rather than thick and cracked. Wash gently two to three times a day with lukewarm water and a fragrance-free liquid soap, using only clean hands, and let the water carry off the dried fluid and old ointment. This also helps with the smell. Pat dry with a clean paper towel rather than a cloth towel, and let it air dry fully for a few minutes before applying anything. Then use a very thin layer of a fragrance-free moisturizer or a tattoo aftercare product. Thick layers of ointment suffocate the skin, trap moisture and bacteria, and make scabs gummy, so less is better. By now most people switch from ointment to a light unscented lotion.

Don't pick, peel or scratch the scabs, even when they get itchy, because pulling them off can take ink with them and leave patchy spots or scars. If itching is bad, gently slapping or tapping the area, or applying a cool clean compress over clean skin, can help. Wear loose, clean, breathable clothing over the area, avoid tight sleeves, and change bedding that touches the arm. Avoid soaking in baths, pools, hot tubs and the sea until it has fully healed, and keep it out of direct sun. Drinking plenty of water and avoiding alcohol also help healing.

Scabs on a dense piece generally flake off over the next one to two weeks. If the smell persists after a good washing routine or gets stronger, or if anything on the warning list appears, contact your tattoo artist for advice or see a doctor.

Market capitalization, usually shortened to market cap, is the total market value of a company's outstanding shares of stock. You calculate it by multiplying the current share price by the total number of shares held by investors. For example, if a company has 100 million shares outstanding and each share trades at 50 dollars, its market cap is 5 billion dollars. Because the share price changes constantly while markets are open, market cap fluctuates throughout the trading day.

Investors use market cap as a quick way to gauge a company's size and how the market values it. Companies are commonly grouped into categories based on this figure. Large-cap companies are generally those worth more than about 10 billion dollars, mid-cap companies fall roughly between 2 billion and 10 billion, and small-cap companies are typically valued between about 300 million and 2 billion. There are also mega-cap companies at the very top, often worth hundreds of billions or even trillions, and micro-cap companies at the bottom. These thresholds aren't fixed rules, and different sources draw the lines slightly differently.

These categories matter because companies of different sizes tend to behave differently as investments. Large-cap firms are usually more established and stable, often paying dividends, while small-cap firms may offer more growth potential but tend to carry more risk and price volatility.

It's worth noting that market cap reflects what investors are collectively willing to pay for a company's equity at a given moment, which isn't necessarily the same as what the company is fundamentally worth or what it would cost to buy it outright. A related measure called enterprise value adjusts market cap by adding debt and subtracting cash, giving a fuller picture of a company's total value from an acquirer's perspective.

Stocks and high-yield bonds can both have a place in a diversified portfolio, but they're different animals when it comes to risk, reward, and taxes. Stocks are basically ownership slices of a company. If the company grows, your shares can gain value over time, but that's not guaranteed, and prices can swing a lot. High-yield bonds, often called junk bonds, are rated below investment grade. They pay more interest than safer bonds to make up for the extra risk, and that higher income comes with a real chance the issuer won't pay you back.

Taxes work differently too. Dividends and capital gains from stocks are taxed at different rates depending on how long you held the stock and what your tax bracket looks like. Regular bond interest is usually taxed as ordinary income, which often hits harder. High-yield bonds can be trickier, since the income might be a mix of interest and capital gains. If you're weighing these, talk to a financial advisor or tax pro about your own situation. Really, the right pick comes down to your goals, how much risk you can stomach, and what the rest of your finances look like. Spreading your money across different types of investments is a good way to keep risk in check.

An LED is a tiny electronic light that works very differently from a filament bulb. Instead of heating a wire until it glows, an LED uses a special crystal that makes light directly when electricity flows through it.

Think of it like a tiny slide for electricity. The crystal has two sides, one with extra little electric "bits" that want to move and one with spaces where those bits can fall into. When electricity pushes the bits across, each one drops into a space and lets go of a small packet of energy. That packet comes out as a particle of light. Lots of these drops happening at once make the LED shine.

The big difference is efficiency. A filament bulb wastes a lot of its energy as heat, because it has to get the wire so hot that it glows, and most of that energy becomes warmth you can feel. An LED skips most of that heating and turns more of its electricity into light, so it uses much less power for the same brightness and lasts much longer. Filament bulbs also burn out when the thin wire snaps, while LEDs just get slowly dimmer over many years.

Several factors can explain why different sources report different closing prices for the same stock. First, sources may draw on different data feeds, since the many providers of stock price information do not always match one another. Second, they may calculate the closing price differently: some treat the final trade of the day as the close, while others average the prices over the last few minutes of trading. Third, sources located in different time zones may base their closing figures on slightly different moments, which can produce small discrepancies. To avoid confusion, it is generally wise to take the closing price from a reputable source, such as a major financial news outlet or a well-known financial data provider.

Academic Marxism is basically Marxism as practiced by people in universities: professors, grad students, researchers who dig into Marx's ideas and use them in history, sociology, economics, political science, and so on. Marxism itself is a way of looking at the world that Karl Marx came up with. His big claim is that society splits into two main classes. On one side you've got the bourgeoisie, who own the means of production like factories and businesses. On the other is the proletariat, the working class, who don't own that stuff and have to sell their labor to survive. Marx argued that the bourgeoisie exploits the proletariat, and that this exploitation sits at the root of a lot of social and economic problems. So academic Marxists use these ideas to make sense of social and economic issues, figure out what's going on, and suggest fixes. They also tend to use Marxist ideas to push back on mainstream theories in their fields, which can get them into some pretty heated debates.

Gene expression programming (GEP) is an evolutionary computation method for evolving computer programs or models. It builds on genetic programming, using genetic-like operators to evolve solutions. Here's the catch, though: the solutions in GEP are stored as tree-like structures called expression trees. Each node is either a function or a terminal, and the branches hold the function's arguments. You can mix and match those functions and terminals in lots of ways to get a full program or model.

So how does it actually work? You start with a population of expression trees, then score each one with a fitness function that tells you how well it handles your problem. The better performers get picked for reproduction, and new trees come out of crossover and mutation. Repeat that loop until something good shows up. People have used GEP for function approximation, symbolic regression, and classification, among other things. It's pretty nice that you can evolve complex solutions with a fairly simple representation and set of operators. The downside is that it can eat a lot of computing power, and you'll often have to fiddle with the settings before you get decent results.

Yeah, there are a few places cruise ships dock around NYC. The main one is the Manhattan Cruise Terminal at West 54th Street and 12th Avenue. Several cruise lines use it as a home port, and it handles both domestic and international departures.

Then there's the Brooklyn Cruise Terminal over in Red Hook. That one's mostly for international sailings.

Cape Liberty Cruise Port is across the water in Bayonne, New Jersey. It's about a 20-minute drive from Manhattan, and a bunch of lines leave from there for the Caribbean and other places.

You'll also see the Staten Island Ferry Terminal mentioned, at the southern tip of Manhattan. Some lines supposedly use it for Caribbean and other trips too, though honestly that one's the odd one out.

Not every cruise line uses every terminal, and which one you end up at depends on where you're headed and who you're sailing with. So just check with your cruise line or travel agent before you book a car or hotel, so you know where you're actually leaving from.

A post is basically a vertical piece of structure that holds up a beam or lintel, and you'll see them all over load-bearing walls and around door and window framing. A lintel, on the other hand, is the horizontal piece that sits across the top of an opening like a window or door and carries the weight above it. They're usually made from concrete, steel, or wood, and their job is to pass that load out to the wall sections on either side.

In a building with load-bearing walls, posts and lintels basically team up. The posts carry the weight from the upper floors and roof down to the foundation, and the lintels pass the load from the walls over to those posts. That way the weight gets spread out evenly, so the walls don't buckle or come down under all that pressure. Lintels can also be decorative, and you can find them in plenty of styles, so they can add some visual interest and fit into the overall look of a building.

The most reliable source for this figure is the Federal Reserve's Survey of Consumer Finances, which is conducted every three years. Its most recent published results, from 2022, found that the median retirement account balance among American families who had such accounts was about $87,000. These accounts include 401(k)s, IRAs, and similar plans. That figure leaves out a large group, though. Only about 54 percent of families reported having any retirement account at all. If you count every household, including those with nothing saved, the median falls dramatically, to a few thousand dollars or close to zero depending on how it is calculated.

Savings rise with age, as you would expect. Among families with accounts in the 2022 survey, the median was roughly $18,900 for those under 35, about $45,000 for ages 35 to 44, around $115,000 for ages 45 to 54, about $185,000 for ages 55 to 64, and roughly $200,000 for ages 65 to 74. For households 75 and older it dropped to around $130,000, since people draw down their savings in retirement.

Several caveats apply. Medians are far lower than averages. The average balance in 2022 was over $330,000 because a relatively small number of very large accounts pull it upward, so the median better reflects a typical household. These numbers also exclude Social Security, traditional pensions, home equity, and other assets that many retirees rely on heavily. Finally, market gains since 2022 have probably pushed current balances somewhat higher. Data from the 2025 survey, expected around late 2026, should give a more up-to-date picture. Other sources, such as Vanguard's annual "How America Saves" report, offer more recent figures, but those cover only participants in employer plans that Vanguard administers.

Pain that severe in the hip and groin, followed by being unable to lift your leg or bear weight the next morning, needs prompt medical attention. Please get evaluated today, ideally at an emergency department or urgent care, rather than waiting to see if it improves.

Several things could cause this. The most common is a serious muscle or tendon injury, such as a strained hip flexor or adductor (inner thigh) muscle, sometimes with a partial or complete tear. A stress fracture of the femur or pelvis is another real possibility, especially if you've recently increased your running distance or intensity, are older, or have low bone density. A hip labral tear or a problem inside the joint can also cause this pattern. Less often, a hip fracture or a problem with blood supply to the hip bone can present this way. Some of these are easy to treat, but others get worse if you keep walking on them, which is why the inability to lift your leg matters so much.

When you're seen, tell the clinician exactly what happened: that the pain started during the run, how it felt when it happened, and that you couldn't lift your leg this morning. X-rays are usually the first step, and an MRI may be needed if the X-rays are normal.

Until you're seen, avoid putting weight on that leg, don't try to force yourself to walk on it, and don't run or exercise. If you can't stand or walk at all, or if you notice numbness, tingling, a leg that looks shorter or turned outward, fever, or severe swelling, call emergency services rather than driving yourself.

Kernel regression is basically a nonparametric way of estimating the conditional expectation of a variable. Think of it as a smoothing method: you use the values of other variables in your dataset to predict the one you care about.

The idea is pretty simple. To estimate the target value at some point, you take a weighted average of the target values at nearby points. The weights come from a kernel function, which just gives each point a weight depending on how far it is from the point you're estimating. Closer points count for more, farther ones count for less.

What I like about it is that it's flexible. It handles nonlinear relationships fine, and you don't have to assume anything about the underlying distribution of your data. You can use it with continuous, categorical, or ordinal variables, too.

You'll see it a lot in machine learning and statistical modeling, and people use it in economics, finance, engineering, and plenty of other places. It's especially handy for time series, where you can predict future values of the target from past observations.

The most likely explanation for a nagging pain under the right shoulder blade after weeks of heavy coughing is muscle strain. Repeated, forceful coughing works the muscles between the ribs, around the shoulder blade and in the upper back very hard, and it is common for one area to become sore, tight or mildly inflamed. Coughing fits can occasionally even bruise or crack a rib. This kind of pain usually feels worse when you cough, take a deep breath, twist or press on the spot, and it tends to ease gradually as the cough settles.

There are other possibilities worth having checked, particularly because your cough has lasted several weeks. A chest infection that never fully cleared, or one that developed into pneumonia, can cause pain in the back of the chest. Pleurisy, inflammation of the lining around the lung, produces a sharp pain that catches when you breathe in. Less often, pain under the right shoulder blade comes from the gallbladder, especially if it is linked to eating fatty food or comes with nausea or discomfort under the right ribs. Rarely, a blood clot in the lung causes chest or back pain with breathlessness. A cough lasting more than three or four weeks after a cold is generally a reason for a doctor to listen to your chest and sometimes arrange a chest X-ray.

You should get seen promptly if you develop a fever, feel short of breath, cough up blood or green or rusty phlegm, have pain that is sharp and worse with every breath, notice the pain getting worse instead of better, or feel generally unwell. Sudden breathlessness or chest pain needs urgent attention.

Your caution about Nolotil is reasonable. Nolotil is metamizole (also called dipyrone), a strong painkiller widely prescribed in Spain and some other countries but withdrawn or restricted in places like the UK and the USA. Its main serious risk is agranulocytosis, a rare but potentially life-threatening drop in the white blood cells that fight infection. This reaction is uncommon, but it can happen at normal doses, and some reports suggest people of British or northern European background may be more vulnerable. If you do take it, the warning signs are fever, sore throat, mouth ulcers or suddenly feeling unwell with signs of infection. If any of those appear, stop the medicine and seek medical help the same day, asking for a blood count. It is generally recommended only for short courses.

It is perfectly reasonable to go back to your doctor or pharmacist and ask whether a different painkiller would suit you. For muscular pain from coughing, paracetamol, or an anti-inflammatory such as ibuprofen if it is safe for you (it is not suitable for everyone, for example people with stomach ulcers, some kidney problems or certain types of asthma), is often enough. Warmth on the area, gentle stretching and movement, and supporting your chest with a pillow or your arm when you cough can also help.

Since the cough has lasted a while and the pain is persistent, the sensible step is to have a doctor examine your chest and back to confirm it is muscular and not something like a lingering infection, and to discuss pain relief you feel comfortable with.

Paracetamol (P-125) should remain your main fever medicine, with Meftal-P kept only as an occasional backup rather than given routinely. Paracetamol is the safest first-choice fever reducer for young children. Meftal-P contains mefenamic acid, an anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) that works well but carries more risk of stomach irritation and kidney strain, especially if a child is not drinking well, is vomiting, or has diarrhoea. It is also best avoided where dengue is possible, because it can increase bleeding risk. Since dengue is common in many parts of India, this matters.

For your daughter at 10 kg, the usual paracetamol dose is 10 to 15 mg per kg, which works out to roughly 4 to 6 ml of P-125 (125 mg per 5 ml). This can be repeated every 6 hours if needed, and she should not get more than 4 doses in 24 hours. The 5 ml you gave was a correct dose. It is normal for paracetamol to take 30 to 60 minutes to work and to bring the temperature down by only a degree or two rather than all the way to normal. A single dose not "working" fully does not mean it has failed.

If the fever stays high (around 102°F or more) and she is uncomfortable despite a proper paracetamol dose, Meftal-P 5 ml (50 mg) can be used occasionally. Give it after some food, keep doses at least 6 to 8 hours apart, give no more than 3 doses a day, and use it only for a day or two unless a doctor advises otherwise. Do not combine or alternate the two medicines on your own schedule unless your paediatrician suggests it, because that increases the chance of dosing mistakes.

The goal of fever medicine is to keep her comfortable, not to keep the thermometer at normal. Plenty of fluids, light clothing, and lukewarm sponging also help. Because she is better now, you don't need to give anything unless the fever returns.

Please have her seen by a doctor if the fever lasts more than 2 to 3 days or keeps coming back. Seek care urgently if she becomes unusually drowsy or very irritable, refuses fluids, passes much less urine, vomits repeatedly, has difficulty breathing, develops a rash or any bleeding, or has a seizure. A check-up can also find the cause of the fever, which the medicines only mask.

The 2011 Major League Baseball All-Star Game took place at Chase Field in Phoenix, Arizona, the stadium of the Arizona Diamondbacks. Phoenix had never before hosted the All-Star Game, and the Diamondbacks served as the home team for the event. Played on July 12, 2011, the contest ended with a 5-1 victory for the National League.

Scientific modelling is the practice of building simplified representations of real-world systems, processes, or phenomena so that scientists can understand, describe, predict, and test them. A model captures the features of a system that matter most for a particular question while leaving out much of the detail, which makes the system easier to reason about and analyze. Models can take many forms, including mathematical equations, computer simulations, physical replicas, diagrams, and conceptual frameworks. A climate model that uses equations to represent the flow of energy through the atmosphere and oceans, a scale model of an aircraft wing tested in a wind tunnel, and the double helix diagram of DNA are all examples of scientific models.

The purpose of a model is to help researchers answer questions that would be difficult, expensive, dangerous, or impossible to address by observing the real system directly. Scientists use models to generate hypotheses, to test how a system would behave under conditions that have not yet been observed, to combine information from different sources, and to guide the design of experiments. Because a model is built from assumptions, its usefulness depends on how well those assumptions reflect reality. Good modelling involves stating these assumptions clearly, checking the model's predictions against empirical data, and revising the model when it fails to match observations.

A well-known saying in the field is that all models are wrong, but some are useful. This recognizes that no model captures reality completely. Its value lies in being accurate enough, for a specific purpose, to offer insight or reliable predictions. Scientific modelling is therefore an iterative process: a model is proposed, tested, refined, and sometimes replaced by a better one as new evidence emerges. It is used across disciplines, from physics and chemistry to ecology, epidemiology, economics, and the social sciences.

I'm sorry your wife is dealing with an eye infection. Pseudomonas can be a tough one to clear, so the most important thing is sticking with whatever plan her doctor gave her. Take the antibiotics exactly as prescribed and finish the whole course, even if her eye starts looking better after a few days. Stopping early is how infections come back.

Keep the area clean and follow any hygiene instructions she was given. Simple stuff helps a lot: wash your hands before and after touching her face or any drops, and don't share towels or pillowcases. Covering your mouth and nose when you sneeze or cough won't hurt either.

Rest and fluids can help her body fight it off, so encourage her to take it easy and drink plenty of water.

Don't skip follow-up appointments. The doctor needs to check that the infection is responding, and it's a good time to ask any questions that have come up. Also know that it can take a while to fully clear, even when treatment is working, so try to be patient. If things get worse or she has new symptoms like increasing pain, vision changes, or swelling, call the doctor right away instead of waiting for the next visit.

Liver inflammation is fairly common and can be triggered by a range of factors, including certain drugs, alcohol, viral infections, and some underlying health conditions. How hepatitis is treated, and how a person fares over time, hinges on what is causing it. When the trigger is short-lived, as with a viral infection or particular medications, the liver may recover by itself after the trigger is gone. When the inflammation stems from a long-term problem, such as heavy drinking or autoimmune hepatitis, continued treatment may be needed to keep the liver from suffering more harm. You should discuss your own circumstances and the exact source of your liver inflammation with a healthcare provider, who can suggest the right course of treatment. Meanwhile, steer clear of alcohol and any other substances that could injure the liver further, and support its health with a good lifestyle, which means a balanced diet and regular physical activity.

Discomfort or pain in the spot where the gallbladder once sat is quite common after a cholecystectomy. Doctors often call this "phantom pain," and it may stem from nerve fibers that were injured during the operation. Those damaged nerves can keep transmitting pain signals to the brain long after the gallbladder has been taken out. Still, your symptoms might have a source other than the gallbladder. The liver sits in the upper right portion of the abdomen, so pain in that region could point to a liver issue. Plenty of other conditions can also cause abdominal pain, such as digestive disorders, muscle strains, and kidney stones. If the pain worries you, it's important to consult a healthcare provider, who can evaluate your symptoms, make a proper diagnosis, and recommend treatment.

Yeah, a high PSA can point to cancer, but it doesn't prove it. PSA is a protein made by cells in the prostate, and the blood test just measures how much is floating around. Plenty of things can push that number up. Prostate cancer is one, sure, but so are an enlarged prostate (BPH), prostatitis (inflammation of the prostate), and even some meds. So a high reading doesn't mean you've got cancer. It just means you need to find out what's going on. That usually means more testing, and a prostate biopsy is the common next step. They take a small tissue sample and check it under a microscope for cancer cells. Definitely bring it up with your doctor, especially if you've got any symptoms. They can walk you through what your numbers mean for you specifically.

Totally normal for some boys to have higher voices than their friends. Nothing medical can change your natural pitch, and you don't need to force it lower just to fit what people expect. Everyone's voice is different, and there's no right or wrong way for one to sound. If it's bugging you, a speech therapist or doctor can listen to it and give you some tips on projecting or communicating in ways you feel good about. And honestly, what other people think of your voice says way more about them than about you.

The most reliable way to pin down when a SWIFT payment was actually sent is to get a copy of the payment message itself from the sending bank. For a standard customer transfer this has traditionally been an MT103, and increasingly, since the industry migration to ISO 20022, it is a pacs.008 message. You can ask the bank that sent the money, or ask the sender to request it from their bank, for the full message including its headers and not just a summary confirmation. Banks routinely provide this as "proof of payment."

In an MT103, the application header (block 2) contains the input time and date, meaning the moment the message was entered into the SWIFT network, expressed in the sender's local time. The receiving bank's copy shows an output date and time, the moment it was delivered to them. Field 32A shows the value date, currency, and amount. The value date is the date funds are meant to be settled, which is not necessarily the date the message was sent. In a pacs.008 message, the equivalent information appears in the group header as the creation date and time (CreDtTm), alongside settlement date fields, and these timestamps usually include a time zone offset, which makes them more precise.

Another very useful tool is the UETR, the Unique End-to-end Transaction Reference. It is a long code that every SWIFT gpi payment carries, which today covers the vast majority of cross-border payments. With the UETR, the sending or receiving bank can look the payment up in the SWIFT gpi Tracker, which records timestamps for each step: when the payment left the originating bank, when each intermediary or correspondent bank received and processed it, and when it was credited to the beneficiary's bank. This is often the clearest way to see exactly where a payment is and when each event happened. Some banks show this tracking directly in online banking. Others will look it up for you on request.

Keep a few caveats in mind. Timestamps can be in different time zones depending on which bank's copy you are reading, so check whether the time is local or UTC. The date a customer submitted the instruction, the date the bank released the message, the value date, and the date the beneficiary was credited can all differ, so be clear about which of these you actually need. If you need the information for a legal or contractual dispute, ask the bank for an officially stamped or signed confirmation of the message details. A screenshot or a simple transaction reference number may not be sufficient.

A letterbox movie is a film shown in its original widescreen aspect ratio, which is wider than the standard shape of a traditional television screen or older monitor. When such a film is displayed on a screen with a more squarish shape, black bars appear along the top and bottom of the picture so the full image fits without being cropped or stretched. The name comes from the resemblance to a mail slot, since the wide image sits in a narrow horizontal frame surrounded by black, much like a letter slipped through a box opening.

The practice dates back to the early days of television, when broadcasters wanted to preserve the director's intended composition rather than cutting off the sides of the image to fill a 4:3 screen. Today, letterboxing is common on widescreen televisions and computer monitors when watching films, and the term is also used for the black bars themselves. Many viewers prefer it because it shows the complete frame as the filmmaker framed it, even though the picture appears smaller on the screen.

Imagine your whole class shares one big box of crayons. Everyone wants the box to last, but some kids want to use lots of crayons right away to finish their pictures, and others want to save them for later. Grown-ups have different ideas about how to share the crayons, and that's where the arguing starts.

Here's the simple version. Taking care of the planet affects everybody, so lots of people do care about it. But fixing problems like pollution or a warming planet often costs money or changes how people earn a living, like for workers at factories, farms, or coal mines. Some people think the fixes should be big and fast, and others worry they'll be expensive or unfair. Different groups also trust different people to tell them what's true, so they may hear different stories about the same problem. When people feel that their jobs, their money, or their way of life is on the line, caring about the planet can get mixed up with picking a team, like picking a favorite sports club.

So yes, almost everyone likes clean air, clear rivers, and animals that stay safe. The fight is mostly about who should pay for protecting them and how quickly we should act. Those are questions people answer differently, and that's why politicians get involved: they're the ones who decide the rules everyone has to follow.

Imagine you're holding one end of a jump rope and your friend is spinning around on a merry-go-round... actually, a better picture is this: imagine you throw a ball at a moving bus. If the bus is rolling toward you and you bounce the ball off its front, the ball comes back faster than you threw it, because the bus is moving and helps push it away. The bus gets a tiny bit slower, but it's so big that you'd never notice.

A spacecraft doing a gravity boost works in a similar way, with Jupiter playing the part of the bus. Jupiter is enormous and it moves through space around the Sun. As the spacecraft flies toward Jupiter, Jupiter's gravity pulls it in and speeds it up, like a ball rolling down a hill. The spacecraft swings around the planet, passing behind it, and then gravity pulls it back the other way as it leaves. The tricky part is that the spacecraft is moving the opposite direction when it leaves than it was when it came in, because it went around the planet, so Jupiter's motion around the Sun gets added to the spacecraft's speed. The spacecraft ends up going faster than when it arrived.

Jupiter loses a minuscule amount of speed in the process, far too little to measure, because the spacecraft is so tiny compared to the giant planet. So the spacecraft gets a free speed boost without needing to burn any fuel. That's why missions like Voyager, Galileo, and Juno used this trick to reach far-off places faster and with less fuel.

Your partner should stop taking the cocodamol now and not take any more, because the rash, nausea, sweating and light-headedness that followed it may be a reaction to the codeine or the paracetamol in it. Please contact NHS 111 today, or his GP surgery, to report this. Tell them exactly what happened and when, and ask them to record it as a suspected drug reaction so he is not given codeine again without careful thought.

Call 999 straight away if he has any swelling of the face, lips, tongue or throat, wheezing, difficulty breathing or swallowing, a racing or pounding heartbeat, confusion, or if he faints or feels he might. While you wait for help, have him sit or lie down with his legs raised if he feels faint, and keep him from standing up quickly.

For the itch, a non-drowsy antihistamine such as cetirizine or loratadine from a pharmacy may help, but check with the pharmacist first, since they can confirm it is suitable given what he has taken. Cool, damp cloths, loose cotton clothing and avoiding hot showers can also ease the irritation. Try not to scratch, as this can worsen the rash.

Even if the symptoms settle, he should be assessed by a doctor soon, because a reaction like this needs checking and it is important to know which medicine caused it.

Think of a game service like a big toy train set that people play with all day. Sometimes you need to stop the trains to fix a broken track, add new cars, or swap in a better engine. Blizzard's games, like World of Warcraft, are very big and very old, and they have lots of pieces that change often. So they pick a quiet time, usually early in the week when fewer people are playing, and they stop the trains for a little while to do their fixing.

PlayStation and Xbox do this too. They just try to do it at times when hardly anyone is looking, or they fix things while the trains keep running, like changing a wheel while the train is still rolling. Their systems are built with lots of spare parts, so one piece can be swapped out without stopping everything. That's why you might not notice when they're working on things. They also have outages sometimes, when something breaks unexpectedly, and you may hear about those in the news.

Blizzard's games are also more likely to need a full stop because they update the actual game world, not just the storage shelves behind it. It's a bit like rearranging the furniture in a playhouse while kids are inside. It's easier to ask everyone to step out for a few minutes.

Nobody knows for sure who first had the idea, because it happened so long ago that no one wrote it down. The best guess is that it was an accident. People long ago cooked meat and animal fat over fires, and some of that fat dripped down onto the ashes below. Ashes from wood contain a substance called lye, which is strong and can mix with fat. When fat, ash, and water mix and heat up, they turn into a sticky, soapy material. Early people may have noticed that pots or hands covered in this mess came out cleaner than before, and then they started doing it on purpose.

The oldest clear evidence of soap making is from ancient Babylon, more than four thousand years ago, where clay tablets describe a mixture of fat and ashes being boiled together. The ancient Egyptians also made soap and used it for washing and for medicine, and the Romans later used it too, though some historians think they mostly used it for skin care and treatments rather than for washing their bodies.

So the simple answer for a five year old would be: people were cooking, a little fat and ash got mixed together by accident, and someone noticed it made things clean. After that, they tried it again and again until they learned how to make it well.

Hello Amit, I'm sorry you've been dealing with this for so long. What you're describing is most likely post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation (PIH), a common complication of laser hair removal, especially in medium to darker skin tones. The laser's heat can inflame the skin, and the pigment cells respond by producing excess melanin. The good news is that PIH is treatable, though it takes patience, particularly after two years, since the pigment may have settled partly into the deeper layer of the skin (the dermis), which fades more slowly than surface pigment.

The most important step is strict daily sun protection, because ultraviolet and even visible light keep darkening the patches and undo any treatment. Use a broad-spectrum sunscreen of SPF 30 to 50 every morning, even indoors or on cloudy days, and reapply if you're outdoors. Tinted sunscreens containing iron oxides are especially helpful for pigmentation because they also block visible light. Caps and shade help too.

For topical treatment, a dermatologist will often start with hydroquinone 2 to 4 percent, sometimes in a combination cream with tretinoin and a mild steroid (the "Kligman" or triple combination formula). This is effective but should be used only under medical supervision and usually for limited periods of a few months, because prolonged unsupervised use can cause a paradoxical darkening called ochronosis. Gentler alternatives that can be used longer include azelaic acid, kojic acid, niacinamide, vitamin C serums, arbutin, and topical tranexamic acid. Retinoids such as adapalene or tretinoin speed up skin turnover and help the pigment shed, but they can irritate at first, so begin a few nights a week with a moisturizer. In some stubborn cases, doctors also prescribe oral tranexamic acid, which requires a prescription and screening for clotting risk.

If creams alone don't give enough improvement after two to three months, in-clinic procedures can help. Superficial chemical peels with glycolic, lactic, or salicylic acid, or a mandelic acid peel, done in a series a few weeks apart, are commonly used for PIH. Low-fluence Q-switched Nd:YAG laser ("laser toning") or picosecond lasers can treat deeper pigment, but since a laser caused your problem in the first place, they must be done conservatively by an experienced dermatologist who understands your skin type. Aggressive settings can make pigmentation worse.

A few practical tips: avoid scrubbing, harsh soaps, and home remedies like lemon juice or bleaching creams bought over the counter, as irritation worsens PIH. Also avoid further hair-removal laser on those areas until the pigmentation has settled. If you shave, use a sharp blade and a soothing gel, since razor irritation can also darken the beard-line area.

I'd strongly recommend seeing a qualified dermatologist rather than a cosmetic chain. They can examine the area, possibly with a Wood's lamp or dermoscope, to judge how deep the pigment is and to rule out other conditions such as melasma or contact dermatitis. With consistent sunscreen use and the right treatment, most people see clear improvement over three to six months, though deeper pigment may take longer. Please don't lose hope; this is a manageable condition.

Inference rules are basically logical shortcuts that let you get from what you already know to something new. You see them all over logic and math, whether you're checking if an argument holds up or working through a problem. There are two main flavors. Deductive ones guarantee the conclusion if the starting info is true. Say you know all mammals are warm-blooded and you also know a certain animal is a mammal. You can't avoid concluding it's warm-blooded. That's modus ponens, a classic deductive rule. Inductive ones are different. They give you conclusions that are probably true, but not certain. If a coin lands heads ten times in a row, you'd start to suspect it's biased toward heads. You could be wrong, but it's a reasonable guess. Either way, these rules are how we move from the facts we have to new ones we can rely on.

I don't think a custodian can refuse a prior-year IRA or HSA deposit that's postmarked by April 15, but the rules are a bit messy, so take this with a grain of salt. The general deadline for prior-year IRA contributions is April 15, and after that you usually can't add money for that year. There are a few exceptions, though. If you got an extension on your tax return, that doesn't automatically extend the IRA deadline, which catches a lot of people off guard. Your custodian is generally required to take deposits made before the actual cutoff, so it's worth checking with them directly about how they handle timing.

Contribution limits also apply and they can change depending on your age and income. A tax pro or the IRS site can tell you the exact cap for your situation.

HSAs work a little differently. The deadline for prior-year HSA contributions is also generally April 15, and an extension on your return doesn't really change that. Limits depend on your age, income, and whether you have self-only or family coverage, so double-check those numbers before you send anything in. Again, a tax professional is the safest bet if you're unsure.

They make stuff for aerospace, defense, and government clients, and they're especially known for radar systems, missiles, and cyber tools. They've got customers all over the world, and a lot of their money goes into R&D to keep their products fresh.
