The gunman was James Earl Ray, a convicted criminal and white supremacist who had escaped from a Tennessee prison. King's death marked a turning point for the Civil Rights Movement and left a deep mark on both the United States and the wider world.

Electrical engineering is a branch of engineering concerned with creating, building, and keeping up electrical systems and the parts that make them up. Practitioners take on many kinds of assignments, such as generating and delivering power, building electrical machines, designing control systems, working on telecommunications, and developing electronic gadgets. Drawing on electrical science and mathematics, they build, test, and assess how well electrical and electronic systems and devices perform. Their work is common in fields like power production and distribution, the automotive and aerospace sectors, telecommunications, and manufacturing. Others find positions in research and development, advisory consulting, or teaching.

To design and examine electrical systems, these engineers rely on an assortment of instruments and technologies, including computer-aided design (CAD) programs, oscilloscopes, and other electronic test equipment. Typical responsibilities involve planning and testing electrical systems, diagnosing and resolving problems, preparing technical reports and specifications, and overseeing projects. They may additionally maintain and repair electrical installations and offer technical assistance to colleagues in other professions. As a wide discipline, electrical engineering encompasses specialties such as power engineering, control engineering, electronic engineering, and computer engineering. Certain engineers focus narrowly on an area like power transmission and distribution, whereas others handle a range of different projects.

You have a few possible routes for dealing with high-interest student loans. One is refinancing, which means taking out a new loan at a lower rate to pay off your existing ones; this can reduce the total interest you pay over time, and banks, credit unions, and online lenders all offer these products, so it pays to compare them. Another is consolidation, which merges several loans carrying different rates into one loan with a single rate that may be lower. This simplifies repayment and can sometimes reduce your monthly bill. Federal student loans also come with repayment plans that adjust your monthly payment to your income and household size, including income-driven plans and extended repayment options. If money is tight, you might be able to pause payments through deferment or forbearance. These pauses offer short-term relief, but interest may accumulate and raise the overall cost over the long run. Finally, certain federal loans qualify for forgiveness programs, which cancel part of the balance once you meet conditions such as working in a particular field or for a specific type of employer. Weigh these choices carefully against your own finances, and consider talking with a financial advisor or student loan counselor to decide which path makes the most sense.

In most cases, no, there isn't a deduction for wages you were owed but never received, at least in the United States. The reason is that most individuals are cash-basis taxpayers, meaning you only owe tax on income you actually receive. If your employer never paid you, that money was never part of your taxable income, so there's nothing to write off. The IRS treats it as income that never existed for tax purposes rather than as a loss. People often expect a bad debt deduction to apply, but the IRS doesn't allow it for unpaid wages or unpaid fees for services, because you have no "basis" in that money. You never paid tax on it or invested it.

What you should do is make sure you aren't taxed on money you didn't get. If your employer issues a W-2 (or a 1099 if you're a contractor) that includes the unpaid amount, ask them for a corrected form, such as a W-2c. If they won't fix it or have gone out of business, you can report only what you actually received and attach an explanation, or use Form 4852, the substitute for a W-2. If you already filed and paid tax on wages you never received, you can file an amended return with Form 1040-X to get that tax back. Also, if Social Security and Medicare taxes were withheld from a check that never reached you, or your employer withheld taxes but didn't send them to the IRS, contact the IRS, since you may still get credit for amounts withheld from your pay.

The more productive route is usually recovering the money itself. You can file a wage claim with your state's labor department or the U.S. Department of Labor's Wage and Hour Division, pursue it in small claims court, or, if the employer has gone bankrupt, file a claim in the bankruptcy case, where unpaid wages get some priority. If you do eventually collect, that money becomes taxable in the year you receive it.

If you're outside the U.S. or your situation is unusual, for example if you run a business that uses accrual accounting and already reported the income, the rules can differ, and a tax professional can tell you exactly how to handle it.

Okay so in the US Army, a specialist (SPC) sits above private first class and just below corporal. It's the fourth enlisted rank. One thing that trips people up is that specialists get lumped in with NCOs, but they don't carry the same responsibilities as sergeants and up. It's kind of its own thing.

Mostly a specialist is doing the actual work in their job field. That could mean running and maintaining equipment, handling admin stuff, or giving technical support, depending on what they do. They might also end up supervising and training newer soldiers, and they take part in unit training exercises like everybody else.

The expectation is that they know more and can be trusted with more than a PFC, so every now and then they get put in a leadership spot within their unit too.

Traditionally, bonds, particularly high-quality government bonds such as U.S. Treasuries, tend to rise in price when stocks crash. This happens because investors move money out of riskier assets like equities and into safer havens, which drives up demand for government debt. As prices climb, yields fall. This inverse relationship is one reason bonds have long been viewed as a diversifier that can cushion a portfolio during equity downturns.

The pattern is not guaranteed, though. Corporate bonds, especially lower-rated "high-yield" or junk bonds, often fall alongside stocks because they carry more default risk and investors sell them in a broad flight from risk. Bonds can also lose value during a crash if the crash is driven by inflation fears or if central banks are raising interest rates, since rising rates push existing bond prices down. The 2022 market, when both stocks and bonds fell sharply, is a notable example of this breakdown in the usual relationship.

Kay, I'm sorry you're dealing with this, and it's understandable to feel scared. Swelling that is getting worse, moving up your legs, and now showing up in other parts of your body is something your doctor needs to know about soon, ideally within the next day or two rather than at your next routine visit. The good news is that the causes can usually be identified with fairly simple tests, and many are very treatable.

Edema happens when fluid leaks out of the small blood vessels and collects in the tissues. Gravity pulls it to the feet and legs first, which is why they are usually the worst. When the swelling is in both legs and also seems to be spreading throughout the body, doctors think first about conditions that affect the whole system. The heart is one possibility: if it isn't pumping as strongly as it should, fluid backs up into the legs, and sometimes the lungs. The kidneys are another: if they aren't filtering properly or are leaking protein into the urine, the body holds onto salt and water. Liver problems can lower the protein levels in the blood that normally keep fluid inside the vessels. An underactive thyroid can cause puffiness throughout the body. Weakened leg veins, low protein from poor nutrition, and high salt intake can also contribute.

Medications are a very common and often overlooked cause. Certain blood pressure drugs such as amlodipine, anti-inflammatory pain relievers such as ibuprofen or naproxen, steroids, some diabetes medicines, hormones, and nerve pain medicines like gabapentin or pregabalin can all cause swelling. Xanax is not a typical cause, though fluid retention has occasionally been reported, so please tell your doctor about every medication and supplement you take, including over-the-counter ones. Stress itself doesn't usually cause this much swelling, but it can lead to changes in eating, sleep, and activity that make fluid retention worse, so it's worth mentioning.

Some symptoms mean you should go to an emergency room or call emergency services right away rather than waiting. These include shortness of breath, especially when lying flat or if you have to prop yourself up on pillows to sleep, chest pain or pressure, coughing up frothy or pink mucus, sudden weight gain of several pounds over a day or two, passing much less urine than usual, confusion, or one leg suddenly becoming much more swollen, red, warm, or painful than the other, which can signal a blood clot.

When you see your doctor, expect them to check your blood pressure, listen to your heart and lungs, and probably order blood tests for kidney function, liver function, protein levels, thyroid, and blood counts, along with a urine test to look for protein. They may also order a heart test such as an echocardiogram. It helps to weigh yourself each morning and jot down the numbers, note whether your urine looks foamy or has changed, and record when the swelling began and how it has progressed.

While you wait to be seen, you can ease some discomfort by elevating your legs above heart level when resting, cutting back on salty foods, and avoiding long periods of sitting or standing still. Please don't start taking water pills or stop any prescribed medication on your own without your doctor's guidance.

You're doing the right thing by paying attention to this. Make that call to your doctor's office, tell them clearly that the swelling is getting worse and spreading, and ask to be seen promptly. I hope you get answers and relief very soon.

So you opened a CD and then realized you need the money sooner than the term allows. Here's what you can do.

First, you could just wait it out. If you can, let the CD mature and take the money then. The catch is that CD terms usually run anywhere from a few months to several years, so this doesn't help much if you need cash now.

Second, you can often make an early withdrawal. Most banks allow it, but you'll pay a penalty, usually a percentage of the principal. How much depends on how long the term is and what the bank's rules say. Just know that an early withdrawal can eat into your returns.

Third, some banks and brokerages let you sell the CD to another investor before it matures. Heads up, though: you probably won't get the full face value, since the buyer wants a discount to make up for the interest they'd be earning.

Last, some banks let you "break" the CD. You close the account and get back the balance, minus any fees or penalties.

Before you pick one, read the terms of your CD closely and think through what each option will cost you. If you're unsure, call the bank or talk to a financial advisor. They can help you figure out the best move for your situation.

Nobody can say for certain what would follow if Catalonia backed independence on November 9th, since the Spanish government does not regard the referendum as legal. As a result, Madrid might refuse to acknowledge the outcome. Should Catalans vote in favor of independence, the Spanish authorities could attempt to stop Catalonia from becoming a separate country, which might spark conflict and perhaps even violence. Alternatively, the two governments might look for a peaceful way to settle the matter, for example by negotiating or by organizing a second vote that has legal recognition. It is worth keeping in mind that a country consists of many groups with differing beliefs and opinions, so reaching a solution acceptable to everyone is rarely simple.

A gasser is a type of hot rod or drag racing car from the 1930s through the 1960s, especially popular in the post-World War II era. The name comes from "gas," meaning gasoline, as opposed to the alcohol or nitromethane fuels used in some racing classes. Gassers were typically older American cars, often from the 1920s to 1940s, stripped of unnecessary weight such as bumpers, fenders, and sometimes doors, and fitted with large, powerful engines, frequently V8s with multiple carburetors or superchargers. Many had their front ends raised and rear ends lowered to improve weight transfer and traction on the drag strip. Gassers were known for their bold, exaggerated look, with a tall, nose-up stance and a rough, minimalist appearance. They became a significant part of drag racing culture and the broader hot rod scene, and they are still celebrated today at car shows and nostalgia drag events.

Masturbation by itself does not usually cause albumin (protein) or red blood cells in the urine, and it does not damage the kidneys. Your normal creatinine, urea, and cholesterol are reassuring, since they suggest your kidney filtering function is preserved. But a urine finding of 15 to 20 red blood cells per field along with protein "++" is abnormal, and it has lasted about five years, so it needs a proper medical workup rather than an assumption about its cause.

Blood in the urine (hematuria) and protein in the urine (proteinuria) can come from several sources. Common ones include urinary tract or prostate infection, kidney stones, inflammation of the kidney's filtering units, and bladder or urethral problems. Protein can also appear temporarily after exercise, fever, or standing for long periods, which is called orthostatic proteinuria and is common in young adults. Less commonly, a condition such as IgA nephropathy, a parasitic infection like schistosomiasis if you have traveled to certain regions, or a structural problem in the urinary tract can be responsible. Vigorous sexual activity can occasionally irritate the urethra and cause blood in the semen or urine for a short time, but that would not explain a persistent pattern for years.

Because this has continued for five years, I'd suggest seeing a doctor, ideally a nephrologist (kidney specialist) or urologist, who will likely want to:

- Repeat a urinalysis on several occasions, preferably a first-morning sample, and do a urine culture to rule out infection.
- Measure your urine protein-to-creatinine ratio or collect a 24-hour urine sample to quantify the protein.
- Check your blood pressure, since high blood pressure can affect the kidneys.
- Do an ultrasound of the kidneys, bladder, and prostate.
- Possibly perform further tests, such as a blood test for kidney antibodies, a specialized urine microscopy, or a cystoscopy if the blood in the urine persists, to look inside the bladder.

Please don't stop or change any habits out of worry, and don't delay the evaluation. Most causes of this pattern are treatable or monitorable, and getting a clear diagnosis is the best way to put your concern to rest.

Okay so here's the rough idea of how people solve a Rubik's Cube fast. You start by scanning the cube for any face that's already mostly sorted, like a white one. Then you work on the edge pieces (the two-colored ones), getting them lined up with the center colors on that face. Once those are in place, you move on to the corners (the three-colored pieces), matching them up with the centers and edges you've already set. At the end you just run a bunch of memorized algorithms, which are basically fixed sequences of moves, to shuffle the leftover pieces into the right spots.

There are lots of different methods for this. The Fridrich method is a popular one, and it's basically a long list of specific algorithms you run in a set order. CFOP is another big one. It stands for Cross, F2L (First 2 Layers), OLL (Orient Last Layer), and PLL (Permute Last Layer), so you can kind of see the steps in the name. Getting under 10 seconds takes serious skill, though. You need to know your algorithms cold and be able to pull them off quickly and cleanly. Honestly it takes a ton of practice, but that's part of the fun.

Using only exponential moving averages, you can judge how strong a resistance level is by looking at which EMA is acting as resistance, how price has behaved around it, and how the EMAs are arranged relative to one another. None of this is a guarantee, but together these clues give a reasonable read on whether a ceiling is likely to hold or break.

The first consideration is the length of the EMA that price is pressing against. Longer EMAs such as the 100 or 200 period tend to be stronger resistance than shorter ones like the 9 or 20, because they reflect a longer stretch of trading and are watched by more participants, especially institutions. Resistance on a higher timeframe, such as the 200 EMA on a weekly chart, generally carries more weight than the same EMA on an hourly chart. When several EMAs converge near the same price, for example the 50, 100, and 200 bunched together just above the current price, that cluster forms a confluence zone that is usually much harder to break than any single line.

The second factor is the slope of the EMA. A resistance EMA that is sloping downward signals that sellers have been in control and that the average is actively pushing down on price, which makes it stronger. A flat EMA suggests balance and weaker resistance, and an EMA that is beginning to curl upward suggests the resistance is losing force and may soon flip into support.

The third factor is the history of touches. Each time price rallies into an EMA and gets rejected, the level gains credibility, so an EMA that has turned price back three or four times is stronger than one tested only once. You should also watch how the rejections look. Sharp reversals with long upper wicks right at the EMA indicate firm resistance, while candles that repeatedly close slightly above the EMA before falling back, or that hug it for many bars, show that the level is being worn down. Rising lows beneath a repeatedly tested EMA are a particular warning that buyers are pressing and a breakout may be near.

The fourth factor is the ordering and spacing of the EMAs. In a bearish stack, where shorter EMAs sit below longer ones (for instance 20 below 50 below 200), the longer EMAs overhead act as layered resistance and the structure favors continued rejection. If the shorter EMAs start crossing above the longer ones, such as the 20 crossing the 50, the resistance above is weakening because momentum is shifting. You can also measure the distance between price and the EMA: when price is stretched far below a falling EMA, a rally into it often stalls, but when price has been consolidating just under a flattening EMA with the faster averages catching up, the resistance is more fragile.

A practical way to combine all this is to score the level informally. Resistance is strongest when it comes from a long period EMA on a higher timeframe, when multiple EMAs converge there, when the EMA slopes downward, when it has produced several clean rejections, and when the EMAs are in bearish order. Resistance is weakest when the EMA is short, flat or rising, has only been tested once or is being repeatedly closed above, and when faster EMAs are crossing above slower ones beneath it. Because EMAs are lagging indicators, it is wise to treat this assessment as one input and, if possible, confirm it with volume or price action before acting on it.

The Church-Turing thesis is a core idea spanning computer science, mathematics, and philosophy. It holds that whatever a person could work out by hand with pencil and paper, a machine can also work out, provided it receives the appropriate instructions. Put differently, the thesis claims that every computation achievable in principle can be carried out by a computer. Its name honors two pioneers of computer science, Alonzo Church and Alan Turing. Church, a logician and mathematician, introduced the notion of "effective calculability" for functions, and this notion became the foundation of the thesis. Turing, also a computer scientist and mathematician, is widely regarded as the father of modern computing. He conceived the "universal machine," a theoretical device capable of carrying out any computation that is possible in principle. The thesis has profoundly shaped computer science and remains a central principle in the discipline. It has also provoked extensive debate among philosophers and computer scientists, since it raises many compelling questions about the nature of computation and the boundaries of what can be computed.

An LED, which stands for light emitting diode, is a light source that operates in a different way from a traditional filament bulb. In a filament bulb, electric current runs through a fine wire known as a filament. That current heats the wire until it glows and gives off light. An LED has no such wire. Rather, it is built from two layers of semiconductor material. When current passes through these layers, the semiconductor emits light, a process called electroluminescence. LEDs have the advantage of being more energy efficient, since they need less electricity to generate the same amount of light. They also tend to outlast filament bulbs, because there is no filament that can burn out.

Candida is a kind of yeast that normally hangs out in small amounts in your body. Sometimes it overgrows, though, and that's when you get candidiasis. Where it shows up affects what you notice. You might get a rash, redness, or itching in the affected spot. With vaginal candidiasis, there's often a white, thick, clumpy discharge. If it's a urinary tract infection, peeing can hurt. Oral thrush can cause blisters in the mouth, and rectal candidiasis usually means itching. Plenty of people also feel wiped out, get achy muscles, or just feel cranky and irritable.

As for probiotics, they're generally considered safe for treating candidiasis. That said, if you have herpes, talk to your doctor before taking them or any other supplement. Some probiotics can interact with medications or make certain conditions worse. Honestly, it's always a good idea to check with a healthcare provider before starting something new.

ESPP is short for Employee Stock Purchase Plan. Moving from Europe to the United States while enrolled in an ESPP may change how your benefits are taxed. A few points are worth keeping in mind. In the US, ESPP benefits are usually taxed when the shares are bought, whether or not you sell them immediately or keep them. This is referred to as "qualifying disposition" tax treatment. Should you sell within two years of the grant date or one year of the purchase date, an "early disposition" tax may apply. It equals the gap between the stock's fair market value at purchase and the price you paid, multiplied by your ordinary income tax rate. Selling after holding the shares more than one year past the purchase date and more than two years past the grant date may qualify you for the more favorable long-term capital gains rate. If you live in a country that has a tax treaty with the United States, you might be able to claim certain treaty benefits, such as a lower tax rate on ESPP income or a full exemption from tax. Since the tax rules for ESPP benefits can be intricate and depend on your personal situation, speaking with a tax professional or financial advisor is advisable to understand how your benefits would be taxed after relocating from Europe to the United States.

Generally, no, not in a thorough or reliable way. Free consumer services like Google Finance and Yahoo Finance get their data from commercial vendors and exchange feeds, and what they display is mostly a cleaned-up summary rather than an audited record of every trade.

Here is how it tends to work in practice. Exchanges and consolidated tape processors do cancel or correct individual trades. When a trade is busted, either under the exchange's clearly erroneous execution rules or by mutual agreement, a cancellation message goes out on the feed. Professional data vendors process those messages and adjust their tick-level histories. The daily open, high, low, close and volume figures that retail sites show are then usually derived from the vendor's data, and those can be revised if the vendor corrects them. So a bust that occurs during the day often does get reflected, particularly if it affected the high or low or the close. But the quality varies, and the free sites do not usually announce or document corrections.

Where things get messier is with after-the-fact fixes. If a bad print slips through and is only discovered days later, or if the vendor's upstream correction never propagates to the downstream site, the error can sit in the historical data indefinitely. Users often notice odd highs or lows, or volume spikes, in Yahoo's history that don't match other sources. Intraday charts frequently keep spurious prints that the official end-of-day record excludes, because the charting feed may be built from unfiltered or lightly filtered ticks.

Adjustments are a separate matter. Splits and dividends are handled through adjusted prices, and those are generally applied, though not always correctly or promptly. Yahoo's "adjusted close" is a well-known example, and there have been periods of errors, missing splits, or inconsistent treatment of special dividends and spin-offs. Different sites can disagree about the same historical series for this reason.

If accuracy matters, for backtesting or research for example, the better route is a paid source such as CRSP, Bloomberg, Refinitiv, or Polygon-type vendors that document their correction policies, or the official exchange and SIP data. It is also wise to cross-check suspicious data points against a second source and to filter outliers yourself instead of assuming the free data has been scrubbed.

Mortgage interest rates are set through a combination of broad economic forces and lender-specific factors. At the most fundamental level, they are shaped by the cost of money in the financial system. Lenders need to raise funds, often by borrowing from depositors or by selling loans to investors, so the prices investors demand for holding long-term debt heavily influence what lenders charge borrowers.

A key benchmark is the yield on long-term government bonds, particularly the 10-year Treasury note in the United States. Mortgages are typically long-term loans, and investors who buy mortgage-backed securities compare them with safe government debt. When Treasury yields rise, mortgage rates tend to follow, and when they fall, mortgage rates usually decline as well. The spread between these two, reflecting the extra risk and the costs of servicing home loans, is also important.

Central bank policy plays a significant role too. When a central bank such as the Federal Reserve raises or lowers its short-term policy rate, or changes its large-scale bond purchases and sales, it influences overall borrowing costs and inflation expectations. Because lenders factor expected future inflation into long-term rates, a sustained rise in inflation generally pushes mortgage rates higher, while confidence that inflation will remain low tends to hold them down.

Economic conditions matter as well. Strong growth and tight labor markets often raise rates, while weakness or recession fears can lower them. Demand for mortgage-backed securities, the overall supply of credit, and market volatility all shift the picture.

Finally, individual borrowers receive different rates based on their own profiles. Credit score, down payment size, loan-to-value ratio, debt-to-income ratio, loan type and term, whether the rate is fixed or adjustable, and whether the property is a primary residence or an investment all affect the rate a particular person is offered. Lenders also add margins to cover their operating costs and profit, and these can vary considerably between institutions, which is why shopping around can produce meaningfully different offers.

I can't see today's market data, so I can't confirm what flows look like right now. But there are several structural reasons why bond mutual funds often don't see the massive, panicky redemptions people expect, even when rates are rising or the economy looks shaky.

First, much of the money in bond funds is sticky. A large share sits in retirement accounts, target-date funds, 401(k) plans, and institutional portfolios that rebalance on fixed schedules rather than reacting to headlines. Target-date funds and balanced funds often buy bonds automatically when stocks rise and bonds fall, because they need to restore their allocation targets. That mechanical rebalancing works against a selloff rather than feeding one.

Second, higher interest rates cut both ways for bond investors. When rates jump, existing bond prices fall, which hurts current holders. But the fund's yield also rises as it reinvests maturing bonds and coupons at the new, higher rates. Many investors see higher yields as a reason to stay or even add money, especially when short-term and intermediate bonds pay more than they have in years. The painful part, the price drop, often happens quickly, and by the time people notice, the forward-looking return has improved.

Third, investor behavior has shifted. Much of the money that once sat in actively managed bond mutual funds has moved into bond ETFs. When someone wants out, they can sell ETF shares on an exchange to another investor, and the fund itself doesn't have to dump bonds. Some outflows that would have shown up as mutual fund redemptions in the past now happen as ETF trading, which looks less dramatic.

Fourth, regulators and fund managers prepared for this scenario after 2008 and the March 2020 "dash for cash," when bond markets briefly seized up. Rules now require funds to keep a portion of assets in highly liquid holdings and to run formal liquidity risk programs. Some funds can use swing pricing or similar tools to pass trading costs to redeeming shareholders. The Federal Reserve has also shown it will step in to support credit markets in a crisis, which makes investors less inclined to run for the exits preemptively.

Finally, there's no single trigger forcing mass liquidation. Big bond fund selloffs usually need a sharp credit scare, a liquidity crunch, or a sudden shock that makes people fear defaults or frozen markets. Gradual rate changes or general economic worry tend to produce steady, moderate outflows or rotation between bond types, for example from long-duration funds into short-term or money market funds, rather than a wholesale exodus. That rotation can be substantial without looking like a crash.

If you're seeing headlines predicting a bond fund collapse and wondering why it hasn't happened, the short answer is that the investor base, the market structure, and the policy backstops have all changed in ways that dampen panic. That doesn't make bond funds risk-free, since duration and credit risk are real, but it does explain why outflows tend to be gradual rather than catastrophic.

Actually, there can be thunder and lightning during a snowstorm. It's just pretty rare, and people call it "thundersnow." But your question is a good one, because it's true that it happens much less often than in rainstorms.

Here's the simple version. Lightning happens when little bits of ice and water inside a big cloud bump and rub against each other, kind of like when you shuffle your socks on a carpet and then zap your sibling. All that rubbing builds up static electricity, and when there's enough of it, it jumps out as a spark. That spark is lightning, and the thunder is the loud noise the air makes when the spark zooms through it.

For that to happen, the cloud needs to be really tall and have lots of strong air going up and down inside it, so the ice and water bits can crash around a lot. Summer rainstorms are great at this. The ground is warm, the warm air rises fast, and it builds enormous, tall clouds, which are perfect for making sparks.

Snowstorms happen when it's cold near the ground. Cold air doesn't like to rise very much, so the clouds are usually flatter and calmer inside. Not much crashing around means not much static electricity, so usually no lightning. Snow clouds are more like a lazy blanket than a bubbling pot.

You're right that rain and snow are basically the same stuff, water, just in different forms. The difference isn't really the water, it's the kind of weather that makes it. Sometimes a snowstorm does get strong, rising air in part of the cloud, and then you can get a flash and a rumble. Thundersnow is also a bit harder to notice, because snow soaks up sound and the falling flakes make everything quiet, so the thunder doesn't carry as far.

So under FCC rules in the US, hams have to ID their station at the start and end of each communication, plus every 10 minutes while you're on the air. It doesn't matter what mode you're using either. Voice, digital, image, whatever, it all counts. The idea is that other hams and government agencies can tell who's transmitting, and that helps keep the whole amateur radio service running in an orderly way.

The ID thing isn't the only rule, of course. You've also got to stay inside the allowed frequency bands, follow good engineering and operating practices, and not cause interference for other people. Also, all of this is the US setup. Other countries have their own rules, so if you're somewhere else, look up what applies where you live before you key up.

Ghana scams and direct deposit scams are both ways crooks try to rip off people and businesses. Ghana scams, aka "419 scams," get their name from the section of the Nigerian criminal code that covers fraud. Usually the scammer pretends to be from Ghana or another West African country and reaches out by email or social media with a huge pile of money they need help moving out of the country. Sounds great, right? Then they ask you for personal or financial info, or for a few hundred bucks to cover "fees" or "expenses" for the transfer. The money doesn't exist, the person doesn't either, and you end up out whatever you sent them.

Direct deposit scams work differently. Someone poses as your employer, payroll department, or a government agency and asks you to switch where your paycheck goes to a different account. They might want your login details for your bank or payroll account so they can make the change themselves. Once they've got in, they redirect your deposit and your money is gone.

Be wary of unsolicited requests for personal or financial info, and of anyone promising big money out of nowhere, especially from people you don't know. If you think you've been hit by either scam, report it to the authorities and lock down your accounts and personal info as quickly as you can.

A search algorithm is a systematic procedure for finding a specific item, or a path to a goal, within a collection of data or a defined space. It works by examining candidates in some organized order, checking each one against the target or goal condition, and stopping when the desired result is found or when it is determined that no such result exists. Search algorithms are fundamental in computer science because so many problems reduce to finding something: a record in a database, a word in a document, a route on a map, or a winning move in a game.

Search algorithms are often grouped by the kind of structure they operate on. Some work on linear collections such as arrays or lists, where a simple linear search checks each element in turn, while binary search is much faster but requires the data to be sorted, since it repeatedly halves the range of possible locations. Others operate on graphs or trees, which represent networks of connected nodes. Common examples there include breadth-first search, which explores all neighbors at one level before moving deeper, and depth-first search, which follows one branch as far as possible before backtracking. When the goal is to find the cheapest path rather than just any path, algorithms such as Dijkstra's algorithm or A* are used, and they rely on the costs assigned to connections between nodes.

The efficiency of a search algorithm is usually described in terms of how the time or memory it needs grows with the size of the input, a measure known as computational complexity. A well-chosen algorithm can make the difference between a search that finishes instantly and one that would take an impractically long time. In artificial intelligence, search algorithms also cover problem solving more broadly, where a program explores possible sequences of actions or states to reach a goal, such as solving a puzzle or planning a sequence of moves in a game.

Jaywalking is when you cross a street in a place or at a time when you're not supposed to. Imagine the road is a big playground just for cars, and there are special doorways where people are allowed to walk across, like crosswalks (the painted stripes on the road) or corners with walk signals. If you dash across the middle of the street, or walk when the little light shows a red hand or a "don't walk" sign, that's jaywalking. The funny name comes from old American slang, where a "jay" meant someone silly or clueless from the countryside who didn't know how city streets worked.

It's against the rules in some places, like many parts of the United States, Singapore, and some other countries, mostly to keep people safe. Cars are big, heavy, and fast, and drivers expect people to cross only at certain spots. If someone pops out from between parked cars, the driver might not see them in time to stop. Having clear crossing places helps everyone know what to expect, a bit like how everyone in class takes turns so nobody bumps into each other. There's also a history part: about a hundred years ago, as cars became popular in America, car companies and city leaders pushed the idea that streets belonged to cars, and they helped make crossing anywhere you like seem wrong and then illegal. Other countries, like the United Kingdom, never made it a crime, and people there can cross wherever they judge it safe, though they're still expected to be careful.

Wandering around a new city, exploring and looking at things, is not jaywalking at all. Walking aimlessly on the sidewalk is perfectly fine, and you can stroll wherever you want. Jaywalking only happens at the moment you step into the road to cross it in the wrong spot or against the signal. So if you're exploring and want to get to the other side of the street, just look for a crosswalk or wait for the walking person light, and you're following the rules. Since rules differ from country to country, and some places like Singapore actually give fines for it, it's smart to watch how the locals cross and do the same, and to always look both ways no matter where you are.

Sure, here are a few tips for budgeting. Start by listing all your income sources and fixed expenses. Fixed expenses are the bills that stay the same month to month, like rent or a mortgage, car payments, and insurance premiums. Then figure out your variable expenses, the ones that bounce around, such as groceries, entertainment, and gas. Look for ways to cut back. You might skip some non-essential purchases, call your providers to negotiate lower rates on bills, or find cheaper options for things you actually need. A budgeting app or spreadsheet makes tracking everything a lot easier and can show you where your money is really going. Make a plan to pay off debt as fast as you can, and go after high-interest debt like credit cards first since it costs you the most. Don't forget to set aside money for the long haul too, whether that's retirement or an emergency fund. Finally, check your budget regularly and tweak it as needed. Your income and expenses change over time, so you've got to keep it current if you want it to keep working for you.

A programming language is a formal language made up of a defined set of instructions that can produce many different kinds of output. Developers use these languages to write programs that carry out particular algorithms. Once written, such programs can run on a computer or other devices to accomplish one task or a series of tasks. Numerous programming languages exist, and each one follows its own rules and syntax for constructing programs. Among the best-known are C, C++, Java, Python, and Ruby. Every language has particular strengths and suits certain kinds of work. Python, for instance, is frequently chosen for web development and data analysis, whereas C and C++ are commonly employed for systems programming and low-level work. A programmer creates a program by typing a sequence of instructions into a text file, following the language's syntax and rules. These instructions might be straightforward, such as displaying a message on the screen, or more intricate, such as arranging a list of numbers in order. After the instructions are complete, a compiler or interpreter converts them into machine code that a computer is able to execute. Programming languages play a vital role in modern computing, powering a broad spectrum of software and systems, from operating systems and mobile apps to websites and beyond.

Buying an ETF is pretty straightforward, but you'll need a brokerage account first. You can open one online through Fidelity, E-Trade, or TD Ameritrade, for example. Once you're set up, just search for the ETF you're interested in and place an order. Heads up, though: you might get hit with a commission on the trade, plus the ETF's annual expense ratio. And it's worth doing some digging on the fund before you pull the trigger, just to make sure it fits what you're trying to do with your money.

A sharp, intermittent pain at the back of the lower ribs after a hit could be a cracked or bruised rib, but several other injuries cause similar symptoms. Ribs in the lower back are more mobile than the front ribs, so pain often flares with sitting, twisting, reaching, or stretching because those movements pull on the rib and the muscles attached to it. A fracture is possible, especially if the pain is sharply localized to one spot and is tender when you press on that area. Bruised rib cartilage or a strained intercostal muscle (the muscles between the ribs) or the back muscles that attach near the lower ribs, such as the latissimus dorsi or the quadratus lumborum, can produce the same kind of sharp, movement-triggered pain. Sometimes the lower rib tip is irritated or the joints where the ribs meet the spine are sore after a blow.

Rib injuries usually improve gradually over four to six weeks, and the fact that your pain has been slowly easing is a reassuring sign. You can often manage it at home by taking over-the-counter pain relievers as directed, using a pillow to support your side when sitting or lying down, avoiding heavy lifting or vigorous twisting, and taking slow, deep breaths (or coughing with a pillow pressed against the area) to keep your lungs clear.

You should see a doctor promptly if you have trouble breathing, shortness of breath, a fever, coughing up blood, numbness or tingling, pain that is getting worse instead of better, visible deformity, or blood in your urine. Those signs can point to a more serious injury, such as a fracture affecting the lung or an injury to a kidney or other organ near the back. Even without those symptoms, if the pain persists beyond several weeks or significantly limits your daily activities, an exam and possibly an X-ray or other imaging can confirm what is going on and rule out complications.

A Master Limited Partnership is a business organized as a limited partnership whose ownership interests, called units rather than shares, trade on a public stock exchange just like ordinary stock. The structure combines the tax treatment of a private partnership with the liquidity of a publicly traded security. Under U.S. tax law, a publicly traded partnership can only keep this status if at least 90 percent of its income comes from "qualifying" sources, which mostly means activities involving natural resources and real estate. As a result, most MLPs operate in the energy sector, especially midstream businesses such as pipelines, storage terminals, and processing facilities, though some are involved in timber, fertilizer, or other areas.

The biggest difference from regular stock is taxation. A typical corporation pays corporate income tax on its profits, and shareholders pay tax again when they receive dividends or sell shares, which is often called double taxation. An MLP generally pays no entity-level federal income tax. Instead, its income, deductions, and credits pass through to the unitholders, who report their share on their own tax returns. Because MLPs usually have large depreciation deductions from their physical assets, much of the cash they distribute is treated as a return of capital rather than taxable income in the year received. That defers taxes, but it also lowers your cost basis in the units, so when you eventually sell, you may owe more tax, and part of the gain may be "recaptured" and taxed as ordinary income rather than at capital gains rates.

The paperwork is also different. Stockholders receive a simple Form 1099, while MLP unitholders receive a Schedule K-1, which tends to arrive later in tax season and can be more complicated to handle. Because the partnership may do business in many states, investors can technically have filing obligations in multiple states. Holding MLPs in tax-advantaged accounts like IRAs can create another wrinkle, since partnership income may count as unrelated business taxable income, which can trigger tax inside the account if it exceeds a threshold. For these reasons, many investors who want MLP exposure use ETFs, mutual funds, or exchange-traded notes that hold MLPs and issue a standard 1099, though these vehicles have their own tax drawbacks.

Ownership and governance differ as well. An MLP has a general partner, often a sponsoring company, that manages operations, and limited partners, the public unitholders, who provide capital but usually have very limited voting rights compared with corporate shareholders. Historically, many general partners held incentive distribution rights that gave them a growing share of cash flow as distributions rose, though many MLPs have since eliminated these arrangements or converted to corporations.

Finally, MLPs are designed to pay out most of their available cash to investors, so they are known for high yields, and their payouts are called distributions rather than dividends. That income appeal comes with exposure to energy markets, interest rate changes, and the need to keep raising capital to fund growth. In short, an MLP trades like a stock but behaves like a partnership for tax and governance purposes, which can offer attractive tax-deferred income but brings added complexity that ordinary stock ownership avoids.

I'm sorry you're going through this. Two years of trying without success is understandable cause for worry, but it's encouraging that your HSG was normal, since that means your fallopian tubes are open and your uterus looks normal in shape. That rules out one of the most common causes of difficulty conceiving.

To complete your own evaluation, the most useful next step is checking whether you are ovulating regularly. This is usually done with a progesterone blood test taken about seven days before your expected period (around day 21 of a 28-day cycle), or by tracking ovulation with urine kits or serial ultrasound scans of the ovaries. Your doctor will likely also order hormone tests early in your cycle, usually on day 2 or 3, including FSH, LH, and estradiol. An AMH test estimates your egg reserve. Prolactin and thyroid tests (TSH) are also important, because imbalances in either can quietly interfere with ovulation. A pelvic ultrasound can look for fibroids, ovarian cysts, or signs of polycystic ovary syndrome. If all these are normal and pregnancy still doesn't happen, a doctor may suggest a laparoscopy to look for endometriosis or pelvic adhesions, which an HSG can miss. Screening for infections such as chlamydia is also reasonable.

Your husband needs a full evaluation too, because a male factor contributes to roughly half of couples' fertility difficulties. The key test is a complete semen analysis, which measures sperm count, movement, and shape, along with the pus cells already found. Ideally it should be repeated after a few weeks, because results vary from sample to sample. A semen culture can identify whether bacteria are present and which antibiotic will work best. Depending on the findings, his doctor may also check his hormones (FSH, LH, and testosterone) or order a scrotal ultrasound to look for problems such as a varicocele, which is an enlarged vein around the testicle that can affect sperm quality.

Pus cells in semen, medically called leukocytospermia or pyospermia, are white blood cells. They signal inflammation somewhere in the male reproductive tract. Common causes include infection of the prostate (prostatitis), the epididymis (epididymitis), or the urethra, and sexually transmitted infections such as chlamydia, gonorrhea, or mycoplasma. Less infectious causes include a varicocele, smoking, heavy alcohol use, long periods without ejaculation, and sometimes no identifiable cause at all. Pus cells can harm fertility because they release substances that damage sperm and reduce their ability to move and fertilize an egg.

Whether this can be passed to you depends on the cause. If a sexually transmitted or bacterial infection is behind it, then yes, it can be transmitted during intercourse. If you are infected, it could affect your own reproductive organs over time even though your HSG is currently normal. For this reason, doctors often treat both partners at the same time when an infection is found. It is also wise to use condoms or avoid intercourse until treatment is finished. If the cause is not infectious, such as a varicocele or smoking, there is nothing to transmit.

As for a guarantee, honestly no doctor can promise pregnancy after any treatment, because conception depends on many factors in both partners. That said, the outlook is often good. When pus cells are caused by an infection that is properly treated with the right antibiotics, usually guided by the culture result, sperm quality frequently improves. A new sperm cell takes about two to three months to develop, so improvement is usually judged by repeating the semen analysis around three months after treatment. Healthy habits can help during this time: your husband should stop smoking, reduce alcohol, eat well, take antioxidants if his doctor recommends them, and avoid excessive heat around the testicles, such as hot baths or laptops on the lap.

If natural conception still doesn't happen after treatment, there are effective options, including ovulation-stimulating medication, intrauterine insemination (IUI), and IVF or ICSI. The best step now is to see a fertility specialist or gynecologist together, with your husband also seeing a urologist or andrologist. That way you can both be investigated fully and treated as a couple. Many couples in your situation do go on to conceive, so please stay hopeful.

The Atari 2600 came out in 1977 from Atari, Inc., and it was one of the first home consoles to play games off swappable cartridges. It was huge in the late '70s and early '80s, and plenty of people still have a soft spot for it. It started life as the Atari Video Computer System (Atari VCS), but got renamed the Atari 2600 in 1982. Under the hood, it runs on a MOS Technology 6507 processor and tops out at 128 bytes of RAM. The graphics chip is pretty basic, and it can only show a handful of colors. You hooked it up to your TV and it came with one joystick. Atari kept it simple and cheap to make, which helped it catch on with developers and turn into a household name. There are over 900 games for it, and a lot of them came from third-party companies. Some of the big ones are "Pac-Man," "Asteroids," "Space Invaders," "Missile Command," and "Pitfall!" People still know and play those today, and the 2600 left a real mark on the industry.

Honestly, I'd get a cyst on your eyebrow looked at by a doctor or other healthcare person. It's tough to tell what's causing it or how to treat it without someone actually checking it out.

What they do depends on the cause. It could be antibiotics, drainage, or in some cases surgery to take it out. If it's infected, or they think it might be, they'll probably put you on antibiotics to clear that up first. Once the infection's gone, or if there wasn't one to begin with, they might drain it. That's basically a tiny cut in the skin and then pressing out whatever's inside. Sometimes that isn't enough and the whole cyst has to be removed surgically.

Whatever you do, don't try to pop it or deal with it yourself. That can make things worse and cause more problems. So yeah, just go get it seen and let them sort out the right treatment.

A sonic boom is created when an object travels through the air faster than the speed of sound, which is roughly 343 meters per second (about 767 miles per hour) at sea level, though the exact value depends on air temperature. As any object moves through air, it pushes the air molecules aside and creates pressure waves that spread outward at the speed of sound, much like ripples spreading from a boat moving through water.

When the object is slower than sound, these pressure waves travel ahead of it and spread out harmlessly. As the object approaches the speed of sound, it begins to catch up with its own pressure waves, and they start to bunch together in front of it. Once the object exceeds the speed of sound, it outruns those waves entirely, and they merge into a single, intense shock wave. This shock wave forms a cone-shaped region trailing behind the object, often called a Mach cone, and it carries an abrupt jump in air pressure.

When that cone sweeps past a person on the ground, the sudden rise and fall in pressure is heard as a loud boom or crack. Aircraft usually produce two shock waves, one from the nose and one from the tail, so people on the ground often hear a double boom in quick succession. A common misconception is that the boom happens only at the moment an aircraft "breaks the sound barrier." In fact, the shock wave is produced continuously for as long as the object stays supersonic, so the boom is dragged along the ground beneath its flight path like a carpet, and each observer hears it when the cone passes over them.

Sonic booms are not limited to aircraft. The crack of a bullwhip is a small sonic boom made by the tip of the whip moving faster than sound, and bullets, re-entering spacecraft, and some meteors produce them as well. The loudness of a boom depends on factors such as the size and shape of the object, its altitude, its speed, and atmospheric conditions, which is why engineers working on modern supersonic aircraft try to shape them in ways that soften the shock wave into a quieter "thump."

Sorry, I can't open or read medical reports, so I'm not much help with the specifics here. Your best bet is to sit down with your mom's doctor or nurse and go through the report together. They can explain what the diagnosis actually means and what the treatment options look like. It also really matters that she sticks to whatever plan her care team sets up, since that's what gives her the best shot at good results. If anything in the report confuses you or worries you, write it down and ask them directly. No question is too small for that conversation.

Hitting for the cycle means a batter gets a single, a double, a triple, and a home run all in the same game. It's a pretty rare thing in baseball, and nobody can give you an exact count of how many times it's happened. Baseball Almanac has logged more than 300 cycles in MLB history, but that number is probably low. It only counts games that got properly recorded, so a few might have slipped through the cracks over the years. Either way, players and fans tend to treat it as a big deal when it happens.

Gerald Ford received the Republican nomination for Vice President at the party's national convention in Kansas City, Missouri, in August 1974. That same month, on August 9, he assumed the presidency of the United States after Richard Nixon stepped down.

A spiral fracture is an unstable break because the bone is twisted apart, so it can shorten, rotate, or shift even when it is casted. Five weeks is not unusual for a metacarpal to still look unhealed on X-ray, since many take six to eight weeks or longer to show solid bridging. Still, seeing only "small healing" at this point is a reason to get a closer look rather than simply wait.

I would go back to the doctor who treated you, or see a hand surgeon or orthopedic specialist soon. Ask them directly whether the fracture is healing on schedule, whether the bones have shifted or rotated, and whether the alignment is acceptable. Rotation matters a lot in the fingers, because even a small twist can cause the finger to cross over its neighbors when you make a fist. Ask them to check for that specifically.

Depending on what they find, options may include continued casting or a splint with repeat X-rays in a few weeks, or surgical fixation. For spiral metacarpal fractures that are unstable, misaligned, or slow to heal, surgeons often use pins (K-wires), an intramedullary screw, or a small plate and screws. Surgery is not always needed, but it is a common recommendation when there is displacement or rotation. If you are a smoker, have diabetes, or have poor bone health, mention that too, since those can slow healing.

In the meantime, avoid gripping, pushing, or using the hand for heavy tasks unless your doctor has cleared you. Seek care promptly if you develop increasing pain or swelling, numbness or tingling, a color change or coldness in the fingertip, or a finger that looks visibly bent or turned. Those signs need prompt attention.

A blood pressure reading of 200/121 mmHg is far from typical. Hypertension, the medical term for high blood pressure, begins at 140/90 mmHg or above, and a value of 200/121 is regarded as severely elevated and potentially hazardous. If your readings are this high, you should get medical help right away. Several factors can contribute to elevated blood pressure. Lifestyle habits such as eating a lot of salt, carrying excess weight or obesity, and being physically inactive all play a role. Underlying health problems, including kidney disease, sleep apnea, and hormone imbalances, can also be responsible. In addition, your current blood pressure medication may not be working well enough, or a new health condition may be driving the increase. Contact a healthcare provider as soon as possible so they can identify the cause and recommend suitable treatment. If high blood pressure is accompanied by chest pain, trouble breathing, or changes in your vision, go to the emergency room or call your doctor without delay.

Bill Gates helped found Microsoft, which stands as the largest maker of personal computer software in the world. Ranked among the most accomplished and influential business leaders globally, he has been a driving force behind the rise of the personal computer. Beyond his role at Microsoft, Gates is widely recognized for his charitable work through the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation, an organization dedicated to tackling challenges in global health and development. He has given billions of dollars to philanthropic causes, earning acclaim for both his technological achievements and his generosity.

Deep structure is a concept from generative linguistics, most closely associated with Noam Chomsky and his theory of transformational-generative grammar, developed in the 1950s and 1960s. It refers to the underlying, abstract representation of a sentence's grammatical and semantic organization, as opposed to its surface structure, which is the actual sequence of words and sounds we hear or read.

The central idea is that sentences that look quite different on the surface can share the same underlying meaning and relationships. For example, "The dog chased the cat" and "The cat was chased by the dog" differ in word order, auxiliary verbs, and the passive construction, yet they describe the same event with the same participants in the same roles. Chomsky's proposal was that both sentences originate from a common deep structure, which captures who is doing what to whom, and that transformational rules then convert this deep structure into the various surface forms. Similarly, an ambiguous sentence like "Flying planes can be dangerous" has two deep structures, which explains why it has two readings even though its surface form is identical.

Deep structure was meant to explain how speakers understand meaning and how they can recognize that different sentences are related. In the late 1960s and 1970s, the notion underwent significant revision. Work by Chomsky himself, through the Extended Standard Theory and later Government and Binding theory, along with critiques from linguists such as Ray Jackendoff and George Lakoff, led to the abandonment of deep structure as a separate level in mainstream syntax. Modern frameworks, including Minimalism, retain the idea that sentences have hidden levels of organization, but they describe them differently, often in terms of movement and traces rather than a distinct deep structure level.

J.B. Danquah was a Ghanaian politician and one of the founders of the United Gold Coast Convention, the UGCC, which was a big part of the push for independence in Ghana. He was born in 1909 in Bekwai, in the Ashanti Region, and went to Achimota College and then the University of London. He was a major name in Ghanaian politics back then and had a hand in the negotiations that eventually got Ghana its independence from British rule in 1957. He served as a member of parliament and held a few ministerial roles too, including Minister of Justice and Attorney General. He died in 1965.

A Turing machine is a very simple imaginary machine that people use to think about what it means to "compute" something. It was dreamed up by a mathematician named Alan Turing in 1936. It was never meant to be built; it is a thought experiment.

Imagine a really long strip of paper, so long it never runs out, divided into little boxes. Each box can hold one symbol, like a 0, a 1, or nothing at all. Next to the paper sits a little robot with a tiny window that lets it look at just one box at a time.

The robot has a small rulebook. Each rule says something like: "If you are feeling like state A and you see a 1, then write a 0, move one box to the right, and switch to feeling like state B." That is all the robot ever does. It looks at the box, checks the rulebook, writes a symbol, steps left or right, changes its mood, and repeats. Eventually it may reach a rule that says "stop," and whatever is written on the paper at that point is the answer.

It sounds too silly to be useful, but here is the surprising part: any problem that a computer can solve step by step, this little robot can solve too, given the right rulebook and enough time and paper. It might be painfully slow, but it can do it. That means your phone, your laptop, and the biggest supercomputers can't do anything, in terms of what is possible to compute at all, that this paper-strip robot can't.

Turing also used the idea to show that some questions can never be answered by any computer, no matter how clever. The most famous one is the halting problem: there is no general method that can look at any program and always correctly tell you whether it will eventually stop or run forever.

So in five-year-old terms: a Turing machine is a patient little robot that follows simple instructions on an endless strip of paper, and it turns out that this is enough to do everything a computer can do.
