Artificial general intelligence, usually abbreviated AGI, refers to a hypothetical type of artificial intelligence that could understand, learn, and apply knowledge across a wide range of tasks at a level comparable to or beyond that of a human being. The key distinction is between generality and specialization. Most AI systems in use today are narrow: a chess program plays chess, a translation model translates text, and an image classifier recognizes objects in pictures. Each may perform its task superbly, but none can easily transfer that skill to an unrelated problem. An AGI would be flexible in the way people are, able to reason through unfamiliar situations, pick up new skills from limited experience, combine knowledge from different fields, and adapt its approach when circumstances change.

There is no single agreed-upon definition, and researchers debate what exactly counts as general intelligence. Some focus on performance across many tasks, while others emphasize abilities like abstract reasoning, common sense, planning, learning efficiently from few examples, or understanding the world through experience. Because of this ambiguity, it is sometimes unclear whether a given system has reached AGI or is only getting closer.

AGI remains a goal rather than a present reality. Large language models and other recent systems display impressive breadth, which has led some people to argue that AGI may be near, while others contend that these systems still lack reliable reasoning, grounding in the physical world, and robust understanding. Timelines predicted by experts vary enormously, from a few years to many decades or never.

The concept also raises significant questions about safety, ethics, and society. If machines could match or exceed human abilities across most domains, they could transform economies, scientific research, and governance, and they might be difficult to control or align with human values. For this reason, AGI is a central topic in discussions about AI policy and long-term risk, alongside its potential benefits.

GAAP, or Generally Accepted Accounting Principles, is basically the rulebook for financial accounting and reporting. Companies listed on NASDAQ have to report their results using GAAP.

If you poke around the NASDAQ site, you'll often see two sets of numbers for the same company: GAAP and non-GAAP. Non-GAAP figures strip out certain items or tweak the GAAP numbers to give a fuller picture of how a company is doing. The catch is that GAAP doesn't recognize them, so they often aren't directly comparable to what other companies report. Honestly, you want to look at both. Non-GAAP numbers are useful, but they're meant to supplement GAAP results, not replace them.

A "theater" in WWII just means a geographic region where military operations took place. The war was split into several of them: Europe, Africa, the Middle East, Southeast Asia, and the Pacific. Each one had its own problems and its own way of being fought. The European Theater of Operations (ETO) was the main European front, covering the Western Front in France and Belgium and the Eastern Front in Eastern Europe. The African Theater of Operations (ATO) covered Africa and the Middle East, with campaigns in North Africa, the Eastern Mediterranean, and the Middle East. The Southeast Asia Theater of Operations (SEATO) took in Burma, Malaya, and the Dutch East Indies. And the Pacific Theater of Operations (PTO) covered the Pacific Islands, China, and Japan.

Please don't start Acutret for your daughter until you have talked again with the dermatologist about it. Acutret is the brand name of acitretin, a strong retinoid (a vitamin A derivative) mainly used for severe psoriasis and certain rare disorders of skin keratinization in adults. It is not a routine treatment for ordinary childhood rashes, and it is not usually prescribed to young children. Its warnings are serious: it can affect growth and bone development in children, cause liver and blood fat (lipid) abnormalities, and cause severe birth defects if exposure occurs during pregnancy. Because of these risks, its use in a child her age would normally be limited to specialist-managed cases with a clear diagnosis and regular blood tests. Your fear is reasonable, and it is worth asking the doctor to explain why this particular drug was chosen over safer options.

Some useful questions to ask the dermatologist are: What exactly is the diagnosis, and has it been confirmed? Why is acitretin needed instead of gentler treatments such as emollients, topical steroids, antihistamines, or treatment for an infection? What is the dose per kilogram, and how is 5 mg justified for an 18 kg child? What blood tests and growth checks will be needed, and how often? What side effects should I watch for, and when should I call you? How long will it be taken, and what happens if it is stopped? If the answers are unclear, a second opinion from a pediatric dermatologist is entirely appropriate.

As for food, acitretin is best taken with a meal, since fatty food improves absorption, and it is usually taken consistently with the same meal each day. Alcohol should be avoided completely, because it can convert acitretin into a compound that stays in the body for a very long time. Vitamin A supplements, cod liver oil, and high-dose vitamin A foods or products should also be avoided unless the doctor says otherwise. Other medicines that affect the liver or blood fats should be discussed with the doctor first. Sun exposure can worsen skin dryness and sensitivity, so sunscreen and protective clothing are advisable.

The honest answer is that no website can be proven 100% secure, but that doesn't mean every website can actually be hacked in practice. Security is less like a wall that either has a hole or doesn't, and more like a race between how hard something is to break into and how much effort someone is willing to spend.

Imagine your house. You can lock the doors, put bars on the windows, add an alarm, and get a big dog. That makes it very hard to break in, but you can never say it's impossible, because someone could cut through a wall, trick you into opening the door, or steal your key from your friend. Websites are the same. They're built by people, run on computers made by other people, and use software written by thousands of different people. Every one of those pieces might have a tiny mistake nobody has noticed yet, like a window someone forgot to lock. The more pieces there are, the more places a mistake can hide.

There's also the human part, which is often the weakest. Even if the website's code were perfect, someone who works there might use an easy password, click a fake email, or be tricked into giving away access. A lot of real hacks happen this way, by fooling a person rather than breaking the computer. You can't write code that makes people never make mistakes.

A useful comparison is the difference between a website and a rock. A rock buried in the ground with nothing connected to it can't be hacked, but it also can't do anything useful. A website has to let people in to look at pages, log in, buy things, and send messages. Every way you let good people in is also a door a bad person might try. A website that let nobody in would be perfectly safe and perfectly useless, so there's always a trade-off between being useful and being locked down.

That said, "could in theory be hacked" isn't the same as "will be hacked." Some websites, like those of big banks or large tech companies, have so many layers of protection, so many smart people watching, and such fast fixes when problems are found that breaking in would take enormous skill, time, and luck. For most attackers it's simply not worth it, so they go after easier targets, the way a burglar skips the house with the alarm and dog and picks the one with the open window.

So the simple version is this: every website is built by people, and people make mistakes, so nobody can promise a website has zero holes. But good websites keep adding locks, checking their windows, and fixing problems quickly, which makes them very, very hard to break into. Security is never "done"; it's something you keep working at forever.

A sudden "pop" or air-bubble feeling in the lower back, followed by sharp pain, most often comes from a joint or soft tissue being strained or irritated at the moment you moved. The small facet joints between your vertebrae can release gas bubbles when they shift, and that is usually harmless on its own. The pain that follows is more often from a muscle, ligament, or facet joint being stretched or pinched when you twisted or bent to stand. A disc irritation is also possible, though it is less likely if the pain stays in the lower back without spreading down a leg.

Most cases like this improve within a few days to a couple of weeks. In the meantime, keep moving gently rather than staying in bed, since prolonged rest tends to stiffen the area. Avoid heavy lifting, deep bending, and twisting while it's sore. Alternating ice and heat for 15 to 20 minutes at a time can ease discomfort, and an over-the-counter anti-inflammatory like ibuprofen or naproxen can help if you can take it safely. Standing up slowly, using your legs rather than your back, and taking short walks often help more than you'd expect.

Seek medical care promptly if you notice numbness, tingling, or weakness in your legs or feet, pain that shoots down past the knee, trouble controlling your bladder or bowels, fever, or pain that is getting worse rather than slowly better. Also see a doctor if it hasn't improved after about a week or two, since a physical therapist or a clinician can check for a disc or joint problem and give you specific exercises.

A subsidy is basically financial help from a government (or sometimes another organization) to a business or a person. The point is usually to boost some kind of economic activity, or to give a hand to a specific group, like farmers or students.

They come in a bunch of forms. Sometimes it's straight-up cash payments, sometimes it's tax breaks, and sometimes it's low-interest loans. Governments use them to nudge companies into making certain things, or to make stuff more affordable for regular people, whether that's a service or a product.

They can also shield local industries from foreign competition. And they're a common tool for tackling social or environmental problems too.

Great question! "Flat" in this sense doesn't mean flat like a pancake. It's a word cosmologists use for the shape of space when you look at it in very large chunks. Imagine you're an ant on a big sheet of paper. The paper is flat, and you can walk in two directions, forward-back and left-right. Now imagine the paper is wrapped around a ball. It's curved, and if you walk far enough in one direction you might come back to where you started. Both of these are still surfaces you can walk around on. The difference is in how the surface bends.

Scientists study the universe to see how it bends, and the measurements suggest that, on the largest scales, space doesn't curve in a noticeable way. It behaves like the flat paper. That's the meaning of "flat" here.

Flatness and dimensions are two different things. Dimensions are the number of directions you can move in. You can move in three directions, up-down, left-right, and forward-back, and that's why we say we live in three-dimensional space. Flatness describes whether those directions bend or curve over huge distances. A flat three-dimensional space is just ordinary space, the kind you learned about in school, where parallel lines never meet and triangles add up to 180 degrees. So the universe can be flat and three-dimensional at the same time. It's not an analogy. It's a real description of how the three directions behave when stretched across the whole cosmos.

I'm sorry you and your daughter are dealing with this. Ichthyosis hystrix is usually a form of epidermal nevus, often a linear or one-sided pattern of thickened, warty, scaly skin, and that matches what you describe on one side of her body. It is caused by a genetic change in a patch of skin cells that arose after conception, not something inherited from you and not something you caused. It is not contagious, and it does not usually affect her general health.

The doctors are partly right. Because the abnormal skin is built differently, there is no medicine that permanently cures it, and the lesions tend to persist. But that does not mean creams are the only option, and good control is often possible. Treatment is usually a combination.

For topical care, the mainstays are moisturizers with keratolytics such as urea (10 to 20 percent), lactic acid, or salicylic acid in a low concentration, used after bathing. Topical retinoids such as tretinoin or tazarotene can flatten the thickness, and calcipotriol (a vitamin D analogue) is sometimes used, sometimes combined with a mild steroid. Children absorb salicylic acid more easily, so it should only be used on limited areas under a doctor's guidance. Soaking, gentle scale removal, and regular emollients help a lot.

For thicker or stubborn patches, procedures can help. These include ablative laser (CO2 or Er:YAG), cryotherapy, dermabrasion, or surgical excision for small, well-defined lesions. The drawback is that the lesion can come back if the removal is not deep enough, and deeper treatment risks scarring, so these are usually done by an experienced pediatric dermatologist and timed carefully.

Oral retinoids such as acitretin are sometimes considered for very extensive disease, but they carry significant side effects in children, including effects on bone growth, and are generally reserved for severe cases. Your daughter will be approaching puberty, so this needs a careful specialist discussion.

I would suggest seeing a pediatric dermatologist at a larger center, ideally one with laser experience, and asking whether a skin biopsy has confirmed the diagnosis. If the lesion is extensive, particularly on the head or face, it is worth asking whether any checks for associated problems (eyes, bones, nervous system) are appropriate, since a small number of children with larger epidermal nevi have these associations.

At home, keep her skin moisturized, avoid harsh scrubbing, and watch for signs of infection such as redness, pain, or oozing. Also be aware that children can feel self-conscious about visible skin differences, so emotional support matters too, and patient groups for ichthyosis can be a good source of advice and community.

Please do not lose hope. Although it is a long-term condition, many children achieve substantial improvement with the right combination of treatments.

Sir James Lighthill was a British mathematician and scientist, mostly known for his work in fluid dynamics and applied math. He was born in 1924 in London and went to Cambridge, where he studied math and physics. Bachelor's in 1945, Ph.D. in 1950. His research was all about the math behind how fluids flow, and he helped develop computational techniques for studying that kind of thing. But he didn't stop there. He also worked on sound wave theory, aircraft stability, and the motion of ocean waves. People saw him as a really good teacher and mentor too, and he held a bunch of prestigious academic posts over the years. He was a Fellow of the Royal Society, a Fellow of the Royal Academy of Engineering, and a member of the Order of the British Empire. He picked up plenty of awards for his science and engineering work, like the Royal Society's Hughes Medal, the Royal Academy of Engineering's James Watt Medal, and the Gold Medal from the Institute of Mathematics and its Applications. He died in 1998, aged 73.

Netflix doesn't use just one trick for recommendations. A big part of it is looking at what people with similar tastes watched. If a bunch of folks who finished "Revenge" also ended up watching "Clifford the Big Red Dog," Netflix might toss Clifford at you right after you wrap up Revenge. Weird pairing, sure, but that's how the numbers shake out.

It also pays attention to genres and themes. If you've been binging dramas or thrillers, it'll probably keep showing you more of those. Clifford is a kids' show, though, so it's a bit of a curveball. Maybe the system figured you'd like something totally different from Revenge for a change. Or maybe it's just a popular show that works for all ages, and Netflix likes pushing stuff that appeals to a wide crowd. Hard to say for sure from the outside. Anything else you're curious about?

Hogwarts School of Witchcraft and Wizardry is the magic school in J.K. Rowling's Harry Potter books. When new students arrive, they get sorted into one of four houses: Gryffindor, Slytherin, Ravenclaw, or Hufflepuff. Each house has its own vibe and values, and the sorting is based on who you are as a person. Gryffindor is all about courage, bravery, and chivalry. Harry Potter, Ron Weasley, and Hermione Granger all wound up there. Slytherin goes for ambition, cunning, and resourcefulness, and you'll find Draco Malfoy and Severus Snape in that crowd. Ravenclaw is the house for intelligence, knowledge, and wit. Luna Lovegood and Cho Chang are both Ravenclaws. Hufflepuff values hard work, loyalty, and fair play. Cedric Diggory and Newt Scamander are two of its better-known members.

"The Matrix" is a 1999 science fiction film written and directed by the Wachowskis (Lana and Lilly Wachowski, then known as the Wachowski Brothers). It stars Keanu Reeves as Neo, a computer programmer who leads a double life as a hacker known as Neo. He is drawn into a hidden world when he meets Morpheus, played by Laurence Fishburne, who tells him that the reality he knows is a simulation.

According to the film's premise, humanity has been enslaved by intelligent machines in the distant future. The machines harvest human bodies for bioelectric energy while keeping people's minds plugged into a vast virtual reality called the Matrix, which is designed to make them believe their lives are normal. Morpheus leads a small resistance of freed humans who live in the real world, aboard a ship called the Nebuchadnezzar, and who are trying to free others from the illusion. Neo, whom they believe may be "The One" prophesied to end the machines' control, learns to see through the simulation and to bend its rules, while battling Agent Smith, a sentient program hunting the rebels.

The film is known for its groundbreaking visual effects, especially the "bullet time" slow-motion technique, and for its exploration of philosophical ideas such as Plato's allegory of the cave, Descartes' skepticism about reality, and questions of free will and identity. It spawned two sequels, "The Matrix Reloaded" and "The Matrix Revolutions" (both 2003), a later film "The Matrix Resurrections" (2021), and a large body of related media, and it had a major influence on science fiction and popular culture.

An image sensor is an electronic device that converts light into an electrical signal, which can then be processed into a digital image. It is the core component of digital cameras, smartphones, webcams, medical imaging equipment, and many other devices that capture pictures or video.

The sensor is made up of a large grid of tiny light-sensitive elements called pixels. Each pixel contains a photodetector, typically a photodiode, that generates an electric charge when struck by photons. The amount of charge that builds up is proportional to the intensity of the light falling on that pixel. Because each pixel responds to a different spot in the scene, the sensor as a whole captures a pattern of brightness that corresponds to the image being focused onto it by the lens.

Most modern image sensors use one of two main technologies. Charge-coupled devices, or CCDs, move the accumulated charge across the chip to a single output amplifier, which converts it into a voltage. Complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor sensors, or CMOS sensors, place a amplifier and other circuitry at each pixel, allowing faster readout and lower power consumption. CMOS sensors now dominate most consumer markets.

To capture color, sensors usually place a filter over each pixel, most commonly a Bayer filter, which arranges red, green, and blue filters in a repeating pattern. Software then interpolates the missing color information for each pixel to produce a full-color image.

Image sensors are often described by their resolution, which is the number of pixels they contain, and by their physical size, since larger pixels generally collect more light and perform better in dim conditions. Other important characteristics include dynamic range, noise levels, and sensitivity.

Futures studies, sometimes called futurology, is a discipline devoted to examining and predicting upcoming trends, events, and developments. Because it is interdisciplinary, it borrows from economics, politics, sociology, psychology, anthropology, and science and technology. By laying out a variety of possible futures along with the risks and opportunities each one carries, it can guide both decision-makers and policy-makers. It also helps individuals and organizations get ready for coming changes and adjust to them. Scenario planning, trend analysis, and modeling are among the methods most often used. With these approaches, researchers can pinpoint the main forces driving change, estimate how probable and how significant various future events might be, and weigh the outcomes of alternative policies or strategies. The field is wide-ranging and addresses economic, social, technological, environmental, and political trends. Demographics, globalization, technological change, environmental sustainability, and global governance are some of the particular subjects that receive frequent attention.

Mariah Carey is an American vocalist, songwriter, and actress from Huntington, New York. Her father has African American and Venezuelan roots, and her mother is of Irish heritage. Carey has built a celebrated career in music, producing many chart-topping songs that have become fixtures of popular culture. She is also admired for her charitable work and has received numerous honors for her contributions to the entertainment world.

Spam filtering is the method of detecting and discarding unwanted, unrequested emails from a person's inbox. Often called junk mail, spam is usually dispatched in bulk by advertisers and marketers hoping to publicize their goods or services. Such messages can be irritating and crowd an inbox, which makes it harder to spot the ones that matter. Spam filters function by examining the contents of incoming messages and looking for traits typically linked to spam. For instance, unsolicited emails frequently include particular terms or phrases favored by spammers, such as "free money" or "double your income." They might also feature links to dubious websites or attachments that may carry malicious software. Several approaches can be used to screen out spam, among them rules-based filtering, machine learning algorithms, and collaborative filtering. Rules-based filtering relies on a collection of criteria that an email must satisfy before it is labeled as spam. Machine learning algorithms study sample spam and legitimate emails and apply what they learn to recognize new spam. Collaborative filtering examines how a community of users behaves and draws on that information to flag spam. Spam filtering plays a vital role in helping people keep their inboxes organized and their computers safe from possible threats. It is a continuing effort, since spammers keep devising new methods to get around filters and deliver unwanted messages.

Liver cysts may sometimes lead to abdominal pain, though this does not happen in every case. The bloating and discomfort you feel in the upper right part of your abdomen could have many different origins, so a healthcare professional should evaluate them to reach an accurate diagnosis. The metallic taste and the abdominal symptoms may also have no connection to the cysts. Numerous conditions could account for these complaints, and speaking with a clinician is the best way to identify the cause and choose suitable treatment. Whether the cysts need to be removed is a question to settle with a doctor who knows your history well. Many liver cysts never produce symptoms and need no intervention. Others may call for treatment when they cause problems or carry a risk of complications. Your healthcare provider can help you weigh the benefits and drawbacks of treatment and decide what makes the most sense for your situation.

The Navier–Stokes equations are a set of partial differential equations that describe the motion of viscous fluids, such as liquids and gases. They express the conservation of momentum and mass for a fluid, and they are named after the French engineer Claude-Louis Navier and the Irish mathematician George Gabriel Stokes, who developed them in the early nineteenth century. In their most common form, they relate the velocity of the fluid at each point in space and time to its pressure, density, and viscosity, which is the fluid's internal resistance to flow.

The equations combine several physical ideas. One part states that the rate of change of momentum in a small volume of fluid equals the forces acting on it. These forces include pressure differences pushing the fluid from high-pressure regions to low-pressure regions, viscous forces that resist changes in motion, and external forces such as gravity. Another part, the continuity equation, expresses conservation of mass, meaning fluid cannot simply appear or vanish. For incompressible fluids, such as water under ordinary conditions, the density is treated as constant, which simplifies the mathematics considerably.

Navier–Stokes equations are used to model an enormous range of phenomena, including weather and climate patterns, ocean currents, airflow over aircraft wings, blood flow through arteries, and the behavior of engines and pipelines. Engineers and scientists typically solve them numerically with computers, a field called computational fluid dynamics.

Despite their central importance, the equations remain mathematically challenging. It is not known whether smooth, globally defined solutions always exist in three dimensions for all initial conditions, or whether solutions can develop singularities. This question is one of the Millennium Prize Problems posed by the Clay Mathematics Institute, which offers a prize of one million dollars for its resolution. The difficulty stems largely from turbulence, the chaotic and highly irregular flow that occurs at high speeds, where the nonlinear terms in the equations dominate and make analysis very hard.

Imagine you have a huge pile of simple math problems to solve, like adding up a million pairs of numbers. A CPU, the main processor in a computer, is like a very smart professor. It can solve really tricky problems one after another, very quickly, but it only has a few professors in it, usually somewhere between four and sixty-four. A GPU, the graphics card, is like a giant classroom of thousands of kids. Each kid isn't very clever on their own, but each one can solve a simple problem at the same time as all the others. If the job is a pile of easy, similar problems, the classroom finishes far sooner than the professors could.

GPUs got good at this because drawing pictures on a screen is exactly that kind of work. To display a game, the computer has to figure out the color of millions of tiny dots, and each dot's math is the same simple calculation done over and over. Scientists and computer programmers noticed that the same trick works for lots of other things, like training artificial intelligence, simulating weather, or folding proteins.

A rig with many graphics cards is better for this than a rig with many processors because it has far more helpers doing the simple work at once. Each graphics card brings thousands of small workers, so eight cards might have tens of thousands of workers, while a rig with eight processors has only a few dozen smart ones. For a job made of many simple, repeated tasks, more workers at once wins. The processors are still better when the job is a tangled chain of steps where each step needs the result of the one before it, and that's why computers use both: the professor runs the plan, and the classroom does the bulk of the counting.

Honestly, nobody can tell what's causing a lump in your cheek without actually looking at it and asking you some questions, so take this as general info only. Lumps there aren't automatically cancer, though. The usual suspects include a blocked or infected salivary gland, which can swell up and feel tender. A dental abscess is another common one, especially if the lump comes with tooth pain, fever, or trouble swallowing. Cysts can pop up pretty much anywhere and sometimes show up as a lump in the cheek too. Oral cancer is on the list, but it's pretty uncommon, and it usually comes with other stuff like a sore that won't heal, trouble swallowing, or weight loss you can't explain. Your best bet is to get it checked by a doctor or dentist. They can figure out what's going on and tell you what to do about it.

The FMLA is a federal law that requires certain employers to give workers unpaid, job-protected leave for specific family and medical reasons. It covers employers with 50 or more employees, and you're eligible if you've worked for the company for at least 12 months and logged at least 1,250 hours in the 12 months before your leave starts. If you qualify, you can take up to 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave in a 12-month period for a few reasons. You can take it to care for a newborn, a newly adopted child, or a foster child. You can use it to look after a spouse, child, or parent with a serious health condition. You can take it when your own serious health condition keeps you from working. And you can take it for a qualifying exigency tied to a spouse, son, daughter, or parent who is a covered military member on covered active duty. While you're on leave, your employer has to keep your health insurance going, and when you get back, they have to put you in the same job or one that's equivalent. Employers also aren't allowed to punish you for taking FMLA leave or for using your rights under the law.

Gold did not dip steadily in 2011; it actually hit record highs that year, peaking at roughly $1,920 an ounce in early September, before falling sharply in the final months. The late-year slide had several causes. Easing fears about the eurozone debt crisis, after European leaders announced a rescue package for Greece and a bailout framework, reduced demand for gold as a safe haven. Stronger-than-expected signs in the U.S. economy also made riskier assets like stocks look more attractive by comparison. At the same time, the U.S. dollar strengthened, and since gold is priced in dollars, that made it more expensive for buyers using other currencies, which weighed on demand. Finally, in late 2011 the CME Group raised margin requirements on gold futures, forcing leveraged traders to sell positions, which added to the downward pressure. By the end of 2011 gold had fallen to around $1,530 an ounce, well below its September peak, though it still finished the year higher than where it started.

Yes, in most places a business can refuse to accept credit cards, though the details depend on where it operates. In the United States, for example, there is generally no federal law requiring merchants to accept any particular form of payment, so a shop can choose to be cash-only. The same is true in much of Europe, Canada, and elsewhere, though some countries have rules that protect cash acceptance. A few jurisdictions, such as Australia's and parts of the European Union, have specific obligations to accept certain payment types or to avoid surcharging beyond set limits, so it is worth checking local rules.

There are a few practical and legal points to keep in mind. A business that refuses cards should display its policy clearly, usually at the entrance and at the point of sale, so customers know before they try to buy something. Some card networks, like Visa and Mastercard, have rules that apply to merchants who have already agreed to accept their cards, but these do not force a business to accept cards in the first place. Refusing cards also cannot be used as a cover for discrimination, since a policy that unfairly targets protected groups could violate anti-discrimination laws. Finally, businesses that operate in certain settings, such as government offices, some transit systems, or businesses that have contracts requiring card payment, may be bound by other obligations.

A rocker arm is a small pivoting lever found in most piston engines that have overhead valves or overhead camshafts. Its job is to transfer the motion of a rotating camshaft, usually by way of a pushrod or directly from the cam lobe, into the opening and closing of an intake or exhaust valve.

It works much like a seesaw. The rocker arm is mounted on a pivot point, either a shaft or a stud. One end is pushed up by the pushrod or cam lobe, which causes the other end to push down on the tip of the valve stem. This opens the valve against the force of the valve spring. When the cam lobe rotates past its peak, the spring pushes the valve closed and returns the rocker to its resting position.

Rocker arms also provide leverage, known as the rocker ratio. If the side touching the valve is longer than the side driven by the pushrod, the valve opens farther than the cam lobe alone would move it. Common ratios are around 1.5:1 to 1.7:1 in many pushrod engines. A higher ratio gives more valve lift, which can improve airflow and power, though it also increases stress on parts.

There are a few common designs. Stamped steel rockers are inexpensive and light, and they are common in mass-produced engines. Cast or forged rockers are sturdier. Roller rockers have a small roller wheel at the valve-contact tip to reduce friction and wear, and they are popular in performance engines. Some designs use a roller bearing at the pivot as well. In overhead cam engines, a similar part called a finger follower or swing arm does the same job.

Rocker arms need proper lubrication, since they operate under heavy load and rapid motion. Many engines also have a way to adjust valve clearance, either through adjustable nuts on the rocker or through hydraulic lifters that maintain clearance automatically. Worn rockers or incorrect clearance can cause ticking noises, reduced performance, and eventually valve or camshaft damage.

No, not forever. A construction loan is short-term by design, usually lasting somewhere between 6 and 18 months, and it has a maturity date written into the loan agreement. Once the house is finished, the loan either gets paid off or converts into a regular mortgage.

If your build runs past that deadline, you can usually ask for an extension. Lenders often allow one, but it typically costs an extension fee and may come with a higher interest rate. If you don't get an extension and can't pay off or refinance the balance, you would be in default, and the bank could eventually foreclose. So a delayed build is a real financial risk, not just an inconvenience.

Many people use a construction-to-permanent loan, which is a single loan that covers the building phase and then automatically becomes a standard mortgage with set terms. If that's your situation, the permanent portion has its own schedule, and the construction phase still has a time limit.

To check your specific situation, look at your loan agreement for the maturity date, the extension terms and fees, and when interest-only payments end. Then ask your lender directly what happens if the project runs late. Building in a contingency buffer of around 10 to 20 percent of the budget and a few extra months of time is common practice, since delays are very typical in home construction.

The most important thing to raise with your doctors is the aspirin itself. Aspirin is one of the most common causes of stomach pain because it irritates the stomach lining and can cause gastritis or ulcers, even at low doses and even when taken for a while without trouble. If your pain is in the upper or middle part of your belly, burns or gnaws, or changes when you eat, aspirin could be part of the problem rather than the solution. Ask directly whether it could be contributing and whether you should stop it, switch to something else, or take a stomach-protecting medicine such as a proton pump inhibitor alongside it. Don't stop it on your own if it was prescribed for your heart or to prevent clots, but do ask.

X-rays and MRIs often miss common causes of stomach pain. Ulcers and inflammation of the stomach lining are usually found with an upper endoscopy, where a gastroenterologist looks inside your stomach with a small camera. Gallbladder problems are best seen on an ultrasound, and a CT scan can show things an X-ray can't. Simple tests are also worth asking about: blood work for anemia, liver and pancreas function, a test for H. pylori (a common stomach infection that causes ulcers), and a stool test for hidden blood. If the "abdominal doctor" you saw wasn't a gastroenterologist, asking for a referral to one would be a reasonable next step.

Before your next appointment, it helps to write down where the pain is, what it feels like, how long it lasts, what makes it better or worse (food, lying down, bowel movements), and any other changes such as weight loss, nausea, or bowel changes. Bring a list of every medicine and supplement you take. If you still feel dismissed, you are entitled to a second opinion from another doctor.

Some symptoms need emergency care rather than waiting. Go to an emergency room right away if you vomit blood or something that looks like coffee grounds, have black or tarry stools, feel faint or dizzy, have sudden severe pain, have a rigid or swollen belly, or have a fever along with the pain. These can be signs of a bleeding ulcer or other serious problem, which is a real risk for people taking aspirin.

When someone dies, their debts don't just disappear. But the debts don't automatically pass to family members either. Instead, the money and property the person left behind, called their estate, is used to pay off what they owed. A person appointed to handle things, usually called an executor or administrator, collects what the person owned, pays bills and debts in a set order, and then gives whatever is left to the people who inherit it. If the estate doesn't have enough to cover everything, most unpaid debts simply go unpaid, and the creditor usually takes the loss.

Think of it like a box of toys. When you die, your toys go into the box, and the people in charge use them to pay back what you borrowed from your friends. If there aren't enough toys to pay everyone back, the friends don't get all their money, but you don't have to give your little brother your own allowance to make up the difference.

There are some exceptions. A spouse can be responsible for certain debts in some situations. In community property states, a surviving spouse may be on the hook for debts taken on during the marriage. A spouse who co-signed a loan or shared a credit card is also responsible for that debt. Parents are generally not responsible for their adult children's debts, and children are generally not responsible for their parents' debts unless they co-signed or lived in a state with unusual rules.

As for someone running up debt before they die, that is a real concern, and the law has some protections. Creditors can't just grab family members' own money. Also, if a person borrows money or buys things right before death with no real plan to pay it back, courts can look at that and sometimes refuse to let the creditor collect. Most people don't do this on purpose, though. Usually debt piles up through illness, job loss, or ordinary spending, and the estate handles it.

Is it fair? Many people think so, because the system is designed so that creditors take the risk of lending, and families are protected from being stuck with a dead relative's bills. Others argue it can be unfair when a spouse shares a debt they didn't fully understand. That's why it's a good idea to know which debts you share and to plan ahead.

When a certified bank check is not cashed, the funds used to pay for it generally remain with the bank rather than returning to the purchaser's account. At the moment of certification, the bank debits the customer's account (or collects the funds) and sets them aside to guarantee payment to the payee. Because the bank has already committed those funds, it is not supposed to release them back to the customer simply because the check was never presented.

Typically, the check stays outstanding until the payee deposits or cashes it, and most banks do not let the check expire in a way that returns the money automatically. If the check is lost or never delivered, the purchaser usually cannot get a refund on their own. Instead, they must request a stop payment or a replacement, which often requires signing an affidavit of loss and sometimes waiting a period of time, such as 90 days, before the bank will issue a refund. The bank may also require an indemnity or other documentation before reissuing the funds.

Unclaimed certified funds can eventually be treated as abandoned property under state unclaimed property laws. After a dormancy period set by the state, typically several years, the bank must turn the money over to the state treasury or unclaimed property office. The original purchaser or payee can still claim the funds from the state, although the process is more involved than cashing the check would have been.

Corpus Christi is a Christian feast honoring the real presence of Jesus Christ's body and blood in the Eucharist, which is also called Holy Communion or the Lord's Supper. Some people call it the Feast of Corpus Christi. The celebration usually takes place on the Thursday following Trinity Sunday, a Christian festival held on the Sunday that comes 50 days after Easter. Many nations treat the day as a public holiday, and it is kept by Catholics as well as certain Protestant groups. In some places it is observed as a purely religious day, whereas elsewhere it has become a cultural occasion, with religious processions, parades, and other ceremonies taking place.

A baby who keeps having eye discharge, a fever, and a cough may be affected by many different things, such as infections, allergies, or other underlying health problems. Several possible explanations for your daughter's symptoms are listed below.

Infections: Many kinds of infection can lead to eye discharge and fever, including respiratory infections like bronchitis or pneumonia, as well as ear and sinus infections. Coughing is a typical sign of a respiratory infection.

Allergies: Reactions to pollen, dust, or pet dander can also produce eye discharge and coughing. Fever is not usually linked to allergies, although it can occur in some instances.

Other medical conditions: Other health issues may also be responsible. Epiphora, which means excessive tearing, can result in eye discharge, while asthma can bring on coughing and trouble breathing.

It is important to take your daughter to a healthcare provider, who can work out what is causing her symptoms and decide on the right treatment. The provider might suggest further tests, such as a chest X-ray or CT scan, to help identify the problem. They might also recommend more medications or other treatments to keep her symptoms under control.

They're all just moisturizers at the end of the day. Their job is to hydrate your skin and keep it soft and healthy. The real difference is what each area of skin needs.

Your hands and feet have thicker skin that dries out easily, so hand and foot creams tend to be richer and more emollient, meaning they give you a more intense dose of moisture. Face skin is more delicate, so face creams are usually lighter and soak in quickly. Body creams sit somewhere in between. They're made for the rest of your body, and they're generally thicker and more moisturizing than face cream.

You can technically use any of them anywhere. Nothing bad will happen if you put body cream on your hands. But a product made for a specific spot will usually work better there. A light face cream probably won't do much for dry, cracked hands, and a heavy body cream on your face can feel like too much.

Escrow is a arrangement that protects both the purchaser and the vendor of a home during the sale. It works like this: the two parties settle on the sale terms, including the asking figure for the house. The buyer then hands over a deposit, known as a "down payment," to an escrow company. That company keeps the down payment along with key paperwork, such as the sales contract and the property's title, until it is time to finalize the deal. Before closing, the escrow company verifies that every condition has been satisfied, for example that a home inspection took place or that the seller has cleared any outstanding mortgage on the property. Once all requirements are met, the escrow company pays the seller the down payment and moves the title into the buyer's name. Escrow matters because it safeguards both sides. The buyer can be confident the down payment is secure until the transaction closes, while the seller can count on receiving it once the sale is final. Escrow also ensures every necessary step has been completed, which can head off complications later on.

There are a number of possible explanations for bumps on the shaft of the penis. Among them are folliculitis, an inflammation of the hair follicles that produces small red bumps, usually after bacteria get into the follicle through a cut or other break in the skin. Molluscum contagiosum is another, a viral infection that creates small, firm bumps which may be pink, white, or the same color as the skin, often with a dimple in the middle. Syphilis, a sexually transmitted infection, can also cause bumps on the genitals. These may not hurt and may resolve on their own, but without treatment the infection can lead to serious health complications. Finally, genital warts are small growths that are flesh-colored or pink and can appear on the genitals or around the anus. They result from certain strains of human papillomavirus (HPV) and spread easily. If you notice bumps on your penis, see a healthcare provider for an accurate diagnosis and appropriate treatment. Until then, practice safe sex and refrain from sexual contact until the problem is resolved.

A sonic boom is a sharp, explosive noise produced when something travels through the atmosphere faster than sound does. Once an object reaches or exceeds the speed of sound, it generates a shock wave in the surrounding air. This wave is a region of tightly compressed air that moves outward at the speed of sound. As it reaches the ground, it produces a loud bang that may be audible across a wide area. People tend to link sonic booms with aircraft, yet other objects, including meteorites and supersonic missiles, can cause them as well.

Prepayment penalties are fairly uncommon on mortgages today, though they're not unheard of. In the United States, federal rules under the Dodd-Frank Act and related regulations generally restrict them, especially on most residential loans. Qualified mortgages can carry a prepayment penalty only in limited cases, typically for fixed-rate loans that aren't higher-priced, and the penalty is capped and phases out within a few years. Many lenders simply don't offer them. Adjustable-rate and jumbo loans, or loans from some non-bank lenders and investment properties, are more likely to include them.

In other countries the picture varies. In Canada, for example, penalties on fixed-rate mortgages can be substantial when you break the term early, while in the United Kingdom early repayment charges are common on fixed-rate deals, though they usually expire at the end of the fixed period. Some countries, such as Germany and Australia in many cases, have historically allowed borrowers to repay with little or no penalty.

If you're considering a specific loan, check the loan estimate or closing disclosure for a prepayment clause, and ask the lender directly whether one applies and how it is calculated. Whether it's normal in your case depends heavily on your country, loan type, and lender.

When we say the air "feels like" a particular temperature, we are really referring to the "wind chill factor." This figure describes how cold the outdoors seems when wind is blowing on you. It combines the air temperature with the wind speed. Stronger winds can make the air seem colder, because moving air draws heat away from the surface of your skin, making you feel chillier. For instance, at -2 degrees Celsius with no wind, the air will feel like -2 degrees Celsius. Add a strong wind, however, and the air can feel far colder than the thermometer reading. In that situation, we might say it feels like -10 degrees Celsius even though the actual temperature is still -2 degrees Celsius. In short, the wind chill factor measures how cold the outdoors feels when wind is present, and that sensation can vary from one person to another.

The Seminole Wars were a string of clashes in Florida pitting the Seminole Native American people against the United States government. Three such wars were fought: the first from 1817 to 1818, the second from 1835 to 1842, and the third from 1855 to 1858. The Treaty of Moultrie Creek brought the first war to a close and set aside a reservation for the Seminoles in central Florida. The second war concluded with the Treaty of Fort Gibson, which created a reservation for the Seminoles in what was then Indian Territory, today's Oklahoma. The third war, often called the Billy Bowlegs War, came to an end when the Seminole leader Billy Bowlegs surrendered and the Seminoles still remaining in Florida were moved to Indian Territory. The final major confrontation between the Seminoles and the government ended in 1858, when the Seminole leader Abraham was captured and the rest of the Seminoles in Florida were forced to leave. Taken together, these wars were complicated and brutal, and they profoundly shaped the history of both Florida and the nation. In the end, they drove the Seminole people from their Florida homeland and resettled them in Indian Territory.

So the subprime crisis, which most people just call the financial crisis, kicked off in the late 2000s and hit the US and Europe pretty hard. What happened was banks and other lenders started handing out mortgages to people who probably couldn't pay them back. Those were called subprime mortgages, since the borrowers were seen as a bigger risk than the "prime" ones. Then the banks bundled a bunch of these loans together and sold them off to investors as securities.

Meanwhile more and more people were piling on debt, and the securities built on those mortgages kept going up in value. That fed a bubble in housing, with home prices climbing and climbing. But bubbles pop, and this one did too. The securities lost most of their value almost overnight.

That set off a chain reaction. Lots of banks had put huge amounts of money into those securities, and suddenly they were worth way less than before. A lot of those institutions were close to going under.

The fallout was ugly. In the US, plenty of people lost their homes and unemployment shot up. Europe got hit hard too, since its banks were also in danger of collapsing. The whole thing pushed economies into a recession, which just means the economy slows down and people lose their jobs. Basically it came down to too much debt and reckless lending, and both the US and Europe paid for it.

Earnest money is basically a chunk of cash a buyer hands over when they make an offer on a house, to show the seller they're serious. It's meant to prove you'll actually follow through. If underwriting falls apart, say the lender decides you don't qualify for the mortgage or the property doesn't meet their financing requirements, you usually get that deposit back and the sale just dies. Same goes if you and the seller can't agree on terms. But if you back out for no good reason or break the contract, the seller may be able to keep some or all of it. The exact rules depend on what's written in the purchase contract, so read that thing closely before you make an offer. Trust me, you don't want to be surprised later.

Human computation is a research area concerned with building systems that pair the abilities of people and machines to tackle problems that neither could handle well alone. Such systems typically draw on the group intelligence and varied skills of many individuals who collaborate on problems or jobs too intricate or lengthy for one person or one computer to finish. Crowdsourcing marketplaces like Amazon Mechanical Turk are a common example, letting businesses farm out small assignments to a large, dispersed workforce. Online games and other interactive platforms that depend on players to solve puzzles, label objects in pictures, or transcribe spoken or written material are also instances. The approach applies to many kinds of problems, including data analysis, natural language processing, image and video recognition, and any domain where human judgment or intuition adds value. It can further support collaboration and communication across large groups, or draw on a community's collective knowledge and expertise to solve problems or reach decisions.

The main aim is to remove or destroy as much of the cancer as possible while keeping side effects manageable. After radiation, a lot of people get wiped out with fatigue, and some notice weakness or numbness in their arms and legs. If your dad is dealing with anything like that, he should tell his team, because they can suggest ways to handle it and make him more comfortable. Beyond the medical side, things like diet changes, physical therapy, and other rehab can also help. Your dad's team is the one to map out what makes sense for him.

Bruises can take a few weeks to fully heal, and the spot often stays tender to the touch for a while longer than you'd expect. That raised, firm feeling you're noticing is probably swelling or scar tissue from the healing process. Still, if it's hurting or puffy after two months, get it looked at. A doctor or other provider can check for any underlying injury or condition and suggest what to do next, whether that's ice or heat, pain meds, or physical therapy. In the meantime, gentle massage might help with the swelling and circulation. Just skip anything that pushes into the pain or strains the area, since that can slow things down or cause more damage.

The United States spends about $13,000 to $14,000 per person each year on health care, according to the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services. In 2022 the figure was roughly $13,493 per person, and it has continued to climb since then, so the most recent estimates are a bit higher. That total covers spending from all sources, including government programs like Medicare and Medicaid, private insurance premiums, and out-of-pocket payments by individuals.

This is considerably more than any other wealthy country. Most peer nations, such as Germany, Japan, Canada, and the United Kingdom, spend somewhere between roughly $5,000 and $8,000 per person, measured in comparable U.S. dollars. The U.S. spending also represents a larger share of the economy, around 17 to 18 percent of GDP, compared with about 10 to 12 percent in most of those countries.

Okay so there are tons of different Christian denominations, and they don't all agree on everything. Here's a rundown of some of the big ones.

Baptists think baptism is really important, basically a public sign that you've committed your life to God. They also put the Bible at the center of what they believe and how they live.

Catholics follow the teachings of the Roman Catholic Church, which is led by the Pope. They believe in the Holy Trinity (God the Father, Jesus the Son, and the Holy Spirit) and place a lot of weight on sacraments like baptism and communion.

Methodists care a lot about social justice and doing what they can to make the world better. They also focus on personal faith and grace, the idea that God's love and forgiveness are freely offered to everyone.

Protestants are a pretty wide group that traces back to the Protestant Reformation, when people pushed to reform the Roman Catholic Church in the 1500s. Most Protestant churches treat the Bible as the ultimate authority and encourage people to interpret scripture for themselves.

Pentecostals emphasize experiencing the Holy Spirit, including the gifts of the Spirit like speaking in tongues and healing. Prayer is a big deal for them, and so is having a personal relationship with God.

Those are just a handful, though. Other major ones include the Orthodox Church, the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints (Mormons), and Seventh-day Adventists.

The biggest percentage stock price gain tends to belong to a smaller company whose shares rose many-fold from a low base, while the biggest dollar gain in market capitalization tends to belong to a mega-cap firm, since even a modest percentage move on a company worth over a trillion dollars adds a huge sum. Market cap is roughly the share price times the number of shares outstanding, so the dollar gain depends on the company's size as well as how far its price moved.

For example, Tesla's shares rose roughly 740% in 2020, which was one of the largest annual percentage gains among large companies, but Nvidia added far more dollar market value in 2024, on the order of a couple trillion dollars, as its valuation climbed past $3 trillion.

Which company "wins" depends heavily on the time period and the universe of stocks you're considering.
