In the comic's version, the water keeps going down and the Earth is so big that it could take a long time to fill or cause a lot of trouble. In real life, though, a hole that deep is almost impossible to make. The rock squeezes in and the drill gets stuck or melts, and the deepest hole people have ever dug is only about 12 kilometers, which is tiny compared to the whole Earth. So the answer is: you would get a lot of steam and a very loud, very hot surprise, but the ocean would not drain away into the middle of the planet.

Siddhartha Gautama, widely known as the Buddha, was a spiritual teacher who lived roughly 2,500 years ago in ancient India. He is regarded as the founder of Buddhism, a faith centered on reaching spiritual awakening through meditation and ethical behavior. In his youth, Siddhartha was a prince who enjoyed a luxurious existence. Yet the suffering he witnessed in the world troubled him deeply, so he gave up his privileged position to seek a way of ending that suffering. For many years he practiced severe asceticism, a lifestyle built on renunciation and strict self-control, hoping to reach enlightenment. Eventually, though, he concluded that extreme asceticism did not lead to awakening, and he instead formed a middle path that avoided both excess indulgence and harsh self-denial. This middle path came to be called the Eightfold Path, a collection of guidelines for ethical and spiritual growth. Although he had once been an ascetic, Siddhartha is frequently shown as a plump figure in Buddhist art, since this is read as a sign of his enlightenment and spiritual fulfillment. The image conveys the idea that awakening comes not through self-denial or bodily hardship, but through inner wisdom and understanding.

Biological vision is the process by which living organisms detect light and use it to build an understanding of their surroundings. It encompasses everything from the physical capture of light by specialized sense organs to the neural processing that turns raw light signals into meaningful perceptions such as shapes, colors, motion, depth, and recognizable objects. The term is often used to distinguish natural sight in animals and humans from computer or machine vision, which tries to replicate some of these abilities with cameras and algorithms.

The process begins with light entering an eye or another light-sensitive structure. In humans and other vertebrates, light passes through the cornea and lens, which focus it onto the retina at the back of the eye. The retina contains photoreceptor cells called rods and cones. Rods are highly sensitive and allow vision in dim light, while cones operate in brighter conditions and enable color perception, with different types of cones responding to different ranges of wavelengths. When light strikes these cells, light-sensitive pigment molecules change shape, triggering a chain of chemical reactions that converts the light into electrical signals. This conversion is known as phototransduction.

Those signals are not simply passed along unchanged. The retina itself performs a considerable amount of processing, with layers of neurons enhancing contrast, detecting edges, and compressing information before it leaves the eye. The signals then travel through the optic nerve to the brain, passing through a relay station called the lateral geniculate nucleus before reaching the primary visual cortex at the back of the head. From there, information spreads to many specialized brain regions. Broadly speaking, one pathway is involved in identifying what objects are, recognizing faces, shapes, and colors, while another is involved in determining where things are and how to interact with them, such as reaching for an object or tracking movement.

An important insight from the study of biological vision is that seeing is an active, interpretive process rather than a passive recording of the world. The brain fills in gaps, such as the blind spot where the optic nerve leaves the retina, keeps colors looking stable under changing lighting, and combines incoming data with past experience and expectations. Optical illusions reveal these assumptions at work by showing cases where the brain's interpretation differs from the physical reality.

Biological vision also varies enormously across the animal kingdom. Insects have compound eyes made of many small units that are excellent at detecting motion. Many birds can see ultraviolet light, some snakes sense infrared radiation, mantis shrimp have an unusually large number of photoreceptor types, and some simple organisms have only light-sensitive spots that distinguish light from dark. These differences reflect how each species' vision has evolved to suit its environment and way of life.

The study of biological vision draws on biology, neuroscience, psychology, physics, and medicine, and it has practical importance in understanding and treating eye diseases and visual disorders. It has also inspired technology, since many ideas in artificial intelligence, particularly the layered structure of neural networks used for image recognition, were loosely modeled on how the visual cortex processes information.

Generally, no. A Form W-9 is used to collect a taxpayer identification number from someone you pay for services, rent, interest, dividends, or other reportable payments, so you can issue them a Form 1099. Buying used equipment from you is not a payment you make to them, so you have no reporting obligation that requires their TIN, and the buyer typically wouldn't need to give you one.

The one thing to think about is whether you're the one sending a 1099. If you sold equipment as a business and the buyer later sends you a W-9 or asks for your TIN, that's a different situation, but it's the buyer's request, not a requirement on you. Also, if the sale was a one-off personal sale of used items, no tax form is usually involved at all. If you sold business assets, the sale may need to be reported on your own tax return (for example, on Form 4797 for depreciable business property), and your accountant can help with that.

If you're unsure about a specific case, such as a large sale or a buyer who insists on a W-9, a quick check with a tax professional is worthwhile.

I'm sorry you've been dealing with pain and a burning feeling in your ankle. A healthcare provider should evaluate it so you get an accurate diagnosis and the right treatment. Several conditions could be behind this, including a sprain, a broken bone, tendon or joint inflammation, irritated nerves, or an infection. Until you can be seen, a few steps may ease your symptoms. Stay off the ankle and avoid walking, running, or anything else that loads it. Keep the ankle raised above heart level to limit swelling and inflammation. Place an ice pack wrapped in a towel on the ankle for 15 to 20 minutes every two to three hours to reduce swelling and dull the pain. Choose footwear with solid arch support and a firm heel so your ankle carries less strain. Over-the-counter nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs such as ibuprofen, or acetaminophen, may also help with pain and swelling. Even so, it's important to see a clinician soon to find out what is causing the pain and to get proper care. They may suggest further options, such as physical therapy or prescription medication.

The best choice depends mostly on the interest rate you'd actually get, how long you'll carry the debt, and how much risk you can accept on your home.

Parent PLUS loans are federal loans taken out in the parent's name. They have a fixed interest rate, currently around 8 to 9 percent for new loans, plus an origination fee of about 4 percent. Approval is easy because credit requirements are lenient, and repayment can be deferred while the student is enrolled. Your home isn't at risk, and you may have access to federal repayment options and forgiveness programs that private debt lacks. The downsides are the high rate and fee, and the fact that the loan can't be paid down without a plan.

A HELOC is a revolving credit line secured by your home. Its rate is usually variable and tied to the prime rate, so it may start lower than a Parent PLUS loan but can rise over time. Most HELOCs have a draw period of about ten years, often with interest-only payments, followed by a repayment period with much higher monthly payments. Closing costs tend to be low, and you only pay interest on what you borrow. The main risks are rising rates and the fact that your house secures the debt.

A home equity loan, sometimes called a second mortgage, is a lump-sum loan secured by your home with a fixed rate and fixed monthly payments. It is more predictable than a HELOC and often has a rate below Parent PLUS, though closing costs are usually higher, commonly 2 to 5 percent of the loan. Like a HELOC, it puts your home at risk if you can't pay.

On taxes, interest on a HELOC or home equity loan is generally deductible only if the money is used to buy, build, or substantially improve the home, so using it for tuition would likely not qualify. Parent PLUS interest may be deductible under the student loan interest deduction, subject to income limits and the cap of $2,500 per year.

In practice, most families should first exhaust grants, scholarships, work-study, and the student's own federal loans, and compare the parent options against each other and against private student loans. If you have a strong rate and a clear payoff plan, a fixed-rate home equity loan is often a sensible middle ground. A HELOC can work well if you're confident you can pay it down quickly before rates rise. Parent PLUS is often the least attractive option on price, but it may be the safest because it doesn't put your home at risk and it offers federal protections.

Before deciding, get written quotes for the total cost, including fees, and model the monthly payment at retirement age, since borrowing against your home or taking on debt late in life can strain your finances.

Diablo 3 came out in 2012 and got a lot of criticism, mostly because of some choices that frustrated players who loved the earlier games. At first, the game required you to be connected to the internet even if you only wanted to play alone, and if the servers had problems, you could get kicked out and lose progress. The auction house let players buy and sell items for real money, which felt like the game was pushing people to pay instead of just having fun finding good stuff. Many people also felt the loot was less exciting, because the rare items they found often were not as special as they hoped. When the game first launched, the way the difficulty and rewards worked made it hard to feel like you were getting better gear in a satisfying way.

The good news is that a lot of these problems have been fixed over time. Blizzard removed the real-money auction house, made the game easier to play offline in many cases, and reworked how loot drops and character power work. Patches also improved the overall balance, and a major expansion called Reaper of Souls added new content and a new class. Many players who gave up on it years ago now say it is much better than it used to be, though some still prefer Diablo 2.

So in simple terms: people were upset because the game made some annoying choices at the start, like needing a connection all the time and letting people buy items with real money. Blizzard has made many changes since then, so it can be fixed, and lots of players now enjoy it.

It depends on what you mean by "trade" and what your goals are, so the honest answer is that there's no universal number. A common guideline in trading and investing is to risk only a small fraction of your total capital on any single position, often cited as 1 to 2 percent. That means if you have $10,000, you'd size each trade so that if it goes wrong, you lose no more than $100 to $200. This is about how much you can afford to lose on one idea, not how much you need to set aside before entering.

If you're thinking about how much cash to have available to make a trade at all, that depends on the instrument. Buying a single share of a stock costs its price, while options, futures, and margin trades involve different capital requirements and risks. Beginners are often better off starting with a small amount they can truly afford to lose, so that emotional pressure doesn't distort their decisions.

It would help to know what you're planning to trade, roughly how much capital you have, and whether you're looking to build savings or grow an existing account. With those details, I can give you a more specific way to think about position sizing.

Gerrymandering means setting the borders of electoral districts so that one political party gains an unfair edge over its rivals. Any country with electoral districts and political parties can face this problem. In the United States, a number of remedies have been proposed or adopted.

One is the independent redistricting commission. Instead of letting the state legislature draw district lines, some states have handed the job to an independent body, which can limit how much politicians shape the process.

Another is the use of fair redistricting criteria. Certain states have established rules that mapmakers must follow, such as requiring districts to be compact and contiguous or to respect the boundaries of existing communities.

A third is court challenges. If a redistricting plan is judged to be excessively partisan, it can be contested in court, and judges may direct the state to redraw the lines more fairly.

A fourth is voter initiatives. In some states, citizens can approve ballot measures that reform how districts are drawn. California voters, for instance, passed such a measure in 2010, which established an independent redistricting commission.

Gerrymandering has long been an issue in the United States. The term comes from Elbridge Gerry, the governor of Massachusetts, who in 1812 signed into law a redistricting plan intended to favor his own party. In recent years, however, improvements in technology and data analysis have made it simpler for politicians to design districts that maximize their party's advantage, which has heightened concern about the practice.

This is a common and often stressful situation, and the answer depends a lot on how the two of them hold title and where you live, but here is the general picture.

If they own the house as co-owners, whether as tenants in common or joint tenants, neither one can normally sell the whole property without the other's agreement. He is free to sell or transfer his own share in many places if they are tenants in common, but a buyer for a partial interest in a house is hard to find, and the price is usually heavily discounted. If they are joint tenants, he may be able to sever the joint tenancy, but that is a legal step worth discussing with a lawyer first.

The first and cheapest route is negotiation. The most workable outcome is often a buyout, where one sibling purchases the other's share, usually based on an independent appraisal. His sister may not want to sell the house, but she might be willing to keep it if she can afford to pay him out, perhaps by refinancing. It helps to find out why she objects. If it is sentimental, a buyout may satisfy her. If it is financial, a longer timeline or a different arrangement might help. Mediation can be useful here and is much cheaper than court.

If that fails, the legal backstop in most places is a partition action, where a court orders the property divided or, more commonly with a house, sold and the proceeds split. In the US this is a partition suit, in England and Wales it is an application under the Trusts of Land and Appointment of Trustees Act, and other countries have equivalents. Courts usually do grant it eventually, but it can be slow, expensive, and damaging to the family relationship. Legal fees often come out of the shared proceeds, and a forced sale can bring a lower price.

Some practical points are worth checking. Look at the deed or title to see exactly how they own it, and whether there is any co-ownership agreement, trust document, or will that affects things. Check the mortgage, since both may be liable regardless of who lives there or pays. Also consider who is living in the house and who pays the costs, because those factors can affect how a court divides proceeds.

Because the details vary by location and ownership structure, he should speak with a real estate or property lawyer before taking any step like listing the house or sending a formal demand. If you tell me the country or state and how the title is held, I can give more specific information.

Managing payroll for a tutoring business involves a few distinct challenges that set it apart from a traditional salaried workplace. Most tutors are paid per session or per hour rather than on a fixed salary, many work part-time or as independent contractors, and schedules often shift week to week. A sound payroll process starts with an accurate record of every session delivered, since pay depends on those records. Many owners use scheduling software or a shared calendar linked to a simple log where tutors confirm completed sessions, along with the student, the subject, the duration, and any cancellations or no-shows, which may or may not be billable depending on your policy.

Once hours are tracked, the next step is to set clear compensation rules and put them in writing. Decide whether tutors earn a flat rate per session, an hourly wage, or a percentage of the fee the client pays, and specify how travel time, preparation time, group sessions, and online tutoring are handled. Written agreements protect both sides and reduce disputes at the end of the month. They should also state the pay schedule, such as biweekly or monthly, and the method of payment.

The classification of your workers is a critical decision. If tutors are employees, you must typically withhold income tax, pay employer contributions such as Social Security and Medicare or their local equivalents, handle unemployment insurance, and follow minimum wage and overtime laws. If they are independent contractors, you generally do not withhold taxes, but you may need to issue Form 1099 or the equivalent in your country and must meet the legal tests for contractor status, which look at how much control you exert over their schedule, methods, and tools. Misclassification can lead to back taxes and penalties, so it is worth confirming the rules with an accountant or employment attorney in your jurisdiction.

For the payroll run itself, you can use dedicated payroll software such as Gusto, QuickBooks Payroll, or a comparable service, which calculates pay, withholds taxes, files reports, and issues pay stubs. For a very small operation with only a few contractors, a well-organized spreadsheet and a standard bank transfer may suffice, though it still requires careful record keeping. Whichever method you choose, reconcile the payroll against your session logs and your bank account each cycle, and keep records for the period required by your local tax authority, typically several years.

Finally, consider the practical side of tutor retention and fairness. Pay on a consistent, predictable schedule, communicate changes in advance, and provide a clear way for tutors to question discrepancies. Reviewing your payroll costs against revenue each quarter will show whether your pricing covers tutor pay and overhead, and it will help you decide when it is time to hire additional staff or adjust rates.

Honestly, a cough and cold while pregnant is miserable, but there's a lot you can do. Start with rest and fluids. Water, juice, and broth all help thin out mucus and keep your throat from getting raw. A humidifier in your bedroom can make a big difference for a sore throat and nighttime coughing.

Before you reach for any medicine, though, check with your doctor or midwife. Plenty of cold and cough products are fine during pregnancy, but some aren't, and it's easy to grab the wrong one from the drugstore shelf. Acetaminophen (Tylenol) is usually the go-to for aches and fever, and saline nasal spray is generally considered safe for congestion. Your provider can tell you what's okay for your specific situation.

Some home tricks help too. Gargling with warm salt water soothes a scratchy throat, and a hot shower or vaporizer can loosen up congestion. Saline spray also clears out your nose nicely.

Keep an eye on how you're doing. If things aren't getting better, or they're getting worse, call your provider rather than waiting it out.

A furlong is 660 feet, or about 201 meters. You'll mostly see it in horse racing and farming. The name comes from Old English "furh" (furrow) and "lang" (long), since it was originally the distance a team of oxen could plow before they needed a break. Pretty neat, right?

So getting a prosthetic limb for an animal takes a few steps. First, the amputated area gets cleaned up and treated so it doesn't get infected. Then a vet or prosthetics maker builds a custom limb sized to fit that particular animal. The prosthetic attaches to the leftover limb through a special socket that wraps snugly around the stump, and straps or other fasteners hold the socket in place. After that comes training, which can mean physical therapy and exercises so the animal gets used to moving on the new limb. Getting the fit right matters a lot, since a loose or badly secured prosthetic can lead to gangrene. That happens when blood flow gets cut off to a limb and the tissue starts to die, which can turn into a dangerous infection. A good fit and secure attachment go a long way toward keeping that risk down.

Metal Gear is a series of video games about soldiers who get trained to sneak into enemy bases and pull off special missions without anyone spotting them. The main guy is Solid Snake, and he gets sent on a whole bunch of missions to stop other soldiers from using this thing called Metal Gear, which is basically a giant robot that can fire nuclear missiles. Over the course of the series he ends up fighting all kinds of enemies and bosses: other soldiers, robots, even members of his own family. The story throws in a lot of twists too, since Snake and his friends keep digging up secrets about the people they work for and the missions they've been sent on. The series is known for its complicated plot, characters you actually care about, and action-heavy gameplay. It's a blast to play, though it can get kind of confusing because there are so many characters and events to keep straight.

Category theory is a field of mathematics that formalizes mathematical concepts and structures using "objects" and "arrows," the latter also called "morphisms." Because it is highly abstract, it serves as a framework for understanding and unifying many different mathematical ideas, including groups, rings, and topological spaces. Within this theory, an object is a basic concept standing for a particular entity or structure. In the category of groups, for instance, the objects are groups and the arrows are group homomorphisms, while in the category of topological spaces, the objects are topological spaces and the arrows are continuous functions. The central idea is to focus on the relationships among objects and on the arrows linking them, instead of on the objects and arrows in isolation. Taking this view makes it possible to approach mathematical concepts and structures in a more general and abstract way, and it helps produce new insights and results. The theory is applied across many areas of mathematics, such as algebra, geometry, topology, and logic, and also in computer science and physics. It is a very technical subject that demands a solid mathematical background and a capacity for abstract thinking, so it is commonly taught at the graduate level.

A drop in the heart's pumping strength (ejection fraction) from 40% to 32% is significant and should be reviewed by his cardiologist soon. Several things could explain it. The most important one to rule out is reduced blood flow to the heart muscle, which can happen if the stented artery has narrowed again (restenosis), a new blockage has formed elsewhere, or he has had a silent heart attack that damaged part of the muscle. Irregular heart rhythms, especially atrial fibrillation or other rapid rhythms, can also weaken the pumping function over time. Other possibilities include uncontrolled high blood pressure, a heart valve that has become leaky or narrowed, inflammation of the heart muscle after a viral illness, thyroid problems, anemia, poorly controlled diabetes, or changes in medication or missed doses of heart medicines. Some of the difference may also reflect normal variation between echo tests, since the measurement depends partly on the person performing it and the image quality, though a drop this size usually deserves investigation rather than being dismissed.

The cardiologist may want to repeat the echo, check his heart rhythm with a Holter or similar monitor, order blood tests (including thyroid function and kidney function), and possibly perform a stress test or a coronary angiogram to check the stent and the other arteries. Based on the results, treatment might involve adjusting his medicines, which often include beta blockers, ACE inhibitors or ARBs, and other heart failure medications, as well as treating any rhythm problem or valve issue. Until he is seen, it helps to make sure he takes all prescribed medicines exactly as directed, limits salt, avoids smoking and heavy alcohol, and keeps up gentle activity only as his doctor allows.

Seek emergency care immediately if he develops chest pain or pressure, shortness of breath at rest or when lying flat, fainting or near-fainting, a racing or pounding heartbeat that does not settle, sudden swelling in the legs or abdomen, or unusual weakness or confusion.

Sure! So picture yourself in a car going around a circular track at a steady speed. Even though your speed isn't changing, you still feel pushed toward the center of the track. That's because the car keeps changing direction as it goes around, and your body has to be pulled along to keep up with that turn. The force doing the pulling toward the center is called centripetal force.

Now say the driver wants to go faster. They have to speed up the car, sure, but if they only do that and the centripetal force stays the same, you'll feel like you're getting shoved out of your seat, since the turning isn't strong enough to keep you on the circle. So to go faster around the track, the driver needs to boost both the speed and the centripetal force. Then you still feel that pull toward the middle, just at a higher speed. Make sense?

Some websites hide the final price until you add an item to your cart because the total you pay often includes extra costs that aren't shown on the product page. Think of it like buying a toy at a store where the sticker shows the toy's price, but at the register they also add a bag fee and a tax. The website does the same thing, but it waits to show you those extra pieces until you're closer to buying.

The main reasons are shipping, taxes, and fees. Shipping cost depends on where you live and how fast you want the item, so the site can't know it until it knows your address. Taxes also change depending on your location. Some sites also add service fees or handling charges. By waiting until you're in the cart, the site can add all of these together and show you a real total.

Some companies also do this on purpose to make the item look cheaper at first, so you click on it and start shopping. This is sometimes called "drip pricing," and some people think it's sneaky, which is probably what the article you read was talking about.

So the short version is: the price you see first is only part of the cost, and the rest gets added once the site knows where you live and what you're buying.

Slugging percentage measures a hitter's power by calculating the average number of total bases a player earns per at-bat. The formula is total bases divided by at-bats, often written as SLG = TB / AB.

To get total bases, you count one for each single, two for each double, three for each triple, and four for each home run. Another way to write this is singles plus two times doubles plus three times triples plus four times home runs. Walks, hit by pitches, and sacrifice flies are not counted, and the denominator uses official at-bats, which exclude walks, hit by pitches, sacrifice bunts, and sacrifice flies.

For example, suppose a player has 500 at-bats with 100 hits: 60 singles, 20 doubles, 5 triples, and 15 home runs. His total bases would be 60 + 40 + 15 + 60, which equals 175. Dividing 175 by 500 gives a slugging percentage of .350.

Despite the name, slugging percentage is not truly a percentage, since it can exceed 1.000. The maximum possible is 4.000, which would mean a home run in every at-bat. A slugging percentage of .500 or higher is generally considered excellent, and the league average usually falls somewhere around .400 to .430, depending on the era.

It is often paired with batting average and on-base percentage, and adding on-base percentage and slugging percentage together produces OPS, a popular all-in-one measure of hitting productivity.

Please don't give your daughter Duavent without a doctor's instruction. It contains fenoterol, a bronchodilator, and ipratropium, an anticholinergic. Both are meant for airway narrowing, such as asthma or wheezing that a doctor has diagnosed. Fenoterol can also cause a fast heartbeat, tremor, and agitation, and children's doses differ from adults'. Without a clear reason, the risks outweigh any benefit. Her doctor or pediatrician can decide whether a nebulized medicine is appropriate after listening to her chest.

A temperature of 37.3°C is normal or only slightly raised, and it isn't a fever by most definitions, which generally start at 38°C. A week of cough with thick phlegm and nighttime coughing is worth having a doctor check, though, especially because it's disturbing her sleep.

Until you can see a doctor, some simple measures often help. Keep her well hydrated with water, warm drinks, or soup. Raise the head of her bed or prop her up with pillows at night. Run a cool-mist humidifier in her room. If she is over one year old, a small spoonful of honey before bed can soothe a cough. Avoid over-the-counter cough and cold medicines for young children unless a doctor recommends them. Saline (salt water) nebulization is generally considered low-risk, but check with her doctor first, since it's still best to know what is actually causing the cough.

Seek medical care promptly if she has fast or labored breathing, wheezing, chest pain, a fever of 38°C or higher that persists, blue or grayish lips, unusual drowsiness or difficulty waking, refusal to drink or signs of dehydration, or if the cough is getting worse rather than better. Call emergency services right away if she is struggling to breathe.

Software contains bugs for several reasons. For one, programs are highly intricate, consisting of numerous interconnected parts and functions that must cooperate properly. Even when each piece has been carefully tested and performs as expected on its own, problems can still emerge once those pieces are joined together and used in unforeseen ways. Another cause is that people write software, and people make errors. Even skilled, meticulous programmers slip up while coding. Such errors vary widely, from minor typos with no real effect on how the program works to serious faults that make it act strangely or crash entirely. Lastly, software is always changing and being revised. Each time new features are introduced or old ones are modified, some parts may fail to work as planned or may create conflicts with other components. In short, bugs are an ordinary part of software development, and most companies have established procedures for finding and correcting them when they surface.

Acute pain in the lower right part of the belly may stem from a number of different sources. Among the more frequent culprits are appendicitis, in which the appendix swells and becomes infected, often bringing on sudden and intense pain that usually starts in the lower right abdomen; kidney stones, which are small hardened deposits that form inside the kidneys and can produce sharp pain in that same region as they travel through the urinary tract; intestinal infections, whether bacterial or viral, which can also trigger belly pain; and constipation, where hard, dry stool is difficult to pass and may cause discomfort, particularly in the lower right area. Anyone experiencing abdominal pain should consult a physician, especially if it is severe or is joined by symptoms such as fever, nausea, or vomiting. A doctor can determine what is causing the pain and suggest suitable treatment.

Whether you can keep a "woman-owned business" status after taking on an investor depends mainly on which certification or designation you mean, because each one sets its own ownership and control rules. The most common are the federal WOSB program (Women-Owned Small Business, used for federal contracting), the Women's Business Enterprise National Council (WBENC) certification, and state or local certifications, which often have their own tests. Most of them focus on two things: that women own at least 51 percent of the company, and that women control its day-to-day operations and long-term strategic decisions. Taking on an investor does not automatically disqualify you, but how you structure the deal matters a great deal.

The main risk is dilution. If you issue equity to an investor and your ownership falls below 51 percent, you will generally lose eligibility. Even if you keep a majority stake, the investor's rights can create problems. Preferred stock, veto rights over major decisions, board control provisions, or the power to remove key executives can all be seen as giving the investor control, which can break the rules even when your ownership percentage is fine. Some programs also look at whether the economic arrangement is fair to the woman owner, such as whether she receives a proportionate share of profits and distributions.

If you want to preserve the status, a few approaches are common. You can raise capital while keeping the equity split well above 51 percent, and make sure the investor's rights are limited to economic protections rather than management control. You can use non-voting or limited-voting equity for the investor if that fits your state's rules, though you should verify this carefully because some programs look past non-voting shares. Alternatively, you can take on debt financing or revenue-based financing, which typically does not transfer ownership at all. Whatever you choose, have the investment terms reviewed by an attorney who works with certification programs, and talk to the certifying body before closing. Many will tell you in advance whether a proposed deal would cause you to lose eligibility, and it is far easier to structure the deal correctly up front than to fix it after the fact.

Bayesian optimization is a strategy for finding the best input to a function when that function is expensive to evaluate, has no convenient formula or gradient you can use, and may return noisy results. The classic example is tuning the hyperparameters of a machine learning model: each trial means training a model, which might take hours, so you can only afford a few dozen attempts. Bayesian optimization tries to pick each attempt as intelligently as possible so that you reach a good answer with very few evaluations.

The core idea is to build a probabilistic model of the unknown function, often called a surrogate model, and update it as you gather data. The most common choice is a Gaussian process, which for any candidate input gives both a predicted value and a measure of uncertainty about that prediction. Near points you have already tested, the uncertainty is low. In unexplored regions it is high. This is the "Bayesian" part: you start with a prior belief about what the function might look like, and each new observation updates that belief into a posterior using Bayes' rule. Other surrogates, such as random forests or tree-structured Parzen estimators, are also used, especially when the search space is large or includes categorical choices.

Once you have the surrogate, you need a rule for deciding where to evaluate next. This rule is called an acquisition function. It scores every candidate point by combining two competing goals: exploitation, which means sampling where the model predicts good values, and exploration, which means sampling where the model is uncertain and a better value might be hiding. Popular acquisition functions include expected improvement, which estimates how much a point is likely to beat the best result found so far; probability of improvement, which estimates the chance of beating it at all; and upper confidence bound, which adds a multiple of the uncertainty to the predicted value to favor promising but uncertain regions. Optimizing the acquisition function is cheap because it only involves the surrogate, not the real expensive function.

The overall process is a loop. You begin with a handful of evaluations, perhaps chosen randomly. You fit the surrogate model to those results, use the acquisition function to choose the most promising next point, evaluate the real function there, add the result to your data, and repeat until you run out of budget or the improvements level off. Over time the model becomes more accurate in the regions that matter, and the search concentrates around the optimum while still occasionally checking unexplored areas.

Bayesian optimization works best when evaluations are costly and the number of input dimensions is modest, typically up to about twenty. In very high dimensions the surrogate becomes hard to fit and the method loses much of its advantage, and if evaluations are cheap, simpler methods like random search or gradient-based optimization are often faster overall. Beyond hyperparameter tuning, it is used in experimental design, materials and drug discovery, robotics control, and engineering design, wherever each experiment is precious and you want to learn as much as possible from every trial.

Leaving Las Vegas (1995), directed by Mike Figgis, starred Nicolas Cage as Ben Sanderson, an alcoholic screenwriter who moves to Las Vegas intending to drink himself to death. Elisabeth Shue played Sera, a sex worker with whom he forms a complicated relationship. Cage won the Academy Award for Best Actor for his performance, and Shue received a Best Actress nomination.

Purdue University is a public research university located in West Lafayette, Indiana, in the United States. Founded in 1869 as a land-grant institution under the Morrill Act, it was named after John Purdue, a local businessman and merchant who donated the land and money that helped establish it. The university has a strong focus on science, engineering, technology, agriculture, and management, and it is well known for its engineering and aviation programs, as well as for its aerospace research. Purdue's main campus is in West Lafayette, and it also operates regional campuses in other parts of Indiana, including Fort Wayne and Northwest in Hammond, along with a presence in Indianapolis through its partnerships and programs. The university enrolls tens of thousands of students, both undergraduate and graduate, and is organized into several colleges and schools. It is a member of the Big Ten Conference in athletics, where its teams are known as the Boilermakers. Purdue is also recognized for its contributions to space exploration, having produced a number of astronauts over the years, and it has been associated with numerous notable inventions and research breakthroughs.

I'm sorry you're dealing with this on top of recovering from surgery. What you describe is very common after an operation under general anesthesia, and there are several likely reasons for it.

Anesthesia and the medicines used around surgery slow down the bowel. Opioid painkillers such as codeine, tramadol, or morphine are a major cause of constipation and gas. Reduced movement, less food and fluid intake, and sometimes nausea medicines or iron and calcium supplements add to it. The result is trapped gas, cramping, bloating, and hard stools. This is usually temporary and improves over several days as you become more active and eat normally.

Things that often help: drink plenty of fluids unless you have been told to restrict them, and eat fiber-rich foods like fruit, cooked vegetables, oats, and whole grains once you are eating normally. Walk around the house several times a day, as even short walks stimulate the bowel. Warm tea, especially peppermint or ginger, and a warm compress on the abdomen can ease cramps. Avoid gas-forming foods for now, such as beans, carbonated drinks, cabbage, and chewing gum. Try not to strain hard on the toilet, and avoid a straining effort in particular because it can raise pressure in the head and ear area, which matters after ear surgery. Placing your feet on a small stool while sitting can make passing stool easier.

Over-the-counter options such as a stool softener (docusate), an osmotic laxative like lactulose or polyethylene glycol, or simethicone for gas are usually safe, but please check with your surgeon or pharmacist first, since they know your full medication list. If you are taking opioids, ask whether you can switch to a non-opioid pain medicine like paracetamol, which often relieves the problem.

Please contact your surgeon or go to emergency care promptly if you have severe or worsening abdominal pain, a swollen hard belly, repeated vomiting, inability to pass any gas or stool at all, fever, blood in the stool, or black stools. Also seek urgent help for severe headache, clear fluid leaking from the ear or nose, neck stiffness, or worsening dizziness, as these can relate to the surgery itself. If there is no bowel movement after three to four days despite the measures above, call your doctor as well.

Since you are only two days out from surgery, it is a good idea to let your surgical team know about the symptoms even if they seem mild, so they can adjust your medications if needed.

Intense discomfort beneath the shoulder blade and in the armpit may stem from several sources, such as strained or spasming muscles, irritated or pinched nerves, and issues with the spine or nearby joints. When the discomfort lasts or becomes severe, consulting a healthcare professional is essential for an accurate diagnosis and appropriate care. The best approach depends on what is causing the pain, and possible options include over-the-counter or prescription medications to reduce swelling and ease discomfort; physical therapy, where guided exercises and stretches build flexibility and strength while easing muscle tightness; massage, which can loosen tense muscles and promote better blood flow; chiropractic care, in which spinal adjustments aim to restore alignment and improve movement; and acupuncture, an ancient Chinese practice that uses fine needles placed at specific points on the body to reduce pain. Following the plan your healthcare provider recommends is important for managing pain and supporting your overall well-being. If you have concerns about your symptoms or your pain does not improve with treatment, be sure to talk with your provider.

Dart's a language you can use to build apps for the web, phones, and desktops. People often call it the language of the future, and it's easy to see why. It's pretty easy to pick up, with a simple syntax that new programmers can start using right away. It also scales well, so you can use it for huge, complicated apps or for small, simple ones. And it keeps getting better. The developers are always tweaking it to make it faster and more efficient, so it's a safe bet it'll stay popular for building modern apps for a while.

Cloud computing is the delivery of computing resources over the internet, such as servers, storage, databases, networking, software, and analytics, on demand and typically on a pay-as-you-go basis. Instead of buying, owning, and maintaining physical hardware and data centers, individuals and organizations rent these resources from a provider like Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure, or Google Cloud, and access them remotely through a web browser or application programming interface.

The main appeal of cloud computing is flexibility and scale. A business can start with a small amount of capacity and expand or shrink it within minutes as demand changes, without large upfront investments. Providers handle the underlying infrastructure, including hardware maintenance, power, cooling, security patches, and physical protection, which frees customers to focus on their own applications and services. Resources are also usually distributed across many geographic locations, which can improve reliability and reduce delays for users around the world.

Cloud services are commonly grouped into three broad models. Infrastructure as a Service provides virtual machines, storage, and networking that the customer configures and manages. Platform as a Service offers a ready-made environment for building and running applications, so the customer does not manage the underlying operating system or servers. Software as a Service delivers complete applications, such as email, file sharing, or customer relationship management tools, that users simply log into and use.

Cloud computing also comes in different deployment arrangements. A public cloud is shared infrastructure operated by a third-party provider, a private cloud is dedicated to a single organization, and a hybrid cloud combines the two so that data and applications can move between them. Many everyday services, including streaming video, online backups, and web-based office software, rely on cloud computing behind the scenes.

I can't suggest a particular treatment for your son's condition without more information. A healthcare provider needs to examine the white patch on his tongue to work out what is causing it and which treatment would suit him best. If a fungal infection turns out to be the cause, an antifungal such as Canesten (clotrimazole) could help. Still, Canesten is not licensed for use inside the mouth, so it should not be put on the tongue. It is also usually prescribed for skin and nail fungus, so it may not work well for a fungal infection in the mouth. Please arrange for your son to see a doctor soon so the cause can be found and treated properly. Until then, keep up good oral hygiene and make sure he doesn't share utensils or drink from anyone else's glass.

Ho Chi Minh (1890–1969) was the founder and leader of the Vietnamese communist movement and the first president of the Democratic Republic of Vietnam, commonly known as North Vietnam. Born Nguyen Sinh Cung in central Vietnam, he spent decades abroad, working in France, the Soviet Union, and China, and he helped found the Indochinese Communist Party in 1930. He led the Viet Minh independence movement against Japanese occupation during World War II and against French colonial rule afterward, and he declared Vietnamese independence in 1945. After the French defeat at Dien Bien Phu in 1954, the country was divided, with his government controlling the north.

During the Vietnam War, which escalated sharply after the United States began large-scale involvement in the mid-1960s, Ho Chi Minh was the political figure at the head of North Vietnam's government and its war effort against South Vietnam and the United States. He did not personally command troops, as the military was directed by figures such as General Vo Nguyen Giap, but he was the symbolic and political leader of the communist side. He died in September 1969, before the war ended in 1975 with the fall of Saigon and the reunification of Vietnam under communist rule. Saigon was renamed Ho Chi Minh City in his honor.

Garry Kasparov is a Russian chess grandmaster, widely regarded as one of the greatest chess players in history. Born in 1963 in Baku, in what was then the Soviet Union, he became the youngest undisputed World Chess Champion in 1985 at the age of 22, when he defeated Anatoly Karpov. He held the title until 2000, defending it several times against Karpov and others, and he was ranked world number one for a remarkable span of years. His aggressive, dynamic, and deeply prepared style made him a dominant force in the game.

Beyond chess, Kasparov became well known as a political activist and critic of the Russian government under Vladimir Putin. He founded or led opposition movements and has written extensively about democracy and human rights, and he has lived in exile for much of the time since the mid-2010s. He is also remembered for his 1997 match against IBM's Deep Blue computer. After losing the 1997 match, he became a prominent voice in discussions about artificial intelligence and human-machine collaboration, and he later promoted the concept of "advanced chess," where humans and computers play together.

There are several reasons a child might refuse to eat at daycare. One is stress or anxiety: a new setting with unfamiliar faces and schedules can unsettle young children, and that unease may suppress their appetite. Another is distraction, since daycare is often busy and noisy, and with other kids around, a child may struggle to concentrate on their meal. Routines can also play a role, as children are often accustomed to particular meal times or habits at home, and the different rhythm at daycare can make eating harder. Finally, appetite naturally fluctuates, and it's normal for a child to eat heartily one day and barely touch food the next. If you're worried, it's worth speaking with your child's caregivers to hear what they've noticed and whether they have any ideas. Packing familiar foods your child already likes can help, and encouraging them with praise, whether for trying something new or for finishing a good portion, can also make mealtimes more positive.

Imagine your classroom has one big box of crayons, and nobody owns any crayons personally. Instead, everything in the box belongs to everyone. The teacher, or a small group of helpers, decides who gets which crayons and how many, so that every kid gets what they need. That is the basic idea of communism: instead of people owning their own stuff, like farms, factories, and shops, the whole community owns them together, and the goods are shared out so that nobody has way too much or way too little.

The people who first wrote about it, especially Karl Marx in the 1800s, noticed that a few rich people owned most of the factories while the workers who ran them were poor. They thought that was unfair. Their dream was a world with no rich and poor, where everyone works and everyone shares in the results, a bit like the saying "from each according to his ability, to each according to his need."

Here is where it gets tricky. When countries like the Soviet Union and China tried it, somebody had to be in charge of deciding who gets what. That usually ended up being a small group of leaders in the government, and they often got very powerful. Sometimes they punished people who disagreed, and in some places the economy did badly or people went hungry. So in real life, communism often turned out very differently from the nice sharing dream.

People still argue about it. Some say the idea is good but was done badly, and others say the idea itself doesn't work because it ignores how people behave, for example that many work harder when they can keep what they earn. Back in the classroom: sharing crayons sounds fair, but what if one kid colors all day and another naps, and they get the same? And what if the teacher keeps the best crayons? Those are the kinds of problems people debate.

Okay, so data mining (some people call it information mining) is basically digging through huge piles of data to find patterns and connections that aren't obvious at first glance. You're using fairly sophisticated algorithms to pull stuff out of all sorts of sources, and the whole point is to get useful insights you can act on. Companies use it to make better decisions, spot trends, and fix problems, and it shows up in science and healthcare too. Most of the time it leans on machine learning methods like clustering, classification, and regression to make sense of the data. It's part of the broader data analytics world, and people often pair it with data visualization so they can actually see what's going on and understand it.

Okay so fire needs three things to keep going: oxygen, fuel, and heat. When you dump water on a fire, the water soaks up heat, which cools the fuel down and also pushes some of the oxygen away. That makes it a lot harder for the fire to keep burning. Water also forms a kind of barrier between the fuel and the air, cutting off the fire's supply of stuff it needs. And when water hits a hot fire, it turns to steam, which shoves more oxygen out of the way around the flames. So basically, water puts out fire by stealing heat, crowding out oxygen, and blocking the fuel from air. Once the fire can't get what it needs, it dies out.

Weather really does swing a lot, though, both day to day and from one spot to the next. A bunch of things drive it: air masses moving around, how much sun and heat an area gets, and things like mountains and big bodies of water. Zubir Said wrote the music for Singapore's national anthem, "Majulah Singapura," in 1958. After Singapore became an independent nation in 1965, the song was adopted as its official anthem. Sheikh Ya'acob bin Mohamed bin Abdullah penned the lyrics; he was a leading Malay figure in Singapore during that period. The anthem is performed in Malay, one of the country's official languages. Its message centers on unity and advancement within Singapore, and it serves as an emblem of the nation's identity and sense of pride.

Imagine a lemonade stand where you don't just sell lemonade, you also recruit your friends to open their own stands. Then you get a small cut of every cup they sell, and they get a cut of what their friends sell. Sounds great, right? The problem is that lemonade only sells so many cups, and there are only so many friends. Eventually the people at the bottom of the pile are trying to sell lemonade to a town that already has plenty of stands, and most of them end up spending more on lemonade mix, cups, and fancy starter kits than they ever earn back.

That's the main reason people are wary of MLMs, which is short for multi-level marketing. The money at the top mostly comes from the people underneath. The company often makes its real profit from selling starter kits, training courses, and monthly "required" purchases to recruits, rather than from customers who actually want the product. Because you earn more by signing people up than by selling to shoppers, the business ends up pushing its members to recruit instead of finding real buyers.

The numbers are the big warning sign. Studies of MLM income disclosures, including a well-known one by the US Federal Trade Commission, have found that the large majority of participants lose money once you count what they spent on inventory and fees. Many earn very little, and a small group at the top does very well. Friends and family also get pulled in, which is why people on Reddit often describe losing relationships along with their money.

Not every MLM is a complete fraud, and some people do make money with them. But because the odds are so poor and the pressure to recruit is so strong, many people see them as something to approach with a lot of caution.

Geothermal energy comes from the heat stored inside the Earth, and that heat has two main origins. The first is primordial heat left over from the planet's formation about 4.5 billion years ago. As dust, rock, and planetesimals collided and accreted to build the Earth, the energy of those impacts was converted into heat. Additional heat was released when dense materials like iron sank toward the center to form the core, a process that turned gravitational energy into thermal energy. Because rock is a poor conductor, much of this original heat is still trapped deep inside the planet.

The second and roughly comparable source is radioactive decay. Elements such as uranium, thorium, and potassium-40, distributed mainly through the crust and mantle, continuously break down and release energy as heat. Estimates suggest that radioactive decay accounts for somewhere around half of the heat currently flowing out of the Earth, with the remainder coming from that ancient primordial reserve.

This internal heat makes the Earth's core extremely hot, with temperatures comparable to the surface of the Sun, and it flows outward through the mantle and crust. In most places the temperature rises by about 25 to 30 degrees Celsius for every kilometer of depth. In certain regions, especially near tectonic plate boundaries, volcanic areas, and hotspots like Iceland, Yellowstone, or New Zealand, molten rock rises closer to the surface and concentrates the heat at shallow depths.

Humans tap this energy mainly through water. Groundwater that seeps down into hot rock becomes heated, sometimes forming steam or hot springs, and wells can bring this hot water or steam to the surface to drive turbines for electricity or to supply direct heating. Separately, shallow ground-source heat pumps take advantage of the fairly constant temperature of the ground just a few meters down, though that near-surface warmth is partly influenced by solar heating rather than purely by heat from the deep interior.

Long ago, there was a brave soldier named Snake. His friend and teacher, Big Boss, was a great hero, but one day Big Boss went bad and started a secret army. Snake had to stop him and his giant walking robot tank called Metal Gear.

Many years later, Snake was sent on a new mission to stop a different Metal Gear robot. Snake had a twin brother, a clone made from his own body, named Liquid. Liquid was bad, and Snake had to beat him too. Later, Snake found out that the whole mess was run by a big computer brain called the Patriots, which secretly controlled the world.

The story then went back in time to show how Big Boss first became a soldier and why he turned against his country. Snake ended up fighting many more battles and clones of himself, and he got very old. In the end, he helped turn off the Patriots' computers so people could be free to make their own choices.

The story has lots of twists and some of the characters even come back from the dead, so it can get confusing. But the main idea is simple: a good soldier fights bad people, learns that the truth is complicated, and tries to make the world a little safer and freer.

When an insect dies, it no longer has the strength or energy to keep itself upright, so it simply topples over and lands on its back. Think of lying down on the ground with your eyes shut: you wouldn't have any say in which way you ended up facing. A dead bug is in the same situation, unable to decide how its body comes to rest.

No, they are related but not the same. Keeping track of your money means recording and monitoring what actually comes in and goes out, so you know where it has been going. It is a looking-backward activity: you review transactions, check bank statements, or use an app to categorize spending. A budget is a plan for the future. It sets intended amounts for spending, saving, and bills before you spend, so you decide in advance how your money should be used.

The two work best together. Tracking gives you the real numbers that make a budget realistic, since you may discover that you spend far more on dining out than you assumed. The budget then gives your tracking a purpose, because you can compare what you actually spent against what you planned and adjust accordingly. You can track money without a budget, and some people do, but tracking alone tells you what happened rather than guiding what you do next.

Yes, it's very normal, and researchers have studied it. People often treat money differently depending on where it comes from, what it's for, or which account it sits in. Economists call this "mental accounting," a term popularized by Richard Thaler, who observed that someone might happily splurge a bonus on a vacation while carefully pinching pennies on groceries, even though money is fungible and a dollar is a dollar. Many people keep a "fun money" category, feel that a tax refund is somehow less real than their paycheck, or hesitate to touch savings they've labeled for emergencies.

These separations can be useful. They help people stick to budgets, avoid spending long-term savings impulsively, and make goals feel concrete. Setting aside money for a specific purpose often makes it easier to actually save. The mental boxes can become a problem when they lead to inconsistent decisions, such as carrying high-interest credit card debt while keeping a large balance in a low-interest savings account, or treating windfalls as free money to waste when they could meaningfully improve your finances.

So the habit itself is common and not a sign of anything wrong. A helpful test is whether your categories serve your goals or work against them. If they keep you on track, they're doing their job. If they lead you to choices you later regret or that don't make sense when you look at the whole picture, it may be worth reexamining them.

Dizziness while pregnant may stem from several causes, such as blood pressure that runs too low, blood sugar that drops too far, or not having enough fluid in the body. In some cases it can point to something more serious, like pre-eclampsia, a blood pressure disorder that develops during pregnancy. If your daughter feels lightheaded, the best step is to have her lie down and take it easy. Offer her something to drink and a small snack to help bring her blood sugar back up. If the dizziness continues, or if she notices other troubling signs such as chest pain or trouble breathing, she should reach out to her healthcare provider for a proper assessment. She should also rest as much as possible and avoid standing for extended stretches. If she struggles to keep liquids down, a visit to her healthcare provider for evaluation and treatment may be necessary.

Lisp is one of the oldest families of programming languages still in widespread use, created by John McCarthy at MIT in 1958. Its name is short for "LISt Processing," reflecting its original focus on manipulating lists, which remain its central data structure. Lisp was among the first languages to support functions as first-class values, automatic memory management through garbage collection, and conditionals as expressions, and it introduced ideas that many later languages adopted.

The language is known for its distinctive syntax, which uses fully parenthesized prefix notation. A function call such as adding two numbers is written as an opening parenthesis, the operator, its arguments, and a closing parenthesis, so an expression like adding 1 and 2 appears as (+ 1 2). This uniform structure makes Lisp programs themselves built from the same nested lists that the language manipulates, a property called homoiconicity. Because of this, Lisp supports powerful macros, which let programmers write code that generates other code and effectively extend the language's own syntax.

Over the decades, Lisp evolved into many dialects. Early versions such as Lisp 1.5 and MacLisp gave way to Common Lisp, a standardized and large dialect published in the 1980s, and Scheme, a smaller and more minimal dialect emphasizing simplicity and elegant design. Other notable members of the family include Clojure, which runs on the Java Virtual Machine and emphasizes immutable data and concurrency, and Racket, which is designed for language experimentation and teaching. Emacs Lisp, the extension language of the Emacs text editor, is another widely used dialect.

Lisp has been applied across many domains, including artificial intelligence research during the 1960s through 1980s, symbolic computation, computer algebra systems, and editor scripting. Although it never became as mainstream as languages like C or Java, its influence is substantial. Ideas such as garbage collection, conditionals as expressions, dynamic typing, and interactive development with a live running environment trace back to Lisp, and many modern languages have borrowed features it pioneered.

Libya, a North African country, has endured considerable conflict and instability in recent years. In 2011, citizens rose up against Muammar Gaddafi, who had ruled the country for over four decades. The revolt was part of the broader Arab Spring, a wave of protests across several Middle Eastern and North African nations calling for greater democracy and liberty. Gaddafi was eventually ousted and killed, but the nation fell into disorder as rival factions and militias battled for control. Two principal blocs now compete for power: the Government of National Accord, which is internationally recognized and based in the capital, Tripoli, and the Libyan National Army, which operates from the eastern city of Tobruk. Matters are made more complicated by numerous other armed groups and by foreign states such as Turkey and Russia, which back opposing sides. The 2013 assassination of the Libyan ambassador, which you brought up, took place in Benghazi, an eastern city, when Jala Al-Abdul Salam Arusi was shot dead by unidentified assailants. Who carried out the killing, and why, remains unclear. Libya's turmoil frequently concerns the international community and the President of the United States, since it affects regional stability, the movement of refugees and migrants, and access to oil supplies. Still, no simple fix exists, and restoring peace and stability will likely require sustained effort from many countries and organizations over a long period.

Civil engineering is the field of engineering concerned with designing, building, and maintaining the built environment, which covers public infrastructure like roads, bridges, water and sewer networks, and buildings. Professionals in this area handle the planning, design, construction, and running of these systems, and they also oversee the management of natural resources and the surrounding environment. Their work might involve transportation projects, such as laying out roads, bridges, and airports, or water-related projects, such as constructing treatment facilities, irrigation networks, and flood defenses. Others focus on the built environment itself, designing buildings, structures, and foundations, or on environmental engineering, creating systems that treat and manage waste and pollution. To analyze and design infrastructure, civil engineers rely on a range of tools and methods, including computer-aided design (CAD) software, and they may use specialized instruments like surveying equipment to collect data and take measurements on site. Beyond technical expertise, success in the profession also requires strong problem-solving, communication, and project management abilities.

I can't say what your brother's spots are without seeing his actual results, but I can explain the usual possibilities and how to find reliable information.

The test matters a lot. If it was a nuclear stress test (a scan using a radioactive tracer), a "dark spot" or "cold spot" usually means an area of the heart muscle that isn't receiving enough blood flow, either during exercise or at rest. That most often points to a narrowed or blocked coronary artery, which is why the next step is a catheterization: the doctors can look directly at the arteries and often fix a blockage with a stent in the same procedure. If a resting scan shows the dark area, it can also mean scar tissue from a past heart attack, sometimes one the person never noticed. On a cardiac MRI, dark or bright areas can reflect scarring, inflammation, or other changes in the muscle. On an echocardiogram, the term is less common, though doctors might describe areas that move poorly. Sometimes spots also turn out to be artifacts, such as tissue like the diaphragm or breast blocking the signal, which is one reason a cath is used to confirm.

Because the cardiologist wants a cath, the likely suspicion is reduced blood flow in the coronary arteries, which is a very treatable and common problem when caught. Concern from the doctor is a reason to follow up promptly, not necessarily a sign of something dire. Your brother should ask the cardiologist directly: which test showed this, what do the spots most likely represent, which part of the heart they are in, and what outcomes they are hoping to learn from the cath. Asking for a copy of the report is reasonable, and he can ask them to walk him through the images.

For reading more, the American Heart Association, the Mayo Clinic, and the Cleveland Clinic all have patient pages on nuclear stress tests, coronary artery disease, and cardiac catheterization. Searching those terms along with "perfusion defect" will take you to the right material.

As for you, twins share much or all of their genes, so family history and inherited risk matter. If he turns out to have coronary disease, your own risk is higher than average, particularly if he is an identical twin. You already have mitral valve prolapse with regurgitation and an enlarged left ventricle, so you presumably have a cardiologist. I'd tell that doctor about your brother's findings, and ask whether you should have a stress test, a coronary calcium scan, or other screening, and whether your cholesterol, blood pressure, and blood sugar are well checked. Seek care urgently if you ever have chest pain or pressure, unusual shortness of breath, fainting, or palpitations that worry you.

I hope his cath goes smoothly and gives clear answers.

You can, and people do it all the time. The catch is that once you pay someone to manage money for you, or take a share of the returns, you've stepped into territory that securities and investment advisory laws regulate heavily, and the rules differ by country. The informal handshake version is the risky one.

In the United States, for example, someone who manages other people's money for compensation generally has to register as an investment adviser, either with the SEC or their state, unless an exemption applies. Taking a share of profits is a performance fee, and those are restricted for retail clients. There are rules about who may be charged them, typically wealthier or more sophisticated investors, and about how they're structured. If the two of you pool money into a common enterprise where you rely on his efforts for returns, that arrangement can also qualify as a security under the Howey test, which triggers registration or exemption requirements. Pooled vehicles may also fall under the Investment Company Act, which is why hedge funds are structured so carefully, with limits on investor numbers or qualifications.

There are also practical reasons beyond legal ones. Custody is a big one: handing someone your money invites fraud, and many Ponzi schemes began as friendly arrangements like this. Loss sharing is awkward, since he may take outsized risks when he only shares in some of the downside, or you may dispute what counts as a loss versus a fee. Taxes get complicated too, because you may have created a partnership, with reporting obligations. And without a written agreement, disputes over withdrawals, valuation, or what he was allowed to buy are hard to resolve.

Legitimate ways to do something similar exist. You can hire a registered adviser who charges a flat or percentage fee. You can invest in a fund run by a manager. You can form a properly documented partnership or LLC with a lawyer's help, particularly if it's just between you and a friend or family member and he's investing his own money too, which changes the analysis. Giving him trading authority over an account that remains in your name at a regulated brokerage is another common route.

So the short answer is that it isn't banned outright, but doing it casually can run afoul of registration rules and leaves both of you exposed. If you're seriously considering it, a short consultation with a securities lawyer in your jurisdiction is worth the cost.

Some leaves are simply easier for us to digest than others. The human body lacks the enzymes needed to break down cellulose, the fibrous material plants use to build their cell walls. Certain plants have softer leaves with lower cellulose content, which allows our digestive systems to process them and absorb their nutrients. Tougher leaves, such as those of grass, contain a great deal of cellulose, so we struggle to digest them effectively. That is why some leaves make good food while others do not. Does that make sense?

A backdoor is a technique for getting around the usual authentication or security safeguards of a computer system, program, or application. Attackers may use one to break into a system without permission or to carry out unauthorized operations once inside. Backdoors can find their way into a system in several ways: a developer may deliberately include one during construction, an intruder who has already gained entry may plant one, or a weakness that was never fixed may effectively create one. Malicious actors often exploit them to reach confidential information or to take remote control of a machine, and they can also be leveraged to slip past protections or perform activities that would ordinarily be blocked. Because backdoors pose a serious threat, it is essential to locate and eliminate any that exist. Doing so requires routine security audits and testing, along with keeping systems and their software current with the latest patches and updates.

Honestly, nobody can say for sure what animals understand about death, since they can't tell us what's going on in their heads. Some scientists think a few animals have at least a basic grasp of it. Elephants are the usual example. They've been seen going back to the bones of dead herd members and seeming to linger over them, which looks a lot like mourning. Chimps do something similar. They'll grieve for group members who've died and sometimes try to comfort each other after a loss. Birds and some fish probably don't think about death the way we do. They more likely just react to cues like the smell of a predator, which keeps them out of trouble. So it really depends on the species, and probably on what each individual animal has lived through.

"Cake and underwear" stocks is a slang term in finance for companies whose products are considered recession-resistant, meaning people keep buying them even when money is tight. The idea is that during an economic downturn, consumers may cut back on big-ticket items like vacations, cars, or new homes, but they still buy small necessities and modest indulgences. Cake (or sometimes "lipstick") represents affordable treats, and underwear represents basic everyday essentials. Companies in this category often include makers of packaged foods, personal care products, discount retailers, and household staples. The term became popular after the 2008 financial crisis, when investors noticed that such firms tended to hold up better than the broader market. The phrase is closely related to the "lipstick effect," the observation that people buy small luxuries like cosmetics when they cannot afford larger ones.

Honestly, I'd build the emergency fund first, before you throw extra money at the mortgage or start stashing cash for retirement. It's just a savings account you can dip into when something unexpected hits, like a medical bill, a car repair, or losing your job. The point is that when life blows up a little, you're not stuck putting it on a credit card or borrowing from someone.

Once that's in place, then you can think about the mortgage or retirement, and which one comes first really depends on your situation. If your mortgage rate is high, paying it down fast can save you a ton in interest, so that might be the better move. If the rate's low, though, you're probably better off putting that money toward retirement instead.

In the end it comes down to your own numbers and what you're aiming for. I'd sit down, figure out what matters most to you, and put together a budget that fits it. And if you're still not sure, talking to a financial advisor wouldn't hurt.

An itch is your body's way of tapping you on the shoulder and saying "hey, something might be on your skin, check it out!" Your skin is covered in tiny nerve endings, like little alarm wires, and some of them have one special job: noticing things that might be bugging you. When they get poked or bothered, they send a message up to your brain, and your brain turns that message into the feeling we call an itch.

A lot of the time, those alarm wires go off because something is touching your skin very lightly, like a crawling bug, a stray hair, or a scratchy sweater. Long ago, it was really useful to feel an itch when a bug landed on you, because brushing it off could keep it from biting you or making you sick. So the itch is a kind of built-in bug detector.

Other times, the itch comes from inside your body. When a mosquito bites you, or when you touch something you're allergic to, your body releases a chemical called histamine. Histamine is like a helper that rushes to the spot to deal with the problem, but it also tickles those alarm wires, and that's why bug bites itch so much. Dry skin can itch too, because when your skin gets thirsty and cracked, the nerves get a little cranky. Healing cuts often itch as new skin grows and the area gets busy repairing itself.

When you scratch, you're giving your skin a tiny bit of pain, and that little pain distracts your brain so the itch feels quieter for a moment. That's why scratching feels so good. The tricky part is that scratching too hard can hurt your skin, and a hurt skin can make even more itchy chemicals, so sometimes scratching makes the itch come back stronger. That's why grown-ups sometimes say "don't scratch it!"

So an itch is really just your skin's alarm system, sometimes catching a real bug and sometimes just going off because your skin is dry, healing, or reacting to something.

Joe's Crab Shack was a U.S. chain of casual restaurants built around a seafood theme. The first location opened in 1991, and in 2006 the chain was purchased by Ignite Restaurant Group, Inc. Ignite went bankrupt in 2017, after which Landry's, Inc. took over Joe's Crab Shack. Landry's runs a wide range of restaurants and hospitality ventures, and it is a private company owned by the billionaire Tilman Fertitta.

When an S corporation deals with shareholder loans and capital contributions, the key is distinguishing between the two, since they're reported very differently on the books and on the tax return.

A shareholder loan is money the shareholder lends to the corporation, or money the corporation lends to the shareholder. A loan from shareholder to corporation is recorded as a liability, usually in an account such as "Loans from Shareholder" on Schedule L of Form 1120-S. Interest paid to the shareholder is deductible by the corporation as an ordinary business expense (subject to reasonableness and the applicable interest rate rules), and the shareholder reports the interest as income.
