Repayments of principal are not deductible and are not taxable to the shareholder, since they simply return borrowed funds. A loan from the corporation to the shareholder is recorded as a receivable, often labeled "Loans to Shareholders," and it also appears on Schedule L as an asset. The IRS scrutinizes these loans, so they should be documented with a promissory note, a stated interest rate, a repayment schedule, and actual repayments. Without that support, the IRS may recharacterize the advance as a constructive distribution or as wages.

A capital contribution is money or property the shareholder contributes to the corporation in exchange for no additional debt, which increases the shareholder's equity. On the corporation's books it is credited to paid-in capital or additional paid-in capital, and on Schedule L it appears in the capital accounts section, not as a liability. Capital contributions are not taxable to the corporation or the shareholder and generally do not generate a deduction. They do increase the shareholder's stock basis, which matters for determining how much in losses the shareholder can deduct and whether distributions are tax-free.

On Schedule K-2 and K-3 and in the shareholder's Schedule K-1, you report the shareholder's stock basis and debt basis information. Under current rules, the shareholder tracks stock basis and debt basis separately, and a loan made directly by the shareholder to the corporation can create debt basis, which allows losses to pass through once stock basis is exhausted. A capital contribution increases stock basis instead. The Form 7203 is used by the shareholder to report basis calculations when required.

Because the treatment depends heavily on documentation, the substance of the transaction, and the shareholder's basis, it is worth confirming the specifics with a tax professional, particularly for larger or unusual transactions.

A frequency comb is a device that produces a sequence of evenly spaced frequencies, or a frequency spectrum that repeats periodically along the frequency axis. The gap between neighboring frequencies is known as the comb spacing, and it usually falls in the range of a few megahertz to a few gigahertz. The term "comb" arises because, when the output is plotted against frequency, the spectral lines resemble the teeth of a comb. These devices play an important role in many scientific and technological fields, including precision spectroscopy, metrology, and telecommunications. They can also produce ultra-short optical pulses, which are valuable in areas such as nonlinear optics and high-precision measurement. Although several approaches exist for creating a frequency comb, one of the most widespread is the mode-locked laser. In this technique, the laser cavity is actively stabilized so that it emits a train of extremely brief, evenly spaced light pulses. The spectrum of each pulse forms a frequency comb, and its comb spacing is set by the pulse repetition rate. Additional techniques for producing frequency combs include electro-optic modulators, nonlinear optical processes, and microresonator systems.

A Tensor Processing Unit (TPU) is a type of application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC) developed by Google to accelerate machine learning workloads, particularly neural network training and inference. Google began using TPUs internally around 2015 and later made them available to outside developers through its Google Cloud Platform. The name refers to tensors, which are multi-dimensional arrays of numbers that form the basic data structure of frameworks like TensorFlow, and which are central to the matrix and vector calculations that deep learning requires.

Unlike general-purpose processors such as CPUs, which handle a wide range of tasks, or GPUs, which were originally designed for graphics but later adapted for parallel computing, TPUs are built specifically for the kinds of operations common in machine learning. Their most distinctive feature is a large matrix multiplication unit, often called a systolic array, in which data flows through a grid of processing elements in a rhythmic, pipelined fashion. This design lets the chip perform huge numbers of multiply-and-accumulate operations efficiently while minimizing the energy and memory traffic needed to move data around. TPUs also typically use reduced-precision number formats, such as bfloat16 or int8, which speed up computation and reduce memory use with little loss in model accuracy.

TPUs are offered in several generations, with each version improving performance, memory capacity, and interconnect speed. Multiple TPU chips can be linked together into larger clusters called pods, allowing very large models to be trained across thousands of chips. Google uses TPUs to power many of its own services, including search ranking, translation, and its large language models, and researchers and companies can rent TPU capacity through the cloud rather than buying hardware.

The Guardian is a British daily newspaper, founded in 1821 in Manchester as The Manchester Guardian by John Edward Taylor. It was renamed The Guardian in 1959 and moved its headquarters to London. Its founding was tied to a reformist, liberal political outlook, and it has long been associated with centre-left and progressive viewpoints, though it describes itself as independent in its editorial stance.

The paper is published both in print and online, and its website is one of the most widely read English-language news sites in the world. It is known for investigative journalism, international reporting, and coverage of environmental issues, and it has won numerous awards, including Pulitzer Prizes for work it published in partnership with others, such as its reporting on mass surveillance based on documents leaked by Edward Snowden.

The Guardian is owned by the Scott Trust, a non-profit trust created to protect the paper's editorial independence and financial stability, so it is not owned by shareholders in the usual way. This structure is part of why the paper has emphasized funding through reader donations and subscriptions in recent years, alongside advertising.

Fever and chills in pregnancy have many possible causes. The most common are infections such as urinary tract infections or kidney infections, which are more frequent in pregnancy because of changes in the urinary tract. Other causes include respiratory infections (flu tests can miss other viruses or pneumonia), infections of the uterus or amniotic fluid, gallbladder or appendix problems, and bloodstream infections. Chills, shaking, and feeling cold often happen as the body's temperature is rising or when it is fighting an infection, so a person can feel freezing while the forehead feels hot. Fever also comes and goes, and medications like acetaminophen or ibuprofen can bring a temperature down enough that it looks normal on a check, even while the infection is still active. So "no fever" in the ER does not rule out a serious infection.

Your friend needs urgent medical attention, and I would not wait for another routine check. At 31 weeks, an unexplained infection can affect both her and the baby quickly, and symptoms that have lasted three days with severe shaking and inability to warm up are concerning. She should tell the hospital team right away that she is pregnant, that she has had fever and chills for three days, and that she still feels very ill. If she is still in the hospital, ask the nurses and doctors to reassess her and to check whether she has had a full infection workup, including blood and urine cultures and an evaluation of the pregnancy.

Call 911 or go to the emergency department immediately if she becomes confused or very drowsy, has trouble breathing, chest pain, a racing heartbeat, fainting, very little urine, a seizure, or a severe headache. Also seek care right away if she has vaginal bleeding, fluid leaking, regular contractions, or notices that the baby is moving much less than usual.

ASP.NET is a web application framework from Microsoft that operates on the .NET platform. Developers use it to create dynamic web applications, websites, and web services. The .NET platform, also created by Microsoft, is a software development environment made up of a runtime, a collection of class libraries, and tools for building, deploying, and maintaining applications. Its framework offers a shared set of APIs and runtime services that any programming language targeting .NET can rely on. ASP.NET sits on top of this framework and supplies libraries and tools tailored to web-based applications. Its features, including server controls, form validation, and data access, simplify web development. To sum up, .NET is a development platform comprising a runtime and a set of libraries and tools, while ASP.NET is a web application framework built on that platform to streamline the creation of web applications.

A company may decide to distribute dividends to its shareholders for a number of reasons. The first is to reward investors for putting their money into the business. When a company pays a dividend, it is in effect passing along part of its profits to the people who own it, which can be viewed as a gesture of gratitude for their support and confidence. A second reason is to show the market that the company is in good financial shape and earns profits consistently. Such a signal can strengthen trust in the company and push up the price of its shares. Dividends also matter to certain investors, especially retirees and those close to retiring, who may depend on them as income. For these shareholders, a reliable flow of dividend payments can strongly influence whether they keep a particular stock. To sum up, paying dividends can benefit a company in several ways: it rewards shareholders, demonstrates financial strength, and supplies income to investors who need it.

The Bad Girls Club is a reality TV show that ran on the Oxygen network from 2006 to 2017. It centered on a set of young women sharing a house and was recognized for their unruly, defiant conduct. A fresh group of women joined the cast for each season, which means a large number of participants have appeared over the years. Because the series ran for more than ten years and included many seasons and cast members, I'm unable to offer a full roster of everyone who took part.

So British Energy Nuclear Power Notes are basically a financial instrument put out by British Energy Group, the company that runs nuclear plants in the UK. What they're worth depends on a few things: how creditworthy British Energy is, what interest rates are doing in the market, and how much investors actually want them.

If you're trying to find the current value, your best bet is a financial news site. You could also ask a financial advisor or a broker, since they can usually look it up quickly. British Energy's own website might have something on it too, and so might the big market data providers.

Nervousness, low confidence, and crying when you feel strong emotions usually come from several things working together. Anxiety is one of the most common sources. When you fear judgment, as you might with a boss or professor, your body can switch into a stress response that tightens the throat, speeds the heartbeat, and makes tears come easily. Early experiences matter too. If you grew up in a home where feelings were criticized, dismissed, or punished, or where you had to be careful around people in charge, you may have learned to hold back your opinions or to become overwhelmed when you're put on the spot. Repeated experiences of being talked over, ignored, or embarrassed can also wear down confidence over time. Some people are also simply more sensitive to emotion, reacting more strongly and more quickly than others, and that trait can be part of who they are rather than a flaw.

Beyond depression, several conditions can produce the pattern you describe. Social anxiety disorder is a strong candidate, since it centers on fear of judgment in situations like speaking to authority figures, and it often includes the physical symptoms of choking up or crying. Generalized anxiety disorder, where worry is constant across many situations, can also make everyday interactions feel draining. Post-traumatic stress disorder or complex trauma can cause intense emotional reactions to situations that feel similar to past threats, even when the present situation is harmless. Emotional dysregulation, which is a core feature of borderline personality disorder but can also occur on its own or alongside other conditions, involves strong emotional reactions that are hard to modulate and can make tears feel like an automatic response. ADHD sometimes includes emotional sensitivity and difficulty managing frustration or disappointment. Autism can affect how people recognize and express their own feelings, which sometimes shows up as difficulty stating preferences or reacting in ways others don't expect. Less commonly, neurological conditions such as pseudobulbar affect cause involuntary crying, though those usually occur alongside other neurological symptoms. Physical factors such as thyroid problems, certain medications, or sleep deprivation can also intensify emotional reactions.

Because several of these conditions look similar from the outside, the most useful next step is a visit with a doctor or a mental health professional who can ask detailed questions and, if needed, rule out physical causes. Be specific about when the crying happens, how long you've experienced it, and whether it started at a particular time. Therapy, especially cognitive behavioral therapy for anxiety or dialectical behavior therapy for emotional regulation, is often very effective for exactly this kind of difficulty, and you can learn practical skills for staying steady in tense conversations. In the meantime, it can help to practice short, low-stakes conversations, to prepare brief sentences in advance for meetings with your boss or professor, and to remember that choking up is something many people experience and can recover from without it defining the interaction. If the crying or lack of confidence is making work or school harder, that is a good reason to reach out for support sooner rather than later.

Okay so a Roth IRA is basically a retirement account that gives you a tax break, and it's named after Senator William Roth, who pushed the law that created it. Here's the gist. You put money in, either as one lump sum or little by little over time. That money counts as after-tax money since you've already paid income tax on it. Once it's in there, it can grow, and you can invest it in stuff like mutual funds, stocks, or bonds. The fun part comes later: when you retire and start pulling money out, you don't owe tax on it, because you already paid taxes going in. There are caps on how much you can put in each year, though. For 2021 it was $6,000 if you were under 50 and $7,000 if you were 50 or older. Hope that helps! Shoot me a message if you've got more questions about Roth IRAs.

A duvet cover is a removable fabric case that encloses a duvet, which is the soft, fluffy insert filled with down, feathers, or synthetic fibers. Its main job is to protect the duvet itself from dirt, body oils, sweat, and stains, so the insert stays clean and fresh. Because the cover is the layer that touches your skin, it can be washed regularly, often weekly, while the duvet itself needs cleaning far less often. This makes bed linens much easier to maintain.

Duvet covers also serve a decorative purpose. They come in a wide range of colors, patterns, and textures, so you can change the look of your bedroom simply by swapping covers, without buying a new comforter. Many people choose them for seasonal updates or to match a particular style.

In addition, the cover helps keep the duvet's filling evenly distributed and prevents it from shifting or clumping inside, which helps the insert last longer and retain its loft.

The answer depends on whether you need broker-provided streaming or raw tick data for analysis, and on your asset class, region, and whether you qualify as a professional.

For streaming quotes through a broker, Interactive Brokers is usually the strongest on price. Its market data subscriptions are priced per exchange and are often waived with a minimum commission, and its API gives programmatic access to real-time feeds. Alpaca is a good low-cost option for US equities and API-driven trading, though its free tier uses the IEX feed, which covers only a fraction of volume, so you'd need a paid plan for full consolidated (SIP) data. Schwab's thinkorswim platform provides free real-time streaming quotes and tick-level time and sales for retail accounts, and Schwab's trading API is now available for programmatic use. Fidelity and E*TRADE also stream real-time quotes for free to retail customers, but their data depth and API access are more limited than the others.

If you need true tick-by-tick history or a dependable feed for backtesting or research, a broker's streaming interface is often not the right tool. Third-party vendors such as Databento, Polygon.io, IQFeed (DTN), and Kibot sell historical and real-time tick data, usually on a per-exchange or per-dataset basis, and their pricing is often more transparent for bulk data.

Costs change frequently, and exchange data fees vary by country and by whether you're classed as a professional or a non-professional subscriber. Before committing, check the current fee schedules on each provider's site and, if the feed matters for execution or research, test a free trial or a small subscription first.

I'm concerned about what you're describing. Pain that has moved into your back and sides, feels like your insides are on fire, and has become constant, along with itching all over and oily stools, can mean a gallstone is blocking a bile duct or that the pancreas is inflamed. Both can become serious quickly, and they need to be assessed now rather than while you wait on a list. Please don't wait for your scheduled surgery.

Go back to the emergency department today, and don't leave until a doctor has examined you and checked your blood tests. Ask for a senior doctor if the first person you see doesn't take your symptoms seriously. You can say something like: "My pain has changed, it's now constant and in my back and sides, I'm itching all over, and my stools are oily. I'm worried about a blocked bile duct or pancreatitis, and I need blood tests for liver function and lipase and an ultrasound." Those tests are the ones that would show whether something is blocking your bile duct or inflaming your pancreas.

Call emergency services (999 in the UK, or 112 or 911 elsewhere) straight away if you develop any of these: yellowing of your skin or the whites of your eyes, dark urine, pale or clay-coloured stools, a high fever or shaking chills, repeated vomiting, fainting or feeling very dizzy, or pain so severe that you can't stay still or it isn't eased by the painkillers you've been given.

Until you're seen, avoid fatty meals, don't drink alcohol, and try to eat only small amounts of plain food. Keep a note of when the pain started, what it feels like, and what you've taken for it, so you can give the doctors clear information.

The discomfort you feel when you contract your muscles may be caused by levator ani syndrome, a form of long-term pelvic pain resulting from spasms in the pelvic floor muscles, including the levator ani muscles that hold up the rectum and anus. This condition can be set off by things like having a bowel movement, sexual activity, or sitting for long periods, and it may produce pain in the rectum, anus, and perineum (the region lying between the anus and the scrotum or vulva). Your pain could also stem from other causes, such as a strained muscle or nerve irritation in the pelvic region. Consulting a healthcare professional is important so that the source of your pain can be identified and appropriate treatment can be started.

Paraconsistent logic is a family of logical systems that tolerates contradictions within a body of statements or beliefs. Classical logic treats a contradiction as an impossibility, so that any statement clashing with another must be false. Paraconsistent logic departs from this view: contradictions need not be false, and a statement may be both true and false at once. The framework emerged as an attempt to capture more faithfully the messiness of natural language and the way people actually reason and argue. It has found uses in philosophy, linguistics, and artificial intelligence. A central tenet is that contradictory claims can exist side by side without cancelling one another, unlike in classical logic, where a contradiction always signals falsehood. Within this framework, a statement may count as true in a given context even though it conflicts with another statement that is also taken as true in that same context. Logicians have pursued many different approaches and devised varied systems and principles for handling contradictions. Among the best-known are dialetheism, the view that some contradictions are genuinely true, and supervaluationism, which permits multiple conflicting statements to coexist without forcing each of them to be either true or false.

So a dynamic Bayesian network (DBN) is basically a probabilistic graphical model that tracks how a set of variables and their possible values change over time. Think of it as a regular Bayesian network that's been extended to handle temporal dependencies. Each variable gets its own node in the graph, and the edges show how variables depend on each other. The nodes are organized into layers, one per time point, so each layer captures the state of the system at that moment. Edges within a layer show dependencies between variables at the same time, while edges between layers show how things at one time affect things at another. That's what makes DBNs handy for systems that evolve, since you can model those links and predict where the system is headed. You'll see them used in all sorts of areas, from natural language processing and bioinformatics to finance.

So basically, options are contracts that give you the right, but not the obligation, to buy or sell some underlying asset at a set price by a certain date. You can use that right any time before the option expires, as long as it's still in the money. The expiration date is the last day you can exercise it. If you don't exercise by then, it just expires worthless.

People use options to hedge risk or to bet on where a price is headed. A call gives you the right to buy the asset, and a put gives you the right to sell it. The underlying can be pretty much anything financial: stocks, bonds, currencies, commodities, or futures contracts.

No exchange-traded fund or common security tracks the 30-year fixed mortgage rate directly, because that rate is a survey average (most often Freddie Mac's weekly Primary Mortgage Market Survey or the daily Mortgage News Daily index) rather than a traded price. What you can do is trade the instruments that mortgage rates are built from, and the choice depends on whether you want something that rises when mortgage rates rise or something that moves in price opposite to them.

The single best benchmark is the 10-year Treasury yield. Although mortgages have 30-year terms, most are refinanced or paid off within about seven to ten years, so lenders price them off the 10-year note plus a spread that has historically been around 1.5 to 2 percentage points and widened to roughly 2.5 to 3 points in 2022 and 2023. You can follow the yield itself through the CBOE ticker TNX, or trade it through 10-year Treasury note futures on the CME. Because the spread moves independently, even a perfect 10-year proxy will diverge from mortgage rates at times.

If you want the actual mortgage component, including that spread, look at agency mortgage-backed securities. ETFs such as the iShares MBS ETF (MBB), Vanguard Mortgage-Backed Securities ETF (VMBS), and SPDR Portfolio Mortgage Backed Bond ETF (SPMB) hold the pools of 30-year mortgages that lenders sell into, so their prices fall when mortgage rates rise and rise when rates fall. They are the most faithful inverse proxy for mortgage rates, though they also include some 15-year loans and are affected by prepayment behavior. Institutional traders use the to-be-announced (TBA) market for Fannie Mae and Ginnie Mae securities, which is where mortgage pricing is effectively set each day.

If you want a security that gains when mortgage rates climb, the FolioBeyond Alternative Income and Interest Rate Hedge ETF (RISR) is probably the closest fit, since it holds interest-only mortgage strips whose value increases as rates rise and refinancing slows. Other options that go up with longer-term rates more generally include the Simplify Interest Rate Hedge ETF (PFIX), which uses options on long-dated rates, and inverse Treasury funds like ProShares Short 20+ Year Treasury (TBF) or the leveraged ProShares UltraShort 20+ Year Treasury (TBT). These track Treasury yields rather than mortgage spreads and, in the leveraged case, suffer decay over time, so they are better suited to short-term hedging than long-term tracking.

In short, for a direct inverse read of mortgage pricing, MBB or VMBS are the cleanest choices; for upside exposure to rising mortgage rates, RISR is the most mortgage-specific; and the 10-year Treasury yield remains the most useful single number for anticipating where 30-year mortgage rates are headed.

Good question! Freshwater fish such as the Northern Pike can turn up in lakes that have no connection to one another, spread across vast regions and sometimes even different continents. This happens through a process known as dispersal, in which an organism, here a fish, travels from one location to another and founds a new population there. Freshwater fish can disperse to new areas in several ways. First, there is natural dispersal. Certain fish swim well enough to cover long distances and reach other bodies of water. Northern Pike, for instance, are powerful swimmers and can move downstream into new lakes or rivers. Second, there is dispersal aided by humans. People sometimes stock a body of water with a new fish species for recreational angling, or they may unintentionally let a fish loose in a new place while moving it for another purpose. Third, there is historical dispersal. In some cases, fish spread into new areas long ago and then became established. During the last ice age, for example, ice blanketed much of the world, and some fish species may have survived in isolated pockets of water. Once the ice melted, those fish could spread out and form populations in new places. In short, dispersal explains how freshwater fish like the Northern Pike can end up in unconnected lakes across enormous regions and even on different continents.

Antibodies are used in a wide range of medical, scientific, and industrial settings, largely because they bind very specifically to particular target molecules. In medicine, they are the basis of many treatments, including monoclonal antibody drugs that block cancer-promoting proteins, neutralize inflammatory signals in autoimmune diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis and Crohn's disease, or prevent viruses from entering cells. Antibodies also play a role in vaccines, which stimulate the body to produce its own protective antibodies, and in passive immunization, where antibodies are given directly to a patient for quick protection against infections like rabies or certain snake venoms.

In diagnostics, antibodies are central to many tests. Pregnancy tests, COVID-19 antigen tests, and HIV screening all rely on antibodies that detect specific hormones, viral proteins, or immune markers. Laboratories use techniques such as ELISA and Western blotting to measure the presence and amount of a substance in a blood or tissue sample. Immunohistochemistry uses labeled antibodies to reveal where particular proteins sit within tissue, which helps pathologists diagnose cancers.

In research, antibodies are indispensable tools for identifying and isolating proteins. Scientists use them in flow cytometry to sort and count cells, in microscopy to visualize structures inside cells, and in immunoprecipitation to pull out protein complexes for study. They are also used to purify proteins and to track molecular processes in living systems.

Beyond medicine and the lab, antibodies have applications in food safety testing, where they detect contaminants like bacteria or allergens, and in environmental monitoring for pollutants or pathogens. Some industrial biosensors also use antibodies to detect specific chemicals with high sensitivity.

Antifungal medications like the one you're using, Monistat 1, can be used to treat vaginal infections that occur during pregnancy. The product is considered safe for pregnant women, but you should follow the directions on the packaging and talk to your healthcare provider if you have questions or worries. Taking a bath after applying Monistat 1 is generally fine. That said, try not to stay in the tub for a long time, because extended soaking could rinse the medication away. If it feels more comfortable, you could take a shower instead. If you no longer have itching or burning after using it, that most likely means the treatment is working against the infection. However, if new symptoms appear, or if your symptoms don't get better after you use the medication, reach out to your healthcare provider so they can evaluate you and recommend further treatment.

Honestly, the research on whether weed makes alcoholic cirrhosis worse just isn't clear yet. What we do know is that alcohol is the main cause of cirrhosis, and heavy drinking seriously ups the odds of getting it. Weed might help with some medical issues, but it's not a treatment for alcoholic cirrhosis and shouldn't replace the stuff your doctor recommends.

If you've been diagnosed, the big thing is to stop drinking completely and stick with your care plan. That could mean meds, lifestyle changes, and in severe cases a liver transplant. Also, if anxiety or other mental health stuff is in the mix, get that dealt with too. It can affect your whole health picture, and there are plenty of options like therapy, medication, and self-care habits that actually help. Your healthcare provider is the best person to figure out what works for you.

Worrying about a lump on your child's chest is completely natural. Any new or unfamiliar lump or bump should be looked at by a healthcare professional. The lump may well be benign (not cancerous) and nothing to worry about, but it still needs to be evaluated so that its cause can be identified and, if necessary, treated properly. A chest lump can arise from many things, such as a cyst, an abscess, a swollen lymph node, or a lipoma, which is a harmless growth of fatty tissue. Only a doctor's examination can establish what is causing it. I suggest booking a visit with your child's pediatrician or with a dermatologist. The doctor will probably ask about your child's medical background and examine the lump by hand. They might also advise further testing, such as a biopsy or imaging, to pinpoint the cause. Until the appointment, keep an eye on the lump and watch for any growth or pain. If it changes, or if your child develops other worrying symptoms such as a fever or trouble breathing, contact your child's doctor immediately.

Scotty McCreery is from Garner, North Carolina, a town just southeast of Raleigh. He grew up there and won Season 10 of American Idol in 2011 at the age of 17, making him the youngest winner in the show's history at that point.

A signature is the way a person writes their own name on a document or other object to indicate that they accept or endorse what it says. In effect it means, "Yes, this is my name, and I agree with everything written here."

For hundreds of years, signatures have served to confirm that a person is who they claim to be and that they are prepared to be held accountable for what they have written or agreed to. Although signatures can be forged or imitated, they remain a meaningful way to confirm someone's identity and to show that they bear responsibility for something. For example, suppose you and a friend promise each other something and both sign a sheet of paper to confirm your agreement. If one of you later claims you never made the promise, the other can point to the paper with both signatures and say, "Look, we both signed it, so we both agreed."

In short, signatures are not completely reliable, but they are still an important means of showing that you accept responsibility for something and stand behind what you say.

Sepp Hochreiter is a computer scientist who teaches AI and machine learning at the Institute for Computer Science and Business Information Systems at the University of Applied Sciences Upper Austria. He's best known for his deep learning work, especially long short-term memory (LSTM) networks. These are neural networks that can hold onto information over long stretches of sequential data, which is a big deal for things like speech and text. He's published tons of papers on this stuff and on machine learning more broadly. He's also picked up some serious awards along the way, including the Erwin Schrödinger Prize for young scientists in 2003 and the Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz Prize in 2013.

Yes, though how much depends on what you mean by "additional." At its simplest, an exchange rate is just the price of one currency in terms of another, and that price reflects the relative demand for each currency, so it carries information about trade flows, capital movements, and what market participants collectively expect. Economists have long used it this way. Interest rate differentials between two countries, for example, are closely tied to expected future exchange rate movements through interest rate parity, so the spot rate and forward rates together can reveal what the market anticipates about future monetary policy and inflation.

Beyond that, exchange rates can signal investor sentiment about political stability, fiscal health, or economic growth, since capital tends to flow toward perceived safe and productive economies. Sharp moves can hint at shocks that have not yet appeared in official statistics. Forward rates and currency options also embed market-implied probabilities and volatility expectations, which some analysts read as a gauge of perceived risk.

There are limits, though. The rate is a noisy aggregate shaped by speculation, central bank intervention, and short-term order flow, so it is a poor guide to some things, such as whether a currency is "fairly valued" in the long run. Purchasing power parity offers a benchmark for that, but it adjusts slowly and often disagrees with market prices for years. So the rate contains real information, but it has to be interpreted alongside other data, and it can mislead when read in isolation.

Market capitalization, usually shortened to market cap, is the total market value of a publicly traded company's outstanding shares. You calculate it by multiplying the current share price by the number of shares outstanding. For example, if a company has 100 million shares and each trades at 50 dollars, its market cap is 5 billion dollars.

The figure is a quick way to gauge a company's size and how the market values it. It differs from measures like revenue or total assets because it reflects what investors are collectively willing to pay for the business, including their expectations about future growth and profits. Because it depends on the share price, it changes constantly as the stock moves during trading.

Companies are commonly grouped by market cap. Large-cap companies, often those worth around 10 billion dollars or more, tend to be established and relatively stable. Mid-cap companies fall roughly between 2 and 10 billion dollars, and small-cap companies are typically below that, often carrying more growth potential but also more risk. The exact cutoffs vary depending on the source. Some classifications also include mega-cap for the very largest firms, such as those worth 200 billion dollars or more, and micro-cap for the smallest.

Market cap has limits. It does not tell you how much debt a company carries, so it is not the same as the price of buying the entire business, which is better captured by enterprise value. It also says nothing on its own about whether a stock is cheap or expensive, since a high market cap may or may not be justified by the company's earnings. Still, it remains one of the most widely used starting points for comparing companies and for building index funds and portfolios.

A fuzzy rule is a conditional statement used in fuzzy logic and fuzzy inference systems, where the conditions and conclusions involve vague or imprecise concepts rather than strict true-or-false values. Its general form is "IF x is A THEN y is B," where A and B are fuzzy sets, meaning they describe categories like "high," "warm," or "fast" that have gradual boundaries. For example, a rule for a thermostat might read "IF the temperature is hot THEN reduce the heating a lot," where "hot" and "a lot" are not sharply defined but are represented by membership functions that assign each value a degree of membership between 0 and 1.

The main appeal of fuzzy rules is that they capture the kind of approximate reasoning people use in everyday decisions. Instead of requiring exact thresholds, a system can handle inputs that partially belong to several categories at once. A temperature of 24 degrees, for instance, might be somewhat warm and somewhat hot at the same time, and the rules fire to different extents accordingly.

Using fuzzy rules in practice usually involves four steps. First, inputs are fuzzified by converting crisp values into membership degrees. Second, each rule's antecedent is evaluated, often by combining multiple conditions with fuzzy AND (commonly the minimum or product) or fuzzy OR (commonly the maximum). Third, each rule's conclusion is scaled or clipped according to how strongly its condition was satisfied. Finally, the outputs of all rules are aggregated and defuzzified, typically by computing a centroid, to produce a single crisp output value that can drive a controller or decision.

Fuzzy rules are widely used in control systems such as washing machines, air conditioners, and automotive transmissions, as well as in decision support, pattern recognition, and expert systems. Their strength lies in producing smooth, interpretable behavior from rules that are easy for humans to write and understand, even when the underlying system is complex or hard to model precisely.

Yes, a mortgage can be structured to cover existing debts as well as the cost of buying a home. This arrangement is commonly called a "cash-out refinance." With this type of loan, you borrow more than what remains on your current mortgage and keep the surplus to settle other obligations. Suppose your mortgage balance is $200,000 and you owe $50,000 on credit cards. You could refinance for $250,000: the extra $50,000 would go toward clearing the credit card debt, while the remaining $200,000 would replace your existing mortgage. A cash-out refinance does not suit everyone. It can be an effective way to consolidate debt, but it also means borrowing more, which may not be wise in every situation. It may also lead to a higher interest rate, since lenders often charge more for cash-out refinances than for standard mortgages. Before choosing this option, weigh your financial circumstances carefully and consult a financial advisor or mortgage lender to determine whether it fits your needs.

A day care, sometimes called a child care center, is a facility where children are looked after and supervised during the hours when their parents or guardians cannot be present. These centers offer a secure and caring setting in which children can learn and play under the watch of trained, experienced staff. Many day care centers provide a range of activities, including arts and crafts, educational lessons, and outdoor play. Meals and snacks are often included as well. Some centers run programs designed specifically for infants, toddlers, or school-age children. Depending on the needs of the families they serve, day care centers may be open during the day, in the evening, or overnight.

In linguistic communication, context means the facts and conditions that frame a conversation or piece of writing. This may encompass the physical setting, the people involved, the reason the exchange is taking place, and any relevant prior knowledge. Context matters because it can shape what words and phrases actually mean. Take the sentence "I'm going to the store." At home, the speaker most likely means a nearby grocery shop, whereas on holiday abroad, the same words might point to a gift shop selling mementos. Context also guides word choice and how formal speech should be. Chatting with friends at a relaxed get-together will usually sound far less formal than speaking during a work meeting. Grasping the context of a discussion or text is essential for interpreting it correctly and answering appropriately, and it helps prevent confusion and communication breakdowns.

The cross-entropy method is an algorithm for optimization that seeks the minimum of a function. It works especially well on functions that traditional approaches, such as gradient descent, struggle to handle. Its core idea is to draw samples from a distribution defined over the function's input space, then adjust that distribution according to how well the samples performed. The adjustment is made so that points near the function's minimum become increasingly likely to be drawn. The cycle repeats until the distribution settles on a point close to the minimum.

A major strength of the method is that it needs no gradient calculations, which can be hard or sometimes impossible to obtain for certain functions. As a result, it serves as a handy optimization tool across many kinds of problems. People frequently use it in reinforcement learning and other parts of machine learning, and also for optimization tasks beyond machine learning. Its applications include tuning complex control systems, optimizing financial portfolios, and designing neural network architectures.

Caffeine in coffee can keep you alert and delay the onset of sleep, whereas the Pavlovian conditioning that comes from drinking coffee at bedtime may leave you feeling calm and prepared to rest. These opposing influences may offset one another, or one may dominate, depending on your personal sensitivity to caffeine and the strength of your conditioned response. Acting as a stimulant, caffeine works by activating the brain and heightening wakefulness, which can disrupt sleep. Its effects can last for several hours, so a cup taken close to bedtime may make it harder to drift off. The Pavlovian response, by contrast, is a form of learning in which a particular cue becomes linked with a certain action or feeling. If you drink coffee before bed every night and have come to link it with sleep, your body may begin to unwind and feel ready for rest as soon as the coffee is in front of you. Ultimately, the outcome hinges on how sensitive you are to caffeine and how strongly you have conditioned the response. Some people may find that the soothing effect of the conditioned response helps them fall asleep despite the caffeine's stimulating influence, while others may stay awake regardless of how relaxed they feel.

Honestly, if you're running a business in Ontario, you probably need to register as self-employed. The CRA considers you self-employed if you run a business on your own, either as a sole proprietor or as a partner in a partnership. That means you'll need to register with them and get a business number. Your business income and expenses go on your personal tax return, and you'll owe tax on the profits. Depending on your situation, you might also have to pay quarterly installments on your estimated tax.

There are some exceptions. If you're just doing something as a hobby or picking up the odd gig now and then, you might not need to register. But if you make more than $5,000 a year from that hobby or occasional work, you'll still have to report the income on your return.

The rules can shift depending on what kind of business you run and your particular circumstances, so don't assume this covers everything. If you're not sure where you stand, talk to a tax professional or check the CRA's website. It's worth getting it right early.

Vinod Khosla is an Indian-born American businessman, engineer, and venture capitalist best known as a co-founder of Sun Microsystems, the computer company that developed Java and the Solaris operating system and was acquired by Oracle in 2010. Born in 1955 in India, he studied at the Indian Institute of Technology Delhi before earning a master's degree in biomedical engineering at Carnegie Mellon University and an MBA from the Stanford Graduate School of Business. He co-founded Sun in 1982 along with Scott McNealy, Andy Bechtolsheim, and Bill Joy.

After leaving Sun, Khosla became a prominent venture capitalist. In 1986 he co-founded Kleiner Perkins Caufield & Byers' sister firm, and in 2004 he founded Khosla Ventures, a Menlo Park, California firm that invests in early-stage companies across areas such as clean energy, climate technology, healthcare, artificial intelligence, and food and agriculture. Among its well-known investments are companies in electric vehicles, biofuels, and AI. He has been an early backer of several notable startups and is known for taking bold, high-risk bets on technologies he believes could have large societal impact.

Khosla is also a public commentator on technology, energy, and the future of work and society. He has advocated for climate solutions, has spoken about the potential of artificial intelligence to displace jobs and reshape industries, and has been a frequent voice in debates over innovation policy. His views and investments have sometimes drawn criticism, but he remains one of Silicon Valley's most influential investors and figures.

Yep, non-residents can invest in the London Stock Exchange, but there are a few hoops to jump through, and it depends on your situation and what kind of visa you're on. If you're living in the UK on a visa, you'll generally need to open a brokerage account with a firm that's authorized to offer investment services there. They'll want ID like a passport, plus proof you live in the UK, such as your visa or a rental agreement. Once that's sorted, you can buy and sell LSE-listed stocks and other securities just like any UK resident.

Don't forget the tax side, though. Depending on your home country's rules and your visa type, you might owe tax on your gains or dividends, and you may have reporting obligations too. Worth checking that before you dive in.

And obviously, investing carries risk, so think hard about your finances and how much risk you can stomach. If you're unsure, talk to a professional adviser before putting money in, since what suits one person can be a terrible fit for another.

Flawless duplicates of currency can't really be made, since governments and financial institutions have methods for spotting counterfeits. Deliberately saturating a market with forged bills also wouldn't necessarily harm another nation's economy as intended. Money's worth rests on the confidence people place in it, so if the public distrusts the counterfeit notes, they simply won't be taken as legitimate payment. Rather than undermining an economy, circulating fake currency might backfire and produce even larger problems, including inflation and a loss of faith in the financial system. It is also worth stressing that purposely trying to hurt another country's economy is neither justifiable nor ethical.

South Beach is located in the southern portion of Miami Beach, which is a separate city from Miami itself, situated on a barrier island east of mainland Miami across Biscayne Bay. It occupies roughly the area from the southern tip of the island, known as South Pointe, northward to about Dade Boulevard or 23rd Street, depending on the definition used.

The neighborhood is bordered by the Atlantic Ocean to the east and Biscayne Bay to the west. To reach it from downtown Miami, you typically cross one of the causeways, most commonly the MacArthur Causeway, which connects to the southern end of Miami Beach near Fifth Street, or the Venetian Causeway a bit farther north.

South Beach is famous for its Art Deco Historic District, much of which lines Ocean Drive, Collins Avenue, and Washington Avenue. Other well known spots include Lincoln Road, a pedestrian shopping and dining street, as well as Lummus Park and the wide sandy beaches along the oceanfront. The area is about a 15 to 20 minute drive from downtown Miami without heavy traffic and roughly 25 to 30 minutes from Miami International Airport.

It's hard to say whether you'll be able to conceive normally without knowing more about your situation. Ovacare and Ovaa Shield are both meds that can help regulate cycles and improve your chances, but they're not a guarantee. Folic acid and Duphaston are also commonly prescribed to women trying to get pregnant. Honestly, though, whether it happens comes down to a lot of things: your health, your partner's health, and any underlying conditions that could affect fertility. If you've been trying and it's not working, it's worth talking to a healthcare provider about your options. They can run tests to figure out what's going on and suggest a plan that fits you. In the meantime, a few lifestyle changes can help, like eating well, keeping a healthy weight, managing stress, and cutting back on tobacco and alcohol.

Happy hour gets its name from the period when restaurants and bars offer discounted drinks and, at some venues, reduced-price food. It is generally a chance for people to unwind and socialize with friends after a day at work or school. Despite the name, it rarely lasts only sixty minutes. The special prices usually run for several hours, giving customers a comfortable window to drop in and take advantage of the offers. Certain establishments run happy hour every day, while others limit it to particular weekdays or set times. In short, the term describes a stretch of time for going out, enjoying yourself, and saving money on drinks and food, rather than a strict one-hour period.

Yeah, you can cover a short with stock you already own, though it's worth being clear about what that actually means. When you short a stock, you borrow shares from someone (usually your broker), sell them, and hope the price drops so you can buy them back cheaper, return them, and pocket the difference. If the price climbs instead, you're stuck buying back at a higher price and eating the loss.

To cover, you need to hand back the same number of shares you borrowed. If you already hold shares of that stock, you don't have to go out and buy new ones. You can just return the borrowed shares and keep your own, which closes out the short. If you don't own any shares, though, you'll have to buy them on the market first, and then you're back to paying whatever the current price is.

Fall became the traditional start for new TV seasons mostly because of how people's lives and habits lined up with television over the decades. Back when TV networks were getting started, school and work schedules restarted in September, so families settled back into routines, and that's when people were most likely to sit down in front of the TV every evening. Networks saved their biggest and newest shows for that window, and over time everyone else followed the pattern, so audiences came to expect new shows in the fall.

You're right that it can make sense to launch some shows at other times. Summer is often quieter, with more people outside and on vacation, so it can be harder to get attention there. But because fewer big shows compete for viewers, a smaller show can sometimes stand out more. Networks do sometimes premiere shows in spring or summer for exactly this reason, and some streaming services release shows whenever they're ready, since they don't depend on a weekly schedule.

So the short version is that fall is a habit that grew out of when people were most likely to watch, and smart networks sometimes break that habit when a different time works better for a particular show.

Using a personal credit card for business expenses is legal and common, especially for sole proprietors and new businesses, but it comes with tradeoffs worth understanding before you make it a habit.

The main problem is commingling. When business and personal charges land on the same statement, bookkeeping becomes harder, and you have to separate everything at tax time. If you're audited, you may struggle to prove which expenses were legitimately business-related, which can put deductions at risk. For LLCs and corporations, mixing funds can also weaken the legal separation between you and the business, which is the basis of your limited liability protection. Courts sometimes cite commingling as grounds for "piercing the corporate veil."

There are other downsides. Business debt on a personal card shows up on your personal credit report, and high balances raise your utilization ratio, which can lower your credit score and make it harder to qualify for a mortgage or car loan. Personal cards also typically offer fewer protections and perks for business use, and the credit limit may be too small. Some card issuers' terms prohibit business use, though enforcement is rare. Also, personal cards often lack employee cards and expense-tracking tools.

That said, there are reasons people do it. If you're just starting out, you may not have the business history to qualify for a business card. Sole proprietors don't have the same liability separation issues as incorporated businesses, so the legal risk is lower. Rewards can also be strong on personal cards.

If you do use a personal card, a few habits help a lot. Dedicate one card solely to business expenses so statements are clean. Keep receipts and note the business purpose of each purchase. Use accounting software that syncs with the card, and pay the balance in full monthly to avoid interest, which is only deductible for the business portion. If you're an employee-owner of a corporation, reimburse yourself through a documented expense reimbursement process rather than just paying personally.

Over time, switching to a business credit card is usually better. Many don't report to your personal credit unless you default, they offer higher limits, and they provide cleaner records and useful rewards categories like office supplies, advertising, and shipping. Most small business cards are easy to get with a personal guarantee, even for a new sole proprietorship with no revenue history.

For tax questions specific to your situation and entity type, a CPA can tell you exactly how to document and deduct these expenses.

"Mazel tov" is a Yiddish (and Hebrew) expression that means "good luck" or "congratulations." Literally, the phrase translates to "good constellation" or "good star," from the Hebrew word *mazal*, which refers to a person's fortune or destiny, believed in older tradition to be determined by the stars. People say it to celebrate happy occasions such as weddings, births, graduations, or engagements. It's often shouted or said with enthusiasm, and in Jewish tradition it's sometimes used as a toast or a blessing for good fortune.

Several things could explain this, and the fact that the pain is positional and limited to your torso is useful. The most likely culprits are a bruised or strained abdominal or back muscle, or a cracked or bruised lower rib. Your abdominal muscles and the muscles of the lower back and hip flexors all work to bend and twist your trunk, so a hard landing can strain them, and each time you sit up or lie down you stretch or compress the injured tissue. Lower rib injuries are a common cause of sharp pain when changing position, because the rib cage moves with breathing and with bending, and the lower ribs sit close to the abdomen, so they can feel like belly pain.

A less common but more serious possibility is an injury to an internal organ, such as the kidney, spleen, liver, or the bowel or bladder, or bleeding in the space behind the abdominal cavity. A fall onto the buttocks can transmit force upward, and these injuries sometimes cause pain that is worse with certain movements, though they usually come with other warning signs.

Because you are still having pain several days later and it is making everyday movements difficult, I would recommend seeing a doctor soon. They can examine you and, if needed, order an X-ray to check for rib fractures or a CT scan or ultrasound to look at internal organs. You should seek care immediately, such as at an emergency department, if you notice any of the following: pain that is getting worse or becoming constant, blood in your urine or black or bloody stools, lightheadedness or fainting, a racing heartbeat, a swelling or bruise that is spreading on your belly or flank, nausea or vomiting, fever, trouble urinating, or shortness of breath. Until you are evaluated, avoid heavy lifting, vigorous activity, and contact sports, and use pain relievers only as directed, keeping in mind that some medications can increase bleeding risk if an internal injury is present.

Artificial neural networks are computer programs built to imitate the workings of the human brain. The brain consists of billions of small cells known as neurons, which link up and exchange signals through a web of connections. Along similar lines, an artificial neural network is composed of many interlinked "neurons" that can handle and pass along information. These neurons are arranged in layers: the input layer takes in information, the hidden layers work on it, and the output layer delivers a result. When data is fed into such a network, it analyzes the information and produces a prediction or decision drawn from what it has learned. Consider, for instance, a network trained to identify pictures of animals; when shown a new photo, it can estimate which animal appears there by drawing on its experience with earlier examples. Neural networks have a broad range of uses, such as recognizing images and speech, translating languages, and even playing games like chess. They are a strong tool for tackling problems too intricate for people to solve unaided.

Land Rover, a British maker of luxury vehicles, belongs to Tata Motors, an Indian multinational automotive firm. Tata bought the brand from the Ford Motor Company in 2008. The company is recognized for building vehicles meant for off-road use and difficult, rugged terrain, such as SUVs, pickups, and 4x4s. Its history stretches back to the early 1950s, and its vehicles have gained a following worldwide thanks to their performance, durability, and luxurious features.

Imagine you have a tiny piece of Lego. Normally you'd think of it as just "stuff," something you can hold. What Einstein figured out is that this stuff is actually a super-squished-up form of energy. Mass and energy aren't two totally different things; they're the same thing in two different outfits. The equation E = mc² is the exchange rate between them, like how many pennies you get for a dollar.

Why the speed of light squared? The speed of light is a gigantic number, about 300,000 kilometers every second, and squaring it makes it unimaginably bigger. So the equation is saying that a tiny bit of mass is worth an enormous amount of energy. If you could turn a single raisin completely into energy, it would be enough to power a whole city for a day or more. That's the big surprise: everyday stuff has a huge amount of energy locked up inside it, we just usually can't get it out.

Where does this show up in real life? The sun is the best example. Deep inside, it squeezes tiny hydrogen bits together to make helium. The helium that comes out weighs just a little less than the hydrogen that went in. That missing bit of mass didn't disappear; it turned into the light and heat that reach Earth and keep us warm. Every sunny day is E = mc² happening.

Nuclear power plants work in a similar way but in reverse: they split big, heavy atoms like uranium into smaller pieces, and the pieces together weigh slightly less than the original. That little missing mass becomes heat, which boils water, spins turbines, and makes electricity. Nuclear bombs use the same idea, just released all at once, which is why they are so powerful. Doctors also use it: some medical scanners, called PET scanners, rely on tiny particles that vanish completely and turn into energy the machine can detect.

It even works in tiny everyday ways. When you burn wood or a battery runs down, a minuscule amount of mass is lost as energy too, but it's so small no scale on Earth could notice.

So the simple version is this: stuff is frozen energy, and E = mc² tells you that even a little bit of stuff holds a really, really big amount of energy.

Predictive analytics is a branch of data analysis that uses historical and current data to estimate the likelihood of future outcomes. Rather than simply describing what has already happened, it tries to answer the question of what is likely to happen next. It combines statistics, data mining, machine learning, and domain knowledge to find patterns in past behavior and apply them to new situations.

The process generally starts with a clearly defined question, such as which customers are likely to cancel a subscription, which transactions may be fraudulent, or how much demand a product will see next quarter. Analysts then collect and clean relevant data, which often takes the most time, since real-world data is messy, incomplete, or inconsistent. Next they select or engineer features, meaning the variables that might carry predictive signal, and choose a modeling technique. Common methods include linear and logistic regression, decision trees, random forests, gradient boosting, neural networks, and time series models. The model is trained on part of the data and tested on another part to see how well it generalizes. Once it performs acceptably, it is deployed so that it can score new data, and it is monitored over time because patterns can drift and accuracy can decline.

The outputs are usually probabilities, scores, or forecasts rather than certainties. A model might say a customer has a 70 percent chance of leaving, which lets a business decide whether to offer a retention discount. This is what separates predictive analytics from descriptive analytics, which summarizes the past, and from prescriptive analytics, which goes further by recommending specific actions.

Applications are widespread. Banks use it for credit scoring and fraud detection. Retailers forecast demand and personalize recommendations. Healthcare providers estimate patient risk of readmission or disease. Manufacturers predict equipment failures so maintenance can be scheduled before breakdowns occur. Insurers price policies, and marketers target campaigns toward people most likely to respond.

There are important limitations. Predictions are only as good as the data behind them, and biased or unrepresentative data can produce unfair or misleading results. Models can overfit, performing well on historical data but poorly on new cases. Correlation found in data does not necessarily mean causation, and sudden changes in the world, such as a pandemic or a new regulation, can make past patterns unreliable. Privacy and transparency are also concerns, especially when predictions affect people's access to credit, jobs, or care. Used carefully, though, predictive analytics helps organizations make more informed, proactive decisions.

Think of it like a lemonade stand that makes money in two ways. A TV station sells lemonade to a few people who pay for each cup they drink, and that's the part that makes the most money. The station is also paid by other companies, like the cable and satellite providers, just for being on their menu. If the station lets everyone drink its lemonade for free at home over the internet, some of those people stop buying the cups or stop asking the other companies for it, and the station's income falls.

More viewers doesn't always mean more money, because the money depends on how the viewing happens. A TV ad on the regular channel is often sold at a higher price than an ad on a streaming app, because the regular channel has a long history of big audiences. Streaming ads can also bring in less per viewer, so a station might get fewer total dollars even with more people watching.

Some shows also come with rules attached. Actors, writers, sports leagues, and music companies often sign contracts that say where and when a show can be shown. A football game might be allowed on TV but not online, or a show might be streamed only after a delay, because the company that owns the rights sold those rights to someone else.

So stations aren't really trying to hide things from people. They're trying to protect the money they already get, and streaming is a new kind of lemonade stand that might make their old business worth less.

Certainly! In air, light moves in straight lines, so we can see objects sharply. Underwater, however, light behaves differently: the water scatters and bends it, so our eyes struggle to make out things clearly. Fish, by contrast, have built-in features that let them see well in this environment. Their eyes have a different shape, and many have a reflective layer called the tapetum lucidum that helps them see in dim light. Fish also contain a pigment called guanine, which they use to see better in the blue light that dominates underwater. That is why we need goggles to see clearly beneath the surface, while fish can see well without them. Does that make sense?

Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty, commonly called the Washington Treaty, forms the basis of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO). It sets out the collective defense commitments shared by member states, declaring that an assault on any one member will be treated as an assault on every member. The text reads: "The Parties agree that an armed attack against one or more of them in Europe or North America shall be considered an attack against them all, and consequently they agree that, if such an armed attack occurs, each of them, in exercise of the right of individual or collective self-defence recognised by Article 51 of the Charter of the United Nations, will assist the Party or Parties so attacked by taking forthwith, individually and in concert with the other Parties, such action as it deems necessary, including the use of armed force, to restore and maintain the security of the North Atlantic area." This clause is central to the treaty, and it has been activated just once, after the terrorist attacks of September 11, 2001 against the United States. Following those attacks, NATO members offered military and logistical assistance to the United States and took part in the wider international campaign against terrorism.

I'm sorry to learn that growth has come back on your chin after a cancerous growth was removed there before. If anything about your health worries you, you should see a healthcare professional. Even though your oncologist didn't say the growth appeared cancerous and didn't offer a biopsy, you should still raise your concerns with them and ask about any testing or treatment that might be needed. Dealing with possible health problems early is always the safer choice. I suggest talking with your oncologist or another medical professional to decide how best to proceed. They can look at the growth, take your medical history into account, and advise on whatever testing or treatment may be necessary.
