Short-term rentals also tend to have more deductible expenses, such as cleaning fees, platform service fees, furnishings, supplies, and utilities you pay on guests' behalf.

Finally, many cities now restrict or require permits for short-term rentals, which isn't strictly a tax issue but can carry fines.

Because these rules interact in complicated ways and depend on your income, how involved you are, and where the property is, it's worth talking to a CPA or tax advisor who works with rental property before you decide, particularly if you're hoping to use depreciation losses to offset other income.

Feelings are a big part of being human, and honestly they're kind of wild when you think about how they work. They're emotions we get in response to stuff that happens around us, like an event, a thought, or a memory. Our brains are packed with billions of neurons, and those little cells talk to each other by firing tiny electrical signals back and forth. So when something hits us, say we're watching a scary movie or hearing a sad song, our brain takes that in and starts sending signals all over the body. Watch a horror flick and your heart might start pounding, and your muscles tense up without you really asking them to. That's why you end up feeling afraid or on edge. Flip it around with a happy song and your brain can tell your muscles to loosen up and your face to smile, and suddenly you feel good. Basically, feelings are our brains making sense of what's going on and reacting to it, and they're a huge part of what makes us who we are.

It isn't fair to claim that everybody dislikes Diablo 3. The game has drawn its fair share of criticism and controversy, yet plenty of players have praised it, and it boasts a sizable community. Certain people may turn away from it for their own reasons, such as disliking how it plays, its visual style, or where the storyline heads. Others may have been put off by bugs or technical trouble, or may believe some mechanics are unjust or poorly balanced. Whether these complaints could ever be fully resolved is hard to say, since each person holds different ideas about what should change. Still, the developers have rolled out many updates and refinements since launch and will likely keep doing so. If you were explaining this to a child, you might say that some people love playing Diablo 3 and think it's wonderful, while others simply don't enjoy it as much for their own reasons. The developers keep trying to improve it, but they can't make everyone happy all the time.

The fastest realistic path to retiring on real estate income combines a high savings rate, aggressive but controlled use of leverage early on, and a deliberate shift toward safety and simplicity as you approach your target. It helps to start with the math. Figure out your annual living expenses, then decide how much net cash flow you need after mortgage payments, taxes, insurance, maintenance, vacancy, capital expenditures, and property management. Many people underestimate these costs, so a common rule of thumb is to assume that roughly 40 to 50 percent of gross rent will go to operating expenses before the mortgage. If you need 60,000 dollars a year and a typical property nets you 300 to 500 dollars a month after everything, you can quickly see you need somewhere between ten and twenty units, or fewer if they are owned free and clear.

The biggest accelerator is not clever deal structure but the gap between what you earn and what you spend. Every extra dollar saved becomes a down payment, and down payments become cash-flowing assets. People who retire within seven to ten years typically save 40 percent or more of their income, live cheaply, and pour that capital into properties. Increasing your income through career moves or a side business matters as much as finding good deals.

House hacking is often the single best starting move. You buy a duplex, triplex, or fourplex with a low down payment owner-occupant loan, such as an FHA loan at 3.5 percent down or a conventional loan at 5 percent, live in one unit, and rent the others. Your housing cost drops to near zero or even turns positive, which dramatically boosts your savings rate. After a year you can move out, keep the property as a rental, and repeat the process with another owner-occupant loan. Doing this several times builds a small portfolio with very little cash.

Another popular accelerator is the BRRRR approach, which stands for buy, rehab, rent, refinance, repeat. You buy a distressed property below market value, renovate it to force appreciation, rent it out, then refinance based on the new higher value to pull most or all of your original cash back out. That recycled capital funds the next deal. This can grow a portfolio quickly, but it demands construction knowledge, reliable contractors, and accurate valuations, and it becomes harder when interest rates are high because refinancing may leave you with weak cash flow.

Some investors speed things up with short-term rentals, small multifamily or commercial properties, or by buying in lower-cost markets where rent-to-price ratios are better. Short-term rentals can produce much higher income but are more like running a hospitality business and face growing local regulation. Cheaper markets often cash flow better on paper but can carry higher tenant turnover, more maintenance, and slower appreciation, so the true return depends heavily on the specific neighborhood.

Once you have a portfolio that roughly covers your expenses, the transition to genuine retirement usually involves reducing risk. Highly leveraged portfolios generate equity growth but thin, fragile cash flow, so many people use a phase where they pay down or pay off mortgages, sometimes by selling a few properties and using the proceeds to eliminate debt on the rest. A smaller number of paid-off properties can produce more reliable income than a large leveraged one. Hiring professional property management is also important if you want the income to be truly passive, even though it costs around 8 to 10 percent of rent.

Tax strategy amplifies everything. Depreciation can shelter much of your rental income from taxes, and in the United States a 1031 exchange lets you sell a property and roll the gains into a larger one without paying capital gains tax immediately. A tax professional familiar with real estate can make a meaningful difference in how quickly you reach your goal.

The honest caveats are that leverage magnifies losses as well as gains, a few bad tenants or a major repair can wipe out a year of profit on a small portfolio, and the timelines people cite online often reflect favorable markets with low rates and rising prices. Keeping healthy cash reserves, ideally six months of expenses per property, buying only deals that cash flow under conservative assumptions, and growing at a pace you can manage will get you there more surely than chasing maximum speed. For most people starting from scratch with a solid income and disciplined spending, ten to fifteen years is a realistic target, with faster outcomes possible for those who combine house hacking, value-add renovations, and a very high savings rate.

Armies have employed camouflage for hundreds of years, yet it has not always been as widespread as it is now. Part of the explanation is that the tools for designing and applying camouflage patterns have only lately reached a level of sophistication that makes them truly effective. Earlier forces typically depended on other means of staying hidden, like taking cover behind natural features of the landscape or releasing smoke to conceal their movements. Camouflage was also not always deemed essential. At times, commanders cared more about appearing conspicuous and intimidating than about avoiding notice. This was particularly the case for forces that leaned on shock and awe, where the spectacle of a large, heavily armed army was intended to dishearten opponents and push them toward surrender. In short, camouflage has changed alongside the tactics and strategies of warfare. Modern militaries now rely on a range of approaches to merge with their environment and evade detection, among them camouflaged uniforms and vehicles, along with advanced technologies such as drones and infrared cameras.

Sudden paleness with pale lips in a child, especially with new tiredness, needs prompt medical attention. Several possibilities are worth raising with her doctor. Anemia, a low red blood cell count or low hemoglobin, is one of the most common causes of pallor and fatigue, and it can result from iron deficiency, blood loss, or other problems. Reduced oxygen delivery is another concern. Her asthma may be flaring or worsening even if she feels fine, and low oxygen levels can show up as pale or grayish lips and exhaustion during simple activities like getting dressed. Heart rhythm or circulation problems can also cause pallor and exertional fatigue, and they need to be checked. Her medications could contribute as well. Clonazepam commonly causes drowsiness and weakness, and risperidone can occasionally affect blood counts or blood pressure. Her Geritol contains iron, so it's worth confirming how much she is actually getting, since both too little and too much iron can cause problems. Infection, low blood sugar, and thyroid problems are other possibilities a doctor would consider.

Because these causes vary a lot in urgency, I'd recommend contacting her pediatrician or doctor today rather than waiting. Ask about a blood count, an iron study, a check of her oxygen saturation, and possibly an electrocardiogram. Tell them exactly what you've seen: when the paleness started, whether her lips look bluish or gray, whether she is breathing harder than usual, and how much effort the dressing takes.

Call 911 or go to an emergency room right away if she has trouble breathing, blue or gray lips or face, chest pain, a racing or irregular heartbeat, fainting or near-fainting, confusion, unusual sleepiness that's hard to wake her from, or if she becomes limp or very weak. Trust your instincts as her parent. If something seems seriously wrong, it is always appropriate to seek emergency care.

Black holes are so densely packed and exert such intense gravity that nothing, light included, can break free once it crosses their boundary. A collision between two of them releases an enormous burst of energy. That energy sends ripples through the fabric of space-time, called gravitational waves. Specialized instruments can pick up these waves, yet spotting them directly is extremely hard. If such a collision took place near Earth, the consequences for our planet could be serious. The released energy might produce intense radiation capable of harming living things. The black holes' gravity could also perturb the orbits of Earth and the other planets in our solar system. Still, the likelihood of this is vanishingly small, since black holes typically lie in the enormous voids of space rather than anywhere near planets like ours.

Truvada is a prescription drug that helps lower the chance of getting HIV for people who face a high risk of exposure to the virus. Its purpose is not to guard against sexually transmitted infections (STIs) apart from HIV. Taken once a day as a pill, it works best alongside other prevention measures, such as using condoms, to cut down on HIV transmission. It has been approved for both men and women and may be used by those who have anal or vaginal sex, as well as by people who could be exposed to HIV through oral sex. Although Truvada can reduce the likelihood of acquiring HIV, it does not ensure that you will avoid HIV or other STIs. Continuing to use condoms and practicing safer sex remains important for further lowering the risk of STI transmission. Regular STI testing and telling sexual partners about your HIV status are also important.

I'm sorry you're dealing with swelling and soreness in your ankle and foot after taking a hit from a softball. If you're in significant pain or are worried about the injury, it's important to see a doctor. Meanwhile, several steps may ease the soreness and swelling. First, rest: stay off the injured foot as much as you can and avoid activities that stress it, since this limits swelling and gives the tissue time to heal. Second, apply ice for 15 to 20 minutes at a stretch to bring down swelling and dull the pain, but wrap the pack in a towel or cloth first so it doesn't cause frostbite. Third, use an elastic bandage to compress the area, which reduces swelling and offers support, though it shouldn't be wrapped so tightly that it restricts blood flow. Fourth, keep the injured area raised above heart level to help fluid drain away. Fifth, an over-the-counter pain reliever such as acetaminophen (Tylenol) or ibuprofen (Advil) may provide relief; follow the directions on the label and never exceed the suggested dose. Finally, if the swelling, pain, or redness continues or gets worse, arrange a follow-up with a healthcare professional for a proper evaluation. Be sure to follow whatever advice your provider gives you, since they can judge how serious the injury is and recommend treatment tailored to you.

Your question, "What is hydrogen in," is incomplete, so I'm not certain what you're asking. Are you asking what hydrogen is in general, what element it is, or how it is used or found in something specific, such as water, fuel, or the human body? If you can tell me the context, I can give you a more precise answer. In the meantime, hydrogen is the lightest and most abundant chemical element in the universe. Its atom has a single proton and a single electron, and it is a colorless, odorless gas under normal conditions. It makes up about three quarters of the ordinary matter in the universe, is a component of water and most organic compounds, and is used in industries such as fertilizer production and petroleum refining.

Karma in Buddhism is basically cause and effect. Every action, whether it's something you do with your body or something that happens in your head, has consequences that shape what comes next for you. What's interesting is that these consequences don't come from some higher power handing out rewards and punishments. They just follow from the way the universe works, kind of like gravity. Every action sets off a chain of events that can help or hurt the person who did it and the people around them. The effects don't stop at this life, either. Buddhists believe in rebirth, so what you do now can carry over into future lives. The goal isn't really to rack up good karma like points, though. It's more about paying attention to what you do and building a compassionate, caring attitude toward all beings, which can eventually lead to enlightenment.

In computing, a byte refers to a chunk of data made up of eight bits. Bits form the most basic unit of information in computers and are commonly used to stand for binary digits, which are ones and zeros. Whenever you save a file on your computer, it occupies a specific number of bytes of storage. A plain text file, for instance, might use up 1 kilobyte (KB), or 1,024 bytes. A high-resolution photo could take several megabytes (MB), which works out to 1,024 KB, or 1,048,576 bytes. A video file may require several gigabytes (GB), equivalent to 1,024 MB, or 1,073,741,824 bytes. Files stored on a hard drive occupy physical room on that device, a small disk that spins inside the computer. Once the hard drive is full, you cannot save anything further until you remove some existing files to create room.

Romani people, sometimes called Gypsies, have a rich and captivating history. Their distinctive culture includes its own music, dance, and customs. For centuries they have traveled and settled in various regions around the globe. Their origins lie in the area that is now India, but over the generations they have dispersed and made homes in numerous countries. One feature that sets Romani culture apart is a deep passion for music and dance. Instruments such as the violin and accordion are common, and their dancing is famous for being spirited and full of energy. Although Romani communities have endured a great deal of discrimination and ill treatment over the years, they have also made significant contributions to the cultures of the places where they have settled. Now, Romani people live in many parts of the world, and they keep celebrating and protecting their distinctive heritage.

Metal's basically a branch of rock built around heavy, crunchy distorted guitar riffs and fast tempos. It borrows from all over the place too, like punk, hardcore, even classical, and the whole thing has this aggressive, high-energy feel to it.

Lyrically, bands go in a bunch of directions. Rebellion is a big one, along with social and political stuff and personal struggles. You'll also see a lot of individualism and giving the finger to authority. Plenty of bands pull from mythology, literature, and fantasy, and they tend to be pretty metaphorical or allegorical about it rather than just saying things straight.

The genre's been around a long time and has splintered into tons of subgenres and subcultures. A lot of that scene has an outsider, rebellious vibe, and I think that's a big part of why fans get hooked. It's just intense and full of energy.

Market basket analysis is basically a data mining trick for spotting which items people tend to buy together. Retailers use it a lot. Say you notice that folks who grab bread also tend to grab butter and jam. You might shelve those things near each other, or run a sale that bundles them. That's the whole idea: once you see the patterns in what customers put in their carts, you can make smarter calls on marketing and sales. It's often paired with other methods, like association rule mining, especially when you're digging through huge datasets.

So the Second Law of Thermodynamics is basically a rule about how heat and energy behave. The simple version is that heat moves from hot stuff to cold stuff, never the other way around on its own. Warm object next to a cooler one? Heat flows from the warm one to the cool one until they even out at the same temperature.

Picture a cup of hot coffee next to a cup of cold water. The coffee's heat drifts over to the water until both are at about the same temp. That's the law doing its thing.

Car engines are another good way to see it. You put gas in, turn the key, and the engine uses the heat from burning that fuel to move the car. But the engine makes extra heat while it runs, and that heat has to go somewhere. According to the law, it flows out of the engine and into the air around it. That's why your engine's hot after a long drive.

So really it's all about how heat and energy move and change around us. It explains why your coffee goes cold, why engines heat up, and why you've got to keep filling the tank to keep the car going.

An ethnic group is a collection of people who share a common cultural background, including language, traditions, customs, and values. Ethnic groups commonly display several defining traits. First, they often possess a shared history, language, and set of cultural practices that set them apart from others. Second, some members may have noticeable physical characteristics, such as skin tone, facial structure, or build, that distinguish them from other populations. Third, they frequently inhabit the same region and feel a sense of belonging to a specific homeland or territory. Fourth, they may organize themselves socially and politically through structures like clans, tribes, or nation-states, which help maintain and define their identity. Finally, they often hold common values and beliefs that shape how they see the world and guide their customs. These traits vary widely from one group to another, and no group is inherently better or worse than any other. Since ethnicity is a social construct, it should never be used as a basis for discriminating against or marginalizing anyone.

There's a small mismatch in your question worth clearing up first. Gastritis usually causes pain in the upper abdomen, above the belly button, while you describe pain just below it. Pain in that lower area that comes and goes is more often related to gas, constipation, or intestinal cramping than to gastritis, though only an exam can say for sure.

If it is gas, there are several reasonable things to try. Over-the-counter simethicone (Gas-X, Mylicon) helps break up gas bubbles and is generally safe. Gentle movement, such as walking, often helps gas move along. Lying on your left side, or pulling your knees to your chest, can also ease trapped gas. A warm compress or heating pad on the abdomen may relax cramping. Sipping warm water or peppermint or ginger tea can help too, though peppermint can worsen reflux if that's a problem for you. For the next day or so, it's sensible to avoid carbonated drinks, chewing gum, very fatty or greasy meals, beans, cruciferous vegetables, and sugar alcohols, and to eat slowly in smaller portions. If constipation seems to be part of it, extra fluids and fiber may help.

If the pain turns out to be gastritis, which would feel more like burning or gnawing in the upper stomach, often worse with eating or on an empty stomach, antacids like Tums or an acid reducer such as famotidine can help. Avoid NSAIDs like ibuprofen and aspirin, alcohol, and spicy foods, since they irritate the stomach lining. Persistent gastritis should be evaluated, as it can be caused by H. pylori infection, which needs treatment.

Please seek prompt medical care if the pain becomes severe or constant, settles in the lower right abdomen, or comes with fever, repeated vomiting, blood in the stool or black stools, vomiting blood, a rigid or very tender belly, trouble passing gas or stool, or unexplained weight loss. Also see a doctor if mild symptoms last more than a few days or keep returning.

Quick heads up before you go off the numbers in that other answer, because they're way off. Massachusetts doesn't use a bracket table for capital gains. Most income, including long-term capital gains, is taxed at a flat 5%. Short-term gains (assets held one year or less) get hit with a higher rate, currently 8.5%. There's also a 4% surtax on income above a threshold that's adjusted every year, so if you're a high earner that part matters too.

The bigger thing is that unrealized gains aren't taxed at all. You only owe anything once you actually sell and lock in the gain. So you don't need to figure out a tax on paper gains that are still sitting in your account.

To work out what you'd owe on a sale, take the difference between what you sold for and what you paid, including any costs, then apply 5% if you held it longer than a year or 8.5% if you didn't. Double-check the current rates and surtax threshold on the Mass DOR website, since they change from year to year.

Insects are drawn to light for many different reasons. Moths, for instance, rely on light as a kind of navigational aid, using it to orient their flight toward or away from a source. Beetles and other species may be lured by light because it leads them to mates or food. Yet an insect's attraction to light is not necessarily advantageous. Flies and similar insects, for example, are often pulled toward blue electric zappers, sometimes called bug zappers, since their bright glow draws insects in. This attraction can injure or kill them. In general, insects have evolved to respond to many features of their surroundings, light included, and such responses do not always improve their chances of survival. Even so, some insects that are drawn to potentially dangerous light sources may still manage to reproduce and pass their genes on to later generations.

Terrorist attacks can really shake the stock market, mostly because they stir up fear and uncertainty. When something happens, investors start worrying about what it'll do to the economy, like fewer people traveling or folks cutting back on spending. So a lot of them sell off to cut their risk, and prices drop.

There's also the direct hit to certain industries and companies. Say an attack targets a major transportation hub. Any company that relies on that hub for its supply chain is going to have trouble operating, and their stock will probably take a beating too.

Basically, the market is jumpy about anything that might hurt the economy or individual companies. So it's pretty common to see it react to news of an attack, even when the attack has nothing to do with the companies actually listed on the exchange.

Honestly, you really should get swelling looked at by a doctor, but I get that's not always easy to do right away. Without knowing what's causing it, it's tough to say exactly what to do. Still, a few general things help. Rest the area and skip whatever seems to make it worse. Ice it for 15 to 20 minutes at a time, a few times a day, which usually takes the edge off both swelling and pain. Over-the-counter stuff like acetaminophen or ibuprofen can help with discomfort too, just follow the label. But if the swelling is bad, or you've got trouble breathing or swallowing, severe pain, or a rash, go to urgent care or the ER right away. Otherwise, get in to see someone so they can figure out what's going on. They might want an X-ray or CT scan to pin down the cause and make a plan.

Blue whales are the biggest animals on the planet, period. They can hit about 100 feet (30 meters) long and weigh up to 200 tons, which is just wild to think about. You'll find them in pretty much every ocean, and they've got that blue-gray color and a long, slender body that makes them easy to spot if you're lucky enough to see one.

They're baleen whales, so no teeth. Instead they've got these long, flexible plates of keratin in their mouths that they use to strain tiny stuff like krill out of the water. Kind of funny that something so huge lives on such small food.

Sadly, they're endangered. Hunting and other human activities knocked their numbers way down. And even though they're so big, they're pretty gentle and aren't a danger to people.

A heart rate of 230 would be unusually high for a 58-year-old. The traditional estimate of maximum heart rate (220 minus age) puts her around 162, and even the more accurate formulas give a value in the mid-160s. So the first question is whether the reading is real.

Wrist-based optical sensors are notoriously unreliable during brisk walking, because arm swing and rhythmic movement can confuse them, and they sometimes jump to implausible numbers. Some chest straps also produce spikes from electrical interference or a loose electrode. A good check is to count your pulse by hand for 15 seconds during one of these spikes and multiply by four, or to look at whether the readings are smooth or erratic on the device's graph. If the number you count is around 150 to 170, the sensor is the likely problem.

If the readings do turn out to be real, that deserves medical attention, even though your quick recovery is reassuring. Brief rapid rhythms such as atrial fibrillation or supraventricular tachycardia can come and go during exertion and then settle quickly afterward, so a normal recovery doesn't rule them out. Before you train harder, I'd recommend talking to your doctor, ideally a cardiologist or someone who works with athletes, and describing exactly what you're seeing. They may want a resting ECG, a Holter or patch monitor to capture episodes during normal activity, or an exercise stress test, which would be a good way to see your heart's behavior at high effort.

Stop walking and seek care promptly if a fast heartbeat comes with chest pain or pressure, lightheadedness, fainting or near-fainting, unusual shortness of breath, or a feeling that your heart is pounding or fluttering and not settling. Those symptoms should never be ignored, even in a fit person.

The British Empire grew bit by bit over about 250 years, through trading companies, settlements, and wars that added colonies all over the world. Then, from the end of the Second World War in 1945 to the 1960s and 1970s, most of those colonies became independent countries, and the empire shrank very quickly.

Think of it like a big pile of blocks that someone stacked slowly over a long time. After the Second World War, Britain was badly weakened. It had spent huge amounts of money and lives fighting, and it owed a lot to the United States. The countries it ruled had also started to want to run themselves. People in India, Africa, and elsewhere had fought for independence, and some had served in the war too, so they felt they deserved a say in their own futures. Britain also decided it could no longer afford the cost of keeping control by force.

So the blocks came down one after another. India and Pakistan became independent in 1947, Ghana followed in 1957, and many African countries became free in the 1960s. Most of the rest of the empire was gone by the 1970s and 1980s. Hong Kong, which was handed back to China in 1997, was one of the last big pieces.

That's why it could be built slowly but fall quickly: the empire was held up by power and money, and once those were gone and the people being ruled demanded freedom, it didn't take long for it to come apart.

The Atanasoff–Berry Computer, usually abbreviated ABC, was an early electronic digital computer built at Iowa State College (now Iowa State University) between 1937 and 1942. It was designed primarily by John Vincent Atanasoff, a physics and mathematics professor, with the help of his graduate student Clifford Berry. The machine was created to solve systems of linear equations, a task that arose frequently in physics and engineering research and that was very laborious to perform by hand or with mechanical calculators.

The computer is notable for several pioneering features. It used vacuum tubes for its logic and computation, which allowed it to operate electronically rather than through slow mechanical parts. It was also binary, storing and processing numbers in base two, and it used a regenerative capacitor-based memory drum, which was an early form of dynamic memory. Its arithmetic was performed by dedicated circuitry rather than by a general-purpose processor, and it separated memory from computation in a way that foreshadowed later architectures. The machine was not programmable in the modern sense, however, since it was built to perform one specific class of calculation.

The ABC was never fully completed in a working state that could be used routinely, and it was largely dismantled after the war. Its significance was long overshadowed by ENIAC, the machine developed at the University of Pennsylvania. A legal case in the 1970s, Honeywell v. Sperry Rand, ruled that ENIAC's patents were invalid partly because of Atanasoff's earlier work and his influence on John Mauchly, one of ENIAC's designers, who had visited Iowa State in 1941. As a result, the Atanasoff–Berry Computer is now widely recognized as a important precursor to the modern electronic computer, and it was officially designated an IEEE Milestone in 1990.

Because it can be hard to work out what is causing a cyst on your eyebrow, and how best to treat it, you should have a healthcare professional look at it. The right approach depends on what lies behind the cyst, and it could include antibiotics, draining the cyst, or removing it surgically. When the cyst is infected, or an infection is suspected, your provider may prescribe antibiotics to clear it up. Once the cyst is free of infection, or the infection has been dealt with, your provider may suggest draining it by cutting a small opening in the skin and pressing out what is inside. Sometimes the cyst has to be removed surgically. You should not attempt to treat the cyst on your own, since doing so may cause additional problems. If you notice a cyst on your eyebrow, make an appointment with a healthcare professional so it can be properly evaluated and treated.

A biological neural network is a set of nervous system cells that interact by means of electrical and chemical signals. It forms the physical basis in the body for how information is processed and passed along. The human nervous system has two principal divisions: the central nervous system, made up of the brain and spinal cord, and the peripheral nervous system, which comprises every other nerve in the body. Its constituent cells, known as neurons, are specially adapted to carry information. Neurons pass messages to one another and to other kinds of cells through synapses, specialized junctions where electrical and chemical signals can be exchanged. Biological neural networks are intricate, ever-changing systems able to handle and combine information arriving from many different sources. They play a part in a broad array of functions, such as sensing, moving, learning, and remembering. Because of how they are built and how they operate, they serve as the foundation for many artificial neural network models used in machine learning and other disciplines.

The Fourth of July, better known as Independence Day, is a federal holiday in the United States marking the approval of the Declaration of Independence on July 4, 1776. That document announced that the 13 American colonies had broken free from British authority and become sovereign, independent states. Representatives of the colonies, meeting as the Second Continental Congress, adopted the Declaration, and 56 notable figures, among them Thomas Jefferson, Benjamin Franklin, and John Adams, put their names to it. Americans have observed the day as a national holiday since the late 1700s, usually with parades, fireworks, and other patriotic events. It is a time for citizens to reflect on their nation's past and on the foundational ideals of liberty, justice, and democracy.

The orchestra's conductor directs the ensemble, standing at the front and using hand and arm movements to signal when musicians should begin or stop, and what tempo to take. They also keep the players synchronized and in tune with one another. An orchestra without a conductor could still perform the piece, but it would likely sound less refined, since the musicians would lack a definite leader to follow. Entrances and endings might fall out of step, and the various instruments could struggle to blend smoothly. In this way, the conductor helps the group maintain a polished and professional sound.

Here's a fun surprise first: we actually do have hovercraft! They're real boats that float on a cushion of air. A big fan blows air down underneath a rubber skirt, and the air pushes the craft up a little so it can glide over water, sand, ice, or mud. Some armies and ferry companies use them. But they're noisy and they only hover a few inches up, so they're not like the cool floating vehicles in Halo.

The Halo kind of hovering is "antigravity," and that's where things get tricky. Gravity is the invisible pull that makes everything fall down. As far as scientists know, there's no way to switch it off or push against it. Nobody has ever found anything that "falls up." So antigravity is a make-believe idea, kind of like a magic wand. It's fun in stories, but we don't know any real science that would make it work.

Now, your magnet idea is a really smart guess, and lots of people have wondered the same thing. Earth really is a giant magnet, which is why a compass needle points north. But Earth's magnetism is super, super weak where we live. A little fridge magnet is about a hundred times stronger right up close than Earth's magnetic field. Imagine trying to lift a car by blowing on it through a straw. That's how weak Earth's magnetic push is compared to how heavy a vehicle is.

There's another sneaky problem. Earth's magnetic field is almost the same everywhere around you, like a calm, even pool of water. A magnet sitting in an even field like that gets twisted to face a certain direction, which is why a compass needle spins, but it doesn't get pushed up or down. To get pushed, you need the field to be much stronger in one spot than another, like being right next to another magnet.

That's exactly how real magnet-floating works! Maglev trains in China and Japan float above their tracks using magnets, but the track itself is packed with powerful magnets too. The train is pushing against the track, not against the Earth. Scientists have even made a little frog float in the air with an enormous magnet, but that magnet was huge and used tons of electricity, and the frog only floated inside a tube.

So the short answer is this: we can make things hover by blowing air down, by using magnetic tracks, or with helicopter-style rotors and drones, but there's no known way to cancel gravity, and Earth's magnetism is way too weak and too even to hold up a vehicle. Maybe someday someone will discover something brand new about how the universe works, and that could be you!

Consolidating or refinancing can be a solid move if you've got a bunch of student loans from different lenders and you're tired of juggling payments, or if you think you can snag a lower interest rate. A few things to think about first.

Interest rate is the big one. If you qualify for a lower rate, you could save a good chunk of money over the life of the loan.

Then there's the term. Stretching the loan out will usually drop your monthly payment, but you'll end up paying more interest in the long run, so don't just look at the monthly number.

Watch for fees too. Some lenders charge them for consolidating or refinancing, and they vary, so compare a few lenders before you commit.

And if you're already struggling to make your payments, refinancing probably isn't the answer. Look into an income-driven repayment plan or a forgiveness program instead.

Whatever you do, go through all your options before you pull the trigger. Talking to a financial advisor or someone who really knows student loans can help too, since the right choice depends a lot on your situation.

Usama Fayyad is a data scientist and entrepreneur who's made a real mark on AI and machine learning. He's known for his work on data mining and ML algorithms, and he's published plenty of papers on those topics in top academic journals. He got his PhD in computer science from the University of Michigan in 1990, and since then he's held a bunch of big roles in the field. He was a researcher at AT&T Bell Labs, then moved into leadership at Yahoo!, where he was Chief Data Officer and Chief Research Officer. He later became Chief Scientist at eBay. Fayyad has also co-founded a few companies, including DigiMine, a data mining and analytics outfit, and DMX Group, a data management and analytics firm. He's picked up a lot of awards along the way, including the SIGKDD Innovations Award, which goes to people who've made serious contributions to data mining and knowledge discovery.

A silent letter is one that appears in the written form of a word but isn't spoken aloud. Such letters can serve to show where a word came from, or to tell apart words that look alike but mean different things. Take the "k" in "knife," for instance: it is silent because it sets the word apart from "nife," which doesn't exist. Likewise, the "g" in "gnome" is silent because it points to the word's roots in the French word "gnome." Learners of a new language may find silent letters confusing, since they break the normal rules of pronunciation. Even so, they form an important part of a language's history and development, and they can help us see where words originated and how they have shifted over the years.

There are a handful of ETFs that track gasoline or crude oil prices, or both. A few you might look at: the United States Gasoline Fund (UGA) gives you exposure to the domestic gasoline market. The United States Brent Oil Fund (BNO) follows Brent crude, which is the go-to benchmark for global oil prices. The United States Oil Fund (USO) tracks West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude, another major benchmark. Then there's the iPath Bloomberg Gasoline Subindex Total Return ETN (GAZ), which is an exchange-traded note rather than a true fund, but it also gives you gasoline market exposure. Before you buy into any of these, think hard about your goals, how much risk you can stomach, and where you stand financially. A financial advisor can help you figure out which of these, if any, actually fits your situation.

Escrow's basically a way to make sure neither the buyer nor the seller gets burned on a house sale. Here's how it goes. The buyer and seller agree on the terms, including the price. The buyer then hands over a deposit, usually called a down payment, to an escrow company. That company holds the money and key paperwork, like the contract and the title, until everything's ready to close. Along the way, they check that all the conditions are met. That might mean a home inspection or confirming the seller has paid off any liens or mortgages on the property. Once it all checks out, the escrow company releases the funds to the seller and transfers the title to the buyer.

It's useful for both sides. The buyer knows their money isn't just sitting in the seller's hands while the deal is still shaky, and the seller knows the money is there and will be released once the sale is final. It also forces everyone to finish the required steps, which saves a lot of headaches later.

Triumph Motorcycles is a British manufacturer founded in 1984, with its headquarters in Hinckley, Leicestershire, England. The firm builds a variety of motorcycles, spanning cruisers, touring machines, sport models, and adventure bikes. Riders across the globe value Triumph for its inventive design and engineering.

Kurt Cobain, who sang lead vocals and played guitar for Nirvana, passed away on April 5, 1994. Although his death has sparked a great deal of debate and speculation, the widely accepted view is that he took his own life. His remains were discovered at his residence in Seattle, Washington, on April 8, 1994, and authorities officially ruled that he had died from a self-inflicted gunshot wound to the head. The manner of his death has left a deep mark on the music world and on his admirers, and he is frequently recalled as one of the most influential and iconic musicians of the 1990s.

A lapping machine is a precision finishing tool used to produce extremely flat, smooth surfaces on parts, often to tolerances measured in millionths of an inch or fractions of a micron. It works by rubbing the workpiece against a rotating plate, called a lap, with a loose abrasive slurry or compound between them. The abrasive particles, often aluminum oxide, silicon carbide, or diamond suspended in oil or water, roll and slide between the lap and the part, removing tiny amounts of material and gradually wearing down high spots until the surface becomes highly flat and uniform.

In a typical single-sided lapping machine, a large flat plate made of cast iron, copper, or another relatively soft material spins horizontally. Workpieces are placed on it inside conditioning rings, which rotate freely as the plate turns. These rings hold the parts in place, help distribute wear evenly across the lap, and keep the plate itself flat over time. Weights or pneumatic pressure can be applied to control how quickly material is removed. Double-sided lapping machines have an upper and lower plate rotating in opposite directions, with parts held in carriers between them, so both faces are finished at once and come out parallel to each other.

Lapping is used wherever parts must seal tightly, mate precisely, or meet very strict dimensional requirements. Common examples include mechanical seal faces, valve components, pump parts, gauge blocks, optical components, silicon wafers for semiconductors, ceramic substrates, and precision bearings. Because the process removes material slowly and evenly, it can correct flatness errors and surface defects left by grinding or machining while producing a fine, often matte finish. A related process called polishing typically follows when an even smoother or mirror-like finish is needed.

On November 7, 1940, the Tacoma Narrows Bridge failed and fell. The structure was a suspension bridge crossing the Tacoma Narrows, a strait in Puget Sound in Washington state, and it linked the city of Tacoma to the Kitsap Peninsula. Its destruction was blamed on a phenomenon called "galloping," in which the wind set the bridge's roadway swaying far more than it should have. The deck twisted and tore apart, and the wreckage finally dropped into the water beneath it. The failure of the Tacoma Narrows Bridge became a famous engineering catastrophe, and it prompted major advances in how suspension bridges are designed and built.

An itch is basically that feeling that makes you want to scratch your skin. Something touches or irritates the skin, and that sends a signal up to your brain. Your brain then tells you to scratch. Pretty simple, really.

Lots of stuff can set one off. Dry skin is a big one. Bug bites too, or an allergic reaction to something you touched or ate. Sometimes it's just your clothes, since certain fabrics rub the wrong way and get you itching.

If you can figure out what's behind it, you've got a better shot at making it stop. Dry skin? Put some lotion on it. Bug bite? A cream made for that can take the edge off.

Scratching does feel good for a minute, I'll give you that. But try not to go overboard, because you can end up damaging your skin, and then you've got a bigger problem than the itch.

Imagine you want to build a tiny toy car, but the only tool you have is your own hands. So you build the car by hand. Then you use that car to help you build a bigger toy, and that bigger toy helps you build an even bigger one. That is basically how the first programs were made.

The very first programs weren't written by another program at all. People wrote them by hand, directly in the only language a computer truly understands, which is just numbers, ones and zeros. Early computers had switches and plugs, and people literally flipped switches or punched holes in paper cards to tell the machine what to do. It was slow and very hard, like talking to someone using only blinks.

Then people got tired of all that blinking, so they used the number language to make a small helper program called an assembler. It let them write short words like "ADD" instead of long strings of numbers, and the assembler turned those words into the numbers for the computer. That first helper was written by hand, but once it existed, writing the next programs got easier.

After that, people used the assembler to build something even friendlier, called a compiler, which lets you write in a language that feels more like English. Later on, compilers were used to build better compilers. There is even a fun trick where a language's compiler gets rewritten in its own language, and the old compiler helps build the new one. It's like a ladder where each rung helps you build the next rung.

So the answer to your question is that the first program was made by a person, with patience and a lot of switches or punched cards. Every program since then has stood on the shoulders of the ones before it. It is amazing, and you're right to be curious about it.

Yes, there are meaningful differences in risk between physical and synthetic replication, though both can track an index closely.

Physical replication means the ETF actually holds the securities in the index, or a representative sample of them, in proportion to their weights. Its main risks are tracking error from transaction costs, dividend timing, and sampling when it holds only part of a large index, along with the ordinary market risk of the underlying holdings. Because it owns the assets, the investor's exposure is direct and easy to understand, and counterparty risk is limited to the custodian and the securities lending program, if the fund lends its holdings.

Synthetic replication, typically done through total return swaps or other derivatives with a counterparty (often an investment bank), means the ETF may hold a different basket of assets, sometimes called a collateral basket, and promises to deliver the index return through a swap agreement. Its distinctive risk is counterparty risk: if the swap provider defaults or fails to pay, the fund may suffer losses, even if the collateral is sound. Regulations generally cap this exposure, often at around 10 percent of net assets for European UCITS funds, and the collateral is meant to cover the rest, but the protection depends on the quality, liquidity, and valuation of that collateral. Synthetic funds can also face conflicts of interest, since the swap provider is often the same institution that issues or sponsors the ETF, and the collateral may differ substantially from the index, creating a different kind of basis risk.

On the other hand, synthetic funds can track indexes that are hard or costly to hold physically, such as commodities, emerging markets with restricted access, or indexes with many illiquid components, and they sometimes achieve lower tracking difference because swap returns are contractually defined. Investors should therefore look at the fund's disclosures on counterparties, collateral composition and haircuts, and the rules on exposure limits, and weigh those against the simpler, more direct risk profile of a physical fund.

It's not just the level of moisture. It's mostly about what part of your body the cream is made for, and that changes what goes in the jar.

Think of your skin like different kinds of clothes. The skin on your face is thin and delicate, like a silk scarf. It also has lots of tiny pores and oil glands, so it can get pimples. Face cream is made light and gentle so it won't clog those pores, and it often skips strong perfumes that could make your face sting or turn red. Some face creams also have extra helpers like sunscreen or ingredients that help with spots or wrinkles.

The skin on your hands is thin too, but you wash your hands all the time, so the cream has to stick around and keep working even after soap and water. Hand cream is usually thicker and a bit sticky-free so you can still pick up your toys, and it often has ingredients like glycerin or dimethicone that make a protective layer.

Feet are like leather boots. The skin on your heels and soles is very thick and tough, and it can get hard and cracked. Foot cream is the thickest and strongest. It often has special ingredients like urea or salicylic acid that soften and gently loosen the dead, rough skin so the moisture can get in.

Body cream is for big areas like arms and legs. It's lighter and spreads easily so you can cover lots of skin quickly without using a whole jar. It's usually cheaper too, which is a big reason it's separate from the others.

So can you swap them? Sort of, but not perfectly. Body cream on your hands will work okay, though it may wear off sooner. Foot cream on your face is a bad idea because it's too heavy and strong, and it might break you out or irritate you. Face cream on your body works fine, but it's a waste of money. Hand cream on your feet helps a little, but it won't fix really rough heels.

The simple rule is that the thicker and stronger the cream, the tougher the skin it should go on. If you only want one cream, pick a gentle, fragrance-free one, and it can do most jobs, though your face and your heels will still be happiest with their own special kind.

Dreams frequently seem startlingly real, and feeling yourself fall is one of the most common dream sensations. Your brain produces it while you sleep as it interprets signals from your body and from the environment around you. It takes in sensory input from many sources, including touch, vision, hearing, and motion, and draws on that information to build the experiences and feelings that appear in your dreams. In your recurring dream about falling, the brain is probably interpreting the feeling of tipping backward in your chair as though it were actually happening. That can make the fall feel vivid and convincing, even though you are only dreaming.

The falling sensation may also be tied to real-life experiences or emotions that your mind is working through during sleep. If you are afraid of falling, or you have taken a fall before, your brain may be using that fear or memory as a way to process those feelings while you rest. All in all, dreaming of falling is a normal and widespread occurrence, and it can result from the brain handling sensory input and past experiences as you sleep.

Honestly, there are a bunch of things that could cause trouble peeing after sex. A UTI is a common one. That's when bacteria get into the urinary system, and you'll usually notice needing to go a lot or really urgently, burning or pain while peeing, and a weak stream. Women get them more often than men, but guys can definitely get them too, especially after unprotected sex. Other possibilities are prostate problems, an STI, or just inflammation somewhere in the urinary tract.

Your boyfriend really should see a doctor so they can figure out what's going on and treat it properly. They'll probably ask for a urine sample to look for bacteria or anything else that shouldn't be there, and depending on what they find, they might want more tests or a different treatment.

Until he gets in, he can drink lots of water and pee often, which helps flush out bacteria and whatever else is in there. And going forward, safe sex is a good idea for both of you, since it cuts down the risk of UTIs and other infections.

I'm not a doctor, so I can't really give medical advice or tell you how to treat this. Cellulitis is a nasty bacterial infection of the skin and the tissue underneath, and it needs prompt treatment. Your dad should stick with whatever plan his healthcare provider gave him and keep following their instructions. If you're unsure about anything he's being given, or you're worried it isn't working, call his provider and ask. They're the best people to explain what's going on and what the next steps should be for him.

Recycling itself is rarely a direct source of tax benefits for individuals, but several related tax incentives and deductions can reward recycling activities, particularly for businesses. In the United States, for example, companies that donate or sell recyclable materials may be able to claim charitable deductions when donating equipment or surplus goods to qualified nonprofits, and some states offer sales tax exemptions on equipment purchased for recycling or waste processing operations. Manufacturers that use recycled content in their products may also qualify for certain credits or accelerated depreciation on recycling equipment, depending on the jurisdiction and the specific provisions in place.

Individuals have fewer options, but a few exist. Households that install solar panels or purchase energy-efficient appliances may receive federal or state credits, though these relate to energy use rather than recycling per se. Some municipalities offer property tax reductions or rebates for composting systems or for participating in waste diversion programs, and certain states provide tax credits for the purchase of recycled-content products or for electronics recycling fees that are already built into purchase prices.

Because these incentives vary widely by country, state, and local government, and because rules change frequently, it is worth checking with a local tax professional or the relevant environmental or revenue agency before assuming a deduction or credit applies. If you tell me your country or region and whether you are an individual or a business, I can point you toward the kinds of incentives most likely to be relevant.

Draining fluid from the lungs of an older adult is usually worth considering when the fluid is causing symptoms or making it harder to breathe. Still, each case calls for an individual judgment that weighs the person's overall health and medical background. Several things shape that choice: what is causing the fluid to build up, how serious the symptoms are, and how the likely benefits compare with the risks of the procedure. Your father's healthcare provider is the right person to talk through the treatment options with, and the decision should rest on their advice and on your father's particular circumstances. Potential complications and possible advantages both deserve attention. His provider can explain the risks and benefits in detail, which will help you reach a well-informed decision.

I'm not your brother's doctor, and nephrotic syndrome can't be diagnosed from one high 24-hour urine protein result, so repeating the test next week is a sensible step. Heavy protein in the urine can also come from fever, intense exercise, dehydration, or an infection around the time of collection, and high blood pressure itself can cause it. Being tall and well built is not a cause, though if he lifts weights or trains hard, he should tell the doctor, since strenuous exercise can temporarily raise urine protein.

Nephrotic syndrome is diagnosed when several findings occur together: a large amount of protein in the urine (usually over 3.5 grams a day in adults), low albumin in the blood, swelling of the feet, legs, or around the eyes, and often high cholesterol. The doctor will probably order blood tests for kidney function, albumin, cholesterol, and blood sugar, a urine routine test, and possibly an ultrasound of the kidneys. Sometimes a kidney biopsy is needed to find the exact cause.

If it does turn out to be nephrotic syndrome, treatment depends on the cause, but the main parts are these. Blood pressure and protein loss are controlled with medicines called ACE inhibitors or ARBs (such as ramipril, enalapril, losartan, or telmisartan), which protect the kidneys. Swelling is managed with diuretics like furosemide and with a low-salt diet. Cholesterol is treated with statins. If the cause is an inflammatory or immune kidney disease, steroids such as prednisolone or other immune-suppressing drugs are commonly used. If it is due to another condition such as diabetes, lupus, or an infection, that underlying problem is treated. Because the blood can clot more easily in this condition, some patients need blood thinners, and doctors also watch for infections.

Diet advice generally includes limiting salt, eating a moderate amount of protein rather than very high protein, and avoiding over-the-counter painkillers like ibuprofen or diclofenac, which can harm the kidneys. Protein supplements and bodybuilding products should also be avoided until the kidneys are assessed.

For now, he should repeat the 24-hour test carefully, collecting every sample for the full day, and avoid heavy exercise beforehand. He should keep checking his blood pressure and take any prescribed medicine regularly. He should see a doctor promptly if he notices swelling of the face or legs, foamy urine, a sudden drop in urine output, shortness of breath, severe headache, or pain and swelling in one leg. A nephrologist (kidney specialist) is the right person to see if the repeat test is still abnormal.

The notion of race, and the sorting of people into racial groups, has a long and tangled past. Many cultures have for centuries grouped people by visible traits like skin tone, eye shape, and hair texture. The formal scientific categorization of races, in the form we recognize today, emerged mainly in the 1700s and 1800s, amid European imperial expansion and colonialism. Numerous European researchers and thinkers during that period tried to sort the world's populations into racial types according to physical features, aiming to rank those races in a hierarchy. Such systems were frequently invoked to justify European colonization and the exploitation of other nations and their people. Race remains a contested subject, since it has repeatedly been employed to back discriminatory policies and beliefs, including racism and eugenics. Today, many scientists and scholars contend that race has no sound biological basis, and that human variety is better understood through patterns of genetic variation.

Recognizing revenue for virtual credits comes down to a single question: when does the company satisfy its performance obligation to the customer? Under ASC 606 in U.S. GAAP (and the closely aligned IFRS 15), the answer is generally when the credits are redeemed or consumed for goods or services, not when the customer pays for them. Cash received for unused credits is a contract liability, sometimes called deferred revenue or customer deposits.

The reasoning starts with the nature of the arrangement. When a customer buys credits, the company has agreed to provide a future benefit, namely the ability to obtain goods or services later. The purchase price is consideration received in advance. Until the customer uses the credits, the company has not transferred control of any good or service, so there is no revenue to recognize. The journal entry at purchase is a debit to cash and a credit to a contract liability.

Recognition then depends on how the credits are used. If a credit is redeemed for a specific item, such as a virtual good, a song download, or an in-app feature, revenue is recognized when that item is delivered and control transfers. The company debits the contract liability and credits revenue at that point.

Several complications require judgment. The first is breakage, meaning credits the customer never uses. ASC 606 allows a company to recognize breakage revenue in proportion to the pattern of rights the customer is expected to exercise, but only if it is probable that a significant reversal will not occur, and only if the company can reasonably estimate the breakage amount. Many companies rely on historical redemption data to make that estimate. If the company cannot reliably estimate breakage, it may have to wait until the likelihood of redemption becomes remote, and then recognize the remaining balance, depending on local unclaimed-property rules.

The second complication is whether the credits are a material right, which is a separate performance obligation. If the credits grant a discount on future purchases that the customer would not otherwise receive, part of the transaction price must be allocated to that right, deferring a portion of the revenue until redemption.

The third is whether the company acts as principal or agent, particularly when credits are used on a third-party platform or to buy items the company does not control. In that case, revenue may be recognized net rather than gross.

Finally, the company should consider whether credits are refundable, transferable, or convertible to cash. Refundable credits may not qualify as revenue at all until the refund right lapses, and any indication that credits are effectively a store of value can affect classification and disclosure. Companies should also disclose the contract liability balance, the revenue recognized from the opening balance during the period, and the significant judgments involved, such as breakage estimates.

In practice, the controlling principle is simple: cash on purchase creates a liability, and revenue follows the customer's exercise of the credits, adjusted for breakage and any material rights. The specific facts of the credit program, including its terms, expiration, and redemption patterns, determine how much judgment is needed.

Pain under the left rib cage in the upper stomach has many possible causes, and several of them fit your situation. Constipation is a very common one. When stool builds up in the colon, particularly the descending colon and the splenic flexure (the bend on the upper left side), it can cause cramping, bloating, and a dull or sharp ache under the left ribs. Gas trapped in that area can add to the discomfort. So your ongoing constipation is a plausible explanation on its own.

Alcohol can also irritate the stomach lining and cause gastritis or heartburn-type pain in the upper abdomen. A heavy weekend of drinking can also inflame the pancreas, which sits behind the stomach and can cause pain that radiates to the left upper abdomen and sometimes to the back. Pancreatitis is less common but more serious, so it's worth knowing about. Warning signs include severe pain that doesn't ease, pain that wraps around to your back, nausea and vomiting, and fever.

Regarding gallstones: once your gallbladder has been removed, gallstones cannot form in the gallbladder itself. However, stones can occasionally form in the bile ducts, which is rare but possible, and the gallbladder removal does not affect your liver or stomach pain sources. Gallbladder-type pain is usually on the right side under the ribs, so left-sided pain makes it less likely, though not impossible.

Other possibilities include muscle strain from coughing, vomiting, or exercise, gastritis or stomach ulcers, a trapped wind pain, or spleen or kidney issues on the left side.

I would suggest seeing a doctor if the pain is severe, persistent for more than a few days, getting worse, or accompanied by vomiting, blood in your stool or vomit, yellowing of the skin or eyes, fever, or pain that spreads to your back or chest. Seek urgent care if you have severe pain that doesn't settle, chest pain, or trouble breathing.

In the meantime, try to drink plenty of water, eat more fibre, stay gently active, and avoid alcohol while the pain settles. If constipation is a persistent problem, a GP can help with a suitable treatment plan.

A credit score is basically a number that sums up how trustworthy you look as a borrower, based on your credit history. Lenders use it to decide whether to give you credit and what interest rate to charge. You usually don't need one to rent an apartment or house, but some landlords and property management companies do pull it as part of screening. It can also come up when you apply for certain insurance, like car or homeowners coverage, and a few employers check it during hiring. Still, it's rarely the only thing they look at. Employment history, rental history, and income usually matter too.

Nikita Khrushchev was replaced as First Secretary of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union by Leonid Brezhnev in October 1964. Khrushchev was also removed from his position as Chairman of the Council of Ministers, the Soviet head of government, and Alexei Kosygin took over that role. Brezhnev and Kosygin ran the country together, though Brezhnev quickly emerged as the dominant leader.

Usama Fayyad is a computer scientist and data science leader best known as a pioneer of data mining and knowledge discovery in databases (KDD). He earned his PhD in computer science from the University of Michigan and built much of his early career on machine learning research at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory, where he worked on automated analysis of large scientific datasets, including astronomical sky surveys. That work helped establish methods for finding patterns in very large collections of data, a problem that became central to the modern field of data science.

He is widely credited with helping to define the term "data mining" and with co-editing the influential 1996 book "Advances in Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining," which helped formalize the field. He also co-founded and led several companies in data analytics and was an executive at firms such as Yahoo, where he served as chief data officer and led data and analytics efforts, and later as a leader in the big data and analytics space. He has been involved with the ACM's SIGKDD community and is frequently recognized as one of the key figures who shaped how organizations collect, analyze, and act on large volumes of data.

Currency markets, also called foreign exchange or forex markets, are where one country's money is bought and sold for another's. A currency's price is expressed as an exchange rate, such as how many dollars one euro buys. The market is decentralized, running around the clock across financial centers like London, New York, Tokyo, and Singapore, with banks, institutional investors, corporations, governments, and individual traders all participating. Most trading happens between large banks in the interbank market, and the rate at any moment reflects the balance of buyers and sellers, just as with stocks or any other asset. When more people want to buy a currency than sell it, its price rises relative to others, and vice versa.

Several underlying forces push that balance one way or the other. Interest rates are among the most influential. When a country's central bank raises rates, deposits and bonds denominated in its currency offer better returns, attracting foreign capital and increasing demand for the currency. Investors chase these yield differentials, which is why currencies often strengthen when rates rise and weaken when rates are cut. Inflation works in a related way: a country with persistently higher inflation sees its money lose purchasing power, and over time its currency tends to depreciate against those with lower inflation. Central banks often respond to inflation by raising rates, which can partly offset this effect in the short run.

Economic performance matters as well. Strong growth, rising productivity, and healthy corporate profits attract foreign investment into stocks, bonds, and real estate, which requires buying the local currency and tends to strengthen it. Weak growth or recession has the opposite effect. Trade balances play a role too. A country that exports more than it imports generally has steady foreign demand for its currency, while a persistent trade deficit means it must keep selling its currency to pay for imports, which can weigh on its value. A country's current account, which includes trade plus investment income and transfers, captures this broader flow.

Confidence and political stability can outweigh the purely economic numbers. Elections, policy uncertainty, sovereign debt concerns, and geopolitical crises can cause investors to pull money out of a country quickly, weakening its currency, while perceived safety draws capital in. This is why currencies like the U.S. dollar, Swiss franc, and Japanese yen often strengthen during global turmoil, a pattern called safe-haven demand. Relatedly, the credibility and independence of a central bank shape how markets interpret its decisions. Governments and central banks also intervene directly, buying or selling their currencies or using capital controls, though such efforts are often limited in size and duration against the enormous daily volume of the market.

Finally, markets are heavily driven by expectations. Currency prices tend to move on news surprises rather than on widely anticipated data, since the market has already priced in what everyone expects. Speculation, hedging by businesses protecting against future exchange rate changes, and algorithmic trading all add to short-term volatility. Over longer periods, interest rates, inflation, growth, trade, and confidence tend to matter most, but in the short run, shifts in sentiment and new information can move currencies sharply in either direction.

HIV/AIDS denialism is the idea that HIV either doesn't exist or doesn't cause AIDS. Scientists overwhelmingly agree that HIV is a real virus and that it causes AIDS, but a small group of people have argued otherwise. Here's why they believe it, explained simply.

Imagine you get sick, and a doctor says a tiny germ you can't see is slowly breaking down your body's defenses, but you won't feel very sick for years. That's hard to wrap your head around. When something is invisible, slow, and scary, some people find it easier to believe a different story, especially one that says "you're not actually in danger" or "the doctors are wrong."

The idea got a big push in the late 1980s from a respected scientist named Peter Duesberg, who studied viruses and cancer. He argued that HIV was a harmless "passenger" virus and that AIDS was really caused by other things: recreational drug use (like amyl nitrite "poppers," which were common in some gay communities at the time), malnutrition, poverty, or even the HIV medicines themselves. Because he was a real expert in a related field, people took him seriously, even though his arguments were tested and shown to be wrong.

Several things made his story appealing. Early HIV drugs like AZT were given in high doses and had harsh side effects, so some people saw patients getting sicker on treatment and concluded the medicine, not the virus, was the killer. In the early years, AIDS mostly showed up in groups who were already treated badly by society, like gay men, drug users, and poor people, so there was real distrust of governments and drug companies, and "they're lying to you" felt believable. There's also the comfort factor: if you've just tested positive, a theory that says the virus is harmless can feel like a lifeline. And some denialists simply misunderstood how science works, pointing to unanswered questions or early mistakes as proof the whole thing was fake.

The most damaging case happened in South Africa around 2000 to 2008, when President Thabo Mbeki and his health minister listened to denialists. Partly out of suspicion of Western drug companies and a feeling that Africa's problems were being blamed on African behavior, the government delayed giving out HIV medicines and promoted things like garlic and beetroot instead. Researchers later estimated this led to over 300,000 avoidable deaths.

So, in short, much like the vaccine-autism scare, it comes from a mix of a credible-sounding expert, real side effects that got misinterpreted, distrust of authorities, and the very human wish for a less frightening answer. Today, the evidence is overwhelming: people with HIV who take modern medicine live long, healthy lives, which is pretty strong proof that the virus is the problem and the medicine is the fix.

Opting out of credit card and insurance offers via optoutprescreen.com doesn't directly change your credit score, but it can have an indirect effect by cutting down the number of hard inquiries on your credit report. Whenever you apply for a credit card or loan, the lender usually reviews your credit report as part of its decision. This review, called a hard inquiry, can lower your score for a short time. Opting out of offers may mean fewer of these inquiries appear on your report, which could eventually benefit your score. Keep in mind that the opt-out on optoutprescreen.com covers only offers sent through the Prescreened Offers program, in which lenders and insurers use certain credit report data to target you with offers. It won't stop you from receiving every credit card or insurance offer, and it won't stop lenders from checking your report when you apply for credit or insurance yourself. To strengthen your credit score, pay your bills on time, keep your balances low, and avoid taking on too many new accounts at once. Reviewing your credit report regularly to confirm its information is accurate is also wise. You are entitled to one free credit report per year from each of the three major credit bureaus (Experian, Equifax, and TransUnion), available through AnnualCreditReport.com.

Okay so if you're on an F1 visa and wondering what to do with your money, you've got a few routes. Mutual funds are probably the easiest starting point. They pool money from lots of people and spread it across stocks, bonds, or other stuff, so someone else is managing it and you're not betting everything on one thing. That makes them a decent pick if you're new to investing.

You can also buy individual stocks, which means owning a small piece of a specific company. It's riskier, since prices can swing a lot, but if you pick well, the upside can be bigger. Just don't put all your eggs in one basket.

ETFs are kind of like mutual funds, except they trade on the stock exchange just like regular stocks. You get the diversification and professional management, plus you can buy and sell whenever the market is open instead of waiting until the end of the day.

If you'd rather play it safe, a savings account or CD is the way to go. The returns are pretty low, but your money is very unlikely to disappear, which matters a lot when you're on a student budget.

Every option carries some risk, though, so do your own homework and think about your goals and how much risk you can actually stomach. Talking to a financial advisor before you commit to anything is also a smart move.

A stock price can climb even when a company reports nothing new, because prices reflect supply and demand for shares, and many forces affect that balance besides the company's own performance.

One of the most common drivers is the broader market. When interest rates fall or are expected to fall, future earnings become more valuable in present terms and borrowing gets cheaper, so stocks across the board tend to rise. Similarly, a general wave of optimism about the economy, inflation cooling, or a rally in a particular sector can lift a company along with its peers. A firm might rise simply because a competitor reported strong results and investors assume the whole industry is doing well.

Money flows matter a great deal as well. When a stock is added to a major index such as the S&P 500, index funds are obligated to buy it, which creates demand regardless of fundamentals. Large institutional investors rebalancing portfolios, pension funds adjusting allocations at quarter end, or heavy inflows into ETFs that hold the stock can all push the price up. Share buybacks by the company itself reduce the supply of shares available and add steady buying pressure.

Market mechanics can also play a role. If many traders have bet against a stock through short selling and the price starts to tick up, they may rush to buy shares to close their positions, which drives the price higher still in what is called a short squeeze. Options activity can have a similar effect, since market makers who sell call options often buy the underlying shares to hedge, amplifying upward moves. Low trading volume can make a stock move sharply on relatively small purchases.

Investor psychology and speculation are another source. Momentum traders buy stocks that are already rising, creating self-reinforcing trends. Social media enthusiasm, online forums, or a well-known investor mentioning the company can spark buying. Rumors of a takeover, a rumored partnership, or a general narrative such as a company being linked to a hot theme like artificial intelligence can raise prices before anything concrete happens. Analyst upgrades or higher price targets can also move a stock even though they are opinions rather than new facts about the business.

Finally, sometimes a price rises because bad news turned out to be less bad than feared, or because pessimism had pushed the stock too low and bargain hunters stepped in. In those cases the absence of disappointment can itself act like good news. It is worth remembering that rises driven by these non-fundamental factors can reverse just as quickly, so they are not necessarily a sign that the company has become more valuable.

In criminal court, an arraignment is basically the hearing where the judge reads you the charges against you. You're asked to plead guilty, not guilty, or no contest. It's a big step, since it's your first formal response to the case and it kicks off the prep for trial if things get that far.
