Think of it like this: a long, long time ago, lots of people in Greece believed in gods like Zeus, Athena, and Poseidon. They prayed to them, built temples, and had festivals. For those people, it was a real religion, just like the religions people follow today.

Over time, things changed. A new religion, Christianity, spread across the Greek and Roman world and eventually became the main one. Once almost everybody stopped worshipping the old gods, the stories about them were still loved, but people began to treat them as stories instead of beliefs. The word "mythology" is mostly what we call the stories of a religion when hardly anyone follows it anymore. So the stories were the same, but the way people saw them changed. It is a bit like how we read about Zeus the way we read a storybook, while the ancient Greeks would have said, "No, he is real, and we must be kind to him so he doesn't get angry."

Also, "mythology" is not really a put-down. It just describes the collection of stories. Many religions have myths, including ones that are alive today. The word gets used for Greek stories mainly because the religion behind them faded away for a very long time.

Now for your second question: yes, some people do practice it today. It is often called Hellenism, or Hellenic polytheism, or sometimes Hellenismos. Some groups also use the name Dodekatheism, which means "twelve gods," after the twelve main Olympian gods. In Greece, the religion has been officially recognized as a "known religion" by the government in recent years, which means its followers can hold ceremonies and be treated like other faiths. These modern followers honor the old gods, celebrate festivals, and make offerings, often trying to follow what ancient Greeks did, though they have to guess at some details because many records were lost.

So the short version: it was a real religion, it became "mythology" when most people stopped believing, and a small number of people today still practice it under names like Hellenism.

Your body isn't actually trying to get rid of a poison when you throw up after a hard run. The vomiting is more like a side effect of your body being very busy with something else.

Think of your body like a classroom with only so much attention to hand out. When you run really hard, your muscles shout, "We need lots of blood and oxygen right now!" So your body sends most of the blood to your legs, arms, heart, and lungs. To make that happen, it pulls blood away from places that aren't urgent at the moment, and your tummy is one of those places. Digesting food is a "later" job, so the stomach and intestines get shortchanged. With less blood, they slow down or nearly stop working, and any food or drink sitting in there just stays put, like a traffic jam. A stomach full of stuff that isn't moving can feel awful and may get pushed back up.

There are a few other helpers in the mix. Hard exercise makes your body release stress chemicals like adrenaline, and these can upset the tummy and also tell the brain's "feeling sick" center to get ready. Your breathing is also heavy and fast, and your belly muscles are squeezing and bouncing around, which can jostle a full stomach. If it's hot, being overheated or a little dried out makes the sick feeling stronger. Also, when you push to your limit, you build up lactic acid and other byproducts in your muscles, and your brain can read all those "I'm in trouble" signals as a reason to feel nauseous.

So the body isn't removing a toxin. It's more that the brain's alarm system gets triggered by the stress, and the stomach is stuck holding food it can't digest at the moment. Vomiting is the stomach's way of saying, "I can't handle this right now."

People can lower the chance of this by not eating a big meal right before hard exercise, sipping water instead of gulping it, staying cool, and building up their effort slowly over time so the body gets used to the work.

Bertrand Russell (1872–1970) was a British philosopher, logician, mathematician, and social critic, widely regarded as one of the most influential thinkers of the twentieth century. Born into an aristocratic family in Wales, he became a Fellow of Trinity College, Cambridge, and spent much of his career there and at other universities in Britain and the United States.

His most significant contributions lie in logic and the foundations of mathematics. Together with Alfred North Whitehead, he wrote the three-volume Principia Mathematica (1910–1913), an ambitious attempt to derive all of mathematics from a small set of logical axioms. He also discovered Russell's paradox, which showed that naive set theory contained a contradiction, and this discovery prompted major reforms in the field. In philosophy, he helped develop analytic philosophy, emphasizing clarity of language and logical analysis. His theory of descriptions, which explained how phrases like "the present King of France" function in sentences, became a model of philosophical method.

Russell was also a prominent public intellectual. He opposed British involvement in the First World War, which led to his imprisonment in 1918, and he later campaigned against nuclear weapons, co-signing the Russell–Einstein Manifesto in 1955 and helping to found the Campaign for Nuclear Disarmament. He wrote widely for general audiences, and his book A History of Western Philosophy (1945) remains popular. His other works include The Problems of Philosophy and Why I Am Not a Christian. In 1950 he received the Nobel Prize in Literature, honoring his varied and important writings in defense of humanitarian ideals and freedom of thought.

Simulation-based optimization is an approach to finding the best settings or decisions for a system when that system is too complex to describe with neat mathematical equations, so its performance has to be estimated by running a computer simulation instead. The core idea is to pair two components: a simulation model that predicts how the system behaves for a given set of choices, and an optimization method that searches through possible choices to find the ones that produce the best simulated outcome.

In classical optimization, you typically have an explicit objective function, such as a formula for cost or profit, and you can often use calculus or well-understood algorithms to find its minimum or maximum. Many real-world systems don't allow this. A hospital emergency department, a manufacturing line, a supply chain, a traffic network, or the airflow around an aircraft wing involves randomness, nonlinear interactions, queues, feedback loops, and physical processes that resist a closed-form description. A simulation can still imitate such a system, either by stepping through events over time, as in discrete-event simulation, by sampling random scenarios, as in Monte Carlo methods, or by numerically solving physical equations, as in computational fluid dynamics or finite element analysis. In simulation-based optimization, the simulation is treated as a kind of black box: you feed in a candidate decision, such as the number of nurses on each shift or the shape of a wing, and it returns an estimate of how well that decision performs.

The optimization side then has to work with these black-box evaluations, which brings several challenges. Each simulation run may be computationally expensive, taking minutes, hours, or even days, so the search must be economical with the number of evaluations. Outputs from stochastic simulations are noisy, meaning the same input can give different results on different runs, so the method must distinguish genuine improvements from random fluctuation, often by repeating runs and using statistical comparisons. Gradients, which tell you which direction improves the objective, are usually unavailable or must be estimated indirectly. For these reasons, practitioners rely on techniques such as metaheuristics like genetic algorithms, simulated annealing, and tabu search; response surface methodology and surrogate or metamodels, which fit a cheaper approximate model to a limited number of simulation results and optimize that approximation; Bayesian optimization, which balances exploring uncertain regions with exploiting promising ones; gradient estimation methods like stochastic approximation and perturbation analysis; and ranking and selection procedures, which statistically choose the best among a finite set of alternatives.

A simple example helps make this concrete. Suppose a bank wants to decide how many tellers to schedule at each hour of the day to minimize staffing costs while keeping customer waiting times acceptable. Customer arrivals are random and service times vary, so there is no simple formula linking staffing to waiting time. The bank can build a simulation of customers arriving and being served, then use an optimization algorithm to try different staffing plans, run the simulation for each, measure costs and waiting times, and gradually converge on a plan that performs well.

Simulation-based optimization is widely used in operations research, engineering design, logistics, finance, healthcare planning, energy systems, and many other fields. Its main strength is that it can handle realistic complexity without forcing oversimplified assumptions, while its main limitations are computational cost and the fact that results are usually approximate, with guarantees of finding the true global optimum being rare. Its outcomes are also only as reliable as the simulation model itself, so careful model validation is an essential part of the process.

Grade 1 left ventricular (LV) diastolic dysfunction means the heart's main pumping chamber relaxes more slowly than normal during the filling phase between beats. The muscle still contracts well, so the heart pumps normally, but it stiffens slightly and needs a bit more time or pressure to fill with blood. It is the mildest form of diastolic dysfunction and is very common, especially with age, high blood pressure, diabetes, obesity, or a history of heart disease. Many people with grade 1 changes have no symptoms at all.

Your doctor suggested a stress echocardiogram to see how the heart behaves under exertion. This test takes ultrasound pictures of the heart at rest and again during or after exercise (or a medicine that mimics exercise). It checks whether the stiffness causes pressure to build up in the heart when it works harder, and whether there is any reduced blood flow to the heart muscle. The result is important because it tells your doctor how serious the finding is, not just the label on the report.

The treatment depends mainly on the cause and on whether you have symptoms such as breathlessness on exertion, swelling of the legs, or tiredness. The main approach is:

Controlling the underlying conditions. Good control of blood pressure is the most important step, since high blood pressure is the most common cause of this problem. Blood sugar control in diabetes, and treatment of obesity, also help.

Medicines. If blood pressure is high, doctors often use drugs such as ACE inhibitors, ARBs, or calcium channel blockers, and sometimes beta blockers. Some patients with diastolic dysfunction and fluid retention may be given a diuretic (water tablet) to relieve congestion. Medicines to control heart rate or treat coexisting problems, such as irregular heart rhythm or angina, may also be used. There is no single medicine that specifically "cures" diastolic dysfunction, and you should not start any heart or blood pressure medicine on your own.

Lifestyle measures. Regular moderate exercise, reducing salt intake, maintaining a healthy weight, limiting alcohol, not smoking, and managing stress are all helpful.

Follow-up. Your doctor will likely repeat the echo periodically to check whether the condition is stable or improving.

Please share your reports and the stress echo result with your doctor, who can tell you what applies to your specific case, including whether any medicine is needed now. If you develop chest pain, severe breathlessness, fainting, or rapid swelling of the legs, seek medical care promptly.

Imagine you're walking on a beach and you find a sandcastle. You'd never think the waves just piled the sand up that way by accident. You'd say, "Somebody built this," because it has towers and walls and a shape that looks planned. That's the heart of intelligent design. The idea is that some things in nature, like the human eye, a living cell, or the whole universe, look so organized and so well put together that they seem more like the sandcastle than like a random pile of sand. So, the argument goes, maybe someone smart made them on purpose.

People who like this idea often point to a few things. One is that living things have parts that all have to work together, like a mousetrap, which stops working if you take away any one piece. They ask how such a thing could build itself slowly, one piece at a time. Another is that the universe's rules seem set just right for life to exist, like a lucky dial landing on exactly the right number. Their conclusion is that a designer, which many people take to be God, must have been involved.

Now here's the other side, which is why grown-ups argue about it. Most scientists say that nature has its own way of building complicated things without a planner, called evolution. Tiny changes happen over a very long time, and the ones that help living things survive get passed on. So the eye didn't pop up all at once. It started as a little patch that could sense light and got better step by step. Scientists also say that "it looks designed" isn't the same as proof that it was designed, and that intelligent design doesn't give tests you could run to show it's right or wrong. Because of that, most scientists don't count it as science, and in the United States, courts have ruled that it's a religious idea rather than a scientific one and shouldn't be taught as science in public school classes.

So the short version is this. Intelligent design says that things look planned, so there must be a planner. Critics say that things can look planned and still be built by slow, natural steps, so we can't jump to a planner. Whether there is a creator is a question people answer differently depending on their beliefs, and intelligent design is one way some people try to explain their answer. It doesn't prove a creator exists in the way a math problem gets proven, which is probably part of why the conversation felt confusing.

Decibels (dB) are the usual unit for measuring sound, and they sit on a logarithmic scale. Because of this, even a slight shift in the decibel figure reflects a far bigger change in how loud the sound really is. For example, a gap of only 10 decibels corresponds to a tenfold change in loudness. The world's quietest room is found at Orfield Laboratories in Minnesota, USA, where the average sound level is -9 decibels, so the room is nearly silent. For comparison, a whisper registers at roughly 30 decibels and an ordinary conversation at about 60. Sound levels can fall below zero because the decibel scale is logarithmic, meaning a small movement in the decibel number stands for a much larger shift in actual volume. Put another way, the gap between -9 and 0 decibels is far larger than the gap between 0 and 9 decibels. So, in answer to your question, sound can have a negative value because it is measured logarithmically, and a small change in decibels can signal a much bigger change in real loudness.

Most cars put the engine up front, and there's a good reason for it. It helps balance the weight so the car is easier to drive, and it's simpler to get at when something breaks. Some luxury cars go the other way and stick the engine in the back. That puts the weight over the rear wheels, which can help with grip when you accelerate hard. The catch is that the weight isn't balanced as nicely, so the car can be trickier to handle. Really, it comes down to what the designers want from a particular car. They're weighing things like top speed, how it handles, and how comfortable it'll be for the people riding in it.

Okay, so a "death bubble" is a hypothetical idea people have floated to explain why we haven't spotted any other intelligent life out there. The notion is that a super-advanced civilization might eventually figure out how to make bubbles of space-time that grow outward at the speed of light and wipe out everything in their path. Those bubbles would come from messing with space-time itself using some kind of advanced tech. But here's the thing: nobody has ever seen one, and there's zero real evidence they exist or could even be built. It's more of a fun thought experiment than anything. If you were explaining it to a five-year-old, you'd probably say it's like a giant invisible ball that zooms around really fast and smashes everything in its way. Scientists and sci-fi writers have played with the idea of what would happen if one showed up, but it's made up, not something actually going on.

A heavy ladder hitting your head, followed by dizziness and chest symptoms, needs prompt in-person medical evaluation today. Please go to an emergency department now rather than waiting for a routine appointment or trying to manage this at home. Chest heaviness and constant central chest pain can signal a heart problem, and a head injury with dizziness needs to be checked for bleeding in the skull or a concussion. Emergency teams can evaluate both at once with an ECG, blood tests, and imaging of the head if needed.

Until you are seen, avoid driving yourself. Ask someone to take you, or call your local emergency number if no one is available. Do not stay alone, and have someone with you if possible. Avoid strenuous activity, and do not take any blood-thinning medicine such as aspirin or ibuprofen unless a clinician tells you to, since they can worsen bleeding from a head injury.

Call emergency services immediately, without delay, if you notice any of the following: worsening or spreading chest pain, pain moving into the arm, jaw, neck, or back, shortness of breath, sweating, nausea, fainting, confusion or unusual drowsiness, severe or worsening headache, vomiting more than once, weakness or numbness on one side, slurred speech, trouble walking, unequal pupils, clear or bloody fluid from the nose or ears, or a seizure.

Please tell the staff exactly what happened: the ladder striking your head, whether you lost consciousness even briefly, the two episodes of dizziness, and when the chest symptoms started. This information will help them decide what tests you need. I hope you feel better soon, and please seek care now.

Carlos Pena Jr. is an actor and singer, most recognized for playing Carlos Garcia on Nickelodeon's "Big Time Rush." That series ran from 2010 to 2013 and centered on four hockey players chosen to become a boy band. Pena Jr. portrayed Carlos, a gifted musician and dancer who serves as the group's "wild card." Before landing "Big Time Rush," he had performed in a number of stage productions and had appeared on television programs such as "ER" and "Judging Amy." Beyond acting, he has released music both on his own and as a member of Big Time Rush.

A statistical model is basically a mathematical way of describing how some real-world process produces data. People use them to figure out how variables relate to each other and to make guesses about what'll happen next. You'll see them everywhere: economics, psychology, biology, engineering, you name it. They're handy for spotting relationships, forecasting outcomes, and working out how likely different events are. There's a whole zoo of them, including linear regression, logistic regression, and time series models. Usually you fit them with techniques like maximum likelihood estimation or Bayesian inference. How good a model is depends a lot on two things: how good your data is and whether the model actually suits that data. Don't just trust one blindly, though. Check its assumptions and limits before you lean on it for predictions or conclusions.

Saint Patrick serves as Ireland's patron saint. A Christian missionary and bishop, he is traditionally credited with introducing Christianity to Ireland during the 5th century. According to tradition, he was born in Britain to a family of Roman descent, and as a teenager he was seized by Irish raiders and carried off to Ireland to be held as a slave. He eventually managed to flee, but he later went back to Ireland as a missionary, where he spread the Gospel and won over many people to the Christian faith. He is honored and commemorated on St. Patrick's Day, a cultural and religious holiday in Ireland that Irish people and communities worldwide celebrate.

Subjective experience refers to the first-person quality of being conscious: the way things feel from the inside. When you see a red apple, taste coffee, feel a pang of sadness, or hear a piano chord, there is something it is like to have that experience for you. Philosophers often call this "what it is like" quality, a phrase popularized by the philosopher Thomas Nagel in his 1974 essay "What Is It Like to Be a Bat?" Nagel argued that even if we knew every physical fact about a bat's brain, we would still not know what its experience is like from the bat's own point of view.

The concept contrasts with objective facts, which can be observed and measured by anyone. A neuroscientist can record the electrical activity in your visual cortex when you look at that apple, but the redness you directly sense is available only to you. Others can infer your experience from your reports and behavior, yet they cannot access it directly in the way you do. This privacy and directness is often seen as the defining feature of subjectivity.

The idea raises some of the deepest questions in philosophy of mind and science. One is the "hard problem of consciousness," a term coined by David Chalmers, which asks why and how physical processes in the brain give rise to subjective experience at all. Solving the easier problems, such as explaining how the brain processes information or controls behavior, would still leave open why any of this processing feels like something. Related debates concern whether subjective experience can be fully explained by physical science, whether it is a fundamental feature of reality, or whether it is in some sense an illusion produced by the brain.

Subjective experience also includes qualities philosophers call qualia, the individual felt characters of experiences, such as the particular sensation of pain or the specific shade of blue. People sometimes wonder whether your experience of blue might differ from mine even when we both call the same object blue, a possibility that is hard to test and therefore central to the debate.

In numismatics, a mule is a coin struck from two dies that were not meant to be paired. Normally a coin is made by pressing a blank between an obverse die and a reverse die that belong together, but when a mint accidentally uses a die from a different coin type or denomination, the result is a mule. For example, a penny might be struck with the obverse die of a dime, or a coin from one year might carry a die from another year. Mules are prized by collectors because they are errors that occurred during minting and are relatively scarce. Their value depends on how rare the pairing is and how dramatic the mismatch appears. Some famous examples include the 1955 "Doubled Die" variety and various Lincoln cent and state quarter mules, though the term "mule" specifically refers to mismatched dies rather than doubling or other error types.

Propositional logic is a branch of formal logic that studies how simple statements can be combined into more complex ones and how the truth of those complex statements depends on the truth of their parts. The basic units of the system are propositions, which are declarative sentences that are either true or false, such as "It is raining" or "Two plus two equals four." Propositional logic does not look inside these statements to analyze their subject or predicate structure, which is why it is sometimes called sentential logic. Each proposition is treated as an indivisible unit that is assigned a truth value.

To build more complex statements, propositional logic uses logical connectives. The most common ones are negation (not), conjunction (and), disjunction (or), implication (if...then), and biconditional (if and only if). Each connective has a defined meaning given by a truth table, which lists the resulting truth value for every combination of truth values of its components. For example, a conjunction is true only when both of its parts are true, while an implication is false only when its antecedent is true and its consequent is false. Using these connectives, one can write formulas such as "(P and Q) implies R," where P, Q, and R are propositional variables standing for arbitrary propositions.

The central purpose of propositional logic is to determine which arguments are valid, meaning that whenever the premises are true, the conclusion must also be true. This can be checked by constructing truth tables, which systematically evaluate a formula under every possible assignment of truth values to its variables. A formula that is true under every assignment is called a tautology, and a formula that is false under every assignment is a contradiction. Propositional logic also provides rules of inference, such as modus ponens, which allows one to conclude Q from "if P then Q" and P, along with other rules for manipulating formulas. Because of its precision and simplicity, propositional logic serves as a foundation for computer science, digital circuit design, mathematical reasoning, and the study of more advanced logics such as predicate logic.

Your cough and cold are common in early pregnancy and do not prevent pregnancy or cause harm to the baby by themselves. A positive test means the pregnancy has already started, so the illness does not change that. Still, you should tell your doctor or an obstetrician that you are pregnant, since many cold medicines are not recommended during pregnancy and your doctor may not have known when they saw you.

For relief, try rest, plenty of fluids, and warm drinks such as soup, broth, or herbal tea without added caffeine. Saline nasal sprays or rinses are safe and can ease congestion. A cool-mist humidifier or steam from a bowl of hot water (leaning over it carefully, not too close) can loosen mucus and soothe your throat. Honey in warm water or tea can calm a cough in adults, and throat lozenges can help. To sleep better, prop your head and upper body up with extra pillows, since this reduces coughing when lying flat.

Acetaminophen (paracetamol) is generally considered the safest over-the-counter pain or fever reliever in pregnancy, but check the dose with a pharmacist or your doctor first. Avoid decongestant pills such as pseudoephedrine or phenylephrine unless a doctor approves them, and be cautious with ibuprofen, aspirin, and combination cold products, which often contain these ingredients or cough suppressants you should not take without advice. Ask a pharmacist to check any cold product against your pregnancy before you buy it.

Please contact your doctor again soon, and ask specifically for a medicine that is safe in pregnancy if the cough keeps you awake or does not improve. Seek care promptly if you have a high fever, trouble breathing, chest pain, coughing up blood, severe headache, or if the cough lasts more than about ten days. You should also book a prenatal appointment to confirm the pregnancy and begin routine care, including an ultrasound to check how far along you are.

So basically a stent surgery is when they put a stent inside a blood vessel or some other hollow spot in your body. Stents are little metal mesh tubes that prop open a vessel that's narrowed or blocked. The doctor usually makes a small cut, then threads a thin flexible tube called a catheter in to reach the spot. There's a tiny balloon on the tip of the catheter, and that's what expands the stent once it's in place.

It's often used for things like coronary artery disease, where the arteries feeding your heart get narrowed. It's also used for abdominal aortic aneurysms, which is when the aorta (the main artery) bulges or gets weak, and for carotid artery stenosis, where the neck arteries that carry blood to your brain get clogged up. Most of the time you go home the same day, no hospital stay needed. It's generally considered safe and works well for a lot of people, but it's still surgery, so there are risks. Your doctor can walk you through the specifics for your situation, which is really the best place to start.

OTCMKTS is the OTC Markets Group's market tier, and it's not an exchange like the NYSE or NASDAQ. There's no central floor. Instead, dealers trade securities directly with one another over a network. So if you spot a company with two OTCMKTS symbols, there are a few likely explanations. The most common is that the company has two classes of stock, each trading under its own ticker, say "ABCD" for one class and "EFGH" for the other. Those classes can differ in voting rights, dividends, or other terms. Another possibility is that the two symbols belong to related entities, like a parent and a subsidiary or two divisions, each with its own listing. And sometimes a company just switched tickers after something like a merger, acquisition, or reorganization, and the old symbol hangs around for a while. Without more details it's hard to pin down which one applies to a given company. Check the filings or the company's investor relations page, and if real money is on the line, talk to a financial advisor before you buy anything.

Anne Frank succumbed to typhus at the Bergen-Belsen concentration camp in 1945, at the age of 15. For two years, she and her family had concealed themselves in a hidden annex in Amsterdam to escape Nazi persecution during the Second World War. In 1944, their hiding place was found and they were taken into custody. Anne and her sister Margot were later transferred to the camp, where both fell ill with typhus. Margot passed away first, and Anne followed only a few days afterward. The diary Anne wrote while in hiding has become a widely read and deeply moving record of the Holocaust and of the suffering and bereavement endured by Jewish people during that era.

Brass instruments use separate mouthpieces for a few reasons, and the big one is that every instrument has a different bore size and shape. A trumpet's bore is pretty narrow compared to a tuba's, which is huge, so the trumpet mouthpiece has to be small and narrow to fit, while a tuba mouthpiece is much larger and wider. Mouthpieces also change how the thing sounds. Shape, size, and material all matter. A softer material tends to give you a warmer, rounder tone, and a harder one usually sounds brighter and more focused. Then there's the practical side. If you're jumping between brass instruments, swapping mouthpieces is way easier than hauling the whole horn around with you. And since you're blowing into these things and they collect saliva, having your own mouthpiece makes keeping things clean a lot simpler.

Chest pain and dizziness can come from a lot of different things, so it's worth getting checked out if you're dealing with both. Heart problems are one possibility, including angina, a heart attack, or an irregular heartbeat (arrhythmia). Panic attacks can cause both too, since they bring on a sudden rush of intense fear or anxiety. Acid reflux is another common culprit, when stomach acid backs up into the esophagus and causes chest discomfort. A pulmonary embolism, which is a blockage in the pulmonary artery, can also cause chest pain and dizziness. And sometimes the problem is in the inner ear, with vertigo being a typical example. Honestly, a doctor is the best person to figure out what's going on, so don't wait on this one. They can pin down the cause and get you the right treatment.

Stocks and high-yield bonds can both play a valuable role in a well-diversified portfolio, yet they differ in risk and reward and are not taxed in the same way. Equities, as stocks are also called, give the holder a share of ownership in a company and can grow in value as the business becomes more valuable. That growth is not assured, however, since a stock's price can swing widely and may never recover its earlier level. High-yield bonds, often called junk bonds, carry credit ratings below investment grade and pay higher interest than investment-grade debt. That added income comes with greater danger, because the issuer is more likely to fail to repay what it owes. When it comes to taxes, earnings from stocks, including dividends and capital gains, are taxed at varying rates based on how long the shares were owned and the investor's income bracket. Bond interest is usually taxed as ordinary income. High-yield bonds can be harder to classify for tax purposes, since their returns may combine interest with capital gains. For advice tailored to your circumstances, speak with a financial advisor or tax professional. In the end, deciding between stocks and high-yield bonds depends on your personal objectives, your comfort with risk, and your broader financial position. Weighing all of these considerations and spreading your investments across different assets can help you manage risk while pursuing good returns.

Sedimentary rocks come about through sedimentation, a process in which layers of material like sand, mud, and small stones accumulate and are pressed together over long periods. Such deposits can build up in many settings, among them rivers, seas, and deserts. Several mechanisms contribute to their formation. In deposition, wind, water, or ice carries sediment elsewhere, lays it down, and eventually packs and bonds it into sedimentary rock. In lithification, sediment that becomes buried under mounting pressure is squeezed tighter and glued together, producing rock in this way. Diagenesis refers to the chemical alterations that take place after lithification, such as minerals precipitating out of solution, which can change the rock's makeup and surface character. Sedimentary rocks typically display layering, known as bedding, that mirrors the original sequence of deposited sediment. They also frequently hold fossils, the preserved traces of plants and animals that were trapped within the rock while it was forming.

A "death bubble" is a hypothetical phenomenon suggested as a possible reason why we see no signs of other intelligent life in the universe. According to this idea, advanced civilizations might someday learn to generate "bubbles" of space-time that spread outward at the speed of light, annihilating everything they touch. Such bubbles would result from advanced technologies that reshape space-time itself. It is worth emphasizing that death bubbles are purely theoretical and have never been detected in reality. They make for an intriguing thought experiment, but no scientific evidence indicates that they exist or could ever be built. To explain the concept to a five-year-old, you might say that a death bubble is like a huge, invisible ball that zooms along incredibly fast and destroys whatever stands in its path, an enormous force nothing can stop. Scientists and science fiction writers have imagined what would happen if such a thing were real, but it is simply an invented idea and not something actually taking place.

No, not all of it, and the answer depends on what you mean by "interest." I'll assume you're asking either about the mortgage interest you pay on your home, or about whether the rental income is taxable. I'll take both, using US rules, since you didn't specify a country.

If you mean mortgage interest you pay, renting out a single room does not make all of it taxable or non-deductible. Instead, you generally split the expenses between personal use and rental use. If the rented room is, say, 15 percent of your home's square footage, then roughly 15 percent of your mortgage interest, property taxes, utilities, insurance, and similar costs can be treated as rental expenses and deducted against the rental income on Schedule E. The remaining 85 percent stays a personal expense, and you can still deduct that portion on Schedule A as usual if you itemize. So you lose nothing by renting; the interest is just allocated between the two uses. Expenses that apply only to the rented room, such as new bedding or a lock for that door, are fully deductible against the rental income.

If you mean the income you receive, rental income is generally taxable. There is an important exception: if you rent out your home, or part of it, for fewer than 15 days during the year, you don't have to report that income at all, under the so-called Augusta rule. Beyond that, you report the income, subtract allowable expenses, and pay tax on the net. Short-term rentals where you provide substantial services, or where the average stay is very short, can also bring in self-employment tax in some cases, though a simple room rental usually does not.

Other points to keep in mind: if you sell your home later, the portion used for rental may affect the home sale exclusion and depreciation recapture, so keeping records matters. State and local occupancy or lodging taxes may also apply, and Airbnb sometimes collects those for you. Platforms may send you a Form 1099-K if you cross the reporting thresholds.

If you are in another country, or if you meant something different by "interest," tell me and I can adjust. For your specific situation, a tax professional can confirm how to allocate expenses.

Your body has built-in sensors that tell your brain where you are and how you're moving. Some of them live in your inner ear, where tiny fluid-filled tubes and little crystals sit inside structures called the vestibular system. When you drop suddenly, those crystals and fluid move in a way that tells your brain "something is falling!" Your brain also keeps track of your body's position using nerves in your muscles and joints. When the floor seems to disappear, all of these signals suddenly disagree or change very fast.

The tingly feeling in your tummy and bottom happens because your brain has a quick alarm system that can make your body ready for danger. When it thinks you might be falling, it can briefly change how your nerves and muscles behave. Your insides are full of nerves that connect to the same parts of your brain that handle these alarms, so a big "uh oh" signal can show up as a fluttery, tingly feeling down low. Your brain is basically making a guess that something is wrong, and that guess gets felt in your belly.

Why only when falling, and not when speeding up? When you accelerate quickly, like being pushed back into a seat, your body is squished against something solid. The seat is still holding you up, and your inner ear and muscles read that as "we're being pushed forward," which feels strong but normal. When you fall, though, the support seems to vanish. Your body feels weightless for a moment, and that surprise is what sets off the alarm. Your brain expects to feel the seat or floor pushing up, and when that push disappears, it notices right away.

So the tingle is your brain's alarm going off because it suddenly feels like it has no support, and your tummy is one of the places that feels that alarm most strongly.

Hamburger Helper is a General Mills product, basically a box of dry pasta and seasoning mix that you cook up with ground beef. It's been around since 1971, and it's still a go-to for plenty of people who want a filling, tasty dinner without much fuss. There are tons of flavors to pick from, and you're not stuck with beef either. Ground turkey works fine, and so do other kinds of meat.

Sorry to hear your daughter's sick! Infants, especially those under 2, can get seriously worse from colds and flu, so if she's got a fever or a cough, get her checked out rather than waiting it out. Until then, a few things might help her feel better.

Keep her drinking. Breast milk or formula if she's still nursing or on a bottle, and water or an electrolyte solution if she's old enough for those. A humidifier can make breathing easier, especially at night. For the stuffy nose, a saline spray or drops work well, and a bulb syringe can gently clear out extra mucus.

If her fever's over 101°F (38.3°C), you can give an age-appropriate dose of acetaminophen (Tylenol) or ibuprofen (Motrin). Just read the label and stick to the dosing instructions. Dress her in light clothes and don't let the room get too hot or cold. A lukewarm bath can also help her feel more comfortable.

If she's not getting better or the symptoms hang around, call her doctor. They can tell you what to do next and whether she needs to be seen.

Oregon Institute of Technology, usually called Oregon Tech, is a public university in Klamath Falls, a small city in south-central Oregon. It is the only public polytechnic university in the state, so its focus is on hands-on, applied education in fields like engineering, health sciences, technology, and business, rather than the broad liberal arts emphasis found at many other Oregon schools.

The campus is relatively small, with a student body of a few thousand, which gives students a close-knit feel and good access to faculty. Many classes are taught with lab work, industry projects, and real-world training in mind. The university is well known for its health professions programs, including nursing and radiologic sciences, and it also has a strong reputation for engineering and technology, particularly in areas like mechanical engineering, civil engineering, and renewable energy.

Oregon Tech also has a second campus in Wilsonville, near Portland, which serves students in the Portland metro area and offers programs geared toward working professionals and some degree completion options. Klamath Falls itself is a quiet, outdoorsy town, so the campus appeals to students who enjoy hiking, skiing, fishing, and other activities in the surrounding mountains and lakes. Campus life is more modest than at large universities, with a focus on clubs, athletics in the NAIA Cascade Collegiate Conference, and student organizations tied to academic interests.

If you are considering it, I would recommend checking the current program offerings, tuition, and campus details on the official Oregon Tech website, since those can change.

A Boolean network is a mathematical tool for describing how a dynamic system behaves, using a network of Boolean variables and functions. Each variable in such a network can take only one of two values, "true" or "false," and the functions dictate how each variable changes its value in response to the values of other variables in the network. Researchers frequently rely on Boolean networks to model complex systems like genetic regulatory networks or social networks. They are especially well suited to systems that show either/or behavior, or to capturing how the different parts of a system influence one another. Within a Boolean network, every variable corresponds to a node, and the functions that govern how each variable updates are depicted as edges linking the nodes. At any moment, the network's state is given by the configuration of its nodes, and its dynamics can be explored by repeatedly updating the nodes according to the rules encoded in the edges. Boolean networks have found use in many fields, including the study of cellular automata, the analysis of biological systems, and the design of computer circuits. They have also been applied to examine social and economic systems, as well as the spread of diseases and information.

Think about what you wear. In winter you might be in a thin shirt inside the house because you took your big coat off at the door, so the house needs to feel cozy to make up for that. In summer you might wear shorts and sandals, so a cooler house feels just right. Your body is happy when it feels comfortable with the clothes it has on, and we dress differently in each season.

Our bodies also get used to the weather outside. After a long hot summer, your body gets good at handling heat, so a room that's a little warm feels fine. After a long cold winter, your body gets used to the cold, and a room that's cooler might feel fine too, but most people don't turn the heat down that far. Even so, the big difference is that in summer people want to escape the heat, so they cool the house down below what the outdoors feels like, and in winter they want to escape the cold, so they heat it up.

Here is the surprising part: the temperatures people choose are actually not that different from season to season. Many people set the air conditioner to about 74 to 78 degrees in summer and the heater to about 68 to 72 in winter. So in many homes, the summer setting is actually a bit warmer than the winter one. If it feels like the winter house is warmer, that might be because the heat in winter feels so good compared to the cold outside, and the cool air in summer feels so good compared to the hot outside.

There is also a money reason. Heating and cooling cost money, and the bigger the difference between inside and outside, the more energy it takes. Many people and businesses try to save money by not cooling too much in summer or heating too much in winter.

Finally, some places really do blast the heat or air conditioning more than they need to, and that is just habit. Some offices are famously freezing in summer, because the people who set the thermostat are dressed in suits and want to stay comfy, and some are very hot in winter. So the simple answer is: we like to feel comfortable in whatever clothes we have on, and our bodies like a nice contrast with the weather outside.

Yeah, there are accounts that are basically built for putting money in and not taking it out the normal way. No debit card, no easy withdrawals. People usually call them savings accounts or deposit accounts, and you can get them from regular banks, credit unions, or online-only banks. Savings accounts are mostly for parking cash long term while it earns a little interest. They might come with a minimum balance or a minimum amount to open one. Some charge fees for withdrawals, and some cap how many you can make in a month.

Deposit accounts are more of a short-term thing. People use them to hold cash for a specific goal or to sit on money they'll spend on something soon. They often have lower minimums and usually don't hit you with withdrawal fees. Both kinds are FDIC-insured, so your money is covered up to $250,000 per depositor at each institution. If the bank goes under, you get reimbursed up to that limit.

A brute-force attack is a method of breaking into a system, account, or encrypted piece of data by systematically trying every possible combination of credentials or keys until the correct one is found. Rather than exploiting a flaw in the software or the logic of the system, the attacker relies on computing power and patience. For example, someone attempting to guess a four-digit PIN could simply try 0000, then 0001, and so on through 9999, which is only ten thousand possibilities and would take very little time for a computer to exhaust.

The effectiveness of a brute-force attack depends heavily on the complexity of the target. Short or common passwords, such as "123456" or "password," can be cracked in seconds, while long, random passwords combining uppercase and lowercase letters, numbers, and symbols can require an impractical amount of time to crack with current technology. Attackers often make their attempts smarter by using dictionary attacks, which try lists of common words and previously leaked passwords first, or by running guesses against stolen password hashes offline, where there is no login system to slow them down or lock them out.

Defenses against brute-force attacks include using long and unpredictable passwords, enabling multi-factor authentication, limiting the number of failed login attempts through account lockouts or increasing delays between tries, and using encryption keys that are long enough to make exhaustive searching infeasible. Many systems also use rate limiting and CAPTCHA challenges to make automated guessing much harder.

I understand how frustrating this is, especially when you feel you are eating a lot and nothing changes. At 17 and 41 kg, whether you are truly underweight depends on your height. For example, if you are around 155 cm, your BMI would be about 17, which is mildly underweight. If you are taller, it would be lower. Either way, it is reasonable to want to gain some healthy weight, and there are practical things that usually help.

Before focusing only on diet, I would recommend a check-up with a doctor, because some medical conditions make weight gain difficult even with good eating. Common ones include an overactive thyroid, intestinal worms, celiac disease or other absorption problems, anemia, and sometimes diabetes. Basic blood tests such as a complete blood count, thyroid function, blood sugar, and a stool examination can rule these out. If you have symptoms like a racing heart, excessive sweating, frequent loose stools, bloating after wheat products, unusual tiredness, or irregular periods, mention them to the doctor. If stress, low mood, or worry about food affects how much you eat, that is worth discussing too, because it is very common and treatable.

If everything is normal, the main issue is usually that the body is burning more energy than you take in, even if it feels like you eat a lot. Most people in your situation need roughly 300 to 500 extra calories a day to gain weight steadily. Large plates tend to fill you up quickly, so it is easier to eat five or six smaller meals and snacks spread through the day than three big ones. Choose foods that pack a lot of energy into a small volume. These include whole milk, curd, paneer, cheese, eggs, peanut butter, nuts and seeds, dried fruits like dates, raisins, and figs, bananas, potatoes, rice, ghee or oil added to dal and vegetables, and lentils and chicken or fish if you eat them. A homemade shake made with milk, a banana, a spoonful of peanut butter, oats, and a few nuts is one of the simplest ways to add 400 to 500 calories without feeling overly full. Try not to drink lots of water or tea right before meals, since that reduces how much you can eat. Many people find it helpful to note down what they eat for a few days, because the actual intake often turns out to be less than it seems.

About exercise, your experience makes sense. Running, cycling, and other cardio activities burn calories and can make you lose weight. What helps a thin person is strength or resistance training. This includes bodyweight exercises like squats, push-ups, and lunges, or light weights done three or four times a week, along with enough food. This builds muscle, and the added weight looks healthy and firm rather than just fat. It also tends to improve appetite over a few weeks. Keep cardio light until you have gained some weight.

Sleep also matters, since growth and muscle repair happen during rest, so aim for seven to nine hours. Manage stress where you can, because anxiety can suppress appetite. Avoid skipping breakfast.

Be patient with the process. A healthy rate of gain is about half a kilogram to one kilogram per month, so check your weight every couple of weeks rather than daily. Please avoid weight-gain powders or appetite-stimulant pills sold without prescription, as some contain steroids that can be harmful. If you have not gained any weight after two to three months of consistent effort, or if tests show any problem, a doctor or dietitian can give you a more personalized plan. Being naturally slim is often genetic and not unhealthy in itself, but with the right approach most people can reach a weight they feel comfortable with.

Severe toothache that worsens at night is most often caused by inflammation or infection inside the tooth's pulp, the soft tissue containing nerves and blood vessels. Common causes include a deep cavity that has reached the nerve, an abscess (a pocket of pus at the root tip or along the gum), a cracked or broken tooth, or gum disease. Night pain is typical for several reasons. When you lie down, blood flows more toward your head, which increases pressure inside the tooth and throbs more. There is also less distraction at night, so the pain feels stronger, and the tooth is often clenched or ground during sleep.

Because your pain has lasted three days and is getting worse, I would recommend seeing a dentist as soon as possible, ideally within the next day or so. A dentist can examine the tooth, take an X-ray, and determine whether the nerve needs root canal treatment, the tooth needs a filling or crown, or an infection needs drainage or antibiotics. Delaying treatment can allow an abscess to spread, so do not wait for the pain to settle on its own.

Until you see a dentist, you can ease the discomfort in a few ways. Over-the-counter ibuprofen or naproxen, taken as directed on the package, is often more effective for dental pain than acetaminophen alone, though you should check with a pharmacist if you have stomach problems, kidney disease, asthma, or take blood thinners. Rinsing gently with warm salt water several times a day can help, and sleeping with your head raised on an extra pillow can reduce throbbing. Apply a cold pack to the outside of your cheek for 15 minutes at a time, and avoid very hot, very cold, or sugary foods and anything that bites down on the painful tooth. Avoid placing aspirin or any pain reliever directly against the gum, since it can burn the tissue.

Seek emergency care right away if you develop facial swelling, swelling under the jaw or in the neck, fever, difficulty swallowing or breathing, or a bad taste with pus. These can signal a spreading infection that needs urgent treatment.

In an artichoke, the "seed" is actually located within the flower bud, not in a separate pit or core. The edible heart sits at the base of the bud, and the fuzzy, hairy choke above it is made up of immature florets. Each floret carries a seed, which is an achene, tucked among those fibers. If the artichoke is left on the plant and allowed to bloom, those florets develop into a striking purple flower, and the seeds form at the base of each floret.

So whole brain emulation, which people also call mind uploading or brain uploading, is basically the idea of copying the information in a biological brain onto a computer or some other device. The goal is either to build an actual artificial intelligence or to make a virtual copy of a person's consciousness. It all rests on the assumption that a brain's structure and function can be understood well enough to be replicated in a machine, and that what the brain does computationally could be simulated in software or hardware.

It's a lot harder than it sounds, though. For one, there's the technical problem of how you'd accurately capture something as messy and complicated as a living brain, both how it's built and how it works. Then you get into the philosophical and ethical stuff, like what consciousness even is, and what happens if we actually succeed in creating artificial intelligence this way.

Some researchers and futurists think it could eventually happen. But right now it's still highly speculative, and plenty of people argue about whether it's even a sensible idea.

Utah became the 45th state of the United States on January 4, 1896, when President Grover Cleveland signed the proclamation admitting it to the Union.

Its path to statehood was long. The region was first settled in large numbers by Mormon pioneers led by Brigham Young, who arrived in the Salt Lake Valley in 1847. The area came under U.S. control in 1848 through the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, which ended the Mexican-American War. Settlers proposed a large State of Deseret in 1849, but Congress instead created the smaller Utah Territory as part of the Compromise of 1850.

Statehood was delayed for decades, mainly because of national opposition to the Mormon practice of polygamy. In 1890, Wilford Woodruff, president of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, issued a manifesto officially ending the practice. Utah then wrote a state constitution banning polygamy, and that cleared the way for its admission in 1896.

Relationships naturally go through highs and lows, and you may simply be in a rough patch with your boyfriend at the moment. Try to pinpoint any deeper issues behind these feelings, and reach out for support if you need it. Several approaches may help. Second, focus on self-care: looking after your body, mind, and emotions can boost your overall wellbeing and may make you feel more in touch with what you're experiencing. Ben Goertzel is not a thing but a person: an American computer scientist, artificial intelligence researcher, and entrepreneur, born in 1966. He is best known for his work on artificial general intelligence (AGI), meaning AI systems that could match or exceed human-level reasoning across a wide range of tasks rather than excelling at only narrow, specific problems. He is widely credited with popularizing the term "artificial general intelligence" in the early 2000s, notably through a book he co-edited with that title.

Goertzel earned a PhD in mathematics from Temple University and has worked in academia, research, and business. He led the development of OpenCog, an open-source software framework intended to serve as a foundation for building AGI by combining several AI approaches, such as probabilistic logic, evolutionary learning, and knowledge representation, within a single cognitive architecture. He has also been involved with organizations such as the AGI Society, which organizes an annual conference on artificial general intelligence.

He is perhaps most visible to the public through his connection with Hanson Robotics, where he served as chief scientist and was associated with Sophia, the humanoid robot that attracted global media attention. He is also the founder and CEO of SingularityNET, a blockchain-based platform meant to let AI services be shared and traded in a decentralized way, with the goal of preventing AI development from being controlled by a few large corporations or governments.

Beyond his technical work, Goertzel is a prominent voice in transhumanist and futurist circles. He has written numerous books and papers on AI, cognitive science, philosophy of mind, and the technological singularity, the hypothetical point at which machine intelligence surpasses human intelligence and triggers rapid, transformative change. He tends to be optimistic about AGI arriving relatively soon and about its potential benefits, though some researchers regard his timelines and claims, including some of the publicity around Sophia, with skepticism. Overall, he is regarded as an influential and colorful figure in the AGI community.

White-box testing is a software testing approach in which the tester is fully aware of the system's internal logic and architecture. This stands in contrast to black-box testing, where the tester knows nothing about the internal structure and interacts only with the system's inputs and outputs. White-box testing is usually applied to examine particular components of a program or to confirm that certain internal operations behave as intended. Because of this, it is frequently paired with black-box testing to form a more complete testing plan. Carrying it out requires the tester to understand in depth the code under examination along with the algorithms and procedures it relies on. The tester designs test cases that target different sections of the code and checks whether the results are accurate. These cases may cover particular execution paths, boundary conditions, and how errors are handled. The advantages of white-box testing include a thorough examination of the software's internal processes, the capacity to uncover concealed or difficult-to-spot defects, and the ability to test code at a very granular level. On the other hand, it tends to be time-intensive and may demand specialized expertise or tools.

There is no single best allocation, because the right mix depends on your time horizon, your tolerance for losses, your other sources of income, and how much you need your portfolio to deliver. But there are well-supported principles that point toward sensible ranges, and I can lay those out.

The core tradeoff is between growth and stability. Stocks have historically delivered higher long-term returns than bonds or cash, which matters because a retirement can last thirty years or more and inflation steadily erodes purchasing power. Bonds and cash reduce volatility and give you a reliable source of money to spend during market downturns, so you are not forced to sell stocks at depressed prices. The danger most specific to retirees is sequence-of-returns risk: a big market drop early in retirement, while you are withdrawing money, does far more lasting damage than the same drop later.

A common starting point is to hold a stock percentage roughly equal to 110 or 120 minus your age, so a 40-year-old might hold 70 to 80 percent stocks, while a 65-year-old might hold 45 to 55 percent. Target-date funds follow a similar glide path, gradually shifting toward bonds as the retirement date nears. Many retirees do well with something like 40 to 60 percent in diversified stocks, 30 to 50 percent in high-quality bonds, and a small cash reserve covering one to two years of expenses. Some research suggests that starting retirement with a lower stock allocation and gradually increasing it can help manage early-retirement risk, though this is debated.

Within stocks, broad diversification matters more than picking winners: low-cost index funds covering US and international markets reduce the risk of any single company or country hurting you. Within bonds, a mix of Treasuries and investment-grade bonds is typical, and inflation-protected securities can help hedge rising prices. Keeping fees low is one of the few reliable advantages you control.

Several personal factors should shift the mix. If you have a pension, Social Security, or an annuity covering your essential expenses, you can afford to take more stock risk. If your portfolio is your only income, a more conservative stance may be wise. Your health, expected longevity, desire to leave an inheritance, and emotional reaction to losses all matter too. A portfolio you will abandon in a panic is worse than a slightly less optimal one you can stick with.

Finally, rebalance periodically, perhaps annually, to keep your allocation near target, and consider the tax placement of assets across accounts. Because the stakes are high and the details personal, it is worth talking with a fee-only fiduciary financial planner who can model your specific situation.

The largest whale is the blue whale (Balaenoptera musculus), which is also the largest animal known to have ever lived. Adult blue whales typically measure between 80 and 100 feet (about 24 to 30 meters) long and can weigh as much as 180 to 200 tons, with the heart alone weighing around 400 pounds. Females are generally slightly larger than males. The largest confirmed individuals have reached lengths of over 100 feet, though measurements of very old whales are rare and most estimates come from whaling records and modern observations.

Blue whales are found in oceans around the world, from polar waters to tropical seas, and they feed almost exclusively on krill, consuming several tons of it in a single day during feeding season. Despite their enormous size, they are filter feeders that take in huge volumes of water and strain out the tiny crustaceans using baleen plates. Their populations were drastically reduced by commercial whaling in the twentieth century, and although protections have allowed some recovery, they remain listed as endangered.

Cu is the symbol used on the periodic table for copper. This soft, malleable, and ductile metal has a reddish-orange hue. Because it conducts heat and electricity so well, it plays a major role in the electrical and electronics sectors. Small amounts of copper are necessary for both plants and animals, and trace quantities are present in the human body. The element occurs naturally in abundance, with major sources including ores like chalcopyrite, bornite, and chalcocite. Its uses are varied: it is made into coins, jewelry, and other ornamental objects, employed in building construction, incorporated into alloys, and used as a catalyst in many chemical reactions.

Prochlorperazine can generally be taken with anti-rejection medicines, but your transplant team should confirm it for your specific regimen before you start. Several things matter here.

Prochlorperazine is processed by liver enzymes that also handle many transplant drugs, such as tacrolimus, cyclosporine, and sirolimus. It can also add to the heart-rhythm (QT) risk that some of these drugs carry, and it can occasionally cause movement side effects or sedation. A pharmacist can check your full list quickly, including any drugs you're taking for breast cancer, since some of those interact with transplant medicines too.

The most important point is about the vomiting itself. If you're throwing up soon after taking your anti-rejection medicine, your body may not be absorbing it properly, which can lead to rejection. Don't skip or change doses on your own. Call your transplant team, let them know about the nausea and vomiting, and ask whether they want a blood level check on your immunosuppressant. Ask them too whether they're comfortable with prochlorperazine or would prefer a different antiemetic. Your oncologist may not have had your full transplant medication list when prescribing it, so it's worth making sure both teams know about each other's prescriptions.

If you vomit repeatedly, can't keep your medicines down, or notice fever, decreased urination, or swelling, contact your transplant team right away rather than waiting for your next appointment.

I'm sorry your daughter is dealing with this. A bumpy, raised, mildly itchy rash that shows up near the end of a cold is very common in toddlers, and it's most often harmless. The usual causes are a viral rash that follows or accompanies a cold, a mild reaction to something she was exposed to (including a product), or dry or irritated skin from all the nose wiping, sweating, and extra rubs.

The one thing worth thinking about in your situation is the products. Baby Vicks rub and Hyland's cold and cough can both occasionally irritate skin or trigger a reaction, especially if the rub got on her chest. Since the rash started after about a week of use and is on her chest and stomach, I would stop the Vicks and the Hyland's for now and see whether the rash improves over the next two to three days. If it does, one of them may have been the trigger, and you can avoid it in the future. Her cough alone doesn't need medicine at this age. Honey (a half teaspoon at bedtime is fine for a child over one), fluids, a cool-mist humidifier, and saline drops for her nose work well.

To soothe the rash and itching, keep her skin cool and moisturized. Lukewarm baths, not hot, for about 10 minutes, with a gentle fragrance-free cleanser, help. Pat her dry and apply a thick fragrance-free moisturizer such as Vaseline, Cetaphil, Aveeno, or CeraVe within a few minutes. Dress her in loose, soft cotton, and trim her nails so scratching doesn't break the skin. Use a fragrance-free, dye-free laundry detergent if you can. If the itch is bothering her, a thin layer of 1% hydrocortisone cream once or twice a day for a few days is generally okay on the body for a child her age, but check with her doctor or pharmacist first, and don't use it on her face or for more than a few days without advice. A pediatrician can also tell you whether an oral antihistamine is appropriate and what dose is right for her weight.

Call her pediatrician soon, or get seen the same day, if the rash spreads quickly, becomes blistered, painful, or oozing, or looks like it's getting infected (warmth, increasing redness, yellow crusting). The same applies if she develops a fever, seems unusually tired or irritable, has swelling of her lips or face, or if the rash doesn't improve within a few days or lasts more than a week. Go to the emergency room or call emergency services right away if she has trouble breathing, wheezing, swelling of the face or mouth, repeated vomiting, or if the rash looks like small purple or red spots that don't fade when you press on them, since that needs urgent evaluation.

If it stays mild, it will most likely fade on its own within several days to a week or two. Since I can't see the rash, a quick visit or a photo sent through her pediatrician's portal is a good idea if you're unsure.

A hardware accelerator is a purpose-built hardware component that carries out a particular function, or a small set of functions, faster and with less energy than a general-purpose computer or processor would. These devices are employed to boost speed on demanding workloads, especially those that call for substantial computing capacity or involve heavy calculation. Their uses span many fields, such as machine learning, scientific computation, video processing, and data compression. An accelerator may exist as a separate unit or be built into other hardware, for example a graphics processing unit (GPU) or a field-programmable gate array (FPGA). Such accelerators operate alongside a central processing unit (CPU), which manages and coordinates the overall activity of a computer system. The CPU hands off particular jobs to the accelerator, which completes them more quickly and efficiently than the CPU could on its own. As a result, the system runs more effectively and certain tasks can see a major gain in performance. Common examples include graphics processing units (GPUs), which render images and handle other visual data work; network interface controllers (NICs), which speed up network communication; and digital signal processors (DSPs), which perform mathematical operations on digital signals.

This sounds most likely like a viral chest infection, such as bronchitis, which often follows a cold and can leave a cough, sore throat, tiredness, and soreness in the chest for a week or more. Thick white phlegm is common in this situation and is not usually a concern by itself. The pain in the middle of your chest is probably muscle strain from coughing hard, which is very common, but because it is new and persistent, it is worth having a doctor check it rather than assuming it is harmless.

In the meantime, rest as much as you can and drink plenty of fluids to keep your mucus thin. Warm drinks, honey and lemon, or a saltwater gargle can soothe your throat. Paracetamol or ibuprofen can ease the pain and any fever, provided you have no reason to avoid them. Avoid smoke and dry, cold air, and a steamy shower may help. A cough suppressant is of limited use for a productive cough, since coughing helps clear the chest, but it can help you sleep.

Seek medical help promptly, ideally the same day, through your GP, NHS 111, or a walk-in or urgent care service, if you have any of the following: chest pain that is severe, spreads to your arm, jaw or back, or comes with breathlessness, sweating, or nausea; shortness of breath, even at rest or when walking short distances; coughing up blood or rust-coloured phlegm; a high fever above 38.5°C or one that does not settle; feeling confused, dizzy, or faint; a fast heartbeat; or symptoms that are getting worse rather than better. Because you have recently travelled, including long journeys or periods of sitting still, it is important to mention this to a doctor if you develop sudden breathlessness or chest pain, as a blood clot in the lung needs urgent assessment. If you call an ambulance or go to A&E for sudden severe chest pain or breathing difficulty, do not wait.

If none of those warning signs apply, arrange a routine appointment with your GP in the next day or two. They can listen to your chest and decide whether you need antibiotics or further tests, such as a chest X-ray. Most people recover from this kind of infection within two to three weeks, but the tiredness can linger for some time, so give yourself permission to take it easy.

HIV/AIDS denialism is the conviction that HIV, the virus responsible for AIDS, either does not exist or does not actually cause the disease. People who reject HIV's existence or its connection to AIDS may have a range of motives, such as a poor grasp of the underlying science, an interest in advancing alternative explanations for AIDS, or general distrust of established scientific thinking. A central claim of denialists is that HIV has never been properly isolated and identified as a distinct virus, and that HIV tests cannot be trusted. In reality, scientists have studied HIV in great depth and have both isolated it and identified it as a distinct virus. Moreover, HIV tests are very accurate and are used successfully in numerous countries worldwide. It is worth stressing that denialism can have grave consequences, since it may keep people from getting treated and from taking steps to avoid spreading HIV. It should also be emphasized that decades of scientific research have firmly established the connection between HIV and AIDS, and that effective treatments for the condition exist.

A type system is basically a set of rules that gives every piece of a program (variables, expressions, functions, whatever) a "type." The whole point is to cut down on type errors that blow up while the program's running, by making sure everything follows those type rules.

There are a few flavors. With a static type system, the checking happens at compile time, before you ever run the thing, so you can catch and fix type errors early. With a dynamic type system, the checking happens while the program's actually running. That means a type error might sit there unnoticed until that exact line executes, and then your program just fails on the spot.

Type systems also differ in how much safety they give you. A type-safe language is one where type errors either can't happen or are really unlikely. A type-unsafe language is the opposite: type errors show up more often, and it's a lot easier to slip one into your code without realizing.

Either way, type systems are a big help for keeping programs reliable and correct, which is why so many languages have one built in.
