The voice in your head has a name, actually: self-talk, or inner speech. It's just the way you think to yourself, or the way you carry on a conversation with yourself without saying anything out loud. That talking comes from activity in your brain, mostly in the areas that handle language and thought. Those areas are full of neurons, or brain cells, that pass signals to each other across connections called synapses.

So to answer your question: the "I" doesn't live in one particular spot in your brain. There's no tiny little person up there doing the talking. The voice is what you get when lots of neurons are firing and linking up with each other. It's your brain processing information, putting thoughts together, and turning them into words.

Lebesgue integration is a way of defining the integral of a function, developed by Henri Lebesgue in the early twentieth century. It extends and generalizes the Riemann integral, which is the approach most people first meet in calculus. The key difference lies in how the two methods slice up the problem. The Riemann integral partitions the domain of a function, the x-axis, into small intervals and approximates the area under the curve by summing rectangles whose heights are taken from the function's values on those intervals. The Lebesgue integral instead partitions the range, the y-axis, into small intervals and asks how much of the domain maps into each of those value intervals. In effect, it measures the sets of inputs at which the function takes values in a given band, weights each band by its approximate value, and sums these contributions.

This change in perspective makes the Lebesgue integral far more robust. It is built on measure theory, which assigns a notion of size, called measure, to sets that can be far more complicated than intervals. Because of this, the Lebesgue integral can handle functions with very irregular behavior, such as the indicator function of the rationals, which takes the value 1 on rational numbers and 0 elsewhere. This function has no Riemann integral because it is discontinuous almost everywhere, yet its Lebesgue integral over an interval is zero, since the rationals have measure zero.

The Lebesgue integral also has much better behavior under limits. The convergence theorems, including the monotone convergence theorem and the dominated convergence theorem, state conditions under which one may interchange a limit and an integral. These results are essential in analysis, probability theory, and many areas of applied mathematics, and they are much harder to establish with the Riemann integral. For this reason, the Lebesgue integral forms the foundation of modern real analysis and of the rigorous treatment of probability, where expectations of random variables are defined as Lebesgue integrals with respect to a probability measure.

You're not imagining it. Competitive bodybuilders really do look different from regular gym-goers, and a few things combine to create that look.

The first is that they lift with a different goal. Most people exercise to be healthy, strong, or fit. A bodybuilder's whole job is to make muscles as big as possible, so they train each muscle like a sculptor working on a statue, hitting it from many angles, many days a week, for years. Muscles grow when you push them hard, eat a lot, and rest, and bodybuilders do all three to an extreme.

The second is food. Think of muscles as a house being built: you need lots of bricks. Bodybuilders eat huge amounts of protein and calories to build size, then later follow very strict diets to strip away almost all their fat. Normal people have a soft layer of fat over their muscles, like a blanket over furniture. On stage, bodybuilders have taken the blanket off, so you see every bump, line, and vein. That's a big part of why it looks strange: we almost never see human bodies with that little fat, and it isn't healthy to stay that lean for long.

The third is stage tricks. Before a show they often cut back on water and salt so their skin looks thin and tight, then eat carbs to make their muscles look full. They put on very dark spray tans because bright stage lights wash out details, and they oil up so the muscles shine. In everyday life they look noticeably softer and less extreme than in competition photos.

The fourth, and the one that explains most of the "unnatural" look at the top level, is drugs. Many professional bodybuilders use steroids, growth hormone, insulin, and other substances. These act like turning up the body's "build muscle" dial far beyond what nature allows. A natural person's body has a limit on how big it can get, and these drugs push past it. That's why some pros have giant shoulders, thick necks, and sometimes swollen-looking bellies from growth hormone and huge amounts of food. These drugs carry real health risks, including heart problems.

So regular exercisers look healthy and normal because they're building a body for living. Bodybuilders look strange because they're building a body for being judged on a stage, using extreme training, extreme dieting, stage tricks, and often drugs to get there.

I'm sorry you're dealing with pain that keeps going on and seems to be getting worse. When pain persists after imaging and treatment, and you feel it's worsening, it's reasonable to keep pushing for answers, even when you've been told it's nothing serious.

First, get emergency care right away if you notice black or tarry stools, vomiting blood or material that looks like coffee grounds, fainting or dizziness, a rigid or very swollen belly, fever with pain, pain that suddenly becomes much more intense, or chest pain or shortness of breath. Aspirin can irritate the stomach lining and cause ulcers or bleeding, so these symptoms matter even more while you're taking it.

Because you're on aspirin, ask your doctor directly whether it's still the right medicine for you, whether you should take it with food, and whether a stomach-protecting medication such as a proton pump inhibitor would be appropriate. Don't stop aspirin on your own if you take it for a heart or stroke-prevention reason, but do ask whether a different pain reliever would be safer for your stomach.

Next, ask for specific answers rather than general reassurance. You might say, "I'd like to know what you think is causing this, what has been ruled out, and what the next step is if it doesn't improve." Useful questions include whether you've been tested for H. pylori (a common and treatable cause of stomach pain), whether blood tests for liver, pancreas, and gallbladder function have been done, and whether an upper endoscopy or colonoscopy has been considered. If you're not getting clear answers, ask for a referral to a gastroenterologist, which is the specialty most suited to ongoing stomach pain. Seeking a second opinion from another doctor is also completely reasonable.

It also helps to keep a simple log for a few weeks: when the pain happens, how severe it is on a scale of 0 to 10, what makes it better or worse (food, movement, time of day, bowel movements), and any other symptoms such as weight loss, nausea, changes in appetite, or changes in bowel habits. This gives your doctors concrete information and makes it harder for symptoms to be dismissed.

Finally, your sense that something is getting worse deserves to be taken seriously. If your doctors aren't listening, you can say so clearly, and it's appropriate to seek another opinion.

Yes, there are a few things you can start tonight that will help, though home measures usually ease oral thrush rather than fully clear it, so plan on calling your doctor tomorrow as well.

The most important step is changing how you use your Flovent. Thrush is a common side effect of inhaled steroids because some of the medicine settles in the mouth and throat and lowers local immunity there. After every puff, rinse your mouth thoroughly with water, gargle, and spit it out rather than swallowing. If you have a spacer, use it, since it reduces how much steroid lands in your mouth. Don't stop the Flovent on your own, especially while you're recovering from a respiratory illness. Your prescriber can decide whether to adjust it.

For soothing and helping clear the infection, rinse several times a day with warm salt water (about half a teaspoon of salt in a cup of warm water) or a baking soda rinse (about half a teaspoon in a cup of water), swishing and spitting. Brush gently with a soft toothbrush, and replace that toothbrush once the infection clears so you don't reintroduce yeast. If you wear dentures, clean them carefully and leave them out overnight. Cutting back on sugary foods and drinks can help, since yeast feeds on sugar. Plain unsweetened yogurt with live cultures is a reasonable addition, though the evidence for it is modest. Cool, soft foods and drinks may feel better on a sore throat in the meantime.

Even with these measures, thrush linked to inhaled steroids usually responds best to a prescription antifungal, such as nystatin liquid, clotrimazole lozenges, or sometimes fluconazole pills. These are quick and inexpensive to get, often through a phone or telehealth visit, and they typically clear things up within one to two weeks. It's also worth confirming that this is thrush. It usually looks like creamy white patches on the tongue, cheeks, or throat that can be wiped off, leaving a red or slightly raw surface underneath.

Seek care sooner if swallowing becomes painful or feels like food is sticking, since that can mean the infection has spread into the esophagus and needs oral medication. The same applies if you have a fever, if the patches spread or bleed significantly, if you have diabetes or a weakened immune system, or if your flu symptoms return or your breathing worsens. Your pharmacist can also be a helpful resource tonight if you want guidance on products or on rinsing technique with your inhaler.

When Pluto was found in 1930, nobody knew much about it. It was the only thing out there past Neptune that anyone could see, and it looked like a small dot that moved around the sun. Astronomers were looking for a ninth planet, so when they found something, they called it a planet. They didn't have a "dwarf planet" box to put it in because nobody had a reason to make one yet.

Over the years, people learned that Pluto was much smaller than first thought. It's even smaller than our Moon. Then, starting in the 1990s, telescopes got better and astronomers began finding lots of other icy things out in the same faraway neighborhood, called the Kuiper Belt. Pluto wasn't alone out there. It was just one of many. In 2005 they found one called Eris that was about the same size as Pluto, even a little heavier.

That made people ask a question: if Pluto is a planet, is Eris a planet too? And what about the next one, and the next? We might end up with dozens or hundreds of planets. So in 2006 a group of astronomers called the International Astronomical Union decided to write down clear rules for what counts as a planet.

Think of it like a club with three rules. First, you have to go around the sun. Second, you have to be big enough that your own gravity pulls you into a round ball. Third, you have to have cleared your path, meaning you're the boss of your orbit and have swept up or flung away the other stuff near you. Pluto follows the first two rules, but it shares its orbit with lots of other icy objects, so it fails the third. Because it's round and orbits the sun but hasn't cleared its path, it got a new name: dwarf planet.

So Pluto didn't change at all. It's the same little world it always was. What changed is that we learned more, and we made clearer rules for naming things. It's a bit like calling a whale a fish for a long time, then learning more and deciding it fits better in a different group. Some people still wish Pluto were a planet, and that's okay, but it's still a wonderful, interesting world.

Saint Patrick's the patron saint of Ireland, and he's usually credited with bringing Christianity there in the 5th century. He was a missionary and bishop. The story goes that he was born in Britain to Roman parents, then got snatched by Irish pirates as a teenager and hauled off to Ireland as a slave. He eventually got away, but he went back as a missionary, preaching and converting a lot of people. Today he's remembered on St. Patrick's Day, a holiday that's part cultural, part religious, and gets celebrated by Irish folks and communities all over the world.

Cloud computing refers to an arrangement in which many internet-connected machines work together to supply computing capacity whenever it is requested. Rather than executing programs or keeping files on a personal computer or in-house server, people can reach these capabilities online through a cloud vendor. Adopting this approach offers a number of advantages. It can lower costs compared with maintaining your own servers or hosting applications yourself, since you pay only for what you consume. It also makes growing or shrinking your resources straightforward, with no need to purchase additional equipment. Reliability is another strength, as providers usually maintain backup systems so that applications stay online even if one machine fails. In addition, providers generally employ strong security protections to safeguard information and software. Cloud computing comes in several forms. The most fundamental is Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS), where the provider rents out underlying hardware such as servers, storage, and networking. Platform as a Service (PaaS) supplies a ready-made environment, including operating systems, databases, or development tools, on which customers can construct and run their own software. Software as a Service (SaaS) delivers complete applications that users simply access over the internet. Well-known providers include Amazon Web Services (AWS), Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud Platform.

Phobias can indeed be overcome. A phobia is an irrational fear of a particular thing, and one effective treatment is known as "exposure therapy." In this approach, you slowly and deliberately confront whatever frightens you, under safe and controlled conditions. Someone who fears bugs, for instance, might begin by viewing photos of them, then progress to touching one, and finally to staying in a room where one is present. The process can feel frightening and hard, yet it teaches your brain that the object of your fear isn't really a threat. As you keep practicing over time, the fear fades and you become less anxious. Remember that being afraid of things is perfectly normal, but it's worthwhile to work on your fears so they don't limit your life. If you're dealing with a phobia and would like to try exposure therapy, it's wise to team up with a mental health professional, who can guide you in confronting your fears in a safe and effective way.

"Deep structure" is a concept from linguistics, most closely associated with Noam Chomsky and the early versions of his transformational-generative grammar, especially as presented in his 1965 book Aspects of the Theory of Syntax. It refers to an abstract, underlying level of representation of a sentence that captures its basic grammatical relationships and core meaning, as opposed to the "surface structure," which is the actual form of the sentence as it is spoken or written.

The central idea is that sentences that look different on the surface can share the same deep structure, and sentences that look identical on the surface can have different deep structures. For example, "The dog chased the cat" and "The cat was chased by the dog" differ in word order and form, yet in both the dog is the one doing the chasing and the cat is the one being chased. Chomsky proposed that both sentences derive from a common underlying representation, and that rules called transformations (such as the passive transformation) convert that representation into the different surface forms. Conversely, a sentence like "Flying planes can be dangerous" is ambiguous: it can mean that the act of flying planes is dangerous or that planes which are flying are dangerous. The theory explains this by saying one surface string corresponds to two distinct deep structures.

Another classic illustration contrasts "John is eager to please" with "John is easy to please." On the surface they appear structurally parallel, but in the first John is the one who wants to please others, while in the second John is the one who is pleased by others. Deep structure was meant to make such hidden differences explicit.

In the original theory, deep structure was generated by phrase structure rules and the lexicon, and it was the level where semantic interpretation was thought to take place, while transformations mapped it onto surface structure, which was then given a phonological form. This view was influential partly because it suggested that human languages share deep, universal organizing principles even when their surface grammars differ greatly.

Over time the concept was revised and eventually abandoned in Chomsky's own work. Debates in the late 1960s and 1970s, notably with the generative semantics movement, questioned exactly where meaning was determined. Later frameworks renamed the level "D-structure" to strip away popular misconceptions that it meant something profound or psychologically "deep," and the Minimalist Program of the 1990s eliminated D-structure altogether as a distinct level of representation. Nonetheless, the term remains historically important and is still used informally to describe the idea that the meaning and structure underlying a sentence can differ from its visible form.

The phrase has also been borrowed in other fields. In psychology and therapy, particularly neuro-linguistic programming, it refers loosely to the full underlying experience or meaning behind what someone says, and in literary theory and anthropology it sometimes denotes underlying patterns beneath surface narratives or cultural practices, though these uses are looser adaptations of the linguistic concept.

Automated reasoning is a branch of computer science and artificial intelligence concerned with building programs that can draw logical conclusions, verify claims, and solve problems through formal deduction, without a human walking through each step. The core idea is to represent knowledge and problems in a precise logical language, such as propositional logic, first-order logic, or some more specialized formalism, and then use algorithms to derive whether a statement follows from a set of assumptions or whether a given property holds.

The field has several main kinds of tools. Theorem provers attempt to prove mathematical statements or properties of software and hardware systems by constructing formal proofs. Satisfiability (SAT) and satisfiability modulo theories (SMT) solvers decide whether a logical formula can be made true by some assignment of values, and they are widely used because many practical problems, from scheduling to circuit design, can be encoded this way. Model checkers explore all possible states of a system to confirm that it never reaches a bad state, which is useful for catching subtle concurrency bugs. Proof assistants such as Coq, Isabelle, and Lean combine human guidance with automated search to build machine-checked proofs of complex results.

Automated reasoning has practical applications in hardware verification, software security, cryptographic protocol analysis, and the configuration of cloud and network policies. For example, companies use these techniques to mathematically confirm that access-control rules do what they are intended to do. It also supports research in mathematics, where computers have helped settle certain long-standing problems.

Because the underlying problems are often computationally hard, much of the work involves designing clever heuristics and efficient search strategies so that solvers can handle realistic inputs in reasonable time. In short, automated reasoning aims to make logic itself a tool that machines can apply reliably and at scale.

Transfer learning is a machine learning approach in which a model developed for one job is adapted to a different but related job. This typically means starting with a pre-trained model and adjusting its weights on new data so it fits the new objective. The underlying premise is that characteristics a model picks up while solving one problem can prove helpful on other problems. Consider a model that has learned to identify patterns in pictures of animals: with further tuning, it could also learn to identify patterns in pictures of plants. Rather than beginning from zero and mastering image recognition all over again, the model can draw on what it already knows. This method is frequently applied when the data available for the new task is scarce and insufficient for training a model from the ground up. It can also raise a model's performance on a new task by leveraging features acquired during the earlier one. In short, transfer learning is a strong technique that helps practitioners create more accurate and efficient models, particularly when data is limited.

An arraignment is a formal court proceeding in which a person accused of a crime is brought before a judge to hear the specific charges against them. During the arraignment, the defendant is usually asked to enter a plea, such as guilty, not guilty, or sometimes no contest. The judge may also address matters like bail or bond, confirm that the defendant has or will have a lawyer (or appoint a public defender if they cannot afford one), and set dates for future hearings or the trial. The purpose is to make sure the accused understands the charges and their rights, and to move the case forward. Arraignments typically take place shortly after an arrest or formal charging, though the exact timing and procedures vary by jurisdiction.

A body of land entirely encircled by water is called an island. Islands may be large or small, and no bridge or similar link joins them to other land. A continent, by contrast, is a vast area of land that water does not wholly enclose, since bridges, tunnels, or other links attach it to neighboring land. Australia counts as an island because water surrounds all of it, and no bridge or other kind of connection ties it to any other land.

Sure thing! The American election system is a bit tangled, but here's my best shot at making it clear. Every four years, Americans vote for who they want as President. You have to be at least 35 and born in the U.S. to qualify. On Election Day, people head to polling places and cast their ballots. Whoever gets the most votes in a state wins that state's electoral votes, and each state's count depends on its population. A candidate needs at least 270 of the 538 electoral votes to win and become President. That's the core of it, but there's a lot more to the rules, and there are also races for other offices like Congress and state governors. Hope that clears things up a little! Got any other questions about how it all works?

Early retirement in the UK is possible through several routes, though each carries trade-offs around income, tax, and eligibility, so it is worth understanding the main options before making decisions.

The most important figure to know is your State Pension age, which is currently 66 for most people and is scheduled to rise to 67 between 2026 and 2028, and later to 68. You cannot draw the State Pension before this age, so anyone retiring earlier must fund the gap from other sources. Your personal State Pension forecast is available through the government's online service, and it is a sensible first check.

For workplace pensions, the normal minimum pension age is 55, rising to 57 from April 2028. Defined contribution pots, such as a personal pension or a workplace pot, can usually be accessed from this age, and up to 25 percent of the pot can typically be taken tax-free, with the rest taxed as income. Taking money early can significantly reduce the long-term value of the pot, and it can trigger the Money Purchase Annual Allowance, which limits how much you can subsequently contribute to pensions while still getting tax relief. Defined benefit schemes, often final salary schemes, may offer early retirement with a reduced pension, sometimes with a penalty, or in some cases without one if you retire at a specific age or have longer service. Your scheme administrator can explain the exact terms and the cost of early payment.

Some people retire before the normal pension age by using a stakeholder or personal pension arrangement combined with savings, such as ISAs, which are free of income and capital gains tax and have no age restriction. Taxable savings, cash, and investment portfolios can bridge the gap, and careful drawdown planning can keep you in lower tax bands. Those with a spouse or partner may also consider how each person's allowances and pensions can be used together.

A few special cases exist. Ill health early retirement may be available through a workplace pension scheme if you can no longer work because of a medical condition, and the rules vary by scheme. Some public sector schemes, such as the armed forces or police pension schemes, allow retirement at earlier ages with a defined benefit income.

Practical steps include checking every pension you have, including old workplace schemes you may have forgotten, requesting a statement of the benefits each would pay at different ages, and building a realistic budget that covers the years before State Pension age. Because tax, pension rules, and benefits change, and because the decisions are hard to reverse, speaking with a regulated financial adviser or using the free Pension Wise service, offered by MoneyHelper for people with defined contribution pensions aged 50 and over, can be valuable. Anyone with complex circumstances or a large pension should seek regulated advice before acting.

Yeah, you can't really get cash off a credit card without paying for it. Cards are built for buying stuff, not pulling out cash. If you need cash, your best bet is usually an ATM or a withdrawal from your checking or savings through your bank or credit union.

If you really do have to use the card, you can take a cash advance at a bank or ATM. Just know it'll cost you. There's usually a fee, the interest rate is often much higher than your regular purchase rate, and there's no grace period, so interest starts piling up the second you take the money out. Honestly, it's rarely a good deal. Stick with a debit card or your bank account whenever you can, since those don't come with fees or interest.

Okay so birds don't digest stuff like we do. They skip the long intestine most mammals have and rely on a short one, plus a gizzard, which is basically a muscular chunk of the stomach that grinds up whatever they've eaten. Pretty neat setup.

The white part is the thing people usually ask about. Birds don't pass solid poop like dogs or humans do. Instead they make uric acid, a whitish paste, and it gets mixed in with the solid waste as it leaves. That's the white stuff you see on your car. Mammals mostly pee out their nitrogen waste as urea in liquid form, so they don't have that white goop. Their solid poop tends to be brown instead.

Inside an artichoke's fruit, which is the part of the plant people eat, you will find the seed. Several layers of edible flesh surround it, and you can get to them by peeling off the outer layers of the artichoke. The seed is usually small and hard, and it sits at the very center of the fruit. People generally do not regard it as something to eat. If you want to take the seed out, begin by stripping away the fruit's outer layers, either with your fingers or with a knife. When the center is exposed, the seed should be visible. Gently pull it free with your fingers or a small spoon. Take care not to harm the seed, since it plays an important role in the plant's life cycle and is what is used to grow new artichoke plants.

Insurance offers a means of safeguarding yourself and your belongings against unforeseen events. Suppose another driver collides with your car: your auto policy can contribute toward the cost of fixing your vehicle. Rather than covering every repair bill entirely on your own, your insurer may pay for all or part of it. Consider how costly it would be to bear the full expense of every possible misfortune yourself. Insurance spreads the financial burden of such events across a large pool of policyholders, so that no single person has to absorb the entire cost. You can picture it as a kind of shared fund. By signing up (purchasing a policy), you commit to paying a modest regular amount, known as the premium. If a covered incident occurs, such as a car accident, the pool helps pay for the loss. Over time, this arrangement can keep you from spending a great deal of money.

Imagine a big group of kids sharing one big box of toys, and everyone agrees the toys should be fair. Communism is the big idea behind that: a world where nobody is rich and nobody is poor, and the people who make things own them together. Marx was the thinker who first wrote down this idea in the 1800s. He thought that workers were being treated unfairly by bosses who owned the factories, and he dreamed of a future where workers would take over and share everything equally. Marxism is just the name for his original ideas.

Lenin was a leader in Russia who wanted to make Marx's dream happen. He believed that a small group of very dedicated people, called a party, had to lead the workers and run things at first, because he thought regular people might not be ready to do it on their own. He took power in 1917 in a revolution, and that way of doing things is called Leninism.

Stalin came after Lenin and ran the country with a very tight grip. He wanted total control, and he punished or removed anyone who disagreed with him, even people who had once been his friends. Stalinism means that kind of harsh, one-person rule, and it caused a lot of suffering. It is not a fair way to share toys, so many people think it went badly wrong.

Trotsky was another leader who worked with Lenin, but he lost the fight with Stalin and was eventually forced out of the country and killed. Trotskyism is his version of the idea. Trotsky believed the revolution should spread to other countries around the world, not just stay in one place. He also wanted workers to have more say, not just a single strong leader.

So the main idea is the same for all of them: share things fairly. They just disagree about how to get there and who should be in charge along the way.

Self-determination theory is a broad framework in psychology that examines human motivation, personality, and well-being. Developed in the late 1970s and 1980s by psychologists Edward Deci and Richard Ryan, it starts from the premise that people have innate psychological needs that drive them toward growth, integration, and meaningful engagement with the world. Rather than seeing motivation as a simple matter of rewards and punishments, the theory holds that humans are naturally active and curious, and that their behavior is shaped largely by whether those underlying needs are satisfied.

The theory identifies three basic psychological needs that it considers universal. The first is autonomy, the sense that one's actions are self-endorsed and chosen rather than imposed or controlled by others. The second is competence, the feeling of effectiveness and mastery in what one does. The third is relatedness, the experience of feeling connected to, cared for by, and belonging with other people. When these three needs are met, people tend to be more engaged, resilient, and psychologically healthy. When they are frustrated, people may become apathetic, anxious, or defensive.

A central distinction within the theory concerns the types of motivation. Intrinsic motivation refers to doing something for its own sake because it is interesting or enjoyable. Extrinsic motivation refers to doing something to obtain an outcome, such as a reward or to avoid punishment. Self-determination theory does not treat extrinsic motivation as wholly negative. It describes a continuum along which external motives can become more internalized and self-endorsed over time, moving from simple compliance toward genuine personal value. The theory suggests that environments supporting autonomy, competence, and relatedness foster this internalization better than environments relying on pressure, control, or constant evaluation.

Self-determination theory has been applied widely in areas such as education, workplace management, healthcare, sports, parenting, and psychotherapy. Research within this framework has generally found that autonomy-supportive approaches, such as giving people meaningful choices and acknowledging their perspectives, tend to produce better learning, performance, and well-being than controlling approaches.

So the false positive rate is basically how often a test says "yes, this is present" when it really isn't. You get it by taking the number of false positives and dividing by the total number of actual negatives.

Think of a medical test for some disease. The false positive rate would be the share of people who test positive even though they don't have the disease. Strictly speaking, it's out of everyone who's truly healthy, not out of everyone who tested positive, which trips a lot of people up. So the formula is just: false positive rate = false positives / total negatives.

If the rate's high, the test is throwing up a lot of false alarms. If it's low, you can trust a positive result a bit more, or at least it's less likely to be wrong in that direction.

You'll usually see it paired with the true positive rate, which is also called sensitivity or recall. Looking at both together gives you a much better picture of how well a test or any measurement method actually performs.

Yes, though the trick usually works in the opposite direction from what the phrase suggests. Ignoring sunk costs is the correct way to make decisions: money already spent cannot be recovered, so only future cash flows should matter. But that principle can be exploited when someone frames a decision so that the past spending quietly disappears from view while the benefits of continuing are highlighted.

A common example is a project manager asking for approval to finish a half-built venture. The pitch emphasizes that "only the remaining $2 million is at stake," which is technically a sunk-cost-consistent argument, but it omits whether the completed project will generate enough future returns to justify that $2 million. The original $10 million, which may have been wasted, is excluded from the presentation, so the investment looks cheap even though it may be a poor use of resources. Similarly, a seller of a used asset might point out that its marginal cost of keeping it running is low, while glossing over that its expected future earnings are below what a replacement would produce.

The deception works because the future-only framing is accurate in isolation. The misleading part lies in selective framing: the analysis compares the cost of continuing against nothing, rather than against the best alternative, which might be abandoning the project and redeploying the money elsewhere. The right question is never "what have we already spent?" but also not just "what is the next dollar costing us?" It is "given everything we could do with the next dollar, is this the best option?"

To guard against this, decision-makers should ask for the full comparison of alternatives, check whether the projected future returns are realistic, and be wary of presentations that emphasize how little remains to be spent without showing what the finished result will be worth.

The short answer is that the share price is always set by buyers and sellers trading with each other. Profit never flows directly into the share price. A company earning X dollars doesn't mechanically add anything to the stock's value on the exchange. What profit does is change what buyers and sellers are willing to pay, and that is how earnings end up influencing the price.

The key idea is that markets are forward-looking and prices reflect expectations. If analysts and investors widely expected the company to earn X dollars, they will already have been buying and selling with that number in mind for weeks or months. By the time the company announces it earned exactly X, the information is "priced in," so the announcement itself often causes little movement. The earlier rise in the share price, as people came to expect the profit, is where the effect of that profit showed up, and it happened through investors bidding the price up in anticipation.

What moves a stock sharply on an earnings announcement is the surprise. If the company earns more than expected, buyers suddenly see the business as more valuable than they thought and are willing to pay more, while sellers demand more to part with their shares, so the price jumps. If it earns less than expected, even if it is still a healthy profit, the price can fall, because the shares had been priced for a better result. This is why you sometimes see a company report record profits and its stock drop: the market wanted even more. Guidance about future quarters often matters as much as the reported number, since investors care about future earnings more than past ones.

Underneath this, profit matters because a share is a claim on the company's future earnings, whether paid out as dividends, reinvested to grow the business, or used for buybacks. Investors estimate what that stream of future cash is worth today and trade accordingly. So the honest way to put it is that profits drive value, expectations of profits drive investor behavior, and the actual price at any moment is simply the level where the buyers and sellers meet. Earnings matter only insofar as they change the minds of those buyers and sellers.

Delaware was one of the original 13 colonies that broke away from Great Britain and helped form the United States. People call it the "First State" because it was the first to ratify the Constitution, doing so on December 7, 1787, before any other state signed on. That made it the first state to officially join the new federal union. The motto, "Liberty and Independence," ties back to that history and to the state's part in founding the country. You'll also see "The First State" printed on Delaware license plates, and plenty of folks there are pretty proud of it.

I'm sorry you've been struggling with this for two years. Compulsive cleaning is one of the most common forms of OCD, and the encouraging part is that it is very treatable.

Whether you need lifelong treatment varies from person to person. OCD is generally considered a chronic condition, meaning it tends to come and go over time, but that does not mean you will be stuck with severe symptoms or on medication forever. Many people reach a point where their symptoms are minimal or absent for long periods, and some stay well without any ongoing treatment. Others find that symptoms return when they stop medication or when they are under stress, so they continue a low-maintenance plan. It is better to think of it as something that can be managed very well rather than a condition with a single permanent cure, though full remission is realistic for many people.

The most effective treatment combines medication with a specific kind of therapy called cognitive behavioral therapy, in particular exposure and response prevention, often shortened to ERP. In ERP, you gradually face the situations that trigger your urge to clean, such as leaving a room slightly untidy, and you practice not performing the cleaning ritual. Over time the anxiety falls on its own and the urge loses its power. Studies show that people who learn ERP often keep their gains long after therapy ends, and it lowers the chance of relapse, including after medication is reduced. If you are only taking fluoxetine and have not tried ERP, adding it could make a major difference.

On fluoxetine, OCD usually needs higher doses than depression and takes 8 to 12 weeks at an adequate dose to show its full effect. If you have been on it for a while without enough improvement, your doctor can adjust the dose, switch to another medication, or add a second one. Please do not stop it suddenly or on your own, since that can cause withdrawal symptoms and a return of symptoms. If you and your doctor decide to stop eventually, it is usually done slowly after a year or more of stable improvement.

Some practical steps can help in the meantime. Try delaying a cleaning urge by a few minutes and then lengthening the delay, and notice that the anxiety rises and then fades without the ritual. Avoid seeking reassurance from family, and try to keep a regular routine for sleep, exercise, and stress. Talk to your psychiatrist about how well your current treatment is working and ask for a referral to a therapist trained in ERP. If your symptoms ever make you feel hopeless or like harming yourself, seek help right away.

Your question makes sense, and the answer is that you're right about evolution but a little off about what insects are "supposed" to learn. Evolution doesn't make animals smart or give them a rule book. It only shapes behavior that worked well enough in the past. Insects are attracted to light because of a simple built-in trick. Most flying insects that live at night use the moon and stars to navigate, and they keep a steady angle to a bright light source so they fly in a straight line. A distant light like the moon stays at the same angle no matter how far you fly, so this works well. A nearby bug zapper is different. When an insect flies toward a light that is close, the angle changes quickly, and the insect spirals inward instead of flying straight. It's like a sailor using a lighthouse that suddenly moves close to the ship.

Evolution hasn't fixed this because the zapper is very new in evolutionary terms, and the mistake doesn't usually stop an insect from having babies. Most of the insects drawn to lights would have been fine in the wild, and the few that get caught are a tiny fraction of the population. Evolution only works on what matters for survival and reproduction, and this trap rarely changes those numbers enough to matter.

As for insect brains, they are small and simple, with far fewer nerve cells than ours, so they run on fixed instincts rather than learning from mistakes like this. A fly doesn't think "that light hurt my friends last time." It just follows its built-in navigation rule, which is almost always helpful and only occasionally fatal.

Most stoplights stack the colors vertically, with red on top, yellow in the middle, and green on the bottom. Red means stop. Yellow is your heads-up that red is coming, so start getting ready to stop. Green means it's clear to go. Pretty much everywhere uses the same setup, so you don't have to relearn anything when you drive somewhere new.

Brett Favre started 297 consecutive regular-season games for the Green Bay Packers, from September 20, 1992, through the 2007 season. Including playoff games, his streak reached 321 consecutive starts, which is often cited as the NFL record for quarterbacks. Favre's streak ended on December 2, 2007, when he was sidelined in a game against the Packers' opponents with a sprained ankle... wait, let me correct that: he did not miss a game because of injury in that stretch, and the streak ended when he was benched during a game against the Jets in 2010 instead.

Honestly, there's no hard rule on this. Some people grab cash for small stuff because it's fast and simple, while others swipe because it's easier to track spending and they like the rewards. It really comes down to what works for you.

A few things are worth thinking about. First, cost: some cards tack on fees for certain transactions, like foreign transaction fees or cash advances, so if your card does that, paying small amounts with it might not make much sense. Second, the merchant matters too. A lot of small shops would rather get cash for tiny purchases since card processing eats into their margins and cash is less hassle for them. If you can pay with cash, that's often a nice gesture. Basically, keep the fees and the shop's situation in mind, and go with whatever's easiest for you and them.

Actually, solar has gotten much better, but it took a long time because it started out very expensive, and people only buy big things when they are cheap enough.

Imagine the first toy of its kind costs as much as a house. Nobody buys it except people with lots of money who really need it. The first solar panels, made in the 1950s, were like that. They were used on satellites in space because nothing else would work there, and cost was not the main worry. For everyday use, they cost hundreds of times more than electricity from coal or gas, so almost nobody bought them.

Then the prices slowly came down. Every time more panels were made, factories learned how to make them cheaper and better, a bit like how you get faster at building with blocks the more you practice. Since the 1970s, the price of solar panels has dropped by more than 99 percent. In the last ten to fifteen years, it dropped so fast that solar became the cheapest way to make new electricity in many places. That is why you now see panels on roofs and in big fields all over the place. In many countries, solar is growing faster than any other kind of power.

So why does it still feel like it is only "in the talks"? There are a few reasons. First, the sun goes away at night and hides behind clouds, so you need batteries or other power sources to fill in the gaps, and batteries only recently became cheap enough. Second, the old power system was built around big power plants, and changing wires, rules, and habits takes a long time. Third, oil, gas, and coal companies were already big and powerful, and some governments protected them. Fourth, for many years the support for solar went on and off, because leaders kept changing their minds about helping it.

Also, electricity is only part of all the energy we use. Cars, planes, ships, and factories use a lot of energy too, and those are harder to switch over.

So the short version is this: solar was too expensive for a long time, then it got cheap very quickly, and now the world is catching up. The change is happening, just slower than the hopeful talk made it sound.

Newton's universal law of gravitation states that every particle of matter in the universe attracts every other particle with a force that is directly proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between their centers. In symbols, this is written as F = G m1 m2 / r², where F is the magnitude of the gravitational force, m1 and m2 are the two masses, r is the distance separating them, and G is the gravitational constant, approximately 6.674 × 10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg².

Several things follow from this. The force is always attractive, never repulsive. It acts along the straight line joining the two objects, and the two objects pull on each other with equal and opposite forces, in accordance with Newton's third law. Doubling either mass doubles the force, while doubling the distance reduces the force to one quarter of its original value.

The law is called universal because it applies everywhere: it explains why an apple falls to the ground, why the Moon orbits the Earth, and why planets orbit the Sun. It also underlies Kepler's laws of planetary motion and the tides.

Newton's law works very well for most everyday and astronomical situations, but it was later refined by Einstein's general theory of relativity, which describes gravity as the curvature of spacetime caused by mass and energy. The Newtonian version remains accurate enough for most purposes except where gravity is extremely strong or precision is very high, such as near black holes or in the orbit of Mercury.

At the most basic level, a stock's price goes up when more people want to buy it at the current price than want to sell it, so buyers have to offer more to get shares. That is only the mechanics, though. The more useful question is why buyers become willing to pay more, and company performance is a big part of the answer, but not all of it.

A share of stock is a claim on a fraction of a company's future profits, whether those profits are paid out as dividends, reinvested to grow the business, or used to buy back shares. In theory, a stock is worth the present value of all the cash it will generate for owners over its lifetime. So when a company earns more, or when investors come to believe it will earn more in the future, the stock tends to rise. Over long periods, this is the dominant force. Broad stock indexes trend upward mainly because the economy grows, companies sell more, and their profits rise along with population, productivity, and inflation. Companies also typically retain part of their earnings and reinvest them, which compounds the value of each share.

The key word, though, is expectations. Prices reflect what investors already anticipate, so a stock moves on news that changes those expectations rather than on good or bad performance as such. A company can report record profits and see its stock fall because investors expected even more, while a struggling company's stock can jump if results are less bad than feared. This is why prices often seem disconnected from current results: they are forward-looking bets on what comes next.

Interest rates are another major factor. Because future profits have to be translated into today's value, the rate used to discount them matters a lot. When interest rates fall, safe alternatives like bonds and savings accounts pay less, so stocks look relatively more attractive, and distant future earnings are worth more today. When rates rise, the opposite happens. This is why stock markets often react sharply to central bank decisions even when nothing about the companies themselves has changed.

Inflation plays a role too. Since companies sell goods at nominal prices, rising prices tend to lift nominal revenues and profits over time, so some of the long-run increase in stock prices simply reflects the declining value of money rather than real gains.

Beyond fundamentals, there are flows of money and human psychology. When more savings flow into the market, for example through retirement contributions that automatically buy index funds, that steady demand supports prices. Companies buying back their own shares reduce the supply and increase each remaining share's claim on profits. In the short run, sentiment, fear, greed, hype, momentum trading, and news headlines can push prices well above or below what fundamentals justify, which is how bubbles and crashes happen. Risk appetite matters as well: when investors feel confident, they accept lower expected returns and pay higher prices for the same earnings.

So the short answer is that stocks go up over the long term mostly because companies grow their profits and the economy expands, but in any given day, month, or year, prices move because of changing expectations, interest rates, money flows, and investor mood, which can overwhelm the underlying business performance for quite a while.

It is entirely typical for certain boys to speak with a higher pitch than their peers. No medication or therapy can alter a person's inherent vocal pitch, and there is no need or benefit in attempting to modify a natural voice to fit social norms. Every individual is distinct, and no voice is inherently correct or incorrect. If your voice worries you, consulting a speech therapist or a medical professional may help. They can evaluate your voice and offer information and methods to support clear communication. Additionally, other people's views and judgments about your voice have no bearing on your value as a person.

Having two periods about two weeks apart in one month is not usually a sign of anything serious, but it is worth paying attention to, especially since it's a change from your normal pattern. Bleeding that occurs twice in a month can happen for several reasons. Hormonal fluctuations are the most common cause, particularly around stress, significant weight change, illness, travel, or a shift in sleep routine. Hormonal changes linked to perimenopause, the years before menopause, often cause irregular cycles and closely spaced bleeding. Thyroid problems, polycystic ovary syndrome, and certain medications, including some hormonal contraceptives, can also disrupt cycles. Uterine polyps or fibroids sometimes cause bleeding between periods, and infections of the cervix or uterus can as well.

Since you have not had intercourse for two months, pregnancy is unlikely, but a home pregnancy test is still a simple way to rule it out, and it is worth doing if your cycles are changing. Pregnancy can occasionally cause bleeding that is mistaken for a period.

You should see a doctor soon, rather than waiting, if the bleeding is very heavy (soaking a pad or more every hour or two), lasts longer than usual, is accompanied by severe pain, dizziness, fever, or unusual discharge, or if it happens repeatedly. Bleeding after menopause, or any bleeding you're unsure about, also warrants prompt evaluation.

A doctor may ask about your cycle history and symptoms, and may recommend blood tests for hormone and thyroid levels, pregnancy, and blood count, and sometimes an ultrasound of the uterus and ovaries. Keeping a record of the dates and flow of your bleeding will help that visit be more useful. Most people with this kind of irregularity find that it is manageable once the cause is identified.

Okay, so FMLA gives eligible employees up to 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave for certain family and medical reasons. It does more than just protect your job, though. One big perk is that your employer has to keep your group health insurance going while you're out. You keep the same coverage you had before, so you don't have to scramble to find and pay for something else during your leave.

It also covers a bunch of different situations. You can take time off to care for a seriously ill family member, to bond with a new baby, or to deal with your own serious health problem. That can make it a lot easier to juggle work and family, and it gives you room to take care of yourself or the people you love.

And yes, your job is protected. When you get back, you're entitled to return to the same position or an equivalent one. That's a big relief, since you won't be stuck hunting for a new gig after you've been out.

Nope, there's no rule saying a president can't have facial hair. It's just that most of the recent ones have gone without beards or mustaches. Part of it is probably image. Some folks figure facial hair looks too casual or kind of unprofessional, so when you're in a big, formal job, staying clean-shaven feels like the safer move. And then there's the personal stuff. Plenty of people just don't like how a beard feels, and others have skin that gets irritated by shaving, so they'd rather skip it. At the end of the day, though, it's really up to each person whether they want to grow it out or not.

Benedict Arnold died of dropsy, a historical term for edema, the swelling caused by fluid buildup in the body, which at the time was often linked to heart or kidney failure. He died on June 14, 1801, in London, where he had lived in exile after defecting to the British during the American Revolution. He was 60 years old.

The Late Heavy Bombardment is thought to have occurred roughly 4.1 to 3.8 billion years ago, and the Moon was heavily struck by asteroids and comets during this interval. Impacts were frequent and often enormous, excavating large basins such as Imbrium, Serenitatis, Nectaris, and Orientale, many of which were later partly filled with lava. The bombardment reshaped the lunar surface, churning the upper crust into a thick layer of fragmented rock and dust called regolith, and creating the highland terrain of overlapping craters that still covers much of the Moon's far side.

Some of the evidence for this period comes from samples returned by the Apollo missions, which included impact-melted rocks dated to around 3.9 billion years ago. Scientists debate whether the bombardment was a sharp spike in impact rates or a more gradual decline from the early Solar System's high debris population, and the exact timing and intensity remain active research questions. Whatever its precise profile, the period left the Moon's surface heavily scarred and recorded in its rocks a dramatic chapter of early Solar System history.

Honestly, a painless lump in the right arm near the shoulder can have a few different causes, and most of them are harmless. The usual suspects are a lipoma, which is a benign fatty lump that's soft and easy to move around under the skin. Then there are cysts, which are sac-like pockets that can hold fluid or other stuff and can pop up almost anywhere on the body, usually without hurting. A ganglion cyst is another option. It's a fluid-filled sac that shows up most often on the wrist, hand, or foot, but it can happen in the arm too, and it's typically painless and movable. Bursitis is a bit different. That's when the small fluid-filled sacs that cushion your joints get inflamed, and it can cause a lump and some discomfort around the shoulder. If the lump sticks around or starts bugging you, get it checked by a doctor. They can figure out what it is and tell you what to do about it.

Erytop cream is a topical medicine containing erythromycin, an antibiotic used to treat acne and certain other skin infections. It can help reduce the number of pimples, but it should be applied as your healthcare provider instructs or as stated on the product label. If you apply Erytop cream at night to treat pimples, be sure to rinse it off in the morning. Keeping the cream on the skin for long stretches may raise the chance of side effects like irritation or dryness. Washing your face in the morning with a mild cleanser is also important, since it helps prevent your skin from drying out.

Beyond using Erytop cream, several other habits can improve your skin and reduce breakouts. Wash your face twice daily with a gentle, oil-free cleanser, and avoid harsh scrubbing, which can inflame the skin and encourage more pimples. Do not pick or squeeze your pimples, as this may cause scarring and additional irritation. Choose a moisturizer designed for acne-prone skin that is labeled non-comedogenic, meaning it won't clog pores. Select oil-free makeup and hair products, especially those marked "non-comedogenic" or "oil-free," since they are less likely to trigger breakouts. Finally, eating a balanced diet rich in fruits, vegetables, and healthy fats may support healthier-looking skin.

If you have questions about your skin or your current treatment, it is always wise to consult a healthcare provider or dermatologist. They can offer tailored advice based on your particular needs and medical history.

A person with a supraclinoid aneurysm may have symptoms that resemble those of trigeminal neuralgia (TN). Even so, the two are distinct conditions, and an accurate diagnosis of the underlying cause is essential before deciding on treatment. Trigeminal neuralgia is a form of facial pain resulting from irritation or injury to the trigeminal nerve, the nerve that carries sensation from the face. It usually produces short, intense bouts of facial pain set off by everyday triggers such as talking, chewing, or touching the face. Patients often describe the pain as sharp and stabbing, and it can be strong enough to disrupt daily life. An aneurysm, by contrast, is a bulging or ballooning of a blood vessel that can develop in any part of the body. Supraclinoid aneurysms form in blood vessels situated above the clinoid process, a bony projection within the skull. These aneurysms may produce headache, neck pain, and changes in vision, and they can be fatal if they burst. If you suspect your symptoms could stem from a supraclinoid aneurysm or TN, consult a neurosurgeon or another qualified clinician for a thorough evaluation. They can then recommend a treatment plan suited to the actual cause of your symptoms.

Imagine you have a favorite toy box at a friend's house. You don't own it, you just get to play with it. Your friend's parents can rearrange it, take toys out, or add new ones whenever they want, and they don't have to ask you. That's roughly the situation with Windows, iOS, and YouTube. You use them, but the companies decide what they look like, and they make those choices based on what's good for them, not always what's good for you.

A big reason is money. YouTube makes money when you keep watching and see ads. A "most viewed" list lets you pick what you want and leave, but a recommendation feed run by a computer is designed to keep you scrolling for as long as possible. So the tool that helped you got pushed aside for the tool that helps them. (YouTube did bring back a "Popular" sort button on channel pages after people complained, but searching everything by view count is still gone.) Windows is similar: when Microsoft collects information about how you use your computer and shows you suggestions or ads, that helps their business, so they make it harder to turn those things off.

Another reason is that companies design for the "average" person, not for people like you who like control. Most people never touch settings, and some who do accidentally break things. So companies hide or remove options to keep things simple and reduce support calls. Forced updates in Windows are a good example. Lots of people used to never update, their computers got viruses, and Microsoft got blamed. So Microsoft took the choice away. It protects careless users, but it annoys careful ones.

There's also a cost to keeping old features around. Every button has to be tested and fixed every time something else changes. If only a small slice of users touch a feature, the company may decide it's cheaper to delete it than keep it working.

Finally, a little bit of it is how our brains work. We notice when something we loved disappears much more than we notice small improvements we got for free, so updates can feel worse even when some parts got better.

So, in five-year-old terms: the toys belong to the company, the company wants to make money and keep things easy for most kids, and you happen to be one of the kids who liked the old toys better. Your feelings are reasonable, it's just that the people making the decisions are listening to different things than you are.

A soft bump that appears a day after a blow to the nose bridge is most often a hematoma (a collection of blood under the skin) or just localized swelling from bruised tissue. Your doctor's advice is sound, and for most people this kind of injury settles on its own with simple home care.

For the first 48 to 72 hours, keep using the cold compress as your doctor said. Wrap the ice in a thin cloth rather than putting it directly on the skin, and avoid pressing hard on the bridge. After about two or three days, you can switch to a warm, damp compress for 10 minutes once or twice a day, which helps your body reabsorb the pooled blood and reduces leftover swelling and bruising. Keep your head slightly elevated, including when you sleep, since this limits swelling around the face.

Some other things help. Avoid touching, squeezing, or massaging the bump early on, and do not try to drain it yourself, as that can cause infection or scarring. Avoid contact sports, heavy lifting, and anything that could bump the nose again until it has healed. Be careful with glasses, since pressure on the bridge can slow healing, so rest them on a soft pad or wear contacts if you can. For pain, acetaminophen (paracetamol) is generally preferred in the first couple of days, because ibuprofen and aspirin can slightly increase bleeding and bruising. Check with your doctor if you take other medications.

As for timing, a small soft bump usually shrinks noticeably within one to two weeks, and bruising (which may turn purple, green, then yellow and may drift toward the eyes) typically fades over two to three weeks. A firmer lump can take a few weeks longer to fully flatten. If the bump is still there after about three to four weeks, or if it feels hard and is not shrinking, ask your doctor to re-examine it, since it could be a small fracture or cartilage or bone swelling that has changed the shape of the nose.

Go back to a doctor promptly if you notice any of these: a bump that keeps growing or feels tense, bulging, or very painful inside the nose (which could be a septal hematoma that needs drainage), difficulty breathing through one or both nostrils, ongoing nosebleeds, clear fluid draining from the nose, a visible crooked shape, vision changes, worsening headache, or signs of infection such as spreading redness, warmth, pus, or fever.

If your doctor has already examined it and was not concerned, continuing the ice routine and being patient is usually all that is needed.

So a psychoactive drug is basically any chemical that acts on the central nervous system and messes with brain function, which then changes how you perceive things, what your mood is like, how alert you are, how you think, or how you act. Put simply, it's a drug that affects how your mind works. To count as psychoactive, it has to be able to shift your mental state or change how you see reality. That usually happens through changes in brain chemistry, like bumping certain neurotransmitters up or down.

CBD (cannabidiol) is a compound in the cannabis plant. It can have some psychoactive effects, but it doesn't really produce the mind-altering stuff people usually link with drugs like THC. CBD doesn't bind directly to the same brain receptors that THC does, so you don't get the same intoxication or "high." Instead, it seems to work with the body's endocannabinoid system in ways that might help with things like sleep or feeling less anxious or stressed. Researchers are still figuring out how well that works, though.

I'm sorry your mother is going through this. A severe rash that started when her risperidone dose was increased needs to be checked by her doctor, and I'd recommend contacting them today rather than relying on creams alone.

Topical steroid creams like MyloCORT can calm inflammation and itching on the skin, and an antihistamine cream such as Mepyramine (Allergex) may give some relief. But creams treat the symptoms, not the cause. If the rash is a reaction to risperidone, it can keep coming back as long as she takes it. Antihistamine creams can also irritate the skin or cause allergic sensitivity themselves, so they should not be put on broken or weeping skin without a doctor's approval. Oral antihistamines are sometimes used for drug rashes, but many, especially diphenhydramine, can worsen confusion and drowsiness in people with dementia, so她 doctor or pharmacist should choose any such medicine carefully.

Please tell her doctor clearly that the rash returned when the dose went up to 1 mg, and ask whether risperidone should be avoided in future and whether another antipsychotic might be safer. Ask them to note the reaction in her medical records.

Seek emergency care right away if the rash comes with fever, blistering or peeling skin, sores in the mouth or eyes, swelling of the face or lips, trouble breathing, or a sudden change in alertness. These can be signs of a serious drug reaction.

Please do not stop or change her risperidone on your own, since abruptly stopping antipsychotics can also cause problems. Let her care team guide any change.
