Bogleheadian World ETFs and index funds are investment vehicles designed to mirror the returns of a specific market benchmark, such as the S&P 500 or the MSCI World Index. The name honors John Bogle, who founded Vanguard and helped pioneer the concept of index investing. Numerous asset managers issue these products, which investors can buy through brokers or online trading platforms. Their appeal lies in low costs and broad diversification, giving investors wide exposure to the global stock market.

Optical sorting is a method of automatically separating items, such as food products, recyclable materials, minerals, or manufactured parts, by examining their optical properties and rejecting those that fail to meet set criteria. Machines that do this are often called optical sorters or color sorters. They are widely used in industries where large volumes of material must be inspected faster and more consistently than people could manage by hand.

The process generally has four stages. First, the material is fed onto a conveyor belt or sent down a chute so that the items are spread out in a thin, single layer and pass the inspection zone one at a time or in a controlled stream. Second, the items are illuminated and observed by sensors. These can be ordinary color cameras, but many systems also use near-infrared sensors, hyperspectral imaging, lasers, X-ray transmission, or ultraviolet light. Different sensors reveal different things: color cameras detect surface color and visible defects, near-infrared can identify plastics or organic compounds by how they reflect light, lasers can detect shape, structure, or fluorescence, and X-rays can reveal density or internal flaws such as foreign objects.

Third, software analyzes the sensor data in real time. It compares each item against programmed thresholds or trained models, which may use machine learning, to decide whether the item is acceptable or should be removed. Finally, an ejection mechanism acts on that decision. Most commonly, a bank of fast air jets fires short bursts to deflect the unwanted item into a separate bin, though mechanical flaps or paddles are sometimes used. Because the timing is measured in milliseconds, the system can handle many tons of material per hour.

Applications are varied. In food processing, optical sorters remove discolored grains, rotten nuts, stones, glass, and plastic fragments from products like rice, coffee, potatoes, and frozen vegetables. In recycling, they separate plastics by polymer type and color, sort paper from cardboard, and recover glass and metals. In mining, they separate ore from waste rock before expensive processing. They are also used for pharmaceuticals, tobacco, and quality control of small manufactured components.

The main advantages are speed, consistency, improved product quality and safety, reduced labor cost, and the ability to detect characteristics that the human eye cannot see. Limitations include high equipment cost, the need for careful calibration and maintenance, difficulty when items overlap or are dirty, and imperfect accuracy when materials look very similar to the sensors.

Joe's Crab Shack is owned by Ignite Restaurant Group's former parent chain history, but today the brand is held by Landry's, Inc. The Houston-based company is owned by billionaire Tilman Fertitta, who also owns the Houston Rockets and runs the Golden Nugget casinos and a large portfolio of restaurant brands such as Landry's Seafood House, Rainforest Cafe, and Chart House.

The ownership history is a bit tangled. Joe's Crab Shack was founded in 1991 in Houston and was later owned by Landry's, which sold it to Ignite Restaurant Group (the parent of Brick House Tavern + Tap) in 2006. Ignite filed for bankruptcy in 2017, and Joe's Crab Shack was acquired by Landry's, which meant it returned to Fertitta's company. Over the following years the chain shrank considerably, with many locations closing, though some remain open under Landry's, and a few are operated by franchisees or licensees.

For the most current details, it's worth checking the company's website or recent news, since corporate holdings and restaurant counts can change.

A parallel random-access machine (PRAM) is a theoretical model of a computer capable of carrying out several operations at the same time. Researchers use it to analyze how complex algorithms are and to build efficient parallel ones. The model consists of n processors that can exchange information with one another and reach a shared memory. These processors run instructions simultaneously, and any of them can access any part of the memory at any moment. Several versions of the PRAM exist, differing in how they handle communication and synchronization between processors. A widely studied version is the concurrent-read concurrent-write (CRCW) PRAM, which lets many processors read from and write to the same memory location at once. Another is the exclusive-read exclusive-write (EREW) PRAM, where a memory location can be accessed by only one processor at a time. PRAM algorithms are crafted to exploit the parallelism the model offers, and they can frequently be run on actual parallel machines like supercomputers and parallel clusters. Still, the PRAM is an idealized abstraction, so it may not precisely capture how real parallel computers behave.

There's no single answer because tax residency is defined separately by each country, and often by each state or province within a country. That said, some patterns are very common.

The most widely used benchmark is the 183-day rule. Many countries, including Canada, Australia, much of Europe, and others, treat you as a tax resident if you are physically present for 183 days or more within a tax year or a rolling twelve-month period. Crossing that threshold usually means you owe tax on your worldwide income in that country, not just on what you earn there.

Day counting is rarely the whole story, though. Many countries also look at your ties to the place, such as where your permanent home is, where your spouse and children live, where you work, where your bank accounts and belongings are, and where you intend to return. You can be considered a resident with far fewer than 183 days if your life is clearly centered there, and some places, like the United Kingdom with its Statutory Residence Test, combine day counts with these ties in a detailed formula.

In the United States, federal rules use the substantial presence test for non-citizens. You are generally a resident if you are present at least 31 days in the current year and the weighted total over three years reaches 183 days, counting all days this year, one third of last year's days, and one sixth of the year before. US citizens and green card holders are taxed as residents regardless of where they live. Individual US states set their own rules, often treating you as a resident if it's your domicile or if you maintain a home there and spend more than 183 days in the state.

When two countries both claim you as a resident, tax treaties usually contain tie-breaker rules that look at your permanent home, center of vital interests, habitual residence, and citizenship to decide which one gets primary taxing rights.

If you tell me which country or state you're asking about, I can give you the specific rules that apply. For anything involving significant income or a move between countries, it's worth confirming with a tax professional or the relevant tax authority.

Imagine you touch a cold ice cube and then touch a cold metal spoon. The air might be the same temperature as both, but the spoon feels colder, right? That's because things don't just feel the temperature around them. They also feel how quickly they lose heat from your body.

Your body is always making heat, a little like a tiny campfire inside you. When it's cold outside, your body gives off heat to the air around you. If the wind is blowing, it whisks that warm air away super fast, so your body keeps losing heat quickly and you feel colder than the thermometer says. The thermometer just measures the air. It doesn't know about the wind blowing on your skin or how wet you are.

That's why weather reports say something like "feels like negative ten." They're giving you a guess at how cold your body will actually feel once the wind and other things are counted in. The real air temperature is still negative two.

You're also right that feelings are different from person to person. Some people feel cold more easily than others, depending on how thick their body is, how much they've been moving, and what they're wearing. So the "feels like" number is really an average guess for a typical person, not an exact answer for everybody.

ECML PKDD, which stands for the European Conference on Machine Learning and Principles and Practice of Knowledge Discovery in Databases, is a series of conferences focused on machine learning and the discovery of knowledge from databases. The European Community on Machine Learning and Data Mining (ECML/PKDD) organizes it every year. Its goal is to gather scholars, professionals, and users from universities, companies, and public institutions to examine recent progress in machine learning, data mining, and knowledge discovery, as well as how these fields are applied across different areas. Researchers and practitioners use it as a venue to share their findings, trade ideas, and learn from one another. Typical program elements include invited speeches, tutorials, workshops, and presentations of accepted papers covering a broad range of topics in these areas. Well established and widely respected in the discipline, ECML PKDD draws a large volume of submissions from researchers worldwide. It offers researchers and practitioners a valuable chance to keep up with the latest developments, build connections with peers, and present their work to a wide and varied audience.

That feeling is basically your body's autonomic arousal kicking in. It's an automatic response that happens when something stressful or exciting hits you, like suddenly feeling like you're falling. Your autonomic nervous system runs a lot of the stuff you don't think about, like breathing and heart rate, so when your body decides something's up, it can make your heart race or your blood pressure jump. Blood flow can also shift toward certain areas, including the genitals, and that can cause a tingly sensation like the one you're describing. It's totally normal, and it doesn't have to be tied to any particular emotion or feeling.

As for why you only feel it in your bowels when you're falling, my guess is that the position or movement of your body in that moment sends the blood flow that way. It could also just be that the area's more sensitive, so you notice it more there. Hope that helps explain what's going on.

Okay, so here's the basic difference between the two. A defined contribution plan is where you and your employer both put a set amount of money into the plan on a regular basis. Usually your part comes straight out of your paycheck, and the company often matches some of it. What you end up with at retirement depends on how much went in and how well those investments did. A defined benefit plan works differently. The employer promises you a specific monthly payout once you retire, and that amount is typically based on things like your salary and how many years you worked there. The company handles all the contributions and has to invest the money well enough to cover those promised payments.

Both have their upsides. With a defined contribution plan, you get more say in how your money is invested, which some people love. The downside is that the risk is all on you, so if the market tanks right before you retire, your balance takes the hit. Defined benefit plans give you that guaranteed check, which is nice for peace of mind, but you don't get much control over the money or much flexibility if your plans change.

An MLP, or master limited partnership, is basically a hybrid. You get the tax setup of a partnership, but the units trade on a public exchange like a regular stock, so you can buy and sell them whenever. Most of them are in energy, running things like pipelines, storage facilities, and natural resource extraction.

So yeah, they're a lot like plain stock in that you can trade them on an exchange. But there are a few big differences.

Taxes are the first one. An MLP doesn't pay corporate income tax at the entity level. The income gets passed through to the partners, and each of them pays tax on their own share. That can leave you with a lower tax bill than you'd have owning regular stock.

Then there's the payout. MLPs have to distribute a chunk of their income to partners, and those are called distributions. They work kind of like dividends, but the tax treatment is different. They're generally treated as a return of capital, so you're not taxed on them as ordinary income right away. Instead they lower your cost basis in the units, which means you can end up owing tax when you finally sell.

Ownership is the last piece. Units do make you a part owner, similar to owning shares. But your voting rights are usually weaker, since the general partners typically keep the management and control.

Before you buy in, I'd think hard about the tax side and what you're giving up in ownership rights. Talking to a financial advisor or a tax pro is a smart move too, since they can walk you through the pros and cons for your situation.

Honestly, there's a bunch of reasons bugs go for light. Moths use it for navigation, kind of like a compass, so they fly toward or away from it. Beetles might be drawn to it because it leads them to mates or food. But being drawn to light isn't always good news for them. Bug zappers are the classic example: those blue lights pull flies and other insects in, and plenty of them end up dead. Bugs have evolved to respond to all sorts of stuff in their environment, light included, and that response doesn't always work out. Still, an insect that gets fried by a zapper might have already reproduced, so the trait can stick around in the population anyway.

The First World War lasted from July 28, 1914 until November 11, 1918, and it spread across much of the planet, drawing in most nations, among them Europe's leading powers and the United States, which joined the fighting in 1917. Although the assassination of Austria-Hungary's Archduke Franz Ferdinand on June 28, 1914 served as the immediate trigger, the war's roots ran much deeper, lying in long-standing rivalries among the great powers and in disputes over economics, territory, and colonies. The conflict cost millions of lives and left lasting effects on the countries involved and on the wider world.

Okay so the Great Chicago Fire ran from October 8 to October 10, 1871, and it wrecked a huge chunk of the city. It killed around 300 people, destroyed about 3.3 square miles, and left more than 100,000 folks without a home. Nobody knows for sure how it started. The popular story blames a barn owned by Patrick and Catherine O'Leary, supposedly because a cow knocked over a lantern, but that's never been proven. Chicago was mostly wooden buildings packed tightly together, and strong winds made everything worse, so the flames jumped from block to block. Firefighters and volunteers fought it hard, but it kept going for more than two days before anyone got it under control.

It's natural to be worried, and it's good that you're asking before the procedure. An angiogram is a common test that uses a thin tube, usually inserted through an artery in the wrist or groin, with dye to show how blood is flowing through the arteries. It's routinely done on people in their 60s, including people with diabetes, and serious complications are uncommon.

The results depend on why the test is being done. For someone who has been on warfarin for a long time, it's often because of a heart problem, such as a irregular heartbeat, a heart valve issue, or concern about blocked arteries. The results could be normal, could show narrowed or blocked arteries that might be treated with medicine, a stent, or sometimes bypass surgery, or could show something else that explains his symptoms. Many people leave with a clear plan and feel better once they know what's going on.

Stopping warfarin for four days is usually a deliberate step so the blood can clot properly during the procedure. Doctors normally check his INR (a blood clotting test) beforehand and may give him a different medicine in the meantime if his condition needs protection against clots. Because the warfarin was for a serious reason, it's worth confirming with his team that they know he's been on it for a long time, when he should restart it, and whether he needs any bridging treatment. Also check whether his diabetes medicines or eating and drinking instructions have been explained, since fasting can affect blood sugar.

Some questions you could ask the team tomorrow or beforehand are why the angiogram is being done, what they hope to find, what happens afterwards, how long he'll need to rest, and when the results will be discussed with him.

After the procedure, it's important to watch for bleeding or swelling at the puncture site, and for any new chest pain, shortness of breath, weakness or numbness, trouble speaking, or a leg that becomes cold, pale, or painful. Those need urgent medical attention.

Most people get through an angiogram without problems, and whatever it shows, the team will explain the next steps. Your dad's doctors will be the best people to answer questions about his specific situation, so don't hesitate to ask them directly.

Manifold regularization is a technique in machine learning, especially semi-supervised learning, that uses the geometric structure of the data to guide a model toward better predictions. The core idea is that high-dimensional data often lies close to a much lower-dimensional manifold, a curved surface embedded in the larger space. Points that are close to one another along this manifold are likely to share the same label, so a good prediction function should vary smoothly across the manifold rather than jumping erratically between nearby points.

In practice, the method adds a penalty term to the learning objective that discourages the function from changing rapidly along the data's underlying structure. To estimate that structure, the algorithm typically builds a graph whose nodes are the data points and whose edges connect points that are similar, often through nearest-neighbor relationships. The graph Laplacian, a matrix derived from this graph, then serves as a way to measure how much the prediction function varies across connected points. Adding this measure to the loss function encourages predictions that are consistent with the graph's connectivity.

This approach is especially valuable when labeled data is scarce but unlabeled data is plentiful. The unlabeled points reveal the shape of the data distribution, and the regularization term lets the model exploit that information even though it has few labels to learn from. A well-known example is Laplacian regularized least squares, and the broader framework is often associated with work by Belkin, Niyogi, and Sindhwani, who developed it in the early 2000s.

Inverse problems are a broad class of problems in science, engineering, and mathematics in which the goal is to determine the causes or underlying properties of a system from observed effects or data. They are the reverse of forward problems, which start with a known cause or model and predict the outcome. In a forward problem, you know the structure of a system and its parameters and compute what you will observe. In an inverse problem, you have the observations and must work backward to infer the hidden quantities that produced them.

A classic example is medical imaging. In computed tomography (CT), the scanner measures how X-rays are attenuated as they pass through the body from many angles. Predicting those measurements from a known tissue distribution is the forward problem. Reconstructing the internal image of tissues from the measurements is the inverse problem. Similar issues arise in geophysics, where scientists infer the structure of the Earth's interior from seismic waves recorded at the surface, and in astronomy, where researchers deduce properties of distant objects from the light they receive.

Inverse problems are often difficult for several reasons. They are frequently ill-posed in the sense defined by Jacques Hadamard: a solution may not exist, may not be unique, or may not depend continuously on the data. Small amounts of noise in the measurements can lead to large errors in the recovered solution. To handle this, practitioners use regularization, which adds constraints or prior assumptions, such as smoothness or sparsity, to stabilize the answer. Bayesian methods are another common approach, treating the unknown quantities as random variables and combining the observed data with prior knowledge to compute the most probable explanation.

Inverse problems appear across many fields, including image processing and deblurring, machine learning, electrical impedance tomography, groundwater flow estimation, and parameter estimation in differential equations. Understanding them is essential for turning indirect measurements into meaningful knowledge about hidden structures.

A 529 plan is a tax-advantaged savings account designed for education expenses. You contribute after-tax money, and the investments grow without federal income tax. When you withdraw the money for qualified education costs, the withdrawals are also federal tax-free. Many states add their own benefits, such as a state income tax deduction or credit for contributions, though the specifics vary, and some states offer these perks only if you use their own plan.

The money can cover a wide range of costs beyond tuition, including fees, required books and supplies, room and board for students enrolled at least half-time, and computers or related technology used for school. Qualified expenses also include tuition for K through 12 private or religious schools, up to an annual limit, and certain apprenticeship program costs. Because the account stays in your name, you control it even after your child turns 18, and you can change the beneficiary to another family member if your child doesn't attend college or receives a scholarship.

Contribution limits are generous, since each plan sets its own cap, often several hundred thousand dollars per beneficiary. Gift tax rules also let you front-load up to five years of annual gift exclusions in a single year, which can jump-start the account. Most plans offer age-based portfolios that automatically shift toward more conservative investments as college approaches, which helps manage risk without much effort on your part.

Before opening one, compare your home state's plan with others, paying attention to fees, investment options, and any state tax benefits. Unused funds can be rolled into a Roth IRA for the beneficiary under certain conditions, which adds some flexibility if plans change. A fee-only financial advisor or your plan's website can help you run the numbers for your situation.

Natural language processing, usually abbreviated NLP, is a branch of artificial intelligence and computer science concerned with enabling computers to understand, interpret, and generate human language. Human language is messy: it is full of ambiguity, idioms, context-dependent meaning, slang, and grammatical variation. NLP attempts to bridge the gap between how people naturally communicate and how computers process information, which is typically structured and precise.

The field draws on linguistics, statistics, and machine learning. Early NLP systems relied on hand-written rules crafted by linguists, such as grammars and dictionaries. Over time, statistical methods took over, learning patterns from large collections of text. In recent years, deep learning and large neural network models have become dominant, allowing systems to capture subtle relationships between words and sentences.

Common NLP tasks include breaking text into words or sentences, tagging parts of speech, recognizing names of people, places, and organizations, determining the sentiment of a review, translating between languages, summarizing documents, answering questions, and holding conversations. Many everyday technologies depend on NLP, including search engines, spam filters, voice assistants, autocomplete on phones, and chatbots.

There are a number of potential reasons why the scrotum might become swollen. Among the more frequent ones are the following. A hydrocele occurs when fluid collects around a testicle, leading to enlargement; this is generally painless and may result from inflammation or an injury to the testicle. A varicocele is an enlarged vein within the scrotum that can produce swelling and a sensation of heaviness in the testicle. Like a hydrocele, it typically doesn't hurt, and it tends to arise from irregular blood circulation to the testicles. Infections affecting the testicle or nearby tissue may also cause swelling and pain, and common examples include epididymitis, orchitis, and prostatitis. Testicular torsion is a medical emergency in which the testicle twists within the scrotum, cutting off its blood flow; it can bring on intense pain and swelling. Anyone experiencing scrotal swelling should consult a healthcare provider so the problem can be properly diagnosed and treated. A clinician can identify the underlying cause of the symptoms and suggest suitable treatment.

A backdoor in computing is a method of bypassing the normal authentication or security mechanisms of a computer system, program, or device to gain access that would otherwise be restricted. It is a hidden or undocumented way in, and it can be created deliberately or arise from a mistake in the design or implementation of software.

Backdoors can take many forms. Some are secret accounts or passwords built into a system, such as a hardcoded credential that a developer uses for testing and forgets to remove. Others are malicious code inserted into a program, often by an attacker who has compromised the software supply chain or the developer's environment, which lets them return later and control the machine remotely. Malware frequently installs backdoors, sometimes called remote access trojans, so that an attacker can keep access even after the initial intrusion is discovered and closed. Backdoors may also be hidden in hardware or firmware, where they are particularly difficult to detect and remove.

The purposes behind backdoors vary. Attackers use them to maintain persistent access, steal data, or launch further attacks. Some organizations or governments have sought lawful access mechanisms, often called lawful intercept or exceptional access, which critics argue inevitably weaken security because any intentional entry point can be discovered and exploited by others. Developers sometimes leave backdoors for maintenance or debugging, which is generally considered poor practice.

Because backdoors are hidden by design, they are hard to find. Defenses include code review, security audits, limiting the privileges of software, monitoring network traffic for unusual connections, and keeping systems updated. Notable historical examples include the Dual_EC_DRBG random number generator, which was suspected of containing a government-influenced backdoor, and the 2024 discovery of a backdoor planted in the XZ Utils compression library, which was caught before wide deployment.

Shiva is the seven-day period of mourning in Jewish tradition that begins after the funeral, and several customs shape it. Mourners, usually the immediate family, typically stay at home and sit on low stools or chairs rather than regular seating, a reminder of their loss and of the lowliness the mourning period calls for. Mirrors in the home are often covered, and mourners traditionally refrain from leather shoes, bathing for pleasure, and sexual relations. Prayer services, usually morning and evening, are held in the home, and a minyan of ten adults is gathered when possible so that the Mourner's Kaddish can be recited.

Visitors, known as comforters, come to pay respects and offer consolation. The traditional greeting is simply "HaMakom yenachem etkhem," meaning "May God comfort you among the other mourners of Zion and Jerusalem." It is customary not to speak until the mourner speaks first, so the visitor can follow the family's lead. Guests bring food, since it is considered a mitzvah to feed the mourners and relieve them of cooking during this time. Common offerings include bagels, salads, desserts, and fruit platters. Visitors often arrive during set hours and may stay for a short while, though the family may welcome longer conversations about the person who died.

Guests traditionally do not wear leather shoes when visiting, and it is customary to perform a small act of tearing or to make a small tear in a garment, called keriah, which is typically done by the mourners at the funeral. Visitors often leave with a brief parting phrase, and some families share memories, stories, and reflections throughout the week. Practices vary considerably among Orthodox, Conservative, Reform, and secular families, so it is worth asking the family if you are unsure what they expect.

So you stand up too fast after sitting or lying down for a while and your vision goes gray or black for a few seconds? Happens to a lot of people. It's usually called postural or orthostatic hypotension, and it basically means your blood pressure dips when you go from lying or sitting to standing. Your brain gets a little less blood flow for a moment, and that's what causes the dizziness or the vision cutting out. It's usually harmless and passes on its own within seconds. That said, certain medical conditions and medications can make it more likely, so if it keeps happening, or if it comes with fainting or chest pain, get it checked by a doctor. A few things that help: stand up slowly and give yourself a moment before walking off. Compression stockings can improve circulation, which helps. Staying hydrated makes a difference too. Eating a balanced diet with plenty of fruits, veggies, and whole grains supports healthy blood pressure, and regular exercise helps your circulation work better overall. Cutting back on alcohol and caffeine is worth trying as well, since both can mess with blood pressure regulation.

There are several ways to put money into US stocks as an Indian resident. One is to open a brokerage account with a firm that accepts foreign investors and lets them trade American shares; well-known choices include Charles Schwab and Interactive Brokers. Another is to buy a mutual fund or exchange-traded fund (ETF) that follows a collection of US equities, since these funds trade on Indian exchanges and can be bought through a broker or online platform. You could also acquire American Depositary Receipts (ADRs), which are certificates representing shares of a foreign company, through an Indian brokerage account, as ADRs trade on US exchanges. Finally, cross-border trading platforms such as DealTimer or TradeZero let investors from India open an account and trade US stocks directly. Keep in mind that international investing brings extra risks, including currency exchange fluctuations and political uncertainty. Before committing any money, it's wise to think carefully about your investment goals and how much risk you can comfortably accept.

I Bonds are savings bonds issued by the U.S. Department of the Treasury, and they're pretty low-risk. If you want to stash money away for the long haul and earn a bit of interest along the way, they can be a decent pick. The interest rate has two parts. There's a fixed rate, which stays the same for the life of the bond, and an inflation-indexed rate, which moves up and down with the Consumer Price Index (CPI).

The fixed rate gets set by the Treasury when the bond is issued and doesn't change after that. It depends on market conditions and how much the Treasury needs to borrow. They usually announce a new fixed rate twice a year, in May and November, and it applies to bonds bought during the following six months.

The inflation part is also set by the Treasury, but it gets adjusted every six months based on CPI changes. Its whole job is to protect your money from losing value. When prices go up, the rate goes up too, so your bond keeps up with the cost of living. So basically, the fixed rate is locked in from day one, while the inflation rate shifts with prices every half year.

Blood in a kid's loose stools can come from a lot of things, like infections, inflammatory bowel disease, or other digestive problems. Honestly, though, you should get your child seen by a doctor for this, since it can be a sign of something serious that needs treatment. In the meantime, make sure they're drinking plenty of fluids so they don't get dehydrated, which is a real risk with this kind of thing. If they've got belly pain, a child-safe pain reliever might help, and just keeping them comfortable goes a long way. If you're worried, call their pediatrician. They can look at the symptoms and tell you what to do next.

Throwing up during or after a really hard workout isn't normal, really, and sometimes it's a sign of something serious like heat stroke or just pushing way past what your body can handle. That said, there are a few common reasons people end up feeling sick or puking after exercise.

Dehydration is a big one. You sweat a lot when you work out, and if you're not replacing that fluid you can get dehydrated, which easily leads to nausea and vomiting.

Eating too much right before you train can do it too. If you've just had a huge meal, your body's trying to digest all that food while you're also asking it to run, lift, whatever, and it doesn't handle both well. Stomach gives up, and out it comes.

Then there's plain old overexertion. If you go too hard, your body can't keep up, and feeling sick or vomiting is kind of its way of telling you to stop and cool off.

Sometimes it's something else entirely, like heat stroke, low blood sugar, or some underlying health issue you don't know about yet.

So drink plenty of fluids and don't push yourself into the ground every session. If it keeps happening, though, go talk to a doctor so you can figure out what's actually causing it and get it treated properly.

Ken Jennings won 74 games in a row on "Jeopardy!" back in 2004, which is still a record. He got pretty famous from it and took home over $2.5 million in prize money along the way. His streak finally ended in game 75 when he lost to Nancy Zerg, and he missed out by just $51.

White coat hypertension (some people call it office hypertension) is when your blood pressure runs high at the doctor's office or a clinic but comes back down to normal when you check it at home or anywhere that isn't medical. Usually it's down to nerves or stress about being in that setting. If yours is really bad and you can't get a normal reading at any clinic, you'll want to work with your doctor to figure out what makes sense for you.

There are a few things that can help. A home blood pressure monitor is a big one, since it gives you more accurate readings and a fuller picture of what your numbers actually look like day to day. Relaxation stuff like deep breathing or progressive muscle relaxation can take the edge off the anxiety. Lifestyle changes help too, like eating better, exercising regularly, and keeping stress in check, and those can bring your pressure down and make you healthier in general. And sometimes medication gets recommended, but that's a call to make with your doctor based on your situation.

Keep seeing your doctor so they can keep an eye on things. Regular check-ups and readings let you know whether your plan is working, and they can tweak it if it isn't.

A gynecologist's office laboratory is usually a small, point-of-care space focused on the tests that can be done quickly while the patient is still in the office. The core equipment is a microscope, often a good-quality light microscope with at least 10x and 40x objectives (and sometimes oil immersion for higher magnification), used to examine slides for things like vaginal discharge, yeast, bacterial vaginosis clues, trichomonas, and cells from Pap smears or cervical samples. Nearby there is typically a supply of glass slides, cover slips, saline and potassium hydroxide solutions for wet mounts, stains such as Gram stain or Papanicolaou-type stains where used, and a sink or basic handwashing station for preparing samples. Many offices also keep a refrigerator for reagents and specimens that need cold storage, and a centrifuge for certain urine or fluid preparations.

Beyond microscopy, the lab often includes rapid testing supplies. These can include pH test strips or nitrazine paper for checking vaginal pH, rapid antigen or antibody kits for conditions like group B strep or chlamydia, urine dipsticks for checking urine for infection, pregnancy test kits, and sometimes a point-of-care glucose or hemoglobin meter. Some practices also have a small hematology or chemistry analyzer for quick blood counts or basic blood chemistry, though many send blood samples out to an outside commercial or hospital lab instead.

The space also needs collection materials such as swabs, transport tubes and media, specimen containers, and sharps and biohazard disposal containers, along with personal protective equipment like gloves, gowns, and eye protection. Because the lab handles biological samples, it must follow infection-control and safety rules, and in the United States it falls under CLIA (Clinical Laboratory Improvement Amendments) regulation, which determines what tests the office may perform and requires certificates, quality control logs, and staff training for each test category. Samples that exceed the office's capabilities, such as cultures, many molecular tests, and full blood panels, are generally packaged and sent to a reference laboratory.

Living with damp and mold can mess with your health in a few different ways. The big one is breathing trouble. Mold and dampness can bring on coughing, wheezing, and shortness of breath, and if you've got asthma or some other lung condition, you'll probably feel it more than most people.

Allergies are another common thing. Mold can set off sneezing, itchy eyes and skin, and a runny nose, and again, people who already deal with allergies or asthma tend to get hit harder.

Your skin can react too. Some people get irritation or rashes from damp, moldy surroundings, especially if they already have eczema or similar skin problems.

There's also some research suggesting that mold and damp might weaken the immune system, which could leave you more open to infections and other health issues. That one's less settled than the others, though.

How bad it gets really depends on a bunch of stuff: what kind of mold you're dealing with, how long you've been around it, how heavy the exposure is, and things like your age, your general health, and even your genes. If you're worried about it, I'd talk to a doctor who can give you advice that fits your situation.

Imagine a neighborhood where lots of families wanted to buy houses, and banks were happy to lend them money. Some of those families had very little savings or steady income, so they were given loans that were risky, with low starting payments that would jump later. These were called subprime loans. As long as house prices kept rising, everyone seemed fine: if a family couldn't pay, they could sell the house for more than they owed.

The trouble started because banks didn't want to keep these risky loans on their own books. Instead, they bundled thousands of loans together and sold them as investments, packaged into complicated products with fancy names like mortgage-backed securities and collateralized debt obligations. Rating agencies, which were supposed to judge how safe these products were, often gave them top grades they didn't deserve. Investors all over the world bought them, thinking they were safe. Meanwhile, the people selling and packaging the loans often got paid up front and didn't have to worry if the loans later failed. That gave everyone a reason to keep the party going while ignoring the danger.

Then house prices stopped rising and began falling, starting around 2006 and 2007. Families with jumping payments couldn't pay, and they couldn't sell their homes for enough to cover their debts. Defaults spread, and the bundled products lost value quickly. Nobody knew exactly who was holding the bad pieces, so banks stopped trusting each other and stopped lending. In 2008, the large investment bank Lehman Brothers collapsed, and panic spread through the whole financial system.

In the United States, the government stepped in with huge rescue programs to keep banks from failing, and the Federal Reserve cut interest rates to near zero. Millions of people lost their homes to foreclosure, millions lost their jobs, and unemployment rose sharply. Many people felt the rescues helped bankers more than ordinary families, which fueled anger that later showed up in politics. New rules were passed, such as the Dodd-Frank Act, to make banks hold more money in reserve and to watch risky lending more closely.

Europe was hit too, partly because European banks had bought many of the same American products. Some major banks in countries like Britain, Germany, and Switzerland had large losses and needed government help. The crisis then turned into a European debt crisis around 2010. Countries such as Greece, Ireland, Portugal, Spain, and Italy had borrowed heavily, and when the economy slowed and the government had to rescue its banks, investors began to doubt they could repay. Greece in particular needed large bailouts from other European countries and the International Monetary Fund, along with harsh spending cuts that caused long recessions and high unemployment. The euro itself was under threat, and the European Central Bank eventually promised to do whatever it took to hold the currency together.

In short, people borrowed too much on risky terms, a complicated system spread that risk around the world while hiding it, and when the bubble popped, banks, governments, and ordinary people on both sides of the Atlantic paid a heavy price.

Honestly, the reason people snort drugs is usually speed and punch. Swallow a pill and it has to go through your digestive system before it gets into your bloodstream, which can take forever, especially if you've just eaten. Snort it and it soaks through the lining of your nose straight into your blood, so you feel it way faster. But there's a catch. Snorting wrecks the inside of your nose over time and can cause other health problems too. Unless a doctor has told you otherwise, it's just safer to take meds the way they're meant to be taken.

Trouble breathing can stem from a wide range of causes, so it is important to consult a doctor who can identify the exact reason and recommend the right treatment. Among the possible causes are the following. Asthma is a frequent culprit, especially among young people, because it narrows the airways and makes breathing more laborious. Allergies may lead to swelling within the airways, which can also make breathing hard. Infections, including the common cold and pneumonia, can inflame the airways and make it difficult to get air. Heart conditions such as a heart attack or heart failure may likewise bring about breathing problems. Anxiety and panic attacks can interfere with breathing as well, because stress or anxiety may trigger hyperventilation, meaning rapid, shallow breaths. Anyone who has difficulty breathing should see a doctor, since the symptom may point to a more serious condition underneath. A doctor can evaluate your symptoms, work out what is behind your breathing trouble, and offer suitable treatment.

Intraday prices are the prices a security trades at while the market is open, whereas end-of-day (EOD) highs and lows are the maximum and minimum prices it reached during a given session. Intraday figures often don't match the EOD highs and lows, because prices can swing considerably over the course of a day in response to factors such as supply and demand, news events, and investor sentiment. When intraday prices and EOD highs and lows seem to conflict, you might apply technical analysis to look for patterns or trends that could support better-informed trading decisions. Tools like moving averages may also be useful, since they smooth out short-term fluctuations and give a clearer view of a security's trend over a longer period. Additionally, it helps to keep up with news and developments that could affect the price of the security you are trading, and to let that information guide your decisions.

Great question, and nobody knows the full answer yet, not even the scientists who study brains. Here is the simple version.

Think of your brain like a huge orchestra. Each musician is a group of neurons playing a tiny part, and no single musician plays the whole song. The music you hear is what happens when they all play together. The voice in your head is a bit like that song. It isn't stored in one spot, like a single instrument hidden in a corner. It shows up from lots of parts working together.

Scientists have found that certain areas help with talking to yourself, remembering things, and imagining, like the front part of your brain and some areas toward the middle and back. When you think in words, these areas pass messages back and forth very quickly. So the voice is more like a conversation between many helpers than a single person sitting in a room.

As for where "you" are, that's a puzzle people have wondered about for thousands of years. Some people think the "I" is just the pattern of all those helpers working together, the way a whirlpool is a pattern in water rather than a thing separate from the water. Others think there's something more to it that we don't understand yet.

So the honest answer is that you are probably not in one tiny spot. You're more like the song the orchestra plays, and that song is made of the whole brain working together.

Okay, so the palatine canal is basically a little tunnel running through the roof of your mouth, the palate. It starts at the incisive foramen, which is a tiny opening just behind your front teeth, and heads back to the nasopalatine duct, a small passage that links the palate up to the nose. Inside it you'll find the nasopalatine nerve and some blood vessels, and those handle sensation and blood supply for the palate and the tissue around it. It's a pretty important little structure in the head and neck area, and it plays a part in taste, speech, and swallowing too.

Not really. Banks don't let a home-building arrangement run on indefinitely, though the exact limits depend on what kind of financing you have.

If you mean a construction loan, these are short-term by design. They typically last somewhere between six months and eighteen months, sometimes up to two or three years for larger custom builds. During that period you usually pay only interest on the money that has been drawn so far, and the bank releases funds in stages as inspectors confirm work is done. When the term ends, the loan has to be paid off, usually by converting it into a regular mortgage (a "construction-to-permanent" loan does this automatically) or by taking out a separate mortgage. If construction drags past the deadline, you may be able to get an extension, but banks generally charge fees for it, may raise the rate, and will want a convincing explanation and a realistic completion date. Repeated delays can lead the lender to stop funding or call the loan, because an unfinished house is risky collateral.

If you mean a mortgage on a finished home, that also has a fixed end date, commonly fifteen to thirty years, with some countries offering terms up to thirty-five or forty years. You can, however, keep borrowing against a home for most of your life by refinancing, moving to a new mortgage when you buy another house, or taking a home equity loan. Some people effectively carry mortgage debt for decades this way, but each loan still has its own payoff schedule, and interest-only arrangements eventually require the principal to be repaid or refinanced.

If you're thinking about building slowly over many years, owner-builders often avoid long construction loans entirely and instead build in phases with cash, or finish enough of the house to get it appraised and qualify for a standard mortgage, then continue work later. If you tell me which country you're in and what your situation looks like, I can give more specific guidance.

Four Thirds is a digital camera system standard introduced in 2002 by Olympus and Kodak, later joined by Panasonic, Leica, Sigma, and others. It was designed from scratch for digital photography rather than adapting older film-based designs. The name refers to the 4:3 aspect ratio of the sensor, which is squarer than the 3:2 ratio found in 35mm film and most APS-C and full-frame cameras. It also loosely refers to the sensor's size, which has a diagonal of about 22mm, with an imaging area of roughly 17.3 by 13 millimeters. That is about half the diagonal of a full-frame sensor, giving a 2x crop factor, so a 25mm lens frames a scene like a 50mm lens would on full frame.

The original Four Thirds system used a DSLR design with a mirror and optical viewfinder, and it had its own lens mount, also called Four Thirds. Olympus made cameras like the E-1, E-510, and E-5, and Panasonic and Leica made a few as well. The system emphasized compact lenses, and the lens designs were meant to be telecentric, sending light to the sensor at a nearly perpendicular angle, which helps image quality at the edges.

In 2008 the companies introduced Micro Four Thirds, which keeps the same sensor size but removes the mirror and optical viewfinder, allowing a much shorter distance between lens and sensor. This made cameras and lenses considerably smaller and lighter. Micro Four Thirds became far more successful than the original system, and the original DSLR line was effectively discontinued. Today when people mention Four Thirds cameras, they usually mean Micro Four Thirds bodies from Olympus (now OM System) and Panasonic's Lumix G series, along with lenses from those makers and others like Sigma, Tamron, and Laowa.

The main appeal is portability, a wide selection of lenses, and good in-body image stabilization. The trade-offs are that the smaller sensor generally gives somewhat more noise in low light and less ability to produce very shallow depth of field compared with larger sensors.

Gastritis is inflammation of the stomach lining, and pain from it is usually felt in the upper middle abdomen, above the belly button. Common suggestions include antacids such as calcium carbonate or magnesium hydroxide for quick relief, and acid reducers like famotidine (an H2 blocker) or omeprazole (a proton pump inhibitor) for longer-lasting effects. Eating smaller, bland meals, avoiding alcohol, caffeine, spicy or fatty foods, and smoking, and not lying down right after eating can also help. Doctors generally advise against ibuprofen, naproxen, and aspirin when the stomach is irritated, since these can make gastritis worse.

Your pain is just below the belly button, which is less typical for gastritis, and it sounds like it may be gas. For bloating and gas, simethicone (sold as Gas-X or Mylicon) is a common over-the-counter option that helps break up gas bubbles. Peppermint oil capsules may ease cramping, and a warm heating pad on the belly can be soothing. Gentle walking often helps move trapped gas along, while cutting back on carbonated drinks, chewing gum, and foods that commonly cause gas may prevent recurrence. Acetaminophen (Tylenol) is generally a safer choice than NSAIDs if you need something for pain.

Because the pain comes and goes, it is worth keeping an eye on it. You should contact a doctor promptly, or seek emergency care, if you develop severe or steadily worsening pain, pain that moves to the lower right side, fever, vomiting (especially blood or material that looks like coffee grounds), black or bloody stools, yellowing of the skin or eyes, trouble swallowing, chest pain or shortness of breath, or unintended weight loss. These can signal conditions that need evaluation, such as appendicitis, an ulcer, or gallbladder problems. If your symptoms persist beyond a few days or keep returning, a medical visit is a good idea.

A biological system consists of a set of interconnected living organisms or their parts that cooperate to carry out one particular function or several functions. These systems vary widely in scale and intricacy, ranging from a lone cell up to a complex organism such as a human being. Examples include the circulatory system, which carries oxygen, nutrients, and hormones to cells and clears waste products away from the body; the digestive system, which breaks food down and takes up nutrients from what we eat; the nervous system, which organizes and governs the body's reactions to internal and external stimuli; the respiratory system, which helps oxygenate the blood and expel carbon dioxide; and the endocrine system, which releases hormones that control a range of bodily processes. To keep a steady internal environment, known as homeostasis, biological systems frequently depend on feedback mechanisms. Body temperature is a good illustration: the endocrine system releases hormones that keep it within a narrow band. If the body becomes overheated, the sweat glands secrete sweat, and its evaporation cools the skin. If the body becomes too chilly, the muscles generate heat to raise the temperature again. In short, biological systems are fundamental to living organisms and are central to sustaining an organism's health and proper functioning.

Young investors typically benefit from spreading their money across a mix of stocks and bonds. The ideal balance depends on how much risk you can handle and what you hope to achieve, but a popular strategy is to hold a larger share of stocks early on and slowly move toward bonds as the years pass. The reason is that stocks can deliver higher gains over time, though they also swing up and down more sharply, whereas bonds usually fluctuate less and offer more modest returns. When it comes to choosing specific holdings, index funds or exchange-traded funds (ETFs) that follow a broad benchmark like the S&P 500 are worth considering, since they provide wide diversification at a simple, inexpensive cost. Adding international exposure through global index funds or ETFs may also be sensible. Keep in mind that every investment carries some risk and you could lose money, so be ready for that possibility. Still, a well-diversified portfolio can produce solid returns over the long run. Finally, check your portfolio from time to time to confirm it still matches your objectives and comfort with risk.

The false positive rate describes how often a test or other measurement method wrongly signals that a certain condition or attribute is present. It is calculated by dividing the number of false positive results by the total number of actual negative cases. Take a medical test for a given disease as an example. Its false positive rate would be the share of people who receive a positive result even though they do not have the disease. The formula is: False positive rate = (Number of false positives) / (Total number of negatives). When the false positive rate is high, the test tends to produce many false alarms, whereas a low rate means such erroneous results are less likely. Evaluators commonly pair the false positive rate with the true positive rate, which is also called the test's sensitivity or recall, to judge how well a test or measurement procedure performs overall.

Ethanol, a form of alcohol, is frequently blended into gasoline to cut down on emissions and boost fuel performance. Being self-employed means you'll owe self-employment tax on top of regular income tax. That covers your Social Security and Medicare contributions, which an employer would normally split with you. The total rate is 15.3%, made up of 12.4% for Social Security and 2.9% for Medicare. Heads up though: in 2021, only the first $142,800 of your self-employment income is hit with the Social Security part.

Figuring it out isn't too bad. Start with your net self-employment income, which is what you earned minus whatever business expenses you can legitimately deduct. Multiply that number by 15.3% and you've got your self-employment tax bill. Income tax is a separate thing and depends on your total income and filing status, so you'll want to check the IRS tax rate schedules for that part.

Keep in mind this is just the rough picture. Plenty of other factors can change what you actually owe, so if your situation is messy, it's worth talking to a tax pro or running everything through tax software.

So Bernoulli numbers are this sequence of rationals that pop up in all sorts of expansions. Jacob Bernoulli, a Swiss mathematician, was the one studying them back in the 1600s. People usually split them into two types, even and odd. The even one, B2n, is the coefficient of x^(2n) in the Taylor series of e^x/(e^x + 1), and the odd one, B2n+1, is the coefficient of x^(2n+1) in that same expansion. The first few go like this: B0 = 1, B1 = -1/2, B2 = 1/6, B3 = 0, B4 = -1/30, B5 = 0, B6 = 1/42, B7 = 0, B8 = -1/30. They show up all over the place. They're in the Taylor series for sine and cosine, and you can use them to write the Riemann zeta function at even integers. Apparently they also link to Fibonacci numbers and Euler numbers, though I'd double-check that one before relying on it.

A stochastic process is a mathematical framework for describing a series of events or quantities that change over time in a random fashion. It belongs to the broader category of random processes, and its defining feature is the presence of chance or uncertainty. Typically, such a process is specified through a probability distribution spanning a collection of possible results or states. These results or states might capture the value of some variable at various moments, or they might capture the possible endings of a chain of events. The share price of a firm, for instance, can be treated as a stochastic process because it moves up and down over time without a fixed pattern. Likewise, weather can be regarded as one, as conditions shift from one day to the next in ways that cannot be fully foreseen. Fields such as economics, finance, and engineering rely heavily on stochastic processes to model and study random phenomena. Through them, analysts can represent and examine the uncertainty and randomness that are built into many real-world systems.

The word "baptism" comes from the Greek noun "baptisma," which derives from the verb "baptizein." That verb means "to dip," "to immerse," or "to submerge," and it was used in ordinary Greek for things like dyeing cloth by dipping it into a vat or sinking a ship. The root connects to the older verb "baptein," which carried a similar sense of dipping or plunging. Early Christian writers adopted the term to describe the ritual of immersion in water that marked a person's entry into the Christian community, and the word eventually passed into Latin as "baptismus" and then into Old French and Middle English, giving us "baptism."

Computational complexity is basically the study of how many resources an algorithm needs to solve a problem, mostly time and space. It's a way of measuring how efficient an algorithm is, and it helps you figure out whether an algorithm is practical for a given problem. Time gets measured in steps or operations, and space gets measured in how much memory the thing eats up. An algorithm counts as efficient if it finishes in a reasonable amount of time and memory for the size of the input. If it needs an absurd amount of either, it's considered inefficient. There are a few flavors of this: time complexity looks at how long things take, space complexity looks at memory, and then there's the combined view that considers both. The field matters because it tells you where the limits of efficient computation are and helps you design algorithms that get as close to those limits as possible. It also helps you weigh trade-offs between different approaches and pick the right one for the job.

Bayesian optimization is basically a smart way to hunt for the best value of some function you don't know much about. People use it a lot for tuning hyperparameters in machine learning models, since the search space is usually huge and every single evaluation costs you a ton of compute.

Here's how it goes. You build a surrogate model of the unknown function from the points you've already tried. It's a probabilistic model, so it's really just capturing what you currently believe the function looks like. Then, at each step, the algorithm picks the next point to test by looking at where the surrogate predicts the biggest expected improvement. Try that point, update the model, repeat.

One big plus is that it copes with constraints and with noisy evaluations, which is handy because real-world results are rarely clean. You can also feed in prior knowledge about the function's shape to steer the search in a better direction. So if your function is complicated and expensive to evaluate, it's a really solid, efficient option.

Largely yes, but with important caveats. Implied volatility is the market's consensus estimate of how much an asset's price will move over the life of an option, backed out of the option's price. Because traders know about scheduled events like earnings reports, central bank meetings, FDA decisions, or elections, they bid up options that span those dates, and that expectation shows up in the implied volatility. You can often see this directly: IV typically rises into an earnings announcement and drops sharply right after, a phenomenon often called volatility crush. Term structure also reveals it, since an expiry that includes a known event will usually carry higher IV than a neighboring expiry that doesn't.

That said, implied volatility does not capture everything. It reflects the expected size of moves, not their direction, so it says nothing certain about whether the event will be good or bad. It also only prices what market participants anticipate. Genuinely unforeseen events, such as sudden geopolitical shocks or surprise fraud revelations, can't be priced in beforehand, though markets do carry some general premium for the possibility of unknown shocks, which is partly why IV often exceeds subsequently realized volatility. That gap is known as the volatility risk premium.

Further, implied volatility is not a pure forecast. It is shaped by supply and demand, such as demand for portfolio hedges pushing up put prices, along with dealer positioning, liquidity, and risk aversion. So it can overstate or understate the true expected move. Also, the figure is derived from a model, typically Black-Scholes, which assumes things like constant volatility and lognormal returns that don't hold in practice. That is why you see skew and smile patterns across strikes.

Finally, an event's impact is only as well priced as the market's understanding of it. If participants underestimate how disruptive an outcome could be, IV will be too low, and if they overreact, it will be too high. So implied volatility is best viewed as an efficient but imperfect summary of known and anticipated information, plus a risk premium, rather than a complete or unbiased accounting of the future.

The single most effective step is to freeze your credit at the three major bureaus, Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion. In the United States this is free, and it stops anyone, including a thief with your Social Security number, from opening new credit in your name. You can temporarily lift the freeze online in minutes when you actually need to apply for a loan or card. Many people also freeze with smaller agencies such as ChexSystems, which banks use when opening accounts.

Next, secure your online accounts, especially email, since your email is the key that resets everything else. Use a password manager so every account has a long, unique password, and turn on two-factor authentication wherever it's offered. An authenticator app or a hardware security key is safer than text-message codes, because phone numbers can be hijacked through SIM-swapping. It's also worth calling your mobile carrier to add a PIN or port-out lock to your account for that reason.

Be skeptical of unsolicited contact. Most identity theft starts with phishing emails, texts, or calls that impersonate banks, the IRS, delivery services, or tech support. Legitimate organizations rarely ask you to confirm passwords, Social Security numbers, or verification codes. If something seems urgent or alarming, hang up or close the message and contact the company directly using a number or website you look up yourself.

Monitor what you can. Check your bank and credit card statements regularly and set up transaction alerts so you're notified of charges right away. You can pull your credit reports for free at AnnualCreditReport.com, which now offers them weekly, and look for accounts or inquiries you don't recognize. Paid identity monitoring services exist, but much of what they offer you can do yourself for free.

Protect physical documents and information too. Shred papers containing account numbers or personal details before discarding them, collect your mail promptly, and keep your Social Security card at home rather than in your wallet. Give out your Social Security number only when it's truly required, and ask why when someone requests it. Be careful about what you post on social media, since birthdays, pet names, and hometowns often answer security questions.

Keep your devices updated, since software updates patch security holes, and avoid logging into sensitive accounts on public Wi-Fi without a VPN. Lock your phone and computer with a strong passcode.

Finally, there are a couple of tax-specific protections. The IRS offers an Identity Protection PIN to anyone who wants one, which prevents someone else from filing a fraudulent return using your Social Security number. If you ever do become a victim, IdentityTheft.gov, run by the Federal Trade Commission, walks you through a personalized recovery plan, and acting quickly makes a big difference in limiting the damage.

Cancer can produce many different signs and symptoms, which depend on the particular type of cancer and where it is located in the body. Among the more frequent ones are the following. Unexplained weight loss can happen because cancer speeds up the body's consumption of energy and nutrients. Fatigue, which can be severe, may be brought on by the disease itself or by its treatments. Pain can arise either directly from the tumor or as a side effect of therapy. Shifts in bowel or bladder function, such as constipation, diarrhea, or needing to urinate often, may also occur. Sometimes lumps or bumps develop under the skin or elsewhere on the body. Changes in the skin, including new moles or alterations to existing ones, are another possibility. Finally, a cough or hoarseness that refuses to go away can be a sign. These symptoms, however, have many other possible causes and do not automatically indicate cancer. Anyone experiencing them should consult a healthcare provider for a proper assessment and diagnosis.

In Massachusetts, capital gains are treated as ordinary income and therefore face the same tax rates that apply to other income. The state uses a progressive system, meaning the rate applied to your capital gains depends on your total taxable income for the year. For the 2021 tax year, the rates were as follows: taxable income of $0 to $1,000 was taxed at 5.05%; $1,001 to $2,500 at 6.10%; $2,501 to $5,000 at 7.00%; $5,001 to $10,000 at 7.05%; $10,001 to $15,000 at 7.10%; $15,001 to $20,000 at 7.15%; $20,001 to $25,000 at 7.20%; $25,001 to $30,000 at 7.25%; $30,001 to $40,000 at 7.30%; $40,001 to $150,000 at 7.75%; and $150,001 or more at 8.95%.

To work out your tax on unrealized capital gains, first determine your total taxable income for the year, including any gains you have actually realized during that period. Then apply the matching rate to that taxable income to find your liability. Keep in mind that these rates and brackets are applied to your federal taxable income after any deductions or exemptions have been claimed. Also, Massachusetts imposes a separate tax on short-term capital gains, meaning gains from assets held for less than one year, and those are taxed at a flat 12% rate.

Generally, no, at least not as income in the way wages are taxed. Tax systems typically tax realized income, meaning money or property received in exchange for something, and the value of your own labor applied to your own property is usually not treated as a receipt. If you build a deck on your house or grow vegetables in your garden, you have created value, but you have not received income from anyone, so there is nothing to tax at that moment. This is one reason economists often point to "imputed income," such as the rental value of an owner-occupied home or the value of household work, as something the tax code largely ignores.

There are important exceptions and nuances, however. Many jurisdictions do tax certain self-produced goods when they are converted into a form of income. A farmer who consumes some of their own crop may face questions about whether that consumption counts as income, and in many countries it is not taxed, though business inventory rules can apply when goods are sold or transferred. Self-created assets can also trigger tax when they are disposed of. Someone who renovates a property and later sells it realizes a gain, and the capital gains calculation may reflect the value of their own work in the cost basis or, depending on the rules, may not. Similarly, if a business owner takes goods from their company for personal use, that withdrawal is often treated as a taxable distribution or deemed sale.

Some countries also tax noncash benefits in ways that look similar, such as fringe benefits or the personal use of company property, though these generally involve an employer or business rather than pure self-labor. Barter and in-kind exchanges are taxable, but a purely self-directed effort without any transaction usually falls outside the net.

Because the answer depends heavily on the country, the type of activity, and whether the output is consumed, sold, or used in a business, anyone facing a specific situation should consult a local tax professional or the relevant tax authority.

Bill Gates is an American business magnate, software developer, and philanthropist, best known as a co-founder of Microsoft, the technology company that created the Windows operating system and the Microsoft Office software suite. He was born William Henry Gates III in Seattle, Washington, in 1955, and he founded Microsoft with his childhood friend Paul Allen in 1975. Under his leadership as chief executive, the company became one of the most successful and influential in the personal computer industry, and Gates was for many years one of the richest people in the world.

He stepped down as Microsoft's CEO in 2000 and later left his day-to-day role at the company in 2008 to focus on charitable work. In 2000 he and his wife, Melinda, established the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, one of the largest private charitable organizations in the world. The foundation concentrates on global health, including efforts to fight diseases such as malaria and polio, improve access to vaccines, and advance agricultural and educational development, particularly in poorer countries. Gates has also written books and has been outspoken on issues like climate change and public health. In 2024 he announced plans to wind down the foundation by 2045.

Computation time, also called run time or execution time, is just how long a computer takes to finish a task or a set of tasks. You can measure it in seconds, milliseconds, microseconds, whatever fits the job. Lots of things affect it: how complicated the task is, how fast the processor is, how much memory is free, and how well the algorithms and programs are written. Generally, anything that needs more processing power or simply takes longer will have a bigger computation time. It matters a lot in computer science and engineering since it can really shape how well a system performs. If you're trying to hit performance targets or make things feel snappier for users, you'll often end up tweaking algorithms and code to cut that time down.

Okay so if you're just starting out with investing, the big thing is getting a diversified portfolio that fits your money situation and goals. Here's how I'd approach it.

First, figure out what you're actually investing for. Retirement? A house down payment? Something else? Once you know, it's a lot easier to make decisions that line up with your plans.

Next, think about how much risk you can stomach. Different investments swing around in different ways. If you're pretty conservative, you might lean toward bonds or funds holding blue-chip stocks, which tend to be steadier. If you're more aggressive, you might be fine with bumpier rides in exchange for a shot at bigger returns.

Then decide on your asset allocation, which is just the mix of stuff you own. A common setup is some stocks, some bonds, and some cash or short-term stuff. Within that, it helps to spread things around: domestic and international stocks, different kinds of bonds like corporate, government, or municipal, and a bit of cash.

After that, you can start picking actual investments. That could be individual stocks, mutual funds, ETFs, or index funds. Index funds and ETFs are popular with beginners since they give you a lot of diversification in one purchase.

Finally, check in on your portfolio every so often. Life changes, and your goals might too. When your mix drifts away from what you wanted, you'll probably need to sell some things and buy others to get back on track.

Animal rights is a philosophical position holding that animals, because they are sentient, possess moral entitlements that deserve consideration and safeguarding. Supporters of this view contend that animals should be met with respect and compassion, and that people should not use or exploit them for their own gain. According to them, animals can feel pleasure, pain, and a range of other emotions, which means they should not be made to endure needless suffering or injury. Advocates maintain that animals are entitled to live without human intrusion or exploitation, and to live in ways that suit their natural needs and their species. Some also argue that animals deserve protection from human practices that threaten their welfare, including hunting, intensive factory farming, and animal testing.
