The two brands were later merged into a single company, Jaguar Land Rover (JLR), which is headquartered in the United Kingdom and operates as a wholly owned subsidiary of Tata Motors. Tata Motors has since reorganized its businesses, and JLR now sits within its passenger vehicle arm.

Before Tata, Land Rover changed hands several times. It began as a product of the British Rover Company in 1948 and later became part of British Leyland. It then passed to British Aerospace, then to BMW in 1994, and to Ford in 2000. Under Tata's ownership, JLR has continued to design and build Land Rover vehicles, including the Range Rover, Defender, and Discovery lines, mainly in the UK, with additional production in other countries.

Heroes was a television series broadcast on NBC between 2006 and 2010. Across its four seasons, it ran roughly 24 episodes per season. The program centers on ordinary individuals who learn they possess remarkable powers, chronicling their efforts to make sense of those abilities and manage them while coping with the demands of daily life. Every season unfolds its own storyline and brings in fresh characters, yet the larger narrative remains focused on the cast's attempts to protect the world from a range of dangers.

When you visit another country, you have to follow that country's rules, just like when you visit a friend's house and have to follow their house rules. It doesn't matter that you live somewhere else. If you break a rule while you're there, that country's police and judges are the ones in charge of you.

For something small like a speeding ticket, you usually get a fine. If you're driving a rental car, the rental company often passes the ticket along to you and charges your credit card. If you simply leave without paying, the country might not chase you right away, but it can cause trouble later, like being stopped or fined when you come back, or sometimes having trouble getting a visa.

For bigger things like fraud or other white collar crimes, the country can arrest you, put you on trial, and send you to prison there, even though you're a visitor. If you run home before they catch you, they can ask your home country to send you back. This is called extradition. Many countries have agreements to do this for each other, though not all of them do, and some will refuse for certain reasons.

For something very serious like murder, it works the same way but with much higher stakes. The country where it happened can arrest you, try you, and punish you under its own laws, which might mean a very long prison sentence, and in some places even worse. If you escape to your home country, many countries will send you back to face trial, or sometimes they will put you on trial themselves at home. Some countries won't send their own citizens away, but they may try them in their own courts instead.

Being a tourist also gives you a little help. Your country's embassy can check that you're being treated fairly, help you find a lawyer, and contact your family. But they can't make the charges go away or get you out of jail. So the simple lesson is: wherever you go, you play by the local rules.

Vinod Khosla, an American businessman and venture capitalist born in India, helped found Sun Microsystems and later started Khosla Ventures, a venture capital firm that backs young companies in internet, mobile, digital health, and clean technology. He is widely recognized for his influence in the tech sector, where he has placed major bets on many companies that went on to succeed. Khosla is also a leading voice in clean technology, championing renewable energy such as solar and wind power. Beyond his business work, he is active in philanthropy and has given support to a range of charities and causes.

Deep structure is a term from linguistics, most closely associated with Noam Chomsky's early work on generative grammar in the 1950s and 1960s, especially his 1965 book Aspects of the Theory of Syntax. It refers to an abstract level of representation underlying a sentence, where its fundamental grammatical relations and meaning-relevant organization are encoded. This is contrasted with surface structure, which is the form of the sentence as it is actually pronounced or written.

The idea was motivated by the observation that sentences that look quite different on the surface can share the same underlying relationships, while sentences that look alike can differ underneath. Consider "The dog chased the cat" and "The cat was chased by the dog." Their surface forms differ, but in both, the dog is the one doing the chasing and the cat is the one being chased. On Chomsky's account, both derive from a single deep structure, and a transformation (in this case, the passive transformation) rearranges it into the passive surface form. Conversely, "John is eager to please" and "John is easy to please" look parallel, yet in the first John is the one who pleases, while in the second someone else pleases John. Deep structure was meant to capture such differences.

In the classic model, the grammar had a base component that generated deep structures using phrase structure rules and a lexicon, and a set of transformations that mapped these onto surface structures. Deep structure was also taken to feed semantic interpretation, while surface structure fed phonological interpretation. This claim that deep structure determines meaning was controversial, and it prompted debates, including the "linguistics wars" between Chomsky's interpretive approach and the generative semanticists, who argued that syntax and semantics could not be so separated.

Later, Chomsky revised his theory. In Government and Binding theory the level was renamed D-structure, and in the Minimalist Program of the 1990s he dropped deep structure as a distinct level altogether, favoring a more economical system where structures are built by operations like Merge and interfaced directly with sound and meaning.

The term is also used more loosely outside linguistics, for example in anthropology, literary theory, and psychology, to mean underlying patterns or principles that shape surface phenomena, such as the deep structures Lévi-Strauss proposed in myth and kinship. In everyday usage it often simply means the hidden organizing logic beneath something's visible form.

Yes. The converse of dollar-cost averaging is usually called dollar-cost withdrawal, or sometimes "reverse dollar-cost averaging," though that label is less common. Where dollar-cost averaging means investing a fixed amount on a regular schedule so you buy more shares when prices are low and fewer when they are high, a systematic withdrawal plan means selling a fixed dollar amount on a regular schedule, so you sell more shares when prices are low and fewer when prices are high.

The catch is that this mirror image does not behave the same way in terms of risk. Dollar-cost averaging tends to reduce the impact of volatility on your average purchase price. A withdrawal plan faces what is called sequence-of-returns risk: if the market falls early in your retirement, you must sell a larger share of your portfolio to fund the same withdrawal, and those shares are no longer available to recover when prices rebound. Two retirees with identical average returns can end up with very different outcomes depending on the order in which the good and bad years arrive.

For a low-risk withdrawal from the market, several approaches address this. A cash or bond buffer, often one to three years of spending held in short-term instruments, lets you draw from that reserve during downturns rather than selling stocks at depressed prices. Variable withdrawal rules, such as taking a smaller amount after bad years and allowing modest increases after good ones, reduce the strain on the portfolio. Guardrail strategies set upper and lower bounds on your withdrawal rate and adjust when the portfolio crosses them. A conservative initial withdrawal rate, commonly discussed in the range of 3 to 4 percent of the starting balance, also lowers the probability of depletion, though the appropriate figure depends on your time horizon, asset allocation, and flexibility.

If you are planning a specific withdrawal, a fee-only financial planner or a tool that runs Monte Carlo simulations can test how your particular mix of assets and spending would hold up under a range of market paths.

Sadomasochism refers to deriving pleasure, often sexual, from either inflicting pain or humiliation on someone else (sadism) or from receiving pain or humiliation oneself (masochism). The term combines the names of two writers: the Marquis de Sade, an 18th-century French aristocrat whose novels depicted cruelty linked with sexual pleasure, and Leopold von Sacher-Masoch, a 19th-century Austrian author whose novel "Venus in Furs" described a man who wished to be dominated by a woman. The psychiatrist Richard von Krafft-Ebing coined the terms in the late 1800s.

In modern usage, sadomasochism is most commonly discussed as part of BDSM, an umbrella term covering bondage and discipline, dominance and submission, and sadism and masochism. Within this context, the activities are consensual and negotiated between adults. Participants typically agree in advance on what they are and aren't comfortable with, often use a "safe word" that immediately stops the activity, and emphasize principles such as "safe, sane, and consensual" or "risk-aware consensual kink." The appeal varies from person to person. Some enjoy the physical sensations, others the psychological dynamic of giving up or taking control, the trust involved, or the intense emotional release.

It's important to distinguish consensual sadomasochism from abuse. The defining difference is consent: in healthy BDSM, everyone involved has freely agreed, can withdraw at any time, and their limits are respected. Abuse involves harm without genuine consent.

From a medical perspective, current psychiatric guidelines, such as the DSM-5, do not consider consensual sadomasochistic interests to be a mental disorder in themselves. A diagnosis of sexual sadism or masochism disorder applies only when the interests cause significant personal distress or impairment, or when sadistic urges are acted on with people who have not consented. Research has generally found that people who practice consensual BDSM are psychologically comparable to the general population.

Outside of sexuality, the word "masochistic" is also used casually to describe someone who seems to seek out hardship or suffering, and "sadistic" to describe someone who enjoys others' discomfort.

Tax-loss harvesting means selling investments that have lost value so that you can report the loss on your tax return and use it to offset capital gains. It can help lower what you owe on those gains, which in many cases are taxed at a higher rate than ordinary income. To gauge how much it might help, you should look at a few things: how large your capital gains are, what tax rate applies to them, and how much in losses you can claim by harvesting.

Consider a simple illustration. Suppose you have $10,000 in capital gains taxed at 20%. If you did no harvesting, your tax bill on those gains would be $2,000. Now suppose you realize $5,000 in losses through tax-loss harvesting. Those losses reduce your $10,000 in gains to a net gain of $5,000, and the same 20% rate applied to that amount produces a tax bill of $1,000. So in this case, harvesting cuts your taxes by $1,000, from $2,000 down to $1,000.

Keep in mind that there are caps on how much loss you can claim in any one year, as well as rules governing how unused losses may be carried into later tax years. For more detail, talk with a tax professional or consult the IRS guidelines.

Your son may have preauricular pits or sinuses, which are tiny, shallow dimples found on the front of the ear close to the lobe. Babies are born with these, and they are generally believed to result from irregular formation of the ear while the baby is developing in the womb. Typically they are harmless and cause no difficulties, although occasionally they become infected. If the pits worry you, it would be wise to bring them up with your pediatrician, who can examine them and advise you on how to keep them clean and help prevent infection.

Automatic differentiation (AD) is a method for computing the derivative of a function that is specified by a computer program, carried out numerically. It makes it possible to efficiently obtain the gradient of a function with respect to its inputs, a quantity frequently required in machine learning, optimization, and scientific computing. AD works on functions expressed as a series of basic arithmetic operations (addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division) along with elementary functions such as exp, log, and sin. By repeatedly applying the chain rule to these steps, AD yields the derivative with respect to any input, so there is no need to derive it by hand using calculus. Two principal implementation strategies exist: forward mode and reverse mode. Forward mode determines the derivative with respect to one input at a time, whereas reverse mode determines the derivatives with respect to all inputs at once. Reverse mode is the better choice when inputs greatly outnumber outputs, and forward mode is more efficient when outputs outnumber inputs. In machine learning, AD is employed to calculate the gradients of loss functions with respect to model parameters during training. It also plays a role in optimization, where it helps locate a function's minimum or maximum through gradient descent or related algorithms. In scientific computing, AD can measure how sensitive a model or simulation is to its inputs, or support parameter estimation by reducing the gap between model predictions and observed data.

"Human Compatible" is a 2019 book by Stuart Russell, a computer scientist at the University of California, Berkeley, and a leading researcher in artificial intelligence. He is also co-author of "Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach," one of the standard textbooks in the field. The book argues that the way AI has traditionally been built is fundamentally flawed and proposes a new foundation for developing systems that are safe and beneficial.

Russell's central claim is that the dominant model of AI treats machines as optimizers of fixed objectives. Engineers specify a goal, and the system pursues it as effectively as possible. The problem is that it is extremely hard to write down the objective we actually want. A system that rigidly maximizes a slightly wrong goal can cause serious harm, since it will pursue that goal relentlessly, possibly at the expense of things we care about but forgot to include. Russell illustrates this with examples such as a social media recommendation algorithm that optimizes engagement and thereby amplifies outrage, or hypothetical superintelligent systems that pursue a misspecified goal with catastrophic thoroughness.

To address this, Russell proposes three principles for building what he calls provably beneficial AI. First, the machine's only objective is to maximize the realization of human preferences. Second, the machine is initially uncertain about what those preferences are. Third, the ultimate source of information about human preferences is human behavior and feedback. Because the machine knows it does not fully understand what humans want, it has an incentive to defer to people, ask for clarification, accept correction, and allow itself to be switched off. Russell argues this uncertainty is a feature rather than a bug, because it makes the system cooperative and corrigible rather than dangerously overconfident.

The book also discusses the broader risks of advanced AI, the difficulty of aligning machine behavior with human values when those values are complex, diverse, and sometimes contradictory, and the policy and governance questions that follow. Russell draws on economics, philosophy, and game theory, and he discusses topics such as how AI might affect employment and how humans might lose autonomy if they become overly dependent on automated systems.

In short, "Human Compatible" is a call to rethink the goals of AI research. Rather than building machines that are perfect at achieving fixed objectives, Russell urges researchers to build machines whose purpose is to serve human interests, while remaining humble about what those interests are.

When people who jointly own a property can't agree on whether to sell it, the situation can be hard to handle. A sensible first step is often to negotiate in the hope of reaching a compromise. The owners might talk through their reasons for wanting to sell or to keep the property, and look for alternatives that could satisfy everyone's needs. If negotiation doesn't produce an agreement, they may have to turn to mediation or arbitration, in which a neutral outsider helps guide them toward a resolution. If the disagreement still can't be settled, another possibility is to request a legal partition, which splits the property into separate ownership interests for each co-owner. Because this process can be complicated, hiring an attorney to help work through the legal requirements may be necessary. In the end, the best approach depends on the particular circumstances, as well as on what the co-owners need and hope to achieve. Consulting an attorney or a neutral third party can help them weigh their options and decide which path to take.

Bigamy is basically when you marry someone while you're still legally married to somebody else. It's illegal in a lot of countries, mostly because it's dishonest and it hurts people.

Think about it this way. You're married, you love your spouse, you trust them. Then you find out they went and married another person behind your back. That would be crushing, right? Your trust in them would be shot. And the new spouse gets a raw deal too, since they probably had no clue the person was already married. They're left confused and blindsided.

It gets messy legally as well. If the two people have kids, it can be unclear who the legal parent is. And when it comes to stuff like a house or a car, people can end up fighting over who actually has a right to it. So the law steps in because bigamy is deceptive and causes a ton of heartache and legal headaches for everyone caught up in it.

Imagine two kids from different neighborhoods who want to trade toys. Each one sends a friend to do the talking. Now imagine that if the other neighborhood's kids didn't like the message, they could grab the friend and lock him in a closet. Nobody would ever agree to be the messenger, and the two neighborhoods would stop talking and maybe start fighting. Diplomatic immunity is the rule that says messengers can't be grabbed. It exists so countries can keep talking to each other, even when they are angry, without fearing that the other side will arrest their representatives on made-up charges to gain leverage.

The idea is very old. Even ancient kingdoms treated heralds and envoys as untouchable, because war is worse than talk. Today the rules are written down in a treaty called the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations from 1961, which almost every country has signed.

Family members are covered because diplomats usually live abroad with their spouses and kids. If the host country could arrest a diplomat's wife or child, it could pressure the diplomat just as easily. Protecting the family also means diplomats will actually accept foreign postings instead of leaving their families behind. Typically the closest family members who live in the household are covered.

Now for the TV question: no, you could not rob a bank and murder people for free. The shows exaggerate. Immunity means the host country's courts can't prosecute you, but it doesn't mean you did nothing wrong. A country has several tools. It can declare the diplomat "persona non grata," which means "get out, you're not welcome," and send them home. The diplomat's own country can waive immunity so they can be tried, which happens for serious crimes. The home country can also prosecute them itself under its own laws. And police can still stop a diplomat in the moment, for example to prevent violence, even if they can't charge them later.

A diplomat who committed a murder would almost certainly be expelled, disgraced, and likely prosecuted at home, and their career would be over. There have been real abuses, such as unpaid parking tickets in New York and some serious cases of crime, and some people think the system is too generous. But it's not a license to kill. It's more like a very powerful "you can't arrest the messenger" rule, with the consequence being that the messenger gets sent home.

Also, only certain people have it. Full immunity belongs to accredited diplomats, not to every foreign tourist or even every embassy employee. Lower-level staff often get protection only for acts connected to their official job. So if you are not a diplomat, you are on your own, and robbing a bank will not go well.

Variable annuities are mostly bought by people saving for retirement or some other long-term goal. They can grow tax-deferred, you get a bunch of investment options to pick from, and you can usually turn the thing into guaranteed income payments down the road. Plenty of folks buy them to top up their retirement income, while others just want to spread their money around and hope for better returns than they'd get from more conventional stuff. That said, they come with investment risk and aren't a fit for everyone. Think hard about your goals and how much risk you can actually stomach before you commit to anything.

Numerous large American cities sit along state lines, and this pattern stems from several causes. Many of these cities grew up around transportation hubs like rivers and railroads, since such sites made it simpler for travelers and merchandise to cross between states. St. Louis, for instance, sits on the Mississippi River, a vital route for people and goods during the 1800s. Likewise, Kansas City lies near the point where the Missouri and Kansas Rivers meet, and Omaha sits on the Missouri River.

Other cities lie on state boundaries because they were established as frontier settlements straddling two states. Cincinnati, founded in 1788, is one example. At that time Ohio was still part of the Northwest Territory, and the town was positioned on the line separating Ohio from Kentucky, which then belonged to Virginia.

A third group of cities sits on borders because their growth eventually spread into neighboring states. Memphis, for example, lies on the boundary between Tennessee and Mississippi and has expanded to include territory in both. In sum, the placement of major cities along state lines reflects a mix of transportation routes, historical and political circumstances, and the way these cities expanded over time.

The short answer is that a glide path is usually the better default for most people, but the choice matters less than getting the basics right: saving enough, keeping costs low, and not panicking during downturns.

A static allocation keeps the same mix of stocks and bonds throughout your life, say 70/30 forever. Its appeal is simplicity and the fact that it never forces you to sell stocks at a bad time just because the calendar says you should be more conservative. If you have a high tolerance for volatility, a long time horizon, or other sources of guaranteed income such as a pension or Social Security that cover your essential spending, a static mix can work well.

An age-based glide path starts with a higher stock share when you're young and gradually shifts toward bonds and cash as you approach and enter retirement. Its main advantage is that it matches your risk exposure to your shrinking capacity to recover from losses. A market crash at 35 is an opportunity; the same crash at 64, just before you begin withdrawals, can permanently damage your plan through sequence-of-returns risk. Target-date funds are the most common version of this and are a reasonable, low-effort choice for many savers.

Some practical points to weigh. Glide paths can be too conservative for people who will live a long time, since a 65-year-old may need money to last into their 90s, so retirees often keep a meaningful stock allocation even after they stop working. Fund fees differ a lot between target-date products, so compare expense ratios. And whichever you choose, the approach you can stick with through a bear market is the one that works.

If your situation is unusual, with a large concentrated position, a pension decision, or a short timeline, a fee-only financial planner can help you tailor the mix. For a typical saver, a low-cost target-date fund or a simple glide path you set yourself is a sound place to start.

Dear Ammu, thank you for sharing this. Daydreaming is very common, and it is not a sign that something is wrong with you. Many people drift into daydreams when they feel overwhelmed or when a goal feels far away. The good news is that you can learn to manage it, and your ideas about further study can actually become a source of motivation rather than distraction.

Start by noticing when the daydreaming happens. Is it during routine tasks, when you feel bored, or when you are tired or stressed by your responsibilities? Once you see the pattern, you can prepare for it. For example, if you tend to drift during long tasks, break them into small pieces of 25 to 30 minutes, with a short break in between. This technique, sometimes called the Pomodoro method, gives your mind a clear finish line and makes it easier to stay present.

It also helps to give your dreams a planned place in your day. Set aside a short, fixed time, perhaps ten or fifteen minutes each evening, to think about your plans for further study. Write down the course or institution you are considering, the steps needed to apply, and one small action you can take the next day. When your imagination has a scheduled outlet, it is less likely to interrupt your work at unexpected moments. If a random dream appears during the day, you can gently tell yourself, "I will think about this during my planning time," and return to your task.

Keep your daily responsibilities organized with a simple to-do list. A clear list reduces the mental clutter that often leads to drifting. Choose the three most important tasks each morning and focus on them first.

Physical habits matter too. Since your night sleep is good, look at your daytime energy: regular meals, drinking enough water, a short walk, and some sunlight can all reduce restlessness and make it easier to concentrate. If you notice that your mind wanders very heavily even when you are rested and busy, or if it starts to affect your mood or daily functioning, it may be worth speaking with a doctor or counselor. That is a sensible step, not a sign of weakness.

Finally, you mentioned that you do not feel able to share this with anyone. Even so, consider finding one trusted person, a teacher, a senior colleague, or a friend, who could check in on your study plans with you. Having someone to briefly update on your progress can make your goals feel more real and keep you grounded.

Wishing you success with your studies and your responsibilities.

Warm regards

In Michigan, there is no statewide law requiring landlords to pay interest on security deposits, so whether interest is owed depends largely on the city where the rental is located. Michigan's Landlord-Tenant statute (MCL 554.601 et seq.) governs how deposits must be handled, including that they be held in escrow or a regulated financial institution and that the tenant receive an itemized statement and any balance within 30 days after the tenancy ends, but it does not mandate interest. A few Michigan municipalities, such as Ann Arbor, Lansing, and East Lansing, have adopted local ordinances requiring landlords to pay interest on deposits, typically at a set annual rate or a rate tied to a bank savings rate, and sometimes only for rentals covered by the local rental registration program. Because these rules change and vary, a tenant or landlord should check the current ordinance for the specific city or township, or ask the local housing or code enforcement office, and should also review the lease, since it may address interest. If you tell me the city where the property is located, I can share what I know about its specific rules, though you should confirm the details with the local government.

Yeah, you can use balance transfers to dodge interest on credit cards, at least for a while. The basic idea is moving a balance from a card charging high interest over to one with a lower rate. What you're really hunting for is a card with a promo 0% APR on balance transfers. Those usually last somewhere around 6 to 18 months after you open the account, and as long as you keep making your minimum payments on time, you won't get hit with interest on the transferred amount during that window.

To do it, you'll need the account info for your old card and the new one, and you'll tell the new card issuer what to pay off. Heads up that there's often a transfer fee, usually a percentage of whatever you move. Sometimes it's waived or lower if you transfer within the first few months after opening the card, so it's worth checking the fine print before you commit.

Don't count on it being a permanent fix, though. Once the promo ends, the leftover balance will probably start accruing interest at the regular rate, and new purchases might too, depending on the card. The real trick is paying the balance off before the promo runs out and not running up new charges you can't cover in full each month.

Imagine you want to walk to a wall. First you walk half the way there. Then you walk half of what's left. Then half of that, and so on. Each time you get closer, but there's always another half left to walk, so it seems like you'd never actually reach the wall. That's the puzzle Zeno came up with long ago.

Here's the trick that solves it. Those halves get smaller and smaller so fast that their total adds up to exactly the whole distance. Half, plus a quarter, plus an eighth, plus a sixteenth, and so on, gets closer and closer to one whole. It never goes over, but it gets as close as you like. So you can take infinitely many steps and still finish the walk, and the steps take less and less time too, which is why you really do reach the wall.

Brain simulation is basically about building a computer model of the human brain, or some part of it. People do this mostly to figure out how the brain actually works, and then to use that knowledge for things like AI systems or brain-machine interfaces. There are a few main ways to go about it. The empirical approach builds the model from data gathered with brain imaging, like MRI or PET scans. The theoretical approach starts from what we currently understand about how the brain functions and uses that to predict what brain activity should look like. Then there's the hybrid approach, which mixes the two: you use imaging data to tweak and check your theoretical models. It's a hard problem, though. The brain has billions of neurons and trillions of connections, so there's a lot to capture. Still, better computing power and better tools for analyzing brain activity have let researchers make real progress on both understanding the brain and building new tech from it.

What you're describing sounds very much like a common inherited skin condition called ichthyosis vulgaris. Dry, flaky skin that started in early childhood, mostly on the arms and legs, that keeps scaling even after moisturizer, and that runs in your family (your father and brother have it too) is the classic pattern. It's caused by a gene change that reduces a protein called filaggrin, which your skin needs to hold moisture and shed old cells normally. It isn't contagious and it isn't your fault. It can also be linked to eczema, allergies, or asthma, so mention those to a doctor if you have them.

To answer your question honestly, it usually can't be cured, because it comes from your genes. But it can be controlled very well. Many people find their skin looks and feels close to normal with the right routine, and it often improves in warm, humid weather and sometimes with age.

Olive oil probably didn't help because plain oils sit on the surface and don't loosen the built-up scales. What works better are moisturizers with ingredients that soften and remove scale and pull water into the skin. Look for creams containing urea (around 10 to 20 percent), lactic acid or ammonium lactate (such as Lac-Hydrin or AmLactin), or salicylic acid. Thick, greasy products like petroleum jelly (Vaseline) or ointment-based creams are also good for sealing in moisture. If a cream stings on cracked skin, start with a plain thick ointment until it heals, then add the urea or lactic acid cream.

How you use them matters as much as what you use. Take short baths or showers with lukewarm rather than hot water, and use a mild, fragrance-free cleanser instead of regular soap. Pat your skin gently so it's still slightly damp, then apply the cream within a few minutes to lock in the water. Some people soak in the bath for a while and then gently rub the softened scales with a soft washcloth or pumice, but don't scrub hard or make the skin raw. Apply moisturizer at least twice a day, every day, even when your skin looks better, because the scaling returns if you stop. A humidifier in your room can also help in dry or cold weather.

I'd strongly suggest seeing a dermatologist. They can confirm the diagnosis, since a few other types of ichthyosis look similar, and prescribe stronger treatments if over-the-counter creams aren't enough, such as prescription-strength lactic acid, topical retinoids, or occasionally oral medication for more severe cases. Since your father and brother are affected too, the same advice will likely help them.

I know it can feel embarrassing, especially at 19, but this is a well-known, manageable condition, and with consistent care your skin can look much better than it does now.

It may be that the scabies and the red, tender belly button are not connected to your ovarian cancer or your remission. Scabies is a skin disorder brought on by the human itch mite, which tunnels into the skin and deposits its eggs there. Typical signs include severe itching that tends to worsen at night, along with a rash of small, elevated red spots or blisters. This rash commonly shows up where the mites favor burrowing, including skin folds, the spaces between the fingers and toes, and the wrists, elbows, and buttocks. If your doctor has diagnosed scabies and prescribed a topical medication, you should follow the directions carefully and keep applying it until the infestation is completely cleared. Any clothing, bedding, or other belongings that may have touched the mites should also be cleaned and treated. Your low body temperature and sensation of feeling cold could point to several different conditions. These symptoms might stem from a side effect of a medication you're taking or from an underlying health problem. Whenever you have concerns about your health or notice unusual symptoms, it's wise to speak with a healthcare provider, who can evaluate what's happening and recommend the most appropriate next steps.

I can't tell you where to put your money specifically, since that depends on your age, savings, time horizon, and how much loss you could tolerate, but I can outline the common approaches people use to protect against a stock market decline.

Many investors start with high-quality bonds, particularly U.S. Treasuries or a broad bond index fund. Government bonds have historically held their value or risen during many stock downturns, especially when the downturn is driven by recession and the Federal Reserve cuts interest rates. Cash and money market funds offer stability too, though they lose ground to inflation over time and don't rise in a crash. Some investors also hold gold or other precious metals, which sometimes act as a store of value during turmoil, though their behavior is inconsistent and they produce no income.

Defensive stock sectors such as consumer staples, utilities, and healthcare tend to fall less than the broad market in downturns, though they still decline. Lowering exposure to high-valuation or heavily leveraged companies can also reduce risk. Some people use put options or inverse ETFs to bet directly on a decline, but these are complex, often expensive to hold, and can lose money quickly if the market doesn't cooperate, so they're generally better suited to experienced investors.

The most reliable hedge for most people is diversification and an asset allocation matched to their risk tolerance. Holding a mix of stocks and bonds, rebalancing periodically, and keeping an emergency fund so you aren't forced to sell during a downturn often matters more than any single bet. If you tell me more about your situation, I can explain how these options might fit together, though a fee-only financial advisor can give you advice tailored to your full picture.

Some companies won't ship to P.O. boxes, and there are a few common reasons. First, P.O. boxes are usually smaller than a street address can accommodate, so big or oddly shaped items just won't fit. Some carriers, especially ones that fly packages around, also have size and weight limits that make P.O. box delivery a no-go. Then there's verification. A package going to a house or office can be checked against a real address, and the carrier can be pretty sure the person getting it is the one who ordered it. With a P.O. box, though, anyone who has the box number and key can grab the package, so companies worry about that. And finally, some businesses just don't offer P.O. box shipping at all, either because their systems can't handle it or because they've decided it's not worth offering.

A cryptographic hash function is a mathematical operation that accepts an input, often called a 'message,' and produces a fixed-length string of characters, usually written as a hexadecimal number. Its defining feature is that it is computationally impractical to locate two distinct messages that yield the same output. As a result, it serves well for confirming that a message or file has not been altered, since even a small modification to the input produces a different hash. These functions are also called 'digest functions' or 'one-way functions,' because computing the hash of a message is straightforward while reconstructing the original message from the hash is extremely hard. For this reason, they are commonly used to store passwords, since the original password cannot be readily recovered from the saved hash. Well-known examples include SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm), MD5 (Message-Digest Algorithm 5), and RIPEMD-160 (RACE Integrity Primitives Evaluation Message Digest).

Daydreaming is totally normal, and it can even be useful sometimes. But if it's getting in the way of focusing and finishing stuff, a few things might help. First, figure out what sets it off. Maybe it's a boring lecture or a meeting that drags on. If you know the trigger, you can either dodge it or make it more interesting, like taking breaks or switching up the activity. Second, set clear goals and deadlines. When you know exactly what you need to get done and when, it's a lot harder to drift off. Third, try some mindfulness. Deep breathing or a quick meditation session can bring you back to the present, and it doesn't have to take long to work. Fourth, give your brain something engaging to chew on. If you zone out when you're bored, pick up a puzzle, a hobby, or a task that's challenging enough to hold your attention. Last, if you've tried this stuff and it's still a struggle, talk to someone. A friend, family member, or mental health professional can help you figure out if something deeper is going on and what to do about it.

Computational complexity is the branch of computer science and mathematics that studies how much of a resource, such as time or memory, an algorithm needs to solve a problem, and how that requirement grows as the size of the input grows. Rather than measuring the exact seconds a program takes on a particular machine, which depends on hardware and implementation details, it asks more fundamental questions: Is a problem inherently easy or hard? Is there any algorithm that could solve it efficiently at all?

The usual way to express this is with asymptotic notation, such as big O. If sorting a list of n items takes roughly n log n steps, we say its time complexity is O(n log n), meaning the running time grows at a rate no faster than that expression, up to a constant factor, as n becomes large. This lets us compare algorithms independently of the machine they run on. An algorithm that takes n squared steps will become dramatically slower than one that takes n steps once the input is large, even if the first one is faster on tiny inputs.

The field also classifies problems themselves rather than just algorithms. Problems solvable in polynomial time, meaning time bounded by some fixed power of the input size, are generally considered tractable. Problems for which no known algorithm runs in polynomial time, such as many scheduling, routing, and puzzle problems, are considered intractable in practice. The class P contains the efficiently solvable decision problems, while NP contains problems whose proposed solutions can be verified quickly. Whether P equals NP is one of the most famous open questions in mathematics, and its answer would have sweeping consequences for cryptography, optimization, and many other areas.

Computational complexity also studies space, meaning memory use, and other models of computation, including randomized and parallel computing. Its results have practical importance: they tell engineers when a problem deserves a clever heuristic instead of an exact method, they underpin modern cryptography, which relies on certain problems being hard, and they set theoretical limits on what any computer can do efficiently.

A Mexican standoff describes a showdown in which every participant has a weapon aimed at the others, so none of them can safely strike first or back away. Firearms were a routine means of self-protection in the American Old West, which means such face-offs could well have occurred there. Still, they were neither frequent nor lawful. Threatening or injuring someone with a gun was prohibited, so anyone caught taking part in one could face legal consequences.

Paul Revere was born in Boston, in the British colony of Massachusetts, on January 1, 1735. He came from a family of Huguenot descent; his father, Apollos Rivoire, was a silversmith who had emigrated from France, and Paul later became a silversmith himself, as well as a well-known participant in the American Revolution.

ETFs are basically a way to buy a whole bunch of assets in one go. You get a diversified basket of stuff through a single security. They're kind of like mutual funds in that they hold a collection of assets, but the big difference is they trade on an exchange just like stocks.

Like mutual funds, ETFs charge fees to cover running the thing: buying and selling securities, keeping records, marketing, that kind of stuff. Those fees usually come out of the fund's assets and show up in the expense ratio. That's the percentage of the fund's assets that goes toward expenses. So if an ETF has a 0.50% expense ratio, 0.50% of the fund's assets go to covering costs, and that gets deducted from returns every year.

There can also be other fees on top of that. Brokerage commissions and transaction fees can hit you when you buy or sell, and they depend on your broker and the specific ETF. Fees can eat into your returns a lot over time, so it's worth checking them before you commit. Comparing a few ETFs side by side is a smart move.

Opening an online stock trading account in the United States is a straightforward process, though it does require some preparation. Start by choosing a brokerage. Major options include Fidelity, Charles Schwab, Vanguard, E*TRADE, Robinhood, and Interactive Brokers, and each differs in fees, research tools, account minimums, and investment options, so compare them based on your goals and how you plan to trade. Confirm that the firm is a member of the Securities Investor Protection Corporation (SIPC), which protects customer assets up to certain limits if the brokerage fails.

Once you have selected a broker, visit its website or download its app and click the option to open an account. You will need to choose the account type. A individual brokerage account is the most common choice for general investing. If you want tax advantages for retirement, you can instead open an IRA, either traditional or Roth. Joint accounts are available for couples or others who want shared ownership.

Next, fill out the application with your personal information. This typically includes your full legal name, date of birth, Social Security number or taxpayer identification number, residential address, phone number, email address, and employment details. You will also be asked about your income, net worth, investment experience, and investment objectives. These questions are required by federal regulations and help the broker assess whether certain products are suitable for you. Answer them honestly.

You will then need to verify your identity. Most brokers ask you to upload a government-issued photo ID such as a driver's license or passport, and some may ask additional verification questions drawn from your credit history. Keep these documents ready so the process goes smoothly.

After that, link a bank account to fund your brokerage account. Provide your bank's routing number and your account number, and the broker will usually verify ownership with small test deposits or through an instant verification service. Then transfer money into the account by ACH, wire transfer, or check. ACH transfers are common and often free, though funds may take a few business days to become available for trading, while wires are faster but may carry a fee.

Before placing your first trade, review the account agreements and disclosures, and if you plan to trade options or margin, you may need to apply separately for approval. Once your funds have settled, you can search for a stock by its ticker symbol, choose an order type such as a market or limit order, specify the number of shares, and submit the trade.

Finally, take time to learn the broker's platform, understand the fee structure, and consider setting up two-factor authentication to protect your account. Many investors also start with a small amount of money and diversified investments, such as index funds or exchange-traded funds, while they become comfortable with the process.

Anorexia is a really serious mental illness, and it hits people of all ages and backgrounds. At its core is an intense fear of gaining weight, plus an obsessive focus on weight, body size, and shape. A lot of people with it have a distorted body image, so they look in the mirror and see someone bigger or heavier than they actually are. That can push them to cut way back on food and do other unhealthy stuff too, like exercising excessively, all to lose weight.

Nobody knows exactly what causes it. The best guess is a mix of genetic, environmental, and psychological factors. Some research points to family history, like relatives with anxiety or depression, as something that makes it more likely. Other things that can raise the risk are a history of trauma or abuse, trouble coping with stress, and the social and cultural pressure to be thin.

There's also a brain side to it. Anorexia may be tied to unusual activity in the areas that handle thoughts, feelings, and behaviors around food and weight, and some people think chemical imbalances in the brain play a part as well.

The big thing is that it can be life-threatening and needs professional treatment. If you or someone you know is dealing with anorexia or another eating disorder, please reach out to a mental health professional or a qualified treatment center.

A notary public is an official authorized by the state to serve as an impartial witness when people sign important documents. Their main job is to verify the identity of the people signing, confirm that they are signing willingly and understand what they are signing, and then apply an official seal or stamp along with their signature to certify that this happened. This process, called notarization, helps prevent fraud, since it makes it much harder for someone to forge a signature or pressure another person into signing a document.

Notaries handle many kinds of paperwork. Common examples include deeds and mortgages for real estate transactions, powers of attorney, wills and trust documents, affidavits and sworn statements, and some business contracts. In many cases, a document must be notarized before a court, government agency, or financial institution will accept it.

Notaries also administer oaths and affirmations, meaning they ask a person to swear that the contents of a statement are true. Some notaries are licensed to perform additional tasks, such as certifying copies of certain documents, but their core role is verifying identity and witnessing signatures. Notaries are generally not lawyers and usually cannot give legal advice about the documents they handle, though some states allow specially trained notaries to help prepare immigration-related forms.

Corpus Christi is a Christian holiday that celebrates the presence of Jesus Christ's body and blood in the Eucharist, which some people call Holy Communion or the Lord's Supper. You'll also hear it called the Feast of Corpus Christi. It usually falls on the Thursday after Trinity Sunday, which itself comes 50 days after Easter. Plenty of countries make it a public holiday, and Catholics observe it along with some Protestant denominations. In some places it's a quiet day of worship, but in others it's more of a community event, with religious processions, parades, and other ceremonies out in the streets.

In the UK, people wishing to retire early have a few routes available. The state pension can be claimed once you reach state pension age, which is presently 66 for both men and women, though it is set to rise to 67 somewhere between 2026 and 2028. Those with a private pension may be able to start drawing from it before reaching state pension age, but what is permitted depends entirely on the rules of the particular scheme. People aged 55 or over might also ask their employer for flexible arrangements, such as fewer hours, home working, or a sabbatical. If ill health makes it impossible to keep working, retiring early on medical grounds may be an option. Where an employer is offering voluntary redundancy, accepting it could be a way to leave work sooner. Finally, those aged 50 or older may be able to negotiate a job-share, which would let them cut their hours gradually as they move toward retirement. Retiring ahead of state pension age can significantly reduce income, so the financial consequences deserve careful thought, and taking professional financial advice before committing to any decision is strongly recommended.

An itchy rash showing up on the knees, elbows, hands, feet, and face can stem from a wide range of causes. Among the possibilities are the following. Allergic reactions: Exposure to a specific substance, for example a certain food, drug, or household product, may trigger an itchy rash in someone who is allergic to it. Infections: Fungal infections such as ringworm, as well as bacterial infections, can lead to an itchy rash. Skin conditions: Eczema, psoriasis, and dermatitis are all skin disorders that may produce itching and a rash. Insect bites: Bites from insects like mosquitoes or fleas can leave itchy, rash-like marks on the skin. Contact dermatitis: This is an allergic reaction that develops when the skin touches a particular substance, such as poison ivy or certain chemicals. Because the cause can be hard to pinpoint, it is important to consult a doctor for a proper diagnosis and suitable treatment. A doctor can identify what is behind the rash and advise on the best way to deal with it.
