In the United States, Nevada is the only state where prostitution is legal, and even there it is permitted only in a limited form. State law allows counties with populations under 700,000 to license brothels, so legal prostitution exists only in licensed brothels in certain rural counties. It remains illegal in Clark County, which includes Las Vegas, and in Washoe County, which includes Reno, as well as in Carson City. Street prostitution and any sex work outside a licensed brothel are illegal everywhere in the state, and licensed workers must undergo regular health testing.

A couple of other states are worth knowing about because of related legal history or recent changes. Rhode Island had a legal loophole from 1980 to 2009 under which indoor prostitution was not explicitly prohibited, but the legislature closed it in 2009. Maine passed a law in 2023 that decriminalized selling sex while keeping the purchase of sex and activities like pimping illegal, an approach often called the Nordic or equality model. That makes it partially decriminalized rather than legalized. In every other state, both buying and selling sex are criminal offenses.

If you meant countries rather than U.S. states, prostitution is legal and regulated in some form in places such as Germany, the Netherlands, New Zealand (which fully decriminalized it in 2003), parts of Australia, and several others, though the specific rules vary widely.

The figure of 306 bones is a common textbook number for an adult human skeleton, but the count is not fixed. Adults typically have 206 bones, while babies are born with roughly 270 to 300 bones, many of which fuse together as the child grows. The number 306 likely appears in some sources because it counts certain structures differently, such as including some sesamoid bones or counting bone pieces that are separate in certain individuals. For most purposes, the standard answer is 206 bones in the adult human skeletal system.

There's no good evidence that eating Mentos, or any mint or candy, reduces sperm count. The idea seems to be a rumor. Mentos are sugar-based mints with flavoring, coloring, and sometimes gelatin or other additives, and none of those ingredients is known to affect sperm production. Sperm count is mainly influenced by things like hormone levels, testicular health, infections, smoking, heavy alcohol use, excess body heat, obesity, certain medications, and genetic factors. Occasional or even frequent candy eating isn't on that list.

That said, eating a lot of Mentos can cause other issues. The sugar can contribute to weight gain and tooth decay, and the mint can irritate the mouth or stomach if you eat large amounts. If you've been eating them in large quantities, it may be worth cutting back for those reasons, and it's worth paying attention to whether you're using them to replace meals or to cope with stress or cravings.

If you're worried about your fertility, the most useful step is a semen analysis with a doctor, especially if you're trying to conceive or have other symptoms such as pain or swelling in the testicles, changes in libido, or erectile problems. A doctor can check your actual numbers instead of leaving you to guess based on a rumor.

Norway has actually tried to join twice, in 1972 and in 1994, and both times the government was in favor but the people voted no in a referendum. Both votes were close, with "no" winning by roughly 53 to 47 percent. So it's less that Norway as a country refuses and more that a slight majority of ordinary Norwegians said "no thanks" when asked.

Imagine a big club where everyone shares toys and agrees to the same rules. Norway looked at the club and thought, "We already get to play with most of the toys, and if we join we'd have to share some of our favorite things and follow rules we didn't make." That's the heart of it.

Oil is part of the story, but not all of it. Norway found huge amounts of oil in the North Sea starting around 1969 and saved the money in an enormous national fund. Being rich made it easier to say no, because Norway didn't need the EU's help or money. As a member it would probably have paid more into the EU budget than it got back.

Fish matter just as much. Fishing is very important to Norway, especially in the north, and EU members share access to each other's fishing waters under common rules. Many Norwegians didn't want boats from other countries fishing in their seas or decisions about their fish made in Brussels. Farmers felt similarly. Norway protects its farms with high subsidies and import limits, because farming in a cold, mountainous country is hard, and EU rules would have exposed them to cheaper competition.

Then there's independence. Norway only became fully independent in 1905, after centuries under Denmark and then in a union with Sweden. Many people are wary of handing power to a larger union again. Rural areas, the political left, and some on the right all had reasons to be skeptical, which is why the "no" side was such a mixed coalition.

The key detail is that Norway isn't really outside. Through the European Economic Area agreement, it's part of the EU's single market, so goods, services, money, and people move freely between Norway and the EU. It's also in the Schengen passport-free zone. In exchange, Norway pays money to the EU and adopts most EU market rules, but it doesn't get a vote on making them. Critics call this "fax democracy," since Norway just receives the rules. Supporters say it's a good deal because fish, farming, and oil stay under Norwegian control.

So it's not really self-righteousness. It's a mix of being wealthy enough not to need membership, protecting fishing and farming, valuing hard-won independence, and already getting most of the benefits through a side door. Polls have shown a clear majority against joining for many years, so it's unlikely to change soon.

Imagine your body is like a little campfire that is always making warmth. Your skin is a blanket that keeps that warmth close, and a thin layer of warm air sits right against your skin, like a cozy jacket made of air. When there is no wind, that warm air jacket stays put and does a good job of keeping you warm.

When the wind blows, it pushes that warm air jacket away and replaces it with new, cold air. Your skin has to warm up the new cold air, and that takes energy, so your body loses heat faster. It's kind of like someone keeps taking off your blanket and putting a cold one on you instead.

That is why it can feel much colder outside when it's windy, even if the thermometer says the same number. The wind doesn't actually make the air colder, but it steals your warmth more quickly, so you feel colder.

Every four years, the International Federation of Association Football (FIFA) organizes the Women's World Cup, a soccer competition. The latest edition occurred in 2019, when the United States national team took the title by beating the Netherlands 2-0 in the final. That victory gave the American squad its fourth championship in the event, following earlier wins in 1991, 1999, and 2015.

Mark Zuckerberg is the CEO of Facebook, or more precisely of Meta Platforms, the parent company that was renamed from Facebook, Inc. in 2021. He co-founded Facebook in 2004 while a student at Harvard and has led the company ever since. He is also its chairman and controlling shareholder. Meta owns Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, Messenger, and the Quest virtual reality line.

Sparse coding is a method for representing data, such as images, sounds, or signals, as a combination of a small number of active elements chosen from a larger set. The core idea is that each input is described by only a few components being "on" at any given time, while most of the components are "off" or near zero. This contrasts with dense representations, where many components contribute to every input.

In a typical formulation, one learns a dictionary of basis vectors, sometimes called atoms or features, and then expresses each input as a weighted sum of a few of these atoms. The learning process balances two goals: reconstructing the input accurately from the chosen atoms, and keeping the number of nonzero coefficients small. The sparsity constraint is often enforced by adding a penalty term to the objective, such as the L1 norm of the coefficients, which tends to drive many of them exactly to zero.

The approach was popularized in neuroscience in the 1990s by Bruno Olshausen and David Field, who showed that training such a model on small patches of natural images produced basis functions resembling the oriented, localized edge detectors found in the primary visual cortex of mammals. This suggested that sparse representations might reflect how biological sensory systems compactly encode the world.

Sparse coding has several practical advantages. Sparse representations are often easier to interpret, since each input is explained by a few meaningful parts. They can also be more efficient to store and compute with, and they tend to be robust to noise and useful for tasks like denoising, compression, and feature extraction. In machine learning, the idea connects to related techniques such as sparse autoencoders, compressed sensing, and dictionary learning.

There are a number of advantages and drawbacks to weigh when choosing between purchasing physical gold outright and putting money into a gold exchange-traded fund (ETF). The main considerations are outlined below.

On the upside, buying gold directly means you hold the actual metal and can keep it somewhere secure, like a safe deposit box. Owning it outright can bring a feeling of control and peace of mind, since you always know where your investment sits. Gold also has a long record as a store of value, and its price may rise over the years. If you expect that increase, buying the metal itself could suit your strategy.

On the downside, storing gold directly requires a safe place to keep it, which can be inconvenient and expensive if you have to rent a safe deposit box. Selling large quantities of physical gold quickly can also be hard, because you must find a buyer willing to pay your asking price. That difficulty can grow worse during market turmoil or an economic slump.

Gold ETFs have their own strengths. They trade on stock exchanges, so buying and selling them is quick and simple, which helps during periods of volatility. They also let you gain exposure to gold without owning it physically, a convenient way to diversify a portfolio and potentially reduce risk. Their costs are usually lower too, since you avoid paying for storage and insurance.

Gold ETFs carry drawbacks as well. You depend on the fund to hold the physical gold and manage it responsibly, so you face counterparty risk should the fund default or mismanage its assets. In addition, an ETF is designed to follow the price of gold but does not always match it exactly, creating tracking error, so its returns can diverge from those of the underlying metal.

Ultimately, the better choice between buying gold directly and investing in a gold ETF depends on your goals and tolerance for risk. If you want a tangible asset you can hold and that may gain value over time, purchasing gold directly may fit. If you prefer the convenience and liquidity of a publicly traded product, a gold ETF may be the better option. As with any investment, weigh the pros and cons carefully and consult a financial advisor before deciding.

The three primary colors in the subtractive color model are cyan, magenta, and yellow. This model is used in color printing and painting, where pigments or inks absorb certain wavelengths of light and reflect others. Mixing these three together in theory produces black, which is why printers also add black ink (the K in CMYK) for deeper, more accurate shadows.

Calling them "ghost cities" isn't really fair. That term makes it sound like these places are abandoned, and that's not the case. Yeah, some new developments in China have had trouble filling up, but it's not everywhere, and there's a lot going on behind it. Some of these areas are in regions that aren't very populated to begin with, or they just don't have enough infrastructure like transit, schools, and hospitals to pull people in. In other cases, the housing is priced higher than what most people can actually afford, so nobody's buying or moving in. China has also been urbanizing and building at a crazy pace, and it takes years for a place to fill out. So you often get a gap where the buildings are finished but the residents haven't shown up yet. Point is, there's no single explanation, and you'd be jumping to conclusions if you judged the whole country based on a few examples.

Circumpolar constellations are basically the ones that never seem to set. If you're at a certain latitude, they just hang above the horizon all year long, circling around the sky without ever dipping below it. Which ones do this depends on where you're standing. The Big Dipper (Ursa Major) is circumpolar if you're above 44 degrees north, for example. Flip to the southern hemisphere and the Southern Cross (Crux) stays up for anyone below 30 degrees south. There are plenty of others too. Cassiopeia is circumpolar above 74 degrees north, Draco above 65 degrees north, and Polaris, the North Star, only stays up for folks above 89 degrees north, so basically the North Pole.

A bank might choose a lower all-cash offer over a higher one that relies on conventional financing for several reasons.

Speed: Cash deals tend to close faster, because they don't hinge on the buyer winning mortgage approval or on a lender being happy with the property's condition and value. This can matter a great deal to a bank that has had the property listed for some time and wants it off its books.

Risk: An offer that depends on a traditional loan exposes the bank to more uncertainty. The sale only works if the buyer secures financing and the property appraises high enough to justify the loan amount. If either condition isn't met, the transaction may collapse, pushing back the sale and possibly forcing the bank to put the property on the market again and start over.

Other considerations: Additional factors can also tip the balance toward a lower cash bid. The buyer might have a solid financial history, or might offer non-monetary perks such as a longer closing window or a willingness to handle certain repairs or renovations. In the end, whether a bank takes a lower cash offer instead of a higher financed one depends on the particulars of the sale and how it weighs the risks and benefits of each bid.

Most vaccines have a few main parts. The big one is the antigen, which is the piece of the virus or bacteria that gets your immune system to make antibodies. Usually it's either a killed or weakened version of the germ, or just a bit of its genetic material like DNA or RNA.

Some vaccines also include adjuvants. These give the immune response a boost, so the body makes more antibodies and other immune cells, which can make the shot work better.

Preservatives are added to some vaccines to keep bacteria or fungi from growing in them. Nobody wants a contaminated shot.

Stabilizers do what the name says: they keep the vaccine from breaking down or losing potency over time.

Then there are excipients, which are the inactive stuff that gives the vaccine the right consistency, pH, and so on. You'll see things like salts, sugars, or oils. They're there to help the vaccine last longer and be easier to handle.

So really, the antigen is the key ingredient that does the work. The rest are extras that either help it work better or keep it in good shape until it reaches your arm.

Erie's a town in northern Colorado, mostly in Weld County, about 25 miles northwest of Denver. It's been growing like crazy and has something like 25,000 people now. People like it for the small-town feel and all the outdoorsy stuff nearby, plus you can get to Denver and the other bigger cities around there pretty easily.

Yes, the tax treatment can differ quite a bit, and the biggest factor is usually how long guests typically stay. In the U.S., a traditional long-term rental (generally a lease of 30 days or more) is treated as passive rental income. You report the income and deduct expenses such as mortgage interest, property taxes, insurance, repairs, and depreciation, typically on Schedule E. Passive loss rules often limit how much of a loss you can use against your other income.

A short-term rental like Airbnb can be treated differently. If the average guest stay is seven days or less, the IRS generally does not classify the activity as a rental for certain purposes. Depending on how much personal services you provide, such as daily cleaning, linens, or concierge-style support, the income may be treated as a business and reported on Schedule C, which can bring self-employment tax into play. If you materially participate in managing the property, short-term rental losses may also be treated as nonpassive, meaning they can potentially offset your wages or other ordinary income. That can be a significant advantage in the early years, when depreciation and furnishing costs are high.

Short-term rentals also tend to bring more expenses. Cleaning, supplies, platform fees, utilities, furnishings, and higher wear and tear are common, and you may need to track them carefully. Many cities and states also impose occupancy or lodging taxes on short-term stays, and some platforms collect these on your behalf while others leave it to you. Local registration, permits, or zoning restrictions may also apply, and some areas limit or ban short-term rentals altogether.

Rules vary significantly by country, state, and municipality, so if you're seriously considering this, it's worth talking with a CPA or tax professional who knows short-term rental rules in your area. They can help you model the after-tax difference between the two approaches for your specific situation.

Your symptoms need prompt medical attention, ideally today. Bleeding in the upper GI tract combined with severe upper abdominal pain, gas without passing it, inability to keep anything down, and violent vomiting can signal a blockage or serious injury to the stomach or small intestine. Please go to an emergency room now rather than waiting for a routine appointment, and tell them about your pelvic radiation in 2005 to 2007. If you vomit blood or material that looks like coffee grounds, pass black or tarry stools, feel faint or dizzy, or your pain becomes constant and severe, call 911.

Radiation given to the pelvis can cause long-term damage to nearby bowel, including scarring that narrows the intestine, chronic inflammation, and fragile blood vessels that bleed. Some people also develop ulcers, and the bowel can become partially or fully obstructed. Because your symptoms overlap with several conditions, the team will need to find the exact source before treating it. They will likely check your blood counts and iron levels, do imaging such as a CT scan, and perform an upper endoscopy, which lets them see the bleeding site and sometimes treat it directly, for example by cauterizing a vessel, placing clips, or dilating a narrowed area.

Treatment depends on what they find. Bleeding may be managed with acid-reducing medicines, sucralfate, endoscopic therapy, and blood transfusions if the loss is significant. Ongoing iron deficiency is often handled with intravenous iron, as you have already received. Radiation-related injury is sometimes treated with hyperbaric oxygen therapy, which can help tissue heal, though it is not right for everyone. A blockage or severe stricture may require hospitalization, bowel rest, or surgery. Once the acute problem is controlled, a dietitian can help you find foods that your bowel tolerates, and your oncologist or a gastroenterologist can coordinate long-term follow-up for radiation effects.

Please also avoid aspirin, ibuprofen, naproxen, and similar pain relievers unless a doctor approves them, since they can worsen bleeding. Bringing a list of your medications and a summary of your past treatment to the emergency room will help them act faster.

"Wikipedia:Citation needed" refers to the template and tag that Wikipedia editors use to flag a statement in an article that lacks a reliable source to support it. When someone adds the tag, it appears as a small superscript note, typically reading "[citation needed]" in bracketed text placed right after the questionable sentence or claim. Readers and other editors then know the information has not been verified by a citation and may need one before it can be trusted.

The tag serves several purposes. It signals to readers that a claim should be treated with some caution, it invites other editors to find a credible source that backs up the statement, and it helps maintain Wikipedia's standard that material should be verifiable. Wikipedia's policy on verifiability requires that information be attributable to reliable, published sources, so an unsourced claim is considered a weakness that should be addressed.

Editors add the tag to a wide range of content, from a single statistic or date to an entire paragraph of unsupported assertions. The tag is usually a prompt rather than a judgment that the claim is false. Often the information is accurate but simply has not yet been linked to a source. If an editor finds a suitable reference, they can add it and the tag is removed. If no source can be found after a reasonable period, the content may be deleted, since Wikipedia does not keep material that cannot be verified.

Because the tag is so common, it has also become a bit of a cultural touchstone. Many people encounter it while reading, and the phrase is sometimes used humorously online to point out weakly supported claims elsewhere on the internet.

Moving money from India to the United States can be done in a few different ways. One approach is a bank transfer, in which you send funds from your Indian bank account to an American one. This is usually carried out as a wire transfer, which can involve fees and may take several days to go through. Another approach is to use a money transfer company such as Western Union or MoneyGram. These providers generally let you send money either online or in person, and they often advertise competitive exchange rates and quick delivery. A third approach is an online payment platform like PayPal, which lets you send money straight to another person's account or pay for purchases online. Keep in mind that every one of these methods may charge fees, and the exchange rate can differ from one service to another. Before you send anything, it is wise to compare rates and fees so that you get the best possible deal.

In double-entry accounting, capital gains and losses get recorded as revenues or expenses, and which one depends on whether they're realized or unrealized. If you've actually sold the asset and got the cash (or whatever you received), the gain or loss is realized, so it goes on your income statement. Sell a stock at a profit and you record that profit as revenue. Sell it at a loss and that loss goes in as an expense. Unrealized stuff works differently. If you still own the asset, the gain or loss doesn't hit your income statement at all. Instead, the change in value shows up as a change in equity on your balance sheet. So if your stock goes up while you're still holding it, equity goes up; if it drops, equity goes down. Also, capital gains and losses are taxed differently from ordinary income, so you'll probably want to track them separately come tax time. A tax pro or your local tax rules can tell you exactly how to handle them where you live.

Applied science is the branch of science concerned with using scientific knowledge and methods to solve practical problems and create useful technologies. Where basic or pure science seeks to understand how the natural world works, often without a specific goal in mind, applied science starts with a concrete need or objective and draws on established theories and discoveries to meet it. Engineering, medicine, agronomy, and computer science are common examples, since each takes principles from physics, chemistry, biology, or mathematics and turns them into devices, treatments, crops, or software that people can use.

The work of applied science typically involves identifying a problem, researching what is already known, designing and testing solutions, and refining them based on results. A materials scientist developing a stronger, lighter alloy for aircraft, or a pharmacologist designing a drug to treat a specific disease, is practicing applied science. The distinction between basic and applied research is not always sharp, because discoveries made for purely theoretical reasons often later find practical uses, and practical problems can reveal new questions that advance fundamental understanding. Still, the defining feature of applied science is its orientation toward real-world application and its aim of improving health, safety, efficiency, or quality of life.

Mitral valve prolapse (MVP) is a widespread condition in which one of the heart's valves fails to shut completely. Pregnancy can sometimes aggravate MVP symptoms because of the rise in blood volume and shifts in hormone levels. Any questions about your MVP should be raised with your obstetrician or primary care doctor. If you notice more frequent palpitations or extra heartbeats while pregnant, you should inform your healthcare provider. Your provider might suggest changes to your daily habits or prescribe medication to keep your symptoms under control. For instance, they could advise you to steer clear of caffeine, alcohol, and tobacco, since these can occasionally set off palpitations. They might also encourage relaxation methods like deep breathing or meditation to lower stress and relieve symptoms. Medication may occasionally be needed to treat MVP symptoms, but many drugs are unsafe during pregnancy, so you should go over your options with your healthcare provider. They can determine the most suitable treatment plan for you, taking into account your individual needs and how far along your pregnancy is. Ultimately, staying in close contact with your healthcare provider is essential for managing your MVP and related symptoms throughout pregnancy, as they can help you make the best choices for your health and your baby's.

Creditworthiness data is among the most sensitive personal information people have, because it determines access to loans, housing, insurance, and sometimes employment. Most people want it shared as narrowly as possible: with lenders they're actively applying to, for purposes they've agreed to, and not sold or repurposed for marketing or profiling without clear consent.

If you're in the United States, the Fair Credit Reporting Act gives you several concrete controls. You can get a free credit report from each of the three major bureaus (Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion) at AnnualCreditReport.com. You can place a free credit freeze with each bureau, which blocks most new creditors from accessing your file unless you temporarily lift it. You can also opt out of prescreened credit and insurance offers, which are the preapproved mailers and marketing lists, either at optoutprescreen.com or by phone. A fraud alert is a lighter option that requires creditors to take extra verification steps but doesn't block access.

If you're in the European Union or UK, the GDPR gives you rights to access your data, correct errors, object to certain processing, and request erasure in some circumstances. You can ask credit reference agencies such as Experian UK, Equifax UK, or CRIF for a copy of your file and ask them to explain how it's used. In other places, such as Canada, Australia, or Brazil, there are similar consumer reporting laws with access and correction rights, though the details differ.

Beyond legal rights, it helps to decide what you're comfortable with in practice. You might be fine with lenders checking your score during an application but object to data brokers selling a derived "risk score" to marketers. You might want alerts whenever your file is pulled, or you might want to limit which apps and fintech services can connect to your bank or credit data through open banking permissions. Reviewing those connections periodically and revoking ones you no longer use is one of the more effective steps.

Pain that shows up when you laugh is usually tied to the sudden, forceful changes in breathing and chest pressure that laughing creates, so the most likely explanations involve your airways, the lining of your lungs, or the muscles and cartilage of your chest wall. Given that you've had a dry cough for a few days, the most common culprit would be irritated or inflamed airways from a mild viral infection or early bronchitis. When the airways are inflamed, the deep, rapid exhalations of laughing can trigger a tight, squeezing sensation, and sometimes a bit of bronchospasm, which is a temporary narrowing of the airways similar to what happens in asthma. Smoking, even occasionally, and alcohol can both make the airways more reactive, so a weekend of drinks and cigarettes on top of a cough could plausibly set this off.

Another frequent cause is strain of the chest wall. Coughing over several days can tire or slightly strain the muscles between your ribs, or inflame the cartilage where the ribs meet the breastbone, a condition called costochondritis. That kind of pain often feels worse with laughing, coughing, twisting, or pressing on the sore spot, and it tends to be reproducible if you push on the area. Pleurisy, an inflammation of the lining around the lungs that can follow a viral illness, is also possible, though it usually feels sharp or stabbing with deep breaths rather than like pressure.

There are a few less common but more serious possibilities worth keeping in mind. A collapsed lung, or pneumothorax, can come on suddenly and is more likely in smokers and in tall, thin young people; it typically causes sharp pain on one side and shortness of breath. And because you describe the pain as pressure or tightening, it's important not to completely dismiss the heart, since laughing is a mild exertion and cardiac pain is classically described exactly that way, especially if you have risk factors like high blood pressure, high cholesterol, diabetes, or family history.

You should seek emergency care right away if the pressure comes on with exertion or at rest and doesn't go away, spreads to your arm, jaw, neck, or back, or comes with shortness of breath, sweating, nausea, lightheadedness, a racing or irregular heartbeat, or coughing up blood. If none of that is happening and the pain only appears when you laugh or cough, it's reasonable to rest, avoid cigarettes and heavy drinking while you recover, stay hydrated, and see a doctor in the next few days, sooner if the cough worsens, you develop a fever, or the pain persists beyond a week. A doctor can listen to your lungs, and if needed check a chest X-ray or an ECG, which can quickly sort out which of these explanations fits.

The short answer is that the fund's name describes its investment strategy, not a promise that its own distributions will rise every year. Vanguard Dividend Growth Fund (VDIGX), managed by Wellington Management, looks for companies with the financial strength and commitment to raise their dividends over time. Those companies often have fairly modest current yields, so the fund's payout is small relative to its share price, and the per-share amount you see on Yahoo Finance can look flat or bumpy rather than steadily climbing.

Several factors produce that pattern. The manager regularly buys and sells holdings, and if a higher-yielding stock is sold and replaced with a lower-yielding but faster-growing company, the fund's total income per share can stall or drop even though every company in the portfolio is raising its own dividend. The fund also passes through only what is left after its expenses, and the timing of when underlying companies pay relative to the fund's semiannual distribution dates can shift income between periods, making individual payments look uneven. Over a long horizon the fund's income has generally trended upward, but not in a smooth year-over-year line.

Yahoo Finance's presentation can make this worse. Its dividend history and yield figures for mutual funds are sometimes incomplete or inconsistent, occasionally mixing in or omitting capital gains distributions, or showing a trailing yield that falls simply because the share price rose. A rising share price with a modestly rising payout produces a flat or declining yield percentage, which can look like a lack of dividend growth when it isn't.

If you want a clearer picture, Vanguard's own website lists the fund's full distribution history, separating income dividends from capital gains. Comparing total income dividends per share over five or ten year spans, rather than looking at individual payments or the current yield, gives a better sense of whether the strategy is delivering the growth its name implies.

Honestly, better focus can make a real difference when you're deciding things, so here's what tends to help. Find a quiet spot to work or study, and turn off your phone and anything else that'll pull you away. Set a specific goal for each session so you know what you're aiming for. A timer is handy for breaking work into smaller chunks, which keeps you sharp and stops you from burning out. Take breaks regularly so your brain gets a chance to rest. Deep breathing or meditation can help you stay present. Sleep and exercise matter more than people think for concentration, and multitasking is a trap, since it makes it harder to focus on anything. And don't beat yourself up when you zone out. It happens to everyone. If you're stuck, step away for a bit and come back fresh.

As for making bad calls, it helps to look at how you're actually deciding. Ask yourself what problem you're really trying to solve, what your options are, and what could realistically happen with each one. Check your gut too, and think about what you care about most in the situation. Slowing down enough to ask those questions usually leads to better choices.

There are a number of possible explanations for a lump beneath the armpit. One is a swollen lymph node, a small, round, bean-shaped part of the immune system. These nodes tend to enlarge when the body responds to an infection, inflammation, or another kind of injury. Another option is a cyst, a sealed sac that holds fluid, pus, or other matter. Cysts can develop almost anywhere on the body and are typically harmless rather than cancerous. They may form for various reasons, such as an infection, inflammation, or a blocked gland or duct. The lump could also be a hematoma, meaning blood that has leaked out of a damaged vessel and collected in the tissue. Hematomas often follow trauma, such as a blow to the area, or a surgical procedure. Because the cause is not obvious, a healthcare provider should examine the lump to identify it and recommend treatment if needed. The provider will probably conduct a physical exam, ask about your medical history and any recent injuries or infections, and might order further tests, such as blood work or imaging, to pinpoint the cause.

Cold reading is a method some individuals use to create the impression that they possess psychic powers or can perceive what others are thinking. Such performers rely on vague inquiries and remarks that might fit a great many people, then progressively sharpen their guesses according to how the listener reacts. Consider a cold reader who opens with a general statement such as "I sense you have gone through a lot of change lately," a claim that could describe almost anyone. If the listener nods or confirms it, the reader may move on to a narrower assertion, perhaps "I get the feeling you have recently relocated or taken on a new job." Should the listener agree once more, the reader might go further still, suggesting "I feel you are struggling to settle into your new surroundings and are a little overwhelmed." This approach can be remarkably persuasive, since it is difficult to demonstrate that the performer lacks psychic ability, and people frequently wish to believe that such gifts exist. Nevertheless, it is essential to recognize that cold reading is merely a trick and not a genuine psychic skill.

Money-counting devices rely on sensors to notice when a banknote enters the feed and to determine where it sits. Once a note is detected, a mechanism such as rollers or suction pulls it in and carries it along the internal path. These machines count quickly because they never need to deliberate; they simply repeat a fixed sequence of steps for each note that passes through. An apt comparison is a factory conveyor belt, which carries goods down a predetermined route while workers beside it pick items off to process them. A currency counter operates on the same principle, except that the items it handles and tallies are bills rather than manufactured products.

Trying to sprint across water at the speed of sound would fail, since sound travels too slowly for that to work. Sound moves at roughly 343 meters per second, which is about 767 miles per hour, a pace far below what most people can run. Even at that speed, a person would still sink, because water is a fluid that cannot bear the weight of a heavy body. Attempting to run on water would simply leave you submerged and soaked!

A boat or raft, on the other hand, could travel across the water at the speed of sound given a powerful enough engine. Its hull rests on the water's surface, and the engine drives it forward. So if your goal is to move quickly over water, a boat or raft is the better choice.

I can hear that this is really upsetting for you, and feeling embarrassed when people comment on your voice is hard. Many boys have higher or lighter voices, especially before puberty finishes, and that doesn't mean anything is wrong with you or that you are not a boy.

Voice changes during puberty, usually between about 12 and 16 years old. The larynx (voice box) grows, the vocal cords get longer and thicker, and the voice drops over several months. Some boys go through this later than their friends, and their voices stay higher for a while. Genetics play a big role too, so if your father or other male relatives had a late voice change, yours may follow the same timing. Hormones such as testosterone drive this change, and a doctor can check them with a simple blood test if you are worried about delayed puberty.

There is no safe medicine that will deepen your voice on purpose. Some people try to force a lower voice by straining it, and that can damage the vocal cords, so please avoid it. What you can do is talk to a parent or another trusted adult, and ask a doctor, such as a pediatrician or an endocrinologist, to check whether everything is developing normally. If you want, a speech therapist or voice coach can teach you techniques to project your voice more strongly and speak with a lower, steadier tone.

Also remember that people's voices vary a lot, and comments from others don't define who you are. If people tease you, telling a trusted adult can help. You are a boy, and your voice will likely continue to change as you grow.

A Tensor Processing Unit (TPU) is a purpose-built accelerator created to boost the speed of machine learning workloads. Because it handles matrix computations with high efficiency, it is particularly suitable for accelerating jobs such as training deep neural networks. TPUs are built to operate alongside Google's TensorFlow machine learning framework. They support a range of machine learning activities, including training deep neural networks, generating predictions from trained models, and carrying out other machine learning-related operations. TPUs come in several forms: standalone units intended for data centers and cloud environments, and compact units suited to mobile devices and other embedded systems. They are highly efficient and can deliver substantial performance gains over conventional CPUs and GPUs when running machine learning workloads.

A league is a measure of distance, most often applied to the space between two locations at sea. It corresponds to roughly 3 nautical miles, or about 3.45 statute miles. More broadly, the word can also describe a fleet of vessels traveling in company, or an alliance of nations or organizations that cooperate in some fashion.

In most cases, it makes sense to build an emergency fund before you put money toward your mortgage or begin saving for retirement. This fund is a savings account set aside for unplanned costs like a medical bill, a car repair, or losing your job. With one in place, you are less likely to fall into debt or need to borrow when a financial crisis hits. After your emergency fund is established, you can decide whether to pay down your mortgage or start saving for retirement, based on your own circumstances and goals. For instance, if your mortgage carries a high interest rate, it may be wise to pay it off as fast as you can in order to cut down on interest costs. If the rate is low, however, putting your money toward retirement savings may be the better choice. In the end, the right approach depends on your particular finances and objectives. It helps to take the time to review your priorities and draw up a budget that reflects them. If you're unsure how to proceed, consider getting advice from a financial professional.

Voir dire is the name for jury selection, the process of picking the people who will sit on a jury for a particular trial. The point is to end up with a fair jury, so anyone who might be biased or who couldn't judge the case fairly based on the evidence gets dropped. A jury is supposed to be ordinary folks who hear what's presented in court and decide based on that. It matters because it's a big part of keeping the system fair. Lawyers and prosecutors do try to steer the outcome during voir dire, but it's not always that way. Sometimes jurors are picked more or less at random from an eligible pool the court has put together. Other times it's more hands-on, with attorneys asking questions to figure out whether a given person is a good fit. Either way, the goal is the same: a jury that's fair and unbiased, and a justice system that's as fair as it can realistically be.

The wake-sleep algorithm is an unsupervised learning method for training generative models, particularly the Helmholtz machine, which was introduced by Peter Dayan, Geoffrey Hinton, Radford Neal, and Richard Zemel in the mid-1990s. Its central goal is to learn a model of the data and, at the same time, an approximate way of inferring the hidden causes behind each observation, without needing any labeled examples.

The model has two sets of connections. A recognition model, sometimes called the bottom-up or inference network, maps observed data to a distribution over hidden variables. A generative model works in the opposite direction, taking hidden variables and producing a distribution over the data. The difficulty is that for many useful models, computing the exact posterior over hidden causes given the data is intractable, so the recognition network is trained to approximate it.

The algorithm alternates between two phases. In the wake phase, the system takes real data from the environment, uses the recognition network to infer hidden states, and then adjusts the generative weights so that the model becomes better at reconstructing the data from those inferred states. In the sleep phase, the system runs the generative model on its own to produce fantasy samples of both hidden states and data, which gives it known ground truth. It then adjusts the recognition weights so that the recognition network can better recover the hidden states that generated those fantasy samples.

The appeal of this scheme is that each phase uses simple local learning rules and avoids computing gradients through the full model, which made it feasible in the 1990s. Its main drawbacks are that it does not optimize a single consistent objective, so convergence is not guaranteed, and the recognition network may be biased because it is trained on samples from the generative model rather than from the true posterior. These limitations were later addressed by variational autoencoders, which optimize a single evidence lower bound using the reparameterization trick, and by other methods such as reweighted wake-sleep.

Sulfas are medications built around sulfonamide, a synthetic compound that fights bacteria. Doctors use them against many kinds of infection, particularly those of bacterial origin. They are commonly given for infections of the urinary tract, the respiratory tract, and the skin, and for certain sexually transmitted infections. Patients can take them as tablets, capsules, or liquids. Side effects of sulfas may include nausea, vomiting, and allergic reactions. Because they can also interact with other drugs, you should tell your doctor about every medication you take before you begin a sulfa. Thanks to the arrival of newer and more effective antibiotics, sulfonamides, sulfas among them, are not used as widely as they once were. Even so, a doctor may still prescribe them in some circumstances, for example when other antibiotics fail to work or when the infection is caused by bacteria resistant to other antibiotics.

The Italian ocean liner SS Andrea Doria sank on the morning of July 26, 1956. The previous night, July 25, it collided with the Swedish liner MS Stockholm in heavy fog off the coast of Nantucket, Massachusetts, while bound for New York. The ship listed badly after the collision and finally capsized and sank about eleven hours later, at roughly 10:09 a.m. Thanks to a large rescue effort involving several ships, including the Île de France, more than 1,600 people were saved, though 46 people aboard the Andrea Doria and 5 aboard the Stockholm died. The wreck now lies in about 240 feet of water and has become a well-known, though dangerous, site for deep-sea divers.

These dreams sound frightening and exhausting, and waking up crying and unable to fall back asleep would wear anyone down. Dreams often reflect emotional states rather than predict anything. Recurring nightmares are common with depression, anxiety, grief, stress, or past trauma, and they can feed a cycle: anxiety disturbs sleep, poor sleep intensifies mood problems, and the dreams keep returning. Checking yourself for injuries after waking is also a known response when a dream feels that real. Your body reacts to the fear as if it were happening.

The goodbye letters are the part I most want to ask about. Do you ever feel that your family would be better off without you, or that you don't want to keep living? In the US you can call or text 988, and if you're somewhere else, findahelpline.com lists free services by country. If you feel you might act on these thoughts, call your local emergency number or go to the nearest emergency room.

Whatever the answer, it's worth telling a doctor or therapist about the nightmares and the trouble sleeping afterward. Nightmares are very treatable. Imagery rehearsal therapy, for example, has a good track record for recurring nightmares, and treating depression or anxiety often calms the dreams too.

Individuals and organizations have a number of options for putting other people's money to work in investments or business ventures. Some common examples follow.

Partnership: In a partnership, two or more people join forces to run a business and divide its gains and losses. Every partner supplies money, property, labor, or expertise, and the partnership agreement determines how profits and losses are split.

Limited liability company (LLC): An LLC is a business structure that pairs the liability protection of a corporation with the tax advantages of a partnership. Members put money or property into the company and divide profits and losses as set out in the operating agreement.

Joint venture: A joint venture is an arrangement in which two or more individuals or organizations collaborate on a particular project or business activity. Each party provides money, property, or other assets, and the joint venture agreement governs how profits and losses are shared.

Crowdfunding: Crowdfunding raises money for a project or business by gathering small contributions from many people, usually via an online platform. In return for contributing, backers generally receive either a reward or an equity stake in the project.

Angel investing: An angel investor is a person who offers financial support to a startup or small business. In return, the angel usually gets an ownership share in the company.

Venture capital: Venture capital is financing that investors supply to startups and small businesses with strong growth prospects. Venture capital firms generally invest substantial amounts and receive ownership equity in the companies they back.

Public offerings: A public offering involves selling securities to the general public. Companies can raise funds this way by offering stocks or bonds to investors.

A SATA power connector is the standardized plug used to deliver electrical power from a computer's power supply unit to storage devices and some other internal components. It was introduced alongside the Serial ATA (SATA) data interface in the early 2000s as a replacement for the older four-pin Molex connector that had powered hard drives and optical drives for decades. Although it was designed with SATA drives in mind, it has since become a general-purpose internal power connector used for many kinds of hardware.

Physically, the SATA power connector is a thin, flat, L-shaped plug with 15 pins. It is noticeably wider than the SATA data connector, which has only 7 pins, and the two sit side by side on the back of a typical hard drive or SSD. The L-shape acts as a key so the plug can only be inserted one way. Unlike the old Molex plug, which required a fair amount of force and often had to be wiggled loose, the SATA power connector slides on and off fairly easily, though its plastic tab can be fragile if bent sideways.

The connector supplies three voltages: 3.3 volts, 5 volts, and 12 volts. Each voltage is carried on three pins, and the remaining pins are mostly ground connections, with one pin in some versions reserved for features like staggered spin-up or power disable. Using multiple pins per voltage spreads the current so that each individual contact carries less load. Historically, 12 volts powered the spinning motors in hard drives, 5 volts ran the drive's electronics, and 3.3 volts was included for future low-power devices, although in practice many drives never used the 3.3-volt line. Some pins are also slightly longer than others, which allows the ground and pre-charge contacts to connect first, making the connector suitable for hot-plugging, meaning a drive can be connected or disconnected while the system is running if the controller and operating system support it.

Today SATA power connectors are found on cables coming from virtually every desktop power supply, usually several on a single cable in a daisy-chain arrangement. Besides 2.5-inch and 3.5-inch hard drives and SSDs, they commonly power optical drives, case fan hubs, RGB lighting controllers, PCIe riser boards, and various expansion cards. A typical connector is rated for roughly 4.5 amps per voltage rail, so it is not intended for very high-power loads, and users are generally advised to avoid cheap adapters, especially Molex-to-SATA converters with molded plastic, because poorly made ones have been known to short and cause fires.

It is worth noting that newer storage devices such as M.2 NVMe SSDs do not use a SATA power connector at all, since they draw power directly from the motherboard slot they are installed in. Even so, the SATA power connector remains one of the most common and important cables inside a modern PC.

The patient should consult a healthcare provider so that the reason behind their shortness of breath, anxiety, and headache can be identified and the right treatment chosen. The provider will probably perform a physical exam and look over the patient's medical history along with any test results, including the TMT (stress test) findings. If the TMT comes back positive even though the patient has no history of high blood pressure, diabetes, or similar conditions, the provider may order additional testing to find out why the result was positive. Such testing might involve imaging like an echocardiogram or cardiac MRI, or other assessments of how well the heart and blood vessels are working. The treatment plan will hinge on what is causing the symptoms. When the TMT is positive and an underlying heart or vascular problem is present, the provider may suggest medications or lifestyle adjustments to control it. For anxiety, the provider might propose therapy or medication. For headaches, they could recommend over-the-counter or prescription pain relief, or offer ways to manage stress or other possible triggers. The patient should stick to the provider's recommendations and seek medical care promptly if symptoms get worse or if any new concerns arise.

Ehud Shapiro is a computer scientist and professor at the Weizmann Institute of Science in Rehovot, Israel. His work centers on theoretical computer science and artificial intelligence. He has contributed to logic, verification, and automated reasoning. He has also taken part in building practical automated reasoning tools, including the automatic theorem prover EQP. Shapiro is a member of the Israeli Academy of Sciences and Humanities, and his work has earned several honors, among them the ACM SIGPLAN Robin Milner Young Researcher Award and the Israel Prize in Computer Science.

The exponential moving average, or EMA, is a technical analysis tool that smooths price movements so trends are easier to see. To calculate it, a weighting factor is applied to the current period's price and combined with the EMA from the prior period.

Traders commonly use the EMA to judge how strong a stock's resistance level is. Resistance is a price at which the stock has historically had trouble moving higher. How strong that level is can be measured by how many times the stock has attempted to climb past it and been turned back.

One approach is to plot the EMA on a stock chart and watch how the price behaves as it nears resistance. If the EMA is rising and the price keeps rebounding off the resistance level, that may signal strong resistance. Conversely, if the EMA is sloping downward and the price manages to push through the level, the resistance may be weaker.

Keep in mind that the EMA is only one of many indicators that can help assess resistance, and relying on it alone is unwise. It is generally wise to combine several indicators and also carry out fundamental analysis, which gives a fuller picture of a stock's trend and its possible future direction.

James Cameron directed "The Terminator," a science fiction film released in 1984. Arnold Schwarzenegger plays the title character, a cyborg assassin dispatched through time from a future ruined by catastrophe. Its target is Sarah Connor, portrayed by Linda Hamilton, a woman carrying a child who will one day lead humanity's resistance against the machines. As the Terminator hunts Sarah, Kyle Reese, a soldier who has also come from the future and is played by Michael Biehn, works to shield her and halt the cyborg. The movie achieved both box office and critical triumph, and it gave rise to a franchise encompassing sequels, television series, and merchandise.

Computational science is basically the field where people use computers and algorithms to simulate, analyze, and figure out complicated systems. Researchers build computational models and simulations to tackle problems in science, engineering, and plenty of other areas. It pulls from a bunch of fields, like math, computer science, physics, chemistry, biology, and engineering, so it can be applied to all kinds of problems. You can use it to study how fluids move, how materials are put together, how biological systems evolve, how economies behave, and a lot more. Lately it's become a bigger deal because many problems have gotten too large and messy for traditional analytical methods to handle. It lets researchers run experiments and dig into data in ways that would be impractical or flat-out impossible otherwise. It's also opened the door to studying things that used to be too hard to crack, like large-scale biological systems or financial markets.

There are a bunch of financial data points analysts look at when they're sizing up a stock and deciding whether to recommend it. The big ones tend to be these.

Earnings come first for most of them. They'll check earnings per share and compare it against the company's own history and its industry, and they'll look at revenue, operating income, and net income to see how healthy the business really is. Valuation is next. Analysts lean on ratios like the price-to-earnings and price-to-book ratios to figure out whether a stock looks cheap or expensive next to its peers.

If you're buying for income, dividends matter a lot. Analysts will look at the dividend yield, the payout ratio, and how consistently the company has paid out over time. Then there are the financial statements themselves: the balance sheet, income statement, and cash flow statement, which together show where the company stands, how profitable it is, and whether it can cover its bills.

Analysts also zoom out to the bigger picture, including the economy, industry trends, and the broader market, to gauge risks and opportunities. In the end they usually blend all of this with softer stuff like competitive advantage, the management team, and growth prospects. They'll also think about how risky the stock is, how bad things could get, and whether it even fits into your portfolio.

Imagine you have a piggy bank with ten coins in it. Every time you play a game, you have to pay a little coin, and the game never gives you more coins than you put in. So no matter how clever your game is, you can't end up with more coins than you started with, and because the game always takes a few coins for itself, you'll actually end up with fewer. That's basically what nature does with energy. You can move energy around, change it from one kind to another, and pass it from one toy to another, but you can't make new energy from nothing. That's the first rule, and it means a machine can't give you more work than the energy you put in.

Now, some people say, "Fine, then my machine doesn't need to make extra energy. It just needs to keep going forever with what it already has." That's where the second rule comes in. Think of a ball rolling across the floor. It slows down and stops, because it rubs against the floor and the air, and a little of its pushing energy turns into tiny bits of warmth that spread out into the room. Once that warmth is spread out everywhere, you can't gather it up and make the ball roll again. Every real machine has rubbing, bending, heating, and air pushing, and each one leaks a little energy into warmth that is lost for good. So a machine that only gives back what it started with is already losing a bit each turn, and eventually it runs out and stops.

As for why people don't believe you, there's a reason that's worth knowing for your own sanity. Their machines usually look as if they should work, because the trick is hidden somewhere in the drawing. Maybe the weights on one side look farther from the middle, or a magnet seems to pull a little more in one place. Spotting the hidden catch is like finding the mistake in a magic trick, and people who are in love with their idea often don't want to see it. So instead of explaining the rules, try asking them to follow the energy: "Where does the energy come from at this step, and where does it go?" Or ask them to draw a box around the whole machine and count what goes in and what comes out. Also, if their device really did work, it would be the biggest discovery in history, and every careful test of it so far has failed. That helps them see that the rule isn't just your opinion, it's what nature has done every single time anyone has checked.

There are a number of possible explanations for a painless lump in the right arm close to the shoulder. Among the most frequent are the following. A lipoma is a noncancerous growth composed of fat cells; it usually feels soft, causes no pain, and can be moved under the skin. A cyst is a sac-like pocket that may hold fluid, pus, or other material. Cysts can form virtually anywhere on the body and are generally painless. A ganglion cyst is a fluid-filled sac most often found on the wrist, hand, or foot, though it can also develop elsewhere, including the arm. These cysts are typically painless and can be shifted around. Bursitis refers to swelling of the bursae, which are small fluid-filled sacs that cushion and protect the joints. It can produce a lump and discomfort around the shoulder. If a lump in your arm lasts or causes concern, it is worth consulting a doctor, who can identify the cause and suggest suitable treatment.

A blood clot could be responsible for swelling in the ankle and foot along with a lump in the groin. If you think a clot might be present, you should get medical help as quickly as you can, since clots can be dangerous and may lead to serious complications when they go untreated. Swelling in the ankle and foot can also come from other sources, including inflammation, an injury, or a buildup of fluid, so a medical professional should examine it to pinpoint the cause and recommend suitable treatment. The swelling and the groin lump might also be connected to the procedure your mom underwent to have stents put in. Be sure to follow the directions given by her healthcare team, and let them know about any new or unusual symptoms. They can evaluate her condition and give her the care she needs.

Temporal difference, usually called TD learning, is a family of methods in reinforcement learning for estimating how good it is to be in a particular situation, without waiting until the end of an episode to find out how things turned out. The core idea is that an agent can learn from the difference between successive predictions over time. Instead of comparing a prediction to a final, true outcome, it compares a prediction made now with a slightly better-informed prediction made one step later, and nudges the earlier estimate toward the later one.

To make this concrete, imagine an agent that keeps a value estimate V(s) for each state s, representing the total future reward it expects to collect starting from that state. Suppose it is in state s, takes an action, receives an immediate reward r, and lands in a new state s'. At that moment it has a new, partly grounded guess for the value of s: the reward it just got plus the discounted value it currently believes s' has, written as r + γV(s'), where γ is a discount factor between 0 and 1 that makes future rewards count somewhat less than immediate ones. The gap between this new guess and the old estimate, δ = r + γV(s') − V(s), is called the TD error. The agent then updates its estimate with V(s) ← V(s) + αδ, where α is a small learning rate. If things turned out better than expected, the TD error is positive and the value of s goes up; if worse, it goes down.

This approach sits between two older ideas. Like Monte Carlo methods, TD learning learns directly from raw experience and does not need a model of how the environment works. Like dynamic programming, it uses bootstrapping, meaning it updates estimates partly on the basis of other estimates rather than waiting for complete returns. This combination lets it learn online, step by step, and handle tasks that never terminate or have very long episodes. It also tends to have lower variance than Monte Carlo methods, though the bootstrapping introduces some bias, especially early on when the estimates it relies on are still poor.

The simplest version described above is called TD(0) because it looks only one step ahead. A generalization called TD(λ) blends information from many future steps using a parameter λ, smoothly interpolating between one-step TD at λ equals 0 and Monte Carlo at λ equals 1, often implemented with a mechanism called eligibility traces that assigns credit to recently visited states. TD ideas also underpin well-known control algorithms such as Q-learning and SARSA, which learn values of state-action pairs rather than just states, and they are central to deep reinforcement learning systems like DQN.

The concept was developed largely by Richard Sutton in the 1980s, building on earlier work, and became famous through Gerald Tesauro's TD-Gammon, a backgammon program that reached expert level by playing against itself. Interestingly, TD learning also has a notable connection to neuroscience: the firing patterns of dopamine neurons in the brain closely resemble a TD error signal, spiking when rewards are better than predicted and dipping when they are worse, which suggests that biological learning may use a similar principle of learning from prediction errors over time.

Puce is a brownish-purple color, often described as a dusky, muted pinkish-purple or a grayish reddish-brown. Its exact shade varies depending on the source, which is part of why people find it confusing. Some interpretations lean toward a pale pinkish-mauve, while others are darker and closer to a deep purplish-brown. A commonly cited web version is the hex code #CC8899, which appears as a soft, dusty pink-mauve.

The name comes from the French word "puce," meaning "flea." The color became fashionable in France in the late 18th century, and a popular story holds that Marie Antoinette wore a gown of this shade and King Louis XVI remarked that it was the color of a flea. The idea is that it resembles the color of a flea, or according to some accounts, the color of the bloodstains fleas left behind on linens.

Because the word sounds a bit like "puke," many English speakers assume it's a sickly greenish-yellow, but that is a common misconception. Puce is firmly in the purple, pink, and brown family.

Multilinear subspace learning (MSL) is a machine learning approach that seeks low-dimensional representations of high-dimensional data lying in a multilinear subspace, meaning a space that can be built from the tensor product of several linear subspaces. Broadly, MSL tries to find a compact description of a high-dimensional data set that preserves its underlying structure. Such a description is useful for tasks like dimensionality reduction, data compression, and data visualization. A common strategy relies on tensor decomposition methods, for example the canonical polyadic decomposition (CPD) or the Tucker decomposition, which break the data tensor into a combination of low-dimensional subspace components. Those components can then be used to rebuild the original tensor while keeping much of its structure and information. Other MSL techniques include multilinear principal component analysis (MPCA) and multilinear independent component analysis (MICA), which extend conventional linear methods for dimensionality reduction and data analysis. They look for a set of low-dimensional subspaces that represent the structure of the data in a multilinear way. In sum, MSL is a strong tool for analyzing and making sense of high-dimensional data sets, and it can be used in many areas, such as image and video processing, natural language processing, and social network analysis.

Yes, the prescription your husband received is standard and appropriate. Doxycycline 100 mg twice daily is the usual adult dose for Lyme disease, and his age doesn't require a higher amount. As for length, current guidelines from the Infectious Diseases Society of America recommend about 10 to 14 days for the typical early form of Lyme disease (the expanding "bull's-eye" rash and flu-like symptoms). Longer courses, around 14 to 21 days, are used for some other presentations, and about 28 days for Lyme arthritis. Three weeks is therefore at the generous end for early disease. Studies have not shown that courses longer than this improve outcomes, and they do increase side effects. If his doctor knows which stage or symptoms he has, the 21-day plan fits within accepted practice.

How he takes the medication matters a lot. He should swallow each capsule with a full glass of water and stay upright, sitting or standing, for at least 30 minutes afterward. Doxycycline can cause painful irritation or ulcers in the esophagus if it lodges there, especially when taken right before bed. Taking it with food is fine and reduces nausea. However, dairy products, calcium, antacids, iron, magnesium, and zinc supplements, including many multivitamins, bind to doxycycline and reduce absorption, so he should keep those at least two to three hours away from each dose. Doxycycline also makes skin much more prone to sunburn, so sunscreen, a hat, and long sleeves are wise while he's on it.

The probiotic is reasonable and may help prevent antibiotic-associated diarrhea. Spacing it a couple of hours from the doxycycline doses makes sense. Turmeric is generally safe, but it has mild blood-thinning effects and can occasionally upset the stomach, so mention it to his doctor or pharmacist. It isn't a treatment for Lyme disease itself, so the antibiotic is what's doing the real work.

Some people feel a bit worse in the first day or two of treatment, with fever, chills, or aches, which is usually a temporary reaction to the bacteria dying off. Fatigue, mild aches, or brain fog can also linger for weeks or even a few months after treatment is finished. This usually improves on its own and doesn't by itself mean the infection persists or needs more antibiotics.

He should contact his doctor promptly if he develops drooping on one side of the face, a racing, irregular, or very slow heartbeat, fainting or chest discomfort, a severe headache with a stiff neck, new swollen joints, a rash or hives suggesting an allergy, or frequent watery diarrhea, especially if it is severe or bloody. Otherwise, completing the full course as prescribed and following up with his doctor if symptoms don't improve is the best plan.

Finally, avoid posting your email address publicly in health forums, since it can attract spam.

I'm sorry you're dealing with this. Waking up aching all over and struggling through the day is exhausting in itself, and it's frustrating when blood tests come back normal and you still feel unwell. Normal bloods rule out some causes, but they don't explain everything, so it's reasonable to keep looking.

Widespread aching, tiredness and tenderness that persists for weeks or months can come from several sources. Sleep is a common one. Even if you think you sleep enough, poor sleep quality from snoring or sleep apnea, irregular hours, stress, or alcohol can leave you unrefreshed. Stress and anxiety themselves often cause muscle tension and aches, and can disrupt sleep in ways you may not notice. Physical factors matter too: a sudden increase in activity, a physically demanding job, or a period of inactivity can all leave muscles sore and fatigued. Viral illnesses, including ones you may have had weeks earlier, sometimes leave lingering fatigue and muscle pain. Conditions such as fibromyalgia, chronic fatigue syndrome, an underactive thyroid (which a standard blood test would usually detect, though some people need additional tests), vitamin D deficiency (which is sometimes not included in routine bloods), or inflammatory conditions like rheumatic disorders can also cause this pattern, and some of them need specialist assessment.

Since your bloods were normal, I'd suggest going back to your GP and describing the symptoms in detail: when they started, whether they're worse in the morning, whether you have joint swelling, rashes, fevers, low mood, changes in appetite or weight, snoring, or any change in your sleep. Ask whether they would check vitamin D, a fuller thyroid panel, inflammatory markers, or whether a sleep assessment would be useful. It's also worth telling them if you feel low or anxious, as that's relevant too.

In the meantime, it may help to keep a simple diary of sleep, activity, stress and symptoms for a couple of weeks, since patterns often show up that help a doctor pin things down. Gentle daily movement, a consistent sleep schedule, and cutting back on alcohol can also help some people.

If you develop fever, significant swelling of joints, unexplained weight loss, chest pain, shortness of breath, or weakness in your limbs, seek medical attention promptly rather than waiting for your next appointment.

Imagine you own a big toy store, and the front door of your store is the only way people can get to the toys. If you build that door yourself, you get to decide what people see first when they walk in, which signs they read, and which aisles they're nudged toward. If someone else builds the door, they get to make all those choices instead. A web browser is that front door to the internet, and Microsoft would much rather own the door than let Google own it.

The biggest reason ties back to the Bing point you already understand. A browser picks the default search engine, so when Edge ships with Bing, lots of people search with Bing simply because it was already there. Chrome naturally pushes Google search, so every person using Chrome is a person Microsoft probably won't earn ad money from. Owning the browser is the most reliable way to keep people searching on Bing. It's like a lemonade stand whose cups only fit its own straws.

The second reason is information. Whoever makes your browser can learn a lot about what kinds of things people do online, what they shop for, and what they click on, even if it's in a general, anonymized way. That knowledge helps a company improve its products and sell better-targeted ads. Microsoft would rather that knowledge flow to Microsoft than to Google.

The third reason is that Edge is a shelf where Microsoft can display its other stuff. Inside Edge, Microsoft can promote its Copilot AI assistant, its shopping and coupon features, its news feed (which shows ads), Microsoft 365, OneDrive, and its rewards program. Every one of those either makes money directly or keeps you inside Microsoft's world, where you're more likely to keep paying for Microsoft things.

The fourth reason is control and competition. If almost everyone uses Chrome, Google gets a huge say in how the web works, which features websites build for, and which services feel "normal." That gives a rival a lot of power over Microsoft's own customers on Microsoft's own operating system. Businesses matter here too: companies that run Windows computers often like Edge because it plugs neatly into Microsoft's security and management tools, which helps Microsoft sell those bigger business packages.

So in kid terms: the browser is the doorway, the doorway decides where you go first, and wherever you go first is where somebody makes money. Microsoft wants to be the one standing at the door instead of Google.

Your mouth and your cut feel different things because they have different kinds of skin and different kinds of nerves. The inside of your mouth is covered in a soft, wet lining that is built to handle food, drinks, and hot or cold stuff, so the nerves there are pretty tough and used to a lot of different tastes. A cut, on the other hand, is an open spot where the protective outer layer of skin is gone, so the sensitive nerves underneath are exposed. Alcohol touching those exposed nerves makes them send a "hey, something's wrong here!" signal to your brain, and that signal feels like a sting.

Alcohol also pulls water out of things it touches, and it can irritate the tiny bits of tissue in a cut. When you drink it, your mouth is wet and busy with saliva, which dilutes the alcohol and washes it along, so it doesn't bother the nerves in the same way.

So it's really about where the alcohol lands: on exposed nerves in a cut, it stings, but in your mouth, your body is ready for it.

Virtual reality, usually called VR, relies on a headset that fits over your eyes and shows images directly in front of them. Sensors inside the headset follow the motion of your head, so the virtual scene shifts whenever you turn. Lenses in the headset bring the displayed images into focus for your eyes, while magnets assist those sensors in picking up head movements. Grasping how our minds can make sense of a VR environment is easier if we first consider how we experience the physical world. Through sight, hearing, and touch, our brains continuously gather information and assemble an internal picture of our surroundings. A VR headset feeds our brains a similar flow of input, except it originates from a computer instead of the physical world. Our brains handle this input in the same manner, building a mental model of the virtual space just as they would with a real one.

Computer Go refers to the field of programs designed to play the board game Go. Go is an old game that began in China and is played on a 19x19 grid of intersections. Players try to enclose a larger area of the board than their opponent does. The game is famous for combining straightforward rules with great strategic depth. For artificial intelligence, Computer Go is a difficult problem because it demands sophisticated strategic reasoning, planning far into the future, and the capacity to judge positions without complete information. Building effective Computer Go algorithms calls for a mix of AI techniques, including machine learning, search, and pattern recognition. In recent years the field has advanced considerably, and the top programs can now defeat the best human players. Even so, the game continues to pose a challenge for artificial intelligence, and a great deal of work remains to improve what Computer Go programs can do.

Profit by itself doesn't directly raise a share price. What moves the price is the buying and selling of shares, but profit influences how buyers and sellers behave, so the two ideas are connected rather than opposed.

A share price is set by supply and demand. At any moment, the price is whatever level a willing buyer and a willing seller agree on. If more people want to buy than sell, the price rises until the two sides balance. If more want to sell, it falls. In that literal sense, it is always the buyers and sellers who set the price.

Profit matters because it changes what investors believe the company is worth. A company's value is roughly the profits it is expected to earn in the future, so when a company reports earnings, investors compare them with what they had expected. If a company was expected to earn, say, 5 dollars per share and actually earns 7, that is a positive surprise. Investors then revise their view of the company upward, more people want to buy, and the price rises. If it earns exactly what was expected, the price often barely moves, because the expectation was already built into the price. If it earns less than expected, the price commonly falls, even if the company still made a profit.

This is why you sometimes see a company report a record profit and its share price drop. The profit was good, but the market had hoped for even more.
