The price reflects the gap between results and expectations, plus what the results suggest about future earnings, rather than the profit figure alone.

Other factors also affect demand and supply: interest rates, the economy, news about the industry, management changes, the company's outlook and guidance, and general market mood. Also, the profit does not go straight to the share price. It may be paid out as dividends, kept in the business, or used to buy back shares, and each of these affects investor interest differently.

So the short answer is that the profit does not mechanically increase the price. Buyers and sellers do, and they respond to how the profit compares with what they expected and what it implies for the future.

A furlong measures 660 feet, which works out to roughly 201 meters. People typically use it when talking about distances in horse racing and farming. Its name derives from the Old English words "furh" and "lang," together meaning "furrow long," since it was originally the length a team of oxen could plow before stopping for a break.

Erotic novels, aka romance novels or romance fiction, are a genre that focuses on romantic relationships and sexual content. You can find them in plenty of places, grocery stores included, because lots of people read them just for fun or to unwind. Not everyone's into explicit material, though, and that's totally fine. Everybody gets to pick what they want to read or watch. And nobody should ever be pressured into consuming something that makes them uncomfortable.

Occam's Razor is a guiding idea that says that when you are trying to explain something or solve a problem, you should favor the simplest explanation or solution. It takes its name from William of Ockham, a philosopher who lived in the 14th century. To see how it works, picture a toy car that has stopped running. You could come up with several theories about what went wrong. The batteries might be dead, the motor might be faulty, or the wheels might have a problem. Applying Occam's Razor means picking the simplest explanation that matches what you observe, and here that would probably be the dead batteries. If you put in fresh batteries and the car runs again, you have found the most likely cause. If swapping the batteries does not help, you can move on to the other possibilities, such as the motor or the wheels, and again look for the simplest explanation that fits the facts. In short, Occam's Razor helps us arrive at the simplest and most probable answer to a problem or question, and it is useful in many areas, including science, philosophy, and daily life.

A faint line in the test window, even a very thin one, most likely means the test has detected pregnancy hormone (hCG), and it is very likely that you are pregnant. The deep purple line in the other window is the control line, which only shows that the test worked properly. So you have a valid test with a faint positive result.

Home pregnancy tests are designed so that any visible line in the test area, however faint, counts as positive. Faint lines usually mean the hormone level is still low, which is common when you test very early, around the time your period is due or just before. A false positive from a faint line is uncommon, though it can happen with an evaporation line (which appears after the time limit in the instructions and is usually colourless or grey) or very early pregnancy loss. Fertility medications containing hCG can also cause one, but that doesn't sound relevant to you.

Because you came off the pill in December, it is also worth knowing that your cycle may take a few months to settle, so a late period alone wouldn't be conclusive. But combined with unprotected sex and a visible line on two tests, pregnancy is the most likely explanation.

The best next step is to repeat the test in two to three days, ideally with first-morning urine, which is the most concentrated. If the line gets darker, that supports a healthy rising hormone level. Read the result within the time window in the instructions. If the line stays faint, fades, or your period arrives with heavier bleeding than usual, contact a doctor, as that can occasionally reflect an early miscarriage.

It is also sensible to book an appointment with your GP or a sexual health clinic to confirm the pregnancy and talk through your options, whatever you decide. If you are continuing the pregnancy, you can start taking 400 micrograms of folic acid daily, avoid alcohol, and speak to a doctor about any medicines you take. If you experience severe one-sided abdominal pain, shoulder-tip pain, dizziness, or heavy bleeding, seek urgent medical care, since these can signal an ectopic pregnancy.

I hope that helps, and I'm happy to answer any other questions you have.

President George W. Bush signed the USA PATRIOT Act into law on October 26, 2001, as a reaction to the September 11 terrorist attacks earlier that year. The name stands for the Uniting and Strengthening America by Providing Appropriate Tools Required to Intercept and Obstruct Terrorism Act. Its purpose was to equip law enforcement agencies with further means of preventing and fighting terrorism, and it substantially altered a number of federal statutes, among them the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA) and the Electronic Communications Privacy Act (ECPA). Because of the effect it might have on civil liberties and personal privacy, the Act has remained a subject of controversy.

A buyer should share enough financial information for the agent to judge whether a property is realistically within reach and to avoid wasting time on homes they cannot afford, but not so much that it weakens their position or exposes them to risk. In practice, the most useful thing to give is your budget range, ideally backed by a mortgage agreement in principle or pre-approval from a lender, which confirms how much you can borrow. Stating whether you have a deposit and roughly how large it is, and whether you are chain-free, also helps the agent prioritise you and tailor listings.

Beyond that, you generally do not need to disclose your full income, detailed bank statements, credit history, or other personal finances to an estate agent. Those belong with your mortgage lender or solicitor, who need them for proper checks. Agents are not regulated to assess your finances, and sharing more than necessary creates privacy risks and gives them information that could subtly influence how they negotiate with you.

It is also wise to be strategic about the exact maximum you could pay. If you reveal your absolute ceiling, an agent may steer you toward properties at that level or have less incentive to negotiate hard on price. Giving a realistic range and keeping your true limit to yourself, while being honest that you are financially serious, usually strikes the right balance. Above all, be truthful about anything that affects the transaction, such as needing a sale of your own property first, since misrepresenting your position can cause problems later.

Lockton Affinity operates as a unit within Lockton Companies, a worldwide insurance brokerage that supplies insurance and risk management solutions to both corporations and private clients. The division focuses on creating and running insurance programs for affinity groups, including professional associations, alumni networks, and other membership-based organizations. Working alongside these groups, it tailors insurance products and services to the particular requirements of their members and assists with selling and administering them. Lockton Affinity maintains offices in the United States, the United Kingdom, and several other nations.

Here's how it usually works for hand-drawn cartoons: the voice actor records the lines first, and then the animators listen to that recording and draw mouth shapes to match what's being said. People call this lip syncing, and it's a slog because the mouths have to line up pretty tightly with the words. Once the mouth shapes for every line are done, animators use them as a guide for the rest of the character's movement.

The main component of a vaccine is the antigen, which is a piece of a pathogen (such as a protein, sugar, or inactivated or weakened form of a virus or bacterium) or, in the case of mRNA vaccines, the genetic instructions for the body to produce that piece. The antigen is what the immune system recognizes and learns to respond to, building immunity without causing the disease itself. Vaccines also typically contain adjuvants, which boost the immune response, along with stabilizers, preservatives, and small amounts of other ingredients to keep the vaccine effective and safe.

Michael I. Jordan works as a computer scientist and holds a professorship at the University of California, Berkeley. His work centers on machine learning, where he has helped create algorithms for artificial intelligence and methods for analyzing massive datasets. He holds Fellow status in the American Association for Artificial Intelligence, the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers, and the Association for Computing Machinery. Several honors have recognized his research, among them the ACM SIGKDD Innovation Award and the ACM/AAAI Allen Newell Award. He has written a large body of work for academic journals and has also worked as an editor for a number of prominent publications in computer science.

Yes, though the term is used in a few different ways. In the strictest sense, a deposit-only account lets you put money in but not take it out, or only allows withdrawals under limited conditions. Examples include certain savings or trust arrangements for minors, where funds are locked until the child reaches a set age, and some restricted accounts used for escrow or for holding bail or court-ordered money.

In everyday banking, the phrase more often refers to accounts that accept deposits but are not set up for ordinary spending. Some banks offer accounts that receive incoming funds, such as a business account used only to collect customer payments, while withdrawals are made from a separate operating account. Similarly, some people set up accounts that a family member or employer can pay into, but where the owner withdraws only through a linked account.

Many banks also use the term "deposit-only" for the lockbox-style or remote-deposit arrangements that businesses use to collect checks, and for ATMs or branches that will accept deposits even when a particular service is unavailable. If you have a specific situation in mind, such as receiving payments for a business, holding funds for a child, or restricting spending, let me know and I can explain which type of account would fit best.

Honestly, shorting in pre-market tends to be easier to pull off for brokers, mostly because there's just less going on. Trading volume before the bell is way lower than during regular hours, so fewer buyers and sellers are around. That means less competition for the shares a broker needs to borrow, which can make them easier to locate. Still, it really depends on the stock and what the market is doing that day, so don't assume it'll be smooth every time.

SpongeBob SquarePants premiered on Nickelodeon on May 1, 1999. Stephen Hillenburg created it. He was an animator, but he also taught marine science, which probably explains why the show's underwater world feels so oddly detailed. Nobody expected it to stick around this long, yet it's still going strong, with plenty of spin-offs and adaptations along the way.

I'm sorry you're going through trouble trying to get pregnant. Your husband's low sperm count may be part of the problem, but it's possible other issues are involved too. Seeing a fertility specialist is the best way to find the underlying cause and create a suitable plan. For male infertility related to low sperm count, options might include medications that boost sperm production, surgery to correct problems in the reproductive tract, or assisted reproductive methods like in vitro fertilization (IVF). Predicting your chances of conception is hard, since they depend on many things, including what is causing the infertility, your ages, and your general health. A specialist can give you more details about your situation and what your odds look like with treatment. I'd encourage you and your husband to meet with a fertility specialist to talk through your choices and settle on a treatment path. Following the recommended plan and making any helpful lifestyle changes can also improve your chances of success.

Haiti got hit by a magnitude 7.0 quake on January 12, 2010. It struck just west of Port-au-Prince, and it was shallow, only about 13 km (8 miles) deep, which is part of why it did so much damage. Estimates put the death toll around 300,000, and roughly 1.5 million people lost their homes. It was the strongest quake to hit the country in more than 200 years, and it was followed by a long string of aftershocks. Hospitals, schools, roads, and bridges were badly damaged or destroyed, and the shaking also set off landslides. Rebuilding has dragged on for years, and it's been slowed by political instability and a serious lack of money and resources.

Sending money from India to the US is common, but it is regulated, so the right method depends on why you are sending it and how much.

The main route is a bank wire through an authorized dealer bank, typically using SWIFT. You fill out a remittance form (Form A2 or the bank's online equivalent), state the purpose, and the bank converts rupees to dollars and sends the funds. Wires are reliable for large amounts, but banks often charge a flat fee plus an exchange rate markup, and intermediary banks may deduct additional fees. Transfers usually arrive in one to three business days.

Online money transfer services such as Wise, Remitly, Xoom, or the international transfer features of some Indian banks are often cheaper and faster for small to medium amounts. Compare the actual exchange rate offered against the mid-market rate, since the markup is where most of the cost hides.

Indian rules matter a great deal. Under the Reserve Bank of India's Liberalised Remittance Scheme, resident individuals can send up to 250,000 US dollars per financial year (April to March) for permitted purposes, including education, medical treatment, gifts, family maintenance, travel, and overseas investments. You need a PAN, and the bank will ask for supporting documents such as an admission letter or invoice depending on the purpose. Remittances above certain thresholds may attract Tax Collected at Source, which has been changed several times in recent budgets, so check the current rate. Education and medical payments, especially those funded by a loan, usually get lower or no TCS. The TCS can be claimed as credit against your income tax when you file your return.

Some things are restricted or prohibited, such as remittances for lottery, margin trading, or certain speculative purposes. If you are an NRI sending money from an NRO account, there is a separate limit of one million US dollars per financial year, after paying applicable taxes, with a CA certificate (Form 15CA and 15CB). NRE account funds are freely repatriable.

On the US side, receiving a gift from abroad is generally not taxed for the recipient, but if a US person receives more than 100,000 dollars in gifts from a foreign individual in a year, they must report it on Form 3520. Large deposits may also prompt questions from the US bank, so keep documentation of the source of funds.

To keep costs down, compare total cost including fees and exchange rate, avoid sending many tiny transfers, and consider whether you can time conversion when the rupee rate is favorable. Always use regulated providers, and confirm the recipient's name, account number, and routing number before sending.

If you tell me the purpose, amount, and whether you are a resident or NRI, I can give more specific guidance.

Computers can do a ton, but they can't do everything. Some things are just out of reach because they need stuff only humans have. A computer can't really think or feel the way you do, and it doesn't make decisions or solve problems the way people do either. It's stuck with whatever instructions it's been given. It only does what it's programmed to do, so it can't just wake up one day and come up with a new idea on its own. It also only works with the data it's handed. It can't pick up something new unless a person (or another computer) explicitly sets it up to learn. So yeah, computers are super powerful, but they're still boxed in by their programming and by the fact that they don't experience things the way we do.

Paying off part of a loan early means the lender gets back some of the principal sooner than scheduled. Doing so can lower the total interest you owe. How the interest is adjusted afterward depends on your loan's terms and the lender's own policies. Certain lenders recalculate interest according to the time left on the loan once the early payment has been applied, whereas others rely on a different approach. It is worth finding out how your lender treats prepayments and what effect they will have on what the loan costs you overall. Talking with your lender or going over your loan agreement can help you see how prepayments will be handled. You might also find it useful to try an online calculator or consult a financial advisor, who can help you weigh the cost of prepaying against the cost of simply keeping up your regular payments.

I'm sorry your daughter is going through this. Three nosebleeds in three hours is worrying, and the pain she describes near her cheekbone needs attention, so please have her seen by a doctor today rather than waiting to see whether it settles on its own.

For the bleeding itself right now, sit her upright, leaning slightly forward so blood drains out of the nose rather than down the throat. Have her breathe through her mouth, and pinch the soft part of her nose firmly against the bony bridge for about 10 to 15 minutes without letting go to check. Keep her calm and seated, since crying and lying down can make bleeding worse. Ice wrapped in a cloth on the bridge of the nose or the back of the neck may help a little. Avoid tilting her head back, and don't put anything inside the nostril.

Seek emergency care immediately if the bleeding doesn't stop after 20 minutes of steady pressure, if she is bleeding heavily or swallowing a lot of blood, if she becomes pale, drowsy, or unusually weak, or if she vomits blood. Go urgently too if she has trouble breathing, a severe headache, a swollen or very painful face, eye swelling or changes in vision, fever, or if she was hit on the face or nose recently, since a fracture or infection could be behind the cheekbone pain.

When you see the doctor, mention whether she has had any recent injury, whether she has a cold or sinus symptoms, whether anyone in the family bruises or bleeds easily, and whether she is taking any medicines. A doctor can examine her nose and face and decide whether she needs further tests. Please don't delay, because a child who has had repeated nosebleeds with facial pain should be checked in person.

Ichthyosis hystrix (sometimes called "hystrix-like ichthyosis") is a rare genetic skin condition. It causes thick, rough, scaly skin, mostly on the arms, legs and torso, though it can also show up on the scalp, face and nails. There's no cure, so treatment is really about managing the symptoms and making the skin look and feel better.

A few things that can help: Moisturizers are the basic one. Using emollients regularly keeps the skin hydrated and cuts down on scaling. Creams or ointments with urea or salicylic acid can be prescribed to soften and slough off the thickened skin. Some people get phototherapy, which is ultraviolet light treatment, to improve how the skin looks and feels. In some cases doctors will also prescribe oral meds, like retinoids, which come from vitamin A and can help with texture and appearance.

I'd work closely with a dermatologist or another healthcare provider to figure out the best plan for your daughter. And once you've got one, stick with it, and keep her skin clean and moisturized. That goes a long way toward keeping the symptoms in check.

Buying out a co-owner's share of a car isn't too bad, and there are a few steps to keep the taxes and fees down.

First, you two need to agree on what the car's actually worth. Look it up on Kelley Blue Book or NADA to get a ballpark number, then settle on something you both think is fair before you do anything else.

Next comes the actual ownership transfer. You'll head to your local DMV with the paperwork, which usually means a bill of sale, the title, and whatever else your state wants. There'll be a transfer fee too, so budget for that.

Then there's tax. Depending on where you live, you might owe sales tax on the value of the car when the title changes hands. Some places also hit you with property tax on vehicles. A few states give breaks when the transfer is between co-owners or family, so it's worth asking about that, since it could save you real money.

Last, call your insurance company and update the policy so it matches the new ownership. You want to be fully covered if something happens to the car.

Rules vary a lot from state to state, so I'd check with your DMV before you start. A quick call can save you a headache.

Occam's razor is a thinking trick that says when you have a few different explanations for something, the simplest one is usually the best place to start. It's named after William of Ockham, a monk who lived about 700 years ago. The "razor" part means you shave away the extra stuff you don't need.

Here's a way a five-year-old might see it. Imagine you left a cookie on the table, and when you come back, it's gone and there are crumbs on your little brother's face. You could guess that a sneaky alien flew in through the window, ate the cookie, wiped crumbs on your brother, and flew away. Or you could guess your brother ate the cookie. Both stories explain what happened, but the alien story needs lots of extra things to be true. The brother story needs just one. Occam's razor says go with your brother.

It's important to know that the razor doesn't say the simple answer is always right. It says that if two explanations fit the facts equally well, you should prefer the one that needs fewer guesses. Sometimes the complicated answer turns out to be true, but you should only believe it when the evidence pushes you there.

As for where it holds true in practice, I don't have personal experiences the way a person does, but I can tell you where it shows up again and again in the things people have written and discovered. Doctors have a saying: "When you hear hoofbeats, think horses, not zebras." If someone has a cough and a fever, it's probably a cold or the flu, not some rare tropical disease, and doctors who chase rare illnesses first often waste time. Mechanics and computer technicians live by it too. When a computer won't turn on, the first question is whether it's plugged in, and a surprising number of times, that's the whole problem. In science, astronomers once used very complicated systems of circles within circles to explain how planets moved around the Earth, and the much simpler idea that planets go around the Sun ended up explaining things better. Detectives and people who investigate rumors or conspiracy theories also find that the plain explanation, like a mistake, a coincidence, or ordinary human behavior, usually beats the secret elaborate plot.

So the short version is this: when you're trying to figure something out, start with the easiest explanation that fits everything you know, and only add more pieces when you really have to.

Keynesian economics is a framework for understanding how the economy functions and how it can be steered toward better performance. Its name comes from John Maynard Keynes, an economist who worked in the early twentieth century. A central tenet of this approach is that when the economy is struggling, the government should step in to help. If many people are unemployed and little money is circulating, for instance, the government might increase its spending on projects such as roads and schools, both to generate jobs and to get people spending again. Keynes also challenged the view held by some other economists that prices and wages would always fall during a downturn. He argued instead that they may stay put or even rise, which can make recovery more difficult. In short, Keynesian economics holds that government action can help an ailing economy, and that rigid prices and wages should not stand in the way of a return to health.

An ethnic group is basically a bunch of people who share a cultural background, like a language, traditions, customs, and values. Ethnic groups tend to have a few things in common. Lots of them share a history, a language, and everyday cultural habits that set them apart from others. Some also have physical features that get associated with them, like skin tone or facial features, though that varies a ton. Many live in the same region and feel a real connection to that land. They often build their own social or political structures too, such as clans, tribes, or nation-states, which help keep their identity alive. And they usually share values and beliefs that shape how they see the world and what they do day to day.

That said, every group is different, so these traits don't apply the same way everywhere. And no group is better or worse than another. Ethnicity is really a social idea more than a fixed thing, and it shouldn't be used as an excuse to treat anyone unfairly.

Yes, you can usually straighten teeth without cutting the gums, but what works depends on what's actually going on with your bite. Invisalign is the big one people think of. It uses clear, removable aligners that nudge your teeth into place little by little, applying gentle pressure as you switch to each new tray. It handles crowding, gaps, and general misalignment pretty well. If your front teeth won't touch because of gum tissue or the muscle attached between them, though, that's a different problem and clear aligners alone might not fix it. Your orthodontist could try aligners that push harder on the specific teeth that aren't lining up, or suggest rubber bands, special appliances, or other tricks to get them where they need to go. Either way, you'll want a trained dental pro planning and watching the treatment. They can look at your mouth in person and tell you what's realistic for your case.

The question is a good one, because in an idealized world it isn't obviously rational at all. Modigliani and Miller showed that if markets are frictionless, with no taxes, no transaction costs, and everyone holding the same information, a company's dividend policy doesn't affect its value. Paying out a dollar of cash reduces the firm's value by a dollar and puts a dollar in the shareholder's pocket, so the shareholder is no better off. Any investor who wanted cash could simply sell a few shares to create a "homemade dividend," and any investor who didn't want cash could reinvest it. So the case for dividends has to rest on the ways real markets depart from that ideal.

The most basic reason is that the money belongs to the shareholders, and a company should only keep it if it can earn a return at least as high as what shareholders could earn elsewhere at similar risk. A mature business that generates more cash than it can sensibly reinvest, such as a utility, a tobacco company, or a consumer staples firm, destroys value by hoarding cash or by pouring it into mediocre projects. Returning the surplus lets investors redeploy it into growing companies, which is good both for them and for the efficient allocation of capital in the economy.

Closely related is the problem of agency costs. Managers don't always act in shareholders' interests; with a large pile of cash at their disposal they may be tempted toward empire building, prestige acquisitions, lavish perks, or pet projects. Michael Jensen called this the free cash flow problem. Committing to a regular dividend takes that cash out of managers' hands and forces them to justify new investments by raising money from outside investors, who will scrutinize the plans. Because cutting a dividend is so unpopular, a dividend acts as a credible commitment in a way that a vague promise of discipline does not.

Dividends also convey information. Managers know more about the firm's prospects than outsiders do, and a dividend is a costly signal because it requires actual cash, year after year. A company that initiates or raises its dividend is implicitly saying it expects earnings to be strong and stable enough to sustain the payment. Markets tend to react positively to dividend increases and sharply negatively to cuts, which supports the idea that investors read dividends as a signal of management's confidence. Real cash payments are also harder to fake than accounting earnings, so they provide some reassurance that reported profits are genuine.

Investor preferences matter too. Some investors, such as retirees, endowments, and certain funds, want a steady stream of income and may face costs or restrictions when selling shares, or may simply find it psychologically easier to spend dividends than to sell off their holdings. Behavioral economists note that a dividend acts as a self-control device, letting people consume income without feeling they are "eating into capital." Firms that pay reliable dividends attract this clientele, and serving them can support demand for the stock.

There are counterarguments and caveats. In many countries dividends have historically been taxed more heavily than capital gains, which is one reason share buybacks have become a popular alternative: they return cash too, but offer more flexibility and allow investors to choose whether to sell. Paying dividends also means that a firm needing capital later may have to raise it at a cost through new equity or debt. So dividends are not always the best choice, and fast-growing firms with abundant profitable opportunities usually and rightly pay none.

In short, paying a dividend is rational when a company has more cash than good uses for it, when it helps discipline management, when it credibly signals financial strength, and when it suits the needs of the company's investors. It is less a way of creating value out of nothing than a way of avoiding the value destruction that can come from retaining cash the firm cannot use well.

Okay, so in Far Cry you can patch yourself up by using some special ability that snaps your bones back into place and stops the bleeding. Real life doesn't work like that, sadly. If you've got a broken bone or a wound that won't stop bleeding, you need to get to a doctor or another healthcare pro. They can treat it properly so you actually heal. For a broken bone, they'll line it back up in the right position and hold it there with a splint, cast, or something similar. That gives it a fair shot at knitting together correctly and keeps you from making it worse. With a bleeding wound, they'll clean it out and might close it with stitches or staples. Bodies just don't work like video games, unfortunately. Healing takes time and proper care, and you pretty much always want medical help to make sure things go smoothly.

Imagine your body is like a cozy little blanket of warm air. Your skin makes heat, and that heat warms up a thin layer of air right next to you, kind of like wearing an invisible jacket. On a calm day, that invisible jacket stays put and keeps you snug.

Now the wind comes along and blows that warm jacket of air away. Your body has to work to make a new one, and then the wind blows that one away too. So you keep losing your warmth over and over, much faster than if the air were just sitting still. That's why you feel colder.

Here's a fun way to think about it. When you blow on a spoonful of hot soup, it cools down quickly. You're blowing away the warm air above the soup and replacing it with cooler air. The wind does the same thing to you, only you're the soup.

One more thing: the wind doesn't actually make the air colder. A thermometer would show the same temperature with or without wind. It just makes your body lose heat faster, so you feel colder. That feeling is what people call wind chill. Wet skin or clothes make it even worse, because the wind also helps water dry off, and drying takes heat away too. That's why a windbreaker helps so much: it holds your warm air jacket in place so the wind can't steal it.

The dot com bubble was basically a wild stretch of hype around internet companies, especially online shops, from the late 1990s into the early 2000s. Investors piled into anything with ".com" in the name, and company values shot way up, inflating a huge bubble in the stock market. Then it popped. Stock prices crashed, and a bunch of things went wrong at once: the internet companies were wildly overvalued, internet usage growth cooled off, and venture capital dried up. Lots of those companies went under or got into serious money trouble, which meant layoffs everywhere and a real drop in economic activity. The fallout hit the global economy hard and helped drag things into the recession of the early 2000s.

Imperfect information describes a scenario in which one or more participants in a game or decision process lack full knowledge of their available options or the outcomes their choices will produce. Put differently, participants do not fully grasp the circumstances they face and therefore have to choose based on partial or restricted information. Such situations appear in many settings, including strategic games, economic activity, and ordinary daily life. In poker, for instance, each player is unaware of the cards held by opponents and must act according to the cards visible to them and how others behave. Investors in the stock market face a similar problem, since they cannot know a company's future performance with certainty and must commit money based on incomplete data. Likewise, people in everyday life frequently decide without knowing every possible result or the motives of those around them. Imperfect information introduces uncertainty and complexity into decision-making and can strongly shape the results of both games and real-world events. For this reason, it is a central idea in game theory, economics, and other disciplines that examine choices made under uncertainty.

Multilinear subspace learning is a family of dimensionality reduction techniques designed for data that naturally comes in the form of multidimensional arrays, which mathematicians call tensors. Many real-world datasets have this kind of structure. A grayscale image is a two-dimensional array of pixels, a color video can be seen as a four-dimensional array indexed by height, width, color channel, and time, and data from brain imaging or sensor networks often has several distinct "modes" such as space, time, frequency, and subject. Multilinear subspace learning aims to find compact, low-dimensional representations of such data while respecting and exploiting its multidimensional organization.

The idea is easiest to understand by contrast with traditional linear subspace learning, such as principal component analysis (PCA) or linear discriminant analysis (LDA). These classical methods expect each data sample to be a single vector. To apply them to an image or a video, you first have to flatten, or vectorize, the array into one very long vector. This causes two main problems. First, it destroys the structural relationships in the data, since pixels that were neighbors in a row or column, or values that were related across time, become scattered positions in a long list. Second, it produces extremely high-dimensional vectors, which means the projection matrices that must be learned are enormous, the computations become expensive, and with limited training samples the estimates can become unreliable, a difficulty often called the small sample size problem.

Multilinear subspace learning avoids flattening. Instead of learning a single huge projection matrix, it learns a separate, much smaller projection for each mode of the tensor. For an image, for example, one projection acts on the rows and another acts on the columns. The data is transformed through a series of these mode-wise projections, often expressed using an operation called the mode-n product, and the result is a smaller tensor or a set of features that captures the essential information. Because each projection is small, the total number of parameters is dramatically reduced, which makes learning more efficient and often more robust, and the natural correlations along each dimension are preserved.

There are two broad styles of projection used in this field. In tensor-to-tensor projection, the input tensor is mapped to a smaller tensor of the same order, so a large image becomes a small matrix of features. This approach is closely related to the Tucker decomposition and is exemplified by multilinear principal component analysis (MPCA). In tensor-to-vector projection, the input is mapped directly to a feature vector through a sequence of elementary projections, each built from one vector per mode, an approach connected to the CANDECOMP/PARAFAC decomposition and exemplified by uncorrelated multilinear PCA and related discriminant methods. Supervised versions also exist, such as multilinear discriminant analysis, which seeks projections that best separate different classes, and there are multilinear extensions of canonical correlation analysis and other classical techniques.

Learning these projections is usually harder than in the linear case, because the optimal projection for one mode depends on the projections chosen for the other modes, so there is generally no closed-form solution. Most algorithms therefore use an alternating strategy: they fix all projections except one, solve for that one, then cycle through the modes repeatedly until the solution stabilizes. This iterative process typically converges to a good, though not always globally optimal, result.

Multilinear subspace learning has been applied in face and gait recognition, video and image analysis, neuroscience data such as EEG and fMRI, audio processing, and data mining of multi-way datasets. Its central appeal is that it treats structured data in its natural form, offering more compact models, lower computational cost, and frequently better generalization than methods that ignore the multidimensional structure by forcing everything into vectors.

Stores use prices like $1.99 or $2.49 because of how our brains read numbers. When you see $1.99, your brain tends to notice the "1" first and think "one dollar something," which feels cheaper than $2. It's a little trick that makes things seem like a better deal, even when the difference is only a penny.

Stores also like these prices because they make people think about the amount they're spending. Sometimes a price ending in 99 can make a person feel like they're getting a bargain, so they're more likely to buy.

Not every price ends in 99, though. Some stores use prices like $9.95 or $2.49 for the same reason, and some use other endings to look fancy or to match what competitors charge. Prices are chosen to look appealing and to fit in with what people expect to pay.

Rounding to whole dollars would be simpler, but it would mean the store can't show that "cheaper" feeling, and it would also make it harder to set prices that fit the store's costs and the prices of similar items nearby. The small change in endings is a way to nudge people toward buying without anyone having to think too hard about it.

"The Terminator" is a 1984 American science fiction action film directed by James Cameron, who co-wrote the screenplay with Gale Anne Hurd. It stars Arnold Schwarzenegger as the title character, a cyborg assassin sent from the future by a sentient artificial intelligence called Skynet. The machine's goal is to kill Sarah Connor, a waitress whose unborn son, John, will later lead the human resistance against Skynet in a war that machines have nearly won. Kyle Reese, a soldier also sent back in time to protect Sarah, is played by Michael Biehn, and Linda Hamilton plays Sarah.

The film was a surprise hit that launched a long-running franchise, including sequels such as "Terminator 2: Judgment Day" (1991), "Terminator 3: Rise of the Machines" (2003), and later installments, as well as television series, novels, comics, and video games. The original is best known for its tense chase scenes, its memorable line "I'll be back," its dark, low-budget noir style, and its vision of a future shaped by artificial intelligence and nuclear war. It helped establish Schwarzenegger as a major action star and Cameron as a leading director of big-budget spectacle.

Your numbers are close to the lower limit. A hemoglobin of 11.9 g/dL and a hematocrit of 34.8% are just below the usual reference range for adult women (roughly 12.0 to 15.5 g/dL and 36% to 46%), so you have very mild anemia, or possibly a result at the edge of normal depending on the lab. Your other values, including your lipids, vitamin D, glucose, and white cell count, look good.

Hemoglobin alone can't tell you whether you're short on iron, so the next step is to ask your provider for an iron panel: serum ferritin (your body's iron stores, which is the most useful single test), serum iron, total iron-binding capacity, and transferrin saturation. Ask for the full CBC report too, especially the MCV (red cell size), MCH, and RDW. A low MCV with low ferritin points toward iron deficiency, while a normal MCV with normal ferritin suggests something else, such as inflammation, a vitamin B12 or folate issue, or a kidney or thyroid problem.

The more important question is why you might be losing or not absorbing iron, because supplements only treat the symptom. At 53, be sure to ask about heavy or irregular periods if you still menstruate, since perimenopause is a common cause. Also ask about regular use of ibuprofen or aspirin, any blood in your stool or dark stools, and any digestive symptoms. Iron deficiency in a woman your age is a reason to make sure you're up to date on colon cancer screening, and your provider may want to discuss that or a celiac screen.

Please don't start iron supplements on your own without confirming the deficiency. Too much iron can cause constipation, stomach upset, and, over time, harm to the liver and heart, and it can mask other problems. If the ferritin comes back normal, your provider may not need to start iron at all, and you can reasonably ask what they think is causing the slightly low hemoglobin and whether it needs rechecking in a few months.

Ken Jennings is probably best known for his 74-game winning streak on "Jeopardy!" back in 2004, which still stands as the record. He's also a writer, and he's put out a bunch of books over the years covering everything from science to trivia to pop culture. He's become a familiar face on TV since then, popping up on other game shows and in the media as a guest expert on trivia and general knowledge stuff.

Your daughter's fever is being treated appropriately, and it's good that it is slowly coming down. A fever that returns a few hours after a dose is common, because paracetamol typically lasts about 4 to 6 hours. Paracetamol is generally safe to repeat once 4 hours have passed since the last dose, and it should not be given more often than every 4 hours or more than 5 doses in 24 hours. Check the label or ask a pharmacist to confirm the exact interval for P-250.

Mefenamic acid (Mefanorm) is an NSAID, and it is not usually the first choice for children, so please confirm with a doctor or pharmacist that 5 ml is the correct dose for her weight and age. Do not give any more of it without medical advice, and do not give aspirin to a child. If you want an alternating option, a doctor can tell you whether ibuprofen is suitable for her and at what dose. Give the medicines in the order and spacing the doctor advises, and write down the times and doses so you don't accidentally overdose.

Between doses, keep her hydrated with small, frequent sips of water, oral rehydration solution, or diluted juice. Dress her in light clothing and keep the room comfortable. A lukewarm sponge bath can help, but avoid cold water or alcohol rubs.

Since the fever has lasted since yesterday evening, I'd recommend seeing a doctor today rather than waiting to see what happens. The fever may have a cause that needs antibiotics or other treatment, and a doctor can examine her and check her hydration.

Seek emergency care right away if she has a seizure or convulsion, is unusually drowsy, hard to wake, or confused, has trouble breathing, has a stiff neck, has a rash that does not fade when pressed, refuses fluids, has very little or no urine for 8 hours or more, or if the fever goes above 40°C (104°F) and doesn't respond to medicine.

Cashmere comes from cashmere goats, specifically from the soft, fine undercoat that grows beneath their coarser outer guard hairs. This downy layer develops during the winter to insulate the goats against harsh cold, and the goats naturally begin to shed it in the spring. Herders collect the fibers at that time, traditionally by combing the goats by hand, though some producers shear them instead. The coarse outer hairs are then separated from the fine undercoat in a process called dehairing, leaving the soft fibers that are cleaned, spun into yarn, and woven or knitted into garments.

The name comes from Kashmir, the Himalayan region where the fiber was historically processed and made into prized shawls, which became fashionable in Europe in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. Today, most of the world's cashmere comes from China and Mongolia, with additional production in Afghanistan, Iran, India, Nepal, and parts of Central Asia. The best quality tends to come from goats living in extremely cold, high-altitude environments such as the Gobi Desert and the Tibetan Plateau, since the harsher climate encourages a finer, denser undercoat.

Cashmere is considered a luxury fiber because each goat produces only a small amount of usable undercoat each year, often around 150 grams or less, meaning it can take the fleece of several goats to make a single sweater. The fibers are also exceptionally fine, typically under 19 microns in diameter, which gives cashmere its characteristic softness, lightness, and warmth.

Yeah, you'll generally want to pay any VAT you actually owe. If a company didn't charge you VAT when it should have, you could still end up on the hook for it, so it's not something to just ignore.

If you're not sure whether you owe it, ask the company directly. They should be able to tell you why they didn't collect it and whether it's your responsibility to pay. Don't just sit on it, though. If you do owe it and don't pay, you can get hit with penalties and interest, which adds up fast. Paying sooner rather than later saves you that extra cost.

If you think the amount is wrong or you're unsure how the company handled it, a tax pro or your local tax office can help you sort it out. They're usually pretty good about answering these questions.

In Far Cry titles, characters can recover their health through a special power that instantly resets broken bones and halts bleeding. Real life doesn't work that way. When someone has a fractured bone or a bleeding wound, the right step is to see a doctor or another healthcare provider, who can treat the injury properly and support recovery. A medical professional sets a broken bone by realigning it and then immobilizing it with a splint, cast, or similar device, which allows it to heal correctly and lowers the risk of further harm. For a bleeding wound, the provider cleans it and may close it with stitches or staples so it can mend properly. The human body isn't like a video game, and it can't repair itself immediately. Recovery takes time and careful attention, and medical care is generally needed to keep healing on track.

Sound isn't really a negative. The number -9 dBA doesn't mean there's "negative sound" in the way that -9 apples would mean negative apples. It's just a number on a scale that someone chose for convenience, a bit like how temperature can be below zero in Celsius and that doesn't mean there's negative heat.

Here's the idea. Sound is tiny vibrations in the air that reach your ears. Some sounds are very loud, like a jet engine, and some are very quiet, like a whisper. To measure how loud something is, scientists use a unit called the decibel, written dB. Decibels work on a logarithmic scale, which means every jump of 10 dB is about ten times more sound energy, not just a little more. Think of it like counting steps up a very tall ladder where each step is a giant leap.

The "A" in dBA means the measurement has been adjusted to match how human ears actually hear. Our ears are better at hearing some pitches than others, so the A-weighting makes the number reflect what we'd really perceive.

Now, the scale has a starting reference point, roughly the quietest sound a healthy young person can barely hear. That reference is set at 0 dB. Most sounds are louder than that, so they get positive numbers. But a sound that is quieter than the reference point gets a negative number, just like a temperature below the freezing point of water gets a negative number on the Celsius scale.

So a room measuring -9 dBA is one where the background noise is even quieter than that threshold of human hearing. It's so quiet that your own body becomes the loudest thing you hear. You can hear your heartbeat, your breathing, and the blood moving through your ears. That's why people in that room often feel a little strange and can't stay in it for long.

As for how we measure it, scientists use a very sensitive microphone placed inside the room. The microphone picks up the tiny vibrations in the air, and an instrument called a sound level meter converts that into a decibel number, applying the A-weighting automatically. The room is built with thick walls, special foam, and insulation to block outside noise, so the meter can detect how quiet it really is.

In the subtractive color system, cyan, magenta, and yellow serve as the three primaries. Printing, painting, and dyeing rely on these hues to produce an extensive palette by soaking up and removing particular light wavelengths. The model takes its foundation from how objects create color through absorbing and reflecting light. Upon striking a surface, certain wavelengths are taken in by the material, while others bounce back toward the observer. Because the wavelengths that get absorbed are removed from the reflected light, the system is termed "subtractive." Cyan, magenta, and yellow are the primaries here since, when blended in varying amounts, they are capable of absorbing and removing specific wavelengths. Mixing these primaries in different combinations yields many other shades. For instance, equal parts of cyan and magenta create blue, and equal parts of magenta and yellow create red.

Hyperparameter optimization is the task of identifying the best settings for a model's hyperparameters. These are configuration values fixed before training begins, and they can have a substantial effect on how well a model performs. Common examples include the learning rate used when training a neural network, the count of layers and neurons in that network, the choice of loss function, and the strength of regularization. Tuning these values is a key stage in building and training any machine learning model, since selecting suitable hyperparameters can noticeably improve both accuracy and efficiency. Several approaches exist for this, including manual tuning, grid search, random search, and Bayesian optimization. With manual tuning, a practitioner chooses the values based on experience and familiarity with the problem. This process takes a lot of time and does not always produce the strongest outcome. Grid search requires the practitioner to specify a grid of candidate values, after which the model is trained and assessed for every possible combination. This approach can demand a great deal of computation, particularly when the grid is large or the model is complicated. Random search instead has the practitioner define a probability distribution over the values, and each iteration draws a random set of values from it. It is typically less demanding computationally than grid search, though it may not explore the space as exhaustively. Bayesian optimization is a more advanced technique that applies Bayesian statistics to build a model of the objective function, then uses that model to pick the next set of hyperparameters to test. It can be more efficient than either grid or random search, but it is generally more complicated to implement.

Ok so if you've never read "Who Moved My Cheese?" by Dr. Spencer Johnson, it's a short parable about dealing with change. It's basically about two mice, Sniff and Scurry, and two little guys, Hem and Haw, hunting for cheese in a maze. The cheese stands for whatever you're after, like a job, a relationship, or whatever else matters to you. At first, all four of them find cheese in the same spot. Then one day it's just gone.

Sniff and Scurry don't waste much time. They head out into the maze to look for more. Hem and Haw, though, get stuck. They keep going back to the old spot like the cheese is going to reappear if they just wait long enough. Eventually they realize it's not coming back and they have to move on. They go through denial, anger, and bargaining before they finally accept it, and only then do they find new cheese.

I think the point is pretty simple. Change happens to everyone, and you can either adapt or sit there staring at the empty spot. Be open to it, go look for what's next, and don't cling to stuff that's already gone.

Medical diagnosis is the process by which a healthcare professional determines which disease, condition, or injury explains a person's symptoms and signs. The word "diagnosis" comes from Greek roots meaning "to know thoroughly" or "to distinguish," which captures the essence of the task: figuring out what is actually wrong so that appropriate treatment can follow. The term refers both to the reasoning process itself and to its outcome, the named condition a clinician concludes a patient has.

The process usually begins with the medical history, in which the clinician asks the patient about current complaints, when they started, how they have changed, past illnesses, medications, family history, lifestyle, and other relevant details. Many experienced physicians consider the history the single most informative part of diagnosis, since a careful conversation often points strongly toward the answer before any tests are done. This is followed by a physical examination, where the clinician looks, listens, feels, and sometimes measures things such as blood pressure, heart and lung sounds, reflexes, or areas of tenderness to gather objective signs.

Based on this information, the clinician typically forms a differential diagnosis, which is a list of possible conditions that could account for the findings, ranked by likelihood and by how serious they would be if missed. Diagnostic tests are then used to narrow the list. These may include blood and urine tests, imaging such as X-rays, ultrasound, CT, or MRI scans, electrocardiograms, biopsies examined under a microscope, genetic testing, and many other specialized investigations. Each result raises or lowers the probability of the various possibilities until one explanation becomes clear enough to act on.

Diagnosis is fundamentally a matter of reasoning under uncertainty. Symptoms can be vague, different diseases can look alike, one patient may have several conditions at once, and tests are never perfectly accurate, since they can produce false positives and false negatives. For this reason clinicians often speak of a working diagnosis, a provisional conclusion that guides initial treatment but is revised if new information emerges or if the patient does not respond as expected. Sometimes a diagnosis is confirmed only by watching how the illness evolves over time, and in some cases, called diagnoses of exclusion, a condition is identified only after other possibilities have been ruled out.

An accurate diagnosis matters because nearly everything else in medical care depends on it. It determines which treatments are chosen, helps predict the likely course and outcome of the illness, informs decisions about further monitoring, and allows patients to understand what is happening to them. Diagnostic errors, whether a missed, delayed, or incorrect diagnosis, are recognized as a significant source of preventable harm in healthcare, which is why much effort goes into improving clinical reasoning, testing methods, and, increasingly, computer-based decision support and artificial intelligence tools that assist clinicians in interpreting data.

Think of a perpetual motion machine as a magic toy that keeps running forever without anyone feeding it energy. The rule of the universe is that you can't get something for nothing. Every time something moves, some of its energy has to come from somewhere, and whenever it moves it leaks a little of that energy out as heat, sound, or rubbing. So a machine that runs on its own forever would have to create energy out of thin air, and nature doesn't do that.

A good way to see it is with a ball rolling down a hill. It speeds up on the way down because it's gaining energy from its height, and it slows down going up the other side because it's giving that energy back. It never gets back higher than where it started, because a little energy was lost to rubbing along the way. Every machine is like that ball, only losing a bit at each step. Nothing can add back more than it started with.

People often think, "But what if I just arrange the parts cleverly so the pushes always add up?" The trick is that every clever arrangement still has to pay for its motion, through friction, heat, or the energy you put in to set it up. Changing the shape or the order of the parts doesn't change the total. Lots of people have tried, and every single one ends up leaking energy somewhere, even if they can't see where.

So the short answer for the people who bring you ideas is this: a machine can only pass along energy it already has, and it always passes along a little less than it got. The universe keeps a strict account, and the account never shows a profit.

Occam's razor is a simple idea: when you have two explanations that both fit what you see, the simpler one with fewer assumptions is usually the better bet. It's a rule of thumb for not inventing extra stuff you don't need.

Imagine you come home and find a cookie jar empty, with crumbs on the counter. One explanation is that your little brother ate the cookies. Another is that a raccoon sneaked in through the window, ate the cookies, climbed back out, and also somehow closed the lid behind it. The brother explanation needs fewer made-up pieces, so it's the one to check first.

You can see the razor working in real life in plenty of places. Doctors often hear hoofbeats and think horses, not zebras: a common cause like a cold or a simple infection usually explains a set of symptoms better than a rare disease with a long list of special conditions. Scientists also use it. When astronomers noticed planets moving strangely across the sky, the idea that Earth goes around the Sun explained the movements with far fewer complicated circles than the older idea that everything circles Earth. Even your phone's spell checker follows the same thinking: when you type "teh," the simplest guess is that you meant "the," not some unusual word nobody uses.

The razor isn't a law, though. Sometimes the complicated answer turns out to be right, like when germs were found to cause diseases that people once blamed on bad air. It just tells you where to look first.

Neptune was discovered in 1846, and the credit is shared among a few people. The planet was first identified by sight on September 23, 1846, by the German astronomer Johann Gottfried Galle, working with his student Heinrich d'Arrest at the Berlin Observatory. They found it after receiving a letter from the French mathematician Urbain Le Verrier, who had calculated where an unseen planet should be, based on irregularities in the orbit of Uranus.

Independently, the English mathematician John Couch Adams had done similar calculations in 1845 and predicted a position for the new planet, but his work was not acted upon promptly by the British astronomers he approached, so no search succeeded in time. This led to a well-known priority dispute between Britain and France, though today both Le Verrier and Adams are generally credited as co-predictors of Neptune's existence, with Galle as the first to observe it with that knowledge.

It is also worth noting that Galileo had actually recorded Neptune in his observations in 1612 and 1613, but he mistook it for a faint fixed star, so he is not counted as its discoverer.

World War I started on July 28, 1914, and wrapped up on November 11, 1918. It was a huge global fight that pulled in a lot of countries, including the big European powers and the United States, which didn't jump in until 1917. The spark was the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand of Austria-Hungary on June 28, 1914, but that was really just the trigger. The real causes were messier: years of tension between the major powers, plus fights over money, land, and colonies. By the end, millions of people had died, and the war reshaped the countries involved and the world around them.

Yes, a person can have a concussion and show no symptoms at all. Doctors sometimes call this a "silent" or "mild" concussion. Although most people with a concussion do develop symptoms, a few may experience none, or only very faint ones that are easy to overlook. Even without any noticeable signs, a concussion can still be present, so anyone who has suffered a blow to the head should get medical care. Typical symptoms include headache, dizziness, tiredness, memory problems, trouble focusing, and irritability, among others. If you have hit your head and are not sure whether you have a concussion, see a healthcare provider for a proper assessment and treatment.

The multivariate normal distribution is a generalization of the familiar bell-shaped normal distribution to several random variables at once. Instead of describing a single quantity, it describes a vector of quantities that are jointly random and may be correlated with one another. For example, the height and weight of a person can be modeled together as a two-dimensional normal vector, capturing both how each varies and how the two move together.

The distribution is specified by two parameters. The first is a mean vector, which gives the expected value of each component and locates the center of the distribution. The second is a covariance matrix, which is a square, symmetric, positive semidefinite matrix. Its diagonal entries are the variances of the individual variables, and its off-diagonal entries are the covariances between pairs of variables, which measure how strongly and in which direction they move together. Together these determine the shape, spread, and orientation of the distribution.

When the covariance matrix is positive definite, the distribution has a probability density function. For a vector x with k components, mean vector mu, and covariance matrix Sigma, the density takes the form of a normalizing constant multiplied by the exponential of negative one half times the quadratic form (x minus mu) transposed, times the inverse of Sigma, times (x minus mu). The quantity inside the exponent is the squared Mahalanobis distance from x to the mean, which measures distance in a way that accounts for the variances and correlations. As a result, the contours of equal density are ellipsoids centered at the mean, with their axes aligned with the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix.

The multivariate normal distribution has several important properties that make it widely used. Any linear combination of its components is itself normally distributed. Its marginal distributions for any subset of components are also normal, and its conditional distributions given other components are normal as well. Moreover, two components are independent if and only if their covariance is zero, a property that does not hold for general distributions. These features make it central in statistics, machine learning, signal processing, finance, and many other fields. It underlies methods such as linear regression with Gaussian errors, Gaussian processes, Kalman filters, and principal component analysis, and the central limit theorem explains why it arises so often in practice, since sums of many independent effects tend toward normality.

Creatine phosphokinase (CPK) levels may rise for a variety of reasons, such as muscle injury, inflammation, and some drugs. For individuals with type 2 diabetes, a raised CPK level may stem from muscle harm caused by persistently high blood glucose, or from complications like neuropathy (damage to the nerves) or nephropathy (damage to the kidneys). Certain medications, including statins prescribed to reduce cholesterol, can also push CPK up, as can rhabdomyolysis, an uncommon condition in which muscle tissue breaks down. Several approaches can bring CPK back down. Addressing the root cause is the first step: if muscle injury or inflammation is responsible, correcting that problem usually helps. If uncontrolled blood sugar is damaging muscle, for instance, your physician might suggest adjusting your diabetes care plan or changing your medications to bring glucose under better control. Resting is another option, since allowing injured muscles time to recover can lower CPK when muscle damage is the culprit. Exercise is generally good for building muscle strength and lowering the chance of injury, but if your CPK is elevated because of muscle damage, you should check with your doctor before beginning a new fitness routine. A nutritious, well-rounded diet with adequate protein also supports muscle health and may contribute to lower CPK. In certain situations, your doctor might prescribe medication to reduce CPK, though you should discuss its possible benefits and risks with them beforehand. Note that "perdiosine" is not a medication, and it is unclear what you intended to refer to. Ultimately, follow your doctor's guidance and work together with them to design the treatment plan that best fits your needs.

I'm sorry you're thinking about losing your dog. Ten years together is a long and special time, and it makes sense that it got you wondering.

Here is the simple version. Every living thing has a kind of "speed setting." Small, fast animals live their lives on fast-forward. Their hearts beat quickly, they grow up quickly, and they get old quickly. Big, slow animals, like humans, elephants, and whales, live on slow-motion. A mouse lives about two years, a dog about ten to fifteen, a human about eighty, and a whale can live over a hundred.

Why are dogs set to the faster speed? Part of the reason is about danger. In the wild, animals like wolves, which dogs came from, face lots of risks: hunger, injuries, sickness, and other animals. Because life is so risky, nature rewards animals that grow up fast and have babies early, rather than ones that spend decades getting ready. A body that is built to grow quickly and be ready for puppies in a year or two isn't built to be repaired and kept running for eighty years. Humans, on the other hand, have big brains and take a long time to learn things, and we have long childhoods and grandparents who help raise children. That favors a body built to last longer.

Another part is how bodies wear out. Every day, the cells inside a body get tiny bits of damage, a little like scratches on a toy. Bodies can fix a lot of that, but not forever. A dog's body grows fast and ages fast, so those scratches pile up sooner. Also, bigger dogs tend to live shorter lives than small dogs, because growing so big so quickly is hard on the body.

A rough rule people use is that one dog year is like several human years, though it isn't exact. So your ten-year-old dog is a bit like a person in their sixties or seventies. That doesn't mean he's about to go, since many dogs live several more years, but it does mean he is an older gentleman now.

The kind part of the answer is this: dogs live their whole lives at full speed, and they love completely in the time they have. The best thing you can do is what you're probably already doing, which is giving him good walks, good food, vet checkups, and lots of cuddles. That's what makes a short life a very happy one.

A brute-force attack is a form of cyberattack where the attacker attempts to discover a password or key by systematically testing every possible character combination until the right one turns up. Attackers commonly use this method to break into password-protected systems or to decrypt data that has been encrypted. To carry it out, the attacker runs a program or script that automatically produces and tests large numbers of character combinations in search of the correct password or key. The program may work through a list of frequently used passwords, or it may simply try every combination that is possible.

Because these attacks usually take a long time, they are often impractical against long or complex passwords. They can still succeed, though, when the passwords are short or weak, or when the attacker has powerful computing resources capable of testing many combinations rapidly. Defending against brute-force attacks calls for strong, complex passwords and for protective measures such as two-factor authentication, which adds an extra step to the login process. Another sensible precaution is to cap the number of failed login attempts permitted before the account is locked.

Since you're a Resident Alien for tax purposes, you might qualify for exemptions under the India-US tax treaty, but you'll need to meet the requirements of a specific treaty provision. The treaty exempts certain income types, like business profits, dividends, interest, and royalties. Each one comes with its own conditions, which could mean being a resident of one of the treaty countries, having a particular kind of business or investment in the other country, or something else entirely. Keep in mind that treaty benefits only apply when they're more favorable than what the Internal Revenue Code already gives you. If the Code already offers a better exemption, the treaty won't help, so you might not be able to use it. If you think you could qualify, talk to a tax pro or read through the treaty's provisions carefully to see what you'd need to meet.

The Guardian is a British daily newspaper, and it is one of the most widely read and influential news outlets in the English-speaking world. It was founded in Manchester in 1821 as The Manchester Guardian by the cotton merchant and journalist John Edward Taylor, with backing from a group of businessmen who supported liberal political reform. It was renamed The Guardian in 1959 as its reach expanded beyond its home region, and it later moved its operations to London.

The paper is generally associated with centre-left and liberal editorial positions. It tends to cover topics such as social justice, climate change, civil liberties, and international development with particular emphasis, and its opinion pages often reflect progressive viewpoints, though it publishes a range of columnists. It is known for its investigative journalism. Notable examples include its reporting on the phone-hacking scandal at News of the World, which led to major inquiries and the closure of that tabloid, and its publication of material leaked by Edward Snowden in 2013 revealing mass surveillance by the United States and British governments. It shared a Pulitzer Prize for Public Service for the Snowden coverage.

Ownership is unusual. The paper is owned by the Scott Trust Limited, set up in 1936 to protect its editorial independence and ensure it would not be subject to the control of a proprietor or commercial interests. Profits are reinvested in journalism rather than paid out to shareholders. Its sister paper, The Observer, is the world's oldest Sunday newspaper, and the two share resources.

The Guardian has also been a pioneer in digital publishing. Its website, theguardian.com, attracts a very large international audience, with editions focused on the UK, the US, Australia, and other regions. Unlike many competitors, it has kept its online content free to read rather than placing it behind a hard paywall, instead asking readers to contribute voluntarily through donations and memberships. The print edition is published in a compact Berliner-sized format, which it adopted in 2005.

Nuance has additionally taken on work in the automotive field, where it has built voice recognition technology for in-car infotainment systems.

Honestly, there's no single right time to pull money out of your investments. It really comes down to what you're investing for, what you need the cash for, and how much risk you can stomach.

People usually cash out for a handful of reasons. Maybe there's a big purchase coming up, like a down payment on a house or a kid's college bill. Maybe something unexpected hits and you need money fast, like an emergency. Some folks pull money out to rebalance, so their mix of stocks and bonds and whatever else stays where they want it. Others try to catch opportunities in the market, buying low or selling high, though that's a lot easier to say than do. And of course, once you hit retirement you'll be withdrawing to live on.

Most people say you're better off thinking long term, since that gives your money more time to grow and maybe earn higher returns. That said, don't just set it and forget it. Take a look at your portfolio every so often to make sure it still fits your goals and your comfort level with risk, and tweak it if it doesn't. And if you're about to make a big change, it's probably worth talking to a financial advisor first.

Land Rover's a British luxury brand, but it's actually owned by Tata Motors, the big Indian automaker. Tata bought it from Ford back in 2008. They're best known for off-road vehicles built to handle rough terrain, so you've got SUVs, pickups, and 4x4s.
