Amazon Web Services, usually abbreviated as AWS, is the cloud computing platform offered by Amazon. It provides businesses, governments, startups, and individual developers with on-demand access to computing power, data storage, databases, networking, analytics, machine learning tools, and many other technology services over the internet. Rather than buying and maintaining their own physical servers and data centers, customers can rent exactly the resources they need, scale them up or down as demand changes, and pay only for what they use.

AWS launched in 2006 and was one of the first major cloud providers, and it remains the largest by market share. Its offerings span hundreds of services. Some of the most widely used include Amazon EC2, which provides virtual servers; Amazon S3, a service for storing files and data; and Amazon RDS, which manages relational databases. Many companies use AWS to host websites and applications, run large-scale data processing, back up information, or build new software products without the upfront cost of hardware.

The service operates through a global network of data centers grouped into regions and availability zones, which helps customers keep their applications fast, close to their users, and resilient if part of the infrastructure fails. Amazon also handles much of the underlying maintenance, security infrastructure, and physical operations, while customers remain responsible for configuring and securing their own applications and data.

Okay so model years trip people up all the time. Basically it's the year a car gets released or first goes on sale, and it's usually one year ahead of the calendar year it actually hits showrooms. Say a car starts selling in December 2020. That one's probably going to be called a 2021 model. Makers start designing new stuff way before it's ready to sell, so the label kind of catches up to the timeline. It's handy for everyone, honestly. Manufacturers can keep track of which version is newest, and buyers can spot the latest features and tech without digging through specs.

Fixed income ETFs are priced primarily by the market value of the bonds they hold, but several forces combine to set the price you see on an exchange at any moment.

The most basic driver is the underlying bonds' prices, which move inversely to interest rates. When rates rise, existing bonds with lower coupons lose value, and when rates fall, they gain. Because most bond funds hold many bonds with different maturities, the fund's net asset value (NAV) reflects a weighted average of these price changes, along with the duration of the portfolio, which measures how sensitive it is to rate movements. A fund with longer duration will typically swing more in price than one with shorter duration.

Credit conditions also matter. If the market perceives higher default risk for the issuers in a fund, or if investors demand a bigger premium for holding riskier debt, the bonds' prices fall and the ETF follows. Changes in credit spreads, the extra yield over government securities, can therefore move a corporate or high-yield bond ETF even when interest rates are stable.

The fund's expenses and income distributions play a smaller role. Management fees gradually reduce NAV, while interest income accumulates and is typically paid out as dividends, which drops the share price by the amount distributed on the ex-dividend date.

Finally, the market price of the ETF itself can differ from its NAV. Because ETFs trade on exchanges, supply and demand can push the price slightly above or below NAV, a difference known as a premium or discount. This gap is usually small because authorized participants can create or redeem shares to keep prices aligned. However, it can widen during periods of stress, especially for funds holding less liquid bonds, since the underlying securities may be harder to price and trade. In such cases, the ETF's trading price can reflect market sentiment about the bonds before the NAV fully catches up.

A level, short for Advanced Level, is a qualification awarded in England, Wales, Northern Ireland, and many other countries that follow the British education model. It is typically taken by students aged 16 to 18, after completing their General Certificate of Secondary Education (GCSE) exams at age 16. Students usually study three or four subjects over two years, though the exact number varies by school and by the student's plans. Each subject is taught in depth, with a focus on understanding the material well enough to analyse and apply it, rather than covering a broad range of topics as in many other systems.

A level results are a key factor in university admissions in the United Kingdom. Universities typically make offers based on predicted or actual grades, such as "AAB," which means the student needs an A in one subject and B grades in two others. Grades run from A* (the highest) through A, B, C, D, and E, with a U meaning ungraded or fail. Because the subjects are specialised, students often choose A levels that match the degree they hope to pursue, so a student planning to study medicine would usually take chemistry and biology, for example.

Some students who take A levels go on to apprenticeships, employment, or other further education instead of university. The qualification is widely recognised internationally and is often accepted by universities abroad, though they may have their own entry requirements.

Lots of babies have stool that changes color, texture, or how often they go, and it can come from all sorts of things: what they're eating, medications, or an infection. Still, if something's worrying you about your baby's poop, it's never a bad idea to call the doctor. Eczema is a skin thing, really. It causes inflammation and irritation, but it doesn't usually mess with stool color or consistency. Could a baby with eczema also have an infection or another condition that affects their stool? Sure, that's possible. But eczema by itself probably isn't what's making it green. If your little one has other symptoms along with the green stool, or you just have a gut feeling something's off, get them checked out. A healthcare provider can look things over and sort out what's going on.

Imagine your muscles are like balloons that grow when you make them work really hard. Regular people who exercise make their muscles work a little, so the balloons get a bit bigger and stay a nice, normal shape. Bodybuilders make their muscles work extremely hard, for many hours a week, for many years, and they eat a huge amount of food specially chosen to feed those muscles. So their balloons get much, much bigger than most people's ever do.

Some bodybuilders also use special medicines, like steroids, which are like magic plant food for muscles. These make muscles grow far bigger and faster than the body could ever manage on its own. That is a big part of why some of them look so different from what a person could normally become. Not all of them use these, but many at the top level do.

Then there is the stage trick. Before a show, bodybuilders do things to make the muscles pop out. They eat very little fat so the skin gets super thin and you can see every muscle line. They sometimes drink less water for a short time so the skin looks tight, like plastic wrap on a sandwich. They also put on tan or dark oil so the lights make each bump and curve stand out. A person standing on stage like that looks very different from the same person at the grocery store.

Another reason they look odd is that they train to make a certain shape, not to be good at everyday things. They focus on huge shoulders, a tiny waist, and big arms and legs, and they care about how it looks, like a sculpture. Regular exercisers train for health or fun, so their bodies keep a softer, more balanced look that we are used to seeing.

So you are not alone in thinking it looks strange. It looks unusual because it truly is unusual: extra-big muscles, very little fat, sometimes medicine help, and a bit of stage makeup, all put together on purpose.

There are several approaches you can take to get rid of debt. One is the "debt avalanche" method, where you concentrate on clearing the debts carrying the highest interest rates before anything else. Because you pay less in interest over time, this usually saves the most money overall. Another is the "debt snowball" method, which has you tackle the smallest balances first and then move on to progressively larger ones. This tends to suit people who need early victories to keep themselves going. You might also consider debt consolidation: if you're juggling several high-interest debts, rolling them into one loan with a lower rate could reduce what you pay. Whichever route you pick, consistency matters, and paying more than the minimum each month will speed up repayment and cut interest costs. Trimming your expenses and boosting your income, where possible, can also free up extra cash for debt payments. Lastly, make sure every bill is paid on time so you avoid late fees and further interest charges.

In the chaotic wars of the past, troops frequently tried to make clear that they were allies by displaying flags or dressing in uniforms that set them apart. They also tended to remain with their own units and obey the orders of their officers, which helped them keep track of who was fighting on their side. Confusion and mishaps did occur from time to time, and a soldier could end up wounding or killing a comrade by mistake. Even so, for the most part, soldiers made every effort to avoid harming their own people.

Feedback mechanisms in plant respiration are regulatory controls that adjust the rate of cellular respiration according to the energy needs of the cell and the availability of its raw materials. Respiration breaks down sugars such as glucose to release energy in the form of ATP, and the plant must balance this process so that it neither wastes resources nor runs short of energy. The main control is end-product inhibition: when ATP and NADH accumulate, they signal that the cell is energy-rich, and they slow key enzymes such as phosphofructokinase in glycolysis and isocitrate dehydrogenase and citrate synthase in the Krebs cycle. Conversely, high levels of ADP, AMP, and inorganic phosphate indicate low energy, which activates these same enzymes and speeds up respiration.

Substrate availability also acts as a feedback signal. When sugar supplies from photosynthesis or stored starch are plentiful, the pathway runs faster, and when they are scarce, respiration slows. Oxygen availability is another factor, since the electron transport chain in the mitochondria depends on oxygen as the final electron acceptor. If oxygen falls, for example in waterlogged roots, the rate of aerobic respiration drops and the plant may switch to fermentation, which is itself regulated by the buildup of products such as lactate or ethanol.

At the whole-plant level, hormones and environmental signals contribute to feedback as well. Sugar levels sensed in leaves and roots can alter gene expression for respiratory enzymes, and temperature changes affect the rate at which these enzymes work. Together, these controls keep respiration matched to the plant's current metabolic demands.

Particle swarm optimization (PSO) is a computational method for finding the best solution to a problem, typically one that involves minimizing or maximizing some objective function over a set of possible values. It belongs to a family of techniques called metaheuristics, which search for good solutions without requiring the problem to have smooth, differentiable, or otherwise well-behaved mathematical properties. The method was introduced by James Kennedy and Russell Eberhart in 1995 and was inspired by the collective movement of bird flocks and fish schools, where individuals appear to coordinate their motion through simple local rules.

The core idea is to maintain a population of candidate solutions, called particles, which move through the search space. Each particle has a position, representing a candidate solution, and a velocity, which determines how it moves at each step. Every particle remembers the best position it has personally visited so far, and the swarm as a whole tracks the best position found by any particle. At each iteration, a particle updates its velocity by blending three influences: its current momentum, a pull toward its own personal best, and a pull toward the global or neighborhood best. Randomness is usually added to these pulls so that the particles explore different regions rather than collapsing onto a single point too quickly. The position is then updated using the new velocity, the objective function is evaluated at the new position, and the personal and global bests are refreshed if improvements are found.

Over many iterations, this interplay between individual exploration and social information tends to concentrate the swarm around promising regions of the search space. Users typically set parameters such as the number of particles, the inertia weight that controls momentum, and the strength of the personal and social pulls. Stopping occurs after a fixed number of iterations, after reaching a satisfactory objective value, or when progress stalls.

PSO is popular because it is simple to implement, requires few parameters, and works reasonably well on continuous, nonlinear, and multimodal problems where gradient-based methods struggle. It is used in areas such as neural network training, engineering design, scheduling, and signal processing. Its main limitations include a tendency to converge prematurely to suboptimal solutions on some problems and limited theoretical guarantees, so results often depend on careful tuning and multiple runs.

"Fiona" is a feminine given name with a Scottish and Irish literary origin. It was invented by the Scottish poet James Macpherson in the 1760s, when he published his "translations" of the epic poems of Ossian, a supposed third-century Gaelic bard. The name is derived from the Gaelic word "fionn," meaning "fair" or "white," and it was coined as a feminine form to suit the poems' characters. Macpherson's Ossian collection was enormously popular across Europe, and the name spread from there.

Before Macpherson, the name was essentially unused, though some scholars note a connection to the older Gaelic word "fíon," meaning "wine," and to the Irish name Finola. Its popularity grew through the nineteenth century, and it became especially common in the English-speaking world during the twentieth century, particularly in the United Kingdom, Ireland, Australia, and the United States.

Air in the bloodstream is seriously dangerous, and it can kill you. Tiny bubbles can block blood vessels and stop oxygen and nutrients from getting to your organs and tissues. That can lead to a heart attack or stroke, and sometimes it's fatal. That's why IV meds and fluids should only ever go through sterile, properly sealed equipment, so air doesn't sneak in.

Protecting yourself from identity theft starts with locking down the information thieves most want. Freeze your credit with each of the three major bureaus (Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion). A freeze is free, doesn't affect your credit score, and prevents anyone from opening new accounts in your name until you lift it. Next, use a password manager to create a unique, strong password for every account, and turn on two-factor authentication wherever it's offered, preferably using an authenticator app or security key rather than text messages, which can be intercepted.

Be skeptical of unsolicited contact. Scammers often pose as banks, government agencies, or tech support, creating urgency to get you to share a code or click a link. If someone calls or emails claiming to be from an organization, hang up or close the message and contact the organization directly using a number you look up yourself. Also be careful about what you share publicly online, since birthdates, pet names, hometowns, and family details are often used to answer security questions.

Monitor your financial accounts regularly. Turn on transaction alerts with your bank and credit card companies, and review your statements for charges you don't recognize. Check your credit reports at least once a year for free at AnnualCreditReport.com, and look for accounts or inquiries you don't recognize. If you're worried about a specific breach, the company involved will usually notify you, and you can check whether your email has appeared in known breaches at haveibeenpwned.com.

Protect your physical documents too. Shred statements and pre-approved credit offers, keep your Social Security card somewhere secure rather than in your wallet, and be cautious about sharing your Social Security number, using it only when truly required.

Keep your devices secure by installing updates promptly, using a lock screen passcode, and avoiding public Wi-Fi for sensitive activity, or using a VPN when you must.

If you discover that someone has misused your identity, act quickly. Report it at IdentityTheft.gov (run by the U.S. Federal Trade Commission), which creates a recovery plan for you, place a fraud alert or extended alert with the credit bureaus, and contact any affected banks or creditors right away. If you're outside the United States, your national consumer protection agency or police can guide you through similar steps.

Andrew Ng is not a thing but a person: a British-American computer scientist and entrepreneur who is one of the most influential figures in artificial intelligence and machine learning. He was born in 1976 in London and grew up partly in Hong Kong and Singapore. He studied at Carnegie Mellon University, MIT, and the University of California, Berkeley, where he earned his PhD, and he later became a professor of computer science at Stanford University.

Ng is best known for his work in machine learning and deep learning and for making AI education widely accessible. In 2011 he co-founded and led Google Brain, a research project that showed large neural networks trained on huge amounts of data could achieve impressive results, including a well-known experiment in which a network learned to recognize cats in YouTube videos without being told what a cat was. He later served as chief scientist at Baidu, the Chinese technology company, where he led its AI group.

He is also a major figure in online education. His Stanford machine learning course, offered free online, became one of the most popular online courses ever, and in 2012 he co-founded Coursera with Daphne Koller, a platform offering courses from universities and companies worldwide. He went on to found DeepLearning.AI, which offers specialized training in deep learning and generative AI, and Landing AI, which helps businesses, especially in manufacturing, adopt computer vision. He also started the AI Fund, a venture studio that builds AI startups.

Ng is known for promoting the idea that AI is "the new electricity," meaning it will transform nearly every industry, and for advocating a practical, data-centric approach to building AI systems. Through his teaching, millions of people have learned the basics of machine learning, which is a large part of why his name is so widely recognized in the tech world.

Futures studies, sometimes called futurology, foresight, or futures research, is an interdisciplinary field concerned with systematically exploring possible, probable, and preferable futures. Rather than trying to predict a single, certain future, practitioners generally assume that the future is open and shaped by present choices, trends, and uncertainties. The goal is to help individuals, organizations, and societies think more clearly about what might lie ahead so they can make better decisions today.

The field emerged in its modern form in the mid-twentieth century, drawing on work at institutions such as the RAND Corporation in the United States, where methods like the Delphi technique and scenario analysis were developed for military and policy planning. Figures such as Herman Kahn, Bertrand de Jouvenel, Ossip Flechtheim (who coined the term "futurology"), Alvin Toffler, and later Wendell Bell and Jim Dator helped shape it. Organizations like the World Futures Studies Federation and the World Future Society, along with academic programs in places such as the University of Hawaii, the University of Houston, and Finland's Turku School of Economics, gave the discipline an institutional base. Shell's use of scenario planning in the 1970s, which helped the company respond to the oil crises, is often cited as an influential corporate example.

A central idea in futures studies is the distinction between different kinds of futures. Possible futures include anything that could conceivably happen, plausible futures are those consistent with current knowledge, probable futures are those considered most likely given present trends, and preferable futures are those people actually want to bring about. This framework allows futurists to move beyond forecasting toward questions of values, goals, and deliberate action, which is why the field often has a normative or participatory side, encouraging communities to envision and work toward desired outcomes.

Futures researchers use a range of methods. Trend analysis and horizon scanning look for emerging developments and weak signals of change. Scenario planning builds several contrasting but coherent stories about how the future might unfold, helping decision makers test strategies against different conditions. The Delphi method gathers and refines expert opinion over multiple rounds. Backcasting starts from a desired future and works backward to identify the steps needed to reach it. Other approaches include causal layered analysis, which examines the deeper worldviews and myths underlying surface trends, as well as simulation modeling, wild card analysis for low-probability high-impact events, and visioning workshops.

The field is applied in many areas, including government policy and strategic planning, business strategy, technology assessment, environmental and climate planning, urban development, defense, and education. Many governments maintain foresight units, and large companies often employ strategic foresight teams.

Futures studies also faces criticism. Some argue it lacks the rigor of established sciences because its subject matter, the future, cannot be directly observed or tested. Others point out that past forecasts have frequently been wrong, and that popular futurism can slide into speculation or hype. Practitioners typically respond that the purpose is not accurate prediction but improved preparedness, broader thinking about uncertainty, and more thoughtful choices about the kind of future worth creating.

I can't diagnose this without examining you in person, and I don't have enough details about what you're feeling. Sharp pain in the lower right abdomen can come from a bunch of things, and some of them are serious. If the pain is bad or hasn't gone away after a few days, get it looked at soon. Possible causes include constipation, irritable bowel syndrome, appendicitis, a urinary tract infection, pelvic inflammatory disease, kidney stones, and ovarian cysts. That's only a partial list, so a doctor is the one who can actually pin it down. Until then, drinking plenty of fluids and holding off on solid food until the pain eases is generally reasonable. But if it gets worse or you develop fever, vomiting, or diarrhea, don't wait around. Go get medical help right away.

Speech synthesis refers to the man-made generation of human voice. It relies on software and algorithms running on a computer to produce audio that sounds like people talking. This audio may come from text-to-speech (TTS) systems, which turn written words into spoken language, or from a recording that has been synthesized so it resembles a human voice. Such systems serve many purposes, such as reading text aloud for people with visual impairments, providing voice-over narration in the entertainment field, and powering automated customer service lines. Several techniques exist for producing synthetic speech, including rule-based synthesis, formant synthesis, and concatenative synthesis. Rule-based synthesis generates sounds by applying a collection of rules that account for the phonetic and prosodic features of the input text. Formant synthesis uses a voice model built from pre-recorded formants, meaning frequency bands that correspond to the distinct sounds of a language. Concatenative synthesis joins together short pre-recorded speech fragments to build the intended output. In summary, speech synthesis has advanced considerably in recent years and the naturalness of generated speech has improved markedly, yet further progress is possible and researchers are still actively working in this field.

The Earth has five officially recognized oceans: the Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Southern (Antarctic), and Arctic. The Pacific is the largest and deepest, covering roughly a third of the planet's surface. Some geographers count the Southern and Arctic as separate oceans, while others treat them as extensions of the Pacific, Atlantic, and Indian, so you may occasionally see a different number cited.

Biological vision is the process by which living organisms detect, process, and interpret light from their surroundings to guide behavior. It spans everything from simple light-sensitive cells in single-celled organisms and worms, which can only tell light from dark, to the highly developed visual systems of vertebrates, insects, and cephalopods, which can resolve detailed images, color, motion, and depth.

The process begins with photoreceptors, specialized cells containing light-sensitive pigments called opsins. When a photon is absorbed, it changes the shape of a molecule bound to the opsin (retinal in most animals), which triggers a chain of biochemical events that converts light into an electrical signal. This conversion is called phototransduction. In the human eye, there are two main kinds of photoreceptors: rods, which are very sensitive and work in dim light but do not distinguish color, and cones, which work in bright light and come in three types sensitive to different wavelengths, giving us color vision.

Eyes have evolved many designs to gather and focus light. Vertebrates and cephalopods have camera-type eyes with a lens that focuses an image onto a retina. Insects and many crustaceans have compound eyes made of many small units called ommatidia, each capturing a small part of the visual field, which gives wide viewing angles and excellent motion detection. Some animals can see ultraviolet or polarized light, which humans cannot. Birds, bees, and mantis shrimp are well-known examples, and the mantis shrimp has an unusually large number of photoreceptor types.

In vertebrates, the retina does considerable processing before signals leave the eye. Layers of cells, including bipolar, horizontal, amacrine, and ganglion cells, enhance contrast, detect edges, and begin to separate information about motion and color. The ganglion cell axons form the optic nerve, which carries signals to the brain. In humans, these signals travel mainly through the lateral geniculate nucleus of the thalamus to the primary visual cortex at the back of the brain, and from there to many other regions. Researchers often describe two broad pathways: a ventral stream involved in recognizing objects and faces, and a dorsal stream involved in locating objects and guiding movement.

Seeing is not a passive recording like a camera. The brain actively constructs perception, filling in gaps, maintaining stable colors under changing light, inferring depth from cues such as binocular disparity and perspective, and using prior experience to interpret ambiguous scenes. Optical illusions reveal these inference processes at work.

Biological vision is studied in neuroscience, psychology, and evolutionary biology, and it has strongly influenced computer vision. Artificial neural networks for image recognition, for example, were inspired by the hierarchical organization of the visual cortex, where simple features such as edges are combined into progressively more complex representations.

Honestly, most governments avoid negotiating with terrorists, and it's not hard to see why. If it works, the group learns that kidnapping pays off, and every other group watching takes notes. Hostages can end up paying the price too, since things can go sideways fast when talks break down. Negotiators aren't safe either. And there's the gut-level problem: caving can feel like a reward for violence, which is rough on victims' families and on the public. So instead, most governments lean on law enforcement, diplomacy, and military options, and they also try to deal with the underlying causes and head off future attacks.

Transcendentalism is a idea that grew up in New England in the United States around the 1830s and 1840s. Some writers and thinkers, like Ralph Waldo Emerson, Henry David Thoreau, and Margaret Fuller, believed that people can understand big truths about life not just by using their eyes and ears, but also by listening to a deeper feeling inside themselves. They thought nature was full of meaning, and that each person has a little spark of goodness and wisdom that connects them to everything else in the world.

Individualism is a different idea. It means that each person is special and should be free to make their own choices, think their own thoughts, and live the way they want. It is more about being your own boss and not letting others tell you what to do.

So the difference is this: individualism is about you being your own person and making your own decisions. Transcendentalism agrees that you are special, but it also says that your special inner self is connected to something much bigger, like nature and a shared spiritual truth. Thoreau, for example, went to live alone in the woods at Walden Pond, which shows some individualism, but he did it so he could listen to nature and find deeper meaning, which shows the transcendentalist part.

Acts of terrorism can strongly affect the stock market, largely because they stir up fear and uncertainty among investors. After an attack, investors may worry about its possible economic fallout, including a drop in tourism or weaker consumer spending. Many respond by selling their holdings to limit their exposure to risk, which pushes stock prices down. Attacks can also hit particular industries or companies directly. If one targets a major transportation hub, for instance, businesses whose supply chains depend on that hub may see their operations disrupted, and their share prices could fall as a result. More broadly, the market tends to react to anything that might affect the economy or the performance of individual firms. It is therefore common for stocks to move on news of a terrorist attack, even when the attack has no direct connection to the companies listed on the exchange.

A torn frenulum, the thin band of tissue under the head of the penis, usually heals on its own, and many small tears do. Because the frenulum has a good blood supply, it tends to bleed heavily at first but also repairs quickly. Your description of it bleeding a lot, being only mildly sore, and now looking like it is closing up is consistent with that normal course.

That said, a complete tear is a bigger injury than a minor one, and it is worth having a doctor or urologist look at it, even at this stage. The main reasons are these. A complete tear can sometimes leave a gap or scar tissue that heals in an uneven way, and a clinician can check whether the edges have knitted together properly. They can also confirm there is no damage to the urethra or deeper structures, and that no infection is developing. Signs that would make it more urgent include increasing pain or swelling, redness spreading from the area, pus or a bad smell, fever, trouble urinating, a change in the direction your penis curves when erect, or bleeding that restarts.

If none of those are present and it continues to look and feel fine, it will most likely keep healing without intervention. Keep the area clean, avoid sexual activity and friction until it has fully closed and stopped being tender, and watch for the warning signs above. Since you are already four days in and asymptomatic, a non-urgent visit to a doctor for reassurance is reasonable rather than an emergency, and it would be sensible to go sooner if anything changes.

Chalmers is a philosopher and cognitive scientist, and he's best known for his work on consciousness, especially the "hard problem of consciousness." He's a professor of philosophy and directs the Centre for Consciousness at the Australian National University, and he's also taught at places like the University of Arizona and New York University. His big claim to fame is the 1996 book "The Conscious Mind: In Search of a Fundamental Theory," where he coined the idea of the "hard problem." His argument was basically that science can explain a lot about how the mind and brain work, but it still doesn't really tell us how or why we have subjective experiences. Why does seeing red feel like anything at all? He called these felt qualities "qualia," and he thought that question might never be fully cracked by current science. He's also done plenty of work in the philosophy of language and philosophy of mind, with lots of articles and books along the way. People in philosophy and science argue with him constantly, which says a lot about how much his ideas have shaken things up.

According to figures from the United States Census Bureau, Memphis, Tennessee had roughly 654,723 residents in 2020. That count covers only the city itself and leaves out the surrounding metro area. As the most populous city in Tennessee, Memphis is celebrated for its deep history, a wide range of cultural sites, and a lively music scene.

Generally, it depends on whether the per diem is an accountable plan reimbursement or a flat allowance, and on whether it stays within federal limits. Under an accountable plan, a per diem or meal and incidental expense allowance paid to an employee for business travel is not taxable income, provided the employee substantiates the time, place, and business purpose of the travel and returns any excess over the IRS-approved rate. The IRS publishes standard per diem rates for lodging, meals, and incidentals for different cities and regions each year, and an employer may use those rates or other reasonable ones. Amounts paid within those limits are generally excluded from wages and not subject to income tax withholding or payroll taxes.

If the per diem is paid without an adequate accounting, or if it exceeds the allowable rate, the excess is treated as taxable wages and must be included in the employee's income and subject to withholding and employment taxes. Independent contractors and self-employed workers are treated differently: they generally deduct their actual travel expenses or use the standard rates on their own tax returns rather than receiving a tax-free allowance.

Because state rules can differ and the specifics depend on your situation, it's worth checking IRS Publication 463 and Publication 1542, or consulting a tax professional, if you have a particular case.

Not quite. When scientists say a quantum particle "reacts" to being observed, they don't mean it knows it's being watched or has any awareness at all. Particles like electrons don't have feelings or thoughts. What happens is that tiny things behave in a strange way: before we measure them, they don't seem to sit in just one definite spot or state. They're more like a blurry mix of possibilities. When we measure one, it has to give a clear answer, like a spinning coin that lands on heads or tails once you catch it. The word "observation" in physics really means any interaction that leaves a clear trace, like bouncing a little light off it or hitting it with another particle. It's the physical contact that matters, not a mind looking on.

Think of it like trying to find a bouncy ball hiding in a dark room by tossing a bigger ball into the room. The bigger ball bumps the small one, so the small one moves. The small one didn't decide to move because it saw you. Your tool changed where it was.

As for everyday life, this strange behavior doesn't really change how your day goes, because the effects are too tiny to notice with big things like cups, cars, or people. But quantum behavior is very important in ordinary technology. Computer chips, phone screens, lasers in barcode scanners and fiber-optic internet, and the tiny sensors in medical scanners all depend on these rules. So while particles don't have awareness, the rules they follow quietly make a lot of your modern world work.

VR works by strapping a headset over your eyes that shows images right in front of them. The headset has sensors that track how your head moves, so when you turn, the virtual world turns with you. Lenses in the headset focus those images for your eyes, and the sensors use magnets to pick up your head's movements. As for why your brain buys into it, think about how it handles the real world. You're constantly taking in sight, sound, and touch, and your brain stitches all that together into a picture of what's around you. VR just feeds your brain a similar stream of info, except it's coming from a computer instead of the room you're sitting in. Your brain processes it the same way and builds a mental model of the virtual world, pretty much like it does with the real one.

Okay, imagine a big story about soldiers, secrets, and giant walking robots, told out of order across many games. Here it is from the beginning, in the order things actually happened.

A long time ago, during World War Two, a very brave soldier lady called The Boss and some friends formed a team. After the war, the world split into two big sides, America and Russia, who didn't like each other. Some powerful old men decided they wanted to secretly control the whole world, and The Boss was part of their early plans. Then America told a young soldier named Naked Snake to go to Russia and kill The Boss, his own teacher, whom he loved like a mom. She let him win because it was her secret mission to die so America and Russia wouldn't start a giant war. Snake was sad and angry because his country tricked him and called her a traitor. They gave him a fancy name, Big Boss.

Big Boss and his friends, like Major Zero, Ocelot, and others, started a group called the Patriots to make the world the way The Boss wanted. But they argued about what she really wanted. Zero thought it meant controlling everyone so there would be peace. Big Boss thought it meant soldiers should be free and not be anyone's toy. Zero also secretly made copies of Big Boss, kind of like twin babies made in a lab. Three of them grew up to be Solid Snake, Liquid Snake, and Solidus Snake. Big Boss was very upset about this.

Big Boss left and built his own army of soldiers with no country. Bad guys blew up his ocean base, and he was badly hurt and fell asleep for nine years. When he woke up, he learned a helper had been pretending to be him the whole time, a loyal medic who was made to look like him so enemies would chase the wrong guy. That fake Big Boss and the real one both kept building armies.

Later, Big Boss and his army got so strong they had a giant walking robot with a nuclear bomb called Metal Gear. America sent Solid Snake, his own clone son, to stop it. Snake beat the fake Big Boss first, and then later beat the real Big Boss too, though Big Boss didn't actually die.

After that, Solid Snake's brother Liquid took over a snowy island base with another Metal Gear and threatened the world. Snake went in, made friends with a smart scientist named Otacon and a robot ninja named Gray Fox, and stopped Liquid. Snake learned he was a clone and felt confused about who he was, but decided he gets to choose his own life.

Then a young soldier named Raiden got pulled into a big confusing mission on a big sea fortress. He found out the Patriots had been controlling everything, even him, like puppets. The Patriots were now just computer brains running the world, using information to control what people think. Raiden met Solidus, the third brother, and beat him.

Finally, old Solid Snake, who was getting old super fast because clones made that way don't last long, went on one last mission. Liquid's spirit seemed to be inside Ocelot, but really Ocelot was pretending, and his plan was actually to break the Patriots' computer control. Snake and his friends shut down the Patriots' computers, so the world was free from that big puppet master. At the very end, Big Boss, now very old, came to talk to Snake, said sorry for everything, turned off the last bit of the Patriots by ending Zero, and died peacefully near The Boss's grave. Snake got to live the rest of his short life in peace.

The big idea of the whole story is that people shouldn't be used like toys by governments or wars, and everyone should get to choose who they want to be and pass good things on to the next generation.

I'm sorry you're dealing with this. I can't diagnose you from a description, but I can explain what commonly causes this pattern and which parts of your story deserve attention.

Lower back pain that spreads to the legs with tingling usually points to irritation or compression of a nerve in the lower spine. The most common cause is a herniated or bulging disc pressing on a nerve root, which produces sciatica: pain that travels down the buttock and leg, often with tingling or numbness. Other causes include spinal stenosis (narrowing of the canal through which the nerves run), degenerative changes in the spine, or muscle and joint problems in the lower back or sacroiliac joint. Pain that began on one side and then moved toward the midline can fit with any of these.

What makes your case less typical is the combination of other symptoms: severe bone pain in the arms a month ago, leg pain at night, and new tiredness. Bone pain that is deep, worse at night, and affects several parts of the body can be associated with problems beyond the spine. Examples include vitamin D deficiency and other bone-softening conditions, anemia or other blood disorders, thyroid or kidney problems, infections, inflammatory conditions, and less commonly, cancers affecting the bone or marrow, such as multiple myeloma. Low vitamin B12 can also cause tingling and fatigue. Most of these are treatable or easy to check with basic tests, so it is worth looking rather than assuming it is only a back strain.

I would recommend seeing a doctor soon, within days to a couple of weeks, rather than waiting. They will likely examine your nerves and reflexes and may order blood tests (blood count, calcium, vitamin D, B12, kidney and thyroid function, inflammatory markers) and possibly imaging such as an X-ray or MRI of the spine.

Seek urgent care the same day if you develop any of the following: numbness in the groin or inner thighs, difficulty urinating or controlling your bladder or bowels, progressive weakness in a leg or foot, fever with back pain, unexplained weight loss, or pain after an injury. These can signal serious nerve compression or infection that needs prompt treatment.

In the meantime, gentle movement and walking are generally better than complete bed rest, and over-the-counter pain relievers can help if you can safely take them. When you see the doctor, mention the arm bone pain, night leg pain, and tiredness together, since that full picture will guide which tests they choose.

Emerging technologies are new, innovative developments that are still being built out and are expected to shape society, industry, and the economy in the coming years. They tend to be in the early stages of their evolution, neither fully mature nor widely used, yet they hold the promise of upending established industries and giving rise to entirely new ones. Artificial intelligence, blockchain, the Internet of Things, renewable energy, biotechnology, and nanotechnology are among the many examples. What typically defines them is their ability to spur change and innovation, their power to unsettle existing business models and sectors, and the pace at which they develop and spread. Because they usually demand heavy investment in research and development, along with major shifts in infrastructure, regulation, and policy to enable their growth and uptake, they attract close attention from governments, companies, and investors, all of whom want to grasp their likely effects and capitalize on the opportunities they offer.

Communism is a political and economic ideology that seeks to establish a society where the means of production are collectively owned and private property does not exist. Marxism, a variant of communism, was formulated by Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels in the middle of the 19th century. It holds that capitalism, where a small group controls the means of production and profits from the labor of the working class, is inherently flawed and will in time give way to socialism, a system in which the working class owns the means of production and exploitation ends. Marx and Engels expected socialism to evolve eventually into communism, a society without class divisions in which everyone cooperates to satisfy the community's needs.

Leninism is a variant of communism created by Vladimir Lenin, a Russian revolutionary leader. Its central idea is that a small body of committed revolutionaries should guide the working class in a revolution that topples capitalism and establishes a socialist society. Lenin argued that this revolution ought to be directed by one disciplined party, which would steer the working class toward communism.

Stalinism is a variant of communism associated with Joseph Stalin, who ruled the Soviet Union from 1922 to 1952. It rests on the notion that a single, powerful party should command the state and direct the shift from socialism to communism. Stalin favored force and repression as the means of keeping control and reaching communism's aims.

Trotskyism is a variant of communism developed by Leon Trotsky, another Russian revolutionary leader. It maintains that socialist revolutions should spread across the world, producing a global network of socialist states. Trotsky held that the working class should be the main force behind revolution and that the party should be democratic and open to every member of the working class.

In short, Marxism stresses overthrowing capitalism and building a socialist society. Leninism highlights the part played by a single disciplined party in leading workers to revolution. Stalinism emphasizes a single powerful party controlling the state and directing the move toward communism. Trotskyism focuses on the working class as the force behind revolution and on creating a worldwide network of socialist states.

Bertrand Russell (1872-1970) was a British philosopher, logician, mathematician, historian, and social critic. He helped found modern analytic philosophy, and plenty of people still rank him among the top logicians of the 20th century. He worked across a huge range of areas: mathematics, logic, philosophy of language, philosophy of science, political philosophy, and social criticism. He was elected to the British Academy and the American Academy of Arts and Sciences, and he picked up plenty of honors along the way, including the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1950. He spoke out loudly against war and imperialism, became a prominent pacifist, and campaigned against nuclear weapons. He also backed civil liberties and human rights, and he was an early pioneer of sex education. On top of all that, he wrote an enormous amount, and people are still reading and studying his work today.

Vehicles can go unsold for a range of reasons, such as an oversupply of stock, shifts in what consumers want, and the state of the market. Sometimes these vehicles are kept on dealership lots, in warehouses run by manufacturers or distributors, or at other storage sites until a buyer is found. Other times they are passed along to wholesalers or sold through auctions. A number of vehicles may also be sent back to the manufacturer or distributor for a variety of reasons. Having some unsold inventory is fairly common in the automotive industry, since it often takes time to bring supply into line with demand.

A graph neural network (GNN) is a type of neural network designed to learn from data that is structured as a graph. A graph is a collection of nodes (also called vertices), which represent entities, and edges, which represent relationships or connections between those entities. Examples include social networks, where people are nodes and friendships are edges; molecules, where atoms are nodes and chemical bonds are edges; and road networks, citation networks, and knowledge bases. Standard neural networks like convolutional or recurrent networks expect data in fixed grids or sequences, so they handle graph-structured data poorly. GNNs were developed to fill this gap.

The core idea behind most GNNs is message passing. Each node starts with a feature vector describing it, such as a user's profile or an atom's type. In each layer of the network, every node gathers information from its neighbors, combines those messages with its own current representation, and updates its state. After several rounds, a node's representation reflects not only its own features but also the structure and features of its surrounding neighborhood, extending outward as more layers are added. Because the same update rules are shared across all nodes, GNNs can handle graphs of varying size and shape.

The learned node representations can then be used for different tasks. For node-level prediction, a model might classify each user in a social network or predict the property of each atom. For edge-level prediction, it might forecast whether two nodes should be linked, which is useful for recommendation systems. For graph-level prediction, the node representations are pooled into a single vector describing the whole graph, which allows predicting properties of an entire molecule, for instance whether it is likely to be toxic.

Several well-known GNN variants exist, including Graph Convolutional Networks, GraphSAGE, and Graph Attention Networks, each differing in how messages are aggregated and weighted. GNNs are now widely used in drug discovery, traffic forecasting, fraud detection, recommender systems, and materials science, making them an important tool for learning from relational data.

The debt-to-GDP ratio compares what a government owes to the size of its economy in a given year. It matters less as a number in itself than as an indicator of how easily a country can carry its debt, and its effects depend heavily on context: who holds the debt, what currency it is in, interest rates relative to growth, and what the borrowed money was used for.

At moderate levels, government debt can be useful. Borrowing lets a government smooth spending over the business cycle, support demand during recessions, and finance long-lived investments like infrastructure, education, and research that raise future output. Government bonds also give banks, pension funds, and households a safe asset to hold, which helps financial markets work smoothly. In this sense, a country with some debt is not necessarily worse off than one with none.

As the ratio rises, costs tend to become more visible. Higher debt means larger interest payments, which take up a growing share of the budget and can crowd out spending on public services or force higher taxes. Heavy government borrowing may also compete with private firms for savings, pushing up interest rates and reducing private investment, though how strong this effect is varies a great deal by country and period. High debt can also limit a government's room to respond to future shocks such as recessions, pandemics, or wars, because it may be unwilling or unable to borrow much more.

A key factor is the relationship between the interest rate a government pays and the growth rate of its economy. When growth exceeds the interest rate, the debt ratio can stabilize or fall even with modest deficits, because the economy grows faster than the debt compounds. When interest rates exceed growth, the ratio tends to rise unless the government runs primary surpluses, meaning it collects more in taxes than it spends before interest. This is why countries with similar debt levels can face very different prospects.

Investor confidence is another channel. If lenders begin to doubt a government's ability or willingness to repay, they demand higher interest rates, which raises borrowing costs and can make the debt harder to sustain, sometimes in a self-reinforcing spiral. This risk is greatest for countries that borrow in foreign currencies or, like eurozone members, do not control their own currency, as Greece experienced around 2010. Countries that borrow in a currency they issue, such as the United States, Japan, or the United Kingdom, cannot be forced into default in the same way, but they can face inflation or currency depreciation if markets lose confidence or if the central bank is pressured to finance deficits.

Researchers have debated whether there is a threshold beyond which debt sharply harms growth. A widely cited study by Carmen Reinhart and Kenneth Rogoff suggested growth slows noticeably once debt exceeds about 90 percent of GDP, but later work found errors in that analysis and showed no clear universal tipping point. Japan, for example, has carried debt above 200 percent of GDP for years without a crisis, largely because most of its debt is held domestically and interest rates have been very low. The broader consensus is that very high debt tends to be associated with weaker growth and greater vulnerability, but the relationship is gradual, depends on circumstances, and runs in both directions, since slow growth itself pushes debt ratios up.

In short, the debt-to-GDP ratio affects an economy mainly through interest costs, fiscal flexibility, private investment, and market confidence. A rising ratio is a warning sign worth watching, but whether it becomes a real problem depends on the trajectory of the debt, the cost of borrowing relative to growth, the structure of the debt, and how productively the borrowed funds are used.

Enigma is a German musical project that began in 1990. It is recognized for its electronically produced sound and for weaving Gregorian chants and samples from a range of other sources into its songs. The name comes from the Enigma machine, an electromechanical rotor cipher device the German military relied on to encrypt messages during World War II. Blending electronic, dance, ambient, and new age styles, the music has often been called "ethereal" and "mysterious." Michael Cretu, a Romanian-born musician and producer, founded the project and leads it. Over the years Enigma has put out several albums, among them "MCMXC a. D." (1990), "The Cross of Changes" (1993), "Le Roi est mort, vive le Roi!" (1996), and "The Fall of a Rebel Angel" (2016).

Optical sorting is a technology that separates materials, products, or objects based on their visual or optical properties. A machine uses sensors, typically cameras, lasers, or infrared or hyperspectral detectors, to inspect each item as it moves past on a conveyor or in a free-falling stream. The system compares the detected characteristics, such as color, size, shape, texture, or chemical composition, against a set of programmed criteria. When an item fails to match the acceptable profile, the machine ejects it from the stream, usually with a rapid burst of compressed air, though some systems use mechanical or other methods.

The technology is widely used in agriculture and food processing to remove defective, discolored, or foreign produce, such as rotten grains, stones, or diseased fruit, from harvests. It is also central to recycling, where it identifies and separates different plastics, paper, glass, and metals so they can be processed more efficiently. Mining and minerals processing use optical sorters to distinguish valuable ore from waste rock, and some industries use them for quality control in manufacturing.

The main advantages of optical sorting are speed, consistency, and accuracy compared with manual inspection, which allows it to process large volumes of material continuously while improving product quality and reducing labor costs. Its effectiveness depends on the quality of the sensors, the lighting conditions, and how well the sorting criteria are calibrated for the specific material being handled.

Lactare is generally considered low-risk for most mothers, but I can't give you a definitive answer on six more months without knowing its exact ingredients, so check the label. Many Indian galactagogues contain fenugreek, shatavari, fennel, or ajwain. Fenugreek can cause stomach upset, loose stools, or a maple-syrup smell in your urine or sweat, and it can lower blood sugar, so watch for shakiness or sweating if you are diabetic or take diabetes medicine. Shatavari is usually well tolerated but can rarely cause allergic reactions, such as rash, itching, or swelling. Any herb can occasionally cause an allergic reaction, so stop the capsule and seek care if you notice hives, facial swelling, or breathing difficulty. Since long-term safety studies on these combinations are limited, it's wise to pause or reassess after a few months rather than assuming six more months is fine.

Before continuing, I'd recommend talking to your doctor, pediatrician, or a lactation consultant. They can check whether the supply problem has a fixable cause, such as a shallow latch, feeding too infrequently, not emptying both breasts, or a medical issue like thyroid disease or retained placental tissue in the early months. They can also confirm your baby is gaining weight well, which is the best measure of whether your milk supply is adequate. Often, feeding on demand, at least 8 to 12 times in 24 hours, and pumping after feeds if needed will improve supply more reliably than supplements alone.

Please seek medical advice promptly if you have heavy bleeding, fever, severe breast pain or redness, or if your baby seems to be feeding poorly, has fewer wet diapers, or is losing weight.

Supervised learning is a branch of machine learning in which a model learns to map inputs to outputs using a dataset of labeled examples. Each training example pairs an input, such as an image, a sentence, or a row of numbers describing a customer, with the correct output, called the label or target. The model makes predictions on these examples, compares them to the known correct answers, and adjusts its internal parameters to reduce the gap between its predictions and the labels. Over many rounds of this process, it learns a general rule that can be applied to new, unseen inputs.

There are two main kinds of supervised learning problems. In classification, the label is a category, such as whether an email is spam or not, or which digit a handwritten image depicts. In regression, the label is a continuous numerical value, such as predicting a house's price from its size and location. Common algorithms include linear and logistic regression, decision trees, random forests, support vector machines, and neural networks.

The key idea is that the "supervision" comes from the labels, which act like an answer key guiding the learning. The quality of a supervised model depends heavily on the amount and accuracy of its labeled data, and on whether it generalizes well to new examples rather than simply memorizing the training set. To check this, practitioners typically hold back a portion of the data as a test set and evaluate the model on it.

Dmitri Mendeleev was a Russian chemist who lived from 1834 to 1907, and he is best known for creating the periodic table of the elements. In 1869 he arranged the known chemical elements in order of their atomic weights and noticed that elements with similar properties appeared at regular intervals. He grouped them into rows and columns based on these repeating patterns, which is the basic idea behind the periodic table used today.

What made his work especially famous is that he left gaps in his table for elements that had not yet been discovered, and he predicted their properties. When elements such as gallium, scandium, and germanium were later found, they matched his predictions remarkably well, which convinced scientists that his system was correct. The element mendelevium, number 101, is named in his honor.
