People do wonder about it, and a few have actually seen it. There just aren't many good pictures, for some pretty simple reasons.

Imagine trying to take a photo inside a giant, invisible blender. A tornado's winds can spin faster than a race car, and they carry dirt, rocks, broken wood, and pieces of houses. Anything that goes inside, a person, a car, or a camera, gets smashed, flipped, or thrown away. So the first problem is that getting there usually means getting destroyed.

The second problem is that tornadoes are sneaky and hard to aim for. They pop up suddenly, wiggle around, change direction, and often last only a few minutes. You can't park in the right spot and wait, because you don't know where the right spot will be. Even storm chasers who do this for a living usually see a tornado from a distance, not from the middle.

The third problem is that even if you got inside, there might not be much to see. The tornado is often wrapped in rain, dust, and darkness from the huge storm cloud above. A camera in there would mostly record a blurry, swirling mess of gray and brown, not a neat view of a hollow tube.

But some people have seen the middle. Back in 1928, a Kansas farmer named Will Keller said a tornado passed right over him, and when he looked straight up he saw a hollow, spinning tube with walls of cloud, lit up by flickering lightning. Another man, Roy Hall, told a similar story about a Texas tornado in 1948, describing a calm-ish space inside with smooth, swirling walls. Those are stories, not photos, but they match what scientists think the inside looks like.

In more recent years, scientists and filmmakers tried on purpose. A man named Sean Casey built an armored car called the Tornado Intercept Vehicle, which is basically a tank with thick windows, and drove it into tornadoes to film them for a movie called Tornado Alley. A scientist named Tim Samaras placed special sturdy probes with cameras in a tornado's path, and in 2003 one of them captured footage from inside a tornado in South Dakota. So there are some videos, but they're rare, short, and often not very clear, which is why a quick search doesn't turn up much.

So the short answer is that the middle of a tornado is very dangerous, very hard to find in time, and very hard to see even when you're there. A few brave people and tough machines have managed it, but it's one of the hardest pictures in the world to take.

Belief revision is a area of formal epistemology and artificial intelligence concerned with how a rational agent should change its set of beliefs when it receives new information. The central question is how to incorporate new evidence that may conflict with what the agent already accepts, while keeping the overall system of beliefs as coherent and well-motivated as possible.

The field is usually traced to the work of Carlos Alchourrón, Peter Gärdenfors, and David Makinson, whose 1985 paper gave the subject its standard framework, often called the AGM theory after their initials. In that framework, an agent's beliefs are modeled as a logical theory, a set of sentences closed under logical consequence. The theory addresses three main kinds of change. Expansion adds a new belief to the set without removing anything, which is possible only when the new information is consistent with what is already believed. Contraction removes a belief, along with enough other beliefs to prevent it from being logically derivable. Revision is the most demanding case: the agent must accept a new belief that may contradict existing ones, so it must give up some older beliefs to keep the set consistent.

A key insight of the theory is that revision is not arbitrary. The AGM postulates impose rationality constraints, such as requiring that the new information be accepted after revision, that the revised set remain consistent when the input is consistent, and that changes be minimal. Gärdenfors's work on epistemic entrenchment provides an ordering of beliefs according to how willing the agent is to give them up, which guides which beliefs are retained. Later work extended the theory to iterated revision, where the agent revises repeatedly, and to belief bases rather than full logical closures, since a finite set of foundational beliefs is more realistic than an infinite set of consequences.

The ideas have wide application. In philosophy they bear on questions about rational change of mind and the nature of knowledge. In computer science and AI they underlie systems for knowledge representation, database updating, and reasoning under uncertain or changing information. Belief revision is closely related to, but distinct from, Bayesian updating, which handles degrees of belief through probability rather than all-or-nothing acceptance and rejection.

Dividend reinvestment basically means you take the dividends a stock pays you and use them to buy more shares of that same stock, instead of getting the cash. So if you own a stock that pays a dividend and you've signed up for reinvestment, that money goes straight into buying more of the stock. Over time, that's a painless way to build up your holdings without having to send in new cash yourself.

Here's how it plays out. Say you own shares of a company that declares a dividend, and you've enrolled in its dividend reinvestment plan, often called a DRIP. When the payout date comes, the dividend amount is figured out, but you never actually see it as cash. Instead, it buys more shares at the current market price, and your account shows you own a few more than before.

Just don't skip the fine print. Some DRIPs charge fees or have rules you might not expect, so read the terms before you sign up. And if you don't want to go all in, some companies let you split things up, taking part of the dividend as cash and reinvesting the rest.

Khrushchev got booted out in 1964, and Leonid Brezhnev took over. Khrushchev had been running the Soviet Union since Stalin died in 1953, but it was a coup led by Brezhnev and other top Soviet leaders that finally pushed him out. Brezhnev stayed in charge for 18 years, until he died in 1982.

I'm sorry you're dealing with this. Your symptoms are worth getting checked by a doctor fairly soon, within the next several days rather than waiting weeks, because several possible causes overlap and a few need to be ruled out.

Since you know you have diverticula, diverticulitis is an obvious possibility. It happens when one or more of those pouches becomes inflamed or infected, and it classically causes pain in the lower left abdomen. It often comes with tenderness, changes in bowel habits, nausea, or fever, though early or mild cases can feel like a dull ache and fullness. Having had no trouble before doesn't rule it out, since many people's first flare comes in their fifties or later. Constipation, gas, and irritable bowel can also cause left-sided bloating and pressure that sometimes seems to reach the back.

The other area to consider is your ovaries. A partial hysterectomy usually removes the uterus but leaves the ovaries. If yours are still there, they can develop cysts or other growths that cause one-sided pelvic fullness, bloating, and pain spreading to the lower back. In a woman in her early fifties, persistent bloating, a feeling of fullness, pelvic or back pain, and sometimes getting full quickly when eating are recognized early warning signs that doctors take seriously for ovarian problems, including ovarian cancer. Most of the time the cause turns out to be benign, but this combination of symptoms is exactly what should prompt a pelvic exam and usually a pelvic or transvaginal ultrasound. Your doctor may also order a blood test such as CA-125, and possibly a CT scan, which is also the main test for diverticulitis. Kidney or urinary problems, such as a stone or infection, can cause flank and lower back pain with abdominal discomfort too, so a urine test is reasonable.

The emotional ups and downs you describe, crying for no clear reason, are very common at your age, and retained ovaries are a big part of why. Without a uterus you don't get periods to signal perimenopause and menopause, so the hormonal swings can sneak up on you and show up as mood changes, irritability, tearfulness, poor sleep, hot flashes, or anxiety. Tell your doctor about this too. There are effective options, including hormone therapy and other treatments, and depression is also worth screening for so it doesn't get overlooked.

Go to urgent care or an emergency department right away if you develop a fever or chills, severe or worsening pain, vomiting, inability to keep fluids down, blood in your stool or urine, a hard swollen abdomen, or you feel faint. Otherwise, call and book an appointment soon. Describe the location, how long it has been going on, the bloating and fullness, the back pain, your diverticula, your hysterectomy history (and whether your ovaries were left in), and the mood changes. Keeping a few days of notes on when the pain and bloating occur, any bowel changes, and your appetite can help the doctor sort through the possibilities more quickly.

Pulmonary hypertension occurs when the pressure inside the arteries that carry blood to the lungs rises above normal. This serious condition often threatens life and can progress to heart failure or other complications. In many cases the precise trigger remains unidentified, though it may arise from several sources, such as particular medical problems (including lung disorders, congenital heart defects, and blood conditions), contact with certain drugs or chemicals, and inherited predispositions. Common warning signs include breathlessness, tiredness, chest discomfort, and feeling faint or dizzy. Management may consist of medication, changes to daily habits, and, occasionally, surgical intervention. Patients should maintain close collaboration with their medical team to control the disease and avoid complications.

Technical analysis is basically a way of judging stocks and other securities by looking at what the market has been doing, mostly past prices and trading volume. Analysts lean on charts and various tools to spot patterns that might hint at a good time to buy or sell. There are tons of indicators out there, but a few get mentioned a lot as leading indicators.

Moving averages are one of the big ones. They smooth out price action by averaging prices over a set stretch, say the last 50 days. They're handy for spotting trends and can also throw off buy and sell signals.

Then there's the relative strength index, or RSI. It tracks how big recent price moves have been to figure out whether something's overbought or oversold. Above 70 it might be overbought, and below 30 it might be oversold.

MACD (moving average convergence divergence) uses two moving averages to catch trend changes, and it can generate buy and sell signals too.

Bollinger Bands are bands drawn around a moving average that show how volatile a security is. When price pushes outside the bands, that can mean a trend is shifting.

One thing to keep in mind: don't rely on any single indicator. Most people combine several before making a trade. And remember that past performance doesn't guarantee anything going forward. Technical analysis is just one tool among many.

Yes, taking too much methylprednisolone could plausibly be contributing to what you're seeing, and it's worth getting her prescriber involved soon. If her prescription is one and a half 4 mg tablets (6 mg a day) and she's been taking six tablets (24 mg a day), that is four times the intended dose.

Corticosteroids like Medrol commonly affect mood and energy, and higher doses raise the risk. Many people get energized, irritable, or unable to sleep at first, but depression, emotional flatness, and fatigue are also well-recognized effects. Higher doses can also cause muscle weakness, especially in the thighs and upper arms, which can feel like exhaustion. They can raise blood sugar, sometimes significantly, and high blood sugar causes tiredness and lethargy. They can lower potassium, which causes weakness and fatigue. And the longer she's been on the higher dose, the more these effects tend to build.

There's another possibility to keep in mind. If she has been taking the higher dose for a while and then ran out early, skipped doses, or cut back on her own, her body may not be producing enough of its own cortisol. Steroids suppress the adrenal glands, and a sudden drop can cause profound fatigue, depression, weakness, nausea, dizziness, and low blood pressure. This can become dangerous. Running out early, which is likely if she's been taking four times the prescribed amount, makes this more of a concern.

For that reason, she should not simply stop the medication or drop abruptly back to the lower dose without guidance. Call her prescribing doctor or pharmacist today. Explain how many tablets she's actually been taking, for how long, and what symptoms she has. It helps to count the remaining pills and check the refill dates so you can estimate how much she's really been taking. The doctor will likely want to check her blood sugar and electrolytes and give a safe plan for getting back to the right dose, which may involve a gradual taper. It's also worth asking what the steroid is treating, since the underlying condition can sometimes cause fatigue too.

Seek emergency care right away if she becomes confused or very hard to wake, faints or is extremely dizzy, has severe weakness, vomiting, or abdominal pain, has signs of very high blood sugar such as intense thirst and frequent urination, or expresses any thoughts of harming herself. Steroid-related depression can occasionally be severe, so take any mention of hopelessness or suicide seriously and call 988 (in the US) or emergency services.

Since the dosing mix-up happened accidentally, a pill organizer or a clearly written daily schedule may help prevent it from happening again.

Imagine you want to call your friend Sam, but you only remember his name, not his phone number. Phones need numbers to connect, not names. So you look Sam up in a big book that says "Sam = 555-1234," and then you dial the number. That's basically what DNS does for the internet.

Every website lives on a computer somewhere, and every one of those computers has a number-like address called an IP address, something like 142.250.80.46. Computers talk to each other using those numbers. But people are bad at remembering numbers and good at remembering names like google.com. DNS, which stands for Domain Name System, is the helper that turns the name you type into the number the computer actually needs.

Here's what happens when you type a website name. Your computer first asks, "Do I already remember this one?" If you visited recently, it keeps a little note and uses it right away. If not, it asks a helper server, usually run by your internet provider or a company like Google or Cloudflare. That helper also checks its own memory. If it doesn't know, it goes asking around, like a kid running through a school looking for the answer.

The asking works in steps, because nobody has the whole book in one place. First the helper asks a "root" server, which is like the school office. The office doesn't know where google.com is, but it says, "Ask the people in charge of .com." So the helper asks them, and they say, "Google's own address keeper knows." The helper asks that last one, which finally replies with the number. The helper hands the number back to your computer, remembers it for a while in case someone asks again, and your computer connects to the website.

All of this takes a tiny fraction of a second, and it happens every time you visit a new site. So the phone book idea is right, except it's really many smaller books spread around the world, each one pointing you to the next until you find the exact number you need.

So you're freelancing and wondering how taxes work? Honestly, the big thing is to set money aside through the year instead of waiting until April and getting hit with a huge bill plus possible penalties. One way to handle that is making estimated tax payments. These are payments you send to the government during the year to cover what you expect to owe, usually in four installments based on your projected income.

To make them, you'll fill out Form 1040-ES, Estimated Tax for Individuals. It comes with a worksheet that helps you figure out your expected tax for the year based on your income and deductions. Then you pay using that form and a payment voucher.

Here's the catch: if you don't pay enough during the year, you can get hit with a penalty. You can usually avoid it by paying at least 90% of this year's tax bill or 100% of last year's. (Last year's number is often the easier target.)

Another option is asking your clients to withhold taxes from what they pay you. Some will agree to this, especially if you've worked with them for a while. You'd give them a Form W-9, which asks for your Social Security number or ITIN. They'd then take out the right amount and send it to the government for you.

I shouldn't recommend particular medications or alterations to your sister's treatment without knowing far more about her medical history and the details of her condition. Managing pain can be complicated, and the right approach depends on what is causing the pain, how severe it is, and whether she has any other health problems. Your sister should talk about her pain with her healthcare provider, who can evaluate what she needs and settle on the most suitable plan. That plan might blend medications with non-drug therapies, such as physical therapy, as well as changes to her daily habits. She should also understand the possible risks and side effects of any medication she takes, and tell her provider about anything that worries her. Asking about the benefits and risks of any treatment is always wise, as is raising any questions or concerns with a healthcare professional.

Chest discomfort combined with trouble breathing may stem from a range of causes, several of which can be dangerous or even fatal. If you notice both chest pain and shortness of breath, you should get medical care promptly, since this combination can signal an emergency. Among the possible explanations are the following. A heart attack can produce chest pain alongside breathlessness, particularly when the pain is intense and spreads to the arms, neck, or jaw; sweating, nausea, and lightheadedness may also occur. A pulmonary embolism involves a blood clot blocking the artery that carries blood from the heart to the lungs, and it can lead to chest pain, labored breathing, and a racing pulse. Asthma, a chronic airway condition, may cause chest tightness, breathlessness, and wheezing. Pneumonia, a lung infection, can bring on chest pain, difficulty breathing, and a productive cough. Finally, a panic attack, which is a sudden surge of intense fear or anxiety, can also produce chest pain and breathing problems. Because these symptoms may point to a serious condition requiring urgent treatment, it is essential to see a doctor quickly. A physician can identify the underlying cause and recommend suitable treatment.

Cancer can cause all sorts of signs and symptoms, and what you notice depends a lot on the type of cancer and where it is in the body. Some of the more common ones: you might lose weight without trying, because cancer can burn through your energy and nutrients faster than usual. Fatigue is another big one, and it can come from the cancer itself or from treatment. Pain can show up too, either from the tumor or from the treatments. Bowel or bladder habits may shift, so you could get constipation, diarrhea, or needing to pee way more often. Sometimes lumps or bumps form under the skin. Skin changes are possible as well, like new moles or existing ones looking different. And a cough or hoarseness that just won't go away can be a sign.

That said, these things are caused by plenty of other stuff, so they don't automatically mean cancer. But if you've got any of them and they're hanging around, it's worth getting checked out by a doctor or other healthcare provider so they can figure out what's going on.

Buying or selling a house comes with a bunch of fees, and what you'll actually pay depends on where you live and the details of your deal. Here are the usual suspects.

Agent commissions are the big one. Most people work with a real estate agent, and the agent gets paid a percentage of the sale price. That commission usually gets split between the seller's agent and the buyer's agent.

Then there are closing costs, which is kind of a catch-all for the fees tied to the purchase or sale itself. Think title insurance, attorney's fees, and assorted other little charges that add up.

If you're buying, you'll probably want an inspection too. You pay a pro to look the place over and make sure there aren't any nasty surprises. Expect a few hundred dollars, more or less depending on how big and how old the house is.

If you're getting a mortgage, the lender may hit you with an origination fee. That's normally a percentage of the loan amount, and it covers processing and underwriting. The lender will also usually want an appraisal to confirm the house is worth what you're borrowing against it, and the borrower typically picks up that tab.

And don't forget moving costs. Packing, shipping, and storing your stuff can cost more than you'd think.

Scottsdale's a city in the eastern part of Maricopa County, Arizona, so it's technically part of the Greater Phoenix area and the wider metro. People mostly know it for its luxury resorts, golf courses, and spas. You'll also find plenty of art galleries and museums, plus a steady calendar of cultural events. It's got around 255,000 residents and sits roughly 20 miles northeast of downtown Phoenix.

A stun grenade, sometimes called a flash-bang, is a small metal canister that makes a very loud bang and a very bright flash when it goes off. Inside, there is a small amount of powder that burns very fast, a bit like a tiny firecracker. The powder makes a big puff of hot gas and sound all at once. The metal shell is shaped so that the flash and bang come out quickly, and sometimes little pellets are added to make the bang even louder.

When the flash and bang happen close to you, they overload your senses for a few seconds. Your eyes get a huge burst of light, so they can't see well for a moment, like when a camera flash goes off right in your face and you see spots. Your ears get a sudden blast of noise. Inside your ears there are tiny parts that help you balance and hear, and the loud bang shakes them so hard that your brain gets confused. That is why people who hear one can feel dizzy, wobbly, or unable to think clearly for a short time.

The good news is that these effects don't last long. Once the flash and noise are over, your eyes and ears return to normal within seconds to a few minutes. Stun grenades are used by police and soldiers because they can make people pause and stop moving for a moment without causing permanent harm, although they can still hurt if used too close to someone, which is why they must be handled carefully.

When somebody dies, their debts don't just vanish. The money they owe gets sorted out through probate, which is a court process. The court names a personal representative, usually a family member or a close friend, to handle the person's affairs and make sure the bills get paid. That person collects whatever the deceased owned, pays off the debts, and then passes what's left to the beneficiaries named in the will. If there's no will, the leftovers go to heirs based on state law.

If the debt is bigger than the estate, creditors often don't get everything they're owed. Usually they just eat the loss. Family members aren't generally on the hook for a parent's credit card bill or medical debt, which surprises a lot of people. The exception is when someone co-signed a loan or opened an account jointly with the person who died. Then that co-signer can be stuck paying. So if you're thinking about co-signing anything, it's worth reading the fine print and asking yourself whether you could cover the whole thing if you had to.

Congratulations on your new bike! Those two sets of levers work together, so let's make it simple.

Think of the left-hand lever as the "big gear" switch. It has 3 positions, and it changes how hard your legs have to push. Use the small setting when you're going up hills, because it makes pedaling easier, like having a little helper. Use the big setting for flat roads or going downhill, when you want to go fast.

The right-hand lever is the "fine-tuning" switch with 7 positions. It changes the gear within whichever setting the left lever picked. Click it toward one side to make pedaling harder and go faster, and toward the other side to make it easier, like a slide on a playground.

Here's the main trick: pedal steadily while you shift, and ease off the pedals for a moment if the chain doesn't click over smoothly. You don't need to stop. Start in a easy gear before you pull up to a hill or stop, so it's simple to get going again.

If you're not sure, try clicking one lever at a time while riding on a flat, quiet road and notice how your legs feel. Soon it will feel natural!

The user asks about stocks that have only one really high peak. This is ambiguous: it could mean stocks with a single dominant price spike in their history (a one-time bubble peak), or stocks whose price chart shows one dominant peak with a long decline afterward. I should explain the concept and give examples, in plain prose with no formatting.

A stock with only one really high peak typically describes a price history where the stock surged to a dramatic high, often during a speculative bubble or a hype cycle, and then fell substantially and never recovered to that level. Many companies fit this pattern. Cisco Systems is a classic example: during the dot-com bubble in March 2000 it briefly became the most valuable company in the world, and its share price has still not returned to that peak in the decades since, though it has grown in other ways and paid dividends. Lucent Technologies, Pets.com, and many other internet-era companies followed similar arcs, rising to a single spectacular high and then collapsing. Among more recent cases, many meme stocks and pandemic-era darlings such as Peloton and Zoom spiked dramatically and then fell far below their highs, though Zoom's pattern is closer to a boom followed by a long retreat.

If you're looking for these in a screener or chart tool, you would typically look for stocks whose all-time high is far above their current price, where the high occurred many years ago, and where the price has stayed well below it for a long stretch. Keep in mind that a stock being far below its peak doesn't by itself mean it's a bad investment, since some companies recover and others were simply overvalued at the top.

If you meant something different, such as a specific chart pattern or a particular stock you've noticed, let me know and I can address that more precisely.

Renal carcinoma is just kidney cancer, plain and simple. It's sneaky because it usually doesn't cause symptoms until it's gotten pretty far along, so it often gets caught late. If your friend's urologist says he has renal carcinoma and the tumor is hooked to the kidney by a little stalk of tissue, he most likely has renal cell carcinoma (RCC). That's the most common kind, making up roughly 90% of kidney cancers.

Treatment depends on the stage and grade of the cancer, plus how healthy he is overall. Options can include surgery to take out the affected kidney, radiation to kill cancer cells, and chemo, which is used less often for kidney cancer but can still help slow it down. Some people get targeted therapy or immunotherapy, which works by getting the immune system to go after the tumor. He should definitely talk through everything with his care team so they can figure out what makes sense for his situation. And sticking with whatever plan they land on really matters for his chances.

Gerrymandering is when the people who draw the lines for voting districts pick the lines on purpose to help one political party win. Imagine you and your friends are dividing up a box of crayons so that your team gets more of the red ones. You could draw the lines so all the red crayons end up in your group, even if your team is not really the favorite. That is a little like what happens with voting districts.

People have come up with several ideas to fix this. One idea is to let a group of neutral people, not politicians, draw the lines instead. Some states already do this with independent commissions. Another idea is to use computer programs that draw lines by following simple rules, like keeping neighbors together and keeping the shapes neat, so nobody can secretly pick the lines to win. Some people want strict rules written into the law that say how districts must look, such as they must be squarish and must not split up towns. Others want to change the voting system itself, so that more than one representative is picked from each larger area, which makes it harder for the lines to be used to shut out voters. Finally, some people think the courts should be able to step in and throw out unfair maps, and the Supreme Court has had some back and forth on whether federal courts can do that.

Other countries do have similar problems, though many handle them differently. Some countries, like Canada and the United Kingdom, use independent boundary commissions to draw the lines, so politicians have less say. Many countries with list-based systems avoid the problem altogether, because voters pick a party and the party gets seats in proportion to its votes, so there are no small districts to play with. Still, unfair line-drawing can happen in other places too, and some countries have had scandals about it.

Yes, it has been a problem for a very long time. The word itself comes from 1812, when Massachusetts Governor Elbridge Gerry signed off on a strangely shaped district that looked a bit like a salamander. A newspaper cartoonist called it a "gerry-mander," and the name stuck. Politicians have been drawing lines to help themselves ever since, and both major parties have done it whenever they had the chance to control the process. It has gotten more powerful over time because computers now make it much easier to predict how people will vote in each neighborhood.

Your blood is a bit like a special kind of paint that is inside your body, and every person's paint has a slightly different recipe. The little markers on the outside of your blood cells are like name tags, and different people have different name tags. Your body's defense team, the immune system, looks at these tags, and if it sees a tag it doesn't recognize, it thinks the blood is an intruder and gets upset. That is why doctors have to match blood carefully before giving someone a transfusion.

Why do people have different name tags? Nobody decided it on purpose. Long, long ago, our ancestors' bodies copied their blood recipes from their parents, and over many thousands of years, small changes happened by chance in the copying. Some of those changes stuck around in families and spread out, so now there are several main types, the most famous being A, B, AB, and O. Having different types may have helped people survive different germs in different places, so the variety has been kept over time.

Animals have blood types too. Dogs, cats, horses, cows, and many other animals each have their own name tags, and their blood types are different from ours. A dog's blood is not the same as a cat's, so the two can't safely share blood. Even among dogs there are many different types. Scientists who care for animals have to be careful to match blood for them, just as doctors do for people.

Those big square boxes are called matte boxes, and they do a few helpful jobs for the camera. The main one is blocking stray light. When sunlight or a bright lamp shines at the front of the lens from the side or above, it can bounce around inside the lens and make the picture look washed out or add odd spots and streaks. The matte box casts a shadow over the lens, like holding your hand over your eyes to keep the sun out.

The box also has slots at the front where people can slide in filters. A filter is like a colored or tinted window that changes how the picture looks, for example making the sky darker or cutting down glare off shiny surfaces. Because the filters sit in a holder instead of screwed onto the lens, the filmmaker can swap or adjust them easily, and can even use several at once.

Finally, the flaps on the sides and top, called barn doors, let the person filming fine-tune exactly where the shadow falls, so the light hits the lens just right. The whole thing is a bit like a sun visor with a built-in photo filter holder, which is why it looks so big and boxy.

There are several possible explanations for leg tremors that occur when someone is lying in bed. One is restless leg syndrome (RLS), a neurological condition that produces a compelling need to move the legs, frequently with tingling, crawling, or pulling sensations. Although RLS is more prevalent among adults, children can have it too. Another is growing pains: children experiencing a growth spurt may feel aches in their legs, which can lead to trembling when they rest. These aches typically come with additional signs such as stiffness, soreness to the touch, and tiredness. Muscle cramps are a third possibility. These are involuntary tightenings of one or more muscles that cause pain and discomfort, and they may stem from dehydration, a shortage of certain minerals, or excessive exertion. Finally, sleep disorders such as periodic limb movement disorder (PLMD) or sleep-related leg cramps can also cause shaking in the legs during sleep. If your child is experiencing leg shaking while lying down, particularly when it is paired with pain or other symptoms, it is important to consult a healthcare provider. They can identify the underlying cause and recommend suitable treatment.

Pi (π) is basically the ratio you get when you take a circle's circumference and divide it by its diameter. Measure around the edge, measure straight across through the middle, divide, and you'll land on roughly 3.14 every time, no matter how big or small the circle is. People call it "infinite," and that's the reason: its decimal digits never end and never settle into a repeating pattern. You can keep going forever. It starts 3.14159265358979323846264338327950288419716939937510... and it just keeps on rolling. Because of that, nobody can write pi out exactly, so we use approximations. Still, they're good enough for pretty much everything you'd actually need, whether you're figuring out a circle's area or the length of a pipe wrapped around a drum.

Sorry you're dealing with chronic liver trouble and other gut issues, that sounds miserable. The main thing is to stick with the treatment plan your doctor gave you, since they know your situation way better than any of us do. But if you're not getting better on it, bring that up with them. Getting a second opinion from a different doctor is totally reasonable too.

Besides the treatment itself, a few lifestyle things might help your symptoms and be easier on your liver. Try eating a balanced diet that's light on processed and fried stuff and heavy on fruits, veggies, and whole grains. Cut out alcohol or at least cut way back. Get some regular exercise, keep your weight in a healthy range, and find ways to chill out, like meditation or yoga.

One more thing: don't start any over-the-counter meds or supplements without checking with a doctor or pharmacist first. They can clash with your prescriptions or make your symptoms worse.

Hope that helps. I'm not a medical professional, so this isn't medical advice or a diagnosis. If you're worried about anything health-wise, definitely talk to a qualified provider.

A change from 930 to 937 is essentially no change at all. Ferritin measurements routinely vary by several percent from one blood draw to the next because of normal lab variability, time of day, hydration, and minor fluctuations in the body. So her ferritin did not really go up. It stayed the same. And it would not be expected to drop quickly after stopping supplements. Ferritin reflects the iron stored in the body, mainly in the liver, and once those stores are built up they come down very slowly, over many months, unless the iron is actively removed, for example by drawing blood.

The more important question is why her ferritin is high in the first place. A level around 930 is well above normal (roughly 15 to 150 or 200 ng/mL for women, depending on the lab) and deserves a proper workup. Ferritin is not only a marker of iron. It is also an "acute phase reactant," meaning it rises with inflammation even when iron stores are normal. Common causes of a high ferritin include chronic inflammation or infection, liver conditions such as fatty liver disease, hepatitis, or alcohol-related liver injury, metabolic syndrome (often seen alongside high blood pressure, excess weight, or diabetes), kidney disease, autoimmune conditions, certain cancers, and true iron overload. Taking iron supplements for a long time can contribute, but in most people the body limits how much iron it absorbs, so a ferritin this high from supplements alone raises the possibility of an underlying tendency to absorb too much iron, such as hereditary hemochromatosis.

To sort this out, her doctor will usually check serum iron, total iron binding capacity, and especially transferrin saturation. A high transferrin saturation (often above 45 percent) suggests genuine iron overload and would typically lead to genetic testing for hemochromatosis (the HFE gene). A normal saturation with high ferritin points more toward inflammation, liver, or metabolic causes. Other helpful tests include liver function tests, inflammatory markers like CRP, a complete blood count, kidney function, and sometimes a liver ultrasound or MRI to estimate liver iron. If true iron overload is confirmed, treatment is usually regular therapeutic phlebotomy (removing blood), which is very effective at bringing ferritin down.

It would also be worth asking why she was taking iron to begin with. If it was started for anemia, it's important to know whether that anemia has resolved or has a different cause, because some types of anemia are not due to iron deficiency and iron will not help them.

Her plantar fasciitis is unlikely to be related, though joint pain in general can sometimes accompany hemochromatosis. Her hypertension may be relevant if it's part of a broader metabolic picture. The best next step is to share both results with her doctor and ask specifically for iron studies with transferrin saturation and liver tests if they haven't been done. Avoiding iron supplements, vitamin C supplements, and alcohol until the cause is clear is generally reasonable. If she develops yellowing of the skin or eyes, abdominal swelling, significant fatigue, or unexplained weight loss, she should be seen sooner.

Okay, so WTC 7 was a 47-story skyscraper in New York that came down on September 11, 2001. It wasn't hit by a plane. What got it was debris from the Twin Towers falling after they'd been hit by hijacked planes earlier that morning. That debris started fires on several floors, and those fires burned for hours with no way to put them out.

Here's the basic chain of events. The fires got hot enough to weaken the steel beams and columns holding the building up, and they warped them too. Eventually the structure couldn't carry its own weight anymore, so the upper floors started to fall. Once that began, each floor came down onto the one below, and the whole thing went.

No, it wasn't a controlled demolition, whatever you've heard from conspiracy circles. The damage and the fire did it. Engineers and scientists have gone over this in detail, and their findings line up with what I just described.

A straw man argument occurs when someone deliberately distorts another person's argument or viewpoint so that it becomes easier to criticize or defeat. The name comes from the image of a flimsy straw figure, which is far simpler to knock over than a real opponent. Imagine you argue that we should recycle more because it benefits the environment. A person using a straw man response might reply, "So you believe we should just dump all our garbage into the ocean since it's natural?" This reply is a straw man because it twists your original point about recycling into something foolish or extreme. Straw man arguments belong to the family of logical fallacies, meaning they lack solid reasoning. People often rely on them to win a debate by making their opponent's view seem absurd, instead of offering evidence and sound logic to support their own position. In discussions and debates, it is important to notice these distortions and avoid using them, and to concentrate on engaging with the arguments that were actually made.

Corpus linguistics is a discipline that examines large bodies of authentic language material, called corpora, to uncover the recurring patterns and rules that govern how language is employed. These collections may be assembled from many kinds of sources, such as written documents, recordings transcribed from speech, or even posts made on social media. Researchers in this area rely on computer-based tools and procedures to process the information held in corpora, aiming to learn how people use language in everyday situations and how that usage evolves across time. The discipline is applied in many fields, including language instruction, translation, natural language processing, and general linguistic study. Among the principal methods are counting how often words occur, concordancing, which means locating particular words or phrases within a corpus, and applying statistical tests to linguistic patterns. Through these approaches, corpus linguistics sheds light on variation and change in language, as well as how it functions in different settings, and its findings can guide the creation of language technologies like spell checkers and machine translation systems.

Let's start with what the word "proves" meant in the old days. It didn't mean "shows something is definitely true." It meant something closer to "tests." When you test a bridge, you see whether it holds up. So "the exception proves the rule" originally meant "the exception tests the rule," and that's a much more sensible idea.

Here's the trick. If someone says "all birds can fly," and you point to a penguin, you've found an exception. But notice what the exception actually did: it showed that the rule was a rule at all. A rule is a general statement that says things usually or always go a certain way. The only way to notice an exception is to have an expectation first. Nobody says "penguins are an exception to the rule that fish can fly," because fish flying was never a pattern anyone expected. The penguin stands out precisely because the rule is there to stand out against.

So the saying is really about recognizing that exceptions only exist relative to a pattern. Finding one doesn't make the pattern more true. It shows that the pattern was strong enough to be noticed when something broke it.

The saying is also a little misleading today, and a sharp person in an argument might point that out. An exception to a rule usually means the rule is false as stated, at least in that case. If "all birds fly" is your claim, the penguin really does disprove it. The better version of the rule would be "most birds fly," and then the penguin is an exception to a rule that still holds in general.
