That's a good question. It may sound odd at first, but the very first program didn't require any other program to create it. A person wrote it using a programming language, which is a set of instructions a computer can understand and carry out. Much as we rely on words and sentences to talk with one another, we rely on programming languages to talk to computers and direct what they do. So the first program came from a person who used such a language to put together a list of instructions for the machine to follow. That person then ran those instructions through a special tool called a compiler, which converted them into a form the computer could understand and run. I hope that clears things up! If you have any more questions, feel free to ask.

There are several reasons people often don't pay for a car outright, even when they could afford to. The biggest is opportunity cost: cash tied up in a vehicle is cash that isn't earning returns elsewhere. If you have $35,000 sitting in savings or investments, the money might grow through an index fund or pay meaningful interest in a high-yield account, and a car loan at a low interest rate, especially one offered as a promotional deal, can leave you ahead by financing and investing the difference.

Liquidity matters too. Money spent on a car is hard to get back, and a car loses value quickly, often a significant share in the first few years. Keeping cash on hand gives you a cushion for emergencies, job loss, or medical bills, which can be far more painful to face without savings than with a monthly car payment.

Taxes and incentives can also tip the balance in some places. Certain business owners can deduct vehicle loan interest or depreciation, and some dealers offer financing deals, such as 0 percent APR, that effectively give you free money to hold onto your cash.

Finally, credit history is a consideration. Paying cash doesn't build a credit record the way an installment loan does, which can matter if you plan to take out a mortgage soon.

That said, paying in full has real advantages, and many financial planners consider it the best choice when the car is affordable relative to your savings and you don't carry high-interest debt. It avoids interest entirely, eliminates monthly payments, simplifies budgeting, and gives you negotiating leverage at the dealership. The right answer depends on your interest rates, your emergency fund, and how much peace of mind a debt-free purchase gives you.

Buying a foreclosed home can be a smart way to acquire property for less money, though it comes with its own set of risks and difficulties. If you're considering this route, keep the following in mind. Start by investigating the property thoroughly: look into its past, including any liens or claims against it, and assess its current state and what repairs it might need. Hiring a qualified inspector to evaluate the building is often worthwhile. Next, learn the legal procedures, since foreclosure rules differ from state to state. Speaking with a real estate attorney can help you move through these requirements safely. Keep in mind that foreclosed homes tend to sell fast, so you should have your financing arranged in advance and be ready to submit an offer on short notice if you want to win the property. A real estate agent who has experience with foreclosures can also be a helpful ally, guiding you through the steps and negotiating with the lender or seller for you. Finally, watch out for hidden expenses, such as overdue taxes or unpaid homeowners association dues. Include these in your budget when deciding how much you can realistically spend. In short, a foreclosed property can offer real savings, but thorough research and preparation for the obstacles ahead are essential.

Think of a video game character like a little robot pet that has to decide what to do next. Game AI is mostly a set of rules and tricks that the programmers wrote to make the character seem smart. Usually it doesn't "think" the way you do. It looks at what is happening right now and picks something from a list of things it knows how to do.

For example, imagine a game where a monster chases you. The programmer might write a simple rule: if the player is close, run at them; if the player is far away, wander around; if the monster's health is low, run away. The computer checks these rules many times every second. That's why the monster seems to react to you. It isn't watching you with feelings. It is just checking "where is the player?" and "how healthy am I?" and then following the matching rule.

So are there preprogrammed responses? Yes, many of them. Game makers often write out a set of possible actions for each character, and sometimes they use a little map of choices, like a flowchart, where each answer leads to the next step. Some games use a technique called a "behavior tree," which is like a set of nested questions. Other games use a "state machine," where the character is always in one mode, such as patrolling, chasing, or hiding, and it switches modes when something changes.

Does the computer have a strategy? In a sense, yes. A strategy is just a plan for choosing actions to reach a goal. In a chess or strategy game, the computer may look ahead at possible moves, score how good each outcome is, and pick the best one. Some newer games use machine learning, where the computer plays against itself thousands of times and slowly learns which moves tend to win. Even then, it is still following patterns it was built to find, not inventing things from nothing.

The short version: game AI is a bunch of clever if-then rules and scoring tricks, and it feels smart because the rules are chosen well and the game reacts quickly to what you do.

A digital image is a visual picture, like a photograph, that has been converted into a grid of pixels and saved in a computer's memory. These images can be saved in many file formats, among them JPEG, PNG, and GIF, and image editing software can be used to alter them. They show up in numerous settings, including websites, social media, and print materials. One of their main benefits over conventional printed photographs is that they can be shared and modified with little effort.

Honestly, it's not surprising the closing price looks different from site to site. A few things usually cause it. Different sites pull from different data feeds, and those feeds don't always match. Some sources use the last trade of the day as the close, while others average the final few minutes of trading, so you can get different numbers. And if a site is in another time zone, it might be stamping the close at a slightly different moment, which can throw things off by a bit. If you need one number you can trust, go with a reputable source like a major financial news outlet or a well-known data provider.

An AI accelerator is a specialized piece of computer hardware designed to run artificial intelligence workloads, especially machine learning and neural networks, much faster and more efficiently than a general-purpose processor can. The term covers a family of chips and systems built specifically to handle the kinds of mathematical operations that dominate AI, rather than the broad mix of tasks an ordinary computer processor is built for.

The reason these devices exist comes down to the nature of the math involved. Training and running neural networks consists overwhelmingly of multiplying and adding enormous arrays of numbers, operations known as matrix multiplications and tensor operations. A conventional CPU is optimized for flexibility. It executes a wide variety of instructions one after another very quickly and handles complex branching logic well, but it has relatively few processing cores. AI workloads benefit far more from doing thousands or millions of simple arithmetic operations simultaneously, so hardware that offers massive parallelism and high memory bandwidth can deliver dramatically better performance per watt and per dollar.

Several kinds of hardware fall under the AI accelerator umbrella. Graphics processing units, or GPUs, were originally built for rendering video game graphics, which also involves heavy parallel math, and they turned out to be well suited to deep learning. Companies like NVIDIA have since added dedicated features such as tensor cores to make them even better at AI. Beyond GPUs, there are application-specific integrated circuits, or ASICs, which are chips designed from the ground up for AI. Google's Tensor Processing Unit is a well-known example, as are chips from companies like Cerebras, Graphcore, and Groq, along with Amazon's Trainium and Inferentia. Field-programmable gate arrays, or FPGAs, offer another option, since they can be reconfigured after manufacturing to implement custom AI circuits. Many smartphones and laptops now also include neural processing units, or NPUs, which are small, power-efficient accelerators for running AI features like image recognition, voice assistants, and photo enhancement directly on the device.

AI accelerators often use techniques that trade some numerical precision for speed. Neural networks tend to tolerate lower-precision numbers well, so accelerators frequently support formats like 16-bit, 8-bit, or even 4-bit arithmetic instead of the 32-bit or 64-bit formats common in scientific computing. This lets them pack more calculations into the same chip area and move data more quickly. They also typically feature large amounts of fast on-chip or closely attached memory, because shuttling data between memory and processing units is frequently the real bottleneck.

It is common to distinguish between accelerators aimed at training and those aimed at inference. Training is the process of teaching a model by adjusting its parameters over huge datasets, which demands immense computing power and is usually done in data centers on clusters of high-end accelerators. Inference is the process of using an already trained model to make predictions or generate output, and it can range from large server deployments answering chatbot queries to tiny chips in phones, cameras, and cars where low power consumption matters most.

In short, an AI accelerator is hardware purpose-built to make artificial intelligence computations faster and more energy-efficient, and the rapid progress in AI over the past decade has been closely tied to advances in this kind of specialized hardware.

An itch is a sensation that gives you the urge to scratch your skin. It starts when something irritates the skin and a signal travels to the brain. The brain responds by telling you to scratch the spot. Many different things can trigger an itch. Dry skin, for instance, often feels itchy, and so do insect bites and allergic reactions. Even certain clothes or fabrics rubbing against the skin can set off an itch. It helps to work out what is behind your itch so that you can deal with it. If the cause is dryness, you can apply a moisturizing lotion. If an insect bit you, a cream can help ease the itching. Scratching may bring brief relief, but you should avoid doing it too much, since it can harm your skin.

Chest pain with trouble breathing can come from a lot of things, and some of them are really serious. If you're having both, don't wait it out. Get medical help right away, ideally by calling emergency services if the pain is severe or you feel faint.

A heart attack is one of the big ones. The pain can feel crushing and spread to your arms, neck, or jaw, and you might also be sweating, nauseous, or dizzy. A pulmonary embolism, which is a clot blocking a blood vessel in the lungs, can cause similar chest pain and breathlessness, often with a racing heart. Asthma can do it too, usually with wheezing. Pneumonia, an infection in the lungs, tends to bring chest pain, shortness of breath, and a cough that brings up phlegm. And panic attacks can cause chest tightness and breathlessness, even though they're not dangerous in themselves. Since it's hard to tell these apart at home, a doctor really needs to check you out. They can figure out what's going on and get you the right treatment.

You can buy an ETF through any brokerage account, which is the same kind of account you'd use to buy individual stocks. The basic process starts with choosing a broker. Well-known options in the United States include Fidelity, Charles Schwab, Vanguard, and brokerage apps like Robinhood or Webull, and many banks also offer investment accounts. Compare them on fees, account minimums, the range of investments available, and the quality of their app or website. Most major brokers now charge no commission for trading ETFs online.

Once your account is open and funded by transferring money from your bank, you need to find the ETF you want. Each one has a ticker symbol, such as VOO for an S&P 500 index fund or VTI for the total US stock market. You can search for the ticker in your broker's platform, and the listing will show the fund's price, expense ratio, holdings, and historical performance. It's worth reading the fund's objective and checking its expense ratio before buying, since fees compound over time.

To place the order, you select the ETF, choose how many shares to buy or how much money to invest, and pick an order type. A market order buys at the current price right away, which is usually fine for widely traded ETFs. A limit order lets you set the maximum price you'll pay, giving you more control, especially with less popular funds. ETFs trade throughout the market day like stocks, so the price can move during the day, unlike traditional mutual funds that price once daily. Some brokers also let you buy fractional shares or set up automatic recurring purchases, which can be a convenient way to invest gradually.

If you're new to investing and unsure which ETF suits you, a broad index fund that tracks a large market index is a common starting point, and a fee-only financial advisor can help you decide if you want personalized guidance.

Lucy Stone died on October 18, 1893, in Dorchester, Massachusetts (now part of Boston). She was 75 years old. She was a prominent American abolitionist and suffragist, and she is remembered as the first woman from Massachusetts to earn a college degree and for keeping her own surname after marriage. She died of stomach cancer, and she is notable also as one of the first people in the United States to be cremated.

In *The Intelligent Investor*, Graham's defensive-investor stock selection criteria rely on a multi-year average rather than the most recent year's earnings. The key figure is the average earnings per share over the past three years. The price-to-earnings test requires that the current price be no more than 15 times that three-year average. Graham chose an average because it smooths out the year-to-year swings that can make a single year's earnings misleading.

Other earnings-related criteria also apply. Graham requires positive earnings in each of the past ten years and earnings growth of at least one-third over the decade, measured using three-year averages at the start and end of the period, so the test does not hinge on a single unusually good or bad year.

Electronic transfers often seem slow because the money doesn't move in one step. Each bank has its own internal ledger, and moving funds between banks means updating several records that belong to different institutions, each with its own checks and schedules.

Much of the delay comes from batch processing. In many countries, interbank transfers such as ACH in the United States or BACS in the UK are collected and settled in batches at scheduled times, not handled instantly one by one. A transfer submitted on a Friday afternoon may not be processed until the next batch window, and batches generally don't run on weekends or bank holidays. A three-day window is common because the transfer must pass through the originating bank's cutoff, the clearing system's processing cycle, and the receiving bank's posting, with each step possibly adding a business day.

Settlement also takes time because banks need to confirm that the money is actually available and that the transaction is legitimate. Banks run fraud screening, compliance checks such as anti-money-laundering rules, and reconciliation to make sure the debit and credit match. Reversing a mistake is costly, so institutions prefer a buffer period in which errors and disputes can be caught before funds are final. Many electronic transfer rules also allow customers to dispute a payment within a set period, which adds to the time before a transfer is treated as fully settled.

Finally, the underlying infrastructure is older than many people assume. Clearing systems were designed around business days and end-of-day netting, where the net positions between banks are calculated and settled through a central bank at set times. Some newer systems, such as instant payment networks like FedNow, RTP in the US, or Faster Payments in the UK, settle in seconds, but adoption varies, and many transfers still use the older rails.

Some currencies get treated as safe havens when things go sideways, mostly because people see them as stable places to park money. The usual suspects are the US dollar, the Japanese yen, and the Swiss franc. Investors and traders tend to pile into these when the markets get jittery, since they're seen as fairly safe bets. Why do they have that reputation? Mostly because they come from countries with strong, steady economies, which makes a collapse or default less likely. The countries also tend to have solid, transparent regulatory systems, and that helps calm nervous investors. On top of that, central banks around the world hold these currencies in their reserves, so they're widely accepted and traded, which keeps them steadier and less prone to wild swings. That said, no currency is totally safe. A currency's stability can shift over time as economic and political conditions change, so anyone investing should think carefully and keep the risks in mind.

If an option's entire price consists of its intrinsic value, the option is described as "in the money." In other words, exercising it would immediately produce a gain equal to that intrinsic value. This does not guarantee a profit, but it does mean you would at least avoid a loss. Keep in mind that options expire, so the option must be exercised before its expiration date to capture the intrinsic value; if it lapses unexercised, it expires worthless and neither a gain nor a loss results. Even when an option is in the money, the underlying asset may still fall in price, which could leave you with a loss if you sell the asset after exercising.

You may have pulled a muscle in your lower back, which can lead to pain and discomfort. This often results from a sudden, awkward movement or from activities that strain the back muscles, such as lifting heavy loads or exercising without a proper warm-up. Several approaches may ease the pain. First, rest and steer clear of activities that could make it worse. Second, apply heat, since warmth can relieve muscle spasms and improve blood flow, both of which help reduce pain; a heating pad, hot water bottle, or warm compress works well. Third, consider an over-the-counter pain reliever. Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), such as ibuprofen or naproxen, can reduce both inflammation and pain. Finally, try gentle stretching, which may ease discomfort and improve flexibility in the lower back. If the pain continues or grows worse, see a healthcare provider for a proper evaluation and treatment.

Honestly, there are a few situations where taking out a loan beats paying cash. If you don't have enough cash sitting around for a big purchase or a serious expense, a loan can cover the gap. If the interest rate is lower than what you'd earn by investing that cash, borrowing and investing the money might actually make sense. And if the loan lets you buy something that makes money or gains value over time, it can be a smart move. Timing matters too. When you need to pay for something quickly, a loan can be faster and easier than saving up for months. Just make sure you read the terms closely and can really handle the monthly payments. It's also worth shopping around and comparing offers from different lenders, since rates and terms can vary a lot.

Puffy eyelids can come from all sorts of things, like allergies, inflammation, or infections. Talking to a healthcare provider is the best way to figure out what's actually going on and how to treat it. Since your 4-year-old has already seen a doctor and had tests to rule out nephrotic syndrome, that's a good sign you're on the right track. A few other common culprits in kids are allergies, infections, and inflammation. Allergies can make swelling pop up around the eyes, so if you suspect allergies, try to figure out what's triggering them and cut back on exposure. The doctor might also suggest an antihistamine. Infections are another possibility. A sinus infection or an eye infection can both cause puffiness, and if that's the issue, antibiotics are often part of the fix. Inflammation is a big one too. Pink eye (conjunctivitis) is a classic example, and it can leave the eyelids looking swollen. Depending on the case, the doctor might prescribe eye drops, ointment, or oral meds to calm things down. Either way, keep up with the follow-up visits. Getting the cause nailed down is what gets you the right treatment.

Folliculitis and asthma may be connected, though scientists do not yet fully understand how. Folliculitis involves swelling of the hair follicles, leading to red, itchy bumps on the skin. Asthma is a long-term lung disorder in which the airways become inflamed and constricted, making it hard to breathe and causing coughing and wheezing. If your doctor has diagnosed you with folliculitis and you notice red, itchy bumps, it is essential to stick with the treatment plan they recommend. That might involve applying creams or ointments such as benzoyl peroxide and keeping the affected skin clean and dry. Steering clear of irritants that can aggravate the condition, such as very hot water or particular fabrics, may also help. If the folliculitis does not improve with treatment or is causing considerable discomfort, it is worth talking with your doctor about other options. Likewise, you should keep following your healthcare provider's instructions for managing asthma, since poorly controlled asthma can worsen folliculitis symptoms.

Honestly, pain in the shaft of a 4 year old's penis isn't normal, so I'd get him seen by a doctor soon. It could be that the infection didn't fully clear up, or that something new is going on. The provider can examine him, ask about his symptoms, and figure out what's causing the pain and discoloration. They might suggest treatment or tests depending on what they find. Until then, keep the area clean and dry, and try not to fiddle with it.

Deciding between refinancing for a longer term with extra in the kitty and a shorter term where you just make the scheduled payments comes down to a few things. The first is the interest rate on the new loan. If it's lower than what you're paying now, the longer term with a buffer could save you money over time, since you'd pay less interest overall even on the same amount borrowed.

Your own money situation matters a lot too. If you've got cash to spare and don't mind bigger monthly payments, the shorter term is probably the smarter move. You'll clear the loan faster and pay less interest along the way. But if money's tight or you'd rather keep the monthly bill low, the longer term with some extra set aside might suit you better.

Honestly, the right call depends on your situation and what you're aiming for. Run the numbers both ways and see which one saves you more in the long run. And if you're still torn, a financial advisor or loan officer can look at your specifics and give you a more tailored answer.

A surveyor's wheel, also called a measuring wheel or trundle wheel, is a hand-pushed measuring instrument used to determine distances over relatively flat ground. It consists of a small wheel of known circumference attached to a handle, often with a mechanical or digital counter that records the number of revolutions and converts them into a distance reading. To measure, the user simply rolls the wheel along the path being measured, from one point to another, and reads the total distance from the counter. Many models can be reset to zero at the start of each measurement and some have adjustable counters that allow the user to select units such as feet, meters, or yards.

Surveyor's wheels are commonly used in land surveying, construction, landscaping, road work, and property assessment, particularly when a quick and reasonably accurate measurement is needed over long or irregular distances where a tape measure would be cumbersome. While they are not as precise as electronic total stations or GPS equipment, they are inexpensive, portable, and easy to use, which makes them a practical tool for many everyday measuring tasks.

Picking up a language alongside someone who speaks another one can be a little challenging, yet it is entirely achievable. One approach would look like this: to begin, the pair could rely on gestures and sketches to get their points across. Suppose one person wants to convey "I'm hungry." They might sketch a figure with a small line rising from its belly. Afterward, the two could turn to a translation app or website, since these tools convert words and phrases from one tongue into another. Lastly, they could enroll in language lessons together, which would let them pick up the fundamentals of each other's languages and practice speaking and listening. Progress may demand patience and time, but through consistent practice and effort, the two can learn to understand one another across their different languages.

Mariah Carey is American. She was born in 1969 in Huntington, New York, to an African American mother, Patricia Hickey, who was of Afro-Venezuelan descent, and a white father, Alfred Roy Carey, an Irish American engineer. Her heritage is mixed, and she has spoken about growing up with both sides of her family and the cultural influences that came with them. Her musical style draws heavily on African American traditions such as R&B, soul, gospel, and hip-hop, which shaped much of her career.

A stock price can rise without any good news or strong results for several reasons, mostly tied to how markets move rather than to the company itself. One common cause is simple supply and demand: if a large buyer, such as an index fund, a pension fund, or a wealthy investor, decides to accumulate shares, the extra buying pressure can push the price up even when nothing about the business has changed. Short squeezes work similarly. When many investors have bet against a stock by short selling, they are forced to buy shares to close their positions if the price starts climbing, and that buying can drive the price higher still.

Speculation and momentum also play a large role. Traders often buy a stock because it is already rising, expecting the trend to continue, and this self-reinforcing behavior can carry a price well past what fundamentals would justify. Social media, online forums, and viral attention can amplify this, drawing in retail investors who pile into a name that is getting talked about.

Broader forces matter too. Falling interest rates tend to lift stock valuations generally, since future earnings become worth more when discounted at lower rates. Strong performance in a whole sector, or optimism about the economy, can lift a company's shares along with its peers. Sometimes a stock rises because of takeover rumors, an activist investor taking a stake, or hope for a future product or deal, even before anything is confirmed.

Finally, there are technical and structural factors, such as a stock being added to a major index, low trading volume that lets modest orders move the price, or the company buying back its own shares, which reduces the supply available to the public. Any of these can lift a price in the short term without any change in the underlying business.

Whether you pay anything for holding stocks overnight depends on how you hold them. If you buy shares outright in a regular cash brokerage account, there is normally no overnight or holding charge. You own the shares, and you can keep them for a day or decades without paying anything per night. Some brokers do charge account maintenance, custody, or inactivity fees, and some in Europe or the UK charge a small percentage-based platform fee, but these are general account costs, not overnight charges.

Overnight charges come into play when you use borrowed money or derivatives. If you buy stocks on margin, the broker lends you part of the purchase price and charges interest on the borrowed amount. That interest is usually calculated daily and billed monthly. The rate is typically a benchmark rate plus a markup that shrinks as the loan size grows, and it varies widely between brokers. Some discount brokers charge well under ten percent a year, while others charge noticeably more.

If you trade contracts for difference or spread bets, which are common in the UK, Europe, and Australia but not allowed for retail traders in the US, you pay an overnight financing fee, sometimes called a swap or rollover fee, for each night a leveraged position stays open past the daily cutoff. It is usually based on a benchmark interest rate plus a broker markup of around two to three percent a year, applied to the full position value rather than just your deposit. Wednesday nights often carry a triple charge to cover the weekend. Short CFD positions may earn a small credit or incur a charge depending on interest rates.

Short selling actual shares has its own costs. You pay a borrow fee to the lender of the shares, which can be tiny for widely available stocks but very high for hard-to-borrow ones. You also owe any dividends paid while you are short.

Day trading accounts that close all positions before the market closes avoid these overnight financing costs entirely. That is one reason some traders prefer not to carry leveraged positions overnight.

In practice, if you are a long-term investor buying shares with your own cash, overnight fees aren't a concern. If you use margin, CFDs, or shorting, check your broker's published financing or margin rate schedule, because over weeks or months these costs can add up to a large share of your returns. If you let me know which broker or country you're dealing with, I can give a more specific idea of what to expect.

Symbolic AI is basically the branch of AI that works with symbols and logic instead of raw data. People also call it "classical AI" or "good old-fashioned AI (GOFAI)," which tells you it's been around a while. The idea is that you solve a problem by manipulating symbols according to a set of rules. The symbols stand for concepts or things in whatever domain you're working in, and the rules spell out how those things relate to each other. Say you want a program to solve a puzzle. You'd represent each piece as a symbol, then use rules to shuffle those symbols around until you hit a solution.

Most of these systems lean on first-order logic, which lets them talk about objects and the relationships between them. That makes them a good fit for stuff that needs real logical reasoning, like natural language processing, planning, or theorem proving. The downside is that they're a pain to build. Someone usually has to hand-encode a huge amount of knowledge into the system, and they can be pretty rigid. They also tend to struggle with uncertainty, or with tasks that involve tons of data or sensory input. That's why you'll often see symbolic methods mixed with machine learning and neural networks these days. Together they can do better than either one alone.

Honestly, you can't really pump a stock's price by buying shares from yourself at a higher price. The market is pretty tightly watched, and that kind of trading would stick out like a sore thumb to regulators, so you'd be asking for legal trouble. Prices come down to supply and demand, shaped by things like how the company is doing, the broader economy, and how investors feel about it. A single person can nudge a price for a moment by trading a big chunk of shares, but they can't hold it there. If you're hoping to get more for your shares, your best bet is usually to sit tight and let good news about the company or the market do the work. You could also just sell to another buyer willing to pay your price. Just keep in mind that stocks can drop as easily as they climb, so don't count on any particular number.

What you're describing sounds most like a viral upper respiratory infection or early acute bronchitis, which is by far the most common cause of a new productive cough in a healthy adult. Small streaks of red in the mucus are usually not alarming in this situation. Repeated coughing fits can break tiny blood vessels in the airways, throat, or nose, and a little blood from postnasal drip or irritated nasal passages can also mix into what you cough up. Dry indoor air, frequent nose blowing, and the force of the coughing itself all make this more likely.

The dizziness has a few common explanations. Coughing fits can briefly raise pressure in the chest and reduce blood flow back to the heart, which can cause lightheadedness during or right after a spell. Mild dehydration from being a little under the weather, poor sleep from coughing, an inner ear or sinus involvement from congestion, and some over-the-counter cough and cold medicines can also cause it.

As for how long it lasts, coughs from viral infections often linger longer than people expect. Most improve within one to three weeks, though some take up to three or four weeks to fully settle because the airways stay irritated after the infection clears. In the meantime, staying well hydrated, using a humidifier, drinking warm liquids with honey, and avoiding smoke or other irritants can help. Standing up slowly and sitting down during coughing fits can reduce the dizziness.

You should see a doctor promptly if you cough up more than streaks of blood (for example, a teaspoon or more, clots, or mucus that is mostly red), or if the blood keeps increasing. Also get checked if you develop fever, shortness of breath, chest pain (especially sharp pain with breathing), a fast heartbeat, or wheezing, or if you have one-sided leg swelling or pain. The same applies if the dizziness becomes severe, causes fainting or near-fainting, or happens even when you aren't coughing, or if the cough lasts beyond about three weeks without improving. Unexplained weight loss or night sweats are also worth reporting. Chest pain or sudden breathlessness together with coughing up blood should be treated as an emergency. Recent long travel, surgery, birth control pills or other estrogen, smoking, or a history of lung problems would also lower the threshold for getting evaluated sooner.

Since you otherwise feel well and the blood is only occasional streaks, this is most likely a passing infection. Because blood in sputum and dizziness together are worth a professional look, it would be reasonable to call your doctor or visit an urgent care clinic for a quick listen to your lungs and some reassurance, especially if things aren't clearly improving over the next several days.

I can share the usual pediatric dosing, but your daughter needs to be seen by a doctor today before you start a new steroid. She has had a rash for 7 days that hasn't responded to antihistamines or to deflazacort, which is itself a corticosteroid. The doctor needs to examine her and confirm the diagnosis, since persistent urticaria in a child can have causes that steroids could mask or make harder to treat. Switching steroids without that review isn't standard practice, and the prescriber should decide whether to change the plan.

For reference, prednisolone for urticaria in children is typically 1 to 2 mg per kg per day, given once in the morning. For a 19 kg child that works out to about 19 to 38 mg daily, and the prescriber will choose a dose within that range. Courses are usually short, around 3 to 5 days, and are often tapered rather than stopped abruptly if they run longer. Please don't use these numbers on your own. The exact dose and duration depend on her examination and history, and the prescriber should also check whether the deflazacort should be stopped first.

Seek emergency care immediately if she has swelling of the lips, tongue, face, or throat, difficulty breathing or swallowing, wheezing, fainting, or extreme drowsiness. Also get urgent help for a rash that doesn't fade when you press a glass against it, fever, joint pain, blood in the urine or stool, or a rash that spreads rapidly.

A biological system is basically a group of connected living things, or parts of living things, that work together to do a particular job. These can be pretty small or really complex. A single cell counts, and so does a whole human body. Some common examples are the circulatory system, which moves oxygen, nutrients, and hormones around to your cells and hauls away waste. Then there's the digestive system, which breaks down your food and pulls nutrients out of it. The nervous system handles coordinating your body's reactions to whatever's going on inside and outside you. The respiratory system gets oxygen into your blood and gets rid of carbon dioxide. And the endocrine system makes hormones that keep all sorts of things running.

Biological systems also tend to use feedback loops to keep things steady, which is called homeostasis. Body temperature is a good example. The endocrine system releases hormones that help keep your temperature in a fairly narrow range. If you get too hot, your sweat glands kick in and the sweat cools you off as it evaporates. If you get too cold, your muscles generate heat to warm you back up. Pretty neat, honestly. These systems are what keep a living thing healthy and functioning.

Sir James Lighthill (1924–1998) was a British applied mathematician, best known for his work in fluid dynamics and for a 1973 report that shaped the history of artificial intelligence research. The name refers to a person, not a concept or object, and the "Sir" reflects the knighthood he received in 1971.

Michael James Lighthill was born in Paris to English parents and showed exceptional mathematical talent early, entering Trinity College, Cambridge, at a young age. During the Second World War he worked at the National Physical Laboratory on aerodynamics. He later became a professor at the University of Manchester, then director of the Royal Aircraft Establishment at Farnborough, and eventually held the Lucasian Professorship of Mathematics at Cambridge, the chair once held by Isaac Newton and later by Stephen Hawking. From 1979 to 1989 he was Provost of University College London.

His most celebrated contribution is the theory of aerodynamic sound, often called Lighthill's acoustic analogy, published in the early 1950s. It explained mathematically how turbulent airflow, such as the exhaust of a jet engine, generates noise, and it founded the field of aeroacoustics. This work helped engineers design quieter jet engines and is still used today. He also made important contributions to nonlinear wave theory, including the Lighthill–Whitham–Richards model of traffic flow, which treats cars on a road somewhat like a fluid, as well as work on biological fluid dynamics such as how fish swim and how microorganisms move, and on the mathematics of physiological flows like blood circulation.

Outside of fluid dynamics, Lighthill is widely remembered for the Lighthill Report, formally titled "Artificial Intelligence: A General Survey," which he wrote in 1973 for the British Science Research Council. In it he argued that AI research had failed to deliver on its grand promises, particularly because many approaches broke down when faced with the "combinatorial explosion" of possibilities in real-world problems. The report led to sharp cuts in government funding for AI in the United Kingdom and contributed to what is often called the first "AI winter," a period of reduced interest and investment in the field. It also prompted a televised BBC debate in which Lighthill argued against prominent AI researchers including Donald Michie and John McCarthy.

Lighthill was known as an energetic and adventurous personality. He was a keen long-distance swimmer who swam around the island of Sark in the Channel Islands many times, and he died in 1998 while attempting that swim at the age of 74. He received numerous honors, including election as a Fellow of the Royal Society and the Royal Medal, and he is regarded as one of the leading applied mathematicians of the twentieth century.

Imagine your game is a book. With old cartridge games like The Legend of Zelda on the NES, the book came with its own little notepad glued inside the back cover. That notepad was a tiny memory chip inside the cartridge, often kept alive by a small watch battery, and it let the game write down where you were. Every cartridge had its own notepad, so you never needed anything extra.

Then games started coming on CDs, like on the PlayStation. A CD is more like a printed book that you can read but can't write in. The information is pressed into the shiny disc at the factory, and the console has no way to scribble new things onto it. So there was nowhere on the game itself to keep your save. The fix was to give players a separate little notepad they could plug into the console, and that's the memory card. One card could hold saves for lots of different games.

You might ask why the console didn't just have a notepad built in. Back then, memory chips were pretty expensive, and companies wanted to keep the console's price low. Selling the memory separately meant the console was cheaper, and people who needed more space could buy more cards. CDs were also much cheaper to make than cartridges, partly because they didn't need a chip inside, so the save system moved off the game and onto the card.

One small correction about the Nintendo 64: not literally all of its games saved on the cartridge. Many did, but some, like certain sports and racing games, used a plug-in Controller Pak that went into the controller, which was basically Nintendo's version of a memory card. Adding a save chip to every cartridge cost money, so some publishers skipped it.

Later on, memory got cheap enough that consoles started including built-in storage and hard drives, which is why today your games just save to the system itself and memory cards mostly disappeared.

There are a few steps you can take to get your income into your personal finance balance. First, figure out where the money is coming from, whether that's your job, investments, or something else, since knowing the source makes tracking way easier. Next, write it down. A finance app, a spreadsheet, or even a notebook works fine, as long as you log the date, the amount, and where it came from. Once that's recorded, update your budget so you can see how much you actually have to spend and save. Then keep an eye on your spending so you don't blow past your budget and you're still putting enough aside. Finally, check in on your finances every month or every few months and tweak things as needed. It's a lot easier to stay on top of things when you look at them regularly.

Honestly, a lot of it comes down to size, metabolism, environment, and genetics. Dogs and cats are way smaller than us, and their bodies just run differently. They age faster, and their cells don't hold up as long. Usually bigger animals live longer than smaller ones, since their cells aren't working as hard and don't wear out as quickly.

Then there's the danger factor. Pets are more likely to run into stuff like disease, accidents, and predators. Lifestyle matters too. An outdoor cat is going to be way more prone to accidents and injuries than one that stays inside.

Genetics plays a part as well. Some dog and cat breeds are known for living longer than others, kind of like how some human families seem to have a lot of long-lived relatives.

So basically, it's their size, their metabolism, the environment they live in, and their genes that all add up to shorter lives than ours.

Ethanol is a kind of alcohol, the same family of chemicals found in drinks, but the kind put in gasoline is made mostly from corn and is not meant for drinking. Adding about 10 percent of it to gasoline does a few helpful things. First, it helps the fuel burn more completely, which cuts down on some of the smoke and pollution that comes out of the car. Second, it acts a bit like a booster for the octane in the fuel, which helps the engine run smoothly and avoid knocking, that rattling sound engines can make. Third, it's a way of using a plant-based fuel instead of relying only on oil that comes out of the ground. Farmers grow the corn, and that gives them another market for their crops.

So when you see that "10% ethanol" sign, it just means that about one tenth of what's in that pump is a plant-made fuel mixed in with the gasoline, helping your car run cleaner and making use of crops grown on farms.

You may have hurt your tailbone, also known as the coccyx. This is the small triangular bone at the bottom of the spine, just above the buttocks. A fall onto your backside can occasionally damage it, leading to pain when you sit, stand, or walk around. Another possibility is that the fall caused you to strain or pull a muscle in your abdomen. Whichever it turns out to be, you should go easy on yourself and steer clear of any activity that triggers pain until the soreness fades. If the pain lingers or gets severe, it would be wise to have a healthcare provider examine you. They can work out what is causing the pain and suggest suitable treatment, such as rest, ice or heat, over-the-counter pain relievers, or physical therapy.

Basically, in a communist system you've got one party running the show. It holds the power and makes the big decisions for the whole country. The party's usually led by a fairly small group of people, who get picked either by the party members or through some kind of election process, though how democratic that really is can vary a lot.

The idea behind it all is that property should be owned collectively, and that the country's wealth and resources should be shared out equally among everybody. So the party ends up in charge of setting economic, social, and political policy, and it's also on the hook for making sure those policies actually get carried out and enforced across the country.

Pigs are omnivores, meaning they are able to consume both plants and animals. Wild pigs search for many kinds of food, such as roots, fruit, insects, and small creatures. Pigs raised on farms usually eat a manufactured feed designed to supply the nutrients necessary for growth and good health. Such feed is generally made from grains like corn and soybeans and may be fortified with vitamins and minerals. Farm pigs may also receive extras like vegetables, fruit, and even leftover food from the kitchen. Providing a well-rounded diet is essential to keeping pigs healthy and comfortable.

Spending more than you earn without borrowing is possible, but only by drawing on resources you already have rather than creating new debt. The most common way is to use savings. Someone who has built up a cash cushion can cover a month or a year of excess spending by withdrawing from it, and the gap closes as the money runs out. Selling assets works the same way: converting stocks, a car, jewelry, or property into cash funds spending beyond income. Other sources include inheritances, gifts from family, insurance payouts, tax refunds, lottery or bonus windfalls, and the proceeds of a sale of a business.

These arrangements are temporary, though. Once the savings or assets are gone, the gap has to be closed by earning more, spending less, or borrowing. So a household that consistently outspends its income is either slowly depleting its wealth or is about to fall into debt. Someone who appears to live beyond their means without debt is usually living off accumulated resources, which may be invisible to others.

Retirees are a good example of this in a legitimate form. Many spend more than their current paycheck would allow, which is fine because they are drawing down savings they built over decades, and they plan for that money to last.

QFC, short for Quality Food Centers, is a grocery chain up in the Pacific Northwest, mostly in Washington and Oregon. As of 2021 they had around 65 stores across those two states. It's owned by Kroger, which is one of the biggest grocery companies in the US. I can't say how many stores they have today, though. My info only goes up to 2021, so the count could have changed since then.

Arthur C. Clarke, born in 1917 and dying in 2008, was a British author of science fiction and popular science, as well as a futurist. He is chiefly remembered for his science fiction novels and short stories, numerous of which were turned into movies and television series. His scientific reputation rests as well on his ideas in satellite communication and space exploration. He is frequently credited as a co-writer of the screenplay for "2001: A Space Odyssey," the landmark film directed by Stanley Kubrick. His novels include "Childhood's End," "Rendezvous with Rama," and "The Fountains of Paradise." A prolific writer, he saw his books translated and published in countless countries. He belonged to the British Interplanetary Society and earned many honors for his work in science fiction and science.

It depends on what you mean by unfulfilled paychecks, and the answer differs for employers and employees. I'll assume you're in the US.

If you're an employee whose employer failed to pay you, there generally isn't a deduction for wages you earned but never received. The reason is that most individuals report income on the cash method, meaning you only owe tax on money you actually (or constructively) receive. If you were never paid, you don't report that income, so there's nothing to write off. The loss is effectively handled by not being taxed on it. If you already reported it, for instance because a W-2 was issued showing wages you never received, you should ask the employer for a corrected W-2c, or report the correct amount and attach an explanation. If you later collect the back pay, it's taxable in the year you receive it, and in some cases you can use special rules for lump-sum back pay or a claim-of-right adjustment if you repay amounts.

Also, if a paycheck bounced or the employer withheld taxes but didn't pay you, you may still be credited for the withholding shown on your W-2, so check your wage statement carefully. You can also file a wage claim with your state labor department or the US Department of Labor, which is often the more useful route than any tax strategy.

If you're a business owner or self-employed and a client didn't pay you, the cash-method rule applies similarly: unpaid invoices are not income until collected, so no write-off is needed. If you use the accrual method and already counted the income, you may be able to claim a bad debt deduction once the amount is truly worthless, and you must have previously included it in income.

If you're an employer who issued paychecks that were never cashed, the wages are generally still deductible when paid, but uncashed checks may be considered unclaimed property that must eventually be turned over to the state. If you're asking about payroll you couldn't make, unpaid wages on an accrual basis have specific deduction timing rules, usually requiring payment within about two and a half months after year-end.

If you tell me whether you are the employee, the employer, or a freelancer, and what exactly happened, I can be more specific. For a large amount, a CPA or tax professional is worth consulting.

A conductor is like the traffic director and the coach of a big musical team all at once. An orchestra has many musicians playing many different instruments, and each one is watching music written on paper. The conductor stands in front of them and uses their hands, arms, and face to show everyone when to start, how fast or slow to play, when to play loudly or softly, and when to come in after a quiet part. They also help everyone stay together, so the whole group moves as one instead of each person going their own way. Some conductors also talk through their ideas about how the piece should feel before they start, and they fix small problems during rehearsals, like telling the violins to play a little gentler.

Would you notice a difference without one? Yes, most people would. Without a conductor, the music would likely start a little messily, and the musicians would probably drift out of step with each other over time, especially in long pieces or fast, tricky parts. Some parts might speed up or slow down unevenly, and the big swells and quiet moments might not line up as neatly. Still, a really well-practiced group of musicians who know a piece by heart can play together without a conductor. Some chamber groups and a few orchestras do this on purpose, and they often sound lively and close-knit. But for a large group of players, the conductor is what keeps everybody together and makes the music feel like one shared idea.

He first went on the program in 2000 and has since made many returns, among them a spot in the "Jeopardy! All-Star Games" tournament in 2019. Rutter is also a philanthropist who has given large sums to a range of charities.

The multi-armed bandit problem is a well-known challenge in reinforcement learning. In this setup, a decision-maker, referred to as an "agent," picks from a number of options, called "arms," with the aim of earning as much reward as possible. Every arm has its own probability distribution of rewards, but the agent has no prior knowledge of these distributions and must discover them through repeated trials. The name "bandit" comes from the tension the agent faces between exploration, which means testing various arms to better understand their rewards, and exploitation, which means selecting the arm that currently appears to offer the highest expected payoff given what is already known. The agent's objective is to strike the right balance between these two strategies so that its total reward accumulates as much as possible over time. Despite its simplicity, the multi-armed bandit model is a powerful tool that has informed the study of many decision-making scenarios, such as online advertising, clinical trials, and resource allocation. Researchers have also used it to examine how humans and animals behave when faced with comparable choices.

Metal is a style of rock music usually built on heavy, distorted guitar riffs and rapid tempos. It frequently borrows from other genres, including punk, hardcore, and classical music, and has a reputation for an aggressive, high-energy sound. In their lyrics, metal bands commonly deal with rebellion, social and political concerns, and personal hardships. The genre has a long, diverse history and has branched into numerous subgenres and subcultures. Recurring themes include rebellion, individualism, and resistance to authority. Plenty of bands also look to mythology, literature, and fantasy for inspiration, and their lyrics are often metaphorical or allegorical. Metal is generally linked with a rebellious, outsider outlook, and many of its fans are attracted to it because of its intensity and energy.

Tugain is a brand name for minoxidil, a drug prescribed to address hair loss. It comes as a liquid or foam that is massaged into the scalp to encourage hair regrowth. Although minoxidil is usually well accepted by the body, it can produce certain side effects. Some users notice dryness, itchiness, or flaking on the scalp; a gentle shampoo and not leaving the product on longer than instructed can help ease these issues. In rare cases, a person may have an allergic response, with signs such as a rash, hives, trouble breathing, or swelling of the face, lips, tongue, or throat. Anyone who experiences these should stop the medication and get medical help right away. Minoxidil can also bring on dizziness, lightheadedness, or a racing heartbeat. If any of these occur, the medication should be discontinued and a healthcare provider contacted. Following the instructions given by your provider is essential, and if you have worries about side effects or are already experiencing them, speak with your provider, who can recommend the most suitable approach to treating your hair loss.

A graph neural network (GNN) is a neural net built to work on graph-structured data, the kind of data you get when you store things as nodes and the connections between them as edges. Graphs are great for showing how things relate to each other, and GNNs are especially good at spotting patterns in those relationships and making predictions from them. Each node represents some object or entity you care about, and each node carries a set of features. Those features can be learned or fixed. Edges can have their own features or weights too. The network uses all of this to pick up on patterns in the structure and make calls based on what it finds.

You'll see GNNs pop up in social network analysis, recommendation systems, and predicting how proteins interact, among other things. They also show up in natural language processing and computer vision, anywhere your data can be shaped into a graph. There are lots of flavors. Convolutional ones (CNNs), recurrent ones (RNNs), and graph attention networks (GATs) are a few names you'll run into. Which architecture makes sense really depends on what your graph looks like and what you're trying to do with it.

Chronic stuffiness can come from a bunch of different things, so it's worth narrowing it down. The big one is allergies. Pollen, mold, pet dander, that kind of stuff can keep your nose clogged for months if you're around it a lot.

Then there's non-allergic rhinitis, which is basically your nose reacting to irritants instead of actual allergens. Smoke, perfume, strong smells, even swings in temperature or humidity can set it off.

Sinusitis is another common one. That's inflammation in your sinuses, and it can come from allergies, infections, or even the shape of your nose.

You could also have nasal polyps. They're soft, non-cancerous growths in the lining of your nose, and they can make it hard to breathe through it. And there's a deviated septum, where the bone and cartilage dividing your nostrils is off-center. That alone can leave you congested and struggling to get air through.

Honestly, I'd see a doctor to figure out which one it is, since the fix depends on the cause. They might do allergy testing, imaging, or just take a look up your nose to see what's going on.

Imagine you have a box with a wall down the middle. On the left side there are lots of bouncing balls, and the right side is empty. Now you pull out the wall. The balls start bouncing around, and before long they spread out and are roughly evenly mixed across both sides. You never see them all wander back to the left side on their own. That one-way behavior is the heart of the Second Law.

Here is the idea behind it. Things tend to move from arrangements that are unusual and special to arrangements that are ordinary and common. There are far more ways for the balls to be scattered evenly than for them all to be huddled on one side, so when they bounce around randomly, they almost always end up in the mixed-up, evenly spread state. Physicists have a name for this measure of how many ordinary ways a situation can be arranged: entropy. The Second Law says that in a closed system, entropy tends to stay the same or go up, which means things drift toward the more common, more spread-out state.

Think of a messy bedroom. Toys can be arranged neatly in one particular way, but there are countless ways for them to be scattered across the floor. If you let things happen on their own, with nobody tidying up, the room gets messier, not tidier. Tidying takes effort, and that effort uses up energy and makes the surroundings warmer, which adds to the total mess of the universe.

That last part is important. Your room can become neat, but only because you spent energy, and that energy ended up as heat spreading into the air. Add up the tidy room and the warm air, and the total disorder went up. So the Second Law is not saying that nothing can ever become orderly. It is saying that the overall amount of disorder in the universe never goes down on its own, and getting order in one place always costs some disorder somewhere else.

That is the whole idea: things naturally spread out and mix, because spread-out and mixed-up is what almost all possible arrangements look like.

Sound's usually measured in decibels, and the dB scale is logarithmic. That just means a small change in the number is a much bigger change in actual loudness. Every 10 dB is a tenfold difference, for example.

The quietest room in the world is at Orfield Laboratories in Minnesota, and it averages around -9 dB. So yeah, it's basically dead silent in there. For comparison, a whisper is about 30 dB and a normal conversation is somewhere around 60.

As for how you can have negative decibels at all, it comes back to the log scale. Zero doesn't mean "no sound," it's just a reference point, and you can go below it. Because of the logarithm, the gap between -9 and 0 is a way bigger deal than the gap between 0 and 9, at least in terms of the actual sound level involved.

So to answer your question, sound can be "negative" because decibels are on a logarithmic scale, and a tiny shift in the number can mean a big shift in how loud something really is.

Pain with turning your neck after a multilevel fusion is common, because the muscles around the spine tighten up and guard, and the levels above and below a fusion (C3 and C7 in your case) take on extra load, which can make those herniations more irritable. Physical therapy is usually still worthwhile even when movement hurts, but it should not mean pushing through pain. Ask the therapist to start gently. Early work often involves posture correction, gentle range of motion within a comfortable range, isometric exercises (tightening muscles without moving the neck), shoulder blade strengthening, and soft tissue work. Tell them about your fusion hardware, your radiculopathy, and the double crush so they avoid aggressive manipulation, traction, or end-range stretching unless your surgeon has cleared it. It is reasonable to ask your surgeon for specific precautions to give the therapist in writing.

For pain relief at home, heat (a warm shower or heating pad for 15 to 20 minutes) often helps tight muscles, and some people prefer ice in the first stretch after a flare. Pacing your activity, avoiding prolonged looking down at phones or screens, and using a supportive pillow that keeps your neck neutral can help. Over-the-counter options like acetaminophen or an anti-inflammatory such as ibuprofen may be fine, but check with your doctor, since anti-inflammatories are sometimes restricted after fusion surgery. Your doctor may also consider a muscle relaxant for short-term use, or medications aimed at nerve pain such as gabapentin or duloxetine, which can help with radiculopathy symptoms. If the pain stays severe, options like targeted injections near the irritated nerve roots or trigger point injections can be discussed with a pain specialist.

For the nerve problems, the EMG and nerve conduction study should help clarify how much is coming from the neck versus compression at the wrist or elbow, since a double crush means both sites contribute. Treating the peripheral site, with night splints or sometimes a release surgery, can improve hand function even while the neck is being managed. Hand therapy can also help maintain strength and dexterity in the meantime.

Because you are already having hand symptoms, certain changes need prompt attention: worsening weakness or numbness, dropping things more often, trouble walking or balance problems, loss of bladder or bowel control, severe new pain, fever, or trouble swallowing. Contact your surgeon right away or go to the emergency room if any of these occur.

If turning your neck hurts too much to start therapy, tell your doctor that now rather than waiting. They may adjust your pain medication first, or have the therapist begin with the gentlest approaches.

Ayn Rand's philosophy is called Objectivism. Its big idea is that the most important thing a person can do is live for their own happiness and work to achieve their own goals, and that reason is the best tool we have for figuring out what is true. She thought people should be proud of what they make, should not sacrifice themselves for others just because others ask, and should not force others to do things for them. In The Fountainhead, Howard Roark stands for this: he refuses to compromise his designs even when the world pushes him to, because he believes his work should come from his own mind and not from what other people want.

Many people frown on her ideas for a few reasons. Some think she goes too far in saying that helping others is bad or that selfishness is always good, when most people see kindness and cooperation as valuable parts of a good life. Others point out that her heroes are often portrayed as perfect and her villains as weak or evil, which makes her books feel more like lectures than real stories. Critics also argue that her view of capitalism ignores how luck, family, and social help affect who succeeds. Many philosophers say her arguments are not very rigorous, even if her stories are exciting. And some people dislike how strongly her followers have sometimes promoted her ideas, which has made the philosophy seem rigid.

So your feeling makes sense. You can enjoy the story and the stronger points about independence and creativity while still questioning the parts that seem too extreme. Plenty of thoughtful readers do exactly that.

Before changing anything about your medication, please talk with your healthcare provider first. They can assess your particular circumstances and recommend the most suitable approach to your back pain. Cymbalta (duloxetine) is prescribed mainly for depression and anxiety, though it is sometimes also used for long-term pain, including back pain. It is generally not the first choice for chronic pain, and other medications may work better.
