They can guide a safe reduction in dose and help manage any withdrawal symptoms. Once more, please check with your healthcare provider before altering your medication routine, since they are best placed to advise you based on your own situation.

In artificial intelligence and machine learning, a fuzzy rule is a statement describing how a group of input variables relates to a single output variable. The term "fuzzy" reflects the fact that such rules accommodate vagueness and imprecision in both the inputs and the output. Fuzzy rules form the foundation of fuzzy logic systems, a category of nonlinear mathematical models used to represent and reason about intricate systems containing many variables that may conflict with one another or be uncertain. These systems appear in many domains, such as control engineering, decision support, and pattern recognition. A fuzzy rule generally has two parts: a condition, which identifies the input variables, and a conclusion, which identifies the output. The condition is commonly phrased as an if-then statement, with the conclusion following the "then." Consider a basic example: if the temperature is hot, the air conditioning should be switched on. Here the input is the temperature and the output is the air conditioner's state. When the temperature is hot, the rule directs that the conclusion be carried out, namely activating the air conditioning. Fuzzy rules are often combined with other methods, such as fuzzy inference systems, to build decision-making or control mechanisms that operate on data which may be inexact or unclear. They are especially valuable where conventional true-or-false Boolean reasoning falls short, and they help model complicated systems in which many variables interact.

Fatty liver basically means there's too much fat building up in your liver. How it gets treated really depends on what's causing it. Common culprits are obesity, high triglycerides, drinking a lot of alcohol, and losing weight too fast. Some medications get used for it. Udiliv 300 (ursodeoxycholic acid) helps dissolve cholesterol in the liver and is sometimes prescribed when high cholesterol or triglycerides are behind the problem. Rose day 10mg (rosiglitazone) is mostly for type 2 diabetes, but it can cut down liver fat too. Febutaz 40 (febuxostat) is meant for high uric acid, and it may also help with liver fat. Statins, which lower cholesterol, are another option, and so is vitamin E, which has helped in some studies. If you're working abroad and worried about your liver, talk to a doctor there about what makes sense for you. They can look at what's causing it and how healthy you are overall. Either way, keeping your weight in check, moving around regularly, and eating well goes a long way toward getting it under control.

Yeah, that hematoma (basically blood pooling outside the vessels) in your thigh could well be from damage to the small blood vessels when the muscle pulled. Other stuff can cause them too, like a bump or bruise, bleeding disorders, or meds that thin your blood. Sometimes they point to something bigger going on, so if you notice bleeding or bruising that won't go away or keeps showing up, get it checked out. A doctor can look at what's happening and tell you what to do next.

The term "fifth generation computer" refers to a major national research initiative launched in the early 1980s, most prominently by Japan's Ministry of International Trade and Industry (MITI) through the Institute for New Generation Computer Technology (ICOT), founded in 1982. The project aimed to create computers that would move beyond the conventional von Neumann architecture and the traditional programming paradigms of earlier machines. Its goal was to build systems capable of knowledge processing, logical inference, and natural language understanding, essentially machines that could reason and interact with humans in a more intelligent way.

The project was built around logic programming, especially the Prolog language, and it envisioned massively parallel hardware designed to run inference engines efficiently. Researchers hoped these machines would use large knowledge bases to draw conclusions, solve complex problems, and support applications such as expert systems, machine translation, and advanced database querying. The name signaled ambition: the first generation of computers used vacuum tubes, the second used transistors, the third used integrated circuits, and the fourth used microprocessors and very large scale integration, so the fifth generation was meant to represent a fundamental leap in intelligence rather than merely faster hardware.

The project ran for about ten years, ending in 1992. It is generally regarded as a commercial and technical disappointment. The hardware and software did not achieve the broad capabilities its proponents had hoped for, and conventional processors, which kept improving rapidly, outpaced the specialized machines the project produced. Nevertheless, the initiative had lasting effects. It spurred related research in parallel computing, logic programming, and knowledge representation in Japan, the United States, and Europe, and it is often cited as an example of how ambitious government-led technology goals can fall short when the underlying science is not yet mature. The term is also sometimes used more loosely to describe future computing concepts involving artificial intelligence, quantum computing, or neuromorphic hardware.

Okay so data scraping is basically when a program pulls info off a website. It sends a request to the site's server, grabs the HTML, then digs through that code to find the stuff it actually wants. That stuff could be text, pictures, or other media. People do it for all kinds of reasons. A company might want to see what competitors are charging for their products. A journalist could use it to collect numbers for a story, and a researcher might need a big pile of data for a study. You can do it by hand with a browser and a text editor, but most people automate it with scripts or specialized software. There are also services that will do the whole thing for you: you paste in a URL and they hand back the data as a spreadsheet or through an API. Just be careful, though. Scraping can break a site's terms of use, and plenty of sites actively block it. It can also hammer a server, which slows things down for everyone else trying to use the site.

The Baykar Bayraktar TB2 is an unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) from Turkey, built by Baykar Makina, a Turkish firm focused on designing, developing, and manufacturing drones, robotics, and automation systems. It is a medium-altitude, long-endurance (MALE) drone suited to many tasks, such as intelligence gathering, surveillance, and reconnaissance (ISR), border monitoring, and disaster relief. Equipped with an array of advanced sensors and payloads, the TB2 carries high-resolution electro-optical and infrared cameras, laser designators, and radar. It can stay airborne for more than 24 hours at a stretch and reaches a top speed of roughly 180 km/h. In recent years the aircraft has drawn considerable attention after the Turkish Armed Forces used it successfully in several military operations, including in Syria and Libya. It has also been sold to various countries worldwide, among them Ukraine and Qatar.

Identifying what is causing your red, itchy spots is the first step toward treating them successfully. Since I don't have more details, I can't suggest particular medications with confidence. That said, several possible causes of red, itchy patches on the face may apply to your situation. One is contact dermatitis, a form of skin irritation that develops after the skin touches certain substances. Makeup, skincare products, and fabrics can set it off, as can irritants such as pollution and harsh chemicals. If contact dermatitis seems likely, try steering clear of whatever appears to provoke your symptoms and apply a fragrance-free moisturizer to calm the skin. An over-the-counter hydrocortisone cream may also help ease inflammation and itching. Another possibility is seborrheic dermatitis, a condition that produces red, flaky rashes on the face, scalp, and other parts of the body. Itching often comes along with it, and hormonal shifts, stress, and some medications can all contribute. If this seems to be the issue, an over-the-counter antifungal cream or shampoo may help keep it under control. However, if the spots don't get better with home care, or if you develop other symptoms like fever, trouble breathing, or swelling, you should consult a healthcare provider, who can pinpoint the cause and recommend the right treatment.

Ensemble averaging is a technique in machine learning and statistics where multiple models are trained independently, and their predictions are combined, usually by averaging for regression tasks or by majority vote for classification. The core idea is that individual models make different errors, and when their predictions are pooled, those errors tend to cancel out or reduce, producing a result that is more accurate and stable than any single model would achieve on its own.

The technique works because of a basic statistical principle: averaging reduces variance. If each model has some random error around the true value, and these errors are not perfectly correlated, the average of the models will have a smaller overall error. This is why ensembles are especially useful for high-variance models, such as deep decision trees or neural networks, which can fluctuate significantly depending on the training data or initialization.

Ensemble averaging can be implemented in several ways. The models might be the same type trained on different random subsets of the data, as in bagging, or they might be different kinds of models altogether. The averaging can be uniform, giving every model equal weight, or weighted, where models that perform better on validation data receive more influence. Random forests are a well-known example of averaging many decision trees.

The main tradeoff is cost. Training and running several models requires more computation, memory, and time than using a single model, which can matter in production systems with strict latency requirements. Even so, ensemble averaging is a reliable way to improve predictive performance and robustness, and it is widely used in competitions and real-world applications.

Zero-interest intro offers are out there, but nobody can promise you'll get one. Whether you're approved depends on things like your credit score, your credit history, and your overall financial picture. What helps most is keeping your credit in good shape: pay your bills on time, don't max out your cards, and try to keep your credit utilization (how much of your limit you're actually using) low. If a zero-interest deal doesn't come through, look for a card with a low regular rate instead. Shop around and compare what different issuers offer. And read the fine print before you apply, because fees and other costs can sneak in even on a card that looks great at first glance.

Not necessarily. Many stocks trade on only one exchange, but a company can choose to list its shares on more than one exchange, and this is fairly common among large multinational firms.

When a company lists on two exchanges, it's usually called a dual listing. For example, some large companies are listed both on an exchange in their home country and on a major foreign exchange such as the New York Stock Exchange or the London Stock Exchange. Companies do this to reach a wider pool of investors, increase liquidity, raise their international profile, or make it easier for investors in different countries to buy shares in their local currency and during their local trading hours. Royal Dutch Shell, Toyota, and many Canadian companies that trade on both the Toronto Stock Exchange and a U.S. exchange are well-known examples.

Another common arrangement is the depositary receipt. Instead of listing its actual shares abroad, a foreign company can arrange for a bank to hold its shares and issue certificates representing them in another market. In the United States these are called American Depositary Receipts, or ADRs, and they let American investors buy stakes in companies like Alibaba, Sony, or Novo Nordisk on U.S. exchanges in dollars. Global Depositary Receipts serve a similar purpose in other markets.

Within a single country the picture can also be more complicated than one stock, one exchange. In the United States, for instance, a stock is formally listed on one exchange, such as Nasdaq or the NYSE, but it can actually be traded on many different venues, including other exchanges, alternative trading systems, and broker-dealer platforms. So the place where a stock is listed and the places where it trades are not always the same.

Because the same company's shares can trade in multiple markets, their prices tend to stay closely aligned after accounting for exchange rates and any conversion ratios, since traders will quickly exploit any meaningful price differences through arbitrage.

Your description points most strongly to a soft tissue injury on the little-finger side of the wrist, which plain X-rays often don't show. The bony bump you feel on the outer wrist is the ulnar styloid, and pain there that worsens with twisting, along with clicking and grinding, is a common pattern after punching or sparring impacts.

The most likely candidate is a tear or injury to the triangular fibrocartilage complex (TFCC), a cushion of cartilage and ligaments between the end of the forearm bones and the wrist bones. It is frequently hurt by a sudden twisting or impact load, and it classically causes pain on the pinky side with rotation and sometimes clicking or a sense of instability. Another possibility is an injury to the extensor carpi ulnaris tendon, which runs along that same side of the wrist and can become irritated, inflamed, or slip out of its groove, producing pain with twisting and a snapping or clicking feeling. A small fracture of the ulnar styloid or a subtle injury to the distal radioulnar joint, where the two forearm bones meet near the wrist, can also be missed on a standard X-ray, as can a bone bruise. Because you are hurting on the outer side and not the thumb side, injuries to the scaphoid or the scapholunate ligament are less likely, though a doctor should still consider them if symptoms change.

Since you're still symptomatic, I'd suggest going back to your doctor and asking specifically about an MRI or an ultrasound, which are better at showing cartilage, ligaments, and tendons. A referral to a hand or wrist specialist or a sports medicine clinic is also worthwhile. In the meantime, avoid sparring, heavy bag work, and any movement that reproduces the pain, and consider a wrist splint or brace for support. Ice and rest can help with irritation.

Seek prompt care if you notice significant swelling, a visible deformity, numbness or tingling in your fingers, a marked loss of grip strength, or pain that is getting worse rather than better. Your persistence in following this up is reasonable, as a clinical exam and further imaging can often clarify what's going on.

Multilinear subspace learning is a family of techniques in machine learning and signal processing for finding low-dimensional representations of data that naturally have the form of multidimensional arrays, called tensors. Examples include grayscale images (a second-order tensor, height by width), color images or video clips (third- or fourth-order tensors, adding color channels and time), and hyperspectral or fMRI data. It extends classical linear subspace learning methods such as principal component analysis (PCA), linear discriminant analysis (LDA), and canonical correlation analysis to this kind of data.

The motivation is that traditional methods require each sample to be a vector. To apply PCA to a 100 by 100 image, you would flatten it into a 10,000-dimensional vector. This has several drawbacks. It discards the structure of the data, since neighboring pixels in rows and columns, or frames across time, are no longer treated as having special relationships. It produces very high-dimensional vectors, so the projection matrices are huge and expensive to compute and store. It also invites overfitting, because the number of parameters is large compared with the number of training samples, which is the small-sample-size problem.

Multilinear methods instead learn a separate projection for each mode of the tensor. For a second-order tensor, one projection acts on the rows and another on the columns, so the reduced representation is obtained by multiplying the data along each mode by its own matrix. The number of parameters then grows with the sum of the mode sizes rather than their product, which reduces computation and memory and often acts as a helpful regularizer.

There are two broad approaches. The first is based on tensor decompositions, such as the Tucker decomposition (also called higher-order SVD) and the CANDECOMP/PARAFAC decomposition. These are used for exploratory analysis and compression, and for data that arises from multiple factors, for example faces varying by identity, pose, and illumination. The second consists of multilinear generalizations of specific learning criteria. Multilinear PCA (MPCA) and its relatives maximize the variance captured in the projected tensor. Multilinear discriminant analysis maximizes class separation. Others include tensor rank-one decomposition methods, uncorrelated multilinear variants, and tensor-based canonical correlation analysis.

Because the optimization over all projection matrices at once is generally not solvable in closed form, most algorithms use alternating optimization. One fixes all projections except one, solves for that one (often an eigenvalue problem), and cycles through the modes until convergence. Results can depend on initialization, and convergence is typically to a local optimum.

Applications include face and gait recognition, video and action analysis, medical imaging, chemometrics, and other computer vision tasks, as well as general dimensionality reduction as a preprocessing step before classification. The main caveat is that the multilinear model assumes the data's structure is well captured by separable per-mode projections, which may not hold for every dataset.

I'm sorry you're still bleeding after giving birth. Heavy bleeding, known as hemorrhage, can be serious and needs prompt medical care. Please keep in touch with your healthcare provider, and seek care right away if the bleeding is heavy or you notice any other worrying symptoms. The right treatment depends on what is causing the bleeding and how severe it is. Possible options include the following. Medication: your provider may prescribe drugs to stop the bleeding, such as tranexamic acid or other agents that help blood clot. Suture repair: if a tear or laceration in the cervix, vagina, or perineum is responsible, your provider may close it with stitches. Uterine artery embolization: a thin catheter is threaded through an artery in the leg up to the uterus, where tiny beads are released to block blood flow to the uterus and slow the bleeding. Hysteroscopy: a slim, flexible tube fitted with a camera is passed through the cervix into the uterus so the inside can be examined, and any abnormal tissue or foreign material can be removed. Dilation and curettage (D&C): the cervix is widened and a spoon-shaped instrument called a curette is used to clear tissue from the uterus. This may be needed if bleeding comes from retained placental tissue or an incomplete abortion. Please continue following up with your provider, and bring up any concerns or questions you have about your treatment. Also, report any heavy bleeding or other alarming symptoms to your provider without delay.

He held the title from 1985 until he retired from pro chess in 2000. Beyond the board, he's known for his chess theory work and his politics. He's written a bunch of chess books, and he's been a loud critic of Vladimir Putin.

A flame is a bright, burning form of fire. It forms when a blend of gases, such as oxygen and a fuel like wood or gasoline, catches light and begins to combust. As the fuel burns, it releases heat and illumination. People make use of this heat for cooking meals, staying warm, or running engines and other equipment. The glow can light up dark places or serve as a way to send a message. Although flames are lovely to watch, they pose real risks when not managed with care, which is why anyone working near them should be cautious and observe safety guidelines.

A classic tequila sunrise is made with tequila, orange juice, and grenadine. The tequila and orange juice are poured over ice in a tall glass, and then the grenadine is slowly added so it sinks to the bottom, creating the gradient of red fading into orange and yellow that resembles a sunrise. Some recipes include a splash of lime juice or a dash of triple sec for extra flavor, but the core ingredients are those three.

Picture yourself in a room defined by three measurements: length, width, and height. From where you stand, you can step ahead or behind, to either side, or go up or down. Next, suppose a fourth dimension exists, a direction of movement entirely distinct from the first three. Picturing it clearly is tough, since our minds are built around three-dimensional space and struggle to grasp anything outside ordinary experience. Still, one helpful approach is to imagine moving through time the way you move through the other three dimensions, so that you could travel forward into the future or backward into the past. Time differs from those three spatial directions, though, because you cannot wander through it in the same physical sense. It is better understood as a way of tracking how events unfold. People have also considered other possible fourth dimensions beyond time, yet offering a concrete example of what they would be like is hard. Some scientists and philosophers have suggested that extra dimensions beyond the three we experience daily may exist, but no one can say with certainty what those dimensions would be like or how they would function.

Apple Computer, Inc. was founded in 1976 by Steve Jobs, Steve Wozniak, and Ronald Wayne, and it was a technology firm. The company gained a reputation for its groundbreaking products and easy-to-use interfaces, becoming one of the most prosperous and influential tech firms globally. In 2007, it shortened its name to Apple Inc., reflecting that it had grown well past computers alone. Even now, Apple remains a leading force in the technology sector, placing considerable emphasis on hardware, software, and services.

The United States government typically refuses to bargain with terrorists, meaning it does not seek deals or arrangements with groups or individuals who rely on violence and fear to pursue their aims. Part of the reasoning is that such negotiations can end up rewarding terrorists with the very things they demand, which may motivate them to keep resorting to violence. Such concessions could also create a risky precedent, leading other groups to believe that terrorism is a workable route to their objectives. Negotiation is further complicated by the difficulty of identifying who truly holds authority within an organization and what they actually want. Confidence that any group or person would honor a settlement is also hard to establish. In the end, refusing to negotiate is meant to make clear that violence and terrorism will not be accepted, and to deter others from adopting such methods.

David Rumelhart was a cognitive psychologist and computer scientist who made important contributions to artificial intelligence and cognitive modeling. Born in 1941, he earned his doctorate in psychology from Stanford University in 1967. He is chiefly remembered for his research on artificial neural networks, computer programs built to mimic the way the human brain handles information. He was among the leading figures of the connectionist movement, which aimed to explain how the brain functions by constructing computational models of the neural links that support thought. Rumelhart played a major role in developing the backpropagation algorithm, a method now widely used to train artificial neural networks. He also co-wrote the influential volume "Parallel Distributed Processing," which popularized the idea of distributed representation: the notion that the brain holds information spread across many neurons and connections instead of in one specific place. Rumelhart served as a professor at the University of California, San Diego, and in 1990 he received the National Medal of Science, the highest scientific honor in the United States. He died in 2011.

Think of bread like a sponge full of tiny water bubbles and a wall of starchy stuff. When bread is fresh, the starch inside is soft and loose, and the water is spread out nicely. As the bread sits, the starch slowly tightens up and squeezes out the water, a bit like a sponge that dries out and gets stiff. That tightening is what makes bread go stale and hard.

Baguettes go stale so fast for a few simple reasons. First, they are mostly just flour, water, salt, and yeast, with no fat, no milk, and no sugar. Those extra ingredients in other breads act like little helpers that keep the starch soft and the moisture locked in. Baguettes don't have those helpers, so their starch tightens up quickly.

Second, baguettes are thin and have a lot of crust compared to the soft inside. The crust is hard and dry, and it can pull moisture out of the inside, which speeds up the drying.

Third, the crust of a baguette is very crispy, and the inside is very open with lots of air holes. That means more surface area is exposed to the air, so the bread loses moisture faster.

So a baguette is like a small, simple, airy sponge with no protective extras, and that's why it turns hard so quickly. Keeping it in a paper bag on the day you buy it, or warming it briefly in an oven, can help it feel nicer for a little longer.

So a cryptographic hash function is basically a math function that takes some input (called a message) and spits out a fixed-length string, usually written as a hex number. The big thing is that it's computationally infeasible to find two different messages that give you the same output. That's why it's handy for checking whether a file or message has been tampered with, since even a tiny change gives you a totally different hash. People also call these "digest functions" or "one-way functions," because computing the hash is easy but going backwards from the hash to the original message is really hard. That's why they're used for storing passwords: you can keep the hash without anyone being able to easily pull the original password out of it. Some common examples are SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm), MD5 (Message-Digest Algorithm 5), and RIPEMD-160 (RACE Integrity Primitives Evaluation Message Digest). Though, fair warning, MD5 is pretty broken at this point and shouldn't be trusted for anything security-sensitive.

So basically, stereo vision is a way for computers to figure out the 3D shape of a scene using two or more 2D photos taken from cameras sitting a known distance apart. You compare how things shift between the images, and that tells you how far away each point is. It's used all over the place: robotics, self-driving cars, 3D mapping, AR, you name it. People use it to build 3D models of objects or whole landscapes, and it can also help track and recognize things in real time.

Getting it to work means calibrating the cameras first. You need to know each camera's intrinsics (things like focal length and the principal point) and the extrinsics, which tell you how the cameras are positioned and angled relative to each other. Once that's done, you rectify the images so matching points line up along the same row, which makes finding depth way easier. For the depth calculation itself, there are a bunch of options: block matching, semantic segmentation, and deep learning methods are the usual suspects. Which one you pick really depends on how messy your scene is and what your application needs.

Actually, the premise needs a correction: Apple is in the Dow Jones Industrial Average, and has been since March 2015, when it replaced AT&T. Microsoft, Amazon, Salesforce, Nvidia, and several other major tech names are in it as well. Google's parent company, Alphabet, is the notable exception, and so is Meta, along with Tesla and Berkshire Hathaway.

The reasons for those absences come down to how the index is built and managed. The Dow is not a mechanical index based on size. It consists of just 30 stocks chosen by a committee at S&P Dow Jones Indices, which looks for companies with an excellent reputation, sustained growth, and wide investor interest. There is no strict market-capitalization rule, so the committee has a lot of discretion, and with only 30 slots, many large companies are simply left out.

The more important quirk is that the Dow is price-weighted rather than weighted by company value. A stock with a high share price has more influence on the index than one with a low share price, regardless of the company's actual size. This makes very high-priced stocks awkward to include, because a single one could dominate the index. Alphabet's share price was historically very high, and Amazon's was too until stock splits brought it down, which is part of why Amazon only joined in 2024 after splitting its shares. Companies often get added after a stock split makes their price more compatible with the index. Apple itself did a 7-for-1 split in 2014 shortly before joining.

Other factors play a role too. The committee tends to make changes sparingly, so it doesn't turn over members quickly. Alphabet has a complicated share structure with multiple classes, and Tesla's inclusion has been questioned partly because of its volatility and, in earlier years, its lack of consistent profitability. Berkshire Hathaway's Class A shares cost hundreds of thousands of dollars each, which would break a price-weighted index. Meta has simply not been picked yet.

Because of all this, many analysts view the S&P 500 or the Nasdaq-100 as better representations of the overall market, since they weight companies by market capitalization and include far more firms.

Atherosclerotic heart disease, also called coronary artery disease, is a condition in which the arteries that supply blood to the heart muscle become narrowed or blocked by a buildup of fatty deposits, called plaques. These plaques are made up of cholesterol, calcium, inflammatory cells, and other substances that accumulate within the artery wall over many years. As the plaque grows, it reduces the space available for blood to flow, and the heart receives less oxygen and nutrients than it needs, particularly during physical exertion or stress.

The disease often develops silently for decades before symptoms appear. When blood flow to the heart is restricted, a person may experience chest pain or pressure, known as angina, or shortness of breath. A more serious complication occurs when a plaque ruptures, triggering a blood clot that can suddenly block the artery. This can cause a heart attack, where part of the heart muscle is damaged or dies.

Risk factors include high LDL cholesterol, high blood pressure, smoking, diabetes, obesity, physical inactivity, a family history of early heart disease, and advancing age. Treatment typically involves lifestyle changes such as a heart-healthy diet, regular exercise, and quitting smoking, along with medications like statins to lower cholesterol, blood pressure drugs, and antiplatelet agents. In some cases, procedures such as angioplasty with stenting or coronary artery bypass surgery are needed to restore blood flow.

Yes, Tennessee offers a principal residence exemption for property taxes. Under state law, homeowners can qualify for a property tax break when the property serves as their principal residence, meaning the place where they live for most of the year. Qualifying can lower the amount of property tax a homeowner must pay on the home.

To qualify for this exemption in Tennessee, homeowners need to satisfy several conditions. The property must be the owner's principal residence, in other words the place where they live for the majority of the year. The owner must submit an application by the deadline, which is usually November 1 or earlier in a given year. The owner must also supply proof of ownership and residency, such as a driver's license or another government-issued ID, utility bills, or other documents showing the owner's name and the property's address.

Once a homeowner meets these conditions and the exemption is approved, their property tax bill goes down. The size of the reduction depends on the property's value and the tax rate in the local jurisdiction where the home sits.

It's also worth knowing that the principal residence exemption is only one of several property tax exemptions that might be available in Tennessee. Others may depend on factors like the owner's age, disability status, military service, or how the property is used. To learn which exemptions apply in your area, it's a good idea to contact your local county assessor's office or tax collector's office.

In the UK, property landlords must pay tax on the rental income they collect. Previously, they could deduct certain costs tied to their rental homes from that income, including mortgage interest, insurance, and repair and upkeep expenses, which lowered their tax bill. Recent changes to the tax system, however, have greatly cut the relief available to them. In 2017, the government altered how landlords could claim relief on mortgage interest. Before this, they could claim relief on the entire interest amount at their marginal tax rate. Under the new rules, relief was gradually reduced, beginning with a 20% cut for those earning between £50,000 and £100,000, and rising until relief was entirely removed for those earning more than £200,000. The government also brought in what is called the "section 24" tax, which cut relief even further. Landlords can no longer deduct a range of costs, such as repairs and maintenance, insurance, and some other expenses. Taken together, these measures have considerably shrunk the tax relief available on rental properties, making it harder for landlords to earn a profit from their investments. Those affected may need to raise their rents or look for other ways to cut costs in order to stay profitable.

Your husband's regimen matches standard guidelines. The Infectious Diseases Society of America recommends doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 10 to 21 days for most adults with early Lyme disease, and 21 days is common when the infection has spread or the diagnosis is less certain. Doxycycline is generally well tolerated at 79, and because it is not cleared mainly by the kidneys, it usually doesn't need adjustment for age-related changes. Because he takes no other medications, interactions are unlikely to be a concern.

To get the most from the course, he should take each dose with a full glass of water and stay upright for at least 30 minutes afterward to lower the risk of esophageal irritation. He should take it at least two hours apart from dairy products, calcium supplements, antacids, iron, magnesium, or multivitamins with minerals, since these can reduce absorption. Doxycycline also makes skin more sensitive to sunlight, so he should use sunscreen and cover up outdoors.

On the turmeric, there is no good evidence that it helps treat Lyme disease or speeds recovery, so it shouldn't replace or be considered an add-on to the antibiotic. Turmeric can thin the blood somewhat and may interact with other medications, so it's worth mentioning to his doctor. A probiotic is generally harmless and may ease antibiotic-related stomach upset or diarrhea. Taking it a few hours apart from the doxycycline is a sensible precaution.

Some symptoms can linger for weeks after finishing antibiotics, including fatigue, aches, and mild joint discomfort. This is common and does not usually mean the infection persists, and extra or longer courses of antibiotics are not recommended for it. However, he should contact his doctor promptly or seek urgent care if he develops a severe or worsening headache, facial drooping or weakness, neck stiffness, heart palpitations or dizziness, new joint swelling, a spreading rash, persistent fever, or severe or bloody diarrhea.

Finally, since a blood test alone can sometimes be unclear early in infection, it's worth confirming with his prescriber that the diagnosis and plan are right for his specific symptoms.

People fail to save more for a mix of practical constraints and psychological tendencies, and it is hard to separate the two in any individual case.

The most basic reason is that many people simply don't have much left over. Housing, food, transportation, healthcare, childcare, and debt payments absorb most of a typical household's income, and for lower earners they can absorb all of it. Wages for many workers have grown more slowly than the cost of things like rent, tuition, and medical care, so the room to save has shrunk even for people who are careful. Irregular income makes it worse, since a person who cannot predict next month's earnings has to keep cash on hand and can rarely commit to a steady savings habit.

Beyond constraints, behavioral economics has documented several consistent biases. People tend to value present rewards much more than future ones, a pattern called present bias, so spending today feels more compelling than a retirement that is decades away. Retirement also feels abstract, and many people struggle to picture their older selves as people whose interests they should look after. Inertia matters too: saving usually requires an active decision, such as opening an account, choosing investments, or setting up transfers, and people often put these off. This is why automatic enrollment in workplace retirement plans raises participation so dramatically.

Social and informational factors play a role as well. Consumer culture and comparison with peers encourage spending, and easy credit makes it possible to consume now and pay later. Many people also lack financial literacy, so they underestimate how much compounding can help or how much they will need in retirement. Others are overconfident, assuming they will earn more later and can catch up then.

There are also rational reasons not to save in some cases. Means-tested benefits can penalize people who accumulate assets, high-interest debt may make paying down balances a better use of money than saving, and people who expect support from family or Social Security-type programs may reasonably save less. Some people also distrust financial institutions or markets, especially if they have been burned before or come from communities with a history of exclusion from banking.

In short, many people can't save more, some could but are pulled by psychology and habit, and a few are making defensible choices given their circumstances. That is why the most effective policies tend to combine higher incomes and lower costs with defaults that make saving automatic.

In linguistics, "context" refers to the circumstances surrounding a piece of language use that help determine its meaning. Language rarely carries its full meaning on the surface of the words alone; listeners and readers draw on additional information to interpret what is said or written. This information can be divided into several overlapping kinds. The linguistic context, sometimes called co-text, is the surrounding words, sentences, or discourse in which an expression appears. The meaning of a word like "bank" or "bat," for instance, often becomes clear only from the words around it. The situational context includes the physical setting, the time and place of an utterance, and the activity taking place, so that "Look at that!" can point to very different things depending on where it is said. The social context concerns the relationships between speakers, their roles, social norms, and the institutions involved, which shape how formal or polite an utterance should be. Finally, the cultural and background context consists of shared knowledge, beliefs, and assumptions that speakers presuppose without stating.

Context matters for several areas of study. Pragmatics examines how context contributes to meaning beyond literal semantics, including implicature, where a speaker suggests something without saying it directly, as when someone answers "Do you want coffee?" with "It's late," implying no. Discourse analysis looks at how context shapes larger units of text and conversation. Sociolinguistics studies how social context influences variation in language, such as differences in dialect or register. Context also shapes the interpretation of deixis, the words whose meaning depends on who is speaking, where, and when, such as "here," "now," and "you." In short, context is the broad set of conditions that allow speakers and hearers to understand language as it is actually used, rather than as an abstract system of words and rules alone.

Honestly there are a few reasons soccer gets tagged with fan violence more than other sports. First off, it's a global sport with a massive following, so you've got way more people packed into stadiums, and that just gives trouble more chances to happen. The fans are also super passionate, and when emotions run that high, arguments can blow up pretty fast.

Then there's the hooliganism thing. In some countries it's been a problem for decades, with organized groups of fans who actually plan fights and show up ready to brawl. For some people, getting violent is a way of showing loyalty to their club, or of letting rival fans know they're not scared of them.

Alcohol plays a big part too. Lots of fans drink before the match and during it, and that tends to make the whole atmosphere rowdier and more aggressive.

That said, most soccer fans aren't violent at all, and clubs, leagues and governments have been doing plenty to cut down on trouble at matches. It's still an issue in some places though, and it's not something that should just get ignored.

The saying "the exception proves the rule" means that when a rule has an exception, that exception actually serves to confirm the rule's existence. For instance, suppose there is a rule stating that all birds can fly. Penguins, however, are an exception, since they cannot fly. The existence of this exception (penguins being unable to fly) is what lends support to the rule (all birds can fly). Put another way, the penguins demonstrate the rule by showing that it is not universally true, so the exception points to the rule's existence. Does that make sense? High blood pressure can make people feel tired, and it can also bring on shortness of breath, headaches, and dizziness. Imagine the air above us is like a giant blanket that moves around, and sometimes it gets pulled from warm places, like the south, up toward where you live. In winter, cold air usually comes down from the north, but sometimes a big pocket of warm air gets pushed up instead, the way a warm breeze can sneak into a room when a window is open. Winds high up in the sky, called the jet stream, act like a wavy road that steers weather. When that road bends in a way that lets warm air flow north and parks there for a while, places get much warmer than usual for the season.

Sometimes a big bubble of high pressure settles over an area and acts like a lid. It holds the warm air in and keeps cold air from coming in, so the days stay mild and sunny for a long time.

Earth is also slowly getting warmer overall because of gases people add to the air by burning fuel. That doesn't cause every warm day, but it makes warm days like this more likely and makes them a little warmer than they would have been.

So 68 degrees on Christmas Eve is a warm "wrong-way" day: warm air got steered north, a weather lid may be holding it there, and a warmer planet makes it a bit more likely. Your local weather forecaster can tell you how long it will last.

Testing shows only what's in your body at the moment of the test. If you're both clean and neither of you has been exposed to anything since, then you're starting from a good place. But if one of you, or both, has been with someone else in the past, an infection can sometimes take a while to show up on a test. Some infections have a "window period," meaning the test can miss them for days, weeks, or even months after exposure. So a clean result from a while ago doesn't fully guarantee you're clean today.

Also, some infections spread through skin-to-skin contact and not just fluids. Herpes and HPV, for example, can pass between partners even when no one has symptoms, and standard STD tests don't always check for them. Condoms help a lot with these, but they don't cover every area of skin, so they lower the risk rather than removing it.

If you and your partner have only been with each other, have both been tested recently, and have no symptoms, the chance of picking something up is quite low. Getting tested again after a few months, or before you stop using protection, is a simple way to stay sure. A doctor or clinic can also tell you which tests fit your situation.

This let them switch off the console and return later, resuming right where they had stopped. Because the cards were compact and easy to carry, a player could bring their saves along and use them on another console.
