The Church-Turing thesis is one of those ideas that sits at the crossroads of computer science, math, and philosophy. Basically, it says that anything a human could work out with pen and paper, following a clear set of steps, can also be done by a machine, as long as you give it the right instructions. So the thesis is really claiming that every computation that's possible in principle can be carried out by a computer. It's named after Alonzo Church and Alan Turing. Church was a logician and mathematician who came up with the idea of "effective calculability" for functions, and that became the foundation for the whole thing. Turing was a mathematician who's often called the father of modern computer science. He came up with the "universal machine," a theoretical device that can run any computation that's possible at all. The thesis has had a huge impact on computing, and it's still a big deal today. It's also kicked off plenty of arguments among philosophers and computer scientists, since it raises tough questions about what computation actually is and where its limits lie.

Error messages are written by people. Every program on your computer, whether it's a game, a web browser, or the operating system itself, was made by programmers who typed out instructions telling the computer what to do. While they write those instructions, they also try to imagine what could go wrong, and for each problem they think of, they write a little note the computer should show if it happens.

Think of it like a parent leaving a babysitter a list that says "if the baby cries, check the diaper" and "if the power goes out, the flashlight is in the drawer." The babysitter doesn't make those notes up. They were written ahead of time by someone who guessed what might happen. When your computer shows "File not found," it's reading a note a programmer wrote years ago for exactly that situation.

So why are some messages so strange? Programmers often write them in a hurry, and they write them for other programmers, not for regular people. A message like "Segmentation fault" or "Exception 0x0000005" makes sense to someone who knows how the inside of the computer works, a bit like a mechanic's shorthand. To everyone else it sounds like gibberish.

Sometimes the problem is something nobody planned for. In that case the computer falls back on a very general, catch-all message, like "An unknown error occurred," because there's no specific note for that situation. It's like the babysitter's list ending with "if anything else goes wrong, call me."

Those long codes full of numbers and letters are like labels on a filing cabinet. They don't mean much to you, but a programmer or tech support person can look one up and find out exactly which part of the program got stuck. That's why searching an error code online often leads you to an answer.

And every now and then a programmer adds a joke or a weird message just for fun, assuming hardly anyone will ever see it. So when an error sounds silly or confusing, it's usually because a real person wrote it quickly, for themselves, a long time ago.

Your spelling is fine, and your question is a good one! The word you want is "ascetic," which means someone who gives up comforts like tasty food to focus on their mind.

The round, smiling figure you're thinking of is usually not Siddhartha himself. In China, Japan, and nearby places, people often picture a jolly, pot-bellied monk called Budai. Lots of people believe he was a real monk who loved children, carried a big sack, and was always happy. Because he looks so cheerful and full, people started to see him as a symbol of good luck, plenty, and being content. Some traditions also connect him with Maitreya, the future Buddha who is yet to come.

Siddhartha himself is often shown as thin and calm in artwork that shows his years of hard fasting, and many statues from ancient India show him that way. The later, plumper statues are a different idea. They show the peace and happiness that come after you have found what you were looking for, so the artists made him look well-fed and relaxed.

Tennessee's path to statehood began with its settlement by European Americans in the 1760s, when pioneers crossed the Appalachian Mountains from Virginia and North Carolina. The region was then part of North Carolina, which ceded its western lands to the federal government in 1790. Before that, the settlers had already formed their own governments, including the short-lived State of Franklin in the early 1780s, which sought recognition from Congress but never gained it.

In 1790 Congress organized the area as the Southwest Territory, with William Blount as governor. As the population grew past the threshold set by federal law, residents called a constitutional convention in 1796. That convention drafted a state constitution, and the territorial legislature approved the plan. Congress then admitted Tennessee to the Union on June 1, 1796, making it the sixteenth state and the first to be carved out of federal territory west of the original states. Its name came from the Cherokee town of Tanasi, and John Sevier was elected its first governor.

Credit card convenience checks can be handy for making payments or borrowing money when you need it, but they carry risks and costs that deserve careful thought. A few points to keep in mind follow.

First, these checks usually carry higher interest rates and fees than ordinary credit card purchases, so review the terms and conditions closely and make sure you understand what using one will actually cost you. Second, writing a convenience check raises your credit utilization ratio, meaning the share of your available credit that you are using, and a higher ratio can drag down your credit score. Third, because a check can be stolen and cashed by someone else, store it somewhere secure and avoid leaving it out in the open. Finally, look at whether other options, such as moving money from a savings account or taking out a personal loan, might serve you more affordably. In short, weigh the advantages against the drawbacks and stay alert to the risks and expenses involved before you use a credit card convenience check.

Think of a big toy box that many people share. When the company that owns the box wants to make more money, it often adds new toys that it can sell, shows you ads, or collects information about what you play with. Sometimes the toys you liked get moved to a harder-to-find shelf, or taken out entirely, because fewer people used them or because they don't make money the way the new things do.

Companies also change things to match what they think most people want. If the company looks at its numbers and sees that most people watch videos recommended to them rather than searching for the most popular ones, it may hide or remove the "most viewed" list to make room for the recommendations it wants you to see. That can feel like a loss to someone who liked the old way.

Windows and iOS work a bit like this too. Their makers want every computer or phone to be safe and up to date, so they turn on updates automatically and make it harder to switch them off. They believe that keeps people protected from viruses and bugs, and that is a good reason. But it also means you get less say in when things change, and the company gets to decide more of the settings for you.

Another part is that these programs are very large, with thousands of people working on them at once. Changing one thing can affect many others, so sometimes they add new features that people didn't ask for, and sometimes they remove old ones that a few people still depend on.

So in short, companies change their products to make money, to keep everyone safe in the same way, and to chase what most people seem to use, and those choices don't always match what you personally want. Your frustration is very common, and many people feel the same way.

Each year, Burning Man takes over a stretch of desert in Nevada, USA, where people gather to honor art, self-expression, and community. Participants construct a temporary metropolis called "Black Rock City," which is full of art installations, live music, and things to do. A defining moment of the event is the burning of a huge wooden figure shaped like a man, carried out on the final night. The ritual marks the close of the gathering and represents releasing one's attachment to physical belongings. Attendees are invited to channel their creativity and self-expression in any way they choose, whether by dressing in elaborate costumes, taking part in art projects, or simply soaking up the surroundings. Known for its one-of-a-kind and nonconformist character, Burning Man is often described by attendees as a transformative experience. It offers a space where people can set aside their daily routines and become whoever they wish to be.

Bayesian optimization is an approach for finding the best value of a function whose form is unknown, and doing so with few evaluations. It is especially well suited to tuning the hyperparameters of machine learning models, since the space of possible settings is frequently huge and testing any single configuration demands a great deal of computation. The technique begins by using the points already evaluated to construct a surrogate model of the unknown function. This surrogate is probabilistic, so it captures our present belief about what the function looks like. In each round of the optimization, the algorithm chooses the next point to test according to the improvement in the function value that the surrogate model expects. A major strength of the approach is its ability to cope with constraints as well as noisy measurements of the function. It can further make use of existing knowledge about the function's shape to steer the search. In short, Bayesian optimization is an effective and economical way to optimize functions that are complicated and costly to evaluate.

Tom M. Mitchell is an American computer scientist and academic, best known for his foundational contributions to machine learning. He is the Founders University Professor at Carnegie Mellon University, where he has long been affiliated with the Machine Learning Department, which he helped establish as one of the first departments of its kind in the world.

Mitchell's most widely cited contribution is his 1997 textbook, Machine Learning, which became a standard introduction to the field for students and researchers. In it he offered a well-known formal definition of machine learning: a computer program is said to learn from experience E with respect to some class of tasks T and performance measure P, if its performance at tasks in T, as measured by P, improves with experience E. This definition remains a common reference point in discussions of the field.

His research has spanned several areas, including machine learning methods, the use of neural imaging data such as fMRI to study how the brain represents meaning, and the application of learning systems to natural language processing. He has also worked on the NELL (Never-Ending Language Learning) project, which aimed to build a system that continuously learns to read the web.

Mitchell has received numerous honors for his work, including election to the National Academy of Engineering and the American Association for the Advancement of Science, and he is a Fellow of the Association for the Advancement of Artificial Intelligence. He has also served as a past president of the International Machine Learning Society.

Pretty simple, really. First thing, your associate has to sign the back of the cheque, since it's made out to them. Without that endorsement the bank probably won't touch it. Some people also write "pay to the order of [your business name]" above the signature so it's clear who's getting the money.

After that, take it to your business bank's branch and deposit it. A lot of banks let you do it through their mobile app or online banking too, so you might not even have to leave the house. Depending on the bank, they may ask for ID or some proof that you own or run the business, especially when the cheque isn't in your name. Banks can be picky about that stuff, so bring something just in case.

Then you wait for it to clear. It can take a few business days before the funds are actually available, so don't count on the money right away.

Every bank does things a bit differently, and there can be rules depending on where you live, so it's worth checking your bank's own procedure. If you're not sure about anything, just call them or ask an accountant or someone who knows the finance side.

Nobody has found the plane, and it's still one of the biggest mysteries in aviation. In March 2014, Malaysia Airlines Flight 370 took off from Kuala Lumpur with 239 people on board, headed for Beijing. About an hour later, someone turned off its tracking signals, and the plane turned away from its route and flew west over the Indian Ocean. Satellites picked up a few faint pings from it for several hours after that, which suggested it ended up somewhere in a very remote part of the southern Indian Ocean, but no one knows exactly what happened to it.

Think of it like a toy that suddenly vanished from a room while the lights were off. We know roughly where it was last seen, but not where it ended up.

Searchers spent years combing the bottom of the ocean in that area, covering an enormous stretch of seafloor, and came up empty. Some pieces of wreckage did wash up on beaches thousands of miles away, including a wing part found on the island of Réunion, and experts confirmed they came from this plane. But those pieces didn't tell investigators why the plane went off course or where the main part of it is.

As for why it happened, no one has a definite answer. Some theories suggest a fire or a loss of air pressure that disabled the crew, while others point to deliberate action by someone on board. Investigators never reached a firm conclusion.

You're right that the news coverage faded. Big stories tend to fade when there's no new information, and the search was called off in 2017. A private company tried again in 2025 with a no-find, no-fee deal, and as far as I know that search also didn't locate the wreckage. Families of the passengers still want answers, and a few people keep looking into it, but for most of the world the story has quieted down. Since news moves fast, you may want to check a recent source for any developments after my information ends.

The body produces warmth through a series of chemical reactions known as metabolism, which is how it turns the food we eat into usable energy. Every activity the body carries out, including maintaining its internal warmth, depends on this energy. When food is consumed, the body breaks its molecules apart and rebuilds that chemical energy into forms it can use, and heat is released as a side effect of this work. That heat helps hold the body near its usual temperature of roughly 98.6 degrees Fahrenheit, or 37 degrees Celsius. In short, metabolism is the process of converting food into energy, and the heat it gives off is what keeps us warm.

Taking two emergency contraceptive pills like the i-pill within the same week is not dangerous to your health. The i-pill contains levonorgestrel, a hormone that is considered very safe, and the World Health Organization says it can be used more than once, even within the same menstrual cycle, without causing serious harm or affecting your future fertility. So you have not damaged your body by doing this.

You took both pills within about two days of each act of intercourse, which is good timing, since the pill works best the sooner it is taken and is meant for use within 72 hours. Each pill only covers the intercourse that happened before it. The first pill did not protect you during the second encounter, so taking the second one was the right decision.

The main effect of taking two doses close together is that your hormones may be temporarily unsettled. You may notice nausea, headache, tiredness, breast tenderness, lower abdominal discomfort, or spotting and irregular bleeding over the next few days or weeks. Your next period may also come earlier or later than usual, sometimes by up to a week. These changes are temporary and should settle within a cycle or two.

No emergency pill is 100 percent effective. If your period is more than about a week late, or is unusually light or strange, take a home urine pregnancy test, ideally at least three weeks after the last unprotected sex (so around mid-July). If you have severe lower abdominal pain, especially on one side, or very heavy bleeding, see a doctor promptly.

The i-pill is meant for emergencies and is less effective than regular contraception, and frequent use tends to make periods unpredictable. If you are sexually active, it would be worth talking to a gynecologist about a regular method, such as daily birth control pills, an IUD, or an injection. Condoms are also a good choice because they protect against sexually transmitted infections as well as pregnancy. You also have every right to decide when you have sex and to insist on protection, and you should never feel pressured. If you ever feel unsafe or forced in your relationship, please reach out to someone you trust or a doctor.

Having a lot of albumin in your urine (it's called albuminuria) can mean your kidneys are damaged or that you've got some kind of kidney disease, nephrotic syndrome being one example. Definitely see a doctor so they can figure out what's actually causing it and what to do about it.

Treatment usually starts with dealing with whatever's behind it. If it's high blood pressure or diabetes, getting those under control can really cut down on further damage to your kidneys. Your doctor might also put you on medication to reduce how much protein you're losing in your urine and to protect your kidneys. Sometimes they'll suggest lifestyle stuff too, like changing your diet or getting more exercise.

Stick with whatever your doctor recommends, and keep getting your albumin levels and kidney function checked on a regular basis so you know it's being managed properly.

Predictive analytics is a branch of data analysis that uses historical data, statistical methods, and machine learning techniques to forecast what is likely to happen in the future. Rather than simply describing what has already occurred, it looks for patterns and relationships in past data and applies them to new situations to estimate future outcomes, such as customer behavior, equipment failures, sales volumes, or the likelihood of a loan default.

The process typically begins with gathering relevant data and preparing it for analysis, which may involve cleaning errors, handling missing values, and selecting the variables most likely to influence the outcome. Analysts then build a model, using techniques such as regression, decision trees, neural networks, or time series methods, and train it on past examples where the result is already known. The model is tested on separate data to check how accurately it performs before being used to make predictions on new cases.

Organizations use predictive analytics across many fields. Retailers use it to anticipate demand and recommend products, banks use it to assess credit risk and detect fraud, hospitals use it to identify patients at risk of complications, and manufacturers use it for predictive maintenance so that machines can be serviced before they break down. Its value lies in helping decision-makers plan ahead and allocate resources more effectively, though its predictions are probabilities rather than certainties and depend heavily on the quality of the data and the assumption that future conditions will resemble past ones.

Imagine you want to send a secret note to a friend across the playground, but you don't want anyone to know it came from you. So you fold the note inside three envelopes, one inside another. You hand it to a kid named Alice. Alice opens the outer envelope and sees "give this to Bob," so she does. Bob opens the next envelope and sees "give this to Carol." Carol opens the last envelope and finally sees the actual note and who it's for, and she delivers it.

Here's the clever part. Alice knows the note came from you, but she has no idea what it says or where it's really going. Carol knows where it's going and can read it, but she has no idea it came from you, because she only got it from Bob. Bob knows almost nothing at all. Nobody in the chain knows both who sent the note and where it ended up.

That's basically how Tor works on the internet. Tor stands for "The Onion Router," and it's called that because your message is wrapped in layers like an onion, or like those nested envelopes. Each of the kids passing the note along is a "Tor node." A node is just a computer, usually run by a volunteer somewhere in the world, that agrees to help pass these wrapped-up messages along. Your internet traffic usually hops through three of them.

The "exit node" is the last kid in the chain, Carol in our story. It's the computer that takes off the final layer and sends your request out onto the regular internet, like to a website you want to visit. When that website looks to see who's visiting, it sees the exit node, not you. That's how Tor helps keep people private.

There are a couple of grown-up details worth knowing. Because the exit node unwraps the last layer, it can sometimes see what's being sent if the website itself isn't using encryption (the little padlock you see in your browser). So Tor hides who you are, but it doesn't automatically hide what you're saying unless the website also protects it. And because people who run exit nodes look like the source of all that traffic, they sometimes get blamed or get complaints for things other people did, which is why fewer volunteers run exit nodes than the other kinds.

Imagine someone tied your hands behind your back, made you kneel in a row, and stood a person with a gun right behind you. Even if there were lots of you, trying to jump up would mean being shot before you got two steps. Most of the men in these videos are in that exact spot. Their hands are tied, they're kneeling, and the armed men are close and ready.

They've also often been locked up for a long time before the video was made. Many were hungry, sick, hurt, or scared for weeks or months, and that makes it very hard to move quickly or think clearly. Some were probably told or shown that resisting would make things worse for them or their families.

There's also a problem that makes it hard for a group to act together. Everyone is thinking, "If I move, I'll get shot first, so maybe I'll wait and see if someone else does something." When nobody moves first, nobody moves at all.

Finally, the videos are edited and carefully arranged, so we only see a small part of what happened. What we see is a moment when resisting was almost certainly hopeless.

The ones you see moving up and down in fields are called pumpjacks, or "nodding donkeys." They're not really rigs at all. A rig is the tall tower you see drilling into the ground to find oil, but the pumpjack is what's left after the oil is found and the well is ready to pump it out.

Think of it like a giant straw. Oil sits deep underground, under lots of rock and dirt. Someone drills a long hole down to it, and then they need a way to pull the oil up through that hole. The pumpjack is the machine that does the pulling.

Here's how it works. A motor, usually powered by electricity or natural gas, turns a big wheel at the bottom of the machine. A metal arm is attached to that wheel, off-center, so as the wheel spins, the arm goes up and down, like a seesaw. The top of the arm is the "head" that bobs up and down, which is why it looks like it's nodding. That up-and-down motion moves a long metal rod, called a sucker rod, that runs all the way down the well pipe to the oil. At the bottom of the rod is a pump that acts like a plunger in a syringe. Each time the rod goes up, the pump sucks oil in from below. Each time it goes down, a valve closes so the oil gets pushed up the pipe and out.

So the whole thing is just a slow, steady pump, pumping oil one stroke at a time, over and over, day and night. It's a bit like pumping a playground swing or working a water pump by hand, just done by a machine that's much bigger and stronger.

Sorry to hear your dad's been dealing with this, that sounds rough. An enlarged liver (hepatomegaly) and fatty liver can both cause belly pain, plus stuff like tiredness, weakness, and weight loss. The first step is figuring out what's behind the enlargement and the fat, since that decides how it gets treated. Treatment usually comes down to a few things. Lifestyle changes are often the big one: tweaking his diet, getting more movement in, and cutting back on alcohol can help the liver work better and lower the chance of complications. Depending on the cause, his doctor might also prescribe medication to keep things under control. Surgery is less common but can be needed to remove damaged or diseased tissue. In some cases, things like weight loss surgery or even a liver transplant come up. Whatever the plan is, he should stick with his doctor's advice and get seen fast if the symptoms get worse or just won't let up. Dealing with any underlying issues, like obesity, high blood pressure, or diabetes, matters a lot too, since those often feed into liver problems.

An axiomatic system is a way of organizing a body of knowledge, most often in mathematics and logic, by starting from a small set of statements called axioms and deriving everything else from them through logical reasoning. Axioms are taken as true without proof, or more precisely, they are accepted as the starting assumptions of the system, and their truth is not something the system itself tries to justify. Theorems are then statements proven from these axioms using inference rules, and each step of a proof must follow from the axioms or from previously proven results.

The purpose of this approach is to make reasoning explicit and rigorous. By stating exactly what is assumed, mathematicians can check that every conclusion truly depends only on those assumptions, and they can compare different systems by seeing how changing the axioms changes the results. Euclid's Elements is the classic historical example: he began with definitions, postulates, and common notions about points, lines, and circles, and built a large body of geometry from them. Modern examples include Peano's axioms for the natural numbers and the Zermelo-Fraenkel axioms for set theory.

Axiomatic systems are generally judged by a few key properties. Consistency means the system never proves both a statement and its negation. Independence means no axiom can be derived from the others. Completeness means every meaningful statement in the system can be either proved or disproved. Gödel's incompleteness theorems showed that any sufficiently powerful consistent system of arithmetic cannot be both complete and able to prove its own consistency, which was a landmark result about the limits of axiomatic methods.

A tequila sunrise is a drink that combines tequila, orange juice, and grenadine syrup, and it is usually presented in a tall glass with an orange slice and a cherry as garnish. The ingredients you need are 1 1/2 ounces of tequila, 4 ounces of orange juice, and 1/2 ounce of grenadine syrup. Start by filling a tall glass with ice. Add the tequila and orange juice, then stir them together. Next, pour the grenadine in slowly so that it sinks to the bottom of the glass. As it blends with the rest of the drink, the grenadine produces a "sunrise" look. Top it off with an orange slice and a cherry, and it is ready to serve. The tequila sunrise comes in plenty of variations, and some recipes include extras like lime juice, triple sec, or a splash of soda water. You can try out different combinations until you find the one that suits your taste best.

If you live in the Eurozone and are thinking about putting money into US dollars (USD), several factors deserve attention. To begin, look at the euro-to-dollar exchange rate, since it shapes both the value of your dollar holdings and any gains you might make. When the rate works in your favor, the timing may be good for buying dollars; when it does not, you might hold off until it improves or explore other options. The health of the economies on both sides of the Atlantic matters too. Strong US economic conditions could make dollar investments attractive, whereas weak ones may suggest waiting or looking elsewhere. Lastly, weigh your own finances and objectives. Can you handle the risk that comes with dollar investments? Is your portfolio already well diversified? Does your horizon span months or decades? Your answers to these questions will help clarify whether investing in USD suits you.

Pilots pulling hard G's can black out if the force on their body gets too strong. Under high G, blood gets shoved down toward the legs and away from the head, so the brain doesn't get enough of it and you lose consciousness. That same pull can change how the face looks. Muscles tense up and strain while you're fighting to stay awake, and the skin can go pale or flushed as blood moves around. Pilots aren't left to figure this out on their own, though. They get special training on how to handle G-forces safely, since they're genuinely dangerous.

LTE, short for Long-Term Evolution, is a cellular standard that enables wireless communication, linking devices such as phones and tablets to the internet. Compared with earlier cellular systems, it offers several advantages. For one, it operates at higher speeds, so tasks like downloading files and streaming video happen more rapidly. It also reaches farther, allowing a connection from greater distances. In addition, it draws less power, which extends how long a device runs before it needs recharging. All told, LTE improves the speed and dependability of internet access, making it simpler to remain in touch with the people and content you care about.

Imagine your school has one big playground, and one group of kids in the corner says, "We want our own playground and our own rules." The principal says, "No, this is all one playground, and you can't just decide that by yourselves." That's roughly what is happening in Spain.

The vote on November 9th (2014) was not a real, binding vote. Spain's Constitutional Court suspended the official referendum the Catalan government had planned, because the Spanish constitution says Spain is indivisible and only all Spaniards together can decide such a thing. So Catalonia held a scaled-down "participation process" run largely by volunteers instead. It was more like a big poll than an official election. Even if most people said yes, it would have no legal power.

So if Catalans vote yes, they cannot simply break away. Nothing would automatically change. Spanish courts, police, tax offices, and the army would all keep working as before, and no other country would recognize Catalonia as independent. Countries generally don't recognize a region that leaves without its parent country's agreement, and the European Union has suggested a new state would have to apply to join from scratch.

What a yes vote does do is create political pressure. The Catalan leaders could point to it and say, "Look how many people want change, so let's negotiate." Madrid could respond by ignoring it, saying it didn't count, or even taking legal action against the organizers, which it in fact did later. Catalonia could also try to declare independence anyway, but without Spain's agreement and international recognition, that would mostly be symbolic and could land the leaders in trouble with the law.

So the short version is this: a yes vote is a loud shout, not a door that opens. Real independence would need either an agreement with Spain, which Madrid says it won't give, or a much bigger and more difficult confrontation that nobody can easily predict.

Buying local just means getting your stuff from businesses that are close to where you live or work. And there are a few good reasons to do it.

For one, it helps the local economy. When you spend money at a local shop, you're helping create jobs and income for people in your own community, and that money tends to keep circulating around town instead of disappearing somewhere else. That's good for the whole area's prosperity.

It's also usually just more convenient. These places are nearby, so you don't have to go far to get what you need, which saves you some time and a bit of money on gas or transport.

Then there's the environmental side. Local businesses often don't need as many resources to get products to you. Nothing has to be shipped halfway across the world, so you cut down on fuel use and carbon emissions.

And honestly, it's nice for building a sense of community. When you shop local you actually get to chat with the owners and employees, and that helps you feel more connected to the people around you.

So basically, buying local supports the local economy, it's handier, it's easier on the environment, and it helps make your community feel more like a community.

Honestly there are a bunch of things that can cause fever and chills when someone's pregnant. The most common culprits are infections, like urinary tract infections or respiratory ones, since pregnant women are a bit more prone to them. Preterm labor can also do it, and it's labor that starts before 37 weeks. That usually comes with contractions, vaginal bleeding, or belly pain too. Problems with the placenta, like placental abruption or insufficiency, can cause it as well. And some other medical conditions, including autoimmune disorders or cancer, can show up with fever and chills during pregnancy.

Your friend really needs to see a healthcare provider soon so they can figure out what's going on and get her the right treatment. Her low potassium might be part of the picture, but it could also be an infection or something else entirely. A doctor can sort that out pretty quickly.

A digital signature is a means of confirming that a digital document or message is genuine and has not been altered. It relies on cryptography: a private key generates a distinctive signature for a document, and a matching public key is used to check that signature. Digital signatures are routinely employed to protect electronic correspondence such as email and to confirm who sent a message. They can also establish that digital files, including contracts, invoices, and legal papers, are authentic. To sign a document, the sender relies on a digital certificate, which holds their public and private keys, to attach a unique code to the file. The private key produces the signature, while the public key allows it to be verified. Upon receipt, the recipient uses the sender's public key to check the signature and make sure the content has not been changed in transit. Because they offer strong protection, digital signatures are widely adopted in fields like finance, healthcare, and government. They provide a secure, efficient method of verifying the sender's identity and preserving the document's integrity.

People talk about saving money "in this economy" because they feel that the normal rules of getting ahead have become less reliable, and the advice to save is a response to that uncertainty. Several pressures tend to show up together. Prices for groceries, rent, insurance, and childcare rose sharply after the pandemic and have stayed high even where inflation has cooled, so people's paychecks don't stretch as far as they used to. Borrowing has also gotten more expensive, since interest rates rose to fight inflation, which makes credit card balances, car loans, and mortgages costlier and makes it harder to cover an emergency by borrowing. At the same time, many households feel less secure about their jobs, with layoffs in some sectors and a sense that a single income loss could be hard to recover from.

There is also a broader shift in what people expect. Many folks feel that wages haven't kept pace with the cost of housing, and that homeownership or a comfortable retirement is harder to reach than it was for their parents. In that context, saving becomes less about planning for a vacation and more about having a cushion against shocks, which is why the message is so prominent.

Some of the urgency is also amplified by media coverage, social media, and financial companies that benefit from a worried public. Surveys regularly find that a large share of Americans, for example, couldn't cover an unexpected $1,000 expense without difficulty, so the advice resonates with real vulnerability rather than just abstract worry.

Whether the situation is as dire as the rhetoric suggests depends on your own circumstances, your region, and your income, and economists disagree about how widespread the hardship really is. But the reason the phrase keeps coming up is that many people genuinely feel squeezed and want a buffer against whatever comes next.

Being completely debt free is a sound goal for many people, but whether it's the smartest move depends on what kind of debt you're talking about and what else you could do with the money.

High-interest debt, such as credit card balances or payday loans, is almost always worth eliminating quickly. Interest rates on those often run 20 percent or more, which is a guaranteed drain that few investments can reliably beat. Paying those off is one of the clearest financial wins available.

Low-interest debt is less clear-cut. A fixed-rate mortgage at 3 percent, for example, might be cheaper to keep while you invest the extra cash in a diversified portfolio that has historically returned more over the long run. Some people also keep a mortgage deliberately to preserve liquidity, since cash tied up in a house is harder to access in an emergency. Likewise, student loans with low rates or federal protections like income-driven repayment can be worth keeping rather than rushing to repay.

The trade-off with being fully debt free is that it can mean sacrificing other goals, such as building an emergency fund, contributing to retirement accounts that offer employer matches, or saving for something important. Aggressively paying off a 3 percent loan while skipping a 401(k) match, for instance, would usually be a mistake.

There are also real non-financial benefits. Many people find that having no debt reduces stress, gives them flexibility to change jobs or take risks, and makes budgeting simpler. Those benefits are worth something, even if the math alone would favor keeping a cheap loan.

A reasonable approach is to eliminate high-interest debt first, make sure you have an emergency fund and get any employer retirement match, and then decide about low-interest debt based on your interest rates, your comfort with carrying it, and how much peace of mind being debt free would give you. Being debt free is smart when it fits into that bigger picture, not as an automatic rule.

Indeed, a number of websites cover the bonus features that come with credit cards. A good first step is to check the websites of the card issuers, since they frequently give thorough details on what each of their cards offers and the perks that come with them. Sites such as Credit Karma, NerdWallet, and Bankrate are also worth a visit, as they supply tools for comparing cards along with reviews that describe bonus features. They can be especially helpful when you want to weigh different cards against one another and see what each one provides. Before settling on a card, it's wise to do some research so that you pick the one that best suits your needs and know what to expect from it.

Squash is a racquet sport played indoors by two players (or occasionally two teams of two, in doubles) in a four-walled court. The players take turns hitting a small, hollow rubber ball against the front wall, and the ball may bounce off the side and back walls as well. The goal is to hit the ball so that your opponent cannot return it before it bounces twice on the floor, or cannot return it cleanly at all.

The game is fast and demanding, requiring quick footwork, stamina, and precise shot control. Players use a racquet with a strung head that is smaller and lighter than a tennis racquet. Matches are typically played to 11 points per game, with the best of five games deciding the winner, although the scoring system has changed in recent years and now uses a point-a-rally format in most professional play.

Squash originated at the Harrow School in England in the early nineteenth century, where students reportedly developed it by hitting balls against the walls of a court that had a gap in the wall, which gave the game its name. It later spread through the British Empire and became popular across Europe, North America, and Asia. Today it is played in many countries and is recognized for its health benefits, and it has been proposed for inclusion in the Olympic Games.

The most widely known tsunami of 2005 was the Indian Ocean tsunami, which struck on December 26, 2005, after a magnitude 9.1 to 9.3 earthquake off the west coast of northern Sumatra in Indonesia. The waves spread across the Indian Ocean and caused devastation in Indonesia, especially Aceh province, as well as in Sri Lanka, southern India, Thailand, the Maldives, Myanmar, Malaysia, and parts of East Africa, including Somalia, Kenya, and Tanzania. More than 225,000 people died across the affected countries, making it one of the deadliest natural disasters in recorded history.

Several factors can explain why some people feel nothing the first time they use weed, or marijuana. To begin with, bodies differ, and certain individuals are simply more responsive to the active compounds in the plant than others. As a result, two people taking the same dose may experience very different intensities. Another factor is potency, which varies considerably. Strains differ in strength, and even within a single strain, the concentration of active compounds can change from batch to batch. So the experience you have one time may not match the next, even with the same strain. Lastly, the person may simply not have consumed enough, or may not have taken it in an effective way. Feeling the effects depends on using an adequate quantity and on a method that lets the active compounds enter the bloodstream. Smoking or vaporizing, for instance, usually works more reliably than eating, since compounds pass into the body much faster through the lungs. I hope this clarifies why some people don't notice anything on their first attempt. Please feel free to reach out if you have further questions.

Tracking your personal finances through accounting offers a number of benefits. First, it sharpens your financial planning: recording what comes in and what goes out gives you a clearer picture of where you stand and what you need to do to reach future goals. You might discover spending you could trim, or find that your income must grow to meet your objectives. Second, it raises your awareness of spending habits and how money actually flows through your life, which can lead to smarter choices down the road. Third, a clear view of your finances supports better decisions about allocating money, such as opening a retirement account or setting aside funds for a home down payment. Fourth, accounting helps you build a workable budget; by monitoring income and expenses, you can spot places to cut back and direct your money more efficiently. Finally, it strengthens your financial security. When you know exactly how much you have saved and how much you owe, you are better equipped to handle surprises like a job loss or a medical emergency.

Congratulations on planning ahead. Having PCOS and a recent bout of cystitis doesn't rule out pregnancy, but a few things need to be addressed first.

The most important point is about YAZ. It is a combined birth control pill, so while you take it, it prevents ovulation and pregnancy. Your doctor likely prescribed it to regulate your cycles and reduce the effects of PCOS, such as irregular periods and excess androgens, before you try to conceive. Don't stop it on your own, but do ask your OB when to stop it and when to start trying. After stopping, periods can take a few weeks to a few months to become regular again, and this is normal. Your doctor may also want to check your ovulation and hormone levels before you start trying.

Since you're underweight at 40 kg (about 4'11"), it's sensible that your OB advised against dieting. Being at a low body weight can disrupt ovulation, and for women with PCOS, reaching a healthy weight often improves cycle regularity and fertility. Rather than cutting calories, work with your doctor or a dietitian to build a nutritious eating plan that supports gradual, healthy weight gain. If you have a higher body weight in the future, a gentle, sustainable plan with medical guidance would also help.

Regarding the cystitis, a urinary tract infection by itself usually doesn't affect your ability to conceive, but it should be fully treated and checked before pregnancy. Make sure you've completed your course of antibiotics and that the infection has cleared. Some antibiotics are avoided in pregnancy, so tell your doctor you're planning a pregnancy so they can choose safer options if you need treatment again. If you get recurrent infections, ask about prevention strategies such as hydration, urinating after intercourse, and any preventive medication. Seek care promptly if you develop fever, back or side pain, or blood in your urine, since untreated kidney infections can be serious in pregnancy.

Several other steps will help. Start a prenatal vitamin with folic acid, usually 400 micrograms daily or more if your doctor recommends it, at least one month before you start trying. Track your cycles, and if your periods remain irregular, ask about ovulation tests or basic blood work such as thyroid function, prolactin, and androgen levels. If you don't ovulate regularly, your doctor may discuss medications such as metformin, letrozole, or clomiphene. Many women with PCOS conceive with this kind of support.

If you have not become pregnant after about 12 months of regular unprotected intercourse, or sooner if your cycles remain very irregular, ask for a referral to a reproductive endocrinologist or fertility specialist. Given your PCOS, early evaluation is reasonable.

Please keep your OB involved in every step, since they know your full history and can tailor the timing of YAZ, your nutrition plan, and any fertility treatments to your health.

Carter G. Woodson died on April 3, 1950, in Washington, D.C., at the age of 74. He is often called the "father of Black History" for founding the Association for the Study of Negro Life and History and launching Negro History Week, the precursor to Black History Month.

The phrase is most often traced to Frederick R. Barnard, an advertising executive who used it in a 1921 trade publication article, "One Look Is Worth A Thousand Words," in Printers' Ink. He attributed it to a Chinese proverb, but no such proverb has been found, so its true origin is uncertain. Some versions of the idea also trace back to earlier sayings, such as one attributed to Confucius, though that attribution is likewise doubtful.

Think of your mouth and your throat like a garden hose with a little gate at the top. Your mouth is where the water starts, and your stomach is where it needs to end up. But there's a tricky part in between: your throat has two tubes side by side. One tube is for air, which you need to breathe, and the other is for food and drink, which go down to your tummy.

When you're not swallowing, that air tube is open so you can breathe. If water just poured in from the top, it could slip into the air tube by mistake, and then you'd cough and sputter, like when you giggle while sipping juice and it goes up your nose.

So swallowing is like closing the gate to the air tube and opening the gate to the food tube at the exact right moment. Your tongue pushes the water back, a little flap called the epiglottis folds down over the air tube, and muscles in your throat squeeze in a wave that carries the water down to your stomach. That squeezing wave happens all by itself once it starts, which is why you can't really stop halfway through a swallow.

Your stomach is at the bottom of the hose, and gravity helps, but the squeezing muscles do most of the work, so you can even swallow while sitting on your head, though that's a silly thing to try!

Category theory is a branch of mathematics that studies mathematical structures in terms of relationships and transformations rather than their internal details. Its basic building blocks are objects and morphisms (also called arrows): an object can be anything of interest, such as a set, a group, or a topological space, and a morphism is a structure-preserving map between two objects. A category is simply a collection of objects together with morphisms between them, subject to two rules: morphisms can be composed end to end, and every object has an identity morphism that leaves other morphisms unchanged when composed with them. Composition must also be associative.

What makes category theory powerful is its focus on how things relate. Instead of asking what a set of numbers looks like inside, it asks how it maps to other sets, and which properties can be described purely through those maps. Concepts such as products, coproducts, limits, and colimits are defined by their universal properties, meaning they are characterized by how they interact with every other object in the category, not by any particular construction. This lets mathematicians recognize the same pattern across very different fields.

Category theory was introduced in the 1940s by Samuel Eilenberg and Saunders Mac Lane, who developed it to clarify connections between algebraic topology and abstract algebra. Since then it has become a unifying language across mathematics and has found uses in theoretical computer science, particularly in type theory and functional programming, as well as in physics and logic. Functors, which map one category to another while preserving structure, and natural transformations, which relate functors to each other, are among its central tools for moving between mathematical worlds.

Vomiting after brushing teeth may stem from several different sources. One possibility is that some dental anesthetics, such as nitrous oxide (commonly called laughing gas), can cause nausea and vomiting as side effects, which would be relevant if you received sedation during a dental appointment. Another possibility is the gag reflex, a normal response triggered by stimulation at the back of the throat. A particularly sensitive gag reflex, or dental tools that set it off during your procedure, could explain the symptoms. Vomiting can also point to an underlying condition, such as an infection, food poisoning, or a problem with the digestive system. If your saliva has a small amount of brown tint rather than being clear white, that may result from blood or food debris mixed in, or from certain medications or substances in your body. If your symptoms persist, or if you notice further vomiting or changes in your saliva's color, you should consult a doctor or dentist, who can evaluate your condition and suggest suitable treatment.

Your son might have preauricular pits, also called sinuses. These are small, shallow dimples on the front of the ear, usually near the earlobe. They're there from birth because of how the ear forms in the womb. Most of the time they're harmless and never cause any trouble, though now and then one gets infected. If you're worried about it, bring it up with your pediatrician. They can take a look and tell you how to keep it clean so it doesn't flare up.

The earliest computer programs were composed in machine code, a set of instructions the central processing unit (CPU) can carry out directly. These instructions were typically expressed as numbers and were quite elementary, such as ordering the computer to save a value in memory or carry out a calculation. In the first days of computing, programmers entered these machine code instructions manually, using switches and buttons on the machine itself. The process consumed a great deal of time and invited mistakes, so people soon began searching for a more efficient approach. One answer was assembly language, a programming language that resembles human language more closely and is simpler for programmers to read and write. Assembly language remains very low-level and is tied to a specific type of computer, yet it is far easier to work with than machine code. As computers grew more powerful and sophisticated, writing programs in assembly became increasingly cumbersome. This prompted the creation of higher-level languages, such as C and FORTRAN, which are closer to human language and more abstract than either machine code or assembly. A compiler is a program that converts code written in a high-level language into machine code the computer can execute. Therefore, when you write a program in a high-level language like C, a compiler translates your code into machine code the computer can understand. I hope this is helpful! Feel free to ask if you have any other questions.

Yes, an insect bite can lead to a boil-like swelling with burning. This usually happens either as a local reaction to the bite itself or, more often, when bacteria (commonly Staphylococcus or Streptococcus from the skin) enter through the bite, especially after scratching. That can produce a boil (abscess) or a spreading skin infection called cellulitis, which typically causes redness, warmth, swelling, tenderness, and a burning or stinging feeling. Since you say the problem is spreading, infection is a real possibility and should be checked by a doctor soon rather than waiting to see if it settles.

There is another important possibility at her age: herpes zoster, or shingles. In a 62-year-old, a burning, painful patch on one side of the body that is spreading should raise this suspicion. Shingles often begins with burning, tingling, or pain, followed by a cluster of small fluid-filled blisters on a red base, usually in a band-like strip on one side only. It is often mistaken for an insect bite or boil in its early stage. If the lesion looks like grouped small blisters rather than a single raised lump with a pus head, please mention this to the doctor, because antiviral medicines such as acyclovir or valacyclovir work best when started within about 72 hours of the rash appearing.

Her low body weight of 41 kg is also worth noting, as being underweight can reduce resistance to infections. Even if her routine reports are normal, the doctor may want to check blood sugar specifically, since diabetes makes boils and skin infections more common and harder to heal.

Until she is seen, keep the area clean with mild soap and water and avoid squeezing, pricking, or scratching the boil. A warm compress for 10 to 15 minutes a few times a day can help a true boil soften and drain on its own. Paracetamol can be used for pain if she has no reason to avoid it. You can draw a pen line around the edge of the redness so you can tell whether it is spreading. Please avoid applying random steroid creams, as these can worsen infections.

She should see a doctor promptly if the redness is spreading, if she develops fever, chills, or weakness, if red streaks run up the leg, if the pain becomes severe, or if blisters appear. Depending on what is found, treatment may include oral antibiotics for cellulitis, drainage of the boil if it becomes large and soft, or antivirals if it turns out to be shingles. A clear photo shown to a doctor can also help in making the diagnosis quickly.

I can't diagnose this from a description, but I can explain what commonly causes it and when it matters.

A hard fall onto the buttocks sends a jolt up through the tailbone, pelvis, and spine, and the force can reach the abdomen even though you didn't land on it. The most common explanation is a strained or bruised abdominal wall muscle. Muscles like the rectus abdominis and obliques tighten hard when you brace or twist during a fall. This fits your pattern well: pain when going from lying or sitting to standing, and sharp pain in certain lying positions, are classic signs of a strained core muscle, because those movements engage the abdominal muscles. Other possibilities include a bruised or strained hip flexor or pelvic muscle, a rib or lower spine injury that refers pain to the front of the torso, or a small compression injury to a vertebra. The lack of back pain makes a spinal problem less likely but doesn't rule it out.

Less common but more serious causes include injury to internal organs such as the spleen, liver, kidney, or bowel, which can happen after blunt trauma. A fall onto the buttocks is an unlikely way to injure these, but it's not impossible, and delayed symptoms are a known feature of some of these injuries.

Because the pain has persisted for days and is sharp with certain positions, it's reasonable to get examined soon, especially if it isn't clearly improving. Seek urgent care or the emergency room if you notice worsening or constant severe pain, a hard or swollen belly, fever, vomiting, blood in your urine or stool, dizziness or fainting, a racing heart, pain in the left shoulder tip, numbness or weakness in your legs, or trouble urinating or controlling your bowels.

In the meantime, you can rest, avoid heavy lifting and twisting, and use an ice pack for the first couple of days, then gentle heat. Acetaminophen is usually a safer choice than anti-inflammatories if you're worried about internal bleeding, though ibuprofen is commonly used for muscle strains. To get up more comfortably, roll onto your side and push up with your arms rather than sitting straight up. A muscle strain typically improves noticeably within one to two weeks, so if yours isn't getting better, or if you're unsure, a doctor can examine you and order imaging if needed.

Bonds are usually seen as a steadier, lower-risk bet than stocks. When a recession hits, stock prices often drop as nervous investors dump their holdings, and bond prices often climb because people pile into fixed-income stuff they see as safer. That said, bonds aren't bulletproof. If the economy gets rough, companies and governments can struggle to make their payments, and that default risk can drag bond values down. Interest rates matter too: when rates go up, existing bonds with lower rates lose value. So bonds can help cushion a portfolio, but calling them recession-proof would be a stretch. Weigh the risks and returns, and build a mix that fits your goals and how much risk you can actually stomach.

A life insurance policy is a contract between you and an insurance company in which you pay regular premiums, and in return the insurer agrees to pay a specified sum of money, called the death benefit, to your chosen beneficiaries when you die. The purpose is to provide financial protection for people who depend on your income, such as a spouse, children, or other family members, by covering expenses like everyday living costs, mortgage payments, education, and funeral costs.

There are two main categories. Term life insurance covers you for a set period, such as 10, 20, or 30 years, and pays the benefit only if you die during that window. It is generally the least expensive option and is often chosen to cover a specific need, like raising children or paying off a loan. Permanent life insurance, which includes whole life, universal life, and variable life, remains in force for your entire life as long as premiums are paid. These policies also build a cash value component that grows over time on a tax-deferred basis and can be borrowed against or withdrawn, but they cost considerably more than term coverage.

When choosing a policy, it helps to consider how much coverage you need, how long you need it, your budget, and your health and age, since these factors strongly affect premiums. Insurers typically require an application and often a medical exam, and they review your history to determine eligibility and rates. It is also wise to compare quotes from several companies, check the insurer's financial strength ratings, read the policy's exclusions (such as suicide within the first two years or deaths from certain hazardous activities), and name beneficiaries carefully and update them after major life events. If you have a specific situation in mind, a licensed insurance agent or financial adviser can help you weigh the options.

Swollen, tender lymph nodes in the armpit are very common and most often reflect the body responding to something minor. Your lymph nodes act as filters for the immune system, and they tend to enlarge and become sensitive when they are fighting an infection or reacting to irritation nearby. Common causes include a cold or other viral illness, a skin infection or small cut, an ingrown hair or irritated hair follicle in the armpit, a recent vaccination (particularly in the arm on the same side), shaving or waxing that causes irritation, and deodorant or antiperspirant irritation. Hormonal fluctuations related to your menstrual cycle can also make nodes feel more noticeable, and tenderness in the breast or armpit area is a frequent, benign finding around ovulation or before a period. Tender nodes that come and go, especially if they are soft, movable, and resolve within a few weeks, are usually reassuring.

There are some features that make a lump worth having checked by a doctor. These include a node that keeps growing, becomes hard, fixed in place, or feels rubbery and does not move under the skin. Concern also rises if the swelling lasts longer than about two to four weeks without a clear cause, if it appears without any preceding illness or irritation, or if it is accompanied by unexplained fevers, night sweats, significant weight loss, or persistent fatigue. Redness, warmth, or spreading skin changes suggest infection and warrant prompt evaluation. Any new lump in the breast or underarm area should be assessed, since breast tissue extends into the armpit and a firm, painless lump there deserves a clinical look even if it is probably benign.

Some practical guidance may help you tell the difference. Check both armpits so you know what is normal for you, ideally at a similar point in your cycle, because your baseline may shift. Note when you first noticed the swelling, whether it has changed in size, and whether you have any recent illness, shaving, or skin problems. Normal tenderness usually fades on its own. If the node has been present for more than a few weeks, is getting larger, or has any of the concerning features above, make an appointment with your primary care provider. They can examine you and, if needed, order blood work or an ultrasound. Most swollen nodes at your age turn out to be harmless, but a quick check is a sensible way to get peace of mind.

Investing in mutual funds in India for long-term goals such as retirement, a child's education or buying a home is a sensible approach, because time in the market tends to smooth out volatility and let compounding work. The first step is to define each goal, its time horizon and the amount you will need, adjusted for inflation. A goal more than seven years away can take significant equity exposure, while one within three years should lean toward debt funds or other low-risk options.

For long horizons, equity mutual funds are the main growth engine. Index funds tracking the Nifty 50 or Nifty Next 50 are low-cost and a good core holding, since many actively managed large-cap funds struggle to beat their benchmark consistently. Flexi-cap or multi-cap funds can add diversification across company sizes, and mid-cap and small-cap funds can be added in modest proportions if you can tolerate sharp falls of 30 to 50 percent in bad years. Hybrid funds such as balanced advantage or aggressive hybrid funds suit people who want some automatic rebalancing and lower volatility. For stability, you can use short-duration or corporate bond funds, and for retirement specifically, options like the National Pension System sit alongside mutual funds.

The most practical method is a Systematic Investment Plan, where you invest a fixed amount monthly. It builds discipline, averages your purchase cost, and removes the temptation to time the market. Increasing the SIP amount each year, a step-up SIP, helps your investments keep pace with rising income. Lump sums can be invested when you have them, though staggering them over a few months reduces timing risk.

Costs matter a great deal over decades. Direct plans have lower expense ratios than regular plans because they carry no distributor commission, and the difference can add up to a substantial sum over 20 years. You can invest in direct plans through the AMC websites, platforms like Kuvera, Groww or Zerodha Coin, or MF Central. If you prefer advice, a SEBI-registered investment adviser who charges a flat fee is better than someone paid through commissions.

Before starting, complete your KYC, which is a one-time process using PAN and Aadhaar, and make sure you have an emergency fund of six months of expenses plus adequate health and term insurance. Mutual funds should come after these basics.

On taxation, as per recent rules, gains on equity funds held over one year are long-term capital gains taxed at 12.5 percent above an annual exemption of 1.25 lakh rupees, while gains within a year are taxed at 20 percent. Debt fund gains are taxed at your income tax slab rate. These rules change from time to time, so check the current position or consult a tax professional.

Finally, review your portfolio once or twice a year rather than reacting to market news. Rebalance if your equity and debt split drifts well away from your target, avoid stopping SIPs during downturns, and gradually shift money from equity to safer funds as a goal approaches. Past returns do not guarantee future results, and mutual fund investments are subject to market risk, so choose an allocation you can stay committed to through a full market cycle.

A computer scientist is a professional who studies computers, computation, and the information processes that underlie them. The field asks fundamental questions about what can be computed, how efficiently problems can be solved, and how information can be represented, stored, and transmitted. Computer scientists work on both the theory behind these questions, such as algorithms, complexity, and formal languages, and the practical design of systems, including software, hardware architectures, networks, databases, and artificial intelligence.

The work spans a wide range of activities. Some computer scientists are primarily researchers who develop new algorithms, prove mathematical results about computation, or explore emerging areas like machine learning and quantum computing. Others focus on building and improving systems, designing programming languages, creating operating systems, or ensuring that software is secure and reliable. Many also apply computational methods to problems in other fields, such as biology, medicine, economics, or the social sciences.

Computer scientists typically hold degrees in computer science or a closely related discipline, and many pursue graduate study, especially for research positions in universities or industrial labs. The role is distinct from a software developer or programmer, though the boundaries overlap. A programmer usually writes code to implement a specified solution, while a computer scientist is more likely to determine what the solution should be, why it works, and how well it performs.

Ever get asked "debit or credit?" at the register and freeze up a little? Here's the deal. Debit means your card pulls money straight from your checking or savings account at your bank or credit union. The cash moves from your account to the store's account. Credit is different. You're borrowing from the card company, and you'll have to pay it back later, plus interest if you don't clear the balance in time.

So which one should you pick? If the money's already sitting in your account and you want to pay right now, debit is usually the simple choice. If you're short on cash this month, or your credit card gives you rewards or other perks you actually use, credit might make more sense. Just make sure you can cover the bill when it comes due.

They've been involved with early computers, the development of the internet, and new materials and tech. They also take on projects for private companies, universities, and other groups all over the world.

Honestly, there are a bunch of things that can cause blood pressure that just won't budge with treatment, so your husband really should sit down with his doctor and figure out what's going on in his case.

A few things to think about. First, are the meds actually being taken the way they were prescribed? Missing doses or taking them at odd times can totally keep the numbers up. Second, there could be something else going on that hasn't been caught or isn't under control. Kidney disease, sleep apnea, and an overactive thyroid can all push blood pressure higher, and if he's got one of those, it'll probably need treating before his BP comes down much.

Stress matters too, so finding some healthy ways to deal with it can help. Then there's the usual lifestyle stuff: too much salt, not moving around enough, smoking or other tobacco. Changing those can make a real difference.

So he should stick with the plan his doctor gives him and make whatever lifestyle changes are needed. And if his BP is still high even then, the doctor might switch his meds or tweak the doses of what he's already on.
