A year-round runny, clogged nose that has lasted for years, especially in someone who already has known allergies, usually comes from one of a handful of causes, and often from more than one at once.

The most likely explanation is that your allergic rhinitis is not fully controlled or has become perennial. Seasonal and pet allergies are the ones you know about, but many people with those also react to indoor allergens that are present all year: dust mites, mold spores, cockroach droppings, and the dander that lingers in a home even after a pet is gone. Bedding, carpets, and humid rooms are common sources. Allergy testing, either skin prick or blood tests, can show whether something like dust mites is driving your symptoms, and that changes what you can do about it, such as using mattress and pillow covers, washing bedding in hot water, and reducing humidity.

A second possibility is non-allergic rhinitis, sometimes called vasomotor rhinitis. Here the nasal lining reacts to irritants and triggers that are not allergens: temperature changes, strong smells, smoke, perfume, dry air, spicy food, or pollution. It can coexist with allergies, and antihistamines do little for it, which might explain why your medicine isn't fully working.

Third, medication itself can be a factor. If you use a decongestant nasal spray such as oxymetazoline for more than a few days, it can cause rebound congestion that persists for as long as you keep using it. Some oral medications can also cause nasal stuffiness.

Structural problems are another common cause of chronic blockage. A deviated septum, enlarged turbinates, or nasal polyps can keep one or both sides clogged. Chronic sinusitis can also cause congestion and drainage that lasts for months, often with facial pressure, reduced smell, or thick discharge. Polyps in particular are associated with allergies and asthma.

Less commonly, a persistent clear runny nose on just one side, especially after head injury or surgery, can occasionally be a cerebrospinal fluid leak, and a persistent one-sided blockage with bleeding deserves prompt evaluation. These are rare but worth mentioning if they match your situation.

Since this has gone on for more than a decade and your current treatment isn't working, it makes sense to see an allergist or an ear, nose and throat specialist. They can examine your nasal passages, often with a small camera, test for specific allergens, and consider imaging if needed. In the meantime, a daily steroid nasal spray such as fluticasone, used consistently, is more effective for chronic congestion than oral antihistamines alone, and saline rinses with distilled or boiled water can help. Allergy shots or under-the-tongue immunotherapy are also options if testing confirms specific allergies.

Truvada (emtricitabine/tenofovir disoproxil fumarate) is an HIV medication, and its preventive use is called PrEP, or pre-exposure prophylaxis. It is effective at reducing the risk of acquiring HIV through sex, and that protection applies to any sexual activity where HIV could be transmitted, not only anal intercourse. Receptive anal sex carries a higher HIV risk than other activities, which is why it is often highlighted, but PrEP is not limited to men who have anal sex. It is prescribed to anyone at substantial risk of HIV, including people of any gender, people who inject drugs, and partners of people living with HIV. Oral sex carries a much lower HIV risk, and PrEP is not usually prescribed for it alone, but a clinician would consider the whole pattern of someone's sexual behavior when deciding whether PrEP is appropriate.

PrEP does not protect against other sexually transmitted infections. Truvada has no effect on gonorrhea, chlamydia, syphilis, herpes, human papillomavirus, hepatitis B or C, or others. Someone taking it can still catch these infections from anal, oral, or vaginal sex, and many of them are quite common among men who have sex with men. Some of these infections can be serious, and many have no symptoms, so regular testing is important. Condoms still reduce the risk of all of these infections, and vaccines exist for hepatitis A and B and HPV, which are worth discussing with a provider.

So no, PrEP does not guarantee that you will not catch an STD. It greatly lowers the risk of HIV when taken consistently, but it does nothing for most other infections. Taking it requires HIV testing before starting and periodic testing while on it, along with kidney function checks and STI screening. A doctor, sexual health clinic, or local health department can review your specific situation and explain your options.

I'm sorry your daughter is dealing with this. Repeated nosebleeds in young children are usually caused by dry air, nose picking, a cold or allergies, but three in a few hours with pain in the cheekbone area deserves attention, so I'd suggest having her seen by a doctor today, especially if she may have bumped her face or had anything pushed into her nose.

To stop a nosebleed at home, keep her sitting upright and leaning slightly forward, not lying down or tilting her head back, so the blood doesn't run down her throat. Pinch the soft part of her nose, just below the bony bridge, firmly with your thumb and finger and hold it continuously for 10 to 15 minutes without letting go to check. Have her breathe through her mouth. A cold cloth across the nose or cheek can help, and keeping her calm and quiet matters, since crying raises blood pressure in the face. Afterward, avoid nose blowing, picking, and rough play for a day or so.

To help prevent further bleeds, dab a small amount of petroleum jelly or saline nasal gel just inside each nostril once or twice daily, use saline spray, run a humidifier in her room at night, and keep her fingernails short.

The cheekbone pain is the part that concerns me. It could simply be sinus congestion or irritation from a cold, but it could also reflect an injury, a sinus infection, or an object in the nose. A doctor can look inside her nose and check for these things. Occasionally, frequent bleeding is also checked with blood tests if there are other signs, such as easy bruising, bleeding gums, or a family history of bleeding problems.

Go to the emergency department right away if a bleed lasts more than 20 minutes despite proper pressure, if the bleeding is heavy, if she looks pale, drowsy, or limp, if she had a fall or blow to the face or head, if there is swelling or bruising of the face, if she has fever, or if there is a foul-smelling discharge from one side of the nose, which can suggest a foreign body.

Please don't give her aspirin. If she seems uncomfortable, a child-appropriate dose of acetaminophen is fine. I'd call her pediatrician today for an in-person check.

Whether you receive US income depends on what kind of income you have, where it comes from, and who pays you. The general idea is that the United States taxes its citizens and residents on income from anywhere in the world, while nonresident aliens are generally taxed only on income that has a US source. So the first question is usually whether you are a US citizen, green card holder, or someone who meets the substantial presence test, since those statuses bring you into the worldwide tax system. If you are none of those, the focus shifts to the source of each payment.

For wages, the source is generally where the work is physically performed, so pay for work done while you were physically in the US counts as US-source income even if the employer is foreign. For interest and dividends, the source usually depends on whether the payer is a US person or company. For rent from US real estate, the property's location determines the source. For business income, it generally matters whether you have a US trade or business and whether the income is effectively connected with it. Royalties, capital gains, and other categories each have their own rules, and some payments that look domestic, such as certain US bank interest, are specifically exempt from tax for nonresidents.

If you tell me more about your situation, such as your citizenship or visa status, where you live, what types of payments you receive, and from whom, I can walk through the likely answer for your case. For a definitive determination, especially if real money or a filing obligation is involved, a tax professional who handles cross-border matters is worth consulting.

Lactare is an herbal supplement whose main ingredient is shatavari (Asparagus racemosus), a plant used for a long time in Ayurvedic medicine to support breast milk production. It is generally considered safe for breastfeeding mothers, and many women take it for several months without problems. That said, there is limited good-quality research on its long-term use, so it is sensible to continue it with your doctor's knowledge rather than entirely on your own.

Side effects are usually mild and uncommon. Some women notice stomach upset, bloating, gas, loose stools, or mild weight gain. Allergic reactions such as rash, itching, or breathing difficulty are rare, but you should stop the capsule and see a doctor if they happen, especially if you are allergic to asparagus. Shatavari may slightly lower blood sugar and has a mild diuretic effect, so mention it to your doctor if you have diabetes, kidney problems, or take other regular medicines. Because it has mild hormone-like activity, women with hormone-sensitive conditions should also check with their doctor. If you have had no problems in the last two months, you are unlikely to develop new side effects by continuing at the same dose.

Since you plan to breastfeed for at least six more months, it helps to remember that no supplement replaces the main driver of milk supply, which is frequent and effective removal of milk. Feeding your baby on demand (around 8 to 12 times in 24 hours in the early months), making sure the latch is good, offering both breasts, feeding or pumping at night, and pumping after some feeds if needed will usually do more than any capsule. Drinking enough fluids, eating well, resting when you can, and managing stress also help.

It is also worth checking whether your supply is actually low. Many mothers feel their milk is insufficient when it is not. Good signs that your baby is getting enough include steady weight gain on the growth chart, about six or more wet diapers a day, regular stools, and a baby who seems satisfied after feeds. If these are fine, you may be able to reduce or stop Lactare gradually and see whether your supply stays steady. If your baby's weight gain is slow, a lactation consultant or your pediatrician can look at feeding technique and check for problems such as thyroid issues, anemia, or retained placenta, which can affect supply.

In short, you can usually continue Lactare at two capsules a day for the next several months if it suits you, but review it with your doctor, watch for any side effects, and focus mainly on frequent feeding. Once your baby starts solid foods at around six months, the demand pattern changes, and that is a good time to reassess whether you still need it.

Doritos and Mtn Dew became the snacks and drinks of gaming because of a mix of history, marketing, and the way people played games together. Here's the story in simple terms.

Back in the 1990s and early 2000s, video games were mostly played at home on the couch, often late at night or during long sessions with friends. People wanted something to munch on and something to keep them awake, and those two things were easy to grab. Doritos are crunchy and cheesy, so they're fun to eat without needing a plate, and they leave bright orange dust on your fingers, which made them feel like a "gamer snack." Mountain Dew is a very sugary, very caffeinated soda with a bright green color and a strong, fizzy taste that feels exciting and energetic, so it seemed like the perfect drink to keep you going.

Once gaming became a big business, companies started looking for ways to connect with the young people who played. Mountain Dew and Doritos both had money to spend on advertising, and they figured out that gamers were a group they could reach. They sponsored video game tournaments, put their logos in games, made commercials that showed people gaming with their products, and even created special flavors and packaging. Over time, the link between the snacks and the games got stronger because the advertising kept repeating it.

Then came competitive gaming and streaming. When big tournaments started showing games on TV and online, and when popular players began broadcasting their games live, viewers saw these snacks and drinks everywhere. Players often had cans of Mountain Dew and bags of Doritos on their desks, and that image spread quickly. People copied what they saw, and the habit became part of gaming culture.

So in short, the snacks and drinks were easy and fun for long play sessions, companies noticed gamers and bought ads to reach them, and the image spread as gaming grew into tournaments and streaming. Put together, it made these two brands seem like they belonged to gaming itself.

Okay, so a hyperspectral imager is basically a remote sensing instrument that measures how much light a surface reflects across a whole bunch of wavelengths, usually from visible light into the near-infrared. You'll find them on satellites, planes, and sometimes drones, mostly taking pictures of the ground. What makes them special is that they capture a lot of narrow spectral bands, so you get a detailed fingerprint for each pixel. That's how you can tell minerals, plants, water, and other materials apart just by their spectral signatures. People use them for mineral exploration, crop monitoring, mapping land use, keeping an eye on the environment, and even military surveillance. Basically, you get a pretty detailed picture of what's actually sitting on a surface and how it's spread out.

For now, rest the leg and avoid putting weight on it if walking hurts. Keep it elevated when you sit or lie down, and if you use ice, wrap it in a thin towel and hold it on lightly for 10 to 15 minutes at a time, or skip the ice if contact itself is too painful. Over-the-counter pain relievers like ibuprofen or acetaminophen can help with discomfort, provided you have no reason to avoid them, such as stomach problems, kidney disease, or a bleeding risk. Avoid tennis and any running or jumping until it has settled.

Some causes of shin pain, like a stress fracture or a blood clot in the deep veins of the leg, can be serious, so get medical care promptly, ideally today, if you notice any of the following: significant swelling, warmth, or redness along the shin or calf; the leg looking discolored or feeling cool; pain or swelling in the calf, especially if it's one-sided; fever; a wound or break in the skin; numbness or weakness; inability to bear weight; or pain that is getting worse rather than better. If none of those apply, a doctor or urgent care visit is still reasonable given how severe the pain is and how sudden its onset was. They can examine the leg and order an X-ray or ultrasound if needed. Please don't wait it out for several days if the pain isn't clearly improving.

Some people choose not to pay for a car all at once for several reasons. First, a full upfront payment may simply be out of reach for many buyers, since not everyone has enough savings to cover the entire price in a single payment. Second, a person's credit score may be too low to secure a car loan with good terms, and in that situation, paying the full amount upfront might be the only realistic route. Third, tying up a large sum in a vehicle can carry an opportunity cost: that money might instead be invested, or used to clear debts that carry higher interest, potentially producing greater returns over time. Finally, financing can be simpler on a monthly basis, because it spreads the expense across a longer period and makes the payments easier to handle. In the end, the decision between paying in full and taking out a loan depends on each person's financial circumstances and goals.

Thomas Hobbes's main work is Leviathan, published in 1651. Its full title is Leviathan, or The Matter, Forme and Power of a Common-Wealth Ecclesiasticall and Civil. In it, Hobbes argues that without government, human life would be a "war of all against all," which he famously described as "solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short." To escape this state of nature, people enter a social contract and submit to a sovereign with absolute authority. The book is one of the foundational texts of modern political philosophy and social contract theory.

Nope, they're not the same thing at all. Cap rate (short for capitalization rate) is a real estate thing. It tells you the expected return on a property, and you get it by dividing the property's net operating income (NOI) by its current market value. Higher cap rate, higher expected return. So if a property's worth $100,000 and has an 8% cap rate, you're looking at about $8,000 a year.

Net profit margin is a different animal. It's about how profitable a company is. You take net income and divide it by net sales. Net income is basically revenue minus expenses, and net sales is revenue minus returns and allowances. The higher the margin, the more profitable the company. Say a company has a 10% net profit margin on $100,000 in net sales. That works out to $10,000 in net income.

Both are ways of sizing up how well an investment or a business is doing, sure, but they're calculated differently and they tell you different things. Cap rate is just for real estate investments, while net profit margin is for measuring how profitable a business is.

Using a line of credit to invest is a strategy known as leveraged investing. It can magnify gains, but it magnifies losses just as much, so it deserves careful thought before you try it.

A line of credit is a revolving loan with a set limit. You borrow what you need, pay interest only on the balance, and can reborrow as you repay. Rates are usually variable, tied to a benchmark such as the prime rate, and a home equity line of credit (HELOC) is typically cheaper than an unsecured line because your home is collateral. That collateral is also the main danger: if investments sour and you cannot service the debt, your home is at risk.

The basic math is simple. If your investments return more than your after-tax borrowing cost, you come out ahead. If they return less, or lose money, you still owe the full debt plus interest. With rates at, say, 7 to 9 percent, you need consistent returns above that just to break even, and equity markets do not reliably deliver that over short periods. Because the rate is variable, your costs can also rise at the worst moment.

Tax treatment varies by country. In Canada, interest on money borrowed to earn investment income is often tax deductible, provided the investment can reasonably produce income such as dividends or interest. In the United States, investment interest is deductible only up to your net investment income and only if you itemize. In other places the rules differ again, so check with a tax professional.

Several practical points are worth weighing. Make sure you can comfortably make payments from your regular income even if the portfolio drops 30 to 40 percent. Avoid concentrated or speculative bets with borrowed money; broad, diversified holdings are safer. Compare the line of credit against alternatives such as simply investing monthly from cash flow, or paying down higher-interest debt first, which is a guaranteed return equal to the interest rate. Also consider whether you have an emergency fund separate from the credit line, since lenders can reduce or freeze limits during downturns, just when you might need them.

Leveraged investing tends to suit people with stable, high income, a long time horizon, and a strong tolerance for volatility. For many people, the risk is not worth the added return. The right choice depends on your numbers, but here is how the three generally compare for paying for a child's college.

A HELOC is a revolving line of credit secured by your home. Rates are variable, usually tied to prime plus a margin, so your cost can rise over time. Its main advantages are flexibility and low upfront cost: you borrow only what you need each semester, pay interest only on what you've drawn, and closing costs are often minimal. The drawbacks are rate risk, the possibility that the lender freezes or reduces the line in a downturn, and the fact that your house is collateral. Interest is deductible only if the money is used to buy, build, or substantially improve the home, so college use generally gets no deduction.

A second mortgage, usually a fixed-rate home equity loan, gives you a lump sum at a fixed rate with a set repayment term. It suits someone who wants predictable payments and knows the total cost upfront. The downsides are that you pay interest on the whole amount from day one, even if you won't spend it until later years, closing costs can be higher, and it is also secured by your home. A cash-out refinance is a related option, but it resets your whole first mortgage, which is rarely worth it unless your existing rate is higher than current rates.

Parent PLUS loans are federal loans in the parent's name. Rates are fixed but typically higher than home equity rates, and there is an origination fee of over 4 percent. They are unsecured, so your home isn't at risk, and they offer federal protections: income-driven repayment options (through consolidation, with limits), deferment, forbearance, and discharge on death or disability. Approval requires no adverse credit history, not a minimum income or equity. Private parent loans can sometimes beat PLUS rates if your credit is excellent, but they lack federal protections.

As a rough rule, if you have substantial equity, strong credit, and stable income, home equity borrowing is often cheaper, with the HELOC better for spreading costs over four years and the fixed home equity loan better if you want certainty. If your job is less secure, your equity is thin, or you value the safety net, Parent PLUS is the safer choice even though it costs more. Putting your home at risk for education debt is a serious trade.

Before borrowing, it's worth exhausting cheaper sources: scholarships, grants, the student's own federal loans (which have lower rates and fees than PLUS and are in the student's name), work-study, and payment plans from the school. Having the student take the federal direct loans first is usually better than parental borrowing. Also consider whether you can afford to repay before retirement, since taking on debt late in your working life can hurt your retirement savings more than the education helps.

If you're new to investing, it's essential to begin with a diversified portfolio suited to your financial circumstances and objectives. You can build one by following these steps. First, define your investment goals: what are you hoping to accomplish? Are you saving for retirement, a home down payment, or another financial milestone? Clear goals make it easier to choose investments that fit your broader financial plan. Next, gauge your risk tolerance. Investments vary widely in risk, so pick ones that match how much volatility you can handle. Conservative investors might favor lower-risk options like bonds or funds holding blue-chip stocks, while aggressive investors may accept greater risk in pursuit of higher potential returns. Then, decide on your asset allocation, meaning how you divide your money among different asset types. A popular strategy is to split your holdings among stocks, bonds, and cash or other short-term instruments. A well-diversified portfolio usually spreads money across several asset classes, including domestic and international stocks, various bond types such as corporate, government, and municipal, and cash or similar short-term holdings. After that, select specific investments. With your goals, risk tolerance, and allocation in mind, you can start picking individual stocks, mutual funds, exchange-traded funds (ETFs), or index funds. Finally, review and rebalance periodically. As your circumstances or objectives shift, adjust your portfolio accordingly, which may mean selling some holdings and buying others to restore your target allocation. I hope this helps! Certainly! The Monty Hall problem is a well-known probability puzzle, named for the man who hosted a TV game show. The show features three doors. A prize, typically a car, sits behind one of them, while the other two hide nothing. You choose a door, and then the host, Monty Hall, opens one of the two doors you didn't pick, showing that the prize isn't behind it. He then offers you the chance to change your selection to the one remaining closed door. The question is whether you should switch or keep your first pick.

Suppose you choose door number 1. Since there are three doors and only one hides the prize, your chance of having chosen correctly is 1/3. Monty then opens door number 2 and shows it is empty. This means the prize must be behind either door 1 or door 3, and the only other closed door is door 3. Because the prize is now known to be behind door 3 if it isn't behind your door, switching to door 3 means you lose only if your first guess was right, which has a probability of 1/3. By contrast, if you keep door number 1, you lose with a probability of 2/3, since there is a 2/3 chance that the prize is somewhere other than door 1. So switching gives you a better chance of winning than staying put. It may feel counterintuitive at first, but it is true!

Implied volatility reflects the market's collective expectation of future price movement as priced into options, so it tends to incorporate events that are widely known and scheduled, such as earnings announcements, central bank meetings, or product launches. Traders typically bid up options ahead of these events, and that demand pushes implied volatility higher, sometimes creating a visible "event premium" in the options chain.

However, implied volatility is only as good as the market's information and judgment. It cannot price in events nobody knows about, such as an unannounced fraud, a sudden regulatory action, or a geopolitical shock. It also may not fully capture the magnitude or direction of a known event, since the market can misjudge how much a result will move the price. Uncertainty about timing matters too: an event whose date is unclear may be only partly reflected. Finally, implied volatility can be distorted by supply and demand imbalances, such as heavy hedging or speculative buying, so it sometimes overstates or understates the risk that will actually materialize.

In short, implied volatility reflects the known and anticipated events the market has noticed and judged important, but it is an estimate rather than a complete accounting of everything that could happen.

Geothermal energy is a renewable resource that is produced and held within the Earth. It arises naturally from the heat of the planet's core, which is sustained by the ongoing decay of radioactive elements. That heat travels toward the surface by means of conduction, convection, and radiation, and people can capture it to produce electricity or to warm and cool buildings. There are several ways to make use of it. Geothermal power plants are one option, and they draw on the Earth's internal heat to generate electricity. Geothermal heat pumps are another, relying on the steady temperature near the Earth's surface to keep buildings warm or cool. A third approach taps geothermal reservoirs, which are natural underground pools of water warmed by the heat from the Earth's core. The water in these reservoirs can drive electricity generation, supply heat to buildings, or feed thermal baths and spas. All in all, geothermal energy is a dependable and sustainable resource that could contribute substantially to the shift toward renewable energy.

High historical tax rates were usually far less punishing in practice than their headline figures suggested. In the United States, the top marginal rate was 91 percent for much of the 1950s and reached 94 percent in the early 1940s, but these rates applied only to income above a very high threshold, often several hundred thousand dollars in mid-century money, which put them out of reach for nearly all households. Most taxpayers faced rates in the teens or twenties. The top brackets also captured a narrow slice of the population, so they raised a modest share of total revenue even though they were politically prominent.

The gap between marginal and effective rates was often wide. Wealthy people with high salaries or business profits could reduce their liability through deductions, exclusions, and preferential treatment of capital gains, which were taxed at much lower rates than ordinary income. Income splitting through family partnerships, trusts, and closely held corporations let earners shift income to lower brackets or defer it. Many high earners also used tax-sheltered investments such as real estate losses and oil and gas drilling deductions. Estimates of average effective rates for the very richest households in the 1950s often fall in the 40 to 50 percent range, which is high but well below the statutory top rate.

Britain offered a similar picture with an even more layered structure. Through the 1960s and 1970s, the top rate on earned income was around 83 percent, and a separate investment income surcharge could push the combined rate on unearned income close to 98 percent. Such figures pushed many wealthy people to leave the country, shelter income offshore, or convert income into forms taxed differently, and critics argued that the system drove talent and capital abroad while raising relatively little. Partly for these reasons, Britain and the United States both cut top rates sharply in the 1980s, while broadening the tax base by closing many shelters.

Administration mattered as much as the law. Withholding at the source, introduced in the United States in 1943, dramatically improved collection by turning the tax into a pay-as-you-go system for wage earners. Wartime high rates were often accepted as temporary and patriotic, but peacetime rates faced more resistance, and the political coalition supporting them depended on the perception that rich people were paying their share. When rates were high but loopholes were many, the outcome was often a system that looked steep on paper and was porous in operation, which contributed to the push for reform.

A bus adapter is a piece of hardware that plugs into a computer's bus, enabling the machine to talk to other devices or peripherals. Acting as an intermediary between the computer and those devices, it makes it possible for data to move back and forth between them. Several varieties exist. PCI (Peripheral Component Interconnect) bus adapters link components such as sound cards, network cards, and graphics cards to the motherboard. USB (Universal Serial Bus) adapters attach devices like printers, scanners, and external hard drives to the computer. SCSI (Small Computer System Interface) adapters connect hard drives and tape drives. IEEE 1394 (FireWire) adapters are used for devices such as digital cameras and camcorders. Overall, bus adapters are valuable for extending what a computer can do and for letting it interface with a broad variety of hardware.

China operates as a one-party communist state, meaning the Communist Party of China alone wields all political authority. Governance rests with a body of top officials known as the Politburo, which is led by the Communist Party's General Secretary. Beijing restricts speech through several mechanisms. Among them is the Great Firewall, a collection of technical tools that block or filter online material the authorities deem unsuitable or a danger to national security. Traditional outlets such as television and newspapers are also controlled, since the state determines what may be printed or aired. Furthermore, the government frequently penalizes people and groups who criticize it or voice opinions that diverge from the party's official line.

Nuance Communications was an American software company headquartered in Burlington, Massachusetts, known primarily for its speech recognition and artificial intelligence technologies. Founded in 1994 as a spin-off related to speech recognition research, the company became one of the leading providers of voice-based software for both consumers and businesses. Its best-known consumer product was Dragon NaturallySpeaking, a dictation program that allowed people to convert spoken words into written text on their computers. The company also powered voice assistant features in various products, and its technology was used in automated phone systems, customer service applications, and interactive voice response systems.

In the healthcare sector, Nuance became especially prominent. It developed medical transcription and clinical documentation tools, including speech recognition systems that help physicians dictate patient notes directly into electronic health records. Its health care division grew substantially over the years, and the company built a large customer base among hospitals and medical practices.

Nuance also made acquisitions to expand its capabilities, the most significant being its 2011 purchase of Dragon's parent company, ScanSoft, which had already been integrated into its operations. In 2021, Microsoft announced it would acquire Nuance in a deal valued at roughly 19.7 billion dollars, and the acquisition was completed in March 2022. Following the deal, Nuance's technologies were folded into Microsoft's cloud and AI offerings, particularly its healthcare and Azure-related services.

Imagine a big playground where a few kids own all the toys and everyone else has to work for them just to get a turn. Communism is the idea that the toys should belong to everybody, and that no one should be the boss of the sandbox. The different kinds of communism are mostly arguments about how to get there and who should be in charge along the way.

Marxism is the original idea, from Karl Marx. He said that the kids who own the toys will always take advantage of the kids who do the work, and that eventually the workers will get fed up and take over. After that, everything would be shared, and eventually you wouldn't even need a government. Marx mostly described the problem and the big picture, and he didn't give a detailed instruction manual.

Leninism is what happened when Vladimir Lenin tried to actually do it in Russia. He said the workers were too busy and too scattered to organize themselves, so a small, disciplined group of dedicated leaders, the Communist Party, should lead the revolution for them and run things afterward. So Leninism is Marxism plus a leadership team that steers the ship.

Stalinism is what happened after Lenin died and Joseph Stalin took over the Soviet Union. Stalin said the country should build communism by itself, without waiting for revolutions elsewhere, and he did it with extreme control. The government ran the whole economy, pushed factories and farms very hard, and punished anyone who disagreed, often brutally. Millions died from famine, prison camps, and executions. Think of a class monitor who takes total control and punishes anyone who talks back.

Trotskyism comes from Leon Trotsky, who lost the power struggle to Stalin. He believed the revolution had to spread to other countries, because one country alone couldn't make communism work. He also thought Stalin had betrayed the original idea by letting a bossy bureaucracy take over, and wanted more democracy among workers. Stalin had him exiled and eventually killed.

So in short: Marx had the dream, Lenin added a leader-run party to make it happen, Stalin made it a strict one-man-rule system in one country, and Trotsky said the dream should go worldwide and stay more democratic. Plenty of other versions exist too, like Maoism in China, but these four are the classic ones people compare.

Bryophytes are a group of small, simple land plants that include mosses, liverworts, and hornworts. They are often called the amphibians of the plant kingdom because, although they live on land, they still depend on water to complete their life cycle. They typically grow in moist, shady places such as forest floors, damp rocks, tree bark, and stream banks, though some species are remarkably tolerant of drought and can survive long periods of desiccation before reviving when water returns.

One of their most defining features is the absence of true vascular tissue. Bryophytes lack xylem and phloem, the specialized tissues that transport water and nutrients in higher plants. Because of this, they absorb water and minerals directly through their surfaces and move them by diffusion and capillary action, which limits their size. Most bryophytes are only a few centimeters tall. They also lack true roots, stems, and leaves. Instead, they are anchored by thin, thread-like structures called rhizoids, which hold the plant in place but play little role in absorption. In liverworts and hornworts the body is often a flat, ribbon-like thallus, while mosses have leaf-like and stem-like structures that only superficially resemble those of vascular plants.

Their life cycle shows a clear alternation of generations, but unlike in ferns and seed plants, the dominant and long-lived stage is the gametophyte, which is haploid and photosynthetic. The green plant you see when looking at a moss carpet is the gametophyte. The sporophyte, which is diploid, is small, short-lived, and remains attached to and nutritionally dependent on the gametophyte for its entire life. It usually consists of a foot, a seta or stalk, and a capsule in which spores are produced by meiosis.

Sexual reproduction in bryophytes involves multicellular sex organs. The male organ, called the antheridium, produces flagellated sperm, and the female organ, called the archegonium, is flask-shaped and contains a single egg. Because the sperm must swim to reach the egg, fertilization requires a film of water, which is one reason these plants are tied to moist habitats. After fertilization, the zygote develops into an embryo within the archegonium, a trait that places bryophytes among the embryophytes along with all other land plants. When spores are released and germinate, many mosses first form a filamentous stage called the protonema, from which the leafy gametophyte later grows.

Bryophytes also reproduce asexually through fragmentation and through specialized structures such as gemmae, small clusters of cells often held in cup-like structures on liverworts that can be splashed away by raindrops to form new plants. They do not produce flowers, seeds, or fruits, and they disperse solely by spores.

Ecologically, bryophytes are important pioneer species that help colonize bare rock and soil, contributing to soil formation and preventing erosion. They retain water effectively, and peat mosses in particular form vast peatlands that store significant amounts of carbon. Their cell walls are made of cellulose, they store food as starch, and they contain chlorophyll a and b, characteristics they share with green algae and other plants, reflecting their evolutionary position as some of the earliest lineages of land plants.

David Lorge Parnas is a computer scientist and software engineer who is widely recognized for his work in software engineering, particularly on modularity and information hiding. He holds the title of professor emeritus at the School of Computer Science at the University of Waterloo in Canada, and he has also taught at other institutions, among them the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT). His contributions have earned him many awards, including the ACM SIGSOFT Outstanding Research Award and the ACM SIGPLAN Robin Milner Young Researcher Award. He is a Fellow of both the Association for Computing Machinery (ACM) and the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE). Parnas is also a pioneer of modularity in software design, an approach that breaks a large system into smaller, more manageable modules that can be built and tested separately. This makes software systems easier to structure, maintain, and reuse.

Oregon Tech, formally the Oregon Institute of Technology, is a state-supported polytechnic university in Klamath Falls, Oregon. It is the sole polytechnic school in the Pacific Northwest. The university concentrates on applied science, applied technology, and professional studies, granting bachelor's and associate's degrees in areas including engineering, health sciences, business, and applied sciences and technologies. Its curriculum places heavy weight on practical, real-world training, and many of its programs incorporate internships, cooperative education placements, or other forms of experiential learning. The student population is varied, and the school is recognized for a welcoming atmosphere, modest class sizes, and close individual attention from its professors and staff. The campus sits in the scenic southern Oregon countryside, ringed by forests and mountains.

So basically, companies usually book revenue from selling virtual credits when the customer buys them. The customer gets the benefit right then, since they can spend the credits later on stuff or services. Say a company sells credits you spend on items in an online game: the company recognizes that money as revenue at the moment of purchase. You've got the ability to buy items in the game, so the company has met its obligation to you. That said, depending on your industry and what exactly the credits do, there may be specific accounting rules you have to follow. Companies really need to check those carefully so their revenue gets reported correctly.

Short answer: a kid under 18 generally can't just own stock outright, so if your dad wants to give shares to your son, it has to go through some kind of legal setup. The two main ways are a custodial account or a trust.

A custodial account is basically an account in the child's name that an adult runs for them. That adult is the custodian, and they get to make the investment decisions, but they're legally required to act in the kid's best interest. Once your son hits the age of majority, which is usually 18 or 21 depending on your state, the assets are his, no strings attached.

A trust is a bit more involved. Your dad (the grantor) puts the shares into the trust and names a trustee to manage them for the beneficiary, which would be your son. The trustee has the same kind of duty to act in the child's best interest. The difference is that the trust terms decide when your son actually gets the assets. That could be at the age of majority, or whenever the trust says.

Which one makes sense depends on your situation, so I'd talk to a lawyer or a financial advisor before doing anything. They can also make sure the transfer follows the rules where you live.

Melissa & Joey ran on ABC Family (later Freeform) from 2010 to 2015, and it's a pretty fun watch if you like sitcoms with a bit of heart. Melissa is a local politician and Joey is a former bachelor who's now doing entertainment stuff. They end up as roommates and co-guardians of Melissa's teenage niece and nephew after a family crisis, so they're suddenly raising kids together whether they planned to or not. The show mixes comedy and drama and keeps coming back to family, friendship, and romance, while both leads juggle their own work and personal messes. Melissa Joan Hart and Joey Lawrence play the two title characters.

A sonic boom is that big, explosive crack you hear when something travels through the air faster than sound does. Once an object hits the speed of sound or goes past it, it builds up a shock wave, which is basically a zone of super compressed air that moves along at the speed of sound. When that wave reaches the ground, you get the boom, and it can carry over a pretty wide area. Most people think of planes when they hear about sonic booms, but other stuff can cause them too, like meteorites or supersonic missiles.

I'm sorry you're going through this. Being switched off a medication you relied on, losing your doctor, and now feeling sick from withdrawal is a lot to handle. Let's start with what matters most right now, then get to the back pain.

The sick feeling you have is very likely opioid withdrawal, and you don't have to tough it out alone. Call the pain management clinic today, tell them plainly that you are in withdrawal, and ask to be seen or to speak with the prescriber. If you can't reach them or you feel very unwell, go to urgent care or an emergency room. That's especially important if you have vomiting or diarrhea you can't keep up with, can't keep fluids down, feel faint, or have chest pain. Emergency departments can treat withdrawal symptoms, and many can start or adjust buprenorphine on the spot. If you're in the United States, the SAMHSA National Helpline at 1-800-662-4357 is free, confidential, and open 24 hours, and can connect you to nearby help. If at any point you feel hopeless or think about hurting yourself, call or text 988.

A few things can keep this from getting worse. Methadone stays in the body a long time, and switching from it to Suboxone is tricky. If Suboxone is taken too soon after methadone, it can actually bring on sudden, severe withdrawal, and that may be part of why it felt like it did nothing or made you feel worse. That doesn't necessarily mean Suboxone can't work for you. It may mean the timing or dose needs adjusting, so tell your doctor exactly when you last took methadone and when you started Suboxone. Please don't try to manage this by taking extra doses, mixing in other medications, or using anything from the street, because the risk of overdose is real, particularly as your tolerance changes. Sipping fluids with electrolytes, resting, and eating light foods can ease things in the meantime, and doctors can prescribe medications such as clonidine for the aches, anxiety, and stomach symptoms. If the taste was the problem, ask about alternatives. Suboxone comes as a film and tablets, there are other buprenorphine forms including monthly injections, and staying on methadone through a clinic may also be an option. Buprenorphine does relieve pain for many people, often when it's given in split doses through the day, so it's worth telling your doctor directly that your pain isn't controlled.

On the back pain itself, there's honestly no single permanent cure that works for everyone, because back pain has many different causes, such as disc problems, arthritis, nerve compression, or muscle and posture issues. What usually helps most is finding the specific cause through an exam and possibly imaging, then combining treatments. Physical therapy and a regular stretching and strengthening routine are among the best-supported long-term approaches. Others include non-opioid medications like anti-inflammatories or certain nerve-pain medicines, injections, heat, weight management, and therapies like acupuncture or massage. For some structural problems, surgery is an option. Many people get real, lasting improvement this way, even if the pain doesn't vanish completely.

Right now, the most important step is to call your clinic or get seen today for the withdrawal. You're doing the right thing by reaching out, and this situation can get better with the right care. If it would help, I'm glad to suggest what to say when you call your doctor.

It's actually been tried, so your idea isn't crazy. But it's much harder and less effective than it sounds. Here's the simple version.

Imagine your class uses special stickers as money to trade for snacks. If you secretly printed a big pile of fake stickers and dropped them on the playground, more stickers would be floating around, and kids would start asking for more stickers per cookie. That's inflation. So far, so good for your plan. The trouble starts when you try to do it to a whole country.

The first problem is that "perfect copies" are really, really hard to make. Modern money has special paper, tiny hidden pictures, threads, color-shifting ink, and secret features that only banks and governments know about. Countries change their bills often to stay ahead of copiers. Even a powerful nation that tries will probably make bills that are almost perfect, and almost perfect gets caught by bank machines.

The second problem is that once people notice fake money, the target country fights back. It can print new bills that look different and tell everyone to trade in their old ones at banks, where the fakes get spotted and thrown away. Your giant pile of fake stickers suddenly becomes worthless paper, and you've wasted all your effort.

The third problem is that you'd need an enormous amount. Most money today isn't paper at all. It's numbers in bank computers, like points in a video game. A big country has trillions of dollars, mostly digital, so even a huge truckload of fake bills is like pouring a bucket of water into the ocean. You'd also have to sneak all that cash into the country and get people to spend it, which is slow and risky.

The fourth problem is that it can backfire. Fake money doesn't stay where you put it. It travels across borders, and if your own country trades with the enemy, the mess can come back to you. And if you get caught, other countries will be furious, because messing with someone's money is treated as a serious act of hostility. It also teaches everyone that your country plays dirty, and they may do the same thing back to you.

As for history, during World War II, Nazi Germany ran a secret project called Operation Bernhard to make fake British pounds. They made millions of very good fakes, but they never managed to flood Britain with them, and Britain eventually replaced its bills. Napoleon tried something similar against Russia, and the British did it against the American colonists during the Revolution. The American case did contribute to their money becoming nearly worthless, but that worked mostly because the colonists' money was already weak and easy to copy, and the colonists had printed way too much themselves. Against a strong country with modern money, it hasn't really worked.

So you might want to tell The Great Leader that the idea has a long history, but it's expensive, easy to undo, mostly ineffective against modern digital money, and likely to start a fight you'd regret. Maybe pitch a better snack-sticker economy at home instead.

Oakhurst, New Jersey lies within Monmouth County, which sits along the Atlantic coast in the central part of the state. Ocean County forms its southern boundary, while Middlesex County lies to the northwest and Mercer County to the northeast. Freehold serves as the county seat. The county contains many different communities, and Oakhurst is one of them, situated in the county's central area.

Stuart J. Russell is a computer scientist who holds a professorship in electrical engineering and computer science at the University of California, Berkeley. His research in artificial intelligence (AI) is well regarded, especially his role in advancing probabilistic programming and his work examining the constraints and possible dangers of AI systems. Russell earned a bachelor's degree in physics from Oxford University and a doctorate in computer science from Stanford University. His efforts have earned him many honors, among them the ACM Karlstrom Outstanding Educator Award, the ACM-AAAI Allen Newell Award, and the ACM SIGAI Autonomous Agents Research Award. He is also a Fellow of the Association for Computing Machinery, the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers, and the American Association for Artificial Intelligence.

Yes, a strategy exists that works in the opposite direction from dollar-cost averaging, known as value averaging. Rather than putting the same sum into an investment at set intervals, value averaging has you invest a varying amount based on how far your portfolio's current value falls short of a target value you've chosen. Suppose your target is $100,000 and your portfolio is worth $90,000; you would add $10,000 to lift it to the target. If the portfolio then grows to $110,000, you would take out $10,000 to return it to the target. This approach may appeal to people who are averse to risk and hope to shield their portfolio from market swings. Still, it demands careful watching and frequent changes to your holdings, so it won't suit everyone. Before making any investment decisions, it's always wise to weigh your goals and tolerance for risk closely.

A painless lump like this is most often a benign growth or a harmless local change. A lipoma, a slow-growing fatty lump that feels soft and moves slightly under the skin, is one of the most common causes in the upper arm and shoulder area. An epidermoid cyst, a small sac under the skin that can feel firm and sometimes has a tiny opening or dark spot, is another frequent possibility. Enlarged lymph nodes can also appear in the arm region, especially if there was a recent scratch, insect bite, or minor infection in the arm or hand. The occasional slight muscle ache you describe could come from a minor strain, from pressing on the area, or from the lump sitting over muscle tissue. Less commonly, a small blood collection from a bump or a fibrous knot in the muscle can cause a similar picture.

Because the lump has stayed the same size for more than a week, is not red or warm, and causes little or no pain, these reassuring features are encouraging. Still, it is worth having a doctor examine it, not because it is likely serious but because only an in-person exam can tell a lipoma from a cyst or a lymph node, and a clinician can judge whether it needs imaging or a simple removal.

You should seek medical care sooner if the lump grows noticeably, becomes hard, fixed in place, or irregular, or if it becomes painful, red, hot, or drains fluid. Also see a doctor promptly if you develop fever, night sweats, unexplained weight loss, fatigue, or additional lumps elsewhere, such as in the armpit, neck, or groin, since these symptoms warrant a more thorough evaluation.

A physical neural network is a type of neural network in which the computation is carried out by a physical system rather than by simulating the network's mathematics on a conventional digital computer. In an ordinary artificial neural network, the weighted sums and nonlinear activations are performed as arithmetic instructions executed by processors such as CPUs or GPUs. A physical neural network instead uses the natural behavior of some material or device, such as light passing through optical components, electrical currents in analog circuits, mechanical vibrations, or the electrical resistance of certain materials, to perform the operations that a neural network needs. The physical system itself becomes, in effect, the network.

The basic idea is that many physical processes already perform operations resembling matrix multiplication or nonlinear transformation. For example, when light beams interfere with one another in a programmable optical mesh, the resulting intensities can represent weighted combinations of inputs. In a memristor-based circuit, the conductance of each element can store a weight, and applying voltages to the array yields currents that sum the products of inputs and weights according to Ohm's and Kirchhoff's laws. Training such a system typically involves adjusting physical parameters, such as phase shifts, voltages, or material properties, so that the device's output moves closer to the desired result.

The motivation for physical neural networks is mainly efficiency. Digital hardware spends considerable energy moving data between memory and processors and on performing many separate arithmetic operations. Physical systems can perform large parallel computations at very low energy cost and very high speed, sometimes in a single pass through the device. Researchers hope this can lead to faster and more energy-efficient artificial intelligence, particularly for tasks where the cost of conventional computing has become a major concern.

There are challenges as well. Physical devices are often affected by noise, manufacturing variability, temperature changes, and drift over time, which can reduce accuracy. They are also harder to program and reconfigure than software, and training methods must account for the imperfections of the hardware. Because of these issues, physical neural networks are still largely an active area of research, with prototypes demonstrated in optics, electronics, and other fields, rather than a widely deployed technology.

Microsoft Money was discontinued in 2009, so you'll need a different personal finance app on your Mac. Several strong options exist, and the best fit depends on whether you want desktop software or a web-based service and how much you value automatic bank syncing.

Quicken is the closest match in spirit to Money. It's a full desktop-style personal finance program with budgeting, investment tracking, bill reminders, and reports, and it has a Mac version. It's a subscription now, and it's the most feature-rich option, though it can feel heavy if you only need basic tracking.

If you want something simpler and free, GnuCash is a free, open-source double-entry accounting program that runs on macOS. It's powerful but has a steeper learning curve and doesn't sync automatically with banks, so you'd enter or import transactions yourself.

Moneydance is another Mac-compatible desktop option with a one-time purchase model rather than a subscription. It offers budgeting, investment tracking, and bank downloads, and it feels reasonably familiar if you're coming from Money's style of organizing accounts and categories.

If you'd prefer a cloud-based service that works from any browser, YNAB (You Need A Budget) is popular for zero-based budgeting and has a subscription fee, while Monarch Money is a subscription service focused on tracking accounts, budgets, and goals across institutions.

For a quick start, Moneydance is probably the closest in feel to Money at a reasonable price, and Quicken is the choice if you want the most complete feature set. If you tell me whether you care more about budgeting or investments, and whether you're comfortable with a subscription, I can narrow it down further.

So natural-language understanding, or NLU, is basically a branch of natural-language processing (NLP). The whole point is getting a computer to actually make sense of human language, not just shuffle words around. You feed it messy, unstructured text or speech, and it pulls out the meaning so it can do something useful with it, like answer a question, write a reply, or carry out a command.

Under the hood, these systems borrow from linguistics, computer science, and AI all at once. They'll work out the grammatical structure of a sentence, figure out what individual words and phrases mean, and dig out the key info from the text or speech.

You see it all over the place: chatbots, voice assistants, translation tools, search and information retrieval systems. It's still a really active research area too, and a lot of people think it could completely change how we interact with computers.

Nosebleeds can be frightening, particularly for small children, yet they are typically harmless and can be handled at home. Here is what you can do when your daughter gets one. First, have her sit up straight and tilt her head slightly forward. This keeps blood from running down the back of her throat, which could make her feel sick or cause her to vomit. Next, have her pinch the soft part of her nose just beneath the bony bridge. The pressure helps seal the blood vessels and stops the bleeding. She should keep holding her nose this way for at least 5 to 10 minutes.

If the blood is still flowing after 10 minutes, you could try a saline nasal spray, or rub a thin coat of petroleum jelly inside her nostrils. Either one moistens the nasal lining and can make later nosebleeds less likely.

Call your healthcare provider if the bleeding won't stop or if she keeps getting nosebleeds. You should also get in touch if she has other symptoms, such as a fever, a headache, or pain in her face.

In the meantime, try to keep the air in your home moist, either with a humidifier or by setting a bowl of water near a heat source, since dry air can bring on nosebleeds. Also steer her away from anything that could irritate the inside of her nose, like picking it or blowing it too hard.

I hope this helps. If you have more questions or concerns, please don't hesitate to reach out to your healthcare provider.

Okay so "Judas" by Lady Gaga came out April 15, 2011. It's the second single off her second album, Born This Way. Critics were split on it when it dropped, but it still did well commercially and hit the top ten in a bunch of countries. Pretty sure it's one of her most famous tracks at this point.

Warren Buffett's a big name in investing, and honestly most people would call him one of the best ever at it. He's the chairman, CEO, and biggest shareholder of Berkshire Hathaway, a huge holding company based in Omaha, Nebraska. He started out as a stockbroker in the 1950s, then set up his own investment partnership, which eventually turned into Berkshire. His thing is value investing: find companies that are trading for less than they're really worth, with real growth potential, and then just hold on to them for years. He's made plenty of good calls over the decades, with stakes in Coca-Cola, American Express, and Wells Fargo. He's also bought whole companies, like GEICO, Duracell, and the railroad Burlington Northern Santa Fe. Beyond investing, he's pulled in money from his salary as Berkshire's CEO and from dividends and buybacks. Even with all that, he's known for living pretty modestly and giving away a big chunk of his fortune.

Birds digest food differently from most animals. Rather than a lengthy intestine as seen in humans and other mammals, birds possess a brief intestine along with an unusual organ known as the gizzard. This gizzard is a muscular section of the stomach that works to crush the food a bird swallows. Their waste is also unlike that of mammals. Birds do not pass solid feces; instead, they excrete uric acid, a white liquid that combines with their solid waste to make up their droppings. Consequently, the reason bird droppings look white is that a liquid called uric acid makes up much of them. Animals with other digestive arrangements, by contrast, release solid feces that are usually brown.

I'm sorry your daughter is having this discomfort. Foul-smelling gas and on-and-off belly pain in a 5-year-old are common, and they often come from diet, constipation, or an intestinal infection. Since the Cyclopam and Colicaid haven't helped, she should be examined by her pediatrician, who can work out the cause and choose the right treatment. Please don't keep adding medicines on your own, and don't give adult doses of anything.

Until you see the doctor, some simple steps may help. Make sure she drinks enough water and eats fiber from fruits, vegetables, and whole grains, since constipation is a very common cause of gas and pain. Limit fizzy drinks, chewing gum, juices high in fructose such as apple and pear juice, and foods that often cause gas, like beans, cabbage, and sugar-free sweets. Encourage her to sit on the toilet after meals so she doesn't hold stool in. If you suspect milk is the trigger, try cutting back on dairy for a short time and tell the doctor what you notice.

Take her to a doctor promptly, rather than waiting for a routine visit, if she has blood or mucus in her stools, persistent diarrhea, vomiting, fever, weight loss, or poor appetite. Also seek care if the pain is severe, wakes her at night, stays in one spot on the lower right side of her belly, or has lasted more than two weeks. Signs of dehydration, such as little urine, dry lips, or unusual drowsiness, need urgent attention.

When you see the doctor, tell them when the pain happens, what she eats, how often and how hard she passes stools, which medicines you've given and how they affected her, and whether anyone else at home has similar symptoms. The doctor may recommend a stool test to check for parasites such as Giardia, which is a common cause of smelly gas and cramps in children, and may treat constipation or other causes if they're found.

So the capital market is basically where long-term debt and equity-backed securities get bought and sold. Think stocks, bonds, and other debt instruments, usually issued by governments, municipalities, and corporations. They're not backed by physical assets, either.

Don't mix it up with the money market, though. That one deals in short-term debt, with maturities of a year or less.

Why does it matter? Well, it's a big part of how capital gets spread around an economy. Companies use it to raise money for running things and growing, and investors get a chance to earn a return by putting their money into those companies.

There are two main kinds. The primary market is where new securities get issued, so that's where companies and governments actually raise the money. The secondary market is where people trade securities that already exist, buying and selling among themselves.

The light-independent reactions of photosynthesis, commonly called the Calvin cycle or dark reactions, have no need for light to proceed. Rather, they draw on the energy held in the chemical bonds of ATP and NADPH, both generated during the light-dependent stage of photosynthesis. In this stage, carbon dioxide is captured and built into organic molecules such as glucose through a sequence of chemical steps. These steps take place in the stroma of the chloroplasts and rely on a number of enzymes to drive each reaction. In brief, carbon dioxide first attaches to a molecule called ribulose bisphosphate (RuBP), a reaction catalyzed by the enzyme ribulose bisphosphate carboxylase/oxygenase (RuBisCO). The product of this step, 3-phosphoglycerate (3-PGA), is then converted into glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate (G3P) by way of reactions involving glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate dehydrogenase and triose phosphate isomerase. A portion of the G3P goes toward regenerating RuBP, and the remainder serves as raw material for building compounds like glucose, amino acids, and lipids. All in all, these reactions are vital for producing the organic compounds that plants need to grow and develop. They also matter greatly for the global carbon cycle, since they allow plants to pull carbon dioxide out of the atmosphere and lock it away in organic form.

Temporal difference learning, usually abbreviated TD learning, is a family of methods in reinforcement learning for estimating how good it is to be in a given situation, based on experience gained while interacting with an environment. It was developed most prominently by Richard Sutton in the 1980s, and it combines ideas from two other approaches: Monte Carlo methods, which learn from sampled experience without needing a model of the environment, and dynamic programming, which updates estimates based on other estimates rather than waiting for a final outcome.

The central idea is bootstrapping. Suppose an agent wants to learn the value of each state, meaning the expected total future reward it can collect starting from that state. A Monte Carlo method would wait until an entire episode finishes, look at the actual total reward received, and then adjust its estimates for every state visited. A TD method does not wait. After each single step, the agent observes the reward it just received and the state it landed in, and it uses its current estimate of that next state's value as a stand-in for everything that will happen afterward. It then nudges its estimate for the previous state toward this slightly better-informed target.

The simplest version, called TD(0), updates the value like this: the new estimate of the state's value equals the old estimate plus a learning rate times the TD error. The TD error is the reward received plus the discounted value estimate of the next state, minus the old estimate of the current state. In other words, it is the difference between what the agent predicted and what it now thinks, one step later, which is where the name "temporal difference" comes from. If the error is positive, things turned out better than expected and the value is raised; if negative, it is lowered.

This approach has several practical advantages. It can learn online, after every step, and so works in continuing tasks that never end. It usually learns faster than Monte Carlo methods because the targets have lower variance, although they introduce some bias since they rely on imperfect estimates. It also needs no model of how the environment works.

TD ideas underlie many well-known algorithms. Sarsa and Q-learning apply TD updates to action values so that an agent can learn what to do, not only how good states are. TD(λ) blends updates over multiple time steps using eligibility traces, interpolating between one-step TD and full Monte Carlo. Deep Q-networks and actor-critic methods use TD errors with neural networks, and Tesauro's TD-Gammon, which learned backgammon at a high level, was an early famous success.

TD learning has also drawn interest in neuroscience, because the firing of dopamine neurons appears to resemble a TD error signal, responding to unexpected rewards and shifting to earlier predictive cues as learning proceeds.

Imagine a big group of people who decide they want to run their own neighborhood, with their own rules, their own leaders, and their own way of doing things. When enough people agree, and they can actually keep the neighborhood working, other neighbors start to say, "Okay, you're in charge of your own place now." That is roughly how a new country is born. It needs people living in a certain piece of land, a government that can make rules and be obeyed, and enough control to keep order. Then the other countries in the world have to decide whether to say hello and treat it as a real member of the neighborhood. Some countries say yes right away, some wait, and some never agree. Being recognized is a bit like being invited to the playground: the more friends who let you join in, the easier it is to have fun and get things done.

Once a new country is up and running, it has a lot to figure out, kind of like a new family moving into a house. First, it has to keep everyone safe, which means having some way to protect itself and to stop fights inside its borders. Second, it needs to make rules and a fair way to settle arguments, like a school with a principal and a playground monitor. Third, it has to take care of its people by making sure they have food, clean water, homes, and doctors, and by building roads and schools so kids can learn and grow up healthy. Fourth, it needs money, so it can pay its helpers, buy things, and trade with other countries, the same way you need allowance to buy snacks. Fifth, it must make friends with other countries, talking with them, agreeing on how to share the playground, and keeping promises. Finally, it has to decide who is a citizen, who gets to vote, and how everyone gets a say in running things, so that everybody feels like they belong to the team.

I can't really give medical advice or recommend treatment without examining you or seeing your history, so I'd stick with what your doctor tells you. They know your health situation best. If something about the treatment they've suggested bugs you, bring it up with them directly. They can explain their reasoning and answer whatever you're wondering about.

The 2005 tsunami struck the Indian Ocean, particularly near the coast of Sumatra in Indonesia, though its origin dates to 2004. On December 26 of that year, a huge undersea earthquake shook the Indian Ocean floor and generated a series of destructive waves that hit nations along the ocean's rim, among them Indonesia, Sri Lanka, India, and Thailand. More than 230,000 people died in the catastrophe, and the surrounding regions suffered extensive harm to their infrastructure, homes, and economies. Ranking among the most lethal natural disasters on record, the tsunami led to a wide-scale international effort to deliver humanitarian relief to the survivors.

The Mansfield Amendment was added to the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961, the U.S. federal law governing economic and military aid to other nations. It takes its name from its sponsor, Montana Democrat Senator Mike Mansfield. Under the amendment, the President must confer with Congress before offering military aid or selling military equipment to any country outside NATO, the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. The President must also submit a report to Congress explaining why the aid or sales are being provided and what effect they are expected to have on the recipient country's military capabilities. The amendment's goal is to give Congress a voice in decisions about American military assistance and sales abroad, especially when the recipients are not NATO allies. It is meant to encourage openness and accountability in how military aid is provided, and to keep Congress fully aware of what such assistance could mean.

Imagine a corner, like the corner of a book or a slice of square toast. When two edges meet to make that perfect corner, we call it a right angle. Now imagine a triangle with one of those corners. It has two short sides that hug the corner, and one long slanty side across from it. That long side is the sneaky one, and the Pythagorean theorem is a secret about how long it is.

Here is the secret. Build a square on each side of the triangle, like putting a blanket flat against each edge. You get two small blankets on the short sides and one big blanket on the long side. The magic is that if you cover the big blanket with little tiles, you need exactly the same number of tiles as it takes to cover both small blankets put together. Small blanket plus small blanket equals big blanket. That is the whole idea.

For a number example that preschoolers can count, use a triangle with short sides of three and four. The three-side blanket has nine tiles, because three rows of three make nine. The four-side blanket has sixteen tiles, because four rows of four make sixteen. Nine and sixteen together make twenty-five. The big blanket on the long side is five tiles across and five tiles tall, and five rows of five make twenty-five. It fits perfectly, every time.

For your picture book, I would suggest a few ideas. Make the triangle a character, maybe a cozy little triangle with a square corner like a cap. Give each side a colored square: red, blue, and yellow. Show a child pouring the tiles or sand from the red and blue squares into the yellow one, and it fills up exactly, with nothing left over and nothing spilling. Repeat a simple refrain on each page, such as "Two small squares make one big square," because young children love repetition.

You can also add a gentle caution for older kids reading along: this only works for triangles with that square corner. A floppy, pointy triangle will not play the game. Preschoolers do not need the formula, but if a grown-up wants it, it is a squared plus b squared equals c squared, which just means small square plus small square equals big square.

A fun last page could invite children to find square corners around them, in doors, windows, books, and crackers, and imagine the secret hiding there.
