CFD stands for "contract for difference," and basically it lets you bet on which way a price will move without ever owning the thing itself. You're trading on margin, so you can control a bigger position than your cash would normally cover. That's the appeal, but it cuts both ways. Leverage can magnify your gains, and it can also magnify your losses, to the point where you can end up owing more than you put in if the market goes hard against you.

Making money here comes down to calling the direction right. If the price moves the way you guessed, you profit. If it moves the other way, you take a loss. Simple on paper, but it's a high-risk game and not for everyone. Before you put real money in, make sure you actually understand the risks and have a plan you can stick to.

I can't diagnose your son, but I can walk you through the most likely possibilities and what would make this more urgent.

In a healthy teenager, pain in the lower ribs that worsens with movement and breathing usually comes from the chest wall rather than anything deeper. A common cause is a muscle strain between the ribs (the intercostal muscles). Even a mild cough can strain these muscles, and so can sports, lifting, or twisting awkwardly, often without your son remembering any specific injury. Another frequent cause is costochondritis, an inflammation of the cartilage connecting the ribs to the breastbone. It causes sharp or aching pain that is often tender to the touch and worse with deep breaths or movement. A related condition, slipping rib syndrome, affects the lower ribs specifically and can cause a clicking or popping feeling with sharp pain. Teens also sometimes get precordial catch syndrome, brief stabbing pains on the left side when breathing in, which is harmless and passes on its own.

Because he has a cough, his lungs are also worth considering. Pleurisy, an irritation of the lining around the lungs often following a viral infection, causes sharp pain with breathing. A mild pneumonia can sometimes show up with little or no fever, especially early on. Less commonly, a small collapsed lung (pneumothorax) can happen spontaneously in teenagers and causes sudden sharp chest pain and shortness of breath.

The lower left rib area also sits over the spleen. If he has recently been tired, had a sore throat, or been around someone with mononucleosis, an enlarged spleen could cause pain there and needs medical attention, especially before any contact sports. Stomach and kidney problems can occasionally cause pain in that region too, though usually with other symptoms like nausea or urinary changes.

A simple check you can do at home is to gently press on the sore spot. If pressing reproduces the pain exactly, a muscle or cartilage problem becomes more likely. Rest, a heating pad, and an over-the-counter pain reliever like ibuprofen, taken as directed, often help in those cases.

You should take him to urgent care or the emergency room right away if he becomes short of breath, has trouble breathing, has a racing heart, feels faint, coughs up blood, develops a fever, has lips or skin with a bluish tint, or if the pain becomes severe or suddenly worse. At his weight, a blood clot in the lung is uncommon at his age but not impossible, which is another reason not to ignore breathing difficulty. Even without those warning signs, it is reasonable to have his pediatrician see him within a day or two, since pain with breathing plus a cough deserves a listen to his lungs. If the pain has not improved in a few days, definitely get him checked.

An operating system, usually abbreviated OS, is the core software that manages a computer's hardware and provides services for the programs that run on it. When you turn on a computer, phone, or tablet, the operating system is the first major piece of software to load, and it stays active the whole time the device is on. Common examples include Windows, macOS, Linux, Android, and iOS.

Its most basic job is to act as an intermediary between hardware and applications. Programs such as web browsers or games do not need to know the details of how a particular hard drive, keyboard, or graphics card works. Instead, they ask the operating system to perform tasks like reading a file, drawing something on the screen, or sending data over a network, and the operating system handles the specifics through software components called drivers. This makes it possible for the same application to run on many different hardware configurations.

The operating system also manages shared resources. It decides which program gets to use the processor at any moment, switching between them so quickly that many programs seem to run at once. It allocates memory to each program and keeps them from interfering with one another, so a crash in one application does not usually bring down the whole system. It organizes data into files and folders on storage devices, and it controls access to peripherals like printers and network connections.

Security and user management are another part of the role. The operating system handles user accounts, passwords, and permissions, determining who can read or change particular files and what programs are allowed to do. It also enforces boundaries that protect the system from faulty or malicious software.

Finally, the operating system provides a way for people to interact with the machine. This may be a graphical interface with windows, icons, and menus, or a text-based command line. Many operating systems also include utilities for tasks like managing files, configuring settings, and installing updates.

At the center of most operating systems is the kernel, the part that directly controls hardware and core functions. Around it sit system libraries, services, and the user interface. Together these give developers a stable foundation for building software and give users a consistent way to use their devices.

Intractability, sometimes called complexity, describes how hard it is to solve a problem or finish a task with a computer algorithm. Certain problems can be handled quickly by a computer, whereas others are far harder and might require an enormous amount of time or, with today's technology, may be unsolvable in practice. The root of intractability can lie in how large a problem is, how many steps it takes to reach a solution, or how much in the way of resources, such as time or memory, is needed. It may also stem from the problem's intrinsic complexity, for instance when it demands heavy computation or when its definition is vague. The traveling salesman problem, the shortest path problem, and the knapsack problem are commonly cited examples of intractable problems. They are hard to crack either because they call for extensive calculation or because a great many candidate solutions must be examined. In computer science, intractability matters a great deal, since it can shape how algorithms and computer systems are designed and built. By grasping how complex a problem is, researchers and engineers can judge whether it is realistically solvable with current tools and can guide the creation of new algorithms and methods for tackling difficult challenges.

Bayes' theorem is a formula for updating the probability of a hypothesis when new evidence comes in. It's named after Thomas Bayes, an 18th-century mathematician and statistician who first proposed it. The formula looks like this: P(H|E) = (P(E|H) * P(H)) / P(E). Here's what each piece means. P(H|E) is the probability that hypothesis H is true, given the evidence E. That's usually the thing you're trying to figure out. P(E|H) is the probability of seeing evidence E if H is true. P(H) is the prior, meaning how likely H was before you looked at any evidence. And P(E) is how likely the evidence is overall, regardless of H. Basically, you start with what you believed going in, then adjust it based on what you actually observed. It's a neat way of revising your beliefs as you learn more. People use it all over the place now, in statistics, machine learning, and AI, for making predictions and decisions from data. It's a really handy tool for reasoning when you don't have certainty.

Shorting a stock under $5 can be tricky, and there are a few reasons for that. Stocks in that range tend to be more volatile and risky, so a lot of brokers don't want to deal with them. Plenty of firms have rules that either ban or limit shorting them, mostly to protect customers from the bigger swings and losses that come with these stocks. If your broker allows it, you might be able to do it through a margin account. Just keep in mind that shorting is risky and isn't right for everyone, so think hard about whether it fits your situation before you jump in.

Another route is buying put options on the stock, which can also let you profit if the price drops. A put gives you the right, but not the obligation, to sell the stock at a set price (the strike price) by a certain date (the expiration date). If the stock falls below the strike before expiration, you can exercise the put and sell at that higher strike price, pocketing the difference. Same deal as shorting, though: options carry their own risks and aren't for everybody.

There is no known time when the world will end on May 21, or on any other date. No credible scientific evidence points to a global end on that day. When that passed uneventfully, he revised his prediction, and the day came and went like any other.

If you heard about May 21 from a specific video, post, or website, it's worth checking who made the claim and whether they offer any evidence. Predictions of this kind almost never hold up. If something about the claim is worrying you, I'm happy to talk through it.

Hard, painless lumps behind the ear and near the base of the skull in a young child are most often lymph nodes. The lymph nodes in those areas swell in response to a minor infection, such as a cold, an ear or scalp infection, or a scratch or skin irritation, and they can stay firm for several weeks after the infection has cleared. Some children simply have more noticeable lymph nodes than others. Another common possibility is a small cyst, such as a sebaceous or epidermoid cyst, or a lipoma, which is a soft fatty lump. These are usually harmless too.

Because you noticed them recently and they are new to you, it's a good idea to have her pediatrician take a look, though this is not usually an emergency. The doctor can tell whether the lumps are lymph nodes or cysts by feeling them, and may simply recheck them in a few weeks. A visit sooner is worthwhile if the lumps grow, become red, warm, or tender, or feel fixed and rock-hard, or if she develops a persistent fever, night sweats, unexplained weight loss, fatigue, or other new symptoms. Those signs are uncommon in children with these lumps, but they are the reason doctors like to evaluate new lumps rather than wait.

On the blood clots: axitinib can plausibly be linked to clots, though I can't confirm it was the cause in his case. Axitinib and related drugs (VEGF pathway inhibitors) carry a recognized risk of both venous clots, such as pulmonary embolism, and arterial clots. In the clinical trials the rates were a few percent, so it is a known side effect. However, advanced kidney cancer itself raises clot risk considerably, as does reduced mobility, surgery, or dehydration. Doctors often can't say for certain which factor was responsible, and it may be a combination. His treating team is best placed to say how likely the drug was the cause.

On other treatments: there is no single "best" drug, but options for metastatic kidney cancer have expanded a lot. Immunotherapy is now central. Combinations such as nivolumab with ipilimumab, or a checkpoint inhibitor (pembrolizumab, nivolumab, avelumab) paired with a targeted drug, are common first-line choices. If he has already had axitinib (possibly with an immunotherapy drug), other options include cabozantinib, lenvatinib combined with everolimus, tivozanib, sunitinib, pazopanib, or belzutifan. Several of these also belong to the same VEGF-targeting family as axitinib, so they can carry a similar clot risk, which is why his doctors will weigh that carefully. Immunotherapy drugs work differently and have a different side effect profile, though they have their own risks, such as immune-related inflammation. Which one fits depends on his kidney cancer subtype, risk group, what he has already received, how the cancer responded, his other health conditions, and how he is managing the clots.

Some questions worth asking his oncologist: Was the clot most likely related to axitinib, and does it rule out all similar drugs? Is he on blood thinners now, and for how long? Would he be a candidate for immunotherapy or belzutifan? Is a clinical trial an option? Would a second opinion at a major cancer center be useful? A second opinion is reasonable and common in this situation.

Please also make sure he follows the clot treatment plan closely, and that he seeks urgent care for new shortness of breath, chest pain, coughing blood, or leg swelling.

I hope he finds a good next step.

Basically, margin is the collateral you have to put up to get into a derivative contract. It's there as a safety net for the other side, so if you can't make good on your obligations, they're not left holding the bag.

How much you have to post depends on a few things: what kind of derivative it is, what the underlying asset is, and whatever the contract specifically says. Sometimes it's just a fixed percentage of the contract's value. Other times it's based on how creditworthy the parties are, or on how jumpy the underlying asset's price tends to be.

It matters because it keeps people honest, more or less. If everyone has skin in the game, the odds of someone defaulting drop quite a bit. Traders also use it to manage how much risk they're taking on and how much leverage they're running in their positions.

What you're feeling is really the outcome of a bodily reaction known as "autonomic arousal." It occurs automatically whenever you face something stressful or thrilling, such as a sudden drop. The autonomic nervous system oversees many of your body's involuntary processes, including your breathing and your heartbeat. If your body interprets a situation as stressful or exciting, this system can trigger physical changes like a pounding heart or higher blood pressure. Another change that may occur during autonomic arousal is greater blood flow to particular areas of the body, the genitals among them. That extra flow can produce a tingling feeling there, similar to what you've described. This reaction is normal, and it doesn't necessarily have anything to do with a specific emotion or feeling. As for why you only notice it in your bowels while falling, the particular posture or motion of your body during a fall may be sending blood toward that region. Alternatively, the feeling may just stand out more there because the area is more sensitive. I hope this clears up the physical sensation you're experiencing.

A graphical model, often called a probabilistic graphical model, is a way of representing a complex probability distribution over many random variables using a graph. Each node in the graph stands for a random variable, such as a patient's symptom, a pixel's color, or a word in a sentence, and the edges between nodes encode how those variables depend on one another. The key idea is that the structure of the graph tells you which variables are conditionally independent of which others. This lets a huge joint distribution be broken down, or factorized, into a product of smaller, local pieces that are much easier to specify, store, and compute with.

There are two main families. Directed graphical models, usually called Bayesian networks, use arrows to point from one variable to another, and they are natural for describing cause-and-effect or generative processes. For example, a network might have an arrow from "season" to "rain" and from "rain" to "wet grass," and the full distribution becomes the product of each variable's probability given its parents in the graph. Undirected graphical models, known as Markov random fields or Markov networks, use plain edges without direction and are suited to situations where influences are symmetric, such as neighboring pixels in an image tending to have similar colors. In these models the distribution is expressed as a product of potential functions defined over groups of connected nodes, called cliques, normalized by a constant. There are also hybrid forms, such as factor graphs, which make the factorization explicit, and conditional random fields, which model the distribution of some variables given others.

Graphical models support two central tasks. Inference means answering questions like "given that the grass is wet, how likely is it that it rained?" by computing marginal or conditional probabilities, using exact algorithms such as variable elimination and belief propagation, or approximate ones such as Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling and variational methods. Learning means estimating the parameters of the model, and sometimes the graph structure itself, from data.

The value of graphical models lies in combining probability theory with graph theory to handle uncertainty in a structured, interpretable way. They underlie many well-known techniques, including hidden Markov models for speech recognition, Kalman filters for tracking, topic models for text, and diagnostic systems in medicine, and they remain an important conceptual framework in machine learning, statistics, and artificial intelligence.

Several factors may explain why soccer supporters can be more inclined toward violence than followers of other sports. One is that soccer is played and watched all over the world, so stadiums frequently hold very large crowds, which creates more chances for trouble to break out. Another is that soccer inspires intense devotion, and that passion can push emotions to a boil and spark confrontations. In certain countries, hooliganism, meaning violent conduct by fans, has long been an entrenched issue, with some groups becoming notorious for planning and taking part in brawls. Some supporters also turn to violence to demonstrate their loyalty to their club or to show opponents that they cannot be intimidated. Alcohol plays a role as well. Many fans drink before and during games, which can make the mood rowdier and more hostile. It should be stressed that most soccer fans are not violent, and soccer bodies and governments are taking numerous steps to curb disorder at matches. Even so, the problem persists in some places and still requires attention.

In short, exercising an ISO or QSO early leaves you better prepared for the real event or project and makes better outcomes more achievable.
