Starting a side business is a solid way to bring in some extra money, chase something you're into, or just see if an idea has legs. If you want to ease into it, here's how I'd go about it.

First, figure out what you could actually offer. Brainstorm a product or service, and think about what you're good at, what you enjoy, and what you've already got experience in.

Once you've got an idea, do a bit of homework on the market. Is there real demand? Check out similar businesses, work out who you'd be selling to, and see what the competition looks like.

Then put together a simple plan. Nothing crazy, just your goals, your target customers, how you'll market yourself, and some rough financial numbers. It keeps you organized and stops you from drifting.

Depending on what you're doing, you might need to sort out the legal side too. That could mean registering with the government, getting licenses or permits, and picking a structure like sole proprietorship, LLC, or corporation.

Before you sink a ton of time and money in, try the idea out on a small scale. You'll spot problems early and can tweak things before you're fully committed.

And keep it part-time. Sure, you've got to take it seriously, but it's a side gig. Start small, then put in more time and money as it starts to take off.

Be patient, stay smart about it, and you can slowly turn it into something that really pays off.

A feeding tube can be put straight into the duodenum (the first bit of the small intestine) for someone with esophageal cancer, usually when the cancer or its treatment has damaged the esophagus enough that swallowing becomes hard or impossible and they can't get enough nutrition by mouth. The duodenum sits right after the stomach, so a tube there lets food skip the damaged esophagus and go straight to the small intestine, where the body can absorb it.

The procedure is called a duodenostomy. The surgeon makes a small cut in the belly and threads the tube through it into the duodenum. Doctors sometimes go with this over a stomach tube (gastrostomy) because the duodenum is closer to the liver and can be better at absorbing nutrients. The duodenal wall is also thinner than the stomach's, so it might be less irritated by the tube, though that's not the whole story.

A feeding tube isn't the only way to get nutrition in this situation, though. Depending on the case, people might switch to a liquid diet, take medications to make swallowing easier, or get a stent placed in the esophagus to hold it open. What works best really depends on the patient, and the healthcare team is the one who figures that out.

A high ferritin level (the technical word is hyperferritinemia) can mean there's too much iron in the body, but not always. A few things can cause it. One is a hereditary condition that makes you store too much iron, like hemochromatosis. Another is taking too many iron supplements. And sometimes the body just makes extra ferritin because of some other medical condition. Inflammation or liver damage can also push it up, so it's not always an iron thing at all.

Your mom should really talk to her doctor about this to figure out what's behind it and what to do next. They'll look at her medical history and stuff like her diet and any meds she's on, then go from there with a treatment plan.

One more thing: if she stops the iron supplements, don't expect her ferritin to drop right away. The body can keep holding onto the extra iron for a while after she quits, so it may take some time to come down.

A hardware accelerator is a specialized piece of computer hardware designed to perform a particular task or class of tasks much faster or more efficiently than a general-purpose processor, such as a central processing unit (CPU), could do on its own. Rather than relying on the CPU to handle every operation through software instructions, the system offloads specific workloads to a dedicated component built with circuitry tailored to that job.

The core idea is that general-purpose processors are flexible but not optimized for every kind of computation. A hardware accelerator trades that flexibility for speed and energy efficiency by implementing common, computationally heavy operations directly in silicon. Familiar examples include graphics processing units (GPUs), which were originally built to render images and are now widely used for parallel computations such as training machine learning models; video encoding and decoding chips that compress or decompress video streams; cryptographic engines that speed up encryption; and neural processing units (NPUs) or tensor processing units (TPUs) designed specifically for artificial intelligence workloads. Field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs) and application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs) are also used to build custom accelerators for specialized needs in areas like networking, scientific computing, and telecommunications.

In practice, a hardware accelerator usually works alongside the CPU. The CPU prepares the data, sends the demanding portion of the work to the accelerator, and then receives the results. Because the accelerator can process many operations in parallel or use circuits optimized for one function, the overall task often completes far sooner and consumes less power than it would in software on the CPU alone. The tradeoff is that accelerators are typically less versatile, and they add cost, design complexity, and the need for software that knows how to use them.

I'm sorry you're dealing with this. The combination you describe deserves attention, so I'll walk through the possibilities and what I'd suggest doing.

With diverticulosis, the most obvious concern is mild or early diverticulitis, since the sigmoid colon sits in the lower left abdomen and is where diverticula most often become inflamed. Dull ache, fullness, bloating, and pain radiating to the back fit that picture, even if you've never had a problem before. Having diverticula for years without symptoms doesn't protect you from a first flare. Fever, worsening pain, nausea or vomiting, a change in bowel habits, or blood in the stool would make this more likely and more urgent.

Because you had a partial hysterectomy, it matters whether your ovaries were left in place. If they were, an ovarian cyst or, less commonly, an ovarian mass can cause one-sided lower abdominal bloating, fullness, and back pain. Persistent bloating in a woman over 50 is something doctors take seriously for this reason, and it's worth getting checked with a pelvic exam and usually an ultrasound or CT. Other possibilities include constipation or gas, an irritable bowel flare, a urinary tract or kidney problem (a kidney stone or infection can cause flank and back pain), and pelvic adhesions from your earlier surgery.

The mood changes may be a separate issue or a related one. At 51, you're right in the perimenopausal or menopausal window. If you still have your ovaries, hormone fluctuations can cause tearfulness, irritability, and anxiety, and these can also come with bloating. If your ovaries were removed, you would already have been through surgical menopause, so a new change now would point elsewhere, such as thyroid problems, depression, anxiety, poor sleep, or stress. It's reasonable to mention both symptoms together, since a doctor may find a connection or want to test thyroid and hormone levels.

I'd recommend seeing your doctor within the next few days rather than waiting it out, since the symptoms are persistent and involve a specific area. Expect an exam, blood work, a urine test, and possibly imaging. Go to urgent care or the ER promptly if you develop fever, severe or worsening pain, repeated vomiting, inability to pass stool or gas, blood in the stool, or a rigid, very tender abdomen. In the meantime, drink plenty of fluids, eat lighter foods, and avoid anything that seems to worsen the pain. Please don't start heavy NSAID use without checking with your doctor, as it can irritate the bowel.

If you can tell me whether your ovaries were kept, whether you have a fever, and what your bowel habits have been like, I can help you narrow things down further.

Okay, so American English is basically the version of English people speak in the US. It's pretty close to British English, but the two differ in vocabulary, spelling, and pronunciation. Take words like elevator, which Americans use while Brits say lift, or soccer versus football (flip those depending on who you ask). And chips in Britain are what Americans call French fries.

Spelling is where you'll notice it most. Americans write "color," Brits write "colour." Americans also tend to use "z" in lots of words where Brits use "s," so you get "organize" in the US and "organise" in the UK.

Pronunciation varies too. Americans often pronounce the vowels in "cot" and "caught" differently, while many British speakers make them sound the same. And Americans usually pronounce the "r" in words like "hard," whereas a lot of British accents drop it.

Anyway, American English is pretty varied and keeps changing, shaped by all sorts of cultural and historical stuff. Millions of people speak it around the world, and it's a big part of American culture.

Non-monotonic logic is a family of formal logical systems designed to model reasoning in which conclusions can be retracted when new information arrives. In classical logic, the relation of logical consequence is monotonic: if a conclusion follows from a set of premises, it still follows if additional premises are added. Adding information can never invalidate something already proven. Human reasoning often works differently. If we learn that Tweety is a bird, we might conclude that Tweety can fly, but if we later learn that Tweety is a penguin, we withdraw that conclusion. Non-monotonic logics were developed in the 1970s and 1980s, notably by researchers in artificial intelligence, to capture this kind of defeasible or default reasoning.

Several well-known formalisms exist. Default logic, introduced by Raymond Reiter in 1980, extends classical logic with default rules of the form "if A is true and B is consistent with what we believe, then conclude C." Circumscription, developed by John McCarthy, minimizes the extension of certain predicates, effectively assuming that the only objects with a given property are those that must have it. Autoepistemic logic, associated with Robert Moore, formalizes reasoning about one's own beliefs and lack of knowledge. Logic programming with negation as failure, as in Prolog and answer set programming, is another practical branch, where a statement is treated as false if it cannot be proven.

The central feature across these systems is that the set of conclusions is not simply growing as premises accumulate. Reasoning becomes a matter of choosing the most plausible or preferred set of conclusions given what is known, and that choice can change when new facts appear. This makes non-monotonic logic valuable for commonsense reasoning, knowledge representation, database systems with incomplete information, and the design of intelligent agents. It also raises technical challenges, such as ensuring that the resulting inference relation behaves sensibly and that the systems remain computationally tractable.

Honestly, just do what your doctor told you and keep icing your nose like they said. It really does help with the swelling. You can also prop your head up with an extra pillow when you sleep, and if it's sore, something like acetaminophen or ibuprofen should take the edge off.

If the bump's still there after a few days, or you get really bad pain, trouble breathing, or anything else that feels off, call your doctor and get it looked at. Don't just wait it out.

Also, try not to bump it again. Be careful with it so you don't make things worse. A lot of the time the bump goes down by itself in a few days or a couple of weeks, but if anything's worrying you, it's always fine to check in with your doctor.

Steam is a digital distribution platform and software client developed by Valve Corporation, the American video game company best known for Half-Life, Portal, and Counter-Strike. Launched in 2003 as a way for Valve to deliver updates to its own games, it grew into the largest PC gaming storefront in the world. Users create an account, buy or download games, and have them automatically updated, while the Steam client also handles friends lists, voice and text chat, community forums, workshop content for mods, cloud saves, and achievements.

Beyond buying games, Steam also offers a marketplace for trading and selling in-game items, a hardware line called the Steam Deck (a handheld PC), and Steam Machine and Steam Controller products. Although it began on Windows, it now runs on macOS and Linux as well, and many games are compatible with Valve's Proton compatibility layer, which lets them run on Linux. Steam is often praised for frequent sales, a large library of indie and AAA titles, and its ecosystem of community features, though it has also faced criticism over its revenue cut for developers and its handling of certain content policies.

Nope, you can't build a magnet motor that runs forever. It breaks conservation of energy, which is basically the rule that energy never gets made or destroyed, just moved from one form to another. A motor needs energy coming in to keep going, whether that's fuel in a car engine or electricity in a fan. To get a perpetual motion machine with magnets, you'd have to keep it running with no energy input at all, and that just doesn't happen. Energy can't come out of nothing.

Think about a toy car with a battery. The battery supplies the energy that moves the car, and once it's dead, the car stops. You can't keep it going without swapping in a new battery or finding some other power source. Same deal with a magnet machine. It'll coast for a while, but it can't go forever without some kind of energy going in. Those videos are fun to watch, though, I'll give you that.

Gordon Bell is an electrical engineer and computer scientist whose work has had a considerable impact on computer architecture and digital hardware design. He is most widely recognized for his role in creating the VAX computer system and for his part in developing the SPEC benchmarks, which are used to gauge how well computer systems perform. Bell has also been a leading figure in the growth of high-performance computing, and his achievements have earned him many honors, among them the IEEE Computer Society's Computer Pioneer Award and the ACM SIGARCH Maurice Wilkes Award. At present, he works as a researcher at Microsoft Research and holds the title of professor emeritus at Carnegie Mellon University.

Dmitri Mendeleev was a Russian chemist and inventor, and he's mostly remembered for coming up with the periodic table. If you haven't seen one in a while, it's basically a chart that lines up all the known elements in an orderly way, going by their atomic structure and chemical properties. His work on it ended up laying a lot of the groundwork for modern chemistry, which is why he's often named among the most influential scientists ever. He didn't stop there, though. He also did some pretty significant work in thermodynamics and in petroleum production.

Aircraft are engineered with their mass carefully distributed so that they remain even and steady while airborne. This matters for several reasons: it allows the aircraft to fly safely and efficiently, and it reduces strain on the aircraft's various parts. Airlines and manufacturers rely on a range of methods to balance a plane whose rows contain an odd number of seats. For instance, heavier items like baggage and freight may be positioned near the middle of the fuselage to even out the load. Weight sensors can also be used to gauge the load in each row, with adjustments made as necessary to keep the aircraft balanced. In short, keeping an odd-seated plane balanced is a key concern for airlines and manufacturers, who employ several techniques to keep the aircraft evenly loaded and stable in flight.

Honestly, acne comes down to a mix of things: hormones, genetics, and your environment. Some people just get it more because their hormone levels run higher, or because they inherited genes that make breakouts more likely. If your parents had bad skin, there's a decent chance you will too.

Then there's the stuff you can actually control, like the makeup or skincare products you use (some of them clog your pores) or not washing your face properly. And some people just get lucky and barely deal with it at all, which, yeah, doesn't seem fair.

The twelfth cycle of America's Next Top Model was won by Teyona Anderson, who received the crown during the finale broadcast on December 4, 2009. Judges commended Anderson for a powerful and adaptable portfolio, along with her consistent ability to produce high-quality photographs throughout the competition. Amanda Babin, Fo Porter, and Allyson Lewis were the other finalists. America's Next Top Model is a reality television contest in which hopeful models compete through a range of challenges and photo shoots, aiming to be declared the next top model.

A data warehouse is basically a central place where you dump data from all over the place so you can run reports and analysis on it. It's built so end users and analysts can query it quickly without bogging down the systems the data came from. Most of the data comes from things like transactional databases, log files, and other operational systems. It gets pulled out of those sources, cleaned up and reshaped to fit the warehouse's schema, and then loaded in. The whole thing is meant to be fast and scalable, since you've got lots of data and plenty of people hitting it at once. It also works with analysis tools like OLAP and data mining, which let you poke around the data in ways that would be a pain otherwise. For businesses and analysts, it's a big deal because it helps you actually see what's going on and make smarter calls.

Honestly, nobody can give you an exact number for Muslims in the UK, since the country doesn't actually collect religion statistics the way some others do. The best we've got comes from the Office for National Statistics and the Pew Research Center, and they both land around 5% of the population. That works out to roughly 3.45 million people. Worth knowing too that the community is really varied, with folks from all sorts of ethnic and national backgrounds.

Your pain might be caused by pregnancy, though a number of other explanations are possible. Lower back and abdominal pain commonly result from a strained muscle, constipation, trapped gas, or a urinary tract infection. The discomfort could also be tied to your menstrual cycle, or to some other health problem, whether or not it involves the reproductive system. If you are hoping to conceive and suspect you may be pregnant, you should have this confirmed, either by a medical professional or with a home pregnancy test. And if you are pregnant and have had unprotected sex, you should contact a healthcare provider as soon as you can to go over your options and make sure you get the right prenatal care. In general, it is wise to see a healthcare provider whenever you have pain you cannot explain or any other unusual symptoms. They can work out what is behind your symptoms and suggest suitable treatment.

A secret agent is a person whose job is to find out things that other countries or groups want to keep hidden. Imagine your neighbor has a locked treasure box and you want to know what's inside. A secret agent is like someone who quietly makes friends with the neighbor, listens carefully, and maybe gets a peek, all without the neighbor knowing why they're really there. Governments do this to learn about plans, weapons, or dangers so they can keep their own people safe.

Most real spies don't sneak around with guns. The people who work for agencies like the CIA in America or MI6 in Britain are usually called intelligence officers, and they mostly work by talking to people. They go to parties, meetings, and embassies, and they try to persuade someone who has access to secrets, like a government worker or a military officer, to share information. Those helpers are called agents or sources, which is a confusing detail: the officer is the one who recruits, and the agent is the person who actually passes along the secrets. Other spies spend their days reading newspapers, studying satellite pictures, listening to intercepted messages, or breaking codes. Much of the job is patient, boring paperwork, because a lot of small clues have to be put together like a jigsaw puzzle.

James Bond is mostly fantasy. The real world has no spies with a license to kill who race exotic cars, wear tuxedos at casinos, and blow up villain lairs. Real spies try very hard not to be noticed, so a famous drink order and a fancy name would be terrible for the job. Still, a few bits are based on truth. Spy agencies have made clever gadgets, such as hidden cameras, tiny listening devices, and disguised containers for passing secret notes. Some operatives have also been involved in dangerous actions like sabotage, and in history there were cases of assassination plots. Ian Fleming, who created Bond, actually worked in British naval intelligence during World War Two, so he borrowed ideas from real life and then made them much more exciting.

Spying is absolutely still done today. Nearly every country has intelligence services, and they now also work with computers, hacking, phone data, and satellites, which makes it less about trench coats and more about screens. Much of what they do stays secret, but a lot has come out over the years through declassified documents, which are files released after enough time has passed, as well as court cases, leaks, and books by former officers. So we know the general picture well, even though the details of current missions are kept locked away.

Thinking about hiring a freelancer? You'll want to get a handle on your tax duties as the business owner. Generally, you're on the hook for withholding and paying taxes on what you pay them for their work. That covers federal income tax, Social Security, and Medicare. If you're hiring someone in the US and you pay them $600 or more in a calendar year, you'll need to send them a Form 1099-MISC. It reports that miscellaneous income to the IRS, and you file it by January 31 of the following year. If the freelancer isn't a U.S. citizen or resident alien, you might also have to withhold and pay tax on what you send them. That's called "backup withholding." Honestly, your best bet is to talk to a tax pro or check the IRS website for the details on your situation.

China has given the world many inventions that shaped human history. The most famous are often called the Four Great Inventions: papermaking, printing, gunpowder, and the compass. Paper was refined around 105 CE by Cai Lun, a court official of the Han dynasty, though earlier forms existed before him. Woodblock printing appeared during the Tang dynasty, and the oldest surviving dated printed book, a copy of the Diamond Sutra, comes from 868 CE. Around 1040, during the Song dynasty, an artisan named Bi Sheng created movable type using baked clay characters.

Gunpowder was discovered by Chinese alchemists, probably in the ninth century, while they were searching for elixirs of immortality. It was soon used in fireworks, fire arrows, early bombs, and eventually primitive guns. The magnetic compass began as a divination tool made from lodestone and was later adapted for navigation, and by the eleventh century Chinese sailors were using it at sea.

Beyond these four, China produced silk, which was cultivated from silkworms thousands of years ago and became so valuable that it gave the Silk Road its name. Porcelain, a fine, hard, translucent ceramic, was perfected in China and was so closely associated with the country that English speakers came to call it "china." The Chinese also developed cast iron centuries before Europe, along with the wheelbarrow, the seismoscope designed by Zhang Heng in 132 CE to detect distant earthquakes, and the sternpost rudder for steering ships.

Other notable contributions include paper money, which emerged during the Tang and Song dynasties, the crossbow, kites, tea cultivation and preparation, the umbrella, lacquerware, and the abacus as a calculating tool. Many of these innovations spread westward through trade and cultural exchange and went on to influence science, warfare, commerce, and daily life around the world.

Metal music is a genre of rock that emerged in the late 1960s and early 1970s, with bands like Black Sabbath, Led Zeppelin, and Deep Purple often credited as its founders. Musically, it is defined by heavily distorted electric guitars, powerful and often fast drumming, prominent bass, loud volume, and a sense of intensity and force. Guitar riffs are usually the backbone of a metal song, and many styles feature virtuosic guitar solos.

In terms of themes, metal covers a wide range of subjects, but it tends to gravitate toward the darker, more dramatic, or more extreme sides of human experience. Common topics include war, death, mortality, injustice, alienation, mental struggle, religion and its critique, mythology, fantasy, history, horror, and the occult. Some bands write about social and political issues, while others focus on personal pain, anger, or resilience. Despite its reputation, much metal is less about being evil and more about confronting difficult emotions and ideas head on, often finding empowerment, catharsis, or even a kind of triumph in that confrontation.

The genre has split into many subgenres, each with its own sound and focus. Heavy metal in the classic sense, represented by Iron Maiden and Judas Priest, often features soaring vocals and epic storytelling. Thrash metal, from bands like Metallica and Slayer, is fast and aggressive, frequently dealing with war and social anger. Death metal uses guttural vocals and extreme brutality, often with gory or existential themes. Black metal, associated with Norway, emphasizes raw atmosphere and often anti-religious or nature-focused imagery. Doom metal is slow and heavy, centered on despair and gloom, while power metal is upbeat and fantastical, full of heroes and dragons. Progressive metal emphasizes complex song structures and musicianship, and newer styles like metalcore and nu metal blend metal with punk, hardcore, or hip hop influences.

Beyond the music itself, metal is also a culture and community. Fans often value authenticity, loyalty, musical skill, and a sense of belonging among outsiders. Concerts are a big part of the experience, with headbanging, mosh pits, and a strong shared energy. For many listeners, metal offers an outlet for frustration and a source of strength, and despite its aggressive sound, its fan communities are often known for being welcoming and supportive.

Magic Kingdom is a theme park at Walt Disney World Resort in Bay Lake, Florida, near Orlando. It opened in 1971 and was the second Disney park built after Disneyland in California, and it is the most visited theme park in the world. The park is organized around themed "lands," including Main Street, U.S.A., Adventureland, Frontierland, Liberty Square, Fantasyland, Tomorrowland, and Storybook Circus, and it is known for its iconic castle, Cinderella Castle, which serves as the centerpiece of the park. Guests can ride attractions such as Space Mountain, Pirates of the Caribbean, and Seven Dwarfs Mine Train, watch parades and fireworks, and meet Disney characters.

A surname is a person's family name, the name they share with their relatives and that is usually passed down through generations. It is often the last part of a full name in Western naming conventions, such as "Smith" in "John Smith."

A given name is the name chosen for a person at birth or later, used to identify them individually within their family and social circle. It is also called a first name or forename in many contexts, such as "John" in "John Smith." In some cultures the order is reversed, with the family name coming first, as in much of East Asia, where "Wang Wei" would have Wang as the surname and Wei as the given name.

Okay, so an upper ontology is basically a formal vocabulary that gives you a shared set of concepts and categories for representing knowledge. It's meant to be general enough to work across lots of different domains, which is why people often use it as a starting point before building more specific domain ontologies for a particular subject or app. The whole point is to have a common language you can use to represent and reason about knowledge. You can use its broad concepts to sort and organize the more specialized stuff in your domain ontology, and that helps cut down on confusion, since everyone's describing things with the same standardized terms. People usually build these with formal methods like first-order logic, and implement them with tools like OWL or RDF. You'll see them show up in knowledge management, natural language processing, and AI, among other places.

Yes, appendicitis can come on very suddenly. Pain often starts around the belly button or in the middle of the abdomen and then moves to the lower right over several hours, but it can also be sharp and intense from the start. Sudden sharp pain in the lower right abdomen has several possible causes, including a kidney stone or ureter stone, which can begin abruptly and sometimes feels worse when you move. A urinary tract infection or kidney infection can also cause this, and an inguinal hernia can cause sharp pain on one side.

Because you're male and this started suddenly, you should also think about testicular torsion, where the testicle twists and loses its blood supply. It can cause pain in the lower abdomen or groin before the testicle itself hurts much, and it's an emergency where treatment within a few hours makes a big difference. Check whether your right testicle is swollen, very tender, or sitting higher or at a different angle than usual.

I'd recommend going to an emergency department now rather than waiting to see if it passes. Doctors can examine you and do a urine test, blood tests, and often an ultrasound or CT scan to tell these causes apart. Don't eat or drink much until you've been seen, in case you need surgery. Call emergency services instead of getting a ride yourself if the pain becomes severe, you vomit repeatedly, you develop a high fever, you feel faint, or you notice testicle pain or swelling.

Sharp, random pains in the wrists, arms, and hands are often nerve-related. They can come from pinched or irritated nerves in the neck or shoulder, from repetitive strain, or from joint hypermobility, which is common in people with POTS and can be linked to connective tissue conditions like Ehlers-Danlos syndrome. Poor circulation or fluctuating blood pressure can also cause tingling or sharp sensations in the extremities. Your POTS may well be connected to these symptoms, even if it doesn't seem like it.

The new right-sided head pain and the lump together are the parts I'd take most seriously. A lump that appears overnight could be a swollen lymph node responding to an infection, a cyst, an insect bite, or an injury you don't remember. Combined with two days of head pain, it's worth having someone examine it soon, ideally within the next day. Please don't wait for it to resolve on its own.

Seek emergency care right away if you develop a sudden or severe headache, weakness or numbness on one side of the body, trouble speaking, vision changes, confusion, fainting, a stiff neck with fever, or if the lump becomes rapidly larger, very red, hot, or painful.

When you see a doctor, mention all your symptoms together, including the arm and hand pain, the headache, and the lump, along with when each started and whether anything makes them better or worse. Let them know about your POTS and any medications you take, since some can affect headaches and blood flow. Keeping track of your fluid intake and any dizziness or heart rate changes can also help, since dehydration can trigger headaches in POTS.

I'm doing well, thanks for asking, and I'm glad the dry socket pain has finally eased. A tender lump near the stitched area three weeks after surgery is fairly common and often part of normal healing, but because it's painful it's worth having your surgeon look at it.

There are a few likely explanations. Stitches can leave a firm knot of scar tissue as the flap heals, and this granulation or scar tissue usually softens and shrinks over several weeks to a few months. If your stitches were dissolvable, part of one may not have fully dissolved, or a knot may be stuck in the tissue, causing a small inflammatory reaction that feels like a tender bump. Another possibility is that your cheek, swollen and tender from surgery, keeps getting bitten or rubbed against your teeth, which irritates it further. A small blocked minor salivary gland, called a mucocele, can also appear after oral trauma or surgery. It tends to feel like a soft, fluid-filled bubble and is usually more annoying than painful. Less often, the lump is a localized infection or small abscess, especially since you had a dry socket. A small bone fragment working its way out of the socket can also feel like a hard, sore lump.

You should contact your oral surgeon soon, ideally within a few days, if the lump is getting larger or more painful. The same applies if it feels warm, looks red, or has pus or a bad taste coming from it. Fever, swelling in your face or jaw, difficulty opening your mouth, or swollen glands under your jaw are other reasons to call, as is a lump that hasn't improved after another week or two. Any trouble swallowing or breathing, or rapidly spreading swelling, needs urgent care right away.

In the meantime, warm salt water rinses several times a day can calm irritated tissue and keep the area clean. Try not to poke at the lump with your tongue or fingers, chew on the opposite side if you can, and use an over-the-counter pain reliever like ibuprofen if it's safe for you.

Most lumps like this turn out to be harmless healing tissue or a leftover stitch, and both are easy for your surgeon to check and resolve, often with a quick snip or reassurance. Since you've already had one complication, a short follow-up visit is a reasonable step for peace of mind.

In the beloved children's book "The Wizard of Oz," penned by L. Frank Baum and released in 1900, the central figure is an enigmatic man living in the Land of Oz who possesses considerable magical abilities. He goes by the plain name the Wizard of Oz. In the well-known 1939 movie version of the story, the role of the Wizard is played by Frank Morgan.

Imagine your neighborhood has lots of different houses, each with its own family, its own rules, and its own way of doing things.

Nationalism is like saying, "Our house comes first." People who lean this way believe each country should look out for its own people, keep its own traditions, and make its own decisions without outsiders telling it what to do. They often care a lot about things like a shared language, culture, and history, and they tend to want strong borders and to protect local jobs and businesses. The good side of this is that people feel proud and connected to one another, and a country can run itself the way its citizens want. The worry is that it can slide into treating outsiders unfairly, or into countries clashing with each other.

Globalism is like saying, "We all live on the same street, so we should work together." People who lean this way believe countries should cooperate through trade, shared agreements, and international groups like the United Nations, because many problems, such as pollution, diseases, and wars, don't stop at borders. The good side is that cooperation can make goods cheaper, spread ideas, and help solve big problems together. The worry is that people may feel their own community's voice gets lost, that far-away organizations make decisions for them, or that some workers lose jobs when work moves overseas.

Most people aren't fully one or the other. Someone can love their country and still want to trade and cooperate with others. The real debate is usually about how much: how much should a country decide things for itself, and how much should it share decisions with the rest of the world?

One more thing worth knowing: the word "globalist" is sometimes used as an insult, and "nationalist" can be too, depending on who is speaking. So when you hear either word, it helps to ask what the speaker actually means by it.

A robo-advisor like Betterment can be preferable to buying a single index fund like SPY for several reasons, though the tradeoffs matter. SPY tracks only the S&P 500, which means it holds large U.S. companies and nothing else. A robo-advisor typically builds a diversified portfolio across U.S. and international stocks, bonds, and sometimes real estate, using low-cost ETFs, so the investor gets broader exposure and can manage risk more deliberately. For someone who wants to avoid the decision of how much to allocate to each asset class, the service handles that based on a questionnaire about goals, time horizon, and risk tolerance.

Robo-advisors also automate behaviors that are easy to neglect on your own. They rebalance the portfolio when market moves push allocations away from targets, and many perform tax-loss harvesting, selling investments at a loss to offset gains elsewhere, which can improve after-tax returns in taxable accounts. Some also handle dividend reinvestment and cash deposits automatically. For investors who might otherwise panic-sell during downturns or make impulsive changes, the automation and a set plan can enforce discipline.

Accessibility is another factor. Many robo-advisors have low or no account minimums and allow fractional share purchases, so someone with a few hundred dollars can build a diversified portfolio that would otherwise be difficult to assemble. They also tend to offer goal-based accounts and simple interfaces that make it easier to track progress.

The main counterpoint is cost. Betterment charges an annual advisory fee, historically around 0.25 percent of assets under management, on top of the expense ratios of the underlying funds. Buying SPY directly or a comparable broad fund through a brokerage can cost only the fund's expense ratio, which for SPY is about 0.09 percent. Over decades, that fee difference compounds meaningfully. So a robo-advisor is most valuable to someone who would not otherwise diversify, rebalance, or stay disciplined, and less so to a investor who is comfortable managing a simple portfolio of a few low-cost funds themselves. It's also worth checking current fee schedules, since they change.

If you are in the United States, a gift of nearly $10,000 from a foreign person usually requires no declaration at all, but it depends on who gave it and how the money reaches you.

The recipient of a gift does not owe U.S. income tax or gift tax on it. Gift tax, where it applies, falls on the giver, and a foreign person giving money that is not tied to U.S. property generally has no U.S. gift tax obligation either. You do not report the gift as income on your Form 1040.

The IRS form for foreign gifts is Form 3520. You must file it only if the gifts you received during the tax year from a nonresident alien individual or foreign estate total more than $100,000. Gifts from related people are added together toward that limit. Gifts from a foreign corporation or foreign partnership have a much lower threshold, roughly $20,000 and adjusted annually for inflation, so check the current figure in the Form 3520 instructions. For a single gift of just under $10,000 from an individual, you would not file Form 3520 unless other gifts that year push you over the threshold. If you are required to file and do not, the penalties can be steep, so it is worth adding up all foreign gifts for the year.

How the money arrives matters separately. If you or someone else physically carries cash or certain monetary instruments worth more than $10,000 into or out of the U.S., you must declare it to Customs on FinCEN Form 105. Carrying it is legal; failing to declare it can lead to seizure. A bank wire carries no such requirement, though your bank may ask about the source of the funds, and you should keep records such as a gift letter, the sender's details, and transfer confirmations. If you deposit more than $10,000 in physical cash, the bank files a Currency Transaction Report automatically, which is routine and not a problem. Deliberately splitting deposits or transfers to stay under $10,000 to avoid that reporting is a federal crime called structuring, even if the money itself is entirely legitimate, so do not break the gift into smaller pieces for that reason.

If the money stays in a foreign bank account in your name and your foreign accounts together exceed $10,000 at any point in the year, you would need to file an FBAR (FinCEN Form 114), and possibly Form 8938 at higher balances.

The giver should also check their own country's rules, since some countries tax gifts or restrict money sent abroad.

If you are in a different country, or the gift is tied to a business, trust, or U.S. property, the rules differ, and a tax professional can confirm what applies to you.

Palpitations that feel like a single hard beat, a thump, or a skipped beat are most often caused by premature beats, either premature atrial contractions (PACs) or premature ventricular contractions (PVCs). The beat comes slightly early, the heart then pauses briefly, and the next normal beat is stronger because the chamber has had extra time to fill. That is why you feel one hard heartbeat. Having this 3 to 6 times a day for two weeks is very common, and in people with structurally normal hearts these beats are usually benign.

Common triggers include caffeine, energy drinks, alcohol, nicotine, stress and anxiety, poor sleep, dehydration, and some medications and supplements such as decongestants, asthma inhalers, ADHD drugs, and thyroid medication. Medical causes worth ruling out include an overactive thyroid, anemia, low potassium or magnesium, and less often an underlying heart condition such as valve disease, cardiomyopathy, or other rhythm problems. A recent illness, fever, or a period of heavy exertion can also bring them on.

Catching an episode on your Holter monitor is useful, because the recording will show whether the sensation lines up with a premature beat or with something else. Be aware that consumer devices and their automated readings can be unreliable, so have the tracing reviewed by a doctor, ideally a cardiologist, rather than relying on the device's interpretation. Bring the full recording, with the time you felt the symptom marked.

A typical evaluation includes a history and physical exam, a 12-lead ECG, blood tests (blood count, thyroid function, electrolytes, sometimes magnesium), and often an echocardiogram to check the structure and function of the heart. If the beats turn out to be frequent, a longer monitoring period may be used to measure how many you have in total.

Meanwhile, you can keep a diary of when episodes occur and what you had beforehand, and cut back on caffeine, alcohol, and nicotine to see if it helps.

Seek urgent care if the palpitations come with chest pain or pressure, shortness of breath, fainting or near-fainting, marked dizziness, or a sustained racing or irregular heartbeat that does not settle. Also see a doctor sooner if you have a family history of sudden cardiac death or heart disease, or known heart problems yourself.

In summary, what you describe is most likely benign premature beats, but because it has lasted two weeks and you have a recording, it is reasonable to get it checked with an ECG and basic tests to confirm.

You can take a shower or bath now. Since you used the one-day Monistat on Friday night, the medication should be finished, and the usual advice to avoid tub soaking during treatment no longer applies. Gentle washing with water is fine, and you don't need to avoid water while you're recovering. Pat the area dry afterward and wear breathable cotton underwear. Some providers suggest skipping bubble baths or harsh soaps, since they can irritate the vulva.

Because you're at 9 months, please call your OB or midwife to let them know you were treated and that your symptoms have cleared. They may want to confirm the infection is gone or check whether you need further treatment, especially since yeast infections can return near delivery. Monistat is generally considered acceptable in pregnancy, but your provider should know what you used.

Also contact your provider right away, or go to labor and delivery, if you notice fluid leaking or a gush from the vagina, which can be hard to tell apart from vaginal discharge at this stage. Other reasons to call promptly include regular contractions, bleeding that's more than light spotting, fever, a foul-smelling discharge, or new burning, itching, or pain. Using pads is a reasonable way to keep track of what you're noticing, so keep an eye on the color and amount of any discharge.

Eurodollar futures are a derivative contract that lets you lock in a deal to buy or sell a set amount of U.S. dollar deposits sitting in banks outside the States, the so-called Eurodollars. They trade on exchanges like the Chicago Mercantile Exchange (CME). People use them to hedge against moves in the interest rate on those deposits, or to bet on where rates are headed. They can also help manage the risk that the dollar's value shifts against other currencies.

Each contract is for $1,000,000, and the smallest price move, the tick, is 0.01, which works out to $25 per contract. Nothing gets delivered at the end. It settles in cash, based on the London Interbank Offered Rate (LIBOR) at the close of the contract period. Banks, companies, and hedge funds use them a lot to manage interest rate exposure and as a reference point for other instruments. Some individual traders also use them to speculate on rates and currency moves, though it's not really a beginner product.

The term "commonwealth" can mean a few different things depending on context, so it helps to separate them.

In the United States, four states officially call themselves commonwealths: Kentucky, Massachusetts, Pennsylvania, and Virginia. Despite the different name, they are legally and politically the same as any other state. They have the same constitutional powers, the same representation in Congress, and the same relationship with the federal government. The word is mostly a historical holdover. In the colonial and Revolutionary era, "commonwealth" was a term drawn from English political thought, meaning a political community founded for the common good, and it carried a republican, anti-monarchical flavor. Those states simply chose it in their early constitutions and kept it.

The word has a separate and more substantive meaning for certain U.S. territories. Puerto Rico and the Northern Mariana Islands are called commonwealths, and this is a distinct status. They are self-governing, with their own constitutions and local governments, but they are not states and remain under U.S. sovereignty. Their residents are U.S. citizens but generally cannot vote in presidential elections while living there and have no voting representation in Congress.

Then there is the Commonwealth of Nations, usually just called the Commonwealth, which is a voluntary association of about 56 countries, most of them former territories of the British Empire. Members such as Canada, Australia, India, and Nigeria are fully independent. The association promotes cooperation, shared values, and development, and the British monarch serves as its symbolic head. Some members, like Australia, officially use "Commonwealth" in their own name as well, referring to the federal union of its states.

So if someone says a state is a commonwealth, in the U.S. context it is mainly a matter of name and tradition rather than any difference in power or status.

The American Civil War began on April 12, 1861, when Confederate forces opened fire on Fort Sumter, a Union-held fort in the harbor of Charleston, South Carolina. The Union surrendered the fort two days later.

You generally can't lock a mortgage rate five years in advance. Lenders usually hold a rate for a set period, often 30 to 60 days, sometimes up to 90 or 120 days for a fee, and only once you have a specific loan application and property. Pre-approvals typically expire within 60 to 90 days. So the practical question is which loan structure fits a five-year horizon.

If you're buying a home now and expect to sell in about five years, a 5/1 adjustable-rate mortgage is worth a close look. It keeps the rate fixed for the first five years, usually at a lower initial rate than a 30-year fixed, and then adjusts annually after that. If you sell on schedule, you never face an adjustment. The risk is that you stay longer than planned or can't sell, and the rate then resets based on market conditions, with caps that limit how much it can climb at each adjustment and over the life of the loan.

A 30-year fixed mortgage is the safer choice if you want payment certainty, even if you plan to move. It costs a bit more up front, but you can sell in five years without worrying about resets. Ask about prepayment penalties too, since some loans charge a fee for paying off or selling early.

If you already have a fixed-rate mortgage and are asking how to keep that rate until you move, you're already locked in. Refinancing would only be worth considering if current rates fall well below yours and you plan to stay long enough to recoup closing costs.

If you're not yet ready to buy, you can use the time to improve your credit score, save for a larger down payment, and pay down debt, since these improve the rate you'll be offered later. Some lenders also offer temporary buydowns or rate-lock extensions, which are worth asking about when the time comes.

So the Romani, who a lot of people call Gypsies (though that word's considered offensive by many Romani folks these days), have a really interesting history. They're known for their own culture, with music, dance, and traditions that are all their own.

They've moved around a lot over the centuries and ended up living all over the world. Originally they came from the area that's now India, and over time they spread out into tons of different countries.

One thing that really stands out is how big music and dance are in the culture. You'll often see violins or accordions, and the dancing is super lively and energetic.

They've dealt with a ton of discrimination and mistreatment throughout history, which is pretty awful. Still, they've added a lot to the cultures of the places they've lived. Today you can find Romani communities pretty much everywhere, and they keep celebrating and holding on to their culture.

What you're describing is very common in teenagers and young adults, and in a healthy, active person it's most often harmless. The feeling of not getting a satisfying breath, relieved by a deep breath or a sigh, is sometimes called sighing dyspnea or "air hunger," and it's frequently linked to how we regulate our breathing rather than to a problem in the lungs or heart.

The most likely explanation is a habit of subtle over-breathing or tension in the breathing muscles. Stress, anxiety, tiredness, or even just paying attention to your breathing can make the chest and neck muscles tighten and make each breath feel shallow. You then take a big breath to compensate, which can briefly blow off too much carbon dioxide and leave you feeling you still aren't getting enough, so the cycle continues. Poor posture, like slouching over a phone or desk, can add to the tight feeling in the chest and neck. The faster breathing you notice fits this pattern too.

Other possibilities worth knowing about include mild exercise-induced asthma or allergies, which can cause a feeling of tightness, especially during or after activity or in certain seasons. Low iron or anemia is also common in teenage girls, particularly with periods, and can cause breathlessness and fatigue. Acid reflux can sometimes cause a tight feeling in the chest and throat as well.

As for the childhood heart murmur, most murmurs in children are "innocent" and harmless, and they often disappear with age. Since yours was described as very minor and you're active without trouble, it's unlikely to be the cause, but it's worth mentioning to a doctor so they have the full picture.

A few simple things may help. Try slow breathing, in through the nose for about four seconds and out for about six, letting your belly rise rather than your upper chest. Practice it a few minutes a day. Stretch your neck and shoulders, keep active, sleep well, and notice whether the feeling gets worse when you're stressed.

It's reasonable to see a doctor if this continues or bothers you, since they can listen to your heart and lungs and check for things like anemia or asthma with simple tests. Seek care promptly if you have chest pain, fainting or near-fainting, a racing or irregular heartbeat, blue or gray lips, breathlessness that comes on suddenly or happens at rest and doesn't settle, swelling in your legs, or if you can't keep up with activities you used to manage easily. Based on what you've told me, though, nothing sounds alarming.

Honestly, a burning feeling down there with brown and white discharge can come from a bunch of things. Infections are the usual suspects: STIs, bacterial vaginosis, or a yeast infection. Irritation or an allergic reaction is another common one, especially from soap, laundry detergent, or other hygiene products that touch that area. Hormone shifts can change discharge and sometimes cause burning too.

Please don't try to diagnose or treat this yourself, though. Get it checked by a healthcare provider so they can figure out what's actually going on and what treatment makes sense. And don't take AF kit tablets before you've talked to one, because you could end up masking the real problem.

California's domestic partnership law is found in the Family Code, and to qualify, two people must meet a set of basic requirements. Both partners must be at least 18 years old and cannot be related by blood in a way that would bar marriage between them under California law. Neither person can be married to someone else or already be in another domestic partnership, and each must be capable of consenting to the partnership. Historically, the two people had to share a common residence, though that requirement was removed in recent years. The partners must also be members of the same sex, or, if they are of different sexes, at least one partner must be 62 years of age or older. That age rule was added to give older couples a way to register without marrying, since they may have concerns about Social Security or pension benefits.

To register, the couple files a Declaration of Domestic Partnership with the California Secretary of State. Both partners must sign it, and they must agree to the mutual obligations described in state law, such as sharing basic living expenses and being responsible for each other's support. Because the rules and forms can change, it is worth checking the Secretary of State's website or consulting an attorney before filing, particularly because eligibility rules and the consequences of registration can affect taxes, benefits, and property matters.

Honestly, it makes sense when you think about it. People always need mattresses, so there's steady demand. Plus there are tons of types out there, memory foam, innerspring, hybrid, and some stores focus on just one of those, so they don't all compete head to head. Competition is a big part of it too. Every shop is trying to lure you in with sales or discounts, which keeps prices in check. And honestly, it's convenient. You can hop from store to store, lie down on a few beds, compare prices, and find the one that feels right. So even in a small area, those stores can keep going because people need mattresses, there's variety to shop around, stores are competing for your business, and buyers like having options nearby.

There are a few ways to get money from India to the US, and which one works best kind of depends on how much you're sending and how fast you need it there.

The most obvious one is a bank transfer. You can wire money straight from your Indian bank account to a US account. It works fine, but banks usually charge fees for it and it can take a few days to go through.

Then there are money transfer companies like Western Union and MoneyGram. You can use them online or walk into a location and do it in person. They often have decent exchange rates and the transfers tend to be pretty quick.

You could also go with an online payment service like PayPal. You can send money right to someone's account, or just use it to pay for stuff online.

Whichever way you go, expect some fees, and the exchange rate will change depending on the service. So it's worth comparing rates and fees before you hit send. A little checking around can save you a decent chunk of money.

Greek belongs to the Indo-European family of languages. It serves as the official language of Greece and holds official status alongside another language in Cyprus. Communities of Greek speakers are also found across the globe, with notable populations in places such as Albania, Italy, and Turkey. The language boasts a lengthy and distinguished past, stretching back to the first written texts produced by the ancient Greeks in the 14th century BCE. Its alphabet descends from the Phoenician script and ranks among the oldest and most widely used writing systems anywhere. Greek contributed greatly to the growth of Western literature, science, and philosophy, and it shaped many other languages, English among them. It is additionally one of the official languages of the European Union.

You've assumed "IDL" means LDL, and an LDL of around 168 mg/dL is moderately high. Whether medicine makes sense depends less on that one number than on your overall chance of a heart attack or stroke over the next ten years. Your healthy weight, regular walking, yoga, normal blood pressure and sugar, and lack of family history all work in your favor. Age, however, is the strongest single driver of cardiovascular risk, and at 69 to 70 it pushes your risk up even when everything else looks good.

Doctors usually estimate that ten-year risk with a calculator such as the ACC/AHA Pooled Cohort Equations. It uses age, sex, total cholesterol, HDL, systolic blood pressure, whether you take blood pressure medicine, diabetes, and smoking. From your ratios, your HDL is probably in the high 40s and your total cholesterol in the mid-250s. For a non-smoking man of 70 with those numbers and normal blood pressure, the estimated ten-year risk often comes out around 15 to 20 percent. For a woman it might be closer to 8 to 12 percent. Under current American guidelines, a risk of 7.5 percent or more is "intermediate," and a moderate-intensity statin is generally considered reasonable after a discussion with your doctor. At 20 percent or more, a statin is more clearly recommended. An LDL in the 160 to 189 range is itself listed as a "risk-enhancing factor" that tips the balance toward treatment. So many people in your situation would be offered a statin, but it isn't automatic.

If you and your doctor are unsure, a coronary artery calcium (CAC) scan can help. It's a quick, low-radiation CT scan of the heart.

- A score of zero suggests low near-term risk, and many doctors would reasonably hold off on medication and recheck in a few years.
- A score above zero, and especially above 100, favors starting a statin.

Some doctors also check lipoprotein(a), a largely inherited factor that can raise risk even in otherwise healthy people.

Whatever you decide about medication, diet can lower LDL by roughly 10 to 20 percent:

- Cut back on saturated fat from ghee, butter, full-fat dairy, coconut oil, and fatty or processed meats.
- Eat more soluble fiber from oats, barley, beans, lentils, and psyllium.
- Include nuts, especially almonds and walnuts.
- Use plant sterol-fortified foods, which add a further modest reduction.

Keep up your walking and yoga, since they help in other ways even if they don't move LDL much.

If you do start a statin, a low or moderate dose of a drug like atorvastatin or rosuvastatin is typical. Most people tolerate it well. Muscle aches occur in a minority, and liver tests and blood sugar are checked periodically.

I can't make the decision for you. I'd suggest asking your doctor to calculate your ten-year risk and discussing whether a calcium score would help clarify things. That conversation should settle whether a statin is worthwhile for you.

Basically, communism is a way of running a society where everybody works together and shares what they make. The government owns the stuff used to produce things, like factories, farms, and offices, and there's no private property. Houses, cars, even phones would technically belong to everyone, at least in the pure version of the idea.

The thinking is that everybody should be equal, so nobody gets left out and nobody ends up with way more than anyone else. The goal is a society where everyone has what they need and there's no real divide between rich and poor. The government plans how the country's resources get used, and people work together to make what the country needs. It also provides education, healthcare, and other services.

In theory, that means everyone gets an equal shot at succeeding, and nobody has to worry about going hungry or skipping the doctor because they can't afford it.

In practice, though, communist governments have run into a lot of problems and haven't always done well. Some people say it just can't work because it goes against human nature, since folks aren't really willing to share equally. Others say it failed because it was carried out badly, or because other countries worked against it and tried to crush it.

Severe toothaches at night can come from a few different things. The most common is a cavity, those little holes that form when plaque and bacteria build up. They tend to hurt more at night because you produce less saliva while you sleep, and saliva is what normally helps neutralize the acid bacteria make. An infection is another possibility. Bacteria can get into the tooth through a cavity or a crack and settle into the tooth or the gum around it. Gum disease can do it too. That's an infection of the gums that causes inflammation and pain in the teeth and gums. Then there's tooth grinding, or bruxism, which a lot of people do without knowing it, usually while asleep. Grinding can leave your teeth sore enough to ache all night. Finally, trauma like a chipped or cracked tooth can absolutely hurt, especially when you lie down. If the pain is bad, get to a dentist as soon as you can. They can figure out what's actually going on and fix it, whether that means a filling, treating an infection, or repairing a broken tooth. Until then, an over-the-counter painkiller can take the edge off.
