Think of sound loudness like a ruler where zero doesn't mean "no sound at all." It just means "the quietest sound a normal person can barely hear." Scientists picked that spot as the starting line, the way we pick a spot on a thermometer and call it zero degrees. Zero degrees doesn't mean there's no heat, and zero decibels doesn't mean there's no sound.

So when a room is at minus nine decibels, it means the room is even quieter than the quietest thing a person can normally hear. Just like a day can be below zero degrees outside, a room can be below the "barely hearable" line. There is still a tiny bit of sound in there, such as air molecules jiggling around, but it's too faint for your ears to notice.

Decibels are also a special kind of measuring stick. Instead of counting up one, two, three, each step up means the sound is a lot stronger, roughly ten times more energy for every ten decibels. Going the other way, minus ten would mean ten times less energy than the zero starting point. So a negative number just means "a fraction of that starting amount," which is perfectly fine for this kind of math.

How do we measure it? We use a very sensitive microphone connected to a machine called a sound level meter. The microphone feels the tiny pushes of air that make up sound, and the machine turns those pushes into a number. For a super quiet room, the microphone has to be extra special, because ordinary ones make their own little hiss that would drown out the quiet. The room itself is built with thick walls, springs, and foam wedges that soak up sound, so almost nothing from outside gets in and nothing bounces around inside.

The "A" in dBA just means the machine pays more attention to the sounds that human ears are good at hearing and less to ones we can't hear well, so the number matches what a person would actually experience.

One fun side effect is that in such a quiet room, people start to hear their own heartbeat, their breathing, and even their stomach gurgling, because there's nothing else to listen to.

Historical price-to-earnings (P/E) ratios for small-cap and large-cap shares can fluctuate considerably across different periods, and comparing them directly can be misleading because the two groups differ in fundamental ways. Companies with a market value under $2 billion are classified as small-cap, and they generally carry more risk and price swings than large-cap companies, which are valued at $10 billion or more. Because of this, investors may accept a higher price relative to earnings in exchange for the expansion potential that small-caps offer, pushing their P/E ratios upward. Large-cap companies, by contrast, are usually more mature and steady, with longer histories of growing profits and revenue. Consequently, their P/E ratios often run lower, since investors are less inclined to pay a premium for growth that is already more predictable. P/E ratios should not be judged on their own, however. A company's financial strength, industry conditions, and broader economic climate also shape its P/E ratio and should be weighed alongside it.

The Lord of the Rings is a fantasy novel by J.R.R. Tolkien, and it came out in three volumes across 1954 and 1955. It follows a hobbit named Frodo Baggins who has to destroy the One Ring. That's a seriously powerful, nasty piece of work that the Dark Lord Sauron made so he could conquer and enslave everybody in Middle-earth. It's easily one of the most popular fantasy books out there, and it's held up for decades. People have turned it into tons of films, TV series, and other stuff too.

Okay so a "crypto mule" is basically someone who gets paid to move crypto from one place to another, and it's usually part of a bigger scheme to steal or launder money. Scammers tend to recruit these people with a job offer or some other sales pitch, and most of the time the mule has no clue they're part of anything illegal. The name comes from the idea that they're a middleman or go-between, hauling funds from point A to point B without really knowing what's going on. They might be told they're just moving money for some legit business, when the funds are actually stolen or dirty. Here's the thing though: even if you didn't know, acting as a mule is still a serious crime and can land you in real legal trouble. So if a job or business opportunity smells off, look into it carefully before you agree to anything.

Living in a damp house can affect health, and what you describe is worth taking seriously. Mouldy clothes and a musty smell in the wardrobes mean mould is growing somewhere in your home, even if you can't see it on the walls. Mould releases spores and tiny fragments, along with volatile compounds that cause the smell, and these get breathed in and settle on skin. Damp also encourages dust mites, which are a major trigger for allergy and eczema.

The main health effects of damp and mould are respiratory. People commonly get a persistent cough, wheezing, a tight chest, a blocked or runny nose, sore throat and watery or itchy eyes. Damp housing is linked in research to a higher risk of developing asthma, and to making existing asthma worse. In some people mould exposure can cause allergic reactions or irritation without any history of asthma, so a cough lasting weeks that you can't shake is quite consistent with it, though many other things can cause that too, including lingering viral infections, postnasal drip, reflux, and some medications. Because it has gone on for several weeks, it is sensible to see your GP, who can check your chest and rule out other causes. Seek help sooner if you have breathlessness, coughing up blood, chest pain, fever, night sweats or unexplained weight loss.

For your daughter, the link with eczema is plausible but not straightforward. Eczema is driven mainly by skin barrier problems and genetics, but flare-ups are often triggered by environmental factors. Dust mites thrive in damp, warm homes, and mould exposure has been associated with worse eczema in some children. Smelly, mouldy clothes against the skin may also irritate it. It is unlikely to be the only cause, but reducing damp could help her symptoms, and it is worth mentioning the damp to her doctor or dermatologist so they can consider allergy triggers and review her treatment.

Children, older people, those with eczema or asthma, and anyone with a weakened immune system are most affected. Healthy adults usually have milder symptoms, though they can still be unpleasant.

There are practical steps you can take. Find the source of the moisture, since it could be a leak, rising or penetrating damp, condensation from poor ventilation, or drying laundry indoors. Wardrobes against external walls are often a hotspot. Pull furniture a few inches from walls, leave wardrobe doors open sometimes, and avoid overfilling them. Ventilate daily, use extractor fans when cooking and bathing, and avoid drying clothes on radiators if you can. A dehumidifier can help keep indoor humidity around 40 to 60 percent, and a cheap hygrometer will show you the level. Wash mouldy clothes hot where fabric allows, or dry-clean them, and discard anything badly affected. Wipe small areas of mould with detergent and water rather than stirring it up, and avoid dry brushing.

If you rent, your landlord is responsible for fixing the underlying damp and you should report it in writing, keeping photos and a record of your health problems. In the UK, your council's environmental health team can inspect if the landlord doesn't act. If you own the home, a damp specialist or surveyor can identify the cause, since treating the symptoms without fixing the source usually means it returns.

I can't say for certain that damp is behind your cough or your daughter's eczema, but it is a reasonable suspect and worth addressing for both. Raise it with your GP when you go about the cough.

A surname is basically the family name, the one that gets handed down from generation to generation. A given name is the personal one you get at birth or when you're pretty young. People also call it a first name or a forename, depending on where they're from. In a lot of cultures the surname goes last and tells you which family or bigger social group someone belongs to. The given name is what people actually use when they're talking to you or about you. Take "John Smith" for example. John's the given name, Smith's the surname. Not everybody does it in that order, though. Some cultures put the surname first and the given name after it.

Try not to worry too much, because this is a very common situation and it rarely prevents an MRI. Most orthognathic hardware from the mid-1990s was titanium, and titanium is not ferromagnetic, so it is generally considered MR conditional or safe. Titanium plates and screws for jaw surgery were in wide use by then, having largely replaced older stainless steel systems through the late 1980s and 1990s. Some surgeons still used stainless steel in that era, and some used wires or other fixation, so it isn't guaranteed, but titanium is the most likely answer. Even stainless steel implants of this type are usually weakly magnetic and are commonly scanned without trouble, though they can cause image distortion near the metal.

There are a few practical ways to find out. The most reliable is to request your operative report from the surgeon or the hospital where you had the surgery. Operative notes usually name the fixation system and manufacturer, and sometimes list the implant lot numbers. Hospitals are generally required to keep records for a long time, though 1996 records may be in archives and take a few weeks to retrieve. If your surgeon has retired, the hospital's medical records department should still be able to help. Your oral surgeon's office or orthodontist may also have notes or images on file.

Another option is imaging. A panoramic dental X-ray or a CT of the face can show the number, size, and position of the plates and screws. Radiologists can often tell a lot from the appearance, though X-rays cannot definitively identify the metal alloy. If you tell the MRI facility about the hardware, the radiologist can review any prior imaging and decide whether it is acceptable.

Most importantly, tell the MRI center now, well ahead of your appointment, so they can sort it out. They will have you complete a screening form, and they may ask for the records or an X-ray. Facilities commonly scan patients with jaw hardware, especially when it is titanium. For a breast MRI, the area of interest is far from your jaw, so any image distortion from the hardware would be unlikely to affect the study, and heating risk is minimal with non-ferromagnetic implants.

If the records can't be found, the radiology team can still make a judgment based on an X-ray and the known low risk of these implants. Don't postpone or cancel the MRI on your own. Call the imaging center, explain the surgery, and let them guide you through the next steps.

Okay, so in physics, a configuration space is basically the set of every possible arrangement a system can be in: positions, shapes, orientations, all of it. It's an abstract math space that packs in where all the particles could be. It shows up a lot in classical mechanics for describing how a bunch of particles move. Take a single particle zipping around in 3D space. Its configuration space is just 3D space itself, and each point is one possible spot the particle could sit. Things get more interesting with more particles. Two particles in 3D would need six dimensions, since each point in that space tells you where both of them are. Quantum mechanics uses the idea too, though people often call it the "Hilbert space" or "state space" there. Either way, it's a handy tool for figuring out how physical systems behave, and it comes up all over physics.

A PC is basically a computer built for one person to use, whether it's a desktop sitting on your desk or a laptop you carry around. People use them for all sorts of things: typing up documents, surfing the web, gaming, keeping track of their bank stuff. At the heart of it is a microprocessor, the CPU, which runs instructions and does the number crunching. It's not alone in there, though. You've also got memory (RAM), storage like a hard drive or SSD, a monitor, and the keyboard and mouse you use to control everything. Plenty of them come with extras too, like a touchscreen, a webcam, or built-in speakers.

I cannot determine what is causing your symptoms without more details and a physical exam, so it is essential that you see a healthcare provider for a thorough assessment and proper care. Severe stomach pain and a reduced appetite may stem from many possible problems, such as digestive disorders, infections, or hormone-related changes. Headaches and absent menstrual periods can likewise arise from numerous sources, and pinpointing the root cause is necessary before any suitable treatment can be chosen. Keep in mind that some of your symptoms, including skipped periods and food sensitivities, may point to pregnancy. Taking a pregnancy test and discussing the results with a medical professional is an important step in ruling this out.

Similarity learning is a branch of machine learning concerned with learning a function that measures how similar or related two objects are. Instead of predicting a class label or a numeric value for a single input, the model takes a pair (or sometimes a triplet or larger group) of inputs and outputs a score indicating how alike they are. The objects can be images, text passages, audio clips, user profiles, molecules, or anything else that can be represented in a numerical form.

The motivation is that many practical problems are really about comparison rather than classification. Face verification asks whether two photos show the same person. Recommendation systems ask which items resemble ones a user liked. Search engines ask which documents are closest to a query. In these settings the set of possible classes may be huge, constantly changing, or unknown in advance, so a standard classifier is awkward. A learned similarity function can generalize to new identities or categories never seen during training, which is why it is often associated with few-shot and one-shot learning.

There are several common formulations. In metric learning, the goal is to learn a distance function, such as a Mahalanobis distance, so that similar items are close together and dissimilar ones are far apart. In representation or embedding learning, a neural network maps each input to a vector, and similarity is computed with a simple measure like cosine similarity or Euclidean distance in that embedding space. Training usually relies on labels indicating whether pairs are similar or not, or on ranking information such as "A is more similar to B than to C."

Typical architectures and losses reflect this. Siamese networks use two identical networks with shared weights to embed both inputs. Contrastive loss pulls matching pairs together and pushes non-matching pairs apart beyond a margin. Triplet loss uses an anchor, a positive example, and a negative example, requiring the anchor to be closer to the positive than to the negative by some margin. More recent approaches, such as contrastive self-supervised methods (SimCLR, CLIP and similar), learn similarity without manual labels by treating different views or paired modalities of the same item as positives and other items as negatives.

Challenges include choosing good negative examples, since easy negatives teach little and overly hard ones can destabilize training, as well as defining what "similar" means for a given task, since similarity is often subjective or context-dependent. Scalability matters too, because comparing every pair is expensive, which is why embeddings are often combined with approximate nearest neighbor search.

Applications include face and fingerprint recognition, image and product retrieval, semantic text search, duplicate detection, recommendation, drug discovery, and clustering.

HSBC Hong Kong's Deposit Plus is a dual currency investment, a short-term structured product that HSBC markets alongside its time deposits. Despite the name, it is not a deposit. It is an investment product, it is not protected by the Hong Kong Deposit Protection Scheme, and your principal is not guaranteed in its original currency. You place funds in a base currency, such as Hong Kong dollars, US dollars, or Australian dollars, and choose a linked or alternate currency together with a conversion rate, often called the strike. In exchange you receive a higher interest rate than an ordinary time deposit of similar length. Tenors are usually short, often one week to a few months, and HSBC sets a minimum investment that you should confirm on its current product page or with a branch, since thresholds and available currency pairs change.

At maturity, the outcome depends on where the exchange rate stands relative to the conversion rate on the fixing date. If the base currency has not weakened past the strike against the linked currency, you get your principal back in the base currency plus the enhanced interest. If it has, the bank converts your principal and interest into the linked currency at the pre-agreed strike, which will be worse than the prevailing market rate at that moment. In effect you have sold the bank a currency option, and the extra yield is the premium for that option. The upside is capped at the stated interest, while the downside can be substantial if the linked currency falls sharply against your base currency, because you end up holding the weaker currency at an unfavourable rate. Returns are fixed at the outset, early withdrawal is generally not allowed or is costly, and the bank's pricing includes a margin, so the yield you receive is less than the full theoretical option value.

The most important strategy is to pair only currencies you would genuinely be content to hold. Deposit Plus works best for someone who already has a future need for the linked currency, such as tuition in Australia, property in the UK, or regular travel or business costs in renminbi or US dollars. For that person, being converted is not a loss but simply a way to acquire the currency they wanted at a price they chose, while earning extra yield if conversion doesn't happen. Following from this, set the conversion rate at a level you would be happy to transact at anyway, almost like placing a limit order that pays you interest while you wait. A strike close to the current spot rate pays more but makes conversion more likely, while a strike further away pays less but offers a larger buffer. Choosing between them is really a choice about how much conversion risk you want to accept for each extra percentage point of yield.

Short tenors are usually wiser for most investors because they limit exposure to large moves, let you reassess frequently, and allow you to adjust strikes as the market changes. Some investors stagger several placements across different maturities and strikes so that no single fixing date determines their whole outcome. Pay attention to the economic calendar, since central bank decisions, inflation releases, and elections can cause sharp currency moves. The higher quoted yields around such events reflect higher volatility rather than a free gift. It also helps to compare the Deposit Plus yield with what you could earn from a plain time deposit in either currency. If the premium over the higher of the two is small, the risk may not be worth taking.

If you do get converted, avoid automatically converting back at a loss. Many users instead place the new currency into a Deposit Plus that is linked back to the original currency, with a strike near or better than their earlier rate, effectively "wheeling" between two currencies while collecting yield. This only makes sense if both currencies are ones you are comfortable holding for a while. Finally, keep emergency funds and money needed by a fixed date in a specific currency out of the product, and don't commit more than you could tolerate seeing converted. Understand the Hong Kong dollar's peg to the US dollar, which makes HKD and USD pairings low-yield because there is little volatility. Read the term sheet and the bank's risk disclosures carefully, as HSBC will typically require a suitability and risk-profile assessment before you invest. Because terms, rates, and eligibility change, confirm current details directly with HSBC, and consider independent financial advice if you are unsure whether the product fits your circumstances.

Okay so the learning rate is basically a hyperparameter that tells the optimizer how big a step to take when it updates the model's parameters. It's a big deal in neural network training because it controls how fast the model learns, or how slow. You usually pick it before training starts and then leave it alone. Bigger learning rate means bigger updates each step, smaller means smaller nudges.

There are a few ways people go about setting it. You can just pick a fixed number and hope for the best, but that's tricky since the ideal value can change a lot depending on your model and data. Way more common is using a learning rate schedule, where the rate changes over time, often based on how the model is doing. A typical pattern is to start high and then taper off as training goes on.

Picking a good one matters. Too high and the model can blow up and diverge, too low and training crawls along and wastes your time. Getting that balance right is pretty much the whole game when you're training a model.

Drug design, sometimes called rational drug design, is the practice of discovering and creating new medicines on the basis of detailed knowledge of a biological target. The idea is to maximize a drug's therapeutic value while keeping its possible harmful effects as low as possible. Scientists rely on several methods, including computer modeling, to work out how the target is built and how it functions, and to pinpoint candidate compounds that will interact with it in a precise, intended manner. The aim is to create a molecule that attaches to the target so that it either switches the target's activity on or shuts it down, according to the therapeutic outcome being sought. After a promising candidate has been found, it goes through a sequence of preclinical studies and clinical trials that assess its safety, effectiveness, and likely side effects. When the candidate proves both safe and effective, it can receive approval to be used as a medicine. Ultimately, drug design is meant to produce new, effective therapies for many different diseases and health conditions, among them cancer, infections, heart and blood vessel disease, and disorders of the nervous system.

Dealing with student loan debt collectors depends a lot on whether your loans are federal or private, so the first step is figuring out which kind you have. Federal loans are held by the Department of Education or its contractors, and private loans are held by banks or private lenders. You can check your federal loans at StudentAid.gov, and your credit report at AnnualCreditReport.com will show both types.

If you have federal loans, you have more options than you might expect. You can ask for an income-driven repayment plan, which sets your monthly payment based on your income and family size and can bring it to zero if your income is low. You may also qualify for deferment or forbearance if you are facing financial hardship, or for loan rehabilitation, which involves making a series of on-time payments to bring a defaulted loan back into good standing and remove the default from your credit history. Consolidation is another option, though it can reset some progress toward forgiveness. Some borrowers qualify for Public Service Loan Forgiveness or Teacher Loan Forgiveness if they work in qualifying jobs. Federal collectors must follow the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act, so you can tell them in writing to stop contacting you at work or to communicate only in writing, and they cannot harass you or misrepresent the debt.

If your loans are private, your options are more limited but still real. You can ask the lender about hardship programs, reduced interest rates, or temporary forbearance. You can also consider refinancing if your credit has improved. Like all debt collectors, private collectors are covered by the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act, so you can request written validation of the debt, which requires them to prove the amount and that they have the right to collect it. If the debt is not what they claim, you can dispute it in writing.

Whatever type of loan you have, avoid ignoring the calls and letters, because the debt can lead to wage garnishment or tax refund offsets, and the collector may sue. It is also wise to be cautious of companies that promise to fix your loans for an upfront fee, since legitimate help with federal loans is free through StudentAid.gov. If your situation is complicated, a nonprofit credit counselor or a student loan attorney can review your specific case, and your state attorney general's office can help if you believe a collector has broken the law.

A sociopath is a person whose brain works a little differently when it comes to feelings about other people. Most of us feel a kind of invisible tug inside when we hurt someone, like a tummy ache of guilt that makes us want to say sorry and do better. A sociopath usually doesn't feel that tug very strongly, or sometimes hardly at all. They know the rules, like "don't take your friend's toy," but the rules feel more like suggestions to them, and breaking them doesn't make them feel bad the way it would for you. Doctors don't actually use the word "sociopath" much anymore; they usually call it "antisocial personality disorder," but people still say sociopath in everyday talk.

Some common things you might notice are that they lie a lot, even about small things, and don't seem bothered when they get caught. They often break rules or promises over and over. They might be very charming, like the kid on the playground who is super fun and says all the nice things, but who is really being nice because they want your snacks. They can get angry quickly, do risky things without thinking, and blame everyone else when something goes wrong. When someone is sad or hurt, they might not seem to care, or they might pretend to care because they've learned that's what people expect. They also tend to use people like tools to get what they want, and then lose interest once they've gotten it.

Can you spot one easily? Usually not. That's one of the tricky parts. Many sociopaths are good at acting normal, and some are even extra friendly and likable at first, so you can't tell just by looking at someone or talking to them once. It's a bit like a cake that looks yummy on the outside, and you only find out what's inside after a while. The best clue is to watch what a person does over a long time instead of what they say. If someone keeps lying, keeps hurting people, never says sorry and means it, and always makes it someone else's fault, that's a pattern worth paying attention to.

It's also important to remember that everyone fibs sometimes, everyone gets grumpy, and everyone is a little selfish now and then. That doesn't make them a sociopath. Only a doctor who knows a lot about how minds work can really say if someone has this condition, and even then it takes careful checking. So the grown-up lesson is simple: you don't need to label people, but if someone keeps treating you badly and never feels sorry, it's okay to keep your distance and stay safe.

Brain zaps are a common discontinuation symptom. They are brief, electric-feeling jolts that happen when the brain is adjusting to a drop in serotonin activity, and they are most common with SSRIs like citalopram (Celexa), especially when the dose falls quickly. Your recent symptoms probably have several overlapping causes. Cutting Celexa from 40 mg to 20 mg is a sizable change, and stopping both medications for two days can bring on withdrawal effects such as anxiety, irritability, restlessness, sweating, chills, nausea, and flu-like aches. Those withdrawal symptoms can look a lot like a cold, and the cold itself can make anxiety worse. Wellbutrin can also cause jitteriness or anxiety in some people, and stopping it can unmask or add to those feelings. Your zaps easing is a good sign, but it doesn't mean the medication change is finished being felt.

I would not simply push through this on your own. Stopping both medications abruptly, and then continuing to stop them, can make withdrawal harder to manage and can make it harder to tell what is causing what. Please call your prescriber or a pharmacist today. Tell them what you have described: the dose change, the cold, the two days off both medications, and the anxiety. They can tell you whether to restart at a dose that's easier on you, how to taper more slowly, and whether your cold needs to be checked. Don't restart or change doses on your own without that guidance, because the right step depends on your history.

Slow breathing, rest, fluids, and reducing caffeine can help with anxiety in the meantime. Seek urgent care or call emergency services if you have chest pain, fainting, confusion, trouble breathing, a high fever that won't come down, or any thoughts of harming yourself. If you have thoughts of suicide or feel unsafe, contact a crisis line or emergency services right away.

A process calculus, sometimes called a process algebra, is a family of formal mathematical languages used to describe and reason about concurrent systems, meaning systems made up of many independent components that run at the same time and interact with one another. Where ordinary programming languages and classical models like the lambda calculus focus on sequential computation, process calculi focus on communication, synchronization, and the way separate processes affect each other over time. They give computer scientists a precise, compact notation for writing down how a system behaves and a set of rules for proving things about that behavior.

The central idea is that a system is built from processes, which are abstract agents that perform actions. Most process calculi share a small core of operators for combining processes. Sequential composition or action prefixing lets you say that a process performs some action and then continues as another process. Parallel composition lets you place two processes side by side so they run concurrently. Communication is usually modeled through named channels, where one process sends a message on a channel and another receives it, and the two synchronize at that moment. Choice lets a process behave in one of several ways depending on which action becomes possible. Restriction or hiding lets you make a channel private so that only certain processes can use it. Recursion or replication allows processes to repeat behavior indefinitely, which is essential for modeling servers, protocols, and other long-running systems.

Several well-known process calculi emerged in the late 1970s and 1980s. Robin Milner developed the Calculus of Communicating Systems, known as CCS. Tony Hoare created Communicating Sequential Processes, known as CSP, which strongly influenced practical languages such as Occam and later the concurrency model of Go. Jan Bergstra and Jan Willem Klop developed the Algebra of Communicating Processes, ACP. Milner, together with Joachim Parrow and David Walker, later introduced the pi-calculus, which added the powerful ability to pass channel names themselves as messages, allowing the structure of communication between processes to change dynamically. This made it suitable for modeling mobile systems and networks whose connections evolve over time. Many variants followed, including the ambient calculus for mobility across locations, the spi calculus for cryptographic protocols, and stochastic calculi for modeling biological systems.

A key concern in process calculi is deciding when two processes should be considered equivalent. Because concurrent systems can interleave and branch in complicated ways, simply comparing outputs is not enough. Researchers developed notions such as bisimulation, which says two processes are equivalent if each can match every step the other takes while remaining equivalent afterward, as well as trace equivalence and testing equivalences. These equivalences let one prove that an implementation correctly matches a specification, or that replacing one component with another will not change the observable behavior of a larger system.

Process calculi have practical value in verifying communication protocols, security protocols, distributed algorithms, and hardware designs, and they underpin tools for model checking and formal verification. They have also influenced the design of programming languages and type systems for concurrency, such as session types, which use ideas from process calculi to guarantee that communicating programs follow agreed-upon protocols. In short, a process calculus is to concurrent and interacting systems roughly what the lambda calculus is to functions: a minimal, rigorous foundation for describing and reasoning about how such systems compute.

Yeah, banks can require pre-approval for a checking account, or keep a kind of white-list of who's allowed to open one. With pre-approval, you have to apply and get the okay before you can actually open the account. That usually means handing over personal and financial info like your Social Security number, where you work, and proof of income. The bank looks it over and decides yes or no.

A white-list is basically a list of people who are cleared to open an account at that particular bank. To get on it, you'd typically need to meet certain requirements, like a decent credit score, steady income, or whatever else the bank sets. If your name isn't on the list, you're out of luck at that bank. Not every bank works this way, though, so don't assume. Shop around and compare what different accounts offer and what they require before you settle on one.

The Bellman equation is a mathematical expression that captures the dynamic programming approach to certain optimization problems. Richard Bellman, who developed dynamic programming in the 1950s, is the namesake of the equation. Under this approach, a problem is divided into smaller subproblems, each subproblem is solved, and the answers are then merged to produce the overall best solution. The equation is central to this method because it lets the optimal value of a subproblem be written in terms of the optimal values of smaller subproblems. Its general form is V(S) = max[R(S,A) + γV(S')]. In this expression, V(S) denotes the value of being in state S, R(S,A) is the reward received for performing action A in state S, γ is a discount factor that sets how much weight future rewards carry, and V(S') is the value of the successor state S' reached by taking action A in state S. The "max" signifies that the goal is to find the largest possible V(S) by evaluating every action A available in state S. Bellman's equation applies to a broad range of optimization problems across economics, control theory, and machine learning. It is especially well suited to sequential decision-making, where the best choice at each stage hinges on the choices made earlier.

Transcendentalism is a philosophical and literary movement that began in the United States during the early 1800s. Its core ideas include self-reliance, individualism, the natural goodness of both people and the natural world, and the value of intuition and personal growth. Individualism shares some of this ground, since it too stresses the significance of the individual along with a person's rights and freedoms. Transcendentalism, though, reaches further than simply prizing the individual. It also focuses on the spiritual and transcendent side of human experience, including the bond between a person and the divine, or between a person and the universe as a whole. Picture yourself as a small boat drifting on a broad, open river. Individualism is about steering your own boat and making your own choices. Transcendentalism asks you not only to steer your boat but also to feel connected to everything around you, such as the river, the trees, and the sky. It means looking past your own experiences and wants to discover a deeper purpose in life.

Amitriptyline is generally considered one of the better-studied tricyclic antidepressants in pregnancy, and there is no strong evidence that it causes birth defects or that taking it through pregnancy is dangerous. Many obstetric and psychiatric guidelines treat continuing it as reasonable, especially when stopping would risk a relapse of anxiety or depression. So the fact that you've taken it throughout your pregnancy is not in itself a cause for alarm.

The reason some clinicians suggest stopping near delivery is that babies exposed to tricyclics late in pregnancy can occasionally show temporary withdrawal or adaptation symptoms after birth, such as jitteriness, irritability, feeding difficulty, or trouble settling. These are usually mild and short-lived, and the baby is simply monitored. Because of this, some teams prefer to lower the dose before delivery, while others advise staying on it, since an abrupt stop can cause problems for you. Either approach can be legitimate, but the decision should be made with your care team, not by guessing.

What concerns me is that you stopped suddenly after four years at 50mg. Abrupt discontinuation can cause discontinuation symptoms: insomnia, vivid dreams, nausea, headaches, restlessness, flu-like feelings, and a rebound of anxiety. Your sleep trouble may well be that. Poor sleep and a surge of anxiety right before labor are also not ideal for you.

My practical advice is not to settle this on your own, but also not to sit with it. Contact your midwife, obstetrician, or the maternity unit's advice line today, since they are available around the clock at 39 weeks, and tell them exactly what you told me: you stopped two nights ago and are now struggling to sleep. Ask whether you should restart the 50mg, or taper, and ask them to flag it to the pediatric team so they know to watch the baby for any adaptation symptoms. Your prescriber or pharmacist can also advise quickly.

Restarting it in the meantime is commonly what clinicians recommend when someone has stopped abruptly and is having symptoms, but I'd get that confirmation from someone who has your full chart. If you cannot reach anyone and are feeling quite unwell, go to the maternity assessment unit. Also seek help promptly if your anxiety or mood worsens significantly, or you have any thoughts of harming yourself.

You haven't done anything wrong by staying on your medication. Being well and rested matters for both you and your baby.

Thank you for describing this so clearly. What you are experiencing is a fear response that has become attached to many different everyday situations: buildings, new people, riding a bike, the movement of a fan, lifts, and showrooms. When fear spreads like this and lasts for a year, it is usually an anxiety condition, most often a set of specific phobias or an anxiety disorder with avoidance. It is not a sign of weakness or of madness, and it is very treatable. Anxiety of this kind often works like an alarm that rings at the wrong times. The brain learns to treat harmless things as dangerous, and each time you avoid them, the fear becomes stronger.

The most useful fact here is that you have not yet found relief with treatment. That may mean the treatment so far has been only tablets, or that it was not matched to this kind of problem. The most effective treatment for these fears is usually cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT), which includes gradual exposure: step by step, you face the feared situation while using calming skills, until your brain learns that it is safe. Medicines such as certain antidepressants can reduce the baseline anxiety and make this therapy easier, but they work best combined with therapy. I would suggest asking your doctor directly for a referral to a psychiatrist or a clinical psychologist who treats anxiety and phobias, and telling them exactly what you told me: the list of fears, how long they have lasted, and that previous treatment has not helped.

While you arrange that, there are some things you can start doing yourself. When fear rises, slow your breathing so that the out-breath is longer than the in-breath, and remind yourself that the feeling will peak and then pass, usually within a few minutes. Avoid the situations completely only when you truly must; in small, planned steps, approach one mildly uncomfortable thing a day, such as standing near a building entrance or watching a fan from a distance, and stay until the fear drops a little. Cut back on caffeine, tea and coffee, energy drinks, and alcohol, since these often increase anxiety. Keep regular sleep and meal times. It would also help to have your physical health checked, including thyroid function, blood sugar, haemoglobin, and heart rhythm, because some of these problems can cause or worsen anxiety.

If at any point the fear turns into sudden panic with chest pain, breathlessness, or feeling you might faint, or if you have thoughts of harming yourself, please get medical help urgently. In India you can call Tele-MANAS at 14416 or 1-800-891-4416 at any time for free, confidential support.

Ovex is a drug prescribed for threadworms, sometimes called pinworms. Its active ingredient, mebendazole, stops the worms from producing energy, which leads to their death. Following the directions on the Ovex packaging closely and giving the proper amount matters a great deal. Typically, a single dose is advised, and the medicine should not be taken for more than three days in a row. If your child has received one dose and still has symptoms after a few days, you should consult a healthcare provider for further guidance. Ovex usually kills threadworms within a few days, but symptoms can take several weeks to fully disappear, since the body still has to eliminate the dead worms and eggs. During this time, good hygiene, such as frequent handwashing and keeping the affected area clean, helps stop the infection from spreading. If you have concerns about your child's symptoms or questions about using Ovex, speak with a healthcare professional, who can recommend the most suitable treatment based on your child's individual situation.

In an artichoke, the seeds are not in a spot you would normally notice, because the part people eat is actually an immature flower bud. The structures that would become seeds sit at the base of the bud, in the area known as the heart, underneath the fuzzy, hairy fibers called the choke.

If you cut an artichoke open and pull away the tough outer leaves, you reach the thistle-like choke covering the top of the heart. Each of those hairs is part of an individual tiny floret, and each floret has an ovary at its base that would develop into a seed (technically a small fruit called an achene) if the bud were left to mature. In a mature plant that has been allowed to flower, the bud opens into a large purple-blue bloom, and the seeds form at the base of the florets, much like the seeds of a sunflower or thistle.

In a store-bought, harvested artichoke, the seeds are still undeveloped, so you generally see only the fuzzy choke, which is scraped out with a spoon before eating the heart. If you want actual seeds for planting, you let the artichoke bloom and dry on the plant, then collect the hard seeds from the base of the dried flower head.

Machine perception refers to a machine's capacity to make sense of sensory input from its surroundings, including visual images, audio, and other signals. It relies on artificial intelligence methods, such as machine learning and deep learning, which allow machines to detect patterns, categorize objects and occurrences, and reach conclusions from that information. Its aim is to let machines comprehend the world around them in a manner resembling human perception. This capability supports many applications, such as image and speech recognition, natural language processing, and autonomous robotics. Achieving it is difficult, since machines must process and interpret vast quantities of data accurately, adjust to shifting conditions, and decide quickly as events unfold. For these reasons, machine perception remains a vibrant research topic in both artificial intelligence and robotics.

A thigh gap is a space between the upper parts of your two thighs when you stand with your feet together and your legs touching at the knees. Some people see it as a sign of being very thin, and that's a big part of why it caught on.

People find it attractive mostly because it became a trend, not because most people have a natural preference for it. Trends like this often spread because they're easy to picture and easy to copy. Around the early 2010s, social media sites like Tumblr, Instagram, and Pinterest made it simple to share photos of bodies with a particular look, and posts about thigh gaps spread quickly. Once a lot of people were talking about it, it started to seem like something everyone wanted, even though it was really just a popular idea.

It also got attention because of how it was framed. Some online communities promoted extreme dieting and presented a thigh gap as a goal to chase, which worried doctors and body-image experts. Many of them point out that a thigh gap depends mostly on bone structure, like the width of your hips and pelvis, not just on how much you weigh. So lots of people who are healthy and fit simply won't have one, and trying to get one can lead to unhealthy habits.

So it became popular because it was a visible, easy-to-share image that got passed around a lot online, not because it reflects a universal standard of beauty. Plenty of people never cared about it, and fashion and attitudes about bodies keep changing.

Upper belly pain that gets worse when you cough, laugh, or sneeze could come from a few different things. One common culprit is just a strained or spasming abdominal muscle, since all that coughing or laughing puts extra stress on those muscles. Gastroenteritis is another possibility. That's inflammation of the digestive tract, usually from a virus or bacteria, and it can bring pain along with nausea and vomiting. Gallbladder problems, like gallstones, can also cause upper abdominal pain, especially after you've eaten. And then there's pancreatitis, which is inflammation of the pancreas and can cause pain plus nausea and vomiting. Honestly, though, you really should see a healthcare provider to figure out what's going on. They can examine you, run some tests if needed, and help you get a diagnosis and a plan.

Starting a side business slowly is one of the smartest ways to do it, because it lets you learn what works without risking your income or burning out. Here is how I would approach it.

Begin by picking an idea that fits skills you already have and problems you can see people paying to solve. Talk to five or ten potential customers before you spend money. Ask what they currently do, what frustrates them, and what they would pay for. If nobody shows interest in a conversation, they probably won't show it at a checkout page either.

Next, set a small and sustainable time commitment, perhaps five to eight hours a week, and protect it on your calendar like an appointment. Consistency matters far more than intensity. Many people start with a burst of energy, exhaust themselves in a month, and quit. A modest weekly rhythm can carry you for years.

Then test the idea in the cheapest way possible. Offer the service to one or two people, sell a handful of products, or put up a simple one-page site describing the offer. The goal is to earn your first dollar quickly, since that proves someone values what you do. Don't spend time on logos, business cards, or elaborate branding until you have that proof.

Keep the admin simple but not neglected. Check whether your employer's contract limits outside work or competing activity. Look into the registration, tax, and licensing rules where you live, and open a separate bank account so the business money stays distinct from personal funds. Track income and expenses from day one, even in a basic spreadsheet. Setting aside a portion of earnings for taxes will save you stress later.

For example, after six months you might ask whether you are earning a steady amount, enjoying the work, and seeing growth. Ezekiel was a priest and prophet in the Hebrew Bible who lived in the sixth century BCE. He was among the Jews deported to Babylon during the Babylonian exile, around 597 BCE, and he received his prophetic call while living by the Chebar River in Babylonia, in a vision of God's glory that he describes at the start of the book that bears his name.

His ministry, recorded in the Book of Ezekiel, spans roughly 593 to 571 BCE. Much of his message concerns the reasons for Judah's fall and Jerusalem's destruction in 586 BCE, which he presents as the consequence of Israel's idolatry and unfaithfulness. He also delivers messages of hope, including the famous vision of the valley of dry bones, which symbolizes national restoration, and the closing vision of a rebuilt temple and a renewed land. Ezekiel often communicates through dramatic symbolic acts, such as lying on his side for many days or building a model of a siege.

He is also considered one of the major prophets, and his name, meaning "God strengthens" or "God will strengthen," appears in various forms in Jewish and Christian tradition.

So in an automatic, those 1, 2 and 3 settings are mostly for special situations, or sometimes for squeezing a bit more efficiency out of the car. 1st is for really low speeds, like crawling up a steep hill or trying to get some traction on a slippery surface. It sends the most power to the wheels, so the car moves off more easily in those conditions. 2nd is for slightly higher speeds, like on a flat road or when you're pulling away from a stop and accelerating. It gives the wheels a bit less power than 1st, but it's still handy for getting the car going. 3rd is for higher speeds again, say on the highway. You get less power to the wheels than in 1st or 2nd, but the car can go faster and burn less fuel while it's at it. Most of the time, though, you should just leave it in "D" (drive). That lets the transmission pick the right gear for whatever you're doing. Dropping into 1, 2 or 3 yourself can help in certain spots, but you really don't need it for everyday driving.

So the biggest stock price gain is basically how much a single stock's price went up over some stretch of time, shown as a percentage. Say a stock goes from $100 to $200. That's a 100% gain. Simple enough.

The biggest market cap gain is different. That's about the total value of all the shares a company has out there. You get market cap by multiplying the number of outstanding shares by the current price of one share. So a stock can shoot up in price and still not move the market cap much if there aren't many shares floating around. Flip it around, and a company with tons of shares could see only a small price bump and still add a huge chunk of market cap.

If you want to ask for a lower credit limit on your credit card, you can reach out to your card issuer straight away. This is usually possible by dialing the customer service number printed on the back of your card, or by signing in to your account on the web or through the issuer's mobile app. When you get in touch, let them know you're looking to reduce your credit limit. Have your name, account number, and any other identifying details ready, since the issuer may need them to find your account. Keep in mind that the issuer makes the final decision on whether to accept your request. They might lower your limit based on several considerations, including your credit score, credit history, and broader financial picture. Should your request be granted, your credit score could be affected. A lower limit may raise your credit utilization ratio, meaning the share of your total available credit that you're currently using. A high utilization ratio can hurt your credit score. Still, if you pay off your card balances in full every month, this shouldn't be a major worry.

Yes, it is possible to become pregnant while taking anti-tubercular medicine, and you should not assume that pregnancy is impossible during treatment. The good news is that the standard first-line TB drugs, including rifampicin (which Rcinex contains), isoniazid, ethambutol, and pyrazinamide, are generally considered safe in pregnancy. Untreated tuberculosis is usually more dangerous to both mother and baby than the medicines themselves, so stopping treatment because of pregnancy is not recommended. Pregnancy is not an absolute reason to avoid the drugs, but it does need careful medical supervision.

There are a few practical points to keep in mind. Rifampicin can reduce the effectiveness of oral contraceptive pills, hormonal patches, and hormonal implants, so if you rely on any of these, please discuss a backup or alternative method with your doctor. A copper IUD or condoms are not affected by rifampicin. If you do become pregnant, or think you might, tell your physician promptly so they can check your liver function and adjust monitoring, since some of these drugs can affect the liver. Your doctor may also recommend vitamin B6 supplementation during treatment.

Because you are only two months from finishing, it would be sensible to ask your physician whether it is better to wait until the course is completed and your condition is confirmed to be fully resolved before trying to conceive. Pregnancy planning is also much easier when your health status is clear. Please raise this with your doctor at your next visit so they can give advice based on your specific diagnosis and history.

Apple Computer was started in 1976 by Steve Jobs, Steve Wozniak, and Ronald Wayne. It began as a personal computer maker, but it didn't stay that way for long. Over the years it branched out into all kinds of consumer gadgets, like smartphones, tablets, music players, and smartwatches. People loved the products, and a lot of that came down to how simple and intuitive they were to use, so Apple grew into one of the biggest and most influential tech companies around. The company dropped "Computer" from its name in 2007 since computers were no longer the whole story. These days it's still a huge name in tech, with its hands in hardware, software, and services.

The sooner you report it, the better your chances of getting the money back, though recovery isn't guaranteed. If the wrong payment is returned or recovered, you can apply it to your balance, but paying the correct amount now limits the added cost. Keep records of the original payment, your communications with the bank, and any confirmation numbers so you can show what happened if the IRS asks.

If the payment was a check instead of an electronic transfer, contact your bank about stopping payment, and then send a new payment through the correct channel.

No U.S. state has fully legalized prostitution. It is illegal throughout the country, with one notable exception: certain counties in Nevada allow licensed brothels. Nevada is the only state where prostitution is legal in any form, and even there it is restricted to licensed brothels in rural counties that have opted in, while it remains illegal in Las Vegas, Reno, and Clark County, where most of the state's population lives. Brothels in those permitted counties are regulated by county and state authorities, and individual workers must obtain health cards and work within licensed facilities.

Outside the United States, several countries have taken different approaches. New Zealand decriminalized prostitution in 2003, and Australia's approach varies by state, with New South Wales and the Northern Territory decriminalizing it in some form. Germany and the Netherlands have regulated or legalized sex work in various ways, though the Netherlands has moved toward restricting some aspects in recent years. Because laws change, it's worth checking current local regulations if you need up-to-date specifics.

Ben Goertzel is an entrepreneur and researcher working in artificial intelligence (AI). He established Hanson Robotics and serves as its CEO; the company builds humanoid robots equipped with sophisticated AI. He also founded the OpenAI Research Institute and chairs it, an organization devoted to furthering AI and the ways it can be applied. Goertzel's training spans mathematics, computer science, and cognitive science, and his research centers on creating intelligent systems able to learn and adjust to unfamiliar situations. Regarded as an authority on AI, he has written many papers and articles on the topic along with several books. He is also a popular speaker, having delivered talks on AI and related subjects at conferences and events across the globe.

Imagine you have a box of shoes, but every person in the world has feet of different sizes, and sometimes their left foot is a different size than their right foot. If the shoe store only sold shoes in matching pairs, they'd need a pair for every possible combination of left and right sizes. That would be a giant, messy store. Windshield wipers are a lot like that.

On many cars, the wiper on the driver's side is a different length than the wiper on the passenger's side. One might be 26 inches and the other 16 inches. Every car model mixes and matches different lengths, so there are tons of possible combinations. If stores sold wipers only in pairs, they'd have to stock a package for every combination, which would take up huge amounts of shelf space. Selling them one at a time means the store just keeps one stack of each length, and you grab the two sizes your car needs. It's simpler for the store and makes it more likely they'll have what you need.

There are also some other reasons. Some cars have only one wiper on the front, and lots of cars have a separate wiper on the back window, often a different size again. Selling singles works for all of those. And sometimes people really do replace just one, maybe because one broke, got torn, or wears out faster. The driver's side wiper usually gets more attention because that's the side you look through, so some people replace only that one when it starts streaking.

But you're doing the normal and recommended thing. Most people, and most mechanics, replace both front wipers at the same time, because they're the same age, have been through the same sun, ice, and rain, and usually wear out at about the same pace. The single packaging isn't a hint that you should replace them one at a time. It's mostly because the sizes are often different and stores want to keep things simple.

Most people are advised to keep an emergency fund in a safe account that they can get to quickly, so they can pay for unplanned costs when they come up. High-yield checking accounts often pay more interest than standard checking accounts, but you should look closely at their terms and fees before you commit. A few points are worth weighing when you decide whether this kind of account suits your emergency fund.

Interest rate: Seek out an account with a competitive rate, and compare it against other choices so you know you're earning the best return available. Fees: Certain high-yield checking accounts charge for particular services, including ATM use or monthly maintenance. Read the fine print thoroughly so you know exactly which fees might apply. Accessibility: Confirm that you can reach your money easily and take it out without major delays or restrictions. Account stability: Pick a well-regarded financial institution that has a solid history of stability.

In general, it pays to look at several options and compare them before choosing. Speaking with a financial advisor or doing your own research could help you identify the best account for your emergency fund.

Paul Avery covered the Zodiac case for the San Francisco Chronicle back in the late '60s and early '70s. The Zodiac killer went on a string of murders up in Northern California during that stretch, and nobody ever caught him. The case is still open, and people are still arguing about it. Avery got really deep into it and spent a lot of time trying to track the guy down. The killer sent him several threatening letters, and one of them came with a piece of one of the victims' bloody shirts. Avery's reporting fed the public's obsession with the case, and it's still one of the best-known unsolved serial killer cases out there.

The Human Brain Project was a large-scale European scientific research initiative that ran from 2013 to 2023. It was one of the European Union's Future and Emerging Technologies Flagship projects, which were designed to fund ambitious, long-term research efforts with the potential for major scientific and societal impact. The project received roughly one billion euros in funding over its ten-year lifespan, shared between the European Commission and participating countries, and it involved hundreds of scientists at more than a hundred universities, hospitals, and research institutions across Europe.

The project was originally conceived by neuroscientist Henry Markram of the École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne in Switzerland, who had previously led the Blue Brain Project, an effort to build detailed computer simulations of parts of the rodent brain. His central ambition for the Human Brain Project was to use supercomputers to build a detailed digital simulation of the human brain, integrating data from many levels of biological organization, from genes and molecules up through cells, circuits, and whole-brain systems. Supporters hoped this would deepen understanding of how the brain works, help researchers study neurological and psychiatric diseases, and inspire new forms of computing modeled on the brain.

The project became controversial early on. In 2014, more than 800 neuroscientists signed an open letter criticizing its scientific direction and governance. Critics argued that the goal of simulating an entire human brain was premature given how much remained unknown about brain function, that the project had sidelined cognitive neuroscience and other experimental approaches, and that decision-making was too centralized. An independent mediation process followed, and the project was substantially restructured. Its leadership and management were reorganized, and its focus shifted away from the headline goal of a full brain simulation toward building shared research infrastructure and supporting a broader range of neuroscience.

Following these reforms, much of the project's lasting work centered on a digital research platform called EBRAINS, which provides scientists with tools, datasets, brain atlases, modeling and simulation software, and access to high-performance computing. EBRAINS has continued to operate after the project formally ended and is intended to serve as a long-term European research infrastructure for brain science. The project also produced detailed multilevel brain atlases, advanced work in neuromorphic computing through systems such as SpiNNaker in Manchester and BrainScaleS in Heidelberg, contributed to research on epilepsy and consciousness, and generated thousands of scientific publications. It also included a notable program on neuroethics, examining the social and ethical questions raised by brain research and related technologies.

In assessing its legacy, many observers regard the Human Brain Project as a mixed success. It did not come close to achieving its original promise of simulating the human brain, and its early years are often cited as a cautionary example of overpromising in large science projects. At the same time, it fostered unprecedented collaboration in European neuroscience, produced valuable data and tools, and left behind infrastructure that continues to support research. It is often discussed alongside other large national brain initiatives that emerged around the same time, such as the BRAIN Initiative in the United States and the Brain/MINDS project in Japan.

Your brother asked a great question. The short answer is that the United States has a general policy of not giving in to terrorists, but in practice it has sometimes talked with them, especially to free hostages or end conflicts. So the idea in the movie is a simplified version of a real debate.

Here is why the policy exists. Imagine a bully at school who takes someone's lunch money and threatens to keep doing it. If the kids who are being bullied hand over their money every time, the bully learns that taking things works, and then the bully just keeps coming back for more. Terrorist groups work the same way. If a government gives them what they want when they kidnap people or set off bombs, the groups learn that kidnapping and bombing pay off, so they are likely to do it again, and they may hurt more people. Governments also worry that paying ransom or making deals can put more people in danger, because it makes everyone a target.

But talking is not always forbidden. Sometimes it is smart to talk, the way a grown-up might calmly talk a scared kid down from a tall tree. Leaders may talk to a group to rescue hostages, to get information, or to end a fight without more people getting hurt. Even when they talk, they usually try not to hand over what the terrorists demand, because that is what keeps the bullying from starting again.

So the rule is more like "we try very hard not to reward bad behavior, but we will sometimes talk when it helps keep people safe."

Lots of people have the same experience, and it usually comes down to a few simple things. Your body has to learn how to notice the effects. The main ingredient in weed, THC, works on a system in your brain that controls feelings like relaxation, hunger, and how time and sensations feel. The first time you try it, your brain doesn't really know what to look for, so the feeling can be faint or easy to miss. Over a few tries you start to recognize what it's like, and the effects seem to show up more clearly.

Another reason is that many first-timers don't take in enough smoke or edible to feel it, or they hold back because they're nervous. If you're tense, it's harder to relax into the feeling. Breathing in deeply and holding it a bit longer can help with smoking or vaping, and with edibles it takes time to kick in, so people often take more before the first dose has worked and then feel a surprise.

The strength of the plant matters too. Different strains and products vary a lot in how much THC they have, so one person's experience may be very different from another's just because of what they tried.

So it's normal that it took a few attempts. If it helps, try a comfortable setting with people you trust, start small, and give it time before deciding how it's working for you.

A redshirt freshman is a college football player who is in his second year at a school but his first year of actual playing eligibility. The term comes from "redshirting," which is the practice of having an athlete sit out of competition for a season so that it doesn't count against the limited number of years he's allowed to play.

Under NCAA rules, a player generally has five years to complete four seasons of competition. That extra year gives room for a redshirt season. During that year, the player is enrolled in school, attends classes, practices with the team, lifts weights, and studies the playbook, but he doesn't appear in games, or at least not enough to use up a season of eligibility. When he returns the following year, he's academically a sophomore but athletically a freshman, so he's called a redshirt freshman. The same idea continues with labels like redshirt sophomore, redshirt junior, and redshirt senior.

Coaches redshirt players for several reasons. Many freshmen arriving from high school aren't yet physically ready for the size and speed of college football, so a year of strength training and development can make a big difference. A redshirt year also helps when a team already has experienced players ahead of a newcomer on the depth chart, since it saves the younger player's eligibility for later when he's more likely to contribute. Players recovering from injuries can also be redshirted.

Since 2018, the NCAA has allowed football players to appear in up to four games in a season and still keep their redshirt status. This lets coaches give young players some real game experience, fill in when injuries occur, or reward hard work in practice without costing the player a full year of eligibility.

The name itself traces back to the red practice jerseys that some non-playing athletes historically wore to distinguish them from the regular players, though today it's simply a general term for sitting out a season to preserve eligibility.

Drug design is the process of discovering and creating new medications based on knowledge of a biological target, usually a protein such as an enzyme, receptor, or ion channel whose activity is involved in a disease. The central idea is that a molecule can be deliberately shaped so that it binds to that target and changes its behavior, for example by blocking an overactive enzyme or by mimicking a natural signaling molecule. The term "design" distinguishes this rational approach from older methods that relied heavily on chance discovery, such as screening natural products for any observable effect.

The process generally begins with identifying and validating a target, meaning researchers gather evidence that modulating it will have a therapeutic benefit. Next they look for "hit" compounds that interact with the target. These may come from screening large libraries of chemicals, from studying natural substances, or from building molecules from scratch. Hits are then refined into "leads," and the leads are optimized through repeated cycles of design, synthesis, and testing. Optimization aims to improve potency and selectivity for the target while also improving properties such as solubility, stability in the body, absorption, and low toxicity. A compound that binds tightly but is quickly destroyed by the liver or harms healthy tissue is of little use.

There are two main strategies. Structure-based drug design uses the three-dimensional structure of the target, determined by methods like X-ray crystallography, cryo-electron microscopy, or NMR spectroscopy, to design molecules that fit into its binding site much as a key fits a lock. Ligand-based drug design is used when the target's structure is unknown; it relies instead on the properties of known active molecules, building models of what features are needed for activity, such as pharmacophore models or quantitative structure-activity relationships.

Computers play a large role, an area often called computer-aided drug design. Techniques include molecular docking, which predicts how a molecule will sit in a binding site, molecular dynamics simulations, which model how molecules move and interact over time, and increasingly machine learning, which can predict activity or propose novel structures. These tools help narrow down enormous numbers of possible compounds before costly laboratory work begins.

After a promising candidate is found, it moves into preclinical testing in cells and animals, and then into clinical trials in humans to establish safety and effectiveness. Despite advances, drug design remains difficult, time-consuming, and expensive, and most candidates fail along the way. Notable successes of the rational approach include HIV protease inhibitors, kinase inhibitors such as imatinib for certain leukemias, and many modern antiviral and cancer therapies.

Thanks for describing this so clearly. Feeling like you're not getting enough air, needing a deep breath now and then, and sometimes breathing faster are common experiences, and in a healthy, active teenager they are often harmless. Still, since you had a heart tumour as a child, it's worth mentioning to a doctor so they can take that history into account.

Some of the more common, usually benign causes include shallow or irregular breathing that often happens with stress, anxiety, or tension in the chest and neck muscles. Poor posture, especially from long periods hunched over a phone or desk, can make it harder for the chest to expand fully, which can create the sense that you need a big breath. Sometimes the feeling comes from simply being aware of your breathing, which makes it seem more noticeable than it is. Dehydration, low iron, or a recent cold or allergy flare can also contribute. Exercise and hard breathing can leave you with a lingering urge to sigh or breathe deeply afterward.

Because of your childhood heart history, I'd suggest seeing a doctor, especially if you notice any of the following: breathlessness during light activity or at rest, chest pain or pressure, dizziness, fainting or near-fainting, a racing or pounding heartbeat, swelling in your legs, or symptoms that are getting more frequent or intense. A doctor can check your heart and lungs, and if needed, refer you to a cardiologist for a basic heart check such as an ECG or echocardiogram. If you ever have sudden severe chest pain, trouble breathing, or fainting, get medical help right away.

Blind people usually get around with a white cane or a guide dog, and the cane is the one most folks picture. It's a long, thin stick they hold in front of them and tap along the ground as they walk. That tapping picks up bumps, drop-offs, and changes in the surface, so they know about obstacles or where a sidewalk or staircase begins and ends. Finding a Braille sign works pretty much the same way. They'll sweep the cane or reach out with a hand until they hit the sign, and they'll often use their ears or nose too. Maybe they hear a sound coming from the sign, or catch a smell from a shop right next to it. Once they've found the spot, they run their fingertips over the raised dots. Braille is just a system of raised dots standing in for letters, numbers, and symbols, and readers learn to recognize the patterns by feel. It's slower than skimming a sign with your eyes, sure, but with enough practice it becomes second nature and they can read it about as easily as anyone else.

The Matrix came out in 1999 and was written and directed by the Wachowskis, who were still going by the Wachowski Brothers back then. Turns out they've taken over the world and built this simulated reality, the Matrix, just to keep humans docile and under control. People also use "league" for a group of ships sailing together, or for a group of nations or organizations that have teamed up for some shared purpose.
