Software engineering is the discipline of designing, building, testing, deploying, and maintaining software systems in a systematic, disciplined, and measurable way. Rather than treating programming as simply writing code, it applies engineering principles to the entire lifecycle of a software product, from gathering requirements from users and stakeholders, through architecture and implementation, to ongoing operation and eventual retirement. The goal is to produce software that is reliable, efficient, secure, maintainable, and delivered on time and within budget.

The field draws on a range of practices and tools. These include requirements analysis, system design, version control, code review, automated testing, continuous integration and deployment, documentation, and project management methodologies such as Agile, Scrum, or more traditional waterfall approaches. Software engineers also think carefully about trade-offs, such as performance versus readability, speed of delivery versus long-term quality, or flexibility versus simplicity, and they use established patterns and principles to manage complexity as systems grow.

Because software often outlives its original authors and must adapt to changing needs, software engineering places strong emphasis on collaboration and maintainability. Teams work together across roles like developers, testers, designers, and product managers, and they aim to write code that others can understand, modify, and extend over many years. In this sense, software engineering is as much about managing people, processes, and long-term consequences as it is about the technical work of writing programs.

In World War II, a "theater" (also called a theatre of war) was a large geographic region in which military operations were organized and conducted as a distinct campaign zone. Rather than meaning a place of stage performance, the term referred to a broad area of land, sea, and air where opposing forces fought, and each one typically had its own commanders, strategy, and logistics. The major theaters included the European Theater, which covered Western and Central Europe and the Atlantic and North African approaches; the Mediterranean Theater, centered on North Africa, Sicily, and Italy; the Eastern Front, where Germany and the Soviet Union fought across Eastern Europe; the Pacific Theater, covering the war against Japan across the Pacific islands and Asian mainland; and the China-Burma-India Theater, where Allied forces supported Chinese resistance and fought in Burma. Dividing the war this way helped the Allies and Axis powers coordinate forces, supply lines, and command structures across vast distances.

Raw fish and raw chicken can both make you sick, since they can carry bacteria that cause food poisoning. Raw fish often gets a pass as the safer of the two, though, mostly because fish swim in water that rinses off a lot of the germs they pick up. Chickens are stuck on land, rolling around in whatever bacteria their surroundings have, so they tend to be the bigger worry. Fish has its own issue too. Salmon and tuna can carry parasites, and cooking kills those while eating the fish raw doesn't. So if you're eating sushi or sashimi, buy from a place you trust and make sure the fish was handled and prepared properly.

Born in Urbino, Italy, on April 6, 1483, Raphael was a painter and architect from Italy. He ranks among the most significant figures of the High Renaissance, and he earned renown for his paintings, frescoes, and architectural plans. His work strongly shaped how art developed throughout both the Renaissance and the Baroque eras, and he is widely regarded as one of the finest artists in the history of Western art.

Dungeness crabs (Metacarcinus magister) live along the Pacific coastline of North America, ranging from the Aleutian Islands in Alaska south to central California. They usually inhabit rocky or muddy seafloors, found in bays, estuaries, and out on the open coast. Their preferred water temperature falls between 10 and 15 degrees Celsius, and they are most often encountered at depths of 10 to 50 meters. Because they travel widely, Dungeness crabs shift to deeper or shallower water as the seasons turn and temperatures change. They are also present in parts of the Pacific Northwest, such as Washington, Oregon, and British Columbia.

Using other people's money, often shortened to OPM, simply means financing an investment or business with capital that isn't yours. The appeal is straightforward: if you can earn a higher return on money than it costs you to obtain it, you keep the difference, and you can pursue opportunities far larger than your own savings would allow. Nearly every large company, real estate portfolio, and investment fund runs on this principle. The money generally comes in one of two forms, debt or equity, and the tradeoffs between them shape how the whole arrangement works.

Debt means borrowing. A bank loan, a mortgage, a line of credit, bonds, or a loan from a private lender all fall into this category. You agree to pay back the principal plus interest on a schedule, and the lender doesn't own any part of your business or asset. If a real estate investor buys a $500,000 property with $100,000 down and a $400,000 mortgage, and the property rises 10 percent in value, the investor's $100,000 stake has gained $50,000, a 50 percent return. That magnification is called leverage. The catch is that leverage works in both directions. If the property falls 20 percent, the investor's entire stake is wiped out, and the loan still has to be repaid. Debt also demands regular payments whether or not the business is doing well, which is why overleveraged companies and investors are the first to fail in downturns.

Equity means selling a share of ownership in exchange for capital. Startups raising money from angel investors or venture capitalists, small businesses taking on partners, and real estate syndications where a sponsor pools money from many investors are all equity arrangements. There are no fixed repayments, so equity is less dangerous to the business in hard times, but you give up a portion of the profits and often some control. If a founder sells 30 percent of a company for $1 million and the company later sells for $50 million, the investors receive $15 million. That's expensive compared to a loan, but the investors also would have lost everything if the company had failed, so they are paid for taking that risk.

Many arrangements blend the two. In a typical real estate syndication, a general partner finds and manages a deal while limited partners supply most of the cash. The limited partners might receive a preferred return, say 8 percent annually, before the sponsor gets anything, and then profits above that are split, perhaps 70 percent to investors and 30 percent to the sponsor. Private equity and hedge funds work similarly, with the manager typically charging an annual management fee plus a share of the profits, commonly described as "two and twenty." Convertible notes and SAFEs in the startup world start out resembling debt and later convert into equity.

Getting access to other people's money depends almost entirely on trust and track record. Lenders want collateral, steady cash flow, good credit, and evidence that you can repay. Equity investors want a compelling opportunity, a credible plan, and confidence in the person running it. This is why most people start small, using their own money or modest loans, build a history of results, and then attract larger pools of capital. Relationships matter enormously; a lot of early funding comes from people who already know and trust the person asking.

There are serious obligations attached. When you take investors' money, you typically owe them fiduciary duties, meaning you must act in their interest, disclose material information honestly, and avoid self-dealing. In the United States, raising money from investors usually involves selling securities, which falls under SEC rules and state laws. Most private raises rely on exemptions such as Regulation D, which have specific requirements about who can invest and how the offering can be advertised. Getting this wrong can lead to investors demanding their money back, regulatory penalties, or fraud liability, so anyone raising outside capital should work with a securities attorney. Personal guarantees on business loans can also put your own assets at risk even if the business is structured as a corporation or LLC.

The core logic, then, is that other people's money lets you scale beyond your own resources, either by paying a fixed cost for borrowed funds or by sharing the upside with partners. It can accelerate wealth building dramatically when the underlying investment is sound, but it amplifies mistakes just as much, and it brings legal and ethical responsibilities to the people whose money you are using. The investors who succeed with it tend to be conservative about how much leverage they take on, transparent with their backers, and disciplined about only deploying capital into opportunities they genuinely understand.

Warehouse spreadsheets are used to organize, track, and analyze the many moving parts of storing and shipping goods. They are especially common in small and mid-sized operations that don't have a dedicated warehouse management system, though larger facilities often use them alongside formal software for reporting and quick analysis.

Their most common use is inventory tracking. A spreadsheet can list every item by SKU or part number, along with its description, quantity on hand, storage location (aisle, rack, bin), unit cost, and supplier. Staff update the counts as stock comes in and goes out, so the business knows what it has and where it is. Formulas can flag items that fall below a reorder point, helping prevent stockouts, and can highlight slow-moving or obsolete stock that ties up space and money.

They are also used to record receiving and shipping. Incoming shipments can be logged with dates, purchase order numbers, quantities, and any discrepancies or damage, while outgoing orders can be tracked through picking, packing, and dispatch, often with carrier and tracking information. This creates a record that helps resolve disputes with suppliers or customers and shows how quickly orders move through the building.

Spreadsheets also support cycle counts and physical inventory audits, where workers count stock and compare it with recorded figures to find shrinkage, theft, or data entry errors. Warehouse managers use them for space and layout planning, mapping which products sit in which locations and assigning fast-moving items to easier-to-reach spots. They also handle labor and operations tasks such as staff schedules, shift assignments, productivity metrics like picks per hour, equipment maintenance logs, and safety inspection checklists.

Finally, spreadsheets are valuable for reporting and analysis. Managers can calculate inventory value, turnover rates, order accuracy, on-time shipping percentages, and storage costs, then build charts or pivot tables to spot trends and support decisions about purchasing, staffing, or expansion. Their appeal lies in being inexpensive, flexible, and familiar to most people. Their drawbacks are that they rely on manual entry, are prone to errors, and become hard to manage as a warehouse grows, which is why many businesses eventually move to barcode-based inventory or warehouse management software.

Masturbation is not causing this. It is a normal activity and does not damage the kidneys or cause blood and protein to leak into the urine over years. The one small exception is that ejaculation shortly before a urine test can occasionally leave a little semen in the sample, which can slightly affect the result. So it is sensible to avoid ejaculation and heavy exercise for a day or two before your next urine test. But that would not explain a finding that has persisted for five years.

What concerns me is the combination of 15 to 20 red blood cells per high-power field and albumin at 2+ that has lasted this long. Blood and protein together in the urine, persisting over time, usually point to a problem with the kidney's filtering units, called the glomeruli. In a young man, the most common cause is IgA nephropathy. Other possibilities include thin basement membrane disease, Alport syndrome (which is often linked with hearing problems or a family history of kidney disease), or other forms of glomerulonephritis. Sometimes the bleeding comes from elsewhere in the urinary tract, such as a stone, but the protein makes a kidney filter problem more likely.

Normal creatinine and urea are reassuring because they mean your kidney function is currently preserved. They do not mean the kidneys are completely healthy. Creatinine often stays normal until a significant amount of kidney function has been lost. Ongoing protein leakage is itself a sign of kidney stress and a risk factor for slow damage over time. That is why this should not simply be watched for years without a diagnosis.

You should see a nephrologist, a kidney specialist, if you have not already. They will likely want to measure exactly how much protein you are losing with a urine protein-to-creatinine ratio or a 24-hour urine collection. They may also look at the urine under a microscope for misshapen red cells or casts, which suggest a kidney origin, and calculate your eGFR. Checking your blood pressure is important too, since high blood pressure is common in these conditions. Other likely tests include a kidney ultrasound and blood tests such as complement levels, ANA, and hepatitis B, hepatitis C and HIV screening. If protein loss is significant, a kidney biopsy is often recommended because it gives a definite diagnosis and guides treatment.

The good news is that many of these conditions can be managed well when caught early. Treatment often includes blood pressure medicines such as ACE inhibitors or ARBs, which also reduce protein leakage and protect the kidneys. Further treatment depends on the specific cause. In the meantime, avoid painkillers like ibuprofen and diclofenac, keep your salt intake moderate, don't smoke, and have your blood pressure checked. Please let go of the guilt about masturbation and put your energy into getting a proper kidney evaluation.

Capital gains and losses are recorded in double-entry accounting by treating the disposal of an asset as a set of linked debits and credits that remove the asset from the books, recognize any cash or other consideration received, and record the difference as a gain or a loss.

When an asset is sold, the first step is to remove its carrying value from the balance sheet. This means crediting the asset account for its original cost and crediting any accumulated depreciation or amortization account associated with it, which together bring the asset's net book value to zero. Next, the cash or receivable received from the buyer is recorded as a debit, typically to the Cash account or Accounts Receivable. The difference between the proceeds and the net book value is the gain or loss. If the proceeds exceed the net book value, the difference is a credit to a Gain on Sale of Asset account, which appears on the income statement as other income. If the proceeds fall short, the difference is a debit to a Loss on Sale of Asset account, which is an expense.

As an illustration, suppose a company sells equipment that originally cost 10,000 with accumulated depreciation of 6,000, for cash of 5,500. The net book value is 4,000. The journal entry would debit Cash for 5,500, debit Accumulated Depreciation for 6,000, credit Equipment for 10,000, and credit Gain on Sale of Equipment for 1,500. The debits total 11,500 and the credits total 11,500, so the entry balances. If the same equipment sold for 3,000 instead, the entry would debit Cash for 3,000, debit Accumulated Depreciation for 6,000, debit Loss on Sale of Equipment for 1,000, and credit Equipment for 10,000.

For investments such as shares or bonds, the same logic applies, with the carrying amount of the investment replacing the asset's net book value. Companies also need to account for transaction costs such as brokerage fees, which typically reduce the proceeds or increase the loss. Where the asset was held in a foreign currency or was revalued through other comprehensive income, additional reclassification entries may be needed to move previously recognized amounts into retained earnings or profit or loss, depending on the applicable accounting framework.

At the end of the period, the gain and loss accounts are closed to the income summary or retained earnings, so they begin the next period at zero. For tax purposes, the gain or loss is often computed separately using the tax basis of the asset, which can differ from the book value and create deferred tax entries.

Yes, there are ways to bring a period earlier or delay it, though the options differ in safety and effectiveness, and it helps to know what is actually happening in the body before choosing one.

To bring a period on earlier, the most commonly used approach is a progestin-only pill or a combined oral contraceptive taken to shift the cycle, usually started a few days before the expected date and stopped when the bleeding should begin. Some people take a higher dose of progesterone for a few days, which can trigger withdrawal bleeding once the dose stops. These methods work best when used at the right point in the cycle and are most reliable when a doctor prescribes the exact dose and timing. Many herbal or folk remedies are promoted for this purpose, but they are not well studied, can be unpredictable, and some can cause harm, so it is better to avoid them unless you have spoken with a clinician.

To delay a period, yes, there are tablets that can do this. Progestin-based medicines such as norethisterone or medroxyprogesterone are commonly prescribed to postpone bleeding for a short time, often starting a few days before the expected period and continuing until you want the bleeding to begin. Some combined oral contraceptives can also be used this way, by skipping the placebo or inactive pills and moving straight into a new pack. These are generally safe for short-term use in healthy women, but they are not suitable for everyone, particularly those with a history of blood clots, migraine with aura, certain liver conditions, breast cancer, or unexplained vaginal bleeding.

Because the right choice depends on your health history, the reason you want to change your period, and whether you are trying to avoid pregnancy, please see a doctor or gynecologist. They can prescribe the appropriate medicine and explain the correct dosing and timing. Also remember that these medicines do not protect against pregnancy in the way contraceptives do, unless they are a contraceptive pill used as directed, and a missed period when you are sexually active should always be checked with a pregnancy test.

The Turing Test assesses how well a machine can display intelligent conduct that matches, or cannot be told apart from, that of a human being. Alan Turing, a British mathematician and computer scientist, devised it in 1950 and gave it his name. In the procedure, a human evaluator holds written exchanges in natural language with both a person and a machine, then tries to identify which party is which. When the evaluator cannot dependably distinguish the machine from the human, the machine is considered to have passed. People frequently use the test as a standard for judging whether a machine possesses artificial intelligence, though it falls short of being a flawless gauge. Some critics contend that its scope is too narrow, since it only evaluates a machine's skill at imitating human dialogue and ignores other kinds of intelligent behavior. Others find it too subjective, because the outcome depends on the opinions of particular human judges. Even so, the Turing Test continues to be a broadly recognized and influential idea in artificial intelligence.

Symbolic computation, sometimes called symbolic algebra or algebraic manipulation, is a area of mathematics that works with algebraic expressions and equations by transforming and simplifying them through symbolic methods. Rather than relying on numerical values, this form of computation uses symbols to stand in for mathematical quantities and operations. It can tackle a broad range of problems, including algebraic, differential, and integral equations, and it can also carry out operations on polynomials, matrices, and other kinds of mathematical objects. A key benefit is that it often reveals more about the structure of a problem and how different quantities relate to one another than numerical approaches do. This is especially valuable in fields with complex or abstract ideas, where the underlying structure can be hard to grasp through numerical methods alone. Several software packages and programming languages are built specifically for symbolic work, including Mathematica, Maple, and Maxima. These tools let users enter algebraic expressions and equations and manipulate them symbolically to find solutions or simplify them.

In 1964, Leonid Brezhnev took over leadership of the Soviet Union from Nikita Khrushchev. Khrushchev had held that position since Joseph Stalin died in 1953, but Brezhnev and other Soviet leaders orchestrated a political coup that forced him out. Brezhnev then governed the Soviet Union for 18 years, remaining in office until he died in 1982.

A straddle is an options trade where you buy both a call and a put with the same strike price and expiration date, betting that the underlying stock will make a big move either way before expiry. Some ETFs try to copy that return pattern by holding a mix of calls and puts on a stock or index. They can get pretty complicated, though, and they aren't a fit for everyone. Before putting money into one, think hard about what you're after and how much risk you can stomach. Options in general are risky too. You can lose a lot, so make sure you understand what you're getting into before you jump in.

It is commonly regarded as typical for blood pressure to run a little higher in those who exercise regularly, since their hearts grow stronger and pump blood more efficiently. Even so, a healthcare provider should check your blood pressure to confirm that it falls within a healthy range for you. This is particularly important if you notice symptoms that might point to high blood pressure, including headaches, dizziness, shortness of breath, or chest pain. Regular check-ups are also worthwhile even when you feel fine, as they can catch potential health problems early and make timely treatment possible if needed.

When you buy a home without a buyer's agent, the paperwork is usually handled by a few professionals, and the right one depends on where you live, since the rules differ by state or country.

In the United States, the key professional is a real estate attorney or a title company. In some states, such as New York, Massachusetts, Georgia, and a handful of others, attorneys are required or customary for closings, so you should hire one. In most other states, a title company or escrow officer conducts the closing, and you may not need an attorney at all, though having one review the contract is still a smart investment, often a few hundred dollars. Your lender will also provide much of the mortgage paperwork, and the closing agent will prepare the settlement statement and deed transfer. Because you have no agent looking out for you, a flat-fee attorney to review the purchase contract, title commitment, and closing documents is worth considering.

If you are in the United Kingdom, Ireland, Australia, or another country with a conveyancing system, you will typically hire a conveyancer or solicitor. They handle the contract exchange, property searches, title checks, and the transfer of funds and ownership. You can find licensed conveyancers through professional bodies such as the Law Society or the Conveyancing Association, and it is wise to get quotes from several before choosing.

Whatever your location, a few tips help. Ask for a fixed fee quote in writing. Confirm that the professional is licensed and carries professional liability insurance. Ask whether they represent only you or also the lender or seller, since that creates a conflict of interest you should avoid. Finally, have them review the inspection report and title search, because those documents are where costly surprises usually hide.

Imagine a big truck driving from country to country, and every time it crosses a border, the guards at that border have their own rules about guns. One country says guns are fine, another says you need special paperwork, and another says if you bring a gun in, you go to jail. A cargo ship has the same problem, only worse, because it might stop at a dozen ports in different countries on one trip. Every port can check what's on board, and carrying weapons can mean huge fines, the ship getting held up for days or weeks, or the crew getting arrested. For a shipping company, that hassle and risk often seemed worse than the pirate risk.

There's also the question of who would use the weapons. Sailors are trained to drive and fix ships, not to fight. Handing a gun to someone who isn't trained can make things more dangerous, because pirates who see the crew shooting back might start shooting to kill instead of just trying to take hostages. Back then, pirates mostly wanted to capture the ship and the people on it so they could ask for ransom money, and they usually didn't want to hurt anyone because a hurt hostage is worth less. Companies worried that arming the crew would turn a scary but usually survivable kidnapping into a deadly gunfight.

Insurance and law played a part too. If a sailor shoots someone, who is responsible? The captain, the company, the country whose flag the ship flies? Lawyers and insurance companies got very nervous about those questions, so the safe answer for a long time was simply "no guns."

Instead, ships used other tricks: going very fast, steering in zigzags so small pirate boats couldn't climb aboard, spraying fire hoses at attackers, putting barbed wire along the sides, and having a locked safe room where the crew could hide and wait for the navy to come help.

The interesting part is that things changed after the period shown in Captain Phillips, which happened in 2009. As the attacks kept coming, many shipping companies started hiring professional armed security guards, often former soldiers, to ride along through dangerous waters near Somalia. Countries worked out rules to allow it, and guards would sometimes get on and off at special stops so the weapons didn't have to enter ports. Along with navy patrols, this helped make pirate attacks in that area drop a lot. So the short answer is that ships weren't totally forbidden from having weapons, it was just complicated, risky, and messy enough that most companies avoided it until the pirate problem got bad enough to make it worth the trouble.

Income earned from selling covered calls is usually treated as a short-term capital gain, since the underlying shares typically have not been held for more than a year. When the shares have been held longer than a year, that income may instead qualify as a long-term capital gain, which usually carries a lower tax rate than short-term gains. Put simply, a capital gain is the profit made when a capital asset, such as a stock, is sold for more than its purchase price. How much tax applies depends on both how long the asset was owned before the sale and the seller's tax bracket. Gains on assets held one year or less are taxed as ordinary income, whereas gains on assets held beyond one year receive a reduced rate. Because covered call writing can have intricate tax consequences, anyone with such income should consider consulting a tax professional for guidance on reporting and paying the correct taxes.

Okay, so a fuzzy rule is basically a statement linking some input variables to an output variable. The "fuzzy" part is because it handles uncertainty and fuzziness in those values instead of demanding exact yes-or-no answers. You'll see these rules in fuzzy logic systems, which are nonlinear mathematical models for reasoning about messy, complicated systems with lots of uncertain or conflicting variables. People use them for control systems, decision-making, pattern recognition, and plenty more.

Most fuzzy rules have two halves: a condition part that lays out the inputs, and a conclusion part that gives the output. The condition usually shows up as an if-then statement. Here's a simple one: "If the temperature is hot, then turn the air conditioning on." The input is the temperature, the output is the state of the AC, and when the temperature counts as hot, you follow the conclusion and switch it on.

You can pair fuzzy rules with other tools, like fuzzy inference systems, to make decisions or run controls based on data that's fuzzy or incomplete. They shine when plain true/false logic just doesn't cut it, especially with systems where a bunch of variables interact in tangled ways.

Mincemeat is a blend of chopped dried fruit, strong alcoholic spirits, spices, and, in some versions, beef or venison. Bakers commonly use it to fill pies and tarts. Classic recipes typically combine raisins, currants, and apples with suet, the hard fat found around the kidneys of beef or mutton, and warm spices like cinnamon, nutmeg, and cloves. Certain recipes add brandy or another spirit to help preserve the mixture. People can prepare mincemeat in their own kitchens or buy it already packed in jars or tins. Although it is usually a sweet, rich filling for desserts, it can also serve as a topping for savory dishes like crostini or be incorporated into other baked goods.
