Imperfect information is a concept from game theory, economics, and decision theory that describes situations where participants do not have complete knowledge about the state of the world or about the actions others have taken. In such settings, a player may be uncertain about past events, current conditions, or the strategies and intentions of other players. This contrasts with perfect information, where everyone can see the full history of moves and the complete state of the game at every point.

A useful way to understand the idea is to compare familiar games. Chess is a game of perfect information because both players can see the entire board and every move made so far. Poker, by contrast, is a game of imperfect information, since each player keeps their cards hidden and must infer what the others might be holding from their betting behavior. Note that imperfect information is related to but distinct from incomplete information, which refers to uncertainty about the payoffs or characteristics of other players, though the two terms are often used together in the literature.

In economics, imperfect information is central to many real-world problems. A used car seller typically knows more about the car's quality than the buyer does, which can lead to adverse selection, where low-quality goods drive out high-quality ones. Insurance companies face similar challenges because they cannot fully observe how careful a customer will be, which gives rise to moral hazard. Financial markets, job hiring, and political decision-making all involve participants acting on partial information.

Economists and game theorists study these situations using tools such as Bayesian games, signaling models, and screening mechanisms, which help describe how people form beliefs under uncertainty and how they might reduce information gaps. In short, imperfect information means that decisions must often be made with incomplete or uncertain knowledge, and much of strategic and economic reasoning deals with how to act sensibly under those conditions.

You can take money out of a Roth 401k to buy your first home, though a few rules and limits apply. In many cases, such a withdrawal is free of taxes and penalties if you satisfy certain requirements. The main points to keep in mind are these: your Roth 401k must have been open for at least five tax years; the funds must go toward buying a principal residence for you, your spouse, or your children, grandchildren, or parents; the withdrawal must take place within 120 days of the purchase; and the total you can take for a first-time home purchase from all of your Roth IRAs (including Roth 401ks) is capped at $10,000. If you fail to meet these conditions, you might still be allowed to withdraw from your Roth 401k for this purpose, but you could owe taxes and/or penalties on the amount. Before making any decisions about pulling money from your retirement accounts, it's wise to speak with a tax professional or financial advisor.

The director is often the one who takes the story the writer created and brings it to life on screen. Working with the actors, they shape how each character delivers their lines and how they move, and they coordinate with the teams responsible for sets, costumes, and visual effects to ensure everything appears as intended. In a way, the director resembles an orchestra conductor, pulling the various elements together so the film comes across as a unified whole. Put simply, the writer creates the story and its characters, while the director turns that material into a living production and keeps all the moving parts running smoothly. Does that make sense?

Imagine you built a really tall tower out of blocks, and it's sitting on a crowded table right next to your friends' block towers. If you knocked it over, it would crash into everyone else's towers. So what do you do instead? You take it apart carefully, one block at a time, starting from the top. That's basically how most skyscrapers in crowded cities get demolished.

Workers start at the very top floor and work their way down. They use smaller machines, sometimes cranes lift little bulldozers or "nibbler" machines right up onto the roof. These machines chew through the concrete and cut the steel beams on one floor, and the pieces get lowered down by crane or dropped through a chute inside the building, kind of like a garbage slide. When that floor is gone, they move down to the next one and do it again. It's slow, but it's safe, because nothing big ever falls outside the building.

To keep dust and little bits from flying around, they often wrap the building in big nets or sheets, like putting a blanket around it. They also spray water to keep the dust down, the way you might wet sand so it doesn't blow everywhere.

Some clever companies in Japan even invented a way to take buildings apart from the bottom. They hold the building up with giant jacks, remove the lowest floor, then gently lower the whole building down a little, and repeat. From far away, it looks like the building is slowly shrinking into the ground! They also put a "hat" over the top to keep everything quiet and clean inside.

You might have seen videos of buildings being blown up with explosives so they fall down in a big whoosh. That's called implosion, and the explosives are placed very carefully so the building collapses straight down into itself, like a sandcastle slumping into its own footprint. It's fast, but it shakes the ground and makes huge clouds of dust, so it's usually used only when there's enough empty space around. In a really packed city full of tall buildings, people almost always choose the slow, careful, piece-by-piece way instead.

A deep learning processor is a processor built specifically to carry out the intricate mathematical computations that deep learning requires. Deep learning, a branch of artificial intelligence (AI), teaches a computer to spot patterns in data and reach decisions based on them. This is usually achieved with neural networks, a design loosely modeled on the human brain, consisting of stacked layers of linked "neurons" that handle and pass along information. Deep learning processors are engineered to perform the matrix multiplications and other operations needed to train and run these models very efficiently. They can be built into many kinds of hardware, from desktop and laptop computers to dedicated devices such as graphics processing units (GPUs) and tensor processing units (TPUs). Several notable examples exist. NVIDIA, a major graphics processing unit manufacturer, produces GPUs that are widely employed in deep learning because they can execute many calculations at high speed in parallel. Google's Tensor Processing Units are chips designed in-house for deep learning workloads, optimized to run the matrix operations involved in training and inference. Intel Nervana is another deep learning processor from Intel, built to handle the demanding calculations deep learning involves. These processors support a broad range of applications, such as image and speech recognition, natural language processing, and autonomous driving.

Okay so VAT is basically a tax on most goods and services in the UK. Businesses collect it when they sell something and then hand it over to the government. For the cultural industry it works pretty much the same way as anywhere else, but there are a few quirks. The big one is that admission to things like concerts, plays and exhibitions is usually VAT-exempt, so no VAT gets charged on those tickets or passed on.

It gets a bit messier with imports. If a UK cultural business buys stuff from overseas, it might end up owing VAT on those purchases. The reason is that the zero-rating or exemption tends to apply mainly to supplies within the EU, so anything coming from outside it can trigger VAT. Worth double-checking the current rules though, since they've shifted over the years.

Honestly, if you're running a business in this area, it's worth knowing these rules inside out and making sure you're actually following them. And if you've got specific questions, a tax pro or HMRC is the best bet for a proper answer.

People start smoking for all kinds of reasons, even though it's bad for you. Some think it looks cool, or their friends and family smoke so it seems normal. Others pick it up to deal with stress or to fit in with a crowd. Plenty of people just get curious, or figure it'll help them chill out. But smoking really does wreck your health. It can lead to lung cancer, heart disease, and stroke, and that's just the serious stuff. You also get bad breath, yellow teeth, and skin that wrinkles faster. It gets expensive too, since you keep buying packs for as long as you smoke. If you're thinking about starting, weigh those risks first. There are better ways to handle stress or find your people than picking up a habit that's going to hurt your body down the line.

The premise needs a small correction first: the main constraint on shorting penny stocks is not really a rule that brokers apply to every sub-$5 stock. Brokers restrict shorting for a variety of reasons, including low liquidity, thin borrow supply, high volatility, and regulatory requirements like the SEC's and FINRA's rules on hard-to-borrow securities. Many brokers do decline to short very low-priced or illiquid names, but the price threshold is one factor among several rather than a universal bar. Also, the reverse is closer to the truth: companies that fall below roughly $1 typically face exchange listing rules, since Nasdaq and the NYSE require a minimum bid price and will issue deficiency notices if a stock stays below it.

As for why companies don't split their stock down into sub-$5 territory, the main reason is that a stock split changes only the number of shares and the price per share, not the company's total value. If a $400 stock splits 10-for-1, it becomes a $40 stock with ten times as many shares, and the market capitalization stays the same. So a split doesn't create value, and it doesn't make the company any more or less attractive on a fundamental basis.

Companies also have several reasons not to push the price very low. Many institutional investors and index funds have mandates or preferences against low-priced stocks, and some funds are barred from holding them. Brokerages and market makers can be less interested in covering very cheap stocks, and wider bid-ask spreads in percentage terms can make trading more expensive for shareholders. Low-priced stocks also tend to attract a reputation for speculation, which can affect how analysts and the broader market view the company. Finally, a split is generally undertaken to bring a share price into a more typical trading range, and companies usually split when the price has risen a lot, not as a way to chase a particular number.

So the short answer is that splitting doesn't change underlying value, and there are practical and reputational reasons companies often keep their share prices in a moderate range rather than pushing them as low as possible.

Liver tenderness could come from a bunch of things, like inflammation, damage to the liver, or a mass or growth on it. A healthcare provider can figure out what's actually going on and what to do about it.

Metformin is primarily prescribed to treat type 2 diabetes. It helps lower blood sugar levels by reducing the amount of glucose the liver produces, improving the body's sensitivity to insulin, and decreasing how much sugar the intestines absorb from food. It is often the first medication doctors recommend for type 2 diabetes, and it can be used alone or combined with other diabetes drugs.

Beyond diabetes, doctors sometimes prescribe metformin off-label for conditions such as polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), where it can help regulate insulin resistance and menstrual cycles, and for prediabetes to help prevent progression to type 2 diabetes. Some clinicians also use it to manage weight gain associated with certain antipsychotic medications. Metformin is taken by mouth, usually in tablet form, and it should only be used under a healthcare provider's guidance, since they can determine the right dose and check for any reasons it may not be suitable.

In principle, implied volatility reflects everything market participants know and expect about a stock's future movements over the life of an option, including scheduled events. In practice, saying it "factors in all known events" holds only in a loose sense and comes with important caveats.

Implied volatility is not a forecast someone calculates from a list of upcoming events. It is backed out of an option's market price using a pricing model like Black-Scholes. Whatever traders are willing to pay for the option, the model translates into a volatility number. So to the extent traders know about an earnings report, an FDA decision, a central bank meeting, or an election and expect it to move the stock, they bid up options that expire after that event, and implied volatility rises. You can see this clearly in the term structure: options expiring just after an earnings date often carry noticeably higher implied volatility than those expiring just before it. After the event passes, implied volatility typically drops sharply, a phenomenon traders call "IV crush." Traders can even use the difference between expirations to estimate the size of the move the market is pricing in for the event itself.

However, several limitations apply. First, the market can know an event is coming and still misjudge how big the move will be. Earnings reactions frequently turn out much larger or smaller than options implied. Pricing an event in means the market has assigned it a consensus expectation, not that the expectation is correct.

Second, implied volatility includes more than an expectation of future movement. It typically contains a volatility risk premium, because option sellers demand compensation for taking on risk. Historically, implied volatility has on average exceeded the volatility that actually materializes. Supply and demand pressures, such as heavy hedging demand or speculative call buying, can also push implied volatility around for reasons unrelated to any specific event.

Third, implied volatility compresses a lot of information into a single number. An option's implied volatility blends ordinary day-to-day fluctuation with any event-driven jumps, and it assumes a distribution of returns that real markets don't follow neatly. This is why implied volatility varies across strike prices, producing the "skew" or "smile." Traders price in the risk of large downside moves or jumps in ways a single volatility figure can't fully capture.

Fourth, unknown or unscheduled events cannot be priced individually, though markets do charge a general premium for tail risk. Surprises such as a sudden acquisition announcement, a fraud revelation, or a market-wide shock are only partly reflected through that broad premium, not as specific anticipated events.

Finally, liquidity matters. For thinly traded options, prices can be stale or distorted by wide bid-ask spreads, so the implied volatility may not reflect a well-informed consensus.

In short, implied volatility is the market's best collective attempt to price known future events plus a buffer for risk and uncertainty. Scheduled events are generally reflected in it, often visibly, but that reflection is an estimate that can be wrong, is mixed with risk premiums and supply-demand effects, and cannot account for genuine surprises except in a general way.

Your eyes are great at bending light so it lands in the right spot on the back of your eye. They do this bending mostly at the front surface of the eye, where the clear part meets the air. When you're underwater, water surrounds that front surface instead of air. Water bends light almost as much as your eye does, so the light doesn't get bent the right amount anymore and everything looks blurry. A mask or goggles keeps a small pocket of air in front of your eyes, so your eyes can do their usual bending and you can see clearly again.

Fish don't have this problem because their eyes are built for water. Instead of relying on the front surface to bend light, a fish's eye has a round, bulgy lens that does nearly all the bending by itself. Since the lens does the work, it doesn't matter that the water is outside the eye. Fish eyes are also shaped to focus by moving the lens closer to or farther from the back of the eye, the way a camera does, rather than by changing the shape of the front surface like ours do.

Azoospermia just means there's no sperm in the semen. A bunch of things can cause it: hormone problems, genetic stuff, or a physical issue in the reproductive system. What they do about it really depends on which one it is.

If it's a physical problem like a blockage, surgery might fix it and get things working again. If it's hormonal, you'd probably be put on hormone therapy to get your sperm production back on track. And if none of that works, there's IVF and similar assisted reproduction options.

Honestly, the first step is getting a proper workup from a fertility specialist so you know what's actually going on. Your wife should get checked too, since there could be something on her end that needs sorting out as well. Whatever you decide, it's worth working with a doctor who can look at your specific situation. Hope that helps, and good luck with it all.

Okay so Pringles are basically potato flakes and corn flour mashed together, then pressed into that famous saddle shape. The thing people don't always realize is that when they prep the potatoes, you end up with little bits left over. Those scraps are usually too small or the wrong shape to work in the mix, so they don't make it into the cans. Most of the time they get sent off for stuff like animal feed or fertilizer.

Yes, opening a new credit card and shutting down another one can both influence your credit score. Applying for a new card usually triggers a credit check by the lender, which may cause a slight, short-lived drop in your score. The lender reviews your credit history and the details in your credit reports, and every time someone checks your credit, it can leave a minor negative mark on your score. Closing a card can matter too, particularly if it has been open for a long time or carries a high credit limit. Once the card is closed, its available credit disappears, which can push up your credit utilization ratio. That ratio compares how much credit you are using with how much you have available, and it is one of the elements that shapes your score. A significant jump in this ratio after closing a card can pull your score down. Managing your cards responsibly matters here, which means paying bills on time and keeping your utilization as low as you reasonably can. If you're thinking about opening a new card or closing an existing one, weigh how it could affect your score and make sure the choice suits your situation.

Mt. Ka'ala, the tallest point on Oahu, rises 4,025 feet (1,227 meters) above sea level in the Waianae mountain range. It is the loftiest peak of the Waianae Range and the highest spot in the whole state of Hawaii. The mountain lies inside the Ka'ala Natural Area Reserve, which shelters a wide array of plants and animals, among them numerous endangered and threatened species. Hikers also flock to the mountain, which is recognized for its demanding trails and the spectacular views available from its summit.

Dubai is a metropolis in the United Arab Emirates (UAE), a nation in the Middle East situated on the Arabian Peninsula. To the south and west, the UAE shares its borders with Saudi Arabia, while Oman lies to its east. Abu Dhabi serves as the country's capital, and Dubai is among the seven emirates that together form the federation. The city is renowned for its contemporary architecture, upscale shopping, and lively nightlife.

RFID tags can draw their power in several distinct ways. Passive tags have no built-in power supply; instead, they wake up when they receive radio frequency energy from the RFID reader. That energy powers the tag's microchip and lets it send its stored information back to the reader. Active tags carry their own power source, typically a small battery, which runs the microchip and handles transmitting the stored data to the reader. Semi-passive tags also contain a small battery that powers the microchip, but they still depend on the reader's radio frequency energy to activate. In this case, the reader's energy boosts the signal coming from the tag's chip, so it can be detected from farther away. In short, the appropriate power source for an RFID tag hinges on the particular tag type and the purpose it is meant to serve.

In the late nineteenth century, two competing electrical systems were under development: direct current (DC), championed by Thomas Edison, and alternating current (AC), championed by Nikola Tesla. DC electricity moves in a single direction, travelling from a positive terminal to a negative one, and it powers many electronic gadgets, including batteries and mobile phones. AC electricity, by contrast, reverses its flow periodically, usually 50 or 60 times per second (measured in hertz), and it supplies the majority of homes and offices. The dispute between the two camps focused on which system was superior for carrying power across great distances. Edison maintained that DC was preferable because it was simpler to distribute and operate. Tesla, however, contended that AC was the better choice, since it could travel far greater distances at higher voltages and therefore with greater efficiency. In the end, AC prevailed and is now the dominant form of electricity worldwide, yet DC remains essential in batteries and electronics. Consequently, both forms continue to be used today.

Keith Whitley was an American country singer and songwriter, born July 1, 1955, in Ashland, Kentucky. He's best known for hits like "Don't Close Your Eyes," "When You Say Nothing at All," and "I'm No Stranger to the Rain." His career was short, but it was a good one, and fans still talk about his music. He died on May 9, 1989, at just 33, from alcohol poisoning.

Corpus linguistics is basically the study of huge piles of real language data, called corpora, to figure out how people actually use words and what patterns show up. These corpora can come from all sorts of places: written texts, transcripts of speech, even social media posts. Researchers use computer tools to dig through this stuff and see how language gets used in everyday situations and how it shifts over time. It's useful for a lot of things, like teaching languages, translation, natural language processing, and plain old linguistic research. Common techniques include word frequency counts, concordancing (basically searching for a particular word or phrase and seeing it in context), and statistical checks on patterns. You can learn a lot from it about language variation, change, and how usage differs depending on the situation. It also feeds into tools you probably use already, like spell checkers and machine translation systems.

As of the most recent figures I'm aware of, roughly 290 to 295 million motor vehicles are registered in the United States. That total includes passenger cars, light trucks such as pickups, SUVs and vans, and heavy trucks, buses, and motorcycles. The Federal Highway Administration's annual Highway Statistics reports are the best source for the exact current number, since the count changes every year as new vehicles are added and older ones are scrapped.

Mike, a tooth infection like this usually needs dental treatment, not just antibiotics. Antibiotics can calm the spreading infection, but the abscess itself has to be drained, or the source treated with a root canal or extraction. Until you see a dentist, the most helpful steps are to keep taking ibuprofen as directed (with food, and not exceeding the label's daily maximum), rinse gently with warm salt water several times a day, avoid chewing on that side, and avoid putting aspirin directly on the gum, since it can burn the tissue.

I would not switch to clindamycin on your own. Amoxicillin is a reasonable first choice for dental infections, and clindamycin is usually reserved for people who are allergic to penicillin-type drugs. Switching without a prescriber's guidance can add side effects, especially diarrhea, and clindamycin carries a risk of a serious bowel infection. Also, if you take the two drugs at the wrong times or doses, you could mix up your treatment. Instead, call your dentist's office today and say you have a suspected tooth abscess and are already on amoxicillin. Many dentists will see urgent cases the same day or next day, and if you can't reach one, an urgent care clinic or dental emergency service can help. Ask them directly whether you should change antibiotics.

If the amoxicillin is working, you should usually notice some easing of pain and swelling within 24 to 48 hours. Improvement that's slow or partial is common with dental infections, but you should not see steady worsening. If you have no improvement after about 48 to 72 hours, or if things get worse, get seen promptly.

Go to an emergency department or call emergency services right away if you develop swelling that spreads to your cheek, neck, or under your jaw, trouble swallowing or breathing, difficulty opening your mouth, a high fever or chills, a racing heartbeat, confusion, or unusual drowsiness. These can signal a serious spreading infection that needs immediate care.

I'm sorry your daughter is so uncomfortable. A widespread itchy rash with pus-tipped bumps, blisters between the toes, and involvement of the scalp in a toddler has several common possibilities, and a doctor should look at her soon, ideally within the next day or so.

The most likely causes include a bacterial skin infection such as impetigo, which often causes crusted or pus-filled spots and can spread quickly. Scabies is another strong possibility: it causes intense itching that is often worse at night, can affect the hands, feet, and scalp, and spreads easily to other family members. Fungal infections can cause blisters between the toes and itchy patches. Chickenpox, hand, foot and mouth disease, eczema that has become infected, and an allergic reaction to a new soap, food, medicine, or insect bites can also look similar. Because some of these are contagious and some need prescription treatment, it is worth getting an accurate diagnosis rather than guessing.

While you wait for the appointment, you can help her feel more comfortable. Keep her fingernails short and clean so she causes less damage if she scratches. Use a cool, damp cloth on itchy areas, and give lukewarm rather than hot baths, then pat her dry gently. A plain, fragrance-free moisturizer can soothe the skin. Dress her in loose cotton clothing and avoid new detergents or harsh soaps. Children's acetaminophen or an age-appropriate antihistamine can ease itching, but check the dose with her doctor or pharmacist first, since antihistamines are not always suitable for toddlers.

Seek medical care promptly, the same day if possible, if she has a fever, seems unusually sleepy or fussy, has spreading redness or warmth, the blisters or sores are increasing, she is not drinking well, or she is breathing with difficulty or has swelling of the face or lips. If anyone else in the household is also itchy, mention that to the doctor, since scabies and some infections spread between people.

Greece ended up with so much debt because it kept spending more than it brought in. Think of it like earning $100 a week but regularly spending $110. Eventually you're stuck owing money and struggling to pay it back. That's pretty much what the Greek government was doing for years. On top of that, a lot of people and businesses weren't paying their taxes, and the economy wasn't growing much, so there wasn't much extra money coming in to cover the bills. Put all that together and paying the debt back got really hard.

If you're selling one home and buying another in quick succession, the main thing to understand is that the proceeds from the old sale are usually needed to close on the new purchase, so the timing and paperwork matter a great deal.

The most common approach is to use the sale proceeds directly as your down payment or to pay off the remaining mortgage on the old house. When you sell, the closing agent or title company calculates your net proceeds after paying off the existing mortgage, real estate commissions, closing costs, and any outstanding taxes or liens. That net amount is typically wired or sent as a check to you on closing day. If your new purchase closes the same day or shortly after, you can ask your agent or attorney to coordinate so the funds flow straight into the new transaction, which avoids having to hold a large sum yourself.

If the closings don't line up, you have a few options. You can arrange bridge financing, which is a short-term loan that covers the gap between buying the new home and receiving the old home's proceeds. Some lenders offer this, though it can be costly and is less common now. Alternatively, you can make a contingent offer on the new house, meaning it's conditional on selling your current home, though sellers often prefer offers without that condition. Another route is a "double closing" or simultaneous closing, where both transactions close on the same day with the funds passed between them, which requires close coordination among your agents, lenders, and title companies.

Some practical steps help. Talk to your mortgage lender early so they know about the pending sale and can structure your new loan accordingly, since they may need to see proof of the sale proceeds. Ask your real estate agent and closing attorney to plan the timing and funds transfer in advance. Keep in mind that if you're taking a new mortgage while still holding the old one, lenders may count the old debt against you, so the sale should ideally close first or on the same day. Finally, once the money arrives, you can apply it to your down payment, closing costs, renovations, paying down debt, or investments, depending on your goals and any tax considerations.

For a specific situation, a real estate attorney or a mortgage advisor can review your timeline and recommend the safest sequence.

Yes, and it happens more often than people realize. The principle itself is sound: money already spent and unrecoverable shouldn't influence a forward-looking decision, because no choice you make today can change it. The problem is that the principle can be applied selectively, stretched beyond its proper scope, or used as cover to avoid scrutiny.

The most common abuse is mislabeling costs as sunk when they aren't. Suppose a company owns a building or piece of equipment and proposes using it for a new project. An analyst might treat the asset as free because it was paid for long ago. But if the building could be sold or leased to someone else, its value is an opportunity cost, and that cost belongs in the analysis. Treating it as sunk inflates the project's apparent return. The same goes for committed spending that could still be cancelled, renegotiated, or redirected. Only truly irrecoverable costs are sunk.

A second abuse involves breaking a bad project into pieces. A manager who knows a full proposal would be rejected can ask for a modest first phase, then argue at each later stage that the previous spending is sunk and the next increment looks profitable on its own. Each step can be technically correct while the whole sequence destroys value. This is sometimes called salami-slicing, and it exploits the fact that incremental analysis says nothing about whether the overall venture should have been started.

There is also an accountability problem. Sunk costs are irrelevant to the decision about whether to continue, but they are highly relevant to judging how reliable the people making forecasts are. If a project has run triple its budget so far, that history is evidence that the remaining cost estimates may also be too optimistic. Someone who says "forget the past, look only at what's ahead" may be steering attention away from a track record that should lower confidence in the new projections.

Finally, the framing can be used rhetorically to make continuation sound like the only rational choice, when the real comparison should include alternatives such as abandoning the project, selling it, or redeploying the people and capital elsewhere. An incremental return that looks attractive in isolation may still be worse than the best available alternative.

The safeguards are fairly straightforward. Decision-makers should verify that anything treated as sunk truly has no salvage or alternative-use value, require a full life-cycle analysis of the project alongside the incremental one, approve staged projects against a complete budget rather than one slice at a time, and use past cost overruns to stress-test future estimates. Conducting post-audits of completed projects also helps, because it makes clear who forecast well and who didn't. Used honestly, ignoring sunk costs leads to better decisions; used strategically, it can make a weak investment look far better than it is.

A computer scientist is someone who has trained in computer science, the field that examines the theoretical underpinnings of information and computation, along with how these ideas are put into practice and used in computing systems. These professionals design, build, and evaluate the software, hardware, and algorithms that make computers operate. They also apply computing tools to tackle problems in science, engineering, and business. Their work spans many areas, such as artificial intelligence, software engineering, computer systems and networks, data science, and human-computer interaction. Some also help create emerging technologies like virtual reality, machine learning, and the Internet of Things. Beyond technical expertise, computer scientists typically bring strong problem-solving, analytical, and communication abilities to their work. They can be found in universities, private companies, or government agencies, where they may take part in research, development, or teaching.

QFC is a grocery chain owned by Kroger, operating primarily in the Pacific Northwest, mainly in Washington state. As of my most recent information, it had roughly 100 stores, though that number changes as locations open and close, so for the current count you should check Kroger's store locator or QFC's website.

There are a handful of approaches for moving money from a website you run into your UK bank account. One is to rely on a payment processor such as PayPal or Stripe, which many sites use to process online payments; these providers can send the funds from your site to your UK account. Another is to connect your bank account straight to the website, if the platform supports it, so that money can be transferred directly from the site to your bank. A third option is a money transfer service that focuses on moving funds between countries, such as TransferWise or Xoom, which can also get your website earnings into your UK account. Keep in mind that these services often carry fees, so weigh the costs carefully before deciding how to move your money.

Simulation-based optimization tackles optimization problems by running computer simulations to assess how well various candidate solutions perform. The technique is especially helpful when the objective function or constraints are hard or impossible to write in analytical form, or when the problem concerns complex systems or processes that resist straightforward mathematical modeling. A computer model of the system or process in question produces simulated results for each candidate solution, and the optimization algorithm relies on those results to steer its search toward the best option. The main benefit is that the algorithm can explore a broad range of potential solutions instead of being restricted to those that can be stated analytically. The approach is widely used in fields such as engineering, operations research, and economics, and it can address many kinds of problems, among them resource allocation, scheduling, logistics, and design. A number of algorithms and strategies are available for this purpose, including evolutionary algorithms, genetic algorithms, simulated annealing, and particle swarm optimization. In general, these methods search iteratively for better solutions, with the simulated outcomes directing the search toward improved results.

It's great that you're thinking about how to make the most of a small amount of money. There are a few directions you could go. You could save it in an emergency fund or a high-yield savings account, which gives you a cushion for surprise bills and keeps the cash easy to reach. If you're comfortable with some risk and can leave the money alone for a while, you could put it into a diversified mix of stocks, bonds, or mutual funds. That can grow more over time, but it can also lose value, so don't go in expecting a sure thing. If you're carrying high-interest debt, like credit card balances or a personal loan, paying some of it down is often a solid move since you'll cut the interest you're paying every month and shrink what you owe overall. And if you don't have any pressing goals or bills, you could always spend it on something you've been wanting. Just pause and ask yourself whether it's really worth it, and try not to blow the whole thing. What makes the most sense really depends on your situation, so it might help to sketch out a quick budget and see where the money does the most good for you.

Overlapping toes are usually a mild, mostly cosmetic or positional problem, and most cases are managed without surgery. The usual approach starts with conservative care. Shoes with a wide, deep toe box and soft materials reduce pressure and friction. Silicone or foam toe separators and padding between the toes can help keep them apart and protect the skin. Gentle taping or strapping, which a podiatrist or physiotherapist can teach, may hold the toes in a better alignment, especially in infants and young children whose feet are still soft and flexible. Regular inspection of the skin between the toes is important, since overlapping areas can develop calluses, blisters, or infections, and nail care needs attention because ingrown nails are common in these toes.

Surgery is generally reserved for toes that are rigid, painful, causing skin breakdown, or interfering with walking or shoe fitting. When it is needed, it is often delayed until the child is older, partly because the foot is still growing. The procedure may involve releasing tight soft tissue or tendons, correcting bone alignment, or in some cases removing a small piece of bone or the involved joint.

Because the deformity is bilateral and the child is undernourished and small for age, a thorough medical evaluation would be appropriate. Overlapping toes can occur as an isolated finding, but they are also seen in some genetic and connective tissue conditions, and poor growth can point to an underlying systemic problem. Nutritional status should be assessed and addressed, and the child should be referred to a pediatrician, and possibly a genetics service or pediatric orthopedics, for further workup. As a student, documenting the findings and sharing your concerns with your supervising nurse would be a sound step.

It's essential to address shin pain promptly so it doesn't get worse or lead to further injury. There are several steps you can take to ease the discomfort and swelling in your lower leg. First, rest by steering clear of high-impact activities like running or tennis until the pain fades. Second, apply an ice pack wrapped in a towel to your shin for 15 to 20 minutes at a time, repeating several times daily; this can lessen swelling and dull the pain by numbing the area. Third, wrap the area with an elastic bandage or wear a compression sock to reduce swelling and provide support. Fourth, keep your shin raised above heart level to help draw off excess fluid. Finally, over-the-counter nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), such as ibuprofen or naproxen, can help ease pain and inflammation. If the pain lasts or becomes severe, see a doctor for an accurate diagnosis and proper treatment, since it could be a shin splint or a stress fracture, both of which need more targeted care.

Lisp (short for "List Processing Language") is a family of languages built around lists, and they're famous for treating code as data. It's one of the oldest programming languages around, going back to the late 1950s. It's dynamically typed and homoiconic, meaning source code and data both look like lists, so you can manipulate code with the same tools you'd use on any other data. That makes Lisp programs pretty concise and expressive. It's had a long run in AI research and has shaped a lot of other languages. People still use it today, though it's nowhere near as popular as some newer options. You'll mostly see it in projects that need a lot of flexibility, like machine learning, natural language processing, and symbolic computing.

Basically, a medical diagnosis is just figuring out what's causing someone's symptoms. Usually that's a doctor, nurse practitioner, or physician assistant who does a physical exam, asks about your medical history, and maybe orders some tests. The goal is to pin down the specific condition or disease behind the symptoms so you can actually get the right treatment.

It tends to go in a few steps. First comes gathering info, so they take a thorough history, examine you, and look over any records or test results you've got. Then they start identifying the problem. They think through what it could be and narrow the list down to the most likely options. After that, if they need to be sure, they'll confirm it with more tests, like bloodwork, imaging (X-rays, CT scans), or other procedures. Once the diagnosis is confirmed, they'll recommend a treatment plan that fits whatever you've been diagnosed with.

It's not always that clean, though. Sometimes it takes several rounds, and a few different healthcare professionals might weigh in. And sometimes the answer just isn't obvious right away, so you end up needing more testing or a follow-up visit.

Tracking your personal finances with accounting has a lot going for it. For one, it makes planning easier. Once you see what's coming in and going out, you can spot where you might cut back or realize you need more income to hit your goals. It also makes you more aware of your spending habits, which helps you make smarter choices down the road. Knowing exactly where you stand lets you decide how to put your money to work, whether that means opening a retirement account or saving up for a house down payment. A good record also makes budgeting much less of a guessing game, since you can see which categories are eating your cash and move money around accordingly. And if something goes sideways, like a job loss or a surprise medical bill, you'll be in a much better spot. When you already know your savings and debt levels, you can handle a setback without scrambling.

The answer depends heavily on what kind of company you work for and what form the equity takes, so the first thing to find out is whether you're being offered stock options, restricted stock units, or actual shares. Options give you the right to buy shares at a fixed price, called the strike price, so they only have value if the company's share price rises above that. RSUs are a promise of shares delivered to you later, usually as they vest, and they are taxed as income when they arrive. Restricted stock or outright grants are less common but come with their own tax wrinkles, including something called an 83(b) election in the US that can matter a lot.

Expect a vesting schedule. The most common setup is four years with a one-year cliff, meaning you get nothing if you leave before year one, then 25 percent at the cliff, and the rest monthly or quarterly afterward. Ask whether vesting accelerates if the company is acquired, and what happens to unvested equity if you're laid off.

Pay attention to the numbers that give the grant meaning. A grant of 10,000 shares is meaningless without knowing the total number of shares outstanding, which tells you your ownership percentage. For options, ask for the strike price, the most recent valuation, and the preferred versus common share distinction, since investors often have liquidation preferences that come ahead of you. Ask about dilution from future funding rounds too.

If the company is private, be realistic about liquidity. Your shares may be worth nothing in practice until an IPO, acquisition, or tender offer, which can take many years or never happen. Many startup equity packages end up worthless, so treat it as a lottery ticket on top of fair salary rather than a substitute for it. Also ask about the post-termination exercise window. Many companies give you only 90 days after leaving to buy your vested options, which can require a large cash outlay and a tax bill on shares you can't sell. Some companies offer longer windows, and that's worth negotiating.

Taxes deserve attention before you act. In the US, incentive stock options and non-qualified options are taxed differently, and exercising ISOs can trigger the alternative minimum tax. RSUs at public companies are taxed at vest, often with shares withheld to cover it. A session with a tax professional before exercising is usually money well spent.

If the company is public, things are simpler: RSUs vest and you can generally sell, though there may be trading windows and blackout periods.

You can and often should negotiate. Ask about the size of the grant, the vesting terms, refresh grants, and the exercise window. Request the equity plan document and grant agreement in writing and read them, since the details there override what anyone tells you verbally.

If you tell me the company type, the kind of equity, and your country, I can get more specific.

A fever that keeps coming back after a few days, and returned after antibiotics a couple of weeks ago, means something is still going on. Fevers are the body's response to an infection or inflammation, and when one returns repeatedly, it usually means the cause hasn't been fully identified or treated. Common possibilities at this age include ear infections, urinary tract infections, pneumonia (sometimes not obvious at first), sinus or throat infections, or a viral illness that is causing a longer course. Less often, the fever can come from an abscess, a problem with the immune system, or an infection that needs different treatment. Teething doesn't cause fevers over 101 degrees. Only a doctor can tell which of these it is, which is why the fever needs to be looked at again.

Please call your pediatrician today, and don't wait for the fever to break on its own. Tell them exactly what you've told me: the fever has lasted four days, it returns after the medicine wears off, and it happened before and went away with antibiotics. They may want to see him in person, check his ears, lungs, and urine, and possibly run tests. If you can't reach the office, or it's after hours, go to an urgent care or emergency room.

Go to the emergency room right away if he has any of the following: a temperature of 104°F (40°C) or higher that doesn't come down with medicine, unusual sleepiness or difficulty waking, limp or floppy movement, trouble breathing or fast breathing, a rash that doesn't fade when pressed, a seizure, repeated vomiting, a soft or bulging spot on top of his head, a stiff neck, or very few wet diapers (fewer than about three in 24 hours) or refusing to drink.

For the medicine, alternating acetaminophen (Tylenol) and ibuprofen (Motrin) is generally acceptable at his age, but dose strictly by his current weight and the label or your doctor's instructions, and keep track of the times you give each one so you don't give too much. Never give aspirin to a child. Medicine can lower the fever, but it doesn't treat the underlying cause, so a fever that keeps returning needs medical evaluation even if he seems to improve between doses.

The UK government has made several changes to tax relief for private landlords over the past decade, and the most significant shift concerns mortgage interest. Until April 2017, landlords could deduct all of their finance costs from rental income before calculating income tax. From April 2017, this was phased out and replaced with a basic rate tax reduction of 20 per cent of the finance costs. The change was introduced gradually over four years, with the full restriction applying from April 2020. The effect is that higher and additional rate taxpayers, who previously gained relief at 40 or 45 per cent, now receive only a 20 per cent credit, which can push some landlords into a higher tax bracket because their rental profit is calculated before interest relief.

Alongside this, the government abolished the 10 per cent wear and tear allowance for furnished residential properties in April 2016. Landlords can now claim the actual cost of replacing furnishings, or use a replacement of domestic items relief, which covers the cost of replacing items such as beds, sofas, and kitchen appliances, but not improvements.

Stamp Duty Land Tax also changed. From April 2016, a higher surcharge of 3 per cent applies to purchases of additional residential properties, including buy-to-let homes and second homes, on top of the standard residential rates. This surcharge was temporarily reduced during the pandemic and in later years, so the current rate should be checked against official HMRC guidance before any purchase.

Finally, the Renters' Reform and wider policy discussions have focused on tenancy rules rather than tax, but landlords should also monitor the Chancellor's budgets, since allowances, rates, and reliefs are reviewed regularly. Because these rules are complex and change often, landlords are advised to check the latest position on GOV.UK or consult a qualified accountant, particularly where they hold multiple properties or are close to a tax threshold.

Yeah, as a UK resident you can totally freelance for a Swiss company. There's nothing stopping you. A few things are worth sorting out first, though.

Tax is the big one. Since you're living in the UK, you'll owe UK tax on what you earn. But Switzerland might want a piece too if you're actually providing the services over there, so it's worth paying a tax professional to look at your situation and make sure you're covered on both sides.

Then there's the contract. Read it properly and get clear on payment terms, how long it runs, and any other obligations you're signing up for. Get it all in writing so nobody ends up arguing later about what was agreed.

Last thing is communication. If you're working remotely, set up a clear way of keeping in touch with them early on. That way you know you're meeting their expectations, and if something goes wrong it gets sorted quickly instead of dragging on.

It can be a really good gig, and the money can be great, but do your homework and make sure you're following all the rules on both ends.

American English is the version of the English language spoken in the United States. Although it resembles British English, the variety used in the United Kingdom, the two differ in their vocabulary, spelling, and pronunciation. For instance, Americans say "elevator" where the British say "lift," and "soccer" where the British say "football," while the Americans' "football" is the British "american football" equivalent. Likewise, what the British call "chips," Americans call "french fries." Spelling also varies: the word "colour" in British English becomes "color" in American English, and where British writers often use an "s" in words like "organise," Americans typically write a "z," producing "organize." Pronunciation differs as well. Americans pronounce the vowels in "cot" and "caught" differently, whereas British speakers generally pronounce them alike. Furthermore, Americans usually sound the "r" in words such as "hard" and "hark," while British speech often drops it. On the whole, American English is a varied and evolving language shaped by many linguistic and cultural influences, and millions of people worldwide speak it, making it a significant part of American culture.

Film ratings are assigned by bodies such as the Motion Picture Association of America (MPAA) and the British Board of Film Classification (BBFC). Their reviewers view the picture and determine which audience age range it fits, based on what it contains. A film may carry the label "not yet rated" because it hasn't yet been submitted to these raters, since it may still be in production. The process can take some time, as reviewers must watch the whole film and then deliberate with colleagues before agreeing on a rating. In short, "not yet rated" simply means the rating body hasn't reviewed the film yet, and a rating will be issued before it reaches cinemas or home viewers.

Honestly, there are a ton of reasons people don't save more, and a lot of them overlap.

The big one is just not making enough. If your paycheck barely covers the basics, there's nothing left to put aside, no matter how disciplined you are. And even people who earn a decent amount get squeezed by housing, food, and transportation, which eat up most of it before you can blink.

Debt is another huge thing. When you're stuck paying off credit cards or student loans, it feels like you can't start saving until those are gone, and that can take years.

Then there's the knowledge side. Plenty of people never really learned how to save or how to make their money work for them, so they don't know where to start. Some folks also just lean toward short-term thinking, like spending on stuff that feels good now instead of worrying about the future. It's human nature, really.

And finally, surprise expenses. If you haven't built up a cushion, a medical emergency or a car repair can wipe out whatever you did manage to save, or push you right into debt.

So it's usually a mix of these, and if you're trying to improve your own saving habits, it helps to figure out which ones are actually hitting you.

If an option's whole price is made up of its intrinsic value, people call it "in the money." That means exercising it would hand you an immediate profit equal to that intrinsic value. You won't necessarily walk away with a profit, though, since you've only got a guarantee of not losing money. And don't forget the expiration date: you have to exercise before it runs out, or the intrinsic value is gone and the option just expires worthless. Even when it's in the money, the underlying asset could still drop in price, so if you exercise and then sell that asset, you could still end up losing money.

Yeah, it's tough when co-owners can't agree on selling. I'd start by just talking it out. Sit down and get into why one person wants to sell and the other doesn't, and see if there's some middle ground that works for everybody. Sometimes the real issue isn't the sale itself, and once that comes out you can find another way forward.

If talking doesn't get you anywhere, you could bring in a neutral third party. That's what mediation and arbitration are for. They help the two sides reach a resolution without it turning into a total mess.

And if that fails too, there's always a legal partition, where the court basically splits the property into separate ownership interests. Fair warning, it can get complicated, so you'll probably want an attorney to walk you through it.

Really, what's best depends on your situation and what each of you is after. Talking to an attorney or some other neutral person early on can help you figure out which route makes the most sense.

Solar panels turn sunlight into electricity using tiny particles of light and a special kind of material. Sunlight is made of little packets of energy, and when those packets hit a solar panel, they knock loose some tiny bits of stuff inside it called electrons. The panel is built with two layers of special material arranged so that the loose electrons are pushed to flow in one direction, like kids lining up and walking down a hallway together. When many electrons flow along a wire, that flow is electricity, and it can power lights, toys, and the fridge in the kitchen.

Civil engineering is the branch of engineering concerned with designing, building, and maintaining the physical infrastructure that society relies on. It is one of the oldest engineering disciplines, and its scope covers the structures and systems that shape everyday life, such as roads, bridges, tunnels, dams, railways, airports, water supply networks, sewage systems, and large buildings.

At its core, civil engineering applies principles of physics, mathematics, and materials science to ensure that these structures are safe, durable, functional, and economical. Engineers in this field analyze how loads such as weight, wind, earthquakes, and water pressure affect a structure, and they choose materials like concrete, steel, timber, and asphalt accordingly. They also consider environmental factors, so that projects minimize harm to ecosystems and manage resources like water and land responsibly.

The field is usually divided into several specializations. Structural engineers focus on the strength and stability of buildings and bridges. Geotechnical engineers study soil and rock to determine how the ground will support foundations and slopes. Transportation engineers plan and design roads, railways, and traffic systems. Water resources engineers manage rivers, flood control, and drinking water and wastewater systems. Environmental engineers address pollution control and sustainability, while construction engineers oversee the planning and execution of building projects.

Civil engineers typically work on a project from start to finish: they survey and study a site, develop designs using software and technical standards, estimate costs, coordinate with architects, contractors, and government agencies, and then monitor construction to make sure the work meets specifications. Because their work affects public safety and well-being, civil engineers are usually required to hold a degree in the field and, in many countries, a professional license.

Bird poop isn't really white because birds are special in color; it's white because of how birds get rid of waste. Mammals, like us and dogs, pee and poop as separate things. Their urine is watery and their poop is solid, and the brown color in poop comes from bile and broken-down blood cells, which get processed by the liver and gut.

Birds don't have a separate bathroom. Everything comes out through one opening called the cloaca, so pee and poop leave together. To save weight so they can fly, birds turn the waste they make into a thick paste, and they pull most of the water out of it before it leaves their body. The part that is pure white is uric acid, a substance birds use to store nitrogen waste. Uric acid doesn't dissolve in water well, so it comes out as a white chalky paste. The darker parts you sometimes see in bird droppings are the leftover poop bits mixed in.

So the white color is simply the leftover from how birds handle their pee, and the brown in other animals is from the digestive stuff in their poop.

Changes in an infant's stool color, texture, and how often they pass it are quite common. Many things can cause these shifts, including what the baby eats, certain medications, and infections. Even so, if you're worried about your baby's stool, it's always wise to consult a healthcare provider. Eczema, by contrast, is a skin condition marked by inflammation and itchiness, and it doesn't usually affect how stool looks or feels. An infant with eczema could still have an infection or another medical issue that alters their stool, but eczema alone is unlikely to be the reason for green stool. If your baby has other symptoms alongside the green stool, or if you have broader concerns about their health, you should reach out to a healthcare professional, who can evaluate your child and recommend treatment if necessary.

You may have dermatitis, a broad label for skin inflammation. Many things can trigger it, such as allergic reactions, exposure to irritating substances, or an underlying health problem. A dermatologist can determine the exact cause and recommend the right treatment, so an appointment is worthwhile. Until then, an over-the-counter cream containing hydrocortisone may ease the dryness and itchiness. Wearing loose-fitting clothes, keeping the area clean, and making sure it stays dry can also help. However, if the rash becomes painful, spreads quickly, or is accompanied by a fever or other symptoms, you should contact a doctor immediately.

A solar eclipse happens when the Moon passes directly between the Earth and the Sun, casting its shadow onto part of Earth's surface. Because the Moon has to be on the same side of Earth as the Sun, solar eclipses can only occur during a new moon, the phase when the Moon's sunlit side faces away from us.

There isn't an eclipse at every new moon, though, because the Moon's orbit is tilted about five degrees relative to the plane of Earth's orbit around the Sun. Most months the Moon passes slightly above or below the Sun from our point of view. An eclipse only happens when a new moon falls near one of the two points where the Moon's orbit crosses Earth's orbital plane, called the nodes. The Sun lines up with these nodes roughly twice a year, creating windows of about five weeks known as eclipse seasons. Because these seasons shift slightly earlier each year, eclipses don't happen in the same months every year.

As a result, there are at least two and at most five solar eclipses each year somewhere on Earth. They come in several types. A total eclipse occurs when the Moon completely covers the Sun. An annular eclipse happens when the Moon is farther from Earth and appears too small to cover the Sun fully, leaving a bright ring. A partial eclipse occurs when the alignment is imperfect or when you're outside the path of the Moon's central shadow. A rare hybrid eclipse shifts between total and annular along its path.

Any single location on Earth sees a total solar eclipse only about once every 375 years on average, which is why people often travel long distances to see one. Astronomers can predict eclipses centuries in advance, so if you want to know about upcoming ones, NASA's eclipse website and similar resources list dates and paths of visibility.

Yeah, you can use a mortgage to pay off other debts, not just to buy the house. People usually call this a cash-out refinance. Basically you borrow more than you still owe on your current mortgage and pocket the difference to clear other stuff, like credit cards.

Say your mortgage balance is $200,000 and you've got $50,000 in credit card debt. You could refinance for $250,000. The $200,000 pays off your old mortgage, and the extra $50,000 goes to the cards. Easy math, but the catch is you've now got a bigger loan secured by your house.

It's not for everyone, though. It can be a handy way to consolidate debt, but you're turning unsecured debt into debt tied to your home, and that's a real risk if money gets tight. Rates on cash-out refis also tend to run a bit higher than standard mortgages, so check the numbers carefully. Before you commit, talk to a financial advisor or a mortgage lender who can look at your actual situation and tell you whether it makes sense.

The Millennium Prize Problems are seven mathematical problems that the Clay Mathematics Institute, a private nonprofit based in Cambridge, Massachusetts, announced in 2000. The institute chose them as especially deep and important questions that had resisted solution for decades, and it offered a prize of one million US dollars for the correct solution of each one. The problems span several areas of mathematics, including number theory, algebra, geometry, and mathematical physics.

The seven problems are the Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture, which relates the number of rational points on an elliptic curve to the behavior of an associated function; the Hodge conjecture, which concerns how certain geometric shapes can be built from simpler pieces; the Navier-Stokes existence and smoothness problem, which asks whether solutions to the equations describing fluid flow always remain well behaved; the P versus NP problem, which asks whether every problem whose solution can be quickly checked can also be quickly solved, and which is central to computer science; the Poincaré conjecture, which concerns the characterization of the three-dimensional sphere; the Riemann hypothesis, which predicts where the nontrivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function lie and has deep consequences for the distribution of prime numbers; and the Yang-Mills existence and mass gap problem, which asks for a rigorous mathematical foundation for a quantum field theory that underlies particle physics.

Only one of the seven has been resolved so far. Grigori Perelman proved the Poincaré conjecture in 2002 and 2003, building on Richard Hamilton's work on Ricci flow. The Clay Institute awarded him the prize in 2010, but Perelman declined both the money and the associated recognition. The other six problems remain open, and a correct solution to any of them would earn the million-dollar prize, subject to publication in a reputable journal and a waiting period set by the institute.
Algoma, Wisconsin had a population of 3,176 at the 2010 United States Census. That figure is for the city of Algoma in Kewaunee County, on the Lake Michigan shore.

Health care refers to the services, practices, and resources that are provided to maintain, improve, diagnose, treat, or restore people's physical and mental health. It covers a wide range of activities, from routine checkups, vaccinations, and screenings that aim to prevent illness, to the treatment of injuries and diseases, to long-term management of chronic conditions such as diabetes or heart disease. It is delivered by many kinds of professionals, including doctors, nurses, pharmacists, dentists, therapists, and other specialists, and it takes place in settings such as hospitals, clinics, pharmacies, and people's own homes.

Health care systems are the organized arrangements through which these services are financed, delivered, and regulated. Different countries structure them in different ways. Some rely primarily on government-run programs that cover most residents, while others depend largely on private insurance, employer-sponsored plans, or out-of-pocket payments. Questions about access, cost, quality, and fairness are central to debates about how health care should be organized, and they remain among the most significant public policy issues in many societies.

So here's how shareholder loans and capital contributions usually work with an S-corp. Loans from the shareholder to the company show up as a liability on the S-corp's books, and the loan terms decide whether it's current or long-term. Capital contributions go into equity as paid-in capital instead. On the shareholder's side, contributions raise your basis in the S-corp, which matters for deducting losses later. A loan the corp makes to you is generally not income, but it needs to be a real loan with repayment terms, or the IRS may treat it as a distribution or wages. Keep good records of both, since they affect the tax picture for you and the company. If you've got a specific situation, a CPA or tax pro can sort out the details for your setup.

Gordon Moore helped found Intel Corporation and is best known for formulating Moore's Law. In 1965, he predicted that the number of transistors packed onto a computer chip would roughly double every two years, which would drive computing power up exponentially while bringing costs down. That forecast has held up for about fifty years and has shaped the growth of the modern computer industry in profound ways. Born in San Francisco, California, in 1929, Moore earned a bachelor's degree in chemistry from the University of California, Berkeley, in 1950. He went on to earn a doctorate in chemistry and physics from the California Institute of Technology in 1954. In 1968, he and Robert Noyce co-founded Intel. Moore led the company as CEO until 1975 and then served as chairman until 1997. For his contributions to technology, he has received many honors, among them the National Medal of Technology and Innovation and the IEEE Medal of Honor.

A Switchblade drone is a small, loitering munition, sometimes called a "kamikaze drone" or "suicide drone." It is manufactured by AeroVironment, an American company. The name comes from its folding wing design, which lets it be packed into a tube about the size of a shoulder-fired rocket launcher and then deployed quickly by a soldier. Once launched, its wings unfold and its electric motor propels it silently over a target area.

The drone is designed to be operated by infantry and special forces units at short range. It carries a small explosive warhead and a camera, so an operator can fly it, watch a live video feed, search for enemy positions or vehicles, and then crash it into a target. Some versions can also be recovered and reused if they are not used for a strike. There are two main variants: the Switchblade 300, which is a lighter model meant to target individuals and small objects, and the Switchblade 600, which is larger, carries a heavier warhead, and is intended to attack armored vehicles.

Switchblade drones have been used by the United States and some allied militaries, and they gained wide public attention during the war in Ukraine, where they were supplied to Ukrainian forces. They represent a broader trend in modern warfare toward inexpensive, portable unmanned systems that give small units precise strike capability and real-time surveillance.

Dart: The Friendly Helper Language

Dart is a computer language made by Google. Think of it like a set of building blocks that helps grown-ups make apps, the programs you tap on phones and computers. Some people say it could be a language of the future, but that's more of a hopeful guess than a settled fact. Its main reason for being exciting is a toolkit called Flutter, which also comes from Google. With Flutter and Dart, a builder can write one set of instructions and make the same app work on a phone, a tablet, a web page, and a computer. That's like writing one recipe that makes a cake in four different kitchens.

Dart is also easy to read, a bit like a picture book for computers. It can check mistakes before the app runs, so fewer surprises pop up later. And it has a trick called hot reload: when a builder changes something, they can see the change almost right away, without starting over. That makes making things feel fun and quick.

So Dart isn't magic. It's a handy, friendly tool that lets people build apps in many places with less effort, and that's why many people think it has a bright future.

Criminal organizations such as mobs and the mafia consist of people who take part in illegal enterprises, organized crime among them. Such groups can be found in any country, and they are occasionally referred to as "gangs." Historically, a number of them held considerable power and had control over many unlawful activities in the regions where they operated. Nowadays, though, law enforcement has dismantled many of these organizations, making it far harder for them to function. Although it remains possible for such groups to exist, they are neither as widespread nor as influential as they used to be.

TMZ stands for "Thirty Mile Zone." The name refers to the studio zone around Hollywood, a 30-mile radius centered on the intersection of West Beverly Boulevard and North La Cienega Boulevard in Los Angeles. Entertainment industry contracts, including those for union workers, have historically used this zone to define where film and television crews work and how they are paid, with travel pay and other rules changing for work outside that radius.

The celebrity news website TMZ launched in 2005 as a joint venture between AOL and Telepictures, and it took its name from that industry term as a nod to its focus on covering stars and happenings within the Hollywood entertainment world. Harvey Levin, a former attorney and TV legal reporter, founded it and has long been its public face. The brand later expanded into a syndicated TV show, TMZ Live, and other programming, and it is now owned by Fox Corporation.

Imagine your enemy's country is a big playground where all the kids trade toys using special stickers. Now imagine you sneak in and hand out millions of extra stickers. It sounds like it would wreck their playground, and it can, a little. But here are the reasons it's much harder and less useful than it seems.

First, making perfect copies is very hard. Real money has special paper, color-shifting ink, tiny hidden patterns, and security threads, and the people who make it keep upgrading these tricks. Even countries with lots of resources have only managed "super notes" that get caught by banks and machines over time. Once people know fakes are around, they get careful, and the fakes get thrown out or tracked down.

Second, you would need an enormous amount. A big economy has trillions of dollars' worth of money moving around. To push prices up noticeably, you would have to print and sneak in a mountain of fake bills, and getting that much into the country without anyone noticing is nearly impossible. A small number of fakes is just a nuisance, like a few extra stickers on a huge playground.

Third, a lot of money today isn't paper at all. Most of it lives in bank computers as numbers. You can't hand out fake numbers in a bank account. Cash is only a small slice of the whole, so flooding the country with paper barely touches the main system.

Fourth, the playground boss fights back. The enemy's central bank can change the design of the bills, call in the old ones, tighten the rules, and adjust interest rates to cool prices down. They can also work with police and other countries to hunt down where the fakes come from.

Fifth, it can backfire on you. Counterfeiting another country's money is treated as an attack and a serious crime, and if you get caught, other nations may punish you with sanctions or worse. Also, fake money floats around the world, and some of it could come back to hurt your own people or your trade partners. Your own country's money can lose trust too, if you're known as the one cheating.

Finally, there's a history lesson. Countries have tried this before. Nazi Germany's Operation Bernhard made fake British pounds in World War II, and it didn't bring Britain down. Other attempts have caused headaches but never collapsed a large economy.

So the simple answer for The Great Leader is that the plan costs a lot, is easy to detect, barely affects digital money, can be countered, and risks big trouble for your own country. Better ways to help your nation are usually building your own strong economy and making good trade friends.

Inductive logic programming (ILP) is a branch of artificial intelligence and machine learning concerned with creating algorithms and systems that can automatically derive logical rules and models from data. Its aim is to learn logical rules that can predict outcomes or categorize instances according to a collection of input features. Such rules are usually written in a logical formalism like first-order or propositional logic, and they are acquired from examples or training data through an inductive procedure. At its core, ILP combines logical reasoning with induction to extract rules from data. Induction means drawing general principles or patterns out of specific observations or instances. Within ILP, this involves analyzing a set of training examples to derive logical rules that can then be applied to predict or classify new cases. ILP has been used across many fields, such as natural language processing, biomedical informatics, and robotics. It has also helped develop expert and knowledge-based systems in areas like medicine and biology.

Chest tightness and a left arm ache for two weeks in a 17-year-old are most often caused by something non-cardiac. Common culprits include muscle strain from exercise, poor posture or sitting at a screen, inflammation of the cartilage where the ribs meet the breastbone (costochondritis), reflux, asthma, and anxiety or stress, which can cause real physical tightness and arm discomfort. A recent viral infection can also cause chest symptoms, and the swabs you had suggest the A&E team was considering that possibility.

Your normal ECG and clear blood tests are reassuring, but one ECG doesn't rule out every heart condition, particularly ones that come and go or that need an echocardiogram (heart ultrasound) or a longer-term heart rhythm monitor to detect. Because your symptoms have lasted two weeks, please book an appointment with your GP soon, even though the hospital didn't find anything. Tell them exactly what you told me: how long it has lasted, whether it's constant or comes and goes, what brings it on or eases it, and whether it's linked to exercise, breathing, eating, or stress. Ask whether you need further tests such as an echo or a monitor, and whether they'd like to check for asthma or reflux.

Seek emergency help straight away, by calling 999 or 112 or going to A&E, if you get chest pain that is severe, crushing, or squeezing, or that spreads to your jaw, neck, or back; if you have pain with breathlessness, sweating, nausea, dizziness, or fainting; if you have a racing, pounding, or irregular heartbeat that doesn't settle; or if the pain comes on with exertion and doesn't go away with rest.

Okay so "Mama Told Me (Not to Come)" was written by Randy Newman, but the version most people know is by Three Dog Night. It came out in 1970 and was a pretty big hit, making it into the top 40 on the Billboard Hot 100. What makes it stick is the bouncy, upbeat tune paired with funny lyrics. It's about a guy who really doesn't want to go to a party, since his mom warned him about all the wild stuff that goes on there.

Okay, so your relatives can cut down on what they have to pay out of pocket for your dad's estate in a few ways. First, get all the paperwork together: the will, any trust documents, property deeds, and financial statements. Keeping it all in one place makes the whole process smoother and helps avoid wasted costs. Next, they'll need an executor. That person runs the estate and makes sure everything goes to the people your dad wanted, so it's worth picking someone organized, responsible, and trustworthy. That can head off a lot of headaches and extra expenses. They should also list every asset, from property and investments to personal stuff, and figure out what each one is worth so things can be divided properly. Then there are the debts. The executor should pay off whatever your dad owed when he died, like credit cards, the mortgage, and any other bills, because leaving those hanging only adds to the cost. A financial planner can be a big help too. They can walk your relatives through the decisions and make sure things get split up the way your dad intended, ideally in a tax-friendly way.
