Pelvic pressure by itself doesn't cause premature birth, but it can sometimes be a sign that something is happening that could lead to it, so it's worth taking seriously and getting checked rather than waiting it out.

In a second pregnancy, pelvic pressure is very common and usually harmless. The baby's weight, stretched ligaments, and muscles and joints that have already been through one pregnancy all tend to make the pressure show up earlier and feel stronger than it did the first time. Round ligament pain, the baby sitting low, constipation, and urinary tract infections can all feel like pressure too. Many women are surprised by how different a second pregnancy feels, so the fact that you had no symptoms the first time doesn't mean something is wrong now.

That said, pressure can also be a warning sign of preterm labor or of a cervix that is softening or opening early (sometimes called cervical insufficiency). Family history can play a role too. Premature birth running in your family, especially on your side of the family tree, is a recognized risk factor worth mentioning to your provider, though a father's side history is considered a weaker link than your own or your mother's history, and it certainly doesn't mean it will happen to you. Being under 20 is also a minor risk factor on its own.

Since you're not at full term, please call your doctor, midwife, or the labor and delivery unit soon, and tell them exactly what you told me, including the family history. They can check your cervix, sometimes with an ultrasound measurement of its length, and test for infection. If it's all fine, you'll have peace of mind, and if not, there are treatments that can help, such as progesterone or monitoring.

Go in the same day if you notice any of these: regular or tightening contractions, more than about four to six in an hour, lower back pain that comes and goes, cramping like period pain, a change in vaginal discharge (watery, mucus-like, or bloody), leaking fluid, or reduced baby movement. Also go in if the pressure feels like the baby is pushing down or is getting steadily worse.

Don't worry about bothering anyone. Providers would much rather check a false alarm than miss early labor, and pressure like this is a completely legitimate reason to call.

Stainless steel doesn't really stain the way a T-shirt does. It's actually very good at resisting rust and stains, but it has a weakness: it shows fingerprints, water spots, and smudges very easily, and that makes it look dirty even when it's clean.

Here's the simple idea. Stainless steel is mostly regular steel mixed with a bit of chromium. The chromium makes a super thin, invisible layer on the surface that protects the metal from rusting. That layer is what keeps it shiny and strong. But the surface is also not perfectly smooth. It has tiny grooves and lines left over from how it was made and polished, and those little bumps and grooves catch oils from your skin, grease from cooking, and tiny bits of water. When light hits all those oily or wet spots, they show up as marks.

Water is a big culprit. When water dries, it leaves behind minerals from the water, which look like cloudy spots. Cooking oil and fingerprints do the same thing by catching dust and reflecting light differently.

The good news is that it's usually not permanent. A soft microfiber cloth with a little warm water or a few drops of dish soap will clean most marks. For a nice shine, use a stainless steel cleaner or a tiny bit of olive oil or baby oil on a cloth, and always wipe in the direction of the grain, which is the faint lines you can see on the surface. Avoid harsh scrubbing pads, which can scratch the finish and make future smudges show even more.

A domain ontology is a formal, structured description of the concepts, entities, properties, and relationships that exist within a specific field of knowledge or area of activity, such as medicine, finance, law, or manufacturing. It defines the vocabulary used in that domain and the rules that govern how those terms relate to one another, so that people and computer systems can share a common, unambiguous understanding of the subject matter.

The purpose of a domain ontology is to capture what is meaningful within a particular field. For example, an ontology for healthcare might define terms like "patient," "diagnosis," "medication," and "treatment," specify that a patient can have many diagnoses, and state that a medication must be prescribed by a licensed practitioner. By making these definitions explicit and machine-readable, the ontology helps reduce confusion between different organizations or software systems that might otherwise use the same words to mean different things.

Domain ontologies are typically built using formal languages such as OWL (Web Ontology Language) or RDF Schema, which allow logical reasoning over the stored knowledge. They are widely used in areas like semantic web applications, knowledge management, data integration, artificial intelligence, and information retrieval. A domain ontology is distinguished from a more general, or upper-level, ontology in that it focuses narrowly on one subject area rather than attempting to describe concepts that apply across all fields.

A tumor attached to an organ by a narrow stalk is usually described as pedunculated (or polypoid when it bulges into a space). That describes the tumor's shape, not a type of cancer, which is probably why your searches turned up nothing. Renal cell carcinoma can grow this way, so your friend's urologist's suspicion is reasonable. The exact type and whether it has spread will be determined by imaging such as a CT or MRI, and sometimes a biopsy.

Treatment depends mainly on the tumor's size, its stage, and whether it has spread. For a small, localized tumor, options include active surveillance (monitoring with regular scans), thermal ablation (destroying the tumor with heat or cold, usually guided by imaging), or a partial nephrectomy, which removes only the tumor and preserves as much healthy kidney as possible. For larger localized tumors, a radical nephrectomy, which removes the whole kidney, may be recommended, though partial removal is often preferred when feasible. If the cancer has spread, treatment typically involves systemic therapy, such as immunotherapy alone or combined with targeted drugs, with the choice guided by the cancer's features and the patient's overall health. Some patients with limited spread may also have surgery to remove the primary tumor along with other treatment.

Since the right approach depends heavily on details that only his care team can assess, I'd encourage your friend to ask his urologist for a referral to a urologic oncologist or a kidney cancer specialist, and to ask about the tumor's size, its exact pathology, the staging results, and all treatment options, including which ones are appropriate for him. A second opinion at a comprehensive cancer center is also worthwhile for kidney cancer.

A long, long time ago, people lived in small groups, kind of like a big family camping together. Everyone knew everyone, so if someone said "Go get Tom," there was only one Tom, and everybody knew who that was. Nobody needed a last name because there just weren't many people around to confuse.

Then, over thousands of years, people started building villages, and the villages grew into towns and cities. Now there were lots of people, and that caused a problem: there might be five different Toms! If you said "Tom owes me a chicken," everyone would ask, "Which Tom?" So people started adding a little extra description to tell them apart.

These extra descriptions usually came from a few simple ideas. Sometimes they talked about who your dad was, so Tom whose father was John became "Tom Johnson," meaning John's son. Sometimes they talked about your job, so Tom who made horseshoes and tools from metal became "Tom Smith," and Tom who baked bread became "Tom Baker." Sometimes they talked about where you lived, so Tom who lived by the hill became "Tom Hill," and Tom who lived near the woods became "Tom Wood." And sometimes they described what you looked like or how you acted, so Tom with brown hair might become "Tom Brown," and a very small Tom might be "Tom Little."

At first, these extra names didn't stick. Tom Baker's son might be a farmer, so he'd get a different name. But later, rulers and governments wanted to keep track of everybody, mostly so they could collect taxes and know who owned which land. They started writing names down in big books, and it was much easier if a family kept the same name over and over. So kids began keeping their parents' last name, even if they didn't bake bread or live by a hill anymore. That's how it became a family name that gets passed down.

This happened at different times in different places. China started using family names thousands of years ago, while in England it became common less than a thousand years ago, and some countries, like Iceland, still mostly use the "son of" or "daughter of" style instead of a fixed family name.

As for first names, people have probably had those for a very, very long time, maybe as long as people have been talking, because even in a small group you need a way to call someone over. Last names came much later, when there were simply too many people to keep straight.

"Heroes," the NBC science fiction drama created by Tim Kring, ran for four seasons, premiering in September 2006 and concluding in February 2010. A fifth season was planned but was cancelled before it could be produced, which is why the series ended after four. There was also a 2015 revival titled "Heroes Reborn," which ran for a single season on NBC.

The Netflix Prize was a open competition launched by the online DVD and streaming company Netflix in October 2006. Its goal was to improve the accuracy of Netflix's recommendation system, known as Cinematch, which predicted how much a user would enjoy a movie based on their past ratings. Netflix offered a grand prize of one million dollars to any team that could beat Cinematch's prediction accuracy by at least 10 percent, measured by root mean squared error on a held-out test set of ratings.

To support the contest, Netflix released a large dataset of roughly 100 million anonymized movie ratings from about 480,000 subscribers across nearly 18,000 films. Teams from around the world, including both academic researchers and hobbyists, submitted algorithms, and the competition drew enormous attention and participation. Progress was tracked on a public leaderboard, and a "progress prize" of 50,000 dollars was awarded annually to the leading team that had not yet reached the full goal.

The competition ended in 2009 when a combined team called BellKor's Pragmatic Chaos surpassed the 10 percent threshold, and it received the million-dollar prize. The contest is widely remembered for accelerating research in collaborative filtering and matrix factorization techniques, which influenced recommendation systems across many industries. It also became noteworthy for a privacy controversy: researchers showed that the supposedly anonymized data could sometimes be linked to individuals using information from public sources such as IMDb reviews. Following a lawsuit, Netflix canceled a planned second competition.

Born in Haifa, Israel, he earned his doctorate in history at the University of Oxford. Today he holds a professorship at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, where he teaches world history. Beyond his scholarly work, he is also a sought-after public speaker, appearing at conferences and events across the globe. Readers and critics have widely praised his books for their lucidity, depth, and skill in presenting intricate ideas to general audiences. They have been published in over 50 languages and have sold millions of copies around the world.

There's no single right answer, since it depends on your interest rates, employer benefits, and how secure your income is, but there's a sensible order most people can follow. Start with the emergency fund, typically three to six months of essential expenses in a readily accessible savings account. Without it, an unexpected job loss or medical bill can force you to borrow at high rates or sell investments at a bad time, which undermines everything else you're trying to do. If your income is unstable or you have dependents, aim for the higher end of that range.

Once you have that cushion, prioritize any retirement contributions that your employer matches. A match is effectively an immediate return on your money, often 50 to 100 percent, which beats almost anything else you could do with it. Beyond the match, retirement accounts with tax advantages are generally worth funding, especially if you're early in your career, since compound growth over decades is powerful.

Paying extra on your mortgage makes the most sense once those steps are covered and your mortgage rate is fairly high, say above 6 or 7 percent, or if you value the guaranteed, risk-free return and the peace of mind that comes with owning your home outright. If your mortgage rate is low, you may do better investing the extra money, since long-run stock returns have historically been higher, though with more volatility and no guarantee.

So a practical sequence is: build the emergency fund, capture any employer match, then split extra money between retirement investing and mortgage payoff based on your mortgage rate and how much risk and peace of mind matter to you. If you share your rough numbers, such as your mortgage rate, savings, and employer match, I can help you think through the specific tradeoff. A fee-only financial planner can also give tailored advice.

An Army specialist is an enlisted rank in the United States Army, designated E-4. It sits above Private First Class (E-3) and below Corporal (E-4 in some branches, though Corporal is a non-commissioned officer rank in the Marine Corps and some Army career paths) and Sergeant (E-5). In the Army, specialist is a rank that is also a career track: soldiers who advance to it are recognized for technical skill and competence in their job, or military occupational specialty (MOS), such as mechanic, medic, or intelligence analyst, rather than for supervisory duties. Specialists are generally expected to master their specific job and may begin to take on some responsibility for training junior soldiers, but leadership of a squad or team typically comes with promotion to sergeant. The rank is commonly abbreviated as SPC, and it is often the first rank where a soldier has completed initial training and has a few years of service behind them.

You may be dealing with patellar subluxation or dislocation, a condition in which the kneecap (patella) slips out of its usual place in the groove at the front of the thigh bone (femur). This can lead to pain, a feeling of instability, and trouble walking. Other conditions that could explain pain and difficulty walking related to air in the knee joint include: a knee joint effusion, meaning a buildup of extra fluid inside the joint, which may result from inflammation, an injury, or another underlying problem; a fracture, or break, in one of the knee's bones, such as the patella, femur, or tibia (shinbone); torn knee ligaments, such as the anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) or medial collateral ligament (MCL); and osteoarthritis, a degenerative joint disease that can cause pain and make walking difficult. It is important to see a doctor for an accurate diagnosis and suitable treatment, since the approach will depend on the exact cause of your symptoms. In the meantime, avoid activities that provoke pain and apply ice to the area to help ease swelling and inflammation.

A deep belief network (DBN) is a kind of artificial neural network employed for unsupervised learning. Its architecture consists of several stacked layers of interconnected "hidden" units, where every successive layer acquires the ability to pick out more abstract features from the raw input. DBNs are initially trained through a procedure known as unsupervised pretraining, during which each layer learns to rebuild the input it receives, relying on a method called contrastive divergence. After this pretraining stage, the network can be refined with supervised techniques, such as backpropagation, so that it handles a particular job like image classification or language translation. Such networks have found use in many areas, including image recognition, natural language processing, and speech recognition. They are especially effective when working with vast quantities of unlabeled data, since they can identify useful features within that data and apply them to form predictions or decisions.

Adversarial machine learning is a branch of machine learning devoted to developing methods for training models that can withstand adversarial examples. These are inputs that have been deliberately altered so as to deceive a model and push it toward an incorrect prediction. The field matters because it helps keep machine learning systems dependable and resilient, even when they encounter malicious or accidental input. This is particularly critical in settings where a model's predictions carry serious consequences, such as cybersecurity and autonomous vehicles. Researchers have pursued a number of strategies. One is adversarial training, in which a model learns from a dataset that contains adversarial examples. Another is defensive distillation, which makes a model sturdier against such examples by using a "softened" version of the original model's output as the training label. Further strategies include using optimization algorithms to generate adversarial examples, and creating techniques to detect them and defend against them.

Dr. Joseph Boakye Danquah (1895–1965), usually known as J.B. Danquah, was a Ghanaian statesman, lawyer, scholar, and politician who is regarded as one of the founding figures of Ghanaian nationalism. He was born in Bepong, in the Kwahu area of the Gold Coast, and belonged to the Akyem Abuakwa royal family; his half-brothers included Nana Sir Ofori Atta I, a prominent paramount chief.

He studied in London, where he earned a law degree and then a doctorate in philosophy at the University of London, becoming one of the first Gold Coast Africans to receive a doctorate there. He returned to the Gold Coast in the 1920s and became active in journalism and public life. He founded the Times of West Africa, the country's first daily newspaper, in 1931, and he helped establish the Gold Coast Youth Conference, which pushed for greater African participation in governance.

His best-known role came in 1947, when he was a leading founder of the United Gold Coast Convention (UGCC), the first major political movement aimed at self-government. He invited Kwame Nkrumah home from abroad to serve as its general secretary. The two later fell out, and Nkrumah broke away in 1949 to form the Convention People's Party, which pursued immediate independence. Danquah and his allies favored a more gradual approach. After the 1948 Accra riots, he was among the "Big Six" detained by the colonial government.

Danquah is also credited with proposing the name "Ghana" for the independent country, drawing on the medieval Ghana Empire, and he wrote extensively on Akan culture, religion, and philosophy. His works include The Akan Doctrine of God and Gold Coast: Akan Laws and Customs.

After independence in 1957, he became a leading opposition figure against Nkrumah's government. He ran against Nkrumah in the 1960 presidential election and lost. He was detained under the Preventive Detention Act in 1961, released, and then detained again in 1964. He died in Nsawam Prison in February 1965, which is widely seen as a symbol of the political repression of that era. He is considered a founding father of the Ghanaian opposition tradition, and his political legacy is often associated with the modern New Patriotic Party.

What you're describing is usually called a cash-out refinance or a delayed financing mortgage, and the right path depends on how soon after the cash purchase you want to borrow.

If you want to borrow right away, look at delayed financing. Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac allow a lender to give you a mortgage on a property you bought with cash within the previous six months, and treat it like a rate-and-term refinance rather than a cash-out loan, which usually means better pricing. The conditions are that the original purchase was an arm's-length transaction, there were no mortgage liens on the property at the time of purchase, and the source of the cash can be documented, for example through bank statements, a HELOC you've since paid off, or gift funds. The new loan amount generally can't exceed what you actually paid, plus closing costs and prepaid items. You'll need your settlement statement showing the cash purchase.

If more than six months have passed, you'd apply for a regular cash-out refinance. Many conventional lenders also impose a seasoning period, often six months of ownership, though some lenders and loan types are more flexible. Loan-to-value limits are typically lower for cash-out, often 75 to 80 percent for a primary residence and lower for investment properties.

The application process itself looks like any mortgage. First, shop several lenders, since delayed financing is not offered or understood equally by all of them, and ask directly whether they do it. Second, gather documents: the closing disclosure from your cash purchase, proof of where the funds came from, two years of tax returns and W-2s or 1099s, recent pay stubs, two months of bank statements, and identification. Third, submit the application, receive a Loan Estimate within three business days, and lock your rate. Fourth, the lender orders an appraisal and title work, and underwriting reviews your income, credit, and debt-to-income ratio. Finally, you close, and funds are disbursed, with a three-day right of rescission for primary residences.

A few practical notes. Expect credit score and debt-to-income requirements similar to other mortgages, with a score of around 620 or higher for conventional loans and better rates above 740. Investment properties often need larger down payments or equity and higher reserves. If the lender balks, a non-QM or portfolio lender, or a DSCR loan for rental properties, may be an alternative. Also ask about costs, since closing costs commonly run 2 to 5 percent of the loan, and compare that against what you'd save by getting the money back out.

If you tell me whether the property is a primary home or an investment, and how long ago you closed, I can be more specific about options.

Sudden paleness in a kid with asthma and autism could be a bunch of things. Anemia is one possibility, or low oxygen in the blood, or even a heart problem. It might also be a breathing issue like an asthma flare-up, or a side effect from a medication they're on. I'd get them seen by a doctor if you notice it come on suddenly, because it can point to something serious. The doctor can look at the rest of their symptoms, figure out what's behind it, and get them the right treatment.

A decision tree is a model used in machine learning and statistics to make predictions or classifications by repeatedly splitting data based on feature values. It is structured like an upside-down tree: it begins with a root node that contains the full dataset, and each internal node asks a question about one feature, such as "Is the applicant's income above 50,000?" Based on the answer, the data is directed along one of several branches to another node, where another question is asked. This continues until the data reaches a leaf node, which holds the final output, such as a predicted class label or a numeric value.

The tree is built during training by an algorithm that searches for the splits that best separate the data according to the target outcome. Common measures used to choose these splits include Gini impurity, entropy, and information gain for classification tasks, and variance reduction for regression tasks. The process generally continues until the leaves are sufficiently pure or until some stopping criterion, such as a maximum depth, is reached. Because an overly deep tree can memorize noise in the training data, practitioners often apply pruning or limit the tree's growth to improve how well it generalizes to new data.

Decision trees are popular because they are easy to interpret and visualize, require relatively little data preparation, and can handle both numerical and categorical features. They can, however, be unstable, since small changes in the data can produce quite different trees. For this reason, they are often combined into ensemble methods such as random forests and gradient boosted trees, which average or sequence many trees to achieve greater accuracy and robustness. Decision trees are also used outside machine learning, for example in operations research and business analysis, where they help map out choices, probabilities, and expected outcomes.

A statistical model is a mathematical description of a real-world process that produces data. Researchers use it to characterize how variables relate to one another and to forecast results that have not yet been observed. Such models appear across many disciplines, among them economics, psychology, biology, and engineering. Their applications include clarifying links between variables, anticipating future outcomes, and gauging how likely various events are. Common varieties include linear regression, logistic regression, and time series models. Analysts usually fit these models with statistical methods like maximum likelihood estimation or Bayesian inference. How well a model performs hinges on both the quality of the data used to build it and how suitable it is for that data. Before relying on a model to make predictions or reach conclusions, it is essential to scrutinize its underlying assumptions and shortcomings.

Double jeopardy is a rule that stops the government from trying someone again for the same crime after they have already been tried and either found not guilty or convicted. It exists so that the government cannot keep hitting a person with repeated trials until it gets the result it wants, and so that people can get on with their lives once a case is finished.

So yes, in the basic version of the rule, if a jury or judge found someone not guilty, the government generally cannot bring that same charge again, even if strong new evidence turns up later. Think of it like a game that has ended: once the final whistle blows, you don't get to replay it just because someone finds a better camera angle.

There are some important exceptions, though. In the United States, if a trial ended in a hung jury, where jurors could not agree, the case can usually be tried again, because no final verdict was reached. If the defendant asked for a new trial or appealed and won, that is also usually allowed, since the defendant chose to reopen the case. And some legal systems allow a retrial after a not-guilty verdict in limited situations, such as when new evidence shows the verdict was obtained through jury tampering or fraud. Many countries, including the United Kingdom, have changed their rules in recent years to allow retrials for certain serious offenses when compelling new evidence appears, which is a direct answer to the situation you describe.

So the short version is: the rule is strong and does block most retrials after an acquittal, but it is not absolute, and the exact answer depends on where the case is happening.

A painful, swollen, dark red area at a blood draw site that is growing over a couple of days is not the usual pattern of a bruise, and it can sometimes signal a complication such as a hematoma that is expanding, an infection (cellulitis or an abscess), or in rare cases a clot or a reaction in the vein. Most of these are treatable, but they are easier to manage when caught early.

Seek care right away, or go to an emergency department, if you notice any of the following: the redness spreads quickly or streaks up your arm, you develop fever or chills, the area feels hot, the swelling is rapidly increasing, your fingers or hand become numb, cold, pale, or bluish, you have new shortness of breath, chest pain, or a fast heartbeat, or you feel generally unwell or faint. If you are on a blood thinner or have a bleeding disorder, you should be seen sooner rather than later.

When you call or visit, tell them the date of the blood draw, that the area is dark red, growing, painful, and swollen, and whether you have any fever. Avoid squeezing or massaging the area, and you can use a cool cloth for comfort, but do not apply heat yet. Keep your arm elevated when you can.

Doctors generally advise against giving any drug, Septilin included, to infants younger than six months unless a healthcare professional has directed it. Septilin has not been shown to be safe or effective for babies in that age range. Parents should follow their child's provider's guidance and give only those medicines prescribed specifically for the child. Dosing instructions from the provider or the product label should also be followed closely. Anyone with questions about giving Septilin or another medication to their child should consult the child's healthcare provider.

Yeah, you actually can get past a phobia. A phobia is basically an irrational fear of something, and the go-to treatment is exposure therapy. You slowly face the thing you're afraid of, in a safe and controlled way, a bit at a time. Say you're terrified of bugs. You'd maybe start by just looking at pictures of them, then work up to touching one, and eventually you'd be able to sit in a room with one without freaking out.

It's not fun, and it can be pretty rough while you're going through it. But what it does is teach your brain that the thing isn't really dangerous. Stick with it and the fear fades, and you get way less anxious around it.

Being afraid of stuff is totally normal, by the way. The goal is just to keep the fear from running your life and holding you back. If you want to try exposure therapy, I'd go with a mental health professional rather than winging it. They can walk you through it safely so you're not just throwing yourself into the deep end.

Think of an economy like a huge game of passing money and trust around. Most of the time, people keep paying each other, businesses keep hiring, and everyone assumes tomorrow will be about as good as today. A crash happens when that shared assumption breaks all at once, and everyone starts doing the same thing at the same time.

Here is a simple way to see it. Imagine you lend your friend some money because you believe they will pay you back, and they borrow from someone else with the same belief. Now suppose one friend suddenly doubts they can pay. They stop spending and try to collect what they are owed. Their creditor now has less money, so they stop paying their own bills too. The doubt spreads down the line like a row of dominoes. Economists call this a chain reaction of debt, and it is one of the main ways crashes spread.

Crashes often begin with something that makes people worry. It might be a bubble, where prices of houses or stocks have been rising far above what they are really worth, fueled by borrowed money. When people realize the prices cannot keep climbing, they rush to sell before the price falls, which makes the price fall even faster. Other triggers include a bank failing, a sudden shortage of a key resource like oil, a war, or a pandemic that closes shops and factories.

Once fear takes hold, people behave in ways that make things worse for everyone, even though each person is only trying to protect themselves. Families cut back on buying things, so shops sell less, so shops cut staff, so those workers spend even less. Banks become scared to lend, so businesses cannot borrow to pay their workers or buy supplies. This loop of fear feeding into less spending, which feeds into more fear, is what turns a small problem into a large crash.

Governments and central banks try to stop this loop. They can lend money to banks so they do not collapse, lower interest rates to make borrowing cheaper, or spend public money to keep people working. When these steps work, confidence returns and the dominoes stop falling.

So in the simplest words: an economy crashes when many people lose trust at the same time, pull back their spending and lending, and each person's caution pushes others to be cautious too.

Okay, so the Atanasoff-Berry Computer (ABC) was an early electronic computer that physicist John Atanasoff and engineer Clifford Berry designed and partly built in the 1930s. It was the first computer to use electronic switches (vacuum tubes) instead of mechanical ones like relays or mechanical calculators, and it was also the first to use binary digits, or bits, to represent data. The whole point was to solve systems of simultaneous linear equations, which show up a lot in science and engineering. It read data from punched cards, and it had vacuum tube circuits that could add, subtract, and multiply. It never got finished, though. Still, the ideas Atanasoff and Berry worked out while building it ended up mattering a lot for later computers. In 1973, the US Patent Office called the ABC "the first computer to use electronic switches and binary digits in its calculations, and the first machine to use punched cards as a program medium." That same year, Atanasoff and Berry got the US National Medal of Technology and Innovation for the work.

Trouble urinating after sex can have a number of different causes. One of them is a urinary tract infection (UTI), which occurs when bacteria get into the urinary system. Typical symptoms include a frequent or sudden urge to urinate, pain or a burning sensation while passing urine, and a weak stream. Although UTIs occur more often in women than in men, men can develop them too, particularly after unprotected sex. Other potential explanations for difficulty urinating following intercourse include problems with the prostate, sexually transmitted infections (STIs), and inflammation within the urinary system. Your boyfriend should see a doctor so the cause of his symptoms can be identified and properly treated. The doctor will most likely suggest a urine test to look for bacteria or other abnormal substances, and, depending on what is causing the symptoms, may suggest additional tests or treatments. Meanwhile, he can drink lots of fluids and urinate often, which may help wash bacteria or other substances out of his urinary system. Both of you should also practice safe sex to lower the chance of UTIs and other infections.

I am sorry to learn that you formed a kidney stone after using OxyELITE Pro. Dietary supplements, weight loss products among them, carry potential hazards and are not suitable for everyone. Several factors, such as diet, how much fluid a person drinks, and existing medical conditions, can lead to kidney stones. Whether OxyELITE Pro actually caused yours is uncertain, but it is wise to approach any new supplement with caution and watch closely for adverse effects. If you are thinking about resuming OxyELITE Pro or taking another dietary supplement, speak with a healthcare provider beforehand. They can help you balance the possible risks against the benefits and decide whether the product fits your personal health history and needs. Paying attention to your overall diet and lifestyle, and maintaining a healthy mix of exercise, hydration, and nutrition, is also worthwhile.

"Astronomically large" is a phrase that refers to something enormous in scale, especially when measured against objects or distances commonly encountered on Earth or within our solar system. People often apply it to distances, sizes, or quantities that are hard for most individuals to picture or grasp. The observable universe, for instance, is believed to be astronomically large, measuring roughly 93 billion light-years across. That dwarfs any distance humans have ever covered or are realistically likely to cover in the foreseeable future. Likewise, the star count of the universe is considered astronomically large, with estimates spanning from 100 billion to a trillion or more. Overall, the phrase describes things so vast that they are nearly impossible to fully comprehend, and that overshadow even the biggest scales familiar to us on Earth.

Banks often ask small businesses to open a dedicated business account for several reasons. First, many countries legally require companies to keep their business activities in a separate account, which keeps the company's money distinct from the personal funds of its owner or owners. Second, a separate account simplifies bookkeeping, allowing a business to monitor its income and expenses more easily at tax time. That clarity helps the company report its profit or loss accurately and pay the correct amount of tax. Third, a business account lends a small company a more polished image and makes it smoother to handle payments with suppliers and customers. Finally, it streamlines day-to-day financial management, since these accounts often come with conveniences such as checkbooks, online banking, and merchant services. In short, a business account is a valuable tool that helps small companies organize their finances, comply with the law, and project credibility to clients and partners.

Imagine your neighborhood is like a big family, and everyone in it has a special job. One person bakes bread, one grows apples, one fixes shoes. When you buy from them, you give them a few coins, and then they use those coins to buy things from other people in the neighborhood too. The money keeps going around and around like a game of tag, and that helps everybody in your neighborhood have enough to live happily.

When you buy things that come from far away, the coins zoom off to a faraway place and don't come back. So buying nearby keeps more of the coins close to home, and it helps people near you keep their shops open and their jobs safe.

Food from nearby is also fresher. An apple from a farm down the road doesn't have to ride in a truck or a ship for days and days, so it tastes better and crunches more. Because it travels a shorter way, it also uses less gas, and that is kinder to the air and the planet we all share.

Buying locally can also be a chance to make friends. You can say hello to the person who made your bread, ask them how they did it, and they might remember your name. That feels warmer than picking something off a shelf where you never meet anybody.

Finally, local shops often sell special things you can't find everywhere, like a funny-shaped jam jar or a handmade toy, so your town stays interesting and doesn't look exactly like every other town.

Now, you don't have to buy everything locally, and sometimes things cost a bit more. But even a few little choices, like getting your eggs or fruit from a nearby farm, can help your neighborhood grow strong, like watering a garden you get to live in.

Fred Brooks (Frederick Phillips Brooks Jr., 1931–2022) was an American computer scientist and software engineer best known for his work on the IBM System/360 family of mainframe computers in the 1960s, which he managed as project manager. The experience of leading that large, complex project shaped his thinking about software development, and he became one of the most influential writers on the subject.

His most famous book, The Mythical Man-Month: Essays on Software Engineering, published in 1975, collects his reflections on the difficulties of managing software projects. It contains the observation known as Brooks's Law, which holds that adding manpower to a late software project makes it later, because of the communication overhead that grows as more people join and because new team members need time to get up to speed. The book also includes his influential essay "No Silver Bullet," which argues that no single technology or technique will produce an order-of-magnitude improvement in software productivity, since the core difficulty lies in the essential complexity of the problems themselves rather than in accidental difficulties of implementation.

Brooks was also a professor at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, where he founded the computer science department and later became known for his work in computer graphics, virtual environments, and interactive systems. He received the Turing Award in 1999, among many other honors, for his contributions to computer architecture, operating systems, and software engineering. His ideas remain widely taught in software engineering courses and continue to be cited in discussions about project management and team organization.

Ayn Rand's big idea, which she called Objectivism, is basically this: you matter, your own life is your highest purpose, and the best way to live is to use your mind, work hard at something you love, and not apologize for succeeding. She thought selfishness, in the sense of pursuing your own happiness and rational goals, is a virtue, and that forcing people to sacrifice for others (through government or social pressure) is wrong. In The Fountainhead, Howard Roark is the picture of this: he builds what he believes in, refuses to compromise his vision, and won't let the crowd tell him what to do.

If I explain it like you're five: imagine a kid who builds an amazing Lego castle. Rand says the kid should be proud of it and keep it, and that nobody should force him to break it up and share the pieces just because others want them. She also thought the kids who just copy others or whine about the castle are kind of sad.

Plenty of people like parts of this, and it's not wrong to have enjoyed the book. Its appeal is real: it celebrates creativity, integrity, and independence. But there are reasons it gets criticized.

First, many philosophers think her arguments are weak. She claimed to derive her ethics from pure logic ("A is A"), but critics say she jumps from "you should pursue your own life" to "altruism is evil" without really proving it. Academic philosophy mostly doesn't take her seriously as rigorous work.

Second, her world is black and white. In her books, the heroes are brilliant and virtuous, and the villains are weak, envious, and collectivist. Real life is messier. People are shaped by luck, family, health, and timing, not just effort. Someone born poor or disabled isn't necessarily a "moocher," yet her framework tends to treat need with contempt.

Third, critics argue her ideal society ignores how much successful people depend on others: roads, schools, workers, and customers. Roark seems to build everything alone, which isn't how it works.

Fourth, some dislike how she treated people. Her movement was known for being cult-like, with strict loyalty and expulsions of those who disagreed. Her views on certain topics, and the way her heroes sometimes behave (Roark's famous scene with Dominique is widely read as rape-like), also bother many readers.

Finally, her ideas got tied to political debates about taxes, welfare, and regulation, so people who dislike those politics often dislike her too.

So you didn't necessarily miss something. A good way to read her is to take what inspires you, like self-reliance and sticking with your work, while questioning the claims that compassion is a weakness or that everyone gets what they deserve. Reading a critic or two alongside her can help you see both sides.

A frequency comb is basically a device that spits out a bunch of evenly spaced frequencies, kind of a spectrum that repeats across the frequency axis. The gap between neighboring frequencies is the comb spacing, and it's usually somewhere in the megahertz to gigahertz range. The name makes sense once you plot it: the spectrum looks like the teeth of a comb.

They're pretty handy tools. People use them for precision spectroscopy, metrology, and telecom, among other things. They can also crank out ultra-short optical pulses, which is useful in nonlinear optics and precision measurement work.

There are a few ways to make one, but the most common is a mode-locked laser. The idea is to actively stabilize the laser cavity so it emits a train of very short, evenly spaced pulses. Each pulse has a spectrum that's a comb, and the spacing between the teeth is set by how often the pulses repeat. Other routes exist too, like electro-optic modulators, nonlinear optical processes, and microresonator setups.

You're right to question the ringworm idea. Ringworm is a fungal infection that slowly spreads outward and doesn't disappear on its own and reappear elsewhere within a day. Rings that come and go, especially in a child, point toward a few other conditions worth having a doctor look at.

One strong possibility is urticaria multiforme, sometimes called annular hives. It is common in children and is basically an unusual form of hives. The spots are itchy, raised, and often form rings or target shapes with a dusky purple or bluish center, which can look a lot like ringworm. Individual spots usually fade within a day and new ones appear elsewhere, and the hands, feet, and face are often involved, sometimes with puffy swelling. It is frequently triggered by a recent viral infection or by a medication, especially antibiotics like amoxicillin, so think back to whether she has been sick or taken anything in the past few weeks.

A related condition is erythema multiforme, which also produces target-shaped spots on the hands, feet, elbows, knees, and sometimes the face. Its spots tend to stay put for several days or longer rather than vanishing within hours. It is often triggered by a cold sore (herpes simplex) or by mycoplasma, a bacterial chest infection. It is usually mild, but it should be evaluated, particularly if there are any sores in the mouth, eyes, or genital area.

Another possibility is a serum sickness-like reaction. This usually appears one to three weeks after starting an antibiotic and causes ring-shaped hives along with joint pain or swelling and sometimes fever. A less likely cause is IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schönlein purpura), which causes raised purplish spots, typically on the legs and buttocks. It is not usually very itchy, but purple spots in a child are worth mentioning to the doctor so it can be ruled out.

I'd recommend having her seen by her pediatrician in the next day or two. Because the rash comes and goes, take clear photos of the spots, including the purple ones on her face, so the doctor can see what they looked like at their worst. In the meantime, a non-drowsy antihistamine such as cetirizine dosed for her age often helps the itch and can shrink hive-type spots. Stop any new medication only after checking with the doctor, and avoid hot baths and scratchy fabrics.

Seek care urgently if she develops swelling of the lips, tongue, or throat, or any trouble breathing or swallowing. The same applies if she gets sores in her mouth or around her eyes, blisters, skin peeling, high fever, swollen or painful joints, belly pain, or bloody urine. Purple spots that look like bruises and don't fade when you press on them also need prompt attention.

Imagine electricity is water flowing through a garden hose. Volts are like how hard the water is pushed, the pressure. Amps are how much water is actually flowing through the hose each second. Volts push, and amps are the flow that does the work.

For a person, the flow is what does the harm. Electricity moving through your body can mess with the tiny electrical signals that tell your heart when to beat. A current of about one tenth of an amp (100 milliamps) passing through the chest can make the heart beat chaotically, which is often deadly. Even much smaller amounts, around 10 to 20 milliamps, can make your muscles clamp down so you can't let go of whatever you're holding. There isn't one exact "deadly number" because it depends on the path the electricity takes through the body, how long it lasts, and the person's health.

Voltage matters because it's what pushes the current through your body. Your body resists the flow a bit, like a narrow pipe. Household electricity, around 120 or 230 volts, is strong enough to push a dangerous current through a person, especially if the skin is wet, which lowers the body's resistance. That's why water and electricity are a dangerous mix.

So the simple version is this: volts are the push, amps are the flow, and the flow through your body is what can hurt you. Electricity should always be treated with respect, and it's best to leave any wiring work to a professional.

Starting a side business slowly is often the smartest way to do it, because it lets you test ideas, build skills, and earn early income without betting your stability on something unproven. The key is to treat it as a series of small experiments rather than a single big launch.

Begin by choosing something that fits the time and energy you actually have, not the time you wish you had. If you work full time, you might realistically have five to ten hours a week. Look for ideas that draw on skills you already possess, such as freelance writing, design, bookkeeping, tutoring, crafts, photography, or consulting in your field. Starting from existing skills shortens the learning curve and lets you get paid sooner.

Before investing much money, validate demand. Talk to potential customers, offer your service to a few people at a modest price, or create a simple listing on a marketplace like Etsy, Upwork, or a local Facebook group. The goal is to learn whether people will actually pay, what they value, and what they're willing to spend. A handful of real sales teaches you more than months of planning.

Keep costs low in the beginning. Use free or inexpensive tools, avoid buying inventory in bulk, and resist spending on branding, fancy websites, or equipment until you've proven the idea works. Many successful businesses started with a basic social media page and a payment app. Reinvest early profits gradually as the business shows it can sustain growth.

Set clear boundaries so the side business doesn't erode your health, relationships, or primary job. Block specific times on your calendar, check your employment contract for any restrictions on outside work or conflicts of interest, and avoid using your employer's time or equipment. Consistency matters more than intensity, so a few steady hours each week will usually beat occasional all-night bursts that lead to burnout.

Handle the basic administrative pieces early so they don't become problems later. Keep business income and expenses in a separate bank account, save receipts, and set aside a portion of earnings, often 25 to 30 percent depending on where you live, for taxes. Look into whether you need a local business license, and consider forming an LLC or similar structure once revenue becomes meaningful, though many people start as sole proprietors.

Finally, track what's working and adjust. Note where customers come from, which offerings sell best, and how much you earn per hour of effort. Over time, you can raise prices, narrow your focus to the most profitable work, and decide whether to keep it as supplemental income or grow it into something larger. Moving slowly gives you the freedom to make that choice based on evidence rather than hope.

I'm sorry you've been through this. Nine years of trying and a surgery that didn't help can be very discouraging. The good news is that azoospermia, meaning no sperm in the ejaculate, no longer means you can't have a biological child. There are several realistic options, and the right one depends on why the sperm are absent.

The first step is to find out which type of azoospermia you have, if this hasn't already been done. In obstructive azoospermia, the testes make sperm normally but a blockage stops them from reaching the semen. In non-obstructive azoospermia, the testes themselves produce very few or no sperm. A urologist or andrologist usually tells these apart with blood tests for FSH, LH, testosterone and prolactin, a semen analysis that includes semen volume and fructose, a scrotal ultrasound, and genetic tests such as a karyotype and Y-chromosome microdeletion testing. If a blockage seems likely, cystic fibrosis gene (CFTR) testing is also done. Ideally you would see a specialist in male infertility rather than a general urologist, because the next steps are quite specialized.

If the cause turns out to be hormonal, which is less common, medication such as hCG, FSH, or drugs like clomiphene can sometimes restart sperm production. If you have ever used testosterone or anabolic steroids, tell your doctor, because these suppress sperm production and stopping them can sometimes reverse the problem.

For most men with azoospermia, the main route to a biological child is surgical sperm retrieval combined with IVF using ICSI, where a single sperm is injected directly into each egg. In obstructive cases, sperm can usually be collected fairly easily with needle procedures called PESA or TESA, and success rates are high. In non-obstructive cases, the best technique is micro-TESE, in which a surgeon uses an operating microscope to search the testicular tissue for small pockets of sperm production. Sperm are found in roughly 40 to 60 percent of men with non-obstructive azoospermia, even when hormone levels look poor. Because your wife is 31 and healthy, her eggs give you a favorable chance of success with ICSI if sperm are found. Any sperm retrieved can also be frozen for future IVF cycles.

If no sperm can be retrieved, or genetic testing shows a condition that rules out retrieval, such as certain complete Y-chromosome deletions, the main alternatives are donor sperm, used through IUI or IVF, and adoption. Many couples find either path deeply fulfilling.

My practical suggestion is to see a reproductive urologist or andrologist, ideally at a fertility center that does micro-TESE and ICSI, and bring all your previous reports, including your semen analyses, hormone results and surgery notes. Your wife should also have a basic fertility check, such as an AMH level and an ultrasound, so the IVF can be planned efficiently. Genetic counseling is worth considering too, since some causes of azoospermia can be passed on to a son.

Since your wife's age is currently in your favor, it's best not to wait too long before moving forward. Wishing you both success.

Fairness in machine learning basically means the model should treat everyone equally and not discriminate against any particular group. It matters because models can pick up on biases already baked into their training data and then repeat or even amplify them. Say a model learns from data that's unfair to some group of people. It might end up making decisions that hit that group harder. This could happen with lending, hiring, or any situation where a model predicts how likely someone is to succeed and uses that to decide whether they get a chance at something.

There are a few ways to make models fairer. You can clean up or adjust the data before training to reduce bias, use evaluation metrics that actually check for fairness, or build fairness constraints right into the training process. But it's not a simple fix. Fairness touches on social questions as well as technical ones, and it's really hard to get right. That's why people are still actively researching it.

It seems you might have experienced a serious injury to your leg. Until you're able to consult a healthcare provider, it's best to keep weight off the leg and give it time to rest. Raising the leg can also help bring down swelling. Pain relievers available without a prescription, like acetaminophen (Tylenol) or ibuprofen (Advil), could ease your discomfort. Still, you should get to a doctor quickly so the injury can be properly evaluated and the right treatment chosen. Meanwhile, keep the leg as motionless as you can and steer clear of anything that could make the damage worse. If you experience intense pain or find you cannot put any weight on the leg, go to emergency care right away.

Inner speech is the silent voice we hear in our minds when we talk ourselves through things. People rely on it to sort out their feelings and thoughts, reach decisions, and work through problems. It exists because it lets us gain insight into who we are and what is happening around us. As for why it keeps going and won't stop, the reason is that our minds are constantly active, always occupied with some topic. Having a busy inner voice is perfectly ordinary, and it is generally beneficial, since it aids us in making sense of our thoughts and emotions. Still, if that voice feels overwhelming or keeps pulling your attention away, you can try methods like meditation or slow, deep breathing to quiet your mind.

Your guess is a good one, but the answer is a little different. Animals usually don't wear their prosthetics all the time, and the goal is to keep the leg from squeezing the skin too hard, not to make it stay on forever.

Think of blood like a delivery truck that brings food and oxygen to the leg. Gangrene happens when the truck can't get through, so the skin and tissue start to die. A prosthetic can block the truck in two ways. One is squeezing: if a strap or socket is too tight, it pinches the skin and muscle so blood can't flow. The other is rubbing: a spot that rubs all day can break open, and the wound can get infected. So the trick is to make the fit snug enough to hold on, but loose enough to let the blood keep moving, and to spread the pressure out over a wide, padded area instead of one tiny spot.

That's also why the prosthetic is usually removable. Vets and caretakers take it off every day to wash the stump, look for red or sore spots, and let the skin breathe. Because an animal can't tell you "my leg hurts," someone has to check for them. The socket is also shaped to fit the leg, and as the leg heals and changes shape, the fit gets adjusted or remade.

So the simple version is: the prosthetic holds on with straps or a snug cup, it's kept loose enough for blood to flow, it's padded so nothing rubs too hard, and somebody takes it off often to make sure the skin is healthy.

Stomach pain and cramping during dialysis can have several underlying causes. One is an imbalance in electrolytes such as potassium, sodium, and calcium, since dialysis can shift these levels in the body and trigger cramps and other symptoms. Another possibility is medication: certain drugs taken alongside dialysis, including phosphate binders and acid reducers, may irritate the stomach and lead to cramping. An infection, whether bacterial or viral, can also produce abdominal pain and cramps. Finally, an ulcer, which is a sore in the lining of the stomach or intestine, may be responsible.

If your husband is having stomach pain or cramps during dialysis, he should talk with his healthcare provider. The provider can identify what is causing the symptoms and suggest suitable treatment, which might involve changing his medications or prescribing others to ease the pain and cramping.

Mid-back pain that wraps around toward the ribs can come from a bunch of things, and with your history of degenerative spine disease and spinal stenosis, that's probably the main suspect. Stenosis means the spinal canal has narrowed and is pressing on the nerves running through it, which can cause pain, numbness, and weakness. If the nerve roots or spinal cord are getting squeezed in the mid-back, the pain can show up along the ribs. Muscle strain, herniated discs, and fractures can also cause mid-back pain, so it's worth getting it checked out properly. A doctor can look at your specific situation and figure out what's going on. Treatment might include pain meds, physical therapy to build up the muscles that support your spine, or in some cases surgery to take pressure off the nerves or stabilize things. Good posture and regular movement help too, and cutting back on heavy lifting or anything else that really strains your back can keep things from getting worse.

The Green Bay Packers are from Green Bay, Wisconsin, a city on the western shore of Green Bay (an arm of Lake Michigan) in the northeastern part of the state. The team is the only NFL franchise owned by its community rather than by an individual or corporation, and it has been based in Green Bay since its founding in 1919.

Released in 1999, "The Matrix" is a science fiction action movie created by the Wachowski siblings, who wrote and directed it and were then credited as the Wachowski Brothers. Keanu Reeves plays Thomas Anderson, a computer programmer who finds himself pulled into a revolt against machines. These machines have seized control of the planet and built a simulated world, known as "the Matrix," to keep humanity docile and under their control. The movie delves into questions about reality, consciousness, and what it means to exist, and it has since become a classic that has had a lasting influence on science fiction.

El Morro, formally called Castillo San Felipe del Morro, is a citadel dating from the 1500s in Old San Juan, Puerto Rico. Recognized as a UNESCO World Heritage Site, it draws many visitors to the island. Built to guard San Juan against seaborne assaults, the fortress stands on a rocky headland overlooking the harbor's entrance. Its imposing design spans six levels and features a moat along with several artillery batteries that once repelled enemy vessels. Visitors can join guided tours of the site, which offer a chance to explore the fort's past and the broader story of San Juan.

Movies get rated by groups like the MPAA in the US or the BBFC in the UK. They watch the whole film and decide what age group it's suitable for based on the content. If a movie says "not yet rated," it usually just means it hasn't been through that process yet. Sometimes the film isn't finished, so there's nothing for the raters to watch yet.

It can also take a while, since somebody has to sit through the entire thing. Then the raters talk it over and agree on a rating together. So "not yet rated" doesn't mean the movie is missing a rating forever. It just means the rating hasn't happened yet, and it'll get one before it hits theaters or shows up for home viewing.

Rent and home prices move for a bunch of reasons, and the two don't always follow the same logic. On the rental side, demand is a big one. When lots of people want to rent in an area, landlords can usually get away with charging more. When demand dries up, they often have to drop prices to fill units. Costs matter too. If property taxes, utilities, or repairs get more expensive, landlords tend to pass some of that along to tenants.

Home prices are driven by a different mix of things. The general state of the housing market plays a role: tight supply and lots of buyers push prices up, while a flood of listings and few buyers pull them down. Interest rates matter a lot. Cheap borrowing makes buying easier, so more people jump in and prices climb. When rates go up, borrowing gets pricey, fewer people can afford to buy, and prices often soften. The economy in general counts as well. A strong job market and rising incomes bring more buyers in, while a shaky economy makes people hold off.

Location can make a huge difference. A house in a neighborhood with good schools, plenty of jobs nearby, and a nice vibe will usually cost more than a similar place somewhere else. So there's no single answer here. What's pushing prices in one city might be totally irrelevant in another, and it really depends on the local market.

Moravec's paradox is an idea in artificial intelligence (AI) and robotics, put forward by Hans Moravec, a robotics researcher at Carnegie Mellon University. It holds that computers find tasks that are hard for people, such as intricate mathematical computation, comparatively easy, whereas tasks people perform effortlessly, like identifying objects or moving through a messy room, are far harder for machines. The reason is that effortless human tasks depend on common sense, pattern recognition, and other kinds of high-level thinking that are hard to reproduce in a machine. The paradox shows that although computers can sometimes outperform humans in speed and accuracy on certain jobs, many others remain difficult for them. Consequently, AI researchers have concentrated on building methods that let computers handle high-level cognitive work, including natural language processing, machine learning, and pattern recognition.

Okay so the kanji for "language" is 言語, read as げんご. It's two characters stuck together. 言 means "to speak," and 語 means "word" or "language." Put them side by side and you get 言語, which is just the normal Japanese word for language.

A "cycle" in baseball is when one batter hits a single, a double, a triple, and a home run in the same game. It is a rare feat, and Major League Baseball has recorded it roughly 320 times in its history, though the exact count depends on how one counts certain cases, such as the 19th-century years when records and rules differed. The first recorded cycle came in 1882, and the feat has become more common in recent decades as offensive play has increased. Since the number changes slightly as new cycles happen, checking an up-to-date source such as Baseball-Reference or MLB.com will give you the current total.

Animal cognition describes the mental abilities of creatures other than humans. It covers how animals take in information, notice and focus on stimuli, acquire and retain knowledge, work through problems, and reach decisions. Scientists believe these faculties depend on brain activity, and research in this area aims to uncover the neural and psychological processes that make them possible. Investigations have been carried out on many kinds of animals, among them mammals, birds, reptiles, and fish. Such work has shown that numerous species possess advanced mental skills, including the capacity to solve problems, learn, and choose between options. Some animals, for instance, can fashion and use tools, exchange signals with one another, and find their way through intricate surroundings. Studying animal cognition can shed light on how thinking abilities evolved in people and other species, and it can also guide more humane approaches in areas like animal welfare, conservation, and therapy involving animals.

A data warehouse serves as a centralized storage system for information used in reporting and analysis. Its architecture is built to let end users and analysts query and examine data efficiently. Typically, it gathers information from many origins, such as transactional databases, log files, and other operational systems. This information is pulled from those sources, then transformed and cleansed so it matches the warehouse's structure, and finally loaded in for reporting and analysis. Because businesses and analytical applications often involve huge volumes of data and many simultaneous users, data warehouses are engineered to be quick, efficient, and scalable. They also accommodate specialized analytical methods like OLAP (Online Analytical Processing) and data mining, enabling users to probe and interpret data in innovative and powerful ways. In short, data warehouses are a vital resource for companies, organizations, and analysts, helping them derive insights and reach well-informed decisions from their data.

Voting to table a motion means putting it aside or delaying its consideration. Members usually take this step when the motion isn't yet ready for discussion or when other urgent business needs attention first. A tabled motion is not dropped or forgotten; it is merely set aside for the time being and can be revived for consideration later if needed. In most cases, approving a motion to table requires a majority vote.

Futures studies, also called futurology, foresight, or strategic foresight, is the systematic and interdisciplinary study of possible, probable, and preferable futures. It is not about predicting the future with certainty, which most practitioners regard as impossible. Instead, it aims to help people understand the forces that shape change, imagine a range of alternative outcomes, and make better decisions in the present by taking those outcomes seriously.

The field draws on many disciplines, including economics, sociology, political science, technology studies, ecology, psychology, and design. Its roots lie in the twentieth century, when military planners, corporations, and intellectuals began to look for more disciplined ways to anticipate change. Early landmarks include the RAND Corporation's work on forecasting and the Delphi method in the 1950s and 1960s, Herman Kahn's scenario planning, Bertrand de Jouvenel's writing on the "art of conjecture" in France, and Shell's use of scenarios in the early 1970s, which helped it respond to the oil shocks. Later figures such as Wendell Bell, Jim Dator, and Sohail Inayatullah helped develop the field's theoretical foundations, and institutions like the World Future Society and the World Futures Studies Federation gave it an organized community.

Practitioners use a variety of methods. Scenario planning builds several coherent stories about how the future might unfold, often organized around key uncertainties. Horizon scanning looks for weak signals of emerging change in technology, culture, or politics. Trend analysis extrapolates from existing data, while the Delphi method gathers and refines the judgments of expert panels over several rounds. Backcasting starts from a desired future and works backward to identify the steps needed to reach it. Causal layered analysis examines not only surface events but also underlying systems, worldviews, and myths. Simulation, modeling, and design fiction are also used.

A central idea is that there is not one future but many, often described as a cone of possibilities that widens with time. Some futures are possible, a smaller set are plausible, some are probable, and others are preferable according to particular values. This framing encourages people to ask who defines the desirable future and whose interests are served, making the field as much about ethics and power as about analysis.

Futures studies is applied in government planning, business strategy, urban development, education, environmental policy, and the military. Its value lies less in accuracy than in expanding imagination, exposing hidden assumptions, and preparing organizations and societies to adapt. Critics point out that forecasts often fail, that the field can be dominated by Western or corporate perspectives, and that it can drift into speculation or hype. Many contemporary practitioners respond by stressing humility, pluralism, and the inclusion of diverse cultural viewpoints in imagining what comes next.

Low libido can have a lot of causes, so it's worth looking at whatever physical or mental health stuff might be behind it first. Before you reach for something like Manforce, though, think about the side effects and risks. Taking it long-term without a doctor keeping an eye on things isn't a great idea. Manforce and other options, like sildenafil (Viagra), can cause problems and aren't right for everyone. If your libido has dropped and you're thinking about treatment, talk to a healthcare provider. They can help figure out what's going on and suggest something that fits, whether that's medication, lifestyle changes, or therapy. Plus, the causes can be all over the place: physical health, medications you're already on, stress or mental health, relationship stuff, and more. Working with a provider is the best way to find the real cause and build a plan that actually works for you.

Fiona is a given name with Scottish roots, and it is a fairly recent invention as a personal name. It comes from the Gaelic word "fionn," meaning "white," "fair," or "pale," which appears in many older Celtic names such as Fionn mac Cumhaill (Finn McCool) of Irish legend. The feminine form, Fiona, was essentially created by adapting that element into something that sounded like a woman's name in English.

The name was popularized by the Scottish writer William Sharp, who published works under the female pseudonym "Fiona Macleod" in the 1890s. Sharp used it as a literary persona for his Celtic Twilight style writing, and the name caught on as a real given name in Scotland and then across the English-speaking world during the twentieth century. Some earlier uses of Fiona do exist, including in James Macpherson's Ossianic writings in the eighteenth century, but Sharp's usage is generally credited with making it widespread.

There is also a separate Latin-sounding association, since the ending resembles names like Fiona's cousin forms in Italian and Romance languages, but this is coincidental rather than the source. In Irish and Scottish contexts, Fiona is sometimes treated as an anglicized equivalent of names like Fionnghuala (Fionnuala), though that is a different name with its own history, meaning "white shoulder."

Today the name is common in Scotland, Ireland, England, Australia, and North America, and it has gained additional familiarity through figures such as Princess Fiona in the Shrek films and the singer Fiona Apple.

The outlook for someone with a leaking heart valve hinges on several variables, such as how serious the leak is, which valve or valves are affected, and how healthy the individual is otherwise. Every patient is unique, and outcomes can differ considerably, so the best next step is to talk through her specific case with her healthcare provider, who can offer fuller information and direction.

Some companies skip stock splits for a few reasons. The big one is perception: a high share price can make a company look successful and valuable, and splitting it can sometimes make the stock seem cheaper or less prestigious. Liquidity can also matter. More shares outstanding can make it harder to move a large block at once, which may thin out the market a bit. And then there's cost. Issuing new shares means legal and accounting fees, and for smaller companies those can be a real chunk of change. In the end, it really comes down to the company's financial situation, what the market looks like, and what management is aiming for.

Yes, a checking account can be set up to require pre-approval, or a bank may maintain a white-list of approved account holders. Under pre-approval, a person must apply and receive authorization before being allowed to open an account. The application typically asks for personal and financial details, such as a Social Security number, employment history, and proof of income, which the bank or financial institution then evaluates before deciding whether to accept it. A white-list, by contrast, is a roster of individuals cleared to open a checking account at a specific bank or financial institution. To be placed on it, a person usually has to satisfy certain conditions, such as maintaining a good credit score, having steady income, or meeting other standards the institution sets. Anyone not on the white-list cannot open an account there. Keep in mind that many banks and financial institutions impose neither pre-approval nor white-list requirements for checking accounts. Before choosing one, it is wise to compare the features and requirements of various accounts to find the best match for your needs.
