The cerebral cortex forms the outer shell of the cerebrum, the brain's largest region. Built from folded sheets of neural tissue, it governs many of the brain's advanced abilities, such as perceiving the world, thinking, remembering, and deliberately moving the body. Anatomically, it is split into four lobes: frontal, parietal, temporal, and occipital. Each one specializes in particular tasks. The frontal lobe handles movement, planning, and choices. The parietal lobe interprets sensory input like touch and temperature. The temporal lobe deals with hearing and memory. The occipital lobe is dedicated to vision. Additionally, the cortex is separated into left and right hemispheres, which communicate through a thick band of nerve fibers known as the corpus callosum. Typically, the left hemisphere takes the lead on language and logical reasoning, whereas the right is more involved in spatial awareness and creative thought. In short, the cerebral cortex is a vital structure that underpins much of our thinking and movement.

Lean manufacturing is basically a production mindset focused on cutting waste and squeezing out as much value as possible. The idea is to build a process that gets top-quality products to customers fast, using as few resources as you can. Toyota came up with it in the 1950s, built on what they called the Toyota Production System. Taiichi Ohno is the guy most people credit with building that system, and a lot of folks call him the father of lean. The basic approach is to kill waste, cut down on variation, and boost efficiency by standardizing how work gets done and then constantly tweaking it. Since then, industries from cars and aerospace to healthcare and electronics have picked up these ideas. Service businesses like banks, insurers, and government offices have tried it too, hoping to get things running smoother.

A SATA power connector is the standard connector a computer's power supply uses to deliver electricity to storage drives and similar devices that use the Serial ATA interface. That includes hard disk drives, solid state drives with a 2.5 inch or 3.5 inch form factor, and optical drives such as DVD and Blu-ray players. It is separate from the SATA data connector, which carries the actual information between the drive and the motherboard. A SATA drive therefore needs two cables: one for data and one for power.

Physically, the power connector is a flat, L-shaped plug that is about 15 pins wide, roughly 4.5 centimeters across. The L-shaped keying means it can only be inserted in the correct orientation. The data connector, by comparison, is much smaller with seven pins.

The 15 pins are grouped to supply three different voltages: 3.3 volts, 5 volts, and 12 volts. Each voltage uses three pins, which helps carry more current and reduces the load on any single contact. There are also pins for ground, plus a pin for staggered spin-up and one for power management. The staggered spin-up feature lets the system start multiple drives one after another instead of all at once, which avoids a large surge of power at boot. In practice, the 3.3 volt line is rarely used by modern drives. Hard drives mainly use 12 volts for the spindle motor and 5 volts for the electronics, while SSDs primarily use 5 volts.

Compared with the older Molex connectors used for IDE drives, SATA power connectors are thinner, easier to plug and unplug, and carry the additional 3.3 volt line. Some power supplies include adapters between Molex and SATA, though cheap adapters have occasionally been a reliability and fire concern, so good quality ones are recommended.

Note that M.2 SSDs and NVMe drives do not use a SATA power connector, since they draw power directly through the motherboard slot they plug into.

Ebola is a virus that causes a severe, often deadly illness in humans and monkeys, apes, and other primates. It's thought to jump to people from animals like bats or monkeys, and then it spreads from person to person through direct contact with an infected person's blood or other bodily fluids. How likely someone is to survive depends on a bunch of things: which strain it is, the person's age and general health, and whether they can get good medical care. So no, it's not true that only 10% of people survive. In some outbreaks survival has been as high as 90% or more, while in others it's been much lower. There's also no known genetic defense that only a small slice of people have that lets them shrug it off. Some people might have a stronger immune response or other factors working for them, sure, but that's not a magic shield. Getting care fast really matters, though. Things like IV fluids to fight dehydration and medications to ease symptoms can give someone a much better shot at pulling through.

The Uberman sleep pattern replaces a single long stretch of nighttime sleep with a series of brief naps spread across the day. Its premise is that a person can meet their full sleep needs through these multiple naps instead of one extended period at night. In practice, a person on this schedule takes six naps, each lasting 20 to 30 minutes, at intervals of roughly every four hours. Nighttime sleep is either skipped entirely or limited to 30 minutes or less. The routine is meant to be kept every day, weekends included. Advocates say it leaves them feeling more alert and productive during waking hours. Still, most sleep specialists advise against it, since it conflicts with the body's natural sleep rhythms. Adequate nighttime sleep matters because it supports the body's repair and the mind's recovery, and keeping a consistent sleep routine helps regulate the internal clock and improves overall sleep quality.

Kernel regression is a nonparametric method for estimating the relationship between an input variable and an output variable without assuming a specific functional form, such as a straight line or polynomial, for that relationship. Instead of fitting a fixed model with a set of parameters, it estimates the value at any given point by averaging nearby observed data, with closer observations receiving more weight than distant ones. The "kernel" is the weighting function that determines how quickly this influence falls off with distance.

The basic idea works like this. Suppose you have a set of data points, each consisting of an input x and an observed output y, and you want to predict the output for a new input value x0. Kernel regression computes a weighted average of the observed y values, where each weight depends on how close its corresponding x is to x0. A common choice of kernel is the Gaussian function, which gives weights that decline smoothly as distance increases. Another frequent choice is the Epanechnikov kernel, which has compact support, meaning it assigns zero weight to points beyond a certain distance. The Nadaraya-Watson estimator is the most widely used form of kernel regression, and it normalizes the weights so they sum to one, making the result a true weighted average.

A crucial parameter in this method is the bandwidth, often denoted h. The bandwidth controls the width of the kernel and therefore how much smoothing occurs. A small bandwidth makes the estimate follow the data closely and can produce a wiggly curve that overfits noise. A large bandwidth produces a very smooth curve that may miss important patterns and underfit the data. Choosing the bandwidth is therefore a central task, and it is commonly done with cross-validation, which evaluates how well different bandwidths predict held-out data.

Kernel regression has several strengths. It is flexible enough to capture nonlinear trends, it requires few assumptions about the underlying shape of the relationship, and it is conceptually intuitive. Its main drawbacks are that it can be computationally expensive for large datasets, since each prediction involves all the training points, and that it becomes less reliable in high-dimensional input spaces, where data become sparse and distances lose meaning. It is closely related to other smoothing techniques, such as local regression (including LOESS), and to kernel density estimation, which uses the same kind of weighting to estimate probability densities rather than regression curves.

Sharp pain in your lower back when you sneeze or cough can come from a few different things, like a muscle strain, kidney stones, or a UTI. Since you've dealt with interstitial cystitis and chronic UTIs before, one of those could be behind it, but it might be something else altogether. Until then, a heating pad on the spot, an over-the-counter pain reliever, and plenty of water can help take the edge off.

I'm sorry you're going through this. Abdominal pain together with bleeding that has lasted all day should be checked by a doctor today, so please don't wait for it to settle on its own.

Heavy drinking can cause several conditions that fit your symptoms. Alcohol irritates the stomach lining and can cause gastritis or an ulcer, which can bleed. Heavy drinking with vomiting can tear the lining of the gullet or stomach, which causes pain and bleeding. Alcohol can also inflame the pancreas (pancreatitis), which causes serious upper abdominal pain. Blood when you wipe usually points lower down, to something like haemorrhoids or an anal fissure, which are often triggered by straining, vomiting, or constipation after drinking. Less commonly, the bleeding could come from elsewhere in the digestive tract or from the urinary or reproductive system. Only an examination and some blood tests can tell which it is, and some of these causes can become serious if left untreated.

Go to A&E or call emergency services now if you notice any of the following: vomiting blood or material that looks like coffee grounds, black or tarry stools, passing a lot of blood or clots, dizziness or fainting, a racing heartbeat, feeling very weak or pale, a fever, pain that is getting worse or is severe, or a swollen or rigid belly. If you are a woman and could possibly be pregnant, tell the doctor, as that changes what they need to check.

If none of those apply and the bleeding is small, you should still see a GP, urgent care, or an out-of-hours service today. Tell them exactly what you drank, how much, whether you vomited, and when the bleeding started and how it has changed. Avoid more alcohol and painkillers like ibuprofen or aspirin until you've been seen, because they can make bleeding worse.

Long ago, soldiers mostly fought in big crowds, close together, and the bright colors helped them do three things. First, they helped soldiers tell friend from foe in the smoke and noise. Second, they helped officers see where their own soldiers were. Third, they made the army look big and scary. Being easy to see also didn't matter as much back then, because the guns were not very accurate. A soldier with a musket could hardly hit anything far away, so hiding was not very useful. Staying in a neat line was more important, since that's how they kept their courage up and followed orders.

Things changed when guns got much better at long distances. Once a single sniper or machine gun could hit someone from far away, being easy to see became very dangerous. That's when armies started using dull colors like khaki, brown, and green, and patterns that blend into the ground. Some older armies did use something like camouflage. Hunters and scouts often wore natural colors, and a few groups fought in dull clothes long before modern times. But the big push came in the 1900s, when people realized that a colorful uniform was like waving a flag that said "shoot here!"

Before taking any supplement aimed at supporting brain repair or memory, it is wise to speak with a medical professional. Your doctor or other healthcare provider can suggest treatment approaches that fit your particular circumstances and needs. Research on certain supplements and their effects on brain function and memory is limited, but a few examples are worth knowing about. Omega-3 fatty acids, which are abundant in oily fish like salmon, may reduce inflammation in the brain. Ginkgo biloba is a herb that has long been used to sharpen memory and thinking skills, though the scientific support for it is inconsistent. B vitamins, such as B6, B12, and folic acid, play an important role in brain health and may aid memory and cognition. Acetyl-L-carnitine, an amino acid, has improved memory and thinking abilities in some studies. Curcumin, a compound found in turmeric, has anti-inflammatory properties and may enhance memory and cognitive performance. Keep in mind that these supplements may not work for everyone and can carry potential side effects. Speaking with a healthcare professional before beginning any new supplement routine is always the safest choice.

Your question touches on a real and contested debate, so let me give you the simple version of the different views, keeping in mind that people disagree strongly about this.

Iran has a nuclear program, and the U.S. and many other countries worry it could be used to build a bomb. Iran says its program is only for peaceful things like electricity and medicine, which is allowed under international rules. The key question is whether Iran is secretly trying to build a weapon. Some reports, including ones from the International Atomic Energy Agency, which is the United Nations nuclear watchdog, have found that Iran has enriched uranium to much higher levels than peaceful power needs, and that it has not fully explained some old nuclear work. U.S. intelligence assessments have said that Iran halted its formal weapons program in 2003, though the intelligence community has also said Iran has been keeping the option open. So the reports are mixed rather than all saying the same thing.

As for why the U.S. is so focused on Iran, there are a few reasons people point to. Iran is an enemy of Israel and a major backer of armed groups in the Middle East, such as Hezbollah and militias in Iraq and Syria. Iran's government has also been repressive toward its own people and has been involved in attacks and plots abroad. Critics of U.S. policy argue that Washington sometimes exaggerates threats, points to the flawed Iraq war intelligence as a warning, and that a hostile stance pushes Iran closer to building a weapon as a deterrent. Supporters of a hard line say that Iran's behavior justifies the pressure.

So the honest answer is that there is a real dispute over how much danger Iran poses and whether U.S. statements match the evidence. If you want to judge for yourself, it helps to check the IAEA's public reports and U.S. intelligence summaries directly rather than relying only on news summaries from either side.

A fuzzy system is a computer system built on fuzzy logic, which is a kind of math logic that handles uncertainty and fuzziness by allowing partial truth values. People use these systems to make decisions or predictions, and you'll find them in control systems, AI, image processing, and data analysis. The big difference from classical Boolean logic is that Boolean logic only says something is true or false, while fuzzy logic lets things be partly true. That's where membership values come in. They run from 0 to 1 and tell you how much a value belongs to a set or category. So if "hot" has a membership of 0.7 for some temperature, that temp is pretty hot. If "cold" gives it 0.3, it's only kind of cold.

Here's how it works in practice. A fuzzy system takes input data and runs it through a bunch of rules that say how to handle it. It also uses membership functions to turn raw inputs into those membership values. At the end, you usually get a crisp value, one single number that acts as the final decision or prediction. These systems shine when your data is messy or incomplete, or when you've got competing goals you need to balance. Control systems are a big example: they can keep a process steady or tweak settings on the fly as things change.

Blizzard takes the servers down on a regular schedule for a few reasons. The big one is that devs just have to do maintenance to fix bugs and push updates. Without it the game wouldn't run nearly as smoothly, and players would notice pretty fast.

Also, game servers are like any other servers. They get overloaded or hit problems that can only be fixed by shutting them down for a bit. That's even more true when the player base is huge, since way more people are trying to connect at once.

The timing matters too. Studios usually pick a time when fewer people are online so not as many players get annoyed. That's probably why Blizzard goes with Tuesdays, since it's likely a quieter day.

PSN and XBL are a different story. They might not need maintenance as often, or they've just got more resources to keep things running without going offline.

A spatial index is a data structure for storing and querying data that describes objects located in a geometric space. Its purpose is to support spatial queries, meaning queries that return results according to how objects relate to one another in space. One might use a spatial index, for instance, to rapidly locate every object within a given distance of a particular point, or to identify the object closest to that point. Geographic information systems (GIS) and other applications that work with spatial data rely on spatial indexes heavily. Several data structures can be used to build them, including quadtrees, R-trees, and k-d trees. Which one is best depends on what the application needs, such as the kind and volume of data, the sorts of spatial queries to be run, and the level of performance required. By cutting down the number of objects that must be checked, spatial indexes can greatly speed up spatial queries. Suppose a large collection of points is held in a spatial index. A query for all points within a certain distance of a given location can then be answered by inspecting just a small portion of the points instead of the whole dataset. Doing so can substantially lower the time and resources the query consumes.

Of course! When a country adheres to international drug treaties, it commits to observing specific rules and regulations on drugs, marijuana among them. These rules exist so that nations can cooperate in tackling drug-related problems and make sure drugs aren't produced or consumed in damaging ways. Should Canada legalize marijuana without honoring these treaties, the country could face adverse consequences. Other nations might object to the decision and choose to end their cooperation with Canada on drug matters. Such a development could strain Canada's relationships with those countries and make it harder for Canada to secure the help it needs to deal with drug-related difficulties. Ignoring the treaties could also cause other countries to doubt that Canada will abide by the rules set up to handle drug issues. That loss of trust might complicate Canada's collaboration with other nations on many topics, not just those involving drugs. In short, it matters that countries cooperate and keep to the rules they have agreed on, both to deal with drug-related problems effectively and to preserve good relations with one another.

Section 8 housing is the common name for the Housing Choice Voucher Program, a federal program run by the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) and administered locally by public housing agencies. It helps low-income individuals, families, seniors, and people with disabilities afford decent, safe, and sanitary housing in the private rental market. The name comes from Section 8 of the U.S. Housing Act of 1937, the law that authorized the program's earlier forms.

Under the voucher system, a participant finds a rental unit, typically a house or apartment owned by a private landlord, and the local housing agency pays a subsidy directly to the landlord. The tenant generally pays about 30 percent of their adjusted monthly income toward rent and utilities, and the voucher covers the rest up to a payment standard set by the agency based on local market rents. The unit must pass a housing quality inspection, and the landlord must agree to participate in the program.

Eligibility is based primarily on household income relative to the median income for the area, with priority usually given to the lowest-income applicants. Because demand far exceeds available vouchers, waiting lists are often long, sometimes lasting years, and many agencies close their lists for periods of time. Applicants should contact their local public housing authority to learn about current openings and requirements.

Dizziness, blurred vision, and a numb or cold feeling in the hands, feet, and face that reliably follow chocolate or a fizzy drink deserve a proper look, especially while you are on an antidepressant. I can't diagnose you, but there are several likely explanations, and which antidepressant you take matters a lot.

Caffeine is the most obvious common factor, since chocolate and most fizzy drinks, especially colas and energy drinks, contain it. Some antidepressants slow the body's breakdown of caffeine. Fluvoxamine is the strongest example, but others can have a smaller effect. Even a modest amount can then cause jitteriness, a racing heart, dizziness, and anxiety-like symptoms. Caffeine and anxiety can also cause rapid or deep breathing without your noticing, and that over-breathing commonly produces exactly the numb, tingly, or cold sensation in the hands, feet, and around the face, along with lightheadedness and blurry vision.

A second possibility is blood sugar. Sugary foods and drinks cause a quick rise in blood sugar, and in some people a drop follows an hour or two later. That drop can bring shakiness, dizziness, blurred vision, cold or clammy extremities, and tingling. If your symptoms come an hour or two after eating rather than immediately, this becomes more likely.

The antidepressant itself may also contribute. Many cause dizziness or lower blood pressure, particularly on standing, and a few, such as tricyclics, can blur vision. Something else may simply be adding to that background effect.

One situation needs urgent attention. If you take an MAOI, such as phenelzine, tranylcypromine, isocarboxazid, or selegiline, foods and drinks containing tyramine or certain stimulants can cause a dangerous spike in blood pressure. Warning signs are a pounding headache, palpitations, stiff neck, sweating, or nausea. If you're on one of these drugs, contact your doctor promptly.

Please seek emergency care if an episode ever includes weakness or numbness on one side of the body, difficulty speaking, facial drooping, chest pain, fainting, a severe sudden headache, or confusion. The same applies if you develop fever, muscle twitching, agitation, and heavy sweating, which can signal serotonin toxicity.

For now, it would help to keep a short diary noting what you ate or drank, how long afterward symptoms started, how long they lasted, and whether you were standing or breathing quickly. Try avoiding caffeinated and very sugary items for a week or two to see whether the episodes stop. Then share the diary with your prescriber or GP, along with the name and dose of your antidepressant and any other medicines or supplements. They can check your blood pressure lying and standing, your blood sugar, and possibly blood tests such as a blood count, thyroid function, and B12. Don't stop or change your antidepressant on your own, because stopping suddenly can cause its own dizziness and discontinuation symptoms.

Metronidazole does pass into breast milk, but in amounts that are generally considered low and acceptable for breastfeeding. Major references such as the American Academy of Pediatrics and LactMed classify it as compatible with breastfeeding, and it is commonly prescribed to nursing mothers. Your baby is 6 months old, so she is past the newborn period when metronidazole exposure is a bigger concern. The most important thing is to let your doctor know you are breastfeeding, which they may already be aware of. Stopping breastfeeding is usually not necessary. Some clinicians suggest a small precaution, such as timing feeds so that the baby nurses just before your dose and waiting a few hours before the next feed, since milk levels peak a few hours after a dose. Ask your doctor whether this is worth doing. Watch your baby for diarrhea, fussiness, unusual sleepiness, rash, or white patches in the mouth (thrush), and report any of these to her pediatrician. Also avoid alcohol while taking metronidazole and for at least 48 to 72 hours after your last dose.

As for alternatives, I would not switch medicines on your own. Metronidazole is the standard and most effective treatment for amoebiasis, especially when the infection has spread beyond the gut. Tinidazole is generally advised against during breastfeeding. Other options such as paromomycin, which is poorly absorbed and often considered compatible with breastfeeding, are used mainly for infections limited to the intestinal lumen, so they are not a direct replacement for a full course in every case. Your doctor can decide which treatment fits your diagnosis and whether an alternative is appropriate.

Finally, since amoebiasis spreads through contaminated food, water, and hands, make sure you and your family wash hands carefully, especially after using the toilet and before handling food or feeding your baby. Ask your doctor whether your daughter should also be tested or treated, particularly if she develops symptoms.

In the United States, the FCC rules (47 CFR 97.119) require an amateur station to identify with its call sign at the end of each communication, and at least every 10 minutes during a communication. So if you are in a long conversation or a net, you need to give your call sign at least once every ten minutes, and again when you finish. You don't need to ID at the start, though most operators do so out of habit and courtesy.

You can identify using voice in English, or using CW (Morse code) or a digital mode appropriate to the one you're operating. Phonetics are allowed and encouraged, and ideally should be standard ones, though that's not strictly required.

A few related points: if you're using a repeater, the repeater typically handles its own identification, but that doesn't replace your obligation to ID your own station. If you're operating with a reciprocal or temporary authorization, or as a different class of license, there may be extra identifiers to add. When you're sending a test transmission or just keying up briefly, you still need to ID at the end of that transmission. Special cases like remote control of models or space stations have their own rules.

Other countries have similar requirements, though details differ. Many follow ITU guidance and require identification at the start and end of a contact and periodically during it, often about every 15 minutes in some places, so check your own country's regulations if you're outside the US.

Oregon Tech is a public polytechnic university up in Klamath Falls, Oregon. It's the only polytechnic school in the Pacific Northwest, which is a big deal if you're into hands-on stuff. The focus is on applied sciences, applied technologies, and professional studies, and you can get bachelor's and associate's degrees in things like engineering, health sciences, business, and tech-based fields. Most programs push real-world experience hard, with internships, co-ops, and other kinds of experiential learning built in. Class sizes are small, so you actually get to know your professors and staff, and the student body is pretty diverse. The campus sits in southern Oregon, surrounded by forests and mountains, so the scenery's hard to beat.

So you're trying to conceive while dealing with cystitis and PCOS on both ovaries. Definitely stick with whatever your doctor prescribed for both, since that's the foundation. Lifestyle stuff helps too: eat reasonably well, move your body regularly, and try to keep your weight in a healthy range. That last one matters a lot with PCOS, since extra weight can make symptoms worse and make getting pregnant harder.

Tracking your cycle is worth doing. Ovulation predictor kits and basal body temp charts can show you when you're most likely to ovulate, so you can time sex around those days instead of guessing. If you've been at it for a year or more without luck, bring it up with your doctor about fertility treatment options. They can look at your specifics and give you much better advice than any forum post can.

Hope that helps. Feel free to ask if anything's unclear.

Google Voice Search is a feature of Google's search technology that lets you look things up by speaking instead of typing. You activate it by tapping the microphone icon in the Google app, the Google search bar, or Google Chrome, or by saying a voice command such as "Hey Google" on devices that support it. Your spoken words are converted into text using speech recognition, and Google then processes that text as a normal search query, returning web results, answers, or other information just as it would for typed input.

The feature is available on smartphones, tablets, computers, smart speakers, and other devices that have Google services installed. Beyond simple searches, it can be used to open apps, set reminders, get directions, check the weather, or control smart home devices, depending on the device and settings. Google has refined its speech recognition over the years using machine learning, which has improved its accuracy across many languages and accents.

Voice Search is designed for convenience, particularly when your hands are busy or when typing is slow or inconvenient. Users can usually review or delete their voice search history through their Google account settings, and voice recordings may be stored to help improve the service, so privacy controls are worth checking if that matters to you.

You are not alone in this, and it's good that you're asking about it. What you're describing, a recurring worry that you'll develop a serious illness in a particular part of your body, with nervousness and tension that show up physically, is a form of health anxiety. It is common, it is real, and it can be treated. It is not a sign that something is wrong with you or that you are "crazy." A doctor or counselor can help you sort it out, and it's worth talking to one, especially since the worry keeps coming back and is making you feel stressed.

As for prostate cancer, you almost certainly cannot get it at your age. It is very rare in people under 40 and mostly affects men in their 60s and older. The feeling of anxiety in your genital area is also very common in teenagers and adults with health anxiety. Anxiety can create tension, pressure, or odd sensations in the body, and once you focus on an area, you notice it more, which then feeds the worry. The sensation is real, but it's usually anxiety, not disease.

Some things that can help: tell a parent, relative, school nurse, or your family doctor what you've been feeling, so you're not carrying it alone. A doctor can examine you and reassure you, and can refer you to a counselor if needed. Cognitive behavioral therapy is very effective for health anxiety. It's also helpful to limit searching symptoms online, since that often increases fear rather than easing it.

If the worry ever becomes overwhelming, or you start having thoughts of hurting yourself, please tell someone you trust right away or contact a local emergency service or crisis line.

Imagine you own a lemonade stand, and you notice that when you sell lemonade, a few kids buy it, but when you give out cookies, the whole street lines up. You would start making a lot more cookies. That is basically what happened to these channels.

Cable channels make money in two ways: they get a small fee from every home that has cable, and they sell advertising during the shows. Advertisers pay more when lots of people watch, so the channel wants shows that bring in the biggest crowds. In the 1990s, a documentary about black holes or ancient Rome could do fine. But when channels tried shows like Gold Rush, Deadliest Catch, or American Chopper, far more people tuned in, and they kept watching week after week. Those shows were also cheap to make compared to a big science documentary with expensive animation, experts, and years of research. Cheaper to make and more people watching is a very happy math problem for a company.

There is also a thing called reality television, where you follow regular people around with cameras. You do not need actors, writers, or scientists. You just need an interesting situation with some drama, like will the boat sink or will the gold be found. People get hooked on the drama and the characters, which science lectures have a harder time doing.

Then the world changed. Streaming and YouTube arrived, and many people now go there for science. Cable channels began losing viewers, which made them even more nervous and even more likely to chase whatever was a sure hit. Also, the companies that own these channels got bought and merged. National Geographic is now owned by Disney, and Discovery is part of Warner Bros. Discovery. Big companies tend to care a lot about numbers on a spreadsheet, and less about the original mission of teaching.

So it is not that the people running the channels hate science. It is that the cookies sell better than the lemonade. The good news is that science shows have not disappeared. They have mostly moved to places like YouTube, PBS, and streaming services, and National Geographic still makes some excellent documentaries, though you may have to hunt for them.

Disputes and disagreements between nations are fairly common. The United States and Iran share a complicated past, and their relationship has been strained for a long time. Tension between them stems from a number of issues, among them American sanctions against Iran, Iran's nuclear program, and Iran's role in conflicts around the region. Washington has charged that Iran is seeking to build nuclear weapons, a worry that stems from the enormous destruction and suffering such weapons can bring. Iran, though, rejects the claim that it is trying to develop them and maintains that its nuclear activities serve peaceful aims alone. International inspections exist to help confirm that the program is not being turned toward military uses. When looking at any conflict, it is valuable to try to understand each side and to stay open to the idea that an issue can be viewed from more than one angle. It is equally important to seek peaceful ways of settling disputes and to pursue solutions that are fair to everyone involved and respect all parties.

Magnetic resonance imaging, usually called MRI, is a medical imaging technique that produces detailed pictures of the inside of the body without using ionizing radiation such as X-rays. It works by taking advantage of the magnetic properties of hydrogen atoms, which are abundant in water and fat and therefore throughout human tissue.

When a patient lies inside an MRI scanner, a powerful magnet creates a strong, uniform magnetic field. This field causes the hydrogen nuclei in the body to align with it, much like tiny compass needles. Radio-frequency pulses are then sent into the body, temporarily knocking these aligned nuclei out of their alignment. As the nuclei return to their original orientation, they release small amounts of energy in the form of radio signals. The scanner detects these signals, and computers process them, using additional magnetic gradients that vary across the body to determine where each signal originated. The result is a cross-sectional image, which can be combined into three-dimensional views.

Different tissues return to alignment at different rates and carry different amounts of hydrogen, so they appear with different brightness in the final image. This allows MRI to show soft tissues such as the brain, spinal cord, muscles, ligaments, and internal organs with great clarity, often better than other imaging methods. Doctors use it to diagnose conditions including tumors, strokes, joint injuries, and neurological disorders.

Some contrast agents, often containing gadolinium, can be injected to highlight specific structures or blood vessels. MRI is generally considered safe, but the strong magnet means that people with certain metal implants, pacemakers, or other devices may not be able to undergo the scan. The procedure can also be loud and requires the patient to remain very still for periods that may last from several minutes to an hour.

Second Life is basically a 3D virtual world that Linden Lab launched back in 2003. You make an avatar and then hang out, chat, and meet people from all over the planet. You can also build and sell your own virtual stuff, plus services, and there are tons of activities and events going on inside the world to jump into.

To get in, you download a client program. It runs on Windows, macOS, and Linux, so most people are covered. Once it's installed you sign up for an account and tweak your avatar until it looks the way you want. After that you're free to wander around, talk to other users, and join in on things like concerts or classes.

It's not just a social thing, either. Businesses and schools have used it for virtual conferences, training simulations, and even e-commerce.

There are several possible explanations for a spinning feeling in the head accompanied by head pressure. One is benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV), a condition that brings on dizziness and a spinning sensation when the head shifts into particular positions. Another is inner ear disorders, where inflammation or damage in the inner ear can produce dizziness, vertigo, and the feeling of spinning. Migraines can also be responsible, since this type of headache may cause spinning, head pressure, and other symptoms. High blood pressure is a further possibility, as elevated readings can occasionally create a feeling of pressure in the head. Beyond these, a number of other conditions, including vestibular neuritis, labyrinthitis, and Meniere's disease, can lead to dizziness and spinning. Your grandmother should see a doctor for a proper diagnosis and treatment, which will depend on what is causing her symptoms. Until then, she should avoid sudden head movements and activities that could provoke dizziness or vertigo, such as reading in a moving vehicle or getting up too quickly.

Optical sorting is a technique in which sensors and advanced software algorithms automatically separate objects according to how they look. It is commonly applied in manufacturing and recycling to sort materials such as plastics and metals by color, shape, size, and other visual traits. A typical optical sorting system has a conveyor belt or similar moving surface that carries the items past a set of cameras or other sensors. The sensors record images of each object and pass them to a computer, which analyzes them and decides how to sort them according to criteria programmed in advance. The system then sends the objects to separate destinations or bins, using mechanical arms or other automated devices. This approach handles large volumes of items quickly and efficiently, and it can be more precise and consistent than sorting by hand. It also has less environmental impact than certain alternative methods that rely on chemicals or other hazardous substances. On the downside, optical sorting equipment can be costly to buy and maintain, and it may be poorly suited to objects that are hard to tell apart by appearance.

Computer Go is the field of artificial intelligence devoted to creating computer programs that can play the ancient board game Go. Go originated in China more than 2,500 years ago and is played on a grid, usually 19 by 19 lines, where two players take turns placing black and white stones with the goal of surrounding more territory than the opponent. Although the rules are simple, the game is extraordinarily deep, and for decades it was considered one of the greatest challenges in game-playing AI.

The difficulty comes mainly from the enormous number of possible positions and moves. A typical chess position offers around 35 legal moves, while a Go position often offers 200 or more, and the number of possible board configurations exceeds the number of atoms in the observable universe. Just as important, it is very hard to write a formula that judges who is winning in a given Go position. In chess, counting material and evaluating piece positions works reasonably well, but in Go the value of a stone depends on subtle, long-range relationships across the whole board. Because of this, the brute-force search techniques that let Deep Blue defeat world chess champion Garry Kasparov in 1997 were far less effective for Go, and for many years the best programs played only at an amateur level.

A major breakthrough came in the mid-2000s with Monte Carlo Tree Search. Instead of relying on a handcrafted evaluation function, these programs estimated a move's strength by simulating many random or semi-random games to the end and seeing how often each move led to a win. Programs such as MoGo, Crazy Stone, and Zen used this approach to reach strong amateur levels, though they still fell short of top professionals.

The decisive leap came from DeepMind, a company owned by Google, with its program AlphaGo. AlphaGo combined Monte Carlo Tree Search with deep neural networks, one network suggesting promising moves and another evaluating board positions. These networks were trained first on records of human expert games and then improved through reinforcement learning by playing millions of games against itself. In 2015 AlphaGo defeated the European champion Fan Hui, and in March 2016 it beat Lee Sedol, one of the world's strongest players, four games to one in a widely watched match in Seoul. In 2017 it defeated Ke Jie, then ranked number one in the world. DeepMind later released AlphaGo Zero and AlphaZero, which learned entirely from self-play with no human game data and became even stronger.

Today computer Go programs, including open-source projects like Leela Zero and KataGo, far surpass the best human players. They have become valuable study tools for professionals and amateurs, and they have changed how humans understand the game, popularizing new opening ideas and overturning some long-held conventions. Beyond Go itself, the field matters because the techniques developed for it, particularly the combination of deep learning, self-play, and search, have influenced AI research in areas such as protein structure prediction, scientific discovery, and other complex decision-making problems.

A US citizen buying a house in Canada should keep several special factors in mind. First, immigration and citizenship: if you intend to live in Canada for a long stretch, you might need a visa or permanent residency. An immigration lawyer or the Canadian government can help you work out the right path. Second, currency: because the purchase must be made in Canadian dollars, you will have to convert US dollars, and since exchange rates move constantly, a currency exchange service may help you secure a better rate. Third, taxes: non-residents often face tax rules that differ from those applied to Canadian residents, so a tax professional can clarify what you owe. Fourth, financing: lenders may view non-residents as a greater risk, which can mean a larger down payment or a search for alternative loan options. Fifth, insurance: you will need coverage for the property, such as homeowner's insurance and possibly flood insurance, so it's wise to compare quotes from several providers. Finally, legal matters: a lawyer can explain the requirements for buying property in Canada and make sure the transaction is handled correctly.

Brad Rutter is an American former game show contestant best known for his record-setting performance on the quiz show Jeopardy!. Born in 1979, he rose to fame in the early 2000s, winning the show's Tournament of Champions in 2001 and building a reputation as one of the most successful contestants in the program's history. His most notable achievement came in 2011, when he competed in the famous Jeopardy! match against IBM's Watson computer system. That televised exhibition, which Watson won, was a landmark moment in the public history of artificial intelligence. Rutter also holds the record for the largest total winnings in Jeopardy! history, having earned more than three million dollars across his various appearances, including tournaments and special events. Beyond quiz shows, he has pursued other interests and appeared in a number of media projects, but he is primarily remembered for his extraordinary trivia knowledge and his role in the Watson matchup.

Business intelligence, or BI, is basically the set of tools, tech, and processes companies use to gather data, dig into it, and show it in a way that helps them make better decisions. It works with all kinds of data, like sales numbers, financial records, or market research. Once you've got BI in place, you can spot trends, catch opportunities before anyone else does, and make calls based on actual numbers instead of gut feeling. That usually means smoother operations and more profit.

There's a huge range of BI tools out there. Data visualization software, dashboards, and reporting programs are the common ones. Plenty of teams also lean on data mining, statistical analysis, and predictive modeling to find patterns that aren't obvious at first glance. BI folks often team up with data analysts, data scientists, and others to build setups that actually fit what the organization needs.

I can't recommend a specific replacement for Udiliv without knowing your liver tests, ultrasound or FibroScan results, blood sugar, cholesterol, and uric acid levels. No medicine is proven to cure fatty liver. Udiliv (ursodeoxycholic acid) is used mainly for cholestatic liver conditions, and major liver guidelines do not recommend it as routine treatment for fatty liver. Some doctors do prescribe it, so ask your doctor why it was chosen for you and whether it is still needed. Rosuvastatin (Rozat or Rosday 10 mg) is generally considered safe in fatty liver and is used to control cholesterol. Febuxostat (Febutaz 40) lowers uric acid, which is often raised in fatty liver. Don't stop or switch any of these on your own. Changes should be made with your prescribing doctor.

For the second question, the most effective treatment is lifestyle change. Losing about 7 to 10 percent of your body weight can reduce liver fat and inflammation. Eat less refined sugar, sugary drinks, fried food and white bread, and more vegetables, fruit, whole grains, and protein. Aim for at least 150 minutes of brisk walking or similar activity each week, and avoid alcohol completely. Abroad, a regular work schedule can make this harder, so plan simple habits such as packing home-cooked meals, walking during breaks, and avoiding late-night fast food.

Medical follow-up matters at your age, too. Find a local general physician or gastroenterologist and bring your prescriptions and past reports. They can check for other causes of fatty liver, such as hepatitis B or C, thyroid problems, or autoimmune liver disease, and can measure liver enzymes, HbA1c for diabetes, lipid profile, uric acid, and liver stiffness (FibroScan). Those results will show whether your current medicines are working and whether you need anything more.

The battle was between British troops and colonial militia, and the colonists ended up having to pull back in the end.
