Making your first million basically means getting your net worth to one million dollars, whether that comes from your paycheck, investments, or other money moves. People treat it as a big milestone, a kind of benchmark for how well you're doing financially. You'll hear it tossed around a lot in personal finance circles, usually when someone's talking about building wealth slowly over the years.

Your wife should not stop or change any of these medicines without talking to her doctor, because untreated tuberculosis is a serious risk to both her and the baby. The question is which drugs carry risk, and how much.

Isoniazid is one of the most commonly used TB drugs in pregnancy and is generally considered safe for the fetus. Doctors usually prescribe extra vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) alongside it to protect the mother from nerve side effects, and that supplement is commonly given during pregnancy.

Ethambutol is also generally considered acceptable in pregnancy when it is needed. The main concern with ethambutol is eye damage (optic nerve irritation causing blurred vision or colour changes) in the mother, so her vision should be checked periodically. Serious harm to the baby has not been established.

Ofloxacin, a fluoroquinolone, is the drug doctors are most cautious about in pregnancy. Animal studies raised concern about effects on developing cartilage, and human data are limited. For this reason fluoroquinolones are usually avoided when other effective options exist. They are sometimes still used when the infection is drug-resistant and no safer alternative is available, and in that case the benefit of treating the mother is weighed against the possible risk to the baby.

Some points are worth raising with her doctor. Standard first-line TB treatment for lymph node TB is usually about six months, and she has been on treatment since August 2009, so the doctor should confirm how much longer the course is meant to run and why ofloxacin is part of it. Ofloxacin is not part of the usual first-line regimen, which may mean the doctor is treating drug-resistant TB or has a specific clinical reason. The doctor should also monitor her liver function and eyesight during treatment.

Her obstetrician and TB doctor should work together, and the baby should be checked after birth. If she is still taking isoniazid or other TB drugs when the baby is born, the newborn may need to be evaluated for TB and may need preventive treatment, and the timing of the BCG vaccine should be decided by the doctors. Family members who have close contact with the mother and baby may also need screening.

Honestly, it's not normal to see sperm when you pee, so it's worth getting checked out. One possibility is retrograde ejaculation, where semen goes backward into the bladder instead of out the tip during orgasm. Certain meds, nerve damage, or conditions like diabetes can cause it. A doctor can run a urine test or imaging to figure out what's going on and what treatment makes sense, which might be meds or something else depending on the cause.

Also, the two-holes thing is a separate issue. Penile duplication (diphallia) is a rare condition you're born with, and it has nothing to do with retrograde ejaculation. If that's something you're worried about, bring it up with a doctor too so they can take a look and walk you through it.

Both individuals and companies in India must pay tax on the income, profits, and capital gains they receive. Whether you owe tax there turns on three things: your residency status, the kind of income you have, and how much you earn. Residents of India are taxed on their global income, so earnings from foreign sources must be reported and taxed alongside what they make inside the country. Non-residents, by contrast, owe tax only on income that is earned in India or received there. That covers wages from work performed in India, profits from a business operating in India, and rent from property situated in India. Keep in mind that Indian tax law offers a range of exemptions and deductions, which can lower the amount you ultimately owe. To work out what your obligations are, it is advisable to speak with a tax professional or ask the Indian tax authorities for guidance.

Most cruises in New York City dock at one of two main terminals, with a third option used by a few lines.

The primary one is the Manhattan Cruise Terminal, on the west side of Manhattan along the Hudson River, roughly between West 46th and West 54th Streets (Piers 88, 90, 92, and 94). It's the closest to Midtown, Times Square, and Hell's Kitchen, so passengers can walk or take a short cab ride to many attractions. Lines such as Princess, Holland America, Norwegian, and Cunard often use it, particularly for Canada and New England itineraries and transatlantic crossings.

The other major terminal is the Brooklyn Cruise Terminal in Red Hook, Brooklyn, which opened in 2006. Carnival, Royal Caribbean, and some other lines sail from there, and it's the home of Cunard's Queen Mary 2 transatlantic crossings. It's a bit farther from the main sights, so most people take a taxi, rideshare, or ferry to reach Manhattan, since the subway isn't conveniently close. The views of the Statue of Liberty and the Manhattan skyline as ships depart are a highlight.

Many Caribbean and Bahamas sailings also depart from Cape Liberty Cruise Port in Bayonne, New Jersey, which is often marketed as a New York departure. It's about 30 to 45 minutes from Manhattan by car, and it's used heavily by Royal Caribbean and others.

Because lines shift ports from season to season, it's best to check your cruise documents for the exact terminal and pier before you travel.

Honestly, there's no single best allocation for a retirement portfolio. It comes down to your own situation: how old you are, how many years you've got before you retire, how much income you'll need once you do, and how well you can stomach the market tanking without panicking and selling.

The usual advice is that as you get closer to retirement, you shift toward something more conservative. That means leaning more on income-producing stuff like bonds and dividend-paying stocks. The idea is to get a steadier stream of money coming in while you hold on to the capital you've built up.

You also want to spread things across different asset classes, so stocks, bonds, and some cash. That helps manage risk and might even improve your returns over the long haul. Diversifying softens the hit when the market gets rocky, and it means one asset class going south won't wreck you.

Keep in mind that none of this guarantees a profit or protects you from losses. Nothing does. What helps is checking in on your portfolio regularly and rebalancing, so it still matches your goals and how much risk you can handle. And if you're feeling unsure, talking to a financial professional is a good move. They can help you build a plan that actually fits you.

Okay, so to stay at the same weight, you just need to eat about as many calories as your body burns in a day through normal activity and exercise. If two people share the same height, age, and activity level, they can eat the same amount and hold steady. But if one person is 60 kg and the other is 80 kg, their needs will probably differ. Heavier folks tend to burn more energy at rest, since there's more body to run, so they usually need more calories to keep their weight where it is.

A few things change how many calories someone needs. Age is a big one: metabolism slows as you get older, so you often need fewer calories than you did at 20. Gender matters too, since men generally have a higher metabolic rate and tend to need more food than women. Height plays a part as well, because taller people usually carry more muscle and body mass, which pushes their needs up. And then there's activity level. If you're on your feet all day or hitting the gym regularly, you're burning way more, so you'll need to eat more to stay put.

So, to answer your question: two people with the same height, age, and activity level can eat the same calories and keep the same weight, even if they weigh different amounts. Once any of those things differ, though, the number they need will likely differ too.

Dr. Carter G. Woodson died on April 3, 1950, in Washington, D.C., at the age of 74. He died of a heart attack at his home. Woodson is often called the "Father of Black History" because he founded the Association for the Study of Negro Life and History in 1915 and launched Negro History Week in 1926, which later grew into Black History Month.

Judgment as a matter of law (often abbreviated JMOL, and called a directed verdict when made during trial) is a ruling by a judge that decides a case or a particular issue in a case without letting the jury reach a verdict on it. The judge can grant it when, after considering the evidence in the light most favorable to the non-moving party, no reasonable jury could find for that party. In other words, the evidence is so one-sided, or so lacking, that the outcome is legally required regardless of what a jury might think.

It is made under Rule 50 of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure in federal court, and most state courts have similar rules. A party usually moves for it at the close of the other side's evidence or at the end of the trial, and it can be renewed after the jury returns a verdict, in which case it is called judgment notwithstanding the verdict (JNOV). The judge does not weigh credibility or choose between competing reasonable inferences; those are jury tasks. The question is purely whether the evidence is legally sufficient to support a finding.

In criminal cases, a similar motion is called a motion for acquittal, and it is governed by different standards because of constitutional protections such as double jeopardy.

Not every teenage boy is obsessed with phallic imagery, and plenty of people of all genders are curious about bodies in general. That said, some teen boys do seem especially drawn to it, and there are a few likely reasons. Puberty is a huge shift. Bodies change fast, hormones are all over the place, and it's pretty normal to get more curious about your own body and other people's. That curiosity can sometimes tip into a kind of fixation on certain body parts, genitals included. Some boys may also lean into this stuff to feel more masculine or to fit in with friends. Plenty of cultures push boys toward certain behaviors and interests, and this can be one of them. Honestly, the reasons vary a lot from person to person and aren't always simple. Everyone's different, and it's fine to be into different things.

The OTC Markets Group, commonly called OTCMKTS, is a financial marketplace that works over the counter (OTC). This means it does not rely on a centralized exchange such as the New York Stock Exchange or NASDAQ. Instead, it is a network of dealers who trade securities directly with one another.

When a company is listed under two OTCMKTS symbols, one possibility is that it has issued two distinct classes of stock, each trading under its own ticker. For instance, one class might trade as "ABCD" while the other trades as "EFGH." Such classes can differ in voting rights, dividend entitlements, or other terms. Another possibility is that the company owns two subsidiaries or divisions, each with its own ticker on the OTCMKTS. In that case, the symbols would represent two separate businesses linked through ownership or some other commercial arrangement. A third possibility is that the stock previously traded under one symbol and was later reassigned a new one, perhaps after a merger, acquisition, reorganization, or other corporate event. Without further details, it is hard to determine precisely what distinguishes the two symbols for a given company. Anyone considering an investment should conduct their own research and consult a financial advisor or professional first.

A chronograph watch is a timepiece with a built-in stopwatch function, allowing the wearer to measure elapsed time independently of the watch's regular timekeeping. It typically has one or more additional pushers (buttons) on the case that start, stop, and reset the stopwatch hands, which are usually separate from the main hour and minute hands. Many chronographs also have subdials, small secondary dials on the watch face that track elapsed minutes and hours, along with the running seconds.

The term comes from Greek words meaning "time" and "writing," reflecting the original purpose of recording durations. Chronographs were historically valued by pilots, race car drivers, athletes, and scientists who needed precise timing of events. Today they are popular both as practical instruments and as fashionable luxury watches, and they come in mechanical as well as quartz varieties.

Sores in the mouth that come with blood clots may point to a number of different conditions, so seeing a doctor or dentist is important for finding the cause and getting proper treatment. Several things could be responsible. Canker sores are small, shallow ulcers that form inside the mouth, commonly on the tongue, gums, or inner cheek. They tend to be round or oval with a red edge, and they can hurt enough to make eating or talking difficult. Cold sores, also called fever blisters, are small, painful blisters that typically show up on the lips or the skin around the mouth. The herpes simplex virus causes them, and they are contagious. They usually clear up by themselves within a few days to a week. Oral cancer is another possibility, since a mouth sore with blood clots can be one of its signs. This cancer affects the mouth, throat, or head and neck area, and it may also bring a sore throat that won't go away, trouble swallowing, and a lump or mass in the mouth or throat. If you notice a mouth sore with blood clots, see a healthcare provider as soon as you can so the cause can be identified and treated. Meanwhile, a few steps may ease the discomfort: rinse your mouth with warm salt water, take an over-the-counter pain reliever such as acetaminophen or ibuprofen, stay away from acidic, spicy, or salty foods, and use a topical anesthetic or a pain-relieving mouthwash. Good oral hygiene also matters, meaning regular brushing and flossing and avoiding tobacco and alcohol. Following these habits can help prevent mouth sores and other oral problems.

Gordon Plotkin is a logician and computer scientist recognized for his work in programming language theory and for his part in developing the calculus of communicating systems (CCS), a mathematical model describing how concurrent systems behave. He now holds the title of professor emeritus at the University of Edinburgh, where he spent many years both conducting research and teaching. Plotkin is likewise noted for his research on categorical semantics, an area of mathematical logic concerned with the meaning of programming languages and the constructs they contain. He has produced a number of influential papers and books on these subjects, among them "A Structural Approach to Operational Semantics" and "Categories for the Working Mathematician." Beyond his academic research, Plotkin has worked as an editor for several journals and belonged to a variety of professional organizations. His contributions to the field have earned him many awards and honors, including the ACM SIGPLAN Robin Milner Young Researcher Award and a Fellowship of the Royal Society of Edinburgh.

People say it because a lot of households have felt squeezed over the last few years, and the phrase has become shorthand for that feeling. The main driver was the burst of inflation that began in 2021 and peaked in 2022. Prices for groceries, rent, car insurance, and energy rose quickly, and even though the rate of increase has slowed, prices did not fall back. Wages have in many cases caught up on average, but people don't experience averages. They remember what a carton of eggs or a month of rent used to cost, and the gap still stings.

Interest rates add to it. To fight inflation, central banks raised rates sharply, which made mortgages, car loans, and credit card balances much more expensive. Housing is especially painful: high home prices combined with high mortgage rates have put buying out of reach for many people, and rents are high too. Student loan payments resuming in the US after a pandemic pause hit many budgets as well.

There are also worries about the future. Layoffs in some industries, talk of recession, tariffs and trade disputes, and general political and global uncertainty make people nervous about job security. When people feel uncertain, advice to build an emergency fund and cut spending sounds sensible.

Social media amplifies all of this. "In this economy" became a meme, often used jokingly to justify skipping a restaurant or to mock high prices, and trends like "no-buy years," "loud budgeting," and frugality content spread it further. Financial influencers, news outlets, and retailers all have incentives to keep the topic in front of you, whether it's to get clicks or sell a budgeting app.

That said, the picture is mixed. In many countries unemployment has stayed relatively low and the stock market has done well, so some people are doing fine while others struggle, particularly renters, young people, and those with lower incomes. Saving money is generally good advice in any economy, but the urgency you hear is partly real pressure and partly the way a catchy phrase and constant online repetition make everyone feel the same anxiety. How much it applies to you depends on your own income, debts, and job stability.

Some internal combustion engines use rocker arms, which are mechanical parts that carry motion from the camshaft to the valves. The name comes from the way they rock, or pivot, on a shaft or pivot point when the camshaft lobes press against them. In a typical engine, the camshaft sits in the cylinder head, and its lobes are shaped to open and close the valves at the right moments in the engine cycle. A pushrod links the camshaft to each rocker arm, and the rocker arm passes the camshaft's force on to the valve. As the camshaft rotates, it presses on the pushrod, which then pushes on the rocker arm, making it pivot and open the valve. Rocker arms come in several varieties, among them solid, hydraulic, and roller designs. The solid type is the simplest and is made from one piece of metal. Hydraulic rocker arms rely on oil pressure to lessen friction and wear in the valve train, while roller rocker arms have a roller at the tip that cuts friction and wear even further. Because rocker arms are a key part of an engine, they are built to withstand heavy loads and high speeds.

Ovex is a medicine for threadworms, also called pinworms. The active ingredient is mebendazole, which starves the worms of energy so they die off. Read the Ovex packet carefully and get the dose right. Usually it's a single dose, and you shouldn't keep taking it for more than three days in a row. If your kid still has symptoms a few days after one dose, call a healthcare professional rather than just waiting it out.

Most of the time Ovex kills the worms within a few days. The symptoms can hang around for several weeks, though, since the body still has to clear out dead worms and eggs. Meanwhile, keep up the hygiene stuff: wash hands often and keep the bottom area clean to stop it spreading. And if you're worried or have questions about using Ovex, ask a doctor or pharmacist. They can tell you what makes sense for your child's situation.

Honestly, wiping out the whole planet would be really hard for us to do. Earth is huge and tough, and you'd need an insane amount of effort to do permanent, total damage. That said, we're definitely capable of wrecking a lot of it. We could poison the air, water, and soil until plants and animals struggle to survive anywhere. Nuclear weapons could cause massive destruction and leave radiation behind for a long time. Still, this is our only home, so it makes way more sense to look after it than to go out of our way to trash it. Protecting it for the people who come after us seems like the better play.

Okay, so the Wizard of Oz is a kids' book by L. Frank Baum, which came out in 1900. The title guy is a mysterious figure living in the Land of Oz, and he's got a lot of magic going for him. Everyone just calls him the Wizard of Oz. Fun fact: in the 1939 movie, Frank Morgan played him.

Thermal energy is a kind of energy, and whenever a warm object touches a cooler one, that energy flows from the warm object into the cool one. It always travels from the hotter location toward the colder one. A freezer relies on a special fluid called refrigerant, which switches easily between liquid and gas forms. As the refrigerant turns from liquid into gas, it soaks up heat, and the freezer makes use of this by drawing heat away from whatever is stored inside. The refrigerant repeatedly cycles between liquid and gas, and with every change it removes a bit more heat from the freezer. A compressor drives this back-and-forth motion by squeezing the refrigerant, which raises its temperature. The heated refrigerant then passes through tubes where it releases its heat and condenses back into a liquid. The liquid then returns to the freezer compartment, and the entire sequence begins again. Because the compressor requires a great deal of electricity to operate, freezers consume a considerable amount of power. Still, the benefit is considerable, since freezers keep food fresh, store ice cream, and serve many other purposes.

Sorry you're dealing with this, back pain is miserable, and it's even worse when nothing seems to help. Honestly, the best thing you can do is work with a doctor or other healthcare pro to figure out a plan that fits you. There's just no single permanent cure that works for everybody. What's causing the pain varies a lot from person to person, and so does what actually helps.

Most plans end up being a mix of things: medication, physical therapy, and some lifestyle changes like regular exercise and finding ways to manage stress.

If you're having withdrawal symptoms from the medication you were prescribed, don't wait on it. Talk to a healthcare provider as soon as you can. Coming off stuff like methadone or suboxone can actually be dangerous, so it really should be managed by someone trained to do that.

So bring all of this up with your provider, your worries and whatever symptoms you're having. They can help you work out what to do next and get you the support and treatment you need. It also helps to lean on friends, family, or a support group while you get through this. It's a rough stretch, and you shouldn't have to go through it alone.

Getting near the center of a tornado to photograph or film it is difficult, since these storms are extremely dangerous and capable of widespread destruction. A tornado forms when warm, humid air climbs while cool, dry air descends, producing a rotating column of wind that may exceed 300 miles per hour. Once it reaches the ground, it can lift debris such as trees and parts of buildings and hurl them through the air, which puts anyone nearby at serious risk. For this reason, people should keep their distance from tornadoes and avoid trying to approach them. If you spot one, seek shelter right away and stay put until the storm has passed before going outside again. It is also wise to heed the guidance of local officials, including emergency services and meteorologists, who can tell you how to remain safe while a tornado is in the area.

A Solo 401(k) for Schedule C income and an employer 401(k) from a W-2 job can coexist, but the employee deferral limit is shared between them, while the employer contribution limit is not.

The employee deferral limit under IRC 402(g) applies to you as an individual across all 401(k) plans you participate in, not per plan. For 2025 that is $23,500, plus a $7,500 catch-up if you are 50 or older (and a higher catch-up of $11,250 if you are 60 through 63). If your W-2 employer's 401(k) already receives $23,500 of your deferrals, you cannot make any additional employee deferrals to your Solo 401(k). Employer matching contributions from your W-2 job do not count toward this limit.

The employer side of the Solo 401(k) is calculated only from your self-employment income. As a sole proprietor, the profit-sharing contribution is generally up to 25 percent of your net self-employment earnings, which works out to roughly 20 percent of Schedule C net profit after you deduct one-half of self-employment tax and the contribution itself. For example, with $100,000 of Schedule C net profit, you could contribute roughly $18,700 as an employer contribution. Your W-2 wages do not increase this amount.

The overall annual addition limit under IRC 415(c) is $70,000 for 2025, excluding catch-up contributions. This limit applies separately to each employer, so your W-2 employer's contributions and your own business's contributions do not reduce each other, provided the two employers are not under common control. If you own an S corporation that pays you W-2 wages, the controlled-group rules become more complicated and you should get professional advice.

Putting it together, if your W-2 job already uses up the full deferral limit, you can still make a sizable employer contribution to the Solo 401(k) from Schedule C income. If your W-2 deferrals are small, you can use the remaining room for employee deferrals to the Solo plan, up to your self-employment earnings. Roth deferrals are available in many Solo 401(k) plans and are also subject to the same shared deferral limit.

Two practical points: the Solo 401(k) must be established by December 31 of the tax year for employee deferrals to be made for that year, while employer contributions can be made up to your tax filing deadline, including extensions. Also, all these figures are indexed and change most years, so confirm the current year's limits before making contributions.

The Lord of the Rings was originally written by J.R.R. Tolkien and published as three volumes between 1954 and 1955. The Fellowship of the Ring and The Two Towers came out in 1954, and The Return of the King followed in 1955.

If you mean the famous film trilogy directed by Peter Jackson, those movies were released one per year from 2001 to 2003. The Fellowship of the Ring premiered in 2001, The Two Towers in 2002, and The Return of the King in 2003, with the last one winning eleven Academy Awards, including Best Picture.

There was also an earlier animated film by Ralph Bakshi released in 1978, and more recently the Amazon series The Rings of Power, set in the same world, began streaming in 2022.

Think of it like a recipe for a sandwich box. Before anyone builds a lunchbox, the people who design it decide how big it can be, how the lid closes, and how the latch works. They don't have to build a thousand boxes first to know the rules. The rules are the plan, and the boxes are made to follow the plan.

SDXC works the same way. The standard is a written set of instructions about how the card's memory is organized and how the computer talks to it. One of those instructions is about addresses. Every bit of storage gets a numbered spot, like houses on a street, and the address numbers are written with a certain number of digits. With 32 bits of address space, you can count up to about 4 billion spots, and when each spot holds 512 bytes, that comes to about 2 terabytes. So the 2 TB limit isn't a guess about what engineers will manage to build. It's a math result from how many address numbers the standard allows.

That also answers the "what if it's really much lower" worry. The limit is a ceiling, not a promise that every card will hit it. A 2 TB card is possible only because the math allows it, and the people making memory decide what size to actually sell based on cost and technology. Today's largest SDXC cards are much smaller than the ceiling, and nobody has yet made one at the full 2 TB. If future engineers find a better way to build memory, they can move to a newer standard, called SDUC, which uses bigger address numbers and allows up to 128 TB.

So the short version: the standard sets the biggest size the design can ever hold, using counting rules everyone agrees on, and then real products grow up to that size over time.

Yep, there are a few online tools that can handle cost basis for a stock that's had dividend reinvestments and splits. The easiest one is probably your brokerage's own cost basis calculator. Most brokers have one, and you just punch in your buys and sells, plus any reinvested dividends or splits, and it spits out the basis for you. Some financial websites and software programs also have standalone cost basis calculators that work pretty much the same way, so they're worth a look if your broker's tool is clunky or you hold shares at more than one place.

Fair warning, though, this stuff can get messy fast. Make sure you've got accurate records of every purchase, sale, reinvestment, and split, because one wrong number throws off everything after it. If you're not sure about something, or the numbers just aren't adding up, a financial advisor or tax pro can save you a headache.

Basically a software subscription is just a recurring payment that gets you access to some software or service for a set period, usually monthly or yearly. You pay the fee at regular intervals and that's it.

How you report it really depends on who you are and why you're paying for it.

If it's just for personal use, you'd only need to mention it on your personal tax return if there's some deduction or credit tied to it. Most of the time there isn't, but it's worth checking.

If you're running a business and the software is part of your operations, then yeah, it probably goes on your business tax return. You'd list the cost as a business expense, and that's often deductible.

And if you're the one selling the subscriptions, like a software company, you'd report the revenue on your financial statements. That could mean how many subscriptions you sold, how much money they brought in, and whatever expenses go along with them.

Whichever bucket you're in, keep good records. Hang onto the subscription dates, what you paid, and any tax or financial paperwork connected to it. It makes reporting a lot easier later, and it keeps you on the right side of whatever tax or reporting rules apply to you.

It's possible to pull in extra money through Social Security, but you can't count on getting an extra $15,978 a year. What you actually get depends on a bunch of things: how long you've worked, how much you've earned, and when you decide to start collecting. Social Security is a federal program that pays retirement, disability, and survivors benefits, but you have to qualify first. That means working and paying Social Security taxes for a set number of years. Your benefit is based on your average earnings over your working life, and claiming early or late can change the monthly check quite a bit. If you're thinking about it, poke around the Social Security Administration's website or talk to a financial advisor. They can run the numbers for your situation, which is way more useful than guessing.

ECML PKDD (short for European Conference on Machine Learning and Principles and Practice of Knowledge Discovery in Databases) is a conference series focused on machine learning and knowledge discovery in databases. It runs every year and is organized by the European Community on Machine Learning and Data Mining (ECML/PKDD). The whole point is to get researchers, practitioners, and users from academia, industry, and government in the same room to talk about where the field is heading and how these methods get used in all sorts of areas. It's basically a place to show off your work, swap ideas, and pick up tricks from people who've been doing this longer than you. You'll usually find invited talks, tutorials, workshops, and paper presentations covering a wide range of machine learning and data mining topics. It's a well-established, pretty well-respected event, and it pulls in a huge number of submissions from all over the world. If you're into this stuff, it's a great chance to catch up on the latest developments, meet people in the field, and get your own research in front of a broad crowd.

The main issue is when you became a US tax resident. Once you're a US resident (through a green card or the substantial presence test), the US taxes your worldwide income, including ESPP shares, regardless of where you were when the shares were granted or purchased. In the year you move, you'll usually be a part-year resident, and the split between US and foreign income for that year needs careful handling.

If your employer's ESPP is a US "qualified" plan under Section 423, the US tax treatment depends on how long you hold the shares. In a qualifying disposition, where you sell at least two years after the offering date and at least one year after the purchase date, part of the gain is taxed as ordinary income (the lesser of the actual gain or the discount measured at the offering date, which is capped at 15%), and the rest is taxed as long-term capital gain. In a disqualifying disposition, where you sell earlier, the discount at purchase is taxed as ordinary income and any further gain or loss is capital, short-term or long-term depending on the holding period. Your employer should provide Form 3922 for transfers, and the ordinary income portion may show up on your W-2 or need to be reported based on that form, so check that it matches your records.

The European side is often the complicating factor. Many European countries tax ESPP benefits at purchase, at vesting, or at sale, and some tax a portion based on the period you worked there. If you were taxed in Europe on the same income, you can usually claim a foreign tax credit on Form 1116 to avoid double taxation, and the US-Europe tax treaty may include rules for allocating income in a year when you changed residency. The timing mismatch between the two systems can create real differences in how much tax you ultimately pay, so it's worth working through the specific dates.

There are also reporting obligations to keep in mind. If you hold foreign bank or brokerage accounts with a combined balance over $10,000 at any point in the year, you'll need to file an FBAR, and you may need Form 8938 under FATCA. If you still hold European-domiciled investment funds after becoming a US resident, those are often PFICs, which carry punitive US tax treatment, so consider that when deciding what to hold. Shares of the US-listed employer stock don't have this problem.

Given the overlapping rules, it's worth paying for a preparer or advisor with cross-border experience. Keep records of each offering date, purchase date, fair market value on those dates, and purchase price, because you'll need them to compute the correct basis and ordinary income for each lot.

I'm sorry your husband is going through this. I can't confirm from here that axitinib caused his lung clots, but his care team can. Axitinib's prescribing information does list venous blood clots, including pulmonary embolism, as a possible serious side effect, so the explanation is plausible. Cancer itself also raises clot risk, and other factors such as immobility, recent surgery, or other medications can contribute. Ask his oncologist directly whether they consider axitinib the likely cause, what the clots' treatment plan is (usually blood thinners for a period of time), and whether he needs to avoid any particular drugs because of them.

As for other treatments, there are several options for metastatic kidney cancer after a period on axitinib, and the best choice depends on his overall health, how the cancer has responded, and his prior treatments. Some commonly used options include other tyrosine kinase inhibitors such as cabozantinib, lenvatinib combined with everolimus, or sunitinib and pazopanib. Immunotherapy drugs such as nivolumab, often combined with ipilimumab, are also used, sometimes in combination with a targeted drug. For patients whose disease has progressed after both targeted and immune treatments, belzutifan is an option. Each of these carries its own side effects, and some, including several of the tyrosine kinase inhibitors, can also affect clotting, so that history should shape the decision.

I'd suggest asking his oncologist for a scan review to see how the cancer is doing now, whether his cancer is responding or has progressed, and which next-line treatments fit his situation best. If the current team isn't offering options you're comfortable with, a second opinion at a larger cancer center or a kidney cancer specialist can be very helpful. Clinical trials are also worth asking about, since they sometimes offer newer drugs. Bring a written list of his questions and his medication history to the appointment.

A leading voice in the American women's rights movement, she also holds the distinction of being the first Massachusetts woman to receive a college degree. Committed to equality and women's rights, she devoted tireless effort to winning women the right to vote. She passed away on October 18, 1893, at 75 years old.

Andrew Ng is a British-American computer scientist and entrepreneur best known for his work in artificial intelligence, machine learning, and online education. He is a professor of computer science at Stanford University, where he has taught and conducted research in areas such as deep learning, robotics, and natural language processing. He is also known for co-founding Google Brain, a research team at Google that helped advance large-scale deep learning, and for serving as chief scientist at Baidu, where he led efforts in AI research.

Ng is widely recognized for his role in making AI education accessible. He co-founded Coursera, one of the largest online learning platforms, and created its popular Machine Learning course, which has introduced millions of learners around the world to the field. He also founded DeepLearning.AI, which offers courses and specializations on deep learning, and he has launched AI Fund, an investment firm that backs AI startups. Through these ventures, he has been a prominent advocate for democratizing AI skills and encouraging its responsible use across industries.

Sorry to hear about the pain and burning in your ankle, that sounds miserable. Honestly, you should get it looked at by a doctor or other healthcare provider so they can figure out what's actually going on. It could be a sprain, a fracture, tendon or joint inflammation, nerve irritation, or even an infection, and those need different treatment. Until you can get in, a few things might help take the edge off. Try to rest it and avoid walking or running on it. Prop it up above heart level when you can to cut down on swelling. Ice helps too: wrap an ice pack in a towel and put it on for 15 to 20 minutes every two or three hours. Supportive shoes with good arch support and a firm heel can ease the strain. Over-the-counter painkillers like ibuprofen or acetaminophen may also take the edge off. Just don't skip the appointment. A provider can pin down the cause and might suggest physical therapy or prescription meds if it's needed.

The cross-entropy method, often abbreviated CE method, is a Monte Carlo technique introduced by Reuven Rubinstein in the late 1990s. It was originally designed for estimating the probabilities of rare events and was later adapted into a general-purpose tool for optimization. Its central idea is to iteratively adjust a sampling distribution so that it concentrates more and more of its probability mass on the region of interest, whether that region is a rare event or the neighborhood of an optimal solution.

For rare-event estimation, suppose you want to estimate the probability that some random quantity exceeds a very high threshold. Naive simulation would almost never produce such an event, so the estimate would be useless. Importance sampling fixes this by drawing samples from a different distribution under which the event is common, then reweighting the results by a likelihood ratio. The difficulty is choosing a good alternative distribution. The CE method does this by restricting attention to a parametric family, such as Gaussians or Bernoullis, and picking the member that minimizes the Kullback-Leibler divergence, also called cross-entropy, from the ideal but unknown optimal importance distribution. Because that ideal distribution cannot be sampled directly, the method approximates it through an iterative procedure.

For optimization, the procedure works like this. You want to maximize a function S(x). You start with a parametric distribution over candidate solutions, for example a Gaussian with some mean and variance. At each iteration you draw a batch of samples, evaluate S on each, and keep the top fraction, called the elite samples, often the best 5 to 10 percent. You then refit the distribution parameters to the elite samples by maximum likelihood, which is equivalent to minimizing the cross-entropy between the empirical elite distribution and the parametric family. For a Gaussian, this just means setting the new mean and variance to the sample mean and variance of the elites. Often the update is smoothed, mixing old and new parameters, to avoid premature collapse. The process repeats until the distribution becomes concentrated near a single point, which is taken as the solution.

The method is appealing because it is simple, requires no gradients, and handles continuous, discrete, and combinatorial problems. For combinatorial problems like the traveling salesman problem or max-cut, the distribution might be over binary vectors or transition probabilities. It has also been used in reinforcement learning and control, where it appears as a policy search method and as a planner in model-based approaches, where action sequences are sampled and refit to the best-scoring ones.

Its limitations include sensitivity to the choice of distribution family, sample size, and elite fraction, a tendency to converge prematurely to local optima when the variance shrinks too quickly, and poor scaling in very high dimensions. It is closely related to evolution strategies and estimation-of-distribution algorithms.

The foreign exchange market ranks as the most actively traded market globally, with the stock market coming in second. Forex is where currencies are exchanged, and it stands as the biggest financial market anywhere, handling more than $5 trillion in transactions each day. Equities are also very easy to trade, as shares worth billions of dollars change hands daily. Futures and options markets likewise rank among those with high liquidity.

Foamy stools may result from several causes, such as irritation of the intestinal lining, shifts in how much or what kind of digestive fluid the intestines release, and excess gas. For a pneumonia patient taking antibiotics, these drugs may alter the balance of bacteria in the gut, which can lead to irregular bowel movements and frothy stool. Dehydration, poor absorption of nutrients, and certain medications can also play a role. Anyone noticing changes in their bowel habits should talk with a healthcare professional, who can offer tailored advice on identifying and addressing the cause. For a patient recovering from pneumonia, it is especially important to confirm that the infection has cleared and that they are eating well and staying properly hydrated.

Metal is a genre of rock music known for heavy, aggressive sound: distorted, low-tuned guitars, powerful drumming, often fast tempos, and vocals that range from clean and soaring to guttural growls and screams. At its core, it's about intensity and power, and fans tend to value virtuosity, dramatic energy, and a sense of catharsis or release.

The themes in metal vary widely depending on the subgenre. Classic heavy metal from bands like Black Sabbath and Judas Priest often dealt with rebellion, fantasy, mythology, and the darker side of life. Thrash metal, pioneered by groups like Metallica and Slayer, tended toward social critique, war, and anger. Death and black metal went further into horror, violence, nihilism, and sometimes mysticism or anti-religious imagery. Power metal leans toward epic fantasy and heroism, while progressive metal bands like Dream Theater explore complex song structures and sometimes philosophical or personal subjects. Many metal bands also write about personal struggles like depression, alienation, and heartbreak.

Beyond the lyrics, metal is also a culture. Its fans often form tight communities around concerts, festivals, album art, fashion such as leather and band shirts, and a shared appreciation for musicianship. Many listeners find that the music helps them process difficult emotions or simply feel energized, and the genre is often misunderstood by outsiders who hear only the noise rather than the craft and feeling behind it.

So HSBC Hong Kong's Deposit Plus is basically a savings account where you earn interest on whatever you've got parked in it. The rate is tiered, so the more you put in, the better the rate you get. If you want to make the most of it, the obvious move is to keep your balance high. That might mean saving a bit more each month, or folding a few separate accounts into one Deposit Plus account so everything counts toward the higher tier.

Definitely read the terms and conditions before you jump in, though. Check for fees. Some accounts will hit you with a charge if you pull money out too early, or if you make too many transactions in a month, and that can eat into whatever interest you're earning.

If you're thinking about moving somewhere new for your first job after graduating, there are several factors worth weighing first. Start with living costs: look up what everyday expenses look like in the city or town you're considering, so you can work out how much you'd need to earn to keep your current lifestyle. Next, explore the housing situation. If you plan to rent, pay attention to typical rent prices, how many apartments are actually available, and the overall condition of the buildings. Think about getting around, too. Is public transit convenient and reasonably priced, or would you need a car, and is owning one practical and affordable there? Consider the social and cultural side of life as well. Identify the activities that matter most to you, such as dining, live music, museums, or sports, and find out what the new area offers. Finally, check the job market in your target location to confirm that your field has solid openings, and think about whether those opportunities will continue to grow over time. A move for your first job out of college can be an exciting and rewarding step, but thorough research and readiness for the difficulties and adjustments that come with settling somewhere new will make it go much more smoothly.

Frederick Phillips "Fred" Brooks Jr. was an American computer scientist, software engineer, and author whose work greatly advanced computer science and computer engineering. He is chiefly remembered for his role in building the IBM System/360, the first line of computers built to serve a wide spread of uses, and for "The Mythical Man-Month," a book examining the difficulties of running large software projects. Brooks earned his bachelor's degree in electrical engineering at Duke University, then went on to complete his master's and doctoral degrees in computer science at Harvard University. Over many years at IBM he rose to lead the System/360 project, one of the most successful and influential computer undertakings in history. Later he became a professor at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, where he kept contributing to the discipline. Brooks received wide acclaim and many awards, among them the Turing Award, considered the top prize in computer science, and the National Medal of Technology and Innovation. He was additionally named a Fellow of both the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) and the Association for Computing Machinery (ACM).

If a person drilled a deep shaft into the planet and linked it to the sea, seawater would pour down into the opening and keep filling it until the water's pressure matched the pressure of the surrounding crust, at which point the inflow would cease. Disregarding sunk costs might, in theory, be a way to make an investment look more appealing, but doing so is usually unwise. Sunk costs are expenses that have already been paid and cannot be gotten back. To ignore them is to leave out the money already put into an investment when deciding whether to keep funding it. Although this can make an investment look better in the short run, it may produce bad decisions over time. The reason is that sunk costs ought not to factor into the choice to continue investing in something. The choice should rest instead on what the investment is expected to return in the future. Suppose, for instance, that you have put $10,000 into a company that is doing poorly. If you set aside that $10,000 and keep investing because you believe the company will eventually recover and begin to do well, you may lose even more money down the road should it fail to improve. Overall, it is important to weigh all the relevant information carefully when making an investment decision, including the costs already incurred and the anticipated future returns. Overlooking sunk costs can result in poor investment choices and may cost you additional money.

There are several factors to weigh when deciding whether to purchase the home you rent from your landlord. If a mortgage is necessary, determine whether you would qualify for a loan and what its terms would look like. Next is location. Honestly, there are a few things that could cause swelling of the foreskin with red patches after sex, and the only way to know for sure is to get it checked by a doctor or clinic. The most common suspects are infections. STIs like gonorrhea, chlamydia, and syphilis can make the foreskin and penis swell and turn red, and you might notice burning when you pee. Herpes is another one, and it often shows up as redness, swelling, or little blister-like sores in the genital area.

It could also be an allergic reaction. Condoms, lube, or other products you used during sex can irritate things pretty badly, and that usually comes with itching and stinging. Plain irritation or inflammation is possible too. That's called balanitis, and it can happen from poor hygiene, tight clothing, or contact with certain chemicals. A yeast infection is worth mentioning as well. It's caused by an overgrowth of Candida, causes swelling, redness, itching, and burning, and is usually easy to treat with antifungal meds.

Don't try to guess which one it is. Get seen soon, especially if you have sores, discharge, fever, or pain that's getting worse.

Historically, small-cap stocks have tended to trade at higher price-to-earnings ratios than large-cap stocks, though the gap has varied considerably over time and depends heavily on how the categories and earnings are defined. Using the Russell 2000 as a small-cap benchmark and the S&P 500 or Russell 1000 for large caps, small caps have often carried trailing P/Es in the high teens to mid-20s during stable periods, while large caps have often sat in the high teens to low 20s. The difference is frequently modest on a trailing basis, but on a forward basis small caps have sometimes looked considerably more expensive, partly because their earnings are more volatile and often depressed during downturns, which inflates their P/E at the bottom of a cycle.

A notable feature of the history is that small-cap P/Es can spike sharply during recessions and earnings collapses, when the denominator shrinks. Many small companies also have negative earnings, which are excluded from the calculation, so the reported median or aggregate P/E for the index can be misleading. Analysts therefore often prefer to compare the weighted harmonic mean P/E or use forward estimates, and to look at the premium or discount of small caps relative to large caps over time rather than the absolute levels.

For precise, current figures, the best sources are data providers such as FactSet, Morningstar, or the index providers themselves (FTSE Russell for the Russell indexes, S&P Dow Jones Indices for the S&P family), since the numbers shift daily and methodologies differ. If you tell me the time window or specific indexes you care about, I can help you frame the comparison more precisely, though I would recommend verifying exact values against those sources.

Pain in the right upper abdomen that comes and goes and changes with position can have several causes, and your pattern gives some useful clues. Pain that gets worse when you stand and eases when you lie down often points to a mechanical or muscular source rather than a digestive one. A small hernia, such as a ventral or hiatal hernia, can bulge or pull more when you are upright. Strained or irritated abdominal wall muscles, or inflamed rib cartilage (costochondritis), can also flare with posture and movement. Sometimes the liver or gallbladder is involved, since gallbladder pain tends to come in episodes, often after meals, but it can occur without an obvious trigger. Acid-related problems like reflux or an ulcer are also possible, though they more often feel worse lying down. A kidney stone or kidney problem on the right can cause pain in this area that shifts with position, but it usually comes with more intense pain, urinary changes, or pain that spreads toward the back or groin.

Because the pain is intermittent and you have no digestive changes, a doctor will usually start with a physical exam and may order blood tests, such as liver enzymes and a complete blood count, along with an abdominal ultrasound. Those tests can identify gallbladder, liver, kidney, and many hernia-related causes fairly quickly.

You should seek medical care promptly if you notice fever, yellowing of the skin or eyes, dark urine, pale stools, vomiting blood or material that looks like coffee grounds, black or bloody stools, unexplained weight loss, pain that becomes severe or constant, pain that spreads to your chest or back, shortness of breath, or a lump in the abdomen or groin. Go to an emergency department right away if the pain is suddenly severe or you feel faint.

In the meantime, keep a brief log of when the pain starts, how long it lasts, and what you were doing, which will help your doctor narrow things down. Avoid heavy lifting or straining until you have been evaluated. Since this has been recurring, it is worth booking an appointment rather than waiting for it to resolve on its own.

Lean manufacturing is a production approach centered on cutting out waste and increasing the value delivered. Its aim is to build a production system that is both highly efficient and effective, getting top-quality products to customers as quickly as possible while consuming as few resources as possible. Toyota Motor Corporation created lean manufacturing in the 1950s, drawing on the Toyota Production System (TPS). Taiichi Ohno, frequently called the father of lean manufacturing, developed TPS. This system seeks to remove waste, lessen variation, and boost efficiency by standardizing work procedures and refining them on an ongoing basis. In the years since, industries as varied as automotive, aerospace, healthcare, and electronics have embraced lean principles. The approach has also reached service sectors like banking, insurance, and government agencies, where it has been used to make operations more efficient and effective.

Homeschooling is when a kid learns at home instead of going to a regular school building. Usually a parent acts as the teacher, but sometimes families use online classes, tutors, co-ops where several homeschooling families take turns teaching each other's kids, or community college classes for older students. The family picks the books and lessons, decides the schedule, and keeps track of what the child has learned. Every place has its own rules. In the United States, each state sets them. Some states ask almost nothing of families, while others want parents to send in a notice, keep records, teach certain subjects, or have the child take tests now and then to show they're learning.

As for the diploma, it's a bit like this: in a regular school, the school is the one that says "you finished!" and hands you a diploma. In homeschooling, the parents are usually the school, so the parents are the ones who make and sign the diploma. In many U.S. states, that parent-issued diploma is perfectly legal and counts just like any other. Some families instead use an accredited online or correspondence program that issues its own diploma, and some students take a test like the GED to get a high school equivalency certificate. There isn't one single "official homeschool degree" from the government. It depends on how the family does it and where they live.

Do colleges accept homeschooled students? Yes, very much so. Most colleges in the U.S., including very famous ones like Harvard, Stanford, and MIT, accept homeschoolers and often have special instructions for them. Since colleges can't compare a homeschool to a school they already know, they look at other things to understand what you learned. They usually want a transcript the parent writes up listing your courses and grades, a description of what you studied, test scores like the SAT or ACT, and sometimes extra proof such as AP exams or community college classes. Letters of recommendation from people outside the family, like a tutor, coach, or class instructor, also help a lot.

Does homeschooling hurt your chances? Not really, as long as you can show what you learned. Colleges care about whether you're ready to do the work and whether you're an interesting, motivated person. Homeschoolers who keep good records, get solid test scores, and do things they're passionate about, like volunteering, building projects, sports, music, or starting a small business, often do just as well as other students, and sometimes they stand out because their path was unusual. Where it can get harder is if there's very little proof of what the student studied, because then the college has a tough time trusting the grades. So the simple version is: homeschooling is fine for college, but you have to show your work.

Think of your body like a car, and sugar in your blood as the gas. Insulin is like a key that lets the gas get into the engine cells. In type 1 diabetes, the body can't make its own insulin, so people have to put it in from the outside, with shots or a pump. The trouble is that a person has to guess how much insulin to give, and sometimes they give too much. Too much insulin pushes too much sugar out of the blood and into the cells, and the blood runs low on sugar. That's a low blood sugar, and it can make a person shaky, confused, or even faint.

Now, you're right that glucagon is the body's rescue helper. When sugar gets low, glucagon tells the liver to open its sugar storage closet and release some into the blood. But there are a few reasons it doesn't always save the day in type 1 diabetes.

First, the glucagon response often gets weaker over time. In type 1 diabetes, the alpha cells that make glucagon don't react as well to low sugar, so the rescue signal can be late or too small.

Second, the liver's closet may be nearly empty. Glucagon can only release sugar that's been stored. If the person has exercised a lot, skipped meals, or had low sugars recently, there may not be much left to release.

Third, the insulin is already in the body and keeps working. Injected insulin can't be switched off the way a healthy pancreas turns its own insulin down. So even if glucagon is shouting "release sugar!", the extra insulin is shouting "put sugar away!" at the same time, and insulin can win. Glucagon is also slower than eating sugar.

So when blood sugar drops, eating or drinking fast sugar, like juice or glucose tablets, is the quickest and most reliable way to fix it. It goes straight into the blood within minutes and doesn't depend on a tired or weak backup system. Glucagon is a nice helper, but in type 1 diabetes it can't always be counted on, which is why people keep sugar nearby, and why some also keep emergency glucagon medicine for severe lows.

The medicines you mention treat only part of the problem. Recurrent dysentery with blood needs a clear cause. A normal colonoscopy is reassuring, since it makes ulcerative colitis, Crohn's disease, polyps and cancer in the colon less likely, but it doesn't exclude everything. Ask about stool tests for infections and parasites (especially amoebiasis, Giardia and bacterial infection), a stool calprotectin test, and a check for hemorrhoids or anal fissures, which are common sources of blood. Blood in the stool can also come from higher in the digestive tract, so an upper endoscopy may be worthwhile given your acidity.

For the liver, "chronic liver problem" is too general to treat. You should have liver function tests (ALT, AST, ALP, bilirubin, albumin), an abdominal ultrasound, and viral hepatitis tests (hepatitis B and C). Depending on the results, doctors often also check for fatty liver, alcohol-related damage, autoimmune liver disease and iron or copper disorders. Treatment depends entirely on which of these is present. If you haven't had these done, ask for them, and consider seeing a gastroenterologist or hepatologist rather than relying on general treatment alone.

Some things help in nearly all cases. Avoid alcohol completely. Avoid unnecessary painkillers, herbal or "liver tonic" products, and supplements, since some can harm the liver. Eat regular, small, simple meals, limit fried, spicy and very oily food, and don't lie down right after eating. Drink clean, safe water, and wash your hands carefully, because recurrent dysentery often comes from contaminated food or water. If you are overweight, gradual weight loss improves fatty liver and acidity. Don't stop your anxiety medicine suddenly, as that can cause withdrawal symptoms.

Seek medical care urgently if you notice heavy or continuing bleeding, black stools, vomiting blood, yellowing of the skin or eyes, swelling of the abdomen or legs, severe abdominal pain, fever, unintended weight loss, or marked weakness or dizziness.

Take your colonoscopy report and all previous test results to your next appointment, and ask directly, "What is the exact diagnosis, and what tests are still pending?" If you don't get a clear answer, a second opinion from a gastroenterologist is reasonable.

Think of a bullet like a little pebble you throw. The "mm" number tells you how wide the bullet is, like the width of the pebble. A 9 mm bullet is about 9 millimeters across, which is roughly the width of a pencil eraser.

A wider bullet isn't automatically more dangerous, though. How hard a bullet hits depends on three things: how wide it is, how heavy it is, and how fast it travels. It's like comparing a tennis ball thrown gently with a baseball thrown hard. The wider one isn't always the one that hurts more. A 15 mm bullet would be wider than a 9 mm, but whether it's more powerful depends on how heavy and fast it is. Also, 15 mm is an unusual size for common firearms, so the comparison is less useful in practice.

The ".308" is a different kind of measurement. It uses inches instead of millimeters. A .308 bullet is about 0.308 inches wide, which is roughly 7.8 mm, so it's actually a little narrower than a 9 mm. But .308 is a rifle bullet, and it's usually launched from a long gun with a lot more gunpowder behind it. It travels much faster and carries much more energy than a 9 mm handgun bullet. So even though it's slightly thinner, a .308 rifle round is generally considered far more powerful.

In short, the number tells you about width, but the power comes from the whole package: the size, the weight, the speed, and the gun it's fired from.

So a Turing machine is basically a made-up machine that Alan Turing came up with. He was a famous mathematician and computer scientist, in case you haven't heard of him. The point of it is to show how a computer could work using just a handful of really simple instructions.

Picture a long strip of paper that you use to store stuff. You can write numbers or letters on it and read them back later. Now picture a little machine that slides along the strip, reading and writing as it goes. That's your Turing machine.

It runs on a set of rules (you'd call that an algorithm) that tell it what to do next. Say it reads a number off the paper, adds one, and writes the new number back. It just repeats that over and over, same rules every time, and by stacking up enough of those little steps you can get it doing way more complicated things.

The big idea is that with the right instructions, a Turing machine can do anything a regular computer can do. That's why people in computer science care about it so much. It gives us a simple way to think about how computers work and what kinds of problems we can actually solve with them.

There are a few ways to split a mortgage and living costs fairly, and the best one really depends on your situation. Here are some options.

First, you could split things in proportion to what each person put into the purchase. If one person paid 60% of the price and the other paid 40%, the 60% person would cover a bigger chunk of the mortgage payments. Pretty straightforward.

Second, you could just split it 50/50 no matter who paid what. This can feel fairer if one person has a lot more money to put in than the other, since it keeps things even.

Third, think about who actually lives there. If one person is in the place full-time and the other is there part-time or not at all, it might make sense to base the split on how much each person uses it. The full-time resident would usually cover more of the mortgage and bills, and the other person pays less.

And if you're stuck, talk to a financial planner or a lawyer. They can look at your numbers and help you land on something that works for both of you.

Yes, index funds are capable of paying dividends. An index fund is a kind of mutual fund or exchange-traded fund (ETF) that follows a specific market index, like the S&P 500 or the Dow Jones Industrial Average. Certain index funds aim to replicate the index's performance as precisely as possible, and that includes passing along any dividends the index's member companies pay out.
