Earning $250,000 through trading, investing, or launching a business within five years is achievable, though it takes hard work, commitment, and some good fortune. Several steps can improve your odds. First, educate yourself by building a firm grasp of how financial markets and businesses work, since this lets you make well-informed choices. Next, set clear goals by deciding precisely what you want to accomplish and how much you hope to earn, which keeps you motivated and focused. Then create a plan for reaching those goals, whether that means designing a trading or investment strategy, starting a company, or doing both. Patience matters too: trading and investing can be unpredictable, and results may take a while to appear, so don't lose heart if success doesn't come right away. You should also be willing to take calculated risks, but weigh the possible downsides and payoffs carefully before you commit to any decision. Keep your attention on your long-term objectives, because it is tempting to chase the newest trends or hot tips. Finally, think about getting advice from a financial advisor or a mentor experienced in your field of interest, who can offer useful perspective and help you stay on course. Keep in mind that trading, investing, and entrepreneurship come with no guarantees. Be realistic and avoid being swept up by hype. With diligence, determination, and a little luck, reaching your financial goals is possible.

Buying physical gold directly, such as bullion bars or coins, offers a tangible asset that you hold outright. It has no counterparty risk in the sense that you are not relying on a fund manager or custodian's paper promise, and it can serve as a hedge in scenarios where financial systems are disrupted. Physical gold also carries no annual expense ratio, though you pay a premium over the spot price when buying and often a markup again when selling, and dealers may charge spreads of several percent on smaller coins. The drawbacks are significant: you must arrange secure storage, either at home, which brings theft and insurance concerns, or in a vault, which adds fees. Selling can be less convenient than clicking a button in a brokerage account, you may face sales tax in some jurisdictions, and the collectible premium on popular coins can make them a poor value for pure investment purposes. Record-keeping for taxes is also more cumbersome.

Gold ETFs like GLD, IAU, and SGOL trade on exchanges like stocks, so you can buy or sell in seconds during market hours, in any quantity, with minimal friction and often a tight bid-ask spread. They are easy to hold in an IRA or brokerage account, and they avoid storage and insurance hassles. The costs are an annual expense ratio, which is about 0.25 percent for GLD, 0.25 percent for IAU, and 0.17 percent for SGOL, and you do not own the metal itself but a share of a trust that holds it. That introduces some counterparty and structural risk, since you depend on the custodian and the trust's terms, and in extreme scenarios redemption for physical metal is limited to large authorized participants. Tax treatment also differs: in the United States, physical gold and many gold ETFs are generally taxed as collectibles, with a maximum long-term rate of 28 percent, which is higher than the rate on ordinary long-term stock gains. ETFs are typically taxed this way as well, though some structures differ, so checking the specific fund matters.

In practice, ETFs suit most investors who want exposure to gold as a portfolio component because they are cheap to hold, liquid, and simple to manage. Physical gold appeals more to those who want direct ownership, a deliberate hedge against systemic risk, or a holding outside the financial system, and who are willing to accept higher transaction costs and storage burdens to get it. Among the ETFs, SGOL has the lowest expense ratio, while IAU is often cited for its lower share price, which makes it easier to buy fractional amounts.

Okay so the UN was set up after WWII mainly to encourage countries to work together and hopefully stop wars from breaking out again. It's got a bunch of different bodies and agencies covering stuff like peace and security, human rights, and development. A big part of what it does is push diplomacy, basically getting countries in a room to talk through their problems and hopefully land on a peaceful fix. It also runs peacekeeping missions, where troops get sent to places at risk of fighting or already in the middle of it. Those missions keep an eye on things and try to stop the violence from getting worse.

That said, it doesn't always work. Conflicts and wars still happen all the time, and the UN can't force anyone to behave, especially if countries just refuse to cooperate or ignore what it recommends. Where it can still step in is humanitarian help, like getting food, water, and medical supplies to people caught up in the mess, and pushing for a peaceful way out.

On a standard traffic light, the colors are arranged vertically, with red on top, yellow in the middle, and green on the bottom. In some countries or on certain signals, the lights are arranged horizontally instead, with red on the left, yellow in the center, and green on the right.

The Globe Theatre, located in London, England, was constructed in 1599 by a group of actors with William Shakespeare at its head. Shaped like a circle and open to the sky, it featured a thatched roof and three tiers of galleries, and it hosted theatrical productions, particularly the plays Shakespeare wrote. A fire consumed the building in 1613, after which it was reconstructed, but in 1642 it was shut down because Puritans were opposed to theater.

Hair testing is a drug testing method that can reveal whether a person has used certain substances over a much longer period than urine or blood tests allow. As hair grows, drugs and their metabolites from the bloodstream become incorporated into the hair shaft, where they remain stable. Because hair typically grows about a half inch to an inch per month, a standard sample of roughly 1.5 inches cut close to the scalp can usually provide a history of drug use covering about 90 days. Laboratories analyze the sample for substances such as cocaine, methamphetamine, opiates, amphetamines, cannabis metabolites, and some prescription medications.

The test can indicate what substances were present in the body and roughly when exposure occurred, since segments of hair closer to the scalp reflect more recent use. It is often used by employers, courts, child custody evaluators, and in some medical or rehabilitation settings. Its main advantages are the long detection window and the difficulty of tampering with a sample compared with urine.

There are limitations to keep in mind. Hair testing generally cannot show the exact timing of a single use or how recently someone used a drug within the past week or so, because hair needs time to grow out of the scalp before it can be collected. Results can also be affected by hair treatments like bleaching or dyeing, and by external contamination such as secondhand smoke exposure, which has been a concern particularly with cannabis. Body hair can be used when scalp hair is unavailable, though it grows more slowly and has a different timeframe. Hair tests also do not measure impairment, so they cannot confirm whether someone was intoxicated at a particular moment. Interpretation of results usually requires a careful review by qualified professionals, and confirmatory testing is standard practice when a result is positive.

A single hard or "thumping" heartbeat that happens a few times a day, as you describe, is most commonly caused by an extra beat called a premature contraction. These come in two main types: premature atrial contractions (PACs), which start in the upper chambers, and premature ventricular contractions (PVCs), which start in the lower chambers. What you feel is often not the early beat itself but the pause after it, followed by a stronger-than-normal beat as the heart refills more completely. These extra beats are very common and, in people with an otherwise healthy heart, are usually harmless, even when they persist for weeks or come and go for months.

Several things often trigger or increase these beats: caffeine (coffee, tea, energy drinks), alcohol, nicotine, stress or anxiety, poor sleep, dehydration, heavy meals, intense exercise, and some medications or supplements such as decongestants, asthma inhalers, thyroid medication, or stimulants. Medical conditions can also contribute, including an overactive thyroid, anemia, low potassium or magnesium, fever, and, less commonly, underlying heart disease such as valve problems, cardiomyopathy, or prior heart damage.

Capturing an episode on your Holter monitor is very useful, because the main question is what rhythm was happening at the moment you felt the symptom. I would recommend bringing or sending that recording, along with the time you felt the palpitation, to your doctor or a cardiologist for interpretation. If it shows isolated PACs or PVCs, the usual next steps are simple blood tests (thyroid function, blood count, electrolytes such as potassium and magnesium) and often an echocardiogram to confirm the heart structure is normal, particularly if the extra beats are frequent. If everything is normal, treatment is usually reassurance and reducing triggers, with medication such as a beta blocker reserved for cases where symptoms are bothersome or the beats are very frequent.

If you'd like, you can describe what the Holter report or tracing says, or share the summary numbers such as heart rate and any labeled beats, and I can help explain it. In the meantime, try cutting back on caffeine and alcohol, staying well hydrated, and getting enough sleep, and note whether the palpitations change.

You should seek urgent care right away if palpitations come with chest pain, fainting or near-fainting, significant shortness of breath, or severe dizziness, or if you have a sustained rapid or irregular heartbeat lasting more than a few minutes. Also see a doctor sooner if you have known heart disease, a family history of sudden cardiac death at a young age, or if the palpitations happen mainly during exercise.

Imagine the universe is like a ball sitting in a small dip on a hill. It's resting in a dip that isn't the lowest place it could be. Physicists think the "dip" is a kind of energy state that all of space could be in. A ball in a small dip can stay there for a very long time, but it isn't truly settled. Every so often, a tiny random jiggle, called quantum tunneling, could push a small piece of it over the edge into a lower, more stable spot.

When that happens, a little bubble of the new, lower state forms. Inside it, the laws of physics and the basic building blocks of matter would be different, so nothing that exists now could survive there. The bubble then grows outward, very fast, close to the speed of light. You can't outrun it, and you can't see it coming until it arrives. That's why it's called a "death bubble" or vacuum decay.

Are they stable? The bubble itself is not stable at all. Once it forms, it keeps expanding and can't be stopped. The dip the universe sits in is what physicists call "metastable," meaning stable for an extremely long time but not forever. For the bubble to form, though, is incredibly unlikely, and the odds for any particular region in any particular year are tiny. Current measurements suggest our universe may or may not be in such a dip; scientists are still working that out. So there's no sign it's happening now, and nobody expects it to happen during human lifetimes.

The book's point is about deep time. If a bubble has a tiny chance of starting in any given place, then across billions of years and enormous amounts of space, one eventually will. That's a sobering idea for a civilization that hopes to last forever.

Night sweats, low energy, and weight loss can come from a lot of different things, so it's worth getting checked out rather than guessing. Since you're diabetic, keeping an eye on your blood sugar and sticking to your meds matters a lot here. Your knee replacement and the aspirin could be playing a part too, and so can blood pressure swings, which often show up as sweats and tiredness. Tell your doctor everything you're taking and exactly what you've been noticing, since that helps them narrow things down. And if the symptoms are severe or just won't let up, don't wait. Get seen sooner rather than later.

Okay so cloud computing basically means a bunch of internet-connected computers working together to give you computing resources whenever you need them. You don't have to run apps or store your stuff on your own machine or server. You just log in and use whatever you need from a cloud provider.

There are a few reasons people go with it. First, it's often cheaper, since you only pay for what you actually use instead of buying and maintaining your own servers. Second, it's really easy to scale up or down when your needs change, and you don't have to buy new hardware to do it. Third, providers usually have backup systems running, so your apps stay up even if one server goes down. And fourth, they tend to have pretty strong security in place to protect your data and apps.

There are also a few different flavors. Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS) is the most basic one: the provider rents you the raw stuff like servers, storage, and networking. Platform as a Service (PaaS) goes a step up and gives you a platform, like an operating system, a database, or dev tools, so you can build and run your own apps on top. Software as a Service (SaaS) is the most hands-off: you just use a finished app through your browser. Big names in the space include Amazon Web Services (AWS), Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud Platform.

Far-right politics describes an ideology that places a firm emphasis on conventional social and cultural norms, favors strong authority, and resists progressive or liberal movements. Adherents often hold that their own group or nation is superior and tend to distrust outsiders and minority communities. Such ideologies may also show contempt for democratic institutions and back authoritarian or dictatorial systems of rule. Certain versions, including fascism and Nazism, have been tied to violence, racial hatred, and the persecution of minorities. These positions are generally regarded as falling well outside mainstream political thought, and the great majority of people reject them.

Honestly there are a handful of ways people manage to spend more than they bring in without ending up in debt. The obvious one is dipping into savings or other money they've already got stashed away. Some folks sell stuff they don't need, like old furniture, electronics, or even a car, to cover the gap. Others cut back for a while, skipping the nonessentials and haggling down bills or calling their providers to get better rates. A lot of people pick up side gigs or freelance work to bring in extra cash. And yeah, some borrow from friends or family, though that can get messy fast and strain the relationship if it isn't handled carefully.

All of that can keep you out of debt for a while, but none of it really fixes the underlying problem. You can only patch a spending gap so many times before you run out of stuff to sell or savings to tap. The long-term answer is living within your means: sticking to a budget, setting aside some money every month, and paying down whatever you already owe.

Pain in the upper left chest, neck, and upper back can come from a bunch of different places. It's often muscle or joint trouble, and fibromyalgia can cause widespread aches and tenderness too. But the heart can be behind it as well, including angina (chest pain from reduced blood flow to the heart) or even a heart attack, so don't brush it off. Lung issues like pneumonia or pleurisy (inflammation of the lining of the lungs) can cause it, and so can digestive stuff like acid reflux or gallstones.

Honestly, you really should see a doctor to figure out what's going on and get it treated properly. Until then, over-the-counter stuff like acetaminophen or ibuprofen might take the edge off, and a heating pad or ice pack on the sore spot can help too. If the pain is severe, comes with shortness of breath, sweating, or nausea, or spreads to your arm or jaw, get emergency help right away.

It's wonderful to have you here today, and I'm glad to help with your questions. Your first question concerns lumbar lordosis, which describes the typical curve in the lower portion of the spine. A healthy spine shows a natural inward bend in this lower region, called lordosis. When that curve becomes straighter, sometimes described as flattening or loss of lordosis, it can be worth looking into, since it may point to an underlying problem such as weak muscles, a spinal disorder, or poor posture. Please discuss this observation from your MRI report with a healthcare provider so you can decide on the right next steps. Regarding acne, a range of over-the-counter and prescription creams and ointments can help, including products containing benzoyl peroxide, salicylic acid, or retinoids. Choosing something suited to your skin type and following the directions closely matters. If several products haven't worked for you, a dermatologist or another healthcare professional can offer further guidance and alternative treatments. Acne can also be influenced by factors such as hormonal shifts, certain medications, and some skin care products. If you have PCOS (polycystic ovary syndrome), that may contribute to breakouts as well. Working with a healthcare professional to address any underlying causes and build a treatment plan that suits you is the best approach.

Secret agents, or spies, are basically people who work for a government or some other organization and collect information on the quiet. Sometimes they're trying to figure out what other countries or groups are up to, and sometimes they're keeping tabs on what's going on inside their own country. How they do it varies a lot. They might watch people, intercept communications, or lean on high-tech tools to pull in data.

The James Bond type, which came from Ian Fleming's novels, isn't really realistic. Some of the gadgets might be loosely based on real equipment, but most of what happens in the Bond movies is heavily dramatized and has little to do with how the job actually works.

Spying is still very much a thing, though, and plenty of governments and organizations around the world do it. The catch is that the details are mostly kept under wraps, so it's hard to say exactly what agents do day to day or how they operate.

Imagine a big, empty playground where lots of kids from many different families moved in, one after another. The land was already home to many Native American peoples, who had lived there for thousands of years, so it wasn't really empty, but the newcomers from Europe and elsewhere arrived with their own ideas, tools, and hopes. Over a few hundred years, these families built a huge neighborhood, and it grew very strong for a few main reasons.

First, the land itself was a treasure chest. It had rich soil for growing food, big rivers for moving goods, forests for building homes and ships, and lots of coal, iron, oil, and other things for making machines and power. Having so much to use gave the country a head start.

Second, the people who came were a mix of many cultures, and they had a habit of building new things. The country also made rules, called a constitution, that tried to protect everyone's right to speak, work, and try new ideas. When people feel free to invent and start businesses, lots of good inventions happen. The light bulb, the telephone, and the computer are examples of things that came from this kind of place.

Third, the country was lucky to be far away from the big wars that kept happening in Europe for a long time. Oceans acted like a moat around a castle, so it could grow without being bombed or invaded often. Then, when it did join big world fights in the 1900s, it helped win them and came out with a strong economy while others were broken.

Fourth, it grew very rich. Factories, farms, banks, and companies sold things all over the world, and the money they made let the country build more schools, roads, and research labs. Smart people from all over the world also came to study and work there, which made it even better at science and business.

Finally, after World War II, it became one of the two biggest powers on Earth, and then the leading one when the other big power fell apart. Its money, its companies, its movies and music, and its ideas about freedom and democracy spread around the world, so many people came to know it well.

So, in short: it started with lots of good land and resources, got a mix of people who loved building things, stayed out of many wars, grew very rich, and became the big kid on the playground that everyone else pays attention to.

Azoospermia means that a man's semen contains no sperm at all. Several things can lead to it, such as hormonal imbalances, genetic disorders, and structural problems in the reproductive system. How it is treated depends on what is behind it. When a physical problem is responsible, for example a blockage in the reproductive tract, surgery may be able to fix it and bring back fertility. When hormones are the cause, hormone therapy may be suggested to correct the imbalance and boost sperm production. If those approaches do not work, assisted reproductive technologies like in vitro fertilization (IVF) may be recommended. A fertility specialist should carry out a thorough evaluation to identify the cause of your azoospermia and the treatments best suited to you. Your wife's fertility should be assessed too, so that any underlying issues on her side can be dealt with. I hope this is useful. Working with a healthcare professional is always wise when deciding on the best treatment for your particular circumstances.

A Boolean network is basically a way to model a dynamic system as a bunch of on/off variables linked together by rules. Each variable can only be true or false, and its functions decide how it flips based on what the other variables are doing. People use these a lot for complex stuff like gene regulatory networks or social networks. They're especially handy when a system acts in a yes-or-no way, or when you want to see how different parts of something interact. Each variable gets its own node, and the rules for updating it show up as edges between nodes. At any moment, the whole network is just the current pattern of those nodes, and you can watch how things evolve by repeatedly applying the update rules. Boolean networks pop up in all kinds of places, from cellular automata and biological systems to designing computer circuits. Folks have also used them to look at social and economic systems, and even how diseases or information spread.

When a bank is selling a property, usually a foreclosed home it now owns (often called REO, or real estate owned) or a short sale where it has to approve the price, it cares less about the headline number and more about how much money it will actually net and how certain and fast that money is. A cash offer that looks lower on paper can easily come out ahead once those factors are weighed.

The biggest factor is certainty of closing. A financed offer depends on the buyer getting final loan approval, and loans fall through more often than people expect. The buyer's job situation can change, the underwriter can find a problem with their credit or income, or interest rates can move. If the deal collapses after thirty or forty-five days, the bank has to relist the property and start over, having lost time and possibly other interested buyers. A cash buyer removes that risk almost entirely.

Appraisal risk is closely related. A lender will only lend based on the appraised value, so if the appraisal comes in below the contract price, the financed buyer often renegotiates down, asks the seller to cover the gap, or walks away. That higher offer can shrink to the same level as the cash offer or lower, just weeks later and after the property has been off the market. Cash buyers generally don't need an appraisal, so the price they offer is the price the bank gets.

Property condition also plays a role. Foreclosed homes are frequently in poor shape, with missing appliances, water damage, mold, or code issues. Conventional, FHA, and VA loans have minimum property standards, and a house with serious defects may simply not qualify for financing until repairs are made. Banks typically sell as-is and don't want to make repairs, so a cash buyer who can take the property in any condition is far more attractive.

Speed matters because holding a property costs the bank money every day. It pays property taxes, insurance, utilities, maintenance, security, and HOA dues, and vacant homes are vulnerable to vandalism and squatters. A cash deal can close in a week or two instead of a month or more, which saves real carrying costs. Banks also aren't in the business of owning houses; regulators and their own accounting treat these as nonperforming assets they want off the books, so quick liquidation has value beyond the dollars.

Finally, financed offers often come with extra strings that reduce the bank's net proceeds, such as requests for the seller to pay closing costs, longer inspection periods, or repair requests. Cash offers tend to be cleaner, with fewer contingencies. When the bank's asset manager compares offers, they look at the net amount after concessions, adjusted for the probability that each deal actually closes and how long it will take. A modestly lower cash offer frequently wins that comparison, though if the financed offer is substantially higher and the buyer is well qualified with a strong preapproval and a sound property, the bank may well choose it instead.

Ayn Rand's philosophy is called Objectivism, and the simplest way to put it is this: you should be the hero of your own life. She believed that reality is real and knowable, that your own mind and reason are your best tools, and that the most moral thing you can do is pursue your own happiness through your own effort. In her view, people should trade with each other fairly, value for value, and nobody should be forced to live for someone else or have their work taken from them. That's why Howard Roark in The Fountainhead refuses to change his buildings to please committees. To Rand, he's a good person precisely because he stays true to his own vision and doesn't sacrifice himself to what other people want.

Imagine you build an amazing sandcastle. Rand would say it's yours, you should be proud of it, and nobody should be allowed to stomp on it or force you to build it their way just because there are more of them. She called her ethics "the virtue of selfishness," which sounds shocking, but she meant something closer to "self-respect" than "being a jerk." She thought the idea that you owe your life to others, which she called altruism, was the real villain, because it lets the group bully the individual.

So why do many people frown on her? One big reason is that critics think she goes too far. Most people agree you shouldn't be a doormat, but Rand argued that helping others out of duty or sacrifice is actually wrong, and many find that cold. Going back to the sandcastle, a lot of people would say: what about the kid who has no bucket, or who is sick and can't build at all? Rand's answer was that charity is fine if you personally want to give, but nobody should be forced to. Critics argue that real life is full of people who are struggling through bad luck rather than laziness, and that her worldview doesn't leave much room for them.

Another reason is politics. Rand supported pure, unregulated capitalism with almost no government help programs. People on the left often see that as a defense of the rich and powerful, and her books have been popular with some politicians who wanted to cut social programs, which made her a symbol people react to strongly.

Philosophers also tend not to take her very seriously, partly because she mostly wrote novels and essays rather than careful academic arguments, and they think some of her big leaps, like going from "reason is important" to "selfishness is a virtue," aren't well proven. Her characters are often seen as cartoonish too: the heroes are geniuses who are always right, and everyone who disagrees is weak or envious, which critics say isn't how real people work. Some also point to her personal life and the cult-like circle around her, where disagreeing with her could get you kicked out, as at odds with her praise of independent thinking.

So you didn't necessarily miss anything. Plenty of thoughtful people find her ideas about integrity, creativity, and not living for others' approval genuinely inspiring, especially in The Fountainhead, which is often considered her most likeable book. The disagreement is mostly about how far she pushes those ideas and what they mean for people who can't easily stand on their own. A good way to think about her is to take what resonates, like being true to your work, while also asking where her ideas might leave others behind.

Okay so scientific modeling is basically building a stand-in for some real-world system or phenomenon, using assumptions and principles that come from what we already know in science. The whole point is to figure out how the thing works and then guess how it'll act under different conditions. Models come in all sorts of forms: math equations, computer simulations, physical prototypes, even just sketchy conceptual diagrams. You can use them for pretty much anything, from chemistry and biology to economics or how people behave in groups.

Usually the process goes something like this. First you pin down what you're studying, then figure out which variables matter and how they interact with each other. Next you build a model that captures all that. Then comes the testing part: you run experiments, compare against observations, and tweak things when the model misses. And if new data shows up later, you change the model again. It's a pretty messy, iterative thing honestly. Still, it's a huge deal across science and engineering, and it's one of the main ways people make sense of complicated systems and decide what to do next.

A defibrillator (the correct spelling) is used when someone's heart has stopped or is beating in a dangerously irregular way, most commonly in cases of ventricular fibrillation or pulseless ventricular tachycardia. The person will typically be unconscious, unresponsive, and not breathing normally. Before using one, the rescuer should check that the person is unresponsive and not breathing or only gasping, call emergency services or have someone else do so, and begin CPR while getting the device. Automated external defibrillators (AEDs) are designed for use by laypeople: they analyze the heart rhythm and only deliver a shock if one is needed, and they give spoken instructions. Trained professionals use manual defibrillators in hospitals and ambulances. If you are unsure whether to use one, start CPR and use the AED anyway, since it will not shock someone whose heart does not need it. Anyone with a serious concern should call emergency services right away.
As of 2022, Louisiana's two senators are John Neely Kennedy and Bill Cassidy. Both are Republicans, and both won their current terms back in 2020.

Management science is a discipline that applies statistical, mathematical, and computational methods to examine and improve business activities and the choices managers make. It is frequently paired with operations research, a closely related field centered on mathematical modeling and analysis for enhancing decisions and solving problems within intricate systems. Practitioners apply these methods to a broad array of business challenges, such as allocating resources, creating schedules, generating forecasts, and choosing courses of action when outcomes are uncertain. Such approaches enable managers to decide more wisely, operate more efficiently, and raise profits. Industries like manufacturing, finance, healthcare, and transportation rely on them routinely. The field draws on a diverse toolkit that includes linear programming, network analysis, decision analysis, and simulation, and it depends on computer software and other advanced technologies to process data and build decision-making models. In short, management science aims to help organizations reach better decisions and strengthen their operations through rigorous analytical techniques.

Peter Dayan is a British neuroscientist and computational biologist, and these days he runs the Max Planck Institute for Biological Cybernetics in Tübingen, Germany. He's also a professor of computational neuroscience at the University of Tübingen. He got his undergrad degree in physics at Oxford, then picked up a PhD in theoretical physics at Edinburgh. After that he did a postdoc at the University of Sussex and then moved to the Salk Institute in San Diego, where he worked with Terry Sejnowski on computational models of the nervous system. His interests cover computational and theoretical neuroscience, machine learning, and decision making. He's done a lot to show how the brain processes information, learns, and makes decisions, and his models of learning and decision making have been pretty influential. He's also a Fellow of the Royal Society and a Fellow of the Academy of Medical Sciences.

An insect bite may sometimes lead to a boil that feels like it is burning. Boils, which are also called abscesses, are tender, red, swollen patches of skin that result from an infection. They can show up on any part of the body, and they frequently come with additional symptoms like fever, chills, and tiredness. A bite can irritate the skin, trigger inflammation, and allow infection to set in, and this chain of events may end in a boil. When a boil is growing larger or is causing a great deal of discomfort, the patient should see a healthcare provider to get a proper diagnosis and treatment. After examining the boil, the provider can work out what caused it and recommend the best way to treat it.

Human evolution is the gradual development of our species over time, and it has not stopped. Our present form results from a mix of inherited genetic changes accumulated across countless generations and the environmental pressures our ancestors endured. One mechanism driving this change is natural selection, in which traits spread through a population because they improve the chances of their carriers surviving and having offspring. Individuals who were more skilled at locating food and steering clear of threats, for instance, were more likely to reach adulthood and raise children, who in turn carried those advantageous traits forward. As generations passed, such traits grew increasingly widespread. Today, though, people enjoy far longer lifespans than their predecessors did and have built many safeguards against the hazards they once faced. As a result, natural selection may exert less influence on human evolution than it formerly did. Even so, evolution continues, as we keep adjusting to our surroundings through other means, including shifts in what we eat and how we live.

A pilot study is a limited-scale research effort designed to assess how practical a larger study would be, how it should be structured, and what results it might produce. Researchers typically carry it out ahead of the principal project so they can spot potential problems and adjust the design or methods before moving forward. Although pilot studies are most often found in medicine, psychology, and the social sciences, they are also used in areas such as engineering, education, and business. A pilot might gather data from a small group of participants, run a small experiment, or try out a new measurement instrument or intervention. These preliminary studies help researchers judge whether a full-scale study is likely to succeed and allow them to fine-tune its design. They can also offer useful insight into factors that could shape the findings of the main study, including the characteristics of participants, the appropriate sample size, and the measurement methods used.

It's possible the scabies and the red, sore navel have nothing to do with your ovarian cancer or your remission. Scabies is caused by the human itch mite, which burrows into the skin and lays eggs there. You'll usually notice intense itching, especially at night, and a rash of small raised red bumps or blisters. It tends to show up where the mites like to dig in: skin folds, between the fingers and toes, and on the wrists, elbows, and buttocks. If you've been diagnosed and prescribed a cream, stick with it and keep using it until the infestation is fully cleared. Don't skip it just because you feel better. You'll also want to wash and treat any clothing, bedding, or other stuff that's touched your skin. As for the low body temperature and feeling cold, that could point to a bunch of different things. It might be a side effect of your meds, or it could be something underlying. Either way, it's worth getting it checked by a doctor, especially with symptoms that feel off. They can look at everything together and tell you what to do next.

Fleas live mostly on the bodies of warm-blooded animals, such as dogs, cats, rodents, rabbits, and birds, where they feed on blood. Adult fleas spend most of their time on the host, living in the fur or feathers close to the skin. However, most of a flea's life happens away from the host. Eggs usually fall off the animal and land in bedding, carpets, cracks in floors, and soil or nesting areas, where the larvae develop. The larvae feed on organic debris, including adult flea droppings, before spinning cocoons and becoming adults. Because of this, a flea infestation in a home is often concentrated in the pet's sleeping spots and the carpets or furniture nearby.

A signature is basically a person writing their name on a document or item to show they agree with it or approve of what it says. You're kind of saying, "Yep, that's me, and I'm fine with everything written here."

People have been signing things for centuries to confirm who they are and that they're willing to back up what they wrote or agreed to. Sure, signatures can be forged or copied, but they still matter a lot for proving identity and showing someone is on the hook for something. Say you and a friend make a promise. You both sign a piece of paper, so if one of you later claims you never agreed to anything, the other can point at the page and say, "Look, we both signed it."

So no, signatures aren't foolproof. But they're still a big deal, because they show you're willing to take responsibility and stand behind your word.

In American football, the defensive line is usually just called the "D-line," and it's made up of the defensive linemen who line up directly across from the offense's linemen at the line of scrimmage. The players in this group are typically defensive tackles, who line up toward the middle, and defensive ends, who line up on the outside edges. A defensive tackle positioned directly over the center is often called a nose tackle or nose guard. Together with the linebackers behind them and the secondary (cornerbacks and safeties) further back, they form the overall defense. The defensive line's main jobs are to stop running plays and to pressure or sack the quarterback, which is why pass-rushing linemen are sometimes collectively referred to as the "pass rush." Teams with especially famous defensive lines have earned nicknames, such as the Steelers' "Steel Curtain," the Vikings' "Purple People Eaters," and the Rams' "Fearsome Foursome."

If you meant soccer (association football), the comparable group is the defense or back line, made up of defenders such as center-backs and full-backs, and the deepest line of defenders is often simply called the "back four" or "back three," depending on how many players are used.

Honestly it's hard to say what's behind that "frozen" feeling on the right side of your head without knowing more. It could be a brief dip in blood flow to the brain, or maybe a problem with the nerves that give sensation to that side of your head. It could also be something more serious, like a stroke or a TIA (a mini-stroke, basically).

Because of that, I'd get it looked at by a doctor, especially if it's new, weird, or worrying you. They can do a proper exam and work out what's going on, and they might want a brain scan or some other tests to pin down the cause. Then you can sort out the right treatment.

I'm not Dr. Bhatti, and I can't evaluate you, but chest tightness is a symptom you should take seriously, so please don't wait on it.

Clindamycin and oxycodone/acetaminophen are not well-known causes of chest tightness, though each can rarely contribute. Oxycodone can slow breathing, cause flushing, or in rare cases cause chest discomfort. Clindamycin can trigger allergic reactions, and its most serious known risk is severe diarrhea from C. difficile. Chest tightness also has causes unrelated to these medications, some of them serious. Blood clots in the lungs are a concern after surgery, especially if you've been less active, and heart problems can also present this way.

Call 911 or go to the nearest emergency department now if the tightness is severe or getting worse, or if it comes with shortness of breath, pain spreading to your arm, jaw, or back, sweating, dizziness or fainting, a racing or irregular heartbeat, coughing up blood, or swelling or pain in one leg. Also seek emergency care right away if you notice hives, facial or throat swelling, or trouble swallowing or breathing, which could signal an allergic reaction.

If none of those apply and the symptom is mild and stable, call your surgeon's office or a pharmacist today. Tell them exactly what you're experiencing, when it started, and that you've taken the medications three times. Don't stop or change your pain medication on your own without guidance, since uncontrolled pain has its own risks. Also check the acetaminophen content of your pain pills and make sure you're not taking other acetaminophen-containing products, because exceeding the daily limit can damage the liver.

Basically, a warehouse spreadsheet is just a way to keep tabs on what's coming into the warehouse, what's sitting there, and what's heading back out. You can use it for a bunch of stuff.

When a shipment shows up, you log it, so you've got the quantity, where it got put, and any other details you care about. That same sheet can track your current inventory too, like how much of each product you have and which spot it's stored in.

Orders are another big one. You can list what's been ordered, how many, and when it's supposed to ship. Once stuff actually leaves, you can note the quantities and where it's going, so you've got a record of everything moving out the door.

Some people go further and use spreadsheets for the day-to-day running of the place. Think employee schedules, equipment maintenance, or figuring out how to divvy up storage space.

So really, it's a simple tool that helps you stay organized and makes it a lot easier to store and ship things efficiently without screwing up the counts.

Scientific modeling involves building a representation or approximation of a real-world system or phenomenon, drawing on assumptions and principles grounded in scientific knowledge. Its aim is to comprehend and account for how the modeled system or phenomenon behaves, and to forecast its behavior under varying circumstances. Models come in many forms, including mathematical equations, computer simulations, physical prototypes, and conceptual diagrams. They are applicable to a broad spectrum of systems, spanning physical, chemical, biological, and social domains. Typically, the modeling process unfolds in several stages: pinpointing the system or phenomenon under investigation, identifying the pertinent variables and how they interact, and building a model that captures those variables and interactions. Afterward, the model undergoes testing and refinement through experiments and observation, and it may be altered or revised as fresh information emerges. Across many branches of science and engineering, scientific modeling is essential, serving as a key means of grasping complex systems and supporting well-informed decisions.

Functional programming is a style of software development that treats computation as the evaluation of mathematical functions. Instead of describing a sequence of steps that change the state of a program, a functional program is built by combining functions that take inputs and produce outputs, with the aim of making the flow of data clear and predictable. The idea has roots in mathematical logic, particularly the lambda calculus developed by Alonzo Church in the 1930s, and languages such as Lisp, ML, Haskell, and Erlang are often cited as examples of the approach.

Several core ideas define the style. Functions are treated as first-class values, meaning they can be stored in variables, passed as arguments to other functions, and returned as results. Many functional languages also emphasize pure functions, which always return the same output for the same input and produce no side effects such as modifying global variables, writing to a file, or changing data in place. Immutability is closely related: rather than altering an existing value, a functional program creates new values when something changes. Higher-order functions such as map, filter, and reduce are common tools for transforming collections without writing explicit loops.

The appeal of this approach lies in its consequences. Because pure functions do not depend on hidden state, they are easier to test, reason about, and run in parallel, since there is no risk of one part of the program interfering with another. Many programmers also find that code written this way is more concise and easier to verify. Functional programming is not an all-or-nothing choice, however. Many mainstream languages such as Python, JavaScript, Java, and C# now incorporate functional features like lambdas and stream operations, allowing developers to adopt the ideas gradually while still using imperative or object-oriented techniques where they are more natural.

The Arctic Circle is an imaginary line of latitude that circles the Earth at approximately 66.5 degrees north of the equator (more precisely, about 66°34′ N). It marks the southern boundary of the Arctic region, and everything north of it up to the North Pole is considered to lie within the Arctic.

What defines the line is sunlight. North of the Arctic Circle, the sun stays above the horizon for at least one full 24-hour period around the June solstice, a phenomenon often called the midnight sun, and stays below the horizon for at least one full day around the December solstice, known as the polar night. The farther north you go from the circle, the longer these periods last, until at the North Pole there are roughly six months of continuous daylight followed by six months of darkness.

The Arctic Circle passes through eight countries: Norway, Sweden, Finland, Russia, the United States (Alaska), Canada, Denmark (via Greenland), and Iceland, where it just touches the small island of Grímsey off the northern coast. It also crosses the Arctic Ocean, the Norwegian Sea, the Barents Sea region's margins, Baffin Bay, and the Bering Strait area. Well-known places near the line include Rovaniemi in Finnish Lapland, which promotes itself as the official hometown of Santa Claus, and Bodø region in Norway, where the circle is marked by monuments and visitor centers.

The circle's position is not perfectly fixed. Because the tilt of Earth's axis wobbles slightly over time, the Arctic Circle is currently drifting northward by about 14 to 15 meters per year.

So Springer Nature is basically one of the big names in research and academic publishing. If you work in science, tech, medicine, or even the social sciences, you've probably bumped into their stuff. They put out books, journals, and other material, both in print and online. The company came together in 2015 when Springer Science+Business Media merged with Nature Publishing Group. Their audience is pretty broad: researchers, professionals, and students, whether they're in universities, industry, or government jobs. Beyond just publishing, they also do some research services, like helping out with peer review, and they've been pushing open access so that more people can actually read the research without hitting a paywall.

MediaFire and MegaUpload are both file hosting services where people can upload files and share them with others, but their histories differ, and so has the way law enforcement has dealt with them. MegaUpload enjoyed great popularity in the late 2000s, yet in 2012 the U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) and the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) shut it down. The authorities argued that the site enabled copyright infringement by letting users distribute pirated movies, music, and other protected material without authorization. Consequently, they brought criminal charges against MegaUpload's owners and employees and took control of the site's servers. MediaFire, by contrast, has never faced a criminal investigation or legal action from the DOJ or FBI. So far as anyone knows, it has run within the law and has not been accused of promoting copyright infringement at anything like MegaUpload's scale. For that reason, law enforcement has not closed it down, and it is still available online. I hope this clears up how the two sites differ and why one was taken offline while the other continues to operate. Feel free to ask if you have further questions.

The answer depends on which Roman Empire you mean and where you start counting, because the state changed form many times over its history.

If you count from 27 BCE, when Augustus became the first emperor, the Western Roman Empire lasted until 476 CE, when the last western emperor, Romulus Augustulus, was deposed by the Germanic leader Odoacer. That is about 500 years. The Eastern Roman Empire, usually called the Byzantine Empire by modern historians, continued after that and ended in 1453 when the Ottomans captured Constantinople. Counting from 27 BCE to 1453 CE gives roughly 1,480 years.

If you include the Roman Republic, which began in 509 BCE according to tradition, then Roman rule as a continuous state lasted about 2,000 years, from the Republic's founding to the fall of Constantinople. Some people go back even further to the legendary founding of Rome in 753 BCE, which would add another few centuries.

There are also other ways to date the end. The Holy Roman Empire claimed to be a continuation of Rome and lasted from 800 or 962 until 1806, though most historians don't treat it as the same state. The Ottoman sultans also took the title "Caesar of Rome" after 1453, but that is likewise a claim of succession rather than continuity.

The most common short answer is that the Roman Empire lasted about 500 years in the West and nearly 1,500 years if you include the Eastern half.
In 2011, the mayor of Chicago was Rahm Emanuel. He took office in May 2011, succeeding Richard M. Daley, who had served as mayor for 22 years. Emanuel was re-elected in 2015 and served until 2019.

Debt-to-GDP is basically how much a country owes compared to how much it produces in a year (that's the GDP part). People use it to get a feel for whether a government's finances are sustainable. When the ratio gets really high, it can signal trouble, and it might mean the country is at risk of not being able to pay what it owes. That can hit the economy in a few ways.

First, there's interest. The more debt you carry, the more of the budget goes to paying interest, and that money has to come from somewhere. Usually it means less for things like education, healthcare, and infrastructure.

Then there's the stability problem. If investors start doubting a country can pay its debts, they lose confidence, and that can push the value of its currency down.

Growth takes a hit too. Heavy debt limits how much a country can borrow and invest in stuff that actually grows the economy, so you can end up with slower growth and a lower standard of living.

So a high ratio can be a big deal, and it's generally treated as a key sign of financial stability, or the lack of it. But it's only one piece of the puzzle. You also have to look at how strong the country's institutions are, how developed its economy is, and what the business environment looks like.

Honestly, it's pretty normal for blood pressure to run a bit higher in people who work out regularly. Your heart gets stronger and more efficient, and that can nudge the numbers up a little. That said, you still want a healthcare provider to check it and tell you whether it's in a good range for you specifically. Get it looked at sooner if you're having things like headaches, dizziness, shortness of breath, or chest pain, since those can point to high blood pressure. Even if you feel fine, regular check-ups are worth it. They catch problems early, and that makes them much easier to deal with.

Dear Vijay, I understand why you are worried, and it is wise to get this checked rather than wait. Pain in the upper right abdomen, just below the chest, can have several causes, and some of them need prompt medical attention. Because you completed tuberculosis treatment and drink alcohol, your doctor will want to rule out problems with the liver, gallbladder, stomach, or lungs, and also check whether the tuberculosis has returned.

Please see a doctor soon, ideally within the next few days. If you cannot wait, go to an emergency department right away if the pain becomes severe, you vomit blood or material that looks like coffee grounds, your stools turn black or pale, your skin or eyes look yellow, you have fever, chills, a persistent cough, coughing up blood, weight loss, or shortness of breath, or you feel confused or very drowsy.

Until you see a doctor, try to stop drinking alcohol completely, since it can damage the liver and irritate the stomach and pancreas. When you visit the doctor, tell them about your past tuberculosis treatment, the date you finished it, how much and how often you drink, any medicines you take, and exactly where and when the pain occurs. The doctor may order blood tests for liver function and infection, an ultrasound of the abdomen, and a chest X-ray. These are simple, common tests, and most causes of this pain are treatable once identified.

Please do not feel alarmed before you have been examined. Getting checked promptly is the right step, and it will give you a clear answer.

An A level, short for Advanced level, is a qualification awarded in the United Kingdom, the Isle of Man and the Channel Islands, and it is usually taken by students aged between 16 and 18. It is available in a broad range of subjects, such as mathematics, the sciences, English, history and modern languages. Universities and employers treat A levels as a standard measure of academic ability, and they frequently serve as an entry requirement for university study in Britain. The qualification is split into two components: the AS (Advanced Subsidiary) level and the A2 level. The AS level is generally completed during the first year of the course and covers roughly half of the content of the full A level. The A2 exams are normally sat at the close of the second year. Results are awarded on a grading scale running from A* at the top to E at the bottom. Grades A* and A are usually regarded as excellent, whereas grades B, C and D are seen as good. A grade of E counts as a pass, though it is not generally viewed as a strong result. Apart from traditional A levels, students may also pursue alternatives such as the International Baccalaureate (IB) or the Cambridge Pre-U, which universities likewise accept as a route to admission.

Excess cash is the portion of a company's cash balance that is not needed to run the day-to-day operations of the business, and it is typically subtracted from enterprise value (or added to equity value in the bridge) because a buyer effectively acquires it. Since it is not a precise line item on the balance sheet, analysts usually start with reported cash and cash equivalents and then adjust downward for the amount deemed operating.

The first step is to find cash and cash equivalents on the balance sheet, which generally includes currency, bank deposits, and highly liquid short-term investments with original maturities of three months or less. Short-term marketable securities are sometimes included as well, depending on how liquid and cash-like they are. Restricted cash, such as collateral for letters of credit, escrow balances, or cash held in foreign jurisdictions subject to repatriation limits, should generally be excluded from excess cash because the company cannot freely use it.

The second step is to estimate minimum operating cash, the amount the business needs to keep on hand to meet payroll, payables, and other routine obligations. A common approach is to express this as a percentage of revenue (often somewhere between 2 and 5 percent, though this varies widely by industry) or as a number of days of operating expenses. Some practitioners look at the historical low point of cash balances over a period, or at the industry norm, to set this figure. Companies in industries with large working capital needs or seasonal swings generally require higher operating cash.

The third step is to subtract the operating cash estimate from total cash and cash equivalents. The remainder is excess cash. If the result is negative, the company has no excess cash and the adjustment is zero.

Analysts should also be cautious about a few related issues. Debt-like items, such as trapped cash that cannot be easily distributed or cash needed to fund pension deficits or deferred obligations, may need further adjustment. Cash held offshore may carry repatriation taxes that reduce its value to a buyer. Consistency matters too: if the enterprise value is calculated using a multiple applied to EBITDA, the treatment of cash should align with the assumptions in that multiple. Finally, the figure should be taken from the most recent balance sheet date, and any significant cash movements since then, such as large dividends or acquisitions, should be considered.

Nerve growth factor (NGF) is a protein that is essential for the growth, upkeep, and survival of the body's nerve cells, known as neurons. It belongs to the neurotrophin family of growth factors, a group that also includes brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) and neurotrophin-3 (NT-3). Several types of cells produce NGF, among them nerve cells, glial cells (the non-neuronal cells that support and shield neurons), and some immune cells. NGF binds to particular receptors on the surface of neurons, which are proteins that recognize specific signaling molecules and relay the signal into the cell, thereby switching on pathways that encourage these cells to grow and survive. The protein takes part in many physiological processes, such as the formation and maintenance of the nervous system, the control of pain sensitivity, and the reaction to nerve damage. It is also implicated in some disease states, including neurodegenerative disorders and cancer. In recent years, NGF has attracted considerable research interest because of its possible therapeutic uses across a range of illnesses. It has been studied, for instance, as a potential treatment for neuropathic pain, Alzheimer's disease, and Parkinson's disease, along with other conditions. Nevertheless, further research is required to fully clarify NGF's role in these and other disorders, and to establish whether NGF-based therapies are safe and effective.

There's no real science showing that eating Mentos does anything to sperm count. Sperm production is a complicated process run by hormones and a bunch of other body stuff, and a candy isn't going to nudge it one way or the other. Age, general health, lifestyle habits, and certain medical conditions are what actually matter for fertility. If you're worried about yours, your doctor is the person to talk to, not a packet of mints.

Pretty much not easily at all. Think of Earth like a giant, very sturdy rock ball. It's so heavy that even all the people in the world, pushing as hard as we could, couldn't move it or crack it. Destroying it would take far more energy than we have ever made or could make.

We could hurt the planet a lot, though. We have enough nuclear bombs to cause a "nuclear winter," where smoke blocks the sun for a long time, crops fail, and many people get sick or starve. We could also wreck the air and water with pollution or cause big changes to the weather. That would be terrible for people and for lots of animals and plants.

But even then, Earth would keep spinning, and life would most likely bounce back. Tough little things like bacteria and some insects can survive almost anything, and over a long enough time, nature tends to fill empty places again. Think of it like a sandcastle after a big wave: the wave can wash away the castle, but the beach is still there.

So the honest answer is that we could make the world a very bad place for ourselves and many other living things, but we couldn't blow up the planet itself.

The United States spends far more on health care per person than any other country. According to the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, national health expenditures reached about 4.9 trillion dollars in 2023, which works out to roughly 14,570 dollars per person. That total was about 17.6 percent of the country's gross domestic product, and spending grew about 7.5 percent from the year before, faster than in the immediately preceding years.

The figure covers all health spending from every source, including private insurance, Medicare, Medicaid, other government programs, and out-of-pocket payments. Hospital care is the largest share, at around 30 percent of the total, followed by physician and clinical services and then prescription drugs.

Compared with other wealthy nations, U.S. spending stands out. OECD data show that countries such as Germany, Switzerland, and Norway, among the next-highest spenders, typically spend somewhere around 7,000 to 9,000 dollars per person when adjusted for purchasing power, and the average across OECD countries is roughly half of the U.S. level or less. Despite this higher spending, the United States tends to lag peer countries on measures like life expectancy and infant mortality, a gap that is often attributed to higher prices for services and drugs, administrative costs, and differences in insurance coverage rather than to Americans using much more care.

If you need the most current numbers, CMS updates its National Health Expenditure data each year, usually in December, and those projections suggest per-person spending will keep rising over the coming decade.

A quasi-judicial agency is a government body that is not a court but has powers and procedures that resemble those of a court. It is usually part of the executive branch or created by legislation, and it is given authority to hear disputes, interpret and apply laws or regulations to specific cases, and issue decisions that are binding on the parties involved. The prefix "quasi" means "to some degree" or "resembling," so the term reflects that these agencies perform judge-like functions without being formally part of the judiciary.

Typical powers include holding hearings, taking evidence, summoning witnesses, examining documents, making findings of fact, and issuing orders, penalties, or rulings. Many also have rule-making powers and enforcement functions, which means one agency may combine legislative, executive, and judicial-type roles within a particular field of regulation.

Examples vary by country. In the United States, bodies such as the Securities and Exchange Commission, the National Labor Relations Board, the Federal Trade Commission, and the Federal Communications Commission exercise quasi-judicial powers, as do administrative law judges within many agencies. In the Philippines, the term is commonly used for bodies like the National Labor Relations Commission, the Securities and Exchange Commission, and the Civil Service Commission. In other countries, tax tribunals, immigration appeal boards, competition authorities, and labor boards play similar roles.

There are several important features. Quasi-judicial agencies are generally expected to follow due process, meaning they must give notice, allow parties to be heard, and base decisions on evidence. Their procedures are usually less formal and faster than those of regular courts, and they often have specialized expertise in the subject matter, such as securities, labor, or utilities. Their decisions can generally be appealed or reviewed by regular courts, which check whether the agency acted within its authority, followed fair procedures, and did not abuse its discretion.

The main advantage of these agencies is efficiency and expertise: they can handle large volumes of technical disputes more quickly and cheaply than courts. Critics point out the risk of concentrating investigative, prosecutorial, and adjudicative functions in one body, which may raise concerns about bias, so judicial review serves as an important safeguard.

Sexual assault in prisons is a grave issue that can occur for many different reasons. Overcrowding is one factor, since when facilities hold more inmates than they were built for, staff struggle to monitor every area. Another factor is the presence of aggressive or violent inmates, which can leave officers hesitant to step in for fear of harm to themselves. A further problem is that some incumbents may use money or threats to pressure guards into ignoring mistreatment. Stopping or fully controlling these assaults is difficult, yet steps can be taken to lower how often they happen, such as adding surveillance cameras, increasing staffing levels, and training employees to identify and head off abuse.

Nasdaq.com shows both, depending on where you look. The default figures on a stock's summary and earnings pages are typically the non-GAAP (adjusted) numbers that companies report to the market and that analysts use for consensus estimates, so headline EPS and the "actual vs. estimate" comparisons usually reflect those adjusted figures. The company's GAAP results, which follow generally accepted accounting principles and include items like stock-based compensation, restructuring charges, and amortization of acquired intangibles, appear in the financial statements sections (income statement, balance sheet, cash flow), which are presented on a GAAP basis.

Because the site pulls from data providers and company reports, the labeling can vary by page and by company, so it's worth checking the specific line item. If you need a precise comparison, look at the company's earnings release, which usually includes a reconciliation between the GAAP and non-GAAP figures, and confirm which basis the number you're reading is based on.

A strawman argument happens when someone deliberately twists another person's position so it's easier to knock down. It's called a "strawman" because the attacker swaps in a weak, flimsy version of the argument, like a scarecrow that falls over at the slightest push. Say you argue, "We should recycle more because it helps the environment." Someone replies, "Oh, so you think we should just dump all our trash in the ocean because it's natural?" That's a strawman. They've bent your point about recycling into something absurd so they can mock it instead of dealing with what you actually said.

It's a type of logical fallacy, so it doesn't rely on sound reasoning. People reach for it because making the other side look ridiculous is often easier than making a real case for their own view. The fix is to stick to what the other person actually claimed and respond to that, not to whatever cartoon version is more fun to hit.

Mortgage interest rates come from a mix of broad economic forces and factors specific to each borrower and loan. At the broadest level, rates follow what investors demand to lend money over long periods. In the United States, most mortgages are bundled into mortgage-backed securities and sold to investors, so mortgage rates track the yields on those securities. Those yields move closely with the 10-year Treasury yield, because the typical mortgage is refinanced or paid off within about ten years. When Treasury yields rise, mortgage rates usually rise too. Mortgage rates typically sit a couple of percentage points above Treasuries, and that gap widens or narrows with market volatility, prepayment risk, and lenders' operating costs and profit margins.

Central bank policy shapes this environment, though not as directly as many people assume. The Federal Reserve sets a short-term rate, the federal funds rate, which most directly affects credit cards, home equity lines, and adjustable-rate mortgages. Long-term fixed mortgage rates respond more to expectations about where the economy and inflation are heading. The Fed can still have a strong indirect effect through its signals about future policy and through buying or selling mortgage-backed securities, which changes demand for them.

Inflation is one of the most important underlying drivers. Lenders want to be repaid in money that hasn't lost much purchasing power, so when inflation is high or expected to rise, they demand higher rates. Economic growth matters as well. A strong economy with robust hiring tends to push rates up, while a weakening economy or a financial scare often sends investors toward safe assets like Treasuries, lowering yields and mortgage rates with them.

Within that market-wide baseline, the rate you are offered depends on how risky the lender judges your loan to be. Your credit score is a major factor, with higher scores earning lower rates. Your down payment, expressed as the loan-to-value ratio, matters because borrowers with more equity are less likely to default. Lenders also look at your debt-to-income ratio, the stability of your employment, and your documented income. The loan itself matters too. Fifteen-year loans usually carry lower rates than thirty-year loans, adjustable-rate loans often start lower than fixed-rate loans, and jumbo loans, investment properties, and cash-out refinances may be priced differently from standard owner-occupied purchases. Government-backed programs such as FHA, VA, and USDA loans have their own pricing structures.

Borrowers also have some direct influence. You can pay discount points, an upfront fee, to buy down your rate. Rate locks protect you from market movements between approval and closing. And because lenders have different costs, appetites for risk, and competitive strategies, quotes for the same borrower on the same day can vary noticeably, which is why shopping among several lenders is one of the most effective ways to get a better rate.

Honestly, having several current accounts with different banks usually isn't a great idea. Juggling multiple logins, account numbers, and statements gets old fast. Fees can stack up across accounts too, and those costs eat into whatever interest you're earning on your deposits. Keeping tabs on balances and transactions across several places is also a lot harder than doing it in one spot.

That said, there are cases where it can make sense. If you run a business with several locations or separate income streams, giving each one its own account can make the books way easier to sort out. Just weigh the hassle and costs against the benefits before you open anything, and pick accounts that actually fit how you use your money.

Here's a simple way to think about it. Gender is mostly about how a person experiences themselves and how they want to live in the world: what name they go by, how they dress, what roles they take on, and how they feel inside. Those things are about personal expression and inner sense of self, and society has long let people shape them in many ways. Race is different because it is mostly tied to ancestry and to how other people see and treat you. Your race is largely about where your family comes from and the physical traits that come with that history, and those facts exist whether or not you agree with them. A person can choose how they present themselves, but they can't change the family tree they were born into.

That is why many people see the two as different. Gender identity is about how you understand yourself, while race is about facts of heritage and how others categorize you.

Some people push back on this, and it's a fair debate. Critics point out that race is also partly a social category, not just biology, and that people sometimes do take on cultural identities or describe themselves in ways that don't match their background. Others argue that gender also involves physical facts, so the line isn't perfectly clean. Thoughtful people land in different places on how far these comparisons go, but the core distinction most people draw is between an identity centered on inner self-understanding and one rooted in ancestry and external recognition.

Ichthyosis hystrix, sometimes called "hystrix-like ichthyosis," is an uncommon inherited skin disorder marked by thickened, rough, scaly skin, most often on the arms, legs, and trunk. The scalp, face, and nails can be involved as well. The condition cannot be cured, so care centers on controlling symptoms and improving how the skin looks and feels. Possible treatments include several approaches. Moisturizers: applying emollients or moisturizing products regularly helps keep the skin hydrated and lessens scaling. Topical medications: creams or ointments containing urea or salicylic acid may be prescribed to soften thickened skin and help remove it. Phototherapy: treatment with ultraviolet light may be used to improve the skin's look and texture. Oral medications: in some cases, medicines taken by mouth may be prescribed to ease symptoms, including retinoids, which come from vitamin A and can improve the skin's appearance and texture. It is important to work closely with a dermatologist or another healthcare provider to settle on the most suitable treatment plan for your daughter's ichthyosis hystrix. Sticking to the recommended plan, and keeping the skin clean and moisturized, will also help control symptoms and improve how the skin looks.

Transfer learning is a machine learning technique in which a model trained on one task is reused as the starting point for a different but related task. Instead of training a model from scratch, which often requires large amounts of labeled data and computing power, the practitioner takes knowledge the model has already acquired and adapts it to the new problem.

The underlying idea is that many tasks share common structure. A neural network trained to recognize objects in millions of photographs, for example, learns general visual features such as edges, textures, and shapes in its early layers. Those features are useful for many other image tasks, such as identifying medical scans or classifying plant species. Transfer learning lets a developer keep those learned features and retrain only some portion of the model, or fine-tune the whole network gently, using a much smaller dataset specific to the new task.

The approach is especially valuable when labeled data is scarce or expensive to obtain. It also shortens training time and often yields better performance than training from scratch on the small dataset alone. In natural language processing, large pretrained language models are a prominent example: they learn broad patterns of language from huge text corpora and are then adapted to tasks like sentiment analysis, translation, or question answering.

Direct marketing is a form of advertising in which a business communicates directly with individual consumers or specific target customers, rather than broadcasting a general message to a mass audience through intermediaries like television networks, billboards, or general-circulation magazines. The defining feature is that the message is addressed to a particular person or household and usually invites a specific, measurable response, such as making a purchase, calling a phone number, visiting a website, requesting information, or redeeming a coupon.

The channels used for direct marketing have evolved over time. Traditional forms include direct mail (catalogs, letters, postcards, and flyers sent to a home or business address), telemarketing (sales calls to individuals), and door-to-door selling. Modern forms include email marketing, text message (SMS) campaigns, personalized social media messages, push notifications from apps, and targeted online ads that are tailored to an individual's browsing or purchase history. Direct response television, such as infomercials that urge viewers to "call now," is sometimes included as well because it seeks an immediate, trackable reaction.

A central element of direct marketing is the customer database. Companies collect and analyze information about people, such as names, contact details, demographics, past purchases, and interests, so they can segment their audience and send tailored offers to those most likely to respond. Because each message can be tracked, businesses can measure results precisely, for example by counting how many people opened an email, clicked a link, or used a promotional code. This makes it relatively easy to test different versions of an offer and calculate the return on investment.

The main advantages of direct marketing are its precision in targeting, its personalization, its measurability, and its potential cost-effectiveness for smaller businesses that cannot afford large mass-media campaigns. It also helps build ongoing relationships with existing customers through loyalty offers and reminders.

There are drawbacks and concerns as well. Many people view unsolicited direct marketing as intrusive, which is why terms like "junk mail" and "spam" exist. Poorly targeted campaigns can damage a brand's reputation, and response rates for some channels can be low. Privacy is a major issue, since direct marketing relies heavily on personal data. As a result, many countries regulate it through laws such as the General Data Protection Regulation in the European Union, the CAN-SPAM Act and the Telephone Consumer Protection Act in the United States, and "do not call" registries, which generally require consent, honest identification of the sender, and an easy way for recipients to opt out.

In short, direct marketing is about reaching the right individual with a personalized message and prompting them to take a specific action, with results that can be directly tracked and measured.

So in California, a domestic partnership is basically a legal setup for two people who aren't married but live together as a household and are committed to each other emotionally and financially. To qualify, both of you need to be at least 18. You also can't be related by blood or marriage, and neither of you can be married or in another domestic partnership.
