You've got to share a home, and you both have to agree to look out for each other's basics like food, housing, and medical care. And you need to register the partnership with the California Secretary of State.

Just know it's not the same thing as marriage. You don't get every legal protection that married couples do. That said, registered domestic partners end up with a lot of the same rights and responsibilities under California law, so it's not nothing.

Think of it like a flipbook with a soundtrack. A cartoon is made of lots of drawings shown one after another, very fast, so they look like they move. Each second of a cartoon usually has about 24 drawings, and each one is a tiny bit different from the last.

Before any drawing happens, the voice actor records their lines first. Then someone listens to the recording over and over and writes down exactly when each word starts and which mouth shape goes with each sound. Long ago, artists did this by hand, but the idea is the same today. An "oo" sound makes a round mouth, an "ee" sound makes a wide smile-like mouth, and "mmm" closes the lips.

The artist then draws the character's mouth on the right frames so the drawn mouth matches the sound. If the character says "hello," the artist draws the mouth opening for the "h," then changes to the "eh" shape, then the "l," and so on, using the timing marks as a guide. Sometimes the artist draws a few extra frames to make the motion look smooth, and sometimes they reuse the same mouth drawings to save time.

Finally, all the drawings get put together in order and played alongside the recording, so when the mouth looks like it's saying a word, the sound of that word plays at the same moment. That's how the voice and the picture stay in sync.

Imagine your brain is like a team of helpers who pass messages to each other to get things done. When you want to pay attention to something, like a story at circle time, the helpers have to pass the important message along and keep the other noisy messages quiet. For most kids, this works pretty smoothly. For kids with ADD, the helpers sometimes get distracted, pass the wrong messages, or run off to chase every shiny thing in the room, so it's harder to stay focused on the one thing you need to do.

So how does one kid have it and another not? Everybody's brain is a little different, like how some kids are taller or better at drawing. Doctors think ADD comes from a mix of things in the brain, and genes, which are the instructions passed down from parents, play a big part. The helpers in the brain use special chemicals to send messages, and in kids with ADD those chemicals may not be balanced quite the same way. It's not because the kid tried harder or was naughty. It's just how their brain is built.

Doctors also know that a kid with ADD isn't broken. Their brain just needs different kinds of help, like breaking big jobs into small steps, taking movement breaks, or sometimes medicine that helps the helpers work together better. Lots of kids with ADD are creative, energetic, and very good at things that grab their interest.

Imagine you have a giant pile of math homework, and every problem is simple, something like "add these two numbers" or "multiply these two numbers." There are millions of these problems, and none of them depends on the others.

A regular computer processor, the CPU, is like a small group of really smart professors, maybe eight or sixteen of them. Each professor can solve very hard, tricky problems, switch quickly between different kinds of tasks, and make clever decisions. But there are only a few of them, so with millions of easy problems they still have to work through the pile a handful at a time.

A graphics card, the GPU, is like a huge classroom of thousands of kids. No single kid is as smart or as fast as a professor, and they all have to do pretty much the same kind of problem at the same time. But because there are so many of them, they can finish an enormous pile of simple problems far faster than the few professors could. Each kid grabs a problem, everyone works at once, and the whole pile disappears quickly.

GPUs were built this way because drawing pictures for video games needs exactly this kind of work. A screen has millions of tiny dots, and the computer must figure out the color of each one many times every second. Each dot is a simple calculation, and they can all be done at the same time. People later noticed that lots of other jobs look the same way: training artificial intelligence, simulating weather, cracking codes, mining cryptocurrency, or crunching scientific data. All of these involve doing the same simple math over and over on huge amounts of numbers.

So a machine stuffed with graphics cards is like having many giant classrooms of kids, while a machine stuffed with processors is like having many small rooms of professors. For millions of simple, similar problems, the kids win because there are just so many more of them, and they also tend to give you more total math done for the money and electricity spent. The professors still win when the work is complicated, full of decisions, or has to happen step by step where each answer depends on the last one. That's why computers have both: the CPU acts as the boss that handles the tricky stuff and hands out work, and the GPU acts as the huge team that plows through the repetitive number-crunching.

A sociopath is a person whose brain works a little differently when it comes to caring about other people's feelings and following rules. The more official name for this is antisocial personality disorder, and doctors don't actually use the word sociopath as a formal diagnosis, but people use it a lot in everyday talk. Imagine a kid who takes a toy from another kid, sees them cry, and just doesn't feel bad about it. They understand the other kid is sad, but it doesn't tug at their heart the way it would for most of us.

Some common traits are these. They often lie easily and don't feel guilty about it. They can be charming and friendly when they want something, like a person who smiles a lot to get you to give them your cookie. They may break rules or laws without worrying about it, act without thinking about what happens next, get bored easily, get angry quickly, and blame other people when things go wrong. They may use people like tools and then drop them. Many don't keep promises or hold steady jobs or relationships for long.

Can you spot one easily? No, and that is the tricky part. Many of them are very good at seeming nice, funny, and normal. Also, plenty of people do some of these things sometimes without being sociopaths. Everybody tells a fib or gets grumpy. What matters is a long pattern, starting from when someone is young, of hurting others and not caring, across many parts of life. Only a trained professional can really tell.

A few gentle warning signs are worth knowing: someone who keeps lying even when caught, who never seems sorry, who makes you feel sorry for them to get what they want, or who repeatedly hurts people or animals without concern. If you notice a pattern like that, the smart move is to be careful, set firm boundaries, and talk to a trusted grown-up or counselor rather than trying to diagnose anyone yourself.

One last thing: most people with these traits aren't dangerous criminals like in movies. Many are just difficult to be around. And since labeling people is risky, it's usually better to judge by how someone treats you over time than by guessing what's going on inside their head.

The effective interest rate is the rate actually paid on a loan or earned on an investment once the compounding of interest over time is factored in. It offers a way to compare the real cost of borrowing, or the real return on an investment, by accounting for how often interest is compounded. A bifurcated interest rate is one that is split into two portions, each carrying a different rate. A loan might, for instance, charge a lower rate during its first year and then a higher rate for the rest of its term. In that situation, the effective rate would be a weighted average of the two rates, with each weighted by how long it applies. Calculating it requires knowing the loan's terms: both interest rates, the period over which each one is in force, and the compounding frequency. With that information, you can use a financial calculator or spreadsheet software to work out the effective rate. Keep in mind that the effective rate differs from the nominal rate, which is simply the stated rate and ignores the impact of compounding. Because it reflects interest compounding over time, the effective rate is generally higher than the nominal rate.

Imagine your class is voting on whether recess should be inside or outside. Ten kids want outside and eight want inside. Normally outside wins. But suppose the teacher who likes inside recess gets to split the class into small groups, and each group's majority counts as one vote. If she's clever, she can pack lots of outside-lovers into one group, where they win big but still only get one vote, and spread the rest thinly so inside-lovers win most of the other groups. Inside recess wins even though fewer kids wanted it. That's gerrymandering: drawing the lines around voting areas, called districts, so one side wins more seats than its number of voters would suggest.

There are several ways people try to fix this. The most popular is to take the crayon away from the politicians. Instead of letting the people who will run in elections draw their own districts, some states, like California, Arizona, and Michigan, have independent commissions made of regular citizens from different parties who draw the maps together. Another idea is to give the mapmakers strict rules, like keeping towns and counties whole, making districts compact instead of weird snake shapes, and not using information about how people voted before. Courts can also step in and throw out maps that are unfair. They do this for maps that hurt voters because of their race, but in 2019 the Supreme Court said federal courts can't decide whether a map is too unfair to one political party, so those fights now happen mostly in state courts and state constitutions. Some people suggest bigger changes, like computer programs that draw neutral maps, or electing several representatives from each larger area so seats match the share of votes each party gets, which is called proportional representation. That last one makes the line-drawing trick much less powerful.

Other countries mostly have less of this problem, but not none. Many countries, like the Netherlands and Israel, use proportional systems where there aren't really small districts to cheat with, so the trick doesn't work. Countries that do use districts, like the United Kingdom, Canada, and Australia, usually hand the job to neutral, nonpartisan boundary commissions, which has made gerrymandering rare there. Canada actually had serious gerrymandering problems in the past and fixed them this way in the 1960s. Some places still struggle with it, such as Hungary, where critics say the ruling party redrew districts to help itself, and Northern Ireland historically, where lines were drawn to give one community more power than the other.

In the United States, it's been a problem from the very beginning. The name comes from Elbridge Gerry, a governor of Massachusetts who in 1812 signed off on a district shaped so strangely that a newspaper said it looked like a salamander, and they called it a "Gerry-mander." Even before that, there were accusations about lines drawn to keep James Madison out of Congress in 1788. What has changed is how good people are at it. Long ago, mapmakers worked with paper maps and guesses. Today they use powerful computers and detailed information about voters, so they can draw lines with incredible precision, which is why many people feel the problem is worse now than it used to be, and why both major parties have done it whenever they had the chance.

I can't diagnose you from a description, but some of what you're describing deserves prompt medical attention, so please don't wait this out for long.

Pain in the lower abdomen that gets worse with urinating and also with passing stool, combined with foamy urine, could have several explanations. A urinary tract infection or prostatitis (in men) can cause pain with urination and lower abdominal discomfort. Pain during bowel movements along with urinary symptoms can point to inflammation in the pelvis, such as diverticulitis, which affects the colon, or a pelvic infection. Kidney stones can cause severe pain that changes with position and sometimes comes with blood in the urine. Foamy urine is often caused by protein in the urine, which can happen with kidney problems, but it is also common and harmless when you are dehydrated or urinating forcefully. Other possibilities include sexually transmitted infections, which can cause both urinary pain and pelvic pain, and inflammatory bowel conditions.

The fact that the pain happens with both urinating and passing stool suggests the problem may be in the pelvic area, where the bladder, bowel, and reproductive organs are close together. That is worth having checked.

I'd recommend seeing a doctor within the next day or two. If you develop a fever or chills, severe or worsening pain, vomiting, blood in your urine or stool, difficulty urinating, inability to pass urine, or confusion or dizziness, go to an emergency department right away. A urine test and basic blood work can identify many of these causes quickly.

Cutting back on soda and beer is a good idea in general, and drinking more plain water can help if an infection or stones are involved. However, reducing your drinks won't resolve an underlying infection or other condition, so please get evaluated rather than relying on dietary changes alone.

So an image sensor basically turns light into a digital picture. You'll find one in digital cameras, scanners, and pretty much anything else that captures images. The sensor is a grid of photodiodes, tiny light-sensitive spots that turn incoming light into an electrical current. When light hits the sensor, each photodiode spits out a current that matches how bright that spot is. The camera then converts those currents into digital data, and the image processor turns that data into the picture you actually see.

There are two main flavors. CCDs cost more to make but usually give you cleaner images with less noise. CMOS sensors are cheaper and sip less power, though they can get noisier. Either way, the sensor is the part that takes the light coming in and turns it into something a device can store and edit.

Market basket analysis is a data mining method for uncovering links between products that tend to be bought at the same time. Retailers typically rely on it to find goods that shoppers often pick up together, which lets them shelve those goods side by side or promote them as a bundle to boost sales. Suppose a store finds that people who buy bread also tend to buy butter and jam. It could then stock these products near each other or feature them together in a promotion. Recognizing such habits in purchasing behavior helps retailers sharpen their marketing and grow revenue. The technique is frequently combined with other methods, such as association rule mining, to detect recurring patterns in large volumes of data and guide sound decisions about marketing and sales.

South Africa hosted the 2010 FIFA World Cup from June 11 to July 11, 2010, and Spain came away as the champions. In the final, played on July 11, the Spaniards beat the Netherlands 1-0 after extra time. The win gave Spain its first World Cup title, and it also marked the first occasion on which a European side claimed the trophy in Africa.

"Discovery (observation)" is a term from the philosophy of science and the study of how knowledge is produced. It refers to the process of finding something new about the world through careful watching, recording, and noticing, as opposed to deliberately testing a hypothesis through a designed experiment. An observational discovery happens when a researcher, or sometimes an ordinary person, notices a pattern, object, event, or anomaly that was not specifically anticipated and then recognizes its significance.

Classic examples include Galileo's telescopic observations of the moons of Jupiter, Edward Jenner's noticing that milkmaids who had contracted cowpox seemed resistant to smallpox, and the astronomical discovery of Uranus by William Herschel, which came from systematically surveying the sky. In each case, the discovery came from paying close attention to what was seen rather than from confirming a prediction.

The term is often contrasted with discovery through experiment, where the researcher manipulates variables to test a specific idea, and with theoretical discovery, where a new idea or law is reached through reasoning or mathematics. Observational discovery is especially important in fields such as astronomy, geology, biology, and ecology, where many phenomena cannot be controlled or reproduced in a laboratory.

Philosophers of science have debated how much observation is shaped by prior theory, since what a person notices depends partly on what they are looking for and what concepts they already hold. Nonetheless, the idea of observational discovery remains a central concept for understanding how unexpected findings lead to new knowledge.

I can't verify exactly what is in your product, so please check the label. Lactare is an Indian brand of herbal lactation supplement, and formulations typically contain galactagogue herbs such as shatavari, fenugreek, fennel, ginger, or similar. The general picture for these herbs is below, but the exact ingredient list matters.

Most people tolerate these supplements reasonably well, and there is no strong evidence of serious harm from taking them for months. That said, the evidence is also limited. Herbal galactagogues have not been studied rigorously over long periods, products are not tightly regulated, and the benefit for milk supply is modest and inconsistent. So I would not call them proven safe for six more months, only that serious problems are uncommon.

The side effects people most often report are digestive: gas, loose stools, bloating, or heartburn. Fenugreek can cause a maple-syrup smell in sweat and urine, can lower blood sugar (relevant if you have diabetes or take diabetes medicine), and may cause loose stools or gas in the baby. It can also worsen asthma or cause allergic reactions in people sensitive to peanuts, chickpeas, or related plants. Fenugreek has been linked to thyroid effects in some reports, so tell your doctor if you have a thyroid condition. Watch your baby for fussiness, rash, unusual stools, or colic-like symptoms, and stop if these appear.

An important point is that supplements work best when milk removal is also optimized. Milk supply is driven mainly by how often and how effectively milk is removed from the breast. At 3 months, it is worth checking that you are feeding on demand, at least 8 to 12 times in 24 hours, that the latch is good, and that you are offering both breasts. Adding a pumping session after feeds can help. Enough sleep, fluids, and food matter too. Sometimes a baby who seems unsatisfied is actually getting enough, so the real test is the baby's growth, wet diapers (about six or more a day), and regular weight checks.

Since you have already taken it for two months, I would ask yourself whether it has actually helped. If supply has not improved noticeably, continuing for another six months is unlikely to add benefit. If it has helped, you can usually continue for a while, but it is reasonable to review with your doctor or a lactation consultant every month or two rather than committing to six months upfront. Also consider that if low supply persists despite good breastfeeding technique, there may be an underlying cause, such as thyroid problems, anemia, retained placental tissue, hormonal contraceptives, or insufficient glandular tissue, and these are worth checking.

Please speak to your doctor or a lactation consultant before continuing long term, particularly if you have other health conditions or take other medicines. Contact them sooner if your baby is not gaining weight well, has fewer wet diapers, or seems unwell.

Your inner voice feels like it's coming from the top or front of your head mostly because that's where your brain tells you "I" live. Your eyes are in the front of your face, your ears are on the sides, and your brain is stuck in the middle building a picture of the world. Your brain makes a guess about where you are, and for most people that guess lands somewhere behind the eyes and up high, since that's where we look out from. The thoughts feel like they're happening at that spot because it's the spot your brain picked as "home base." It's a bit like how a movie seems to come from the screen even though the sound is really coming from speakers around the room.

It isn't really coming from a place at all. When you think in words, parts of your brain that handle speech and hearing light up softly, as if you were talking out loud but with the volume turned all the way down. These include areas on the sides of your brain, like those near your ears, and areas that plan speech, which are toward the front. The frontal lobe does help, because it handles planning, choosing what to think about, and holding ideas in mind. But it's a team effort, not one single spot.

As for why you can't move it, that's because the location is a feeling your brain makes up, not a real speaker you could slide around. Some people actually can shift it a bit with practice, for example by imagining the voice coming from their chest or from across the room, and others find it just stays put. Most people never try, so it never changes. Also, people differ a lot. Some hear a clear voice, some think in pictures, and some have no voice at all.

And no, it has nothing to do with lacking discipline. Discipline is about choosing what to do, and this is about how your brain draws the map of where "you" are. It's like asking why you can't make your nose feel like it's on your elbow. It's just how the map got drawn. If you're curious, you can play with it by picturing the voice somewhere else, and see if it feels different. If it doesn't budge, that's perfectly normal.

Mild discomfort or soreness after masturbating is common, but if the pain is significant, you should talk to a healthcare provider. Several things could be behind the pain you describe, such as an infection, inflammation, or irritation. For problems involving the scrotum and anus, a primary care provider or a urologist is usually the best person to see. They can examine you and may order tests to work out what is causing the pain. They can also suggest treatments, which might include medication, changes to your daily habits, or other therapies. Dealing with this matters, since pain that does not go away can point to a more serious underlying problem. For that reason, you should get medical attention as soon as you can so the cause can be identified and you can receive the right treatment.

Asthma does not directly cause folliculitis, but the two conditions are linked in a few indirect ways. People with asthma often have other allergic or atopic skin conditions, such as eczema, which can cause small bumps on the arms, thighs, and back. These bumps are sometimes mistaken for folliculitis, and the difference matters because they need different treatment. Some asthma medicines can also play a role. Oral steroids taken for a severe flare can sometimes trigger folliculitis, and inhaled steroids rarely do. If you take either, mention it to your doctor.

Since benzoyl peroxide and AHA soap haven't helped, the bumps may be a different type of folliculitis, or something that looks like it. Fungal folliculitis (caused by Malassezia yeast) is a common cause of itchy, uniform small bumps on the back and arms, especially in hot, humid weather or after sweating. If that's the case, an antifungal treatment such as ketoconazole or selenium sulfide shampoo, used as a body wash and left on the skin for several minutes, often works much better than benzoyl peroxide. Keratosis pilaris, a harmless condition that causes rough, bumpy skin on the arms and thighs, responds better to urea or salicylic acid lotions than to antibacterial treatments. A dermatologist can often tell these apart with a simple skin scraping or exam, so it's worth asking your doctor for a referral or a follow-up visit to confirm the diagnosis before trying more creams.

In the meantime, several habits can help. Shower soon after sweating or exercising, wear loose, breathable cotton clothing, avoid thick oils and occlusive creams on the affected areas, and use a clean towel and fresh razor blades if you shave. Warm compresses can soothe the skin, but try not to squeeze or pick at the bumps, since that spreads infection and can leave scars.

See your doctor promptly if the bumps spread, become painful, fill with pus, or come with fever, or if they don't improve after a few weeks of a corrected treatment. Those signs can mean a bacterial infection that needs oral antibiotics.

Massachusetts does not tax unrealized capital gains. A gain is only taxable once it is realized, meaning the asset has been sold or otherwise disposed of in a taxable transaction. Until then, any increase in the value of an investment is simply not reported as income on a Massachusetts return.

Once a gain is realized, Massachusetts taxes it under its income tax system, which has two rates. Short-term capital gains, generally from assets held one year or less, are taxed at 8.5 percent. Long-term capital gains, from assets held more than one year, are taxed at 5 percent. Collectibles gains are taxed at the higher rate, and the state's surtax on income above a threshold (the 4 percent surtax funded by the 2022 millionaires' tax amendment, which applies to taxable income over roughly one million dollars) also applies to large capital gains, bringing the effective rate on high earners' gains higher.

The calculation for a realized gain starts with the sale proceeds minus the adjusted cost basis, which is generally the purchase price plus any commissions or improvements, adjusted as the rules require. The resulting gain is then reported on the Massachusetts return, typically Schedule D and the Form 1 return, and taxed at the applicable rate. Capital losses can offset gains, and net losses can reduce other income up to the limits set by state law, with unused losses carried forward.

Because the rules involving basis, holding periods, and the surtax can be detailed, anyone with significant realized gains should check current Department of Revenue guidance or consult a tax professional.

Roughly 60 nations around the world have designated English as an official language. Still, the meaning of "official language" differs from one country to another, and some countries recognize several languages as official at once. In many of the countries where English holds this status, it serves as a lingua franca, a shared tongue that people with different native languages use to communicate with one another. Consequently, English is often not the first language of most residents, yet it plays a major role in government, schooling, and other public spheres. The countries where English is official include Antigua and Barbuda, Australia, the Bahamas, Barbados, Belize, Botswana, Cameroon, Canada, Dominica, Fiji, Gambia, Ghana, Grenada, Guyana, India, Ireland, Jamaica, Kenya, Kiribati, Lesotho, Liberia, Malawi, Malta, the Marshall Islands, Mauritius, Micronesia, Namibia, Nauru, New Zealand, Nigeria, Pakistan, Palau, Papua New Guinea, the Philippines, Rwanda, Saint Kitts and Nevis, Saint Lucia, Saint Vincent and the Grenadines, Seychelles, Sierra Leone, Singapore, the Solomon Islands, South Africa, Sudan, Swaziland, Tanzania, Tonga, Trinidad and Tobago, Tuvalu, Uganda, the United Kingdom, the United States, Vanuatu, Zambia, and Zimbabwe.

Yes, they still exist, but they look different than they did in old movies.

Think of a mob or mafia as a big secret club of people who make money by breaking the rules. They might sell things that aren't allowed, scare people into paying them "protection" money, cheat at business deals, or hurt people who get in their way. Long ago, especially in big American cities around the 1920s to the 1970s, some of these clubs were very powerful and everyone knew about them.

The Italian mafia is still around. In Italy there are several big groups: the Sicilian Mafia, the 'Ndrangheta from Calabria, and the Camorra from Naples. The 'Ndrangheta is especially strong today and makes huge amounts of money moving drugs around the world. In the United States, the old Italian-American families, like the famous "Five Families" of New York, still exist, but they are much smaller and weaker. Police spent decades catching their leaders and putting them in jail, so they're kind of like an old toy that still works but isn't the shiny new thing anymore.

The Russian mob, which people sometimes call the Bratva (meaning "brotherhood"), grew a lot after the Soviet Union fell apart in the early 1990s. Things were messy then, and these groups grabbed money and power. Today they are often mixed up with business, computers, and hacking, so they're less about tough guys on street corners and more about stealing money in sneaky ways.

The Irish mob was famous in American cities like Boston and New York. A well-known boss was Whitey Bulger in Boston. These groups are much smaller now. In Ireland itself there are still crime gangs, like the Kinahan group, which police around the world are trying to stop.

There are also many others you might not hear about as much. Mexico and Colombia have very powerful drug cartels. Japan has the Yakuza, though it's shrinking. China has groups called Triads. Some of these are actually much bigger and scarier today than the old Italian mob ever was.

So the short answer is yes. The bad-guy clubs never really went away. Some got smaller because police got better at catching them, and some new ones got bigger. Many have also learned to hide better by using computers, fake businesses, and money moved around the world, so they're harder to see than they used to be.

Oakhurst, NJ is in Monmouth County. That's in central New Jersey, right on the Atlantic coast. Ocean County sits to the south and Middlesex is up to the northwest, and Mercer's over to the northeast. The county seat's Freehold. There are a ton of different towns in the county, and Oakhurst's one of them, sitting more or less in the middle of it all.

Car companies give their cars a model year, like 2009, that can be a year ahead of when the car first shows up in stores. Think of it like a birthday party held before the big day, or like a magazine that comes out in the middle of the month but has next month's date on the cover. The idea is that the car stays "new" for as long as possible.

Here is why it works that way. Carmakers like to unveil their new cars in the summer or fall of one year, and then sell them through the next year. If a car arrives in showrooms in late 2008, calling it a 2009 model makes it sound fresher and more up to date for most of the time it's on sale. When 2009 arrives, a buyer in early 2009 will think, "Oh, this is the newest one!" instead of thinking it's already old.

It also helps keep things tidy. Factories often change small things partway through the year, and a new model year gives them a clean point to show off those updates. So the year on the car is more like a version name than a calendar date, a bit like how a new phone is called "Model 12" even though it came out at a certain time.

A PAN card is a permanent identifier used for tax filings, bank accounts, loans, and many financial transactions, so a scanned copy in the wrong hands carries real risk. Someone holding it could try to open bank or demat accounts, take out loans or credit cards, or file tax returns in your name. They could also combine the PAN with your name, date of birth, and address, which are often visible on the card, to pass verification checks or to build a fuller identity profile for phishing and social engineering. Scanned copies can also be shared with third-party background-verification agencies, stored insecurely, or leaked in a data breach, after which they circulate on the internet.

Most of this risk comes from how the copy is handled rather than from the fact that you shared it. Legitimate employers usually need the PAN only at the offer or onboarding stage, not during interviews. If you are asked for it early, it is reasonable to ask why and how it will be stored, who will see it, and when it will be deleted if you don't join. Under India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, companies must have a lawful purpose for collecting personal data, must limit its use to that purpose, and must protect it, so you can cite those principles when asking questions.

To reduce your exposure, you can share a watermarked copy, writing the company name and the purpose on it (for example, "Provided to ABC Ltd for employment verification only"), or mask some digits where the format allows. Sharing it through a secure channel rather than casual email or messaging apps is also safer. Keep a record of what you shared and with whom.

If you suspect misuse, check your credit report and Form 26AS or your income tax account for unfamiliar transactions, and consider enabling alerts with your banks. You can report identity misuse to the cybercrime portal at cybercrime.gov.in or call 1930, and you can raise a complaint with the Income Tax Department if PAN is used fraudulently. If the company mishandled your data, you can also file a grievance under the DPDP framework once its rules are fully in force.

Okay so if you're on SSDI and your money situation gets better, you might have to pay back some or all of what you got. That can happen if you're no longer considered disabled under the Social Security Administration's definition, or if you've picked up other income or assets that make you ineligible. Either way, it's worth knowing about.

Best move is to tell the SSA as soon as things change. Reporting it early can keep you from building up an overpayment that you'd have to repay later. They'll review your case and figure out whether you still qualify based on your current situation. If you don't qualify anymore because your finances improved, you could owe back whatever you got after the change. They'll mail you a notice spelling out how much you owe and how to pay it.

Also, if you're receiving SSDI, you're required to report changes to your income, assets, and employment status. Don't skip that. Not reporting can lead to overpayments, and then you're stuck paying it back down the road.

Adversarial machine learning is the study of how machine learning systems can be attacked, deceived, or manipulated by intelligent opponents, and of how to build systems that resist such interference. Most standard machine learning assumes that the data a model sees in deployment resembles the data it was trained on and that nobody is deliberately trying to make it fail. Adversarial machine learning drops that assumption and treats the model as something an attacker may probe, exploit, or corrupt.

The best-known type of attack is the evasion attack, which uses adversarial examples. These are inputs altered in tiny, often imperceptible ways that cause a model to make a confident mistake. A classic example is an image of a panda with a faint layer of carefully computed noise added, which a neural network then labels as a gibbon even though a human sees no difference. Attackers typically find such perturbations by using the model's gradients to determine which small change most increases the error, as in methods like the fast gradient sign method or projected gradient descent. Physical versions exist too, such as stickers placed on a stop sign that cause a vision system to misread it.

A second category is poisoning, where the attacker interferes with the training data. By inserting mislabeled or crafted examples, they can degrade overall performance or plant a backdoor, meaning the model behaves normally except when a particular trigger pattern appears, at which point it produces the attacker's chosen output. This is a serious concern when models are trained on data scraped from the internet or contributed by many parties.

A third category concerns privacy and intellectual property. Model extraction attacks involve querying a model repeatedly to reconstruct a copy of it. Model inversion and membership inference attacks try to recover information about the training data, for example determining whether a specific person's record was used to train the model. More recently, large language models face prompt injection and jailbreaking, where crafted text causes the system to ignore its instructions or reveal restricted content.

Attacks are often categorized by how much the attacker knows. In white-box settings the attacker has full access to the model's architecture and parameters, while in black-box settings they can only observe outputs. Notably, adversarial examples often transfer between models, so an attacker can craft them against a substitute model and use them against a target they cannot inspect.

Defenses are an active and difficult area. Adversarial training, which augments training data with adversarial examples, is among the most effective approaches, though it costs more computation and can reduce accuracy on clean inputs. Other strategies include input preprocessing, anomaly detection, certified robustness methods that provide mathematical guarantees within a bounded perturbation, differential privacy to limit information leakage, and careful data vetting against poisoning. Many proposed defenses have later been broken by adaptive attacks, so the field is something of an arms race.

The topic matters because machine learning is used in security-sensitive settings such as malware detection, fraud prevention, autonomous driving, biometric authentication, and content moderation, where adversaries have real incentives to cause failures. It also reveals that models can be accurate on ordinary data while relying on fragile patterns that differ from human perception, which makes it relevant to understanding model reliability more broadly.

The IEEE Computer Society is basically a branch of the IEEE, the big professional engineering organization, and it's focused on computing and information processing, both the theory side and the practical side. It's been around since 1946, and these days it's one of the largest and most influential groups in the field. What it does for people in computing is pretty broad: publications, conferences, technical committees, and professional development stuff. The journals and conference proceedings it puts out are well regarded, and it sponsors a ton of conferences and workshops every year. It's also a global community, made up of computing professionals who want to push the state of the art forward. Members do all sorts of things, like research, education, and career development, and plenty of them volunteer their time and expertise to help the field move ahead.

Andrew Ng is a British-born American computer scientist and entrepreneur, widely known as one of the most influential figures in modern artificial intelligence and machine learning education. He was born in 1976 in London and grew up partly in Hong Kong and Singapore before pursuing his studies in the United States. He earned a bachelor's degree at Carnegie Mellon University, a master's at MIT, and a PhD at the University of California, Berkeley.

He spent many years as a professor at Stanford University, where he worked on machine learning, robotics, and deep learning. His research contributed to early work on reinforcement learning for autonomous helicopter flight, and he was a key advocate for using graphics processing units to train large neural networks, which helped accelerate the deep learning revolution.

In industry, he founded and led the Google Brain project in 2011, which applied deep learning at large scale, including the well-known experiment in which a neural network learned to recognize cats from unlabeled YouTube videos. He later served as chief scientist at Baidu, where he led a large AI group, before leaving in 2017.

Ng is also famous for democratizing AI education. He co-founded Coursera in 2012 with Daphne Koller, and his Stanford-based Machine Learning course became one of the most popular online courses ever, introducing millions of people to the subject. He later created the Deep Learning Specialization and founded DeepLearning.AI, which offers courses and resources for learners and professionals.

He has founded or led other ventures as well, including Landing AI, which focuses on bringing AI to manufacturing and industrial settings, and AI Fund, a venture studio that builds AI startups. He has promoted the idea of data-centric AI, which emphasizes improving the quality of training data rather than only refining model architectures. He has also popularized the phrase that AI is "the new electricity," reflecting his view that it will transform nearly every industry.

Common sense reasoning is the ability to make inferences and judgments about everyday situations using broad, largely implicit knowledge of how the world works. It draws on things most people learn through ordinary experience rather than formal study: that objects fall when dropped, that people get hungry and tired, that a glass of water left on a table will not suddenly float away, or that if someone says they are going to the store they will probably come back with groceries. This kind of knowledge is usually so familiar that people do not consciously think about it, yet it shapes nearly every decision and interpretation they make.

What makes common sense reasoning distinctive is its flexibility and its reliance on context. Humans can fill in gaps in incomplete information, anticipate likely consequences, interpret ambiguous language, and recognize when a rule does not apply to an unusual case. For example, if someone asks you to "grab a seat" at a crowded event, you understand that they mean any available chair, not that you should take one from a person already sitting in it. Such inferences come easily to people but have historically been very hard to program into computers, which is why common sense reasoning has long been considered a central challenge in artificial intelligence.

In philosophy, psychology, and AI research, the term refers to this body of practical, default knowledge and the processes that use it. Researchers study how people reason about physical objects, social behavior, time, and cause and effect, and how to represent such knowledge in machines so they can respond sensibly to situations their designers never explicitly anticipated.

A shaped charge is a type of explosive that is designed to focus its blast into a narrow jet, instead of spreading it out in all directions. Here is the basic idea.

Imagine you have a bowl of explosive with a cone-shaped hollow carved into the front, and a thin metal liner, often copper, lining that cone. When the explosive goes off, the blast squeezes that metal liner inward so hard that it folds in on itself and shoots forward as a fast, thin stream of metal. Think of it like squeezing a tube of toothpaste from the back: the paste gets pushed out the front in a concentrated stream. In the case of a shaped charge, the "toothpaste" is metal moving at very high speed, so it can punch through thick armor.

The shape is the important part. A plain block of explosive pushes its energy out evenly, so most of it is wasted in the air. By hollowing out the front and lining it with metal, the explosive's energy is aimed and focused into one direction, much like a magnifying glass focuses sunlight into a bright spot. That focus is what lets a relatively small charge make a hole through something very tough.

So in short: a shaped charge uses the shape of the explosive to squeeze a metal cone into a fast, narrow jet that can cut through hard targets.

New Guinea sits in the southwestern Pacific Ocean, lying east of Indonesia. As the second-largest island on Earth, it is split along political lines between two nations: Papua New Guinea claims the eastern portion, while the Indonesian province of Papua holds the western portion. Situated directly to the north of Australia, the island forms part of the broader area called Melanesia.

The Church–Turing thesis is a foundational principle in computer science and mathematical logic stating that any function that can be computed by an effective procedure, meaning a step-by-step mechanical method that a human could carry out with paper and pencil in principle, can also be computed by a Turing machine. Equivalently, it claims that the intuitive notion of "computability" coincides with the formal notion of Turing computability.

The thesis is named after two logicians who proposed closely related ideas in the 1930s. Alonzo Church introduced lambda calculus and, in 1936, proposed that effective calculability is captured by the lambda-definable functions. Alan Turing, in the same year, introduced the Turing machine, an abstract device with a tape, a read/write head, and a finite set of rules, and argued that it captures every mechanical computation. Soon after, it was shown that lambda calculus and Turing machines define exactly the same class of functions, and many other formalisms, such as recursive functions and register machines, turned out to be equivalent as well. This convergence of independently designed models strongly supported the thesis.

It is important to understand that the Church–Turing thesis is not a mathematical theorem that can be proved, because "effective procedure" is an informal concept. Instead, it is a hypothesis about the nature of computation, supported by evidence rather than by formal proof. Its implications are significant: it implies that there are well-defined problems, such as the halting problem, that no computer program can solve, and it suggests that a Turing machine can serve as a universal model of what any computer, from a laptop to a supercomputer, can do in principle. Some researchers have explored variants, such as the physical Church–Turing thesis, which asks whether physical processes in our universe can compute anything beyond Turing machines, but these remain open and debated questions.

If you co-sign a loan and the main borrower stops making payments, you can be held liable for the balance. By co-signing, you have committed to sharing responsibility for repaying the loan should the primary borrower default. If the co-signer refuses to pay, supply needed information, or hand over the asset, you might have to pursue legal remedies to recover what is owed. Speaking with an attorney can help you understand your options and choose the most suitable approach for your circumstances. Sometimes the co-signer or the lender can be persuaded to reach a settlement that everyone accepts. If that fails, though, you may need to sue for compensation or seek to have the co-signer released from the loan. Keep in mind that litigation can take a long time and cost a good deal of money, and it is not always the wisest path. Weigh the advantages and disadvantages carefully before deciding whether to go to court.

Double-reporting usually happens when the same payment shows up on two different information returns, most often a 1099-K from a payment processor and a 1099-MISC or 1099-NEC from the business that paid you. The IRS matches these forms against your return, so the goal is to report the income once while making sure both forms are accounted for.

The key principle is that a 1099-K reports gross payments processed through a platform such as PayPal, Venmo, Stripe, or an online marketplace, while a 1099-MISC or 1099-NEC reports payments a specific client or company made to you for services. If the same dollars appear on both, you are not supposed to count them twice. Instead, you report the underlying income once on the appropriate schedule and then adjust for the overlap.

For self-employment income, the usual approach is to report the gross receipts on Schedule C, using whichever form reflects the actual source of the money. If a 1099-K includes personal payments, such as reimbursements from friends, sales of personal items at a loss, or transfers between your own accounts, those amounts are not income and should be removed. You can document them in your records and, if needed, explain the difference with a statement attached to your return. Many tax preparers handle this by entering the 1099-K gross amount, then subtracting nontaxable items, so the net taxable figure matches what you actually earned.

If a client issued you a 1099-NEC or 1099-MISC for the same work that a payment app also reported on a 1099-K, compare the amounts carefully. Often the payment app reported money you received from that client, so the client's form and the app's form describe the same earnings. Include the income once, and keep the matching documentation so you can show the IRS why the totals line up. Do not omit a form altogether, because the IRS computer matching will flag the mismatch.

A few practical steps help. Gather every 1099 you received and reconcile them against your bank deposits and invoices. Separate business payments from personal ones throughout the year, since this makes the reconciliation far easier. Keep records of fees, refunds, and chargebacks, which can often be deducted as business expenses or subtracted from gross receipts. If the numbers still don't match after reconciliation, consider consulting a tax professional, because the correct treatment depends on your specific facts, and the IRS allows corrections through amended returns if an error comes to light later.

Property tax serves several interrelated purposes. Its chief role is to raise revenue for local governments, which rely on it to fund public services such as schools, police and fire protection, road maintenance, parks, libraries, and sanitation. Because it is typically levied on real estate, and the value of that property is tied to the local public services and infrastructure nearby, it is often seen as a reasonable way to pay for the services that make a place desirable to live in.

Property tax also provides a stable and predictable source of income for localities. Unlike sales or income taxes, which can swing with economic conditions, property values tend to change more slowly, so communities can plan budgets and long-term investments with greater confidence. Many local governments depend on it heavily, in some cases for the majority of their own-source revenue.

Beyond raising funds, property tax can serve as a tool for land use and fairness. It is generally tied to the value of a property, so it aims to distribute the cost of public services according to the wealth that property represents. Some economists also argue that it encourages efficient use of land, since it is harder to avoid than many other taxes and does not directly discourage productive activity the way taxes on income or labor might. Critics note that it can burden people with limited incomes who own valuable homes, which is why many jurisdictions offer exemptions, caps, or deferrals to address that concern.

I'm not aware of "cake and underwear stocks" as an established term in finance or investing, so I can't point to a single definitive meaning. It may be a phrase from a particular article, commentator, country's market slang, or social media discussion that I'm not familiar with. If you can tell me where you encountered it, I can help interpret it more precisely.

That said, the phrase resembles some well-known ideas about consumer spending as an economic signal. One is the "men's underwear index," popularized by former Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan, which holds that sales of men's underwear are usually very stable. When they drop noticeably, it suggests households are under enough financial strain to postpone even basic, unseen purchases, which can signal a downturn. Another is the "lipstick effect," the observation that during recessions people cut back on big-ticket luxuries but keep buying small, affordable indulgences such as lipstick, chocolate, or desserts, which gives a lift to companies selling those treats.

Taken together, "cake and underwear" stocks could plausibly describe companies selling inexpensive everyday necessities and small comforts, such as basic apparel makers, bakeries, snack and confectionery firms, and similar consumer staples. Investors sometimes see these as defensive holdings because demand tends to stay steady, or even rise slightly, when the broader economy weakens. Again, that's an informed guess based on related concepts rather than a confirmed definition, so the source where you saw the phrase would be the best guide to what the author actually meant.

The 2010 Haiti earthquake was a shallow, strike-slip earthquake, meaning the ground moved mostly sideways as two blocks of the Earth's crust slid past each other along a fault. It occurred on January 12, 2010, with a magnitude of about 7.0, and its epicenter was near Léogâne, west of the capital, Port-au-Prince. It struck along the Enriquillo-Plantain Garden fault system, which forms part of the boundary between the Caribbean and North American tectonic plates. Because the quake was shallow, at roughly 13 kilometers deep, its shaking was intense near the surface, contributing to the enormous destruction and loss of life in the region.

EThe freedom to provide services across the European Union (EU) lets individuals and companies based in one EU member state offer their services temporarily in another member state, with no need to set up a business there or pay taxes in that host country. For example, if you live in an EU country and wish to offer services in Germany for a limited period, you can do so without paying German taxes, provided you satisfy the requirements that apply under this freedom. Nevertheless, income earned from services performed in Germany may still be taxable in your home EU country. To understand your tax obligations on such income, you should review the tax rules of your home country. It is also advisable to consult a tax professional or financial adviser to confirm that you are meeting every applicable tax requirement.

In computer science, a type system is a collection of rules that attaches a property known as a "type" to the different elements of a programming language, including variables, expressions, and functions. Its goal is to lower the chance of type errors occurring at runtime by making sure that the rules concerning types are respected while a program runs. Type systems come in several varieties, among them static and dynamic ones. A static type system carries out type checking at compile time, prior to the program's execution, so type errors can be found and corrected before the program ever runs. A dynamic type system, by contrast, checks types at runtime while the program is executing. As a result, type errors may stay hidden until the program is run, and they can make it fail during execution. Type systems also differ in how much type safety they offer. In a type-safe language, type errors either cannot happen or are highly improbable. In a type-unsafe language, such errors occur more often and can be introduced into a program more easily. In short, type systems are a valuable means of ensuring that programs are reliable and correct, and they form an essential component of many programming languages.

A deep belief network (DBN) is a kind of neural network used for unsupervised learning. It's made up of several layers of interconnected hidden units, and each layer picks up higher-level features from the raw input. You train them in two stages. First comes unsupervised pretraining, where each layer learns to reconstruct its input using contrastive divergence. After that, you can fine-tune the whole thing with supervised methods like backpropagation so it handles a specific job, say image classification or translation. People have used DBNs for all sorts of things, including image recognition, natural language processing, and speech recognition. They really shine when you've got tons of unlabeled data, since they can pull out useful features from it and use those to make predictions or decisions.

Association rule mining is a data mining technique for finding relationships between variables in big datasets. You can use it to spot patterns that help predict when certain things will happen or guide decisions. Rules usually look like "if-then" statements. The "if" part is a set of items (an itemset) that show up together in a transaction, and the "then" part is an item that's likely to be bought along with them. So a rule might say, "if a customer buys bread and milk, they'll probably buy butter too."

To find these rules, algorithms measure how strongly the items in the "if" and "then" parts are linked. One of the main measures is support, which counts how many transactions contain the items together. If a rule has high support, it shows up often in the data, so you can trust it more. People use association rule mining for all sorts of things, like market basket analysis, catching fraud, and building recommendation systems. It's a handy way to dig out relationships in data and get insights that can actually shape business choices.

You can work out the best price at which to buy a stock by examining market depth, a measure of how many orders exist for a given stock at various price levels. The CSE Atrad tool is a trading platform that offers this information, letting you view the volume of orders at each price level for a chosen stock. To find the best buying price with CSE Atrad, take the following steps: open the tool and choose the stock you want to purchase. Then review its market depth data, which typically appears as a "buy ladder" and a "sell ladder." The buy ladder lists the volume of orders placed by buyers at each price level, whereas the sell ladder lists the volume of orders placed by sellers at each level. Find the price level in the buy ladder that has the largest order volume. That level reflects the best buying price, since demand for the stock is strongest there. Bear in mind that market depth data changes all the time, so you should check it often to keep your picture of the best buying price for a stock current. Before deciding to buy, it is also important to weigh other factors, such as general market conditions and the stock's fundamental performance.

Night sweats, fatigue, and unexplained weight loss can stem from a wide range of causes, so it's wise to see a healthcare professional when these show up. They may point to an underlying condition that deserves attention. Since you have diabetes, keeping a close eye on your blood glucose and sticking to your prescribed medication schedule matters. Your recent knee replacement and daily aspirin use may also be playing a role. Shifts in blood pressure are another possible source of sweating and tiredness. Your doctor can review your symptoms alongside every medication you take, evaluate your general health, and suggest treatment or lifestyle adjustments where needed. If the symptoms are severe or don't go away, get medical care promptly.

An angiogram uses x-ray imaging to make the blood vessels, both arteries and veins, inside the body visible. Doctors usually order it to diagnose and treat circulation problems, such as blocked or narrowed vessels. During the procedure, a slender, flexible tube known as a catheter is threaded into a blood vessel, typically in the arm or leg, and a contrast dye is released that shows up on x-rays. Warfarin is a drug that keeps blood clots from forming by blocking the creation of certain proteins needed for clotting. Doctors commonly give it to patients who face a higher risk of clots, including people who have previously had a heart attack, a stroke, or particular irregular heart rhythms. If your father has taken warfarin for an extended period and recently stopped it ahead of the angiogram, his blood may clot more easily than normal. That doesn't automatically mean the procedure will be dangerous or lead to complications. The medical team will take precautions to keep him safe, such as checking his vital signs and giving medications when necessary. Your father should carefully follow the pre-procedure instructions he receives and make sure everyone involved knows about all his medications, warfarin included.

An elevated PSA is not a diagnosis of cancer. It is a marker that tells your doctor something needs a closer look. Many men with raised PSA levels turn out to have no cancer, and the common alternatives include benign prostate enlargement and prostatitis (inflammation or infection of the prostate). Your recent antibiotic course fits that picture, since prostatitis is one of the conditions cipro is used to treat, and an infection can raise PSA for weeks. Recent ejaculation, vigorous cycling, a urinary catheter, or a prostate procedure can also temporarily raise it.

Your numbers do deserve attention, though. Going from 2.9 to over 5 in under a year is a meaningful rise, and doctors pay closer attention to how quickly PSA is climbing than to a single reading. That trend is why a biopsy is a reasonable next step, even though it doesn't mean cancer is present. Biopsy is the only way to answer the question directly.

Before the biopsy, it would be worth asking your urologist or primary care doctor a few things. Would they like a repeat PSA now that the antibiotic course is finished, since infection can falsely elevate the number and a recheck after it clears can help clarify things? Would an MRI of the prostate before biopsy be appropriate? An MRI can guide the biopsy toward suspicious areas and may reduce the need for a random biopsy. They may also look at the free-to-total PSA ratio and PSA density, which help estimate the likelihood of cancer.

If the biopsy does show cancer, it is important to know that many prostate cancers grow slowly and can be managed in several ways, including active monitoring, so a result like that would not necessarily mean immediate, drastic treatment. Try to hold off on worrying until you have the actual results, and bring your questions to the appointment.

There are several approaches you could take to find trailing 5-year stock returns for the 1980s. One option is to turn to an online financial database or website. Platforms like Yahoo Finance, Google Finance, and Bloomberg let you pull up historical stock data for individual companies or indices, so you can look up the trailing 5-year returns for a given security during that decade. Another option is to use a financial calculator or spreadsheet program. With either tool, you can compute the trailing 5-year returns yourself by entering the historical prices for the stock or index across the five-year window. If you run into trouble locating the data or are unsure how to do the calculation, a financial advisor or other professional may be able to supply the figures or help you work them out. Keep in mind that the historical data you can access depends on the source. Some providers only go back a limited number of years, while others offer more extensive records. The accuracy and completeness of the data can also differ, so it's wise to cross-check your figures against more than one source.

Amazon Web Services, usually called AWS, is the cloud computing division of Amazon. It provides on-demand access to computing resources over the internet, such as servers, storage, databases, networking, and a wide range of software tools, on a pay-as-you-go basis. Instead of buying and maintaining their own physical hardware and data centers, individuals, companies, and governments can rent these resources from AWS and scale them up or down as their needs change.

AWS began offering services publicly in 2006, starting with Simple Storage Service (S3) for storing files and Elastic Compute Cloud (EC2) for running virtual servers. The idea grew partly out of Amazon's own experience building large-scale infrastructure for its retail business, and the company realized that other organizations could benefit from the same kind of reliable, flexible computing capacity. Since then AWS has expanded to offer hundreds of services and has become the largest cloud provider in the world, competing mainly with Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud.

The services AWS offers cover many areas. Its compute services let customers run applications on virtual machines, in containers, or through "serverless" functions like AWS Lambda, where code runs only when triggered and the customer doesn't manage servers at all. Its storage and database services include options for files, backups, traditional relational databases, and specialized databases for large-scale or real-time data. It also provides networking tools, security and identity management, analytics, machine learning and artificial intelligence services, tools for developers, and support for things like video streaming, Internet of Things devices, and data warehousing.

AWS operates data centers grouped into geographic "regions" around the world, each containing multiple isolated locations called availability zones. This structure allows customers to place their applications close to their users and to design systems that keep running even if one facility has a problem.

Many well-known companies rely on AWS, including streaming services, social media platforms, banks, and startups, as do government agencies and universities. The main appeal is that customers avoid large upfront hardware costs, can launch new projects quickly, and pay only for what they use. AWS is also a major source of Amazon's profits, often generating a large share of the company's operating income despite being smaller in revenue than its retail business.

Think about a friend who says they'll bring you a toy tomorrow. You believe them, so you trust them. But before you hand over your allowance for it, you might peek in the box to make sure it's really the toy you wanted. Peeking doesn't mean you think your friend is lying. It just means you want to be sure.

The phrase "trust, but verify" is about that exact idea. It comes from an old Russian proverb, and it became famous when a U.S. president used it during arms control talks with the Soviet Union. The point is that you can give someone a good-faith start, believing they mean well, and still check the important things, because even people who mean well make mistakes, and sometimes people try to fool you.

So it isn't really a contradiction. Trust is how you begin, and verifying is how you keep things honest. You don't have to choose between them. A grown-up who trusts a bank still checks the bank statement once a month, and nobody thinks that means they don't trust the bank. Checking just means the trust is sensible instead of blind.

Imagine you built a really tall tower out of blocks, and now you want to take it down, but your tower is squished right between lots of other towers you love. You can't just knock it over, because it would smash the others. So instead, you take it apart carefully, piece by piece, from the top down, like unstacking the blocks one at a time.

That's mostly how real skyscrapers get demolished in crowded cities. Workers don't blow them up, because an explosion in a crowded place would throw dust and chunks everywhere and could hurt people and buildings nearby. Instead, they start at the very top and work their way down, floor by floor.

First, the building gets cleaned out. Workers take out the furniture, windows, wires, pipes, and anything dangerous like asbestos, which is a harmful old insulation material. Then they wrap the building in thick protective screens and nets, a bit like a big blanket, so that dust and falling bits stay put. Sometimes they build a protective roof over the sidewalks and streets below.

Next comes the taking apart. Small machines, like mini bulldozers and mini excavators, get lifted by a giant crane onto the roof. They break up the concrete with tiny hammers and crushers and push the pieces down special holes cut in the floors, where other machines gather them up. Then a floor is removed, the machines get lowered, and the work continues on the next floor down. The building slowly gets shorter and shorter, kind of like a pencil being sharpened.

Some buildings use a clever trick: they're held up by a central column of strong supports, and workers take the building apart from the top using a big frame that holds the machines and slides down as the building shrinks. This keeps everything covered and safe.

Workers also spray lots of water to keep dust down, and put up sound blankets to make the noise quieter for neighbors. They use sensors to check that nearby buildings aren't shaking too much.

It takes much longer than an explosion, often many months, but it's safe. The only time people use explosives is when there's lots of empty space around, so the building can fall neatly without hurting anything.

The name is a little misleading. "Stainless" doesn't mean nothing will ever show up on it. It means the metal won't rust or get eaten away the way regular steel does. The "stain" in the name is about rust, not fingerprints and smudges.

Think of the surface like a super smooth, shiny mirror. When you touch it, your fingers leave behind a tiny bit of oil, like an invisible smear of butter. On a dull or bumpy surface, you'd never notice. But on a smooth, shiny metal, that oil changes how light bounces off it, so every fingerprint shows up like a little drawing. Water does something similar: when a drop dries, it leaves behind the minerals that were in it, and those make chalky spots and streaks.

Stainless steel also has a "grain," tiny lines brushed into it in one direction, like the fur on a dog. If you wipe against those lines, or use a wet rag and let it air dry, you push the oil and water into the grooves and leave streaks that make it look even dirtier.

So your appliances aren't broken or cheap. They're just really good at showing off every touch. To keep them looking nice, wipe with a soft microfiber cloth in the same direction as the lines, use a little warm water with a drop of dish soap or a stainless steel cleaner, and dry it right away. A tiny bit of stainless steel polish or even a drop of mineral oil on a cloth afterward leaves a thin coating that makes new fingerprints harder to see and easier to wipe off. Some newer appliances come with a "fingerprint resistant" coating for exactly this reason, because so many people have the same complaint you do.

In legal and insurance disputes, pain and suffering describes the bodily and emotional hardship a person goes through because of an injury or another harmful event. It may encompass physical discomfort, emotional anguish, and psychological distress, along with the loss of pleasure in life and the inability to take part in hobbies or activities the person once enjoyed. When deciding how much compensation to grant, a court or insurer may weigh several considerations, such as how serious and long-lasting the injury is, the degree of any physical or emotional impairment, and how much the injury has disrupted the person's everyday routine and general well-being. Because pain and suffering is personal and hard to measure, it is typically evaluated individually in each case and may rely on testimony from the injured person, medical professionals, and other witnesses.

A language model is a system that learns the patterns of a language well enough to estimate how likely a given sequence of words, or pieces of words, is. At its core, it answers a simple question: given some text so far, what is the probability of each possible next word or token? By repeatedly predicting the next piece and adding it to the text, a language model can generate sentences, paragraphs, or entire documents. Early language models were statistical, counting how often word sequences appeared in large collections of text. Modern ones are typically neural networks, most often based on the transformer architecture, which can capture long-range context, grammar, facts, and even some reasoning patterns from training on enormous amounts of data.

Language models are used for many tasks, including translation, summarization, answering questions, writing assistance, code generation, and speech recognition. Large language models, often abbreviated LLMs, are simply language models trained on very large datasets with very many parameters, which allows them to perform a wide range of tasks when given instructions in plain language. Although they can produce fluent and useful text, they learn from patterns in their training data rather than from direct experience of the world, so they can make mistakes, state false information confidently, or reflect biases present in that data.

It is always wise to heed your doctor's advice and undergo any medical tests or treatments they consider necessary. A liver function test (LFT) is a blood draw that gauges the amounts of certain substances produced by your liver. These substances, known as liver enzymes, may show up at higher-than-usual concentrations in your blood when the liver is not working as it should. As you noted, raised bilirubin can point to liver injury or illness. Still, elevated bilirubin can also stem from other causes, including some medications or conditions that disrupt how red blood cells are broken down. Because a two-year-old can't legally own and manage shares in his own name in most countries, your dad will usually need to transfer them into some kind of arrangement where an adult controls the shares on your son's behalf until he comes of age. The exact options depend on where you live, so here are the most common approaches in the US and UK, plus some general points.

In the United States, the simplest route is a custodial account under the Uniform Transfers to Minors Act (UTMA) or the older Uniform Gifts to Minors Act (UGMA). Most brokerages offer these. Your dad, or you, would open the account with an adult named as custodian and your son as the beneficial owner, and your dad can then transfer existing shares directly from his brokerage account into the custodial account, usually by an in-kind transfer so nothing has to be sold. The gift is irrevocable, and your son gains full control at the age set by your state, typically 18 or 21. Gifts above the annual gift tax exclusion (about $19,000 per recipient in 2025) require your dad to file a gift tax return, although actual tax is rarely owed because of the large lifetime exemption. Your son also takes on your dad's original cost basis, so if the shares have grown a lot, that embedded gain will eventually be taxed when they're sold. Investment income in the account may be subject to the "kiddie tax" rules above a certain threshold. If your dad wants more control over when and how your son receives the money, a formal trust drafted by an attorney is the alternative, and a 529 plan is worth considering if the goal is education, though that would mean selling the shares and contributing cash.

In the United Kingdom, the common choices are a bare trust or a Junior ISA. With a bare trust, your dad transfers the shares to trustees (often himself or you) to hold for your son, who becomes absolutely entitled at 18. Because the gift comes from a grandparent rather than a parent, the income is taxed as your son's, which can use his personal allowance. For inheritance tax, the gift is a potentially exempt transfer, meaning it falls outside your dad's estate if he survives seven years. Transferring shares also counts as a disposal for capital gains tax purposes, so your dad may owe CGT on any gain since he bought them. A Junior ISA is tax-free but only accepts cash contributions up to an annual limit, so the shares would need to be sold first, and the account must be opened by a parent or guardian.

Regardless of country, it helps to call the brokerage or share registrar holding your dad's shares and ask what forms they need for a gift transfer to a minor's account, and to keep a written record of the date and value of the gift. Given the tax implications, especially around capital gains and estate planning, a short consultation with an accountant or financial adviser before making the transfer is well worth it. Call 911 or your local emergency number right away if you have chest pressure, tightness, or squeezing, especially if it lasts more than a few minutes or comes and goes; shortness of breath; sweating, nausea, or lightheadedness; pain spreading to your jaw, neck, or arm; or unusual fatigue or a sense that something is wrong. Yes, but not as a simple transfer of the same shares. Moving money from a regular (taxable) brokerage account into a Roth IRA is treated as a contribution, not a transfer, and the IRS rules apply. Vanguard allows you to do this in a couple of ways.

The second option is to sell the shares in the taxable account and contribute the cash to the Roth IRA. This is often simpler, though selling may trigger capital gains tax in the taxable account if the shares have appreciated.

Your annual Roth IRA contribution is capped (for 2024 and 2025 the limit is $7,000, or $8,000 if you're 50 or older), and the cap applies to the total of all contributions across your IRAs for the year. Contributions can be made up to the tax filing deadline of the following year.

Atoms are extraordinarily tiny, far smaller than the width of a knife's blade. They are so minute that no human eye could ever make them out. Splitting an atom requires a distinct form of energy called nuclear energy, which dwarfs the energy used when cutting something with a knife and demands specialized equipment to produce. When nuclear energy is used to break an atom apart, the process is known as "nuclear fission." Because fission releases a great deal of energy and can also generate harmful radiation, it is tightly regulated and reserved for particular uses, such as nuclear power plants and certain medical treatments.
