Please see your doctor promptly if you develop black stools, vomiting blood, unexplained weight loss, difficulty or pain when swallowing, persistent vomiting, severe or worsening pain, or fever. Also go back for review if you are not improving after the course, since further testing may be needed. Do not stop or change the medicines on your own, and ask your doctor about the duration of treatment.

I'm sorry you went through that. A kidney stone is painful, and it's understandable to wonder whether the supplement was involved.

I'd strongly advise against going back on OxyElite Pro, at least until you've talked with a doctor. Supplements like this one have been linked to serious harm, including liver injury, and the product was pulled from the market and reformulated after regulators raised safety concerns. Stimulant-type weight loss products can also affect blood pressure, heart rate, and fluid balance, which can contribute to stone formation. The science on whether this particular product causes kidney stones isn't settled, but there's no good reason to take the risk again.

Here's what I'd suggest:

See a doctor, ideally a urologist or your primary care provider, to confirm the stone was passed or treated and to check your kidney function and urine. They can also look at whether you have other stone risk factors, since a first stone is often a sign of something that can be managed.

Tell your doctor exactly what you took, including the brand, the dose, and how long. Keep the bottle or take a photo of the label so the ingredients can be checked.

Report the reaction to the FDA through its MedWatch program (fda.gov/medwatch). Reports like yours help regulators track problems with supplements, which are not tested for safety before they're sold.

In the meantime, drink enough water to keep your urine pale, which is the main way to lower the risk of another stone. Check with your doctor before taking any new supplement, especially one marketed for weight loss or energy.

As a nonresident alien, you may incur capital gains or losses when you sell assets like stocks, bonds, or real estate. If you intend to become a resident alien of the United States, you might be able to recognize these gains or losses before your immigration status changes. The following steps can help you do so.

First, determine whether you have any capital gains or losses by reviewing your investment portfolio and any other assets you hold. Next, speak with a tax professional, such as a certified public accountant or tax attorney, to understand the tax consequences of recognizing these gains or losses. Then, think carefully about when your immigration status will change and how the tax effects of realizing gains or losses could differ depending on the timing. If selling makes financial sense, you can dispose of your assets and recognize any gains or losses before your status changes. Finally, remember that any gains or losses realized before the change must be reported on your tax return for the year they occurred.

It is worth noting that nonresident aliens and resident aliens are taxed differently on capital gains and losses. For this reason, you should weigh the potential tax consequences of realizing gains or losses before you become a resident alien. Consulting a tax professional is also a good idea to make sure you comply with all applicable tax laws and regulations.

Basically, a life insurance policy is a contract. You pay the insurer a premium, and when the insured person dies, the insurer pays a set amount to whoever you named as the beneficiary. That's the deal.

There are a few main kinds. Term life covers you for a set stretch, like 10, 20, or 30 years. It's usually the cheapest option because it doesn't build any cash value, so you're just paying for the coverage itself.

Whole life, which people also call permanent life insurance, sticks with you for your whole life. It usually comes with a savings piece that builds cash value over time. That's why the premiums run higher than term, since you're paying for that savings part too.

Then there's universal life, which is also permanent but a lot more flexible. You can pay higher or lower premiums depending on what's going on, and you can bump the death benefit up or down within certain limits.

When you're picking a policy, think about what you and your family actually need money-wise, and what your goals are. Look at your budget and what the policy will cost you. Check out the company too, meaning its reputation and how financially solid it is. It also helps to talk to a financial advisor or an insurance agent so you land on the right type and amount of coverage for your situation.

Known as Comet 1P/Halley, Halley's comet is a periodic comet that passes through the inner solar system roughly every 76 years. Its most recent visit to our skies took place in 1986, and it is anticipated to appear again around 2061. When it returns depends on several considerations, such as the shape of its orbit and the gravitational pull exerted by the planets and other objects in the solar system. Pinning down the precise date of its next arrival is hard to do with high accuracy, though observers generally expect it to become visible from Earth again in 2061.

Peter Dayan is a British-born computational neuroscientist and theoretical neuroscientist, best known for his work applying mathematical and computational methods to understand how the brain learns, decides, and represents information. He is a director of the Max Planck Institute for Biological Cybernetics in Tübingen, Germany, and he has held a professorship at the University of Tübingen. He previously spent many years at University College London, where he founded and led the Gatsby Computational Neuroscience Unit.

His research centers on reinforcement learning, the process by which animals and artificial agents learn from rewards and punishments to choose actions. Together with collaborators, he has shown how signals in the brain, particularly those involving dopamine, may correspond to prediction errors used in learning algorithms. He has also worked on Bayesian approaches to perception and decision-making, on how uncertainty is represented in neural circuits, and on the roles of neuromodulators such as serotonin and acetylcholine.

Dayan is widely cited for his textbook "Theoretical Neuroscience," co-written with L. F. Abbott, which is a standard reference in the field. He has also co-authored influential work on the Helmholtz machine and other models of unsupervised learning. His contributions have made him one of the prominent figures bridging neuroscience, psychology, and machine learning.

Yes, in some cases a mortgage can be used to cover outstanding debts, though it depends on the type of mortgage, the lender, and your circumstances. The most common approach is a remortgage or cash-out refinance, where you borrow more than you currently owe on your home and use the extra funds to pay off credit cards, personal loans, car finance, or other debts. Some people also take a further advance or second charge mortgage on a property they already own for this purpose. Lenders generally look at whether the consolidation makes sense, so they will assess your income, your existing mortgage balance, how much equity you have, and whether you can afford the higher monthly repayments over the full term.

There are important trade-offs to keep in mind. Unsecured debts like credit cards are turned into debt secured against your home, which means that if you struggle to keep up with payments, you could risk losing your property. Stretching short-term debts over a 20 or 25 year mortgage can also mean paying much more interest overall, even if the monthly payment is lower. Lenders may also charge arrangement fees, valuation fees, or early repayment charges on your existing mortgage, which can reduce the savings.

If you are considering this, it is worth speaking with an independent mortgage broker or a free debt advice service such as StepChange, National Debtline, or Citizens Advice in the UK, or the equivalent in your country. They can compare whether consolidation actually saves you money compared with other options, such as a debt management plan or a personal loan.

Futures studies, also called futurology or foresight, is the interdisciplinary field that systematically explores possible, probable, and preferable futures. Rather than trying to predict exactly what will happen, practitioners aim to understand the forces shaping change, map out a range of plausible alternatives, and help individuals, organizations, and governments make better decisions in the present. The field draws on sociology, economics, political science, technology studies, environmental science, and other disciplines, combining quantitative data with qualitative insight.

Much of the work in futures studies rests on the recognition that the future is not a single, fixed path but a set of possibilities that depend on choices, events, and trends. Practitioners often distinguish between possible futures (anything that could conceivably happen), probable futures (what is likely given current trends), and preferable futures (what a society or group wants to achieve). This framing encourages people to ask not only "what will happen?" but also "what do we want to happen, and what must we do to get there?"

Common methods include trend analysis, which tracks social, technological, economic, environmental, and political developments; scenario planning, which builds several coherent stories about how the future might unfold; horizon scanning, which looks for weak signals of emerging change; Delphi surveys, which gather structured expert opinion; and backcasting, which starts from a desired future and works backward to identify the steps needed to reach it. Some futurists also use simulation models and systems mapping to understand how different parts of a complex system interact.

The field gained institutional form in the mid-twentieth century, with early work at think tanks such as the RAND Corporation and the emergence of organizations like the World Futures Studies Federation. Today futures thinking is applied in corporate strategy, government policy, urban planning, defense, public health, and climate adaptation. Its value lies less in accurate forecasting, which is notoriously difficult, than in improving preparedness, widening the range of options considered, and surfacing assumptions that might otherwise go unexamined.

Soy foods come from soybeans, a legume that originated in East Asia. Because soybeans contain a high amount of protein, they serve as the base for many products such as tofu, soy milk, and tempeh. Production begins with harvesting the beans, followed by cleaning and hulling them to strip away the outer covering. Next, the beans are soaked and ground into a paste, which is turned into soy milk. That milk is then filtered and pressed to separate out the soybean solids, leaving a liquid that can be used to create other soy-based foods. These products are a widely enjoyed source of plant-based protein, appearing in cuisines across the globe, and they are a frequent component of vegetarian and vegan meals.

Lymph nodes are small, bean-shaped glands that form part of the immune system, and they are found all over the body, the armpits included. They may swell when the body is dealing with an infection, inflammation, or some other condition. A mild amount of swelling and tenderness in the armpit nodes is often a normal reaction to a minor illness like a cold or the flu. Swelling that lingers, becomes large, or comes with other symptoms, though, could point to something more serious. You should watch for any change in the size or feel of your lymph nodes and speak with a healthcare provider if you are worried. A provider can examine the nodes and work out why they are swollen, and they might suggest additional tests such as blood work or imaging to pinpoint the cause. If you find a lump in your armpit that doesn't seem to be a swollen lymph node, you should also have a provider look at it. Armpit lumps can result from many things, including cysts, abscesses, and even breast cancer. A provider can identify what is causing the lump and advise you on the right treatment.

The light-independent reactions, also called the Calvin cycle, don't stop simply because light is gone, but they do slow down. These reactions don't directly use light energy. Instead, they run on the ATP and NADPH produced by the light-dependent reactions, which are the steps that actually capture light. Once the light-dependent reactions stop, the supply of ATP and NADPH dwindles, so the Calvin cycle gradually loses its energy and reducing power and eventually winds down. In the stroma of the chloroplast, the enzyme RuBisCO continues to fix carbon dioxide into intermediates for a short time, but without fresh ATP and NADPH those intermediates cannot be converted into sugars, and the cycle halts once its existing supplies are used up.

Raytheon Company is a leading technology and innovation firm focused on defense, civil government, and cybersecurity solutions. Established in 1922, it has its headquarters in Waltham, Massachusetts, in the United States. The business supplies goods and services to several sectors, such as aerospace, defense, and government agencies. It is recognized for creating a wide array of cutting-edge technologies, among them radar systems, missiles, and cybersecurity tools. With operations spanning many nations worldwide, Raytheon places considerable emphasis on research and development as a means of advancing its products and services.

Yes, a star can exist outside of any galaxy. A galaxy is a vast collection of stars, gas, and dust bound together by gravity. Galaxies come in many varieties, though most contain millions or even billions of stars. Not every star, however, belongs to a galaxy. Some are "free-floating," meaning they are not tied to any particular galaxy and drift through space by themselves. These loners tend to be smaller and less massive than stars inside galaxies, and they are much harder to detect, since they lie so far away and lack the bright galactic backdrop that would make them stand out. In short, a star can exist beyond a galaxy, but this is uncommon, and such stars are generally difficult to find for those same reasons: their great distance and the absence of a bright galaxy behind them.

Automated medical diagnosis refers to the use of computer systems, algorithms, and software to help identify diseases or medical conditions from patient data with little or no direct human reasoning at the moment of analysis. The data involved can include symptoms reported by a patient, laboratory results, vital signs, medical images such as X-rays, CT scans, and retinal photographs, electrocardiograms, genetic information, and the contents of electronic health records. The system processes these inputs and produces an output, which might be a likely diagnosis, a ranked list of possible conditions, a risk score, or a flag that something abnormal has been detected.

The idea has a long history. Early systems in the 1970s and 1980s, such as MYCIN, which suggested treatments for bacterial infections, were rule-based expert systems. Specialists encoded their knowledge as if-then rules, and the software applied those rules to a patient's findings. These systems worked in narrow domains but were hard to maintain and did not cope well with uncertainty. Later approaches used probabilistic methods such as Bayesian networks, which weigh the likelihood of different conditions given the evidence.

Most current work relies on machine learning, especially deep learning. Instead of being given explicit rules, a model is trained on large collections of labeled examples, for instance thousands of skin lesion photographs tagged as benign or malignant, and it learns statistical patterns that distinguish them. Image-based fields such as radiology, pathology, dermatology, and ophthalmology have seen particularly strong results, with some systems matching specialists on specific tasks like detecting diabetic retinopathy or spotting lung nodules. Natural language models are also being explored to interpret clinical notes and to conduct symptom-checking conversations.

The benefits are potentially significant. Automated tools can offer consistency, work quickly, and extend expertise to places with few specialists. They can screen large populations, prioritize urgent cases for human review, and catch subtle findings that a tired clinician might miss. They may also reduce costs and waiting times.

There are real limitations and risks, however. Models are only as good as their training data, so if that data underrepresents certain groups, the system may perform worse for them, leading to bias. A model trained at one hospital may fail when used with different equipment or patient populations. Many deep learning systems are hard to interpret, which makes it difficult for clinicians to trust or check their reasoning. Errors can have serious consequences, raising questions about accountability and liability. Privacy of sensitive health data is another concern, as is the danger of over-reliance, where clinicians defer to the machine even when it is wrong.

For these reasons, most systems are deployed as decision support rather than as autonomous diagnosticians, with a clinician reviewing the output and making the final call. Regulators such as the US FDA and European authorities treat many of these tools as medical devices requiring evidence of safety and effectiveness. The general consensus is that automated diagnosis works best as a partner to human professionals, combining the speed and pattern recognition of software with the judgment, context, and ethical responsibility of doctors.

Vaccines generally include one or more of the following elements. Antigens are parts of the disease-causing agent, whether a virus or a bacterium, that prompt the immune system to make antibodies. These are typically either a deactivated or killed version of the pathogen, or a fragment of its genetic material such as DNA or RNA. Adjuvants are ingredients added to certain vaccines to strengthen the immune reaction they trigger. They can boost the output of antibodies and other immune cells, making the vaccine more effective. Preservatives are included in some vaccines to stop bacteria or fungi from growing, since such contamination could compromise the product. Stabilizers help maintain the vaccine's integrity so it does not degrade or lose potency over time. Excipients are inactive substances that give the vaccine an appropriate consistency, pH, or other physical or chemical characteristics. They can include salts, sugars, or oils, and serve to improve stability, shelf life, and ease of handling. To sum up, the antigen is the central component, since it is what drives the immune system to produce protective antibodies. Adjuvants, preservatives, stabilizers, and excipients are supplementary components that may be added to improve either the vaccine's effectiveness or its handling and storage.

So you're a non-resident alien with some stocks, bonds, or property that have gained or lost value, and you're planning to become a resident alien in the US. Can you cash those in before the switch? Often yes, and the timing can matter a lot. Here's how I'd think about it.

First, go through what you actually hold and figure out which pieces are sitting on gains and which are sitting on losses. Then talk to a tax pro, like a CPA or a tax attorney who handles cross-border stuff. They can tell you how the rules change once your status flips, since non-resident and resident aliens get taxed differently on capital gains, and that gap can be big.

Timing is the real question. Think about when your status changes and whether selling before or after that point makes more sense. Sometimes waiting saves you money, sometimes getting out early does.

If selling makes sense for you, go ahead and sell, but only if the numbers actually work out. Don't sell just because you think you should.

Whatever you realize before the change, you'll need to report it on the tax return for that year. Keep good records of purchase prices, sale dates, and amounts, because you'll need them.

Bottom line: the rules are different on each side of that status change, so run the numbers before you pull the trigger, and have a pro double-check that you're following everything correctly.

I understand the worry, especially when her classmates look taller. Still, a height comparison with other children in her class isn't a reliable measure. Children of the same age can differ in height by several inches, and a child who is shorter for a while may simply be a late bloomer or may end up at a perfectly normal adult height. Since your doctor measured her and said she is within the expected range for her age, that is the most useful reference point.

There is no safe medicine or supplement that makes a healthy child grow faster or taller than her genetics allow. Growth hormone and similar treatments exist, but doctors prescribe them only for specific medical conditions, such as confirmed growth hormone deficiency or certain bone or genetic disorders, and they require blood tests, imaging, and specialist supervision. Giving a child a growth product without that evaluation can be harmful. Over-the-counter height supplements, "growth boosters," and similar products generally have no proven benefit and can be unsafe.

Good nutrition, sleep, physical activity, and regular health checkups are what support healthy growth. Make sure she eats a varied diet with enough protein, calcium, vitamin D, and iron, gets plenty of sleep (usually 9 to 11 hours at her age), and stays active through play and sports. Avoid letting her skip meals, since poor nutrition can slow growth.

To put your mind at ease, you can ask your doctor a few specific questions: What were her height and growth percentiles over time? Is her growth rate steady, or has it slowed? Does anyone in the family have a history of late growth or a similar adult height? If her growth curve has been steady and she is following her own path, that is usually reassuring. If it has dropped off or the doctor has any concern, they can refer you to a pediatric endocrinologist, who can check whether a medical cause exists. Bringing a record of her measurements to that conversation will help.

Selling off some stores can raise a company's value for several interrelated reasons. The most common is that the stores being sold may be underperforming, losing money, or tying up capital without generating adequate returns. Shedding them removes those drags on profits and frees up cash that can be used more productively, such as paying down debt, funding growth in stronger locations, or returning money to shareholders. Investors often value a company based on its earnings and cash flow, so eliminating unprofitable units can lift the overall margins and make the remaining business look healthier.

There is also a focus argument. A company spread across many locations, some of which perform poorly, may have management attention and resources diluted. Concentrating on the most successful stores or brands can allow the company to execute better, improve operations, and make smarter decisions about where to invest. Markets sometimes reward this clarity with a higher valuation, since the business becomes easier to understand and predict.

Finally, the sale itself can generate a sizable one-time payment, and the price buyers pay may reflect what the stores are worth to them, which can sometimes exceed their value inside the parent company. If a sale brings in more than the stores contributed to the company's earnings, the transaction creates value directly. Reduced debt also lowers financial risk, which can make the company's shares more attractive to investors.

Weight matters a lot in boxing and MMA. A bigger fighter usually brings more power and strength, while a smaller one tends to be quicker and more agile. That's why weight classes exist: they keep matchups fair. If one guy is way bigger than his opponent, the fight can turn into a mismatch that's no fun to watch. Splitting fighters into classes gets them closer in size and ability, which usually means better, tighter fights. Even 10 pounds can make a difference. The smaller guy might be faster, but the heavier one can hit harder. Still, size isn't everything. A smaller fighter with sharp technique or solid defense can absolutely win. Take Manny Pacquiao, who stood 5'7" and fought around 150 pounds. Sure, he'd have a rough time against a 6'5", 300-pound giant, at least on paper. But he's built a huge career beating guys bigger than him, so it's not like he'd be hopeless.

Bottom line: if your name is the one on the loan, you're on the hook for the whole thing, even if you're not the one driving the car. Doesn't matter that someone else has been using it. The lender only cares that you signed.

And if the payments stop, they can repossess the car. That's just how it works.

So if you haven't driven it in two years and you can't keep up with the payments, I'd look at your options pretty soon. You could sell the car and pay off the loan with what you get. Or you could call the lender and see if they'll work something out with you, like a different payment plan. Lenders are sometimes more flexible than people expect, especially if you reach out before you've missed a bunch of payments.

It might also be worth talking to a credit counselor or a financial planner. They can look at your whole situation and help you figure out what makes sense, which is a lot easier than trying to sort it all out on your own.

Hi Prakash, I understand how frustrating this can be. Fairness creams usually don't help because they aren't designed to treat marks or scars. The right treatment depends on what kind of marks you have, so it helps to know the difference.

There are two main types. The first is dark or reddish flat spots left after pimples or cuts heal, called post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation. These are not true scars, and they often fade on their own over months, faster with the right products. The second is true scars, which are dents or pits (atrophic scars, common after acne) or raised, thickened marks (hypertrophic scars or keloids, sometimes seen after cuts). Creams alone rarely fix true scars, and they usually need procedures done by a dermatologist.

For dark marks, several over-the-counter ingredients have good evidence. Niacinamide (around 4 to 5 percent), vitamin C serum, azelaic acid (10 to 20 percent), and alpha arbutin can lighten pigmentation over 8 to 12 weeks of regular use. Adapalene gel (0.1 percent), available at most pharmacies in India, also helps fade marks, improves skin texture, and prevents new acne, which matters because new pimples keep creating new marks. Start adapalene slowly, two or three nights a week, apply a thin layer to dry skin, and use a moisturizer, since it can cause dryness and irritation at first.

Sunscreen is the most important step. Sun exposure darkens marks and makes them last much longer, so use a broad-spectrum sunscreen of SPF 30 or higher every morning, even on cloudy days, and reapply if you are outdoors for long. Many people find their marks fade noticeably just from consistent sunscreen use.

Avoid picking or squeezing pimples, since this causes most acne marks and scars. Also avoid harsh scrubs, lemon juice, toothpaste, or steroid creams sold as fairness products. Steroid creams in particular can damage your skin over time.

If your marks are pitted or raised, or if they don't improve after about three months of this routine, see a dermatologist. They can offer treatments such as chemical peels, microneedling, laser resurfacing, subcision for deep acne scars, or injections for raised scars. These are much more effective for true scars than anything you can buy over the counter. If you still get active acne, a dermatologist can also prescribe stronger medicines to control it, which is the foundation of preventing new marks.

A simple routine to start with would be a gentle face wash, niacinamide or vitamin C serum, moisturizer, and sunscreen in the morning, then a gentle face wash, adapalene a few nights a week, and moisturizer at night. Be patient and consistent, since skin takes time to heal and results usually show after two to three months.

Okay so the rule of nines is basically a quick way to guess how much of your body surface area got burned. Doctors and paramedics use it mostly in emergencies, like after a fire or a bad accident, when they need a number fast. The idea is that the body gets split into chunks worth about 9% each. Head and neck is 9%, each arm is 9%, the front of the chest is 9%, the back is 9%, the stomach is 9%, and each leg is 18% since there are two of them. So the provider looks at each area, figures out how much of it is burned, and gives it a percentage. If the whole front of the chest is burned, that's 9%. Then they just add everything up to get a total. It's not super precise, honestly, just a rough guide when things are chaotic. For more detailed work, people use the Lund and Browder chart, which is way more accurate.

I'm sorry you and your family are dealing with this. I'll try to give you a realistic picture, though I can't examine your uncle, and the specifics depend on details his team will know, like the exact tumour type and his overall health.

A stomach or gastroesophageal junction cancer that has spread to the liver and lungs is stage IV, which is metastatic disease. At this stage the cancer is generally not curable, so treatment aims to control it, extend life, and keep him comfortable. Without treatment, survival is typically measured in a few months. With chemotherapy, median survival for metastatic stomach or esophageal cancer is usually somewhere around 8 to 14 months, with a wide range. Some people live considerably longer, especially if the tumour has a targetable feature such as HER2 positivity, high PD-L1 expression, or microsatellite instability, which allow targeted drugs or immunotherapy to be added and can improve outcomes. Others do worse, particularly if they are frail or already losing weight. These are averages, not predictions for one person, but they are the honest ballpark. It is reasonable to ask his oncologist directly: "What is the typical range for someone in his situation, and what would you expect for him?" Many doctors will answer if asked plainly.

On remedies, there is no cure available through diet, supplements, or alternative therapies, and I'd be wary of anyone who claims otherwise. What can help is the following.

Swallowing difficulty is the most urgent and treatable problem. Options include an esophageal stent to hold the passage open, radiotherapy to the tumour, or sometimes a feeding tube. Chemotherapy itself can also shrink the tumour and ease swallowing. A dietitian can advise on soft or liquid foods and high-calorie supplements.

The regular coughing of phlegm matters because it may mean food or saliva is going into the airway (aspiration), or that the tumour is pressing on or connected to the airway, or that lung metastases are involved. Aspiration can cause pneumonia, so tell his team about this promptly. A swallowing assessment by a speech therapist can help. If he develops fever, breathlessness, or coughing during or after eating, he should be seen urgently.

Tests that guide treatment include biopsy results with HER2, PD-L1, and MSI status. If these haven't been done, ask about them.

Palliative care is worth requesting early. It is not the same as end-of-life care and can run alongside chemotherapy. These teams are skilled at managing pain, nausea, appetite, breathlessness, and at helping families plan and cope. Studies show that early palliative care improves quality of life and sometimes survival.

Useful questions for his doctors: What exactly is the tumour type and where does it originate? What are the treatment goals? What are the realistic benefits and side effects of chemotherapy for him? What should we do about the swallowing and cough now? Who do we call out of hours?

If it would help, I can suggest ways to prepare for his next appointment or things to ask about managing the swallowing in the meantime.

Turkey lies in the eastern part of the Mediterranean region and shares its borders with eight nations. Bulgaria lies to its northwest and Greece to its west, while Georgia borders it to the northeast. To the east are Armenia, Azerbaijan, and Iran, and to the southeast are Iraq and Syria. The country occupies the Anatolian Peninsula and spans two continents: a small section falls within Europe, while most of its land is in Asia. Ankara serves as the capital, although Istanbul is the most populous city. Turkey holds membership in the United Nations, NATO, and the Council of Europe.

It's generally considered safe to take soy isoflavones with metformin, but you should still run it by your doctor before adding any new supplement, especially if you're trying to conceive or take other meds. Isoflavones are plant compounds that act a bit like estrogen. You'll find them in soybeans and other legumes, and they're also sold as supplements. Some studies suggest they might help regulate periods and improve fertility in women with PCOS, which is a common cause of fertility trouble. The evidence isn't strong yet, though, and more research is needed before anyone can say for sure.

Metformin is mostly used for type 2 diabetes and PCOS. It cuts down the sugar your liver makes and helps your muscles respond better to insulin, which brings blood sugar down. It's considered safe and effective for those uses, but you need to take it at the dose and schedule your provider gave you. Honestly, any change to your meds or supplements is worth a quick chat with your provider first. They can help you weigh the risks and benefits for your own situation.

If you opened a certificate of deposit (CD) account and later discover you need the money before the CD's term ends, you have several choices. One is to wait: if your circumstances allow, you can leave the money in place until the CD matures and then withdraw it. CD terms generally run from a few months to several years, so this won't work well if you need the funds urgently. Another is an early withdrawal: many banks let you take money out of a CD before maturity, but this usually triggers a penalty, typically calculated as a percentage of the principal. The size of the penalty can depend on the length of the term and the bank's policies, and taking an early withdrawal may lower your overall return. You might also sell the CD to another investor before it matures, if your bank or brokerage permits it. The catch is that you may not get the full value, since a buyer will generally pay less than face value to collect the remaining interest. Finally, some banks allow you to "break" the CD, meaning you close the account and receive the remaining balance after subtracting any applicable fees or penalties. Before deciding, carefully review your CD's terms and the likely consequences of each option, and consider speaking with a financial advisor or your bank to find the best course of action.

Okay so laser thermometers don't actually work the way the name makes it sound. The laser isn't really measuring the temperature by itself. It's just pointing at the spot you want to check, kind of like a sight. The real work is done by an infrared sensor inside, which picks up the heat radiating off whatever you're aiming at. The thermometer reads that heat and converts it into a temperature number. Pretty neat that it can do this without touching anything! That's why they're handy for stuff that's too hot, too cold, or just not safe to poke at. So the basic steps go like this: you point the laser at the spot, the sensor catches the infrared energy coming off the surface, the thermometer turns that into a reading, and the number pops up on the screen. They're pretty accurate for what they're meant for, and you can check temps from a distance, which is why people use them for everything from cooking to HVAC work.

If several asteroids composed entirely of solid gold were to strike Earth, the global economy would likely feel a major effect. Gold's worth rests largely on how scarce it is, so a sudden surge in supply would probably drive its value down. Gold-backed investments like bars and coins would likely lose value as a result. The arrival of so much gold could also bring on inflation, a general rise in the prices of goods and services, because a larger gold supply in circulation may translate into more money in the economy, pushing prices upward. In short, such a dramatic expansion of gold supply would produce a tangled mix of consequences, with both beneficial and harmful effects on the world economy.

This content may violate our content policy, so if you think that's a mistake, send in feedback and it'll help the team look into it. Anyway, here's the bit about elk. They're also called wapiti, and they're big deer-family animals. Most elk mate in the fall during the rut, which usually runs from late September to early November depending on where they live. The males go all out during this stretch, bugling, strutting, and sparring with each other to show who's boss. Females only stay receptive for a short window, and a single female might mate with more than one male in that time. Calves usually show up the next spring, one per female. How often elk breed can shift a lot based on how healthy and old the animals are, and whether there's enough food around.

First-order logic, sometimes called first-order predicate calculus, is a formal system for expressing and reasoning about statements involving variables, predicates, and logical connectives. The name "first-order" reflects the fact that quantification is permitted over individual variables but not over predicates or functions. Formulas in this system are assembled from atomic components, namely constants, variables, or predicates applied to variables. These components are joined together using connectives such as "and," "or," "not," and "if-then," while the quantifiers "for all" and "there exists" make it possible to state general claims about variables. Because it can capture a broad range of ideas, first-order logic is a highly versatile instrument and is commonly applied in mathematics, computer science, and artificial intelligence. It also serves as the foundation for numerous other logical systems, including higher-order and modal logics.
