The Jacquard loom is a weaving machine invented by the French inventor Joseph Marie Jacquard, whose design was presented in 1804 and became a landmark in both textile manufacturing and the history of computing. Its key innovation was the use of punched cards to control the pattern produced by the loom. Before this, complex woven designs such as brocades and damasks required a skilled weaver and an assistant to manually select which threads were lifted at each step, a slow and expensive process. The Jacquard mechanism automated this selection: each punched card corresponded to one row of the pattern, with holes indicating which hooks or threads should be raised, and a chain of cards linked together could direct the loom through an entire design. Changing the pattern meant simply changing the cards, which made intricate fabrics far faster and cheaper to produce.

The idea of using punched cards to store instructions had a lasting influence. Charles Babbage admired the Jacquard principle and considered it when planning his Analytical Engine, and the concept of programmable control through punched media later shaped early computing, including the work of Herman Hollerith on tabulating machines. Today the term "Jacquard" is also used for a type of intricately patterned fabric, and the Jacquard attachment remains a recognized component in textile machinery.

Sure thing! Gears on a bike make pedaling easier or harder depending on what you're riding over. The shifters on the handlebars control them. On the right one, the indicators usually run from 1 to 7, and on the left, they usually go from 1 to 3. Going up a hill and the pedals feel like they're fighting you? Shift to a lower number on the right and a higher number on the left. That makes things easier. For a harder push, go the other way: higher on the right, lower on the left.

Here's how it works in practice. On a hill, you'd hit the right shifter to drop the chain onto a smaller cog on the back wheel, and at the same time hit the left shifter to move it onto a larger chainring up front. The chain pulls on a bigger cog, so the pedals turn more slowly and you're not grinding away. On flat ground when you want more speed, you go the opposite way. Use the right shifter to move up to a larger cog and the left to drop to a smaller chainring. It's harder to pedal, sure, but the bike goes faster since the pedals are spinning quicker.

Just try to shift smoothly and don't yank the pedals or the bars while you do it. It feels clunky at first, but you'll get the hang of it pretty quick.

Malware, viruses, and trojans are all nasty software that hackers tend to create and spread. A hacker is basically someone who uses computers and the internet to get into other people's systems without permission, usually to cause trouble or steal stuff. They've got plenty of ways to get their malware out there. They might send it as an email attachment, or hide it on a website you'd never think twice about visiting. Once it's on your machine, the hacker can dig through your files, grab your personal info, or just wreck things. McAfee makes software that tries to keep malware off your computer, and so do plenty of other security companies. But those companies aren't the ones writing and spreading the bad stuff in the first place.

A complex number is made up of two parts: a real number and an imaginary number. A real number is one you can measure or count, such as 3 or 10. An imaginary number, as the passage describes it, is one you can't measure because it is too large or too small, infinity being an example. Put a real number and an imaginary number together and the result is a complex number. These numbers are useful in many real-world settings. Engineers and scientists rely on them to tackle problems in areas such as electrical engineering and physics, where they help explain how electric current moves through circuits and how waves travel through space. Computer graphics also makes use of complex numbers to produce the images you see on a screen. They can even help researchers work out how certain diseases spread and how to halt them. In short, complex numbers let us understand and solve real-world problems that would be out of reach without them. You can think of them as a special tool for making sense of things that are otherwise very difficult to grasp.

So the universal law of gravitation is basically Newton's way of describing the pull between any two objects. The force gets bigger the more massive the objects are (it's proportional to the product of their masses), and it drops off fast as they get farther apart, specifically with the square of the distance between them.

Written as a formula, it's F = G * (m1 * m2) / r^2. Here F is the gravitational force between the two objects, and m1 and m2 are their masses. r is the distance between them. G is the gravitational constant, which scientists had to figure out through experiments. It comes out to roughly 6.674 x 10^-11 N·m^2/kg^2.

Newton first put this together in 1687, and it's still a core piece of how we study gravity and the motion of planets and other celestial stuff today.

Font size is usually measured in points, and one point is 1/72 of an inch. So a 12 point font is 12/72 of an inch tall, which works out to about a sixth of an inch. 12 is the standard size for most documents, mostly because it's a nice middle ground. It's small enough that you can fit a decent amount of text on a page, but big enough that it's easy on the eyes.

Here's the catch, though: two fonts that are both "12 point" won't necessarily look the same size. Every typeface is designed differently. Some have wider or narrower letters, some have taller lowercase letters, and some have more space between the lines. So a 12 point font in one typeface can look noticeably bigger or smaller than a 12 point font in another one.

Honestly, if you've got hepatitis C or any kind of liver disease, most doctors will tell you to skip the alcohol. It inflames the liver and can cause scarring, and that just makes whatever damage is already there worse. So quitting is probably going to help your liver, and there's a decent chance your enzyme levels will come down too.

That said, alcohol isn't the only thing that moves those numbers. How advanced your liver disease is matters, and so can other health problems you might have. So don't assume that cutting out drinking will fix everything on its own. Your best bet is to stick with what your doctor tells you and work with them on managing the hep C and anything else going on.

I'm pretty sure a googol is 1 followed by 100 zeros, so 10^100. People use it when they need a way to talk about really huge numbers, like the atoms in the observable universe or the combinations on a lock with 100 digits. In math it's written as 10^100, and some folks abbreviate it as "G." Say you wanted to express the atoms in the observable universe, which is estimated to be around 10^80, in googols: that works out to 1.0 x 10^-20 G, since 10^80 is a tiny fraction of 10^100. Same idea for a 100-digit lock with 10 options per digit: that's exactly 1 x 10^100 combinations, or 1 googol. Also, the googol isn't an official unit of measurement, and you won't see it in scientific work. It's mostly just a handy way to make giant numbers easier to wrap your head around.

Automated reasoning is basically getting a computer to draw its own conclusions from a pile of statements or axioms you give it. It's a branch of AI and computer science, and it's all about building algorithms that can think logically and make decisions based on what they already know. People use it for theorem proving, diagnosis, planning, and even natural language processing. You'll see it in math, engineering, and AI work, mostly for jobs that would take a person forever or just wouldn't be practical by hand. There are a bunch of approaches: rule-based systems, resolution-based systems, model-based systems, and hybrids that mix them. They can run on different logic setups like propositional logic, first-order logic, or higher-order logics to represent and reason about stuff. So yeah, it's a computer reasoning logically from known facts, and it's a pretty handy tool for hard problems that would be a nightmare to do manually.

The visual cortex is the part of your brain that handles visual information. It sits in the occipital lobe, right at the back of your head. Its job is to take what your eyes pick up and turn it into a coherent picture of the world. It's split into several areas, and each one handles a different piece of the job. Some areas pull apart the basics like color, shape, and contrast, while others stitch together info from different parts of your field of view and build a 3D sense of what's around you. Everything starts with the retina, the light-sensitive tissue at the back of your eye. Light hits it, gets converted into signals, and those travel to the brain through the optic nerve. The visual cortex then processes that input and passes signals along to other regions, which is how you actually end up seeing and making sense of stuff.

Yes, you can conceive while taking these medicines, and becoming pregnant during treatment is not considered harmful to the baby. Rcinex 600 contains rifampicin and isoniazid, two first-line anti-tubercular drugs. Both have been used in pregnant women for many decades, and international guidelines from the WHO and the CDC consider them safe to continue during pregnancy. They have not been shown to cause birth defects. An unplanned pregnancy during this treatment is therefore not a reason for worry or termination, and you should never stop your TB medicines on your own because you have become pregnant, since incomplete treatment is a far greater risk to both you and the baby.

That said, because you have only about two months of treatment left, the more comfortable option, if you are able to wait, is to finish the course first and then try to conceive. This lets you start pregnancy with the infection fully treated. It also avoids a small added concern: liver side effects of isoniazid and rifampicin are somewhat more common during pregnancy and just after delivery, so your liver function would need closer monitoring.

If you do conceive during treatment, a few precautions are important. Isoniazid can deplete vitamin B6, so pregnant women on it should take pyridoxine (vitamin B6) daily, usually 10 to 25 mg. Ask your doctor about this if you are not already taking it. You should also start folic acid now, ideally before conception, as all women planning pregnancy should. If rifampicin is still being taken near delivery, doctors usually give vitamin K to the newborn, and sometimes to the mother in late pregnancy, to prevent bleeding problems. Please inform your physician and your gynecologist as soon as you know you are pregnant so they can monitor you together.

Rifampicin significantly reduces the effectiveness of hormonal contraceptives such as birth control pills, patches, and some implants. If you decide to wait the two months, use a non-hormonal method such as condoms or a copper IUD during treatment and for a few weeks afterward.

Tuberculosis in the abdomen sometimes also involves the fallopian tubes or the lining of the uterus, which can affect fertility. If you have trouble conceiving after a reasonable period of trying, typically six months to a year at your age, ask your gynecologist about checking your tubes and pelvic organs.

Breastfeeding is also safe while taking these medicines, should treatment overlap with that time. Please discuss your plans with your treating physician, who knows your full history and can tailor this advice to you.

Thank you for sharing this. At 17, weighing 41 kg with visible hip bones is a real concern, and it deserves a proper medical check rather than only diet tips. Being thin since childhood can be part of your build, but when someone cannot gain weight despite eating, and exercise makes them lose more, a doctor should look for the cause. Possible reasons include thyroid problems, malabsorption conditions such as celiac disease, diabetes, digestive disorders, anemia, or hormonal changes. Some of these are easy to test for and treat.

Please book an appointment with your doctor soon. Ask for a basic check-up with blood tests, and tell them exactly what you eat in a typical day, how much you exercise, and how long this has been happening. Be fully honest about your eating habits, including any anxiety about food, weight, or body shape, because that information helps them find the right cause. If you can, ask for a referral to a dietitian, who can build a high-calorie plan that suits you.

While you wait for the appointment, try to eat three regular meals plus two or three snacks, even when you are not hungry. Choose calorie-dense foods such as nuts, nut butters, whole milk or yogurt, eggs, cheese, avocado, oats, rice, potatoes, lentils, and healthy oils added to your cooking. Drinking some of your calories, such as milk shakes or smoothies, can help if solid food feels hard to finish. For now, keep exercise light, such as walking or gentle stretching, rather than intense workouts, since your body seems to be using up what you take in.

Seek medical help promptly if you feel dizzy or faint, notice your periods have stopped or become irregular, feel unusually weak or cold, have chest pain or a racing heartbeat, or if your weight keeps dropping.

Finally, if you find that you feel distressed about eating or gaining weight, or that you avoid food or feel strong fear of getting fat, please mention this to your doctor as well. These feelings are common and treatable, and you do not have to manage them alone.

The highest point on Oahu is Mount Ka'ala, which rises about 4,003 feet (1,220 meters) above sea level. It sits in the Wai'anae Range on the western side of the island. The summit is a relatively flat, boggy plateau, and it is often shrouded in clouds and mist, which helps support unique native plant communities.

Hikers can reach the area via the Wai'anae Kai or Kaʻena side routes, though the main road to the top, which leads to an FAA radar installation (a large white dome visible from much of the west side), is closed to the public. Because the terrain is steep, muddy, and frequently slippery, it's a demanding trek.

The highest point in the Ko'olau Range, on the island's eastern side, is Pu'u Konahuanui, at about 3,150 feet (960 meters), which is a popular but difficult hike above the Nu'uanu and Ko'olau Valley area.

Simulated annealing is a heuristic for finding the global minimum or maximum of a function, and it's named after the metallurgy process where you heat metal up and then cool it slowly to make it purer and stronger. The idea is that you start with a random solution and keep nudging it with small random changes. Whether you keep a change depends on a probability tied to how much better or worse the new solution is compared to the current one. Early on, the algorithm accepts a lot of changes, even bad ones, which helps it avoid getting stuck. As it runs, it gets pickier and accepts fewer bad moves, so it settles down. People reach for it when a problem is too messy for other methods, like lots of variables or an objective function that isn't smooth or differentiable. It's also handy when there are tons of local minima, since it can climb out of those dips and check other parts of the search space. That said, it can be pretty slow, and there's no guarantee it'll find the true global best. A lot of people pair it with other optimization techniques to speed things up and get better results.

Mild changes like these are usually not an emergency, but they deserve a follow-up with a doctor rather than being ignored.

Start with the H. pylori result. A "reactive" blood test means your body has antibodies to the bacterium. That shows you have been exposed at some point, but it doesn't reliably tell whether the infection is active now. Blood antibody tests can stay positive for months or years after treatment. To confirm an active infection, doctors usually use a urea breath test, a stool antigen test, or an endoscopy with biopsy. If the infection is confirmed and you have stomach symptoms, treatment with a combination of antibiotics and acid-reducing medicine is effective. Please don't start antibiotics on your own, because the correct combination depends on local resistance patterns and your other medicines.

Your liver results are only slightly outside the usual range. An ALT of 42 is near the upper limit of normal for many labs, and a bilirubin of 1.72 is mildly raised. In a slim young man, the most common cause of an isolated mild rise in bilirubin is Gilbert's syndrome, a harmless inherited condition that can be made worse by fasting, dehydration, poor sleep, stress, or illness. Your doctor will usually check whether the raised bilirubin is mostly the "indirect" type, which points toward Gilbert's, or the "direct" type, which needs more investigation. Other possible causes include a recent viral hepatitis infection, alcohol, certain medicines or supplements, and gallbladder or bile duct problems. The multivitamin you took the day before is unlikely to explain these results, since a single day's dose rarely causes liver changes, but tell your doctor exactly what you took, including any high-dose vitamin A or niacin products, and stop taking supplements you don't need until you've been reviewed.

A reasonable next step is to see a doctor, who will likely repeat the liver tests with a fractionated bilirubin, check for hepatitis A, B, and C, review any medicines or supplements, and possibly arrange an abdominal ultrasound. Avoid alcohol while your liver results are being evaluated.

Seek medical care promptly if you notice yellowing of your skin or the whites of your eyes, dark urine, pale stools, persistent or worsening abdominal pain, vomiting blood, black or bloody stools, unexplained weight loss, fever, or extreme tiredness.

Your instinct about films is partly right, but the real explanation is also fascinating. The main idea is that electricity needs a path to flow through, and a person working on a live line can be set up so that no current flows through their body.

Power line workers are often said to be "bonded" to the line. They wear conductive suits made of fine metal threads woven into fabric, and they connect that suit to the wire with a metal cable. When the worker touches the line, they are at the same voltage as the wire, so there is no voltage difference across their body. Electricity only hurts you when it flows through you from one point to another at a different voltage, like from the wire to the ground. If you are already at the wire's voltage, there is nothing pushing current through you. The suit also acts like a shield, carrying any stray current around the body rather than through it.

A helicopter case works similarly. A helicopter flying near a line can pick up an electrical charge, and it is typically grounded to the earth through its landing gear or a special discharge system. When the worker is lowered in, the helicopter and worker can be brought to the same voltage as the line, so there is no difference that would make a spark jump between them. The worker is often lowered in on a rope or insulating line and may be connected to the wire before they touch it. Engineers carefully manage the timing and the connections so the voltages stay matched.

Arcs do happen sometimes, which is why the procedures are so strict. Workers are trained to keep everything at the same potential, and the whole process is planned so that the one thing that could hurt them, a voltage difference across the body, is kept at zero.

So it is not that the electricity is ignored. It is that the worker is made part of the electrical circuit at the same voltage as the wire, so nothing flows through them.

Generally, yes. Holding a visa does not usually stop you from investing in the London Stock Exchange or in UK-listed funds, shares, and bonds. Your immigration status governs whether you can work, study, or live in the UK, not whether you can buy financial assets. Most UK brokers will open an account for anyone with a valid UK address and a passport, though some ask for proof of residence and a National Insurance number or tax identifier, and a few platforms restrict certain products or limit services for people on temporary visas, so it is worth checking each broker's eligibility rules before signing up.

The more important issues are tax and the source of your funds. If you are a UK tax resident, you may owe capital gains tax on profits and tax on dividends and interest, and your residence status for tax purposes depends on the Statutory Residence Test rather than your visa type alone. If you are on a short-term visa or plan to leave the UK, you should also consider whether you will become non-resident, since that can change your tax position and how gains are treated when you leave. Funds you bring from abroad should be legitimately sourced, and some banks will ask questions about large transfers.

Because the details depend on your nationality, visa category, how long you plan to stay, and where you pay tax, it is sensible to speak with a regulated UK financial adviser or a tax accountant before investing significant sums.

I'm sorry you've been dealing with this for two years. The combination you describe (weight loss, night sweats, widespread itching, persistent swollen neck glands, a recurring scaly red rash, rising liver enzymes, low red cell count with a low MCV, and a raised CEA) deserves a thorough, targeted workup rather than reassurance. I can't diagnose you, but I can explain what doctors usually think about with this pattern and what to push for.

The first group of possibilities is lymphoma. Persistent lymph node swelling, drenching night sweats, weight loss and generalized itching are classic "B symptoms" and itch. A scaly rash that comes and goes for years, especially with lymph node involvement, raises the question of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (mycosis fungoides or Sézary syndrome), which is often mistaken for eczema or psoriasis for a long time. It can also involve the liver and cause anemia. Hodgkin lymphoma commonly causes itching, night sweats and weight loss as well. Diagnosis needs a skin biopsy (sometimes repeated, since early biopsies can be non-diagnostic) and an excisional lymph node biopsy, not just a needle sample, plus imaging such as a PET/CT.

The second group is chronic inflammatory or infectious conditions. Sarcoidosis can cause skin lesions, swollen nodes, liver enzyme elevation and weight loss. Tuberculosis, HIV, hepatitis B or C, and syphilis can all cause this combination. Autoimmune disease such as lupus or primary biliary cholangitis (which causes itching and liver enzyme changes) is also possible. Drug reactions, including a DRESS-type reaction, can cause rash, nodes and liver changes, so review all medications and supplements.

The third group is a solid cancer or other malignancy. CEA at 12.69 is clearly elevated (normal is generally under 3 to 5). CEA is not a diagnostic test, and it can be raised by smoking, liver disease, inflammation and infection, but it is most associated with cancers of the colon, lung, breast, pancreas and others. A low MCV anemia with weight loss can point to chronic blood loss and iron deficiency, so a colonoscopy and endoscopy are reasonable if they haven't been done. Liver enzymes rising could also reflect liver metastases or bile duct problems, which is why imaging of the abdomen matters.

Things worth asking your doctor for: a full blood count with differential and a blood smear, ferritin and iron studies, LDH, ESR and CRP, a full liver panel including ALP and bilirubin, hepatitis B and C and HIV testing, an ANA and antimitochondrial antibody, a chest X-ray or CT, a CT or PET/CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis, a colonoscopy if not recently done, a skin biopsy of an active rash patch, and an excisional biopsy of an enlarged lymph node. Ask for a referral to a hematologist or oncologist, and a dermatologist experienced in cutaneous lymphoma if the rash stays unexplained.

You say everything "checks out well," but with these symptoms and a raised CEA, tests so far clearly haven't explained the picture. It is reasonable to say plainly that you have lost weight, have night sweats, and have had swollen glands for two years, and ask what the plan is to find the cause. If you get no movement, request a second opinion or a referral to a hospital-based specialist clinic. If you develop severe fatigue, jaundice, black or bloody stools, fever, or rapidly growing lumps, seek care promptly.

If you want, tell me your age, medications, and which tests and scans have already been done, and I can help you work out what gaps remain.

The Democrats did not so much lose the 1968 presidential election as fracture, and several interlocking factors contributed to Hubert Humphrey's narrow defeat to Richard Nixon. The most consequential was the Vietnam War. Lyndon Johnson's escalation of the conflict had made it deeply unpopular, and by 1968 the war had sparked massive antiwar protests, divided the party's base, and fueled the insurgent candidacy of Eugene McCarthy and then Robert Kennedy. Johnson's decision in March 1968 not to seek reelection reflected how badly the war had damaged him, but the party he left behind carried the burden of that unpopularity into the fall.

The party's internal division was closely tied to the war. Kennedy's assassination in June, following the earlier challenge from McCarthy, removed the most charismatic anti-war figure from the race. Humphrey, as Johnson's vice president, was seen by many liberals as too tied to the administration's policies, and he struggled to distance himself from Johnson while still needing the president's support and the party machinery. He did not publicly break with Johnson's Vietnam policy until late in the campaign, a delay that cost him support among young voters and activists who had been alienated from the party.

The chaos of the Democratic National Convention in Chicago also hurt the party badly. Violent clashes between police and protesters outside the convention, shown on national television, created an image of disorder that many voters associated with the Democrats and with the broader social unrest of the period. The convention's bitter fights over the platform and the nomination process further exposed the party's divisions.

Nixon, meanwhile, ran a disciplined campaign that appealed to what he called the "silent majority." He promised law and order in response to urban riots and campus protests, and he offered a strategy for ending the war that seemed credible to voters weary of conflict. His "Southern strategy" also drew many white Southern voters who had been drifting away from the Democrats since the civil rights legislation of the mid-1960s. George Wallace's third-party candidacy further split the traditional Democratic coalition in the South, drawing away votes that might otherwise have gone to Humphrey.

Finally, the broader coalition that Franklin Roosevelt had built was under strain. Economic concerns, racial tensions, urban unrest, and generational conflict all pulled at the New Deal alliance of labor, urban voters, Southerners, and liberals. Humphrey narrowly lost the popular vote, and a late shift in his campaign helped him close the gap, but the combination of these forces left him short of the victory he needed.

Onions and garlic owe their pungent taste and smell to sulfur-based compounds. After we eat them, these compounds pass into the bloodstream and leave the body through the lungs, which is why our breath takes on an unpleasant odor. Some of the same compounds also come out through perspiration, so a person's sweat may smell of onion or garlic after a meal containing them. Brushing teeth and rinsing with water does not fully get rid of this smell, and chewing aromatic herbs such as parsley or mint does little better. The reason is that these compounds evaporate easily and drift through the air, so they can be noticed even by someone standing some distance away.

A bus adapter is basically a piece of hardware that plugs into your computer's bus and lets it talk to other devices or peripherals. Think of it as a middleman: it sits between the computer and whatever you're hooking up, so data can move back and forth. There are a few common types you'll run into. PCI (Peripheral Component Interconnect) bus adapters are what you'd use to hook up things like sound cards, network cards, and graphics cards to the motherboard. USB (Universal Serial Bus) adapters handle printers, scanners, and external hard drives. SCSI (Small Computer System Interface) adapters are for hard drives and tape drives, and you'll mostly see them on older or server gear. Then there's IEEE 1394, better known as FireWire, which was popular for digital cameras and camcorders. Honestly, a bus adapter is a handy thing to have if you want to add capabilities to a machine and connect it to all sorts of gear.

A hyperspectral imager is a camera-like instrument that captures images across many narrow, contiguous bands of the electromagnetic spectrum at once, rather than just the three broad bands (red, green, and blue) that an ordinary color camera records. Where a standard camera might divide light into three channels, a hyperspectral imager may record dozens or even hundreds of channels, each corresponding to a small slice of wavelength, often spanning visible light and extending into the near-infrared or shortwave infrared.

The result is a three-dimensional data set often called a hypercube. Two dimensions represent the spatial layout of the scene, as in a normal image, and the third represents the spectrum. Each pixel therefore contains a full spectral signature, a detailed record of how much light that point reflects or emits at each wavelength. Because different materials absorb and reflect light in distinctive ways, this spectral signature can reveal information invisible to the eye, such as the chemical composition, moisture content, mineral type, or health of vegetation.

Hyperspectral imagers are used in remote sensing from satellites, aircraft, and drones to map crops, monitor forests, survey minerals, and track pollution or oil spills. They also appear in agriculture, food inspection, pharmaceutical quality control, medical diagnostics, art conservation, and forensics. Compared with multispectral imagers, which capture fewer and broader bands, hyperspectral systems provide far finer spectral detail, but they also produce much larger data volumes and generally require more complex processing to interpret.

Gerrymandering is basically when whoever's drawing the district lines does it in a way that tilts things toward one party. It can happen in any country that has districts and parties, but in the US there are a few ways people try to fix it.

One is independent redistricting commissions. Some states took the map-drawing job away from the legislature and handed it to a separate commission, which cuts down on politicians picking their own voters.

Another is setting fair criteria for the maps. Some states require districts to be compact and contiguous, or to keep communities together instead of splitting them up.

Courts are another route. If a plan looks way too partisan, it can be challenged, and a court can order the state to redraw it more fairly.

Then there are voter initiatives. In some states, voters can just pass a ballot measure to change the process themselves. California did this in 2010 and ended up with an independent commission.

The problem's been around a long time, too. The name comes from Elbridge Gerry, the Massachusetts governor who signed a plan into law in 1812 that was designed to help his party. These days it's arguably worse, since better technology and data let politicians draw lines that squeeze out every bit of advantage for their side, which is why people have been worrying about it a lot more lately.

Yes, but the protection is mostly indirect and depends heavily on where you live. In general, a private loan between two people is a contract, and courts will enforce it if it has the usual elements: an offer and acceptance, consideration (the money lent and a promise to repay), and an intention to create legal obligations. If a borrower refuses to pay, the lender can usually sue in small claims or civil court, and a judgment can lead to wage garnishment or a lien, depending on local enforcement rules. Written agreements make this much easier to prove, and many jurisdictions require a writing for loans above a certain amount or for loans that will not be repaid within a year.

The law also limits what private lenders can do. Most places cap interest rates, and charging above those caps can make a loan partly or fully unenforceable, or in some cases expose the lender to penalties. Some jurisdictions treat frequent informal lending as regulated lending if it is done as a business, so occasionally lending to friends is different from repeatedly lending to many people for profit. Debt collection harassment is restricted for professional collectors, and in many places those rules can apply to individuals who collect debts in a similar manner, though casual reminders between friends are generally fine. Borrowers also have protections: a loan obtained through fraud or duress can be voided, and in some places a borrower can challenge unconscionable terms.

Practical points matter as well. Statutes of limitations limit how long a lender has to sue, often somewhere between three and ten years depending on the jurisdiction and whether the agreement was written. Gifts can be confused with loans, so if you want repayment, it helps to document the terms in writing, including amount, due date, interest if any, and signatures. For specific situations, especially larger sums, real estate, or disputes, a local attorney or consumer protection office can tell you exactly what applies where you are.

Kernel methods are a family of techniques in machine learning and statistics that let algorithms find complex, nonlinear patterns in data while still using relatively simple mathematical tools designed for linear relationships. The central idea is to implicitly map data into a higher-dimensional feature space, where patterns that were tangled together in the original space may become linearly separable or easier to model, and to do so without ever computing the coordinates of the data in that larger space.

The trick that makes this practical is the kernel function. A kernel is a function that takes two data points and returns a number representing their similarity, and it corresponds to an inner product between the two points after they have been transformed into the higher-dimensional space. Because many algorithms, such as support vector machines, ridge regression, and principal component analysis, can be rewritten so that they depend only on inner products between data points, one can replace those inner products with a kernel evaluation. This substitution is often called the kernel trick. It means the algorithm behaves as though it were working in a very high, or even infinite, dimensional space, while the actual computation remains manageable.

Common kernels include the linear kernel, the polynomial kernel, which captures interactions between features up to a chosen degree, and the radial basis function or Gaussian kernel, which measures similarity based on distance and can correspond to an infinite-dimensional feature space. The choice of kernel and its parameters encodes assumptions about what kind of similarity matters for the problem at hand.

Kernel methods are valued because they combine flexibility with a solid theoretical foundation, drawing on functional analysis and reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces, and because they often work well with modest amounts of data. Their main drawbacks are that training can become expensive as the number of data points grows, since the kernel matrix scales quadratically with the sample size, and that selecting an appropriate kernel and tuning its parameters can require careful experimentation.

When you sell an asset like a stock, property, or collectible, your capital gain is the sale price minus your "cost basis," which is usually what you paid plus certain costs like commissions or improvements. If you don't know the original purchase price, the tax authority doesn't simply let you skip the calculation. In the United States, the IRS puts the burden on you to prove your basis, and if you can't, it can treat your basis as zero. That means the entire sale price would be taxed as a gain, which is usually the worst possible outcome. So it's well worth reconstructing the number as best you can.

For investments, start with your brokerage. Brokers have been required to track and report cost basis for stocks bought since 2011, and for mutual funds and many other securities since 2012, so the figure may already be on your Form 1099-B or in your account history. If the shares were transferred from another firm, the old broker may still have records, and you can request old statements. If you know roughly when you bought the shares, you can look up the historical price for that date or period using financial websites, newspaper archives, or the company's investor relations department. For older holdings, dividend reinvestment records, stock splits, mergers, and spinoffs all affect the basis, and services exist that specialize in reconstructing this history for a fee.

For real estate, useful sources include the closing statement from the purchase, county property records (which often show the recorded sale price or transfer tax paid), old tax returns, mortgage documents, and receipts for improvements, which add to your basis. Insurance records and appraisals can also help.

How you acquired the asset matters a great deal. If you inherited it, you generally don't need the original purchase price at all, because in the US the basis is "stepped up" to the fair market value on the date of the previous owner's death. Estate documents, an appraisal, or historical price data for that date establish the figure. If you received the asset as a gift, by contrast, you usually take over the giver's original basis, so you'd need to find out what they paid, though special rules apply if the value had fallen below their basis at the time of the gift.

If records truly can't be found, courts have sometimes allowed taxpayers to use a reasonable estimate when there's credible evidence supporting it, a principle known from the Cohan case. However, the estimate needs a rational basis, such as the approximate purchase date combined with historical prices, and courts tend to resolve uncertainty against the taxpayer. Document your reasoning and sources thoroughly in case you're ever questioned.

Also keep in mind that how long you held the asset determines whether the gain is short-term, taxed at ordinary income rates, or long-term, taxed at lower rates, so establishing the approximate purchase date matters too.

Rules differ in other countries. The UK, Canada, and Australia have their own approaches, including special valuation dates for assets held before certain years. If the amount involved is significant, a tax professional can help you reconstruct the basis and choose a defensible method.

Machine perception is basically a machine's ability to make sense of sensory data like images, sounds, and other inputs from the world around it. It's built on AI techniques, mostly machine learning and deep learning, which let machines spot patterns, sort out objects and events, and decide what to do based on what they see or hear. The idea is to get machines to take in their surroundings roughly the way people do. That opens the door to all sorts of things, from image and speech recognition to natural language processing and self-driving robots. It's not easy, though. Machines have to chew through huge piles of data accurately, adjust when conditions shift, and make calls in real time. Which is why it's still a hot research area in both AI and robotics.

"The Guardian" most commonly refers to the British daily newspaper, one of the most widely read and influential news organizations in the English-speaking world. It was founded in 1821 in Manchester as the Manchester Guardian by John Edward Taylor, a cotton merchant. The paper was established in the aftermath of the Peterloo Massacre of 1819, when cavalry charged a crowd of peaceful pro-reform protesters, and from the beginning it took a liberal, reformist stance. It dropped "Manchester" from its name in 1959 and moved its main operations to London in 1964.

Politically, The Guardian is generally regarded as centre-left. It is known for its coverage of social justice, the environment and climate change, civil liberties, and international affairs, as well as for its arts, culture, and opinion sections. It has a reputation for investigative journalism, most notably its 2013 reporting, led by Glenn Greenwald and others, on the global surveillance programs revealed by Edward Snowden, which earned it a share of the Pulitzer Prize for Public Service. It also played major roles in reporting on the WikiLeaks diplomatic cables, the News of the World phone-hacking scandal, the Panama Papers, and the Cambridge Analytica affair.

One unusual feature of The Guardian is its ownership. Since 1936 it has been owned by the Scott Trust, named after its long-serving editor C. P. Scott, and the trust became a limited company in 2008. The arrangement exists to secure the paper's financial and editorial independence in perpetuity and to protect it from commercial or political interference by owners. C. P. Scott is also remembered for a famous line from a 1921 essay: "Comment is free, but facts are sacred."

The Guardian is also notable for its digital strategy. Unlike many newspapers, it does not put its online content behind a paywall. It relies instead on voluntary reader contributions and memberships, along with advertising, and this model helped it return to operating profitability after years of losses. It runs dedicated editions for the United States and Australia, giving it a large international readership. Its sister Sunday paper is The Observer, which it acquired in 1993; in 2024 and 2025 The Observer was sold to Tortoise Media. The print edition of The Guardian is currently published in a tabloid format, having moved from broadsheet to the mid-sized "Berliner" format in 2005 and then to tabloid in 2018.

The name "The Guardian" can also refer to other things depending on context. Several other newspapers carry the name, including The Guardian in Nigeria and the Guardian in Trinidad and Tobago. It is also the title of a 2006 American film starring Kevin Costner and Ashton Kutcher about Coast Guard rescue swimmers, and of a 2001 to 2004 American legal drama television series. If you had one of these other meanings in mind, I'd be happy to explain that instead.

Race as a way of sorting people by things like skin color, eye shape, and hair texture has been around in plenty of cultures for centuries. The scientific version most of us picture, though, really took shape in the 1700s and 1800s, when European empires were expanding across the globe. Scientists and scholars back then tried to sort the world's peoples into racial boxes and rank them from "higher" to "lower." That ranking got used to justify colonization and the exploitation that came with it. Race has been a touchy subject ever since, because it's been leaned on to back up racism and eugenics. Plenty of scientists today say race isn't biologically solid, and that human diversity makes more sense when you look at genetic variation instead.

Lightheadedness is common in early pregnancy. Blood vessels widen and blood volume rises, which can lower blood pressure. Low blood sugar from skipped meals or vomiting, dehydration, and anemia are also frequent causes, and shakiness with a racing heart often points toward low blood sugar. Standing up too fast or staying upright too long can make it worse.

Even so, almost fainting with shakes and a racing heart during pregnancy should be evaluated by a clinician today, not just watched at home. Less common causes, such as an irregular heartbeat, low blood pressure from dehydration, thyroid problems, or a complication of the pregnancy itself, need to be ruled out, and the absence of bleeding doesn't exclude an ectopic pregnancy. Please call her OB or midwife now, or a nurse advice line if her provider's office is closed. If you can get a heart rate reading, a fingertip pulse monitor or a smartwatch is useful to report.

She should go to the emergency department right away, or call 911, if she faints, has chest pain, trouble breathing, a heart rate that stays very fast or irregular, confusion, severe abdominal or shoulder pain, vaginal bleeding, or if she feels worse instead of better. Keeping her lying down, sipping fluids, and having her eat something with sugar and protein while she waits is a reasonable step in the meantime.

Imagine you find a box of old letters written in a secret code that nobody speaks anymore. You can't just read them, but you can still figure out a lot by being a clever detective.

First, linguists look for patterns. If a word shows up over and over at the end of sentences, it might be a "stop" or "the end" kind of word. If a word changes its ending depending on what's happening in the sentence, that tells them the language has grammar rules for showing who did what. Think of how we say "I walk" but "she walks." Ancient writers did the same kind of thing, so the endings give clues.

Second, they compare languages that are related. Languages often come from a common family, like cousins in a family tree. Hittite, Tocharian, Latin, Greek, and English all share a very distant ancestor called Proto-Indo-European. Even though nobody spoke that ancestor language in a way we can hear, scholars can compare words across the cousins. If "father" sounds like "pater" in one and "fadar" in another, they can guess the old form and how sounds changed over time. Knowing those rules helps them read words they've never seen before.

Third, they use bilingual texts. Sometimes the same message was written in two languages, like a translation on a school handout. The Rosetta Stone is the famous example for Egyptian. When a language we already partly know sits next to an unknown one, we can match up the words.

Fourth, they study the context. Pictures, clay tablets used for trade, lists of goods, and religious rituals all give hints about what the words mean. If a text shows a list of animals next to a word, that word probably means one of those animals.

For Hittite, the breakthrough came partly because it was written in cuneiform, a script that was already well understood, and because scholars recognized its grammar looked like other Indo-European languages. For Tocharian, which was spoken in ancient Central Asia, scholars found manuscripts in a language that wasn't known at all, then realized it belonged to the Indo-European family by comparing its verbs and nouns with cousins like Latin and Sanskrit.

Put simply, linguists are like someone putting together a jigsaw puzzle with no picture on the box: they match shapes, compare with other puzzles that look similar, and slowly work out what the whole picture must look like.

SWIFT (Society for Worldwide Interbank Financial Telecommunication) is basically the network banks all over the world use to send each other info about financial transactions, and it's secure and standardized so everyone's speaking the same language. So when a bank "issues a SWIFT," it's really just sending a message over that network to another bank, usually to kick off some kind of transaction. If you want to know exactly when it went out, your best bet is to ask the bank that sent it. They'll have records or internal systems that track their SWIFT messages, so they should be able to give you the date and time. You might also be able to figure it out yourself by looking at the message, since it should have the date and time it was sent right there in it.

So the bid-ask spread is just the gap between what a market maker will pay for a security (the bid) and what they'll sell it for (the ask). The bid is the highest price a buyer's willing to pay, and the ask is the lowest price a seller's willing to take. At the open things can swing around pretty fast, since traders are still sizing up the market and tweaking their bids and asks as they go. But the bid's almost always lower than the ask, because market makers want to buy low and sell high, that's how they make their money. So when the market opens, you'll typically see the bid sitting below the ask. Say a stock's bid is $50 and the ask is $51. The spread is $1, which just means the market maker will buy it from you at $50 and sell it to you at $51.

Go is a board game with origins in China that stretch back over 2,500 years. The board is a grid made up of 19 horizontal and 19 vertical lines, and each player begins with a supply of stones in one color, either black or white. The aim is to enclose a greater portion of the board with your stones than your opponent manages with theirs. The players alternate turns, setting one stone at a time on the points where lines cross, and play concludes once both of them pass, signaling that neither wants to move again. Go is famous for combining straightforward rules with deep strategy and great complexity. It enjoys particular popularity in East Asia, where professionals compete in countries including China, Japan, and South Korea. The game has also attracted fans elsewhere in the world, and international tournaments take place on a regular basis. People widely admire Go for the distinctive challenges it poses and for the mental discipline and focus it demands.

Formal reasoning is a kind of logical argumentation governed by a defined set of rules and conventions. It is a methodical procedure in which conclusions are drawn logically from statements or propositions taken as true or accepted as starting points. Within formal reasoning, arguments can be built either deductively or inductively. Deduction begins with a broad statement or principle and applies it to arrive at a particular conclusion, whereas induction starts from particular observations or instances and uses them to establish a broader conclusion. This mode of reasoning is employed across numerous disciplines, such as mathematics, computer science, philosophy, and law. It serves as a valuable instrument for assessing and comprehending intricate systems and for arriving at well-founded decisions through logical analysis.

A 30% share in a business means you own 30 percent of the company's equity, so you are entitled to a proportional slice of its profits, assets, and value. The exact meaning depends on the business structure and the agreement behind it. In a corporation, a 30 percent shareholder typically receives 30 percent of any dividends the board declares and holds roughly 30 percent of the voting power, unless the shares are non-voting or the bylaws say otherwise. In a partnership or LLC, the share usually governs your portion of profits, losses, and distributions, and it may be set out in an operating or partnership agreement.

Owning 30 percent is often enough to block certain major decisions that require a supermajority, such as selling the company or amending its charter, though it is not enough to control the business alone. Minority holders at this level may also have rights to financial information, and the governing documents may include protections such as tag-along rights, preemptive rights to avoid dilution, or limits on how the majority can pay itself.

If you are considering acquiring a 30 percent stake, or you have been offered one, it would be wise to review the shareholder or partnership agreement, confirm how the company is valued, and ask about debts and liabilities. A business attorney or accountant can help you understand what the stake is actually worth and what protections come with it. Heart palpitations and blood in the stool are not directly connected, though both can point to underlying health problems. If you notice any new or worrying symptoms, it is important to talk with a healthcare provider, who can work out what is causing them and recommend the right treatment. Palpitations are feelings that your heart is racing, skipping beats, or fluttering. A range of factors can produce them, such as stress, caffeine, alcohol, smoking, certain medications, and medical conditions like anemia, thyroid problems, and heart disease. Blood in the stool has its own possible causes, including inflammatory bowel disease, hemorrhoids, anal fissures, and cancer of the colon or rectum. Because it can signal something serious, you should see a healthcare provider if you notice it. Your palpitations and bloody stool could conceivably share an underlying cause, but only a proper evaluation can confirm that. A provider can identify the source of your symptoms and guide you toward appropriate care.

Dimples are little dents in your cheeks, and whether you have them comes from the genes you got from your mom and dad. Genes are like instruction books inside your body that decide things like your hair color and how tall you'll grow. Some instruction books say "make a dimple here," and some don't say that at all. So if your parents had dimples and passed that instruction along, you might have them too. If not, you won't.

Dimples happen because a tiny bit of muscle in your cheek is attached to the skin in a special spot. When you smile, that muscle pulls the skin inward a little, making a small dent. Lots of people's cheeks don't have that exact attachment, so their skin stays smooth when they smile.

As for why they show up in different places, it's because everybody's face is built a little differently, like how no two sandcastles look exactly the same even when people build them with the same bucket. Some people's muscles attach a bit higher, lower, or further out on the cheek, so the dimple lands in a different spot. Some people even get dimples on their chin, which happens for the same kind of reason. It's all part of what makes each person's face unique.

Getting cash from a credit card almost always costs you something. These cards are meant for buying goods and services rather than for withdrawing money. When you need cash, a bank or credit union is usually the better choice, whether you use an ATM or take money out of your checking or savings account. If a credit card is your only option, you can take a cash advance at a bank branch or from an ATM. That route typically brings fees and steep interest, so it rarely makes financial sense. Interest on a cash advance also starts right away, since these transactions carry no grace period. In most situations, it is wise to steer clear of credit cards for cash. A debit card or a withdrawal from your bank account is generally preferable, because neither carries fees or interest.

Hydrogen's the lightest element there is, atomic number 1, symbol H. It's also the most common one in the universe, around 75% of all the elemental mass out there. At room temperature and pressure it's a gas, but you can cool it or squeeze it hard enough to get it to a liquid or even a solid. It burns easily too, with a pale blue flame.

It's about as simple as atoms get: one proton, one electron. In nature you'll mostly find it bonded to other things, like in water (H2O) or in the hydrocarbons that make up a lot of fuels and plastics. On its own it's rare on Earth because it escapes into space so easily.

People use it for plenty. It powers some vehicles, including fuel cell cars that turn it into electricity. It's a key ingredient in making ammonia and methanol, and refineries use it to process petroleum. It also shows up in steel production, in cleaning up certain metals, in some food processing, and in making certain plastics.

Breastfeeding while on metronidazole is usually discouraged, since the drug passes into breast milk and could potentially harm the infant. Even so, the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) regards metronidazole as compatible with breastfeeding, so the decision should be made carefully with your healthcare provider by comparing the possible risks and benefits. If you take metronidazole and plan to keep nursing, watch your baby for possible side effects such as fussiness, vomiting, diarrhea, or unusual drowsiness. Other drugs can also treat amoebiasis in nursing mothers, including antibiotics like paromomycin or tinidazole. The best option depends on the type and severity of your infection and on the risks and benefits for both you and your baby, so review these choices with your provider, who can recommend the most suitable treatment for your situation.

Fairness in machine learning refers to the goal of ensuring that automated decision-making systems do not produce outcomes that systematically disadvantage individuals or groups based on characteristics such as race, gender, age, or socioeconomic status. As machine learning models are increasingly used in areas like lending, hiring, criminal justice, healthcare, and content moderation, concerns have grown that these systems can reproduce or even amplify existing social inequalities, sometimes in ways that are hard to detect because the models appear objective.

A central difficulty is that fairness has no single agreed definition. Researchers have proposed many formal criteria, and several of the most prominent ones cannot all be satisfied at once. One common criterion, demographic parity, requires that the rate of positive outcomes, such as loan approval, be equal across groups. Another, equalized odds, requires that error rates such as false positives and false negatives be similar across groups. A third, calibration, requires that a given predicted score mean the same probability of the outcome regardless of group membership. Mathematical results have shown that when base rates differ between groups, it is generally impossible to satisfy calibration and equal error rates simultaneously, so developers must choose which notion of fairness matters most in a given context, often a value judgment rather than a purely technical one.

Unfairness can enter a system in several ways. Training data may reflect historical discrimination or underrepresent certain populations. The choice of features or labels may encode biased proxies; for example, using arrest records as a measure of crime reflects policing patterns as well as behavior. The model's objective may optimize overall accuracy while neglecting performance for minority groups. Deployment context matters too, since a tool built for one population may be used on another.

To address these problems, practitioners use approaches at different stages. Pre-processing methods modify training data, in-processing methods add fairness constraints during model training, and post-processing methods adjust outputs after prediction. Auditing, documentation, and testing across demographic subgroups are also common, as is involving affected communities and domain experts in design decisions. Fairness is closely tied to related concerns such as transparency, accountability, and privacy, and it intersects with law, including anti-discrimination statutes in many countries.

Overall, fairness in machine learning is best understood as an ongoing sociotechnical challenge rather than a problem with a single technical fix. It requires clarifying what fairness means in a particular setting, measuring its trade-offs, and recognizing that statistical improvements alone may not resolve deeper questions about whether a system should be used at all.

"Information mining" is not a standard, widely established term, so its meaning depends on context. In most cases, people using the phrase are referring to data mining, the process of discovering patterns, relationships, and useful insights within large collections of data. Data mining draws on statistics, machine learning, and database techniques to sort through information and identify trends, such as customer buying habits, anomalies in financial transactions, or correlations in scientific measurements.

Some writers use "information mining" more loosely to mean the broader activity of extracting useful knowledge from information sources, which can include text, documents, and web content. In that sense it overlaps with text mining, web mining, and information retrieval, where the focus is on pulling structured meaning out of unstructured material like articles, emails, or social media posts.

Having two periods in one month, roughly two weeks apart, is fairly common and in most cases is not a sign of anything serious. A normal cycle can range from about 21 to 35 days, and it's not unusual for a cycle to occasionally be shorter than expected. If your cycles are normally on the shorter side, two bleeds can sometimes fall within a single calendar month even when nothing is wrong. Since you haven't had intercourse in two months, pregnancy-related bleeding is very unlikely, which removes one of the things doctors usually want to rule out first.

The most common cause of an occasional early or extra bleed is a temporary hormonal fluctuation. Stress, poor sleep, illness, significant changes in weight, intense exercise, travel, or changes in diet can all affect the hormones that control ovulation and the timing of your period. Sometimes ovulation doesn't happen in a given cycle, or happens early, and this shifts when bleeding occurs. Some women also notice light spotting around ovulation, which falls roughly midway between periods and can be mistaken for a second period.

Other possible causes are worth knowing about, especially if this keeps happening. These include thyroid problems, polycystic ovary syndrome, uterine fibroids or polyps, starting or stopping hormonal contraception or other medications, and, in women approaching their forties, the hormonal changes of perimenopause. Infections of the cervix or uterus can also cause irregular bleeding, though they often come with other symptoms such as unusual discharge or pelvic pain.

If this has happened once and you otherwise feel well, it is reasonable to keep a record of your cycles for the next two or three months, noting the start and end dates of bleeding, how heavy it is, and any other symptoms. Often the pattern returns to normal on its own. You should see a doctor if irregular bleeding continues for more than a couple of cycles, if the bleeding is very heavy (for example, soaking through a pad or tampon every hour or two, or passing large clots), if it lasts longer than about seven days, or if you have significant pain, fever, dizziness, tiredness or paleness that might suggest anemia, bleeding after any future intercourse, or unusual discharge. A doctor may suggest blood tests for hormones, thyroid function, and blood count, and possibly a pelvic ultrasound to look at the uterus and ovaries.

In short, a single month with two periods is usually not a cause for alarm, but tracking your cycles and getting checked if it persists or comes with other symptoms is the sensible approach.

Yes, lots of people get these, so you're definitely not alone. Here's the simple version.

Inside your foot are tiny muscles, kind of like little rubber bands that help you wiggle your toes and hold up your foot. Sometimes one of those rubber bands gets confused and squeezes really hard all at once, and it won't let go. That's a cramp. The sharp, stabbing feeling is the muscle clenching like a tight fist.

Why does the muscle get confused? A few common reasons. Your body might be low on water, or low on minerals like potassium, magnesium, or calcium, which are like the messages that tell muscles when to squeeze and when to relax. The muscle might be tired from a long day of standing, walking, or exercise. Shoes that squish your foot or don't support it well can make it worse. Staying in one position for a long time, like sleeping with your toes pointed down, is another trigger, which is why night cramps are so common. Cold temperatures can also make muscles grumpy.

What can you do in the moment? Gently stretch the muscle. Pull your toes back toward your shin, or stand up and press your foot flat on the floor. Rubbing the spot and putting something warm on it helps too. Walking around a little often makes it let go.

To make them happen less, drink enough water, stretch your feet and calves before bed, wear comfortable shoes, and eat foods with potassium and magnesium, like bananas, potatoes, nuts, and leafy greens.

One grown-up note: if the cramps happen very often, last a long time, come with swelling, numbness, or weakness, or started after a new medication, it's worth seeing a doctor. Sometimes cramps are a sign of something like a nerve issue, circulation problem, or medication side effect. But for most people, they're just an annoying, harmless muscle tantrum.

Sure thing! So DNA is basically a set of instructions for your body, kind of like a recipe that tells it how to grow and develop. When your cells divide, they copy the DNA so every new cell gets the same instructions. Then cells use those instructions to make proteins, which are like tiny machines doing different jobs. Some proteins help build stuff like bones and muscles, while others speed up chemical reactions or pass signals between cells. Proteins can get pretty complicated, and they shape your body in all sorts of ways. Take blood vessels and neurons, for example. Blood vessels carry blood everywhere, and neurons are the cells in your brain and nerves that help you think, feel, and move. Both depend on DNA's instructions to form and work properly. A random forest is a machine learning method that combines many decision trees to make predictions more accurate and reliable than any single tree could achieve. Each tree in the forest is trained on a different random sample of the training data, drawn with replacement, which is a technique known as bootstrap sampling. In addition, at each point where a tree decides how to split the data, it considers only a random subset of the available features rather than all of them. These two sources of randomness make the trees differ from one another, so their individual errors tend to cancel out when they are combined.

To produce a prediction, the forest asks every tree for its answer. For classification tasks, such as deciding whether an email is spam, the final output is determined by majority vote among the trees. For regression tasks, such as estimating a house price, the forest averages the numerical predictions of all the trees. Because many diverse trees contribute to the result, the method is less prone to overfitting, which is the common problem of a model memorizing noise in its training data instead of learning general patterns.

Random forests are popular because they usually perform well with little tuning, handle both numerical and categorical data, and can rank features by how useful they were for prediction. They are also fairly robust to outliers and missing values. Their main drawbacks are that the models can be large and slow to make predictions when the forest contains many deep trees, and that they are less interpretable than a single decision tree. The technique was formalized by Leo Breiman in 2001 and is widely used in fields such as finance, medicine, ecology, and many areas of data science.

Google Now was a virtual personal assistant developed by Google for Android and iOS devices. Its purpose was to deliver information users might want at a given moment and place, including traffic conditions, weather forecasts, and sports results. To do this, the app drew on a mix of the user's search history and location data to surface relevant content and suggestions. Google introduced it in 2012, and in 2016 it was superseded by Google Assistant.

Personally identifiable information (PII) refers to any data that can point to a particular person. Examples include a person's full name, home address, telephone number, email address, national identification or social security number, and other distinctive identifiers. Organizations commonly gather and process PII to confirm who someone is, to get in touch with them, or to maintain records of their actions. Legal frameworks exist to control how PII is collected, used, and safeguarded. Although the specifics differ from one jurisdiction to another, these rules generally obligate organizations to treat PII securely and responsibly. Depending on the rules, an organization might have to get permission before gathering PII, keep it protected and private, and erase it once it is no longer required. Overall, people should think carefully before disclosing personal details online or to companies, since such information could be used to monitor their behavior, commit identity theft, or otherwise undermine their privacy. Staying aware of what you share and taking measures to protect your personal data is a wise practice.

Think of a font size like the size of a box that a letter sits inside. Long ago, printers set each letter on a little metal block, and the size number described how tall that block was. The letter itself doesn't fill the whole block, though. There's a bit of empty space above and below it, the same way a tiny toy sits inside a shoebox with room to spare. So when you pick "12," you're choosing the height of the box, not the exact height of the letter.

The unit used for that number is called a point. A point is about 1/72 of an inch, which is a very tiny amount. So 12 points means the box is about 12/72 of an inch tall, roughly the size of a sixth of an inch. That part is a real measurement.

The reason two size 12 fonts can look different is that every font designer decides how big to draw the letters inside that box. One font might make its letters tall and fill most of the box, while another makes its letters small and leave lots of empty space. Some fonts also have a big x-height, meaning the lowercase letters are taller, so they look bigger even at the same number. It's a bit like two cookie cutters both labeled "medium": they might cut out cookies of slightly different shapes and sizes.

As for why 12 is the standard, it's mostly tradition and comfort. Twelve points is about the size that's easy for most people to read on a printed page without squinting or wasting space. Early typewriters and word processors used it as a default, and people kept using it because it worked well. It's a convention, not a law of nature, so you can use 11, 14, or anything else you like.

So COMPAS (it stands for Correctional Offender Management Profiling for Alternative Sanctions) is a piece of software made by a company called Northpointe. Criminal justice agencies across the US use it to predict how likely someone is to reoffend or skip a court date. Judges and probation officers lean on it when they're making calls about bail, sentencing, and parole.

It works by running a proprietary algorithm that spits out a score for each person, based on stuff like their personal background, criminal history, and other info. The higher the score, the higher the supposed risk of reoffending or not showing up in court. The catch is that nobody outside the company really knows how the algorithm works or exactly what factors it weighs, since Northpointe owns it and keeps it under wraps.

It's been pretty controversial, too. Some studies found a racial bias, where Black defendants were more likely than white defendants to get wrongly flagged as high risk. People have also questioned how accurate it even is. Some research suggests its predictions aren't much better than what you'd get from human experts just making a judgment call.

Sure! So the Halting Problem asks a pretty simple question: can you write a program that takes any other program and tells you whether it'll run forever or eventually stop? Think of it like a toy robot you can program. Say you want the robot to check any program you hand it and tell you if that program loops forever or finishes. Can it be done? Nope. Some programs run forever, some stop, and there's no general way to tell which is which without actually running them and waiting. That's the Halting Problem, and it matters a lot in computer science because it shows there are hard limits on what computers can figure out.

Christianity has many branches, and they mostly differ in how they organize their churches, how they worship, and how they understand a few key beliefs. Let's start with the biggest group, the Catholic Church, which is the largest Christian church in the world. Catholics have a Pope in Rome who leads the whole church, and they believe the Pope and bishops are like a line of leaders passed down from the very first apostles of Jesus. Catholics celebrate seven special moments called sacraments, like baptism and communion, and they pray to Mary and to saints who they believe are helping them from heaven.

Eastern Orthodox churches, which include Greek, Russian, and many other national churches, are very close to Catholics in their history and rituals. They have their own leaders called patriarchs instead of one Pope, and their services often feature beautiful singing, icons (special painted pictures of holy people), and incense. Orthodox churches are led by groups of bishops who work together.

Then there are Protestants, a huge family of churches that began about five hundred years ago when a man named Martin Luther questioned some practices of the Catholic Church. Protestants believe that people should be able to read the Bible for themselves and that faith in Jesus is what saves us, not just doing good works or following rules. Because they don't have one central leader, Protestant churches have split into many different kinds.

Baptists are one kind of Protestant. They believe that baptism should happen only for people old enough to choose it for themselves, so they usually dunk a person fully under water rather than sprinkling them as a baby. Each Baptist church runs itself, and members vote on important decisions.

Methodists are another Protestant group, started by John Wesley in England. They care a lot about helping poor people and living a holy life, and their churches are organized with bishops and other leaders who guide many local congregations together.

Lutherans follow Martin Luther's teachings. They love singing hymns and believe that God's grace, a free gift, is what saves people. They keep many traditions similar to Catholics, like baptizing babies and having a service that looks a lot like a Mass.

Presbyterians and Reformed churches are led by groups of elders instead of one pastor alone. They believe God has already decided who will be saved, an idea called predestination, and they think a church should be guided by careful rules found in the Bible.

Anglicans, sometimes called Episcopalians in America, come from the Church of England. They blend Catholic-style worship with Protestant beliefs. Their churches are led by bishops, and they use a famous prayer book for their services.

Pentecostals are a more recent group, starting in the early 1900s. They focus on the Holy Spirit and believe that people can receive special gifts like speaking in other languages, which they call speaking in tongues. Their services are often lively, with lots of singing, clapping, and dancing.

Many other groups exist too. Mormons, whose church is officially called The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, believe they have additional scripture called the Book of Mormon and see their church as a restoration of the original church. Seventh-day Adventists worship on Saturday, the biblical Sabbath, and look forward to Jesus's return. Quakers meet in quiet worship, waiting for the Holy Spirit to speak, and have no paid clergy in many communities. Church of Christ and Churches of Christ emphasize going back to the simple teachings of the early church and often avoid using musical instruments in worship.

So, in a nutshell, all these churches love Jesus and read the Bible, but they disagree about who leads the church, how to baptize, how worship should look, and some deep questions about salvation. Think of them as one big family with many different houses, all sharing the same main family name.

A day care, also called a child care center, is basically a place where kids get looked after and supervised while their parents or guardians are at work or otherwise busy. You drop them off, they spend the day with trained caregivers in a safe, nurturing spot, and you pick them up later. Most of them have a bunch of stuff going on: arts and crafts, learning activities, outdoor play, that sort of thing. Many also serve meals and snacks, which saves you a packing job. Plenty of centers split things up by age, with separate programs for infants, toddlers, and school-age kids. Hours vary too. Some run during the day, some stretch into the evening, and a few even stay open overnight, depending on what the families in the area need.

Oakhurst, New Jersey is in Monmouth County. It is an unincorporated community within Ocean Township, which is located in the central part of the state near the Jersey Shore. The area is close to Asbury Park and Long Branch, and it is known for Deal Lake and for being a largely residential suburb.

A Mexican standoff is when nobody in a group can safely shoot or back off, because everyone has a gun pointed at everyone else. Guns were everywhere in the Old West, so it's totally possible people ended up in situations like that. That said, these weren't really common, and they weren't legal either. Using a gun to threaten or hurt someone was against the law, so anyone caught in one could've ended up in trouble with the authorities.

Smirnoff is owned by Diageo, the British multinational drinks company headquartered in London. Diageo acquired the brand's rights in the 1990s as part of its wider portfolio of spirits, which also includes Johnnie Walker, Guinness, and Baileys.

Zach Thomas went to Texas Tech. He played for the Red Raiders from 1992 to 1995, and he was a beast at linebacker there. He made first-team All-American twice and was a finalist for the Butkus Award, which goes to the best linebacker in college ball every year. After college, the Miami Dolphins took him in the fifth round of the 1996 draft. He turned out to be a great pick, too.
