Imagine a big family living in one house, called Spain. One of the kids, Catalonia, has its own room, speaks its own language at home, and has its own traditions. Some people in that room feel they would be happier moving out and having their own house. So they say, "Let's take a vote in our room about whether we should move out." But the parents, the Spanish government in Madrid, say, "You can't decide that alone. The house rules, the Spanish Constitution, say that the whole family is one family and nobody can split off without everyone agreeing."

That is the heart of it. Even if most Catalans voted yes, the vote would not automatically make Catalonia a new country. Spain's courts ruled the referendum illegal, so in Spain's eyes a yes vote would be like a kid writing "I live alone now" on a piece of paper. It might show how the kid feels, but it doesn't change who owns the house. Catalonia could not just walk out, because to be a real country you need things like control of your borders, your own money and taxes, and other countries agreeing that you exist. The European Union and most governments said this was Spain's internal matter and that they would not recognize a breakaway that broke Spain's laws. A new Catalonia would also have found itself outside the EU, which would be scary for its businesses.

So the realistic idea behind the vote was not "vote yes and we're instantly free." It was "if lots of us vote yes, it shows how strongly we feel, and that puts pressure on Madrid to negotiate," maybe for more self-rule, more control over taxes, or eventually a proper, legal referendum like Scotland got from the UK.

Here is what actually happened. Because the courts blocked the official referendum, the Catalan government held a softer, unofficial "consultation" on November 9th, 2014, run largely by volunteers. Around 2.3 million people took part and about 80 percent said yes to independence, but only a little over a third of eligible voters showed up, since many people who wanted to stay in Spain stayed home because they saw it as illegal or meaningless. Nothing legally changed. Catalonia's leader, Artur Mas, was later put on trial, fined, and banned from holding office for a while for going ahead with it.

The story didn't end there. In 2017 Catalonia held another referendum that Spain called illegal, and police tried to stop it, sometimes roughly. Catalonia's parliament then declared independence, but no country recognized it, and Spain used a constitutional power to take direct control of the Catalan government, called new elections, and arrested several leaders, while the Catalan president Carles Puigdemont fled to Belgium. Some of those leaders were later pardoned, and Spain has since passed an amnesty law, but Catalonia is still part of Spain today.

So the five-year-old version is this: voting yes was a way of shouting "we want to leave," but leaving for real needs either the family's permission or the neighbors agreeing you're your own house, and Catalonia had neither.

Great question! Let's start with you. When you think, it often feels like words are running through your head, like a little voice. But that's only part of thinking. Lots of thinking happens without words at all: picturing where you left your keys, imagining how a ball will bounce, feeling that a song is sad, or knowing how to tie your shoes without saying the steps. Your brain has ways of holding ideas that aren't words.

Deaf people think the same way. Many Deaf people think in sign language, and their inner voice is made of hands and movements instead of sounds. Others think in pictures or feelings, just like hearing people do sometimes. A Deaf person who never learned any language early on still has a busy mind full of wants, memories, and plans.

Feral children, who grew up with little or no human contact, are a bit different. Researchers have found that they often had trouble learning language later, especially grammar, which suggests there's a window in early childhood when the brain is best at picking up language. But they could still think. They could feel hungry, scared, or happy, remember where food was found, and figure out how to get something they wanted. Some even learned to solve problems in clever ways.

So the simple answer is that thinking doesn't need words. Words are a tool we use to share thoughts and to organize them, kind of like a map. A person without words still has the land, the places they've been, and the things they want to reach. They just find their way around without the map.

Dr. Joseph Boakye Danquah, usually called J.B. Danquah, was a Ghanaian lawyer, scholar, writer, and nationalist politician, widely regarded as one of the founding fathers of modern Ghana. He was born on 18 December 1895 at Bepong in the Kwahu area of what was then the British colony of the Gold Coast, and he came from a prominent royal family of Akyem Abuakwa. His half-brother was Nana Sir Ofori Atta I, the influential paramount chief of Akyem Abuakwa.

Danquah studied in Britain at the University of London, where he earned a law degree and later a doctorate in philosophy in 1927, making him one of the earliest West Africans to obtain a PhD there. He was also called to the bar at the Inner Temple. After returning home he practiced law, founded the newspaper The Times of West Africa in 1931, and became a leading intellectual voice. His scholarly work includes The Akan Doctrine of God (1944), an important study of Akan religious thought, and he also wrote plays such as The Third Woman. He is often credited with promoting the adoption of the name "Ghana" for the country at independence, drawing on the ancient West African empire of that name.

In politics, Danquah was a central figure in the movement for self-government. In 1947 he co-founded the United Gold Coast Convention, the first major nationalist party, and he and his colleagues invited Kwame Nkrumah to return from abroad to serve as its general secretary. After the 1948 Accra riots, Danquah was arrested along with Nkrumah and four other leaders, a group remembered as "The Big Six," who are honored on Ghana's currency today. Nkrumah later broke away to form the Convention People's Party, and the two men became political rivals. Danquah, who favored a more gradual and constitutional path along with liberal democratic and free market ideas, ran against Nkrumah in the 1960 presidential election and lost decisively.

Under Nkrumah's increasingly authoritarian government, Danquah was detained without trial under the Preventive Detention Act, first in 1961 and again in 1964. He died in detention at Nsawam Prison on 4 February 1965. His political legacy lives on through the Danquah-Busia tradition, which is the ideological foundation of Ghana's New Patriotic Party, and he is commemorated in Ghana as a champion of democracy, the rule of law, and individual liberty.
Rahm Emanuel was mayor of Chicago from 2011 to 2019. He got replaced by Lori Lightfoot, who took over in May 2019 and has been running the city since then.

Knives with sharp blades are best kept out of the dishwasher, since the machine can harm them. During a wash cycle, a knife can knock against plates and other utensils, which may dull its edge. Cleaning knives by hand is the gentler option. A soft sponge or cloth can remove food and grime, and you should hold the blade carefully so it doesn't strike anything. More broadly, sharp tools such as knives deserve caution, because they can pose a danger when they are not used or handled correctly.

On January 12, 2010, a magnitude 7.0 earthquake struck Haiti. Its epicenter lay just to the west of the capital, Port-au-Prince, and because it was shallow, at roughly 13 kilometers (8 miles) deep, its shaking was especially destructive. The disaster was catastrophic: an estimated 300,000 people lost their lives and 1.5 million were rendered homeless. It was the most powerful quake to strike Haiti in over two centuries, and a string of aftershocks followed. Numerous structures were either harmed or demolished, among them hospitals, schools, roads, and bridges. The quake additionally set off landslides and inflicted further environmental harm. Rebuilding efforts have continued for many years, hampered by a range of obstacles, such as political unrest and insufficient resources.

Oral thrush is common with inhaled steroids like Flovent, and it usually responds well to simple measures. Here is what you can start tonight, though home care alone often isn't enough, so I'll also cover when to call your doctor.

The most important habit is to rinse your mouth thoroughly after every Flovent dose. Swish with water, gargle, and spit it out rather than swallowing. Brushing your teeth and tongue gently afterward helps even more. If you use a spacer, that reduces how much medicine lands in your mouth and throat. Keep using the inhaler as prescribed, since stopping an asthma controller on your own can set you up for a flare, especially when you're recovering from the flu.

For comfort and some help with the yeast, you can rinse with warm salt water (half a teaspoon of salt in a cup of warm water) several times a day, or use a baking soda rinse (half a teaspoon in a cup of warm water). Plain unsweetened yogurt with live cultures is harmless and soothing, though evidence that it clears thrush is weak. Avoid sugary foods and drinks for now, since yeast feeds on sugar, and skip alcohol-based mouthwashes, which can irritate the sore tissue. If you wear dentures, take them out at night and clean them well. Replace your toothbrush, since it can harbor yeast and keep reinfecting you.

Honestly, home remedies are mostly supportive. Thrush that appears while you're on an inhaled steroid generally needs an antifungal, such as nystatin liquid or clotrimazole lozenges, or sometimes a single fluconazole pill. These require a prescription in most places, but this is a quick call to your doctor's office or a telehealth visit, and they can often prescribe without an in-person exam. Since you've been sick for ten days and have a sore throat, it's worth having someone look at it, partly to confirm it's thrush and partly because it may extend into your throat or esophagus.

Contact a doctor sooner if you have trouble or pain when swallowing, a fever, white patches that spread or bleed, or if you have diabetes or a weakened immune system. Also mention it to whoever prescribes your Flovent, because they may adjust your dose or technique to prevent recurrence.

Pimples on the penis can come from all sorts of things: bacteria, plain old skin irritation, or even an STI. Honestly, if you're worried about them, get them checked, because some STIs can cause real trouble if they go untreated. In the meantime, there are a few things you can try. Keep the area clean and dry by washing it gently with warm water and a mild soap, and skip scented products since they tend to irritate things. Wear loose clothing so the skin can breathe and you're not rubbing against it all day. A warm, damp cloth held on the spot for a few minutes can take the edge off the swelling and soreness. Over-the-counter creams with benzoyl peroxide or salicylic acid can dry out the bumps and calm redness. But if they stick around, or you notice pain, discharge, or trouble peeing, make an appointment with a healthcare provider. They can figure out what's going on and treat it properly. And since these bumps can sometimes be a sign of an STI, it's smart to practice safe sex and get tested regularly, for your own sake and your partners'.

These are most likely preauricular pits, a common and usually harmless birth feature. They form in early pregnancy, when the small bumps that become the outer ear fuse together. If the fusion is incomplete, a small dimple, pit, or tiny opening can remain. They often run in families, and they appear on one or both ears in a sizable share of people.

The occasional substance that comes out is typically a thick, cheesy material from the lining of the pit, similar to a small sebaceous secretion. It's not unusual for these pits to drain now and then. The main concern is infection, which can cause redness, swelling, warmth, tenderness, pus, or a fever. If you notice any of those, or if the area becomes a firm, painful lump, see your pediatrician promptly, since these can develop into an abscess that may need treatment. Meanwhile, gently clean the area, avoid squeezing or trying to dig out the contents, and don't let anyone attempt to remove the pit at home.

Because the kidney x-ray was done at birth, it may be worth asking your pediatrician whether any other features need attention. In rare cases, ear pits occur alongside a genetic condition called branchio-oto-renal syndrome, which can involve hearing loss and kidney problems. This is uncommon, and most children with ear pits never have it. It would be reasonable to mention it if there's a family history of hearing loss or kidney disease, if your son has any ear shape differences or other unusual features, or if he has had any concerns with hearing or kidney function. A hearing check is a simple way to put your mind at ease if you have any doubts, though many babies pass the newborn screen and go on to have normal hearing.

The World of Coca-Cola opened in Atlanta, Georgia, on May 6, 2007, in Pemberton Place near the Georgia Aquarium and Centennial Olympic Park. It replaced an earlier Coca-Cola museum, the Coca-Cola Museum, which had operated at the company's headquarters area since 1990. Note that "built" could refer to the construction of the building or its opening date; the attraction was designed and constructed in the years leading up to its 2007 opening.

Neptune got found on September 23, 1846, by a team at the Berlin Observatory led by Johann Gottfried Galle. But honestly, the real credit goes to the French mathematician Urbain Jean Joseph Le Verrier, who figured out where to look in the first place. He'd been studying the orbit of Uranus, the seventh planet, and noticed something was tugging on it. Basically another planet nobody had seen yet was pulling on it with its gravity. So he crunched the numbers and predicted the mass, size, and position of this mystery planet. He's also the one who named it Neptune, after the Roman god of the sea.

Galle and his team took Le Verrier's predictions and pointed their telescope at the spot. They found it on the very first night, within about one degree of where he said it'd be. Pretty wild when you think about it. They looked at it through the telescope and confirmed it was a planet and not just some star.

People made a big deal of it back then, and for good reason. It was the first planet found through math rather than just somebody spotting it in the sky, and it was a huge step in how we understand the solar system.

A key-agreement protocol is a cryptographic procedure that lets two or more parties establish a shared secret key over a communication channel that an adversary may be able to observe. The defining feature is that the key is not simply picked by one side and sent to the other. Instead, each party contributes information, and the final key is computed from those contributions, so that no single party fully determines it in advance. This distinguishes key agreement from key transport, where one party generates a key and encrypts it for delivery to the other.

The classic example is Diffie-Hellman key exchange, published in 1976. Both parties agree on public parameters, such as a large prime and a generator of a group. Each then chooses a private random number and sends the other a public value derived from it by modular exponentiation. Each side combines its own private number with the other's public value and arrives at the same result. An eavesdropper sees only the public values and would have to solve the discrete logarithm problem, which is believed to be computationally infeasible for properly chosen parameters, to recover the key. A variant using elliptic curves (ECDH) achieves the same result with smaller keys and is widely used today.

The shared secret that results is typically passed through a key derivation function to produce one or more symmetric keys, which are then used with fast ciphers such as AES for encrypting and authenticating the actual data. This is why key agreement is a core building block of protocols like TLS, SSH, IPsec, and Signal.

Basic Diffie-Hellman by itself is vulnerable to man-in-the-middle attacks, because nothing proves who is on the other end. An attacker can run separate exchanges with each party and relay messages between them. Practical protocols therefore add authentication, using digital signatures, certificates, pre-shared keys, or passwords (as in password-authenticated key exchange protocols such as SRP or OPAQUE). Authenticated key agreement ensures each party knows with whom it has established the key.

Important security properties include forward secrecy, meaning that compromise of long-term keys later does not reveal past session keys, which is achieved by using fresh ephemeral values in each session. Others include resistance to key-compromise impersonation and to unknown key-share attacks. Newer work also addresses quantum threats, since Shor's algorithm would break Diffie-Hellman and elliptic-curve variants on a large quantum computer. Post-quantum key-agreement mechanisms, such as lattice-based schemes like ML-KEM (Kyber), are being deployed, often in hybrid combination with classical exchanges.

Pregnancy can occur from intercourse at any point in the menstrual cycle, even while you are menstruating. The chances are typically lower during a period, but they are not zero. Because sperm can live inside the female reproductive tract for several days, having sex toward the end of your period and then ovulating (releasing an egg) soon afterward could result in conception. To help avoid an unplanned pregnancy, it is important to rely on a dependable form of contraception, such as condoms or birth control pills. If your menstrual cycle is irregular or you are worried you might be pregnant, consider speaking with a healthcare provider, who can evaluate your situation and offer guidance.

Honestly there are a few reasons someone might buy a bond yielding 0%, even though it sounds kinda nuts at first.

The big one is safety. If the issuer has a strong credit rating, a lot of people see the bond as way less risky than stocks or real estate, so they'll take a lower return just to sleep better at night.

Diversification is another one. Bond returns tend not to move in lockstep with other asset classes, so having some in your portfolio can smooth things out.

Then there's liquidity. You can usually turn these into cash pretty easily, which is handy when markets get weird or you've got a bill or some other obligation to cover.

And some folks buy for inflation reasons. Inflation eats away at what your money can buy, so if you think it's going to run high, you might take the 0% to hold onto some of that purchasing power. Though honestly that logic is a bit shaky, since 0% in an inflationary stretch still loses ground in real terms.

Whether it makes sense really comes down to your own goals and how much risk you can stomach. It won't fit everybody, and if you're unsure, talking to a financial advisor before you put money in is probably a smart move.

Jamestown was established in 1607 and was the first lasting English colony in the territory that later became the United States. The Virginia Company, a joint stock firm granted a royal charter by King James I of England, founded it with the aim of setting up North American colonies for commercial gain and territorial growth. The town stood on the shores of the James River, in the area that is now Virginia, and it took its name from the king.

So HIV is basically a virus that goes after your immune system, the thing that's supposed to protect you from getting sick. It mostly spreads through sex, but you can also get it from sharing needles that have the virus on them, or a mom can pass it to her baby during pregnancy, birth, or breastfeeding.

What it does is infect immune cells, especially CD4+ T cells (some people call them T helper cells). Those are the ones that help coordinate your body's response when an infection or some other invader shows up. The longer HIV goes on, the more of those cells it kills off, and that makes it harder and harder for your body to fight off infections and diseases.

If it's left untreated, it can turn into AIDS. That's when your immune system is badly damaged and you're open to all kinds of serious infections and illnesses. There's no cure for HIV right now, but with the right treatment, people living with it can have long, healthy lives.

Hillary Clinton has served the United States as First Lady, as a senator from New York, and as Secretary of State. In 2016 she won the Democratic nomination for president but lost the general election to Donald Trump. Her career in public life spans many years and has placed her at the center of American politics. Before she became First Lady, she practiced law and focused on the rights and welfare of children and women. During her time in the White House, she pushed for healthcare reform and played a role in establishing the Children's Health Insurance Program. In the Senate, she devoted herself to healthcare, education, and foreign affairs. As Secretary of State, she directed American foreign policy and oversaw the nation's relations with other countries. Many admire Clinton for her intellect, her wealth of experience, and her commitment to public service, and she remains a powerful voice in American political life.

IRBBB stands for incomplete right bundle branch block. It describes a small delay in the electrical signal traveling through the right side of the heart, which shows up as a specific pattern on an ECG. It is one of the most common ECG findings in children and young adults, and in healthy, athletic kids it is usually harmless. Many people with it never know, and it often comes and goes or stays stable for life without causing problems. By itself, it does not mean the heart is weak or damaged.

Your son's shortness of breath during endurance sports deserves to be looked at, though. Mild breathlessness during hard basketball can be normal for a kid who is out of shape or pushing hard, and it may have nothing to do with the heart. But it's the kind of symptom doctors want to evaluate alongside an ECG finding, so it's good that you have an appointment already.

For next week, it may help to bring a list of questions and details. Ask whether the doctor thinks the breathlessness is typical for his fitness level or needs further testing. Ask whether he should have an echocardiogram (an ultrasound of the heart) to check its structure and pumping, and whether an exercise stress test makes sense. Be ready to describe any chest pain, dizziness, fainting, racing or skipping heartbeats, or unusual tiredness, even if it seems minor. Tell the doctor about any family history of heart problems, unexplained fainting, or sudden death at a young age, since that is one of the most important things they will ask about.

Most of the time, an IRBBB finding in an active kid turns out to be a benign variant, and the reassurance from a good workup can be a relief. Try not to assume the worst before you have the results, and don't hesitate to ask the doctor to explain anything that's unclear.

It is hard to say whether you will be able to conceive naturally without more information about your particular circumstances. Ovacare and Ovaa Shield are medications that can help balance menstrual cycles and raise the odds of getting pregnant, yet neither offers any guarantee. Folic acid and Duphaston are also frequently prescribed to women who are trying to conceive. Still, whether pregnancy happens depends on a range of factors, including your general health, your partner's health, and any underlying conditions that could affect fertility. If you have been trying without success, it would be worthwhile to talk with a healthcare provider about your choices. A provider can run tests to identify the source of any fertility problems and suggest a treatment plan suited to you. Meanwhile, certain lifestyle changes may improve your prospects, such as eating well, keeping a healthy weight, managing stress, and steering clear of tobacco and alcohol.

So if you tried to buy something online with a debit card that didn't have enough money in it, the bank will usually decline the charge. The payment just doesn't go through and the purchase doesn't happen. Sometimes, though, it'll show up as pending on your account or on the store's side for a while. That usually means the merchant hasn't actually gotten the money yet. If that's your situation, you'll need to sort it out with the merchant or your bank to get the transaction cancelled.

Honestly, the easiest way to avoid this mess is to check your balance before buying anything online. If you come up short, your bank might hit you with an overdraft fee, and those can really sting. If you can't get things sorted with the merchant or the bank, try reaching out to a financial advisor or a consumer protection agency. They can walk you through your options and make sure you know what rights you have.

The seasons are caused by the tilt of Earth's axis, not by changes in our distance from the Sun. Earth's axis is tilted about 23.5 degrees relative to the plane of its orbit, and that tilt stays pointed in the same direction in space as the planet travels around the Sun over the course of a year. As a result, for part of the year the Northern Hemisphere leans toward the Sun, and for the other part it leans away, with the Southern Hemisphere experiencing the opposite.

When your hemisphere is tilted toward the Sun, two things happen that make it warmer. First, sunlight strikes the ground at a steeper, more direct angle, so the same amount of solar energy is concentrated on a smaller area and heats it more effectively. Second, the days are longer, giving the Sun more hours each day to warm the land and air. This combination produces summer. When your hemisphere is tilted away, sunlight arrives at a shallow, glancing angle that spreads its energy thinly, and the days are short, which produces winter. Spring and autumn occur in between, around the equinoxes, when neither hemisphere is tilted toward the Sun and day and night are roughly equal everywhere.

A common misconception is that summer happens when Earth is closest to the Sun. In fact, Earth's orbit is nearly circular, and it is actually closest to the Sun in early January, during the Northern Hemisphere's winter. The fact that the two hemispheres have opposite seasons at the same time is strong evidence that tilt, rather than distance, is the real cause. Places near the equator experience little seasonal temperature change because the Sun's angle there stays fairly high all year, while places near the poles see the most extreme variation, including periods of continuous daylight in summer and continuous darkness in winter.

Sado-masochism, which is also called BDSM, describes a range of practices in which people either cause pain or take pleasure in experiencing it. The activities may be physical, mental, or emotional in nature, and they sometimes include role-play, dominance and submission, or other arrangements built around power differences. Although the practice is frequently misunderstood and can provoke controversy, some individuals regard it as a significant part of who they are and how they express their sexuality. It is worth stressing that sado-masochism must always be consensual and respectful, and it should never involve abuse or any behavior to which a participant has not agreed.

Stress could be part of what's going on with your symptoms, but it's worth keeping other causes in mind too. Leg pain, night sweats, bleeding gums, and headaches can all come from lots of things, and stress is only one of them. Bloating and losing your appetite have plenty of possible causes as well: digestive problems, hormone shifts, or certain meds. And that bruise or red pinprick on your skin could point to something else entirely.

If these symptoms keep hanging around or get worse, see a doctor. Don't wait on it if you're worried. They can ask you more specific questions about what's happening and your history, and run whatever tests make sense to figure out the cause and treat it if needed.

Yes, in many cases you can, but the rules depend on your country. I'll assume you're in the United States, since that's the most common context for this question, and note where other countries differ.

In the US, a self-employed person can deduct home office expenses if they use a part of the home regularly and exclusively as their principal place of business. "Exclusively" is the strict part: a spare bedroom that doubles as a guest room or a corner of the living room you also use for watching TV generally won't qualify. A dedicated room, or a clearly separated area used only for your development work, usually will. Your home also needs to be your principal place of business, meaning you do your main administrative and income-producing work there, or you meet clients there regularly.

There are two ways to calculate the deduction. The simplified method lets you deduct $5 per square foot of the office, up to 300 square feet, for a maximum of $1,500. It's easy and requires little record-keeping. The regular method lets you deduct the business percentage of your actual home costs, such as mortgage interest or rent, property taxes, homeowners insurance, utilities, repairs, and general upkeep. To find the percentage, divide the office square footage by the home's total square footage. This method takes more records but often produces a larger deduction, especially if your home costs are high. You can usually switch between methods from year to year.

You report the deduction on Form 8829 if you use the regular method, or on the Schedule C line for simplified home office deductions, and it applies to your self-employment income. Note that if you're an employee of someone else, the home office deduction is generally no longer available federally, so your freelance status matters here.

If you work from home but also have a traditional office elsewhere, the rules get stricter, so check the details. Also, depreciation recapture can apply if you sell the home later, which is worth knowing about if you use the regular method.

In the UK, Canada, Australia, and other countries, the rules differ. For example, the UK allows a flat-rate deduction for working from home without requiring exclusive use, and Canada is stricter about what qualifies. If you tell me your country, I can give you more specific guidance. For a definite answer on your situation, a tax professional or your local tax authority's guidance is worth consulting.

Intellectual property (IP) covers the products of human creativity, including inventions, literary and artistic works, and the symbols, names, and images that businesses use in trade. The law safeguards these creations by granting their owners specific exclusive rights to use them and profit from them. Several forms of intellectual property exist. Copyright shields original literary, artistic, musical, and other creative output, like novels, films, songs, and paintings. Trademarks guard the brands and logos a business uses in commerce, including company names, emblems, and taglines. Patents cover inventions and discoveries, such as novel products, methods, and technologies. Trade secrets protect private business information, like recipes, formulas, and internal processes, that gives a firm an edge over rivals. The goal of intellectual property law is to strike a balance between creators and society: it lets creators reap rewards from their work while ensuring the public can still access new ideas and knowledge.

Putting money into mutual funds is a sound approach for reaching long-term objectives like retirement savings or steady wealth accumulation. A mutual fund gathers contributions from a large number of investors and uses the combined sum to purchase a varied collection of stocks, bonds, or other securities. Investors benefit from expert management, spread-out risk, and a chance to share in the possible growth of various markets. In India, mutual funds come in several main categories: equity funds, debt funds, and hybrid funds. Equity funds put most of their money into stocks. They may deliver higher returns over an extended period, though they also involve greater risk than other fund types. Debt funds focus on fixed-income instruments such as bonds. They generally see less volatility and lower risk than equity funds, but their potential returns are smaller as well. Hybrid funds blend stocks and bonds, aiming to strike a balance between return potential and risk. Selecting a fund requires attention to your financial goals, how much risk you can accept, and the particular characteristics and fees of the fund. Many people find it helpful to consult a financial advisor or carry out their own research so they can identify a fund that matches their objectives and suits their broader financial plan. It is also wise to spread your money around rather than placing everything in a single fund or asset class. Doing so helps control risk and may lead to better long-term results.

The Tacoma Narrows Bridge collapsed on November 7, 1940, in Washington State. The suspension bridge, which spanned the Tacoma Narrows strait of Puget Sound, had opened to traffic only about four months earlier, on July 1, 1940.

The bridge was nicknamed "Galloping Gertie" because its deck visibly moved up and down in even moderate winds. On the morning of the collapse, winds of roughly 40 miles per hour set off a severe twisting motion that the structure could not withstand, and the main span tore apart and fell into the water below. The failure is usually explained as aeroelastic flutter, in which the wind and the bridge's own movement reinforce each other until the motion becomes destructive.

No people died in the collapse, though a dog named Tubby, left in a car on the bridge, was killed. The event was captured on film and became a famous case study in engineering, leading to major changes in how suspension bridges are designed and tested for aerodynamic stability. A replacement bridge opened in 1950, and a second parallel span was added in 2007.

Homeschooling means that instead of going to a school building every day, a kid learns at home, usually with a parent as the main teacher. The parent picks what to teach, either by buying a ready-made set of lessons called a curriculum, by using online classes, by mixing in classes at a local co-op where homeschool families share teaching, or by putting together their own plan. Kids still learn reading, writing, math, science, and history, but they can go faster or slower than a regular classroom, and they can spend extra time on things they love. Rules differ a lot by state in the U.S. and by country. Some places want you to tell the government you are homeschooling, keep records, or take tests, and other places barely ask for anything.

About the diploma: in most places, there is no single official high school diploma handed out by the state for homeschoolers. Instead, the parent usually issues the diploma and keeps a transcript, which is a record of the classes taken and the grades earned. That is perfectly legal in most U.S. states. Some families instead enroll in an accredited online school or a umbrella school, which gives a diploma from a recognized institution. Some students also take the GED, which is a test that gives a state-recognized equivalency certificate, though many homeschoolers skip it.

Colleges do accept homeschoolers. Most colleges, including very famous ones, have clear steps for homeschooled applicants. They usually want a transcript, a list of books and courses, and often scores from tests like the SAT or ACT. Some also ask for letters from outside teachers or an interview. Many homeschoolers also take community college classes in high school, which gives colleges a grade from a school they already trust.

Does it hurt your chances? Not by itself. Colleges care about whether you are ready for college work, and homeschoolers often do as well as other students, sometimes better. The tricky part is that colleges can't just assume what your parent's grades mean, so you need to prove your learning in other ways: good test scores, outside classes, clear records, projects, and activities. If a family keeps solid records and shows real, challenging coursework, homeschooling is usually not a disadvantage. If records are messy or the courses seem too easy, it can make things harder. Also, if you plan to join the military or apply for certain scholarships, check their specific rules, since those can be pickier about diplomas.

A graph neural network (GNN) is a kind of neural network built to work with data organized as a graph. Graphs are a natural way to capture connections between various objects or entities, and GNNs excel at tasks that require examining and forecasting these connections. Within a GNN, nodes stand for the objects or entities being studied, while edges indicate how those objects relate to one another. Every node carries a collection of features or attributes, which can either be learned during training or set in advance, and edges may likewise carry features or weights. The network draws on these features to detect patterns within the graph's structure and then produces predictions or decisions based on what it finds. GNNs are applied widely, in areas such as social network analysis, recommendation engines, and predicting protein-protein interactions. They also appear in natural language processing, computer vision, and any other field where data can be expressed as a graph. Several varieties exist, including convolutional neural networks (CNNs), recurrent neural networks (RNNs), and graph attention networks (GATs). The particular design of a GNN depends on the characteristics of the graph data and the problem to be solved.

Kobe Bryant won the NBA Most Valuable Player award one time, for the 2007–08 season, when he led the Los Angeles Lakers to a strong record and the team reached the NBA Finals that year. He was also named MVP of the 2008 NBA Finals and won the Finals MVP award in 2009 and 2010, but those are separate honors from the regular-season MVP, so his regular-season MVP total is one.

I'm sorry you're dealing with this, especially after everything you went through with your own lymphoma. It makes total sense that your mind jumps there. Still, swollen lymph nodes have a lot of possible causes, and most of the time they turn out to be nothing serious. In kids, the usual culprit is a viral infection like a cold or the flu. The nodes swell up as the immune system does its job. Bacterial infections, allergies, and minor injuries can cause it too. Since your son just had a cold and is cutting his molars, that's probably what's going on here. Even so, if something still bugs you, go with your gut and talk to his doctor. They can actually examine him, figure out what's behind the swelling, and tell you whether anything needs treating. If you're not satisfied after that, ask again, or get a second opinion from another pediatrician or a pediatric specialist.

Afghan cuisine is hearty and flavorful, shaped by its location at the crossroads of Central and South Asia and the Middle East. Rice is the centerpiece of most meals, and the national dish, kabuli pulao, is a fragrant rice cooked with oil, carrots, raisins, and almonds or pistachios, usually topped with tender lamb or beef. Another staple is mantu, steamed dumplings filled with spiced minced meat and onions and served with a yogurt sauce and tomato-based sauce. Bolani, a thin flatbread stuffed with potatoes, leeks, or pumpkin, makes a popular snack or side. Kebabs are also common, especially chapli kebab, a flat, spiced minced meat patty, and seekh kebab, which is grilled on skewers.

Afghans eat plenty of bread, with naan being the everyday loaf baked in tandoor-style ovens. Soups and stews such as aush, a noodle and herb soup topped with yogurt and sometimes beans, appear often, especially in colder months. Yogurt, known as mast, is used widely, both as a side and in dishes and drinks like doogh, a savory yogurt drink flavored with mint. For dessert and tea, Afghans enjoy sweets like firni, a creamy rice pudding flavored with cardamom and rosewater, along with green tea, often served with cardamom and sugar.

Mark Zuckerberg and several of his fellow students at Harvard University launched Facebook in 2004. At first the business went by the name "TheFacebook," and its purpose was to serve as a social networking website aimed at college students. Its appeal grew rapidly, and it spread to additional universities before it became available to anyone in 2006. Now, Facebook ranks among the biggest and most influential social media services anywhere, counting its users in the billions worldwide.

The cross-entropy method (CEM) is a general-purpose stochastic optimization and rare-event estimation technique. It was developed by Reuven Rubinstein in the late 1990s, and it works by iteratively adjusting a probability distribution so that it concentrates more and more of its mass on good solutions to a problem.

The basic idea goes like this. You start with a parameterized probability distribution over possible solutions, often a Gaussian for continuous problems or a Bernoulli or categorical distribution for discrete ones. In each iteration, you draw a batch of candidate solutions from the current distribution and evaluate how well each one performs according to the objective you care about. You then keep only the top fraction of these samples, often called the elite set, which are the best performers. Finally, you update the parameters of the distribution to fit the elite samples, for example by recomputing the mean and variance of the elite set. The next round of sampling then draws from this refined distribution, so the search gradually focuses on promising regions of the solution space.

The name comes from the fact that the parameter update can be derived by minimizing the cross-entropy, or equivalently the Kullback-Leibler divergence, between the current sampling distribution and a distribution concentrated on the elite samples. This connection to importance sampling is what gives the method its theoretical grounding, and it was originally used to estimate the probabilities of rare events, which is where Rubinstein first applied it.

The method has been applied to a wide range of problems, including combinatorial optimization such as the traveling salesman problem, continuous black-box optimization, training of policies in reinforcement learning, and planning tasks. Its appeal lies in its simplicity: it requires no gradients of the objective, it is easy to implement, and it is fairly robust to noisy evaluations. Its main drawbacks are that it can converge prematurely to a local optimum if the distribution collapses too quickly, and that it can be sample-inefficient in high-dimensional problems, which is why variants that add smoothing or adaptive elite fractions are commonly used in practice.

Power Loaders are imaginary machines invented for the 1986 film "Aliens." They don't exist outside the movie, since they were designed solely as entertainment. Real-world equipment can lift and transport heavy loads, but it's usually smaller and less sophisticated than the Power Loaders shown on screen. There is currently no practical demand for machines of that scale, and building one would be so costly that it isn't financially feasible at present.

Automatic investing is an arrangement in which a set sum of money is moved on a recurring basis, usually each month, from a checking account or a paycheck into a brokerage account or mutual fund. People often use this approach to grow their savings over the long term through dollar-cost averaging, meaning they put the same amount in at regular intervals no matter what the investment's price happens to be. An automatic investment fee is what a brokerage or mutual fund company charges for handling this service. Such fees can be levied per transaction or calculated as a percentage of the money invested. Anyone considering this kind of plan should know what fees apply and how they could reduce overall returns. Because some firms offer automatic investment plans without any fees, it can pay to compare several providers and choose the one that best fits your situation.

A 529 plan is a tax-advantaged investment account designed specifically for education savings, and its main appeal is the way it lets your money grow without being eroded by taxes. You contribute after-tax dollars, the investments grow tax-deferred, and withdrawals are entirely free of federal income tax as long as they're used for qualified education expenses. Over 15 or 18 years of compounding, avoiding taxes on dividends and capital gains can add up to a meaningful difference compared with saving in an ordinary brokerage account.

Many states add their own incentives. Over thirty states offer a state income tax deduction or credit for contributions, usually when you use your own state's plan, though a handful give the break no matter which state's plan you choose. Because of this, it's worth checking your home state's plan first, then comparing its fees and investment options with plans elsewhere.

The definition of qualified expenses is fairly broad. It covers college tuition, fees, books, supplies, required equipment, computers, and room and board for students enrolled at least half time, at most accredited colleges, universities, community colleges, and trade schools in the U.S. and many abroad. You can also use up to $10,000 per year for K-12 tuition (rising to $20,000 starting in 2026 under recent federal legislation), pay for registered apprenticeship programs, and put up to $10,000 over the beneficiary's lifetime toward student loan repayment.

Most plans offer age-based or target-enrollment portfolios that automatically shift from stocks toward more conservative investments as your child approaches college, which makes the account fairly hands-off. Anyone can contribute, so grandparents and other relatives can give directly to the account for birthdays or holidays, and there are no income limits on who can open or fund one. Contribution limits are high, often several hundred thousand dollars per beneficiary depending on the state, and gifts fall under the annual gift tax exclusion, with a special option to front-load five years' worth of exclusions in a single year.

A 529 is also relatively favorable for financial aid. When a parent owns the account, it's counted as a parental asset on the FAFSA, which is assessed at a maximum of about 5.64 percent, far less than the rate applied to assets held in the student's name. You, as the account owner, keep control of the money rather than it passing to your child at a certain age.

Flexibility is better than many people assume. If your child gets a scholarship, chooses not to attend college, or has money left over, you can change the beneficiary to another family member, including a sibling, cousin, or even yourself. You can withdraw up to the amount of a tax-free scholarship without the usual penalty, paying only income tax on the earnings. And since 2024, unused funds in an account open at least 15 years can be rolled into a Roth IRA for the beneficiary, up to a $35,000 lifetime limit and subject to annual Roth contribution limits.

The main drawback is that if you withdraw money for non-qualified purposes, the earnings portion is subject to income tax plus a 10 percent penalty, and you may have to repay any state tax deduction you claimed. Investment options are also limited to the menu the plan offers, and you can typically change investments only twice a year.

For most families, starting early and contributing consistently, even modest monthly amounts, is the most effective way to use a 529. It may also help to look at your state's plan details or talk with a financial advisor about how it fits alongside your retirement savings, since it's generally wise not to shortchange retirement in favor of college funding.

Okay so fuzzy logic is basically a kind of logic for reasoning that's approximate instead of exact. It's built around the idea of partial truth, where something can be somewhere between totally true and totally false. People use it all over the place, like in AI, control systems, and decision-making stuff. Instead of just yes or no, a statement gets a truth value that's any real number from 0 to 1, with 0 meaning completely false and 1 meaning completely true. That gives you a lot more room to deal with fuzzy or fuzzy-ish info. Say you have "It is very cold outside." You might give that a 0.9. "It is slightly cold outside" could land at 0.5 or so.

Fuzzy systems run on fuzzy rules that help them decide things from messy or incomplete data. The rules look like IF-THEN statements. The IF part is a fuzzy set, and the THEN part is a crisp value. For example: IF temperature IS cold THEN heater ON. Here "cold" is a fuzzy set describing how cold it is, and "heater ON" is a specific action. The system checks how cold it is and picks the action from that.

It's especially handy when the relationships between variables are hard to pin down exactly, or when the data is really uncertain or imprecise.

There are a few ETFs that track mortgage-backed securities, which are basically bonds backed by a pool of mortgages. They're issued by government agencies like Ginnie Mae (the Government National Mortgage Association) or by government-sponsored enterprises like Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac.

For 30-year MBS, the one people usually point to is the iShares MBS ETF (MBB). It follows a market-weighted index of investment-grade mortgage-backed securities, with an average maturity around 30 years. One thing to know is that the index leaves out Ginnie Mae securities, the ones backed by the full faith and credit of the U.S. government.

Another option is the VanEck Vectors Mortgage REIT Income ETF (MORT). It's a different animal, though. It tracks a market-weighted index of mortgage REITs, meaning companies that invest in mortgages and MBS. The index holds a mix of maturities, 30-year stuff included.

Neither of these tracks mortgage rates directly. They follow how mortgage-backed securities perform, and that's affected by a bunch of things, rates being just one of them. So don't expect the ETF's price to move in lockstep with mortgage rates.

Also, they won't be a fit for everybody. Look at the risks and the fees before you put money in.

Computational creativity is basically about designing algorithms and systems that can produce stuff people would call creative. It's a mashup of computer science, AI, philosophy, psychology, and the arts, so people coming at it from different backgrounds tend to see it differently. Most of the work aims at systems that come up with new ideas, products, or solutions. That could mean new music or visual art, or it could mean clever fixes for problems in science and engineering.

There's no single way to go about it. Some folks train machine learning models on existing data, then let them spot patterns and generate new material from what they've learned. Others stick with older AI tools like rule-based systems and decision trees. Either way, the hard parts keep coming up. Getting a system to make things people find beautiful or meaningful is tough, and so is getting it to work well within the limits of a specific field or area of expertise.

A Dynamic Bayesian Network (DBN) is a probabilistic graphical model used to represent systems that evolve over time. It extends the ordinary Bayesian network, which describes a set of random variables and their conditional dependencies using a directed acyclic graph, by adding a temporal dimension. In a DBN, the variables at each time step are represented as nodes, and the model specifies how variables at one time slice depend on variables at earlier time slices, as well as on other variables within the same slice.

The structure of a DBN is typically defined by two components. The first is an initial network, which describes the joint distribution of the variables at the starting time point. The second is a transition network, sometimes called a two-slice temporal Bayesian network, which describes how the variables at time t depend on variables at time t and t-1. Because the same transition structure and conditional probability distributions are reused at every time step, a DBN can be unrolled into a single large Bayesian network spanning as many time steps as needed, while keeping the number of parameters compact.

DBNs are useful because they capture both the uncertainty and the temporal dependencies present in real processes. Common applications include speech recognition, where they can model phonemes and words evolving over time; bioinformatics, for example modeling gene regulatory networks from time-series expression data; robotics and tracking, where they support state estimation; and finance and medicine, for monitoring patients or forecasting variables. A well-known special case is the Hidden Markov Model, which can be viewed as a DBN with a single hidden state variable and a single observed variable per time step. Another important case is the Kalman filter, which corresponds to a DBN with continuous Gaussian variables and linear dependencies.

Inference and learning in DBNs are typically performed with algorithms such as filtering, smoothing, and prediction, often implemented through exact methods like the forward-backward algorithm when the model is small, or approximate methods such as particle filtering and variational inference when the state space is large.

Tugain is a brand of minoxidil, and the most common side effects are scalp itching, dryness, redness, or flaking where it's applied. Some people also get a temporary increase in shedding in the first few weeks, which is often a sign it's working but can be alarming. Less common effects include unwanted hair growth on the face or nearby areas, a fast or pounding heartbeat, dizziness, or swelling in the hands or feet. These usually happen when the product gets onto the face or is absorbed more than expected, so applying it carefully to the scalp only helps. Serious reactions are rare, but you should stop and contact a doctor if you notice chest pain, fainting, or an irregular heartbeat.

About your hair: hair grows only about 1 cm a month, and after a big shedding episode, the hair that regrows takes months to show visible length. So four months of no visible change in length can be normal, especially if you've been trimming or if your hair was thinner and the new growth is fine and short. However, stopping minoxidil does cause the new growth it produced to fall out over the following few months, so it's possible you're seeing the hair you had before the treatment rather than new growth.

Since your hair loss was sudden and severe, I'd strongly suggest going back to the same doctor or seeing a dermatologist rather than restarting on your own. They can check for causes that a medicine alone won't fix, such as low ferritin (iron stores), thyroid problems, low vitamin D or B12, or a recent illness, stress, or crash diet that triggered the shedding. If you restart, your doctor may recommend the lower 2% strength, which is often used in women, and can tell you how to apply it safely and what to watch for. Please don't stop or start any medicine without that guidance.

Mark Jackson spent 17 seasons in the NBA, playing point guard. Along the way he suited up for the New York Knicks, Los Angeles Clippers, Indiana Pacers, Denver Nuggets, Toronto Raptors, Utah Jazz, and Houston Rockets. He earned three All-Star selections and stepped away from playing in 2004. Afterward, he moved into coaching, serving as head coach of the Golden State Warriors and the Indiana Pacers.

Probably not forever, but the answer depends on what you mean. I'm guessing you're asking about a construction loan, where the bank pays out money in stages while the house is built, and whether you can keep that arrangement going indefinitely.

In most cases, no. Construction loans are short-term by design, typically twelve to eighteen months. During that period you usually pay interest only on the amount drawn so far. When the build is finished, the loan has to be converted into a regular mortgage or paid off. If the project drags on past the loan's term, you generally need an extension, which banks may grant for a fee and with conditions, but they won't let it run open-ended. Lenders also inspect the work before releasing each draw, so they expect steady progress. If building stalls, they can charge higher rates, refuse further draws, or in the worst case call the loan due and begin default proceedings.

If you meant something else, the picture changes. If you're worried about being in debt on the house for a very long time, a standard mortgage commonly runs fifteen to thirty years, and you can sometimes refinance or extend, but it does eventually end if you keep paying. If you meant whether the bank owns the house until you finish paying, then yes, in effect the bank holds a lien on the property until the loan is repaid, but you are the owner and can live there, sell it, or refinance.

If you're planning a slow build, perhaps doing the work yourself over many years, it's often better to use a different approach: pay as you go from savings, use a short construction loan only for the main phases, or take a loan that converts to a mortgage once the home is habitable. It's worth talking to the lender early about their term limits and extension policies so there are no surprises.
