Chloe Dao took the title in the second season of Project Runway. A fashion designer based in Houston, Texas, she became the first Asian-American winner in the show's history. Her rewards included $100,000 to launch her own clothing line, a feature in Elle magazine, and a chance to sell her collection on bluefly.com.

Yes, though they are uncommon and usually appear in specialized forms rather than as standard retail checking. The closest examples are accounts that restrict who can pull money out or send payments into them. In the United States, for instance, some banks offer "positive pay" arrangements, which are mainly used by businesses. The company gives the bank a list of checks it has issued, and the bank only honors checks that match that list. Similarly, "debit blocks" or "ACH debit filters" let an account holder approve or reject specific merchants or direct debits before they clear, so a payment from an unapproved source is refused.

Some institutions also offer accounts with restricted payee lists, sometimes called approved-payee or whitelist controls, where transfers can only go to pre-registered recipients. These features are more common in business treasury services, trust accounts, and accounts set up for minors or for people under a court-supervised arrangement, such as a conservatorship. Certain prepaid and custodial accounts follow similar logic.

If you have a particular goal in mind, such as protecting an elderly relative's money, controlling a child's spending, or limiting fraud on a business account, tell me more and I can suggest the most practical option. Availability varies by bank and country, so it's worth asking a specific institution what controls it supports.

Burgundy is a deep, dark red with a slight purplish or brownish tint. It takes its name from the Burgundy wine region in France, where wines of this color are produced. The shade is rich and somewhat muted, sitting between true red and maroon, and it is often associated with wine, autumn, and formal or luxurious styles.

Murder and manslaughter both involve causing another person's death, yet they differ in important ways. Murder is the unlawful killing of a person with intent. In other words, the perpetrator deliberately planned to kill the victim and then followed through. Most jurisdictions split murder into two levels: first-degree and second-degree. First-degree murder is the gravest form and is generally premeditated, whereas second-degree murder is typically not planned in advance but still carries an intent to kill.

Manslaughter, by contrast, is also an unlawful killing, but it is neither premeditated nor intentional. It comes in two main forms: voluntary and involuntary. Voluntary manslaughter occurs when someone kills in the heat of the moment, overwhelmed by intense emotions such as anger or fear. The person did not plan the killing and may not even have meant to cause death, but reacted impulsively. Involuntary manslaughter is an accidental killing that happens during the commission of a crime or through reckless conduct. The person had no intention of killing the victim, but their behavior was so careless or reckless that it led to the victim's death.

An analogy with a baseball bat may help. Murder is like deciding in advance to strike someone with a bat and then doing it. Voluntary manslaughter is swinging the bat in a rage without meaning to hit anyone in particular. Involuntary manslaughter is hitting someone by accident while recklessly waving the bat around.

Bumps like these are most often one of a few harmless things. Small white-tipped bumps with a hair in the center are typically folliculitis, which is inflammation of a hair follicle, or an early ingrown hair. Friction and irritation during sex or masturbation, along with any recent shaving or trimming, can trigger this, and it often clears on its own over a few weeks, which fits what you're seeing. Pearly penile papules are another common cause. They're small, smooth, evenly spaced bumps around the head or base of the shaft, but they don't usually have hairs and aren't caused by sex. Fordyce spots, which are normal oil glands that can look like small white or yellowish dots, are also harmless and not related to sexual activity.

Molluscum contagiosum is worth knowing about because it can spread through skin contact and sometimes shows up after sex. It causes small, firm, pearly bumps, sometimes with a tiny dimple in the center. It usually lasts for months rather than fading in two weeks, so it's less likely given your timeline, but it's one reason to get a proper look if the bumps change.

To keep things settled, avoid squeezing or picking at them, wash gently, let the area breathe, and hold off on shaving or hair removal until it has cleared. Use lubricant during sex and avoid friction that seems to irritate the skin.

Since these appeared right after sexual contact, I'd recommend seeing a doctor or a sexual health clinic, even if they seem to be fading. Get checked sooner if they grow, multiply quickly, become painful, bleed, ulcerate, or develop a cauliflower-like texture, or if you notice discharge, fever, or swollen lymph nodes in the groin. A clinician can usually identify these bumps by sight, and if you're unsure about your partner's health or your own sexual exposures, a standard STI screen is a simple way to rule out anything else.

Tabling a motion just means you're setting it aside and pushing off discussion on it for later. People usually do this when the motion isn't ready yet or when something more urgent has to get dealt with first. It doesn't mean the motion is dead or forgotten, though. It's just parked, and it can come back up whenever the group wants to revisit it. In most cases, a simple majority vote is all it takes to table something.

Saint Patrick, often called "St. Patty" in casual speech, was a fifth-century Christian missionary and the patron saint of Ireland. He was born in Roman Britain, possibly around 386 CE, and as a teenager he was captured by Irish raiders and taken to Ireland as a slave. He spent several years herding sheep before escaping and returning home. Later he felt called to go back to Ireland as a missionary, and he spent much of his life there spreading Christianity, establishing churches, and ordaining clergy. Legend credits him with driving the snakes out of Ireland, though snakes never lived there in the first place, and he is also said to have used the shamrock to explain the Christian Trinity. He died around 461 CE, and March 17, the traditional date of his death, became his feast day. That day is now celebrated worldwide as St. Patrick's Day, with parades, green attire, and festivities honoring Irish culture.

Dragons show up in mythology all over the world, across tons of cultures and time periods. They're usually big, reptile-like, winged, with sharp teeth, and sometimes they breathe fire. Nobody knows for sure why they keep popping up everywhere, but there are a few theories floating around. One is that they were inspired by real animals from the past, like dinosaurs or other reptiles. The idea goes that ancient folks might have dug up fossils and figured they belonged to dragons. Another idea is that dragons were just a way to explain stuff people couldn't figure out, like storms or earthquakes. Some cultures might have blamed dragons for those. And then there's the simplest explanation: people just like telling stories, and dragons make great stories. Ideas could have spread from one group to another through trade, travel, or just swapping tales. So there's probably no single answer. It's more likely a mix of all of these, real animals, trying to make sense of the natural world, and good old storytelling.

Blood pressure bounces around over the course of a day, so one reading doesn't always tell the whole story. That said, a jump like the one you described is worth taking seriously, especially if you've got peripheral artery disease (PAD) and you're on lisinopril. Call your doctor about it. They might want to tweak your meds or suggest some lifestyle changes, and they may ask you to track your numbers for a while to spot any patterns. Until then, keep taking your medication the way it's prescribed and follow whatever else they've told you about managing your pressure.

To know precisely when a SWIFT message was issued by a bank, you need to look at the evidence the network and the bank itself produce, because the date on a payment instruction or a customer advice is not always the same as the moment the message left the bank.

The most reliable source is the SWIFT message itself, specifically its header and trailer data. In the traditional MT format, the output header (Block 2) shows the input time and the message input reference, known as the MIR. The MIR contains the date, the logical terminal of the sender, the session number and the sequence number. The trailer block can include a PDE (possible duplicate emission) or a delivery notification, and the network acknowledgment (ACK) confirms the time SWIFT accepted the message. In the newer ISO 20022 MX format, the business application header carries a creation date and time, and the network also adds its own timestamps, so you can compare when the message was created against when it was actually sent.

Next, ask the sending bank for a SWIFT copy or a proof of payment such as an MT103 or, for newer payments, a pacs.008 message, and also for the UETR, the unique end-to-end transaction reference. The UETR lets you trace the payment through SWIFT gpi Tracker, which shows each step with timestamps as the payment passes through each bank, including when it was released by the originator and when it was credited. Your bank can look it up for you, and in many cases the receiving bank can too.

It also helps to distinguish between the different dates involved. The value date is when funds are meant to settle, which can differ from the day the message was sent. The message creation time is when the bank's system generated it, while the network input time is when it was actually transmitted to SWIFT. Messages can also sit in a bank's internal queue for compliance screening or approval before release, so the true issue time is the network acceptance time, not the time you instructed the payment. Also check time zones, since SWIFT timestamps are generally in UTC while bank statements use local time.

If you need formal certainty, for example in a dispute or for legal evidence, ask the bank for an official confirmation signed or stamped by the bank, including the MIR, the UETR and the ACK time. If the bank is uncooperative, the receiving bank's incoming message record, which shows its own output time, provides independent corroboration.

There are several possible reasons why the skin in the genital area and on the buttocks might look darker or become hyperpigmented. Among the more common ones are friction, where tight clothing or constant rubbing and chafing irritate the skin and cause it to darken; hormonal shifts, since rises in certain hormones such as testosterone can boost melanin production and darken the skin; genetics, as some individuals are simply more predisposed to hyperpigmentation; sun exposure, because too much sunlight can cause pigmentation in exposed areas, including the buttocks and genitals; and certain medications, such as birth control pills, which can have darkening of the skin as a side effect.

If you are dealing with darkening or dullness in these areas, you could try the following: wear loose, breathable clothing to lessen friction and irritation; clean the area with a gentle, unscented soap and pat it dry instead of rubbing; apply a moisturizer to keep the skin hydrated; and protect the skin from the sun by covering up or using a broad-spectrum sunscreen with an SPF of 30 or higher. If these steps don't improve the appearance of your skin, or if you have other concerns, it's important to see a dermatologist or healthcare provider, who can help identify the cause and recommend appropriate treatment.

Biomarkers of aging are biological signals that allow researchers to gauge how far the aging process has progressed. They can reveal how well different organs and tissues are working and help clarify how aging affects the body. Several widely studied examples exist. Telomere length is one: telomeres, the protective tips of chromosomes, wear down every time a cell divides, and shorter ones tend to go along with a greater chance of age-related illness and a reduced lifespan. Chronic inflammation is another, since it is a defining feature of aging and is linked to conditions such as heart disease, cancer, and neurodegeneration. DNA methylation, a chemical tag on DNA that helps control which genes are switched on, shifts with age, and these shifts are believed to play a role in aging itself. Mitochondria, often described as the cell's energy producers, lose efficiency over time, and this decline is tied to many age-related disorders. Hormone levels such as testosterone and estrogen also fall with age, touching many aspects of health. Bone density drops as well, raising the odds of osteoporosis and broken bones. Grip strength, a measure of muscle power and function, usually weakens with advancing years. Beyond these, many other biomarkers exist, and scientists continually work to identify new and more precise ones in order to understand aging and its impact on the body more fully.

Honestly, opening a bunch of new cards with big limits and just letting them sit there isn't really the best way to bump your score. A high limit can help, sure, but lenders care more about whether you pay on time and manage what you borrow responsibly. One big piece of the score is your credit utilization ratio, meaning how much of your available credit you're actually using. Lower is generally better, since it tells scoring models you aren't leaning hard on your credit. So yeah, a bigger total limit can push that ratio down and possibly help. But that trick only goes so far, and it's not really a long-term plan. The better move is paying everything on time and not borrowing more than you can comfortably pay back. It's also worth checking your credit report now and then to make sure everything on it is accurate. Errors happen, and catching them early lets you fix anything that might be dragging your score down.

The seasons are caused by the tilt of Earth's axis, not by changes in its distance from the Sun. Earth's rotational axis is tilted about 23.5 degrees relative to the plane of its orbit around the Sun, and this tilt stays pointed in nearly the same direction in space (toward the star Polaris) as the planet travels around its yearly path.

Because of this fixed tilt, different parts of Earth lean toward or away from the Sun at different times of year. When the Northern Hemisphere is tilted toward the Sun, as it is around June, sunlight strikes it more directly, like a flashlight shone straight down rather than at a slant. The energy is concentrated over a smaller area, so the ground and air heat up more. The Sun also appears higher in the sky and stays up longer, so days are longer and there is more time for warming. That produces summer. At the same time, the Southern Hemisphere is tilted away, receiving slanted, more spread-out light and shorter days, which brings winter. Six months later the situation reverses.

Spring and autumn occur in between, when neither hemisphere is strongly tilted toward or away from the Sun, around the equinoxes in March and September, when day and night are nearly equal in length everywhere.

A common misconception is that summer happens when Earth is closest to the Sun. In fact, Earth is closest in early January, during Northern Hemisphere winter, and farthest in early July. The distance change is small, about 3 percent, and its effect is much weaker than that of the tilt. Evidence for the tilt explanation is that the two hemispheres have opposite seasons at the same time, which distance alone could not explain.

The tilt also explains why regions near the equator have little seasonal variation, since they receive fairly direct sunlight all year, while regions closer to the poles experience dramatic swings, including months of continuous daylight in summer and darkness in winter.

There's no single inventor of medicine, since healing practices developed gradually across many human societies over tens of thousands of years. Early humans likely treated injuries and illnesses using plants, splints, and wound care long before anyone wrote anything down. Some of the earliest known medical knowledge comes from ancient Mesopotamia, Egypt, India, and China. The Edwin Smith Papyrus from ancient Egypt, dating to around 1600 BCE, describes surgical cases, and Mesopotamian clay tablets record diagnoses and remedies. In India, the Ayurvedic texts attributed to figures like Charaka and Sushruta date to roughly the first millennium BCE, and Chinese medical writings such as the Yellow Emperor's Inner Classic emerged around the same era.

Hippocrates, a Greek physician who lived around 460 to 370 BCE, is often called the father of Western medicine. He is important because he moved medical thinking toward observation and natural explanations for disease rather than purely supernatural ones, and the Hippocratic Corpus, a collection of texts associated with him and his followers, shaped medical ethics for centuries. However, he built on earlier traditions rather than starting from nothing, and many of the texts attributed to him were likely written by others.

Imagine a town where everyone wants a house, and houses cost a lot, so people borrow money from a bank to buy one and promise to pay it back a little at a time. Normally the bank is careful and only lends to people it thinks can pay. In America in the early 2000s, banks stopped being careful. They lent money to people who had shaky jobs, little savings, or a history of not paying bills. These risky loans were called "subprime" loans. Some even started with tiny payments that suddenly got much bigger a couple of years later.

Why would a bank do something so silly? Because the bank didn't keep the loans. It sold them. Big Wall Street firms bought thousands of these home loans, mixed them together like a giant bag of candy, and sold pieces of the bag to investors all over the world. The idea was that even if a few people couldn't pay, most would, so the bag was safe. Companies whose job was to grade how safe things were gave many of these bags the best possible grade, a gold star, even though they were full of bad candy. Since the lender got paid as soon as the loan was sold, it didn't care much whether the borrower could ever pay it back.

Everyone also believed house prices would keep going up forever. If you couldn't pay, no problem, you could just sell the house for more than you paid. But around 2006 and 2007, house prices stopped rising and began to fall. Suddenly lots of people couldn't make their payments, couldn't sell their houses for enough, and lost their homes. The bags of loans that everyone thought were safe turned out to be full of rotten candy, and nobody knew exactly how much rotten candy was in whose bag.

That is when the real panic started. Banks lend money to each other every day, a bit like kids lending each other lunch money. When nobody knew which banks were holding rotten loans, they stopped trusting each other and stopped lending. Many banks had also borrowed huge amounts to buy these investments, so even a small loss could wipe them out. In September 2008 a giant bank called Lehman Brothers collapsed, and a huge insurance company called AIG, which had promised to cover losses on these loans, nearly collapsed too. The whole money system froze, like the blood in a body's veins suddenly stopping.

In the United States, the consequences were painful. The government and the central bank, the Federal Reserve, spent enormous sums rescuing banks and car companies because they feared that letting everything fall would be even worse. Interest rates were pushed down to almost zero to get money moving again. Even so, millions of people lost their jobs, millions lost their homes, and many families lost a big chunk of their savings and retirement money. This long slump became known as the Great Recession. Lots of people were angry that the banks that caused the mess got rescued while ordinary people suffered. Afterward, Congress passed new rules, the Dodd-Frank Act, to make banks keep more money as a safety cushion and to protect borrowers.

Europe got hit in two ways. First, many European banks, especially in Germany, Britain, Ireland, and elsewhere, had bought those same bags of American loans, so they lost money directly. Some countries also had their own housing bubbles, especially Ireland, Spain, and Britain, which popped at the same time. Banks there needed rescuing too; Britain, for example, took over banks like Northern Rock and the Royal Bank of Scotland.

Second, and this is the part that hurt Europe for longer, the crisis turned into what is called the euro crisis. When governments rescued their banks and their economies shrank, they had to borrow a lot. Investors started to worry that some countries, like Greece, Ireland, Portugal, Spain, and Italy, might not be able to pay their debts back. Greece turned out to have hidden how much it already owed. Because these countries shared the euro, they couldn't just print their own money or make their currency cheaper to help themselves, and their troubles worried the whole group. Other European countries and the International Monetary Fund lent them rescue money, but with strict conditions: cut spending, raise taxes, and shrink the government. This was called austerity. It was very hard on ordinary people. In Greece and Spain, about one in four workers had no job at one point, and for young people it was around one in two. Wages and pensions were cut, and there were large protests. The European Central Bank eventually promised in 2012 to do "whatever it takes" to save the euro, which calmed things down, and Europe later created new shared rules for watching over its big banks.

So in very simple terms: people were lent money they couldn't pay back, those loans were dressed up as safe and sold around the world, house prices fell, the loans went bad, banks stopped trusting each other, and the whole system nearly broke. America suffered a deep recession and huge job and home losses, then recovered somewhat faster. Europe suffered the same shock and then a second wave of debt troubles that lasted years longer, left deep scars in countries like Greece and Spain, and caused a lot of anger toward banks and politicians on both sides of the Atlantic.

Parking spaces and garage boxes can make sound investments, though the outcome depends on several considerations. When judging the investment potential of one of these properties, the following factors deserve attention. First, location matters a great deal: spaces in busy urban districts where parking is scarce tend to hold more value than those in quieter, less crowded areas. Second, physical condition plays a role, since a space that is well kept will generally be worth more than one that has fallen into disrepair. Third, local demand influences value, as a space in an area where many people want parking may command a higher price or rent. Fourth, cost is important, because if the purchase or lease price is low relative to the return you could reasonably expect, the space may prove a worthwhile investment. In the end, whether a particular parking space or garage box is a good investment depends on its specific circumstances and calls for individual assessment. Doing some research and speaking with a financial advisor or real estate professional can provide useful guidance.

Water can actually work as a moisturizer, it just depends on how you use it. Like, when you hop in the shower and wash up with soap, you're stripping away a lot of your skin's natural oils, and that's why it ends up feeling dry and tight afterward. That's the reason a lot of people slap on moisturizer right after, to put those oils back and keep their skin soft and hydrated. But if you're just splashing your face with water, or spritzing it with a facial spray that's mostly water, that can actually help hydrate your skin and make it feel more moisturized. So really it comes down to how you're using it and what else you're pairing it with.

A swelling and sore at the corner of the mouth can have several causes. Common ones include impetigo, a bacterial skin infection that often forms crusty, honey-colored sores around the mouth and nose. Angular cheilitis, an irritation or infection where the lip corners stay moist, is another possibility, often from drooling, lip licking, or a yeast or bacterial overgrowth. A cold sore (herpes simplex) usually starts as a cluster of small blisters, not one large sore. An abscess or boil can form after a bite, scratch, or hair follicle infection. An allergic or contact reaction, such as to a lip balm, toothpaste, food, or the medication itself, can also cause swelling. The fact that Benadryl reduces the swelling suggests an allergic or histamine-driven component, though that alone doesn't identify the cause.

Your doctor prescribing penicillin suggests they suspected a bacterial infection, possibly impetigo or a skin infection. However, you're right to be concerned that the swelling hasn't gone down after two days. Antibiotics for a skin infection often start to show improvement within 48 hours, so lack of improvement could mean the diagnosis is off, the bacteria aren't responding, or she may be reacting to the drug.

Please call her doctor or the urgent care clinic and tell them the swelling is not improving and that Benadryl only helps temporarily. Ask whether the penicillin could be causing a reaction, whether she should stop it, and whether a different antibiotic or a swab culture is needed. A pediatrician or dermatologist can also take a closer look if it persists.

Seek emergency care right away if she develops swelling of the lips, tongue, or throat, trouble breathing or swallowing, hives spreading across her body, fever that is rising, rapidly spreading redness, or unusual sleepiness or confusion.

Jay McCarroll won season 2 of Project Runway... actually, let me correct that: Jay McCarroll won season 1, which aired in 2004. Season 2, which aired in 2005, was won by Chloe Dao. Daniel Vosovic and Nick Verreos were the other finalists who showed collections at Bryant Park that season, and Santino Rice was also a notable contestant, though he did not make the finale. Chloe Dao, a Houston-based designer, won the prize package that included funding to launch her line, a spread in Elle magazine, and a car.

So at a dim sum place you usually end up at a big shared table, and servers wheel carts around with little plates of food on them. That's the "dim sum" part. It's a Cantonese thing, basically lots of small dishes like dumplings, buns, and other bite-sized stuff.

Ordering is easy. You just wave down someone with a cart and pick whatever looks good. Some places also have a menu you can order from instead, or on top of the carts. Either way, the server marks what you got on a tally sheet, and if it's something made to order, they bring it out when it's ready.

A lot of these restaurants run on a kind of point system, where what you pay depends on how many dishes you took. Besides the dim sum itself, you'll often find other things too, like soups, noodles, and rice dishes, and some spots have desserts and drinks as well. It's usually a pretty loud, social kind of meal, and the best part is you get to try a bunch of different dishes and flavors in one sitting.

Sorry, but I haven't heard of any big changes in programming at Discovery Channel or National Geographic. Could be that what you're seeing is just a temporary shift in the schedule. Or maybe your own viewing habits have changed, so you're running into those kinds of shows more often now. It's also possible you're remembering the old days a little differently than how they really were, and those channels have always had a mix of stuff, science shows and not-so-science shows alike. If you want a better feel for what they actually put out, I'd try watching a bunch of different programs on both channels and see what you think.

So basically, emerging technologies are the new stuff that's still being developed but is expected to shake things up pretty soon, whether that's in society, industry, or the economy. They're usually still early-stage. Not fully mature, not widely used yet, but they've got the potential to disrupt whole industries and even create brand new ones.

Think artificial intelligence, blockchain, the Internet of Things, renewable energy, biotech, nanotechnology, and a bunch of others. What they tend to have in common is that they drive change and innovation, they can wreck existing business models, and they're evolving and getting adopted really fast.

They also don't come cheap. Most need a lot of investment in research and development, plus big changes to infrastructure, regulation, and policy before they can really grow and catch on. That's why governments, businesses, and investors keep a close eye on them. Everybody wants to figure out what the impact could be and grab a piece of the opportunity.

Great question! Bytes do take up real space, just not the kind of space you can hold in your hand as a little blob of stuff.

Think of your hard drive as a huge row of tiny light switches. Each switch can be in one of two positions, on or off. A byte is a group of eight of these switches, and by setting each one on or off, you can make 256 different patterns. Those patterns are how computers store letters, pictures, songs, and everything else.

So what are the switches actually made of? On a traditional hard drive, the switches are tiny spots on a spinning metal disk. Each spot is magnetized one way or the other, north or south, and that magnetic direction is the on or off. A little arm with a reader zips over the disk to check which way each spot points. On a solid state drive, which is the kind in most laptops now, the switches are tiny electrical traps built into a computer chip. Each trap either holds a bit of electric charge or doesn't.

So a byte occupies a real, physical spot on the drive. It is just an incredibly small one, far smaller than a grain of sand. Your 1 TB drive has about a trillion of these tiny switch-groups lined up, each holding one byte, and that is why it is called "1 terabyte."

Tennessee has no general principal residence or homestead exemption like the ones in Florida or Texas. Homes are taxed at their assessed value, and the state doesn't reduce that value for owner-occupied property across the board.

It does offer a targeted property tax relief program for qualifying homeowners. Homeowners who are at least 65, or who are totally and permanently disabled, and who meet an income limit can have part of their property taxes on their primary residence reduced. Veterans with a service-connected disability may also qualify under related provisions. You apply through your county property assessor or trustee's office, and the eligibility rules, income thresholds, and benefit amounts are set by statute and change periodically, so check the current details with your county or the Tennessee Comptroller's office.

On the income tax side, Tennessee no longer taxes wages or most investment income, since the Hall income tax was fully repealed effective 2021. That means no state tax on gains from selling a home either. The federal home sale exclusion under Section 121 still applies, generally excluding up to $250,000 of gain for a single filer or $500,000 for a married couple filing jointly who have owned and lived in the home for at least two of the prior five years.

Okay so computer simulation is basically using a computer to model how some system or process behaves. You build a mathematical model of the thing, then run the computer through it to see what happens. The whole point is to copy the real behavior as closely as you can so you can learn stuff, make predictions, or check whether an idea holds up. People use it everywhere: engineers test how aircraft handle, epidemiologists guess how a disease might spread, economists poke at market trends. It's especially handy when doing the real experiment would be impossible, dangerous, or just way too expensive, since it's often cheaper to simulate a design than to build and break a bunch of prototypes. Simulations come in all shapes too. Some are tiny models with a handful of variables, and others are huge tangles of interacting parts. Some let you tweak things live and watch the results change, while others just run on their own and spit out graphs, charts, or tables for you to dig through. All in all, it's a really useful tool for wrapping your head around complicated systems and making better calls.

Tony Hoare is a British computer scientist, and honestly one of the big names in the field. He's best known for his work on ALGOL, and he's made a lot of contributions to programming, computer science theory, and the whole idea of software engineering as its own discipline. In 1980 he won the ACM Turing Award, which people often call the "Nobel Prize" of computing. It was for his work on defining and designing programming languages, and CSP (communicating sequential processes) is a big part of that story too. He's also a Fellow of the Royal Society, and yeah, he's got the OBE as well.

The thin layer you notice around the edges of cooked eggs is often called a film or skin. It appears when the proteins in the eggs begin to cook and set. As heat is applied, the proteins in both the whites and the yolks denature, meaning they unfold, and then coagulate, meaning they thicken and firm up. While coagulating, they may cling to the sides of the pan and create a thin film.

Several approaches may keep this film from forming. First, cook in a non-stick pan. Its special coating keeps food from sticking, which can lessen the film. Second, add a small amount of oil or butter to the pan before the eggs go in, since this also discourages sticking and film formation. Third, use a silicone or rubber spatula to scrape along the pan's edges as the eggs cook, which can stop the film from developing. Finally, keep the heat low. With gentler heat the proteins cook more slowly, so they have less time to attach to the sides of the pan.

Of course! Talking with a distant spacecraft, such as Rosetta, which journeyed more than 300 million miles from Earth, relies on large radio antennas here on the ground that beam signals up to the craft, while the spacecraft's own antenna transmits signals back down to us. These radio waves cross the vast emptiness of space and are picked up by the antenna on the other end. The messages may carry instructions telling the spacacraft to carry out particular activities, or they may contain data the craft has gathered. To ensure the signals are strong enough to make the long trip, Earth-based stations use extremely powerful transmitters, and the spacecraft is equipped with highly sensitive receivers. Engineers also apply special methods so that the signals are not cut off or garbled by interference from other radio sources or from objects in space. I hope this clarifies how we manage to communicate with spacecraft located so far from home! Feel free to ask if anything else comes to mind.

Several common conditions can cause nausea, vomiting, and dizziness that are worse when you lie down, and I can't tell which one is behind your symptoms without an examination. The pattern you describe, especially waking up suddenly nauseated, points toward a few possibilities.

One is benign positional vertigo, where tiny crystals in the inner ear shift and trigger brief spinning dizziness with changes in head position, often in bed. Another is a vestibular migraine, which can cause dizziness and nausea with or without headache. Acid reflux is also worth considering, since lying flat lets stomach acid move upward and can wake you with nausea. Sleep apnea can cause nausea, morning headaches, and disrupted sleep, and it's more common than people expect in young men, particularly if you snore or wake gasping. Heavy cannabis use can cause cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome, which produces repeated vomiting and nausea, sometimes relieved by hot showers. Less often, problems like delayed stomach emptying, inner ear disorders such as Ménière's disease, or medication side effects can be responsible.

Because symptoms have lasted several months, you should see a doctor soon, ideally a primary care physician who can order basic tests and refer you to an ENT or neurologist if needed. Before the visit, it helps to keep a short log of when episodes happen, what you ate or drank, any cannabis or alcohol use, your sleep quality, and any medications you take. Tell the doctor about any snoring or daytime sleepiness too.

Seek emergency care right away if you have a severe or sudden headache, vision changes, double vision, weakness or numbness, slurred speech, trouble walking, confusion, fainting, blood in your vomit, chest pain, or vomiting that prevents you from keeping fluids down. These are uncommon causes, but they need prompt evaluation.

So type 1 diabetes is basically when your immune system gets confused and attacks the cells in your pancreas that make insulin. Insulin is the hormone that regulates your blood sugar (glucose), and it's what lets your body actually use that glucose for energy. Without enough of it, the sugar just hangs around in your blood and your levels climb way too high.

People with type 1 don't make enough insulin on their own, so they have to replace it, either with injections or an insulin pump. That lets the body use the glucose in their blood the way it's supposed to.

Even with treatment, though, it doesn't always work out perfectly. Insulin needs can shift, like when you're exercising or sick, or you might eat more sugar than your body can handle at that moment. When that happens, someone with type 1 may need to eat some sugar or other carbs to get their blood sugar back in balance.

Hope that helps! Ask away if you've got other questions.

Therapy may help ease the stiffness and improve the use of your husband's hand following a stroke. Still, how well therapy works depends on several things, such as how severe the stroke was, where it occurred, how long ago it happened, and his general health and fitness. Consulting a healthcare provider, such as a physical or occupational therapist, is the best way to decide on the right approach for him. These professionals can evaluate what he is currently able to do, identify what he needs, and build a plan designed around his particular goals. Keep in mind that stroke recovery often takes a long time and tends to move forward slowly and unevenly. Patience and a hopeful outlook matter, since even modest gains can make a meaningful difference in daily life.

You're definitely not alone. Foot cramps are really common, and lots of people know exactly that sharp, grabbing pain you're describing. You're not out of luck, either, because there are things that usually help.

Here's the simple version of what's happening. Your muscles are like little rubber bands that squeeze and then let go. Normally your brain tells them "squeeze" and then "relax." During a cramp, a muscle gets stuck on "squeeze" and won't let go. It clenches as hard as it can all by itself, and that's why it hurts so much and why your toes might curl or point in weird directions.

Nobody knows every reason this happens, but some common ones are being a little low on water, being low on certain minerals your muscles use to relax (like magnesium, potassium, and calcium), muscles that are tired from lots of standing or exercise, muscles that are tight because you haven't stretched them, shoes that squish your feet, or sitting or lying in one position for a long time. Cramps also tend to happen more at night, as people get older, during pregnancy, and with some medicines.

When one hits, the best trick is to gently stretch the muscle the opposite way it's pulling. If your toes are curling down, pull them back up toward your knee, or stand up and put your weight on that foot. Rubbing the spot, walking around, or using warmth like a warm towel or a bath can help the muscle remember how to relax.

To make them happen less often, drink enough water through the day, eat foods with those minerals (bananas, potatoes, leafy greens, nuts, yogurt), stretch your feet and calves before bed, and wear comfy, supportive shoes. Some people also find that rolling their foot over a ball helps.

If the cramps happen a lot, are getting worse, come with numbness, weakness, swelling, or color changes in your foot, or started after you began a new medicine, it's worth telling a doctor. Sometimes cramps are a clue that something else, like a circulation, nerve, or mineral problem, needs checking. But most of the time they're just annoying muscles having a tantrum, and stretching plus water goes a long way.

Yes, phobias can be overcome, and many people with a fear of bugs get much better over time. The most effective method is something called exposure therapy. The idea is simple: your brain learns that bugs are not dangerous by seeing that nothing bad happens when you are near them. You start small, like looking at a picture of a bug, then maybe watching a video, then looking at a bug through a window or in a jar, and slowly working your way closer. Each step, you stay calm for a little while, and your body learns that the fear is bigger than the actual danger.

Your heart skipping is your body's alarm system going off. It's a normal reaction, a bit like a smoke alarm that goes off when someone burns toast. Over time, with practice, the alarm gets less sensitive. Some people also find it helpful to take slow, deep breaths when they feel the fear start, breathing in for a count of four and out for a count of four. This tells your body it's safe to calm down.

A doctor, school counselor, or therapist can help you with this, especially someone who knows about exposure therapy. You don't have to do it all at once, and you can go at your own speed. Taking small brave steps is how most people beat a fear like this.

Smart traffic lights are signals fitted with sensors, cameras, and other devices that let them respond to shifting traffic patterns and enhance the flow of vehicles. They are able to exchange information with neighboring signals and with cars on the road in order to fine-tune green light timing and cut down on holdups and gridlock. At intersections, these lights rely on sensors to spot vehicles, pedestrians, and cyclists as they approach and move through. Using that data, they can alter green light durations according to how heavy traffic is, how fast cars are moving, and other conditions. For instance, when a busy road has many vehicles stacked up behind a red light, the signal might lengthen the green phase so that more cars can get through the crossing. Communication is also carried out through dedicated short-range communications (DSRC), a wireless standard built for transportation, which lets signals and vehicles work together to keep traffic moving smoothly and to boost safety. The overall aim of smart traffic lights is to make traffic more efficient, reduce congestion and delays, and protect everyone using the roads, whether they are walking, cycling, or driving. As cities seek better transportation systems and lower vehicle emissions, these signals are becoming more widespread in urban areas worldwide.

China's a one-party communist state, so the Communist Party of China holds all the political power. The top leadership is the Politburo, and it's run by the Communist Party's General Secretary. As for censorship, the big one is the Great Firewall, a set of technical controls that block or filter online content the government sees as inappropriate or a security risk. Traditional media gets the same treatment: TV and newspapers can only publish or broadcast what the state allows. And if someone speaks out against the government or pushes views that clash with party policy, they can face punishment, sometimes serious.

Imagine your wall outlet is like a garden hose with a small trickle of water. It can fill a bucket slowly, but it can't shoot a big splash all at once. A railgun needs a huge splash of energy in a tiny fraction of a second, and the outlet just can't deliver that fast enough.

Here's the idea. A railgun pushes a metal piece along two metal rails using electricity. To make it go really fast, you need a enormous jolt of power for a very short time, like a giant gulp instead of a sip. Capacitors are like a big bucket you fill up slowly over time and then dump all at once. The outlet fills the bucket, and then the bucket gives the big splash to the railgun.

Plugging the rails straight into the outlet would be like trying to make a huge splash by just turning on the tap. The wall outlet might only supply around 15 amps at 120 volts in a home, which is far too little for a railgun. Also, if you tried to pull that much power directly, you would likely trip the breaker, blow a fuse, or overheat the wiring. So the capacitors act as a middleman that stores energy quietly and then releases it all in one burst.

That's also why railguns need recharging between shots. The bucket has to be refilled before it can splash again, and that takes time.

Howard H. Aiken (1900–1973) was an American physicist, computer pioneer, and Harvard University professor best known for designing the Harvard Mark I, also called the IBM Automatic Sequence Controlled Calculator (ASCC). Completed in 1944 in collaboration with IBM engineers, the Mark I was an electromechanical computer that could carry out long sequences of arithmetic operations automatically by reading instructions from punched paper tape. It was one of the first large-scale automatic digital computers built in the United States and played a role in wartime calculations for the U.S. Navy.

Before building the machine, Aiken had worked on the problem of solving complex differential equations used in physics and engineering, and he envisioned a machine that could perform such calculations without constant human intervention. His ideas drew on earlier work with mechanical calculators and on Charles Babbage's Analytical Engine, which Aiken admired and studied. He later oversaw the Harvard Computation Laboratory and designed subsequent machines, including the Mark II, Mark III, and Mark IV, which advanced the development of electronic computing in the postwar period.

Aiken is remembered as an important figure in the history of computing, helping to bridge the mechanical calculating devices of the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries and the electronic stored-program computers that followed. He also trained many students who went on to influential careers in the field.

Toasting makes bread taste better mostly because of a chemical change called the Maillard reaction, plus a bit of caramelization. When the surface of bread gets hot enough, usually above about 300 degrees Fahrenheit, the sugars and proteins in the bread start reacting with each other. This creates new flavor molecules that smell and taste toasty, nutty, and a little sweet. Regular bread doesn't have these flavors because it never gets hot enough for this reaction to happen.

Think of it like this: bread is a bit like a cookie dough that never got baked all the way. Heat turns the outside into something new and more interesting.

Toasting also dries out the surface. Less moisture means the bread crisps up instead of staying soft and chewy, and crispy things often taste stronger because the flavors are more concentrated. The crunch itself feels good too, which makes the whole thing more enjoyable to eat.

Finally, toast is warm, and warm food usually smells stronger. Since much of what we taste is actually smell, that warm, toasty aroma makes the bread seem tastier.

Grocery stores offer cash back mostly because it's convenient. If you're paying cash and come up a bit short, or just want some extra bills on hand, you can grab it right at the register instead of hunting down an ATM. It also helps the store out a little. Timing the market means trying to guess when prices will go up so you can buy, and when they'll go down so you can sell first. The problem is that nobody can guess that reliably. Prices move because of news, surprises, and the mood of millions of people, and those things can't be predicted. It's like trying to know exactly when it will rain next week. Some people get lucky once, but doing it again and again is very hard.

Here's the tricky part: the market's best days often happen right next to its worst days. When prices suddenly jump, they often do it during a scary drop, when many people have already run away. If you sold because you were scared and then missed the big bounce back, you lost out. Studies have found that missing just a handful of the best days over several decades can cut someone's total gains in half or more.

Feelings make it worse. When prices are falling, people get scared and sell, which often means selling at the lowest price. When prices are rising fast, people get excited and buy, which often means buying near the top. So many investors end up doing the opposite of what would make money: buying high and selling low.

Trading a lot also costs money. Every trade can come with fees, and selling investments you held for less than a year can mean paying more tax. These small costs add up and quietly eat into gains.

That's why many people who keep their money invested steadily for a long time, and don't jump in and out based on guesses, tend to do better. The stock market has gone up over long periods, but the path is bumpy, and the people who lose are often the ones who try to skip the bumps.

Here is some free, practical budgeting advice you can start using right away.

Begin by tracking everything you spend for at least a month. Check your bank and card statements, or simply jot purchases in a notebook or a free app. Most people are surprised by where their money actually goes, and you can't plan well without that picture.

Next, list your income and fixed expenses such as rent, utilities, insurance, debt payments, and subscriptions. Subtract those from your take-home pay to see what remains for flexible spending like groceries, dining out, and entertainment. If the numbers come out negative, look first at subscriptions you no longer use, then at recurring costs you could reduce, like switching phone plans or cooking more meals at home.

A popular starting framework is the 50/30/20 rule: roughly half your after-tax income for needs, about 30 percent for wants, and 20 percent for savings and debt repayment. Treat it as a rough guide rather than a strict law, and adjust the percentages to your situation, especially if you have high rent or heavy debt.

Build a small emergency fund before aggressively paying extra on other goals. Even one month of essential expenses set aside in a savings account can keep a car repair or medical bill from turning into credit card debt.

If you carry high-interest debt, such as credit cards, consider either the avalanche method (paying the highest interest rate first) or the snowball method (paying the smallest balance first for quick wins). Either works; the best one is the one you will stick with.

Automate what you can. Set up automatic transfers to savings on payday so saving happens before you have a chance to spend the money. Automating bill payments also helps you avoid late fees.

Finally, review your budget monthly and adjust it. Your budget is a living plan, not a one-time exercise. Celebrate small milestones, and be patient with yourself if a month goes over. The goal is steady progress, not perfection.

Many of the technologies that shaped the world came out of ancient and medieval China. Papermaking, traditionally credited to Cai Lun during the Han dynasty around 105 CE, spread from China across Asia and eventually to Europe. Printing followed, first with woodblocks and later with movable type, which Bi Sheng developed from clay characters around 1040 CE, centuries before Gutenberg's press in Europe. The compass, first used for divination and later for navigation, was refined in China and became essential to maritime travel. Gunpowder emerged from alchemical experiments during the Tang dynasty and was later used in weapons, fireworks, and early rockets.

China also contributed the seismograph, invented by Zhang Heng in 132 CE to detect distant earthquakes, and the south-pointing chariot, an early mechanical device that maintained a fixed direction. Silk production, which dates back thousands of years, was a closely guarded technique for much of antiquity. Other notable inventions include the abacus for calculation, the umbrella, the wheelbarrow, cast iron metallurgy, porcelain, the kite, and the crossbow with a trigger mechanism. Acupuncture and various herbal medicine practices also developed over many centuries, and chess-like games and early forms of paper money were likewise Chinese innovations.

A breeze can make you feel chillier because it speeds up how quickly your body loses heat. Your body is constantly releasing warmth, and that warmth escapes into the surrounding air. In calm conditions, this loss happens slowly, but when the air is moving, as it does on a windy day, the loss happens more quickly. That is why a windy day can feel colder than a still one, even when the thermometer shows the same reading.

Picture yourself standing outside on a cold day in a warm coat. The coat holds a thin layer of heated air close to your skin, and this layer helps you stay comfortable. If the wind picks up, however, it can sweep that warm layer away and bring in colder air in its place. As a result, you feel colder, even though the actual temperature has not shifted at all.

Wind chill is a measure of how much colder the wind makes the air feel. It combines the air temperature and the wind speed to produce a "feels like" temperature. For instance, if it is 10 degrees Fahrenheit outside and the wind is blowing at 20 miles per hour, the wind chill would be -9 degrees Fahrenheit, meaning it would feel about 19 degrees colder than the real temperature.

Film colorization refers to the act of adding color to a film or video that is in black and white, grayscale, or already partly colored. It can be carried out by hand or with computer programs, with the aim of producing a version that appears as though it had been filmed in color from the start. Several methods exist, such as painting each frame individually, relying on specialized software to colorize the footage automatically, or combining the two approaches. Supporters contend that colorization can enrich the experience by introducing visual appeal and helping the work connect with contemporary viewers. Critics, however, argue that it can weaken the historical and artistic significance of a monochrome film and that the original form should be kept as its creators intended. Whatever one's view, colorization remains a contested and polarizing practice, and the decision rests ultimately with the filmmakers or whoever holds the rights to the work.

In California, a domestic partnership refers to a legal arrangement between two people who are not married but live together as a household and are emotionally and financially committed to each other. To qualify as domestic partners in the state, both people must satisfy several conditions. Each must be at least 18 years old. Neither can be related by blood or marriage to the other, and neither can be currently married to, or in a domestic partnership with, anyone else. They must share a common home and maintain an emotional and financial bond. They must also agree to take on joint responsibility for each other's essentials, including food, housing, and healthcare. Finally, both must be prepared to register their partnership with the California Secretary of State. A domestic partnership is not equivalent to marriage and does not carry the identical legal benefits and protections. Nevertheless, registered domestic partners hold many of the same rights and duties that married couples have under California law.

When a fighter pilot pulls hard into a sharp turn, the force of acceleration pushes their blood down toward their legs and away from their head and eyes. Their brain starts running low on blood and oxygen, and the body reacts in a few ways that can make the face look strange.

First, the muscles in the face and neck tense up as the body fights to keep blood flowing to the brain. Pilots also clench their jaw, scrunch their eyes, and grimace, partly because they are trying to strain against the force, and partly because the body is in a kind of emergency mode. Some pilots even make a grunting or straining sound, which is part of the same effort.

Second, the lack of blood to the brain and eyes affects how the face and eyes look. Vision starts to narrow and go gray or dark, and the skin can look pale or stretched because the blood is being pulled away from the head. The pressure also pushes the cheeks, lips, and eyelids in odd directions, so the face can look squished or pulled.

So the funny-looking face is basically the body's way of struggling. The pilot's muscles are working hard, their blood is rushing the wrong way, and their brain is running out of the fuel it needs. That is why the face looks so strange just before they pass out.

I'm sorry you're in this much pain. A tooth with an unfinished root canal and a lost temporary filling needs dental care soon, but there are steps you can take today to ease the discomfort while you arrange that visit.

The most important step is to contact a dentist or endodontist (root canal specialist) as soon as possible, ideally today or tomorrow. Many dental offices keep emergency slots, and if yours cannot see you quickly, ask them for a referral to an emergency dental clinic or an after-hours urgent dental service. If you develop facial swelling, fever, trouble swallowing or breathing, or swelling that spreads toward your eye or neck, go to an emergency department right away, because an infection can become serious.

While you wait, you can try a few things. Rinse gently with warm salt water (half a teaspoon of salt in a glass of warm water) several times a day to keep the area clean. Avoid chewing on that side and keep food and drink that is very hot, very cold, or sugary away from the tooth. Sleeping with your head slightly raised can also reduce throbbing.

For pain, if you have no reason to avoid them, ibuprofen or naproxen are often more effective for dental pain than acetaminophen alone. You can also combine ibuprofen with acetaminophen, taking them at staggered times, but follow the package directions and do not exceed the maximum daily dose of either. Check with a pharmacist first if you have kidney, stomach, or liver problems, take blood thinners, are pregnant, or take other medications. Do not place aspirin or other pain tablets directly against the gum, as this can burn the tissue.

You can cover the exposed opening with a temporary dental filling material sold at pharmacies, or with a small piece of sugar-free gum, to keep food and air out of the tooth. This is only a short-term measure and does not replace seeing a dentist. Clove oil applied to the area may also numb it briefly.

Because the root canal was never completed, the tooth likely needs the treatment finished or, in some cases, extraction, so it is important that a dentist assess it soon rather than waiting for the pain to pass on its own.

Your symptoms could stem from a range of sources, such as underlying illnesses, daily habits, or the medications you take. Constant exhaustion and a racing heartbeat during activity may be linked to several possibilities. Heart-related problems, including heart disease, hypertension, or anemia, can leave a person tired and short of breath when exerting themselves. Lung conditions like asthma or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) can make breathing harder and bring on fatigue during physical effort. An underactive thyroid, known as hypothyroidism, can also produce tiredness and reduced stamina. Poorly controlled diabetes is another potential contributor. Everyday factors, including too little sleep, a poor diet, or overdoing physical activity, may also add to fatigue and make exercise harder. Finally, some medications, such as sedatives or antihistamines, are known to cause drowsiness and lower physical capacity. Because the cause can be difficult to pin down, it is worth consulting a healthcare professional who can identify the source of your symptoms and recommend suitable treatment.

Banks lose money on foreclosures mainly because the property they end up holding is worth less than what the borrower still owes, and the bank has to absorb the difference after all the costs of getting the home back and selling it.

The process starts with a loan that is secured by the house as collateral. When a borrower stops paying, the bank may spend months or years trying to collect before it can foreclose, and during that time it often stops receiving interest and principal while still paying property taxes, insurance, and sometimes homeowners association fees on the property. Legal fees for filing and prosecuting the foreclosure add up, and court costs vary widely by state. If the home is vacant when the bank takes possession, it may need to pay for locks, cleaning, trash removal, and basic repairs to keep the property from deteriorating further.

The biggest loss usually comes from the sale itself. Foreclosed homes often sell at a discount because they are sold quickly, sometimes at auction or in an as-is condition, and buyers know the seller is motivated. Homes that sat empty for a long time may have suffered damage from weather, vandalism, plumbing failures, or stripped fixtures, which lowers their value further. Real estate agent commissions, closing costs, and any outstanding liens or unpaid taxes that must be cleared before a sale also come out of the proceeds.

When the sale price does not cover the remaining loan balance plus all these expenses, the bank records a loss. In many cases, banks have already set aside reserves for expected losses on troubled loans, so the impact shows up in their financial statements over time. Whether the bank can recover the shortfall from the borrower depends on state law. Some states allow deficiency judgments that let the lender pursue the former owner for the gap, while others prohibit this, leaving the bank to bear the full loss.

The question is ambiguous because several civil wars have occurred in different countries, so I'll assume you mean the American Civil War, the best-known one. It was triggered primarily by the dispute over slavery and whether it would be allowed to expand into the western territories and new states. Tensions had built for decades through events such as the Missouri Compromise, the Compromise of 1850, and the Kansas-Nebraska Act of 1854, which let settlers decide slavery's status locally and led to violent conflict in Kansas. The Supreme Court's Dred Scott decision in 1857 further inflamed the North by ruling that Black Americans could not be citizens and that Congress could not ban slavery in the territories.

The immediate trigger came with Abraham Lincoln's election as president in November 1860. Lincoln opposed slavery's expansion, and though he did not promise to abolish it where it already existed, many Southern leaders viewed his victory as a threat to their way of life. South Carolina seceded in December 1860, and by early 1861 six more Deep South states had followed, forming the Confederate States of America. When Confederate forces attacked Fort Sumter in April 1861, and Lincoln called for troops to suppress the rebellion, four more states seceded and the war began.

If you meant a different civil war, such as the Spanish Civil War or the Russian Civil War, let me know and I can explain its causes.

Ever notice how so many things cost $9.99 instead of a nice round $10? That's called charm pricing, and stores lean on it because it works. The idea is that a price ending in 99 cents looks like it's sitting just under a whole dollar amount, so your brain reads it as a better deal. $9.99 feels closer to nine bucks than ten, even though you're only a penny off.

Retailers also use it for a few practical reasons. Say a store wants to charge $10 but doesn't want the item to look pricey. Dropping it to $9.99 can make it feel more affordable without really changing much. Shoppers tend to respond to that, so sales often go up. It's a small trick, but it's a popular one.

Think of college like a big club where you have to show a ticket to get in, and then you have to keep showing you're doing your part to stay in good standing. Getting in is one step, and grades are one way the school checks how you're doing with the work it asks of you.

Here's the simple idea. Your high school grades were like a ticket that said, "I can handle learning." Once you're in, college wants to see that you actually learn the things you're studying. Grades are how teachers keep track of that. They also help you figure out what you understand and what you still need to practice.

Grades matter after you get in for a few reasons. Many colleges have rules that you must keep a certain grade average to stay enrolled, and if it drops too low you can be put on probation or even asked to leave. Some majors, like nursing or engineering, require you to pass certain classes with a decent grade before you can move on to harder ones, because each class builds on the last. And when you finish, employers and graduate schools often look at your grades to see what kind of student you were.

So the high school grades got you through the door, and college grades show whether you're keeping up once you're inside and whether you'll be ready for what comes next.

Blue Brain is a research initiative that seeks to build a digital replica of the human brain through sophisticated computer simulations. Started in 2005 at the École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne (EPFL) in Switzerland, it receives partial funding from the Swiss government and the European Union. The project aims to uncover how the brain is organized and how it operates in far more depth than conventional experimental methods allow. Researchers believe that a digital model of this kind could shed light on how the brain functions and lead to new therapies for neurological disorders. To do this, the project combines experimental measurements with computational modeling. The team relies on high-resolution microscopy and other methods to examine brain tissue at the cellular level, then feeds these findings into a digital model that captures neurons, synapses, and other structures. Blue Brain has made notable advances in understanding the brain's structure and function and has produced many scientific papers and patents. Even so, the work is ongoing, and a complete digital reconstruction of the brain still requires a great deal more effort.

Great question! Imagine you have a big wall covered in little bumpy dots, and you want to find the one spot where a message is written. Blind people have a few helpful tricks for this.

First, Braille signs are usually put in places that are easy to find by touch. Many are placed right beside a door handle, on the wall at about the height of a hand, or on the door itself. A blind person can run their fingers along the wall or door frame until they feel the bumps. Sometimes there are also raised lines or special textured strips on the floor that lead people straight to the sign's spot, kind of like a bumpy road map.

Second, Braille has a clear starting point. Each line of Braille begins at the same side, the left, just like how we start reading a book at the top left corner. So once someone finds the first bump, they know to start there and move from left to right. When they reach the end of a line, they slide their finger down to the next row and start again at the left edge.

Third, lots of people who read Braille get very good at feeling the patterns of the dots quickly, almost like how you can recognize your name on a page without sounding out each letter. Their fingers learn the shapes, so finding and reading a short sign becomes quick and natural.

Finally, many signs are short, like "Exit" or "Restroom," so there isn't a long sentence to hunt through. And when a sign is hard to find, a blind person can always ask someone nearby for help, just like you might ask a friend where the bathroom is.

Human height is typically measured with a stadiometer, a vertical ruler or rod fixed to a wall or floor, often with a movable headpiece that rests on the top of the head. The person stands barefoot with heels together, back against the rod, and looks straight ahead with the head held so that the line of sight is horizontal, a position sometimes called the Frankfort plane. Shoulders should be relaxed and the arms hanging at the sides. The measurer lowers the headpiece until it presses firmly on the crown, compressing the hair as little as possible, and then reads the height in centimeters or inches.

When a stadiometer is unavailable, a simpler method uses a tape measure fixed to a flat wall, with a book or flat object placed on the head and pressed against the wall to mark the reading. Self-reported height, such as from a driver's license or a personal estimate, is common in surveys but tends to be somewhat inaccurate, often overstating height for men and sometimes for women as well, so measured values are preferred in clinical and research settings.

Height can also vary slightly over the course of a day, since spinal discs compress under gravity and decompress overnight, so measurements are usually taken at a consistent time, often in the morning, for the most reliable comparisons.

What you're describing is almost certainly a fake invoice scam, one of the most common frauds aimed at website and small business owners. Scammers scrape domain registration records, business directories, and contact forms, then send official-looking "past due" notices for SEO, search engine submission, domain listing, or website maintenance services you never ordered. The fact that several different companies are contacting you with the same claim is a strong sign, because legitimate vendors don't appear out of nowhere demanding payment for work you didn't request. The urgency, threats of late fees, collections, or your website being "deactivated," and vague descriptions of the services are all designed to pressure you into paying before you think it through.

Start by checking your own records. Search your email, bank and credit card statements, and any contracts for the company names or invoice numbers. If you or someone on your team never signed an agreement or received services from them, you don't owe anything. If you run a business with multiple people, quickly confirm that no colleague hired an SEO firm, but if nobody recognizes it, treat it as fraudulent.

Don't pay, don't reply, and don't click any links or open attachments in these messages. Links can lead to phishing pages that steal login or payment details, and attachments can carry malware. Replying, even to dispute the charge, confirms your address is active and usually leads to more messages. If you want to verify a company, look it up independently instead of using the contact details in the email, though you'll often find nothing or only complaints from other recipients.

You can report these messages to cut down on them and help others. In the United States, report to the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov, and forward phishing emails to reportphishing@apwg.org. In the UK, forward them to report@phishing.gov.uk or report through Action Fraud. Most email providers also let you mark the messages as phishing or spam, which trains the filter. If you happen to have already paid one, contact your bank or card issuer right away to dispute the charge and ask about blocking further transactions, and change any passwords you may have entered on a linked site.

To reduce future contacts, check whether your domain has privacy protection turned on with your registrar, since exposed WHOIS contact information is a common source for these mailing lists. Using a separate address for public listings or contact forms can also keep your main inbox cleaner. If any message includes specific information that makes you think there might be a real account involved, such as an actual contract you signed, you can ask the company in writing for a signed agreement and an itemized record of work, but genuine scams will rarely be able to produce one.

Honestly it depends on where you are. The first weekend of September isn't a holiday everywhere, but a few holidays land on or close to it in different parts of the world.
