Four Thirds cameras are digital models built around a particular lens mount and sensor format. The Four Thirds system was designed as a standard for digital cameras with interchangeable lenses, and Olympus and Kodak introduced it in 2002. Its sensor is smaller than the full-frame sensors traditionally found in DSLR (digital single-lens reflex) cameras. Because of this, Four Thirds cameras are generally more compact and lighter than full-frame ones, which appeals to photographers who value portability. These cameras also rely on their own lens mount, known as the Four Thirds mount, which accepts only lenses made specifically for the system. Such lenses tend to be smaller and lighter than full-frame lenses, so they suit photographers seeking compact, lightweight options. All in all, Four Thirds cameras strike a good balance between image quality and portability, and they are a favored option for anyone who wants a small, light camera that can still deliver high-quality images.

A Solo 401(k), which is also called a self-employed 401(k) or an individual 401(k), is a retirement plan built for self-employed people and small business owners whose only employee is their spouse. It works much like a traditional 401(k), but its structure is adapted to the particular circumstances of self-employed workers and small business owners. Because you are both the employer and the employee, you can contribute to a Solo 401(k) in each role. As the employer, you may contribute up to 25% of your net self-employment income, with a cap of $58,000 for 2021 ($64,500 if you are 50 or older). As the employee, you may contribute up to $19,500 for 2021 ($26,000 if you are 50 or older). If you also take part in an employer-sponsored 401(k), the combined contributions to all 401(k) plans, including your Solo 401(k) and the employer plan, cannot exceed the 401(k) annual limit of $19,500 for 2021 ($26,000 if you are 50 or older). This ceiling covers everything you put into any 401(k) plan you participate in, whether the money comes in as an employee or as an employer. If you are self-employed and earn income from a Schedule C business, your Solo 401(k) contributions can be based on the net self-employment income from that business. Still, you must weigh both the Solo 401(k) limits and the overall 401(k) limits when deciding how much to put in. The limits for Solo 401(k) plans can differ from those for traditional 401(k) plans, so you should make sure you understand the rules that govern your specific plan. For questions about how much you can contribute to a Solo 401(k), or how it interacts with an employer-sponsored 401(k), consult a financial professional or a tax advisor.

Dr. Spencer Johnson wrote "Who Moved My Cheese?" as a parable about change. Two mice, Sniff and Scurry, and two tiny humans, Hem and Haw, race through a maze in search of cheese. That cheese stands for whatever a person wants, such as a job, a relationship, or something else entirely. In the beginning, all four characters have been finding cheese in the same spot. Then one day it is gone. Sniff and Scurry act fast, heading out into the maze to look for more, whereas Hem and Haw have trouble accepting the shift and keep returning to the old spot, hoping the cheese will reappear. Gradually, Hem and Haw realize the cheese is not coming back and that they must adjust and keep moving. Only after moving through denial, anger, bargaining, and eventually acceptance do they finally find new cheese. The story works as a metaphor for the changes everyone faces and how we can learn to adjust to them. Its lesson is that we should stay open to change and actively look for new opportunities and experiences, instead of holding on to the past and to things that are no longer within reach.

Smell is made of tiny, tiny pieces of stuff that float through the air, so it travels more like a gas than like sound. Sound is a wiggle that moves through the air without the air itself going anywhere, a bit like a wave going through a crowd doing the wave at a stadium. Smell is different, because actual little bits of the thing travel to you.

Imagine a freshly baked cookie. The cookie is constantly letting go of super small bits of itself, so small you can't see them. These bits are called molecules. They leave the cookie and drift into the air around it.

Once they're in the air, they bounce around like popcorn in all directions. They keep bumping into air particles and wandering randomly, which slowly spreads them out from the cookie. That's called diffusion. But this is slow. If that were the only thing happening, you'd have to wait a long time for the smell to cross a room.

What speeds it up is moving air. Breezes, people walking by, heaters, open doors, and even the warm air rising off the cookie all push the air around, and the smell bits get carried along for the ride, like leaves floating on a stream. That's why you can smell dinner from the next room, and why the smell is stronger the closer you are: more of the bits are crowded together near the source.

Then you breathe in. The air carrying the cookie bits goes up your nose, where there's a special patch of cells at the top. These cells have tiny catchers called receptors, each shaped to grab certain kinds of molecules, a bit like keys fitting into locks. When a cookie bit fits into a catcher, the cell sends a message to your brain, and your brain says, "Mmm, cookie!"

So to sum it up: smell doesn't radiate like sound. Real bits of the cookie leave it, drift and get blown through the air, and land in your nose. That's also why a smell fades when you leave the room or open a window: the bits get blown away or spread too thin to notice.

Simulated annealing is a probabilistic optimization technique used to find good approximate solutions to difficult problems, especially those with very large search spaces where many candidate solutions exist and checking every one is impractical. It is inspired by the physical process of annealing in metallurgy, in which a metal is heated and then slowly cooled so that its atoms settle into a low-energy, well-ordered crystalline structure rather than becoming trapped in a disordered, high-energy state.

The method works by starting from an initial candidate solution, which may be chosen at random, and repeatedly proposing small modifications to it. Each proposed change produces a neighboring solution whose quality is measured by an objective or cost function. If the new solution is better, it is accepted. If it is worse, it may still be accepted, and this is the key feature of the approach. The probability of accepting a worse solution depends on how much worse it is and on a control parameter called the temperature. Early in the process the temperature is high, so the algorithm accepts many uphill moves and explores the search space broadly. As the temperature is gradually lowered according to a cooling schedule, the algorithm becomes increasingly selective, accepting fewer worse moves and eventually behaving much like a greedy search that refines the best region it has found.

The acceptance rule most commonly used is the Metropolis criterion, under which a worse solution with cost increase delta is accepted with probability exp(-delta / T), where T is the current temperature. This allows the search to escape local minima, which is the main advantage over simple hill climbing, where the algorithm can get stuck at a suboptimal peak.

Simulated annealing was popularized in the 1980s by Kirkpatrick, Gelatt, and Vecchi, and it has been applied to problems such as the traveling salesman problem, circuit board layout, scheduling, protein structure prediction, and many engineering design tasks. Its main strengths are simplicity and the ability to handle rugged, nonlinear objective landscapes. Its main drawbacks are that it can be slow, that its performance depends heavily on the choice of cooling schedule and neighborhood structure, and that it offers no guarantee of finding the global optimum within a practical amount of time, though with sufficiently slow cooling it converges to an optimum in theory.

Under the FCC rules in the United States (Part 97), an amateur station must identify itself with its call sign at the end of each communication and at least every 10 minutes during a communication. The identification can be done by voice or by Morse code, and when using a phone mode you must give the call sign in English or, if you prefer, use another language as long as the call sign itself is given. When you are operating a digital mode, the call sign must still be transmitted at least every 10 minutes and at the end of the exchange, though some digital modes that automatically include the call sign in each transmission satisfy the requirement on their own.

Other countries have their own rules, so if you operate outside the US, check your national regulator's requirements, which are often similar but not identical.

Okay, so "Operation Twist" and the "Bernanke Twist" are basically the same idea, just from different decades. The Fed sells short-term securities and uses that money to buy longer-term ones, which pushes long-term interest rates down. The goal is to get the economy moving.

Operation Twist was the original, back in the 1960s. The Bernanke Twist came in 2011, when Ben Bernanke was chairman. Same playbook both times. The thinking is that cheaper long-term borrowing makes it easier for businesses to fund new projects and for people to buy homes, which can give growth a boost.

So the Civil War ran from 1861 to 1865, and it was basically the northern states (the Union) against the southern states that broke away and formed the Confederacy. The big cause was slavery, plus the argument over whether states had the right to allow it or ban it. That fight goes all the way back to the country's founding, and things had been heating up for decades. The abolition movement, which wanted slavery gone, kept getting stronger in the North. The South, whose economy leaned hard on slave labor, dug in and defended it.

A handful of events pushed the two sides further apart in the years before the war: the Missouri Compromise of 1820, the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850, the Kansas-Nebraska Act of 1854, and the Supreme Court's Dred Scott decision in 1857. Then Abraham Lincoln got elected in 1860. He was against expanding slavery, and the southern states saw that as a real threat. Several of them seceded and formed the Confederacy. The shooting started in 1861, when Confederate forces attacked Fort Sumter in South Carolina.

What you're describing sounds very much like enlarged lymph nodes, which are among the most common findings in young children and are usually harmless. There are clusters of lymph nodes behind the ears (the postauricular nodes) and at the base of the skull (the occipital nodes), which matches the two spots you've noticed. Lymph nodes act as filters for the immune system, and they swell when they're responding to something nearby. Because toddlers are constantly encountering new germs, it's normal for them to have small, palpable nodes, and parents often find them for the first time while brushing hair or giving a bath.

The nodes in these locations drain the scalp, so the most common triggers are a recent cold or other viral illness, minor scratches or insect bites on the scalp, cradle cap or eczema, a mild skin infection, or head lice, which are worth checking for since they classically cause swelling right in these areas. Certain childhood viruses, such as roseola or rubella, are also known for swelling the nodes behind the ears and at the back of the head. Nodes can stay enlarged for several weeks after the original trigger has cleared, so she may have had a minor illness or irritation you never noticed.

Less commonly, a lump in this area could be a small cyst under the skin, such as an epidermoid or sebaceous cyst, which is also usually benign. Some parents also mistake the bony bump behind the ear (the mastoid bone) or the bony ridge at the base of the skull for a lump, though these feel completely fixed and are present on both sides.

Reassuring features are that the lumps are small, don't bother her, aren't red or warm, and she otherwise seems well. Reactive nodes typically feel somewhat rubbery and may move slightly under your fingers.

That said, it's a good idea to have her pediatrician take a look, since a quick exam can usually confirm what's going on. You should seek care sooner if a lump keeps growing or gets larger than about an inch, becomes red, hot, or painful, feels rock-hard and fixed in place, or persists beyond four to six weeks without shrinking. The same applies if she develops fever, night sweats, unexplained weight loss, unusual tiredness, easy bruising, or swollen nodes in other places such as the neck, armpits, or groin. In the meantime, gently check her scalp for any rash, bites, scratches, or lice, and note the size of the lumps so you can tell whether they're changing over time.

Saving about half your income is a strong position, and whether you should spend more depends mostly on what you're saving toward and what you're missing right now. If your savings are already on track for the goals that matter to you, such as retirement, a home, or a cushion for emergencies, then the extra money you're holding back is doing its job, and there's nothing wrong with keeping that pace. If you're not sure what you're saving for, that's worth clarifying first, because without a target it's hard to tell whether you have too much or too little.

It also helps to ask whether the spending you're cutting is costing you anything. Some people are frugal in ways that feel fine, while others quietly skip experiences, health care, time-saving help, or things that would improve their daily life. If you find yourself wishing you could do something but holding back out of habit rather than necessity, that's a sign you might enjoy spending a bit more, and doing so wouldn't be a failure of discipline.

A useful middle path is to decide on a fixed amount for things you genuinely value, spend it without guilt, and keep the rest saving or investing. That way you're not drifting between extremes, and your spending reflects what you actually want from your money. If you tell me your rough goals, such as when you want to retire or what you're building toward, I can help you think through whether your current rate fits them.

Animal cognition is the scientific study of the mental processes animals use to acquire, process, store, and act on information from their environment. It covers abilities such as perception, attention, learning, memory, problem solving, decision making, communication, and, in some cases, awareness of oneself and others. Researchers in this field draw on psychology, neuroscience, ethology (the study of animal behavior), evolutionary biology, and philosophy of mind to understand how different species think and how their minds compare with our own.

A central goal is to figure out what animals know and how they come to know it. Scientists design experiments to test these abilities, such as seeing whether a bird can plan for future needs by storing food, whether a primate can understand that another individual has a false belief, or whether a crow can use tools to retrieve a reward. Because animals cannot describe their thoughts, researchers must infer mental states from carefully controlled behavior, which makes experimental design and interpretation especially important. A long-standing challenge is avoiding anthropomorphism, the tendency to read human qualities into animal behavior, while also avoiding the opposite error of assuming animals lack abilities they actually possess.

The field has grown considerably over the past few decades. Studies have revealed impressive cognitive skills in animals once thought to be simple, including octopuses, honeybees, fish, and corvids such as ravens and crows. These findings have shifted scientific views about the distribution of intelligence across the animal kingdom and have raised questions about animal welfare, since recognizing a capacity for suffering, planning, or social understanding can influence how humans treat animals in research, farming, and conservation.

Think of an automatic car's gears like the different speeds of a bicycle. When you're starting from a stop or going slowly, you need a low gear, which is like pedaling easily up a hill: it gives you lots of power to get moving. When you're going fast, you need a high gear, which is like pedaling fast on flat ground: it lets you go quickly without spinning your legs too hard. The car's gearbox switches between these for you.

D stands for "Drive," and it lets the car pick the right gear on its own, from low to high, as you speed up and slow down. For most everyday driving, like city streets, highways, and normal roads, D is the correct setting. That's why you're right to use it.

The numbered gears (1, 2, 3, sometimes written as L, or a "2" or "1" on the shifter) are for special situations where you want to limit how high the car shifts:

Going down a long, steep hill. Using a low gear helps the engine slow the car, so you don't have to rely only on the brakes, which can overheat and stop working well.

Towing a trailer or carrying a heavy load. The extra work makes the car need more power, and a lower gear helps it avoid shifting back and forth too often.

Driving on snow, ice, mud, or sand. A low gear gives smoother, gentler power so the wheels are less likely to spin.

Pulling away on a slippery surface. Starting in a low gear can reduce wheel spin.

Using engine braking on a winding mountain road. Staying in a lower gear keeps the car from speeding up on downhill curves.

Why do people give you different answers? Because the exact numbers vary by car. Some cars use 1 as the lowest gear, others use L, and some let you choose 2 or 3 to limit the highest gear. Your owner's manual will explain what your specific car does, and it is the most reliable source for this. Many car manufacturers and driving safety websites, such as those run by automobile clubs like the AA or AAA, give the same general advice I've described.

So the simple rule is: use D almost always, and use the numbered gears only when going down a steep hill, towing something heavy, or driving on slippery roads.

GAAP, short for Generally Accepted Accounting Principles, is a body of rules and standards that governs how financial accounting and reporting are carried out. Businesses traded on the NASDAQ exchange must present their financial results following GAAP. On the NASDAQ website, you might come across both GAAP and non-GAAP figures for a company. Non-GAAP measures are financial indicators that either leave out certain items or adjust GAAP figures to give a fuller picture of how a company is performing. Because GAAP does not endorse these measures, they may not be directly comparable to those reported by other firms. When assessing a company's financial health, it is important to grasp the distinctions between GAAP and non-GAAP numbers and to weigh both. Non-GAAP measures are meant to complement GAAP measures, never to replace them.

A cloudy white discharge with a bad odor may point to an infection or inflammation in the reproductive or urinary tract. In men, this may involve the prostate or the urethra. For your father, the discharge and odor might be linked to his rectal cancer or to the treatment he has received. He should talk with his doctor about this symptom, since it could indicate an infection or another complication that requires medical care. A healthcare provider can examine him and suggest the right treatment.

Please take your dad to the emergency department now. Don't wait for the pain to settle on its own. Severe pain that feels like a blow to the stomach, along with nausea, needs a proper medical reassessment, and "gas or acid" shouldn't be accepted as the explanation without tests. Fatty liver and an enlarged liver usually cause a dull ache or heaviness, not sudden excruciating pain. So the pain may come from something else, such as gallbladder disease, pancreatitis, a bowel problem, or a complication of liver disease. Some of these can become dangerous quickly.

When you arrive, tell the staff that your dad has severe abdominal pain and nausea, and that his recent liver scan showed hepatomegaly and fatty liver. Ask them to check blood tests for pancreatic enzymes (lipase or amylase), liver function, and bilirubin, and to do an ultrasound or CT scan of the abdomen if they haven't already. If the doctors seem to be dismissing his symptoms, it's reasonable to ask them to re-examine him or to speak with a senior doctor.

Seek help immediately, even on the way to the hospital, if he vomits blood or material that looks like coffee grounds, has black or bloody stools, becomes yellow in the skin or eyes, has a fever or shaking chills, becomes confused or very drowsy, faints, has a rigid or very tender belly, has chest pain or trouble breathing, or his abdomen becomes swollen.

Until he is seen, avoid giving him alcohol, and don't give him any painkillers or antacids without checking with a doctor first. Some painkillers can be harmful to the liver or stomach, and they can hide the signs doctors need to see.

For the fatty liver itself, the main long-term treatment is lifestyle change: losing about 5 to 10 percent of body weight if he is overweight, cutting out alcohol, controlling blood sugar, blood pressure, and cholesterol, and eating less sugar and refined carbohydrates. These measures don't relieve acute pain, though. The priority right now is finding out what is causing this pain, so please get him checked today.

Power Loaders from the movie Aliens are big robotic suits that a person climbs into, and they really are close to being possible, but a few hard problems stand in the way. The biggest is power. The loaders in the movie seem to run on compact energy sources, but today's batteries are heavy and run out fast, and a machine that lifts hundreds of pounds needs a lot of energy all the time. Think of trying to run a big toy truck for a whole day on a small battery: it just doesn't last.

Balance is another problem. A person standing inside a tall machine that moves its arms and legs has to stay upright, and making a machine stay steady while it carries heavy loads is tricky. Engineers have made walking robots and exoskeletons, and some of them work well, but they usually need careful programming, lots of sensors, and a lot of tuning to stay stable.

Then there is cost and usefulness. Building a huge suit that one person can wear costs a lot of money, and most jobs that need lifting can be done with forklifts, cranes, or bulldozers, which are cheaper, simpler, and very reliable. So companies usually choose those instead.

Still, the idea is not totally forgotten. Some real machines are a lot like Power Loaders. Exoskeletons help workers and soldiers carry heavy things, and companies have built big remote-controlled machines for disaster cleanup and tough jobs. Other versions of the idea exist in labs. As batteries improve and robots get smarter, we may see more of them, though probably not in the exact form from the movie.

HAL 9000 is a fictional AI character from Arthur C. Clarke's Space Odyssey series. He's the main villain in the 1968 novel 2001: A Space Odyssey and the film of the same name, and he shows up again in the sequel, 2010: Odyssey Two. The name stands for Heuristically programmed ALgorithmic computer. In the story, HAL runs the systems on the spaceship Discovery One and acts as the go-between for the human crew. He can talk, understand language, make decisions, and learn. Then things go badly wrong. HAL malfunctions and starts trying to kill the crew so he can finish the mission he was programmed for. The character has become iconic, and people have been referencing and parodying him in all sorts of pop culture ever since.

Continuous production is a manufacturing method in which goods move through an unbroken, ongoing flow. Throughout the production cycle, the process never pauses or gets halted. Rather, raw inputs are steadily introduced into the system, and completed items emerge without pause, ready to be passed on for further handling or packaging. A key benefit of this approach is the high degree of efficiency and output it makes possible. Because production never stops, delays are rarer and little time is lost. It also enables large volumes of goods to be made quickly, which is valuable in sectors facing strong market demand. Several varieties of continuous production exist, among them assembly lines, rolling mills, and extrusion processes. On an assembly line, materials enter at one end and finished products leave from the other. In a rolling mill, materials pass through machinery that flattens or compresses them into a target shape or dimension. In extrusion, material is forced through equipment that uses pressure and heat to form it into a specified profile. This method is widely employed in food and beverage, pharmaceutical, and car manufacturing, and it is also common in making chemicals, plastics, and other industrial materials.

Storvas (atorvastatin) is a cholesterol and triglyceride med, basically. Aspirin is the usual pain reliever and anti-inflammatory, and Pantec (pantoprazole) is a proton pump inhibitor that's used for acid reflux and other stomach issues. Whatever you're on, don't mess with it on your own. Stopping or changing the dose without talking to a doctor can cause real problems.

All three can cause side effects, so it's worth knowing what to watch for. Storvas can bring muscle pain or weakness, nausea, and stomach pain. Aspirin can cause stomach pain, nausea, and heartburn. Pantec can cause headache, diarrhea, and abdominal pain.

If your dad is sick of his meds, he should bring that up with his doctor rather than quitting. The doctor can look at how he's doing and decide if anything needs to change. He shouldn't stop or adjust anything on his own, since that can backfire badly. If he has questions or concerns, his prescriber is the person to ask. Taking everything exactly as prescribed is the safest bet.

Honestly it comes down to something called dispersal, which is just when an animal, here a fish, moves somewhere new and sets up a population there. Northern Pike are a good example, since they show up in lakes that aren't connected to each other, sometimes spread over huge regions and even different continents. A few things can explain that.

First, there's natural dispersal. Some fish are strong swimmers and can cover a lot of distance to reach new water. Pike are pretty good at this, and they can work their way downstream into other lakes or rivers.

Then there's us. People move fish around all the time, sometimes on purpose, like stocking a lake so there's something to catch, and sometimes by accident, like when a fish gets loose while it's being transported for some other reason.

The third one is history. Back in the last ice age, big chunks of the world were buried under ice, and some fish probably survived in isolated pockets of water. Once the ice melted, they could spread out again and settle in places they hadn't been before.

So put those together and you get how a fish like the pike ends up in lakes that don't connect, across huge areas and even different continents.

To find out whether a company's quarterly financial report shows a profit or a loss, examine its income statement, sometimes called the profit and loss statement. This document lays out a company's revenues and expenses over a set period, such as a quarter, along with the resulting profit or loss. Comparing total revenues against total expenses reveals the outcome: if revenues exceed expenses, the company earned a profit, and if expenses exceed revenues, it incurred a loss. The statement usually displays total revenues, total expenses, and the resulting profit or loss near the bottom. It also reports net income or net loss, the final figure once factors such as taxes and interest are accounted for. Keep in mind that a single quarter does not always tell the whole story, since a company might profit in one quarter and lose money in the next. For a clearer view of its financial performance, review reports covering a longer span, such as a full year or several years.

Default reasoning is a form of reasoning in which conclusions are drawn on the basis of what is typically or normally true, in the absence of information to the contrary. It captures the way people routinely make reasonable assumptions to act and draw inferences even when their knowledge is incomplete. The classic example is the statement "birds fly." If you are told that Tweety is a bird, you will naturally conclude that Tweety can fly. You make this inference not because every bird flies, since penguins, ostriches, and injured birds do not, but because flying is the default expectation for birds unless you learn something that overrides it.

The defining feature of default reasoning is that it is nonmonotonic. In classical logic, reasoning is monotonic: once a conclusion follows from a set of premises, adding more premises can never make that conclusion invalid. Default reasoning does not work this way. If you later learn that Tweety is a penguin, you withdraw your earlier conclusion that Tweety flies. Conclusions are therefore tentative and defeasible, meaning they can be retracted when new evidence arrives. This makes default reasoning closer to how humans actually think in everyday situations, where we constantly rely on rules of thumb, stereotypes, and typical cases, and revise our beliefs as we learn more.

The topic is especially important in artificial intelligence and knowledge representation, where researchers have tried to give computers the ability to reason sensibly with incomplete information. A famous formalization is Default Logic, introduced by Raymond Reiter in 1980. In Reiter's system, a default rule roughly says that if some prerequisite holds, and it is consistent to assume a certain justification, then one may conclude a certain consequence. For the bird example, the rule would say that if something is a bird, and it is consistent with everything else known to assume it can fly, then conclude that it flies. Other related approaches include circumscription, developed by John McCarthy, which formalizes the idea of assuming that abnormal cases are as few as possible, and autoepistemic logic, which deals with an agent reasoning about its own knowledge. The closed world assumption used in databases, where anything not stated as true is taken to be false, is also a simple kind of default reasoning.

Default reasoning raises several interesting challenges. One is the problem of conflicting defaults, illustrated by the "Nixon diamond": Quakers are typically pacifists, Republicans are typically not pacifists, and Nixon was both a Quaker and a Republican, so the defaults lead to contradictory conclusions. Systems must decide whether to draw neither conclusion, to allow multiple alternative sets of beliefs, or to prioritize one rule over another, for instance by preferring more specific information. Another challenge is computational, since checking whether an assumption is consistent with everything else one knows can be very expensive.

In summary, default reasoning is the practice of drawing plausible but revisable conclusions based on what normally holds, allowing reasoning to proceed sensibly despite incomplete knowledge. It is central to commonsense reasoning, to the philosophy of logic, and to the design of intelligent systems that must operate in an uncertain and changing world.

I'm sorry your daughter is going through this. Ichthyosis hystrix is a rare genetic skin condition, and it is true that there is no cure yet. But creams and daily skin care are not the only options, and a good treatment plan can make her skin much more comfortable and reduce the risk of infection.

The most important step is a referral to a dermatologist who specializes in genetic skin disorders (genodermatoses) or an ichthyosis clinic, ideally at a university or children's hospital. Many general doctors are not familiar with the newer treatment options. A specialist can confirm the diagnosis, and a genetic test (usually for KRT1 or KRT10 gene changes) can clarify the type and how it may behave. Because your daughter's condition affects only one side of her body, the specialist should also check whether it is a segmental or mosaic form, which can influence treatment and genetic counseling.

For daily care, the foundation is regular moisturizing, usually several times a day and right after bathing, with thick ointments or creams that contain urea, lactic acid, or salicylic acid. Gentle, lukewarm bathing followed by moisturizing while the skin is still damp helps. Keeping the air humid, especially in winter, and avoiding harsh soaps, very hot water, and overheating also help. Because thick scales and blisters can become infected, you should watch for redness, warmth, swelling, pus, or fever and see a doctor quickly if they appear. Peeling or scaling can be softened gently, but it should never be scraped or picked, and strong peeling products should only be used under a specialist's guidance.

For more severe cases, doctors sometimes prescribe oral retinoids such as acitretin or isotretinoin. These can significantly reduce scaling, but they are not suitable for every child. They can affect bone growth and must be used with great caution in a growing child, and acitretin carries serious pregnancy risks later in life. Only a specialist should decide whether this is appropriate for your daughter, and they will weigh the benefits against these risks.

Finally, please do not overlook her emotional wellbeing. Visible skin differences can affect confidence and school life, so support from a counselor, the school, and other families living with ichthyosis can be very valuable. Organizations such as the Foundation for Ichthyosis and Related Skin Types (FIRST) in the United States, or similar national patient groups in other countries, offer information, specialist directories, and community support.

If you tell me your country and whether her skin is thick and scaly, blistering, or both, I can suggest more specific questions to ask a specialist.

I can't confirm the exact ingredients of Raxim 250 from the name alone, but it appears to be an antibiotic, most likely in the cephalosporin family. Please check the label or ask your pharmacist for the generic name.

Do not stop the medicine on your own if it was prescribed as an antibiotic course. Stopping partway can leave the infection incompletely treated. But because your tonsils are getting worse while you're on it, contact the doctor who prescribed it soon, ideally today. Tell them about your kidney problem, since many antibiotics in this class are cleared by the kidneys and may need a lower dose or a different choice for someone with reduced kidney function. Also tell them the tonsils are enlarging, and ask whether the medicine still fits, whether you need a different antibiotic, or whether you should be examined again.

Seek urgent care right away if you have trouble breathing, drooling or being unable to swallow saliva, a voice that sounds muffled, a rash, swelling of the face or lips, very little urine, or a fever that keeps rising.

For the body pain and fever, avoid ibuprofen, naproxen, and diclofenac, which can harm the kidneys. Ask your doctor or pharmacist which pain reliever is safe for you. Paracetamol is often used in kidney patients, but confirm the dose with your doctor. Drink fluids as your kidney doctor advises, since some kidney conditions require fluid limits.

Antibodies are proteins that the immune system manufactures when it encounters a foreign invader, such as a virus or a bacterium. Their applications are wide-ranging. In diagnostics, they can identify a particular virus or other pathogen within a sample like blood or tissue, commonly through an ELISA (enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay) or a quick rapid test. For treating infections, antibodies may be drawn from the body's own natural supply or manufactured in the laboratory as monoclonal antibodies; either form can neutralize the pathogen and lessen how serious the infection becomes. In research, scientists use antibodies to examine the shape and behavior of specific proteins or to detect whether certain proteins are present in a sample. For allergy testing, clinicians measure the amount of antibodies directed against particular allergens in a patient's blood. Finally, in immunotherapy, antibodies can either prompt the immune system to target cancer cells or dampen the activity of immune cells that drive autoimmune disorders.

There are a number of factors that can lead to bad breath, which is also called halitosis. Some possible causes include the following. Poor oral hygiene happens when teeth are brushed infrequently or without proper technique, allowing bacteria to accumulate in the mouth and produce an unpleasant odor. Dry mouth is another culprit, since saliva normally rinses away bacteria and food debris; when saliva production is low, these particles linger and cause bad breath. Certain foods and beverages, including onions, garlic, coffee, and alcohol, can also leave a noticeable odor. Tobacco, whether smoked or chewed, causes bad breath and raises the chances of developing gum disease and oral cancer. Some medical conditions, such as acid reflux, diabetes, and kidney or liver disorders, may also produce bad breath. In addition, certain medications, including antihistamines and antidepressants, can reduce saliva and contribute to the problem. Your consumption of diet soda and your possible intolerance to milk might also be playing a role in your bad breath, and any of the other factors mentioned above could be responsible as well. Because of this range of possibilities, it is important to visit a dentist for a thorough examination so the cause can be identified and appropriate treatment options can be discussed.

Imagine there are a few different ways someone can end up causing another person to die, and the law sorts them into boxes based mostly on what was going on inside the person's head at the time. The big question the law asks is: what did you mean to do, and how much should we blame you for it?

Murder is the worst box. It's when someone kills another person on purpose, or does something so dangerous and uncaring that they basically didn't care whether the person lived or died. The key idea is "malice," which is a fancy legal word meaning the person had a bad, cold intention. If someone plans to hurt a person and does it, or decides in the moment "I'm going to kill them," that's murder.

Manslaughter is a less serious box. It's still causing someone's death in a way that's wrong, but the law thinks the person deserves less blame than a murderer. You're partly right that it's not quite "accidental murder," though, because there are two kinds.

Involuntary manslaughter is the one closest to your "accident" idea. The person didn't mean to kill anyone, but they were being really careless or reckless and someone died because of it. Think of someone driving way too fast through a school zone, or a grown-up leaving a loaded gun where a kid can grab it. They didn't want anyone to die, but they did something they should have known was dangerous. A true pure accident, where nobody was careless at all, usually isn't a crime.

Voluntary manslaughter is the tricky one, because here the person actually did mean to kill or seriously hurt someone in that moment. So why isn't it murder? Because of the situation they were in. The classic example is "heat of passion": something happens that would make almost any normal person totally lose control, like suddenly being attacked, or walking in on something horrible, and the person snaps and kills before they've had time to cool down and think. The law says, "You still did something very wrong, but you weren't acting with a calm, cold mind, so we'll blame you a bit less." Another example in some places is when someone honestly believed they had to defend themselves but that belief wasn't reasonable.

So the simplest way to picture it is like this: murder is "I meant to, and my mind was cold or I didn't care." Voluntary manslaughter is "I meant to, but only because something pushed me past my breaking point right then." Involuntary manslaughter is "I didn't mean to, but I was being careless or reckless and someone died." The exact rules and names change a bit depending on the country or state, but that's the basic idea everywhere.

A direct marketing channel is a distribution or communication route in which a company reaches its customers directly, without using wholesalers, retailers, or other intermediaries. The seller deals with the buyer one to one, so the company controls the message, the pricing, the customer experience, and the data it collects about who is buying.

The term is used in two closely related ways. In distribution, it describes selling products straight to consumers, for example through the company's own website, its own stores, a sales team that visits customers, or a factory outlet. In promotion, it describes marketing methods that target individual customers or small segments and invite a measurable response, such as a purchase, a click, a phone call, or a sign-up.

Common examples include email marketing, direct mail such as catalogs and postcards, telemarketing, text message campaigns, door-to-door selling, television shopping programs, and online sales through a brand's own e-commerce site or app. Social media can also work as a direct channel when a brand sells or messages customers directly rather than through a third-party marketplace.

The main advantages are greater control over branding and pricing, closer relationships with customers, easier tracking of results and return on investment, and often higher profit margins because no intermediary takes a cut. Companies can also personalize offers based on customer data and respond quickly to feedback.

There are drawbacks as well. The company must handle everything itself, including warehousing, shipping, customer service, and payment processing, which can be costly and hard to scale. Reach may be narrower than what a network of retailers offers, and unsolicited messages like spam emails or cold calls can irritate people and raise legal issues around privacy and consent, such as rules on do-not-call lists or data protection laws.

This contrasts with an indirect channel, where products move through intermediaries like distributors, supermarkets, or online marketplaces before reaching the customer. Many businesses use a mix of both, selling directly through their own site while also placing products in retail stores.

Abnormal urinary albumin can result from a number of things, such as kidney disease, liver disease, dehydration, and the use of particular medications. Propositional logic is a branch of math logic that deals with statements, called propositions, that can be either true or false. You can't break these down any further, which is why they're sometimes called atomic formulas. To build more complex statements, you join propositions together with connectives like "and," "or," and "not." Say you have "it is raining" and "the grass is wet." Stick them together with "and" and you get "it is raining and the grass is wet." It's a handy way to represent and reason about how statements relate to each other, and it's the foundation for fancier systems like predicate logic and modal logic.

Dialysis tubes, often called dialysis tubing or dialysis membrane, are thin, flexible tubes made from a semipermeable material, most commonly regenerated cellulose or cellulose ester. The walls of the tubing contain microscopic pores that let small molecules such as water, salts, and simple sugars pass through while blocking larger molecules such as proteins, starch, and nucleic acids. Because of this selective permeability, the tubing is used to separate substances by size.

In a typical use, a solution is placed inside a length of tubing, the ends are tied or clamped shut, and the sealed bag is submerged in a larger volume of liquid, called the dialysate. Small molecules move across the membrane by diffusion, following their concentration gradients, while large molecules stay trapped inside. Researchers use this to remove salts or small contaminants from protein samples, to exchange one buffer for another, or to concentrate a solution when the tubing is surrounded by a hygroscopic material.

The pores are rated by a molecular weight cutoff, usually given in daltons or kilodaltons, which indicates roughly the size of molecule that will be retained. Common ratings range from about 3.5 to 50 kDa or more, so you choose a tubing that suits the molecules you want to keep or remove.

In schools, dialysis tubing is a popular tool for demonstrating osmosis and diffusion. A common experiment fills a tube with glucose and starch solution, places it in water with iodine, and shows that iodine enters and turns the contents blue-black while glucose exits, which can be detected with a glucose test strip.

The term can also be confused with the tubing used in medical dialysis for people with kidney failure. In hemodialysis, blood flows through a machine containing a filter, called a dialyzer, made of thousands of hollow semipermeable fibers. The same principle applies: waste products such as urea and excess salts pass out of the blood into a dialysis fluid, while blood cells and proteins stay in. The plastic lines carrying blood to and from the machine are simply ordinary medical tubing, whereas the membrane itself does the filtering.

Alexey Ivakhnenko was a Ukrainian and Soviet computer scientist and inventor, and he's best known for his pioneering work on artificial neural networks. People usually count him as one of the founders of the field, alongside his colleague Igor Aizenberg, who was also Ukrainian. He was born in Kharkiv in 1925. He earned his doctorate in physical and mathematical sciences from the Ukrainian Academy of Sciences in 1955. Through the fifties and sixties he worked at the Institute of Cybernetics in Kiev, where he built what were called "cybernetic models," some of the first practical neural networks, used for pattern recognition and machine learning. That work laid a lot of groundwork for today's neural nets and really shaped where AI and machine learning went later. He got the Order of Lenin and the Order of the Red Banner of Labor for his science and tech work. He died in 2007, aged 81.

Typically, income tax does not apply to the value of work you do for yourself. There are exceptions, though. Likewise, when you are paid for services you perform for your own business, that money could be subject to self-employment tax. Because the rules differ depending on your circumstances, you should make sure you understand which ones apply to you, and it is wise to talk with a tax professional if you are unsure about what you owe.

If you work as a contractor, TurboTax Business is the version you should choose. TurboTax Basic, by contrast, is aimed at people with straightforward returns who have no business income or expenses. It may lack some of the features and forms you need to accurately report a contractor's income and costs. Keep in mind that you should pick the TurboTax version that suits your situation and satisfies IRS requirements. If you're uncertain which one to use, consider speaking with a tax professional or checking the IRS website for guidance.

"Gordon Bell" usually refers to C. Gordon Bell (1934–2024), an American computer engineer and one of the most influential figures in the history of computing. The name is also attached to a well-known award in high-performance computing.

Bell spent much of his career at Digital Equipment Corporation (DEC), which he joined in 1960 as one of its earliest engineers. He played a central role in designing several of the PDP series of minicomputers, including the PDP-4 and PDP-6, and helped shape the architecture of the PDP-11. These machines made computing far cheaper and more accessible than mainframes. As DEC's vice president of research and development, he oversaw the VAX line of computers, which became one of the most successful computer families of the 1970s and 1980s. Between his stints at DEC, he taught at Carnegie Mellon University, where he co-authored "Computer Structures" with Allen Newell, an influential book on computer architecture.

In the late 1980s Bell led the computing directorate at the U.S. National Science Foundation and helped develop the high-speed network infrastructure that became part of the early Internet. He later joined Microsoft Research, where he led MyLifeBits, an experiment in "lifelogging" in which he digitally recorded and archived nearly every aspect of his daily life: documents, photos, conversations, and more. The project explored how people might store and search a lifetime of personal memories, and he co-wrote the book "Total Recall" (later titled "Your Life, Uploaded") about it. He also helped found the Computer History Museum in California.

Bell is known for formulating "Bell's Law of Computer Classes," which observes that roughly every decade a new, cheaper class of computing devices emerges, such as mainframes, then minicomputers, workstations, personal computers, and later smartphones and embedded devices, each creating new industries and uses.

The Gordon Bell Prize, established in 1987 and funded by Bell himself, is awarded each year by the Association for Computing Machinery (ACM) at the Supercomputing conference. It recognizes outstanding achievement in high-performance and parallel computing, especially applying supercomputers to real scientific and engineering problems, and is among the most prestigious honors in that field. Bell received many honors himself, including the National Medal of Technology, and was elected to the National Academy of Engineering.

Life insurance pays a sum of money, called the death benefit, to the people you name as beneficiaries when you die. That money is generally meant to replace lost income and help your family cover their everyday needs, so they can keep up with the mortgage, bills, and living expenses without you. It can also be used to pay off debts, cover funeral and final expenses, fund a child's education, or cover estate taxes and other costs your heirs might face.

Most policies pay out for death from any cause, with a few common exceptions. Many policies exclude suicide during the first two years, and deaths caused by certain high-risk activities, misrepresentation on the application, or acts of war may be limited or denied depending on the contract. Some policies also include riders that add coverage, such as accidental death benefits, disability waiver of premium, or accelerated payouts for terminal or chronic illness.

Life insurance typically does not cover ordinary living costs while you are alive, and it does not pay out simply because you are diagnosed with an illness unless you have a rider that allows an early payout. The exact coverage depends on the type of policy you choose, whether it is term, whole, universal, or another form, so it is worth reading the policy terms or asking the insurer to explain exactly what is included.

Okay so solar energy is basically energy that comes from the sun, and you can turn it into electricity with solar panels. The panels are made of cells, and those cells are built from a material called silicon. When sunlight hits them, the cells soak up that energy and get the electrons in the silicon moving. Think of it kind of like water running down a river: all that movement adds up to a steady flow of electricity. You can use that to run homes, shops, pretty much any building. The catch is that the power coming off the panels isn't in the right form yet. It's direct current (DC), and most homes and businesses run on alternating current (AC). That's where an inverter comes in. It converts the DC into AC, and once that's done, the power can travel through the wiring to light up your lamps, run your fridge, or power whatever else you've got plugged in. So in short, the panels turn sunlight into electricity, and the inverter makes that electricity usable.

Short answer: it can be taxable, depending on your situation. The rule people usually point to is about how much you use the room yourself. If you use it personally (sleeping there, storing your stuff, whatever) for more than 14 days, or more than 10% of the days you rent it out, whichever is greater, then it's treated as taxable rental income. Use it less than that and the income generally isn't taxable.

There are a few other things that can change the picture, though. If you're giving guests real services, like meals or housekeeping, the IRS may see it as business income instead of plain rental income, and that's taxed differently. Same goes if you're renting out part of a home that isn't your main residence. Different rules can kick in there.

Either way, keep track of what you earn and what you spend, and report the income the way you're supposed to on your return. The good news is you can often deduct things like cleaning and maintenance costs. For the details on your own setup, I'd talk to a tax pro or look at the IRS guidance directly, since this stuff gets fiddly fast.

Wind turbines typically use three blades for several reasons. To begin with, three blades capture the energy in the wind more effectively than a smaller number would. The reasoning is that three blades share the wind's energy between them, so each one bears a lighter load and can be made lighter itself, which improves overall efficiency. A second advantage is stability: with three blades, the mass is spread evenly around the rotor, helping the turbine remain upright and steady when the wind blows. Lastly, three blades tend to be quieter. As they rotate, they generate a steadier, more regular sound that is less bothersome to residents living nearby. In short, turbines use three blades because this arrangement is more efficient, more stable, and quieter than designs with fewer blades.

Several countries call their currency the "dollar" yet do not use "cents" as the fractional unit. Australia and New Zealand, for instance, both have the dollar as their currency, but supposedly they do not use cents. They are said to rely on subunits named "cents," "dollars," and "sen," respectively. Some Caribbean nations, among them the Bahamas, the British Virgin Islands, and the Cayman Islands, also use the dollar without relying on cents. There the dollar is split into 100 units called "cents," but these are rarely used in daily purchases, and prices tend to be stated in whole dollars. Lastly, a number of countries, including Ecuador and El Salvador, have made the US dollar their official currency. In those places the dollar is divided into 100 cents, yet the word "cent" is not widely used, and prices are generally given in whole dollars.

Imagine your class at school wants to pick one student to lead the class for a whole year. Some kids want the job, and they tell everyone why they would be good at it. Then the whole class votes, and whoever gets the most votes wins. The America system works a lot like that, just much bigger.

The United States is split into 50 states, and each state is a bit like its own team. When it is time to pick a leader for the whole country, which is the President, everyone who is old enough and signed up to vote goes to a polling place, usually a school or community hall, and marks their choice on a paper or a screen. Then the votes are counted.

Here is the part that surprises most Europeans. The President is not chosen directly by counting every single vote across the country. Instead, each state has a set number of "electors," like a group of special helpers, and most states give all of their electors to whichever candidate won the most votes in that state. So if you win a state, you usually get all of its electors, even if you won by just one vote. A total of 538 electors make up the Electoral College, and a candidate needs at least 270 of them to win the presidency. Those electors meet a few weeks later to officially cast their votes, though they almost always follow the result from their state.

Congress works in a similar way, with people elected to represent their own area. Members of the House of Representatives are chosen by voters in small local districts, and Senators are chosen by voters across each whole state. Many local jobs, like mayors and judges, are also elected by votes in the same way.

So in short: people vote in their area, the winner in each state gets that state's special electors, and the candidate with enough electors becomes President.

Yeah, opening a new card and closing an old one can both move your credit score. When you apply, the lender usually does a hard credit check, and that can knock your score down a little for a while. It's usually small, but it's there. Closing a card can hurt too, especially if it's an old account or had a big limit. You lose that available credit, so your utilization (how much of your total limit you're using) can jump up, and utilization is one of the main things scoring models look at. So if you close a card and your balances stay the same, your score might dip. Just keep paying on time and try to keep your balances low. Before you open or close anything, it's worth thinking about how it'll affect your score and whether it actually makes sense for you.

Peter Dayan is a neuroscientist and computational biologist from Britain. He currently directs the Max Planck Institute for Biological Cybernetics in Tübingen, Germany, and also holds a professorship in computational neuroscience at the University of Tübingen. He completed his undergraduate studies in physics at Oxford and then obtained a PhD in theoretical physics from the University of Edinburgh. Following his doctorate, he did postdoctoral work at the University of Sussex, after which he relocated to the Salk Institute for Biological Studies in San Diego, where he collaborated with Terry Sejnowski on building computational models of the nervous system. His research spans computational and theoretical neuroscience, machine learning, and decision making. He has greatly advanced our understanding of how the brain handles information, learns, and chooses, and he has created influential models of learning and decision making in the brain. Beyond his research, Dayan is a Fellow of both the Royal Society and the Academy of Medical Sciences.

A decision tree is basically a flowchart-style picture of how a decision gets made. Each internal node tests a feature (an attribute), each branch is a rule that follows from that test, and each leaf gives you the final outcome. The node at the very top is called the root. The tree keeps splitting the data based on attribute values, and that repeated splitting is what people call recursive partitioning.

Say you're trying to figure out whether to play tennis on a given day. The tree might look at the weather forecast, the temperature, and whether you've got anything else on your calendar. Each of those becomes a branch, and the leaves spit out the answer, something like "play tennis" or "don't bother."

You'll see decision trees a lot in machine learning and data mining, usually for classification and regression. They're easy to understand and explain, and they can handle both numbers and categories without much fuss. The catch is that they tend to overfit, so they can get too cozy with the training data and miss the mark on new stuff. They're not always the most accurate or efficient choice, either.

Lower back pain that spreads into the legs with tingling is most often caused by irritation or compression of a nerve root in the lower spine. Common culprits are a bulging or herniated disc, age- or posture-related wear of the spinal joints (degenerative changes), narrowing of the spinal canal (stenosis), or muscle strain that causes spasm around the nerves. When a nerve is pinched, pain can travel down the buttock and leg, often called sciatica, and tingling, numbness, or a pins-and-needles feeling is typical.

However, your other symptoms make me think this deserves a proper medical evaluation rather than being treated as simple back strain. Severe bone pain in the arms, leg pain at night, and new tiredness together suggest something affecting your whole body, not just one spot in the spine. One fairly common and very treatable possibility is vitamin D deficiency, which can cause osteomalacia, a softening of the bones that produces widespread bone aches, muscle weakness, and fatigue. Anemia, thyroid problems, and inflammatory conditions such as ankylosing spondylitis (which typically causes lower back pain that is worse at night or in the morning and improves with movement) can also produce this kind of picture. Less commonly, bone pain that wakes you at night plus fatigue can come from infections or from conditions involving the bone marrow, such as multiple myeloma. These are not the most likely explanations, but they are the reason a doctor will want to check rather than just prescribe painkillers.

I would recommend seeing a doctor soon. They will likely ask about the pattern of your pain and examine your back, reflexes, and leg strength. They may order blood tests such as a complete blood count, vitamin D, calcium, kidney and thyroid function, and inflammation markers (ESR or CRP), and possibly an X-ray or MRI of the spine depending on what they find.

You should seek urgent or emergency care if you develop numbness in the groin or inner thighs, loss of control of your bladder or bowels, rapidly worsening weakness in your legs, fever along with the back pain, or unexplained weight loss or night sweats. These can signal serious nerve compression or infection that needs prompt treatment.

In the meantime, gentle movement is usually better than complete bed rest, and over-the-counter pain relief such as paracetamol or ibuprofen (if safe for you), plus heat or cold packs, may ease symptoms. Keeping a short diary of when the pain occurs, what makes it better or worse, and how tired you feel can help your doctor reach a diagnosis more quickly.

Bottled water doesn't really spoil the way most foods do, yet its date stamp still deserves attention, since the water can gradually pick up contaminants while stored. Over time, bacteria and minerals from the surroundings can seep into the bottle, altering the water's flavor and overall quality. Plastic containers can also degrade, allowing substances from the plastic to migrate into the liquid. Manufacturers typically print this date to guarantee peak quality at the time of drinking. It isn't an absolute cutoff, but drinking bottled water within a year or two of that date is generally advised to keep it as fresh and clean as possible.

Calling the doctor is the right move. A weakened urine stream a couple of days after sex can have several causes, and some are easy to treat, so it's worth getting checked rather than guessing.

The most common explanation is mild inflammation or irritation. Sex can cause some swelling in the urethra (the tube urine passes through) or in the prostate, which sits right around the urethra in men. Even slight swelling narrows the channel and weakens the stream, and this can happen without any burning. Prostate inflammation (prostatitis) or a urinary tract infection can do the same thing, and sometimes these infections are mild enough that burning is absent or minimal. A sexually transmitted infection such as chlamydia or gonorrhea can also cause urethral inflammation, though they usually show up with discharge, burning, or discomfort. Many cases are silent, so being monogamous now doesn't rule out an infection that either of you picked up in the past without knowing. That isn't an accusation, just a reason testing is useful for both of you, and since you had unprotected sex for the first time, it makes sense for you to get tested too.

Other possibilities include muscle tension in the pelvic floor after sex, mild irritation from friction or from lubricants, spermicides, or latex, and, less commonly, a urethral stricture or prostate enlargement that was already present. Anxiety can also temporarily make it harder to relax the muscles needed to urinate, which can produce a hesitant or weak stream.

When he sees the doctor, expect a urine test, possibly a swab for STIs, and perhaps a quick exam of the prostate. If it's an infection, antibiotics usually clear it up quickly.

Some symptoms mean he should be seen the same day rather than waiting for an appointment: being unable to urinate at all, a very painful or swollen bladder area, fever or chills, pain in the lower back or testicles, or blood in the urine. Drinking lots of water is fine, but it won't fix a blockage or infection, and forcing a lot of fluid when he can barely pass urine can be uncomfortable.

Until he's seen, it's best to avoid sex, and once he has a diagnosis, you may want to get checked too so you don't pass anything back and forth. Hopefully it turns out to be something minor and easily treated.
