Lee Sedol is a South Korean professional Go player, widely regarded as one of the strongest and most creative players of the modern era. Born in 1983 on Bigeum Island in South Korea, he turned professional at the age of twelve and rose to the highest rank of 9-dan. Over his career he won 18 international titles, second only to fellow Korean Lee Chang-ho at the time, and he was known for an aggressive, unconventional style of play and an exceptional ability to read complex fighting positions.

He is best known internationally for his 2016 match against AlphaGo, an artificial intelligence program developed by Google DeepMind. Held in Seoul in March 2016, the five-game match drew enormous global attention because Go had long been considered far too complex for computers to master at a top human level, given the astronomical number of possible board positions. AlphaGo won the match four games to one, a result many experts had not expected for another decade. The match is often cited as a landmark moment in the history of artificial intelligence.

Lee's single victory, in the fourth game, became famous in its own right. His 78th move, sometimes called the "divine move" or "hand of God," was a brilliant and unexpected play that AlphaGo had estimated a human would choose with very low probability, and it led the program into a series of errors. That game remains the only official win by a human against that version of AlphaGo.

In 2019 Lee Sedol retired from professional Go, explaining in interviews that the rise of AI had changed his view of the game, saying that even if he became the best human player, there was now an entity that could not be defeated. His story is featured in the 2017 documentary "AlphaGo," and he remains a symbolic figure in discussions about the relationship between human skill and artificial intelligence.

Okay so a feedforward neural network is basically a type of artificial neural network used for classification and prediction. It's made up of a bunch of layers of connected "neurons" that process and pass along information. Each layer takes input from the one before it, does its thing, and sends the result forward. Whatever the last layer spits out is the network's prediction or classification.

The first layer is the input layer, and its neurons just receive the raw data. The middle layers are called hidden layers, and they crunch the data using weights and biases. The final one is the output layer, which gives you the answer.

Why "feedforward"? Because info only moves one way, from input to output, and never loops back. That's different from recurrent neural networks, which can feed information back into themselves. You'll see feedforward nets everywhere: image and speech recognition, language stuff, predictive modeling, you name it. They're pretty powerful, honestly, and a lot of modern AI systems wouldn't exist without them.

Investing in mutual funds is one of the most practical ways for Indian investors to build wealth for long-term goals such as retirement, a child's education, buying a home, or achieving financial independence. The key is to match your investments to your time horizon, risk tolerance, and the specific goal, and then stay disciplined for many years.

Begin by defining each goal clearly with a target amount and a timeline. A goal that is ten or more years away can usually tolerate the ups and downs of equity markets, while a goal three to five years away may need a mix of equity and debt, and anything shorter is better suited to debt or liquid funds. Remember to account for inflation, since education costs in India have historically risen faster than general inflation, often around eight to ten percent a year. Before investing, keep an emergency fund of about six months of expenses in a savings account or liquid fund, and have adequate term life and health insurance so you never have to break your investments in a crisis.

For horizons beyond seven to ten years, equity mutual funds have historically offered the best potential for beating inflation. A simple and effective approach is to use a low-cost index fund tracking the Nifty 50 or Sensex as the core of your portfolio, since many actively managed large-cap funds have struggled to consistently beat their benchmarks after expenses. Flexi-cap funds give the fund manager freedom to invest across large, mid, and small companies and can work well as a single diversified holding. Mid-cap and small-cap funds can deliver higher returns over long periods but come with sharper volatility, so they are usually best kept to a modest portion of the portfolio for investors who can stomach steep temporary declines. ELSS funds offer a tax deduction under Section 80C with a three-year lock-in, though this benefit applies only if you use the old tax regime. Balanced advantage or aggressive hybrid funds can suit those who want some built-in cushioning from debt.

A Systematic Investment Plan, or SIP, is the most popular way to invest because it builds the habit of regular saving and spreads your purchases across market highs and lows through rupee cost averaging. Starting early matters enormously because of compounding. For example, investing ten thousand rupees a month for twenty years at an assumed twelve percent annual return could grow to roughly one crore, whereas the same amount over ten years would reach only around twenty-three lakh. Using a step-up SIP, where you raise your monthly amount by ten percent or so each year as your income grows, can significantly boost the final corpus.

Choose direct plans rather than regular plans whenever you are comfortable selecting funds yourself, since direct plans have lower expense ratios and the difference compounds into a meaningful sum over decades. You can invest in direct plans through the AMC websites, MF Central, or platforms such as Zerodha Coin, Groww, Kuvera, and Paytm Money. When comparing funds, look at the expense ratio, consistency of performance over five to ten years relative to the benchmark and category, the fund house's reputation, and the portfolio's risk profile, rather than simply chasing whichever fund topped last year's returns.

Keep the portfolio simple. Three to five well-chosen funds are usually enough, and owning many funds in the same category often just duplicates holdings. Review your investments once a year, rebalance if your equity and debt mix has drifted far from your target, and avoid stopping SIPs during market crashes, as those periods often turn out to be the best times to accumulate units. As a goal approaches, typically in the last two to three years, gradually move money from equity to debt or liquid funds to protect what you have built.

On taxation, long-term capital gains on equity funds held over twelve months are currently taxed at 12.5 percent on gains above 1.25 lakh rupees in a financial year, while short-term gains are taxed at 20 percent. Gains on debt funds purchased after April 2023 are taxed at your income slab rate regardless of holding period. Tax rules change periodically, so it is worth checking the latest provisions.

Finally, mutual fund investments are subject to market risk and past performance does not guarantee future returns. If your situation is complex, consider consulting a SEBI-registered investment adviser who charges a fee rather than earning commissions, so that the advice you receive is aligned with your interests. Patience, consistency, and low costs are ultimately the biggest drivers of long-term success.

Moravec's paradox is one of those AI ideas that sounds backwards at first. Hans Moravec, a robotics researcher at Carnegie Mellon, pointed out that computers find hard human stuff easy and easy human stuff hard. Crunching complicated math? No problem for a machine. Recognizing a cup on a messy desk or walking across a cluttered room without tripping? Surprisingly brutal. The reason is that things we do without thinking, like using common sense, spotting patterns, and handling the physical world, rely on a ton of high-level cognition that's really tough to copy in a machine. So computers can be faster and more accurate at plenty of things, but plenty of everyday tasks still stump them. That's a big reason AI researchers have spent so much time on things like natural language processing, machine learning, and pattern recognition.

In the United States, FCC rules (47 CFR 97.119) require an amateur station to transmit its call sign at least once every 10 minutes during a communication and again at the end of the communication. There's no requirement to identify at the start of a contact, although most operators do so out of habit and courtesy. When you're exchanging transmissions with another station, you only need to give your own call sign. Saying the other station's call is customary but not required, except in certain cases such as third-party traffic involving foreign stations.

The identification must be sent in English by voice or in Morse code (CW) at no more than 20 words per minute, or in the same digital or image mode being used, provided the mode is one the FCC recognizes for identification. Repeaters and auxiliary stations follow the same 10-minute rule, which is why repeaters automatically send their call sign in CW or voice at regular intervals. Stations under remote or automatic control, such as beacons and digipeaters, have similar obligations, sometimes satisfied through the digital protocol itself.

If you're operating under reciprocal privileges or in another country, the rules may differ somewhat. Many countries follow similar intervals, but some, including parts of Europe and Canada, have their own specific wording, such as Canada's 30-minute interval. So check the local regulations if you're operating outside the US.

Land Rover is owned by Jaguar Land Rover, which is a British subsidiary of the Indian conglomerate Tata Motors. Tata Motors acquired Jaguar and Land Rover from Ford in 2008 for about $2.3 billion. Jaguar Land Rover operates as a separate company within the Tata Group, and its headquarters remain in the United Kingdom, in Coventry, England.

I'm not certain about the exact current terms of HSBC Hong Kong's "Deposit Plus" product, since bank deposit offerings change frequently and I may not have up-to-date details. As I understand it, dual-currency or structured-deposit style products of this kind generally pair a fixed-term deposit with an embedded currency option, so the return depends on whether an exchange rate reaches a specified level at maturity. Because the principal can be converted into another currency at maturity, you may receive less than you deposited in your original currency, even though the stated interest rate looks attractive. These products are typically not protected by the Hong Kong Deposit Protection Scheme in the same way as ordinary savings deposits, which is an important point to confirm with the bank.

As for strategies, the most sensible approach is to start by reading the product term sheet closely: identify the strike rate, the currency pair, the tenor, the early-withdrawal rules, the minimum amount, and the maximum possible return and loss. Compare the advertised yield with what a standard fixed deposit or a high-interest savings account would pay over the same period, since the premium is compensation for the risk you are taking. Only commit funds you will not need before maturity, and size the position so that a worst-case conversion would not materially harm your finances. If you already hold the target currency for business or travel reasons, the product may serve as a hedge or a way to earn yield on money you expect to convert anyway; if you do not, you are effectively making a directional bet on exchange rates, and it is worth asking whether that bet fits your goals. Finally, speak with an HSBC relationship manager or an independent financial adviser, ask for a written explanation of the downside scenarios, and make sure you understand the product's risk rating before buying.

I'm sorry to hear your daughter is dealing with stomach pain and smelly gas. A number of conditions could be behind these symptoms, so it's important to have a healthcare provider examine her to find the cause and choose the right treatment. In children, stomach pain and foul-smelling gas can be caused by constipation, a food intolerance or allergy, or an infection such as gastroenteritis. A provider will want to learn about her medical history, perform a physical exam, and may order tests to pinpoint the problem. Treatment will depend on the cause and could involve medication, changes to her diet, or other measures. In the meantime, a few home measures may ease her discomfort. Encourage her to drink plenty of fluids, such as water, clear broth, or electrolyte drinks, to prevent dehydration. Offer bland, easy-to-digest foods like toast, crackers, rice, or mashed potatoes. Hold off on high-fiber or fatty foods, since they are harder to digest and can make symptoms worse. Also avoid caffeine and artificial sweeteners, which can irritate the digestive tract, as well as drinks or foods that are very hot or very cold. Again, please have her seen by a healthcare provider so the cause can be identified and she can get the proper care. I hope this helps.

Hello Laxman. A painful swelling on the eyebrow that has grown over four days is most often an infected epidermoid or sebaceous cyst, or a boil (furuncle) from an inflamed hair follicle. Both are common in young men and usually respond well to treatment. Because it is still growing despite what you have taken, though, you should see a doctor in person soon, ideally within the next day or two.

Amoxicillin alone is often not the best choice for this kind of infection. Skin abscesses and infected cysts are usually caused by Staphylococcus bacteria, and many strains are resistant to plain amoxicillin. A doctor will commonly switch to something like amoxicillin with clavulanic acid, cephalexin, or, depending on local resistance patterns, doxycycline or clindamycin. Please do not change antibiotics on your own. Let a doctor examine the swelling and prescribe the right one. The tetanus injection was reasonable, and paracetamol is fine for pain. Ibuprofen can also help with pain and swelling if you have no stomach problems or other reason to avoid it.

If the swelling has become soft and filled with pus, which feels like a fluid-filled, tender lump sometimes with a yellowish point, antibiotics alone often will not cure it. The usual treatment is a minor procedure called incision and drainage, done under local anaesthesia in a clinic, which releases the pus and gives quick relief. After the infection settles completely, usually a few weeks later, a cyst can come back unless its wall or sac is removed. A small, planned surgical excision at that stage prevents recurrence, and a surgeon or dermatologist can do this with a neat, small scar.

Until you see a doctor, apply a clean warm compress, a cloth soaked in warm water, for about ten to fifteen minutes three or four times a day. This eases pain and helps the swelling either settle or come to a head. Do not squeeze, prick, or try to burst it yourself. The area around the eyes and upper face has veins that connect to deeper areas near the eye and brain, so pressing an infection there can occasionally spread it. Keep the area clean and avoid touching it.

Go to a doctor or emergency department urgently if you notice swelling spreading to your eyelid so the eye starts to close, pain when moving your eye, blurred or double vision, high fever, chills, severe headache, or redness spreading quickly across the forehead or face. These can be signs of the infection spreading toward the eye, which needs prompt treatment.

With proper antibiotics, drainage if needed, and later removal of the cyst if it is a true cyst, this problem is usually cured completely. Please get it checked soon rather than waiting to see if it keeps growing.

Buying your first home is exciting, but the financing side can feel like a maze. Here's what helped me figure it out, and what I'd tell a friend.

Start with your budget. Figure out what you can actually afford before you go house hunting. Look at your income, your existing debts, and how much cash you've got saved for the down payment and closing costs. Don't skip this part, because it keeps you from falling in love with a place you can't really pay for.

Then look at your loan options. You've got traditional mortgages, government-backed loans like FHA and VA loans, and some less common routes like owner financing or rent-to-own deals. Each one has its own rules and tradeoffs, so compare them against your situation instead of just grabbing the first one you hear about.

Get pre-approved early. Once you have a lender look at your finances, you'll know roughly how much they'll let you borrow, which makes your search way more focused. Sellers also tend to take offers more seriously from buyers who are pre-approved, so it's worth doing before you start making offers.

Don't forget the extras. The purchase price isn't the whole story. Closing costs, property taxes, homeowners insurance, and maintenance all add up fast. Build them into your numbers now, or they'll sneak up on you later.

Finally, consider working with a lender or mortgage broker. A good one can explain the loan types in plain language, help with the paperwork, and hunt for better rates and terms than you might find on your own. It's worth talking to a few before you pick one.

Setting up your first investment portfolio can feel overwhelming, but the core process is simpler than most people expect. Start by getting your financial foundation in order: build an emergency fund covering three to six months of essential expenses in a high-yield savings account, and pay off high-interest debt such as credit cards, since no investment reliably beats a 20 percent interest rate. Once that's in place, decide what you're investing for and when you'll need the money. Money needed within three to five years generally belongs in cash or short-term bonds, while money you won't touch for ten years or more can reasonably be invested in stocks, which historically have grown faster than inflation but swing considerably in the short term.

Next, choose the accounts that will hold your investments. If your employer offers a 401(k) with a matching contribution, contribute at least enough to get the full match, since that is an immediate return on your money. In the United States, a Roth or traditional IRA is a common next step, and in other countries similar tax-advantaged retirement accounts exist. A regular taxable brokerage account works for goals beyond retirement. Many beginners find that low-cost brokerages make opening and funding these accounts straightforward.

For the investments themselves, beginners often do well with broad, low-cost index funds or target-date funds rather than picking individual stocks. A total U.S. stock market index fund and a total international stock index fund provide wide diversification, and a bond index fund can add stability. A target-date fund does much of this automatically: you choose the fund whose year matches your expected retirement, and it gradually shifts from stocks toward bonds as that date approaches. Pay attention to expense ratios; a fee of 0.03 to 0.20 percent is excellent, while many actively managed funds charge over 1 percent, which compounds into a substantial difference over decades.

A simple starter allocation might be 80 percent in a total stock market fund and 20 percent in a total bond fund, or a single target-date fund if you prefer hands-off simplicity. Your appropriate mix depends on your age, income stability, and how well you could handle watching your balance drop 30 percent in a bad year without selling. Younger investors with long horizons can typically hold more stocks.

Once invested, set up automatic monthly contributions so investing happens consistently regardless of market news. Rebalance once a year, meaning you bring your percentages back to your target if one asset class has drifted significantly. Avoid checking your balance obsessively, and be wary of anyone promising guaranteed high returns or pressuring you to act quickly.

Finally, educate yourself gradually. Reputable resources include books like "The Simple Path to Wealth" by JL Collins and the Bogleheads wiki. Because tax rules and account options vary by country and personal situation, consider consulting a fee-only fiduciary financial advisor for a one-time review of your plan once you have a clearer picture of your finances.

Eliezer Yudkowsky is an American artificial intelligence researcher, writer, and public commentator, best known for his work on AI alignment, the problem of ensuring that advanced AI systems pursue goals that are beneficial to humans. Born in 1979, he is largely self-taught in formal academic terms, and he rose to prominence in the late 1990s and 2000s through online writing about rationality, decision theory, and the long-term future of artificial intelligence.

In 2000 he co-founded the Singularity Institute for Artificial Intelligence, which was later renamed the Machine Intelligence Research Institute (MIRI). The organization focuses on theoretical research into how to build AI systems that remain reliably aligned with human values, even as they become more capable than their creators. Yudkowsky has been one of the most prominent voices arguing that advanced AI could pose an existential risk to humanity if developed carelessly, and in recent years he has become a leading advocate for slowing or halting the development of frontier AI systems until safety can be better understood.

He is also well known for the "Sequences," a large collection of blog posts written between 2006 and 2009 on the LessWrong website, which he founded. These essays cover cognitive biases, Bayesian reasoning, and the art of rational thinking, and they helped build a community of readers often called rationalists. He additionally wrote *Harry Potter and the Methods of Rationality*, a widely read fan fiction that retells the Harry Potter story with its characters applying scientific and rational thinking.

Yudkowsky's views are controversial in some circles. His warnings about AI risk are considered alarmist by some researchers, who argue that the dangers are overstated or too speculative, while others regard him as one of the earliest and most important thinkers on the subject. Regardless of where one stands, he remains an influential figure in discussions about AI safety, rationality, and the future of technology.

Smirnoff is owned by Diageo, the British multinational beverage company headquartered in London. Diageo acquired the brand through its predecessor companies; it came into the fold when Grand Metropolitan merged with Guinness in 1997 to form Diageo, and Grand Metropolitan had gotten Smirnoff by acquiring Heublein in 1987.

The brand's origins go back to Russia in the 1860s, when Pyotr Smirnov founded a vodka distillery in Moscow. After the Russian Revolution, the family lost the business, and Vladimir Smirnov, a family member, eventually reestablished production in Europe. The American rights were sold to Rudolph Kunett, who began making Smirnoff in the United States, and Heublein later bought the rights in 1939 and helped turn it into one of the best-selling vodkas in the world.

Diageo also owns many other well-known spirits brands, including Johnnie Walker, Captain Morgan, Tanqueray, Guinness, and Don Julio.

In computing, pattern matching means examining a sequence of tokens to determine whether it contains the parts that make up a given pattern. Unlike pattern recognition, the pattern being searched for is precisely specified in advance. The technique appears across many areas, such as computer science, data mining, and machine learning. Analysts commonly rely on it to pull information out of data, verify that data is valid, or locate particular structures within it. Numerous algorithms and methods exist for this purpose, and which one is appropriate depends on the demands of the task. Widely used approaches include regular expressions, finite automata, and string search algorithms like Boyer-Moore and Knuth-Morris-Pratt. Certain programming languages also build pattern matching into the language itself, letting a programmer define the shapes that data must fit and break the data apart accordingly. This makes it possible either to extract pieces of information or to carry out different operations based on the exact structure of the data.

A new lump in the armpit combined with pins and needles in the fingers of the same arm is worth getting checked promptly, and I'd not wait until next Tuesday if you can avoid it. Please call your midwife, obstetrician, or GP today rather than deciding on your own. You've been on amitriptyline for four years, and stopping it suddenly can cause withdrawal symptoms such as poor sleep, nausea, dizziness, irritability, and a rebound of anxiety. The advice you were given to stop near term is probably about the baby. Amitriptyline crosses the placenta, and taking it close to delivery can occasionally cause effects in newborns, such as sleepiness, feeding difficulties, or temporary withdrawal symptoms. Your team will weigh that against the risks of stopping, which in your case include your sleep and your anxiety. They may suggest a different approach, a taper, or a plan for restarting after the birth, so tell them exactly what has happened over the last two nights.

Don't restart or change the dose without speaking to them first, and don't simply continue without checking, since they need to know you've stopped and how you're feeling. While you wait for advice, avoid alcohol and other sedatives, and let someone know how you're coping.

Seek urgent help the same day, through your maternity unit, NHS 111 or your local equivalent, or emergency services if needed, if you have a racing or pounding heartbeat, confusion, severe agitation, hallucinations, thoughts of harming yourself, or any signs of labour or reduced baby movements.

Devaluing a nation's currency can meaningfully affect the prices of its stocks. When Mexico's government introduced a package of economic reforms in 1994, one element was a devaluation of the peso of roughly 50%. Mexican equities fell sharply as a result, since the lower currency value made them less appealing to overseas investors. Several mechanisms explain how devaluation can push stock prices down. To begin with, it erodes the purchasing power of investors who hold shares denominated in the local currency: when the peso loses value, a given amount of goods or services costs more pesos, so the worth of those holdings shrinks. Devaluation can also squeeze corporate profits. A firm that sells abroad and collects foreign currency will earn fewer local-currency units once those receipts are converted, and its share price may drop accordingly. Lastly, devaluation can dent equity prices by undermining confidence in the broader economy. If investors read a devaluation as a signal that the economy is in trouble and that further hardship may follow, they may sell off shares. In sum, the effect of devaluation on equity markets is intricate and hinges on many factors, so investors should weigh the risks and consequences of currency movements carefully before making decisions.

Direct marketing is a form of advertising where companies speak to consumers directly, using channels like email, text messages, and social media. Its purpose is to reach people personally and hold their attention, usually in the hope that they will buy something or carry out another particular action. Campaigns of this kind generally rely on targeted lists of consumers who have shown interest in a given product or service. Such lists may be built from several sources, among them customer databases, data on website visitors, and records of past purchases.

A major benefit of direct marketing is that companies can measure how well their campaigns perform, using figures such as open rates, click-through rates, and conversion rates. With this information, businesses can see which approaches succeed and which fall short, then adjust their plans as needed.

Direct marketing takes several forms. Email marketing means sending promotional messages or newsletters to a set of email addresses. SMS marketing means delivering text messages to a set of phone numbers. Social media marketing means promoting products or services on platforms such as Facebook, Twitter, and Instagram. Direct mail means posting promotional items, such as brochures or catalogs, to consumers. Telemarketing means phoning consumers to present products or services.

All in all, direct marketing can be a useful way for businesses to connect with consumers and engage them, as long as it is carried out with respect for their privacy and their preferences.

A googol is a unit of measurement equal to a 1 followed by 100 zeros. People often use it to express enormous quantities, such as the number of atoms in the observable universe or the number of possible combinations on a combination lock. Mathematically, a googol is written as 1 x 10^100 and abbreviated "G." For instance, to express the number of atoms in the observable universe, estimated at about 10^80, in googol units, you would write 1.0 x 10^20 G. Likewise, a combination lock with 100 dials, each with 10 possible values, could be expressed as 1 x 10^100 G. Note that the googol is not an officially recognized unit and is not used in scientific or mathematical work. Its main purpose is to make very large numbers easier to grasp.

Yeah, an emergency fund should sit somewhere safe where you can grab the money fast if something blows up, like a car repair or a surprise medical bill. High-yield checking accounts can pay better interest than regular checking, but read the terms and fees before you jump in, because some of them have catches.

Here's what I'd look at. First, the interest rate. Don't just take the first one you see, compare a few and make sure it's actually competitive. Second, fees. Some of these accounts charge for things like ATM use or monthly maintenance, so read the fine print and know what you'd be paying. Third, access. You want to be able to pull your money out without waiting around or running into weird restrictions, since that's the whole point of an emergency fund. And last, the bank itself. Stick with a reputable one that's been stable for a long time.

So shop around and compare before you pick. If you're not sure, talk to a financial advisor or just do some digging on your own to figure out what fits best.

COMPAS, which stands for Correctional Offender Management Profiling for Alternative Sanctions, is a commercial risk assessment tool used in the United States criminal justice system. It was originally developed by a company called Northpointe, which later rebranded as Equivant. The software is used by courts, probation departments, and corrections agencies in many states to estimate the likelihood that a defendant or offender will commit another crime or fail to appear in court, and to help guide decisions about bail, sentencing, parole, and supervision.

The tool works by having a defendant answer a long questionnaire and by drawing on information from their criminal record. The questions cover things like prior arrests, age at first arrest, employment history, substance use, family background, social relationships, residential stability, and attitudes toward crime. COMPAS then produces scores, typically on a scale from one to ten, that place a person into low, medium, or high risk categories for outcomes such as general recidivism and violent recidivism. It also includes a needs assessment intended to identify areas where rehabilitation programs might help. The exact formula used to compute the scores is proprietary, meaning the company does not publicly disclose how the inputs are weighted.

COMPAS became widely known after a 2016 investigation by the news organization ProPublica. Reporters analyzed the scores of thousands of people arrested in Broward County, Florida, and compared them with whether those people actually reoffended over the following two years. They concluded that the tool was biased against Black defendants, finding that Black defendants who did not go on to reoffend were nearly twice as likely as white defendants to have been wrongly labeled high risk, while white defendants who did reoffend were more likely to have been mislabeled low risk. Northpointe disputed the analysis, arguing that the scores were equally accurate across racial groups in the sense that a given score corresponded to roughly the same probability of reoffending regardless of race.

This disagreement turned out to be important beyond COMPAS itself. Researchers in computer science and statistics showed that when two groups have different underlying rates of recidivism, it is mathematically impossible for a risk score to satisfy several intuitive definitions of fairness at the same time, such as equal calibration across groups and equal false positive and false negative rates. The COMPAS debate therefore became a central case study in the field of algorithmic fairness and in broader discussions about the ethics of using machine learning and automated decision tools in high-stakes settings.

Other criticisms have focused on accuracy and transparency. A 2018 study by Julia Dressel and Hany Farid found that COMPAS predicted recidivism with roughly 65 percent accuracy, about the same as untrained people recruited online and no better than a simple model using only age and number of prior convictions. Critics also argue that because the algorithm is a trade secret, defendants cannot fully examine or challenge the basis of a score that may affect their liberty. This issue reached the Wisconsin Supreme Court in the 2016 case State v. Loomis, where a defendant argued that the use of COMPAS at sentencing violated his due process rights. The court allowed the use of the tool but ruled that it could not be the determining factor in a sentence and that judges must be given written warnings about its limitations.

In short, COMPAS is both a practical tool still used in parts of the justice system and a landmark example in public debates about whether, and how, algorithms should be trusted to inform decisions about people's lives.

The United States President leads the federal executive branch and serves as commander-in-chief of the country's armed forces. Charged with carrying out federal law, the President oversees how the government is run. The office includes authority to negotiate treaties with other nations and to name federal judges and other officials, whose appointments require Senate approval. The President speaks for the nation internationally and guides its overall course. In addition, the President may put forward and veto legislation and issue pardons for federal crimes.

I'm sorry your father is dealing with this pain and discomfort. An enlarged liver, known medically as hepatomegaly, and fatty liver can both lead to abdominal pain, along with symptoms like tiredness, weakness, and unintended weight loss. Identifying what is causing the enlarged liver and the fatty buildup is essential so that the right treatment can be chosen. Several approaches may help. Lifestyle adjustments, such as changing eating habits, becoming more physically active, and cutting back on alcohol, can improve liver function and lower the chance of complications. Depending on the underlying cause, a doctor might prescribe medication to keep the condition under control. In certain situations, surgery may be needed to take out tissue in the liver that is damaged or diseased. Some people may also be advised to consider other options, such as weight loss surgery or a liver transplant. It is important for your father to follow his doctor's guidance and to get medical care promptly if his symptoms get worse or fail to improve. Treating any related conditions that may be contributing to liver disease, such as obesity, high blood pressure, or diabetes, is also important.

Sorry to hear about your dad's kidney problem. Treatment really depends on what's causing it and how bad it is, so I can't really say much about his meds without knowing more about his history and where he's at right now. I'd just keep him on the plan his doctor gave him and take everything as directed. If something about the meds or the plan worries you, bring it up with his healthcare provider. They know his case and can walk you through what's going on, which is way more useful than anything a stranger online can tell you.

Raphael, the Italian Renaissance painter, was born on March 28, 1483, in Urbino, Italy. Some sources give his birth year as 1483 with the exact date sometimes cited as April 6, but March 28 is the date most commonly given. He died on April 6, 1520, in Rome, at the age of 37.

It's not normal for redness around the penis to stick around, so you should really get it checked by a doctor. Vaseline might calm things down for a bit, but it won't fix whatever's causing it. There are a bunch of possible culprits: plain old irritation, a fungal or bacterial infection, an STI, or an allergic reaction to something like soap, detergent, or condoms. A doctor can figure out which one it is, and they may run some tests or prescribe a cream or pills to clear it up. Until then, keep the area clean with warm water every day and try to avoid tight underwear or pants that rub, since that can make things worse.

The largest whale, and in fact the largest animal known to have ever lived, is the blue whale (Balaenoptera musculus). Adults typically reach lengths of 24 to 30 meters, or about 80 to 100 feet, and the biggest recorded individuals have been close to 30 meters long. They commonly weigh between 100 and 150 tonnes, and exceptionally large specimens may have approached 180 tonnes or more. To put that in perspective, a blue whale's heart can be about the size of a small car, and its tongue alone can weigh as much as an elephant.

Despite their enormous size, blue whales feed almost entirely on tiny shrimp-like crustaceans called krill. During the feeding season, a single adult can consume several tonnes of krill in a day by lunging into dense swarms and filtering the water through baleen plates in its mouth. They are found in oceans around the world, migrating between cold, productive feeding grounds and warmer waters where they breed.

Blue whales were hunted heavily in the 20th century, and their numbers collapsed to a small fraction of their original population before international protection began in the 1960s. Populations have been recovering slowly since, though the species is still considered endangered. Threats today include ship strikes, entanglement in fishing gear, ocean noise, and changes in krill availability tied to climate change.

The second largest whale is the fin whale, which can reach about 25 meters, while the largest toothed whale is the sperm whale, with males reaching around 16 to 20 meters.

I'm sorry you've been dealing with this for two years. The combination you describe, with unexplained weight loss, night sweats, itching all over, swollen neck glands, a recurring red scaly rash, anemia with low MCV, rising liver enzymes, and an elevated CEA, is a pattern doctors take seriously. It deserves a focused workup soon rather than more waiting. I can't diagnose you, but I can explain what these symptoms together can point to so you can push for the right tests.

The most important possibility to rule out is a lymphoma, a cancer of the lymphatic system. Weight loss, drenching night sweats, and fevers are called "B symptoms" and are classic for lymphoma. Persistent generalized itching is a well-known feature of Hodgkin lymphoma, and lymphoma can involve the liver and cause anemia. One type, cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (mycosis fungoides or its more advanced form, Sézary syndrome), shows up as red, scaly patches that come and go and are often misdiagnosed for years as eczema or psoriasis. It can later involve lymph nodes and blood. Given your rash and swollen glands, this is worth specifically asking about.

Other conditions can cause a similar mix. Chronic infections such as HIV, hepatitis B or C, or tuberculosis can cause swollen glands, weight loss, night sweats, and liver changes. Sarcoidosis can affect the skin, lymph nodes, and liver. Autoimmune liver diseases like primary biliary cholangitis cause intense itching and rising liver tests. Celiac disease can cause iron deficiency (which fits a low MCV), weight loss, abnormal liver enzymes, and an itchy blistering rash. A low MCV most often means iron deficiency, and in an adult that raises the question of slow blood loss from the gut. Your mildly raised CEA fits that concern, though CEA can also rise from smoking, liver disease, or inflammation.

The tests that usually get answers are a biopsy of a swollen lymph node, ideally removing a whole node rather than just a needle sample, since that is the best way to diagnose or exclude lymphoma. A biopsy of the rash by a dermatologist is also key, and it helps to have it taken when the rash is active. Other useful steps include a CT scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis, a blood smear and flow cytometry, iron studies, tests for HIV and hepatitis, a celiac antibody test, and possibly an endoscopy and colonoscopy to check for bleeding or a gut source of the CEA.

When you see your doctor, say plainly that you have had two years of weight loss, night sweats, whole-body itching, persistent swollen neck glands, and a recurring scaly rash, along with worsening anemia, liver numbers, and an elevated CEA. Ask directly whether you can be referred to a hematologist and whether a lymph node biopsy and skin biopsy can be done. If you feel you are not being heard, it is reasonable to ask for a second opinion, ideally at a larger hospital or academic center. Many of these conditions, including lymphomas, are very treatable, especially once properly diagnosed. If you develop high fevers, yellowing skin or eyes, severe weakness, shortness of breath, or black or bloody stools, go to an emergency department.

Inflation describes how quickly the overall price level of goods and services climbs, which in turn means that each unit of money buys less than it did before. To keep the economy on an even keel, central banks work to hold inflation down while also preventing deflation, a sustained fall in prices. One common yardstick is the Consumer Price Index (CPI), which tracks how much, on average, the prices consumers pay for a fixed set of goods and services change over time. Because it captures what people genuinely spend their money on, the CPI is frequently relied upon to gauge inflation. The pace of inflation shifts across the years and differs from nation to nation. Prices generally trend upward over the long run, though the speed of that increase can rise and fall. Many governments target an annual inflation rate near 2%, a level regarded as modest and steady, yet some countries experience rates well above or below that mark. Since your question does not specify a particular country or period, a precise answer is hard to give without further details.

Buying a first home is usually the largest financial commitment a person makes, and the costs reach well beyond the sticker price.

The most visible expense is the down payment. Many buyers aim for 20 percent of the purchase price, which avoids private mortgage insurance on conventional loans, but plenty of loans accept much less. FHA loans in the United States allow as little as 3.5 percent down, and some conventional programs accept 3 percent. A smaller down payment means a larger loan, higher monthly payments, and more interest paid over time, plus mortgage insurance premiums until you build enough equity.

Closing costs are the next surprise for many first-time buyers. These typically run 2 to 5 percent of the loan amount and cover lender fees, appraisal, title insurance, inspections, attorney fees, and prepaid items like property taxes and homeowners insurance. Some sellers agree to cover part of these, and certain first-time buyer programs offer grants or assistance.

The monthly payment consists of principal, interest, property taxes, and insurance, often abbreviated PITI. Your interest rate matters enormously: on a 30-year loan, a one-point difference in rate can change the payment by roughly 10 percent and the lifetime interest by tens of thousands of dollars. A shorter loan, such as 15 years, costs more per month but dramatically reduces total interest. A common guideline is to keep housing costs below about 28 percent of gross monthly income, and total debt payments below about 36 to 43 percent, though lenders may approve more than is comfortable.

Ongoing ownership costs are where budgets often break. Maintenance and repairs commonly average 1 to 2 percent of the home's value per year, and a failed roof, water heater, or HVAC system can cost thousands at once. Utilities are usually higher than in an apartment, and condos or planned communities add homeowners association fees. Property taxes can also rise after purchase, particularly if the home is reassessed at your purchase price.

Your credit and savings position shape the terms you get. A higher credit score lowers your rate, so paying down card balances and avoiding new debt before applying is worthwhile. You should also keep an emergency fund after closing, ideally three to six months of expenses, so that one repair or job disruption does not become a crisis.

On the positive side, each payment builds equity, and over long periods homes have often appreciated, though not reliably, and not in every market. Mortgage interest and property tax deductions can help, but only if you itemize, and with higher standard deductions many buyers no longer benefit. There may also be first-time buyer programs, tax credits, or down payment assistance worth researching locally.

Finally, consider liquidity and flexibility. A home is hard to sell quickly, and selling typically costs 6 to 10 percent of the price after agent commissions and fees. If you might move within about five years, renting can be the better financial choice. Getting a mortgage pre-approval, comparing multiple lenders, and running a realistic budget that includes all of these costs will give you the clearest picture before you commit.

"Dialysis tubes" can mean two different things depending on context: a laboratory material used in science classes and research, or the tubing used in medical dialysis for people with kidney failure.

In the laboratory sense, dialysis tubing is a thin, flexible tube made of a semi-permeable membrane, usually regenerated cellulose or cellophane. It has tiny pores that let small molecules such as water, salts, and glucose pass through while blocking larger molecules like starch, proteins, or DNA. Manufacturers rate it by a "molecular weight cutoff," which indicates roughly how large a molecule must be before the membrane holds it back. Scientists use it to purify proteins, remove salts from samples, or exchange one buffer solution for another. In schools it is a common way to demonstrate diffusion and osmosis, often as a model of a cell membrane or the small intestine: students fill a bag of tubing with a starch and glucose solution, place it in water, and test which substances pass through.

In the medical sense, dialysis tubes are the tubing and access devices used during dialysis treatment, which filters waste and excess fluid from the blood when the kidneys can no longer do so. In hemodialysis, blood flows out of the body through plastic tubing called bloodlines, passes through a filter called a dialyzer, and returns through more tubing. The dialyzer itself contains thousands of hollow fibers made of semi-permeable membrane, working on the same principle as laboratory dialysis tubing. Patients usually connect to the machine through a fistula or graft in the arm, or through a catheter, a soft tube placed into a large vein, often in the neck or chest. In peritoneal dialysis, a catheter is surgically placed in the abdomen so that cleansing fluid can be drained in and out, using the lining of the abdomen as the natural filter.

Both uses rely on the same basic idea: a membrane that separates substances by size, letting small waste molecules and water move across while keeping larger molecules in place.

Swelling after surgery is pretty common, especially in the feet and ankles. It can come from the surgery itself, certain meds, or some underlying health issues. The big thing is to follow whatever your doctor or nurse told you to do. Usually that means keeping your feet up above heart level as much as you can, especially when you're resting or sleeping. Gravity does a lot of the work there, pulling fluid away from your ankles. Compression stockings or wraps can help too, since they add gentle pressure to the area. Try to move around when your provider says it's okay. Even small bits of movement get your circulation going. If you have to stand or sit for a long stretch, take breaks and walk around a bit. And drink plenty of water, since staying hydrated helps your body flush out extra fluid. If the swelling sticks around even after you've done all this, call your provider. They may want to check for something else going on and figure out the best next step.

A 529 plan is a tax-advantaged savings account that helps families set aside money for higher education costs. These plans come in two forms: prepaid tuition plans and college savings plans. With a prepaid tuition plan, you can buy tuition credits at participating colleges and universities at current prices and redeem them in the future. States or educational institutions usually sponsor these plans, and they may be limited to particular schools. A college savings plan, by contrast, lets you put money into an investment account to cover your child's educational costs. The funds grow without being taxed and can pay for tuition, fees, room and board, and other qualified expenses at any accredited college or university in the United States. Both kinds of plans provide tax advantages, including tax-free withdrawals when the money goes toward qualified education expenses, and in some cases state tax deductions or credits for contributions. To start a 529 plan, you select a plan and sign up through its administrator. You'll be asked for some personal and financial details, and you can either pick your own investments or choose a pre-set investment portfolio. After that, you can contribute regularly or make a single lump-sum payment. Because they offer the possibility of tax-free growth and tax-free withdrawals for qualified education expenses, 529 plans can be a helpful way to save for your child's college education. Still, it's wise to weigh your options carefully and do your own research to decide whether a 529 plan suits you and your family.

Its more than 600,000 main entries include definitions, etymologies, and quotations that show words being used in context. The dictionary also records pronunciation, grammar, and regional differences in usage. Available in both print and digital form, the OED is revised regularly to keep pace with developments in English. The French don't have a law that makes answering emails after 6 pm illegal. In 2017 France passed a "right to disconnect" rule. It requires companies with 50 or more employees to negotiate rules about when workers are expected to be reachable after hours. Some firms set quiet times, and others just agree that no one has to reply at night. It's more of a workplace agreement than a hard ban, and the exact rules vary by company.

On productivity, the short answer is yes. Think of it like a sports team. A player who runs hard for 30 minutes can accomplish more than someone who jogs around the field for three hours. France counts its output per hour worked, and that number is among the highest in Europe and comparable to or above the United States. The French work fewer hours in total, roughly 1,500 a year on average versus about 1,800 in the US, but they get a lot done in each one.

The economy doesn't collapse because it isn't built on hours alone. It depends on how much each hour produces, which comes from good training, strong public services, modern equipment, and a large, varied economy. Working fewer hours doesn't mean doing less, as long as each hour is productive. France also has some real downsides, like higher unemployment and tighter rules for hiring and firing, so the trade-offs are real and debated.
