Okay, so the disk defragmenter basically rearranges the stuff on your hard drive so each file sits in one continuous chunk instead of being scattered all over the place. That can make your computer run a bit smoother, since the drive doesn't have to hunt around for every piece of a file. When a drive gets really fragmented, it can take noticeably longer to pull up what you need, because the read head has to jump between a bunch of spots. Defragging cuts down on that wandering and can give the whole machine a bit of a boost.

Here's how to run it. Open the Start menu and type "defragment" into the search bar. Pick "Defragment and Optimize Drives" from the results. That opens the tool, and you can choose whichever drive you want to work on. Hit "Analyze" first if you're curious how messy it is, then click "Optimize" to actually start. How long it takes really depends on how big the drive is and how fragmented it was to begin with, so don't be surprised if it runs for a while.

The "AI effect" is a term used in the field of artificial intelligence to describe a recurring pattern in how people judge AI achievements. Once a task that was once considered a hallmark of intelligence is accomplished by a machine, people tend to redefine intelligence so that the accomplishment no longer counts as genuinely intelligent. The goalposts keep moving, so that AI is always defined as whatever has not yet been achieved.

The classic example comes from chess. For decades, playing chess well was widely regarded as a deep demonstration of human reasoning, and computer programs that could beat strong players were seen as a major milestone. When IBM's Deep Blue defeated world champion Garry Kasparov in 1997, many observers responded not by admiring the machine's intelligence but by arguing that brute-force search was not real thinking. Similar reactions followed with other feats, such as machines recognizing speech, translating text, or defeating champions at Go. Each time, the achievement was discounted as mere computation or pattern matching rather than true understanding.

The term was popularized by computer scientist Larry Tesler, who reportedly said that "intelligence is whatever machines haven't done yet." Whether or not that exact phrasing originated with him, the idea captures the phenomenon well.

The AI effect matters for several reasons. It shapes public expectations, making it hard to know when AI systems have truly reached a given capability. It can also make progress seem less impressive than it is, since successful techniques often get absorbed into ordinary software and stop being labeled as AI. At the same time, it raises legitimate philosophical questions about what intelligence actually means and whether we have clear criteria for recognizing it.

Java is a general-purpose, object-oriented programming language that was developed by James Gosling and his team at Sun Microsystems and released publicly in 1995. Its central design goal was "write once, run anywhere," meaning that a program written in Java can run on any device or operating system that has a Java runtime environment, without the programmer needing to rewrite or recompile the code for each platform. It achieves this by compiling source code into an intermediate form called bytecode, which is then executed by the Java Virtual Machine (JVM), a software layer that translates bytecode into instructions the host machine understands.

The language is known for its syntax, which resembles C and C++ but removes many of the more error-prone features of those languages, such as manual memory management and direct pointer manipulation. Java uses automatic garbage collection to reclaim memory no longer in use, and it emphasizes object-oriented concepts like classes, inheritance, encapsulation, and polymorphism. It also includes a large standard library that provides support for networking, data structures, input and output, concurrency, and graphical interfaces.

Since its release, Java has been widely used for enterprise server applications, large-scale web back-end systems, Android mobile applications, and embedded systems, among many other domains. Oracle Corporation acquired Sun Microsystems in 2010 and now owns the Java trademark and the primary implementation, though open-source implementations such as OpenJDK are also widely used. The language continues to evolve through regular releases, with newer versions adding features such as lambda expressions, modules, records, and pattern matching while maintaining a strong emphasis on backward compatibility.

Swollen, tender lymph nodes in the armpit are very common and, in a 25-year-old woman, they are usually a sign that your immune system is doing its job rather than a sign of something serious. Lymph nodes act as filters for the lymphatic fluid draining from the arm, the side of the chest wall, and the breast. When they encounter something they need to respond to, such as bacteria or irritation, they enlarge and often become tender. Tenderness is generally a reassuring feature because it suggests inflammation or infection rather than cancer, which more often causes painless lumps.

There are many everyday reasons the armpit nodes in particular might swell on and off. Shaving can cause tiny cuts, ingrown hairs, or folliculitis that the nodes respond to. Deodorants and antiperspirants can irritate the skin. Minor infections or scratches on the hand or arm, a cold or other viral illness, and recent vaccinations, including flu and COVID-19 shots, commonly cause temporary swelling. Many women also notice that breast and armpit tissue changes with the menstrual cycle, becoming fuller, lumpier, or more tender in the days before a period, and some have small amounts of breast tissue extending into the armpit that behave the same way. If your swelling comes and goes, is tender, and settles within a few weeks, these explanations fit well.

A normal reactive node is usually small (under about one centimeter, roughly the size of a pea or small bean), soft or rubbery, movable under the skin when you press on it, and often tender. It tends to appear in response to something and shrink back within two to four weeks. A lump that deserves a doctor's evaluation is one that keeps growing, stays enlarged longer than about two to four weeks without an obvious cause, is larger than about one to one and a half centimeters, feels hard, or seems fixed in place rather than sliding under your fingers. It is also worth getting checked if the swelling comes with unexplained fevers, drenching night sweats, unintentional weight loss, or persistent fatigue, if nodes are swollen in several areas of the body at once (such as the neck and groin as well), or if you notice changes in the breast on the same side, such as a new breast lump, skin dimpling or redness, nipple changes, or nipple discharge. Redness, warmth, and significant pain over a node can signal an infection or abscess that may need treatment.

A practical approach is to get familiar with what your own body feels like. Check your armpits and breasts at the same point in your cycle each month, ideally about a week after your period starts when hormonal swelling is lowest, so you can more easily tell what is new. When you notice a swollen node, it can help to jot down when it appeared, roughly how big it is, and whether you had anything that might explain it, like a shaving nick, an illness, or a vaccine. If it is gone or clearly shrinking within a few weeks, that is typical reactive swelling.

Because yours recur often, it is reasonable to mention them at your next routine checkup even if nothing feels alarming. A doctor can examine the area, help you learn what is normal for you, and look for patterns such as a skin condition or recurrent infection. If any node shows the concerning features above, they may order an ultrasound, which is quick and painless and the usual first test at your age. Overall, though, recurrent tender armpit nodes in a healthy 25-year-old are most often benign.

No website is 100 percent secure, and no one can honestly promise that a website can never be hacked. But that doesn't mean every website is easy to break into. Some are very hard to hack, and some are very easy.

Imagine a website is a big toy castle that you build out of blocks. You put doors and windows in it so friends can come in and play. Every door and window is a place where someone could sneak in if the lock is bad. Now imagine the castle is built from thousands of blocks that you didn't make yourself. Other people made them and gave them to you. If one of those blocks has a tiny crack nobody noticed, a sneaky person might find it and push their way in.

That is basically why websites can be hacked. They are built by people, and people make mistakes. A website is made of lots of parts: the code the owners wrote, software made by other companies, the computers it runs on, and the people who use and manage it. A mistake in any one of these can become a hole. Sometimes the hole is a bug in the code. Sometimes it is a password that is too easy to guess, like "1234." Sometimes a person gets tricked into handing over their key, like when someone pretends to be a friend and asks for it. That last one is very common, and it has nothing to do with the code at all.

Another reason is that the people trying to break in only need to find one weak spot, while the people protecting the castle have to guard every single one, all the time. Also, new cracks keep getting discovered in old blocks, so a castle that was safe yesterday might not be safe today.

So why aren't all websites broken into constantly? Because owners can do a lot to make it hard. They can use strong locks, keep their blocks updated and patched, watch for strange visitors, only give keys to people who need them, and hire friendly experts to test the castle by trying to sneak in and then report the weak spots. A well-protected website can be so hard to break into that most thieves give up and go find an easier one.

Think of it like a bank vault compared with a cardboard box. Neither is perfectly safe, but one takes a huge amount of effort to open. The goal of security isn't being unbreakable, because that is impossible. It is making it so hard and costly to get in that it is not worth trying, and noticing quickly if someone does.

Private companies get a reputation for being more efficient than government agencies, and a lot of that comes down to profit. If a company wants to make money, it has to find cheaper and faster ways to make its products or deliver its services. Government agencies don't really face that same squeeze, since they're paid for by taxpayers no matter how they perform. That said, it's not a simple call. Companies might chase profits at the expense of the public, while government groups tend to answer more directly to voters and are usually more open about how they make decisions. So choosing between the two for any given service means weighing those tradeoffs. Take the military and NASA, for example. They both work with firms like Boeing and SpaceX because those companies have the know-how and hardware to build the complicated systems involved. Still, the government has plenty of its own agencies and contractors building and maintaining the stuff it relies on.

A changed itinerary is one of the stronger grounds for a refund, but the right route depends on where you bought the ticket, where you're flying, and whether you accepted the change. If you tell me those details, I can be more specific.

Start by documenting the change. Save the original confirmation, the notice of the schedule change (screenshot it and keep the email), and any record of what you were told by phone or chat, with dates and names if possible. Compare the original and new itineraries carefully. Many rules care about how much the departure or arrival time moved, whether you lost a connection, or whether you changed cities or airports. In the US, the Department of Transportation generally requires a refund if the airline makes a significant change and you decline the alternative it offers. In the EU, UK, and some other regions, similar rules apply, with compensation possible for long delays or cancellations, though the thresholds and exceptions differ.

Next, request the refund from the party you paid. If you booked directly with the airline, submit a refund request through its website or customer service and state that you did not accept the change and are entitled to a full refund under the applicable rules. If you booked through an online travel agency, a consolidator, or a third-party merchant, contact them first, since they are usually the ones who process the refund, but make clear that the airline initiated the change. Keep the tone factual and reference the specific change. Note the date and any reference numbers, and follow up in writing if you're given only verbal assurances.

If the merchant or airline refuses, or stalls for several weeks, you can file a chargeback with your credit card issuer. Most card networks allow disputes for services not rendered as described or for a significant unauthorized change, and the window is often around 60 to 120 days from the transaction or from when you discovered the problem, so don't wait too long. Your card issuer will ask for your evidence, so the documentation you gathered earlier will matter. In the US, a billing error dispute under the Fair Credit Billing Act has to be raised in writing to the card issuer within 60 days of the statement showing the charge. If you paid by debit card or another method, ask your bank about its dispute process, which may have different timelines.

If none of that works, you can escalate to a regulator or consumer agency, such as the DOT's complaint portal in the US, the aviation authority or consumer body in your country, or a small-claims court for the amount in dispute. Filing a regulatory complaint often prompts a faster response from airlines.

If you share where you bought the ticket, your country, whether you accepted the new schedule or were already traveling, and what the airline has told you so far, I can help you figure out which rules apply and draft a specific refund request or chargeback explanation.

Pain in the kidney area and testicle can have a few different causes. The usual suspects include kidney stones, a urinary tract infection, testicular torsion, and prostatitis (inflammation of the prostate). You really should see a doctor to figure out what's going on. Kidney stones can hurt like crazy and often need to be removed somehow. UTIs are painful too, but they usually clear up with antibiotics. Testicular torsion is an emergency, though, since it needs surgery fast or the testicle can get permanently damaged. Prostatitis can be managed with medication and some lifestyle changes. Acidity meds might take the edge off for a bit, since acid can sometimes add to that discomfort, but they won't tell you what's actually causing it. Get it checked out.

I'm sorry you're dealing with this after your surgery. Stomach cramps, gas, and trouble passing stool are very common in the first few days after surgery, especially when general anesthesia has been used, since anesthesia and reduced movement slow the bowel down. Pain medications, particularly opioids, can also make constipation worse. Even so, you should let your surgical team know, because they can check whether anything else is going on and suggest a safe remedy.

In the meantime, gentle steps often help. Try to walk around a little several times a day as your team allows, since movement helps the bowel start working again. Drink plenty of fluids unless you have been told to restrict them. Eat small, simple meals with fiber such as soft fruits, cooked vegetables, oats, or rice, and avoid heavy, greasy, or very gassy foods for now. Warm drinks and gentle abdominal massage may ease trapped gas. Do not start any laxative or stool softener without checking with your doctor first, because some are unsuitable after ear surgery or while you are on certain medications. Your surgeon or pharmacist can recommend a suitable option.

Contact your doctor or go to emergency care promptly if you have severe or worsening belly pain, a swollen or hard abdomen, persistent vomiting, no passage of gas or stool for several days, blood in your stool, a fever, or any new dizziness, facial weakness, severe headache, fluid or bleeding from the ear, or sudden hearing change. Those symptoms need urgent attention.

Norah Jones was born Geethali Norah Jones Shankar on March 30, 1979, in New York City. Her father is Ravi Shankar, the Indian sitar virtuoso and composer who became one of the most famous Indian musicians in the world and who influenced Western artists such as George Harrison of the Beatles. Her mother is Sue Jones, a concert producer and nurse from the United States.

Her parents were not married, and the relationship ended when she was young. Norah grew up in Grapevine, Texas, near Dallas, raised mainly by her mother, and had little contact with her father during her early years. She has said she didn't really know him well until later, and they reconnected more as she got older, particularly as her own music career took off. Her father died in December 2012.

She has a half-sister, Anoushka Shankar, who is also a sitar player and a well-known musician, and another half-sister, Shubhendra's family line aside, from her father's side. Her father also had a son, Shubho, from his marriage to Sukanya Rajan, but Anoushka is the one most closely associated with Norah in public. Norah took her professional name by dropping the Shankar surname and using her mother's name, Jones.

Penn State's main football stadium is Beaver Stadium, located on the university's University Park campus in State College, Pennsylvania. It sits on the south side of campus and is one of the largest stadiums in the United States, with a capacity of roughly 106,000 people, making it among the biggest in the Western Hemisphere.

Action selection is the problem of deciding what an agent should do next, given that it has many possible things it could do. The term is used across several fields, including psychology, neuroscience, robotics, artificial intelligence, and ethology, and in each of them it refers to the same basic puzzle: at any moment an agent with multiple goals, drives, and options must resolve the competition among them and commit to one behavior, or a compatible set of behaviors, so that it can act coherently.

The problem arises because an agent's body and resources are limited. An animal cannot flee a predator, eat, and groom at the same moment, and a robot cannot drive forward and turn left at once. Even when actions are not strictly incompatible, switching between them too rapidly wastes effort, a failure sometimes called dithering. So a good action selection mechanism needs to choose sensibly in light of the current situation and internal needs, stay with a choice long enough to make progress, and still be able to interrupt it when something more urgent, like a threat, appears.

In ethology, researchers such as Niko Tinbergen and Konrad Lorenz described hierarchical systems of instincts and drives, where motivations compete and the strongest one given the stimuli and internal state wins. Later work looked at how animals trade off feeding, mating, and safety, often in terms of costs and benefits.

In neuroscience, a prominent view holds that the basal ganglia play a central role. In this account, many cortical and subcortical regions generate competing action proposals, and the basal ganglia normally keep them all suppressed through tonic inhibition. When one proposal gains enough support, the inhibition on that channel is lifted, allowing it to proceed while the others stay inhibited. This works as a kind of gating or winner-take-all mechanism.

In artificial intelligence and robotics, action selection covers a range of approaches. Some are reactive, mapping sensory input directly to behavior, as in Rodney Brooks's subsumption architecture, where higher layers can override lower ones. Others use explicit planning, searching ahead over possible action sequences to reach a goal. There are also utility-based methods that score options by expected value, and reinforcement learning, in which an agent learns a policy that picks the action expected to yield the greatest long-term reward. Cognitive architectures and behavior trees, common in games, offer further structured ways to organize the choice.

Across these approaches, designers face recurring trade-offs between speed and deliberation, between flexibility and stability, and between exploiting known good actions and exploring new ones. Action selection is therefore best understood not as a single technique but as a central question in understanding any autonomous, goal-directed system.

Imagine you are standing on the side of a road, and a big truck is driving past you. Now imagine you throw a tennis ball at the truck. The ball bounces off the front of the truck and comes back at you much faster than you threw it, because the truck was already moving and gave the ball an extra kick. A gravity boost works a bit like that, except the truck is a giant planet like Jupiter, and instead of bouncing, the spacecraft swings around the planet.

Jupiter is not sitting still. It is racing around the Sun at about thirteen kilometers every second. When a spacecraft comes close to Jupiter, Jupiter's gravity pulls on it. The spacecraft falls toward the planet, curves around it, and then flies away again. If the spacecraft comes in behind Jupiter and swings around in front of it, it gets dragged along in the direction Jupiter is traveling, like a kid on a sled being pulled by a rope tied to a speeding car. When the spacecraft lets go and flies off, it is moving faster than before, as seen from the Sun.

You might wonder where the extra speed comes from, since nothing in space is free. The answer is that Jupiter pays for it. The spacecraft steals a tiny bit of Jupiter's motion, so Jupiter slows down a little. But Jupiter is so enormously heavy compared to a spacecraft that the change is far too small to ever notice, like a bug hitting a bus windshield and nudging the bus.

Another thing that may seem odd is that the spacecraft speeds up as it falls toward Jupiter, but then slows down as it climbs away, just like a ball rolling down a hill and up the other side. From Jupiter's point of view, the spacecraft leaves at the same speed it arrived. The trick is that the direction changes, and because Jupiter itself is moving, that change in direction turns into a real gain in speed when you measure it against the Sun.

Engineers love this trick because rockets are expensive and fuel is heavy. Using a planet's gravity lets a spacecraft get a big speed boost without carrying extra fuel. Probes like Voyager, Galileo, and New Horizons all used it to reach far-off places much faster and more cheaply than they could have otherwise.

Secret agents, often called spies, work for governments or other organizations and collect information in secret. Some focus on learning what foreign countries or groups are up to, while others look into events taking place inside their own nation. To obtain this information, they can rely on many techniques, such as watching people covertly, intercepting messages and calls, or employing sophisticated technology to collect data. The James Bond type of agent, a fictional creation of Ian Fleming, does not give an especially accurate picture of the profession. Although a few of the gadgets and devices Bond uses may draw on real equipment, most of the events and scenarios in the Bond films are heavily dramatized and have little basis in reality. Espionage and covert intelligence work remain common practices for many governments and organizations across the globe. Even so, the details of how this work is carried out are usually kept confidential, which makes it hard to know precisely what secret agents do or how they go about it.

Yes, though with some qualification, since almost every dollar-denominated currency is divided into 100 cents. The clearest examples of exceptions are Brunei and Taiwan.

The Brunei dollar is divided into 100 sen, and the coins are inscribed with "sen" rather than "cents," since Malay is the official language. In English the unit is sometimes still called a cent, and the Brunei dollar is interchangeable at par with the Singapore dollar, which does use cents. So Brunei officially uses a different name for its fractional unit, but "cent" remains a common English equivalent.

The New Taiwan dollar is the stronger case in everyday practice. Officially it is divisible into 100 cents, or 10 jiao and 100 fen in Chinese terms. In reality those fractional units no longer exist as coins, and prices and transactions are handled in whole dollars. The smallest coin in circulation is one dollar. Taiwan therefore uses the word "dollar" in English while effectively having no fractional units at all.

Hong Kong is a partial case. Its dollar is officially divided into cents, but in Cantonese the units have local names, such as "ho" for ten cents. The official English terminology is still cents, so it doesn't really count as an exception.

If you're looking for a country whose dollar has no cent subdivision in official use, Taiwan comes closest. If you're looking for a different official name for the fractional unit, Brunei's sen is the best example.

Howard Hathaway Aiken (March 8, 1900 – March 14, 1973) was an American physicist and computer scientist, mostly known for the Harvard Mark I. That machine got built at Harvard in the 1930s and 1940s. Aiken was born in Hoboken, New Jersey, and he got his undergrad degree in electrical engineering from Columbia in 1923. He later picked up a PhD in physics from Harvard in 1939. He was really into using computers for scientific and engineering math, and he worked closely with IBM to build the Mark I, which was finished in 1944. It was an electromechanical machine used for all sorts of scientific and military work, including early hydrogen bomb development. Aiken kept working on computer projects at Harvard and was also involved in UNIVAC, the first commercial computer. Honestly, he was a real pioneer, and the Mark I shaped how computers developed in the 20th century. He's remembered as a key figure in computing history, and he picked up plenty of awards and honors along the way.

Creams for the hands, feet, face, and body all fall under the moisturizer category, meaning products meant to hydrate and nourish the skin. They supply the moisture skin requires to remain healthy and feel soft and smooth. What sets these creams apart is the particular needs of the skin in each area. The skin on the hands and feet, for instance, is thicker and dries out more easily, so creams made for these areas are typically richer in emollients (moisturizing ingredients) and deliver deeper hydration. Because facial skin is more delicate, face creams tend to have a lighter texture and are made to absorb easily. Body creams are generally intended for the remainder of the body, and they are usually thicker and more moisturizing than face creams. Any moisturizer can technically be applied anywhere on the body, but a product designed for the needs of a given area will probably work better there. Putting a light face cream on your hands, or a heavy body cream on your face, may give less satisfying results than a product made specifically for those spots.

Question answering is a field within computer science, specifically in natural language processing and information retrieval, concerned with building systems that automatically answer questions people ask in ordinary human language. Rather than returning a list of documents or links the way a traditional search engine does, a question answering system tries to give a direct, precise answer. For example, if you ask "Who wrote Pride and Prejudice?", the ideal system replies "Jane Austen" instead of showing you ten web pages that might contain that fact.

These systems are often classified by where their knowledge comes from. Some draw on structured data such as databases or knowledge graphs, translating a natural language question into a formal query, much like converting a sentence into SQL, and retrieving the matching fact. Others work with unstructured text, such as Wikipedia articles, news, or a company's internal documents, where the system must locate relevant passages and extract or compose an answer from them. A common distinction is also made between closed-domain systems, which specialize in a particular area like medicine or legal documents, and open-domain systems, which attempt to answer questions about nearly anything.

Another useful distinction is between extractive and generative approaches. In extractive question answering, the system identifies the exact span of text within a given passage that answers the question, a task popularized by benchmark datasets such as SQuAD from Stanford. In generative question answering, the system writes the answer in its own words, which is the approach taken by large language models like ChatGPT. Many modern systems combine the two ideas through a technique called retrieval-augmented generation, in which the system first searches for relevant documents and then uses a language model to produce an answer grounded in what it found.

Historically, question answering dates back to the 1960s with programs like BASEBALL, which answered questions about baseball statistics, and LUNAR, which answered questions about moon rock samples from the Apollo missions. A famous milestone came in 2011 when IBM's Watson defeated human champions on the quiz show Jeopardy!. Since then, advances in deep learning and transformer models such as BERT and GPT have dramatically improved the accuracy and flexibility of these systems.

Question answering is used today in virtual assistants like Siri and Alexa, customer support chatbots, search engines that display direct answer boxes, medical and legal research tools, and educational applications. Ongoing challenges include handling ambiguous questions, reasoning across multiple pieces of information, keeping answers up to date, and avoiding confidently stated but incorrect answers, a problem often called hallucination in language models.

What you describe sounds like aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease (AERD), also called Samter's triad: nasal polyps, asthma, and sensitivity to aspirin and other NSAIDs. Aspirin desensitization followed by daily high-dose aspirin is a recognized treatment for it, and your good response at 600 mg twice daily suggests it is working.

The symptoms you get when you lower the dose are typical. The benefit of aspirin therapy is dose-dependent, so nasal congestion and polyp symptoms often return when the dose drops too far. Desensitization also only lasts as long as you keep taking aspirin consistently. If you skip doses or drop very low, especially for more than a day or two, your body can lose its tolerance, and the next dose can trigger a reaction. The hives you developed at 60 mg may be a sign that your tolerance was partly slipping. For that reason, please do not adjust, reduce, or stop your aspirin on your own. If you have missed doses for more than about 48 hours, talk to your allergist before restarting, because re-desensitization under supervision may be needed.

Some patients can eventually reduce their dose, often to about 300 to 325 mg twice daily after six to twelve months of stable control. This is done gradually and under your allergist's guidance, not by experimenting at home. If lower doses don't control your symptoms, staying on your current dose is a reasonable choice as long as you tolerate it, but long-term high-dose aspirin has risks you should discuss with your doctor. These include stomach irritation and ulcers, so many people take a stomach-protecting medicine such as a proton pump inhibitor, as well as bleeding risk and occasional effects on the kidneys. Tell any surgeon or dentist you are on it.

If the high dose becomes hard to tolerate, or you want to come off aspirin, other options exist. Leukotriene-blocking medicines such as montelukast, or zileuton in some countries, help many people with AERD. Steroid nasal sprays or rinses help too. Biologic injections such as dupilumab, omalizumab, or mepolizumab are now approved for nasal polyps and work very well in AERD, sometimes allowing people to stop aspirin altogether.

The best next step is to book a follow-up with the allergist or ENT specialist who started your desensitization. Tell them exactly what happened when you lowered the dose, including the hives, and ask about the right long-term dose, stomach protection, and whether a biologic might suit you. Seek urgent care if you ever develop wheezing, chest tightness, throat swelling, or widespread hives after a dose.

Hilary Putnam (1926–2016) was an American philosopher widely regarded as one of the most influential thinkers of the twentieth century. He made foundational contributions to philosophy of mind, philosophy of language, philosophy of mathematics, philosophy of science, and metaphysics, and he was also known for his work in epistemology and his later engagement with pragmatism and ethics. Born in Chicago, he studied at the University of Pennsylvania and later taught at Harvard, Princeton, and MIT, where he spent much of his career.

Among his best-known ideas is functionalism in the philosophy of mind, the view that mental states are defined by their causal roles rather than by the physical material that realizes them, so that a mind might be realized in a brain, a computer, or some other system. He also developed the "Twin Earth" thought experiment, which argued that meaning is not simply "in the head," since the reference of words like "water" depends partly on the environment and the substances people are actually in contact with. This line of thought helped launch the externalist turn in philosophy of language.

In the philosophy of mathematics, Putnam worked with Martin Davis and Julia Robinson on mathematical logic, and he co-developed, with Willard Quine, the Quine-Putnam indispensability argument for the existence of mathematical objects. Later in his career he became a prominent critic of metaphysical realism and developed "internal realism," and he wrote extensively on pragmatism, drawing on figures like William James and John Dewey. He also wrote on ethics, philosophy of religion, and the relationship between fact and value.

Putnam's work is known for its wide range and for his willingness to revise his own positions over time, and he remains a major reference point across many areas of contemporary philosophy.

Amazon Mechanical Turk (MTurk) is an online marketplace, created and run by Amazon, through which companies and other organizations can hand off small jobs to a worldwide group of contributors. Because it draws on the output of a large crowd rather than a single staff member or contractor, it is commonly described as a crowdsourcing platform. The assignments posted there, known as Human Intelligence Tasks (HITs), span from basic data entry and transcription to more intricate work that calls for human judgment, such as reviewing content or rating search results. The people who take on these assignments, called Turkers, pick whichever tasks interest them and receive a modest payment for each one completed. Organizations across the globe rely on MTurk to get fast, dependable outcomes for work that would be hard or slow to do internally. For individuals, it also offers a way to earn supplemental income by working on tasks during their free time.

Franklin D. Roosevelt was first elected president of the United States in November 1932, defeating incumbent Herbert Hoover. He took office on March 4, 1933. He was subsequently reelected three more times, in 1936, 1940, and 1944, making him the only president to serve more than two terms.

A nautical mile is exactly 1,852 meters, which is about 6,076 feet or roughly 1.15 statute miles. This length was adopted as an international standard in 1929 and is now used by the International Hydrographic Organization and most countries for sea and air navigation.

The unit has its origin in the geometry of the Earth. It was historically defined as one minute of latitude, which is one sixtieth of a degree, measured along a meridian. Because the Earth is not a perfect sphere, the length of a minute of arc varies slightly with latitude, so the fixed value of 1,852 meters was chosen to approximate the average. This connection to latitude is why nautical miles are so convenient for navigation, since distances can be read directly from the latitude scale on a chart.

Speed at sea and in the air is measured in knots, where one knot equals one nautical mile per hour.

"The Matrix" is a 1999 science fiction action film written and directed by Lana and Lilly Wachowski. It stars Keanu Reeves as Thomas Anderson, a computer programmer who leads a double life as a hacker under the alias "Neo." Alongside him are Laurence Fishburne as Morpheus, Carrie-Anne Moss as Trinity, and Hugo Weaving as the menacing Agent Smith. The film became a major cultural phenomenon and is widely regarded as one of the most influential movies of its era.

The story begins with Neo sensing that something is fundamentally wrong with the world around him. He is contacted by Morpheus, a mysterious rebel leader, who offers him a choice between a blue pill, which would let him return to his ordinary life with no memory of the encounter, and a red pill, which would reveal the truth. Neo chooses the red pill and awakens to discover that the world he believed was real is actually a computer simulation called the Matrix. In reality, the year is far later than he thought, and humanity has been conquered by intelligent machines. Most humans are kept unconscious in vast fields of pods, where their bodies are harvested as an energy source while their minds are plugged into the simulated world to keep them docile and unaware.

Morpheus and his crew are among the few free humans, and they believe Neo is "the One," a prophesied figure capable of manipulating the Matrix and ending the war against the machines. Much of the film follows Neo as he learns to bend the rules of the simulation, battles the Agents who police it, and gradually comes to believe in his own abilities.

The film is celebrated for several reasons. Its visual effects were groundbreaking, especially the technique known as "bullet time," in which the action appears to slow down dramatically while the camera seems to sweep around a scene at normal speed. Its fight choreography, influenced by Hong Kong martial arts cinema and supervised by Yuen Woo-ping, set a new standard for Hollywood action. Its stylish aesthetic of black leather, sunglasses, and green-tinted digital code became instantly iconic.

Beyond its action, The Matrix is known for its philosophical depth. It draws on ideas such as Plato's Allegory of the Cave, René Descartes' question of whether our senses can deceive us, and Jean Baudrillard's writings on simulation and reality. It also incorporates religious themes, particularly messianic imagery surrounding Neo. Many viewers have also read it as an allegory about personal awakening and identity, and the Wachowskis have since acknowledged that it can be understood as a transgender allegory. The "red pill" concept in particular has entered everyday language as a metaphor for confronting an uncomfortable truth.

The film's success launched a franchise that includes the sequels The Matrix Reloaded and The Matrix Revolutions, both released in 2003, as well as The Matrix Resurrections in 2021. It also expanded into The Animatrix, a collection of animated short films, along with video games and comics. Today, The Matrix remains a touchstone of popular culture and a frequent reference point in discussions about technology, virtual reality, and the nature of reality itself.

Lyme disease itself can cause a range of symptoms, and the treatment, usually antibiotics, has its own side effects. Early symptoms of the infection often include fever, chills, headache, fatigue, muscle and joint aches, and swollen lymph nodes, frequently accompanied by a characteristic circular, expanding skin rash called erythema migrans, which may look like a bull's-eye. If the infection is untreated, it can spread to the joints, causing arthritis that tends to affect the knees, and it can affect the nervous system, leading to facial palsy (drooping on one side of the face), meningitis-like symptoms, or nerve pain and numbness. Less commonly, it can affect the heart, causing irregular heartbeat or heart block.

The antibiotics used to treat Lyme disease, most often doxycycline, amoxicillin, or cefuroxime, can cause side effects. Doxycycline commonly causes nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, stomach upset, and sensitivity to sunlight, so it's wise to use sunscreen and protective clothing. Amoxicillin and cefuroxime can cause diarrhea, nausea, and rashes or allergic reactions. Any antibiotic can cause yeast infections or, rarely, a serious bowel infection called C. difficile, so report severe or persistent diarrhea to your doctor. Seek emergency care for signs of a serious allergic reaction, such as swelling of the face or throat or difficulty breathing.

Some people experience a temporary flare-up of symptoms in the first day or two after starting antibiotics, known as a Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction. It is caused by the immune response to dying bacteria and usually resolves on its own.

If you have a tick bite or symptoms that concern you, see a healthcare provider promptly, since early treatment works best. They can tailor the medication and monitor for side effects.

Norway has voted against joining the European Union twice, once in 1972 and again in 1994, and the reasons go deeper than oil or simple stubbornness. Many Norwegians care a great deal about controlling their own laws, fish, and farmland. The EU has rules on fishing and farming, and fishing communities in particular worried that joining would let other European countries fish in waters they had fought hard to protect. Farmers worried about losing subsidies and facing cheaper imports. Many people also valued their independence after centuries of being ruled by Denmark and then Sweden, and they did not want to hand decisions to a large body where they would have little say.

Oil does play a part, but not in the simple way people often assume. Norway already has a comfortable economy, so it did not feel desperate to join for money. Its wealth gives it the option to stay outside, which is different from being forced to stay outside.

Norway is still very closely connected to the EU. Through the European Economic Area agreement, it belongs to the EU's single market, follows most of its rules, pays into its funds, and takes part in many programs, all without having a vote on the rules it accepts. Supporters of joining call this a kind of rule-taker arrangement, while opponents see it as a sensible middle path that keeps Norway independent while still trading freely with its neighbors.

During his time in office, George W. Bush, the 43rd U.S. President, relied on more than one national security advisor. Condoleezza Rice held the post first, from January 2001 until January 2005. Stephen Hadley then took over from her and remained National Security Advisor from January 2005 through January 2009.

Entropy is a way of quantifying how much disorder or randomness exists within a system. Its main application is in thermodynamics, the field that examines how thermal energy moves from one body or system to another. Picture two containers holding the same gas. In one, the gas particles are crowded together in a neat arrangement, while in the other they are scattered about in a loose, chaotic fashion. The first container has lower entropy because its particles are orderly, whereas the second has higher entropy because its particles are more disordered. Entropy matters in thermodynamics since it sheds light on how heat travels between objects. When two objects differ in temperature, heat naturally flows from the warmer one to the cooler one until both reach a common temperature, a condition called thermal equilibrium. The amount of heat exchanged, though, depends on the temperature gap between the objects as well as the entropy present in the system. Put simply, entropy measures how mixed up or jumbled something is, and scientists use it to understand how heat moves and how hot or cold things become.

So AI is basically a machine doing stuff that normally needs a human brain, like learning, solving problems, or making calls. An AI system is just a program or machine built to act smart in that way. People usually split them into two buckets: narrow and general. Narrow AI does one specific job, like recognizing faces or translating text, and it gets trained on huge piles of data to get good at that job. General AI, on the other hand, would be able to handle a much wider range of tasks, and that's the part that's still mostly theoretical. There are a bunch of ways to build these things: rule-based systems, decision trees, neural networks, and machine learning. You can use them on their own or mix them together. AI is already everywhere, from speech recognition and photo or video analysis to self-driving cars and natural language processing. It's only going to keep creeping further into everyday life and into just about every industry, so it's worth paying attention to.

The most likely explanation is a mild respiratory infection, usually acute bronchitis or the tail end of a viral cold. These often begin with a cough that produces clear or white mucus and can linger for one to three weeks, sometimes up to four. Coughing in fits is irritating to the airways, and small streaks of blood are common in this setting. Forceful coughing can break tiny blood vessels in the airway lining or the throat, and irritated, inflamed bronchial tissue can bleed slightly. Streaks mixed into otherwise clear mucus, in a person who feels well, are usually harmless and tend to resolve as the cough settles.

Other possibilities include irritation from dry air, allergies, postnasal drip, or a nosebleed or sinus bleed draining down the back of the throat. Reflux can also cause a cough. Less common causes include pneumonia, which would usually come with fever, shortness of breath, or feeling ill, and more serious problems like a blood clot in the lung, tuberculosis, or a lung lesion. These are much less likely given how well you feel, but they are why blood in the sputum deserves some attention if it persists.

The dizziness is nonspecific. It could come from mild dehydration, congestion affecting the ears or sinuses, a lingering viral illness, or lightheadedness from coughing fits. It is worth noting how it behaves: whether it happens when standing up, after coughing, or constantly.

You should seek care promptly, the same day or at an emergency department, if you cough up more than streaks (such as a teaspoon or more of blood), if the blood is bright red and increasing, or if you develop shortness of breath, chest pain, a racing heart, fainting, fever, calf pain or swelling, or leg swelling. Risk factors matter too: recent long travel or surgery, estrogen-containing birth control, smoking, recent weight loss, night sweats, or exposure to tuberculosis would make me want you to be seen sooner.

Otherwise, a reasonable plan is to rest, drink plenty of fluids, use a humidifier, and try honey or a throat lozenge. Avoid smoke. If the dizziness continues or the red streaks persist beyond a few days, book a visit with your doctor, who can listen to your lungs, check your oxygen level and blood pressure, and consider a chest X-ray. Even if everything seems fine, any cough lasting more than three weeks, or blood in the sputum that keeps recurring, is worth evaluating.

As for timing, most cases of bronchitis-type cough improve noticeably within one to two weeks and fully clear by about three weeks. Since yours started four days ago, expect it to keep going for a while longer, but it should steadily improve.

Many grooming essentials are suitable for men. Among them are moisturizers, which keep skin hydrated and can be applied to the face, hands, and body. Sunscreen is equally important, since it shields men's skin from harmful UV rays, and a product with a high SPF is advisable. Shampoo and conditioner help keep hair and the scalp clean and healthy. A quality razor makes it possible to get a neat, smooth shave. Face wash works to clear away excess oil, dirt, and sweat from the skin. Deodorant leaves men feeling fresh and clean while helping to control body odor. Beyond these products, men can enhance their appearance by caring for their skin and hair through a consistent skincare routine, a nutritious diet, and regular exercise. Adequate sleep and stress management matter as well, since both can significantly affect overall health and how a person looks.

Talk to a doctor about the allergic asthma, the bronchitis, and the swollen lymph nodes in the chest, since they'll need to sort out what's actually going on. Bronchitis is basically inflamed bronchial tubes, usually from an infection or some irritant, and it can bring on coughing, shortness of breath, and chest pain. Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy just means the lymph nodes near the middle of the chest are enlarged on both sides. That can come from infection, inflammation, or sometimes cancer, so it's not something to guess at. For allergic asthma and bronchitis, treatment often includes inhaled corticosteroids to calm the airways, bronchodilators to open them up, and sometimes leukotriene inhibitors. Your sister's doctor might also suggest avoiding known triggers, keeping up with vaccines to ward off respiratory infections, and washing hands and covering coughs. Some cases need more tests, like imaging or a biopsy, before they know the cause and how to treat it. Stick with the plan and don't skip follow-up visits. Her doctor can give much more specific advice once they know her full history, so bring up every question you have.

Recurrent painless scrotal swelling that comes back every few months deserves a proper medical evaluation, even though it doesn't hurt. I can't diagnose the cause from a description, but I can walk through the most likely possibilities so you know what a doctor will be looking for.

Several common causes fit this pattern. A hernia is one of the most likely. An inguinal hernia, where a loop of intestine or fat pushes through a weak spot in the lower abdominal wall, can descend into the scrotum. It often appears as a soft swelling that may get bigger when you stand, strain, or cough, and it may shrink or disappear when you lie down. The location you describe, near the base of the penis on one side, is consistent with this. Hernias usually don't resolve on their own and sometimes need repair, so this is worth prioritizing.

A varicocele is another possibility. This is a enlargement of the veins within the scrotum, most often on the left side, though yours is on the right. Varicoceles can come and go and are often felt as a "bag of worms." Right-sided ones are less common and occasionally warrant imaging to check for a blockage elsewhere.

A hydrocele, which is fluid collecting around the testicle, can cause painless swelling that fluctuates over time. Epididymal cysts, which are small fluid-filled lumps near the testicle, can also come and go.

Less commonly, swelling can reflect infection, an injury, or in rare cases a testicular growth. Because a testicle lump is the one thing that should never be dismissed, you should see a doctor promptly if you notice any firm lump, a change in testicle size or texture, or if the swelling becomes painful, red, warm, or is accompanied by fever or nausea. Those would be reasons to be seen urgently.

Since this has happened three times in six months, I'd recommend seeing a primary care doctor or urologist soon. Describe the timing and whether the swelling changes with standing or straining, as those details help narrow things down. An exam is usually enough to identify a hernia or varicocele, and an ultrasound can confirm the rest if needed.

Dmitri Mendeleev, a Russian chemist and inventor, is most famous for creating the periodic table of elements. This chart organizes every known chemical element in a systematic way, grouping them according to their atomic structure and chemical properties. His work on the table laid the groundwork for modern chemistry and earned him a place among the most influential scientists in history. Beyond the periodic table, Mendeleev also made important contributions to thermodynamics and to the production of petroleum.

Not every sci-fi story makes humans look dumb or weak next to other intelligent beings. Plenty of them have humans as the main characters, and those characters are usually brave, clever, and able to pull off some pretty impressive stuff. That said, it's pretty common for humans to run into aliens or other beings who are way ahead of us technologically or who can do things we can't. In those stories, people can come across as clumsy or outmatched, mostly because they're behind on tech and lack those abilities. Writers use this a lot to poke at what it means to be human and to think through how we'd handle finding other intelligent life. It's also a handy way to talk about power, culture clashes, and what intelligence even is. So it really depends on the story and what the writer is going for. Some show humans as tough and capable, and others make them look small next to whatever else is out there.

Honestly, there are a bunch of reasons not everyone uses tax havens to cut their tax bill. For one, tax havens get tied up with money laundering and tax evasion, so using one can seriously hurt a company's reputation. Plus, a lot of countries have laws that make it illegal to use tax havens just to dodge taxes. Then there's the hassle. Setting one up takes serious legal and financial know-how, and keeping a presence there isn't cheap. And many countries have tax treaties that let them swap information about financial activity, so hiding money offshore is harder than it used to be. Also, sure, tax havens can lower your tax burden, but they usually come with lighter regulation and oversight, which is its own kind of risk for businesses.

Tofu is made from soybeans. The process starts by soaking dried soybeans and grinding them with water to make a liquid called soy milk. That mixture is then cooked and strained to separate the milk from the solid pulp, called okara. A coagulant is added to the hot soy milk, such as calcium sulfate, magnesium chloride (nigari, traditionally derived from seawater), or a acid like vinegar or lemon juice. The coagulant causes the soy proteins to curdle and form curds, which are pressed into blocks of varying firmness. So the basic ingredients are soybeans, water, and a coagulant, though commercial versions may include small additions such as preservatives or stabilizers.

Bronchitis and allergic asthma are often treated along similar lines. For bronchitis, the cause matters. If it is viral, which is most common, it usually settles in one to three weeks with rest, fluids, and symptom relief such as paracetamol for fever or pain, and cough medicine for comfort. Antibiotics don't help viral bronchitis and are only given when a bacterial infection is suspected. Inhaled bronchodilators like salbutamol can open the airways and ease wheezing and breathlessness. For allergic asthma, the usual long-term treatment is a daily inhaled corticosteroid, which reduces airway inflammation and is the most effective way to prevent attacks. Avoiding your triggers, such as dust mites, pollen, smoke, pets, or cold air, makes a large difference. Your doctor may also check whether an antihistamine or other allergy treatment would help. Stopping smoking and getting a yearly flu vaccine are also important.

The part of your report that needs the most attention is the bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy. This means the lymph nodes near the centre of the chest, on both sides, are enlarged. It is a finding, not a diagnosis, and it can have many causes. Some are harmless and related to infection or allergy, which often settle on their own. Others need proper investigation, including sarcoidosis, tuberculosis, and, less commonly, lymphoma. Because of this, please don't assume it is serious, but don't ignore it either. Ask your doctor to explain exactly what the radiologist saw, and ask whether you need a CT scan, blood tests (including a TB test and inflammatory markers), or a referral to a lung specialist (pulmonologist). Repeat X-rays after a few weeks are also common to see whether the nodes shrink.

You should see a doctor promptly, and go to emergency care right away if you have severe breathlessness, blue lips, chest pain, coughing up blood, high fever with weight loss, or night sweats that persist. Bring your X-ray report and a list of your current medicines to your appointment.

Your sister's allergic asthma should also be reviewed by a doctor, ideally with a written asthma action plan and a check of her inhaler technique, since poor technique is a common reason asthma stays uncontrolled.

When intraday data and end-of-day (EOD) highs and lows disagree, the first step is to figure out why, because the cause determines the fix. The most common reason is that the two sources are built differently. Intraday bars may come from a tick feed that includes every trade, while the EOD file may be derived from an official exchange settlement or a consolidated daily summary. Some vendors also exclude or include extended-hours trading, so a pre-market spike can show up in the intraday data but not in the daily high. Check whether both datasets use the same session definition, time zone, and trade filter, and whether the daily bar is anchored to the regular session close or to midnight UTC.

Next, verify whether the discrepancy is real or a construction artifact. Aggregate your intraday bars yourself into a daily bar (first open, maximum high, minimum low, last close, summed volume) and compare that to the vendor's EOD record. If your aggregation matches the intraday data but not the EOD file, the vendor's daily series is using a different rule, such as official auction prices or adjusted values. If the mismatch appears only on certain days, look for halts, corporate actions, splits, or data gaps that day.

Corporate actions deserve special attention. If the EOD series is split- or dividend-adjusted and the intraday series is not, highs and lows will appear inconsistent even though both are correct. Confirm the adjustment status of each source and apply adjustments consistently before comparing them.

Bad ticks are another frequent culprit. A single erroneous print can create an extreme intraday high or low that the EOD file filtered out. Exchanges and vendors usually remove such trades, so the intraday feed may need cleaning. Common approaches include flagging prints that deviate sharply from neighboring trades, comparing against the bid and ask, or applying a rule that rejects prints outside a percentage band around the prior close. Be careful not to remove genuine extreme moves, especially in volatile or thinly traded instruments.

For practical use, decide which source is authoritative for each purpose and document the choice. Backtests and reporting generally should use the EOD series, since it is the official record and is typically what other participants reference. Intraday analysis, such as stop-loss simulation or execution studies, should use the tick or bar data, but you can reconcile it to the EOD record by forcing the daily aggregate to match the official high and low when they differ only slightly, or by flagging the day for manual review when they differ substantially. Whatever you choose, log the discrepancies, because systematic differences often point to a specific vendor issue or a recurring data rule you need to account for.

The Tacoma Narrows Bridge in Washington State collapsed on November 7, 1940, just four months after it opened to traffic on July 1, 1940. The bridge had earned the nickname "Galloping Gertie" because of how much it swayed and undulated in even moderate winds. On the day of the collapse, winds of roughly 40 miles per hour set the main span into a twisting motion known as torsional flutter, which grew in amplitude until the center span broke apart and fell into Puget Sound. Remarkably, the only fatality was a dog left in a car that had been abandoned on the bridge. The event was captured on film and became a famous case study in engineering, leading to major changes in how designers account for aerodynamic forces on suspension bridges. A replacement bridge opened in 1950.

If a child has watery stools containing blood, the cause could be one of several things, such as an infection, inflammatory bowel disease, or another digestive problem. Medical evaluation is important in this situation, because it may point to a serious illness that needs treatment. While you arrange care, focus on keeping your child well hydrated by offering frequent drinks. If your child has stomach pain, a pain reliever that is safe for children may help, and making them as comfortable as possible is worthwhile. Preventing dehydration matters a great deal, since it can become a dangerous complication. If you have concerns about your child's health, reach out to their healthcare provider for advice. They can assess the symptoms and suggest the right treatment.

An operational definition explains a concept or variable by describing the way it is measured or put into practice within a study. Researchers rely on these definitions because they offer a precise, specific, and objective method for measuring something. Doing so helps guarantee that the concept is measured the same way and with accuracy across various studies and by different investigators. Consider a researcher examining intelligence: they could operationally define it as the score an individual receives on a standardized intelligence test. Here, the definition makes clear exactly how intelligence was assessed in that particular study. Such definitions matter because they make research replicable, so that other scientists can repeat the study with the same operational definitions and obtain comparable outcomes. Replicability, in turn, strengthens confidence in the validity and reliability of the findings.

She also did "What's Luv?" with Fat Joe, which came out in 2002. Then there's Nelly, with "Body On Me" from 2015. Flo Rida worked with her on "Good Time" in 2010, and Akon on "Baby" in 2007.
