Using credit cards for everyday purchases makes it easy to lose track of spending, because the money never leaves your account in the moment. Swiping feels painless, so small purchases add up unnoticed until the statement arrives. A few changes can help you regain control.

Start by making your spending visible in real time. Turn on transaction alerts from your card issuer so every purchase triggers a notification, which creates a small pause and a running sense of what you've spent. Many people find that checking the app once or twice a week, rather than only when the bill comes, makes a large difference.

Next, consider separating your budget from your card entirely. One popular method is to decide on a monthly spending amount for categories like groceries, dining, and fuel, and then withdraw that amount in cash or move it to a debit account or prepaid card for those categories. When the money runs out, you stop. Another option is to keep the credit card for bills and planned purchases only, paying it off in full each month, and handle daily spending from a checking account.

It also helps to set a hard limit on the card itself. Many issuers let you lower your credit limit or set spending caps through their app, which can prevent overspending without relying on willpower alone.

Finally, track your categories with a simple spreadsheet or a budgeting app that links to your cards. Reviewing the totals once a month shows where the money goes, and you can adjust your plan based on real numbers rather than guesses. If the balance is already growing and you're only making minimum payments, it may be worth looking into a balance transfer or a nonprofit credit counseling service for advice on a repayment plan.

The sulfas, or sulfonamides, are a class of synthetic antibiotics first developed in the 1930s, and they were among the first drugs widely used to treat bacterial infections in humans. The original breakthrough came from a red dye called Prontosil, which was found to be broken down in the body into the active compound sulfanilamide. Sulfonamides work by interfering with the bacteria's ability to make folic acid, which they need to grow and reproduce, so they are described as bacteriostatic, meaning they slow bacterial growth rather than directly killing the organisms.

Common examples include sulfamethoxazole, often combined with trimethoprim in the drug Bactrim or Septra, which is prescribed for urinary tract infections, certain skin infections, and some respiratory infections. Sulfadiazine is used in some cases of toxoplasmosis and has historically been used for certain parasitic and eye infections. Sulfasalazine is a related compound used mainly for inflammatory bowel disease and rheumatoid arthritis rather than for infections.

Sulfonamide antibiotics can cause side effects such as rashes, allergic reactions, nausea, and in rare cases serious skin reactions like Stevens-Johnson syndrome. People with a known sulfa allergy are usually advised to avoid them. Because of the rise of antibiotic resistance and the availability of newer drugs, they are used less often today than in the mid-twentieth century, but they remain useful for specific conditions.

It is generally acceptable to withdraw money from investments once you have reached the point the money was meant for, and the right timing depends largely on what the money is for and how soon you will need it. Your time horizon is the length of time between when you invest and when you expect to spend the funds. A common rule of thumb is that money you will need within about three to five years should not be in volatile assets like stocks, because markets can fall sharply and take years to recover. Money with a horizon of five to ten years can hold a balanced mix, and money you won't touch for ten years or more can usually bear the greater short-term swings of equities in exchange for higher expected long-term growth.

Some withdrawals are tied to specific life events, such as a home purchase, a child's education, or a planned retirement date. In those cases, it makes sense to gradually shift the money into safer holdings like high-yield savings accounts, certificates of deposit, or short-term bonds as the date approaches, so that a market downturn does not coincide with the moment you need cash. Retirement is a special case because withdrawals may stretch over several decades, so people often keep a portion invested for growth even after they stop working, while drawing down at a sustainable rate.

Certain accounts also carry rules about when withdrawals are allowed without penalty. Retirement accounts such as 401(k)s and IRAs typically impose penalties and taxes on withdrawals before about age 59 and a half, with some exceptions. Withdrawing early can also forfeit years of tax-advantaged compounding, so it is worth checking the rules and costs before taking money out.

Finally, an emergency fund should exist separately from long-term investments. Having three to six months of expenses in cash means you are less likely to be forced to sell investments during a downturn to cover an unexpected bill. If you are unsure about your specific situation, a fee-only financial planner can help you match each goal to an appropriate time horizon and withdrawal strategy.

Swallowing is the act of transferring food or drink from the mouth into the stomach. When we take a sip of water, it enters the mouth, and our tongue pushes it toward the back of the throat. That action sets off an automatic response known as the "swallow reflex," which carries the water down toward the stomach. This reflex matters because it keeps food or liquid from going down the wrong way and causing choking. It also limits how much air we take in along with what we swallow, since excess air can leave us feeling uneasy or bloated. As we swallow, the muscles of the throat and tongue cooperate to send the food or liquid into the esophagus, a long tube linking the mouth and stomach. Muscles lining the esophagus alternately tighten and loosen, moving the contents along to the stomach. Once there, the water mixes with stomach acid and other digestive fluids, which break it into smaller molecules the body can absorb and use for energy and nutrients. In short, we swallow so the body can carry food and drink from the mouth to the stomach, where it can be digested and turned into usable energy and nutrients.

Okay so a year is basically how long it takes Earth to go around the sun, which works out to about 365.24 days. That's what gives us the seasons, and it's a big deal for climate and weather. Earth's orbit also messes with the length of a day a bit, since the sun and moon's gravity tugs on the planet's spin. Over the course of a year you get all sorts of weather, from temperature swings to humidity and rain or snow. A lot of that comes down to how far Earth is from the sun, the tilt of its axis, and of course the spin itself. Then there's the cultural side: holidays, festivals, and other events that line up with the calendar year. Those can shape societies pretty heavily, socially, economically, and politically, depending on where you live.

A spiral fracture of the ring finger is typically treated by immobilizing it in a splint or cast so the bone can knit back together. Doing so can ease discomfort and shield the finger during recovery. If the fracture remains visible after five weeks in a cast, the bone may be healing more slowly than anticipated. Your physician might then suggest other approaches, such as extending the immobilization period, undergoing physical therapy to restore movement and strength, or performing surgery to fix the break. Keeping to your doctor's advice and attending scheduled follow-up visits is important. If you have questions about your care or notice new symptoms, such as worsening pain or swelling, reach out to your doctor for further assessment and direction.

Voir dire, the process of jury selection, is how a group of people is chosen to serve as jurors in a given trial. Its goal is to produce a fair and impartial jury and to screen out anyone who may be prejudiced or who cannot reach an objective verdict based on the evidence heard in court. A jury is meant to consist of ordinary citizens who listen to what is presented in the courtroom and reach a decision based on that testimony and those exhibits. This procedure matters because it helps keep the justice system equitable and free of bias. Although experienced attorneys and prosecutors sometimes try to sway who ends up on the jury during voir dire, that does not always happen. In certain cases, jurors are picked at random from a pool of eligible people the court has already assembled. In other cases, the process is more structured, with lawyers and prosecutors posing questions and using other techniques to decide whether a given juror is appropriate for the case. In short, jury selection aims to produce a fair and unbiased jury and, in doing so, to make the justice system as fair and unbiased as it can be.

Sharp thigh pain together with a burning feeling in the lower leg can come from a number of sources. Here are some of the possibilities.

A muscle strain or injury is one. If you fell a month ago and your leg was heavily bruised, you may have strained or damaged a muscle in either the thigh or the lower leg.

Irritation or compression of a nerve is another. The burning in your lower leg and foot might result from a nerve being irritated or squeezed, which can happen because of an injury, a condition such as multiple sclerosis, or a pinched nerve.

A blood clot could also be responsible for both the sharp thigh pain and the burning lower leg sensation. Clots can form in the leg veins and often bring pain, swelling, and warmth in the area they affect.

Various other conditions might produce similar symptoms as well, among them myositis (muscle inflammation), tendinitis (tendon inflammation), and arthritis (joint inflammation).

You should see a doctor to find out what is behind your symptoms and to receive suitable treatment. The doctor will review your medical history and examine you physically to work out the cause and suggest the right course of treatment. Sometimes additional tests are necessary to reach a diagnosis.

So the Uberman schedule is basically chopping your sleep into a bunch of short naps instead of one long stretch at night. The idea is you get all the rest you need from naps alone. In the usual version, you take six naps of about 20 to 30 minutes each, spaced every 4 hours around the clock. Some folks cut night sleep out entirely, others keep a tiny bit of it, maybe 30 minutes or less. And you're supposed to stick to it every single day, weekends included.

Plenty of people who try it say they feel sharper and more productive during the day. That said, most sleep experts aren't fans, since it runs against how our bodies are wired to sleep. Real nighttime sleep does a lot of the work of repairing your body and brain, and keeping a steady sleep routine helps your internal clock stay on track and makes your sleep better overall. So if you're thinking about trying it, go in with eyes open.

So communism, basically, is the idea that everybody shares ownership of the means of production and there's no private property. Marxism is the version Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels came up with in the mid-1800s. Their take was that capitalism, where a small group owns the factories and so on and lives off the labor of the working class, is a flawed system that'll eventually get replaced by socialism. That's where the workers own the means of production and nobody's being exploited. They figured socialism would then lead into communism, where there are no classes and everyone pitches in to meet the community's needs.

Leninism is Vladimir Lenin's spin on it. He was a Russian revolutionary leader, and his idea was that a small group of dedicated revolutionaries should lead the working class in overthrowing capitalism and building a socialist society. He thought one disciplined party should run the show and steer the workers toward communism.

Stalinism comes from Joseph Stalin, who led the Soviet Union from 1922 to 1952. The core of it is that one powerful party controls the state and guides the shift from socialism to communism. Stalin was big on force and repression to keep control and hit the goals of communism.

Then there's Trotskyism, from Leon Trotsky, another Russian revolutionary leader. He wanted socialist revolutions to spread worldwide, with a global network of socialist states. He also thought the working class should drive the revolution, and that the party should be democratic and open to any worker.

So to sum it up: Marxism is about overthrowing capitalism and building a socialist society. Leninism puts the focus on a single disciplined party leading the workers to revolution. Stalinism stresses one powerful party controlling the state and guiding the move to communism. Trotskyism is more about the working class driving the revolution and building a worldwide network of socialist states.

Sounds like it could be dermatitis, which is basically a catch-all term for skin inflammation. It can come from allergies, irritants, or some underlying condition. You really should get a dermatologist to take a look so you know what you're dealing with. Until then, an over-the-counter hydrocortisone cream can take the edge off the dryness and itching. Try to skip tight clothes and keep the spot clean and dry. If the rash hurts, spreads fast, or comes with a fever or other symptoms, don't wait on the derm appointment. Get to a doctor right away.

Software bugs are errors that programmers introduce while writing code, and they can make a program act in unexpected ways or stop it from working entirely. Bugs can creep in through many channels. A programmer may leave out a necessary line of code, or use the wrong kind of data in a calculation. At other times, faulty reasoning is the culprit: the code is written in a way that does not accomplish what the programmer meant. Writing bug-free software is hard, since programming is an intricate process with many stages that demands careful attention. Mistakes come easily, particularly when the program being built is large and complicated. Moreover, it is rarely practical to test every possible situation and combination of inputs, which means some bugs can stay concealed until real users run the software. To limit bugs, developers commonly rely on methods like testing, debugging, and code reviews to find and correct problems before release. Even so, some bugs still get past these safeguards and only surface once the program is in use.

A binary classifier is a type of machine learning model that sorts inputs into one of two categories. The name reflects the fact that there are exactly two possible outcomes, often labeled as positive and negative, or as 1 and 0. Common examples include an email spam filter that decides whether a message is spam or not spam, a medical test that determines whether a patient has a particular condition or does not, and a fraud detection system that flags a transaction as fraudulent or legitimate.

The model works by learning patterns from labeled training data, where each example already has its correct category attached. During training, the classifier adjusts its internal parameters to reduce its errors. Once trained, it takes a new, unseen input and produces a prediction. Many binary classifiers actually compute a score or probability, such as a 0.87 likelihood that an email is spam, and then apply a threshold, like 0.5, to convert that score into a final yes or no decision.

Several algorithms are commonly used for this task, including logistic regression, decision trees, support vector machines, and neural networks. Because the outcome has only two states, performance is typically evaluated with metrics such as accuracy, precision, recall, and the F1 score, along with tools like the confusion matrix and the ROC curve. These metrics matter because a classifier can appear accurate while performing poorly on the less common class, which is a frequent issue when one outcome is much rarer than the other.

Legal financing is the provision of monetary support to people or companies to pay for the legal fees and costs tied to a legal dispute. These costs may include retaining a lawyer, covering court filing charges and fees for expert witnesses, and other expenses involved in bringing or defending a claim. Such funding comes in several forms, including loans, legal funding agreements, and contingency fee arrangements. Under a legal funding agreement, a firm or individual advances money in return for a share of whatever is recovered or settled in the case. With a contingency fee arrangement, a person can retain an attorney who is paid only if the case succeeds, receiving a portion of the money won or agreed upon in settlement. This kind of financing can help those who cannot afford the upfront expense of pursuing a legal matter, or who lack the means to keep paying legal bills over time. It can also be valuable in cases expected to be intricate or lengthy, since it lets parties concentrate on their dispute rather than the financial strain. Anyone considering legal financing should closely examine the terms of the agreement and weigh its possible risks and rewards. Likewise, the fees and conditions charged by any attorney or legal service provider should be reviewed carefully, as they can differ considerably.

Traditional mincemeat is a sweet, spiced filling for pies, and despite its name it usually contains no meat at all in modern versions. Its base is a mix of dried fruits such as raisins, currants, and sultanas, often combined with chopped apples and candied citrus peel. These are bound together with sugar or honey and a generous amount of suet, the hard fat from around beef or mutton kidneys, which gives it richness and body. Brandy, rum, or sherry is typically stirred in as a preservative and for flavor, along with warm spices like cinnamon, nutmeg, cloves, and ginger, and sometimes lemon or orange zest and juice. Older recipes did include real minced meat, usually beef, cooked with the fruit and spices, which is where the name comes from. Vegetarian versions substitute vegetable suet, and the meat has largely disappeared from the recipe over the past century or two.

The Atari 2600 is a home video game console released by Atari, Inc. in 1977 under the name Atari Video Computer System (Atari VCS). It was one of the first widely successful consoles to use interchangeable game cartridges, which meant players could buy new games for the same machine rather than being limited to games built into the hardware. It connected to a television set and was controlled with a joystick, and it became a defining product of the early home video game era.

The console's hardware was relatively simple, built around a MOS Technology 6507 processor, which allowed it to be sold at a price accessible to many families. Its graphics were modest by later standards, with blocky sprites and limited color, but programmers developed clever techniques to get the most out of the system. Popular titles included Space Invaders, Pac-Man, Pitfall!, Adventure, and Missile Command, along with many games based on arcade hits and original concepts.

The Atari 2600 enjoyed enormous popularity through the late 1970s and early 1980s and sold tens of millions of units. Its success helped establish the home video game market, but the industry also experienced a severe crash in 1983, partly due to a flood of low-quality games and oversupply. The system remained in production into the 1990s and is remembered today as an important and iconic piece of gaming history.

There are a few ways to make passive income from real estate, and what works best really depends on your goals, how much money you've got to put in, and how much risk you can stomach.

The classic one is buying properties and renting them out. You can go with regular long-term tenants, or try short-term rentals like Airbnb if you want something different.

Then there are REITs. These are companies that own and run income-producing real estate like apartment buildings, office buildings, and shopping centers. You buy in and get a cut of the profits those properties bring in, without ever dealing with a leaky faucet.

Crowdfunding platforms are another route. Basically a bunch of investors pool their money to fund real estate projects, like building new developments or renovating existing places. It's a decent way to get some exposure to real estate without owning or managing anything yourself.

You could also buy a vacation rental. These can bring in solid income, especially if they're in a popular tourist spot. You own it, manage it, and rent it out to travelers.

As for the fastest way to retire on real estate income, there's no single answer. It comes down to the kinds of properties you pick, how much demand there is for them, and how well you can manage them. Look carefully at your options and do your homework before you put any money down.

The Democratic defeat in 1968 came from several overlapping pressures, and the most important was the Vietnam War. Lyndon Johnson's escalation had divided the party badly. The Tet Offensive in January 1968 undermined official claims that the war was being won, and Eugene McCarthy's strong showing in New Hampshire, followed by Robert Kennedy's entry into the race, exposed how deeply Johnson was disliked within his own party. Johnson's decision in March not to seek re-election left the party without a unifying leader. Hubert Humphrey, as vice president, was tied to an unpopular policy and was slow to distance himself from it, which alienated antiwar voters and left him looking like a continuation of the administration.

The second major factor was the chaos surrounding the nomination. Robert Kennedy was assassinated in June, just after winning the California primary, and with his death the party lost the one candidate who might have united working-class whites, minorities, and young antiwar voters. Humphrey then won the nomination without entering a single primary, which many insurgents saw as illegitimate. The Chicago convention in August made matters worse. Violent clashes between police and protesters outside, along with bitter fights over the war plank inside, were broadcast on television and made the party look divided and unable to keep order.

Third, the Democratic coalition was fracturing along racial and cultural lines. The civil rights legislation of 1964 and 1965, urban riots, rising crime, and the assassination of Martin Luther King Jr. in April fed a white backlash, especially in the South and among some blue-collar northern voters. George Wallace's third-party campaign pulled five Southern states and about 13 percent of the national vote, taking support from traditional Democratic territory. Nixon's "law and order" message and his Southern strategy appealed to voters who felt the country was spinning out of control, and he cast himself as representing a "silent majority."

Finally, Nixon ran a disciplined campaign and Humphrey's started late, with little money and a divided party organization. Humphrey recovered considerably in October after he broke somewhat with Johnson on bombing halts, and the final popular vote was very close, with Nixon winning by under one percentage point. Still, the combination of war, party disunity, racial and cultural backlash, and a weak start was enough to hand Nixon the presidency.

Formal verification is basically proving, with math and logic, that a system does what it's supposed to do. The system could be a program, a chip design, whatever. You start by writing down exactly what the system should do, then turn those requirements into a bunch of logical statements that have to hold true. Automated theorem provers and other mathematical tools then check whether they do. If they do, you've got solid evidence the system meets its spec. If they don't, you've probably caught a bug or a security hole before it bit anyone. It's used in computer science, engineering, and math, and it works on software, hardware, or both. It's especially handy for high-stakes stuff, where one small mistake could cause real trouble.

Not every science fiction story depicts humans as silly or feeble next to other thinking creatures. Plenty of these tales put people at the center as courageous, clever characters capable of remarkable achievements. Still, it is a familiar pattern for humans to meet aliens or other intelligent beings that have superior technology or powers humans lack. In such narratives, people can appear foolish or fragile beside these beings, simply because they are less advanced and lack comparable abilities. Writers often use this kind of portrayal to examine what it means to be human and to imagine how our species might respond to contact with other forms of intelligent life. The same device can also address topics like power, cultural difference, and the meaning of intelligence. In the end, how humans are shown in science fiction depends on the individual story and the message its author hopes to share. Some works present people as strong and capable, while others cast them as less advanced or weaker than the intelligent beings they encounter.

In science, a discovery is basically when someone finds something new that helps us understand the world better. It might be a brand new phenomenon, or a connection between things we already knew about but never saw as linked. Sometimes it's just fresh evidence that backs up an old hypothesis, or knocks it down.

Discoveries come out of all kinds of work: running experiments, crunching data, simply observing things, or digging through existing literature. And they're a huge part of how science even works, since that's how we keep expanding what we know.

They tend to spark new ideas and theories, and they can lead to big leaps in areas like medicine, technology, and environmental science. There's a practical side too. A discovery might end up as a new product, or change policies and the way people do things. At the end of the day, discovery is how we learn what's really going on in the world, and that lets us make better decisions and act on what we actually understand.

Apple operates roughly 530 retail stores worldwide as of the most recent figures I have, which are from around 2024. The United States has the largest share, with about 270 stores. The rest are spread across more than 25 other countries and regions, including China (with around 50 or more locations), the United Kingdom, Canada, Japan, Australia, France, Germany, Italy, and others.

The exact total shifts from year to year because Apple regularly opens new stores, relocates existing ones to larger spaces, and occasionally closes locations. Apple has also expanded into new markets in recent years, with stores opening in places like India (Mumbai and Delhi in 2023), and online stores are available in additional countries where there is no physical presence. For the current count, Apple's website has a store locator and a retail store list that reflects the latest numbers.

Her period arriving three days after sex is a reassuring sign. A period means the cycle restarted, so pregnancy is unlikely from that act. Some bleeding after emergency contraception is common, and levonorgestrel pills like Unwanted 72 can shift the timing of a period, so a bleed that comes early isn't a perfect guarantee. Still, if her period came on or near its expected date, the chance of pregnancy from this incident is low. Taken within 72 hours, levonorgestrel reduces the chance of pregnancy from a single act of unprotected sex by roughly 80 to 90 percent, and it works best the sooner it's taken. If she took it promptly, her overall risk is small.

The best way to be sure is to watch for her next period. If it's late, she should take a pregnancy test about three weeks after the incident, or at least two weeks after the missed period date. A test done too early can miss a pregnancy, so if the first result is negative but her period still doesn't come, she should test again or see a doctor.

If she does turn out to be pregnant, the decision about what to do is personal, and the legal situation depends on where you live. In many countries, early medical abortion using pills is available through a licensed clinic or doctor, and it is safest and simplest when started early. The best step at that point would be to contact a local doctor, a family planning clinic, or a women's health service. They can explain the options and what is legal where you are, and they can give her confidential care without judgment.

For the future, condoms should be checked before use, and used with a second method such as the pill, an IUD, or an implant if you want more protection. If a condom breaks again, emergency contraception is most effective when taken as soon as possible.

There isn't one universal "normal," since it depends heavily on where you live, your income, and your household size, but there are useful benchmarks.

For food, average US spending runs roughly 10 to 13 percent of household income. In dollar terms, that is often around 60 to 100 dollars per week for a single adult buying groceries, and 150 to 300 dollars per week for a family of four, depending on region and how much you cook at home. Eating out adds to this: many people spend 25 to 75 dollars a week on restaurants and takeout, though plenty spend much more or less. The USDA publishes monthly food plans (thrifty, low-cost, moderate, liberal) that make a handy reference if you want a specific number for your household.

For entertainment, which includes streaming, hobbies, events, outings, and often drinks out, the typical range is about 5 percent of income or less. That works out to perhaps 20 to 60 dollars a week for many people, though it varies a lot with lifestyle. A single person who goes out often might spend well above that, while someone with mostly free hobbies might spend almost nothing.

For clothing, households typically spend around 2 to 4 percent of income, which is often 10 to 30 dollars a week on average. In practice, clothing spending is lumpy, so it is easier to think of it monthly or yearly, such as 500 to 1,500 dollars a year for many adults.

A common framework is the 50/30/20 rule: about 50 percent of after-tax income for needs (including groceries), 30 percent for wants (dining out, entertainment, clothing beyond basics), and 20 percent for savings and debt repayment. To apply it, take your weekly take-home pay and see whether your wants fit inside roughly 30 percent of it.

The best approach is to look at your own spending for a month or two, compare it with these ranges, and adjust based on your priorities and whether you are meeting your savings goals. If you tell me your approximate income, location, and household size, I can give you more tailored numbers.

Yep, you can probably deduct home office costs as a freelance software developer, but you've got to meet a few conditions. The big one is that you need to use a specific part of your home exclusively and regularly for work. That means no mixing in personal stuff. The room (or corner, or whatever) has to be strictly for business. You'll also need to show it's your main place of business, or that you regularly meet clients there. If you check those boxes, you can write off a slice of your home costs, things like mortgage interest, property taxes, insurance, utilities, and repairs. The rules have some fine print and limits, though, so either talk to a tax pro or check the IRS guidelines before you claim anything.

Psychedelic art is a style of visual art that seeks to depict or evoke the altered states of consciousness associated with psychedelic experiences, such as those produced by LSD, psilocybin, mescaline, or DMT. It is characterized by vivid, saturated colors, swirling or fractal patterns, melting or morphing forms, kaleidoscopic symmetry, and an overall sense of movement and visual vibration. Artists often blend realistic and abstract elements, so that familiar objects, faces, or landscapes appear to dissolve, multiply, or merge into one another.

The style emerged prominently in the 1960s, when the counterculture embraced psychedelic drugs and music. Its visual language was shaped by concert posters from venues like the Fillmore in San Francisco, album covers for bands such as the Grateful Dead, Jefferson Airplane, and the Beatles, and underground comics and magazines. Artists like Victor Moscoso, Rick Griffin, Wes Wilson, and Stanley Mouse developed the lettering and imagery that became iconic, often using intricate, hard-to-read typography and bold, clashing colors. Light shows at concerts, which projected moving liquid patterns onto screens, also contributed to the aesthetic.

Beyond the 1960s, the term has expanded to cover later movements such as the 1990s psytrance and rave scenes, and digital psychedelic art created with software and computer-generated fractals. Many contemporary artists continue the tradition, and the style remains popular in posters, tattoos, clothing, and album art. Some works aim to recreate the experience of a trip, while others are simply playful or decorative explorations of color and pattern.

No, it is not riskless, even though the spread can look tempting. The gap between the market price and the tender price is the market's way of pricing several risks, and a persistent gap usually means the market sees some real chance you won't get the full tender price on all your shares.

The first risk is proration. If the company offers to buy, say, 20 percent of its shares and holders tender more than that, the company takes only a fraction of each holder's tendered shares. You get the tender price on those, but you are left holding the rest, and those shares often trade down toward or below the pre-offer price once the tender is done. So your blended return can be well below the headline spread, or even negative.

The second risk is that the offer can be withdrawn, extended, or fail. Many tender offers are conditional on financing, minimum tender levels, regulatory approval, no material adverse change, or the absence of litigation. If a condition fails, the offer can lapse and the stock may fall back sharply. In a takeover tender the spread also reflects the chance the deal is blocked or the bidder walks away.

Third, there is time and opportunity cost. Tender offers usually stay open for at least 20 business days and are often extended, and payment comes after expiration. Capital is tied up, and if the spread is small, an annualized return may be modest compared with the risk.

Fourth, there are market risks during the holding period. The stock can drop if the broader market falls, if the company releases bad news, or if the offer looks less likely to close. Hedging with a short position in a merger-arbitrage setup can reduce some of this, but it adds costs and its own risks.

Fifth, there are practical and legal details. You must tender correctly and on time through your broker, which often sets earlier deadlines than the official one. Shares tendered are typically locked up and may not be sellable, though withdrawal rights usually exist before expiration. Taxes matter too, since a tender can be treated as a sale or as a dividend depending on how much of your position is taken and whether you are a continuing holder, and that can change your after-tax return. Odd-lot holders (under 100 shares) are often exempt from proration, which is one case where the math is notably better.

So the right framing is that it is a risk-adjusted bet, not free money. Professional arbitrageurs do this routinely, but they study the offer documents, financing, proration odds, and downside price, and they accept that the spread compensates for risks that sometimes materialize.

Okay, so the sequester is basically an automatic spending cut the U.S. government set up to bring down the national debt and the budget deficit. When it kicks in, certain federal agencies have to trim their budgets. Sometimes the cut hits everything in an agency by the same percentage, and sometimes it's targeted, so some programs take a bigger hit than others. It can touch a lot of areas, like education, defense, and healthcare, and that can mean things like fewer teachers in classrooms or fewer military personnel. Most people see it as a last-resort kind of move, since it can really hurt important programs and the folks who depend on them.

Poetry translates better than people expect, mostly because what matters in a poem is often the feeling, not the exact dictionary meaning of each word. Poets lean heavily on figurative stuff like metaphors and symbols, and those can usually be carried over into another language so the mood survives. The structure helps too. Even when every word changes, you can often keep the syllable count of each line. Take the old rhyme "Roses are red, violets are blue, sugar is sweet, and so are you." You could keep the AABB rhyme and the line lengths and still end up with something that works in Spanish: "Las rosas son rojas, / Los violetas son azules, / El azúcar es dulce, / Y tú también lo eres." The words are all different, but the rhythm and rhyme still hold, so it still feels like the same little poem.

A vector space is one of the central structures in mathematics, especially in linear algebra. It is a collection of objects, called vectors, that can be added together and multiplied by numbers, called scalars, in such a way that the results stay inside the collection and behave according to a familiar set of rules.

More precisely, a vector space over a field F (most often the real numbers or the complex numbers) is a set V equipped with two operations: vector addition, which takes two vectors and produces a third, and scalar multiplication, which takes a scalar and a vector and produces another vector. These operations must satisfy several axioms. Addition must be associative and commutative, there must be a zero vector that leaves any vector unchanged when added to it, and every vector must have an additive inverse, so that adding a vector to its negative gives zero. Scalar multiplication must be compatible with multiplication in the field, meaning that multiplying by a and then by b is the same as multiplying by the product ab. Multiplying by the scalar 1 must leave a vector unchanged. Finally, scalar multiplication must distribute over both vector addition and addition of scalars.

The most familiar example is the plane, R², whose vectors are pairs of real numbers such as (2, 3). You add them componentwise and scale them by multiplying each component. The same idea extends to R³ and to Rⁿ for any n. This matches the geometric picture of arrows with direction and length, which can be placed tip to tail or stretched and shrunk. But the abstract definition covers much more. The set of all polynomials of degree at most three forms a vector space, as does the set of all continuous functions on an interval, the set of all m by n matrices, and the set of solutions to a homogeneous linear differential equation. In each case the objects are not arrows, yet they obey the same rules.

Several key concepts arise within this framework. A linear combination of vectors is a sum of scalar multiples of them. A set of vectors is linearly independent if none can be written as a combination of the others, and it spans the space if every vector is some combination of them. A set that is both independent and spanning is a basis, and the number of vectors in a basis is the dimension of the space. Once you pick a basis, every vector in a finite-dimensional space can be described uniquely by a list of coordinates. A subspace is a subset that is itself a vector space under the same operations, such as a line or plane through the origin in R³.

Maps between vector spaces that preserve addition and scalar multiplication are called linear transformations. These are represented by matrices in finite dimensions and underlie a huge range of applications, from solving systems of equations to computer graphics, quantum mechanics, signal processing, and machine learning. Extra structure can also be added, such as an inner product to measure angles and lengths, or a norm to measure distance, leading to inner product spaces, Banach spaces, and Hilbert spaces.

Stephen Hawking was a celebrated physicist and cosmologist, often considered one of the most gifted and influential scientists of his era. He advanced theoretical physics in significant ways, especially in his work on black holes and the beginnings of the universe. Born in Oxford, England, in 1942, Hawking studied physics and mathematics first at University College, Oxford, and then at the University of Cambridge. At 21, he was diagnosed with ALS (commonly called Lou Gehrig's disease), a motor neuron disease that left him paralyzed and unable to speak. Even so, he kept working and went on to become a professor at Cambridge. His research centered on comprehending the nature of the cosmos and the fundamental laws that shape it. Among his many breakthroughs was the theoretical prediction that black holes emit radiation, now called Hawking radiation. He also authored several popular science books, most notably "A Brief History of Time," which became a bestseller and made the intricacies of theoretical physics accessible to a broad readership. Hawking died in 2018 at the age of 76, yet his scientific contributions and legacy remain widely acknowledged and honored.

Chronic nasal congestion, sometimes called chronic rhinitis, can stem from a number of different causes. Among the most common are the following. Allergies to substances such as pollen, mold, and pet dander can lead to persistent stuffiness. Non-allergic rhinitis results from environmental irritants like smoke, perfumes, or strong odors, and shifts in temperature or humidity can trigger it as well. Sinusitis, an inflammation of the sinuses, may be brought on by allergies, infections, or structural abnormalities inside the nose. Nasal polyps are benign growths on the lining of the nose that can block airflow and make breathing difficult. A deviated septum, which is a structural problem in the bone and cartilage separating the two nostrils, can likewise cause congestion and trouble breathing. Because the underlying cause varies, you should see a healthcare provider to identify what is behind your congestion and to decide on the most suitable treatment. The provider might suggest allergy testing, imaging studies, or a physical exam to help pinpoint the source of your symptoms.

Trouble breathing can come from a ton of different things, so honestly the best move is getting a doctor to figure out what's going on and treat it properly. But here are some of the usual suspects.

Asthma is a big one, especially in younger people. Your airways narrow down and it gets harder to pull air in. Allergies can do something similar, since they make the airways swell up.

Infections count too. Anything from a plain old cold to pneumonia can inflame your airways and make breathing feel like work. Then there's the heart stuff, like a heart attack or heart failure, which can leave you short of breath as well.

And don't rule out anxiety. Panic attacks can make you hyperventilate, meaning that fast, shallow breathing you get when you're stressed out, and that can feel awful even when nothing's wrong with your lungs.

Anyway, if you're struggling to breathe, get it checked out. It could be a sign of something more serious going on underneath. A doctor can go over your symptoms, work out the cause, and get you the right treatment.

Water jet propulsion basically means pushing a boat along with a fast jet of water. The system pulls water in at the stern, shoves it through a narrow nozzle at the back, and that stream of water drives the vessel forward. You'll find it on fast boats, jet skis, and some larger ships. The big perk is the shallow draft, so the boat can run in water that would ground a propeller-driven one. It's also pretty quiet and smooth, which is why a lot of recreational boaters like it. Maintenance is fairly simple, and it can sip fuel more efficiently than other setups. The catch is that it usually costs more to install and fix than a conventional propeller system.

China's got a seriously long history of coming up with stuff. Paper is probably the big one. The Chinese get credit for inventing it back in the Han Dynasty (202 BC to 220 AD). Printing came from there too, and they developed the first printing press, which got used for books, posters and all sorts of other materials. Then there's the compass, which they're credited with as well. It was used for navigation and ended up being a pretty important tool for exploring by sea.

Gunpowder showed up in China during the Tang Dynasty (618 to 907 AD), and later on it fed into the development of firearms. Silk is another one, supposedly dating back to the Shang Dynasty (around 1600 BC to 1046 BC). Tea was first cultivated there too, and it's been a huge part of Chinese culture for thousands of years. Porcelain is worth a mention as well. It's a fine ceramic they used for dishes, vases and other decorative pieces.

On the medicine side you've got acupuncture, a traditional Chinese practice where thin needles go into specific points on the body to ease pain and help healing. And Kung Fu, which is basically Chinese martial arts, is a system of physical, mental and spiritual training that started in China. They also made a bunch of martial arts weapons like the staff, spear and sword, which people used for self-defense and for ceremonial stuff too.

A SIM-only mobile plan does not affect your credit rating by itself. Your credit rating, often called your credit score, reflects how trustworthy you are as a borrower, based on your past borrowing and repayment record. Lenders, landlords, and other parties use it to judge the risk involved in lending to you or renting property to you. Still, a phone contract can influence your rating indirectly in a few ways. First, your payment history matters: paying your phone bill on time shows lenders that you handle payments dependably, which can help your rating, whereas missed or late payments can hurt it. Second, there is credit utilization, meaning the share of your available credit that you are using. A large outstanding balance on a phone contract could raise this share and possibly drag your rating down. Third, applying for a new contract often triggers a credit check by the provider, which may appear on your credit report as a "hard" inquiry, and accumulating several of these within a short span can lower your score. Overall, the best approach is to pay bills promptly, keep balances low, and avoid applying for credit too frequently, since this helps maintain a healthy rating and improves your odds of approval for credit or loans down the road.

Stevie Wonder's full name is Stevland Hardaway Judkins. He was born Stevland Hardaway Morris on May 13, 1950, in Saginaw, Michigan, and took the surname Judkins from his stepfather's family later on, before he began performing under the name Stevie Wonder.

Hydrocortisone and thyroxine aren't usually used to treat high blood pressure, so that's not really what they're for. Sinemet (carbidopa and levodopa) can sometimes make blood pressure drop, though. It's most likely when you're just starting it or when you're taking it alongside other meds that lower blood pressure. If you're noticing a big drop after taking your meds, talk to your doctor. They might tweak your doses or add something else to keep things steady. Blood pressure that's too high or too low can both cause real problems, so it's worth getting it sorted.

Raccoons usually have litters of somewhere between one and seven babies, though three or four is the most common. How big a litter gets depends on a few things: how old and healthy the mom is, how much food is around, and what kind of habitat they're living in. Breeding happens in spring and early summer, and some raccoons manage more than one litter a year. The babies (kits, or cubs, if you want to be fancy) are born blind and totally helpless, so mom does pretty much everything for them for quite a while.

Of course! DirectX is basically a collection of tools that developers rely on when building games and other programs for Windows. Its job is to help software communicate more effectively with your computer's hardware, such as the graphics card and the sound card. Sometimes a newly released game is built to use a more recent version of DirectX than the one installed on your machine. That's the reason an update may be necessary: it gives the game access to the newer tools so it can perform better on your computer. Does that clear things up?

The North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA), which took effect in 1994 and was among the United States, Canada, and Mexico, was designed to eliminate or reduce barriers to trade and investment among the three countries. Its main goals were to remove tariffs on most goods traded across the borders, to make it easier for businesses to move products, services, and capital between the member nations, and to protect intellectual property and establish clearer rules for resolving trade disputes. Supporters argued that it would boost economic growth, create jobs, lower consumer prices, and make North America more competitive globally by integrating supply chains across the region. Critics raised concerns about job losses in certain industries, particularly manufacturing, and about the effects on wages and labor and environmental standards. In 2020 NAFTA was replaced by the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA), which kept many of its core features while updating rules on areas such as digital trade, autos, and labor.

Whether paying a dividend is rational depends on which theory you start from, and the honest answer is that it is rational under some conditions and not others.

The baseline is the Modigliani-Miller result. In a world without taxes, transaction costs, or information problems, dividend policy is irrelevant. A dollar paid out is a dollar the firm no longer has, so the share price falls by the dividend, and shareholders who want cash can create their own "homemade dividends" by selling a few shares. So any case for dividends must rest on a departure from that frictionless world.

The first departure is agency costs. Managers with idle cash tend to build empires, overpay for acquisitions, or fund marginal projects. Paying out cash commits the firm to return surplus funds and forces it to raise external capital when it needs more, which subjects management to market scrutiny. For a mature firm with few good investments, a dividend is rational because it moves cash to owners who can deploy it better. This is Jensen's free cash flow argument.

The second is signaling. Managers know more about future prospects than outside investors do. Because cutting a dividend is costly and punished by the market, initiating or raising one credibly signals confidence that earnings will be sustained. A firm that is not truly strong cannot easily mimic this, so the dividend carries information that cheap talk cannot.

The third is investor clienteles. Some investors, such as retirees, endowments, and certain institutions, prefer regular income, face rules against spending principal, or find it cheaper and more convenient than selling shares. Firms may rationally cater to them, and tax-exempt holders may be indifferent or favor payouts. Behavioral explanations add that investors use dividends as a self-control device.

Against all this stand the costs. Where dividends are taxed more heavily than capital gains, or taxed earlier, paying them destroys value relative to buybacks or retention. Dividends also reduce flexibility, and a firm with profitable growth opportunities should retain earnings rather than pay them out and then issue costly new equity.

So the rational rule is roughly this: pay dividends when the firm lacks investment opportunities that earn more than the shareholders' required return, when governance concerns make retained cash risky, when the signal or clientele benefits outweigh tax and flexibility costs. Otherwise, retain the cash or use buybacks. That is why young growth companies rarely pay dividends and mature, cash-rich ones usually do.

So Ehud Shapiro is a computer scientist who teaches at the Weizmann Institute of Science in Rehovot, Israel. He's known for work in theoretical computer science and AI, mostly around logic, verification, and automated reasoning. He's also been involved in building practical reasoning tools, like the automatic theorem prover EQP. He's a member of the Israeli Academy of Sciences and Humanities, and he's picked up a few awards along the way, including the ACM SIGPLAN Robin Milner Young Researcher Award and the Israel Prize in Computer Science.

Il Divo is a multinational operatic pop group that Simon Cowell put together back in 2003. The lineup is Urs Bühler, a Swiss tenor, Carlos Marín, a Spanish baritone, David Miller, an American tenor, and Sébastien Izambard, a French pop singer and songwriter. They've put out nine studio albums and sold more than 30 million records worldwide, which makes them one of the most successful classical crossover acts ever. They've toured all over the place and have a pretty loyal fanbase.

The mind-body problem is a philosophical puzzle concerning the connection between the mind and the body. For centuries it has stood at the heart of philosophical inquiry, shaping how we think about consciousness, selfhood, and the link between the mental and the physical world. One approach asks whether the mind is a separate entity from the body or whether it is merely a byproduct of physical bodily processes. Those who take the first position, known as dualists, hold that mind and body are distinct substances that nonetheless influence one another, rather than being one and the same. A different approach regards mind and body as two facets of a single underlying reality. This position, called monism, maintains that mind and body are not truly separate, but are instead two different ways of describing the same thing. Many philosophical theories have been advanced to resolve the mind-body problem, yet it continues to be a matter of active debate and discussion.

Sorry you're dealing with a toothache. Honestly, you want to get this looked at soon, since a root canal that didn't fully work can let infection creep in and do more damage. In the meantime, a few things might take the edge off. Rinse with warm salt water to calm down swelling and irritation. Over-the-counter painkillers like acetaminophen or ibuprofen can help too, just follow the directions on the package. Hold a cold compress against the outside of your cheek near the sore tooth; it cuts swelling and numbs things a bit. Skip anything super hot or cold, since that tends to make it worse. If the pain sticks around or gets bad, call a dentist right away. They can figure out what's going on and fix it. Until then, go easy on the tooth and don't chew on that side. Hope you feel better soon!

I can't verify the exact ingredients of those brands, and some of them don't look like hair-loss medicines. Dazit is usually an antibiotic (azithromycin), and Zinetac is usually an acid reducer (ranitidine). Ask your doctor or a pharmacist to confirm what each one contains before you buy it.

Hormonal hair loss is commonly treated with medicines whose generic versions are much cheaper. Minoxidil, available as a topical solution or foam in 2% and 5% strengths, is widely sold as a generic and is one of the most studied options for both men and women. Finasteride is a generic oral medicine often used for male pattern hair loss, and spironolactone is sometimes prescribed to women with hormone-related thinning. Both need a doctor's prescription and monitoring, and finasteride must not be taken by women who are or may become pregnant. Ask your doctor whether a generic version of any of these would suit you, since generic names are usually far cheaper than branded products with the same active ingredient.

Your doctor may also want to check blood levels of thyroid hormones, ferritin (iron stores), vitamin D, and sometimes vitamin B12 and androgens. Correcting a deficiency or thyroid problem can improve hair loss, and it tells you whether an expensive supplement is actually needed. Biotin helps only when you are deficient, so taking it without a deficiency is unlikely to make a difference.

Some practical steps can also help at low cost. Eat enough protein, and include iron-rich foods, though avoid megadosing supplements without a test. Reduce harsh chemical treatments, tight hairstyles, and heat styling. Manage prolonged stress and poor sleep where possible. Results from any treatment usually take three to six months to appear, so give a medicine a fair trial before judging it, and go back to your doctor if you see no improvement after that.

There's a small mismatch in your question: the title mentions pain above the belly button from gastritis, but your message describes pain just below it that you suspect is gas. These can feel similar but are treated a bit differently, so I'll cover both. The location matters because gastritis usually causes burning or gnawing pain in the upper middle abdomen, while gas pain tends to move around, comes in waves, and often eases after passing gas or having a bowel movement.

If this is gas, over-the-counter simethicone (sold as Gas-X, Mylanta Gas, and similar brands) is a common, gentle option that helps break up gas bubbles. Activated charcoal helps some people, though the evidence is mixed. Walking, lying on your left side, or gently massaging your abdomen in a clockwise direction can help gas move through. Sipping warm water or peppermint, ginger, or chamomile tea may ease cramping, though peppermint can worsen heartburn in some people. For the rest of the day, avoid carbonated drinks, chewing gum, drinking through straws, and gas-producing foods like beans, onions, cabbage, broccoli, and dairy if you're sensitive to lactose. Eating slowly also reduces swallowed air.

If it turns out to be gastritis, the approach is to reduce stomach acid and irritation. Antacids such as Tums or Maalox give quick, short-term relief. Famotidine (Pepcid) or a proton pump inhibitor like omeprazole (Prilosec) reduces acid for longer. Avoid NSAIDs like ibuprofen, naproxen, and aspirin, as these commonly cause or worsen gastritis. Acetaminophen is generally safer for the stomach if you need a pain reliever. Alcohol, coffee, spicy food, and acidic foods are worth avoiding, and smaller, bland meals are easier on the stomach. If gastritis keeps coming back, a doctor may test for H. pylori, a common bacterial cause that needs antibiotics.

It's also important to know when this might be something else. Pain that starts near the belly button and moves to the lower right side of the abdomen can be an early sign of appendicitis. Seek prompt medical care if the pain becomes severe or constant, or if you develop fever, vomiting, a rigid or very tender belly, blood in your stool or black tarry stools, vomiting blood, or inability to pass gas or stool. You should also get checked if the pain lasts more than a few days or keeps recurring.

For now, since your pain is mild and comes and goes, trying simethicone, gentle movement, and light food is a reasonable first step while you watch how it develops.

Many toddlers eat differently in group care than at home, and there are several common reasons this might be happening with your daughter. Daycare is a busy, social, and stimulating place, and at two years old children are often more interested in playing, watching their friends, and exploring than in sitting still to eat. Mealtimes there may also be rushed, with a set window after which food is cleared away, so she may simply not have enough time to settle in and eat. Some toddlers also feel shy or unsure about eating in a room full of other children, or they may be seated with children they don't feel close to, which can dampen appetite. The sensory environment matters too: the noise, the smells, the seating, or the feel of the plates and utensils can all be different from home, and a sensitive child may find that off-putting.

It's also worth considering that toddlers often eat more at home because the food is familiar and they have a parent's attention and encouragement. At daycare, the adults are caring for several children at once, so one-on-one coaxing is limited. Because she is happy there and eats well on other days, this pattern looks more like a context issue than a sign of a medical problem or a broader feeding difficulty. Still, drinking milk without eating solids is worth keeping an eye on, since milk can fill a toddler up.

To figure out the cause, you could ask the caregivers what she does at mealtimes. Do they see her refuse food, or does she simply not touch it? Does she eat any snacks there? Is she sitting with other children, and how long is the meal window? You might also ask whether they can offer small portions of a few familiar foods, let her serve herself, or give her a little more time. Sending a few foods she particularly loves, and keeping meals at daycare calm and low-pressure, often helps. If she continues to eat very little there for several weeks, or if you notice weight loss, unusual fatigue, or distress, it would be sensible to talk with your pediatrician.

I'm so sorry your family is going through this. Wanting a straight answer about what you're facing is completely reasonable, so I'll be as honest as I can while recognising that only his own medical team can speak to his specific case.

What you're describing is stage 4 (metastatic) stomach cancer, likely involving the junction where the stomach meets the oesophagus. Once it has spread to both the liver and lungs, it is generally considered incurable, and treatment shifts toward controlling the disease, extending life where possible, and keeping him comfortable. No diet, herbal remedy, or alternative therapy can shrink or cure this kind of tumour, and some can interfere with treatment, so please be cautious about anything promising otherwise.

On life expectancy, these are rough averages from large groups of patients, and individuals can do better or worse. Without any active cancer treatment, people with this stage of disease often live a few months, commonly around three to six. With chemotherapy, the average extends to roughly ten to fourteen months. If his tumour tests positive for certain markers, such as HER2 or PD-L1, adding targeted drugs or immunotherapy can push that average somewhat further, and a minority of people live well beyond two years. The biggest factor is how well he is overall: if he is still fairly active, eating some, and able to look after himself, he is more likely to tolerate treatment and benefit from it. If he is already weak, losing a lot of weight, and spending much of the day resting, the timeframe tends to be shorter, and chemotherapy may do more harm than good.

The swallowing difficulty and phlegm are important and very treatable symptoms, even if the cancer itself isn't curable. Doctors can place a stent, a small mesh tube, through the narrowed area to open it up, often with quick relief. Short courses of radiotherapy can shrink the tumour enough to ease swallowing, and chemotherapy sometimes helps too. If eating remains very hard, a feeding tube may be offered. The coughing up of phlegm may be saliva and mucus that can't pass the blockage, but it can also mean food or fluid is going into the lungs, which risks pneumonia, so please tell his team about it promptly. A dietitian can help with soft or liquid nutrition in the meantime.

I'd strongly encourage asking for a referral to palliative care now, not just at the very end. Palliative teams specialise in managing swallowing problems, pain, breathlessness, and nausea, and they support families too. Research suggests early palliative care can improve quality of life and sometimes even length of life.

When you next meet his oncologist, it's fair to ask directly whether they would be surprised if he were still alive in six months or a year, what treatment is realistically expected to achieve for him in particular, whether his tumour has been tested for HER2, PD-L1, and similar markers, and what can be done right now for his swallowing. Doctors are often more forthcoming when the family makes clear they want honest information.

I hope he gets relief soon, and that you all have support through this.
