It's worth clarifying that not every Republican turns away from science. Still, some Republicans do dispute particular scientific ideas or results, such as evolution and climate change. Part of the explanation is that some people, Republicans among them, hold religious or ideological convictions that clash with the evidence. Someone might hold that the Earth is only a few thousand years old, for instance, even though the evidence points to an age of billions of years. Likewise, some people believe humans occupy a unique position in the universe and are exempt from the natural processes that shape other living things, a view that runs against the evidence for evolution. A second factor is skepticism toward the scientific method and the way researchers reach their conclusions. Some people assume scientists are biased or that the process is fundamentally broken, and so they are more inclined to dismiss findings they find disagreeable. Finally, some people, Republicans included, reject scientific concepts because they lack accurate information or have encountered misinformation. A person who has heard false or misleading claims about climate change, for example, may come to doubt that it is happening at all. In short, the reasons are varied. Science is an ongoing process of learning and refining understanding, and approaching its questions with an open and curious mind is important.

When you sell shares bought through an employee stock purchase plan (ESPP), you typically owe tax on the gain you earned from the sale, known as a capital gain. If you kept the shares for over a year before selling, that gain is taxed at the long-term capital gains rate, which is usually lower than the rate for ordinary income. If you kept them for a year or less, the gain is taxed at the short-term capital gains rate, which matches your ordinary income tax rate. The sale must be reported on your US tax return, and any tax owed must be paid. If you are a US citizen or a resident alien living overseas, you might be able to exclude all or part of your foreign earned income and housing costs from your taxable income. To understand your exact tax obligations and whether you qualify for any exclusions or credits, speak with a tax professional.

There isn't one universally agreed number, because it depends on how "official language" is defined (de jure national status versus official use at the regional or state level) and on which sources and classifications are used. Commonly cited figures range from about 55 to around 60 sovereign countries where English holds official or de facto official status. English is also an official language in many dependent territories and in subnational units such as individual U.S. states or Indian states, which pushes the broader count considerably higher. If you need a precise figure for a specific purpose, it is worth checking a current authoritative list, such as the one maintained by the relevant government or international organization.

Diet alone usually can't change facial structure. Your bone architecture, the shape of your eye sockets, and how much fat sits under your eyes are mostly set by genetics, age, and bone development, and food doesn't reshape them. Eating well does help skin quality, hydration, and general health, but it won't necessarily make sunken eyes look fuller. Two eggs a day is a good protein source, but protein alone won't change the look of the eye area.

At your height, 6'2" and 70 kg gives a BMI of about 20, which is on the lean side. Being slim can make the cheeks and under-eye area look hollow, so a modest increase in healthy body weight, through balanced meals and strength training, may make your face look fuller. Strength training also improves posture and overall appearance.

Sunken or dull-looking eyes often come from factors you can control. Poor or short sleep is the most common cause, so aim for 7 to 9 hours on a regular schedule. Dehydration, high salt intake (which causes puffiness and then hollowing as fluid shifts), smoking, alcohol, and long sun exposure without protection all make the eye area look tired. Daily sunscreen, and a moisturizer or eye cream with ingredients like caffeine or retinol, can improve the appearance of the skin over time. Allergies with eye rubbing also contribute, so treating them can help.

See a doctor if the sunken look appeared suddenly, if you have persistent dark circles, fatigue, dizziness, or weight loss, or if you have never had your thyroid, iron, or vitamin levels checked. These can affect the eyes and skin. If you're bothered by the appearance after you've addressed these basics, a dermatologist or cosmetic specialist can discuss options such as under-eye fillers, which can soften hollows in a targeted way. Setting realistic expectations matters too: you can make your face look healthier and brighter, but you can't fully change its underlying structure.

Okay, so time dilation is basically when two things are moving relative to each other and time seems to run at different speeds for each of them. Picture this: you're standing on a platform, and your friend zooms past on a really fast train. From where you're standing, their clock looks like it's ticking slower than yours. Their movements seem slowed down to you, so time looks like it's crawling for them.

Here's the weird part, though. Your friend would say the exact same thing about you. From their side, they're the one standing still and you're the one flying by, so your clock looks slow to them. Neither of you is wrong. It just depends on who's doing the measuring and how fast the two of you are moving relative to each other.

So that's really all it comes down to: relative speed changes how time looks from different viewpoints. Everyone's perspective is different, and the faster things move relative to each other, the bigger the difference gets.

Triumph Motorcycles is a British bike maker, founded in 1984 and based in Hinckley, Leicestershire, England. They make all sorts of bikes: cruisers, touring machines, sportbikes, and adventure bikes. People tend to love them for the design and engineering, and riders all over the world have picked up a Triumph at some point.

Genetic algorithms are optimization methods modeled on the way species evolve in nature. They are typically applied to locate good answers to optimization and search tasks. Within such an algorithm, candidate solutions, referred to as "individuals" or "chromosomes," are encoded as strings of bits or numbers, and these strings are altered by a collection of rules known as "operators." The main operators are selection, crossover (sometimes called recombination), and mutation. As the algorithm runs, each individual in the population is scored with a fitness function that gauges how good the solution it encodes is. Individuals with higher scores are more likely to be chosen to contribute to the next generation. Chosen individuals then undergo crossover, where portions of their bits or numbers are merged with those of another individual to produce an offspring. Next, the offspring is passed through mutation, which randomly alters some of its bits or numbers. These steps are repeated across many generations, with the expectation that the population will gradually converge on increasingly strong solutions. Genetic algorithms are valuable because they can explore a vast set of possible solutions and often identify good ones even when the problem is intricate and the search space is huge. Nevertheless, they demand substantial computation and cannot guarantee that they will find the globally optimal solution.

Stock price is usually derived from equity value, not directly from equity and debt separately, so the approach depends on what you are given. The core idea is that the enterprise value of a company (the value of its operations) is split between debt holders and equity holders. So if you know the total firm value and the debt, equity value is what remains, and the stock price is equity value divided by the number of shares outstanding.

In the simplest case, where you are given the equity value directly, you just divide it by shares outstanding. If equity value is 500 million dollars and there are 100 million shares, the price is 5 dollars per share.

If instead you are given the total value of the firm (sometimes called enterprise value or total asset value) and the amount of debt, subtract the debt from the firm value to get equity value, then divide by shares outstanding. For example, if the firm is worth 800 million and has 300 million in debt, equity is 500 million, and with 100 million shares the price is again 5 dollars.

A slightly more refined version uses net debt, which is total debt minus cash and cash equivalents, since cash also belongs to the owners. Equity value equals enterprise value minus debt plus cash. Preferred stock and noncontrolling interests, if present, are subtracted in the same way.

If you are given the debt-to-equity ratio and the total capital instead, you can solve for equity first. If total capital (debt plus equity) is 1,000 million and the debt-to-equity ratio is 0.6, then equity is 1,000 divided by 1.6, which is about 625 million, and debt is about 375 million. Divide equity by shares outstanding to get the price.

Finally, if you are working with market values, remember that the debt figure should ideally be its market value, and the resulting equity value reflects the market's current assessment. Dividing by diluted shares, which include options and convertible securities, gives a more conservative per-share figure than using basic shares alone.

A virtual assistant is basically a software program that helps you get stuff done. You can ask it questions, get recommendations, have it handle little tasks for you, that kind of thing. Under the hood it's running on AI and machine learning to figure out what you're asking, and it uses natural language processing so you can just talk to it like a normal person instead of typing in commands. The big ones you've probably heard of are Apple's Siri, Amazon's Alexa, and Google Assistant. Most people use them through a smartphone or a smart speaker, and they can do a surprising amount. Setting reminders, playing music, turning your smart home gadgets on and off, and plenty more.

Hi Amit, I'm sorry this has been bothering you for two years. Post-laser pigmentation is frustrating, but it is often treatable, and the fact that it has persisted this long means it's worth having it properly evaluated rather than trying random creams.

Since the pigmentation is on your cheeks after beard laser treatment, it is most likely post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, meaning the skin darkened in response to heat or irritation from the laser. Sometimes it can also be a melasma-like pattern triggered by heat, or a combination. A dermatologist can distinguish these with a simple examination, sometimes with a Wood's lamp, and that distinction guides treatment.

The usual approach starts with topical treatments prescribed by a dermatologist. These commonly include hydroquinone or alternatives such as azelaic acid, kojic acid, arbutin, or tranexamic acid, often combined with a retinoid like tretinoin and a mild steroid for a limited period. Strict daily sunscreen with broad spectrum protection (SPF 30 or higher, reapplied outdoors) is essential, because sun exposure will keep the pigment dark and can worsen it. Visible light and heat can also darken pigment, so avoid picking at the area and be cautious with hot water and harsh scrubs.

If creams alone are not enough after a few months, a dermatologist may consider procedures such as chemical peels (glycolic, mandelic, or Jessner's), microneedling, or low-fluence Q-switched or picosecond laser toning. Laser treatment for pigment should be done only by an experienced doctor, because treating over-pigmented skin with the wrong settings can make it darker. Since your pigmentation followed a laser procedure, it would also be sensible to tell the treating dermatologist about it.

I would recommend seeing a board-certified dermatologist in person, preferably one who is not only the clinic that performed the original laser. Bring photos showing how the area looked before and now, and a list of any products you have already used. Please avoid self-prescribing strong bleaching creams, especially those containing high-dose steroids or unregulated hydroquinone, as these can cause rebound darkening, thinning of skin, or other side effects.

If you tell me your skin type, whether the patches are brown or grey, and what you have already tried, I can suggest what to discuss with your dermatologist.

A duvet cover is basically a removable outer layer that goes over your duvet, the soft, fluffy comforter stuffed with down, feathers, or synthetic fill. It slides over the duvet and gets fastened with buttons, snaps, or a zipper. The best part is that you can pull it off and throw it in the wash whenever you want, which means the duvet underneath stays clean and doesn't take the hit from stains, dirt, and everyday wear. Most covers are cotton, linen, or some mix of natural and synthetic fibers, so they feel nice against your skin. They also come in pretty much every color, pattern, and style you can think of, so you can match your room or just add a bit of personality to your bed. Honestly, it's one of the cheapest ways to freshen up your bedding without buying a whole new duvet. They're handy for travel too, since a light cover packs down small and comes along easily.

Elk, also called wapiti, are big mammals from the deer family. Most of them breed in autumn during what is called the rut, which in most of their range runs from late September into early November. Over this stretch, males vie for mates by showing off their strength through bugling calls, posturing, and fights with rival bulls. A female is only ready to mate for a short window, and during that time she may be bred by more than one male. Females generally deliver one calf the following spring. How often elk breed depends on several things, including the health and age of each animal and how much food and other resources are available.

Cancer is basically when cells in your body start growing and multiplying out of control. When they bunch together into a mass or tumor, doctors can often cut it out with surgery. The catch is that cancer cells can spread, or metastasize, to other parts of the body, and then just removing the original tumor might not cure it.

Take testicular cancer. If it has already spread to places like the lymph nodes or lungs, taking out the testicle (that's called an orchiectomy) isn't enough on its own. The person would usually need more treatment, like chemo or radiation, to wipe out any cells that got away and keep the cancer from coming back. That said, plenty of testicular cancers get caught early, and surgery alone can handle those. Honestly, though, if you or someone you know is dealing with this, talk it through with a doctor, since the best plan really depends on the specifics.

Imagine you're playing tag at recess with two big teams. How do you know who's on your side? Mostly, you stay close to your friends and you all run the same direction together. Old battles worked a lot like that.

The biggest trick was simply staying in a group. Soldiers stood in tight lines or blocks, shoulder to shoulder with the people they'd trained and marched with for weeks or months. They knew those faces. When the two armies met, your team was beside you and behind you, and the enemy was in front of you. As long as everyone kept their spot, "who's the bad guy?" was mostly answered by "whoever is facing me."

Armies also used big, easy-to-see signs. Flags and banners were held high so everyone could find their group, and soldiers were trained to follow them. Many armies wore something colorful to tell sides apart, like a sash, a ribbon, a feather, a cloth band on the arm, or a painted symbol on a shield. Sometimes they even stuck a plant sprig in their helmet that morning. Later armies wore uniforms in a team color, a bit like sports jerseys.

They used sounds, too. Each side had its own drums, horns, and battle cries, and sometimes a secret password or shout. If someone ran up yelling your army's word, he was probably a friend.

But here's the honest part: it didn't always work. When lines broke apart and things got messy, especially in fog, smoke, dust, or at night, soldiers did sometimes hurt their own side by accident. This happened in plenty of real battles. That's exactly why generals worked so hard to keep their soldiers in neat groups. A tidy team is much less likely to get confused than a scattered one.

A gift of stock that has risen in value to a social club exempt under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) section 501(c)(7) spares the club from paying tax on that increase. The donor may, however, be able to deduct the stock's full fair market value from their income tax return, within certain limits. Claiming that deduction requires the donor to satisfy the charitable deduction rules in IRC section 170. Those rules cover the donor's adjusted gross income, the kind of organization receiving the gift, and the kind of property given. Generally, a donor can deduct the fair market value of donated property if it goes to a qualified charitable organization. Because a social club exempt under IRC section 501(c)(7) is treated as a qualified charitable organization, the donor may be able to deduct the fair market value of appreciated stock given to one. The donor must also get a written acknowledgment from the club. That document should describe the donated property and state whether the club gave anything in return. The donor should keep it for their records and attach it to their tax return when claiming the deduction. Charitable deductions are also capped based on the donor's adjusted gross income and the type of property donated. To find the maximum deduction allowed for a gift of appreciated stock to a social club, the donor should consult a tax professional or review IRS guidance.

The prostate is a small gland in male reproductive system, roughly the size and shape of a walnut, that sits just below the bladder and in front of the rectum, surrounding the urethra (the tube that carries urine out of the body). Its main job is to produce fluid that forms part of semen. This fluid is slightly alkaline, which helps neutralize the acidity of the vagina and so supports sperm survival and movement, and it also contains enzymes and nutrients that nourish sperm. During ejaculation, muscles in the prostate contract to push this fluid into the urethra, mixing it with sperm from the testes and fluid from the seminal vesicles to form semen.

Because the prostate wraps around the urethra, it also plays a role in urinary control. Its muscular tissue helps keep urine from leaking during ejaculation and helps regulate the flow of urine when you urinate.

The prostate's health matters because it is prone to certain conditions as men age. Benign prostatic hyperplasia, a noncancerous enlargement, can squeeze the urethra and cause urinary difficulties, while prostatitis is inflammation or infection of the gland. Prostate cancer is also common in older men, which is why screening discussions often come up with a doctor after middle age.

The short version is that the government treats corn and sugar very differently, and the difference is what makes corn syrup cheap and sugar expensive.

Start with sugar, because that is where most of the price gap really comes from. The United States protects its sugar farmers. It limits how much foreign sugar can come into the country by using quotas, and it adds high taxes (tariffs) on imports beyond those quotas. It also runs a loan program that sets a kind of price floor, so sugar can't get too cheap. Because less sugar comes in from places like Brazil, where it is made very cheaply, American buyers pay more. So sugar in the US usually costs about double what it does on the world market. That is not a subsidy in the sense of handing out money. It is more like building a fence around the market so the price stays high.

Now corn. Corn farmers do get subsidies in the more familiar sense. The government helps pay for crop insurance, and it gives payments when prices or revenues fall below certain levels. This lets farmers keep growing lots of corn even when it is not very profitable, so there is a big supply, and a big supply means low prices. Corn is also grown very efficiently in the Midwest, which helps too. High fructose corn syrup is made from that plentiful, cheap corn, so it ends up cheap.

Put those together and you can picture it like this. Imagine two lemonade stands. The government helps one stand keep its lemons coming in huge piles so lemons are cheap. For the other stand, the government keeps outside lemon sellers away, so the lemons stay pricey. Naturally, the lemonade from the first stand costs less.

There is one honest caveat. Economists argue about how much the corn subsidies themselves lower the price of corn syrup, because the sugar protections do much of the work. Even without corn subsidies, corn syrup would likely still be cheaper than American sugar, simply because sugar is held artificially high. So when people say "because of subsidies," the fuller story is that corn is supported and made plentiful, while sugar is protected and made scarce.

Coke Zero and Pepsi One contain no calories since they rely on artificial sweeteners rather than ordinary sugar. These sweeteners taste intensely sweet, yet the body doesn't break them down the way it does sugar, so they add no energy to the diet. Whether these beverages are a healthier choice depends on an individual's health objectives and situation. For some people, swapping in artificial sweeteners makes it easier to cut back on added sugar and calories, which can support weight control. Still, the long-term health effects of artificial sweeteners remain under debate, and certain studies have linked them to possible health concerns. Anyone trying to decide what suits them best should consult a healthcare provider.

Ayn Rand was a philosopher who was big on individual rights, reason, and capitalism. She wrote Anthem, The Fountainhead, and Atlas Shrugged, and all three are novels that dig into those ideas. In Anthem, the main character rebels against a society that puts the group above the individual (that's collectivism), and he ends up discovering what individuality and personal freedom are actually worth. The Fountainhead follows an architect who won't go along with the traditional way of doing things and builds in his own style instead. Atlas Shrugged is about a bunch of people who go on strike because they see their society as oppressive. Basically, Rand thought people should be free to think and act for themselves, and that the government shouldn't have too much say over how people live.

Anorexia is an illness where a person becomes so afraid of gaining weight that they eat very little, even when they are hungry and even when they are getting sick. It is not just about wanting to look pretty. It is more like the brain's alarm system getting stuck on "danger" when there is no real danger.

Think of your brain as a helpful robot that keeps a list of things to worry about. In someone with anorexia, the robot starts treating food and body size as the biggest emergency in the world. It keeps shouting, "Don't eat, don't eat!" and it becomes very good at finding reasons to obey. Scientists think a few things add up to make this happen. Some people are born with brains that are more sensitive to worry and perfectionism. Genes play a part, and anorexia often runs in families. Stressful life events, teasing, or pressure to be perfect can set it off. Starving also changes the brain itself. When a person doesn't eat enough, their brain chemistry shifts, which makes them more anxious and more fixated on food and rules, so the illness feeds itself.

As for the "fat girl in the mirror" picture, the brain normally builds a picture of your body by combining what your eyes see with feelings and memories. In anorexia, that picture gets bent. The brain's body map becomes distorted, and the person sees themselves as bigger than they really are, even when they are very thin. It's a bit like a funhouse mirror that the brain itself is holding up, and the person can't easily tell it's warped. That is why arguing with someone who has anorexia, saying "You're not fat!", often doesn't work. Their brain is convinced of what it sees.

Why the illness exists at all is still not fully understood. Scientists don't think it was designed to help us survive. It seems to be a mix of inherited sensitivity, the way the brain handles anxiety and reward, and the environment, all going wrong together.

If this topic feels close to you, whether you're noticing it in a friend or wondering about your own thoughts, talking to a doctor, a counselor, or an eating disorder helpline can make a real difference. Recovery is possible, and nobody has to figure it out alone.

No, "folio" is not generally an accepted contraction of "portfolio." The two words are related, since "portfolio" comes from Italian roots meaning to carry papers, and "folio" itself refers to a leaf of paper or a page number, or a book size made from sheets folded once. In everyday and professional use, "portfolio" is the standard term for a case or collection of work, and writing "folio" in its place would likely read as an error or an unfamiliar usage. The one exception is in specialized contexts such as bookbinding, publishing, or library cataloguing, where "folio" has its own established meanings, but those do not make it a shortened form of "portfolio."

The metric system is a measurement framework adopted by the majority of nations worldwide. It rests on the International System of Units (SI), a standardized set of units used to quantify attributes such as length, mass, and time. Many people regard the metric system as better than the imperial system, which is still used in the United States and a few other places. One advantage is its foundation in the number 10, which keeps it simple to grasp and apply. In the metric system, the meter serves as the base unit of length, and all other measures scale by powers of 10. Thus, for distances beyond a meter, one might use decimeters (ten centimeters), centimeters (one hundred millimeters), or kilometers (one thousand meters). A second advantage is its grounding in science. Its units draw on constants such as the speed of light and the mass of a specific kind of atom, which makes the system well suited to scientific work. Lastly, the metric system makes conversion straightforward. Changing meters into kilometers, for instance, only requires dividing the number of meters by 1000. By contrast, the imperial system relies on feet, inches, and pounds, whose relationships are not based on multiples of 10, so converting among them is often awkward. In short, the metric system is considered superior because it is easy to understand, rooted in scientific principles, and simple to convert.

The Green Bay Packers are a professional American football franchise headquartered in Green Bay, Wisconsin. Within the National Football League (NFL), they compete in the North Division of the National Football Conference (NFC). Established in 1919, the club has taken part in the NFL since 1921. Their 13 league titles are the most of any team in league history, reflecting a long record of winning. Home games are held at Lambeau Field, situated in Green Bay.

Blog-style websites can earn money in a few main ways, and none of them involve selling a product or service. The most common is advertising. A blogger signs up with an ad network, which places ads on the pages, and the site earns a little money each time someone sees or clicks an ad. The more people who visit the blog, the more the ads pay. Think of it like a sign on a lemonade stand that a friend pays you to put up, except the friend pays a tiny bit every time someone walks by and notices it.

Another way is affiliate links. A blogger writes about a book or a toy they like and includes a special link to where it can be bought. If a reader clicks the link and buys something, the blogger gets a small share of the price. The blogger doesn't sell the item themselves; they just point people toward it, like recommending your favorite candy shop to a friend and getting a thank-you coin when your friend goes there.

Some bloggers ask readers for support directly. They might have a donation button, or a membership where fans pay a small amount each month to get extra posts or early access to stories. This works a bit like a fan club, where people who enjoy your writing chip in because they want more of it.

Sponsored posts are another option. A company might pay a blogger to write about a topic or mention something in a post. Readers usually need to be told when a post is sponsored, so it stays honest, a bit like a friend telling you, "I got paid to say this, but I really do like it."

Finally, some bloggers earn money by writing for others, such as getting paid to write articles for a magazine or website, or by publishing a book based on their blog posts. Their blog then acts like a showcase that gets them noticed.

Most successful blogs combine a few of these methods, and it usually takes a long time and many readers before the money adds up.

Soft computing is an umbrella term for a family of computational techniques designed to solve complex real-world problems that are difficult or impractical to handle with traditional, exact methods. The term was popularized in the early 1990s by Lotfi Zadeh, the mathematician who also invented fuzzy logic. The central idea is that many problems in the real world involve uncertainty, imprecision, partial truth, and approximation, and that insisting on perfectly precise, rigorously provable solutions can make those problems intractable or prohibitively expensive to solve. Soft computing deliberately tolerates these imperfections in exchange for tractability, robustness, low solution cost, and a closer resemblance to the way humans reason and make decisions.

It is usually defined in contrast to "hard computing," which refers to conventional computation based on exact binary logic, crisp numerical analysis, and deterministic algorithms. Hard computing works very well when a problem can be modeled precisely, such as calculating a payroll or solving a well-defined system of equations. However, many tasks, like recognizing a face, controlling a vehicle in changing traffic, predicting stock movements, or diagnosing an illness from vague symptoms, do not fit neatly into precise mathematical models. Humans handle such tasks routinely using approximate reasoning, and soft computing tries to capture that same flexibility.

The main components traditionally grouped under soft computing are fuzzy logic, artificial neural networks, evolutionary computation, and probabilistic reasoning. Fuzzy logic allows variables to have degrees of truth between completely true and completely false, so that a temperature can be "somewhat warm" rather than strictly hot or cold, which makes it useful for control systems in appliances, cars, and industrial processes. Neural networks are inspired by the structure of the brain and learn patterns from data, making them powerful for classification, recognition, and prediction tasks. Evolutionary computation, which includes genetic algorithms, mimics natural selection by evolving a population of candidate solutions over many generations to find good answers to optimization problems. Probabilistic reasoning, including Bayesian networks, handles uncertainty by working with likelihoods rather than certainties. Related methods such as swarm intelligence, rough set theory, and chaos theory are also often included.

A key feature of soft computing is that these techniques are seen as complementary rather than competing. They are frequently combined into hybrid systems, such as neuro-fuzzy systems, where a neural network learns the rules for a fuzzy controller, or neural networks whose structure or weights are optimized by a genetic algorithm. Each method compensates for the weaknesses of the others: fuzzy logic offers interpretable reasoning, neural networks provide learning ability, and evolutionary methods provide global search.

Soft computing has been applied widely in engineering, robotics, medicine, finance, image and speech processing, data mining, and consumer electronics. Its overall philosophy can be summarized as exploiting tolerance for imprecision and uncertainty to achieve practical, efficient, and human-like solutions to problems where exact answers are either unattainable or not worth their cost.

So osteophytic lipping is basically when you get little bony outgrowths, called osteophytes (bone spurs), along the edges of bones in a joint. They can hurt, make the joint feel uncomfortable, and limit how far you can move it. They usually show up because the joint's been taking a beating over time, or because of something else going on like osteoarthritis or rheumatoid arthritis.

Surgery to remove them can be an option, but usually only after the non-surgical stuff, like physical therapy and medication, hasn't done enough for the pain or function. A doctor should really look at your situation before you decide. They'll think about how bad it is, what the risks and benefits of surgery are, and what you actually need and want out of it.

If you're thinking about surgery, talk it through with your doctor and weigh the pros and cons carefully. And keep in mind it doesn't always work, and it might not get rid of all your symptoms. Sometimes simpler changes do the trick, like adjusting what you do at work or wearing better shoes, and that can be enough to keep things manageable and cut down the pain.

A Truth-in-Lending Disclosure is a legally required document that lenders must give borrowers when they take out a loan. Its purpose is to present clear and accurate details about the loan's terms, such as the annual percentage rate (APR), the finance charge, and the loan's total amount. Calculating the APR requires knowing the interest rate, how many payments will be made over the loan's duration, the size of each payment, and any fees added to the loan, such as origination fees or closing costs. The finance charge is worked out from the same set of details: the interest rate, the number of payments, the payment amount, and any added fees or charges. The total amount of the loan, meanwhile, depends on the principal, meaning the sum being borrowed, along with the finance charge already calculated. Several formulas and methods exist for determining the APR, finance charge, and total loan amount. A financial calculator or spreadsheet program can perform these computations, or you can use an online calculator or seek help from a financial professional. Reading and understanding your loan terms carefully is essential so you can make well-informed decisions about your finances.

A little soreness or discomfort after masturbating is pretty common, so that part on its own isn't a big deal. But if the pain is really bad, or it keeps coming back, go talk to a doctor about it.

What you're describing could come from a few different things. An infection, some kind of inflammation, or just plain irritation are all possible. For pain around the scrotum and anus, your best bet is either a regular primary care doctor or a urologist. They can examine you, and they might order a few tests to figure out what's actually going on. Once they know the cause, they can go over treatment with you. That could be medication, some changes to your habits, or other therapies, depending on what they find.

I wouldn't just sit on this one. Pain that sticks around can sometimes point to something more serious going on underneath, so it's worth getting checked out soon rather than waiting and hoping it goes away. The sooner you find out what's causing it, the sooner you can get it treated.

Oklahoma is best known for its energy production, particularly oil and natural gas, which have long been the backbone of its economy. The state is one of the leading producers of natural gas in the country and sits atop the Anadarko Basin and the Woodford Shale, among other formations. Oklahoma also produces coal, though in smaller quantities than in past decades, and it has a growing wind energy sector, with large wind farms across the western and central parts of the state.

Agriculture is another major contributor. Oklahoma is a significant producer of cattle and beef, and the state raises substantial numbers of hogs, poultry, and dairy cows. On the crop side, wheat is the most prominent, with Oklahoma regularly ranking among the top wheat-producing states. Other crops include hay, soybeans, corn, sorghum, cotton, and peanuts, and the state is also known for its pecan orchards and for producing a variety of fruits and vegetables.

Manufacturing and other industries round out the state's output. Oklahoma has aerospace and defense manufacturing, with a notable presence around Tinker Air Force Base in Oklahoma City, along with machinery, food processing, and chemical production. Its forests and timber industry, along with the mining of minerals such as gypsum, helium, and crushed stone, add further variety to what the state produces.

Being the primary borrower on a car loan means you're legally responsible for the debt no matter who has been driving or holding the car. The lender doesn't care who has the keys. If payments are missed, it's your credit that takes the hit, and the lender can pursue you for the balance, repossess the vehicle, and send any remaining deficiency to collections or court. So even though it feels unfair if someone else has had the car for two years, acting quickly is in your interest.

Start by getting a clear picture of where things stand. Call the lender or log into the account to find out the current balance, whether payments are behind, how far behind, and whether the account has been sent to collections or charged off. Pull your free credit reports at annualcreditreport.com to see how the loan is being reported. Find out where the car actually is and what condition it's in, because the car itself is your main asset for getting out of this.

Your next steps depend on who has the car and why. If it's an ex-partner, family member, or friend, the cleanest solution is usually for them to refinance the loan in their own name, which removes you entirely. If they can't qualify, the next best option is often selling the car and using the proceeds to pay off the loan. If the car is worth less than what's owed, you'd need to cover the gap or negotiate with the lender. If the person refuses to cooperate, you may be able to retrieve the car yourself if your name is on the title, though you should check local laws and avoid confrontation. Involving a lawyer or using small claims court to recover what they owe you is another option. If the car was part of a divorce decree that assigned it to your ex, that agreement doesn't bind the lender, but you can go back to family court to enforce it.

If payments have been missed and you can't catch up, talk to the lender before repossession happens. Lenders will sometimes agree to a payment plan, a deferral, or a voluntary surrender. Voluntary surrender still hurts your credit but usually less than a forced repossession, and it can reduce fees. If the debt has already gone to collections, you may be able to negotiate a settlement for less than the full amount. Get any agreement in writing before paying.

If you can tell me a bit more, I can give more specific advice. Who has the car, is the loan current or behind, is your name on the title, and is anyone else on the loan as a co-signer?

Putting together a taxable investment portfolio means weighing several factors so that you earn the best possible returns while keeping your tax bill as low as you can. The following steps can help you build one properly.

Define your investment goals. Any portfolio starts with a clear sense of what you want to achieve, including how long you plan to invest and how much risk you can accept. These answers point you toward the kinds of investments that suit your situation.

Create an asset allocation strategy. After settling on your goals, decide how to divide your money among different asset types, such as stocks, bonds, and cash. The proportions you pick should reflect your risk tolerance and your time horizon.

Take your taxes into account. With a taxable account, the tax consequences of each decision matter. For instance, you might place tax-advantaged holdings, like municipal bonds, in this account to reduce what you owe.

Spread your investments around. Diversification helps control risk and improve returns, so try to hold a variety of asset classes, sectors, and industries.

Check in and rebalance regularly. Because your goals and circumstances will shift over time, periodically review the portfolio and rebalance it so it still matches your aims. Doing so could mean buying or selling certain investments or changing how your assets are distributed.

Keep in mind that constructing a taxable portfolio involves many complicated issues, so working with a financial professional can help you make well-informed choices.

Bigamy is illegal in most Western countries mainly because marriage is a special promise between two people, and the law is set up to protect that promise and the people who make it. Here's the simple version.

Think of marriage like a game where the rules say each player has one partner at a time. When someone secretly has two partners, the other people in the game can get hurt, because they were promised something that wasn't true. The law steps in to protect them.

There are a few main reasons governments give:

First, it protects the people who got married. If you marry someone believing they're only yours, and you later find out they already had a husband or wife, you may have been tricked. Bigamy laws help keep people from being fooled like that.

Second, it protects the family. Marriage often comes with rights about money, property, inheritance, and children. When one person has two spouses, it gets very confusing who gets what and who is responsible for whom. Keeping things to one spouse at a time makes these questions much easier to sort out.

Third, it keeps records clear. Governments keep official records of who is married to whom. If someone could be married to several people at once, those records would be a tangle.

Finally, many Western countries have built their marriage laws on a tradition where marriage is a partnership between two people. That idea has deep roots in history and religion, and lawmakers have kept it as the standard.

So in short, bigamy is illegal because it's a bit like cheating at the marriage game, and the law wants to make sure everyone plays fairly and knows the rules.

Yeah, there can be tax stuff to deal with if you rent out a unit on Airbnb. Rental income is generally taxable, though exactly how it works depends on your situation and where you live. Basically, you'll need to report whatever you earn on your tax return.

Keep good records, both of what you take in and what you spend on the place, like cleaning or repairs. You can often deduct some of those expenses, which brings down what you owe.

How it's treated can also change depending on how long and how often you rent it out. Say you only rent out a room in your home once in a while. That might count as plain "rental income," taxed at your normal income tax rate. But if you're hosting all the time, it could get treated as "business income" instead, and that comes with different rules.

Your best bet is to talk to a tax professional, or at least read up on the tax laws where you live, so you know what actually applies to you.

A disk defragmenter is a utility that reorganizes the data on a storage drive so that the pieces of each file are stored in contiguous blocks. When files are repeatedly created, edited, resized, and deleted, they often get split into scattered fragments across the disk. This fragmentation can make the drive work harder to read a file, since the read head of a traditional hard disk drive must jump between locations, which can slow down performance. The defragmenter rearranges these fragments so that files sit together in continuous sections, which can speed up access times.

Windows includes a built-in tool called Defragment and Optimize Drives for this purpose. On macOS and Linux, fragmentation is far less of a concern because those systems' file systems are designed to minimize it, so such tools are rarely needed. Defragmentation is also generally unnecessary for solid-state drives, since they can access any location at nearly the same speed, and running a defragmenter on an SSD adds wear without a meaningful benefit. Modern versions of Windows recognize the drive type and typically apply TRIM or other optimization routines to SSDs instead of traditional defragmentation.

An ant trail is a path that ants repeatedly travel between their nest and a food source, water, or another destination. It is formed through chemical communication. When a forager ant finds food, it returns to the colony and lays down a trail of pheromones, chemical signals that other ants can detect with their antennae. Ants that encounter this scent are drawn to follow it, and as more ants walk the route and reinforce the pheromone with their own deposits, the trail becomes stronger and more clearly defined. Over time, the path can become a well-worn highway of ants moving in both directions, with outbound workers heading to the food and returning ones carrying pieces back to the nest.

This system is an efficient example of collective behavior. The strength of the trail reflects the quality and distance of the food source. Shorter routes get traveled more often, so pheromone builds up faster on them, while longer or less productive paths gradually fade as the scent evaporates and ants stop reinforcing it. Because of this, colonies can find the most efficient routes without any single ant having a map or overall plan. Scientists studying this process have used it as inspiration for computer algorithms, known as ant colony optimization, which help solve problems such as network routing and delivery planning.

Bob Seger was born on May 6, 1945, so he's 77 now. He's an American singer-songwriter known for hits like "Old Time Rock and Roll," "Like a Rock," and "Turn the Page." He's been at it for more than five decades, and his bluesy rock and roll sound is pretty much his trademark.

The price of a fixed income exchange-traded fund (ETF) depends on several elements, such as the worth of the bonds it holds, the balance between buyers and sellers of the fund, and the general condition of the financial markets. Among these, the value of the underlying bonds plays a central role. A bond's value hinges on factors like the issuer's credit quality, its coupon rate, when it matures, and the current level of interest rates. When an issuer's credit standing strengthens or rates fall, the bonds held by the ETF tend to gain value, which pushes the ETF's price up. On the other hand, a weakening issuer credit profile or rising rates usually reduce the bonds' value and, in turn, the ETF's price.

Supply and demand for the ETF itself also influence its price. When more investors want to buy than sell, the price tends to rise, while an excess of sellers over buyers often drives it down. Broader market conditions matter as well. In a favorable environment, investors are generally more eager to buy fixed income ETFs, which can boost demand and lift prices. In an unfavorable environment, that eagerness fades, demand softens, and prices may fall.

The cheapest route almost always depends on how your state (or country) treats transfers between people who are already on the title. Many jurisdictions see removing a co-owner differently from an ordinary sale, so before anything else call or check the website of your DMV or motor vehicle agency and ask specifically about "removing an owner from a title" or "transfer between co-owners." In the United States, many states either exempt these transfers from sales or use tax or tax only the portion of the vehicle actually changing hands, so a 50 percent share purchase is taxed on half the value rather than the whole thing.

Look at how the names appear on the current title. If they are joined by "or," either owner can often sign the vehicle over alone, which can make the paperwork simpler. If they are joined by "and," both of you must sign. Either way, the departing owner releases their interest and a new title is issued in your name alone. That usually costs only a standard title fee, typically somewhere between roughly 15 and 100 dollars depending on the state, and often avoids new plates or re-registration because the vehicle stays with an existing owner.

Several exemptions can eliminate tax entirely. Transfers between spouses, parents and children, or other close family members are frequently tax exempt. Transfers required by a divorce decree or legal separation are almost always exempt, and you would bring a copy of the decree to the DMV. Some states also exempt transfers where no money changes hands, which is why some people structure the buyout as a gift. Be honest on the forms, though. Writing a false price or calling a paid transfer a gift to dodge tax is fraud in most places and can bring penalties. If you really are paying your co-owner, report the actual amount paid for their share, which is often lower than full market value anyway.

On the federal side in the US, a gift of a partial vehicle interest is rarely a concern because the annual gift tax exclusion (19,000 dollars per recipient in 2025) covers most shares, and even larger gifts just require filing a form rather than paying tax. The seller usually owes no income tax because personal vehicles generally sell for less than their original cost, so no capital gain arises.

If there is a loan on the car, the lender holds the title and must agree to any change. Typically you refinance the loan into your name alone, which pays off the joint loan and releases the other person. Shop around, since some credit unions charge little or nothing to refinance, and ask whether your current lender will simply release the co-borrower, which is sometimes allowed if you qualify on your own income. Refinancing may trigger a title fee to record the new lien, but usually no sales tax because the ownership change is between existing owners.

In practice, the steps are to agree on a price for the share, write a simple bill of sale or release describing the share and amount paid, have both people sign the title or the state's specific co-owner removal form (some states require notarization), handle any lender requirements, and submit everything to the DMV with any applicable exemption form or supporting document. Finally, update your insurance to remove the other person, and make sure they take the car off their own policy so they stop paying for it and aren't liable for it going forward.

Imagine two kids who both run lemonade stands where people can leave their things for a while. One kid just lets people store stuff and takes it down when a grown-up politely asks. The other kid is actually helping people trade stolen toys and getting rich from it. The police are much more interested in the second kid. That is basically the difference between MediaFire and MegaUpload.

MegaUpload was shut down in 2012 because the US government said it was not just a neutral storage place but a business built around piracy. Prosecutors pointed to internal emails where employees seemed to talk openly about infringing files, and they said the company paid people rewards based on how many times their uploads were downloaded, which in practice encouraged uploading popular movies and music. They also said that when a takedown request came in, the company often removed only the single link rather than the underlying file, so the pirated copy stayed available. On top of that, the company made huge money from ads and premium subscriptions, and the charges included racketeering and money laundering, not just copyright infringement.

MediaFire, and sites like Dropbox or Google Drive, mostly try to fit into what the law calls a safe harbor. In the US, the DMCA says a service is generally not responsible for what users upload if it responds quickly to takedown notices, removes repeat offenders, and does not knowingly encourage piracy. Those companies have no famous trail of evidence showing they were designed around piracy, and they do not pay uploaders for popular pirated content.

There are a few other things going on. Prosecutors can't chase everyone, so they tend to pick the biggest and most blatant example to send a message. MegaUpload was enormous, with a flashy founder, Kim Dotcom, and a lot of money to point at. Timing and politics mattered too, since the entertainment industry was pushing hard at the time.

Also worth knowing, many people felt the MegaUpload case was heavy-handed, and the legal process was messy, with questions about whether the raid in New Zealand was done properly. The case dragged on for years. So the short version is that it was not that one site was breaking rules and the other wasn't being noticed, but that investigators believed one was knowingly running a piracy business and the other was playing by the takedown rules.

Usually a spiral fracture of the ring finger gets treated with a splint or cast so the bone can knit back together. That takes the pressure off and keeps the finger still while it heals. If you've been in a cast for 5 weeks and the fracture still isn't looking better, it might be healing slower than it should. Your doctor could suggest keeping the immobilization going longer, starting physical therapy to get your movement and strength back, or in some cases doing surgery to fix the bone. Make sure you keep up with your follow-up appointments and do what your doctor tells you. And if the pain or swelling gets worse, or anything new shows up, give them a call right away instead of waiting for your next visit.

Imagine you are carrying a heavy backpack that is full of stuff on top of your shoulders. Bugs are a bit like that. Most bugs have a body that is heavier on top, where their back is, and they have skinny little legs that hold them up from underneath. While the bug is alive, its legs are strong and work like tiny stilts, keeping its body balanced so it doesn't tip over.

When a bug gets sick or is poisoned, like from bug spray, its muscles start to go wobbly and then stop working. The legs get weak and curl up toward the belly. Now the heavy part of the body has nothing strong to hold it up, so the bug tips over, and its curled legs can't push it back upright. It's like a table that loses its legs. Once it's flipped, it stays that way.

There is another reason, too. When a bug is dying, its body often twitches and its legs flail around. All that wiggling can make it flop over onto its back. A bug that is on its back and too weak to flip itself over just stays there, even after it stops moving.

Also, think about bugs that die on their feet. Their legs may stiffen and curl, and they might fall over later. So you mostly notice the ones on their backs because those are the ones that end up looking like the classic "dead bug" pose.

So the short answer is that bugs have heavy backs, skinny legs that curl up when they die, and nothing left to hold them upright, so they roll over and stay that way.

Imagine a big ship on the ocean as a giant floating toy box that belongs to lots of different countries. When the ship goes into a port, the people in charge of that port have to check on it, and every country has its own rules about what can be brought in and out. Guns are a very serious thing, so there are strict rules about who is allowed to have them and where they can go.

Ships also sail under a flag, which tells everyone which country's rules the ship follows. If a ship carries weapons, it can run into trouble in many places, because some countries will not let armed ships into their waters or ports at all. Carrying guns could get the whole crew arrested or stop the ship from delivering its cargo, which is the whole reason it exists.

There is another problem too. Many ships have crews who are not trained to use weapons safely, and a gun on a ship can cause accidents or get used by the wrong person. Some people also worry that if a ship has weapons, it might start fights instead of avoiding them, which could make things even more dangerous.

Because of all this, shipping companies usually choose other ways to stay safe. They can sail farther from dangerous areas, travel faster, build high fences and barbed wire around the deck, use water hoses to spray attackers, and lock themselves in a secure room called a citadel until help arrives. In some places, navies send warships to escort cargo ships, and some countries allow trained security guards who are approved by the government to be on board. So the ship is not totally defenseless, but the rules are set up so that guns are handled by people whose job is to use them carefully and legally.

An artificial brain is a computer system or model designed to replicate, simulate, or draw inspiration from the structure and function of the biological brain. The term covers a range of efforts, from software that mimics how neurons process information to large-scale hardware projects that attempt to reproduce brain-like activity. It is important to note that the phrase is often used loosely, and most current systems described this way are far simpler than a real brain, which contains roughly 86 billion neurons connected by trillions of synapses.

There are several broad approaches. One is neuromorphic computing, which builds chips whose circuits are organized to behave like networks of neurons, often processing information in short electrical spikes rather than the continuous calculations used in conventional processors. Another is brain simulation, in which researchers use supercomputers to model the activity of neurons and their connections in detail, sometimes for a small part of the brain such as a cortical column or a fruit fly's neural circuitry. A third approach is the development of artificial neural networks in software, the machine learning systems behind modern image recognition and language models. These are loosely inspired by biological neurons, but they are mathematical abstractions rather than accurate copies of brain tissue.

Researchers pursue artificial brains for several reasons. They hope to build more energy-efficient computers, since the human brain runs on roughly 20 watts while comparable artificial systems can consume far more. They also want to understand how biological brains work by testing theories through simulation, and they hope to develop medical applications such as better brain-computer interfaces or treatments for neurological disease.

Despite impressive progress, true artificial brains that match human intelligence, consciousness, or the full complexity of biological neural tissue do not yet exist. Major challenges include our incomplete understanding of how the brain actually works, the enormous computing power required for realistic simulation, and difficulties in designing hardware that can learn and adapt the way biological systems do. The field therefore sits at the intersection of neuroscience, computer science, and engineering, and its goals range from practical technology to a deeper understanding of the mind itself.

The US government generally doesn't negotiate with terrorists, meaning it won't make deals with groups or people who use violence and intimidation to get what they want. Why? Mostly because caving can reward the behavior. If a group gets concessions through attacks, it has every reason to keep attacking. And other groups notice. Suddenly terrorism looks like a workable strategy, which is exactly what policymakers want to avoid.

There's also the practical headache. Figuring out who actually runs a group, or what they really want, is often murky. Even when a deal gets signed, it's hard to trust that the other side will stick to it. Put together, the policy is basically a signal: violence won't buy you a seat at the table, and it's meant to discourage others from trying the same thing.

Yoshua Bengio is a Canadian computer scientist widely regarded as one of the pioneers of modern deep learning, the branch of artificial intelligence that uses multi-layered neural networks to learn from large amounts of data. Born in France in 1964 and raised partly in Morocco, he later moved to Canada and built his career at the Université de Montréal, where he has long led research in machine learning. He is a professor there and founded the Montreal Institute for Learning Algorithms (MILA), which has become one of the world's leading centers for AI research.

Bengio is best known for foundational work in neural networks, particularly on sequence modeling, language models, and representation learning. His research helped lay the groundwork for many technologies that power today's AI systems, including speech recognition, machine translation, and large language models. Along with Geoffrey Hinton and Yann LeCun, he received the 2018 Turing Award, often described as the highest honor in computer science, for their contributions to deep learning.

In recent years he has also become a prominent voice on AI safety and governance. He has expressed concern about the risks of advanced AI systems, including misuse and loss of human control, and has called for careful regulation and research into safe development. He is one of the most cited researchers in computer science, and his views on these topics carry considerable weight in both academic and policy circles.

Yeah, you can totally catch a cold or the flu from someone with a runny nose and cough, especially if you're close to them or they sneeze or cough right on you. How bad it hits you and how likely it is to spread really depends on which virus or bacteria is going around and how you were exposed. With finals coming up, it's worth taking some precautions. Wash your hands often with soap and water; it really does cut down on germs. Try to avoid getting too close to sick people, and if you can't avoid it, aim for about 6 feet of space. Cover your mouth and nose when you cough or sneeze so you're not passing stuff along. If you'll be around a lot of people for a long stretch, a face mask can help too. And don't skimp on sleep or good food, since that keeps your immune system in better shape. If you're really worried about getting sick, though, a doctor or nurse is the best person to ask.

Raised readings of SGOT (serum glutamic-oxaloacetic transaminase) and SGPT (serum glutamic-pyruvic transaminase) may signal that the liver is damaged or diseased. Consulting a healthcare provider is essential to find out what is driving these elevated values and to begin suitable treatment. Among the common culprits are viral hepatitis, excessive alcohol consumption, and certain drugs. Adopting a wholesome diet and lifestyle can help bring these levels down. In terms of eating, aim for a balanced intake heavy in fruits, vegetables, and whole grains while keeping saturated and trans fats low. Steer clear of processed and fried items, since they often contain unhealthy fats and additives. Opt for lean protein such as chicken, turkey, fish, or plant-based options. Cut back on sugar and sweetened beverages, and keep well hydrated by drinking plenty of water. Abstaining from alcohol and exercising regularly are also important. If any medication you take could be contributing to the elevated enzymes, follow your doctor's directions on how to take it. Finally, comply with any further treatment or monitoring your doctor recommends.

Survival instinct is a built-in drive shared by people and animals alike, and it is what keeps us alive and out of harm's way. Yet at times individuals choose to set this drive aside and take actions that endanger them, such as giving up their lives for others or ending their own lives. Many factors can shape a person's decision to go against this instinct. Someone might feel a powerful loyalty or obligation toward others, or they might be enduring emotional anguish so severe that it feels impossible to bear. When a person sacrifices themselves for others, like throwing themselves onto a grenade to shield their fellow soldiers, they are often driven by a deep sense of duty or selflessness. They may conclude that saving their companions matters more than their own survival. When someone takes their own life, for instance by hanging, they may be in the grip of overwhelming emotional pain and feel that no other escape exists. Their feelings can seem to engulf them, leading them to believe death is the only way to end their suffering. These choices usually stem from complicated psychological and emotional forces, and they are rarely simple to comprehend or explain. If you or someone you know is wrestling with thoughts of self-harm or suicide, please reach out to a mental health professional or a trusted friend or family member.

Oral thrush is a fungal infection of the mouth and throat. Several things can bring it on, including some medications, among them inhaled corticosteroids such as Flovent. If you have developed oral thrush even though you have been using your Flovent inhaler as prescribed, you should talk to your healthcare provider, who can suggest the most suitable treatment for your circumstances. Meanwhile, a few home measures may ease the symptoms. Rinse with salt water: stir half a teaspoon of salt into 8 ounces of warm water and swish it around your mouth several times daily, which may lessen swelling and soreness. Run a humidifier: adding moisture to the air at home can relieve dryness in the mouth and throat, which may contribute to thrush. Steer clear of acidic or sugary foods: they can irritate the throat and aggravate thrush symptoms. Keep up good oral hygiene: brush twice daily with a soft-bristled toothbrush and floss every day to clear away food debris and plaque that could be irritating your mouth. Drink plenty of fluids: water, clear broths, and other beverages keep you hydrated, help keep your mouth moist, and guard against dryness. Keep using your Flovent inhaler as directed until your healthcare provider tells you to stop. If your symptoms fail to get better or become worse, contact your healthcare provider for further evaluation and treatment.

American football is a game between two teams of eleven players each, and the goal is to get an oval ball into the opposite team's end zone, which is the strip at each end of the field. Getting the ball there scores points. A touchdown, where you carry the ball into the end zone or catch it there, is worth six points. After a touchdown the team can try a kick through the tall yellow goalposts for one extra point, or run or throw it in for two. A field goal, kicked through the goalposts from farther away, is worth three.

The reason it feels confusing is that the game is broken into short plays, and each play is a little fight. The team with the ball is called the offense, and it gets four tries, called downs, to move the ball at least ten yards toward the end zone. If it succeeds, it gets four new downs. If it fails after the fourth try, it has to hand the ball over to the other team, usually by punting, which means kicking it far down the field so the other team starts farther from scoring. The defense is trying to stop the offense from gaining those ten yards and to take the ball away.

Each play starts with the two teams lined up facing each other, and the ball is snapped, meaning passed backward from the center to the quarterback, who is the team's leader on offense. From there the quarterback either hands the ball to a running back, throws it to a receiver, or runs with it himself. The offensive linemen, the big players in the middle, try to block the defensive linemen so the quarterback has time. The defense tries to tackle the ball carrier to the ground, which ends the play, and the spot where he ends up becomes the starting line for the next play.

That is why Madden feels so hard. The game is actually a series of puzzles: on every play, the offense picks a trick and the defense picks a counter, like guessing what the other person is going to do. The game is paused between plays so you can pick the next move, which is the part you are supposed to think about.

If you want an easy way to watch it, pick one game and just track the down number and the yards needed for a first down. Everything else is just players trying to push the ball forward ten yards at a time.

Unfortunately, I don't know of any programming changes at Discovery Channel or National Geographic. What you're noticing could just be a short-term change in the schedule, or it may be that your own viewing habits have shifted, making you more inclined to watch those kinds of shows. Another possibility is that your memory of the past isn't quite accurate, and these networks have always offered a blend of science-focused and other types of programs. To get a better sense of what these channels generally provide, I suggest sampling a wide range of their shows.

Good Friday is a Christian observance that remembers the crucifixion of Jesus Christ and his death at Calvary. It falls during Holy Week, on the Friday before Easter Sunday, and ranks among the holiest days of the Christian year. People in many countries around the world keep the day, typically with solemn ceremonies and church services. A lot of Christians treat it as a time of fasting, repentance, and prayer, and some attend special services or take part in devotional practices such as the Stations of the Cross, which involves meditating on the 14 events of Jesus' journey to the Cross. The day invites believers to reflect on the sacrifice Jesus made for the salvation of humankind and to recall the suffering and death he endured. It is also an occasion to think about the significance of forgiveness and the power of love to transform lives.

I'm sorry your granddaughter is going through this. Two weeks after a concussion, improving headaches are a good sign, but irritability, mood swings, and anxiety are common during recovery and deserve attention too. Please keep her doctor involved, since they should be following her recovery and can check whether her symptoms are on track.

Start by making sure she has a doctor's follow-up if one hasn't happened recently. A clinician can assess her symptoms, rule out complications, and advise on when it is safe to return to school and sports. Concussion recovery in teens often involves a gradual return to activity, and a doctor or a sports medicine specialist can guide that process step by step.

For the headaches, ask the doctor before she takes any pain medication. Ibuprofen and similar drugs are sometimes avoided in the early recovery period, and the doctor can tell you what is appropriate. Rest, hydration, regular sleep, and limiting screen time, bright lights, and loud noise often help. Many teens need a temporary reduction in schoolwork and screen use, so talk with her school about accommodations such as extra time on tests, reduced homework, or a lighter course load. Teachers are usually willing to help once they know about the concussion.

For the mood changes and anger, a few things can help. Keep her sleep and meals as regular as possible, since both strongly affect mood after a concussion. Give her space to vent without judgment, and let her know that irritability is a recognized symptom of a brain injury, not a character flaw. If the anger, anxiety, or low mood continue or get worse, ask her doctor about a referral to a counselor or psychologist. Cognitive behavioral therapy is effective for teens dealing with stress and worry, and some clinicians specialize in concussion recovery.

Her worries about grades and sports are understandable, and they can feed into the anger and stress. Reassure her that most teens recover fully from concussions, and that a careful return to sports, done under medical guidance, gives her the best chance of playing again. Setting small, concrete goals, like finishing one assignment a day or a short walk, can give her a sense of progress.

Seek medical care promptly if she has a severe or worsening headache, repeated vomiting, confusion, unusual drowsiness, trouble waking, slurred speech, weakness or numbness, or any thoughts of harming herself. Those signs need immediate attention, and if she ever talks about hurting herself, treat it as urgent and contact a crisis line or emergency services right away.

Imagine you're sitting in a car traveling at a steady speed around a circular track. Even though the speed never changes, you still feel a sensation of being pressed toward the middle of the circle. That happens because the car keeps turning as it moves around the track, so your body has to be pulled inward to follow that continual change in direction. The inward force responsible for this is known as centripetal force. Suppose the driver then wants to take the track faster. Doing so means raising the car's speed. If the speed goes up but the centripetal force stays the same, though, you'll feel yourself thrown outward against the door, since the turning force isn't strong enough to keep the car on its curved path. To go faster around the track, the driver must therefore increase both the car's speed and the centripetal force. That way, you still feel pulled toward the center, and the car moves more quickly. Does that make sense?

It depends on what the company is asking for and whether you're a business or a private customer. I don't know your exact situation or country, so here is the general picture, which is based mainly on UK-style VAT rules.

The VAT is owed to the tax authority, not to the company as a favour to you. If a supplier should have charged VAT and didn't, they are usually still liable for it, and they may try to recover it from you by issuing a supplementary invoice. But you generally aren't obliged to pay extra VAT just because they forgot to add it, unless your contract or the original terms say the price is exclusive of VAT and VAT is payable on top. Ask them to explain in writing exactly what they're claiming, why, and under which rule or contract term.

If you're a VAT-registered business, paying may be worth considering, because you can usually only reclaim input VAT with a valid VAT invoice. A correct invoice might therefore be useful to you, and the cost could be neutral in the end. If you're a private customer, you typically have less reason to pay, and you can reasonably push back, especially if the delay was the company's error and you were never told the price would change.

Before deciding, check the original invoice and contract, confirm whether the amount they want is correct, and find out whether the time limit for correcting the error has passed. If the sum is significant, a short consultation with an accountant or a VAT adviser is worthwhile, and HMRC's guidance or Citizens Advice can help if you're in the UK.

A lot of today's vehicles come with a smart key system, which lets the driver unlock and start the car without putting a key into the ignition. The driver only needs to have the smart key on their person, and they can open the doors and start the engine by pushing a button, either on the key itself or on the car.
