Hilary Putnam was a philosopher and mathematician whose work had a major impact on philosophy of mind, philosophy of language, and philosophy of science. Born in Chicago in 1926, he earned his undergraduate degree in mathematics at the University of Pennsylvania. Following his service in the U.S. Army during the Second World War, he completed a PhD in philosophy at Princeton University. Putnam is chiefly remembered for his philosophy of language and mind, where he contended that mental states and words are not private, inner items accessible only to their owner, but public and objective things that others can share and comprehend. He also contributed substantially to philosophy of science, especially on scientific realism and the character of scientific explanation. Over his long career he wrote prolifically and took part in many philosophical debates. He taught at several universities, among them Harvard, MIT, and the University of California, Los Angeles, and he was elected to the American Academy of Arts and Sciences. Putnam died in 2016.

A stop loss set at your purchase price is a common way to protect against losing money on a trade, but it works a little differently than many people expect. You place a stop order that triggers a sale if the price falls to your entry level. Once triggered, it typically becomes a market order, so you sell at whatever price is available at that moment, which may be below your purchase price if the stock gaps down or moves quickly. In a fast-moving market, the fill can be meaningfully worse than the stop price, so the result is not guaranteed to break even.

It is also worth remembering that a stop at your purchase price turns a position into a near-break-even trade rather than a profit-locking one. Many traders use this approach after a stock has risen, moving the stop up to the entry price so that a winning trade cannot turn into a losing one. Used this way, it limits downside while still letting the position run.

If you are considering this, check a few things first. Confirm whether your broker supports stop orders and whether it offers a stop-limit alternative, which sets a minimum sale price but risks not filling at all. Also consider normal price volatility: a stock that routinely swings a few percent may hit a stop at its entry price on ordinary noise and sell you out before the trade has had room to work. Setting the stop slightly below entry, or using a percentage or support level, can sometimes suit the stock better.

The ex-dividend date is the day when a stock begins trading without the right to the declared dividend attached to it. This means that anyone who purchases shares on or after this date will not be paid the dividend the company has announced for its shareholders. The payable date, by contrast, is when the dividend actually reaches the shareholders. The payable date can come before the ex-dividend date, because the ex-dividend date is tied to the record date, the cutoff the company uses to decide which shareholders qualify for the payment. Companies generally set the record date a few days ahead of the ex-dividend date so they have time to compile the list of eligible holders. Since the record date falls a few days before the ex-dividend date, the payable date may end up earlier than the ex-dividend date. I hope this clears things up. Feel free to ask if you have any other questions.

Mostly, yes, though it happens automatically rather than as a separate recalculation. On a standard amortizing loan, interest accrues each period on the outstanding principal balance. When you prepay, you reduce that balance, so all future interest is calculated on a smaller amount. The effect is the same as having borrowed a smaller sum or a shorter term. Your rate doesn't change. You either keep paying the same amount and finish early, or ask the lender to re-amortize so your payment drops while the end date stays the same.

There are two exceptions to check in your loan agreement. Some older or precomputed loans, particularly certain auto and consumer loans, calculate the total interest up front and allocate it across payments using a method like the Rule of 78s. With these, an early payoff saves less interest than a simple-interest calculation would, because much of the interest was front-loaded. Also, some loans carry a prepayment penalty, which can offset the savings.

To confirm how your loan works, look for the terms "simple interest" or "precomputed" in your loan documents, or ask the lender how a principal-only payment will be applied and whether there's a penalty.

When weighing whether to refinance a vehicle over a longer term while keeping some spare cash on hand, or to take a shorter term and simply stick to the scheduled payments, several considerations come into play. The first is the rate on the new loan. When that rate falls below what you currently pay, a longer term paired with extra cash set aside may end up saving money over time, since a lower rate means less interest paid across the loan's life, even on the same principal.

Your personal finances matter just as much. If you have spare funds and feel comfortable with heftier monthly payments, a shorter term with the regular payments could be the wiser route. It lets you clear the debt sooner and cut the total interest you pay. On the other hand, if your budget is stretched or you would rather keep monthly costs low, the longer term with a cash reserve may suit you better.

In the end, the right choice depends on your particular circumstances and objectives. Take the time to weigh each option carefully and run the numbers to see which one keeps the most money in your pocket over the long haul. Speaking with a financial advisor or loan officer can also provide guidance tailored to your situation.

Yes, a food allergy can cause itchy rashes on the arms, chest, and side. Hives (urticaria) are the most common form, and they typically appear as raised, red or skin-colored welts that can be itchy, may move around or change shape, and often fade within hours, though new ones can keep appearing. Foods like shellfish, nuts, eggs, milk, wheat, soy, and fish are common triggers, and so are medications and additives. Sometimes a food can also cause a reaction a few hours after eating, so the culprit may be something you had earlier today or yesterday. Stress, heat, infections, and other triggers can cause hives too, so a food isn't the only possibility.

Your description of a rash that spreads, shows up in several places, and comes and goes is consistent with hives. Whether it's from food or something else, a few things matter. Get medical care right away if you notice swelling of the lips, tongue, face, or throat, trouble breathing or swallowing, wheezing, dizziness, fainting, vomiting, or a feeling that your heart is racing. Those can signal anaphylaxis, which is an emergency, so call emergency services (911 in the US) immediately.

If you don't have those symptoms, it's still worth seeing a doctor or urgent care soon, especially if the rash lasts more than a day or two, keeps spreading, or comes back repeatedly. A doctor can examine it, consider your recent foods and medications, and may recommend an antihistamine or allergy testing. Until then, keep a short log of what you ate and drank in the hours before each outbreak, since that's often the most useful clue. Avoid scratching if you can, and an over-the-counter antihistamine like cetirizine or loratadine may help with the itch, though check with a pharmacist if you take other medicines.

Metal music is a broad genre that grew out of hard rock in the late 1960s and early 1970s, with Black Sabbath, Led Zeppelin, and Deep Purple often credited as its pioneers. What defines it most is sound: heavily distorted guitars, powerful and often fast drumming, thick bass, and vocals that range from soaring operatic singing to gritty shouting to guttural growls. Riffs, the repeated guitar phrases that drive a song, sit at the center of the style, and many metal musicians place a high value on technical skill, with fast solos and complex rhythms.

As for what it is about lyrically, the range is wide. Early metal drew on darkness, horror, war, and social unease, partly because Black Sabbath came from a gritty industrial English city. Since then, different subgenres have taken different directions. Heavy metal and power metal often lean toward fantasy, mythology, heroism, and epic storytelling. Thrash metal, which emerged in the 1980s with bands like Metallica and Slayer, tends to address political corruption, war, injustice, and personal anger. Death metal often explores violence, mortality, and gore, while black metal is associated with atheism, anti-Christian themes, nature, and isolation. Doom metal dwells on despair and grief, and progressive metal may take on philosophy or abstract concepts. Many bands also write about personal struggles, addiction, mental health, and alienation.

Beyond the lyrics, metal is also a culture. Fans tend to be loyal and form tight communities around concerts, festivals, and shared aesthetics like black clothing, band shirts, and long hair. Many people find the music cathartic, a way to process anger, sadness, or frustration in a controlled and even joyful setting. Despite its reputation for being menacing, the metal community is often described as welcoming and supportive, and the dark imagery is usually theatrical or expressive rather than literal.

If you want to explore it, a gentle path might be starting with classic acts like Black Sabbath, Iron Maiden, or Metallica, then branching out into whichever subgenre catches your ear.

Soap is a cleaning product created by combining fats or oils with an alkaline substance, such as lye. This chemical reaction, known as saponification, has been practiced for thousands of years. The earliest documented record of soap production comes from ancient Babylon, dating to about 2500 BC, though people almost certainly made soap well before that. Long ago, soap was typically produced by blending animal fats or plant oils with wood ash, yielding a mixture suitable for washing clothes and skin. Who first thought to heat animal and vegetable fats into soap is unknown, but the method probably emerged gradually through repeated trial and error. As people came to understand how different oils cleansed and softened skin, they likely tested various oils in their soap-making. Over time, they found that some oils performed better than others and began relying on those more often.

Rugby's pretty simple at its core: two teams of 15 players each, one oval ball, and the goal is to outscore the other side. Kickoff gets things going. One team kicks the ball to the other, who catches it and tries to run it back toward the far end. You can move the ball by running with it, passing it to a teammate, or kicking it ahead to someone.

Scoring happens when you get the ball over the other team's goal line and ground it there. That's called a try, and it's worth 5 points. After a try, the team gets a shot at kicking it between the posts for 2 more. If someone breaks a rule, the other side gets a free kick or penalty kick. The game's split into two halves, and whoever has more points at the end takes it. Hope that helps! Got any other rugby questions?

Object detection is a computer vision task in which a system identifies and locates objects of interest within an image or video. Unlike image classification, which only answers the question of what is in a picture, object detection answers both what objects are present and where they are. For each object it finds, the system typically outputs a bounding box, a rectangle that encloses the object, along with a class label such as "car," "person," or "dog" and a confidence score indicating how certain the system is about its prediction.

The task is challenging because objects appear in many sizes, orientations, lighting conditions, and positions, and they may be partially hidden or crowded together. A detector must handle all of these variations while also deciding how many objects are present, which can be zero or many.

Modern object detection is dominated by deep learning. Early approaches relied on hand-crafted features and sliding windows, but since the mid-2010s, convolutional neural networks have driven major advances. Two broad families of detectors exist. Two-stage detectors, such as the R-CNN family, first propose candidate regions that might contain objects and then classify and refine them. Single-stage detectors, such as YOLO and SSD, predict boxes and classes in one pass over the image, trading some accuracy for speed. More recently, transformer-based models like DETR have reframed detection as a direct set prediction problem.

Object detection is widely used in applications including autonomous driving, surveillance, medical imaging, retail inventory tracking, robotics, and augmented reality. It is often a foundation for further tasks such as object tracking, instance segmentation, and activity recognition.

IQ is basically a score from a standardized test meant to gauge things like problem-solving and critical thinking. Some folks argue that average IQ scores differ across racial groups because of genetics, but that claim doesn't hold up. There's no solid scientific evidence that race determines IQ. Most researchers think environment, schooling, and life experiences play a big role in the scores people get. Intelligence isn't locked in either. People can build their cognitive skills over time through learning and practice, whatever their background. So assuming someone's IQ is set by their race just isn't accurate.

Your symptoms, erection problems for two years, watery and reduced semen for four months, and an undescended testis, together deserve a proper medical evaluation, ideally with a urologist or andrologist (a specialist in male reproductive health). Some of this can be treated well, and the combination is worth checking rather than assuming one cause.

The first step is usually blood tests for testosterone, prolactin, thyroid function, fasting blood sugar or HbA1c (diabetes can damage erections), and lipids. A doctor will also want to know your medications and any use of alcohol, tobacco, or recreational drugs, since all of these affect erections. A semen analysis is important because watery semen with low volume can reflect inflammation of the prostate or seminal vesicles, an infection, a blockage, or problems with the ejaculatory pathway. A urine test and screening for sexually transmitted infections are reasonable to include. Because of your undescended testis, the doctor should examine your testes and may order a scrotal ultrasound and hormone levels such as FSH and LH. A history of undescended testis is linked to reduced sperm production and a somewhat higher lifetime risk of testicular cancer, so regular self-checks and follow-up matter, and the testis may need further assessment.

Regarding your sexual habits, frequent masturbation by itself rarely causes lasting erectile dysfunction or permanent changes in semen, and abstaining is not a treatment for these problems. However, if you have developed anxiety about performance, or if you feel you rely on masturbation in a way that bothers you, that is worth discussing. Anxiety and past sexual experiences are common contributors to erection problems in men your age, and psychosexual therapy or cognitive behavioral therapy works well for them. If there is tension in your relationship, couples counseling can also help.

Once the cause is clear, treatment options may include a PDE5 inhibitor such as sildenafil or tadalafil for erections, treatment of any infection or prostate inflammation with antibiotics or anti-inflammatory medicines, hormone correction if levels are low, and surgical or hormonal options for the testis if needed. Lifestyle changes help in any case: regular exercise, a healthy weight, good sleep, reduced alcohol, and stopping smoking.

Please see a doctor soon rather than waiting, and seek care urgently if you notice blood in your semen or urine, testicular pain or swelling, fever, a new lump, or pain during urination or ejaculation. Most of these conditions respond well to treatment, and a thorough evaluation will usually give you a clear plan.

Ten-year Treasury yields and mortgage rates move together mainly because both reflect the same underlying forces in the bond market, and because mortgages compete with Treasuries for the same pool of investors.

A 30-year fixed mortgage is a long-term loan, and the people who fund it, mostly large investors and government-backed entities, are constantly weighing it against other long-term, relatively safe investments. The 10-year Treasury is the most common benchmark for that comparison. If a lender can earn a certain yield on a 10-year government bond with essentially no default risk, it will demand a higher yield on a mortgage, which carries prepayment and default risk, before it will lend. So when Treasury yields rise, mortgage rates tend to rise with them, and when yields fall, mortgage rates usually follow.

Much of the mortgage market works through mortgage-backed securities. Lenders typically sell the loans they originate to investors, often through Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, or Ginnie Mae, which package them into bonds. Those bonds are priced against Treasuries, so their yields track Treasury yields closely. The rate a borrower is offered is essentially the yield investors require on those securities plus a spread covering the lender's costs and risks.

Both Treasury yields and mortgage rates also respond to shared expectations about inflation, Federal Reserve policy, and economic growth. Investors who expect higher inflation or stronger growth demand higher yields on long-term debt of all kinds, pushing both up. That shared sensitivity is why the 10-year Treasury is often cited as a useful guide to where mortgage rates are heading.

The link is not perfect. The spread between mortgage rates and Treasury yields widens and narrows with conditions such as market volatility, demand for mortgage securities, and changes in lender competition. In recent years that spread has been unusually wide at times, so mortgage rates have not always moved one-for-one with the 10-year yield.

"I think, therefore I am" is the famous line from the French philosopher René Descartes. People usually just call it the "Cogito," since "cogito" is Latin for "I think."

The idea is pretty simple. If you're thinking, you must exist. You can doubt pretty much everything else, like whether the world is real or whether your senses are fooling you, but you can't doubt that you exist, because doubting is a kind of thinking. Something has to be around to do the doubting in the first place.

So basically, the fact that you can think at all is proof you're there. Does that make sense?

Could be a hernia, honestly. Pain in the right groin when you're standing, or when you're talking in a higher voice than usual, fits with that. Hernias can cause pain, discomfort, or just a weird feeling of pressure down there. Standing and talking both bump up the pressure in your belly, and that can make the hernia push out more, so you notice it more at those times.

That said, it might not be a hernia at all. Something like a strained inguinal ligament or a pulled muscle can cause the same kind of pain and even a lump. Hard to tell from the outside.

I'd get it looked at by a doctor so you actually know what's going on and can get the right treatment. They'll probably do a physical exam, and they might send you for imaging if they can't tell from that alone.

So nitrites and nitrates are both compounds made of nitrogen and oxygen, and you'll find them in a lot of cured stuff like ham. They help preserve the meat and give it that particular cured flavor.

The main difference is just the oxygen count. Nitrites have two oxygen atoms, nitrates have three. Sounds tiny, but that one atom can change how they act in your body when you eat them.

For curing meat, nitrites are the ones doing the real work. Only a small amount is needed to keep the color and flavor in good shape. Nitrates aren't nearly as good at preserving meat, so they don't get used as much in the food industry.

So if the ham you bought lists nitrites, that's just the preservative that keeps it fresh and gives it its flavor.

Institutional racism describes the manner in which social institutions treat certain groups of people unfairly. It can appear in many shapes, and several American laws and policies have drawn criticism as examples. Drug laws, for instance, have been said to be enforced far more heavily against racial minorities, producing higher incarceration rates for those communities. Voter suppression is another concern: measures such as voter identification requirements or the purging of voter rolls have been faulted for falling hardest on racial minorities and complicating their ability to cast ballots. Immigration policies, including detention and deportation practices, have likewise been criticized for weighing disproportionately on racial and ethnic minority groups. Finally, redlining, a practice once common among banks and other financial institutions, involved refusing loans or financial services to residents of certain neighborhoods because of their racial or ethnic composition. It helped entrench racial segregation and made it harder for people of color to obtain credit and financial opportunities.

There is no single fixed dollar amount. The answer depends on the jurisdiction, and in the United States, which is the most common context for this question, the rules changed significantly in recent years. Under the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017, businesses generally lost the ability to deduct entertainment expenses entirely, so a corporation can spend as much as it likes on entertainment, but the cost is not deductible for federal income tax purposes. Before 2018, corporations could deduct 50 percent of qualifying entertainment costs, subject to the requirement that the expense be ordinary, necessary, directly related to or associated with the active conduct of the business, and not lavish or extravagant under the circumstances.

Even where the expense is not deductible, the company should still track it carefully. Meals with clients, for example, generally remain 50 percent deductible if they meet the business meal rules, and the separate categories of entertainment, meals, and gifts each have their own treatment. Gifts to any one individual are generally limited to a deduction of $25 per year. Companies should also be mindful of internal policies, shareholder expectations, and any applicable rules for employees, such as fringe benefit treatment for employee entertainment, which can create taxable income for the recipients.

Other countries have their own limits. Some tax systems cap deductible entertainment at a percentage of revenue or a set amount, and some disallow it entirely. If you tell me the country and the type of expense you have in mind, I can give you a more specific answer. For a definitive ruling on a particular situation, a tax professional should be consulted.

Candida is a yeast that normally lives in the body in small quantities. Certain conditions, however, can allow it to multiply excessively, resulting in an infection called candidiasis. The signs of candidiasis depend on where the infection occurs. Common symptoms include a rash, redness, or itchiness in the affected area; white, thick, or lumpy discharge (with vaginal candidiasis); painful urination (with a urinary tract infection); blisters in the mouth (with oral thrush); and itching around the rectum. People with candidiasis also frequently report fatigue, muscle aches, and irritability. Regarding the use of probiotics to address candidiasis, this is generally considered safe. Nevertheless, anyone with herpes should speak with their healthcare provider before taking probiotics or any other dietary supplement, since some probiotics can interact with medications or aggravate certain health conditions. Consulting a healthcare professional before beginning any new treatment is always the wisest course.

A digital image is a representation of a visual scene or picture stored as numerical data that a computer or other electronic device can process, store, transmit, and display. Unlike a traditional photograph, which records light on chemical film or paper in a continuous way, a digital image breaks the scene into a finite grid of tiny elements and assigns numbers to each one.

The most common kind is the raster image, sometimes called a bitmap. It is made up of a rectangular array of picture elements, or pixels. Each pixel holds a value describing its brightness or color. In a grayscale image, a single number per pixel indicates how light or dark it is, often on a scale from 0 (black) to 255 (white) when 8 bits are used. In a color image, each pixel usually carries several numbers, commonly red, green, and blue components in the RGB model, which combine to produce a wide range of colors. Other color models exist too, such as CMYK for printing or HSV for certain editing tasks. The number of bits used per pixel, called bit depth, determines how many distinct shades or colors can be represented.

Resolution describes how much detail an image holds. It is often given as the pixel dimensions, such as 4000 by 3000, or as pixels per inch when relating the image to a physical size. More pixels generally allow finer detail, though they also mean larger files.

The other major type is the vector image, which does not store individual pixels but instead describes shapes using mathematical definitions such as points, lines, curves, and fills. Because these instructions can be recalculated at any size, vector graphics scale without losing sharpness, which makes them well suited to logos, icons, and technical illustrations.

Digital images are created in several ways. Cameras and scanners use sensors, such as CCD or CMOS chips, that convert light into electrical signals which are then digitized. Images can also be generated entirely by software, as in digital painting, 3D rendering, or computer-generated graphics. Medical scanners, satellites, and microscopes similarly produce digital images from other kinds of measurements.

Because raw image data can be very large, images are often compressed and saved in file formats. JPEG uses lossy compression, discarding some information to shrink files considerably. PNG and GIF use lossless methods that preserve every pixel exactly, and TIFF is popular in professional and archival work. SVG is a common vector format.

The digital nature of these images allows easy copying without degradation, editing, enhancement, analysis, and sharing. It also underpins fields such as computer vision, medical imaging, remote sensing, and photography, where algorithms can filter, sharpen, recognize patterns, or extract measurements from the numerical data.

COMPAS, which stands for Correctional Offender Management Profiling for Alternative Sanctions, is a proprietary risk assessment software developed by Northpointe, a company later renamed Equivant. It is used in parts of the United States criminal justice system to estimate the likelihood that a person accused or convicted of a crime will reoffend (commit another crime) or fail to appear in court. The software generates risk scores, typically on a scale from one to ten, by analyzing answers to a lengthy questionnaire covering topics such as criminal history, age, employment, education, family background, substance use, and attitudes. Its outputs are intended to assist judges, parole boards, probation officers, and corrections staff in making decisions about bail, sentencing, parole, and supervision levels, though the software is meant to supplement rather than replace professional judgment.

COMPAS has drawn significant public attention and criticism since 2016, when the investigative news organization ProPublica published an analysis of its scores in Broward County, Florida. ProPublica reported that the software was more likely to incorrectly label Black defendants as high risk when they did not go on to reoffend, and more likely to label white defendants as low risk when they did later reoffend. Northpointe disputed these findings, arguing that the scores were equally accurate across racial groups when measured by a different standard, namely whether a given score predicted the same probability of reoffending regardless of race. This disagreement sparked a broader debate among researchers about the mathematical impossibility of satisfying several fairness criteria at once when base rates of reoffending differ between groups.

Beyond the fairness debate, COMPAS has been criticized for its lack of transparency, since its underlying algorithm is a trade secret and defendants often cannot examine how their scores were calculated. Critics also question whether the tool generalizes well across jurisdictions and whether judges place excessive trust in numerical scores. Some courts, including the Wisconsin Supreme Court in State v. Loomis (2016), have allowed its use while requiring that judges be warned about its limitations, whereas other jurisdictions have restricted or reconsidered its role. The controversy around COMPAS has become a prominent example in discussions about algorithmic decision-making, bias, and accountability in the justice system.

The stock market is a marketplace where people trade shares of stock in publicly traded companies. Purchasing a share means acquiring a small slice of ownership in that business; owning a single share, for instance, gives you a very tiny piece of the company. Stocks can be traded in several ways, but one of the most popular is opening a brokerage account, which works much like a bank account except that it is designed for buying and selling securities. To set one up, you select a brokerage firm and complete its application process, which typically means filling out forms and perhaps supplying identification. Once the account is open, you can place trades through the firm's website or mobile app. Buying a stock is essentially a wager that the company will perform well over time. If it does, and the share price rises, selling can produce a gain. If the company struggles and the price falls, however, you could end up losing money. Keep in mind that investing in stocks is risky, and you should be ready for the possibility of losses. It is also wise to conduct your own research and speak with a financial advisor before committing your money.

A husband-and-wife LLC has a federal tax choice that affects whether Form 7004 applies at all. By default, an LLC with two members is treated as a partnership, so it must file Form 1065 each year. If the couple needs more time to file that return, they file Form 7004 by the original due date, which is March 15 for calendar-year filers. The extension moves the deadline to September 15, giving six more months to file. The extension covers only the filing deadline, not payment, so any tax owed at the owner level still needs to be paid by April 15.

Spouses in a community property state (Arizona, California, Idaho, Louisiana, Nevada, New Mexico, Texas, Washington, Wisconsin, or Alaska if they opt in) may instead elect under Revenue Procedure 2002-69 to treat the LLC as a disregarded entity. Under that election, the business reports on Schedule C or Schedule F and Schedule SE like a sole proprietorship, and no Form 1065 is filed. In that case Form 7004 is not needed, because there is no partnership return to extend. Couples who do not qualify for or do not choose that election must file the 1065.

Form 7004 does not extend the owners' personal returns. Each spouse's Form 1040 is still due April 15 and needs a separate extension on Form 4868 if more time is needed. Because the partnership's K-1s feed into those personal returns, the couple should keep the 1065 timing in mind when planning. The LLC's state filing requirements may also differ from the federal rules, so it is worth checking those separately.

La Palma is not in Africa. The name usually refers to La Palma, one of the Canary Islands, a Spanish archipelago in the Atlantic Ocean off the northwest coast of Africa. It lies roughly 100 kilometers west of Morocco and the Western Sahara, and it belongs to Spain even though it is geographically close to the African continent. If you meant a different place called La Palma, such as a town in Panama or a locale in Colombia, let me know and I can tell you more about it.

So the range of a function is basically just the set of every output it can spit out. You've got a function f(x), you feed it x, and whatever comes out is f(x). The range is all the f(x) values you get as x runs through the domain. Take f(x) = x^2. Whatever you plug in, the result can't be negative, so the range is all non-negative reals.

You can also write the range as an interval on the number line. If you restrict f(x) = x^2 to x in [-3, 3], the outputs stay between 0 and 9, so the range is [0, 9]. Pretty straightforward once you see it.

People also use "range" for something a bit looser: the set of values a variable is allowed to take. If x can only be 1, 2, or 3, then the range of x is {1, 2, 3}.

A coordinate measuring machine, or CMM, is a computer-controlled measuring machine that checks the physical dimensions of manufactured parts and assemblies. It's basically a precision probe sitting on a movable platform, and the platform's position gets tracked by linear and angular encoders, so the machine can map out an object's geometry very accurately. Factories use them all the time for quality control, mostly to make sure parts actually hit their tolerances and match the design. You'll also see them in R&D labs and reverse engineering work, anywhere someone needs solid measurements of a physical object.

Gibraltar is a small rocky peninsula at the southern tip of Spain, and Britain has held it since 1713, when it was handed over under the Treaty of Utrecht. Britain's reasons for keeping it go beyond the wishes of the people who live there.

The most important reason is location. Gibraltar sits right at the entrance to the Mediterranean Sea, where the water narrows to a strait only about 13 kilometres wide between Europe and Africa. Whoever controls that spot can watch and guard the route between the Atlantic Ocean and the Mediterranean. During the age of sailing, and again in the two World Wars, this made it a key stopping point for warships and merchant ships. Britain has a large naval base and airfield there, and the Royal Navy has long used it to keep an eye on the sea.

Gibraltar also gives Britain a foothold in the region for trade and military planning. Ships can refuel, repair, and resupply there, and its harbour has been important for commerce for centuries.

It is also a symbol. For many British people, holding Gibraltar is a sign of their country's long history as a naval and imperial power, and giving it up would be seen as a loss of pride.

Finally, the British government has said it will not transfer sovereignty without the consent of Gibraltar's people. Under the 1967 referendum and later laws, the population has repeatedly voted to stay British, so the UK has treated that choice as a deciding factor.

In medical diagnostics, two key metrics, sensitivity and specificity, are used to assess how well a diagnostic test works. Sensitivity is the share of truly positive cases that the test picks up. Put simply, it measures how well a test can detect people who actually have a given disease or condition. When sensitivity is high, the test catches most individuals who are ill, whereas a test with low sensitivity overlooks a substantial number of those cases. Specificity, by contrast, is the share of truly negative cases that the test correctly labels as negative. It reflects how reliably a test clears people who do not have the disease. A test with high specificity will rightly clear most healthy individuals, but one with low specificity will wrongly flag many people as sick when they are not. Both measures matter because a highly sensitive test will identify most real cases, while a highly specific test will correctly rule out most cases where the disease is absent. A test that performs well on both counts is regarded as dependable and accurate.

Lots of things can cause a lump under the armpit. The most common is a swollen lymph node. Those are small, bean-shaped bits of your immune system, and they swell up when you've got an infection or some kind of inflammation going on. It could also be a cyst, which is basically a closed sac filled with fluid, pus, or other gunk. Cysts can pop up pretty much anywhere and are usually harmless, often from a blocked gland or duct. Another option is a hematoma, which is just blood that's leaked out of a damaged vessel and pooled under the skin. Those usually come from a bump, a knock, or even a recent procedure.

That said, you really should get it looked at by a doctor or other provider so they can figure out what's going on and whether it needs treatment. They'll probably examine it, ask about your history and any recent injuries or infections, and might order a blood test or imaging if they need more info.

Hilary Putnam was a philosopher and mathematician who did a lot of important work in philosophy of mind, philosophy of language, and philosophy of science. He was born in Chicago in 1926 and got his undergrad degree in math at the University of Pennsylvania. After serving in the U.S. Army during World War II, he earned his PhD in philosophy from Princeton. He's best known for his work on language and the mind. He argued that mental states and linguistic expressions aren't private, subjective things locked inside your head. They're public and objective, something other people can share and understand. He also had plenty to say about science, especially scientific realism and what makes an explanation scientific. He wrote constantly and jumped into all sorts of debates. He taught at a bunch of schools, including Harvard, MIT, and UCLA, and he was a member of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences. Putnam died in 2016.

Stocks and high-yield bonds (often called junk bonds) both sit on the riskier end of the investment spectrum compared with Treasuries or investment-grade bonds, but they carry different kinds of risk and reward, and the tax treatment can meaningfully change which one makes more sense for you.

On risk and reward, stocks represent ownership in a company. Their returns come from earnings growth, dividends, and changes in valuation, so they have historically delivered higher long-run returns, roughly 9 to 10 percent annualized for the broad U.S. market over the last century, though with severe drawdowns such as the 50 percent or more declines seen in 2008 and 2000 to 2002. Stockholders are residual claimants, meaning they are paid last if a company fails, and their outcomes are highly variable. High-yield bonds are loans to companies rated below investment grade, typically yielding several percentage points above Treasuries, often in the 6 to 9 percent range depending on the market environment. Their upside is capped at the coupon and principal, so the best case is limited, but they are senior to stock in the capital structure and pay predictable interest. Their main risk is default, which tends to rise in recessions, and in default they often recover only part of their face value. Historically, high-yield bonds have been less volatile than stocks but more volatile than investment-grade debt, and they tend to fall alongside stocks during economic stress, so they offer less diversification than many investors expect.

Taxes are where the comparison gets more nuanced. Qualified dividends from stocks and long-term capital gains are generally taxed at preferential federal rates of 0, 15, or 20 percent depending on income, plus a possible 3.8 percent net investment income tax at higher incomes. Stock held in a taxable account also gives you control over timing, since you can defer gains indefinitely by not selling. High-yield bond interest, by contrast, is taxed as ordinary income at your marginal rate, which can be as high as 37 percent federally, plus state tax in most places. Bond funds also often distribute income and short-term gains that are taxed in the year received, even if you reinvest them. Because of this, high-yield bonds are frequently better held in tax-deferred accounts such as traditional IRAs or 401(k)s, while stocks, particularly those paying qualified dividends or held for long-term growth, are often more efficient in taxable accounts. Municipal bonds are not a substitute here, since most high-yield munis are rare and carry their own liquidity and credit concerns, though some investors do use them in high tax brackets.

In practice, the after-tax comparison depends on your bracket, account type, and time horizon. A high-yield bond yielding 7 percent may deliver only about 4.5 to 5 percent after tax in a high bracket held in a taxable account, which narrows the gap with stocks considerably. Holding high-yield bonds in tax-advantaged accounts and stocks in taxable accounts is a common approach that captures the tax advantages of each. As always, the right mix depends on your personal circumstances, and a tax professional or fee-only advisor can help you model your specific situation.

I'm sorry you're dealing with this. Pain and swelling in the perineum (the area between the scrotum and anus) that comes on after masturbation and lasts a few hours can have several causes, and it's worth getting it properly evaluated, especially since your doctors haven't yet found the cause.

Since you've already seen doctors without a result, the most useful next step is usually a urologist, a doctor who specializes in the male genital and urinary system. If you can, tell them exactly what you told me: the pain is in the area between the scrotum and anus, it feels like swelling, it lasts two to three hours after masturbation, and the scrotum turns red during the episodes. Describing the timing carefully often helps narrow things down. A general practitioner can refer you, and if the area is painful to touch, a proctologist or colorectal specialist can check the anal and perineal region, since the pain sits close to that area.

Some possibilities your doctor may want to check include friction or irritation from lubricants, soaps, or rough handling, a small skin problem such as an infected hair follicle or cyst, a pelvic floor muscle that tightens and aches with repeated ejaculation, prostate inflammation (prostatitis), or a hernia or varicose vein in the groin or scrotum. Sexually transmitted infections can also cause this kind of pain, so testing may be part of the workup even if you feel well otherwise.

While you wait for an appointment, you can reduce irritation by using gentle, unscented soap, avoiding lubricants that irritate, letting the area rest between sessions, and applying a cold pack wrapped in cloth for 10 to 15 minutes if it feels swollen.

Seek care urgently, the same day if possible, if you notice severe or rapidly worsening pain, fever, a lump that is hard or very tender, blood in the urine or semen, pain when urinating, trouble passing urine, or swelling that spreads or doesn't go down. Those signs need prompt attention.

A credit rating is basically a grade for how likely someone is to pay back what they owe. It can apply to a person, a company, or a government. Independent companies called credit rating agencies usually hand these out after looking at the borrower's risk. Lenders and investors lean on them a lot, since they give a quick sense of how risky it is to lend money or buy debt from a given borrower. A high rating usually means the borrower is unlikely to default and will probably pay on time. A low rating flips that: more risk, and a real chance they might miss payments. Ratings are typically shown as letters, with "AAA" at the top and "D" at the bottom. Exact systems differ from agency to agency and depend on what kind of borrower is being rated, so don't assume every scale looks the same. Also, ratings aren't set in stone. If someone keeps paying their debts reliably, their rating can climb. If they start struggling with payments or hit money trouble, it can drop.

Finding the value of British Energy Nuclear Power Notes depends first on working out exactly what instrument you hold, because the name is not a standard security title. British Energy was the UK nuclear generator that restructured in 2002 and was bought by EDF in 2009. During the restructuring, creditors received a package that included new bonds issued by British Energy plc (often called the new bonds or the Nuclear Liabilities Fund-linked entitlements), plus shares. If your notes are old paper certificates, they may be pre-restructuring Eurobonds that were exchanged in 2005 and have no current value except as collectibles.

Start by checking the certificate or statement for an ISIN, CUSIP, or SEDOL code, the issuer name, the coupon, and the maturity date. With an identifier you can search on the London Stock Exchange site, Bloomberg, Morningstar, or the Financial Times markets data. If the identifier returns no active listing, the bond has probably matured, been redeemed, or been cancelled.

Next, contact the registrar or the broker that holds the notes. For UK securities, the registrar may be Computershare or Equiniti. Companies House records for British Energy Limited and EDF Energy filings can also tell you what happened to the debt. If the holding is old and forgotten, the UK Unclaimed Assets Register or the Gretel service can help trace it, and the registrar can tell you whether any redemption proceeds went unclaimed.

If the notes are still outstanding and traded, value them using the latest market price from a broker or data provider, multiplied by the face amount held, plus accrued interest. If they are illiquid, ask a bond dealer for an indicative quote, or estimate value by discounting the remaining coupons and principal at a yield comparable to similar-rated debt. EDF-guaranteed or EDF-related paper would be priced off EDF credit spreads.

If the notes are collectible certificates, value comes from the scripophily market. Auction sites such as eBay, and specialist dealers in historic share and bond certificates, show what comparable items sell for, usually modest sums.

If you tell me what is printed on your notes, such as the issue date, coupon, and any codes, I can help narrow down what they are and the best route to a valuation. For a significant holding, a financial adviser or a bond broker can give a formal valuation.

Imagine every house in a giant city has a number painted on it, like 4827-1193. That number is how the mail carrier actually finds the house. But nobody wants to remember a big jumble of numbers for every friend they want to visit. You'd much rather say "I want to go to Grandma's house."

Computers on the internet are like those houses. Each one has a number address, called an IP address, something like 142.250.80.46. Your computer needs that number to find the website you want. But you don't type numbers. You type a name like google.com, because names are easy for people to remember.

DNS is the helper that turns the name into the number. When you type google.com, your computer basically asks, "Hey, where does Google live?" and DNS answers, "Google lives at 142.250.80.46." Then your computer goes to that number, and the website shows up.

The part that trips people up is that there isn't one single giant phone book. The internet is too big for that. It's more like asking around a neighborhood. Your computer first asks a helper nearby, usually run by your internet provider. If that helper doesn't know, it asks a big boss helper that knows where all the ".com" addresses are kept. That one says, "I don't know Google's exact house, but go ask the .com helper." The .com helper says, "Go ask Google's own helper." And Google's own helper finally gives the exact number. It's like asking a grown-up, who asks the mayor, who points you to the right street, where someone tells you the exact house.

Because all that asking takes a little time, everyone along the way remembers the answer for a while. This is called caching. So the next time you visit Google, your computer or the nearby helper already knows the number and doesn't have to ask the whole chain again. That's why websites usually load quickly after the first visit.

So the simple version is this: you know the name, the computer needs the number, and DNS is the friendly helper that asks around until it finds the number for you.

Railguns fire metal projectiles using electromagnetism, and the whole trick is that a big electric current running through the rails pushes the projectile down the barrel. So you need a serious power source. Most of the railgun videos you've seen use large capacitors, which can hold a huge charge and dump it all at once. You could also hook one straight into a wall outlet, since that's a steady supply of electricity. The problem is that railguns pull a ton of current and throw off a lot of heat, and the wiring in most homes and buildings isn't built for that kind of load. Plug one in that way and you could fry the wiring or start a fire. That's why people use capacitors or other special power setups instead. They're built to handle the massive current and heat, and they're a lot safer.

Weighing the tax consequences before buying any security or asset usually makes good sense, since taxes can meaningfully reduce what you ultimately earn. Whether investing in a security based in a country that does not tax dividends is the better choice depends on many things, including your own tax circumstances and the particulars of the investment. If you live in a country that taxes dividends, a security from a jurisdiction with no dividend tax may let you retain a larger share of your income. That said, the full tax picture needs careful review, because other levies may apply, such as capital gains taxes or taxes on interest. The rules on dividends and other investment income also differ widely between countries, so you should look into the specific laws of any country where you plan to invest. Finally, speaking with a tax professional or financial advisor can help you make well-informed investment decisions.

The 2001 Chevrolet Monte Carlo came with two engine options. The base model used a 3.4-liter V6 (the L82 in most trims), producing about 180 horsepower. The Monte Carlo SS, the performance trim, had a 3.8-liter V6 (the L36) rated at roughly 240 horsepower. Both were paired with a four-speed automatic transmission.

I'm sorry you're dealing with this. Pain and fullness in the lower left abdomen that spreads to the back deserve a prompt medical evaluation, especially given your history of diverticulosis. Pringles crisps are produced by combining potatoes, corn flour, and various other components, which are then processed and molded into the recognizable Pringles form. During the preparation of the potatoes for this blend, some tiny fragments may be left over. Because these fragments are usually too small or irregularly shaped for the Pringles manufacturing line, they do not end up in the finished snack. Rather, such leftover bits are commonly repurposed as livestock feed or fertilizer.

Within biology, the term family refers to a rank in taxonomy. A family consists of related organisms that have certain traits in common and are placed together inside a broader group, such as an order or a class. In the system used to classify living things, families sit below the order and above the genus. Members of a family are usually defined by a shared set of features or characteristics. The family Felidae, for instance, contains every species of cat, including lions, tigers, and house cats. The family Canidae covers all species of dog, among them wolves, foxes, and domestic dogs. The family Rosaceae takes in plants like roses, apples, and strawberries. Grouping organisms into families is useful because it lets scientists recognize and examine the relationships among different sets of organisms. It also offers a means of sorting and arranging organisms so that they can be studied and discussed more easily in science.

A mechanical calculator is a device that carries out arithmetic using physical parts like gears, levers, and dials instead of electronic circuitry. These machines were the earliest calculators ever built, appearing several centuries before electronic versions existed. Their first use dates to the early 1600s, and their popularity grew steadily through the 1800s and into the early 1900s. People relied on them for many kinds of computation, such as adding, subtracting, multiplying, and dividing. Most were run manually, often with a crank or lever that rotated gears or other components to produce a result. Electronic calculators, which rely on circuits and electronic parts, eventually took over their role. Even so, a few mechanical calculators remain in use for teaching purposes or are valued by collectors.

Ayn Rand was a writer who believed that the best way to live is through reason, purpose, and self-interest. Her core idea is objectivism, which holds that reality exists independently of our wishes, that we can understand it through our minds, and that each person should live for their own happiness and not sacrifice themselves for others or for society's demands. She believed that creative and productive people, the ones who build and invent things, are the heroes of human life, and that a free society lets them do their work without being held back. Her books explore these ideas through characters who choose to stand up for what they believe, even when everyone around them disagrees.

In The Fountainhead, the main character is Howard Roark, an architect who designs buildings his own way and refuses to compromise his vision to please critics or clients. The story follows his struggles and his refusal to bend, and it treats his independence and integrity as the highest virtues. Atlas Shrugged is a much bigger book about a group of talented business leaders, inventors, and thinkers who grow tired of a society that punishes them for their success and expects them to hand over their achievements to others. They withdraw from the world in a hidden valley to show what happens when the people who make things stop working. The book is about the value of individual genius and the cost of a world that treats it as something to take away.

Since you've read The Anthem, you may notice the same themes: a single person who thinks for himself, a rejection of group thinking, and a belief that the individual mind is the source of progress.

Honestly, I can't give you medical advice, so the best move is to see a dermatologist about the pigmentation. They can look at your skin and figure out what makes sense for your case.

Which one's right for you really depends on your skin, so that's a conversation for the doctor.

Several things might explain why high blood pressure fails to improve with treatment. Your husband should talk with his healthcare provider to pinpoint the exact cause and decide on the right approach for his situation. Possible reasons for resistant high blood pressure include the following.

Incorrect use of medication: Blood pressure drugs need to be taken exactly as a healthcare provider prescribes. If your husband is not following the directions, that may be keeping his blood pressure high.

Underlying conditions that have not been diagnosed or properly controlled: Illnesses such as kidney disease, sleep apnea, or an overactive thyroid can raise blood pressure. If he has any of these, treating them may be necessary to bring his numbers down.

Stress: Stress can push blood pressure up, so finding healthy ways to cope with it is important.

Lifestyle habits: Eating a lot of salt, getting little exercise, and using tobacco can all raise blood pressure. Changing these habits may help reduce it.

Your husband should stick to the treatment plan his healthcare provider recommends and make whatever lifestyle changes are needed to lower his blood pressure. If it stays high even with treatment, his provider may switch him to other medications or alter the doses of the ones he already takes.

The Navier-Stokes equations are a collection of mathematical relations that govern how fluids, including liquids and gases, move. The name honors the French engineer and physicist Claude-Louis Navier and the Anglo-Irish scientist George Gabriel Stokes. These equations capture the connections between a fluid's velocity, pressure, and other characteristics, along with how each of them evolves over time. Engineers and scientists apply them to forecast fluid behavior across many fields, such as aerodynamics, weather prediction, and the design of airplane wings and engines, and they also help explain blood circulation in the body and the movement of seas and rivers. Their foundation lies in the conservation laws for mass, momentum, and energy. Mathematically, they form a system of coupled partial differential equations that has to be solved all at once to reliably describe fluid motion. Finding these solutions is difficult, and it remains a vibrant topic of study in both mathematics and engineering. Even with their broad use and significance, many features of fluid dynamics are still poorly understood and continue to be investigated.

A flame is what you see when something is burning, and it's actually a kind of gas that is glowing hot. Think about a candle. The wax near the wick melts, then turns into a vapor, which is a gas. That gas mixes with oxygen from the air, which is the part of the air that burning needs. When the gas and oxygen get hot enough, they react together very quickly, and that reaction releases energy as heat and light. The glowing, hot gas is the flame you see dancing above the candle.

Here's a fun way to picture it: a flame is a little party of tiny bits of gas that are so excited they give off light. The energy that was stored up in the wax, or in wood, or in a gas stove's fuel, gets set free in the form of that light and warmth. That's why a flame needs three things to keep going: fuel to burn, oxygen to mix with it, and enough heat to keep the party started. Take away any one of them and the flame goes out. That's why blowing on a candle works, since you blow the heat away, and why putting a lid on a pan can smother a grease fire, since you cut off the oxygen.

So the short answer for a curious eleven-year-old is this: a flame is hot, glowing gas, made when fuel and oxygen combine fast enough to release energy as heat and light.

Online referral systems reward existing customers or users for bringing in new ones. The basic idea is simple: a person who already uses a product or service shares it with someone they know, and when that friend signs up or buys, both parties, or sometimes just the referrer, receive a benefit such as a discount, credit, free months, or cash.

The mechanics usually work through a unique link or code. When a company enrolls a user in its referral program, the system generates a personal identifier, often embedded in a URL or a short promo code like "SARAH20." The user shares this link by email, text, social media, or word of mouth. Tracking software, typically using cookies, URL parameters, or the code entered at checkout, records that the new visitor came from that specific referrer. If the visitor completes the qualifying action, such as creating an account, making a first purchase, or staying subscribed past a trial period, the system credits the referrer's account and often gives the new customer an incentive as well.

Many programs are designed with safeguards. Companies set conditions like minimum purchase amounts, expiration dates on rewards, caps on how much a person can earn, or waiting periods before a reward becomes available. They also try to prevent fraud, such as people referring themselves with fake accounts, by checking things like device identifiers, email domains, payment details, and patterns of suspicious activity.

From the business side, referral systems are attractive because they bring in customers who are often more likely to stay, since a personal recommendation carries trust. The company pays only when a referral actually converts, which makes the cost easier to control than traditional advertising. Popular examples include ride-sharing apps offering credit for each friend who takes a first trip, cloud storage services giving extra space for invitations, and subscription platforms offering free months to both the referrer and the new subscriber.

Broadcast television stations are eager to reach larger audiences and earn more advertising income, yet they must also weigh what it costs to make their programming available online. Delivering video over the internet demands substantial bandwidth, and that can add up to a significant expense for a station. Moreover, many stations have agreements with cable and satellite companies that pay the stations to carry their signals. Offering the same content for free on a station's website or a streaming platform could breach those agreements and jeopardize that income. Stations may also restrict streaming to guard against piracy. When content is easy to access online, it becomes harder to stop unauthorized copies from spreading across the internet. Limiting where and how content appears gives stations greater control over its distribution. Overall, broadcasters aim to strike a middle ground: reaching as many viewers as possible while safeguarding their material and keeping revenue strong.

Our brains and stomachs are linked through what is known as the gut-brain connection. When strong emotions arise, the brain can pass signals to the stomach, producing sensations we can physically feel. Sadness or anxiety, for instance, may leave us with a "knot" in the stomach, while embarrassment or regret can create a "sinking" sensation there. Such feelings result from changes that take place in the body whenever we go through intense emotions. They are simply one way our bodies react to what is happening around us.

You can find S&P 500 historical data from several free and paid sources. FRED, the economic database run by the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis, also carries S&P 500 index series, which are useful if you want to combine market data with economic indicators. Biologists study living things and the processes that keep them going. You'll find them in research labs, field stations, hospitals, and government agencies. Some are chasing basic questions about how life works, while others take that knowledge and build new products, treatments, or technologies that people actually use. Day to day, a biologist might run experiments to test an idea and collect data, crunch the numbers and figure out what they mean, write up reports or papers, work with other scientists, teach and mentor students, advise policymakers on science issues, or keep an eye on natural resources like forests, wetlands, and wildlife habitats. Many focus on a particular area such as genetics, evolution, ecology, or physiology, depending on what grabs them. Others zero in on a specific group of organisms, whether that's plants, animals, or microbes.

A strawman argument is when someone argues against a version of what another person said that is easier to beat, instead of the actual thing they said. It's called a strawman because it's like setting up a scarecrow made of straw and then knocking it down, pretending you've defeated a real opponent.

Here's a simple example. Imaybe your friend says, "I think we should have a little more homework time on weekends." You reply, "So you want us to never have any fun and to work all the time?" You've twisted what your friend said into something extreme and then argued against that exaggerated version. Your friend never said they wanted no fun at all, so you haven't really answered their actual idea.

So yes, you can call it a strawman argument or just a strawman. Both mean the same thing. People use it when someone misrepresents another person's point to make it look weaker or sillier than it really is.

You can usually find the complete list of open bids and asks for a stock on a stock exchange or via a brokerage platform. Exchanges generally present this information in what is known as an "order book," which lists every pending order for a given security. For each entry, the order book gives the bid or ask price along with the number of shares available at that price. Customers who hold an account with a brokerage may be able to see the full set of open bids and asks through the firm's trading platform or website. Certain brokerages also offer real-time streaming quotes, which may show the bids and asks for a stock together with the latest trade price and trading volume. Keep in mind that an order book or quote stream can shift quickly, since orders are constantly being submitted, canceled, or executed. For that reason, the data you see may not always be current or fully complete.

When you change the volume on your television, you are really changing how strong the sound is that comes out of the speakers. The volume control lets the TV raise or lower the amount of electrical power sent to the speakers, and that is what makes the sound get louder or quieter. Pressing the "up" button on the remote or on the TV itself tells the set to send more electricity to the speakers, so the sound becomes louder. Pressing "down" does the opposite: it instructs the TV to send less electricity, and the sound becomes softer. The TV can produce a range of volume levels, and it determines whether to step up or down based on the signal it gets from the remote or the buttons on the set. Because it can adjust in small steps, you can fine-tune the volume to suit you. I hope this is helpful! Feel free to ask if you have any other questions.

It isn't really accurate to say that home internet is "priced by speed" while mobile data is "priced by amount." The truth is that these are two separate kinds of services, usually sold by different kinds of companies, and each is priced in its own way. With home internet, providers commonly sell a series of speed tiers at different prices, and the quicker tiers tend to cost more. Higher speeds let you do more online, such as watching high-definition video or playing online games, both of which need a large amount of data to move in a short span of time. Mobile data plans, by contrast, are usually priced according to how much data you are allowed to use in a month. That is because wireless carriers must pay to operate the networks that connect your phone to the internet, and they have to recover those expenses. The more data customers use, the more it costs the carrier, so heavier usage means a higher bill. In short, the distinction isn't simply that internet is priced by speed and phones by data. These services are used in different ways and cost different amounts to provide, and that is why their pricing differs.

He's also a Fellow of the ACM, the IEEE, and the American Association for Artificial Intelligence.
