Things that should not be done include making him vomit, giving him anything to neutralize the acid such as baking soda, vinegar, or lemon juice, giving him activated charcoal, or forcing him to drink water or milk. These can cause further harm.

If you are not sure whether he is receiving appropriate care, you can call your local poison control center or emergency number and ask to speak to the treating team. Continued vomiting of blood is an emergency, so it should be reported to the doctors immediately if it is not already being managed.

I'm sorry you're feeling this way, and I believe you. You know your body, and what you're describing deserves to be taken seriously. Feeling unwell since a bad IUD infection in October, with a tender abdomen, night sweats, chills, body aches, a rash, and cuts that won't heal, is not something to manage with home remedies. It needs to be looked at by a doctor, and soon.

An IUD infection can sometimes spread into the uterus, fallopian tubes, or pelvis (pelvic inflammatory disease) or form an abscess that lingers for months if it wasn't fully cleared. A temperature of 96.5 may seem reassuring, but an unusually low temperature together with sweats, chills, pain, and feeling "not myself" can sometimes mean the body is struggling with an infection. Slow-healing cuts can also point to things like blood sugar problems or a weakened immune response, which a simple blood test can check. A rash on top of all this is another reason to be seen in person rather than wait.

Please go to an emergency room today if you notice any of the following: abdominal pain that is getting worse or becoming severe, a fever above 100.4 or a temperature that keeps dropping, a racing heart, fast breathing, dizziness or fainting, confusion, a rash that spreads quickly or looks like purple or dark spots that don't fade when pressed, unusual vaginal discharge or bleeding, vomiting that stops you keeping fluids down, or simply feeling much worse. If none of these apply, try to get an urgent care or same-day doctor appointment rather than waiting weeks.

Since you feel no one has been listening, it helps to go in prepared. Write down a short timeline starting with the IUD infection in October: what treatment you got, whether the IUD was removed, and how you've felt since. List every symptom, including the sweats, chills, rash, slow healing, and abdominal tenderness. Take photos of the rash in case it changes. You can say directly, "I had a serious IUD infection in October and I haven't been right since. I'm worried the infection never fully cleared, and I'd like a pelvic exam, blood work including a blood count, inflammation markers, and blood sugar, and possibly a pelvic ultrasound." Bringing a friend or family member as support can also help you be heard.

Until you're seen, rest, drink plenty of fluids, and eat small, simple meals if you can. Acetaminophen (Tylenol) or ibuprofen, taken as directed on the package, can ease the aches and headache, but they may also hide a fever, so note your temperature before taking them. Keep any cuts clean and covered. Please don't take leftover antibiotics or try to treat this yourself, because the right treatment depends on finding the cause.

You are not overreacting. Ongoing symptoms after a pelvic infection are a real medical concern, and you deserve answers. Please reach out for care today, and if the first place doesn't take you seriously, it's okay to go somewhere else or ask for a second opinion.

Yes, in Canada you can generally deduct hobby expenses up to the amount of hobby income, but the rules are a bit more specific than that. Under the Income Tax Act, an activity that is a hobby (one carried on without a reasonable expectation of profit) is not a business, so its losses cannot be deducted against your other income such as employment income. Instead, the Canada Revenue Agency allows you to deduct hobby expenses only against income from that same hobby, and only to the extent that the hobby generated income in the year. In practice, this means your expenses can offset the hobby income, bringing the net to zero, but they cannot create a loss that reduces your other income.

Some points to keep in mind. Hobby income is generally reported as "other income" on your return, and the related expenses are claimed in a way that limits them to that income. Expenses you can't deduct in the current year because they exceed the income generally cannot be carried forward to future years, which is a key difference from a business, where non-capital losses can be carried back or forward. There are also certain items, such as capital cost allowance on property used in the hobby, that follow their own rules and may be restricted.

Whether an activity is a hobby or a business depends on the facts, including the intention to earn a profit, the way the activity is carried on, the time and effort invested, and its history of profits or losses. If you have a particular situation, especially one involving significant expenses or a possible business classification, it's worth confirming the treatment with the CRA guidance or a tax professional.

A spoiler mounted at the back of a front-wheel drive car serves to lower lift and build up downforce over the rear axle. Doing so improves grip and steadiness, particularly when travelling quickly. A wing fitted to the nose of the car might achieve something comparable, though the result would hinge on the wing's particular shape and on how it works together with the rest of the body. Still, wings and spoilers are typically found at the back rather than the front, since the rear end generally tends to suffer more lift owing to how the vehicle's weight is spread out.

Your stomach and your feelings are connected through your nervous system, kind of like a phone line running between your brain and your belly. Your brain has a part that handles big feelings, like being scared or sad. When you feel those strong feelings, that part sends messages down the line to your tummy.

Your belly has its own little group of nerves, so it can feel things and react on its own, too. When those messages arrive, the muscles in your stomach can tighten up, squeeze, or move differently, and your body may make less or more of the juices it uses to digest food. That's why you might feel fluttery, queasy, or like you have a knot in there.

Your body also has a "get ready to run or hide" system. When you feel upset, it can slow down or speed up things in your belly to save energy for other jobs. Long ago, that helped people survive scary moments, but now it just makes your tummy feel funny when you're sad or sorry about something.

So your tummy turns because your brain is talking to it, and it's listening closely to how you feel.

Self-determination theory (SDT) is a theory of human motivation and personality about how our basic psychological needs connect to well-being and mental health. The basic idea is that people have an innate drive to grow and develop, and that the social and physical environments around us can either help that along or get in the way. SDT names three basic needs. Autonomy is feeling in control of your own life and making choices that fit your values and goals. Competence is feeling effective and capable at the things you do. Relatedness is feeling connected to and supported by other people. When these needs get met, people tend to feel better, with more positive emotions and better mental health. When they don't, things tend to go the other way, with more negative emotions and mental health problems. You'll find SDT applied in plenty of places, like schools, healthcare, and workplaces, usually as a way to understand and boost well-being.

Spain took the 2010 World Cup, which was hosted in South Africa from June 11 to July 11. They beat the Netherlands 1-0 in the final on July 11, and it took extra time to get it done. That was Spain's first World Cup title ever, and it was also the first time a European team had won the thing on African soil.

It's hard to say what's going on without seeing it in person, honestly. A few things could cause a swollen inner cheek that's peeling and sore. An oral infection is one possibility, like a staph infection or thrush. You might also be having an allergic reaction to something you ate or touched, which can cause swelling and irritation. Physical trauma is another common one, like accidentally biting your cheek. And if your mouth is really dry, the skin can get swollen and start peeling.

I'd get a doctor or dentist to take a look so you know what you're dealing with and can get the right treatment. Meanwhile, a warm saltwater rinse can help keep things clean and calm the inflammation, and you might want to skip spicy or acidic foods for a bit so you're not irritating it more.

Labeled data refers to data that has been tagged, or annotated, with a class or category. In other words, every item in the dataset is given a label that states what it depicts or which group it falls into. A collection of animal images, for instance, could carry labels like "cat," "dog," or "bird" to identify the animal shown in each picture. Such data is commonly used to train machine learning models, since the labels give the model a means of learning how different data points relate to one another and of making predictions about new data that has no labels. Here, the labels serve as the "ground truth" for the model, enabling it to learn to classify fresh data points correctly according to their features. Labeled data may be produced by hand, with people annotating the data, or it may be created automatically through methods such as data preprocessing or data augmentation. To train a high-quality machine learning model, it is important to have a large and varied collection of labeled data.

The words "bourgeois" and "bourgeoisie" refer to members of the middle class, and they are frequently applied to people who are focused on earning money and acquiring property. Yet they can also carry an insulting meaning, implying that a person is materialistic, self-absorbed, and disconnected from the everyday worries of ordinary people. This negative sense stems from the notion that the middle class cares more about defending its privileges and social standing than about contributing to the welfare of society at large.

A frozen or numb feeling on one side of the body that lasts about 20 minutes, especially at your age, needs prompt medical attention, even though it has gone away. The most important possibility is a transient ischemic attack (TIA), often called a "mini-stroke." This happens when blood flow to part of the brain is briefly blocked, and the symptoms can resolve completely within minutes to an hour. A TIA is a warning sign that a full stroke may follow, so it should be evaluated quickly, typically within 24 hours.

Other possible causes include a migraine with aura, since some people have sensory or numbing symptoms before or without a headache. Your history of right-sided migraines makes this a consideration, but because your migraines stopped at 65, a new episode at 71 should still be checked rather than assumed to be migraine. Other possibilities include a brief seizure, low blood sugar, or, less commonly, a problem with a nerve or the neck rather than the brain.

Please see your doctor soon, ideally today or tomorrow. They will likely examine you, check your blood pressure, heart rhythm, and blood sugar, and may order a brain MRI or CT scan, an ultrasound of the neck arteries, an ECG, and heart rhythm monitoring, since irregular heartbeat can cause clots. Tell your doctor exactly what you felt, how it started, and how long it lasted.

Call 911 right away if you have any of these symptoms, even if they seem to be getting better: sudden weakness, numbness, or drooping on one side of the face, arm, or leg; trouble speaking or understanding speech; sudden vision loss or double vision; loss of balance or coordination; or a sudden severe headache. Do not drive yourself. Note the time when any symptoms start, because treatment for stroke works best when given quickly.

I'm sorry you're dealing with this from so far away. Worrying about someone you love when you can't be there is hard, and your concern is reasonable. Weeks of severe nosebleeds along with nausea, dizziness, and sensitivity to light and sound deserve a proper medical workup.

Several things could explain this combination, and many are far more common than leukemia. Afghanistan's dry air, dust, smoke, and high altitude in many areas often cause repeated nosebleeds by drying and cracking the blood vessels inside the nose. The light and sound sensitivity, nausea, and dizziness, however, point strongly toward something affecting the brain, and in a deployed service member one of the first things doctors think about is a concussion or mild traumatic brain injury. Blast exposure, even from a distance and even without being knocked out, can cause exactly these symptoms, and many soldiers don't realize a blast affected them. Migraines can also cause light and sound sensitivity, nausea, and dizziness. High blood pressure, which stress, poor sleep, and energy drinks or supplements can worsen, can cause both nosebleeds and headaches with dizziness. Frequent ibuprofen, common among deployed troops, makes bleeding easier. Significant blood loss from repeated nosebleeds can itself cause dizziness and lightheadedness.

Blood disorders, including leukemia or low platelets, can cause nosebleeds that are hard to stop, usually along with easy bruising, tiny red or purple dots on the skin, bleeding gums, unusual fatigue, paleness, fevers, night sweats, frequent infections, or weight loss. About your family history: most leukemias are not strongly inherited, so his father's leukemia raises his risk only modestly, and the absolute risk stays low. Still, it's worth mentioning to his doctors, and the good news is that a simple, inexpensive blood test called a complete blood count (CBC) can detect most signs of leukemia and other blood problems. That test is available at nearly every military medical facility, including many deployed ones.

The most useful thing your husband can do is ask his medical providers directly for a CBC, a blood pressure check, and a concussion or TBI evaluation. He should tell them about his father's leukemia, describe how long his nosebleeds last and how much they bleed, and mention any blast exposure or head impacts, however minor. Asking for specific tests often moves things faster than describing symptoms generally. If he isn't getting answers, he can ask to be seen by a higher level of care or raise it with his chain of command.

From home, you have options too. His unit's Family Readiness Group or rear detachment can relay concerns and help you understand what's happening. Military OneSource can guide you through the system, and if you truly feel his care is being neglected, your congressional representative's office handles military constituent concerns and can sometimes move things along. The American Red Cross is mainly for emergency communication but can help in serious situations.

He should seek urgent care right away if a nosebleed won't stop after 20 to 30 minutes of firm pressure, if he faints, has a severe sudden headache, confusion, slurred speech, weakness or numbness, vomiting that won't stop, or chest pain or trouble breathing.

Most likely this has a treatable explanation, but pushing politely and persistently for basic tests like a CBC is the right instinct, and it's the fastest way to either catch something serious early or put your mind at ease.

Public companies may hold off on secondary stock offerings for a few reasons. First, these offerings can be costly, since companies usually need to hire investment banks to underwrite them and must also pay legal and other expenses. That expense can weigh heavily on a firm, particularly when it has no urgent need for more capital. Second, issuing new shares spreads ownership across a larger number of shares, which reduces existing shareholders' stakes. This is especially troublesome if current shareholders oppose dilution, or if the share price has dropped considerably since the previous offering, leaving investors with less value per share. Third, timing matters. If the broader stock market is struggling or investors have little interest in new issues, a company may decide to wait for better conditions before proceeding. Finally, firms may have other ways to raise money, such as bank loans or debt issues, which they can pursue instead of selling new stock. Overall, secondary offerings are a useful way for companies to raise capital, but they are not always the best choice in every circumstance.

Defined contribution and defined benefit pension plans are two distinct kinds of retirement arrangements that employers may provide to their workers. In a defined contribution plan, both the worker and the employer put a set sum of money into the plan at regular intervals. The worker's share typically comes out of their paycheck, while the employer's share usually takes the form of a matching contribution. Retirement income under this kind of plan depends on the amounts deposited, along with whatever returns those deposits earn through investment. A defined benefit plan, by contrast, is one in which the employer promises the worker a particular monthly payment once they retire. That payment is generally calculated from factors such as the worker's salary, length of service, and similar considerations. The employer alone funds the plan and manages its investments, making sure enough money is available to cover the promised payments when they come due.

Each type of plan has advantages and drawbacks. Defined contribution plans give workers greater command over their retirement savings, since they can decide how their contributions are invested. Yet this freedom also brings added risk, because the size of the eventual retirement benefit rises and falls with how the investments perform. Defined benefit plans provide the reassurance of a guaranteed payment, but they offer less authority over investment choices and less flexibility than defined contribution plans do.

Dubai's a city in the United Arab Emirates, which sits in the Middle East on the Arabian Peninsula. The UAE shares borders with Saudi Arabia to the south and west and with Oman to the east. Abu Dhabi is the capital, and Dubai is just one of the seven emirates that make up the country. People mostly know Dubai for its sleek modern skyline, big-name shopping, and nightlife that never really slows down.

Dextromethorphan lozenges are hard to find now, but you can get similar relief from other options. You're right that slow dissolution matters, since a lozenge coats the throat for a long time. Many cough drops work this way even without a cough suppressant.

Several lozenges are widely available. Those with menthol or eucalyptus, such as Halls, Ricola, or Vicks VapoCool, soothe irritation and make coughing feel less urgent. Lozenges with benzocaine or phenol, such as Cepacol or Chloraseptic, numb the throat and are useful when the cough is raw or painful. Honey-based or pectin-based drops also coat the throat, and plain honey in warm tea is well supported for cough relief in adults and children over one year old.

If you want a suppressant that works like dextromethorphan, you can use dextromethorphan in liquid or gel form. Delsym and store-brand dextromethorphan syrups are long-acting and widely sold. If your cough is wet or congested, guaifenesin (Mucinex or store brands) thins mucus, and it is often more useful than a suppressant in that case.

A few cautions apply. Check labels for duplicate ingredients, since many cold products already contain dextromethorphan or acetaminophen. Dextromethorphan should not be combined with MAOI antidepressants. Ask a pharmacist if you take other medications, have heart, liver, or kidney problems, or are giving medicine to a child. See a doctor if the cough lasts more than three weeks, comes with high fever, causes shortness of breath or chest pain, or coughs up blood or discolored mucus that persists.

Lending and borrowing between individuals generally falls outside the body of rules that governs loans made by banks and other financial institutions. Even so, certain legal principles can come into play depending on the particulars of a given arrangement. Suppose one person lends money to another and collects interest: that arrangement may fall under state usury statutes, which cap the rate of interest a lender may legally charge. Should the borrower fail to repay as promised, the lender can also generally pursue a lawsuit to recover the outstanding amount. Finally, these arrangements can carry tax consequences, which depend on the type of transaction and how much money changes hands. When a person lends a substantial sum and earns interest in return, that interest may be taxable income. Anyone with questions about the tax side of personal lending or borrowing would be wise to consult a tax professional.

Afghan cooking draws on both Middle Eastern and Central Asian traditions. Among its typical staples and dishes are the following. Rice is a cornerstone of the cuisine and usually accompanies the main course. Naan, a flatbread widely eaten across Afghanistan, is commonly served alongside meals. Kebabs are another favorite, consisting of grilled meat, most often lamb or chicken, and presented with either rice or naan. Bolani is a flatbread stuffed with vegetables such as potatoes, onions, or leeks, and it is typically accompanied by yogurt or chutney. Ashak consists of boiled dumplings packed with a filling of leeks and ground beef, topped with a yogurt sauce. Qabili palaw is a rice dish cooked with lamb and frequently decorated with raisins and carrots. Aush is a soup containing noodles, meat, and vegetables, often served with a side of yogurt. Finally, Afghanistan produces a wide range of fresh fruits and vegetables, such as melons, grapes, pomegranates, apples, apricots, and tomatoes, which appear in many local recipes or are simply enjoyed as snacks.

When Pluto was found in 1930, it was labeled a planet because astronomers believed it resembled the other planets of our solar system in both size and makeup. As our knowledge of Pluto grew, and as more objects were spotted in the distant outer regions of the solar system, scientists came to see that Pluto differs quite a lot from the other planets. A key reason it was demoted to dwarf planet status is its size, since it is far smaller than the planets around it. Worlds such as Earth and Mars measure thousands of kilometers across, whereas Pluto spans only about 2,377 kilometers (1,475 miles). Pluto's path around the Sun also sets it apart. The other planets travel along orbits that are fairly close to circular, but Pluto's orbit is far more stretched out and inclined. As a result, Pluto frequently lies much farther from the Sun than the other planets do, and a single trip around the Sun takes it considerably longer. Given its small size and unusual orbit, scientists chose in 2006 to reclassify Pluto as a dwarf planet. In other words, it remains a celestial body that circles the Sun, but it is no longer regarded as a full planet like the eight others in our solar system.

Okay so Spades is a trick-taking card game for four players. You use a standard 52-card deck, ranked Ace high down to 2. Players sit across from their partner, making two teams. Everyone gets dealt 13 cards, and the leftover cards just sit out the game.

The player to the left of the dealer leads off with any card they want. Everyone else has to follow suit if they can. If you can't, you're free to play whatever you like. Highest card of the suit led takes the trick and leads the next one, but if a spade gets played, the highest spade wins it instead. Keep going until all 13 tricks are gone.

Scoring is a bit fiddly. Your team gets points for tricks taken, and the other team picks up points for certain cards they've won in their tricks. Most games go to 500 points, and the first team there wins. Also, plenty of house rules float around, so the exact details can shift depending on who you're playing with.

Remastering an old movie basically means taking the original film or video and cleaning it up so it looks decent on modern screens. It works for movies shot on actual film and for ones originally recorded on video. If you want a high-def version like Blu-ray, you first need to track down the best source you can find. That could be an original film print or a digital copy someone made from the film.

Once you've got the best version, you deal with scratches, dust, and other damage. Special software can pull out a lot of those blemishes and sharpen things up. After that, the movie needs to go digital. You'd scan the film into a computer or convert the existing digital file into a different format.

Now that it's digital, you can tweak it a lot more. Color correction is a big one, getting the colors looking right instead of faded or yellowed. Some people also add effects to make it feel more modern, though that's a bit more controversial. Last step is converting it to a high-def format like Blu-ray, then either burning it to a disc or putting it up for streaming. Hope that makes sense! Let me know if you've got more questions.

Several factors could explain why your follicular study isn't showing the growth you were hoping for, even though you're undergoing IUI (intrauterine insemination). One possibility is ovarian dysfunction, which may stem from hormonal imbalances, a natural drop in fertility with age, or particular medical conditions that interfere with how the ovaries work. Another is a weak response to medication: some people don't respond well to certain fertility drugs, such as the ovitrop HP 75 injection, and this can hold back follicle development. Abnormalities of the uterus or cervix may also make it harder to conceive. Finally, lifestyle habits like overexercising, ongoing stress, and an unbalanced diet can influence both fertility and follicle growth. The best step is to speak with your fertility specialist, who can identify the exact reason growth is lacking in your situation and go over suitable treatment options. They might change the dose or the type of medication you're using, or they may propose different fertility treatments altogether.

A defibrillator (the word is often misspelled "defibulator") is used when someone is in cardiac arrest with a heart rhythm that can be corrected by an electric shock. The person will be unresponsive, not breathing or only gasping abnormally, and have no detectable pulse. In that situation you should call emergency services, start CPR, and use the device as soon as it is available.

The two rhythms a defibrillator can treat are ventricular fibrillation, where the heart quivers chaotically instead of pumping, and pulseless ventricular tachycardia, where it beats too fast to pump blood effectively. You don't need to identify these yourself. An automated external defibrillator, or AED, analyzes the heart rhythm after you attach the pads and only delivers a shock if one is appropriate. It will say "no shock advised" if the rhythm isn't one it can treat, and it won't let you shock someone who doesn't need it.

Anyone can use an AED, including people with no training, because the devices give clear voice instructions. The basic steps are to turn it on, expose the chest, attach the pads as shown in the pictures (one on the upper right chest, one on the lower left side), let the device analyze, make sure nobody is touching the person, and press the shock button if prompted. Then resume CPR right away until help arrives or the person starts to move or breathe normally.

There are a few practical points. Do not use one on someone who is conscious, breathing normally, or has a pulse. If the chest is wet, dry it first, and if there is a lot of chest hair, shave or clip the pad area if a razor is provided. Move the person away from standing water, and remove any medication patches from the pad area. For children under about eight, use pediatric pads if available; if not, adult pads can be used, placed on the front and back of the chest so they don't touch. Pacemakers or implanted devices just mean placing the pad a few centimeters away from the bump under the skin.

Speed matters a great deal, since survival chances drop roughly 7 to 10 percent for each minute without defibrillation, so don't hesitate if you suspect cardiac arrest.

Pressure or tightness in the chest when you laugh is most often caused by the muscles and cartilage of the chest wall. Laughing involves forceful, repeated contractions of the diaphragm and the muscles between your ribs, and a few days of coughing can strain or irritate those same muscles and the cartilage joining your ribs to your breastbone. Inflammation of that cartilage (costochondritis) is a common cause of this kind of pressure, and it tends to worsen with deep breaths, laughing, or coughing.

Your dry cough deserves attention too. A lingering cough can be due to a viral infection or bronchitis, and inflammation of the lining of the lungs or chest wall (pleurisy) can cause pain that gets worse with deep breathing and laughing. Less commonly, a small collapsed lung or a blood clot in the lung can cause chest pain with breathing, so the pattern matters.

Your occasional smoking and drinking are worth mentioning to a doctor, since they can irritate the airways and affect heart and lung health, but they aren't likely to explain a sudden new symptom on their own.

Chest pain is hard to judge without an examination, so please seek emergency care right away if you have pressure that spreads to your arm, jaw, neck, or back, or if it comes with shortness of breath, sweating, nausea, dizziness, fainting, a racing or irregular heartbeat, coughing up blood, a fever, or swelling or pain in one leg. Call emergency services if the pressure comes on at rest or doesn't go away.

If none of those apply, it's still sensible to see a doctor within the next day or two, especially since the symptom is new and your cough has been going on for several days. They can listen to your lungs and heart and, if needed, order a chest X-ray or other tests to rule out anything serious.

Chest pain plus an itchy lump on your back could have a bunch of different causes, and honestly I can't tell which one it is without more info and someone actually examining you. If your chest pain is severe or you're having trouble breathing, don't wait on this: head to the ER right away. If it's milder, or the lump is just annoying rather than painful, your primary care doctor or a dermatologist can take a look. Make sure you tell them about any other symptoms you've got and every medication you're on, since that stuff can really help narrow things down. And don't try to tough it out or treat it yourself if something's worrying you. Get it checked.

A millwright is a skilled tradesperson who installs, maintains, and fixes industrial machinery and equipment. You'll find them working on conveyor systems, pumps, motors, and generators, and they often handle machine tools and other manufacturing gear too. Most spend their days in factories or power plants, though some end up in other industrial settings. The job can be tough. You might be squeezed into a confined space, working at height, or dealing with rough conditions. Tools range from basic hand tools to power tools and precision measuring instruments. You need a solid grasp of mechanical and electrical systems, plus good problem-solving skills and an eye for detail. Being able to read blueprints and technical drawings helps a lot. Some millwrights also pick up formal training or certification in areas like welding or pneumatics, depending on the work they want to do.
Orono's a town in Penobscot County, Maine. That's where you'll find it.

A button-down shirt is a style of shirt featuring buttons on the front placket and at the collar points, which let the collar be fastened flat. These shirts are usually crafted from cotton or a cotton blend, and they fall somewhere between casual and semi-formal in dress code. People commonly pair them with trousers or jeans, and they can be styled up or down to suit the occasion. Because they work in so many settings, from a day at the office to a relaxed weekend outing, button-down shirts remain a timeless and adaptable piece of any wardrobe.

World Trade Center 7 (WTC 7), a 47-story office tower in New York City, came down on September 11, 2001, after a fire had burned inside it for several hours. Debris from the Twin Towers, which terrorists had crashed hijacked planes into earlier that morning, set the fire off. No conspiracy was behind the collapse; instead, it resulted from the blaze combined with the structural harm the building had already suffered.

In simpler terms, falling wreckage from the Twin Towers hit the outside of WTC 7 and started fires on several floors. Those fires raged for hours, weakening and warping the steel beams and columns holding the structure up. Once the metal could no longer carry the building's weight, the upper floors began to give way. Each floor then dropped onto the one beneath it, a chain reaction that eventually brought down the whole building.

Notably, WTC 7 was not brought down by a controlled demolition, an idea some conspiracy theorists have put forward. The damage and fire were what caused it to fall. Engineers and scientists have examined the collapse in depth, and their conclusions match the explanation given here.

The cross-entropy method is a general-purpose Monte Carlo technique for solving two closely related kinds of problems: estimating the probabilities of rare events, and finding good solutions to difficult optimization problems. It was introduced by Reuven Rubinstein in 1997, originally as an adaptive way to do importance sampling for rare-event simulation. It was later recognized as a simple and effective method for both combinatorial and continuous optimization. Its name comes from the cross-entropy, or Kullback-Leibler divergence, a measure of how different two probability distributions are, which the method uses to update its sampling distribution.

The core idea is to treat optimization as a problem of learning a probability distribution. Suppose you want to find the input that maximizes some objective function, and the function is too complicated, noisy, or non-differentiable for gradient-based methods. The cross-entropy method keeps a parameterized probability distribution over candidate solutions, such as a multivariate Gaussian for continuous problems or a set of independent Bernoulli probabilities for binary problems. It repeats a simple loop. First, it draws a batch of random samples from the current distribution. Second, it evaluates the objective function on each sample. Third, it keeps the best-performing fraction, often called the elite samples, for example the top 10 percent. Fourth, it refits the distribution's parameters to those elites. Over many iterations, the distribution concentrates more tightly around high-performing regions of the search space, and ideally it collapses onto an optimal or near-optimal solution.

The connection to cross-entropy comes from how the parameters are updated. Ideally, you would want your sampling distribution to match the unknown distribution concentrated on the good solutions. The method chooses new parameters that minimize the cross-entropy between that ideal target, approximated by the elite samples, and the parameterized family. For common families such as Gaussians or Bernoulli distributions, this minimization has a closed-form answer that amounts to maximum likelihood estimation on the elites. With a Gaussian, for instance, you simply set the new mean and covariance to the sample mean and sample covariance of the elite points. In practice people often add smoothing, blending the new parameters with the old ones, to keep the distribution from collapsing too quickly onto a suboptimal point.

In its original rare-event setting, the goal is to estimate a very small probability, such as the chance that a communication network fails or a financial portfolio suffers an extreme loss. Plain simulation is hopeless because the event almost never occurs in the samples. Importance sampling fixes this by sampling from a different distribution under which the event is common and then reweighting the results. The difficulty is choosing a good alternative distribution. The cross-entropy method finds one adaptively. It gradually raises a threshold over several iterations so that the rare event is approached in stages, and at each stage it updates the sampling parameters by minimizing cross-entropy with respect to the optimal, zero-variance importance sampling distribution.

The method is popular because it is easy to implement, needs no gradients, handles noisy objectives reasonably well, and has few tuning parameters: mainly the sample size, the elite fraction, and the smoothing factor. It has been applied to the traveling salesman problem, graph partitioning, scheduling, neural network training, and especially reinforcement learning and robotics. In model-based control, for example, it is often used to search for good action sequences by sampling candidate trajectories from a model. Its main limitations are that it can converge prematurely to a local optimum if the distribution shrinks too fast, it may need many function evaluations, and simple distribution families can struggle in very high-dimensional or highly multimodal spaces. It belongs to the same broad family as estimation-of-distribution algorithms and evolution strategies such as CMA-ES, all of which improve solutions by iteratively reshaping a search distribution.

I'm glad you reached out, because at 71 any new or unusual sensation involving one side of the head deserves prompt medical attention, even if it went away on its own.

A "frozen" or numb feeling on one side of the head can have several causes. Since you have a history of right-sided migraines, one possibility is a migraine aura without headache. Some people whose migraine headaches fade with age still get the aura part later in life, sometimes called "late-life migrainous accompaniments." These episodes often last 15 to 60 minutes, which fits what you describe. Other possibilities include irritation of a nerve in the scalp or face, circulation changes, or, less commonly, a small seizure.

The most important possibility to rule out, though, is a transient ischemic attack (TIA), often called a mini-stroke. A TIA happens when blood flow to part of the brain is briefly blocked. Symptoms go away completely, usually within minutes to an hour, which can make it easy to dismiss. But a TIA is a serious warning sign: the risk of a full stroke is highest in the days right after one. Your age, and the fact that this has happened more than once, make it especially important to get checked. A TIA and a migraine aura can look very similar, and a doctor can't safely tell them apart without examining you and possibly doing tests such as a brain scan, an ultrasound of the neck arteries, a heart rhythm check, and blood work.

My advice is to contact your doctor today and describe exactly what happened, or go to an urgent care or emergency department if you can't be seen quickly. Tell them it was a one-sided frozen feeling lasting about 20 minutes, that it has happened once or twice before, and that you have a history of right-sided migraines. It also helps to mention any other symptoms you noticed during the episodes, even subtle ones. These might include numbness or tingling in your face, arm, or leg, weakness, trouble speaking or finding words, vision changes, dizziness, or confusion. Bring a list of your medications and any conditions like high blood pressure, diabetes, high cholesterol, or heart rhythm problems.

If the feeling comes back and doesn't go away, or if you ever experience sudden weakness or numbness on one side of the body, facial drooping, slurred or confused speech, sudden vision loss, severe sudden headache, or loss of balance, call 911 (or your local emergency number) immediately. Don't drive yourself.

There's a good chance this is related to your migraine history and is not dangerous, but it's important to confirm that rather than assume it. Please don't wait on this one.

Spam filtering is basically how your email tries to weed out the junk nobody asked for. Spam (aka junk mail) gets blasted out in huge batches by advertisers and marketers trying to sell something, and it can bury the messages you actually care about. Filters look at incoming mail and flag stuff that resembles known spam. Spammers often lean on certain phrases like "free money" or "double your income," and they'll stuff messages with sketchy links or attachments that might carry malware.

There are a few main ways filters do this. Rules-based filtering checks mail against a list of criteria, and if a message hits enough of them, it gets tagged as spam. Machine learning systems learn from big piles of examples, both spam and legit mail, and then use what they picked up to spot new junk. Collaborative filtering watches how a whole bunch of users behave, like who's marking what as spam, and uses that to catch messages that many people are flagging. It's a constant cat-and-mouse game, though. Spammers keep finding new tricks to slip past filters, so the filters have to keep getting updated.

The Baykar Bayraktar TB2 is a medium-altitude, long-endurance (MALE) armed drone, or unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV), developed by Baykar, a Turkish defense company based in Istanbul. It entered service in the Turkish Armed Forces around 2014 and has since become one of the most widely exported combat drones in the world.

The aircraft is a fixed-wing design with a relatively simple, robust airframe. It can stay airborne for roughly 24 hours and typically operates at altitudes of up to about 8,000 meters (around 26,000 feet). It is controlled remotely from a ground station by operators who can monitor its sensors in real time, and it is usually launched from a runway or a short catapult-style rail. It carries electro-optical and infrared cameras for surveillance and targeting, along with laser designators and a range of precision-guided munitions such as MAM-series small smart munitions and laser-guided missiles.

The TB2 gained international attention for its use in several conflicts. It was employed by Turkey in operations in Syria, Libya, and Nagorno-Karabakh, and by Ukraine in its war with Russia beginning in 2022. Its relatively low cost compared with larger drones and manned aircraft made it attractive to many governments, and it has been exported to a number of countries including Azerbaijan, Poland, Qatar, Morocco, and others. Its performance in some of these conflicts was widely discussed, and analysts have debated both its battlefield effectiveness and the implications of such drones for modern warfare.

Paul Revere came into the world in Boston, Massachusetts, which was then part of the British colonies in North America. His birth took place on January 1, 1735, in a home on North Square. That house now operates as the Paul Revere House, a museum devoted to his life and achievements. Revere worked as a silversmith and craftsman, and he was also a patriot who had an important part in the American Revolution. He is most remembered for his midnight ride, in which he alerted colonists that British soldiers were on their way, just before the Battles of Lexington and Concord in 1775.

Stuart J. Russell is a British computer scientist and one of the most prominent researchers in artificial intelligence. He is a professor of computer science at the University of California, Berkeley, where he has taught since the 1980s and where he directs the Center for Human-Compatible Artificial Intelligence. He earned his undergraduate degree at Oxford and his PhD at Stanford.

He is best known for co-authoring, with Peter Norvig, the textbook "Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach," which has been one of the most widely used references for teaching AI at universities around the world since its first edition in the 1990s. His research has spanned machine learning, probabilistic reasoning, reinforcement learning, and the theoretical foundations of intelligent agents.

In recent years Russell has become a leading voice on AI safety. He has argued that the central challenge of advanced AI is ensuring that machines pursue objectives aligned with human values, and that systems should be designed to be uncertain about what humans want and to defer to them accordingly. He wrote about these ideas in the book "Human Compatible" (2019), aimed at a general audience, and he has advocated for careful regulation and research into controllable AI. He has also served on various advisory bodies and has testified before governments on the topic.

A line of credit is a form of borrowing that lets you take out funds whenever you need them, as long as you stay under a set maximum. People use these lines for many purposes, and investing is one of them. If you're thinking about funding investments this way, keep a few points in mind.

First, look at the terms of the line of credit. Be sure you understand its interest rate, any fees, and the conditions for paying it back.

Second, think about your investment strategy. Ask whether borrowing this way fits with your broader goals and approach. For instance, if you intend to hold your investments for a long time, a line of credit may be a poor choice, since it usually costs more in interest than a conventional loan.

Third, consider your capacity to repay. Have a clear plan for clearing the balance, because failing to do so can lead to serious problems, such as a lower credit score and extra charges.

Weigh all of these factors carefully before using a line of credit to invest, since doing so can be a risky financial move. Talking to a financial professional may help you understand both the possible risks and the benefits.

Heart disease is usually caused by damage to the heart or its blood vessels over time, and the most common form, coronary artery disease, develops when the arteries that supply blood to the heart heart muscle become narrowed or blocked. The main culprit is atherosclerosis, a process in which fatty deposits called plaque build up along the artery walls. These deposits can grow, rupture, and trigger blood clots that suddenly block blood flow, leading to a heart attack.

Several factors raise the risk of developing this damage. High blood pressure strains and injures the arteries, high LDL cholesterol contributes to plaque formation, and smoking damages the blood vessel lining and accelerates buildup. Diabetes and prediabetes, obesity, physical inactivity, and a diet high in saturated fat, trans fat, sodium, and processed foods also play significant roles. Excessive alcohol use, chronic stress, and poor sleep can contribute as well. Age and family history matter too, since men generally face higher risk earlier in life and a close relative with early heart disease increases susceptibility.

Other types of heart disease have different causes. Heart valve disease can result from birth defects, infections such as rheumatic fever, or simply wear and tear with aging. Cardiomyopathy, which weakens the heart muscle, may be inherited, caused by long-term high blood pressure, linked to alcohol or certain toxins, or triggered by viral infections. Arrhythmias, or irregular heartbeats, are often tied to structural problems, aging, or conditions like atrial fibrillation, and congenital heart defects are present from birth due to abnormal development in the womb.

Many of the most common causes are preventable or manageable through regular checkups, blood pressure and cholesterol monitoring, a heart-healthy diet, regular exercise, not smoking, and maintaining a healthy weight. If you have concerns about your own risk, a doctor can assess your personal factors.

The user's message is terse: "Bid price… sudden Drop". They likely mean a stock or asset's bid price dropped suddenly, and want to know what that means or why. I should give a helpful plain-prose answer without markdown, and ask briefly for context.

A sudden drop in the bid price means that the highest price buyers are currently willing to pay for a security has fallen quickly. This can happen for several reasons. The most common is new information that changes how people value the asset, such as an earnings miss, a news announcement, a regulatory action, or a macroeconomic data release. Sometimes the cause is a large seller who places a big sell order that consumes existing bids and pushes the price down, or a wave of stop-loss orders being triggered as the price falls through key levels. Liquidity can also play a role: when few buyers are active, even a modest sell order can knock the bid down sharply, and this is more common in thinly traded stocks, options, or crypto assets, and during off-hours or market openings and closings.

It helps to check whether the drop is broad or specific. If the whole sector or market fell, the cause is likely macro or market-wide. If only one asset moved, look for company or asset-specific news. It is also worth distinguishing a drop in the bid from a drop in the last traded price, since the bid can fall while the last trade stays higher if buyers simply pulled their orders.

If you tell me which asset you are looking at, what market it trades in, and roughly how big the move was, I can help you narrow down the likely cause.

Random pain in the wrists, arms, and hands can stem from several sources. One is repetitive strain injury, which develops when the same movement is repeated over and over, such as typing or working a mouse for extended stretches. Another is carpal tunnel syndrome, where the median nerve, running from the forearm into the hand, gets squeezed as it passes through the wrist, producing pain, numbness, and tingling in the wrist, hand, and fingers. Tendinitis, meaning inflammation of the tendons (the fibrous bands that connect muscles to bones), can also be responsible, often from overuse or injury, and it causes soreness in the affected area. A fracture, or broken bone, will likewise cause pain in the injured spot. Finally, arthritis, a condition that inflames the joints, can bring on both pain and swelling. If these symptoms are troubling you, it's worth consulting a healthcare provider who can make an accurate diagnosis, assess what you're experiencing, and suggest the right treatment. Be sure to mention your POTS diagnosis as well, since it may affect how you should be treated.

Amazon Mechanical Turk, or MTurk for short, is a platform Amazon built and still runs. It lets companies and organizations farm out small jobs to a huge pool of workers spread all over the world. People call it a crowdsourcing platform because you're getting results from a big crowd instead of one employee or contractor. The tasks, called Human Intelligence Tasks (HITs), can be pretty basic, like data entry or transcription, or they can get more involved, like moderating content or rating search results. Workers, known as "Turkers," pick whatever tasks they want and get paid a small amount for each one. Businesses use it when they need quick, reliable results for stuff that would be a pain to do in-house. For a lot of people, it's just a way to make some extra cash in their spare time.

Bond fund investors have mostly stayed put for several reasons, and the first is that much of the pain has already been absorbed. When rates rose sharply in 2022, bond funds took their worst losses in decades, and the people most likely to panic sold then or shortly after. The ones who remain tend to be more patient or more resigned to holding through volatility.

Second, yields are now high enough to act as a cushion and a lure. When a fund yields 4 to 5 percent or more, income covers a meaningful share of any price decline, and investors see a reason to keep holding or even add money. Compared with the near-zero yields of a few years ago, bonds look like a real investment again, and cash-like alternatives such as money market funds, while popular, have not drained bond funds as dramatically as some expected.

Third, the nature of the losses matters. Most bond fund declines come from interest rate moves rather than credit problems. Investors in Treasury and high-quality funds understand, or are told, that prices recover as bonds approach maturity and as older low-coupon holdings roll into higher-yielding ones. That makes the losses feel temporary rather than a sign of underlying failure, which tends to reduce panic selling.

Fourth, the investor base is sticky. A large share of bond fund money sits in retirement accounts, target-date funds, and advisor-managed portfolios, where allocations are rebalanced on a schedule rather than driven by headlines. Automatic contributions also keep inflows steady, offsetting some redemptions.

Fifth, market conditions have been orderly. Redemption waves usually come with a shock, such as a credit scare or a liquidity freeze like March 2020. Without a crisis, there is little trigger for a rush to exit. The Federal Reserve's rate path has also become more predictable, and many investors expect cuts eventually, which would help bond prices, so they are reluctant to sell near what they see as a turning point.

Finally, there is a lack of obvious alternatives for people who want income and diversification. Stocks are richly valued by many measures, and bonds offer a hedge against a slowdown. That said, the calm is not guaranteed. If inflation reaccelerated or long-term yields spiked again, outflows could pick up quickly, especially in riskier categories like high-yield or long-duration funds.

Keeping a formal record of your personal finances gives you a clear picture of where your money actually goes. Many people have a rough sense of their spending, but tracking every transaction often reveals surprises, such as forgotten subscriptions, frequent small purchases that add up, or categories that consume far more than expected. That awareness is the first step toward making deliberate choices rather than letting spending drift.

Accounting also makes budgeting far more realistic. When you have actual historical data on income and expenses, you can set targets based on how you really live instead of how you hope to live. You can see seasonal patterns, such as higher utility bills in winter or holiday spending in December, and plan for them in advance so they don't derail your finances.

Good records support long-term goals as well. Tracking net worth over time, meaning the difference between your assets and liabilities, shows whether you are moving in the right direction. It also helps you measure progress toward milestones like paying off debt, building an emergency fund, or saving for a home or retirement, and it keeps you motivated by making improvement visible.

Organized financial records are valuable in practical situations too. They make tax preparation easier, help you substantiate deductions, and provide documentation if you apply for a loan, mortgage, or insurance. In the event of a dispute with a bank or merchant, or after a death or emergency in the family, well-kept records can save considerable time, stress, and money for you or your loved ones.

Finally, the discipline of regular accounting tends to encourage better financial habits overall. Reviewing your finances on a schedule makes you more mindful of purchases, more likely to compare prices, and quicker to catch fraudulent charges or billing errors. Over time, this steady attention can translate into meaningfully better financial outcomes.

Many such growths are benign, such as seborrheic keratoses, cysts, or scar tissue, but a clinician can only tell by examining it, and when there's doubt, by taking a biopsy. Your oncologist's comment that you could have it checked if it would make you feel better is a reasonable answer to the question of whether it's needed, but it doesn't rule out cancer, and not offering a biopsy doesn't mean the growth was judged to be benign. Target-date funds are basically a "one-stop shop" kind of fund. They can be mutual funds or ETFs, and they hold a mix of stocks, bonds, and other stuff. The mix is set by the year you plan to retire, so the fund gets more conservative as that date gets closer.

Most people see them as a safe, easy option if you just want a diversified portfolio that's built around retirement. But they're still investments, so there's some risk. How much depends on the specific fund and how it's run.

As for the Fed ending quantitative easing, I wouldn't expect that to hit target-date funds directly. QE is just the Fed's way of boosting the economy by pumping up the money supply and pushing interest rates down. Ending it could shake up financial markets a bit, sure, but that's not a direct threat to these funds.

Still, you should look at what you're actually buying. Check the fund's strategy and what it holds, and know what kind of risk and returns you're signing up for. And every so often, take another look at your portfolio to make sure it still fits your long-term goals.

UK VAT on cultural businesses that deal with overseas customers and suppliers turns mainly on two questions: where the supply is treated as taking place, and whether the customer is a business or a consumer. For most business-to-business services, such as licensing rights, commissioning freelance designers, or selling exhibition or production services to a foreign company, the place of supply is generally where the customer belongs. If a UK business supplies services to a VAT-registered business overseas, the supply is usually outside the scope of UK VAT rather than zero-rated. You do not charge UK VAT, but you should still keep evidence that the customer is overseas and in business, typically a valid foreign VAT or business registration number and the customer's address. Because it is outside scope rather than zero-rated, you can generally still recover the input VAT you incur on costs connected with those sales.

Where the overseas customer is a consumer, the rules differ. Event admissions, for example, are generally taxed where the event takes place, so tickets to a UK event sold to foreign visitors normally carry UK VAT, subject to any relevant exemption. Digital services such as online streaming, downloads, or e-books sold to private individuals are taxed where the consumer is located, so a UK supplier selling to EU or other overseas consumers needs to consider the rules of those countries, and a UK consumer buying from an overseas digital provider may face UK VAT charged by that provider or at the border.

When a UK cultural business buys services from overseas, such as a foreign artist's licence, a translation service, or software, the UK business usually has to account for VAT itself under the reverse charge. The VAT is declared as output tax and reclaimed as input tax on the same return, so the net effect is often neutral for a fully taxable business, but it must be recorded correctly. Goods exports, such as physical artworks, books, or merchandise sent abroad, are generally zero-rated, provided you hold proof of export.

The treatment of admissions and cultural services also depends on whether the provider is a commercial business or an eligible non-profit body. Many museum, gallery, theatre, and concert exemptions in UK law apply only to certain bodies, so commercial operators often must charge VAT on admissions, though there are exceptions for specific cases.

Because these rules involve several overlapping regimes and have been revised since the UK left the EU, the specifics for a particular transaction, especially involving digital services or consumer sales into the EU, should be checked against current HMRC guidance or confirmed with a VAT adviser. If you can describe the particular type of cultural activity and the countries and customer types involved, I can help you work through the likely treatment in more detail.

A year is the span of time Earth needs to complete one trip around the sun, roughly 365.24 days. This interval matters because it sets the seasons and strongly shapes the planet's climate and weather. Earth's journey around the sun also affects the length of a day, since the rotation of Earth on its axis is influenced by the gravitational pulls of both the sun and the moon. Over the course of a year, Earth goes through a variety of weather and climate conditions, with shifts in temperature, humidity, and rainfall. Several factors drive these changes, among them how far Earth is from the sun, the angle of its axial tilt, and its spinning motion on that axis. Beyond the orbit itself, a year is also defined by the arrival of many astronomical and cultural occasions, including holidays and festivals. Such occasions can carry considerable social, economic, and political consequences for communities across the globe.

Feature engineering is the practice of devising and constructing the inputs that machine learning models learn from. Each feature captures a particular trait or property of the data used in training. Its aim is to pull the most pertinent and valuable information out of raw data and reshape it into a format that learning algorithms can readily work with. Doing this involves choosing and merging various data elements and applying a range of transformations and methods to surface the most helpful features. When done well, feature engineering can markedly boost model performance, since it highlights the factors that most strongly shape the model's output and filters out noise or data that doesn't matter. It forms a key stage of the machine learning workflow and demands a thorough grasp of both the data and the problem at hand.

Almost every website can be attacked in some way, but "hackable" doesn't mean the same thing everywhere. Think of a website like a house with lots of doors and windows. Some houses have strong locks, alarms, and a guard dog. Others have a flimsy door that anyone can push open. A website is the same: the people who build it try to lock every door, but there are so many parts (the program, the computer it runs on, the internet connection, and the people who log in) that it's very hard to make sure none of them has a small mistake.

Can a website be 100% unhackable? No one can honestly promise that. The reason is that software is written by people, and people make mistakes. Even very careful teams miss something. Also, the computers and networks a site runs on are made by many different companies, and new weaknesses are discovered all the time. Someone can also trick a person into giving away a password, which no amount of locks on the computer can stop.

That said, some systems are extremely hard to break into. Very careful designs, with few parts, constant updates, strict limits on who can get in, and experts testing for problems, make a site much safer. Banks and military systems work hard at this. But "very, very hard" is not the same as "impossible."

So the simple answer is: yes, nearly all websites have some possible holes, and the goal of security is to make those holes so hard to find and use that attackers give up or move on to easier targets.

The Dartmouth workshop, sometimes called the Dartmouth Conference or the Dartmouth Summer Research Project on Artificial Intelligence, took place in the summer of 1956 at Dartmouth College in Hanover, New Hampshire, in the United States. John McCarthy, Marvin Minsky, Nathaniel Rochester, and Claude Shannon organized it, and it was among the earliest gatherings devoted to artificial intelligence (AI). It marked a turning point in the field's history: the phrase "artificial intelligence" was coined there, and AI was formally recognized as a discipline. Researchers who were curious about whether intelligent machines could be built came together, and the event produced many foundational ideas and methods that AI research still relies on. Participants debated a variety of AI-related subjects, such as natural language processing, problem solving, and learning. The workshop also helped lay the foundation for LISP, the first AI programming language, which McCarthy and Minsky went on to develop. Today the Dartmouth workshop is widely regarded as a pivotal moment in AI's history and is frequently identified as the starting point of modern AI research.
