The United States Constitution was drafted in 1787. Delegates to the Constitutional Convention in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, signed it on September 17, 1787, and it became operative on March 4, 1789. As the highest law of the nation, it is the oldest written national constitution still in force anywhere in the world. It set up the structure of the federal government and has been changed through amendment 27 times since its adoption. The document specifies the authority and responsibilities of the legislative, executive, and judicial branches of the federal government, and it lays out the basic rights held by American citizens.

There is no set cap on how much a corporation may spend on entertainment. Still, the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) sets rules governing how entertainment costs are treated for tax purposes. Under IRS guidance, entertainment, amusement, and recreation expenses are usually not deductible as business costs, though a few exceptions apply. One example: if the entertainment is directly tied to the business and takes place during business activities, it may qualify as a deductible expense. Suppose a company brings clients to a baseball game as part of a business discussion; the ticket costs could then be deductible. Likewise, entertainment regarded as "ordinary and necessary" for the business may also qualify. Even when an entertainment expense meets these criteria, however, the IRS allows only half of the cost to be deducted. So if a company spends $100 on entertainment, its tax return can claim just $50. Corporations should also take care not to use entertainment costs as a means of dodging taxes. The IRS enforces strict rules against such abuse and may reject deductions or impose penalties if it finds that entertainment expenses are being misused.

The Roman Empire is usually dated from 27 BCE, when Augustus became the first emperor, to 476 CE, when the Germanic leader Odoacer deposed the last western emperor, Romulus Augustulus. That gives it roughly 500 years in the West.

The story doesn't end there, though. The Eastern half, usually called the Byzantine Empire by historians though its people called themselves Romans, continued until 1453, when the Ottoman Turks captured Constantinople. Counting from Augustus, the Roman state lasted about 1,480 years in total, which makes it one of the longest-lasting polities in Western history.

In boxing and mixed martial arts (MMA), body weight matters because it can give a fighter an edge over an opponent. A heavier fighter often brings more power and strength, whereas a lighter one may move faster and be more nimble. Weight classes exist to keep bouts balanced and fair. If one competitor is far bigger than the other, the size and strength gap could make the contest lopsided and dull to watch. Grouping fighters by weight helps organizers pair people who are closer in size and ability, which tends to produce tighter, more thrilling bouts. Even a 10-pound difference can affect how a fight unfolds. The lighter fighter may be quicker and more agile, while the heavier one may hit harder and hold more strength, which can tip the balance. Still, size alone does not decide a fight. A smaller competitor can still win with sharp technique or a solid defense. Manny Pacquiao, who stands 5'7" and weighs about 150 pounds, might struggle against a 6'5", 300-pound opponent. Yet, as before, size is not the only thing that determines the result. Pacquiao enjoyed a highly successful career and defeated opponents who outweighed him, so it is not necessarily the case that he would have no chance against a bigger opponent.

Stocks can go up even when there's no good news or earnings behind it, and there are a few usual reasons why.

One is plain old demand. If enough people want to buy a stock, the price climbs, news or no news. That can come from investor mood or just speculation about how the company might do down the road.

Another is a short squeeze. Say a bunch of investors have bet against a stock, which is what short selling is. Then some good news hits, or buying picks up, and those short sellers scramble to close out their positions by buying shares. That buying pushes the price up even faster, and that's the squeeze.

Then there's manipulation. Sometimes a price gets pumped up on purpose, like with pump and dump schemes or insider trading. That's illegal, and people caught doing it can end up in serious trouble.

Prices get pushed around by a lot of things, and nobody can predict them perfectly. So do your own homework and keep in mind that investing in stocks carries real risk.

A capital market is a financial market in which long-term funds are raised and traded, typically through instruments with maturities of more than one year. It connects those who have surplus savings, such as households, institutional investors, pension funds, and insurance companies, with those who need long-term finance, such as businesses and governments that want to invest in factories, infrastructure, research, or other productive assets. In this way, the capital market channels savings into investment and plays a central role in economic growth.

The main instruments traded in capital markets are equity shares, which represent ownership in a company, and debt securities such as bonds and debentures, which represent loans that the issuer must repay with interest. Other instruments include preference shares, government securities with long maturities, and various hybrid or derivative products linked to these securities.

Capital markets are usually divided into two parts. The primary market is where new securities are issued for the first time, for example when a company makes an initial public offering or a government sells new bonds. The money raised goes directly to the issuer. The secondary market is where existing securities are bought and sold among investors, most commonly on stock exchanges such as the New York Stock Exchange, the London Stock Exchange, or the Bombay Stock Exchange. The secondary market does not provide new funds to the issuer directly, but it gives investors liquidity, meaning they can convert their holdings into cash, and it helps determine the market price of securities.

The capital market differs from the money market, which deals in short-term funds and instruments maturing within a year, such as treasury bills and commercial paper. While the money market meets temporary working capital needs, the capital market supports long-term growth and capital formation.

Capital markets are generally regulated by government bodies to protect investors and ensure fair, transparent trading. Examples include the Securities and Exchange Commission in the United States and the Securities and Exchange Board of India. Overall, a well-functioning capital market mobilizes savings, allocates resources efficiently, provides opportunities for wealth creation, and contributes to the overall development of an economy.

The Pythagorean theorem is a mathematical idea that lets us calculate the length of a missing side in a right triangle, which is a triangle containing a 90 degree angle. To apply it, you must already know the lengths of the other two sides, which are known as the "legs" of the triangle.

Here is how it works. Picture a right triangle whose legs measure 3 units and 4 units. Our goal is to find the length of the third side, called the "hypotenuse." The theorem states that if you square the length of the hypotenuse, the result equals the sum of the squares of the two legs. Written as a formula, it is: (length of hypotenuse)^2 = (length of leg 1)^2 + (length of leg 2)^2.

In our example, we substitute the leg lengths into the formula: (length of hypotenuse)^2 = 3^2 + 4^2, which becomes (length of hypotenuse)^2 = 9 + 16, and then (length of hypotenuse)^2 = 25. The last step is to take the square root of 25. Since that equals 5, the hypotenuse is 5 units long.

So that is the Pythagorean theorem. When you know the lengths of two sides of a right triangle, it gives you a way to work out the length of the remaining side.

Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is a diagnostic technique that relies on a magnetic field and radio waves to generate detailed pictures of the body's organs and tissues. Because it avoids ionizing radiation like x-rays, it is considered a non-invasive method of looking inside the body. In a typical MRI exam, the patient lies within a powerful magnet, and radio waves stimulate the protons found in the body's cells. When these protons settle back into their resting state, they release a signal that the scanner picks up and converts into detailed internal images. Physicians can review these images on a computer to identify a broad array of conditions, such as injuries, diseases, and structural abnormalities. As a diagnostic tool, MRI is highly effective at imaging the brain, spine, joints, and other organs and tissues. It is frequently employed to detect disorders of the nervous system, including strokes and brain tumors, as well as conditions affecting the musculoskeletal system, such as injuries and degenerative changes. Additionally, it helps in diagnosing and tracking the progression of cancer, heart disease, and other illnesses.

The Bayraktar TB2 is a Turkish drone built by Baykar Makina, a company that makes UAVs, robotics, and automation systems. It's a medium-altitude, long-endurance (MALE) model, so it's meant for things like intelligence gathering, surveillance, reconnaissance, border patrol, and disaster response. It carries a pretty solid set of sensors: high-res electro-optical and infrared cameras, laser designators, and radar. It can stay up for more than 24 hours at a stretch and tops out around 180 km/h.

It's gotten a lot of attention lately, mostly because the Turkish military has used it in real operations in places like Syria and Libya. Plenty of other countries have bought it too, including Ukraine and Qatar.

Taste in music, movies, and art is pretty subjective. What one person loves, another might not even care about. Our tastes get shaped by all sorts of things: what we've lived through, where we grew up, what era we happen to be living in. Still, we tend to talk about "good" and "bad" taste like it's a fact, mostly because we feel strongly about the stuff we're into or can't stand. It's totally normal to want to share your favorite bands or films and get into it with people. But those "good" and "bad" labels are really just opinions dressed up as facts. Everyone's taste is different, and it's fine to love something others don't get. You can have strong opinions too, as long as you're cool about other people having theirs.

Inductive programming is a subfield of AI and machine learning where computer programs automatically build and refine machine learning models from data. The idea is to automate model building and selection so you end up with models that are more accurate and generalize better to new data. It usually leans on techniques like genetic programming, neural networks, and decision trees to dig through big datasets, spot patterns and relationships, and then use those to predict outcomes or classify new stuff. The real payoff is that you can get decent predictions or decisions without spending forever on manual tuning or hand-crafting features. It's used all over the place, from natural language processing and image and video recognition to predictive modeling in finance, healthcare, and marketing. It could speed up model development a lot and make it easier for people without deep technical chops to get useful results.

You can ask your card issuer to lower your credit limit by calling the number on the back of your card, logging into your account online or in the mobile app, or sending a secure message through the bank's website. Most issuers let you request a decrease through one of these channels, and the request usually takes effect quickly.

When you contact them, you might say something like: "I'd like to request a decrease in my credit limit on this account from its current amount to a new amount of [figure]. I'd appreciate it if you could confirm once the change is made and let me know whether it affects my rewards or interest rate." Stating a specific figure makes the request easier to process.

It may help to know why you're asking before you call, since the issuer may ask. Common reasons include reducing the temptation to overspend, lowering the risk of fraud exposure, or preparing for a period of tighter budgeting. Keep in mind that a lower limit can increase your credit utilization ratio, which may lower your credit score if your balances stay the same. If your goal is to protect your credit score, you could instead ask for the limit to stay the same and simply keep your balance low.

Ezekiel appears in the Hebrew Bible as a prophet, and the Book of Ezekiel, which bears his name, is included in both the Hebrew Bible and the Christian Old Testament. Tradition holds that he wrote it himself. A priest as well as a prophet, he lived in the 6th century BC. Born in Jerusalem, he was taken to Babylon with other Jews by the Babylonian king Nebuchadnezzar II following Jerusalem's fall in 586 BC. During his exile, God gave Ezekiel visions and appointed him to deliver prophetic messages to the Israelites living in Babylon. His prophecies dealt mainly with God's approaching judgment on the Israelites because of their sins, and with the eventual restoration of the nation of Israel. He also foretold that the temple in Jerusalem would be rebuilt and that the Jews would go back to their homeland. The book combines prophecies, parables, and symbolic acts, all of which Ezekiel used to communicate God's message to his people. Both Judaism and Christianity regard it as an important and influential work.

Yes, a hernia is a real possibility, and what you describe fits fairly well with an inguinal hernia. This type happens when a bit of fat or intestine pushes through a weak spot in the lower abdominal wall near the groin, producing a bulge and an ache or pulling sensation on that side. The classic pattern is that the lump and discomfort appear or worsen when pressure inside the abdomen rises, and ease when you lie down. Standing for long periods raises that pressure somewhat, and speaking in a louder or higher-pitched voice involves tightening the diaphragm and abdominal muscles, which can increase it further, much like a mild cough or strain. That would explain why the pain shows up in those situations and why the lump may be more noticeable or tender at those times.

There are other possibilities worth knowing about. A swollen lymph node in the groin can feel like a small tender lump, often after an infection or a small skin irritation in the leg, genital, or lower abdominal area. A strained muscle or tendon at the top of the inner thigh (a groin strain) can hurt with prolonged standing. Less commonly, a femoral hernia, a cyst, or in men a problem in the testicle or spermatic cord can cause similar symptoms. Nerve irritation in the area can also produce intermittent pain.

You can do a rough check yourself. Stand up, cough or bear down gently, and feel the area with your fingers; a hernia often bulges out when you do this and can sometimes be pressed back in when you lie down. That is not a substitute for an exam, though, and a doctor can usually diagnose a hernia by physical examination, sometimes confirmed with an ultrasound.

Because you have both a lump and recurring pain, it is sensible to see a doctor soon rather than wait it out. Hernias do not heal on their own, and while many are not urgent, they can occasionally become trapped (incarcerated) or have their blood supply cut off (strangulated), which is an emergency. Seek urgent care if the lump becomes firm, very painful, discolored red or purple, cannot be pushed back in, or if you develop nausea, vomiting, fever, or trouble passing stool or gas. Until you are seen, avoid heavy lifting and straining, and try not to stand in one position for very long periods.

Bloemfontein is in South Africa, in the central interior of the country on the Free State plateau. It sits roughly in the middle of the nation's northern-central region, about 400 kilometers south of Johannesburg and about 1,000 kilometers north-east of Cape Town. Buying your first home is a huge money move, probably the biggest one most people ever make, so it's worth knowing what you're getting into.

First, the down payment. Most lenders want at least 5% of the purchase price up front. The more you can put down, the smaller your mortgage ends up being, and that usually means lower monthly payments and maybe a better interest rate too.

Then there are closing costs, which catch a lot of people off guard. They can add up to several thousand dollars and cover things like lender fees, title insurance, property taxes, and other odds and ends.

After that you've got the monthly mortgage payment. It normally covers principal and interest, and how much you pay depends on the size of the loan, your rate, and how long the term is.

Maintenance and repairs are on you now, too. That can get pricey, especially if the house is older or needs major work.

And don't forget property taxes. Most homeowners have to pay them, and the amount depends on what the home is worth and the tax rate where you live.

So before you jump in, think hard about all of this and make sure you've actually got the cash to cover it.

Paying a dividend can be rational for several interrelated reasons, though the answer depends on what the company and its shareholders are trying to achieve.

The most basic argument comes from the idea that a firm should return cash it cannot invest profitably. If a company has no projects that earn more than the return shareholders could get elsewhere, holding onto the cash simply lets management use it poorly. By paying it out, the firm hands the money back so investors can deploy it in better opportunities. In this view, a dividend is a disciplinary tool that limits the risk of managers building empires or funding wasteful acquisitions.

Dividends also serve as a signal. Because managers generally know more about the firm's prospects than outside investors do, a steady or rising dividend can convey confidence that future earnings will support the payment. Cutting a dividend is often read as bad news, which gives managers a strong incentive to pay one only when they expect to sustain it. This signaling role makes dividends informative even though, in an idealized world, they should not change a firm's value.

Shareholders may also value dividends for practical reasons. Some investors, such as retirees, need a regular stream of cash and would otherwise have to sell shares, incurring transaction costs and possibly disturbing their holdings. Others, including certain institutions, have mandates that favor income-producing assets. For these investors, a dividend provides a predictable return without requiring them to time sales.

Finally, dividends can attract a particular class of investors and build a reputation for reliability. Firms with a long record of paying dividends often develop a shareholder base that expects and values them, and that loyalty can lower the firm's cost of capital and reduce volatility in its stock price.

Against these arguments, the classic Modigliani and Miller analysis holds that, in a world without taxes or frictions, dividend policy should not affect firm value, since shareholders could create their own "homemade" dividends by selling shares. Taxes, transaction costs, and information asymmetry are what make dividends matter in practice, and that is why paying one can be a rational choice.

A 30% share in a business basically means you own 30% of the company. So if there are 100 shares of stock and you hold 30 of them, you've got a 30% stake. Pretty straightforward on paper.

What it actually gets you depends a lot on the setup. In a corporation, shareholders usually get to vote on big stuff like electing directors or approving major decisions, and your voting power generally tracks your percentage, so 30% gets you roughly 30% of the votes. Your share also usually determines how much of the profits (or losses) you get, and how much exposure you have on company debts, though that second part depends heavily on the type of entity. Ownership structures can look wildly different from one business to another, since they're shaped by all sorts of legal and contract terms. If you're trying to figure out exactly what your rights and obligations are, talk to a lawyer. It's worth the cost.

When pilots are exposed to intense gravitational forces, known as G-forces, they can black out if those forces press too hard on the body. Under high G, blood is driven downward, away from the head and toward the lower body. This reduces the amount of blood reaching the brain and can result in unconsciousness. Because blood is drawn away from the face, it may look twisted or deformed. Facial muscles can also tighten and strain as the individual fights to stay conscious, and the skin may turn pale or red as blood circulation shifts. Since G-forces carry real risks, pilots receive specialized training to learn how to manage them safely.

Fleas live in two places at once, in a sense. Adult fleas spend most of their lives on a host animal, usually a warm-blooded mammal or bird, where they feed on blood. Common hosts include dogs, cats, rats, mice, rabbits, squirrels, and birds, and some fleas will bite humans when their preferred host isn't available. On an animal, fleas tend to gather where the fur is thick and warm, such as around the neck, the base of the tail, the belly, and behind the ears.

The rest of the flea's life cycle happens in the host's environment rather than on the host itself. Female fleas lay eggs on the animal, but the eggs fall off easily and land wherever the animal spends time. That's why flea eggs, larvae, and pupae are usually found in places like pet bedding, carpets, rugs, upholstered furniture, cracks in floorboards, animal nests and burrows, and shady, moist spots in yards or under porches. The larvae feed on organic debris, including the dried blood excreted by adult fleas, and then spin cocoons where they can wait for weeks or even months until they sense vibrations, warmth, or carbon dioxide from a passing host before emerging and jumping on.

Because only a small fraction of a flea population is typically on an animal at any given moment, getting rid of an infestation usually means treating both the pet and the home or yard. Fleas thrive in warm, humid conditions, so they are most common in summer and in milder climates, though indoor heating lets them survive year-round in many houses.

So people long ago needed something everyone agreed was worth having, something you could trade for anything. Shells, salt, beads, and shiny metals all got used this way. Eventually people settled on coins and paper bills, because they're easy to carry, hard to fake, and everybody agrees they count as payment. Money is really just a way of saying "I trust that other people will accept this for the things I need."

Nobody sat down and invented money all at once. It grew up slowly over thousands of years in many places, starting around 5,000 years ago or more in Mesopotamia, where people kept track of grain and debts on clay tablets. Early coins showed up around 2,600 years ago in the kingdom of Lydia, in what is now Turkey. Later, governments and kings started stamping coins so everyone could tell how much they were worth, and eventually banks and governments began printing paper money. So the answer to who made money is: lots of ordinary people, traders, and rulers, over a very long time, all working out a better way to trade.

Go is a board game that started out in China something like 2,500 years ago, maybe more. You play on a 19 by 19 grid, and each person gets a pile of stones in their color, black or white. The point is to end up surrounding more of the board with your stones than your opponent manages with theirs. You take turns putting a stone down on the intersections of the lines (not in the squares, which trips up a lot of beginners), and the game wraps up when both players pass because neither one wants to make another move.

What's wild about it is how simple the rules are compared to how deep the strategy gets. You can learn the basics in a few minutes and still be figuring things out decades later. It's huge in East Asia, and there are pro players in China, Japan, and South Korea. It's picked up fans in other parts of the world too, and there are international tournaments on a regular basis. People tend to love it for the odd challenges it throws at you, and honestly for the focus and mental discipline it demands.

Bread tastes different after it's toasted because the process alters its appearance and texture. The toaster's heat turns the surface of the bread crisp and crunchy. On top of that, toasting releases a faintly nutty, toasty smell, which can boost the bread's flavor even further. In short, toasting changes how bread looks, feels, and smells, and all of these changes work together to create a better overall taste.

An inference rule is a formal pattern for drawing a conclusion from one or more statements that are already accepted as true or assumed for the sake of argument. Each rule specifies a form that premises must take and a form that the conclusion may then take, so that whenever the premises hold, the conclusion must hold as well. Inference rules are the basic tools of logic and mathematical proof, where they let a reasoner move step by step from axioms or assumptions to new truths without relying on intuition alone.

A classic example is modus ponens, which states that if a statement "if P then Q" is true and P is true, then Q must be true. Another is modus tollens, which allows one to conclude that P is false from "if P then Q" together with the falsity of Q. Other familiar rules include conjunction introduction, which lets one infer "P and Q" from separate statements P and Q, and disjunctive syllogism, which lets one infer Q from "P or Q" together with the falsity of P.

Inference rules are usually written in a notation with the premises placed above a horizontal line and the conclusion below it, though they can also be stated in words. In formal systems such as natural deduction or sequent calculus, a proof is simply a sequence of statements in which each one either is an assumption or follows from earlier lines by an inference rule. Because the rules are mechanical, a computer can check such proofs, which is why they are central to automated reasoning and to the foundations of mathematics.

Volodymyr Zelenskyy is a Ukrainian politician and former entertainer who has served as the President of Ukraine since May 2019. He was born on 25 January 1978 in Kryvyi Rih, in what was then the Soviet Union, into a Russian-speaking Jewish family. He trained as a lawyer, earning a law degree, but he never practiced and instead pursued a career in comedy and television.

Before entering politics, Zelenskyy was a well-known actor, writer, and producer. He performed with the comedy troupe Kvartal 95, which he helped found and which grew into a successful production company. He also won the Ukrainian version of Dancing with the Stars in 2006 and voiced Paddington Bear in the Ukrainian dubbing of the films. His most famous role was in the television series Servant of the People, in which he played a schoolteacher who unexpectedly becomes president after a video of him ranting about corruption goes viral. The show's title was later adopted by his real political party.

In 2019 he ran for president as an outsider promising to fight corruption, end the war in the Donbas region, and renew the political class. He defeated incumbent Petro Poroshenko in a landslide, winning about 73 percent of the vote in the runoff, and then called early parliamentary elections in which his party won an outright majority.

His presidency was transformed by Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Rather than leaving Kyiv, he stayed and appeared in widely shared video messages, famously rejecting an offer of evacuation by saying he needed ammunition, not a ride. He became a global symbol of Ukrainian resistance, addressing foreign parliaments, lobbying for military and financial aid, and meeting with world leaders. Time magazine named him Person of the Year in 2022.

His record has also drawn criticism. Domestically, critics have pointed to concerns about corruption, the concentration of power, restrictions on media and opposition during martial law, and the postponement of elections, which martial law legally requires. Internationally, his relationship with the United States became a focus of attention, including a contentious Oval Office meeting with Donald Trump in February 2025 amid debates over peace negotiations and continued support.

The legal doctrine of double jeopardy holds that, within the criminal justice system, an individual may not be prosecuted again for an offense for which they have already been acquitted (declared not guilty) or convicted. Under this rule, once a person has stood trial and been found not guilty, the state is barred from prosecuting them again, even if fresh evidence emerges indicating they actually committed the crime. In the same way, a person who has already been convicted cannot be retried, even if new evidence surfaces that could establish their innocence. The purpose of this protection is to shield individuals from being repeatedly targeted by the government and to stop the state from exploiting its authority in an effort to reach a different result in the same case.

George Forsythe was a mathematician, computer scientist, and academic whose work advanced both computer science and numerical analysis. Born in New York City in 1917, he earned his undergraduate mathematics degree from Columbia University in 1938, then completed a PhD in mathematics at Brown University in 1941. Over the course of his career, he was a pioneer in computing, contributing to early computer systems and creating algorithms for scientific computation. He was instrumental in the development of the FORTRAN programming language and helped found Stanford University's Computer Science Department, which he chaired for many years. As a teacher, he was recognized for his creative and rigorous methods, and his influence on the discipline endured through both his research and his educational work. He held fellowships in the American Academy of Arts and Sciences and the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers, and he was a member of the National Academy of Sciences. He died in 1972 at the age of 55.

Porcupines are plant-eaters, so their diet consists mainly of vegetation. Out in nature, they chiefly consume tree bark, young twigs, and other plant matter. The soft inner bark is their favorite, and they reach it by chewing through the tougher outer layer. Depending on what their surroundings offer, they also eat leaves, shoots, and nuts. Their menu is broad and includes conifers such as pine, spruce, and fir, as well as deciduous trees like oak, maple, and beech. Fruit trees, including apple and pear, are also on the list, since porcupines will strip the bark and nibble the shoots. Although they sometimes eat insects or other small creatures, this makes up only a minor share of their diet. Porcupines are not typically aggressive or predatory, and they do not go out hunting other animals for food.

Google Now was a mobile virtual assistant and information service developed by Google. It launched in 2012 as part of Android 4.1 Jelly Bean and was also available as an app on iOS. Its main idea was to deliver proactive, personalized information to users before they asked for it. By analyzing data from a user's search history, location, calendar, email, and other Google services, it displayed "cards" on the screen showing things like current weather, traffic conditions on the way to work, upcoming appointments, sports scores for favorite teams, flight status, and reminders.

Users could also interact with it by voice, using commands such as "OK Google" to ask questions, set alarms, send messages, or get directions. In this sense it competed with Apple's Siri and Microsoft's Cortana.

Over time Google expanded and refined the service. Its functionality was gradually folded into the Google app and, more significantly, into Google Assistant, which Google introduced in 2016 as its successor. Google Now's card-based, predictive feed was largely replaced by the more conversational and broadly capable Assistant, and the Google Now name was phased out in the following years, though the feed-style features lived on in the Google app for a time.

Yes, you still need to report it. The $600 threshold determines when a company must send you a 1099-MISC, not whether the income is taxable. All income is reportable, whether or not you receive a form.

Where you enter it depends on how you earned it. If you were an employee and the company simply failed to issue a W-2, report it as wages and contact the IRS or the company, since a missing W-2 is their problem to fix. If you were an independent contractor or did freelance or gig work, don't put it in general or "other" income. Enter it as self-employment or business income (Schedule C if you're using a 1040 form, or the self-employment section in tax software). Otherwise you may miss self-employment tax, which applies once your net earnings reach $400. If the work was a one-time or hobby activity, it can go under "other income," but it's still taxable.

Keep your invoices, bank deposits, and any payment records to support the amount, since the IRS can ask for them even without a 1099. If you expect to owe tax on this income, you may also need to make quarterly estimated payments to avoid an underpayment penalty.

Think of a TV channel like a lemonade stand. It needs customers, and customers are the people who watch, who the advertisers pay to reach. Long ago, these channels made lots of slow, careful nature and science shows, and not many people watched them, so the money was thin.

Then they noticed that shows about people doing something exciting, like hauling crab in a storm, fixing old junk to sell, or buying gold, got lots of viewers. Those shows are also cheap to make. You don't need expensive filming in faraway places or teams of scientists. You put a few cameras on regular people and let them talk and argue. Advertisers like that, because lots of people are watching at the same time.

The channels also have bills to pay. Cable TV has been losing viewers to Netflix, YouTube, and other streaming, so they chase whatever keeps people from changing the channel. Science shows still exist, but they cost more and bring in fewer viewers, so they get pushed to the side or moved to smaller channels.

So it isn't really that they stopped caring about science. It's that the shows that make the most money are the ones that are cheap and popular, and those happen to be the reality shows. If you want more science on TV, watching and supporting those shows, or streaming them elsewhere, tells the channels that there's an audience for them.

A direct marketing channel is a way for a company to sell its products or services straight to customers without using intermediaries such as wholesalers, distributors, or retailers. In this model, the business controls the entire relationship with the buyer, from promoting the offer to completing the sale and handling after-sale service. Common examples include company-operated websites and online stores, catalogs and mail-order sales, telemarketing, door-to-door selling, email campaigns, and sales through company-owned stores or a direct sales force. Brands that sell through their own apps or subscription services, such as many software and meal-kit companies, also use this approach.

The main advantages are greater control over pricing, branding, and the customer experience, along with richer data about customer preferences and buying behavior that can be used to target future offers. The trade-offs are that the company must bear the costs of marketing, logistics, and customer service itself, which can be expensive, especially for businesses without an established reach. This contrasts with indirect channels, where products pass through independent resellers who share the work and the margin.

Getting hit with a taser sends an electrical current through your body, and your muscles start contracting and relaxing over and over, fast. That can leave you temporarily unable to move. The current messes with the nerves that normally carry the brain's signals to your muscles. Your brain tells a muscle to tighten or loosen so you can move, but the current gets in the way and makes the muscles jerk around on their own. Tasers are risky, so they should only be used by trained people in certain situations. If you've been tasered, get medical attention, since there can be other effects that need checking.

Law enforcement refers to the activities carried out by government agencies and their personnel to maintain public order, prevent and detect crime, and ensure that laws are obeyed. It is the practical side of the legal system, the part that turns written laws into real-world action. Its core functions include patrolling communities, responding to emergencies, investigating crimes, gathering evidence, arresting suspects, and supporting the courts by bringing cases forward for prosecution.

The people who do this work include police officers, sheriff's deputies, state troopers, federal agents such as those at the FBI or Drug Enforcement Administration, and specialized units that handle areas like traffic, narcotics, cybercrime, or organized crime. Many countries also have their own national police forces or gendarmeries, each with its own structure and authority.

Law enforcement agencies operate under legal limits meant to protect individual rights. In many places, officers must have probable cause or a warrant before making certain searches or arrests, and their conduct is subject to oversight by courts, internal review boards, civilian commissions, and the media. The balance between effective policing and respect for civil liberties is an ongoing subject of public debate.

In short, law enforcement is the system of institutions and officials responsible for keeping society safe and making sure the law is applied in daily life.
