There is nothing unusual about finding Tim and Eric, or any other comedian, unfunny, and everyone is entitled to their own sense of what makes them laugh.

Supplements are unlikely to be a major part of recovery. No supplement has been shown in good clinical trials to restore memory, retrieval, or motor skills after a stroke. Most of the meaningful recovery comes from the brain's natural rewiring in the first several months, and that is driven mainly by rehabilitation: physical, occupational, and speech therapy, and cognitive exercises that are practiced consistently. Intensive, repeated practice of the specific skills you want back is the most effective tool available.

A few supplements have some research behind them, though the results are modest or mixed. Citicoline has shown small benefits for stroke recovery in some studies and is sometimes used in Europe and Asia. Omega-3 fatty acids may support overall brain and vascular health, but evidence for stroke recovery is inconsistent. Vitamin D and B vitamins are worth checking with a blood test, since correcting a deficiency is useful, but taking them when levels are normal has not been shown to help. Ginkgo biloba is popular for memory, but large trials have not shown benefit, and it has been linked to seizures and bleeding in some reports.

Safety matters a great deal here. After coiling, the patient is often on antiplatelet medication such as aspirin or clopidogrel, and fish oil, ginkgo, vitamin E, turmeric, and garlic supplements can add to bleeding risk. St. John's wort can reduce the effectiveness of many medications, including some anti-seizure drugs and blood thinners. Any supplement should be cleared with the neurologist or neurosurgeon, and a pharmacist can check for interactions with the current prescriptions.

The things with the strongest evidence for protecting the brain after this kind of event are controlling blood pressure, cholesterol, and blood sugar, avoiding smoking and excess alcohol, regular aerobic exercise as cleared by the medical team, good sleep, a Mediterranean-style diet, and treating any depression, which is common after stroke and can worsen memory and motivation. Keeping the seizure medication schedule consistent and reporting any changes in seizure pattern promptly is also essential. Ask the care team for a referral to outpatient rehabilitation and neuropsychology testing, which can pinpoint specific memory and motor deficits and guide targeted therapy.

Emerging technologies are technologies that are currently being developed or have only recently become available, and whose full potential, practical uses, and social impact are still uncertain. The label is relative and shifts over time. Something that counted as emerging a few decades ago, such as the commercial internet, is now simply part of everyday infrastructure, while fields like quantum computing or certain forms of gene editing still sit firmly in the emerging category.

Researchers who study the topic usually point to a handful of shared characteristics. These technologies tend to be radically novel, meaning they depend on new principles or combine existing knowledge in unfamiliar ways. They grow relatively fast, though sometimes unevenly, with periods of hype followed by disappointment and then more steady progress. They are also marked by uncertainty and ambiguity: it is not clear how they will be used, who will adopt them, what rules will govern them, or what side effects they will produce. Finally, they often have the potential to be disruptive, changing industries, labor markets, or the way people live and communicate.

Commonly cited examples include artificial intelligence and machine learning, especially generative models; biotechnology such as CRISPR gene editing and mRNA therapies; quantum computing; advanced robotics and autonomous vehicles; renewable energy and battery technologies, including next-generation storage and fusion research; nanotechnology and new materials; blockchain and related distributed systems; augmented and virtual reality; the Internet of Things; and space technologies such as reusable rockets and satellite constellations. Many of these overlap and reinforce each other, as when AI accelerates drug discovery or robotics research.

Emerging technologies matter because they can drive economic growth, solve long-standing problems in medicine, energy, and transportation, and shift the balance of power between companies and countries. They also raise difficult questions. Issues like privacy, bias, job displacement, security risks, environmental costs, and unequal access often appear before laws and norms are ready. This gap is why governments, companies, and researchers invest in technology assessment and foresight, trying to anticipate consequences early enough to guide development responsibly.

It is also worth remembering that predictions about emerging technologies are frequently wrong. Some that seem promising fade away, while others take far longer than expected to mature or end up being used in ways their inventors never imagined. For that reason, the term is best understood not as a fixed list but as a description of a stage in a technology's life, when it is promising, unsettled, and still taking shape.

Joe's Crab Shack is owned by Landry's, Inc., the Houston-based restaurant and hospitality company controlled by billionaire Tilman Fertitta. Landry's acquired the chain in 2017 after its previous owner, Ignite Restaurant Group, filed for bankruptcy and sold off its brands.

That purchase was actually a return to familiar territory, since Landry's had operated Joe's Crab Shack in its earlier years before selling it to Ignite in 2006. Under Fertitta's ownership, the chain sits alongside many other Landry's brands, including Rainforest Cafe, Bubba Gump Shrimp Co., Saltgrass Steak House, and Morton's The Steakhouse.

Ownership details can change over time through sales or restructuring, so if you need the most current information for business or legal purposes, it's worth checking a recent news source or the company's official website.

Optimal control theory is a branch of applied mathematics that deals with finding the best way to control a dynamical system over time. A dynamical system is anything whose state changes as time passes, such as a rocket moving through the atmosphere, a chemical reactor, an economy, or a population of animals. Optimal control asks which inputs or decisions should be applied to such a system so that some measure of performance is as good as possible, whether that means minimizing fuel use, reaching a target in the shortest time, maximizing profit, or keeping a process stable at the lowest cost.

The theory rests on three basic ingredients. The first is a mathematical model of the system, usually a set of differential or difference equations that describe how the state evolves in response to the control inputs. The second is a control variable, the quantity the decision-maker can choose at each moment, which may be constrained by physical or practical limits such as maximum thrust or valve openings. The third is a cost function or objective, which assigns a numerical penalty or reward to trajectories of the system, often combining an accumulated cost over time with a terminal cost at the end.

Several classical methods solve these problems. The calculus of variations, developed in the eighteenth century, provided early tools for optimizing functionals. Pontryagin's maximum principle, formulated in the 1950s by a Soviet team led by Lev Pontryagin, gives necessary conditions for optimality by introducing an auxiliary function called the costate and a Hamiltonian that must be maximized along the optimal path. Richard Bellman's dynamic programming offers another approach, based on the principle of optimality, which leads to the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation, a partial differential equation whose solution yields the optimal cost from any initial state. Numerical methods, such as direct collocation and shooting methods, are widely used when closed-form solutions are unavailable.

The theory has many practical applications. It guides spacecraft trajectory design, such as the planning of lunar transfer orbits, and it underpins the design of autopilots for aircraft and missiles. In engineering, it informs chemical process control and robotics. In economics, it is used to model optimal investment, resource extraction, and taxation over time. In medicine and biology, it helps design drug dosing schedules and models of disease treatment. Closely related fields include model predictive control, which repeatedly solves finite-horizon optimal control problems in real time, and reinforcement learning, which can be seen as a data-driven relative of dynamic programming.

Bayesian optimization is a strategy for finding the maximum or minimum of a function that is expensive to evaluate, when you cannot easily compute its gradient and often know nothing about its internal structure. Typical examples include tuning the hyperparameters of a machine learning model, where each trial may require hours of training, designing a physical experiment, or choosing parameters for a chemical process or an engineering simulation. In these settings you can only afford a limited number of evaluations, so each one needs to be chosen carefully.

The method works by building a cheap statistical model of the unknown function and using that model to decide where to evaluate next. The model is called a surrogate, and the most common choice is a Gaussian process, though random forests and Bayesian neural networks are also used. After each evaluation, the surrogate is updated using Bayes' rule, combining a prior belief about what the function looks like with the observed data to produce a posterior. This posterior gives, for any untested input, both a predicted value and a measure of uncertainty about that prediction. Points near previously observed ones have low uncertainty, while regions far from any observation have high uncertainty.

The second key ingredient is an acquisition function, which converts the surrogate's predictions and uncertainties into a score for how promising each candidate point is. The central idea is balancing exploitation, meaning sampling where the model predicts good values, against exploration, meaning sampling where the model is uncertain and might be hiding something better. Popular acquisition functions include expected improvement, which measures how much better than the current best result you expect a point to be, probability of improvement, and upper confidence bound, which favors points with high predicted value plus a bonus for uncertainty. Because the acquisition function is cheap to compute, it can be optimized thoroughly with standard methods to select the next point.

The overall loop is simple. You start with a few initial evaluations, fit the surrogate, maximize the acquisition function to choose the next input, evaluate the true function there, add the result to the data, and repeat until your budget runs out. The best point found is then returned.

Bayesian optimization tends to be much more sample-efficient than grid search or random search, which is its main appeal. It does have limitations. Gaussian processes scale poorly with large numbers of observations, and the method becomes harder in very high-dimensional spaces, typically beyond a few dozen dimensions. It also depends on modeling assumptions, such as smoothness, that may not hold. Extensions address many of these issues, including approaches for parallel evaluations, noisy measurements, constraints, categorical variables, and multiple objectives.

The American Civil War, which lasted from 1861 to 1865, pitted the northern states, called the Union, against the southern states that broke away to form the Confederacy. At its core, the war arose from a dispute over slavery and over whether individual states had the right to permit or prohibit it. Slavery had been a divisive question in the country since its beginning, and for decades the friction between the two regions kept growing. In the North, the abolition movement, which aimed to end slavery, grew stronger, whereas the South, whose economy depended heavily on enslaved labor, vigorously defended the practice. Several important events and controversies in the years before the war deepened the divide between North and South, among them the Missouri Compromise of 1820, the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850, the Kansas-Nebraska Act of 1854, and the Supreme Court's 1857 ruling in the Dred Scott case. In the end, the southern states viewed the 1860 election of Abraham Lincoln, who opposed extending slavery into new territories, as a danger to them. Several of them responded by leaving the Union and establishing the Confederacy. The war itself started in 1861, when Confederate troops attacked Fort Sumter in South Carolina.

Menstrual cycles naturally differ in how many days bleeding lasts and how heavy the flow is, and periods often become lighter as a woman ages. Still, if you notice changes in your cycle or experience unusual symptoms, you should consult a healthcare provider who can assess your situation and offer guidance. Many things can influence your cycle, such as stress, shifts in body weight or physical activity, certain medications, and underlying health conditions. A provider can work out what is behind any changes and recommend suitable treatment or management. Using contraception is also important to prevent unplanned pregnancy, even when your periods are irregular or light.

A cough combined with pain beneath the right shoulder blade can stem from a number of causes. Among the more common are the following. Bronchitis is an inflammation of the bronchial tubes and may lead to coughing as well as chest pain. Pneumonia, a lung infection, can bring on a cough, chest pain, and trouble breathing. Pleurisy refers to inflammation of the membrane lining the lungs and chest cavity, and it can produce chest pain and coughing. Asthma is a long-term respiratory disorder that may result in coughing and breathing difficulty. Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) occurs when stomach acid travels back up into the esophagus, causing heartburn and, at times, chest pain and a cough. It is important to have a doctor determine what is behind your cough and pain. Nolotil (metamizole) is a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) used to ease pain, yet it carries the potential for serious side effects, such as a greater risk of bleeding and ulcers. You should not take Nolotil unless you have first consulted a doctor.

Titanium was commonly used for jaw surgery hardware by the mid-1990s. Titanium and titanium alloys, such as Ti-6Al-4V, had become the standard for maxillofacial plates and screws by then, largely replacing earlier stainless steel and cobalt-chrome (Vitallium) systems. Some surgeons still used stainless steel in 1996, though, so titanium isn't certain. Either way, the metals used in jaw plates and screws are nearly always non-ferromagnetic or only weakly magnetic, and these materials are generally considered safe for MRI. Even so, the material should be confirmed rather than assumed.

The most reliable way to find out is to ask for your surgical records. Contact the oral and maxillofacial surgeon who performed the operation, or the hospital where it was done, and request the operative report or implant record. Surgeons often note the hardware manufacturer and material, and some hospitals keep implant logs. If you were given an implant card or sticker at the time, check your papers for it. Your dentist or oral surgeon's office may also be able to find the information in old files. Existing X-rays or CT scans of your jaw can show whether the hardware is still present, though they cannot reliably identify the metal.

Regarding your MRI, you should not assume you're disqualified. Most MRI facilities screen for implants by asking what you have and, when needed, reviewing the implant's material and documentation. Plates and screws in the jaw are usually not a barrier to a breast MRI. The breast is far from the jaw, so any metal-related imaging artifact should not interfere with the scan. Tell the imaging center about the surgery when you schedule, and bring whatever records you can find. If the facility needs more certainty, the radiologist can make the decision with the surgeon's information. Your situation is very likely fine, and the MRI you need should not be delayed because of the 1996 surgery.

Acquiring business credit is a crucial move for many small enterprises, since it opens doors to financing and helps build a company's credit reputation. Several actions can help you apply for and obtain business credit. First, create a business credit profile: applying requires a credit file for your company, which you can set up by registering with credit bureaus like Dun & Bradstreet, Experian, and Equifax. Securing a business license and a tax identification number can also help establish this profile. Second, keep personal and business credit apart, both to safeguard your personal credit score and to create a distinct credit record for the company. Third, open a dedicated business bank account, which separates personal and company finances and simplifies tracking your business's transactions and credit activity. Fourth, develop a solid credit history by paying bills promptly, using credit wisely, and maintaining low balances, all of which improve your odds of approval. Fifth, select the appropriate credit product. Options include credit cards, loans, and lines of credit, and the right choice depends on your needs and on factors like interest rates, fees, and repayment terms. Sixth, prepare your paperwork in advance. Applications typically call for financial statements, tax returns, and a business plan, and having these ready streamlines the process. Finally, compare offers from several lenders to find the most favorable terms, and read the conditions of any product carefully before committing. By taking these steps and actively managing your business credit, you can improve your chances of approval and secure the funding needed to grow your business.

Yes, computers have limits, and some of them are really interesting. Imagine you have a very fast helper who follows instructions perfectly, but only the instructions you write down exactly. A computer is like that. It can do lots of things very quickly, like adding numbers, playing music, or showing you pictures. But there are some things it just cannot do, no matter how good it gets.

One big limit is that a computer can only follow clear rules. If something is confusing, mixed up, or hard to describe step by step, the computer gets stuck. For example, it is hard for a computer to truly understand how you feel or to know what a joke means the way a person does, because those things don't come with simple rules.

Another limit is that some questions have no answer a computer can find in a fixed amount of time. Think about a puzzle that would take a computer longer than the whole age of the universe to solve. The computer is not broken, it just cannot finish in any useful way.

There is also a famous kind of problem that computers can never solve for every possible case. Imagine trying to write a program that can look at any other program and always tell you whether it will finish or run forever. Smart mathematicians proved that no computer program can do this perfectly for every case. It is like asking someone to predict every single outcome of a game they've never played, and no one can do that in general.

Finally, computers don't have feelings, wishes, or a sense of what is right and wrong. They can copy the words people use about these things, but they don't truly experience them.

So computers are amazing at following clear, careful instructions, but they cannot understand everything, feel things, or solve every puzzle in the world.

Belize sits along the eastern edge of Central America. Mexico lies to its north, while Guatemala borders it on both the west and the south, and the Caribbean Sea washes its eastern shore. The nation is recognized for its warm tropical weather, lovely coastline, and varied cultural heritage, shaped by indigenous, Maya, and Afro-Caribbean traditions. English is the official language, but Spanish, Kriol, and several indigenous tongues are spoken as well. Belmopan serves as the capital, though it is not the largest city.

Mortgage points, also called discount points, are fees you pay to the lender at closing in exchange for a lower interest rate on your loan. One point equals one percent of the loan amount. So on a $300,000 mortgage, one point would cost $3,000.

The trade-off works like this: by paying points upfront, you reduce your monthly payment and the total interest you pay over the life of the loan. Buying points makes the most sense if you plan to keep the mortgage long enough to recoup the upfront cost through monthly savings, a point where you've "broken even." Someone who plans to sell or refinance within a few years usually won't benefit much.

There's also a separate type called origination points, which are fees a lender charges for processing the loan. These don't lower your rate. They're simply part of the lender's compensation, and they're sometimes negotiable.

When comparing loan offers, it helps to look at the annual percentage rate (APR) as well as the interest rate and points, since the APR reflects the total cost of borrowing including fees. Your lender can show you the exact trade-off for different point options.

Shiva is the seven-day mourning period in Jewish tradition that follows the death of a close relative. People sitting shiva usually take it easy: they sit on low stools or benches and let visitors come by to offer condolences. Mourners generally skip work, leisure, and other distractions for the week. Many recite the Mourner's Kaddish, which is a prayer praising God, and some also say other traditional prayers or spend time studying Torah for comfort. Friends and family often bring food over, since the mourners usually aren't up to cooking for themselves. Customs can vary quite a bit from person to person and community to community, so the best move is to follow whatever the mourners and their family want.

Okay, so an LED (light emitting diode) works quite differently from the old filament bulb. A filament bulb runs electricity through a thin wire, the filament, which gets so hot it glows. That glow is the light. An LED skips the wire entirely. It's built from two layers of semiconductor material, and when current flows through them, the material gives off light. People call this electroluminescence. The nice part is that LEDs use way less electricity for the same brightness, and they last a lot longer since there's no filament sitting there waiting to burn out.

Targeted advertising means tailoring ads to a particular group of people or a defined audience. Its aim is to reach consumers who are most likely to be drawn to a given product or service, judged by their demographics, interests, and online activity. Companies rely on data and analytics to pinpoint and divide up their audience, and that information can be gathered from many places, including customer databases, social media profiles, and website analytics. Armed with these insights, advertisers can build ads that feel more relevant and compelling to the people they want to reach, which raises the odds of a sale or other desired action. These ads can appear through search engines, social media platforms, and websites, in formats such as banner ads, sponsored posts, or personalized emails. Compared with traditional untargeted advertising, the main advantage is greater effectiveness in reaching and engaging the right people. It can also lower advertising costs, since companies can direct their money and effort toward a specific segment instead of attempting to reach a vague, broad crowd. Still, businesses must be open about their practices and respect consumer privacy when they gather and use data for this purpose.

Emergency contraception pills, often called "morning-after pills" or "Plan B," are meant to be taken as soon as possible following unprotected sex or a failure of regular contraception, in order to lower the chance of an unintended pregnancy. They are generally safe, but they should not be relied on as an ongoing method of birth control. If unprotected sex occurred within the last 72 hours (3 days), taking the pills can reduce your risk of becoming pregnant. Once more than 72 hours have passed, the pills will no longer work. If you have already used one dose and then have unprotected sex again, you may take another dose. Still, repeated doses within a short span are not advised, since they may offer no added benefit and can bring side effects such as nausea, vomiting, and irregular bleeding. It is important to use a dependable method of contraception, such as condoms, which protect against both pregnancy and sexually transmitted infections. If unintended pregnancy worries you, talk with a healthcare provider about your options for regular contraception. They can help you choose a method that is both safe and effective for you.

When colleges look at applicants, they're trying to figure out who'll actually fit in at their school and add something to the campus. The admission essay (some people call it the personal statement) is one of the main ways they get a feel for you beyond your grades. So the whole point is to show the committee who you are and why you'd belong there.

Here's what they're usually hoping to see. First, your personality. They want to meet you as a person, so let that come through instead of writing something stiff and generic. Second, your goals and interests. What are you into? What do you want to study, and why? Third, your experiences. Maybe something that really shaped you, like a community service project, a job, or just something personal that stuck with you.

Your writing matters too, since the essay is a chance to show you can write. Keep the grammar and punctuation clean, and aim for something clear that's actually fun to read. And then there's fit. Why this school in particular? What is it about the programs, the campus, or the community that clicks with you?

At the end of the day, the essay is your shot at showing them who you are and why you'd be a good match. Be honest and genuine about it, and lean on your real strengths and experiences instead of trying to sound like someone else.

Honestly, there's no single "best" Roth IRA for a 21-year-old with $1,500. It really comes down to what you want out of it, how much risk you're comfortable with, and what the provider actually offers. A few things are worth checking before you pick one.

Fees come first. Low fees matter a lot because they chip away at your returns year after year, and with a small balance they can hurt even more.

Next, look at the investment options. You'll want a provider that lets you hold a good mix of stocks, bonds, and mutual funds so you can spread your money around and cut down on risk.

Also, make sure the app or website is easy to use. If managing your account feels like a chore, you're less likely to keep up with it.

Finally, check out customer service. You'll probably have questions early on, so it helps to know you can get a real person on the phone or a quick answer when you need one.

It's worth comparing a few providers before you commit. And if you want a second opinion on your specific situation, a fee-only financial planner can help you map out a strategy.

An artificial brain is basically a machine built to copy what the human brain does: learning, solving problems, making decisions, and taking in the world around it. People use the term loosely for pretty much any advanced AI meant to act smart in a human-like way. There's no single recipe for building one, so you'll see all sorts of approaches. The main tools right now are machine learning, neural networks, and natural language processing. Honestly, the whole idea is still mostly theoretical, but AI has moved fast in the last few years, so it feels closer than it did a decade ago. People talk about it being useful in robotics, healthcare, and education. Still, if we're going to build something that can think like us, we'd better think hard about the ethics of it too.

So the multivariate normal, also called the multivariate Gaussian, is just a distribution over a random vector where all the components are jointly continuous and normally distributed. Think of it as the one-variable normal curve grown up to handle several variables at once. Its density, with mean vector $\boldsymbol{\mu}$ and covariance matrix $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$, looks like this: $$f(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{1}{(2\pi)^{n/2}|\boldsymbol{\Sigma}|^{1/2}}\exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})^\top\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})\right)$$ Here $\mathbf{x} = (x_1, \dots, x_n)^\top$ is the random vector, $n$ is how many components it has, and $|\boldsymbol{\Sigma}|$ is the determinant of the covariance matrix. The mean vector tells you where the distribution is centered, and the covariance matrix tells you its shape, like how stretched or tilted it is. People use it all the time in statistics and machine learning because it's flexible enough to capture lots of different relationships between variables. It also shows up a lot in Bayesian work, since the posterior for many models ends up being roughly multivariate normal.

Great question! Think of your skin like a set of different playgrounds, and each cream is made to fit the playground it's built for.

Your face, hands, feet, and body have different skin. Face skin is thin and sensitive, and it works hard, so face creams are usually gentler, lighter, and often include extras like ingredients to help with wrinkles, oil, or redness. Hand cream is often thicker and richer, because hands get washed a lot and need a strong protective layer. Foot cream is usually the thickest of all, since the skin on your heels is very thick and dry and needs heavy-duty softening. Body cream is often a middle option, a bit lighter than foot cream but made to cover large areas of skin without being too greasy.

So yes, a lot of the difference is how much moisture and how heavy the cream feels. But it's not only that. The face creams usually avoid ingredients that might irritate delicate skin, and foot creams often contain things like urea or salicylic acid that help break down rough, hard skin.

Can you use them interchangeably? Often you can, and nothing terrible will happen. A thick foot cream on your face might feel greasy and could clog pores for some people. A light face cream on your heels might not be enough to soften them. So you can swap them in a pinch, but each one works best in its own playground.

The seasons are caused by the tilt of Earth's axis, not by its distance from the Sun. Earth's rotational axis is tilted about 23.4 degrees relative to the plane of its orbit around the Sun. As Earth travels around the Sun over the course of a year, this tilt keeps pointing in the same direction in space, so at different points in the orbit, one hemisphere is tilted toward the Sun while the other is tilted away.

When a hemisphere leans toward the Sun, sunlight strikes it more directly, and the days are longer, so it receives more concentrated energy and warms up. That is summer for that hemisphere. Six months later, the same hemisphere is tilted away from the Sun, sunlight arrives at a lower angle and is spread over a larger area, and the days are shorter, producing winter. The opposite hemisphere experiences the reverse, which is why Australia has summer in December while the United Northern Hemisphere is in winter.

Earth is actually closest to the Sun in early January, during the Northern Hemisphere's winter, which shows that distance plays little role in the seasonal cycle.

Yes, balance transfers can be used to avoid paying interest on major credit cards. A balance transfer means moving debt from one credit card to another that charges a lower interest rate. This can save you money if you carry a costly, high-interest balance and cannot clear it in full every month. To take advantage of this, you should look for a credit card offering a promotional 0% rate on balance transfers. Such offers typically last a limited time, often somewhere between the first 6 and 18 months after you open the account. While the promotion runs, the transferred balance accrues no interest, provided you keep up with your minimum payments on schedule. Completing a transfer requires the account details of both your current card and the card receiving the balance. You may also have to pay a transfer fee, which is usually a percentage of the amount moved. That fee is often waived or lowered if the transfer happens soon after opening the new account. Keep in mind that balance transfers are only a temporary fix. When the promotional window closes, the rate on the transferred amount will likely rise, and new purchases on the card may begin accruing interest as well. The most reliable way to avoid interest altogether is to pay your balances in full each month and borrow only what you can comfortably repay.

Your brain has a part that makes words for you to think with, and it's a bit like a little talker that works inside you. Most of that talking happens in the front part of your brain, which is good at planning and speaking, so the front of your head gets some of the credit. But the feeling of where the voice sits is a guess your brain makes, not a map it reads. When a sound comes from outside, your ears notice which side it reached first and how loud it is, so you know where it is. Your inner voice doesn't send any sound to your ears, so your brain just picks a vague spot, often near the front or top of your head where thinking feels like it happens.

You can't move it because it isn't a real object you can point at. You can change what you pay attention to, and that can change how the voice feels, but the location is more like a feeling than a dial you can turn. Your brain also tags the voice as "mine" by sending itself a copy of the instructions it used to make the words, which quiets it so it doesn't sound like someone else talking. That's why it feels like it's inside you, but not exactly in a spot you can steer.

So no, it isn't a lack of discipline. The front of your brain helps, but many parts work together to make and place that voice, and none of them are controlled by willpower over where it seems to sit.

Taking two emergency contraceptive pills (i-Pill contains levonorgestrel 1.5 mg) in the same week is not dangerous. It will not cause serious or lasting harm, and it will not affect your future fertility. The main effects you may notice are temporary: nausea, headache, tiredness, breast tenderness, lower abdominal cramps, dizziness, and most commonly a change in your next period. It may come early, late, or be heavier, lighter, or have spotting beforehand. Because you took it twice, these irregularities may be a bit more noticeable than usual.

The bigger issue is that the pill is less reliable than people assume, and especially so when repeated. It works best when taken within 72 hours (ideally 24 hours) of sex, and it only protects against the one act of sex it follows. It does not give ongoing protection. Sex on the 20th and the pill on the 22nd was reasonably timed, but that pill would not protect you from sex on the 24th. Your second pill on the 26th was two days after that, so it should still help for that act, but effectiveness drops the longer you wait. Also, if you have had sex more than once between the pills, the chance of pregnancy is not zero. Emergency pills reduce the risk but do not eliminate it.

Because of this, I would suggest the following. If your period is more than a week late, take a urine pregnancy test. Do not rely on the pill alone as your regular method, since it is less effective than regular contraception and hormonally heavier. Consider a regular method such as condoms, or talk to a doctor about birth control pills, an IUD, or other options. Condoms also protect against sexually transmitted infections, which the pill does not. If you want extra reassurance about infections, a check-up can be arranged.

See a doctor sooner if you have severe lower abdominal pain, very heavy bleeding, fainting, or vomiting within two hours of taking a pill (in which case the dose may need repeating). Severe one-sided pain with a missed period should be checked promptly to rule out an ectopic pregnancy, which is rare but important.

Finally, please do not feel afraid or guilty. This is a common situation, and the safest step now is to plan reliable contraception going forward so you are not relying on repeated emergency pills.

Okay so if you want to figure out what interest rate you'd need to break even against an insurance policy, you basically need three things: how much you're putting in, how long you're holding it, and what the policy costs. Plug those into this: required interest rate = (insurance cost / investment amount) * (1 / number of years).

Say you've got $10,000 invested for 5 years and the policy runs $500 a year. That works out to ($500 / $10,000) * (1 / 5) = 0.05, so you'd need about a 5% annual return just to cover the premiums. Keep in mind this ignores taxes and fees, which will eat into your returns, and it assumes the policy stays in force the whole time. Also think about risk. A riskier investment might swing hard enough to wipe out the gains you were counting on, so don't just look at the number on paper.

The Clay Mathematics Institute (CMI) has named seven mathematical problems, known as the Millennium Prize Problems, that it regards as among the most significant open questions in the field. The problems were chosen for their difficulty and for their importance across many branches of mathematics and science. A prize of one million dollars is offered for a correct solution to each. The first problem asks whether every question whose yes-or-no answer can be verified quickly by a computer can also be answered quickly by one. The Hodge Conjecture concerns the topology of algebraic varieties, which are geometric shapes that emerge from algebraic geometry. The Poincaré Conjecture addresses the topology of three-dimensional manifolds, objects that can be understood as higher-dimensional analogues of surfaces. The Riemann Hypothesis deals with how prime numbers, the whole numbers greater than one that have no divisors other than one and themselves, are distributed. The Yang-Mills Existence and Mass Gap problem concerns the behavior of subatomic particles, in particular the force that binds quarks together within protons and neutrons. The Navier-Stokes Equations address the behavior of fluids, including how they move and the forces acting on them. The Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer Conjecture concerns elliptic curves, mathematical objects that can be used to model certain kinds of equations. As of 2021, only one of the seven problems, the Poincaré Conjecture, had been solved, so six remain open, not just the P versus NP problem as the original text stated.

Dave Mason wrote "Feelin' Alright" when he was with Traffic, and the band first recorded it for their 1968 self-titled album. It's gone on to become a classic rock staple, and tons of artists have covered it over the years. Joe Cocker's version was the big one, hitting it out of the park in 1969.

To keep your weight steady, your calorie intake has to match the energy you expend through everyday movement and exercise. Two people who share the same height, age, and activity level should therefore require the same daily calories to stay at their current weight. If, however, one person weighs 60 kg and another weighs 80 kg, their calorie requirements will probably differ, since a heavier person generally has a higher metabolic rate and therefore burns more energy to maintain their weight. Several factors shape how many calories someone needs to hold their weight. Age matters because metabolism tends to slow as we grow older, so older individuals often need fewer calories. Gender plays a role as well, since men usually have a higher metabolic rate than women and may need to consume more. Height is another factor, as taller people often have greater muscle mass and a higher metabolism, which can mean a larger calorie need. Finally, activity level is significant: those who are more physically active burn more energy through exercise and movement, so they generally need more calories. In short, two people of the same height, age, and activity level can eat the same number of calories and keep the same weight even if their body weights differ. When height, age, or activity level differ, however, their calorie needs may differ as well.

Imagine a big playground where kids trade candy. In the US, banks wanted to give out lots of loans to buy houses, even to families who probably couldn't pay them back. These risky loans were called subprime loans. Many came with low payments at first that jumped up later, and people figured house prices would keep rising, so if trouble came they could just sell the house for more.

Then the banks did something clever but dangerous. They bundled thousands of these loans together into packages and sold slices to other banks and investors all over the world. Rating agencies stamped many of these packages as very safe, even though they were full of shaky loans. It was like mixing a few rotten apples into a basket, calling it a basket of great apples, and selling it to everyone. Banks also borrowed huge amounts of money to buy more of these packages, so they had very little of their own money cushioning them if something went wrong.

Around 2006 and 2007, house prices stopped rising and began falling. People who couldn't pay their loans couldn't sell their houses for enough either, so they lost their homes. The packages lost value, and nobody knew which banks were holding the rotten apples. So banks stopped trusting and lending to each other. In 2008 the investment bank Lehman Brothers collapsed, and panic spread. Credit froze, meaning businesses and people couldn't easily borrow.

In the US, the consequences were severe. Millions lost their homes and jobs, the economy shrank sharply in what became known as the Great Recession, and the government spent hundreds of billions bailing out banks and other big firms like the insurer AIG. Stock markets plunged and many families lost savings. Recovery was slow, and anger at banks and bailouts fed political frustration for years.

Europe got hurt in two ways. First, many European banks had bought those American packages or had borrowed heavily themselves, so they suffered losses too. Some needed rescues, such as in Britain, Germany, Belgium, Ireland, and others. Second, the crisis exposed weaknesses at home. Countries like Ireland and Spain had their own housing bubbles that burst. Greece, Portugal, and others had borrowed a lot and suddenly investors worried they couldn't repay. This became the eurozone debt crisis starting around 2010. Countries that share the euro couldn't print their own money or devalue it to recover, so they received bailout loans from the EU, the European Central Bank, and the IMF, in return for austerity, meaning budget cuts and tax rises. That made recessions deeper, pushed unemployment very high, especially among young people in Greece and Spain, and caused lasting political tension between richer northern and poorer southern countries.

Afterward, governments tightened bank rules so banks must hold more of their own money as a cushion, and central banks kept interest rates very low for years to help growth. The big lesson is that when everyone takes risks they don't understand, and everyone is tied together, one problem can topple the whole playground.

Inductive logic programming (ILP) is a subfield of AI and machine learning about building systems that can automatically pull logical rules out of data. The goal is pretty straightforward: learn rules you can use to make predictions or sort new examples based on some input features. Those rules usually live in a logical language like first-order or propositional logic, and they get learned from examples or training data through an inductive process. The core idea is to combine logical reasoning with induction. Induction just means inferring general patterns from specific observations, so in ILP you feed the system a batch of training examples and it tries to come up with a set of logical rules that work on new cases too. People have used ILP for all sorts of things, including natural language processing, biomedical informatics, and robotics. It's also been used to build expert and knowledge-based systems in fields like medicine and biology.

There are several reasons someone might reasonably decide against an umbrella policy, and most of them come down to cost, need, and practicality.

The most obvious is cost. Umbrella policies are relatively inexpensive for the coverage they provide, often a few hundred dollars a year for a million dollars of protection, but that is still an ongoing expense. A person on a tight budget may feel the money is better spent on higher-priority needs like emergency savings, retirement contributions, or adequate primary coverage.

A second reason is having few assets to protect. Umbrella insurance exists mainly to shield savings, home equity, investments, and future earnings from a large judgment. Someone with little net worth, few prospects of being a lucrative target, and perhaps limited wages that could be garnished may feel there is little to lose. In some situations, the person is effectively "judgment proof," so the policy offers less value to them.

Third, the policy has requirements and limits that can make it less appealing. Insurers typically require minimum liability limits on underlying auto and homeowners policies, such as 250,000 dollars per person for auto, and raising those limits can increase premiums. Umbrella coverage also has exclusions. It generally does not cover intentional acts, business activities, professional liability, or damage to your own property, so a person with those exposures would need other policies anyway. Some people feel the exclusions make it less useful than it first appears.

Fourth, there is the matter of perceived risk. Some people believe their chance of causing a catastrophic accident or being sued is very low, particularly if they have no pool, no dog, no teenage drivers, and a quiet lifestyle. They may view the premium as paying for an unlikely event. People also sometimes rely on state protections that exempt certain assets, such as homestead exemptions or retirement accounts, and conclude they are already partly shielded.

Finally, there are practical factors. Insurers can decline or surcharge applicants with poor driving records, multiple claims, or high-risk exposures, so some people cannot get affordable coverage. Others simply have not considered it, find the topic confusing, or already have sufficiently high limits on their primary policies. Still, for anyone with meaningful assets or income, many advisors suggest that the low price relative to the protection makes the policy worth serious consideration.

Malware, viruses, and trojans are made mostly by people who want to make money or cause trouble. Some are criminals who run online scams, steal passwords, or lock up people's computers and demand a ransom to unlock them. Others are hackers who do it for fun, to show off, or to spy on someone. Some are paid by companies or governments to build tools for spying or attacking other countries. Most of the bad software you hear about comes from criminal gangs, often in groups that work like businesses, with workers who write the code, sell it, and share profits.

They spread it in many ways. A common one is tricking people with fake emails, text messages, or websites that ask you to click a link or open a file. Some spread through downloads from shady websites, pirated games, or fake apps. Others sneak into computers through weaknesses in software that hasn't been updated. Once a bad program is on one computer, it can sometimes copy itself to others on the same network or to people in the same email contacts.

As for McAfee, it is not one of the makers. McAfee is a company that makes antivirus software, which is a tool that tries to find and stop the bad programs. So the bad guys are the hackers and criminal groups, and the good guys who try to catch them include companies like McAfee, along with many other security firms and researchers. Think of it like germs and doctors: the germs are not made by the doctors, even though the doctors work hard to stop them.

Index funds handle dividends in a fairly simple way: the stocks they hold pay dividends, and the fund collects those payments and passes them along to shareholders, usually on a quarterly schedule. You can take the money as cash, or you can set the fund to reinvest the dividends automatically, which buys additional shares and lets your holdings compound over time. Most long-term investors reinvest, since it puts the money back to work without any action on their part.

A few details are worth knowing. Dividends are taxable in a regular brokerage account even if you reinvest them, so you'll owe tax on them each year, with qualified dividends generally taxed at the lower long-term capital gains rate. Inside tax-advantaged accounts like an IRA or 401(k), that tax drag doesn't apply in the same way. Also, the dividend yield on broad index funds is typically modest, often in the range of about 1 to 2 percent a year depending on the market, so dividends are usually a smaller part of your return than price appreciation, though they still add up over decades. Finally, the fund's expense ratio is already netted out of the figures you see, so you don't pay it separately from the dividend payments.

The defensive line in football is commonly called the defensive line, or simply the "D-line." It is the group of players who line up closest to the opposing offensive line at the start of a play, and it typically includes defensive ends and defensive tackles. Their main job is to rush the quarterback, stop the run, and disrupt the offense at the line of scrimmage. In some formations, a nose tackle, who lines up directly over the center, is also considered part of this unit.

So a pleural effusion is basically when extra fluid builds up in the space between the lung lining and the chest wall. That fluid can crowd the lungs and make it harder to breathe. Common culprits include infections, heart failure, cancer, and kidney or liver disease. You'll usually notice shortness of breath, coughing, chest pain, or just feeling worn out. Doctors typically start with a physical exam, then order a chest X-ray or CT scan to confirm it. Treatment often means draining the fluid with a procedure called thoracentesis, and treating whatever's causing it. Sometimes surgery is needed if the underlying problem can't be fixed any other way.

A grist mill stone is a flat, circular stone that is used to turn grain into flour. Grain is spread over the bottom stone, known as the bedstone, and the top stone, called the runner stone, rests above it. As the runner stone turns, it crushes the grain between the two surfaces. These stones are typically cut from tough, long-lasting materials like granite or quartz. Grist mills were a common sight in the countryside, where they processed grain into flour and other goods. They formed a key element of the farming economy and were essential to producing food.

A stun grenade, also called a flashbang, is basically an explosive device built to throw people off balance for a few seconds. It works by setting off a loud bang and a blinding flash of light all at once. Inside there's a small charge that goes off when it's triggered, and that's what makes the noise and light. The whole point is to startle people so badly they can't think straight or make out what's happening around them.

Usually it gets tossed into a room or an area where people are standing. The bang and flash hit anyone nearby hard, and it's pretty disorienting. How long the effects stick around varies a lot, from a few seconds to a few minutes, depending on the person and the situation.

Cops and military folks use them to get crowds under control or to grab suspects, but they've also shown up in other situations where you need to quickly knock people off their game. Just know they can seriously hurt someone if they're used carelessly.

A red spot on a newborn's tongue can have several causes. The most common harmless ones include a small blood vessel cluster (a superficial vascular lesion or capillary malformation), a tiny cyst or mucus-filled sac (such as a ranula or mucocele), a minor injury from birth or a bite, or a small tissue bump like an Epstein pearl, though those are usually white or yellowish. Infantile hemangiomas can appear on the tongue, but they are less common there than on the skin of the face or scalp.

Your description makes a hemangioma less likely, though not impossible. Infantile hemangiomas often aren't fully visible at birth, usually appear in the first few weeks, and then grow during the first several months before slowly fading. A spot that was present on day two and has stayed the same size for a month doesn't fit that pattern well. It could still be an early or slow-growing hemangioma, or it could be one of the other harmless lesions above. Only an examination can tell them apart.

If it is a hemangioma, most small ones on the tongue cause no lasting harm. The main concerns are growth that could interfere with sucking, feeding, swallowing, breathing, or later speech, and ulceration, where the surface breaks open, bleeds, or becomes painful. Treatment is often just watchful waiting, and when treatment is needed, options such as the medication propranolol are effective.

Abdominal pain, regurgitation of stomach contents, nausea, and colicky pain that have lasted three months suggest a chronic upper digestive problem. The most common causes are gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), functional dyspepsia (persistent indigestion without a structural cause), gastritis or peptic ulcer, and irritable bowel syndrome if the colicky pain is lower in the abdomen and linked to bowel habits. Gallbladder disease can also cause colicky pain, especially after fatty meals. Poor sleep is common with these conditions, since lying down or nighttime reflux worsens regurgitation, and pain itself disrupts sleep. Stress and anxiety can both cause and worsen these symptoms.

The medicines you listed are typical for this kind of problem. Tinitapride is a prokinetic that helps the stomach empty and reduces nausea and bloating. Rabeprazole (the "t.rbp" listed) is a proton pump inhibitor that lowers stomach acid and helps reflux and ulcer-type pain. The syrup you listed appears to be an antacid or acid-reducing or antispasmodic preparation, and the tablets labeled "Phycam" and "Kinpride" are less clear to me from the names alone, so please check the packaging or ask your pharmacist for their exact generic ingredients and purpose. Prescriptions like this usually run for a set period and are adjusted based on how you respond, so the exact duration should come from the doctor who prescribed them.

Because your symptoms have lasted three months, you should have a proper medical evaluation if you have not already had one. A doctor may want blood tests, a stool test, or an endoscopy to look for ulcers, infection such as H. pylori, or other problems, and an ultrasound if gallbladder disease is possible. You should seek urgent care right away if you have vomiting blood or material that looks like coffee grounds, black or bloody stools, unintended weight loss, trouble swallowing, pain that is severe or spreads to the chest or back, fever, yellowing of the skin or eyes, or difficulty breathing.

Please do not stop or change these medicines on your own. Discuss any side effects, how long you should take each one, and whether your treatment is working with your prescribing doctor or pharmacist.

A peptide sequence is the specific order in which amino acids are linked together in a peptide or protein. Amino acids are the building blocks of these molecules, and when they join through peptide bonds (a type of covalent bond formed between the carboxyl group of one amino acid and the amino group of the next), they form a chain. The sequence describes which amino acid sits at each position along that chain, starting from one end, conventionally the N-terminus (the end with a free amino group), and reading toward the C-terminus (the end with a free carboxyl group).

Because there are twenty standard amino acids, the order in which they appear can vary enormously. Even a short peptide of just five residues can take on 20 to the fifth power different arrangements, which is over three million possibilities. Each unique order produces a molecule with different chemical properties, so changing even one amino acid can alter how the peptide folds, what it binds to, and what biological function it performs.

Scientists usually write peptide sequences using either three-letter codes (such as Gly-Ala-Ser) or one-letter codes (such as GAS). The sequence is important because it largely determines the three-dimensional structure of the molecule, and that structure in turn determines its function. Knowing the sequence is therefore a key step in understanding a protein's role in the body, identifying mutations linked to disease, or designing synthetic peptides for research and medicine.

Imagine you're at a party and a song you like is playing, but you don't know its name. Shazam is like a super-smart friend who can listen for a few seconds and tell you exactly which song it is. Here's how it does that, in simple steps.

First, your phone listens to a little bit of the music through its microphone, maybe ten or fifteen seconds of it. Think of it like taking a quick photo of the sound.

Next, the app doesn't try to remember the whole song. Instead, it picks out the most special bits, like the high points where the sound is loudest or the notes that stand out the most. It turns these bits into a kind of sound fingerprint, which is a short code that's unique to that moment in the song.

Then the app sends that little fingerprint over the internet to a huge library. This library has fingerprints for millions of songs, all stored and ready to check.

The computer looks through the library very quickly and finds the fingerprint that matches yours. Even if the music is noisy, like at a party with people talking, the matching still works, because the fingerprint only keeps the strongest, most important parts.

Finally, it tells your phone the name of the song and who sings it, usually in just a few seconds.

So in short, your phone takes a sound snapshot, makes a fingerprint from it, and asks a giant song library, "Whose fingerprint is this?"

So dialysis tubes are basically tubing made from a special kind of membrane, and they're used in dialysis. That's the treatment people get when their kidneys can't clear out extra waste and fluid on their own anymore. The tubes get filled with a special solution and hooked up to a machine, and the membrane does the filtering, pulling the excess waste and fluid out of the patient's blood. Once it's cleaned up, the blood goes back into the body. You'll mostly see it used for people with kidney failure or really serious kidney damage.

I'm sorry you're dealing with pain in your shoulder and chest. Worrying that it could be a heart attack is completely natural. That said, pain in these areas has many possible sources, and many of them have nothing to do with the heart. One frequent culprit is heartburn, also called acid reflux, which happens when stomach acid travels up into the esophagus and produces a burning feeling in the chest and throat. Sometimes that discomfort also radiates into the shoulder and neck. Other potential explanations include strained or sprained muscles, nerve problems, and even stress or anxiety. However, if your chest pain is intense, comes on suddenly, or comes with symptoms like difficulty breathing, sweating, or nausea, you should get medical help immediately, since these can point to a serious problem such as a heart attack. Meanwhile, try to relax and breathe slowly and deeply, which may ease any tension or anxiety you're feeling. If heartburn seems likely, over-the-counter antacids or acid blockers may relieve your symptoms. If the pain continues or gets worse, or if you have ongoing concerns about your health, please see a healthcare professional for a proper evaluation and treatment.

Halley's Comet is next expected to reach perihelion, its closest point to the Sun, in late July 2061. It last passed through the inner solar system in 1986, and its orbit takes it around the Sun roughly every 75 to 76 years, so it will be visible from Earth again in mid-2061, though it will be most favorably placed for viewing in the Southern Hemisphere, as it was in 1986 when it appeared low in the sky for northern observers. Living in the UK does not stop you from freelancing for a company based in Switzerland. Still, several matters deserve your attention before you begin.

Taxes: Think about how your earnings will be taxed. Because you live in the UK, your income is subject to UK tax. If your services are delivered in Switzerland, though, Swiss tax may apply too. Consulting a tax specialist is wise, so that you meet the requirements of both countries' tax rules.

Legal matters: Be sure you fully understand the terms of your contract with the Swiss company, such as how and when you will be paid, how long the agreement lasts, and any other legal duties it places on you. Putting everything in a written agreement helps prevent misunderstandings.

Communication: Set up clear channels of contact with the Swiss company, particularly when you work remotely. Doing so helps you meet their expectations and lets you resolve any problems quickly.

All in all, freelancing for a Swiss company can be both satisfying and financially rewarding, but you should do your homework and make sure you follow every applicable law and regulation.

Fifth generation computers, or 5G computers as some people call them, were a class of machines developed in the 1980s and early '90s. The goal was pretty ambitious: build computers that could handle tasks normally needing human-level smarts. They were supposed to reason, learn, and adapt to new situations, kind of the way people think through problems.

What set them apart was their use of AI techniques like expert systems, natural language processing, and machine learning. That let them tackle jobs that demand a lot of knowledge and decision-making. They were also built to be highly parallel, so they could juggle lots of tasks at once and chew through big piles of data without breaking a sweat.

A couple of well-known examples: the Japanese Fifth Generation Computer Systems (FGCS) project, a research effort funded by the Japanese government in the '80s to build advanced AI systems, and IBM's Deep Blue, which beat the reigning world chess champion in 1997. Plenty of today's computers get counted as fifth generation or beyond, since they pack serious AI and machine learning and can handle all sorts of tasks that once needed a human brain.

At 5 to 6 weeks, an ultrasound often shows only the gestational sac, and the embryo and its heartbeat may not be visible yet. This can happen for a few reasons. Sometimes the pregnancy is simply earlier than the dates suggest, because ovulation or conception happened later than expected. Sometimes the embryo is just too small to see with the scan, especially if it's done through the abdomen. Doctors generally don't diagnose a miscarriage from a sac alone until it reaches a certain size without an embryo, and even then they usually confirm with a repeat scan. Your normal hCG level, your closed cervix, and the fact that your sac is still growing are all encouraging signs.

The usual next step is a repeat ultrasound, typically in about one to two weeks, and sometimes a repeat hCG blood test in the meantime. Your hCG should rise, and the scan is likely to show the embryo and a heartbeat by then. Please ask your doctor, midwife, or early pregnancy unit when your repeat scan is booked and what result they're looking for, so you know what to expect.

Get medical help urgently, rather than waiting for the next appointment, if you have heavy bleeding that soaks pads, severe pain on one side of your abdomen, pain in your shoulder tip, dizziness, fainting, or feeling faint. Hello Rochan, thank you for your question. I'm not your treating doctor and can't examine you, but I can explain what this term means and help you think through the decision about surgery.

Osteophytic lipping describes small bony outgrowths, called osteophytes or bone spurs, that form along the edges of a joint. On an X-ray they look like a lip or ledge of extra bone at the joint margin. They are usually a sign of wear-and-tear arthritis (osteoarthritis). When the cartilage that cushions a joint thins, the body responds by laying down extra bone at the edges. In the foot, this most often affects the big toe joint (often called hallux rigidus), the joints of the midfoot on top of the foot, or the heel. The spurs themselves can cause pain by rubbing against shoes, pressing on nerves or soft tissue, or blocking normal joint movement, and the underlying arthritis also causes pain and stiffness.

Your situation explains a lot. Standing for nine or more hours a day puts constant load on the foot joints. Flat shoes, though sensible in many ways, often give little arch support or cushioning, so they don't protect the joints much.

Whether surgery is worth it depends on several things: which joint is affected, how much arthritis there is beyond the spurs, how much the pain limits your life, and whether you have properly tried non-surgical treatment. For many people, conservative measures give real relief. These include supportive shoes with good cushioning and a stiff or rocker-bottom sole, which reduce bending at a painful big toe joint. Custom or good-quality off-the-shelf orthotic insoles help, as do cushioned anti-fatigue mats at work and pain relief such as anti-inflammatory medication if it is safe for you. Physiotherapy, weight management if relevant, and sometimes a steroid injection into the joint can also help. If you can, ask your employer whether you could sit for part of your shift or take short breaks off your feet.

Surgery becomes reasonable when pain persists despite a fair trial of these measures, usually a few months, and it is seriously affecting your work and daily life. The type of operation matters a great deal. Removing the spurs (cheilectomy, for the big toe) is a relatively small procedure with fairly quick recovery and good results when arthritis is mild to moderate. Advanced arthritis may need a joint fusion, which is very effective for pain but permanently stiffens the joint and takes longer to recover from. With a standing job, you would likely need several weeks to a few months before returning to full duties, so plan for that.

Before you agree to surgery, it would help to ask your surgeon some questions. Which joint is affected, and how severe is the arthritis? What exactly will be done, and what success rate do they expect for someone like you? How long until you can stand for a full shift again? What happens if you delay or don't have surgery? Have you exhausted the non-surgical options? If you feel uncertain, getting a second opinion from a foot and ankle specialist (an orthopaedic surgeon or podiatric surgeon) is entirely reasonable, since this is usually not an emergency operation.

In short, osteophytic lipping is a sign of arthritis in your foot joints. Surgery can be very worthwhile if your pain is significant and hasn't improved with proper footwear, orthotics and other treatment, but it's best chosen after those options have been tried and once you clearly understand the procedure and recovery time. I hope your feet feel better soon.

Honestly, I'm not sure there's a solid link between folliculitis and asthma, though some people do wonder about it. Folliculitis is when your hair follicles get inflamed, and you end up with red, itchy bumps on your skin. Asthma is a long-term lung condition where your airways get inflamed and narrow, so you get trouble breathing, coughing, and wheezing.

If you've been diagnosed with folliculitis and you're dealing with those red, itchy bumps, stick with what your doctor recommended. That might mean a topical cream or ointment like benzoyl peroxide, and keeping the area clean and dry helps too. Try to avoid stuff that makes it worse, like really hot water or certain scratchy fabrics. If it isn't clearing up or it's really bugging you, ask your doctor about other options. And don't drop your asthma care while you're dealing with this, since poorly controlled asthma can make the skin stuff worse too.

No, opting out at optoutprescreen.com won't affect your credit score, either up or down. That site, run by the major credit bureaus, lets you stop prescreened credit and insurance offers, the preapproved mailers and some marketing based on your credit file. Your score is calculated from the information in your credit reports, such as payment history, balances, credit utilization, length of credit history, and recent applications. Opting out doesn't change any of that.

The main benefit is fewer unsolicited offers in the mail, and it can reduce the chance that someone opens credit in your name using a preapproved offer that was intercepted. It's free, and you can opt out for five years or choose to make it permanent by providing more information.

If you want to improve your score, the things that actually matter are paying every bill on time, keeping credit card balances low relative to their limits, avoiding unnecessary new applications, and checking your reports at annualcreditreport.com for errors you can dispute.

Lucy Stone, the American abolitionist and women's suffrage leader, died on October 18, 1893, at her home in Dorchester, Massachusetts, which is part of Boston. She was 75 years old and had been suffering from stomach cancer. Her last words to her daughter, Alice Stone Blackwell, are often reported as "Make the world better." She was also the first person in New England to be cremated.

A home equity line of credit, or HELOC, lets you borrow against the equity you've built up in your house, which serves as the collateral. How much you can take out generally depends on what your home is worth and how much equity you hold. Parent PLUS loans, sometimes called parental student loans, are federal loans that parents can obtain to cover their child's educational costs. They carry fixed interest rates and tend to cost more than most other student loan options. A second mortgage is a loan taken in addition to the main mortgage on a property. People usually use it to raise a substantial amount of cash, for instance to fund renovations or tuition for a child. Because lenders view them as riskier, second mortgages tend to come with higher interest rates than first mortgages. Overall, a HELOC or second mortgage can be a sensible choice when you need a large sum and your home has enough equity to back the loan. Parent PLUS loans can suit parents who want to help finance their child's schooling and accept the extra cost of a higher interest rate. Whichever you consider, review the terms and conditions of each loan carefully before deciding which fits your situation.

Weak artificial intelligence, also called narrow AI, refers to systems designed to perform a specific task or a limited set of tasks, without possessing general understanding, consciousness, or the ability to think across domains the way humans do. The term "weak" does not mean the systems are unimpressive or ineffective; rather, it describes their scope. A weak AI can be extremely capable within its domain, such as recognizing faces in photographs, translating text between languages, recommending films based on viewing history, or playing a game like chess or Go at a superhuman level. However, it cannot transfer that skill to unrelated problems. A chess engine, for example, cannot hold a conversation or drive a car, and a language model that writes fluent prose does not truly comprehend the world in the way a person does.

The concept is usually contrasted with strong artificial intelligence, sometimes called artificial general intelligence, which would be a hypothetical system capable of understanding, learning, and reasoning across any intellectual task a human can perform, possibly including genuine awareness. Every AI system in use today falls into the weak category, regardless of how sophisticated it appears. The distinction was popularized by the philosopher John Searle, who used it in discussions about whether machines could truly think or merely simulate thinking.

What you're describing deserves attention, and I'd recommend getting it checked by a doctor today or tomorrow rather than waiting to see if it goes away. A normal bruise after a blood draw usually shows up within a day, is purple, blue, or yellowish, and slowly fades. A dark red area that keeps spreading, along with growing pain and swelling, points to something else, most commonly a skin infection (cellulitis) or inflammation of the vein (phlebitis). Both are usually easy to treat, but cellulitis in particular can spread quickly if ignored, and it often needs antibiotics.

A simple step that helps both you and your doctor is to trace the edge of the red area with a pen. If it moves past the line over the next several hours, it's spreading. Until you're seen, keep the arm elevated when you can and avoid squeezing or pressing on the spot. A warm compress may ease discomfort, but it shouldn't replace an evaluation.

You should go to urgent care or the emergency room right away, rather than waiting for an appointment, if you develop a fever or chills, if red streaks start running up your arm from the site, if the redness spreads quickly, if the area becomes very hot, hard, or pus-filled, if the pain becomes severe, or if you feel generally unwell, dizzy, or confused. Faster care is also wise if you have diabetes, a weakened immune system, or circulation problems, since infections can progress faster in those situations.

This isn't necessarily something to panic about, but it isn't something to ignore either. Calling your doctor's office, the place that drew your blood, or an urgent care clinic and describing what you told me is a good next step.

Opting out through optoutprescreen.com won't change your credit score directly, but it can help indirectly. The thing is, every time you apply for a card or loan, the lender pulls your credit report, and that hard inquiry can knock your score down a bit for a while. Fewer prescreened offers usually means fewer of those applications, so over time it could help a little.

Just know what the opt-out actually covers, though. It only stops offers that come through the Prescreened Offers program, where lenders and insurers use certain credit report info to pick who gets a pitch in the mail. You'll still see plenty of offers from other sources, and lenders can still pull your report whenever you apply for something yourself.

If you really want your score to move in the right direction, the basics matter most: pay on time, keep balances low, and don't go applying for a pile of credit all at once. It's also worth checking your credit report now and then for mistakes. You can get a free report from Experian, Equifax, and TransUnion once a year at AnnualCreditReport.com.

Westlife is not a single singer. It is an Irish pop boy band formed in Sligo, Ireland, in 1998 through the television talent show Boyzone's... actually, the band was formed in 1998 by Louis Walsh and Ronan Keating's management team, with members chosen from an audition process. The group's best-known members include Shane Filan, Nicky Byrne, Kian Egan, Mark Feehily, and Brian McFadden, who left in 2004. Shane Filan is often considered the lead vocalist and the face of the group, and the band had many chart-topping singles, including "Flying Without Wings" and "You Raise Me Up." Westlife disbanded in 2012 but reunited in 2018 and has continued to perform and record.

Dark spots on the skin may stem from several causes, such as injuries to the skin, acne, and exposure to the sun. If facial dark spots have developed after a skin injury, you can take several steps to make them less noticeable. Start by keeping the area clean: wash it gently with mild soap and water, which helps guard against infection and supports healing. You might also apply a natural moisturizer, since aloe vera or coconut oil can calm the skin and ease redness. Over-the-counter creams containing hydroquinone or kojic acid can help brighten dark spots, but they are not right for everyone, so read the label carefully and follow the directions closely. If the spots do not improve with home care or store-bought products, consider seeing a dermatologist, who can suggest stronger options such as chemical peels or prescription creams. Finally, shield your skin from further injury and sun exposure so new dark spots do not form. Apply a broad-spectrum sunscreen with an SPF of at least 30, and wear protective clothing whenever you spend time outdoors.

Think of a web browser like the front door to the internet. Whoever owns the front door gets to decide what people see first when they walk in, like which shops are right by the entrance. Microsoft wants its own front door, Edge, so that when people come in, they see Microsoft things first, like Bing search, Microsoft's online shopping, and its other services.

Edge is also built on the same engine as Chrome, so websites work the same in both. That means Microsoft can offer nearly everything Chrome does without people having to learn something new. It just wants you to be using its door instead of Google's.

Why does that matter? Every time someone uses Edge, Microsoft can show them its own search engine and ads, which earns money. It also keeps people inside Microsoft's world, using its accounts, its cloud storage, and its Office apps. Once you're comfortable there, you're more likely to keep paying for Microsoft products.

Chrome is Google's front door, and Google makes most of its money from ads shown through it. So Microsoft pushing Edge is really about not wanting Google to be the only one standing at the entrance to the internet.

Animal rights is basically the idea that animals are sentient beings with moral rights of their own, and those rights deserve to be taken seriously and protected. People who hold this view think animals should be treated with respect and kindness, and that using or exploiting them for human benefit is wrong. The core argument is pretty simple: animals can feel pleasure, pain, and other emotions, so they shouldn't be made to suffer for no good reason. Advocates often say animals should be able to live free from human interference and exploitation, in ways that fit their natural needs as a species.
