Rather than describing a single random outcome, it describes an entire family of random variables, one for each point in the index set, which together capture how the randomness unfolds. The index is often time, so the process might track the daily price of a stock, the number of customers arriving at a store, or the position of a particle undergoing random motion. The index can also be discrete, such as the integers, in which case the process is a sequence of random variables, or continuous, such as the non-negative real numbers, in which case the process is defined at every instant.

To make this concrete, consider flipping a fair coin repeatedly and keeping a running total of heads minus tails. At each step the value is random, and the sequence of these values over time forms a stochastic process, often called a simple random walk. Each individual value is a random variable, but the process as a whole describes how those variables depend on one another across time.

Stochastic processes are characterized by properties such as their state space (the set of possible values), their index set, and the probabilistic rules linking the variables, such as independence, stationarity (whether the statistical behavior stays the same over time), or the Markov property (whether the future depends only on the present and not the past). Common examples include Markov chains, Poisson processes for counting random events, Brownian motion for continuous random movement, and martingales used in finance and gambling theory.

Stochastic processes are widely used in physics, biology, economics, engineering, queueing theory, and many other fields wherever systems involve uncertainty that changes over time.

Arthur C. Clarke (1917–2008) was a British science fiction writer, inventor, and futurist, best known for his novels and short stories that imagined humanity's future in space. He was born in Minehead, England, and served in the Royal Air Force during World War II, where he worked on radar systems. In 1945 he published a paper in the magazine Wireless World proposing that communications satellites placed in geostationary orbit could relay signals around the globe, an idea that later became the foundation of modern satellite communications.

As a writer, Clarke is most famous for 2001: A Space Odyssey, which he co-developed with filmmaker Stanley Kubrick and published as a novel in 1968 alongside the film's release. He wrote many other celebrated works, including Childhood's End, Rendezvous with Rama, and The City and the Stars, and he received numerous awards, including Hugo and Nebula honors. His writing often combined scientific plausibility with philosophical ideas about human evolution and the contact between humanity and alien intelligence.

Clarke is also remembered for formulating three adages known as Clarke's laws, the most famous being that any sufficiently advanced technology is indistinguishable from magic. He spent much of his later life in Sri Lanka, where he lived until his death, and he was an active promoter of space exploration and science education throughout his career.

When an in-the-money stock option reaches expiration, its value does not simply vanish if the holder takes no action, but the answer depends on the brokerage and the type of option. In the United States, most brokers and the Options Clearing Corporation follow an automatic exercise rule: a listed equity option that is in the money by a small threshold at expiration, commonly $0.01 per share, is exercised automatically. The brokerage then delivers or receives the underlying shares, or settles the cash difference, according to the contract terms. Many brokers, however, set their own thresholds and may not auto-exercise positions unless they are in the money by a larger margin, so a holder should check the firm's policy.

Because of this, the owner is not always protected. A brokerage may decline to exercise an option the holder wants exercised, and a holder who lacks the funds or margin to take delivery of shares may face a forced liquidation or a rejected exercise. Some brokers also charge fees for exercise or assignment. Holders who want to be certain of the outcome usually submit an exercise instruction before the deadline, which is often earlier than the official expiration time, or they sell the option in the market before it expires so they capture its remaining value without relying on automatic processing.

Honestly, a sudden drop in the bid price can come from a bunch of things. Usually it's one of these:

Bad news or rumors about the company or its industry can make buyers pull back fast. A credit rating downgrade does the same thing. Sometimes it's just a shift in the broader market or a change in how investors feel about the stock. Technical stuff matters too, like a big wave of sell orders hitting the market at once. And if insiders are selling, or there's some other odd trading activity, that can spook people.

Quick reminder on the terms, since they get mixed up a lot. The bid is the highest price a buyer is willing to pay, and the ask is the lowest price a seller will take. The gap between them is called the spread. When the bid drops suddenly, it usually means buyers have less appetite for the security. When it jumps, it's the opposite: more people want in.

Imagine two kids who used to be friends until one day there was a huge fight, and ever since, neither trusts the other. Every time one does something, the other assumes the worst. That's a lot of what's going on between the U.S. and Iran.

The bad feelings go back a long way. In 1953, the U.S. helped overthrow Iran's elected leader and put a king (the Shah) back in charge, and many Iranians resented that for decades. In 1979, Iranians overthrew the Shah, and a new religious government took over that saw the U.S. as an enemy. That same year, Iranian students took over the American embassy and held 52 Americans hostage for over a year. Americans were furious, and the two countries have basically been in a long grudge match ever since.

On the nuclear question, you're partly right. U.S. intelligence agencies have said for years that Iran stopped its organized effort to build a bomb around 2003 and hasn't decided to build one since. But that's not the whole picture. Iran has enriched uranium to about 60 percent purity, far more than it needs for power plants and fairly close to the roughly 90 percent used in weapons. It has also sometimes limited what international inspectors can see. So the worry isn't usually "Iran is building a bomb right now." It's "Iran is getting itself into a position where it could build one quickly if it decided to," which some people call being a threshold state. Reasonable people disagree about how dangerous that is and how to respond to it.

There are also reasons beyond nukes. Iran funds and arms groups like Hezbollah in Lebanon, the Houthis in Yemen, and militias in Iraq and Syria, some of which have attacked American troops, shipping, or U.S. allies. Iranian leaders have often said very hostile things about Israel, which is a close U.S. partner. Saudi Arabia and other Gulf countries, also U.S. allies, see Iran as their main rival. Iran sits next to the Strait of Hormuz, where a large share of the world's oil passes through, so it can cause big trouble if it wants to.

You're also not wrong that politics plays a role. Being "tough on Iran" is popular with many voters and politicians, some allies push the U.S. to take a hard line, and governments everywhere tend to describe their rivals in the scariest possible terms. Sometimes claims get exaggerated, and the memory of the Iraq War, when the U.S. was wrong about weapons of mass destruction, is a good reason to be skeptical. Iran, for its part, describes the U.S. in pretty outlandish terms too.

So the simple version is that it's a mix of real disagreements, real dangers, old grudges, and political theater on both sides. The truth usually sits somewhere between "Iran is totally innocent" and "Iran is about to nuke everyone."

Law enforcement is basically the set of agencies that make sure laws get enforced and public order holds up. Most of them are in the business of preventing and investigating crimes, though a lot also handle general public safety and other community services. You've got your local police departments and sheriff's offices, then federal outfits like the FBI and the DEA, plus smaller groups like campus security and park rangers. At the end of the day, their main job is protecting people by enforcing laws, responding to emergencies, and chasing down crimes.

Pain that gets worse with coughing, laughing, or sneezing usually means the problem is irritating the lining of the chest or abdomen, or the muscles and bones of the chest wall, because those actions briefly raise pressure and jolt these structures. Several things can do this. A strained chest wall muscle or inflamed rib cartilage (costochondritis) is common after a bout of coughing and often hurts when you press on the area. Pleurisy, inflammation of the lining around the lungs, can cause sharp pain with breathing and coughing, and it can be a sign of a lung infection such as pneumonia. A cracked rib can cause the same pattern. Problems in the upper abdomen can also produce this pain. Gastritis or a stomach ulcer can cause upper abdominal pain, though these usually relate more to meals. Inflammation of the pancreas (pancreatitis) can cause pain that spreads across the upper abdomen and worsens when lying flat or moving. Gallbladder problems, a splenic issue, or a hernia can also be involved. Less commonly, a blood clot in the lung can cause pain that worsens with breathing, and heart-related inflammation can cause chest or upper abdominal pain, so these shouldn't be ruled out by the pattern alone.

Because the pain began only yesterday, is spreading, and isn't responding to medication, I'd recommend getting it checked by a doctor today rather than waiting to see whether it settles. Contact your GP, a nurse line, or an urgent care clinic, and tell them exactly what you told me, including the timing, the spread, and what medication you've taken. They may want blood tests, a urine test, or imaging such as a chest X-ray or ultrasound to find the cause.

Seek emergency care immediately, calling 999 in the UK or 911 in the US, if you have chest pain or pressure, trouble breathing, a racing or irregular heartbeat, fainting or near-fainting, a fever with chills, vomiting blood or material that looks like coffee grounds, black or bloody stools, a rigid or very tender belly, severe pain that keeps getting worse, sweating or nausea with the pain, or a swollen, painful calf or sudden shortness of breath.

The answer depends on how you define the Roman Empire, but the most common figure is about 500 years for the Western Empire and nearly 1,500 years if you include the Eastern Empire.

The Roman Empire is traditionally dated from 27 BCE, when Octavian took the title Augustus and became the first emperor, ending the Roman Republic. The Western Roman Empire is usually said to have fallen in 476 CE, when the Germanic leader Odoacer deposed the last western emperor, Romulus Augustulus. That gives the empire in the West a lifespan of roughly 500 years.

The Eastern Roman Empire, often called the Byzantine Empire by modern historians, continued long after the West collapsed. Its people considered themselves Romans, and it lasted until 1453, when the Ottoman Turks captured Constantinople. Counting from 27 BCE to 1453 CE, the Roman Empire in some form endured for about 1,480 years.

If you go back further and include the Roman Kingdom (traditionally founded in 753 BCE) and the Roman Republic (founded around 509 BCE), Roman civilization as a political entity spans more than 2,000 years.

Milky white discharge with a bad smell usually means something's infected or inflamed, either in the reproductive or urinary system. For men, that often means the prostate or urethra. With your dad, it could be tied to the rectal cancer or to the treatment he's getting, though that's not certain. Either way, he should bring it up with his doctor soon, since it might be an infection or another complication that needs looking at. A provider can examine him and figure out what's going on and what to do about it.

Bounded rationality is a notion from behavioral economics and the study of decision-making holding that the reasoning people apply to choices is restricted by the mental and emotional limits of the human mind. In other words, individuals do not always reason in a perfectly logical manner; their choices are often swayed by prejudices, feelings, and other cognitive shortcomings. Economist Herbert Simon introduced this idea in the 1950s, arguing that actual human decisions deviate from the standard of perfect rationality found in conventional economic theory. Rather, these decisions are molded by the restricted mental capacity people possess and by whatever information happens to be within their reach. The concept matters for understanding real-world decision-making, since it recognizes that people often act without full rationality or complete information. It is likewise significant in areas such as management and public policy, where choices are frequently made on the basis of partial or uncertain data.

Path planning is basically figuring out how a robot or self-driving vehicle gets from where it is to where it needs to go, without hitting anything and while playing by its own rules. You've got to look at the environment first: where the obstacles are, what shape they are, how big the robot is, and anything else that might get in the way. The robot's own limits matter too. It might be running low on battery, have a speed cap, or need to stick to a particular route. There's no single method for this. People use graph-based approaches, sampling-based approaches, and heuristic ones, and which one you pick really comes down to the problem you're trying to solve and what the application needs. Still, it's one of the core pieces of robotics and autonomous systems. Without it, a robot can't really get around a messy, changing space in any useful way.

Certainly! The imaginary turtle on a sunny island is a thought experiment meant to examine the idea of infinity. It goes like this: picture a turtle on a small island in the middle of the sea, perched atop an enormous pillar so tall that its peak disappears into the sky. The turtle holds a little feather in its grip. It begins to release the feather so that it drifts slowly toward the ground, and while the feather descends, the turtle takes one minuscule step down the pillar. The puzzle asks whether the feather will ever touch the ground before the turtle does. The answer is no: however long the feather takes to fall, the turtle can always manage one more tiny step down the pillar before the feather lands. Since the turtle can take an endless number of these tiny steps, the feather never gains on it. The experiment illustrates infinity, the notion of something without any end or limit. Here, the count of tiny steps is infinite, which is why the feather never catches up to the turtle.

The word "baptism" comes from the Greek "baptizo," which means "to dip" or "to immerse." Today it names a Christian sacrament where someone gets dunked in water or has water poured over them. It's meant to symbolize being cleansed and welcomed into the faith. The roots go back to older Jewish practice, and the New Testament describes Jesus himself being baptized and telling his followers to do the same. Plenty of languages have borrowed the word, and Christians everywhere still use it for the ritual.

Salesforce is a cloud-based software company best known for customer relationship management, or CRM, tools. Its core idea is to give businesses a single place to track and manage everything related to their customers, including contact details, sales opportunities, support requests, marketing campaigns, and purchase history. Because the software runs over the internet and is sold by subscription, companies don't have to install and maintain their own servers or large software packages, which was a novel approach when founder Marc Benioff launched the company in 1999.

Over the years it has grown from a sales-tracking tool into a broad suite of products. Sales Cloud helps sales teams manage leads and deals, Service Cloud supports customer service and help desks, and Marketing Cloud handles email, advertising, and campaign automation. Commerce Cloud powers online storefronts, and Data Cloud brings together customer data from many sources so it can be used across the other products. Salesforce also owns Slack, the workplace messaging platform, and Tableau, a data visualization tool, as well as MuleSoft, which connects different software systems together.

Beyond ready-made products, Salesforce offers a platform for building custom business applications, which lets companies tailor the system to their own processes without starting from scratch. More recently it has added artificial intelligence features under the Einstein and Agentforce names, which can do things like draft emails, summarize customer interactions, predict which sales leads are most promising, and carry out routine tasks through automated agents.

Its customers range from small businesses to some of the largest corporations and government organizations in the world, and it is one of the biggest enterprise software companies globally. The company's domain was originally salesforce.com, and while the brand is now often simply called Salesforce, the website remains its main online presence.

A bank selling a foreclosed or repossessed property (what's called REO, or real estate owned) is usually trying to turn the asset into cash quickly and with as little risk as possible, not to squeeze out the highest possible price. A cash offer helps with nearly every part of that goal.

The biggest factor is certainty of closing. A conventional loan buyer has to go through underwriting, and the deal can fall apart if the buyer's credit or income changes, if the lender finds problems with the file, or if the appraisal comes in below the contract price. When an appraisal falls short, the deal has to be renegotiated or it dies, and the bank is back at square one after weeks of wasted time. A cash buyer has no lender and no appraisal contingency, so the sale is far more likely to actually happen.

Speed matters too. Cash deals can often close in two weeks or so, while financed deals typically take thirty to forty-five days or longer. Every month a bank holds a property costs it money in property taxes, insurance, maintenance, utilities, and sometimes HOA fees. A property sitting vacant also risks vandalism, deterioration, and code violations. Those carrying costs can easily eat up the difference between a lower cash offer and a higher financed one.

Banks also care about how the asset appears on their books. Nonperforming assets and REO inventory draw regulatory attention and can affect capital requirements and internal performance metrics, so getting them off the balance sheet by quarter or year end has real value to the institution.

Condition is another consideration. Many distressed properties will not qualify for FHA, VA, or other conventional financing because of repair needs, and even a property that does qualify may face lender-required repairs that complicate the deal. Cash buyers typically buy as is, which spares the bank from negotiating repairs or credits.

Finally, cash offers tend to come with fewer contingencies and less back and forth. There is no financing contingency and often no lengthy inspection renegotiation, so the bank's asset managers spend less time and take on less risk.

The same logic applies to individual sellers too, who may favor a lower cash offer when they need to move fast or want to avoid the risk of a collapsed deal. For a bank, the "net" outcome after time, costs, and risk is what counts, and a slightly lower cash price can easily beat a higher but shakier one.

First-order logic (also called first-order predicate calculus) is a formal system for representing and reasoning about statements that involve variables, predicates, and connectives. The "first-order" part means you can quantify over individual variables, but not over predicates or functions. Formulas get built from atoms, which are constants, variables, or predicates applied to variables. You glue those together with connectives like "and," "or," "not," and "if-then." Quantifiers, "for all" and "there exists," let you make general claims about variables. It's a pretty powerful tool, and you'll see it everywhere in math, computer science, and AI. It's also the foundation for a lot of other logics, like higher-order and modal ones.

Andy Griffith was born June 1, 1926, in Mount Airy, North Carolina. He was an actor and comedian, and most people know him as Sheriff Andy Taylor on "The Andy Griffith Show." He also starred as the lead in the legal drama "Matlock." Griffith died on July 3, 2012, at 86.

Honestly it depends on a few things: what kind of drill you're using, what you're drilling through, and what the water's doing down there.

For really deep work, the go-to is a submersible drilling rig. Those are built to work at around 10,000 feet (about 3,000 meters), and people use them for oil and gas exploration, construction, and scientific research. You can also use other stuff like diamond core drills at depth, but they generally don't do the job as well as a proper submersible rig.

What you're drilling into matters too. Solid rock usually means a more powerful drill or some specialized techniques, while sand or mud is a lot easier to get through.

Then there's the environment. Water pressure, temperature, and currents all make it harder for a drill to keep working the deeper you go.

So there's no single number. It comes down to the specific equipment and methods, plus whatever the material and conditions happen to be where you're drilling.

Index investing is one of the most tax-efficient ways to build wealth, and the reasons come down to how index funds are structured and how they trade. A traditional index fund tracks a benchmark such as the S&P 500 by holding the same securities in roughly the same proportions, and because it rarely needs to buy or sell, it generates few capital gains distributions. Actively managed funds, by contrast, frequently sell positions to chase performance or meet redemptions, and those sales can push realized gains out to shareholders who may not have sold a single share themselves. Over long holding periods, that difference in turnover can meaningfully reduce the drag taxes place on returns.

Much of the tax advantage also stems from the buy-and-hold discipline that indexing encourages. Because the investor is not trading in response to market movements, gains accumulate unrealized and compound without interruption until the shares are sold. Long-term capital gains rates, which apply to assets held more than a year, are generally lower than ordinary income rates, so holding index positions for extended periods can further improve after-tax outcomes. Investors can also practice tax-loss harvesting, selling a position at a loss to offset gains elsewhere and then reinvesting in a similar but not substantially identical fund to maintain market exposure while respecting wash-sale rules.

Location matters as well. Placing tax-inefficient assets such as bonds or high-dividend funds inside tax-deferred accounts like traditional IRAs or 401(k)s, while holding broad equity index funds in taxable accounts, can improve overall efficiency. Exchange-traded index funds often have an added edge over traditional mutual funds because of their in-kind creation and redemption process, which lets them shed low-basis shares without triggering taxable sales inside the fund.

Investors should still weigh expense ratios, fund-specific distribution histories, and their own tax brackets before committing. Tax efficiency is one component of sound investing, not a substitute for appropriate asset allocation and risk management. Consulting a qualified tax professional can help tailor these principles to an individual's circumstances.

A stochastic process is basically a math model for something that changes over time in a random way. Think of a sequence of events or values where you can't know exactly what comes next. These models usually work by assigning a probability distribution to the possible outcomes or states. Those states could be the value of something at different points in time, or the possible results of a series of events. Stock prices are a good example: they bounce around unpredictably, so you can model them this way. The weather works too, since it shifts from day to day in ways nobody can nail down. People in economics, finance, and engineering use stochastic processes all the time to study random stuff. They're handy for capturing the uncertainty that shows up in so many real-world systems.

Christian tradition holds that Mary, the mother of Jesus, was still a virgin when she gave birth to him, since God intended Jesus to enter the world in an extraordinary way. The Bible recounts that the angel Gabriel appeared to Mary and announced that she would bear a child, although she was a virgin who had never been intimate with a man. Gabriel told her that the child would be the Son of God and that he should be named Jesus. Some people interpret the account of Mary's virginity as a symbol of how special and miraculous Jesus' birth was. It may also be understood as a way of stressing that Jesus was born free of sin, because he was not conceived through human sexual union.

Bell's palsy is a disorder that leads to temporary weakness or paralysis of the muscles on one side of the face. Doctors do not know precisely what triggers it, though it is believed to involve swelling of the facial nerve. Treatment generally combines medication with physical therapy, aiming to restore muscle function and calm inflammation. The drugs your wife's physician prescribed, Benfomet Plus and Evion LC, are commonly given for these same purposes in people with Bell's palsy. Ecosprin, which is aspirin, is frequently used to lower inflammation and enhance blood circulation to the affected region. If your wife developed vertigo after starting these medications, she should stop taking them and speak with her doctor right away. Vertigo can stem from many different underlying problems, so identifying its cause is essential before it can be treated properly. The doctor might suggest a different treatment approach for her Bell's palsy. Physical therapy may also be part of the plan, since targeted exercises can strengthen and restore function to the affected side of the face. A therapist may additionally show her facial massage or other methods to support muscle recovery. Most people with Bell's palsy get better on their own within a few weeks to several months. Still, following the doctor's treatment plan and continuing physical therapy as directed gives her the best chance of making a full recovery.

You can do several things to guard against identity theft. First, keep your personal details secure. Treat your social security number, birth date, and similar information as private, and share it only when it is truly needed and only with organizations or people you trust. Second, look after your passwords. Give each account its own strong, unique password, never reveal your passwords to anyone, and turn on two-factor authentication wherever it is offered.

Third, be careful when you are online. Avoid clicking links or opening downloaded attachments that come from sources you do not know, and install security software to shield your computer and devices from malware and other dangers. Fourth, keep an eye on your accounts. Review your bank and credit card statements on a regular basis for charges you did not authorize, and think about setting up alerts that warn you of suspicious activity.

Fifth, stick to secure websites when you shop or handle money online. Check that the URL begins with "https" and that a padlock icon appears in the address bar. Sixth, safeguard your mail by using a mailbox that locks or by having it sent to a post office box, and shred any papers containing personal information before you throw them away. Finally, be cautious about handing out personal information by phone or over the internet, particularly to organizations or individuals you do not know. Following these suggestions can greatly lower your chances of becoming a victim of identity theft and help keep your information safe.

I'm sorry you're dealing with this. Lower back pain a couple of months after an Implanon insertion is worth taking seriously, so it's good that you're looking for options, and it's also worth getting it checked properly.

The first thing to do is book an appointment with your GP or the clinic that placed the implant, and tell them exactly what you've told me: when the pain started, where it is, what it feels like, and that ibuprofen (Nurofen) and ketoprofen (Oruvail) haven't helped. Your doctor can examine you and decide whether anything else is needed. Implanon is a small plastic rod placed under the skin of the upper arm, so it is unlikely to cause back pain directly, but the doctor will want to rule out other causes, such as a muscle strain, a kidney or urinary problem, or something related to the spine. If the pain is severe, comes with fever, blood in your urine, pain when passing urine, numbness or weakness in the legs, or problems controlling your bladder or bowels, seek urgent medical help the same day.

Your doctor may suggest a different painkiller, a muscle relaxant, a short course of physiotherapy, or a referral if it turns out to be a back problem. They can also check whether you need a different type of pain relief, since some medicines are better suited to certain kinds of pain. In the meantime, gentle movement, a warm pack, and staying as active as you comfortably can often help back pain more than rest does. Please don't change or stop any prescribed medicine without speaking to your doctor first.

The Arctic Circle is an imaginary line of latitude at about 66.5 degrees north of the equator. It encircles the northernmost part of the planet, surrounding the North Pole. Land and water inside this line make up the Arctic region, which includes parts of northern Canada, Alaska, Greenland, Iceland's northern edge, Scandinavia, Finland, and Russia. The line sits roughly parallel to the equator and marks the boundary where the sun can stay above the horizon for at least one full day in summer and remain below it for at least one full day in winter.

Okay, so the "ageing clock" idea basically means there's some kind of biological clock inside us (or any living thing) that sets how fast we age. People use it to explain why some creatures live way longer than others, or why certain folks seem to get old faster or slower than their peers. Plenty of stuff seems to play into it: genes, what your environment throws at you, and how you live day to day. A lot of scientists think certain genes control how quickly cells divide and fix themselves, and that those genes could account for the differences in lifespan we see across species and between individuals. Is it a neat, single clock? Nobody's sure yet, and researchers are still arguing about it. What most people agree on, though, is that the pace of aging isn't locked in stone. Diet and exercise have been linked to slowing things down in some studies, and other work has pointed to certain gene mutations or treatments that might stretch lifespan.

"A Change Is Gonna Come" was sung by Sam Cooke. He recorded it in 1964, and it was released as a single shortly after his death that December. The song was written by Cooke in response to racial injustice in America and to personal experiences of discrimination, and it has since become one of the most celebrated civil rights anthems. Otis Redding and many other artists have covered it, but the original is Cooke's.

Honestly, it's pretty possible your neurologist is looking at other things besides MS, based on your symptoms and whatever tests you've had so far. The blood work helps rule out stuff that can look a lot like MS, like lupus, rheumatoid arthritis, Sjogren's, and a few others. It could also just be part of confirming the MS diagnosis itself, so don't read too much into it either way.

MS isn't usually pinned down by one single thing. Doctors put it together from your medical history, a physical exam, and a mix of tests: blood tests, imaging, nerve conduction studies, that kind of thing. And it can take a while to get there. A lot of people are stuck waiting for a bit while everything gets sorted out, which is frustrating, I know.

If anything's worrying you about the diagnosis or the treatment plan, just ask your neurologist or another healthcare provider directly. They can tell you what each test is actually for.

Alaska was a U.S. territory before it became a state in 1959, but before that it actually belonged to Russia. The Russians got a foothold there in the late 1700s, and by the middle of the 1800s they pretty much had the whole region under their control. That lasted until 1867, when Russia sold it to the U.S. for $7.2 million. The U.S. took it over and made it a territory, and that's how it stayed until statehood.

Radio waves given off by cellphones have the potential to disrupt the electronic equipment aboard an aircraft. That equipment plays a key role in navigation, communication, and other functions the plane needs in order to operate safely. Once a phone is switched on, it transmits a signal as it searches for a nearby cell tower to link up with. Because that signal may interfere with the aircraft's electronics, passengers are asked to power their phones down while in flight. Still, certain newer planes come with specialized systems designed to shield against interference from phones and other electronic devices, so using a phone during a flight could become possible down the road.

Mixing yellow and blue paint produces green because of how colors behave. Every color corresponds to a particular mix of light wavelengths. When two colors are combined, their wavelengths blend to form a different color. Yellow paint mainly bounces back yellow light and soaks up the rest, while blue paint mainly bounces back blue light and soaks up the rest. In a mixture, the yellow pigment absorbs the blue light and sends back yellow, and the blue pigment absorbs the yellow light and sends back blue. Those two reflected colors then combine into green. At the molecular level, the pigments are made of tiny molecules that interact when mixed. This interaction changes how each pigment absorbs and reflects different wavelengths, producing the green you see. I hope this clarifies why yellow and blue make green. Is there anything else you'd like to know?

Could be a few things going on with why the text looks different on your TV versus your monitor. For one, your TV probably just has a lower display quality than your computer screen. TVs and monitors use different tech and features that change how text gets rendered, like the panel type (LCD, OLED, and so on), pixel density, and refresh rate. Also, your computer might be running text at a higher resolution than the TV is, and that can make things look sharper and more defined. And don't forget distance: if you're sitting too close to a big screen, the text can look pixelated, so try backing up a bit and see if that helps.

Apple Computer was the original name of the American technology company now known as Apple Inc. It was founded on April 1, 1976, by Steve Jobs, Steve Wozniak, and Ronald Wayne to build and sell personal computers. Its first product, the Apple I, was a hand-built circuit board sold as a kit, and the company soon followed it with the Apple II, a fully assembled machine that became one of the most successful early personal computers and helped popularize the industry.

The company went public in 1980 and grew quickly through the 1980s, introducing the Macintosh in 1984, which popularized the graphical user interface and mouse for many users. Financial troubles and internal conflict in the 1990s led to a period of decline, and Jobs returned in 1997. Under his leadership the company shifted its focus toward consumer electronics and software, launching products such as the iMac, iPod, iPhone, and iPad.

In January 2007, the company dropped "Computer" from its name to reflect its broader range of products and services, becoming Apple Inc. Today it is known for devices like the iPhone and Mac computers, as well as software, online services, and its App Store. The name change marked the transition from a computer maker to a much wider consumer technology company.

Yes, an insect bite can lead to a boil-like lesion with burning, but it is only one of several possibilities, and the fact that it is spreading matters more than the original cause.

An insect bite can cause a red, swollen, painful or burning lump. If the skin is scratched, bacteria (usually Staphylococcus aureus) can get in and form a true boil or abscess, or spread into the surrounding skin as cellulitis. Spreading redness, warmth, increasing pain, and a burning feeling all point toward a bacterial skin infection rather than a simple bite reaction. A burning, blistering, or band-like rash on one leg can also be shingles (herpes zoster), which is quite common at age 62, especially in someone who is thin or run down. Shingles often starts with burning or pain before or along with small clustered blisters. Fungal infections and contact dermatitis are other possibilities, though they are less likely to look like a boil.

Because she is 62 and underweight at 41 kg, her body may handle infection less well, so I would not wait long. She should see a doctor, ideally a dermatologist or a general physician, within a day or two, and sooner if any of the following appear: fever or chills, red streaks moving up the leg, rapidly expanding redness, severe pain, pus, a hard painful swelling, dark or blistering skin, or feeling generally unwell. In those cases she should be seen the same day.

Until she is examined, keep the area clean and dry. Applying a warm, clean compress for 10 to 15 minutes a few times a day can help a boil come to a head. Do not squeeze or pierce it, since that can push the infection deeper. Wash hands after touching it, and use her own towel. For discomfort, paracetamol is generally safe. Avoid applying steroid creams or home remedies to the area until the diagnosis is clear, since steroids can worsen an infection or shingles.

The doctor will likely examine it and, if it is bacterial, prescribe an oral antibiotic and perhaps a topical one. A larger boil may need to be drained. If it looks like shingles, an antiviral medicine works best when started within about 72 hours of the rash appearing, which is another reason to be seen promptly. Normal blood tests are reassuring, but they do not rule out a local skin infection, so examination of the lesion itself is what will settle the cause.

Buying a house three ways is workable, but it hinges on getting the legal and financial structure right before anyone signs anything. The most important early step is a candid conversation about what each person is contributing and what each expects to get out of the arrangement. Are you splitting the down payment equally, or is one person putting in more? Will the monthly mortgage, property taxes, insurance, and repairs be divided equally, or in proportion to ownership? Do all three want to live there, or is one person an investor who may eventually want to sell? Answering these questions in writing saves a lot of resentment later.

Next, decide how the title will be held. In many places, co-owners can hold property as joint tenants, which gives equal shares and a right of survivorship, or as tenants in common, which lets you hold unequal shares and leave your portion to heirs. Tenants in common is often the better choice when contributions differ. The title choice affects what happens if one owner dies, divorces, or wants out, so it's worth confirming with a real estate attorney in your jurisdiction.

Financing is the next hurdle. Mortgage lenders typically want every co-borrower to qualify, so each person's income, credit, and debt will be scrutinized. Some lenders cap the number of borrowers, and not all will approve three unrelated people, so ask lenders early whether they handle multi-party purchases. Everyone on the loan is generally liable for the full amount, not just their share, which is a significant risk to understand.

Then put everything in a co-ownership agreement drafted by an attorney. This document should cover how expenses are split and paid, what happens if someone can't pay their share, how decisions about repairs, renovations, or selling are made (majority vote, unanimous consent, or some other rule), how a departing owner's share is valued and bought out, what happens if someone wants to move out or stops paying, and how disputes will be resolved. Many co-buyers also agree on a rule about first right of refusal, so that a departing owner's share is offered to the remaining owners before going to an outsider.

Finally, consider practical matters: set up a shared bank account for household costs, keep records of contributions, get adequate title and liability insurance, and plan for an exit strategy from the start, including a timeline for when someone might sell. Treating the arrangement like a small business partnership, with clear roles and written terms, tends to keep friendships intact.

Flies are crazy fast and can switch direction in a split second, mostly because they've got a bunch of tiny muscles in their wings that let them make really quick adjustments. Their vision's great too, so they spot a threat early and are gone before you know it. They're also super agile, and can shift their weight around to turn on a dime. So when you go to swat one, it picks up on the movement and just takes off before your hand gets anywhere near it. That's why it feels like the thing is dodging you on purpose. Basically, flies have evolved to be really good at staying alive, which is why they slip away even when you're sure you've got them cornered.

At the open, quotes come first, and the trades come out of them. In a continuous market the bid and ask are standing limit orders, so there is always a quote before there is a trade. A trade happens only when someone crosses the spread, either by sending a marketable order or by having an auction match orders. So in that sense the bid and ask exist before the first print.

What actually happens at the open depends on the exchange. On most major venues, such as the NYSE, Nasdaq, and the London and European exchanges, there is an opening auction or cross. Orders accumulate before the open, including limit orders, market-on-open orders, and so on. Indicative prices and imbalance information are often published during this period, but the book is not matched continuously. At the scheduled time the exchange computes a single price that maximizes executable volume, usually with tie-breaking rules based on imbalance and a reference price, and executes all matchable orders at that price. That is the official opening print. Only after the auction does continuous trading begin, with the remaining unexecuted limit orders forming the opening bid and ask.

So the sequence is: orders are entered pre-open, the auction determines the opening price and trades, and the continuous-session bid and ask are then formed from what is left in the book plus new orders. Pre-market quotes may exist as well, and they can differ from the post-auction spread.

A few caveats are worth knowing. The first trade you see in data may be the auction trade, which is not at the bid or ask and can sit outside the pre-open quoted spread. Spreads right after the open are often wider and more volatile because of uncertainty and thin books. Data feeds can also mislabel or time-stamp quotes and trades slightly differently, which creates apparent trades before quotes. For a market maker or dealer market without an auction, the dealer posts quotes first and then trades against incoming orders.

In short, quotes are logically prior to trades, but at an auction-based open the first trade is set by the auction and the post-open bid and ask are then what remains in the book.

Extreme right wing, often called the far right, refers to political ideologies and movements that sit well beyond the mainstream conservative spectrum. People on the far right typically reject liberal democratic norms or core principles such as equal rights for all citizens, pluralism, and the rule of law, though the precise boundaries vary by country and by who is doing the defining.

The term covers a range of views. Some far-right movements emphasize strong nationalism and a desire to preserve what they see as a nation's traditional culture, ethnic identity, or religious heritage, often opposing immigration and multiculturalism. Others are openly authoritarian, favoring strongman leadership, restrictions on dissent, or the concentration of power. At the most extreme end are groups that embrace white nationalism, racial hierarchy, or neo-fascism, and some of these have been linked to violence and terrorism.

It is worth distinguishing the far right from the broader right. Mainstream conservatives generally work within democratic institutions and accept electoral outcomes, while far-right actors are more likely to attack those institutions, promote conspiracy theories, or advocate for policies that would undermine minority rights. Critics sometimes apply the label loosely to any conservative they disagree with, so context matters when encountering the term. Scholars who study politics usually use it more precisely, drawing on criteria such as opposition to democratic pluralism and advocacy of exclusionary or hierarchical political communities.

Go is an abstract strategy board game for two players, generally considered one of the oldest board games still played today. It originated in China more than 2,500 years ago, where it is called weiqi, and it later spread to Korea, where it is known as baduk, and to Japan, where it took the name igo, from which the English word "Go" derives. In ancient China it was regarded as one of the four essential arts of a cultivated scholar, alongside calligraphy, painting, and playing the guqin.

The game is played on a board marked with a grid of lines, most commonly 19 by 19, although smaller boards of 13 by 13 and 9 by 9 are popular for beginners and quick games. One player uses black stones and the other uses white stones. Players take turns placing a single stone on an empty intersection of the grid, with Black traditionally moving first. Once placed, stones do not move, though they can be removed if captured.

The central objective is to surround and control more territory than the opponent. Stones of the same color that are directly connected along the grid lines form groups, and the empty points adjacent to a group are called its liberties. When a player surrounds an opposing stone or group so that it has no liberties left, that stone or group is captured and removed from the board. A rule called ko prevents players from endlessly repeating the same position by immediately recapturing back and forth, and placing a stone where it would have no liberties is generally forbidden unless the move captures enemy stones. The game ends when both players pass consecutively, at which point the score is counted based on controlled territory and captured stones, with White usually receiving a compensation called komi to offset Black's advantage of moving first.

Despite its simple rules, Go is famous for its extraordinary depth and complexity. The number of possible board positions vastly exceeds the number of atoms in the observable universe, and the game rewards a blend of tactical calculation, long-term strategic planning, intuition, and a sense of balance between attack and defense. Players often speak of the game in almost philosophical terms, and a common saying holds that it takes minutes to learn but a lifetime to master.

Go has a well-developed professional scene, particularly in China, Japan, Korea, and Taiwan, with ranked players, major tournaments, and organizations that train young talent from childhood. Amateur players are ranked using a system of kyu grades for beginners and intermediates and dan grades for advanced players, and a handicap system allows players of different strengths to enjoy competitive games by giving the weaker player extra stones at the start.

The game gained worldwide attention in 2016 when AlphaGo, an artificial intelligence program developed by DeepMind, defeated the top professional Lee Sedol in a five-game match. This was considered a landmark achievement, because Go had long been viewed as far more difficult for computers than chess due to its enormous search space and reliance on intuitive judgment. Since then, AI programs have become a major tool for study and have influenced how even top professionals think about the game.

Norway stays out of the EU mostly because a majority of Norwegians have said no to it, twice, and the reasons are more practical and historical than oil or smugness.

The two times Norway voted on it were 1972 and 1994. Both times the "no" side won, narrowly. In 1994 it was about 52 to 48. Since then, polls have bounced around, and at times a majority has favored joining, but the political parties that dislike the idea have enough clout that no government has wanted to start another fight over it. The issue splits parties internally, so most leaders just leave it alone.

Now the why, in simple terms. Imagine Norway is a kid who only got their own toys in 1905, when they separated from Sweden, and before that spent centuries under Denmark and then Sweden. Being told "come share your toys with a big group and let the group make some of the rules" feels uncomfortable to a lot of people there. Sovereignty matters to them, and the memory of being run from elsewhere is not that old.

Then there are the toys themselves. Fishing and farming are the big ones. Norway has a huge fishing industry and a lot of small farms in remote areas that get strong government support. Joining the EU would mean going along with the EU's common fisheries and agricultural policies, and many rural Norwegians feared losing control of their waters and their subsidies. That is why the "no" vote is strongest in the countryside and the north.

Oil does play a part, but not as a simple "we're too rich to need you." Norway has a giant savings fund built from oil money, and having it means the country feels financially safe on its own. It also means Norwegians worry about having to share or answer to outsiders about how they manage it. So oil makes staying out feel less risky, but it isn't the main reason people vote no.

What makes the whole thing easier is that Norway doesn't really lose much by staying out. Through the European Economic Area agreement, Norway gets access to the EU single market and follows a large share of EU rules anyway, and it is also in the Schengen travel zone. The catch is that it pays into EU programs and has to adopt many rules without having a seat at the table where they are made. Critics call that the worst of both worlds, while supporters of staying out say it gives most of the benefits with more freedom.

So it's not really misguided self-righteousness. It's a mix of recent independence, fish and farms, a comfortable economy, and a deal that already gives Norway most of what it wants.

Honestly, any website can be hacked in theory, but some are way harder to crack than others. A lot of it comes down to how well the site was built and how well somebody keeps up with it afterward. I don't think any site is ever 100% secure, or even close to it. Hackers keep finding new ways in, and developers keep patching the holes they find. It's basically cat and mouse, and it never really stops. Even the best-protected sites can get broken into if the attacker is skilled enough and has the time and money to keep at it. So if you run a site, check your security regularly and fix whatever problems turn up. You won't make it bulletproof, but you can make it a real pain for anyone trying to get in. No site is totally safe, but you can still do a lot to make yours a tougher target.

Okay, so if you want to open an online stock trading account in the US, here's roughly how it goes. First, figure out what kind of account you need. You've got individual accounts, joint accounts, and retirement accounts like a traditional or Roth IRA. Next, shop around for online brokers. Look at fees, what you can invest in, how good their customer service is, and whether their website or app is easy to use.

Then gather your paperwork. Depending on the broker and account type, they'll likely ask for your name, address, and Social Security number, plus some financial info like your job, income, and rough net worth. You'll also need an ID such as a driver's license or passport.

Fill out the online application and agree to their terms. Once that's done, fund the account. Most brokers let you transfer money electronically from your bank, though some still take paper checks by mail.

After your account is funded and approved, you can start trading. Take some time to poke around the platform and check for any fees or restrictions before you place your first trade. Every broker has its own quirks, so read their instructions closely. And if you're unsure about anything, talking to a financial advisor or tax pro before you invest is never a bad idea.

A defibrillator is a machine that gives the heart a short, strong jolt of electricity. Your heart works like a pump that squeezes in a steady rhythm, and that rhythm is controlled by tiny electrical signals, a bit like how a drummer keeps a beat. Sometimes the signals get scrambled and the heart starts quivering or beating chaotically instead of pumping blood. A defibrillator sends one big electrical pulse through the chest, which briefly stops all the heart muscle at once. That gives the heart's natural built-in drummer a chance to restart the steady beat on its own.

Defibrillators do not usually start a heart that has completely stopped with nothing going on. In that case, the heart is often quivering in a state called ventricular fibrillation, and the shock is what can reset it. If the heart has stopped altogether, the machine is less helpful, and people need CPR to keep blood moving while they wait.

As for doing it repeatedly, yes, it is possible, and it is often done. If the first shock does not work, the machine can be charged and used again, and rescuers usually keep giving CPR between shocks. Some devices can be worn or implanted and will shock the heart automatically whenever they detect a dangerous rhythm, which can happen more than once over time. Each shock is carefully timed and measured so it does the least harm needed to reset the rhythm.

I get why you're worried about your son and the way he's acting. Getting upset or defensive yourself usually makes things worse, so try to stay calm and come at it with some empathy. A few things that might help:

Set clear boundaries and tell him what they are. That could mean not putting up with threats or disrespect, full stop.

Keep the door open. Let him know you want to hear what's going on with him, and then actually listen, even when it's hard to hear.

If it's getting too much to handle on your own, a therapist or counselor can be a big help. They're neutral, which means your son might open up to them more easily than to you.

Don't forget about yourself. If things get too stressful, take a break or lean on friends or family. You can't help him well if you're running on empty.

It's also worth asking what's driving the behavior. Is he overwhelmed? Stressed about something? Is there an underlying mental health issue that needs attention? Figuring that out can make it a lot easier to figure out how to support him.

Coke Zero and Pepsi One don't have calories because they don't use the usual sugar that regular soda uses. Your body gets energy from calories, and regular soda is packed with sugar, which is a big source of them. Instead, these drinks use special sweeteners like aspartame or sucralose. These sweeteners taste very sweet, but your body either can't break them down for energy or only needs a tiny amount of them to make things sweet. So they make your tongue happy without adding much fuel for your body.

Are they healthier? It's a bit complicated. Compared to regular soda, they are generally a better choice, because they don't give you the big sugar load that can lead to weight gain, tooth decay, and blood sugar spikes. If you're trying to cut back on sugar, they can be a helpful swap. But they aren't magic health drinks. Scientists are still studying whether sweeteners affect appetite, gut bacteria, or cravings for sweet things, and the research isn't fully settled. Plain water is still the healthiest thing to drink. Diet sodas are best thought of as a step better than regular soda, not as a health food.

Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) is an uncommon condition in which the immune system wrongly targets the nerves. It can lead to muscle weakness and paralysis, and it may become life-threatening if the muscles needed for breathing are affected. Confirming a GBS diagnosis usually involves a physical exam, a review of the patient's medical background, and laboratory tests along with imaging. A clinician may also carry out a nerve conduction velocity (NCV) test, which gauges how quickly electrical signals pass along a nerve. NCV is frequently reduced in GBS. Additional tests that can help verify the diagnosis include a lumbar puncture (spinal tap), in which a small amount of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) is drawn from the lower back; an abnormal protein level in this fluid may point toward GBS. Electromyography (EMG) measures muscle electrical activity, helping to establish nerve damage and how severe the weakness is. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) can reveal abnormalities in the brain or spinal cord that might account for the symptoms. Because symptoms differ considerably between individuals, diagnosing GBS can be difficult, so healthcare providers weigh all available information before reaching a conclusion.

Elevated albumin in the urine, a condition called albuminuria, may indicate kidney damage or a kidney disorder such as nephrotic syndrome. You should consult a healthcare provider to find out what is causing the raised albumin levels and to decide on the right treatment. Addressing the underlying problem, for example by keeping high blood pressure or diabetes under control, is often part of the treatment and can limit further harm to the kidneys. Your provider might also prescribe medication that lowers the amount of protein lost in the urine and helps safeguard the kidneys. Sometimes lifestyle adjustments, such as altering your diet or exercise habits, may be advised as well to help control the condition. Be sure to follow your provider's guidance and to have your albumin levels and general kidney function checked regularly, so that the condition stays well managed.

Microsoft Windows XP came out on October 25, 2001, which means it has been around for more than two decades. For many years it was a widely adopted operating system, remaining in common use until Microsoft ended its support on April 8, 2014. Since the company no longer releases security patches or offers technical assistance for the system, running Windows XP today is discouraged, as it may be vulnerable to threats.

A driverless vehicle, which may also be called a self-driving or autonomous car, is able to perceive its surroundings and move along a route without a person controlling it. To collect information about the world around them and decide how to proceed, these cars rely on a range of tools, including cameras, radar, and lidar. Artificial intelligence (AI) algorithms then analyze that information and choose the most suitable action. Such vehicles could transform how people travel by making roads safer, traffic more efficient, and mobility easier for more people. Because many crashes stem from human mistakes, autonomous cars may prevent some of them, ease congestion, and give independence to those who cannot drive because of age, a disability, or similar circumstances. Nevertheless, doubts remain about whether these vehicles are safe and dependable, and people continue to argue about how strictly they should be regulated and supervised.

Tugain is a brand name for minoxidil, the stuff people use to fight hair loss. It comes as a liquid or foam you put right on your scalp to help hair grow. Most people handle it fine, but it can cause some side effects.

The most common one is scalp irritation. You might notice dryness, itching, or flaking. A gentle shampoo usually helps, and so does not leaving it on longer than the directions say.

Allergic reactions are rare, but they happen. Watch for rash, hives, trouble breathing, or swelling in your face, lips, tongue, or throat. If you get any of those, stop using it and get medical help right away.

It can also cause dizziness, lightheadedness, or a racing heartbeat. If that happens, stop and call your doctor or pharmacist.

Use it exactly as your provider told you to. If you're worried about side effects or already having some, talk to them. They can help you figure out what's best for your hair loss.

Chris Cornell fronted Soundgarden as lead singer and guitarist, one of the big names in the American rock scene. He also played in Audioslave and Temple of the Dog. Soundgarden was one of the early bands behind grunge in the late '80s and early '90s, and they put out a bunch of critically loved records, including "Badmotorfinger" (1991) and "Superunknown" (1994). Cornell's voice was something else. He could go from a deep, gravelly growl to a huge, soaring falsetto that sounded almost operatic. He died in 2017.

Traffic signals typically display their three colors stacked vertically, with red at the top, amber in the center, and green at the bottom. Red generally tells drivers to halt, whereas yellow serves as a caution that the signal is about to change to red, prompting drivers to get ready to stop. Green means drivers may move forward safely. Because these colors and their meanings follow international standards, drivers can read the signals easily no matter which country they happen to be in.

A tsunami is a huge wave set off by something happening underwater, like an earthquake or a volcanic eruption. When the seafloor suddenly shifts or blows up, it shoves the water around and sends a wave rolling across the ocean. These waves are wild because they're incredibly long and can carry a ton of energy. Some of them move at up to 500 miles per hour, which is faster than a jet airliner. All that energy comes from whatever set the thing off, whether that's a quake or an eruption dumping its power into the water. Once a tsunami hits shore, it can wreck buildings and roads, and it can flood the coast and chew away at the land. They're seriously dangerous, so if you live somewhere they're likely to hit, it's worth knowing what to do before one shows up.

When an ECG shows an anteroseptal infarct, it means blood flow has been cut off to the front and middle portion of the heart muscle, including the septum. A clot in one of the coronary arteries that nourish the heart is a common reason for such a blockage. Without prompt treatment, the affected heart tissue can be injured or die, a condition called a myocardial infarction, or heart attack. When several ECGs taken at different times point to an anteroseptal infarct, and an echocardiogram also reveals a thickened septum, it is very likely that the infarct truly took place. People who have suffered a heart attack often continue to have symptoms or ECG abnormalities, because the damage to the heart muscle may not be completely reversible. Anyone experiencing possible heart attack symptoms, including chest pain, breathlessness, or discomfort in the neck, jaw, arms, or back, should get medical help. Doctors should also exclude indigestion and other noncardiac sources of chest discomfort, since correctly identifying and treating the true cause of the symptoms is essential.

If you're in the US and shoot and kill someone in Mexico, Mexican authorities get jurisdiction over the case since the crime happened on Mexican soil. That means you'd be under Mexican law, and you could be arrested, charged, and tried in a Mexican court. If convicted, you could face prison or other penalties under their system. Honestly, the big takeaway is that you can't harm someone and expect to be shielded by the fact that you're a US citizen, so always follow the laws wherever you happen to be.

Yes, you can take emergency contraception again if you have another unprotected sexual encounter, but it is meant for occasional emergencies rather than regular use. Levonorgestrel (sold as Plan B and similar brands) is generally considered safe to repeat, though it is less reliable the more often it is used and it can disrupt your cycle. Ulipristal (ella) is usually not recommended to be repeated within the same cycle, because it can interfere with hormonal contraception taken afterward. Either way, the pill is most effective when taken as soon as possible, ideally within 24 hours, and levonorgestrel works only up to 72 hours after sex while ulipristal works up to 120 hours. The copper IUD is the most effective form of emergency contraception and can be fitted up to five days after unprotected sex.

Because you have had unprotected sex more than once in a short period, I would strongly suggest seeing a pharmacist, doctor, or family planning clinic soon. They can talk you through which option suits you, help you start a regular method such as the combined or progestin-only pill, an injection, or an implant, and advise on condoms, which protect against sexually transmitted infections as well as pregnancy.

If your period is late, or has not come when you expected, take a pregnancy test. Tests are most accurate about three weeks after unprotected sex, though a test a few days after a missed period is also reliable. If the test is positive or you are unsure, see a doctor promptly. Emergency contraception does not end a pregnancy that has already begun, but a doctor can discuss your options with you.

I was sorry to learn about your neck pain and your other health problems. Many things can lead to neck pain, such as strained muscles, a pinched nerve, or degeneration or injury of the spine. Because of this, you should work with a healthcare professional who can identify the source of your pain and design a treatment plan suited to your particular situation. Options for treating neck pain can include physical therapy, medication, injections, and, in certain cases, surgery. Physical therapy aims to stretch and strengthen the muscles of the neck and upper back, which can ease pain and make it easier to move your neck. Doctors may prescribe medications like nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and muscle relaxants to bring down inflammation and calm muscle spasms. Injections, including corticosteroid injections and nerve blocks, can also be used to lessen inflammation and relieve pain. When neck pain is severe, or when conservative treatments fail to help, your healthcare provider might suggest surgery. Several surgical procedures exist for neck pain, among them fusion surgery, in which two or more vertebrae are joined together to steady the spine. You should stick to the treatment plan your provider recommends and let them know about any worries or changes in your symptoms. It is also wise to take preventive measures against neck pain, including maintaining good posture, using ergonomic equipment, and pausing regularly during activities that put strain on the neck.

Mary Matalin is married to James Carville, the political consultant who managed Bill Clinton's 1992 presidential campaign. The two are a well-known bipartisan couple, since Matalin is a Republican strategist who worked for George H.W. Bush and Dick Cheney, and they have co-authored a book and appeared together often in media. They married in 1993 and have two daughters.

I'm sorry you're dealing with this on top of recovering from surgery. Stomach cramps, gas, and difficulty passing stool in the first few days after an operation are very common and usually not dangerous. The main causes are general anesthesia, which temporarily slows the bowels; pain medicines, especially opioid painkillers like tramadol, codeine, or morphine-type drugs, which are strongly constipating; reduced eating and drinking around the time of surgery; and spending more time lying in bed than usual. Some patients also receive anti-nausea medicines that can slow digestion.

Avoiding straining matters more for you than for most patients. After ear surgery for a glomus tympanicum, heavy straining, forceful nose blowing, and similar pressure-raising efforts can increase pressure in the middle ear and head and may disturb the healing area, packing, or graft. So the goal is to soften the stool and get things moving gently rather than pushing hard on the toilet.

Simple measures help most people. Drink plenty of fluids, such as water, warm water, soups, and clear juices, unless your doctor has restricted fluids. Warm drinks in the morning often stimulate the bowel. Eat soft, fiber-containing foods such as papaya, prunes or prune juice, pears, cooked vegetables, oats, and whole-grain foods, and reduce gas-forming foods like beans, cabbage, cauliflower, onions, fizzy drinks, and heavy fried items for a few days. Gentle walking around the room or house several times a day, if your surgeon allows it, is one of the best ways to relieve gas and restart bowel movement. Sitting on the toilet with your feet raised on a small stool can make passing stool easier without straining.

For medication, a gentle stool softener or osmotic laxative is commonly used after surgery. Examples include lactulose syrup, polyethylene glycol powder, or isabgol (psyllium husk) taken with plenty of water. Simethicone tablets or drops can ease gas and bloating. Please check with your surgeon or pharmacist before starting any of these, especially since they know which painkillers and other medicines you were given. If you are taking an opioid painkiller, ask whether you can switch to paracetamol or another non-constipating option, since this alone often makes a big difference.

Call your doctor promptly or go to the hospital if you develop severe or worsening abdominal pain, a swollen, hard belly, repeated vomiting, inability to pass any gas at all, fever, blood in the stool, or no bowel movement for more than three to four days despite these measures. Also contact your ENT team if you notice new dizziness, worsening hearing, fluid or bleeding from the ear, facial weakness, or severe headache, as these relate to the surgery itself rather than the stomach.

In most cases, the bowels return to normal within a few days once you are eating, drinking, and moving more. Wishing you a smooth recovery.

In daily life, objects usually act in ways we can anticipate. If you let go of a ball, for instance, you can be fairly sure it will drop to the ground because of gravity. That's because the world around us obeys certain rules, or laws, which let us forecast how things will behave. Quantum physics is the area of physics devoted to the behavior of extremely small things, such as atoms and subatomic particles. These tiny things don't always follow the same predictable patterns as ordinary objects. An atom, for example, can be in several places at once, or spin in two opposite directions simultaneously. That may sound odd, but numerous experiments have shown it to be true.

Quantum computers are machines that rely on the principles of quantum physics to carry out certain calculations far more quickly than conventional computers. Conventional computers store and process information using bits. A bit works like a switch that is either "on" or "off," shown as a "1" or a "0." Quantum computers instead use "quantum bits," or "qubits," which can stand for a "1," a "0," or both together. Because of this, quantum computers can handle many calculations simultaneously, which makes them much faster than conventional machines for particular tasks.

So the word "quantum" in quantum physics, quantum computers, and related terms points to the strange and unpredictable behavior of very small things like atoms and subatomic particles. The laws of quantum physics describe this behavior, and they differ from the laws governing everyday objects. Quantum computers take advantage of these principles to perform certain calculations much faster than normal computers.

Get medical help right away if someone has swallowed toilet cleaner or any other possibly toxic stuff. Toilet cleaner is seriously dangerous. It can burn the mouth and throat, cause stomach pain and vomiting, make it hard to breathe, and in bad cases it can kill someone. If a person swallowed a lot, doctors might do a gastric lavage, sometimes called a stomach wash. That means passing a tube through the mouth or nose into the stomach and flushing it out with a special solution. Depending on the symptoms and how much got swallowed, they might also give meds for nausea and vomiting, provide support to help with breathing and keep vital signs steady, or even operate if there's damage. Just do what the medical team tells you, and don't wait around if someone's swallowed something toxic.

Generally, a person owes tax in the country where they are physically located and generating income. If you work for an Indian company while living physically in the UK, you could end up owing tax in both nations, since each has the authority to levy tax on individuals who are present there and earning money. Because tax regulations differ considerably between countries, it is wise to consult a tax advisor or the revenue authorities in both places to pin down your exact obligations. They can supply more specific guidance on the rules that apply to your circumstances and clarify what you are required to do.

The Nintendo 64 is a cherished gaming console that launched in 1996. At the time it enjoyed great success, and many people look back fondly on the hours they spent playing it with friends and relatives. Although it is now quite old, enthusiasts still like to discuss it and recall the enjoyable moments it provided. Titles released for the system, such as Super Mario 64 and The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, are regarded as classics and continue to be played and appreciated. These games keep the console alive in people's minds and stir up nostalgia for it.

Signatures are old, and they're not great at proving who someone is, but people keep using them because they're quick, familiar, and good enough for a lot of everyday jobs. Think of it like a name tag. Anybody can write a name on a piece of paper, so a signature alone doesn't prove much. What it does do is show that the person was there, saw the paper, and agreed to what it says. That's useful when you're signing for a package or agreeing to a school trip.

The reason they seem unreliable is that a signature is just a squiggle, and squiggles are easy to copy. Banks and courts know this, which is why they often check signatures against other things, like an ID card, a witness who watches you sign, or a stamp.

For important things, people have switched to stronger tools. Computers can use secret codes, fingerprints, face scans, or special digital keys that only one person has. These are much harder to fake than a handwritten name.

So signatures stick around because they're simple, cheap, and most people already understand them. They work well when the stakes are low, and when the stakes are high, we add extra checks to make up for their weak spots.

Generally speaking, the money sitting in your bank account is not taxed. Still, the interest that account generates can sometimes be taxed. In the U.S., for instance, the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) treats savings account interest as ordinary income, and the rate applied depends on your tax bracket and on whether the account is taxable or tax-exempt. Rules differ in other countries, so it's wise to consult your local tax office or a tax advisor to learn what applies to your situation. Some nations also cap how much interest can be earned tax-free each year, and any amount above that cap may be taxed.
