Anti-inflammatory drugs are meds that calm down inflammation, the body's reaction to injury or illness. You know the signs: swelling, redness, heat, and pain. It's normal and part of how your immune system works. But when inflammation sticks around too long, it can feed into things like heart disease, cancer, and autoimmune disorders.

There are a few main types. NSAIDs, like ibuprofen and naproxen, block the production of prostaglandins, the chemicals that drive a lot of the inflammation process. Corticosteroids, like prednisone and hydrocortisone, are much stronger. They shut down parts of the immune system, which is why doctors reach for them for severe flare-ups or for people with autoimmune conditions.

People take these for all sorts of things: headaches, toothaches, sore muscles, arthritis, and other inflamed areas. You can get them as pills, capsules, gels, creams, or shots. Whatever you're taking, go by what your doctor or pharmacist tells you, and keep an eye out for side effects like stomach upset, nausea, or allergic reactions. If something feels off, don't just tough it out.

A lapping machine is a piece of equipment used to produce extremely flat, smooth surfaces on a workpiece, or to achieve very precise thickness and fine surface finishes. It works through a process called lapping, which is a gentle abrasive machining method. Instead of cutting aggressively like a grinder or milling machine, it removes tiny amounts of material by rubbing the workpiece against a flat plate, called a lap, with a loose abrasive slurry or paste between the two surfaces.

In a typical setup, a large, precisely flat rotating plate, often made of cast iron or another relatively soft material, serves as the lap. Abrasive particles such as diamond, silicon carbide, or aluminum oxide, suspended in a liquid or paste, are applied to the plate. The workpieces are held in carriers or conditioning rings that sit on the plate and move across it as it turns. The abrasive particles roll and scrape between the plate and the part, gradually wearing the part down evenly. Many machines use a planetary motion so that the workpieces travel in varied paths, which helps keep both the part and the plate flat over time.

Lapping machines come in single-sided and double-sided versions. Single-sided machines work on one face of the part at a time, while double-sided machines lap both faces simultaneously, producing parallel surfaces with tight thickness control.

They are used wherever very tight tolerances matter. Common applications include precision bearings and seals, valve components, gauge blocks, pump and compressor parts, semiconductor wafers, optical components, ceramic parts, and watch components. Lapping can achieve flatness within fractions of a micrometer and very low surface roughness.

Compared to grinding, lapping is slower and removes much less material, so it is usually a finishing step performed after rougher machining. Its advantages are high accuracy, a uniform finish, little heat generation, and minimal stress or damage to the part, which makes it suitable for hard, brittle, or delicate materials.

The chance of pregnancy from this is lower than with ejaculation inside the vagina, but it isn't zero. Pregnancy requires sperm to reach an egg, and pre-ejaculate (the fluid released before ejaculation) can sometimes contain sperm, especially if sperm was left in the urethra from earlier ejaculation. Partial erection and pulling out before ejaculation reduce the risk considerably, but they don't eliminate it, and a broken condom adds some uncertainty. Your actual risk depends mostly on where you are in your cycle. If you ovulated recently or are near ovulation, the risk is meaningfully higher than if you're at the start or end of your cycle.

If you want to lower the risk, emergency contraception is the most useful step, and it works best the sooner you take it. Levonorgestrel pills (sold as Plan B and generics) are available without a prescription in many countries and are most effective within 72 hours, though they can work up to about five days in some cases with reduced effectiveness. Ulipristal (ella) requires a prescription in some places but works up to five days. A copper IUD inserted by a clinician within five days is the most effective option. Pharmacists can help you choose and check whether anything interacts with medications you're taking.

To find out whether you're pregnant, wait about two to three weeks after the encounter, or until a missed period, and then take a home pregnancy test. Testing too early can give a false negative. Since you've been feeling unwell, keep in mind that fatigue, nausea, and similar symptoms can come from many causes, including pregnancy, so symptoms alone won't tell you much. If your period is late or you want certainty sooner, a doctor or clinic can do a blood test.

Since the condom broke, you may also want to consider STI testing, and a clinic can advise you on that too.

The Switchblade is a family of small, portable loitering munitions made by the American company AeroVironment. Often called "kamikaze drones," they are designed to be carried by a soldier, launched from a tube, and flown to a target, where they detonate. The name comes from the way the wings spring open after launch, much like a switchblade knife opening.

There are two main versions. The Switchblade 300 is the smaller one, weighing roughly 2.5 kilograms, with a range of around 10 kilometers or more depending on conditions. It is intended mainly for use against personnel and light targets. The Switchblade 600 is larger, weighing about 15 kilograms, with a much longer range of several tens of kilometers and a longer flight time of around 40 minutes. It carries a warhead capable of damaging armored vehicles and other harder targets, similar in role to an anti-armor weapon.

The key concept is the loitering munition: unlike a conventional missile that flies directly to a pre-set target, the drone can circle or hover over an area while its operator watches live video from an onboard camera. The operator can select a target, adjust the flight path, and even abort the attack and recall the drone to attack later, which reduces the risk of collateral damage compared with many unguided weapons. Operators control it using a handheld ground station, and the system is electric-powered and relatively quiet.

The Switchblade is used by the US Army, Marine Corps, and special operations forces, and it has been exported to other countries. It drew wide public attention when the United States supplied hundreds of Switchblade 300s and later 600s to Ukraine after Russia's 2022 invasion. Reports from the conflict suggested mixed results: the weapons were useful in some situations, but they were also affected by electronic warfare, jamming, and the challenge of striking well-defended or moving targets.

Supporters argue that such systems give small units precise, affordable, on-demand firepower, while critics raise concerns about the growing autonomy of weapons and the ethics of lethal drones. In the Switchblade's case, a human operator is still responsible for selecting targets and authorizing the strike.

Robot navigation is a robot's capacity to travel through a given setting, steering clear of obstructions while working toward a chosen destination. Several techniques make this possible: sensor-driven methods rely on instruments that spot and dodge obstacles, while map-based methods depend on a previously built representation of the surroundings to direct movement. The capability matters across many robotic fields, such as self-driving cars, military machines, rescue robots, and personal assistant devices. Achieving it demands combining sensors, control systems, and algorithms so the robot can move through varied environments both effectively and efficiently. Navigation approaches generally fall into three categories: reactive, deliberative, and hybrid. A reactive approach has the robot respond to what is directly around it, using sensors to identify and avoid nearby obstacles. A deliberative approach has the robot chart a route to its target using a map of the area and then carry out that route. A hybrid approach blends the two, letting the robot adjust to shifting conditions while still pursuing its objectives. Overall, navigation is a intricate and demanding undertaking, since the robot must sense and interpret its surroundings, reach decisions from that information, and perform actions in a coordinated, efficient way.

A sensible habit is to decide in advance how much money you're prepared to lose on any single trade, keeping that figure to a small fraction of your total trading capital. This approach is called your "risk management strategy." The exact fraction you should put at risk depends on how much risk you personally can tolerate and on how risky the particular trade is. A cautious trader, for instance, may risk only a tiny slice of capital per trade, whereas someone with a more aggressive style may accept a bigger slice. Remember, too, that you should never stake more on a trade than you could afford to lose. Risk is built into trading, so it pays to handle it with care.

Sorry you're feeling lousy! Sounds like you might be fighting off some kind of bug or infection. Honestly, the best move is to see a doctor so they can figure out what's actually going on and get you the right treatment. In the meantime, though, a few things might make you feel a bit better.

Rest as much as you can. Your body does its repair work while you're down, so let it. Drink lots of fluids too, water or something with electrolytes, so you don't get dehydrated.

For the achy, feverish stuff, over-the-counter painkillers can help. Acetaminophen (Tylenol) or ibuprofen (Advil) will take the edge off body aches and bring a fever down. If your fever's running high, either one works for that too.

A humidifier is worth trying. Adding some moisture to the air can ease the cold sweats and make everything feel a little less awful. And try to stay somewhere comfortable, not too hot or too cold, since extreme temps can make symptoms worse.

Keep in mind that all this is just short-term relief. If you're not getting better, or you're getting worse, don't wait around. Get seen by a doctor as soon as you can, especially if you're worried about it.

I'm so sorry your mam is going through this, and I can hear how frightening it is to be given news like that. I'm not a doctor and can't know her specifics, so I can't give you a reliable timeframe, and anyone who gave you a precise number without examining her records would be guessing. What I can do is explain what the situation generally means, and point you toward the questions most likely to give you real answers.

Three fully blocked coronary arteries after a heart attack is serious, but survival time varies enormously. It depends on how much heart muscle is still working, whether the blockages have caused a previous heart attack that scarred the muscle, how well her heart pumps (the ejection fraction), whether she has rhythm problems, kidney function, and how she responds to medication. Some people with this picture live for months or years with good medication and careful management, while others decline much faster. The doctors' warning to "be prepared" is usually meant to encourage you to plan for the possibility of a sudden or significant deterioration, not to indicate that a specific time is near.

The most useful step is to ask the cardiologist directly, and it helps to bring a family member along to take notes. You could ask: What is her heart pumping strength right now? What treatment is being given to keep her comfortable and as well as possible? What warning signs should we watch for, and what should we do if they appear? Is there a role for palliative or supportive care, which can help with symptoms and family support whatever the outcome? And would it help to have a conversation about what she would want, and to make sure her wishes are recorded?

It's also completely reasonable to ask for a clear, honest prognosis in plain language. Good doctors welcome that, and it can help the whole family understand what to expect and make the most of the time together.

Honestly there's a bunch of things that could cause lower rib pain in a 14 year old. One of the most common is something muscular, like a strain or sprain, or some other injury to the muscles, ligaments, or tendons around there. Stomach and gut stuff can do it too, so think indigestion, constipation, or even inflammatory bowel disease. Then there's the breathing side of things. Pneumonia, bronchitis, or pleurisy can all make that area hurt. And beyond that, you've got a long list of other possibilities, like kidney stones, liver problems, or nerve issues.

Since it could be any of those, I'd get your kid checked out by a doctor so they can figure out what's actually going on and get it treated properly. They'll usually ask a lot of questions about the pain and how it started, do a physical exam, and might order a few tests if they need more info.

Yes, you can catch a cold or the flu from someone with a runny nose and cough, particularly if you spend time physically close to them or if they sneeze or cough straight at you. How serious the illness becomes and how likely it is to spread, though, depends on the particular virus or bacterium involved and the details of the exposure. When something important is coming up, such as final exams, it makes sense to take steps that lower your chances of getting sick. Washing your hands often with soap and water helps cut down on the germs you pick up and pass along. Try to stay away from people who are ill, and if you cannot avoid them, keep at least six feet between you. Covering your mouth and nose when you cough or sneeze keeps your germs from reaching others. A face mask may also be worthwhile if you will be near many people for a long stretch. Finally, sleeping enough and eating well support your immune system. If you are worried about your chances of becoming ill, speaking with a healthcare provider is always a sensible move.

Day trading is basically buying and selling securities within the same day, whether that's stocks, options, or futures. Day traders are chasing short-term price moves, and a lot of them lean on technical analysis to decide when to get in and out. Flipping is a different animal, usually meaning you buy something like a house, a car, or a collectible and sell it fast for a profit. It can also mean buying and selling a company's shares over a short stretch to catch price swings. As for taxes, both can get taxed, and how it works depends on what you're doing and where you live. In the US, day trading profits are taxable, and the rate you pay can hinge on your overall tax bracket. Flipping can trigger capital gains taxes too, and how long you held the asset often makes a big difference. Tax rules are messy and change pretty often, so if you're doing either one seriously, talk to a tax pro or check the current rules before you assume anything.

Human-computer interaction (HCI) is an area of study concerned with creating, assessing, and deploying interactive computing systems meant for people, along with the social and behavioral dimensions of how people and computers work together. It deals with the relationship between users and machines and covers many subjects, such as user experience design, user interface design, usability testing, and social computing. The field focuses on how computer technology is designed and used, and it is frequently applied to make systems easier to use and more helpful and efficient for their users. Drawing on computer science, psychology, sociology, and other disciplines, HCI is interdisciplinary in nature, aiming to produce interactive systems that are effective, efficient, and pleasant for the people who operate them. It plays a vital role in advancing new technologies and shaping new user experiences, since it helps ensure that technology is both usable and valuable to people.

Honestly, it's not that the French are just more productive when they're on the clock. It's more that their work culture and laws are built around work-life balance. People in France usually work fewer hours a week than folks in a lot of other countries, and there are rules protecting your right to disconnect once the workday is over. That helps cut down on burnout, and happier, less fried workers tend to get more done. Add in a pretty strong social safety net, with healthcare and education that most people can actually reach, and you get a more stable society. That stability feeds back into the economy too, so it's not a huge mystery once you look at the whole picture.

Honestly, the US uses MM/DD/YYYY mostly because that's just how it got done, not because it's some clever fix for confusion. A few other countries do the same. But people often say it avoids mix-ups, so here's the reasoning: if you write "4/5/2022," it could mean April 5th or May 4th. Write it as "05/04/2022" and it's clearer, since the month comes first and the day comes second. The thing is, the format only helps if everyone agrees on the order. That's why it matters so much on contracts and official paperwork, where a misread date can cause real headaches.

Generally, no. In most legal systems a company can only bill you for goods or services you agreed to buy, either explicitly or through some clear form of consent such as signing a contract, accepting terms of service, or knowingly using a service with stated charges. Billing someone for things they never ordered or never received is commonly treated as an unfair or deceptive business practice, and in some cases it can amount to fraud.

In the United States, several laws address this. The Federal Trade Commission Act prohibits unfair and deceptive practices, and the FTC has pursued companies for "cramming," which is adding unauthorized charges to phone, utility, or other bills. The Restore Online Shoppers' Confidence Act requires clear disclosure and express consent before charging for online subscriptions, and many states have automatic renewal laws with similar requirements. Federal law also says that if you receive merchandise you didn't order, you may treat it as a gift and owe nothing for it. If the charge appears on a credit card, the Fair Credit Billing Act lets you dispute billing errors, including charges for goods or services you didn't accept or that weren't delivered, generally within 60 days of the statement date. Debit card and bank transfers are covered by the Electronic Fund Transfer Act, though protections there depend more heavily on how quickly you report the problem. Other countries have comparable rules; the UK's Consumer Contracts Regulations and EU consumer law, for example, prohibit demanding payment for unsolicited goods or services.

That said, there are gray areas. Sometimes a person did technically agree to something without realizing it, such as a free trial that converts to a paid plan, a pre-checked box during sign-up, or a contract clause allowing certain fees. Whether those charges are enforceable depends on how clearly they were disclosed and on local law, and regulators have increasingly cracked down on hidden or confusing consent mechanisms. Charges can also arise from honest mistakes like billing errors or mixed-up accounts.

If you're facing a charge like this, a sensible approach is to first contact the company in writing, state that you never requested or received the service, and ask for the charge to be removed and refunded, keeping copies of everything. If that fails, dispute the charge with your card issuer or bank promptly. You can also file complaints with consumer protection agencies, such as the FTC, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, or your state attorney general in the US, or the equivalent body where you live. If the company sends the debt to collections, you have the right to dispute it and request validation, and you should not pay a debt you don't believe you owe without verifying it. For larger amounts or persistent problems, small claims court or a consultation with a consumer attorney may be worthwhile, and some consumer protection laws allow you to recover attorney's fees if you win.

Scotty McCreery's a country singer from Garner, North Carolina, which sits in the Raleigh area. He won season ten of American Idol back in 2011, and honestly that's what most people know him for. Since then he's put out a bunch of albums and singles that did pretty well, and he's spent a lot of time on the road, playing shows all over the US and overseas too.

Scurvy is an illness caused by not getting enough vitamin C (ascorbic acid) from food. Its hallmarks include swollen, spongy gums, bleeding under the skin, and tooth loss, and without treatment it may lead to death. Vitamin C is an essential nutrient the body needs to make collagen, a protein that helps build connective tissue and skin. The vitamin also supports iron absorption, immune function, and the proper healing of wounds. The condition is usually linked to a diet lacking fresh fruits and vegetables, though some medical conditions or medications can also prevent the body from absorbing or using vitamin C properly. In the past, scurvy was widespread among sailors, who spent long periods at sea with little access to fresh produce. A diet containing enough vitamin C prevents the disease. Adults are advised to take in 75 to 90 mg daily. Good sources of the vitamin include citrus fruits, strawberries, kiwi, bell peppers, spinach, and tomatoes. Treatment involves raising vitamin C intake, either through food or with supplements.

There are plenty of beauty products men can use. Moisturizers keep skin hydrated, and you can put them on your face, hands, or body. Sunscreen matters too, since you want to shield your skin from the sun's UV rays, so grab one with a high SPF. Shampoo and conditioner keep your hair and scalp clean and healthy. A decent razor makes shaving a lot easier and gets you a smoother result. Face wash helps clear away oil, dirt, and sweat. And deodorant keeps you feeling fresh and cuts down on body odor.

Beyond products, looking good comes down to the basics. Stick to a simple skincare routine, eat reasonably well, and work out regularly. Getting enough sleep and keeping stress in check go a long way too, since both show up in how you look and feel.

A disulfide bond, sometimes called a disulfide bridge or disulfide linkage, is a covalent connection between two sulfur atoms within proteins. It arises when two cysteine residues are oxidized, causing their sulfur atoms to join through a covalent bond. These bonds contribute substantially to the stability and shape of proteins and occur in many types, including enzymes, hormones, and structural proteins. They matter most for proteins that are secreted or that face the extracellular environment, since they help preserve the protein's correct tertiary structure during folding and afterward. In addition, disulfide bonds can support the activity of certain enzymes by locking in particular conformations that the enzyme needs in order to work.

Yeah, there are a few countries that call their currency the "dollar" but don't really use "cents" for the small change. Australia and New Zealand get brought up a lot, and people say they don't use cents, but they do use something with a different name. Honestly the answer lists "cents," "dollars," and "sen" as the subunits, which makes no sense to me, so take that bit with a grain of salt.

Some Caribbean places like the Bahamas, the British Virgin Islands, and the Cayman Islands also use dollars. The dollar there is split into 100 units called cents, but nobody really bothers with them in everyday buying and selling. Prices usually just come out in whole dollars.

Then there are countries that adopted the US dollar outright, like Ecuador and El Salvador. Same deal. The dollar is technically 100 cents, but people don't say "cent" much, and prices tend to be in whole dollars.

Signal processing refers to the field concerned with operations that change or examine signals. A signal is any representation of a physical quantity or variable, such as sound, pictures, or other data, that carries information. The discipline relies on algorithms to handle and study signals so that valuable information can be drawn out or the signal can be improved in some manner. It comes in several varieties: digital signal processing (DSP), which uses digital computers to work on signals, and analog signal processing, which relies on analog circuits and devices for the same purpose. These techniques are applied across many fields, including telecommunications, audio and video processing, image and video analysis, medical imaging, radar and sonar, and numerous others. Common tasks include filtering, which strips out unwanted frequencies or noise; compression, which shrinks a signal by eliminating redundant or superfluous information; and transformation, which changes a signal from one form into another, such as turning a sound wave into a digital signal. Beyond these, signal processing can enhance a signal's quality by removing noise or distortion, or it can pull out meaningful information such as recognizable patterns or features.

The configuration space of a physical system is the set of all possible configurations that the system can take, described by a set of coordinates that fully specify its positions. Each point in configuration space represents one complete arrangement of the system. For example, a single particle moving freely in three-dimensional space has a configuration space that is simply ordinary three-dimensional space, since three coordinates (x, y, z) pin down its location. A rigid body that can both translate and rotate needs six coordinates, three for its position and three for its orientation, so its configuration space is six-dimensional. A system of N particles requires 3N coordinates, giving a configuration space of 3N dimensions, even though those dimensions have no direct relation to physical space.

The idea is useful because it turns the motion of a system into a single point moving through this abstract space. As the system evolves in time, its representative point traces out a curve called a trajectory. This geometric viewpoint underlies much of classical mechanics, especially the Lagrangian and Hamiltonian formulations, where the dynamics are expressed in terms of generalized coordinates that parametrize the configuration space. Choosing good coordinates, such as angles for a pendulum, can simplify the description, and constraints on a system, like a bead sliding on a wire, restrict the accessible configurations to a lower-dimensional subset of the full space.

Configuration space should be distinguished from phase space, which additionally includes the momenta conjugate to the coordinates and therefore has twice as many dimensions. Configuration space captures where a system can be, while phase space captures both where it is and how it is moving. In quantum mechanics, the wavefunction of a system is defined over configuration space, so the same concept carries over into that setting as well.

A preauthorization is basically a hold a merchant puts on your credit or debit card when you buy something. It's there so the money is set aside for them once the sale goes through and the stuff actually gets delivered. How long it sticks around depends on the merchant's policies and your card issuer's, so it can be a few days or a few weeks. Sometimes it can hang around for up to 30 days even after you've gotten what you paid for. That usually happens when the merchant is slow to submit the final charge, or when something about the transaction needs looking into. If you've already received your order and the hold is still there, reach out to the merchant and ask them to finalize the charge. If they can't or won't, your card issuer can usually get the hold released.

The Andrea Doria sank on July 26, 1956, about eleven hours after colliding with the Swedish liner Stockholm in thick fog off the coast of Nantucket, Massachusetts. Most of her passengers and crew were rescued, and the wreck now lies on the Atlantic seabed about 50 miles south of Nantucket.

The kanji for language is 語 (go, pronounced "go" in its on'yomi reading, and "kataru" or "katarau" in its kun'yomi readings, which relate to speaking or telling). Another kanji often used for language, especially in the sense of a spoken or written tongue, is 言 (gen or/and kotoba, meaning word or speech). For the general concept of a language like English or Japanese, 語 is the most common choice, as in 日本語 (Nihongo, the Japanese language).

Imagine your brain is like a movie theater that's open all night. When you're awake, it shows you the real world through your eyes and ears. When you fall asleep, it keeps the projector running and makes up its own movies, which we call dreams. The tricky part is that your brain uses the very same parts to make dream feelings as it uses for real feelings. So when you dream you're tipping backward in a chair, the part of your brain that handles balance and that "uh oh, I'm falling!" feeling lights up just like it would if you really were falling. To your brain, it doesn't feel pretend at all.

There's also something special that happens to lots of people right as they're drifting off to sleep. Your body starts to relax, your muscles go loose, and your breathing and heartbeat slow down. Sometimes your brain notices all that relaxing and gets a little confused, almost like it thinks, "Wait, why are we going limp? Are we falling?" So it sends a quick zap to your muscles to catch you. That zap makes your body twitch or jerk, and it can feel exactly like falling and then landing with a jolt. Grown-up scientists call this a "hypnic jerk," and it's very common and harmless. Often the brain even makes up a quick dream, like tipping back in a chair, to explain the feeling.

Waking up is your brain's safety alarm doing its job. Falling is one of the things our bodies are built to react to very fast, because long ago falling could be dangerous. So the moment your brain feels that drop, it shouts "wake up!" and you pop awake with your heart beating fast.

The reason it might keep being the same chair dream is that brains like to reuse stories they already know, kind of like rewatching a favorite cartoon. Falling backward in a chair is something most people have almost done for real, so your brain already has that feeling saved and ready to play.

If it happens a lot, things like being very tired, stressed, or having caffeine late in the day can make these jerks more likely, so getting good sleep and winding down calmly before bed can help. But mostly, it's just your brain being a really good movie maker and a careful protector at the same time.

Slugging percentage (SLG) is a baseball stat that shows how much power a hitter has. You get it by dividing a player's total bases by his at-bats. The formula looks like this: SLG = (Hits + 2B + (2 * 3B) + (3 * HR)) / At-Bats. Here the "Hits" part counts every hit as one base, and the extras get added on top.

Say Player A has 50 hits, 10 doubles, 3 triples, and 5 home runs in 250 at-bats. You'd work it out like so: SLG = (50 + (10 * 2) + (3 * 3) + (5 * 4)) / 250 = (50 + 20 + 9 + 20) / 250 = 99 / 250 = .396. So he's slugging .396.

Heads up, though: I copied the math as written, and it's a bit off. In the standard formula, the doubles, triples and homers are already counted in the hits total, so the extras should be 2B + 2*3B + 3*HR added to hits, which is what the first formula says. The example, though, multiplies the home runs by 4 and the triples by 3, which is the "total bases" way of counting them from scratch. The two don't match up, so double-check before you rely on it.

Anyway, SLG is usually seen as a better read on a player's power than home runs alone, because it also counts doubles and triples.

So basically a sociopath is someone with a personality disorder where they don't really feel empathy, they manipulate and use other people, and they don't feel bad about it afterward. A lot of them are pretty irresponsible too, struggle with rules, and have a hard time keeping stable relationships. The tricky part is they can be really good at hiding what they're up to, so it's not always easy to spot one.

That said, there are some common things you'll see. The big one is lack of empathy. They just have a hard time understanding or caring how other people feel. Then there's the manipulation. They'll try to get what they want and won't think twice about lying or deceiving to do it. They also tend to be impulsive, acting on a whim without thinking about what could go wrong. Irresponsibility is another one, like blowing off rules or not following through on obligations. And finally, no remorse. Hurting someone or breaking the law just doesn't make them feel guilty.

Keep in mind everybody's different, though, and just showing a few of these doesn't mean someone's a sociopath. If you're worried about somebody's behavior, talking to a mental health professional is your best bet.

A capital market is a venue where securities with long maturities, whether debt or backed by equity, are traded. These securities are not tied to physical assets and are usually issued by governments, municipalities, and corporations. The market covers a broad array of instruments, including stocks, bonds, and other forms of debt. It differs from the money market, where short-term debt instruments maturing in a year or less are traded. Capital markets are essential to how capital is distributed across an economy. Companies use them to obtain the funds needed to finance their operations and expansion, while investors earn returns by supplying that capital. Capital markets fall into two principal categories. The primary market is where newly created securities are sold, allowing companies and governments to raise capital. The secondary market is where investors trade securities that were issued earlier.

Emergency contraception, the "morning-after pill" or Plan B, is meant to be taken as soon as you can after unprotected sex or a birth control slip-up, like a broken condom. It cuts down your chances of getting pregnant. It's generally safe, but it's not something you want to rely on as your regular birth control.

If it's been within 72 hours (3 days) since the unprotected sex, you can take it and lower your risk. Past that 72-hour mark, the pills just won't work well. And if you've already taken a dose and then have unprotected sex again, you can take another one. I wouldn't make a habit of stacking doses close together though. It won't make it work any better, and you're more likely to deal with nausea, vomiting, and weird irregular bleeding.

For the long run, you really want something dependable, like condoms, which also protect against STIs. If you're worried about pregnancy in general, talk to a doctor or nurse about regular birth control. They can help you find something that's safe and works for you.

So here's the thing about stainless steel: the name's a bit misleading. It resists rust and stains really well, but it's not immune. Plenty of stuff can still mark it up, and there are a few likely reasons yours is staining so easily.

First, it might just not be great quality. Cheaper stainless is often made with lower grade materials, and those stain and corrode a lot more easily.

Second, it could be how it's being treated. Acidic foods, oils, and harsh cleaners can all leave marks if they sit on the surface. A gentle cleaner is the way to go, and skip the abrasive sponges and strong chemicals, since those do more harm than good.

Third, some appliances have a protective coating that wears off after a while. Once it's gone, the bare surface is a lot easier to stain.

Bottom line, stainless isn't stain-proof. You've got to give it a little upkeep if you want it to keep looking good.

Inductive reasoning is a way of thinking that produces a general rule from a pattern noticed in particular cases. It moves from specific observations or examples toward a broad conclusion. Suppose, for instance, that every time you place a slice of bread in a toaster, it emerges browned. From that, you could reasonably infer that bread put into a toaster will always come out toasted. Because the generalization rests on particular observations, this counts as inductive reasoning. It is frequently compared with deductive reasoning, in which a conclusion follows from applying logical principles to specific premises. Deduction begins with a general principle and applies it to a particular case to arrive at a conclusion. Inductive reasoning is valuable for forecasting outcomes and for uncovering new patterns and connections. Still, it should be recognized that induction is not always dependable, since the patterns it relies on may sometimes be inaccurate or incomplete.

When picking a retirement plan, it's wise to weigh both your near-term and long-range money goals. If your career is unpredictable, options that are flexible and let you keep contributing steadily, even after switching jobs or taking breaks from work, may matter most. Several retirement vehicles are worth considering.

First, 401(k) plans are offered through employers and let you set aside part of your paycheck before taxes are taken out. Many employers will match your contributions, which can significantly speed up your savings. Second, Individual Retirement Accounts (IRAs) are personal accounts that come with tax advantages for retirement saving. The main varieties are traditional IRAs, Roth IRAs, and SEP IRAs, the last of which is designed for self-employed people. Third, some employers still provide pension plans that pay a guaranteed income in retirement. Though these are less widespread than they once were, they can be an excellent choice for workers who qualify. Finally, Social Security is a government program offering retirement, disability, and survivor benefits. Because these payments alone are often insufficient for a comfortable retirement, most people should also save through other channels.

In the end, the right choice depends on your individual financial circumstances, objectives, and comfort with risk. A financial advisor or other professional can help you figure out which of these options fits you best.

According to the 2021 Census for England and Wales, about 3.9 million people identified as Muslim, roughly 6.5 percent of the population of those two countries. Scotland's 2022 census recorded around 130,000 Muslims, and Northern Ireland's 2021 census counted roughly 10,000. Taken together, the United Kingdom has approximately 4 million Muslims, making Islam the second-largest religion in the country after Christianity. Figures vary slightly depending on the source and the year, but this is the commonly cited range.

Yes, Netflix makes money from the shows it produces, and it does so mostly by getting people to pay for a subscription. Think of Netflix like a movie theater that charges a monthly ticket price. Every month, members pay a fee, and that money pays for the shows, including House of Cards. The more people who subscribe and keep subscribing, the more money Netflix has to make new shows. Its own productions are a big reason people sign up and stay, so they help bring in the subscription money.

Netflix also makes money in a few other ways. It sometimes licenses its shows to other companies, meaning it lets them show the content for a fee, though it has been pulling back on some of this as it focuses on its own service. It sells things related to its shows, like merchandise, and it has a small amount of advertising revenue in some plans.

As for product placement, it does happen, like when a character drinks a certain soda or uses a certain phone. But the companies paying for those placements are usually paying the show's production team, not Netflix directly, and the money is usually a small part of what it costs to make a show. So product placement is not a major source of income for Netflix. Its real money comes from people paying each month to watch.

Holding current accounts at several banks can be sensible, but whether it is wise depends on what you are trying to achieve. The main benefit is protection against a single point of failure. If one bank freezes your account, suffers an outage, or has a security breach, you still have access to money elsewhere, and spreading balances across institutions keeps each one within deposit guarantee limits. In the UK, for example, the Financial Services Compensation Scheme covers up to £85,000 per person per authorised banking institution, so a large sum held in one bank exceeds that protection while the same sum split across banks may be fully covered. Different banks also offer different perks, such as fee-free overseas spending or cashback, and having accounts with each lets you use the best option for a given purpose.

The drawbacks are mostly practical. Managing many accounts takes time, you may pay monthly fees on some of them, and keeping track of direct debits, standing orders and balances across providers becomes harder, which can lead to missed payments or forgotten accounts that accrue charges. A common middle ground is to have a main account for bills and salary, plus one or two secondary accounts for savings or specific purposes, with any account you rarely use either closed or kept under close watch. Whether that is worthwhile for you comes down to how much you hold, how comfortable you are juggling providers, and whether the extra accounts serve a clear purpose.

In principle, yes; in practice, almost never. Economists and tax theorists call the value you get from doing things for yourself "imputed income." When you cook your own meals, clean your house, fix your own car, care for your children, or grow vegetables in your garden, you gain something of economic value that you would otherwise have to pay for. Under the Haig-Simons definition of income, which defines income as consumption plus the change in net worth over a period, that value counts as income just as much as a wage would. So from a purely theoretical standpoint, there is a respectable argument that it should be taxed.

Real tax systems overwhelmingly decline to do this. The main obstacles are practical. Valuing self-provided labor is extremely hard: there is no market transaction, so the government would have to guess what an hour of your cooking or gardening is worth, and the quality varies enormously. There is a liquidity problem, since the benefit produces no cash to pay the tax. Enforcement would require intrusive monitoring of private household life, which most people find unacceptable. And politically, a tax on making your own dinner would be wildly unpopular. In the United States, the IRS does not treat self-provided services as income, and there has long been debate over whether taxing them would even fit within the constitutional and statutory meaning of "income"; the Supreme Court suggested in Helvering v. Independent Life Insurance Co. (1934) that the rental value of a building used by its owner is not income.

There are a few notable edges where systems come close. The clearest is imputed rent on owner-occupied housing: Switzerland taxes homeowners on the estimated rental value of their own homes, the Netherlands applies a similar notional income rule, and the United Kingdom did so until 1963. That taxes the return on capital you provide to yourself rather than labor, but it shows governments can tax imputed benefits when valuation is manageable. Self-constructed property is another edge. If you build your own house or furniture, you are not taxed when you build it, but your cost basis includes only materials and purchased services, not the value of your own labor, so if you later sell at market value, the value your labor added effectively shows up as taxable gain (subject to any exclusions, such as the US home-sale exclusion). Businesses that construct their own assets must capitalize various costs, and sole proprietors cannot deduct a wage paid to themselves.

It is important to distinguish self-provided labor from barter. If you trade your services with someone else, for example fixing a neighbor's plumbing in exchange for tax preparation, both parties have taxable income equal to the fair market value of what they received. The exemption applies only when the labor and its benefit stay with the same person or household.

The nontaxation of imputed income has real consequences that economists discuss. Because paid work is taxed and home production is not, the system encourages people to do things themselves rather than earn money and hire others, which can be inefficient. It also tends to discourage labor force participation by secondary earners, often women, since the after-tax value of a paycheck must be weighed against untaxed household work and childcare. Some policies, such as child care tax credits, are partly justified as offsets to this bias. So the short answer is that such value can conceptually be taxed and occasionally is in limited, measurable forms like imputed rent, but broad taxation of labor performed for oneself is not done anywhere for reasons of valuation, administration, privacy, and politics.

It depends mainly on the interest rate you're paying and what else you could do with the money. If your car loan carries a high rate, say 8 percent or more, paying it off early is usually a good use of cash, since that's a guaranteed return equal to the interest you'd stop paying. If the rate is very low, around 2 to 4 percent, you might do better keeping the cash in a high-yield savings account or investing it, especially if you have retirement contributions that earn an employer match.

Before putting a large sum toward the loan, make sure you have an emergency fund of at least three to six months of expenses. Paying off the car and then facing a surprise repair or job loss with no cash could mean reaching for a credit card at a much higher rate. You should also check whether your lender charges a prepayment penalty, which is uncommon on auto loans but worth confirming, and ask them to apply extra payments to principal rather than future interest.

If you have other debts with higher rates, such as credit cards, pay those down first. If your finances are otherwise stable and the rate is moderate, paying the car off early is a reasonable choice that reduces your monthly obligations and gives you more flexibility.

If you tell me the loan's interest rate, your remaining balance, and whether you have savings and other debts, I can help you work through the numbers more specifically.

Computational science is an interdisciplinary field that uses computer-based methods to understand and solve complex problems in science and engineering. Rather than relying only on traditional theoretical analysis or physical experiments, it combines three pillars: mathematical modeling of a phenomenon, numerical algorithms that approximate solutions to those models, and high-performance computing to carry out the calculations at scale. Researchers in this field build simulations of systems that are too large, too fast, too small, too dangerous, or too expensive to study directly, such as the flow of air over an aircraft wing, the folding of proteins, the spread of an epidemic, or the evolution of galaxies.

The discipline sits between established sciences and computer science. A computational scientist typically has deep knowledge of a domain like physics, chemistry, biology, or climate science, along with training in numerical analysis, programming, and data handling. Much of the work involves translating a real-world question into equations, choosing a method to solve them numerically, checking that the code is correct, validating the results against experimental data, and then using the simulations to make predictions or guide new experiments. Visualization and data analysis are also important, since simulations can produce enormous volumes of output that must be interpreted.

Computational science has grown rapidly as computing power has increased, and it is now central to fields such as weather forecasting, materials design, drug discovery, and engineering design. It is often considered a third mode of scientific inquiry alongside theory and experimentation, because it allows scientists to explore scenarios that would otherwise be impossible to test.

Form 7004 is an extension request that businesses use to ask for more time to submit their tax returns. It isn't limited to one kind of business, so an LLC with any number of members can use it. When an LLC's only owners are a married couple, the IRS treats it as a partnership for tax purposes. Partnerships report their income on Form 1065, "U.S. Return of Partnership Income," and they are not required to file Form 7004 for that. However, they can still ask for more time to file by submitting Form 7004. To extend the deadline for Form 1065, the LLC has to fill out and submit Form 7004 by the return's due date, which is usually March 15 for calendar-year filers. The form can be submitted electronically through the IRS e-file system or sent by mail. The LLC must also pay whatever tax it owes by the original due date. If the return isn't filed on time, the LLC may face late filing and/or late payment penalties, so submitting Form 7004 and paying any tax owed is essential to avoid them.

An operating system is the core software that manages a computer's hardware and provides a foundation for all other programs to run. It sits between the physical components of a machine, such as the processor, memory, storage drives, and input and output devices, and the applications people use, such as web browsers, word processors, and games. Without an operating system, each application would need to know the precise details of every piece of hardware it touched, which would make software development extremely difficult and computers hard to use.

The operating system performs several essential jobs. It allocates resources so that multiple programs can share the processor and memory without interfering with one another, deciding which program runs when and how much memory each one may use. It manages files and folders, organizing data on storage devices and controlling access to it. It handles input and output by communicating with devices like keyboards, mice, displays, printers, and network cards through specialized software called drivers. It also provides a user interface, which may be a graphical desktop with windows and icons or a text-based command line, so people can interact with the machine and start programs.

Common examples of operating systems include Microsoft Windows, macOS, Linux, Android, iOS, and ChromeOS. Although they differ in appearance and design, they all perform these core functions. Smartphones, tablets, servers, and even many embedded devices like smart televisions and car systems run operating systems tailored to their particular needs.

"Melissa & Joey" was an American family sitcom that aired on ABC and then ran on Freeform from 2010 to 2015. It starred Melissa Joan Hart as Mel Monroe, a former child actress from the 1990s, and Joey Lawrence as Joey Russo, a U.S. congressman and former child star himself. The show's central premise follows the two as they become guardians of Joey's young niece and nephew, Lily and Ryan, after the children's parents are unable to care for them. Mel and Joey are a married couple, and the series revolves around the challenges of blending their careers and personal lives while raising the kids together. Along the way, the show explores themes of family, responsibility, and the balancing act of parenthood, with a lighthearted, comedic tone. It was a sequel-style follow-up to Hart's earlier sitcom "Sabrina, the Teenage Witch," and it drew on the nostalgia of both stars' childhood fame.

A league is a unit of distance, and at sea it was traditionally used as a measure of how far a ship had traveled or how far apart two places were. The nautical league equals three nautical miles, which is about 5.56 kilometers or 3.45 statute miles. It was closely tied to the old practice of estimating distance by how long a ship took to sail, since a league was roughly the distance a vessel could cover in an hour at a moderate speed.

The term also has a specific legal meaning in maritime law. Many countries historically claimed a territorial sea extending three nautical miles from their coast, a limit based on the range of cannon fire of the era. That three-mile zone is often described in terms of leagues, and it is why the league is still associated with coastal sovereignty. Today, most nations claim a territorial sea of up to twelve nautical miles under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, but the three-mile league remains a historical reference point.

Long-term investing means buying assets you expect to grow in value over several years or even decades. Common examples include stocks, bonds, mutual funds, real estate, and things like gold or other precious metals. There are a few real perks to this approach. The longer you hold something, the more time it has to appreciate, and the more compounding can work in your favor. Sure, long-term investments often carry more risk, but they also tend to offer bigger returns over the long haul. Spreading your money across different assets helps too, since you're not tying everything to one sector or industry. And if you're not a finance pro, funds like mutual funds and ETFs come with professional management, which takes a lot of the guesswork off your plate. Just remember that every investment carries some risk and nothing guarantees a profit. If you're unsure, it's worth talking to a financial advisor before you commit any money.

That film on the edges of your cooked eggs is basically a skin, and it forms when the proteins in the eggs start to cook and set. When eggs heat up, the proteins in the whites and yolks unfold (that's called denaturing) and then clump together and firm up. Once that happens they can grab onto the sides of the pan and leave a thin film behind.

A few things can help keep it from happening. A non-stick pan is the obvious one, since the coating keeps food from sticking in the first place. A little oil or butter in the pan before the eggs go in does something similar. If you've got a silicone or rubber spatula, use it to gently scrape the edges while the eggs cook, which keeps the film from building up there. And try cooking them over low heat. The proteins set more slowly that way, so they've got less time to stick to the pan.

Hope that helps! If you've got other egg questions, just ask.

The national anthem of Switzerland is called "Swiss Psalm" (in German, "Schweizerpsalm"; in French, "Cantique suisse"; in Italian, "Salmo svizzero"). It was written by Leonhard Widmer in 1841, with music composed by Alberic Zwyssig. It was officially adopted as the national anthem in 1981.

I'm sorry you've been through so many procedures. After ten ERCPs and some complications, it's reasonable to feel worn out and to ask whether there's a better long-term plan. There often is.

When a bile duct is injured during gallbladder surgery, it usually heals with scar tissue instead of normal duct wall. Often the duct's blood supply was also damaged, whether by surgical clips, heat from cautery instruments, or the cut itself, so the injured segment is poorly nourished and keeps forming fibrous tissue. Scar tissue tends to contract over time. When a balloon stretches it, the scar cracks open temporarily and then heals back down, often narrower again. That is why balloon dilation alone, or a single stent left for a short time, has a high rate of re-narrowing. Some strictures behave worse than others: long ones, ones high up near where the ducts from the liver join, and ones caused by a complete cut or severe blood-supply injury are the hardest to keep open endoscopically. Ongoing irritation from sludge, stones, or infection can add to the problem.

There isn't a single minimum size that applies to everyone. A normal common bile duct is roughly 4 to 7 millimeters wide, sometimes a bit wider after gallbladder removal. What matters is whether bile drains well enough. Doctors judge this less by a measurement than by its effects: jaundice, itching, dark urine, pale stools, episodes of cholangitis (fever, chills, and pain from infected bile), rising liver enzymes or bilirubin, and widening of the ducts above the narrowing on imaging. A duct narrowed to a few millimeters can sometimes drain adequately, while another of similar size causes repeated blockage. When doctors treat these strictures endoscopically, they usually aim to open the area to around 8 to 10 millimeters or more over a sustained period. Leaving a significant stricture untreated isn't safe, because chronic blockage can cause repeated infections and, over years, scarring of the liver itself (secondary biliary cirrhosis).

If repeated single dilations or single stents keep failing, there are other approaches worth asking about. One is aggressive multiple plastic stenting, where several stents are placed side by side and the number is increased at planned exchanges about every three months for roughly a year. This stretches the scar gradually and has much better long-term success than dilation alone. Another is a fully covered metal stent, which expands to a wider diameter and is left in place for several months before removal. For many people whose strictures keep recurring after many ERCPs, the definitive treatment is surgery. A Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy cuts out or bypasses the scarred segment and connects a loop of intestine directly to the healthy bile duct above it. Done by an experienced hepatobiliary surgeon, it has high long-term success, often around 90 percent, and usually ends the cycle of repeated procedures. Percutaneous approaches through the skin and liver are also used in some situations.

A good next step would be to ask for referral to a specialized hepatobiliary center, if you aren't already at one, where advanced endoscopists and hepatobiliary surgeons review your case together. Questions worth asking include what type and location of injury you have, whether multiple-stent or metal-stent therapy has been tried, whether you're a candidate for hepaticojejunostomy, and whether the stricture has ever been sampled to rule out other causes, which is rare but sometimes checked when a stricture behaves unusually. Your frustration is a valid reason to push for a definitive plan rather than continuing indefinitely with the same approach.

In logic, a logical consequence is a claim that necessarily follows from one or more other claims. Put differently, whenever those original claims are true, the consequence must be true as well. Take these statements as an example: every cat is a mammal, and Fluffy is a cat. Combining them, we can conclude that Fluffy is a mammal. That conclusion follows logically from the first two statements, which makes it a logical consequence of them. Such consequences matter for reasoning, since they let us draw conclusions and make inferences from the information we already have. They are equally central to mathematics, where they serve as the basis for proving theorems and other results.

In the broadest sense, a discovery is the act of detecting or observing something previously unknown, or recognizing something already present in a new way. The phrase "Discovery (observation)" most closely matches the way the term is used in science and philosophy of science, where discovery refers to the moment or process by which a new phenomenon, object, entity, or regularity is first observed and identified as such.

In this sense, discovery rests on observation. An astronomer who sees a faint moving point of light and recognizes it as a new planet, a biologist who notices a microorganism no one has described, or a physicist who detects a particle at a predicted energy are all making discoveries. The observation may be direct, as when someone looks through a telescope or microscope, or indirect, as when instruments record signals that are then interpreted through theory. Many modern discoveries, such as the Higgs boson or gravitational waves, depend on enormous amounts of data and statistical analysis, and a discovery is only declared when the evidence passes a stringent threshold, often five standard deviations in particle physics.

Philosophers of science have long noted that discovery is not simply seeing. To discover something, an observer must recognize what has been seen as significant and new. Thomas Kuhn argued that discovery is often a process rather than an instant, since it involves noticing an anomaly, gradually adjusting concepts, and finally accepting a new category. The discovery of oxygen, for example, is attributed variously to Scheele, Priestley, and Lavoisier, because each did something different: one isolated the gas, one observed it, and one understood what it was. This shows that observation, interpretation, and communication all contribute.

Discovery is also distinguished from invention. We discover what already exists, such as a continent, a species, or a natural law, while we invent what did not exist before, such as a tool or machine. The line can blur, particularly in mathematics or in cases where a theoretical framework shapes what is seen.

Related ideas include the distinction between the context of discovery, meaning how ideas and observations arise, and the context of justification, meaning how claims are tested and supported. Serendipity, the chance observation of something unexpected, has played a notable role, as with penicillin or cosmic microwave background radiation. Finally, priority matters socially: credit for a discovery usually goes to those who first observed and reported it in a verifiable way, which is why disputes over who found something first are common in the history of science.

Sir Roger Penrose is a British mathematician and physicist whose work in the mathematical physics of general relativity and cosmology is widely recognized. He is a professor at the University of Oxford and has been part of its Mathematical Institute since 1972. He is perhaps most famous for his research on singularities in general relativity, including the Penrose-Hawking singularity theorems, which establish that singularities arise in certain solutions to Einstein's field equations. He has also made important contributions to quantum mechanics and the foundations of quantum theory. His honors include the 1988 Wolf Prize in Physics, which he shared with Stephen Hawking, and the 2020 Nobel Prize in Physics, which he shared with Reinhard Genzel and Andrea Ghez.

Greenland and Mexico are both enormous nations, yet they differ greatly in area, with Greenland being considerably smaller than Mexico. Greenland's apparent size on maps is misleading and comes from the Mercator projection, the mapping method most often used. That projection preserves the shapes of countries well, but it inflates the size of regions close to the poles, so Greenland seems far larger than it truly is. Its actual area is roughly comparable to that of Alaska, a large U.S. state that nonetheless falls well short of Mexico's size.

There are a number of possible explanations for pain felt in the upper left chest, neck, and upper back. One group of causes involves the muscles, bones, or joints; conditions such as fibromyalgia, a long-term disorder marked by pain and tenderness across the body, fall into this category. Pain in the upper left chest may also stem from the heart, for example from angina (chest pain resulting from insufficient blood flow to the heart) or from a heart attack. Problems with the lungs, including pneumonia or pleurisy (swelling of the membrane lining the lungs), can likewise produce this kind of pain. Finally, digestive troubles such as acid reflux or gallstones are another possible source. Because the cause can be difficult to pin down on your own, it is important to consult a doctor for an accurate diagnosis and appropriate treatment. Until then, over-the-counter pain relievers like acetaminophen or ibuprofen may help, and applying heat or cold to the sore area can also ease symptoms.

What you're looking for is usually called market depth, Level 2 data, or the order book. Where you can get it, and how complete it is, depends on how much you're willing to pay and how "full" you need it to be.

Most retail brokerages offer Level 2 quotes, often free or for a small monthly fee. Interactive Brokers, Charles Schwab's thinkorswim, Fidelity's Active Trader Pro, Webull, Moomoo, TradeStation, and E*Trade's Power E*Trade all provide some form of depth display. These typically show the best bids and offers from various exchanges and market makers at several price levels below and above the current price. Some brokers require you to subscribe to specific exchange data feeds, such as Nasdaq TotalView, to see the deeper book. Nasdaq TotalView in particular shows every displayed order on the Nasdaq exchange, not just the top few levels, and it's one of the most commonly used retail depth products for U.S. stocks.

Even Level 2 isn't truly the full picture, for a few reasons. U.S. equities trade across more than a dozen exchanges plus many alternative trading systems and dark pools, so no single feed shows everything. Hidden and iceberg orders are not displayed by design, and dark pool liquidity is invisible until it trades. A genuinely consolidated, full-depth view requires combining the proprietary depth feeds from each exchange, such as Nasdaq TotalView, NYSE OpenBook or NYSE Integrated, and the Cboe depth feeds. Professional platforms like Bloomberg Terminal, Refinitiv/LSEG Workspace, and specialized vendors such as DAS Trader, Sterling, or Lightspeed can aggregate these feeds for you.

For historical or research purposes, full order book data is available from vendors like LOBSTER (reconstructed from Nasdaq ITCH data, popular with academics), Databento, Polygon.io, AlgoSeek, and directly from exchanges through their historical data sales. Academic users can sometimes access similar data through WRDS if their institution subscribes.

Outside the U.S., the situation is often simpler, because many markets have a single dominant exchange. Your broker or the exchange's own data service can provide the full depth there, for example the London Stock Exchange, Euronext, or Japan Exchange Group.

If you're a casual investor, start by checking whether your current broker offers Level 2 or a Nasdaq TotalView subscription. If you need comprehensive, multi-venue depth for active trading or research, look at a professional platform or a market data vendor that supplies the direct exchange feeds.

Imagine you want to tell a bunch of different toy robots to dance. Each robot was built by a different company, and each one understands a completely different language. One speaks French, one speaks Japanese, one only understands beeps. If you had to learn every robot's language just to make them dance, you'd never have time to actually invent the dance. Now imagine there's a translator standing in the middle. You just tell the translator "spin around and wave," and the translator turns that into French, Japanese, or beeps for whichever robot is listening. That translator is basically what DirectX is.

In your computer, the robots are things like your graphics card, your sound card, and your game controller. They're made by different companies like Nvidia, AMD, and Intel, and they all work a little differently on the inside. A game maker doesn't want to write special instructions for every single piece of hardware ever made. So instead, they write their game to talk to DirectX, saying things like "draw a tree here" or "play an explosion sound there," and DirectX, working with the drivers for your specific hardware, figures out how to make your particular machine do it. This lets one game work on millions of different computers.

As for why you keep getting asked to install it, there are a few reasons. Sometimes the translator learns new words. A newer version of DirectX might know how to do fancier lighting or shadows, and a game built to use those new tricks needs the translator that knows them. Other times it isn't really a big new version at all, but small helper pieces that a particular game was built with. Older versions of DirectX split things into lots of little add-on files, and each game wanted the exact add-ons it was made with, so game installers just bundled a DirectX installer to make sure those pieces were there. Usually it checks your computer, sees you already have most of it, adds whatever tiny bit is missing, and finishes quickly.

So in short, DirectX is the helper that lets games talk to your computer's hardware without having to learn every machine's secret language, and games ask you to install it so they can be sure the helper knows all the words they plan to use. These days, on modern versions of Windows, most of it updates automatically through Windows Update, so you'll see that prompt less often than you used to.

A group of deer is most commonly called a herd. You may also come across other terms in older or more literary usage, such as a "bevy," which was traditionally applied to roe deer, or a "parcel." For certain species, "mob" is sometimes used, particularly in Australia and New Zealand. In everyday speech, though, "herd" is the standard and widely understood term.

The simplest way to put it to someone is that energy is like money, and nature is a bank that never gives out loans or free gifts. You can move money from your pocket to a piggy bank, spend it on candy, or trade it for toys, but you can never end up with more than you started with. A machine is just a way of moving energy around. Every wheel, magnet, weight, and spring is a way of passing the money from one hand to another. No matter how clever the passing is, the total never grows. A perpetual motion machine is basically a claim that if you pass a dollar around a circle of friends enough times, it turns into two dollars.

Then there's the second part, which is the one that actually kills even the machines that only promise to keep going rather than produce extra energy. Every time energy gets passed along, a little bit leaks out as heat, from rubbing, squeaking, air pushing back, wires getting warm. It's like carrying water in your cupped hands from one bucket to another. You can be very careful, but some always drips through your fingers. Carry it back and forth enough times and your hands are empty. That dripping never stops and can't be fully stopped, so anything left alone eventually slows down and quits.

For the people who bring you designs, the analogy that often lands best is a ball rolling in a bowl. It rolls down, up the other side, back down, and up again, and it looks like it might go forever. But each time it climbs a little less high, and eventually it sits still at the bottom. Every perpetual motion design is a fancier bowl. The magnets, ramps, and floating balls are just a more complicated shape, but there is always a "bottom" where things settle, and the machine finds it.

As for why they don't accept your explanation, it usually helps to stop arguing about the physics in general and instead ask them to follow the energy in their own design step by step. Ask where the push comes from at each stage, and what it costs to reset the machine to where it started. Almost every design hides the cost in the reset: the magnet that pulls the ball up also pulls it back when it tries to leave, the weight that falls has to be lifted again, the float that rises has to be pushed back underwater. When they find that hidden cost themselves, it sticks far better than being told. And if they still believe it works, the kindest and most convincing answer is simply to suggest they build it, because the universe is a much more patient explainer than any of us.

So there are a few things a US citizen should think about before buying a house in Canada. First, immigration. If you want to spend a lot of time up there, you'll probably need a visa or permanent residency, and it's worth talking to an immigration lawyer or checking with the Canadian government about what works for you. Second, money. You'll have to convert US dollars into Canadian dollars, and exchange rates move around, so it pays to look into a currency exchange service and shop for a decent rate. Third, taxes. Non-residents often get treated differently than Canadian residents, so a tax professional can help you figure out what you actually owe. Financing is another headache. Lenders tend to be pickier with non-residents, so expect to put more money down or hunt for alternative loan options. Insurance matters too. You'll need coverage for the property, including homeowner's insurance and maybe flood insurance, so get several quotes before picking one. And finally, get a lawyer who knows Canadian property law. They can walk you through the legal requirements and make sure the deal closes cleanly.

Quantum particles such as electrons and photons can behave in peculiar ways when someone observes or measures them. A widely discussed feature of quantum mechanics is that such a particle can occupy several states or positions at once, a condition called superposition. Yet when we observe or measure the particle, it appears to "select" one specific state or position. Physicists call this the "collapse of the wave function." Put differently, the act of looking at the particle forces it to "collapse" into a single definite state, instead of remaining in many states at the same time. This effect has no bearing on daily life, since it arises only at extremely small scales involving minute particles. It is a fascinating and puzzling part of the quantum world, yet it has no noticeable impact on us.

Functional programming is a paradigm, meaning a way of organizing the structure and components of computer programs, in which computation is treated as the evaluation of mathematical functions. It rests on immutability: once a piece of data has been created, it can never be altered. Functions are first-class citizens in this approach, so they can be given to other functions as arguments, returned from other functions as results, and stored in variables. Functions are also free of side effects. They neither change the program's state nor interact observably with the outside world, for instance by writing to the console or editing a file on disk. To carry out complicated computations, functional languages frequently rely on recursion, where a function calls itself. They also commonly make use of higher-order functions, which either accept other functions as arguments or produce functions as their output. The origins of functional programming lie in lambda calculus, a formal system created in the 1930s by the mathematician Alonzo Church to investigate the notion of a function. The paradigm has shaped the design of numerous languages, among them Lisp, ML, and Haskell. By contrast, imperative programming is built on altering the program's state through statements that carry out actions and change variables. C, C++, and Java are examples of imperative languages.

Stephen Hawking was one of the most famous physicists and cosmologists of his era, and honestly one of the sharpest minds in the field. He did a lot of important work in theoretical physics, especially on black holes and how the universe got started. Hawking was born in Oxford, England, in 1942, and he studied physics and math at University College, Oxford, before heading to the University of Cambridge. At 21, he was diagnosed with ALS (also called Lou Gehrig's disease), a motor neuron disease that left him paralyzed and unable to speak. He didn't let that stop him. He kept working and ended up as a professor at Cambridge. His research was all about figuring out how the universe works and what fundamental laws run it. One of his biggest breakthroughs was predicting that black holes give off radiation, which we now call Hawking radiation. He also wrote popular science books, and "A Brief History of Time" became a huge bestseller that made tough physics way more accessible to regular people. Hawking died in 2018 at 76, but his work is still hugely respected and talked about.

Several factors could bring on short-term memory loss lasting around 8 hours. Because memory problems can accompany many different medical conditions, it's essential to consult a healthcare professional who can identify the cause and recommend suitable treatment. A concussion or other head injury is one possibility. Concussions are a form of traumatic brain injury that may cause temporary memory loss along with symptoms like dizziness, nausea, and headache. After any head injury or other trauma, seeking medical care is important to assess how serious it is and to get proper treatment. Stress and anxiety are another potential cause. Intense stress or anxiety can impair the brain's capacity to take in and hold onto new information, leading to brief memory lapses. In such cases, tackling the underlying stress or anxiety and learning ways to cope with it may help restore memory function. Additional possible causes include lack of sleep, alcohol or drug use, and certain medical conditions such as a stroke or transient ischemic attack (TIA), sometimes called a "mini-stroke." A temporary disruption to your sleep-wake rhythm during travel, such as on vacation, could also affect your ability to recall events. Again, a healthcare provider can ask questions and run tests to pinpoint the cause of your symptoms and create an appropriate treatment plan.

They're way more useful than they sound, too. Engineers and scientists lean on them all the time for stuff like electrical engineering and physics. So yeah, they let us solve real-world problems we'd get stuck on otherwise. Think of them as a special tool for making sense of things that are really hard to wrap your head around.

Refinancing a federal loan with a private lender can lower your rate, but it permanently gives up those protections, so it's usually worth doing only if you're confident you won't need them. If it's a private loan, refinancing is often the main route to a lower rate. Shop among several lenders, including credit unions, and compare fixed and variable rates, fees, and terms. Whichever type you have, you can reduce the total interest you pay by making extra payments. Directing extra money to the highest-rate loan first (the "avalanche" method) saves the most. Make sure the extra goes toward principal, and ask your servicer to confirm that. If you receive a raise, bonus, or tax refund, putting part of it toward the loan can shorten the repayment period considerably. Some employers also offer student loan repayment assistance, which is worth asking about.
