Buying a first home is usually the largest financial commitment a person makes, and its implications go well beyond the purchase price. Understanding the full picture helps you decide whether you're ready and how much you can comfortably afford.

The most visible upfront cost is the down payment. Twenty percent of the purchase price is the traditional benchmark because in many countries it lets you avoid mortgage insurance, but many first-time buyers put down far less through low-down-payment or government-backed loan programs. A smaller down payment gets you into a home sooner, but it means a larger loan, higher monthly payments, and often an added insurance premium. On top of the down payment come closing costs, which commonly run between two and five percent of the price. These cover loan origination fees, appraisal, title insurance, legal or escrow fees, inspections, prepaid property taxes and insurance, and in some places transfer taxes or stamp duty. Moving expenses and the cost of furnishing and repairing a new home also add up, so it's wise to keep a separate cash cushion rather than draining your savings to close.

The ongoing costs are often larger than buyers expect. Your monthly mortgage payment includes principal and interest, and frequently property taxes and homeowners insurance held in escrow. You may also owe homeowners association or condo fees. Maintenance and repairs are the cost most often underestimated; a common rule of thumb is to budget one to two percent of the home's value each year, since roofs, furnaces, water heaters, and appliances eventually need replacing and there's no landlord to call. Utilities are often higher than in an apartment as well. Lenders typically want your total housing costs to stay around 28 to 31 percent of gross income and your total debt payments under roughly 36 to 43 percent, but staying below those limits leaves more room for savings and surprises.

The interest rate and loan structure have a huge effect over time. On a thirty-year mortgage, the total interest paid can rival or exceed the original loan amount, and a difference of even one percentage point changes the monthly payment and lifetime cost substantially. Fixed-rate loans offer predictability, while adjustable-rate loans may start cheaper but carry the risk of rising payments. Your credit score directly influences the rate you're offered, so improving it before applying can save a meaningful amount of money.

On the benefit side, homeownership builds equity. Each payment reduces the principal, and if the property appreciates, your net worth grows. This forced saving is one of the main ways many households accumulate wealth. Owning also provides stability, since your principal and interest payment on a fixed loan won't rise the way rent can. In some countries there are tax advantages, such as deductions for mortgage interest and property taxes or exclusions on capital gains when you sell a primary residence, though the value of these depends on your tax situation and local law.

There are also real risks and trade-offs. A home is illiquid, so you can't easily access that money in an emergency without borrowing against it or selling. Selling involves its own costs, often six to ten percent of the price once agent commissions and fees are included, which is why buying generally makes more sense if you plan to stay at least five years or so. Home values can fall, and if you have little equity you could owe more than the home is worth. There's also opportunity cost: money tied up in a down payment and maintenance could otherwise be invested elsewhere, and in some markets renting and investing the difference can produce comparable or better financial results.

Before buying, it helps to have stable income, an emergency fund covering several months of expenses even after closing, manageable existing debt, and a realistic budget that includes maintenance rather than just the mortgage. Getting preapproved, comparing offers from multiple lenders, researching first-time buyer assistance programs, and running a rent-versus-buy comparison for your specific market will give you a much clearer sense of whether the purchase strengthens your finances or stretches them too thin.

Anonymous doesn't have a central leadership or membership list, so there's no single office that writes and approves statements the way a company's press department would. Instead, statements usually come from people who identify themselves as part of Anonymous and post them on places the group has used for years, such as imageboards like 4chan, certain Twitter or YouTube accounts, or sites that act as announcement hubs. Often a video is posted with the familiar Guy Fawkes mask, and the message is read or typed out. Because anyone can do this, the media has to decide which messages seem credible. Reporters usually look at whether the account has a track record, whether the message matches past Anonymous actions, and whether other people in the loose network repeat or support it.

So yes, in a practical sense, almost anyone can issue a statement in Anonymous's name. Nobody can stop them, and nobody has to approve it. That's also why journalists often write "a statement purportedly from Anonymous" or say they couldn't verify who was behind it. Some statements are genuine expressions of views held by many people in the movement, some are made by a few individuals acting on their own, and some are fakes or pranks meant to make the group look bigger or more dangerous than it is.

A sonic boom is created by an object moving through air faster than the speed of sound, which is roughly 343 meters per second (about 767 miles per hour) at sea level at 20 degrees Celsius. As an aircraft or other object travels, it pushes air out of its way, creating pressure waves that spread outward in all directions at the speed of sound. When the object itself moves faster than those waves can travel, they can no longer get out ahead of it. Instead, they overlap and merge, forming a cone-shaped shock wave that trails behind the object, with its tip at the nose and its edges extending to the ground.

The boom is the sound heard when this shock wave passes over a listener. Because the pressure changes sharply, the air reaches the ear as a sudden, loud crack or thump rather than a gradual rise and fall in pressure. A supersonic aircraft produces two booms, one from the shock wave at the nose and another from the tail, which is why a boom often sounds like a double clap. The strength of the boom depends on factors such as the aircraft's size, shape, altitude, and speed, and the boom is typically heard on the ground in a narrow band beneath the flight path rather than everywhere the aircraft flies.

Osteophytic lipping refers to the formation of small, bony outgrowths called osteophytes, or bone spurs, along the edges of a joint. It is a common sign of osteoarthritis, which is wear and tear of the joint cartilage. When cartilage thins or is damaged over time, the body responds by laying down extra bone at the joint margins, which gives the edge a "lipped" appearance on an X-ray. In the feet, this most often affects the big toe joint, the midfoot, the ankle, and sometimes the heel. Long hours of standing, previous injuries, foot shape, and age all contribute. The spurs themselves are not always painful. Pain usually comes from the underlying arthritis, inflammation of the joint, or the spurs rubbing against shoes, tendons, or nerves.

Whether surgery is worth it depends on several things, and I cannot decide that without knowing which joint is involved and how severe the changes are. In general, surgery is considered only after conservative treatment has been given a proper trial and has failed. Many people improve substantially without an operation. Options to try first include supportive footwear with a roomy toe box and a cushioned, slightly stiff sole (flat shoes with thin soles are often not ideal for arthritic feet), custom or off-the-shelf orthotic insoles, anti-inflammatory medication or topical anti-inflammatory gels if you can safely take them, physiotherapy and calf and foot stretching, weight management if relevant, and activity pacing with short sit-down breaks during your shift. Anti-fatigue mats at work can help. A corticosteroid injection into the affected joint can give relief for weeks to months and also helps confirm which joint is the source of pain.

Surgery becomes reasonable when pain is persistent and disabling despite these measures, and especially when it threatens your ability to work. Procedures range from removing the spurs (cheilectomy), which works well for early big toe arthritis, to joint fusion or, less commonly, replacement for more advanced disease. Recovery can take several weeks to a few months, often with time off standing work, and results vary. Risks include infection, stiffness, persistent pain, and slow healing, so it is a decision to weigh carefully.

Questions worth asking your surgeon are which exact joint is being treated, what the expected improvement and recovery time are, how much time off work you would need, what the success rate is for people with jobs like yours, and what happens if you wait. Getting a second opinion from a foot and ankle specialist is entirely reasonable, particularly if you have not yet tried orthotics, injections, and physiotherapy.

If you have severe night pain, swelling, redness, numbness, or a sudden worsening, see your doctor promptly. Otherwise, I would suggest trying the conservative measures for a few months and discussing with your surgeon whether surgery is truly necessary now.

Wishing you relief,
Dr.

Sounds like the person you're describing has abdominal pain and headaches that nobody has been able to explain with neurological or blood flow problems. So it's probably worth looking at other causes. A kidney stone is one possibility, since those can cause belly pain and sometimes headaches too. Inflammatory conditions like Crohn's or ulcerative colitis could be in the mix, and so could a gut infection. To narrow it down, they'd likely need more imaging, like a CT or MRI of the abdomen, plus blood and urine tests to look for infection or inflammation. A detailed history and a physical exam would help too, since small clues can point the way. Honestly, without more details it's hard to say what's going on, so the best move is to get it checked out by a doctor who can actually examine them.

Nope, a stock can totally be listed on more than one exchange. It's called cross-listing. A company might be on the NYSE and the NASDAQ, plus a few others on top of that. The main perks are better liquidity and a bigger pool of investors who can get at the shares. It also gives people more choices about where to buy and sell.

Sometimes a company is listed on an exchange in its home country and then trades on exchanges abroad too. That usually happens when it does a lot of business in those countries and wants local investors to be able to buy in easily.

One thing to keep in mind, though: even if a stock is listed in several places, it's usually only actively traded on one of them at any given moment. That one is called the primary listing exchange.

The area you describe, between the scrotum and anus, is called the perineum. Pain or a feeling of swelling there after ejaculation is common in young men, and it usually points to a problem with the prostate or the pelvic floor muscles rather than something dangerous. The most likely causes are chronic pelvic pain syndrome (sometimes called chronic prostatitis), tight or spasming pelvic floor muscles, or mild inflammation of the prostate or epididymis. Congestion of the area after arousal without full release, or very frequent or forceful masturbation, can also trigger it. Redness of the scrotum during the pain suggests some inflammation or irritation, which is worth taking seriously.

The doctor to see is a urologist, ideally one who works in men's health or andrology. If the first doctors you saw were general physicians, a urologist is the right specialist. Since you were told nothing was found, ask for specific checks: a urine test and urine culture, a semen or prostatic fluid culture to look for infection, a scrotal and perineal ultrasound, and a physical exam of the prostate. A test for sexually transmitted infections such as chlamydia is also reasonable. If everything comes back normal, ask about a pelvic floor physiotherapist, because muscle tension is a very common cause of exactly this pattern and is often missed.

In the meantime, some things may help. Take a warm bath or sit in warm water for 15 to 20 minutes after the pain starts. Avoid long periods of sitting, and avoid cycling or hard seats. Stay hydrated, and cut back on alcohol, caffeine, and spicy food, which can irritate the bladder and prostate. Try to masturbate less often and avoid stopping partway or holding back ejaculation. Gentle stretching and deep relaxation breathing can ease pelvic muscle tension. An over-the-counter anti-inflammatory like ibuprofen can help if you can safely take it, but check with a doctor first.

See a doctor urgently if you develop fever, severe or sudden testicular pain, a hard or very swollen testicle, blood in the urine or semen, pain with urination, or discharge. Sudden severe testicular pain in particular can be testicular torsion, which is an emergency.

Because the pain has been happening repeatedly and you have already had one consultation without answers, getting a second opinion from a urologist is a sensible next step.

When you sell an asset but can't recall or document what you originally paid for it, you can still work out your capital gain or loss by treating the asset's fair market value as your basis. Fair market value means the price a willing buyer would agree to pay a willing seller, after weighing all the relevant circumstances, including the asset's condition and the market where it is being sold. To figure out your gain or loss, take the sale price and subtract the asset's fair market value at the time of the sale. A sale price above the fair market value produces a capital gain, while a sale price below it produces a capital loss. Keep in mind that fair market value may serve as the basis only when the original purchase price is unknown. If you do know what you originally paid, that amount must be used as the basis for your calculation.

No, generally an employee does not have the right to pay their own federal and state income and payroll taxes in place of having the employer withhold them. Under federal law, employers are required to withhold income tax and the employee's share of Social Security and Medicare (FICA) taxes from wages, and to match the Social Security and Medicare contributions themselves. The withholding requirement is mandatory, and an employer that fails to withhold can be held liable for the unpaid amounts. Most states impose similar requirements for state income tax and unemployment insurance contributions.

An employee can still take steps that affect how much is withheld. The most common is filing a new Form W-4 with the employer to adjust withholding, such as claiming additional withholding, so that less tax is taken from each paycheck and the balance is paid at tax time. An employee can also make estimated tax payments directly to the IRS and state tax agencies, which is often done by people with self-employment income, investment income, or other income not subject to withholding. Some workers can also request a withholding exemption if they had no tax liability in the prior year and expect none in the current year, though this is limited to specific situations.

If an employee is actually treated as an independent contractor rather than an employee, then the worker is responsible for paying self-employment tax and estimated income tax directly. However, misclassification is a serious issue, and whether someone is an employee or contractor depends on the facts of the working relationship, not just the label the parties use. Rules vary by state, so anyone with a specific situation should consult a tax professional or the relevant tax authority.

Tax-loss harvesting means selling investments that have fallen below their purchase price to realize a capital loss, then using that loss to offset capital gains elsewhere in your portfolio or, to a limited extent, ordinary income. The estimated benefit comes from the tax you avoid paying now, and the deferral it creates, rather than from any change in your overall investment return.

A reasonable way to estimate the impact starts with the size of the realized loss. Suppose you harvest $10,000 in losses this year. If those losses offset $10,000 of short-term gains taxed at a 35 percent federal rate plus state tax, the immediate saving could be roughly $3,500 to $4,000. If they offset long-term gains taxed at 15 or 20 percent, the saving is smaller, perhaps $1,500 to $2,000. Losses in excess of gains can reduce ordinary income by up to $3,000 per year, with the remainder carried forward indefinitely, so the value of carryforwards depends on whether you will generate enough future gains to use them.

The most important caveat is that harvesting creates a lower cost basis in the replacement holding, so much of the benefit is a deferral rather than a permanent saving. If you sell a position for a $10,000 loss and buy a similar but not substantially identical fund, you have traded a tax liability you would have faced later for a smaller one. The deferred tax is worth less than the immediate saving only to the extent that you can invest the money you would otherwise have paid, and the timing advantage compounds over long holding periods. If you hold until death, the basis may step up and the deferred gain may disappear entirely, which makes the benefit larger in that scenario.

Several factors reduce the realized benefit. Transaction costs and bid-ask spreads eat into the saving, and you must avoid wash sales. Under the wash-sale rule, if you buy a substantially identical security within 30 days before or after the sale, the loss is disallowed and added to the new position's basis. Replacing an S&P 500 index fund with a different provider's S&P 500 fund may be treated as substantially identical, so many investors choose a related but distinct index, such as a total market or a different benchmark.

To put a rough number on your own situation, multiply the harvested loss by your expected marginal rate on the gains it offsets, then subtract the value of any deferred gain you are effectively postponing, adjusted for the time value of money and your expected future tax rate. Automated direct-indexing and robo-advisor platforms can harvest continuously and often report estimated annual savings, which is a useful cross-check, though those estimates usually assume the benefit is permanent and should be discounted accordingly.

Similarity learning is an area of supervised machine learning, closely related to regression and classification, whose goal is to learn a function that measures how similar or related two objects are. Instead of predicting a label for a single input, a similarity learning system takes a pair (or sometimes a group) of inputs and produces a score indicating how alike they are. It is widely used in ranking, recommendation systems, visual identity tracking, face verification, speaker verification, and information retrieval.

The core idea is that what counts as "similar" depends on the task. Two photos might be similar because they show the same person, the same object category, or the same scene, and a generic measure such as raw pixel distance rarely captures the notion that matters. Similarity learning therefore uses examples to teach a model what similarity should mean in a particular context. Training data typically comes as pairs labeled similar or dissimilar, as numeric similarity scores for pairs, or as triplets in which an anchor example is said to be more similar to one example (the positive) than to another (the negative).

Several common formulations exist. In regression similarity learning, the model is given pairs with real-valued similarity scores and learns to predict those scores. In classification similarity learning, pairs are labeled simply as similar or not, and the model learns to make that binary judgment. In ranking similarity learning, the model learns from relative comparisons such as triplets, which is often easier to obtain and more natural, since people find it easier to say "A is more like B than like C" than to assign exact scores.

A closely related idea is metric learning, which aims to learn a distance function that satisfies the mathematical properties of a metric, such as non-negativity, symmetry, and the triangle inequality. A classic example is learning a Mahalanobis distance, where a matrix is learned that reweights and correlates the input features so that distances reflect the desired notion of similarity. Methods such as Large Margin Nearest Neighbor and Information Theoretic Metric Learning follow this approach.

In modern deep learning, similarity learning is usually done by training a neural network to map inputs into an embedding space, a vector representation in which similar items lie close together and dissimilar items lie far apart. Siamese networks process two inputs with identical shared-weight networks and compare their outputs, while triplet networks handle anchor, positive, and negative examples together. Loss functions such as contrastive loss and triplet loss encourage the right distances in the embedding space. Face recognition systems like FaceNet are a well-known example: once trained, they can compare faces of people never seen during training simply by measuring distances between embeddings. Contrastive self-supervised methods such as SimCLR and CLIP extend these ideas by generating similar and dissimilar pairs automatically, for instance by treating two augmented views of the same image, or an image and its caption, as a positive pair.

A major practical advantage of similarity learning is its ability to generalize to new classes. Because the model learns how to compare rather than memorizing fixed categories, it supports tasks like one-shot or few-shot learning, where a new item can be recognized from only one or a few examples by finding which known examples it most resembles. Challenges include choosing informative training pairs or triplets, since easy examples teach little, and scaling to large datasets where the number of possible pairs grows rapidly.

Your body is a bit like a busy kitchen that has to juggle two jobs at once. When you run hard, your legs and heart need a huge amount of blood and oxygen, so your body quickly sends blood away from your stomach and intestines to your muscles. Your stomach is then working with less blood than it normally gets, and it gets grumpy about it. Food you ate earlier may still be sitting there, and it doesn't get mixed and moved along as smoothly as usual.

Your body also bounces around a lot when you run, which can jiggle a full stomach and make it feel squishy and upset. On top of that, hard exercise can make your body release stress hormones, which can slow down digestion and make your stomach feel queasy.

So the body isn't really trying to get rid of something poisonous. It's more like a tummy that feels crowded, not getting enough help, and getting shaken around, so it decides the easiest fix is to empty out. That's why eating a big meal right before exercise, or running while dehydrated, makes it more likely. Giving yourself time to digest and sipping water along the way usually helps keep things calm.

Masturbating once a day is within the normal range for many adults, and on its own it does not cause sexual problems or harm your sexual life. Many people masturbate daily, and it is generally considered a healthy part of sexual expression. It doesn't reduce your ability to enjoy sex with a partner, and it doesn't cause infertility or permanent damage. The real question is whether it feels like a choice you make or something you feel pulled into against your wishes. If you enjoy it and it fits comfortably into your life, there is usually nothing to worry about. If you find yourself wanting to cut back and struggling, that is worth paying attention to, and it can help to talk with a doctor or counselor who works with sexual health.

Your second concern sounds like it may be urinary, and it is worth getting checked. Needing to urinate often, especially every hour or so, can have several causes, including a bladder or urinary tract infection, an overactive bladder, drinking a lot of fluid, especially caffeine or alcohol, or in men, prostate changes. Sitting or lying in a relaxed, reclined position can also make it easier to feel the urge, or to notice it more, since the body changes how fluid is distributed. Feeling the urge while watching a movie does not necessarily mean it is linked to masturbation, and the two are not the same physical sensation, though the feeling of arousal can sometimes make you more aware of your body.

I would suggest seeing a doctor, preferably a primary care physician or urologist, who can check your urine, review your fluid intake and medications, and see whether something treatable is going on. It would also help to note how much you drink, when the urges happen, and whether you pass only small amounts each time. Most of these causes are easy to manage once identified.

If you're worried about the habit or the urination, please don't hesitate to speak with a healthcare provider in person. They can give you advice tailored to your body and situation.

Institutional racism is when a rule or system treats people differently by race, or hurts some racial groups more than others, even if no one in charge is personally prejudiced. Here are some examples people point to, though whether each one counts is still argued about.

Think of a school that says every kid must bring a pencil case. That sounds fair, but if the only shop that sells cases is across town and most kids in one neighborhood can't get there, that rule hits those kids harder. Lawyers call this "disparate impact," and it's one of the main ideas behind the examples below.

Some states still take away voting rights from people who have been convicted of felonies, sometimes for life. Because Black Americans are arrested and convicted at higher rates, these rules remove a larger share of Black adults from voter rolls, even though the rule never mentions race.

Zoning laws in many cities allow only single-family homes on most of the land. Many of these rules were written in the early 1900s with the open goal of keeping Black families out of certain neighborhoods. Today the rules don't mention race, but they still make it expensive to build apartments in wealthier areas, which keeps neighborhoods divided by income and race.

Schools are often funded largely by local property taxes. Rich neighborhoods, which are often mostly white, raise more money for their schools than poor ones, which are often mostly Black or Hispanic. The law doesn't say "give less to Black kids," but the result is that schools serving different races get very different amounts of money.

Cash bail can keep people locked up before trial just because they can't pay a set amount. Since Black and Hispanic defendants tend to have less money on average, they are more likely to sit in jail while white defendants with the same charges go home.

Some people think these are clear examples of racism built into the system. Others argue that the rules are about money, crime, or property rather than race, and that the gaps come from other causes. Courts in the United States also generally require proof that a law was intended to discriminate before they strike it down under the Constitution, which is why many of these examples are still legal even when their effects are unequal.

So a HELOC is basically a loan where you borrow against the equity in your house, meaning the part you actually own. How much you can get usually depends on what the home's worth and how much equity you've built up. Parent PLUS loans are something else entirely. They're federal loans parents can take out to cover a kid's college costs. The rates are fixed, but they tend to cost more than other student loans. A second mortgage is just a loan on top of your main mortgage. People usually use them for big stuff, like renovating the house or paying for a kid's tuition. They generally have higher rates than your first mortgage, since the lender's taking on more risk if things go south. If you need a big chunk of cash and you've got enough equity to back it up, a HELOC or second mortgage could make sense. Parent PLUS loans might work if you're mainly trying to help pay for your kid's education and you're okay with the higher rate. Either way, read the terms carefully on whatever you're looking at before you pick one.

An alkali is basically a substance that gives a pH above 7 when you dissolve it in water. Most alkalis are strong bases, and they'll react with acids to make a salt and water. So what happens when you add one to a liquid? It depends on what the liquid is and how strong the alkali is, but there are a few usual results.

First, it neutralizes acids. Alkalis react with acids to form a salt and water. Toss sodium hydroxide into hydrochloric acid, for example, and you get sodium chloride (regular table salt) and water.

Second, it raises the pH. The alkali soaks up any acid that's around and releases hydroxide ions, so the more you add, the higher the pH climbs.

Third, it can dissolve some stuff. Fats and oils are a classic example. The hydroxide ions react with the fatty acids in them and break them into simpler compounds, which is why drain cleaners and soap-making involve this stuff.

Last, it can change colors. Litmus paper is the easy one to remember: it shifts color when it meets an alkali, because the alkali sets off a reaction that changes the dye's appearance.

Just keep in mind that the exact outcome really depends on which alkali and which liquid you're working with.

Think of a maple seed, the kind that spins like a little propeller as it falls from a tree. It doesn't plummet; it twirls down slowly. A helicopter's rotor can do the same thing, and that's autorotation.

Normally the engine pushes the rotor blades around, and the blades bite into the air and push it downward, which lifts the helicopter up. When the engine quits, the pilot immediately lowers a lever so the blades are flat and not fighting the air. Then the helicopter starts to fall. But as it falls, air rushes up through the rotor from below, and that rising air keeps the blades spinning, a bit like wind spinning a pinwheel you hold up in front of you. So the falling itself keeps the rotor turning, without any engine.

A spinning rotor is a big wing going around in circles, and spinning wings make lift. So instead of dropping like a rock, the helicopter descends fairly slowly and the pilot can still steer. The spinning blades are also heavy, so they store energy, the way a spinning top or a merry-go-round keeps going after you stop pushing.

Now for the landing. Just before touching the ground, the pilot pulls the nose up a little to slow the forward speed, then raises the lever to make the blades bite the air harder. That uses up the stored spinning energy all at once to make a big burst of lift, which cushions the helicopter right at the end, like a soft pillow. The helicopter settles onto the ground gently, usually sliding or rolling a short way if it has skids or wheels.

The tricky part is timing. If the pilot uses that last bit of stored energy too early or too late, the landing gets hard. That's why helicopter pilots practice autorotations a lot, and why it's a standard part of their training. So a helicopter isn't a brick without its engine; it's more like a very big maple seed with a skilled person steering it.

Hans Moravec is a roboticist and AI researcher, best known for his work on autonomous robots. He's a professor at Carnegie Mellon University and has written a few books on the subject, including "Mind Children: The Future of Robot and Human Intelligence" and "Robot: Mere Machine to Transcendent Mind." He's especially interested in the idea of human-level AI. He's also the namesake of "Moravec's paradox," which says that computers find things humans consider hard, like crunching huge numbers fast, pretty easy. The stuff we do without thinking, like seeing the world and moving around in it, is what really trips them up. His work has shaped robotics and AI a lot, and plenty of people count him among the pioneers of autonomous robots.

Occam's razor is a rule that says when you have a few different explanations for something, the simplest one is usually the best place to start. It doesn't mean the simple answer is always right. It just means you shouldn't add extra pieces to a story when you don't need them.

Here's a five-year-old version. Imagine you come into the kitchen and the cookie jar is empty, and there are crumbs on your little brother's shirt. One explanation is that your brother ate the cookies. Another is that a secret team of tiny cookie-loving squirrels sneaked in through the window, ate them, and then got away, and your brother just happened to spill crumbs on himself. The squirrel story needs a lot of extra stuff to be true: squirrels, a window, a getaway, a coincidence. The brother story needs almost nothing extra. So you check the brother first. The word "razor" is because you shave away the extra parts of the story you don't need.

As for where it holds up in practice, doctors use it all the time. If a kid has a runny nose and a cough, the doctor thinks it's probably a common cold rather than some very rare disease. There's even a saying in medicine: when you hear hoofbeats, think horses, not zebras. Most of the time the common, simple cause is the right one.

It also shows up in science. For a long time people thought the planets moved in complicated loops around the Earth, with circles stacked on circles to make the math work. When people realized the planets orbit the Sun, the explanation became much simpler and fit what they saw better.

Everyday troubleshooting works the same way. If your toy or lamp stops working, you check whether it's plugged in or needs a new battery before you assume something strange is wrong inside it. Detectives, mechanics, and computer programmers all start with the simple likely cause because it saves time.

One last thing: sometimes the simple answer turns out to be wrong, and then you move on to the more complicated one. Occam's razor is a good place to start looking, not a promise about where you'll end up.

The most important next step is to check blood pressure carefully. A 16-year-old with severe headache, irritability, sweating, and abdominal pain should have BP measured in both arms and a leg, with repeated readings and ambulatory monitoring if needed. Hypertension would explain the headaches and would link them to the kidney finding. Since the MRI, angiography, and thyroid studies were normal, the next investigations should focus on whether the right ureteropelvic junction (PUJ) obstruction is causing secondary hypertension, and on ruling out a catecholamine-secreting tumour.

For the kidney, obtain serum creatinine and electrolytes, eGFR, urine routine and microscopy, and urine culture. A diuretic renogram (MAG3 or DTPA scan) will show the degree of obstruction and the split renal function on each side. Plasma renin activity and serum aldosterone (renin-aldosterone ratio) help assess renin-mediated hypertension, which can occur with unilateral obstruction. Repeat ultrasound with Doppler and a check for stones or crossing vessels will clarify the cause of the narrowing.

Because episodic headache, sweating, irritability, appetite change, and abdominal pain together with hypertension strongly suggest a pheochromocytoma or paraganglioma, measure plasma free metanephrines or 24-hour urinary fractionated metanephrines and catecholamines. Adrenal imaging with CT or MRI of the abdomen should follow if these are raised. A complete blood count and inflammatory markers are also reasonable to exclude other causes of fever, pain, and sweating.

The probable diagnosis is right-sided PUJ obstruction with hydronephrosis, most likely a congenital or acquired narrowing, possibly causing intermittent colicky or flank-referred abdominal pain and, potentially, renin-mediated hypertension responsible for the headaches and sweating. Pheochromocytoma must be excluded before any surgery, and the headache and sweating could also reflect a separate functional or psychosomatic component, though that diagnosis should only be made after organic causes are excluded.

Treatment depends on the findings. If hypertension is confirmed and the obstruction is significant (poor drainage on renogram, declining split function, or recurrent pain and infection), pediatric urology should consider pyeloplasty, which is usually curative for PUJ obstruction. Blood pressure should be controlled in the meantime, typically with an ACE inhibitor or calcium channel blocker, while watching renal function and potassium. If metanephrines are elevated, alpha blockade with phenoxybenzamine or doxazosin must be started first, followed by beta blockade if needed, and the tumour should be localised and surgically removed by an endocrine surgical team. Symptomatic relief of headache and abdominal pain can be given with simple analgesics, with attention to avoiding frequent use, which can itself cause rebound headache. Follow-up should include serial renal function, blood pressure, and imaging, and the patient should be referred jointly to paediatric nephrology or urology and endocrinology.

Chest pain might be linked to taking Clindamycin and Oxycodone, but other possible explanations should also be kept in mind, including heart problems and other underlying medical conditions. Because chest pain can signal a serious problem that needs treatment, you should talk to a healthcare provider if you have it. Until then, keep following your provider's directions and let them know about any side effects you notice. If you have trouble breathing or the chest pain is severe, get medical help right away.

Sure thing! Air is easy for our eyes: light goes in a nice straight line and we see stuff clearly. Underwater is a different story. The water scatters and bends the light, so everything gets blurry for us. Fish have some tricks for this. Their eyes are shaped differently, and many have a reflective layer called the tapetum lucidum that helps them see in dim light. Some fish also have a special pigment called guanine that helps them pick up the blue light that dominates down there. That's why you need goggles to see anything underwater, while fish just get on with it. Makes sense, right?

Hello Sushma, I'm sorry you're dealing with this. Severe pain after breakfast that doesn't respond to Eno but eases with buttermilk can have several causes, and some are worth getting checked promptly. Acidity or gastritis is possible, and buttermilk often soothes it, but pain that is severe and recurrent should not be assumed to be simple gas or acidity. Gallbladder problems, peptic ulcers, pancreatitis, irritable bowel syndrome, and sometimes infections or food intolerances (such as lactose intolerance, which would be odd given that buttermilk helps, but still worth considering) can all produce similar symptoms.

Please see a doctor soon for an examination and basic tests. These usually include a blood count, liver and pancreatic enzymes, an ultrasound of the abdomen, and sometimes a test for H. pylori infection. Seek urgent care right away if you notice pain that becomes sudden and intense, pain that spreads to your back or chest, vomiting that won't stop, blood in vomit or stool, black stools, yellowing of the eyes or skin, fever, fainting, or difficulty breathing.

In the meantime, while you wait for your appointment, you may find it helpful to eat smaller, more frequent meals rather than one large breakfast, to avoid lying down right after eating, and to keep a short diary noting what you ate and when the pain started. Plain foods like oats, boiled rice, bananas, plain curd or buttermilk, and well-cooked vegetables are generally gentle on the stomach. Try to avoid fried or very oily foods, tea or coffee on an empty stomach, carbonated drinks, and alcohol, and avoid smoking if you smoke. Avoid taking painkillers such as ibuprofen or aspirin regularly without medical advice, since they can irritate the stomach.

Please don't rely on home remedies alone for this kind of recurring severe pain. A doctor, ideally a gastroenterologist or your general physician, can identify the cause and recommend the right treatment. I hope you feel better soon.

Think about everyday stuff for a second. If you drop a ball, it falls. You can basically bet on it, because gravity and a bunch of other rules make the world pretty predictable. Quantum physics is the branch of physics that looks at really tiny things like atoms and subatomic particles, and those don't play by the same rules. An atom can be in more than one place at once, or spin in two opposite directions at the same time. Sounds nuts, I know, but experiments have backed it up again and again.

Quantum computers take advantage of that weirdness to do certain calculations way faster than a normal computer can. A regular computer stores and processes info in bits, which are like little switches that are either "on" or "off," a 1 or a 0. A quantum computer uses quantum bits, or "qubits," and a qubit can be a 1, a 0, or both at once. That lets the machine work through lots of calculations at the same time, so for certain tasks it's much faster.

So when people say "quantum" in quantum physics, quantum computers and so on, they're pointing at that strange, unpredictable behavior of very small things. The laws of quantum physics describe it, and they're different from the ones that govern everyday objects. Quantum computers just put those principles to work to speed up certain calculations compared to normal computers.

Multilinear subspace learning, or MSL, is basically a way of learning low-dimensional representations of high-dimensional data that lives in a multilinear subspace. If that sounds abstract, a multilinear subspace is just a space you can build from the tensor product of several linear subspaces. The goal is to find a compact version of your data that still captures its underlying structure, which comes in handy for things like dimensionality reduction, compression, and visualization.

A really common way to do it is with tensor decomposition, like the canonical polyadic decomposition (CPD) or the Tucker decomposition. You break the data tensor down into a combination of low-dimensional subspace components, and then you can use those to rebuild the original tensor without losing much of its structure or information.

There are other methods too. Multilinear principal component analysis (MPCA) and multilinear independent component analysis (MICA) are basically extensions of the traditional linear techniques for dimensionality reduction and data analysis. They try to find a set of low-dimensional subspaces that capture the data's structure in a multilinear way instead of a flat linear one.

It's a pretty powerful tool for making sense of high-dimensional data, and people use it in all sorts of areas, like image and video processing, natural language processing, and social network analysis.

Dreams like this can really get under your skin, and it's pretty common to wake up feeling anxious or low after one. Lots of things can feed into them: stuff you've been through, things you want or fear deep down, even physical stuff like how your body feels while you sleep. With a recurring dream about getting shot and saying goodbye to people you love, one guess is that it's tied to feeling vulnerable or scared of losing someone close. Another possibility is that it's picking up on something unresolved in your waking life, some conflict or worry you haven't really dealt with yet. That said, dreams aren't always a direct window into your real life, so try not to read too much into any single one. If they're messing with your sleep or how you get through the day, though, it's worth talking to a therapist or counselor. They can help you figure out what's going on underneath and work through it with you.

Bayesian inference is a statistical approach that applies Bayes' theorem to revise the probability of a hypothesis whenever new evidence arrives. Bayes' theorem is a formula for calculating the likelihood of an event using prior knowledge of circumstances that may be connected to it. Under this framework, a hypothesis's probability is continually adjusted as fresh evidence emerges. By contrast, classical (frequentist) inference does not revise the probability of a hypothesis in light of data; instead, that probability is treated as fixed, and the data are used to put the hypothesis to the test. At the heart of Bayesian thinking is the idea that both the data and the hypothesis can be modeled as random variables, with the connection between them captured through probability theory. This makes it possible to form probabilistic predictions about a hypothesis from the data and to refine those predictions as more data comes in. Bayesian methods are widely used in machine learning and data analysis, where they help forecast the behavior of complex systems from limited information. They also appear in fields such as economics, psychology, and biology, where they support conclusions about uncertain outcomes drawn from observations.

Chest pain and shoulder blade pain can come from all sorts of things, and there's no way to know what's going on without a proper medical evaluation. Right-sided chest pain could be a muscle strain or a bruised rib, but it could also be something serious like a heart attack. Shoulder blade pain has its own list of possibilities: a pulled muscle, an injury, a pinched nerve, or a problem with the spine. If you've got chest pain and shoulder blade pain along with cold or flu-like symptoms, get in touch with a doctor or other healthcare provider soon. The flu could be behind it, but other causes need to be ruled out too. A provider can examine you, maybe order some tests, and figure out what's actually causing the pain and how to treat it. And if you ever have severe chest pain or trouble breathing, don't wait around. Get medical help right away, because those can signal something serious.

Running at the speed of sound would be a fun thing to imagine, but it wouldn't let you walk on water. Here's why. Water holds you up because it is pushed hard from underneath when you press down on it, and that push depends on how fast you move and how much of your body is touching it, not on any special speed. A person running on a lake is really just a person pushing down on water with their feet, and the water pushes back for a moment before it gives way and you sink in.

The speed of sound is also much, much faster than anybody can run. Sound moves through the air at about 343 meters per second, or roughly 767 miles per hour. The fastest human sprinter reaches about 12 meters per second, so you would need to go nearly thirty times faster than the world's best runner. At that speed your feet would hit the water so hard and so often that it would act a bit more like a solid surface for a split second, but it would still break apart under you. Pushing down that hard would also break your legs long before you got anywhere near the speed of sound.

So the short answer is that you would sink, and the faster you tried to run, the harder and quicker you would sink. Water only feels solid to fast-moving things like a skipping stone, which is why flat rocks can bounce across a pond when thrown with enough speed and the right angle.

Lots of people in Australia feel like everyday life has gotten harder while the things that make life feel secure have gotten more expensive. Imagine your family's allowance stays the same but the price of bread, rent, and petrol keeps climbing. You'd be upset too, even if nobody was trying to hurt you.

The biggest worry for many people is housing. Home prices and rents rose very fast over the past decade, so it's now much harder for young people to buy a house than it was for their parents. Many people also worry that interest rates will rise, which makes their mortgage payments bigger.

Then there's the cost of living more generally. Groceries, electricity, gas, insurance, and fuel all cost more than they used to, and wages haven't always kept up. When a family has to choose between paying the power bill and buying good food, that's stressful, and stress often turns into anger.

People also get frustrated with the services they rely on. Waiting for a doctor, a hospital bed, or a specialist can take a long time, and some areas have too few doctors. People feel the government should be fixing these things faster.

Many people also don't trust politicians. They feel that the people in charge don't understand their problems or are more interested in arguing with each other than solving them. That distrust makes every other problem feel worse.

Finally, there are big arguments about the future, like how fast to change energy sources, how many people should move to Australia each year, and how to treat the country's First Nations people. Different groups feel strongly about these, and the arguments can get heated.

So "numerous issues" really means a bunch of worries that stack on top of each other. If you tell me which article or topic you read, I can explain the specific part that's causing the most anger.

Malware, viruses, and trojans are categories of damaging software typically built and distributed by hackers. Hackers are individuals who use computers and the internet to break into other people's machines or networks without authorization, frequently aiming to do damage or steal data. They can spread malicious programs in several ways, including through email attachments or by hiding them on websites that users are likely to browse. After malware infects a person's computer, the attacker may exploit it to access the owner's files, take personal details, or create other kinds of trouble. McAfee is a firm that develops programs designed to shield computers from malware and other dangers. Although McAfee and similar security companies work to defend people against malware and hackers, they do not originate or distribute the malware themselves.

The Late Heavy Bombardment (LHB) was a stretch of early solar system history, roughly 4.1 to 3.8 billion years ago, when the inner planets, Earth and the Moon included, got hit by asteroids and comets way more often than usual. The usual explanation is that the giant planets shifted their orbits, which knocked loads of small bodies out of their paths and sent them crashing into the inner worlds. The Moon took a huge beating during this time, and a lot of those craters are still sitting on its surface. Plenty of the oldest ones have been wiped out by later impacts, but some survived well enough that astronomers and spacecraft missions can still study them. It was a big deal for how the terrestrial planets and their atmospheres developed. It probably helped shape the Moon's surface too, including the dark basaltic plains called maria and the bright, rugged highlands. Some people also think the bombardment might have delivered water and other raw ingredients for life to the young Earth, though that's still debated.

Because I don't know a retired couple's specific finances, goals, or risk tolerance, I can only offer a general framework, and a fee-only fiduciary financial planner or a certified financial planner can tailor the details to your situation.

For most retired couples, the central goal is to generate reliable income that lasts as long as both spouses live, while protecting against the two biggest threats: running out of money in a long retirement and losing too much in a market downturn. Because one or both spouses may live into their nineties, a portfolio usually still needs some growth, so keeping a meaningful allocation to stocks is typically wise even after retirement, though the exact share depends on how much risk you can tolerate and how much you need to withdraw.

A common approach is to divide savings into buckets by time horizon. The first bucket holds roughly one to three years of planned withdrawals in cash, money market funds, or short-term Treasuries, so you are never forced to sell stocks during a slump. A second bucket, covering about the next three to ten years, might hold high-quality bonds and bond funds to provide steady income and stability. The third bucket, for needs beyond a decade, can remain in diversified stock index funds to keep pace with inflation and support long-term growth. Rebalancing once or twice a year keeps the mix near your targets.

Withdrawal rates matter greatly. Many planners use a starting withdrawal around 3.5 to 4.5 percent of the portfolio in the first year, adjusted annually for inflation, though a more flexible approach that trims spending after bad market years can improve sustainability. Couples should also coordinate Social Security claiming strategies, since delaying benefits for the higher earner often increases lifetime income and provides more protection for the surviving spouse.

Other considerations include keeping costs low through index funds and low-fee accounts, planning for taxes by thinking about which accounts to draw from first and when to convert traditional IRA money to Roth, maintaining an emergency reserve, considering inflation-protected Treasuries (TIPS) as a stable base, and reviewing health care costs, including Medicare premiums and potential long-term care needs. Estate documents, beneficiary designations, and a plan for the surviving spouse's finances should be up to date as well.

If you share more details, such as total savings, annual spending needs, expected Social Security or pension income, and your comfort with market swings, I can help you think through a more specific allocation and withdrawal plan.

A furlong is a unit of length in the imperial and US customary systems equal to one eighth of a mile, which is 220 yards or 660 feet, or roughly 201 meters. The name comes from the Old English words for "furrow" and "long," reflecting the length of a furrow an ox could plow before resting. It is most commonly used today in horse racing, where distances are often given in furlongs, and in land measurement.

After the stitches come out, it's typical for the treated spot to be puffy and sore. A firm or bumpy feeling in that area is also common for a time while the tissue repairs itself. As the swelling subsides and healing progresses, these sensations should gradually ease. If the uneven appearance of your lips or the firm lump you're noticing worries you, it's a good idea to talk with your healthcare provider. They can examine the site and advise you on managing any swelling or discomfort, and they may suggest further treatment or recommendations to support healing. Soreness, exhaustion, and aching across the body can stem from a wide range of sources. Among the likely explanations are overexertion, where physical activity is too intense or unfamiliar to your body and leads to muscle soreness and fatigue. Inadequate fluid intake can also leave you drained and sore. Similarly, a diet lacking essential nutrients may leave you feeling worn out and achy. Insufficient sleep often produces fatigue and muscle discomfort, while ongoing stress can cause muscle tightness and tiredness. Finally, certain infections, such as influenza, frequently bring on muscle aches and exhaustion. Because the underlying cause matters for treatment, it is wise to consult a healthcare provider, who can recommend the right approach for your situation. Meanwhile, resting adequately, drinking plenty of fluids, and eating well may help ease your symptoms.

When you rise abruptly after being seated or lying down for a long stretch, you might notice a brief loss of vision, a kind of "blackout," lasting only a few seconds. This frequent occurrence is called "postural hypotension" or "orthostatic hypotension." It happens when blood pressure falls suddenly upon standing, temporarily reducing blood flow to the brain and leading to lightheadedness or momentary vision loss. Although postural hypotension is usually harmless and resolves by itself within seconds, certain medical conditions or medications can contribute to it. For that reason, it is wise to consult a healthcare provider if the problem recurs often or comes with other symptoms, such as fainting or chest pain. Several measures can help prevent it. Rise slowly, particularly after prolonged sitting or lying down. Consider wearing compression stockings, which can improve circulation and lower the chance of this problem. Keep up your fluid intake, since adequate hydration supports healthy blood pressure. Eat a balanced diet rich in fruits, vegetables, and whole grains to help keep blood pressure stable. Exercise regularly to strengthen circulation. Finally, limit alcohol and caffeine, as both can disrupt blood pressure regulation and raise the risk.

In linguistics, "deep structure" means the underlying meaning and organization of a sentence or phrase. It is considered the origin of the surface structure, which is the form in which the sentence is actually spoken or written. Noam Chomsky and his followers introduced the idea as part of their transformational grammar, a theory holding that a series of rules converts a sentence's deep structure into its surface structure. On this view, deep structure is made up of the syntactic and semantic relationships that exist among the words and phrases of the sentence. It is regarded as the source of the many surface forms a sentence may take, which vary with the context of use and with the rules applied to transform it. Take the sentence "The cat sat on the mat." Its deep structure is simple, made up of a subject ("the cat"), a verb ("sat"), and an object ("the mat"). Its surface structure is the particular way it is expressed, with the words in a certain order and with specific inflections added to the verb. Deep structure matters in linguistics because it helps account for how a sentence conveys meaning and for how several different surface structures can come from one deep structure. It also forms a central part of many theories about language and about how the brain processes it.

"Astronomically large" just means something huge, like way bigger than anything you'd run into on Earth or even in our solar system. People use it for distances, sizes, or numbers that are honestly hard to wrap your head around. Take the observable universe, which is roughly 93 billion light-years across. Nobody has traveled anywhere near that distance, and nobody's going to anytime soon. Same deal with stars: estimates for the number in the universe run from around 100 billion to a trillion or more. That's the kind of thing that's almost impossible to picture, and it dwarfs pretty much every scale we deal with day to day.

Yes, it is possible, though it depends on the fund's strategy, its time horizon, and the investors it serves. Hedge funds are not required to report returns on any particular schedule, and many do report and calculate performance monthly, since that is the standard convention for most managers and the basis for most industry databases. Quarterly results are nonetheless common in practice, particularly for funds that hold illiquid assets such as private credit, real estate, private equity-style positions, or certain distressed debt, where valuing holdings more frequently is difficult or costly. Funds with long lock-up periods, where investors cannot redeem for a year or more, may also see little reason to publish monthly figures.

Quarterly reporting is usually a matter of the fund's offering documents and its investor agreements rather than a legal mandate. Investors in a fund typically receive statements or capital account updates on whatever schedule the partnership agreement specifies, and the fund's administrator, auditor, and board or general partner oversee how and when valuations are struck. Some funds report quarterly to investors while still calculating net asset value monthly internally, and others only produce audited annual statements alongside periodic letters. Whatever the frequency, a fund that wants to be taken seriously by sophisticated investors and by allocators who track performance will generally disclose enough information for the returns to be verified and compared.

Gordon Moore (1929–2023) was an American chemist, physicist, and businessman who became one of the most influential figures in the history of the semiconductor and computer industries. He earned his doctorate in chemistry and physics from the California Institute of Technology in 1954 and then worked at Johns Hopkins University's Applied Physics Laboratory before joining William Shockley's semiconductor company in 1956. When Shockley's firm faced internal difficulties, Moore and several colleagues, including Robert Noyce, left to found Fairchild Semiconductor in 1957. Moore and Noyce later left Fairchild as well and co-founded Intel in 1968, where Moore served as chief executive and then chairman, helping to shape the company into a dominant force in microprocessors.

He is best known for Moore's Law, an observation he made in a 1965 article, in which he noted that the number of components on an integrated circuit was roughly doubling every year. He revised this in 1975 to a doubling about every two years. Although it was never a physical law, it became a guiding principle and benchmark for the semiconductor industry, shaping research, investment, and product planning for decades, and it is often cited as a driver of rapid progress in computing power and falling costs.

Moore was also known for his philanthropy. Through the Gordon and Betty Moore Foundation, which he established with his wife Betty, he supported scientific research, environmental conservation, and patient care initiatives, giving away billions of dollars over his lifetime.

A deep belief network (DBN) is a type of generative neural network made up of several layers of stochastic hidden units, typically built by stacking restricted Boltzmann machines (RBMs) on top of one another. Each RBM is a two-layer model with a visible layer that represents the input data and a hidden layer that learns features of that data, with connections only between the layers and not within them. This restriction makes training far more tractable than for general Boltzmann machines.

The network is usually trained in two phases. In the first, each RBM is trained one at a time in a greedy, layer-by-layer fashion. The first RBM learns to model the raw input, its hidden activations then serve as the input for the next RBM, and so on up the stack. This unsupervised pretraining gives the network a good initial set of weights that capture hierarchical structure in the data, from simple low-level patterns in the bottom layers to more abstract concepts in the higher ones. In the second phase, the whole network can be fine-tuned for a specific task. For classification, for example, a output layer is added and the weights are adjusted with backpropagation or a similar supervised method, often using the pretrained weights as a starting point rather than random initialization.

Deep belief networks were popularized by Geoffrey Hinton and colleagues around 2006, and their success in training deeper networks helped spark the renewed interest in deep learning that followed. They were applied to tasks such as handwritten digit recognition, speech recognition, and motion capture modeling. Although they have largely been superseded in many applications by architectures trained end to end, such as convolutional networks and transformers, DBNs remain an important milestone in the history of deep learning and are still studied as a model of hierarchical probabilistic representation.

Think of it like a club with rules. Each of these religions has its own big set of beliefs, and some of those beliefs contradict each other, so it's hard to hold all of them at once.

Here's the simplest way to see it. All three religions believe in one God and trace their story back to Abraham, which is why they're called Abrahamic. But they disagree about important things. Jewish people believe God gave them a special set of laws, and they're still waiting for a promised messiah who hasn't come yet. Christians believe that messiah already came in the person of Jesus, and that he is God's son. Muslims believe Jesus was an important prophet but not God's son, and they believe the final and most important messenger was Muhammad, who received the Quran.

So if you said "I believe Jesus is the messiah" and "I believe the messiah hasn't come yet" at the same time, those two statements cancel each other out. A person can't hold both as true at once, the same way you can't be both at home and at school at the very same moment, or believe that a light is both on and off.

Some people do mix ideas from different traditions, and some communities try to blend them, but usually they end up choosing one main faith, because the core beliefs don't fit together neatly.

I'm sorry you're thinking about your dog getting older. Ten years is a lot of shared life, and it makes sense that it brings up big questions.

Here's the simple idea. A body is a bit like a toy that gets used every day. Every time cells in the body copy themselves to grow, heal, and keep going, a tiny bit of wear happens. Over time, the copies get a little less perfect, and the body has more trouble fixing itself. Animals with fast-beating hearts and quick growing bodies, like dogs and cats, do all of this work faster, so they wear down sooner. Their bodies grow up in a year or two, and they hit their "grown-up" stage much faster than we do.

Size matters too. Bigger dogs often don't live as long as small ones, and scientists think that's because big bodies grow very fast and make lots of cells, which gives more chances for things to go wrong.

Humans are different. Our bodies take many years to grow, and we have strong ways of fixing small problems, so we tend to live much longer. Animals just have a shorter time on the clock.

Because of all this, the best thing you can do now is enjoy the time you have. Regular vet checkups, good food, exercise, and lots of belly rubs can help him feel his best for as long as possible. If you ever want to talk through what to watch for as he gets older, I'm happy to help with that too.

Russian rule lasted until 1867, when the territory was purchased by the United States for $7.2 million. The Americans then assumed ownership and organized Alaska as a territory.

Ezekiel was a Hebrew priest and prophet who lived in the sixth century BC and is the central figure of the Book of Ezekiel in the Old Testament. He was the son of Buzi and belonged to a priestly family, which shaped much of his outlook, especially his concern with the Temple, purity, and the presence of God. In 597 BC he was taken into exile in Babylon along with King Jehoiachin and thousands of other leading people from Judah, during the first Babylonian deportation. He settled among the exiles by the Kebar River, and it was there, around 593 BC when he was about thirty, that he received his call to be a prophet.

His call came through an overwhelming vision of God's glory, in which he saw a fiery storm cloud, four living creatures, and wheels within wheels, with a throne above them. This showed that God was not confined to the Jerusalem Temple but was present with his people even in a foreign land. God commissioned him as a watchman for Israel, charged with warning the people of their responsibility.

Ezekiel's ministry falls into broad phases. Before Jerusalem fell in 586 BC, he delivered stern messages of judgment, condemning idolatry, injustice, and the corruption of the Temple. He often communicated through dramatic symbolic acts, such as lying on his side for many days to represent the siege of the city, shaving his head, and acting out exile. After Jerusalem's destruction, his message turned toward hope and restoration. The best-known passage is the vision of the valley of dry bones, in which God breathes life into a heap of bones as a picture of Israel's renewal. He also spoke of God as a shepherd who would gather scattered sheep, and promised a new heart and a new spirit for his people. The book closes with a detailed vision of a restored Temple and the glory of the Lord returning to it.

Ezekiel is known for his vivid, strange imagery and his emphasis on individual responsibility, God's holiness, and the phrase "then they will know that I am the Lord." His visions have influenced Jewish mysticism and Christian thought, and he is regarded as one of the major prophets, alongside Isaiah and Jeremiah.

Tofu's basically bean curd, made from soybeans, and it's a staple in a lot of East and Southeast Asia. You soak the soybeans, grind them into a fine paste, then mix that with water and a coagulant so the solids (curds) split off from the liquid (whey). Heat it, let the curds form, press them into blocks or whatever shape you want, then cool and chill it until it's ready to eat. It's a solid source of protein and pretty low in fat and calories, and it's got iron, calcium, and magnesium too. You can grill it, fry it, or stir-fry it, and it works in soups, stews, stir-fries, salads, pretty much anything.

Tearing down a skyscraper can be done in a number of ways, though each one requires dismantling the structure bit by bit. One approach uses a crane fitted with a wrecking ball. The crane swings the heavy ball against the building, breaking off sections of concrete and steel. Another option is a hydraulic excavator, a machine with a long arm that ends in a large bucket. Its operator uses the arm to seize parts of the building and tear them away. Whichever technique is chosen, demolishing a skyscraper demands great care, particularly when other buildings stand nearby. Workers must proceed cautiously so that neighboring structures are not damaged. They may also set up barriers or rely on specialized equipment to keep people in the vicinity safe.

The short answer is cold water, at least under normal conditions. Water that has already been cooled to near freezing has less thermal energy to remove before it reaches the freezing point, so it naturally gets there sooner than water starting at room temperature.

Hot water, though, can sometimes freeze faster in practice, and this is known as the Mpemba effect. Several factors may contribute. Hot water evaporates more quickly, and evaporation carries heat away, which can speed cooling. It also loses heat faster to its surroundings because the temperature difference is larger, and convection currents inside the container may be more vigorous when the water starts hot. Dissolved gases, which come out of solution more readily in hot water, may also play a role in some experiments.

The effect is real in some experiments but not reliably reproducible, and scientists still debate its causes. So for a typical comparison, pre-chilled water will freeze first, but whether hot water can beat cold water depends heavily on the specific conditions.

Labeled data is data that has been tagged with one or more meaningful labels, tags, or classes that describe what each example represents or what the correct answer for it should be. In machine learning, a labeled dataset pairs each input, such as an image, a sentence, an audio clip, or a row of numbers, with an output that a human or a reliable process has assigned. For example, a photo of a cat paired with the label "cat," an email paired with the label "spam" or "not spam," or a house description paired with its actual sale price are all instances of labeled data.

The main purpose of labeled data is to train and evaluate supervised learning models. In supervised learning, an algorithm studies many input-label pairs and tries to learn the relationship between them, so that it can later predict the correct label for new inputs it has never seen. The labels act as the "ground truth" or answer key that guides the model during training and lets researchers measure how accurate the model's predictions are during testing.

Labels can take different forms depending on the task. In classification problems, the label is a category, such as identifying whether a medical scan shows a tumor. In regression problems, the label is a continuous number, such as a temperature or a price. More complex tasks may require richer labels, such as bounding boxes drawn around objects in an image, the part of speech assigned to every word in a sentence, or a transcript matched to an audio recording.

This stands in contrast to unlabeled data, which consists of raw inputs without any accompanying answers, like a large collection of photos with no captions or descriptions. Unlabeled data is much easier and cheaper to collect, and it is used in unsupervised learning, where algorithms look for patterns or groupings on their own, and in self-supervised learning, where the model generates its own training signals from the structure of the data. Semi-supervised learning combines a small amount of labeled data with a large amount of unlabeled data.

Creating labeled data is often expensive and time-consuming because it usually requires human annotators, and sometimes domain experts such as doctors or lawyers, to examine each example carefully. The quality of the labels matters a great deal, since inconsistent, biased, or incorrect labels can lead a model to learn the wrong patterns. For this reason, organizations often invest heavily in annotation guidelines, quality checks, and tools to make the labeling process more efficient and reliable.

So ETPs (that's ETFs and ETNs) trade on an exchange just like stocks, and they charge fees to cover running costs like managing the portfolio, marketing, and admin. When you buy or sell one, your broker may charge its own transaction fee, which varies by broker and by the specific product. That usually just comes straight out of your account.

The bigger ongoing cost is the expense ratio. It's a percentage of the fund's assets that gets deducted every year. Say an ETP has a 0.50% expense ratio and you hold $10,000 of it. You'd pay about $50 a year in fees.

Those fees generally show up in the fund's net asset value (NAV), which is basically the value of the underlying assets minus liabilities. The NAV feeds into the price you see on the exchange. So the market kind of prices the fees in: a higher-fee ETP may trade lower to reflect that drag, and a cheaper one may trade a bit higher.

The first weekend of September is usually tied to Labor Day in the United States and Canada. Labor Day falls on the first Monday of September, so it creates a long holiday weekend that many people treat as the unofficial end of summer. It honors the contributions of workers and the labor movement, and it is commonly marked with barbecues, parades, travel, and end-of-summer sales.

The exact dates shift each year. If September 1 falls on a Monday, Labor Day is that day, and the "first weekend" holiday is actually the weekend just before it, which technically falls in late August. In other years the holiday weekend runs from the first Saturday through the first Monday of the month.

Other countries observe different things around then. Labour Day in many places is on May 1 instead, so this timing is mostly specific to North America. If you're asking about a particular country or religious observance, let me know and I can give you a more specific answer.

In Ontario, HST relief comes through two credits, and both are claimed when you file your income tax return.

The federal GST/HST credit is a quarterly payment from the Canada Revenue Agency for lower- and modest-income individuals and families. You don't need a separate form. Just file your T1 return on time and answer the questions about your marital status and number of children. The CRA calculates your eligibility from your adjusted family net income, and if you're eligible, payments begin the month after you file. If you're not sure whether you've been receiving it, you can check your CRA My Account or call the CRA.

The Ontario component is the Ontario Sales Tax Credit, which is delivered as part of the Ontario Trillium Benefit. You claim it on Schedule ON-BEN, which is filed with your provincial return. The form asks for your net income and family information, and it calculates the amount you qualify for. If you qualify, you receive the benefit in monthly payments throughout the year. If your return shows you're eligible, the payments start automatically.

To make sure you receive both, file your return by April 30 of the following year, even if you owe no tax or have little income. If you use tax software, it will generally prepare Schedule ON-BEN for you. If your situation is complicated, a tax preparer or the Ontario Ministry of Finance's tax credit information can help you confirm the amounts.

Automatic differentiation (AD) is a way to get the derivative of a function that's defined in a computer program. You don't have to work out the calculus by hand. It basically breaks the function down into simple arithmetic steps (addition, subtraction, multiplication, division) and basic functions like exp, log, or sin, then applies the chain rule to each piece, so you end up with the derivative with respect to any input you care about. That makes it really useful for getting gradients quickly, which comes up a lot in machine learning, optimization, and scientific computing.

There are two main ways to do it: forward mode and reverse mode. Forward mode works out the derivative with respect to one input at a time. Reverse mode gets the derivatives with respect to all the inputs in one pass. So if you have way more inputs than outputs, reverse mode is the better choice. If it's the other way around, with more outputs than inputs, forward mode tends to win.

In machine learning, AD is what lets you compute how a loss function changes with each model parameter during training. It's also handy in optimization, where you can use those gradients to hunt for a minimum or maximum with gradient descent or something similar. And in scientific work, people use it to see how sensitive a simulation is to its inputs, or to fit parameters by shrinking the gap between predictions and real observations.
